## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of All the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers Who Flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III; a Chronological Reprint of All Existing Monuments of Catholic Tradition through the First Twelve Centuries of the Church, According to the Most Accurate Editions, Collated with One Another and with Certain Manuscripts.**

Most carefully corrected; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the most extensive editions produced in the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following either individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters properly set within the text itself, and also with headings marking the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, provided they possess some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two full general indexes: the first, an index of subjects, by consulting which one may see at a glance whatever each of the Fathers has written upon any topic; the second, an index of Holy Scripture, by which the reader may readily discover which Fathers have commented upon individual texts of individual books of Scripture, and in what places in their works.

A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others, if one considers: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and number of reprinted works, the exceptionally convenient form of the volumes, uniformly maintained throughout the whole course of the work, the modest price, and above all this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and small works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time brought together in our library, from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Clergy Library, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been issued in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin.—The two hundred and sixty volumes of the Latin edition are sold for 1,300 francs; the 1,300 volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for 1,800 francs.—The wholly Latin edition embraces every author, Western as well as Eastern; the latter, however, are supplied there in Latin translation alone.

## [The Complete Works of Ivo]

[Col. IX]

## Historical Notice

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. VIII, col. 1126, under the bishops of Chartres.)

[Col. IXA] After Geoffrey had been removed from the see of Chartres by the judgment both of Ivo and of the supreme pontiff, and Urban had empowered the clergy of Chartres to appoint another in his place, Ivo was elected by the unanimous vote of all. He was born in the district of Beauvais, of a family far from noble, as he himself testifies in Letters 3, 12, and 22. His father was Hugh of Auteuil, if Fronton is to be believed; his mother was Hilemburgis, whose name is entered in the necrology of Saint-Quentin of Beauvais on 10 February.

After completing his studies in humane letters and philosophy at Paris, he devoted himself to theology in the monastery of Bec under Blessed Lanfranc. According to our Sammarthani, in their collections, he was first a canon of Nesle. Subsequently, summoned by Guy, bishop of Beauvais, he was placed as superior, that is, provost or abbot, over the regular canons of Saint-Quentin [Col. IXB], an abbey founded outside the walls of his city by that bishop. Ivo not only conveyed to this house certain estates from his patrimony, but also, in accordance with the practice then customary in monasteries, taught theology there. Already most skilled in the canons, he gave certain constitutions to his brethren, and is therefore not undeservedly regarded as an organizer of regular canons.

At that time he also compiled a collection of canons, or concise *Decretum* drawn from the canons of the saints, which jurists used before Gratian’s time. In it he followed Burchard, bishop of Worms, so exactly that he copied even Burchard’s errors into his own work, just as Burchard himself had copied those of Regino. [Col. IXC]

Ivo had already spent many years in office when, unsuspecting anything of the sort, he was canonically elected in the place of the deposed Geoffrey by clergy and people, in accordance with the instructions of Pope Urban. Though resisting, he was presented to the king, from whom he received the pastoral staff, but not episcopal consecration as well. For Richer, archbishop of Sens, who supported the deposed Geoffrey, never wished to set a day for Ivo’s consecration, although the clergy requested and pressed him to do so. Ivo complains of this in Letter 8, where he addresses Richer, archbishop of Sens, as follows:

> “You accuse me of having sought blessing elsewhere. Yet, truth being witness, I shall speak the truth: I sought neither the bishopric nor episcopal blessing from you, nor from anyone else. But when I had first been presented to the king by the clergy’s contrivance, and afterwards by their force, and when, after the pastoral staff had been forced upon me by the king, I had been brought to the church of Chartres, and you were unwilling, despite the requests and urgent entreaties of the clergy, to appoint any day for my consecration, my intention meanwhile was not to give unqualified assent to their election, until I had become certain both concerning Geoffrey’s deposition and concerning the will of the supreme pontiff. When I came to him, I was compelled by apostolic authority, at the request of the church of Chartres, and was thus consecrated bishop.”

Concerning this consecration, perhaps performed on 23 November 1090 itself, Pope Urban issued letters at Capua on 24 November, the eighth day before the Kalends of December, to the clergy and people of Chartres, that they should receive Ivo as bishop in place of the deprived Geoffrey. On the following day he wrote to Richer, archbishop of Sens, informing him that Ivo, canonically elected, had been consecrated by himself because Richer had refused to lay hands upon him; he asked Richer to receive Ivo kindly and give him his assistance in governing his church.

Yet Richer did not rest even then. Let us hear Ivo again, in Letter 12:

> “The archbishop of Sens, misled by the counsel of the bishop of Paris, brought with him that same bishop of Paris and two others of like folly, the bishops of Meaux and Troyes, and this year at Étampes accused me rather irregularly concerning the ordination which I had received from you. He said that I had offended against royal majesty by presuming to receive consecration from the Apostolic See. Therefore, when they attempted to restore the deposed Geoffrey to his former condition contrary to your decree, and to pronounce upon me a sentence of deposition, I appealed to the Apostolic See; and by apostolic decrees I recalled them from their presumption, although they feared those decrees only for the future. Yet they did not deign either to pursue the appeal [Col. XC] or to have full peace with me.”

We think that this letter, as well as the council held at Étampes, belongs to the year 1091. In an old charter preserved by the Sammarthani Ivo is mentioned as bishop:

> “Done in the year 1091, indiction XIV, in the reign of Philip, while Ivo, formerly abbot of the church of Blessed Quentin, was then bishop of the people of Chartres.”

He also occurs in a charter of the monastery of Vendôme, dated 1091, indiction XIV, Friday of Easter week, 18 April; in that year, having been ordained, he received an agreement, in the capacity of abbot, between Garnald of Charismot and the monks, before the head church of Vendôme. Hence it is rightly concluded that Urban’s letters both to the clergy and people of Chartres—issued at Capua on 24 November—and to Richer the metropolitan—issued on 25 November—must be assigned to 1090.

Having obtained the bishopric of Chartres, Ivo did not therefore relinquish the care of the community of Saint-Quentin at Beauvais. Its canons resisted this, and he wrote them Letter 17, asking them to appoint another [Col. XIA] abbot for themselves. At last he obtained this result, as is clear from Letters 31 and 32, when he wholly resigned the office of superior into the hands of Fulk, bishop of Beauvais.

In 1092 he subscribed Robert of Bellême’s charter for the monks of Marmoutier. In the same year he was grievously persecuted because of the hatred of King Philip. Philip had brought Bertrada, wife of Count Fulk of Anjou, into the lawful marriage-bed of his wife Bertha, while certain bishops of Gaul supported or even disgracefully connived at this act. Ivo, a man steadfast in justice and unable to ignore such enormous wickedness, was harassed in cruel ways, especially by Hugh, lord of Le Puiset. Hugh held him in prison for nearly a year and repeatedly kept him even without bread. Ivo opposed, with great strength and constancy of spirit, the mistress who had corrupted the king and the king’s lust.

Concerning this union and the king’s wrath, Ivo remonstrates with Philip in Letter 22 in these words:

> “Since, through the preceding grace of God, I have been raised by your hand from the dunghill of the poor to the throne of princes, I acknowledge that, after God, I owe you to the extent of my power all things fitting for your honour and welfare. But because, angered by the salutary admonitions which I addressed to your Serenity with the utmost loyalty and charity, you have withdrawn your trust from me and exposed the goods of the episcopal household to be plundered by our enemies, I have suffered grave and great hardships as a result. At present I can neither safely nor honourably attend the royal court. I therefore beseech your Majesty meanwhile to bear with me in royal gentleness, until I can [Col. XIC] recover a little breath and repair, at least in part, the losses inflicted upon me almost to the point of want of bread.”

He wrote this after being released from prison, perhaps through the intervention of Rainald, archbishop of Reims, and his suffragans, to whom Pope Urban had written for the liberation of the bishop of Chartres on 27 October 1092.

On 1 July 1093 he granted freely to Eustace, abbot, and the monks of Saint Peter at Chartres six altars: those of Bruerolles, Ermentières, Roheria, Buxet, Cruciac, and Castellaria. On either 24 or 22 August of the same year he consecrated Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme. Yet in Letter 21 he still says that he was shut in prison when the body of Saint Julian was translated. This translation is said to have occurred on 17 October 1093, in the eighth year of the ordination of Hoel, bishop of Le Mans, who was ordained on 21 April 1085. Accordingly, 1092 should perhaps be read instead of 1093, since that year agrees perfectly with the ordination.

Besides the matters already mentioned, in November 1093 Ivo entered Rome peacefully with Pope Urban and left him there in January. On returning, he settled in 1094 the dispute between the monks of Bec and those of Molesme concerning the cell of Pexiac. Summoned to the council of Reims, held on 17 September of that year, concerning the king’s marriage and the deposition of Ivo, who opposed it, he refused to attend. Richer, archbishop of Sens, who was hostile to him, presided over the council in some fashion. Ivo wrote to Richer on the matter in Letter 35.

On 3 January he gave the Cluniac monks permission to build a monastery outside the city. He attended the council of Clermont on 8 November 1095, and the council of Tours in 1096, where he subscribed Urban II’s decree subjecting the abbot of Cormery to Saint Martin. In that same year he wrote to the pope concerning William, bishop-elect of Paris, whom he consecrated at Chartres together with Walter, bishop of Meaux, and Sanction, bishop of Orléans. On 11 February, at the beginning of 1096, he subscribed the charter of foundation of the abbey of La Rote.

In 1097 he was present when Count William of Nevers gave the church of Saint Stephen at Nevers, which he had restored, to the abbot and monks of Cluny; and he cursed all who should in any way dare to oppose that gift. He consecrated that same church on 13 December. In the same year he persuaded Count Geoffrey of Preuilly, of Vendôme, to acknowledge the rights and privileges of the monastery of the Most Holy Trinity, and reconciled him with its abbot. He also wrote to Urban II concerning the consecration of Daimbert, bishop-elect of Sens; and, at the beginning of the following year, 1098, against the election of John of Orléans.

On 13 May he granted, without redemption of the vicarage, to the monks of Marmoutier the altars of Basenville, Bisconcellis, and Boveniville. At the beginning of that same year, he wished to lay aside the episcopal burden and therefore wrote Letter 67 to Pope Urban in these terms:

> “Behold, now that seven-year period having passed, I have cultivated to the best of my ability the vineyard committed to me, but I have not found the fruit which I sought. Let liberty therefore be granted in the eighth year, that I may enter upon this beginning of the true octave; that I may be able to keep sabbath for myself, gather the sweet fruits of contemplation, and taste beforehand the joys of that octave. But if I do not now do this with your permission, necessity will nevertheless compel me to do it because of the king’s renewed hostility toward me on the old account, and because of my parishioners, who despise God’s word and are inclined to long only for earthly things.”

At the pope’s urging, he did not resign his episcopal care. Indeed, amid the greatest storms and the shameful condition of the Gallican Church at that time, he sustained it most praiseworthily. The many letters in which he deals with the appointment of cathedral churches and bishops, and with restraining the arrogance of legates and envoys from the papal side—by whom the Gallican Church was often burdened—bear witness to this.

Letter 133, addressed to Richard, bishop of Albano and apostolic legate, should be read. Richard had sharply rebuked Ivo as guilty of public simony. Ivo replied that the dean, the cantor, and some others in the church of Chartres exacted several payments when canons were admitted. He had tried unsuccessfully to abolish them, because they defended themselves by the example of the servants of the Roman curia, among whom everything was for sale. Meanwhile, in 1099 Bishop Ivo established in the church of Saint John in the Valley regular canons summoned from Saint-Quentin, and bestowed many gifts upon them.

[Col. XIIIA] He attended the synod of Étampes in the same year and granted the monks of Marmoutier permission to build a church at Francheville. In 1100 he confirmed under anathema the royal decree expelling the monks and restoring canons to the church at Poissy. About this time, burdened with care for all the churches, he wrote to Walter, bishop of Meaux, concerning the incontinence of the nuns of Saint Fara, admonishing him either to correct them or to place monks in their stead.

By a bull issued on 14 February of that same year, Paschal II exempted from every form of plundering, customarily carried out at that time after a bishop’s death, the house of the bishops of Chartres which Ivo had built at great expense, in accordance with the decree of the council of Clermont.

[Col. XIIIB] In the records of Saint Peter, the year of the Incarnation 1104 is equated with the fourteenth year of Ivo’s episcopate and the forty-fifth of King Philip. In that year he attended the council of Troyes on 2 April and subscribed Count Hugh of Champagne’s charter for the monastery of Molesme. He was also present at the synod for the king’s reconciliation at Baugency, held at Ivo’s earnest request on 30 July.

Another council was held at Paris, with Ivo present, on 2 December, indiction XIII, in the sixth year of Paschal II, to reconcile and absolve King Philip, who, together with Bertrada, swore to live separately. At the council of Poitiers in the same year, the judgment of the council of Bordeaux concerning Marestais, rendered on behalf of the monks of Saint-Jean-d’Angély against the monks of Saint-Maixent, was entrusted to Ivo for examination and was confirmed by him and his colleagues.

On 12 April 1104 Paschal II confirmed the church of Saint Nicasius of Meulan which Ivo had given to the monks of Bec. In the following year Count Henry of Blois and his wife Adela, at Ivo’s request, made the episcopal house free from the evil custom of plundering its furnishings. King Philip confirmed their benefaction by his authority in the forty-sixth year of his reign. In the same year Ivo ratified, at the request of Countess Adela, the liberty of the church of Bourg-Moyen; and he attended the election of Ralph as abbot of Saint-Quentin on the feast of the Dedication.

By command of Paschal II, in 1106 he settled the dispute involving Ivo of Curvaville, Viscount Hugh, and Count Rotrou of Perche, who were disturbing the peace while preparing to depart for the holy war. Invited by Ivo, Pope Paschal celebrated Easter at Chartres in 1107.

In the same year Ivo confirmed the place given to Bernard by Count Rotrou for the construction of a monastery and consecrated its cemetery. On 25 August he issued letters concerning the controversy over the church of Villemeux between the monks of Coulombs and the nuns of Saint-Avit.

In 1108 he attended the funeral of King Philip; immediately afterwards he celebrated the sacred rite for King Louis at Orléans, despite the fruitless opposition of the clergy of Reims. Concerning this he wrote apostolic Letter 189. In 1109 he subscribed King Louis VI’s ordinance regarding the freedom of the servants of the church of Paris to make wills and to wage war.

On 3 February 1110, together with the chapter, he granted a carucate of land in the territory of Garzay, beside the river Thironne, for building a monastery. He subscribed King Louis’s diploma for the canons of Saint Geneviève on 12 March 1111. Summoned to the councils of Vienne and Anse in 1112, he excused himself.

In the same year he subscribed King Louis’s letters in favour of the monks of Fleury. In 1113, together with many bishops, he strengthened by his subscription that prince’s charter for the foundation—or rather the endowment—of Saint Victor at Paris. Along with Arnald, dean, and the entire church of Chartres, he approved the newly established abbey of Tiron, granted it many privileges on 3 February, and in the preceding year affixed [Col. XIVB] his seal to the instrument confirming those privileges by Conon of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See.

On 3 February 1114 he granted the monks of Marmoutier the church of Hanches, held by Pagan the canon, and whatever was given them by that man’s brothers. In the same year, on 28 October, Paschal II confirmed a decree previously issued by Ivo against provosts who oppressed the chapter, harassed lesser churchmen with forced services, and violated other regulations established by him. Angered by that bull, the provosts attempted to stir King Louis against Ivo and secured letters from the king to him. Ivo replied in Letter 265. On this matter see Souchet, *New Observations on the Letters of Ivo*, pp. 252 ff.

[Col. XIVC] In an instrument of the church of Saint Nicholas, cited by Souchet, p. 254, the twenty-fifth year of Ivo’s ordination is linked with the sixteenth of Paschal II and with the year of the Incarnation 1114:

> “This charter was made in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1114, in the sixteenth year of the ordination of Lord Pope Paschal, and in the twenty-fifth year of the ordination of Lord Ivo, bishop of Chartres, etc.”

Souchet also reports a bull of Paschal II, issued at Rome on 14 March and addressed to Ivo of Chartres and Ralph of Saintes. Both had attended the council of Clermont. The bull ordered, in accordance with the council’s decree, that altars possessed by monks for thirty years and subject to the redemption of vicars should remain free to them.

In 1115, indiction VIII, Ivo granted to the brethren of Saint John the church of Saint Nicholas returned by Ivo of Curvaville. He had a serious dispute with Bernard, abbot of Bonneval, which the author of Robert’s *Life* indicates was settled by Robert of Arbrissel shortly before Robert’s death, said to have occurred at the end of 1116, now reckoned 1117. For the chronicle of Saint-Albin of Angers says:

> “In the year 1116 Robert of Arbrissel died on 26 February.”

The most learned Pagi adds another argument of no less weight: Letter 275 of Ivo mentions Count William of Nevers, captured in 1116 according to the chronicles of Fécamp and Vézelay, and those who captured him being excommunicated. Pagi therefore concludes that the letter belongs to 1117.

Mabillon, however, following Alberic, Helinand, the ancient calendar of Saint-Quentin, and others, holds that Ivo died toward the end of 1116. Yet, with due respect to such great men, I would say that this cannot be reconciled with the method of reckoning years employed in charters of Geoffrey, Ivo’s successor, who, as will be stated, began his episcopate at the beginning of 1116. Moreover, the disagreement of the chronicles concerning Ivo’s death demonstrates their carelessness. Finally, I think that greater deference and reverence are due to the necrologies of churches in which bishops died and were buried than to those of churches generally far removed. In the necrologies of the cathedral church and of Saint John in the Valley, Ivo’s death is assigned to 23 December 1115.

[Col. XVB] Ivo was buried in the choir of the church of Saint John in the Valley; but in the sixteenth century the hostile fury of heretics impiously scattered his pious ashes to the winds. By a bull dated 18 November 1570, Pius V permitted the Regular Canons of Saint John Lateran to celebrate his feast annually. The Sacred Congregation of Rites extended this faculty to the canons of Chartres on 28 November 1648, through the efforts of Father Natalis, a Minim of Chartres then living at Rome, at the request of J.-B. Souchet, canon of Chartres.

Philip of Alençon, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, composed this epitaph for him:

> Affection made him a father; learning, a teacher;  
> The rule, a canon; his rank, a bishop.  
> Integrity made him renowned, nature humble,  
> Austerity of life venerable, long and chaste old age holy.  
>
> When a bishop died, it had formerly been the custom  
> For the prince to take his possessions; Ivo bought off this custom from the prince.  
> The injured received his aid; the common people, his teachings; the evil king, restraint;  
> The poor experienced his resources; God, his prayers for the flock.

The Sammarthani report another poem from old papers belonging to the most illustrious Barnabé Brisson, president of the Parliament of Paris:

> In mind, hand, tongue, learning, and bodily service,  
> Wise, generous, excellent, useful, blameless,  
> A firm pillar of the house of the Lord, which by salutary law  
> He cherished, fortified, equipped, and continually enlarged  
> By counsel and writings, showing in what order it should live and act.  
> The sick freely experienced his assistance, the poor his bounty.  
> Ivo, memorable bishop and crown of this city,  
> Lies in this tomb awaiting the coming of the Judge.

It is also fitting to report the following verses in the manner of an epitaph, which were read in the church of Saint John before its destruction:

> Here lies buried the body of Bishop Ivo,  
> Whose honour strikes at either threshold of heaven.  
> This bishop read through the decrees of the sacred canons  
> And set forth the principles of the laws in briefer form.  
>
> Elsewhere, O king, are mysteries celebrated for you at Reims;  
> You depart, called king and counsellor of your people.  
> Count Hugh, attacking the walls of Chartres, captures him;  
> The devout people redeem him at countless cost.  
>
> At his own expense and through his own labour he renewed the bishop’s house,  
> He strengthened the abbey of John, where he lies buried,  
> And formed and enlarged the deanery of Andrew.  
> Under your leadership the pulpit of Mary’s church was made.  
>
> He laid the foundations of the priory of Belles;  
> Here he prepared the church of Magdalene.  
> For twenty [f. 25] and two years without fault  
> He governed the see with upright conduct and faith.

To these should be added the words of the Martyrology of Chartres:

> “23 December. On this same day, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1115, Father Ivo, bishop of this most sacred see, died: a man of great religious devotion, most prudent in ecclesiastical and secular affairs, gentle in speech, outstanding in patience, eminent in chastity, and most learned both in divine matters and in philosophy. [Col. XVIB] He gave six fine copes, seven capes, three mitres, and three tapestries for the adornment of this church; he gave a missal, an epistolary, a Gospel-book, and one matutinal lectionary, and had them all furnished with silver. He constructed a pulpit of wonderful beauty, established schools, and rebuilt from the foundations the episcopal house, which he had found mean and wooden, enslaved at the death or departure of bishops by certain evil customs violently introduced by the counts of Chartres. He made it splendid and of stone, and freed it, together with everything belonging to it, movable and immovable, from servitude; and he confirmed this liberty by the guarantee of privileges of the Roman See, king, and count, which are kept in the archives of this church. [Col. XVIC]
>
> “He also acquired from the vidame a tract of land adjoining that house, for enlarging it, and enclosed it with a wall. Near the bridge of Godin he built other houses for episcopal use, and improved the same town in many respects. He converted the abbey of Saint John from secular to regular status, established and enlarged it; through his counsel and aid the monastery for the sick at Beaulieu was founded. He converted all the junior prebends of this church, and its precarial benefices, to common uses; and by his own privilege and apostolic privilege he forbade their future distribution to individuals. By the same privileges he prohibited forced services, unjust exactions, and the abusive circuits of officials conducted through the provostships. [Col. XVID] He gave this chapter the authority which he possessed to grant the provostship of Ébrardville and all its appurtenances. He caused the fixed charges for burials to cease throughout the bishopric of this church. At his death, to increase the altar fund, he left one hundred measures of wine, and in many other matters he did much good for his church and clergy.”

The necrology of Saint John in the Valley likewise reads:

> “On 23 December, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1115, died Ivo, bishop of Chartres, of blessed memory. He established in this church the order of Regular Canons and enlarged it with his own property, giving for the use of the brethren the church of Saint Stephen with its possessions, the church of Lucé, the church of Pont-Godin, and land beyond the pond; likewise thirty volumes from his library and many other things.” [Col. XVIIA]

Almost all historians of his age praise Ivo. Cardinal Baronius honourably calls him “the lamp of the West, the glory of the world, the ornament and splendour of the Gallican Church.” Certainly distinguished by profound and outstanding learning, by knowledge of divine and human law, and by monuments of works destined to endure through the ages, and possessing virtues eminent and wholly suited to the supreme pontiff, he outshone in his own time not only the other bishops of the kingdom, but also, if it may be said, all bishops of the church of Chartres.

Besides the *Decretum* which he compiled, he left many letters, in which everything relating to canon law may be found. Mabillon added two new letters in the fifth volume of his *Annals* to the 288 already published. Many of them also contain material shedding great light on the history of the Gallican Church, indeed upon that of the universal Church. Among his works are also twenty-four sermons, of which the fourth is attributed by some to Fulbert.

Further information on Ivo is found in the edition of his works published in 1647. The curious reader may consult J.-B. Souchet’s preface to the *Life of Saint Bernard, Abbot of Tiron*, and his *Defence of Truth*, published at Chartres in 1651. Baronius, *Annals*, volumes XI and XII; Spondanus; Possevinus; Bellarmine; and others should also be consulted.

## § 1. History of Saint Ivo

[Col. XVII]

Ivo [Note: [Col. XVIIA] Baronius, year 1092, no. 2; Ivo, Letters 92, 102; *Life*, no. 1.], the light and oracle of the Church of France in his time—and one might even say of the whole West—was born in the territory of Beauvais around the year 1040. His father was named Hugh of Auteuil, and his mother Hilemburgis. The common opinion is that his family was noble; but Ivo himself attests the contrary in several of his letters [Note: [Col. XVIIA] Letters 3, 12, 22.].

From his earliest youth he devoted himself to the study of the liberal arts. After receiving instruction in them in his native country [Note: [Col. XVIIA] *Life*, ibid.], or even at Paris according to others [Note: [Col. XVIIA] Egas, *Bullarium*, vol. I, p. 613; Robert of Torigni, addition to Sigebert, p. 750.], he went to Bec to perfect his knowledge of them and to study ecclesiastical disciplines. There the celebrated Lanfranc was his teacher, and a great many young men distinguished by birth and character were his fellow students; several of them were afterwards raised to the highest dignities of the Church. This must therefore have been before 1062, when Lanfranc left Bec and went to Caen to assume the abbacy of Saint Stephen.

The love of learning and piety which Ivo acquired at Bec, he cultivated with as much success as care. When he reappeared in the world, his entire occupation was the study of ecclesiastical antiquity and the practice of virtue. Evidence for this is found in the writings he left to posterity and in the honour he brought to every rank which he held.

At first he was a canon of Nesle, an illustrious collegiate church in Picardy [Note: [Col. XVIIA] *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. VIII, p. 1126.]. His merit then caused him to be called away to govern the new house [Note: [Col. XVIIA] *Gallia Christiana vetus*, vol. IV, pp. 773–774.] which Guy, bishop of Beauvais, had just founded for clerics at the gate of his episcopal city. This establishment began not in 1078, as most writers assert, but as early as 1067; it was completed two years later under the patronage of Saint Quentin the martyr. Ivo had already been its superior for several years before 1079: first with the title of *praelatus* (“superior”), then with that of abbot, although in his letters he styles himself only a simple priest.

This new community soon acquired an extraordinary reputation. Ivo not only increased its revenues by transferring to it some estates from his patrimony [Note: [Col. XVIIIA] *Nova*, ibid.; Ivo, *Life*, no. 2.], but also caused a discipline in every respect conforming to the ancient canons to be observed there, and opened a celebrated school in which he personally took care to give lectures in theology. This manner of life, established at Saint-Quentin, has caused Ivo to be regarded as one of the most illustrious founders of the order of Regular Canons.

That order had already been known at Rome and Reims for several years [Note: [Col. XVIIIA] *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. VII, pp. 522, 578.], but Ivo brought it to perfection. During his lifetime he had the consolation of seeing his house serve to extend it in various places in France, and of seeing his school furnish excellent bishops to several churches. It was in the tranquillity of his retirement that he composed the two collections of canons [Note: [Col. XVIIIA] Ivo, *Life*, ibid.], one shorter and the other more extensive, which survive under his name and of which fuller discussion will be given below.

These writings, together with the care he himself took in teaching, earned him even then the title of a renowned doctor, among the most renowned in the Church of France: *Inter praecipuos Franciae doctores eruditione litterarum, tam divinarum quam saecularium floruit*—“He flourished among the foremost doctors of France through learning in letters, both sacred and secular” [Note: [Col. XVIIIA] Ibid., no. 2; Orderic Vitalis, book X, p. 810.].

Apart from this, he did not yet play a great part in the Church. The council of Issoudun, held in 1081, was the only notable public action in which he was seen to take part [Note: [Col. XVIIIA] Ivo, Letter 181; Mabillon, *Annals*, book LXIV, no. 107.].

He had governed the abbey of Saint-Quentin for about fourteen or fifteen years when Geoffrey I, bishop of Chartres—twice deposed by Pope Gregory VII on account of simony, and guilty besides of other crimes—acknowledged himself unworthy of the episcopate and resigned it. [Note: [Col. XVIIIA] Councils, vol. X, pp. 420, 430; Ivo, letters 1, 2, 8.] Pope Urban II, who induced him to take this course, wrote at the same time to the people of Chartres, inviting them to elect another bishop, and indicating to them the venerable abbot of Saint-Quentin, whose merits he fully knew. When the election had fallen upon him, they took hold of his person, lest his humility should cause him to flee, and presented him to King Philip, from whom he received the pastoral staff. [Note: [Col. XIX] Ivo, letter 322.] But Richer, archbishop of Sens and metropolitan of the province, to whom by right belonged the ordination of the newly elected bishop, refused his ministry on various pretexts. In truth, he was aggrieved that Geoffrey had been deposed without his participation. Seeing matters in this state, Ivo wished to renounce his election [Note: [Col. XIX] Letter 3.], and wrote accordingly to the Roman pontiff. He was nevertheless persuaded to go to the pope with delegates from the church of Chartres [Note: [Col. XIX] Letters 1, 2.], who brought him their complaints concerning their archbishop’s refusal. To settle the matter promptly, Urban himself ordained the new elect and sent him back with two letters, dated 24 and 25 November: one to the people of Chartres, the other to Archbishop Richer.

Almost all our writers disagree concerning the exact year and place of this ordination. But Dom Mabillon proves by unanswerable evidence [Note: [Col. XIX] Mabillon, ibid., book LXVIII, no. 27.] that it took place at Alatri, where the pope then was [Note: [Col. XIX] In his letter 36 Ivo himself mentions this place, where he was then in the pope’s retinue. But instead of *Alatri*, the editors read *a latere*, which makes no sense here.], at the end of November 1091. Although ordained bishop of Chartres [Note: [Col. XIX] Ivo, letter 31.], Ivo still retained the abbey of Saint-Quentin, and only after some time resigned it into the hands of Fulk, bishop of Beauvais. He then wrote to the Regular Canons who served there, permitting them to elect another abbot and exhorting them to make a good choice. [Note: [Col. XIX] Letter 32.] Nevertheless, he continued to protect it throughout his life. [Note: [Col. XIX] Letter 193.]

On returning from his journey from Italy to France, he took possession of his church by virtue of the king’s investiture and the pope’s ordination, attested by the latter’s letters. [Note: [Col. XIX] Letters 1, 2, 6.] But Richer, his metropolitan, far from recognizing him as bishop, wrote him a letter full of bitterness, contempt, and insults, treating him as nothing less than an intruder. [Note: [Col. XIX] Letter 8.] Ivo replied politely, yet with great firmness, offering to justify himself canonically. For this purpose he appeared at the council of Étampes, where Richer and the bishops of Paris, Troyes, and Meaux had concerted his deposition and Geoffrey’s restoration. [Note: [Col. XIX] Letter 12.] Their pretext was that, in having himself ordained elsewhere, he had acted against royal authority and violated the rights of the Gallican Church. [Note: [Col. XIX] Life, ibid., no. 3.] But Ivo halted the proceedings by an appeal to the Holy See, and the pope found the means of restoring peace in the matter. Ivo was maintained in his see, while Geoffrey was confined to that portion of the diocese of Chartres which lay under the dominion of Robert, duke of Normandy. [Note: [Col. XX] Letter 6.]

Yet scarcely had our prelate begun to enjoy this calm when he had the misfortune to fall into his sovereign’s disgrace. [Note: [Col. XX] Letters 13–17.] Unable in conscience or honor to give the least sign of approval to the king’s scandalous marriage with Bertrade, countess of Anjou, he generously refused to attend it, although the king had invited him. He went further: in letters to several bishops he openly censured him, and wrote to the king himself with a vigor worthy of a bishop of the earliest centuries, without nonetheless exceeding the bounds of respect due to royal majesty. This was in 1092, and from that time this apostolic zeal cost the generous prelate his liberty. [Note: [Col. XX] Letters 19, 21, 22; Alberic, Chronicle, part II, p. 143; Suger, *Life of Louis*, p. 300.] Hugh, lord of Le Puiset and viscount of Chartres, seized him and shut him up in the castle of Le Puiset itself, seeking to break his spirit and thereby curry favor with King Philip. Ivo only became firmer, and God did not leave him without consolation in his bonds. Among others, William of Ros, abbot of Fécamp, visited him through letters in which he congratulated him on suffering for the same cause as Elijah and Saint John the Baptist of old. [Note: [Col. XX] Ivo, letter 19.] The people of Chartres, for their part, deeply attached to their bishop, formed the plan of going to free him by force of arms. [Note: [Col. XX] Letter 20.] But when the peaceable prelate was informed of this, he stopped the attempt by an admirable letter. Hoel, bishop of Le Mans, also came to his aid and acted so effectively with Pope Urban that they succeeded in securing his release. [Note: [Col. XX] Letters 21, 23, 25; Councils, ibid., p. 463.] Ivo, moreover, took proper measures to ensure that his flock would not suffer from his absence. [Note: [Col. XX] Ivo, letters 17, 44.]

Restored to his church, he found it in extreme want because of the ravages committed by the king’s men upon the estates of the bishopric, and he saw himself further burdened with false accusations. [Note: [Col. XX] Letter 22.] Secure in his innocence, he wrote to Philip, offering to justify himself legally, whether in a council or before the prince’s own court. Some time afterwards, however, he refused to attend the council held at Reims in 1094, although he had been invited, because he ought not to be judged outside his own province. [Note: [Col. XX] Letter 35.] Apparently on the same principle, he would not promise to attend another council summoned at Troyes for the Sunday after All Saints’ Day without first receiving Pope Urban’s advice. [Note: [Col. XX] Letter 46.] This council is otherwise unknown, and it is not known whether our prelate attended it. We know only that the archbishops of Reims, Sens, and Tours were to be present, and presumably the bishops of their provinces.

In 1095 the great council of Clermont in Auvergne was held, at which the pope himself presided. [Note: [Col. XX] Letter 38.] Ivo was among the bishops composing it and, after the assembly, had the honor of accompanying the Roman pontiff as far as Tours. [Note: [Col. XX] Councils, ibid., p. 603.] Urban held another council there, which Ivo attended, as he had all the other assemblies held by that pope on his journey. The council of Tours was held in March 1096; and the following year Ivo was in the Nivernais, though it is unknown on what occasion, unless again for some council. [Note: [Col. XX] Mabillon, ibid., book LXIX, no. 76.] During this journey he solemnly dedicated the church of the monastery of Saint-Étienne, assisted by Guy, the diocesan bishop; Gautier of Châlons-sur-Saône; and Humbaud of Auxerre.

[Col. XXI] Hardly anything important occurred in the Church of France during his episcopate in which he did not play a major part. He attended the council of Étampes in 1099 and that of Poitiers the following year, where King Philip and Bertrade were again excommunicated, and where the worthy bishops had much to suffer from the count of Poitiers. [Note: [Col. XXI] Councils, ibid., pp. 716, 720, 722; Ivo, letters 95–100.] When the legate Richard, bishop of Albano, convened another council at Troyes in 1104, Ivo at first excused himself from going, but nevertheless attended it. [Note: [Col. XXI] Councils, ibid., p. 740; Ivo, letter 141.] The subject of the assembly was the king’s absolution, which was nonetheless deferred to another time. On 30 July of the same year another council was held at Beaugency on the same subject. Ivo attended it as well and reported to Pope Paschal II what had occurred there. [Note: [Col. XXI] Ivo, letter 144.] When the king’s absolution was again postponed, Ivo urged the supreme pontiff to hasten it and to show some indulgence toward that prince. In this way he cleared himself of the reproach some laid upon him, that he had had the greatest share in the king’s excommunication. Previously he had furnished proofs to the contrary, since he had acted with Urban II to suspend execution of this design and had caused notice of it to be given to the king through the chief officer of his court. [Note: [Col. XXI] Letter 23.] Finally Philip was solemnly absolved at Paris at the beginning of December 1105, and he wished Ivo to take part in the ceremony. [Note: [Col. XXI] Councils, ibid., p. 742.] Before that date he had already restored Ivo to his favor, as appears from a diploma granted at Ivo’s request for the church of Chartres. [Note: [Col. XXI] *Spicilegium*, vol. XIII, pp. 296–297; Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, p. 831.]

Three years later, when this prince died on 29 July 1108, his son Louis the Fat was advised immediately after the funeral to have himself crowned without delay. [Note: [Col. XXI] Suger, ibid., p. 293.] “It was Ivo,” says Abbot Suger, “that prelate so worthy of respect and so full of wisdom,” who proposed this counsel. Accordingly Daimbert, archbishop of Sens, was summoned, and he performed the ceremony at Orléans on 2 August following, assisted by all his suffragans, among whom was our prelate. Hardly had it ended when the delegates of the church of Reims, which claimed to possess the sole right to crown our kings, arrived and lodged their protest. Ivo undertook to answer them and to justify Louis’s coronation. [Note: [Col. XXI] Ivo, letter 173.] He did so in a fine circular letter addressed to the Roman Church and to all churches acquainted with the complaint of the clergy of Reims, showing that its claim was founded neither upon reason, custom, nor law. Nor did Ivo’s devotion to his sovereign end there. He also urged him to marry, for the strengthening of the royal house and the tranquility of Church and state. [Note: [Col. XXI] Letter 239.]

In 1112 Joscerand, archbishop of Lyons, indignant—as were several others—at the treaty concluded in the preceding year between Pope Paschal and Emperor Henry V concerning the concession to that prince of the right of investiture, wished to assemble a council at Anse to oppose it. [Note: [Col. XXII] Mabillon, ibid., book LXXII, no. 23.] Having invited the bishops of the province of Sens, Ivo did not think they ought to attend, and in fact they did not. He doubtless feared to rekindle a fire that appeared extinguished and that soon afterward flared up again. Unable to bring any other remedy, he wrote in moving terms to Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, whom he knew to possess great influence at the imperial court, asking him to employ it in ending a schism which for more than thirty years had divided priesthood and empire. [Note: [Col. XXII] Ivo, letter 214.]

This zeal and pastoral solicitude for the welfare of the Church in general appeared on every occasion involving the violation of good order, even by popes and their legates. [Note: [Col. XXII] Letter 18.] We have various proofs in the collection of his letters. In circumstances of this kind, love of the rules prevailed over every consideration, and Ivo spared not even his closest friends. He was closely connected with Hugh, archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Holy See, and had shown him tokens of attachment when Pope Urban restored him to the latter dignity, of which Victor III had deprived him. [Note: [Col. XXII] Letter 24.] Yet when Hugh took it upon himself to halt the consecration of Daimbert, archbishop of Sens, until he had acknowledged the primacy of Lyons over that other metropolis, Ivo wrote to him on the matter with truly episcopal vigor. [Note: [Col. XXII] Letter 60.] Hugh took offense and complained of it to the pope, who consequently grew cold toward our generous bishop. [Note: [Col. XXII] Letter 67.] But Ivo only became firmer, as appears from his letter to the pontiff; and he took the opportunity to show that he held the episcopate solely in order to uphold the honor and right of the churches. This firmness might perhaps have drawn upon him the displeasure of pope and archbishop had not Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, then at Rome, justified Ivo before the Roman pontiff and, passing through Lyons on his return to France, reconciled him with Legate Hugh. [Note: [Col. XXII] Geoffrey of Vendôme, book II, letter 18.]

After some time Ivo learned that Stephen of Garlande, whose incapacity and other faults he knew, was intended for bishop of Beauvais. He employed every means to thwart his election and prevent his consecration, and succeeded. [Note: [Col. XXII] Ivo, letters 87, 89, 97, 98.] On the other hand, he supported with all his power the subsequent election of Galon, abbot of Saint-Quentin, whose merit he knew perfectly well. [Note: [Col. XXII] Letters 102, 104, 105, 110.]

The generous fearlessness of our prelate appeared not only in maintaining the canons and ecclesiastical discipline in spiritual matters; it also showed itself in matters concerning the temporal customs or duties owed by churches to sovereigns. Ivo left striking examples of this. King Philip ordered him to appear with the troops of the church of Chartres at a certain place where the king was to meet Henry, king of England and duke of Normandy; but as he attached unusual conditions to the order, Ivo took the liberty of making representations to him that were as firm as they were respectful. [Note: [Col. XXII] Letter 28.] Similarly, when Stephen, count of Chartres and Blois, demanded an unprecedented due from the church of Chartres, Ivo opposed him with a vigor worthy of a bishop devoted to his church’s interests. [Note: [Col. XXII] Letter 49.]

The many occasions on which he gave conspicuous proofs of his ability in every kind of affair, of [Col. XXIII] his love and zeal for the maintenance of good order, caused his reputation to spread abroad. Rome, which knew him better than others, feared and respected him at the same time. England revered his learning and virtue, and often resorted to his counsel. This appears from Ivo’s connections with King Henry I, Queen Matilda, and several bishops of the realm. Matilda in particular held the pious bishop in singular esteem, of which great evidence appears in the letters he wrote her. [Note: [Col. XXIII] Letters 107, 142, 174.] Out of regard for him she made the church of Chartres a rich gift of bells, for which the prelate knew how to thank her in a manner of excellent taste for that age.

If the whole Church and foreign countries drew such assistance from Ivo’s episcopate, the Church of France in particular, and especially the diocese of Chartres, drew even more. To convey a just idea of it, one would here have to give almost a complete analysis of his collection of letters. In his counsels and decisions addressed to persons of every rank, one would see that he was in his time the adviser of bishops and the oracle of ordinary faithful people. In their instructions and explanations, one would see how much he loved purity of faith and morals, the observance of sound discipline, and how much he labored for both. It is no exaggeration to say, to his credit, that his care was especially responsible for the kind of renewal then occurring in the Gallican Church among clergy and laity alike, and that his writings later helped to sustain it.

However strict Ivo may have been in his decisions on questions of morals and discipline, his conduct was full of enlightenment, wisdom, moderation, and gentleness. By this means he knew how to win the hearts of those whose passions he had opposed. An example may be observed in the person of Philip I, king of France. Another appears in Stephen, count of Chartres and Blois, who, after having had several disputes with the zealous prelate, regained his favor so completely that, at Ivo’s request, he abolished the pernicious custom established by his predecessors of pillaging, upon the death of a bishop of Chartres, the episcopal residence and all the estates dependent upon it. [Note: [Col. XXIII] Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, pp. 621–622.] But his gentleness never extended to tolerating vice. Among other proofs, he showed this particularly in the steps he took to end the scandalous conduct of a lord in his diocese named William and Adelaide, a close relative of Countess Adela of Chartres. [Note: [Col. XXIII] Ivo, letter 5.] By his wisdom and gentleness he opened the eyes of the unfortunate Roscelin, who, after renouncing his errors, embraced penance, as has been seen in his history. [Note: [Col. XXIII] Letter 7.]

To so many excellent qualities Ivo also joined a compassionate heart toward those under oppression or any other kind of affliction. On such occasions he took pleasure and found merit in employing on their behalf the influence he possessed with the powerful. Among the many examples of this beneficent generosity furnished by the letters of the tender-hearted prelate, it is enough to say that Saint Geoffrey, bishop of Amiens, Geoffrey, archbishop of Rouen, and Hubert, bishop of Senlis, when circumstances required it, experienced its happy effects: [Note: [Col. XXIII] Letters 253, 254, 258, 264.] the first with Louis the Fat, the other two with Pope Paschal II. When that pontiff was compelled to take refuge in France, Ivo had the honor of receiving him in his own house, where Paschal celebrated Easter in 1107; Ivo retained him there as long as he could. [Note: [Col. XXIII] Orderic Vitalis, book X, pp. 762, 810.] Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, compelled to leave his monastery by the vexations of the local lord, found with our generous bishop a retreat as gracious as it was honorable. [Note: [Col. XXIII] Mabillon, *Annals*, book LXIX, no. 92.]

But nothing surpassed the care Ivo took for instructing his clergy and people, as far as the needs of Church and state, to which he was obliged to attend, allowed him. [Note: [Col. XXIII] Ivo, letters 6, 12.] As soon as he had taken possession of his church, he set himself to instructing, correcting, uprooting, and planting. He had both the talent and zeal for it, and found ample opportunity to exercise both. The sermons that remain to us, both printed and manuscript, and which are apparently only the smallest part of those he preached to his people, attest that he often distributed to them the bread of the word. Not content to address them orally, he also sometimes issued pastoral letters to them, of which the collection of his other letters contains a fine example. [Note: [Col. XXIV] Letter 44.]

As for his personal conduct, however occupied he was by the care of his flock and by so many external affairs, he was as inwardly recollected in God as when he lived at Saint-Quentin of Beauvais. [Note: [Col. XXIV] Baillet, 23 December, p. 288.] Robert of Torigni did not fail to emphasize this piety in his praise of the great bishop. It made Ivo complain, from the beginning of his episcopate, that he was obliged to give himself to tumultuous occupations which deprived him of intimate union with God and of that lovable tranquility required by prayer. [Note: [Col. XXIV] Robert, additions to Sigebert, p. 750; Ivo, letter 6.] This same piety inspired him to support so many devout foundations in which God was to be served in spirit and truth. Besides what he had already done for Saint-Quentin of Beauvais, he newly founded, outside the gate of his episcopal city, the abbey of Saint-Jean-en-Vallée for Regular Canons. [Note: [Col. XXIV] Life, no. 16.] The celebrated Bernard, monk of Saint-Cyprien at Poitiers, having withdrawn to the diocese of Chartres and obtained from the local lord land on which to build a monastery, Ivo applied himself to the undertaking with such zeal and success that he deserved to be regarded as its founder jointly with Blessed Bernard. [Note: [Col. XXIV] Letter 283; Mabillon, ibid., book LXXI, nos. 39, 111.] The monastery was called Tiron, after the small neighboring river, and later became the head of an order. The convent of nuns at Hautes-Bruyères, of the Order of Fontevraud, also owed its foundation to the same prelate. He likewise established a hospital for the sick, was a benefactor of the Order of Cluny [Note: [Col. XXIV] Ivo, Life, ibid.], and of the abbeys of Marmoutier, Bonneval, and Bourgmoyen at Blois. [Note: [Col. XXIV] Letter 211; Mabillon, ibid., no. 16.]

In his pious benefactions Ivo did not forget his own church. [Note: [Col. XXIV] Robert, additions to Sigebert, ibid.; Ivo, Life, no. 2.] Mention has already been made of the notable service he rendered it by freeing it from those crying customs, which were veritable plunderings. He took care to embellish the cathedral and supply it with books and ornaments. He renewed and considerably enlarged the episcopal residence, adding to it a country house for the various uses of the [Col. XXV] bishops. The schools had been very well attended since the time of Saint Fulbert, and the place where they were held had to be very spacious. Ivo rebuilt it entirely, and left his church and canons various other tokens of his generous goodwill. Finally, he took some part in the foundation of the abbey of Saint-Victor at Paris, established in 1113. [Note: [Col. XXV] Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. VI, p. 219.] At least his subscription is read at the foot of the charter of King Louis the Fat for that foundation.

It remains to say something concerning the connections of our holy prelate. Without speaking of popes, kings, princes, and princesses, he was connected with almost all the great persons of his age. Most appear in the addresses of his letters; but we shall recall here only those with whom he was more intimately associated. Among them were Saint Bernard of Tiron, already mentioned, and Blessed Robert of Arbrissel. He had given the former the abbatial blessing; and out of regard for both men he had furthered the foundation of Tiron Abbey and the monastery of Hautes-Bruyères. Having become friends with Saint Anselm while studying at Bec, they continued their union after Anselm became first abbot and then archbishop of Canterbury. [Note: [Col. XXV] Ivo, letter 39.] They had the mutual consolation of seeing one another when, in 1103, Anselm came to France in order to go thence to Rome. [Note: [Col. XXV] Eadmer, *Historia novorum*, book II, p. 66.] Taking the route through Chartres, Anselm was received with much honor by Bishop Ivo, who, together with Countess Adela, persuaded him to wait until autumn for this long journey, in order to avoid the summer heat. On his return at the end of June 1105, Anselm again passed through Chartres and had the pleasure of seeing his good friend once more. [Note: [Col. XXV] Pp. 70.2, 71.1; Bernier, *History of Blois*, appendix, p. 8.] Indeed, he stayed there for a considerable time: having subscribed a charter for the canons of Bourgmoyen at Blois on 24 June, he did not leave until 22 July following, when he departed for L’Aigle.

There was likewise a close union between Ivo and Lambert, bishop of Arras, as appears from a letter of the former inserted among those of the latter. Lambert wrote one of his own letters to thank Ivo for a notable service he had just rendered the Church of Arras, and for others it had already received from him on different occasions. [Note: [Col. XXV] Ivo, letter 33; Baluze, *Miscellanies*, vol. V, pp. 286, 356.] From the time our prelate blessed Geoffrey as abbot of Vendôme—on 23 September 1093—a lasting friendship arose between them, attested by the first nineteen letters of the second book of Geoffrey’s collection, all written to the bishop of Chartres. [Note: [Col. XXV] Labbe, *New Library*, vol. I, p. 289.] The epistle by which Hugh of Sainte-Marie, monk of Fleury and one of the learned men of his century, dedicated to him in 1110 his great chronicle shows that they were connected by literary pursuits. [Note: [Col. XXV] Mabillon, ibid., no. 98.]

Ivo lived to old age and died full of glory and merit, in the odor of sanctity. [Note: [Col. XXV] Ivo, letter 254.] But ancient and modern writers differ greatly concerning the exact day and year of his death. Some place it as early as 1114; others assign the following year. Some date it 1 January 1116; others, such as Robert of Torigni, postpone it to 1117; and still others fix it on 23 December. [Note: [Col. XXV] This chronology shows how far Bernard de la Guionie departed from the truth when, speaking in praise of our prelate, he placed him only under [Col. XXVI] Pope Anastasius IV, about the middle of that century, and made him a disciple of Gilbert de la Porrée. André Thevet, in his *Cosmography*, was even further from the truth, assigning him to the end of the fifteenth century, under Charles VIII, king of France. [ [Col. XXV] Muratori, *Italian Writers*, vol. III, p. 240.].] The opinion fixing his death on 23 December 1116 deserves preference, since it is that of the historians Helinand of Froidmont and Alberic of Trois-Fontaines. [Note: [Col. XXVI] *Historia Chronica*, p. 454, 1; Ivo, *Life*, nos. 2, 18; *Cistercian Library*, vol. VII, p. 178; Robert, additions, ibid.; Alberic, Chronicle, part II, p. 228; Mabillon, ibid., book LXXII, no. 125; Egasse du Boulay, vol. I, p. 613; Cave, p. 541.] Ivo may then have been in the seventy-seventh year of his age, and had spent twenty-five years and one month in the episcopate, counting from the day of his ordination. He was buried in the choir of the abbey church of Saint-Jean-en-Vallée, of which, as has been said, he was the founder. [Note: [Col. XXVI] Robert, additions, ibid.; *Old Gallican Chronicle*, vol. III, p. 488, 2; Bollandists, ibid., p. 248.] Three epitaphs have been dedicated to his memory. One was composed by Philip, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, but the authors of the other two are unknown. The one copied here, preferred to the others because it better expresses the character of this great bishop, was taken from an ancient manuscript of President Barnabé Brisson and has been printed in various collections.

## Epitaph

In mind, hand, tongue, learning, and bodily practice,

Prudent, generous, affable, helpful, blameless;

A firm pillar of the house of the Lord, which by salutary right

He cherished, fortified, instructed, and continually enlarged,

By counsel, writings—how it should live in order—and resources;

The sick freely experienced his help, the needy his means.

The glory of this city, Bishop Ivo, worthy of remembrance,

Lies in this tomb and awaits the coming of the Judge.

Besides these three epitaphs, which contain an outline of our prelate’s history, Father Fronteau, a Regular Canon of Sainte-Geneviève, composed his life. It is printed at the head of his *Decree* in the latest edition, and Bollandus’s successors included it in their great collection of the Acts of the Saints, with certain remarks of their own. [Note: [Col. XXVI] Bollandists, 20 May, pp. 247–252.] M. Baillet, for his part, published another on 23 December among his *Lives of the Saints*. [Note: [Col. XXVI] Baillet, ibid., pp. 282–288.] Finally, about the same time, a third writer produced a small duodecimo volume bearing the title: *The Spirit of Ivo of Chartres in the Government of His [Col. XXVII] Diocese and at the Courts of France and Rome*. The work was printed at Paris by Anisson in 1701 and gives, in fourteen chapters, a fairly good portrayal of Ivo’s conduct in the three different spheres announced by its title page. Bibliographers and other writers who have spoken of this excellent bishop are almost innumerable. We have profited from the best things they have said of him, but without confining ourselves to complete Lives, in which we did not find everything necessary, in our judgment, to represent him as he was. We have composed another account, drawn chiefly from his own writings and, for the rest, from contemporary authors.

Ivo became as distinguished by holiness of life as by great learning: *nec minus sanctitate quam scientia venerandus*, “worthy of reverence no less for holiness than for learning.” [Note: [Col. XXVII] Trithemius, *Writers*, ch. 349.] His learning is sufficiently known from the writings that remain by him; and his holiness, from the earliest times, attracted great veneration from the people, especially the people of Chartres. [Note: [Col. XXVII] Ivo, *Life*, nos. 1; 2–2, 20.] Yet for several years no feast was celebrated in his honor, and it appears to be unknown whether he was ever canonized in due form. Pope Pius V merely issued a bull in 1570 transferring to 20 May the feast then observed in his memory on 23 December, because that latter day always falls in Advent and is unsuitable for the solemn celebration of feasts. Another indication of his sanctity is the treatment inflicted upon him by the Calvinists in the time of their ravages, when they reduced his relics to ashes along with those of the other saints.

Moreover, Ivo, bishop of Chartres, must not be confused with another Ivo, a cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso, formerly a Regular Canon of Saint-Victor at Paris, who died in 1142 or the following year. [Note: [Col. XXVII] Ibid., no. 18; Aubery, *History of the Cardinals*, vol. I, pp. 127–128.] The same distinction must be made regarding a third Ivo, surnamed “of Chartres” and styled Doctor, who had studied under Gilbert de la Porrée, later bishop of Poitiers. The latter cited him in his defense at the council of Reims in 1148, together with Rotrou, another of Gilbert’s disciples, then bishop of Évreux and later archbishop of Rouen.

It has been said above that Ivo, bishop of Chartres, had the consolation, before his death, of seeing some of his disciples raised to the highest dignities of the Church; but we have particular knowledge only of the following. John, a Roman by birth, received instruction for some time from Ivo at Saint-Quentin of Beauvais [Note: [Col. XXVII] Hugh of Flavigny, *Chronicle*, p. 261.]. After leaving there, he became a monk at Le Bec and was subsequently made bishop of Tusculum and legate of the Holy See. Another disciple, bearing the same name as the preceding, after perfecting under him what he had already learned at the school of Utrecht, became bishop of Thérouanne and lived so saintly a life in the episcopate that the Church counts him among the saints whom she honours [Note: [Col. XXVII] Bollandists, 27 January, p. 796, nos. 1–2.]. From the manner in which Ivo recommends to Pope Urban II and to Richer, bishop of Sens, William, elected bishop of Paris in 1095, it appears that he regarded him as one of his pupils [Note: [Col. XXVII] Ivo, letters 43, 50.]. Galon, William’s successor, likewise had the advantage, as has been shown in the article devoted to him, of being trained in the same school. Wulgrin, first chancellor of the church of Chartres and then elected bishop of Dol at the council of Troyes in 1107, is acknowledged as one of his disciples [Note: [Col. XXVIII] Letters 176, 178.]. Samson of Mauvoisin, archbishop of Reims, who died in 1161, is also included among them [Note: [Col. XXVIII] Marl., *Metropolis Remensis*, vol. II, p. 329.]. Odo, successively a regular canon and then abbot of Saint-Quentin of Beauvais after Galon, clearly calls himself a pupil of our saintly prelate in a fairly long letter addressed to him, in which he lays before him the state of his conscience [Note: [Col. XXVIII] Ivo, unnumbered letter, p. 230.].

Thevet, in his *History of Learned Men*, believed that he had given us a life-like portrait of Bishop Ivo, which he had engraved in copperplate from another supplied to him by an old book in the library of Cardinal Georges d’Amboise [Note: [Col. XXVIII] Thevet, vol. II, p. 125.]. Ivo is represented there with hair falling to his shoulders, a skullcap covering almost his entire head, and a full, long robe to which a hood is attached, hanging down behind.

## § 2. HIS WRITINGS

[Col. XXVII]

Robert of Torigni, abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel, writing in the century in which Ivo of Chartres died, attests in the brief eulogy he composed for him that this prelate had left many illustrious monuments of his learning and ability [Note: [Col. XXVIII] Robert, addition to Sigebert, p. 750.]; yet he specifies none of them. The anonymous author of Melk, who published about the same period his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers, names four of these works [Note: [Col. XXVIII] Melk, *Writers*, ch. 95.]; and Sigebert, earlier than either of them because he was Ivo’s contemporary, reduces them to his *Decree* and the collection of his letters [Note: [Col. XXVIII] Sigebert, *Writers*, ch. 167.]. Subsequently, however, a crowd of scholars interested in the fame of this great bishop investigated the matter and discovered several others. The principal works have been printed; the rest still survive only in manuscript. Here is their enumeration, beginning with those already printed.

1. The most celebrated of all is his collection of canons, concerning which several observations must be made. Most—indeed, nearly all—the writers who have undertaken to discuss it recognize only one collection; but two must be distinguished and admitted, for the reasons now to be seen.

While Ivo was still abbot of Saint-Quentin of Beauvais, and made the study of ecclesiastical antiquity one of his principal occupations, he perceived how useful a good collection of canons and other rules in force in the Church would be. Several had already existed before that time, as we observed when discussing those of Regino of Prüm and Burchard of Worms, in the article on Olbert, [Col. XXIX] abbot of Gembloux. But Ivo, knowing their defects—though he did not himself avoid them all—and judging them insufficient, conceived the design of another collection and seriously set about carrying it out. The method he adopted to accomplish it is noteworthy, and we learn it from himself in the rather extensive preface which he placed at its head [Note: [Col. XXIX] Ivo, *Decree*, preface.]. Having assembled into one body, with labour such as may be imagined, extracts from ecclesiastical rules which could be supplied to him by the letters or decretals of the popes, the acts of councils, the treatises of the Fathers, and the constitutions of Catholic kings, he then arranged them in a certain order. The motive that led him to undertake this arduous labour was to serve the public, enabling those who did not possess these writings to draw from his collection whatever suited their needs. In order that everyone might readily find what he sought, he observed the following order: he says that he will treat first of faith, which he calls the foundation of Christian religion; then of the sacraments; next of the conduct of morals; and finally of matters concerning the various affairs—that is, those belonging to the Church’s jurisdiction. To these four principal heads the author refers everything which he judged should be discussed in his work, under various books or parts subdivided into several titles.

Foreseeing that readers might not sufficiently understand what he said, or might think they detected contradiction in it, he takes care to warn them not to be hasty in blaming it, but attentively to consider what is said according to the strictness of law or according to indulgence, since all ecclesiastical government is founded upon charity. By this principle, he adds, explaining it at considerable length, the Church at one time adheres to the severity of the rules and at another relaxes them out of condescension [Note: [Col. XXIX] Doujat, bk. III, ch. 28, no. 1; Poss., *Appendix*, vol. II, p. 306; Baillet, 23 December, p. 283.]. What Ivo says here concerns the method he followed in his collection, inserting under the same subject canons of both kinds, that is, strict and moderate ones. But lest anyone suppose that such condescension or moderation could apply in every case, he observes that there are two kinds of precepts, just as there are two kinds of prohibitions. Some are of divine law, established by the eternal law; others are merely disciplinary, established by men for the sake of a greater good [Note: [Col. XXIX] Doujat, bk. III, ch. 28, no. 1; Poss., *Appendix*, vol. II, p. 306; Baillet, 23 December, p. 283.]. The former, he says, are immutable and consequently admit of no moderation; but the same is not true of the latter.

Such, in general, is the plan upon which Ivo directed his two collections. He gave the first the title *Pannormia*, formed from two words, one Greek and the other Latin, as though to express a body comprising all laws or rules of ecclesiastical law [Note: [Col. XXIX] Doujat, bk. III, ch. 28, no. 1; Poss., *Appendix*, vol. II, p. 306; Baillet, 23 December, p. 283.]. Certain purists, excessively fastidious in this matter, would have it read *Pannomia*; but the ancient manuscripts do not permit this. Others, more numerous, have attempted to deprive Ivo of the credit for this work, claiming that he composed no other work on the subject than his *Decree*; but they will never persuade informed persons of this. The reasons on which they base their opinion are far too weak. They say, on the one hand, that at the end of this work there are several matters taken from the decretals of Calixtus II and Innocent, his successor after Honorius, who became popes only several years after Ivo’s death [Note: [Col. XXIX] Doujat, ibid., no. 4.]. They further allege that the *Pannormia* is nothing other than an abridgement of our author’s *Decree*, made in his own time by a certain Hugh, described as bishop of Châlons-sur-Marne, as Vincent of Beauvais reports.

Nothing could be weaker than these supposed reasons. With respect to the first, it is no wonder that the *Pannormia* underwent what so many other original works have suffered in every age: after leaving their authors’ hands, they received extraneous additions, at least in several of their copies. This is precisely what happened to the *Pannormia*, as can readily be established by the two very ancient manuscripts of this collection which Dom Mabillon attests that he saw in the abbeys of Anchin and Blandinberg [Note: [Col. XXIX] Ibid.]. Both bear the name of Ivo of Chartres and contain none of the alleged additions. The same proof is found in the old manuscript of Saint-Victor and in another possessed by Dom Antonio Augustinus [Note: [Col. XXX] Baluze, *On the Emendation of Gratian*, preface, no. 23.].

The other reason upon which this work is disputed from him is no more solid. It was not a Hugh, bishop of Châlons, who made the abridgement in question, since this church had no bishop of that name after the time of Ivo of Chartres; rather, it was Haimond of Bazoches, who governed it in the middle of the twelfth century [Note: [Col. XXX] Alberic, *Chronicle*, part II, p. 320.]. Far from this abridgement being identical with the *Pannormia*, as is supposed, it proves the opposite: it shows that the *Pannormia* already existed, because it was drawn from it, and not from the same author’s *Decree*. Alberic of Trois-Fontaines attests this, and deserves all the more credit because we know with certainty that in his *Chronicle* he speaks only on the authority of historians who preceded him. “This Bartholomew, bishop of Châlons,” says Alberic under the year 1151, “died on his pilgrimage to Jerusalem; and Haimond of Bazoches, archdeacon, a man distinguished by nobility and virtue, was elected bishop, and he made the manual of decrees according to the *Pannormia* of Ivo of Chartres.” This testimony is as clear as it is decisive and requires no commentary.

That of Vincent of Beauvais, correctly understood, is no less so, except that in place of Haimond he names Hugh, bishop of Châlons, as abridger of our prelate’s work [Note: [Col. XXX] Doujat, ibid., no. 2.]. For after speaking of the latter’s work, which he also calls an abridgement in relation to the sources from which it had been drawn, he adds that the author entitled it *Pannormia*; but because it was not a work of small compass, the bishop of Châlons undertook to abridge it and made a small portable book, entitled the *Summary of Ivo’s Decrees*. This is precisely the *Manual* or *Enchiridion* of which Alberic speaks as drawn from the *Pannormia*, and which was consequently very different from it.

The learned M. Baluze had already proved this by another argument [Note: [Col. XXX] Baluze, ibid., no. 20.]. The abridgement made by the bishop of Châlons, he says, on the testimony of Vincent of Beauvais just cited, bore the title *Summary of Ivo’s Decrees*. Now the *Pannormia*, in three old manuscripts of the abbey of Saint-Aubin at Angers and a fourth in the library of Saint-Victor at Paris, is uniformly entitled everywhere *Pannormia*, and never *Summary of Decrees*. The same is true of the editions published of it, showing that the manuscripts used retained the same title. We ourselves saw it similarly entitled in another old manuscript of the abbey of Saint-Ouen at [Col. XXXI] Rouen. In all this there is another observation which settles the difficulty finally: the manuscript of Saint-Victor is older than the abridger, whoever he was. It is therefore beyond dispute that his writing is not the *Pannormia*, and that there is no reason to deny it to Ivo of Chartres, its true author.

Another question is also raised concerning it: whether it preceded the *Decree* of the same prelate, or came only afterward [Note: [Col. XXXI] Doujat, ibid., no. 9.]? M. Doujat appears to favour the second alternative and brings forward some weak reasons; but M. Baluze openly declares for the first, which deserves preference, since the *Decree* is not only more extensive but also better worked out than the *Pannormia*, and displays much greater order [Note: [Col. XXXI] Baluze, ibid.]. A historian from the latter part of the very century in which Bishop Ivo died, who, like Alberic of Trois-Fontaines, wrote only from those who preceded him, informs us that Ivo published his *Decree* in 1090, exactly one year before he was elevated to the episcopate [Note: [Col. XXXI] Pagi, under the year 1117, no. 15]. By this reckoning, the *Pannormia* must already have left its author’s hands some years earlier.

We should not, however, believe that Ivo had before him all the original books which he generally indicates in his preface as the sources from which he drew what he reports [Note: [Col. XXXI] Ivo, *Decree*, preface, 1.]. Books were then too scarce for it to be possible to assemble such a great number in two, three, or four libraries. He drew the greater part from collections preceding his own: specifically from that of the famous Isidore, compiler of the false decretals, and from those of Regino, Burchard, and perhaps others besides [Note: [Col. XXXI] Doujat, ibid., no. 2.]. He carried this out in such a way that he copied even the errors of those compilers. Isidore had arranged his decretals according to the chronological order of the popes whom he represented as their authors. Ivo changed that order and preferred an arrangement by subjects. The constitutions of Catholic kings which he employs, as he announces in his preface, are the Theodosian Code, Justinian’s Code, Digest or Pandects, and the Capitularies of our kings [Note: [Col. XXXI] ch. 27, no. 3.].

The *Pannormia* is divided not into ten books, as some writers have claimed, but into only eight, each book subdivided into titles or articles. At times there are as many as sixteen titles, the highest number. It circulated among men of letters even after the author had published his *Decree*. We have seen that Haimond of Bazoches abridged it, and there is thought to be evidence that Gratian drew for his compilation from the *Pannormia* rather than from the *Decree* [Note: [Col. XXXI] Conc., 28, no. 5.]. Moreover, the preface at its beginning being the same as that read before the *Decree*, the two writings have very often been confused with one another [Note: [Col. XXXI] No. 10.].

We have two editions of the *Pannormia*: one in quarto, published at Basle in 1499 under the care of Sebastian Brant [Note: [Col. XXXII] Ibid.; Baluze, ibid., no. 23; Cave, p. 541, 2.]. But it is full of errors. The other, in octavo and much more correct, appeared at Louvain in 1557, published by Étienne Valère for Antoine-Marie Bergagne [Note: [Col. XXXII] *Library of Saint-Florent of Salm*.]. It was supervised by Melchior de Vosmedian, doctor of arts and theology, who took care to provide the text in its integrity. Yet he confused its title with that of our prelate’s *Decree*, which would suggest that he belonged to those who confused the two works.

2. Ivo, seeing the favourable reception given to his *Pannormia*, conceived the plan of a more extensive work on the same subject and soon carried it out by composing what is called his *Decree* [Note: [Col. XXXII] Baluze, ibid., no. 24.]. The *Pannormia* served as his outline in this second undertaking. He merely altered somewhat the order of its subjects, treated them much more fully, and added new ones. Thus he extended this new compilation to seventeen books or parts, each divided into a great number of chapters—sometimes as many as 378 or even 435, as in the fifth and sixth parts. It is true that these chapters are generally very short, although some, especially in the first and second parts, occupy one or two full pages. In other respects, the author retained the entire preface of the *Pannormia*, which, as observed, has occasioned the confusion of the two works. This preface begins with the words *Excerptiones regularum ecclesiasticarum*—“Extracts of ecclesiastical rules”—from which the title of the work was formed in some manuscript copies [Note: [Col. XXXII] Trithemius, *Writers*, ch. 349.]. Ivo himself uses the equivalent phrase to designate it when referring to it in his letters, calling it *collectiones canonum*, “collections of canons” [Note: [Col. XXXII] Ivo, letter 262.].
