In an old manuscript of Saint-Victor at Paris, the work bears neither title nor author’s name at its beginning [Note: [Col. XXXII] Baluze, ibid.; Doujat, ibid.]. At the end one reads only: *Explicit liber canonum*—“Here ends the book of canons.” On the following leaf, a later hand notes that this collection of canons belongs to Ivo, formerly bishop of Chartres, and is called *Decreta Ivoniani*; here an obvious error is apparent, the copyist having written *Ioviniani* in place of *Ivoniana*, “the decrees of Ivo.” Yet the work is scarcely known except by the name *Decree*, the title it bears in printed editions, apparently in conformity with the manuscripts from which it was published.

At the beginning, after the preface, comes the table of the seventeen books or parts according to which the author judged it proper to distribute the subjects he undertakes to discuss [Note: [Col. XXXII] Ivo, *Decree*, preface, pp. 6, 2, 7.]. Ivo himself took care to arrange this table, and the first editor praised it for the fine order prevailing in it. He might also have praised it for the accurate idea it affords of the range and variety of matters treated there. The author’s method consists in setting under each title or chapter passages from the Fathers of the Church and other ecclesiastical writers, from ecumenical and provincial councils, from papal decretals, and sometimes from ordinances of Catholic princes relevant to the matter. Thus, if it possessed as much discrimination and accuracy as it does research and learning, it would be an inestimable repertory. It was nonetheless of very great usefulness to learned people, who could not, without considerable expense, acquire—or without distaste read—all the books which our author [Col. XXXIII] excerpted and arranged in order. Indeed, it was regarded as the most perfect work of its kind that had appeared up to that time. It therefore enjoyed the greatest currency, along with the same author’s *Pannormia*, until the celebrated collection of Gratian, which became known only more than sixty years later, gained the ascendancy. M. de Marca counts our prelate’s work as the first collection of both laws—civil and canon law—made in the West [Note: [Col. XXXIII] Marca, *Concord of Priesthood and Empire*, bk. III, ch. 6, no. 2.]. It is nevertheless certain that Regino of Prüm had included several passages of civil law in his own.

Some writers hold that Ivo drew the greater part of his work from that of Burchard of Worms, excepting the second and penultimate parts [Note: [Col. XXXIII] Doujat, ibid., no. 8.]. Others maintain that this seems true only insofar as both copied the same canons or decrees. Yet it would be very difficult fully to defend Ivo from the charge, since he is seen copying Burchard’s errors, sometimes even in the titles. There is likewise much reason to think that Ivo also drew from Regino, from whom Burchard himself, according to M. Baluze, took about 670 chapters to enrich his compilation.

Some writers, including Dom Beaugendre, have wished to take the credit for this work from Ivo of Chartres and transfer it to Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans and afterward archbishop of Tours. They base their claim on what Hildebert says in one of his letters, where he speaks of a collection of decrees which he had undertaken to reduce into one volume but had not been able to finish because of his occupations. Dom Beaugendre concludes from this that Hildebert must at least have begun the work, *saltem inchoaverit* (“at least have initiated it”), and that Ivo of Chartres, a studious and industrious prelate, added the finishing touch to it [Note: [Col. XXXIII] *Excerptiones autem decretorum quas in unum volumen ordinare disposuimus, ad suum finem nondum perductae sunt. Opus enim hoc liberum curis pectus desiderat, etc.*—“But the extracts of decrees which we have proposed to arrange into one volume have not yet been brought to their completion. For this work requires a mind free from cares, etc.”]. For, adds Hildebert’s editor, it is inconceivable that two authors fairly distant from each other should have undertaken the same work without communicating with one another and should have coincided so completely as to employ the same words. To overthrow this claim beyond recovery, we need only the letter cited against us: it is the twenty-seventh of the second book [Note: [Col. XXXIII] Hildebert, *Works*, pp. 123–124.]. It was written at the end of 1118 or the beginning of 1119, upon the death of Matilda, queen of England, which occurred in 1118. These dates are certain and established by Dom Beaugendre himself. “It is in this letter that Hildebert speaks of the work he had undertaken and which his occupations had not allowed him to finish” [Note: [Col. XXXIII] Ibid., p. 124, note.]. The work, therefore, was not finished when Hildebert wrote at the end of 1118 or the beginning of 1119. Let them now tell us how Ivo of Chartres, who had died two years earlier—that is, in 1117 at the latest—could have added the finishing touch to Hildebert’s work, which had only been begun, at the earliest, by the end of 1118. Such reasons are unanswerable and make the addition of others unnecessary.

Let us therefore conclude that it is wrongly sought to credit Hildebert with Ivo of Chartres’s *Decree*; and that, if the bishop of Le Mans composed a work of this kind, it has not come down to us, whether because he never gave it its finishing touch or because it has been lost.

As for the prologue to the *Decree*, found at the end of Hildebert’s letters in all editions of the Fathers and which, according to Dom Beaugendre, belongs to the bishop of Le Mans, we need only the editor’s admission to overthrow this claim. For since this prologue, as Dom Beaugendre himself acknowledges, is found in no manuscript of Hildebert, on what ground can it be attributed to him or he believed to be its author? Presumably on the basis of the letter of which we have spoken, which we have shown proves precisely the contrary. In a word, Ivo of Chartres’s work was finished in 1116, while Hildebert’s was still unfinished in 1118 when he wrote the twenty-seventh letter. It is therefore evident that Ivo could not have inserted into his writing something that had not yet come from the bishop of Le Mans’s pen.

We have only two editions of Ivo of Chartres’s *Decree*: the first issued in 1561 by Jean du Moulin, doctor of canon law at the University of Louvain; the second published at Paris in 1647 by Fr. Fronteau, regular canon of Sainte-Geneviève.

3. Of all Ivo’s works, the most substantial and, rightly, most highly esteemed by scholars is the collection of his letters.

These letters number 289, including a charter of Ivo [Note: [Col. XXXIII] Ivo, letters, pp. 1, 124.] and a rather long letter [Note: [Col. XXXIV] It appears that Juret appended this letter of Hugh of Pontigny and Saint Bernard to Ivo’s letters only because he believed that the bishop of Chartres mentioned in the letter was Ivo himself. But this is certainly an error, for the bishop of Chartres in question is none other than Geoffrey II, the immediate successor of Saint Ivo in the bishopric of Chartres.] from Hugh, abbot of Pontigny, and Saint Bernard to Odo, abbot of Marmoutier, found at the end as an appendix. All were written during his episcopate, except no. 287, written while he was still an abbot.

It is evident that the person who took care to arrange this collection did not always preserve chronological order exactly. Besides the fact that no. 287 should be first for the reason just given, several others are misplaced. For example, no. 7, to Roscelin, was certainly written only after several of those that follow it, since the author had already been bishop for several years when he wrote it. The same must be said of no. 25, to Pope Urban II, which was written only after the seventh year of his episcopate. Conversely, no. 277, addressed to Hildebert, newly elected bishop of Le Mans, ought to be placed much earlier, since it dates from 1097. At the head of the collection are placed two letters of Pope Urban II concerning Ivo’s ordination, serving as an introduction to all those which follow.

All scholars agree that this collection of letters is among the most precious monuments of ecclesiastical learning available to us for the end of the eleventh and beginning of the twelfth century. M. Baillet, the celebrated critic, speaks of it thus in the author’s life [Note: [Col. XXXIV] Baillet, 23 December, p. 287]:

> “In Ivo’s collection of letters we have the principal points of the doctrine, morals, and discipline of his time, and above all many excellent decisions upon various cases of conscience and various questions of law proposed to him. Everywhere one sees a profound knowledge of the affairs of the Church, a marvellous uprightness of heart, learning and ability of very great range, and a zeal for the purity of faith and morals and for the observance of the canons—always most ardent, yet always enlightened, prudent, and tempered by an admirable moderation and wisdom.”

During the author’s lifetime, Sigebert spoke of it as a collection of very useful letters [Note: [Col. XXXV] Sigebert, *Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 167.]. In particular, identifying letter 60, written in 1099 to Hugh, archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Holy See in France, he says that this letter, though brief in words, is full of citations, canons, and authorities from the holy Fathers, which make it highly instructive. Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines, presents this collection as a work everywhere inspiring love of good and justice and hatred of evil and injustice [Note: [Col. XXXV] Alberic, *Chronicle*, part II, p. 228.]. Among other books bequeathed about 1150 to Soissons Cathedral by Bishop Anculf, Ivo of Chartres’s *Decree* and letters are listed, showing the esteem in which this prelate held both works [Note: [Col. XXXV] Dormay, *History of Soissons*, p. 161.].

It would be desirable to enter into detail concerning at least the most important and curious contents of so excellent a collection. But since this would carry us far beyond the limits we have set ourselves, and since M. Dupin has anticipated us in this matter by providing a fairly accurate account of the contents of each letter [Note: [Col. XXXV] Dupin, twelfth century, pp. 3, 78.], we shall content ourselves with observing that what makes this collection still more precious is the various points of both civil and ecclesiastical history of France which would be sought elsewhere in vain.

From this source above all must be drawn the principal circumstances and unhappy consequences of the disastrous divorce of King Philip I from Queen Bertha, his lawful wife, and of his scandalous marriage to Bertrade of Montfort, whom the prince had carried off from the count of Anjou, her husband [Note: [Col. XXXV] Ivo, letters 13, 14, etc.]. It is chiefly there, too, that one may learn the reasons of state which led King Louis VI to have himself crowned in 1108, not at Reims but at Orléans [Note: [Col. XXXV] Letter 189.]. There are even some letters that may be of great service for the genealogies of various old French houses: namely, letter 45 for the genealogies of the houses of Meulan and Crépy; letter 129 for the genealogies of the house of Vendôme and of the viscounts of Blois; and letter 211 for that of the counts of Flanders and the counts of Rennes.

It should be added that there are two letters on the Eucharist: no. 251, to Manasses, bishop of Meaux, from which the gentlemen of Port-Royal drew the fourth lesson of their forty-third Office of the Blessed Sacrament; and no. 287, to Haimery, abbot of Anchin, in which he decides that the apostles received at the Last Supper the passible body of Jesus Christ as it then was, whereas we now receive it in communion as impassible, as it has been since his resurrection. This latter letter seemed so important to Jean Ulimier, prior of the regular canons of Saint-Martin at Louvain, that he judged it appropriate to append it to the treatises on the Eucharist by Lanfranc, Alger, Guitmund, Adelman, and Peter the Venerable, in a collection printed at Louvain in 1561, in octavo [Note: [Col. XXXV] *Library of Saint-Vincent of Cenre*]: from there it passed into Margarin de la Bigne’s *Library of the Fathers*, and into other collections as well [Note: [Col. XXXV] *Library of the Fathers*, vol. I, pp. 485, 488].

Concerning no. 276, it is important to know that it was written not to John, archbishop of Lyons, as the printed editions state, but to Joscerand, archbishop of the same city [Note: [Col. XXXV] Mabillon, *Annals*, bk. LXXII, p. 3, and vol. V, appendix, p. [Col. XXXVI] 682.]. This observation is necessary lest one persist in enlarging the catalogue of archbishops of Lyons with a supposed John who never existed. With regard to no. 277, in which Saint Ivo accuses Hildebert, newly elected bishop of Le Mans, of having led a licentious life since becoming archdeacon, it should likewise be known that François Juret, in his notes upon this letter, claimed that it was written not to Hildebert, as stated in the first printed edition, but to another man called Aldebert, as an old manuscript of Saint-Victor reads. But, to refute Juret’s claim, it is enough to observe that Hildebert is not called Aldebert only in the address of this letter; he is also so named in one of the poems of Baudri, his contemporary and friend [Note: [Col. XXXVI] Duchesne, vol. IV, p. 271.]. In any case, this letter cannot in any way prejudice the reputation of the illustrious bishop of Le Mans, since Ivo says that all he advanced to Hildebert’s disadvantage was known to him only from persons who had neither wished to advise nor to consent to his election, and who therefore had an interest in disparaging him [Note: [Col. XXXVI] Mabillon, *Annals*, bk. LXIX, no. 59.].

If Ivo’s collection of letters is a precious monument of his ecclesiastical learning, it is no less a monument of his modesty and humility. No doubt through the effect of this modesty, when writing his twenty-eighth letter to King Philip he gives himself no title except that of humble clerk, or chaplain, of His Majesty. In the greater number of his other letters, he styles himself only the humble minister or servant of the church of Chartres [Note: [Col. XXXVI] Letters 32 and following.].

Letter 118 shows that his knowledge of geography was not very extensive, and that he scarcely knew the antiquity of the metropolitan sees of France except through a superficial glance at the ancient *Notitiae* of Gaul [Note: [Col. XXXVI] Le Beuf, dissertation on the history of Paris, vol. II, p. 172.].

One must not forget that his letters are no less full than his *Decret* of citations from the *Pandects*, the *Code*, the *Novels*, and the *Institutes* of Justinian. [Note: [Col. XXXVI] Pasq., *Recherches de la France*, p. 880.]

Three different editions have been produced of the complete collection of the letters of our holy and learned prelate. The first appeared at Paris from Sébastien Nivelle; some copies bear the date 1584 and others 1585. I do not know whether any bear 1583 as well, [Note: [Col. XXXVI] *Bibliothèque Bigot*, part II, p. 181.] since Father Le Long expressly gives that date. [Note: [Col. XXXVI] Le Long, *Bibliothèque française*, p. 331, no. 2.] François Juret issued this quarto edition, as is evident from his undated dedicatory epistle to Pierre Pithou. The privilege is dated 1578, which might lead one to believe [Col. XXXVII] that there had already been a previous edition; but it is certain that none preceded this one. The second likewise appeared in Paris, from Sébastien Cramoisy, in 1610, in quarto. [Note: [Col. XXXVII] *Bibliothèque Caumartin*, p. 44.] Lipenius places it in the preceding year, 1609. [Note: [Col. XXXVII] Lip., *Bibliotheca theologica*, vol. I, p. 606.] It was again Juret who issued this edition, as appears from a new dedicatory epistle addressed to Jacques-Auguste de Thou, First President of the Parlement of Paris. It is preferable to the first, for besides correcting several errors and filling several lacunae in the earlier edition, Juret added learned observations which elucidate the text and greatly assist in clarifying the author’s history and identifying the persons to whom the letters were addressed. There are also notes by Jean-Baptiste Souchet, supplementing what was lacking in Juret’s. We owe the third edition to Father Fronteau, a regular canon of Sainte-Geneviève, who followed Juret’s second edition throughout in his general edition of our prelate’s works, published at Paris by Laurent Cottereau in 1647, folio. [Note: [Col. XXXVII] *Bibliothèque de Saint-Vincent de Cen...*]

Besides these three editions of the complete collection, several others have appeared containing a certain number of letters, whether gathered together or printed separately. We shall not enumerate here all those found in Baronius’s *Annals*, [Note: [Col. XXXVII] Bar., year 1100, etc.] or in the collection of councils; [Note: [Col. XXXVII] *Councils*, vol. X, pp. 486, 490, etc.] the detail would be tedious. We shall say only that André Duchesne inserted in his collection of French historians all those concerning the history of France, regarding them as excellent monuments and original sources for historical use. [Note: [Col. XXXVII] Duchesne, vol. IV, pp. 217–247.] They number forty-six.

One of the most considerable among those in Duchesne is no. 1897 of the great collection. This letter, dealing with the anointing and coronation of our kings, was printed separately: first in Latin, under the title *De consecratione Ludovici regis* (“On the Consecration of King Louis”), at Sens in 1561, in quarto, through the care of Claude Goust, lieutenant-general of that city; then translated into French at Chartres in 1594, likewise in quarto. [Note: [Col. XXXVII] Le Long, *Bibliothèque française*, p. 155, no. 1.] This French edition appears to have been made on the occasion of King Henry IV’s coronation. The same letter is also found, both in Latin and French, in M. Godefroi’s French ceremonial, vol. I, pp. 127 and 130. Letter sixty, written in 1099 to Hugh, Archbishop of Lyons, concerning the investiture of bishops and abbots—the only one, as seen above, which Sigebert specifically mentioned—was printed through the care of Melchior Goldast among the apologies of Emperor Henry IV, published by Goldast at Hanover in 1611. [Note: [Col. XXXVII] Gold., *Apologiae*, pp. 183–187.] It should be noted that Archbishop Hugh made a reply to this letter, which M. Baluze brought to light and published in his *Miscellanea*.

We have seen above that letter 287, to Haimeri, Abbot of Anchin, was also printed separately by Ulimmier and by Margarin de la Bigne. We learn from Lambecius that the Emperor’s library at Vienna preserves an excellent manuscript of the letters of Ivo of Chartres, by means of which, he says, a large number of errors in the printed editions could be corrected. [Note: [Col. XXXVII] Lamb., *Bibliotheca*, vol. II, p. 933.] This manuscript is apparently the same one mentioned by Possevin, which in his day was kept at Vienna by Wolfgang Lazius and seems to have been particularly valued. [Note: [Col. XXXVIII] Poss., *Apparatus*, vol. II, p. 307.] Dom Montfaucon indicates another manuscript containing only 274 letters, but distinguished by the presence, at its end, of a rhymed prose beginning: *Alpha et omega, magne Deus*—“Alpha and Omega, great God.” [Note: [Col. XXXVIII] Montf., *Bibliotheca*, p. 1238.] If our prelate himself compiled the ancient collection of his letters, as there is reason to believe, he may well have added this prose as an epilogue, to dedicate the entire work to God.

However much effort Juret took to gather all Ivo’s letters, three escaped him; they deserve to be joined to the rest when a new edition is made. They are: letter 20 of book II of the letters of Geoffrey of Vendôme, which treats of the repetition of extreme unction; another addressed to Pope Paschal II, in support of the Abbey of Saint-Pierre at Chartres, which Dom d’Achéry drew from the Abbey of Évron in Maine and inserted in his notes on Lanfranc, p. 360; and finally one addressed to Adela, Countess of Blois, concerning that princess’s plan to restore the ancient monastery of Saint-Martin-en-Vallée. [Note: [Col. XXXVIII] Mab., *De re diplomatica*, pp. 364, 652; *Annals*, bk. LXVIII, no. 60.] Dom Mabillon gave us this last letter not only in print but also engraved from the original in his great work on diplomatics. Sanderus speaks of a fourth letter, on the mysteries of the Mass, among the manuscripts of the Abbey of Saint-Amand, [Note: [Col. XXXVIII] Sand., *Bibliotheca Belgica*, part I, p. 42.] but, as he says nothing further about it, we cannot provide fuller information.

In addition to letters absent from Juret’s collection, three charters of our prelate are also lacking from it. The first, issued for the benefit of the regular canons of Bourgmoyen at Blois, is dated at Chartres, 24 June 1105. It is noteworthy because, among other witnesses, it was subscribed by the great Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, who was consequently then at Chartres. [Note: [Col. XXXVIII] Bernier, *History of Blois*, proofs, p. 8.] We owe this document to Jean Bernier, who published it among the documentary proofs of his *History of Blois*. The second is the foundation charter of Tiron Abbey, dated 3 February 1110, written in the name of the Church of Chartres, and subscribed first by Ivo in his capacity as bishop. [Note: [Col. XXXVIII] Mab., *Annals*, vol. V, appendix, pp. 680–681.] The opening of this document recounts the visions and extraordinary apparitions which preceded the arrival at Chartres of Blessed Bernard, founder and organizer of this house, who had come to ask Ivo and his canons for the ground on which he wished to build it. The subscriptions show what dignities were then established in the Church of Chartres: there were six archdeacons and several provosts. Dom Mabillon, having found it in the cartulary of Tiron, placed it among the documents constituting the appendix to the fifth volume of his *Annals*. The third charter is a public instrument in favour of Bonneval Abbey, addressed to Abbot Bernier, which Dom d’Achéry published at the end of his notes on Guibert of Nogent. [Note: [Col. XXXVIII] Guib., notes, p. 664.]

[Col. XXXIX] Among the omissions from Juret’s collection of letters may also be counted two judgments of Ivo, which Jacques Petit printed after the *Penitential* of Saint Theodore, Archbishop of Canterbury. [Note: [Col. XXXIX] Theod., *Poenitential*, vol. II, pp. 551–555.] The first is a sentence pronounced by Ivo against three provosts of his cathedral, who grievously harassed the canons, their fellow members, and the poor. The second is a judgment rendered by him, as commissioner of the apostolic legate Hugh, Archbishop of Lyons, concerning the dispute then existing between the monks of Marmoutier-les-Tours and those of Saint-Martin-des-Champs at Paris over possession of the church of Hienville, situated in the parish of Le Puiset, in the diocese of Chartres. By this judgment the church of Hienville was awarded forever to the monks of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, and the monks of Marmoutier were entirely dismissed from their claims.

Finally, one might add to the letters of Ivo of Chartres the regulation which he made for his cathedral, mentioned in the necrology of that Church in these terms: *Junioratus omnes hujus Ecclesiae et precarias in communes redegit usus, et eas in posterum personis distribui tam suo quam apostolico privilegio, vetuit*—“He converted all the juniorates of this Church and its precariae to common use, and by both his own and an apostolic privilege forbade their future distribution to persons.” [Note: [Col. XXXIX] Du Cange, *Glossarium*, new ed., vol. III, p. 1595.] From M. du Cange’s explanation of the words *junioratus* and *precaria*, it appears that Saint Ivo ordained that all vicariates dependent upon his cathedral, and all the labour-services owed to them, should enter the common manse; and that henceforth no one should receive them under title of a *personatus* or benefice. [Note: [Col. XXXIX] Ibid., vol. V, p. 803.] He took care to have this regulation confirmed by a papal rescript; but neither the regulation nor the rescript appears to have survived.

To return to the printed collection of Ivo’s letters: certain proof that it perhaps contains only the smaller part of those he wrote during his episcopate is that almost all the letters composing book II of Geoffrey of Vendôme’s correspondence are addressed to this prelate. Yet there is only one from him—namely, letter 20 of the same book. Is it likely that Ivo made only this one reply to Geoffrey, and remained silent concerning that abbot’s other letters?

Before ending this article, it is proper to observe, lest the writings of the Bishop of Chartres be multiplied without reason, that the work entitled in a manuscript of Saint-Amand Abbey, *Ivonis Carnot[ensis]. De excommunicatis, nisi denuntiati fuerint, non vitandis*—“Ivo of Chartres: On Excommunicated Persons Not to Be Avoided Unless They Have Been Denounced”—is nothing other than his letter 186 to Lawrence, monk of La Charité, in which this point of ecclesiastical discipline is expressly established. [Note: [Col. XXXIX] Sand., *Bibliotheca Belgica*, part I, p. 33.]

**4.** After Ivo’s letters, the 1647 edition of his works gives us a collection of his sermons, numbering twenty-four. [Note: [Col. XL] Ivo, *Sermons*, pp. 259–304.]

The first six are rather short works or separate treatises than simple sermons. Thus the author himself, when citing the fifth, in which he discusses the relationship between the old and new priesthoods, calls it nothing but a little book: *In libello, quem composui de convenientia veteris et novi sacerdotii*—“In the little book which I composed on the correspondence of the old and new priesthood.” [Note: [Col. XL] Ep. 231.] Likewise, manuscripts almost always designate them by the title of books or treatises. For example, a manuscript of Liessies Abbey in Hainaut lists them thus: *De sacramentis dedicationis liber unus; De sacris ordinibus liber unus*—“One book on the sacraments of dedication; one book on holy orders.” [Note: [Col. XL] Sand., ibid., part II, p. 28.] Nevertheless, because the first three are said to have been delivered in a full synod, there can be no doubt that they are discourses delivered by our pious and learned prelate for the instruction of his clergy, not so much in the form of sermons as in that of a master’s lessons to his disciples.

Since these first six sermons or brief treatises are the most substantial of all and seem to have brought our prelate much credit, we cannot avoid giving at least a general account of them.

In the first, entitled *De sacramentis neophytorum* (“On the Sacraments of the Newly Baptized”), the author, after surveying the mysteries wrought in the first six ages of the world and noting the institution of baptism, undertakes to explain all the ceremonies employed by the Church in administering this sacrament and to unfold their mystical and spiritual meanings. [Note: [Col. XL] Ivo, *Sermons*, pp. 259–202 [sic].] He does so with much clarity, order, and precision. In the second, entitled *De excellentia sacrorum ordinum, et de vita ordinandorum* (“On the Excellence of Holy Orders and the Life of Those to Be Ordained”), after identifying the signs of a genuine calling to the clergy and explaining the meaning of the word *cleric*, he explains in detail the seven ecclesiastical orders: doorkeeper, reader, exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, deacon, and priest. He marks with great exactitude the duties of each order and the obligations of those promoted to it; furthermore, he maintains that there is not one of these seven orders which Jesus Christ himself did not in some manner personally exercise during his mortal life. It is noteworthy that, distinguishing priests from bishops, he says that the former are successors and vicars of Christ’s seventy disciples, and the latter successors of the apostles. In the third, entitled *De significationibus indumentorum sacerdotalium* (“On the Meanings of Priestly Vestments”), after speaking of the origin of priestly garments, which he says were instituted on the model of those under the old law, he gives their mystical reasons and dwells upon the virtues represented and figured by these holy vestments. It appears that the garments of deacons, priests, bishops, and cardinal-priests were then the same as those still used today, although their form has changed in the course of time. Reading these first three sermons, one perceives that they form a sequence: the second presupposes the first, and the third supplements what is lacking in the second.

The purpose of the fourth, entitled *De sacramentis dedicationis* (“On the Sacraments of Dedication”), is to show that all the religious ceremonies employed by the Church in the consecration of its material temples are only mysterious images of what baptism accomplishes in consecrating spiritual temples, namely the faithful. It is a sermon certainly worthy of its author’s learning and piety. The fifth, entitled *De convenientia veteris et novi sacrificii*—one should read *sacerdotii*—“On the Correspondence of the Old and New Priesthood,” is a genuine treatise in which the author extensively proves that the priesthood of the old law had no other purpose than to prefigure and represent that of the new, and that the coarse worship rendered to God by the Synagogue was merely an image of the truly religious worship now rendered to him by the Church. This discourse alone would suffice to convince us that Ivo was among the most profound scholars of his age in understanding [Col. XLI] the great mysteries contained in the Scriptures of both Testaments. Finally, the aim of the sixth, entitled *Cur Deus natus et passus est* (“Why God Was Born and Suffered”), is to prove the necessity of the incarnation and death of the Son of God. The author’s principal argument is that, if God had saved sinful humanity, as he was able, solely by his will and without the sacrifice of his Son, he would indeed have manifested his limitless power; but he would not have satisfied his sovereign justice, which required, on the one hand, that the sinner should not remain unpunished and, on the other, that the devil should not be deprived of the rights he had acquired over humankind through the victory he had won over it, without deserving to be stripped of them. Ivo develops and extends this argument and adds several matters showing that he was as capable in theological subjects as he was learned in law. Ivo appears to have composed this sixth discourse—much shorter than the preceding ones and having no appearance of a sermon—on the model of Saint Anselm’s celebrated treatise, *Cur Deus homo?* (“Why Did God Become Man?”). We may add that the writing of the Bishop of Chartres is only a précis and abridgment of that by the holy Archbishop of Canterbury.

The library of the King of England preserves a manuscript headed: *Ivonis Carnot[ensis] episcopi, De sacramentis ecclesiasticis, libri quatuor*—“Four books by Ivo, Bishop of Chartres, on ecclesiastical sacraments.” [Note: [Col. XLI] *Royal Library of England*, p. 152; VIII, 12.] Might these four books be the first four sermons of Ivo just discussed? They are indeed like four separate books, to which that title would suit very well, if by “sacraments of the Church” one understands not what we properly call the Church’s seven sacraments, but, more generally—as our author does—all sacred signs which the Church employs in its ceremonies and in all the external worship it renders to God. These are apparently also the first four sermons designated by the title *Book of Sacraments*, mentioned by several bibliographers, [Note: [Col. XLI] Sand., part I, p. 359; Montf., *Bibliotheca*, p. 1359, etc.] and presented about the year 1130 by Guy, Bishop of Le Mans, to his cathedral [Note: [Col. XLI] Mab., *Annals*, vol. III, p. 348.] together with the *Decret* of our Ivo of Chartres. The author of Bishop Guy’s life says: *Ecclesiae nostrae decreta cum libro De sacramentis, quae Ivo, Carnotensis episcopus, abbreviavit, noscitur contulisse*—“He is known to have bestowed upon our Church the decrees, together with the book *On the Sacraments*, which Ivo, Bishop of Chartres, compiled in abridged form.” Perhaps, nonetheless, this *Book of Sacraments* is nothing other than the first sermon, *De sacramentis neophytorum*. After this necessary brief digression, let us return to our subject.

As to the remaining eighteen sermons of our prelate, fifteen are short but lucid and solid instructions on the principal feasts of the year: Advent, the Nativity of the Lord, the Circumcision, the Purification, Septuagesima, the beginning of the fast or Ash Wednesday, Lent, the Annunciation, Palm Sunday, the Lord’s Supper or Maundy Thursday, Easter, the Ascension, Pentecost, and the Chair of Saint Peter. [Note: [Col. XLI] Ivo, *Sermons*, pp. 286–304.] The last three are instructions on the Lord’s Prayer, the Apostles’ Creed, and adulterous, or worldly, attire among men as well as women. From one of these sermons, one learns that the rule of continence during Lent for married persons was still in force at that time, at least in the Church of France. The opening of the sermon on the Lord’s Supper seemed so important to the gentlemen of Port-Royal that they made it the fifth lesson of their forty-third office of the Blessed Sacrament. It should be noted that, in a manuscript belonging to the King of England, the Advent sermon is entitled *De distinctione Adventus Domini* (“On the Distinction of the Lord’s Advent”), because it treats of the twofold coming of Jesus Christ: in the humility of his mortal flesh in the fullness of time, and in all the glory of his divine majesty at the end of time. [Note: [Col. XLI] *Royal Library of England*, p. 152, VIII, 13.]

The first to undertake publication of Ivo’s sermons was Melchior Hittorpius, who included the first twenty-one in his collection of ancient writings on the liturgy, printed at Cologne by Gervin Calenius in 1568, folio, [Note: [Col. XLII] *Bibliotheca Minorum Centuriatorum*] and reprinted at Rome in 1591 and Paris in 1624. [Note: [Col. XLII] *Bibliotheca theologica*, II, p. 702.] In this collection they bear the title: *B. Ivonis Carnot[ensis] episcopi, De ecclesiasticis sacramentis et officiis, De praecipuis per annum festis, sermones nunc primum editi*—“Sermons of Blessed Ivo, Bishop of Chartres, on ecclesiastical sacraments and offices, and on the chief feasts of the year, now published for the first time.” This title confirms the already noted observation that the book, or four books, of sacraments bearing Ivo’s name in certain manuscripts are only the first sermon, or the first four sermons, of his collection. From Hittorpius’s collection the same sermons passed into the general edition of Ivo’s works prepared at Paris in 1647 through the care of Father Fronteau. [Note: [Col. XLII] *Bibliothèque de Saint-Vincent de Cen...*] The editor added three other sermons, the first of which—on adulterous attire—had already been published by Juret from a Saint-Victor manuscript, after the letters of our venerable prelate.

The twenty-four sermons in Father Fronteau’s edition are not the only ones Ivo composed.

The most recent editors of Saint Augustine inform us that the sermon for a martyr beginning *Triumphalis B. martyris N.*—“The triumphal [feast] of Blessed Martyr N.”—belongs to him. [Note: [Col. XLII] Aug., *Sermon Appendix*, p. 368; *Patrologiae*, vol. XXXIX, *Works of Saint Augustine* V, part II, col. 2158.] This sermon, which in the Roman Breviary bears Saint Augustine’s name, formerly stood as no. 44 among the sermons which that holy doctor composed for saints; it is now no. 223 in the appendix to the third volume of his works. The same editors state that they found it in an ancient manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés Abbey, where it occurs between other sermons of Ivo of Chartres.

It should be noted that this sermon is not the only one certainly belonging to our blessed prelate which has been honoured by being regarded as a work of Saint Augustine. Three others of his occur in the same appendix: namely, no. 64, which is his twenty-second sermon on the Lord’s Prayer; no. 74, which is his twenty-fourth sermon on adulterous attire; and no. 247, which is his sixth sermon, “Why Jesus Christ Was Born and Suffered.” The Benedictines state in the errata to their eleventh volume of Saint Augustine that these three sermons occur in Father Fronteau’s edition with some errors, corrected in their appendix to the fifth volume of Saint Augustine.

Besides the sermon for a martyr falsely attributed to Saint Augustine, Ivo composed three more which have never been published. The first is on the Cross, and occurs in two manuscripts, one [Col. XLIII] belonging to the King of England and the other to Thomas Theyer in London. [Note: [Col. XLIII] *Royal Library of England*, ibid.; *Catalogue of English Manuscripts*, part IV, no. 662.] The second is on the feast of Saint John the Evangelist, also found in two manuscripts, one from Cambron Abbey and the other from Lobbes Abbey in Hainaut. [Note: [Col. XLIII] Sand., ibid., part I, p. 359, and part II, p. 359.] The third is on the marriage of Jesus Christ and is found in a manuscript noted by Dom Montfaucon. [Note: [Col. XLIII] Montf., *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum*, p. 319, B.]

If we accepted the conjectures of Jean Prévost, a canon of the Church of Rouen, we would be inclined to believe that Ivo of Chartres was also the author of six other sermons on the duties of pastors, [Note: [Col. XLIII] Joan. Abr., *De officiis ecclesiasticis*, pp. 444–487.] which Jean Prévost himself published at Rouen in 1679 after the treatise on the offices of the Church by John, Bishop of Avranches and later Archbishop of Rouen, [Note: [Col. XLIII] *Literary History*, vol. VIII, pp. 64, 74.] discussed in its proper place.

These sermons having been found without an author’s name in a five-hundred-year-old manuscript in the library of the Messrs Bigot, Jean Prévost conjectured that they might be by Ivo of Chartres. [Note: [Col. XLIII] Joan. Abr., ibid., preface, pp. 9–10.] His reasons are: (1) the same manuscript contains three sermons of that prelate which have already appeared several times under his name; (2) the style and manner of thought of the author of these six sermons closely resemble Ivo’s style and manner of thought in sermons unquestionably his, especially in the sermon he composed on the Chair of Saint Peter; and (3) finally, they cannot be denied to be the work of some bishop, since their author addresses his priests as their superior and as one charged, in that capacity, to answer to God for their conduct. This shows that they are synodal discourses.

But reasons no less forceful are advanced against these arguments, plausible though they may appear. For, it is said: (1) if these six sermons truly were by Ivo of Chartres, is it possible that, among the prodigious multitude of manuscripts of his works still preserved in libraries, not even a few should be found in which the sermons are expressly attributed to him? (2) We have seen above that the first three of the twenty-four printed sermons are synodal discourses intended thoroughly to instruct his clergy in all matters concerning their offices and duties. This being so, how likely is it that he would have wished to compose six other synodal discourses on the same subject, in which he would have done little but repeat what he had said in the preceding ones? (3) It is known that, with synodal instructions, bishops are not accustomed to multiply writings on the same subject without necessity. (4) It must be carefully observed that the author of these six sermons invariably begins each with a scriptural text as the theme of his entire discourse. Ivo of Chartres, by contrast, never does this in any sermon certainly his. Thus, even if the style of the author of these six sermons resembles that of our prelate, there is at least a considerable difference in the preaching method of the two. As for Jean Prévost’s statement that this author’s manner of thought closely resembles Ivo’s, we do not see what inference can be drawn from it. The Bishop of Chartres did not have a manner of thought peculiar and distinctive to himself. In that age there was almost only one manner of thought on all questions concerning religion; it was only after Ivo that the Church had the sorrow of seeing itself inundated by a multitude of different opinions, in dogma as well as morals and discipline.

Besides, whoever may be the author of these six sermons, he appears to have been a judicious man, highly versed in the study of Scripture, the Fathers, and the councils; he possessed piety, discernment, and a great knowledge of all his obligations, and wrote well enough for the age in which he lived. All these traits, joined to other circumstances, suggest to us that the sermons may well have been by Hildebert, Bishop of Le Mans. This may be examined in the article on the latter.

**5.** The final work published under Ivo’s name in the 1647 edition of his works is a short chronicle of the kings of France, beginning with Pharamond and ending with Philip I. [Note: [Col. XLIV] Ivo, *Chronicle*, pp. 308–307 [sic].]

It is surprising that François Juret, who first drew this chronicle from the dust of libraries, did not realize that it cannot be by our prelate. The proof is certain, since it speaks of Henry I, King of England, as a prince then in the thirtieth year of his reign. Now the thirtieth year of this prince’s reign—he ascended the throne in 1100—coincides with the year 1130 of the Christian era. How, then, could Ivo, who died as early as 1116, be the author of a chronicle written about fourteen years after he was no longer in the world?

It is true that some have wished to say that the passage of this chronicle concerning Henry I, King of England, is an addition made by another hand. [Note: [Col. XLIV] Cave, p. 541, no. 2; Oud., vol. II, p. 875.] But what proofs can they offer? Is this alleged addition not found in every manuscript? Moreover, it follows very naturally from what precedes: since the author had immediately before spoken of William the Conqueror and William Rufus, Henry I’s predecessors on the English throne, it was natural that he should not omit the latter prince, who was certainly reigning when the author wrote. To this must be added that no bibliographer is known to have attributed this chronicle to the Bishop of Chartres. We shall discuss the chronicle in the article on Hugh of Sainte-Marie, monk of Fleury, who is its true author.

Besides, scholars now agree that this chronicle is very slight and highly defective. [Note: [Col. XLIV] Le Long, *Bibliothèque française*, p. 341, no. 2.] According to Abbé Le Gendre, its author relates many things that do not accord with contemporary historians.

It has already been observed that François Juret was the first to publish this chronicle, in the two editions of Ivo of Chartres’s letters which he issued: [Note: [Col. XLIV] *Bibliothèque Caumartin*, p. 44; Le Long, ibid.] the first at Paris in 1584 or 1585, in quarto; the second, likewise at Paris, in 1610, in octavo. Marquard Freher took the trouble to reprint it in 1613, [Note: [Col. XLIV] Le Long, ibid.; Fab., *Bibliotheca Latina*, bk. VI, p. 559.] in the first part of his collection of French historians. From Juret’s first two editions it again passed into the Paris folio edition of Ivo’s works of 1647. [Note: [Col. XLIV] *Bibliothèque de Saint-Vincent de Cen...*]

We shall here give an account of this last edition, so as not to return to it. Although it is advertised [Col. XLV] as containing all the writings of Ivo of Chartres, it certainly contains only part of them: the *Decret*, the Letters, the Sermons, and the short Chronicle just mentioned. Added are François Juret’s and Jean-Baptiste Souchet’s notes on the letters, together with the author’s Life, which was reprinted by the Bollandists under 20 May. At the beginning, in the copy in the library of Saint-Vincent Abbey at Le Mans, are two different dedicatory epistles, both addressed to Jean Lescot, Bishop of Chartres. The first is by Father Fronteau, regular canon of Sainte-Geneviève at Paris, who presents himself as editor and dedicates the volume to the Bishop of Chartres in both his own name and that of his congregation. The second is by Jean-Baptiste Souchet, who likewise claims to be editor of the same edition, asserting it to be his own work and one for which Father Fronteau vainly sought honour for himself and his congregation. This produced between the two scholars a most contemptible literary lawsuit, whose history we do not undertake to give here. We shall say only that Cave [Note: [Col. XLV] Cave, p. 541, no. 2.] and Oudin [Note: [Col. XLV] Oud., p. 875, no. 2.] attribute it to Souchet, apparently because they had seen only his dedicatory epistle, whereas Messrs Dupui [Note: [Col. XLV] Dupui, *Catalogue of Canon Law*, p. 133.] and Dupin [Note: [Col. XLV] Dupin, p. 83.] attribute it to Father Fronteau.

**6.** Besides the short chronicle just discussed, another and far more extensive chronicle has also been attributed to Ivo. It begins with Ninus, founder of the Assyrian monarchy, and is divided into two parts. The first ends in Charlemagne’s final year; the second extends to about the year 1034, or rather to the reign of Louis XI. [Note: [Col. XLV] Cave, ibid.; Oud., pp. 875–876; Lamb., *Bibliotheca*, vol. II, pp. 856, 860.]

Gérard-Jean Vossius says that he saw this chronicle at Amsterdam, in a manuscript of Guillaume Oomsius, where it bore the title: *A Brief History of the Deeds of Certain Assyrian Kings, of the Deeds of All Roman Emperors, and Finally of the Deeds of Charlemagne and All His Successors, Composed by the Venerable Ivo, Bishop of Chartres.* [Note: [Col. XLV] Vossius, *Hist. Lat.*, bk. II, ch. 47.] It occurs with the same title in a manuscript of Mr. Cotton at London. [Note: [Col. XLV] *Bib. Cott.*, p. 97, no. VIII, 22.] On the authority of a third manuscript, Marquard Freher had part of it printed under the name of our learned prelate in his collection of French historians, published at Hanover in 1613. [Note: [Col. XLV] Fabricius, *Bib. Lat.*, bk. VI, p. 559.]

The attribution of this chronicle to Ivo of Chartres must be very ancient, since it is expressly cited as his in a letter which Nicholas, a monk of St Albans in England, wrote around the year 1176 to Peter of Celle, abbot of Saint-Remi: “The venerable Ivo, bishop of the people of Chartres, wrote in his *Chronicles*,” it is said in this letter, [Note: [Col. XLV] Peter of Celle, bk. IX, ep. 9, p. 184.] etc.

It is likely that this chronicle is not different from a book which, in the inventory made in 1458 of the books of Gauthier de Shiginpton, canon of Chartres, is entered thus: “Ivo, bishop of Chartres, *On a Collection of Ecclesiastical Histories*, a meagre table,” [Note: [Col. XLV] *Monastic. Angl.*, vol. III, p. 363, I.] etc. It should be noted in this connection that the same chronicle is in fact described as an ecclesiastical history in several ancient manuscripts, such as that of Saint-Denis cited by Dom Mabillon. [Note: [Col. XLV] Mabillon, *Ann.*, bk. 74, no. 48.] Might it also be the same work as a history found in one of the manuscripts of the abbey of Saint-Evroul in Normandy—the fifty-fourth quarto—with the title: *History of Master Ivo*?

But although, as we have just seen, the attribution of this chronicle to Ivo of Chartres is both very ancient and very widespread, it is nevertheless certain that this work is not his. [Note: [Col. XLVI] Lambecius, ibid.; Oudin, ibid.; Sanderus in Vossius, p. 42; Mabillon, ibid.; Alexandre, *Instr. ecclés.*, vol. VI, p. 515, 2; Dupin, ibid., p. 83.] All scholars now agree that it belongs to Hugh of Sainte-Marie, monk of Fleury, or Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire. He composed its first part in 1110, at the request of Adela, countess of Blois and Chartres, and then its second part at the request of Queen Matilda, wife of Henry I, king of England, as will be seen in the article on that writer.

What apparently caused the mistake was [Note: [Col. XLVI] This letter is found at the head of the testimonies of the ancients concerning Ivo of Chartres, collected at the beginning of the 1647 edition of his works. It is discussed in Dom Mabillon, *Ann.*, bk. LXXIV, no. 48.] a letter from this same Hugh of Sainte-Marie to our prelate, in which he sends him his work and asks him kindly to take the trouble of reviewing and correcting it. Since this letter stood at the head of the chronicle, superficial readers or inattentive copyists, without examining the letter further, may have concluded, on seeing Ivo’s name in it, that he was the author of the chronicle. It was all the easier for them to fall into this error because the author’s name was little known, whereas Ivo’s was famous everywhere. Those familiar with manuscripts know that errors of this kind were only too common before the invention of printing.

**7.** If our prelate cannot be considered the author of the two preceding chronicles, the same is apparently not true of a *Life of Saint Augustine* which bears his name. This *Life*, hitherto unknown to all bibliographers, occurs in two manuscripts: one in the library of Mr. Cotton in London, where it bears the title, “*Life of Blessed Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, by Ivo, Bishop of Chartres*”; [Note: [Col. XLVI] *Bib. Cott.*, p. 93, no. 13.] and the other in the church of St Peter’s, Cambridge, where it is entitled: “*Extracts of the Venerable Ivo, Bishop of Chartres, from the Confessions and Life of Blessed Augustine, Bishop of Hippo*.” From the latter title it appears that this *Life* is composed of passages drawn from Saint Augustine’s *Confessions* and from the life of that holy doctor written by Possidius, bishop of Calama.

**8.** In the enumeration of Ivo of Chartres’s works made by the anonymous writer of Melk, published by Dom Pez, he lists a *Martyrology of the Saints*; [Note: [Col. XLVI] Anonymous of Melk, *Script.*, ch. 9, p. 155.] but this martyrology may well be an imaginary work, since absolutely nothing about it is found elsewhere.

**9.** When, in our eighth volume, we spoke of the *Micrologus on Ecclesiastical Rites*, we knew certainly that this excellent work was by a bishop who lived before the end of the eleventh century; [Note: [Col. XLVI] *Hist. litt.*, vol. VIII, pp. 320, 323.] but we did not know with the same certainty that this bishop was Ivo of Chartres. We [Col. XLVII] are indebted to Henry Wharton for having made known to us this important fact in such a manner that it can no longer be doubted. [Note: [Col. XLVII] Fabricius, *Bib. Lat.*, bk. IX, pp. 607–608.] The same author further informs us that this work is only a detached part of a more extensive work which Ivo composed on the offices of the Church, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, of which there is a very fine manuscript, almost as old as the author, in the library of Lambeth in England.

This work of Ivo on the offices of the Church, as Wharton presents it, consists of seventy-one chapters. The first eight treat respectively of matins, lauds, prime, terce, sext, none, vespers, and compline. The following sixty-two form the *Micrologus*; and the last, which is not in the *Micrologus*, treats of the authors of the Mass and of each of its parts. It is clear from this that it is among the most substantial and extensive ancient works composed on the liturgy.

Those who desire a more exact and detailed account of it may satisfy themselves by reading what was said in the eighth volume of the literary history about the *Micrologus*, which forms a considerable part of our prelate’s work on the offices of the Church. We shall only observe here that this work on ecclesiastical offices, of which Ivo is the author and which would well deserve to be printed in its entirety, is manifestly none other than the work listed by the anonymous writer of Melk under the name *Sentences on the Divine Offices*, which he expressly attributes to our holy prelate.

Besides the Lambeth manuscript indicated by Wharton, there are two further manuscripts: one in the library of All Souls College, Oxford, and the other in that of St Benedict’s College, Cambridge. [Note: [Col. XLVII] *Cat. mss. Angl.*, pt. II, no. 1435, and pt. III, no. 1444.] To these four English manuscripts must be added one kept at Rome in the Vatican Library, which belonged to the Queen of Sweden. [Note: [Col. XLVII] Montfaucon, *Bib. bib.*, vol. I, p. 48, no. 1522.]

**10.** One of the works which, in all likelihood, would do Ivo most honour if it were printed is his commentary on the Psalms. [Note: [Col. XLVII] Le Long, *Bib. sac.*, vol. VII, p. 810, 2.] It is found in two manuscripts: one in the library of Mr. Colbert, numbered 1473, in two folio volumes; and another in the library of Saint-Allire at Clermont in Auvergne, in one folio volume; and in a third manuscript in the Low Countries, mentioned by Sanderus. [Note: [Col. XLVII] Sanderus, pt. II, p. 28.]

**11.** In several manuscripts, both French and English, there is a book under the name of Ivo of Chartres entitled: *On the Manifold Distinction of the Scriptures*. [Note: [Col. XLVII] Montfaucon, *Bib. bib.*, p. 135, C.] It is not easy to determine what this book is. In one manuscript belonging to the public library of Cambridge, its title is explained as though the book were nothing other than the collection itself of Ivo’s letters. [Note: [Col. XLVII] *Cat. mss. Angl.*, pt. III, no. 2230.]

Here is the title: “Ivo, bishop of Chartres, *On the Manifold Distinction of the Scriptures Contained under One Appearance of Chaste Utterances*; or, as another has noted it, *The Letters of Ivo*.” Conversely, in another manuscript belonging to Sir Cotton, [Note: [Col. XLVII] *Bib. Cott.*, ibid.] the title is expressed as though the book were nothing other than our prelate’s *Panormia*: “The Book of the *Panormia* of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, *On the Manifold Distinction of the Scriptures Contained under One Appearance of Chaste Utterances*.” In a third manuscript of Hereford Cathedral, the same book is designated only by the general title *Distinctions of Ivo of Chartres*. [Note: [Col. XLVIII] *Cat. mss. Angl.*, pt. IV, no. 1702.] It is for those who may one day undertake to publish a new edition of this great prelate’s works to bring this writing to light and make it known to the public. They should be informed that a copy is found among the quarto manuscripts of the abbey of Mont-Saint-Michel, no. 165.

**12.** Possevino speaks of a work by our prelate entitled *Book on Determining the Decrees of the Fathers*, which in his day was at Vienna in Austria, together with Saint Ivo’s letters among the manuscripts of Wolfgang Lazius. [Note: [Col. XLVIII] Possevino, vol. II, p. 307.] This work is even less known to us than the preceding one, unless it is either the *Panormia*, the *Decretum*, or perhaps some fragment of one or the other.

**13.** We are likewise ignorant what another book is, entitled *Book on the Sacraments of Devotion*, which some are said to attribute to Ivo, but which Father Combefis claims, on the authority of Blessed Peter Damian, to be by Saint Fulbert. [Note: [Col. XLVIII] Fabricius, *Bib. Lat.*, bk. VI, p. 642.]

**14.** Finally, we are still ignorant what a *Gospel of the Blessed Virgin* is, said to survive in manuscript with Ivo’s sixtieth letter to Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, in the library of Caius-Gonville College, Cambridge. [Note: [Col. XLVIII] *Cat. mss. Angl.*, pt. III, no. 746, 5.]

**15.** The same is not true of a discourse or treatise *On the Matter, Order, and Truth of the Sacraments of Jesus Christ and of the Church*, which is reported to be at London in a manuscript of Thomas Bodley, [Note: [Col. XLVIII] Ibid., pt. I, no. 2014.] for the place occupied by this discourse in the same manuscript gives every reason to think that it is nothing other than the first sermon of Saint Ivo, entitled *On the Sacraments of the Neophytes*. As to another discourse in the same manuscript, under the title *On the Clerical State and Its Office*, it is manifestly our prelate’s sermon which treats of the excellence of sacred orders and the duties of those raised to them. [Note: [Col. XLVIII] Ibid.]

**16.** Sixtus of Siena speaks of a Humbert, bishop of Chartres, who about the year 1100 wrote a treatise against the Jews on the words of Genesis, chapter XLIX: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah,” [Note: [Col. XLVIII] Sixtus Senensis, *Bib.*, bk. IV, p. 333, 1.] etc. Since our Ivo was certainly bishop of Chartres in 1100, someone may perhaps imagine that he was the author of this treatise, especially since no bishop of Chartres named Humbert is found. But it is certain that this supposed Humbert is none other than Saint Fulbert, who did in fact write against the Jews the treatise in question. [Note: [Col. XLVIII] *Hist. litt.*, vol. VII, p. 273.] See his article in our literary history.

**17.** To omit nothing concerning the writings of Ivo of Chartres, we shall observe that Antoine l’Oisel cites a manuscript of Sigebert’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, in which, he says, [Col. XLIX] there are things not found in the printed edition of Aubert le Mire. [Note: [Col. XLIX] L’Oisel, *Hist. de Beauv.*, p. 133.] L’Oisel himself suspects that this manuscript belonged to, or was even copied by, Ivo when he was still only abbot of Saint-Quentin of Beauvais. This would imply that our learned prelate was the author of the additions to Sigebert’s book found in this manuscript. But to be assured that this suspicion or conjecture of Antoine l’Oisel has no basis, one need only observe that Sigebert did not publish his book on ecclesiastical writers until near the end of his life, and that Ivo of Chartres survived him by scarcely more than four years. This gives every reason to doubt whether the latter ever knew the former’s book, since these two scholars were hardly in a position to communicate their works to one another.

After the enumeration we have just made of all the productions of Saint Ivo’s pen, we believe that we may affirm that there was no scholar in the eleventh and twelfth centuries who wrote more than he, or on a greater number of subjects pertaining to ecclesiastical learning; although it must be acknowledged that our holy and learned prelate distinguished himself principally in matters concerning discipline and liturgy. We shall add that there were scarcely any who treated each subject with more order, clarity, solidity, and learning than he; so that he was, without question, one of the greatest and most able men of his age, in almost every field.

[Col. XLIX]

# DISSERTATION ON THE *DECRETUM* ATTRIBUTED TO IVO AND ON OTHER ANCIENT COLLECTIONS OF CANONS PRIOR TO GRATIAN

(Augustine Theiner, *Critical Investigations into the Principal Collections of Canons and Decretals, or a Continuation of Galland’s Collection of Dissertations on Ancient Collections of Canons.*—Rome, 1836, quarto, 139 pages.)

[Col. XLIXA] Among the questions commonly discussed in the history of canon law, one of no slight importance concerns Ivo’s *Decretum* and its authenticity. For not only is the plan of this work altogether singular and plainly different from other collections of the same kind, and there is moreover a complex connection between it and the *Panormia*, which is certainly a genuine work of Ivo; but the facts reported by historians are uncertain and are not always rightly understood. Thus doubts have arisen concerning this *Decretum* at every period, and learned men have endeavoured, with arguments of sometimes lighter, sometimes weightier force, either to defend or to attack it.

What frequently occurs in questions of this kind—namely, that, in order to uphold the authenticity of one work, another work attributed to the same author is denied to him—has also happened in this controversy over the author of this *Decretum*. Many, misled by the *Decretum*’s magnitude, as might very readily happen, denied that the *Panormia* was Ivo’s work [Col. XLIXB] and asserted that it was nothing other than a kind of abridgment of the same *Decretum*. Others, on the contrary, attempted with certainly stronger arguments to show that both collections ought to be attributed to Ivo. They said that he had been moved to publish the *Decretum* chiefly because he wished to augment with new materials what he had briefly collected in the *Panormia*, and to recast it into a fuller and more perfect form.

This opinion, precisely by the appearance of truth which it presented, must be said to have led its proponents into error. It was indeed [Col. LA] entirely possible that Ivo himself, when he more maturely considered the circumstances of his time and situation, recognized that very much was lacking in a work which, as the very name *Panormia* indicates, ought to embrace all ecclesiastical materials. He might therefore have revised it with renewed care and elaborated it into a fuller form. The most learned brothers Ballerini had long ago indicated with many arguments, and arguments not to be despised, that Ivo had in fact done this. [Note: [Col. XLIXB] *Treatise on Ancient Collections and Collectors of Canons down to Gratian*, pt. IV, ch. 16, pp. 661–666, in the collection of the more distinguished works [Col. LB] illustrating canon law, vol. XV, Mainz, 1790, quarto.] In our own times the exceedingly learned Savigny appears to have established it so certainly that he must be said to have entirely removed all controversy on the matter. For, relying upon that very collection of canons which the Ballerini seemed not to have sufficiently appreciated, Savigny discovered and explained with the greatest clarity both the origin of that *Decretum* and the manner in which it was compiled. [Note: [Col. LB] *History of Roman Law in the Middle Ages*, vol. II, p. 286 ff.]

Yet from this same collection, which demonstrates the origin of the *Decretum* so clearly, it can at the same time be proved most conclusively—though this may rightly seem surprising—that Ivo [Col. LB] could in no way have been the author of that work. In order to demonstrate this with every suitable kind of argument, we must examine more closely the collection just mentioned. Because of the particular arrangement in which it presents its various sources, we shall henceforth call it the *Tripartite Collection*. We shall first compare it with certain other collections of canons; then with Ivo’s *Panormia* and *Decretum*; and finally with Gratian’s collection.

# CHAPTER ONE. The Relation of the Tripartite Collection to Other Collections of Canons

[Col. LI]

[Col. LIA] We must rightly distinguish two methods which different authors of ancient collections employed in gathering legal materials. Some went directly to the sources themselves and extracted from the canons of councils, the letters of Roman pontiffs, and the works of the Fathers such materials as they then arranged in their collections in whatever form best suited the end which they or others had set before themselves. Others, however, turned not to the sources themselves but to the works of earlier collectors. They either arranged the materials found there in another order, more or less their own, or selected only those materials which seemed better suited to the compilation of a new collection. It is worth while to illustrate this method of proceeding among collectors by several new examples, since there are many collections of canons not yet published, which we have been able to examine more carefully.

[Col. LIB] **§ I.** In the Vienna Library there is preserved a tenth-century codex (*Jus can.* no. 81, folio) containing a collection of canons very similar to that first published by Jean Petitus [Note: [Col. LIB] *Penitential of Theodore of Canterbury*, vol. I, pp. 97–280. Paris, 1677, quarto.] and previously more fully elucidated by Coustant [Note: [Col. LIB] *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs from Saint Clement I to Innocent III*. Paris, 1721, folio, vol. I, p. 709 ff.] and subsequently by the brothers Ballerini. [Note: [Col. LIB] *On Ancient Collections*, etc., pt. IV, ch. 7, § 2, pp. 611–616, cited edition.] For both collections flow from the same sources, and nothing is added in the Vienna collection which is not found in the other. The individual chapters, divided into sixty-four headings, are arranged in almost the same order and sequence as in Petitus’s collection. Nevertheless, letters of Gregory the Great to Eleutherius of Lyons (bk. IX, ep. 106, pp. 1106–1111) and to Queen Brunhild (bk. IX, ep. 109, pp. 1014–1016), [Note: [Col. LIB] Benedictine edition, Paris, 1705, vol. II, folio.] as well as certain other extracts from Isidore’s books, occur within the collection, though they are not assigned to their headings as they are in Petitus’s collection.

The compiler appended to the end of the collection Gregory the Great’s letter to Augustine, archbishop of Canterbury; the chapters of Gregory the Younger and his capitulary or letter of instruction to Martinianus, Gregory, and Dorotheus, travelling with God’s help into Bavaria; [Note: [Col. LIB] Mansi, *Most Extensive Collection of Holy Councils*, vol. XII, pp. 257–260.] then Saint Jerome’s two letters to Oceanus and Amantius on how clerics ought to live in this world; and finally the little book *On Remedies for Sins*, commonly attributed to Bede. Anyone who compares our collection somewhat more carefully with that published by Petitus will readily convince himself that the latter arose from the former. [Note: [Col. LIB] It is sufficient to indicate the headings.—“Here begin the chapters extracted from books of canons.”

[Col. LIC] I. That nothing apart from the canonical Scriptures is to be read in the Church, and what canonical Scripture is. II. That a synod is to be held twice every year. III. What kind of person cannot come to the priesthood or sacred orders. IV. What kind of person, and in what manner, may come to the priesthood or sacred orders. V. That a province is by no means to be divided between two metropolitans. VI. That there are not to be two bishops in one city, and concerning bishops’ vicars. VII. That the ordinations of bishops ought not to be long delayed. VIII. Concerning bishops ordained but not received. IX. That it is not fitting to ordain anyone without a title. X. Concerning a slave who, without his master’s knowledge, has been ordained. XI. That a cleric may not minister in two cities, [Col. LID] nor abbots possess several monasteries or cells. XII. That a bishop or cleric is not to pass from one place to another without the bishop’s authorization. XIII. Concerning travelling bishops and clerics. XIV. Concerning travellers’ letters and clerics travelling without letters. XV. What person, or for what offences, is degraded from priestly office or the clergy according to canonical institutions. XVI. Concerning one expelled from the Church, excommunicated, or condemned from his office. XVII. Concerning ecclesiastical order and the office of the Mass. [Col. LIIB] XVIII. Concerning relics of saints and rural oratories. XIX. That no altars are to be consecrated except those made of stone. XX. Concerning baptism. XXI. Concerning confirmation with chrism; that meals are not to be held in church; and that on the Lord’s Day people are not to bend the knee in church. XXII. Concerning the Lord’s Day of Easter and the other feasts. XXIII. Concerning fasting, Lent, or litanies. XXIV. That eminent feasts are to be celebrated publicly only in cities or public villages. XXV. Concerning offerings made at the altar, taken to [Col. LIIC] the priest’s house, or given as an oblation. XXVI. That all the faithful are to communicate and remain for the Mass; otherwise they are to be excommunicated; and that no food is to be taken before the sacrifice. XXVII. Concerning preaching. XXVIII. Concerning guests. XXIX. Concerning tithes. XXX. Concerning widows, young women, and the poor. XXXI. How a bishop ought to administer or govern the property of the Church; how gifts made upon the altar are to be divided; that parishes and oratories are in the bishop’s authority; and concerning ruined churches in parishes. XXXII. That a bishop’s successor is not to take away property which a priest gave to clerics or servants. XXXIII. Concerning property given to churches or priests. XXXIV. Concerning Church property taken away or disputed. XXXV. Concerning litigants and judges. [Col. LIID] XXXVI. That clerics are not to be contractors, are not to neglect their office, and are to refrain from secular concerns. XXXVII. That a cleric is not to live with unrelated women. XXXVIII. Concerning a priest’s widow. XXXIX. Concerning clerics who practise usury or give surety, and concerning drunkards, obscene songs, and idle words. XL. Concerning bishops and orders, the rules governing clerics, and their clothing. XLI. Concerning hunters. XLII. That bishop, priest, or deacon ought not to beat sinful believers. [Col. LIIIA] XLIII. Concerning lots and auguries. [Col. LIIIB] XLIV. Concerning clerics, monks, and abbots who do not remain faithful to their profession. XLV. Concerning monks. XLVI. Concerning monasteries. XLVII. Concerning women consecrated to God and monasteries of girls. XLVIII. Concerning abductions. XLIX. Concerning incestuous persons and adulterers, and those who dismiss their wives. L. Concerning forgers, perjurers, murderers, and captives. LI. Concerning those at discord. LII. Concerning abandoned children. LIII. Concerning freed persons. LIV. Concerning those who flee to the church. LV. Concerning Jews, and that Christians are neither to share with them, nor be subject to them, nor be slaves of Jews. LVI. Concerning clerics who abstain from meat. LVII. Concerning heretics and pagans. [Col. LIIIC] LVIII. Concerning conspiracies. LIX. That a pall is not to be placed upon a body, and that divine ministries are not to be performed for weddings. LX. Concerning demoniacs. LXI. Concerning chrism. LXII. Concerning those who act against the canons. LXIII. Concerning the bishops who assented to and confirmed the aforesaid canons. LXIV. Concerning the fallen and penitents.”]

**§ II.** Although the collection of which we have spoken is of little [Col. LIIIA] importance, it was nevertheless reduced to an epitome by some unknown student of this discipline. There is, in fact, in the Paris Library a codex (no. 3859), written near the end of the ninth or beginning of the tenth century, which presents a collection of canons compiled with the aid of one or another of the collections mentioned above. It bears the following prefixed title: “Here begins a brief capitulary collected from the canons of various councils, whose places and names are made known in the following statements under their own headings,” divided into thirty headings. [Note: [Col. LIIIC] I. That a synod is to be held twice every year. II. What person, according to canonical authority, cannot come to the priesthood or sacred orders, and for what offences a person is degraded from office or the clergy. III. Gregory on pastors who do not walk rightly. IV. Concerning episcopal ordinations. V. That no one ought to be ordained without a title. VI. That [Col. LIIID] a bishop, priest, deacon, or any cleric is not to pass or migrate from one place to another. VII. That a cleric ought not to be received without commendatory letters. VIII. Concerning the condemned, excommunicated, and expelled, and for what offences, according to canonical institution, a person is degraded from priestly office or the clergy. IX. How a bishop ought to govern or administer Church property and gifts made upon the altar, and concerning property given to churches. X. Concerning the canons of each council. XI. Concerning the honour due to a monk; that none of them is to attempt to disturb ecclesiastical or secular affairs; that none is to receive another’s slave because of the slave’s master’s conscience; concerning clerics and monks who come to the imperial city of Constantinople against their bishop’s will; and concerning monasteries and abbots. [Col. LIVA] XII. Concerning forgers, perjurers, murderers, and thefts. [Col. LIVB] XIII. Concerning women consecrated to God and monasteries of girls; incestuous persons and women; those who dismiss their wives; and abduction. XIV. Saint Augustine’s treatise *On Penance*. XV. In the decretal of Pope Gelasius, ch. 20: that those who join themselves to consecrated virgins and enter into incestuous unions cannot communicate unless perhaps they have undergone public penance. XVI. That widows, as stated above, are not to be veiled; and if, having professed continence, they trample it underfoot by changing their purpose, they themselves must render an account to God for their violations; and concerning virgins if they go astray. XVII. Concerning litigants and accusers, judges, those who accuse the innocent, and how a cleric is to approach secular courts. XVIII. Concerning usury and avarice, fornicators, and penitents. [Col. LIVC] XIX. Concerning those at discord, freed persons, abandoned children, sacrilegious persons, and auguries. XX. Concerning Jewish banquets, confessions, their slaves, and various relations between Jew and Christian, so that Christians are not subject to Jews. XXI. Concerning Church property taken away or disputed, and that it is to be preserved. XXII. That clerics are not to be contractors, are not to neglect their office, are not to be contumacious, and are to refrain from secular concerns. XXIII. That no cleric is to live with unrelated women. XXIV. Concerning clerics who practise usury or give surety, drunkards, secular banquets, obscene songs, and idle words. XXV. Concerning bishops, the rules and orders of clerics, their clothing, and hunting. XXVI. That a synod is to be held twice each year; what persons may and may not enter sacred orders; that none are to be ordained without a title; and that a bishop or cleric is not to pass from one place to another. [Col. LIVD] XXVII. Concerning travellers’ letters, clerics travelling without letters, those expelled from the church, the condemned, and adulterers. XXVIII. Concerning relics of saints, oratories and rural churches, baptism, confirmation, Easter and the Lord’s Day, the Lenten fast, and eminent festivals. XXIX. Concerning Patrick’s synod. XXX. Concerning bishops who assented to and confirmed the aforesaid canons: 233 canons through 26 councils.] Under each of these headings are contained several chapters, which the author extracted with incredible completeness from the sources already known. To these he added certain other materials drawn from the collection of Dionysius Exiguus, especially from the second part of that collection, or the decretal letters of Roman pontiffs, without any change at all and with the same inscriptions [Col. LIVA] found in the Dionysian work. [Note: [Col. LIVD] Siricius, *Decretals*, chs. 5, 14, 15; heading XVIII, chs. 17, 18, 19. Innocent, *Decretals*, chs. 7, 22, 34; heading XVIII, chs. 20, 21, 22. Celestine, *Decretals*, ch. 15; heading XVIII, ch. 23. Gelasius, *Decretals*, chs. 12, 19, 23, 27, 28; heading XII, ch. 4; heading XV; heading IX, ch. 8; heading XXI, ch. 11; heading XVI, ch. 34.]

**§ III.** More highly than the others, however, another collection seems deserving of esteem. It is contained in a tenth-century codex of the Royal Paris Library, no. 4280 A, and presents a recension of Cresconius’s *Breviary* arranged in a definite order. In compiling it, the author evidently had regard to the work of Martin of Braga. This collection is divided into twelve headings, each containing more or fewer chapters. Throughout the entire work, however, the chapters are numbered in one continuous numerical sequence, reaching 354. The chapters correspond to the subjects of the headings; thus they have been taken and collected from different parts of Cresconius’s work.

The collection itself begins with a preface copied from Cresconius. This is followed by an index of the headings and chapters, [Col. LVA] and finally by the text of the chapters themselves. Cresconius had arranged his work in the same way. Hence not a few persons were led into error and separated from the *Concord of Canons* such an index, entitled *Abridgment of Canons*, thinking it to be a work distinct from that collection. [Note: [Col. LVB] Ballerini, cited work, pt. IV, ch. 3, pp. 383–387. Pithou first published the abridgment in 1581; then T. Chifflet in the works of Fulgentius Ferrandus, pp. 24–54, Dijon, 1649, quarto. Pithou published it again: *Ancient Code of Canons of the Roman Church*, Paris, 1687, folio, pp. 314–326. Justel published the abridgment in *Library of Canon Law*, vol. I, pp. 456–466, [Col. LVC] and the *Concord* in vol. I, appendix, pp. XXXIII–CXII.] In order to understand the plan of both collections, it will suffice to give the headings of our collection, noting beside their titles Cresconius’s chapters.

R. I. Chapters proper to bishops, cc. 1–72. Cresc. cc. 151, 152, 164, 228, 16, 37, 38, 18, 36, 40–42, 142, 145–150, 153, 154, 157–160, 162, 169, 192, 209, 218, 244, 245, 256, 259, 260, 267, 270, 279–283, 287, 232, 144, 200, 203, 170, 210–96.

R. II. Likewise, matters proper to bishops, presbyters, and deacons, cc. 73–101. Cresc. cc. 5–7, 10, 194, 8, 9, 11, 27, 30, 29, 8, 31, 35, 43–45, 49–52, 110, 143, 248, 254, 300, 177, 251, 246, 193.

R. III. Likewise, matters proper to presbyters, cc. 102–125. Cresc. cc. 2, 76, 4, 33, 81, 93, 97, 108, 111, 117, 119, 191, 217, 229, 252, 257, 276.

R. IV. Likewise, matters proper to presbyters and deacons, cc. 126–137. Cresc. cc. 17, 34, 91, 98–109, 190, 196, 239, 285.

[Col. LVD] R. V. Likewise, matters proper to deacons, cc. 138–145. Cresc. cc. 95, 120, 82, 92, 94.

R. VI. Likewise, concerning subdeacons and clerics of the lower grades, cc. 146, 154. Cresc. cc. 171, 172, 175, 173, 168, 169, 167.

LVIB] 263–265, 273–275, 278, 177.
