The manuscript codex of Cresconius’s work preserved in [Col. LVIC] the library at Vercelli appears to have certain distinctive features. G. Andres, *Lettera sopra alcuni Codici delle Biblioteche capitolari di Novarra e di Vercelli*, Parma, 1802, octavo, p. 49.

Moreover, the author of our collection altered scarcely anything in the chapters taken from Cresconius’s work; but for the few which he omitted he substituted others, apparently drawn from Gallican compilations. For, besides canons borrowed from Gallican councils, the *Statuta Ecclesiae antiquae* occur very frequently, and, according to the testimony of the Ballerini brothers, these are found only in collections compiled in Gaul. From this it is permissible to infer that the collection of which we are speaking was prepared in Gaul.

He also cites certain passages from the Council of Clement.

> [Note: Col. LVIC.] Rubric I, cc. 50–55. Fourth Council of Carthage, cc. 34, 84, 25, 26, 27.

These agree entirely with the canons of the Fourth Council of Carthage and were received into Gratian’s *Decretum* [Col. LVB] under the name of that council.

> [Note: Col. LVIC.] Distinction XCV, c. 9; Distinction I, c. 67; *On Consecration*, Distinction XC, cc. 6 and 7; Cause 15, question 7, c. 6. The Ballerini brothers first published the *Statuta Ecclesiae antiquae* among the documents of ancient canon law, no. 3, pp. 654–668, in *Opera S. Leonis Magni*, vol. III, folio, Venice, 1757. Compare the same authors, *Dissertatio de antiquis canonum collectionibus*, part 2, c. 3, §4, pp. LXXXVIII–XCI; Mainz edition, pp. 353–358.

## § III

Another collection, surviving in Paris, in codex no. 3859 of the Royal Library, is of lesser importance. It contains 341 chapters.

> [Note: Col. LVIC.] In this little work too, a table of contents precedes the collection itself, under this heading: “Here begins a list of chapters drawn from various councils and judgments.” The collection itself bears the title: “Here begins a breviary compiled from the canons [Col. LVID] of various councils, ecclesiastical rule, the canons of the Apostles, and chapters concerning the ordination of presbyters, deacons, or readers.”

These chapters were taken from the collections both of Dionysius Exiguus and of Pseudo-Isidore, with no order of chronology or subject matter preserved. The author begins with Dionysius’s collection, drawing certain passages from both its first and second parts; he concludes their sequence with the constitution of Gregory the Younger. Then, proceeding at chapter 155 to another collection of Pseudo-Isidore, he appends certain excerpts from it, though he does not everywhere preserve their sequence.

Moreover, he incorporated into his collection several canons drawn from the councils held at Paris in 557 and 615, as well as from the Council of Tours of 813. This seems to indicate that it was compiled in Gaul. Nothing certain can be determined concerning the date of the collection; nevertheless, the codex appears to have been copied no later than the end of the ninth century.

> [Note: Col. LVID.] Under Abbot Godo, who succeeded Walderic, the manuscript came to the monastery of Bonneval near Chartres, as is clear from the verses copied before the collection:
>
> Godo, the humble monastic abbot of Bonneval,  
> gives this work of the holy canons contained in this codex  
> to the blessed Peter and Marcellinus.  
> And may whoever removes it be punished with harsh punishment,  
> shut in the lowest depth of hell together with the reprobate,  
> unless fitting restitution first restores what was taken.
>
> J. Mabillon, *Annales O. S. Benedicti*, book LXVIII, §39, pp. 297 ff., Paris, 1713, folio, vol. IV; and the Samarthani, *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, p. 1237, examined the codex.

This certainly demonstrates how highly Pseudo-Isidore’s collection was already valued at that time.

## § IV

Yet nowhere are clearer evidences of this fact to be found than in the book entitled the *Collection Dedicated to Anselm*, which was compiled in the period between the year 883 and the year 897. This collection comes closer to that which, as we said above, consists of three parts and of which, in accordance with the purpose of our work, more must shortly be said. Meanwhile, it will be useful to discuss this collection itself, especially since those learned men who have hitherto elucidated it were ignorant of the very features that distinguish it most sharply from other works of this sort.

> [Note: Col. LVID.] Ballerini, cited work, part IV, c. 10, pp. 623–630; Savigny, *History of Roman Law*, III, vol. II, p. 274 ff.

The sources consulted by its author may be reduced to four. Above all, beyond doubt, he used the works of Dionysius and Pseudo-Isidore, since he received them almost entire into his collection, though arranged in a distinct and wholly peculiar manner. Wherever he found that Dionysius possessed the same letters of Roman pontiffs as Isidore presents, he almost abandoned Isidore in order to follow Dionysius’s tracks in every respect. Accordingly, he took all the decretals of Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Gelasius, and Anastasius from Dionysius, without changing even a letter, retaining the same titles and division into chapters.

As regards the letters of Boniface, Hilary, Simplicius, Felix, Symmachus, and Hormisdas, he borrowed them from Pseudo-Isidore’s collection; whence we may readily infer that he used the authentic recension of Dionysius. No trace of Adrian’s chapters occurs, and he again took the letters of Gregory the Great from Isidore himself. In that part of his work also which presents the canons of councils, he used the Dionysian rather than the Isidorian collection, especially in excerpting the canons of Greek councils, which he drew from the Isidorian recension or translation only very rarely and in a few isolated chapters.

Moreover, in arranging those letters of Roman pontiffs which he took from the Isidorian compilation, he seems to have imitated Dionysius. He arranged the decretal letters themselves so that, while retaining chronological order, all decretals of each pontiff—if he issued more than one—were divided into more or fewer chapters. He carried the series from the letters of St Clement to those issued by Zachary. Although the chapters are numbered in an uninterrupted sequence, they are inserted separately in different places of the collection according to diversity of subject.

Thus, for example, anyone wishing to assemble the ninety-eight chapters into which our author divided the five decretals of St Clement, and compare them with the text of the decretals themselves, would find that every individual portion follows in such a way that the chapters of the first decretal are followed, in their natural order and continuous numerical sequence, by the chapters of the second, third, fourth, and fifth decretals.

> [Note: Col. LVIIC.] I considered that almost all the decretal letters ought to be examined in this manner, and I found that in all of them the author followed the same method. To avoid undue length, I refrain from citing the chapters.

This arrangement of materials is wholly distinctive, and the author does not appear to have borrowed it from any earlier collector. Yet, with respect both to materials drawn from Dionysius and to those drawn from Isidore, he observed chronology no more than other collectors did, and repeatedly inserted several passages in continuous succession from one and the same decretal.

> [Note: Col. LVIIC.] For example, part VIII, cc. 1–24 contains fragments of the decretals: Clement, cc. 20, 21, 22; Alexander, cc. 2, 10; Xystus, c. 2; Hyginus, c. 1; Soter, c. 1; Eutychian, cc. 1, 2; Gaius, c. 5; Miltiades, cc. 1, 2, 3, 16; Damasus, c. 2. Chapters 26–40: Clement, cc. 64, 65; Anacletus, c. 13; Alexander, c. 6; Celestine, cc. 4–11. Chapters 40–60: Clement, cc. 21, 24, 41, 65, 68, 69, 77, 78, 91; Pontian, cc. 5, 7, 8, 10; Eutychian, c. 5; Marcellinus, c. 2; Marcellus, cc. 3–6; Eusebius, cc. 6, 8, 16; Dionysius, c. 1; Victor, c. 1; Clement, cc. 72, 74–76; Felix, cc. 7, 16, 17, 19, 20. From these few examples, it seems to me clear that the author cared little for order.

Or from one and the same council.

> [Note: Col. LVIID.] The same must be said of the councils. Part XII, cc. 19–25: Council of Laodicea, cc. 6, 7, 8, 32, 33, 34. Chapters 27–41: Council of Gangra, cc. 2, 3, 5, 6, 10–18, 20. Part VII, cc. 11–15: African Council, cc. 31, 49, 42, 23. Part II, cc. 185–197: African Council, cc. 85–88, 90, 32, 54, 55, 67, 75, 91, 98, 100. Part III, cc. 86–88: African Council, cc. 97–99. Part XII, c. 26 presents the entire Council of Ephesus together with Cyril’s letter, which the author took from Pseudo-Isidore’s work.

It is therefore apparent that neither order nor method was of much concern to him. He himself brings forward nothing from the Fathers or other ecclesiastical writers, nor does one find in him decretals of pontiffs later than Gregory the Younger and Zachary. Hence it is clear that, apart from the many materials he took from the letters of Gregory the Great and from Justinian’s collections, he drew all the rest from the compilations of Dionysius and Pseudo-Isidore.

Meanwhile, the collection possesses such abundance and variety of material that it could scarcely have escaped the notice of subsequent collectors of canons. Burchard of Worms must certainly be said to have valued it highly for this reason, since he drew the greater part of his work from it.

> [Note: Col. LVIID.] To establish this, we compared the latter six books of the collection with Burchard’s work. In this labor we used the Sorbonne codex at Paris, no. 481, marked B.E.; see P. Coustant, *Dissertatio de antiquis canonum collectionibus*, §§CLXIX and CLXX, in Galland, vol. I, p. 152 ff., cited edition; and F. Salmon, *De l’étude des conciles et de leurs collections*, part II, c. 1, Paris, 1724, quarto, pp. 173–178.
>
> Burchard, book I, cc. 25, 41, 67, 88, 128, 131. A, part X, c. 56; part XI, c. 2; part VII, c. 21; part XI, c. 24; part VII, c. 98; part X, c. 89.
>
> Burchard, book III, cc. 19, 28, 31, 33. A, part VI, c. 18; part X, cc. 67, 15, 41, 34; A, c. 11; Gregory, cited passage, cc. 60, 67; A, part X, cc. 87, 102, 94, 95; A, part XII, cc. 30, 31, 107, 137, 139, 140, 142, 144, 145, 147, 184, 185, 187, 195, 203; A, part X, cc. 38, 19, 29, 70, 71, 77, 78, 44, 54, 53, 55, 52, 51, 41, 209–211; A, part XII, cc. 22, 25; part X, c. 185.
>
> Burchard, book IV, cc. 2, 4, 5, 9–12, 15, 18–20, 22, 23. A, part IX, cc. 10, 11, 15, 30, 27, 19, 20; I, 59, 17, 58, 24, 25, c. 29; A, part X, c. 92; cc. 31, 32, 36, 38, 44, 45, 53, 54, 56, 63, 65, 69; A, part X, cc. 41, 32, 31, 40, 34, 33, 60, 61, 23, 6, 37, 38, 81–85; A, part XII, cc. 56, 58, 61, 63, 60.

> From this comparison it is clear that Burchard also drew the letters of Gregory the Great from this collection, designated by us with the letter A, “Dedicated to Anselm.”

He altered passages taken from it so slightly that he copied them with the same headings and summaries. At that time, indeed, Germany possessed no collection of canons, apart from the meagre work of Regino of Prüm, capable of meeting every need. Burchard therefore seems to have been prompted to prepare a larger and richer compilation through the assistance of this collection of ours, which he found while staying in Italy and recognized to be of great importance. Thus it may also readily be explained whence that highly esteemed book of Burchard, whose origin had hitherto been obscured by darkness, arose.

Whoever wishes to prepare a new and more accurate recension of Burchard’s work should turn his attention to the collection entitled *Dedicated to Anselm*. It is truly remarkable that even such eminent men as Francis Salmon, P. Coustant, and the Ballerini brothers were wholly unaware of the close bond joining this collection with Burchard’s work. Furthermore, they erred seriously in maintaining that Regino had used it.

> [Note: Col. LIXC.] *De antiquis canonum collectionibus*, part IV, c. 11, p. 632, cited work.

For the author of our collection, as we observed above, followed the Dionysian recension alone in citing Innocent’s decretals, and imitated none at all of his predecessors. Yet this would by no means be true if one examines the passage from Regino cited by the Ballerini brothers, book I, c. 117.

After Burchard had composed his work from the collection named after Anselm, the collection itself became so obsolete that neither Anselm of Lucca nor any other later collector of canons resorted to it. They considered that everything should be drawn from Burchard’s work, for no other reason than that he had arranged the copious and unorganized mass of his predecessor in order and method.

[Col. LIXB] §§ V–VI. Another collection of canons, preserved at Vienna in the Imperial Library (*Jus canonicum*, no. 99, quarto), approaches the Tripartite Collection much more closely than that of which we have just spoken, since we find it already divided into three parts. The first part presents eighty chapters drawn from the spurious Isidorian collection, containing fragments of decretals of Roman pontiffs—Clement and those who follow him down to Gregory the Younger—arranged according to chronological succession. To these are added certain decrees of Nicholas I, excerpted from his letters addressed to Salomon, bishop of Constance, and Charles, archbishop of Cologne.

> [Note: Col. LIXC.] In Mansi, vol. XV, pp. 454 ff., 434–448 ff. The Third Council of Lyons, held in 583, in [Labat], *Collection of the Councils of Gaul, both published and unpublished, arranged in chronological order from A.D. 177 to A.D. 1563, by the monks of the Congregation of Saint-Maur* (*Collection des conciles de la Gaule, tant édités qu’inédits, disposée dans l’ordre chronologique depuis l’an 177 jusqu’à l’an 1563, par les moines de la congrégation de Saint-Maur*), Paris, 1789, folio, vol. I, p. 1287.

At the head of this first part the author placed Pseudo-Isidore’s order for celebrating a council, together with certain fragments taken from its preliminary notices. These bear the title: “Origin of General Councils and Notice of the Synods whose acts are contained in this Pseudo-Isidorian codex.” Our author nevertheless extended this notice as far as the twenty-fourth council: “likewise, the Council of Lyons, in which twenty Fathers decreed, among whom Priscus, bishop of Lyons, was especially prominent.”

> [Note: Col. LIXC.] Rubric LXX in Petitius’s edition, vol. I, p. 264; rubric LXIII in the Vienna codex. Compare Gratian, [Col. LIXD] Distinction 16, c. 11, who received this passage into the *Decretum*.

The author also appended a catalogue of Roman pontiffs, whose sequence begins with St Sylvester and extends down to Gregory the Younger. Beside each pontiff’s name he wrote the number corresponding exactly to the place each held in the succession of pontiffs.

> [Note: Col. LIXD.] “Pope Sylvester, the thirty-fourth from Peter, having assembled 277 Fathers in the city of Rome with the counsel of the Emperor Constantine, condemned Arius and the other heretics after the Synod of Nicaea, and undertook to establish many constitutions necessary for the Church. Siricius, the fortieth from Peter, wrote fifteen decretal chapters concerning certain necessities, at the counsel of Bishop Himerius. … Innocent, the forty-second from Peter, wrote certain letters to bishops of diverse provinces, containing fifty-six decretal chapters. Pope Zosimus, the forty-third from Peter, wrote a decretal letter to Hesychius, bishop of Salona, marked with three chapters. … Pope Hilary, the forty-eighth from Peter, in the presence of forty-five bishops and presbyters, established six synodal chapters, containing twenty-two chapters. … Pope Felix, the fiftieth from Peter, in the presence of eighty-one bishops and presbyters, established twenty-four chapters of canons concerning bishops, presbyters, and deacons in Africa who were to be rebaptized. … Pope Gregory II, the ninety-first from Peter, wrote seventeen chapters to be observed by the whole Church, together with thirty-three Fathers; these he commends under the bond of anathema.”
>
> This catalogue, in preparing which the author used the works of Pseudo-Isidore, Dionysius, and others, contains some matters wholly peculiar to itself.

To these are then added the Council of Tribur, held in 795, certain canons from Greek and Latin synods, and certain fragments excerpted from the capitularies of Frankish kings. Although fewer and less important, these constitute the second part of the collection. The third part, finally, is fuller and more orderly. In it the author assembled ninety-eight chapters, excerpted from the Fathers, decretals, and canons. Under the title, “Here begin chapters from the canons of eighty-eight Fathers,” he arranged them without joining one to another in any way, so that they present the appearance of collections frequently called *Deflorationes canonum* (“Selections of Canons”). The codex appears to have been written in the ninth century; experts in such matters maintain that the recension of the Council of Tribur presented by the collection was prepared at the very time when the council itself was held.

Yet, although this collection is of lesser importance, later compilers of canons appear to have used it. If the codex presenting it was indeed written in the ninth century, Regino must have been the first to use it, since he composed his work about the year 906. For almost all the chapters of its third part are found in him.

> [Note: Col. LXC.] The following chapters of our collection occur in Regino: cc. 3–5, 2, 8–11, 13, 14; Regino, book II, cc. 6–9, 49, 50, 61, 68, 92, 63. [Col. LXD] Cc. 18–30; Regino, book II, cc. 167–170, 174, 176, 178, 182, 183, 185, 188, 189, 192. Cc. 31, 32; Regino, book II, c. 196. Cc. 36–32 [as printed]; Regino, book II, cc. 111, 112, 117, 118, 176, 282.

The sequence of subjects is the same as in our codex, and the titles are the same. If, however, anyone should challenge the date of the codex, it would be necessary to say that this collection of ours was derived from Regino’s compilation.

## § VII

Thus far we have examined most of the ancient compilations of canons. We now turn our hand to that with which we are chiefly concerned; and since all the questions we have proposed bear upon it, it seems necessary to describe it somewhat more carefully.

This collection, as we have noted above, is wholly divided into three parts. The first comprises letters of Roman pontiffs; the second, canons of councils; [Col. LXC] and the third, finally, passages excerpted from works of the Holy Fathers and other ecclesiastical writers, as well as from Roman and Frankish collections of law. Following the practice of other compilers, the author prefixed a short preface to his collection, in which he both explains the object of the work and indicates the nature of the sources from which he drew.

> [Note: Col. LXD.] “Since the decretals of certain Roman pontiffs are earlier in time than synodal assemblies, they fittingly claim the first place in the little work of our selection. For from the episcopate of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, down to the time of the most serene Emperor Constantine, whether because bishops were few or because of the fury of persecutors, either no councils of pontiffs, or scarcely any, are believed to have been celebrated. Moreover, the canons of the Apostles are held to have lower authority than the Nicene canons and most others, since they are read as belonging to some of those apostles. Hence, what could be done more freely and, so to speak, more conveniently, the apostolic men conveyed to their partners in faith by letters, making known what they ought to seek, what to avoid, [Col. LXIB] what to hold, and finally what to reject.
>
> “But when the religion of Christianity began, through the favor of the devout prince Constantine, to spread far and wide throughout the world, assemblies of bishops likewise began to be held freely. Although such assemblies have not ceased to be held by the prelates of the holy Church throughout the four quarters of the world, the council said to have been convened by St Sylvester in the city of Nicaea in Bithynia and celebrated by 318 bishops is nevertheless reported to hold the foremost rank of authority, although it is not first in chronological order.
>
> “But amid these matters it should be noted that, although thirty-two pontiffs are counted from the pontificate of Peter, prince of the apostles, to the episcopate of Sylvester—Linus and Cletus being omitted because they exercised the episcopate while Peter the apostle was still alive—none of them failed to establish certain rules through his decretals, except Chrysogonus alone, who is counted as the twenty-eighth from Peter the apostle. Again, although thirty-two prelates are likewise counted from St Sylvester to blessed Gregory, all are said to have issued decretals except Mercury alone, who held the episcopate as the sixty-second after Peter the apostle.
>
> “Let us now consider what is the meaning of the name *decretal*. Therefore, a decree (*decretum*), derived from the verb *decerno*, ‘I decree,’ produces from itself another name, namely *decretale*, whose plural is *decretalia*; it is understood as an ordinance or constitution. Hence decretals may be understood as ordinances or constitutions. But let us at last imprint upon the page the necessary judgments of these decretals. Here ends the prologue. Here begin the chapters.”
>
> The collection appears in this form in a Vatican manuscript and in four codices of the Royal Library of Paris (nos. 3858, 3858 A, 3858 B, 4282). In the Berlin codex (Latin manuscript no. 104, folio), Ivo’s prologue is prefixed to this prologue; it is copied there with the following note added: “Here ends the first prologue. Likewise, the prologue of the following work.”
>
> The manuscript begins with the *Order for Celebrating a Council*, which agrees throughout with that copied by Burchard of Worms at the end of the Council of Seligenstadt, though it is presented by the scribe of our codex in a more complete form than by Burchard. It is followed by the notice, *Admonition to Priests*, which St Anselm of Lucca attributed to Leo and included in his collection under the heading: “Here begins the sermon composed by St Pope Leo, to be delivered in a synod.”
>
> The *Ordo Romanus* in Melchior Hittorp, *De divinis Catholicae Ecclesiae officiis in mysteriis, varii vetustorum aliquot Ecclesiae Patrum ac scriptorum ecclesiasticorum libri*, Paris, 1610, folio, p. 174 ff., closely resembles our text and contains the same admonition. Compare J. Mabillon, *Museum Italicum*, vol. II, pp. 373–397, Paris, 1724, quarto; E. Martène, *De antiquis Ecclesiae ritibus*, book III, c. I, p. 867 ff., Antwerp, 1736, folio, vol. II. Burchard’s fragment was received into all collections of councils: Labbe and Cossart, vol. IX, pp. 848–833 [as printed]; Coleti, vol. XI, pp. 1133–1138; Hardouin, vol. VI, part I, pp. 829–834; Mansi, vol. IX, pp. 400–406; Hartzheim, *Concilia Germaniae*, vol. III, pp. 9–16.
>
> Yet the Berlin codex is distinguished above all by a title wholly its own and peculiar, of which we shall say more shortly. It reads:
>
> “Book of the monastery of the Blessed Virgin Mary at the Lake, containing a method for the observance of a synod. Likewise, the book of canons of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, of the Order of Canons Regular of blessed Augustine, collected into one from the judgments of supreme pontiffs, general councils, and holy Fathers, and divided into ten books.”
>
> In Paris codex no. 3885 A, the following verses were copied by the scribe:
>
> Joyful company of God’s faithful, pray to the Son  
> that by his mercy he may lead us to the joys of heaven;  
> may joy above all things and abundance of good things be ours  
> through God’s grace, by whom solemn observances  
> may take place in the Church without sorrow.
>
> [lacuna]
>
> O God, be merciful to me, William, a sinner.
>
> Whatever harms the Church, whatever troubles it,  
> the decrees excellently teach and at once make plain.  
> The writer of this distinguished work is to be praised.  
> Christ, you will be judge for William of Abbini.  
> Then you will enjoy good peace, when you receive  
> the promised rewards of the kingdom, shining in everlasting light.
>
> The Vienna Library codex (*Codex theologicus* no. 355, folio) is defective and begins with part III, title 22.

In preparing the first and second parts of his work, he used no collection other than Pseudo-Isidore’s, employing its Gallican recension. Yet very many features are peculiar to himself and distinguish his work from other such productions of earlier ages. In the first part, he extended the succession of Roman pontiffs—which Pseudo-Isidore ends with Gregory the Younger—down to Urban II, who died in 1099. He then placed the *Exceptions of St Sylvester* immediately after the decretals of Miltiades, inserting nothing between them, although Pseudo-Isidore inserted the canons of councils between them.

Moreover, he names two Roman pontiffs, Chrysogonus and Mercury, of whom we know absolutely nothing and for whom not even Blanchini—learned and tireless in the study of antiquity, and editor of the *Lives of the Pontiffs* written by Anastasius—could find any trace in history.

> [Note: Col. LXIID.] Rome, 1731–1735, 4 vols., folio, vol. I, pp. 30 and 90.

In assigning the names of individual pontiffs, he carefully indicates the number or place that each occupies in the succession of pontiffs.

> [Note: Col. LXIID.] “Pope Anacletus, third from Peter,” etc.

In this he seems to have imitated the collector whose manuscript codex, as we have said, is preserved in the Vienna Library. The pontiffs’ decretals were taken from the Pseudo-Isidorian collection without disturbing their order and were divided into chapters. These successive chapters follow one another in an uninterrupted numerical sequence, so that the chapters of the final decretal are joined in their natural order to the chapters of the first. The author also notes repeatedly where he proceeds from one decretal to another.

> [Note: Col. LXIID.] “Clement in his first letter,” c. 11; “Clement in his second letter,” c. 20; “Clement in his third letter,” c. 32; “Clement in his fourth letter,” etc. The chapters following one another from the first through the eleventh are all taken from the first decretal, a fact repeatedly indicated by the words: “Likewise, from the same letter.”

He followed this method of division in arranging each pontiff’s letters so that the chapters of all the letters of the same pontiff are numbered separately and are wholly distinct from chapters of the letters both of earlier and later pontiffs.

In marking out the second part, the author followed the same method. He inserted each council into his collection in the order in which Pseudo-Isidore had arranged it, and distinguished the canons of each by numbers in such a way that the canons of each council are reckoned in a separate numerical sequence and are not joined with the canons of the following council. He begins the Greek councils with the First Council of Nicaea and the Latin councils with the First Council of Carthage. He ends the former series with the Council of Chalcedon and the latter with the Second Council of Seville.

He generally retained the headings or summaries attached by Pseudo-Isidore, as well as the numbers by which Pseudo-Isidore himself distinguished the conciliar canons; but he arranged the Greek councils in almost the same manner as he had arranged the decretals of Roman pontiffs in the first part. To the Council of Chalcedon he appended several canons from the Quinisext, or Trullan, Synod, held at Constantinople in 692, prefacing them with certain passages taken from books of the Venerable Bede and other ecclesiastical writers, as well as from the acts of that council itself.

Moreover, the translation of the canons differs in many respects from that found in collections of councils.

> [Note: Col. LXIIIB.] Mansi, vol. XI, pp. 939–988.

It more closely approaches the Greek texts.

> [Note: Col. LXIIIB.] By way of example, we reproduce here the translation of those canons which passed into neither Ivo’s nor Gratian’s works:
>
> “C. 8 (canon 20). It is not permitted for a bishop to preach in a city that does not belong to him. A bishop is not permitted publicly to preach in another city that does not belong to him. But if anyone is found doing this, let him cease from the episcopal office; let him do what belongs to presbyters.”
>
> “C. 9 (canon 21). Concerning bishops. Those who have been irreproachably deposed because of their offenses and reduced to the rank of laypersons, if they voluntarily turn to the Lord and renounce the sin for which they were deposed, and wholly separate themselves from it, are not to lose the clerical tonsure. But if they adhere to sin, let them wear their hair long like laypersons, because they have preferred a worldly manner of life to the heavenly life.”
>
> “C. 11 (canon 26). Concerning presbyters bound in non-lawful marriage. We decree that a presbyter bound in a marriage not lawful may retain his seat, but must abstain from office. Such indulgence is sufficient for him, because it is not fitting for one who ought to heal his own wounds to bless others. For a blessing is the conferral of sanctification. But how shall one who lacks this because of the offense of ignorance confer it upon others? Let him bless neither publicly nor privately; let him not distribute the body of the Lord to others, nor minister in any other manner. Let it suffice him that he presides (*ἀρκούμενος τῇ προεδρίᾳ*, ‘being content with the presidency’) and begs the Lord that the iniquity of his ignorance may be forgiven him. It is clear, however, that such an unlawful marriage must be dissolved, so that he may have no access whatever to the woman on account of whom he was deprived of sacred ministry.”

The Second Council of Nicaea, held in 787, and the Eighth Synod, celebrated in 869 and 870, are then appended; once again, certain fragments excerpted from their acts are prefixed. Finally, to every series of canons—both those drawn from Latin and those drawn from Greek councils—are added certain chapters taken from the works of the Holy Fathers and other writers.

The third part of the collection, which alone bears the appearance of a collection of canons, presents passages excerpted from the Fathers, ecclesiastical writers, and compilations of Roman and Frankish laws. These are arranged in twenty-nine rubrics, each of which is then divided into several chapters distinguished by a numerical sequence never interrupted. Yet other fragments, both of decretals and of canons, are intermingled with these chapters.

We know neither the author of this collection nor the time when it was compiled. Yet because it extends the succession of Roman pontiffs no further than Urban II and presents no canons of later councils, we reasonably believe that it was composed in the time of this pontiff. The author completed his work with such great and remarkable zeal in gathering documents that, if he had possessed or known of later documents, he would surely have inserted them.

Since in the course of this little work we must very frequently have recourse to this collection, we think it necessary to present a clear outline of it, lest, whenever we cite it, readers should not sufficiently understand us. Accordingly, in a note we append an index of all the contents of the collection. Retaining the division into three parts, and distributing the decretals of each pope and the canons of each council into an equal number of titles, we have followed exactly the chronological order observed by the author in his collection [Col. LXIVB]. As for the two appendices which, as we have said, are attached to the canons of both Greek and Latin councils, we distinguished the first by this designation: “Part Two, Appendix A”; the other by this: “Part Two, Appendix B”; and numbered them together with the other titles.

[Col. LXVA] We must now see whether, and which, predecessors the author of our collection followed. With respect to the first and second parts, it may seem doubtful whether in arranging them he imitated earlier collectors or not. For the manner in which he excerpted the Pseudo-Isidorian collection is his own and distinctive. He differs very greatly from the author of the collection dedicated to Anselm. For he never departs from Pseudo-Isidore: he presents fragments of decretals in precisely the same order in which they stand in the Pseudo-Isidorian collection; nor does he separate them from one another or insert them in different places in his own collection. Yet he drew from it far fewer chapters, and selected ones, whereas the other gathered into his compilation almost the whole Pseudo-Isidorian work indiscriminately and without any selection.

Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that there is a very great resemblance between our collection and that other one [Col. LXVB] preserved in the Vienna manuscript, of which we have recently spoken. The first part of our collection is arranged exactly as in the Vienna manuscript, though in a fuller form. In both, all the chapters are taken solely from Pseudo-Isidore, and each pope is assigned a notice stating how far he stands, in the succession of pontiffs, from blessed Peter. Finally, almost all the chapters [Note: [Col. LXVIC] Chapters 3, 14, 18, 27, 38, 39, 40, 42. Tripartite Collection, Part I, title I, ch. 22; title II, ch. 19; title III, ch. 3; title V, ch. 1; title XII, chs. 1 and 3; title XIII, ch. 3. Chapters 47, 51, 52, 56, 59, 63. LXVIC] Chapters 4, 5, 10, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17. Tripartite Collection, Part I, title I, chs. 20–21; title II, chs. 5, 9, 10, 11, 13, 23, 24. Chapters 28–32, 25, 37, 41, 54, 55, 58. Nor should it seem surprising that the author of a collection which is indeed extremely extensive followed that small and meagre Viennese work, since even great works not infrequently derive both their model and their enlargement from very small ones. As regards the second part, the author needed no other guide or teacher, since everything had already been made ready for him by Pseudo-Isidore. Finally, in arranging the third part of his work, he had before him Burchard of Worms’s *Decree* alone [Note: [Col. LXVIC] Here are some examples: Part III, title I, chs. 12–16 [Col. LXVID]: Burchard, book IV, chs. 13, 16, 50, 51; title II, chs. 2–6: Burchard, book V, chs. 15, 16, 20, 21, 47; title III, chs. 9–12, 27, 28, 30, 31: Burchard, book III, chs. 9–12, 142, 146, 159, 160; title VI, chs. 1–3: Burchard, book III, chs. 126–128; title X, chs. 7–9, 12–16: Burchard, book II, chs. 181, 182, 184, 185–187, 191, 192; title XII, chs. 1–8: Burchard, book VIII, chs. 10, 19, 22, 23, 37, 54, 58; title XIII, chs. 1–5: Burchard, book VIII, chs. 65, 68, 86, 96, 98; title XV, chs. 63–68, 70–78: Burchard, book IX, chs. 3, 4, 46, 47, 51, 54, 59, 60, 61, 65, 66, 74, 75, 81, 82; title XVI, chs. 9–13, 19–29: Burchard, book VII, chs. 2, 3, 10, 15, 17; book XVII, chs. 9, 12, 13, 22–24, 33, 34, 45, 46, 49; title XX, chs. 53–55: Burchard, book VI, chs. 21, 22, 42; title XXVIII, chs. 7–10, 16–18: Burchard, book XVIII, chs. 14, 16, 20, 21; book XIX, chs. 11, 12, 15; title XXIX, chs. 1, 3–17: Burchard, book XIII, chs. 8–11, 22, 29, 30, 34–37, 40, 44.], while accepting almost all the other material. [Col. LXVIB] Yet, while gathering a harvest from it, he wished to employ the same freedom that Burchard had used when harvesting the compilations of his predecessors.

## CHAPTER II. The Difference between the Tripartite Collection and the Works of Ivo

[Col. LXV]

[Col. LXVB] Rather than linger any longer in reporting the opinions of others [Note: [Col. LXVID] These opinions appear in Caspar Oudin, *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, pp. 873–876, Leipzig, 1722, folio; *Literary History of France*, vol. X, p. 102; and the Ballerini brothers, cited work, p. IV, ch. 16.] concerning Ivo’s works, and approving or refuting them, let us turn to our collection and compare it with Ivo’s works. Thus it will become clear that Ivo can be called author of the *Panormia* alone, and that he constructed it with the aid of our collection; whereas the *Decree* must be attributed not to Ivo but to someone else who lived much later [Col. LXVC].

Almost all learned men acknowledge that the *Panormia* is genuinely Ivo’s work—even those who maintain that it was composed before the *Decree* and consequently is by no means an abridgment of the *Decree*. All manuscripts, both ancient and later, containing the *Panormia*—of which I have had occasion to inspect innumerable examples, especially in the libraries of France—bear Ivo’s name and are preceded by his familiar prologue. Most of them, including the best, contain no decretal letter older than Leo IV’s decree on the election of a pope. Moreover, in most manuscripts there is no appendix concerning the canon of what books are to be read in church and at what time, nor the canons of the Second Lateran Council held under Innocent II. Nearly all scholars agree that the latter were added to the *Panormia* at a later date. It also seems no less certain that another canon concerning books to be read was further added, both because it has no authority, being drawn from some ritual book, and because the same title occurs elsewhere in the same collection [Note: [Col. LXVIIB] I use the octavo edition published at Louvain in 1557. It is divided into chapters; for this reason, although the division was made less correctly, it was used by the Roman correctors, as also by Antonio Agustín, Baluze, and others. Moreover, it reproduces the Brandian edition without any alteration whatsoever.].

### § I

Whoever carefully compares Ivo’s *Panormia* with the Tripartite Collection and considers how closely these two compilations are connected will easily understand that the *Panormia* somehow emerged wholly from it—fashioned from its vast and unorganized mass [Col. LXVIIB] and reduced to a kind of order. In the individual parts and rubrics likewise, a very great similarity between the two collections may be discerned, especially evident in the third part of that collection. For from it Ivo took not merely certain individual chapters, but whole rubrics [Note: [Col. LXVIIB] To make clear how closely these two collections are connected, I shall note from each part of the *Panormia* the principal chapters which Ivo drew from the Tripartite Collection and not from some other collection. To each chapter of the *Panormia* [Col. LXVIIC] I have appended the corresponding chapters of the Tripartite Collection.

LXVIIIB] 14, 15, 16, 17, 22, 25, 26, 34, 35, 38, 39, 40, 44, 48–54, 56–59, 60; Tripartite Collection, Part III, title XX, chs. 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 14, 16, 17, 18, 21, 22, 23, 26, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 36, 38, 39–45, 46–49, 51. From this it can also be proved that Ivo took much from the first part, which contains the decretals, in composing his work [Note: [Col. LXVIIIC] Ivo, *Panormia*, Part I, chs. 18, 22; Tripartite Collection, Part I, title XLIII, ch. 44; title IV, ch. 71. — Ivo, *Panormia*, Part II, chs. 170, 174, 177; Tripartite Collection, Part I, title LV, ch. 50; title VI, ch. 1; title XXXVIII, ch. 3. — Ivo, *Panormia*, Part III, chs. 13, 43, 94, 55, 164, 165, 189, 145, 146; Tripartite Collection, Part I, title XLIII, ch. 36; title XXXVIII, chs. 11, 21; title XLVI, chs. 31, 26, 27, 14; title LV, chs. 56, 77. — Ivo, *Panormia*, Part IV, [Col. LXVIIID] chs. 1, 4, 8, 10, 22, 25, 26, 29, 74, 75, 76, 100, 112, 113, 118, 136; Tripartite Collection, Part I, title XXX, ch. 8; title II, ch. 20; title LXII, ch. 4; title II, chs. 15, 16, 17; title IX, chs. 3, 4, 5, 6; title LXII, ch. 74; title XVIII, chs. 11, 12; ch. 1; title XXXII, ch. 2; title XXI, ch. 1; title XII, ch. 2; title IV, ch. 2; title XI, ch. 1. — Ivo, *Panormia*, Part V, chs. 12, 13, 106, 134, 135; Tripartite Collection, Part I, title LXII, chs. 60, 61, 34, 65, 66. — Ivo, *Panormia*, Part VII, chs. 14, 15, 68; Tripartite Collection, Part I, title LXII, chs. 24, 54; title LV, ch. 111. From the very words with which the decretal fragments begin, it is apparent that they were taken, without any alteration, word for word from the Tripartite Collection. For example: Ivo, *Panormia*, Part IV, ch. 118: “Alexander, fifth pope from Peter, in the first of his decretals,” etc.].

As for the second part, although Ivo may have borrowed it from the work of Pseudo-Isidore no less than did the author of the Tripartite Collection, it is nevertheless perfectly clear that in this part too Ivo did not depart from his predecessor. For from him he copied the canons of the Quinisext Council, the Second Council of Nicaea, and the Eighth Ecumenical Council, which are absent from Pseudo-Isidore’s work and first occur in the Tripartite Collection. He then received into the *Panormia* certain fragments from the acts of those same synods, which in the Tripartite Collection are prefixed to the synods themselves; and finally those chapters which, as we have said, are attached in the form of appendices to Greek and Latin councils alike. From all this, no one can fail to see that our opinion is beyond all possibility of doubt.

But from Ivo’s letters no less than from the *Panormia*, it is established that the Tripartite Collection was known to him and that he used it. We have noted only those passages [Note: [Col. LXVIIID] Letter 47: Tripartite Collection, Part I, title XLVI, ch. 2. Letter 60: Tripartite Collection, Part I, title XXXIX, ch. 2; Part I, title XLVI, ch. 35; Part III, title III, ch. 26. Letter 61: Tripartite Collection, Part I, title LXIV, ch. 3; Part I, title LXII, ch. 74. Letter 99: Tripartite Collection, Part III, title XV, chs. 20, 2, 3. Letter 119: Tripartite Collection, Part III, title XV, ch. 95. Letter 135: Tripartite Collection, Part III, title XXIX, [Col. LXIXC] ch. 115. Letter 147: Tripartite Collection, Part III, title XV, ch. 36. Letter 184: Tripartite Collection, Part III, title III, ch. 25; Part III, title VII, chs. 3, 4, 5. Letter 212: Tripartite Collection, Part III, title XXIX, ch. 218. Letter 213: Tripartite Collection, Part I, title I, ch. 23. Letter 222: Tripartite Collection, Part III, title VI, ch. 5. Letter 241: Tripartite Collection, Part I, title XXXII, ch. 1. Letter 242: Tripartite Collection, Part III, title XVI, ch. 42. I use the edition of Ivo’s works published at Paris in 1647, in two folio volumes; the *Decree* is contained in the first volume.] which were not received into the *Panormia*, and which therefore prove [Col. LXIXA] that in writing them he had the Tripartite Collection before his eyes. If, disregarding the considerations we have thus far adduced in support of our view, anyone should still insist that Ivo did not follow that collection in composing his *Panormia*, indeed that it was wholly unknown to him when he made his work, he must necessarily maintain that the Tripartite Collection was drawn from the *Panormia*. Though this assertion would be altogether absurd, it would at the same time prove that the collection had likewise been drawn from the *Decree* commonly attributed to Ivo, since that *Decree* is connected with it by precisely the same relation that we have shown to exist between the *Panormia* and the Tripartite Collection.

Yet we do not think it worthwhile to linger longer over this matter, since we have sufficiently established our opinion: namely, that Ivo fashioned the *Panormia* upon the model of, and from the materials of, the Tripartite Collection.

[Col. LXIXB] Meanwhile, the mass of that collection was so great that Ivo’s book, compared with it, appeared deficient in many respects and was by no means sufficient for resolving every ecclesiastical question. Ivo had certainly left uncollected much material from his predecessor’s collection, and he could have enlarged the various rubrics of his own collection with more chapters and increased it by adding other new rubrics, without deserving rebuke for an excessive and disorderly eagerness to collect. What Ivo had neglected, however, others did. For there were two collectors of canons who, by repeated labor, enlarged Ivo’s *Panormia* from the Tripartite Collection and at nearly the same time—or at least a little later—compiled new collections of canons, yet neither took anything from the work of the other. The name of the first is wholly unknown; the second either deliberately assumed Ivo’s name, or, what is more likely [Col. LXXA], came down to posterity under that name through the ignorance of scribes and the error of editors.

Both works must now be examined more carefully.

### § II

The Vienna manuscript (Canon Law, no. 91, quarto) contains a collection comprising a new recension of Ivo’s *Panormia*, divided into ten parts. The author seems to have adopted this division so as in constructing his work to come closer to the Decalogue, and thereby to follow the character of his age and the intention of his contemporaries. Otherwise, imitating the *Panormia* in its entirety, including its division into books and chapters, he received it into his own collection with almost the same form preserved; yet he arranged its chapters in a fashion peculiar and distinctive to himself. He does not divide individual chapters by numbers and insert them one after another; instead, he combines several that treat the same subjects and reduces them, as it were, to a single chapter imitating titles or rubrics. Thus he distinguishes the subsequent material from the first chapter by adding one or more points, according as it stands at a greater or lesser distance from the beginning [Col. LXXB]. To make ten parts, he divided the third part of the *Panormia* into two and added a tenth, which deals with penance. Its materials, entirely omitted by Ivo, he drew both from the Tripartite Collection (III, 28) and from Burchard of Worms’s *Decree*. The Tripartite Collection presented itself to him in somewhat the same manner as it had presented itself to his predecessor [Note: [Col. LXIXC] Part IX, ch. 6, preface, §§ 1–2; ch. 7, preface, §§ 1–2; ch. 8, preface, §§ 1–2; ch. 9, preface, §§ 1–7; ch. 10, preface, §§ 1–7; ch. 11, preface, §§ 1–4, copied from Ivo’s *Panormia*, Part VIII, chs. 6–33, etc. Chapters 22, preface, §§ 1–7, and 23, preface, §§ 1–9, from the Tripartite Collection, Part III, title XXII, chs. 1–18, etc.].

He prefixed two prefaces to his work: one expounds the plan of the whole work; the other he took from Ivo’s *Panormia*, so that it might itself—using the author’s words—be “the gate and guide of the entire sanctuary, under whose direction anyone may explore its mysteries.” Accordingly, he placed Ivo’s prologue before his own preface [Note: [Col. LXIXC]

> Most reverend Father, I have complied with your wish as far as I was able. Having examined with diligent curiosity the libraries of many churches, I have gathered piecemeal the judgments of the holy Fathers from the acts of councils, the decrees of Roman pontiffs, and also the treatises of illustrious and orthodox men; and I have reduced this collection, in an ordered arrangement, to the body of one volume [Col. LXIXD], so that whoever might find it difficult to possess all those works from which these materials have been gathered, or to read what he judges useful to himself, may find it here more easily. After the account of the Roman pontiffs and their times, let the diligent reader find, read, and understand, as a lamp, the treatise of the venerable Lord I., bishop of Chartres, which he composed in an exceptionally lucid style on the harmony of the canons; and thus let him traverse with unimpeded step the inner chambers of the following little work and all its hidden places. For I have endeavoured to arrange the whole structure of the same work in such a way that it may in every respect seem suited to serve as its preface.
>
> Moreover, in order that the same little book might correspond also in the number of its parts to the sacred Decalogue of the law, I divided the sum of the whole volume into ten parts, and I added to the treatise of the aforesaid man a suitably concise summary of the contents of each part, so that what should be sought in each part might be more easily apparent. Furthermore, I took care to note, in order, the proper titles of the distinctions within each chapter, so that the reader need not traverse the whole volume in search of a decision in any case, but need only note the chapter with the number prefixed which concerns his business, and investigate in continuous reading the judgments placed under it.
>
> To prevent the frequent insertion of material on one and the same subject from producing difficulty for the inquirer and weariness for the reader, avoiding a prolixity hateful to most people, I compressed these materials with such brevity that I did not assign a separate title to every separate chapter, but often placed several chapters under a single title and repeatedly subdivided those titles by subordinate divisions. I indicated the number of those subdivisions by the number of points appended, both in the titles and in the titled chapters.
>
> As to the fact that I have often inserted some discordant judgments, less suitable to our times, I did not do this in order that I myself should judge by them or suggest that others ought to judge by them; rather, I thought it proper to show that different persons had held different opinions, and to leave to the judgment of the prudent reader which of them should be followed [Col. LXXD]. I therefore entreat you, by the mercy of God, to render above all this return for my labors: that you may deign to intercede for my sins before him who takes away the sins of the world.
>
> “The first part contains: on faith; on certain heresies; on baptism; on the ministry of baptizing those to be baptized; on the preparation and distribution of chrism; on confirmation; on the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord; on the offering and reception of the Eucharist; on the veneration of sacred vessels.
>
> “The second part contains: on the constitution of the Church; on the offerings of the faithful; on the dedication of churches; on burial; on the consecration of altars and the manner in which churches are possessed by priests; on tithes; on lawful possession; on those who flee to a church; on sacrilege; on freed persons, the property of the Church, and their alienation; on authentic and apocryphal Scriptures and councils [Col. LXXIB]; on customs; on fasting and almsgiving.
>
> “The third part contains: on the election and consecration of the pope and bishops; on examination and ordination; on certain persons, for various causes, to be ordained or not ordained; on the transfer of ordinands; on ordained persons not to be reordained; on the continence of the ordained; on simoniacs; on heretics; on those fallen while in holy orders; on clerics who are murderers and usurers; on slaves unknowingly ordained; on vicious clerics; on abbots and monks; on veiled virgins and widows and abbesses.
>
> “The fourth part contains: on the Rule of blessed Augustine and its observance; on archbishops and bishops to be ordained; on those expelled; on unknown persons; on persons at variance—what they are to do in churches and throughout parishes [Col. LXXIC]; on their ministers; how they are to be in harmony with princes and restrain evil men; on property; on sobriety; on poverty; on freedom; on witnesses against bishops; on deceased bishops; on episcopal and ecclesiastical property; on where and how priests and clerics should live or instruct others; on their possessions.
>
> “The fifth part contains: on the primacy and dignity of the Roman Church; on councils to be convoked; on the establishment of a province; on the authority of primates and metropolitans; on where cases of clerics are to be heard; on those who have been despoiled and must be reinvested; on accusation—by what procedure, by which persons, and against whom it ought or ought not to be made; on witnesses—who, how, how many, and in what matter ought or ought not to give testimony; on truces, when and for how long they are granted; on those who evade proceedings, how long and on what grounds they are to be awaited; on what kind of persons judges ought to be and when they should pronounce judgment; on appeal, when and how it is made [Col. LXXID], and on those who appeal improperly; on appointed judges; on condemned bishops and clerics whose cases have been decided.
>
> “The sixth part contains: how clerics accused solely by public ill repute are to clear themselves; on the cases and legal affairs of laymen; on the power to bind and loose; on summoning the excommunicated; on excommunication; on absolution; on those bound by fidelity or oath to excommunicated persons; on heretics to be excommunicated after death; and that communion is to be had with persons not excommunicated by name; on unlawful, unjust, and hasty excommunication.
>
> “The seventh part contains: on marriages—at what time, between what persons, and on what grounds they should be contracted; on the three things that make a marriage complete; on complete and incomplete marriage; on concubines; on spouses, one of whom, without the other, vows continence or assumes the religious habit; on wives who, after their husbands were taken captive, married other men; on what marriage is among persons of the same religion, that is, among Gentiles [Col. LXXIIB] and among Jews; on what grounds marriage is not to be dissolved; on what union does not make a marriage; on separation of marriage for a cause other than fornication.
>
> “The eighth part contains: on marriage not being dissolved except for fornication; on fornication with sisters and blood-relatives, and that no one should marry as wife a woman whom he previously committed adultery with; on killers of their own spouses; on adultery; on Lothair and Theutberga; on spiritual fornication; on reconciliation of spouses; on the formalities of accusation, separation, and reconciliation; on the submission owed by wives to husbands; why and who are forbidden or commanded to marry; on consanguinity and its enumeration, observance, proof, accusation, calculation, and investigation; on its degrees arranged in direct and collateral order [Col. LXXIIC].
>
> “The ninth part contains: on homicides; on those who have killed themselves, bishops, or other ecclesiastics; on parricides and killers of spouses and penitents; on homicides committed voluntarily, involuntarily, or by counsel; on one who strikes a pregnant woman and causes miscarriage; on certain homicides committed without sin; on incantations, divinations, and various kinds of magical art; on the nature of demons; on lots; on the observance of days and months; on the eight different kinds of lying; on oaths, whether they must be kept or ought not to be kept because unlawful; on exacting an oath and deception; on certain oaths and the companions of oath-taking; on every kind of lying.
>
> “The tenth part contains: on penance and penitents, and on the distinction to be observed among them; how clerics are to do penance; on confession of sins; on satisfaction and reconciliation; on greater [Col. LXXIID] and lesser faults; on penitents at the point of death; and on the correction of all crimes and the commutation of fasts.”]

This is followed by an index of the parts [Col. LXXIA], from which it can be seen better than from a lengthy description in what manner he used his predecessor’s book.

Besides the materials which he excerpted from the two collections of which we have spoken, he added certain other documents; and in doing so he followed the example of no predecessor. These include a great many canons drawn from the Council of Pavia of the year 1100, the Council of Toulouse of 1119, the Council of Beauvais of 1120, the Second Lateran Council under Calixtus II, and finally the Synod of Nantes of 1127; likewise, many letters of Ivo, Paschal II, and Calixtus II. At the end of Part Four, after the formularies of Acacius’s letters, he added two others which the author himself seems to have composed, one of which is addressed to Ivo. Both bear the year 1130.

Although neither the author of this collection nor the time at which it was compiled is known, we are confident that both may be conjectured with plausible reasoning. [Col. LXXIB] As regards the date of the Collection, the matter is more easily settled: from the more recent documents added, and especially from those two letters [Col. LXXIIA] bearing the year 1130, we rightly infer that the collection itself was compiled either in that very year or at least in the year following. By no different reasoning do learned men infer from the formal letters written in the year 906, which Regino of Prüm received into his *Decree*, book I, chs. 448 and 449, the time at which he composed that work. From the same grounds which indicate the date of our collection, we believe that its author also may be discovered.

Hildebert, first bishop of Le Mans and then, from 1130, archbishop of Tours, who died in 1134, relates in a certain letter which he addressed in 1118 or 1119 to Gilbert, bishop of Limerick in Ireland, that he was occupied in compiling a collection of canons; that he had not yet completed it, but would send it to him immediately upon its completion.

> “The extracts from the decrees which we have resolved to arrange in a single volume have not yet been brought to their conclusion. For this work requires a mind free from cares, from which the episcopate has not exempted us. Yet we have already completed part of it, and, in order to finish what remains, we shall lay aside the bishopric. When completed, it will come into your hands; nor will it be necessary for your legate to weary himself by coming all the way to us to carry it. It shall be our duty to have it sent to you by one of our own.”  
> Book II, letter 27, p. 124, *Works*, ed. J. Beaugendre, Paris, 1708, folio.

In another of his letters is found a preface which he intended to place before this collection, though it is neither complete nor anything other than a section taken from Ivo’s prologue.

> “St Hildebert, archbishop of Tours, on his extracts concerning ecclesiastical rules, on the manifold kinds of divine commandments.”  
> Book II, letter 161, cited work.

If these facts are compared with the characteristics of our Collection, it may with good reason be affirmed that Hildebert was its author. [Col. LXXIIIA] Indeed, the preface which we find in our Collection, composed by its author himself, answers every request made by Gilbert, bishop of Limerick, to whom it is moreover addressed. It is also evident from its very opening—indeed, from the whole preface—that it was written by a man distinguished by ecclesiastical rank to another man of the same condition. Furthermore, the canons of the Council of Nantes, held in November 1127 under Hildebert’s presidency, prove that he was the author of the Collection into which they were received. If we add that Ivo’s prologue to the *Panormia* occurs among Hildebert’s letters, we may rightly conclude that he wished to prefix it to his own Collection. Since we see this done in our Collection, we rightly attribute it to Hildebert.

This also makes it easy to discern why the copyist who transcribed the manuscript could have forgotten the true author’s name: seeing only Ivo’s prologue, he thought that the second preface also had been written by Ivo. It is likewise clear why the copyist who wrote the Berlin manuscript, in which the Tripartite Collection is found—

> Compare chapter 1, note 260, of this Dissertation. [Col. LXXIIIC]

—also attributed this Collection to Ivo: surely for no other reason than that Ivo’s prologue likewise stood at the beginning of the Collection in that codex. Nor need it seem surprising that the same copyist states that Ivo divided his work into ten parts, and entitled the codex with Ivo’s name, although it contains only that Tripartite Collection. If we reflect carefully, either the copyist himself or the person at whose command he prepared the manuscript could very easily have known that there existed a collection of canons divided into ten parts which, whether because of its great resemblance to Ivo’s *Panormia*, or merely because Ivo’s prologue had been prefixed to it, was also commonly attributed to Ivo.

[Col. LXXIVA] We therefore rightly and without any doubt attribute the Collection of which we are speaking to Hildebert. Because of his ardent desire to preserve ecclesiastical discipline, he could not possibly have neglected those new documents which set forth altered or enlarged rules of that discipline, and which earlier collectors neither possessed nor could have possessed, since they had completed their works before those documents appeared. Yet by receiving documents of this sort into his Collection he did not depart from the practice of his predecessors, since all of them eagerly inserted into their collections whatever new material suitable to their own times they discovered.

For this reason we cannot attribute to Hildebert either the collections commonly called the Caesaraugustana and Tarraconensis, or that which is to be traced to Anselm of Lucca as its author, as some have done; for all these collections contain no letters later than those of Urban II. Certain most learned men of the Congregation of Saint Maur, Benedictines in France—

> “Despite all the investigations and discussions we have been able to make, it is very difficult to decide with certainty what ought to be thought of the collection of canons made by Hildebert. The collection which bears the name of Yves of Chartres cannot be the work of the bishop of Le Mans; that is evident. If he were author of that of Tarragona or of Saragossa, as Antonio Agustín and, after him, M. Dujat conjecture, would it be possible for the work of a bishop of France to be found only in the libraries of Spain? We shall not pause to show that he cannot be the author of the collection bearing the name of Anselm of Lucca, nor to refute those who have attributed it to him . . . . Finally, all that we can say with certainty on this subject is that Hildebert undertook to make a collection of canons; that he partly carried out his design; but that the duties attached to the episcopate caused him to interrupt his work until 1118. He then resolved to resume it; but we do not know whether he put the finishing hand to it; and, if he did finish this collection, we do not know whether it exists or has been lost; at least, it is unknown to us.”  
> *Histoire littéraire de France*, vol. XI, p. 409; generally pp. 406–410.  
> It would be needless to observe that Hildebert is by no means the author of the Tripartite Collection, since Ivo, who died in 1115, had already used it, while Hildebert composed his work in 1118 or 1119. [Cols. LXXIIIC–LXXIIID]

—endeavoured very admirably and subtly to examine the various opinions current concerning Hildebert’s collection of canons. They pointed out the errors on which such opinions rest; but, believing it sufficient to demonstrate the truth of what Hildebert says about his own collection of canons, they supplied nothing at all certain by which the question could be conclusively resolved.

### § III. On the other compiler

As to the other compiler, who, by reworking the *Panormia*, produced the *Decretum* which, as we shall shortly endeavour to prove, is falsely attributed to Ivo, we may be briefer. We need only show clearly in what manner this work was compiled.

The author divided his work into seventeen parts. We give their headings in the notes, so that it may more easily be compared with the preceding collections, and especially with the Tripartite Collection.

> **Part I.** On faith and the sacrament of faith—that is, baptism—and the ministry of those baptizing and those baptized; of those being confirmed and those confirmed; and on the observance of each matter; also, what baptism confers and what confirmation confers.  
> **Part II.** On the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord; its reception and observance; the Mass; and the holiness of the other sacraments.  
> **Part III.** On the Church, ecclesiastical property, and their reverence and observance.  
> **Part IV.** On the observance of feast days and lawful fasts; canonical Scriptures and customs; and the celebration of a council.  
> **Part V.** On the primacy of the Roman Church; the right of primates, metropolitans, and bishops; their ordination; and episcopal eminence.  
> **Part VI.** On the conduct, ordination, correction, and cases of clerics.  
> **Part VII.** On the separate life and quiet of monks and nuns; and the recall and penance of those who transgress their profession of continence.  
> **Part VIII.** On lawful marriages; virgins and unveiled widows; those who abduct them and their separation; concubines; violation of marriage; and the penance of each offender.  
> **Part IX.** On incestuous unions and various kinds of fornication; the degree of relationship in which the faithful ought to marry or separate; and the correction and penance of each offender.  
> **Part X.** On voluntary and involuntary homicides; parricides and fratricides; the killing of lawful wives, lords, and clerics; the proposition that not everyone who kills a human being is a murderer; and their penance.  
> **Part XI.** On enchanters, auguries, diviners, sorcerers, casting lots, the various delusions of the devil, and the penance of each offender.  
> **Part XII.** On lying and perjury; accusers; judges; advocates and false witnesses; and the penance of each offender.  
> **Part XIII.** On robbers, thieves, usurers, and moneylenders; hunters; revilers and quarrelsome persons; revelries and drunkenness; mad persons; Jews and their correction.  
> **Part XIV.** On just and unjust excommunication: for what causes and in what order it is to be imposed.  
> **Part XV.** On the penance of the healthy and the sick, and the substitutions by which penance may be mitigated.  
> **Part XVI.** On the duties and cases of laypersons.  
> **Part XVII.** Containing speculative judgments of the holy Fathers concerning faith, hope, and charity. [Cols. LXXIIID–LXXVC]

So far as one may infer from the work itself, the author seems to have kept two things in view. In general, he never wished to depart from Ivo; but although he imitated the form which Ivo had used in arranging the *Panormia*, he departed from it in many respects, particularly where the fuller material of the Tripartite Collection required a different procedure. For Ivo, as we have also said above, had omitted to excerpt much from that Collection which he could, and indeed ought, to have excerpted in order to enlarge and perfect his work. Thus we have shown that, in the other Collection which we attribute to Hildebert, Ivo’s work was enlarged and more fully developed from the Tripartite Collection.

The author of the *Decretum*, whom we call Pseudo-Ivo, divided each part of the *Panormia* into two, since, as we shall shortly see, the *Decretum* was by no means composed by Ivo. He added a seventeenth part which, apart from certain passages taken from Augustine’s works, is wholly derived from Burchard of Worms’s *Decretum*. I believe this also explains why this final part is wholly absent from a certain Paris manuscript, and was altogether omitted by the epitomizers of the same *Decretum*: neither the plan nor the method of the *Panormia* or of the Tripartite Collection required such a part.

As to the headings of the parts themselves, Pseudo-Ivo followed the Tripartite Collection rather than Ivo’s *Panormia*. The first and second parts are certainly taken from the *Panormia*; but the following parts, from the third through the sixteenth, although the author looked to Ivo in arranging them, mostly imitate the Tripartite Collection, which set out more distinct particular headings. He therefore combined several headings of the third part of that Collection into one, as the structure of his work required. Thus the third part of the *Decretum* comprises the third heading of the Collection; the fourth, headings four, five, six, and seven; the fifth, headings eight and nine; the sixth, heading ten; the seventh, headings eleven, twelve, thirteen, and fourteen; the eighth, heading fifteen; the ninth, headings sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, and nineteen; the tenth, heading twenty; the eleventh, heading twenty-one; the twelfth, heading twenty-two; the thirteenth, headings twenty-three through twenty-six; and finally the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth parts comprise headings twenty-seven, twenty-eight, and twenty-nine, the last headings of the Tripartite Collection.

Pseudo-Ivo followed not only the genuine Ivo in constructing his work, but also drew the material itself from the same sources from which Ivo had drawn it, adding material that Ivo had already added to passages excerpted from elsewhere. Thus he again consulted Burchard’s *Decretum* and the Tripartite Collection, which Ivo had used in particular, and excerpted still more from them. To these collections he added the *Panormia*, which he used not only as a source but also as a model. He received in the same form as Ivo those chapters drawn from the Tripartite Collection which Ivo had combined into one or modified.

> To make these points clearer, we append a synoptic table recording, for each part of Pseudo-Ivo’s *Decretum*, the chapters taken in the same preserved sequence from Burchard’s *Decretum*. Yet the author used these works so ineptly that one must say that he lacked every skill in arranging and ordering such material, and did nothing except heap together into an unordered and undigested mass whatever he found in those three collections. It is incredible how everything is mixed together, arranged without order, and scattered here and there, as if sown broadcast, with no discrimination of places. Whatever he found in his predecessors, without excepting even trifles, he incorporated into his Collection. He laboured so anxiously to gather these materials that, in order not to interrupt the sequence in which individual chapters had been arranged by his predecessors, he admitted the same documents into his Collection twice and three times, according as he found them in the two or three collections at hand.
