These passages, mostly taken from Burchard’s *Decretum*, had been somewhat modified both by the author of the Tripartite Collection and by Ivo in the *Panormia*. Yet Pseudo-Ivo, who did not even notice the modification, inserted them into his Collection in the same form which they had in those sources.

Since we have thus shown how the *Decretum* was compiled, we believe that we have also proved that Ivo can in no way be called its author. For how could a man of the highest intelligence and learning—such as history attests Ivo to have been—utterly destroy a work composed with such care and clarity from the works of Burchard and Anselm of Lucca, as well as from the Tripartite Collection, a work connected in every part and elaborated with wonderful order and method; and then compile another work anew from his own work and those of the same predecessors, in which an incredible confusion and complete absence of order appear, apparently for no other reason than to accumulate a certain undigested and wholly unworked mass of materials? No one, surely, would easily persuade himself of this, and still less would anyone undertake to prove that Ivo acted thus.

As for the opinion of the most distinguished Savigny, who maintains that Ivo himself, after completing the *Panormia*, compiled the *Decretum*, and was induced to complete it especially by the discovery of the Tripartite Collection, which he had earlier not known: we have no reason to disagree with him when he admits that the *Decretum* was drawn from that Collection. But when he recognizes Ivo as its author, we demonstrate his error by this single argument: the *Panormia* had already been arranged according to the plan of the Tripartite Collection and drawn from it.

The fact that Ivo has hitherto been considered the author of the *Decretum* seems to have arisen from an error. For its author, since, as we have seen, he had little ability to arrange the documents of his Collection and made only a shapeless mass out of three compilations already ordered and arranged according to a fixed plan, did not dare even to preface his work or explain its design. He therefore judged it best, and at the same time shortest, to prefix Ivo’s prologue to the work. I am strongly confirmed in this opinion after carefully examining two manuscripts, one Vienna manuscript and the other London manuscript, both of which contain the *Decretum* divided into seventeen parts. Nowhere in these codices is the *Decretum* attributed to Ivo, although his prologue occurs in each and is so placed that it is altogether clear that the author of the *Decretum* was then not as unknown as he is seen to be today.

The opening of both manuscripts is:

> “Here begins the prologue of Lord Ivo, bishop of Chartres, before the collection of ecclesiastical rules, concerning their agreement and dispensation.”

By the word *before* in this title, the copyist sufficiently indicates that he did not regard Ivo as the author of this *Decretum*.

Moreover, Ivo’s name appears neither at the beginning nor at the end of the individual parts; and, what is more remarkable, it does not appear even at the end of the whole work, where copyists were nevertheless accustomed to write the author’s name. In another Paris manuscript, in the Royal Library under no. 3874, which contains the same *Decretum* but omits the seventeenth part, the *Decretum* and the *Panormia* are treated as one and the same work. For the manuscript bears this title:

> “The *Panormia* of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, collected from the authoritative books of decrees, canons, Roman laws, and the books of the orthodox Fathers.”

I therefore think there can be no doubt that the *Decretum* was attributed to Ivo solely because Ivo’s prologue preceded it. If it is added that the *Decretum* is not only very similar to the *Panormia*, but that the evidence for this similarity can be derived only from the Tripartite Collection, which remained unknown for a long time, one can easily understand how the *Decretum* came to be regarded as a recension of the *Panormia*. Thus the Tripartite Collection alone, which entirely explains the origin of the *Decretum*, also plainly proves that Ivo was by no means its author.

If anyone wished to deny this because Ivo, in a letter, speaks of his collections of canons, and not of one collection alone, namely the *Panormia*, he can very easily be refuted by the fact that Ivo himself, when speaking of Burchard of Worms’s work, also employs the plural.

> “I have sent you the collections of canons which you requested from me, and my smaller works which you wished added to them.”  
> Letter 262, to Pontius, abbot of Cluny; *Works*, vol. II, p. 112 ff., cited edition. [Col. LXXIXC]
>
> “But in the collections of Burchard, bishop of Worms, it is found written thus, etc.”  
> Letter 80, p. 40.  
> Of all Ivo’s contemporaries, none says more clearly that he was author of only one canonical work than Sigebert: “Ivo, bishop of Chartres, composed an outstanding volume of canons.” *De script. eccl.*, c. 167, p. 113, J. A. Fabricius, *Bibliotheca ecclesiastica*, Hamburg, 1718, folio. [Cols. LXXIXC–LXXIXD]

Moreover, the author of this *Decretum* took such care in his compilation that, since he added no more recent document, he did not reveal the time at which he composed it. Content with material which his predecessors had admitted into their collections, he inserted nothing in his Collection later than the time of Urban II. That he fashioned his work soon after Ivo’s death is shown especially by the fact that, already in an age close to Ivo’s, an epitome of it existed, of which we shall shortly say more.

Before proceeding to the third chapter of this little work, it will be worthwhile to add a few observations here in order to dispel the obscurity surrounding what has reached us concerning the *Summa Decretorum* of Ivo. We are confident of being able to satisfy everyone in this matter, because, remarkably enough, each of the collections of which we have spoken found its own epitomizer. Such an ardour for cultivating legal learning seized men at the beginning of the twelfth century that, while it contributed greatly to advancing the study of letters, then gradually reviving, it aroused and encouraged everywhere the desire to possess an epitome of works of any importance.

### § IV

[Col. LXXXB] The London manuscript preserved in the Cottonian Library and designated Cleopatra CVIII contains an extract from the Tripartite Collection. Its distinctive feature is that its author, although he took it wholly from the Tripartite Collection, departed from its arrangement and returned to the division observed by Pseudo-Isidore. Thus, interrupting the series of decretal letters after the letters of Miltiades, he placed the canons of councils after them. Their sequence begins with the canons of the Council of Nicaea and ends with the Second Synod of Seville; he then again added the decretals of the Roman pontiffs down to Gregory the Great, and finally appended extracts drawn from the third part of the Tripartite Collection.

> “Thus far I have endeavoured to glean, as I believed might benefit my slowness, from the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs, beginning only with the apostolic office of Peter, prince of the apostles, and continuing to the episcopate of blessed Sylvester. Henceforth I shall endeavour to transfer all my effort to the synodal canons of the holy Fathers, so that from these also I may be able to satisfy the desire of my littleness. Yet after making a selection from the various councils, I shall endeavour to return to the decrees of the subsequent Roman pontiffs, that is, from the times of Saint Sylvester to blessed Gregory. But first let us consider what a canon is, what a synod is, what a council is, and what an assembly is.
>
> “Other decrees of the Roman pontiffs. Since, beginning with the episcopate of Peter, prince of the apostles, we have judged it fitting to set forth briefly and summarily whatever seemed suitable to this little work, not only from the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs but also from the holy canons of councils—namely Greek, Gallican, and Spanish councils—we ought now, beginning with Pope Sylvester’s time, to survey with a discerning eye the remaining pontiffs down to Gregory of blessed memory, in case something suitable to our selection may also be found in their statements. For most of them seem not to issue general decrees, but rather to write familiarly to private persons; whereas in the present compendium I wish to insert nothing except what is general. Therefore their writings should generally be passed over; yet if anything general can be found in them, it should suitably be adapted to our little work.”
>
> Similar extracts were later also prepared from collections of decretals. On this point see my dissertation, *Recherches sur plusieurs collections inédites de décrétales du moyen âge*, Paris, 1832, p. 26. [Cols. LXXIXD–LXXXD]

> “Thereafter, more fully from the little works of the holy Fathers.” [Col. LXXXD]

At this point in the work he inserted certain new documents, though none is later than those contained in the Tripartite Collection. Among them are some letters of Fulbert of Chartres—

> To Leutherius, letter 25, p. 36; to Theodoric, letter 61, p. 62; to King R., letter 85, p. 81; and to the monks of Saint-Médard, p. 70; ed. C. de Villiers, Paris, 1608. [Col. LXXXD]

—which seem to indicate that it was compiled in France. [Col. LXXXC] The manuscript was written in the middle of the twelfth century.

The Berlin manuscript, catalogued as MS Lat. quarto 106, contains a certain epitome, wholly excerpted from Ivo’s *Panormia* and entitled the *Summa decretorum* of Ivo. The author borrowed both the order of the books and that of the chapters from the same collection [Col. LXXXIA].

III, p. 671—have asserted to contain Ivo’s epitome, contains nothing other than a certain unpublished treatise on ecclesiastical matters written by Ivo. The Berlin manuscript contains certain portions of Ivo’s unpublished treatise.]

From history we know that Hugh [Note: Col. LXXXIC. Vincent of Beauvais says something concerning Ivo’s work, yet does not indicate which of his works he is speaking about. It is nevertheless clear that he speaks of none other than the *Panormia*: “This book of Ivo’s Decrees is found among us in a great many places; because it is itself also of no small bulk, it is not easily portable.” Hugh of Châlons is said to have composed from the same abbreviated volume a portable little book, which likewise exists among us and is called the *Summa decretorum* of Ivo. *Speculum historiale*, book XXVI, chapter 84. There is scarcely a library in France in which one or two copies of the *Panormia* are not found, whereas, by contrast, you will find no more than four manuscripts of the *Decree*.] and Haimo [Note: Col. LXXXID. “Haimo, archdeacon, a noble and devout man of the Basoches, was elected bishop of Châlons; he made an *enchiridion* in the Decrees according to Ivo’s *Panormia*.” ALBERIC OF THREE FOUNTAINS, under the year 1153, in Leibniz, *Accessions to History*, vol. II, p. 320. The statements found in Werner of Rollewink seem to have been drawn from this testimony: “Ivo, bishop of Chartres, abridged and compiled the apostolic Decree after Isidore; after him came Hugh of Châlons, and after him Gratian.” *Fasciculus temporum*, under the year [Col. LXXXIIB] 1104; J. Pistorius, *Writers of German Affairs*, vol. II, p. 545, Regensburg, 1726, folio.]—both men of Châlons—excerpted Ivo’s work. But since, as we shall demonstrate in the following paragraph, the present collection cannot be attributed to Haimo, we judge that it should be ascribed to Hugh.

Hugh himself, whom we know from Ivo’s letter to Urban II to have been Ivo’s friend [Note: Col. LXXXIIB. Letter 95, p. 45 of the *Works*, vol. II, Paris, 1647, folio.], was bishop at Châlons during the period between 1100 and 1113. At this very time, namely shortly after Ivo had completed the *Panormia*, he compiled his collection. The manuscript likewise was written in the twelfth century and comprises no more than fourteen folios; for this reason it could rightly be called a portable little book.

§ V. No less worthy of notice is the little work contained in Paris manuscript no. 4377, which includes an epitome of that collection divided into ten books and drawn from Ivo’s *Panormia*, of which we spoke above [Col. LXXXIB]. At the beginning the little book gives a series of those popes who, more than others, issued laws; then a catalogue of Roman Pontiffs from St Clement [Col. LXXXIIA] to Adrian IV (d. 1161). Further, this type of catalogue names Chrysogonus between Caius and Marcellus, following the example of the *Collection in Three Parts*.

After these two prefaces, which provide such a catalogue of pontiffs, follow passages in which it states the purpose and arrangement of the work. Certain excerpts from Ivo’s prologue are added, namely from the first chapter through the sixth; to these it gives the headings: “How the canons agree with one another,” and “On mutable and immutable precepts.” At the end follows:

> We have copied these brief remarks on the interpretation of the canons. If they do not suffice for the reader, let him consult the more extensive little work which the venerable bishop of Chartres wrote on these same rules of the canons; there he will find treated at greater length what we have briefly set forth here.

Finally, the proper prologue of the little work is added; it bears the author’s name in its heading, and we transcribe it in the note.

[Note: Col. LXXXIIB. “Haimo, by God’s grace, what he is.” Prologue to the book called the *Summa decretorum*.

The commands or prohibitions of the canons, handed down to us by apostolic men, Roman pontiffs, and the other orthodox Fathers, are shown by evident reason, and confirmed by the weightiest authority of the Fathers, to be both salutary and necessary for the Church of God. For by them we are ruled and governed as by a special form of government; by the canons themselves, I mean, we are restrained, as by stricter rules, from everything unlawful and dishonourable; through them we are taught to devote attention to ecclesiastical discipline [Col. LXXXIIC] and diligence to divine matters. In accordance with them almost all administrations of churches are conducted; and, to use the words of Pope Leo IV, they are those through whom bishops judge—indeed, through whom bishops and clerics alike are judged.

Therefore, because of their manifold efficacy, or usefulness; because of the instruction in faith and sacraments which they fully contain; and likewise because of certain admonitions and precepts necessary for the public library of the Church, they deserved to be placed there, reckoned among authoritative pronouncements, and entitled by this special name, “decrees of pontiffs.” From that time they began to have force as ecclesiastical laws, to be read by elders, and to be held in honour and reverence.

But the volumes of these books have increased to such a boundless extent that they could scarcely be acquired because of their expense, written because of the labour, or read because of weariness. For, as Roman pontiffs succeeded one another, so many and such extensive materials were added, partly from their general councils [Col. LXXXIID] and partly from their letters or those of other eminent men, that they exceeded all human memory. To omit other councils—namely those of Constantinople, Ephesus, Chalcedon, Antioch, Laodicea, Sardica, Carthage, and many others—we find that at the Council of Nicaea alone, held under 318 bishops, seventy chapters were promulgated after the pattern of the seventy disciples. How many, then, do you suppose were issued by innumerable other councils, when so many were inserted into this one alone?

Accordingly, because of this vast multitude of books, which could scarcely be read or retained in memory, the teachers of the Church, by prudent understanding, sound counsel, and provident caution, resolved to make a lucid abridgement of them all. The venerable bishop of Chartres, Ivo of glorious memory, with painstaking care arranged certain chapters from the aforesaid rules of the canons and commendably reduced them to a compendium of no fewer than ten books. But since that book is immense [Col. LXXXIIIB] and has not yet been abbreviated so that it may rightly be called an *enchiridion*, I have attempted to make a summary of it and reduce its volume to a handbook.

Yet, lest anyone charge me with arrogance, I offer this in my defence: I make this little work only for myself, not for publication or public circulation, but that it may remain hidden with me alone. Since I am occupied with ecclesiastical cases, because disputes and lawsuits fall within my responsibility, I may have at hand—or in my hands—whether indoors or outdoors, at home or on a journey, wherever ecclesiastical business may arise, the means by which such matters can be examined or judged. But enough of this. Let us now pursue our purpose.]

He excerpted in order the ten books of that collection and prefixed to them the same summaries [Col. LXXXIIB]. There can be no doubt whatever that Haimo, bishop of Châlons, was the author of this little work. Yet, since he occupied that see scarcely a full year and died in 1153, it is quite possible that he composed it when he was only archdeacon; this may also be inferred from the words which we noted at the end of the preface. In any event, the manuscript was written within the twelfth century itself.

It may certainly seem surprising that Haimo attributes to Ivo the collection in ten books which he reduced to an epitome. Yet he could very easily have fallen into this error because he found Ivo’s prologue prefixed to it. Alberic, who seems to have had this work of Haimo in his hands, similarly erred; hence, as we saw above, what he relates concerning Haimo’s work must be understood only of this little work itself. The more learned Benedictine brethren, however, did indeed assign the same work to Haimo, but made no mention of this issue.

[Note: Col. LXXXIIIB. *Literary History of France*, vol. XII, p. 427.

“Another, more important writing of Haimo, which has not yet appeared, is his Abridgement [Col. LXXXIIIC] of the *Panormia* of Yves of Chartres. We shall not repeat here what has been said elsewhere (*Literary History*, vol. X, pp. 120–121): the *Panormia* itself is not his work, as M. Doujat thought. The abridgement of which we speak belongs incontestably to him, on the authority of all the manuscripts, supported by that of Alberic of Trois-Fontaines. In a manuscript of the King’s Library it is entitled: *The Sum of Haimo’s Decrees*.

“The author begins with a list of the popes who left decrees on ecclesiastical matters, beginning with St Peter. He then lays down rules for understanding these decrees. First, he requires attention to be paid to the purpose of ecclesiastical laws; then he explains how they are reconciled with one another; after that, he treats of mutable and immutable precepts. All this serves only as preliminary matter to the *Summa*. It opens with a prologue in which the author says that ecclesiastical laws having grown to a number [Col. LXXXIIID] almost infinite, the books containing them form a library which few persons can afford to acquire; that even those who possess them cannot retain all that they contain; that for this twofold reason several learned persons undertook to furnish abridgements of them; that among these abbreviators Yves of Chartres is one of the most distinguished; but that the *Summa decretorum*, being contained in ten books, still cannot be regarded as a manual. This moved him to reduce the work of that able man to the form of a portable book.

“He then asks the reader not to attribute his work to any feeling of arrogance, because he made it only for his private use and not at all with the intention of giving it to the public. . . . From this it is apparent that Haimo was performing the duties of archdeacon when he composed this writing. See vol. XIII, p. 127; *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 882, cited edition.”]

But if anyone should think that the words of the prologue, “he reduced [them] to a commendable compendium of no fewer than ten books,” must be understood [Col. LXXXIIIB] as meaning that Haimo compressed that collection [Col. LXXXIVA] into at least ten books and not into more, rather than that he completed his own work within the narrow bounds of a compendium of ten books—the obvious meaning of those words, as anyone may easily see—these same words would repeatedly demonstrate and prove how uncertain, even from those times onward, were the reports circulating about Ivo’s genuine work.

§ VI. But let us finally come to the epitome of the *Decree* itself, which, as we have seen, is falsely attributed to Ivo. Nothing remains to be said about the character of this work, since it was composed by exactly the same method as the others discussed so far. Ivo’s prologue, together with a catalogue of the individual parts into which the *Decree* itself is divided, is prefixed to the work [Note: Col. LXXXIVB. “Preface of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, to collections of ecclesiastical rules.”]; the parts themselves, in the order in which they were originally joined together, have been reduced to a compendium, while each retains its own title. The final part, however, is wholly lacking.

[Col. LXXXIVB] I was able to examine two manuscripts of this little work: the first is preserved at Vienna (University MS no. 789, folio), the other in London (British Museum, Harleian Library, no. 3090, pressmark LXIII B) [Col. LXXXVA]. Moreover, I learned from the distinguished Biener, formerly my colleague at Berlin, that another manuscript of the same collection exists at Leipzig, specifically in the municipal library. The manuscripts which I examined, however, agree completely with one another; at the end they give a catalogue of Roman pontiffs extending to Callixtus II, the years of whose pontificate are precisely specified.

We rightly infer from this that this epitome was composed about that time, and therefore not later than 1126. Both manuscripts seem to have been written about the middle of the twelfth century. No traces occur concerning the author of the collection or others who used this work.

§ VII. At approximately the same time, three other collections seem to have been made; they were, however, excerpted from other collections and present their epitomes. In Savigny’s most select library at Berlin there is a unique manuscript [Col. LXXXVB]. It contains a collection in which Anselm of Lucca’s celebrated compilation—used by Gratian more than any other—has been abridged into an epitome in the same fashion as the *Decree* attributed to Ivo in the collection just mentioned.

This compilation is divided into thirteen books after the model of Anselm’s thirteen books, from whose order it departs very rarely. Thus books II, III, IV, V, VI, VII, VIII, IX, X, and XII correspond exactly to Anselm’s books III, IV, V, VI, VII, VIII, IX, X, XI, and XIII [Col. LXXXVIA], and their chapters are excerpted only from those books. Books I, II, XI, and XIII, however, are drawn not from Anselm’s collection but from Burchard’s *Decree*, which the author carefully followed in everything that he did not take from Anselm.

[Note: Col. LXXXVIC. It will suffice to append here a synoptic table of one book, so that the relationship of the two collections may be evident. The noted chapters are taken from Anselm: Book VIII (chapters 1–26); Anselm, Book IX (chapters 1–52): chapters 1–4, 6, 7, 11, 12, 13, 20, 21, 24–27, 30, 32, 33, 35, 37, 38, 40, 41, 52.]

Nevertheless, it also contains other documents which it did not draw from Burchard, Anselm, or any other known compilation. Both the time when this epitome was made and its author are wholly unknown. But since it contains no documents later than the time of Urban II (d. 1098), we may reasonably maintain that it was compiled shortly after Anselm’s work. Those documents which, as we have said, the author added anew for the most part passed into Gregory’s collection called the *Polycarpus*, and Gregory undoubtedly used our collection in compiling his own. For, since he drew chiefly from Anselm, it seems very likely that he also consulted the works of those who made new collections from Anselm [Col. LXXXVIB] and added new documents. Gregory completed his work after 1125; it would follow that the Savignian collection was made in the period between 1098 and 1125.

Gratian too seems not to have disregarded this epitome, since he received into his *Decree* very many materials, including those not at all found in Gregory.

We say nothing here of another collection, excerpted from the work of Anselm of Lucca, which is preserved in the Vienna library (Canon-law MS 39, folio). The work, divided neither into books nor titles, comprises a vast mass of chapters, all excerpted from Anselm’s collection, and often in the same sequence. It contains very many documents, and ones of the greatest importance, which have hitherto been unpublished.]

I shall offer more concerning this collection when time allows me to write a treatise on Anselm’s collection and its connection with Gratian’s *Decree* [Col. LXXXVIIA]. There I shall discuss more fully both this collection itself and the relationship it bears to the collections of Anselm, Bonizo, and Gregory.

The author of a certain compilation preserved in the Royal Library at Paris under no. 4283, and made in the thirteenth century, took a more convenient course. For it is entirely drawn from Burchard of Worms’s *Decree* [Note: Col. LXXXVIIC. The books are arranged in the same order as Burchard’s. It is therefore enough to note those chapters which the epitomizer retained from Burchard’s *Decree*.

The author of the collection found in a manuscript of the library of Sainte-Geneviève at Paris, compiled from the decrees of Burchard and Pseudo-Ivo, imitated his predecessors far less closely. It is wholly divided into four parts, each of which is distributed into several books.

[Note: Col. LXXXVIIIB. Part I: Book II, “On the sacrament of baptism,” chapters 1–105. Book III, “On the sacrament of the altar,” chapters 1–153. Book IV, “On churches,” chapters 1–96.

The manuscript, numbered 2, seems to have been written near the end of the twelfth century. Baluze examined it closely, since from Part IV, Book I, chapter 101, he published Adrian’s decree addressed to the bishop of Châlons. Baluze attributed this decretal to Adrian II (867–881), from which it would follow that it was issued to Bereo (878–885).

[Note: Col. LXXXVIIID. *Miscellanies*, vol. V, p. 488. Cf. *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, col. 869, cited edition.]

Nevertheless, if we inspect the style of that decretal somewhat more closely, we shall say that it should rather be attributed to Adrian IV (1154–1157), and that it was addressed to Bishop Boso (1151–1161).

[Note: Col. LXXXVIIID. *Gallia Christiana*, cited place, col. 882.]

Accordingly, the collection itself should be judged to have been made about the same time. Besides, it must also be observed that this letter seems to have been written and added to the manuscript by a hand of a later age.

As the printers press us, we publish the *Decree* first, intending, God willing, to publish the *Panormia* below. Editors.]

[Col. 0009]

## Dedicatory Letter to the Most Illustrious and Most Reverend Lord James Lescot, Bishop of Chartres
Of the flamens, priests, druids, and whatever other names the ancients gave to the governors of sacred rites, it was the custom—if it lay within their power, most illustrious Bishop—everywhere among lands and nations, to reconcile the rights of God and of men, and to move between both in so tempered a fellowship that at one moment, like the heavenly gods, they inspire terror, thunder, and stand eminent; at another, enrolled among those upon earth (*epichthoniois*), they pray, groan, and prostrate themselves as suppliants at the altars. For he who performs the office of priest in some measure puts on both God and man, made a mediator (*mesitēs*) between the two, so that there is nothing so great that he does not dare, nothing so low that he avoids.

Therefore, those raised to this office had to be most skilled in divine and human affairs, so that, discerning the tendencies of things above and below, and attending to the purposes of the former and the advantages of the latter, they might adapt themselves to both by ready obedience and conform themselves by an easy flexibility in either direction. Indeed, among the ancients—especially the Egyptians, among whom “the class of priests was permitted leisure” (*epheitē scholazein to tōn hiereōn ethnos*) [Note: [Col. 0009] Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, I]—priests acquired and made sciences illustrious. But now those divinely appointed to priesthoods ought to be leaders in learning before they are leaders in sacred things. There, as the Philosopher testifies [Note: [Col. 0009] *Metaphysics*, I], priests were the parents of sciences; here, learning is a kind of preliminary approach (*proodia*) and almost a definite summons (*proklēsis*) to priesthood.

As for the French, most illustrious Bishop, their love, by which they honour the citizens and senators of the republic of letters and set them over sacred affairs, is no recent one. Long ago among them “there were certain philosophers and theologians honoured beyond measure” (*philosophoi te tines eisi kai theologoi perittōs timōmenoi*) [Note: [Col. 0009] Diodorus, book V]. And—what I cannot help wondering at—there was once among them a custom “to perform no sacrifice without a philosopher” (*ethos autois mēdena thysian poiein aneu philosophou*); I add, “nor without a theologian,” for what follows supports this: “For they say that thank-offerings must be offered to the gods through those experienced in the divine nature, as through certain persons who speak with them in one voice, and through these they think that good things must be requested” (*dia gar tōn empeirōn tēs theias physeōs, hōsperei tinōn homophonōn, ta charistēria tois theois phasi dein prospherein, kai dia toutōn oiontai dein ta agatha aiteisthai*).

Thus the priests of the Gauls, and indeed of Chartres, were teachers of wisdom, says an ancient author [Note: [Col. 0009] Pomponius Mela, book III, chapter I]; and because they devote themselves to contemplating the heavens, they profess to know what the gods desire. Hence we need not wonder if they worship her whom the stars promise will come; or if, while they pursue the stars with anxious gaze, they find the Virgin—not merely the ear of grain, as the common herd of astrologers does, but Bread itself being brought forth for the world. So great a thing it is for priests to cultivate wisdom and fix their attention upon heaven.

These men were called Druids [Note: [Col. 0009] Pliny, book XVI, chapter 44], undoubtedly from the oak (*apo tēs dryos*), because they held nothing more sacred than its mistletoe, and performed no rites without its foliage. And because it aids women’s conception and childbirth [Note: [Col. 0009] Pliny, book XXIV, chapter 4; Matthiolus on Dioscorides], you might say that by it they sought to hasten the birth of her whom they worshipped as about to give birth. And why, further, are they called *Semnotheoi*, “revered gods,” by Laërtius [Note: [Col. 0009] In the Prologue], unless because among them also there was a *Semnē thea*, a “revered goddess”? For *semna* are “the mysteries of the Virgin” (*ta tēs parthenou mystēria*) [Note: [Col. 0009] Hesychius]; and *semnē*, in its native meaning, denotes what is modest and chaste [Note: [Col. 0010] Ancient Glossary; Hesychius].

Or rather, while they worship the Virgin who was to give birth, they are said to celebrate and venerate what human reason cannot penetrate: *ta semna*, that is, “the unspeakable and inexplicable mysteries” (*ta arrhēta kai anexēgēta mystēria*) [Note: [Col. 0010] *Etymologicum Magnum*]; or, as another has it, things “wonderful and unsearchable.” And of them it is indeed written [Note: [Col. 0010] Pomponius Mela, book III, chapter 1, ancient recension] that they taught many things secretly, in caves or hidden groves. This divinity made them *siōpēlon*, “silent,” which is the same as *semnon*, “revered” [Note: [Col. 0010] Greek scholiast on Aristophanes, *Clouds*], and consequently made them also *semnotheoi*. Therefore the priests of the Gauls were theologians.

Nor did the practices of the ancient Church depart from this. For as formerly the same men were judges of peoples who were kings, so in the earliest years of the Church the same men were bishops (*episkopoi*) and teachers (*didaskaloi*); nor does the Golden Mouth of Antioch call his patriarch more often, or by a more emphatic designation, than “teacher” (*didaskalos*) [Note: [Col. 0010] Chrysostom, *Homilies to the People of Antioch*]. Why is it that among the few who hold first place in their own kind, bishops too are sceptre-bearers (*skēptouchoi*)? Surely because, according to the ancients, “the sceptre was a sign of kingship, discourse, and justice” (*sēmeion basileias kai logōn kai dikēs kata tous palaious to skēptron ēn*) [Note: [Col. 0010] Eustathius]. Although all three may in some manner belong to a bishop, the middle one especially and properly belongs to him, whence he has the right to carry a staff.

[Col. 0011] And if we read again the beginnings of things, the consecration of bishops in the Church succeeded that initiation by which, among the Hebrews, men were promoted to the office of teacher. This was performed by certain stages, and was finally completed by the laying on of hands (*cheirothesia*) and prescribed words; nothing was afterwards held by them to be more exalted. We therefore have reason to congratulate France, which, wholly inspired by a divine genius, has caused the heads of her academies to be bishops of churches. Ancient times return; we emulate the practices of the ancients; and we leave to posterity a great example, either to imitate or to admire.

Thales urged Pythagoras, who was studying under him, “to sail over to Egypt and confer with the priests at Memphis, especially those of Zeus” (*proetrepsato eis Aigypton diapleusai, kai tois en Memphei, kai Dios malista symbalein hiereusi*) [Note: [Col. 0011] Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras*, book I, chapter 2]: this is the most ancient glory of priests. More fortunate is France, which does not send abroad those whom she wishes to be instructed in sacred matters, but possesses hierarchs so full of learning that their houses may be schools (*didaskaleia*).

But the city of Chartres surpasses all others in this praise and goes beyond Memphis itself, whether we consider ancient or later times. There was once the seat of sacred theologians (*hierotheologoi*); there bishops flourished, outstanding by far in piety and learning. Fulbert, Geoffrey, John of Salisbury, and others bear witness to this, men whose published works, offices they held, or most celebrated authors establish their authority. You yourself, most wise Bishop, are a witness: the latest of all, yet their equal—reverencing all as your elders, yet not inferior to them; worthy of the episcopate long before you became bishop. You possess every ornament of letters, and are yourself their ornament; a foster-child and father of sacred and venerable theology.

Many Churches desired you, but that Church prevailed which ought to have prevailed; and since several cannot possess one and the same man, they desire what they can: one like him. Happy are the academies which furnish rulers to Churches! Happy are the Churches which receive Fathers from academies! Is it burdensome to you that I should rank and compare myself with such great bishops of Chartres? I shall comply with your modesty; I come to another witness—yet I fear that I may still seem to speak of you.

The witness is Ivo, whom we here present, a witness beyond every exception: no doctrine could be more solid than his, no piety more sincere, no spirit greater or stronger. Perhaps someone will ask what he knew. Everything that a bishop ought to know. He was so versed in the Fathers, councils, canons, and customs that he fought with these alone and almost exclusively spoke and wrote of them. Someone will ask what kind of virtue he possessed. Virtue altogether ancient and canonical, which he cultivated with the greatest candour and most effectively commended to its devotees. Someone will ask what strength of character he possessed: strength that overcame crimes, even royal crimes; that compelled men, even princes, to better conduct; that gave courage to the weak and fearful, even to bishops.

To whom ought this man, at last made to live again by those who are at once his own and yours, to have been dedicated, if not to him who causes his authority and conduct to revive in himself? You will not, I think, despise this gift, because it contains what makes you surpass others—consummate learning; what you love most—the observance of canons; what you seriously embrace—the care and solicitude of Churches; and what you commend to all, in part by word and in part by deed—piety and the practice of the fullest virtue.

We acknowledge you as set between God and men, speaking with them in one voice (*homophonon*), and therefore through you offer our thank-offerings (*charistēria*) to God: namely, Ivo’s toils, vigils, and labours, long since given to God and now justly demanded back by Him from us. You have that which invites and draws us to desire this service from you. It was customary for ancient priests to claim for themselves the insignia of their gods—bows, fillets, sceptres, spears, rays, and whatever else might win them the veneration of the people. Made priest of the great God born from a Virgin, what emblem will you receive from Him? There are no thunderbolts there, no spears, no darts for you to assume. There is only milk, suckled by the Son and supplied by the Mother.

Ivo confirmed in us one part of that symbol: namely, whiteness. You too confirmed it, even as abbot of regular canons; for the restoration of canonical observance to the monastery of All Saints at Châlons owes everything to you and your exertions, so that not even in this respect can we call you unlike Ivo. Bishops have reserved for themselves the sweetness of milk. Relying on this alone, most illustrious Bishop, I have dared to approach your threshold and, in the name of the regular canons who are under your jurisdiction, to dedicate this work to your name.

Of your most illustrious lordship,  
the most humble and devoted,  
F. J. FRONTO,  
Regular Canon of St Geneviève, Paris.

[Col. 0011]

# Life of St Ivo

[Col. 0011A] Among those called Ivo in France, Ivo of Chartres far surpassed all. Born in the district of Beauvais, he drew a noble spirit from noble blood [Note: [Col. 0011A] In an ancient document of St Quentin of Beauvais]. His father was Hugh of Auteuil, and his mother was named Hilemburgis. Having been instructed in liberal letters as a young man and having pursued philosophy [Col. 0012A], he devoted himself to sacred theology at the monastery of Bec under Lanfranc, abbot and teacher of Bec; when he became older, he taught it there himself [Note: [Col. 0011A] Master Peter the Chanter, in his manuscript *Summa* [Col. 0012A] in the monastery of St John of the Garden, Regular Canons].

As he applied himself seriously to reading the Fathers and councils, and gathered ecclesiastical decrees from diverse sources, he was distressed that canons should fall so far short of their own canon [Col. 0013A]. At the opportune moment Guy of Beauvais appeared. Formerly dean of the church of St Quentin at Vermand, he became bishop of Caesaromagus, or Beauvais, and built a monastery in memory of St Quentin, endowing it with estates and establishing canons there in 1078. Set over them, Ivo enlarged the monastery with his paternal possessions; and, that he might assist it with every resource, he drew up laws for that purpose and introduced the regular life—being most expert in the canons and most ardent in zeal for their observance.

Regular canons had indeed long existed here and there in France and in other provinces. Long before, Chrodegang [Note: [Col. 0013D] He was nephew by a sister of King Pepin. SIGEBERT] had composed a special rule for his canons of Metz. At the Council of Aachen, Louis the Pious caused a rule to be published for all through the agency of the deacon Amalarius [Col. 0013B], and sent it to be observed in every province [Note: [Col. 0013D] These things are written by Ademar the monk]. This rule contains, for the most part, the Rule of Chrodegang. But when discipline had relaxed with the passage of time, many laboured to restore it, and among them Ivo’s efforts excelled those of all others.

He presided over the aforesaid monastery for about fourteen years: at one time as its superior, as in the privilege of King Philip; at another as provost, as in the bull of Gregory VII; and at another as abbot, as he is more often called. Here, without doubt, while enjoying holy leisure, he compiled the Collection of Canons which Hugh of Châlons later abridged [Note: [Col. 0013D] I found the name of the author of this abridgment in the History of the monastery of Hérivaux under the year 1091] and called the *Panormia* or *Pannormia*. He also taught theology, for it was then customary for the study of sacred theology to flourish chiefly in monasteries [Col. 0013C]; nor did the abbots of monasteries themselves evade that burden, as we have previously seen in Lanfranc and here in our Ivo. This office which Ivo discharged accounts for his being called master and doctor in the most ancient records.

So great was the reputation of that monastery and of Ivo himself for piety and canonical observance [Note: [Col. 0013D] See St Anselm, book III, letter 106] that many monasteries were either founded or restored by canons summoned from there, and some of these attained distinguished episcopates.

Meanwhile Geoffrey held the see of Aictrici, or Chartres [Note: [Col. 0013D] Joseph Scaliger writes “Aictrici” twice. Others, however, write “Auctricum”]. Gregory VII had long before summoned him to Rome on a charge of simony; but because witnesses were lacking to establish so serious a matter, he was sent back and allowed to retain his see. Urban II, however, when he was again accused before him and finally convicted of many crimes, removed him from his see; and among the clergy and people of Chartres, by his admonitions, as Ivo himself states, brought it about that they chose our Ivo, distinguished for learning and piety.

Ivo did not immediately yield to their wishes, loving peace and not coveting dignities; but at the command of King Philip he was compelled to obey [Note: [Col. 0014D] See letters 1, 2, 8, and 40]. Yet Richer, archbishop of Sens, supported by several of his suffragans, refused either to subscribe to the election or to lay hands upon the elect [Col. 0014A], claiming that Geoffrey’s deposition had been effected contrary to his right, since it belonged to him, as the nearest judge, to hear and judge the case [Note: [Col. 0014D] See Sirmond on the letter of Geoffrey of Vendôme].

The clergy and people of Chartres long pressed and petitioned him, but, finding themselves unsuccessful, they arranged for Ivo to meet Urban. Having departed for Italy with the intention of freeing himself from these difficulties, he received the laying on of hands (*cheirothesia*) from Urban at Capua, willing or unwilling, at the end of 1092. From this arose serious conflicts between him and the aforementioned bishops. Claiming that an injury had been done to the majesty of the king and that Ivo had violated the rights of France, they assembled at Étampes and undertook to reject Ivo and restore Geoffrey to his see. Their zeal was doubtless directed against an innocent Ivo, though it was by no means novel, being supported by many examples both before and after that time [Note: [Col. 0014D] See Ralph Glaber, book II, chapter 4, and the abbot of Stade in his *Chronicle*; indeed Ivo himself throughout his letters].

Ivo, on the other hand, appealed to the Apostolic See and loudly complained that its authority had been spurned and violated—a man otherwise in no sense servile and no flatterer even of the highest powers. But when that which is supreme, and religion itself, are involved, all else must yield. Richer was therefore forbidden the use of the pallium, Geoffrey was again expelled, and Ivo was installed in his see.

What he accomplished there is told by his letters to supreme pontiffs, kings, cardinals, legates, primates, bishops, and leading men; it is told by all the histories written from his own time onward. While he upheld authority on the one hand and cultivated virtue on the other, he made himself conspicuous not merely to France but to the whole Church. And he had especial need of both, both to resist vices rampant everywhere [Col. 0014C] and to endure the evils which he himself brought upon his head by his ardent zeal and his refusal to tolerate public errors, if they were serious.

Philip, then king of France, captivated by love for Bertrada, took her from her husband Fulk, count of Anjou; or at least married her while she was secretly withdrawing herself from Fulk. Some bishops of France connived, others remained silent; so easy is it to comply with majesty wherever it inclines. Other bishops even resigned their sees because they did not wish to have as either friend or enemy a king acting contrary to divine law [Note: [Col. 0014D] See Paulus Aemilius on Philip I].

Ivo was ordered to go to Paris to attend the celebration of the marriage, but he refused to go. In speech and in letters written to the king himself, the supreme pontiff, and the bishops of France, he steadfastly denounced the unlawful marriage [Col. 0014D]. This brought upon him the most bitter hatred of Philip and Bertrada. Yet he also incurred the hatred of one by whom he would not have wished to be loved. Against Philip, however, he so moderated his fervour that, though he sharply restrained his lust, he nevertheless showed himself compliant with royal majesty in other matters and deeply devoted to the king’s interests, indeed to those of the whole kingdom.

For a long time he avoided the king’s presence and refused, even when summoned, to come to court, lest, if he were present and silent, he should seem to approve; but if he spoke in opposition, he should seem to offend the king. That great frankness (*parrhēsia*) was not without cost to him [Col. 0015A]. There were bishops too who accused him of rash obstinacy while themselves submitting to shameful compliance. The king’s ministers, bound to him through right and wrong alike, plundered Ivo’s property, intercepted the revenues of his Church, and afflicted him by every means and with every precedent, so that he had not even bread to eat.

But foremost among them in this matter was Hugh of Le Puiset, lord and viscount of Chartres. While he accommodated the king and ingratiated himself with adulterers, or even incestuous persons, he cast our Ivo into prison and held him long in a certain castle, intending to break his spirit—unless it should prove harder than stone. [Col. 0015B] Yet Ivo remained everywhere unconquered. When word reached him that the leading men and citizens of Chartres wished to free him by arms, he forbade it [Note: [Col. 0015D] Letter 20], refusing to obtain freedom purchased by the blood and loss of his own people. This patience was wholly worthy of praise and in no respect unlike that of the ancient defenders of the Church and most holy men.

Why should I not reckon him equal to them, when William, abbot of Fécamp, his contemporary (*homēlix*), compared him with John and Elijah? He would not have lacked all assistance if there had been another Ivo in France to act for him against Viscount Hugh as Ivo himself did somewhat later for Hildebert of Le Mans against Count Rotrou [Note: [Col. 0015D] Hildebert, letter 39], who had likewise imprisoned Hildebert. After prayers had been used in vain, Ivo pronounced an anathema and devoted Rotrou to curses.

While doing this, the great man could not escape slander (*diabolē*), the enemy of great souls (*megalōn psychōn*) and their perpetual persecutor. Perhaps there will be someone, above all, who thinks that Ivo indulged anger and suspicion too much, because he provoked the indignation and thunderbolt of the supreme pontiff against the king. Yet although those who attempt to lessen or wipe away the stains rashly placed upon the name of kings may seem to me to deserve well of kings, no one would dare to declare Philip entirely innocent; nor can anyone have sufficient grounds for showing that Ivo was insufficiently favourable to Philip or his kingdom.

As regards Philip, his action had precedents and was followed by many examples, though not wholly similar examples, and ones which conceal his sin more than excuse it [Col. 0015D]. For even if it be granted that his divorce from Bertha was not subject to blame—which ought nevertheless to have been established to the satisfaction of Ivo and others, so that they would not call it into question—the marriage contracted with Bertrada certainly cannot in any way be excused. She had not withdrawn from Fulk by any judgment of the Church; and she should have been kept from Philip by the same bond of consanguinity which might have been alleged in relation to Fulk.

[Col. 0016A] And, to pass over contemporary (*synchronoi*) authors—great men and eyewitnesses of events—who praise and extol Ivo in remarkable fashion [Note: [Col. 0015D] Hildebert, Abbot Geoffrey, Anselm, Lisiard, Geoffrey Malaterra, Geoffrey Grossus, Suger. The author of the ecclesiastical history in the monastery of Hérivaux calls Ivo a saint], and to note that no one spoke against him in this matter, though he had enemies and accusers: Philip and Bertrada themselves, when they received absolution from excommunication from Lambert, bishop of Arras and acting vicar of the Roman pontiff, confessed themselves guilty and promised never thereafter to meet one another in the presence of bishops. I myself read this in a manuscript letter [Note: [Col. 0015D] It is in the hands of Father Sirmond] of that Lambert to Paschal II, supreme pontiff.

There were princes and bishops who flattered the king—of course, of that kind of men whose custom is to praise every act of rulers, honourable and dishonourable alike. For if there was any reasoning in them [Col. 0016B], why did they not protest while these things and so many others were done in attestation of an unlawful marriage? Why did they not defend the king’s innocence by hand or voice? Everything invited them: the king, innocence under attack, precedents, Ivo’s excessive fervour, his freedom in accusing. Yet they were silent and said nothing against Ivo. Did so many bishops, cardinals, legates, and princes, assembled so often, see nothing, when with one voice they condemned the king’s sin but never excused, lessened, or concealed it?

Moreover, when Ivo states [Note: [Col. 0016D] Letter 144] that Philip promised Richard, bishop of Albano and legate of the supreme pontiff, that he would separate from Bertrada until the Roman pontiff should grant a dispensation—and this separation occurred in the year of the Lord 1102—and when Ivo himself asks the supreme pontiff to deal leniently with the king and grant a dispensation; and since it is otherwise certain from Lambert’s cited letter that no dispensation was granted [Col. 0016C], this is evidence that those nuptials were investigated again and that no ground whatsoever for a dispensation was found.

I add that Ivo had no reason to wish King Philip ill, since he knew himself bound to him by many benefits, and he did not deny it. More than once he acknowledged that he owed his episcopal rank to Philip. If he had been subject to ordinary human feeling and possessed the disposition common to the multitude, because of this he ought especially to have complied with the king and his desires. Even before he reached the episcopate, he owed the king very much. When the monastery of St Quentin had been built and regular canons placed there, the king, by granting a privilege, confirmed with royal authority both their establishment and the gifts made to it [Col. 0016D]. Later, at Ivo’s request, he sent a letter to the canons of St Quentin at Vermand asking that they grant a prebend to their namesake church at Beauvais.

Since both royal documents are unpublished, I thought they should be inserted here, lest they be wanted. The first has the following words [Note: [Col. 0016D] From an ancient manuscript codex of St Quentin of Beauvais. Ivo mentions these letters, which he calls a Pragmatic Sanction, in letter 193 to Geoffrey, bishop of Beauvais. They are found composed in this form in a very ancient parchment]:

“It is the office of royal eminence not to violate, but to preserve inviolate, and to command to be preserved by those present and future—without any part of the law objecting—royal enactments and public or private ecclesiastical or secular affairs confirmed without any legal controversy by the command and authority of former kings [Col. 0017A]. Therefore we wish it to be known to all orthodox sons of the Church,” etc. See above, under Philip I, at the year 1106.

The second reads as follows [Note: [Col. 0017D] Rescript of King Philip to the chapter of the church of St Quentin at Vermand, concerning the prebend which the Quentinian canons of Beauvais possess in that church by the grant of Philip himself. Given, it is believed, in 1089]:

> Philip, by the grace of God king of the Franks, to O., dean, and the other canons of our Church of St Quentin: greeting and our favour.
>
> We make known to you that Ivo, abbot of the Church of Blessed Quentin at Beauvais, has approached the ears of our clemency, entreating us, both in person and through our faithful men, that we grant to the Church committed to him one prebend in your Church, to be held in perpetuity for the salvation of the soul of my father and of my mother. We have willingly granted this petition because we have heard from some of you that you had already approved it in your chapter [Col. 0017B]. Therefore we command you to make, through the aforesaid abbot, to the aforesaid Church the investiture that pertains to you, as has been determined among you. Farewell.

From these facts everyone can see that Ivo ought to have shown Philip more deference than any other, unless recalled from this by something higher than human judgment and royal dignity. He thereby made many enemies, who set about injuring his reputation both with the king and with the supreme pontiffs. When, attacked by calumnies before Urban—his “spiritual Father” (*pneumatikon autou Patera*)—he wished to counter them by no arguments other than resigning his episcopate; but the supreme pontiff forbade it. For the episcopate (*hē episkopē*) needed Ivo, not Ivo the episcopate (*Ivo tēs episkopēs*).

After Urban died [Col. 0017C] and affairs continually worsened [Note: [Col. 0017D] See the letters of Geoffrey of Vendôme, book II], Ivo resolved to go to Rome, intending to cast off every burden; but, learning that ambushes had been laid for him among the Alps, he turned back. Paschal, the supreme pontiff, knowing his intention, commanded him to remain at his post. Still, he could not avoid incurring Paschal’s displeasure as well: knowing perfectly the difference between deference and flattery, he rendered the former and dismissed the latter; and this does not always please.

When his own canons were accused of simony before Richard, bishop of Albano and legate of the Holy Roman Church, he repelled the charge in such a way as simultaneously to show that the ministers of the supreme pontiff should be charged with the same crime, since they exacted truly enormous sums from bishops, abbots, and others under the pretext of paying for documents and other petty matters of that kind [Col. 0017D] [Note: [Col. 0017D] Letter 133].

It must indeed be admitted that at that time, and shortly before it, the crime of simony had grown so entrenched among clerics, and the supreme pontiffs had laboured so much to uproot it, that whatever bore even its shadow came under suspicion. Yet no one casts a weapon who willingly suffers the same weapon to be cast against himself; and it has always seemed a weak form of defence to retort an accusation. Ivo did not do this, but frankly reported what the canons answered.

Almost everyone acknowledges that Ivo alone, or nearly alone, stood forth in that age against the torrent of overflowing vices [Col. 0018A]. He laboured to the utmost with Hugh of Lyons, legate of the Roman pontiff, to prevent John the archdeacon, a man of ill repute, from becoming bishop of Orléans [Note: [Col. 0017D] Letter 66]. He resisted the elevation of Stephen of Galar to the see of Beauvais [Note: [Col. 0018D] Letter 87]. And lest France be too narrow a field for his virtue, he complained to Paschal II and Count Robert of Meulan [Note: [Col. 0018D] Letters 154 and 157] that Ranulf, bishop of Durham, had seized the Church of Lisieux by a new kind of invasion, setting his sons—still boys—over it in Jewish fashion, one to succeed the other.

He wrote once and again to Henry, king of England [Note: [Col. 0018D] Letters 55, 60, 87, 109, and 110], both concerning many other matters and that the king might not bind his daughter in an incestuous marriage. With supreme pontiffs, though always modestly, he remonstrated concerning the avarice of so-called legates *a latere*, and the importunate appeals to the Apostolic See of persons bound by the judgments of their own pastors. Being most devoted to that See, he bore it ill that it should everywhere be disparaged [Note: [Col. 0018D] Letters 46, 250, 259]; hence he wished, so far as possible, to cut away the occasions of disparagement.

Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, then flourished, a man truly simple and good, and friendship bound him to Ivo. Yet Geoffrey writes to Paschal II [Note: [Col. 0018D] See the letters of Geoffrey of Vendôme, books I and II, letter 195] that he suffered much from the bishop of Chartres, namely our Ivo. From the letters of both men, it can be seen that a certain enmity had arisen between them over the exemption of the monastery of Vendôme from episcopal authority [Col. 0018C]. This has from ancient times been a most fertile root of conflicts of this kind, even among all persons distinguished for sanctity and learning. And just as no authority, even of the most devout men, had thus far been able to put an end to such conflicts, so this one did not appear to detract in any degree from the integrity and holiness of either disputing party [Note: [Col. 0018D] Letters 11, 25, 60].

But while Ivo attacks the vices of all men on every side, what wonder if he was a burden to some and hateful to others? Who could calmly hear that trumpet perpetually sounding? If certain men had risen to higher rank and authority (*hē exousia*) [Col. 0018D], who would not be angry, or fail to avenge a dignity so often wounded? Certainly, anyone attentive to the morals of men in that age will wonder, not that Ivo cried out, but that he alone cried out and that so many others could be silent when a mighty cry was necessary to rouse men from lethargy.

Yet do not imagine Ivo to have been an austere, iron-hearted man, provoking renown and destiny by obstinacy and an empty boasting of liberty [Note: [Col. 0019D] Letter 23]. Whoever reads his letters will recognize a moderate man. He often tempered the rigor of the canons or advised others to temper it. He often dissuaded pontiffs, their legates, and other bishops from pronouncing anathema. Finally, he tolerated far more than he reproved, so that we may say of him what was once said of a pontiff, though a pagan: “of no servile judgment willingly the author, and whenever necessity pressed, wisely moderate.”

When Urban II pronounced an anathema against Philip, Ivo wished it to remain concealed for a long time, from a certain goodwill and inclination toward the prince, lest disturbance arise in the kingdom. When the clergy of Beauvais asked whether they should arraign a certain accused canon before an ecclesiastical tribunal, as canonical law required [Col. 0019B], or before a civil or royal tribunal, as the king himself commanded, Ivo judged the former better and more lawful, but that the latter should nevertheless be done because of the evils that threatened, unless they had patience hardened and prepared for everything.

He wrote much the same to Turgis, the ingenuous bishop of Avranches, who was uncertain whether to obey the legate of the supreme pontiff or the king. He says that obedience should indeed be rendered to the legate; but if Turgis did not have sufficient courage and did not wish to have the king angry with him, he should send persons to the supreme pontiff to excuse an act performed against the pontiff’s will. Before Conon, bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Holy Apostolic See, Ivo prayed that the bishop of Bayeux should not be branded by ecclesiastical censure, since he was held under another’s jurisdiction, which he was necessarily bound to serve.

[Col. 0019C] But among the proofs of his moderation and goodwill toward his superiors, we must not omit what Orderic says of him. I shall give his words:

> “In the year 1103 Pope Paschal came into Gaul. . . . At that time the venerable Ivo, bishop of the city of Chartres, flourished among the foremost doctors of France through his learning in letters, both divine and secular. At Ivo’s invitation the pope celebrated the solemnity of Easter at Chartres.”

Moreover, while he diligently attended to these matters, while on the one hand he asserted ecclesiastical discipline and on the other, when circumstances required, proved its greatest moderator, he did not neglect what he owed to king and country. Although he was the most vigorous defender of the sacred rights of the Apostolic See, he never committed, or permitted to be committed, anything against the rights of the Gallican Church. In preserving and defending both, he was remarkably prudent and circumspect [Col. 0019D].

Louis VI perceived this as soon as he began to reign. A few days after Philip’s death, Ivo suspected that many men, from a desire for innovations, intended to delay the king’s sacred anointing [Note: [Col. 0019D] Letter 189]. He therefore insisted that it be performed as soon as possible at Orléans, despite the futile objections of the clergy of Reims; and in this matter he undoubtedly took thought for both king and kingdom.

What need is there to mention the care with which he acted to prevent King Louis from staining himself with a marriage of insufficient honour [Col. 0020A] [Note: [Col. 0019D] Suger, *Life of Louis VI*, chapter 13], such as Count Hugh of Troyes advised, and to ensure that he joined without delay the bride intended for him, so that hope of an heir might restrain the impending divisions of the realm [Note: [Col. 0019D] Letter 209]? Certainly the king valued him highly, so that Ivo was his counsellor before all others. He judged that a man struck with anathema, yet made a participant at the king’s table, ought to be received by the bishop, and he received him himself [Note: [Col. 0020D] Letter 239]; so much did he value being acceptable to the king.

When Paschal II commanded Ralph, designated for the see of Reims, not to bind himself to the king by any oath, Ivo wrote that the command had not been obeyed [Note: [Col. 0020D] Letter 190], because it was contrary both to the custom of the bishops of Gaul and to the king’s right; and because it proceeded from nothing other than that which is fleshly (*sarkikon*) in men and seeks the things of the flesh (*ta sarkos*), not the things of God.

Writing to the same supreme pontiff [Note: [Col. 0020D] Letter 6], he asks that he never rashly depart from friendship with the king of France, lest he give France—otherwise most religious and most devoted to the Roman pontiff—a cause for the dissension and schism by which Germany was then miserably torn. He therefore held that human affairs could not remain safe and secure unless kingdom and priesthood agreed with one another; and for this purpose it is necessary that each sometimes yield something of its own to the other.

But there is no matter in which Ivo’s talent and wisdom shone more brightly than in the question of what are called investitures. At that time it was debated with such heat between emperors, kings, and popes that neither now nor then could one say on which side the victory stood. In pronouncing upon these matters, Ivo—though he now pleased, now displeased Baronius—nevertheless argued in such a way that he allowed no stigma of heresy, error, schism, or cowardice to be branded upon either the Roman pontiff or kings and emperors. For this was not a matter of heresies and errors; and the other points, where there was no division, could, according to place, time, and other circumstances, be diminished, increased, removed, or added, and might subsequently receive varying acceptations and designations. Thus he judged that investitures made by princes were not therefore to be condemned; that those permitted by supreme pontiffs were by no means to be rejected; that, by the nature of the matter, if the good of peace so required, they should be received from the supreme pontiff alone; but that previously they had often been given and received not without kings. This, I say, he judged and vigorously affirmed—and, if one consults our own times, not to be regretted. He was unwilling for ecclesiastical liberty to be subjected to secular powers, nor, on the other hand, to raise itself so high as to despise or offend them. From this one might say that Ivo was different from the man whom I described above as rebuking and thundering. Yet he was the very same man: impartial toward all, had all been impartial toward him; certainly moderate, if at that time there had been any moderation in luxury, ambition, and avarice. He boldly deterred King Louis and his courtiers from plundering the Church’s goods, by threats or censures; yet he abstained from the censures when he judged the threats sufficient. Thus he tempered mildness with severity—unless perhaps when he so sternly restrained Louis himself, who was asking some paltry thing from him, because he demanded trifles from a bishop, that one might say he had put on a royal spirit because he was addressing a king.

Though occupied with these very great concerns, he did not neglect lesser matters. Above all, that he might always have his brethren with him and enjoy their fellowship, he granted to them the church of Saint Vincent, near the city of Chartres, built around A.D. 1038 by a certain priest named Realdo, where a body of canons lived; and he added the collegiate church of Saint Stephen. In A.D. 1099, with the consent of his canons, he built for them a cloister and church dedicated to Saint John the Forerunner, from which the monastery derived the name of Saint John of Valliac. [Note: [Col. 0021D] Sirmond, in his notes on Geoffrey of Vendôme’s second sermon, writes “Valiacensis.”] It survived until 1568, when it suffered the fate common to many others through the fury of the seditious and heretics. The religious canons therefore withdrew into the city and lived in the buildings of the aforesaid Saint Stephen—or rather, if one prefers, among their ruins: so broken were all things by age and squalor, and so near collapse. At last, in A.D. 1624, through the efforts of the most illustrious Lord d’Estampes, then bishop of Chartres, regular canons were summoned there. These had recently reformed themselves at Senlis to a better and holier life through the counsel and authority of the eminent Cardinal de La Rochefoucauld, bishop of that city; they rebuilt the same house from its foundations.

[Col. 0021C] Furthermore, with the consent of his chapter, he placed over the college the dean of the church of Saint Andrew in the same city, namely Lord Odo, a venerable man well educated in ecclesiastical and secular matters, to act in his place. Ancient documents call him “abbot”; since that title was formerly common to canons and monks, even after secular canons had been separated from regular canons, it is sometimes given to both classes. During his life he had as friends Robert of Arbrissel, founder of the order of nuns of Blessed Mary of Fontevraud, and Bernard of Saint Cyprian of Quinçay near Poitiers, likewise founder and abbot of certain monks. He is said to have built monasteries for them in his diocese: for Bernard’s monks, the monastery of Tiron; and for Robert’s women, that called Hautes-Bruyères. He built for lepers the house of Great Beaulieu. To the Cluniacs he gave the priory of Saint Mary Magdalene of Little Beaulieu, and he assigned Charité—[Col. 0022A] a town in the diocese of Auxerre—to their monastery. [Note: [Col. 0021D] But all these things are uncertain unless they are established by examining and comparing the foundation charters.] He had the ambo of the church of Chartres elegantly decorated, according to the style of that age, with histories of the Old and New Testaments.

Finally, having deserved exceedingly well of the Church, he fulfilled his last destiny on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, A.D. 1115—contrary to the opinion of Matthew Paris or Papirius Massonius. But the necrologies both of the Church of Chartres and of the Monastery of Saint John, whose eulogies are copied below, establish the fact. [Note: [Col. 0022D] The obituary of Saint Quentin at Beauvais places his death in 1116, because January belonged to that year. But since the tenth day before the Kalends of January falls on 23 December, he properly died in 1115.] I am not unaware that some have counted our Ivo among the cardinals, but they were deceived because at nearly the same time there flourished a Cardinal Ivo, who was also legate in France for Pope Innocent II in A.D. 1142.

These are the things I had to say about Ivo. Whoever reads his letters will discover more. Let no one seek a fuller praise of him here. He followed the road that leads to heaven. Great among those with whom he lived, yet greater to posterity, because he spoke no ill of them. Equal to many in lineage and rank, inferior to some, but greatest of all in virtue and learning. In station and obedience indeed subject to princes and supreme pontiffs; but in loftiness and constancy of spirit not their equal merely, but, if anything, their superior. Born for the highest things, and worthy to have been supreme, had it not been somewhat difficult to deal with those who were supreme. He neither despised nor sought the favor of kings; he valued their goodwill because he wished them well. Nobleman, theologian, canon, abbot, bishop: so that in a manner he belongs to all, being so great, and no one may envy another anything on his account. Belgium gave him a place for his birth, Celtic Gaul for his dignity, and all France, Italy, and England for his merit. Faithful and useful to kings and princes, yet not always pleasing, because both are difficult. A most devoted son of the supreme pontiffs; yet sometimes almost their father, as men, so loftily did he raise his spirit when circumstances required. In short, he conducted himself on earth so as almost to touch heaven; and, freed from the body, he undoubtedly attained it. Christians have always venerated his memory, though for many years they celebrated it on no feast day. Yet after his death heretics assailed him and his bones, as they usually do only saints. And Pope Pius V, of most happy memory, [Col. 0022D] permitted the regular canons of the Lateran Congregation to celebrate his feast on 20 May, by a bull issued 18 December 1570, in the fifth year of his pontificate.

[Col. 0023]

## TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING IVO

To the glorious and wise Ivo, bishop of Chartres, Brother Hugh, monk of the Benedictine monastery of Fleury, wishes the enjoyment of everlasting peace and happiness.

[Col. 0023A]

[Note: [Col. 0023D] From the old Chronicle of P. Petau, senator of Paris.] Behold, most excellent Father and lord, I send you two little works of my humility, so that, if you see in them anything unseemly or unpolished, you may correct and adorn it with the file of your prudence, and may strengthen and confirm whatever pleases you. These little works which you now see are my weapons against idleness; for I prefer to be occupied in study than to pass my life in idleness and torpor like a useless beast. But I desire that all these things be examined by your judgment and seasoned by your wisdom, since that which the bond of your authority has once strengthened cannot waver. Yet perhaps someone will say to me: “Why were you not ashamed to send such cheap and useless things to a prudent man seated on the highest summit [Col. 0023B] of philosophy, when you know it is written that prayer and poetry have little grace unless their eloquence is supreme?” To this I answer that I prefer to be approved by the just judgment of a wise man rather than condemned by the opinion of arrogant men. Yet it is laborious, most honorable Father, to apply the additions and deletions of your integrity to this volume; but charity, the fruit of labor, is more precious than gold. Farewell.

Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, in his book *On the Life of Louis the Fat, King of the French*.

Therefore the matter was conducted with deliberation, and especially at the prompting of the venerable and most wise man Ivo, bishop of Chartres: that they should assemble at Orléans as quickly as possible to refute the scheme of the wicked, and should hasten diligently to promote his elevation.

Accordingly, Daimbert, archbishop of Sens, was invited and came with his suffragans: namely Galon [otherwise Walon], bishop of Paris; Manasses of Meaux; John of Orléans; Ivo of Chartres; Hugh of Nevers; and Humbald of Auxerre [otherwise Altissiodorensis].

The same author, shortly afterward.

When the prelates of the Church departed—the archbishop of Sens, the bishop of Orléans, and the venerable Ivo of Chartres, who had been held in prison, which he had been compelled to have painted in that same castle for many days.

Andrew, an ancient writer, Book III of the *History of the Franks*, addressed to the bishop of the Church of Arras.

[Note: [Col. 0023D] From an ancient manuscript codex.] In the year of the Lord 1109, the bishops who had gathered for the funeral rites of King Philip assembled at Orléans immediately after the funeral. Having received salutary counsel because of the disturbers of the kingdom, they anointed as king the young Louis, a lover of religion, gentle in character, vigorous in arms, most valiant in war, on the day of the Invention of the Protomartyr Stephen, before the altar of the Holy Cross. Daimbert, archbishop of Sens, placed the royal crown upon his head, together with Ivo of Chartres, John of Orléans, Hubert of Senlis, [Col. 0024A] Walon of Paris, Manasses of Meaux, Hugh of Nevers, and the bishop of Auxerre.

The same words occur in a manuscript copy of another ancient author, who adds the following: “Moved by the numerous examples of other kings, who were consecrated by different bishops in different places because of impending disturbances.”

Sigebert, in the *Chronicle*, under the year 1078.

From this time the canonical order began to flourish again in the Church of Blessed Quentin at Beauvais, first regularly established by the apostles and later by Blessed Augustine the bishop, under Master Ivo, the venerable provost of that same church and later bishop of Chartres.

The same, under the year 1092.

[Col. 0024B] Lord Ivo, provost of Saint Quentin at Beauvais, consecrated by Pope Urban, became bishop of Chartres.

The same, Book *On Illustrious Writers of the Church*, chapter 168.

Ivo, bishop of Chartres, wrote to Hugh, archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, a letter [Note: [Col. 0024D] He means Letter 60.] not very long, but greatly fortified by canonical and Catholic testimonies, concerning the dissension between kingdom and priesthood and the unprecedented decrees of the Roman Church. He also wrote very useful letters to various friends and compiled a distinguished volume of canons.

Matthew Paris of England, under William II, in the year of the Lord 1093.

[Col. 0024C]

In this same year Ivo, provost of Beauvais, was consecrated bishop of Chartres by Pope Urban.

The same, under Henry I.

In the year of the Lord 1117, the venerable Ivo, bishop of Chartres, fully learned in the sacred Scriptures, ended his final day.

Robert of Torigni, in his continuation of Sigebert, under the year 1114.

After Ivo, who illumined the Church of Chartres by his life and teaching, and who among his other works usefully compiled that volume called Ivo’s *Decrees*, Geoffrey, venerable by merit of life and prudence, governed the Church of Chartres.

William of Nangis, in the *Deeds of Philip III the Bold*, under the year 1275.

For, as is read in a certain letter [Note: [Col. 0024D] Letter 189.] of Ivo, formerly bishop of Chartres.

An ancient anonymous writer of the chronology of Auxerre, under A.D. 1154.

Ivo of Chartres, most skilled in decrees and laws, [Col. 0025A] establishes this in his letters [Note: [Col. 0025D] Letter 189.] both by arguments and by examples.

From an ancient manuscript codex of the Church of Laon.

On the vigil of the Nativity of Holy Mary, before Vespers, they came to Chartres and were received with the highest honor by Lord Ivo, bishop of Chartres. The entire procession of canons met them outside the city as far as the vineyards, and the bier was placed in the principal church upon the altar of Saint Mary.

Priscus, monk of Marmoutier, concerning the privilege granted by Pope Urban II at the Council of Clermont in 1093.

Besides these, Lord Hugh, legate and primate of the Gauls, who was also archbishop of Lyons, was seated there; likewise Lord Amatus, legate and [Col. 0025B] archbishop of Bordeaux; Renaud, archbishop of Reims; Richer, archbishop of Sens; Hildebert, archbishop of Bourges; Roland, archbishop of Dol; the archbishop of Narbonne; the archbishop of Aix; the archbishop of Toledo and legate of the Spains; Hoel, bishop of Le Mans; Geoffrey, bishop of Angers; the bishop of Nantes; the bishop of Poitiers; Ivo, bishop of Chartres; John, bishop of Orléans; Roger, bishop of Beauvais. There was also a very great multitude of bishops, abbots, nobles, and persons of diverse ranks, whose number is uncertain, all crying, for the authority and confirmation of our privilege: “Let it be done! Let it be done!”

From the Martyrology of Chartres.

[Col. 0025C] On the Ides of December, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1115, died Father Ivo, bishop of this most holy see: a man of great religious devotion; most prudent in ecclesiastical and secular affairs; gentle in speech; remarkable in patience; eminent in chastity; and most learned both in divine matters and in philosophy. For the adornment of this Church he gave six fine pallia, seven copes, three mitres, and three tapestries; he gave a book of Masses, a book of Epistles, a text of the Gospels, and one morning lectionary, all fitted with silver. He built a pulpit of wondrous beauty and established schools.
