He rebuilt from the foundations the episcopal residence, which he had found mean and wooden, and enslaved at the deaths or removals of bishops [Note: [Col. 0025D] See Letter 94.] by certain evil customs forcibly imposed by the counts of Chartres; he made it handsome and of stone, and rendered it free from servitude, with all its appurtenances, movable and immovable. He confirmed that liberty by the supporting guarantees of privileges of the Roman See, the king, and the count, preserved in the archives of this church. He also acquired from the viscount a plot adjoining the house, enlarging its site, and enclosed it with a wall. At the Gaudin bridge he built other houses for episcopal use and improved the same village in many respects. He converted the abbey of Saint John from secular into regular status, established it, and endowed it. By his counsel and assistance the monastery for the sick at Beaulieu was founded. [Col. 0026A] He converted all the diminished benefices and precarious holdings of this church to common uses, and by both his own and apostolic privilege forbade their future distribution among individual persons. [Note: [Col. 0026D] Mention is made in Letter 271.] By the same privileges he forbade compulsory services, unjust exactions, and wrongful burdens imposed upon servants through the provostships. To increase the altar’s provision, at his death he left one hundred measures of wine; and in many other matters he conferred many benefits upon his Church and clergy.

From the ancient Calendar of Saint Quentin at Beauvais.

On the Kalends of January died Master Ivo, of venerable memory, a distinguished teacher above others of his age, first abbot of this church and afterward [Col. 0026B] bishop of Chartres. He gave us thirty volumes, four chalices, a golden Gospel-book, a golden cross, four reliquaries, four silver and gilded crosses, the right hand of Blessed Pope Callixtus, and two silver censers. This great man died in the year of Christ’s Incarnation 1116, for whose soul we give as alms one half-measure of wheat.

From the Calendar of the Church of Saint John in the Valley at Chartres.

On the tenth day before the Kalends of January, in the year from the Incarnation 1115, died Ivo, bishop of Chartres, of good memory. He established in this church the order of regular canons and enlarged it with his possessions, giving for the brothers’ use the church of Saint Faith [Note: [Col. 0026D] See Letter 286.], the church of Saint Stephen [Col. 0026C] with its appurtenances, the church of Lucé, the church of Pontgouin, land beyond the pond, thirty volumes from his library, and many other things.

From the same Calendar.

When one hundred thousand years, less one, had run their course,

This place first flourished in the canonical order.

Epitaph of Ivo of Chartres from an old parchment of Barnabé Brisson.

In mind, hand, tongue, learning, and bodily service,  
Prudent, generous, affable, useful, blameless—  
The chief pillar of the house of the Lord, which by salutary right  
He cherished, fortified, furnished, and continually enlarged  
By counsel, writings, the rule by which it should live, and possessions.  
[Col. 0026D] The sick freely experienced his help; the needy, his resources.  
Ivo, the bishop, memorable crown of this city,  
Lies in this tomb awaiting the coming of the Judge.

Nicholas of Clamanges, cantor of Bayeux, in his letter to Cardinal Galiot de Pietramala, beginning *Quod in superiore*, in which he seeks to prove against Petrarch’s saying that France had never lacked eloquent men.

If historians of deeds are required, take Gregory of Tours and Sulpicius Severus, the splendid narrator of the deeds of the most blessed Martin. I could name very many others, both ancient and recent: among the ancient, Irenaeus of Lyons, Hilary of Arles, Gennadius [Col. 0027A] of Marseilles, Ralph of Flavigny, Prosper, and Cassian. Among the more recent, Bernard comes first to mind, then Hildebert of Le Mans, Ivo of Chartres, Odilo, Hugh, and Peter the Venerable, abbots of Cluny; finally Hugh and Richard, canons who followed the rule of Saint Augustine.

Abbot Trithemius, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

Ivo, bishop of Chartres, formerly provost of Saint Quentin at Beauvais, of the order of regular canons of the holy Father Augustine, was a man practiced in the divine Scriptures and a most cautious interpreter of the canons of the holy Fathers and of general councils. He was no less worthy of reverence for holiness than for learning, and magnificently reformed his order, which had long fallen into decay. After Burchard, bishop of Worms, he wrote from the sacred canons a concise *Decree*, [Col. 0027B] used by jurists before Gratian’s time, which he titled *Pannonia* [*Pannomia*, alternatively *Pannormia*], in ten books; a single book of letters to various persons; and certain other works. He flourished under Henry IV, A.D. 1110.

Among other works written by Ivo, we find these: twenty-one sermons *On Ecclesiastical Sacraments and Offices, and the Principal Feasts throughout the Year*; and a brief *Chronicle of the Kings of France*, which we have appended to the letters from the book of P. Massonius, doctor of civil law.

To the foregoing should also seem to be added passages of Hildebert of Lavardin, bishop of Le Mans, who mentions the bishop of Chartres. Although he does not name him, it is probable that Ivo is meant, since letters to Hildebert himself appear in this book.

Hildebert, Letter 26, to a countess.

[Col. 0027C]

You have, it is said, provided an escort for the bishop of Chartres as he was setting out for a council. If so, I beg you to share with me the benefit of this favor.

The same, Letter 39, to the clergy, when he had been cast into prison by Count Hubert.

Count Rotrou was kept in chains in the tower of Le Mans. [Note: [Col. 0027D] Ivo mentions him in Letter 168 and following.] The count’s mother received me with a kiss and applauded the testament. And shortly afterward: Moreover, in the castle where these things occurred was the bishop of Chartres, a man of venerable authority; but among the authors of the crime, authority had no authority. Meeting Hubert in spirit—for this is the name of the prince of the Pharisees—he first flattered that [Col. 0027D] beast; but a beast does not admit reason. Then he freely accused him of sacrilege, pleaded with him at the proper time, reproved him out of season. Finally, he delivered him to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, bound as he ought to be by the bond of anathema.

The same, Letter 61, to the monks.

You too sinned against the doors, when you closed your doors to the bishop of Chartres, when you shut out Christ, the Christ of Jesus, forgetting alike the good of hospitality and its reward. Both the road had compelled him to pass through you, and the exigency of the moment to lodge with you. Approaching night and foul weather urgently pressed the pontiff to seek lodging. [Note: [Col. 0027D] First published now from an old parchment of Saint Quentin at Beauvais.]

A distinguished eulogy excerpted from the letters of a certain association or confraternity which the regular canons of Saint John in the Valley near Chartres entered into with the likewise regular canons of Saint Quentin at Beauvais four hundred years ago.

[Col. 0028A]

To all Christ’s faithful and to those who shall inspect this present document: Guarinus, abbot of the Church of Blessed John of the Valley at Chartres, and the whole convent of that place, greeting in the Lord. Since, according to the Apostle, we are all one body in Christ, yet individually members one of another, just as the body ought not to be reckoned alien from the head, so neither ought members to be reckoned alien from the body by members of the head. Since, therefore, from times long past we were propagated from the womb of our mother church of Blessed Quentin at Beauvais, and have drawn streams from her as from a fountain of sacred religion [Col. 0028B] through the venerable Father Ivo of venerable memory—who, while the new planting of religious life under the Rule of Blessed Augustine flourished in that same church and nobly served Almighty God, presided as abbot over the brethren serving God there—the outstanding holiness of so great a father, like a city set upon the summit of virtues, could not remain hidden by day. Indeed, the celebrated fame of his religious life spread far and wide; with God’s will leading the way, he attained the see of the Church of Chartres and became patron and founder of our church. Among the other benefits which he bestowed upon us with paternal affection, at last, as a sign of love and an everlasting covenant, he honored our church with the treasure of his body and the presence of his burial. Therefore, since our pious father, founder, and patron loved us with the affection of inward love, as was shown at the end, it was fitting that the canons of Saint Quentin, his spiritual sons, should not degenerate from the deeds of their father, etc. Done in the year of the Lord 1228.

Epitaph of Ivo, written by Philip, abbot of Bonne-Espérance.

His affection made him a father; learning, a master;  
The rule, a canon; and rank, a bishop.  
Virtue made him renowned; nature, humble;  
His serene life, venerable; long and chaste old age, holy.  
Of old it was customary for a ruler, when a bishop died,  
To take his possessions; Ivo bought out this ruler’s custom.  
The injured experienced his aid; the people, his teaching; the wicked king, restraint;  
The needy, resources; God, prayers offered for the flock.

Another epitaph, which Severtius took from a manuscript of Tavelli and copied into his *Chronology*.

[Col. 0028D]

In mind, hand, tongue, learning, and bodily service,  
Prudent, generous, excellent, useful, blameless—  
The steadfast pillar of the house of the Lord, which by salutary right  
He cherished, fortified, furnished, and continually enlarged  
By counsel, writings, the rule by which it should live, and possessions.  
The sick freely experienced his help; the needy, his resources.  
Ivo, the bishop, memorable crown of this city,  
Lies here awaiting the coming of the judgments.

[Col. 0029]

## TO THE MOST REVEREND IN CHRIST AND MOST GOD-LOVING FATHER AND LORD, F. BERNARD DE FRESNEDA, CONFESSOR IN THE INNER COUNSELS OF HIS CATHOLIC MAJESTY, MY MOST HONORED LORD AND PATRON, JOHN MOLINAEUS, PROFESSOR OF THE SAME DECREES AT LOUVAIN: GREETING.

[Col. 0029A] Whenever I recall the most calamitous condition of the Catholic Church, and those times which, while the dissensions of the Christian religion had not yet been settled, afforded both the origin and progress of those troubles, most reverend and devout Father Confessor, such amazement seizes me, such stupefaction comes over me, that I think faith itself would once have failed regarding these events—events of which all of us today are not so much readers or hearers as spectators. Not indeed because the name of heresy or schism is, or ever has been, among us—alas!—new or unusual, given humanity’s great and almost natural inclination and capacity for disagreement. For Paul, that vessel of election, foretold and perceived that these evils would be not merely familiar or domestic to God’s Church, but necessary, so that they might be believed altogether inevitable [Col. 0029B] (1 Cor. 11:19). Rather, it is because no sect has ever had an origin more difficult, or a success more extensive, than the Lutheran.

Certainly, if, from the first establishment of religion—and especially after the apostles and Christ’s first disciples, that is, “the eyewitnesses and hearers of the Word” (*τοῖς αὐτόπταις καὶ αὐτηκόοις τοῦ λόγου*), had been taken up into heaven—all things were full of errors and disputes, no one, I think, ought greatly to wonder, especially if he considers first how arduous and difficult are the beginnings of all great and memorable things; then how great an undertaking it was, amid so many vain, perverse, and indeed false superstitions and cults of the false gods, received for many preceding centuries, [Col. 0029C] to found and establish the one true knowledge and religion of the true God—unknown and unheard of, overthrowing every established religion, and, not to mention the disgrace of the cross and the Crucified alone, scarcely credible or plausible. I pass over the fact that its first heralds and architects were, in human judgment, neither famous nor distinguished, nor powerful or wise, but altogether obscure, cheap, and despised men; wholly untrained and ignorant in philosophy, eloquence, polished culture, and every external and common branch of learning; in a word, as Paul says, “the refuse and offscouring of the world” (*περικαθάρματα καὶ περιψήματα τοῦ κόσμου*) (1 Cor. 4:13). For God chose not many wise according to the flesh, nor many powerful, nor many noble; but [Col. 0030A] God chose the foolish things of the world to put the wise to shame, and God chose the weak things of the world to put the strong to shame; and he chose the lowborn things of the world, and things despised, and things that are not, to destroy the things that are (1 Cor. 1:26–28), as he says in writing to the Corinthians—and rightly, for it was written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent” (ibid., 19).

What shall I say of the fact that, owing to the most savage persecution, councils of bishops—wherein the principal safeguard for cutting short the disputes and controversies of faith has always been placed—could not conveniently then be held? What, finally, of the fact that the Roman rulers, whose empire was then most extensive, and whatever other kings there were besides, turned all their forces and their entire power toward the destruction of [Col. 0030B] the Christian name? Nor is this surprising: for who would indulge, spare, or not extirpate persons accused of atheism, Thyestean banquets, and Oedipodean sexual unions—*ἀθεότητος, Θυεστείων δείπνων, καὶ Οἰδιποδείων μίξεων*? These three most atrocious crimes were then charged against our people, though falsely and unjustly.

Moreover, after Constantine the Great, every heresy which the devil, the perpetual enemy of human salvation, introduced in order to disturb the peace and concord of the Church, which had by then recovered breath from external wars, will be found to have arisen from or been defended by emperors or by certain bishops of eminent name. Although their power and efforts were feeble and ineffective for suppressing and extinguishing truth, they nevertheless easily brought it about that synodal decrees lacked, if not force and authority, at least just and lawful execution.

But if you turn your mind now to the heresiarch of our own age, you will find that everything was entirely different when Luther opened the school of his impiety. First, throughout the Christian world there was the fullest agreement in doctrine of faith. There was also an incredible zeal among all rulers and peoples to preserve and defend the ancestral religion which each had received in uninterrupted succession from his forebears. I pass over the fact that no nation ever loved antiquity and ancient institutions more than the German nation, where this standard-bearer of Satan first scattered his poison. What is more, Leo X, then supreme pontiff, not only immediately condemned his doctrines as impious, [Col. 0031A] but also struck down with the dread sword of anathema all who embraced them together with their author.

All directors of studies and academies throughout the world, together with the most devout bishops of the cities, subscribed to this judgment without reluctance. The emperor then reigning, Charles V of most happy memory, father of our king Philip, not content with incorporating the pontifical decrees into imperial constitutions so that they might acquire the force of laws—following the example of the most pious rulers Constantine, Theodosius, Justinian, and others—added besides the most severe penalties for transgressors. Germany, France, Poland, Pannonia, Britain, and, without exception, all Christian [Col. 0031B] kings and princes followed him.

That no one might perhaps suppose that the penalties added to the constitutions had been imposed only to inspire fear—as ecclesiastical history reports was once done by the elder Emperor Theodosius—frequent and no less dreadful punishments soon inflicted upon the accused taught this more than sufficiently. Indeed, punishment was inflicted so freely that, for a long time, even condemned persons who repented and returned to their former faith received neither pardon nor favor in life or goods. It therefore became entirely certain that the anger and hatred of Christian rulers against heretics was greater than that of pagans against Christians and Catholics had ever been. For we read that they were accustomed to soothe persons caught, convicted, condemned, and even led to the place of punishment with words such as: “For what harm is there, Lord Caesar, in speaking, sacrificing, and being saved?”—*τί γὰρ κακόν ἐστιν εἰπεῖν, κύριε Καῖσαρ, καὶ θῦσαι, καὶ σώζεσθαι*? Thus mere denial and renunciation of Christ, even if feigned, delivered those people from danger; whereas for these men repentance for error and seduction, even genuine and sincere, was of no help—no more than for parricides, sacrilegious persons, poisoners, kidnappers, robbers, brigands, or other criminal persons.

What shall I now say of the diligence everywhere exercised by bishops, investigators of the faith, and civil magistrates in searching out the accused? What of the writings of learned men, no less numerous than learned, both in defense and demonstration of the orthodox faith and in refutation and exposure of counterfeit perfidy and diabolical [Col. 0031D] fraud? What, finally, of the diets of all the estates of the empire concerning religion, and the no less frequent conferences of learned men held on both sides? So completely was nothing omitted among all those measures which seemed able to contribute any help toward expelling or restraining this pest [*cruditionis*, reading uncertain] and the ruin of souls; yet it is so far from having been extinguished and abolished that it continually gathered strength and grew without measure.

Certainly, as the outcome of events has shown that the remedies devised thus far have had no effect toward the eradication and destruction of this deadly doctrine, so whether any means remain which might do so is perhaps not equally clear to everyone. It is at least most certainly established that, among a very small number of Christian provinces, there is none that has remained wholly untouched and free from this contagion. Not to mention [Col. 0032A] the very extensive kingdoms and peoples which this plague of souls has so taken from us that scarcely any hope remains of ever recovering them. Indeed, I judge it more to be feared that, stirred by internal tumults and dissensions among themselves—very grave among those who have departed from us—they will destroy one another, than hoped that they will ever be called back from their byways to the road, or, having renounced all errors, will finally embrace Catholic truth. Thus no one can fail justly to cry out with Polycarp the martyr: “O good God, to what times have you preserved me, that I must bear, endure, and permit these things!”

Someone may say: “Then does no plan remain for suppressing this sect (which the last times have produced) [Col. 0032B]? Is there no antidote at all? Is this evil so fated to be incurable that it cannot be overcome by any devices, any force, or indeed any means?” Certainly not! The gates of hell—which expression undoubtedly signifies heresies and schisms—will never prevail against the Church of God. Peter’s little boat is not sunk by the waves. Nor are aids lacking, and these are no less available than they were formerly customary and frequently employed. Why is an ecumenical synod of bishops not convened? Why do we not imitate the Apostles and the ancient Fathers, whom we know always made decisions concerning religious controversies after holding an assembly? For by what other means were the deceits, impostures, and impieties of Arius, Macedonius, Eunomius, Eutyches, and other heretics exposed and condemned? [Col. 0032C]

Moreover, just as it is most certain and fully established that nothing has ever been found more suitable or more powerful than councils—especially universal or “plenary” councils, as they call them—for dispersing the clouds and darkness of heretics, so, because the summoning of such a council does not belong to all persons and never has belonged to them, but today belongs by a special right to the Roman pontiff—and has always belonged to him, at least since the transfer, or rather the division, of the Roman Empire (which lies beyond all possibility of dispute)—it follows that the power to convene or conduct a council belongs not to everyone, but to the Roman pontiff alone.

Therefore someone may rightly ask: “Does no other remedy remain for ending religious disturbances, the power to employ which is shared more widely and does not in any way depend upon the decision of one Apostolic See?” For it belongs to everyone, rightly speaking, if I am not mistaken, not merely to be wise and profess the true faith in God, but also, to the extent of one’s powers, to uphold and defend it and keep it safe and sound. Indeed, it is little—rather, utterly nothing—to have indicated the treatment used by the ancients against new diseases of religion if that treatment cannot presently be obtained. For, according to the familiar maxim of jurists, “not to exist” and “not to appear” are equivalent. [Col. 0032D]

The answer to this question is by no means very difficult. There is indeed another remedy, both for the proscription of heresies and for the strengthening of orthodox faith; and as it is ready at hand and straightforward, so perhaps it is in no respect inferior to the former remedy. [Col. 0033A] For new synods and assemblies of bishops are not so necessary for establishing religion as the diligent observance of those ancient councils hitherto held—councils whose neglect and contempt have never, if I am not mistaken, been greater than they are now, though I cannot say this without deep grief. Hence it comes about that nowhere does even some semblance of the genuine and native Church appear.

Accordingly, those somewhat more expert in human and divine matters, despairing of and lamenting the almost exhausted aid offered by synodal assemblies, have long placed all hope for restoring and ordering the Church in the enactment of ancient ecclesiastical discipline. If their judgment does not deceive them—as indeed it cannot possibly deceive them—then, most reverend Father Confessor, [Col. 0033B] the whole Christian commonwealth owes you, and will forever owe you, an incredible debt: namely, because through your exhortation and under your auspices it has been accomplished that the most ample treasury of ecclesiastical discipline, buried and neglected for more than four hundred years, is now at last, at a time of utmost necessity, set before all for use and benefit.

No writer, whether earlier or later, Greek or Latin, has treated this branch of pontifical learning more fully, elegantly, or successfully than our Ivo did during his lifetime, bishop of the Church of Chartres in Gaul; and his studies relevant to this subject, hitherto unknown to the great harm of the Church, we are now the first to publish—may it be happy and auspicious. [Col. 0033C] I know that many have contended in this arena of learning; but, speaking of our own writers, the four who have won the palm of glory beyond all dispute are and are held to be Isidore of Seville, Burchard of Worms—wrongly called Brocardus by Italians and Frenchmen—Ivo of Chartres, and Gratian. The first three took their surnames from the cities over which they presided as bishops; the last has no surname.

Now Isidore was the first of all Latin writers to patch together canonical letters of Roman pontiffs, acts and canons of councils, beginning with the Constitutions of the Apostles, and to bind together, as it were, the whole pontifical law into a single body. In weaving and arranging it he followed no order but that of times and events, as he himself is a most abundant witness concerning himself; although at times, as though forgetting his own method, he attended, in the course of the work, not so much to the date and consul as to the regions and places in which the Fathers had assembled, after the fashion of Appian of Alexandria, historian of Roman affairs. [Col. 0033D]

Thus one may rightly say that he wrote a history of pontifical law. He carried it down even to his own times, namely to Pope Honorius I, so that he could draw breath at the Sixth Ecumenical Synod, held against the Monothelites at Constantinople in the emperor’s Trullo Palace. It is consequently clear that, although he won some praise for labour and diligence, he can claim none for ingenuity or learning in this matter—although otherwise he was by far the most learned man of his age, as his various little works should demonstrate. [Col. 0034A]

Nearly four hundred years later, Burchard, bishop of Worms, in the times of the emperors Otto III and Henry II of Bavaria, gathered this *hylē* (ὕλη), this mass of Isidore’s canons, under suitable headings and proper places for each subject. He also added judgments of orthodox Fathers such as Basil, Chrysostom, Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, and Gregory of Rome, and arranged the entire body of pontifical law in a more graceful and orderly form. For this service the Catholic Church unquestionably owes him gratitude equal to that which the Roman commonwealth owes to the Emperor Justinian. For just as Justinian arranged the entire law of the Romans first into books, then into titles, and finally into chapters, so Burchard, following as closely as possible the Justinianic method, most elegantly composed the system of the entire pontifical law which we use in twelve books, or volumes. [Col. 0034B]

I said twelve, since the work bearing his name which survives is nothing but an epitome by the author whose name it displays. Although it exceeds the archetype in number of little books, it scarcely reaches one sixth of that work in extent and bulk. Thus Burchard has had the same fate as Ivo: the abridgments of both are commonly regarded and used as their principal writings, since Burchard himself has never been subjected to a printer’s type. We have also resolved shortly to publish him, provided that some gratitude for the present labour expended in correcting Ivo of Chartres is shown by the cultivators of this learning, lest the adornment of the burden which chance has assigned me be lacking. [Col. 0034C]

Burchard, therefore, was the first to reduce the whole of pontifical law to a system. I believe that Isidore’s storehouses supplied him with material and subject matter for commentary; but he himself supplied and added the order of presentation, or arrangement, of those things which lay in Isidore crude, unarranged, and confused. For he distinguished and separated everything into definite classes and places. He accomplished this so successfully that I do not think anyone would have arisen to rework the same material had not heresies subsequently arisen and required some addition to the work. I also judge that this was the sole reason that prompted our Ivo to compose a new rhapsody of canons. [Col. 0034D]

For when, in the intervening period, Berengar disturbed the peace of all the Churches by certain novel and foreign inventions of opinion, Burchard’s work of decrees came to seem defective and mutilated unless the testimonies of ancient Catholic writers, opposed to the paradoxes of innovators, were inserted in suitable places. Nor, to confess frankly, do I see what Ivo contributed to pontifical learning after Burchard beyond this. In every other respect, unless one excepts this appendix of doctrines, one finds everything in Burchard in precisely the same words and not even in a substantially different order of presentation.

For Ivo, in the penultimate book, entitled “On the causes or business of laypersons, though pertaining to the Church,” certainly adduces many testimonies from Roman law, and indeed from every book of the entire civil law—from the Pandects and the Code, from the Institutes and from the Novels, the constitutions of Emperor Justinian. [Col. 0035A] No mention of these occurs in Burchard. Either he omitted all these things because he judged them of little relevance to the present undertaking—as indeed they are of little relevance—or because at that time the laws of Charlemagne were more commonly used than Roman law; or because not merely the force and authority but even all books of Roman law had then disappeared in the West. At any rate Burchard makes no mention whatever of this law, except that once or twice he produces a testimony from the Theodosian Code. This conjecture is further supported by the fact that Lothair II, the emperor said to have called back Roman laws and institutions almost from the underworld, lived several centuries after Burchard. [Col. 0035B]

The reason, then, for the fuller compilation of canons, as it is called, which Ivo of Chartres, a contemporary (*synchronicus*, σύνχρονος) of blessed Bernard, issued more than four hundred years ago while pursuing the remnants of the Berengarian conspiracy, was the one we have mentioned: namely, that the new mists of heretics might be dispersed by the sun of the Church and vanish afar. Consequently, the fortress of decrees eventually rose to the vastness now visible in it. For in the size of the book it surpasses all other rhapsodies and patchworks, not only Burchard’s but also Gratian’s and those of any other compilers of decrees whatsoever. This may be seen most plainly by simple, bare inspection of them all, once the trappings of glosses have been removed. [Col. 0035C] As to method, however, it is entirely the same here as in Burchard, although it is not even more prolix or more copious than Burchard, once the supplement of doctrines is removed.

But since not everyone was equally pleased, as often happens, with the length and bulk of the books, someone was not lacking who at once compressed the entire author into a narrower form. Students made extensive use of this little abridgment, and it easily happened that Ivo’s labours fell into oblivion and nearly perished, so that even to this day everyone has believed that the slender little book, commonly circulated under the title *Pannormia of Ivo*, by an uncertain author—though some suspect Hugh the Catalan—is the very autograph work itself. [Col. 0035D] This had escaped everyone until now, and would still escape notice, had you not, reverend Father Confessor, been the first of all mortals to bring it forth from darkness into light.

Moreover, that this author’s life and memory were shorter than all supposed would be sufficiently demonstrated, even if every other proof were lacking, by the fact that Gratian, who followed about fifty years later and put the finishing hand to this canonical learning, never saw the synopsis of Ivo’s *Decrees*, any more than Burchard’s—although no one can deny that he was aided by abridgments of both. Indeed, if he had drawn from the sacred sources of the canons themselves and their first streams, and not from the dregs of abridgers, then this stranger, but my companion Gratian, [Col. 0036A] and indeed all of us would have drunk more purely and unmixedly. Or, if access to the clearest streams of canons in Burchard or Ivo was truly open, it is astonishing that he did not lead those thirsty and eager for such a drink to the place where he himself might drink far more purely and sweetly.

It is altogether incredible that Gratian ever advanced to such folly as to think that any value would attach to his patchworks and miscellanies so long as the volumes of either Burchard or Ivo remained. Yet Gratian has another defence which readily frees him from every accusation. Those two, understanding the simplest and best method and system for learning and teaching pontifical law, assembled each item under appropriate titles and locations, introducing nothing of their own into the narrative and indulging in no disputation. But when the newer academy—that is, the disputatious academy—had been established, Gratian thought it fine to be the first to introduce it into the sacred precincts of canons. Thus we see that his concern in treatment was not to follow any method or offer a systematic presentation of pontifical law, which had been the sole aim of all earlier authors. Rather, his entire effort is devoted to harmonizing and reconciling, as conveniently as possible, the diversity and antinomy of ecclesiastical constitutions. [Col. 0036B]

Accordingly, he acts everywhere not so much as a selector or compiler of canons, as they say, but as a disputant and examiner, or judge—indeed without precedent even in this: that he breaks up the texture of canons, something that the older writers had considered sacrosanct, by interposing his own opinions. This is confirmed by the original title of Gratian’s Code, which promises neither anything else nor anything more: *The Concordance of Discordant Canons*. [Col. 0036C] At that time dialectical subtleties and quibbles had invaded every kind of learning, and all the liberal arts had begun to be gladiatorial, when nothing had been of greater concern to the ancients than method, ease, and simplicity in teaching.

Therefore those who seek method in Gratian’s volume—without which no one can be *didaktikos* (διδακτικός, capable of teaching)—seem to me not unlike those who hunt dolphins in forests or boars amid the waves; or, to state more closely what I think, those who seek things that exist nowhere. For it is wholly clear that Gratian observed no system of art. Thus I could not help sometimes being vexed by a teacher who, though not altogether bad, was nevertheless exceedingly confused, cumbersome, and disorderly, lacking every grace and skill, so to speak, in treating and teaching. [Col. 0036D]

Nor can I sufficiently wonder by what fate or perversity of judgment it has happened that, while this author alone is retained in the schools, all the others have been so banished that they are not read even privately. Yet it is more certain than certain that the system and path for teaching subjects—what they call method, to say nothing of all else—is better established in these two, Burchard and Ivo, than in Gratian. Nevertheless, if there are people so accustomed to reading Gratian that they refuse to admit another teacher—as perhaps there are people who would not leave acorns behind even after crops had been discovered—we have judged that no contention should be raised even with them, provided they recognize the great benefit and advantage that will thereby accrue to their own teacher: namely, that in him there are innumerable faults and errors, not to mention gaps, and false attributions of authors, which cannot be restored and supplied from elsewhere. [Col. 0037A]

I do not know what happened to others; I shall briefly relate what happened to me. When I first devoted myself to this discipline, and had no teacher other than Gratian, the common teacher of all, I found everywhere so many thorns and such darkness that I altogether despaired of ever reaching the desired goal of my studies under such a guide. Nor did I cease to despair of attaining knowledge of these matters until the Delian swimmers whom I mentioned above, and among them especially our Ivo, came to the aid of this “dark guide” (*skoteinōi hēgemoni*, σκοτεινῷ ἡεμῶνι [sic]). [Col. 0037B] Indeed, I dare affirm that among all the commentaries on Gratian now extant, none can bring him more light and reliability than these Pandects of Ivo’s *Decrees*.

We are therefore so far from wishing that Gratian, who constitutes nearly one entire page of pontifical law, should be expelled from schools or libraries, that through this edition of Ivo of Chartres we may more truly deserve to be called restorers; and our work cannot possibly incur blame, not even among those who have sworn allegiance to the words of Gratian as their sole master. But although I know that no work more important or distinguished for this pontifical discipline, none more useful to the afflicted Church, and none more salutary in these most wretched latter times could have been published by this service of ours—the severity of the disease making us all need this medicine—I nevertheless strongly doubt whether it will be welcome and pleasing to most people. [Col. 0037C]

For just as the doctrinal matters (*ta dogmatika*, τὰ δογματικά), of which there are certainly many here—on the Eucharist, baptism, penance, purgatory, fasts, the Mass, the primacy of the Roman See, and so forth—will undoubtedly not please the heretics of our age, who oppose all these things, so I greatly fear that, amid no less licence than corruption of morals, the moral matters (*ta ēthika*, τὰ ἠθικά) will also displease our people, that is, Catholics nonetheless. [Col. 0037D] For I cannot see whether we have departed farther from ancient virtue, which would be shameful, or whether they have departed farther from the faith and degenerated, so that no trace whatever of antiquity appears anywhere.

There is a fierce controversy over faith on both sides, but it is bare and empty of works; and I fear it is that faith which blessed James aptly called dead, because by itself it is useless for salvation (James 2:20). Thus I sometimes think that a conflict has now flared up among Christians altogether like that which Homer imagined between Trojans and Greeks, fighting over Patroclus—but over Patroclus dead, that is, contending over his corpse. Yet let no one expect me here to enumerate every sin committed everywhere, whether within or without, or to expose anyone’s reproaches and vices after the manner of the accursed Ham.

[Col. 0038A] One thing, however, I cannot possibly leave unspoken: the source from which, as from a spring, all evils are thought to flow—though it is too well known for anyone to be able to conceal it. Among the bishops, leaders of religion, how many—especially throughout Gaul and Germany, the provinces neighbouring us—how many, I ask, have ever discharged even some small portion of their office? Who has anointed altars, dedicated churches, consecrated virgins, laid hands upon penitents or those being confirmed? Who has ever visited and inspected his diocese? Finally, who has ever mounted the pulpit in order to speak divine words to people and clergy?

Do they not cast all these duties—although almost by their very nature they are such that they cannot be delegated—upon the shoulders of others, by a new and unheard-of practice, without any precedent among the ancients? [Col. 0038B] The use of these substitutes is so far from ancient that one can scarcely find even the name of such *topotērētai* (τοποτηρήται, “place-holders” or deputies) in the entire body of pontifical law. For if you attempt to call them bishops or co-bishops, you immediately collide with the Nicene canon, which does not allow more than one bishop to be set over the same city. If you prefer to call them chorepiscopi, you will fare no better, since it is entirely clear that the authority of these men in former times was much narrower than that of today’s pseudo-pontiffs.

Yet Pope Damasus abolished even these chorepiscopi—called from the *chōra* (ἀπὸ τῆς χωρᾶς), as if they were rural or village bishops—lest pontiffs devoted to leisure and repose should transfer even some, though not all, of their duty to these quasi-vicarial functions. He compared them, in a disgraceful and shameful analogy, to prostitutes who, having given birth, habitually send away their children to be reared by someone else. [Col. 0038C] “So these men,” he says, “hand over their children—that is, the peoples entrusted to them—to be brought up by others, so that they may satisfy their desires; that is, so that according to their pleasure they may pursue secular concerns and freely do whatever each of them sees fit.” He immediately adds: “For because of such men souls are neglected, sheep perish, diseases increase, heresies and schisms arise, Churches are destroyed, priests are corrupted, and the remaining evils ensue.”

There blessed and most learned Pope Damasus shows most plainly that heresies, schisms, corruption of clergy and people, the desolation and deformation of the entire Church, and indeed the whole Iliad of evils that surrounds us [Col. 0038D] spring forth, like from a Trojan horse, solely from the sloth, negligence, and utter indolence of bishops.

But to the point: not even the name of chorepiscopi can be adapted to these episcopal vicars, because chorepiscopi were not permitted to consecrate priests, deacons, or virgins. They did not erect altars, dedicate churches, prepare chrism, or mark with it the foreheads of the baptized when it had perhaps been prepared by a bishop. In short, they performed almost no pontifical function, whereas our titular, or Utopian, bishops perform everything. The Latin populace calls them “assistants” or “suffragans,” but this is too absurd to deserve refutation. Perhaps understanding this, the French, having coined another term, thought that they might more correctly be called “portable bishops,” and, in jest, sometimes “potable bishops,” with the *r* omitted. [Col. 0039A] Since they are *apolis* (ἀπόλιδες, without a city), they carry about wherever they travel, without inconvenience, the pontifical documents that alone they possess. If I am not mistaken, this name can indeed be assigned to these episcopal vicars more truly than “suffragans,” though it is plainly more jocular than serious.

For my part, I like them to remain *akōnymoi* (ἀκώνυμοι, without a proper name), since they are *anomimoi* (ἀνόμιμοι, lawless); and, if Pope Damasus is to be believed, the Church cannot be sufficiently safe while they remain safe. Would that no graver charge lay against most bishops than this inactivity and indolence which we have now attacked, although it is by far the gravest, however much long custom may perhaps have made the seriousness of the fault less felt.

Peter, chief of the Apostles, aptly compared the Church in Clement to a ship: its captain is the bishop; its sailors, the clergy; its passengers, the people. [Col. 0039B] Good God! How can this ship avoid shipwreck and not strike rocks and shoals when those sit at the stern and hold the helm who ought not even to have a place in the bilge? Or, what is worse, when they never even board the ship? It is certainly utterly ridiculous to hope that it will ever find harbour unless either others take up the helm or the appointed captains assume an altogether different disposition and concern.

Yet this complaint is not directed generally against all men of this order. For just as it does not pertain especially to those who are truly *episkopountes* (ἐπισκοποῦντες), that is, inspectors and overseers, so it does not touch those who render service either to the Supreme Pontiff, to the commonwealth, or who possess some other just excuse arising from their calling. Indeed, it is understood to strike only those who can offer no necessary—indeed, not even honourable—account of their leisure and time, and who are scarcely anything else, if it is permissible to speak without saying something harsher, than an “useless burden upon the earth” (*etōsion achthos arourēs*, ἐτώσιον ἄχθος ἀρούρης). [Col. 0039C] If no such persons are found, I am content to suffer the penalties due to reckless accusers or complainants.

Nor should anyone tell me that this can easily be corrected, since nothing prevents those whose learning and virtue have first been examined and approved from being appointed to govern churches. This is indeed most earnestly desired by everyone; but how greatly it is to be hoped for, let others judge. I know only this one thing: it is more difficult than many suppose. What Cannae was to the Romans, Capua was to Hannibal. From this it is understood that great men are more exhausted and broken by prosperity than by adversity.

Let us suppose, then, that a candidate for a bishopric has been made perfect to the last detail: let him possess honourable, pious, and holy character; outstanding learning in divine and human affairs; mature age; exceptional favour and acceptance among citizens and all other orders of the commonwealth; in short, let him be complete in every respect and fashioned precisely according to the Pauline ideal. In this dearth of good men and dissolution of morals, such persons are either nonexistent, or, if any exist, are scarcely found. [Col. 0039D] Once such a man sees that everything is subject to his will—not to say his whim—once he knows that he will never have to render an account to anyone for anything he has done or not done, and once he perceives that he alone has acquired an unaccountable and perpetual authority (*aneuthynon exousian*, ἀνεύθυνον ἐξουσιαν), how, I ask, amid this frailty of human nature, amid such licence and impunity in life and every pleasure, and continually surrounded besides by a troop of flatterers, can he fail to become insolent and immediately forget his former moderation? [Col. 0040A]

These, certainly, and many other things give us no grounds whatever to hope for the reformation of the Church; rather, they portend ruin and destruction—would that I were a false prophet! Whoever trusts that all this will be healed and corrected by an ecumenical synod, the signs of which are not yet sufficiently certain, not only is miserably deceived, but also, in my judgment, shamefully betrays ignorance of ecclesiastical antiquity. This is not because a synod ought not to be held—for it would have been most judicious to oppose one to the disease at its birth, before it took such deep roots and spread so far and wide—but because there is no reason to hope that the leaders of factions and their followers will ever return to the point from which they have turned aside. Rather, we must fear that more people will defect from us each day and join the camp of our adversaries, unless bishops have a different care, a different mind, and a different disposition. [Col. 0040B]

For the integrity of those who preside is the safety of those subject to them, and the condition and order of the master’s whole household will waver if what is required in the body is not found in the head, as Leo the Great elegantly says. For as the leaders of cities are, such necessarily are the other citizens. Conversely, nothing can be truer than the ancient Hebrew saying: “As is the people, so is the priest.” [Col. 0040C]

Therefore, for repairing and restoring the Church—which, alas, has never been so afflicted and corrupt—a most diligent selection must above all be made of those to be placed at the head of the Lord’s camp. According to the venerable enactments of the holy Fathers, no one should be judged fit for this summit of ecclesiastical honours unless his whole age, from childhood beginnings to more advanced years, has run through the service of ecclesiastical discipline, so that his past life may provide testimony for each person and no one can doubt his integrity and faith. For, on account of many labours, chaste morals, and energetic deeds, the reward of a higher position is in some measure due to him.

For, as Leo I reasons most elegantly: “If it is unworthy to attain worldly honours without the recommendation of time and without the merit of labour, and if those whom proofs of uprightness do not support are customarily branded as ambitious, how diligent and prudent must be the administration of divine gifts and heavenly dignities, lest apostolic and canonical decrees be violated in any respect and the Church of the Lord be entrusted to the governance of those who know nothing of lawful institutions and are ignorant of all humility—who wish to take their beginning not from the lowest ranks but from the highest? For it is very unjust and absurd that the unskilled should be preferred to masters, novices to veterans, and raw persons to those who have earned their discharge.” [Col. 0040D]

Therefore, since it matters greatly what sort of men are appointed bishops of Churches, everyone sees that no caution can ever be too exacting in choosing them. Closely connected with this is the need that the long-obscured custom of provincial synods be restored to use; otherwise, to say nothing of the Church’s remaining needs which arise daily, bishops will not perform their office, nor will those who have perhaps abandoned it in some respect be compelled into order. I shall add a third requirement: that the hierarchical order at last be restored to its ancient integrity. Thus confusion everywhere will cease, and supreme peace and tranquillity will exist among the Churches and their leaders.

In this matter I should wish the Supreme Pontiff always to remember that he has been appointed defender and guardian of this order, and that it belongs to his religious duty to prevent anyone from disturbing the boundaries and barriers established by the Fathers. [Col. 0041B] Just as it is absolutely certain that the same charge falls upon him if anyone violates the rules of paternal enactments; otherwise the Church of God will be like Penelope’s web. [Col. 0042A] For if it is permitted that one man should pull down and overthrow whatever all others have built, this is, I think, exceedingly ridiculous and no less absurd.

I am not unaware that in this corruption of morals, this fertility of abuses, and this dormancy of paternal constitutions, there are innumerable other matters needing amendment or reform. But once the foregoing provisions have been made, all the rest will follow without resistance. They need not be repeated here, for in these books of *Decrees* they will be before everyone’s eyes.

Receive, then, at last your Ivo, whom we return not without interest. For, reverend Father Confessor, you will have him far more polished and serviceable than when you first redeemed him from barbarians—you know whom I mean. Whatever labour has been expended in revising and correcting him, I willingly dedicate it all to your reverend fatherhood, to whom I have long been devoted. Indeed, if you desire anything else from me, it will be yours to determine what you wish and mine perpetually to execute your commands. I pray that you may long remain blessed and sound in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whose love I wholly give and dedicate myself.

Given at Louvain, on the Kalends of August, 1561.

[Col. 0041]

## ON IVO’S TWO COLLECTIONS

(Extracted from the Ballerini brothers’ *Investigations concerning Ancient Collections and Collectors of Canons*, part IV, chapter 16, *Patrologia*, vol. LVI.)

[Col. 0041C] 1. Ivo was born in the territory of Beauvais about the middle of the eleventh century. In 1078 he was made abbot of the monastery of Saint-Quentin at Beauvais, of the Order of Regular Canons; finally, he was elected bishop of Chartres in 1092 and consecrated by Urban II. He died in 1115, or, as others prefer, in 1117. He was a man distinguished not only for outstanding learning, but also for zeal, prudent steadfastness, faith, and holiness. Therefore Pius V, by a constitution issued in 1570, granted the canons of the Lateran congregation permission to celebrate Ivo’s commemoration on 20 May.

Two collections of canons bearing Ivo’s name appeared. One, divided into eight parts, is called Ivo’s *Pannormia*; the other is Ivo’s *Decretum*, divided into seventeen parts. The *Pannormia* was printed at Basel in 1499 under the care of Sebastian Brant; and Melchior of Vosmediano arranged for it to be reprinted at Louvain in 1557, corrected of errors. The *Decretum* first appeared at Louvain in 1561 through the labour and care of Johannes Molinaeus of Gauda, and was later reprinted at Paris in 1647 with Ivo’s other works, according to the oldest Victorine manuscript. The same preface, entirely identical, is prefixed to both works in the published editions; its style, wholly equal to that of Ivo’s other letters, demonstrates that it is Ivo’s.

2. Let us first set forth the titles of both works. The first part of the fuller work, usually called Ivo’s *Decretum*, treats baptism and confirmation. [Col. 0042C] The second, the sacrament of Christ’s body, the sacrifice of the Mass, the remaining sacraments, and simony. The third, the Church and ecclesiastical property, and their reverence and observance. The fourth, feasts, fasts, canonical Scriptures, customs, and councils. The fifth, the primacy of the Roman Church, and the rank and rights of primates, metropolitans, and bishops. The sixth, the life, rank, and discipline of clergy. The seventh, monks. The eighth, marriage and virginity, abduction, concubinage, and adultery. The ninth, incest and prohibited degrees. The tenth, voluntary and involuntary homicides. The eleventh, magicians, sorceresses, and actors. The twelfth, lying, perjury, and so forth. The thirteenth, theft, usury, hunters, drunkards, madmen, and Jews. The fifteenth, penance. [Col. 0042D] The sixteenth, the office and judgments of laypeople. The seventeenth part contains sayings of the holy Fathers [9], and especially of Gregory the Great, concerning faith, hope, and charity.

3. Now here are the titles of the other collection, entitled Ivo’s *Pannormia*, as the author himself set them forth.

> “The first part of this book contains matters concerning faith and the various heresies; concerning the sacrament, that is, baptism; the ministry of baptizing, consecrating, confirming, and of those confirmed; the observance of each; and what baptism confers and what confirmation confers. Concerning the sacrament [Col. 0043A] of the body and blood of Christ; concerning the Mass and the holiness of the other sacraments.
>
> “The second part contains matters concerning the constitution of the Church and offerings of the faithful; the dedication and consecration of churches and altars; burial, priests, and their churches; tithes and lawful possession; those taking refuge in a church; sacrilege; guardianship of children; alienation and exchange of ecclesiastical property; Scriptures and authoritative councils.”

> “The third part contains [material] on the election and consecration of the pope and of archbishops; on orders; on clerics and laymen to be ordained and not ordained; on the transfer of bishops; on those ordained, who are not to be reordained; on the continence of those ordained; on those ordained and ordainers simoniacally, [Col. 0043B] that they are altogether to be deposed, and that they are to be reconciled mercifully; on the profession of heretics; on those who have fallen while in holy orders, that they ought not to minister, and that they may mercifully be admitted to minister; on clerics who are murderers, that they ought not to minister; on usurers; on slaves ordained through ignorance—who ought to remain in their ordination and who ought not; on drunken and scurrilous clerics; on monks; on the age at which parents may oppose their children’s entry into religion, and at which they may not; on widows and veiled virgins; on abbesses.
>
> “The fourth part contains [material] on the primacy and dignity of the Roman Church; on the calling of councils; on how a province is to be established; on the authority [Col. 0043C] of primates and metropolitan bishops; on the affairs and cases of clerics, where they ought to be handled; on restoring those who have been despoiled; on accusation—by what procedure, by what persons, and against what persons it ought, or ought not, to be made; on witnesses—who, how, how many, and in what matter they ought to testify; on judges—what sort they ought to be and when they ought to pronounce judicial sentence; on appeal—at what time and for what reason it ought to be made, and on the penalty of those who appeal improperly.
>
> “The fifth part contains [material] on clerics accused of infamy alone and without witnesses—by how many hands they ought to clear themselves; on the causes and affairs of laypersons; on summonses of those to be excommunicated; on lawful and unlawful excommunication; on absolution; on those bound to excommunicated persons by fidelity or oath, whether they can be released from that oath without perjury; [Col. 0043D] on heretics to be excommunicated after death; that communion is to be maintained with those not excommunicated by name.
>
> “The sixth part contains [material] on marriage: at what time, between what persons, and for what cause it ought to be contracted; on the three things that make a marriage complete; on complete and incomplete marriage; on concubines; on spouses one of whom, without the other, vows continence or assumes the habit of religion; on wives who, after their husbands have been led into captivity, marry others; that marriage exists between persons of the same religion or faith, but cannot exist between Jews; [Col. 0044A] whereas marriage cannot be contracted between persons who are not of the same religion or faith; on the grounds for which marriage ought not to be dissolved; on what kind of union does not make a marriage; on separation of marriage for a cause other than fornication.
>
> “The seventh part contains [material] on separation of marriage on account of carnal fornication; on a man who commits fornication with another man’s wife, that after her husband’s death he cannot have her as his wife; on killers of their spouses; on spiritual fornication, that a wife may lawfully be dismissed on its account; on reconciliation of spouses; on the marital duties husbands owe their wives and wives their husbands when they are reconciled; on the subjection in which wives ought to be subject to their husbands; on why marriage ought not to be contracted [Col. 0044B] between relatives; on the fact that one man cannot marry two co-mothers in succession; on one whose heading breaks off after “with his goddaughter (*filiola*), or with his co-mother (*commater*)”; or who baptized his own son, or whose wife raised her own son or stepson from the sacred font, or held him at confirmation, and therefore wished to separate. In what branch of consanguinity marriages may be contracted; on accusation of consanguinity, and by what persons it ought to be made; on investigating kinship and incestuous marriage. Diagrams of the degrees of consanguinity arranged in direct and collateral order.
>
> “The eighth part contains [material] on voluntary and involuntary homicide, and on what may be done without sin; on one who kills any cleric, what he ought [Col. 0044C] to make amends for; on one who strikes a pregnant woman and causes miscarriage, whether he has committed homicide or not; on incantations, divinations, and various kinds of magical art; on the nature of demons; on lots; on the observance of days and months; on an oath—whether it ought to be kept or not, and what companions it has; on every kind of falsehood.”

4. No one doubts that Ivo was the author of the earlier collection, called the *Decretum*. But concerning the *Pannormia* a major question is debated among critics. Vincent of Beauvais, *Speculum Historiale*, book XXV, chapter 84, after his notice of Ivo’s *Decretum*, which he declares to be a volume of no small size and not easily portable, adds the following: “Hugh of Châlons is said to have composed from this same volume an abridged little portable book, [Col. 0044D] which I too possess, and which is called the *Summa Decretorum of Ivo*.” From this Sebastian Brandt, who edited the *Pannormia*, was the first of all to suspect that it was rather this *Summa Decretorum of Ivo*, excerpted by Hugh of Châlons from Ivo’s *Decretum*, than a work of Ivo himself. Jean Molinier adopted and defended the same view in his edition of the *Decretum*; the Roman correctors and Father Antoine Pagi subsequently followed them. Others, however, together with Étienne Baluze in the preface to Antonio Agustín’s dialogues on the correction of Gratian, assigned the *Pannormia* to Ivo no less than the *Decretum*. They judge that he first composed the *Pannormia*, and then, when he saw that it was approved by its readers, turned his mind to compiling a fuller collection [Col. 0045A] and gave the same prologue to both works.

5. We shall briefly explain which of these views seems more probable to us. First, it is certain that some collection of canons must be ascribed to Ivo. For not only does Sigebert, who was Ivo’s contemporary, affirm this, writing in book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 168: “Ivo, bishop of Chartres, composed a distinguished volume of canons”; and likewise the Anonymous of Melk, who lived a little after Ivo, says in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 95: “Ivo, bishop of Chartres, wrote among several other works *Excerpts from the Canons*.” Ivo himself also testifies in Letter 262 to Pontius, abbot of the monastery of Cluny: “The collections of canons which you asked of me, and my little works which you wished [Col. 0045B] added to them, I have sent to you.” By these words he seems to indicate a collection arranged by himself.

There may perhaps be those who infer from this testimony that both collections—namely, the *Pannormia* and the *Decretum*—should be assigned to Ivo, since he wrote “collections” in the plural and not “collection.” But Ivo himself similarly says in Letter 80: “In the collections of Burchard, bishop of Worms,” although Burchard’s collection is a single one. Nor are the texts of Sigebert, Robert of Torigni, and other writers, who mention one volume, sufficiently effective to exclude two collections by Ivo. They may perhaps have seen only the collection called *Pannormia*, whose copies are more numerous, and not the other, the *Decretum*, of which rarer [Col. 0045C] manuscripts are found.

6. Secondly, it is certain that the *Pannormia* is not that *Summa Decretorum of Ivo* which Hugh of Châlons is said to have composed: first, because, owing to its division and arrangement differing from the *Decretum*, the *Pannormia* is as far as possible from being an abridgment of that *Decretum*; secondly, because it contains certain things which one would look for in vain in the *Decretum*; and also because in ancient manuscripts it is nowhere entitled *Summa Decretorum*, but *Pannormia* or *Excerpts of Ivo*. Hence the *Summa* arranged by Hugh and mentioned by Vincent of Beauvais was another work, lost through the ravages of time.

Certain decrees copied at the end of the last part [Col. 0045D] from Innocent II, who became pope after Ivo, might, however, create difficulty in assigning the *Pannormia* to Ivo. Yet this difficulty is removed by the ancient manuscripts of the *Pannormia*: because these decrees of Innocent II are not found in them, it is clear that they entered some copies by a later addition.

7. The question seems, moreover, to be decided from the manuscripts. There are few manuscripts of the *Decretum*. Only three have so far become known to us: one from which the first edition appeared; another, the Victorine manuscript, cited by several persons and used for the text of the second Paris edition; and a third, Vatican 1357, of the twelfth century, which we ourselves have seen. All of these contain the preface; but the Vatican manuscript, without the author’s name, bears this title: “Here begins the book of extracts, or excerpts, of ecclesiastical matters, partly from [Col. 0046A] the letters of Roman pontiffs, partly from the acts of councils, Catholic bishops, and kings; and it contains seventeen parts.” The Victorine manuscript, however, presents that preface not at the beginning but, in a later hand, added at the end of the manuscript, with this heading: “The aforesaid book of canons: the decrees of Jovinian, which Ivo, sometime bishop of Chartres, composed; and it contains seventeen principal parts”—as we learn from Baluze, preface to Agustín’s *Dialogues*, no. 21.

There are more copies of the *Pannormia*. One only, cited by Antonio Agustín with the heading *Book of Sacred Canons*, knows neither the preface nor Ivo’s name. The others bear either the preface or a title with Ivo’s name. Baluze cites the very ancient Victorine manuscript and three of Saint-Albin of Angers. [Col. 0046B] François Salmon, in his French treatise *On the Study of Councils*, part II, chapter 1, p. 269, edition of 1726, mentions manuscript F 4 of the Church of Paris. Besides one mutilated copy from Saint-Benedict of Padiliron, we have obtained three others with the preface: one from the Vatican Basilica, 19 G; another, Vatican 1358, with a particular heading to the same preface, *To Father Abbot*—namely, we believe, to Abbot Pontius, to whom Ivo declares in Letter 262 that he sent the collection; and finally the Paduan manuscript of the monks of Saint Justina, shelfmark YY. V. no. 86, in which this title is read: “Excerpts of Ecclesiastical Canons by Ivo, Bishop of Chartres.” The preface follows with the titles of the eight parts into which the *Pannormia* is divided.

This manuscript appears to settle the controversy [Col. 0046C] concerning the author of this work. Though it is believed to be of the fourteenth century, it was copied from an older exemplar, written immediately after Ivo’s death. For it adds a catalogue of Roman pontiffs which ends with Gelasius II in such a way that it omits the years of this pontiff’s reign, years which are separately recorded for the preceding pontiffs. This happened because that catalogue was written under Gelasius himself, when the years of his pontificate could not yet be entered. Gelasius II began his pontificate in 1118 and died in January 1119; Ivo, as we said at the beginning, had died in 1115 or 1117. Therefore the exemplar from which the Paduan manuscript was copied was contemporary with Ivo’s age. This [Col. 0046D] ancient testimony, assigning the *Pannormia* to Ivo, carries such weight with us that, if either work must be doubted, we should think the *Decretum*, rather than the *Pannormia*, the more doubtful.

8. Yet we do not therefore think that the *Decretum* ought to be denied to him. For since the same preface of the *Pannormia* is added to this work also in ancient books, we believe this was done because those ancient scribes had received the tradition that Ivo had composed this work too. Ivo appears first to have written and issued the *Pannormia* with its preface. Hence several copies of the same *Pannormia* were immediately written and disseminated. Later he arranged a more extensive collection, but perhaps did not himself publish it. Thus, when it was found after his death without its own prologue, the prologue from the *Pannormia* was added to it in the rarer [Col. 0047A] copies which were written; accordingly, in the very ancient Victorine exemplar it is copied not at the front but at the end of the *Decretum*, as an addition.

9. The principal source from which Ivo drew his canons was the Isidorian collection. He also sometimes used Regino’s compilation, from which, among other things, he transferred word for word into the *Decretum*, part VI, chapters 433, 434, and 435, the models of *formatae* letters cited by him in book I, nos. [Col. 0048A] 437, 438, and 439. But he took the greater part from Burchard. He himself inserted not a few other materials, for example those set out in the second part of the *Decretum* against Berengar’s errors, and those reported in part XVI from Roman law and from the capitularies of the Frankish kings.

## *Decretum*

[Col. 0048]

## *Decretum of Saint Ivo*

### Prologue to the *Decretum* compiled by its author and arranged in seventeen parts or books

[Col. 0047]

[Col. 0047B] 1. I have taken care, with no little labour, to unite into one body [work] excerpts of ecclesiastical rules: partly from the letters of Roman pontiffs, partly from the Acts of councils of Catholic bishops, partly from the treatises of orthodox Fathers, and partly from the enactments of Catholic kings. Thus, whoever cannot have at hand the writings from which these excerpts are drawn may at least obtain from here whatever he perceives to be of value for the benefit of his case.

Beginning, therefore, from the foundation of the Christian religion—that is, faith—we have gathered under general headings, distinctly arranged, both matters pertaining to ecclesiastical sacraments, matters pertaining to the instruction [establishment] or correction of morals, and matters pertaining to the examination or determination of every kind of case. Thus the person searching need not [Col. 0047C] turn through the entire volume, but need only identify the general heading suitable to his question and read through, without interruption, the chapters placed under it.

In this matter we have thought it appropriate to warn the prudent reader that, if perhaps he does not fully understand what he reads, or thinks it contradicts itself, he should not immediately criticize it. Rather, he should attend carefully to what is said according to strictness, what according to moderation, what according to judgment, and what according to mercy. He who said, “I will sing to you, O Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Psalm 100), and elsewhere, “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 25), did not perceive these things to disagree with one another.

For all ecclesiastical discipline has chiefly this aim: either to destroy every edifice raising itself against the knowledge of Christ; or to build up the edifice of God, consisting in the truth of faith and uprightness of conduct; or, if it has been defiled, to cleanse that same edifice by the remedies of repentance. The teacher of this edifice is charity, which, providing for the salvation of neighbours, commands that [Col. 0047D] each person do to others what he wishes others to render to himself. Therefore, any ecclesiastical teacher who interprets or moderates ecclesiastical rules in such a way as to refer everything he teaches or expounds to the dominion of charity neither sins nor errs, because, in providing for the salvation of neighbours, he intends to reach the end owed to sacred enactments.

Accordingly, blessed Augustine says, while treating of ecclesiastical discipline: “Have charity, and do whatever you will. If you rebuke, rebuke with charity. If you spare, spare with charity.” But in these matters the utmost diligence must be applied, and the eye of the heart purified, so that in punishing or sparing, sincere charity may bring aid for healing diseases; and so that no one may there, after the manner of physicians who trade for gain, seek his own advantage and incur that prophetic rebuke: “They were putting to death souls that did not die, and keeping alive souls that did not live” (Ezekiel 13).

Just as the purpose of bodily medicine is to drive away diseases, heal wounds, preserve health, or increase it; and a physician does not seem inconsistent with himself when, according to the character [Col. 0048C] or severity of the illness or of the patient, he applies now biting, now soothing medicines to the sick person; and now cuts with iron one whom he could not assist by a fomentation, and conversely now assists by a fomentation one whom he did not dare cut with iron: so spiritual physicians—that is, the teachers of holy Church—do not disagree either with themselves or among themselves when they prohibit unlawful things, command necessary things, commend the highest things, and pardon venial things. They impose severe laws of penance according to the hardness of offenders’ hearts, for their correction or for the safeguard of others; or, according to the devotion of those who grieve and desire to rise again, taking account of the fragility of the vessel they bear, they apply the poultice of pardon.

For those who pardon provide for the removal of graver diseases; those who prohibit unlawful things deter from death; those who command necessary things desire to preserve health; while those who counsel strive to increase salvation. The attentive reader who observes this will understand the sacred utterances to have one countenance when he considers distinctly what admonition is, what command is, what prohibition is, and what remission is; and [Col. 0048D] that these neither conflict with one another nor differ from themselves, but dispense to all the remedy of health according to their proper measure. But it must be explained somewhat more fully what force each of these has, to whom each is appropriate, what things are remissible and what irremissible, and when, or for what causes, remissions are to be granted.

[Col. 0049A] First, an admonition does not threaten punishment if someone does not follow it, but promises a reward to those who willingly comply. Thus the Lord says in the second Gospel: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matthew 19). See: this evangelical reading, placing perfection in human choice, does not compel and does not threaten. Nor does that saying which, praising eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven, adds: “Whoever can accept this, let him accept it” (ibid.).

Yet, when someone has bound himself by vow to perfection, or has ascended to a rank which no one ought to ascend without the virtue of continence, what had been voluntary before this ascent becomes necessary and penal if it is not maintained. Therefore the Lord also says: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9). Before the ascent a person could be lower, yet not worse; after the ascent, however, he is lower and worse. This is concerning admonition.

[Col. 0049B] Indulgence, however, in our view, because it does not choose better things, has a remedy indeed but not a reward; but anyone who departs from it deserves a judgment bringing destruction. For example, we know, as we have learned from the Apostle, that marriage was permitted to the human race for the avoidance of fornication (1 Corinthians 7); its violator deserves eternal punishment, as the same Apostle testifies. For he says: “God will judge fornicators and [Col. 0049C] adulterers” (Hebrews 13).

And this state, as we said concerning admonition, compels no one unless he has first bound himself to it. For it is voluntary, not necessary. Otherwise, everyone who did not take a wife would be a transgressor. But after he has bound himself, let him hear the Apostle saying: “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release” (1 Corinthians 7). Likewise, when the same Apostle spoke of marriage, he did not say, “If a woman marries, she earns a reward”; he said only, “If she marries, she does not sin” (ibid.).

Similarly, if someone invites another to daily fasts, he recommends a course worthy of reward to the person who willingly accepts it and perseveres; but the person who does not comply does not become better than himself. Although he remains inferior to the one who does so, he does not become worse than himself. But if [Col. 0049D] he falls (*ceciderit*; variant: *exciderit*, “falls away”) from his vow, he becomes inferior and worse than himself. If, however, he restrains himself within the bounds of sobriety and a simple table, he does not obtain the rewards of the highest things; but if he falls into revelries and drunkenness, he is said to have done something deserving rebuke and shame.

Therefore these two states, the one higher and the other lower, which before a vow are voluntary but after a vow become necessary, have their own modes and institutions. When observed, as has already been said, they obtain a remedy for some and a reward for others; when not observed, they deserve eternal punishment. In these matters, therefore, one must deliberate before undertaking them, but persevere after undertaking them.

Having briefly set forth these matters, something must be said concerning precept and prohibition. [Col. 0050A] Precepts and prohibitions, then, are of two kinds: some mutable, others immutable.

Immutable precepts are those established by the eternal law: when observed, they confer salvation; when not observed, they take it away. Such are: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbour as yourself”; and, “Honour your father and your mother” (Deut. VI; Lev. XIX; Exod. XX); and whatever is similar to these.

Mutable precepts, however, are those which the eternal law has not established, but which the diligence of later persons has devised on grounds of usefulness—not chiefly in order to obtain salvation, but to safeguard it more securely. Such is that saying of the Apostle: “Avoid a heretical person after a first and second correction” (Tit. III): not because conversation with such persons would in itself [Col. 0050B] harm salvation, but because frequent intercourse might indirectly corrupt the simplicity of some persons. You will find many such things in the canonical enactments.

Likewise, immutable prohibitions are those which speak against vices, such as: “You shall not kill”; “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. XX); and the rest. These are the least commandments of which the Lord says: “Whoever shall break them and so teach, shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). Yet one who observes them will not immediately be worthy of the kingdom of God, because these are beginnings, not perfections.

There are other prohibitions such that, if they had not been prohibited, neither would death result nor salvation be endangered. Yet the venerable authority of the holy Fathers decreed them in this manner, so that they should not harm those now living and so that sincere charity might provide for the restraining [Col. 0050C] or avoidance of greater evils. Such is this: “A cleric who has performed penance for a condemnable crime [*damnali*: apparently for *damnabili*] shall not remain a cleric, nor be admitted to the clergy.” As blessed Augustine says (Dist. 50, c. *Ut constituentur*), this was said from the rigour of discipline, not from a despairing refusal of indulgence. Otherwise there would be an argument against the keys of the Church, concerning which it was said: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVI).

But lest a mind swollen with the hope of ecclesiastical honour should perform penance proudly, it was most sternly decided that after penance has been performed no one should become or remain a cleric. This diligence of later persons is not to be regarded as superfluous: where nothing was taken from salvation, they added something to humility, [Col. 0050D] so that salvation might be more securely fortified. I believe that they had experienced the feigned penances of certain persons, prompted by their affected pursuit of the powers of honours. For the experience of many diseases compels the discovery of many remedies.

Such also is that saying in the Gospel: “Let your speech be, Yes, yes; No, no; but what is beyond this is from evil” (Matt. VI)—from the evil not of the one swearing, but of the one compelling another to swear. It is not that it is evil, in human agreements, to swear when necessity requires; but one who never swears is farther from perjury than one who swears on any occasion whatsoever. For it is said even of the Lord: “The Lord has sworn” (Ps. CIX). And the Apostle says: “An oath is the end of all their controversy” (Heb. VI).
