And the same Apostle, swearing, says: “The truth of Christ is in me” (I Cor. XI). And [Col. 0051A] elsewhere: “I die daily, by your grace, brethren” (I Cor. XV).

Therefore, in matters whose observance secures salvation, or whose neglect unquestionably results in death, no dispensation is to be admitted; but all commandments and prohibitions must be kept exactly as they have been established by the eternal law. But in those matters which the diligence of later persons has established for the rigour of discipline or the safeguarding of salvation, if an honourable or useful compensation follows, a dispensation, carefully considered under the authority of those who preside, may take precedence.

For we read that many such things occurred in the Gospel history, in the Acts of the Apostles, and in the proceedings of councils; and we know that they were afterwards confirmed by the authority of apostolic men. Let us therefore take our first example from the Gospel. The Lord, indeed, when sending his disciples to preach, forbade them both bag and purse (Luke X). Since the earthly life of the Lord Jesus is a discipline of conduct, when the time of his Passion was imminent he restored both bag and purse (Luke XXII), first giving an example in himself that, in traditions of this kind, the necessity of the time must be accommodated.

Likewise Paul, though he had promised to pass through Corinth on his way [Col. 0051B] into Macedonia (Acts XX), when he perceived that this would in no way benefit them, changed his arrangement but not his purpose. Thus he excuses himself, saying: “Therefore, when I intended this, did I use fickleness? Or do I plan according to the flesh, so that with me there should be yes and no?” (II Cor. I). For he did not understand himself to have changed his purpose, since both in coming to them and in not coming to them he sought their salvation. Accordingly he says later: “But I call God as witness upon my soul, that it was to spare you that I came no more to Corinth.”

Nor did he consider that he had changed his arrangement according to the flesh, since one who thinks according to the flesh fails to carry out what he has arranged when he defers to more important persons, or is overcome by profit or display. But a spiritual person fails to carry out what was arranged when, for the salvation of those whom he wishes to benefit, he provides something more advantageous.

It was also confirmed at Jerusalem by the common decision of the apostles, and dispatched through Paul and Barnabas to the brethren throughout Asia, that no one coming to the faith should be held subject to the circumcision of the law [Col. 0051D] (Acts XV). The Apostle himself, writing to the Galatians (Gal. V), says: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. II). Yet this same Paul, although he had opposed Peter to his face (Acts XVI), because Peter had consented to the dissimulation of certain Jews who considered circumcision necessary for salvation, nevertheless yielded to the necessity of the time and circumcised Timothy at Lystra, in order to avoid scandal among the Jews dwelling there. By this act he showed what he elsewhere testifies concerning himself: “I became as a Jew to the Jews, that I might gain the Jews” (I Cor. IX).

This must be understood as spoken not with the cunning of one who lies, but with the sympathy of one who shares another’s feeling: desiring to help each person in the way in which he would wish to be helped if he were in that person’s condition.

The rulers of Churches also judge many matters more strictly according to the tenor of the canons; they tolerate many because of the necessity of the times; and they dispense many for the benefit of persons or in order to avoid the ruin of peoples. Many relaxations made by holy Fathers are likewise confirmed by testimonies of Scripture. Thus holy Leo, pontiff of the holy Roman Church, permitted neophytes to rise to the highest priesthood, though Paul endeavoured, by public teaching, to exclude them from that office (I Tim. III). Likewise, after Arians had been converted, we read that they were received in their offices.

Accordingly, the aforesaid Pope Leo writes to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, concerning what must remain unchanged and what must be moderated by discernment:

> “Just as there are certain things which can be overthrown for no reason whatever, so there are many things which ought to be moderated either because of the necessity of the times [Col. 0052B] or with regard to ages. Yet this consideration must always be preserved: in matters which are doubtful or obscure, we must know that what is to be followed is that which is found neither contrary to evangelical precepts nor opposed to the decrees of the holy Fathers.”

Hence Augustine, in a letter to Boniface:

> “In causes of this kind, where through grave fractures of dissension not this or that individual is endangered, but the ruin of peoples lies before us, something must be taken from severity, so that sincere charity may come to the aid of healing greater evils.”

The same author, against heretics in the same work:

> “‘If,’ they say, ‘we must repent of having been outside the Church in order that we may be saved, how do we remain among you as clerics or even bishops after this repentance?’ This would not occur—since in truth, as must be confessed, it ought not to occur—unless it were healed by compassion for peace itself.”

But let them say this to themselves, and grieve with far greater humility, they who lie in so great a death of severance, so that by this, as it were, wound of Mother Catholic they may return to life. For when a branch that has been cut off is grafted in, another wound is made in the tree so that the branch which was perishing apart from the life of the root may be received and live. But when the received branch has grown together with that which receives it, vigour and fruit follow. If it does not grow together, that branch indeed withers, but the life of the tree remains.

There is also a kind of grafting in which, without cutting off any branch within, that which is outside is grafted in; yet not without a wound to the tree, though only the slightest wound. Thus, when these persons come to the Catholic root, even after repentance for their error, the honour of clerical or episcopal office is not taken from them. There is indeed something, as it were, in the bark of the mother tree contrary to the completeness of severity. Nevertheless, since neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, when prayers are poured out for God’s mercy and the peace of the grafted branches grows together, charity covers a multitude of sins.

Concerning this same dispensation in correcting and moderating, Augustine says in the second book *Against the Letter of Parmenian*:

> “Whenever any one of the brethren and Christians established within the fellowship of the Church is detected in such a sin as to be worthy of anathema, let this be done where there is no danger of schism.”

Later in the same work:

> “When a person’s crime is known and appears detestable to all, so that he has either absolutely no defenders or none of such a kind that schism can occur through them, let the severity of discipline not sleep.”

Later:

> “Correction by many cannot be salutary unless the person corrected does not have a multitude as his companion. But when the same disease has seized very many, nothing remains for the good but grief and groaning, so that through that sign revealed to the holy Ezekiel they may deserve to escape unharmed from their devastation.”

Later:

> “Indeed, when the contagion of sinning has invaded a multitude, the severe mercy of divine discipline is necessary. For counsels of separation are both futile and harmful, and sacrilegious, because they become impious and proud and disturb weak good persons more than they correct resolute evil ones. [Col. 0053B] But when there is an opportunity to address the peoples, a crowd of the wicked must be struck by a general rebuke—especially if some scourge from above, sent by the Lord, provides occasion and opportunity, by which they plainly appear to be beaten according to their deserts.”

Likewise, in a letter to Marcellinus:

> “I am accustomed to hear that it lies within the judge’s power to soften a sentence and punish more mildly than the laws do.”

Then Innocent writes to Rufus, Eusebius, and the other Macedonian bishops:

> “It is the law of our Church that those coming from heretics, if they have nevertheless been baptized there, receive communion only as laymen through the laying on of hands, and that none of them be appointed to even the least honour of the clergy. Therefore let your charity see to it that such things have gone no further; and observe that, as you say, necessity indeed commanded this, but that Churches now established in peace should not presume to do so. Yet, as often happens whenever sin is committed by peoples or by a crowd, because punishment cannot be inflicted upon all on account of their number, it is accustomed to pass unpunished.”

The same writer to the same persons:

> “The supreme deliberation of the priests was that those ordained by Bonosus should be received as ordained, lest they remain with him and a not inconsiderable scandal arise. I think we have overcome the ambiguities.”

It is therefore clear that what was established for remedy and the necessity of the time did not exist at first; and that the ancient rules existed, which the Roman Church preserves as handed down by the apostles or apostolic men, and commands to be preserved by those accustomed to heed her. But the necessity of the time urgently required that this be done. Therefore what necessity devised as a remedy ought certainly to cease together with that which compelled it, when the necessity ceases. For one thing is the lawful order, another the exceptional practice to which the present time impels us.

Yet the canons established at Nicaea permitted this to be done in the case of the Novatians (Council of Nicaea, canon 8). The canon first instituted by the Fathers must be set forth, so that we may see what, or in what manner, was intended or commanded by them:

> “Concerning those who call themselves Cathari—that is, the Pure—who at some time come to the Catholic Church: it has pleased the holy and great synod that, having received the laying on of hands, they should thus remain among the clergy.”

By a similar dispensation, blessed Pope Gregory orders that those returning from the Nestorian heresy be received in their ranks. He writes thus to the bishops in Ireland of the Catholic Church:

> “Therefore, whoever return from the perverse error of Nestorius must confess before the holy assembly of your brotherhood the truth of Christ’s birth, anathematizing Nestorius himself with all his followers and the remaining heresies. Let them also promise to receive and venerate the venerable synods received by the universal Church. Then, without any hesitation, let your Holiness receive them into your body, their proper ranks being preserved for them. Thus, while by your carefulness you examine the hidden disposition of their minds, by true knowledge teach them rightly what they ought to hold, and by gentleness cause them no opposition or difficulty concerning their own ranks, you may snatch them from the mouth of the ancient enemy.”

We have something similar from a letter of Cyril sent to Maximus, deacon of Antioch:

> “I have learned from Paul the monk, dear to me, that your Piety refuses even to this day to embrace communion with the most reverend Bishop John, because certain persons in the Church of Antioch either still think wrongly with Nestorius, or did indeed formerly think so but may perhaps have come to their senses. Let your Modesty therefore ascertain whether they ever assemble openly and irreverently in agreement with Nestorius, and converse together; although they may formerly have had a seared conscience, let them now assemble [the Greek has νῦν, ‘now’], and let them do so without having performed penance for the matters in which they were deceived, although perhaps they are ashamed to confess their transgression.”

Later:

> “But lest we be thought to love contention, let us embrace communion with the most reverend Bishop John, granting him indulgence; and, for the sake of dispensation, let his affair not be dealt with too minutely, strictly, or severely, although he recognizes it as concerning himself. For, as I have said, the matter has great need of the favour of dispensation.”

The same Cyril, to Gennadius, priest and archimandrite:

> “Dispensations (1, q. 7, c. *Dispensationes*) sometimes compel some persons to depart a little from what is due, in order that they may gain something greater. For just as men sailing upon the sea, when a storm presses and the ship is in danger, anxiously throw certain things overboard so that the rest may remain safe, so we too, when we have no complete certainty of saving all matters, disregard some things, lest we suffer the loss of all.”

And later:

> “I write this knowing that your Piety is displeased with our most holy brother and fellow minister, Proclus the bishop, a worshipper of God, because he admitted the abbot of Heliensium, whom the laws of the Church do not recognize as set over Palestine.”

And later:

> “Therefore, let not your Piety withdraw from communion with the most holy and God-beloved Bishop Proclus. For his concern and mine were one, and the manner of the dispensation displeased none of the wise.”

By the same moderate discernment the Roman pontiffs permitted episcopal translations—which had previously been strictly forbidden by apostolic and canonical enactments—to be made when providing for the greater good of the Church. Others also restored to their offices certain bishops deposed by their predecessors, because of the worthiness of the persons [Col. 0055A] and the needs of peoples; their names will be found recorded below.

Certain Roman pontiffs also decreed that sons of priests should not be admitted to the priesthood—not because the acceptance of persons has any weight before God, or because nature, the equal mother of all, can be blamed by anyone, or because sons should be condemned for the wrongdoing of their parents. For the Prophet says: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezek. XVIII); and the Apostle: “If God justifies, who is he that condemns?” (Rom. VIII); and blessed Augustine: “Wherever men are born, if they do not follow their parents’ vices, they shall be honourable and saved.” Rather, this was done to restrain the incontinence of certain priests, or more securely to safeguard the continence of others.

But because they recognized that among such persons were some who were not merely religious but necessary to the Church of God, they moderated the decree; and permitted those so born, whose manner of life had been proved in monasteries or religious churches, to be promoted not only to the priesthood but even to the highest priesthood.

And, to say nothing of our own times, as is read in the acts of Roman pontiffs: Felix III, a Roman by nation, son of the priest Felix, was pope from the time of King Odoacer until the time of King Theodoric. Likewise Agapetus, a Roman by nation, son of the priest Gordian, was supreme pontiff. Gelasius, an African by nation, son of Valerius the bishop, sat three years, eight months, and eighteen days. Silverius, a Campanian by nation, son of Hormisdas [Col. 0055C] the Roman bishop, sat one year, five months, and twenty-one days. Deusdedit, a Roman by nation, son of Stephen the subdeacon, sat three years and twenty-three days. Theodore, a Greek by nation, son of Theodore the bishop, sat six years, five months, and twenty-four days.

That a great many bishops were transferred from one city to another because of the necessity or benefit of the times is clear from the following. Perigenes was ordained bishop at Patrae; but because the citizens of that city refused to receive him, the bishop of the Roman city ordered him to be enthroned at Corinth, the metropolis, after its bishop had died; and he presided over that Church until his death. Alexander, bishop of Seleucia, transferred Desideus to Tarsus in Cilicia. Reverentius was transferred from Arcae in Phoenicia to Tyre. John was transferred from Gordolinia to Proconnesus, and presided over that Church. Palladius was transferred from Helenopolis to Aspone. Alexander was transferred from another Helenopolis to Adrianople. Gregory of Nazianzus was first bishop of a city in Cappadocia called Sasima; afterwards, with the consent of blessed Basil and the other bishops, he was installed at Nazianzus. Melenus first presided over the Church of Sebaste and afterwards was made bishop of Antioch. Theusebius was transferred from Apamea in Asia to Eudoxiopolis, which was formerly called Salabria. Polycarp was transferred from the city of Antapristena in Mysia to Nicopolis in Thrace. Hierophilus was transferred from Trapezopolis in Phrygia [Col. 0056A] to Platinopolis in Thrace. Optimus was transferred from Agadarmia in Phrygia to Antioch in Pisidia. Sistuanus was transferred from Philippopolis in Thrace to the Troad.

The following examples also show that many deposed bishops were restored by the Apostolic See. John Chrysostom was condemned by two synods of orthodox bishops, but was restored again. Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, was deposed, but afterwards recovered his own bishopric. Asclepius was condemned by a synod and later recovered his Church. Lucian, bishop of Adrianople, condemned by Pope Julius, recovered the Church of his bishopric. Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, was deposed and afterwards reconciled to his Church. In like manner Pope Sixtus condemned Polycronius, pontiff of the same Church of Jerusalem, and himself again reconciled him. Pope Innocent condemned Bishop Photinus, but afterwards restored him to his own place in his Church. Pope Gelasius, successor of Felix, both communicated with Bishop Misenus, whom Pope Felix had condemned, and restored him to his Church. Leontius was deposed while a priest, but afterwards became patriarch at Antioch. Pope Gregory IV consecrated as bishop of the holy Church of Signia Theodosius, whom his predecessor Eugenius had deprived of priestly rank. Bishop Ibas too was condemned, but the holy synod canonically restored his Church to him. Pope Nicholas reconciled both Rhotadus, bishop of the holy Church of Soissons, condemned by a synod attended by King Charles, and Sophronius, bishop of Piacenza, deservedly rejected.

Thus Pope John VIII restored Photius Neophytus, deposed by Pope Nicholas, to the patriarchate of Constantinople at the intervention of the emperors Basil, Leo, and Alexander. Writing to the aforesaid emperors, he says:

> “You have written to us, most beloved sons, asking us to open the apostolic bowels of compassion, receive all who are subject to censures in the Church among you, and, in the pursuit of peace and unanimity, restore the lord Archbishop Photius himself, communicating with us, to the supreme dignity of priests and the honour of the patriarchate, lest the Church of God remain longer disturbed by schism [Col. 0056D] and scandal. We, therefore, have embraced your petition as just and pleasing to God; rejoicing that we have found the favourable time which we had long desired, we sent our apocrisiaries to carry out your will—although your Piety, before they arrived, forestalled them by restoring the man by force. Nevertheless, we willingly receive this also. Although we possess the authority to do this, we do not wish to restore him by our own authority; rather, we bring forward testimonies from apostolic decrees and paternal constitutions, not dissolving laws anciently given to the Church, but desiring to restore everything to its benefit in matters in which the inflexible observance of favours uproots and scatters the body of the Church.

> “For the Synod of Nicaea says in its second chapter that ecclesiastical persons often happen to transgress the canons either from necessity or in some other way. Pope Gelasius says that where necessity is absent, the decrees of the holy Fathers should remain unaltered. And the most holy Pope Leo commanded in the same spirit, saying: ‘Where necessity is absent, the enactments of the holy Fathers must by no means be violated. But where necessity exists, let him who has authority dispense them for the good of the Church.’ For a change of law is made out of necessity. And Pope Felix says: ‘It must be considered that, where necessity arises, we often transgress the constitutions of the Fathers.’ And the Council of Carthage, chapter 35, says: ‘We command that clerics be received again into the Church, although they were first deposed in a synod.’ One synod also annuls another for the unity and peace of the Church. And Pope Innocent says in the fifth chapter: ‘Let those promoted by the heretic Bonosus be received again, lest scandals spring up in the Church.’

> “Nor has this Apostolic See, striving for ecclesiastical peace, extended a helping hand only to those deposed for heresy; it has also customarily assisted, with its accustomed compassion, orthodox priests and patriarchs fleeing to it, as it has now done for Photius. For you know that the Apostolic See restored to their former honour the great Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria; Cyril and Polycronius of Jerusalem; John, whom your Charity calls Chrysostom; and Flavian, after they had been deposed by a synod. [Col. 0057C]

> “If, therefore, those ordained by Donatists and by Bonosus, and separated from the thresholds of the orthodox Church by a plenary synod, are received by another synod and counted in the catalogue of priests lest the Church suffer diminution or division, how much more ought men of orthodox faith and blameless life not to be despised, but recalled to their former honour? For this Apostolic See, having once received the keys of the kingdom of heaven from Jesus, the first and great high priest, through Peter, prince of the apostles, when he said to him: ‘I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven’ (Matt. XVIII), has universal power to bind and loose, and, according to Jeremiah, to uproot and to plant (Jer. I).

> “Therefore, using the authority of the same prince of the apostles, Peter, together with all our Church, we command you, our most holy brothers the patriarchs of Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem, the other bishops, and the entire body of the Church of Constantinople, in accordance with your petition, to receive into communion Photius the patriarch, our brother and fellow priest.”

Likewise:

> “Receive him without excuse. Let no one make excuse on account of synods held against him; let no one appeal against him to the judgments of my holy predecessors Nicholas and Adrian. For they were deceived concerning him. Let no one make your subscriptions against him an occasion for schism. For we render everything against him as though it had never been done and void; and we place whatever is against him in the hands of the prince of the apostles, and through him upon the shoulders of Jesus Christ, the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world (John I).”

Likewise:

> “We wish you also to confirm this: after the death of our brother Photius, let no one from secular rank rise to pontifical honour; but let one be chosen from the cardinal priests of that same Church, or from its deacons, or from other priests who belong to the Church of Constantinople.”

Likewise:

> “Since, solicitous for the peace of the Church, we receive our brother Photius, just as Pope Adrian received Tarasius, let no one count this as canonical practice. For the privileges of a few do not make a common law. But if anyone henceforth presumes to do such a thing, he shall be without pardon.”

Likewise, although the ancient rules had established that no cleric should keep the company of women unrelated to him, but only of those who excluded every suspicion, blessed Pope Gregory moderated this rigour for English clerics as follows: if any persons outside holy orders could not contain themselves, they should take wives and receive their stipends outside. He understood it to be a lighter fall if the falling were caught by the bond of marriage than if they were swallowed up by the abyss of unbounded lust in wandering concubinage.

Thus other dispensations admitted after salutary deliberation ought also to cease when the necessity ceases. That which usefulness has suggested or necessity has commanded is not to be regarded as law. Hence one reads in a letter of blessed Pope Leo to the bishops of Africa:

> “It remains, brethren, that you receive concordantly these salutary exhortations; doing nothing through contention, but, unanimous in every zeal of devotion, obey the divine and apostolic constitutions. In no respect allow the most provident decrees of the canons to be violated. For what hitherto we have relaxed in consideration of particular causes must henceforth be observed according to the ancient rules, lest what we granted for a time in pious leniency we punish afterward with just retribution.”

Nor is this to be observed only in ecclesiastical rules, but also in laws themselves. Concerning the venerable Roman laws one reads:

> “Whatever the emperor establishes by letter, decrees upon examination, or commands by edict is unquestionably law. These are called constitutions. [Col. 0058D] Certainly, among these are some called personal enactments, which are not drawn into precedent, because the prince does not intend this either. For what he grants to one person on account of merits, or the punishment he imposes upon someone, or the aid he provides to someone without precedent, does not extend beyond the person.”

We might gather very many reasons and examples of this sort, but for an intelligent reader, and one who knows how to understand much from a little, what has been said ought to suffice. Yet what we have already warned, we warn again: if anyone refers what he reads concerning ecclesiastical sanctions or dispensations to charity, which is the fullness of the law, he will neither err nor sin; and when he departs from the utmost rigour for some probable reason, charity will excuse him—provided that he assumes nothing contrary to the Gospel or contrary to the apostles.

But if any statements taken from secular laws have been inserted which contain judgments of blood, they were not inserted so that an ecclesiastical judge should condemn anyone by them, but so that from them he may make an argument in support of canonical decrees. From them he may recognize with how great a penance that crime or shameful act ought to be punished which judges of the world judge worthy of death or mutilation of limbs. For Roman pontiffs frequently introduce this reasoning in support of their decrees: “If secular laws contain this, how much more should divine laws?”

So far on these matters. Next we shall briefly survey the titles of the individual parts, which contain the purpose of the whole volume, so that the prudent reader may thereby observe what he ought to seek as necessary for himself in each part.

# FIRST PART OF THE DECREE OF SAINT IVO, BISHOP OF CHARTRES

Concerning faith and the sacrament of faith, that is, baptism; the ministry of those to be baptized and of those who baptize, of those to be sealed and of those who seal; and the observance of each matter. And concerning what baptism confers and what confirmation confers.

[Col. 0059]

## 7. CHAPTER 1.—Certain things in the Holy Scriptures are set forth so as to be known and believed; certain things are commanded so as to be observed; certain things are prohibited so that they may not be done. From Augustine’s *Mirror*.

[Col. 0059B]

Who is unaware that in the Holy Scriptures—that is, the lawful, prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic writings endowed with canonical authority—some things are so set forth that they are merely to be known and believed? For example: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. I); and: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I); and whatever divine or human deeds are narrated only to be known.

But other things are commanded so as to be observed, and prohibited so that they may not be done. Such are: “Honour your father and mother”; and: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. XX; Eph. VI).

Of those things written in commanding and forbidding, some are veiled in the mysteries of sacraments. Many of these were commanded to be done by that people of the Old Testament; they are not now done by the Christian people, but are required only to be understood and considered. Such are the Sabbath, for visible rest; unleavened bread, in bread without leaven; Passover, in the slaughter of a sheep; likewise the many kinds of sacrifices and prohibited foods, new moons, and annual solemnities which the Jews still observe; and those observances which do not properly pertain to works of righteousness but are understood to signify something.

For what Christian is required in the seventh year to restore a slave to freedom, and, if that slave refuses to depart, to pierce his ear with an awl at the doorpost, [Col. 0059D] and to do the other things of this kind?

Other things, however, must still be done if they are commanded to be done, and must not be done if they are prohibited—such as those I have mentioned: “Honour your father and mother”; and: “You shall not commit adultery.”

Therefore, concerning those matters which are set forth in the sacred writings, whether by commanding, forbidding, or permitting, so that even now—that is, in the time of the New Testament—they pertain to the exercise of a godly life [Col. 0060B] and to moral conduct: I have undertaken to compose this work which I have taken in hand, so that, as far as God helps me, I may gather together all such matters from the canonical books and assemble them into one place, as into a mirror, so that they may easily be inspected.

For our authors had to set them down as they are set down: so that commandments figuratively expressed by narratives or by their own disputations, and plain matters mixed with figurative matters, might be interwoven while the order of events is preserved, or objections are answered, or those who must be taught are instructed, or those who disdain what is ready and open are in some way renewed by the discovery of hidden things.

## CHAPTER 2.—What Catholic expositors have understood to be proper to the divine Trinity. Augustine, Book I, *On the Trinity*, chapter 4.

[Col. 0060C]

(De consecratione, distinction 3, chapter “All whom.”) All those whom I have been able to read, who wrote before me concerning the Trinity, which is God—Catholic expositors of the ancient and new divine books—have aimed, according to the Scriptures, to teach that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit indicate the divine unity by an inseparable equality of one and the same substance. Therefore they are not three gods, but one God. Although the Father has begotten the Son, and therefore the Son is not he who is the Father; and the Son has been begotten by the Father, and therefore the Father is not he who is the Son; and the Holy Spirit is neither Father nor Son, but only the Spirit of the Father and the Son, himself also coequal with the Father and the Son and belonging to the unity of the Trinity. Nevertheless, it was not the same Trinity that was born of the Virgin Mary, crucified and buried under Pontius Pilate, rose on the third day, and ascended into heaven, but the Son alone. Nor did the same Trinity descend in the form of a dove upon Jesus when he was baptized (Matt. 3), or, on the day of Pentecost after the Lord’s Ascension, when a sound came from heaven as though a violent wind were blowing, and divided tongues as of fire sat upon each one of them; but the Holy Spirit alone (Acts 2). Nor was it the same Trinity that said from heaven, “You are my Son” (Mark 1), whether when he was baptized by John (Matt. 3), or on the mountain when three disciples were with him (Matt. 17), or when the voice sounded, saying, “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John 12); but it was the voice of the Father alone addressed to the Son.

Although the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are inseparable, so too they act inseparably. For with what understanding does a human being comprehend God, when he has not yet comprehended the very understanding by which he wishes to comprehend him? But if he has already comprehended this, let him attend carefully and see that in its own nature there is nothing better; and let him see whether he perceives there any outlines of forms, brilliance of colors, spatial magnitude, separation of parts, extension of bulk, movements through intervals of space, or anything of this kind. Certainly we find none of these things in that in which we find nothing better in our nature—namely, in our understanding, by which, so far as we are capable, we apprehend wisdom. Therefore, what we do not find in our better part, we ought not to seek in him who is far better than our better part.

Thus let us understand God, if we can, as good without quality, great without quantity, a creator without need, present without position, containing all things without disposition, wholly everywhere without place, eternal without time, making mutable things without any change in himself, and suffering nothing. Whoever thinks of God in this way, even if he is not yet altogether able to discover what God is, nevertheless piously takes care, as far as he can, not to think of him as something which he is not. Yet he is without doubt substance—or, if this is better called, essence—which the Greeks call **οὐσία**, “being” or “essence.”

## Chapter 3.—Creed of the Council of Ephesus of Two Hundred Bishops

We believe in one God, the Father almighty, Maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten of the Father, only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father: God from God, light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made, **ὁμοούσιον** with the Father, that is, of one substance with the Father, through whom all things were made in heaven and on earth; who for us human beings and for our salvation came down, was incarnate, became man, suffered, rose again on the third day, and ascended into heaven; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. And [we believe] in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was a time when he was not,” and, “Before he was begotten he was not,” or that he was made from things that did not exist, or who say that the Son of God is from another substance or essence, or **τρεπτόν**, that is, changeable, or mutable—the Catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes them.

Therefore, following in every respect the confessions of all the holy Fathers, which they uttered while the Holy Spirit spoke in them, adhering with equal footsteps to the intention present in their minds, and walking the royal road, we confess that the same only-begotten Word of God, born from the very essence of the Father, true God from true God, light from light, through whom all things were made, whether in heaven or on earth, for the sake of our salvation deigned to stoop to self-emptying.

Having been born and become man—that is, having assumed flesh from the holy Virgin and made it his own—he underwent our birth from the womb, proceeding as a man from a woman, without casting off what he was. For although he became so in the assumption of flesh and blood, he nevertheless preserved what he was: remaining God by nature and in truth. Therefore we do not say that the flesh was changed into the nature of the Godhead, nor that the ineffable essence of the Word of God was transformed into the substance of flesh. For he is unconvertible and immutable, ever remaining the same according to the Scriptures.

Yet he was seen as a little child, still laid in a cradle; and, placed in the bosom of his virgin Mother, he filled all creation as God, existing undivided from his Father. For what is divine is known without quantity and without bulk, and is contained by no boundaries. Thus, confessing that the Word of God was united to flesh according to substance, we worship one Son and Lord, Jesus Christ; we do not set apart and distinguish man and God as though joined together merely by a unity of dignity and authority. For this is a novel expression and nothing more.

Nor do we name Christ specially as the Word of God who is from God, and another Christ likewise as the one specially born from a woman; rather, we acknowledge only one Christ: the Word of God the Father with his own flesh. For then, according to us, he was anointed, although he himself bestowed the Spirit upon the worthy, and not by measure, as the blessed evangelist John declares (John 3).

Nor do we say that the Word of God dwelt in the man commonly understood to have been born from the holy Virgin, lest the man Christ be believed to possess God as an indwelling occupant. For though the Word dwelt in us, and it is said that in Christ “all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily” (Col. 2), nevertheless we understand the Word that became flesh not to dwell as he is said to dwell in the saints; nor shall we define such a dwelling as having occurred in him. But, united according to nature and not wholly transformed into flesh, he made for himself such a dwelling as the human soul is believed to have in relation to its own body.

Therefore Christ is one Son and Lord, not as though a man possessed union with God by some conjunction of dignity and authority. For equality of dignity alone cannot unite natures. Peter and John, after all, are equal to one another in dignity, and for this reason are shown to be apostles and holy disciples; nevertheless, the two are not one. Nor do we consider the mode of union to be one of association or connection. For this does not suffice for natural unity, nor does it arise from the effect of participation—as we too, when joined to God, are one spirit with him (1 Cor. 6). Indeed, we rather avoid the word “conjunction,” as not adequate to signify the mystery of unity.

Nor do we assert that the Word of God the Father is God or Lord of Christ, lest we again divide the one Christ, Son and Lord, more manifestly into two and fall into the crime of sacrilege by making God and Lord to himself. For the Word of God, united to flesh according to hypostasis, as we said above, is indeed God of all and Lord of the universe; nevertheless, he is not his own servant or his own Lord, since it is absurd—or rather impious—to think or say this.

Although he called his Father his God, while he himself is God by nature and from the Father’s essence, still we in no way fail to understand that, while remaining God, he also became man, existing under God according to the due law of human nature. But how can he be God or Lord to himself? Therefore, insofar as accords fittingly with the measure of self-emptying, he declared himself to be under God together with us as man. In this sense also he was made under the law, although he himself promulgated the law and existed as God its lawgiver.

We avoid saying of Christ: “Because of the one assuming, I venerate the assumed; because of the invisible one, I worship the visible.” More terrible still is the statement: “He who was assumed is called God together with him who assumed [him].” Whoever says this again divides into two Christs him who is one, assigning the man separately to one part and God likewise to another part. For he plainly denies the unity according to which not one is co-worshiped with another or called God together with another, but one Christ Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God, is understood, to be venerated with one act of worship together with his own flesh.

We also confess that the same one who was born from God the Father, the only-begotten Son, God, although according to his own nature he was free from every suffering, nevertheless suffered in the flesh for us according to the Scriptures. He was in the crucified body, attributing to himself without suffering the sufferings of his own flesh. For “by the grace of God he tasted death for everyone” (Heb. 2), giving up his own body, although by nature he himself is life and the resurrection of the dead.

For, in order that by ineffable power he might trample death down, become firstborn from the dead in his own flesh (Col. 1), and the firstfruits of those who sleep (1 Cor. 15), and make a way for human nature’s return to incorruption, he tasted death for all by the grace of God, as stated above; and, rising on the third day, he despoiled hell. Therefore, although it is said that the resurrection of the dead came through a human being, we understand the Word who is from God and became human; through him the dominion of death was destroyed.

At the appointed times he will come, as the one Son and Lord, in the glory of the Father, to judge the world in righteousness (Ps. 95), as Scripture testifies. We necessarily add this also. For, proclaiming the death in the flesh of the only-begotten Son of God—that is, Jesus Christ—and likewise confessing his resurrection and ascension into heaven, we celebrate in the churches the bloodless sacrificial service. Thus we also approach the mystical blessings and are sanctified, becoming participants in the holy body and precious blood of Christ, the redeemer of us all—not receiving common flesh, far be it! nor the flesh of a man sanctified and joined to the Word by a unity of dignity, or as one possessing a divine indwelling; but flesh truly life-giving and made the very own flesh of the Word himself.

For, being life by nature as God, because he was united to his own flesh, he declared it life-giving. Therefore, although he says to us, “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood” (John 6), we must not think of it as the flesh of merely one human being from among us. For how could a human being’s flesh be life-giving according to its own nature? Rather, it is the very own flesh of him who for our sake became and was called Son of Man.

We do not in any way divide into two hypostases or persons the sayings which our Savior uttered in the Gospels. For the one and only Christ is not twofold, although he is known to have come together indivisibly into unity from two distinct realities. Just as a human being, composed of soul and body, is not twofold but one from both, so, observing that both human and divine sayings were uttered by the one Christ, we think rightly.

When he says most worthily of himself, “Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14), and, “I and the Father are one” (John 10), we understand his divine and ineffable nature, according to which he is one with his Father by reason of one and the same substance, being the image, character, and radiance of his glory. But when, not at all ignorant of the measure of human nature, he addresses the Jews: “Now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you” (John 8), we likewise acknowledge in the measures of his humanity no less him who is in the likeness and equality of the Father, true God.

For if it must necessarily be believed that he who exists as God by nature became flesh—or rather, an animate human being possessing a rational soul—what reason is there for anyone to be ashamed at his sayings, if he uttered things fitting for a human being? But if one rejects sayings appropriate to a human being, what compelled him, according to us, to become human? And when he mercifully stooped for our sake to voluntary self-emptying, why should he avoid sayings worthy of self-emptying?

We therefore attribute all his Gospel sayings to one person, to the one hypostasis or subsistence of the incarnate Word; for, as it is written, “there is one Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 8). When the Apostle calls him “the high priest of our confession” (Heb. 2), as one offering to God and the Father the confession of our faith, which is continually offered by us ourselves through him to God and the Father, we again assign the title and office of priesthood not to some other human being besides him, but to the one who by nature is the only-begotten Son from God.

For he became mediator between God and human beings (1 Tim. 2), and reconciler unto peace, offering himself to God and the Father for us as a fragrant offering (Eph. 5). Therefore he said: “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire; burnt offerings for sin did not please you; but you prepared a body for me. Then I said: Behold, I come. In the head of the book it is written of me, that I should do your will, O God” (Ps. 39). For he offered his own body, not for himself but for us, as a fragrant offering.

For what offering or sacrifice would he have needed for himself, existing as God free from every sin? If all have sinned and need the grace of God (Rom. 5), because, being what we are, we have become more prone to the excess of mutability, human nature became sick with sins; but he did not. Therefore we needed his glory. Why, then, should it any longer be doubtful that the true Lamb was sacrificed for us? But whoever says that he offered himself both for himself and for us (Isa. 53) cannot at all escape the charge of impiety, since he committed no fault whatever and committed no sin at all. What offering, then, did he need, when there was no deed of his own for which, if one had existed, he might most fittingly have offered?

Again, when he says of the Spirit, “He will glorify me” (John 16), rightly understanding this, we confess one Christ and Son, not as though in need of another’s glory, but as receiving glory from the Holy Spirit; for his Spirit is neither better nor greater than he. But because, in performing human works, he used the power of his own Spirit to manifest his Godhead, he is said to be glorified by that Spirit—just as one’s own power or any discipline may glorify a person.

Although the Spirit is his according to substance, and the personal property is understood according to the fact that he is Spirit and not Son, nevertheless he is not alien from him. For he is called “the Spirit of truth” (John 14), and Christ is the truth. Hence he likewise proceeds from this one, as from God the Father. Indeed, this same Spirit, accomplishing glorious miracles through the hands of the holy apostles, glorified the Lord Jesus Christ after he ascended into heaven. For Christ, who exists as God by nature, was believed to work miracles through his own Spirit. Therefore he said: “He will take of what is mine and declare it to you” (John 16).

The same Spirit is not called wise or powerful by participation in another, for he is perfect in every respect and lacks absolutely no good. For he is believed to be the Spirit of the Father’s power and wisdom—that is, of the Son; and therefore he is shown to be power and wisdom in reality and subsistence itself.

Therefore, because the holy Virgin bodily bore God united to flesh according to hypostasis, we confess her to be **Theotokos**, “God-bearer” or “Mother of God.” Not because the nature of the Word received from flesh the beginning of its existence: for “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1); and he is the creator of the ages, coeternal with the Father, and maker of all things. Rather, as we said above, because, uniting human nature to himself according to hypostasis, he underwent birth from the bodily womb.

Nor did he require this birth, which took place in the last times of the age, out of necessity for his own nature, but in order to bless the firstfruits of our substance; so that, when a woman had brought forth God united to flesh, the curse pronounced against the entire human race might cease and might no longer consign our bodies to death. Thus, abolishing the saying, “In sorrow you shall bear children” (Gen. 3), he showed true what he had foretold through the prophet’s voice: “Death has been swallowed up in victory” (1 Cor. 15), and again, “God has taken away every tear from every face” (Rev. 7).

For this reason we say that he, by an act of dispensation, then blessed the wedding itself when he deigned to be present at Cana of Galilee, called together with the holy apostles (John 2). These things we have been taught to believe by the holy apostles and evangelists, by all divinely inspired Scripture (2 Tim. 3), and also by the truth-supported confessions of the blessed Fathers. It is now fitting that your piety agree with all these things and consent without any deceit. Those matters which it is necessary for your piety to anathematize are appended to this our letter.

I. If anyone does not confess that Emmanuel is truly God, and therefore that the holy Virgin is Theotokos—for she bore according to the flesh the Word of God made flesh, according as it is written, “And the Word became flesh” (John 1)—let him be anathema.

II. If anyone does not confess that the Word of God the Father was united to flesh according to substance, and that Christ is one with his own flesh, the same one undoubtedly God and human being together, let him be anathema.

III. If anyone divides the hypostases in the one Christ after the union, joining them merely by an association according to dignity, or even authority or power, rather than by a conjunction effected through natural unity, let him be anathema.

IV. If anyone divides into two persons or hypostases the sayings contained in the Gospel and apostolic writings, or those spoken by the saints concerning Christ or by Christ himself concerning himself; and believes that some of them are to be applied to a human being understood separately apart from the Word of God, while assigning others, as worthy of God, to the Word of God the Father alone, let him be anathema.

V. If anyone dares to call Christ a **θεοφόρον**, that is, “God-bearing,” human being, rather than confessing him truly to be God, as the one Son by nature, according as the Word became flesh and shared likewise with us in flesh and blood, let him be anathema.

VI. If anyone says that the Word of God the Father is God or Lord of Christ, rather than confessing that the same one is God and human being together because, according to the Scriptures, the Word became flesh, let him be anathema.

VII. If anyone says that Jesus as a human being was aided by the operative Word of God, and ascribes the dignity of the only-begotten to another existing apart from him, let him be anathema.

VIII. If anyone dares to say that the assumed human being ought to be co-worshiped with the Word of God and jointly called God as one other with another—for the addition of the single syllable *con-* compels this meaning—but does not rather worship Emmanuel with one reverence and render him one glorification, according as the Word became flesh, let him be anathema.

IX. If anyone says that the one Lord Jesus Christ was glorified by the Holy Spirit as by an alien power which he employed, and from which he received efficacy against unclean spirits and through which he accomplished divine signs, rather than saying that the Spirit is his own, as also [the Spirit] is the Father’s, through whom he worked the signs, let him be anathema.

X. Divine Scripture recalls that Christ was made the high priest and apostle of our confession (Eph. 5). For he offered himself for us to God the Father as a fragrant offering. If, therefore, anyone says that another besides God the Word himself was made our high priest and apostle, when the Word became flesh and human according to us—namely, some distinct human being from a woman besides him—and if anyone says that he offered himself as an offering for his own sake and not rather for us alone (for he who knew no sin needed no offering), let him be anathema.

XI. If anyone does not confess that the Lord’s flesh is life-giving, as the very own flesh of the Word of God the Father, but [treats it] as that of some other being besides him, joined to him according to dignity or because it possessed only a divine indwelling, rather than confessing it, as we have said, to be life-giving because it became the own flesh of the Word of God, to whom it is possible to give life to all things, let him be anathema.

XII. If anyone does not confess that the Word of God suffered in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh, tasted death in the flesh, and became firstborn from the dead—inasmuch as he is life and giver of life as God—let him be anathema.

## Chapter 4.—Augustine in *On Faith to Peter the Deacon*: One God

Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are naturally one God, in whose name we have been baptized. For while Father is one name, Son another, and Holy Spirit another, “God” is nevertheless the one name of the nature of these three. He says in Deuteronomy: “See, see, that I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Deut. 32); and of him it is said: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, God is one” (Deut. 6); and, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matt. 4).

## Chapter 5.—Lord

Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the holy Trinity—are alone by nature the true God and Lord. For, although we may not worship three gods but only one true God, nevertheless, just as the Father is called true God, as the Apostle testifies when he says, “You turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God, and to await his Son from heaven, Jesus, whom he raised from the dead” (1 Thess. 1), so also John the apostle declares the Son to be true God, saying: “We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, that we may know the true God; and we are in his true Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5).

And because he is true God, he is also truth, as he himself teaches us, saying: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). Concerning the Holy Spirit also John the apostle says: “For the Spirit is truth” (ibid.). And one who is truth cannot fail to be true God by nature. The apostle Paul also confesses him to be God, saying: “Your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God, and you are not your own. For you were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6).

## Chapter 6.—Eternal

Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the holy Trinity—are one true God, eternal without beginning. Therefore it is written: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God” (John 1). This eternity is again indicated in the psalm where it is said: “But God is our king before the ages” (Ps. 73). And elsewhere: “His eternal power also and divinity” (Rom. 1).

## Chapter 7.—Immutable

Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that the holy Trinity, the one true God, is, just as eternal, so also alone naturally immutable. This is what he signifies when he says to his servant Moses: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3). To him it is said in the psalm: “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; and all will grow old like a garment. You will change them like a covering, and they will be changed; but you are the same” (Ps. 101).

## Chapter 8.—Creator of All Things

Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that the holy Trinity, the one true God, is the Creator of all things visible and invisible. Of him it is said in the Psalms: “Blessed is he whose helper is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them” (Ps. 143). The Apostle also says of him: “For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory for ages of ages” (Rom. 11).

## Chapter 9.—Three Persons

Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one nature, but are truly three persons. The Father alone is he who said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17); the Son alone is he over whom the voice of the Father alone sounded when, according to his humanity, he was baptized in the Jordan. He is the only-begotten one who alone assumed flesh. The Holy Spirit of the Father and Son alone is he who descended in the form of a dove upon Christ as he was baptized and came up out of the water (Matt. 3), and who, on the fiftieth day after Christ’s resurrection, came in the appearance of fiery tongues and filled the faithful assembled in one place (Acts 1).

But that voice which God the Father alone spoke; that flesh by which the only-begotten God alone became man; that dove, in whose form the Holy Spirit descended upon Christ; and those fiery tongues, in whose appearance he filled the faithful gathered in one place—all are works of the whole Trinity, that is, of the one God who made all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible.

## Chapter 10.—The Son of the Father Alone; the Spirit of Both

Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that God the Son alone—that is, one person of the Trinity—is Son of God the Father alone; but that the Holy Spirit, likewise one person of the Trinity, is not the Spirit of the Father alone, but at once the Spirit of the Father and of the Son. For God, showing that the Son alone is begotten from the Father, says: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3); and shortly afterward: “But whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God” (ibid.).

The Apostle teaches that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit both of the Father and of the Son, saying: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Rom. 8). And he continues: “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (ibid.).

## Chapter 11.—Proceeding Ever from Both

Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that the same Holy Spirit, who is the one Spirit of the Father and the Son, proceeds from the Father and the Son. For the Son says: “When the Spirit of truth comes, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15), where he teaches that he is his own Spirit, because he himself is truth.

Prophetic and apostolic teaching also commends to us that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. Isaiah says concerning the Son: “He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the Spirit of his lips he will kill the impious one” (Isa. 11). And the Apostle says concerning him: “Whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the Spirit of his mouth” (2 Thess. 2). The only-begotten Son of God himself indicates that [the Spirit] is the Spirit of his mouth when, after his resurrection, breathing upon the disciples, he says: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20). John says in the Apocalypse concerning the mouth of the Lord Jesus: “A sword sharp on both sides proceeded” (Rev. 1). The Spirit of his mouth is that very sword which proceeds from his mouth.

## Chapter 12.—God Is Immeasurable in Power, Not in Bulk

Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that the Trinity, God, is immeasurable in power, not in bulk, and that every spiritual and bodily creature is contained by his power and presence. For God the Father says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23). It is said of the wisdom of God, who is his Son: “For she reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8). We likewise read concerning the Holy Spirit: “For the Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” (Wis. 1). And David the prophet says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, or where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 131).

## Chapter 13.—The Son Alone Incarnate

Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that one person of the Trinity—God the Son, who alone was born from the nature of God the Father and is of one and the same nature with the Father—voluntarily, in the Spirit and in the fullness of time, according to the assumption of the form of a servant (Gal. 4), was conceived in the Virgin and born from the Virgin, the Word made flesh. He is the one who was born essentially from the Father and was essentially conceived and born from the Virgin; he is one, of one nature with the Father and of one nature with the Virgin. Of him it is said concerning God the Father: “Before the ages he founded me, and before all hills he begot me” (Prov. 8). The Apostle also said of him: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4).

## Chapter 14.—True God, True Human Being

Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is, as from God the Father, full and perfect Lord; so from Mary the Virgin, full and perfect human being. That is, the Word, the Lord, has true flesh of our race without sin and a rational soul. The Son of God himself clearly showed this when he said of his flesh: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” (Luke 24). He showed that he has a soul by these words: “Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my soul, and I will take it again” (John 10). He also showed that he possesses the understanding of a soul in saying: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11). And God says of him through the prophet: “Behold, my servant shall understand; he shall be exalted and lifted up and shall be very high” (Isa. 52).

For blessed Peter too, according to the prophecy of holy David, confesses flesh and soul in Christ. Speaking of him, blessed Peter says: “Therefore, being a prophet and knowing that God had sworn to him by oath that one from the fruit of his loins would sit upon his throne” (Acts 2), he foresaw and spoke concerning Christ’s resurrection: “For his soul was not left in hell, nor did his flesh see corruption” (Ps. 15).

## Chapter 15.—The One Word Made All Times and Gave the Law, Being Made under the Law

Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that the one and same true God, the Word, who together with God the Father and God the Holy Spirit made all times and gave the law to Moses on Mount Sinai, ordained through angels (Exod. 20), is the very Word, God made flesh, who, when the fullness of time came, was sent by the Father and the Holy Spirit. He alone was made from the woman whom he made; he alone was made under the law which he gave (Gal. 4).

## Chapter 16.—One, Unconfused and Inseparable

Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that two natures remain unconfused and inseparable in the Word of God who became flesh: one truly divine, which he has in common with the Father, according to which he says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10); “Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14); and, “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (ibid.). According to this nature the Apostle called him “the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of his substance” (Heb. 1). The other is truly human, according to which God incarnate himself says: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14).

## Chapter 17.—One Person

Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that God the Word made flesh has one person of his divinity and his flesh. For God the Word deigned truly to unite a complete human nature to himself; and, while his divinity remained, the Word so became flesh that, although by nature the Word is not the same thing as flesh—for the truth of two natures remains in Christ—nevertheless, according to one person, the same Word became flesh from the very beginning of maternal conception.

For God the Word did not assume a human person, but a nature; and into the eternal person of divinity he assumed the temporal substance of flesh. Therefore Christ, the Word made flesh, is one: he who is both from the fathers according to the flesh and “God over all, blessed for ages,” the one Jesus. To him the Father also says: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. IX). Here is signified an eternal birth before all time and without beginning. The evangelist also says concerning him: “His name was called Jesus, as it had been named by the angel before he was conceived in the womb” (Luke 2).

## Chapter 18.—The Word Conceived

Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that Christ’s flesh was not conceived in the Virgin’s womb without divinity, before it was assumed by the Word; rather, God the Word himself was conceived in the assumption of his flesh, and the flesh itself was conceived through the incarnation of the Word of God.

### Chapter 19.—That the Word of God, made flesh, offered Himself as a sacrifice for us.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that the only-begotten God the Word, made flesh, offered Himself for us as a sacrifice and victim to God, for an odor of sweetness [Col. 0071D] (Eph. 5); to whom, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, animals were sacrificed by the patriarchs, prophets, and priests in the time of the Old Testament; and to whom now—that is, in the time of the New Testament—together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, with whom He possesses one divinity, the holy Catholic Church throughout the whole world does not cease to offer the sacrifice of bread and wine in faith and charity.

For in those bodily victims there was a signification of Christ’s flesh, which He, being without sin, was to offer for our sins, and of the blood which He was to shed for the remission of our sins. But in this sacrifice there is thanksgiving and commemoration of Christ’s flesh, which He offered for us, and of the blood [Col. 0072A] which that same God shed for us. Of Him blessed Paul says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to govern the Church of God, which He acquired by His own blood” (Acts 20).

Therefore, in those sacrifices what was to be given to us was signified figuratively; in this sacrifice what has now been given to us is shown openly. In those sacrifices the Son of God, to be slain for the ungodly, was foretold; but in this sacrifice He is proclaimed as slain for the ungodly. As the Apostle testifies: “For while we were still weak, at the appointed time Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. 5); and, “while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son” (ibid.).

### Chapter 20.—The Word always possesses true flesh.

[Col. 0072B] Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that the Word made flesh always possesses that same true human flesh in which God the Word was born from the Virgin; in which He was crucified and died; in which He rose again and ascended into heaven; at the right hand of God, in which He sits; and in which He will also come to judge the living and the dead. Therefore the apostles heard from the angels: “Thus shall He come, as you saw Him going into heaven” (Acts 1). And blessed John says: “Behold, He shall come with the clouds, and every eye shall see Him, even those who crucified Him; and every tribe of the earth shall see Him” (Rev. 1).

### Chapter 21.—Concerning every good creature.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that the Trinity—God, namely Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is by nature the highest and unchangeable [Col. 0072C] good; and that all natures were created by Him. They are indeed good, because they were made by the highest Good; but mutable, because they were made from nothing. No nature is evil, because every nature, insofar as it is nature, is good. But because its good can both diminish and increase, it is called evil to the extent that its good is diminished. For evil is nothing other than the deprivation of good.

Hence it is evident that the rational creature has a twofold evil: one, by which it voluntarily falls away from the highest Good, its Creator; the other, by which it will unwillingly be punished by the punishment of eternal fire. It will suffer the latter justly, because it admitted the former unjustly. And it, having not kept in itself the order of divine institution, will not escape the order of divine retribution.

### Chapter 22.—Nothing besides God is of the same nature.

[Col. 0072D]

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that neither angels nor any other creature are of the same nature as the supreme Trinity, which according to its natural divinity is one God by nature—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For He who made and those things which He made could not be of one nature.

### Chapter 23.—Concerning the immutable and the mutable.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that every creature, naturally mutable, was made by the immutable God; yet that no creature of the holy angels can now be changed for the worse, because they received eternal blessedness in such a way that they enjoy God steadfastly and cannot be deprived of it. But the fact itself that they cannot in any way be changed for the worse from that state of blessedness in which they are blessed is not innate to them by nature; rather, after they were created, it was bestowed by the bounty of divine grace. For if angels had been made naturally immutable, the devil and his angels would never have fallen from their fellowship.

### Chapter 24.—Concerning the difference between rational and irrational beings.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that among every creature, spiritual and bodily, made by the supreme Trinity, only angelic and human spirits have received from God the faculty of understanding. The spirits of brute animals, however, have not received rational intelligence and therefore cannot possess it at all. Hence it is said to human beings: “Do not [Col. 0073B] become like horse and mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31). Therefore neither can the souls of cattle ever pass into human beings, nor the souls of human beings into cattle.

### Chapter 25.—Concerning free choice.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that the first human beings—Adam and his wife—were created good, upright, and without sin, with free choice, by which they could, if they wished, always serve and obey God with humble and good will; and by that same free choice they could, if they wished, sin by their own will. They sinned not by necessity but by their own will; and by that sin human nature was so changed for the worse that not only did death obtain dominion through sin in those first human beings themselves, but sin also passed into all [Col. 0073C] human beings (Rom. 5), together with the dominion of death.

### Chapter 26.—Concerning original sin and its remedy.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that every human being conceived through intercourse between man and woman is born with original sin, subject to impiety and liable to death; and is therefore born by nature a child of wrath, of whom the Apostle says: “We too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2). From that wrath no one is delivered except through faith in the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, who was conceived without sin, born without sin, died without sin, and was made sin for us—that is, was made a sacrifice for our sins. For in the Old Testament the sacrifices offered for sins were called “sins.” [Col. 0073D] In all these there was a signification of Christ, because He is the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world (John 1).

### Chapter 27.—Concerning baptism.

(*On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter “Firmissime.”) Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that not only human beings already exercising reason, but also little children—whether they begin to live in their mothers’ wombs and die there, or, having already been born of their mothers, pass from this world without the sacrament of holy baptism, which is given in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are to be punished eternally with the everlasting punishment of eternal fire. For although they have committed no sin by personal action, nevertheless by bodily conception and birth they have incurred the condemnation of original sin [Col. 0074A].

### Chapter 28.—Concerning judgment.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead in order that, at His coming, He may raise and glorify those human beings whom He here freely justifies by the gift of His grace through faith, and to whom, once justified, He grants perseverance in the faith and charity of the holy Mother Church until the end; and according to His promise may make them equal to the holy angels and bring them to that state in which they are perfectly good, insofar as He grants this to each, and from which perfection they can thereafter no longer change. There will be diverse glory among the saints there, but one eternal life for all.

But the devil and his angels will be sent by Christ into eternal fire [Col. 0074B], where they will never be deprived of the punishment prepared for them by divine justice. Together with the devil, ungodly and wicked human beings will burn, their bodies having been resumed, in the punishment of eternal burning—those of whom Scripture says, “They imitate him who belong to his party” (Wis. 2), because they imitated him in evil works and did not perform fitting repentance before the end of the present life.

### Chapter 29.—Repentance must be performed before the end of the present life.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that the resurrection of the flesh at the coming of the Lord will be common to all human beings, both good and evil; but the recompense of God’s justice will differ for the good and the evil, as the Apostle says: “We shall all [Col. 0074C] rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15). The righteous, who will go into eternal life, will be changed. The Apostle shows this when he says: “The dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (ibid.). And, showing what that change will be, he adds: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (ibid.).

In their bodies will take place what the Apostle himself says: “It is sown in corruption; it shall rise in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor; it shall rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it shall rise in power. A natural body is sown; a spiritual body shall rise” (ibid.). He says this not because the body itself will become spirit, but because, made alive by the Spirit, it will remain immortal and incorruptible. Thus at that time the body is called spiritual, although it is not spirit but remains body, just as it is now called natural, although [Col. 0074D] it is not soul but body.

### Chapter 30.—Concerning martyrdom, repentance, and baptism.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that excepting those baptized in their own blood for Christ’s name, no one will receive eternal life unless in this life he has been converted from his evils through repentance and faith, and has been delivered through the sacrament of faith and repentance—that is, through baptism. Adults must both repent of their evils, hold the Catholic faith according to the rule of truth, and receive the sacrament of baptism. But for little children, who can neither believe by their own will nor repent for the sin which they inherit originally, the sacrament of faith, which is holy baptism, suffices for salvation so long as their age is incapable of reason [Col. 0075A].

### Chapter 31.—Concerning the grace of repentance.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that no human being here can repent unless God has enlightened and converted him by gratuitous mercy. For the Apostle says: “Perhaps God may grant them repentance for the acknowledgment of the truth, and they may return to their senses from the snares of the devil” (2 Tim. 2).

### Chapter 32.—Concerning the grace of obedience.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that a person not prevented by ignorance of letters, by any weakness, or by adversity may indeed either read the holy words [Col. 0075B] of the Law and the Gospel, or hear them from the mouth of some preacher; but that no one can obey the divine commandments unless God has first acted upon him by His grace, so that he may receive in his heart as well as in his body what he hears, and, having received from God good will and power, may both will and be able to perform God’s commandments. For “neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (1 Cor. 3), because He also works in us both to will and to accomplish according to good will (Phil. 2).

### Chapter 33.—God knows all things unchangeably.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that to the immutable God not only all things past, but also all things future, are most fully and unchangeably known; to whom it is said: “You are the knower of hidden things, who know all things before [Col. 0075C] they occur” (Dan. 13).

### Chapter 34.—Concerning knowledge.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that the immutable Trinity, God, is the most certain knower of all things and deeds, both His own and human; and that before all ages He knew to whom He would grant grace through faith, without which no one could, from the beginning of the world to its end, be absolved from the guilt of either original or actual sin. “For those whom God foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son” (Rom. 8).

### Chapter 35.—Concerning predestination.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that all whom God made vessels of mercy by gratuitous goodness were predestined by God before the foundation of the world for adoption as sons of God; that none of those whom God predestined for the kingdom of heaven can perish; and that none of those whom God did not predestine for life can be saved by any means. For predestination is that preparation of gratuitous gift by which, as the Apostle says, we have been “predestined for adoption as sons of God through Jesus Christ unto Himself” [Col. 0075D] (Eph. 1).

### Chapter 36.—Baptism outside the Church does not benefit.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that the sacrament of baptism may exist not only within the Catholic Church but also among heretics who baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; but that it cannot benefit outside the Catholic Church. Indeed, just as salvation is conferred through the sacrament of baptism upon those who rightly believe within the Church, so destruction is increased by that same baptism for those baptized outside the Church if they do not return to the Church. So great is the force of the unity of ecclesiastical fellowship for salvation that one is not saved by baptism when it is not given where it ought to be given.

Nevertheless, baptism is present even in a person baptized outside the Church, but it is present in one who is separated for judgment. Since it is clear that baptism, wherever it has been given, is to be given only once, even if it has been given by heretics in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, it must be reverently recognized and therefore never repeated. For the Savior says: “He who has been washed once does not need [Col. 0076A] except to wash his feet” (John 13).
