### Chapter 37.—On the same subject.

[Col. 0076B] Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that everyone baptized outside the Catholic Church cannot become a participant in eternal life unless, before the end of this life, he has been restored and incorporated into the Catholic Church. For, says the Apostle, “If I have all faith and know all mysteries, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13). For in the days of the flood, we read that no one outside the ark could be saved (Gen. 7).

### Chapter 38.—Concerning heretics and schismatics.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that not only all pagans, but also all Jews, heretics, and schismatics who end their lives outside the Catholic Church, will go into the eternal fire prepared [Col. 0076C] for the devil and his angels.

### Chapter 39.—On the same subject.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that any heretic or schismatic baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit cannot be saved if he has not been joined to the Catholic Church, however many alms he may have given, even if he has shed his blood for Christ’s name. For no baptism, no matter how abundant an almsgiving, and no death suffered for Christ’s name can avail for salvation to anyone who does not maintain the unity of the Church, while heretical or schismatic perversity, which leads to death, persists in him.

### Chapter 40.—Concerning criminal Catholics.

[Col. 0076D]

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that not all who are baptized within the Catholic Church will receive eternal life, but those who, having received baptism, live rightly—that is, who abstain from the vices and desires of the flesh. For just as unbelieving heretics and schismatics will not possess the kingdom of heaven, so criminal Catholics cannot possess it.

### Chapter 41.—Concerning the necessity of forgiveness.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that even righteous and holy persons—except those who died as baptized little children—cannot live here without sin; and that it is always necessary for every person, until the end of the present life, to cleanse his sins by alms [Col. 0077A] and humbly and sincerely seek forgiveness from God.

### Chapter 42.—Concerning foods and marriage.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that every creature of God is good, and that nothing received with thanksgiving is to be rejected (1 Tim. 4). Servants of God who abstain from meat or wine should not reject these things as unclean, since they were made by God, but should abstain from stronger food and drink solely for bodily discipline.

Marriage likewise is divinely instituted and blessed. It is indeed better for anyone to remain unmarried, so that he may more freely and fully consider the things of God and how to please God. Yet for those who have not vowed continence, it is no sin if a woman marries or a man takes a wife [Col. 0077B] (1 Cor. 7). Nor were only first marriages instituted by God; second and third marriages also were allowed because of the weakness of those unable to remain continent. But those who, whether married or free from marriage, have vowed continence to God are exceedingly blameworthy if the former wish to seek marital intercourse, from which they professed by their own free will that they would abstain, or if the latter wish to return to that from which they professed by common consent that they would withdraw.

### Chapter 43.—Concerning baptism.

Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in the least, that the Catholic Church is God’s threshing floor, and that chaff is contained in it, mingled with wheat until the end of the age: that is, good and evil persons are mixed together in communion of the sacraments; and in every profession—whether monks, clergy, or laity—there are good persons and, at the same time, bad ones. The good are not to be abandoned because of the bad; rather, the bad are to be tolerated for the sake of the good, insofar as faith requires and the principle of charity permits: that is, provided that they neither scatter the seed of any unbelief in the Church nor lead brethren to any evil through deadly imitation.

Nor can anyone who rightly believes and lives well within the Catholic Church ever be stained by another’s sin, if he gives neither consent nor approval to anyone’s sins. It is beneficial that bad persons be tolerated by good persons within the Church, if this is done by living well among them and remaining well among them, so that, seeing and hearing what is good, they may reject their own evils; and, knowing that they will be judged by God for their evil deeds, may return to their senses. [Col. 0077D] Thus, forestalled by the gift of grace, they may be ashamed of their iniquities and converted by God’s mercy to a good life.

But good persons established within the Catholic Church ought to be separated from bad persons only by the dissimilarity of their works, so that they may not share the evil deeds by which the others are guilty with those with whom they share the divine sacraments. At the end of the age, however, the good will be separated bodily from the evil, when Christ comes with His winnowing fan in His hand; He will thoroughly cleanse His threshing floor, gather His wheat into the barn, and burn the chaff with unquenchable fire (Matt. 3). Then by just judgment He will separate righteous from unrighteous, good from evil, upright from perverse; He will place the good at His right hand and the evil at His left. By the everlasting and unchangeable sentence issued from His mouth in righteous and eternal judgment, all the wicked will go into eternal burning [Col. 0078A], while the righteous will go into eternal life: the wicked ever to burn with the devil, but the righteous to reign with Christ.

### Chapter 44.—Forty chapters of the true faith to be held most firmly.

For the present, faithfully believe, courageously hold, and truly and patiently defend these forty chapters which pertain most firmly to the rule of true faith. If you discover anyone teaching doctrines contrary to these, flee him as a plague and reject him as a heretic. For these things which we have set forth agree with the Catholic faith in such a way that anyone who wishes to oppose not merely all of them but even a single one, in obstinately resisting any one of these [Col. 0078B] and not hesitating to teach what is contrary to it, evidently proves himself a heretic, an enemy of the Christian faith, and one to be anathematized by all Catholics.

### Chapter 45.—Leo, to all bishops throughout Sicily, concerning baptism (Letter 4).

The power of baptism properly creates a new creature from the old in the death of the Crucified One and in the resurrection from the dead, so that both Christ’s death and life may operate in those reborn. The Apostle says: “Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into His death? For we have been buried with Him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life. For if we have been made one with the likeness of His death, we shall likewise be one with His resurrection” [Col. 0078C] (Rom. 6).

And there are the other things more fully argued by the teacher of the Gentiles in commending the sacrament of baptism, so that from the spirit of this teaching it might appear that, for human children being regenerated and adopted in the Son of God, that day and that time were chosen in which those things done in the members corresponded, through the likeness and form of the mystery, to those accomplished in Christ Himself, the head. For in the rule of baptism, death intervenes through the killing of sin; the threefold immersion imitates the three-day burial; and the lifting from the waters is like the resurrection from the tomb.

Therefore the very character of the rite teaches that the lawful day for the general celebration of grace is that on which both the power of the gift and the form of the action arose. Of great value in confirming this is the fact that the Lord Jesus Christ Himself, after He rose from the dead, gave both the form and authority of baptizing to His disciples—in whom all the rulers of the Churches were instructed—saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” [Col. 0078D] (Matt. 28). He could surely have instructed them about this before His passion, had He not wished it to be properly understood that the grace of regeneration began from His resurrection.

Moreover, the solemn festival of Pentecost, consecrated by the coming of the Holy Spirit, is also added to this observance; it depends upon the occasion of the Paschal feast. Whereas other feasts belong to other days, this one always occurs conspicuously on the day marked by the Lord’s resurrection, extending, as it were, the hand of aiding grace and inviting those whom illness, the length of a journey, or difficulty of sea travel has prevented from coming from Easter Day, so that, though hindered by any necessity, they may obtain the fulfilment of their desire through the gift of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0079A].

### Chapter 46.—The same, on the same matter, the same Letter 4.

That we defend this not from our own persuasion but observe it on apostolic authority, we prove by a sufficiently fitting example, following the blessed Apostle Peter. On the very day when the promised coming of the Holy Spirit filled the whole number of believers, Peter consecrated through the washing of baptism three thousand people converted by his preaching. The holy Scripture containing the Acts of the Apostles teaches this in its faithful history, saying: “When they heard this, they were pierced in the heart and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles: ‘What shall we do, brothers?’ But Peter said to them: ‘Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ for the remission of your sins, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit’” [Col. 0079B] (Acts 2).

### Chapter 47.—The same: baptism is not to be celebrated at Epiphany. Leo, to all bishops throughout Sicily (Letter 4, chapter 6).

(*On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter “Si quis autem.”) If anyone thinks that the feast of Epiphany, which in its proper order is to be venerated with due honor, has the privilege of baptism because some suppose that on that day the Lord came to the baptism [Col. 0079C] of Saint John, let him know that that baptism had a different grace and rationale, and did not belong to the same power by which those are reborn through the Holy Spirit of whom it is said: “Who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God” (John 1).

For the Lord, needing no remission of sin and seeking no remedy of rebirth, wished to be baptized just as He also wished to be circumcised and to have an offering of purification offered for Himself. Thus He who had been made of a woman, as the Apostle says, was also made under the Law (Gal. 4)—a Law which He had not come to abolish but to fulfil (Matt. 5), and, by fulfilling, to bring to its end, as the blessed Apostle proclaims: “For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10). But He established in Himself the sacrament of His own baptism, because, holding primacy in all things, He showed Himself to be the beginning. And He established the power of regeneration when from His side flowed the blood of redemption and the water of baptism [Col. 0079D].

### Chapter 48.—The same Leo I, to Leo, bishop of Ravenna, Letter 38, chapter 1. Concerning persons whose baptism is unknown.

(*On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter “Cum itaque.”) Therefore, when a person desiring regeneration remembers nothing of his baptism, and no other person able to testify knows that he was consecrated, there is no possibility for sin to intrude in this matter, since in this respect of conscience neither the one who is consecrated is guilty nor the one who consecrates.

We know indeed that it is an inexpiable crime whenever, in accordance with the doctrine of heretics and contrary to the institutions of the holy Fathers, anyone is compelled to undergo twice the washing granted once for regeneration; for the Apostolic pronouncement protests against this, proclaiming to us one Godhead in the Trinity, one confession in faith, and one sacrament in baptism [Col. 0080A] (Eph. 4). But in this case no similar danger is feared, because something whose occurrence is wholly unknown cannot incur the charge of repetition.

Therefore, whenever a person of this kind is encountered, first investigate through careful examination; and, unless perhaps death is imminent, inquire over a long period whether there is absolutely no one who can aid the ignorance of the person who does not know by his testimony. When it is established that one needing the sacrament of baptism is prevented solely by an empty suspicion, let him approach without fear to receive grace, of which he knows no trace in himself. Let us not fear to open to him the gate of salvation, which he is never shown to have entered [Col. 0080B].

### Chapter 49.—Gregory, *Morals*, book 4, chapter 2. That among the ancients the same effect was produced by faith, the efficacy of sacrifice, and the mystery of circumcision as baptism produces among us.

(*On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter “Quod autem.”) What the water of baptism accomplishes among us, among the ancients either faith alone accomplished for little children, or the efficacy of sacrifice for adults, or the mystery of circumcision for those descended from Abraham’s stock.

### Chapter 50.—On the same matter. Augustine, to Valerius, against Julian, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, chapter 11.

[Col. 0080C] From the time circumcision was instituted among the people of God, it then functioned as a seal of the righteousness of faith and, as a sign of purification, availed also for little children against original and ancient sin; just as baptism began to avail for the renewal of the human being from the time it was instituted.

### Chapter 51.—First Council of Braga, chapter 23.

It has been decreed that no one shall omit the order of baptism which the metropolitan Church of Braga formerly observed, and which the bishop received in writing, sent to him from the see of the most blessed Apostle Peter, in order to remove the uncertainty of certain persons.

### Chapter 52.—On the same matter. Pope Victor to Bishop Theophilus, chapter 1. That Gentiles coming to the faith are to be baptized by anyone, at any hour, in any river.

[Col. 0080D]

If necessity requires or the danger of death threatens, Gentiles coming to the faith, wherever and whenever it may occur—in a river, in the sea, or at springs—are to be baptized, provided only that their belief in the Christian confession has been made clear. Moreover, the very thing which they promised in baptism must be most carefully observed, lest they be found unbelievers rather than believers. Those, however, who are marked with the stain of unbelief are made infamous and are by no means reckoned among the faithful.

### Chapter 53.—Augustine, *On Seventy Heresies*.

The Lectiani [Selestiani] heretics deny that paradise is visible [Col. 0081A] and do not accept baptism in water.

### Chapter 54.—Haymo on the First Epistle to the Romans.

Perhaps someone will ask why baptism is consecrated only in water and not sometimes in wine. Blessed Ambrose answered him: “For this reason it is uniformly performed in water: so that it may be understood that, just as water washes away the stains of the body or clothing, so that baptism cleanses away the spots of the soul and the filth of vices by purifying them.”

### Chapter 55.—Gregory to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples (to Secundinus, bishop of Taormina).

(Gratian, 18, question 2, chapter “Pridem,” attributes this chapter to Gelasius.) We previously ordered that the baptistery be removed from the monastery [Col. 0081B] of Saint Andrew, which is above Mascalas, because of the insolence of the monks, and that altars be erected in the same place where the fonts are. The completion of this matter has been delayed until now. We therefore admonish your brotherhood to cause no further delay after receiving this present letter of ours; rather, after the place of the fonts has been filled in, let an altar for celebrating the sacred mysteries be erected there without any delay.

### Chapter 56.—Gelasius to Bishop Sabinus.

For a number is not rightly believed to be imposed upon those to be baptized, since however many may perhaps seek baptism or hasten to regeneration are not to be driven away according to another person’s will. Therefore, rejecting the superfluous regulation in every way, we wish each person to be baptized according to the choice of his own mind, either in a church nearby [Col. 0081C] or in one he chooses.

### Chapter 57.—From the *Liber Pontificalis*.

Marcellus established twenty-five titles in the city of Rome, like dioceses, for the baptism and penance of many persons.

### Chapter 58.—Pope Siricius to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, chapter 2.

(*On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter “Non ratione.”) Not on the basis of any authority, but through mere rashness, is it presumed that everywhere and freely, at the Nativity of Christ, at the Epiphany, and also on the festivals of apostles or martyrs, innumerable crowds, as you assert, receive the mystery of baptism; whereas the Lord’s Pascha especially, together with holy Pentecost, claims this privilege for itself among us [Col. 0081D] and among all Churches. Again: We desire that the water of sacred baptism be given with all speed, if necessary, to little children who cannot yet speak because of age, or to persons in any necessity.

### Chapter 59.—Pope Leo to the bishops throughout Sicily, Letter 4, chapter 6.

(*On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter “Duo tempora,” etc., “Non potest.”) You clearly recognize that for chosen candidates for baptism—who, according to the apostolic rule, are to be examined by exorcisms, sanctified by fasts, and instructed by frequent preaching—only two times are to be observed: Pascha and Pentecost.

### Chapter 60.—Council of Girona, chapter 4.

[Col. 0082A]

(*On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter “De catechumenis.”) It has been decreed concerning catechumens to be baptized that they are to come for baptism at the solemnity of Pascha or Pentecost. At other solemnities only the sick are to be baptized.

### Chapter 61.—Gregory to Fantinus, defensor.

If it seems too long or burdensome for Jews seeking baptism to wait for the Paschal solemnity, and you know that they are now hastening to baptism lest—God forbid!—a long delay should turn their minds back, speak with our brother, the bishop of that place, so that, after penance and abstinence have been imposed for forty days, he may baptize them, with the mercy of almighty God protecting them, either on the Lord’s Day or, should a particularly celebrated festival occur, on that day [Col. 0082B].

### Chapter 62.—Gregory answering Augustine (Letter 31).

(Distinction 5, first part, chapter “Baptizari.”) Neither a woman herself who has just given birth nor that which she has brought forth is in any way forbidden to be baptized, if danger of death is pressing: she herself in the very hour in which she gives birth, or the child in the same hour in which it is born.

### Chapter 63.—Gregory to the clergy and people of Tarentum.

(*On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter “Venerabilis.”) Except for those suffering illness, to whom remedies must be provided when danger of death presses, lest they perish eternally, a bishop must not presume to administer the general [variant: “venerable”] sacrament of baptism except at the Paschal and Pentecostal feasts.

### Chapter 64.—Gelasius to bishops throughout Lucania, Bruttium, and Sicily, chapter 9.

[Col. 0082C]

(*On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter “In necessitate.”) Christian laypersons are often permitted to baptize.

### Chapter 65.—Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 100.

A woman must not presume to baptize.

### Chapter 66.—Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book 2, chapter 34.

We read in the Gospel that the right to baptize is permitted neither to private persons nor to clerics [add: “without rank”], but only to priests—granted only to the apostles (John 20).

### Chapter 67.—In the same place.

Likewise: It is established that baptism has been entrusted [add: “to have been”] only to priests, and that even deacons may not perform its ministry without a bishop or presbyter, except when, in their absence at a great distance, the extreme urgency of sickness compels [variant: “necessity”]; this is also often permitted to faithful laypersons, lest anyone be called from this world without the remedy of salvation [Col. 0082D].

### Chapter 68.—Rabanus, *On the Institution of Clerics*, book 1, chapter 7.

The apostles ordained seven deacons, because of the sacrament of the same number, for ministry and service at the altar; these are read to have both preached and baptized not a few.

### Chapter 69.—That an acolyte should not baptize.

From the *Liber Pontificalis*. Boniface III decreed that a Lateran acolyte should not baptize, but that the following deacon and subdeacon should do so.

### Chapter 70.—Ambrose on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 1.

[Col. 0083A]

Greater is it to evangelize than to baptize; therefore the Apostle says that he was sent not to baptize but to evangelize, because in the bishop there is the dignity of all ordinations. For he is the head of the other members. By this also he humbles those to whom the Corinthians attached great importance because they had been baptized by them, so that they might thereby know that baptism is not a great matter, since not everyone who baptizes is fit also to evangelize. For the words spoken in baptism are prescribed formulas. Thus the Apostle Peter ordered believing Cornelius and his household to be baptized, and did not deem it worthy of himself to perform this task while ministers stood by. Had they been absent, he himself would have done it, compelled by necessity.

### CHAPTER 71.—Pope Leo IX, in the synod held at Rheims, chapter 4.

[Col. 0083B]

Let no one demand anything for burial, baptism, the Eucharist, or visitation of the sick.

### CHAPTER 72.—Gelasius, to the bishops established through Campania and Bruttium.

Let no one set any price for baptizing or confirming the faithful; nor, by imposing any contributions whatever, seek to harass those who are being reborn.

### CHAPTER 73.—The Eleventh Council of Toledo, chapter 8.

(1, question 1, chapter *Quidquid*.) Whoever is established in ecclesiastical order and, for baptizing or confirming the faithful, for the conferring of chrism, or for promotions through the ranks, receives any payments or rewards other than voluntary offerings because of such ambition—indeed, if anything of this sort is committed by subjects with the knowledge of the bishop of the place, that bishop shall be subject to excommunication for two months, because he both countenanced known evils and failed to apply the necessary correction. But if any of them, without his knowledge, thinks that he ought to receive anything for the aforesaid matters, then, if he is a presbyter, let him be punished by excommunication for three months; if a deacon, for four. A subdeacon, moreover, or cleric serving these greedy desires, is to be punished both with a fitting penalty and with due excommunication.

### CHAPTER 74.—The Second Council of Braga, chapter 7.

If any offer their infants for baptism, let them be received by the clergy.

### CHAPTER 75.—The same, chapter 1.

(10, question 1, chapter *Placuit omnibus episcopis*.) As bishops travel through the individual churches and dioceses, they should first examine the clergy: how they observe the order of baptism or of the Masses, and how they perform every office in the Church. If they find anything correct, let them give thanks to God. But if not, they must teach the ignorant and command this by every means, as the ancient canons direct: that (On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Ante 20 dies*) twenty days before baptism the catechumens should undergo exorcism for purification; during which twenty days the Creed—“I believe in God the Father almighty”—should be specially taught in its entirety.

### CHAPTER 76.—Augustine, *On Penance*, chapter 2.

[Col. 0084A]

(Book II, chapter 2. Gratian, *On consecration*, distinction 4, chapter *Omnis qui*.) Everyone who has already become master of his own will, when approaching the sacrament of the faithful, cannot begin the new life unless he repents of his old life. From this repentance only infants are exempt when they are baptized, for they cannot yet exercise free choice.

### CHAPTER 77.—Augustine to Seleutiana [Solestianus], letter, chapter 8.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Agunt*.) Before baptism people repent of their former sins; yet they are also baptized, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles, when Peter spoke to the Jews and said: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 2).

[Col. 0084B]

### CHAPTER 78.—Rabanus, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, book I, chapter 27.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Primum*.) First let the pagan be asked whether he renounces the devil and all his damnable works and all his deceits, so that he may first reject error and then approach truth; and so that, according to the Apostle, he may put off “the old man according to the former manner of life” (Ephesians 4), which is corrupted according to the desires of error, renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires (Titus 2).

### CHAPTER 79.—Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book I, chapter 11.

When the levite asked you, “Do you renounce the devil and all his works?”, what did you answer? “I renounce.” “Do you renounce the world and all its pleasures?” What did you answer? “I renounce.” Remember your words, and never let the sequence of your pledge escape you.

[Col. 0084C]

### CHAPTER 80.—Gregory I, Homily 29, on the same subject.

On the day of baptism we promised to renounce all the acts of the ancient enemy and all his pomps. Therefore let each of you turn the eyes of his mind to consider himself; let him consider whether, after baptism, he keeps what he promised before baptism.

### CHAPTER 81.—Rabanus, *On the Instruction of Clerics*.

After the renunciation, the Apostolic Creed is shown to him, and he is asked whether he believes in God the Father almighty, and in Jesus Christ his only Son, our Lord, and in the Holy Spirit, one God in Trinity and unity; whether he confesses that there is one holy catholic Church; and whether he believes in the forgiveness of sins and life everlasting. If, therefore, he truly professes that he believes all these things, he now begins through faith to put on “the new man, created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Ephesians 4); yet he is fully clothed with this when he is regenerated through the washing of baptism.

[Col. 0084D]

### CHAPTER 82.—Chapter 25, book I.

Before baptism, the office of catechizing ought to come first to the person, so that the catechumen may first receive the rudiments of faith. [Variant: “the office ought to come to the person.”]

### CHAPTER 83.

[Col. 0085A]

(Chapter *Ante baptismum*, On consecration, distinction 4.) Likewise: Jesus himself first anointed the eyes of the man born blind with mud made from spittle, and then sent him to the waters of Siloam (John 9), because the person to be baptized ought first to be instructed in faith in Christ’s incarnation, and then, now believing, admitted to baptism, so that he may know in whose grace he shares and to whom he thereafter becomes indebted.

### CHAPTER 84.—Chapter 26.

The saving Creed is delivered to those to be baptized as a reminder of faith and a token of holy confession, so that, instructed by it, they may recognize what manner of persons they ought now to present themselves as for the grace of Christ.

### CHAPTER 85.—Bede, on Ezra, book II.

In the Church the salutary custom of the Fathers’ teaching has fittingly become established: that to those who are catechized the mystery of the four Gospels should be explained and their openings recited.

[Col. 0085B]

### CHAPTER 86.

Likewise, we deliver to hearers of the new life the Creed of faith, which was composed by the twelve Apostles and comprised in an equal number of propositions.

### CHAPTER 87.—Pope Nicholas, to John, Archbishop of Ravenna.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Catechismi*.) The catechisms of those to be baptized may be performed by the priests of each church, as is demonstrably done solemnly in this holy Roman Church—in which, by God’s ordering, we exercise the ministry of our service.

### CHAPTER 88.—Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 9.

[Col. 0085C]

The saving Creed is delivered to the candidates as a reminder of faith and a token of holy confession, so that, instructed by it, they may recognize what manner of persons they ought now to present themselves as for the grace of Christ.

### CHAPTER 89.—Augustine, *On the Creed*, book I, chapter 1.

Receive the rule of faith called the Creed; and when you have received it, write it in your heart and say it daily to yourselves: before you sleep, before you go out, fortify yourselves with your Creed.

### CHAPTER 90.—Rabanus, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, book I, chapter 27.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Postquam*.) After the person to be baptized has, by confession of the true faith, commended himself to the lordship of another, and by renunciation withdrawn himself from service to his former possessor, the savage power is breathed out from him, so that the malignant spirit may flee and yield to the Holy Spirit through the pious ministry of the priest.

[Col. 0085D]

### CHAPTER 91.—Bede, on Kings, book IV.

It is the right order that teachers of truth should first drive every unclean spirit from the hearts of their hearers by exsufflation and catechesis; and then, by instructing them with the saving mysteries, join to the fellowship of the inheritance of the saints those who had been camps of demons but have now become the spiritual possession of Israel.

### CHAPTER 92.—Augustine, *Against Julian*, book IV.

(Augustine, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 31.) Infants are exsufflated in the exorcism before they are baptized.

### CHAPTER 93.—Book IV.

[Col. 0086A]

From those who are reborn in Christ the prince of this world is cast out, as the mysteries signify when infants to be baptized are exorcized and exsufflated.

### CHAPTER 94.—Augustine, *On the Creed*, book I, chapter 1.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Sicut nostis*.) As you know, infants are both exsufflated and exorcized, so that the hostile power of the devil may be expelled from them—the power which deceived the human being in order to possess human beings. Therefore it is not God’s creature in infants that is exorcized or exsufflated, but he under whom those are born who are born under sin.

### CHAPTER 95.—Rabanus, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, book I, chapter 28.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Postea*.) Afterwards the person to be baptized is marked with the sign of the holy cross, both on the forehead

[Col. 0086B]

and on the heart, so that the apostate devil himself, recognizing in his former vessel the sign of his own destruction, may know henceforth that it is alien to him.

### CHAPTER 96.—Augustine, *On the Creed*, book II, chapter 1.

You have not yet been reborn through sacred baptism, but through the sign of the cross you have already been conceived in the womb of holy Mother Church.

### CHAPTER 97.—Rabanus, in the same place.

Then prayers are said over him, that he may become a catechumen.

### CHAPTER 98.—Augustine, *On the Creed*, book IV, chapter 1.

All the sacraments which have been performed and are performed in you through the ministry of God’s servants—exorcisms, prayers, spiritual songs, insufflations, haircloth, bowing of necks, humility of feet—

[Col. 0086C]

this very fear, to be desired above every security: all these things, as I have said, are food that refreshes us in the womb, so that, reborn from baptism, the mother may present you joyfully to Christ.

### CHAPTER 99.—Rabanus, in the same place.

Then blessed salt is given into the mouth of the person to be baptized, so that, seasoned with the typical salt of wisdom, he may be free from the stench of iniquity and no longer decay from the worms of sins, but may rather be kept unharmed for receiving greater grace.

### CHAPTER 100.—Bede, on Kings [Ezra], book II, chapter 9.

(Book I, chapter 27; On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Sal coelestis*.) We are commanded to offer, in all the sacrifices of our works, the salt of heavenly wisdom by which catechumens are initiated.

[Col. 0086D]

### CHAPTER 101.—Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 19.

The Fathers instituted the giving of salt to catechumens in the ministry for this reason: that by its taste they may receive the seasoning of wisdom, neither lose the savor of Christ nor become foolish, looking back like Lot’s wife (Genesis 19).

### CHAPTER 102.—Rabanus, in the same place.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Dehinc*.) Next the devil is again exorcized, so that, recognizing his wickedness and fearing God’s just judgment upon himself, he may depart from the person and no longer strive by his art to overthrow him, lest he attain baptism; but rather, rendering honor to God his Creator, may give back the work to God his Maker.

[Col. 0087A]

### CHAPTER 103.—Gregory, Homily 29, on the Gospels.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Sacerdotes*.) When priests, through the grace of exorcism, lay hands upon believers and forbid malignant spirits to dwell in their minds, what else do they do but cast out demons?

### CHAPTER 104.—Rabanus, in the same place.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Postea*.) Afterwards his nostrils and ears are touched with saliva, and the Gospel word is said to him which Jesus spoke when he healed the deaf and mute man: touching his tongue with spittle and putting his fingers into his ears, he said, “Ephphatha,” that is, “Be opened” (Mark 7). For this sacrament is performed here so that, through the symbolic saliva and the priest’s touch, divine wisdom and power may work the salvation of that catechumen; so that his nostrils may be opened to receive the fragrance of the knowledge of God, and his ears opened to hear God’s commandments and store them in the inward understanding of his heart.

[Col. 0087B]

### CHAPTER 105.—Bede, in book I, Homily 19 (Homily for the Twelfth Sunday after Trinity).

The Church’s custom has become widespread: priests, when preparing those persons to receive the sacraments of baptism, first, among the other beginnings of consecration, touch their nostrils and ears with the saliva of their mouths, saying, “Ephphatha.” By the saliva of their mouths they signify the taste of heavenly wisdom with which those being initiated are to be endowed; by the touching of the nostrils, that, casting aside harmful pleasures, they may always embrace Christ’s fragrance alone.

[Col. 0087C]

### CHAPTER 106.—Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book I, chapter 1.

What did we do on Saturday? Surely, the opening; for the mysteries of opening were celebrated, when the priest touched your ears and nostrils. Our Lord Jesus Christ signified this in the Gospel when a deaf and mute man was brought to him, and he touched his ears and mouth (Mark 7). His ears, because he was deaf; his mouth, because he was mute; and he said, “Ephphatha,” a Hebrew word, which in Latin is called *adaperire*, “to open.” Therefore the priest touched your ears so that your ears might be opened for speech and for the priest’s address. Likewise: Because of the dignity of the gift and rite, the bishop does not touch the mouth but the nostrils, so that you may receive the good fragrance of eternal godliness.

[Col. 0087D]

### CHAPTER 107.—The Council of Nicaea, chapter 14.

Concerning fallen catechumens, the holy and great council has decreed that they shall be among the hearers for three years; after this, however, they shall be with the catechumens.

### CHAPTER 108.—For catechumens: Rabanus, in the same place.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Deinde*.) Then he is anointed by the priest, so that the sacred baptism, received with faith, may be guarded. At that time his breast is anointed with sanctified oil, while his mind is strengthened by invocation of the Holy Trinity. He is also anointed between the shoulders with the same oil, so that he may be defended on every side and strengthened by God’s grace to perform good works.

### CHAPTER 109.—Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book I, chapter 2.

(Book I, chapter 2; On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Venisti*.) You came

[Col. 0088A]

to the font; you entered. Consider whom you saw; carefully recall what you said. The levite met you; the presbyter met you. You were anointed as Christ’s athlete, so that you might approach baptism as a catechumen.

### CHAPTER 110.—Rabanus, in the same book, chapter 28.

The font is consecrated, and the catechumen approaches baptism itself.

### CHAPTER 111.—Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, treatise 2, chapter 5.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Venit*.) The priest comes to the font, says a prayer, invokes the name of the Father and the presence of the Son and Holy Spirit; he uses the heavenly words which are Christ’s: that one be baptized in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.

### CHAPTER 112.—Capitulary, book VI, chapter 77.

[Col. 0088B]

On Holy Saturday of Easter or Pentecost, if anyone wishes to receive consecrated water for sprinkling in his house, let him receive it before the pouring in of chrism.

### CHAPTER 113.—Augustine, *On the Creed*, book I, chapter 1.

(Book II, chapter 1.) This night something was done concerning us which was not done on other nights: each of you was brought out from secret places before the sight of the whole Church. There, with your neck bowed—that neck which had formerly been wrongly lifted up—an examination was performed in you, in the humility of feet and with haircloth spread beneath you; and the proud devil was uprooted from you while the most high Christ was humbly invoked over us.

### CHAPTER 114.—Stephen V, to Stylianus, Archbishop.

[Col. 0088C]

Are not all the charisms of priestly ministry effected by the figure of the cross? Does not the water of baptism remit sins unless consecrated by the cross? And, to pass over the rest, who ascends any rank of priesthood without the sign of the cross?

### CHAPTER 115.—Augustine, *On the One Baptism*, book VI (*Against the Donatists*).

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Si non sanctificatur*.) If water is not sanctified when the person praying pours out certain erroneous words through ignorance, then many brothers, not only evil but also good, do not sanctify water even within the Church itself. For the prayers of many are corrected daily if they are recited to teachers, and much is found in them contrary to the catholic faith. If it becomes known that some were baptized when those prayers had been said over the water, will they be commanded to be baptized again? Why so? Because the devotion of the one praying commonly overcomes the defect of the prayer; and because those certain Gospel words, without which baptism cannot be consecrated, have such force that through them whatever is said in a defective prayer against

[Col. 0088D]

the rule of faith is thus nullified, just as a demon is expelled in Christ’s name. For certainly, if a heretic brings a defective prayer and lacks the good disposition of charity by which that ignorance may be overcome, he is like anyone in the catholic Church who is envious and malevolent, of the kind Cyprian reproves there. Let him also bring, as commonly happens, a prayer in which he speaks against the rule of faith. For many prayers composed not only by ignorant talkers but even by heretics find their way in; and people use them in the simplicity of ignorance, unable to distinguish them and supposing them good. Yet what is perverse in them does not nullify what is right there; rather, it is nullified by it.

[Col. 0089A]

### CHAPTER 116.—Book III.

(Chapter 10. On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Non est aqua*.) Water over which God’s name is invoked is neither profane nor adulterous, even if it is invoked by profane and adulterous persons; for neither the creature itself nor the name itself is adulterous.

### CHAPTER 117.—Book V.

(Chapter 19.) How does a murderer cleanse and sanctify water? How do darknesses bless oil? But if he is present in the sacraments and in his words, through whomever they are administered, then God’s sacraments are everywhere valid, and evil persons, to whom they are of no benefit, are everywhere perverse.

[Col. 0089B]

### CHAPTER 118.—Augustine, *Against Julian*, book IV.

Recall how the mysteries of baptism are celebrated in Christ’s Church, and you will find that infants too renounce through the mouths of those who carry them, just as they believe through the mouths of those who carry them. Likewise:

### CHAPTER 119.

Whoever denies that infants believe through the mouths of those who carry them must also deny that they receive baptism, because they struggle against it in the hands of those who carry them.

### CHAPTER 120.—Augustine, *On Free Will*, book III, chapter 28.

[Col. 0089C]

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Illud perscrutari*.) People commonly inquire what benefit Christ’s sacrament of baptism gives infants, since, after receiving it, they often die before they can have understood anything by it. In this matter it is believed, sufficiently devoutly and rightly, that the faith of those by whom the infant is offered for consecration benefits the infant. And the Church’s most salutary authority commends this: each person should understand from it how his own faith benefits him, when it is advantageous also for the benefit of others who do not yet have power over themselves.

### CHAPTER 121.—Augustine, *On the Remedy of Penance*, chapter 11.

For the consecration and remission of original sin, the faith of those who offer infants benefits them, so that whatever stains of sins they contracted through others from whom they were born may be cleansed also by the questioning of others.

[Col. 0089D]

### CHAPTER 122.—Augustine, on John, tractate 80.

The word of faith has such power in God’s Church that, through the believer who professes it, offers the child, blesses, and anoints, it cleanses even a very little infant, though the infant is not yet able to believe in the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation (Romans 10).

### CHAPTER 123.—Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 28.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Aegrotantes*.) If the sick cannot answer for themselves, let them be baptized when those who know them have testified to their will. The same procedure is to be followed with penitents.

### CHAPTER 124.—Augustine, *On the One Baptism*.

[Col. 0090A]

(*Against the Donatists*, book IV, chapter 24; On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Cum pro parvulis*.) If another answers in baptism for one who is able to answer, it is not valid in the same way. From this principle comes the saying in the Gospel which naturally moves everyone when it is read: “He is of age; let him speak for himself” (John 9).

### CHAPTER 125.—Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, to Pollentius, book I, chapter 28, volume VI of the works.

Not only other catechumens, but even those who, though joined to living spouses, persist in adulterous unions—we do not admit them to baptism while they remain physically well and continue in these unions. Yet if they lie at the point of despair and repent inwardly, and cannot answer for themselves, I think they ought to be baptized, so that this sin too may be washed away with the others by the laver of regeneration.

[Col. 0090B]

For who knows whether perhaps they had determined to remain in the enticement of adulterous flesh only until baptism? But if they recover from that desperate condition and are able to live, they will either do what they had determined, or comply when instructed; or, if they prove contemptuous, the same is to be done concerning them as is customarily done concerning baptized persons of this sort. The same reason applies to baptism and to reconciliation, if the danger of death should overtake a penitent. For Mother Church ought not to will that they leave this life without the pledge of their peace.

### CHAPTER 126.—Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, treatise 2, chapter 7.

You were asked: “Do you believe in God the Father almighty?” You said, “I believe,” and you were immersed—that is, you were buried. Again you were asked: “Do you also believe in our Lord Jesus Christ and in his cross?” You said, “I believe,” and you were immersed. Therefore you were also buried with Christ. For whoever is buried with Christ rises with Christ (Romans 6). Thirdly you were asked: “Do you also believe in the Holy Spirit?” “I believe”; and you were immersed a third time, so that the threefold confession might absolve the manifold fall of the former age.

[Col. 0090C]

### CHAPTER 127.—Pope Gregory III, to Boniface (letter 3).

You have stated that some were baptized without questioning on the Creed by adulterous and unworthy presbyters. In these cases, let your belovedness maintain the ancient custom of the Church: whoever has been baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Matthew 28) must by no means be rebaptized. For he received this gift of grace not in the name of the baptizer but in the name of the Trinity.

### CHAPTER 128.—Canons of the Apostles, chapter 5.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Si quis*.) If any presbyter does not perform the threefold immersion of the one mystery but immerses only once in baptism, which he is commanded to give into the Lord’s death, let him be deposed. For the Lord did not say, “Baptize into my death,” but: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28).

[Col. 0090D]

### CHAPTER 129.—The Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 5.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Propter*.) To avoid scandal among schismatics or the practice of heretical doctrine, let us observe a single immersion in baptism.

### CHAPTER 130.—Gregory, to Bishop Leander (book I, chapter 41).

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *De trina*.) Concerning the threefold immersion in baptism, nothing truer can be answered than what you yourselves have thought: in one faith, differing custom does no harm to the holy Church. We, however, by immersing three times signify the mystery of the three-day burial, so that, when the infant is drawn out of the waters a third time, the resurrection after three days may be expressed. But if anyone perhaps judges that this is done for reverence toward the supreme Trinity, neither does it in any way prevent baptism that the person to be baptized be immersed only once in water. For since there is one substance in three subsistences, it can in no way be blameworthy to immerse an infant in baptism either three times or once: in three immersions the Trinity of persons, and in one immersion the unity of the Godhead, can be signified.

[Col. 0091B]

### CHAPTER 131.—Rabanus, on the Epistle to the Ephesians, book II.

In the same way we baptize into the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and immerse three times, so that the one sacrament of the Trinity may appear. Likewise: although we baptize three times because of the mystery of the Trinity, it is nevertheless reckoned as one baptism.

### CHAPTER 132.—The Council of Auxerre, chapter 25.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Non licet*.) It is not permitted for an abbot or monks to receive children from baptism or to have comothers.

### CHAPTER 133.—Capitulary, book VII, chapter 494.

[Col. 0091C]

Let monks not make for themselves compadres or comothers, nor kiss women.

### CHAPTER 134.—Augustine, First Sunday after Easter, beginning: “This day.”

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Vos ante omnia*.) Before all else, I admonish you, both men and women who have received children at baptism, that you should recognize that you have become sureties before God for those whom you were seen to receive from the sacred font. Therefore always admonish them to preserve chastity, love justice, maintain charity, and do to all what they wish done to themselves; not to observe omens, nor pay vows at trees and springs; to flee enchanters, *caragios* [uncertain term], sacrileges, and amulets as the devil’s poisons; neither to steal nor bear false witness. Above all, both keep the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer yourselves, and teach them to those whom you have received.

[Col. 0091D]

### CHAPTER 135.—Nicholas, to the inquiries of the Bulgarians.

A person ought to love the one who received him from the sacred font as a father. Likewise: Between spiritual fathers and children there is a gratuitous and holy communion, which should not be called consanguinity but rather regarded as spiritual kinship. Hence we judge that no marital union can be contracted between them, since the venerable Roman laws do not permit marriage to be contracted either between those related by nature or those who are children by adoption. Likewise: If marriage is contracted between those whom adoption joins, how much more should those whom regeneration of the Holy Spirit has joined through a heavenly sacrament abstain from carnal cohabitation with one another. Therefore far more fittingly is he called my father’s son or my brother whom divine grace, rather than human will, chose to be my son or brother; and more wisely are we separated from mutual bodily intercourse.

### CHAPTER 136.—The same, to Bishop Salomonius.

You wish to know whether a woman who has lifted from the sacred font a son born to her husband by another daughter may afterwards be joined to that same husband. We decree that they can be joined, because, according to the sacred canons, a spouse ought not to leave a spouse on any pretext of religion except by the consent of both. But it pertains to the grave ruin of a wife who, hating her husband or failing to consider his weakness, performs impiety under a pretext of piety; especially since the Apostle commands: “Do not deprive one another, except by consent for a time, that you may give yourselves to prayer” (1 Corinthians 7). And again: “Return to one another, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control” (ibid.). Therefore, if it is proved that this occurred without the consent of both spouses, let them not deprive one another, but return to one another; especially since the Apostle says: “The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife” (ibid.).

[Col. 0092B]

### CHAPTER 137.—The same, to Salomonius, Bishop of Constance.

Your Holiness asks us whether a man may have two spiritual comothers, one after the other. In this matter your brotherhood must remember what is written: “The two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2). Therefore, since it is established that husband and wife become one flesh through marriage, it follows plainly that a man becomes compadre to the woman to whom his wife, taken in marriage, appeared to be comother; and therefore it is clear that the man cannot be joined in union to the woman who was his comother, with whom he had become one flesh.

[Col. 0092C]

### CHAPTER 138.—The same, to Archbishop Charles and his suffragans.

If anyone has committed fornication with a spiritual comother, he is, as you know, struck by the blows [variant: darts] of anathema. Likewise we decree that he too is to be struck who commits the crime of fornication with her whom he received from the sacred font of baptism, or with her whom he held before the bishop when she was anointed with sacred chrism; nevertheless, if he has a lawful wife, he does not dismiss her.

[Col. 0092D]

### CHAPTER 139.—From the decrees of Gregory the Younger.

If anyone takes a spiritual comother in marriage, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER 140.—Rabanus, in the same book, chapter 28.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Postquam*.) After the baptized person has come up from the font, he is immediately marked on the head by the presbyter with sacred chrism, while prayer is said as well, so that he may become a participant in Christ’s kingdom and be able to be called a Christian from Christ.

### CHAPTER 141.—Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, treatise 2, chapter 7.

[Col. 0093A]

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Emersisti*.) You emerged; you came to the priest. What did he say to you? “God the Father almighty, who regenerated you from water and the Spirit and forgave you your sins, may he himself anoint you unto eternal life.” See where you were anointed: “unto eternal life,” he says.

### CHAPTER 142.—Treatise 3 of the same work, chapter 1.

(Ambrose, *On Those Initiated into the Mysteries*, chapter 6; On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Accipis*.) You receive the mystery—that is, ointment upon the head. Why upon the head? Because the understanding of a wise person is in his head. The spiritual seal follows, which remains after the font, by which perfection is accomplished when, at the priest’s invocation, the Holy Spirit is poured out.

[Col. 0093B]

### CHAPTER 143.—Rabanus, in the same book, chapter 29.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Post baptismum*.) After baptism the Christian is given a white garment, signifying Christian innocence and purity. After the old stains have been washed away, he ought through devotion to holy conduct to keep it spotless, so as to present it before Christ’s tribunal. All those reborn are clothed in white garments for the mystery of the Church rising again. Likewise: The baptized use white garments so that the clothing of second birth may display the glory which the rag of ancient error had darkened in the appearance of their first birth. For after the sacred anointing his head is covered with a mystical veil, so that he may understand that he possesses the diadem of a kingdom and priestly dignity.

[Col. 0093C]

### CHAPTER 144.—Ambrose, *On the Mysteries of Initiation*, chapter 7.

After baptism you received white garments, as a token that you had put off the wrapping of sins and put on the chaste coverings of innocence.

### CHAPTER 145.—Saint Augustine, on the octave of Easter, beginning thus.

Today the Paschal festival is concluded by this celebration; therefore today the attire of the newly baptized is changed. Yet the whiteness which is laid aside in clothing should always be retained in the heart.

### CHAPTER 146.—Gregory III, to Boniface.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Parvulos*.) Infants who have been taken away from their parents, and concerning whom it is unknown whether they have been baptized or not, ought, according to the tradition of the Fathers, to be baptized if there is no one to testify.

[Col. 0093D]

### CHAPTER 147.—The Council of Carthage, chapter 6.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Placuit*.) It has been decreed concerning infants: whenever entirely reliable witnesses cannot be found who can testify without doubt that they have been baptized, and the infants themselves are not old enough to answer concerning the sacraments delivered to them, they are to be baptized without any scruple. The same procedure is to be followed concerning churches whenever there is doubt about their consecration; that is, they are to be consecrated without hesitation.

### CHAPTER 148.—Nicholas, to the inquiries of the Bulgarians, chapter 104.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *A quodam*.) You report that many in your country were baptized by a certain Jew, though you do not know whether he was a Christian or a pagan, and you ask what ought to be done. If they were baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, or even only in the name of Christ, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 2, 10), which are indeed one and the same, as Saint Ambrose explains, it is established that they must not be baptized again.

[Col. 0094A]

### CHAPTER 149.—Gregory III, to Boniface, letter 4.

Those who were baptized amid the diversity and variation of pagan languages nevertheless ought, because they were baptized in the name of the Trinity, to be confirmed by laying on of hands and anointing with sacred chrism.

### CHAPTER 150.—The same, to Boniface.

[Col. 0094B]

Concerning that false bishop of whom you said that he was the son, born in adultery, of an adulterous cleric and a murderer, that he had been reared without discipline, and concerning the other horrible evils which you related individually, and that he consequently consecrated priests like himself: let your reverend brotherhood remember what we have already written three times, that no murderer, adulterer, or fornicator ought to handle the sacred ministry. But concerning those baptized by him and churches consecrated by him, about which your brotherhood inquires: know that the churches which he consecrated in the name of the Holy Trinity, and likewise the infants whom he baptized, whatever the character of the person performing the priestly office, are not to be consecrated again by another, nor are those infants to be baptized again.

### CHAPTER 151.—Pope Anastasius II, to Anastasius.

[Col. 0094C]

(In the Decrees, chapter 7, chapter *Sanctae Ecclesiae catholicae*, distinction 19, first part.) Let the most sacred heart of Your Serenity recognize that no share of harm, on Acacius’s account, touches any of those whom Acacius baptized or whom priests or levites ordained according to the canons; lest the grace of the sacrament administered by an unrighteous person perhaps appear less secure. For baptism, even if conferred far from the Church, whether by an adulterer or a thief, reaches the recipient as an unimpaired gift.

### CHAPTER 152.—The Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 41.

(On consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Non liceat*.) Rebaptizations, reordinations, and translations of bishops must not be performed.

### CHAPTER 153.—Gregory, to Bishop Quirinus in Ireland, book IX, letter 61.

[Col. 0094D]

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “From ancient [tradition].”) From the ancient institution of the Fathers we have learned that those baptized among heretics in the name of the Trinity, when they return to the holy Church, are restored to the bosom of Mother Church either by anointing with chrism, by the laying on of hands, or by profession of faith alone. Thus the West receives Arians by the laying on of hands, whereas the East restores them to entrance into the holy catholic Church by anointing with holy chrism; Monophysites [Monothelites] and others it receives upon their true confession alone. For the holy baptism which they received among heretics then receives in them its power of cleansing, when either the former have received the Holy Spirit through laying on of hands, [Col. 0095A] or the latter have been joined by confession of the true faith to the womb of the holy and universal Church.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “But these.”) But those heretics who are baptized in the name of the Trinity—such as the Bonosiacs and Cataphrygians—when they come to the holy Church are baptized, because the former do not believe Christ to be the Lord, while the latter, in their perverse understanding, believe that the Holy Spirit is a certain wicked man, Montanus. Many others resemble them. Since, being in error, they did not truly receive baptism in the name of the holy Trinity, what they received was not baptism; nor can baptism be called repeated when, as has been said, it had not been administered in the name of the Trinity.

### CHAPTER 154.—Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*, Tractate 9.

[Col. 0095B] A person is not to be said to be in the Church—that is, to belong to the fellowship of the Spirit—merely because he is outwardly mingled with Christ’s sheep while inwardly false of heart. For “the spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wisdom 1). Therefore, all who are baptized in schismatic or heretical congregations—or rather, segregations—although they are not reborn of the Spirit, are like Ishmael, who was born to Abraham according to the flesh, and not like Isaac, who was born according to the Spirit, because he was born through the promise (Genesis 21). Yet, when they come to the catholic Church and are joined to the fellowship of the Spirit—which they undoubtedly did not possess outside—it is not necessary to repeat for them the washing of the flesh. For even outside they did not lack this outward form of godliness; but they lacked that unity of the Spirit in the bond [Col. 0095C] of peace, which can be given only within.

### CHAPTER 155.—From the same author’s Tractate 63.

Heretics and schismatics have made private property for themselves out of the Lord’s estates, and have wished to pasture flocks not of Christ, but their own, against Christ. Yet in their very condemnations [read: dominations] they placed his title upon them, so that their plunder might be defended, as it were, by the title of a powerful owner. What does Christ do when such people are converted, who outside the Church received the title of his baptism? He expels the plunderer, but does not remove the title. Rather, he takes possession of the house, because he finds his title there. What need is there for him to change his own name?

### CHAPTER 156.—Augustine on John, Part I, Tractate 5.

[Col. 0095D]

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “Baptism.”) Baptism is such as he is into whose power it is given, not such as he is through whose ministry it is given.

### CHAPTER 157.—The same, in the same work.

What did John the Baptist know? The Lord. What did he not know? That the authority of the Lord’s baptism would pass from the Lord to no human being, though its ministry certainly would pass on. The authority passes from the Lord to no one; but the ministry passes to good and bad alike. Let not the dove shrink from the ministry of evil men; let it look to the Lord’s authority. What can a bad minister do to you where the Lord is good? What harm can a malicious herald do, if the judge is kindly disposed?

### CHAPTER 158.—The same, in the same Tractate.

[Col. 0096A]

“Neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase” (II Corinthians 3). But if the minister is proud, he is reckoned with the devil; the gift of Christ, however, is not defiled. What flows through him is pure; what passes through him as liquid reaches fertile soil. Suppose that man is stony, because he cannot bear fruit from the water; yet the water passes through a stone channel to the beds. The stone channel produces nothing, but the garden bears abundant fruit.

The same, in the same work. I say—and all of us say—that those through whom baptism is administered ought to be righteous, because ministers of so great a Judge ought to be righteous. Let the ministers be righteous, if they wish. But if those who sit in the chair of Moses do not wish to be righteous, my Master has made [Col. 0096B] me secure—the one of whom his Spirit says: “This is he who baptizes” (Matthew 15).

### CHAPTER 159.—The same, in the same work.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “When baptism.”) Those whom Judas baptized, Christ baptized. Therefore, if a drunkard baptized some, if a murderer baptized some, if an adulterer baptized some, and it was Christ’s baptism, Christ baptized them. I do not fear the adulterer, the drunkard, or the murderer, because I attend to the dove, through whom I am told: “This is he who baptizes” (John 1).

The same. A murderer administered Christ’s baptism; this sacrament is so holy that it is not defiled even when a murderer ministers it.

### CHAPTER 160.—The same, Tractate 6.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “When [a bad man] baptizes.”) When an evil man baptizes through some ignorance or tolerance on the Church’s part—for evil persons are either unknown, or the chaff is tolerated until the threshing-floor is winnowed at the end—what is given is one and the same, not unequal because the ministers are unequal, but equal and alike because of him who baptizes.

(Augustine, *On Ecclesiastical Rules*, chapter 52.) Those baptized among heretics who baptize with confession of the holy Trinity and who come to the catholic Church are indeed to be received as baptized, lest the invocation or confession of the holy Trinity be annulled. But they must be fully taught and instructed in the sense in which the mystery of the holy Trinity is held in the Church. If they consent to believe or agree to confess it, then, cleansed by the integrity of faith, let them be confirmed by the laying on of hands. But if they are children or simple-minded persons who cannot grasp instruction, those presenting them are to answer for them according to the custom of baptism; and thus, fortified by chrism through the laying on of hands, they are to be admitted to the mysteries of the Eucharist.

Augustine’s solution to Orosius’s question (*Dialogue*, book II, question 65). (Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “Baptism.”) Although there is one baptism both of heretics—namely, those who baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and of the catholic Church, nevertheless, because they are baptized outside the Church, they receive baptism not unto salvation but unto destruction. They possess, indeed, the form of the sacrament, but deny its power. Therefore the Church does not rebaptize them, because they were baptized in the name of the Trinity: that is indeed the form of the sacrament. Accordingly, when they return, [Col. 0097A] they receive the power of the Holy Spirit, which those baptized outside the Church do not yet possess.

Augustine, *Against Cresconius the Grammarian*, book XI. This is true, sound, and catholic: that Christ cleanses the consciences of recipients, whether through good ministers of his baptism or through bad ones.

The same, chapter 2. If you ask how those whom the Church has condemned can baptize, I answer: they baptize in the same way as those whom God condemned baptize, before the Church had made any judgment concerning them.

Book III, chapter 6. (Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “If among.”) If, among good ministers, one is better than another, the baptism administered by the better is not better; in no way is that baptism bad which is administered even by a bad minister, when the same baptism is administered. Therefore, through unequal ministers, God’s gift is equal, because it is not theirs but his.

### CHAPTER 161.—Pope Pelagius to Bishop Gaudentius.

Regarding the heretics about whom you judged that we should be consulted through your son Paulinus, a man of highest rank—whether, if some of them wish to return to the catholic faith, they should be baptized or merely reconciled—we desire your Fraternity to observe the practice which we know is observed around Sirmium, Simgidunum, and other neighboring places, where there are many persons of this heresy. Since they assert that they are baptized in Christ’s name alone and with a single immersion, whereas the evangelical precept—handed down by God himself, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ—admonishes us to confer baptism upon each person in the name of the Trinity and with a triple immersion, our Lord saying to his disciples: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28): if indeed those of the aforesaid heretics said to dwell in places neighboring those entrusted to your care perhaps confess that they were baptized only in the Lord’s name, you shall baptize them, without any ambiguity of doubt, in the name of the holy Trinity when they come to the catholic faith. But if the open confession of those who wish to be converted has made clear to you that they were baptized in the name of the Trinity, then, after bestowing only the grace of reconciliation, hasten to reconcile them to the catholic faith. By observing this disposition, nothing may appear to have been done through a spirit of rashness otherwise than evangelical authority commands. [Col. 0097D]

### CHAPTER 162.—Augustine, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, book II, chapter 53.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “It is also customarily asked.”) It is also customarily asked whether baptism administered by someone who has not received it himself ought to be approved—if perhaps he learned out of curiosity how [read: in what manner] it ought to be administered—and whether it makes no difference with what intention the person receiving it receives it: whether with pretence or without pretence. If with pretence, whether he is deceiving, as in the Church or in what is thought to be the Church, or joking, as in a mime. And which is more criminal: to receive it deceitfully in the Church, or without deceit, that is, with an unfeigned mind, in heresy or schism; and whether deceitfully in heresy, or faithfully in a mime, if someone should be moved during the performance by sudden piety. Even if we compare such a person with one who receives it deceitfully in the catholic Church itself, it would be surprising if there were doubt as to which should be preferred to which.

For I do not see what advantage the sincere intention of the administrator gives to a deceitful recipient. But let us suppose even an administrator who is deceitful: when both the giver and the recipient act deceitfully within catholic unity itself, should that baptism be more acceptable, or one administered in a mime, if there should be a recipient who receives it faithfully, suddenly moved? Or does it differ greatly so far as the human beings themselves are concerned, between one believing in a mime and one mocking in the Church, while making no difference to the integrity of the sacrament itself? For if it makes no difference to the integrity of the sacrament within catholic communion whether some perform it deceitfully [Col. 0098B] or sincerely—while both parties nevertheless perform precisely the same thing—I do not see why it should make a difference outside, when the recipient is not cloaked in pretence but changed by religion.

Or do sincere persons among whom it is performed have more force to establish the sacrament than the deceitful persons by whom and among whom it is performed have to frustrate it? Yet, if the deceit is subsequently proved, no one repeats the baptism; rather, the pretence is punished by excommunication or healed by repentance. But it is safe for us not to advance a rash opinion upon matters that have been initiated by no regional council of the catholic Church and settled by no plenary council. It is proper, however, to assert with the confidence of a secure [read: careful] utterance what has been confirmed, under the governance of our Lord Jesus Christ, by the consensus of the universal Church.

Nevertheless, if someone were to press me, perhaps when I was present at a council where such questions were being discussed, in the absence of persons whose views I would prefer to follow, to say what I myself thought—if I were then disposed as I was when I wrote these things—I would not hesitate to hold that those who, wherever and by whomever it was administered, received baptism consecrated with the words of the Gospel without their own pretence and with some faith, possess baptism. Yet it would not benefit them for spiritual salvation if they lacked the charity through which they might be joined to the catholic Church. For, he says, “If I have faith so as to remove mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Corinthians 13).

Likewise, in accordance with earlier decisions of the Fathers, I do not doubt that even those who receive it deceitfully in the Church possess baptism, provided that they receive it either where those in whose fellowship they receive it think the Church to be—those of whom it has been said: “They went out from us” (1 John 2). But where there was neither any fellowship of persons believing in this way nor any such belief on the part of the recipient, but everything was performed playfully, theatrically, and jokingly, whether baptism so administered ought to be approved, I would judge must be sought from divine judgment by the oracle of some revelation, invoked with united prayer and groans. I would certainly wait humbly for those who were to state their opinions after me, should they bring forward anything already investigated and known.

The same work, book I, chapter 1. (Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “It is shown.”) It is shown that those act impiously who attempt to rebaptize the unity of the world, and that we act rightly, who do not dare to reject God’s sacraments even in schism itself. In that in which they agree with us, they are also with us; but in that in which they disagree with us, they have departed from us.

The same, in the same place. The sacrament of baptism is what the baptized person has; and the sacrament of administering baptism is what the ordained person has. For just as a baptized person, if he departs from unity, does not lose the sacrament of baptism, so also an ordained person, if he departs from unity, does not lose the sacrament of administering baptism. No sacrament should be wronged: if he departs from evil persons, he departs from both; if he remains among evil persons, he remains in both. Therefore, if baptism is accepted which the man who departed from unity could not lose, so must baptism be accepted which was administered by one who, in departing, did not lose the sacrament of administering it. [Col. 0099B]

The same work, chapter 12. If someone came deceitfully to baptism, were his sins forgiven him or not forgiven? Let them choose whichever they please; whichever they choose will suffice for us. If they say that they were forgiven, then how did “the Holy Spirit of discipline flee deceit” (Wisdom 1), if he worked remission of sins in this deceitful person? If they say that they were not forgiven, I ask whether, if he later confessed his deceit with a contrite heart and true sorrow, he would be judged to require baptism anew. If it is utterly mad to say so, let them acknowledge that a person may be baptized with Christ’s true baptism, while his heart, persisting in evil or sacrilege, nevertheless prevents absolution from sins from taking place. Thus let them understand that a person may be baptized in communions separated from the Church, where Christ’s baptism is administered and received in the same celebration of the sacrament; but that baptism benefits him for forgiveness of sins only when, reconciled to unity, he is stripped of the sacrilege of dissension by which his sins were held fast and prevented from being forgiven. [Col. 0099C]

### CHAPTER 163.—The same, in the same work.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “How does God hear?” and Peter Lombard, book IV, distinction 4, chapter “But those who.”) For the grace of baptism is hindered from forgiving all sins even if hatred of a brother persists in the mind of the one whose sins are forgiven. For the preceding day is released, and whatever remains of it; likewise the very hour and moment before baptism and in baptism. But afterward he immediately begins to be liable, not only for subsequent days, but also for preceding days, hours, and moments, because all that had been forgiven returns.

The same work, chapter 13. Those things which schismatics or heretics possess and perform no differently from the true Church, we do not correct when they come to us; rather, we approve them. For in the things in which they do not disagree with us, they are not separated from us. Yet, since those things avail them nothing as long as they are schismatics or heretics—because of other matters in which they dissent from the truth, and because of the utterly monstrous crime of separation, whether their sins remain in them or return immediately after being forgiven—we exhort them to come to the salvation of peace and charity. [Col. 0099D]

### CHAPTER 164.—Book III, chapter 10.

[Col. 0100A]

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “Water is not”; Augustine, book III *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, chapter 11.) Christ’s baptism, consecrated with the Gospel words, is holy both through adulterers and in adulterers, although they are unchaste and unclean, because its holiness itself cannot be defiled, and divine power attends its sacrament, either unto the salvation of those who use it well or unto the destruction of those who use it badly.

The same. (Question 1, chapter 1, chapter “Because some”; Augustine, same passage.) For this reason the catholic Church ought not to repeat baptism administered among heretics: lest it seem to judge that what belongs to Christ belongs to them, or that they do not possess what, had they received it within, they certainly could not lose by going out.

The same. (Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “But not.”) But baptism, which belongs to Christ, should not be called theirs in the same way that their heresy is theirs, their error is theirs, and the sacrilege of their dissension is theirs.

The same. (Augustine, chapter 13 of the same book.) Do we say that baptism consecrated by Gospel words is the baptism of heretics? Moved by their deeds, do we wish to attribute even God’s things to them, as though they could have defiled them, or made God’s things their own merely because they themselves refused to belong to God?

### CHAPTER 165.—Book IV, *On Baptism*, chapter 4.

Just as I seem to be pressed when I am asked, “Does a heretic, then, forgive sins?” so I press in turn when I say: “Does one who does not keep the heavenly commandments—a greedy person, robber, usurer, envious person, who renounces the world in words but not in deeds—forgive sins?” If by the power of God’s sacrament, then, just as the former, so also the latter does. If by his own merit, neither the former nor the latter does. For that sacrament is recognized to belong to Christ even among evil people.

The same, in the same chapter. If someone baptized in heresy in the name of the holy Trinity does not become God’s temple unless he withdraws from heresy, then neither does one baptized in the same name amid greed become God’s temple unless he withdraws from greed, which is the service of idols (Ephesians 5). [Col. 0100C]

The same, chapter 5 of the same book.
