But if, as I have said, the sins of both may be weighed equally—the blasphemy of one who is ignorant and the idolatry of one who knows—and judged by the same sentence: the one who, seeking Christ, falls into the plausible discourse of falsehood, and the one who knowingly resists Christ through the Apostle—since “no fornicator, or unclean person, or greedy person, which is idolatry, has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God” (Ephesians 5)—why are baptism and the Gospel words rejected in the former, but approved in the latter, when each is found alien from the members of that dove?

The same, chapter 11. (Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “But no one.”) An unbeliever and blasphemer, if he remains in unbelief and blasphemy, receives forgiveness of sins neither outside the Church nor within it. Or, if by force of the sacrament he receives it for a moment of time, the same power operates outside and inside, just as the power of Christ’s name worked even outside in the expulsion of demons.

The same, chapter 15. (Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “We have sufficiently shown.”) We have sufficiently shown that the error of either the giver or the recipient does not pertain to baptism consecrated with Gospel words, whether he thinks otherwise about the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit than heavenly teaching declares. [Col. 0101A]

The same, chapter 16. Let us then posit two persons in this manner. Let one, for example, think of Christ what Photinus held, and be baptized in his heresy outside communion with the catholic Church. Let the other think the same thing, but be baptized in the catholic Church, supposing that this very belief is the catholic faith. I say that the latter is not yet a heretic unless, when the teaching of catholic faith has been made known to him, he prefers to resist it and chooses what he formerly held. Before that occurs, it is evident that the person baptized outside is worse. Thus in the one case false opinion alone must be corrected; in the other, the division itself must also be corrected. But in neither case is the truth of the sacrament to be repeated.

### CHAPTER 166.—The same, chapter 17.

Baptism can be common to us and to heretics, just as the Gospel can be common to us and to them, although their error differs from our faith: whether they think otherwise than truth teaches concerning the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, or, cut off from unity, do not gather with Christ but scatter (Matthew 12).

### CHAPTER 167.—Book V, chapter 13.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “Since it has so much power.”) Since baptism administered through a contemptible person has as much power as baptism administered through an apostle, it is recognized as belonging neither to the former nor to the latter, but to Christ.

The same. (Chapter 14, book V *Against the Donatists*.) We find the Apostle speaking of “my glory” (1 Thessalonians 2), though certainly in the Lord; and “my ministry,” “my wisdom,” and “my gospel” (Romans 2), though certainly bestowed and given by the Lord. But no one at all has said “my baptism.” For not everyone’s glory is equal; not all minister equally; not all are endowed with equal wisdom; and in preaching the Gospel one person works better than another. Therefore one may be called more learned than another, even in spiritual [read: salutary] teaching; but no one can be said to be baptized more or less than another, whether baptized by an inferior or a superior person.

The same. (Augustine, book V, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 15.) Even if the one who baptizes had no right to baptize, what he gave belongs to Christ, and what the other received belongs to Christ. For many things are given contrary to right, yet are not thereby said either not to exist or not to have been given. [Col. 0101D]

The same, chapter 18. Therefore, since there are dead persons inside—not hidden persons, for Cyprian would not have spoken so strongly about them—who either do not belong, or do not yet belong, to that living dove; and dead persons outside, who more plainly either do not belong, or do not yet belong, to it; and since it is true that one person cannot be made alive by someone who does not himself live: it is evident that those baptized inside by such persons, if they approach with true conversion of heart, are made alive by him whose baptism it is.

The same, chapter 20. What kind of argument is this: that a heretic is thought not to possess baptism because he does not possess the Church? Yet when he is baptized, he is also questioned concerning the holy Church. As though one who inwardly renounces the world not in deeds but in words were not asked the same thing in baptism. Therefore, just as that person’s false answer does not make the baptism he receives cease to be baptism, and just as, if he later truly fulfills what he had falsely answered, baptism is not repeated for him but his life is corrected; so also, if the heretic later comes to the Church about which he gave a false answer when questioned—because he thought that he possessed it when he did not—that Church itself, which he did not possess, is given to him; what he received is not repeated. But why God can nevertheless sanctify oil through words proceeding from a murderer, yet cannot do so upon an altar erected by heretics, I do not know. [Col. 0102A]

### CHAPTER 168.—Book VI, chapter 5.

[Col. 0102B] In a righteous person and in an unrighteous person, baptism is always holy: it is neither increased by anyone’s righteousness nor diminished by anyone’s wickedness.

### CHAPTER 169.—Zacharias to Bishop Boniface.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “In the synod.”) It is known that in the synod of the English a decree and judgment were most firmly commanded and carefully set forth: whoever had been immersed without invocation of the Trinity did not possess the sacrament of regeneration. This is entirely true; for if anyone has been immersed in the font of baptism without invocation of the Trinity, he is not a complete Christian unless he has been baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

You wrote concerning priests who sacrificed bulls or goats to pagan gods, ate sacrifices offered to the dead, possessed a defiled ministry, and were afterwards discovered to be adulterers and then died. It is now unknown whether, when baptizing, they named the Trinity or not; and those still alive fear that they were not baptized under such a ministry. In reply, you ordered all of them to be baptized. The priests also wished this to be observed in the aforesaid synod: that if anyone failed to name even one person of the Trinity in baptism, that baptism could not be true. This is certainly true, because one who has not confessed one name of the holy Trinity cannot be a complete Christian. For one who confesses the Father and the Son but does not confess the Holy Spirit has neither the Father nor the Son. And one who confesses the Father and the Holy Spirit but does not confess the Son has neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit, but is devoid of divine grace. [Col. 0102D]

Meanwhile, your reverend Fraternity wrote that you had discovered a certain priest, a Scot by birth, named Sampson, wandering from the way of truth and declaring and maintaining that someone could become a catholic Christian by the laying on of an episcopal hand without the mystical invocation or the washing of regeneration. But the man who says this is empty of the Holy Spirit and estranged from Christ’s grace, and must be removed from priestly fellowship. For who can be catholic unless baptized according to the Lord’s command (Matthew 28), in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and then consecrated through the laying on of hands? Expel from the holy Church of God this most wicked man who preaches such things as condemned. But with respect to those baptized by heretics, do not fail to carry out, without doubt, the instruction handed down to you according to our predecessor Pope Gregory of blessed memory and the sacred canons, lest they perish eternally, but rather be saved by evangelical consecration. [Col. 0103A]

### CHAPTER 170.—Augustine, *On One Baptism*, book I, chapter 2.

(24, question 1, chapter “If perhaps someone.”) If extreme necessity should compel someone who cannot find a catholic person through whom to receive baptism, and he receives, through someone situated outside catholic unity, what he would have received within catholic unity, while his mind remains established in catholic peace—if he immediately departs this life, we count him as nothing other than catholic. But if he is delivered from bodily death, when he restores himself by bodily presence to the catholic congregation from which he had never departed in heart, we not only do not disapprove what he did, but praise it most confidently and truly. For by unity he preserved the present God in his heart, and did not wish to leave this life without the sacrament of holy baptism—which, wherever he found it, he recognized as belonging not to human beings but to God.

But if anyone, while able to receive baptism in the catholic Church itself, chooses through some perversity of mind to be baptized in schism, even if he later comes to the catholic Church, he is undoubtedly perverse and wicked. For he knows that the sacrament is beneficial there, whereas it can be received elsewhere but cannot be beneficial there; and he is more harmful in proportion as he is more knowing. [Col. 0103C]

### CHAPTER 171.—Augustine’s Letter 23 to Boniface.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “Let this not move you.”) Do not let it trouble you that some bring infants to receive baptism not with the faith that they may be reborn by spiritual grace unto eternal life, but because they suppose that this remedy will preserve or restore their bodily health for the present time. The infants are not thereby prevented from being reborn because they are not offered by such persons with this intention.

### CHAPTER 172.—Augustine’s Letter 203 to Maximinus.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “To rebaptize.”) To rebaptize a heretical person who has received those signs of holiness handed down by Christian discipline is altogether a sin. But to rebaptize a catholic person is a most monstrous crime. [Col. 0103D]

### CHAPTER 173.—Bede, in the *Book of Homilies*, Homily 36, on John chapter 3.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “Whether a heretic.”) Whether a heretic, a schismatic, or any criminal person baptizes in confession of the holy Trinity, one baptized by him may not be rebaptized by good catholics, lest the confession or invocation of so great a name seem to be annulled.

### CHAPTER 174.—Haymo, on the First Epistle to the Corinthians.

Christ retained to himself the authority of baptizing to such an extent that, just as all sins are forgiven to one dipped in water by a holy and innocent man, so they are forgiven to one [Col. 0104A] dipped by a sinful and criminal man—provided only that this is done in the name of the holy Trinity. For the merit of the life of the baptizer or officiant neither benefits nor harms, in this regard, the person who is baptized.

### CHAPTER 175.—Book V of the *Capitula*, chapter 6.

If anyone has been baptized by an unbaptized priest, and the holy Trinity was invoked in that baptism, he has been baptized, as Pope Sergius said; however, he requires the laying on of hands.

### CHAPTER 176.—Augustine, on the First Epistle to the Corinthians.

We know that the Holy Spirit was given by God without laying on of hands, and that an unbaptized person obtained forgiveness of sins. Was Cornelius not invisibly baptized when he received the gift of baptism? [Col. 0104B]

### CHAPTER 177.—Augustine, *On One Baptism*, book IV, chapter 22.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter “Of baptism.”) Blessed Cyprian adduces no slight proof from the thief to whom it was said, although unbaptized, “Today you shall be with me in paradise,” that suffering sometimes fulfills the role of baptism. Considering the matter again and again, I find that not only suffering for Christ’s name may supply what was lacking from baptism, but also faith and conversion of heart, if, amid the constraints of the time, assistance cannot be obtained for celebrating the mystery of baptism. For that thief was not crucified for Christ’s name, but for the deserts of his crimes; nor did he suffer because he believed, but, while suffering, he believed. How much even without the visible sacrament of baptism the Apostle’s words can accomplish—“With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10)—was made evident in that thief. But this is fulfilled invisibly when not contempt for religion but a condition of necessity excludes the mystery of baptism.

The same work, chapter 23. And just as the kindness of the Almighty supplied in that thief what was lacking of the sacrament of baptism, because it was lacking not through pride or contempt but through necessity, so we must believe that the same grace of the Almighty supplies for infants who die baptized what they are unable to do—not by an impious will but through the incapacity of their age—namely, to believe in their heart unto righteousness or confess with their mouth unto salvation. Therefore, when prayer is made for them, so that the celebration of the sacrament may be fulfilled for them, this indeed avails for their celebration, because they cannot themselves respond. For it is another’s act when one believes through another, just as it was another’s act when he sinned in another. [Col. 0104D]

### CHAPTER 178.—Augustine, the same, chapter 23.

But if in the thief, because baptism was lacking bodily through [read: because of] necessity, salvation was complete because it was present spiritually through piety, then likewise, when baptism itself is at hand, if what was present to the thief is lacking through necessity, salvation is completed. This is the tradition held by the universal Church when infant children are baptized; for they certainly cannot yet believe unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation, as the thief could. Indeed, when the mystery is celebrated in them, they interrupt those mystical utterances by weeping and wailing, yet no Christian would say that they are baptized in vain. [Col. 0105A]

The same. By all these considerations it is shown that the sacrament of baptism is one thing and conversion of heart another, but that a person’s salvation is completed from both. Nor, if one of these is lacking, should we suppose that the other must consequently be lacking as well. For the one may exist without the other, as in an infant; and the other could exist without the one, as in the thief, God supplying in either case what was lacking not through the person’s will. But when either is lacking through the will, the person is entangled in guilt. Baptism can indeed be present where conversion of heart is lacking; conversion of heart can indeed be present where baptism has not been received, but it cannot be present where baptism has been despised. In no way may there be said to be conversion of heart to God when God’s sacrament is despised. [Col. 0105B]

### CHAPTER 179.—Gregory to Landulf, Prince of Salerno.

Although we do not doubt that your nobility’s plan to bring Jews to Christian worship proceeds from zeal for devotion, nevertheless, because you seem to act upon it with disordered zeal, we have judged it necessary to send you this letter of admonition. For we do not read that our Lord Jesus Christ compelled anyone violently into his service; rather, by humble exhortation, reserving to each the freedom of his own choice, he recalled from error to eternal life those whom he predestined, not by inflicting punishment, but by shedding his own blood.

The same. Blessed Gregory, in one of his letters, objects to this same people being drawn to the faith by force.

### CHAPTER 180.—To Virgilius and Theodore, Bishops [Bishop] of Marseilles (book I of the *Register of Letters*, chapter 45).

Many men of the Jewish religion residing in this province, and frequently travelling to the region of Marseilles on various business, have brought to your attention that many of the Jews dwelling in those parts have been brought to the font of baptism by force rather than by preaching. I judge such an intention indeed worthy of praise, and declare that it proceeds from love of our Lord. But unless an appropriate effect of holy Scripture accompanies this same intention [read: this intention], I fear that either no work deserving reward will result from it, or that certain losses of souls may follow from some cause—which may it never be. For when anyone comes to the font of baptism not through the sweetness of preaching but through compulsion, he returns to his former superstition and dies more grievously from that by which he seemed to have been reborn. [Col. 0105D]

### CHAPTER 181.—Pope Nicholas, *Responses to the Bulgarians*, chapter 41.

Of those who refuse to receive the benefit of Christianity and sacrifice to idols or bend the knee to them, we can write nothing else to you than that you should persuade them of the true faith by admonitions, exhortations, and reason, rather than by force, refuting the vain notions they entertain. [Col. 0106A]

CAP. 182.—Likewise.

There is to be no sharing of communion with those who do not believe and worship idols. Moreover, no violence is to be inflicted upon them to make them believe; for nothing that does not proceed from free will can be good. In chapter two above, we taught that violence must not be inflicted on a pagan in order to make him a Christian.

CAP. 183.—In the Life of Blessed Gregory, book IV, chapter 42.

Just as Gregory refused to have Jews baptized by force, so he would by no means permit Christians to be subjected to them in any way.

CAP. 184.—Augustine against Julian, book VI, chapter 5.

[Col. 0106B] (On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Si ad matris*.) If the child belonged to the mother’s body, in which he is conceived, so as to be reckoned a part of her, then a child whose mother was baptized while she carried him in her womb, because some danger of death was pressing, would not be baptized. But since the child himself is baptized as well, he will certainly not be regarded as baptized twice. Therefore, while he was in the womb, he did not belong to the mother’s body.

Likewise. (From the same work, book [VI], chapter 6.) If everything that is in a human being when he is baptized and sanctified is thought to be baptized and sanctified, you will say that those things too in him which are processed in the intestines and bladder through the body’s digestion are baptized and sanctified. You will say that a person situated in his mother’s womb is baptized and sanctified if necessity compels the pregnant woman to receive this sacrament, and consequently that the one who is then born ought not to be baptized. Finally, you will say that fevers are baptized and sanctified when the sick are baptized. [Col. 0106C]

CAP. 185.—Isidore, *Sentences*, book I, chapter 18 [22]; book I of *The Supreme Good*, chapter 25.

(On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Qui in maternis*.) Those who are in their mothers’ wombs cannot therefore be baptized with their mothers, because one who has not yet been born according to Adam cannot be reborn according to Christ. Regeneration cannot be said to occur in one whom generation has not preceded. Let those who live wickedly in the Church and do not cease to communicate, thinking that they are cleansed by such communion, learn that it profits them nothing for cleansing.

CAP. 186.—Gregory, replying to Augustine, chapter 10.

[Col. 0106D]

(On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Si quae mulier*.) Why a pregnant woman should not be baptized, I do not know, since fruitfulness of the flesh is no fault in the sight of almighty God.

CAP. 187.—Augustine, to Boniface, Epistle 23.

(On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Nihil est*.) To believe is nothing other than to have faith; and therefore, when the answer is made that an infant believes, though he does not yet possess the disposition of faith, the answer is made that he has faith on account of the sacrament of faith, and that he turns to God on account of the sacrament of conversion, because the answer itself belongs to the celebration of the sacrament.

Likewise. Although the little child does not yet possess that faith which consists in the will of believers, nevertheless the sacrament of that very faith already makes him faithful, just as he is answered to “believe.” For in this way they are called faithful: not by inwardly rejecting the reality itself, but by receiving the sacrament of that reality. [Col. 0107A]

CAP. 188.—Augustine, to Renatus, *On the Soul*, book II, chapter 12.

The mystery of belief in little children is fulfilled through the response of those by whom they are carried.

CAP. 189.—Augustine, *On the Creed*, book II, chapter 1.

You have professed that you renounce the devil, his pomps, and his angels. See, dearly beloved, that you bring this profession of yours before the heavenly court: the names of those making profession are entered in the book of life, not by any human being but by a higher power from heaven.

CAP. 190.—Ambrose on Luke, book X (chapter 88).

[Col. 0107B]

If anyone, whether a heretic or a schismatic, causes a catechumen to be cast forth, as it were, from the womb of a mother, of a soul, or of the Church in labor, he is punished more lightly; if [he does so to] a believer, more severely.

CAP. 191.—Augustine, in the book to Fortunatus.

(On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Sanctum est*.) Baptism given in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is holy in itself, so that in that sacrament there is also the authority of the transmission handed down from our Lord to the apostles, and through them to bishops and other priests, or even to Christian laypeople proceeding from the same origin and stock.

(On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *In necessitate*.) For in a case of necessity, when bishops, priests, or any of the ministers [Col. 0107C] are unavailable, and danger presses upon the person who asks, lest he end this life without this sacrament, we are accustomed to hear that even a layperson may give the sacrament which he has received. For when that story is told, it moves nearly all who hear it to tears. On a certain ship no believer was present except one penitent, and shipwreck began to threaten. There was there a man not forgetful of his salvation and most urgently demanding the sacrament; yet there was no one able to give it except that penitent, for he had received penance for the sin concerning which he was undergoing penance. He had lost the sanctity proper to the elders, but he had not lost the sacrament. For if sinners lose this when they are reconciled after penance, why are they not baptized again? [Col. 0107D]

Therefore he gave what he had received; and, lest the other should end his life in danger unreconciled, he asked the very man whom he had baptized to reconcile him. And it happened: they escaped shipwreck. You know what they did. There was no one among them who did not hold so pious an opinion as to believe that in that danger the Lord was present in their counsels. For a devout and suppliant mind demands the sacrament from a human being and obtains holiness from God.

But if perhaps someone does not wish to believe this story which I have related about those imperiled by an imminent shipwreck—for it is recommended not by the authority of the divine Scriptures but by report from an uncertain author—I shall not dispute it; but I ask: if something of this sort should happen, what is to be done? For no one can say that a person who desires baptism when death is imminent ought to be abandoned; and whoever does not believe that it happened for him to be baptized by a penitent must believe that it can happen. [Col. 0108A]

CAP. 192.—Augustine, *On the Origin of the Soul*, to Victor, book I (chapter 9).

The thief may, by divine judgment, be reckoned among those cleansed by the confession of martyrdom; yet you do not know even whether he was unbaptized. For, leaving aside the belief that, fastened beside the Lord’s pierced side, he could have been drenched with the water and blood that sprang forth together and washed in so holy a baptism—what if he had been baptized in prison? Some were afterward able to obtain this secretly in a time of persecution. What if he had been baptized before he was arrested? For public laws could not on that account spare him, so far as bodily death was concerned, because he had divinely received remission of sins. [Col. 0108B]

CAP. 193.—Augustine, Homily to the Neophytes, beginning: “Every discourse indeed concerning these things.”

Let each one of you, therefore, recall the individual kinds of mysteries which, by our ministry and with the Lord’s gift, you have received; and understand wisely now those things which you then received humbly and faithfully, so that you may preserve them the better through understanding.

First, certainly, we anoint your ears with the oil of blessing. But learn for what reason this is done, according to ecclesiastical tradition, by all Catholic priests of Christ. The entrance of faith and of all holy teaching is admitted to the mind through the ears, and understanding arises from hearing. For no one can know the sacraments of faith unless he hears a preacher. [Col. 0108C]

Likewise. Therefore the holy anointing applied to the ears signifies that they should resist and flee every discourse outside discipline, as though contradicting Christ’s teaching; but they should turn to hearing God’s words alone, because, with that oil applied, they have consecrated their hearing to Christ’s words.

Likewise. But after your ears have been anointed with blessed oil, you have been designated among the number of wise hearers, so that, rightly retaining the words of God—that is, fulfilling what you hear—on the day of judgment you may hear Christ saying to you: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV).

Moreover, do not suppose that we also anointed your nostrils with the oil of blessing idly or without a definite reason of mystery. This is understood to be done so that those who come to baptism may be admonished to preserve the sacrament of so great a mystery inviolate and whole until death: so that, as long as they draw the breath of this life through their nostrils, they may not depart from the worship and service of Christ our Lord. [Col. 0108D]

Likewise. Yet a subtler meaning is signified in the anointing of the nostrils. For the fragrance of that oil, blessed in Christ’s name and power, summons you to spiritual smell, so that you may perceive Christ with inestimable sweetness, not by bodily but by mental senses; and, delighted by knowledge of his fragrance, may follow his footsteps and say that which the chorus of believers speaks to God: “We run after you in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song I). [Col. 0109A]

CAP. 194.—Homily 3.

(On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Prima igitur*.) Thus far we have spoken of the mysteries celebrated by the sacrament in baptism itself. Now we shall speak of those things which are fulfilled by holy institution concerning those already baptized. For after you had given the most certain pledge by which you promised, in descending into the font—the holy font, the font of redemption, the font sanctified by heavenly power—to renounce all the devil’s pomps, works, and every demonic fornication, [Col. 0109B] we began to speak of the inner mysteries themselves, which were celebrated in that holy font.

Likewise. Therefore, in this font, before we immersed you with your whole body, we asked: “Do you believe in God the Father almighty?” You answered: “I believe.” Again we asked: “Do you also believe in Jesus Christ his Son, who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary?” Each of you answered: “I believe.” Again we asked: “And in the Holy Spirit?” You answered likewise: “I believe.” We did this according to the command of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior, who, when he ascended to the Father in heaven, commanded his disciples, that is, the apostles, saying: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII). [Col. 0109C]

Likewise. But when we asked: “Do you believe the holy Church, the remission of sins, and the resurrection of the flesh?” we did not ask this in the way in which one believes in God, as though one believed also in the holy and catholic Church. It is holy and catholic because it rightly believes in God. Therefore, we did not say that you were to believe *in the Church* as in God; rather, understand that you say—and said—that, living in the holy and catholic Church, you believed in God; you also believed in the resurrection of the flesh which is to come.

Likewise. (On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Postquam*.) After you promised to believe, we immersed your heads three times in the sacred font. [Col. 0109D] This order of baptism is performed with a twofold mystical significance. You were rightly immersed three times, because you received baptism in the name of the Trinity. You were rightly immersed three times, because you received baptism in the name of Jesus Christ (Rom. VI), who rose from the dead on the third day. Thus the threefold immersion expresses a type of the Lord’s burial; through it you have been buried with Christ in baptism and risen with Christ in faith, so that, washed from sins, you may live in the holiness of virtues by imitating Christ.

CAP. 195.—Homily.

Thus far we have spoken of the mysteries celebrated through the sacrament in baptism itself. Now we shall deal with those things which, by holy institution, are completed concerning the baptized. For when baptism has been completed, we pour chrism—that is, the oil of sanctification—upon your heads, [Col. 0110A] by which it is shown that royal and priestly dignity is conferred upon the baptized by the Lord. For in the Old Testament those chosen for priesthood or kingship were anointed with holy oil; and by anointing of the head, some received from the Lord authority to reign over God’s people, others authority to offer sacrifices to God.

Likewise. When all the sacraments have been completed, we also give you a command by example and word. For we washed each person’s feet, exhorting you to imitate us—or rather, our Lord and Savior himself—so that, just as we washed your feet, you also ought to wash the feet of brethren and guests.

CAP. 196.—Anastasius to Bishop Epictetus.

Gabriel is sent to Mary, not to a virgin only temporarily, but to a virgin betrothed to a man (Luke II), in order to show the bridegroom that Mary was truly human. Scripture mentions her childbirth and says, “She wrapped the child” (ibid.); “Blessed are the breasts which he sucked” (Luke XI); and a sacrifice was offered because the one who was born opened the womb. All these were indications of a virgin who had given birth. [Col. 0110B]

CAP. 197.—That baptism is not to be administered except at Easter and Pentecost, unless to persons in danger of death. From the letter of Pope Leo, chapter 11.

Since it is most plainly evident that these two seasons, Easter and Pentecost, are the lawful times for the elect who are to be baptized in the Church, we admonish your charity not to mingle any other days with this observance. For although there are other feasts to which great reverence is due in honor of God, yet the mystical and rational pattern of the principal and greatest sacrament must be observed by us. This does not forbid the freedom by which aid is given, through baptism at any time, to persons in danger. Thus we defer until these two festivals, connected with and akin to one another, the free desires of those who are safe and living in the security of peace; but in danger of death, peril of siege, pressure of persecution, fear of shipwreck, we deny this unique safeguard of true salvation to no one at any time. [Col. 0110C]

CAP. 198.—At what time baptism should be celebrated. From the decrees of Pope Victor, to the brethren established throughout Alexandria (Epistle 1 to Theophilus).

[Col. 0110D]

(On Consecration, distinction 3, chapter *Celebritatem*.) Catholic baptism is to be celebrated during the Easter season and Pentecost; but if necessity requires or danger of death threatens, pagans coming to faith are to be baptized wherever and whenever it may occur—whether in a river, sea, or springs—provided only that they are confirmed in belief in the Christian confession. Careful attention must also be given to what they promised in baptism, lest they be found unbelievers rather than believers. Those, however, who are marked by the stain of unbelief become infamous and are by no means reckoned among the faithful.

CAP. 199.—On the two times for baptism. From the decrees of Pope Gelasius X (Epistle 1 to the bishops of Lucania and Bruttium, etc.).

[Col. 0111A]

(On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Baptizandi*.) Let no one suppose that there is any warrant for baptizing indiscriminately at any time, apart from the venerable sacrament of the Paschal feast and Pentecost, except only when a very serious illness strikes, in which case one must fear that, as the danger of sickness grows, the sick person may perhaps be overtaken by death and depart without the remedy of salvation.

CAP. 200.—On the same matter. From the decrees of Pope Siricius, chapter 2 (Epistle to Himerius, Bishop of Tarragona).

(On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Non ratione auctoritatis*.) There follows the blameworthy and corrigible confusion of baptizing different persons according to each one’s pleasure, [Col. 0111B] which, as we say with grief, is presumed by our fellow-priests not by reason of any authority but by sheer rashness: so that, as you assert, innumerable people indiscriminately and freely receive the mystery of baptism on the birthdays of Christ or his manifestation, and likewise on the feasts of apostles or martyrs, although among us and among all Churches the Lord’s Easter, together with its Pentecost, especially claims this privilege for itself.

CAP. 201.—On the same matter. From the council at Compiègne, chapter 4.

That baptism is not to be celebrated outside the times appointed by the canons, namely Easter and Pentecost; for the holy canons forbid this in every way unless some danger is imminent, so strictly that they exclude from ecclesiastical ranks even those who baptize at another time and do not admit them to the clergy. [Col. 0111C]

CAP. 202.—Likewise on the same matter. From the Council of Worms, chapter 9.

Let every believer know that the sacrament of most holy baptism is to be administered only at the Paschal feast and Pentecost, except that those pressed by danger of death must be aided by such remedies, lest they perish eternally.

CAP. 203.—That catechumens are to come twenty days before baptism for purification by exorcism. From the Council of Braga, chapter 4.

(On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Ante dies 20*.) We command this in every way, and the ancient canons order it: catechumens are to come twenty days before baptism for purification by exorcism; and during those twenty days, according to the canonical command, they are both instructed and consecrated. [Col. 0111D]

CAP. 204.—That all persons coming to baptism ought, on Thursday of Holy Week, to recite the faith to the bishop or priest. From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 46.

Those coming to baptism must learn the faith and, on Thursday of Holy Week, recite it to the bishop or priests.

CAP. 205.—That all who are to be baptized are first to be exorcized. From the decrees of Pope Celestine, sent to the bishops of Gaul, chapter 12.

We do not consider idly that which the holy Church uniformly does throughout the whole world concerning those who are to be baptized: whether little children or young persons [Col. 0112A] come to the sacrament of regeneration, they may not approach the font of life until the unclean spirit has been driven from them by the exorcisms and breathings of the clergy, so that it may then truly appear how the prince of this world is cast out.

CAP. 206.—That candidates for baptism, having enrolled their names, should abstain from meat and wine. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 75.

(On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Baptizandi*.) Those to be baptized are to give their names while abstaining from wine and meat, and are to be frequently examined for baptism by the laying on of hands.

CAP. 207.—That neophytes should abstain for a time from richer foods and from spouses. From the same council, chapter 76.

(On Consecration, distinction 5, chapter *Neophyti*.) Let neophytes abstain for some time from more sumptuous meals, spectacles, and spouses. [Col. 0112B]

CAP. 208.—That every priest should have a baptismal vessel. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 7.

(On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Omnis presbyter*.) Every priest unable to have a stone font shall have a suitable vessel exclusively for the office of baptism, which is not to be taken outside the church. Likewise, separate vessels shall be kept for washing the corporal cloth and for the altar coverings, in which nothing else is done.

CAP. 209.—That no priest should baptize except in cities, except for illness. From the same council, chapter 48.

No priest is to presume to baptize except in cities and at the appointed times, unless illness or certain necessity requires it, and [only] in those places which retain the authority and privileges due to them. [Col. 0112C]

CAP. 210.—How baptism is to be conferred upon one who wishes to become a believer. From the decrees of Pope Clement, Epistle 3 sent to all the faithful.

If anyone wishes to become a believer and desires baptism, so that, having put off former evils, he may thereafter, by good works, become heir of heavenly goods, let him approach his priest, give him his name, and hear from him the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. Let him devote himself to frequent fasts and test himself in all things, so that, after completing three months, he may be baptized on a feast day. Let each person be baptized in running water, with the name of the threefold Blessedness invoked over him, having first been anointed with oil sanctified by prayer, so that, consecrated by these means, he may finally receive a place among the saints. [Col. 0112D]

CAP. 211.—On martyrs who underwent martyrdom without baptism. From the sayings of Bishop Augustine. (*On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, chapter 74.)

(On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Catechumenum*.) We do not believe that a catechumen who dies, however good his works, has life, except only if the sacrament of martyrdom completes him. The baptized person confesses his faith before a priest and, when questioned, answers. The martyr does the same before his persecutor: he confesses the faith and, when questioned, answers. The former, after confession, is sprinkled with water; the latter is sprinkled with blood or immersed in fire. The former receives the Holy Spirit by the bishop’s laying on of hands; [Col. 0113A] the latter becomes a dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit, since it is not he himself who speaks, but the Holy Spirit who speaks in him. The former communicates in the Eucharist in commemoration of the Lord’s death; the latter dies together with Christ himself. The former confesses that he renounces the deeds of the world; the latter renounces life itself. All sins are remitted to the former; they are extinguished in the latter.

CAP. 212.—That the sacrament may not be given to catechumens at Easter. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 5.

Likewise, it was resolved that during the most solemn Paschal days the sacrament is not to be given to catechumens, except the customary salt, because during those days the faithful do not change the sacrament, nor ought catechumens to be changed.

CAP. 213.—On removing catechumens from the baptistery. From the First Council of Orange, chapter 13.

[Col. 0113B] Catechumens are never to be admitted to the baptistery unless they have first been baptized.

CAP. 214.—On separating and instructing catechumens. From the same council, chapter 14.

Catechumens, even among household ranks, are to be separated from the blessing of the faithful insofar as it can be guarded against; and they are to be instructed to present themselves separately for signing or blessing.

CAP. 215.—On catechumens who sin. From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 5.

If a catechumen enters the church, he shall stand in the rank of those instructed by the word. If he is discovered sinning, if indeed he kneels, let him hear [the word], so that he may sin no further. But if, while hearing, he sins again, let him be expelled.

CAP. 216.—That those recently baptized should not be promoted. From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 3.

[Col. 0113C]

Concerning those recently enlightened by baptism: it is not fitting that they be promoted to priestly rank.

CAP. 217.—On priests who do not baptize in the Trinity according to the Lord’s command. From Canon 49 of the Apostles.

If any bishop or priest baptizes not according to the Lord’s command in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but in three beginningless principles, or in three sons, or in three paracletes, let him be deposed.

CAP. 218.—That in baptism and confirmation, if necessary, there may be one sponsor. From the decrees of Pope Hyginus, chapter 10.

[Col. 0113D] (On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *In catechismo*.) In catechesis, baptism, and confirmation, one sponsor may serve if necessity compels; this is not, however, the Roman custom, but one person receives each individual.

CAP. 219.—That one male or female sponsor should come forward to receive the infant. From the decrees of Pope Leo at Saint-Médard.

(On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Non plures*.) No more than one person, whether man or woman, is to come forward to receive an infant from baptism. The same is also to be done in confirmations.

CAP. 220.—That one who has not been confirmed may receive no one at baptism. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 2.

(On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *In baptismo*.) In baptism [Col. 0114A] or chrism, one who has not himself been baptized or confirmed cannot receive another as a godchild.

CAP. 221.—That no one may become a sponsor unless he rightly believes. From the Council of Paris.

No one may receive another from the sacred font unless he knows and understands the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed in his own language, recites them before the priest, and all understand the covenant which they have made with God.

CAP. 222.—That priests should require sponsors to know the Creed. From the Council of Worms, chapter 1.

Let priests take care that neither men nor women receive boys or girls from the sacred font unless they have memorized the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer.

CAP. 223.—On publicly reciting the Creed in all churches eight days before Easter. From the Council of Agde, chapter 12 (chapter 13).

[Col. 0114B]

(On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Symbolum*.) It was also resolved that the Creed should be delivered [variant: preached] publicly in church to the candidates by all churches on one day, namely the eighth day before the Lord’s resurrection.

CAP. 224.—On sick pagans, if they desire baptism. Likewise from the same [council], chapter 3.

If pagans desire that hands be laid upon them in the Trinity, and if their life has been honorable in some respect, it was resolved that hands should be laid upon them and that they should become Christians.

CAP. 225.—On baptizing a pregnant woman. From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 6.

[Col. 0114C] (On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Si qua mulier*.) A pregnant woman ought to be baptized whenever she wishes. For the woman giving birth communicates nothing in this matter to the one being born, because each person’s intention is declared in the confession.

CAP. 226.—On baptizing sick little children. From the Council of Girona, chapter 5.

Concerning little children newly brought forth from their mothers’ wombs, it was resolved and established that, if they are ill—as often happens—and do not seek their mother’s milk, they are to be baptized, if brought [for baptism], even on the very day on which they are born.

CAP. 227.—On those baptized during illness. From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 12.

If anyone has been baptized during illness, he ought not to be ordained a priest. For his faith is not voluntary [Col. 0114D] but arises from necessity—unless perhaps his zeal and faith later appear approved, or a shortage of persons compels it.

CAP. 228.—On those who deny that newborn children are to be baptized. From the African Council, chapter 76.

(On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Placuit*.) Likewise, it was resolved that whoever denies that little children newly born from their mothers’ wombs are to be baptized, or says that they are baptized not for remission of sins but that they derive no original sin from Adam requiring expiation by the washing of regeneration—so that it follows that, in their case, the formula of baptism “for remission of sins” must be understood not truly but falsely—let him be anathema. For the Apostle’s statement, “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin [Col. 0115A] death, and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V), must be understood in no other way than the Catholic Church dispersed throughout the world has always understood it. For this rule of faith is why even little children, who have not yet been able to commit any sins in themselves, are truly baptized for remission of sins: so that by regeneration there may be cleansed in them what they derived by generation.

CAP. 229.—On persons baptized while ill, from the Council of Laodicea, chapter 72.

(Chapter 47.) Those who receive baptism during illness ought, once they have recovered, to learn the faith and know in what gift they have become participants.

CAP. 230.—On sick persons who desire baptism and afterward become speechless. From the African Council, chapter 12.

[Col. 0115B]

That sick persons, if unable to answer for themselves, are to be baptized when those who testify to their will say that they desired this on their own account when in danger; and that reconciliation is not to be denied to actors, stage-performers, and other persons of this sort.

CAP. 231.—On not baptizing the dead. From the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 6.

Care must also be taken lest the weakness of the brethren believe that the dead can be baptized, since they observe that the Eucharist is not given to them either.

CAP. 232.—On baptizing one who suddenly becomes speechless, if he has witnesses. From the Council of Orange, chapter 9.

[Col. 0115C] (27, question 6, chapter *Qui recedunt*.) A person who suddenly becomes speechless may, as has been decreed, receive baptism and penance if he has testimony of his previous intention in others’ words, or of his present intention in his own gesture.

CAP. 233.—On those baptized among heretics in the name of the Holy Trinity. From the Council of Rouen, chapter 5.

There is one baptism in the Catholic Church, of which we have been made members, where there is one faith and where it is given in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Therefore those baptized among heretics who baptize in confession of the Holy Trinity and who come to us are indeed to be received as baptized, lest the invocation and confession of the Holy Trinity be annulled. But they are to be taught fully and instructed in the meaning [Col. 0115D] and mystery of the Holy Trinity as held in the holy Church. If they agree to believe, or consent to confess the integrity of purified faith, they are to be strengthened by the laying on of hands. But if they are unintelligent little children who cannot grasp doctrine, those presenting them shall answer for them according to the custom of baptism; they shall thus be questioned so that they may know what they ought to answer, and so receive the laying on of hands.

CAP. 234.—On the same matter. From the Council of Worms, chapter 5.

Whoever has been baptized by heretics in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit must by no means be rebaptized, but is to be purified by laying on of hands alone.

CAP. 235.—That baptism received in the Trinity is not to be repeated. From the First Council of Carthage, chapter 1.

[Col. 0116A]

That baptism received in the Trinity is not to be repeated. Therefore, if it pleases you, let us first consider the heading concerning the rebaptized; and I ask your holiness to direct the gaze of your mind calmly to one descending into the water, questioned concerning the Trinity according to the faith of the Gospel and the teaching of the apostles, and confessing a good conscience toward God through the resurrection of Jesus Christ: may such a person lawfully be questioned again in the same faith and immersed in water again? All the bishops said: “Far be it! Far be it! We decree rebaptism to be unlawful and altogether foreign to sincere faith and Catholic discipline!”

CAP. 236.—On those who do not know in what faith they were baptized. From the decrees of Pope Leo, sent to the bishops established throughout Sicily, chapter 29. (Epistle to Rusticus, chapter 15.)

[Col. 0116B]

(On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Hi de quibus*.) Those about whom you wrote, who know that they were baptized but profess not to know of what faith those who baptized them were: since they received the form of baptism in some manner, they are not to be rebaptized; but, receiving through the laying on of hands the power of the Holy Spirit which they could not receive from heretics, they are to be joined to Catholics.

CAP. 237.—On a priest who did not know grammar but nevertheless baptized in the Trinity. Letter of Zachary to Boniface, Archbishop of Mainz.

[Col. 0116C]

(On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Retulerunt*.) Virgil and Sedulius, religious men living in the province of the Bavarians, have written to us, informing us that your reverend brotherhood was ordering Christians to be rebaptized. Hearing this, we were greatly troubled and fell into some astonishment, if the matter was as reported. For they related that in that same province there was a priest entirely ignorant of the Latin language who, while baptizing, not knowing how to pronounce the Latin tongue, said: “I baptize you in the name of the fatherland [*patria*], and the daughter [*filia*], and the Holy Spirit”; and that for this reason your reverend brotherhood had decided to rebaptize.

Know, most holy brother, that if the one who baptized, not introducing error or heresy, but solely through ignorance of Roman speech and through mangling the language, as we have said above, had spoken while baptizing in this manner, we cannot consent that they be baptized anew. For—as your brotherhood well knows—whoever has been baptized by heretics in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit must by no means be rebaptized, but must be purified by laying on of hands alone. Therefore, most holy brother, if the matter is as it has been reported to us, do not preach this further or anything of that kind; rather, let your brotherhood endeavor to observe what the holy Fathers teach and preach. [Col. 0116D]

CAP. 238.—On those who have some doubt about baptism, that they should be baptized again. From the decrees of Pope Leo [Col. 0117A] to Rusticus, Bishop of Narbonne, chapter 28 (Epistle 90, chapter 15).

(On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Si nulla*.) If among relatives and household members there are no indications, and among clergy or neighbors none, by which it may be shown that those in question were baptized, it must be arranged that they be reborn, lest they plainly perish; for, in their case, reason does not allow what is not shown to have been done to be treated as repeated. Those, however, who can remember that they came to church with their parents may recall whether they received what was given to their parents. But if this too lies beyond their own memory, what is not known to have been conferred appears to be conferable upon them, because where there is the diligence of piety, no rash presumption intervenes.

CAP. 239.—What is to be done concerning infants for whom no wholly certain witnesses can be found as to whether they have been baptized. From the African Council, chapter 39 (Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter 6).

[Col. 0117B]

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Placuit*.) It was likewise decreed concerning infants that, whenever wholly certain witnesses cannot be found to testify without doubt that they have been baptized, and the children themselves, owing to their age, are unable adequately to answer concerning the sacraments administered to them, they are to be baptized without any hesitation, lest this uncertainty cause them to be deprived of the cleansing of the sacraments. For this reason the envoys of your [Moorish] people consulted our brethren, who redeem many such persons from barbarians.

### CHAPTER 240.—Concerning priests through whose negligence someone has died without baptism. From the decrees of Pope Sixtus, chapter 5.

[Col. 0117C] Let priests consider how great a danger it is that, through their negligence, the souls of innocents should perish and the gates of paradise be shut against them. Therefore priests must take the greatest care not, through their own carelessness, to separate from heavenly blessedness souls for whom Christ’s blood was shed. And if—God forbid!—this should happen, the one through whose neglect it occurred shall submit himself, for the days of his life, to the sorrow of severe penance.

### CHAPTER 241.—That no priest may presume to deny baptism to any sick person, whether in his own province or elsewhere. From the decrees of Pope Martian, chapter 3.

Any priest who, in his own province or another, or wherever he may be found, refuses to baptize a sick person entrusted to him, or, while travelling [Col. 0117D] on a journey, makes some excuse, so that the person dies without baptism, is to be deposed.

### CHAPTER 242.—Concerning those led to repeat baptism either by compulsion through fear or by error. From the decrees of Pope Leo to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, chapter 47.

With respect to those concerning whom your charity similarly believes us should be consulted—those who have been led to repeat baptism either under compulsion through fear or through error, and who now recognize that they have acted against the sacrament of the Catholic faith—this moderation must be observed: they are to be received into the unity of communion with our fellowship only through the remedy of penance and the laying on of the bishop’s hand. The duration of their penance, however, is to be moderated according to your judgment, as you perceive the devotion of the converts’ minds; [Col. 0118A] taking account likewise of advanced age and of the necessities arising from any dangers or illnesses. If any of them is so severely pressed that, while still doing penance, there is fear for his salvation, it is necessary to assist him, through priestly care, with the grace common to all.

### CHAPTER 243.—That baptism is not to be denied to a sick little child, even if brought from another parish. From the decrees of Pope Eugenius, chapter 6.

If a sick little child is brought to any priest from any parish for the grace of baptism, the sacrament of baptism is by no means to be denied him. If anyone refuses to grant this ministry to one who asks, let him know that he who has not baptized the child will render an account for that soul and is to be corrected most severely before the synod. [Col. 0118B]

### CHAPTER 244.—That confirmation is not to be repeated. From the Council of Tarragona, chapter 6.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 5, chapter *Dictum est*.) It has been reported to us that certain persons among the laity are confirmed two, three, or even more times by bishops. Therefore it has seemed to us that this same confirmation, like baptism, must by no means be repeated; for it has been decreed that those baptized or confirmed twice or more are to serve most devoutly not the world but God alone, under a religious or clerical habit.

### CHAPTER 245.—That those rebaptized unknowingly cannot be ordained except in great necessity. From the Penitential of Theodore, chapter 14.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Qui bis*.) Those who have unknowingly been baptized twice need not do penance for this, except [Col. 0118C] that according to the canons they cannot be ordained unless some great necessity compels it. But those who were baptized a second time knowingly have, as it were, crucified Christ again: they are to do penance for seven years on Wednesdays and Fridays, and to observe penance through three Lents. If they did this because of some fault, likewise. If they believed it was for purification, they are likewise to do penance for three years.

### CHAPTER 246.—Concerning the souls of little children who die without baptism. From the letter of Pope Gregory to Secundinus, servant of God and recluse.

(In the Register, book VII, letter 53.) At the end of your letter you asked what answer should be given to those who question your charity concerning the souls of little children who die without the grace of baptism. They say: if the body is held by original guilt, how will the soul, which is given by God and has not yet consented with the body to an actual sin, be guilty? But on this matter, sweetest brother, know that no small inquiry concerning the origin of the soul has been debated among the holy Fathers. Yet whether it descends from Adam or is rightly given individually to each person has remained uncertain; and they confessed this to be an insoluble question in this life. For the question is serious and cannot be comprehended by man: if the soul is born with the flesh from the same substance, why does it not also die with the flesh? But if it is bound with the flesh descended from Adam, it is held under sins. Yet, this being so, it is not uncertain that, unless a person has been reborn through the sacred grace of baptism, every soul is bound in the chains of original sin. [Col. 0119A]

For thus it is written: “No one is clean in his sight, not even an infant of one day upon the earth” (Job 14, according to the interpretation of the Septuagint). Thus David says: “I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Psalm 50). Thus Truth himself says: “Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3). Thus the apostle Paul says: “As all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ” (1 Corinthians 15). Why then can an infant who has committed no sin be not clean in the sight of almighty God? Why was the Psalmist, born of lawful marriage, conceived in iniquity? Why these things, unless because one who has not been cleansed by the water of baptism is not clean? Why does every person die in Adam, unless bound by the chains of original sin? But because [Col. 0119B] the human race, in its first parent as in a root, raised up the barrenness of the fathers into the branches, every human being is born with sins, because the first human being chose to remain in sin.

I ought to have spoken more subtly and fully concerning these matters; but while the mass of my concerns presses upon me, and their bearer proved importunate in seeking to be released, I have said little where I owed much.

### CHAPTER 247.—Concerning energumens to be baptized. From the Council of Orange, chapter 13 (chapter 14).

Energumens already baptized, who are concerned for their cleansing, if they commit themselves to the care of the clergy and obey their admonitions, are in every way to receive communion, by the power of that sacrament: either to fortify them against the assault of the demon by which they are harassed, or to cleanse those whose [Col. 0119C] life is already shown to be purer.

### CHAPTER 248.—On the same matter. From the same council, chapter 22 (chapter 15).

In the case of catechumen energumens, provision concerning baptism is to be made insofar as necessity demands or opportunity permits.

### CHAPTER 249.—That communion is not to be shared with those rebaptized. From the Council of Lleida, chapter 14.

Why should devout believers partake with those who have been rebaptized?

### CHAPTER 250.—Concerning a priest who rebaptizes one validly baptized, and does not baptize one invalidly baptized by heretics. From the Council of Lyons, chapter 47.

If a bishop or priest rebaptizes one who has baptism according to the truth, or does not baptize one defiled by the impious and invalidly [Col. 0119D] baptized, he is to be deposed, as one mocking the cross and death of the Lord and not truly distinguishing true priests from false priests.

### CHAPTER 251.—That an unordained person must not rashly presume to baptize. From the decrees of Pope Hormisdas, chapter 4.

If anyone unordained baptizes or rashly performs anything sacred, let him be expelled from the Church and never ordained.

### CHAPTER 252.—That deacons are not to usurp the office of priests. From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, chapter 6.

(Part I, distinction 93, under “deacons,” first part.) We also prescribe that deacons observe their proper measure. We permit them to attempt nothing beyond the scope assigned by the paternal canons, nor to appropriate in any way to their ministry those things which antiquity decreed as properly belonging to the higher orders. [Col. 0120A] They must not dare to baptize without a bishop and priest, unless extreme necessity compels it when those officials are perhaps situated far away; this is often permitted even to Christian laypersons.

### CHAPTER 253.—That priests should admonish the people to present their infants to the bishop for confirmation. From the Council of Worms, chapter 2.

Let priests announce to the people that they should have their infants presented to their bishop for confirmation as soon as possible. If they neglect this, both priest and people are subject to canonical discipline.

### CHAPTER 254.—That all of mature age should come fasting for confirmation. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 6 (chapter 3).

[Col. 0120B]

(Concerning consecration, distinction 5, chapter *Ut jejuni*.) Those of mature age are to come fasting for confirmation; they are to be admonished first to make confession, so that, cleansed, they may be able to receive the gift of the Holy Spirit; and because no one will be a Christian unless he has been anointed with chrism in episcopal confirmation.

### CHAPTER 255.—Whether the sacrament of baptism or confirmation is greater. Pope Melchiades to the bishops of Spain, chapter 6.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter *De his*.) Concerning the matters on which you ask to be instructed—namely, whether the sacrament of the bishops’ laying on of hands or baptism is greater—know that each is a great sacrament. And just as one is from the greater persons, that is, [Col. 0120C] the highest pontiffs, and cannot be performed by lesser persons, so it is to be revered and maintained with greater veneration. Yet these two sacraments are so joined that they can in no way be separated from each other except where death intervenes first, and one cannot rightly be completed without the other.

### CHAPTER 256.—That all Christians should come for confirmation. From the Council of Worms, chapter 3.

Let all devoutly gather for the bishop’s preaching and confirmation, faithfully assist him, and obey him.

### CHAPTER 257.—Likewise concerning the laying on of hands. Pope Eusebius to the brethren established throughout Campania and Tuscany, chapter 22 (letter 3).

(Concerning consecration, distinction 5, chapter *Manus*.) The sacrament of the laying on of hands must likewise be held in great veneration. [Col. 0120D] It cannot be performed by others than the highest priests; nor in the time of the apostles is it read or known to have been performed by any others than the apostles themselves; nor can or ought it ever be performed by any others than those who hold their place. For if it is presumed otherwise, it is to be considered invalid and void, and shall never be reckoned among the ecclesiastical sacraments.

### CHAPTER 258.—Likewise concerning confirmation. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 3.

We command that all should eagerly and devoutly come to receive, through the laying on of the pontiff’s hands, the gift of the Holy Spirit; that they faithfully provide the bishop with what is necessary; and that they obey him in all things and through all things.

### CHAPTER 259.—That all the faithful, having received baptism, ought to receive the heavenly chrism. From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 48.

[Col. 0121A]

Those who are baptized must, after the washing, receive the heavenly chrism and be found participants in the kingdom of Christ.

### CHAPTER 260.—That all reborn at the font of baptism ought to receive the gift of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. From the letter of Pope Antherus, chapter 15 (from the second letter of Pope Urban I).

(Concerning consecration, distinction 5, chapter *Omnes fideles*.) All the faithful ought, after baptism, to receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of bishops’ hands, so that they may be found complete Christians. We receive from the Spirit so that we may become spiritual, because “the natural person does not receive the things that are of the Holy Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2); for when [Col. 0121B] the Holy Spirit is poured in, the faithful heart is enlarged for wisdom and steadfastness. We receive from the Holy Spirit so that we may be wise: to distinguish good from evil, to love what is just, to reject what is unjust, to resist envy and pride, and to withstand lust, diverse enticements, and shameful and unworthy desires. We receive from the Holy Spirit so that, kindled by love and longing for eternal glory, we may be able to raise our minds from earthly things to the things above and to divine things.

### CHAPTER 261.—That bishops should perform confirmation only while fasting. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 3.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 5, chapter *Ut episcopi*.) Bishops are to confer the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands only while fasting, except in the case of the sick and those in danger of death. Just as baptism must be celebrated by fasting persons at the two seasons, namely Easter [Col. 0121C] and Pentecost, so too the conferral of the Holy Spirit ought to be celebrated by fasting bishops.

### CHAPTER 262.—That bishops may, if necessary, confirm in the open field. From the Council of Reims, chapter 10.

A bishop may, if necessary, confirm in the open field.

### CHAPTER 263.—That those baptized are to be sealed only by bishops. From the decrees sent by Pope Innocent, chapter 3.

Concerning the sealing of infants, it is clear that it is permissible for this to be done by no one but a bishop. For priests, although they are second priests, do not possess the summit of the pontificate. This belongs to pontiffs alone: either to seal or to confer the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete. Not only does ecclesiastical custom demonstrate this, [Col. 0121D] but also that reading from the Acts of the Apostles which declares that Peter and John were sent (Acts 8) to confer the Holy Spirit upon those already baptized. (Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Presbyteris*.) Priests, whether apart from the bishop or in the bishop’s presence, may anoint with chrism those whom they baptize; but they may not mark the forehead with that oil consecrated by the bishop, which is reserved to bishops alone when they confer the Paraclete.

### CHAPTER 264.—That priests ought not mark the foreheads of the baptized with chrism. From Gregory’s Register to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, chapter 90 (book III, chapter 9).

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Presbyteri*.) Priests [Col. 0122A] must not presume to mark baptized infants on the forehead with holy chrism; rather, priests are to touch the baptized on the breast, so that bishops may afterward confirm them on the forehead.

### CHAPTER 265.—Concerning priests who demand payment for baptism. From the letter of Pope Gelasius, chapter 5 (chapter 7).

(1 question 1, chapter *Baptizandis*.) Let them set no fees for the baptism or sealing of the faithful, nor seek to harass those being reborn by imposing any exactions whatsoever; for we are commanded to give freely what we have received freely. Therefore they must make no attempt whatsoever to exact anything from the aforesaid persons, lest, driven away by poverty or repelled by indignation, they scorn to seek the means of their redemption. Let them be certain that those found to have committed forbidden acts, or who do not voluntarily correct the acts they have committed, will risk their own office. [Col. 0122B]

### CHAPTER 266.—Concerning priests who presume to baptize with old chrism. From the Council of Lyons, chapter 3.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Si quis de alio*.) If anyone, unless death intervenes first, attempts to baptize with chrism other than the new chrism which he has received through the gift or authorization of his own bishop, he clearly shows that by his bold presumption he has pronounced upon himself the sentence of his own condemnation.

### CHAPTER 267.—That a priest should not go among his people without chrism. From the Council of Vaison, chapter 5.

No priest should ever proceed among the people entrusted to him without chrism, because it has been decreed among us that one who, in baptism, has not been anointed with chrism for any reason whatsoever shall be completed in the priest’s confirmation. [Col. 0122C]

### CHAPTER 268.—Concerning a priest who discovers that he has not been baptized. From the Council held at Compiègne, chapter 5.

[Note: [Col. 0121] In the margin of the royal manuscript, written in a very ancient hand: “Here there is doubt.”]

If any ordained priest discovers that he has not been baptized, let him be baptized and ordained again, and likewise all whom he previously baptized.

### CHAPTER 269.—Concerning how priests ought, at the Lord’s Supper, to deal with chrism, consecrated oil, and oil for the sick. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 1.

At the Lord’s Supper a priest shall carry with him three flasks: one for chrism, another for oil to anoint catechumens, and a third for the sick, according to [Col. 0122D] the apostolic saying: “When anyone is ill, let him summon the priests of the Church” (James 5), etc.

### CHAPTER 270.—On the same matter. From the Council held at Valence, chapter 2.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Presbyteri*.) Priests who govern diocesan churches are to request chrism before the solemnity of Easter, not from just any bishops but from their own bishop; and not through a junior cleric, but in person, or through one of the same order.

### CHAPTER 271.—Likewise on the same matter. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 5.

No bishop or any ecclesiastical minister [Col. 0123A] shall accept, as a gift for holy chrism, a denarius or any small gifts, which are irregularly demanded from priests through bishops’ officials.

### CHAPTER 272.—Likewise on the same matter. From the Council of Vaison, chapter 10.

Throughout every territory priests or ministers are to request chrism each year from bishops, as the solemnity of Easter approaches—not, as they please, from the nearest bishops, but from their own bishops—and through no one else than themselves or representatives of the same order, because it is dishonourable to entrust the highest matters to inferiors. It is best that the one who receives it should himself be the one who will use it in administering it.

### CHAPTER 273.—Concerning priests who customarily come to cities to receive chrism. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 6.

[Col. 0123B]

Concerning priests who customarily come to cities on the Lord’s Supper to receive chrism, it has been decreed that, from among those situated eight or ten miles away, one is to be chosen by the archdeacon, who shall carefully carry the received chrism to himself and his companions. But those who live no more than four or five miles from the city are to come in person, as customary, to receive chrism. For the sake of instruction, however, they are to be summoned to the city at another time, not during Lent, because of the people entrusted to them.

### CHAPTER 274.—Concerning chrism, which must always be kept under lock. From the Council of Tours, chapter 3.

Furthermore, this must in every way be observed: holy chrism and consecrated oil are always to be kept under lock, lest that by which we are incorporated into Christ, by which all believers are sanctified, and by which kings and priests are anointed, [Col. 0123C] be touched by an unbelieving or unclean person, or stolen by a faithless person for the overthrow of God’s judgment—as we have learned by experience.

### CHAPTER 275.—Concerning how Jews are to be examined before baptism. From the Council of Agde, chapter 35.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Judaei*.) Jews—whose faithlessness frequently returns to its vomit—if they wish to come to the Catholic laws, shall enter the threshold of the Church among the catechumens for seven months; and, if they are known to come with sincere faith, only then may they merit the grace of baptism. But if during the prescribed period they happen to incur some danger of illness [Col. 0123D] and are despaired of, let them be baptized.

### CHAPTER 276.—Concerning Jews: that no one ought to compel them by force to believe. From the Fifth Council of Toledo, chapter 8 (Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 5).

(Distinction 45, chapter *De Judaeis*.) Concerning Jews, this holy synod has decreed that henceforth no one is to be subjected to force in believing. For “God has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9). Such persons are not to be saved unwillingly but willingly, so that the form of justice may remain whole. As a human being perished by obeying the serpent through the choice of his own will, so each person is saved through the conversion of his own mind, believing when called by the grace of God. Therefore those who are to be converted and saved are not to be compelled by force, but by the free capacity of choice. Yet those already long ago compelled into Christianity—as occurred in the times of the most religious prince Sisenand—because it is now certain that they have been joined to the divine sacraments, received the grace of baptism, been anointed with chrism, and become partakers of the Lord’s body and blood, must be compelled to keep even the faith which they received by force or necessity, lest the Lord’s name be blasphemed and the faith they received be regarded as cheap and contemptible. [Col. 0124A]

### CHAPTER 277.—That baptized children of Jews must be separated from their society. From the same Fifth Council, chapter 40 (the same Fourth Council, chapter 59).

(28 question 1, chapter *Judaeorum*.) We decree that baptized sons or daughters of Jews be separated from their company, lest they be further entangled in their parents’ errors; and that they be entrusted either to monasteries or to Christian men or women who fear the Lord, so that under their care and manner of life they may learn the practice of faith and, established in a better condition, may advance both in morals and in faith. [Col. 0124B]

### CHAPTER 278.—That Jews converted to the Christian faith are to have no association with others not yet baptized. From the same Fifth Council, chapter 62 (Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 61).

(28 question 1, chapter *Saepe malorum*.) The companionship of evil people often corrupts even the good; how much more those inclined to vices? Therefore Jews converted to the Christian faith are henceforth to have no association with those who still remain in the old rite, lest perhaps they be led astray by participation with them. Whoever henceforth among those who have been baptized does not avoid the society of unbelievers, those persons are to be given to Christians, and the others assigned to public institutions. [Col. 0124C]

### CHAPTER 279.—Concerning Jews who apostatize. From the same Fifth Council, chapter 69 (Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 58).

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Plerique*.) Many who formerly were converted from the Jews to the Christian faith are now found, while blaspheming Christ, not only to have performed Jewish rites but also to have practiced abominable circumcisions. Concerning them, at the counsel of our most pious and religious lord King Sisenand, this holy council decreed that transgressors of this sort, corrected by pontifical authority, be recalled to the worship of Christian doctrine; so that those whom their own will does not amend may be restrained by priestly punishment. [Col. 0124D] Those whom they have circumcised, if they are their children, are to be separated from their parents; if slaves, they are to be granted freedom in recompense for the injury to their bodies.

### CHAPTER 280.—Concerning Jewish slaves. From the same council, chapter 9.

(Distinction 54, chapter *Etsi*.) Likewise, if slaves of Jews who have not yet converted flee to the grace of Christ, they are to be granted freedom.

### CHAPTER 281.—Concerning Jewish slaves who seek refuge for baptism. From the Council held at Clermont, chapter 80.

Although it has already been determined by earlier canons concerning pagan slaves belonging to Jews that, if they flee to a church and request baptism, or if they flee to any Christians, they are to be freed from their master upon payment and tender by believers of a just price, [Col. 0125A] we therefore decree that this very just ordinance be observed by all Catholics.

### CHAPTER 282.—Likewise concerning slaves of Jews, whether Christian or desiring to come to the Christian faith. From the Council of Mâcon, chapter 16.

(Distinction 54, chapter *Praesenti*.) In this present council, with God as author, we decree that henceforth no Christian slave is to serve a Jew. Upon payment of twelve solidi for each sound slave, anyone has permission to redeem that slave, whether for freedom or for servitude. If a slave wishes to become a Christian and is not permitted, the same is to be done; for it is wicked for a blasphemer of the Christian religion to keep in chains one whom Christ the Lord redeemed by the shedding of his blood. [Col. 0125B] If any Jew refuses to comply with what we have decreed, then, so long as he delays receiving the stipulated payment, that slave may live with Christians wherever he wishes.

### CHAPTER 283.—Concerning those who desire to come to the Christian faith from heresy. From the Council of Arles, chapter 9.
