If anyone comes to the Church from heresy, question him concerning the Creed; and if they find that he has been baptized in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, let hands alone be laid upon him so that he may receive the Holy Spirit.

### CHAPTER 284.—Concerning Jews who circumcise a slave. From the Council held at Théodon’s Villa, chapter 4.

[Col. 0125C]

If any Jew purchases and circumcises a Christian slave, or a slave of any other sect, let the slave be removed from that Jew’s power and remain free.

### CHAPTER 285.—What Saint Gregory commands concerning Jews. From Gregory’s Register to John, bishop of Terracina (book I, letter 24).

Joseph, the bearer of this letter, a Jew, informed us concerning a certain place at which Jews living in the fortress of Terracina had been accustomed to gather to celebrate their festivals: your brotherhood had expelled them, and they had moved to another place to observe their festivals in the same way, with your knowledge and consent. They now complain that you have again expelled them even from that place. If this is so, we wish your brotherhood to desist from such harassment, and that they be permitted, as was customary, to gather at the place which, as we have said, they obtained for assembling with your knowledge. For those who differ from the Christian religion must be gathered into the unity of faith by gentleness, kindness, admonition, and persuasion, lest those whom the sweetness of preaching and fear beforehand of the future Judge might have invited to belief should be driven away by threats and terrors. It is therefore fitting that they come kindly to hear from you the Word of God, rather than be terrified by authority extended beyond measure. [Col. 0125D]

### CHAPTER 286.—Concerning those baptized by deacons because of danger of death. From the Council of Tours, chapter 3.

[Col. 0126A]

If any deacon, governing a people without bishop or priest, baptizes persons because death is imminent, the bishop must complete them by blessing and confirmation, in the faith by which each person may be righteous through believing.

### CHAPTER 287.—Concerning those who compel priests to give money for balsam. From the Council of Chalon, chapter [II, chapter 16].

Certain brethren said that in their churches it had been an ancient custom for priests to give two or four denarii for buying balsam to make chrism, or for providing the church’s lights. [Col. 0126B] (1 question 1, chapter *Statuimus*.) Therefore we all decree with one consent that, just as nothing is to be received for dedicating basilicas or conferring orders, so too priests who are to receive chrism are to give nothing for buying balsam or lights. Bishops are to buy balsam from ecclesiastical resources, and each is to provide lights in his own churches.

### CHAPTER 288.—Concerning the chrism-cloth. From the Council held at Beauvais, chapter 8.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 4, chapter *Si quis*.) If anyone wishes to use again a chrism-cloth and place it upon another baptized person, it is not improper.

### CHAPTER 289.—That catechumens ought not eat with the baptized. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 5.

[Col. 0126C] Catechumens must not eat with the baptized or give them the kiss; how much less with gentiles?

### CHAPTER 290.—Concerning the conducting of scrutiny. From the Roman Council, chapter 15.

We have decreed concerning the conducting of scrutiny that it be celebrated by the bishop where there is an assembly of people and clergy and where circumstances permit.

### CHAPTER 291.—Concerning the baptistery. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 9.

The matter of the baptistery and catechumens has been discussed, so that priests may understand more fully how, with due rites, they make a Christian.

### CHAPTER 292.—That one is called a bigamist who had one wife before baptism and another after baptism. From the decree of Pope Innocent, chapter 2 (Letter 22 of Innocent, to the bishops of Macedonia).

[Col. 0126D]

(Distinction 26, chapter *Deinde opponitur*.) It is then asserted that a man ought not be called a bigamist if, while a catechumen, he had and lost a wife, and after baptism took another, because that marriage, together with other sins, was washed away by the sacrament of baptism. If this is said concerning one wife, then certainly, if while still the old man he had three wives, the woman who is fourth after baptism will, according to such interpreters, be the first. A woman taken as the fourth wife will likewise receive the name of virgin. Who, I ask, does not see that this is contrary to the Apostle’s command, who says that a priest must be “the husband of one wife”? (1 Timothy 3.) [Col. 0127A]

But it is objected that in baptism everything done in the old man is dissolved. Tell me—with your leave, I speak—are sins alone forgiven in baptism, or also those things accomplished according to the Lord’s commands and institutions? Is taking a wife a sin, or is it not a sin? If it is a sin, then he who, when joining them in paradise, blessed them so that sins might be committed, will himself be the author of guilt (Genesis 2). But if it is not a sin—because it is wicked to call a sin what God has joined together (Matthew 19), and Solomon added, “A wife is prepared for a husband by God” (Proverbs 19)—how is it believed to have been remitted among sins when it is read to have been consummated by God as author? What judgment is made concerning the children of such persons? Surely they will not be admitted to share in the inheritance, though they were born from her who was the wife before baptism? And will they be called either natural children or illegitimate, because there is no lawful marriage except, as you suppose, that contracted after baptism? [Col. 0127B]

When the Lord himself was questioned by the Jews whether it was lawful to dismiss a wife (Matthew 19), and explained that this ought not to be done, he added: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (ibid.). And lest he be thought to have spoken of marriages contracted after baptism, remember that he was indeed questioned by Jews and answered Jews. Yet I ask—and I ask anxiously—if the same woman is wife to a man who was formerly a catechumen and later a believer, and if he had children by her while a catechumen and others later while a believer, whether they are to be called brothers or not. After their father’s death, will the latter share with the others in the division of the inheritance, though spiritual regeneration is believed to have taken from them the name of sons? Since it is absurd to think and judge so, what reason is there for defending this evil and vaunting it upon an empty opinion rather than establishing it by any authority? For what the law commands and God joins cannot be counted among sins. [Col. 0127C]

If, while a catechumen, someone cultivated virtues, pursued humility, maintained patience, gave alms, rescued persons destined for death by whatever means, and preserved chastity, I ask whether, once he becomes a believer, he loses these things because baptism is thought to remove everything the old man has done. Let us consider Cornelius, a gentile, who saw Peter himself in a revelation because of his prayers and alms (Acts 10). Were these things taken from him by baptism, although baptism seems to have been granted him because of them? If this is believed, believe me, a considerable error is being made; for whatever has been rightly done and kept according to the legal commandments cannot perish for those who do it. Therefore, because the union of marriage is accomplished by God’s command, it cannot be called a sin; and what is not sin should in no way be believed to have been forgiven among sins. [Col. 0127D]

### CHAPTER 293.—Concerning bishops, priests, and deacons who have been rebaptized. From the decrees of Pope Felix III, chapter 1 (letter 3).

[Col. 0128A]

The common grief and general lament is that within Africa we have learned that even bishops, presbyters, and deacons have been rebaptized. This matter has undoubtedly also come to the knowledge of your holiness: how, in the African regions, the cunning of the devil has raged against the Christian people, and by manifold deception has broken out to such a point that he has plunged not merely the incautious multitude but even priests themselves into the depths of death; so that no part of the world has failed to groan and no land has remained ignorant.

Therefore, placed in great sorrow, we cannot disregard the peril of those who are perishing and of the souls for which an account will be required from us. Accordingly, a fitting remedy must be applied to wounds of this kind, lest premature ease in healing should do no good to those seized by the deadly plague; but lest a more slowly prolonged destruction should, through the guilt of an unlawful cure, involve alike the wounded and their healers.

[Col. 0128B]

First, then, the profession and person of one who has been deceived and comes to us seeking a remedy must be carefully examined, so that suitable treatment may be given. One who, in order to make satisfaction to God through penance, has duly grieved that he was rebaptized must be asked whether he ran voluntarily into this crime or came under compulsion. He should know that he who deceives is himself deceived; and that nothing is diminished, by our leniency, from the judgment of the exalted tribunal, to which those things are established which are pious, true, and just. Necessity must be dealt with in one way, intention in another. Worse, moreover, is the case of one who perhaps was induced by payment to perish.

[Col. 0128C]

For the enemy has left nothing unattempted. Help must be given to those entangled, lest he be allowed to rejoice in his capture; the snare of the hunter must be crushed, so that for those lamenting their fall without disguise or deceit there may be an entrance, both through the moderation of justice and through the compunction of mercy, into the court which they had abandoned. Nor should anyone perhaps be ashamed or reluctant, in the prescribed times of fasting and mourning, to obey, or to comply with other commands of more salutary discipline; for grace is given to the humble, not to the proud (1 Pet. 5). Let everyone, therefore, who seeks to be made elect in Christ lie prostrate in sorrow for his fall; and let us deal, through the ministry of our dispensation—which it is fitting to follow in your charity, and which no one may lawfully wish or be able to exceed—with priestly firmness and humanity, with the case of one who, against apostolic teaching, has undergone the ill-fated repetition of baptism, or of one who has craftily thought his own consent excusable by certain arguments.

[Col. 0128D]

Thus may his faith—which, unless it is one, is no faith—by the help of the Lord the Judge be restored to salvation without offence arising from our haste. For when a sinner’s satisfaction is prolonged by us, his mind is found more purified for pardon, to our praise and joy alike.

Remember, therefore, that this is our judgment in these matters: preserving discernment among sinners, not all who have fallen are to be weighed in the same balance. This is to be exacted with greater severity by the discipline entrusted to us in the Lord. (On Consecration, distinction 4, chapter “Those whom.”)

[Col. 0129A]

In order, then, to begin with the leaders of the Church: those who are proved to have been bishops, presbyters, or deacons, and who, whether perhaps willingly or under compulsion, are proved to have cast away that one and saving laver, and to have put off Christ, whom they had put on not only through the gift of regeneration but also through the grace of the rank they had received—since it is established that no one can come to a second washing unless he has openly denied himself to be a Christian and professed himself a pagan—this is detestable in all generally, but in bishops, presbyters, and deacons is shown to be dreadful even to hear or to name.

But because the same Lord and Savior is most merciful and wills no one to perish, they are to remain in penance, if they repent, until the day of their death; nor are they to take part at all in the prayers not only of the faithful but even of catechumens. Lay communion is to be restored to them at death. The care of a most approved priest must diligently investigate and carry this out.

[Col. 0129B]

Concerning monks and clerics, consecrated virgins or laypersons, we command that the rule be observed which the Synod of Nicaea decreed should be observed concerning those who have fallen or may fall: namely, those who, under no necessity and through fear or danger from no circumstance, have impiously yielded themselves to heretics to be rebaptized, provided that they repent from the heart, shall remain three years among the hearers; for seven years they shall submit among penitents to the laying on of priests’ hands; and for two further years they shall by every means be forbidden to offer oblations, but shall be joined in prayer only with the people [or: laypersons]. Nor should one be ashamed to bow the neck to God who did not fear to deny him.

[Col. 0129C]

If, however, as mortals, before the limits of the prescribed time their end of life begins to press upon them, assistance must be given to one who implores it. Whether by the bishop who imposed the penance, or by another who can prove that it was imposed, or likewise by a presbyter, viaticum is not to be denied to one departing from this world.

But to children—whose designation derives from the purity still belonging to their garment—whether clerics or laypersons, and likewise to similar girls, whose age supports their ignorance, communion is to be restored after they have been kept for a while under the laying on of hands; nor is penance to be awaited from those whom the rule exempts from disciplinary coercion. This has been prudently established by us, lest those in whom more or less of the contagion of earthly corruption remains for life should commit sin while still in penance.

[Col. 0129D]

But if anyone, having received the grace of communion before the appointed time of penance because physicians despaired of him on account of evident signs of death, recovers, we are to observe in his case what the Nicene canons ordained: he is to be counted among those who communicate only in prayer, until the period fixed for him has been completed.

Nor do we pass over our catechumens who were baptized after such a confession, because their case is not unlike that, as the same holy canons ordained, of one who in any manner has renounced Christ whom he had once confessed. Let them remain three years among the hearers; afterward let them be permitted to pray with the catechumens, and through the laying on of hands receive the grace of Catholic communion—except only bishops, presbyters, and deacons, who, as we have already said, are to be reconciled only at the time of their death.

[Col. 0130A]

As for the rest—that is, clerics or laypersons, monks of either sex—who are proved to have undergone repetition of baptism under compulsion and danger, or who have said by some manner of evasion [*commento*, perhaps “pretext”] that they are not bound by the guilt of this crime, we decree that they remain in penance for three years and be received into the fellowship of the sacrament through the laying on of hands. In every respect the following is to be observed: none of those who, at whatever age, were baptized or rebaptized anywhere outside the Catholic Church is ever to be permitted to enter ecclesiastical service (1, question 7, chapter “Those who at whatever age”). It must not be enough for them that they have been received among Catholics. Whoever violates these provisions among the bishops shall see what judgment is to be borne concerning his own rank and communion;

[Col. 0130B]

likewise, anyone who does not remove a person whom he discovers has crept from this group into clerical ministry.

Above all, care must be taken and every precaution provided lest any of our brother bishops, or even presbyters, should receive in another city or diocese a penitent, one placed under a priest’s hand, or one who says that he has been reconciled, without the testimony and letters of the bishop or presbyter—whether a presbyter in a parish or a bishop in a city. If this is neglected through any concealment, the fault also touches the clerics residing in places where the matter has received insufficient care.

These matters having thus been duly arranged and, by our deliberation, brought to the knowledge of our churches, it is fitting that you obey.

[Col. 0130C]

Although nothing seems lacking for the restoration of souls, nevertheless, if anything new—something which may have escaped us—has been revealed to anyone, let him faithfully communicate it, according to the blessed apostle Paul, while the first speaker is silent (1 Cor. 14); for “the Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 8), especially when his cause is under discussion. Nor shall we be reluctant to hear it; and, if anything has been omitted, we shall not arrogantly reject it but rationally order it.

Given on the Ides of March, in the consulship of Dinanuus and Sibidius, fourth consulship.

## Chapter 294. Concerning one ordained through ignorance before being baptized. From the statements of Bishop Isidore.

(1, question 1, chapter “If anyone through ignorance”; see the annotation there.) If anyone is ordained through ignorance before being baptized, those baptized by him ought to be rebaptized, and he himself is not to be ordained. But (likewise, *On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter “Romanus”) [Col. 0130D] the Roman pontiff judges not the man who baptizes, but believes that the Spirit of God supplies the grace of baptism, even if the one baptizing is a pagan.

## Chapter 295. Concerning those who attempt to sell the grace of the Holy Spirit. From the Council of Tribur, chapter 22, at which King Arnulf was present.

(1, question 1, chapter “It has been said.”) The holy synod, abhorring and anathematizing the seed of the Simoniacal heresy, declared that in certain places money was customarily given for receiving chrism, and likewise for baptism and communion. It decreed that henceforth nothing whatever should be demanded either for ordination, chrism, baptism, balm, burial, or communion; but that Christ’s free gifts should be bestowed freely through dispensation.

## Chapter 296. By whom the laying on of hands ought to be performed. Pope Urban to all Christians, chapter 7.

[Col. 0131A]

All the faithful ought, after baptism, to receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of bishops’ hands, so that they may be found to be complete Christians.

## Chapter 297. On the same subject. Pope Eusebius to the bishops throughout Campania and Tuscany, chapter 9, letter 3.

(*On Consecration*, distinction 5, chapter “The laying on of hands.”) The sacrament of the laying on of hands must be maintained with great authority. It cannot be performed by others than the chief priests. In the time of the apostles it is read and known to have been performed by none other than the apostles themselves; nor, as has already been said, can or ought it ever to be performed by any others than those who hold their place. [Col. 0131B]

If it is otherwise presumed upon, it is to be considered invalid and void, and shall never be reckoned among the ecclesiastical sacraments.

## Chapter 298. Likewise on the same subject. Bede on the Acts of the Apostles.

(On chapter 8.) Philip, who preached the Gospel to Samaria, was one of the seven deacons. For if he had been an apostle, he surely could himself have laid hands upon them so that they might receive the Holy Spirit. This belongs only to bishops.

[Col. 0131C]

Presbyters, whether apart from a bishop or in the bishop’s presence, may anoint with chrism those who have been baptized, provided it has been consecrated by the bishop; nevertheless, they may not mark foreheads with the same oil, for this belongs only to bishops when they confer upon the baptized the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete.

## Chapter 299. On the same subject. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VII, chapter 20.

Although presbyters are priests, they do not possess the summit of the episcopate: for they neither mark the forehead with chrism nor give the Holy Spirit. The reading in the Acts of the Apostles indicates that these belong only to bishops.

## Chapter 300. Likewise on the same subject: Rabanus, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, book I, chapter 30.

(*On Consecration*, distinction 5, chapter “Finally.”) Finally, through the laying on of the high priest’s hand, the Paraclete is conferred upon the baptized, so that they may be strengthened through the Holy Spirit to preach to others the same gift which they themselves have received in baptism by grace, having been granted eternal life.

[Col. 0131D]

For one who has been baptized is marked with chrism by the priest on the crown of the head; but by the bishop on the forehead. In the former anointing the descent of the Holy Spirit upon him is signified, to consecrate a dwelling-place for God. In the latter it is declared that the sevenfold grace of that same Holy Spirit, with every fullness of holiness, knowledge, and power, comes into the person.

## Chapter 301. What is permitted to a bishop entering another’s church. Haimo on Deuteronomy.

A bishop entering another person’s church may correct or even confirm some persons there, but he may not govern the entire people.

## Chapter 302. A man who has held his stepson or stepdaughter before a bishop for confirmation must be separated from his wife. *Capitulary*, book V, chapter 7.

[Col. 0132A]

If anyone has held his stepson or stepdaughter before a bishop for confirmation, he shall be separated from his wife and shall not take another.

## Chapter 303. One who has been confirmed may not be confirmed again. Gregory II to Boniface.

For a person who has been confirmed by a bishop, repetition of such an act is to be prohibited.

## Chapter 304. Whether a man who unknowingly held his stepson or stepdaughter before a bishop for confirmation must be separated from his wife. Pope Nicholas to Rudolph, bishop of Bourges.

(30, question 1, chapter “Concerning those who.”) [Col. 0132B] Concerning those who hold their stepchildren before a bishop for confirmation—that is, those who hold over themselves, while being chrismated by bishops, the children of their wives by a former husband—if this occurs unknowingly, as is asserted, it is indeed a sin, but it is not to be punished as far as separation of marriage. Nevertheless, let them mourn and, cleansing this by worthy penance, say to the Lord: “Do not remember the sins of our ignorance.”

## Chapter 305. Whether those who receive their own children from the holy font ought to be separated from their wives. From the decree of Pope Deusdedit to Bishop Gordian.

(30, question 1, chapter “It has come to us.”) Deusdedit, bishop of the holy Roman Church and Apostolic See, to Gordian, fellow bishop and dearest brother of the Church of Seville.

[Col. 0132C]

It has come to us, through a deacon of your holiness bringing a letter, that last Easter Saturday certain men and women, amid the great press of people, unknowingly received their own children from the holy font. You therefore wish to know whether, because of such an occurrence, men and women ought to return to their marital intercourse or not. Grieved by this matter, we investigated the statements of our predecessors. We found in the archives of this Apostolic See that such things had already occurred in the Churches of Isauria, Ephesus, and Jerusalem, and that bishops of other churches and cities had asked this Apostolic See whether men and women should return to their own marital bed.

[Col. 0132D]

The most holy Fathers of blessed memory, Julius, Innocent, and Celestine, with the agreement of many bishops and priests in the church of the blessed prince of the apostles, set down and confirmed a prohibition of such things: women and men who, for whatever reason, had received their own children were in no way to resume marriage, but were to separate, lest, through the devil’s persuasion, such a vice should grow throughout the world.

You know that, just as there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, so there are seven gifts of baptism. From the first nourishment of the sacrament of salt and entrance into the Church, through confirmation by chrism—that is, from the first to the seventh—no Christian ought to take his own *commater* (“co-mother,” spiritual co-parent) in marriage. Whoever presumes to do so is to remain bound by the bond of anathema until he has performed worthy penance.

## Chapter 306. Likewise on the same subject. John to Anselm, bishop of the Church of Limoges.

[Col. 0133A]

A certain man named Stephen, coming here to the thresholds of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul for prayer, made known to our episcopal office by petition that, when his son was at the point of death and unwashed by the water of baptism, necessity arising from the absence of priests compelled him to baptize the child, and that he received him while holding him in his own hands. On account of this affair, now made known to you, your reverence, as though burning with zeal for rectitude, judged that the aforesaid man ought to be separated from his wife. This must by no means be done, Scripture saying that a wife is joined to her husband by God, and that “what God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19).

[Col. 0133B]

And the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one can dismiss his wife except on account of fornication” (ibid.). Therefore, relying especially upon the command of such great authority, we say that what necessity brought about should be overlooked and judged blameless. For, according to canonical sanction, even faithful laypersons are freely permitted to perform the work of baptizing if necessity requires it.

Thus, if the above-mentioned father, seeing his son dying bodily, washed him with the sacred water of baptism lest he should allow the soul to perish in everlasting death, rescued him from the power of the author of death and darkness, and unquestionably sent him, now regenerated, into Christ’s kingdom, he is praised for having done well. [Col. 0133C]

Accordingly, we judge that he may remain joined without penalty, as long as they live, to his wife, who had long ago been most properly joined to him; nor ought they in any way to have been separated on this account contrary to the aforesaid divine authorities.

## Chapter 307. No one may take his father’s stepdaughter in marriage; if he has taken her, he must be separated. Pope Zachary to Theodore, bishop of Pavia.

Zachary, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy brother Theodore, bishop of the Church of Pavia. (30, question 3, chapter “Memorandum.”) Your reverend brotherhood presented us with a memorandum (*pytacium*), through which you asked us whether it is lawful for a son to take in marriage the daughter of another person whom his father had received from the sacred font—that is, his father’s spiritual daughter, a thing dreadful even to name. You asserted that this had happened among you in an outrageous manner.

[Col. 0133D]

But your holy brotherhood knows well that the Lord commanded Moses, saying: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father; and you shall not uncover the nakedness of your mother; you shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister, for it is your nakedness” (Lev. 18). “Not to uncover nakedness” is said when we are commanded to abstain from our own blood relationship. All the more, with every occasion or pretext set aside, must we take the utmost care, under strictest restraint, to avoid the spiritual daughter of our father, lest anyone who does not restrain the reins of lust after becoming involved in such a deed incur the wrath of the divine judgment.

[Col. 0134A]

Therefore all must absolutely guard against participation in such a crime, lest they perish eternally. But your brotherhood should strive in every way to separate those who, despising their souls’ salvation, have joined themselves in an impious marriage through this ruinous presumption, and to subject them to worthy penance, so that, by the Lord’s help, you may win their souls by rescuing them from eternal condemnation.

You further reported concerning children proved to have been born from them, whether they may be joined in marriage. But why should these be prohibited from marriage or compelled to perform penance on this account, when they are declared free from condemnation in this matter? For the father shall not bear torments for the son, nor the son for the father. As the Lord says through the prophet: “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine; the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18). But, dearest brother, let it be enough to have said these things concerning them.

[Col. 0134B]

Take care, however, not to permit those subject to you to act otherwise, lest you be found to depart from the right path.

## Chapter 308. In baptism it is not water but the word that cleanses. Augustine on John, tractate 80, homily 26.

The Lord said to his disciples: “Already you are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” (John 17). Why did he not say, “You are clean because of the baptism by which you were washed,” but said, “because of that which I have spoken to you,” unless because the word cleanses even in the water?

## Chapter 309. The apostles were baptized. Augustine, in his letter to Seleucius, letter 308.

(*On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter “When.”) When the Lord Jesus departed from Jerusalem with his disciples into the land of Judaea and remained there with them, he baptized—not himself, but through his disciples, whom we understand already to have been baptized, [Col. 0134C]

either with John’s baptism, as some think, or, what is more credible, with Christ’s baptism. Likewise, the Lord answered Peter: “One who has bathed does not need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean” (John 13). From this it is understood that Peter had already been baptized.

## Chapter 310. On the same subject. Augustine to Vincentius Victor, book III, *On the Soul and Its Origin*, chapter 9.

(*On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter “If those.”) If we maintain that those of whom it is not written whether they were baptized departed this life without baptism, we cast reproach upon the apostles themselves. For, except for the apostle Paul, we do not know when they were baptized. [Col. 0134D]

But it could become known to us that they were baptized from the Lord’s saying to blessed Peter: “One who has bathed does not need except to wash his feet” (John 13).

## Chapter 311. Baptized rich persons are not deprived of God’s kingdom. Augustine to Paulinus, bishop of Nola, concerning Pelagius, letter 106.

Let Pelagius confess that baptized rich persons, even if they do not relinquish their riches and are such as the Apostle describes in writing to Timothy—“Command the rich of this age not to think proudly, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living Lord, who supplies us abundantly with all things for enjoyment; that they may be rich in good works, ready to give, willing to share, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, that they may lay hold on eternal life” (1 Tim. 6)—cannot be deprived of the kingdom of God.

# Second Part of the Decree

Concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, its reception and observance; concerning the Mass and the holiness of the other sacraments.

[Col. 0135]

## Chapter 1. Bread and the cup become Christ’s body not by any consecration whatsoever, but by a definite consecration. Augustine, *On Instructing Beginners*, chapter 1 (book XX against Faustus, chapter 13).

[Col. 0135A]

(Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter “Bread and the cup.”) Bread and the cup become mystical for us by a definite consecration, not by being born. Accordingly, what does not become so for us, although it is bread and cup, is food for refreshment, not a sacrament of religion—except that in every gift of God, not only spiritual but also bodily, we bless and give thanks to the Lord.

Likewise, from the sermon *On the Sacraments*. (*On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter “Because he suffered.”) Because he suffered for us, he commended to us in this sacrament his blood and body, and he made us ourselves this also.

[Col. 0135B]

For we too have been made his body, and through his mercy we are what we have received. Remember: you did not exist, and you were created; you were brought to the Lord’s threshing-floor, threshed by the labor of oxen—that is, of those proclaiming the Gospel. When you were brought as catechumens, you were kept in the granary; you gave your names, and began to be ground by fasts and exorcisms. Afterwards you came to the water, were sprinkled, and became the Lord’s bread. Behold what you have received.

Therefore, just as you see that what has been made is one, so be yourselves one: loving one another, holding one faith, one hope, indivisible charity. When heretics receive this, they receive testimony against themselves, because they seek division while this bread indicates unity. [Col. 0135C]

So too wine was in many bunches of grapes and now is one. In its origin it is one: it is the cup after the pressing of the winepress. And after those fasts, after labors, after humiliation and contrition, you too have now come in Christ’s name, as it were, to the cup; there you are on the table, and in the cup you are with us. For together we receive this, together we drink, because together we live.

Likewise, in the sermon *On Infants*. (In the same place, Gratian.) Thus our Lord Jesus Christ signified us and willed us to belong to him. He consecrated on his table the mystery of our peace and unity. Whoever receives the mystery of unity and does not keep the bond of peace receives the mystery not for himself but as testimony against himself.

[Col. 0135D]

(Peter Lombard, book IV, distinction 9, §a.) No one should doubt in any respect that every one of the faithful becomes a participant in the Lord’s body and blood when, in baptism, he is made a member of Christ; nor is he excluded from the fellowship of that bread and cup, even if he departs from this world before eating that bread and drinking that cup, provided he is established in the unity of Christ’s body.

[Col. 0136A]

For he is not deprived of participation in and benefit from that sacrament when he finds in himself that which the sacrament signifies.

Likewise, from book X of *The City of God*, chapter 20. In the form of a servant, the Lord preferred to be a sacrifice rather than to receive sacrifice, lest anyone, even on this ground, suppose that sacrifice should be offered to any creature. In this he is himself both the priest who offers and the oblation. He willed the Church’s daily sacrifice to be the sacrament of this reality; and since the Church is the body of its head, it learns to offer itself through him.

## Chapter 2. The manna received by the fathers did not free them from death, but he who was prefigured in the manna did. In the sermon *On the Benefit of Doing Penance*.

[Col. 0136B]

“Manna from heaven,” he says, is plainly explained by the Lord himself. “Your fathers,” he says, “ate manna in the wilderness and died” (John 6; Exod. 16; Num. 2). For when they lived, the figure could foretell life, but could not itself be life. “They ate manna,” he says, “and died”: that is, the manna which they ate could not free them from death—not because manna itself was death to them, but because it did not free them from death. But he who was prefigured by the manna was to free them from death. To put it briefly, all who understood Christ in the manna ate the same spiritual food as we do.

## Chapter 3. Although the visible things of the sacraments perish, that which is performed through them cannot perish. In the book *On the One Baptism*.

[Col. 0136C]

“Or,” he says, “does the light of the sun, or even of a lamp, when it is diffused through filthy places, draw any defilement from them? And can Christ’s baptism be polluted by anyone’s crimes? For if we turn our attention to the visible things themselves through which the sacraments are administered, who does not know that they are perishable? But if we turn to that which is done through them, who does not see that it cannot be corrupted? This is so although the persons through whom it is done receive rewards or suffer punishments according to their conduct.”

## Chapter 4. One who says that Christ, impassible and immortal, is daily sacrificed in the sacrament does not lie; and how the sacrament of Christ’s body is to be understood as Christ’s body. In Augustine’s letter to Bishop Boniface, letter 23.

[Col. 0136D] (*On the Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter *Quaeris*, near the end.) “Behold,” he says after much else, “I do as much as I can. May the Lord help me to be able to do what you ask. Surely we often speak in such a way that, when Easter is approaching, we say that the Lord’s Passion will be tomorrow or the day after tomorrow, although he suffered many years ago and that Passion occurred only once. Likewise, on Sunday itself we say, ‘The Lord rose today,’ although so many years have passed since he rose. Why is no one so foolish as to accuse us of lying when we speak in this way? Is it not because we name these days according to their resemblance to those on which these events occurred, so that it may be said, ‘This is that day,’ although it is not that very day, but resembles it by the recurrence of time; and so that it may be said that something occurs on that day because of the celebration of the sacrament, although it occurred not on that day but long ago?

“Was Christ not sacrificed once in himself? Yet in the sacrament he is sacrificed for the people not only at every Easter solemnity but every day; nor does the person who, when asked, answers that he is sacrificed, certainly lie. For if sacraments [Col. 0137B] did not possess some resemblance to the things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all. From this resemblance, moreover, sacraments commonly receive the names of the things themselves. Thus, in a certain manner, the sacrament of Christ’s body is Christ’s body; the sacrament of Christ’s blood is Christ’s blood; and so the sacrament of faith is faith.”

In the book *On the Remedy of Penance* (chapter 7): “This altar which is now in the Church, set upon the earth and exposed to earthly eyes, for the celebration of the signs of the divine mysteries—many wicked persons, too, can approach it, while God in this present time commends his patience, in order that in the future he may exercise [Col. 0137C] his severity.”

(*On the Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *Ut quid paras*; and Peter Lombard, book IV, distinction 9, § a.) “Why,” says blessed Augustine in his exposition of the Evangelist (*Tractate 26 on John*), “do you prepare your teeth and stomach? To believe in him is to eat the living bread: whoever believes in him eats him. He is fed invisibly, because he is born again invisibly. The infant is within; he is new within. Where he is made new, there he is filled.

“For the Lord’s morsel [John 13] was not poison to Judas. When he received it, the enemy entered into him—not because he received something evil, but because, being evil, he received something good wickedly. Therefore, brothers, behold the heavenly bread; eat spiritually; bring innocence to the altar. Even if your sins are daily ones, let them not be deadly. Before you approach the altar, attend to what you say: [Col. 0137D] ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors’ [Matt. 6]. Forgive, and you shall be forgiven. Approach in confidence: it is bread, not poison.

“This is the bread which came down from heaven [John 6]. This bread is signified by the manna; this bread is signified by the Lord’s altar. Those were sacraments: they differ in their signs, but are equal in the reality signified. ‘They all ate,’ he says, ‘the same spiritual food’—certainly the same spiritual food. Their bodily food was different, since they had manna and we have something else; but spiritually they had the same food as we do. ‘And they all drank the same spiritual drink’: theirs was one thing and ours another in visible form, yet the same in spiritual power. For how the same drink? ‘They drank,’ he says, ‘from the spiritual rock which followed them; and the rock [Col. 0138A] was Christ’ [Num. 9; Exod. 13, 14, 16, 17; Num. 20; 1 Cor. 10]. The drink is the same, the bread is the same. The rock was Christ in a sign; the true Christ is in flesh and word.

“This, then, is the bread coming down from heaven [John 6], so that whoever eats of it may not die. This concerns the power of the sacrament, not the visible sacrament: the one who eats inwardly, not outwardly; who eats with the heart, not one who presses with the tooth. ‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life’ [ibid.]. Therefore the person who does not eat this bread and drink this blood does not have that life. Human beings can indeed have temporal life without it. Thus, whoever does not eat his flesh and drink his blood does not have life in himself; and whoever eats his flesh and [Col. 0138B] drinks his blood has eternal life” [ibid.].

“In both cases, however, he answers by saying ‘eternal.’ He therefore wishes this food and drink to be understood as fellowship in his body and members, which is the holy Church. The sacrament of this reality—that is, of the unity of Christ’s body and blood—is prepared at the Lord’s table daily in some places, and at fixed intervals of days in others, and is received from the Lord’s table: for some unto life, for others unto destruction. But the reality itself, of which it is the sacrament, is unto life for every person and unto destruction for no one who has become a participant in it.”

In the creed of the Council of Ephesus (from the Epistle of the Council of Ephesus to Nestorius): “We necessarily add this also: proclaiming according to the flesh the death of the only-begotten Son [Col. 0138C] of God and his resurrection, we celebrate the unbloody service of the sacred rite. For thus we approach the mystical blessings and are sanctified, having become participants in the holy body and precious blood of Christ, the redeemer of us all—not receiving common flesh, far be it! nor the flesh of a sanctified man joined to the Word according to a unity of dignity, or as though it possessed a divine indwelling; but flesh truly life-giving and made the Word’s own. For, naturally existing as life because he is God, when united to his own flesh he declared it life-giving. Therefore, although he says, ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man’ [John 6:54], we nevertheless ought not to suppose it to be the flesh of any ordinary human being. For how [Col. 0138D] could human flesh be life-giving according to its own nature? Rather, it is truly made the own flesh of him who for our sake became and was called Son of Man.”

(Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 65; Gratian, *On Penance*, distinction 1, chapter *In actione*; Peter Lombard, book IV, distinction 20, § c.) “In the exercise of penance, where such an act has been committed that the person committing it must be separated even from Christ’s body, not so much the length of time as the degree of sorrow must be considered. For God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” [Ps. 50].

Hilary, in the book *On the Trinity*: “Concerning those who insert a unity of will between the Father and the Son, I do not even ask whether Christ is in us today through the reality of nature or through harmony of will. For if the Word truly became flesh [John 1], and if we truly receive the flesh of the Word in the Lord’s food, [Col. 0139A] how is he not to be considered as dwelling naturally in us? For, having been born a human being, he assumed the nature of our flesh, now inseparable from himself; and he mingled the nature of our flesh with the nature of eternity in the sacrament of the flesh communicated to us. Thus we are all one, because the Father is in Christ and Christ is in us; these make us one in themselves.

“If, therefore, Christ truly assumed the flesh of our body; if that man who was born of Mary is truly Christ; and if we truly receive under the mystery the flesh of his body, and through this are one, because the Father is in him and he in us: how can a unity of will be maintained, when natural property through the sacrament is the sacrament of perfect unity?

“In matters of God we must not proceed by human or worldly reasoning; nor must perversity be extorted, by force and a foolish exposition of heavenly sayings, toward a foreign and impious understanding. Let us read what has been written, understand what we read, and then we shall discharge the office of faith perfectly. For if we speak of the natural truth of Christ in us without having learned it from him, we shall speak foolishly and impiously. For he himself says: ‘My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him’ [John 6]. No room for doubt has been left concerning the truth of the flesh and blood. For by the Lord’s own declaration and by our faith, it is truly flesh and truly blood; and when these are received and drunk, they bring about this result: that we are in Christ and Christ [Col. 0139C] in us. Is this truth not real? Let it certainly happen to be untrue for those who deny that Christ Jesus is true God.

“Therefore he is in us through flesh, and we are in him, while, according to that which we are, he is in God. This, then, is the cause of our life: that we have Christ, remaining in us who are fleshly, through flesh, and that we shall live through him under the condition by which he himself lives through the Father. If, therefore, we live naturally through him according to the flesh—that is, having received the nature of his flesh—how does he not naturally have the Father in himself according to the Spirit, since he lives through the Father?”

Eusebius of Emesa, from the sermon *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. (*On the Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *Quia corpus*; and book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 8, § b.) “Because he was about to remove the assumed body [Col. 0139D] from our eyes and carry it to the stars, it was necessary that, on the day of the Supper, he should consecrate for us the sacrament of his body and blood; so that what was once offered as the price might be continually worshipped through the mystery. Since an unceasing redemption for human salvation was in progress every day, the offering of redemption had to be perpetual, and that everlasting victim had to live in memory and be always present in grace.

“It is truly to be regarded as the one perfect victim by faith, not estimated by appearance nor judged by external sight, but by inward disposition. Thus heavenly authority confirms: ‘My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.’ Let every ambiguity of unbelief therefore depart, since he who is the author of the gift is also the witness to its truth.

“For the invisible priest, by his word and secret power, converts visible creatures into the substance of his body and blood, saying: ‘Take and eat: THIS IS MY BODY’; and, repeating the sanctification: ‘Take and drink: this is my blood.’ At the command of the Lord who gives the order, the heights of heaven, the depths of the waters, and the expanses of the lands suddenly stood forth from nothing [Gen. 1]. By equal power, in spiritual sacraments, where the power commands, the effect obeys.

“How great, therefore, and how worthy of celebration are the benefits worked by the power of the divine blessing! Consider yourself, you who have been regenerated in Christ, and you will see why it ought not to seem new or impossible to you that earthly and mortal things are converted into Christ’s substance. Once estranged from life, a stranger to mercy and to the way of salvation, inwardly [Col. 0140B] dead, you lived in exile. Suddenly, initiated into Christ’s laws and renewed by saving mysteries, you passed into the body of the Church—not by seeing, but by believing—and by hidden purification deserved to become an adopted child of God from a child of perdition.

“Remaining of visible size, you became invisibly greater than yourself, without any increase of quantity. Though you remained the very same person, you came to be very different through the progress of faith. Nothing was added outwardly, and everything was changed inwardly; and so the human being became a child of Christ, and Christ was formed in the human mind.

“Therefore, just as, without bodily perception, you put off your former baseness and suddenly clothed yourself with new dignity; and just as the fact that God healed wounded life, washed away infection, and cleansed what was defiled was entrusted not to your eyes but to your understanding: so also, when you ascend to the reverend [Col. 0140C] altar to be filled with spiritual food, look upon your God’s sacred body and blood with faith; honor it, marvel at it, touch it with your mind, receive it with the hand of your heart, and above all receive the whole of it in the draught of the inward person.”

## Chapter 5.—That the bread which the Lord broke and gave to his disciples is the body of the Lord Savior; that the cup which he offered them is his blood; and how Christ’s flesh and blood ought to be understood. Jerome to Hedibia.

(Question 2.) “Let us hear that the bread which the Lord broke and gave to his disciples [Matt. 26] is the body of the Lord Savior, he himself saying to them: ‘Take and eat: This is my body’; and that the cup [Col. 0140D] is that of which he again spoke: ‘Drink from this, all of you; for this is my blood of the new covenant, which shall be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins’ [Mark 14]. This is the cup of which we read in the Prophet: ‘I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord’ [Ps. 115]. And elsewhere: ‘My inebriating cup, how glorious it is!’ [Ps. 22].

“If, therefore, the bread coming down from heaven is the Lord’s body and the wine which he gave his disciples is the blood of that New Covenant poured out for the forgiveness of sins, let us reject Jewish fables; let us go up with the Lord to the great upper room, furnished and cleansed; and let us receive from him above the cup of the New Covenant. There, celebrating the Passover with him, let us be made drunk with the wine of sobriety. For the kingdom of God is not [Col. 0141A] food and drink, but righteousness, joy, and peace in the Holy Spirit [Rom. 14]. Moses did not give us the true bread; rather, the Lord Jesus himself is both guest and banquet: he himself eats and is eaten. We drink his blood, and without him we cannot drink.

“Daily, in his sacrifices, we tread the red must from the branch of the true vine and the vine of Sorech, which is interpreted ‘chosen,’ and drink from it new wine in the kingdom of the Father—not in the oldness of the letter, but in the newness of the Spirit [Rom. 7]—singing the new song which no one can sing except in the kingdom of the Church, which is the kingdom of the Father [Rev. 14].”

Likewise, in the Epistle to the Ephesians. (*On the Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *Dupliciter*; and Peter Lombard, book IV, distinction 8, § c.) “Christ’s flesh and blood are understood in the Church in two ways: either that spiritual and divine flesh of which he himself says, ‘My flesh is truly food and my blood is truly drink; and unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not have eternal life’; or the flesh that was crucified and the blood poured out by the soldier’s lance.”

Likewise, on Isaiah, chapter 66. “According to the tropological sense, we may say that all who love pleasures more than God are sanctified in gardens and at thresholds, because they cannot enter the mysteries of truth. They eat foods of piety while they are not holy in body and spirit; neither do they eat the flesh of Jesus nor drink his blood, of which he himself speaks: ‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life’ [John 6]. For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed [1 Cor. [Col. 0141C] 5]; he is eaten not outside, but inside one house.”

Likewise, in a certain homily on Leviticus, chapter 13. “With these points established from Gospel and apostolic authority, see how each person can be shown either clean or unclean. Every person has within himself some food which he offers to his neighbor when that neighbor approaches him. For it cannot happen that, when we human beings come together and engage in conversation, we do not receive or offer some food, as it were from a taste, whether through a question or an answer. If, with the taste of a good mind, we receive someone, we take clean food; but if the one we encounter is unclean, we take unclean food. Hence the Apostle says of such people: ‘With one of this sort, do not even take food’ [1 Cor. 5].

“And, so that these matters may become clearer to you, let us take an example from the greater things and proceed from there to the lesser. The Lord says: ‘Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life; for my flesh is truly food and my blood is truly drink’ [John 6], because all his work is holy and all his speech true. For all humankind is nourished and refreshed by the flesh and blood of the Lamb as clean food and drink.

“In the second place after his flesh, Peter and Paul and all the apostles are clean food. In the third place come their disciples; and thus each person, according to the purity of his merits, becomes clean food for his neighbor. Whoever cannot hear this perhaps turns away his hearing, like those who said, ‘Who can hear him?’ But if [Col. 0142A] you are children of the Church, if you are imbued with the Gospel mysteries, if the Word made flesh [John 1] dwells in you, recognize that what we say belongs to the Lord, lest one who does not know be himself not known. Recognize that the things written in the divine books are figures; therefore, as spiritual and not fleshly persons [1 Cor. 14], understand what is said spiritually.

“For if you receive these things as fleshly, they wound you; they do not nourish you. For there is also a letter in the Gospels which kills [2 Cor. 3]. A killing letter is found not only in the Old Testament; there is also in the New Testament a letter that kills the person who does not attend spiritually. For if you follow according to the letter what is written: ‘Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood,’ this letter kills.

“Do you wish another killing letter from the Gospel to be brought before you? ‘Whoever does not have a sword,’ he says, ‘let him sell his tunic and buy a sword’ [Luke 22]. Behold, this letter is Gospel, yet it kills. But if you understand it spiritually, it does not kill; rather, the Spirit in it gives life. Therefore, whether in the Law or in the Gospels, receive spiritually and judge spiritually what is said.

“As we have said, every person has some food within himself. Whoever takes from it—if he is good and brings forth good from a good treasure—offers clean food to his neighbor. For an innocent and upright-hearted person can appear as a clean animal and offer clean food to one who hears him, like a sheep, which is a clean animal; and likewise in the case of the rest. Therefore, whenever a person speaks to his neighbor, whether he benefits him by his words or harms him, he becomes for him a clean or unclean animal, among which clean animals are to be used and unclean ones are commanded to be avoided.

“If, according to this understanding, we say that the supreme God promulgated laws for human beings, such legislation will appear worthy of divine majesty. But if we cling to the letter and receive what is written according to the way it is said either to Jews or to the common people, I blush to confess that God gave such laws. For the laws of human beings—for example, Romans, Athenians, and Lacedaemonians—will appear more refined.”

## Chapter 6.—That in the Law there was shadow, in the Gospel truth; and that one must approach communion with a devout mind and fear. Ambrose, in the book *On Duties*, chapter 14.

[Col. 0142D] “Those things, therefore, are to be sought by us in which truth is found. Here is shadow, here is image; there is truth. Shadow is in the Law, image in the Gospel, truth in the heavenly things. Formerly a lamb was offered, a calf was offered; now Christ is offered—but he is offered as though a human being, as though undergoing suffering—and he himself offers himself as priest, in order to forgive our sins: here in image, there in truth. There with the Father he intervenes for us as advocate.”

Likewise, on the Epistle to the Corinthians. (On 1 Corinthians, chapter 59.) “He teaches that one must approach communion with a devout mind and fear, so that all may know that they owe reverence to him whose body they approach to receive. For they ought to judge within themselves that he is the Lord whose blood they drink in ministry.”

Likewise, on the Epistle to the Hebrews. (On chapter 5.) “But in this flesh and blood, let the human mind conceive nothing bloody, nothing corruptible; rather, let it conceive a life-giving and saving substance in bread and wine, through which, if they are worthily received, forgiveness of sins is bestowed upon us.”

Likewise, on the same Epistle. (On chapter 10.) “There is one victim of the Church, but theirs were many. For this reason they were not strong, because they were many. What need, tell me, was there of many when one sufficed? Thus, the fact that many were offered shows that they were never purified, just as a powerful, strong, and effective medicine drives away every sickness. If, therefore, applied once, it accomplished the whole cure, it showed its power, so that it should not be applied further. But if it is always applied, it is clear proof that that medicine has been insufficiently strong; for its power consists in being applied once and not frequently—just as here too. For if they had been freed from all sins, no one would have offered sacrifices every day. Therefore there was a remembrance of sin, not absolution, because they, both priests and people alike, were daily cleansed by the same victims.”

(*On the Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *In Christo*; Peter Lombard, book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 12, § g.) “By contrast, in Christ a victim was offered once, powerful for eternal salvation. What then of us? Do we not offer every day? We offer, but for the remembrance of his death; and there is one victim, not many. How is it one and not many? Because Christ was offered once. This sacrifice is the representation of that one: it is always the same; therefore it is one sacrifice. Otherwise, because it is offered in many places, are there many Christs? By no means: Christ is one everywhere, whole here and whole there. For as that which is offered everywhere is one body and not many bodies, so it is also one sacrifice.

“That high priest is the one who offered the victim that cleanses us. We also now offer that same victim which was then offered and cannot be consumed. What we do is done in remembrance of what was done. For he says: ‘Do this in remembrance of me’ [Luke 22]. We do not offer another sacrifice, but always offer the same one; or rather, we perform a memorial of the sacrifice.”

Hence also blessed Augustine, in book ten of *The City of God*, says in nearly the same words: “We vow and render his gifts in ourselves and ourselves also; and on the solemnities, feasts, and appointed days of his benefits, we celebrate and consecrate the memorial, lest ungrateful forgetfulness creep in through the passage of time.” Hence also, in Psalm 80, he says to the brothers: “Behold, Christ has renewed us and granted forgiveness of all sins, when we do not forget the Savior’s gift. Is Christ not sacrificed daily? Yet he was sacrificed once for sins. When we believe, behold the thought. From the remnants of this thought he is thus sacrificed daily for us, as though he renewed us daily, because by his first grace he renewed us.”

## Chapter 7.—That the person who cannot hear “I and the Father are one” stones Christ, just as the Jews, on hearing this, took up stones to stone him; and that the Godhead cannot be seen in the brightness of its truth. Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, book II, chapter 18.

[Col. 0144A] “The Jews, hearing, ‘I and the Father are one,’ took up stones to stone him” [John 10]. “Whoever cannot hear this is a Jew; whoever cannot hear this stones Christ with all the harsher stones of his faithlessness and, if you believe me, wounds Christ. For although he can no longer feel a wound—since we now no longer know Christ according to the flesh [2 Cor. 5]—yet he is stoned by the impiety of the Arians, while he is offered in sacrifice by the piety of the Church. Concerning this sacrificial offering Saint John says in his Epistle: ‘He sent his Son,’ he says, ‘as an atoning offering for our sins’ [1 John 4].”

Likewise, in the sermon on Abel and Cain. “Finally, the Holy Spirit was seen in the form of a dove [Col. 0144B] [Matt. 3], because the Godhead could not be seen in the brightness of its truth. Therefore do not interpret according to nature what is beyond the nature of divinity. For even if you believe that flesh was assumed by Christ and offer the transfigured body upon the altars, nevertheless do not distinguish the nature of the Word from that of the body; and it is said to you: ‘If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.’”

Likewise, in the book *On the Mysteries of Initiation*, chapter 9. “The true flesh of Christ, which was crucified and buried, is truly the sacrament of that flesh.”

Likewise, in the same work. (*On the Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *Ante benedictionem*.) “Before the blessing another kind is named; after the blessing, the body is signified.”

Likewise. (*On the Sacraments*, book IV, chapter 5.) “Christ is in that sacrament.”

Likewise. “Whoever eats this body will receive forgiveness of sins.”

Likewise. “This is not bodily food.”

Likewise. “This is not the bread which enters into the body.”

Likewise. “This food supplies the substance of eternal life.”

Likewise. “With such things he feeds the Church, by which the substance of the soul is strengthened.”

Likewise. (*On the Mysteries of Initiation*, chapter 9.) “Finally, this food strengthens our heart, and this wine gladdens the heart.”

Likewise. (*On the Sacraments*, book IV, chapter 3.) “You have seen the sacraments placed upon the altar and have marveled at the creature itself—yet it is a customary and familiar creature.”

Likewise. (*On the Sacraments*, book IV, chapter 4.) “If there is such power in Christ’s word that things which did not exist began to exist, how much more effective is it that things which existed should continue to exist and be changed into something else?”

Likewise (chapter 5). “As you drank the likeness of death, so you drink the likeness of precious blood.”

Likewise. (*On the Sacraments*, book IV, chapter 2.) “Make this offering acceptable to us, which is a figure of the Lord’s body and blood.”

Likewise. (*On the Sacraments*, book IV, chapter 6.) “The altar is a figure of the body.”

Likewise. “So that there might be no horror at bloodshed, you receive the sacrament in a likeness.”

Likewise. “We offer to you an immaculate victim, a rational victim, an unbloody victim, this holy bread.”

Likewise. (*On the Sacraments*, book IV, chapter 5.) “Before consecration it was not Christ’s body; but after consecration I tell you that it is now the body.”

Likewise. “Hasten to maturity. Abraham had many sons, but he weaned no other; in this son alone he is said to have made a great feast—and rightly great, because this was the time of him whom the hearts of the saints feast upon always.”

In the book *On the Trinity*, addressed to Gratian. (Likewise Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, book II, chapter 7.) “Far be it from anyone to defile himself with such impiety as to say that the Holy Spirit is frequently created, or ever created! For I do not understand why he should seem to be created frequently unless I believe him to die frequently and to be created again frequently.”

Likewise, on the Epistle to the Corinthians (chapter 58). (*On the Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter *Quia morte*.) “Because we have been set free by the Lord’s death, mindful of this fact, in eating and drinking we signify the Lord’s flesh and blood which were offered for us.”

Likewise, in the same chapter: “The blood is witness of the divine benefit, in whose type we receive the mystical cup for the protection of body and soul.”

The Thursday after Theophany. (*On the Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *Singuli*; Peter Lombard, book IV, distinction 12, § e.) “Each receives Christ the Lord, [Col. 0145B] and he is whole in each portion; he is not diminished among the individual portions, but gives himself whole in each.”

Blessed Hilary. (*On the Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *Corpus Christi*.) “The body of the Lord Christ which is received from the altar is a figure, while bread and wine are outwardly seen; but it is truth, while Christ’s body and blood are inwardly believed in truth.”

Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*. (*On the Mysteries of Initiation*, chapter 8.) “Therefore, the sacrament which you receive is not a human but a divine gift, brought forth by him who blessed Abraham, the father of faith, whose grace and deeds you admire. It has been proved that the Church’s sacraments are more ancient; now learn that they are more excellent.

“It is indeed marvelous that God rained manna upon the fathers and that they were fed with the daily food of heaven. Hence it was said: ‘Man ate the bread of angels’ [Ps. 77; Exod. 16; Num. 10]. Yet all who ate that bread died in the wilderness [John 6]. But this food which you receive, this living bread coming down from heaven [ibid.], supplies the substance of eternal life; and whoever eats it shall not die forever, and it is Christ’s body.

“Consider now whether the bread of angels or the flesh of Christ is more excellent—the flesh which, indeed, is the body of life. That manna was from heaven; this is above heaven [Exod. 16]. That was of heaven; this belongs to the Lord of heaven. That was liable to corruption if preserved for the next day; this is free from every corruption. Whoever tastes it devoutly cannot experience corruption. Water flowed from the rock for them [Exod. 17]; blood flows from Christ for you. The water satisfied them for an hour; the blood cleanses you for eternity. The Jew drinks and thirsts; when you have drunk, you cannot thirst. That was in shadow; this is in truth. If that which you marvel at is a shadow, how great is this, whose shadow you marvel at?

“Hear that what was done among the ancients is shadow: ‘They drank,’ he says, ‘from the rock which followed them, and the rock was Christ’ [1 Cor. 10]. ‘But God was not pleased with most of them; for they were struck down in the wilderness. These things happened as a figure for us.’ You have learned what is more excellent. Light is superior to shadow, truth to figure, the body of the Author to manna from heaven.

“Perhaps you say: ‘I see something else. How do you maintain to me that I receive Christ’s body?’ It remains for us to prove this. How many examples, then, shall we use to prove that this is not what nature formed, but what blessing consecrated, and that the power of blessing is greater than that of nature, because by blessing even nature itself is changed?

“Moses held a rod, threw it down, and it became a serpent. Again he seized the serpent’s tail, and it returned to the nature of a rod [Exod. 7]. You see that prophetic grace changed the nature of both serpent and rod twice. The rivers of Egypt were running in a pure flow of water; suddenly blood began to burst forth from the veins of the springs, and there was no drink in the rivers. Again, at the prophet’s prayers, the blood of the rivers ceased and the nature of water returned.

“The Hebrew people were hemmed in on every side: enclosed by Egyptians on one side and shut in by the sea on the other. Moses raised the rod; the water divided and congealed into the appearance of walls, and a footpath appeared amid the waves. The Jordan turned backward and, contrary to nature, flowed back toward the beginning of its own source. Is it not clear that the nature both of sea-waves and of the river’s course was changed?

“The people of the fathers thirsted; Moses touched the rock, and water flowed from the rock. Did not grace work contrary to nature, causing it to pour forth water which nature did not possess? The stream of Marah was most bitter, so that the thirsty people could not drink [Exod. 15]. Moses put wood into the water, and the nature of the water laid aside its bitterness, which the grace suddenly infused tempered.

“Under Elisha, the holy prophet, an iron axe-head slipped from one of the sons of the prophets and immediately sank [4 Kings 6]. The man who had lost the iron asked Elisha, and Elisha put wood into the water, and the iron floated. We certainly recognize that this too occurred contrary to nature, for the substance of iron is heavier than water.

“We observe, then, that grace is greater than nature, although we have so far only been enumerating the gifts of prophetic blessing [4 Kings 1]. If human blessing had such power as to change nature, what shall we say of the divine consecration itself, where the very words of the Lord Savior are at work? For this sacrament which you receive is made by Christ’s word. If Elijah’s word had such power as to bring down fire from heaven, will Christ’s word not have power to change the kinds of the elements? You have read concerning the works of the whole world: ‘He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created’ [Ps. 148]. Therefore, can Christ’s word, which was able to make from nothing what did not exist, not change things which exist into what they were not? For it is no lesser thing to bestow new things than to change natures.

“But why do we use arguments? Let us use his own examples and establish the truth of the mystery by the newness of the Incarnation. Did the normal course of nature precede when the Lord Jesus was born from Mary? If we seek the ordinary order, a woman customarily conceives by union with a man. It is clear, then, that a virgin gave birth contrary to the order of nature, and that what we make is the body from the Virgin. Why do you seek the order of nature in Christ’s body, when the Lord Jesus himself was born of a virgin contrary to nature?

“The true flesh of Christ, which was crucified [Col. 0147A] and buried, is truly the sacrament of that flesh. The Lord Jesus himself cries out: ‘This is my body.’ Before the blessing of the heavenly words another kind is named; after consecration, the body is signified. He himself calls it his blood. Before consecration it is called something else; after consecration, it is called blood. You say: ‘Amen,’ that is, ‘It is true.’ Let the heart feel what the word declares.”

Likewise. (Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book VI, chapter 1.) “As the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, is true God—not as human beings are gods by grace, but as Son from the Father’s substance—so Christ’s flesh, which we receive, is true flesh, as he himself said, and the blood which we drink is true blood. But perhaps you say what Christ’s disciples said at that time when they heard him saying: ‘Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he shall not remain in me nor have eternal life’ [John 6]. Perhaps you say: [Col. 0147B] ‘How can it be true flesh, how true blood, when I do not see the likeness of flesh, nor see the reality of blood?’

“First of all, I spoke to you about Christ’s word, which works so as to be able to change and convert the kinds and established orders of nature. Then, when his disciples could not accept Christ’s saying, but heard that he would give his flesh to be eaten and his blood to be drunk, they departed. Peter alone then said: ‘You have the words of eternal life, and how could I depart from you?’ [John 6].

“Therefore, lest more people should say this, and lest there should be, as it were, a horror of bloodshed, while the grace of redemption remained, [Col. 0147C] you receive the sacrament indeed in a likeness, but attain the grace and power of the true nature. ‘I am,’ he says, ‘the bread which came down from heaven’ [John 6].”

### Chapter 8.—That captive Jerusalem must be delivered from the Babylon of this world; that the visible things are signs of divine realities, while the invisible realities themselves are to be honored in them; and many other points of this kind. Augustine, *On Instructing Beginners in the Faith*

(Chapter 11.) Sometimes, even when everything is truly and rightly said, something not understood, or something harsh because of its novelty in contrast to an opinion or the habit of an old error, offends and disturbs the hearer. If this becomes apparent and shows itself curable through an abundance of authorities and arguments, it must be healed without any delay. But if the offense is hidden, the medicine of God can bring help. If, however, he recoils and refuses to be healed, let the Lord console us by that example in which, when people were offended by his word and fled from it as though it were harsh, he said even to those who remained: “Do you also wish to go away?” (John 6).

For it is fitting that this be held firmly and immovably in the heart: that captive Jerusalem is to be delivered, when the course of time has run, from the Babylon of this world; and that none of her will perish, because whoever perishes was not of her.

Likewise. Concerning the sacrament which he has received, when it has been properly commended to him: the visible things are indeed signs of divine realities, but the invisible realities themselves are honored in them. The appearance sanctified by blessing is not to be regarded as it is in any ordinary use. One must also say what it signifies, and what meaning is enclosed in it by the word which he has heard, of whose reality that thing bears the likeness. Then he must be admonished on this occasion that, if he hears anything even in the Scriptures which sounds carnal, even though he does not understand it, he should nevertheless believe that something spiritual is signified which pertains to holy conduct and to the life to come.

But he should learn this brief rule: whatever he hears from the canonical books which cannot be referred to love of eternity and holiness, and to love of one’s neighbor, he should believe to have been spoken or done figuratively; and he should strive to understand it so as to refer it to that twofold love.

Likewise, *On Instructing Beginners in the Faith*, chapter 9. Concerning the sacrament, it is enough for the more intelligent to hear what that reality signifies; but with the slower, one must sometimes proceed with more words and comparisons, lest they despise what they see.

Likewise, *Against Faustus*, book XIX, chapter 16. For what else are the bodily sacraments, each of them, but certain visible words—holy indeed, but nevertheless changeable and temporal?

Likewise, in book X of *The City of God* (chapter 19). Those who suppose that these visible sacrifices are suitable for foreign gods, while invisible sacrifices are suitable, as it were, for the invisible God, and greater offerings for the greater, better offerings for the better—such as the offices of a pure mind and good will—certainly do not know that these are signs of those realities, just as spoken words are signs of things. Therefore, as when praying and praising we direct significant sounds to him to whom we offer in our hearts the realities which we signify, so, when sacrificing, we should know that a visible sacrifice is to be offered to no one other than him whose invisible sacrifice we ourselves ought to be in our hearts. [Col. 0148C]

Likewise, in book X of *The City of God*. (Chapter 5, *De consecratione*, distinction 2, chapter “Sacrificium”; and book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 1, §1.) A visible sacrifice is the sacrament—that is, the sacred sign—of an invisible sacrifice. And elsewhere: “A sacrament is a visible form of invisible grace.”

Likewise, book II of *On Christian Doctrine*. A sign is a thing which, beyond the appearance it presents to the senses, causes something else to come into knowledge from itself.

Likewise, book III in the same work. Christian liberty, finding people under useful signs, as though nearly discovered, freed them—once the signs to which they had been subject were interpreted—and raised them to those realities of which those signs are signs. From these were made the Churches of the holy Israelites. But those whom it found under useless signs, it deprived not only of servile action under such signs, but also of the signs themselves, and removed everything, so that the nations might be converted from the corruption of a multitude of counterfeit gods—which Scripture often and properly calls fornication—to the worship of the one God. They were no longer to serve even under useful signs, but rather to have their minds stirred up by their spiritual understanding of them.

For he serves under a sign who performs or reveres some thing without knowing what it signifies. But he who performs a divinely instituted sign, whose force and meaning he understands, does not revere what is seen and passes away, but rather that to which all such things are to be referred. Such a person is both spiritual and free in the time of servitude, when those signs, under whose yoke carnal minds must be subdued, ought not yet to be revealed. Such spiritual persons were all the patriarchs and prophets, and all those in the people of Israel through whom he supplied us with the consolations and aids of the Scriptures.

But in this time, after the resurrection of our Lord had shone forth as the clearest token of our liberty, we have not been burdened with the heavy performance even of those signs which we now understand. Rather, the Lord himself and apostolic discipline have delivered a few things in place of many: things most easy to perform, most exalted in meaning, and most pure in observance. Such are the sacrament of baptism and the celebration of the body and blood of the Lord. When anyone has received these, having been instructed as to what they refer to, he recognizes that he is to revere them not in carnal servitude but rather in spiritual liberty. [Col. 0149B]

And a little later (chapters 15, 16): “In figurative expressions,” he says, “a rule of this kind shall be observed: what is read is to be considered with diligent reflection until its interpretation is brought to the kingdom of charity. But if it already conveys a literal meaning, no figurative expression is to be supposed.

“If the expression is preceptive, forbidding either a disgraceful act or a crime, or commanding usefulness or beneficence, it is not figurative.
