But if it seems to command a disgraceful act or a crime, or to forbid usefulness or beneficence, it is figurative. ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man,’ he says, ‘and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves’ (John 6): it appears to command a crime or a disgraceful act. Therefore it is a figure, commanding that one share in the Lord’s passion, and that one sweetly and profitably store in memory that his flesh was crucified and wounded for us.

“Scripture says: ‘If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink’ (Proverbs 25; Romans 12). Here, beyond doubt, it commands beneficence. But what follows—‘For in doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head’—might be thought to command a malicious crime. Therefore do not doubt that it is spoken figuratively; and although it can be interpreted in two ways, one for harming, the other for helping, let charity recall you rather to beneficence, so that you understand the coals of fire to be the burning groans of repentance, by which the pride of the man is healed when he grieves that he was the enemy of a person from whom help is given to his distress.

“Likewise, when the Lord says, ‘He who loves his soul will lose it’ (John 12), he should not be thought to forbid the good by which each person ought to preserve his own soul. Rather, it is said figuratively: ‘let him lose it,’ that is, let him destroy and relinquish the use which it now has—namely, the perverse and disordered use by which it is inclined toward temporal things so that it does not seek eternal things.

“It is written: ‘Give to the merciful man, and do not receive a sinner’ (Ecclesiasticus 12). The latter part of this saying appears to forbid beneficence, for it says: ‘Do not receive a sinner.’ Understand ‘sinner’ to be said figuratively for ‘sin,’ so that you do not receive his sin.”

Likewise, on Psalm 3, treating of Judas, the betrayer of the Lord. “He admitted him to the meal at which he commended and delivered to the disciples the figure of his body and blood.”

Likewise, in the second preface to Psalm 21. (*De consecratione*, distinction 2, chapter “Semel”; book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 12, §g.) “Christ died once, the righteous for the unrighteous” (1 Peter 3); and we know, hold as certain, and retain with immovable hope that “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Romans 6). These are the Apostle’s words. Yet, lest we forget what was done once, it is enacted in our memory every year. Whenever Easter is celebrated, is Christ killed as often? Yet the annual commemoration represents what was done long ago, and thus moves us as though we saw the Lord present upon the cross. [Col. 0150A]

Likewise, in the earlier exposition of Psalm 21. “I will pay my vows”: I will render the sacraments of the body and blood of my Lord. “The poor shall eat and be satisfied”: those who despise the world shall eat, shall be changed, and shall praise the Lord who seek him. The praise of the Lord is the outpouring of their satisfaction; their hearts shall live for ever and ever, for that food is food for the heart. [Col. 0150B]

In the exposition of Psalms 53 and 98. (*De consecratione*, distinction 2, chapter “Prima”; and book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 10, §a.) “The first heresy among Christ’s disciples arose, as it were, from the harshness of his saying. For when he said, ‘Unless anyone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he shall not have eternal life’ (John 6), they, not understanding, said to one another: ‘This saying is harsh; who can hear it?’ (ibid.). Saying that this saying was harsh, they separated themselves from him; he remained with the twelve. When they had gone away, he instructed those who remained: ‘It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life’ (ibid.), that is, they are to be understood spiritually. Have you understood spiritually? They are spirit and life. Have you understood carnally? Even so, they are spirit and life, but not for you. Understand spiritually what I have spoken.”

(The same chapter, and *De consecratione*, distinction 2, chapter “Non hoc.”) “You are not going to eat this body which you see, nor drink that blood which those who crucify me are going to shed. I have commended to you a certain sacrament; spiritually understood, it will give you life; but the flesh profits nothing. But they understood it as they did: for they understood flesh as it is sold in a corpse or cut to pieces in a butcher’s shop.”

Augustine, tractate 27 on John. But Jesus, knowing this, said (ibid.): “Does this offend you because I said to you, I give you my flesh to eat and my blood to drink? What, then, if you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before?” What does this mean? By this he resolved what had troubled them; by this he opened up that by which they had been offended—clearly by this, if they understood. But they thought that he would distribute his body; he said that he would ascend into heaven, certainly whole. “When you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before,” then surely you will see that he does not distribute his body in the manner you suppose; or then you will understand that his grace is not consumed by bites. [Col. 0150D]

Likewise, tractate 50 on John. Until the world comes to its end, the Lord is above; yet the Lord, who is truth, is also here with us. For the body in which he rose must be in one place, but his truth is diffused everywhere. [Col. 0151A]

Likewise, tractate 12 on John. Because Thomas touched the man, he confessed God. And the Lord, comforting us, who cannot touch with our hands Christ now seated in heaven but may touch him by faith, says to him: “Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20).

Likewise, in a sermon on the words of the Gospel. [Note: The beginning of this sermon of Augustine is: “The truth which is Christ.” Col. 0151D.] The Lord invites his servants; he has prepared himself as food. Who would dare to eat his Lord? Yet he says: “He who eats me lives because of me.” When Christ is eaten, life is eaten; nor is he killed in order to be eaten, but, when eaten, he gives life to the dead, because, having been killed, he rose again. Nor, when he is eaten, do we make parts of him; yet in the sacrament this does indeed take place. The faithful know how they eat Christ’s flesh: each receives his own part; he is eaten in parts, yet remains whole and entire. He is eaten in parts in the sacrament; he remains whole and entire in heaven; he remains whole and entire in your heart. [Col. 0151B]

Likewise. What you see upon the altar is bread and a cup, as your eyes themselves report to you. But what faith demands, once instructed, is this: the bread is the body; the cup is the blood. This has indeed been said briefly, perhaps sufficiently for faith; but faith desires instruction. For the Prophet says: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isaiah 6). Therefore you may say to me: “You have commanded us to believe; explain, that we may understand.” For such a thought may arise in someone’s mind:

“We know whence the Lord Jesus Christ received flesh: namely, from the Virgin Mary. He was an infant, was nursed, was fed, grew, came to youthful age, was suspended on the wood, killed, taken down from the wood, buried, and rose on the third day. On the day he wished, he ascended into heaven. He lifted his body there, whence he will come to judge the living and the dead. There he now sits at the right hand of the Father. How, then, is bread his body? And how is the cup, or what the cup contains, his blood?”

These things, brothers, are called sacraments because one thing is seen in them and another is understood. What is seen has a bodily appearance; what is understood has spiritual fruit. [Col. 0151C]

Likewise, book VIII, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 50. He introduces blessed Cyprian as speaking thus: “For when the Lord calls his body bread (John 6), formed from the gathering together of many grains, he indicates our people, whom he bore, gathered together from the nations. And when he calls his blood wine, pressed from many clusters and grapes and brought together into one, he likewise signifies our flock joined together by the mingling of a united multitude.” [Col. 0151D]

Likewise. At present through faith, at present through a sign, at present through the sacrament of baptism, at present through the food and drink of the altar.

Likewise, in the same Gospel. “It was concerning those persons,” he says, “that the Apostle spoke when he said this: those who received the Lord’s body indiscriminately and negligently as though it were any other food” (1 Corinthians 11). And, explaining in what follows what he called the Lord’s body, he says that it must be understood that he had already distributed to them all the sacrament of his body and blood.

And elsewhere: “See: while faith remains, the signs are changed. There, the rock was Christ; for us, Christ is what is placed upon the altar of God. And they, as a great sacrament of the same Christ, drank water flowing from the rock; the faithful know what we drink. If you attend to the visible appearance, it is something different; if to the intelligible signification, they drank the same spiritual drink.” [Col. 0152A]

Likewise, in a sermon on the words of the Gospel, tractate 26 on John. (*De consecratione*, distinction 2, chapter “Quid est”; book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 9, §a.) “What is it to eat Christ? It is not merely to receive his body in the sacrament. For many receive unworthily, concerning whom the Apostle says: ‘Whoever eats and drinks the Lord’s cup unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself’ [cf. 1 Corinthians 11]. But how is Christ to be eaten? As he himself says: ‘He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him’ (John 6). If he abides in me and I in him, then he drinks. But whoever does not abide in me, nor I in him—even if he receives the sacrament—acquires great torment.”

Likewise, from the tractate on the Gospel according to John (sentence 339). Judas was such a man; nevertheless, he entered and went out with the eleven holy apostles and approached with them the very Lord’s Supper. Judas received from the one bread, and Peter received; yet what share has the faithful with the unfaithful? Peter received unto life, and Judas received unto death. [Col. 0152B]

Likewise, in the book of *Sentences* of Prosper. He receives the food of life and drinks the cup of eternity who abides in Christ, whose indweller is Christ. For one who is at variance with Christ neither eats Christ’s flesh nor drinks his blood, even if he daily receives, without distinction, the sacrament of so great a reality unto judgment for his own presumption. [Col. 0152C]

### Chapter 9.—As, by the Lord’s word, things which did not exist began to exist, so by his operation things which do exist are changed into something else; further, that the sacrifice of the Church is made and consists of two things: the visible appearance of the elements and the invisible flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. Lanfranc. (*On the Sacrament of the Body*, chapter 5 and following.)

If such power lies in the word of the Lord that things which did not exist begin to be, how much more effective is it [Col. 0152D] in causing things to be what they were, and to be changed into something else? That they remain what they were is attested according to their visible appearance; but that they are changed according to their inner essence, into the nature of things which previously did not exist.

(De consecratione, distinction 2, chapter *Hoc est quod dicimus*, and Book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 10, § b.) This is what we say and strive by every means to establish: that the sacrifice of the Church is made up of two things and consists of two things—the visible appearance of the elements and the invisible flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, that is, the body of Christ. Thus the person of Christ consists and is constituted of God and man, since [Col. 0153A] Christ himself is true God and true man; for everything contains within itself the nature and truth of those things from which it is constituted. The sacrifice of the Church, moreover, is constituted of two things: the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, that is, the body of Christ. Therefore there is both a sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, namely Christ’s body.

For Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him (Rom. 6:9). But, as the apostle Andrew says: “Although his flesh is truly eaten on earth and his blood is truly drunk, he nevertheless remains whole and living in heaven at the right hand of the Father until the time of the restoration of all things.” If you ask how this can happen, I answer briefly for the present: the mystery of faith can beneficially be believed, but cannot usefully be investigated. [Col. 0153B] “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6); nor, when we eat, do we make parts of him. Far be it from us to understand Christ’s eating in the way in which those understood it who, upon hearing the Lord say, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves,” immediately replied: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” (ibid.). For, as blessed Augustine says in many places, they thought that they would cut the Lord, while he was living on earth, into pieces, and thus eat his flesh either boiled in pots or roasted on spits; or else, if they were unwilling to do this, that they could not be his disciples. Therefore they chose to depart and no longer go with him [Col. 0153C]. May God utterly avert such an opinion from his Church! Thus we eat and drink Christ, who was sacrificed on earth, in such a way that he always remains whole and living in heaven at the right hand of the Father.

(De consecratione, distinction 2, chapter *Dum frangitur*.) While the host is broken and the blood from the chalice is poured into the mouths of the faithful, what else is signified than the immolation of the Lord’s body upon the cross and the pouring forth of his blood from his side?

(De consecratione, distinction 2, chapter *Nos autem*, and Book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 10, § d.) But in the appearance of bread and wine which we see, we honour invisible realities—that is, Christ’s flesh and blood. Nor do we weigh these two appearances in the same way as we weighed them before consecration, since we faithfully confess that before consecration they are bread and wine, formed by nature; but after consecration, they are Christ’s flesh and blood, consecrated by the blessing [Col. 0153D].

Therefore, with respect to that which was sacrificed on the cross, the sacrament of Christ’s body is the Lord Jesus Christ himself. His flesh is that which we receive in the sacrament veiled under the form of bread; and his blood is that which we drink under the appearance and taste of wine. The flesh, namely, is the sacrament of the flesh, and the blood the sacrament of the blood. By the flesh and blood, both invisible, intelligible, and spiritual, is signified the visible and tangible body of our Lord, full of every grace of virtues and divine majesty. When the one is broken and distributed for the salvation of the people, and the other is poured out from the chalice and received by the mouths of the faithful, his death on the cross and the issuing of his blood from his side are represented [Col. 0154A].

Blessed Gregory carefully considered both, and expounded them clearly in Book IV of the *Dialogues*, saying: “For there his flesh is received; his blood is poured out, no longer into the hands of unbelievers, but into the mouths of believers.” Therefore we must consider what kind of sacrifice this is, which continually imitates, for our absolution, the death of God’s only-begotten Son. He said “imitates,” not “effects,” because Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him (Rom. 6).

Thus the flesh and blood by which we are daily nourished in order to obtain mercy for our sins are called Christ’s body and blood—not only because they are so essentially, though they differ greatly in their qualities, but also by that manner [Col. 0154B] of speech in which a thing signifying is customarily called by the name of the thing signified. Nor should anyone rightly be troubled if the same flesh and the same blood are their own sacraments, received in different respects; since the Lord Jesus himself, after his resurrection, bore a type and figure of himself in different temporal respects.

For, when he appeared to the two disciples and spoke with them as much as he judged sufficient, he pretended to be going farther; and, as blessed Augustine says, he thereby signified that he would ascend to heaven after a few days. This journey is far removed from ordinary human life, which was most clearly figured by those two disciples. Therefore Christ is the sacrament of Christ: by pretending to go farther, he was the sacrament of Christ ascending farther, in his own time, into heaven (Luke 24) [Col. 0154C]—the same of the same, yet not altogether the same. For he who pretended and he who ascended was true God and true man. Nevertheless, the pretence of an earthly journey is one thing, and the reality of ascending into heaven another. Nor should anyone be so foolish as, because he signified the true Christ ascending into heaven by the pretence of a longer journey, to dare deny that the one pretending to go farther was the true Christ.

Moreover, in the very letter to Boniface, blessed Augustine calls baptism the sacrament of faith (Letter 23 to Boniface). True baptism, however, consists not so much in the washing of the body as in faith of the heart, as apostolic teaching hands down when it says: “Cleansing their hearts by faith.” And elsewhere: “Baptism saves, not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience to [Col. 0154D] God.” Yet one thing is signified through the other. For by the washing externally applied to the body, the purification of the soul is expressed, which inward faith accomplishes; and faith is called baptism according to that figure of speech by which the mystery is customarily designated by the name of that reality of which it is the mystery.

The reason is the likeness which must always be found in the sacrament and in the reality of the sacrament, as in baptism and faith; for both wash, cleanse, and purify—the one the flesh, the other the mind. Therefore, just as the heavenly bread, which is truly Christ’s flesh, is in its own manner called Christ’s body, although it is in truth the sacrament of Christ’s body—namely, of that body which was visible, tangible, mortal, and set upon the cross—so the very immolation of the flesh, performed by the hands of the priest, is called Christ’s passion, death, and crucifixion, not by the truth of the reality but by the signifying mystery [Col. 0155A]. Likewise, the sacrament of faith, by which baptism is understood, is faith.

(De consecratione, distinction 2, chapter *Semel*, and Book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 12, § g.) Christ was sacrificed once in himself, and yet is daily sacrificed in the sacrament. This must be understood thus: in the manifestation of his body, distinguished in all his members, true God and true man hung only once upon the cross, offering himself to the Father as a living, passible, mortal victim, effective for the redemption of the living and the dead—namely, those whom the depth of the divine counsel judged worthy to be redeemed, predestined, and called in the ways and at the times fitting for this to occur.

How bread [Col. 0155B] becomes flesh and wine is converted into blood, with the nature of each essentially changed, or whether they pass away as ordinary foods do, the righteous person who lives by faith (Habakkuk 2) does not seek to investigate by arguments or comprehend by reason. For he prefers now to place faith in heavenly mysteries, so that he may at some time attain the rewards of faith, rather than labour vainly over matters which cannot be comprehended; knowing what is written: “Do not seek what is too high for you, nor search out what is too strong for you; but always think upon what God has commanded you, and do not be curious about his many works” (Ecclus. 3).

If we believe that the Lord Jesus Christ is truly and beneficially eaten on earth by worthy recipients, then we must most certainly hold that he exists incorruptibly in heaven [Col. 0155C]. For if, in foolishness, you were to say that the widow of Zarephath could not eat the oil with which her lamp was full because, according to sacred history, the lamp’s oil was not diminished—although the same Scripture says, “She went and did according to the word of Elijah; and he and she and her household ate” (3 Kings 17)—you would be burdened with no dissimilar insanity if you endeavoured for that reason to establish that the Church cannot receive the flesh and blood of the Redeemer, because the Apostle says: “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6).

With the bodily mouth we eat and drink whenever we receive from the Lord’s altar, through the hand of the priest, the Lord’s own body. But with the spiritual mouth of the heart it is spiritually eaten and drunk when, sweetly and beneficially, as blessed Augustine says, it is stored in memory that the only-begotten Son of God took flesh for the salvation of the world, hung upon the cross, rose again, appeared, and ascended [Col. 0155D].

“I,” he says, “am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6); but his flesh did not come down from heaven—that is, he assumed flesh on earth from the Virgin. How, then, did the bread come down from heaven, and how is it living bread? Because the same Lord Jesus Christ shares in divinity and in body; and you who receive the flesh partake, in that food, of his divine substance.

Ambrose, Letter 62, Book VIII, to Irenaeus: “You ask me why the Lord God rained manna upon the people of the fathers, and does not rain it now. If you understand, he does rain it, and daily rains manna from heaven upon those who serve him [Col. 0156A]. And that bodily manna is still found today in very many places; but now it is not so great a miracle, because that which is perfect has come—the perfect bread from heaven, the body from the Virgin—concerning which the Gospel sufficiently teaches you how much more excellent these things are than those earlier ones.”

Likewise, in the eleventh homily on Psalm 33: “The Jews approached in order to crucify Christ; let us approach him in order to receive his body and blood. They were darkened by the Crucified One; we are enlightened by eating and drinking the Crucified One.” And shortly afterward: “Truly God is great, and great is his mercy; truly he who gave us to eat his body, in which he endured so much, and to drink his blood.”

Likewise, in the homily on Psalm 65: “The shed blood of the innocent has now been bestowed upon murderers; and the very blood which [Col. 0156B] they shed in madness, they drank by grace.”

Likewise, in the homily on Psalm 28: “Christ received earth from the earth, because flesh is from earth: from the flesh of Mary the Virgin he received flesh; and because in that flesh he walked here and gave that same flesh to be eaten for salvation, no one eats that flesh unless he has first adored it.”

Likewise, in the same work (De consecratione, distinction 2, chapter *Non hoc corpus*): “You will not eat this body which you see, nor drink that blood which those who crucify me will shed: it is indeed the same, and not the same—the same invisibly, not the same visibly.” Hence it is added: “And although it must be celebrated visibly, nevertheless it must be understood invisibly.”

In the sermon to the newly baptized: “Receive in the bread that which hung upon the cross; and receive in the chalice that which [Col. 0156C] was poured out from Christ’s side. For death, not life, shall be his who judges life to be deceitful.”

Pope Leo, in the sermon on the fast of the seventh month: “Beloved, uttering this confession with your whole heart, reject the impious inventions of heretics, so that your fasts and alms may not be polluted by any thought of error. For then the offering of sacrifice is pure and the gift of mercy holy, when those who render these things understand what they do. For, since the Lord says, ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves’ (John 6), you ought so to partake in the sacred Mass that you entertain absolutely no doubt concerning the truth of Christ’s body and blood. For that which is received by the mouth is believed by faith, and ‘Amen’ is vainly said by those who dispute against [Col. 0156D] that which they receive.”

Likewise, in the letter sent to Bishop Anatolius. (Leo I, Letter 40, l., question 1, chapter *In Ecclesia Dei*.) “For in the Church of God, which is Christ’s body, neither are priesthoods valid nor sacrifices true unless the true High Priest reconciles us in the property of our nature and the true blood of the spotless Lamb cleanses us. Though established at the Father’s right hand, he nevertheless performs the sacrament of propitiation in that same flesh which he assumed from the Virgin.”

Likewise, in the sermon *On the Passion of the Lord* (Leo, Sermon 11): “Thus his own malice deceived him: it inflicted punishment upon the Son of God which was turned into a remedy for all the children of men; it shed righteous blood, which, in reconciling the world, might be both reward and cup.”

Saint Gregory, in the [Col. 0157A] Paschal homily. (Homily 22 on the Gospels.) “What the blood of the lamb is, you have learned no longer by hearing but by drinking. That blood is placed upon both doorposts (Exod. 12), when it is drunk not only by the mouth of the body but also by the mouth of the heart.”

(LANFRANC.) Someone will say: “That which you maintain to be the true body of Christ is called in the sacred writings appearance, likeness, figure, sign, mystery, and sacrament. But these terms are relative. Nothing which is relative can be that very thing to which it is referred. Therefore it is not Christ’s body.”

But these terms in no way prescribe against the faith which we believe or the truth which we defend. (De consecratione, distinction 2, chapter *Species*; Book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 9, § c.) For “appearance” and “likeness” are terms belonging to the things which previously were bread and wine [Col. 0157B]. Thus, at the end of a certain Mass, this prayer is said: “Grant, we beseech thee, O Lord, that thy sacraments may accomplish in us what they contain, so that what we now receive under an appearance, we may one day receive in the truth of the realities.” For the priest asks that Christ’s body, now received under the appearance of bread and wine, may at some time be received by manifest vision as it truly is.

Concerning that vision the Lord says in the Gospel according to John (chapter 14): “He who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.” Although it is not implausibly explained in this place that the truth of the flesh and blood is their very effect, namely remission of sins. For by every means the flesh and blood truly exist for those who receive worthily.

Hence Saint Gregory, in Book IV [Col. 0157C] of the *Dialogues* (chapter 59): “Then there will truly be a sacrifice for us before God when we make ourselves a sacrifice.” Christ’s flesh and blood are indeed true also for sinners and unworthy recipients, but in essence, not in saving efficacy. Blessed Augustine bears witness to this in Book V of *On Baptism* (chapter 8), saying: “Just as Judas (De consecratione, distinction 2, chapter *Sicut Judas*, and Book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 9, § b), to whom the Lord handed the morsel, made room for the devil in himself not by receiving something evil but by receiving it evilly, so anyone who receives the Lord’s sacrament unworthily does not thereby make it evil because he himself is evil, nor does he receive nothing because he does not receive it unto salvation. For it was nevertheless the Lord’s body for those to whom the Apostle said: ‘He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself’” (1 Cor. 11) [Col. 0157D].

“Appearance,” “likeness,” and “figure” are also found in place of “truth.” Thus the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “We walk by faith, and not by appearance” (2 Cor. 5). Ambrose, in *On the Sacraments*: “We find that ‘appearance’ is to be understood also in the sense of truth—both of Christ, ‘found in appearance as a man,’ and of God the Father, ‘you have seen neither his appearance.’” The Apostle says to the Philippians: “Made in the likeness of men, and found in outward form as a man” (Phil. 2). And likewise to the Hebrews: “Who, being the brightness of glory and the express figure of his substance” (Heb. 1).

Moreover, these names signify the Lord’s passion, provided that “sacrament” is understood as a sacred sign. Hence blessed Gregory, in Book IV of the *Dialogues* (chapter 58): “For [Col. 0158A] this singular victim saves the soul from eternal destruction, since through a sacrament it renews for us the death of the Only-Begotten One.” And after some intervening words (same work, chapter 59): “We who celebrate the mysteries of the Lord’s passion ought to imitate what we worship.”

That it is called bread follows the customary manner of sacred Scripture, which calls things by the names of those things from which, or which, they are thought to be—even when they are not—or to which they are in some manner similar. Hence blessed Jerome, in the second book of his *Explanations on Hosea* (on chapter 5): “After the earth has returned to its own earth.” And to a proud man the Wise One says: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Ecclus. 10). And Abraham is said to have seen three men, though they were angels (Gen. 18).

And blessed Jerome, in the aforesaid *Explanations [Col. 0158B] on Hosea* (ibid.): “[God] becomes like a moth and decay,” not because God is a moth or decay, but because to those undergoing punishments all these things appear so. And in the Gospel according to Matthew: “If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children” (Matt. 7). On this saying blessed Augustine argues in Book II of *On the Sermon on the Mount*: “How do evil persons give good things?” But he calls lovers of the world evil. The things they give are called good according to their own judgment, because they regard these as good.

Still someone presses the point and says: Ambrose, in *On the Sacraments* (Book IV, chapter 4), says: “Just as you received the likeness of death, so you drink the likeness of the precious blood.” From this he infers and says that there is no true blood in the sacrament, since there is no true death in baptism [Col. 0158C]. But he is mistaken. For adverbs of comparison do not always signify identity or equality. In the Gospel the Saviour says: “Be merciful, as your Father also is merciful” (Luke 6). Yet the same or equal mercy cannot belong to God and human beings. And in the Gospel according to John he says: “The love which thou hast given me, I have given to them, that they may be one as we are” (John 17); and elsewhere: “Thou hast loved them as thou hast loved me” (ibid.).

Hence blessed Augustine says in his exposition of the same Gospel (Tractate 110): “He who says, ‘as this, so also that,’ does not always signify equality. Sometimes it means only that because this is, that also is; or that this is in order that that may be.” There is still another objection: “If bread is converted into Christ’s true flesh, either [Col. 0158D] bread is raised into heaven so that it may there be changed into Christ’s flesh, or Christ’s flesh is brought down to earth so that bread may here be changed into it, or neither is bread raised nor flesh brought down. Therefore it is not true flesh into which bread is changed.”

This conclusion is drawn according to human wisdom and not according to divine wisdom. But the Apostle forbids the investigation of divine works by human wisdom, saying to the Romans: “Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think soberly” (Rom. 12). And to the Corinthians: “My speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of Spirit and power, that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God” (1 Cor. 2). And to the Colossians: “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and vain deceit, according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world” (Col. 2) [Col. 0159A].

And blessed Gregory, in the homily for the octave of Easter (Book of Forty Homilies, Homily 26): “We must know that, if a divine operation is comprehended by reason, it is not wonderful; and faith has no merit where human reason provides proof.” We must do what the lawgiver shows ought to be done, saying: “Do not transgress the ancient boundaries which your fathers set” (Prov. 22).

And blessed Augustine, in Book I of *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*: “Whatever there sounds obscure or absurd, let it not thereby stir up contests of contradiction, but let one pray in order to understand.” And in Book II of *On the Trinity* (chapter 10): “It is useful to me,” he says, [Col. 0159B] “to remember my own powers, and to admonish my brothers to remember theirs, lest human weakness advance farther than is safe.” And in the book against the heretic Felicianus (Augustine, *On the Unity of the Trinity*, addressed to Optatus against the Arian Felicianus, chapter 2): “Content with the authority of the Scriptures, I strive rather to obey simplicity than pride.” And shortly thereafter: “What reason can you offer if you proclaim the birth from a virgin? If you do not deny that sight was restored to the blind? If you show that the buried returned from the dead? Therefore, since both the reason of these things is incomprehensible and their truth evident, in matters of faith testimony is more readily believed than reason investigated.”

With these points set forth, let us now see what follows from the error of those who believe that the bread and wine of the Lord’s table remain unchanged in substance during consecration [Col. 0159C]. If this is so, the sacraments of the Jews were more excellent and more divine than the sacraments of Christians. For who does not know that the manna which the Lord rained from heaven, or the living and sentient creatures which that people was accustomed to consecrate, were more excellent than a small morsel of bread and a little wine? Again, who does not understand that it was more divine to foretell future things than to recount past things? For the former cannot be done except by one filled with God’s Spirit, whereas the latter can be done even by an uneducated or wholly unskilled person.

But let this be far from the heart of believers and Christian understanding! For Ambrose, the soldier of Christ, confirms in the book *On the Mysteries* that the former things are inferior and these superior and more worthy, saying (chapter 8): “We wish to demonstrate with the utmost care [Col. 0159D] that the sacraments of the Church are more ancient than those of the Synagogue and more excellent than manna.” And again, in Book IV of *On the Sacraments* (chapter 3): “Accept what I say: the sacraments of Christians are more divine than those of the Jews.” Therefore the things which you propose are false.

Moreover, if what these people believe and maintain concerning the Lord’s body and blood is true, then what the Church throughout all nations believes and maintains concerning the same matter is false. For all who rejoice to be and to be called Christians rejoice that in this sacrament they receive Christ’s true flesh and his true blood, both taken from the Virgin. Ask all who have acquired knowledge of the Latin language or of our writings. Ask Greeks and Armenians, or any Christians whatsoever of any nation: with one voice they testify that they hold this faith [Col. 0160A].

But if the faith of the universal Church has proved false, either there never was a catholic Church or it has perished. Nothing is more effective for the destruction of souls than pernicious error. Yet no one will agree that the catholic Church either did not exist or has perished; otherwise the promise of Truth to Abraham is void: “In thy seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22). Likewise: “Ask of me, and I shall give thee the nations for thine inheritance, and the ends of the earth for thy possession” (Ps. 2). Likewise: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Ps. 21). And elsewhere: “[Those] whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy, and gathered from the regions—from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea” (Ps. 106).

Likewise, blessed Augustine in the first [Col. 0160B] part of his exposition of the Psalms: “What is the great Church, brothers? Is it some small part of the world? The great Church is the whole world.” Likewise, in the same work (Psalm 39): “I have proclaimed thy righteousness in the great Church.” How great? Throughout the whole world. How great? Among all nations. Why among all nations? “Because their sound went forth into all the earth” (Ps. 18). Likewise, in the third part of the same work: “The body of Christ consists of many believers throughout the whole world.” Likewise, in the same work: “The tabernacle of the Lord is the Church itself, spread throughout the whole world.” And elsewhere: “The body of Christ is now the whole world. The body of Christ sounds in harmony from east to west.” Likewise, in the book *On Christian Combat* (chapter 29): “Let us not listen to those who deny that the holy Church, which is one and catholic, is spread throughout the world” [Col. 0160C].

And the Lord says in the Gospel: “The field is this world” (Matt. 13). And shortly afterward: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind” (ibid.). Against such illustrious testimonies of the Holy Spirit, these people offer this: “The Gospel was preached among all nations, the world believed, the Church came into being, grew, and bore fruit; but it will perish through the ignorance of those who misunderstand it.”

The truth of the Gospel and the inviolable authority of the prophets overthrow this sacrilegious vanity. For the Lord promises his Church, saying: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). Augustine, in the second part of his exposition of the Psalms (on Psalm 64): “The hope of all the ends of the earth—not of one [Col. 0160D] corner, not of Pannonia or Judaea or Africa, not of east or west, but of all the ends of the earth.” Likewise, in the same work (on Psalm 71): “This prophecy was promised because of those who think that the religion of the Christian name will live in this world until a certain time and afterward will no longer exist. But it will remain with the sun—that is, as long as the sun rises and sets.” Therefore what these persons believe and maintain concerning Christ’s body is false. Therefore his flesh which we receive is true flesh, and the blood which we drink is true blood.

## CHAPTER 10.—How Berengar’s profession agrees with the holy Roman Church concerning the Lord’s body and blood. Berengar.

(De consecratione, distinction 2, chapter *Ego Berengarius*.) “I, Berengar, [Col. 0161A] unworthy deacon of the Church of Saint Maurice of Angers, acknowledging the true, catholic, and apostolic faith, anathematize every heresy, especially that concerning which I have hitherto been defamed, which attempts to maintain that the bread and wine placed upon the altar are after consecration only a sacrament, and not the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; nor can they be handled by the hands of priests, broken, or ground by the teeth of the faithful except sensibly, in the sacrament alone.

“But I agree with the holy Roman and apostolic see, and profess with mouth and heart that I hold concerning the sacraments of the Lord’s table the faith which the Lord, the venerable Pope Nicholas, and this holy synod, by evangelical and apostolic authority, have handed down to be held and confirmed for me: [Col. 0161B] namely, that the bread and wine placed upon the altar are after consecration not only a sacrament but also the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and are sensibly handled by the hands of priests, broken, and ground by the teeth of the faithful, not only sacramentally but in truth. I swear this by the holy and consubstantial (*homousion*) Trinity and by these most sacred Gospels of Christ.

“Those who oppose this faith, together with their doctrines and followers, I pronounce worthy of eternal anathema. And if I myself should ever presume to think or preach anything against this, may I be subject to the severity of the canons. Having read and reread this, I have subscribed it voluntarily.”

Pope Nicholas sent throughout the cities of Italy, Gaul, and Germany, and to whatever places the report of Berengar’s depravity had formerly been able to reach, this confession of his faith concerning the Lord’s body and blood, made at Rome before one hundred and twenty bishops; so that Churches which had earlier grieved at one who was hostile and perverse might afterward rejoice at one who had returned and been converted [Col. 0161C].

Likewise, in the homily on Psalm 45, speaking to the Jews (Augustine, *Exposition of Psalm 45*): “Behold, you are baptized in the name of him whom you killed, and your sins are forgiven you. A little later you came to know him; now drink without fear the blood which you shed.”

That holy bread by which the Lord’s body is consecrated is seen and visibly received by the mouth; but the power of God’s Word, or divinity, by which the soul of the recipient is sanctified, cannot be seen. The element of bread is seen, yet it is most truly Christ’s body. Hence the Apostle Paul: “The bread which [Col. 0161D] we break, is it not the body of the Lord? And the cup which we bless, is it not the blood of the Lord?” (1 Cor. 10). We likewise receive visible food; but the sacrament is one thing, and the power of the sacrament another (Augustine, Tractates 26 and 27 on John, chapter 16).

How many receive from the altar and die, and die by receiving unworthily. Truth itself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6). The sign that one eats and drinks is this: if he abides and is abided in; if he dwells and is dwelt in; if he cleaves so as not to be abandoned. If Christ’s words are understood spiritually, they are spirit and life; but if understood carnally, they are indeed in themselves spirit and life, but they are not so for those who understand carnally and do not reverence them in faith [Col. 0162A]. For just as the spirit of a human being—that is, the soul—does not give life except to those members which are held together in the unity of the body, and does not give life to severed members, so also it does not give life except to those who stand in Christ’s body, that is, in the unity of the Church.

For it must be known, and greatly feared, that whatever minister is proud is numbered with the devil, but Christ’s gift is not contaminated. (Book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 11, § 2, h; Augustine, Sermon 28, to the brethren in the desert.) What flows through him flows pure; what passes through him passes clear and reaches fertile ground. Such is the spiritual power of the sacrament: it is received pure by those to be enlightened, and, though it passes through the unclean, is nevertheless not defiled.

## CHAPTER 11.—That every crime is expiated by sacrifices offered to God. From the decree of Pope Julius, sent to bishops throughout Egypt.

[Col. 0162B]

(De cons., dist. 4, c. *Cum omne crimen*. Third Council of Braga, ch. 1.) Since every crime and sin is wiped away by sacrifices offered to God, what thereafter shall be given to the Lord for the expiation of offences when error is committed in the very offering of the sacrifice? For we have heard that certain persons, held fast by schismatic ambition, contrary to the divine ordinances and apostolic institutions, consecrate milk instead of wine in the divine sacrifices; that others present to the people the Eucharist dipped [in the chalice] as the completion of communion; that some offer pressed wine in the sacrament of the Lord’s chalice; and that others preserve throughout the whole year a linen cloth dipped in must, and, at the time of sacrifice, wash a portion of it in water [Col. 0162C] and so offer it.

How contrary this is to evangelical and apostolic teaching, and how opposed to ecclesiastical custom, can readily be proved from the very source of truth, from which the ordered mysteries of the sacraments themselves proceeded. For when the Teacher of truth commended to his disciples the true sacrifice of our salvation, we know that he gave them not milk, but only bread and the cup under this sacrament. For it is read in the truth of the Gospel: “Jesus took bread and the cup, and, having blessed them, gave them to his disciples” (Matt. XXVI; I Cor. XI). Therefore let the offering of milk in sacrifice cease, since the plain and manifest example of evangelical truth has shone forth: that nothing other than bread and wine may be offered.

Nor have those who, for the completion of communion, [Col. 0162D] give the people the Eucharist dipped [in the chalice] received this testimony from the Gospel, where he entrusted his body and blood to the apostles. For the commending of the bread is recorded separately, and that of the cup separately. We do not read that Christ gave dipped bread to others (John XIII), except only to that disciple whom the dipped morsel from the Master identified as the betrayer—not as something signifying the institution of this sacrament.

Moreover, the practice by which the people communicate from a pressed cluster—that is, from grains of grapes—is altogether very confused. But if necessary, the cluster should be pressed in the cup and water mixed with it, because the Lord’s cup, according to the precepts of the canons, must be offered mixed with wine and water: for we see that the people are understood in the water, while the blood of Christ is shown in the wine. Therefore, when water is mixed with wine in the cup, the people are united with Christ, and the multitude of believers is joined and united to him in whom it has believed. This joining and union of water and wine is so mixed in the Lord’s cup that that mixture cannot be separated.

For if anyone offers wine alone, the blood of Christ begins to be without us; but if there is water alone, the people begin to be without Christ. Therefore a cluster alone is offered, in which only the efficacy of wine is displayed, while the sacrament of our salvation, signified by water, is neglected. For the Lord’s cup cannot be water alone or wine alone, unless both are mixed together. And therefore, since from this matter a very great and manifold judgment of the Fathers has already issued, henceforth every such error and [Col. 0163B] presumption must cease, lest the disordered combination of perverse persons weaken the established truth. Therefore henceforth no one shall be permitted to offer anything in the divine sacrifices other than, according to the judgment of the ancient councils, bread alone and a cup mixed with wine and water. Whoever thereafter does otherwise than commanded shall abstain from offering sacrifice until, corrected through the lawful satisfaction of penance, he returns to the office of his rank, which he has lost.

### CHAPTER 12.—That neither pure water nor pure wine ought to be offered in the Eucharist. From the Council of Worms, ch. 2.

(Council of Worms, ch. 4.) In the Eucharist pure water ought not to be offered, as some mistakenly do on the pretext of sobriety, but wine mixed with water; because wine was present in the mystery of our redemption when he says, “I shall not drink of the fruit of the vine” (Matt. XXVI), and because he gave it mixed with water after supper. But water issuing with blood from his side showed wine pressed from the true life of his flesh together with water.

Therefore, when Truth commended to his disciples the true sacrifice of our salvation, we know that he provided only bread and the cup under this sacrament. Accordingly, apart from bread and wine mixed with water, nothing else ought to be offered. [Note: The same is found above, ch. 11, Col. 0163D.] For the Lord’s cup must be offered mixed with wine and water, because we see that the people are understood in the water, while the blood of Christ is shown in the wine. Therefore, when wine and water are mixed in the cup, Christ and the people are united; and the multitude of believers is joined and [Col. 0163D] united to him in whom it has believed. This joining and union of water and wine is so mixed in the Lord’s cup that that mixture cannot be separated; for if anyone offers wine alone, the blood of Christ begins to be without us, but if water alone is present, the people begin to be without Christ. The Lord’s cup cannot be water alone or wine alone unless both are mixed together.

### CHAPTER 13.—On the same matter. From the Third Council of Carthage, ch. 23.

(De cons., dist. 2, c. *Ut in sacramentis*.) In the sacraments of the body and blood of the Lord, nothing more shall be offered than what the Lord himself says—that is, bread and wine mixed with water; nor in firstfruits shall anything further be offered to God than wine and grain.

### CHAPTER 14.—Likewise on the same matter. From the Third African Council, ch. 4.

(De consecr., dist. 2, c. *Ut in sacramentis*.) In the sacraments of the body and blood of the Lord, nothing more shall be offered than what the Lord himself handed down—that is, bread and wine mixed with water. Firstfruits, however—such as honey and milk, which are customarily offered on the single most solemn day of the mystery of infants—although they are offered at the altar, shall nevertheless have their own proper blessing, so that they may be distinguished from the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. Nor shall anything further be offered in firstfruits than what comes from grapes and grain.

### CHAPTER 15.—That the Passion of the Lord is to be joined in the consecration of the body. From the decrees of Pope Alexander, ch. 5.

[Col. 0164B]

(De cons., dist. 2, c. *In sacramentorum*.) In the offerings of the sacraments also, which are offered to the Lord amid the solemnities of Mass, the Passion of the Lord is to be joined, so that where his body and blood are made, his Passion may be celebrated (Luke XXII). Thus, after rejecting the opinions of superstitions, only bread and wine mixed with water are to be offered in sacrifice. As we have received from the Fathers, and reason itself teaches, neither wine alone nor water alone ought to be offered in the Lord’s cup, but both mixed together, because both are read to have flowed from his side in his Passion.

Truth itself instructs us to offer the cup and bread in the sacrament, [Col. 0164C] when it says: “Jesus took bread and blessed it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take and eat; this is my body, which shall be given for you. Likewise, after he had supped, he took the cup and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take and drink from it, all of you, for this is the cup of my blood, which shall be poured out for you for the forgiveness of sins” (Matt. XXVI; I Cor. VI).

For crimes and sins are wiped away by these sacrifices offered to the Lord; therefore his Passion, by which we have been redeemed, is to be commemorated in them, recited often, and these things offered to the Lord. The Lord will delight in and be appeased by such offerings, and by mighty mercy [*ingentia*] will forgive sins.

(De cons., dist. 2, c. *Nihil in sacrificiis*.) Nothing in sacrifices can be greater than the body and [Col. 0164D] blood of Christ, nor is any offering more powerful than this; rather, it surpasses all others. It is to be offered to the Lord with a pure conscience and completed with a pure mind. And just as it is greater than the rest, so it ought to be cultivated and venerated more especially.

### CHAPTER 16.—What kinds of things may be offered at the altar, not for sacrifice but for a simple blessing. From the Canon of the Apostles, ch. 4.

It is not permitted to offer anything at the altar, apart from new ears of grain, grapes, oil for lamps, beans, and incense for burning, at the time when the sacred offering is celebrated.

### CHAPTER 17.—On the same matter. From the decree of Pope Miltiades, ch. 1.

[Col. 0165A]

These kinds of things, which it is not permitted to offer upon the altar, according to the constitution of the apostles and their successors, shall be brought to the house of the priests; and, having been blessed by the priests with a simple blessing, they shall then be taken by the people. Only beans and grapes, new ears of grain, oil, fragrant substances for incense, and the other things established by the apostles are to be offered upon the altar.

### CHAPTER 18.—Nothing is to be offered in sacrifice besides what the Lord established. From the Canon of the Apostles, ch. 3.

If any bishop or presbyter, contrary to the Lord’s ordinance, offers certain other things upon the altar in sacrifice—that is, honey or milk, or *sicera* instead of wine, or prepared foods, or birds, or any animals, or vegetables—acting against the constitution, let him be deposed.

### CHAPTER 19.—That presbyters should have a clean vessel in which the Lord’s body is carefully kept. From the Council of Tours, ch. 4.

Every presbyter shall have a pyx or vessel worthy of so great a sacrament, in which the Lord’s body is carefully stored as viaticum for those departing from this world. This sacred offering alone must be dipped in the blood of Christ, so that the presbyter may truthfully say to the sick person: “May the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ profit you for the forgiveness of sins and eternal life.” It shall always be kept locked upon the altar, because of mice and wicked persons; [Col. 0165C] and it shall always be changed from the seventh day to the seventh—that is, the presbyter shall consume it, and another offering consecrated on that same day shall be substituted in its place, lest, if kept too long, it should, God forbid, become mouldy.

### CHAPTER 20.—That a presbyter should always keep the Eucharist ready for the sick. From the Council of Worms, ch. 5.

(De cons., dist. 2, c. *Presbyter*.) A presbyter shall always have the Eucharist ready, so that whenever anyone becomes ill, or a little child becomes ill, he may communicate that person at once, lest the person die without communion.

### CHAPTER 21.—As many offerings are to be made at the altar as can suffice for the people; and what remains is to be consumed with fear and trembling and the greatest care by the clergy. From the letter of Pope Clement (Letter II to James, the Lord’s brother).

[Col. 0165D] (De cons., dist. 2, c. *Tribus gradibus*.) As many sacrificial offerings shall be made at the altar as ought to suffice for the people. What remains shall not be reserved for the next day, but shall be consumed with fear and trembling through the care of the clergy. Those, however, who consume the remains of the Lord’s body left in the sacristy shall not immediately proceed to take ordinary food, lest they seem to mingle food with the holy portion—that food which, digested through the bowels, is expelled into the privy. Therefore, if the Lord’s portion is eaten in the morning, the ministers who consumed it shall fast until the sixth hour; and if they have received it at the third or fourth hour, they shall fast until evening. Thus the sacraments are to be kept by a hidden and everlasting sanctification.

### CHAPTER 22.—On the same matter. From the Council of Orléans, ch. 4.

[Col. 0166A]

It also seems proper to add that the offerings made upon the altar should always be renewed from Sabbath to Sabbath; for the loaves of presentation, which were placed upon the Lord’s table, were always changed from Sabbath to Sabbath, lest they become mouldy when kept too long and, as some think, be consumed by fire. If anyone, instigated by the devil, presumes to do this, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER 23.—That, in the presence and by the command of a presbyter, a deacon may communicate the people. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, ch. 38.

(Dist. 93, c. *Diaconi*.) If necessity compels, a deacon, when a presbyter is present and commands it, may distribute the Eucharist of Christ’s body to the people.

### CHAPTER 24.—That great discernment is necessary in receiving the body and blood of the Lord. From the letter of Pope Clement (Letter II to James, the Lord’s brother).

[Col. 0166B]

Great discernment must be exercised in receiving the Lord’s body and blood. Care must be taken lest, if it is delayed too long, this lead to the destruction of the soul, as the Lord says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John VI). But if it is received indiscriminately, one must fear what the Apostle says: “Whoever eats and drinks the body and blood of the Lord unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (I Cor. XI). In accordance with the words of the same Apostle: “Let a person examine himself, and thus let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup” (ibid.); that is, by abstaining for some [Col. 0166C] days from the works of the flesh and cleansing body and soul, a person may prepare to receive so great a sacrament. David provides the example: unless he had confessed that he had abstained from marital intercourse since yesterday and the day before, he would by no means have received the loaves of presentation from the priest (I Sam. XXI).

### CHAPTER 25.—On daily reception of the Lord’s body and blood. From the sayings of Augustine (*On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, ch. 53).

(De cons., dist. 2, c. *Quotidie*.) I neither commend nor censure receiving Eucharistic communion daily; nevertheless, I urge communion on every Lord’s Day. (Book IV of the *Sentences*, dist. 12, § h.) Yet if the mind is disposed toward sinning, I say that it is burdened more by reception of the Eucharist than cleansed by it. Therefore, although someone is stung by sin, let him nevertheless have no will to sin thereafter; when about to communicate, let him make satisfaction through tears and prayers, and, trusting in the Lord’s mercy, approach the Eucharist boldly and securely. But I say this of one whom mortal sins do not burden.

### CHAPTER 26.—On the same matter. From the sayings of the same author (Augustine, Letter 118, same distinction 2), to Januarius.

Someone may say that the Eucharist should not be received daily; another may affirm that it should be received daily. Let each person do what he believes, according to his faith, ought to be done. For Zacchaeus and that centurion neither quarrelled with each other nor did either set himself above the other, although one of them joyfully received the Lord into his house (Luke XIX), while the other said, “Lord, I am not [Col. 0167A] worthy that you should enter under my roof” (Matt. VIII). Both honoured the Saviour, though not in one manner; both were wretched through sins; both obtained mercy. This comparison is also relevant: among the first people, manna tasted in each person’s mouth according to that person’s own desire. Thus, in the mouth of each Christian, that sacrament is to be judged according to how it is received.

### CHAPTER 27.—Concerning lay persons: that, if not more often, they should at least communicate three times a year. From the letter of Pope Fabian, ch. 3.

(De cons., dist. 2, c. *Etsi non frequentius*.) Even if not more often, people shall at least communicate three times in the year—unless perhaps someone is prevented by certain graver crimes—namely, at Easter, Pentecost, [Col. 0167B] and the Nativity of the Lord.

### CHAPTER 28.—On the Eucharist: that those who always sin should always receive it. From the sayings of Cyprian and other holy Fathers.

(In the sermon *On the Lord’s Supper*; bk. IV *On the Sacraments*, ch. 6.) Saint Cyprian said: “The Eucharist is received daily as food for salvation.” Saint Ambrose said: “If, whenever Christ’s blood is poured out, it is poured out for the forgiveness of sins, I who always sin ought always to receive it; I ought always to receive the medicine.” Saint Hilary said: “If one’s sins are not so great that one must be excommunicated, one ought not to be separated from the medicine of the Lord’s body.” Hence one must fear lest, being withdrawn from Christ’s body for a long time, one remain alienated from salvation. For it is manifest that those who touch Christ’s body live, [Col. 0167C] the Lord himself saying: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves.” Whoever has now ceased from sinning should not cease from communicating.

### CHAPTER 29.—That the faithful should communicate on every Lord’s Day in Lent. From the decrees of Pope Silverius, ch. 3.

On every Lord’s Day in Lent, except for those who are excommunicated and those who are undergoing public penance, the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood are to be received; and communion absolutely must be received by all on the Lord’s Supper, the vigil of Easter, the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord.

### CHAPTER 30.—That reception of the Eucharist should not be neglected on the Lord’s Supper. From the decrees of Pope Soter, ch. 5.

[Col. 0167D]

(De const., dist. 2, c. *In Coena*.) On the Lord’s Supper some neglect reception of the Eucharist. Since it ought on that same day to be received by all the faithful, except those to whom it has been forbidden because of grave crimes, ecclesiastical usage demonstrates this; for even penitents are reconciled on that day for receiving the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood.

### CHAPTER 31.—Concerning actors: whether they should receive communion with the other faithful. From the letter of Saint Cyprian to Eucratius (Letter 10, bk. I).

(De const., dist. 2, c. *Cyprianus*.) Cyprian to Eucratius, his fellow brother, greetings. In your affection, dearest brother, you have thought it right to consult me, through our mutual regard, what I think about that actor who resides among you and persists in the disgrace of that same occupation, as a master and teacher not of boys to be educated but of boys to be ruined, communicating to others what he has wickedly learned: whether such a man ought to communicate with us. I think that it accords neither with the divine majesty nor with Gospel discipline that the modesty and honour of the Church should be defiled by so shameful and infamous a contagion.

### CHAPTER 32.—How long each person ought to abstain from his wife before holy communion. From the Council of Elvira.

(De cons., dist. 2, c. *Omnis homo*.) Every man ought to abstain from his own wife for three, four, or seven days before holy communion.

### CHAPTER 33.—That a person who has not communicated at Easter, Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord is not to be counted among Catholics. From the Council of Agde, ch. 18.

[Col. 0168B]

(De cons., dist. 2, c. *Saeculares*.) Lay persons who have not communicated at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost are not to be believed Catholic, nor are they to be regarded as among Catholics.

### CHAPTER 34.—That an offering at the altar should be made on every Lord’s Day. From the decrees of Pope Fabian, ch. 5.

We have decreed that on every Lord’s Day an offering at the altar, both of bread and of wine, shall be made by all men and women, so that through these offerings they may be freed from the burdens of their sins.

### CHAPTER 35.—On the same matter. From the decrees of the same pope, ch. 10.

The Christian people should also continually be admonished to make an offering and bread in church, [Col. 0168C] because in that offering there is for themselves and their families a great remedy for souls, and in true peace itself unity of mind and concord are shown.

### CHAPTER 36.—Concerning deacons: that they ought not give communion to presbyters. From the Council of Nicaea, ch. 18.

(Dist. 93, c. *Pervenit ad sanctum*.) It has come to the holy and great council’s attention that in some places and cities deacons offer the grace of holy communion to presbyters. No rule has handed down that those who lack the power to offer should give the body of Christ to those who do offer it. Moreover, it has become known that certain deacons touch the sacred offering before bishops. Therefore let all these practices [Col. 0168D] be cut off, and let deacons remain within their proper measure, knowing that they are ministers of bishops and are regarded as inferior to presbyters. Therefore, in order, let them receive the grace of holy communion after the presbyters, with the bishop or presbyter giving it to them. Nor may a deacon sit among presbyters, since, if this occurs, it is shown to be contrary to rule and order. But if anyone refuses obedience even after these determinations, he must cease from the ministry.

### CHAPTER 37.—Concerning *eulogiae* to be given by the people to presbyters. From the decrees of Pope Pius, ch. 4.

Let the presbyter suitably keep portions, cut up in a clean vessel, from the offerings made by the people and remaining after consecration; or from the loaves which the faithful offer to the church; or indeed from his own supplies. After the solemnities of Mass, those who were not prepared to communicate may receive *eulogiae* from these on every Lord’s Day and feast day. Before giving the *eulogiae*, the presbyter shall bless that from which he is to give them with these words.

A simple prayer of blessing for the *eulogia*:

“Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, deign to bless this bread with your holy and spiritual blessing, that it may be for all a salvation of mind and body, and a protection against every disease and all the snares of enemies. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, the bread of life, who came down from heaven and gives life and salvation to the world, and lives and reigns with you through all ages of ages. Amen.”

### CHAPTER 38.—Concerning the bread which is to be offered. From the decrees of Pope Anicetus, ch. 3.

[Col. 0169B]

The loaves which you offer to God as sacrifice must be made by yourselves or by your children in your presence, cleanly and carefully, and must be diligently guarded. Thus bread, wine, and water—without which Masses cannot be celebrated—shall be handled most cleanly and carefully, and nothing cheap or unapproved shall be found in them, according to what Scripture says: “Let the fear of the Lord be with you, and do everything with diligence” (II Chron. XIX).

### CHAPTER 39.—Concerning presbyters who hand the Lord’s body to women to carry to the sick. From the Council of Rheims, ch. 2.

(De cons., dist. 2, c. *Pervenit*.) It has come to [Col. 0169C] our attention that certain presbyters so greatly disparage the divine mysteries that they hand the sacred body of the Lord to a layman or woman to carry to the sick; and those who are forbidden to enter the sacristy or approach the altar are entrusted with the Holy of Holies. All religious persons perceive how dreadful and detestable this is. Therefore the synod wholly forbids such rash presumption to occur any further; rather, in every case the presbyter himself shall communicate the sick person. If he does otherwise, he shall be liable to danger of losing his rank.

### CHAPTER 40.—That the Eucharist should not be given to the dead. From the Third Council of Carthage, ch. 6.

Likewise, it has been decided that the Eucharist shall not be given to the bodies of the dead. For it is written: “Take and eat” (Matt. XXVI). But corpses can neither receive nor eat. Nor should the negligence of presbyters cause persons already dead to be baptized.

### CHAPTER 41.—That offerings should be made impartially at the greater feasts. From the Second Council of Mâcon, ch. 4.

It was decreed in the Synod of Mâcon that on all Lord’s Days and other feast days every person of either sex who has come to Mass shall make an offering in church; each person making one offering, and, when Mass is finished, the offerings shall be received by the presbyter. Whoever presumptuously seeks through disobedience to nullify this determination shall be struck with anathema.

### CHAPTER 42.—That only ministers of the altar may communicate at the altar. From the Council of Laodicea, ch. 19.

[Col. 0170A]

Only ministers devoted to sacred order may approach the altar and communicate there.

### CHAPTER 43.—That no one ordained below the rank of presbyter may distribute at the altar a thing consecrated by a presbyter. From the decrees of Pope Sylvester, ch. 7.

No acolyte or subdeacon shall distribute to others an item already consecrated by the presbyter, for a minister is one thing and an attendant another; except that he may carry only what the priest has placed upon him, blessed by the priest’s own word.

### CHAPTER 44.—That an illiterate presbyter should not celebrate Mass. From the decrees of Pope Fabian, ch. 10.

A sacrifice is not to be received from the hand of a priest who cannot fulfil, according to the rite, the prayers, readings, and remaining observances of Mass.

### CHAPTER 45.—Concerning those who receive the sacrifice after having tasted something. From the decrees of Pope Eutychian, ch. 2.

[Col. 0170B]

Those who receive the sacrifice after food, or after even the smallest refreshment, unless it is as viaticum, shall do penance: children for three days, adults for a week, and clerics for twenty days.

### CHAPTER 46.—That one person’s offering is not to be despised on behalf of another’s. From the decrees of Pope Eugenius, ch. 17.

A presbyter shall not despise one person’s offering on behalf of another’s.

### CHAPTER 47.—That the offerings of brethren at variance are not to be received. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, ch. 93.

(Dist. 90, c. *Oblationes*.) The offerings of brethren at variance shall be received neither in the sacristy nor in the *azophylacium* (repository).

### CHAPTER 48.—That the gifts of those who oppress the poor are to be refused. From the same council, ch. 93.

(Dist. 90, c. *Eorum qui*.) The gifts of those who oppress the poor are to be refused by priests.

### CHAPTER 49.—Concerning presbyters who have sacrificed [to idols]. From the Council of Ancyra, ch. 1.

(Dist. 50, c. *Presbyteros qui*.) Presbyters who have sacrificed and then again entered the contest, if they have done this not through any pretence but in truth, and have not previously contrived and induced others to suppose that they were being subjected to torments while in fact subjected to them only in appearance and dress—such persons, it has been decided, may retain the honour of their own seat; but they may not offer, address the people, or perform any priestly functions whatever. [Col. 0170D]

### CHAPTER 50.—Concerning deacons who have sacrificed [to idols]. From the same council, ch. 2.

(Dist. 50, c. *Presbyteros qui*.) Likewise, deacons who have sacrificed may retain their honour, but shall cease from every sacred ministry, whether offering the bread or the cup. But if certain bishops, aware of their labour, humility, and gentleness, wish to grant or remove anything further, authority shall rest with them.

### CHAPTER 51.—Augustine, bishop of the English, asks concerning presbyters from whom semen is sometimes emitted while they sleep.

(Dist. 6, c. *Testamentum*; bk. XII of the Letters, ch. 11.) After an emission which customarily occurs in sleep, may any person receive the Lord’s body, or, if he is a priest, celebrate the sacred mysteries?

### CHAPTER 52.—The response of Pope Gregory on the same matter.

The testament of the old law, as we have already said in the preceding chapter, declares such a person unclean and does not permit him to enter the church until evening unless he has washed with water. Yet the spiritual people, understanding this otherwise, will take it in the sense that we have stated: namely, that one is, as it were, deceived in sleep when, tempted toward impurity, one is defiled in thought by vain images. But one must be washed with water, that one may wash away the faults of thought with tears; and unless the temptations have first departed, one must acknowledge oneself guilty, as it were, until evening.

But in this emission there is a highly necessary discernment, by which one must carefully consider from what cause it occurs in the mind of the sleeper. For it sometimes arises from excess of food, sometimes from a natural superfluity or illness, and sometimes from thought. Indeed, when it happens from a natural superfluity or illness, this emission is not at all to be feared, because the mind, unaware of it, ought rather to be grieved at having suffered it than at having done it.

But when the appetite of gluttony is carried beyond measure in taking food, and the receptacles of the humours are thereby burdened, the mind incurs some guilt from this, though not so far as to be prohibited from receiving Christ’s body or celebrating the solemnities of Mass. And when perhaps a feast day requires the mystery to be celebrated, because there is no other priest in that place, then, if necessity compels, he himself may sing after changing his garments. But if others are present who can [Col. 0171C] perform the ministry, the emission caused by excess of food ought not to prohibit him from receiving the sacred mystery; but, in my judgment, he ought humbly to abstain from offering the sacred mystery—provided that the indecency has not disturbed the sleeper’s mind.

For in some persons the emission commonly arises in such a way that their mind, even while the body is asleep, is not defiled by shameful images [or “imaginations”]. In this matter the mind is shown to be guilty, though free in neither your judgment nor its own, when, although it remembers seeing nothing while the body slept, it nevertheless remembers, while awake, having fallen into gluttony. But if the sleeper’s emission arises from a shameful thought entertained while awake, the mind’s own guilt is clear. For the person who knowingly thought what he unknowingly suffered sees from what root that defilement proceeded. Because of such pollution, one ought to abstain from the sacred mystery on that day.

(Eadem distinction, c. *Sed pensandum est*.) But it must be considered whether the thought itself occurred at the stage of suggestion, delight, or—what is greater—sinful consent. For every sin is completed in three ways: namely, suggestion, delight, and consent. Suggestion is made by the devil; delight by the flesh; consent by the spirit. For when the serpent suggested the first sin, Eve, as it were the flesh, was delighted, and Adam, as it were the spirit, consented. Great discernment is necessary, therefore, so that the mind, judge of itself, may preside between suggestion, delight, and consent.

For when an evil spirit suggests sin in the mind, if no delight in the sin follows, the sin has not at all been committed. But when the flesh begins to take delight, sin then begins to be born. If, however, it also descends by deliberation to consent, then the sin is known to be completed. Thus, in suggestion is the beginning [or “seed”] of sin; in delight, its nourishment; in consent, its completion. And it often happens that what the evil spirit sows in thought the flesh draws into delight, while the mind nevertheless does not consent to that delight. Although the flesh cannot take delight without the mind, the mind itself, resisting the pleasures of the flesh, is in some way unwillingly bound in carnal delight, so that it opposes and does not consent by reason; yet it is bound by delight, though it groans intensely that it is bound.

Hence that foremost soldier of the heavenly host groaned, saying: [Col. 0172B] “I see another law in my members resisting the law of my mind and leading me captive under the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. VII). But if he was captive, he was not fighting; therefore he was both captive and not captive, and he was fighting [or “resisting”]. Thus the law in his members resisted the law of his mind. But if he was fighting, he was not captive. Therefore a person is, so to speak, both captive and free: free by the righteousness which he loves; captive by the delight which he bears unwillingly.

### CHAPTER 53.—Concerning rural presbyters: that they must not dare to offer in a city. From the Council of Neocaesarea, ch. 13.

Rural presbyters cannot offer in a city church in the presence of the bishop or presbyters of that city, nor may they give the consecrated bread or present the cup. But if these are absent and the rural presbyters are called upon to give the prayer, they alone ought to give it.

### CHAPTER 54.—On the same matter. From the decrees of Pope Soter, ch. 54.

Presbyters who are not fellow-countrymen may not offer in churches when bishops or city presbyters are present, nor give the bread in prayer or drink the cup. But if the city’s priests are absent and they are invited to the prayer, they alone may give it.

### CHAPTER 55.—Concerning one who vomits the Eucharist through drunkenness. From the Penitential of the presbyter Bede.

(De const., dist. 2, c. *Si per ebriet.*) If anyone vomits the Eucharist through drunkenness or gluttony, let a layperson do penance for forty days; clerics or monks, and likewise deacons and presbyters, for seventy days; bishops for ninety. If they vomit because of illness, let them do penance for seven days.

### CHAPTER 56.—Concerning the case in which something from the chalice of the sacred blood drips. From the decrees of Pope Pius, ch. 3.

(De cons., dist. 2, c. *Si per negligentiam*.) If through negligence something from the Lord’s cup drips upon the ground, it shall be licked up with the tongue and the board scraped. If there is no board, lest the place be trodden upon, it shall be scraped away and consumed by fire; and the ashes shall be placed within the altar, while the priest shall do penance for forty days. If the cup drips upon the altar, the minister shall drink the drop and do penance for three days. If it reaches the altar-cloth and the drop passes to a second layer, he shall do penance for four days; if to a third, for nine days; if [Col. 0173A] to a fourth, for twenty days. The linens touched by the drop shall be washed three times by the minister, with the chalice placed beneath; the water of washing shall be consumed and placed beside the altar.

### CHAPTER 57.—Concerning one who vomits the sacrifice and it is consumed by dogs. From Theodore’s Penitential.

(De cons., dist. 2, c. *Qui non bene*.) Whoever vomits the sacrifice and it is consumed by dogs shall do penance for one year; otherwise, for forty days.
