If on the day on which he has communicated he vomits the sacrifice, if it is before midnight, let him undertake three *superpositiones*; if after midnight, two; if after Matins, one.

### CHAPTER 58.—On the same matter. From the Roman Penitential.

If someone vomits the sacrifice, let him do penance for forty days. If he throws it into the fire, let him sing one hundred psalms. But if dogs lick such vomit, the person who vomited shall do penance for one hundred days.

### CHAPTER 59.—Concerning the Eucharist grown stale. From the Third Council of Arles, ch. 5.

Every sacrifice spoiled by foul age is to be burned in fire, and its ashes buried beside the altar.

### CHAPTER 60.—Concerning those who do not properly keep the body and blood of the Lord. From the same council, ch. 6.

Whoever has not properly safeguarded the sacrifice, and a mouse or some other animal has eaten it, shall do penance for forty days. But whoever has lost it in church, or if a part of it has fallen and has not been found, shall do penance for thirty days. [Col. 0173C] Whoever spills anything from the chalice upon the altar while it is being offered shall do penance for six days; or, if the spillage is more copious, for seven days. But whoever spills it while the solemnity of Mass is being celebrated shall do penance for forty days. If, after Mass has been celebrated, the priest neglects to consume the sacrifice, he likewise shall do penance for forty days. And one who receives the sacrifice while defiled by a nocturnal emission shall do penance for seven days. If a deacon, through forgetfulness, fails to offer the oblation until the cloth is brought forward, when the names of those at rest are recited, he shall likewise do penance. Whoever has been negligent regarding the sacrifice, so that a worm has consumed it and it has come to nothing, shall do penance for three Lents on bread and water. If it is found intact, the worm shall be burned in it, and the ashes [Col. 0173D] shall be placed beneath the altar; and the negligent person shall atone for his negligence with four days. If the sacrifice becomes discoloured through loss of flavour, twenty days shall be completed in fasting; but whoever has immersed one which has become stuck together shall do penance for seven days.

### CHAPTER 61.—On the same matter. From the Roman Penitential.

If the sacrifice falls from the hands of the offerer to the ground, so that it is not trampled underfoot, whatever is found in the place where it fell shall be burned, and the ashes, as above, concealed; and the person to whom this happens shall do penance for half a year. But if the sacrifice is found, the place shall be swept with brooms, and the straw, as above, shall be given to the fire, and the ashes, as above, placed away; and the priest shall do penance for twenty days.

### CHAPTER 62.—On a woman who has given birth, that she may communicate if she wishes. From the Council of Carthage.

[Col. 0174A]

A woman who has given birth may receive communion if she wishes.

### CHAPTER 63.—Those who have incorporated the Passion of the Lord into the priests’ prayer. From decrees of the popes.

Alexander incorporated the Passion of the Lord into the priests’ prayer when Masses are celebrated. Siricius decreed that no priest should celebrate Mass throughout the whole week unless he received the consecrated portion, expressly designated by the bishop of the place, which is called the *fermentum*. Leo the First decreed that, during the action of the sacrifice, the words should be said: “Holy sacrifice,” etc.

### CHAPTER 64.—On the guardians of the sacraments. Clement, in the second epistle to James.

[Col. 0174B]  
(*De consecratione*, distinction 2, chapter “Tribus.”) The sacraments of the divine mysteries have been entrusted to three ranks: namely, priest, deacon, and minister. With fear and trembling they must safeguard the remnants of the Lord’s body, that is, the fragments, for the clergy.

### CHAPTER 65.—The sacred linen cloth is not to be sold. Likewise in the same epistle.

(17, question 4, chapter “Si forte.”) If any priest or deacon should steal and sell the linen cloth or veil of the sanctuary, he shall be judged like Judas Iscariot.

### CHAPTER 66.—What ought to be done with worn-out altar vestments. In the same place.

(*De consecratione*, distinction 1, chapter “Altaris palla.”) If the altar-covering, chair, candlestick, or veil has been worn out by age, it shall be consigned to the fire.

### CHAPTER 67.—Those who offer sacrifice perfectly to God ought to have witnesses with them while sacrificing; a bishop, however, more than others. Pope Anacletus, third from Peter, in his first decretal.

[Col. 0174C]

Those who offer sacrifice perfectly to God, when they sacrifice to the Lord, ought not to do this alone, but should bring witnesses with them, so that they may be shown to sacrifice perfectly to the Lord in places consecrated to God. For the authority of the divine law says: “See that you do not offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see, but in the place which the Lord your God shall choose” (Deut. XII).  
(*De consecratione*, distinction 2, chapter “Episcopus Deo sacrificans.”) A bishop sacrificing to God shall have witnesses with him, as has been stated above, and more of them than another priest. For, as he enjoys a rank of greater honour, so he requires a greater increase of testimony [or: attestation]. [Col. 0174D] On more solemn days, moreover, he shall have with him either four, five, or three deacons, who are called his eyes, together with subdeacons and the remaining ministers. Clothed in sacred vestments, they shall stand before and behind him; and the priests opposite, at his right and left, shall stand with contrite heart, humbled spirit, and bowed countenance, guarding him from evil men and giving their assent to his sacrifice. When the consecration has been performed, all who do not wish to be deprived of the thresholds of the church shall communicate.

### CHAPTER 68.—Water ought to be mixed with wine in the chalice. From the first decretal epistle of Alexander the First.

As we have received from the Fathers, and reason itself teaches, neither wine alone nor water alone ought to be offered in the Lord’s chalice, but both mixed together, because both are read to have flowed from his side [Col. 0175A] in his Passion. Likewise.  
(*De consecratione*, distinction 2, chapter “Nihil in sacrificiis.”) Nothing in sacrifices can be greater than the body and blood of Christ. No offering is superior to this; rather, it surpasses all others. It must be offered to the Lord with a pure conscience and received with a pure mind, and must be venerated by all; and, as it is superior to other things, so it ought especially to be honoured and venerated.  
(*De consecratione*, distinction 3, chapter “Aquam sale.”) We bless water sprinkled with salt for the peoples, so that all who are sprinkled with it may be sanctified and purified; and we command that all priests do this. For if the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled upon the people, sanctified [Col. 0175B] and cleansed them (Heb. IX), how much more does water sprinkled with salt and consecrated by divine prayers sanctify and cleanse the people? And if, through the prophet Elisha, the barrenness of water was healed by sprinkled salt (II Kings IV), how much more does water consecrated by divine prayers remove the barrenness of human affairs, sanctify and cleanse those who are defiled, multiply other good things, avert the snares of the devil, and defend people from the wiles of apparitions?

### CHAPTER 69.—Priests erase and consume the sins of the people by their prayers. From the second decretal of the same author.

(1, question 1, chapter “Ipsi sacerdotes.”) The priests themselves intercede for the people and “eat the sins of the people” (Hos. IV), because by their prayers they erase and consume them. The more worthy they are, the more readily they are heard in the necessities for which they cry out.

### CHAPTER 70.—Sacred vessels are not to be handled by anyone other than persons consecrated to the Lord. Sixtus, sixth pope from Peter, in the first of his decrees: “To all brethren beloved in Christ.”

[Col. 0175C]

(*De consecratione*, distinction 1, chapter “In sancta hac apost.”) It has been decreed by us and the other bishops, and by the remaining priests of the Lord, that sacred vessels shall not be touched by anyone other than persons consecrated and dedicated to the Lord. For it is most unworthy that vessels of the Lord, whatever they may be, should serve human uses and be handled by men other than those who serve the Lord and are dedicated to him, lest, because of such presumption, the angered Lord inflict a plague upon his people.

### CHAPTER 71.—Mass is not to be celebrated at night at any time except at the Nativity of the Lord. Telesphorus, seventh from Peter, in his decretal epistle.

[Col. 0175D]

(*De consecratione*, distinction 1, chapter “Nocte sancta.”) On the holy night of the Nativity of the Lord and Saviour they shall celebrate Masses and solemnly sing in them the angelic hymn, because on that same night it was announced by the angel to the shepherds (Luke II). And below: “And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (ibid.). At other times, however, celebrations of Mass are by no means to take place before the third hour of the day, because at that same hour the Lord was crucified (Luke XV [an apparent citation error]), and the Holy Spirit is read to have descended upon the apostles (Acts II).

### CHAPTER 72.—Women consecrated to God, or nuns, ought not to touch sacred vessels or altar-coverings. Pope Soter, eleventh from Peter, in his second decretal epistle.

[Col. 0176A]

(23, distinction, chapter “Sacratas.” And below, part 3, chapter 265.) It has been reported to the Apostolic See that women consecrated to God, or nuns, among you touch sacred vessels or consecrated altar-coverings and carry incense around the altars. No rightly minded person can doubt that all these things are full of blame and censure. Therefore, by the authority of this holy see, we decree that you eradicate all these practices utterly as quickly as you can.

### CHAPTER 73.—Chrism is to be made each year at the Lord’s Supper. Pope Fabian, eighteenth from Peter, in his second decree.

[Col. 0176B]  
(*De consecratione*, distinction 3, chapter “Litteris vestris.”) Among other things included in your letters, we have found that some bishops of your region depart from your order and ours, and do not make chrism every year at the Lord’s Supper. Below: Those who devise and dare such things err, thinking with a deranged rather than a sound mind. Likewise: As the solemnity of that day itself must be celebrated every year, so the making of that holy chrism must be performed every year, renewed from year to year, and delivered to the faithful. For it is a new sacrament to be renewed yearly on the aforesaid day, while the old chrism is to be burned in holy churches. We have received this from the holy apostles and their successors, and we command you to observe it.

### CHAPTER 74.—The ecclesiastical vestments used in service to the Lord ought to be sacred and honourable. Pope Stephen, twenty-second from Peter, in his tenth decree (Epistle 1, chapter 3).

[Col. 0176C]

(*De consecratione*, distinction 1, chapter “Vestimenta.”) Ecclesiastical vestments in which service is rendered to the Lord ought to be both consecrated and honourable. They must not be used for any purposes other than ecclesiastical offices worthy of God. Nor ought they to be touched or carried by anyone except consecrated persons, lest the divine vengeance that struck Belshazzar (Dan. V) come upon those who transgress in these matters and presume to do such things, and cast them down to the depths.

### CHAPTER 75.—Not only bishops but also priests may anoint the sick with holy oil. Innocent the First, in his first decretal epistle, chapter 7.

[Col. 0176D]

(Distinction 95, chapter “Illud superfluum.”) We see that a superfluous addition has been made, namely, that there should be doubt concerning the bishop in a matter which it is unquestionable that priests may do. For this reason it was said of priests: bishops, hindered by other occupations, cannot visit all the sick. But if a bishop either can or judges someone worthy of being visited by him, he can without delay both bless and touch that person with chrism, for it is his office to make the chrism itself. This cannot be poured upon penitents, because it is a kind of sacrament. For how can one kind be thought capable of being granted to persons to whom the remaining sacraments are denied?

### CHAPTER 76.—Mass is never to be sung in unconsecrated places except in great necessity. Pope Felix IV to all bishops (Epistle 1).

[Col. 0177A]

(*De consecratione*, distinction 1, chapter “Sicut non alii.”) It is better not to sing or hear Mass than to do so in places where it ought not to be done, unless, as has often been said, the highest necessity should occur, when necessity has no law. Hence it is written: “See that you do not offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see, but in the place which the Lord your God shall choose” (Deut. XII).

### CHAPTER 77.—On the order of prefaces according to the Roman Church. Pope Pelagius II, Epistle 4.

Pelagius II, bishop of the Roman Church and Apostolic See, to all the bishops of Gaul and Germany. When, in God’s name, we had assembled in the Roman Church a synod of bishops and other fellow-priests, faithful servants of God, [Col. 0177B] and were carefully considering the ecclesiastical ordinances as they were handed down by the apostles and holy Fathers, your letter arrived. And, so that its request might carry greater authority, living voices also came forward, asking that we communicate to you in our letter the order of prefaces which the holy Roman Church had hitherto possessed. Then, greatly rejoicing in your wish and so good a zeal, we carefully reread the sacred Roman order and the holy ordinances of our predecessors.  
(*De consecratione*, distinction 1, chapter “Invenimus has,” but under the title of Gelasius.) We found that only these nine prefaces had been received [variant: were to be received] into the sacred catalogue, which long-standing antiquity has hitherto preserved in the Roman Church: namely, one for the white garments [Col. 0177C] of Easter, another for the Ascension of the Lord, a third for Pentecost, a fourth for the Nativity of the Lord, a fifth for the Manifestation of the Lord, a sixth for the apostles, a seventh for the Holy Trinity, an eighth for the Holy Cross, and a ninth to be said only in the fast of Lent. The holy Roman Church observes and preserves these prefaces; we command you to observe them.

### CHAPTER 78.—Letter of Gregory to Bishop Januarius concerning the ploughing of someone’s harvest (Book VII of the *Register*, indiction 2, Epistle 1).

(Distinction 86, chapter “Tanta.”) Such wickedness concerning your old age has reached my ears that, unless we still took human frailty into account, we would already strike it with a fixed curse. For I have been told that, on the Lord’s Day, before you celebrated the solemnities of Mass, you went [Col. 0177D] to plough the harvest-field of the bearer of this letter, and, after ploughing it, celebrated the solemnities of Mass. After the solemnities you were not afraid to uproot the boundaries of that estate. All who hear of it know what punishment ought to have followed this deed. Likewise below: Indeed, a sentence of punishment ought to have been launched against you; but because we know your simplicity together with your old age, for the present we are silent. But we decree that those by whose advice you did these things are excommunicated for two months, on the condition that, if anything human should happen to them during that two-month period, they shall not be deprived of the blessing of viaticum. Henceforth, however, beware of their counsels, and carefully guard yourself as well, lest, if you become their disciple in evil—when you ought to have been their teacher in good—[Col. 0178A] we spare neither your simplicity nor your old age any longer.

### CHAPTER 79.—Deacons ought not to serve vocal melody. (Likewise, Book IV of the *Register*, chapter 88, or Epistle 44.)

(Distinction 92, chapter “In sancta.”) In this holy Roman Church, over which divine dispensation has willed that I preside, a very blameworthy custom has long arisen: certain persons are selected as singers for the sacred ministry of the altar and, having been placed in the order of deacons, serve the modulation of their voices, though it would have been fitting for them to devote themselves to the office of preaching and to works of almsgiving. Thus it commonly happens that, while a pleasant voice is sought for the sacred ministry, a fitting life is neglected; and the singer, a minister of the Lord [variant: of God], provokes by his morals [Col. 0178B] while he delights the people with his voice. Therefore, by the present decree I establish that, in this see, ministers of the sacred altar must not sing, but are to discharge only the office of reading the Gospel during the solemnities of Mass. I decree that the psalms and remaining readings be performed by subdeacons or, if necessity requires, by the minor orders. But if anyone attempts to act against this decree of mine, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER 80.—The more authoritative practice of the Church is to be retained. Gregory to Augustine (bishop of the English, chapter 3).

(Distinction 12, chapter “Novit.”) Your brotherhood knows the custom of the Roman Church, in which it remembers that it was nurtured. But it pleases me that, whether in the Roman, Gallican, or any other Church, you find something that can more greatly please almighty God, you should carefully choose it and introduce into the Church of the English, which is still new in the faith, as a pre-eminent institution what you can gather from many Churches. For things are not to be loved for the sake of places, but places for the sake of things. Therefore choose from each and every Church whatever is devout, religious, and right, and, having gathered these things as it were into one bundle, establish them as a custom in the minds of the English.

### CHAPTER 81.—On the number of Masses. Pope Alexander.

It is sufficient for a priest to celebrate one Mass on one day, because Christ suffered once and redeemed the whole world. It is no small matter to perform one Mass, and very blessed is the person who can celebrate one worthily. [Col. 0178D] Yet some celebrate one for the dead and another of the day, if necessary. For whoever, for money or through flattery of secular persons, presumes to celebrate several Masses in one day, I do not think that he escapes condemnation.

### CHAPTER 82.—Married priests are not to be rejected by the people. Reply of Pope Nicholas I to the questions of the Bulgarians converted to the faith, chapter 70.

(Distinction 28, chapter “Consulendum.”) You determine to inquire whether you ought to support and honour a priest who has a wife, or cast him out from among you. To this we reply that, although such men are indeed very blameworthy, you nevertheless ought to imitate God, who, as the Gospel testifies, “makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust” [the printed text has *banos*, evidently for *bonos*] [Col. 0179A] (Matt. V). You ought not to cast him out from among you, because the Lord did not cast Judas, though he was a lying disciple, out of the number of the apostles. But you, being laypeople, must neither judge priests nor investigate anything concerning their lives; whatever the matter may be must be reserved for the judgment of bishops.

### CHAPTER 83.—Defiled priests do not defile the divine sacraments. Likewise, title 11, chapter 5.

When you ask whether you ought to receive communion from a priest who has either been caught in adultery or is merely stained by such a report, we reply: No one, however defiled he may be, can defile the divine sacraments, which cleanse every contamination. Nor can a ray of the sun, passing through sewers and latrines, acquire any [Col. 0179B] contamination from them. Therefore, whatever sort of priest he may be, holy things cannot be defiled. Accordingly, communion must be received from him until he is rejected by the judgment of bishops, because evil men, by administering good things, harm themselves alone. A lighted wax torch indeed causes loss to itself, but supplies light to others in darkness; and the very thing through which it provides benefit to others brings loss upon itself. Receive, therefore, Christ’s mysteries fearlessly from every priest, since all things are cleansed in faith. For “faith is what conquers this world” (I John V). And because it is effected not by the merit of the giver but of the receiver, as blessed Jerome says: “For believing, baptism is complete in every soul, and the body is complete in every priest.” [Col. 0179C] He also says, in agreement with sacred Scripture: “Before you have heard, do not judge anyone” (Ecclus. XI); and before an accusation brought has been tested, suspend no one from your communion, because one who is accused is not immediately guilty, nor is one who is convicted immediately criminal.

### CHAPTER 84.—On simoniacs. From the decrees of Pope Paschal [Pascasius], chapter 18.

Whoever can and yet fails to defend a brother from death incurs the crime of fraternal death. We too, having heard of the grave crime of your Excellency, incur the gravest penalty of guilt if we remain silent, since the Lord testifies dreadfully that one who, by keeping silent, conceals the impiety of the wicked indeed sheds blood. [Col. 0179D] For we have heard—at which we greatly marvel—that sacred orders among you are sold for money [variants: *detrahuntur*, “are taken away”; perhaps *distribuuntur*, “are distributed”]. Since all who attempt anything of this kind are proved altogether heretics, the Holy Spirit declaring through Gregory that whoever is ordained by means of money is promoted in order to become a heretic. (Gregory, Book IV of the *Register*, chapter 99.) And to show that the cause of this little letter of ours was not presumption but fear, the same blessed man continues: “Whoever, according to the position of his office, has not burned vehemently against the heresy of simony and neophytes should not doubt that he will have a share with him who first committed this dangerous [variant: sacrilegious] crime.”

Since, in these words, a person is described as heretical by the heresy of simony and neophytes, [Col. 0180A] it is made entirely clear that this is a crime most worthy of eternal death. The divine oracle declares through Augustine and says: “Hold most firmly and never doubt that every heretic and schismatic, even if he gives many alms or even sheds his blood for Christ, is to be consigned to the burning of eternal fire with the devil and his angels, unless before the end of this life he has been incorporated and restored to the Catholic Church.” (Augustine, *On Faith to Peter*, book, chapter 39.) Hence the Lord drove the sellers and buyers from the temple (Matt. XXI). The earth swallowed Dathan and Abiram as they sought advancement (Num. XVI). Peter condemned Simon when he made his attempt (Acts VIII), and in him condemned all simoniacs with the ecclesiastical missiles of a perpetual anathema. It is exceedingly shameful [Col. 0180B] that the Church, now established with fullest vigour, should succumb to that deadly enemy over whom, in the first beginnings of its infancy, it triumphed with such strength.

But if anyone objects that consecrations are not bought, but the things themselves which result from consecration, he is plainly proved to be wholly foolish. For since neither a material church, nor bishop, nor abbot prospers at all in such a matter without material and external possessions, just as the soul does not live bodily without the body, whoever sells one of these two, without which the other cannot come to exist, does not refrain from selling either. Yet the sacred canon entirely destroys this objection, since it so prohibits the appointment for money of a procurator or defender of a church, or of one subject to a rule, that it also cuts down the intermediaries in this crime with the sword-point of anathema. [Col. 0180C] What more need be said? If simoniacs and neophytes, anathematized and excommunicated, and truly heretics, are separated from the number of the faithful of the Church, who does not see that the Masses and prayers of such priests or clerics provoke the Lord to wrath against the people whom they believe to be appeased by such means?

For it is written: “Everything which is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XIV), and there is no place for a true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church. Hence it is also said: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second admonition” (Titus III). How, then, do we avoid such bishops, abbots, or other clerics if we hear their Masses, when we incur excommunication if we even pray together with them? Indeed, it is wholly [Col. 0180D] erroneous even to believe that such persons are priests, since Peter says to Simon: “May your money be with you unto perdition, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money” (Acts VIII). Since the words “you thought” are used, it is clear that he is condemned not for what he did, but because he believed himself able to do it. Yet it is less to think than to believe, whereas to be a heretic of whatever kind is certain and indubitable condemnation.

What profit was there in having expelled Arians, Sabellians, Photinians, and impious Manichees from the city, if the heresy of simony and neophytes—which, as blessed Gregory says, crept in before all others into the holy Church by diabolical fraud—defiles what is, as it were, the Church’s first and greatest chastity, not only by bodily but by mental pollution? Therefore, in God and for God’s sake, we ask and entreat your [Col. 0181A] Excellency and all Christ’s faithful: if you desire to have a share in Christ, strive with utmost zeal that this savage plague, which by raging everywhere has already condemned innumerable peoples to eternal death, may be utterly destroyed by your authority and example. Thus, may it no longer happen—God forbid!—that sin against the Holy Spirit be forgiven neither in this world nor in the world to come (Matt. XII).

### CHAPTER 85.—The consecrated host must not be administered dipped. From the decrees of Pope Julius.

(The same passage is given above, chapter 11.) Those who, for the completion of communion, distribute to the people an eucharist dipped in the chalice have found no testimony to this practice set forth in the Gospel, where the Lord entrusted his body and blood to the apostles. For the handing over of the bread is commemorated separately, and that of the chalice separately. We do not read that Christ gave dipped bread to others, except only to that disciple whom the dipped morsel marked out as the betrayer of his Master (John XIII), not because it signified the institution of this sacrament.

### CHAPTER 86.—To whom the remnants are not to be given. Likewise, from the second epistle of Pope Clement.

(*De consecratione*, distinction 2, chapter “Tribus.”) We command that fragments of the Lord’s offerings are never to be placed at table for a stranger to the Church or for a layperson. You who indiscriminately bestow the breads of the sanctuary upon the unworthy—how do you know whether they are clean from women? Thus David too, when he asked Abimelech the priest for bread [Col. 0181C] to eat, was asked whether he was clean from a woman; and, professing himself clean for three days, he ate the bread of the Presence (I Kings XXI).

### CHAPTER 87.—No more than one Mass is to be celebrated in a day. Leo to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria.

It is necessary that some portion of the people be deprived of their devotion if, preserving the custom of only one Mass, they cannot offer sacrifice unless they assemble in the earlier part of the day. Therefore we earnestly and affectionately admonish your brotherhood not to neglect, through your own care, that which conforms to our custom according to the pattern of paternal tradition, so that in all things we may agree in faith and deeds. Accordingly, when our son Possidonius the priest returned, we gave him this letter to carry to your belovedness. He has often been present at our professions and actions and, having been sent to us so many times, has learned what the authority of the Apostolic See maintains in all things.

### CHAPTER 88.—The mysteries must not be entrusted to persons afflicted by a demon or illness. Pope Gelasius the First of that name, chapter 21.

(Distinction 33, chapter “Usque adeo.”) We have indeed discovered unlawful practices breaking out to such an extent that persons entangled by demons or other afflictions are allowed to handle the most holy mysteries. If, while they are engaged in this work, some personal necessity should arise, who could be confident concerning his own salvation and that of the faithful, when he sees the ministers themselves of human healing afflicted by such a great calamity? And therefore they must necessarily be removed, lest scandal be produced for any weak persons [Col. 0182A] for whom Christ died. Finally, if the divine law does not permit a person bodily wounded or infirm to touch holy things at all, how much less is it fitting that persons struck in mind—which is worse—should be dispensers of the heavenly gift?

### CHAPTER 89.—The body of the Lord must not be received without the chalice. Gelasius to Bishops Majoricus and John.

(*De consecratione*, distinction 2, chapter “Comperimus.”) We have learned that some people in the same region, having received only the portion of the sacred body, refrain from the chalice of the sacred blood. Since, undoubtedly, they are bound by some superstition which I do not know, they must either receive the sacraments whole or be excluded from them whole; for the division of one and the same mystery cannot occur without great sacrilege.

### CHAPTER 90.—No disreputable priest is to approach the mysteries of the divine sacrament. Gelasius to Bishop Helpidius.

[Col. 0182B]

(1, question 1, chapter “Sacrosancta.”) The most holy religion which maintains [variant: contains] Catholic discipline claims such reverence for itself that no one may dare approach it except with a pure conscience. For how will the heavenly Spirit, invoked for the consecration of the divine mystery, come if the priest who prays for him to be present is reprobate and full of criminal deeds?

### CHAPTER 91.—All things are sanctified by the figure of Christ’s cross. Pope Stephen to Bishops Stilianus, Anastasius, Eusebius, John, Paul, etc.

Are not all the charisms of priestly ministry [Col. 0182C] accomplished by the figure of the cross? Does the water of baptism remit sins unless it has been sanctified by the cross? And, to pass over the rest, what rank of priesthood is entered without the sign of the cross?

### CHAPTER 92.—Nothing is to be demanded from communicants among the faithful. From the Sixth Synod of Constantinople III, chapter 23.

(1, question 1, chapter “Nullus episcopus.”) No bishop, priest, or deacon who administers holy communion shall demand any payment from one receiving the grace of communion. For grace is not sold, nor do we give the grace of the Holy Spirit for a price; rather, we permit worthy persons to partake of the gift without defrauding them. But if any of those counted among the clergy demands any payment from one to whom he administers [Col. 0182D] holy communion, let him be deposed as an imitator of simoniacal fraud.

### CHAPTER 93.—The sacraments of Christ’s Church must always be venerated, even though administered by evil ministers. Augustine, *On the One Baptism* (against the Donatists, Book IV, chapter 4).

It is one thing not to possess something; another not to possess it lawfully, or to usurp it unlawfully. Therefore, Christ’s sacraments and those of the Church are not thereby not sacraments because they are used unlawfully not only by heretics but also by all wicked and impious persons. Such persons, however, must be corrected or punished; the sacraments themselves must be acknowledged and venerated.

### CHAPTER 94.—In the same place.

Just as I seem to be pressed when someone says to me, “Therefore a heretic forgives sins,” so I too press when I say: “Therefore one who does not keep the heavenly commands—a greedy person, [Col. 0183A] plunderer, usurer, envious person, renouncing the world in words but not in deeds—forgives sins.” If it is through the power of God’s sacrament, then, just like the former, so too does the latter; if through personal merit, neither the former nor the latter does so. For that sacrament is recognized as Christ’s even in evil persons. Likewise, in the same work: Thus one baptized in heresy in the name of the Holy Trinity does not thereby become a temple of God if he does not depart from heresy; just as one baptized in the same name while in greed does not become a temple of God if he does not depart from greed, which is the service of idols.

Likewise. (Chapter 5 of the same book; distinction 8, chapter “Frustra.” See part 4, chapter 235.) In vain do some, defeated by reason, object custom to us, as though custom were greater than truth, or as though in spiritual matters one should not follow what has been revealed for the better by the Holy Spirit. This is [Col. 0183B] plainly true: if reason and truth support a custom, nothing ought to be held more firmly. Perhaps a greedy person, a plunderer, coveting the possessions of others, stands beside you among the people of God; you know that he is such, and he is a believer—or rather is called a believer. You cannot cast him from the church. You have no means of correcting him by rebuking and reproving him. He will approach the altar with you: do not be afraid; “each person shall bear his own burden” (Gal. VI).

Likewise. (Augustine, *On the One Baptism against Petilian*, chapter 17.) “How,” he says, “am I to endure someone whom I know to be evil?” Would you not endure him more readily than carry yourself outside? See how you would endure him: attend to the Apostle saying, “Each person shall bear his own burden”; that sentence would free you. For you would not share his greed, but would share [Col. 0183C] Christ’s table with him. And what would harm you if you shared Christ’s table with him? The Apostle says: “For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself” (I Cor. XI): to himself, not to you.

(Augustine, *Sermons on the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 68.) Certainly, if you are a judge, if you have received the power to judge, and if one is accused before you according to ecclesiastical rule and convicted by true documents and witnesses, restrain, rebuke, excommunicate, depose.

(11, question 3, chapter “Omnis Christianus.”) Every Christian, most beloved, who is excommunicated by priests is said to be handed over to Satan (I Cor. V). How? Clearly because the devil is outside the Church just as Christ is in the Church; and therefore one removed from ecclesiastical communion is said as it were to be handed over to the devil. Hence, those whom the Apostle then declares to have been handed over to Satan, he shows to have been excommunicated by himself.

### CHAPTER 95.—One must not communicate with hypocrites and deceivers of the people. Boniface the martyr to Pope Zacharias.

(11, question 3, chapter “Antecessor.”) Gregory, the predecessor of your predecessor of venerable memory, when he ordained me, unworthy as I was, and sent me to preach the word of God to the German peoples, bound me by the sacrament of faith to be a supporter and helper, in word, deed, and consent, of canonical and just bishops and priests. This I strove to fulfil with divine grace. But false priests, hypocrites, and deceivers of peoples I was either to correct to the way of salvation or to avoid and abstain from their communion. [Col. 0184A] I observed this partly; partly I could neither guard nor fulfil it, though I fulfilled the obligation spiritually, because my soul did not enter into their assent or counsel. Bodily, however, I could not wholly abstain from them. When I came to the prince of the Franks, compelled by the necessity of the Churches, I did not find there such persons as I wished; nevertheless, in the holy communion of Christ’s body I did not communicate with them.

### CHAPTER 96.—It is no detriment to associate bodily with deceivers and false priests if one does not consent in will. Pope Zacharias to Boniface the martyr.

(11, q. 2, c. *Quod praedecessor*.) What our predecessor, Gregory of blessed memory, bishop of this Apostolic See, ordained when he sent your brotherhood to preach the word of the Gospel among the regions of Germany and those pagan peoples—namely, that he wished you first to be fortified by a word of promise, so that, if you found orthodox bishops, presbyters, or any others perfect in word and exhortation, you should further strengthen them and hold communion with them—this indeed was done. But if you found deceptive bishops, pseudo-presbyters, or any others straying from the straight path of faith, you were to have no communion with them. You have confessed that, with God alone consoling [or: strengthening] you, you have spiritually observed this until the present. Or if, because of the ruling power and human favour of the Frankish people, when you came among them you could not altogether abstain bodily, owing to the necessity of the Churches of God [Col. 0184C], your soul nevertheless has not been defiled by participation in their counsel and consent. Therefore, because you associated with them without consenting to their wickedness, you suffer no loss before God.

## CHAPTER 97.—That a sacrament offered by the ungodly harms them, not those for whom it is offered. Augustine, Book II against the Letter of Parmenian, chapter 5.

(1, q. 1, c. *Per Isaiam*.) Through Isaiah the Lord says: “The criminal who sacrifices to me a calf is as one who kills a dog; and he who presents fine flour is as one who presents swine’s blood; and he who offers incense is as one who blesses an idol” (Isa. 66). A little later: Whoever, wherever he may be, offers such a sacrifice in heart or deeds, so as to deserve to hear these words [Col. 0184D], brings destruction upon himself, not upon those good persons who receive from them those same sacraments—those who, according to the prophet Ezekiel, groan and mourn over the sins and iniquities (Ezek. 4) committed in their midst, although they do not bodily separate themselves from there.

Likewise, chapter 6: The sacrifices of the ungodly harm the very persons who offer them ungodly. For the sacrifice is one and the same, because of the Lord’s name which is invoked; and it is always holy, but it becomes for each person according to the state of heart with which he approaches to receive it. “For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11). He does not say, “upon others,” but “upon himself.”

And below. (Chapter 10 of the same book.) We warn that this must be understood in almost all questions of this kind: namely, that although all sacraments harm those who administer them unworthily, they nevertheless benefit those who receive them worthily through such persons. [Col. 0185A]

And below. (Chapter 11 of the same work.) The Holy Spirit is present in a ruler or minister of the Church in such a way that, if he is not false, the Holy Spirit works through him, both unto his own reward in eternal salvation and unto the regeneration or edification of those who are either consecrated or evangelized through him. But if he is false, since it is most truly written, “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the false” (Wis. 1), the Spirit is indeed absent from his salvation, withdrawing Himself from thoughts without understanding; nevertheless, He does not abandon that man’s ministry, through which He works the salvation of others by him.

(Chapter 13 of the same work.) Below. (1, q. 1, c. *Quod quidam*.) Each is a sacrament, and each is given to a person by a certain consecration: the one when he is baptized, the other when he is ordained. Therefore, neither may be repeated in the Catholic Church. For when rulers coming even from that party have been received for the sake of peace, after the error of schism has been corrected, and it has seemed right that they should perform the same offices they performed before, they are not to be ordained again. Rather, as baptism remained intact in them, so ordination remained intact; for the defect was in their severance, and it was corrected by the peace of unity, not in the sacraments, which are themselves true wherever they may be.

And when it is judged expedient for the Church that their rulers, coming into Catholic fellowship, should not exercise their honours there, the sacraments of ordination themselves are nevertheless not taken away from them. They remain upon them; and therefore hands are not laid upon them among the people, lest injury be done not to the man but to the sacrament itself. [Col. 0185B]

Below. (A little later in the same chapter.) Concerning those who have separated from the unity of the Catholic Church, there is no longer any question that they both possess the sacraments and can confer them, and that they possess and confer them to their own harm outside the bond of peace.

And below. (After several verses.) Injury must be done to neither sacrament.

Below. Just as one who departs from unity does not possess it rightly, yet nevertheless possesses it, and therefore it is not given back to him when he returns; so also one who departs from unity does not confer it rightly, yet nevertheless confers it, and therefore what one receives from him is not repeated when that person comes to unity.

Below. Just as what he possessed outside is not given again to one returning, so what was received outside must not be repeated for one coming in. Hence it is consequently understood that human perversity must be corrected, but the holiness of the sacraments must be violated in no perverse person. [Col. 0185D] For it is certain that in perverse and criminal persons—whether those inside or those outside—it remains undefiled and inviolable. But in the good it remains unto reward; in the evil, unto judgment.

Below. (Chapter 19 of the same work.) *How.* Catholics do not glorify the Lord by treating His sacraments with the reverence due to them, so that, even if they have been administered by unworthy persons, those persons being condemned by their own perversity, the sacraments may be shown to remain in unimpaired holiness. (Augustine, *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, Book III, chapter 2, §23.)

Below. (Q. 4, c. *Cum quisque*.) Whenever any one of the brethren—that is, Christians established in the fellowship of the Church—is detected in some such sin as to deserve anathema, let this be done where there is no danger of schism; and let it be done with that love concerning which Paul himself elsewhere commands, saying: “Do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother” (2 Thess. 3).

Below. (Same chapter.) When the crime of someone is so known to all and appears so detestable to all that he has either no defenders whatever, or none capable of causing schism, let the severity of discipline not sleep. [Col. 0186A]

## CHAPTER 98.—That the uncleanness of others cannot harm the clean. Augustine against Petilian in the dialogue (*Against the Letters of Petilian*, Book II, chapter 30).

(1, q. 1, c. *Dominus*.) The Lord made clear that, within one assembly of persons receiving the same sacraments, the uncleanness of some cannot harm the clean.

Likewise Petilian said: “Or if someone has memorized the chants of a priest, is he thereby a priest because with sacrilegious mouth he publicly recites the priest’s chant?” [Col. 0186B]

## CHAPTER 99.—On the same matter. Augustine’s reply.

You say this as though we were now asking who is a true priest, rather than what is true baptism. For, in order that anyone may be a true priest, he must be clothed not only with the sacrament but also with righteousness, as it is written: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. 131). But a person who is a priest by sacrament alone, such as Caiaphas, the high priest and persecutor of the one and most true Priest, although he himself is not truthful, nevertheless what he gives is true, provided that he gives not his own thing but God’s.

Likewise, a little later: Therefore, if the Apostle himself bore witness to the testimony of some foreigner, whoever he may have been, because he found it true, why do we not, whenever we find what belongs to Christ and is true in any person—even though that person in whom it is found is perverse and deceitful—distinguish between the defect which the person has and the truth which he possesses not as his own but as God’s? And why do we say, “This sacrament is true,” just as that Apostle said, “This testimony is true”? Do we therefore also say, “That man himself is truthful,” because we say, “This sacrament is true”? [Col. 0186C]

Likewise, in the same chapter: But you must necessarily remain always in error so long as, because of human faults, you violate God’s sacraments, or suppose that we, because of God’s sacraments—which we do not wish to violate in you—also take upon ourselves the sacrilege of your schism.

Likewise. (Augustine, chapter 35 of the same book.) Therefore the purity of baptism is wholly distinct from the purity or uncleanness of the conscience either of the giver or of the receiver. [Col. 0186D]

Likewise. (Chapter 47 of the same work.) Remember that the conduct of evil persons does no harm to God’s sacraments, so as to make them either not sacraments at all or less holy.

Likewise. (Chapter 48 of the same work.) If Saul did not possess the holiness of the sacrament, what did David venerate in him? But if he possessed innocence, why did he persecute an innocent man? For David both honoured him while living and avenged him when slain on account of the most sacred anointing; and because he cut off even a small piece of Saul’s garment, he trembled, stricken in heart. Behold, Saul did not possess innocence, yet he possessed holiness—not the holiness of his own life, for that cannot exist without innocence, but the holiness of God’s sacrament, which is holy even in evil persons.

Likewise. (Chapter 49 of the same work; 23, q. 5, c. *Tu dixisti*.) You said: “The traitor perished by a noose; he left the noose to such men.” This does not concern us at all. For we do not venerate as martyrs those who put a noose around their own necks. [Col. 0187A]

Likewise. (Augustine, chapter 52, Book II *Against the Letters of Petilian*.) We say that the sacrifice becomes for each person according to the kind of person he is when he approaches to offer it, and when he approaches to receive it; and that those eat of the sacrifices of such persons who approach them in the same state as those persons themselves. Thus, if an evil person offers to God and a good person receives from it, it is for each one according to what each is, because it is also written: “All things are clean to the clean” (Tit. 1). By this true and Catholic judgment you also were not defiled by Optatus’s sacrifice, if his deeds displeased you. For surely his bread was bread of mourning, under whose iniquities all Africa mourned; but your shared participation in that bread of mourning is caused by the evil of schism common to all of you. [Col. 0187B]

Likewise. (Chapter 54 of the same book.) Thanks be to God, because at last you have confessed that Christ’s invoked name can avail for the salvation of others even if it is invoked by sinners. Therefore understand from this that, when Christ’s name is invoked, the sins of others do not harm another’s salvation.

## CHAPTER 100.—How great is the dignity of the priestly order. In the book *Questions on the Old Testament*, chapter 11.

(1, q. 1, c. *Dictum est*.) The Lord said to Moses and Aaron in Numbers: “You shall put my name upon the children of Israel, and I, the Lord, will bless them” (Num. 6), so that the grace of transmission may be poured out upon people through the ministry of the ordained person; and the priest’s will can neither harm nor benefit them, but rather the merit of the one seeking blessing. Let us therefore observe from this how great is the dignity of the priestly order.

For it was said among other things concerning the most wicked Caiaphas, murderer of the Saviour: “He did not say this of himself; but, being high priest that year, he prophesied” (John 6). By this it is shown that the Holy Spirit of graces follows not the person of one worthy or unworthy, but the order of transmission; so that, although a person may be of good merit, he nevertheless cannot bless unless he has been ordained to perform the office of ministry. But it belongs to God to grant the effect of the blessing. [Col. 0187C]

## CHAPTER 101.—That one separated from the Church, however laudably he may live, cannot have life. Likewise, in the conciliar letter to the Donatists.

[Col. 0187D]

Whoever has been separated from the Catholic Church, however laudably he may think that he lives, shall not have life because of this crime alone—that he is cut off from Christianity—but the wrath of God remains upon him. But whoever lives well in this Church is not prejudiced by the sins of others, because each person in it shall bear his own burden, as the Apostle says (Gal. 6). Therefore communion with evil persons does not stain anyone by participation in the sacraments, but consent to their deeds does. For if a person does not consent to their evil deeds, the evil person bears his own cause and his own person, and does not prejudice another whom he does not have as a companion in the confession of an evil deed or of guilt.

## CHAPTER 102.—That evil persons do not defile one living among them in two ways: if he does not consent and if he rebukes them. The same, *Sermons on the Words of the Lord*, sermon 18.

[Col. 0188A]

Always be separated from the evil in heart; for the time being, be cautiously joined to them in body.

(A little later.) An evil person does not defile you in two ways: if you do not consent and if you rebuke him; that is, not to communicate is not to consent. For communion occurs when companionship of will or approval is joined to another’s deed.

(After several verses.) Therefore do not consent to evil persons by approving them; do not be negligent by failing to rebuke them; and do not be proud by rebuking them insolently [or: offensively].

## CHAPTER 103.—How “Go out from among them, and touch no unclean thing” is to be understood. In the same place.

“Depart, go out from there, and touch no unclean thing” [Col. 0188B] (Isa. 52)—but with the touch of the heart, not of the body. For what is it to touch an unclean thing except to consent to sins? What is it to go out from there except to do what pertains to their correction, so far as can be done without breach of peace in accordance with each person’s rank and position?

If the fact that someone sinned displeased you, you have not touched the unclean thing. If you rebuked, corrected, and warned him; if, when the matter requires it, you also applied suitable discipline that does not violate unity, you have gone out from there. Moses cried out these things; Isaiah cried out; Jeremiah cried out; Ezekiel cried out. Let us see whether they abandoned God’s people and transferred themselves to other nations. How many things, and how vehemently, Jeremiah reproved among the sinners and criminals of the people! Yet he remained among them: he entered the one Temple with them, celebrated the same sacraments, and lived in the same congregation of criminal persons; but by crying out he went out from there. [Col. 0188C] Therefore this is to go out from there, this is not to touch the unclean thing: not to consent in one’s will and not to spare with one’s speech.

## CHAPTER 104.—What it is to speak a word against the Holy Spirit. Likewise, in the sermon *On the Words of the Lord*.

(Sermon 11, near the end.) A word is spoken against the Holy Spirit when one never comes from dispersion to the congregation which received the Holy Spirit for the remission of sins. Even if someone comes to that congregation through an evil cleric, yet a Catholic one—a rejected and false minister—if he comes with a heart that is not false, he receives remission of sins in that very Holy Spirit. This Spirit works in this Church even at this time, when, as it were, a threshing-floor is being threshed with chaff, in such a way that He rejects no true confession, is deceived by no pretence, and flees the reprobate so that even through their ministry He gathers the approved. [Col. 0188D]

## CHAPTER 105.—That God’s gifts reach those who receive with faith, even if the person through whom they receive is like Judas. Augustine, exposition of Psalm 10.

(1, q. 1, c. *Christus*.) What did Christ do to you, He who bore His betrayer with such patience that He gave him the Eucharist, first consecrated by His own hands and commended by His own mouth, as He gave it to the other apostles (Matt. 26; John 14)? What did Christ do to you, He who sent with the other disciples to preach the kingdom of heaven that same betrayer whom He called a devil, and who before betraying the Lord could not remain faithful even to the Lord’s money-box (John 6; John 12 and 13), except to show that God’s gifts reach those who receive with faith, even though the person through whom they receive is like Judas? [Col. 0189A]

## CHAPTER 106.—That one who has heard the Word of God negligently is no less guilty than one who through negligence has allowed Christ’s body to fall to the ground. Likewise Augustine, Book Fifty Homilies, Homily 26.

(1, q. 1, c. *Interrogo*.) I ask you, brothers and sisters: tell me, what seems greater to you, Christ’s body or Christ’s word? If you wish to answer truthfully, you ought to say that God’s word is not less than Christ’s body. Therefore, with as much care as we observe when Christ’s body is administered to us, so that none of it falls from our hands to the ground, let us observe with as much care that the word of God distributed to us does not perish from our heart while we think or speak of something else. For one who has heard God’s word negligently will be no less guilty than one who by negligence has allowed Christ’s body to fall to the ground. [Col. 0189B]

## CHAPTER 107.—That it cannot rightly be offered except through a righteous and holy priest. The same.

(1, q. 1, c. *Neque potest rite*.) It cannot rightly be offered except through a righteous and holy priest; nor can that which is offered for persons be received except by those for whom it is offered; and it must be without defect, so that it can be offered for cleansing the defective. Certainly, all who wish sacrifice to be offered to God for themselves desire this. [Col. 0189C]

## CHAPTER 108.—That God hates and rejects the festivals of heretics. Jerome on the prophet Amos.

(On Amos, chapter 5; 24, q. 1, c. *Odi*.) “I have hated and rejected your festivals, and I will not receive the smell of your assemblies. For if you offer me your burnt offerings and gifts, I will not receive them, nor look upon the vows of your fatlings.” God hates—and not only hates but rejects—the festivals of those who celebrate not God’s festivals but their own.

And a little later: God hates the sacrifices of heretics and rejects them from Himself; and whenever they are gathered in God’s name, He detests their stench and closes His nostrils. [Col. 0189D] But “to hate,” “not to smell,” and “to reject” are spoken in a human likeness, so that we may recognize God’s disposition through our own forms of speech. Even if they offered burnt offerings—that they might appear to fast, give alms, and promise chastity, which are true burnt offerings—the Lord would not receive them. He judges not the magnitude of sacrifices but the merits and motives of those who offer them. Hence the widow who put two small coins into the treasury is preferred by the Saviour to all others (Luke 22), because the Lord looks not at what is offered but at the will of those who offer.

## CHAPTER 109.—That before God not the judgment of priests but the life of the accused is considered. Likewise, on Matthew, chapter 16.

“Whatever you bind upon earth,” and the rest. [Col. 0190A] Bishops and presbyters, not understanding this passage, assume for themselves something of Pharisaic arrogance, so that they think they may either condemn the innocent or absolve the guilty; whereas before the Lord not the judgment of priests, but the life of the accused, is considered.

## CHAPTER 110.—That priests must approach the sacrifice without blemish. Likewise, on Zephaniah, chapter 3.

(1, q. 1, c. *Sacerdotes*.) Priests who serve the Eucharist and distribute the Lord’s blood to His people act impiously against Christ’s law when they think that the words of one invoking are what make the Eucharist, rather than his life; and that only the solemn prayer, rather than the merits of priests, is necessary. Of them it is said: “The priest in whom there is any blemish shall not approach to offer oblations to the Lord” (Lev. 21).

## CHAPTER 111.—Concerning Easter and Lent, and how they should be observed. Blessed Augustine, in the book *Responses to Januarius*.

[Col. 0190B]

(Epistle no. 119, chapter 15.) In the old Scriptures, no time is prescribed for observing Easter except from the fourteenth to the twenty-first day of the new moon of the first month. But because the Gospel clearly makes known on what day the Lord was crucified, lay in the tomb, and rose again, the observance of those days themselves was added by councils of the Fathers, and the whole Christian world was persuaded that Easter ought to be celebrated in this way.

The forty days of fasting have authority both in the old books, from the fast of Moses and Elijah (1 Kings 19; Exod. 10), and from the Gospel, because the Lord fasted for the same number of days [Col. 0190C], showing that the Gospel does not disagree with the Law and the Prophets (Matt. 4). For in the person of Moses the Law is understood, and in the person of Elijah the Prophets. Between them the Lord appeared glorious on the mountain, so that what the Apostle says of Him might stand out more plainly: “having testimony from the Law and the Prophets.” In what part of the year, therefore, could the observance of Lent have been established more suitably than next to and adjoining the Lord’s passion? For in it is signified this laborious life, which needs this self-restraint so that one may fast from friendship with the world, which assuredly does not cease falsely to flatter, scatter the juices of enticement, and cast them about.

## CHAPTER 112.—That a person must receive the Lord’s body fasting. Likewise Augustine, Epistle 118, to Januarius.

[Col. 0190D]

(*On Consecration*, distinction 1, c. *Liquido*; and Peter Lombard, Book IV, distinction 8, §c.) It is plain that when the disciples first received the body and blood of the Lord, they did not receive while fasting. Is the universal Church therefore to be censured because it is always received by those fasting? For the Holy Spirit was pleased that, in honour of so great a sacrament, the Lord’s body should enter the Christian’s mouth before other food. Therefore this custom is observed throughout the world.

For because the Lord gave it after food, brothers ought not on that account to come to receive that sacrament after breakfast or supper, or, as those whom the Apostle rebukes and corrects did, mix these things with their own meals. Indeed, in order to commend more strongly the depth of that mystery, the Saviour wished to impress it last upon the hearts and memory of the disciples, from whom He was about to depart for His passion. [Col. 0191A] Therefore He did not command the order in which it should thereafter be received, so as to reserve this matter for the apostles, through whom He was to order the Churches.

For if He had instructed them that it should always be received after other foods, I think no one would have changed that custom. But when the Apostle, speaking of this sacrament, said: “Therefore, brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you may not come together for judgment,” he immediately added: “The remaining matters I will set in order when I come.” From this it is made understood that it was too much to set out for them in a letter the entire order of practice, which the Church throughout the world observes as established by him [Col. 0191B], and which is not changed by any diversity of hours [variant: “by variation of customs”].

## CHAPTER 113.—That offerings and prayers do not benefit all persons for whom they are made, but only those for whom, while living, provision is made that they may benefit. Likewise, from the second book *For the Dead*.

(Augustine, *On Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, chapter 18.) Let us not suppose that anything reaches the dead for whom we care except that for which we solemnly pray on their behalf through sacrifices of the altar, prayers, or alms. Yet these things do not benefit all persons for whom they are made, but only those for whom, while they live, it is provided that they may benefit. But because we do not discern who they are, we must do them for all the regenerate, so that none of those to whom these benefits can and ought to reach may be omitted. [Col. 0191C]

For these things will always be better bestowed on those whom they neither harm nor benefit than withheld from those whom they benefit. Yet each person does this more diligently for his own close relations, so that the same may likewise be done for him by his own people.

Whatever is provided for a human body is not an aid to salvation but an office of humanity, according to the affection by which no one has ever hated his own flesh. Therefore one ought, as far as possible, to take care for the flesh of one’s neighbour once the person who cared for it has departed from it. And if those who do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh do these things, how much more ought those who believe to do them, so that the service rendered to a dead body—yet one that will rise again and remain in eternity—may in some way be a testimony to that same faith. [Col. 0191D]

But when anyone is buried beside the memorial shrines of martyrs, this seems to me to benefit the deceased only by increasing the devotion of prayer for him, since he is thereby commended also to the martyrs’ patronage.

## CHAPTER 114.—That a presbyter must communicate as many times as he celebrates Mass in one day. From the Twelfth Council of Toledo, chapter 5.

(*On Consecration*, distinction 2, c. *Relatum est*.) It has been reported to us that some priests do not receive the grace of holy communion as many times as they appear to offer sacrifices in one day. Instead, if they themselves offer to God several sacrifices in one day, they abstain from communion in all those offerings and receive the grace of holy communion only in the offering of the final sacrifice—as though one should not participate as many times in that true and singular sacrifice as the immolation of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ is performed.

For behold, the Apostle says: “Are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar?” (1 Cor. 10). It is certain that those who sacrifice but do not eat are guilty concerning the Lord’s sacrament. Therefore, whoever among the priests henceforth approaches the divine altar to offer sacrifice and abstains from communion shall know that, because he has improperly deprived himself of the grace of communion, he is barred for one year. [Col. 0192A] For what kind of sacrifice will that be in which even the sacrificer himself is known not to participate? Therefore it must by every means be maintained that as often as a sacrificer immolates on the altar the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, so often he presents himself as a participant in receiving Christ’s body and blood. [Col. 0192B]

## CHAPTER 115.—That nothing is to be demanded for balsam, chapter 4.

It has been decided that, for the small quantity of balsam which is blessed and distributed through the churches for the sacrament of baptism, since three tremisses are customarily demanded from each person for it, nothing further shall be demanded. Otherwise, what is consecrated for the salvation of souls through the invocation of the Holy Spirit might be sold by us to our damnation, just as Simon Magus wished to buy God’s gift with money (Acts 8).

## CHAPTER 116.—That it must be feared lest, as in the case of Eli, God’s sanctuary be abandoned because of priests’ vices. The same, in the Letter to a Man Who Says That He Is a Penitent While Living in the World.

[Col. 0192C]

Eli was a holy priest, but he had sons who, as we read in the Hebrew books (1 Kings 4), committed fornication with women in God’s tabernacle and, in a manner like yours, shamelessly claimed God’s ministry for themselves. Therefore the very place of the tabernacle was overthrown, and because of the priests’ vices God’s sanctuary was abandoned. Yet Eli himself also offended God because he was too indulgent toward his sons. May your bishop’s righteousness have such power to deliver you that one must fear lest he fall from his throne because of you and perish beyond remedy.

Uzzah the Levite wished to support, as though it were falling, the ark of the Lord, which he himself ought to have carried, and he was struck down (2 Kings 6). What do you think will become of you, who have tried to cast down the ark of the Lord while it was standing? The more commendable is the bishop who ordained you, the more detestable are you for having deceived so great a man.

We are usually the last to know our own evils and the faults of our children and spouses, while our neighbours sing of them. All Italy knew you; all groaned as they stood before Christ’s altar. Nor were you so cunning as to conceal your vices prudently. So you burned, so lust dragged you, sweating and wanton, this way and that, that you seemed to raise up, from your fulfilled lusts, certain triumphs and the palm-branch of vice. [Col. 0192D]

## CHAPTER 117.—That no presbyter shall celebrate Mass without priestly vestments. From the Council of Rheims, chapter 4.

(Burchard, Book II, chapter 50.) Let no presbyter dare under any circumstances to celebrate Mass without amice, alb, stole, fanon, and chasuble. Let these sacred vestments be kept very clean and placed in a clean location within the church. Nor may a presbyter ever leave the church wearing them, because the divine law forbids this. [Col. 0193A]

## CHAPTER 118.—That every presbyter shall bless water in his church on Sundays. From the Council of Nantes, chapter 5.

On every Sunday each presbyter shall, before the solemnities of Mass, make blessed water in his own church in a clean vessel suitable to so great a mystery [variant: ministry]. The people entering the church shall be sprinkled with this water; the courtyard of the same church shall likewise be sprinkled while processing around it with crosses; and prayer shall be made for the souls resting there. [Col. 0193B] Whoever wishes may take some of that water in small vessels and sprinkle it through houses, fields, vineyards, upon livestock and their fodder, and also upon food and drink.

## CHAPTER 119.—That private Masses should not be celebrated on solemn days. From the sayings of Augustine.

This also must be observed: private Masses performed by priests on solemn days should not be celebrated so publicly that the people are drawn away by them from the public solemnities of Mass canonically celebrated at the third hour. For among some there is a most evil custom: on Sundays or any feast-days, to celebrate Mass at once; and then, even if it is for the dead, when a person has heard it, he departs and spends the entire day from early morning serving drunkenness and feasting rather than God. [Col. 0193C]

The people must be admonished not to approach food before the public office has been completed. Rather, all should assemble at the public solemnities of Mass and preaching of holy mother Church. Priests should celebrate Mass at the third hour, so that the people are not drawn away from the public solemnities. Priests who are in the district around the city, or in the city itself, and the people, as we have said, should gather together for the public celebration of Mass—except consecrated women of God, who customarily do not go out in public but remain enclosed within the cloisters of monasteries [variant: “within closed monasteries”].

## CHAPTER 120.—That on feast-days all presbyters shall instruct the people about the prayers they ought to offer. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 8.

[Col. 0193D]

On Sundays and feast-days, after the sermon delivered within the solemnities of Mass, the priest ought to admonish the people that, in accordance with apostolic teaching, all together should pour out prayers to the Lord for various needs: for the king, bishops, and governors of the Churches; for peace; for plague; for the sick lying in bed within that parish; and for the recently deceased. For each of these prayers, he is to say the Lord’s Prayer silently. The priest, however, shall solemnly complete the prayers appropriate to each individual exhortation. After this the sacred offering shall be celebrated. For the Apostle says: “I exhort first of all that prayers be made,” and so forth (1 Tim. 2).

## CHAPTER 121.—That presbyters shall instruct the people to allow oxherds and swineherds to come to Mass on principal feasts. From the Council of Rouen, chapter 5.

[Col. 0194A]

(Burchard, Book II, chapter 71.) Priests ought to admonish the people subject to them to make or allow oxherds, swineherds, and other shepherds or ploughmen, who constantly live in fields or woods and therefore live after the manner of beasts, to come at least to Mass on Sundays and other feast-days. For Christ also redeemed these persons with His precious blood. If they neglect this, let them know that they will without doubt have to render account for those souls.

Indeed, when the Lord came into this world, He chose not the more honourable and noble persons, but called fishermen [Col. 0194B] and unlearned persons as His disciples, in order to show in deed what He Himself declares in words in the Gospel: “What is exalted among men is an abomination before God” (Luke 16). And, without prejudice to a higher interpretation, the birth of our Redeemer was first announced by an angel to shepherds (Luke 2).

## CHAPTER 122.—Concerning a parishioner of another presbyter. From the Council of Nantes, chapter 19.

(16, q. 1, c. *Cunctis fidelibus*.) On Sundays or feast-days, before celebrating Mass, presbyters shall ask the people whether there is in the church a parishioner of another priest who, having rejected his own presbyter, wishes to hear Mass there. If they find one, they shall immediately expel him from the church and compel him to return to his own parish.

Likewise, they shall ask whether there are any persons at discord who have an irreconcilable quarrel with one another. If such persons are found, they shall immediately be reconciled. But if they refuse to accept peace, they shall be expelled from the church until they return to charity. For we cannot offer a gift or offering at the altar unless we are first reconciled with our brother. Once these matters have been completed, priests shall duly perform the solemnities of Mass. [Col. 0194C]

## CHAPTER 123.—Concerning ordained persons and the rest of the faithful: that they should do nothing without their bishop’s permission. From an Epistle of Pope Clement sent to all the faithful.

Therefore all the faithful, and especially all presbyters, deacons, and other clerics, must take care to do nothing without the permission of their own bishop. No presbyter may celebrate Mass in his parish without his command, baptize, or do anything pertaining to the bishop without his permission.

Likewise, the rest of the people, both greater and lesser, shall do whatever must be done with his permission. They shall not depart from their parish without his permission, nor presume to remain there as visitors. Their souls have been entrusted to him; therefore they must do everything by his counsel and nothing without consulting him. Whoever obeys him obeys God; but whoever does not obey him is unquestionably guilty and reprobate. [Col. 0194D]

## CHAPTER 124.—Concerning priests when an occurrence of illness arises during the time of Mass. From the Seventh Council of Toledo, chapter 2.

(7, q. 1, c. *Nihil contra.*) Nothing contrary to the established order [the established condition of the order] is to be presumed upon through a rash venture; [Col. 0195A] nor are those things held in the highest veneration to be relaxed by even the slightest touch [act] of presumption. For they were commanded to be done only for this reason: that, when they have been begun, they are not known to be interrupted, nor, through the onset of illness, is the soundness of health to be deprived of its strength. Thus provision is made not only for human frailty, but also for due concern for the sacred ministries of God.

We therefore decree that, when the holy mysteries are being consecrated by priests at the time of Mass, if any occurrence of illness should arise by which the begun mystery of consecration cannot be completed, it shall be lawful for a bishop or priest to complete the consecration of the office that has been begun. For nothing else is suitable to supply what has been initiated in the mysteries except the completion of the blessing by either the priest who began it or the one who follows him; and these cannot [Col. 0195B] be regarded as complete unless they are completed in due order. Since we are all one in Christ, diversity produces nothing contrary where unity of faith displays the efficacy of a favorable outcome.

Let all clerics of every order have no doubt that this provision, commanded or allowed, is indivisible for them [or: is to be regarded as indivisible]; but, as has been permitted to those preceding, let others immediately succeed them in order to bring it to completion. Yet let that which is provided for because of the infirmity of nature not be turned into the destructive presumption of abuse. No one, after food or drink, or after consuming anything however small, may celebrate Mass; and no minister or priest, once he has begun, may under any circumstances presume to leave the offices unfinished unless an evident onset of illness occurs. Whoever presumes to violate these provisions shall incur a sentence of excommunication.

### Chapter 125.—Concerning priests afflicted by demons and various disorders: that they may not handle sacred things. From the decrees of Pope Pius, chapter 5.

[Col. 0195C]

(Dist. 33, c. *Communiter.*) It has indeed rightly been determined by the rules of the elders that persons possessed by demons and those entangled in other disorders may not handle the sacred ministries. Applying a considered judgment of reason to this command, we determine in common that none of those who are either cast down upon the ground by demons possessing them, or are driven into frenzy by assaults of affliction of any kind, may dare to minister at the sacred altars or, without examination, intrude themselves into the divine sacraments. An exception is made for those who, subject to bodily infirmities and without such [Col. 0195D] disorders, are shown to have been cast down upon the ground; nevertheless, they too shall be suspended from their office, rank, and place until, after the period of one year, they are found, at the bishop’s discretion, to be free from [delivered from] assaults of demons.

### Chapter 126.—On the same matter. From the decrees of Pope Soter, chapter 8.

(De cons., dist. 1, c. *Ut illud.*) Let each person take care to avoid that warning of the divine oracle which is written: “Woe to one who is alone, for when he falls he has no one to raise him up” (Eccles. 4). We must be especially fearful and vigilant lest, during those hours and times when psalms are sung to God or sacrifice is offered, some destructive disorder or bodily ailment should befall anyone engaged alone in the divine offices, causing either the body [Col. 0196A] suddenly to collapse or the mind to be confused through distraction or terror.

Therefore, taking precautions against cases of this kind, we have judged it necessary to direct that, wherever an abundance of time, place, or clergy permits, whoever is singing to God and offering sacrifice should have behind him the assistance of a neighboring helper. Thus, should he who comes forward to perform the offices be troubled by some mishap or cast down to the ground, he may always have behind him someone who fearlessly performs his part and completes the office that was begun.

### Chapter 127.—That priests are not to celebrate Mass alone. From the same source, chapter 10.

(De cons., dist. 1, c. *Hoc quoque.*) This too has been decreed: no priest may presume to celebrate the solemnities of Mass unless two persons are present [Col. 0196B] and respond to him, so that he himself makes a third. For, since he says in the plural, “The Lord be with you,” and also says privately, “Pray for me,” it is most clearly fitting that his greeting also receive a response.

### Chapter 128.—Concerning those who reject the offering of married priests. From the Council of Agde.

If anyone discriminates against a married priest, as though on account of his marriage he ought not to offer sacrifice, and for that reason abstains from his offering, let him be anathema.

### Chapter 129.—That priests are to communicate whenever they have celebrated Mass. From the Council of Rouen, chapter 2.

It has been reported to us that certain priests, after celebrating Mass, refuse themselves to receive the divine mysteries [Col. 0196C] which they have consecrated, and hand the Lord’s chalice to little women who make offerings at Mass, or to certain laypeople who do not know how to judge the body of the Lord—that is, to distinguish spiritual food from bodily food. How contrary this is to all ecclesiastical religion the piety of the faithful knows.

Therefore we forbid all priests to presume henceforth to do this. Rather, the priest himself is to receive reverently, and is to hand the remaining elements to the deacon or subdeacon, ministers of the altar, to be gathered up. He should take care to communicate them with his own hand. Let him place the Eucharist in the hands of no layman or woman, but only place it in the recipient’s mouth, with these words: “May the body and blood of the Lord avail you for the remission of sins and for [Col. 0196D] eternal life.” Whoever transgresses these provisions, because he has despised Almighty God and dishonored him so far as lies in his power, shall be removed from the altar.
