### Chapter 130.—On the same matter. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 10.

It has been heard that certain priests celebrate Mass and do not communicate at all, although this is read to be forbidden in the canons of the Apostles. Or how can they rightly say, if they have not communicated, “We have received the sacraments, O Lord,” etc. In the same place, chapter 11: If any bishop, priest, deacon, or anyone of the sacerdotal order, after the offering has been made, does not communicate, let him state his reason; and if it is reasonable, let him receive pardon; but if he does not [Col. 0197A] state one, let him be deprived of communion, since he has become a cause of harm to the people.

### Chapter 131.—That the chalice and paten are to be made of gold or silver, or at least of tin, but never of bronze or brass. From the Council of Reims, chapter 6.

(Burchard, book III, chapter 96; De cons., dist. 1, c. *Ut calix.*) The Lord’s chalice, together with the paten, must, if not of gold, certainly be made of silver. Priests must not, under the persuasion of avarice, plead poverty or inability, since a fourth part of all that belongs to the church ought to be expended upon the building works of that church itself. The people too should be exhorted to offer something among the Lord’s gifts, as the ancient people are read to have done under Moses in the Lord’s tabernacle.

But if anyone is so poor, let him at least have a tin chalice. A chalice must not be made of bronze or brass, because the potency of wine produces verdigris and likewise induces vomiting. No one may presume to sing the liturgy using a wooden or glass chalice.

### Chapter 132.—On preserving the table of Christ. From the same source, chapter 5.

The table of Christ—that is, the altar where the Lord’s body is consecrated, where his blood is received, where the relics of saints are deposited, and where the prayers and vows of the people are offered before God by the priest—must be honored with every reverence. It must be most carefully covered with the cleanest linens and coverings. Nothing is to be placed upon it except reliquaries containing relics of saints and the four Gospels. When Mass has been completed, the chalice with the paten and the sacramentary, together with [Col. 0197C] the priestly vestments, are to be stored under lock in a clean place.

### Chapter 133.—That the corporal is to be of the purest linen and of one material. From the same source, chapter 3.

The corporal upon which the sacred offering is immolated is to be made of the cleanest linen. No material of another kind, whether more precious or less precious, is to be mixed into it. It must never remain upon the altar except during the time of Mass, but must either be placed in the sacristy with the book, or stored with the chalice and paten in a very clean place. When it is washed by the priest, deacon, or subdeacon, it must first be washed in the church, in a place and vessel prepared for this purpose, since it is stained by the Lord’s body and blood. Afterwards it is to be placed by the laundry worker in a clean place.

### Chapter 134.—That the sacrifice of the altar is not to be celebrated on silk or dyed cloth. From the letter of Pope Eusebius, chapter 51.

[Col. 0197D]

(De cons., dist. 1, c. *Consulto.*) Here, among the other matters already stated, we decree by the counsel of all that no one may presume to celebrate the sacrifice of the altar upon silk cloth or dyed cloth, but upon pure linen consecrated by a bishop—namely, linen produced from and woven out of earthly flax—as the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was buried in a clean linen shroud.

### Chapter 135.—That women are not to approach the altar or involve themselves in men’s offices. From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 44.

Women ought not to enter the altar area or touch those things assigned to men’s offices.

### Chapter 136.—On the same matter. From the decrees of Pope Gelasius I, chapter 28.

[Col. 0198A]

Moreover, we have heard with impatience that contempt for divine matters has gone so far that women are said to minister at the sacred altars and that all things assigned exclusively to the service of men are performed by a sex to which they do not belong.

### Chapter 137.—That laypeople are not to sit beside the altar. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 13.

Laypeople must not presume to stand or sit beside the altar at which the holy mysteries are celebrated, among the clergy either at vigils or at Mass. Rather, that part which is separated from the altar by railings is to be open only to clergy who chant. Yet, for adoration and communion, the holy of holies is to be open to laymen and women, as is customary.

### Chapter 138.—Concerning those priests who presume to sit in church while the Gospels are being read. From a letter of Pope Anastasius I addressed to the bishops of Germany and Burgundy, chapter 1.

[Col. 0198B]

Anastasius, bishop, to all bishops of the German regions and of Burgundy: greeting in the Lord. Your belovedness, dearest brothers, has requested that we answer your inquiries by the authority of the Apostolic See. Although, because of certain other occupations, we hasten to do this not at length but briefly, nevertheless, if necessary, do not hesitate lovingly to send again, as to the head, concerning these and other needs; for we regard your prayers as acceptable, both now and then.

You report that certain priests sit in church when the Gospels are read [Col. 0198C] and hear the words of the Lord and Savior not standing but sitting; and they say that they received this from the tradition of their elders. By apostolic authority we command that you permit this in no way henceforth. Rather, while the holy Gospels are recited in church, priests and all others are not to sit, but are to stand reverently in the presence of the Gospel, listen attentively to the Lord’s words, and faithfully adore.

### Chapter 139.—That no one may presume to give a chalice, paten, or priestly vestments as security to an innkeeper. From the Council of Reims, chapter 11.

(Burchard, book III, chapter 104.) No priest may presume to give as a pledge to an innkeeper or merchant, or to any layman or [Col. 0198D] woman, a chalice, paten, altar covering, priestly vestment, or ecclesiastical book, unless the most urgent necessity compels it. For so great is the holiness of the sacred ministry that, without prejudice to the higher mystical meaning, even the Lord prohibited through the prophet a priest from going out among the people in the sacred vestments; rather, upon returning from divine communion, he was to leave them within the holy place.

And one who is forbidden by the sacred canons to enter taverns for drinking ought not even to allow things sanctified by the sacred mystery to be touched by the unclean—much less offer them as a pledge. So Saint Stephen, pope and martyr, instructed Saint Hilary in his decrees.

### Chapter 140.—From the Council of Orléans, chapter 9.

No priest or layperson may presume to divert a chalice, paten, [Col. 0199A] or any sacred vessels dedicated to divine worship to other personal uses. For whoever drinks anything other than Christ’s blood, received in the sacrament, from a sacred chalice, or uses a paten for an office other than service at the altar, must be deterred by the example of Belshazzar, who, when he appropriated the vessels of the Lord for common use, lost his life together with his kingdom.

### Chapter 141.—That bishops may, with the counsel of the clergy, provide for their household in need from the church treasury. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 5.

It shall be lawful for bishops, in the presence of priests and deacons, to distribute from the church treasury, according to canonical institution and according to need, to the household and poor people of that church. [Col. 0200A]

### Chapter 142.—That no body being conveyed to burial is to be covered with an altar covering. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 30.

No body, when it is carried to its tomb, is ever to be covered with the covering of the Lord’s body or of the altar; and, while bodies are being honored with a sacred veil, altars are not to be polluted.

### Chapter 143.—That divine furnishings are not to be provided for wedding adornment. From the same source, chapter 8.

(De cons., dist. 1, c. *Ad nuptiarum.*) Divine furnishings are not to be provided for the adornment of weddings, lest, when they are polluted by the touch of wicked persons or by the display of worldly luxury, they seem unworthy for the offices of sacred ministry [mystery].

## Third Part of the Decree: On the Church, ecclesiastical things, and their reverence and observance

[Col. 0199]

### Chapter 1.—The condition of the whole Church is like a great ship which carries men, from various places and regions, over the stormy sea, hastening toward one city of a mighty kingdom. Clement, successor of the Apostle Peter, to James, brother of the Lord, namely bishop of Jerusalem (letter 1).

[Col. 0199B]

The condition of the whole Church is like a great ship which, over the billowing sea, carries men from different places and regions who desire to hasten toward one city of a mighty kingdom. Let the Lord Almighty himself be the master of this ship, and let Christ be its helmsman. Then let the bishop perform the office of the prow-master; let priests hold the place of sailors and deacons that of stewards; let those who instruct catechumens be compared with recruiting officers for the crew; and let the multitude of the entire brotherhood be like the passengers (*epibatae*).

Let this sea be understood as the present world; and let the varieties of winds [Col. 0199C] and whirlwinds be compared with different temptations; persecutions, tribulations, and dangers with waves. The earthly winds, which blow from torrents or valleys, signify the sayings of false prophets, seducers, and corrupt doctrine. Headlands and rocky places signify those judges who hold worldly powers and threaten dangers and death. Let the places called *bitalassa*, beaten by the double tides of deceptive waves, be compared with persons doubtful in mind and wavering concerning the truth of the promises. Let hypocrites and deceitful persons be considered like pirates. And what else are the rushing whirlpool, infernal Charybdis, shipwrecks dashed against rocks, and deadly sinkings to be understood as but sins? [Col. 0199D]

It remains, therefore, that this ship may, on a favorable course and in safety, enter the harbor of the desired city, and thus pour out prayer to God, so that those who sail may deserve to be heard.

### Chapter 2.—That the Church and house of God are to be honored by the people, but are not to be accessible to dogs. From the Council of Reims, chapter 2.

[Col. 0200B]

The Church and house of God are to be honored by the people according to their dignity, but are not to be accessible to dogs. Secular lawsuits, business, or idle talk are not to be carried on in it, because the house of God ought to be a house of prayer, not a den of thieves (Matt. 21), nor a place for women’s assemblies; nor are they to leave before the blessing has been completed.

### Chapter 3.—What the Church is. From the decrees of Pope Julius, chapter 5.

(Isidore, book I, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 1.) *Ecclesia* is a Greek name, translated into Latin as “convocation,” because it calls all people to itself. It is called “Catholic,” that is, universal, because it is established throughout [Col. 0200C] the whole world, or because it is Catholic—that is, general—in one and the same doctrine for instruction.

### Chapter 4.—Why the apostles did not acquire estates in Judaea for building churches. From the decrees of Pope Miltiades, chapter 8: On the primitive Church.

(12, q. 1, c. *Ecclesiam.*) No one who reads the divine Scriptures is unaware that, at the beginning of the Church’s birth, the disciples were gathered together with the multitude of believers, who had one heart and one soul. Selling their estates and possessions, they brought the proceeds and distributed them to each person according to need (Acts 4).

For the apostles foresaw the future Church among the nations, especially [Col. 0200D] because the Lord had foretold to them: “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel” (Mark 16); and because they knew that they would be expelled from Judaea and scattered among the nations, and that the Church would be gathered from [Col. 0201A] an uncultivated people. Therefore they acquired no estates in Judaea, but only the proceeds for supporting the needy. But when, amid the storms and adversities of the world, the Church increased, it came to such a point that not only the nations but also the Roman emperors, who held the monarchy of almost the whole world, flocked to the faith of Christ and the sacraments of baptism.

### Chapter 5.—That priests and the other faithful decided that the fields they had customarily sold would yield greater benefit if they were given to churches, so that the faithful might be supported from their annual revenues, than if they were sold. From the decrees of Pope Urban, chapter 2.

(12, q. 1, c. *Videntes.*) But when priests, Levites, and the other faithful saw that greater benefit could result if they gave the inheritances and fields they were selling to the churches over which bishops presided, because from their revenues they could provide more abundantly and more suitably, both in present and future times, for the faithful living the common life than from their sale price, they began to give to mother churches the estates and fields which they had customarily sold and to live from their revenues. [Col. 0201B]

### Chapter 6.—At what time religious men consecrated themselves to the Lord, building basilicas upon their own estates. From the decrees of Pope Miltiades, chapter 12.

From that time onward, religious men consecrated not only the possessions and estates which they owned, but also themselves to the Lord, building basilicas upon their own properties in honor of the holy martyrs, and monasteries in the cities, in which communities of those serving the Lord might assemble. Finally, kings, governors, and magistrates not only granted adjoining properties but also themselves bestowed their own possessions throughout all the kingdoms of the earth, so that the needy, who possessed nothing in the world, might be supported; churches might be built and restored; and provisions might be granted to those who duly served God and his Church, and to his servants, so that they might be free from need. [Col. 0201C]

### Chapter 7.—That Constantine, the first of the emperors openly to embrace the Christian faith, gave all persons authority to build churches. From the same source, chapter 10.

Among these, the most religious Constantine was the first openly to embrace the faith of truth. He granted permission throughout the world to those dwelling under his empire not only to become Christians but also to build churches, and he decreed that estates should be bestowed. Finally, this aforesaid ruler established immense gifts and the construction of the church of the primary see of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, to such an extent that he left the imperial seat over which the Roman emperors successively presided and granted it for the benefit of blessed Peter and his successors. [Col. 0201D]

### Chapter 8.—That no one may build a church unless a bishop has designated the site for it and he has prepared an endowment. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 3.

(De cons., dist. 1, c. *Nemo ecclesiam.*) No one may build a church before the bishop of the city comes and publicly sets up the cross there and marks out the atrium. Beforehand, the person wishing to build must determine what will suffice for lights, guardianship, and the wages of guardians; and, after the donation has been exhibited, let him build the church. After it has been consecrated, let him sprinkle the atrium of that church with holy water. [Col. 0202A]

### Chapter 9.—Concerning one who wishes to build a church on his own estate. From the Council of Worms, chapter 6.

Whoever wishes to build a church on his own property may do so with the consent and approval of the bishop in whose parish it is located. Nevertheless, the bishop must take every precaution that older churches do not, on account of new ones, lose their dues or tithe, but that payment is always made to the older churches.

### Chapter 10.—That all basilicas built within a bishop’s territory must be subject to his authority. From the First Council of Orléans, chapter 19.

(6, q. 7, c. *Omnes basilicae.*) It has been decreed, in accordance with the rule of the ancient canons, that all basilicas which have been built or are daily being built in various places shall be under the authority of the bishop in whose territory they are situated. [Col. 0202B]

### Chapter 11.—That churches and altars whose consecration is doubtful are to be consecrated. From the same council, chapter 45.

(De cons., dist. 1, c. *Ecclesiae.*) Churches or altars whose consecration is uncertain and concerning which there is doubt are to be consecrated; superfluous altars are to be destroyed.

### Chapter 12.—That churches built in ancient times are not to be deprived of tithes or any possessions in order to give them to new ones. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 46.

Churches built in ancient times are not to be deprived either of tithes or of any possession in order that these may be given to new oratories.

### Chapter 13.—That a church must be consecrated anew if its altar has been moved. From the decrees of Pope Hyginus, chapter 4.

[Col. 0202C]

(De cons., dist. 1, c. *Si motum.*) If the altar has been moved, the church must be consecrated anew. If the walls, but not the altar, are altered, they are only to be exorcised with salt.

### Chapter 14.—That a church must be consecrated anew if it has been polluted by homicide or adultery. From the decrees of the same pope, chapter 6.

(De cons., dist. 1, c. *Si homicidio.*) If a church has been violated by homicide or adultery, it is to be cleansed with the greatest care and consecrated anew.

### Chapter 15.—That a church in which a pagan has been buried may not be consecrated unless he is removed. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 7.

[Col. 0202D]

(De cons., dist. 1, c. *Ecclesiam.*) A church in which a pagan has been buried may not be consecrated, nor may Masses be celebrated in it; rather, he must be thrown out and the place cleansed.

### Chapter 16.—That no altar may be consecrated in a church in which the bodies of the dead are buried; but, if it had previously been consecrated, Mass may be celebrated in it. From the same council, chapter 6.

In a church in which the bodies of the dead are buried, it is not lawful to consecrate an altar. But if it was consecrated previously, Mass may be celebrated in it.

### Chapter 17.—That places once dedicated to God are to remain so permanently. From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 23.

(19, q. 3, c. *Quae semel.*) Places once dedicated to God, or which have been monasteries, are to remain so permanently [Col. 0203A] and may not thereafter become secular dwellings.

### Chapter 18.—That monasteries are not to become dwellings for clerics. From the decrees of Pope Gregory sent to John, bishop of Ravenna (book IV, letter 1 in the Register).

(18, q. 2, c. *Pervenit.*) It has come to my attention that in the churches of your brotherhood certain places consecrated as monasteries have now become dwellings for clerics. While those who belong to the churches pretend to live religiously, they seek to be put in charge of monasteries, and through their manner of life the monasteries are destroyed.

16, q. 1, c. *Nemo.* For no one can serve in ecclesiastical duties and at the same time remain properly within the monastic rule: he who is daily compelled to remain in ecclesiastical ministry cannot himself maintain the strict discipline of a monastery. Therefore let your brotherhood hasten to correct this wherever it has occurred, for I in no way permit sacred places to be destroyed through clerical ambition. [Col. 0203B]

### Chapter 19.—That places long ago consecrated and afterwards defiled are to be restored. From the Council held at Aachen, chapter 6.

It has been decreed that places consecrated long ago but now defiled with filth are, insofar as possible, to be restored to their former condition.

### Chapter 20.—That no one may presume to set up any altar other than one consecrated by a bishop. From the decrees of Pope Hormisdas, chapter 10.

(De cons., dist. 1, c. *Ut nullus.*) No priest may set up another altar in a consecrated church except one sanctified by the bishop of the place or his delegate, so that there may be a distinction between what is sacred and what is not sacred. Nor may he feign a dedication where none exists. If he does so, if he is a cleric, let him be deposed; if a layman, let him be anathematized. [Col. 0203C]

### Chapter 21.—That possessed persons are to sweep the floors of the houses of God. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 111.

Let persons possessed by demons sweep the floors of the houses of God.

### Chapter 22.—That monasteries once dedicated, and the property bestowed upon them, are to remain so permanently. From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 24.

It has been decreed that monasteries once dedicated by the counsel of the bishops who govern the cities are to remain monasteries permanently; the property belonging to them must be preserved for the monasteries and they may not thereafter become secular dwellings. Those who permit this to be done shall be subject to the penalties of the canons. [Col. 0203D]

### Chapter 23.—That a church’s endowment belongs to the bishop’s governance and authority. From the Council of Worms, chapter 5.

Contrary to the decrees of the canons, many people seek to have churches which they have built consecrated on the condition that they judge the endowment they have bestowed upon the church not to belong to the bishop’s governance. This practice is disapproved as regards the past and prohibited for the future; rather, all things are to belong to the bishop’s governance and authority according to ancient custom.

### Chapter 24.—That the annual anniversary solemnities of church dedications are to be celebrated for eight days. From the decrees of Pope Felix (IV, letter 1).

(De cons., dist. 1, c. *Solemnitates.*) The annual solemnities of the dedications of churches and priests are to be celebrated solemnly, the Lord himself providing the example. In giving all a model for doing this, he came with the other people to celebrate the same festival at the dedication feast of the Temple, as it is written: “The Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem, and it was winter; and Jesus walked in the Temple, in Solomon’s portico” (John 10).

That the dedication festival (*encaenia*) is to be celebrated for eight days, you will find after the completion of the Temple’s dedication in the Book of Kings (1 Kings 8; 2 Chronicles 7). Whenever there is doubt about the consecration of churches, and there is neither certain written evidence nor reliable witnesses by whom their consecration may be known, know without any doubt that they must be consecrated. Such hesitation does not entail repetition, for that which is not known to have been done is not shown to have been repeated. [Col. 0204B]

### Chapter 25.—On restoring the fabric of a church if it has been ruined, and whether the solemnity of consecration must be repeated where there are no sanctuaries. Pope Vigilius to his brother Eutherius, chapter 4.

If the fabric of any church has been ruined and must be rebuilt, and if the solemnity of consecration must be repeated in a place where there are no sanctuaries, we judge that no impediment arises if exorcised water is not cast throughout it. For we know that the consecration of any church in which an altar of the Holy Spirit is not placed consists only in the celebration of Mass. Therefore, if any basilica of saints has been renewed even from its foundations, then, without any doubt, once the solemnity of Mass has been celebrated in it, the sanctification of the whole consecration [Col. 0204C] will be fulfilled. But if the sanctuaries which it possessed have been removed, it will again receive the reverence of sanctification by their replacement and by the solemnity of Mass.

### Chapter 26.—That ruined churches are not to be rebuilt larger than can be restored from the resources belonging to them. From the decrees of Pope Hyginus, chapter 5.

For ruined churches which are either more numerous than necessary or too large to be restored from the resources belonging to them, a measure is to be found through the bishop’s foresight by which they may be maintained.

### Chapter 27.—How the matter is to be settled if a dispute arises over the boundaries of two mother churches. From the Council at Aachen, chapter 5.

There cannot be more than one baptismal church within one boundary; there may be only one, together with its dependent chapels. If a dispute arises over the boundaries of two mother churches, the congregations belonging to each are to be distinguished.

### Chapter 28.—That no king or other person may give his own monastery to anyone except another church, exchange it except with another church, or sell it for any advantage. From the decrees of Pope Silverius, chapter 1.

No king or any other person may give his own monastery away except to another monastery, exchange it except with another monastery, or sell it for any advantage whatever. Divine, apostolic, and canonical authority has also decreed this under penalty of anathema. If this is done, it shall not be valid, [Col. 0205A] but the monastery itself is to be restored to its former condition.

### Chapter 29.—That a bishop or abbot may not transfer the property of one church to another, even though both are under his authority. From the Council of Lyons, chapter 5.

A bishop or abbot may not transfer the land of one church to another, even though both are under his authority. Nevertheless, if they wish to exchange their lands, this may be done with the consent of both.

### Chapter 30.—That altars may not be anointed with chrism unless they are stone, and that bishops of the same province must observe the order of their metropolitan. From the Council of Hippo, chapter 10.

(De cons., dist. 1, c. *Altaria, et primo.*) If altars are not stone, they are not to be consecrated with the anointing of chrism. For the celebration of divine offices, the bishops of the same province must observe the order maintained by their metropolitans. [Col. 0205B]

### Chapter 31.—That a monastery is not to be transferred from place to place without the counsel of the bishop or brethren. From the decrees of Pope Boniface, chapter 5.

If anyone wishes to relocate his monastery to another place for its improvement, this must be done with the counsel of the bishop and his brethren; and he must leave a priest in the former place for the ministries of the church.

### Chapter 32.—That all basilicas must be consecrated with Mass. From the decrees of Pope Evaristus, chapter 4.

(De cons., dist. 1, c. *Omnes basilicae.*) All basilicas must always be consecrated with Mass.

### Chapter 33.—That no bishop may forbid a pagan, heretic, or Jew to enter church when the word of God is proclaimed to the people. From the Council at Valencia, chapter 16. (Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 14.)

[Col. 0205C]

(De cons., dist. [?], c. *Episcopus.*) No bishop may forbid anyone—whether pagan, heretic, or Jew—to enter church and hear the word of God, up to the Mass of the catechumens.

### Chapter 34.—That the people who gather to celebrate Mass must not depart until it is ended and they have received the blessing. From the Council of Arles, chapter 1.

Likewise, when the people gather in God’s name to celebrate Mass, they are not to depart before the solemnity of Mass has been completed; and, when the bishop is absent, they are to receive the priest’s blessing.

### Chapter 35.—That those holding ecclesiastical benefices must repair church roofs. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 42.

[Col. 0205D]

Whoever holds an ecclesiastical benefice must give all possible assistance in repairing the roofs of churches or repairing the churches themselves, and must render the monetary payment (*numisma*; printed variant: *nonam*, “ninth”) and the tithe.

### Chapter 36.—How churches established among barbarians are to be administered. From the First Council of Constantinople, chapter 4.

The churches of God established among barbarian peoples ought to be governed and administered according to the custom observed by the Fathers.

### Chapter 37.—That churches of the Arians are to be consecrated as Catholic churches by Catholics. From the decrees of Pope John I sent to the bishops of Italy.

Wherever you find churches of the Arians, consecrate them without any delay as Catholic churches by divine prayers and works. For when we were at Constantinople, prompted and encouraged by the business of King Theodoric, and with the most pious and most Christian orthodox Emperor Justin extirpating the Arians, we consecrated as Catholic churches, with the Lord’s help, whatever churches belonging to them we were able to find in those regions. [Col. 0206A]

### Chapter 38.—What is to be done concerning a diocesan church if it has been left destitute. From the Council of Tarragona, chapter 8.

Experience, taught by many occurrences, has shown us that some diocesan churches have been left destitute. (10, q. [ ], c. *Decrevimus.*) Therefore we have decreed by this constitution that the order of ancient custom be observed: each year dioceses are to be visited by the bishop; and if any basilica is found to be abandoned, it is to be restored under his direction, because we know that it was established by rulers under ancient tradition that a third part of everything is to be received by bishops. [Col. 0206B]

### Chapter 39.—Concerning the transfer of the Church of Minturnae to the Church of Formiae. From Gregory’s Register, to Bacanda, bishop of Formiae.

And temporal necessity presses upon us, and the diminution of persons requires that we ought to assist deserted churches by a wholesome and provident arrangement. And therefore, since we have learned that the church of Minturnae has been utterly left desolate, both of clergy and people, and since we foresee that your petition on its behalf—that it should be joined to the church of Formiae, in which rests the body of the blessed martyr Erasmus and over which your brotherhood presides—is both pious and most just, we have judged it necessary, providing alike for the desolation of that place and for the poverty of your church, to grant, by the authority of this our decree, to the control of your church the revenues of the aforesaid church of Minturnae, or whatever may by ancient or modern law or privilege have belonged or be able in any manner rightfully to belong to it. From the present time, therefore, you are to take thought for it as for a church of your own, and to dispose of what belongs to it; so that henceforth that which until now might have been lost may benefit the poor of the Church and the clergy.

### CHAPTER 40.—Images in church are not to be adored; rather, by them that which is to be adored is to be recalled to the minds of the faithful. From the Council of Elvira, chapter 36.

(*On consecration*, distinction 4, chapter “It has pleased.”) It has pleased us that pictures ought not to be made in churches, lest that which is venerated and adored be depicted upon walls. [Col. 0206D]

### CHAPTER 41.—On the same matter. From the letter of Pope Gregory to Secundinus, servant of God and recluse.

It is one thing to adore an image, another to learn from the narrative represented in an image what ought to be adored. For what Scripture provides to those who read, an image provides to the unlearned who behold it; since in it the ignorant see what they ought to follow, and in it those who do not know letters read. Therefore an image is especially a substitute for reading among the nations. You, who dwell among the nations, ought carefully to have considered this, lest, being incautiously inflamed by a righteous zeal, you should produce scandal in fierce minds. Thus, what had been set in churches not for adoration but solely for instructing the minds of the ignorant ought not to have been broken. And because antiquity has not without reason allowed narratives of the saints to be depicted in venerable places, if you had tempered your zeal with discernment, you could undoubtedly both have obtained beneficially what you intended and not scattered the gathered flock, but rather have gathered it; so that the unstained name of shepherd might shine forth, and the guilt of a scatterer might not rest upon you. [Col. 0207A]

### CHAPTER 42.—A bishop is not to demand any gift as a due for consecration. From the Council of Worms, chapter 3.

It has pleased us that whenever a bishop is invited by one of the faithful to consecrate churches, he should not demand any gift from the founder as though it were owed to him. But if the founder himself should offer something by his own free vow, it is not to be refused. [Col. 0207B] Nevertheless, every bishop should remember that he is not to dedicate a church before first receiving confirmation, by a charter of donation, of the endowment of the basilica and of its provision for service. For it is no slight rashness if a church is consecrated like a private house, without lights or without substantial support for those who are to serve there.

### CHAPTER 43.—It is not lawful to consecrate a church in which the bodies of dead unbelievers have been buried, unless they are removed and its walls stripped. From the Council of Cologne, chapter 3.

It is not lawful to sanctify a church in which the bodies of dead unbelievers are buried. But if it appears suitable for consecration, after the bodies have been removed and the walls and timbers of that place stripped away, it is to be rebuilt. If it was previously consecrated, Masses may be celebrated in it, provided that those buried there were faithful. [Col. 0207C]

### CHAPTER 44.—To what uses the timbers of a dedicated church should be put. From the decrees of Pope Hyginus, chapter 3.

(*On consecration*, distinction 1, chapter “Timbers.”) The timbers of a dedicated church ought not to be applied to another work, except to another church, or to be burned by fire, or for the benefit of brethren in a monastery; they must not, however, be used for the works of laypeople.

### CHAPTER 45.—What a bishop should do if several heirs dispute over one church. From the Council of Trebur, chapter 20.

(16, question 7, chapter “Several.”) If several heirs dispute over a common church, the bishop is to order the sacred relics removed [Col. 0207D] and the church closed, until by common consent and with the bishop’s counsel they appoint for it a priest and determine his means of support.

Likewise Pope Gregory, in his decrees, chapter 5.

(16, question 7, chapter “It must be considered.”) Concerning churches divided among co-heirs, it must be considered whether the co-heirs themselves are willing, in accordance with the bishop’s direction and admonition, to retain and honor them. But if they oppose this, it remains in the bishop’s power whether he permits them to continue thus, or wishes to remove the relics from them.

### CHAPTER 46.—On the same matter. From the Council of Metz, chapter 11.

It has been reported to the holy synod that churches situated upon private property are divided among heirs, [Col. 0208A] and that through this very division such discord arises that one altar is made into four shares, and the individual shares have individual priests. This cannot in any way occur without discord and contention. Therefore it has seemed to us that churches of this sort ought not to be divided among heirs; and if they come into dispute and contentions arise among them through which the priest cannot there perform his office canonically, the bishop of the city is to command that the solemnities of Mass are by no means to be celebrated there until they return to concord, and that church, with equal will and counsel, canonically has a priest who can freely carry out his ministry there.

### CHAPTER 47.—It is good for parish churches to be organized and preserved in the manner of the Roman Church. From the second letter of Dionysius to Bishop Severus.

[Col. 0208B] Concerning parish churches, therefore—regarding which you wished to consult the Apostolic See as to how they ought to be safeguarded throughout the province of Córdoba and provided with priests—nothing seems better for us to make known to your charity than that you follow what is known to have been recently done by us in the Roman Church. We assigned each individual church to an individual priest, and established that each should have its own proper right: namely, so that none may invade the boundaries or right of another’s parish, but each may be content with his own boundaries and so guard the church and people entrusted to him that before the tribunal of the eternal Judge he may render account for all entrusted to him, and receive not judgment but glory for his deeds. This rule also, dearest brother, it is fitting that you and all bishops should follow; and you should make known to all whom you can what is written to you, [Col. 0208C] so that this command may become not special but general.

### CHAPTER 48.—Each priest is to be content with one church. From the Council of Rheims, chapter 3.

Each priest is to be content with the one church to which he was ordained, and no one is to presume to minister in two churches.

### CHAPTER 49.—One church is not to be divided among several priests. From the same council, chapter 9.

(21, question 2, chapter “Just as in every.”) Just as there ought to be one priest in each church, so the church itself, which is called his bride or wife, cannot be divided among several priests, but shall have only one priest [Col. 0208D] to govern her chastely and sincerely. Therefore we forbid anyone to presume to divide a church between two or more persons, because the Church of Christ ought to be a wife and bride, not a prostitute, as Pope Callixtus attests (letter 2, chapter 3).

### CHAPTER 50.—Likewise, each priest is to be content with one church. From the same council, chapter 10.

It has been decreed that each church should have its own priest, wherever the means permit this under the bishop’s provision.

### CHAPTER 51.—Likewise on the same matter. From the Council of Nantes, chapter 8.

For just as a bishop cannot have more than one city, and a man one wife, so a priest may have only one church. Therefore no priest is to presume to have two churches [Col. 0209A] if he desires to remain secure in his rank.

### CHAPTER 52.—No priest, having abandoned his own church, ought to aspire to a more important one. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 10.

(7, question 1, chapter “If anyone.”) If anyone of the sacerdotal order, despising a lesser church, should ambitiously and improperly aspire to a more important one, the canonical determination concerning him is to be maintained: that is, he is to be deprived of both.

### CHAPTER 53.—Just as a wife is not permitted to marry another while her husband lives, so, while a priest lives, the church entrusted to him is not permitted to be judged or administered by another. From the decrees of Pope Callixtus, chapter 4.

(Ibid., chapter “Like another’s.”) Just as another man’s wife is not permitted, while her own husband lives, either to be violated by another, or to be judged or administered by him, so neither may the wife [Col. 0209B] of a bishop or priest—that is undoubtedly understood to be his church or parish—while he lives be judged or administered by another, or enjoy his intercourse. Hence the Apostle says: “A wife is bound by the law so long as her husband lives; when he dies, she is released from the law of her husband” (I Cor. VII). Likewise the church, called the priest’s wife, is bound to him while he lives; when he dies, she is to marry in the Lord, that is, canonically. For if, while he lives, she marries another, she will be judged an adulteress.

### CHAPTER 54.—On churches or saints newly discovered. From the Council of Cologne, chapter 5.

Churches or saints newly discovered are by no means to be venerated in his territory without the authority of the discoverer, unless the bishop approves; while canonical authority in this matter, and concerning all churches, is preserved.

### CHAPTER 55.—A priest ought to perform no service from an endowed holding except ecclesiastical service. From the Council of Worms, chapter 50.

[Col. 0209C]

(23, question 8, chapter “Holding.”) It has been decreed that one full holding, free from every service, be assigned to each church; and that priests established therein perform no service other than ecclesiastical service from tithes, from the offerings of the faithful, from houses, courts, or gardens situated near the church, or from the prescribed holding. If they have anything beyond these, they are to render from it the service due to their lords.

### CHAPTER 56.—No mortal is to compel any priest to pay a rent from an endowed holding, slaves, tithes, offerings of the faithful, or revenues bestowed upon churches. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 8.

[Col. 0209D]

In accordance with synodal decrees, we have ordained that no mortal shall compel any priest to pay any rent from ecclesiastical land, a holding, or slaves; nor from anything which anyone may have bestowed on the Church for a burial-place; nor from tithes and the offerings of the faithful. Nor may anyone, of whatever rank or dignity, withdraw anything from these or demand any temporal payment. If anyone does so, he is to be deprived of communion until he has made satisfaction.

### CHAPTER 57.—No memorial of martyrs is to be accepted as authentic except where a body or certain relics are present, or where the origin of some dwelling, possession, or passion is handed down on wholly trustworthy authority. From the African Council, chapter 50.

[Col. 0210A]

(*On consecration*, distinction 1, chapter “It has pleased.”) Likewise, it has pleased us that altars established here and there in fields and along roads as though they were memorials of martyrs, in which no body or relics of a martyr are proved to have been deposited, should, if possible, be overthrown by the bishops who preside over those places. But if this is not permitted because of popular disturbances, the people are at least to be warned not to frequent those places, so that those of sound judgment may not be held there by any superstition. And absolutely no memorial of martyrs is to be accepted as authentic unless either a body or certain relics are present, or the origin of some dwelling, possession, or passion is handed down on wholly trustworthy authority. For altars established anywhere through dreams [Col. 0210B] and through empty, so-called revelations of any persons whatsoever are altogether to be rejected.

### CHAPTER 58.—No profane person is to dishonor the dignity of martyrs. From the First Council of Carthage, chapter 2.

Let no profane person dishonor the dignity of martyrs, nor reduce to the status of suffering bodies those who have been commanded to be committed to burial solely through ecclesiastical mercy; so as to call by the name of martyrs those driven to death by madness, or separated by some such pact or by another form of sin [“disjunctos,” separated], at a time and for a reason not appropriate to the celebration of martyrdoms. But if anyone, to the injury of martyrs, adds infamy to their renown, it has pleased us that, if he is a layperson, he be subjected to penance; but if a cleric, that after admonition [Col. 0210C] and investigation he be deprived of his rank.

### CHAPTER 59.—The solemnities of Mass are not to take place everywhere, but in places consecrated by the bishop or where he has permitted them. From the Council of Trebur, chapter 4.

(*On consecration*, distinction 1, chapters “Of Masses” and “We permit.”) We decree that the solemnities of Mass are to be celebrated not anywhere whatsoever, but in places consecrated by the bishop or where he has given permission. We also permit that, wherever churches have been set on fire and burned by Northmen, Slavs, Bulgars, wicked Christians, or in any other way—which has happened very frequently as our sins demand—Masses may meanwhile be celebrated in chapels with a consecrated altar-table, until the churches themselves can be restored. For those travelling, if a church is lacking, [Col. 0210D] we permit the solemnities of Mass to be celebrated outdoors or in tents, provided that a consecrated altar-table and the other sacred ministrations belonging to that office are available; otherwise we prohibit it altogether.

### CHAPTER 60.—Except in great necessity, Mass is to be celebrated only in a consecrated place. From the decrees of Pope Felix IV addressed to all bishops (IV, letter 1, chapter 1).

(*On consecration*, distinction 1, chapters “Consecration” and “Tabernacle.”) I have gratefully received your letters, which you sent to the Apostolic See concerning certain questions, as to a head, in order that you might receive answers from that source from which the whole Church received the beginning of all religion; and I have taken care to reply briefly. For it is clear to all who know the precepts of the New and Old Testaments that consecrations of churches and celebrations [Col. 0211A] of Mass ought not, except in great necessity, to take place anywhere but in places consecrated to the Lord. We read that Moses, at the Lord’s command, made the tabernacle and consecrated it with its table, altar, and other vessels and implements for completing divine worship; and we know that he consecrated them not only with divine prayers but also, at the Lord’s command, anointed them with holy oil (Num. VII). How these things were done, and how those sacred objects were handled, carried, set up, and taken down only by priests anointed by unction and consecrated to the Lord in holy vestments, and by Levites, is found in the Law of the Lord, in the ordinances written through Moses at the Lord’s command (Lev. VIII). [Col. 0211B] It is read in the Book of Kings how David, most devout of kings, enlarged the worship of God and wished to build the Temple of the Lord (II Reg. VII), but was forbidden because of the much blood he had shed, although he had himself gathered the funds (I Par. XXII); and how Solomon, his son, by the Lord’s command and aid, accomplished what David had desired to do, consecrating the temple with its altar and the other things for carrying out divine worship (III Reg., throughout).

### CHAPTER 61.—On the same matter. From a letter of Pope Felix IV sent to various bishops.

(Ibid.) The Jews had consecrated with divine supplications the places in which they sacrificed to the Lord, and they offered gifts to the Lord in no places except those dedicated to God. If the Jews, who served the shadow of the law, did this, how much more ought we, to whom truth has been revealed and through Jesus Christ grace and truth have been given (John I), to build temples for the Lord and adorn them as best we can; and devoutly and solemnly consecrate them with divine prayers and holy anointings, together with their altars, vessels, vestments, and the other implements required for divine worship; and not celebrate Masses or offer sacrifices to the Lord in places other than those consecrated to God by bishops—and not by chorepiscopi, who have often been forbidden to do so—except, as stated, when supreme necessity requires it. [Col. 0211C]

(*On consecration*, distinction 1, chapter “Just as no others.”) And when supreme necessity compels this to be done, it is not to be done in houses, because the offering of sacrifices in houses has been prohibited in the sacred canons, but in tabernacles dedicated with divine prayers by bishops, and on tables consecrated to the Lord and anointed with sacred unction by bishops. It is to be done on account of supreme necessity, as stated above, and not for anyone’s pleasure or laziness. It is safer [or: better] not to sing or hear Mass than to do so in places where it ought not to be done, except, as has often been said, when supreme necessity occurs, since necessity has no law. Therefore it is written: “See that you do not offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see, but in the place which the Lord your God shall choose” (Deut. XII). And in Exodus it is read: “You have seen that I have spoken to you from heaven. You shall not make gods of silver, nor shall you make gods of gold for yourselves. You shall make me an altar of earth, and you shall offer [Col. 0212A] upon it your burnt offerings and peace offerings, your sheep and oxen, in every place where there shall be a memorial of my name” (Exod. XX). And just as no others but priests consecrated to the Lord ought to sing Masses or offer sacrifices upon the altar, so it is not lawful [“licebit,” shall not be lawful] to sing Masses or offer sacrifices in places other than those aforesaid consecrated to the Lord.

Thus it is read in chapter 26 of the Council of Laodicea: if those who have not been ordained by bishops cannot exorcize either in churches or in houses, then much more may the ministries of a higher rank neither be exercised, nor offices performed, nor sacrifices offered, except by those consecrated to those ranks which they ought to exercise. And, as was mentioned a little above, offerings ought not to be made in houses; this is prohibited in chapter 58 of the same council as follows. (Distinction 69, “It is not fitting.”) Bishops or priests ought not to celebrate offerings in houses. [Col. 0212B]

### CHAPTER 62.—Likewise on the same matter. From the decrees of Pope Clement (letter 3), chapter 32.

(*On consecration*, distinction 1, chapter “Therefore here, that is.”) Therefore here—that is, while you are placed in the present life—you ought to recognize the will and command of God concerning the place where action and sacrifice are to occur, because it is not lawful to sacrifice or celebrate Masses in places other than those in which the proper bishop has ordered it, or which have been consecrated by a bishop canonically ordained and holding the city. [The text has the variant *consecratus fuerit*, “has been consecrated.”] Otherwise these things must not be done nor rightly celebrated, as the New and Old Testaments teach. The apostles received these things from the Lord and handed them down to us; these we teach, and command you and all those whose duty it is to act to hold and teach them without reproach. [Col. 0212C]

### CHAPTER 63.—Likewise on the same matter. From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 58.

Offerings ought not to be celebrated in houses by bishops or priests.

### CHAPTER 64.—Likewise on the same matter. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 4.

We have heard that certain laypeople command their priests to celebrate Masses in their private houses, so that among the running about of dogs and herds of prostitutes the mysteries of holiness are polluted rather than consecrated. Therefore we command that no priest presume to sing Mass outside a church, unless perhaps necessity of travel requires it. In a tent or outdoors [“sub divo,” under the open sky], in a clean place far removed from every impurity, we permit Masses to be celebrated; and this in no case without a consecrated altar-table. [Col. 0212D]

### CHAPTER 65.—Masses are not to be celebrated before the third hour of the day. From the letter of Pope Telesphorus, chapter 6.

Celebrations of Mass are by no means to be held before the third hour of the day, because at that same hour the Lord was crucified and the Holy Spirit is read to have descended upon the apostles—except on the night of the Nativity.

### CHAPTER 66.—It is lawful to celebrate Masses every day in memory of the faithful departed. From the Second Council of Chalon, chapter 39.

(*On consecration*, distinction 1, chapter “It has further seemed to us.”) It has further seemed to us that in all solemnities of Mass the Lord should at the appropriate place be entreated for the spirits of the dead. For just as no day is excepted on which prayer is not made for the living and for all manner of needs, so likewise no day ought to be excepted on which prayers for the souls of the faithful are not poured out to the Lord in the solemnities of Mass. From ancient times, therefore, the holy Church has maintained this custom: that the spirits of those at rest are commended to the Lord in solemnities of Mass and other prayers. Blessed Augustine says (*On Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, book, chapter 4): “Supplications for the spirits of the dead, which we commend as to be made for all in Christian and Catholic fellowship, are not to be omitted.” The Church has also undertaken the commemoration of departed persons, even persons of such importance, under a general remembrance, so that for those lacking parents, children, or any relatives or friends for these observances, a single common pious mother may render it to them. [Cols. 0213A–B]

### CHAPTER 67.—The Mass of the dead is to be sung for all Christians. From the sayings of Dionysius the Areopagite.

Dionysius the Areopagite says that those who offer Masses for a bad person commit blasphemies against God. Augustine says that it should be done for all Christians, because it either benefits them or profits those who offer it.

### CHAPTER 68.—The rites of Mass in all churches of the province are to follow those in the metropolitan church. From the Council of Girona, chapter 1.

(*On consecration*, distinction 2, chapter “Rites.”) As the rites of Mass are performed in the metropolitan church, so, in God’s name, both the order of Mass itself and the custom of chanting and ministering are to be observed in all churches of the province. [Col. 0213C]

### CHAPTER 69.—Prayers and prefaces not approved in council are not to be used in celebration. From the African Council, chapter 64. (Under Boniface I and Celestine I, chapter 70.)

It has also pleased us that prayers approved in council—whether prefaces, commendations, or impositions of hands—be used by all; and that no others contrary to the faith be uttered at all, but that whatever has been conferred with [variant: “collected by”] the more prudent persons be said.

### CHAPTER 70.—No priest is to dare celebrate Mass alone. From the Council of Nantes, chapter 30.

(17, question 4, chapter “It has determined.”) The holy council has determined that no priest shall presume to celebrate [variant: “sing”] Mass alone. For to whom does he say, “The Lord be with you,” “Lift up your hearts,” or “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God,” when no one is present to respond? Or in the canon, “And of all those standing around,” when no one is there? Or whom does he invite to prayer when he says, “Let us pray,” while no one prays with him? Thus either these words must be entirely omitted—and then the sacrifice will not merely be imperfect, but whoever he may be will incur that terrible sentence: “If anyone takes away from this, may God take away his share from the book of life”—or, if he whispers them to walls and mice, it will be ridiculous. Therefore this dangerous superstition is especially to be banished from the monasteries of monks. Let prelates provide that priests in monasteries and other churches have fellow-workers in the celebration of Masses. [Col. 0214A] Whoever violates this is to be suspended from office.

### CHAPTER 71.—Nothing is to be done in church except that for which it was made. From the sayings of Saint Benedict (chapter 52 of his Rule).

(Distinction 42, chapter “Oratory.”) Let the oratory be what it is called, and let nothing else be done or stored there except what is suitable to divine service.

### CHAPTER 72.—On the same matter. From the sayings of Saint Augustine.

In the oratory, apart from the worship of praying and chanting to God, absolutely nothing is to be done, so that the works continually performed there may accord with its name.

### CHAPTER 73.—Likewise on the same matter. From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 28.

(Distinction 42, chapter “It is not fitting.”) Love-feasts (*agapae*) ought not to be held in divine dwellings, that is, churches; nor ought people to eat or spread couches within the house of the Lord. [Col. 0214B]

### CHAPTER 74.—No one is to establish taverns in a church. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 28.

No bishops or clerics are to feast in a church, unless perhaps travellers are refreshed there because of the necessity of lodging; and the people too are, as far as possible, to be forbidden such feasts.

### CHAPTER 75.—On the same matter. From the Council of Tours.

It has been reported to the holy synod that certain priests establish taverns—an abomination—in churches entrusted to them, and there sell wine through tavern-keepers, or permit it to be sold. Where only prayers, the divine word, and the praise of God ought to resound, there occur banquets and drunkenness, laughter and applause, filthy speech, quarrels, and contentions. How contrary this is to God, the Lord Jesus shows, who, when he came into the Temple, drove from it all the sellers, buyers, and seated money-changers with a cord made into a whip (John II). If he cast out those things that appeared lawfully sold in the Temple and were bought in order to be offered to the Lord in that Temple itself, what do you suppose will become of so pestilential a presumption and contempt for God? And if not only priests but all clerics are commanded not to enter taverns, who can endure that the churches of God should become taverns? Therefore the synod altogether forbids this ever to occur in the future. If it occurs, the priest is to be deposed, and laypeople are to be deprived of communion and expelled from the church which they have dishonored. [Col. 0214C–D]

On the same matter, from the same council, chapter 3. For if the house of God is called a house of prayer (Matt. XXI), it ought to be what it is called, and nothing else ought to be done or stored there. For where the body of the Lord is consecrated, where the presence of angels is not doubted, where deposited relics of saints are venerated, let nothing dishonorable appear that might offend the eyes of those approaching the sanctuary; let nothing be seen there that pertains to temporal gain, but let all things be holy, all things pure, and concerned only with ecclesiastical ministry.

### CHAPTER 76.—Every faithful person may have an oratory in his own house, but Masses may not be celebrated there. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 3.

[Col. 0215A]

(*On consecration*, distinction 1, chapter “To each.”) Every one of the faithful may have an oratory in his own house and pray there, but Masses may not be celebrated there.

### CHAPTER 77.—Lewd song around churches and in church courtyards is altogether to be forbidden. From the First Council of Mainz, chapter 48.

We altogether prohibit shameful and lewd song around churches and in the courtyards of churches, a thing to be avoided everywhere.

### CHAPTER 78.—Relics of saints are not to be placed in rural oratories without the presence of a parish cleric. From the Council of Epaone, chapter 25.

Relics of saints are not to be placed in rural oratories [Col. 0215B] unless perhaps there happens to be nearby a cleric of the parish who may serve the sacred pledges [variant: “ashes”] by frequent chanting of psalms.

### CHAPTER 79.—The seats of bishops may, because of various necessities, be transferred to safer places. From the register of Pope Gregory, to John, bishop of Biletrum (book II, letter 11).

(17, question 1, chapter “The condition of the times.”) The condition of the times admonishes a bishop to transfer episcopal sees, established from ancient times in certain cities, to other places of the same diocese which we judge safer, so that both the inhabitants may live more securely and the danger of barbarians may more easily be avoided. Therefore we command you, John, our brother and fellow-bishop of the city of Biletrum, to move your see thence to the place called Renati, at Saint Andrew the Apostle; [Col. 0215C] so that you may be freer from hostile attack and establish there the customary observance of solemn feasts.

### CHAPTER 80.—There are three reasons for transferring places of saints. Saint Augustine.

(*On consecration*, distinction 1, chapter “For three reasons.”) Places of saints are to be transferred for three reasons. First, when persecution has made their places dangerous. Second, when there is difficulty of location. Third, when they are burdened by the association of evil persons.

### CHAPTER 81.—When martyrs are transferred, honor migrates with them. Saint Jerome.

It should be noted that, when some martyrs are transferred, honor moves with them; but when others are transferred, honor does not cease to remain in their places.

### CHAPTER 82.—The blood of martyrs consecrates a place, not the place the blood. From the sayings of Augustine.

[Col. 0213A]

The blood of martyrs consecrates a place, not the place the blood. If anyone says, “The church is mine,” say to him what is read in the Song: “My dove is one, and my beloved is one” (Song VI); and say to him: “It is manifest: the son was killed in the bosom of his mother and nurse; nevertheless, know that only the nurse was consecrated, though polluted by this pollution, while the son died.”

### CHAPTER 83.—Why it is called a basilica. Isidore.

*Basileon* was the Greek word for “king.” Hence *basilica*, “royal,” because in the earliest times only kings were buried in it. For this reason it received the name. For in those times other people were either burned by fire or buried beneath a heap of stones. [Col. 0216A]

### CHAPTER 84.—On those who make the house of God contemptible. From the Council of Gangra, chapter 5.

(Distinction 30, chapter “If anyone teaches.”) If anyone teaches that the house of God is contemptible, and likewise the assemblies celebrated in it, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER 85.—What is to be done with a bishop who has obtained a church through secular powers. From the Canons of the Apostles, chapter 31.

(16, question 7, “If any bishop.”) If any bishop, having used secular powers, obtains a church through them, he is to be deposed and cut off, together with all who communicate with him.

### CHAPTER 86.—What is to be done with a priest who has driven another priest from the church to which he was lawfully ordained by means of money. From the Second Council of Mainz, chapter 5.

[Col. 0216B]

Any priest who has acquired a church for a price, when he is known to act contrary to the discipline of ecclesiastical rule, and who has by money expelled another priest lawfully ordained to that church and thus claimed it for himself, is in every respect to be deposed.

### CHAPTER 87.—Laypeople are not to eject priests from churches. From the same council, chapter 29.

Laypeople are not to eject priests from churches or appoint them without the consent of their bishops.

### CHAPTER 88.—No one may give or take away a church from a priest without the bishop’s consent. From the Second Council of Chalon, chapter 42.

[Col. 0216C] (16, question 7, chapter “It has been found.”) It has been found that many, through the rashness of their own judgment and—what is more serious—led by greed, give churches to certain priests or take them away from them without the consent of their bishops. Therefore, the canonical rule must be observed: no one may give a church to any priest without the bishop’s consent. If he has acquired it justly, he is not to lose it except because of serious fault and by canonical severity before the bishop.

### CHAPTER 89.—No one is to demand any gift from a priest for entrusting a church to him. From the Second Council of Mainz, chapter 30.

No one whatsoever is to demand gifts from priests for the entrusting of a church.

### CHAPTER 90.—A priest who gives anything to cleric or layperson for investiture with a church is to be deposed. From the Council of Rouen, chapter 5.

[Col. 0216D]

It has been decreed and in every way forbidden that, if any priest is found to give or to have given gifts to any cleric or layperson, or to pay any [variant: “other”] sum of money in order to redeem for a price the vacant church of another priest, he is, for this greed, robbery, presumption, and pursuit of shameful gain, to be expelled from the clergy and regarded as outside the rule.

### CHAPTER 91.—Priests are to admonish women throughout their parishes to prepare altar linens. From the Council of Rheims, chapter 4.

Priests are to preach to the women throughout their congregations that they should prepare linens for the altars.

### CHAPTER 92.—Bishops are to determine what service priests owe their lords on account of churches. From the Council of Arles, chapter 3.

[Col. 0217A]

Bishops are to determine what service priests owe their lords on account of churches.

### CHAPTER 93.—No priest is to give gifts upon entering a church. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 10.

No priest is to give *xenia*—customary gifts of hospitality—upon entering a church.

### CHAPTER 94.—Estates bought by a priest are to belong to the church which he entered possessing nothing. From the Council of Rheims, chapter 6.

It is to be investigated whether a priest who possessed no patrimony when he was advanced to ecclesiastical order has afterward bought estates, and to whose right they belong; for, according to canonical authority, they ought to belong to the church to which he was promoted when he possessed nothing. [Col. 0217B]

### CHAPTER 95.—On the same matter. From the Council of Agde, chapter 54.

(12, question 4, chapter “Priest.”) When a priest holds a diocese, he is to make out documents in the name of the church for the things that he buys, so that they may not depart from the administration of the church which he holds.

### CAP. 96.—That bishops, priests, deacons, and any clerics must leave to the Church the estates which they acquire after being assigned to a church; but that they may dispose as they wish of what they receive by hereditary right or someone’s gift. From the Third Council of Carthage, canon 49.

[Col. 0217C] (12, q. 3, c. *Placuit*.) It was resolved that bishops, priests, deacons, and any clerics who are ordained while possessing nothing, and who, during their episcopacy or clerical office, purchase lands or any estates in their own name, are to be held liable as guilty of encroaching upon the Lord’s property, unless they convey those same things to the church to which they have been assigned. But if anything comes to them through the personal generosity of someone, or by succession from kindred, let them do with it what they wish.

Concerning the same matter. From the same council, canon 48. Let every priest leave to his own church the property which he acquires after the day of his consecration.

Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Toledo. Moreover, if a priest acquires anything after ordination, what has been established in the canons concerning those who are consecrated and possess nothing is to be observed.

From the Council of Rheims, canon 10. Inquiry must be made whether any priest has purchased property, under another name, from the revenues of the church or from the offerings and vows of the faithful; whether he has erected buildings there, or placed there things belonging to the church; whether he has allowed women to frequent the place; or—what is more shameful—whether he has kept there such women as carry on their spinning and manage the household, while the priest himself has frequently come and stayed in the same place. If, contrary to the decrees of the canons, he does this evil—for just as a priest ought not to practise usury either in his own name or in another’s, so much the less ought he to commit fraud with ecclesiastical resources—then it is sacrilege, and he shares the crime [*par crimen*] [Col. 0218A] of Judas, who carried off and stole the sacred offerings.

### CAP. 97.—That parishes assigned to each church by the former disposition must remain unshaken in perpetual security. Gelasius to Bishops Maximus and Eusebius.

(16, q. 3, c. *Licet regulis*.) Although the ancient rules provide that parishes assigned to each church by the former disposition cannot be disturbed on any grounds, lest, through the worst custom and the growing rashness of bad example, universal confusion should arise everywhere, nevertheless, by decrees sent out by us not long ago, we ordered that all things which had been so seized should be restored.

But because the rashness of usurpers thinks that it can generate law for itself, if it adds obstinate retention to its wrongdoing, we desire that you carry out what we decreed between our brother and fellow bishop Constantius, priest of the church of Camiscana, and those sent by the bishop of Ancona. At that time we set down in writing the rule to be followed in other investigations. Therefore we do not permit, by any presumption, the condition of parishes—which has endured with the stability of perpetual antiquity—to be altered. For neither a bishop’s negligence, nor a temporary claim arising perhaps through carelessness, nor consent produced by indolence, nor a petition obtained by stealth, can sever a diocese once established, from which the faithful people have always gathered for regeneration and confirmation.

### CAP. 98.—Concerning the composition for sacrilege, and the ways in which sacrilege may be committed. John VIII, in the book of Gothic law.

[Col. 0218C]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops, counts, viscounts, hundredmen, Catholic judges dwelling in Spain, Gothia, and the provinces, and to all the Catholic people of the West: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

Know, most beloved sons, that for the well-being of God’s holy Church we ordered a synodal council to assemble at the city of Troyes. While we were sitting in council, our son Sinebold, bishop of the holy primatial see of Narbonne, came before us with his suffragan bishops and brought us the book of Gothic law. In it there was nothing concerning sacrileges, [Col. 0218D] while those same laws stated that cases not provided for by those laws were not to be heard by the judges of that land. Thus the right of holy Church was being stifled by the inhabitants of Gaul and the provinces of Spain.

Accordingly, after our Serenity, together with the aforesaid bishops, had examined the Roman laws, in which there was provision concerning sacrileges, we found there a law established by the Emperor Justinian fixing the composition for sacrilege at five pounds of the finest gold. But we ordered that the milder law established by the pious prince Charles concerning the composition for sacrilege be observed: namely, thirty pounds of tested silver—that is, the sum of six hundred solidi in the purest silver. Therefore, whoever is found guilty of sacrilege shall make this milder compensation to those bishops, or [Col. 0219A] abbots, or persons to whom the complaint of sacrilege justly pertains. If the person guilty of sacrilege refuses to do so, he shall remain subject to excommunication until he pays the aforesaid composition of six hundred solidi. And if he dies in this obstinacy, his body shall not be carried to burial with psalms and hymns. We order that this law be written at the end of the code of secular law.

Thus far the pope’s law. Sacrilege is committed if anyone breaks into a church, or violates the thirty ecclesiastical paces surrounding a church; or if, in houses situated within the aforesaid paces, someone plunders or carries anything away from them; or if someone inflicts injury or carries off goods belonging to unarmed clerics, monks, persons devoted to God, or ecclesiastical persons. Chapels situated within the circuit of the walls of fortified places are not included or placed under this observance.

Likewise, sacrilege is committed by taking what is sacred from what is sacred, what is not sacred from what is sacred, or what is sacred from what is not sacred. But taking what is not sacred from what is not sacred cannot be reckoned as the crime of sacrilege; it must be punished according to the judgment of secular laws or according to the custom of the country.

### CAP. 99.—Concerning two bishops disputing over the parish of a certain basilica, and that peaceful possession for thirty years excludes every objection.

(16, q. 3, c. *Inter memoratos*.) A dispute arose between our aforesaid brothers Fulgentius, bishop of Astigi, and Honorius, [Col. 0219C] bishop of Cordoba, concerning the parish of a certain basilica, which one of them asserted to be Celtasensian. Since an action concerning the boundary had hitherto been maintained between the two parties, although its long-standing retention did not produce prejudice to any right, and lest our judgment should further be called into doubt between them, the canons having been produced, synodal decrees were read aloud. Their authority warns that greed must be restrained so that no one may usurp another’s boundaries.

For this reason it was resolved that men be sent by the respective parties to inspect the matter, so that the diocese of the possessing church—provided that a boundary marked by a true sign shows the basilica to lie within it—shall have perpetual dominion, since it has the right of possession. But if a lawful boundary does not enclose that basilica, and yet the exception of prescription through long time is proved, the appeal of the present bishop shall not prevail, because the thirty-year exception bars those who have remained silent. This is also prescribed by the edicts of secular princes and decreed by the authority of the bishops of Rome. But if, within the limits of thirty years, an unjust retention of a basilica beyond another’s boundaries is found, it shall without delay be restored to the right of the bishop reclaiming it.

### CAP. 100.—What is included under the term “immunity,” and what compensation is due for violated immunity. From the Book of Capitularies.

It has come to us that some violators rashly assert that the name of immunity includes no more than the enclosure of a monastery, and that all other things, although belonging to the same churches or monasteries, are outside [Col. 0220A] immunity. Therefore we will and decree that all understand that not only the enclosure of a monastery or church, and the precinct of churches, stand under the protection of immunity, but also houses, estates, estate-enclosures, constructed fisheries, and whatever is surrounded by ditches, hedges, or any other kind of enclosure, are included under the same designation of immunity.

Whatever injury or damage anyone deliberately commits within such defenses, against things belonging by right to those churches or monasteries, is judged a breach of immunity. But if, as often happens, anyone causes damage by chance in fields, open lands, or woods which are uncultivated and in no way enclosed, although the field, open land, or wood belongs to a church or monastery possessing a charter of immunity, immunity is nevertheless not judged to have been broken. Therefore the person convicted of causing disturbance or damage in such a place is to be fined not by the composition of six hundred solidi, but according to the law in force in that locality.

### CAP. 101.—That no payment whatever is to be demanded for a burial place. Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Sardinia (Book VII of the *Register*, letter 55).

(13, q. 2, c. *Quaesta*.) It is exceedingly wicked and far removed from a priest’s office to seek payment for land granted to decay, and to wish to make gain from another’s grief. After, by God’s agency, we had attained the episcopal office, we entirely prohibited this vice in our own church and allowed this wicked custom no longer to be practised. We remembered that when Abraham requested from the sons of Ephron—that is, the sons of Seor—a burial place, at a price, for burying the body of his wife, he refused to accept payment, lest he seem to have gained profit from a corpse (Gen. XXIII).

If, therefore, a pagan man showed such consideration, how much more ought we, who are called priests, not to do this? I therefore admonish you lest this vice of avarice should again be rashly attempted, even in other churches. But whenever you permit someone to be buried in your church, we do not forbid you to receive something if that person’s parents, relatives, or heirs freely wish to offer it for lights. Yet we entirely prohibit anything from being requested or exacted, lest, what would be utterly irreligious, the Church be called venal—God forbid—or you seem to rejoice in human deaths, if you seek by any means to derive gain from their corpses.

### CAP. 102.—That laypersons must not dare expel priests from the churches to which they have been appointed. Leo III to King Charles.

It appears contrary to the rulings of the holy Fathers if a secular person or layman attempts to expel priests from churches in which, at the time of their ordination, they were named or introduced.

### CAP. 103.—That priests may not, in contempt of their bishop, separate themselves from their churches and live privately elsewhere. From the Council of Antioch, canon 5.

If any priest or deacon, disregarding his bishop, separates himself from the church and, gathering people privately around himself, dares to erect an altar, and nevertheless remains disobedient while his bishop exhorts and recalls him once and again, he must in every way be deposed. Let him never hope to obtain a cure of souls or to receive back his former rank. If he persists in disturbing the whole Church, he must be restrained, as a seditious person, by the external civil power.

### CAP. 104.—Concerning the boundaries of cemeteries; that is, how many paces they ought to have. Pope Nicholas, to all bishops.

(17, q. 4, c. *Sicut antiquitus*.) Concerning the boundaries of cemeteries, we establish what was established of old by the holy Fathers: a greater church shall have sixty paces around its circuit; chapels or lesser churches, thirty. Whoever attempts to violate their boundary, or carries away from it a human person or that person’s goods, unless he is a public robber, shall be excommunicated until he makes amends and restores what he carried off.

### CAP. 105.—That subdeacons must not enter the sanctuary or touch the Lord’s vessels, canon 21.

Since subdeacons ought not to have permission to enter the *secretarium* or sanctuary, which the Greeks call the *diaconion*, nor to touch the Lord’s vessels.

### CAP. 106.—That rural parishes must remain within the jurisdiction of the bishop who has governed them for thirty years. From the Council of Chalcedon, canon 16.

[Col. 0221C]

(16, q. 3, c. *Per singulas*.) We decree that, in every church, rural parishes or possessions are to remain immovable with the bishops who retain them, especially those who have possessed and governed them without violence for thirty years. But if a dispute concerning them has arisen, or arises, within thirty years, those who say that they have been injured may bring their suit concerning them before the provincial synod.
