If anyone believes himself oppressed by his own metropolitan, let him pursue judgment before the primate of the diocese or before the see of the city of Constantinople, as has been stated. But if any city has been renewed by imperial authority, or is renewed in the future, then the ecclesiastical ordering of parishes also shall follow the civil and public ordering.

### CAP. 107.—Concerning those who flee to a church because of their offenses: that they are not to be dragged away, whether from the church, ecclesiastical workshops, atrium, bishop’s house, or cloister; nor are they to be handed over to anyone unless security against death and mutilation has been received.

(First Council of Orléans, canon 3; 17, q. 4, c. *Id constituimus*.) At the first Synod of Orléans under King Clovis, at which twenty-four bishops sat, it was established concerning those who flee to church because of their offenses that what the ancient canons decreed and Roman law established must be observed: they may not in any way be dragged from the church’s atria, the bishop’s house, or the cloister, since these are regarded as places of immunity; nor may they be handed over to another unless oaths have been sworn upon the Gospels that they will be safe from death, mutilation, and every kind of punishment. Thus an agreement is to be made concerning satisfaction with the person to whom the accused offender is handed over.

If anyone is convicted of violating his oath, he shall be guilty of perjury and separated not only from communion with the Church and all clerics, but also from the fellowship of Catholics. But if the person against whom the accused has offended refuses to come to terms with him, and the accused himself, driven from the church, departs in fear, he is not to be sought by the church’s clerics.

### CAP. 108.—Concerning an abductor who flees to church with the woman abducted. From the same council, canon 4.

(36, q. 1, c. *De raptoribus*.) Concerning abductors of women, we have judged that this must be established: if an abductor flees to church with the abducted woman, and it is established that the woman herself has suffered violence, she shall immediately be freed from the abductor’s power and restored to her parents. The abductor, however, shall be granted immunity from death or penalties and shall have free permission to depart. But if the woman’s parents refuse to obey ecclesiastical men, let them be excommunicated.

### CAP. 109.—Concerning a slave who flees to church from his master for any fault. From the same council, canon 5.

(17, q. 4, c. *Id constituimus*.) If a slave flees to church for any fault and receives from his master an ecclesiastical oath concerning the offense committed, he shall immediately be compelled to return to his master’s service. After he has been handed over to his master upon that oath, if the accused person is proved to have suffered anything for the same fault, he shall, for contempt of [Col. 0222C] the Church and violation [printed: *privatione*] of faith, be regarded as excluded from communion and from the fellowship of Catholics, as stated above. But if a slave, protected by the church because of his fault, receives from his master, at the clerics’ demand, an oath of immunity, the master may seize him if he refuses to depart.

### CAP. 110.—Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Chalcedon, canon 5.

Likewise, it was decreed at the Synod of Mâcon that those fleeing their enemies, whether to a church, the church atrium, the bishop’s house, or the cloister of regulars, are not to be dragged away. First, security must be received from their persecutors, upon sacred things, against death, mutilation, and every kind of punishment—even if they are slaves of those pursuing them—so that an agreement may be made concerning satisfaction with the person against whom they are criminally liable. But if the person who had first sworn upon sacred things is convicted of violating the oath, as guilty of perjury he shall be deprived of communion until he makes satisfaction.

### CAP. 111.—Again, concerning the same matter. From the Council at Thérouanne, canon 11.

(17, q. 4, c. *Reum ad ecclesiam*.) No one may dare drag away a slave fleeing to church, to the church atrium, to the workshops of regular brethren, to the court, or to the bishop’s house, since these are held to be places of immunity in the ancient canons. Nor may anyone hand him over from there for punishment or death. Let the honor of God and his saints be preserved before all else. Rather, the rulers of churches should strive to secure peace, life, and bodily integrity for him by oath; nevertheless, he must make lawful satisfaction for whatever he has done unjustly. If the pursuer refuses to obey the masters of the Church, let him be bound by canonical discipline.

### CAP. 112.—Again, concerning the same matter. From the Council of Orange, canon 5.

Those who have fled to church must not be handed over, but must be defended through reverence for the place and ecclesiastical intercession. But if any cleric believes that he may seize slaves because his own slaves have fled to church, let him be struck with the most severe condemnation in all churches.

### CAP. 113.—Concerning the immunity of the Church. From the Council of Tribur, canon 6.

[Col. 0223B] (17, q. 4, c. *Si quis in atrio*.) If anyone starts a fight or commits homicide in the church atrium, whatever compensation is owed for violation of immunity shall be paid to the altar, whatever church it may be.

### CAP. 114.—Concerning those fleeing to church. From the Council of Metz, canon 2.

(17, q. 4, c. *Si quis contumax*.) If anyone, stubborn or proud, has no fear of the clergy or reverence for churches, and forcibly drags away his fugitive slave, or anyone whom he has been pursuing, from the church atrium or from porticoes attached to the church in any manner: for violation of immunity, he shall pay nine hundred solidi to the bishop. He himself shall be punished with public penance according to the bishop’s judgment, so that the honor of God and reverence for the saints may endure and the Church of God may always remain unconquered.

### CAP. 115.—That slaves fleeing from their masters to church must seek intercession, not hiding places. Gelasius [Gregory] to Bishop Boniface.

(17, q. 4, c. *Metuentes*.) Slaves who fear their masters, if they flee to the church enclosure, should seek intercession, not hiding places, lest this presumption itself increase the rashness of their resistance through delay. Our son Peter, a man of distinguished rank, complains that his slave has remained too long in the church of Saint Clement. Although Peter arranged for oaths to be provided for him, the slave refused on any ground to leave. Therefore delegates of the aforesaid man are to be sent at once, together with a person whom the slave chooses; when they have given oaths guaranteeing his immunity, he must immediately return to his master by every means. Or, if he perhaps persists in this obstinacy after the oath has been given him, he shall be returned against his will.

### CAP. 116.—Concerning the same matter. The same to Peter, subdeacon of Campania.

If any slaves have taken refuge in the monastery of Saint Severinus or in another church of the city, as soon as it comes to your knowledge, do not permit them in any way to remain there. Instead, let them be brought back to a church within the city. If they have a just complaint against their masters, they must leave the church under an appropriate arrangement; but if they have committed a pardonable fault, after an oath of pardon has been received from their masters, let them be returned without delay.

### CAP. 117.—That no cleric may dare drag his slave or pupil out of church, or presume to scourge him. From the Council of Lleida, canon 8.

[Col. 0224A]

(17, q. 4, c. *Nullus clericorum*.) No cleric may dare drag out, or presume to scourge, his slave or pupil who has fled to church. If he does so, he shall be excluded from the place to which he gave no honor, until he makes worthy penance.

### CAP. 118.—That no one may dare seize the slaves of clerics in exchange for his own slaves who have fled to church. From the Council of Orange, canon 6.

If anyone thinks that he may seize the slaves of clerics in exchange for his own slaves who have fled to church, let him be struck with the most severe condemnation in all churches.

From Book VI of the Code, title 4, chapter 1. Whoever receives a fugitive slave in his house or field without his master’s knowledge shall restore him together with another slave of equal value, or pay twenty solidi.

### CAP. 119.—That bishops must judge those who violate churches unworthy of entering them. Gelasius to Bishop Epiphanius.

We have sent an order to the other bishops that they are to judge persons reported to have violated churches unworthy of access to them.

### CAP. 120.—Concerning the same matter. Gelasius to Bishops Victor, Constantine, Martyrius, Felicissimus, Serenus, and Timothy.

(17, q. 4, c. *Frater et coepiscopus*.) Our brother and fellow bishop Epiphanius reported to us that Benenatus and Maurus, citizens of the municipality of Benevento, had erupted into a most bitter insult to religion and a punishable obstinacy. They did not permit their fellow townsman, who had fled to the church enclosure, to be safe there or secure from injury. With the rashness of their mind they dared to commit an outrage which not even officials or princes had ever been permitted to perpetrate: taking advantage of the priest’s absence, they forcibly dragged away a man standing in the sanctuary, while he resisted and cried out. As far as his report revealed to us, Epiphanius rightly judged them unworthy of holy communion. And if it is truly established that so great a crime was committed, our authority also concurs in this matter.

For a person ought not rightly be admitted to prayer where he did not hesitate to commit sacrilege. Let no one suppose that, within thresholds assigned to such great reverence, both things are permitted him at his own discretion: both to claim humility for himself and to indulge rage. Therefore, dearest brothers, if a manifest complaint establishes the guilt of the aforesaid men, exclude them, by the authority of our command, from all churches of your parishes. Thus, not only may those proved to have rushed into outrage against holy places deservedly receive punishment proportionate to their deed, but others also may be recalled from such presumption through fear of this penalty.

### CAP. 121.—Again, concerning the same matter. From the Council of Toledo, canon 12 (Twelfth Council of Toledo, canon 10).

(17, q. 4, c. *Definivit*.) Concerning those who seek the church through whatever fear or terror, this holy council, with the agreement and command alike of our lord King Ervig, decreed that no one may dare drag away those taking refuge and remaining in a church, or inflict upon persons remaining in a holy place any injury, damage, or spoliation. Rather, those who seek the church shall in every respect be permitted to proceed thirty paces from the church doors; throughout those thirty paces around each church, their reverence shall be protected [printed: *defendantur*]. Yet those who flee there must in no way go into buildings belonging to others or situated at a distance from the church. Going about within the thirty-pace limit, without taking refuge in other people’s houses, they shall have access so that they may go out to suitable places for the necessities of nature, and those who have entrusted themselves to the Lord’s enclosures for protection may not be held under any compulsion arising from necessity.

But if anyone attempts to violate this decree, he shall be subject to ecclesiastical excommunication and struck by the sentence of royal severity. Yet if those who have taken refuge in church are claimed, in accordance with the ordinances of the ancient canons, by persons who give the required oaths, and if the priest of that church does not remove them from the church doors—or if such persons escape—the priest must seek them, or a sentence of damages is to be imposed upon such priests according to the decision of the prince.

### CAP. 122.—Interdiction of communion imposed upon Bishop Boniface unless he quickly restores the person whom he seized from the church. Blessed Augustine’s letter to Boniface (Letter 187).

[Col. 0225C] (17, q. 4, c. *Miror*.) Augustine, bishop, to Boniface, most beloved and distinguished man, son.

I wonder how suddenly the battering ram of the enemy has breached the wall of faith. For I know with what devotion you have always revered the Church of God. At whose instigation did you dare [printed: *facinore facere ausus es?*, uncertain] to seize a man from the Church? If your fugitive, perhaps trusting in your friendship, had done this, he could undoubtedly obtain pardon through the intercession of a mediator. Therefore, if friendship is pleaded, why is God offended? But if authority is presumed upon, consider King Nebuchadnezzar, who on account of pride was changed from a man into an ox (Dan. IV).

I write these things not to shame you, but to admonish you as my most beloved son. Restore unharmed to the Church, then, the man whom you most irreligiously seized. I have forbidden [printed: *indixi*] the clergy to receive an offering from your household. I also bar you from communion until, after you have performed the penance which I have prescribed for your audacity or error, and after a period has been granted for this deed, you offer to God, with a contrite and humbled heart, a worthy sacrifice.

### CAP. 123.—That an accused person fleeing to church, after receiving security against death and mutilation, must lawfully make satisfaction for the wrongs he has committed. From the Book of Capitularies (Book V, chapter 90).

(17, q. 4, c. *Reum ad ecclesiam*.) No one may dare drag away an accused person who flees to church, or hand him over from there for punishment or death, so that the honor of churches may be preserved. Rather, their rulers should strive to secure peace, life, and bodily integrity for him; nevertheless, he must lawfully make satisfaction for what he has done unjustly.

### CAP. 124.—Those who break into a monastery and remove something from it must repay what was taken ninefold, and the immunity threefold. From the decrees of Pope John, canon 10.

[Col. 0226A]

Those who break into monasteries, places consecrated to God, or churches, and remove deposits or any other things from them, shall repay the damage ninefold and the immunity threefold, and, as sacrilegious persons, shall be subjected to canonical sentence.

### CAP. 125.—Concerning those who regard the house of God as contemptible. From the Council of Mainz, canon 7.

(Dist. 30, c. *Communione*.) Whoever, puffed up with the pride of arrogance, regards the house of God as contemptible, and dishonorably treats or presumes to violate possessions consecrated to God and established in God’s honor under the protection of royal immunity; or, with rash boldness, perpetrates burnings [Col. 0226B] or devastations: as an invader and violator of the Church of God, which is the house of the living God, let him be cut off from communion with all the faithful.

### CAP. 126.—Concerning their excommunication. From the Council of Orange.

(11, q. 3, c. *Canonica instituta*.) Following canonical ordinances and the examples of the holy Fathers, by the authority of God and the judgment of the Holy Spirit, we exclude violators of God’s churches from the bosom of holy mother Church and from the fellowship of all Christianity, until they repent and make satisfaction to the Church.

### CAP. 127.—Concerning the penance of those who burn churches. From the decrees of Pope Julius.

(17, q. 4, c. *Si quis*.) If anyone burns a church with fire, let him do penance for fifteen years, diligently restore it, and distribute his own property to the poor.

### CAP. 128.—Concerning ministers of the altar. From the Council of Laodicea, canon 21.

(Dist. 42, c. *Non oportet*.) Ministers of the altar or any clerics who are invited to an *agape* should not take portions, because of the reproach which may on this account be attributed to the ecclesiastical order.

### CAP. 129.—That parish priests, when ordained, must receive from their bishop an official handbook. From the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 26.

(Dist. 38, c. *Quando presbyteri*.) When priests are ordained in parishes, let them receive an official handbook from their bishop, so that they may take charge of the churches assigned to them with instruction, lest through ignorance they err even in the divine sacraments. When they come to litanies or a council, they are to render account to their bishop of how they celebrate the office entrusted to them or perform baptisms.

### CAP. 130.—That priests or deacons, when appointed throughout parishes, ought to make a profession to their bishop. From the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 26.

(Dist. 28, c. *Quando presbyteri*.) When priests or deacons are appointed throughout parishes, they ought to make a profession to their bishop: that they will live chastely and purely in the fear of God, so that, bound by such a profession, they may maintain holy discipline.

### CAP. 131.—That any bishop who has possessed another’s diocese for thirty years without any challenge shall retain it. From the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 33.

(16, q. 3, c. *Quicunque*.) Any bishop who has possessed another bishop’s diocese for thirty years without any challenge shall retain it, because according to legal right the diocese appears to be his. An action to reclaim it is not to be admitted against him. But this applies within one province only; outside it, not at all, lest, while a diocese is defended, provincial boundaries be confused.

### CAP. 132.—Concerning exactions from churches in the province of Galicia. From the Council of Toledo, canon 4.

No bishop of his own province may expect to receive annually from each diocese or individual church more than two solidi, according to the Synod of Braga, [Col. 0227B] with the basilicas of monasteries excepted from this expense of payment. When a bishop visits his diocese, he must not burden anyone by the size of his retinue, must never exceed fifty mounts, and may not remain more than one day in any one place. Any bishop who presumes to act otherwise than we decree shall unquestionably be subject to correction by the canons, as a transgressor of synodal constitutions and corrupter of the decree of the ancient Fathers.

### CAP. 133.—That bishops, while travelling through their parishes, must not exercise tyranny but exact provisions with charity. From the Second Council of Chalon, canon 24.

[Col. 0227C] (10, q. 3, c. *Cavendum est*.) Care must certainly be taken that, when bishops travel through their parishes, they exercise no sort of tyranny, not only toward subjects but toward their fellow clergy; and—God forbid—that they exact provisions from them not with charity, but with the rashness of ostentation, and not with thanksgiving but with a kind of judicial imposition.

It must also be observed in every way that whenever the necessity of travelling through their parishes falls upon them, they give attention to confirming persons, examining matters needing correction, preaching the word of God, and winning souls, rather than plundering and despoiling people and causing scandal to brethren. Whenever they must receive something from brethren or subjects for carrying out their ministry, [Col. 0227D] they must take the greatest care not to scandalize or burden anyone. Such discrimination must be maintained in this matter: the preacher of God’s word may receive from brethren where his own resources are lacking, but those brethren must not be burdened by his power—following the example of the Apostle Paul, who, lest he burden anyone, sought his livelihood by craft and manual labor (II Thess. III).

### CAP. 134.—That archdeacons must exercise no tyrannical domination over parish priests. From the same council, canon 15.

(Dist. 94, c. *Dictum est*.) It has also been stated that in many places archdeacons exercise a kind of domination over parish priests and exact tribute from them. This pertains more to tyranny [Col. 0228A] than to the strength of uprightness. For if, according to the Apostle’s teaching, bishops ought not to lord it over the clergy but should become examples to the flock willingly (I Pet. V), much less should these men do so. Rather, let them be content with regular discipline, keep to their proper measure, and diligently carry out throughout the parish what is imposed upon them by bishops, presuming nothing through greed or avarice.

### CAP. 135.—That, in a dispute, the person found in possession must prevail by oath. Gelasius to Bishop Justus.

(16, q. 3, c. *Dilectio*.) Your Charity, after faithfully seeking the truth of all matters, shall preserve unimpaired a definite decision previously issued concerning the territories from which the dispute is said to have arisen. Otherwise, if nothing has ever been shown to have been determined, let the party which dissents [printed: *fidit*] now furnish an oath concerning the prescription of time; provided, however, that the party reported to have possessed hitherto is permitted to offer the oath.

### CAP. 136.—Concerning what bishops of Sicily may exact from their parish clergy. Pelagius to the illustrious Cresconius.

(10, q. 3, c. *Illud te modis*.) We desire you by every means to ensure that no bishop of Sicily presumes to receive, from parishes belonging to him, more than two solidi under the name of *cathedraticum*, nor compels the priests or clergy of his parishes to prepare banquets for them beyond their means.

### CAP. 137.—That clergy oppressed by their bishop should bring their complaint to the metropolitan. From the Third Council of Toledo, canon 20.

[Col. 0228C]

(10, q. 3, c. *Quia cognovimus*.) Because we have learned that bishops conduct themselves in their parishes not priestly but cruelly, and, although it is written, “Be examples to the flock, not lording it over the clergy” (1 Pet. 5), impose exactions or losses upon their dioceses: therefore we decree that, except for what the ancient constitutions require bishops to receive from parishes, all other things hitherto presumptuously claimed by them shall be denied them. That is, neither presbyters nor deacons are to be harassed in compulsory public services (*angariae*) or in any levies, lest we appear in the Church of God to be called tax-collectors rather than bishops of God. Clerics, whether local or diocesan, who know themselves to be oppressed by their bishop, must not delay in bringing their complaints before the metropolitan; and the metropolitan must not delay to restrain such presumptions. [Col. 0228D]

### CHAP. 138.—Judges may not employ clerics or servants of the Church in their compulsory services, ch. 21.

(12, q. 2, c. *Ecclesiarum*.) We grieve that servants of churches, and of all bishops or clerics, are harassed by judges or public agents in various compulsory services. Therefore the whole council sought from the piety of our most glorious Lord Jesus that he should henceforth prohibit such audacities, and that servants of the aforesaid offices should labour for their own needs or those of the Church. But if any judge or public agent wishes to employ a cleric, or the servant of a cleric or of a church, in public or private business, let him be excluded from the communion of that church to which he causes hindrance. [Col. 0229A]

### CHAP. 139.—Common life ought to flourish among all Christians, especially among those chosen for the Lord’s portion; and the faithful first contributed their money, then their estates, for the support of those living in common. Urban, in his first decretal, to all Christians.

(12, q. 1, c. *Scimus vos*.) We know that you are not unaware that common life has hitherto flourished among good Christians, and still flourishes by God’s grace, especially among those chosen for the Lord’s portion—that is, clerics—as is read in the Acts of the Apostles:

> Now the multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul; nor did any one of them say that anything which he possessed was his own, but all things were held in common among them. [Col. 0229B] And with great power the Apostles bore witness to the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord, and great grace was upon them all. Nor was any one needy among them; for as many as owned fields or houses sold them, brought the prices of what they sold, and laid them at the Apostles’ feet. And distribution was made to each according as anyone had need. Now Joseph, who was surnamed Barsabas by the Apostles—which is interpreted “son of consolation”—a Levite, Cypriot by birth, having a field, sold it, brought the price, and laid it at the Apostles’ feet (Acts 4), etc.

But when the chief priests, Levites, and the other faithful saw that greater benefit could result if they entrusted to the churches presided over by bishops the inheritances and fields that they sold, because from their revenues they could provide more abundantly and fittingly, both in the present and in future times, for the faithful who led a common life than from the sale-price of those properties, they began to convey to the mother churches the estates and fields which they had customarily sold, and to live from their revenues. These properties were, and still are, and must always be in future times remain, under the authority of the bishops of the individual parishes, who hold the place of the Apostles. [Col. 0229C]

From them bishops and their faithful stewards must provide all necessities, as well as they can, for all who wish to live a common life, so that none among them may be found needy. These possessions are called the offerings of the faithful, because they are offered to the Lord. Therefore they must not be diverted to uses other than those of the Church and of the aforesaid Christian brethren or persons in need, because they are the vows of the faithful, the price of sins, and have been entrusted to the Lord for accomplishing the aforesaid work. But if anyone—God forbid—acts otherwise, let him beware lest he incur the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5), and become guilty of sacrilege, as they did who fraudulently withheld the price of the aforesaid possessions. [Col. 0229D]

Through the aforementioned endowments and cultivation, the churches over which bishops preside have so increased, with the Lord’s help, and the greater number of them so abound in resources, that no one living a common life among them is needy; rather, each receives every necessity from the bishop and his ministers. Therefore, if anyone in present or future times attempts to tear this arrangement away, let him be struck by the condemnation already stated. [Col. 0230A]

### CHAP. 140.—Whoever takes away the property of churches and the offerings of the faithful sins against God the Father and the Church the Mother, and therefore must be driven from the thresholds of the holy Mother Church. Pope Lucius I, in his first decree, to all bishops, both Gauls and Spaniards.

(6, q. 1, c. *Sapiens non est*.) No one who harms is wise. Moreover, concerning the property of our churches and the offerings of the faithful—which, you have reported, are being troubled by certain assailants and taken away from us and our churches—this is undoubtedly a most grievous sin, as Scripture testifies when it says (12, q. 2, c. *Qui abstulerit*): “Whoever takes anything from father or mother and says that this is not sin is the companion of a murderer” (Prov. 28). [Col. 0230B] Our Father, then, is without doubt God, who created us; and our mother is the Church, which gave us spiritual birth in baptism.

Likewise: the prophets, the Apostles, their successors, and the decrees of all the Catholic Fathers forbid these acts and judge such presumptions to be sacrileges. (17, q. 4, c. *Omnes raptores*.) Following their examples, together with you we drive from the thresholds of the holy Mother Church, condemn by apostolic authority, and judge to be sacrilegious all such presumptuous persons, plunderers of the Church, and alienators of her resources. And not only them, but all who consent to them; for not only those who do such things are judged guilty, but also those who consent to those doing them (Rom. 1). For an equal punishment embraces both the perpetrators and those who consent. [Col. 0230C]

### CHAP. 141.—The decrees of the Fathers are to be moderated, with careful regard for the necessity of the times. From the general decrees of Pope Gelasius, ch. 1 (ep. 1).

(1, q. 7, c. *Necessaria rerum*.) The necessary ordering [or: dispensation] of affairs obliges us to weigh the decrees of the Fathers’ canons and to measure the commands of the bishops and predecessors who came before us, so that, with careful consideration, we may moderate as far as possible those things which the necessity of present times demands be relaxed for the restoration of churches.

### CHAP. 142.—Where no great necessity presses, the institutions of the Fathers must remain unshaken. The same, ch. 2.

[Col. 0230D] (Dist. 55, c. *Priscis*.) Therefore, while the ancient institutions remain in force out of reverence for them—institutions which, wherever no pressure of circumstances or times urges otherwise, ought regularly to be observed—we grant that periods for instituting and promoting clerical service may be dispensed to those churches that are either wholly deprived of ministers or stripped so completely of sufficient services that they cannot provide the divine offices for the congregations belonging to them.

### CHAP. 143.—Concerning the examination of one who enters clerical office. The same, ch. 3.

(Dist. 77, c. *Si quis de*.) If anyone, even one trained in a religious vocation and monastic discipline, comes forward for clerical office, his life in past times must first be examined: whether he is shown to be stained by no grave crime; whether perhaps he has not had a second wife; and whether he is shown not to have taken a woman left [or rejected] by her husband. [Col. 0231A]

### CHAP. 144.—Whatever is encompassed by the law of thirty years may be claimed as one’s right. The same.

(The same occurs below, ch. 147.) Gelasius, bishop of the Roman Church, to the brethren established in Sicily. We have also thought fit to add that, if—God forbid—the property of the Church and dioceses are possessed by any bishops, they may claim as their right what the law of thirty years has settled. For the authority of our sons, the emperors, has so decreed that after thirty years no one may appeal concerning a matter from which the period fixed by law has excluded him.

### CHAP. 145.—Captives are to be redeemed from ecclesiastical property. Gregory to Demetrius [Demetrianus] and Valerian, clerics of Fermo (book VII of the Register, epistle 14).

[Col. 0231B] (12, q. 2, c. *Sacrorum*.) The ordinances of the sacred canons, and legal authority, permit ecclesiastical property lawfully to be expended for the redemption of captives. Therefore, because you have informed us that about eighteen years ago the most reverend Fabius, bishop of the Church of Fermo, paid eleven pounds of silver from that church to the enemy for the redemption of you, your father Passivus—our brother and fellow bishop, but then a cleric—and your mother; and because you consequently have some fear that what was given may at some time be reclaimed from you: [Col. 0231C] by the authority of this decree we have provided for the removal of your anxiety, establishing that neither you nor your heirs shall at any time suffer any inconvenience from a claim for restitution, nor shall anyone raise any question against you on this account.

### CHAP. 146.—Possession held by another for forty years is not to be reclaimed. Gregory to Peter, subdeacon.

(16, q. 4, c. *Volumnus accedentem*.) If you find that the monastery of Saint Theodore has possessed, for an uninterrupted forty years, the boundaries concerning which litigation has arisen, do not allow it henceforth to suffer any legal challenge, even if something may have belonged to the Roman Church; but secure its peace by every means.

### CHAP. 147.—Bishops must administer the resources of churches, distribute support to widows, orphans, the poor, and clerics; but claim for themselves nothing from them except what belongs to their own use by the law of thirty years. (Gelasius, ep. 2 to the Sicilians, ch. 1.)

[Col. 0231D] Gelasius, bishop of the Roman Church, to his most beloved brethren, bishops established in Sicily and united in unanimous charity in Christ. (16, q. 3, c. *Praesulum*.) Just as the authority of our predecessors has decreed that bishops should have power to govern the resources of the Church, so we establish that they must distribute the support of widows, orphans, the poor, and clerics, while granting them what has hitherto been decreed. Bishops may claim the remainder for themselves, so that, as we have said above, they may be able to give generously to strangers and captives. [Col. 0232A]

We have likewise thought fit to add that, if—God forbid—the property and dioceses of the Church are possessed by any bishops, they may claim as their right what the law of thirty years has settled. For the authority of our sons, the emperors, has so decreed that after thirty years no one may appeal concerning that from which the time fixed by law has excluded him.

### CHAP. 148.—No one who unlawfully squanders property left for the use of the poor can shield himself by any obstacle before Christ’s tribunal; and whoever presumes to confiscate, lay claim to, or seize the property of the Church through dangerous or violent assault is to be struck with an anathema. From the sixth synod of Pope Symmachus.

[Col. 0232B] Nor may anyone who, without any consideration of mercy, unlawfully squanders property left by pious souls for the resources of the poor, fortify himself by any obstacle before Christ’s tribunal. (19, q. 1, c. *In canonibus*.) Likewise, by your exhortation and judgment, we decree that this be made known to all churches and firmly observed by all: since the property of bishops is not doubted to be Church property, if anyone has ravaged their resources with similar cruelty, the invaders of the aforesaid property shall be struck with the aforementioned severity of the canons, so that those who are not corrected by their own conduct or by any chastisement of conscience may at least be pierced by the goads of ecclesiastical and canonical punishment.

In general, whoever presumes to confiscate, claim, [Col. 0232C] or seize ecclesiastical property by dangerous or violent assault, unless he most quickly corrects himself by making satisfaction to the church concerned, shall be struck with perpetual anathema. Likewise, those who retain Church property by command or grant of princes, or of certain powerful persons, or by some invasion or tyrannical power, and leave it to their children or heirs as though hereditary—as we have heard some have already done—unless, admonished by the bishop and acknowledging the truth, they quickly restore God’s property, shall be struck with perpetual anathema. For we judge it unjust that we should be regarded as guardians of documents rather than defenders, as commanded, of the property entrusted to us. [Col. 0232D]

### CHAP. 149.—Concerning invaders of another’s property. Pope John to Zacharias, archbishop.

(12, q. 2, c. *In antiquis*.) It is also decreed in the ancient statutes of the Church that one who invades another’s property is not to go unpunished, but must restore everything with an additional amount. Hence it is written in the Gospel: “If I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19). And the laws of the world provide: “Whoever steals another’s property shall restore to the person whose property was plundered elevenfold what was taken.” And in the divine Law it is read: “Cursed is everyone who removes his neighbour’s boundary-mark”; and all the people say, “Amen” (Deut. 27). Therefore such acts must not be presumed without punishment, nor committed without their condemnation. [Col. 0233A]

### CHAP. 150.—Concerning those who strive to trample ecclesiastical privileges. Gelasius to Majoricus, Serenus, and John, bishops.

(12, q. 2, c. *Qui et humanis*.) Those who, having trampled human laws underfoot in their civil condemnation and cast aside reverence for religion, strive either to trample ecclesiastical privileges or anywhere to rush to the injury of the poor, and who, though at least warned and convicted, refuse to cease from such wickedness and to repair the losses inflicted upon sacred things, must altogether be deprived of participation in the divine gift, so that they may lack the reception of that whose sacred laws they held in contempt.

### CHAP. 151.—A bishop may not by any contrivance alienate Church property; and privileges must in every respect be preserved unimpaired. Gelasius to Justin, archdeacon, and Faustus, defender.

(12, q. 2, c. *Vulteranae*.) We have decreed that the affairs and patrimony of the Volaterran [Wulterran] Church, which we have learned has until now been left destitute or dispersed after the condemnation of Eucharistius, who had corrupted it, be entrusted to your care. With the diligence which we believe you exercise in the interests of the Church, restore the estates to their former cultivation. Recall any slaves who have been sold or given away; likewise recall estates which you find held by the bishops Eumatius and Oppilio, or by others under any claim whatsoever—for Church estates could not be alienated by a bishop through any contrivance, contrary to the decrees of the synod. [Col. 0233B]

Let purchasers have recourse against the person who presumed to dispose of anything from the Church’s resources through an unlawful sale. You are to convey annual payments to the bishop, whose privileges must in every respect be kept intact, so that through his administration the customary shares may be allotted. The bishop is to distribute by his own direction the fourth share that belongs to them, according to his knowledge of each person’s position and merit. Likewise, from the offerings of the faithful, the bishop is to distribute a fourth to the clerics in consideration of his election. The portion for buildings also is to be paid out under the bishop’s knowledge and direction, through your disbursement, so that you may allow no loss at all to arise in any matter. [Col. 0233C]

But if you see your bishop permit anything damaging to your Church, or anything prohibited by our ordinance, report it at once to us, so that we may determine what ought to be done. It has appeared right, both to us and to our predecessors, that tithes are owed in due order only to those communities where the most sacred baptisms are administered. [Col. 0233D]

### CHAP. 152.—Property once consecrated and contributed to God may not be invaded or plundered by concession of any princes. Nicholas to Ado, archbishop of Vienne.

(12, q. 2, c. *De rebus*.) Concerning property once contributed and dedicated to God, but afterwards invaded and plundered by certain persons under the pretext of grants by princes, we decree that the prince must first be consulted in order to remove the presumptuous faction and ascertain whether it is his grant or the invader’s presumption. But if the prince’s grant has been irregular, the prince himself must be reproved for correction. [Col. 0234A]

### CHAP. 153.—Church property is not to be alienated without consultation with the metropolitan bishop. From the Fifth Council of Carthage, ch. 8.

(17, q. 4, c. *Nullus*.) It has also been resolved that no one may sell property of the Church. If some necessity compels this, it must be reported to the primate of the Church, so that he may decide, with a fixed number of bishops, whether it should be done. But if the Church is pressed by such urgent necessity that it cannot consult beforehand, it must at least, after the act, show due diligence: it must first notify the neighbouring bishops and refer these necessities of the Church to the council. [Col. 0234B] If it does not do so, the seller shall be held answerable to the council.

### CHAP. 154.—Concerning those manumitted and entrusted to the Church by testament. From the First Council of Orange, ch. 7.

(Dist. 87, c. *Eos qui*.) If anyone attempts to reduce to slavery, service, or the status of a tenant-farmer those manumitted in the Church and entrusted to the Church by testament, he shall be restrained by ecclesiastical discipline.

### CHAP. 155.—Those who retain the offerings of the dead and delay in restoring them to churches are accounted, in God’s judgment, as murderers of the needy. From the First Council of Vaison, ch. 4.

(13, q. 2, c. *Qui oblationes*.) Those who retain the offerings of the dead and delay in delivering them to churches must be cast out from the Church as unbelievers, because this provocation of divine mercy certainly reaches the emptying-out of faith: both the faithful departing from the body are defrauded of the fulfilment of their vows, and the poor of the consolation of food and necessary support. Such persons are judged worthy, in God’s judgment, to be regarded as murderers of the needy. [Col. 0234C] Hence one of the Fathers included in his writings this fitting judgment: “To take something from a friend is theft; to defraud the Church is sacrilege.” (Jerome, letter to Nepotian.)

### CHAP. 156.—Concerning clerics who presume to conceal, deny, or hand over to adversaries documents by which the possession of the Church is established. From the Council of Agde, ch. 26.

[Col. 0234D] (12, q. 2, c. *Si quis*.) If any cleric, with condemnable and punishable obstinacy, presumes to conceal or deny documents by which the Church’s possession is established, or perhaps to hand them over to adversaries, he shall restore from his own resources whatever loss has been inflicted on the Church through the absence of the documents, and shall be deprived of communion. Those also who, wickedly solicited by traitors to the Church’s detriment, receive anything shall be bound by the foregoing sentence.

### CHAP. 157.—No monk may presume to begin or found a new monastery except with the bishop’s permission. There, ch. 27.

(18, q. [?], c. *De monachis*.) No one among monks may presume to begin or found a new monastery unless the bishop permits or approves it. (16, q. [Col. 0235A] 1, c. *Monachi vagantes*.) Wandering monks are not to be ordained to clerical office either in cities or in parishes unless their abbot has given them testimony. (20, q. 4, c. *Monachum*.) No abbot may presume to receive or retain a monk migrating to another monastery without his own abbot’s permission or consent; wherever he may be, he shall be recalled to his abbot by the authority of the canons. For if it is necessary to ordain a monk as a cleric, the bishop may do so with the abbot’s consent and approval.

### CHAP. 158.—Monasteries of nuns must be placed at a greater distance from monasteries of monks. There, ch. 28.

(18, q. 2, c. *Monasteria*.) Monasteries of nuns must be placed farther away from monasteries of monks, whether because of the devil’s snares or because of people’s slander. [Col. 0235B]

### CHAP. 159.—The Church must, when necessary, protect persons lawfully freed. There, ch. 29.

(Dist. 87, c. *Libertos*.) The Church shall protect, if necessity requires, persons lawfully freed by their masters. But if anyone presumes to seize or despoil them before a hearing, he shall be excluded from the Church.

### CHAP. 160.—A bishop has authority to sell small parcels of land and little vineyards of slight usefulness to the Church. There, ch. 45.

(12, q. 1, c. *Terrulas*.) If necessity requires, a bishop has authority, without a council of the brethren, to sell small plots of land or little vineyards, of minor usefulness to the Church or situated at a distance.

### CHAP. 161.—Presbyters or deacons may not dare exchange or sell Church property entrusted to them; if they do, they are to be deposed from office and restore it from their own resources. There, ch. 49.

[Col. 0235C] (12, q. 2, c. *Diaconi*.) Deacons or presbyters established in a parish may not dare to exchange or sell anything from Church property entrusted to them, since such property is known to be consecrated to God. Likewise, priests may not presume to alienate anything from the property of the Church committed to them, as has been stated above. If they do so, all shall be deposed from office in council and restore from their own resources double the amount of what they are found to have presumed to take.

(12, q. 2, c. *Si quis qualibet*.) Certainly, if anyone under any circumstance presumes to alienate anything from Church property, and contributes from his own resources to the Church as much as he appears to have taken away, only then may that act stand. Yet we order that the Church’s records pursue freed persons whom priests or deacons wish to make from the Church entrusted to them. If they refuse to do this, it has been resolved that they return to their own service. [Col. 0235D]

### CHAP. 162.—Whatever presbyters alienate from parish possessions is to be deemed void, both against purchaser and seller. There, ch. 53.

(12, q. 2, c. *Quidquid parochiarum*.) Whatever a presbyter of a parish alienates from possessions belonging by ecclesiastical right shall be held empty and void, both as regards the purchaser’s purchase and the seller’s action.

### CHAP. 163.—Concerning sales which abbots presume to make. There, ch. 56.

(17, q. 4, c. *In venditionibus*.) In sales which abbots presume to make, the following rule shall be observed: whatever has been sold without the bishop’s knowledge shall be recalled into the bishop’s authority. But slaves given to monks may not be manumitted by the abbot. For we judge it unjust that, while monks perform daily agricultural work, their slaves should enjoy the gift of freedom [variant: leisure]. [Col. 0236A]

### CHAP. 164.—One abbot must not preside over two monasteries, ch. 57.

(21, q. 1, c. *Unum*.) We forbid one abbot to preside over two monasteries.

### CHAP. 165.—New cells of monks may not be established without the bishop’s knowledge. There, ch. 58.

(18, q. 2, c. *Cellulas*.) We prohibit the establishment, without the bishop’s knowledge, of new cells or small monastic communities. [Col. 0236B]

### CHAP. 166.—Clerics may not acquire private title to Church property through long possession. There, ch. 59.

(16, q. 3, c. *Clerici quilibet*.) Clerics, whatever the duration of time for which they have possessed any property of the Church as some recompense [variant: “from the Church”], are not to be called [variant: recalled] into private ownership by prescription of time, provided that it is clear that the property belonged to the Church. Thus bishops also may not appear to have been obliged, upon being ordained, to make lengthy or precarious grants of administration, nor may they transfer into the right of their own ownership resources retained for a long time. [Col. 0236C]

### CHAP. 167.—A bishop may assign revenues of his Church, if they do not greatly burden it, for the support of those living under a rule, strangers, and the needy. From the Third Council of Toledo, ch. 3.

(12, q. 2, c. *Sine exceptione*.) This holy synod grants no bishop permission to alienate Church property, since this is prohibited also by the more ancient canons. But if they give something that does not burden the Church’s welfare, for the support of monks or churches belonging to their parish, let it remain valid. They are permitted, for a time and without prejudice to the Church’s right, to provide what they can for the need of strangers, clerics, and the poor.

### CHAP. 168.—Bishops may dedicate one of their parish churches as a monastery. From the Third Council of Toledo, ch. 4.

(12, q. 2, c. *Si episcopus*.) If a bishop wishes to dedicate one of his parish churches as a monastery, so that a community of monks may live there according to the rule, he shall have permission to do this with the consent of his council. If he also gives to that place something from Church property for their support, provided that it causes no loss to the Church, it shall be stable; for the holy council gives its consent to establish a good work. [Col. 0236D]

### CHAP. 169.—Presbyters, and all persons entrusted with Church property, must assign by charter to the Church whatever they acquire during their administration. From the Ninth Council of Toledo, ch. 4.

(12, q. 4, c. *Sacerdotes*.) Priests, or whoever they may be to whom the care of ecclesiastical property has been entrusted, must arrange that charters be drawn up in the name of the Church over which they preside for whatever they acquire during their administration, if they possess from their own resources anything, however slight or small. For it is unfitting that the Church, which receives a stranger, should make someone rich in another’s property while retaining a defrauder in her own. [Col. 0237A]

### CHAP. 170.—If a bishop wishes to establish a monastery or endow a parish church, he may give there the fortieth or hundredth part of Church property. From the Council of Toledo, ch. 5.

(12, q. 2, c. *Bonae rei*.) To provide for a good work is considered both a support in the present life and the expectation of reward in eternal recompense. Therefore, if any bishop wishes perhaps to construct a monastery in his parish and endow it with the property of the Church over which he presides, he may give to it no more than a fortieth part, so that, by preserving this equitable moderation, he may provide adequate support for that to which he gives, while not inflicting severe losses upon that from which he takes. [Col. 0237B]

But to a church not governed by monastic rules, or which he wishes to enrich with its own written endowments, he may contribute no more than a hundredth part of the income of the Church over which he presides; provided, however, that he observes this safeguard: he may choose only one of these two endowments which he prefers.

### CHAP. 171.—A bishop may contribute one third of the share owed to him from parish churches either to that same church or, if he wishes, to an altar. From the same council, ch. 6.

(12, q. 3, c. *Episcopus si partem*.) Since it is well known from earlier enactments what share of the resources of parish churches is assigned to the bishop, we have nevertheless thought it fitting to decree that if a bishop decides to transfer the third share, which by the same enactment he knows to be owed to him, either to the very church to which the property is shown to belong or to another church of his choice, this shall be lawful and his decision shall have irrevocable force. [Col. 0237C]

### CHAP. 172.—A bishop who sells Church property must restore it from his own resources and, by judgment of bishops, be deprived of his office as one guilty of theft or robbery. From the council of Pope Martin, ch. 14.

(10, q. 2, c. *Si quis episcopus*.) If any bishop, compelled by no necessity recognized by ecclesiastical reason, presumes to sell anything from ecclesiastical property within his clergy or perhaps where there is no presbyter, he shall be compelled to restore the properties themselves to his own Church; after being heard before the judgment of bishops, he shall be deposed and deprived of his office as one guilty of theft or robbery. [Col. 0237D]

### CHAP. 173.—What is to be done with presbyters found to have sold anything from the ministries of the Church. From the same source, ch. 17.

(10, q. 2, c. *Si quis presbyter*.) If any presbyter or deacon is found to have sold anything belonging to the ministries of the Church, since he has committed sacrilege, it has been resolved that he shall not be retained in ecclesiastical orders. Yet he is to be left to the bishop’s judgment as to whether he ought deservedly to be received back in his rank, because often this very matter, in which something from the most sacred altar has been defiled, has been left to the bishop’s discretion.

### CHAP. 174.—Concerning Church endowments and tithes. From the Council of Seville.

Let a whole *mansus*—a standard farmholding—be assigned to every church, free from every service. Let all, rich and poor alike, rightly offer to their churches all first fruits and tithes, both from livestock and from crops. For the Lord says through the prophet: “Bring the whole tithe into my storehouse, so that there may be food for those serving in my house” (Mal. 3). [Col. 0238A] Every farmer and every craftsman must make a just tithe from his trade. For as the Lord gave all things, so he demands a tenth from all things: from the fruits of the field, and from every kind of produce; from bees, and from honey; from lambs, and from fleeces and cheeses; from piglets, and from goats, cattle, and horses; we exact it from lesser as from greater things, and from the rest. But if anyone does not tithe all these things, he is a robber of God, a thief, and a brigand; and the curse pronounced by the Lord against Cain, who did not divide rightly, is heaped upon him. [Col. 0238B] Yet no one may demand from priests any tax or service from any of these things except ecclesiastical service.

### CHAP. 175.—No rent is to be paid by a presbyter. From the Council of Paris.

In accordance with canonical authority and the constitution of Lord Emperor Louis: from ecclesiastical land and a *mansus*, from slaves whom he himself established in his capitularies, or from anything that anyone may have given to a church for a burial place, and likewise from tithes and offerings of the faithful, no one may compel any presbyter to pay any rent; nor may anyone of whatever order or dignity take anything from these, or exact any temporal payment whatsoever. If he does so, he shall be deprived of communion until satisfaction is made and compelled by royal authority to give it back. [Col. 0238C]

### CHAP. 176.—It is culpable to prefer Church treasure to the redemption of captives. Gregory to Lord [Bonum], bishop of Messina (book VI, epistle 35).

(12, q. 2, c. *Sicut omnino*.) Just as it is altogether grievous needlessly to sell ecclesiastical ministrations, so likewise it is culpable, when such necessity is imminent, to prefer even the property of a greatly impoverished Church to its captives, and to delay their redemption.

### CHAP. 177.—No one may accept the gift of a person who wishes to make the Church his heir after disinheriting his son. Augustine, in the second sermon *On the Life of Clerics* (to the brethren in the desert).

(17, q. 4, c. *Quicunque*.) Whoever wishes, after disinheriting his son, to make the Church his heir, should seek another person to accept it, not Augustine; indeed, by God’s favour, let him find no one. How praiseworthy was the deed of the holy and venerable Aurelius, bishop of Carthage! How he filled with praises of God the mouths of all who know of it! For a certain man, having no children and expecting none, gave all his property to the Church while retaining the usufruct for himself. Children were born to him, and the bishop restored to him, though he did not expect it, what he had given. The bishop had power not to restore it, but that was by the law of the forum, not by the law of heaven. [Col. 0238D]

### CHAP. 178.—There also, on the same matter.

(13, q. 2, c. *Si quis irasc.*) If someone grows angry with his son and, when dying, disinherits him—if he were alive, ought I not to reconcile him? Ought I not to reconcile the son to him? How then can I wish him to be at peace with his son whose inheritance I seek? But plainly, if he does what I have often urged: if he has one son, let him regard Christ as a second; if he has two, let him regard Christ as a third; if he has ten, let him make Christ the eleventh—and I will accept it. [Col. 0239A]

### CHAP. 179.—No one rightly possesses earthly property except by divine or human law. The same, in the letter to Vincentius (epistle 48).

(23, q. 7, c. *Quicunque*.) Whoever persecutes you under pretext of this imperial law, not out of love for correction but from the hatred of enmity, displeases us. And although no earthly property can rightly be possessed by anyone except either by divine law (by which all things belong to the righteous) or by human law (which lies in the power of the kings of the earth), and therefore you falsely call your own the things which you do not even possess justly and which, according to the [Col. 0239B] laws of earthly kings, you have been ordered to lose; and although you say in vain, “We laboured in gathering them,” when you read what is written: “The righteous shall eat the labours of the wicked” (Wisdom X): nevertheless, whoever, under pretext of this law which the kings of the earth, serving Christ, promulgated to correct your impiety, greedily covets your possessions, displeases us. Finally, whoever holds, not by justice but by avarice, those very possessions of the poor or basilicas of congregations which you held under the name of Church—though these are owed only to that Church which is the true Church of Christ—displeases us. Whoever receives one expelled by us for some disgraceful or criminal act in the same manner as those are received who, excepting the error by which you separate yourselves from us, have lived among you without offence, displeases [Col. 0239C] us. But you do not easily demonstrate such cases; and even if you do demonstrate them, we tolerate some whom we cannot correct or punish. We do not leave the Lord’s threshing-floor because of the chaff; nor tear the Lord’s nets because of the bad fish; nor abandon the Lord’s flock because of the goats to be separated at the end; nor migrate from the Lord’s house because of vessels made for dishonour.

## CHAPTER 180.—That the Church possesses gold not to keep it, but to distribute it and bring relief in necessities. Ambrose, *On Duties*, Book II, chapter 28.

(12, q. 2, c. *Aurum ecclesia habet*.) The Church possesses gold, not in order to keep it, but to distribute it and bring relief in necessities. What need is there to guard what provides no help? Do we not know how much gold and [Col. 0239D] silver the Assyrians took from the temple of the Lord? Is it not better that a priest should melt it down for the sustenance of the poor, if other resources are lacking, than that a sacrilegious enemy should defile and carry it away? Will not the Lord say: “Why did you allow so many needy persons to die of hunger? Surely you had gold from which you could have supplied them with food. Why were so many captives led away for sale, not redeemed, and slain by the enemy? It would have been better to preserve vessels of the living than vessels of metal”? No answer could be made to this. For what would you say? “I feared that the temple of God would lack its ornaments.” He would reply: “The sacraments do not require gold, nor are those things pleasing through gold which are not bought with gold. The ornament of sacred things is the redemption of captives.” And truly, those are precious vessels which redeem souls from death. That is the true treasure [Col. 0240A] of the Lord which accomplishes what His blood accomplished.

And shortly afterwards: In these three kinds of cases it is permitted to break up, melt down, and sell even consecrated vessels of the Church. Care must be taken that the form of the mystical cup does not pass out of the Church, and that the service of the sacred chalice is not transferred to wicked uses. Therefore, vessels not consecrated were first sought within the Church; then they were broken up; finally, they were melted down, distributed to the needy in small allotments, and used for the ransom-prices of captives. But if new vessels, and vessels clearly not consecrated, are lacking, I consider that everything may piously be converted to the uses mentioned above.

## CHAPTER 181.—On the privileges of churches. From the Council of Toul.

[Col. 0240B] There are perhaps persons who, slighting the privileges concerning places dedicated to God and confirmed by the hands of saints, lessen the excommunications pronounced by saints of the Lord against usurpers of ecclesiastical property and resources, claiming for themselves, because they wish it rather than because they can, that they are not bound by the condemnation inflicted for this—that is, by the bond of anathema. Of them Saint Gregory says in his letter to the patrician Theotista:

> “They themselves,” he says, “bear witness against themselves that they are not Christians, since they suppose that they can dissolve by futile efforts the bonds of the Church; and consequently, if they do not judge her bonds to be effective, neither do they judge the absolution which holy Church grants to the faithful to be real.”

There is no need to dispute longer against such persons, because in every respect they must be despised and anathematized; and by that very truth through which they think to deceive themselves, they are truly bound in their sins. [Col. 0240C]

## CHAPTER 182.—On invaders of ecclesiastical property. Ruling of Pope Symmachus (in the Sixth Roman Synod).

(12, q. 2, c. *Indigne*.) He who dares to invade ecclesiastical property, to possess it unjustly, or to persist in it by inequitable or unjust defence, is unworthy to be permitted to approach the altar of the Lord. Care must nevertheless be taken that admonition precede the binding sentence, and that one who has unjustly taken away property that was usurped, or retains property unjustly taken away, restore it according to the laws, justice being its advocate. But if he neglects this and necessity compels, then, at last, matured priestly severity should strike the robber. For it is exceedingly unjust and a great sacrilege that whatever anyone has bestowed or indeed bequeathed to a venerable church, whether for the remedy of sins or the salvation of [Col. 0240D] souls, should be transferred or turned to another use by those especially bound to preserve it—that is, Christians and persons who fear God. Therefore, whoever has not provided against this, and seeks, receives, or possesses estates conveyed to churches otherwise than as is written, unless he quickly corrects himself, shall be struck with anathema, by which God in His wrath strikes souls; and let there be anathema upon the receiver, giver, and possessor. Let him have continual fellowship with the penalty decreed, and let no defence protect him before Christ’s tribunal who squanders property left by devout souls for the substance of the poor.

## CHAPTER 183.—What is to be done concerning an *oeconomus* [steward] who himself alienates Church property, or who, seeing a bishop alienate it, fails to prevent him. Constitution VII, chapter 1. (Emperor Justinian, Novel Constitution 7.)

No one shall dare to injure any church under Roman rule, or any hospice, poorhouse, hospital, orphanage, home for the aged, foundling-home, or monastery of monks or nuns having an archimandrite or archimandritess. Therefore, none of all these institutions may alienate immovable property—whether house, field, garden, rural slave, or civil bread-ration—nor pledge it to creditors by a special hypothecary title. The term “alienation” includes sale, gift, exchange, and a perpetual [Col. 0241B] emphyteutic contract. Let all priests entirely abstain from such alienation, fearing the penalties threatened by the Leonine constitution: namely, that the purchaser of property belonging to a venerable institution must restore it to the person to whom it had formerly belonged, together with its fruits and all other profits accruing in the intervening time; and that the steward of the Church must make good every gain lost through such prohibited alienation. Or, if he has caused loss to the Church, he is thereafter not to remain steward; and not only he himself but also his successors are to be liable, whether the steward himself alienated the property or, seeing the bishop alienate it, failed to prevent him—and still more if he consented. The notary who drew up such prohibited instruments must be consigned to perpetual exile.

[Col. 0241C] ## CHAPTER 184.—That the emperor may lawfully contract an exchange with the Church, chapter 2.

(Justinian, in the same place.) If the emperor wishes to grant immovable property to a holy place and receive from it another immovable property, thus contracting an exchange, he may do so.

## CHAPTER 185.—That one who has purchased, or received from anyone, immovable property of the Church must restore it with all profits accruing in the intervening time; moreover, as a penalty, he must pay to the venerable institution an additional amount equal to what he received; that no one except the emperor may exchange property with the Church; and that if a creditor has received immovable Church property into physical possession, he must first lose both the principal he advanced and its interest, and then restore the property itself with its profits to the venerable institution, chapter 5.

[Col. 0241D] (Justinian, in the same place.) If anyone, contrary to the most salutary laws of the present constitution, purchases immovable property of a venerable institution, he shall first forfeit the value of the property and restore the property unlawfully bought, together with all its profits accruing in the intervening time; and all shall accrue as profit to the Church or other venerable institution. He shall have no action against the churches, but may bring an action on purchase only against the stewards or other persons of the sellers. For it is equitable that the estates of the sellers be liable to the purchaser, even if the sale was made contrary to the present law concerning immovable property belonging to a venerable institution.

But if a gift has been made, then the person who received the prohibited bounty shall not only convey to the venerable institution the property itself, together with its fruits and appurtenances, but shall also pay to the most holy institution, as a penalty, an additional amount equal to that which he received, where the property of that institution was given away by those who administer its affairs. But if anyone receives the property of a venerable institution under the title of exchange, he must restore what he received and forfeit what he himself gave; while retaining an action against the persons and estates of those who contracted with him—except, of course, the emperor, to whom, according to the division stated above, the exchange of immovable properties with most holy places is permitted.

But if a creditor has received a pledge into physical possession, and the property is immovable and belongs to a church or other venerable institution—for example, a house, [Col. 0242B] meadow, field, garden, civil bread-rations, or rural slaves, since these too are, as it were, parts of immovable property—then whoever has physically received any of these as a pledge must first demand neither the principal which he advanced nor any interest he may have stipulated; and must then restore the property itself with its profits to the venerable institution. In this case too, actions against the steward or other administrators of venerable institutions are available to the creditor. All that we have said must likewise apply in convents or ascetic communities of women.

## CHAPTER 186.—That a venerable institution may borrow money when some necessary and inexcusable cause threatens, chapter 6.

[Col. 0242C] (Justinian, in the same place.) If some necessary and inexcusable cause threatens, so that a venerable institution must borrow money, stewards may also encumber immovable property by the law of pledge, provided that it is not physically delivered to creditors.

## CHAPTER 187.—By what penalty one is to be restrained who, contrary to law, pledges, sells, melts down, or in any manner alienates holy vessels or sacred gifts, chapter 8.

(Justinian, the same Novel Constitution 7.) The same penalties must also restrain one who, contrary to law, pledges, sells, melts down, or in any manner alienates holy vessels or sacred gifts, except, of course, for the redemption of captives.

## CHAPTER 188.—That no one may, by a pragmatic sanction, acquire anything from churches or other venerable institutions, whether movable or immovable property, chapter 9.

(Justinian, the same Novel Constitution 7.) No one may acquire by a pragmatic sanction anything belonging to most holy churches or other venerable institutions, whether it be immovable, or movable yet incapable of alienation. But if the illustrious quaestor dictates such an enactment in writing, or other magistrates receive a notification in the form of a pragmatic sanction, each shall be fined fifty pounds of gold. If devout bishops disregard such pragmatic sanctions, let them know that they do so without danger; for if they accept them, they must not doubt that they will lose even the dignity of their episcopate.

[Col. 0243A] Henceforth no one may contract a wicked sale, gift, or exchange of any monastery whatsoever in which an altar has been placed, sacred Masses celebrated, and monastic life maintained. But if anything of this sort has been done, what has been done shall be deemed undone, and the recipient shall lose the price. The person who sold it shall restore both the property and the price to the most holy Church and to the venerable monasteries whose responsibility it was to restore the monastery unlawfully alienated to its former state. Nor may anyone, whether under the title of pledge or mortgage, encumber a most holy monastery. If anything of this kind has been done, it must be annulled, so that sacred Masses may once again proceed in the most holy monastery.

## CHAPTER 189.—If a venerable institution wishes to exchange immovable property with another venerable institution, it may do so after the benefit to each institution has first been considered, chapter 10.

If a venerable institution wishes to exchange immovable property with another venerable institution—if a church with a church, a poorhouse with a poorhouse, or a church with a poorhouse or monastery; or, to put it simply, if a venerable institution prefers to exchange immovable property with another venerable institution—and if this benefits both institutions, their heads may make the exchange. A decree must first be issued before the metropolitans of the places, after proceedings in which they determine whether the exchange of immovable properties benefits both parties.

[Col. 0243C] ## CHAPTER 190.—That one who builds a church may not appoint in it whatever clerics he wishes, but only those whom the bishop judges worthy. Constitution 49, chapter 2.

(Emperor Justinian, Novel Constitution 57.) If anyone builds a church or gives an allowance to clerics from his own property, he may not make whatever persons he wishes clerics in that church. But if he wishes certain persons to be ordained for himself, he shall present them to the most blessed patriarch; and if the patriarch finds them worthy, he shall ordain them, while if he does not approve them, he shall reject them at his own discretion.

## CHAPTER 191.—That one who has an oratory in his house may not celebrate Masses in it without the bishop’s authorization. Constitution 50, chapter 1.

(Emperor Justinian, Novel Constitution 58.) If anyone has an oratory in [Col. 0243D] his house, he shall not dare to celebrate sacred Masses in it unless he has clerics of the Catholic faith assigned to him by order of the most devout bishop of the city or of the most blessed patriarch. If anyone acts contrary to this, his house shall be adjudged to the rights of the imperial treasury.

## CHAPTER 192.—That no one may dare to build a church or oratory unless, after first consulting the bishop, he determines an endowment sufficient for lights, the care of the oratory, and the maintenance of those who will serve there. Constitution, chapter 1.

(Emperor Justinian, Novel Constitution 67.) No one shall dare to build a church or an oratory until the bishop of the city comes, makes prayers, publicly plants the most holy cross on that site while proceeding there, and makes the matter known to all. Before building, every person shall consult the bishop and fix an amount sufficient for lamps suited to sacred service, the care of the oratory, and the maintenance of those who serve there. If these resources are judged sufficient, he shall first make a donation of them and afterwards build the house. But if what he has specified is not sufficient for maintaining the oratory, it is equitable instead to repair old oratories which perhaps threaten collapse, at the discretion of the most devout bishop of the city.

## CHAPTER 193.—That whatever is of divine law and sacred belongs to no person’s estate. Book II, title 1.

(Emperor Justinian, *Institutes*, Book II, “On the Division and Acquisition of Things,” chapter on divine law.) Sacred, religious, and holy things belong to no one. For whatever is [Col. 0244B] of divine law is included in no one’s estate. Sacred things are those duly consecrated to God by pontiffs, such as sacred buildings and gifts duly dedicated to God’s service; and by our constitution we prohibit these also from being alienated or encumbered, except for the redemption of captives.

Likewise, holy things, such as a wall and gates, are in a certain manner under divine law, and therefore belong to no one’s estate. We call walls holy because the penalty of death is established against those who commit any offence against walls.

## CHAPTER 194.—On divine law and human law. Augustine, Tractate 6 on the first chapter of John.

(Dist. 8, c. *Quo jure*.) By what law do you defend the Church’s estates: divine law or human law? Let them answer: “We have divine law in the Scriptures, human law in the laws of kings.” By what right does anyone possess what he possesses? Is it not by human law? For by divine law, “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Psalm XXIII). The Lord made poor and rich alike from one clay (Genesis II), and one earth bears both poor and rich. Therefore, it is by human law that one says, “This estate is mine; this house is mine; this slave is mine.” Human laws, then, are laws of emperors. Why? Because God distributes these human laws to humankind through emperors and the kings of the age.

A few verses later: Take away the laws of emperors, and who dares say, “That estate is mine, this slave is mine, or this house is mine”? But if kings have made laws so that people may hold these things, do you want us to read the laws, so that you may rejoice? And again: Let the laws be read, in which the emperors plainly commanded that those who, because of communion with the Catholic Church, claim for themselves the name Christian yet refuse peacefully to worship the Author of peace, should dare to possess nothing in the name of the Church. But you say, “What have we to do with the emperor?” Yet, as I have already said, the matter concerns human law; and nevertheless the Apostle wished laws to be obeyed, wished kings to be honoured, and said, “Fear the king” (1 Peter II). Do not say, “What have I to do with the king?” What, then, have you to do with property? Possessions are possessed by the laws of kings. You have said, “What have I to do with the king?” Do not call possessions yours, because you have renounced those very human laws by which possessions are possessed.

[Col. 0245A] ## CHAPTER 195.—That all things offered to God are to be regarded as consecrated. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 7.

Let all things offered to God be regarded as consecrated: vineyards, lands, woods, utensils, clothing, livestock, and other possessions; and likewise all things offered to churches, and thus without doubt to Christ, who is their bridegroom.

## CHAPTER 196.—That tithes must in no way be neglected. From the Council of Rouen, chapter 3.

(16, q. 7, c. *Omnes decimae*.) All the tithes of the land, whether of crops or of the fruit of trees, belong to the Lord and are consecrated to Him. Oxen, sheep, and goats which pass under the shepherd’s rod—whatever comes as the tenth—shall be consecrated to the Lord. Neither good nor bad shall be selected, nor shall one be exchanged for another. If anyone exchanges it, both the animal exchanged and that received in exchange shall be consecrated to the Lord and shall not be redeemed. But because many are found unwilling to give tithes, we decree that, according to the command of our Lord, they be admonished once, a second time, and a third time; if they do not amend, they shall be bound by the bonds of anathema until fitting satisfaction and amendment.

## CHAPTER 197.—On the same matter. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 38.

(16, q. 2, c. *Admonemus*.) We admonish and command that the giving of tithes to God must never be neglected—tithes which God Himself decreed to be given—because one must fear lest anyone who withholds from God what is due to Him may perhaps have his necessities taken from him by God because of his sin.

[Col. 0245C] ## CHAPTER 198.—That bishops and abbots must pay tithes to parish churches from fields and vineyards which they hold for their own use or for the support of the brethren. From the Second Council of Chalon, chapter 19.

(16, q. 1, c. *Questi sunt*.) Certain holy persons further complained that there were bishops and abbots who did not allow tithes to be given to the churches where their tenants hear Mass. Therefore this sacred assembly decreed that bishops and abbots should cause tithes to be conveyed to the churches from fields and vineyards which they hold for their own support or that of the brethren. Their households, however, shall bring their tithes where their children are baptized and where they hear Mass throughout the yearly cycle.

## CHAPTER 199.—That tithes are to be given to God and His priests, demonstrated by the example of the fathers Abraham and Jacob, by the authority of the Old and New Law, and by many arguments. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 8.

(16, q. 7, c. *Decimas*.) Abraham’s acts and Jacob’s promises show that tithes must be given to God and to the priests of God. Then the Law established it, and all holy teachers recall it. Indeed, it was fitting that the Israelites should give to the Lord tithes of livestock, of every crop, and of money: He had delivered them from the ten plagues by which He struck the Egyptians; and in the final plague He destroyed the firstborn of all, while granting His own people the favour that, having obtained wealth, they should despoil Egypt.

Concerning these tithes, the venerable teacher Augustine says: “Tithes are required as a debt. What if God said: ‘Surely the human being is Mine; the land you cultivate is Mine; the seeds you sow are Mine; the animals you make labour are Mine; the warmth of the sun is Mine. Since all things are Mine, you who contribute less would scarcely deserve even a tenth; but I reserve nine for you: give Me a tenth. If you do not give Me the tenth, I shall take away the nine. If you give Me the tenth, I shall multiply the nine.’”
