Therefore, since the Jewish people observed the command concerning tithes with such diligence that, as the Lord Himself testifies, they paid tithes from even the smallest things—rue and cumin—why should the evangelical people not fulfil the same command with greater zeal, they who have a greater number of priests and a more sincere worship of the sacraments? Tithes must therefore be given so that the Lord, propitiated by this devotion, may grant necessities more abundantly, as we have shown above; so that priests and ministers of the Church, relieved of the care and concern of bodily needs without which this life cannot be lived, may be freer for meditation upon the divine law, the administration of teaching, and willing fulfilment of spiritual service; and so that the gift of the people may be offered to the Lord in daily oblation, while canonical provisions may also serve the support of the poor and the repair of churches. For, according to the canons, four portions must be made from the offerings of the faithful: one for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth reserved for the repair of churches.

## CHAPTER 200.—Likewise on tithes. From the Council of Metz, chapter 3. (Council of Mainz, chapter 3.)

[Col. 0246C] (16, q. 7, c. *Decimas*.) Bishops must prohibit the redemption, by any payment whatsoever, of tithes which the people are unwilling to give.

## CHAPTER 201.—That portions must be made from tithes, and what portion belongs to the bishop’s use. From the Council of Cologne, chapter 6.

Likewise, the tithe given by the faithful is to be called God’s tribute and rendered to God in its entirety. A third part of it, according to the canon of Toledo, ought to belong to bishops. We, however, do not wish to use that authority, but wish to receive from it only a fourth part each year, according to the practice of the Roman pontiffs and the observance of the holy Roman Church. If any contentious person, cleric or layman, is found concerning this matter, he shall be deprived of communion and judged by synodal censure.

## CHAPTER 202.—That what is offered to the Church in lands, vineyards, slaves, and livestock belongs to the bishop’s administration; but of what is offered to the altar, two parts belong to the clergy and one part is to be faithfully conveyed to the bishops. From the Council of Toledo. (First Council of Orléans, chapter 17.)

(10, q. 1, c. *De his*.) Concerning things offered to the Church by parishioners in lands, vineyards, slaves, and livestock, the ordinances of the ancient canons shall be observed, so that all things remain under the bishop’s authority. But concerning things offered to altars, one third shall be faithfully conveyed to the bishops and two thirds to the clergy. Of tithes, according to some, one third is to be given annually, or the whole in the third year. Yet we follow the Romans: the bishops shall receive a fourth part each year, or the whole in the fourth year.

## CHAPTER 203.—That portions must be made in every Church from both revenues and the offerings of the faithful, and among whom they are to be divided. Gelasius I, in a letter to the bishops throughout Lucania and Bruttium, chapter 29.

(12, q. 2, c. *Quatuor*.) Four portions should be made, both from revenues and from the offerings of the faithful, according to the resources of each Church, as was reasonably decreed long ago. One shall be for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth assigned to building works. As it is the priest’s concern to pay the full stated amount to the ministers of the Church, so the cleric must know that he is not to demand insolently anything beyond the sum allotted to him.

The restoration of holy places must plainly show that what has been assigned for repairing ecclesiastical buildings has truly been devoted to that purpose. For it is wicked, when sacred buildings are left destitute, for a bishop to divert to his own profit the expenditures assigned to them. Likewise, although he may claim to have distributed the portion allotted to the poor in divine prayers, it must nevertheless, according to what is written, “That they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew V), be made known by present testimony and not left unmentioned in the praises of good repute.

## CHAPTER 204.—On the same matter. From the Council of Nantes, chapter 6.

[Col. 0247C] Priests must be instructed and likewise admonished to know that the tithes and offerings which they receive from the faithful are provisions for the poor, strangers, and pilgrims, and that they must use them not as their own but as things entrusted to them. Let them know that they will render an account before God for all these things and that, unless they administer them faithfully to the poor and to those for whom they are commanded, they will suffer loss. The holy canons prescribe how they must be distributed: four portions are to be made from them—one for relieving the needs of the church building, another distributed to the poor, a third provided to priests or clerics, and a fourth reserved for the bishop, so that whatever he orders from it may be done with prudent counsel.

[Col. 0247D] ## CHAPTER 205.—That disputes arising among Christians must be settled. From the decrees of Pope Marcellinus, chapter 3.

Whatever disputes arise among Christians shall be brought before the Church and settled by ecclesiastical persons. If they refuse to obey, they shall be excluded from the thresholds of the holy Church until they obey.

## CHAPTER 206.—On those who attempt to retain or take away offerings of their parents, testamentary bequests, or gifts which they themselves have made to the Church. From the Council of Agde, chapter 4.

(13, q. 2, c. *Clerici vel saeculares*.) Clerics or laypersons who persist in retaining offerings of their parents, whether donated or left by testament, or who think that what they themselves have given to churches or monasteries may be taken away, shall, as the holy synod has decreed, be excluded from the churches as murderers of the poor until they restore it.

## CHAPTER 207.—That we ought to make God our heir. Saint Isidore.

Augustine says in the book *On Heirs*: “Do not, under the appearance of piety, increase your money by saying, ‘I am preserving these goods for my children.’ Why do you not rather preserve them for Him who made you from nothing, who feeds you, and preserves your children? Will you not store treasure better for your Creator than for your children?” And again: “With what face do you seek an inheritance from Christ when you have defrauded Christ of your inheritance?” He said: “Store up treasures for yourselves in heaven” (Matthew VI).

[Col. 0248B] ## CHAPTER 208.—On those who deny or reluctantly restore the offerings of the dead. From the Council of Valence, chapter 4.

Those who deny to churches the offerings of the dead, or restore them only with difficulty, shall be excommunicated as murderers of the needy.

On the same matter. From the decrees of Pope Urban, chapter 4. For these things are called the offerings of the faithful because they are offered to God. Therefore, they must not be diverted to uses other than ecclesiastical purposes and the needs of the aforesaid Christian brethren or needy persons; for they are vows of the faithful and the prices of sins, delivered to God for carrying out the aforesaid work. But if anyone—may it never be!—acts otherwise, let him take care not to incur the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira and become guilty of sacrilege, as those did [Col. 0248C] who defrauded the proceeds of the aforesaid things, concerning whom the account is thus read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts V).

## CHAPTER 209.—That no one may presume to give or receive Church offerings outside the Church. From the Council of Gangra, chapter 7.

If anyone wishes to receive or give Church offerings outside the Church, without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person entrusted with such duties, and does not wish to act by his counsel, let him be anathema.

## CHAPTER 210.—On the same matter. From the same source, chapter 8.

If anyone gives or receives offerings apart from the bishop or from the person appointed by him to administer mercy to the poor, both the giver and the receiver shall be anathema.

## CHAPTER 211.—That all churches, with their endowments, tithes, and all their property, must remain under the bishop’s authority. From the Council of Chalon, chapter 1.

The holy Council of Chalon decreed that all churches, with their endowments, tithes, and all their property, remain under the authority of their own bishop and always belong to his administration.

## CHAPTER 212.—That thirty years’ possession is secure. From the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 34.

(16, q. 3, c. *Sicut dioecesim*.) Just as thirty years’ possession removes another’s diocese, so possession of territory does not lose a congregation. Therefore newly established basilicas shall undoubtedly belong to the bishop whose congregation they are shown to be.

[Col. 0249A] ## CHAPTER 213.—That no one may be buried in a church unless, by living piously and justly, the deceased has acquired such a place; and that no one buried in a church in ancient times may be removed unless a pagan, but that visible tombs should be sunk to the level of the pavement. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 9.

In these regions there was an ancient practice of burying the dead in churches, and places devoted to divine worship and prepared for offering sacrifices to God were often made into cemeteries or burial-grounds (*polyandria*). We therefore wish this practice henceforth to be discontinued, and that no one be buried in a church, unless perhaps he is a priest or some other just person who, by the merit of his life, acquired such a place for himself by living in such a way before his death.

Bodies buried in churches in ancient times are by no means to be cast out, unless they are those of pagans. But tombs which are visible should be sunk more deeply into the earth, and after pavement has been laid above them, with no trace of the tombs visible, the reverence due to the church shall be preserved. Where there is such a multitude of corpses that this is difficult to do, that place shall be treated as a cemetery: the altar shall be removed and established elsewhere, where sacrifice may be offered to God reverently and purely.

## CHAPTER 214.—That holy places do not free those buried in a church if their sins have not been forgiven; rather, they charge them with the fault of presumption. Augustine.

Those whose sins have not been forgiven cannot be helped by holy places after death. For when persons weighed down by graver sins arrange to have themselves buried in holy places, it remains that they be judged for their presumption: holy places do not free them, but the fault of their rashness accuses them.

## CHAPTER 215.—That nothing is to be demanded for a place of burial; but if relatives and friends of the dead wish to give something for the redemption of the soul, it is to be received with charity. From the Council of Tribur, chapter 16.

(13, q. 2, c. *In ecclesiastico*.) For it is written in the book of Ecclesiasticus: “Do not withhold kindness from the dead” (Ecclesiasticus VII), knowing that we shall all die (Ecclesiasticus VIII). Likewise: “All things that arise from the earth shall return to the earth” (Ecclesiastes III). Do you sell earth to earth? Remember that you are earth and shall go into earth, and that death will come to you: it approaches and does not delay. Remember that the earth does not belong to a human being, but, as the Psalmist declares: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Psalm XXIII). If you sell earth, you will be held guilty of invading another’s property. You received it freely from God; give it freely for His sake. Therefore all Christians without exception are forbidden to sell earth to the dead or to deny due burial, unless perhaps the deceased’s relatives and friends wish freely to give something for the man’s name and the redemption of his soul.

## CHAPTER 216.—That burial in a church is beneficial when grievous sins do not weigh one down; otherwise it tends rather to a greater accumulation of condemnation than to absolution. Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 50.

When those whom grave sins do not weigh down are buried in churches, this is of benefit to the dead: whenever their relatives come to those holy places and behold the burial-place of their own, they remember them and pour out prayers to the Lord for them. But those whom grave sins weigh down have their bodies placed in churches not so much for absolution as for a greater accumulation of condemnation. We shall show this more clearly if we briefly recount events that happened in our own days.

For the venerable Felix, bishop of Porto, was born and brought up in the Sabine province. He testified that there was in that same place a certain nun who possessed continence of the flesh indeed, but did not avoid an insolent tongue and foolish talk. When she died, she was buried in a church. But that night the keeper of that church saw in a revelation that she was brought before the holy altar, cut in two down the middle, and one part of her was burned with fire, while the other part remained untouched. When he rose in the morning, told this to the brethren, and wished to point out the place where she had been consumed by fire, the burning of the flame appeared on the marble before the altar, just as though that woman herself had there been burned bodily by fire. From this it is plainly understood that those whose sins have not been forgiven cannot, after death, be helped by holy places in order to escape judgment.

### CHAPTER 217.—On the same matter. Ibid., chapter 52.

John also, a distinguished man holding the office of prefect in this city, whose truthfulness and gravity we know, testified to me that the patrician Valerian died in the city called Brescia. The bishop of that city, having accepted a price, gave him a place in a church in which he was to be buried. This Valerian, plainly enough, had remained frivolous and dissolute into decrepit old age and had scorned to put a limit to his wickedness.

On the same night on which he was buried, the blessed martyr Faustinus, in whose church his body had been interred, appeared to the custodian and said: “Go and tell the bishop to throw out from here the stinking flesh which he has placed here; for if he does not do so, he himself shall die on the thirtieth day.” The custodian was afraid to disclose this vision to the bishop, and, being admonished again, still evaded it. But on the thirtieth day the bishop of that city, though he had returned to bed at evening healthy and sound, died by a sudden and unexpected death.

### CHAPTER 218.—On the same matter. Ibid., chapter 53.

There are also alive in the present age the venerable old man, Father Venantius, bishop of Luni, and the distinguished Liberius, a man most noble and truthful, who testify that they know—and that their own men were present at—the event which they relate as having occurred in the city of Genoa.  
*(This is mentioned in the Council of Tribur, chapter 17.)*

There, as they say, a man named Valentinus, defender of the Church of Milan, died: a man exceedingly dissolute and occupied with every sort of frivolity. His body was buried in the church of the blessed martyr Syrus. At midnight, however, voices arose in that church, as though persons were being violently driven out of it and dragged outside. At these voices the custodians ran up and saw two utterly hideous spirits who had bound the feet of this Valentinus with some fastening and were dragging him out of the church, while he cried aloud and shouted exceedingly. Terrified, they returned to their beds.

When morning came, they opened the tomb in which Valentinus had been laid and did not find his body. Searching inside the church to discover where he had been cast, they found him laid in another tomb, his feet still bound as when he had been dragged from the church. From this, Peter, infer that those whom grave sins weigh down, if they arrange to be buried in a holy place, must further be judged for their presumption, so that holy places do not free them but rather the guilt of their rashness accuses them also.

### CHAPTER 219.—Ibid., on the same matter, chapter 54.

For a multitude of the dyers who live in this city testify to what happened here. When a certain leading man of their trade had died, his wife buried him inside the church of the blessed martyr Januarius, near the gate of Saint Lawrence. On the following night his spirit began to cry out from that tomb, within hearing of the custodian: “I am burning, I am burning!” When he had uttered these cries for a long time, the custodian reported this to his wife.

His wife sent men of the same trade to the church to inspect carefully, wishing to learn how his body was in the tomb from which such cries came. Opening the tomb, they found his garments intact—garments which are still kept in that church as evidence of this event—but did not find his body at all, as though it had never been placed in that tomb. From this it must be inferred with what punishment his soul was condemned, when even his flesh was cast out of the church. What, therefore, do holy places benefit those who are buried, when those who are unworthy are divinely cast out from those same holy places?

### CHAPTER 220.—That bodies of the dead are not to be buried in a church, but, if necessary, outside around the wall. From the First Council of Braga, chapter 36.

Likewise it has been decided that bodies of the dead are by no means to be buried inside a basilica; but, if necessary, they are to be buried outside around the wall of the basilica. For if the cities of Gaul retain to this day this most firmly established privilege [the reading perhaps means “it remains in the cities”], that the body of no deceased person is buried in any way within the circuit of a city’s walls, how much more ought reverence for the venerable martyrs to be maintained!

### CHAPTER 221.—On the same matter. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 10.

No one is to presume to bury any dead person in a church, as though by hereditary right, except one whom the bishop or priest judges worthy on account of the quality of his conduct and life. Nor is anyone to cast the bones of any dead person out of his tomb or in any manner violate anyone’s burial-place by rash audacity. Rather, let each person be permitted to await the coming of his Judge in the resting-place prepared and granted to him by God.

### CHAPTER 222.—Nothing is to be demanded for burying bodies. From the Council of Nantes, chapter 11; Council of Vaison, chapter 5.

*(13, question 2, canon “Praecipiendum.”)* According to the authority of the canons it must be commanded that they demand no payment for tombs or for the burial of persons, unless perhaps the person being buried, while alive, directed that something from his own property should be given to the church in whose court he is buried; or unless, after his death, something else is demanded from his property by those to whom it was entrusted to give his alms, or by those who preside over the places and villages.

It must also be forbidden, according to the ordinances of the elders, that persons be buried in a church at all, but rather in its court, portico, or exedrae; within the church itself, however, or near the altar where the body and blood of the Lord are consecrated, they are to have absolutely no permission to bury.

### CHAPTER 223.—That it is fitting for a wife to be buried with her husband in the same tomb. Jerome.  
*[Note: Col. 0251. In the Hebrew Questions on Genesis and On Hebrew Places.]*

*(12, question 2, canon “Ebron.”)* Hebron is said to be the city of three men, because three patriarchs were buried there in the double cave with their three wives: namely Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebecca, Jacob and Leah, besides Adam himself and Eve his wife. Tobit says to his son: “When God takes my soul, you shall bury my body; and you shall honor your mother all the days of her life; and when she has completed her time, you shall bury her beside me” (Tobit 4), in one tomb.

### CHAPTER 224.—On the same matter. The same author.

Those whom one marriage joins together, let one tomb join together; for they are one flesh; and: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19).

### CHAPTER 225.—Likewise, on the same matter. Augustine.

*(13, question 2, canon “Unaquaeque.”)* Let every woman follow her husband, whether in life or in death.

### CHAPTER 226.—That burial may not separate those whose mind was one in the Lord. Gregory, *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 34.

The sister of Saint Benedict was buried in the tomb which he had prepared for himself, so that burial might not separate the bodies of those whose mind had always been one in the Lord. Thus, those joined in their first marriage, because they are one and the same flesh, are to be buried in one tomb.

### CHAPTER 227.—That grants at request or exchanges made while churches are vacant are invalid. From the Council of Beauvais, held in the presence of Louis, chapter 10.

That grants at request (*precariae*) and exchanges made during the vacancy of churches by those who had occupied the places of bishops are to be rescinded; and, if they are to be made, they are to be made with ecclesiastical or civil authority.

### CHAPTER 228.—On the same matter. From the same council, chapter 11.

*(10, question 2, canon “Precariae a nemine.”)* No one is to presume to make grants at request from ecclesiastical property, except that, in proportion to a suitable contribution given from one’s own property, double the amount may be received from the property of the church, only in the name of the person who gave, if he wishes to hold both his own property and ecclesiastical property in usufruct. But if he has presently relinquished his own property, let him receive from ecclesiastical property threefold in usufruct, only in his own name; for everyone ought to administer such things as one who is a steward of another’s property, not a dispenser of his own.

### CHAPTER 229.—The same, on the same matter. From the same council, chapter 12.

No authority is to compel anyone to make a grant at request from property dedicated to God and His saints, since reason and practice establish that no one should be compelled to bestow from his own property a benefit granted against his will, contrary to utility and reason.

### CHAPTER 230.—On the same matter. From the same council, chapter 13.

*(10, question 2, canon “Precariae.”)* Grants at request are to be renewed every five years, according to ancient custom and authority.

### CHAPTER 231.—On the donation, sale, or exchange of ecclesiastical property. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 32.

*(12, question 2, canon “Sine exceptione.”)* A bishop’s donation, sale, or exchange of ecclesiastical property shall be invalid without the approval and subscription of the clergy.

### CHAPTER 232.—On exchanges of ecclesiastical property. From the Council of Beauvais.

*(Extra, On exchanges of things, canon “Ut commutationes.”)* Exchanges of ecclesiastical property are to be undertaken with great caution and examined most carefully if they must be made in any way. But exchanges made inconsiderately are to be corrected by the successor, according to the canonical decree of Pope Hilary, where a predecessor bishop unlawfully lost property or where unlawful acts were committed by others.

### CHAPTER 233.—On the same matter. From the Council of Mâcon, chapter 4.

The holy synod has decreed, and imperial authority declares, that no person is to presume to make exchanges of ecclesiastical property or slaves without the permission and consent of the religious authority.

### CHAPTER 234.—On the exchange of ecclesiastical slaves. From the council held at Quierzy [or Senlis], chapter 2.

No one is to exchange ecclesiastical slaves except for freedom; that is, slaves given in exchange for an ecclesiastical slave are to remain in the church’s servitude, while the ecclesiastical slave who is exchanged is to enjoy perpetual freedom. For what has once been consecrated to the Lord can no longer be transferred to human uses. For the Law says: “If anyone exchanges it, then both that which is exchanged and that for which it is exchanged shall be consecrated to the Lord” (Leviticus 27).

### CHAPTER 235.—On the same matter. From the same council, chapter 3.

*(2, question 2, canon “Injustum.”)* It seems unjust and impious that slaves whom faithful men or women have consecrated to God and His saints for the remedy of their souls should again be reduced to secular servitude through the slave given as payment in any transaction or through an exchange, when canonical authority permits only fugitive slaves to be alienated. Therefore all governors of churches must take the greatest care lest one person’s alms become another person’s sin. It is absurd that one leaving servitude through ecclesiastical dignity should become subject to human servitude.

### CHAPTER 236.—On royal mandates concerning ecclesiastical grants at request, which are not to be admitted. From the council held at Saint-Médard, chapter 11.

Neither reason permits nor authority in any way allows royal mandates to be issued concerning ecclesiastical grants at request, because it is judged unworthy that mandates should be confirmed in ecclesiastical law. It is necessary that royal majesty seek such a matter only from an ecclesiastical governor; that is, that the guardian of the church take the greatest care lest, perhaps forgetful of his office and of ecclesiastical exchange, he seek, contrary to authority, the issuance of a royal mandate for the sake of any favor. If he does so, he is not to be heard. But if he obtains it, it is to be rescinded by royal compulsion and episcopal judgment, and the unjust petitioner is to be duly corrected for his unjust suggestion to the prince.

### CHAPTER 237.—On a bishop who wishes to manumit a slave of the church. From the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 67.

*(12, question 2, canon “Episcopus qui.”)* A bishop who wishes to manumit a slave belonging by right to the church, without retaining the church’s patronage, shall offer before the council of the church over which he presides two persons of equal worth and peculium, by way of exchange, with the priests subscribing, so that the decision of the one making the exchange may be found valid and just. For only when he has already acquired as his own property the person whom he proposes to give to freedom may he grant free manumission without patronage.

Such a freedman is to be denied permission to accuse or testify against the church to which he belonged by right. If he presumes to do so, it is decreed that, while the exchange remains valid, he be recalled into the church’s own servitude.

### CHAPTER 238.—That priests who leave their own property to the church, or acquire for the church lands or households, may, if they wish, manumit some persons from the household of that church. From the same council, chapter 68.

The agreement of the whole council has determined that priests who either leave their own property to the church or, although possessing nothing, nevertheless acquire for their churches some lands or households, may manumit some persons from the households of that church, in proportion to the thing contributed, as the ancient canons decreed. They and their descendants, if free-born, are to remain under the church’s patronage together with their peculium, performing, as far as they are able, the services imposed on them.

### CHAPTER 239.—That priests are not to presume to sell church property. From the Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter 4.

*(12, question 2, canon “Placuit.”)* It has likewise been decided that priests are not to sell property of the church in which they are established without the knowledge of their bishops, just as bishops are not permitted to sell church estates without the knowledge of the council or their priests. Therefore, when he has no necessity, not even a bishop may appropriate for his own title property of the mother church without the knowledge of the council or his priests.

### CHAPTER 240.—On the same matter. From the First Council of Braga, chapter 17.

*(Distinction 50, canon “Si quis presbyt.”)* If any priest or deacon is found to have sold anything from the church’s goods without the knowledge of the council, because he has committed sacrilege, it has been decided that he is not to be retained in the church’s office; nevertheless, he is to be left to the judgment of the bishop as to whether he is worthy to be restored to his rank.

### CHAPTER 241.—What is to be done concerning a bishop who has sold church property. From the same council, chapter 31.

*(2, question 3, canon “Placuit.”)* Any priest who attempts in any manner permanently to alienate, as donor, alienator, or seller, gold, silver, gems, vestments, if such exist, or any movable objects added for ornamentation, from the right of his own title, shall be punished by loss of his office.

### CHAPTER 242.—On the same matter. From the same council, chapter 14.

*(10, question 2, canon “Si quis.”)* If any bishop, compelled by no necessity arising from ecclesiastical reason, presumes to sell anything from ecclesiastical property among his own clergy, or where perhaps there is no priest, he is to be compelled to restore those properties to his own church. He is to be heard and deposed by the judgment of bishops, and, being guilty of theft and robbery, is to be deprived of his office.

### CHAPTER 243.—That the amount of ecclesiastical property, just as it grants the remedy of pardon to the contributor, so properly prepares loss for the defrauder. From the Council of Toledo, chapter 33.

Every quantity of ecclesiastical property, therefore, just as it grants the remedy of pardon to the contributor, so properly prepares loss for the defrauder. Therefore no priest or minister is to take away anything from the property which the faithful bestow in any places for the church and attach it to his own right or to the unity of his own see.

But, so that the security of this matter may be more firmly maintained, the relatives of those who built or endowed a church may lawfully exercise this careful concern born of good intention: if they perceive a priest or minister defrauding anything from the property contributed, they are either to restrain him by an honorable conference of admonition or report such acts to the bishop or judge for correction. If the bishop attempts such acts, they are not to delay reporting them to his metropolitan. Yet the heirs themselves are not permitted, in respect of those same properties, to assert authority as though by their own right; they may neither commit nor introduce robbery or fraud nor presume any violence whatsoever. Whoever presumes rashly to violate these warnings shall restore with disgrace what has been wrongly seized and shall undergo a sentence of excommunication for one year.

### CHAPTER 244.—On freedpersons who have departed from the church’s patronage. From the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 70.

*(12, question 2, canon “Liberti.”)* Freedpersons of the church who depart from its patronage and attach themselves to any persons whatsoever, if, after being admonished, they scorn to return, shall have their manumission invalidated, because through contemptuous disobedience they are held guilty of an ungrateful act.

### CHAPTER 245.—On freedpersons of the church. Ibid., chapter 69.

*(12, question 2, canon “Liberti.”)* The freedpersons of the church, because their patroness never dies, are never to depart from its patronage, nor indeed are their descendants, as earlier canons have decreed. And lest their freedom perhaps be unknown in future offspring, and those descendants, relying on their natural free birth, withdraw themselves from the patronage of the holy church, it is necessary that both the freedpersons themselves and those born from them make a profession to their bishop. By it they acknowledge that, though free, they belong to the household of the church and do not abandon its patronage, but render it service or obedience according to their ability.

### CHAPTER 246.—On freedpersons manumitted by anyone. From the same council, chapter 71.

*(Distinction 87, canon “Liberti.”)* Freedpersons manumitted by anyone whatsoever and commended to the church’s patronage are, as the rules of the ancient Fathers established, to be protected by priestly defense from the insolence of anyone, both in their state of freedom and in the peculium which they are known to possess.

### CHAPTER 247.—On persons manumitted in church. From the First Council of Orange, chapter 7.

If anyone attempts to reduce [printed alternate: restore] into slavery, service, or the status of a colonus persons manumitted in church or commended to the church by testament, he shall be restrained by ecclesiastical punishment.

### CHAPTER 248.—On fugitive ecclesiastical slaves. From the Council of Toledo.

Even fugitive ecclesiastical slaves who abandon their homes or households, and who cannot be retained even if recalled, may, for the same reason, be sold by the bishop if he wishes, or if they have so deserved.

### CHAPTER 249.—On bishops who contribute nothing to their church and presume to make persons free from the church’s household. From the same council.

Bishops who contribute nothing of their own to Christ’s church are not to presume, to their own condemnation, to free persons from the church’s households. For it is impious that one who has not contributed his own property to Christ’s church should inflict loss upon the church. Therefore the successor of such a bishop shall recall such freedpersons to the right of the church without any objection.

### CHAPTER 250.—What ought to be read in church. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 3.

Nothing other than writings possessing divine authority and those whose authority the orthodox Fathers have established is to be read or sung in church. Nor are they to worship false names of angels, but only those taught by prophetic and evangelical Scripture: namely Michael, Gabriel, Raphael.

### CHAPTER 251.—Those who read apocryphal books in church are to be excommunicated. From the Council of Elvira, chapter 52.

If anyone is found reading or singing apocryphal and unknown books in church, let him be excommunicated.

### CHAPTER 252.—On women who conceive secretly. From the Council of Mâcon, chapter 6.

This holy council has decreed that every priest shall publicly announce to his people that, if any woman who has been secretly violated has conceived, she is by no means to kill her son or daughter. Rather, by whatever means she can, she is to carry the child before the doors of a church and have it placed there, so that on the following day it may be carried before a priest, received by some faithful person, and nourished. Thus she may escape the guilt of homicide and, what is worse, parricide. For whoever kills a son or daughter is altogether to be designated a parricide.

### CHAPTER 253.—On infants born in adultery and exposed at a church. From the Second Council of Arles, chapter 32.

If an exposed child before a church is taken up through the compassion of anyone, the person who takes it up shall deposit a written declaration, so that, if the child who has been taken up is not sought for and recognized within ten days, the collector may possess the child securely. Certainly, anyone who after the stated time appears as a claimant shall be condemned by ecclesiastical discipline as a murderer, as the authority of the Fathers has established.

### CHAPTER 254.—On the same matter. From the Council of Vaison, chapter 9.

Because a complaint brought jointly by all has arisen concerning exposed children—that children are now exposed not to mercy but to dogs, since human compassion, though inclined toward the commands of mercy, refuses to take them up from fear of lawsuits—the following is to be observed. According to the enactments of the most faithful Augusti and most pious princes, whoever takes up an exposed child shall notify the church and obtain a declaration. Moreover, on the Lord’s Day the minister shall announce it from the altar, so that the church may know that an exposed child has been taken up and may reclaim the exposed child within ten days from the day of exposure.

If anyone proves that he has recognized the child, he shall give the collector at once, as he chooses, something in consideration of those ten days of mercy; or the collector may, if he wishes, possess the child permanently with God’s grace. If anyone appears as a claimant or litigious challenger of exposed children taken up in this prescribed manner, he is to be considered a murderer.

### CHAPTER 255.—If priests remove the offerings of the faithful from the church and turn them to their own uses. From the Council of Toledo, Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 32.

“Avarice is the root of all evils” (1 Timothy 6), and its thirst takes possession even of the minds of priests. For many of the faithful, out of love for Christ and the martyrs, build basilicas in bishops’ parishes and record offerings; the priests take these away and turn them to their own uses. Hence worshippers abandon the sacred places when they lose their support; hence the ruins of collapsing basilicas are not repaired, because priestly avarice takes everything away.

*(16, question 1, canon “Constitutum est.”)* For this reason the present council has decreed that bishops are to govern their dioceses so that they presume to take nothing from the dioceses’ right, but receive a third part, according to the authority of earlier councils, from offerings, tithes, dues, and produce. If they presume anything further, restitution shall be made through the council, upon the complaint of the founders themselves or, if they have already departed this world, of their relatives.

*(10, question 1, canon “Noverint.”)* Let founders of basilicas know, however, that they possess no authority over the property which they confer upon those basilicas; rather, according to the ordinances of the canons, the endowment of a church, like the church itself, belongs to the bishop’s administration.

### CHAPTER 256.—On a certain man vexed by a demon. Pope Gregory, *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 16.

At the same time, a certain cleric of the Church of Aquino was vexed by a demon. He was sent by the venerable Constance, bishop of that church, to many shrines of martyrs so that he might be healed. But God’s holy martyrs would not grant him the gift of health, in order to show how great was the grace in Benedict. He was therefore brought to Benedict, servant of almighty God, who poured out prayers to the Lord Jesus Christ and immediately drove the ancient enemy out of the possessed man.

When the man was healed, Benedict instructed him: “Go, and henceforth eat no flesh; and never presume to approach sacred orders. But on whatever day you presume rashly to violate this prohibition concerning sacred orders, you shall immediately again be made subject to the devil’s power.” The cleric departed healed and, as a recent punishment commonly terrifies the mind, for the time being observed what the man of God had commanded.

But after many years, when all his elders had departed this life and he saw persons younger than himself set over him in sacred orders, he set aside the words of the man of God, as though forgotten through the long passage of time, and entered sacred orders. Immediately the devil who had left him seized him, and did not cease tormenting him until he drove out his soul.

### CHAPTER 257.—On church property sold by priests after the bishop’s death. From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 14.

Concerning property belonging to the church which priests sold when the bishop was absent, it has been decided that the contract be rescinded and the property restored to ecclesiastical rights. But it shall be for the bishop to decide whether the stipulated price ought to be returned, or not, because it often happens that the proceeds of property sold bring back a sum greater than the price received.

### CHAPTER 258.—On one who refuses the offering of a priest who has had a wife. From the Council of Gangra, chapter 4.

Whoever separates himself from a priest who has had a wife, on the ground that one ought not receive from the offering when he ministers, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER 259.—That clergy are not to be allowed to go to the cemeteries of heretics. From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 9.

Clergy are not to be permitted to visit the cemeteries of heretics, or the places which they call shrines of martyrs, for prayer or healing. If such persons are faithful, they are to be deprived of communion for a fixed time; but, when they repent and confess that they have sinned, it is fitting that they be received.

### CHAPTER 260.—That one ought not receive *eulogiae* from heretics. From the same council, chapter 32.

*(1, question 1, canon “Non oportet.”)* One ought not receive *eulogiae* from heretics, since they are curses rather than blessings.

### CHAPTER 261.—That no Christian should go to pseudo-martyrs. From the same council, chapter 34.

No Christian ought to abandon Christ’s martyrs and go to pseudo-martyrs—that is, those of heretics, who are themselves known to have been heretics. For they have been alienated from the Lord. Therefore let those who approach such persons be anathema.

### CHAPTER 262.—That popular psalms ought not to be sung in church. Ibid., chapter 59.

Popular psalms ought not to be sung in church, nor books outside the canon read, but only the sacred volumes of the New or Old Testament.

### CHAPTER 263.—On those who abominate gatherings held at the shrines of martyrs. From the Council of Antioch, chapter 20.

If anyone, under the influence of arrogant feeling, abominates the gatherings celebrated at the shrines of martyrs and execrates the services performed in them together with their commemorations, let him be anathema.

That sustenance be supplied by exorcists to the possessed who sit in the house of God. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 92.

To the possessed who sit in the house of God, daily sustenance shall be supplied by exorcists at a suitable time.

### CHAPTER 264.—That sacred vessels are not to be handled except by consecrated persons. From the decrees of Pope Sixtus.

Let your wisdom know, most beloved brethren, that it is established by us, the other bishops, and the remaining priests of the Lord in this holy apostolic see that sacred vessels are not to be handled by anyone except persons consecrated and dedicated to the Lord. For it is most unworthy that sacred vessels of the Lord, whatever they may be, should serve human uses, and that they should be handled only by men serving and dedicated to the Lord, lest, because of such presumptions, the angry Lord lay a plague upon His people and those who have not sinned suffer evils or perish also; for the righteous person very often perishes because of the ungodly.

Take care not to permit such things henceforth in your churches, lest the flock redeemed by the most precious blood of Christ fall, God forbid, into destruction.

### CHAPTER 265.—On consecrated women who presume to handle sacred vessels and altar-cloths. From a letter of Pope Soter.

*(Distinction 23, canon uncertain: “Idem supra,” chapter 72.)* It has been reported to the Apostolic See that consecrated women or nuns among you touch sacred vessels or sacred altar-cloths [the printed text alternates *sacras* and *sacratas*], offer incense, and carry it about the altars. No right-thinking person can doubt that all these things are full of blame and reproach. Therefore, by the authority of this holy see, we judge that you must cut off all these practices utterly as quickly as possible; and, lest this pest spread more widely through all provinces, we command that it be wiped away most speedily.

### CHAPTER 266.—What is to be done with sacred vessels, altar-cloths, and church veils if worn out by age. From the letter of Pope Clement, letter 20.

*(On consecration, distinction 1, canon “Altaris palla.”)* Concerning sacred vessels, what is to be done with them: if an altar-cloth, chair, candlestick, or veil has been worn out through age, it is to be given to the fire. For things which have been in the sanctuary may not be improperly handled, but are all to be consigned to fire. Their ashes also are to be put into the baptistery, where no passage is made, or cast into a wall or into the trenches of the pavement, lest they be defiled by the feet of those entering.

But altar-cloths and veils which have been soiled in the sanctuary are to be washed within the sanctuary by deacons together with humble ministers. The coverings of the Lord’s table are not to be carried outside the sanctuary, lest perhaps dust from the Lord’s body improperly fall when the linen cloth is carried outside, and this be sin for the one performing the act. Therefore we command the ministers to keep them carefully in the sacristy. The altar-cloths are to be washed in one basin and the veils in another.

### CHAPTER 267.—That incense ought to be placed at the offering of the Lord’s body and blood. From the Council of Rouen, chapter 2.

We decree that, at the time when the Gospel is read and when the offertory has ended, incense is to be placed over the offering, namely in remembrance of the death of our Redeemer.

### CHAPTER 268.—That, as often as the basilica to which people go is filled by the presence of a new body of people, the subsequent sacrifice is to be offered. From Leo’s letter to Dioscorus of Alexandria, chapter 2.

In order that our observance may agree in all things, we also wish the following to be observed: when the celebration of a solemn feast has summoned a larger gathering of people, and a multitude of the faithful has assembled at the same place which one basilica cannot contain, the sacrifice is without doubt to be repeated. Otherwise, if only those who arrived first are admitted to this devotion, those who come together afterwards may seem excluded.

For it is a work of complete piety and prayer that as often as any basilica is again filled by the presence of a new gathering of people, the subsequent sacrifice be offered. But some portion of the people must be deprived of its devotion if, with the custom of only one Mass observed, the sacrifice cannot be offered unless they assemble during the first part of the day.

### CHAPTER 269.—That no priest is to presume to appropriate one title-church in addition to another. From the Council of Nantes.

If any priest dies, a neighboring priest is not, by any entreaty or gift, to obtain that church from the senior lay authority, because the title is already established in itself. Nor is he to obtain a chapel without the bishop’s consultation. If he does so, he shall receive the prescribed sentence pronounced against him, as canonical authority has decreed concerning a bishop: if through ambition he seeks a greater city, he shall lose the one he held and by no means obtain the one which he attempted to usurp.

### CHAPTER 270.—What is to be done with altars in which holy bodies or relics are not found. From the African Council, chapter 1.

Altars in which the sacred bodies or relics of martyrs are not proved to be present are to be destroyed by the bishop of that place.

At an altar at which a bishop has celebrated Mass, no priest is to celebrate on that day. From the Council of Urbicus.

No priest is to presume to celebrate Mass on that day at an altar at which a bishop has sung Mass.

### CHAPTER 271.—That a bishop or priest, after beginning Mass and saying the prayer, may in no way depart from God’s altar before completing the ministry, unless some emergency intervenes. Pope Zacharias, chapter 9.

When a bishop or priest has entered to celebrate the solemnities of Mass, unless some emergency intervenes, he is in no way to dare depart after offering the prayer, so that the solemnities of Mass may be completed by another bishop or priest. Rather, the one who has undertaken the beginning is to complete it to the end, because it is written: “The one who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matthew 10). If anyone presumes to act contrary to what we have set down, he is to be suspended from the sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

### CHAPTER 272.—That no bishop or priest is to presume to go to celebrate the solemnities of Mass with a staff, or to stand before God’s altar with his head covered. From the decrees of the same pope, chapter 13.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 1, chapter “No one.”) Let no bishop, priest, or deacon presume to enter for the celebration of the solemn rites of Mass carrying a staff, or to stand at God’s altar with his head covered [Col. 0261B]; for the Apostle also forbids men to pray in church with the head covered (I Cor. XI). If anyone rashly presumes to do so, let him be excommunicated.

CAP. 273.—That the bodies of saints are not to be transferred from place to place. From the First Council of Mainz, chapter 51.

Henceforth let no one presume to transfer the bodies of saints from one place to another without the counsel of the prince or the permission of the bishops and of the holy synod.

CAP. 274.—Which dead persons may lawfully be buried in a church. From the same, chapter 52.

Let no dead person be buried inside a church, except bishops, abbots, worthy priests, or faithful laypersons.

[Col. 0261C] CAP. 275.—That all faithful people ought to do nothing in church except pray. From the Third Council of Tours, chapter 38.

Priests ought to admonish the faithful that, when they assemble at church, they should enter it without noise or commotion. While they remain there for prayer, they must by no means engage in idle conversation among themselves; but during the celebration of the solemn rites of Mass they must abstain entirely not only from idle and useless words, but also from harmful thoughts.

CAP. 276.—That divine mercy is to be implored with knees fixed upon the ground, except on the greater solemnities. From the same, chapter 37.

It must be understood that, except on Sundays and on those solemnities on which the holy and universal Church customarily prays standing in remembrance of the Lord’s Resurrection [Col. 0261D], we must humbly beg, with knees fixed upon the ground, for the mercy that benefits us and for pardon for our sins. The Lord himself gave us an example of this in the Gospel (Matt. XXVI). The book of the Acts of the Apostles testifies that the martyr Stephen (Acts VII) and the Apostle Paul did likewise (Acts XX). From these things it is understood that a Christian ought humbly to prostrate himself upon the earth, lest perhaps it be said to him: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Ecclus. X).

CAP. 277.—That it is not permitted to kiss the dead. From the Council of Agde, chapter 2.

It is not permitted to kiss the dead, nor to wrap their bodies in the cloths placed upon the altar for the sacrifices [Col. 0262A], nor to lay such cloths over the bier.

CAP. 278.—Where the faithful ought to be buried. From the Council of Tribur, chapter 15.

It remains, because of the pressing necessity which now most urgently confronts us, that, wherever resources and the opportunity of circumstances permit, the burial of those who die should take place at the church where the bishop’s see is situated. But if this seems impossible because of the length of the journey or the nearby difficulty of some impediment, let him await burial in the ground at the place where a holy community of canons, monks, or nuns lives together, so that, commended to his Judge by their prayers, he may come before him and receive through their intercessions the remission of sins which [Col. 0262B] he does not obtain by his own merits. But if this too is judged unsuitable or difficult, let him be buried dead where he paid his tithe while alive.

CAP. 279.—That priests should devote themselves to prayer for a time before they sacrifice. From the decrees of Pope Innocent, chapter 36.

Paul writes to the Corinthians, saying: “Abstain for a time, that you may give yourselves to prayer” (I Cor. VI). If he commands this of laypeople, how much more must priests, whose continual sacrifice is both prayer and sacrificial offering, always abstain from such intercourse. A person defiled by carnal desire—by what shame will he perhaps presume to offer sacrifice, or with what conscience and by what merit will he believe himself heard, when it is said: “To the pure all things are pure; but to the defiled [Col. 0262C] and unbelieving nothing is pure” (Tit. I)?

CAP. 280.—Concerning the churches of monks. From the Council held at Confluences, attended by Kings Henry and Charles, chapter 6.

It was decreed that the churches of monks of whatever kind, within the several parishes of their bishops, should, as is fitting, be subject to divinely ordained governance; that they should diligently render their bishops the due services in carrying out matters of ecclesiastical care; and that the monks themselves should unquestionably obey their bishops in all things.

CAP. 281.—Concerning laymen who possess churches of their own. From the same council, chapter 5.

If laymen possess chapels of their own, it must be regarded as contrary to reason and authority for them to receive the tithes [Col. 0262D] and feed their dogs or breeding bitches from them. Rather, the priests of the churches should receive them and use them to provide for restoration, and should earnestly implore God’s mercy for the holy Church and for the welfare of the kingdom.

CAP. 282.—Concerning the vessels in which the sacred mysteries are celebrated. From the Council of Tribur, chapter 18, attended by King Arnulf.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 1, chapter “The vessels in which.”) The vessels in which the most holy mysteries are performed are chalices and patens. When Boniface, martyr and bishop, was asked whether it was permissible to celebrate the sacraments in wooden vessels, he answered: “Formerly golden priests used wooden chalices; now, on the contrary, wooden priests use golden chalices.” Zephyrinus, the sixteenth Roman bishop [Col. 0263A], decreed that Masses should be celebrated with glass patens. Then Pope Urban, the eighteenth, made all sacred utensils of silver. In this matter, as in the other forms of worship, the splendour of churches increased more and more as time advanced. Therefore, in our times, we who are servants of the householder decree that the honour of Mother Church may not be diminished but rather augmented and enlarged: henceforth no priest is in any way to presume to celebrate the sacred mystery of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ in wooden vessels, lest God be angered by that through which he ought to be propitiated.

CAP. 283.—Concerning a church possessed by several heirs. From the same council, chapter 32.

Whenever a church is possessed by several co-heirs [Col. 0263B], every effort must be made, in harmonious unanimity, lest through any disputes the service of God be diminished and the care of the people be irreligiously administered. But if the joint owners happen to disagree about it and to leave it without the administration of any priest, and consequently quarrels and contentions begin frequently to arise both among themselves and among [Col. 0264A] the clergy—since, according to the Apostle, servants of God ought not to quarrel (II Tim. II)—the bishop shall remove the relics from it and place them honourably elsewhere with great care. He shall close the doors of that church and seal them, and no one shall celebrate the sacred mystery in it until, in harmonious unanimity, all choose one priest fit to administer the most holy place and to preside beneficially over the people of God.

CAP. 284.—That those wishing to give away property of their own must recognize that they cannot transfer a tithe anywhere. From the Council at Confluences, chapter 8.

If any layman, cleric, or person of either sex assigns places or possessions belonging to his or her own property as a donation anywhere, that person shall have no authority to divert from its prior church the revenue of tithes lawfully assigned to it [Col. 0264B]. If he attempts to do so, such a transfer shall be held wholly invalid, and he himself shall be restrained for correction by ecclesiastical censure.

## FOURTH PART OF THE DECREE

Concerning the observance of lawful feasts and fasts; concerning the canonical Scriptures, customs, and the holding of a council.

[Col. 0263]

[Col. 0263C] CAP. 1.—How the Apostle’s saying is to be understood: “You observe days and months and seasons and years; I fear that I have laboured among you in vain.” Ambrose, in his exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter IV.

“You observe days and months and seasons and years” (Gal. IV). Thus they observe days who say, for example: “One must not set out tomorrow; nor should anything be begun the day after tomorrow”; and so they are more readily deceived. They revere months who investigate the course of the moon, saying, for example: “In the seventh moon tools must not be made; in the ninth moon, again, a purchased slave should not be brought home.” Through such observances adversities are more easily wont to occur. They observe seasons in this way when they say: “Today is the beginning of spring; it is a festival. The day after tomorrow [Col. 0263D] is the Vulcanalia. Tomorrow one may not leave home.” They revere years when they say: “At the Kalends of January the year is new,” as though years were not completed every day. Yet they practise this superstition in order to recall the memory of that two-faced Janus; it ought to be far removed from the servants of God. For if God is loved with the whole heart, then, with him gracious, there ought to be no fear or suspicion concerning these things. Whatever is done simply in devotion to God can indeed turn out well.

CAP. 2.—That Easter and Lent derive their authority from the old law, and how Easter is now to be celebrated. Blessed Augustine, in the book *Responses to Januarius* (book II, chapter 15).

In the old Scriptures no time for observing Easter is commanded except from the month of new things, from the fourteenth day of the moon to the twenty-first (Exod. XII). Yet because the Gospel makes clear on what day the Lord was crucified, lay in the tomb, and rose again (John XIX), observance of those very days was added through councils of the Fathers; and the whole Christian world was persuaded that Easter ought to be celebrated in this manner. The forty-day fast has authority both in the old books, from the fast of Moses and Elijah, and in the Gospel, because the Lord fasted for the same number of days (Matt. IV), showing that the Gospel does not disagree with the law and the prophets. For in the person of Moses the Law is understood (Exod. XXXIV), and in the person of Elijah the Prophets (III Kings XIX); between them he appeared glorious on the mountain [Col. 0264D] (Matt. XVII), so that what the Apostle says of him might stand out more clearly: that he has testimony from the Law and the Prophets (Acts XXII). In what part of the year, therefore, could the observance of Lent more fittingly be established than adjoining and contiguous to the Lord’s Passion? For in it is signified this laborious life, which requires self-restraint so that one may fast from friendship with this world—a friendship which never ceases deceitfully to flatter and to scatter and cast about the cosmetics of enticements.

CAP. 3.—That Easter must be celebrated on Sunday. Pius the Ninth [Pius I], from Peter, pope, to all churches, in the first of his decretals.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 3, chapter “We wish you to know.”) We wish you to know that the Lord’s Easter should be celebrated at the annual seasons on the Lord’s Day [Col. 0265A]. In these times Hermes, teacher of faith and Scripture, flourished among us. Although we celebrated it on that same aforesaid day, and some doubted about this, nevertheless, in order to strengthen their minds, an angel of the Lord appeared to Hermes in the guise of a shepherd and commanded him that Easter should be celebrated by all on Sunday at its proper time. Therefore we instruct you by apostolic authority that all must observe the same day, because we too observe it, and you must by no means disagree with the head.

CAP. 4.—On the same matter. Victor XIII, from Peter, pope, to Bishop Theophilus and the brethren established at Alexandria, in his first decretal.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 3, chapter “The celebration.”) Our predecessors have already decreed that the celebration of holy Easter [Col. 0265B] must take place on Sunday; and we command you to celebrate it solemnly on that same day, because it is not fitting for the members to differ from the head or act contrary to it.

CAP. 5.—Concerning the solemnity of the Finding of the Holy Cross. Pope Eusebius, chapter 4 (epistle 3).

(Concerning consecration, distinction 3, chapter “Of the Cross.”) We command you solemnly to celebrate the feast of the Finding of the Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, which was discovered recently, while we held the governance of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Nones of May, on the aforesaid day of the Kalends.

CAP. 6.—Concerning the prohibition of work on the Sabbath. Gregory, by the grace of God bishop, to his most beloved fellow citizens of Rome, book XI of the Register, epistle 3.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 3, chapter “It has come.”) It has come to my attention that certain persons of perverse spirit have sown among you some corrupt teachings contrary to the holy faith, so as to forbid the performance of any work on the Sabbath day [Col. 0265C]. What else shall we call them but preachers of Antichrist, who, when he comes, will cause the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day to be observed free from all work? For because he pretends that he died and rose again, he wishes the Lord’s Day to be held in veneration. And because he will compel the people to Judaize, so as to restore the outward ritual of the law and subject them to the faithlessness of the Jews, he wishes the Sabbath to be observed. Another matter has also been reported to me: that perverse persons have preached to you that no one ought to bathe on the Lord’s Day. Certainly, if anyone desires to bathe for luxury of mind and pleasure, we do not permit this even on any other day [Col. 0265D]. But if it is required for bodily necessity, we do not forbid it even on Sunday.

CAP. 7.—Concerning those who deliberately fast on Sunday. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 64.

(26, question 7, chapter “A priest.”) Whoever deliberately fasts on the Lord’s Day is not to be regarded as a Catholic.

CAP. 8.—Concerning those who, neglecting church, go to spectacles. In the same place, chapter 88.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 1, chapter “Whoever on a solemn day.”) Whoever on a solemn day goes to spectacles after neglecting the church assembly shall be excommunicated.

CAP. 9.—That the greater solemnities are to be celebrated in cities. From the Council of Agde, chapter 21.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 1, chapter “If anyone.”) If anyone wishes to have an oratory in the countryside outside parishes where there is a lawful and ordinary [Col. 0266A] assembly, we permit him, on other feasts, to hold Mass there for the sake of the household’s fatigue, in accordance with due order. But Easter, the Nativity of the Lord, the Epiphany of the Lord, the Ascension, Pentecost, the Nativity of St John the Baptist, and whatever days are greatest among the feasts, they shall observe only in cities or parishes. Any clerics who wish to perform or hold services in oratories on the feasts mentioned above, unless the bishop commands or permits it, shall be excluded from communion.

CAP. 10.—Concerning laypeople who do not come to the city for the greater solemnities. From the same council, chapter 62.

Let citizens who neglect to be present with their bishops at the feasts of the aforesaid solemnities—namely, Easter, the Nativity of the Lord, or Pentecost—although they know themselves to be in cities where they may receive communion or a blessing [Col. 0266B], be deprived of the Church’s communion for three years.

CAP. 11.—That litanies are to be celebrated before the Lord’s Ascension. From the First Council of Orléans, chapter 29.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 3, chapter “Rogations.”) It has pleased us that Rogation days, that is, litanies, should be celebrated before the Lord’s Ascension, so that the three-day fast may be ended after Mass on the solemnity of the Lord’s Ascension. During those three days male and female servants shall be released from work, so that the whole people may assemble more fully; during those days all shall abstain and use Lenten food.

CAP. 12.—That no inhabitant of a city is to celebrate the greater feasts in a country estate. From the same, chapter 27.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 3, chapter “No citizens.”) No inhabitant of a city may celebrate the solemnity of Easter, the Nativity of the Lord, or Quinquagesima at a country estate, unless sickness is shown to have confined him there. It is an irreligious custom that the common people are accustomed to practise on saints’ solemnities. People who ought to attend to divine offices devote themselves to shameful dancing, singing not merely wicked songs but also shouting over the offices of religion. That these practices may be driven out of all Spain, their removal is entrusted to the care of priests and judges by the holy council [Col. 0266C].

CAP. 13.—Concerning Sunday. From the statutes of the Fathers.

On Sunday nothing else is to be done except devotion to God. Let no work be found on that holy day; rather, let the day be spent only in hymns, psalms, and spiritual songs [Col. 0266D].

CAP. 14.—That priests should announce to their congregations the days which are to be kept as holidays. From the Council of Lyons, chapter 3.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 3, chapter “It must be announced.”) It must be announced so that they may know the yearly time for keeping holidays: that is, every Sunday from evening to evening, lest they be caught in Judaism. The following are the annual holidays: the Nativity of the Lord; St Stephen; St John the Evangelist; the Innocents; St Silvester; the Octave of the Lord and Theophany; the Purification of St Mary; holy Easter with the entire week; Rogation Days for three days; the Lord’s Ascension; the holy days of Pentecost; St John the Baptist; the twelve [Col. 0267A] Apostles, especially Saints Peter and Paul, who illumined the world by their preaching; St Lawrence; the Assumption of St Mary; her Nativity; the Dedication of the basilica of St Michael the Archangel; the dedication of any oratory; All Saints; St Martin; and those feasts which individual bishops approve with the people in their own dioceses. These are, however, to be announced to neighbouring inhabitants, not generally to everyone. Other feasts throughout the year are neither to be made obligatory holidays nor prohibited. Whenever an appointed fast is announced, it is to be observed by all.

CAP. 15.—That when priests announce feasts they should not forget fasts and vigils. From the Council of Compiègne, chapter 1.

[Col. 0267B] Likewise, when priests announce holy feasts to the people, they should also admonish them in every way to observe the fast of the vigils wherever it is to occur.

CAP. 16.—Concerning the observance of Sunday, and that neither a market nor a judicial hearing is to be held on it. From the First Council of Mainz, chapter 37.

We decree that all Sundays are to be kept from evening to evening with every reverence and observance, and that unlawful work is to be abstained from. No market is to be held on them, nor a court session in which anyone is judged to death or punishment, nor are oaths to be sworn, except for making peace.

CAP. 17.—Likewise concerning the same matter. From the Council at Saint-Médard, in the presence of Emperor Charles, chapter 5.

[Col. 0267C] We also decree, according to what the Lord commanded in the law, that servile works are not to be performed on Sundays, as my father commanded in his synodal edicts: men are neither to undertake rural work, nor cultivate vineyards, nor plough or reap in the fields, nor cut hay, make hedges, grub up land in the woods, cut trees, or work in stone; nor are they to attend court sessions, hold markets, or engage in hunting.

CAP. 18.—That on Sundays and on the days of Pentecost we are to pray standing. From the First Council of Nicaea, chapter 20.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 3, chapter “Since there are some.”) Since some bend their knees in prayer on Sunday and on the days of Pentecost, the holy synod has therefore decreed that, because a harmonious and fitting custom must be maintained in all churches, we should offer our prayers to the Lord standing [Col. 0267D].

CAP. 19.—That Easter is to be celebrated everywhere on one day and at one time. From the First Council of Arles, chapter 1.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 3, chapter “Concerning the observance.”) Concerning the observance of the Lord’s Easter: let it be observed on one day and at one time throughout the whole world, and in accordance with custom let letters be sent by you to all.

CAP. 20.—What works may be done on Sunday. From the Council at Compiègne, chapter 6.

Three kinds of cart-work may be performed on Sunday: conveyance for military service (*hostilicidia*), carts carrying provisions, and compulsory public transport (*angaria*); and, should need arise [Col. 0268A], the body of any person may be conveyed to burial.

CAP. 21.—Likewise concerning observance of Sunday. From the same council, chapter 7.

Women shall not perform textile work on Sunday: they shall not make garments, sew clothing, or card wool. It is not permitted to beat flax, wash garments, or shear wethers, so that in every way honour and rest may be rendered to Sunday. Rather, all should assemble everywhere for the solemn rites of Mass and praise the Lord for all the goods which he has deigned to bestow upon us on that day.

CAP. 22.—Likewise. From the same council, chapter 8.

No bishop, priest, or cleric shall dare on Sunday to undertake the adjudication of business in any legal case [Col. 0268B], except only that the appointed solemnities may be performed for God.

CAP. 23.—That it matters not how much food or drink a person consumes, but consideration must be given to the eagerness with which it is consumed, and likewise to the ease and serenity of mind with which one can go without it if necessary. Augustine, from the book *Questions on the Gospels*.

The Lord’s saying in the Gospel, “Wisdom has been justified by all her children” (Matt. XI), shows that the children of wisdom understand that righteousness lies neither in abstaining nor in eating, but in equanimity in bearing want and in temperance: not being corrupted by abundance, and taking or declining, as circumstances require, those things whose use is not blameworthy but whose craving is. For it makes no difference at all what kind of food you consume to meet the body’s need [Col. 0268C], provided you conform, in the kinds of food, to those with whom you must live. Nor does the quantity consumed matter greatly, since we see that some stomachs are satisfied sooner, yet those persons greedily, intolerably, and altogether shamefully hanker after the small amount that satisfies them; whereas others are satisfied by a somewhat greater amount, yet bear want patiently and can calmly look upon food set before them, even before the hour for eating, if circumstance, duty, or necessity requires it, without touching it. What matters more, therefore, is not what or how much food anyone takes according to the circumstances of those among whom he lives, his own station, and the necessities of his health, but with how much ease and serenity of mind he can lack these things when it is proper or even necessary [Col. 0268D] to lack them. Thus may be fulfilled in the Christian’s mind what the Apostle says: “I know also how to have little, and I know how to abound; everywhere and in all things I have been instructed both to be full and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer want. I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Phil. IV).

CAP. 24.—That each person should use food and drink not superstitiously but temperately, and should not exceed the bounds of the good people among whom he lives. From the book *On Christian Doctrine*, book III, chapter 12.

Whoever uses passing things more strictly than the customs of those among whom he lives require is either temperate or superstitious. Whoever uses them in such a way as to exceed the bounds of the custom of the good people among whom he lives either signifies something [Col. 0269A] or is immoral. In all such matters, the fault lies not in the use of things but in the desire of the user. (A little later.) Therefore one must carefully consider what is fitting to places, times, and persons, lest we rashly condemn immoral actions. For it can happen that a wise person uses very costly food without any fault of greed or gluttony, while a foolish person burns with the foul flame of gluttony for the cheapest food. Someone may more wholesomely prefer, after the Lord’s example, to eat fish (Luke XXIV) than lentils after the example of Esau, Abraham’s grandson (Gen. XXV), or barley after the manner of beasts of burden. Most animals are not more self-restrained than we merely because they feed on cheaper foods. For in all such matters, what we do is to be approved or condemned not from the nature of the things we use, but from the reason for using them and the manner of desiring them [Col. 0269B].

CAP. 25.—That clerics should abstain from meat and other delicacies for seven weeks before Easter. Telesphorus VII, from Peter, in his first decree to all bishops.

(Distinction 4, chapter “We decree.”) Know that it has been decreed by us and by all the bishops assembled in this holy and apostolic see that, for seven full weeks before holy Easter, all clerics called to the Lord’s portion shall fast from meat. For just as the life of clerics ought to be distinct from the conduct of laypeople, so distinction must also be made in fasting. Therefore let all clerics fast from meat and delicacies during these seven weeks, and let them strive day and night to cleave to the Lord through hymns, vigils, and prayers.

CAP. 26.—[Col. 0269C] Concerning the fast of the Four Seasons. Pope and martyr Callixtus XV, from Peter, sends greetings to his brother and fellow bishop Benedict.

(Distinction 76, chapter “The fast.”) The fast which you have learned is observed among us three times a year, we now decree should more suitably be held at the Four Seasons, so that, as the year turns through four seasons, we too may observe a solemn fast four times, through the four seasons of the year.

CAP. 27.—That one must not fast on Sunday. Pope Melchiades XXVIII, from Peter, in his first decree to the bishops of Spain, chapter 3.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 3, chapter “The Sunday fast.”) No one ought to observe a fast on Sunday or on Thursday, so that there may be a true, not false, distinction between the fasting of Christians and that of pagans, and between those who truly believe and unbelievers and heretics [Col. 0269D].

CAP. 28.—That fasting is rightly observed every Saturday. Innocent I, to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio, chapter 4.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 3, chapter “On Saturday.”) The clearest reasoning demonstrates that one must fast on Saturday. For if we celebrate Sunday, on account of the venerable Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, not only at Easter but also throughout every recurring cycle of weeks, repeatedly observing the image of that day; and if, just as we fast on Friday because of the Lord’s Passion, we ought not to omit Saturday, since it seems enclosed between the sorrow and joy of that time. Certainly it is established that the Apostles were in grief during those two days and hid themselves for fear of the Jews (John XX). There is no doubt [Col. 0270A] that they fasted so strictly during those two days that the Church’s tradition holds that the sacraments are not celebrated at all during them. This pattern must likewise be kept in every week, because the commemoration of that day must always be celebrated. If they think that fasting should occur once and on one Saturday only, then Sunday and Friday likewise ought surely to be celebrated only once at Easter.

CAP. 29.—Concerning Lent. Gregory to Augustine, bishop of the English.

(Distinction 4, chapter “Finally, priests.”) Finally, priests, deacons, and all others adorned by the rank of ecclesiastical office should undertake the intention of fasting from Quinquagesima, so that they may add something to the required observance of the holy institution and, just as they surpass those in the lay order in rank, may surpass them also in religion. But we hesitate what should be said concerning that Sunday itself, since all lay and secular persons on that day seek meat more eagerly than usual, more carefully than on other days; and unless they gorge themselves with a new kind of greed until midnight, they think they cannot otherwise undertake the observance of this holy season [Col. 0270B]. This must surely be attributed not to reason but to pleasure—indeed, to a certain blindness of mind. Hence they cannot be turned away from such a custom, and therefore should be left to their own inclination with indulgence, lest perhaps they become worse if they are forbidden that custom. For Solomon says: “He who presses hard draws forth blood” (Prov. XXX). And a little later: It is likewise fitting that we who abstain during these days from the flesh of animals should also fast from all things that derive their origin from the seed of flesh: namely milk, cheese, and eggs. And a little later: The eating of fish is left to the Christian in such a way that it affords consolation for weakness, not fuel for luxury. While abstaining from flesh, let him by no means prepare for himself more costly banquets of marine creatures [Col. 0270C]. We are permitted to drink wine only in such a way as to avoid drunkenness altogether. Otherwise, it would follow that we might likewise do everything pleasing to the body.

CAP. 30.—Concerning those who condemn people for eating meat. From the Council of Gangra, chapter 2.

(Distinction 30, chapter “If anyone [condemns] meat.”) If anyone believes that a person who eats meat with faith and reverence—apart from blood, things sacrificed to idols, and strangled animals—ought to be condemned as having no hope because he eats such food, let him be anathema [Col. 0270D].

CAP. 31.—Concerning the times of fasts. From the Council of Elvira, chapter 23.

It has pleased us that fasts or abstinences should be observed in each month, except during the days of the two months July and August, because of the weakness associated with them.
