CAP. 32.—That fasts on Wednesday and Friday are not to be relaxed except in grave necessity. From the sayings of St Apollonius (in Palladius, *Life*).

(Concerning consecration, distinction 3, “But the fasts.”) The lawful fasts, namely Wednesday and Friday, are not to be relaxed unless there is some grave necessity, because on Wednesday Judas plotted the betrayal of the Lord [Col. 0271A], and on Friday the Saviour was crucified. Therefore anyone who, without necessity, relaxes the appointed fasts on those days will be seen either to betray the Saviour together with his betrayer or to crucify him together with those who crucified him.

CAP. 33.—Concerning the observance of fasting. From the Council held at Salegonstath, chapter 2.

Concerning the uncertain date of the Four Seasons fast, we establish this rule: if the Kalends of March fall on Wednesday or earlier, it shall be observed in that same week. But if the Kalends of March fall on Friday or Thursday, or extend to Saturday, the fast shall be postponed to the following week. Likewise, if the Kalends of June fall on Wednesday or earlier, the fast shall be celebrated in the following week. If they fall on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday [Col. 0271B], the fast shall be reserved for the third week. It must also be known that, if by the aforesaid rule the June fast should fall on the vigil of Pentecost, it is not to be observed then, but in the solemn week of Pentecost itself, because it is not fitting to observe both a vigil and a fast at the same time. Then, because of the solemnity of the Holy Spirit, deacons shall wear dalmatics, the Alleluia shall be sung, and “Let us bend the knee” shall not be said. The same rule has been established concerning the September fast: if the Kalends of September fall on Wednesday or earlier, the fast is to be observed in the third week; and if they fall on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, fasting shall take place in the fourth week. In December, however, this is to be observed [Col. 0271C]: the fast shall be celebrated on the Saturday nearest before the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, because if the vigil falls on Saturday it is not fitting to celebrate vigil and fast simultaneously.

CAP. 34.—Concerning the observance of Lent. From an epistle of Pope Gregory, book of forty homilies, homily 16.

(Concerning consecration, distinction 5, chapter “Lent.”) Lent must be observed with the utmost care, so that the fast during it, apart from Sundays, which are exempted from abstinence, may in no way be relaxed unless illness prevents someone from observing it, because these days themselves are the tithe of the year. From the first Sunday of Lent to the Lord’s Easter, six weeks are counted, namely forty-two days. When the six Sundays are removed from abstinence [Col. 0271D], no more than thirty-six days remain for abstinence. For example, if the year is said to consist of three hundred and sixty-five days and we afflict ourselves for thirty-six days, we give God, as it were, the tithe of the year. In order to complete the sacred number of forty days, which our Saviour consecrated by his holy fast, four days of the preceding week are added to make up the forty days: namely Wednesday, which is marked as the beginning of the fast, the following Thursday and Friday, and Saturday. Unless we add these four days to the preceding thirty-six, we do not have forty days of abstinence. We are also commanded by almighty God to give tithes of all our goods [Col. 0272A]. Therefore, that every tithe may be duly rendered by us to God, let us take the tithe of the year and in it cleanse away our sins by confessing, correcting ourselves, fasting, keeping vigils, praying, giving alms, and tithing our flesh, so that we may reach holy Easter securely.

CAP. 35.—Concerning the fast of the Four Seasons. From the First Council of Mainz, chapter 34.

We decree that the Four Seasons of the year shall be observed by all people with fasting: in March, the first week; in June, the second; in September, the third; and in December, the fourth full week before the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord. That is, on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, all shall come to church at the ninth hour with litanies for the solemn rites of Mass.

[Col. 0272B] CAP. 36.—At what time “Let us bend the knee” is to be announced at Mass. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 13.

(Distinction 30, chapter “It has pleased us,” and chapter “If any priest.”) Let priests announce to the people that only during Lent and the fast of the Four Seasons ought they to bend the knee during the solemn rites of Mass. On Sundays, by contrast, and on other feasts from evening to evening, they shall not bend the knee but pray standing and bowed. Nor may anyone presume to pray with only one knee touching the ground, as the Jews are read to have done in mockery of the Lord during his Passion; rather, he shall place both knees upon the ground. For the Apostle says: “I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Eph. III).

CAP. 37.—Concerning those who disregard an appointed fast. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 35.

If anyone, through pride, disregards an appointed fast and refuses to observe it with the other Christians, the Council of Gangra commands that he be anathematized [Col. 0272C].

CAP. 38.—On the same matter. From the Council of Gangra, chapter 19.

(Distinction 30, chapter “If anyone.”) If any of those devoted to continence, without bodily necessity and under the impulse of his own opinion, proudly breaks the commonly handed-down fast established by the Church, let him be anathema.

CAP. 39.—How the Major Litany is to be celebrated. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 33.

We have determined that the major litany is to be observed by [Col. 0272D] all Christians on one day, the seventh day before the Kalends of May, as we find established in the Roman Church and as our holy Fathers ordained: not on horseback, nor clothed in costly garments, but sprinkled with ashes and clothed in sackcloth, unless illness prevents it.

CAP. 40.—On the fast of the Rogation Days. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 6.

(The same in Burchard, book XIII, chapter 7.) When, through the sins of the people, the inhabitants of Gaul were cruelly destroyed by the ravaging of wolves and could find no remedy for that scourge, the bishops of Gaul are said to have assembled at the city of Vienne and jointly decreed a three-day fast. [Col. 0273A] When the Lord in mercy removed the plague, these days became an annual observance, to be celebrated throughout the provinces of Gaul before the day of the Lord’s Ascension. Let us also observe these days with the utmost reverence and devotion, with abstinence from flesh and humility of mind and heart, so that we may escape not only the ravaging of visible wolves, but may also be enabled to overcome the temptations of invisible wolves—that is, unclean spirits. Let no one on these days wear costly clothing, since we ought to mourn in sackcloth and ashes. Drunkenness and feasting, which occur among the common people, are to be prohibited. Let no one presume to ride there on horseback; rather, let all proceed barefoot. Let no women lead dances; instead, let all together sing *Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”) and, with [Col. 0273B] contrition of heart, implore God’s mercy for sins, for peace, for plague, for the preservation of crops, and for other necessities; for these are days of abstinence, not of rejoicing.

CAP. 41.—That on the Lord’s Supper and on the remaining days of Lent the fast is not to be broken. From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 50.

It is not fitting during Lent to break the fast on the Thursday of the final week, and thus pass through the whole of Lent without observance; rather, the whole season is to be honoured by a strict fast.

CAP. 42.—That on Holy Saturday the fast is not to be broken before nightfall. From the Council of Orange, chapter 2.

(The same is found in book VII of the Capitularies of the Kings, chapter 328.) On Holy Saturday—that is, the Vigil of Easter—the fast is not to be broken before the beginning of night, except by little children or the sick. Good Friday (*Parasceve*) and Saturday belong to those forty days, and the divine mysteries are not to be celebrated on these two days. For the canons command that the sacraments not be celebrated at all during those two days, namely Good Friday and Saturday.

CAP. 43.—That the feasts of saints are not to be celebrated during Lent. From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 51.

(33, question 4, chapter *Non licet*.) It is not fitting during Lent to celebrate the anniversaries of martyrs; rather, it is appropriate that their holy commemoration be held on Saturdays and Sundays.

CAP. 44.—That alms are to be given on fast days. From the Council of Chalon, chapter 5.

[Col. 0273D] On fast days alms are to be given, and each person should distribute to the poor the food or drink which he would have consumed had he not fasted; for to fast and save the food of the midday meal for supper is an increase not of reward but of food.

CAP. 45.—That the time of the meal is to be observed in Lent. From the same Council of Chalon, chapter 5.

(On consecration, distinction 1, chapter *Solent*.) Many who think themselves to be fasting in Lent eat at the ninth hour as soon as they hear the signal. They are by no means to be considered fasting if they eat before the evening office has been celebrated. For one must go to Mass; and, after hearing the solemn service of Mass and the evening offices, and after giving alms, one should take food. But if anyone is constrained by necessity so that he cannot come to Mass, then, when the estimated evening hour has arrived and he has completed his prayer, let him break the fast.

CAP. 46.—That there should be no quarrels on fast days. From the Council of Pope Liberius, chapter 4.

On these fast days there must be no lawsuits and no disputes, but persistence in God’s praises and in necessary work. Through the prophet the Lord rebukes those who engage in disputes and lawsuits during Lent and who demand debts from their debtors, saying: “Behold, on the day of your fast your own desires are found, and you exact payment from all your debtors. Behold, you fast for quarrelling and contention, and strike wickedly with the fist” (Isa. 58).

CAP. 47.—That married persons should abstain from intercourse during the holy days of Lent. From the same source, chapter 5.

[Col. 0274B] For during the most sacred days of Lent one must abstain from one’s spouse; these days should be passed chastely and devoutly, in a sanctified heart and body, and thus one may arrive at the holy day of Easter. For a fast polluted by marital intercourse is of almost no value, and it is not commended by prayers, vigils, and almsgiving.

CAP. 48.—That clerics who abstain from meat should not regard it as abominable. From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 13.

If any presbyters or deacons among the clergy abstain from meat, it has been decided that they should touch it and then, if they wish, abstain from it. But if they abhor it to such an extent that they judge even vegetables cooked with it [Col. 0274C] not to be eaten, then, as persons who do not assent to the rule, they ought to be removed from their order.

CAP. 49.—That fasts established by priests are not lightly to be set aside. From the decrees of Pope Eusebius, chapter 3.

(On consecration, distinction 5, chapter *Jejunia*.) Fasts established in the Church by priests are not to be set aside without a reasonable necessity.

CAP. 50.—On this matter, should plague or an unhealthy condition of the air occur. There, chapter 2 (from the decree of Pope Liberius).

If famine, plague, an unhealthy condition of the air, or any other tribulation occurs, the Lord’s mercy is immediately to be entreated by fasts, alms, and supplications.

CAP. 51.—That no one is to fast on the Lord’s Day by way of abstinence. From the Council of Gangra, chapter 13.

(Distinction 30, chapter *Si quis tanquam*.) If anyone fasts on the Lord’s Day [Col. 0274D] because of a supposed continence or out of obstinacy, let him be anathema.

CAP. 52.—On the same matter. From the Council of Tours, chapter 57.

(Distinction 30, chapter *Si quis presbyter*.) If anyone, because of public penance received from a priest or for some necessity, fasts on the Lord’s Day as though it were an act of religion, like the Manichaeans, let him be anathema.

CAP. 53.—That secular courts are not to be held on Sundays and other principal feast days. From a council held at Erfurt by order of King Henry, chapter 2.

(15, question 4, chapter *Placita*.) We have decreed that secular courts are not to be held on Sundays, on other principal feasts, or on the days on which the lawful fasts are celebrated, in accordance with canonical ordinance. Moreover, the holy synod decreed that no judicial authority may, on its own authority, summon Christians by public ban to a court on the aforementioned days: namely, the seven days before the Nativity of the Lord until the octave of Epiphany; from Quinquagesima until the octave of Easter; and the seven days before the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist. Thus people may have freer opportunity to go to church and devote themselves to prayer.

CAP. 54.—That fasts established by priests should be observed without the luxury of foods. Augustine, Sermon 65.

(On consecration, distinction 5, chapter *Non dico*.) I do not speak of weekly fasts, doubled fasts, or multiplied fasts; but let us at least spend each individual day without the luxury of foods.

CAP. 55.—That a daily fast should not be without some refreshment. From the sayings of Pimen the hermit. These are read in Jerome’s letter to Eustochium, *On the Guardianship of Virginity*.

(On consecration, distinction 5, chapter *Sint tibi quotidiana*.) Let your fasts be daily, and your refreshment such as avoids satiety. For what profit is it to you, after two or three days have passed, to carry an empty stomach, if it is immediately overwhelmed as well? If fasts are compensated for by fullness? At once the filled mind grows sluggish, and the watered soil of this body brings forth thorns and thistles.

CAP. 56.—On the same matter. Jerome to Nepotian, *On the Life of Clerics*.

[Col. 0275C] Let your fasts be pure, continual, and moderate: that is, hunger every day and dine every day.

CAP. 57.—That fasting heals the wounds of one who has sinned. From the same place.

“Do not,” says the Apostle, “continue to drink water, but use a little wine because of your infirmities” (1 Tim. 5); for fasting heals the wounds of the offender and sanctifies those who have been healed.

CAP. 58.—On a certain Alcibiades, who imposed upon himself a grievous yoke of fasting and was admonished by the Lord that he acted wrongly. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 3.

A certain Alcibiades was among those who were held in bonds for Christ. He led a very severe and austere life, wishing to take no food at all, but [Col. 0275D] using only bread, salt, and water. When, even while confined in prison, he wished to maintain this severity of life, it was revealed to Attalus, a servant of God, that Alcibiades was not acting rightly toward God’s creatures and would leave to others an example of stumbling. Once this was known, Alcibiades began to receive everything with thanksgiving, because the same Spirit who revealed these things to one in order to teach him persuaded the other to follow them.

CAP. 59.—That no one, under the pretext of religion, should impose a fast upon himself without the command of his bishop or priest. From the council at Erfurt, at which King Henry was present.

We absolutely forbid anyone, unless his own bishop or the bishop’s representative consents, to impose fasts upon himself under the pretext of religion [Col. 0276A] by singling out one day above others. We forbid both the act, which displeases us, and its future performance, because it is recognized as being more a cause of divination than a supplement to Catholic law.

CAP. 60.—That no Christian who has sought holy places out of reverence should there be bound by the ban of any public authority. From the same council.

We command that no Christian who seeks a church out of reverence be bound there by the ban of any public authority, lest, while he hastens to church for prayer, he be hindered by a ban from less devoutly seeking the Lord’s mercy for the salvation of his soul.

CAP. 61.—On the order of the books of the Old Testament. Pope Gelasius, at a council held in Rome with seventy bishops.

[Col. 0276B] Genesis, 1 book. Exodus, 1 book. Leviticus, 1 book; and so forth: Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua son of Nun, Judges, Kings, 4; Ruth; Chronicles, 2; Psalms, 150; Solomon, 3; Job; Tobit; Ezra; [Col. 0276C] Esther; Judith; Maccabees.

On the order of the prophets.

Isaiah; Jeremiah, with *Cinoth*, that is, his Lamentations; Ezekiel; Daniel; Hosea; Joel; Amos; Obadiah; Jonah; [Col. 0276D] Micah; Nahum; Habakkuk; Zephaniah; Haggai; Zechariah; Malachi.

CAP. 62.—On the order of the books of the New Testament which the holy Roman Church holds and the universal Church observes.

The four books of the Gospels:

According to Matthew; according to Mark; according to Luke; [Col. 0277A] according to John; Acts of the Apostles.

Fourteen Epistles of Paul:

To the Romans; to the Corinthians, 2; to the Galatians; to the Ephesians; to the Philippians; to the Colossians; to the Thessalonians, 2; to Timothy, 2; to Titus; to Philemon; to the Hebrews; the Apocalypse of John.

The order of the seven Catholic Epistles.

[Col. 0277B] Epistles of the apostle Peter, 2; Epistle of the apostle James, 1; Epistles of the apostle John, 3; Epistle of Jude the Zealot, 1.

CAP. 63.—When and at what time the books of the Old and New Testaments are to be read.

(Distinction 15, chapter *Sancta*.) In Septuagesima they appoint the *Heptateuch* [perhaps *Pentateuch*] until fifteen days before Easter. Fifteen days before Easter they appoint Jeremiah until the Lord’s Supper. At the Lord’s Supper they read three lessons from the Lamentation of Jeremiah: “How the city sits alone” (Lam. 1), etc.; three from Saint Augustine’s exposition on Psalm 54: “Hear, O God, my prayer, and do not despise it”; and three from the Apostle, where he says to the Corinthians: “When you come together in one place” (1 Cor. 11). The second lesson begins: “Likewise also the cup, after he had supped” (ibid.). The third: “Now concerning spiritual gifts, brethren, we do not want you to be ignorant” (1 Cor. 10). On Good Friday, three lessons from the Lamentations of Jeremiah (Lam. 2); three from Saint Augustine’s exposition on Psalm 63: “Hear, O God, my prayer when I make supplication”; and three from the [Col. 0277C] Apostle, where he says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Let us hasten to enter into that rest” (Heb. 4), etc. The second: “For every high priest” (Heb. 5). The third: “Of whom we have much to say” (ibid.). On Holy Saturday, three lessons from the Lamentation of Jeremiah (Lam. 3); three from Saint Augustine’s exposition on the same Psalm 63; and [Col. 0277D] three from the Apostle, where he says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Christ, having come as a high priest” (Heb. 9), etc. The second lesson, where he says: “For a testament” (ibid.), etc. The third: “For the law, having a shadow of good things to come” (Heb. 10). On the Lord’s Easter, homilies appropriate to that day. During the week, homilies. On the octave of Easter they appoint the Acts of the Apostles, the Catholic Epistles, and the Apocalypse, until the octave of Pentecost. On the octave of Pentecost they appoint the books of Kings and Chronicles until the Kalends of August. On the first Sunday of August they appoint Solomon until the Kalends of September; from then they appoint Job, Tobit, Judith, Esther, and Ezra until the Kalends of October. On the first Sunday of October they appoint the books of Maccabees until the Kalends of November. On the first Sunday of November [Col. 0278A] they appoint Ezekiel, Daniel, and the minor prophets until the Kalends of December. On the first Sunday of December they appoint the prophet Isaiah until the Nativity of the Lord. On the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, they first read three lessons from Isaiah. The first lesson: “In the former time it was lightly afflicted,” and the rest. The second: “Comfort ye.” The third: “Awake, awake.” Then sermons or homilies appropriate to that day are read. On the feast of Saint Stephen, a homily for that day; likewise on the feast of Saint John; likewise on the feast of the Innocents; likewise on the feast of Saint Sylvester. On the octave of the Lord, a homily for that day. On the first Sunday after the Nativity of the Lord, they appoint the Epistles of Paul until Septuagesima. At Epiphany, three lessons from Isaiah. The first [Col. 0278B] lesson begins: “All you who thirst.” The second: “Arise, shine.” The third: “I shall rejoice with joy.” Then sermons or homilies appropriate to that day are read.

CAP. 64.—On the authoritative books which the Church receives in addition to those in the canon. From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, on authentic and apocryphal books.

(Distinction 15, chapter *Sancta Romana*.) After those writings of the Old and New Testaments which we regularly receive, the holy Roman Church does not forbid the reception of these writings also: the holy Synod of Nicaea, of 318 Fathers, held through the agency of the most great Emperor Constantine Augustus, in which Arius the heretic was condemned; the holy Synod of Constantinople, held through the agency of the elder Emperor Theodosius [Col. 0278C] Augustus, in which Macedonius the heretic received his due condemnation; the holy Synod of Ephesus, in which Nestorius was condemned with the agreement of the most blessed Pope Celestine, through Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria, and Arcadius, a bishop sent from Italy; the holy Synod of Chalcedon, held through the agency of Emperor Marcian Augustus and Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, in which the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies, together with Dioscorus and his accomplices, were condemned. We have likewise decreed that any councils hitherto instituted by holy Fathers, besides the authority of those four, are both to be preserved and received.

Now there must be added the small works of the holy [Col. 0278D] Fathers which are received in the Catholic Church.

The works of blessed Cyprian, martyr and bishop of Carthage.

Likewise, the works of blessed Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus.

Likewise, the works of blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

Likewise, the works of blessed Basil, bishop of Cappadocia.

Likewise, the works of blessed John, bishop of Constantinople.

Likewise, the works of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria.

Likewise, the works of blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria.

Likewise, the works of blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers.

[Col. 0279A] Likewise, the works of blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan.

Likewise, the works of blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo.

Likewise, the works of blessed Jerome the presbyter.

Likewise, the works of blessed Prosper, a most devout man.

Likewise, the letter of Pope Leo sent to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople: if anyone disputes its text even to a single *iota* and does not receive it reverently in all respects, let him be anathema.

Likewise, the works and treatises of all orthodox Fathers who in no respect departed from communion with the holy Roman Church, nor were separated from its faithful preaching [Col. 0279B] [or faith/preaching], but by God’s grace remained participants in that communion until the last day of their lives—we decree that these are to be read.

Likewise, the decretal letters which the most blessed popes issued at different times from the city of Rome for the consolation [or consultation] of various Fathers are to be reverently received.

Likewise, the Acts of the holy martyrs, resplendent with manifold tortures and with the wondrous triumphs of their confessions. Who among Catholics could doubt that these things are so, and that they suffered great things in their contests, enduring all not through their own strength but through God’s grace and aid? Yet, according to ancient custom, they are not read in the holy Roman [Col. 0279C] Church with special caution, because the names of those who wrote them are wholly unknown, and because they are thought to have been written by unbelievers or by persons called [ignorant], either superfluously or less suitably than the proper order of the matter required—as are the passions of a certain Cyricus [Quiricus] and Julitta, of George, and of others of this sort, which are said to have been composed by heretics. Therefore, as stated, lest even a slight occasion for mockery arise, they are not read in the holy Roman Church. Nevertheless, together with the aforesaid Church, we venerate with every devotion all martyrs and their glorious contests, which are better known to God than to men. Likewise, we receive with every honour the *Lives of the Fathers*—of Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the hermits—which the most blessed man Jerome wrote. Likewise, the Acts of blessed Sylvester, [Col. 0279D] bishop of the apostolic see: although we do not know the name of their author, we have learned that they are read by many Catholics in the city of Rome, and many churches follow this practice because of its antiquity. Likewise, the writing on the finding of the Lord’s Cross, and another writing on the finding of the head of blessed John the Baptist, are recent revelations, and some Catholics read them. But when these writings come into the hands of Catholics, let the saying of the blessed Apostle Paul take precedence: “Test all things; hold fast what is good” (1 Thess. 5). Likewise, the devout man Rufinus published very many books of ecclesiastical work and translated certain writings. But because blessed Jerome criticized him in some matters concerning freedom of the will, we hold what [Col. 0280A] we know the aforesaid blessed Jerome held; and this applies not only to Rufinus but also to all whom that often-mentioned man rebuked out of zeal for God and devotion to the faith. Likewise, we receive for reading certain works of Origen which the most blessed Jerome does not reject. But all the rest, together with their author, we declare must be rejected. Likewise, the Chronicles of Eusebius of Caesarea and the books of his *Ecclesiastical History*: although in the first book of his account he was lukewarm, and later wrote one book in praise and defence of the schismatic Origen, nevertheless, because of their exceptional information concerning matters relevant to instruction, we do not say that they must everywhere be rejected. Likewise, we greatly praise Orosius, a most learned man, because he arranged for us a history very necessary against the slanders of pagans and composed it with remarkable [Col. 0280B] brevity. Likewise, we commend with notable praise the Paschal work of the venerable Sedulius, which he wrote in heroic verse. Likewise, we do not despise the laborious work of Juvencus, but admire it. But the Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church receives in no way whatever the things written or proclaimed by heretics. Of these, we believe that a few which have come to mind and are to be avoided by Catholics should be set down below.

CAP. 65.—A list of apocryphal books condemned by the holy Fathers to everlasting condemnation.

(Distinction 15, chapter *Sancta*.) First, we confess that the Synod of Rimini, convened by Constantius Caesar, son of Constantine, through the agency of the prefect Taurus, was condemned then, is [Col. 0280C] condemned now, and shall be condemned for ever. Likewise, the itinerary in the name of the apostle Peter, called that of Saint Clement, eight [or ten] books: apocryphal. Acts in the name of the apostle Andrew: apocryphal. Acts in the name of the apostle Thomas: apocryphal. Acts in the name of the apostle Peter: apocryphal. Acts in the name of the apostle Philip: apocryphal. Gospel in the name of Thaddaeus: apocryphal. Gospel in the name of Barnabas: apocryphal. Gospel of the apostle Thomas, which the Manichaeans use: apocryphal. Gospel in the name of the apostle Bartholomew: apocryphal. Gospel in the name of the apostle Andrew: apocryphal. Gospels falsified by Lucian: apocryphal. Gospels falsified by Ysius [Esitius or Hesychius]: apocryphal. [Col. 0280D] Book on the Childhood of the Saviour: apocryphal. Book on the Nativity of the Saviour, on Saint Mary, and on the Saviour’s midwife: apocryphal. The book called *The Shepherd*: apocryphal. All books made by Leutius, disciple of the devil: apocryphal. The book called *Foundation*: apocryphal. The book called *Treasure*: apocryphal. The book called *On the Daughters of Adam*, or *Genesis*: apocryphal. The *Centimeter on Christ*, compiled in Virgilian verses: apocryphal. The book called the *Acts of Thecla and the Apostle Paul*: apocryphal. The book called that of Nepos: apocryphal. A book of proverbs written by heretics and marked with the name of Saint Sixtus: apocryphal. The revelation called that of Paul: apocryphal. The revelation called that of the apostle Thomas: [Col. 0281A] apocryphal. The revelation called that of Stephen: apocryphal. The book called the *Passing* [that is, Assumption] of Saint Mary: apocryphal. The book called the *Penance of Adam*: apocryphal. The book of Diogenia [or Ogia], in the name of a Giant, who after the Flood is said by heretics to have fought with a dragon: apocryphal. The book called the *Testament of Job*: apocryphal. The book called the *Penance of Origen*: apocryphal. The book called the *Penance of Saint Cyprian*: apocryphal. The book called the *Penance of Jannes and Mambres*: apocryphal. The book called the *Lots of the Apostles*: apocryphal. The book of Lusam: apocryphal. The book of the Canons of the Apostles: apocryphal. The *Physiologus*, written by heretics and [Col. 0281B] bearing the name of blessed Ambrose: apocryphal. The history of Eusebius Pamphilus: apocryphal. The works of Tertullian, or the African: apocryphal. The works of Postumianus and Gallus: apocryphal. The works of Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla: apocryphal. All works of Faustus the Manichaean: apocryphal. The works of another Clement of Alexandria: apocryphal. The works of Cassian, presbyter of Gaul: apocryphal. The works of Victorinus of Poitiers: apocryphal. The works of Faustus of Riez in Gaul: apocryphal. The works of Frumentius: apocryphal. The letter of Jesus to King Abgar: apocryphal. The Passion of Cyricus and Julitta: apocryphal. The Passion of George: apocryphal. Writings called *Solomon’s Contradiction*: apocryphal. All phylacteries, written not by an angel, as they falsely claim, but rather by a demon: apocryphal.

[Col. 0281C] All these and similar works which Simon Magus, Nicolaus, Cerinthus, Marcion, Basilides, Ebion, Paul of Samosata, Photinus, Bonosus, and those who lapsed into similar error; likewise Montanus with his most obscene followers; Apollinaris, Valentinus or Manichaeus, Faustus, Sabellius, Arius, Macedonius, Eunomius, Novatus, Sabbatius, Callistus, Donatus, Eustathius, Jovinian, Pelagius, Julian and Latiensis [Celanensis], Celestinus, Maximianus, Priscillian of Spain, Lampedius, Dioscorus, Eutyches, Peter and another Peter—one of whom defiled Alexandria, the other Antioch—Acacius of Constantinople with his associates, and also all heresies which they and their disciples or schismatics [Col. 0281D] taught or wrote, whose names we do not retain: we confess that these are not merely rejected but have been eliminated from the entire Roman Church and are condemned forever, together with their authors and the followers of those authors, under the indissoluble bond of anathema.

CAP. 66.—That a custom which is not contrary to the Catholic faith must be maintained. From the letter of Pope Pius I (decree 7).

(Distinction 11, chapter *Consuetudinem*.) Through Hilary, our *chartularius* (registrar), you requested from our predecessor of blessed memory that all the customs of former times should be preserved for you—customs which long antiquity has maintained within the Church until now under the ordinance of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles. And we, according to the tenor of our report, [Col. 0282A] approve the custom, provided that it is recognized as making no encroachment upon the Catholic faith.

CAP. 67.—That ecclesiastical ordinances handed down to the Church by the apostles and apostolic teachers must be kept intact, and that no one should observe them as seems good to himself, but according to ancient tradition. From the decrees of Pope Innocent I, letter 1.

Innocent to Decentius, bishop of Eugubium, greeting. If the priests of the Lord were willing to preserve intact the ecclesiastical institutions as they were handed down by the blessed apostles, no diversity and no variation would occur in the rites and consecrations themselves. But while each person considers that he must observe not what has been handed down but what seems good to himself, different practices are seen to be maintained or celebrated in different places or churches. This becomes a scandal to the people, who, not knowing that the ancient traditions have been corrupted by human presumption, imagine either that they are unsuited to themselves or their churches or that opposition has been introduced by apostles or apostolic men. [Col. 0282B] (Distinction 11, chapter *Quis enim nesciat*.) For who does not know or perceive that what was handed down to the Roman Church by Peter, prince of the apostles, and is preserved until now, ought to be observed by all, and that nothing should be added or introduced which either lacks authority or seems to take its example from elsewhere? Especially since it is evident that no one established churches throughout all Italy, Gaul, Africa, Sicily, and the intervening islands except those whom the venerable apostle Peter or his successors appointed as priests. Or [Col. 0282C] let them read whether any other apostle is found or recorded to have taught in these provinces. If they do not read this because they find it nowhere, they ought to follow what the Roman Church preserves, from which they undoubtedly received their beginning, lest, while pursuing foreign assertions, they appear to neglect the head of institutions. There is no doubt that your affection has often come to the city, gathered with us in church, and learned what practice it observes both in consecrating the mysteries and in performing the other sacred rites. I should have considered this sufficient for the instruction or correction of your Church, had I been fully certain what your predecessors held inadequately or differently, unless you had judged that we should be consulted about certain matters. [Col. 0282D] We therefore answer them, not because we believe you ignorant of anything, but so that with greater authority you may instruct your own people or admonish, or not delay to report, those who stray from the institutions of the Roman Church, so that we may know who they are that introduce novelties or believe that the custom of a Church other than Rome ought to be observed.

CAP. 68.—That ecclesiastical customs must be held as law. Augustine, Letter 86 to the presbyter Casulanus.

(Distinction 11, chapter *In his rebus*.) In matters concerning which divine Scripture establishes nothing certain, the custom of God’s people and the institutions of the elders are to be held as law; and, just as transgressors of divine laws, so also despisers of ecclesiastical customs must be restrained.

CAP. 69.—Likewise, on observing ecclesiastical ordinances. Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, book, chapter 27.

[Col. 0283A]

(Distinction 11, chapter *Ecclesiasticarum*.) Of ecclesiastical institutions, some we have received as handed down in the Scriptures, but others through apostolic tradition in succession and in mystery; while usage has approved others, strengthened by custom. An equal rite and the same devotion of piety are owed to both; of this no one even slightly experienced in sacred Scriptures can doubt. For if we attempt to regard as worthless the customs of the Church handed down by the Fathers apart from the Scriptures, it will become plainly evident to those who consider the matter how great a loss religion would suffer. For what Scripture has taught the faithful to be marked with the sign of the saving Cross? What Scripture has prescribed the words of the lengthy prayer, or even of consecration, spoken over the cup and bread, distributed in three parts? For in the mysteries we say not only what is contained in the Gospel or set down by the Apostle, but we also add many other things which carry, as it were, great force. What written text taught us to pray facing east? We bless the font of baptism with the oil of anointing; in addition, we immerse those whom we baptize three times, anoint them with oil, and instruct them in words to renounce Satan and his angels. From where do these things, and many others of this kind, come, unless from a silent and mystical tradition, preserved in the ministries by the Fathers with more reverent diligence in silence than published in writing?

CAP. 70.—To whom recourse is to be had when the authority of sacred Scripture is not available. From the decrees of Pope Innocent, chapter 18.

[Col. 0283C]

(Distinction 20, chapter *De quibus*.) In cases concerning which no authority for loosing and binding appears in the books of the Old Testament, the four Gospels, or all the writings of the apostles, have recourse to the divine Greek writings. If not in them either, turn to the Catholic histories of the Catholic Church written by Catholic teachers. If not in them either, consult the canons of the apostolic see. If not in them either, consider carefully the examples of the saints. But if, after all these have been examined, the nature of the question cannot be clearly discovered, gather the elders of the province and question them. For what is sought by several elders is more easily found. The Lord, the true promiser, also says: “If two or three of you meet on earth in my name, whatever they ask concerning any matter, it shall be done for them by my Father” (Matt. 18).

CAP. 71.—That what is found in the canon must be held firmly, whereas what is found in the writings of others must be considered carefully. Augustine, prologue to book III, *On the Trinity*.

(Distinction 9, chapter *Noli meis*.) Do not submit to my writings as though they were canonical Scriptures; but in those Scriptures, when you find something you did not believe, believe it without hesitation. In these writings, however, do not hold firmly what you did not know to be certain unless you have understood it to be certain.

CAP. 72.—Which Fathers’ writings are more authoritative. Leo IV to the bishops of Britain.

(Distinction 20, chapter *De libellis*.) It is not proper for anyone to judge from the pamphlets and commentaries [Col. 0284A] of others while abandoning the canons of the holy councils or the rules of decretals—that is, those which we have together with the canon and use in all ecclesiastical judgments: namely, those of the Apostles, Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Carthage, Africa, Laodicea, Chalcedon, and Sardica; together with these, the rules of the Roman pontiffs Sylvester, Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, Gelasius, Hilary, Symmachus, Simplicius, Hormisdas, and Gregory the Younger. These, without exception, are the authorities by which bishops judge and by which bishops and clerics together are judged. But if some unprecedented matter should arise or occur which cannot at all be resolved through these, [Col. 0284B] then, if the statements of those whom you mention—Jerome, Augustine, Isidore, or other similar holy teachers—are found, they must be upheld and promulgated generously; or such matters should be referred to the apostolic see. For this reason I do not fear to declare more clearly and in a loud voice that whoever—bishop, cleric, or layperson—does not without reservation accept the ordinances of the holy Fathers that we have mentioned, which among us are entitled canons, is thereby proved neither to hold nor to believe, usefully, effectively, and for his own benefit [or advancement], the Catholic and apostolic faith or the four holy and true Gospels of Christ.

CAP. 73.—Augustine says that many things in his own works may be censured. Augustine to Vincentius Victor, book II (*On the Soul and Its Origin*, book IV, chapter 1).

[Col. 0284C]

(Distinction 9, chapter *Negare*.) I cannot and ought not deny that, just as in conduct itself, so also in my many works, there are many things which may be censured by a just judgment and without any rashness.

### CAP. 74.—That the writers of the canonical Scriptures, even if they are not understood, must nevertheless not be believed to have erred; but that other writers, if they have demonstrated what they say by authority or reason, are to be noted. Augustine, Letter 19 to Jerome.

*(Dist. 9, c. Ego solis.)* I have learned to render this fear and honour only to those writers who are now called canonical: that I most firmly believe none of them, in writing, made any error. But if I encounter anything in them which seems contrary to truth, I shall not doubt that it is nothing other than a corrupt manuscript, or that the translator has not grasped what was said, or that I myself have understood it least of all. I read other authors, however, in such a way that, however great their holiness and learning, I do not think something true merely because they thought it so, but because they have been able to persuade me—either through those canonical authors or by probable reasons—that it does not depart from truth.

### CAP. 75.—That matters shown to be contrary to the privileges of the universal Church have no validity whatever. Gelasius, *On the Bond of Anathema*.

Lest perhaps they say what they customarily say: that, if the Council of Chalcedon is admitted, all that appears to have been produced there must stand. Let them recognize that it must either be admitted in its entirety or, if it is rejectable in part, it cannot stand firm as a whole. Therefore, since that which was done for communion in the faith and for Catholic and apostolic truth—according to the Holy Scriptures and the tradition of the elders, according to the canons and rules of the Church—for which purpose the Apostolic See deputed that council and confirmed what was done, is unquestionably admitted by the whole Church; whereas the other things there put forward, or rather debated, through incompetent presumption, which the Apostolic See delegated to be handled [perhaps *denegavit*, “refused”], were immediately contradicted by the vicars of the Apostolic See. It is clear that the Apostolic See never approved those matters, even at the request of Emperor Marcian. Anatolius, then bishop of the Church of Constantinople, professed that he had not presumed them himself, and did not deny that they were placed within the power of the bishop of the Apostolic See. Therefore, as has been said, the Apostolic See does not receive them, because things proved contrary to the privileges of the universal Church have no basis whatever [variant: “it does not uphold them”].

For why? Because in the holy books which we certainly venerate and follow, it is reported that certain acts of profanity occur there and wicked deeds are narrated: are they therefore likewise to be venerated or followed by us because they are contained in those holy and venerable books?

### CAP. 76.—That the Constantinopolitan synod held against Photius is not to be received. John VIII to Patriarch Photius.

We declare null and wholly erase the synod held at Constantinople against Photius, both for other reasons and because Pope Adrian did not subscribe to it.

### CAP. 77.—On the same matter. Pope John to his *apocrisiarii* [envoys].

You shall say that we annul those synods held against Photius under Pope Adrian, at Rome or Constantinople, and remove them from the number of holy synods.

### CAP. 78.—At what time the Sixth Synod was held. In the prologue to the history of Anastasius, librarian of the Roman Church.

Some chatter vainly, saying that the capitular forms of the Sixth Synod, which were published abroad, were made after four years. But from the chronological record itself it plainly appears that there were twenty-seven years from the holy universal Sixth Synod to the issued forms.

### CAP. 79.—That Pope Sergius did not subscribe to the synod which Emperor Justinian assembled in the imperial city, because certain chapters were appended outside ecclesiastical usage. From the *Liber Pontificalis*.

In the time of Pope Sergius, Emperor Justinian ordered a council to be held in the imperial city. The legates of the Apostolic See attended it and, having been deceived, subscribed. He also compelled Sergius himself to subscribe; but he did not consent at all, because certain chapters had been appended to them outside ecclesiastical usage. These, as though synodically defined, were entered in the Seventh Synod, subscribed by the three patriarchs—that is, those of Constantinople, Alexandria, and Antioch—and by the other bishops who had then assembled, and confirmed by the imperial hand. They were sent in a small casket, which in popular speech is called *cribrum* [variants: *crebro*, *scebro*], to this city of Rome for confirmation or for subscription in the place above, to Pope Sergius, as head of all priests.

But that most blessed pontiff, as stated, did not yield at all to the same Emperor Justinian, nor did he permit those same tomes to be accepted or opened for reading. Rather, he rejected and cast them aside as invalid, choosing to die rather than consent to the errors of innovations.

Likewise: Under John VII, concerning the tomes which Emperor Justinian Augustus had earlier sent under Lord Sergius, Roman pontiff of the Apostolic See—tomes in which various chapters contrary to the Roman Church had been written—he commissioned two metropolitan bishops. Through them he also sent a sacred letter, by which he adjured and exhorted the aforesaid pontiff to assemble a council of the Apostolic Church, to establish whatever seemed fitting to him, and to annul by rejection whatever was contrary.

### CAP. 80.—That the Council of Sardica was Arian. Augustine, *Against Cresconius the Grammarian*, book III.

Learn what you do not know: the Council of Sardica was Arian.

Likewise, book IV: The Council of Sardica was Arian.

### CAP. 81.—That the history of Sozomen is rejected by the Apostolic See. Fulgentius to the bishops Alexandrinus and Anastasius of Antioch.

In the history of Sozomen certain things are narrated concerning a certain Eudoxius, who is said to have seized the bishopric of the Church of Constantinople. But the Apostolic See also refuses to accept that history, since it tells many lies and praises Theodore in an excessively unusual manner, declaring him a great doctor of the Church even up to the day of his death. It follows, therefore, that whoever receives that history must oppose the synod held in the time of Justinian of pious memory concerning the Three Chapters. But whoever cannot oppose that synod must necessarily reject that history.

### CAP. 82.—That Eusebius’s writings on chronological history are to be received. Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book II, chapter 39.

What Eusebius did concerning chronological history, we accept because questions concerning the divine books require its use.

### CAP. 83.—Concerning a certain king of the city of Edessa. Responses of Pope Adrian against certain objections, concerning Abgar, chapter 18.

Our predecessor, the most holy Lord Pope Stephen of holy memory, once presiding in the aforesaid council, taught this in person while setting forth many truthful testimonies. Nor should this be passed over: we have often learned from reports of faithful persons arriving from the eastern regions that, although the Gospel is silent about these matters, their credibility is by no means wholly contrary to faith; and the Gospel itself confirms this: “Jesus indeed performed many other signs which are not written in this book” (John 20).

Finally, it is reported by those who affirm it that, as the day of his Passion drew near, the Redeemer of the human race replied to a certain king of the city of Edessa who desired to see him bodily, and asked him, fleeing the persecutions of the Jews, to come to him and to impart to him and his people the wonders and cures of which he had heard:

> “If you desire to see my face bodily, behold: I send you the likeness of my countenance impressed upon a cloth, by which you may cool the ardour of your longing and may not judge impossible what you have heard about me. Yet, after I have fulfilled the things written concerning me, I shall send you one of my disciples, who will grant healing to you and your people and lead you to the height of faith.”

### CAP. 84.—That only the person established in God and firm in faith, who cannot be deceived, should be permitted to read books of heretics. Bede, on the Parables of Solomon, book I.

Only the person strengthened by God in the Catholic faith is permitted to read the books of heretics, so that he cannot be separated from that faith by sweetness or craftiness of words.

### CAP. 85.—That he confuses the discernment of readers who thinks they must in every way be forbidden to read secular literature. Bede, on Kings, book II, chapter IX.

*(Dist. 37, c. Turbat acumen.)* He confuses the discernment of readers and causes it to fail who thinks that they must in every way be forbidden from reading secular literature, from which it is permissible to take as one’s own whatever useful things are found anywhere. Otherwise Moses and Daniel would not have permitted themselves to be educated in the wisdom or literature of the Egyptians and Chaldeans, though they abhorred both their superstitions and their luxuries; nor would the teacher of the Gentiles himself have introduced a number of verses of poets into his sayings or writings.

### CAP. 86.—That the laws of emperors are not to be used in every ecclesiastical controversy. Pope Nicholas, at the council near Convicinum (Letter 32, to the bishops of the Synod of Senlis).

*(Dist. 10, c. Lege imperat.)* Imperial law is not to be used in every ecclesiastical controversy, especially since it is sometimes found to conflict with evangelical [variant: “ecclesiastical”] and canonical sanction. The law of emperors is not above the law of God, but beneath it.

### CAP. 87.—That the works of Cyprian, Athanasius, and Hilary are sound and unshaken in no respect. Jerome to Laeta, on the education of her daughter.

May your daughter always keep Cyprian’s little works in her hand; may she run without stumbling through the letters of Athanasius and the books of Hilary. Let her delight in their treatises and their gifts of mind, in whose books the piety of faith does not waver. Let her read the others in such a way that she judges rather than follows them.

### CAP. 88.—That books of Catholic Fathers which describe the lives of saints are not to be rejected. From the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 73.

What book of the holy Catholic Fathers does not sound forth this message: that we may reach our Creator by a straight course? Moreover, what are the Conferences of the Fathers, their institutes, and their lives, as also the Rule of our holy Father Basil, except instruments of virtues for monks who live well and obediently?

### CAP. 89.—That Jerome and Gennadius collected ecclesiastical writers in one volume. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 7.

Jerome and Gennadius, searching throughout the whole world for ecclesiastical writers, treated them in order and gathered their works into a single catalogue-volume.

### CAP. 90.—On the usefulness of the volumes of Dionysius the Areopagite. Bede, on the Acts of the Apostles.

Dionysius the Areopagite, ordained bishop of the Corinthians, governed the Church gloriously and left behind volumes produced by his intellect, many of which concern the benefit of the Church and remain to the present day. He received the surname Areopagite from the place over which he presided, the Areopagus.

### CAP. 91.—On the discernment of the Rule of Saint Benedict. Gregory, *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 36.

Benedict wrote a rule for monks, outstanding for discernment and lucid in expression.

### CAP. 92.—Second session of the Council of Chalcedon.

The glorious judges said: “Our lord the emperor believes according to the canonical letters and the decrees of the holy Fathers—Gregory, Basil, Hilary, Athanasius, Ambrose, and Cyril—and in no way departs from their faith.”

### CAP. 93.—Third session.

The glorious princes said: “The most pious emperor believes according to the decree of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers, the confirmation of the one hundred and fifty Fathers, and the expositions of the holy Gregory, Basil, Hilary, Athanasius, Ambrose, and Cyril; and he in no way departs from their faith.”

### CAP. 94.—On the books of Gelasius. From the *Liber Pontificalis*.

Gelasius composed five books against Nestorius and Eutyches, and also treatises in the manner of Ambrose. Likewise, he composed two books against Arius; he also made prefaces and prayers for the sacraments in careful language, and many letters on the faith in polished language.

### CAP. 95.—On the books of Clement, in the same source.

Clement composed two letters which are called Catholic.

### CAP. 96.—On Gregory’s synodal booklet. Bede, *History of the English*, book II, chapter 1.

Gregory composed a highly useful synodal booklet for the bishops of Italy concerning necessary affairs of the Church.

### CAP. 97.—On Gregory’s forty homilies. Bishop Gregory, prologue to the forty homilies.

Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Secundinus, his fellow bishop. During the sacred solemnities of the Mass, I expounded forty Gospel readings from those passages customarily read in this church on appointed days. The dictated exposition of some was read aloud by a notary to the people present; but I myself delivered the explanation of others before the people, and it was taken down as I spoke.

### CAP. 98.—On their arrangement. In the same place.

I took care to arrange those homilies in the order in which they were delivered, in two codices: namely, the first twenty that were delivered and the following twenty.

### CAP. 99.—Acts of the Fifth Synod, third day.

We follow in every respect the holy Fathers and doctors of the Church: Athanasius, Hilary, Basil, Gregory the Theologian, Gregory of Nyssa, Ambrose, Augustine, Theophilus, John of Constantinople, Cyril, Leo, and Proclus. We accept all that they have set forth concerning the right faith and the condemnation of heretics. We also accept the other holy and orthodox Fathers who, in the holy Church of God, preached the right faith irreproachably to the end of their lives.

### CAP. 100.—On the confirmation of the booklet of Ennodius. The synod and Pope Symmachus.

The synod said: “We ask that the matters contained in the booklet which Ennodius composed by our authority, as they have been read in our presence, be confirmed by your apostolic authority—as has been said—so that they may be strengthened by your own hands and preserved forever.”

Symmachus replied: “Let it be done.”

### CAP. 101.—What the same Ennodius thinks concerning the authority of the Roman pontiff. Pope Nicholas I to Emperor Michael (Letter 2 or 8).

As the great confessor of Christ, Ennodius, bishop of Ticinum, who was sent to Constantinople by Hormisdas of apostolic memory and more than once endured countless sufferings from Greek madness for the faith of Christ and the condition of the Church, recalls concerning such persons from the prophet: “Shall the axe boast against him who cuts with it, or shall the saw exalt itself against him who draws it?” (Isaiah 10).

### CAP. 102.—Likewise on the same matter. John VIII to Abbot Berrarius [Bercarius].

Far be it from devout minds to think ill of the pontiff of the Roman height, since we are taught by the writing of the blessed confessor Ennodius, bishop of the city of Ticinum, that almighty God either raises illustrious persons to such high eminence or certainly makes those whom he has chosen illustrious.

### CAP. 103.—On the commentary of Rhetic(i)us, bishop of Autun, on the Song of Songs. Jerome, in the letter to Florentius beginning, “In that part to me.”

For this reason I myself entreat—and I strongly ask you to request—that he grant you for copying the commentary of the blessed Rheticius, bishop of Autun, in which he discussed the Song of Songs in lofty speech.

### CAP. 104.—On John Scotus: that in certain matters he did not think soundly. Nicholas to King Charles the Elder.

It has been reported to our apostolic office that a certain man named John, a Scot by birth, recently translated into Latin the work of the blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, which he wrote in Greek concerning the divine names and the celestial orders. According to custom, this work ought to have been sent to us and approved by our judgment, especially since the same John, though he is said to possess much learning, was long reported by frequent rumour not to think soundly in certain matters. Therefore let your diligence supply what has hitherto been omitted, and send us the aforesaid work without any delay, so that, when it has been approved by the judgment of our apostolic office, it may be received by all the more readily through our authority.

### CAP. 105.—What in the Apostolic Canons is to be received and what is not. Leo IX, against the letter of Nicetas, abbot of the monastery of Stoudios.

*(Dist. 16, cap. Clementis.)* The holy Fathers numbered the book of Clement—that is, the *Itinerary of the Apostle Peter*—and the Apostolic Canons among the apocrypha, except for fifty chapters, which they decreed should be added to the orthodox rules.

### CAP. 106.—Likewise on the same matter. Sixth Synod, chapter 2. (Constantinople in Trullo, canon 2.)

*(Dist. 16, c. Placuit.)* This holy synod decreed that from now on the eighty-five chapters of the Apostolic Canons are confirmed and valid.

### CAP. 107.—That the Apostolic Canons are to be preferred to other councils. From Isidore’s preface to the work on canons.

*(Same distinction, same chapter.)* Isidore the merchant [variant: “sinner”], servant of Christ, to his fellow servant and parent in the faith, greeting in the Lord. Because of their authority, we have placed above the other councils the canons called Apostolic, although some call them apocryphal, since the common people [variant: “many”] receive them and the holy Fathers have strengthened their judgments by synodal authority and placed them among canonical constitutions.

Likewise: The first order, as has been stated, contains an inserted account concerning the holding of a council; afterwards follows a compendium of the Apostolic Canons, of the decrees of the first apostolic pontiffs—that is, from Saint Clement to Saint Sylvester—and of various councils, preserving its own sequence.

Likewise, on the same matter: Pope Zephyrinus to bishops established throughout Sicily. *(Dist. 16, c. Sexaginta.)* Sixty apostles set forth judgments together with very many other bishops, and decreed that they should be observed.

### CAP. 108.—On the seventy chapters of the Council of Nicaea. Athanasius of Alexandria to Pope Mark.

*(Dist. 16, c. Septuaginta.)* Since the seventy chapters of the Council of Nicaea, which, by command of my lord Alexander and by decree of all the bishops, I brought from the aforesaid synod, have been burned by fire, we desire to be granted copies through the present legates by the authority of the Holy See of your Church.

Likewise: In our presence eighty chapters were discussed in the said synod: forty issued by the Greeks in the Greek language, and forty issued by the Latins likewise in the Latin language. But it seemed good to the three hundred and eighteen bishops, filled with the Holy Spirit and assembled in the aforesaid council, and especially to the already mentioned Alexander and the *apocrisiarii* of the Apostolic See, that ten chapters should be joined to the others and inserted in suitable places, and that, in the pattern of the seventy disciples or of the seventy languages of the whole world, there should be seventy chapters of so great and excellent a council, which would instruct the whole Christian world.

### CAP. 109.—Likewise on the same matter. Pope Mark to Athanasius and all the bishops of Egypt.

Concerning authentic copies of the chapters of the Council of Nicaea, at which you stated in the letters of your brotherhood that you had been present, we inquired more carefully of our own people who had been present together with you. In conversation they explained the entire order to us exactly as your letters had attested, and testified that your letter was wholly true. This was not because we suspected anything adverse on your part, but because we desired that we, you, and they should think one thing in the future without any wavering, and that the holy Roman Church—which has always remained unstained and, through the Lord’s providence and the aid of blessed Peter, will remain so in the future—should continue firm and immovable at all times without any assault of heretics.

When this had been done, we searched carefully in the holy archive [variant: “service”] of our Apostolic See and found intact those same seventy chapters which, as you stated, had been sent to my predecessor Sylvester of holy memory.

### CAP. 110.—Likewise on the same matter. Letter of Isidore at the head of the canons.

We found more than the twenty chapters of the Council of Nicaea which are held among us, and in the decrees of Pope Julius we read that there ought to be seventy chapters of that same synod.

### CAP. 111.—Likewise on the same matter. Pope Julius to Eusebius, Tegneus [Theogonius], Theodore, Berinthus, etc.

The following chapters are from the aforesaid Council of Nicaea: namely, 18, 19, 21, 23, 26, 27, 28, 30, 40, 41, 45, 47, 49, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56, 58, 59, 60, 61, 62, 63, and 66.

### CAP. 112.—That no council should dare either to prefer itself to, or compare itself with, the Council of Nicaea. Leo to Bishop Anatolius (Letter 51).

Let no councils flatter themselves concerning the multiplication of synodal assemblies, nor let any number of priests, however much more numerous, dare either to compare itself with or to prefer itself to those three hundred and eighteen bishops. For the Synod of Nicaea has been consecrated by so great a divine privilege that, whether ecclesiastical judgments are celebrated by fewer or by more persons, whatever departs from [variant: “is different from”] their constitution is entirely devoid of authority.

### CAP. 113.—Likewise on the authority of the Council of Nicaea.

*[After a few words.]* Those holy and venerable Fathers who, in the city of Nicaea, condemned the sacrilegious Arius with his impiety, made laws of ecclesiastical canons which are to endure to the end of the age. They live among us throughout the whole world in their constitutions; and if anything anywhere is presumed otherwise than they decreed, it is annulled without hesitation.

### CAP. 114.—Likewise on the authority of the Councils of Nicaea and Chalcedon. Pope Nicholas to Emperor Michael.

We follow not merely the numerous assembly of holy bishops of the Councils of Nicaea and Chalcedon, and the synodal constitutions of the other holy Fathers, but we venerate their generous, just, and divinely given judgments; nor are they observed by us merely because of their multitude.

### CAP. 115.—On the authority of the four councils. Novella Constitution 115, chapter 1.

Let the canons of the four holy councils be held as laws.

### CAP. 116.—Which the four councils are. Gregory to the clergy and people of Ravenna, Letter 2, book V.

We venerate the holy Synod of Nicaea, in which Arius was condemned; that of Constantinople, in which Macedonius was condemned; the First Council of Ephesus, in which Nestorius was condemned; and the holy Synod of Chalcedon, in which the same Nestorius, Dioscorus, and Eutyches were condemned. But if anyone ever presumes to say anything against the faith of these four synods or against the tome and definition of Pope Leo of holy memory, let him be anathema.

### CAP. 117.—Likewise on the same matter, and on the Fifth Council. Gregory, Letter 24, book I, to John bishop of Constantinople, Eulogius of Alexandria, Gregory of Antioch, John of Jerusalem, and Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch, and their peers.

*(Dist. 15, c. Sicut sancti.)* I confess that I receive and venerate the four councils as I do the four books of the holy Gospel: namely, Nicaea, in which the perverse doctrine of Arius is destroyed; Constantinople, in which the error of Eunomius and Macedonius is convicted; the First Council of Ephesus, in which the impiety of Nestorius is judged; and Chalcedon, in which the depravity of Eutyches and Dioscorus is rejected. I embrace them with complete devotion and guard them with most perfect approval, because in them, as upon a squared stone, the structure of the holy faith rises, and the rule of every life and action is founded. Whoever does not maintain their solidity, though he seems to be a stone, nevertheless lies outside the building.

I also venerate the Fifth Council, in which the letter called that of Ibas, full of error, is rejected. Theodore, by separating the person of the mediator between God and human beings into two substances [variant: “subsistences”], is shown to have fallen into the faithlessness of impiety. The writings of Theodore as well, by which the faith of blessed Cyril is reproached, are refuted as products of mad presumption. I reject all persons whom the aforesaid venerable councils reject; I embrace those whom they venerate. For, since they have been established by universal agreement, whoever presumes either to loose those whom they bind or to bind those whom they loose destroys himself, not them. Therefore, whoever thinks otherwise, let him be anathema.

### CAP. 118.—Likewise on the authority of the four councils and the Fifth. Gregory to Secundinus, enclosed servant of God.

Whenever bishops are ordained in the four principal sees, let them send one another synodal letters, in which they profess that they preserve the holy Council of Chalcedon together with the other general councils. Likewise, we oppose—and judge worthy of punishment by anathema—any persons who presume either to diminish anything in the faith of that synod or to add anything to it. For the synod held generally after it is received by us for this reason: following in all things the tenor of that synod, it preserves its authority.

### CAP. 119.—Likewise on the authority of the Fifth Council. Bede, *On Times*.

The Synod of Aquileia, owing to its lack of learning in the faith, hesitated to receive the Fifth Ecumenical Council until, instructed by the salutary admonitions of blessed Pope Sergius, it too consented with the other Churches of Christ to assent to it.

### CAP. 120.—On the authority of the Sixth Synod. Leo II to Emperor Constantine Augustus.

We received with great joy, rejoicing in the Lord, the legates of this Apostolic See, our mother the Roman Church—the servants of your piety Theodore and George, presbyters, John, deacon, and Constantine, regional subdeacon—together with the other things sent by our predecessor Pope Agatho of blessed memory at the command of your Serenity, as well as your divine letters and the acts of the holy synod.

We have learned that the holy and universal synod recently gathered at Constantinople, by the grace of God and by your imperial command, has held and defined concerning the Catholic faith the same things as the universal synod which met in this Apostolic See and over which our humility presided.

Likewise: Since, as stated, the holy Sixth Synod perfectly proclaimed the definition of the right faith, which the Apostolic See of blessed Peter, though unworthy, reverently received—Peter’s See which we serve—therefore we too, by our constitution, approve the things established in it and confirm them by the authority of blessed Peter. Therefore, just as we receive and firmly proclaim the five holy and universal synods—that is, Nicaea, Constantinople, the First Council of Ephesus, Chalcedon, and likewise Constantinople—all of which the Church of Christ confirms and follows; so we receive with equal veneration this synod recently held at Constantinople under your Serenity, as following and interpreting them, and command that it be worthily counted among them.

### CAP. 121.—Fourth session of the Sixth Synod. Peter, bishop of Nicomedia, said:

*(Dist. 16, cap. Habeo librum.)* “I have a book containing the canons of the holy Sixth Synod.”

The patriarch said: “Some, through ignorance, are scandalized by these canons and ask, ‘Did the Sixth Synod make canons?’ Let them know, then, that the holy Sixth Synod was assembled under Constantine against those who said that in Christ there was one operation and one will. In it the holy Fathers anathematized them as heretics and explained the orthodox faith; and the synod was dissolved in the fourteenth year of Constantine. But four or five years later those same holy Fathers assembled under Justinian, son of Constantine, and promulgated the aforesaid canons, so that no one should doubt them. For those who were in the synod under Constantine were the very same persons who subscribed to these canons under Justinian. It was fitting that an ecumenical synod should promulgate ecclesiastical canons.”

Sixth session, first tome, against the false Seventh Synod: “How can a Seventh Synod be called a seventh when it does not agree with the preceding six universal synods? Everything assigned seventh place must have continuity with the things previously numbered. But if it participates in none of the things previously numbered, it cannot be counted with them.”

Likewise: “The holy and universal Sixth Synod, after it had promulgated its definition against the Monothelites, was gathered again at Constantinople in the fourth or fifth year, by divine inspiration, after the death not long afterward of Emperor Constantine who had convened it, while his son Justinian reigned in his stead; and it promulgated one hundred and two canons for the correction of the Church.”

### CAP. 122.—Likewise on the authority of the Sixth Synod. Pope Adrian to Patriarch Tarasius. Second session of the Seventh Synod.

*(Dist. 16, cap. Sextam syn.)* I receive the holy Sixth Synod with all its canons, among which it says: “In certain paintings of holy images, the Lamb is depicted as pointed out by the finger of the Forerunner; adopted as a type of grace, this Lamb shows beforehand to us, through the Law of Moses, the true Lamb, Jesus Christ our Lord. Therefore, taking leave of the ancient figures and shadows handed down to the holy Church as prefigurations of truth, we prefer grace and truth and receive them as the fulfilment of the Law. Therefore we decree that from now on the true Lamb, who portrays our Lord Jesus Christ according to his human image, shall be painted in images instead of the former lamb.”

### CAP. 123.—Likewise on the same matter. Letter of the Seventh Synod to Justinian, son of Constantine.

*(Dist. 16, c. Quoniam.)* Since the holy and universal Fifth Synod under Emperor Justinian and Sixth Synod under your father, Emperor Constantine, while discussing most fully the mystery of the faith, did not make canons as the other four universal synods did, we, assembled in this imperial city, have written canons.

### CAP. 124.—Likewise on the confirmation of the Sixth Synod. From the *Liber Pontificalis*.

The heretic Philippicus was promoted to the imperial throne. He also assumed the holy see with an execration of his corrupt doctrine, and rejected the councils of the Apostolic See. For this reason, the entire assembly of the city of Rome, inflamed with zeal for the faith, erected in the Church of Blessed Peter an image—which the Greeks call *pan*—containing the six holy and universal synods.

Likewise: Leo the Younger received the holy Sixth Synod, which had recently been celebrated in the imperial city by God’s providence, written in Greek, under the direction and presidency of the most pious and clement great emperor Constantine.

### CAP. 125.—Likewise on the same matter. Bede, *On Times*, chapter 65.

*(Dist. 16, c. Sexta.)* The Sixth Ecumenical Synod was celebrated at Constantinople and composed in Greek, in the time of Pope Agatho, under the direction and presidency of the most pious Emperor Constantine within his palace, with the legates of the Apostolic See and one hundred and fifty bishops likewise sitting.

For the First Ecumenical Synod was assembled at Nicaea against Arius, consisting of three hundred and eighteen Fathers, in the time of Pope Julius under Emperor Constantine. The Second was held at Constantinople, consisting of one hundred and fifty Fathers, against Macedonius and Eudoxius, in the time of Pope Damasus and Emperor Gratian, when Nectarius was ordained bishop of that city. The Third was held at Ephesus, consisting of two hundred Fathers, against Nestorius, bishop of the imperial city, under the great Emperor Theodosius and Pope Celestine. The Fourth was held at Chalcedon, consisting of six hundred and thirty Fathers, under Pope Leo in the time of Emperor Marcian, against Eutyches, leader of the most wicked monks. The Fifth was held at Constantinople, in the time of Pope Vigilius under Emperor Justinian, against Theodore and all heretics. The Sixth is that of which we have spoken above.

Likewise: Emperor Constantine made paintings in the portico of Saint Peter containing the acts of the six holy ecumenical synods. For Philippicus had ordered such paintings, when they existed in the imperial city, to be removed; and the Roman people decreed that the name of the heretical emperor should not be accepted on documents or on the image of a coin. Hence neither his likeness was introduced into the church nor his name pronounced during the solemnities of the Mass.

### CAP. 126.—Responses of Pope Adrian against certain objections, to Charles, chapter 35.

The holy Sixth Synod, faithfully establishing orthodox doctrine through its canons, decreed as follows: “In certain paintings of venerable images, a lamb is portrayed as indicated by the finger of the Forerunner, left as a sign of grace.” And after a few words: “We decree that, according to his human form, he shall now also be represented in images in place of the former lamb.”

### CAP. 127.—On the reception of the Seventh Synod, chapter 60.

Above we have set down the seven irreproachable divine dogmas of the synod, as the works of the principal holy Fathers wonderfully demonstrate. For if anyone says that he differs from the creed of the aforesaid synod, he appears to differ from the creeds of the six holy synods.

### CAP. 128.—On the same matter. Likewise, chapter 30.

We receive that Seventh Synod itself. For if we had not received it, the Greeks would have returned to their former vomit of error; and we should have to render an account for the destruction of so many thousands of Christian souls.

### CAP. 129.—On the praise of Theophanes, in the prologue to the History of Anastasius, librarian of the Roman Church.

I think it sufficient for the praise of Theophanes the chronicler that he was approved by the Apostolic See, when its vicars, together with three hundred and fifty Fathers, assembled a second time in the city of Nicaea and celebrated the universal synod. Indeed, his praise is found in that same holy Seventh Council.

### CAP. 130.—On the Second Council of Nicaea, eighth among the universal councils.

Constantine reigned with his mother Irene for ten years, two months, and two days. In their ninth year, the Second Council of Nicaea was held, consisting of three hundred and fifty holy Fathers.

### CAP. 131.—Likewise concerning the same matter.

In the eighth year of the reign of Irene and Constantine, the most holy Tarasius, archbishop of Constantinople, proceeded to the city of Nicaea, and the holy eighth universal synod was held.

### CAP. 132.—Concerning the eight universal councils: from the *Liber Diurnus*, the profession of the Roman pontiff.

(*Dist.* 16, c. *Sancta.*) I profess that I shall preserve inviolate, down to the smallest point, the eight holy universal councils—namely, the first of Nicaea, the second of Constantinople, the third of Ephesus, the fourth of Chalcedon; likewise the fifth and sixth of Constantinople; likewise the seventh of Nicaea; and also the eighth of Constantinople—and shall hold them worthy of equal honour and veneration; that I shall in every way follow and proclaim what they preached and decreed, and condemn in word and heart whatever they condemned. [Col. 0296B]

### CAP. 133.—Concerning the commendation of the bishops Donatus and Eugenius. John VIII to the Neapolitans, Salernitans, and Amalfitans [Melfitans].

Since we believe that we are speaking to faithful persons who understand the mystery of Christianity, avoiding an extended argument from the testimonies of the sacred Scriptures, we hereby send to your charity the venerable bishop Donatus, whose praise is found in the holy eighth synod [Col. 0296C], and the religious presbyter Eugenius, our beloved faithful men and counsellors.

### CAP. 134.—Which councils and writings of the holy Fathers are authentic. Sixth Synod, chapter 2.

(*Dist.* 16, c. *Quoniam sanctae.*) We confirm the canons and synods of the holy Fathers: namely, those of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, Constantinople, the first Ephesus, Chalcedon, Sardica, Carthage, and Constantinople under Nectarius; and the writings of Theodosius [Theophilus], who was archbishop of Alexandria; likewise those of Dionysius, archbishop of Alexandria Megalopolis; Peter, archbishop and martyr of Alexandria [Col. 0296D]; Gregory the Wonder-worker, bishop of Neocaesarea; Athanasius, archbishop of Alexandria; Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia; Gregory, bishop of Nyssa; Gregory the Theologian; Amphilochius, bishop of Biconium [Iconium]; Timothy, archbishop of Alexandria; Cyril, archbishop of the same Alexandria; Germanus, bishop of Constantinople; Cyprian, bishop of Carthage; and his synod.

### CAP. 135.—Concerning the authority of the Council of Sardica. Nicholas to Photius.

(*Dist.* 16, c. *Quod dicitis.*) Your statement that you neither possess nor receive the Council of Sardica, nor the decretal letters of the holy pontiffs, is not easily granted credence by us [Col. 0297A]; especially since the Council of Sardica was held among you, in your own regions, and is received by the whole Church. On what grounds, then, could it have been fitting for this holy Church of Constantinople to reject it and not retain it, as was proper?

### CAP. 136.—Concerning the authority of the synod held at the city of Soissons. Pope Benedict III to Archbishop Hincmar (letter 1).
