Upon examining in due course the text of the synod which your blessedness arranged to celebrate at the city of Soissons, together with the bishops of your diocese and the archbishops Weleno of Sens and Amalric of Tours, and other bishops, we find that those matters known to promote the holy Church were established and decreed by pious authorities.

Likewise: We declare by apostolic authority that the determinations of your brotherhood [Col. 0297B] and of the other bishops, which you have confirmed in the present synod with your own hands upon apostolic and canonical authorities, shall in every respect remain valid; and we decree that they shall always remain so, so that no question may ever arise from them at any time.

Likewise: And lest anyone presume stubbornly to lay hands against these canonical enactments and decrees of the Roman pontiffs, we prohibit this under the penalty of anathema, by our apostolic authority and that of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

### CAP. 137.—Likewise concerning the same matter. Pope Nicholas to Archbishop Hincmar. (In the Appendix to the letters of Nicholas I, letter 6.)

That synod which was celebrated by you and the venerable bishops and archbishops in the city of Soissons, in the year 853 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first indiction, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May [27 April], and which was confirmed by our predecessor Pope Benedict of blessed memory: as that pontiff of holy memory confirmed it, so we also decree by apostolic authority that it is confirmed, irrefragable, and to remain perpetually so—while preserving in every respect the command and judgment of the Roman see. [Col. 0297C]

### CAP. 138.—That earlier councils are often corrected by later ones. Augustine, *On the One Baptism*, book II, chapter 3.

Later councils are preferred by later generations to earlier ones; and the whole is always, by the best right, preferred to its parts.

Likewise: The very councils held in individual regions or provinces yield without any hesitation to the authority of plenary councils [Col. 0297D] held from the whole Christian world; and even plenary councils themselves are often corrected, the earlier by the later, when some experience of affairs reveals what had been closed and makes known what had been hidden—without any trace of sacrilegious pride.

### CAP. 139.—Concerning the authority of Bishop Mainard and Archbishop John. Alexander II to the bishops and king of the Dalmatians.

We make known that all the chapters established by our venerable fellow-bishops, namely Mainard, our fellow bishop, and John, our archbishop, at Spoleto and other cities, were, when reported in due order, strengthened in the Roman synod by apostolic authority and under the imposition of anathema by our predecessor Nicholas of blessed memory. [Col. 0298A]

### CAP. 140.—Concerning the death of the Apostle Peter. From Ambrose’s address against Auxentius, concerning the surrender of the basilicas.

After Peter had conquered Simon and was sowing God’s commands among the people and teaching chastity, he stirred up the spirits of the pagans. As they sought him, Christian souls begged him to withdraw for a little while; and although he desired martyrdom, he was moved by the entreaty of the praying people. For he was asked to preserve himself in order to instruct and strengthen the people.

Why say more? At night he began to leave the walls; and, seeing Christ meet him at the gate and enter the city, he said: “Lord, where are you going?” Christ replied: “I am coming to Rome to be crucified again.” Peter understood [Col. 0298B] that the divine answer referred to his own cross. For Christ could not properly be crucified again, since by assuming death he had put off the flesh of suffering. “For in that he died, he died once; but in that he lives, he lives unto God” (Rom. VI). Peter therefore understood that Christ was to be crucified again in his servant; and he willingly returned. When the Christians questioned him, he gave the answer; and immediately, seized for the cross, he glorified the Lord Jesus by his own cross.

### CAP. 141.—That Lives of the Fathers written without trustworthy authorities are not to be read. Answers of Pope Adrian to certain objections addressed to Emperor Charles, chapter 17.

[Col. 0298C] Lives of the Fathers are not read in church when they lack trustworthy authors. For those bearing titles from orthodox authors are both accepted and read. Indeed, the sacred canons give even greater approval to accounts of the sufferings of holy martyrs, permitting them to be read in church when their anniversary days are celebrated.

### CAP. 142.—How Origen and other heretics are to be read. Jerome to Tranquillinus.

For my part, I judge that Origen should sometimes be read for the sake of his learning, just as Tertullian, Novatus, Arnobius, Apollinaris, and certain Greek and Latin ecclesiastical writers are read: that we may choose what is good in them and avoid what is contrary.

### CAP. 143.—Concerning the authority of Ecclesiastical History. Cassiodorus, in the prologue to the *Tripartite History*.

[Col. 0298D]

The ecclesiastical history, proved to be most necessary for all Christians, is known to have been wonderfully written by three Greek authors: namely, the venerable bishop Theodoret and the two most eloquent men Sozomen and Socrates. Through Epiphanius the scholastic, clothing them in Latin speech, we judged it necessary, with the Lord’s help, to gather selected portions of their sayings into a work of one style and to make one edition out of three authors.

Likewise: Let the person who, with the Lord’s help, comes to these little works read without fear; he will gain much profit and knowledge, if with careful attention he entrusts to memory the matters set forth in these twelve books.

### CAP. 144.—How many books of letters Gregory left behind. In the *Life of Blessed Pope Gregory*, book IV, chapter 71.

[Col. 0299A]

Gregory left in the archive as many books of letters as the years during which he lived in the episcopate. Accordingly, he left unfinished the thirteenth book of letters, of the seventh indiction, because he did not reach the end of that indiction.

### CAP. 145.—Concerning the book written by Hermas. From the *Liber Pontificalis*.

During the episcopate of Pope Pius, Hermas wrote a book containing the command which the angel of the Lord gave him when he came to him in the guise of a shepherd and commanded him that the Lord’s Passover should be celebrated on Sunday.

### CAP. 146.—Concerning Theodore’s penitential. Bede, *On Times*.

[Col. 0299B] Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Adrian, a man equally learned, were sent to Britain by Pope Vitalian, and enriched many churches of the English with the fruit of ecclesiastical learning. Among these Theodore wonderfully wrote judgments concerning sinners—namely, how many years a person ought to do penance for each sin.

### CAP. 147.—Concerning the rejection of the synod in which images of the saints and paintings in churches were condemned. Leo IX to Patriarch Michael.

Remember that abominable synod which our heresiarchs wished to call the seventh, by whose conspiracy the venerable images of our Lord Jesus Christ himself and of the saints were either delivered to the flames or submerged in water, while paintings were erased from the walls of basilicas. [Col. 0299C] Although the authority of the Roman pontiffs opposed them, yet above all is to be proclaimed everywhere the freedom of the most holy Pope Nicholas, who through his legates closed the church of Holy Sophia over both the sacred images and the deposition of the blessed bishop Ignatius and the installation of the neophyte Photius, until it should submit to the decrees of the holy see.

### CAP. 148.—Likewise concerning the same matter. Session 9 of the Council of Chalcedon.

The papal *apocrisiarii* [legates] said: “A synod in which so many abominable deeds were done ought not to be called a synod; therefore it seems superfluous to reread its proceedings. For if the apostolic pope has annulled all its acts, it is evident that the most blessed pope also received him into communion and judged him worthy to hold the primacy of the Church of Antioch.” [Col. 0299D]

Likewise, Stephen, bishop of Ephesus, said: “Let the things done in the first Ephesian synod be annulled. Furthermore, let the acts against the lord bishop of Antioch be annulled, because the ordination of Maximus, who was made bishop in the Church of Antioch in his place, was received by the most holy Pope Leo and by the universal synod.”

### CAP. 149.—Concerning the burial of John the Evangelist. Augustine, on John, second part, tractate 124.

It is believed that John the Evangelist sleeps alive beneath the earth [Col. 0300A]. It is related—also found in certain writings, though apocryphal—that when he commanded a grave to be made for himself, he was present sound and well; and, when it had been dug and very carefully prepared, he laid himself there as if upon a little bed and immediately died.

### CAP. 150.—That several martyrs have already risen with their bodies. From a sermon of Saint Ambrose on the birthday of martyrs, beginning: “It is fitting and appropriate.”

If the martyrs have not yet been delivered from the lower world, they have been delivered from sins. For this is the first resurrection: to have escaped the darkness of sins and to possess the light of righteousness. (These words are not found there.)

Nevertheless, perhaps many of these blessed martyrs also either attain, or have attained, bodily resurrection with the Lord. For, as we read, at the first feast of the resurrection, when the Lord raised himself, he raised many bodies of the saints; they lived and entered the holy city (Matt. XXVII). [Col. 0300B] Why should we not believe that, as often as the feast of his resurrection is celebrated, the saints too rise? For where the solemn observance of vows is continual, the grace of gifts is continual also.

But perhaps someone will say: “The tombs are closed, the monuments are built: how can they come forth from them?” Leaving aside the fact that all things are possible to God, and that a spiritual body can come forth through the innermost places of a closed tomb; leaving all this aside, we nevertheless have the example of the Apostle John, whom a tomb could close after receiving him, but could not keep. For it lost, rather than received, the body deposited in it. This was taken away by the grace of resurrection through the closed doors of the tomb, so that the burial might be evident but the buried man could not be found. Finally, when priests sought the body in order to honour it, after the entrance was opened the tomb could not restore him whom it had received. [Col. 0300C]

### CAP. 151.—Concerning the non-acceptance of the Life of the Apostle Thomas and of others. Augustine, *Against Faustus*, book II, chapter 2.

[Note: [Col. 0299D] Augustine has this in *Against Adimantus, a Disciple of Mani*, chapter 17, though not in exactly the same words.]

The Manichaeans read apocryphal writings, composed under the names of apostles by I know not what cobblers of fables. These writings would have deserved to be received into the authority of the holy Church in the times of their authors, if the holy, just, and learned persons then alive, who could examine such matters, had recognized that they spoke truthfully. [Note: [Col. 0300D] Again in *The Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, book I, chapter 38.]

Yet there they read that the Apostle Thomas, while a stranger and entirely unknown at a certain wedding feast, was struck with the palm of a servant’s hand, and called down upon the man an unceasing and cruel vengeance. For when he had gone out to the fountain to bring water from it for the guests, a roaring lion killed him; and a dog brought to the tables at which the apostle reclined the hand which had struck the apostle’s head with a light blow, torn from the man’s body—according to the wish and imprecation uttered by that same apostle. [Col. 0301A]

Likewise, chapter 4. [Note: [Col. 0301D] This is found in chapter 23 of the book *Against Faustus the Manichaean*.] That the blessed Mary had as father a certain priest named Joachim, from the tribe of Levi, is not canonical.

### CAP. 152.—Concerning the apocryphal book entitled *The Passing of Blessed Mary*. Jerome to Paula and Eustochium.

If that apocryphal work concerning the passing of blessed Mary should perhaps come into your hands, do not receive doubtful matters as certain, although many Latins, from devotion, embrace it more fondly through eagerness to read it; especially since from these sources nothing else can be established with certainty except that today the blessed Virgin departed from the body.

Likewise: Many among us doubt whether she was assumed together with her body or died after leaving her body. How she departed from the body, by what persons [Col. 0301B] her most holy body was taken away, where it was transferred, or whether she rose again, is unknown—although some wish to maintain that she has already been raised and now clothed with blessed immortality together with Christ.

Very many assert the same concerning blessed John the Evangelist, her attendant—to whom, while both were virgins, the Virgin was entrusted by Christ—because in his tomb, as the report goes, only manna is found, which is also seen to flow forth. Yet which of these things should be judged truer is uncertain. It is better, however, to entrust the whole matter to God, to whom nothing is impossible, than rashly to define by our own authority anything which we do not prove. So too concerning those whom, according to the testimony of the Gospel, we believe to have risen with the Lord (Matt. XXVII): whether they returned to the dust of the earth, we do not know for certain, [Col. 0301C] except that we read that many bodies of saints who had fallen asleep rose, came into the holy city Jerusalem, and appeared to many. Concerning them, indeed, some teachers have thought—and left in their writings—that the everlasting resurrection was already fulfilled in them. For they confess that they would not be true witnesses of Christ unless their resurrection too were true.

### CAP. 153.—That bishops ought to forbid apocryphal books to be read either publicly or privately. Leo to Bishop Turibius.

Care must be taken, and provision made with priestly diligence, that falsified codices and those differing from true and sincere truth be admitted to no use in reading. Apocryphal writings, which under the names of apostles contain a nursery of many falsehoods [Col. 0301D], must not only be forbidden but altogether removed and burned in the fire.

Likewise: If any bishop does not forbid apocryphal books to be kept in houses, or permits in church to be read under the name of canonical books those codices corrupted by the adulterating revision of Priscillian, let him know that he is to be judged a heretic; for whoever does not call others back from error shows himself to be in error.

### CAP. 154.—That those who read defamatory books are to be excommunicated. From Pope Adrian’s letter delivered to Ingelrannus, chapter 62 (Council of Elvira, chapter 52).

(5, q. 1, c. *Si qui inventi.*) If any persons are found reading defamatory books, let them be excommunicated.

### CAP. 155.—How cautiously apocryphal books are sometimes to be read. Jerome to Laeta, on the education of a daughter.

[Col. 0302A]

Let her beware of all apocryphal writings. And if she should at any time wish to read them, not for the truth of doctrines but out of reverence for the signs, let her know that they are not by those whose names their titles bear; that much faulty material has been mixed into them; and that it requires great prudence to seek gold in mud.

### CAP. 156.—That no one may forge a writing or words to damage another’s reputation unless he is willing to prove them. Adrian to Ingelrannus, chapter 49.

Whoever publicly fabricates a writing or insulting words against another’s reputation, and, when discovered, does not prove the writings, shall be flogged. The person who first finds such writings shall tear them up, if he does not wish to incur the liability of the author.

### CAP. 157.—Likewise concerning the same matter. Book VII of the *Capitularies*, chapter 200.

[Col. 0302B]

Those who compose songs to blaspheme another, or who sing them, shall be judged outside the order. For the law commands those who devise or publish defamatory writings to be banished. Anyone who utters an insult while addressing a judge is marked with infamy. Not only the person who speaks a curse or insult becomes infamous, but also the person by whose counsel it is shown to have been done.

### CAP. 158.—Concerning the anathematizing of those who falsified Catholic books. Session 13 of the Sixth Synod.

We command that those who falsified Catholic books be subjected to anathema and anathematized together with heretics. We reject as inventions of heretics the discourse said to be “Against Me, to Vigilius,” and the pamphlets called those of Vigilius addressed to Justinian and Theodora. [Col. 0302C]

### CAP. 159.—Concerning the condemnation of the council held against sacred images. Session 2 of the Seventh Synod. Pope Adrian to Patriarch Tarasius.

Let your Holiness urge the pious and triumphant emperors to anathematize, in the presence of our *apocrisiarii* [legates], that false council which was irregularly held without the apostolic see, contrary to the ordinance of the venerable Fathers, against sacred images.

### CAP. 160.—That a bishop should not read books of pagans. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 16.

(*Dist.* 37, c. *Episcopus.*) A bishop shall not read books of pagans; books of heretics, however, he may read when necessity and time require. [Col. 0302D]

### CAP. 161.—Likewise, concerning the same matter. Gregory, book IX of the *Register*, letter 48, to Desiderius, bishop of Gaul.

(*Dist.* 86, c. *Cum multa.*) It has reached us—something which we cannot mention without shame—that your brotherhood expounds grammar to certain persons.

We received this report so painfully, and rejected it so vehemently, that what had previously been said was turned into groaning and sorrow; for in one and the same mouth the praises of Christ cannot be contained together with praises of Jupiter. Consider for yourself how grave and wicked it is for a bishop to sing what is not fitting even for a devout layman.

### CAP. 162.—That classical authors are to be read by boys, not priests. Jerome to Damasus, on the Prodigal Son, volume III, letter 146.

(*Dist.* 37, c. *Sacerdotes.*) We see priests of God, setting aside the Gospels and the prophets, reading comedies, singing the amorous words of bucolic verses, holding Virgil in their hands, and making into a crime of pleasure what in boys is a necessity. [Col. 0303A]

### CAP. 163.—Likewise concerning the same matter. Jerome to Eustochium, *On Virginity*.

What harmony has Christ with Belial? What has Horace to do with the Psalter? Virgil with the Gospel? Cicero with the Apostle?

### CAP. 164.—Concerning the same matter. Rabanus, *On Ecclesiastical Afflictions*, part two.

(*Dist.* 37, c. *Legimus.*) We read concerning blessed Jerome [Col. 0303B] that, while he was reading a book of Cicero, he was rebuked by an angel because, though a Christian man, he gave attention to the inventions of pagans.

### CAP. 165.—Concerning the same matter. In the *Life of Gregory*, book III, chapter 34.

Gregory utterly forbade all pontiffs to read books of pagans.

### CAP. 166.—Likewise concerning the same matter. Jerome, *On the Epistle to the Ephesians*, book III, on chapter VI.

(*Dist.* 37, c. *Legant episc.*) The Apostle says: “Bring up your children in the discipline and correction of the Lord” (Eph. VI). Let bishops and presbyters who educate their children in secular letters and have them read comedies and sing the obscene writings of mime-actors consider this: perhaps the children are educated at ecclesiastical expense, and what a virgin, widow, or any poor person, pouring out all his substance, offered to the *corbona* [temple treasury] for sin, the grammarian and orator turn into a New-Year’s gift at the Kalends, a Saturnalian gratuity, a Minerva-festival gift, domestic expenses, offerings to a temple, or filthy prostitutes. [Col. 0303C]

### CAP. 167.—Why Christians are forbidden to read poets’ fictions. Isidore, *Sentences*, book III, chapter 13.

(*Dist.* 37, c. *Ideo prohibetur.*) A Christian is therefore forbidden to read the fictions of poets, because through the pleasure of empty tales they stir the mind toward incentives to lust. For sacrifice is offered to demons not only by offering incense, but also by listening more willingly to their utterances.

Likewise: Books of pagans must be avoided, and rejected for the love of the sacred Scriptures. The flavour of grammatical art is not to be preferred to plainer letters. For common and simpler learning, directed solely to the reader’s benefit, is better. That learning, however, is worse which instils into people a ruinous exaltation of mind. Grammarians are better than heretics; for heretics, by persuasion, give people to drink from a draught of deadly juice. (*Dist.* 37, c. *Si quis artem.*) Yet the learning of grammarians can also benefit life when it is applied to better uses. [Col. 0303D]

### CAP. 168.—What an honourable law is. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book V, chapter 20.

(*Dist.* 4, c. *Erit autem lex.*) A law shall be honourable, just, possible, in accordance with nature, in accordance with the custom of the country, suited to place and time, necessary [Col. 0304A], useful, and clear, so that through obscurity it may contain nothing deceptive; written not for any private advantage but for the common benefit of citizens.

### CAP. 169.—That temporal laws, once established, must be observed. Augustine, *On True Religion*, chapter 31.

(*Dist.* 4, c. *In istis.*) In these temporal laws, although people judge concerning them when they establish them, yet once they have been established and confirmed, a judge may not judge concerning the laws themselves, but must judge according to them.

### CAP. 170.—Concerning the book of Theodosius’s constitutions. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book V, chapter 1.

(*Dist.* 7, c. *Fuerunt autem hi.*) Theodosius the Younger Augustus, following the pattern of the Gregorian and Hermogenian Codes, arranged in a code the constitutions issued from the time of Constantine [Col. 0304B], under the title of each emperor respectively, and called it the Theodosian Code after his own name.

### CAP. 171.—Concerning the book called the Code of Justinian, the book of the Pandects, and that called the Code of the Novels. From the *History of the Lombards*, book V, chapter 25.

The Emperor Justinian corrected with remarkable brevity the Roman laws, whose excessive prolixity and useless inconsistency were burdensome. For he compressed into twelve books all the constitutions of emperors, which had certainly been contained in many volumes, and commanded that this volume be called the Code of Justinian.

Again, the laws concerning the various magistrates or judges, which had extended to almost two thousand books, [Col. 0304C] he reduced to fifty books and named this code the *Digesta*, or Pandects. He also newly composed four books of the *Institutes*, in which the whole body of the laws is briefly comprised. He further decreed that the new laws which he himself had established, collected into one volume, should be called the Code of the Novels.

### CAP. 172.—Likewise concerning Justinian’s book called the *Novellae Constitutiones*. From the history of Anastasius, librarian of the Roman Church.

The Emperor Justinian removed conflicting laws, making a single code and calling it the *Novellae Constitutiones*, in which he does not permit a prince in the place over which he presides to hold property, build a house, or inherit from an unrelated person, unless that person is known to be his kinsman. [Col. 0304D]

### CAP. 173.—That whatever the emperor establishes by letter, decrees after judicial investigation, or commands by edict is certainly law. *Institutes*, book I, title 2.

Whatever the emperor establishes by letter, decrees after judicial investigation, or commands by edict is certainly law. These are what are called constitutions. Clearly, some of them are personal and are not drawn into precedent, because this is not what the prince intends; for what he has granted to someone on account of merits, or the penalty he has inflicted upon someone, or assistance which he has afforded someone without precedent, does not extend beyond the person.

### CAP. 174.—Concerning the chapters inserted by Charles into the laws. Preface to the fifth book of the *Capitularies*.

The preceding four little books contain certain chapters of the glorious emperors Charles and Louis. [Col. 0305A]

Likewise: For the love of almighty God, the holy Church of God and its servants, and the benefit of all the people, we have taken care faithfully to seek out those matters which we subsequently learned from the faithful of the holy Church of God concerning Pippin, Charles, and Louis, but which had not been inserted in the books already mentioned; and we have not delayed to gather them separately with their own materials in the three following books, to write them for possession by the most noble kings Louis, Lothar, and Charles—namely, the sons of the most pious Emperor Louis—and to deliver them to all Christ’s faithful.

Likewise: When these matters had thus been completed, at the beginning of the first little book was placed the letter of Pope Zachary, addressed, as it contains, to all bishops and the remaining ranks of ecclesiastical order, and to all dukes and counts, and all who fear God established throughout Gaul and the Frankish provinces. [Col. 0305B] It is followed by the synodal assemblies which Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, legate of the holy Roman Church and apostolic see, acting in place of the aforesaid Pope Zachary, held canonically together with Charles the Great, duke of the Franks, so that all may know that these aforementioned chapters of the princes were especially confirmed by apostolic authority.

### CAP. 175.—Concerning the law of the English promulgated by King Æthelberht. Bede, *History of the English*, book II, chapter 5.

Among the other benefits which King Æthelberht conferred upon his people through his prudent care, he also established for them judicial decrees, following Roman examples and with the counsel of wise men. They were written in the English tongue and are still preserved and observed by that people. [Col. 0305C]

### CAP. 176.—Concerning the chapters added to the laws by Emperor Lothar. Pope Leo IV to Emperor Lothar.

(*Dist.* 10, c. *De capitulis.*) We profess that, by every means possible to us, through Christ’s favour, we shall preserve now and forever, inviolably, the chapters or imperial commands of Your Majesty and also those of the predecessors of us pontiffs. And if anyone perhaps has said or shall say otherwise to you, know with certainty that he is lying.

### CAP. 177.—That the laws of Christian kings are to be received by churches. Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, in the case of King Lothar and his wife.

As peoples differ, so do their laws. If they are Christians, the Church does not reject the laws which establish what is just within their respective orders. [Col. 0305D]

### CAP. 178.—That whatever God commands must be done, even if it is contrary to the custom or agreement of any persons. Augustine, *Confessions*, book III, chapter 8.

(*Dist.* 8, c. *Quae contra.*) Offences against human customs must be avoided according to the diversity of customs, so that no citizen’s or stranger’s desire may violate an agreement confirmed among people by the custom or law of a nation or city. For every part which does not accord with its whole is unbecoming.

But when God commands something contrary to the custom or agreement of any persons, even if it has never been done there, it must nevertheless be done; if omitted, it must be restored; and if it had not been instituted, it must be instituted. For if a king may command something in the city over which he reigns which neither anyone before him nor he himself had ever commanded, and if it is not contrary to the society of his city, he is obeyed—indeed, it would be contrary to that society if he were not obeyed, since it is a general compact of human society to obey its kings—how much more must God, ruler of his whole creation, be served without hesitation in whatever he commands? [Col. 0306A] For as among the powers of human society a greater power is set over a lesser for obedience, so God is set over all.

### CAP. 179.—That no one may despise the laws of princes and the rules or admonitions of the Fathers. Gelasius to the bishops Rufinus and Aprillis.

(*Dist.* 10, c. *Quis autem.*) Who would say that the laws of princes, the rules of the Fathers, or modern admonitions ought to be despised, except one who thinks that his offence may pass unpunished? [Col. 0306B]

### CAP. 180.—Likewise concerning the same matter, to King Theodoric.

It is certain that Your Magnificence wishes, for the increase of your prosperity, to observe with still greater care concerning reverence for blessed Peter the Apostle the laws of the Roman emperors which you have commanded to be observed in human affairs.

### CAP. 181.—That those who despise laws are to be punished by imperial censure. Leo IV to Emperor Lothar.

You have no small recompense before God in this matter, if you chastise and correct, according to your powers, by your imperial censure those who do not observe the doctrines of the ancient law.

Likewise. (*Dist.* 11, c. *Vestram.*) We beseech Your Clemency that, just as Roman law has hitherto flourished free from every storm and is remembered to have been corrupted for the sake of no person whatsoever, so now it may retain its own strength and proper vigour. [Col. 0306C]

### CAP. 182.—Likewise concerning the same matter, to Count Guy.

It is most unworthy—and even contrary to future generations—that so glorious a law, which many emperors formerly observed, should now lose its force and be unjustly condemned.

### CAP. 183.—That ecclesiastical persons may invoke earthly laws for their defence. Augustine, chapter 58, book II, *Against the Letters of Petilian*.

(*Dist.* 10, c. *Si in adjutor.*) If you think that the laws of the earthly empire should be invoked to assist you, we do not blame you. Paul did this when, against men acting unjustly, he declared himself to be a Roman citizen (Acts XXII). [Col. 0306D]

### CAP. 184.—That emperors’ laws must be obeyed. Augustine to Boniface (letter 50).

Whoever refuses to obey the laws of emperors which are enacted for God’s truth incurs a great punishment.

(*Dist.* 9, c. *Imperatores.*) Whoever, therefore, refuses to obey the laws of emperors which are enacted against God’s truth acquires a great reward.

### CAP. 185.—That those who oppose laws may be deprived of communion. Gelasius to Majoricus (John), Serenus, and Bertusus.

(12, q. 2, c. *Qui et divinis.*) Those who, trampling upon human laws under civil condemnation and casting aside reverence for religion [Col. 0307A], strive either to violate ecclesiastical privileges or anywhere to bring loss upon the poor, and who, even when warned and convicted, refuse to suppress such wickedness and repair the injuries inflicted upon sacred things, rightly ought to be deprived of participation in the divine gift, so that they may lack the reception of that which they held in contempt by their sacrilegious audacity.

### CAP. 186.—Likewise concerning the observance of laws. Leo IV to Archbishop Colorado and Bertusus.

(25, q. 1, c. *Ideo permittente.*) By God’s permission we have been made shepherds of people for this reason: that we must by no means exceed what our Fathers established either in the holy canons or in secular laws. For we act against their most salutary institutions [Col. 0307B] if we do not preserve inviolate what they established by divine counsel.

### CAP. 187.—That ecclesiastical laws cannot be dissolved by imperial laws. Pope Nicholas to the bishops gathered in council at Convicinum (letter 32).

(*Dist.* 10, c. *Lege imper.*) Ecclesiastical laws cannot be dissolved by imperial judgment. This is not because we say that the laws of emperors—by which the Church is often assisted against [or: concerning] heretics, often defended against tyrants, and against all manner of wicked persons—are to be wholly rejected. Rather, we affirm that no one can bring any prejudice against the evangelical, apostolic, and canonical decrees, to which those laws must be subordinated.

### Chapter 188.—That Christian emperors need pontiffs for eternal life; while pontiffs, for the conduct of temporal affairs only, make use of imperial laws. [Col. 0307C] Cyprian to Julian. (Pope Nicholas II has this in his letter to Emperor Michael.)

(Dist. 10, ch. *Quoniam*.) Since the same mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, by distinguishing their respective functions and dignities, separated the proper offices of the two powers—willing that human hearts should be raised upward by healing humility and not once again plunged into hell by human pride—so that Christian emperors too might need pontiffs for eternal life, and pontiffs might use imperial laws for the course of temporal affairs only; in order that spiritual activity might remain distinct from carnal incursions, and therefore one serving God might not involve himself in secular business, while conversely one occupied with secular affairs might not appear to preside over divine matters [Col. 0307D].

### Chapter 189.—That no person may employ a privilege to evade the snares of the present law. Book IX, chapter 5, of the Novellae constitutions.

No person may employ any privilege to evade the snares of the present law, even though it be a church, a *xenion* [hospice], an oratory, or any other place revered for the sake of piety. That is: the same law applies whether the fisc, an estate, or any other sacred endowment is sued; and much more so if the person of a powerful man has been summoned to trial, even though he claims a privilege from a sacred rescript.

### Chapter 190.—That it is fitting for a king to be subject to divine laws. Gelasius to Emperor Anastasius.

If, in matters concerning the order of public discipline, [Col. 0308A] the bishops of religion themselves obey your laws, recognizing that your imperial power has been bestowed by heavenly disposition, lest in human affairs they appear to resist judgments from which they are excluded, with what disposition of mind ought you fittingly to obey those to whom has been entrusted the dispensing of venerable mysteries?

### Chapter 191.—That those things prevail in law which accord with the reason of right and law. Pelagius to Count John.

To one who said that he had sacred commands in hand, we replied that he ought to know that the most merciful prince himself has established by general laws that those sacred grants made at an individual’s request prevail and are carried into effect which accord with the reason of right and law. But those which are perhaps obtained by surreptitious means, [Col. 0308B] or false petitions bring no relief whatever to the petitioners.

### Chapter 192.—That all lawsuits are to be determined according to the laws. Book VII, chapter 73, of the Novellae constitutions.

All lawsuits are determined according to the laws and constitutions, even though our command or pragmatic sanction has prescribed the contrary.

### Chapter 193.—That individual cases ought to be concluded according to the general laws. Constitution [101–103], chapter 1.

No judge, whether in a pecuniary or a criminal case, is to fear our pragmatic sanction, or any rescript of whatever kind, whether divine commands, statements of *referendarii*, or orders of an illustrious magistrate. For we command that individual cases be concluded according to the general laws, and that the aforesaid solicitations claim no place for themselves in judicial proceedings.

### Chapter 194.—That long-standing customs approved by the consent of those who use them imitate law. Book I, title 2, of the *Institutes*.

[Col. 0308C]

From unwritten sources comes the law which usage has approved. For long-standing customs, approved by the consent of those who use them, imitate law.

Likewise: Things which each community has established for itself are often changed, either by the tacit consent of the prince [or people], or by another law subsequently enacted.

### Chapter 195.—That practices observed by the whole Church, even if they are not found written down, are to be believed to have been handed down either by the apostles or by apostolic men. Augustine, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, book II, chapter 7.

Many things are not found in the writings of the apostles, [Col. 0308D] nor in the councils of later generations; nevertheless, because they are observed throughout the whole Church, we believe that they were handed down and commended by the apostles themselves alone.

### Chapter 196.—That innovations are not to be presumed upon unless some authority supports them. Leo IV to the judge of Sardinia.

Neither custom nor a recently introduced practice of our Church or of our predecessors has been to presume new or unusual measures contrary to the holy canons. Therefore, we would more devoutly wish to receive your petitions, if in these matters the judgment of the holy Fathers supported us. But because the synodal documents do not appear to favour this course, we cannot presume so great an innovation or depart from that most right path.

### Chapter 197.—That what has been canonically handed down is not to be altered by any innovation. From the book of the pontiffs called the *Diurnus*.

[Col. 0309A]

I profess that I shall diminish or alter nothing of the tradition which I find handed down and observed by my most approved predecessors, nor admit any innovation; but that, zealously, as their true disciple and follower, I shall observe and venerate with all the effort of my mind what I discover to have been canonically transmitted.

### Chapter 198.—On the same matter. Seventh session against the false synod.

We preserve inviolate all ecclesiastical traditions, whether written or unwritten.

Likewise: If anyone violates any ecclesiastical tradition, whether written or unwritten, let him be anathema.

### Chapter 199.—That what the usage of antiquity has established is to be preserved uncorrupted. Gregory to Maurentius, master of soldiers, book VII of the *Register*, letter 70.

[Col. 0309B]

We are altogether grieved that truth did not move you to Theodore’s defence, so that you might freely learn what reason required and ensure the preservation of that which long custom rightly claims for itself; for it is exceedingly grievous for priests to arrogate anything to themselves contrary to ancient usage.

Likewise: Let all things established by the usage of antiquity be preserved uncorrupted in every respect.

### Chapter 200.—On the same matter. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book V, chapter 3.

(Dist. 1, ch. *Mos est*.) Custom is a practice approved by antiquity, or an unwritten law.

Likewise. (Ibid., ch. *Consuetudo autem*.) Custom, moreover, is a kind of law [Col. 0309C] established by manners, accepted in place of law when written law is lacking; nor does it matter whether it rests on writing or on reason.

### Chapter 201.—Likewise on the same matter. Book VIII of the *Code*, chapter 52, title 1.

(Dist. 12, ch. *Consuetudo*.) A preceding custom, and the reason which recommended that custom, must be maintained; and whatever is done against a long-standing custom, the provincial governor shall call back to his attention.

### Chapter 202.—That custom does not have such force as to overcome reason or law. Title two.

(Dist. 11, ch. *Consuetudinis*.) The authority of custom and long-established usage is not slight; nevertheless, its force is not so great that it can overcome either reason or law.

### Chapter 203.—That evil customs must be uprooted very swiftly. Pope Nicholas to Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims.

[Col. 0309D]

(Dist. 8, ch. *Mala consuetudo*.) An evil custom, which must be avoided no less than a destructive corruption, if it is not uprooted promptly and thoroughly, is claimed by wicked persons as a right of privilege. Transgressions and various presumptions, unless swiftly restrained, begin to be revered as laws and continually observed in the manner of privileges.

### Chapter 204.—That a good custom, even if it seems to conflict with reason, is not easily to be changed. Gregory, letter 75, book I of the *Register*, to all the bishops of Numidia.

(Dist. 12, ch. *Nos*.) We permit a custom which is known to introduce nothing contrary to the Catholic faith [Col. 0310A] to remain unchanged, whether concerning the appointment [or preservation] of primates or other matters, excepting those who have come to the episcopate from the Donatists. We entirely forbid such men to be promoted to the dignity of a primacy, even when their rank would otherwise bring them to the same position. Let it suffice for them to have charge of the people entrusted to them; they must not precede in attaining the summit of a primacy those bishops whom the Catholic faith has both taught and brought forth in the bosom of the Church.

### Chapter 205.—That one who violates the statutes of the Roman pontiffs is to be deprived of communion. The same author, letter 7, book II, to John, Bishop of Larissa.

If at any time, on any pretext, or through any surreptitious proceeding, you attempt to act contrary to what we have decreed, [Col. 0310B] know that you are deprived of sacred communion, and that—except at the final time of your life—you shall not receive it unless by a dispensation which we decree is granted by command of the Roman pontiff.

### Chapter 206.—That all things neither established by councils of bishops nor confirmed by the custom of the universal Church, but irrationally varied according to the differing practices of different places, are to be cut away. Augustine, in reply to Januarius’s inquiries, letter 109, chapter 19 (book I, chapter 19).

(Dist. 12, ch. *Omnia talia*.) All such things as are neither contained in the authorities of the holy Scriptures, nor found to have been established by councils of bishops, nor confirmed by the custom of the universal Church, but are varied innumerably according to the different customs of different places—so that the reasons which people followed in instituting them [Col. 0310C] can scarcely, or never at all, be discovered—I judge ought, wherever opportunity is granted, to be cut away without any hesitation. For although it may not be discovered how they are contrary to the faith, they nevertheless burden with servile loads that religion which God’s mercy willed to be free through very few and very manifest sacramental observances; so that the condition of the Jews is more tolerable. For although they have not known the time of liberty, they are nevertheless subject to legal sacraments, not to human presumptions.

### Chapter 207.—That usage ought to yield to authority. Isidore, *Synonyms*, book II.

(Dist. 11, ch. *Usus*.) Let usage yield to authority; let law and reason overcome corrupt usage.

### Chapter 208.—On the same matter. Augustine, chapter 6, book III, *On Baptism against the Donatists*.

[Col. 0310D]

(Dist. 8, ch. *Veritate*.) Once truth has been made manifest, let custom yield to truth. “I answer plainly,” says Augustine: “Who doubts that custom ought to yield to manifest truth?”

Likewise. (Ibid., chapter 8.) Let no one set custom above reason and truth, because reason and truth always exclude custom.

### Chapter 209.—That many things are believed to have been handed down by the apostles which are not written. Likewise, book V.

That custom which was opposed to Cyprian must be believed to have taken its origin from apostolic tradition, just as there are many things observed by the whole Church and, for that reason, rightly believed to have been commanded by the apostles, although they are not found written down.

### Chapter 210.—That one ought not lightly to begin what neither the authority of the prince nor the usage of the Church recommends. Leo IV to Lothair Augustus.

[Col. 0311A]

You commanded us to grant a privilege and pallium to Bishop Altheus. We ask, therefore, that Your Greatness not be displeased in this matter, because we could not do what we do not recall having been done from the time of the most holy Pope Gregory himself down to our own times, nor alter the boundaries established by the Fathers.

Likewise: What just and careful custom does not command us to imitate, from that—as from a great precipice—we ought to keep ourselves.

### Chapter 211.—That nothing enacted by apostolic authority can be impeded by any custom. Nicholas I, letter to Emperor Michael.

(Dist. 11, ch. *Consequens est*.) It follows that what is enacted with full authority by the rulers of this see must not be set aside on the pretext of any custom, merely by following private wills, but must be held all the more firmly and without wavering.

Likewise: Concerning the customs which, writing to us, you seemed to set against us—namely that different Churches have different customs—we judge nothing against them, nor resist them, if no canonical authority opposes them; we neither judge against nor resist customs which we ought to oppose only where such authority requires it.

### Chapter 212.—Likewise on the same matter. To Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims.

(Dist. 12, ch. *Ridiculum*.) It is ridiculous and a sufficiently abominable disgrace that we should allow the traditions which we received of old from the Fathers to be broken.

### Chapter 213.—That a practice contrary to truth must be abolished. Gregory VII to Wimo, Bishop of Aversa. (Augustine, chapters 5 and 6, book III, *On Baptism*.)

[Col. 0311C]

(Dist. 8, ch. *Si consuetudinem*.) If perhaps you set custom in opposition, it must be observed that the Lord said: “I am the truth and the life” (John 14). He did not say, “I am custom,” but “I am truth.” And certainly, to use the judgment of blessed Cyprian, every custom, however ancient and however widespread, must altogether be subordinated to truth; and a usage contrary to truth must be abolished.

### Chapter 214.—That teachers of the liberal arts are to be appointed in every church. Synod of Pope Eugenius, in the time of Louis.

(Dist. 37, ch. *De quibusdam*.) It is reported to us that in certain places neither teachers nor care for the study of letters are to be found. Therefore, every bishop and the people subject to him, and likewise other places where necessity arises, must without fail devote care and diligence to appointing masters and teachers who possess learning in letters and the doctrines of the liberal arts, and who may teach them; for in these, above all, the divine commands are made manifest and explained.

### Chapter 215.—That no falsehood is to be admitted into the sacred Scriptures. Augustine, letter 9, to Jerome.

(Dist. 9, ch. *Si ad Scripturas*.) If even well-meant falsehoods are admitted into the sacred Scriptures, what authority will remain in them? What judgment can finally be pronounced from those Scriptures, by whose weight the wickedness of contentious falsehood would be crushed?

### Chapter 216.—On the same matter, letter 8.

[Col. 0312A]

It seems to me most ruinous to believe that there is any falsehood in the sacred books; that is, to believe that the human beings through whom that Scripture was ministered and written for us lied in anything in their books. It is another question whether a writer of the holy Scriptures ought to have lied; indeed, it is not another question, but no question at all. For once any well-meant falsehood is admitted into a height of authority so great, no part of those books will remain which is not, whenever it seems to someone either difficult in its moral teaching or unbelievable in faith, referred—by that same most destructive principle—to the intention and office of a lying author.

### Chapter 217.—On the care to be taken for the dead. Augustine, *On Care for the Dead*, chapter 6.

[Col. 0312B]

We read in the *Ecclesiastical History*, written in Greek by Eusebius and translated into Latin by Rufinus, that the bodies of martyrs in Gaul were exposed to dogs; that the remains of the dogs and the bones of the dead were burned in fires until completely consumed; and that the same ashes were scattered in the River Rhône, so that nothing whatever might remain as a memorial.

### Chapter 218.—That the Gospel called “according to the Hebrews” is not apocryphal but ecclesiastical. Bede on Luke, book I, chapter 1.

The Gospel called “according to the Hebrews” is to be counted not among apocryphal but among ecclesiastical histories; for Jerome, the interpreter of sacred Scripture, is said both to have drawn many testimonies from it and to have translated it into Latin and Greek.

### Chapter 219.—That despisers of the canons are to be excommunicated. Urban II to Gerard, Bishop of Thérouanne.

Despisers of the canons are to be excommunicated and condemned, since the one who refuses obedience to the sacred canons must be excluded from the holy mysteries of the altar.

### Chapter 220.—That one who does not accept the Apocalypse is to be excommunicated. From the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 17.

If anyone hereafter does not accept the Apocalypse, or does not preach it in church during the liturgies from Easter until Pentecost, he shall incur a sentence of excommunication.

And chapter 18: We believe it must necessarily be added to the rules of the canons that they are not to be promoted to the priesthood.

### Chapter 221.—Eighth session of the Sixth Synod.

Theophanius, priest and abbot, presented two written sheets: one by Saint Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria, and the other by Saint Augustine, Bishop of Hippo.

### Chapter 222.—Likewise on the same matter. From book V *Against Julian the Pelagian*.

The holy synod said: “The venerable priest Theophanius has proceeded splendidly and truly in the written sheets of the holy and wonderful Fathers,” etc.

Likewise: Another written sheet of Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, was again read from the same booklet.

### Chapter 223.—That differing customs, according to place and time, do no harm within one faith. Leo IX to Michael, Emperor of Constantinople.

[Col. 0312D]

[Col. 0313A] (Dist. 12, ch. *Scit sancta*.) The holy Roman Church knows that different customs according to place and time do no harm to the salvation of believers, when one faith working through love commends all alike to the one God.

### Chapter 224.—That Christ’s mother excluded every pretension of carnal nobility. Augustine, *On Instructing Beginners in Faith*, chapter 22.

Christ was born of a mother who, though she conceived untouched by a man and remained always untouched—a virgin conceiving, a virgin giving birth, a virgin dying—was nevertheless betrothed to a craftsman; thus he extinguished every pretension of carnal nobility.

### Chapter 225.—That only two books of Ezra are received. Reply of Pope Adrian against certain persons’ objections, chapter 23 (chapter 7).

[Col. 0313B]

In the second book of Saint Ambrose *On the Holy Spirit*, among other matters Ezra teaches us, saying in the third book:

> [Note: [Col. 0313D] See also in the book *On Tobias*, chapter 20, and in the little work *On the Good of Death*, chapter 10: he adduces testimony from the Fourth Book of Ezra.]

Likewise, the third book of Ezra is not accepted in our codices translated from the Hebrew truth; only two books are accepted.

### Chapter 226.—That antiquity lives unshaken when the authority of the holy Fathers supports it. Pope Zosimus to the bishops of the province of Narbonne.

(25, q. 1, ch. *Contra statuta*.) Not even the authority of this see may establish or alter anything contrary to the statutes of the Fathers. For among us antiquity lives with roots unshaken, and the decrees of the Fathers have established reverence for it.

### Chapter 227.—That the canonical holy Scripture of both Old and New Testament is contained within its fixed bounds, so that there can be no doubt whatever about it; but that letters of bishops may be criticized on the authority of other bishops. Augustine, chapter 3, book II, *On Baptism against the Donatists*.

[Col. 0313C]

(Dist. 9, ch. *Quis nesciat*.) Who does not know that the canonical holy Scripture, both of the Old and of the New Testament, is contained within its fixed bounds, and is set before all later writings of bishops in such a way that it can never be doubted or disputed whether whatever is established as written in it is true or right? But letters of bishops, whether written after the canon was confirmed or written now, may be criticized through the perhaps wiser discourse of any person more expert in the matter, through the weightier authority and more learned judgment of other bishops, and through councils, [Col. 0313D] if in them anything has perhaps departed from truth.

### Chapter 228.—On the authority of the Book of Wisdom. Augustine to Prosper and Hilary, *On the Life of the Saints* (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 14).

The saying of the Book of Wisdom ought not to have been rejected. That book has deserved to be read in the Church of Christ for so many years from the rank of readers in the Church of Christ, and to be heard by all Christians—from bishops down to the humblest faithful laity, penitents, and catechumens—with reverence for its divine authority.

Likewise: Those who desire to be instructed by the opinions of commentators ought to set before all commentators this Book of Wisdom, where it is read: “He was caught away lest malice should change his understanding” (Wisdom 4), [Col. 0314A] because distinguished commentators, even in times near to those of the apostles, likewise set it before themselves. When they adduced it as a witness, they believed that they were adducing nothing but divine testimony.

Likewise: The Book of Wisdom, which has deserved to be read in the Church of Christ for so great a number of years, must suffer no injury, because it opposes those who are deceived concerning human merits.

### Chapter 229.—That it did not please God to save his people through dialectic. Reply of Pope Adrian against certain persons’ objections to Charles, chapter 49.

(Dist. 37, ch. *Omnem vim*.) Heretics place all the force of their inventions [poisons] in dialectical disputation [they establish it in disputation], which is defined, in the judgment of philosophers, as having power not to establish but as an endeavour to destroy. But it did not please God to save his people through dialectic; for the kingdom of God consists in the simplicity of faith, not in contention of speech.

### Chapter 230.—That what is received contrary to the laws is dissolved by the laws. John VIII to Emperor Louis.

(Dist. 10, ch. *Vides*.) You see, dearest son, that what is received contrary to the laws deserves to be dissolved by the laws.

### Chapter 231.—That an emperor may not do anything contrary to divine laws. Sixth Synod.

> [Note: [Col. 0314D] In the Sixth Roman Synod in the time of King Theodoric.]

Pope Symmachus.

(Dist. 10, ch. *Non licet*.) It is not lawful for an emperor, or for anyone who preserves piety, to presume anything contrary to [Col. 0314C] divine commands or to do anything that opposes evangelical, prophetic, and apostolic rules.

### Chapter 232.—How many chapters belong to the Council of Nicaea. Stephen to Luythobius, Bishop of Mainz.

(Dist. 16, ch. *Viginti*.) On the testimony of Athanasius, we do not doubt that seventy chapters of the Council of Nicaea were written, as a figure of the seventy disciples. Of these only twenty are held in the holy Roman Church; but through what neglect the rest have disappeared is uncertain. Many suppose that they were incorporated into the Council of Antioch.

### Chapter 233.—That, concerning a most obscure matter, one must not dispute without the authority of the divine Scriptures. Augustine, in the book *On the Baptism of Infants against the Donatists*.

[Col. 0314D] Where a most obscure matter is disputed, and the definite and clear evidences of the divine Scriptures offer no assistance, human presumption ought to restrain itself, taking no position by inclining to either side.

### Chapter 234.—That, once truth has been made manifest, custom must yield. In the same work, book III, chapter 5.

(Dist. 8, ch. *Qui contempta*.) One who, despising truth, presumes to follow custom is either envious and malicious toward brothers to whom truth is revealed, or ungrateful toward God, by whose inspiration his Church is instructed.

Likewise, chapter 6: For the Lord [Col. 0315A] says in the Gospel: “I am the truth” (John 14). He did not say: “I am custom.” Therefore, once truth has been made manifest, let custom yield to truth.

Likewise, chapter 7: Therefore, once truth has been revealed, let error yield to truth; for Peter also, who previously circumcised, yielded to Paul preaching the truth (Galatians 2).

Likewise, chapter 9: Therefore, since Christ is truth, we ought to follow truth rather than custom, because reason and truth always exclude custom.

### Chapter 235.—On the same matter. Augustine, chapter 4, book IV, *On Baptism* (chapter 5).

(Dist. 8, ch. *Frustra*.) “In vain,” he says, “do some persons who are defeated by reason object custom to us, as though custom were greater than truth, or as though, in spiritual matters, one ought not to follow what has been revealed for the better by the Holy [Col. 0315B] Spirit.” This is certainly true, because reason and truth must be preferred to custom; but when truth supports custom, nothing ought to be retained more firmly.

### Chapter 236.—That bishops’ writings are to be distinguished from the authority of the canon. Augustine, letter 48 to Vincentius.

(Dist. 9, ch. *Noli frater*.) The canonical Scriptures also employ this manner of rebuke: they are spoken, as it were, to all, while the words reach certain persons.

Likewise, there: Do not, brother, seek to collect calumnies from the writings of bishops against so many, so clear, and so indubitable divine testimonies—whether from ours, such as Hilary’s, or from those of the unity itself before the party of Donatus was separated, such as Cyprian’s and Agrippinus’s. First, because [Col. 0315C] this kind of literature must be distinguished from the authority of the canon. For they are not read in such a way that testimony is drawn from them as though it were impermissible to hold a different opinion, if they have perhaps thought otherwise than truth requires [Col. 0315B]. For we belong to that number of persons who do not disdain to accept as addressed even to ourselves the Apostle’s words: “And if in anything you think otherwise, God will reveal this also to you” (Philippians 3).

### Chapter 237.—Likewise on the same matter. Letter to Fortunatianus, Bishop of Cirta.

(Dist. 9, ch. *Neque quorumlibet*.) We ought not to regard the disputations of any persons, even Catholic and praiseworthy persons, as canonical Scriptures, so that it would not be lawful for us—while preserving the honour due to those persons—to disapprove and reject something in their writings [Col. 0315D] if we happen to find that they have thought otherwise than truth holds, whether truth has been understood with divine help by others or by ourselves. I am such in relation to other persons’ writings as I wish interpreters of my own writings to be.

### Chapter 238.—That apostolic enactments are confirmed by God. Pope Agatho to all bishops.

All enactments of the apostolic see are to be received as though they had been confirmed by the voice of the divine Peter himself.

### Chapter 239.—That a particular synod cannot be convened to judge a general synod. Pelagius to the patrician Valerian, among other matters.

(Dist. 17, ch. *Nec licuit*.) Thus it has not been permitted for anyone [perhaps, ever], nor will it be permitted, for a particular synod to be convened to judge a general synod. [Col. 0316A] But whenever some doubt concerning a universal synod arises for certain persons, either those who desire their souls’ salvation should voluntarily approach the apostolic sees to receive an explanation of what they do not understand; or, if they are perhaps—as has been said of such persons, “When the sinner has come into the depth of evils, he despises” (Proverbs 18)—so obstinate and stubborn that they do not wish to be taught, they must by some means be drawn to salvation by those same apostolic sees, or, lest they be the ruin of others, be restrained [oppressed] according to the canons by secular powers.

### Chapter 240.—That a synod of bishops is not to be convened without the authority of the Roman see. Pope Marcellus XXVIII from Peter, in his second decretal.

[Col. 0316B] (Dist. 17, ch. *Synodum*.) Although you may be able to gather certain bishops, you cannot regularly convene a synod of bishops without the authority of this holy see; nor may you condemn before a final judgment proceeds from here the bishop who has appealed to this apostolic see. For if laypersons employ written appeals in public courts, how much more is it lawful for priests to do the same, since they are above laypersons? Of them it has been said: “I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Psalm 81). Therefore no bishop accused of any crimes whatsoever is to be heard or judged except in a lawful synod, convened in its proper time by apostolic or canonical authority, lest an innocent man be condemned or lose communion.

### Chapter 241.—That two provincial councils of bishops are to be held each year. Pope Leo I, letter 82.

[Col. 0316C]

(Dist. 18, ch. *De conciliis*.) Concerning episcopal councils, we prescribe nothing other than what the holy Fathers beneficially ordained: namely, that two assemblies be held every year, in which judgment may be made concerning all complaints which commonly arise among persons of different ecclesiastical ranks. But if, among those who preside themselves, a case involving more serious sins should arise—may it not happen!—which cannot be decided by provincial examination, the metropolitan shall take care to inform Your Fraternity of the whole character of the matter, so that, if the matter is not settled before the assembled Fathers by your judgment, whatever it may be may be transferred to our cognizance.

### Chapter 242.—That councils are not valid without apostolic authority. In the fifth synod of Pope Symmachus.

[Col. 0316D]

(Dist. 17, ch. *Concilia*.) Councils of priests, decreed annually in provinces by ecclesiastical laws, have lost their force because they lack the pope’s presence. Read, you utterly mad persons, whether anything was ever established by them apart from the sanction of the apostolic see, and whether, if anything arose concerning major affairs, it was not reserved for consultation at the discretion of the aforesaid see.

### Chapter 243.—Likewise, that councils of bishops are to be held twice yearly. From the Council of Chalcedon, fifteenth session, chapter 19.

(Dist. 8, ch. *Pervenit ad nostras*.) It has reached our ears that the established councils of bishops in the provinces are rarely held; and it is thereby proved [Col. 0317A] that many ecclesiastical matters needing correction are neglected. Therefore this holy synod decrees, in accordance with the rules of the Fathers, that bishops in every province assemble twice each year, so that every matter which has arisen may be corrected. Bishops who refuse to assemble, while remaining in their cities and especially enjoying bodily health, free also from all other pressing and unavoidable business, may lawfully be corrected by admonitions of brotherly love.

### Chapter 244.—That in the churches of Spain councils are to be held once yearly because of poverty. From the Third Council of Toledo, chapter 18.

This holy and universal synod commands that, while the authority of the earlier canons remains in force—which commands councils to assemble twice [Col. 0317B] each year—having regard to the length of travel and the poverty of the churches of Spain, bishops shall assemble once a year at a place chosen by the metropolitan. The local judges and administrators of fiscal estates, by decree of our most glorious Lord, shall likewise gather with the priestly council, either in spring [or autumn] or on the day of the Kalends of November, so that they may learn how piously and justly they ought to act toward the peoples, lest in forced services or superfluous labour they burden either private persons or the fisc. For bishops are to be overseers [reading uncertain: *prosp.*], according to the royal admonition, of how judges act toward the peoples, so that they may correct the judges after warning them, or make their insolence known to the ears of princes. If they cannot reform them after rebuke, [Col. 0317C] they shall suspend them from the Church and from communion. The bishop and the elders shall determine what judges ought to pay throughout the provinces as a penalty if they do not attend the council. Moreover, the council shall not be dissolved until it has first selected the place at which the council is to meet again at the following time, so that the metropolitan bishop will not thereafter need to send letters to convene a council, if at the previous council the time and place have been announced to all.

### Chapter 245.—How reverently and orderly the priests of the Lord ought to preside in judgments. From the Eleventh Council of Toledo, chapter 1.

(5, q. 4, ch. *In loco benedictionis*.) When seated in the place of blessing, the Lord’s priests must neither [Col. 0317D] make a din with uncontrolled voices nor be disturbed by any tumults; they must not engage in idle talk or laughter, nor—what is worse—pour forth tumultuous voices in obstinate disputes. For if anyone, as the Apostle says, thinks himself religious but does not restrain his tongue, deceiving his heart, that person’s religion is vain (James 1). Justice destroys its own worship when a noisy crowd confounds the silence of judgment, as the prophet says: “The work of justice shall be silence” (Isaiah 58). Therefore whatever is discussed in the deliberations of those seated, or proposed by the accusers’ side, must be presented with the gentlest expression of words, [Col. 0318A] so that neither contentious cries disturb the minds of those hearing nor the tumult weaken the firmness of the judges. Whoever, therefore, in an assembly of the council considers that the foregoing rules should be violated, and, contrary to these prohibitions, disturbs the council by tumult, insults, or laughter, shall, in accordance with the command of the divine law which says, “Cast out the scoffer, and contention will go out with him” (Proverbs 22), be removed with every mark of disgrace from the assembly and bear a sentence of excommunication for three days.

### Chapter 246.—The order begins: how a synod is to be conducted by a bishop.

> [Note: [Col. 0317] Taken from the Council of Salegünstadt. See Isidore’s preface to the collection of canons, and the beginning of the councils.]

At the first hour of the day, before sunrise, all are to be put out of the church. When all the doors have been barred, doorkeepers shall stand at the one entrance through which the clergy must enter. The assembled cardinal priests shall enter together with the bishop [Col. 0318B] and take their seats according to the precedence of their rank. After them the deacons shall enter; having formed a circle before the bishop and priests, they shall stand. Then the visiting presbyters shall enter, standing at a distance from the others in their own order and sitting when commanded. The subdeacons also shall enter whom the fitting order requires for reading or taking down the proceedings. With the doors barred, while the bishop and priests sit in prolonged silence and direct their whole hearts to the Lord, the archdeacon shall say, “Let us pray”; and then the litany shall be performed. Immediately all, bishops and presbyters alike, shall bow down [Col. 0318C], praying for a considerable time in silence, with tears and groans. Then the bishop shall rise while all remain bowed, and shall publicly offer this prayer to the Lord.

### Chapter 247.—Prayer to be said by the bishop in synod.

Here we are, Lord, Holy Spirit; here we are, held indeed by the enormity of our sin, but spiritually gathered in your name. Come to us, be with us, and deign to enter our hearts. Teach us what we are to do, where we are to go, and show what we ought to accomplish, so that, with your help, we may be able to please you in all things. Be the salvation, the counsellor, and the accomplisher of our judgments—you who alone, with God the Father and his Son, possess the glorious Name. Do not allow us, who love supreme equity, to become disturbers of justice, lest ignorance draw us to the left [Col. 0318D], favor bend us, or acceptance of a gift or of a person corrupt us; but effectively join us to yourself by the gift of your grace alone, so that we may be one in you and may not depart from the truth in any respect. Thus, gathered in your name, may we uphold justice in all matters with the moderation of piety, so that our judgment here may in no respect differ from yours, and in the future, for deeds well performed, we may obtain everlasting rewards.

### CHAPTER 248.—That the Gospel Is to Be Read in a Synod, and What Chapters Are to Be Recited.

When this prayer has ended, let all respond: Amen. Then let the archdeacon say again: “Rise.” [Col. 0319A] At once let all rise, and let the Gospel be read by the archdeacon: “The Lord Jesus appointed” (Luke 10), etc. When it has been read, let the bishop and the other [presbyters] sit with reverence and discipline.

Let the deacon, clothed in a dalmatic, bring the book of canons into the midst and read through the chapters of the Council of Nicaea, where the Catholic faith is more fully treated: namely, how all worshippers of Christ ought confidently to venerate one God in Trinity and the Trinity in unity, to believe in their hearts, confess with their mouths, and worship unceasingly; where it is set forth clearly enough how the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are truly one God.

Then let the book of offices be read, so that they may know in what order all ecclesiastical offices are to be performed. After this, let the presbyters be examined as to how they ought to exorcize the possessed, [Col. 0319B] how to conduct the scrutinies and the opening of the ears, and how to baptize them. When these matters have been completed, let the bishop address all the clergy in the following manner.

### CHAPTER 249.—The Bishop’s Admonition.

Therefore, prayers having first been offered to God, I admonish your brotherhood, most beloved sons, with pious exhortation, and I entreat you by the divine name, that you receive with all piety those things which are said to us concerning God, the sacred orders, and holy conduct, and that you strive to carry them out with the greatest reverence. Thus, with the help of heavenly grace, may we diligently and prudently consider all matters which appear to concern our salvation and that of the Christian people committed to us, lest the sheep of our Lord Jesus Christ entrusted to us, though unworthily [Col. 0319C], perish through our negligence—sheep for whom we must render an account on the day of judgment.

Then with like entreaty I adjure or beseech you that none of you, in judging, show partiality toward his brother or any person, or, moved by any favor or gift, knowingly turn away or depart from a just judgment; but that, with the full piety of brotherly love and with fear of God, you willingly apply yourselves with us, so that through teaching and holy admonition we may be able, by the aid of God’s mercy, to bring the sins, errors, and corrupt practices of our sons—committed before us or in our time, through the devil’s instigation, in this city or in our parishes—to the correction of their faults and to the performance of good deeds. Thus, on the last day of judgment, may we not be judged by the Lord for negligences [Col. 0319D] and faults as slothful and wicked servants, but may deserve to receive the reward of eternal blessedness for good deeds and right dispositions. Through the Lord, etc.

### CHAPTER 250.—On the Examination of Faith and Other Virtues.

When these matters have thus been stated, the cardinals, priests, and Levites, as well as the rest, are to be searched and examined: first, concerning belief in the Trinity and unity, that is, concerning love of God and neighbor; second, concerning humility and chastity; third, concerning fasting and prayer; fourth, concerning generosity in almsgiving; fifth, concerning ecclesiastical offices, together with all vices to be avoided and virtues to be acquired.

### CHAPTER 251.—Conclusion of the Council’s First Day.

[Col. 0320A]

These matters having therefore been deliberated on the first day in synodal judgment, let the archdeacon rise and say: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, let us go in peace.” Then let the bishop pronounce the blessing.

### CHAPTER 252.—The Bishop’s Blessing.

May he who gathers scattered Israel guard you here and everywhere. Amen. And may he not only guard you, but make you worthy guardians of his sheep. Amen. So that with Christ, the supreme shepherd, you may rejoice in heaven over the feeding of his flocks. Amen. May he deign to grant this, he who foreknew us as predestined before the foundation of the world and justified before the end of the age, through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

### CHAPTER 253.—Proceedings of the Second Day.

On the second day, when they have entered and all have bowed together, as stated above, the bishop is to say this prayer.

[Col. 0320B]

Bowing the knees of our hearts to you, Lord, we ask that we may carry out the good which is required of us by you: namely, that, proceeding with ready diligence beside you, we may make a subtle judgment of difficult discernment and, loving mercy, may shine forth in endeavors of action pleasing to you.

Then let all respond: Amen. When they have risen, let the Gospel be read: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5); or: “Be merciful” (Luke 6). After this, in order as before, let them sit in their assigned seats, and let the bishop then address them. When the words for the second day have been completed, let those things necessary in the synod be examined and carefully considered. When the sixth or [Col. 0320C] ninth hour has passed, let the archdeacon again proclaim: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, let us go in peace.”

### CHAPTER 254.—The Bishop’s Blessing.

May the Lord grant you increase in the grace of the priesthood, in mind and speech, bodily and spiritual. Amen. And, when you have been placed at his right hand, may he grant you a share in the heavenly kingdom. Amen. May he deign to grant this, he who before, etc.

### CHAPTER 255.—Proceedings of the Third Day.

Then, on the third day, after all things have been performed as stated above, when they have entered the church, let the bishop say this prayer while they are again bowed.

To you, Lord, meanwhile crying aloud with clamorous voices, we unanimously pray that, strengthened by the regard of your grace, we may become fearless heralds of virtue and may be able to proclaim your word with every confidence. [Col. 0320D]

And let all respond: Amen. When all have risen, let the Gospel again be read: “I am the good shepherd” (John 11). After this, let them sit in their seats in order, and let the bishop again address them. These preliminaries having thus been completed, let the remaining matters necessary in the synod be considered. When all these have been completed, let the bishop say this prayer over all the clergy.

### CHAPTER 256.—Prayer.

There is no strength of human conscience, Lord, which can carry out without offense the judgments of your will. Therefore, since your eyes have seen our imperfection (Psalm 138), reckon as perfection those things which we desire you to bring to their perfect conclusion in equity.

We have implored you to meet us at the beginning of our proceedings; we also pray that you may be present at this end of our judgments, especially that you may spare ignorance, pardon error, and grant to perfect vows the perfect effectiveness of the work. And because, rebuked by conscience, we waste away, lest either ignorance have drawn us into error or perhaps headlong will have impelled us to turn aside from justice, for this reason we ask and beseech you: if we have incurred any offense in this synodal celebration, deign to forgive and remit it, so that we who are about to dissolve the assembled synod may first be absolved from every bond of our sins, and thus, as transgressors, obtain pardon and, as confessing to you, attain everlasting recompense. Amen.

### CHAPTER 257.—The Lord’s Prayer Is to Be Added to This Prayer, While All Remain Bowed. The Bishop’s Blessing and the End of the Council.

[Col. 0322A]

May the Son of almighty God, who is the beginning and the completion of the end, grant you charity. Amen. And may he who has enabled you to reach the completion of this synod make you absolved from every contagion of sin. Amen. So that, made freer from every guilt and also absolved through the gift of the Holy Spirit, you may return unharmed in happy journey to the resting places of your own sees. Amen. May he himself, etc.

When all these things have been completed, let the archdeacon say: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, let us go in peace.” Then let all rise together and return peacefully to their own places.

## FIFTH PART OF THE DECREES

Concerning the primacy of the Roman Church, the right of primates, metropolitans, and bishops; their ordination; and episcopal preeminence.

[Col. 0321]

### CHAPTER 1.—The Origin of the Priestly Order. Anacletus, in His Second Decretal (Letter 2 to the Bishops of Italy).

[Col. 0321B]

(Distinction 21, chapter *In the New Testament*.) In the New Testament, after Christ the Lord, the priestly order began with Peter, because to him was first given the pontificate in Christ’s Church. For the Lord said to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16).

He, therefore, first received from the Lord the power of binding and loosing, and first brought the people to faith through the power of his preaching. The other apostles received honor and authority with him in equal fellowship. They wished him to be their chief [Col. 0321C]; and they too, at the Lord’s command, scattered throughout the whole world and preached the Gospel (Matthew 28). When they died, bishops arose in their place; their ordination must be performed in the order and manner previously specified.

Whoever receives them and their words receives the Lord; but whoever despises them despises him who sent them and whose embassy they exercise, and he himself will unquestionably be despised by the Lord (Luke 10).
