Seeing that the harvest was plentiful and the laborers few, the apostles asked the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest (ibid.). Hence seventy disciples were chosen by them; presbyters bear their type and have been established in their place in the Church. Let what has already been said concerning their ordination and that of the remaining ministers suffice. [Col. 0321D]

### CHAPTER 2.—What Is the First See. Anacletus, in His Third Decretal (Letter 3 to All Bishops).

(Distinction 22, chapter *Most Holy*.) The first see, by heavenly favor, is the Roman Church, which, as has been mentioned, the most blessed Peter and Paul consecrated by their martyrdom. The second see is at Alexandria, which was consecrated in blessed Peter’s name by Mark, his disciple and evangelist, because, sent by Peter, he first preached the word of truth in Egypt and received glorious martyrdom there. He was succeeded by the venerable Abilius [“Anianus, and after him Abilius”]. The third honorable see is at Antioch, belonging to the same blessed apostle Peter, because there he lived before coming to Rome (Acts 11), appointed Ignatius bishop, and there the name “Christians” first arose for the new people.

### CHAPTER 3.—On Appeal. To All Beloved Brothers in Christ. Sixtus, Sixth from Peter, in His First Decretal (Letter 2, Chapter 2).

[Col. 0322C] (2, question 6, chapter *If Any One of You*.) If any of you is assailed by some adversity, let him freely appeal to this holy apostolic see and seek refuge with it as with the head, lest an innocent person be condemned or his Church suffer harm. If necessity arises and he does not wish to appeal to it, but is nevertheless summoned by this see, he must not refuse to come; rather, as soon as the summons has been announced to him, he must hasten to come and prudently set out the cases for which he has been summoned. If anything needs correction, let him correct it with those whom he first finds here.

Nevertheless, he is not to return to his Church until he has been fully instructed and cleared by apostolic letters or credentials from here, if there is cause for this. And after he has returned home, let his neighbors know [Col. 0322D] how he has settled here his own case and that of others, so that he may be able to report and proclaim it to everyone without any ambiguity.

For bishops have been commanded to be defended and freed by this holy see, by the holy apostles, so that, just as they were originally established through their arrangement by the Lord’s ordination, so in future times they may always be free from every adversity [“perversity”] under the protection of this holy see, to whose direction they have entrusted their cases and judgments. Therefore those are blamed who have acted otherwise toward their brethren than they knew to please the rulers of this see.

These things having been considered, and with the decrees of the other bishops, bearing, as it were, the care of all by reason of the preeminence of our own see, we decree that no pontiff may presume to excommunicate or judge any bishop stripped of his possessions or expelled from his see, because one already stripped cannot have the privilege by which he might be stripped. But if anyone presumes to act otherwise, let him know that the censure of this see, together with all its members, [Col. 0323A] will not fail to come upon him.

### CHAPTER 4.—Likewise on the Same Matter: That the Case of an Accused Bishop May Not Be Determined without Consulting the Roman Pontiff. Pope Victor, Thirteenth from Peter, in His First Decretal (Letter 1, Chapter 3).

(3, question 6, chapter *Accused*.) It has been decided that a bishop accused or judged by bishops of his own province in any case may freely appeal to and approach the pontiff of the apostolic see, who shall arrange for his case to be reconsidered either in person or through his representatives. While the pontiff is reconsidering his case, no one else may be installed or ordained bishop in his place. For although the bishops of the province may examine the case of an accused pontiff, they are not permitted to determine it without consulting the Roman pontiff.

And elsewhere it is read in the apostolic statutes (2, question 6, chapter *If Anyone Thinks*): “If anyone thinks that he is oppressed by his own metropolitan, let him be judged before the patriarch, or the primate of the diocese, or at the see of the universal apostolic Church.” Such presumption, brethren, is nothing other than transgressing the boundaries of the apostles and their successors and violating their decrees.

### CHAPTER 5.—That Priestly Dignity Excels Imperial Dignity. Gregory Nazianzen Speaks of the Emperors Themselves (in an Oration to the Citizens of Nazianzus).

(Distinction 10, chapter *Do You Accept?*) Do you accept freedom of speech? Do you willingly accept that the law of Christ has subjected you to priestly authority and placed you under these tribunals? For he has given authority to us also, and has given us a rule far more perfect than your sovereignties. [Col. 0323D] Or does it seem just to you that spirit should yield to flesh, heavenly things be overcome by earthly things, or human things be preferred to divine?

### CHAPTER 6.—That the Lord Conferred Primacy upon Peter among the Disciples, So That It Might Thus Be Diffused through the Church. The Most Blessed Pope Leo I to All the Bishops of the Province of Vienne (Letter 87).

(Distinction 19, chapter *Thus the Lord*.) Thus our Lord Jesus Christ, Savior of the human race, established matters so that the truth formerly contained in the proclamation of the Law and the Prophets should go forth through the apostolic trumpet for the salvation of all, as it is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18).

Yet the Lord willed the sacrament of this office to belong to the ministry of all the apostles, and he placed it principally in the most blessed Peter, chief of all the apostles, so that from him, as from a kind of head, he might diffuse his gifts through the whole body. Thus whoever dared to depart from Peter’s firmness would understand himself to be excluded from the divine ministry [“mystery”]. [Col. 0324A] For, having taken him into fellowship in indivisible unity, he wished to call him by what he himself was, saying: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matthew 16), so that the construction of the eternal temple might, by the wondrous gift of God’s grace, stand firm in Peter’s solidity.

Strengthening his Church by this firmness, he ensured that neither human rashness might attack it nor the gates of hell prevail against it. But whoever tries to weaken its authority by yielding to his own desires and by refusing to follow what he received from the ancients, desires with excessively impious presumption to violate the most sacred firmness of this rock, constructed by the Lord’s building, as we have said. [Col. 0324B]

### CHAPTER 7.—That the Emperor Is Not to Be Obeyed If He Commands Anything Contrary to God. Augustine on the Psalms (Psalm 124, on the Verse: “For He Will Not Leave the Rod”).

(11, question 3, chapter *Emperors*.) Julian was an unbelieving emperor; was he not an apostate, a wicked idolater? Christian soldiers served the unbelieving emperor. When the cause of Christ was at issue, they acknowledged no one except him who was in heaven. When he wished them to worship idols and offer incense, they preferred God to him. But when he said, “Lead out the battle line; go against that nation,” they obeyed immediately. [Col. 0324C] They distinguished the eternal Lord from the temporal lord, and yet, for the sake of the eternal Lord, they were subject even to the temporal lord.

### CHAPTER 8.—That No One Superior May Be Subjected to Judicial Decisions by Those of Inferior Dignity or Rank. Nicholas to His Beloved Son Michael, Ever Augustus, Beloved by God (Letter 2, Volume 8).

(Distinction 21, chapter *But Now*.) Now, by divine inspiration, we shall neither be reluctant nor find it impossible to show you—if only you are willing to listen—that no one can lawfully be subjected to judicial decisions by persons of inferior dignity or rank.

Indeed, in the time of the Augusti Diocletian and Maximian, Marcellinus, bishop of the city of Rome, who afterward became an illustrious martyr, was so compelled by pagans that, entering their temple, he placed grains of incense upon the coals. On account of this, when a council of numerous bishops had assembled and an inquiry had been made, that pontiff himself confessed that he had done it. Yet none of them dared to pronounce sentence [against him], while all repeatedly declared to him: “Judge your case with your own mouth, not by our judgment. Do not, they say, be heard in our judgment, but gather your case into your own bosom.” And again: “For from you,” they say, “you will be justified, or by your mouth you will be condemned” (Matthew 12). And again they say: “The first see shall be judged by no one.”

Likewise in the same source. When at one time certain persons attempted to bring charges of evil [“not [Col. 0325A] good”] report against Pope Sixtus, and when it had been stated in a council attended also by the Augustus Valentinian that it was not lawful to pass sentence against the pontiff, that emperor immediately arose and granted the aforesaid pontiff authority to judge his own case. For no pontiff of lesser or inferior cities is found to have been subjected to judgments.

Likewise in the same source. (Distinction 21, chapter *To Such an Extent*.) The holy Fathers at Chalcedon so detested this presumption that, among other reasons, they condemned Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, without any restoration, especially because, setting his mouth against heaven and his tongue passing over the earth (Psalm 72), he pronounced excommunication against the holy Pope Leo. Thus, in the sentence delivered against him, they appear especially to mention this matter, saying that the second offense [“second offenses”] greatly exceeded the first in wickedness: “For he presumed to pronounce excommunication against the most holy and blessed Archbishop Leo of great Rome.”

Do we read that an inquiry was made whether Dioscorus had pronounced that excommunication justly or unjustly? Certainly not. Rather, without any controversy, they punished [“avenged themselves upon”] him for this: that, being inferior, he had attempted to assail a superior with every sort of injury [“insult”], as Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, testifies when he says: “Dioscorus was not condemned because of the faith, but because he excommunicated Lord Archbishop Leo.” [Col. 0325B]

### CHAPTER 9.—That the Roman See Judges the Whole Church, but Itself Is Subject to No One’s Judgment. Gelasius I to Faustus, Performing the Office of Legate at Constantinople (Letter 4).

[Col. 0325C]

(9, question 3, chapter *These Are the Canons*.) They set canons against us while not knowing what they are saying. By this very act they show themselves to be acting against the canons: they refuse to obey the sound and right counsel of the first see. These are the canons which decreed that appeals from the entire Church should be brought to the examination of this see, but established that there should be no appeal whatsoever from it. Accordingly, they decreed that it should judge the whole Church, while it should proceed to the judgment of no one; nor did they ever command that judgment be made concerning its judgment, and they established that its sentence ought not to be dissolved, whose decrees they instead commanded to be followed.

In this very case Timothy of Alexandria and Peter of Antioch—Peter, Paul, John, and others, not merely one but certainly several bearing the name of priesthood—were deposed solely by the authority of the apostolic see.

A little later. (Distinction 22, chapter *By What Tradition*.) By what tradition of the elders do they summon the apostolic see to judgment? Were the bishops of the second and third sees and the other priests, well aware of their own guilt, to be deposed, while one who had proved an enemy of religion was not to be deposed? Let them see, then, whether they have other canons by which to pursue their absurdities. But these canons which are regarded as ecclesiastical and lawful cannot summon the apostolic see to judgment. And should the bishop of the city of Constantinople, which indeed has received no rank among the sees through the canons, [Col. 0326A] having fallen into communion with the faithless, not have been removed?

### CHAPTER 10.—On the Same Subject, in the Fifth Synod of Pope Symmachus (in Ennodius’s Book on the Fourth and Fifth Roman Synods).

(9, question 3, chapter *Of Other Men*.) God perhaps willed that the cases of other human beings should be decided by all; but he reserved the see of this prelate, without question, to his own judgment. He willed that the successors of the blessed apostle Peter should owe their innocence to heaven alone and present an unviolated conscience to the investigation of the most subtle examiner.

### CHAPTER 11.—That Vicars of the Roman See Do Not Possess the Fullness of Apostolic Authority. Gregory IV to the Bishops of Gaul, Europe, and Germany.

The Roman Church has imparted its offices to other Churches in such a way that they are called to share in its care, not to the fullness of its authority. Therefore, may your belovedness, in whose devotion we rejoice, join its care to our directives.

And after much else: Let it not perhaps weary or shame you to obey our commands or comply with the precepts of the apostolic see, because grace is given to the humble, not to the proud (James 4). (Distinction 19, chapter *It Is Lawful for No One*.) For it is lawful for no one either to wish or to be able [“either to wish or to be able”] to transgress the precepts of the apostolic see or the ministry of our ordinance, which your charity ought to follow.

Therefore, let whoever wishes to oppose the apostolic decrees lie prostrate in grief over his own ruin, and let him henceforth have no place among priests, but be excluded from the holy ministry. Let no one afterward concern himself with his judgment, because, having already been condemned by the holy and apostolic see through this authority for his disobedience and presumption, he is beyond doubt condemned by everyone; for one to whom discipline in the holy Church has been entrusted, who ought not only to obey the commands of the aforesaid holy Church but also to warn others not to disregard them, must be expelled by the punishment of a greater excommunication. [Col. 0326C] Let him be excluded from divine and pontifical offices who has refused to obey apostolic commands.

### CHAPTER 12.—That a General Synod Is Not to Be Convened without the Pope’s Command. Pope Pelagius II to the Bishops Gathered at Constantinople.

For it has been reported to the apostolic see that John, bishop of Constantinople, calls himself universal and that, because of this presumption, you have called a general synod. Yet the authority to convene general synods has been entrusted by singular privilege to the apostolic see of the blessed apostle Peter; and no synod has ever been valid unless supported by apostolic authority.

Therefore, by the authority of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and by the voice of the Lord Savior—by which the Savior himself gave blessed Peter the power of binding and loosing (Matthew 16), a power which unquestionably passed also to his successors—I command that everything you have decreed in your aforesaid gathering, since a synod presumed in such a manner could not exist, be null and void, so that henceforth such things may never appear or be discussed [“but be mutilated”].

A little later. Therefore let your charity never call anyone “universal” in its letters, lest, by offering another an honor not due to him, it take away what is due to itself. [Col. 0327A]

### CHAPTER 13.—That the Roman Pontiff Alone May, If He Wishes, Ordain a Cleric from Any Church. Stephen to Walbert, Patriarch.

We are surprised that your prudence refuses to consecrate a pastor for the Church of Como, though you know that you have already been urged to this by apostolic exhortation. If, in his election, there was something [perhaps “something which”] displeasing to you and forbidden by the sacred canons, you ought to have answered us in your apologetic letter.

But now we write to you again, not wishing to infringe the privilege of any Church, although by apostolic prerogative we can ordain a cleric from any Church. Stop delaying, through zeal for anyone, the appointment of Lintward [Litward], elected by the clergy and sought by the people, as bishop of the Church of Como. If you delay and, though repeatedly admonished, do not promptly consecrate him, when he comes to us he will undoubtedly depart consecrated. Although we can do this by apostolic authority, we are prompted by your example, since you presumed, by transgressing the limits entrusted to you, to ordain bishops in the Church of Salona, to the indignity of the apostolic see. Consider for yourself how great a violation this is. [Col. 0327B]

### CHAPTER 14.—That the Election and Consecration of the Roman Pontiff Must Be Conducted Justly and Canonically. Leo IV to the Augusti Lothair and Louis.

(Distinction 63, chapter *Between Us*.) By the terms of the agreement between us and you, it has been established and confirmed that the election and consecration of the future Roman pontiff must take place only justly and canonically. [Col. 0327C]

### CHAPTER 15.—That It Is within the Pope’s Power to Restore Those Unjustly Condemned or Excommunicated. Anastasius, Patriarch, to Pope Felix (among the Letters of Felix I, Letter 1).

(9, question 3, chapter *It Has Always Been*.) Your apostolic see has always possessed the authority to restore, by its sovereign power, those unjustly condemned or excommunicated, to restore all things to them, and to punish by apostolic privilege those who condemned or excommunicated them, as we have learned was done both in our times and in earlier times.

Likewise. (9, question 3, chapter *By Ancient Rules*.) It has been ordained [“sanctioned”] by ancient rules that whatever might be done, even in remote or distant provinces, concerning complaints or accusations against bishops, was not to be dealt with or accepted before it had been brought to the knowledge of your venerable see, so that by its authority, according to its pronouncement, it might be invalidated or confirmed. [Col. 0327D]

### CHAPTER 16.—That the Emperor’s Legates Are Not to Be Awaited in the Election of the Roman Pontiff. Gregory II.

(Distinction 63, chapter *Hadrian*.) When Hadrian II was being brought from the church of God’s Mother, our Lady, called “at the Manger,” to the Lateran patriarchal palace for the Roman pontificate, he was carried with eager rivalry by clergy, nobles, and people. On hearing this, the envoys of Emperor Louis took it badly and were indignant, namely because, although they were present, they had not been invited and had not been permitted to attend the election of the future bishop desired by them. [Col. 0328A]

When they received the explanation that this had been omitted not out of contempt for the Augustus but out of regard for the future, lest through such an occasion the custom of awaiting the envoys of rulers at the election of Roman pontiffs [“bishops”] should become established, they entirely calmed their indignation and themselves humbly approached to greet the man elected.

### CHAPTER 17.—That the Lesser Must Always Seek a Blessing from the Greater. Pope Nicholas to Emperor Michael (Letter 2, or 8).

(Distinction 21, chapter *Finally*.) Finally, if in the Epistle to the Hebrews we read that the lesser is blessed by the greater (Hebrews 7), it follows, certainly, that upon just cause the lesser may also be cursed. Indeed, those who came before us, foreknowing these dangerous times, handed down a prudent custom in the Churches. It is observed without omission even today in the Roman Church, which is the teacher of all Churches: no priest should attempt to bless anything without the assent of a priest who is his superior.

Even one who stands before him to pronounce some reading asks for a blessing, but no inferior person dares bless him. Why is this? Is blessing a sin? Far from it. For the Apostle says that the abusive, not those who bless, will not possess the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6). But this indicates by what restraining curb of discipline every inferior is to be constrained in judging his superiors, if such persons do not possess even the slightest right to bless. [Col. 0328B]

### CHAPTER 18.—That Attention Is Not to Be Given to What Sort of Persons Priests Are, but to What They Say concerning the Lord. Pope Nicholas to Emperor Michael (ibid.).

[Col. 0328C]

(1, question 1, chapter *Not What Sort*.) You must take very great care not as to what sort of persons the priests of the Lord are, but as to what they say concerning the Lord. Nor, in the vicars of the blessed apostle Peter, ought you to consider who they are, but what they strive to accomplish for the correction of the Churches and for your salvation.

For you will not say that they are inferior to the scribes and Pharisees who sit in Moses’ chair, of whom the Lord commanded, saying: “Whatever they tell you, do; but do not act according to their works” (Matthew 23). Therefore, Emperor, if he declared that those who sat in Moses’ chair were to be heard, how much more do you think that those seated upon Peter’s chair ought to be obeyed? [Col. 0328D]

### CHAPTER 19.—That the Judgment of the Apostolic See Is Not to Be Reconsidered by Anyone. Nicholas Again to the Same Person.

(9, question 3, chapter *It Is Clear*.) It is certainly clear that the judgment of the apostolic see, than whose authority there is none greater, is not to be reconsidered by anyone, nor is anyone permitted to judge its judgment. As Pope Boniface wrote to Rufus and the other bishops established throughout Thessaly: “No one,” he says, “has ever boldly raised opposing hands against the apostolic summit, from whose judgment it is not lawful to appeal; nor has anyone been rebellious in this matter except one who wished judgment to fall upon himself.”

And blessed Pope Gelasius says: “The canons never commanded judgment to be made concerning its—that is, the Roman Church’s—judgment, nor established that its sentence should be dissolved, whose decrees they instead commanded to be followed.”

Therefore, while we do not deny—since established practice confirms what we have said—that a sentence of the same see may be altered for the better, where something has been obtained by fraud, or where that see itself has decreed to ordain something by dispensation in view of ages, times, or grave necessities, as we read that the distinguished apostle Paul did certain things by dispensation which he is later read to have disapproved, this must nevertheless be observed: such change is made when the Roman Church itself has chosen it after most discerning consideration, not when it has refused [perhaps “wished”] to reconsider what has been rightly determined. [Col. 0329A]

### CHAPTER 20.—That “Glory in the Highest” Is to Be Said by Bishops on the Lord’s Supper. The Same to Ralph, Archbishop of Bourges (Letter 19, Chapter 7).

[Col. 0329B]

(On Consecration, distinction 1, chapter *Moreover, “Glory”*.) Moreover, according to our custom, “Glory to God in the highest” is to be said by bishops on the Lord’s Supper during the solemnities of the Mass. On that same day, however, only those to whom it has been permitted by the apostolic see may use the apostolic pallium.

### CHAPTER 21.—On the Primacy of the Roman Church. Leo IV to King Charles.

(16, question 6, chapter *If Perhaps*.) If perhaps—which we do not believe—we are judged useless among you, nevertheless the Church over which, by the Lord’s permission, we preside is not useless; rather, it is deservedly called by all alike the head and beginning of all things.

### CHAPTER 22.—That Pope Leo Wished His Case to Be Examined in the Presence of the Emperor’s Legates. Nicholas Again to the Emperor.

[Col. 0329C]

(2, q. 7, c. *Nos si incompetenter*.) If we have acted improperly in any matter and have not maintained the path of just law among our subjects, we wish everything to be corrected by the judgment of you and your envoys; for if we, who ought to correct the faults of others, commit worse things, then certainly we shall be disciples not of truth but, as we say with grief, above all others teachers of error. Therefore we earnestly implore the clemency of your Highness to send into these regions persons suited to investigate the matters we have mentioned—men who fear God in all things and who examine everything diligently, just as if your imperial majesty were personally present [Col. 0329D]. Nor do we ask them to investigate with exactness only these matters which we have mentioned above; but whether lesser or even greater affairs concerning us be brought to their attention, let everything be concluded by their lawful examination, so that henceforth nothing connected with these matters may remain unexamined or undecided.

### CHAPTER 23.—That no mortal may presume to rebuke the Roman pontiff, even if he gravely sins. From the Acts of Boniface, martyr and legate of the Roman Church.

(Dist. 40, c. *Si papa*.) If the pope, neglectful of his own salvation and that of his brethren, is found useless and lax in his duties, and moreover silent concerning what is good—which harms him and all others still more—nevertheless he leads innumerable peoples with himself in crowds, as the first slave of Gehenna, to be scourged with many punishments for ever [Col. 0330A]. No mortal presumes to rebuke his faults here, because he who is to judge all is judged by no one, unless he be found to have strayed from the faith. For the preservation of his enduring state the whole body of believers prays all the more urgently, inasmuch as they perceive that, after God, their own salvation depends more particularly upon his safety.

### CHAPTER 24.—That the primacy of the apostolate is to be preferred above all. Augustine, chapter 1 of Book II, *On the One Baptism against the Donatists*.

(2, q. 7, c. *Puto quod sine*.) I think that Bishop Cyprian may be compared with the Apostle Peter, without any insult to him, insofar as the crown of martyrdom is concerned. [Col. 0330B] Yet I ought rather to fear lest I prove insulting toward Peter. For who does not know that he must be preferred, by the primacy of the apostolate, to any bishopric? But even if the grace of their sees differs, the glory of martyrdom is one.

A little lower in the same place: When Peter is corrected by Paul, who came later, and, with the bond of peace and unity preserved, advances to martyrdom, how much more readily and firmly must that which is established by the ordinances of the universal Church be preferred to the authority either of one bishop or of the council of one province.

### CHAPTER 25.—That no one ought to separate himself from communion with Peter. Bede on Matthew (homily for the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul).

(24, q. 1, c. *Quicunque ab unitate*.) Whoever in any way separates himself from the unity of faith or from communion with the Apostle Peter [Col. 0330C] can neither be loosed from the bonds of sins nor enter through the gate of the heavenly kingdom.

### CHAPTER 26.—Preface of the Council of Nicaea concerning the primacy of the Roman see.

To the most blessed Silvester, bishop of the apostolic see in the city of Rome. Under the augusti Constantine and Licinius Caesar, in the consulship of Paulinus and Julian, most distinguished men, in the 1,036th year from Alexander [306], on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, because of the rising heresies, the Catholic faith was set forth at Nicaea in Bithynia. The holy and most venerable Roman Church embraces and venerates this faith, since three hundred and eighteen Fathers, through Victor and Vincent, most devout priests of the Roman see, and under God’s inspiration, issued it to block [or: destroy] the poisons of Arius [Col. 0330D]. (See also Anacletus, epistle 3.) Certain rules were also appended, which the aforesaid Church, receiving them, confirmed.

(Dist. 22, c. *Sacrosancta*.) All Catholics must certainly know that the holy Roman Church was not placed before other churches by any decrees of synods, but obtained primacy by the evangelical utterance of our Lord and Savior, when he said to the blessed Apostle Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16).

There was also joined in fellowship in the same city of Rome the most blessed Apostle Paul, the vessel of election, who, contending under Emperor Nero, was crowned on one day and at one time with Peter by a glorious death. Together they consecrated the holy Roman Church to Christ the Lord and, by their presence and venerable triumph, set it above all other cities throughout the world. Although the continual prayer of all saints is offered to God for all people, nevertheless the most blessed Paul promises the Romans in these words, written in his own hand: “For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I make remembrance of you always in my prayers” (Rom. 1).

Therefore the first see, by heavenly favor, is that of the Roman Church, which the most blessed Apostles Peter and Paul dedicated by their martyrdom [Col. 0331B]. The second see is at Alexandria, consecrated in the name of blessed Peter by Mark, his disciple and evangelist; for, sent by Peter, he first preached in Egypt the word of truth and received glorious martyrdom. The venerable Abilius succeeded him [“Anianus, and after him Abilius”].

The third honorable see is at Antioch, belonging to that same blessed Apostle Peter, because he lived there before he came to Rome, appointed Ignatius bishop, and there the name “Christians,” of the new people, first arose.

Moreover, because of the reverence due to so great a place, the bishop of Jerusalem is held honorable by all, especially because the most blessed James, called the Just, who was also called the Lord’s brother according to the flesh, was first ordained bishop there by the Apostles Peter, James, and John [Col. 0331C]. Therefore, according to the definition of the ancient Fathers, the first see is by no means said to be in Jerusalem, lest perhaps unbelievers or unlearned persons should suppose that the seat of our Lord Jesus Christ—which is in heaven—is on earth. For heaven is his seat, while earth is the footstool of his feet (Isa. 66), since he is the one through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made (John 1); for from him, through him, and in him are all things, to whom be glory for ages of ages (Rom. 11).

At Ephesus, however, the most blessed Apostle and Evangelist John remained for a long time after the resurrection and ascension into heaven of our Lord Jesus Christ; and there also, by divine inspiration, he wrote the Gospel, rested, and died. For this reason the bishop of Ephesus, in memory of so great an apostle and evangelist, holds in synods a more honorable seat [or: place] than the other metropolitan bishops [Col. 0331D].

### CHAPTER 27.—That the legates of the Roman pontiff, in examining the cases of bishops, exercise the authority of him by whom they are sent. From the First Council of Sardica, chapter 7.

(2, q. 6, c. *Si quis episcopus*.) Bishop Hosius said: It has also seemed good that, if a bishop is accused and all the bishops assembled from that region judge him and depose him from his rank, then, if the one who appears [or: is] deposed appeals and takes refuge with the most blessed bishop of the Roman Church and wishes to be heard, the Roman bishop, if he judges it right for the examination to be renewed, should deign to write to those bishops who are in the neighboring and adjacent [or: other] province, or who are in another province, so that they may diligently investigate everything and decide according to the truth of the matter [Col. 0332A].

But if the person asking that his case be heard again has requested the Roman bishop to send priests from his own side, it shall be within that bishop’s power to decide what he wishes and judges appropriate. If he determines that persons should be sent to sit in judgment in person together with the bishops, they shall also possess the power [or: authority] of the person by whom they were sent, as he shall decide. But if he considers the bishops of the same province sufficient to bring the affair to an end, he shall do what he judges by his most wise counsel.

### CHAPTER 28.—Likewise, that a legate acts in the place of him by whom he is sent. From the Sixth Council of Carthage, chapter 3.

Bishop Aurelius said: Let the memorandum which our brethren and fellow priests recently cited from the Acts be produced; and let the remaining matters that have been done, or are to be done, follow. Daniel the notary read the memorandum.

Zosimus, bishop, to Brother Faustinus and to the sons Philip and Asellus, priests: The matters entrusted to you are not unknown to you. Accordingly, carry out everything as though it were ours—indeed, because our presence is there in you—as completely as possible, especially since you may have this our mandate and the words of the canons which, for fuller force, we have inserted in this memorandum [Col. 0332C]. For thus did our most beloved brethren say in the Council of Nicaea when they decreed concerning the appeals of bishops.

### CHAPTER 29.—That bishops’ decisions ought to be strengthened by apostolic authority. From the same council, chapter 5.

Bishop Faustinus, legate of the Roman Church, said: Your Holiness does not prejudice the Roman Church, either concerning this chapter or concerning others, because our brother and fellow bishop Alypius has deigned to say that the canons are doubtful. But deign to write these very matters to our holy and most blessed pope, so that he too, by investigating the complete canons, may be able to discuss with your Holiness all the matters determined [Col. 0332D]. It is enough that the most blessed bishop of the city of Rome should likewise investigate them, just as your Holiness deliberates among yourselves, lest contention seem to arise among the Churches; rather, you may deliberate in brotherly charity, while he writes back what ought better to be observed.

Bishop Aurelius said: Besides the matters which we have set forth [variant: “brought forth”; elsewhere, “promised”] in the Acts, it is necessary that, by the letters of our own lowliness [variant: “fatherhood”], we fully inform our holy brother and fellow priest Boniface of every matter we discuss. Therefore, if our course of action pleases all, let us learn the mind of all from their voices. The whole council said: It pleases us.

### CHAPTER 30.—That doubtful matters are to be referred to the Roman see. Likewise, chapter 8.

[Col. 0333A]

Bishop Faustinus, legate of the Roman Church, said: In accordance with the declaration of your Holiness, I believe that some matters should be confirmed and that others ought to be confirmed, since the canons themselves have now come into doubt. Therefore it pleases both us and your Blessedness that your Holiness should deign to write to Boniface, the holy and venerable bishop of the Roman Church, so that he too may deliberate on what Saint Augustine has deigned to determine: whether this too should be established or passed over—namely, concerning appeals of an inferior rank. If therefore this chapter is still in doubt, it is right that the bishop of the most blessed Roman see should be informed, if indeed this can be found among the approved canons [Col. 0333B].

### CHAPTER 31.—That decrees of the Roman see are to be accepted as rules of the canons. Alexander II to Philip, king of the Franks.

The wretched do not know that the decrees of this holy see must be received and venerated with such devout faith by the children of Mother Church that they are to be admitted by them without any hesitation as rules of the canons.

### CHAPTER 32.—On the same matter. Pope Hilary to Victorinus and the other bishops.

It has been decreed by the law of Christian rulers that whatever the bishop of the apostolic see has pronounced after his examination for the Churches and their governors, for the peace of all the Lord’s priests, and for the observance of discipline itself in removing disorders, is to be reverently received and steadfastly preserved [Col. 0333C].

### CHAPTER 33.—That one who transgresses the decrees of Roman pontiffs is henceforth to know that pardon is denied to him. Nicholas to the archbishops throughout Gaul.

(Dist. 19, c. *Si Romanorum pontificum*.) If the writings of other commentators are approved or rejected by the decree of Roman pontiffs [variant: “of the Roman pontiff”], so that what the apostolic see has approved is today held accepted and what it has rejected is held ineffective, how much more ought the writings which that see itself has issued at different times concerning the Catholic faith, sound doctrines, the various and manifold needs of the Church, and the conduct of believers, to be accorded every honor and reverently received by all in every circumstance, with dispensation or discernment as teacher [Col. 0333D]. Yet some among you have written that those decretals of former pontiffs are not copied throughout the whole body of the code of canons, although they themselves use them freely whenever they see that they support their own purpose; and only now, to diminish the power of the apostolic see and to increase their own privileges, they declare them less acceptable.

Likewise, in the same place: If they say that decretals of holy pontiffs are not to be admitted because they are not written in the code of canons, then no ordinance or writing of Saint Gregory, or of any other person before or after him, should be received, because it is not written in the code of canons. Let them therefore erase from their books the teachings and enactments of those persons whom every tongue venerates, because they are not written in the code of canons [Col. 0334A]. Why then do they occupy parchment, once they are not accepted? Plainly, why should we delay long, when we no longer receive even the divine Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments, if we say that these persons ought not to be heard? For neither of these is included in the code of ecclesiastical canons.

But those who are always prepared for resistance rather than obedience will answer: “A chapter of Saint Pope Innocent is found among the canons, by whose authority we are taught that both Testaments are to be received, although neither is included in its entirety in those paternal canons.” To this it must be replied that, if the Old and New Testaments are to be received not because they are attached in their entirety to the code of canons, but because the judgment of the holy Father [variant: “pope”] Innocent declaring that they are to be received is seen to have been issued (Pope Innocent I, epistle 3 to Exuperius, final chapter), it necessarily follows that the decretal letters of Roman pontiffs are to be received, even though they are not incorporated in the code of canons. For among the canons themselves one chapter of blessed Leo is known to be interwoven (Pope Leo I, epistle 1, chapter 5), in which it is commanded that all decretal enactments of the apostolic see be observed in such a way that anyone who transgresses them is to know that pardon is denied him [Col. 0334B].

For in the fifth chapter of his decretals he says: “Lest anything should perhaps be thought to have been omitted by us, we command that all decretal enactments, both those of blessed-memory Innocent and of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons, be observed by your Love in such a manner that anyone who transgresses them is henceforth to know that pardon is denied him.”

By saying “all decretal enactments,” he omitted nothing that he did not command to be observed; and again, by asserting “of all our predecessors,” he excepted no Roman pontiff who preceded him whose decretal enactments he did not command all to observe, so that anyone who transgresses them is henceforth to know that pardon is denied him. Therefore it makes no difference whether all decretals, or apostolic enactments, are interspersed among the canons of councils or not [Col. 0334D], since they cannot all be bound together in one body, and since among them are those which give firmness and their own force to those that are absent. This is especially so because the synodal proceedings, among which the canons themselves were enacted, are not contained in the code of canons, yet are venerated by us with every fitting honor.

The most blessed Pope Leo is in agreement with this, as is the most eloquent Pope Gelasius in his decrees (Book I, enacted with seventy bishops), saying: “We decree that decretal letters which the most blessed popes have issued from the city of Rome at various times in response to the consultations of various Fathers are to be received with reverence.” Here it should be noted that he did not say, “The decretal letters which are included among the canons,” nor merely those which modern pontiffs have issued, but those which the most blessed popes have issued from the city of Rome at various times [Col. 0335A]. By saying “at various times,” the holy man included also those times when the increasing persecutions of pagans made it most difficult for the cases of bishops to be brought to the apostolic see.

Having thus set these matters forth, with divine grace assisting, we have shown that there is no difference between the decrees of the bishops of the apostolic see found in the code of canons and those which, because of their multitude, are scarcely discovered separately through the bodies of volumes. For we have proved that the eminent bishops Leo and Gelasius commanded that all decretal enactments of all their predecessors, and decretal letters which the most blessed popes issued from the city of Rome at various times, were to be reverently received and observed [Col. 0335B].

### CHAPTER 34.—That no one may add anything to or take anything from the decrees of pontiffs. Pope Adrian to the synod at Troyes.

If the bishop of the apostolic see, or his decrees, is held in detestation or rejection, then neither the name nor the institution of any of us [variant: “of you”] can remain firm or stable. Indeed, even the doctrines concerning the holy and undivided Trinity which are promulgated by the bishops of the apostolic see may suffer some impairment, if the ordinances of any predecessors—and especially of the pontiffs of the first see—are subjected by any successors, or even inferiors, either to some addition or condemnation (which is impious even to say, and altogether horrible even to hear), or are handed over, by the rash audacity of impiety, even to mere derogation [Col. 0335C].

### CHAPTER 35.—That whoever violates the decrees of Roman pontiffs is anathema. From the council of Pope Leo IV and seventy-two bishops, chapter 5.

If anyone despises doctrines, enactments, prohibitions, or decrees beneficially promulgated by the bishop of the apostolic see for the Catholic faith, ecclesiastical discipline, the correction of believers, the amendment of wrongdoers, or the prevention of present or future evils, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER 36.—That one who refuses obedience to the apostolic see incurs the crime of idolatry. From the decrees of Pope Gregory VII.

[Col. 0335D] Whoever refuses to obey the most salutary command of the apostolic see incurs the sin of idolatry, as Samuel testifies (1 Sam. 15) and blessed Gregory affirms (*On Job*, Book XXXV, chapter 10). For “the sin of divination is disobedience, and the crime of idolatry is unwillingness to comply.” Therefore whoever, while professing to be a Christian, despises obedience to the apostolic see incurs the sin of paganism.

### CHAPTER 37.—That enactments contrary to the canons and decrees of pontiffs have no force. Pope Hilary, presiding at a synod, says (Roman Synod, chapter 1).

(25, q. 1, c. *Nulli fas sit*.) Let no one presume, without danger to his rank, to violate either divine enactments or decrees of the apostolic see.

### CHAPTER 38.—On the same matter. Letter of Pope Adrian delivered to Ingelrannus, bishop of the city of Metz, chapter 38.

[Col. 0336A]

(Dist. 10, chapter *Constitutiones*, where it is attributed to Pope Felix.) Enactments contrary to the canons and decrees of Roman bishops, or to good morals, are to have no force.

### CHAPTER 39.—That one who refuses obedience to apostolic commands is excluded from divine and pontifical offices. Pope Hormisdas said.

Let no one advance against me matters contrary to the canons, contrary to the authority of the apostolic see, or contrary to the three hundred and eighteen Fathers; for I do not doubt that to receive anything said contrary to their definition—in which we believe that the Holy Spirit spoke—is not only rash but dangerous [Col. 0336B].

### CHAPTER 40.—That the see of blessed Peter is head of all Churches, and that all ought to assent to its decrees. Pope Adrian, from the second session of the Seventh Synod.

Let your Holiness represent to the pious and triumphant emperors that that false council, which was held irregularly without the apostolic see and contrary to the ordinance of the venerable Fathers against the sacred images, should be anathematized before our *apocrisiarii* [papal envoys].

Likewise: The see of blessed Peter shines forth as holding primacy throughout the world and is the head of all the Churches of God. Therefore the blessed Apostle Peter himself, feeding the Church by the Lord’s command, has failed in nothing (John 21), but has always held, and still holds, the primacy. If your Holiness adheres to the apostolic throne, which is the head of all the Churches of God, and endeavors, as orthodox and God-worshipping, to preserve its sacred and orthodox order incorruptibly and inviolate, let this be the first sacrifice which you offer to almighty God: fall in my stead at the feet of the most pious emperors, and set before their eyes the dreadful judgment of God, so that they may command the venerable icons to be restored to their former state, observing the traditions of this most holy Roman Church [Col. 0336C].

Likewise: The pope’s *apocrisiarii* said: Let the most holy Patriarch Tarasius tell us whether he consents to the letters of the most holy pope. Patriarch Tarasius said: The Apostle Paul, whom light shone round from heaven (Acts 9), who begot us through his Gospel, wrote to the Romans concerning their faith: “Your faith is proclaimed in the whole world” (Rom. 1). It is necessary to follow such testimony, and it is not prudent to oppose it. What, then, has Adrian, the senior bishop of Rome, written to the pious emperors and to our humility, since he shares in the standing of those to whom the Apostle bears testimony? We have confessed, do confess, and shall confess; we think and confirm his letters.

Likewise: The pope’s *apocrisiarii* said: Let the holy synod say whether it receives the letters of the most holy pope. The holy synod said: We follow, receive, and assent. John, representative of the eastern dioceses, said: Great joy has now arisen at the reading of the holy letters of the most holy Pope Adrian, addressed to our most serene emperors and to the most blessed Patriarch Tarasius [Col. 0337A].

Likewise: Constantine, bishop of Cyprus, said: In every respect I assent to the letters of Pope Adrian which were sent to us and to our emperors, and to that which was sent to Patriarch Tarasius; thus I confess, and in this faith I shall stand before Christ’s tribunal.

### CHAPTER 41.—On the condemnation of the Seventh Synod, because it was held without Roman authority. Sixth session, first volume, against the false Seventh Synod.

How is a synod great and universal when the bishops of the other Churches neither received nor agreed with it, but even consigned it to anathema? [Col. 0337B] It did not have the Roman pontiff, or the priests who are with him, as a collaborator; nor did it have their cooperation by a canonical letter, as is the law in synods. Nor did it have the agreement of the eastern patriarchs—namely, those of Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem—or of the archbishops with them.

### CHAPTER 42.—That the apostolic see has not departed from the way of apostolic preaching or fallen into heretical novelties. From the fourth session of the Sixth Synod.

Pope Agatho to the Augusti Constantine, Heraclius, and Tiberius: By the grace of the Almighty, the apostolic Church is shown never to have departed in any way from the path of apostolic tradition, nor, while resisting the novelties of heretics, to have fallen away. Rather, as it received the Christian faith from its lords and princes from the beginning, so it shall remain without change until the end, in accordance with the divine promise of our Lord and Savior, who said: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has sought you, to sift you as wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22) [Col. 0337C].

Let Your Serenity therefore understand that the Lord, who promised that Peter’s faith would not fail, foretold that Peter himself would strengthen his brethren. It is known to all that the apostolic bishops, predecessors of my lowliness, have always done this confidently; and my own humility, though unequal and least, desires to follow them because of the ministry undertaken through divine power.

### CHAPTER 43.—That councils are authorized by letters of the Roman pontiff. From the proceedings of the Second Council of Ephesus.

[Col. 0337D] Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, said: The letter of the most holy and in every respect most blessed Coelestine, bishop of the holy see and apostolic Church of the Romans, having been received, is read aloud to the holy council with fitting honor. Siricius, notary of the holy Catholic city of Rome, read it in Latin.

Likewise: All the most reverend bishops requested that the letter be translated and read. Philip, priest and legate of the apostolic see, said: Custom has been satisfied by the fact that the letters of the Apostolic See were first read in Latin. But now, since your Blessedness likewise requests that they be read also in Greek, it is necessary to satisfy the desire of your Holiness; we have taken care to do so, so that the Latin utterance may be translated into Greek.

### CHAPTER 44.—That, as an entire door is governed by its hinge, so the welfare of the whole Church is administered by Peter and his successors. Leo IX to Michael, patriarch of Constantinople (epistle 1, chapter 10).

[Col. 0338A]

From the see of the prince of the Apostles, Peter—that is, the Roman Church—through Peter himself and through his successors, the inventions of all heretics have been reproved, convicted, and overthrown; and the hearts of the brethren have been strengthened in Peter’s faith, which hitherto has neither failed nor shall fail until the end.

Likewise: You do injury to the Roman Church—a judgment concerning which neither you nor any mortal is permitted to make. For the most blessed and apostolic Pontiff Silvester, by divine ordinance, and his spiritual son, Constantine, the most devout Augustus, with the whole Council of Nicaea approving and subscribing, decreed that the supreme see should be judged by no one. That privilege was to remain for it inviolate and unshaken: namely, that on the fourth day after his baptism the same prince, in devotion, bestowed upon the Roman pontiff the privilege that throughout the whole world priests should have him as their head, just as all judges have the king as judge [Col. 0338B].

The remaining universal councils embraced this venerable judgment of the holy Fathers, as truly promulgated by divine inspiration rather than human opinion: the First Council of Constantinople, with the consent of the pious Augustus Theodosius the Great; the earlier Council of Ephesus, under Theodosius the Younger, son of Arcadius; the Council of Chalcedon, under the rule of the emperor Martian of revered memory; the Second Council of Constantinople, in the presence of the Augustus Justinian; and likewise the Third Council of Constantinople, at the request and with the consent of the younger Constantine. With unanimous will and harmonious word and writing they confirmed that the holy Roman and apostolic see, after the Lord Jesus, is head of all the Churches of God, and that this must be believed, confessed, and written by all venerators of the Council of Nicaea [Col. 0338C]. A strict anathema was imposed by the five aforesaid councils and all subsequent synods of holy Fathers upon those who despise even one iota of its ordinances.

Likewise: We grieve that, by doing injury to the supreme see, concerning which no human being may make judgment, you have received anathema from all the Fathers of all the holy councils.

Likewise: Constantine, the most prudent ruler of the earthly monarchy, reverently acknowledged with deep consideration the summit of heavenly dignity in blessed Peter and in his vicars. Through blessed Silvester he endowed, not only with imperial power and dignity but also with islands and imperial attendants, all pontiffs succeeding that apostle in the Roman see to the end of the age. He considered it utterly unworthy that those whom the divine majesty had set over heavenly things should be subject to earthly rule [Col. 0338D].

Likewise: Remember that abominable synod which your heresiarchs wished to call the Seventh, through whose conspiracy the venerable images of our Lord Jesus Christ himself and of the saints were either delivered to flames or submerged in water, while paintings were erased from the walls of basilicas. Although the authority of Roman pontiffs always opposed them, especially renowned everywhere is the freedom of the most holy Pope Nicholas, who, through his legates, closed the Church of Hagia Sophia on account both of the sacred images and of the deposition of the blessed bishop Ignatius and the installation of the neophyte Photius, until it submitted to the decrees of the apostolic see [Col. 0339A].

Likewise: Although the Church of Constantinople possesses no privilege, divine or human, making it more honorable or illustrious than other Churches, while Antioch and Alexandria retain rights of dignity among the others because of reverence for the prince of the Apostles, nevertheless the pious mother—the Roman Church—unwilling that her beloved daughter should be wholly without the dowry of honor, took care through our blessed predecessors in several synods to decree that, while the ancient dignity of the principal and apostolic sees remained intact, the bishop of Constantinople should be honored as the royal cities are honored. This was so even though the devout Augustus Justinian had wished to establish by human laws that the bishop of the Church of Constantinople should sit after the Roman pope [Col. 0339B].

Likewise: The holy Roman Church knows that differing customs according to place and time do not harm the salvation of believers when one faith, active through love, commends all to one God.

Likewise: Far be it that devout rulers, or an orthodox, most Christian, and God-devoted city, should think that you ought to be heard in your error. Rather, they ought to compel you by the fear of their authority toward the good of unity.

Likewise: The see of the Roman Church, built through Peter upon the rock, shall not fail now or for ever, because Christ the Lord prays for it, as he himself testifies: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22) [Col. 0339C]. By this saying he showed that the faith of the brethren would be endangered by various failures, but would be governed by the aid of Peter’s unwavering and unfailing faith, as by a firm anchor, and strengthened upon the foundation of the universal Church.

No one denies this unless he openly attacks these very words of truth. For as an entire door is governed by its hinge, so the welfare of the whole Church is administered by Peter and his successors; and as the immovable hinge guides the door, so Peter and his successors possess free judgment over the whole Church, since no one ought to alter their status. Hence his clerics are called “cardinals,” as being more closely attached to that hinge by which the other things are moved [Col. 0339D].

Likewise: All priests, although unequal in merit, are equal in office. What is due to office cannot rightly be denied because of merit. Otherwise the priesthood would not stand, if it were made greater or lesser, or varied according to the differing merits of human beings. On this matter, brethren, would that we did not speak to our own judgment. We certainly are such as Peter was, and we are not such as Peter was; for we are the same in office, but not the same in merit. Whenever we demand milk and wool—that is, maintenance and honor—from the sheep of God, there is no mention of our merit; rather, the recompense due to our office is sought. Thus, although we do not possess Peter’s merit, yet in carrying out Peter’s office we claim the honors due to our office [Col. 0340A].

Likewise: Our most blessed predecessor Gregory said: Let no one despise us because of ourselves in Peter’s place, because from his chair, over which by God’s authority we preside however unworthily, our office claims the rights due to it. For it often happens, as we say, that a powerful person suffers disrespect. Yet when he gives orders through that person to his own people or to outsiders, the person of the servant sent is not despised, because reverence for the sending lord is retained in the heart.

Likewise: Whoever endeavors to nullify or diminish the authority or privileges of the Roman Church schemes not the ruin of one Church but the submersion and destruction of the whole of Christianity.

### CHAPTER 45.—That the Roman Church holds the first place among all, while Alexandria and Antioch hold the second. Nicholas, Pope I, to Michael Augustus (epistle 2, or 8).

[Col. 0340B]

Therefore do not say that you have had no need, in a cause concerning piety, of the Roman Church, which confirms the councils assembled by its authority and safeguards them by its moderation. Hence some of them, because they did not have the consent of the Roman pontiff, lost their validity. Likewise, a little later: The holy apostles Peter and Paul made the Alexandrian Church their own through the blessed Mark, the son and disciple of one of them. For the inheritance of a son lies in the power of his parent, and the glory of a disciple is without hesitation referred back to his teacher. Moreover, by his bodily presence the most blessed Peter had already made the Church of Antioch his own; and, as the blessed pope Innocent says (Epistle 21), it would not yield to the see of the city of Rome, except that the former merited him in his passing through it, while the latter received him and rejoiced that blessed Peter came to his end in its midst. [Col. 0340C] Through these three principal Churches, therefore, the care of all the Churches undoubtedly looks for the governance of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul. For these Fathers we were born as sons, through the divinely supplied increase of grace, and were appointed—though unworthy, though far unequal to them in merits—princes over all the earth and over the whole Church.

Likewise, after much else: Furthermore, lest you say that we have decreed Ignatius or Photius to come to Rome contrary to the law of the Church, know that in this we have followed the example of our ancient Father and predecessor Julius. For, as is found in [Col. 0340D] his letter, he is known to have commanded this to those who had assembled at Antioch; and Theodoret the historian shows the same thing in these words (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, ch. 3; *Tripartite History*, Book IV, ch. 6): “But Eusebius and his companions sent to Julius, Roman pontiff, the calumnies brought against Athanasius. Following ecclesiastical law, he commanded them also to come to Rome and regularly summoned the venerable Athanasius to judgment.” The latter came immediately when summoned [variant: “upon receiving the summons”]. But if you say to this: “He indeed summoned them, but they scorned to come,” hear what follows, and you will see whether this contention [perhaps: “contempt”] was reckoned to their praise or blame. For the same historian added, [Col. 0341A] saying: “But the bearers of calumnies did not go to Rome, knowing that their falsehood could easily be exposed.” Therefore do not say that we have ordered the aforesaid men to come to Rome contrary to the law of the Church, since, as you have just heard from the historian, blessed Julius commanded both the accused and the accusers to come to Rome, and regularly summoned the venerable Athanasius to judgment. But he who possessed a good conscience came without resistance; whereas those who possessed an evil one scorned to do so, knowing beyond doubt, as is there written, that their falsehood could easily be exposed.

## CHAPTER 46.—That, just as it was granted by the Lord to Peter to have precedence over the other apostles, so it was granted to his see. From the decrees of Pope Miltiades, chapter 2, sent to the bishops of Spain.

[Col. 0341B] And the Lord entrusted this privilege solely in his own stead to blessed Peter, the keeper of the keys (Matt. 16); and it rightly passed as a prerogative to his see, to be inherited and held in times to come. For even among the most blessed apostles there was a certain distinction of authority. And although the election of all was equal, it was nevertheless granted to blessed Peter that he should have precedence over the others and prudently dispose the causes and questions which came before a complaint. We believe that this was so ordered by God’s ordinance, lest all their successors should claim everything for themselves; but that the greater causes, such as those of bishops and matters of weightier concern, should always flow to the one see of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, so that they might receive there the conclusion of judgments whence they received the beginning [Col. 0341C] of their institution, lest they at any time depart from their own head.

## CHAPTER 47.—On the authority and discernment of teachers. In the first letter of Pope Clement: Peter’s words concerning Clement.

I hand over to Clement the authority of binding and loosing entrusted to me by the Lord, so that whatever he shall decree on earth concerning anything whatsoever, that decree may stand in heaven. For he will bind what ought to be bound and loose what ought [variant: “is expedient”] to be loosed, as one who knows thoroughly the rule of the Church. Therefore listen to him, knowing that whoever grieves the teacher of truth sins against Christ and provokes God, the Father of all.

## CHAPTER 48.—That with the Lord it is not the sentence of priests but life that is required. Jerome, Book III, on Matthew chapter 16.

[Col. 0341D]

“Whatever you bind on earth,” etc. Bishops and presbyters, not understanding this passage, assume for themselves something of the arrogance of the Pharisees, so that they either condemn the innocent or think that they themselves may absolve the guilty; whereas with the Lord it is not the sentence of priests, but the life of the accused, that is examined.

## CHAPTER 49.—Example of the decree of Emperor Constantine concerning the imperial insignia granted to the Church.

(*Dist.* 96, c. *Constantinus*.) By the testament of our decree, we grant to those holy apostles, our most blessed lords Peter and Paul, and through them [Col. 0342A] also to blessed Sylvester, our father, supreme pontiff and universal pope of the city of Rome, and to all his successors as pontiffs who shall sit in the see of blessed Peter until the end of the world, and we hereby transfer to them our Lateran imperial palace, which surpasses and excels all palaces throughout the whole world. Then also the diadem, namely the crown of our head, together with the Phrygian cap, and likewise the shoulder-band, namely the *lorum* with which the imperial neck is customarily encircled; indeed also the purple cloak and scarlet tunic, and all imperial garments. We grant also the rank of the imperial presiding officers, horses, and imperial [Gratian has: “the imperial horse of the presiding riders, granting to him [Col. 0342B] also the imperial …,” etc.] sceptres, together with all standards, banners, and various imperial ornaments, and all the ceremonial procession of imperial majesty and the glory of our authority.

We decree also that the most reverend men, the clergy serving the same most holy Roman Church in its various orders, shall possess that summit of singular power and preeminence by which our most distinguished senate appears adorned in glory—that is, that they shall be made patricians and consuls; moreover, we decree that they shall be adorned with the other imperial dignities, and that, just as the imperial militia is adorned, so too the clergy of the holy Roman Church shall be adorned.

And a little later: The most blessed pope himself did not permit a crown of gold to be used upon the crown of clerical office which he wears, for the glory of blessed Peter. But we placed with our own hands upon his most sacred head the Phrygian cap, shining with white brightness and signifying the Lord’s resurrection; and, holding the bridle of his horse, we rendered him the service of a groom out of reverence for blessed Peter. We decree that all his successors shall use this same Phrygian cap in processions, as a special privilege, in imitation of our empire. Therefore, lest the pontifical dignity be debased but rather be adorned still more by the glorious power [variant: “glory and power”] than the dignity of earthly empire, behold: we transfer and leave to the most blessed pontiff, our father Sylvester, universal pope, our palace—as has been stated above—as well as the city of Rome and all the provinces, places, and cities of Italy and of the western regions; [Col. 0342D] and we decree, by this our divine sacred and pragmatic decree, that these shall be administered and shall remain granted to the right of the holy Roman Church, under the firm imperial sanction, to his power and dominion and to that of his successors as pontiffs [variant: “to the power and dominion of his successor pontiffs under firm imperial sanction”].

Therefore we considered it fitting that our empire and royal power should be transferred and moved to the eastern regions, and that in the province of Byzantium, in a most excellent place [variant: “in the excellent place of the province of Byzantium,” etc.], a city should be built in our name and our empire established there; because where the primacy of the priesthood and the head of the Christian religion have been established by the heavenly Emperor, [Col. 0343A] it is not just that an earthly emperor should hold power there.

## CHAPTER 50.—Concerning one who brings a forged letter allegedly from the Apostolic See. From the capitularies of Emperor Charlemagne (Council of Tribur, ch. 3).

(*Dist.* 19, c. *In memoriam*.) In memory of the blessed apostle Peter, let us honor the holy Roman and Apostolic See, so that, since it is the mother of our priestly dignity, it ought to be the teacher of ecclesiastical order. Therefore its humanity must be preserved with meekness; and although a yoke imposed by that holy see is scarcely bearable, let us bear it and endure it with devout devotion. But if—what is unfitting—anyone, whether priest or deacon, is convicted of having, by plotting some disturbance and laying snares for our ministry, [Col. 0343B] brought a forged letter from the Apostolic See, or anything else that did not come from there, then, with the faith preserved and humility toward the Apostolic See intact, the bishop shall have power to commit him to prison or some other custody, until he appeals by letter or through suitable envoys of his party to the Apostolic Majesty, so that it may deign, by its holy legation, to determine above all what the Roman law should justly prescribe concerning such persons, so that he may be corrected and restraint imposed upon the rest.

## CHAPTER 51.—The pact of the decree of Emperor Louis I with the Roman pontiffs.

(*Dist.* 63, c. *Ego Ludovicus*.) I, Louis, Emperor Augustus, establish and grant by this pact of our confirmation to you, blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, [Col. 0343C] and through you to your vicar, Lord Paschal, supreme pontiff, and to his successors in perpetuity, that you shall hold and administer, as you have held and administered from your predecessors until now, the city of Rome with its duchy, suburbs, and all its villages and territories, its mountainous and maritime shores and harbors, and all cities, castles, towns, and villages [Gratian reads *villis*, “estates”] in the regions of Tuscany.

Likewise: When, by divine calling, the pontiff of this most sacred see shall depart from this world, no man from our kingdom—whether Frank, Lombard, or of whatever people under our authority—shall have permission to come to Rome either publicly or privately, or to conduct an election; and no one shall presume, on that account, to do any harm in the cities or territories belonging to the authority of the Church of blessed Peter the apostle. Rather, the Romans shall be free, with all reverence and without any disturbance, to provide honorable burial for their pontiff and to consecrate canonically, without any doubt or opposition, the man whom all the Romans, by divine inspiration and the intercession of blessed Peter, shall elect with one counsel and agreement, without any promise, to the order of pontiff. And when he has been consecrated, envoys shall be sent to us or to our successors, the kings of the Franks, to join friendship, charity, and peace between us and him.

## CHAPTER 52.—The decree of the first Henry and the first Otto with the Roman pontiffs.

[Col. 0344A]

(*Dist.* 63, c. *Constitutum*.) We absolutely forbid any of our envoys, by contriving any pretext of hindrance whatsoever, to dare interfere in the election of the Roman pontiff. Likewise, in the same place: In elections of Roman pontiffs neither free person nor slave shall presume to intervene in order to create any impediment for those Romans whom ancient custom, through the ordinance of the holy Fathers, has admitted to this election. If anyone presumes to act against this our decree, let him be handed over to exile.

## CHAPTER 53.—In what cities primates or patriarchs are to be found. Pope Anacletus, in his second decretal.

[Col. 0344B] Provinces were for the most part divided long before the advent of Christ; and afterward this division was renewed by the apostles and by blessed Clement, our predecessor. And in the chief cities of provinces [variant: “it was renewed in the chief cities of provinces,” etc.], where in former times were the secular primates of law and the first judicial authority, to whom those living elsewhere would resort, when necessity required, if they could not or were not permitted to flee to the court of emperors or kings, because of their oppressions or injustices, and whom they appealed to whenever necessary, as was commanded [variant: “written”] in their law—in those same cities or places our divine and ecclesiastical laws ordered patriarchs or primates to be appointed and established, who hold one rank, [Col. 0344C] although their names differ, and to whom bishops might resort and appeal if necessary. They alone were to enjoy the title of primate, and not others.

The remaining metropolitan cities, which had lesser judges, although greater than counties [variant: “than counts”], were to have their own metropolitans, who should rightly obey the aforesaid primates, just as this had been ordered in secular laws. They were to enjoy not the name of primates, but that of metropolitans or archbishops. And although each metropolitan city has its own province and ought to have its own metropolitan bishop, just as previously it had metropolitan secular judges, nevertheless, as has been established, they were ordered to have primates both then and now, to whom, after the Apostolic See, the highest matters should come, so that there those in need might be relieved and justly restored, those unjustly oppressed might be justly reformed and supported, and the causes of bishops and judgments in the greatest affairs might be most justly concluded, while the authority of the Apostolic See remains unimpaired.

## CHAPTER 54.—Who are primates. Pope Anicetus to the bishops of Gaul.

(*Dist.* 99, c. *Nulli archiepiscopi*.) No archbishops are to be called primates except those who hold the chief cities, whose bishops the apostles and successors of the apostles regularly established as patriarchs and primates—unless some people should subsequently [Col. 0345A] be converted to the faith and, because of their multitude, it should be necessary to appoint a primate for them. The rest who have acquired other metropolitan sees are not to be called primates, but metropolitans.

(9, q. 3, c. *Si autem aliquis*.) But if any metropolitan should become puffed up and, without the presence or counsel of all the provincial bishops, wish to transact their causes or other causes—except only those concerning his own diocese—or to burden them, let him be strictly corrected by all, lest he dare presume such things in future. If he appears incorrigible and disobedient to them, his contumacy shall be reported to this Apostolic See, to which it has been commanded that the judgments of all bishops be referred for final determination, so that punishment may be inflicted upon him and the others may be afraid. But if, because of excessive distance, inconvenience of time, or hardship of travel, it is burdensome to bring his case to this Apostolic See, then the case shall be brought to his primate and judged by him with the authority of this holy see. Likewise, if any bishop considers his own metropolitan suspect, he shall be heard before the primate of the diocese or before this Apostolic See.

## CHAPTER 55.—That enemies cannot be accusers. Pope Nicholas to Emperor Michael (Epistle 2, or 8).

It pleased the holy synod of bishops that met at Constantinople that accusers should not be admitted without examination, and that not everyone should be commanded to bring accusations [Col. 0345C] against the stewards of churches. Let us come to the holy Synod of Chalcedon and hear what it relates to us concerning Athanasius, bishop of Perrha. This prelate, summoned three times to the synod and failing to appear, had been canonically condemned by his patriarch. Yet solely because, when he was summoned to the synod, he cried out that the person judging him was his enemy, he was reserved by the holy Synod of Chalcedon for examination of the charges brought against him; and it was judged that, unless he were again convicted, he should recover his own church.

If Athanasius, deposed by his patriarch, was sent back for a renewed judgment because he complained of his enmity, and it was ordered that his Church be restored to him unless manifest crimes stood against him, [Col. 0345D] how much more ought Ignatius—who was not judged by a patriarch, but was himself rather patriarch—not to have been stripped of his own Church by enemies and suspect judges pronouncing sentence? And although this was done, once the judgment of enemies had been annulled, he ought much more than Athanasius to have recovered his Church.

Let our most eloquent Pope Gelasius also come forward, the most vigorous assailant of heretics, and explain to us now what he said, according to his custom, about the bishops of Constantinople, then ill: “I ask,” he says, “where can the judgment they put forward be conducted? Before themselves, so that the same persons may be enemies, witnesses, and judges? But not even human affairs ought to be entrusted to such a judgment.” If human affairs ought not to be entrusted to a judgment in which the same persons are enemies and judges, [Col. 0346A] how much less divine—that is, ecclesiastical—matters? Let him who is wise understand.

Indeed, from this Justinian the emperor is known to have promulgated in his pious [variant: “pious”] laws: “Let a person who has [variant: “considers”] a judge suspect, before the suit begins, be permitted to reject him, so that recourse may be had to another. For it is in some way natural to avoid the snares of suspect judges and to wish to flee the judgment of enemies.” For this reason Saint John Chrysostom refused to enter the assembly of the council gathered against him (John Chrysostom, Epistle 19, ch. 2).

## CHAPTER 56.—On the right of primacies. Nicholas to Radulph, Archbishop of Bourges.

(9, q. 3, c. *Conquestus*.) Brother Sigebodus, Archbishop of Narbonne, complained to our Apostolic See [Col. 0346B] that you compel his clerics, against his will, to come to your judgment; and that, without consulting him, you dispose of matters belonging to his Church as though by a right of your patriarchate. Neither antiquity, to which the Fathers decreed reverence should be shown, recognizes this, nor does the authority of the holy canons permit it at all—unless perhaps they appeal to you as to their patriarch in causes that they cannot determine among themselves, or, if their bishop has died, they wish the property of their Church to be administered by your judgment.

For we determine that primates or patriarchs have no privilege above other bishops except insofar as the sacred canons grant it and ancient custom formerly bestowed it upon them; so that, according to the Nicene rules, the Churches may preserve their privileges, except where the Apostolic [Col. 0346C] See has decreed to honor some Church or its ruler by a particular privilege.

## CHAPTER 57.—That the pope is to be called bishop of the first see. From the African Council, chapter 5 (Third Council of Carthage, chapter 26).

(*Dist.* 99, c. *Primae sedis*.) The bishop of the first see shall not be called prince of priests, or supreme priest, or anything of that kind, but only bishop of the first see.

## CHAPTER 58.—That the order of priests is twofold. From the third letter of Pope Anacletus, sent to all bishops and other priests (chapter 1).

Brothers, the order of priests is twofold, and, as the Lord established it, it must not be disturbed by anyone. You know that the apostles were chosen and appointed by the Lord [Col. 0346D] and afterward dispersed through different provinces to preach. But when the harvest began to increase, seeing that the laborers were few, he commanded seventy disciples to be chosen to assist them (Luke 10). Bishops hold the place of the apostles, and presbyters likewise the place of the seventy disciples (*Dist.* 8, c. *Episcopi non in*).
