Bishops, however, ought not to be appointed in villages or small cities; rather, presbyters ought to be ordained and appointed by bishops in villages, small cities, and rural estates, each nevertheless in his own title. Beyond these two orders of priests, neither have any been bestowed on us by God nor did the apostles teach any.

## CHAPTER 59.—That bishops are to be ordained not from laymen, neophytes, bigamists, or husbands of widows, but from the blameless. From the decrees of Pope Leo I (Epistle 82, chapter 3).

[Col. 0347D]

[Col. 0347A] In cities whose pastors have died, the following rule shall be observed in appointing bishops: the man to be ordained, even if supported by testimony to a good life, shall not be a layman, not a neophyte, nor the husband of a second wife; but he shall be one who has or has had only one wife, and whom he married as a virgin. For the election of priests is so excellent that things not counted as blameworthy in other members of the Church are nevertheless held unlawful in them.

## CHAPTER 60.—That, when a bishop is being elected, if he has opponents, five bishops shall assemble to examine them. From the African Council, chapter 17 (also Third Council of Carthage, chapter 40).

It must also be decreed that, when we assemble to elect [Col. 0347B] a bishop, if any objection arises—since such things have happened among us—three bishops shall not presume to clear the man to be ordained; rather, one or two shall be summoned to make up the number stated above, if they can be obtained, in the same people for whom he is to be ordained, and the persons of the objectors shall first be examined [variant: “two or three … and in the same people for whom he is to be ordained, they shall be examined,” etc.]. Finally, the charges themselves shall also be considered. Once he has been cleared, only then shall he be ordained in public view. If this agrees with the judgment of your holiness, let it be confirmed by the response of your dignity. All the bishops said: “It is entirely agreeable.”

## CHAPTER 61.—That no one is to be ordained bishop against the will of clergy and people. From the decrees of Pope Celestine, chapter 18 (Epistle 2 to the bishops of Gaul, chapter 5).

[Col. 0347C]

(*Dist.* 61, c. *Nullus*.) Let no bishop be given to an unwilling people; the consent and desire of clergy, people, and order are to be sought. Let a man from one Church be chosen for another only if no worthy person can be found among the clergy of the city itself for which a bishop is to be ordained—an event we do not believe will occur. For the persons of that Church must first be rejected before persons from other Churches can rightly be preferred. Therefore let each person receive the fruit of his own service in the Church in which he has spent his life through every office. Let no one intrude upon another’s recompense in another Church, nor dare to claim for himself the reward due to another. Clerics must be free to object if they see themselves oppressed, and they must not fear to reject those whom they recognize as thrust upon them [Col. 0347D] by an indirect route; for, even if they have no claim to the reward of the episcopate, they ought at least to have free judgment concerning the person who is to govern them.

## CHAPTER 62.—That those who are to be ordained bishops must first be examined. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 1.

(*Dist.* 23, c. *Qui episcopus*.) The man to be ordained bishop shall first be examined: whether he is naturally prudent; teachable [variant: “capable of being taught”]; moderate in character; chaste in life; sober; always watchful over his own conduct; humble; approachable; merciful; learned; instructed in the law of the Lord; cautious in interpreting the Scriptures; and practiced in ecclesiastical doctrines. Above all, he shall affirm the articles of faith in plain words: namely, confessing Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be one God, and proclaiming the entire Godhead in the Trinity to be coessential, consubstantial, coeternal, and co-omnipotent; confessing each person in the Trinity [variant: “each and every person in the Trinity”] to be fully God, and all three persons to be one God; believing that the divine incarnation was effected not in the Father or the Holy Spirit, but only in the Son, so that he who in the divinity was the Son of God the Father should become, in humanity, the son of a human mother: true God from the Father, true human from the mother, possessing flesh from his mother’s womb and a rational human soul; both natures, human and divine, united in him; one person, one Son, one Christ, one Lord, [Col. 0348B] creator [variant: “of creatures”], author, ruler, and God of all things that exist, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit; who suffered a true suffering of flesh [variant: “a true suffering of flesh for our salvation”], died a true death of his body, rose by a true resurrection of his flesh and a true resumption of his soul, and in that nature will come to judge the living and the dead.

He shall also be asked whether he believes that one and the same God is the author of the New and Old Testaments—that is, of the Law, the Prophets, and the Apostles; whether the devil became evil not by creation but by his own choice. He shall also be asked whether he believes in the resurrection of this flesh which we bear, and not another; whether he believes that judgment is to come and that each person will receive either punishments or rewards for what he has done in the flesh [variant: “in this flesh”]; [Col. 0348C] whether he disapproves of marriage; whether he does not condemn second marriages; whether he does not censure the eating of flesh; whether he communes with penitents who have been reconciled; whether all sins are remitted in baptism, namely both original sin contracted and those sins voluntarily committed; and whether no one is saved outside the Catholic Church. When he has been examined and found fully instructed in all these things, then he shall be ordained bishop.

## CHAPTER 63.—That bishops are to be tested with the greatest care before they are ordained. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 7 [12].

That bishops shall be promoted to ecclesiastical authority by the judgment of the metropolitans and of the bishops in the surrounding area; namely those who have been tested for a very [Col. 0348D] long time both in the word of faith and in the example of upright conduct.

## CHAPTER 64.—That the people may not themselves make elections of priests. From the Council of Braga, chapter 1.

(*Dist.* 63, c. *Non licet*.) The people may not make by themselves the election of those to be advanced to the priesthood [variant: “promoted”]; rather, it must lie in the judgment of the bishops, so that they themselves, together with the person to be ordained, may determine whether he has been instructed in speech, faith, and spiritual life.

## CHAPTER 65.—That those are not to be regarded as bishops whom neither clergy nor people have elected, nor the bishops of the province consecrated. Leo, to Rusticus, Bishop of Narbonne, Epistle 90.

(*Dist.* 62, c. *Nulla ratio*.) No reasoning permits those to be counted among [Col. 0349A] bishops who have neither been elected by clergy, nor sought by the people, nor consecrated by the bishops of their province with the judgment of the metropolitan. Therefore, since a question often arises concerning an honor improperly received, who can doubt that what is not shown to have been conferred ought by no means to be granted to such men?

(1, q. 1, c. *Si qui clerici*.) But if any clerics have been ordained by these pseudo-bishops in Churches belonging to their proper bishops, and their ordination was performed with the consent and judgment of the presiding bishops, it may be held valid, provided that they remain in those same Churches. Otherwise, the consecration is to be considered void, because it is neither grounded in place nor secured by authority.

## CHAPTER 66.—That no bishop is to be ordained except by agreement. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 2.

[Col. 0349B] No bishop is to be ordained unless the clergy and parishioners have been summoned and are in agreement.

## CHAPTER 67.—That those who become proud after assuming rule are to be called dogs rather than princes. Origen.

Some, having taken charge of the Church and divine affairs, become puffed up and despise everyone with the arrogance of pride; these are called dogs rather than princes.

## CHAPTER 68.—Likewise, concerning proud bishops. From the sayings of Gregory and the apostle Paul.

A bishop ought to be humble, for he has received a rank of meekness, not of pride. Paul says: “Such a man ought to be meek, not exalted, not proud” (Titus 1).

## CHAPTER 69.—That the ordinations of bishops must be performed by all the bishops of the province on apostolic authority. From the second letter of Pope Anacletus, written to the bishops of Italy.

[Col. 0349C]

(*Dist.* 64, c. *Ordinationes*.) Ordinations of bishops are to be celebrated, by apostolic authority, by all those who are in the same province. When they assemble together, they shall conduct a careful examination and observe a fast with fitting prayers. Then, on the Lord’s Day at the third hour, praying and laying hands upon them together with the holy Gospels which they are to preach, and anointing their heads with sacred oil after the example of prophets and kings, according to the custom of the apostles and Moses—because all sanctification consists in the Holy Spirit, whose invisible power is mingled with holy chrism—they shall celebrate the solemn ordination by this rite. But if they cannot all assemble together, they shall nevertheless give their consent by prayers and writings, so as not to be absent in spirit from the ordination.

Furthermore, James, the first archbishop of the Jerusalemites, blessed James who was called Just and named the Lord’s brother according to the flesh, was ordained by the apostles Peter, James, and John. Thus they gave their successors a model: no one is ever to be ordained by fewer than three bishops, with all the rest giving assent, and ordination is to be celebrated with common consent.

## CHAPTER 70.—That a layman may not become bishop before the age of thirty, or before the completion of a year. From the Third Council of Arles, near the end of chapter 1.

No layman shall receive the honor of bishop or presbyter before the completion of a year or before thirty years of age.

## CHAPTER 71.—Concerning not rashly making laymen bishops. From the Council of Sardica, chapter 13.

(*Dist.* 61, c. *Osius episcopus*.) Bishop Hosius said: “I consider it necessary that you deliberate on this with the greatest care. If perhaps a wealthy man, a scholar from the forum, or one from public administration is requested as bishop, he shall not be ordained before he has discharged the office of reader and the duty of deacon or presbyter; and thus, passing through each rank, if he proves worthy, he may ascend to the summit of the episcopate. For by these promotions, which will everywhere require a lengthy period of time, he may be tested as to his faith, modesty, gravity, and self-restraint. And if he is found worthy, let him be adorned with the divine priesthood. For it is neither fitting, nor does reason or discipline permit, that a neophyte should rashly and lightly be ordained bishop, presbyter, or deacon—especially since the blessed Apostle, teacher of the Gentiles, appears to have warned and forbidden that this be done (1 Tim. 3)—but only those whose life has been examined over a long time and whose merits have been proved.”

## CHAPTER 72.—That one must arrive at the office of bishop through ecclesiastical ranks. From the decrees of Pope Celestine sent to the bishops of Gaul (Epistle 2 to the bishops of Gaul, chapter 3).

(*Dist.* 59, c. *Ordinatos*.) Most beloved brothers, we have learned that certain men have been ordained bishops who were not established in any ecclesiastical orders before reaching the summit [Col. 0350C] of so great a dignity, contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, by the usurpation of one who acknowledges having done these things. Yet one ought to attain the episcopate through those ranks which have most frequently been prescribed, so that persons initiated in lesser offices may be confirmed for greater ones. For whoever desires to be a teacher must first be a disciple, so that he may teach what he has learned. Every discipline of life confirms itself for the end at which it aims by this principle. A man who has not devoted himself to letters cannot be a teacher of letters. One who has not advanced through every stage of service cannot attain the rank merited by service. Is the priesthood alone, I ask, more worthless among these things, because it is more easily bestowed while more difficult to fulfill?

Likewise, on the same matter. From the Synod of Benevento under Pope Urban, chapter 1. (*Dist.* 60, c. *Nullus in episcopatum*.) [Col. 0350D] No one shall be chosen to the episcopate unless he is found to be living religiously in sacred orders. By sacred orders we mean the diaconate and presbyterate: for the primitive Church is read to have had these alone, and concerning these alone we have the apostle’s command (1 Tim. 3). We permit subdeacons also, since they serve at the altars and necessity requires it, but very rarely, and only if their religious life and learning have been tested; and this shall not be done without the permission of the Roman pontiff or the metropolitan.

## CHAPTER 73.—That one who has obtained the episcopate through ambition is not to receive even lay communion. From the Council of Sardica, chapter 2.

Bishop Hosius said: “Even if someone should be so rash as perhaps to offer this excuse, asserting that he received letters from the people, it is evident that rather many who lack sincere faith could have been corrupted by payment and reward, so that they might cry out in the Church and appear to request that he be made bishop. I judge that these frauds must be condemned altogether, so that such a man may not receive even lay communion at the end.” If it pleases you all, decree it. The synod replied: “It pleases us.”

## CHAPTER 74.—That he cannot be a bishop who has been consecrated without the knowledge of the metropolitan. From the Second Council of Arles, chapter 6.

Above all, this is clear: a man appointed bishop without the knowledge of the metropolitan ought not, according to the great synod, to be a bishop.

## CHAPTER 75.—That bishops may not obtain a position of rule through the Simoniacal heresy. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 43.

[Col. 0351B]

(1, q. 7, c. *Cavendum.*) Care must be taken, and taken with the utmost vigilance; and, by the power of Christ’s blood, bishops, kings, and all higher authorities, together with all supporters and electors of whatsoever kind, and all who consent to or ordain persons to ecclesiastical rank, must be forbidden that anyone obtain a position of rule through the Simoniac heresy—by any favour, cunning, promise, advantage, or gift, whether personally or through an intermediary. For among other teachings the Holy Spirit speaks through the mouth of Gregory (*Epistle* 110, Book VII): “Why is it not seen, why is it not considered, that a blessing is turned into a curse for him who is ordained in order that he may become a heretic?” [Col. 0351C]

Likewise: Whoever, out of consideration for his office, does not burn vehemently against this Simoniac and neophyte heresy, should not doubt that he has his portion with Simon Magus, who first committed this accursed crime.

And elsewhere (*Epistle* 51, or chapter 95, Book IV): Whoever strives to receive this for a price desires not to be a priest, but only vainly to be called one.

And elsewhere (*Epistle* 9): “Grieving,” he says, “I speak; groaning, I declare: because the priesthood, which has fallen among you inwardly, could not long remain standing outwardly.”

## CAP. 76.—Concerning those who have purchased sacred dignity for a price. From an epistle of Pope Gelasius (*Epistle* 9, chapter 26).

(1, q. 1, c. *Quos constiterit.*) Those who are established to have purchased sacred dignity for a price (Acts VIII), though unworthy of it, must, once convicted, be excluded; for the condemnation of Simon, as sacred Scripture testifies, enfolds alike the giver and the receiver. [Col. 0351D]

## CAP. 77.—On the same matter. From an epistle of Pope Hormisdas (chapter 25, chapter 2).

We therefore join this to the preceding matters: that the blessing through the laying on of hands, which is believed to come from God, may not be bought for a price; for Simon Magus, wishing to buy the Holy Spirit for a price, was struck by the condemnation of the apostle Peter.

## CAP. 78.—Likewise on the same matter. From the Canons of the Apostles, chapter 30 [29].

If any bishop, presbyter, abbot [deacon] obtains this dignity through money, let both he and his ordainer be deposed; and let him be cut off in every way from holy communion [Col. 0352A] and be anathema, like Simon Magus at Peter’s hands.

## CAP. 79.—No mercy is to be extended to Simoniacs. Nicholas the Younger, presiding over a synod in the church of Constantinople, said:

(1, q. 1, c. *Erga Simoniacos.*) We decree that no mercy is to be shown to Simoniacs in preserving their dignity; rather, in accordance with the sanctions of the canons and the decrees of the holy Fathers, we wholly condemn them and establish by apostolic authority that they are to be deposed.

Likewise: Henceforth, if anyone knowingly permits himself to be consecrated by one whom he does not doubt to be a Simoniac, both consecrator and consecrated shall undergo an equal sentence of condemnation. Both shall be deposed, shall do penance, and shall remain deprived of their own dignity.

## CAP. 80.—If a Roman pontiff has been intruded Simonically and without the consent of the cardinals, he is to be excommunicated by them and even expelled from the see by human judgment. Same source, chapter 2.

[Col. 0352B]

If anyone has been enthroned in the Apostolic See by money, human favour, popular or military tumult, without the unanimous and canonical election and blessing of the cardinal bishops and then of the following religious orders, he is to be regarded not as pope or apostolic, but as apostate. The cardinals and bishops, together with devout and God-fearing clergy and laity, may repel the invader from the Apostolic See, even by anathema and by human assistance and effort, and may set over it whomever they judge worthy.

But if they cannot accomplish this within the city, then by our authority, assembled outside [Col. 0352C] the city in whatever place pleases them, let them elect the person whom they discern to be worthier and more useful for the Apostolic See; and let authority be granted to him to govern and dispose matters for the benefit of the holy Roman Church, as seems best to him according to the circumstances of the time, as though he had already been fully enthroned.

## CAP. 81.—How those who have received orders Simonically are to be judged. From the decrees of Pope Gregory VII, chapter 11.

(1, q. 1, c. *Ordinationes.*) We judge to be false those ordinations which are effected through price, prayers, or service rendered to some person with that intention; or which are not made by the common consent of clergy and people according to canonical sanctions, and are not approved by those to whom consecration belongs. For those ordained in this manner do not enter through the door—that is, through Christ—but, as Truth himself testifies, are thieves and robbers (John X). [Col. 0352D]

## CAP. 82.—That the ordainers of Simoniacs are to be condemned together with them. From the Sixth Council of Toledo, chapter 4.

Whoever, as an imitator of Simon and thus a follower of the Simoniac heresy, seeks the ranks of ecclesiastical orders not by worthiness of character but by the expenditure of gifts, and obtains them through presents—though neither the order of reason nor any dignity of character commends him for this—such a person, if found out, must by no means be allowed to attain the heights of sacred orders. And if he has attained them, let him, deprived of communion, be condemned together with his ordainers by the loss of his own goods. [Col. 0353A]

## CAP. 83.—Those who have received offices Simonically from Simoniacs are, if clerics, to be punished by loss of rank; if laypersons, to be condemned by anathema. From the Eighth Council of Toledo, chapter 3.

(1, q. 1, c. *Reperiuntur.*) Whoever is discovered to have offered any reward in order to receive priestly dignity, let him know that from that time he is condemned to the reproach of anathema and excluded from participation in Christ’s body and blood, since he is known to have committed an abominable crime against Christ.

If there is someone who brings an accusation, let the person who gained that order through the giving of gifts be deprived of the rank of honour received and confined in a monastery under perpetual penance. Those, however, who have been receivers of gifts in this matter, if clerics, are to be punished by loss of rank; but if laypersons, are to be condemned by perpetual anathema. [Col. 0353B]

## CAP. 84.—What a bishop ought to vow when he is about to receive orders. From the Ninth Council of Toledo, chapter 10.

Everyone who is about to enter ecclesiastical ranks is not to receive consecration to office before he has promised, by the binding of his pledge, that, preserving the Catholic faith with the devotion of a sincere heart, he will live justly and piously; that in none of his actions will he oppose the canonical rules; and that in all things he will render due honour and reverent obedience to everyone set above him.

## CAP. 85.—No one may, without peril, demand a gift for conferring priestly rank, either before or afterward. From the Third Council of Braga, chapter 7.

[Col. 0353C]

(1, q. 1, c. *Qui per pecuniam.*) Whoever, for conferring upon anyone a priestly rank, has received either any gift whatsoever or a promise of a gift before he is ordained; or, after the person has been ordained, has presumed to be rewarded in any way on that account—whether giver or receiver—shall incur the peril of his rank, according to the judgment of the Council of Chalcedon (chapter 2).

## CAP. 86.—That one kind of simony is by service, another by hand, another by tongue. Gregory, in the collection of Forty Homilies, Homily 4.

(1, q. 1, c. *Sunt nonnulli.*) To sell doves is to give, not according to merit of life but for a reward, the laying on of hands by which the Holy Spirit is given. But [Col. 0353D] there are some who indeed take no monetary reward for ordination, yet bestow sacred orders for human favour, and seek from that bestowal only the recompense of praise. Certainly these do not freely give what they have freely received (Matthew X), because from the service rendered in holiness they seek the coin of favour.

Hence, when the prophet described a just man, he well said: “Who shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isaiah XXXIII). For he does not say, “Who shakes his hands free from a gift,” but adds, “from every.” For one gift is from service, another is from the hand, another from the tongue. A gift from service is undue subjection rendered; a gift from the hand is money; a gift from the tongue is favour. Therefore, the person who confers sacred orders then shakes his hands free from every gift [Col. 0354A] when, in divine matters, he seeks not only no money but also no human favour.

## CAP. 87.—Those sell doves who distribute the laying on of hands for a price. From the same homily.

We have learned that some among you perform ordinations for rewards, sell spiritual grace, and heap up temporal gain, at the cost of sin, from the iniquities of others. Why, then, does the Lord’s commanding utterance not return to your memory: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matthew X)? Why do you not recall before your mind’s eyes that, when our Redeemer entered the temple, he overturned the seats of those selling doves and poured out the money of the money-changers? [Col. 0354B] (Matthew XXI.)

For who are those today in God’s temple who sell doves (John II), if not those who receive a price in the Church for the laying on of hands, through which laying on the Holy Spirit is given from heaven? The dove, therefore, is sold because the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is received, is given for a price. But our Redeemer overturns the seats of those selling doves because he destroys the priesthood of such dealers. Hence the sacred canons condemn the Simoniac heresy and command that those who seek a price for conferring orders be deprived of the priesthood. Thus the seat of those selling doves is overturned when those who sell spiritual grace are deprived of the priesthood, whether before human eyes or before the eyes of God.

## CAP. 88.—On the same matter. Homily 39.

[Col. 0354C]

(1, q. 3, c. *Vendentes.*) Christ drives sellers and buyers out of the temple because he condemns both those who confer the laying on of hands for a gift and those who strive to buy the gift of God.

Likewise, in the same place: Those who sell in the temple are those who give for a reward what is rightfully due to certain persons. For to sell justice is to observe it in return for receiving a reward. Buyers in the temple, however, are those who refuse to render to a neighbour what is just, and who disdain to do what is legally owed; by giving a price [*praemio*, “reward”] to patrons, they purchase sin.

## CAP. 89.—Concerning a bishop ordained Simonically. Gregory to Maximinus [Maximus], presumptuous claimant of the Church of Salona (Register, Book V, Epistle 3).

[Col. 0354D] It has come to us that you were ordained through the Simoniac heresy; and many other things have here been said concerning you, of which one especially required us earnestly to forbid you by our letters to celebrate the solemnities of Mass.

## CAP. 90.—That a person worthy in life and character be chosen for sacred orders. Gregory to Brunhild, queen of the Franks (Register, Book VII, Epistle 5).

May the concern of your Christianity keep careful watch, so that you permit no one under your rule to approach sacred order through payment of money, through the patronage of any persons whatever, or by right of kinship; but let him be chosen for the office of bishopric or another sacred order whom life and character have shown to be worthy. [Col. 0355A]

## CAP. 91.—No one may buy sacred orders, nor may anyone pass suddenly from lay dress into the government of the Church. Gregory to Syagrius, Betherius, Virgilius, and Desiderius, fellow bishops (Register, Book VII, Epistle 3).

By God’s authority, we desire your fraternity to convene a synod; and that there, through the mediation of our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Aregius [Syagrius] and our most beloved son Cyriacus, abbot, all things contrary to the holy canons, as we have stated, be strictly condemned under the imposition of anathema: namely, that no one presume to give any advantage in order to obtain ecclesiastical orders, or to receive anything for advantages given; that no one from lay dress dare suddenly to arrive at a place of sacred government; and that no women live with priests except those permitted by the sacred canons. [Col. 0355B]

## CAP. 92.—Concerning the uprooting of Simoniac depravity. Gregory to Theuderic, king of the Franks (Register, Book IX, Epistle 53).

We urge you again, for the sake of your reward, to command that a synod be convened and, as we wrote previously, that bodily vices among priests and the depravity of the Simoniac heresy be condemned by the judgment of all bishops and cut away from the boundaries of your kingdom.

## CAP. 93.—On the same matter. Gregory to Brunhild, queen of the Franks (Register, Book IX, Epistle 57).

[Col. 0355C] Command a synod to be convened, and among the matters written above zealously forbid from your kingdom, by a conciliar decree, the sin of the Simoniac heresy.

## CAP. 94.—Likewise on the same matter. Gregory to Chlothar, king of the Franks (Register, Book IX, Epistle 55).

Because the Simoniac heresy, the first to arise in the Church, was condemned by the authority of the apostles, we ask that, for the sake of your reward, you cause a synod to be convened, so that, being suppressed and uprooted by the judgment of all priests, it may henceforth find no power there to endanger souls, nor be permitted to arise again under any pretext.

## CAP. 95.—A bishop ordained Simonically gave gold and lost his soul; but the ordainer received money and gave leprosy. Ambrose, in his *Pastoral* work (Book *On Priestly Dignity*, chapter 5).

(1, q. 1, c. *Cum ordinaretur.*) What the bishop gave when he was ordained was gold; and what he lost was his soul. When he ordained another, what he received was money; what he gave was leprosy. These are the dealings of the wicked unto their destruction.

Yet I question our brother and fellow bishop, since I too am a bishop and am speaking with a bishop. Tell me then, brother bishop, briefly: when you gave money, what did you receive?

“I received episcopal grace.”

Therefore I ask you: By what word is this grace called?

He replied: “Why do you ask?”

As I suppose, because what is given freely is for that reason called *grace* (*gratia*). Therefore, if grace is given freely and is not valued in gold, why is grace purchased by you with money?

He replied: “I should not have received it if money had not bought it; nor should I have been ordained bishop if I had not given money.”

Therefore, as is clear from your answers, you did not receive grace when you were ordained, because you did not obtain it freely. And so, brother, if you did not receive grace, how could you become a bishop? For the Lord also said to his disciples: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matthew X). Why then did you judge that you possessed freely given grace for a price? For, as I see, in giving gold you lost [your soul], and did not acquire holy grace. [Col. 0356A]

## CAP. 96.—On the same matter. Ambrose, Book I of *Offices* (*On Priestly Dignity*, chapter 5).

[Col. 0356B]

If you wish faithfully to question Simoniacs as to who made them priests, they will immediately answer and say: “I was recently ordained bishop by an archbishop, and I gave him a hundred solidi, so that I might deserve to obtain episcopal grace. If I had not given them, I should not be a bishop today. Therefore, my lord, I preferred to diminish [or: bring in; *invehere*] gold from the treasury, rather than lose so great [or: the whole; *totum*] a priesthood. I gave gold and bought a bishopric. Yet, if I live, I do not doubt that I shall immediately recover those solidi once more. I ordain a presbyter, consecrate a deacon, and receive gold. Indeed, I trust that I shall demand monetary profit from the other orders as well. Behold: I have recovered in my treasury the gold which I gave, and I received the bishopric for nothing.”

This, surely, is what grieves me: the archbishop made the bishop carnally; for on account of money he ordained him spiritually leprous. “May your money,” he says, “be with you unto destruction” (Acts VIII), because you purchased the gift of the grace of the Holy Spirit for a price and carried on a wretched commerce for the ruin of souls.

And ignorant and unlearned people cry out at their ordinations and say: “He is worthy; he is just.” But the wretched conscience says: “He is unworthy; he is unjust” [variant: “You are worthy, and you are just; but the wretched conscience says, You are unworthy, and you are unjust,” etc.]. For this [or: such a] bishop addresses the people, saying: “Peace be with you.” To carnal eyes he appears a great bishop; but to divine sight he is seen as a great leper. [Col. 0356C]

## CAP. 97.—Likewise on the same matter. Bede, in Book 70 of the Homilies (on John, chapter 2).

(1, q. 3, c. *Non solum.*) Not only are those sellers of doves and makers of God’s house into a house of trade who, in conferring sacred orders, seek a price in money, praise, or even honour; but so too are those who exercise, not with a simple intention but for the sake of some human recompense, a spiritual rank or grace in the Church which they received through the Lord’s generosity. This is contrary to the saying of the apostle Peter: “Whoever speaks, [let him speak] as the utterances of God; whoever ministers, [let him minister] as from the strength which God supplies, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ” (I Peter IV).

Therefore, all who are such, if they do not wish to be removed from the Church when the Lord comes, must remove these things from their actions, lest they make God’s house a house of trade. [Col. 0357A]

## CAP. 98.—In what places bishops, and in what places presbyters, ought to be established. Anacletus, in his third decretal to all bishops (above, chapter 58).

Bishops hold the place of the apostles, but presbyters that of the seventy-two disciples. Bishops ought not to be established in villages or in small cities; rather, presbyters ought to be ordained and appointed by bishops in villages, small cities, and rural settlements, each nevertheless in his own title-church. A bishop is to be ordained not by one bishop but by several; and, as has been said, he is not to be assigned and named for a small city, lest the name of bishop be cheapened, but for an honourable city. A presbyter, however, is to be set over whatever place belongs to the church established there. [Col. 0357B]

## CAP. 99.—That an archbishop’s judgment is invalid without the assent of fellow bishops. Pope Hyginus, eighth from the apostle Peter, in his first decretal to all bishops (chapter 2).

(9, q. 3, c. *Salvo.*) Without prejudice in all things to the privilege of the Roman Church, no metropolitan is to hear the causes of accused persons without the attendance of all the other bishops of the same province; for proceedings conducted otherwise than after examination in the presence of all of them shall be invalid, and he himself, if he does so, is to be restrained by his brethren.

(Chapter 2.) (2, q. 7, c. *Criminationes.*) Accusations against elders are not to be made through others, except by the very persons who bring the charges, provided that they themselves appear worthy and irreproachable, and demonstrate by public records that they are free from every suspicion and enmity, and lead an irreproachable faith and manner of life. [Col. 0357C]

## CAP. 100.—No metropolitan may presume to excommunicate a parishioner of another diocese, or take any action concerning him, without the counsel or judgment of his own bishop. Pope Calixtus, fifteenth from Peter, to Benedict, brother and fellow bishop (*Epistle* 2 to the bishops of Gaul, chapter 3).

(9, q. 3, c. *Nullus primas.*) No primate or metropolitan may presume to excommunicate or judge a diocesan church or parish, or anyone from its parish, or take any action concerning him, without its bishop’s counsel or judgment; but let him observe what has been established by the apostles, Fathers, and our predecessors, and confirmed by us.

## CAP. 101.—That what an archbishop does in another’s parish without his consent is invalid. The same, in the same place.

[Col. 0357D]

If any metropolitan bishop attempts to act outside matters belonging solely to his own parish, without the consent [or: counsel] and will of all the bishops of the same province, he shall be liable to the peril of his rank; and what he has done is to be held invalid and void. But if it is necessary to act or make arrangements concerning the cases of fellow-provincial bishops, their churches, clergy, or the needs of laypeople, this is to be done with the consent of all the bishops of the same province—not with any pomp of domination, [Col. 0358A] but with the humblest and harmonious administration, as the Lord says: “I came not to be served, but to serve” (Matthew XX); and elsewhere: “He who is greater among you shall be your servant” (Matthew XXIII), and the rest.

Likewise, the fellow-provincial bishops themselves are to act with his counsel, except insofar as matters concern their own parishes, in accordance with the ordinances of the holy Fathers, so that with one mind and one voice the holy Trinity may harmoniously be glorified for ever.

No primate, no metropolitan, nor any other bishop may enter another’s city or approach an estate which does not belong to him; nor may he make arrangements, ordain, or judge anything in another bishop’s parish regarding anyone’s [or: its] administration, unless summoned by the bishop whose jurisdiction it is known to be, if he wishes to retain the honour of his rank. [Col. 0358B] But if he presumes otherwise, he shall be condemned—not only he, but also those cooperating with and consenting to him—because, just as ordination, so also judgment and the disposition of other matters are forbidden to them [variant: “him”]. For how shall one who cannot ordain judge? Beyond all doubt, he neither shall nor can judge.

For just as another man’s wife may not be adulterated, judged, or disposed of by anyone except her own husband while he lives, so neither may a bishop’s wife—by which his Church or parish is undoubtedly understood—be judged or governed by another, without his judgment and consent, nor may another enjoy her intercourse, that is, her ordination [variant: “be judged by another’s judgment and will,” etc.].

## CAP. 102.—No one ought to attain the highest priesthood except through ecclesiastical grades. Zosimus, bishop of the city of Rome, to Hesychius, bishop of Salona, chapter 1 (*Epistle* 1, chapter 1).

[Col. 0358C]

(Distinctions 36 and 59, c. *Qui ecclesiast.*) This has been specifically forbidden both by our predecessors and lately by us in letters sent to Gaul and Spain, regions in which this presumption is more customary. Nor is Africa exempt from this admonition of ours, that no one whatsoever, contrary to the commands of the Fathers, may presume to aspire to the highest priesthood of the Church when he has not been trained in ecclesiastical discipline in due order and instructed in divine service through the testing of time. In such a case not only is his ambition to be regarded as ineffective, but his ordainers also are to lose that order which they believed themselves entitled to presume to confer contrary to the commands of the Fathers. [Col. 0358D]

## CAP. 103.—If a bishop seeks a greater see, he is to lose his own and not obtain the other. Leo to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica (*Epistle* 84, chapter 2).

If any bishop, despising the modest status of his own city, seeks the administration of a more celebrated place and transfers himself by any means [or: occasion] to a larger people, let him indeed be expelled from the foreign chair, but let him also lose his own; so that he presides neither over those whom he coveted through avarice nor over those whom he despised through pride. Therefore let each be content with his own bounds and not desire to be enlarged beyond the measure of his jurisdiction.

## CAP. 104.—No bishop may choose a successor for himself. Pope Hilary, presiding over a synod, said, chapter 3 (in the Roman Council).

[Col. 0359A]

Moreover, brothers, new and unheard-of seeds of perversity are continually springing up in certain places, as has reliably been reported to us in letters sent from Spain. Indeed, some believe the episcopate—which is given only upon preceding merits—to be not a divine gift but a hereditary possession; and they think that, just as perishable and mortal goods, so the priesthood can be bequeathed as though by legacy or testamentary right.

For many priests, when placed at death’s threshold, are said to substitute others into their own place by designating their names; plainly, so that a lawful election is not awaited, but the favour bestowed by the deceased is treated as the people’s assent. Consider [or: assess] how grave this is. Therefore, if it pleases you, let us remove this licence generally from the Churches. [Col. 0359B]

## CAP. 105.—Office is not to be seized through ambition or sedition, and hands are not to be laid upon a bishop until he has been carefully examined. Pope Leo to all bishops established throughout Africa (*Epistle* 87, chapter 1).

It was necessary that we express in letters now sent to you the grief of our heart, with which we burn on account of the dangers to the Lord’s flocks. We are astonished that among you, through the opportunity of an unsettled time, either the presumption of ambitious persons or popular tumult has prevailed so greatly that the pastoral eminence and governance of the Church have been entrusted to persons unworthy and situated far outside priestly merit.

This is not to provide for the people, but to harm them; not to supply government, but to increase danger. For the integrity of those who preside is the safety of those subject to them; and where obedience is sound, there the pattern of doctrine is healthy. Yet an office which sedition has extorted or ambition has seized, even if it gives no offence in character and conduct, is nevertheless harmful by the very example of its beginning; and it is difficult for things begun in an evil manner to be brought to a good conclusion. [Col. 0359C]

If in every rank of the Church it is necessary to take provident and intelligent care that in the house of God nothing be disorderly or inverted, how much more must labour be expended so that there be no error in the election of the person placed above all ranks? For the condition and order of the entire household of the Lord will waver if what is required in the body is not found in the head.

Where is that instruction uttered through the Spirit of God by the blessed apostle Paul, by which, in the person of Timothy, the whole body of Christ’s priests is taught, and through which each of us is accordingly told: “Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in the sins of others” (I Timothy V)? What is it to lay hands on someone hastily, except to confer priestly honour upon persons not proved—before the age of maturity, before the time of examination, before merit earned by labour, before experience in discipline? And what is it to share in the sins of others, except for the ordainer to become such a person as the one who did not deserve ordination?

For just as the person who follows [variant: “holds”] sound judgment in choosing a priest gains for himself the fruit of a good work, so he inflicts grave harm upon himself who raises an unworthy person to fellowship in his own dignity. [Col. 0360A] For what is contained in general enactments must not be disregarded in anyone’s case; nor is that honour to be regarded as lawful which has been conferred contrary to the commands of divine law.

(A little later.) The venerable enactments of the blessed Fathers rightly judged, when speaking of the election of priests, that only those were fit for sacred administrations whose whole life, from the beginnings of childhood up to more mature years, had passed through the service of ecclesiastical discipline, so that a prior life might bear witness for each person. Nor can there be doubt concerning the promotion of one to whom, for much labour, chaste character, and vigorous actions, the reward of a higher place is due.

For if it is unworthy to attain worldly honours without the endorsement of time and without merit earned by labour, and those whom proofs of uprightness do not support are customarily marked as ambitious, how diligent and prudent must be the dispensing of divine gifts and heavenly dignities, lest apostolic and canonical decrees be violated in anything, and the Lord’s Church be entrusted to the governance of persons ignorant of lawful institutions and wholly unacquainted with humility—persons who wish to receive [variant: “have”] their beginning not from the lowest ranks by gradual advancement, but from the highest—when it is exceedingly unjust and absurd for the inexperienced to be preferred to masters, the new to the ancient, and the untrained to the tried. [Col. 0360B]

## CAP. 106.—The enactments of the holy Fathers are not to be neglected in ordaining bishops. From the preceding letter to the bishops of Africa (chapter 2).

[Col. 0360C]

It remains, brothers, that with united [variant: “harmonious obedience”] hearts you receive these salutary exhortations; that, doing nothing through contention but being of one mind in every zeal of devotion, you obey divine and apostolic ordinances; and that you permit the most provident decrees of the canons to be violated in no respect.

Those regulations which we have relaxed because of the consideration of particular cases are henceforth to be observed according to the ancient rules, lest what we have granted temporarily through pious leniency be punished afterward with just retribution. We shall be moved especially and more sternly against those who neglect the enactments of the holy Fathers in ordaining bishops and consecrate those whom they ought to reject.

## CAP. 107.—Those who ordain unworthy persons ought to lose the right of consecrating. Same source (the same chapter).

[Col. 0360D]

Therefore bishops who consecrate as priest a man whom it is unlawful for them to consecrate, even if in some way they escape loss of their own honour, shall nevertheless no longer possess the right of ordination; nor shall they ever take part in that sacrament which, disregarding the divine judgment, they conferred upon one unworthy.

We also will that, among all the statutes of the canons, the following concerning priestly dignity be observed: bishops are not to be consecrated in every place, nor in every village, nor where bishops have not previously existed. Where populations and congregations are smaller, the care of presbyters suffices. Episcopal government, however, ought to preside only over larger populations and more populous cities, [Col. 0361A] lest priestly eminence be granted to hamlets, estates, or obscure and isolated townships—something forbidden by the divinely inspired decrees of the holy Fathers.

## CAP. 108.—Concerning the eradication of the Simoniac heresy, and concerning not ordaining someone out of favour to another. Gregory to all bishops established throughout the province of Hellas (Register, Book IV, Epistle 56).

(1, q. 1, c. *Quibusdam.*) From the reports of certain persons I have learned that in those regions no one attains sacred order without giving an advantage. If this is so, I say it weeping and declare it groaning: because when the priestly order has fallen inwardly, it cannot long remain standing outwardly either.

For we know from the Gospel what our Redeemer himself did: entering the temple, he overturned the seats of those selling doves [Col. 0361B] (Matthew XXI). To sell doves is to receive a temporal advantage from the Holy Spirit, whom God Almighty, consubstantial [with himself], bestows upon human beings through the laying on of hands.

From this evil, as I have said, it is already indicated that those who presumed to sell doves in God’s temple had their seats fall by God’s judgment. This error is indeed propagated among subjects with increase, for a man who comes to sacred order through rewards, already corrupted at the very root of his promotion, is more ready to sell to others what he bought.

And where is what is written: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matthew X)? And since the Simoniac heresy was the first to arise against the holy Church, why is it not considered, why is it not seen, that one who ordains another for a price acts, by promoting him, so that he becomes a heretic? [Col. 0361C]

Therefore we exhort you that none of you henceforth permit this to be done. Nor may anyone dare promote persons to sacred orders through another’s favour or supplication, unless the quality of their life and conduct has shown them worthy of it. For if we learn that it has again been done otherwise, know that it shall be restrained by strict canonical punishment.

## CAP. 109.—Nothing is to be received for ordination, a pallium, or documents. From the same author as above.

Following the ancient rule of the Fathers, I establish that nothing whatsoever is to be received for ordinations, whether for the giving of the pallium, the delivery of documents, or the exaction called *pastellum*, a new contrivance devised by ambition.

For when a bishop is ordained, the pontiff lays on his hand; a minister reads the Gospel lesson; and a notary writes the letter of confirmation. Therefore, just as it does not befit the bishop to sell the hand he lays upon the ordinand, so the minister or notary ought not to sell his voice or pen in that ordination.

Accordingly, I forbid the person to be ordained, or the person already ordained, to give anything for ordination, the pallium, documents, or *pastellum*. If anyone should presume to demand or request some advantage under the name of any of the aforesaid things, he shall be liable to guilt at the strict judgment of almighty God.

But if the person ordained, not by agreement and not because he has been compelled or solicited, wishes after receiving the documents and pallium to offer something to any member of the clergy merely as a token of favour, we by no means forbid its acceptance, because his offering bears no stain of guilt when it has not arisen from the importunate solicitation of another. [Col. 0362A]

## CAP. 110.—On the same matter. Gregory to Theuderic and Theudebert, kings of the Franks (Register, Book VII, Epistle 116).

Therefore, that you may be able to offer a great gift to almighty God, command a synod to be convened in which, as we have directed our fellow bishops, in the presence of our most beloved son Cyriacus, abbot, it must be established under the bond of anathema that no one is ever to give or receive anything for an ecclesiastical order.

## CAP. 111.—That no act of a Simoniac has validity, and that he provokes rather than appeases God’s wrath upon the people. Same source, shortly after the beginning.

(1, q. 1, c. *Fertur Simoniaca.*) It is reported that the Simoniacal heresy [Col. 0362B]—which first crept into God’s Church through diabolical deception, and was struck down and condemned at its very birth by the zeal of apostolic vengeance—holds sway within the bounds of your kingdom, although in a priest faith must be chosen together with life. For if life is lacking, faith has no merit, as blessed James testifies when he says: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2). For what works can a priest possess when he is proved to have obtained the honors of so great a sacrament by payment? And a little later: Thus a deadly wound is inflicted not only upon the soul of the ordainer and of the ordained, but your Highness’s kingdom is also grievously burdened by the fault of your bishops—by whose intercessions it ought rather to have been helped. For if he is judged worthy of the priesthood who is supported not by the merits of his conduct but by an abundance of payments, it follows that neither seriousness nor diligence counts for anything in ecclesiastical offices, but the profane love of gold obtains everything. And while honor rewards vices, perhaps the very man who ought to have been punished is introduced in the place of an avenger; thus priests are judged not to advance, but rather to perish. For when the shepherd has been wounded, who will apply medicine to the sheep needing treatment? Or when will he protect the people with the shield of prayer who has exposed himself to be struck by the missiles of enemies? Or what fruit will he produce whose root is infected by a grievous plague? Therefore perhaps a greater calamity is to be feared in those places where such intercessors are brought into positions of rule—men who provoke God’s wrath, whereas they themselves ought to have appeased it for the peoples.

## CHAPTER 112.—Likewise concerning Simoniacs. Gregory to Etherius [Betherius], Siagrius, Virgilius, and Desiderius, bishops of Gaul (Register, book VII, epistle 110)

[Col. 0362D]

When no heed is given to the divine saying [command], “Freely you received; freely give” (Matt. 10), the result is that the contagion of the offence grows and is doubled in one and the same matter: namely, in the buyer and the seller. And since it is clear that this heresy, with its pestilential root, crept in before all others and was condemned at its very origin by apostolic detestation, why is it not considered, why is it not guarded against, that his blessing is turned into a curse, because he is promoted precisely in order to become a heretic?

Likewise, in the same place: Nor should that be counted as almsgiving, if what has been received [Col. 0363A] from unlawful sources is distributed to the poor; for he who wickedly receives with the intention of distributing well is burdened rather than helped.

## CHAPTER 113.—That no bishop is to be ordained without the metropolitan’s consent. Innocent to Victricius, bishop of Rouen (epistle 2, chapter 1)

First, no one may dare to ordain a bishop without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop. For a judgment confirmed by the opinions of many is sound. Nor may one bishop presume to ordain a bishop, lest the benefit conferred seem clandestine. For the Synod of Nicaea also established and decreed this.

## CHAPTER 114.—On the same matter. Pope Hilary to Ascanio and the other bishops of the province of Tarragona (chapter 4)

We wish this first of all to be observed according to the rules of those same Fathers: that no bishop be consecrated in any way without the knowledge and consent of our brother Ascanio; for this was maintained by the ancient order, and this was defined by the authority of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers. Whoever stretches out hostile hands against it acknowledges himself unworthy of fellowship with those whose commands he has opposed.

## CHAPTER 115.—That all Simoniacs are to be removed from order and dignity. Leo IV to the bishops of Britain (epistle 2, chapter 1)

(1, q. 7, c. *Requiritis de his.*) You ask concerning those who do not fear to sell doves in the temple of the Lord for most shameful gain, joining their evil deeds to the heresy of Simon by reckless presumption: whether they may perform penance while remaining in their order, or only outside [Col. 0363C] their order and priestly rank. In the case of those convicted and known to have committed so detestable a crime—already condemned by many councils—we cannot offer the aid of any penance, nor oppose so many spiritual Fathers. Let it be certain to all that I concur in the judgment of those Fathers.

## CHAPTER 116.—How, or by how many witnesses, a bishop is to be condemned. The same

(2, q. 4, c. *Nullam damnationem.*) We judge that there can never be any condemnation of bishops except either before the lawful number of bishops, which is twelve bishops, or by a proved verdict through seventy-two suitable witnesses—men qualified both to accuse and first to take an oath upon Christ’s four holy Gospels that they will utter nothing false—as blessed Sylvester handed down to us and as the holy Roman Church appears to maintain. And if among the persons whom they declare ought to be condemned there is a bishop who has requested that his case be heard in the presence of the bishop of the Roman see, no one may presume to pronounce a final sentence upon him; rather, we decree that he be heard in every respect.

## CHAPTER 117.—How bishops ought to be ordained. From the Council of Nicaea, chapter 4

A bishop ought, if possible, to be ordained by all the bishops in his province. But if this is difficult because of pressing necessity or the length of the journey, at least three bishops must assemble [Col. 0364A] together, holding by letters also the consent of the others who are absent; and thus they shall carry out the ordination. Authority, however, or confirmation, belongs in each province to the metropolitan bishop.

## CHAPTER 118.—To what penalty a bishop or any cleric is subject if ordained for money or promoted to any honors. From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 2

(1, q. 1, c. 1. *Si quis episcopus.*) If any bishop performs an ordination after receiving money, and reduces to a price the grace which cannot be priced, and ordains for money a bishop, chorepiscopus, presbyter, deacon, or anyone else numbered among the clergy; or if, after receiving money, he appoints an *oeconomus*, that is, a defender, or a *paramonarius* [church warden or guardian]: whoever has devised this, if convicted, shall suffer loss of his rank. And the person so ordained shall gain no benefit from such shameful trafficking and appointment, but shall be deprived both of the dignity and of the office into which he entered through money. Moreover, he who acted as an intermediary in so shameful and unlawful a matter, if he is a cleric, shall fall from his own rank; but if he is a layman or monk, let him be anathematized.

## CHAPTER 119.—What is to be done concerning a bishop who has obtained a church through secular power. From the Canons of the Apostles, chapter 31

(18, q. 7, c. *Si quis episcopus.*) If any bishop, using secular powers, obtains a church through them, let him be deposed, and let all who communicate with him be separated.

## CHAPTER 120.—On the same matter. The Seventh Synod, chapter 3

(Dist. 63, chapter *Omnis electio.*) Every election of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon made by rulers is to remain void, according to the canon which says: “If any bishop, using secular powers, obtains a church through them, let him be deposed, and let all who communicate with him be separated.”

## CHAPTER 121.—Concerning one who gave or received the laying-on of hands for money. The Seventh Synod, chapter 20

Every bishop, presbyter, or deacon convicted of having given or received the laying-on of hands for money shall fall from priesthood and rank. Yet some perhaps say: “We do penance for sin, and God forgives it.” It is so: for God receives all who do penance and through penance forgives all sins that have been committed.

Likewise. (1, q. 1, c. *Qui per pecunias.*) Whoever consecrates anyone for money, or is consecrated for money, is excluded from the priesthood.

## CHAPTER 122.—That no ruler or lay power should forcibly intrude into the election of bishops, and what is to be done concerning them if they do so. The Eighth Synod, chapter 11

In agreement with the earlier councils, this holy and universal synod has defined, established, and lawfully promulgated that the promotions and consecrations of bishops are to take place by the election and decree of the clergy and by the college of bishops; and that none of the lay rulers or powerful persons is to insert himself [intrude himself] into the election or promotion [Col. 0365A] of a patriarch, metropolitan, or any bishop, lest disorderly and unsuitable contention or confusion thereby arise—especially since no person in authority, or any other layman, ought to possess any power in such matters. Rather, they should remain silent and attend to themselves until the election of the future pontiff regularly receives its conclusion from the college of the Church. But if any layman is invited by the Church to take part and cooperate, he may, if he wishes, comply respectfully with those who have invited him. For in this manner the Church regularly promotes for its own salvation a worthy shepherd. But whoever among secular rulers, powerful persons, or laymen of any other rank attempts to act against the common, harmonious, and canonical election of the ecclesiastical order, let him be anathematized until he obeys and consents to what the Church shows that it wishes concerning the election and ordination of its own prelate.

## CHAPTER 123.—On the same matter. Canons enacted at Paris under King Louis

(Council of Paris I, chapter 8.) Because ancient custom is neglected in some places and the decrees of the canons are violated, it has seemed good that, in accordance with ancient custom, the decrees of the canons be observed. Let no bishop be ordained against the will of the citizens, except one whom the election of the people and clergy has sought with full consent. Let no one be imposed by the command of a ruler or under any pretext, against the will of the metropolitan city or the bishops of the province. But if anyone, with excessive rashness, presumes by royal ordination to seize the summit of this honor, he shall in no way deserve to be received by the bishops of that place’s province, who recognize him as unlawfully ordained. If any bishop of the province presumes to receive him contrary to these prohibitions, let him be separated from all his brethren and removed from the charity of them all. With regard to former ordinations of pontiffs, it is agreed that the metropolitan [metropolitan see] with the bishops of his province, or such neighboring bishops as he may choose, shall, in the place where they assemble, decide [be decided] everything by common counsel and judgment, according to the ancient statutes of the canons.

## CHAPTER 124.—How bishops are to be consecrated. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 2

(Dist. 23, c. *Episcopus cum.*) When a bishop is ordained, let two bishops place and hold the book of the Gospels over his head and neck; and, while one pours the blessing upon him, let all the other bishops present touch his head with their hands.

## CHAPTER 125.—That a bishop or cleric is not to be transferred to another place. From the same council, chapter 27

(7, q. 1, c. *Episcopus de loco.*) A bishop is not to pass through ambition from an insignificant see to a distinguished one, nor is any cleric of lower order to do so. If, however, the advantage of the Church demands that this be done, let him be transferred in the presence of the synod, after a decree on his behalf has been submitted by clergy and laity to the bishops, and after another bishop has nevertheless been substituted in his place. Priests of lower rank, however, or other clerics, may move to other churches with the permission of their own bishops.

## CHAPTER 126.—That no payment be received for divine sacraments. From the Eleventh Council of Toledo, chapter 8

(1, q. 1, c. *Quidquid invisibilis.*) Whatever is bestowed by the conferral of invisible grace must never at all be sold for gain or for any payments, as the Lord says: “Freely you received; freely give” (Matt. 10). Therefore, whoever hereafter is established in ecclesiastical order and receives any price or payment, other than an offering voluntarily made, for baptizing and confirming the faithful, for administering chrism, or for promotions through the ranks, on account of such an offering [ambition]—if, with the knowledge [Col. 0366B] of the bishop of the place, any such act is committed by subordinates, that bishop shall be subject to excommunication for two months, because he kept silent while knowing of evil and did not apply the necessary correction. But if one of his subordinates, without his knowledge, considers himself entitled to receive anything under any of the aforesaid heads, then, if he is a presbyter, he shall be punished by three months’ excommunication; if a deacon, by two; while a subdeacon or cleric serving these avaricious desires is to be punished with an appropriate penalty and the due excommunication.

## CHAPTER 127.—By what sentence those are to be punished who are Simoniacally elected to a bishopric, or who, once elected, are Simoniacally ordained. From the same council, chapter 9

Many judgments of the Fathers have been issued on this point: namely, that no one should judge the inestimable grace of the Holy Spirit purchasable by gifts or presents. Yet—what cannot be said without great sorrow—the more frequently this has been forbidden by the command of decrees, the more it is known to have been repeated among us by fraud. For those who strive to purchase grace at such a price either anticipate the time of their ordination by a gift, or, after receiving the honor, render to their agents the shameful gain promised as payment. Therefore, so that henceforth the occasion for these and similar devices may be cut off, this holy synod has decreed that, when anyone comes before the Lord’s altar to receive the summit of pontifical office, he shall be bound by a declaration that he has neither given any payment of any kind to any person for the bestowal of the consecration of that honor, nor will ever endeavor to give one in the future. Thus he shall either receive the consecration of pre-eminence free from this contagion, or, if this crime is publicly disclosed and he is plainly exposed, he shall not come before the Church to the honor which he sought to purchase.

Nevertheless, those who hereafter are found to have been ordained after their promotion through payment, we judge must be separated from the Church as true Simoniacs under the prescribed laws of penance: that is, exiled for a period of two years and restrained by worthy satisfaction or by a sentence of excommunication, they should strive with tears to regain and restore the rank of honor which they purchased with payments. Thus, if worthy satisfaction finds them during the time of penance, they are to be restored, once the appointed penance has been completed, not only to communion [“commended, after the appointed period of penance has elapsed, not only,” etc.], [Col. 0367A] but also to the place and to all the functions of the order from which they had been separated.

## CHAPTER 128.—That a bishop is not to ordain anyone for money. From the Second Council of Braga, chapter 3

(1, q. 1, c. *Placuit ut de.*) It has seemed good that bishops receive no gifts for the ordination of clerics, but, as it is written: “What they have received freely by God’s gift, let them give freely” (Matt. 10). Let grace and the laying-on of hands not be sold for any price, because the ancient definition of the Fathers decreed thus concerning ecclesiastical ordinations: “Let the giver and receiver be anathematized.” For many persons, at times burdened with many crimes and unworthy ministers at the holy altar, obtain office not through the testimony of good deeds but through lavish gifts. Therefore clerics ought to be ordained not through the favor of gifts, but first through diligent examination and then through the testimony of many.

## CHAPTER 129.—That a bishop is not to be made through payment or the patronage of persons. Gregory to Antony, subdeacon, Register, book II, epistle 22, or chapter 61

(8, q. 2, c. *Illud quidem.*) Above all, let it be your concern that in this election no bestowal of payments intervene in any manner, nor the patronage of any persons prevail. For if anyone is elected through the patronage of certain persons, then, once ordained, reverence requires him to obey their wishes; and thus both the possessions of that church are diminished and ecclesiastical order is not observed. Therefore, with you urging [admonishing], they ought to choose a person who serves no unsuitable will, but who, adorned with life and character, may be found worthy of so great an order.

## CHAPTER 130.—That in the election of a bishop no one should seek private advantage but the common good. The same to the clergy of Milan (epistle 29, or chapter 68)

(8, q. 2, c. *Dilectissimi.*) Most beloved sons, admonished by the discipline of our office, we urge that, in the matter of receiving a bishop, none of you, neglecting the common advantage, should pursue his own profit. For if anyone seeks private gain, he is deceived by a vain estimation, because a mind bound by covetousness does not examine by free judgment the person to be set over it. Therefore, considering what benefits all, always render most complete obedience in all things to him whom divine grace has set over you. For one who has once been placed over you ought no longer to be judged by you; but he must now be judged with so much greater care, because afterward he is not to be judged.

## CHAPTER 131.—What “neophyte” meant in the primitive Church, and what it means now. The same to Virgilius, bishop of Arles (Register, book IV, epistle 50)

(Dist. 48, c. *Sicut.*) Since the apostle Paul forbids a neophyte to come to sacred orders (1 Tim. 3), we must understand that, just as then a neophyte was called one newly planted in the faith, so now we count among neophytes one who is still new in holy conduct. We know, moreover, that walls which have been built do not receive the weight of beams before they have dried from the moisture of their newness, lest, if they receive loads before being made firm, they bring the entire structure down to the ground.

## CHAPTER 132.—That the guilt of a sold mystery is inexpiable. Ambrose (book IV, on Luke chapter 4, under the heading: “On confirmation of the same point, by the example of Elisha and Naaman”)

“You have received money, and you shall possess from it a field, vineyards, olive groves, flocks; and Naaman’s leprosy shall cleave to you [Col. 0368A] and to your seed for ever” (4 Kgs. 5). You see that, because of the deed of the originator, the succession of the heir is condemned. For the guilt of a sold mystery is inexpiable, and the vengeance of heavenly grace passes to descendants (Deut. 23). Thus the Moabites and others shall not enter the Church of God until the third and fourth generation—namely, as we may interpret it more simply, until the succession of many generations had abolished the guilt of the originators.

But since those who sinned against God through the error of idolatry appear to be punished to the fourth generation, the sentence by which Gehazi’s offspring is condemned forever by prophetic authority for covetousness of possession certainly seems harsher—especially since our Lord Jesus Christ has granted to all the forgiveness of sins through the washing of regeneration—unless you understand “seed” to mean the seed of vices rather than of lineage. For just as those who are children of promise are reckoned as good seed, so also those who are children of error are reckoned as evil seed. For the Jews too are from their father the devil (John 8), certainly not by succession of flesh but by crime. Therefore all covetous persons, all the avaricious, possess Gehazi’s leprosy together with his riches; and by their ill-gotten reward they have amassed not so much an inheritance of possessions as a treasury of crimes, with eternal punishment and brief fruit.

## CHAPTER 133.—That the crime of ambition alone is to be condemned most severely. Gregory to Maximus [Maximianus], usurper at Salona, chapter 20

(Register, book III, epistle or chapter 20.) Although the other merits of anyone’s life may be such that there is nothing in them capable of opposing his priestly ordination, nevertheless the crime of ambition alone is condemned by the most severe rigor of the canons.

## CHAPTER 134.—That no consecration is to be celebrated by excommunicated persons. The same, in the same chapter

We have learned [We learned], therefore, that by a forged [or fraudulently procured] or simulated order of the most pious rulers, although you were unworthy in life, you rushed headlong into the order of priesthood, venerable to all. We believe this without any hesitation, first because your life and age are not unknown to us, and then because we know the mind of our most serene lord the emperor: that he is not accustomed to involve himself in priestly matters, lest he be burdened in any respect by our sins. An unheard-of crime is added: after our prohibition, issued under excommunication against you and those who ordained you, you are said to have been brought forth into the midst by military force, after presbyters, deacons, and the rest of the clergy had been beaten. We can in no way call this act a consecration, because it was celebrated by excommunicated persons. Therefore, since you have violated, without any precedent [Col. 0369A] whatever, so great and such a dignity of priesthood, you and your ordainers are in no way to presume to perform anything of priestly office, nor to approach the service of the sacred altar, until we learn from the letters of our lord or of our representative that you were ordained not by a fraudulent but by a true command.

## CHAPTER 135.—That episcopal ordinations ought not be delayed long. From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 25

(Dist. 75, c. *Quoniam quidam.*) Since certain metropolitans, as we have learned [as has been reported to us], neglect the flocks entrusted to them and delay in performing episcopal ordinations, the holy synod has decreed that episcopal ordinations be celebrated within three months, unless some inexcusable necessity compels the period of delay to be extended [prolonged]. If this is not done, the metropolitan shall be subject to ecclesiastical correction. Nevertheless, the revenues of the vacant church are to be kept intact by the *oeconomus* of that church.

## CHAPTER 136.—That an archbishop must receive his pallium from the apostolic see within three months or lose his dignity. From the decrees of Pope Pelagius, chapter 1

(Dist. 100, c. *Quoniam quidam.*) Since certain metropolitans, refusing to set forth their faith to the holy apostolic see according to ancient custom, neither seek nor receive the use of the pallium, and consequently the consecration of bishops for vacant churches is delayed not without danger, it has seemed good that any metropolitan who, within three months of his consecration, has not sent to the apostolic see to set forth his faith and receive the pallium shall lose the dignity entrusted to him. Other metropolitans shall, after a second and third admonition, have leave, with the counsel of the Roman pontiff, to aid vacant churches by ordaining a bishop.

But if the vacancy of a church continues for more than three months through the negligence of the bishop who is to be consecrated, he shall be deprived of communion until he either withdraws from the post or no longer delays in presenting himself for consecration. If through his own negligence he keeps the church vacant for more than five months, he shall receive the gift of consecration neither there nor anywhere else; indeed, he shall withdraw at the judgment of his metropolitan.

## CHAPTER 137.—How a person ought to be ordained by the bishops of neighboring provinces. From the Council of Sardica, chapter 5

[Col. 0369D]

Bishop Hosius said: If it happens that, in a province in which there are many bishops, all the others are occupied with necessary affairs and one bishop happens to remain outside the province, and the people assemble, the bishops of a neighboring province ought first to approach the bishop residing in that province and show him that the people are asking for a ruler and that it is right for them also to come and ordain a bishop with him. But if, when approached by letters, he remains silent and neglects the matter, giving no reply, then the bishops from the neighboring province are to come and ordain a bishop, in order that the people may be satisfied.

## CHAPTER 138.—That a bishop is not to be consecrated without three bishops. From the Second Council of Arles, chapter 5

[Col. 0370A]

No bishop may presume to ordain a bishop without the metropolitan’s permission; nor may a metropolitan do so without three bishops of the province. The other bishops of the province are to be notified, so that by their reply they may indicate that they consent. If there is any doubt between the parties, the metropolitan is to agree with the greater number in the election.

## CHAPTER 139.—On the same matter; and that, if possible, an archbishop is to be ordained by all the bishops of his province. From an epistle of Pope Anicetus sent to the churches of Gaul

Concerning episcopal ordinations, about which you wished to consult us, we have found certain decrees already set down in writing long ago by our predecessor Anacletus (epistle 2) [The *Volume of Councils* reads: “Long ago, in the ordinations of our holy predecessor Anacletus, certain [matters] already …”]. For we know that the most blessed James, called the Just and also called the Lord’s brother according to the flesh, was ordained bishop at Jerusalem by the apostles Peter, James, and John. But if so great a man was ordained by no fewer than three apostles, it is clearly evident that they handed down, by the Lord’s institution, the rule that a bishop must be ordained by no fewer than three bishops. Yet as the number of bishops has increased, more ought also to be added unless necessity intervenes.

But if an archbishop dies and another archbishop is to be ordained, all bishops of the same province are to come to the metropolitan see, so that he may be elected and ordained by all the bishops. For he who ought to preside over all of them must be elected and ordained by all of them. The remaining bishops of the province, if necessary and with the consent of the others, may be consecrated by three bishops at the command of the archbishop. But it is better if he himself, together with all, chooses one who is worthy, and they all together consecrate the bishop [bishops]. Although this has been permitted when necessity compels, what has been stated and commanded concerning the consecration of an archbishop—namely, that all the suffragans are to ordain him—may in no way be altered. For he who presides over them must be appointed by all the bishops over whom he presides. If otherwise has been presumed, there is no doubt that it lacks force, because his ordination, performed otherwise, will be invalid.

## CHAPTER 140.—Concerning a bishop who forcibly ordained another bishop. From an epistle of Pope Simplicius sent to John, bishop of Ravenna

[Col. 0370D]

If you had given any regard to the norm of ecclesiastical discipline, or if any priestly moderation had remained in you, such punishable transgressions would never have been committed. If no command of paternal rules could restrain you from them, at least the example of your predecessor of holy memory ought to have recalled you, for he, though he sinned less in making a presbyter, nevertheless found the judgment deserved for such usurpation, even though the man was unwilling. Where did you learn these acts which you committed against our brother and fellow bishop Gregory, not from election but from envy? You allowed him to be dragged [*pertram*, perhaps “by force”] to you and harassed by inexcusable violence, so that you might impose so great an honor upon him not with a tranquil mind, but—as must be said—with madness. Such things could not have been done in soundness of counsel. We do not wish to aggravate what has been done, lest we be compelled to judge what is deserved. For he deserves to lose his privilege who abuses the power granted to him.

## CHAPTER 141.—Concerning the rejection of one whom two bishops have presumed to ordain. From the First Council of Orange, chapter 21

(Dist. 64, c. *De abjectione.*) Concerning the rejection of one whom two bishops have presumed to ordain, it has seemed good in our provinces to decree concerning the presumptuous persons that, wherever two bishops happen to consecrate a third, both he and his authors shall be condemned, so that what was established in ancient times may be observed more cautiously.

## CHAPTER 142.—That bishops are not to be ordained for villages and small cities. From the Council of Sardica, chapter 6
