No permission is to be granted for ordaining a bishop either in some village or in a small city for which one presbyter suffices, because there is no need for a bishop to be appointed there, lest the name and authority of bishop be cheapened. Bishops invited from another province ought not to make a bishop, except either in cities that have had bishops or in a city of such a character or such population that it deserves to have a bishop. Does this please everyone? The synod answered: It pleases us.

## CHAPTER 143.—On the same matter. Pope Leo (chapter 2, epistle 87 to the African bishops)

We particularly wish that, among all the statutes of the canons, this provision pertaining to priestly dignity be observed: bishops are not to be consecrated in just any places, nor in any forts or villages where there have previously been no bishops. Where the congregations are smaller and the assemblies fewer, the care of presbyters suffices; episcopal governance, however, ought to preside only over greater cities. For the divinely inspired decrees of the holy Fathers forbade the priestly eminence to be bestowed upon hamlets, estates, or obscure or isolated municipalities, lest the honor to which more eminent matters ought to be entrusted become cheap through its very abundance.

## CHAPTER 144.—Concerning Wamba, king of the Spaniards, who contrary to the canons established a bishopric in a certain small town, and how it was annulled. From the Twelfth Council of Toledo, chapter 4
[Col. 0371D] What else is it to oppose the institutions of the elders and to overthrow the decrees of the holy Fathers than to break the bond of Christ’s fellowship and, by the licence of usurped command [presumption], to dissipate the order of the Church? Accordingly, at the prosecution of the venerable and most holy man, our brother Stephen, bishop of the see of Mérida, a matter arising from the usurpation of a novel presumption was brought forward for examination—one to be overthrown by the judgment of our communion in proportion to the boldness with which it is known to have been perpetrated by your perversity. For he said that he had been compelled by royal violence to establish a new appointment to episcopal rank in the monastery of a small village, where the venerable body of the most holy confessor Pigmenius [Pinevius] rests in the honour due to it.

[Col. 0372A] Therefore, because, with indiscriminate and all-too-ready assent, obeying the unjust commands of Prince Wamba, he introduced there a new and unlawful pre-eminence of an episcopal see, where canonical institution rejects such an act on every ground, the aforesaid man himself, lying prostrate on the ground, asks through the remedy of our ordinance both that pardon be granted him and that, by the sentence of our mouth, it be decided what ought above all to be done concerning the person who had been ordained there. But because we knew truly—indeed, in common—that the aforesaid prince had acted on frivolous counsel, and had not only ordered that someone be made bishop in the aforesaid place, but had also determined this with such obstinacy that he ordained a bishop in the suburb of Toledo, in the Praetorian Church of Saints Peter and Paul, and likewise did the same in other villages or hamlets, [Col. 0372B] therefore, in view of so insolent a licence for this kind of uprooting, we ordered that whatever the canonical enactments contained on this matter should be brought forward.

Then the following were read in their established order [as arranged in order]. First, from the Epistle of Paul, where he instructed his disciple Titus that he ought to appoint bishops in the cities (Titus 1). Likewise, from the Council of Nicaea, title 8 [26, if, as commonly happens, the chapters of the Council of Sardica are added to those of Nicaea], where, among other things, it is prescribed that two bishops must not appear to exist in one city. Likewise, from the Council of Laodicea, title 7, where it is said: “Bishops ought not to be ordained in villages, hamlets, or small rural settlements,” etc. (Second Council of Carthage; 16, question 1, chapter *Felix the Bishop*.)

Likewise, from the Second Council of Africa, title 5, where Felix, bishop of Solensita [Selemselita, [Col. 0372C] elsewhere Selambinita], said: “Also, if this pleases your Holiness, I submit that dioceses which have never had bishops should not have them, but that a diocese which has at some time had one should have its own bishop. In accordance with this submission, it belongs to your Holiness to judge what ought to be done.” Bishop Genedius said: “If the submission of our brother and fellow-bishop Felix pleases you, let it be confirmed by all.” All the bishops said: “It pleases us.” (Third Council of Carthage; 16, question 1, chapter *Multis conciliis*.)

Likewise, from the Third Council of Africa, title 42, where it is stated that a people which has always been subject within a diocese is not to receive another bishop. For Bishop Epigonius said, among other things: “I say that that people which has always been subject within a diocese, and [Col. 0372D] has never had a bishop of its own, ought not to receive a ruler. Therefore, if it pleases the entire most holy assembly, let what I have set forth [pursued] be confirmed.” Bishop Aurelius said: “I do not oppose the submission of our brother and fellow-priest, but I profess that I have done this and will do it.”

Likewise, from the Council of Sardica, where, among other things, it is prescribed: “Permission must not be granted indiscriminately. For if some village or small city, for which one presbyter is sufficient, should suddenly wish to have a bishop ordained for itself, so that the name and authority of bishop may be cheapened, those invited from another province ought not to make a bishop in places where none existed before.”

Likewise, concerning the sentence upon those who make such ordinations, or upon those ordained contrary to these canonical enactments, from the Council of Turin, title 2, where it says: “It has also seemed good that the record [series] of proceedings be written down for perpetual discipline—what the holy synod decreed regarding Octavius, Ursio, Remigius, and Bishop Trefae [and Triferius], who were charged, to their discredit, with a certain usurpation concerning the ordination of priests; and it seemed that this was so granted them that, henceforth warned by this authority, they should attempt to usurp nothing. For they defended themselves in this case with the excuse that they had not previously been summoned. Therefore the holy synod judged that, if anyone should hereafter act against the institutions of the elders, the person ordained should know that he is to be deprived of the honour of priesthood, and the one who ordained him that he will retain no authority in ordinations or in councils. [Col. 0373B] This sentence shall prevail not only in the case of the bishop mentioned, but also in the case of all who, deceived by a similar error, have carried out ordinations of this kind.”

Therefore, opposing these most forceful rules to the accomplished deed, we have chosen in our common determination that from now on no episcopal see shall remain in the place of the aforesaid small village, nor shall a bishop thereafter be established there. Yet this Convildus, who appears to have been installed as bishop there contrary to the decrees of the elders, shall not be visited with any canonical sentence of condemnation, because he was ordained not through ambition but at the prince’s compulsion. Therefore we grant him this humane remedy: that he be transferred to another see when any bishop dies. The aforesaid place, however, is henceforth to remain under monastic [Col. 0373C] institution; it is no longer to enjoy episcopal privilege, but is in every respect to be subject to the rule of an abbot, as it has been hitherto.

Moreover [henceforth], let us enact [we enact] this general decree: if anyone should attempt to act against the prohibitions of the canons by causing a bishop to be elected in places where there has never been a bishop, let him incur anathema in the sight of almighty God [let him be anathema in the sight of almighty God]. Furthermore, both the ordainer and the ordained shall lose the rank of their honour, since they have dared to overthrow not only the decrees of the ancient Fathers but also apostolic enactments.

## Chapter 145.—That a people which has never had a bishop is not to receive one except by consent. From the African Council, chapter 61 (under Boniface and Celestine, chapter 65).

[Col. 0373D]

It also seemed good that peoples which have never had bishops of their own should by no means receive them unless this has been decreed by a plenary council of each province and by its primate [primacy], and with the consent of the person to whose diocese that church belonged.

## Chapter 146.—That a province is by no means to be divided between two metropolitans. From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 12.

It has come to our attention that certain persons, acting contrary to ecclesiastical statutes, have resorted to the civil authorities and, by a pragmatic decree, have divided one province into two, with the result that two metropolitans appear to exist in one province. The holy synod decrees [Col. 0374A] that bishops are henceforth to attempt nothing of this kind; otherwise, whoever attempts it shall be subject to loss of his own rank. But whatever cities have been supported by imperial letters with the honour of the metropolitan title are to enjoy honour only; and the bishop who governs its church is to do so with the privileges of the true metropolis preserved. [The second edition reads: “with the right of the metropolitan bishop’s privilege reserved.”]

## Chapter 147.—Concerning those who are not received by those to whom they are ordained. From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 17.

(Distinction 92, chapter *Si qui episcopi*.) If any bishops have been ordained but are not received by the diocese to which they were designated, and wish to occupy other dioceses and use force against their bishops by stirring up seditions [Col. 0374B] against them, it has seemed good that they be expelled. But if they wish to remain in the rank of presbyter, as presbyters, where they formerly were, they are not to be deprived of their own dignity. Yet if they stir up seditions against the bishops established there, even the honour of the presbyterate is to be taken from such persons, and they are to be marked by condemnation [“made notable”].

## Chapter 148.—Concerning a bishop who neglects to go to the church to which he has been ordained. From the Council of Antioch, chapter 17.

(Distinction 92, chapter *Si quis*.) If any bishop has received a bishopric by the laying on of hands and neglects to undertake the ministry entrusted to him, and does not consent to go to the church committed to him, he ought to be deprived of communion until he accepts the office under compulsion, or at least until the synod of bishops of the same province makes some final decision [Col. 0374C] concerning him.

## Chapter 149.—Concerning a bishop who has not accepted the office entrusted to him. From the Council of Arles, chapter 16.

If any bishop has not accepted the office entrusted to him, let him be deprived of communion until, commending himself to obedience, he consents. But if he proceeds there and is not received, let him nevertheless remain bishop, not because of any ill-will on the people’s part; but let the clergy of the city be deprived of communion because they have not been diligent in instructing disobedient peoples [because they have not been diligent in instructing disobedient peoples].

## Chapter 150.—Concerning a bishop without a see who has seized a vacant church. From the Council of Antioch, chapter 16.

(Distinction 92, chapter *Si quis*.) If any bishop without a see, stealthily invading a church without a bishop, [Col. 0374D] attacks its people without the counsel of the full body, even if the people whom he has misled desire him, he must be regarded as alien to that church. By a complete and perfect council we mean one at which the metropolitan bishop has been present.

## Chapter 151.—Concerning a bishop ordained through popular contention. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 10 (chapter 10 of the book of Martin of Braga, from the Greek synods).

If a bishop has been ordained but, through contention among the people or for some reason not due to his own fault, is not received in the diocese assigned to him, he ought to retain only the honour of the priesthood, so that he may presume nothing for himself from the property of the church to which he comes. Let him await whatever the holy council decides concerning him.

## Chapter 152.—Concerning those promoted to the episcopate who are not received. From the Council of Antioch, chapter 18.

[Col. 0375A]

(Distinction 92, chapter *Si quis episcop.*) If any bishop ordained for a diocese does not go to that for which he was elected, through no fault of his own, because either the people prevent him or for another cause not brought about through his fault, he is to share both in honour and ministry, provided that he does not trouble the affairs of the church where he is known to minister. He must also observe whatever the complete synod of the province decrees in its judgment.

## Chapter 153.—That the authority to convene general councils has been entrusted by special power to the Apostolic See. Isidore, chapter 8.

The authority to convene synods has been entrusted by special power to the Apostolic See, and we read that no general synod is valid unless it has been convened or supported by that authority. Canonical authority attests this, ecclesiastical history confirms it, and the holy Fathers uphold it.

## Chapter 154.—Concerning synods: at what time they are to be held. From the Council of Antioch, chapter 20.

(Distinction 18, chapter *Propter ecclesiasticas causas*.) For ecclesiastical benefit and the resolution of matters that admit doubt and controversy, it has most fittingly seemed good that councils of bishops be held twice every year in each province. The first is to be held after the third week following the feast of Easter, so that the synod meets in the fourth ensuing week—that is, midway between Easter and Pentecost—when the metropolitan has summoned the bishops of his province. [Col. 0375C] The second synod is to be held on the Ides of October, that is, on the fifteenth day of October, which the Greeks call Hyperberetaeus. At these councils presbyters and deacons are to be present, along with all who consider themselves injured, and they are to undergo the synod’s examination. No one may hold councils on his own authority except those entrusted with metropolitan rights.

## Chapter 155.—Concerning convening a synod. From the Council of Clermont, chapter 21 [16].

After all the matters promulgated in this council for the correction of our order have been completed, it has seemed good to determine that every year we should devote ourselves with constant zeal of mind to holding [Col. 0375D] the celebration of the council at the metropolitan see, at the time fixed by the decision of the prince or metropolitan; nor should we dissent on account of any alleged occasions, but on the appointed day on which it has been announced, when all the bishops of the province have assembled at the metropolitan see, the council is to be celebrated under God’s presidency. Any bishop who, except for an unavoidable cause or necessity, absents himself from holding the council shall be punished by exclusion from communion for the space of one year. If thereafter he allows the limit of one year to pass without the celebration of a council, he shall remain liable to the judgment of all the bishops in communion in that province—that is, if, hindered by no authority of the prince, illness, or unavoidable cause, but solely by the inclination of his own [Col. 0376A] will, he has not assembled himself to celebrate the council.

## Chapter 156.—Concerning an archbishop who, in time of peace, neglects for more than two years to announce a synod. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 3.

If, within two years, when divine providence has granted tranquillity of the times, and after his fellow-provincial bishops have urged [been admonished], the metropolitan has not announced a synod and has himself delayed the proceedings, he shall not presume to celebrate Mass for a whole year. And if those summoned, though not detained by bodily illness, have contemptuously neglected to attend through their own abuse, they shall be subject to the same sentence.

## Chapter 157.—Concerning bishops summoned to a synod who disdain to come. From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 40.

(Distinction 18, chapter *Non oportet*.) Bishops summoned to a synod ought not wholly to disregard it, but should go at once and teach or learn what pertains to the correction of the Church or other matters. Whoever disregards this shall condemn himself, unless perhaps illness makes it impossible for him to go.

## Chapter 158.—What sort of letters are to be sent by the metropolitan. From the Council of Tarragona, chapter 13.

(Distinction 18, chapter *Si episcopus*.) The metropolitan is to send letters through the brethren of such a kind that they summon to the council not only presbyters of cathedral churches but also diocesan presbyters, and that they should endeavour to bring with them some lay sons of the Church.

## Chapter 159.—For what reasons bishops summoned to a synod may be absent. From the Council of Agde, [Col. 0376C] chapter 35.

If the metropolitan bishop sends letters to his fellow-provincial bishops inviting them either to the ordination of some brother or to a synod, they are not to delay appearing on the appointed day, setting all else aside except grave bodily illness or a royal command. If they are absent, as the ancient authority of the canons prescribes, they shall be deprived of the charity of their brethren and of communion with the Church until the next synod.

## Chapter 160.—Concerning a bishop who neglects to be present at a synod. From the Council of Seville, chapter 10 (chapter 19, Second Council of Arles).

(Distinction 18, chapter *Si quis autem*.) If any bishop neglects to be present at a synod, or thinks that the assembly of the brethren should be abandoned [Col. 0376D] before the council is dissolved, let him recognize that he is alien from the communion of the brethren; nor may he be received until he has been absolved at the following synod.

## Chapter 161.—Concerning bishops unable through illness to come to a synod. From the decrees of Pope Felix, chapter 11.

(5, question 3, chapter *Si aegrotans*.) If a bishop is ill, or if some grave necessity detains him, he is to send a representative to the synod on his behalf, undertaking, without prejudice to the truth of the faith, whatever the synod decrees.

## Chapter 162.—Concerning bishops summoned to a synod who disdain either to come or to send delegates. From the synod held at Altheim, chapter 11.

It pleased the holy synod severely to rebuke and, for the fault of disobedience, to reprimand bishops who had been summoned from [Col. 0377A] Saxony to the holy council but had not come, nor sent their delegates or vicars in accordance with the sacred canons. Therefore, with brotherly charity, we again invite and summon them to the appointed council. If they also—what we do not wish—should treat this as nothing and refuse to give a just account of their disobedience, Saint Peter, by apostolic authority, and the envoy of Pope Saint Peter, together with the holy synod, forbid them to celebrate Mass until they come to Rome and give a worthy account before the pope [and] the holy Church.

## Chapter 163.—A universal council is to be held only when necessity requires it. From the African Council, chapter 42 (chapter 62).

It seemed good that the brethren should no longer be burdened by the necessity of a universal [Col. 0377B] council; rather, whenever a common cause requires it—that is, if letters concerning the matter have been sent to this see from anywhere in all Africa—a synod is to be convened in whatever province practical convenience recommends. Causes that are not common, however, are to be judged in their own provinces.

## Chapter 164.—That later bishops are not to prefer themselves to their predecessors. From a letter of Pope Lucius sent to the Western bishops.

Bishops in each province are to take care not to prefer themselves, though later, to their predecessors, and not to do anything without consulting them, except insofar as it concerns their own parish; rather, they are all to issue and determine a harmonious decision regarding matters common to them. For acts done otherwise shall have no force [Col. 0377C] and shall not be regarded as ecclesiastical.

## Chapter 165.—That bishops are to observe the time of their rank, each rendering honour to the other. From the Council of Chalon, chapter 6.

(Distinction 18, chapter *Placuit*.) Likewise, it seemed good that, while preserving the primacy of the metropolitan bishop, the other bishops, according to the date of their ordination, should yield the place of sitting to one another [to one sitting]; those ordained later must not dare to place themselves before their predecessors.

## Chapter 166.—That bishops ordained later must not dare to place themselves before their predecessors. From the African Council, chapter 53 (and the Council of Milevis, chapter 13).

Bishop Valentinian said: “If the goodness of your patience permits, I shall set forth what was done in the Church of Carthage in former times and became evident as confirmed by the subscriptions of the brethren; we too profess that we shall observe it. But there, we know, ecclesiastical discipline has always remained inviolate, so that no brother ever dared to place himself before his predecessors; rather, the offices of charity always rendered to predecessors what they were always glad to receive from those following them.”

## Chapter 167.—Concerning doubtful matters arising in councils of bishops. From a letter of Pope Boniface to the bishops of Gaul.

(6, question 4, chapter *Si inter episcopos*.) If doubt arises among bishops of the same council concerning ecclesiastical law or other business, first their metropolitan, considering the matter with certain others in the council, is to decide it; and if neither [Col. 0378A] party accepts the decisions, then the primate of the region shall be heard between them, and shall determine what accords with the ecclesiastical canons and our laws. Neither party may oppose his judgment.

## Chapter 168.—That bishops sitting in synod should first correct matters pertaining to the amendment [commendation] of life. From the Council of Clermont, chapter 1.

First, it has seemed good that whenever the holy synod is convened according to the enactments of the Fathers, no bishop should dare first to introduce any cause before matters pertaining to the amendment of life, the strictness of the rule, and remedies for the soul have been addressed.

## Chapter 169.—Concerning a metropolitan who delays hearing a fellow-provincial bishop in his case. From the decrees of Pope Alexander.

If a metropolitan is appealed to twice by any fellow-provincial [Col. 0378B] bishop in his own case and delays hearing him, the latter shall have leave to pursue his case at the next synod; and whatever his fellow-provincials establish for the sake of justice must be observed.

## Chapter 170.—That bishops should always decide just judgments. From the Council of Reims, chapter 19.

Let bishops and judges distinguish judgments, because some things are to be judged now, while others are reserved for God’s judgment. It is written: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts; and then each shall have praise from God” (1 Corinthians 4). And let them remember this saying: “With whatever judgment you judge, you too shall be judged” (Matthew 7).

## Chapter 171.—That the enactments of the canons are to be duly observed by all, and no one is to presume to judge by his own opinion. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 11.

[Col. 0378C]

Let the enactments of the canons be duly observed by all without prejudice, and in ecclesiastical proceedings or judgments let no one be guided by his own opinion, but by their authority. Moreover, in expounding or preaching the divine Scriptures, let each person follow the understanding of the holy catholic Fathers and of those most approved; in their writings, as blessed Jerome says, “the truth of faith does not waver” (letter to Laeta, *On the Instruction of a Daughter*).

## Chapter 172.—Concerning bishops at variance. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 25.

(Distinction 90, chapter *Dissidentes*.) Let bishops at variance be reconciled, if not by fear of God, then by a synod.

## Chapter 173.—That no bishop is to usurp another’s people. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 19.

[Col. 0378D]

It seemed good that no bishop should usurp another’s people and that no bishop should encroach upon the diocese of his colleague.

## Chapter 174.—That no metropolitan or primate may do anything concerning the clergy or parishes of fellow-provincial bishops, nor concerning their cases, without the counsel of them all. From a letter of Pope Calixtus sent to bishops established throughout Gaul.

Henceforth, brethren, with the privilege of the Roman Church preserved in all things, no metropolitan is to hear anyone’s cases without the attendance of all the other fellow-provincial bishops, because acts undertaken otherwise than after being examined in the presence of them all are invalid. If he does so, let him be restrained by the brethren.

## Chapter 175.—Concerning a diocese possessed for thirty years. From the Council of Worms, chapter 23 (Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 33).

[Col. 0379A]

(16, question 3, chapter *Quicunque episcopus*.) Any bishop who has possessed another bishop’s diocese for thirty years without any challenge, although [because], according to the law, it is judged [appears] to be his diocese, is not to be subject to an action for recovery. But this applies within one parish [province]; beyond it, by no means, lest, while a diocese is defended, the boundaries of provinces be confused.

## Chapter 176.—That bishops who neglect their places are to be admonished by neighbouring bishops to correct themselves. From the African Council, chapter 75 (African Council, canon 88, and Milevis, chapter 24).

[Col. 0379B] (16, question 3, chapter *Placuit*.) Likewise, it seemed good that any bishops who neglect to win to catholic unity places belonging to their see should be approached by neighbouring bishops who love God, so that they may not delay doing this. If they have not accomplished it within six months from the day of admonition, the places shall belong to whoever is able to win them. This is so provided, however, that, if the person to whom they appeared to belong can prove that his deliberate negligence was rather chosen by the heretics, so that they might remain there with impunity, and that his diligence was forestalled, so that his more vigilant care might thereby be impeded, then, when the episcopal judges have recognized this, they shall restore the places to his see. If the bishops between whom the case is being heard belong to different provinces, the matter shall first be decided by the bishop in whose province the disputed place lies. But if by common agreement they choose neighbouring judges, either one or three are to be chosen; and if they choose three, they shall follow either the decision of all or that of two.

## Chapter 177.—Concerning bishops who contend over parishes. From the same source, chapter 71 (chapter 87, and Milevis, chapter 21).

(16, question 6, chapter *Placuit*.) It seemed good that any bishops who claim peoples which they consider to belong to their see should not seek them in such a way as to prosecute their cases before episcopal judges; rather, if they invade them while another resists [retains], whether the peoples consent or not, they shall suffer loss of their claim. And whoever has already done this—if the contention between the bishops has not yet ended, but they still dispute the matter—let the one be removed from it who is found to have invaded it while disregarding ecclesiastical judgments. [Col. 0379D] Let no one flatter himself because he has obtained letters from the primate permitting him to retain it. Rather, whether he has letters or not, let him approach the person who holds it and receive his letters, so that it may be apparent that he has peacefully held the church belonging to him. But if that person raises any question, the case shall be concluded through episcopal judges, whether those whom they themselves have selected as neighbouring judges by mutual agreement.

## Chapter 178.—That a cleric of another diocese is in no way to be ordained in another parish. From the Council of Antioch, chapter 22.

(9, question 2, chapter *Episcoporum non debere*.) A bishop is not to go into another city that is not subject to him; nor is he to approach an estate that does not belong to him; nor is he to presume to perform an ordination there, [Col. 0380A] unless perhaps with the council and consent of the bishop of the region. If anyone attempts anything of this kind, his ordination shall be invalid, and he himself shall be disciplined by the synod.

## Chapter 179.—That a bishop is in no way to pass from one parish to another. From the same source, chapter 21.

(7, question 1, chapter *Episcopum de dioecesi*.) A bishop is by no means to migrate from one diocese to another, neither of his own accord by wholly rushing in, nor compelled by force from the people, nor driven by necessity from bishops. Let him remain in the church first allotted to him by God and not move away from it, in accordance with the former rule established on this matter.

## Chapter 180.—Concerning the presumption of another’s diocese. From a letter of Pope Boniface.

If any bishop, uninvited, comes from one province [Col. 0380B] into another, presumptuously intruding upon the ordination and appointment of clerics and officiously involving himself in matters not belonging to him, all that he has established shall be void and empty. He himself is to be excommunicated with fitting rebuke and rejected by the holy council.

## Chapter 181.—That another’s parish is not to be seized by bishops. From the Canons of the Apostles, title 14 (and the Council of Nicaea, chapter 15, and Antioch, chapter 21).

A bishop may not seize another’s diocese after abandoning his own, even if compelled by many, unless some reasonable cause compels him, as one able to confer greater benefit upon those established there and truly to provide something for the cause of religion. He is not to attempt this on his own initiative, but is to accomplish it by the judgment of many bishops and with earnest petition.

## Chapter 182.—Concerning the same matter and its rationale. From the Second Letter of Pope Evaristus to the brethren throughout Egypt, chapter 4.

Priests perform an embassy in the Church in Christ’s stead; and just as his bride, that is, the Church, is joined to him, so churches are joined to bishops, each to its own share. And just as a man ought not neglect his wife but love her, guard her chastely, cherish her, and govern her wisely, so too a bishop ought to do these things for his church. And as a wife who is under her husband’s authority ought to obey, love, and cherish her husband, so much more should the Church obey her [Col. 0380D] bishop in all things and love and cherish him as her own soul, because the former is carnal and the latter spiritual.

And just as a man ought not commit adultery against his wife, so neither should a bishop commit adultery against his church: that is, he should not abandon the one to which he was consecrated, except under unavoidable necessity and through apostolic or canonical transfer, and join himself to another for the sake of ambition. And just as a wife is not permitted to leave her husband in order to be joined in marriage to another while he is alive, thereby committing adultery against him—even if her husband has committed fornication, but, according to the Apostle, she must either be reconciled to her husband or remain unmarried (1 Corinthians 7)—so the Church is not permitted to leave her husband [bishop] or be separated from him in order to receive another while he lives; rather, she must either have him or remain unmarried, that is, she must not receive another [Col. 0381A] bishop while her bishop lives, lest she incur the crime of fornication or adultery. For if she has been adulterated—that is, if she has joined herself to another bishop, added or caused another bishop to be set over herself, or desired this—then through the most severe penance she must either be reconciled to her bishop or remain unmarried.

## Chapter 183.—Concerning the lawful transfer of bishops for the sake of common benefit. From a letter of Pope Anterus sent to bishops established throughout the provinces of Baetica and Toledo, chapter 14.

(7, question 1, chapter *Mutationes*.) Concerning the transfer of bishops, on which you wished to consult the holy Apostolic See, know that it may lawfully be made for common benefit and necessity, but not at anyone’s whim or by domination. Saint Peter, our master [Col. 0381B] and prince of the apostles, was transferred from Antioch to Rome for the sake of usefulness, so that he might be more effective there. Eusebius too was transferred by apostolic authority from a certain small city to Alexandria.

> [Note: [Col. 0381D] On this matter, see further Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 36.]

Likewise Felix was transferred from the city in which he had been ordained to Ephesus, by the choice of its citizens, on account of his teaching and good life, with the common counsel of bishops and the other clergy and peoples. For one does not pass from city to city when he does this not of his own whim or ambition but because of some benefit or the necessity of others, at the urging and counsel of superiors. Nor is one transferred from a smaller city to a greater who does this not through ambition or his own will, but who has been transferred and enthroned by others—not proudly but humbly—either because he was driven from [Col. 0381C] his own see by force, compelled by necessity, or transferred for the benefit of a place or people; for “man sees what is before his eyes, but God sees the heart” (1 Samuel 16). And the Lord speaks through the Prophet, saying: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain” (Psalm 93).

Therefore, one does not change his see who does not change his mind. One does not change city who changes it not by his own will but by the counsel and election of others. Therefore, one does not migrate from city to city who does not voluntarily leave his own for the sake of greed; but, as has already been said, one has been transferred to another city either because he was driven from his own, compelled by necessity, or transferred by the election or exhortation of clergy and peoples. For just as bishops have authority regularly to ordain bishops [Col. 0381D] and the remaining clergy, so, whenever benefit or necessity requires it, they also have authority, in the manner stated above, to transfer and enthrone them.

## Chapter 184.—That a bishop may not leave his own city and move to another. From Apostolic Canon 6.

(Distinction 28, chapter *Si quis docuerit*.) A bishop must by no means cast off his own wife under the pretext of religion; if he does cast her off, let him be excommunicated; but if he persists, let him be deposed.

## Chapter 185.—Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Sardica, chapter 1.

Bishop Hosius said: “No less an evil custom than a destructive corruption must be uprooted completely, so that no bishop may be permitted to move from his own city to another city. For the reason he attempts this is clear, since no bishop has ever been found in this matter who moved from a greater city to a lesser. Hence it appears that they are inflamed by the fire of greed and serve ambition, in order to exercise dominion. If it pleases everyone, let such perniciousness be judged more severely and harshly, so that a person of this kind may not even have lay communion.” All answered: “It pleases us.”

## Chapter 186.—That a bishop may flee to another church if he has suffered persecution in his own. From the decrees of Pope Calixtus sent to bishops throughout Gaul.

If any bishop is persecuted in his own church, he must flee to another and join it [be consoled there, elsewhere: “is to be associated”], as the Lord says: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matthew 10). But if a transfer is to be made for the sake of usefulness, he is not to undertake it himself; he is to do it at the invitation of the brethren and by the authority of this holy see, not for ambition but for benefit.

## Chapter 187.—Concerning a bishop who neglects the principal seat of his church. From the Council of Rouen, chapter 6.

A bishop is not permitted to neglect the principal seat of his diocese and attend another church in his diocese more frequently.

## Chapter 188.—Concerning the same matter, more carefully. From the Council of Sardica, chapter 15.

[Note: Col. 0382D. The Greek text in the same chapter should be consulted, since the translator has not grasped the sense.] Bishop Hosius said that nothing ought to be omitted. There are certain brethren and fellow-bishops who do not [Col. 0382C] reside in the city in which they appear to have been appointed bishops, because they possess only some small property there, while elsewhere they are known to have suitable estates, or because of affection for relatives, to whom they wish to grant favors. They ought to be permitted to go as far as their possessions and administer or arrange the proceeds of their labor, provided that, after four Lord’s Days—that is, after three weeks—if they must remain, they stay preferably on their own estates; or, if there is a nearby city where there is a presbyter, they go there, unless they are seen to spend the Lord’s Day at church. Thus their household affairs will not suffer loss through their absence, and, by not coming frequently to the city where the bishop resides, they will avoid suspicion of ostentation and ambition. All declared that this pleased them.

### CHAPTER 189.—That a bishop should make a circuit of his parish each year. From the Council of Split, chapter 4.

That each bishop should make a circuit of his parish every year, strengthen and teach the people, forbid what must be avoided, and diligently ensure that what ought to be done is done profitably.

### CHAPTER 190.—Concerning bishops who seldom or never personally visit the congregations entrusted to them. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 5.

That bishops who seldom or never personally visit the congregations committed to them should, in accordance with evangelical, apostolic, and ecclesiastical order—since [Col. 0383A] the Lord says to Ezekiel, “I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel; you shall hear the word from my mouth and announce it to them from me,” etc. (Ezek. 3)—be more severely restrained [corrected] by the bishops of their province.

### CHAPTER 191.—That bishops should diligently examine their presbyters concerning their ministries. From the Council of Braga, chapter 2 (Second Council of Braga, chapter 1).

(10, question 1, canon *Placuit omnibus episcopis*.) It has pleased and agreed with us that bishops, as they go through the individual churches and dioceses, should first examine the clergy as to how they observe the order of baptism and of the masses, how they perform each of the offices in church; and, if they find matters rightly done, they should give thanks to God, but if not, they ought to instruct the ignorant.

### CHAPTER 192.—That bishops should make circuits of their parishes with few attendants. From the Council of Toledo, chapter 5.

[Col. 0383B] When a bishop visits his diocese, he should be burdensome to no one by the size of his retinue; he should never exceed fifty mounts, nor be allowed to remain more than one day at any one basilica.

### CHAPTER 193.—If a bishop cannot visit his parish, he should send men of approved life in his place. From the same source, chapter 6.

If a bishop, detained by illness or entangled in other occupations, cannot complete the visitation of his diocese, he should send presbyters of approved life or deacons to investigate the revenues and repairs of the basilicas and the life of those who minister there.

### CHAPTER 194.—What kind of minister a bishop ought to have beside him. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 3.

[Col. 0383C] That every [perhaps, each] bishop should strive, according to his means, to have beside him such a person as will continually instruct and train the presbyters of the people according to the most sincere and pure understanding of the Catholic Fathers, in faith, observance of God’s commandments, and the teaching of preaching; lest the house of the living God—which is the Church—remain without the lamp of the divine word. Such a man must also be one whom love of money does not trouble, and whom depraved habits and blameworthy conduct do not render contemptible.

Hence, when Moses laid before God the complaint that he could not carry so great a burden as had been imposed upon him, he heard from the Lord: “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders and teachers of the people; [Col. 0383D] and I shall take from your spirit and give it to them, so that they may bear with you the burden of the people and you may not be burdened alone” (Num. 11). What do we understand in Moses except the supreme priesthood? What in the seventy men except presbyters? And the fact that the Lord takes from Moses’ spirit and gives it to them plainly shows that those summoned by the bishop before God to bear with him the burden of the people ought to share the same will and, with the honor imparted to them, cooperate with all their strength. For this is signified by their receiving not another spirit, but the spirit of that same Moses.

### CHAPTER 195.—That a bishop should not appoint a layman as his deputy. From the Council of Braga, chapter 9.

We have learned through a recent proceeding that certain members of our body, contrary to ecclesiastical custom, have appointed laymen as stewards in [Col. 0384A] divine affairs. Therefore, deliberating together, we have chosen that each one of us, according to the decrees of the Fathers of Chalcedon, should appoint as his steward a member of his own clergy. For it is unbecoming that a layman should be the deputy of a bishop, and that secular persons should judge in the Church. In one and the same office there ought not to be a differing profession. This is also forbidden in the divine law, Moses saying: “You shall not plough with an ox and an ass together” (Deut. 22); that is, you shall not associate persons of different professions in one office.

Therefore we must obey both the divine books and the commands of the holy Fathers, establishing that those associated with bishops in the administration of the Church must not differ either in profession or in dress; nor can those whose pursuits and [Col. 0384B] aims are different adhere to and be joined with one another. But if any bishop has chosen [afterward] an ecclesiastical estate to be administered under lay management, or has thought it should be governed without the attestation of a steward, he shall truly be judged both a contemner of the canons and a defrauder of ecclesiastical property; he shall be liable not only to Christ for the goods of the poor, but shall also remain answerable to the council.

### CHAPTER 196.—That, during a bishop’s visitation, all who are in the parishes of the mother churches, except the sick, must come to his synod. From the Council of Rouen, chapter 11.

When a bishop makes a circuit of his diocese, the archdeacon or archpresbyter ought to go before him one or two days through the parishes which he is to visit. Having assembled the people, he must announce the arrival of their own shepherd [Col. 0384C] and order that everyone, except the sick, appear without omission at his synod on the appointed day. By the authority of the holy canons he must command and sternly declare that anyone absent without grave necessity shall without doubt be excluded from Christian communion.

Then, having called to himself the presbyters who ought in that place to render service to the bishop, he should endeavor to correct whatever he can of minor and lighter matters, so that the bishop, when he arrives, may not be burdened with easier business or need remain there longer than the available provisions suffice. For the Lord says to Moses concerning such fellow-workers: “They shall bear with you the burden of the people, and you shall not be burdened alone” (Num. 11). Blessed John the Baptist [Col. 0384D] also ran before the Lord’s coming, preaching and saying: “Repent,” etc. (Matt. 3); and likewise, “Prepare the way of the Lord” (ibid.).

Indeed, a bishop appears to act in Christ’s stead; therefore he must be received by the people subject to him with joy, fear, and the highest reverence, so that what the Apostle says to the disciples may be said of them with praise: “I bear you witness that you received me as an angel of God, as our Lord Jesus” (Gal. 4).

### CHAPTER 197.—That bishops should not read pagan books. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 16.

(Distinction 37, canon *Episcopus gentilium*.) That bishops should not read books of the pagans, but books of heretics when necessity and occasion require.

### CHAPTER 198.—That bishops should adapt preaching to the capacity of the common people, according to the character of their ordinary language. From the Council of Rheims, chapter 11 (chapter 15).

[Col. 0385A]

That bishops should endeavor to preach the sermons and homilies of the holy Fathers in such a way that all may understand, according to the character of the common language.

### CHAPTER 199.—Reproof of a bishop who expounds pagan books from the pulpit. From Gregory’s Register, to Bishop Desiderius, chapter 180 (Book IX, epistle 48).

(Distinction 86, canon *Cum multa*.) When many good reports of your studies had reached us, such joy arose in our heart that we could not allow ourselves to deny what your brotherhood asked to have granted to it. But afterwards there came to us something which we cannot [Col. 0385B] mention without shame: that your brotherhood was teaching grammar and expounding some of the more difficult subjects to certain persons. We received this matter so painfully and rejected it so vehemently that we turned the earlier reports into groaning and sorrow, because the praises of Christ cannot be uttered by the same mouth as the praises of Jupiter. Consider how grave and wicked it is for bishops to sing what is not fitting even for a devout layman.

Although our most beloved son Candidus the presbyter, coming afterwards and being carefully questioned on this matter, denied it and attempted to excuse you, it has nevertheless not yet left our mind; for in proportion as it is detestable for such a thing to be reported of a priest, so it is necessary to ascertain by strict and truthful satisfaction whether it is so or not. Therefore, if possible, [Col. 0385C] we shall endeavor clearly to investigate these reports brought to us, so that, if they are shown to be false and it is established that you have not devoted yourself to frivolities and secular literature, we may give thanks to our God, who has not allowed your heart to be stained by blasphemies in the praises of abominable beings; and we may then deal securely and without any doubt with granting what you request.

### CHAPTER 200.—How great a danger threatens pastors who neglect to preach Christ’s truth. From the decrees of Pope Mark sent to the bishops of Egypt.

Woe to us who have undertaken the burden of this ministry if we neglect to preach the truth of our Savior Jesus Christ which the apostles preached. Woe to us if we suppress the truth by silence, though we are commanded to distribute to the bankers [Col. 0385D]—that is, to instruct and teach Christian peoples. What shall we say at the future judgment of Christ himself if we are ashamed to preach the truth of his word? What will become of us when Christ God, our just Judge, strictly requires from us an account of the souls entrusted to us and of the office we have undertaken?

### CHAPTER 201.—That a bishop ought without interruption to teach and love his Church. From the decrees of Pope Evaristus sent to brethren throughout Egypt.

A bishop ought opportunely and without interruption to teach his Church, prudently govern and love it, and abstain from vices so that he may attain eternal salvation. The Church, moreover, ought to receive his teaching with such great reverence and [Col. 0386A] love him as God’s envoy and herald of truth; for Truth himself bears witness: “Whatever he binds on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever he looses on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 16).

### CHAPTER 202.—Concerning ignorance, which all, especially priests, must avoid. From the Council of Toledo, chapter 5 (Fourth Toledo, canon 24).

(Distinction 38, canon *Ignorantia mater*.) Ignorance, the mother of all errors, must especially be avoided by the priests of God, who have undertaken the office of teaching among the people. For Scripture urges priests to read, Paul the apostle saying to Timothy: “Attend to reading and exhortation” (1 Tim. 4). Teachers should know that they must always persevere in these things. Therefore let priests meditate upon the holy Scriptures and the canons, [Col. 0386B] so that all their work may consist in preaching and teaching, and they may build up all people both by knowledge of the faith and by discipline of works.

### CHAPTER 203.—That a bishop should compel those at variance to make peace. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 26.

(Distinction 90, canon *Studendum est*.) A bishop should strive to urge brethren at variance, whether clergy or laity, toward peace rather than judgment.

### CHAPTER 204.—That no judicial determinations of matters should be made by a bishop on the Lord’s Day. From the Council of Split, chapter 2.

That no bishop, nor anyone subordinate to him, should presume to judge cases on the Lord’s Day.

### CHAPTER 205.—Concerning the domestic and private conduct of bishops. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 5.

[Col. 0386C] The holy synod decreed that the domestic and private conduct of a bishop ought to be made impervious to every reproach and suspicion, so that, according to the Apostle, “we provide what is good not only before God but also before all people” (2 Cor. 8). Therefore priests and clerics of unimpeachable reputation should attend in the bishop’s chamber and in all his more private services; they should continually observe their bishop as he keeps watch, prays, and searches the sacred writings, and should be witnesses and imitators of his holy conduct and proclaimers of it to God’s glory.

### CHAPTER 206.—That a bishop ought to conduct himself as a guest. From the sayings of Augustine.

A bishop ought to be as a guest and have no private [Col. 0386D] house, but should be as a guest, as Christ says: “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9).

### CHAPTER 207.—That bishops should celebrate masses frequently. From the Council of Orange, chapter 3.

We decree that bishops should celebrate masses not only on Sundays and principal feasts, but, whenever possible, should frequently perform the daily sacraments [sacrifices] and not disdain them.

### CHAPTER 208.—That a bishop, corrupted by payment, should not presume to ordain another’s cleric. From the Council of Nantes, chapter 1.

We forbid all ministers of ecclesiastical rank that no one, corrupted by a gift or favor [Col. 0387A] of any kind, should presume secretly and furtively to introduce for ordination a cleric of another parish. If he does so, then, according to the Chalcedonian decree, the person who acted as intermediary, if a cleric, shall lose his own rank; if a layman or monk, he shall be anathematized.

### CHAPTER 209.—On the same matter. From the Council of Paris, chapter 22.

A bishop shall not appoint presbyters or deacons subject to another bishop, unless perhaps with that bishop’s counsel and consent. If anyone attempts to do such a thing, his ordination shall be void, and he himself shall be restrained by the synod.

### CHAPTER 210.—That no bishop should presume to enter another bishop’s parish for the promotion of ministry. From the Council of Antioch, chapter 13.

[Col. 0387B] (9, question 2, canon *Nullum episcopum*.) No bishop from another province may dare to cross into another and ordain persons in churches for advancement to ministry, even though some may appear to give consent, unless he comes at the request of letters both from the metropolitan and from the other bishops who are with him, and thus proceeds to the act of ordination. But if, summoned by no one, he hastens in disorderly fashion to arrange certain ordinations and ecclesiastical affairs that do not concern him, what he does shall indeed be void, and he himself shall undergo punishment for his unruly conduct and irrational audacity, being thereby already condemned by the holy council.

### CHAPTER 211.—That a bishop should not dare boldly to seize a cleric of another Church. From the Council of Nicaea, chapter 17.

[Col. 0387C]

If any bishop boldly seizes a cleric belonging to another place and attempts to ordain him in his own Church without the consent of the bishop from whom he departed, such an ordination shall be declared void.

### CHAPTER 212.—Concerning unlawful ordinations not to be presumed. From the letter of Pope Simplicius sent to Bishops Equitius, Florentinus, and Severus, chapter 1.

Your loving report has informed us, and the sequence of proceedings has more fully made known, that Gaudentius, priest of the Church of Osimo, has performed unlawful ordinations contrary to the statutes of the canons and our commands. We command that all power concerning these ordinations be entirely taken from him. For we have written to Severus, our brother and [Col. 0387D] fellow-bishop, that, if necessary, he himself should perform this office in the aforesaid Church, observing the rules of the Fathers—an office which that man has been convicted of abusing—so that those unlawfully promoted by him may be removed from ecclesiastical ministries.

### CHAPTER 213.—Concerning the deposition of those who received only the imposition of hands from their bishop and the remaining blessing of orders from another presbyter. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 5.

The report of the deacon of Gabrena brought before our tribunal a matter concerning certain [three] clerics of that Church: when one was being consecrated to the presbyterate and two to the ministry of levites, their bishop, hindered by an illness of the eyes, is said only to have laid his hand upon them, while a certain presbyter gave them the blessing contrary to ecclesiastical [Col. 0388A] order. That presbyter, though he could have been condemned by the present judgment for such audacious presumption, if he had still been alive, had already been forestalled by the summons of death.

But since he has been left to divine judgment and cannot be accused before a human court, we decree concerning those who survive and received from him not the title of consecration but rather a badge of disgrace: lest such usurpation give itself license, they shall be deposed from the rank of priesthood or levitical order which they perversely obtained and cast out by an equitable judgment. For such persons have rightly been judged worthy of removal because they were wrongly appointed.

### CHAPTER 214.—That a bishop’s sentence has no force unless confirmed by the presence of his clergy. From the same council, chapter 23 (Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 32).

[Col. 0388B] (12, question 2, canon *Sine exceptione*.) A bishop’s sentence shall be void unless it is confirmed by the presence of his clergy.

### CHAPTER 215.—That a bishop should determine the number of clergy according to the revenues of the churches. And from the Council of Split, chapter 1.

A bishop should not indiscriminately create a multitude of clergy, but should regulate their number according to the means or revenues of the churches.

### CHAPTER 216.—Concerning visiting bishops. From the First Council of Arles, chapter 20.

Concerning visiting bishops accustomed to come into a city, whom we know truly to be bishops: it has been decided that they should be given a place in which to make the offering.

### CHAPTER 217.—That bishops wandering frivolously should be compelled to return to their own places. From Gregory’s Register, to Syagrius, Bishop of Autun, chapter 122 (Book VII, epistle 119, or chapter 117).

[Col. 0388C]

Since the dignity of a priest appears exalted, everyone adorned [ordained] with it ought to show himself an example to all, so that by his own example he may harm no one but rather be able to shape the life of those subject to him. For if conduct disagrees with the title, the more the pontificate raises a person, the more it casts him down [binds him over]. Thus we have learned that a certain Bishop Mennas, who went there from the diocese of our ordination [“from the diocese of the Roman Church by our ordination,” etc.], has shown himself so frivolous that we have greater shame on his account, and the name of bishopric is to him not an honor but a burden.

Because [Col. 0388D] it is a disgrace to us to learn of him things which we utterly censure in priests of other provinces, your brotherhood must not allow him to remain there longer, but must compel him to return to us as soon as possible. At every available opportunity send him on, so that, restrained under the discipline he deserves, he may endeavor to turn secular habits into priestly seriousness. For it is sufficiently harmful and destructive that those who ought to have been built up should be ruined by imitating him. In this matter not only he is culpable, but also anyone who has not resisted him; for the person who does not oppose errors that ought to be cut off appears to consent to the erring person.

Moreover, since it is asserted that a certain Bishop Theodore, of the diocese of our most reverend brother Constantius, Bishop of the Church of Milan, [Col. 0389A] has come there in order to avoid discipline, we urge that, after diligently investigating him also, your brotherhood should send him to his bishop. Since, as it is written, “He who rejects discipline is unhappy” (Wis. 3), do not allow him to remain there under any excuse, so that those who can be deceived by the fault of their frivolity may be freed, and you may obtain a reward for them by preventing their perishing through this folly.

### CHAPTER 218.—How long a bishop ought to remain in a foreign city. From the Council of Sardica, chapter 14.

Bishop Hosius said: You must also decree this: when a bishop comes from one city to another city and, serving ambition more than devotion, wishes to reside for a long time in the other city—perhaps because the bishop of the place is not [Col. 0389B] so well instructed or learned, while the visitor begins to despise him and frequently gives addresses in order to dishonor and weaken his standing—then, under this pretext, he may not hesitate to abandon the Church assigned to him and transfer himself to another … Therefore set limits of time. For it is inhumane not to receive a bishop, yet it is harmful if he remains too long. Provision must therefore be made to prevent this.

I remember that at an earlier council our brethren decreed that, if a layman had not attended the assembly in the city in which he lived for four Lord’s Days—that is, for three weeks—he should be deprived of communion. If these rules were enacted concerning laypeople, then all the more it is neither lawful nor fitting for a bishop, unless some necessity so grave detains him, to be absent from his Church for longer than the aforesaid [Col. 0389C] time. All declared that this pleased them.

### CHAPTER 219.—Concerning the reception of bishops suffering persecution. From the same source, chapter 21.

Bishop Hosius said: At the suggestion of our brother and fellow-bishop Olympius, this too has been approved: if anyone has suffered violence and has been unjustly expelled, fleeing dangers for the sake of discipline and Catholic confession or for the defense of truth, and comes innocent and devoted to another city, he must not be forbidden to remain until he can return or has received redress for the wrong done him. For it is harsh not to receive one who suffers persecution; indeed, generous goodwill and humanity must be shown him.

The whole synod [Col. 0389D] said: Let the Catholic Church throughout the whole world observe all that has been decreed. And all who had assembled subscribed.

### CHAPTER 220.—Concerning those who call themselves bishops. Council of Rheims, chapter 43 (Council of Chalon, chapter 43).

In certain places there are Scots and other errant persons who call themselves bishops and ordain many negligent persons as presbyters and deacons without the permission of their lords or masters. Since their ordination often falls into heresy [perhaps, “is heresy”] and is subject to many errors, we have unanimously decreed that it must in every way be rendered void.

### CHAPTER 221.—How visiting bishops are to be received. From Gregory’s Register, to all bishops beloved throughout Illyricum, chapter 42 (Book I, epistle 43).

[Col. 0390A]

Our most excellent son Jovinus has informed us in his letters through Illyricum that, by imperial rescripts sent out by him, bishops whom hostile violence had expelled from their own places were ordered to be attached, for support and the stipends of this present life, to those bishops who still remain in their own places. Although the imperial command already urges your brotherhood to this, we have a greater command concerning them from the eternal Ruler, by which we are compelled to carry this out with greater fear: that, when opportunity requires, we should love in providing assistance for bodily [Col. 0390B] necessities not only our brethren and fellow-bishops, but even those whom we endure as hostile to us.

You must therefore obey first the heavenly Ruler in this matter and also comply with imperial commands, so that you may gladly receive into shared ecclesiastical support, for consolation and fellowship, our brethren and fellow-bishops whom the distress of captivity and various necessities oppresses. This is not to give them a share in the communion of the episcopal throne or its dignity, but so that they may receive from the Church, according to its means, sufficient sustenance. Thus we prove that we love our neighbor in God and God in our neighbor. We grant them no authority in your Churches, but earnestly urge that you support them by your assistance alone.

### CHAPTER 222.—Unknown bishops or presbyters are not to be admitted to ministry before examination. From the Council of Rouen, chapter 23 [68].

In accordance with canonical caution, we decree that all unknown bishops or presbyters arriving from anywhere shall not be admitted to ecclesiastical ministry before synodal examination.

### CHAPTER 223.—That a bishop driven out by hostility should transfer to another vacant Church. From Gregory’s Register, to Bishop Angelus (Book II, chapter 25; to John, Bishop of Squillace).

(7, question 1, canon *Pastoralis officii*.) The care of pastoral office warns us to appoint proper priests to Churches left destitute, who ought to govern the Lord’s flock with pastoral solicitude. Therefore we have thought it necessary to appoint [Col. 0390D] you, John, bishop of the city of Lisbon, who have been taken captive by enemies, as cardinal priest in the Church of Squillace, so that you may fulfill, in view of future recompense, the care of souls once undertaken. Although the enemy’s threat has driven you from your own Church, you ought to govern another Church, vacant of a pastor—provided, however, that if, under the Lord’s protection, that city should be freed from enemies and restored to its former condition, you return to the Church in which you were first ordained. But if the aforesaid city remains oppressed by the continuing calamity of captivity, you ought to remain in the Church in which we have also incardinated you.

### CHAPTER 224.—Concerning bishops: that all people ought by right to obey them. From the decrees of Pope Clement, chapter 15 (epistle 1, far before the end).

[Col. 0391A]

Peter commanded all rulers of the earth and all people to obey bishops, bow their heads, and assist them, so that all might be shown alike to be faithful persons and fellow-workers in God’s law, lest it be said of them: “All who fight against you shall be confounded and ashamed; those who oppose you shall be as though they were not, and the men who contradict you shall perish. You shall seek your rebellious men and not find them. They shall be as though they were not, like the destruction of a man fighting against you” (Isa. 41). (11, question 3, canon *Si autem vobis contraveniunt*.) Accordingly, he declared all who oppose them condemned and infamous until satisfaction was made, and commanded that, unless they converted, they should be strangers [Col. 0391B] to the thresholds of the Church.

### CHAPTER 225.—That bishops are the keys of the Church. From the same decrees, chapter 37 (ibid., after the middle).

He taught that all ought to preserve the holy Church unstained, saying that bishops are its keys. For they have power to shut heaven and open its gates, because they have become the keys of heaven. He also warned that no one ought to harm them, because they are the eyes of the Lord, and whoever touches them is like one who touches the pupil of his eye (Zech. 2). He said that the Lord himself taught how great a punishment the person deserves who causes them to stumble, when he said: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea” (Matt. 18).

### CHAPTER 226.—That the Lord chose bishops to glorify him. From the same source, chapter 29 (ibid., far before the end).

[Col. 0391C]

The Lord chose bishops to glorify him and to sow and proclaim divine commands. He said that they should not be hindered or troubled, because whoever harms them harms him whose embassy they discharge. He urged them to preach continually and announce the commands of the Lord without interruption. He taught that they should show their good works before people and have a good conscience before God.

### CHAPTER 227.—Concerning bishops: that they ought to love one another. From the same source, chapter 30 (ibid., after the middle).

He said that the Lord taught bishops to govern in the place of the apostles, and indicated that presbyters ought to hold the place of the remaining [Col. 0391D] disciples. He preached that the gravest punishment should be imposed upon anyone who caused one of these to stumble. He taught that all ought to love and assist one another, and that no one should withdraw himself from helping a brother.

### CHAPTER 228.—Nor should one bishop trample upon another. From the First Council of Arles, chapter 17.

That no bishop should trample upon another or presume to accuse or injure him. If he does so, he shall be subject to forfeiture of his rank.

### CHAPTER 229.—Concerning bishops who withdraw themselves from the assistance of their brethren. From the decrees of Pope Alexander sent to all bishops, chapter 22 (epistle 2).

But whoever among your body flees [is] and withdraws himself from your aid will be proved more a schismatic [Col. 0392A] than a priest. “Behold,” says the Prophet, “how good and pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132). Those do not dwell in unity who withdraw themselves from the comfort of their brethren; and worse still are those who lay snares for brethren or prepare traps for them.

Again, a little later: Therefore we who are and desire to be called disciples of the Lord ought to carry the Lord’s cross and suffer with our brethren, not prepare for them whatever snares or pits we may; for the one who prepares a pit for brethren shall receive [deserve] retaliation. Do not be deceived, brethren: God is not mocked (Gal. 6). For this reason the Lord entrusted his Church to you: that you may labor for all and not neglect to bring aid to all the oppressed. Therefore the Lord also speaks through the prophet, saying: “Thus says [Col. 0392B] the Lord: Execute judgment in the morning, and rescue by force those oppressed from the hand of the slanderer, lest my indignation go forth like fire and be kindled, with none to quench it” (Jer. 21). You who have been placed by the Lord on the highest watchtower must therefore attend to and restrain those who stir up seditions and scandals among brethren, lest you perish together with them.

### CHAPTER 230.—Concerning bishops who gnaw one another with a dog’s tooth. From the same writer to the same persons, chapter 13 (the same epistle, shortly before).

But if—may it never be!—you are discordant and begin to gnaw one another with a dog’s tooth, you will not merely fail to overcome them, but will harm yourselves and be overcome by them, and perhaps perish disastrously.

### CHAPTER 231.—Concerning bishops who desire to harm their brethren. From the decrees of Pope Boniface.

[Col. 0392C]

As everyone who loves his brother is from God, so everyone who hates his neighbor is from the devil; for by love alone it is discerned from whom a person is shown to be begotten. John says: “In this the children of God and the children of the devil are manifest: everyone who does not do righteousness and does not love his brother is not from God. For this is the message which you heard from the beginning: that we should love one another” (1 John 3). And shortly afterward: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer; and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him” (ibid.).

Behold, the person separated from brotherly fellowship is convincingly declared a murderer. Even if he does not move his hand to kill, [Col. 0392D] nevertheless, because he is armed [savage; alternatively, “strives”] to harm, he is already held by God to be a murderer. The other lives, yet this man is convicted as already a killer. With these commands the blessed Apostle Paul agrees in harmonious teaching, saying: “Do not let the sun go down on your anger” (Eph. 4), and, “Do not give place to the devil” (ibid.).

Again: We have been informed that certain priests have become so heated in the discord of stubbornness that not only does sunset fail to recall them from anger, but not even the passage of many years inclines them to the good of charity; indeed, Christ himself, the same sun of righteousness, has set in their hearts, so that they can scarcely return to the light of charity [truth]. Therefore we judge that the offerings of these and similar discordant brethren must by no means be received, according to the ancient definition of the [Col. 0393A] canons. Yet we command a specific determination concerning the persons of those at variance: before true reconciliation binds them together, none of them may dare approach God’s altar or receive the grace of holy communion; rather, they shall make recompense by penance for twice the time during which they served discord.

But if one of them, though the other despises him, hastens to make satisfaction in charity, from that time he shall be received as peaceable within the Church, once it is established that he has hastened toward concord. Nevertheless, the foregoing sentence remains in force: he must repay in penitential satisfaction twice the time which he spent in anger.

### CHAPTER 232.—That bishops are to be judged by the Lord alone. From the decrees of Pope Clement, chapter 38.

[Col. 0393B] He said that bishops are to be judged or removed by the Lord alone, and not by others, because they belong to him and not to another. “Who are you to judge another’s servant?” For if human beings do not tolerate these things, neither does the God of heaven [gods] and Lord of lords tolerate them in any way. Therefore he said that the prophets were witnesses for him, through whom the Lord speaks: “Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty. For my own sake I shall act, that I may not be blasphemed, and I shall not give my glory to another” (Isa. 48).

### CHAPTER 233.—That it is greatly to be feared and guarded against that bishops be offended. From the decrees of Pope Evaristus sent to brethren throughout Egypt, chapter 6.

This judgment, brethren, is exceedingly to be feared; and you must take care [Col. 0393C] not to offend those who have received such great authority from the Lord. Therefore they ought rather to be obeyed and loved, not maligned, attacked, or expelled, but borne with and loved; for the Lord himself says: “He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10). Therefore, brethren, we write these things to you and to all the faithful, so that you may beware of such conduct and leave to your descendants not an evil but a good example; for injury done to bishops pertains to Christ, whose office they discharge.

### CHAP. 234.—That an accusation by the sheep against their bishop is not to be received. From the first letter of Pope Calixtus.

Calixtus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, to Benedict, brother and fellow-bishop: greeting in Christ. Let no one entertain accusations against a teacher, [Col. 0393D] because sons ought not rebuke fathers, nor servants attack their masters. All whom teachers instruct, therefore, are their sons; and, as children ought to love their bodily fathers, so should these love their spiritual fathers. For those do not live well who do not believe rightly, or who rebuke or malign their fathers. Teachers, therefore, who are also called Fathers, ought rather to be borne with than rebuked, unless they have erred in the true faith.

Accordingly, let no teacher be accused in writing; nor should he answer any accuser except one who is faithful and lawful, and who also leads an irreproachable life and manner of conduct. For it is unworthy that a teacher should answer, according to his folly, a foolish and unlearned person living reprehensibly; as Scripture says: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly” (Prov. 26). One does not live well [Col. 0394A] who does not believe rightly. A faithful person wills no evil. If anyone is faithful, let him take care neither to speak falsely nor to lay snares for anyone. A faithful person always acts faithfully; but the unfaithful person craftily lays snares and strives to destroy those who are faithful and who live piously and justly, because like seeks its like. The unfaithful person, moreover, is dead in a living body; whereas the words of a faithful person preserve the life of those who hear them.

A Catholic teacher, and especially a priest of the Lord, ought no more to be entangled in any error than to be assailed by any intrigue or greed. Holy Scripture says: “Do not follow your desires, and turn away from your own will” (Ecclus. 18).

### CHAP. 235.—That an unjust judgment made at the command of a king, bishop, or any powerful person is to be held void. The same authority, a little later.

[Col. 0394B]

Whatever is irreproachable, the Catholic Church defends. No emperor, nor anyone who keeps piety, may presume anything contrary to the divine commands. Therefore an unjust judgment or unjust decision, ordered or carried out by judges through royal fear or command, or through that of any bishop or powerful person, shall have no force.

For a religious person it ought to be too little merely not to exercise or increase the enmities of others by speaking ill, unless he also strives to extinguish them by speaking well. Humble confession in evil deeds is better than proud boasting in good ones.

### CHAP. 236.—That no one may usurp another’s boundaries, or judge or excommunicate another’s parishioner. The same, in his second decretal.

[Col. 0394C] Let no one usurp another’s boundaries, nor presume to judge or excommunicate another’s parishioner; for such a judgment, excommunication, or condemnation shall neither be valid nor possess any force, since no one shall be bound or condemned by the sentence of a judge other than his own. Therefore the Lord speaks, saying: “Do not remove the ancient boundaries which your fathers set” (Prov. 22).

### CHAP. 237.—Who ought not to be admitted to make accusations or give testimony against bishops. Pope Anacletus, third after Peter, in his first decretal, to all bishops.

Our blessed predecessor Clement, an apostolic man and filled with the Spirit of God, together with his other holy colleagues, decreed as follows: Permission to accuse or testify [Col. 0394D] shall be denied to those who have neglected the dignity of the Christian religion and name, the rule of their own law or profession, or things forbidden by rule. For a voluntary transgressor of his own law, and those who violate it, are called apostates. Every apostate must be rejected before his return, and must not be received for an accusation against those who act rightly or for testimony.

We know, moreover, that many harass teachers in order to destroy them and fulfill the pleasures of their own will. Nevertheless, teachers ought not, so far as their strength permits, to depart from right zeal and good intention, knowing that “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5). Nothing is more miserable than that shepherd who glories in the praise of wolves. If he wishes to please them [Col. 0395A] and chooses to be loved by them, great destruction will thereby come upon the sheep. No shepherd, therefore, can please wolves and flocks of sheep alike. Those who offer sacrifice perfectly to God ought not to be vexed, but borne with, consoled, and venerated by all.

### CHAP. 238.—The same matter stated more expressly. The same, in his second decretal, to the bishops of Italy.

(2, q. 7, c. *Accusatio*.) The accusation concerning which you asked our counsel must be made only by suitable and thoroughly approved men, free from suspicions and crimes. For the Lord did not wish the ministers of his sacred body to be defamed or calumniated by base, rejected, and unsuitable persons; rather, he himself cast sinful priests out of the temple with his own scourge. Hence it is clear that the high priests—that is, bishops—are to be judged by God; they are not to be attacked by men, or by persons of depraved life, but rather borne with by faithful people. The Lord himself set the example when he personally, and not through another, cast from the temple the priests who were selling and buying (Matt. 21).
