For, I think, none among us would wish his servant to be judged by anyone other than himself. If this were presumed, he would either become greatly angry in indignation or rather seek vengeance upon that person. Therefore the Lord says through the prophet: “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zech. 2).

And a little later: If detractors of any persons are severely judged and fall into the snare of destruction, much more are the attackers, detractors, and accusers of God’s servants condemned; [Col. 0395C] unless they amend themselves and do worthy penance by suitable satisfaction to those persons, they undoubtedly go into the abyss and are burned in avenging flames.

Considering these and other dangers, the apostles decreed that the pillars of God’s holy Church—who are rightly called apostles and their successors—should not lightly be disturbed, attacked, or accused. But if anyone has been stirred up against them or their churches, or has grounds for complaint, let him first have recourse to them in a spirit of charity or in private conversation, so that they may heal what has been disturbed and charitably amend whatever they recognize ought justly to be amended. But if any persons presume, before doing this, to attack, accuse, or harass them, let them be excommunicated and by no means absolved until they have done worthy penance by satisfaction, as has already been stated; for injury to them pertains to Christ, whose embassy they discharge.

Likewise: As was mentioned above, the Lord reserved to himself the expulsion of high priests, although he granted their election to good priests and spiritual peoples.

### CHAP. 239.—That those who were enemies the day before yesterday, or three days ago, cannot be accusers and witnesses. The same, in his third decretal.

(3, q. 5, c. *Accusatores*.) Those who were enemies the day before yesterday or three days ago cannot be accusers or witnesses, lest in anger they desire to harm, or, having been injured, wish to avenge themselves. Therefore an unoffended disposition in accusers and witnesses must be sought, not a suspect one.

[Col. 0396A] And somewhat below: Those, indeed, who corrupt the life and morals of superiors are worse than those who ruin the property and estates of others. They are condemned by the judgment upon Ham, Noah’s son: like Ham, who did not cover his father’s nakedness but exposed it for mockery (Gen. 9). If a shepherd of the Church departs from the faith, he is to be corrected by the faithful; but on account of blameworthy morals he is rather to be tolerated than harshly dealt with, for the rulers of the Church are to be judged by God, as the Prophet says: “God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he judges gods” (Ps. 81).

Likewise: Both priests and all the remaining faithful ought to take the greatest care for those who perish, so that through their rebuke they may either be corrected from their sins or, [Col. 0396B] if they prove incorrigible, be separated from the Church.

### CHAP. 240.—That a bishop is not to be reproved or accused by the people or by common persons. Pope Evaristus to the bishops of Africa (letter 2).

(2, q. 7, c. *Non est a plebe*.) A bishop, even if he is disorderly, is not therefore to be reproved or accused by the people or by common persons; for the life of rulers is ordered according to the merits of their subjects. Therefore, if there are any revilers or accusers of bishops or other priests, they ought not to be heard by the judges of the Church until the suspicion or reputation concerning their standing has been examined: with what intention, faith, rashness, manner of life, conscience, or merit they presumed these things—whether for God’s sake, or for vain [Col. 0396C] glory, enmity, hatred, or greed.

And a little later: (2, q. 7, c. *Deus omnipotens*.) Almighty God, in order to restrain us from precipitately pronouncing judgment, although all things are naked and open to his eyes, nevertheless did not wish to judge the evils of the Sodomites merely upon hearing them, before he had manifestly learned whether what was said was true. Hence he himself says: “I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the outcry which has come to me; and if not, I shall know” (Gen. 18). Almighty God, from whom nothing is hidden, but to whom all things are manifest even before they occur, deigned personally to investigate these matters and many others—which we have not inserted here to avoid prolixity—for no other reason than to give us an example, so that we might not be hasty in examining and judging cases.

### CHAP. 241.—On a confession extorted by force. Pope Alexander, fifth after Peter, in his first decretal sent to all bishops.

[Col. 0396D]

If any writings have in any way been extorted from priests or agents of the Church through fear, fraud, or force, or have been written or devised by them through any contrivance in order that they might free themselves, we judge that they are of no force to their prejudice or injury. Nor do we permit them ever, by the authority of God and the holy apostles and their successors, to suffer from them any infamy, calumny, or separation from their goods.

A little later: In such matters confession must not be compelled but voluntary; for every confession made from necessity is not faith. Accordingly, in such matters a confession must not be extorted, but must be made voluntarily [profiteri, “professed”]. For it is most wicked to judge anyone from suspicion or an extorted confession, since the Lord is more the examiner of the heart than of the deed.

A little later: A person whom the Lord has reserved for his own judgment cannot be condemned by human examination. For if all things were avenged in this world, divine judgments would have no place.

And a little later: I think that no evil is worse than Christians’ envy of their own priests.

### CHAP. 242.—In what order primates or other judges are to be approached. The same.

If anyone believes that he has any just complaint against a bishop or the agents of a church, he should not first approach primates or other judges, but should meet privately with those [Col. 0397B] by whom he believes himself injured—not once, but very frequently—in order to receive either justice or an explanation from them. If he acts otherwise, let him be deprived of communion by them and by others, as one who despises the apostles and the other Fathers.

### CHAP. 243.—That neither sheep may rebuke their shepherd, nor the people accuse their bishop, nor the crowd charge him. Pope Pius (I), ninth after Peter, to all Churches.

(6, q. 1, c. *Oves pastorem*.) Let sheep not rebuke their shepherd, let the people not accuse their bishop, and let not the crowd charge him; for “a disciple is not above his master” (Matt. 10). Bishops, whom God chose as his own eyes, are to be judged by God. They are not to be reproved, accused, or attacked by subjects [Col. 0397C] or persons of depraved life.

And in what follows: No one who does good wishes to harm another in word or deed. How much less should a faithful person come under suspicion of saying or doing what he himself does not wish to suffer? For every suspicion ought rather to be rejected than approved or received.

Likewise the same, in his second decretal: (17, q. 4, cap. *Sicut qui Ecclesiam*.) As one who ravages the Church of God and plunders and seizes its estates and gifts becomes sacrilegious, so also one who persecutes its priests is held guilty of sacrilege and is judged sacrilegious. And as a sin committed against God is graver than one committed against a human being, so committing sacrilege is graver than fornication.

A little later: (11, q. 1, c. *Si quis sacerd.*) If any priest or other cleric is disobedient to his bishop, lays snares for him, or brings insult or calumny against him, and can be convicted, let him immediately be handed over to the court and receive the penalty for his unjust deed.

### CHAP. 244.—On avoiding uncertain judgments, and that not even true matters are to be believed unless proved by certain indications and made public in judicial order. Pope Victor to the brethren living at Alexandria (letter 1, ch. 2).

We have heard that various judgments are made among you and yours, and that uncertain matters are judged. Dearest brethren, let us by no means judge uncertain matters, until the Lord comes, who will bring hidden things into the light, illuminate the concealed things of darkness, and reveal the counsels of hearts (1 Cor. 4). For although they may be true, they are nevertheless not to be believed [Col. 0398A] unless they are established by manifest indications, proved by manifest judgment, and made public in judicial order.

Likewise, a little later: (These matters occur above, ch. 4.) It has been decreed that a bishop accused or judged by fellow-provincial bishops in some case may freely appeal and approach the pontiff of the Apostolic See, who shall arrange for his case to be reconsidered either personally or through his representatives. While the pontiff is hearing his case in a renewed judgment, no other bishop is to be put in his place or ordained, because, although fellow-provincial bishops may examine the case of an accused bishop, they are not permitted to decide it without consulting the Roman pontiff.

And elsewhere it is read in the Apostolic statutes (Clement, letter 1): If anyone considers himself oppressed by his own metropolitan, let him be judged before the patriarch [Col. 0398B] or primate of the diocese, or before the see of the universal Apostolic Church. Such presumption, brethren, is nothing other than transgressing the boundaries of the apostles and their predecessors [variant: “successors”] and violating their decrees.

### CHAP. 245.—How a bishop is to be judged, and by how many witnesses he is to be convicted. Pope Zephyrinus, fourteenth after Peter, in his first decretal, to all bishops throughout Sicily.

(2, q. 1, c. *Primates accusatum*.) Patriarchs or primates examining an accused bishop shall not pronounce a final sentence until, supported by apostolic authority, either he has confessed himself guilty or has been convicted by innocent witnesses examined according to rule. Their number must be no fewer than those disciples whom the Lord commanded to be chosen to assist the apostles—namely, seventy-two.

(3, q. 4, c. *Detractores*.) We also exclude from episcopal accusation or testimony detractors, who by divine authority must be rooted out, and instigators [variant: “agents”] of enemies. Let no one of the higher rank be assailed or ruined by the accusations of inferiors; let no certain sentence be judged in a doubtful matter; and let no judgment be held valid unless it has been conducted in due order.

(3, q. 9, c. *Absens vero*.) Let no one be judged in absence, for both divine and human laws forbid this. Their accusers must be wholly free from suspicion, because the Lord wished his pillars to stand firm, not to be shaken by anyone whatsoever. For no sentence not pronounced by his own judge may bind any one of them, since the laws of the world likewise command this.

(5, q. 4, c. *Duodecim*.) If necessary, any accused bishop may choose twelve judges, by whom his case may be judged justly. Nor may he be heard, excommunicated, or judged until they have been selected by himself, and, after he has been duly summoned first to an assembly of his own bishops, his case is justly heard and reasonably determined by them. The final disposition of his case, however, shall be referred to the Apostolic See, to be decided there.

### CHAP. 246.—That despoiled bishops need not answer unless the property taken from them is first restored. The same, in his second decretal to the brethren throughout Egypt.

It has been reported to the Apostolic See through your *apocrisiarii* [envoys] that certain of our brethren, namely bishops, are being expelled from their churches and proper sees, their furnishings [Col. 0399A] taken from them, and then summoned to judgment naked and despoiled. This is wholly without reason, since the enactments of the apostles and their successors, the commands of emperors, and the constitutions of laws alike forbid it, and the authority of the Apostolic See prohibits it from being done.

Accordingly, it is commanded in ancient statutes that expelled bishops and those despoiled of their possessions should regain their own churches; that all their goods should first be returned to them; and only then, if anyone wishes justly to accuse them, that this should be done at equal risk. It is decreed that the judges are bishops who act rightly [variant: “wisely”] and assemble in the Church, where the witnesses of each person who appeared oppressed are present. Nor ought they to answer before all their goods have been restored in the most complete legal manner to them and to their churches.

### CHAP. 247.—That persons unjustly condemned must be restored. Pope Sixtus, twenty-third after Peter, in his second decretal to the brethren throughout Spain.

[Col. 0399B]

(22, q. 3, c. *Fratres quos*.) Know that the brethren whom you unjustly condemned through earthly fear have been justly restored by us. By the authority of Saint Peter and apostolic authority, we command that everything taken from them be returned to them in full, unless you wish both yourselves and your rulers to be separated from our college and from the members of the Church.

For by the just judgment of God, authority by which sinners persecute his saints is often granted to those sinners, so that those who are aided and guided by the Spirit of God may become more illustrious through trials of suffering. Yet those who do this by no means escape punishment, because, as the Lord says: “Woe to him through whom scandal comes” (Matt. 18).

Likewise, a little later: Let us not judge uncertain matters until the Lord comes, who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts (1 Cor. 4). And although they may be true, they are nevertheless not to be believed unless established by certain indications, proved by manifest judgment, and made public in judicial order. No one, therefore, may be condemned by human examination whom God has reserved for his own judgment. All these things must be most carefully guarded against, lest we seem presumptuous.

Nor is an accusation against bishops to be readily received, for the Lord says: “Do not receive a lying report” (Exod. 23); and the Apostle says: “An accusation against an elder is not to be received except on the evidence of two or three suitable witnesses” (1 Tim. 5). If these precautions apply to presbyters [Col. 0399D] or the other faithful, how much more do they apply to bishops?

### CHAP. 248.—That a bishop need not answer the charges of accusers or come to a council unless property taken from him is first restored; and what sort of persons accusers ought to be. Bishop Felix, to the bishops of Gaul, in his second decretal.

(3, q. 2, c. *Si episcopus suis fuerit*.) If a bishop has been despoiled of his own goods or those of the Church entrusted to him, or—God forbid, a thing which ought to be alien to all the faithful—has been expelled from his own see, or separated from his flock by some detention, then he must first be restored canonically to his former condition with every privilege of his rank; and all things taken from him through the plots of his enemies [Col. 0400A] must be restored in full according to law. He cannot be summoned or judged unless he himself chooses of his own accord to appear for his own necessity, though in no way to be judged.

Therefore, no one whatsoever may compel him before all that he had lost through the instigations of his enemies has been restored in the legal order to his control by an honorable council. The bishop must be restored with all honor to his former condition; and after he has freely and securely possessed his goods for a considerable time, arranging and regulating them, then, within four, five, or seven months according to his ability, and not before, let him be summoned at the appointed time to a lawful and canonical council, to answer the charges of his accusers, if this seems just.

Likewise: If both parties come together to state their case—for one should not be heard without the other—it must be investigated in court what manner of life, faith, and reputation the accusers have, and with what intention they act. They must not be admitted unless they are men of good conduct and sound faith, wholly free from suspicion, distinguished by the reputation of a good life, and not infamous.

(3, q. 10, c. *Si accusatorum*.) But if the persons of the accusers appear blameworthy in the judgment of bishops, let them not be admitted to bring charges, unless they wish to assert their own causes, though not criminal or ecclesiastical ones.

(3, q. 7, c. *Infamis persona*.) For an infamous person can be neither procurator nor legal representative.

(3, q. 9, c. *Absente adversario*.) When the opposing party is absent, the accuser must not be heard; nor shall a judgment pronounced by a judge while the other party is absent have any validity.

(3, q. 9, c. *Absens per alium*.) Nor can an absent person accuse or be accused through another, nor may a related witness be admitted. No one, therefore, ought to be brought from province to province or before the imperial court, except upon referral by the judge to whom an appeal has been made—that is, the plaintiff must always follow the defendant’s forum.

(2, q. 6, c. *Si quis judicem*.) But if anyone believes that a judge is opposed to him, let him make an appeal, which must be denied to no one.

(3, q. 6, c. *Peregrina*.) We prohibit foreign tribunals by general enactment, because it is unworthy that one should be judged by outsiders who ought to have fellow-provincial judges chosen by himself.

### CHAP. 249.—That bishops summoned to a council ought not come until they have had as much time as they were deprived of their churches or goods. Pope Eusebius, in his second decretal, to the brethren throughout Alexandria and Egypt.

[Col. 0400D]

(2, q. 2, c. *In scripturis*.) In your writings we have found that certain bishops in your regions have been accused by their own flocks—some, indeed, on suspicion and others on definite grounds—and that some have consequently been despoiled of their goods, while others have been driven from their own sees. Know that they can neither be summoned to a fellow-provincial or general synod, nor judged in any matter, before everything taken from them has been restored to their control according to law.

(5, q. 2, c. *Prius ergo*.) First, therefore, all things must be restored to them by law, and the churches taken from them restored with every privilege; afterward, they must be granted not a narrow interval of time, but as much time as they appear to have been despoiled or expelled, before they are summoned to a synod and heard by all the bishops of their province. For a person who has been despoiled or expelled cannot be summoned to trial or judged, because a person already stripped bare has no privilege by which he can be despoiled.

Therefore it was anciently decreed that, before the contestation of a suit, the possessor or chief recipient must restore to the owner all possessions, everything taken from him, and all fruits received.

Likewise: (12, q. 2, c. *In antiquis*.) It is decreed in the ancient statutes of the Church that one who seizes another’s property shall not go unpunished but shall restore everything with multiplication. Hence it is written in the Gospel: “If I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19). And secular laws provide: “Whoever steals another’s property shall restore elevenfold to the person whose property was plundered what was taken.”

### CHAP. 250.—That bishops are not to be reproved by their sheep unless they err in faith. From the letter of Pope Anacletus written to all priests of Christ, ch. 1 (letter 3).

But if a teacher or shepherd of the Church departs from the faith, he is to be corrected by the faithful; but because of blameworthy morals he is rather to be tolerated than harshly treated, because rulers of Churches are to be judged by the Lord, as the Prophet says: “God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he judges gods” (Ps. [Col. 0401C] 81).

Therefore, if any faithful person sees or learns that his people are swelling up against their shepherd, or that the clergy [variant: “the clergy,” alternatively “against the clergy”] are occupied with detractions, he should strive, so far as he can, to root out and prudently correct this vice. If they prove incorrigible, he must not presume to associate with them in any business before they have been reconciled to their teacher. For both priests and all the remaining faithful ought to take the greatest care for those who perish, so that through their rebuke they may either be corrected from their sins or, if they prove incorrigible, separated from the Church.

### CHAP. 251.—On the same matter. From the decretals of Pope Clement (letter 1).

If bishops themselves depart from the proper way, they are not to be reproved or charged by these persons, but borne with, unless they err in faith. Thus these are above those, not those above these, because a greater person cannot be reproved or judged by a lesser. Let no one exalt himself against his teachers and masters, because a disciple cannot and ought not be above his master (Matt. 10). Let no one wish to be called holy before he is so; but let him first be holy, so that he may be called so more truthfully. It is necessary daily to fulfill the commands of the Lord and the deeds of teachers and masters, and to pray in Christ’s name for one’s enemies.

### CHAP. 252.—On the same matter. From the letter of Pope Eusebius, ch. 20 (Anacletus, letter 3, ch. 5).

It is necessary that rulers be feared by their subjects and corrected by them, so that those who do not fear divine judgments may fear to sin through human fear. [Col. 0402A] (6, q. 1, c. *Deteriores*.) Those who corrupt the life and morals of teachers are worse than those who plunder the property and estates of others. The latter take away things outside us, though they are ours; but our detractors, corrupters of our morals, and those who arm themselves against us properly deceive us ourselves. Therefore they are justly infamous and deservedly become exiles from the Church.

### CHAP. 253.—That those who rebuke the life of prelates and malign their conduct are infamous. From the decretals of Pope Caius, ch. 7 (Eusebius, letter 2 to the bishops of Alexandria).

The sheep entrusted to their shepherd ought neither to rebuke him unless he departs from the true faith, nor can they accuse him in any manner, because the deeds [Col. 0402B] of shepherds are not to be struck with the sword of the mouth, even though they appear deserving of rebuke.

### CHAP. 254.—On bishops not to be reproved. From the decretals of Pope Evaristus sent to all brethren throughout Egypt, ch. 18.

(3, q. 2, c. *Audivimus*.) We have heard that certain bishops have been defamed and attacked by you, driven from their own cities—for bishops cannot be established elsewhere except in cities of no small importance—and that others have been established in those places while the former bishops are still alive. Therefore we write these things to you so that you may know that this must not be done, but that the proper bishops ought to be recalled and restored in full.

But those who hold their spouses—which we understand by the established terminology also to be their wives—in adulterous defilement, we command to be expelled as adulterers and made infamous, and to be excluded from ecclesiastical honors. If, however, you have any complaint against them, after these matters have been accomplished it must be investigated and concluded by the authority of this holy See.

### CHAP. 255.—On bishops defamed, attacked, and expelled from their own cities without Roman authority. From the decretals of Pope Stephen to all bishops, ch. 65 (letter 2, ch. 1).

No bishop, while despoiled of his goods or driven from his own see for any reason, ought to be accused, nor may a charge be brought against him by anyone, before he has been restored in full, all things taken from him by whatever contrivance have been restored according to law, and he himself has been restored in due order to his own see and former condition. Thus the primates and synod must wholly restore, before an accusation is formally brought, to the bishop concerned all possessions, all estates unjustly taken from him, and all fruits; for not only ecclesiastical laws but also the laws of the world prohibit this from being done otherwise.

Nor may any agent [variant: “author”] or defender of one of them or of their churches be accused by anyone before he has been approached charitably two or three times by those who consider themselves injured or wish to rebuke them for some faults, in order that he may receive from them either a private amendment or a just explanation. Whoever presumes otherwise shall be excluded from the thresholds of the Church until worthy satisfaction is made.

### CHAP. 256.—That a bishop despoiled of his goods is not to be judged. From the decretals of Pope Felix sent to the bishops throughout Egypt, ch. 10.

(2, q. 2, c. *Nullus episcop.*) No bishop who has been despoiled of his goods or driven from his own see by force or terror can be accused, summoned, judged, or condemned before everything taken from him has been restored by law, he has peacefully enjoyed his honors for a year or more, and has been restored in due order to his own see, according to canonical institution.

### CHAP. 257.—That accused bishops may freely appeal to the Apostolic See, and that they cannot be judged without the Roman pontiff or his representative. From the decretals of Pope Julius sent to the eastern bishops, ch. 18. (Sixtus II has this in letter 1.)

(2, q. 6, c. *Omnes episcopi*.) Let all bishops who are accused or charged in certain graver cases, whenever necessary, freely appeal to the Apostolic See and flee to it as to a mother, so that they may be piously supported, defended, and delivered by it, as has always been the case. Ancient authority of the apostles, their successors, and the canons has reserved to its disposition all greater and ecclesiastical causes and judgments of bishops. For bishops are blameworthy if they act toward their brethren otherwise than the pope of that See has decreed should be done.

It has been decreed that a bishop accused or judged by fellow-provincial bishops in some case may freely appeal and approach the pontiff of the Apostolic See, who shall arrange for his case to be reconsidered either personally or through his representatives. While the pontiff [Col. 0403C] hears his case in a renewed judgment, no other bishop is to be substituted, installed, or ordained in his place. For although fellow-provincial bishops may examine the case of an accused bishop, they are not permitted to decide it without consulting the Roman pontiff, since the Lord said to the blessed apostle Peter—not to any other, but to Peter himself—“Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 16).

(2, q. 6, c. *Si quis putaverit*.) If anyone considers himself oppressed by his own metropolitan, let him be judged before the primate of the diocese or before the pope [variant: “see”] of the universal Apostolic Church. Accusations which the laws of the world do not admit, we also unanimously exclude, lest impiety arise through lax proof, whereas the sentence of judgment ought to be right in its reading.

If anyone believes that he has a personal case against a bishop or agents [variant: “authors”] of a church, let him not approach judges before having recourse to them in a spirit of charity, so that, being admonished in private conversation, they may heal matters brought forward as grounds of complaint. If he acts otherwise, let him be deprived of communion.

Henceforth let no pontiff presume to excommunicate any bishop despoiled of his goods or expelled from his see, because a person already stripped bare has no privilege by which he can be despoiled. In the same terms we decree that an accuser who presents a case while the opposing party is absent is not to be believed before both parties have been heard, and that accusers or witnesses who are unsuitable are not to be admitted.

It has been decreed that, if an accused or condemned bishop appeals to the Roman pontiff, that which he judges justly shall be established. We judge infamous all who arm themselves against the Fathers, and we hold that those who associate with enemies are not to be received for accusation or testimony. It has been decreed that, in accusations against clerics, the person, faith, life, and conduct of the slanderers must always first be investigated. For faith must precede all human acts, since one doubtful in faith is unfaithful. No confidence at all is to be placed in those who do not know the faith of truth and do not lead a life of upright conduct, because such persons readily and indiscriminately attack and accuse those living rightly and piously. Therefore their suspicion must first be examined and corrected; nor should accusations be believed that are suspect or that proceed from the households of enemies.

### Chapter 258.—That the case of a bishop who has been assailed is to be judged by episcopal judges. From the Council of Spalato, chapter 8 (Spalato I).

If any bishop is attacked by anyone, or if he himself brings forward some question, the case shall be judged [settled] by episcopal judges—whether those appointed for them by their primates or neighbouring bishops chosen by their own agreement.

### Chapter 259.—That no one may challenge episcopal judges. Likewise from the same council, chapter 9.

No one may challenge the episcopal judges whom they have chosen by common agreement. Whoever is proved, through obstinacy, unwilling to obey the judges, once this has been proved to the bishop of the first see, shall give letters ordering that no bishop communicate with him until he obeys.

### Chapter 260.—That bishops of the same province are not to allow foreign tribunals. From the decrees of Pope Fabian sent to Bishop Hilary, chapter 26 (Epistle 3, chapter 2).

(3, question 6, chapter *Peregrina judicia*.) While preserving in all respects the authority of the Apostolic See, we prohibit foreign tribunals by a general enactment. It is improper that a person should be judged by outsiders when he ought to have judges from his own province and chosen by himself, unless an appeal has been made. Therefore, if any bishop is accused of particular crimes, he must be heard by all the bishops of his province, because an accused person ought not to be heard anywhere other than in his own forum.

### Chapter 261.—That a bishop charged with a crime may freely appeal to the Apostolic See if he regards the judge as suspect. From the decrees of the same pope, to the same bishop.

[Col. 0404D]

(2, question 6, chapters *Liceat* and *Si quis*.) If any bishop regards his judge as suspect and sees himself being oppressed, let him freely appeal to the Apostolic See. No affliction or injurious detention [deception] in custody shall be imposed upon one appealing; rather, the appellant may remedy a prejudiced case through the relief of appeal. It is also permissible to appeal in criminal cases, and the right of appeal shall not be denied to one whom a sentence has consigned to punishment.

### Chapter 262.—By how many bishops a bishop, presbyter, or deacon is to be heard. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 12 (Carthage II under Siricius, chapter 10).

(15, question 7, chapter *Felix episcopus*.) Bishop Felix said (3, question 8, chapter *Suggero*): “In accordance with the rulings of the ancient councils, I propose [Col. 0405A] that, if any bishop—though we do not wish it—falls into some accusation, and has an urgent necessity such that he cannot assemble many bishops, then, lest he remain under the charge, he shall be heard by twelve bishops; a presbyter by seven bishops together with his own bishop; and a deacon by three.”

### Chapter 263.—Concerning a bishop, if bishops of the same province disagree in examining him. From the Council of Antioch, chapter 14 (Antioch I under Julius I).

If a bishop is judged concerning particular crimes, and it happens that the bishops of the same province disagree concerning him—so that he is believed innocent by some who have judged him but considered guilty by others—then, to resolve this uncertainty, the holy synod decreed that the metropolitan bishop should summon other judges from a neighbouring province [Col. 0405B] to remove the dispute, and that, through them together with the bishops of the same province, whatever appears just should be approved.

### Chapter 264.—That no layperson may dare bring a charge against bishops or anyone in holy orders. From the decrees of Pope Sylvester, chapter 1 (in the epilogue of the Second Roman Council under Sylvester).

(2, question 7, chapter *Nullus laicus*.) By the agreement and subscription of all it was established that no layperson may bring any accusation against a bishop or anyone in holy orders. Nor may a presbyter bring a charge against a bishop, a deacon against a presbyter, a subdeacon against a deacon, an acolyte against a subdeacon, an exorcist against an acolyte, a reader against an exorcist, or a doorkeeper against a reader. Nor shall [Col. 0405C] a prelate be condemned except on the testimony of seventy-two qualified witnesses.

### Chapter 265.—That bishops must be the judges of bishops who are accused. From the decrees of Pope Damasus, chapter 3.

We decree that the judges of accused bishops shall be bishops who are wise and live justly and uprightly.

### Chapter 266.—Concerning the lawful summons of an accused bishop. From an epistle of the same pope to Stephen and to the Council of Africa (Epistle 4, chapter 4).

(5, question 2, chapter *Vocatio ad synodum*.) In accordance with the canonical decrees of the Fathers, the summons to a synod of one who is being charged must be made by reasonable written notices over a suitable and canonical period. For unless he has been summoned canonically, at the proper time and in the canonical manner, [Col. 0405D] even if necessity of whatever kind brings him to the assembly, he shall in no way answer his plotters unless he wishes to do so voluntarily. For not even secular laws permit this; how much less do divine laws?

### Chapter 267.—That primates shall not pronounce a sentence of condemnation upon an accused bishop before he either confesses himself guilty or is canonically convicted by innocent witnesses. From an epistle of Pope Felix sent to Bishop Paternus, chapter 4 (Felix I, Epistle 1).

(2, question 1, chapter *Primates*.) Likewise, let primates examining an accused bishop not pronounce a sentence of condemnation before, relying on apostolic authority, he either confesses himself guilty or is lawfully convicted through innocent witnesses examined according to canon. Otherwise we judge the condemnation of bishops to be invalid and unjust, and therefore to be reconsidered by the synod, [Col. 0406A] so that in every case assistance may be given in all respects to the oppressed.

### Chapter 268.—How and where a primate is to be appointed. From the register of Gregory to Gennadius, patrician and exarch of Africa (book I, Epistle 73).

The council of Catholic bishops is instructed that it is not to make a primate according to the rank of the place while disregarding the merits of his life; for with the Lord not the more splendid rank, but the conduct of the better life, is approved. The primate himself shall reside, not indiscriminately through villages as is customary, but in one city, according to their election.

### Chapter 269.—That the bishops of each people should know who among them is first. From an epistle of Pope Anacletus to all bishops (Epistle 3, chapter 3).

(Distinction 22, chapter *Sacrosancta*.) The blessed apostles also established among [Col. 0406B] themselves that the bishops of each people should know who among them was first, so that their greater concern might belong to him. For there was a certain distinction among the blessed apostles. Although all were apostles, nevertheless primacy was granted by the Lord to Peter. They themselves wished that Cephas—that is, Peter—should preside over all the other apostles, so that Peter might hold the primacy of the apostolate; for they handed down the same model to be observed by their successors and by the other bishops.

This was established not only in the New Testament but also in the Old Testament. Hence it is written: “Moses and Aaron among his priests” (Psalm XCVIII [98]); that is, they were first among them. Yet, although it is so ordained, no one should seek what is his own, but what belongs to another; therefore the blessed Apostle Paul says: “Let each one please his neighbour for his good, unto edification” (Romans XV [15]). And as the Saviour himself says to his apostles: “He who is greater among you shall be your servant” (Matthew XX [20]; Mark X [10]); and so forth.

### Chapter 270.—That an accused bishop is not to be deprived of communion unless he refuses to appear on the appointed day. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 8 (Carthage III, chapter 7).

(4, question 5, chapter *Quisquis primates*.) Bishop Aurelius said: “Whoever of the bishops is accused, the accuser shall bring the case before the primate of that province. The person against whom a charge is made shall not be suspended from communion unless, summoned by letter to state his case on an appointed day before chosen judges, he fails altogether to appear—that is, within one month from the day on which it is established that he received the letter.

“If he proves any genuine [true] necessity that clearly made it impossible for him to appear, he shall have full opportunity to state his case within another month. But after the second month [for so long], he shall not communicate until he has been examined [cleared]. If he refuses to appear at a general council within the space of a year, so that his case may at least be concluded there, he shall be judged to have pronounced a sentence of condemnation upon himself. During the time when he does not communicate, neither shall he communicate in his own church or parish.

“But if his accuser has never been absent on the days for stating the case, he shall not be removed from communion; if, however, he has at any time been absent by withdrawing himself, then, once the bishop has been restored to communion, the accuser himself shall be removed from communion. Nevertheless, he shall not be deprived of the opportunity to carry through the case if he proves that he did not refuse, but was unable, to appear on the appointed day.

“It was further resolved that, when he begins proceedings before the judgment of bishops, if the accuser’s person is blameworthy, he shall not be admitted to prosecute—unless he wishes to assert his own cases, though not ecclesiastical ones.”

### Chapter 271.—Concerning Bishop Maximus, defamed by various crimes and repeatedly summoned to a synod, who neglected to appear and excuse himself. From the second epistle of Pope Boniface to the bishops of Gaul.

Bishop Boniface, to Patroclus, Remigius, Maximus, Hilary, Severus, Valerius, Julian, Castorius, Leontius, Constantine, John, Montanus, Marinus [Mauritius], and [Col. 0407B] the other bishops established throughout Gaul and the Seven Provinces.

The clergy of the city of Valence approached us, presenting a petition and crimes which, with the whole province as witness, they assert Maximus has committed. They report that, although an investigation had been delegated so many times, he had always evaded the appointed tribunals; nor, trusting his conscience, had he hastened—if innocent—to clear himself once all matters had been examined. We have learned from the records of your [our] documents that these proceedings were so often decreed.

On the contrary, he has proved against himself the things alleged, because, to refute them, though they were innumerable, a provincial inquiry was delegated by my predecessors [to him]. He is also said to have avoided the assembly and to have been wholly unwilling to attend. No one doubts that the guilty person evades judgment just as the innocent person seeks it in order to be acquitted. Yet the crafty sophistry of those who believe that they must proceed by devious counsels will never acquire the name of innocence. For anyone who thinks he can evade judgment by delays thereby confesses everything.

Yet at some time that man, of whom such things are reported, will come before the court. It does not [will not] profit him to have hidden so often, to have evaded so often: wherever he flees, his deeds and offences pursue him—the crimes alleged against him, if they are true. I ought indeed already to have rendered a fitting sentence in our judgment for the conduct of one accused, who by repeatedly avoiding inquiry and a decreed trial thought to mock it. But lest anyone perhaps judge it premature and say that we had reserved nothing for him—though absent, he has been sought—[Col. 0407D] we preferred, granting an interval of time, to defer it, especially since his accusers also asserted that, concerning whose [their] intentions and conduct a decree is [secure], Maximus was committing acts deserving condemnation all the more because he appeared more slowly before the appointed court.

They accuse him of having been enveloped in Manichaean darkness, of having so long defiled his mind by a shameful sect that he cannot cleanse it. As proof of the charge they produce synodal records; they allege that he was entangled on every side in crimes, showing no regard for soundness of mind; and, in his madness and insane recklessness, they charge that he even came before the tribunals of secular judges, subjected to interrogation—something most disgraceful in a person of low station—and they assert, producing the records in court, that he was condemned for homicide.

[Col. 0408A] They complain with profound grief that such a man, after such grave and numerous offences, still claims for himself in his hiding-places the title of bishop, bringing infamy upon a city not his own and wishing, by arrogating the holy name to himself, to defile it. Therefore, dearest brethren, because he refused to present himself here for a hearing, we have granted a postponement, so that, if perhaps convicted by the clergy accusing him, he may at last, when brought before episcopal judgment, receive the fitting sentence of a proper pronouncement. Yet when these matters have been established, we know that he must forfeit this title, since he is said never to have possessed the decency [Latin *podorem*, perhaps *pudorem*] of priesthood and not to have preserved his position even for a short time.

We have decreed that the judgment must be yours within the province, and that a synod be assembled before the Kalends of November [1 November], [Col. 0408B] so that, if he wishes to appear and is confident, he may answer in person to the charges. But if he neglects to appear, he shall not gain a postponement of sentence by his absence. For it is evident that the person confesses the crime who does not use the opportunity, granted and repeatedly assigned, to clear himself by judgment. It makes no difference whether all that has been alleged is proved at a hearing in his presence, since his repeatedly procured absence itself plainly stands as a confession [reading uncertain: *pro confessione*].

We shall send letters throughout all the provinces, so that he may not claim ignorance as an excuse, and he shall be compelled to come into the province and present himself there before the appointed tribunal. Whatever your charity judges should be decreed in this matter, once it has been reported to us, must—as is fitting—be confirmed by our authority.

### Chapter 272.—Concerning a bishop charged with a crime who, summoned to a synod, has scorned to appear. From the synod held at Altheim [Alcheum], chapter 10.

We, by the authority of Saint Peter—I, John, vicar of the Apostolic See—again summon and command Bishop Richuvinus, who contrary to the enactments of the holy canons seized the Church of Strasbourg. We invited him by our letters to the holy synod, but he scorned to come and did not even send his representative. By command of the holy synod, we order that he come to the council, that is, to Mainz, convoked by his metropolitan bishop, before the venerable Archbishop Heriger and his fellow bishops, [Col. 0408D] there to render a just account of his disobedience and perversity. But if he negligently treats even this as unimportant, he shall abstain from his own rank until, coming to Rome, he renders an account before the lord pope and the holy Church.

### Chapter 273.—Who are primates and who are metropolitans. From chapters of the Council of Nicaea added by Pope Felix.

Those, and no others, are primates who were established in the Nicene Synod. The others who hold metropolitan sees are called archbishops, not primates, while in all respects preserving the dignity of the Apostolic See, granted to it by the Lord himself and afterwards confirmed by the holy Fathers.

### Chapter 274.—That accused persons must be denied permission to accuse before clearing themselves of the crime which oppresses them. [Col. 0409A] From the decrees of Pope Stephen sent to all bishops, chapter 11 (Stephen I, Epistle 2, chapter 7).

(3, question 11, chapter *Neganda est*.) Accused persons must be denied permission to make accusations before they have cleared themselves of the crime with which they are burdened. For their testimony against others is not to be believed while they are implicated in crimes, unless they first prove themselves innocent, since the declaration of an accused person against anyone is dangerous and must not be admitted. Nor should persons who are intimate associates, those who have confessed voluntarily, or those entangled in crimes be admitted; nor those who were enemies yesterday, the day before [the previous day], or earlier.

### Chapter 275.—That accusations against teachers are not to be received. From the decrees of Pope Eusebius, chapter 17.

Although these general statements may suffice [Col. 0409B] both to avoid errors and to preserve Catholic principles, nevertheless we know it was established by the apostles and their successors that accusations against teachers ought not to be received, that foreign tribunals ought not to be held, and that no one should be bound by the judgment of a judge other than his own.

### Chapter 276.—On the same matter. From the Council of Spalato, chapter 3.

Let no one receive accusers against a teacher, because one whom the Lord has reserved for his own judgment cannot be condemned by a human examination.

### Chapter 277.—That no one may accuse a bishop before secular authorities. From an epistle of Pope Felix sent to the Egyptians, chapter 1.

No one may accuse a bishop before secular judges, but only before the highest primates.

### Chapter 278.—On the same matter. From an epistle of Pope Boniface to the bishops of Gaul.

[Col. 0409C]

(11, question 1, chapter *Nullus episcopus*.) No bishop may be brought or produced before any judge, civil or military, whether for a civil or a criminal cause. Any magistrate who dares command this shall be punished by condemnation to loss of his belt of office.

### Chapter 279.—That a bishop is not to be accused by criminals. From the epistle of Pope Felix sent to the bishops mentioned above, chapter 18.

Whenever a bishop is accused of particular crimes, if the accusers are such persons as may justly and canonically be received, then, when a lawful synod has been assembled at the proper time, he shall be heard canonically by all the bishops [Col. 0409D] in the province. But if the accusers are not lawful persons who may justly and canonically be received, the bishop is not to be harassed; for priests ought to be free for offering sacrifice, not for litigation. Those who are called the thrones of God should not be disturbed by the plots of wicked men, but should freely serve Christ the Lord (Daniel VII [7]).

### Chapter 280.—That no bishop may be summoned for judgment outside his own province. From the decrees of Pope Julius, sent to the eastern bishops, chapter 18 (compare 3, chapter 17).

No bishop may be summoned for judgment outside his own province. Rather, after he has been canonically summoned to a suitable place, at the synodal time he shall be heard by all the bishops of the same province, who must pronounce upon him a unanimous and canonical sentence. [Col. 0410A] For if this has been granted to lesser persons, both clerics and laypeople, how much more must it be observed in the case of bishops? If he regards the metropolitan or the judges as suspect, or perceives them to be hostile, he shall be judged before the primate of the diocese or before the pontiff of the Roman See.

### Chapter 281.—Within how many days an appeal must be made. Extracts from the Theodosian laws interpreted by Paul, chapter 35.

(2, question 6, chapter *Propter superfluam*.) Because of the excessive licence of appellants, lest they should seem to possess unrestricted discretion in reconsidering or reversing judgments, both periods for appeal and penalties were established. Thus whoever appeals before the judge who heard his case and wishes to challenge the decision before another judge must appeal within [inside] five days; and during those same five days he must arrive, without any evasion, before the judge to whom he has appealed. The very day on which he received the letters shall be counted specifically among those five days. If the journey is longer, then, in addition to those five days, the number of days needed to make the journey shall be counted.

### Chapter 282.—Concerning the receipt of letters of appeal, chapter 36.

(2, question 6, chapter *Ab eo*.) From the judge from whom appeal has been made, letters of dismissal are to be sent to the person who will examine the appeal. These letters are commonly called an *epistola* (“letter of appeal”), and their request and receipt must be made officially within the fifth day. This has already been interpreted above under the title concerning securities and penalties of appeals. Those who fail within the prescribed periods to request, receive, or submit the letters of dismissal shall be excluded from pursuing the action by rescript and compelled to bear the penalty for appeal.

### Chapter 283.—Which appeal is to be accepted and which is not, chapter 37.

(2, question 6, chapter *Quicunque*.) Whoever appeals not because he is confident of a just case, but in order to cause delay and prevent a sentence from being pronounced against him, or whoever, having confessed his deed, wishes to appeal lest he be adjudged liable—such appeals are not received.

### Chapter 284.—What is to be done concerning the possession of an appellant, chapter 38.

(2, question 6, chapter *Quoties*.) Whenever, after a case has been heard, the possessor in the litigation appeals, the fruits of the possession [Col. 0410D] in dispute are properly sequestrated while the outcome of the second hearing remains uncertain. For if the claimant appeals, this cannot be demanded from him, because what he does not possess cannot be sequestrated. If an appeal concerns urban estates or slaves, their rents or freight charges [freight], even where a ship is concerned, are customarily deposited.

### Chapter 285.—That one who appeals unjustly must repay the opponent’s expenses fourfold, chapter 39.

(2, question 6, chapter *Omnimodo*.) Whenever an appeal is declared unjust, it must in every case be penalized [approved] by compelling the appellant to repay, not simply but fourfold, the expenses incurred by the opposing party while pursuing the case.

### Chapter 286.—That before formal inscription no one is to be considered criminal. From book nine of the same laws.

[Col. 0411A]

Before the formal lodging of the accusation (*inscriptio*), no one shall be made a criminal defendant. Once the inscription has been made in due order, the defendant is then to be received by the judge and committed to custody together with the accuser. This must be done, however, with regard to the status of both accused and accuser; before investigation, the judge shall cause each to be guarded in a manner appropriate to his birth or rank.

Certainly, persons who have confessed their own crimes under examination are not to be believed by a judge if they wish to speak about others. For right and law establish that, by voluntarily confessing, an accused person cannot make another a defendant, and that one who has confessed himself criminal is not to be believed concerning another.

### Chapter 287.—What delays are to be granted to accused bishops. From the decretal epistle of Damasus (Epistle 4, chapter 8).

[Col. 0411B]

(3, question 3, chapter *Induciae accusatis*.) In criminal matters, accused bishops must be granted delays of six months, or even longer. For no person instructed in secular law is ignorant that this is permitted even to laypeople; how much more to priests, who are unquestionably their superiors?

### Chapter 288.—That one who has confessed concerning himself is not to be believed in another’s accusation. Dionysius to Severus, fellow bishop (Epistle 2).

(15, question 3, chapter *Nemini praeterquam*.) No one who has confessed concerning himself can be believed concerning another’s crime, because his declaration concerning himself and every other matter is dangerous and must not be admitted. Likewise, we cannot and must not receive one who is an associate in another’s error, who voluntarily departs from the course of his own professed purpose, or who is disobedient to the sacred rules and enactments of the Fathers.

### Chapter 289.—Which accusers and witnesses of bishops are to be received, and which are not. From the decrees of Pope Callixtus to the bishops established throughout Gaul, chapter 17 (Epistle 2, chapter 5).

Therefore all who are suspect in the right faith are not to be received in accusations of priests or of those whose faith is not doubted, and they are to be regarded as doubtful witnesses. Therefore the testimony of those whose faith is doubted must be invalidated; those ignorant of the right faith are not to be believed at all.

(2, question 7, chapter *Quaerendum est*; and Carthage IV, chapter 96.) It must therefore be investigated at trial what kind of conduct and faith belong to both the accuser and the accused. For those who lack right faith and conduct, whose lives are blameworthy, are not permitted to accuse persons [Col. 0411D] whose faith, life, and freedom are known; nor are persons of low status to be admitted to accuse them.

(3, question 8, chapter *Accusatorum*.) The persons of accusers must be investigated in detail. They are received with difficulty without a written document, but never by written document; for no one can accuse or be accused by writing. Each person must present his accusation in his own voice and in the presence of the person whom he wishes to accuse; nor is an accuser to be believed when the person he wishes to accuse is absent.

(3, question 9, chapter *Testes*.) Similarly, witnesses shall not give testimony by any written document, nor shall they testify regarding other cases or business matters, except concerning matters known to have occurred in their presence. Accusers who are blood relatives shall not testify against [Col. 0412A] them, nor their household associates nor persons coming from their houses. But if they wish and mutually agree, relatives alone may testify between themselves, and not against others. Nor are suspect accusers or witnesses to be received, because the attachment arising from kinship, familiarity, and domination commonly obstructs truth.

### Chapter 290.—On the same matter. From the decrees of Pope Damasus sent to Stephen and all bishops of Africa, chapter 17 [10] (Epistle 4, chapter 3).

(2, question 7, chapter *Testes absque ulla*.) The accusers of bishops and the witnesses concerning whom you have asked must be free of all infamy, suspicion, and manifest stain, fully instructed in the true faith, and such persons as divine authority commands to be chosen for the priesthood. For, as ancient authority teaches, persons unable or forbidden to be advanced to the same rank cannot accuse priests or testify against them.

### Chapter 291.—Which persons are infamous. From an epistle of Pope Stephen to Hilary (Epistle 1, chapter 1).

(6, question 1, chapter *Infames*.) We call infamous those persons marked by infamy on account of some fault: namely, all who reject the rule of Christian law and despise ecclesiastical enactments. Likewise thieves, sacrilegious persons, and all entangled in capital crimes; violators of tombs; those who willingly violate the sacred enactments of the apostles, their successors, and the holy Fathers; and all who take arms against the Fathers, who throughout the world are branded with infamy. Likewise incestuous persons, murderers, [Col. 0412C] perjurers, abductors, sorcerers, poisoners, adulterers, deserters from public wars, those who seek to hold positions unworthy of them, those who unjustly remove the resources of the Church, those who slander or accuse brethren and do not prove their charges, those who provoke the minds of rulers to anger against innocents, all who have been anathematized or expelled from the Church for their crimes, and all whom ecclesiastical or secular laws declare infamous.

Such persons may not be promoted to sacred orders: neither slaves before lawful manumission, penitents, bigamists, persons serving on a municipal council, those not physically whole, those lacking a sound mind or understanding, persons disobedient to holy decrees, or persons shown to be insane. None of all these may be advanced to sacred ranks; nor may these persons, freedmen, suspects, or persons lacking right faith or worthy conduct accuse the highest priests.

### Chapter 292.—That no bishop may be condemned without the authority of the Roman pontiff. From the decrees of Pope Felix sent to the bishops throughout Gaul, chapter 9 (Felix I, Epistle 2).

If any bishop is accused by accusers who may be received, after they have charitably approached him so that he may amend the matter itself, and he refuses to correct it, then—not earlier, but only then—his case is to be referred canonically to the highest primates. They must regularly convene a council at a suitable place within that province [Col. 0413A] and at a suitable season, namely spring [autumn] or summer, so that he may be heard there by all the bishops of the same province. He too, having been lawfully summoned, must be present unless illness or some other grave necessity restrains him. For permission to accuse beyond the provincial boundaries does not exist before a hearing is requested.

If this is presumed in any way, it has been decreed that, before his own place and all his possessions have been restored to him according to law, he is not to be accused or charged by anyone at all, nor, unless he freely chooses, to answer anyone concerning such matters. But after he has been restored as set out above and all his possessions have been restored to him according to law, once he has arranged and put in order his affairs, he shall be granted ample time to prepare his case. Afterwards, if necessary, he shall come to trial when canonically summoned and, if it seems just, answer the accusers’ allegations with the support of his brethren.

For no principle permits anything to be objected against him while his property or the resources of the Church are for a time held by enemies or anyone else; nor can anything, great or small, be brought against him in any way while he lacks his churches, property, or authority.

Likewise, from an epistle of Pope Julius sent to the eastern bishops (Epistle I, chapter 4): “If from this day onward anyone presumes to condemn a bishop, or expel him from his own see, apart from the judgment of this holy see, let him know that he is irretrievably condemned and shall forever lose his own rank. Know that those condemned or expelled without the judgment of this holy see receive, by the authority of this holy see, their former communion [Col. 0413C] and are restored to their own sees. For these privileges were granted to this holy see previously, namely from the time of the apostles; and afterwards, at the aforementioned Nicene Synod, they were unanimously confirmed by all on account of the harassment of wicked people, the persecutions of heretics, and the machinations of brethren who lay snares, so that each may take greater care not to dare perpetrate such acts.”

### Chapter 293.—That no person’s accusation may be received in writing while the accused is absent. From the second epistle of Pope Stephen to all bishops, chapter 4.

(2, question 8, chapter *Per scripta*.) No accuser’s accusation is to be received in writing while the accused is absent. Instead, if the accuser is a lawful and qualified person, he must make it in his own voice and in the presence of the person whom he wishes to accuse; for no absent person can either be accused or bring an accusation. Yet no man of the aforesaid order may be accused or be obliged to answer his accusers until he has been lawfully summoned by his own primate and given a place in which to defend himself or investigate in order to clear the charges.

### Chapter 294.—That more difficult cases are to be referred to the summit of the Roman See, to be concluded by apostolic judgment. From an epistle of Pope Anacletus to all bishops.

If more difficult cases arise among you, refer them to the summit of this holy see, as to the head, so that they may be concluded by apostolic judgment. For that God so wills, and that it has been so established by him, is declared by the preceding statements. This Apostolic See was made hinge and head by the Lord, not established by another; and just as a door is governed upon its hinge, so all Churches, by the Lord’s ordinance, are governed by the authority of this holy see.

### Chapter 295.—That all bishops may appeal to the Roman See in emergencies. From the decrees of Pope Callixtus sent to Stephen in Africa.

All ought, when necessary, to appeal to it and be supported by its aid. For, as you know, it is not canonical for a synod to be held without its authority. Nor may a bishop be definitively condemned except in a canonical [lawful] synod, assembled at the proper time by apostolic summons; and no councils are ever recorded as valid [Col. 0414B] unless supported by apostolic authority.

### Chapter 296.—What kind of delays must be granted to bishops charged with crimes. From an epistle of Pope Felix sent to brethren throughout Egypt, chapter 15 (Felix, Epistle 2, book 1, chapter 20).

(3, question 3, chapter *De induciis*.) Concerning the delays for bishops about which you have consulted us, we find various rules established by the Fathers. Some ordered that a year and six months be granted, to ward off the machinations of the unskilled, prepare their answers, confirm witnesses, and seek the counsel of bishops and friends. Others ordered a year, an opinion with which most agree. I find no period shorter than six months, since such delays are allowed even to laypeople; how much more to the priests of the Lord!

[Col. 0414C] Our predecessors and the other holy Fathers have also often forbidden anyone to harass the priests of the Lord with slanders not arising from the root of charity. “Be at rest,” they say, “and do not persecute those who minister perfectly to God: by their prayers even earthly wars are calmed; the assaults of angels departing from God are driven away; and by the constancy of prayer they put to shame all demons, corrupters [variant: those who have been corrupted].”

Delays must be granted not within a narrow period but over a long interval, so that the accused may prepare themselves, meet all their fellow communicants established in the provinces, prepare witnesses, and fully arm themselves against plotters.

(Ibid., chapter 21.) Judges and accusers must be persons entirely [Col. 0414D] free from suspicion and desirous of delivering their judgment from the root of charity.

### Chapter 297.—What is to be done concerning a bishop who refuses to conduct his case in a synod. From the Council of Africa, chapter 54 (under Celestine and Boniface).

Concerning Quodvultdeus of Centuriae also: because his adversary had asked to be admitted to our council, he was asked whether he wished to have the matter tried with him before bishops. At first he promised; on another day he replied that this did not please him, and departed. It pleased all the bishops that no one should communicate with Quodvultdeus until his case reached whatever conclusion it could. For no Christian could rightly think that his episcopate ought to be taken from him before the outcome of his case was evident.

### Chapter 298.—Judgment concerning a bishop who, deposed from office for a crime, afterwards seizes a bishopric like a robber. From the register of Gregory to John, bishop of Prima Justiniana (book X of the Register, Epistle 33).

[Col. 0415A]

When evils that must be cleansed by the tears of repentance are increased by further transgressions, greater correction must be applied to offenders, so that they themselves may recognize their crime, at least when punishment exacts vengeance for it, and so that fear of ecclesiastical protection may restrain others from unlawful acts. (2, q. 7, ch. *Lator*.) Accordingly, our most beloved bearer of these presents, Nemesion, coming to us, reported—as the copies of the proceedings which he brought contained—that Paul, bishop of the city of Declanena [Deaclina, elsewhere Doclevena], among other evils, had fallen into a bodily crime [“a bodily crime”]; that he had been accused by his own clerics; and that, upon an investigation having been held, the matter had become so clear—as we cannot say without [Col. 0415B] sorrow—that, moreover, after he was convicted, he even presented that document in which he confessed that the charges brought against him were true. For this reason we judged that he had been deposed from the episcopal office, and that you had been ordained bishop in his place with the consent of your fraternity.

But we have now learned that this same Paul came with the assistance of secular judges, entered as bishop in the manner of a robber, and, having violently carried off the Church’s property, drove you out and brought you almost to the utmost outrage and to death. Since the perversity of so great a wickedness is neither to be concealed nor lightly reproved, let your fraternity take care diligently to establish all these facts. And if the truth is as we have learned, [Col. 0415C] let it compel the aforesaid Paul by strict enforcement [“excuse”] to restore, without any delay or excuse, whatever he has taken away. But if he says that he took nothing belonging to the Church, but his own property, although it was grave and unjust that he should not have sought this from you or from his metropolitan, but should have presumed, in rash audacity, to act by force, nevertheless, if he took anything of his own, it must be established under the examination of your fraternity whether this is true.

It must also be diligently investigated whether he squandered anything improperly from the Church’s property, so that he may be compelled by every means to repair and make satisfaction for this out of what he has now taken. But if he attempts delay, he is to be sent into a monastery until he restores everything which he squandered or took from the Church’s substance, so that, being compelled, he may return what he did not fear wickedly to take away. And if perhaps—which we do not believe—after his deposition he should, with shameless and deranged mind [“shamelessly and with a perverse mind”], speak in any way of the episcopate and again presumptuously attempt to aspire to it through any persons [“attempt it by any presumptuous aspiration,” etc.], let the full vigor of your fraternity be kindled against his wickedness; and take care that, deprived of communion in the Lord’s body and blood, he be confined in a monastery until the day of his death [Col. 0415D] to perform penance, so that he may learn to amend with fitting tears the stains of the crime he committed—stains which he more wickedly desires to increase to the destruction of his own soul.

But our above-mentioned most beloved brother Nemesion is undoubtedly to be restored to his place and episcopal office; and you must be diligent that he suffer no renewed disturbance or molestation on this account. For this plainly tends not only to his protection but also to the correction of others, so that the presumption of wicked men may in no way hereafter dare to attempt anything contrary to the enactments of the sacred canons or to ecclesiastical discipline.

### CHAPTER 299.—Why the holy apostles and their successors wished the accusation of bishops [priests] to be difficult.

From the decrees of Pope Fabian sent to the Eastern brethren, chapter 19 (letter 2, chapter 2).

The holy apostles and their successors, filled with the Spirit of God, considering these matters, foreseeing wicked people and taking account of the simple, wished accusations against priests to be difficult, or never possible, lest they [Col. 0416B] might be driven away or removed by evil men. For if this were easily granted to secular and wicked persons, either none, or scarcely very few, would remain; since it always was, is, and—what is worse—flourishes excessively, that the wicked persecute the good and the carnal harass the spiritual. Therefore, as has been said, they decreed that bishops should not be accused; or, if it could not be otherwise, that their accusation should be made exceedingly difficult, and not presumed by those persons mentioned above, nor that bishops should be expelled from their own sees or churches.

### CHAPTER 300.—Concerning an expelled bishop, if he dares to enter the city.

From the letter of Pope Boniface to the bishops of Gaul (read in the decrees, chapter 6).

If an expelled bishop dares to enter the city from which he was expelled, or to leave the place in which he was ordered to reside, [Col. 0416C] we command that he be handed over to a monastery established in another province, so that one who sinned in the priesthood may be corrected while living in a monastery.

### CHAPTER 301.—That bishops who wish to choose successors during their lifetime may not do so.

From the Council of Antioch, chapter 23 (under Julius).

(8, q. 1, ch. *Episcopo non licere*.) A bishop is not permitted to appoint a successor for himself on his own authority, even if he has reached the end of life. If anything of this sort has been done, such an appointment is void. Ecclesiastical law, however, must be preserved, which provides that this may not be done otherwise than with a synod and the judgment of bishops, who, after the death of the one at rest, have authority to promote whoever proves worthy.

### CHAPTER 302.—That no one be superordained while a bishop lives.

From the Council of Arvernum, chapter 13 (in the fragments of the Second Council of Arvernum, under Vigilius, chapter 2).

[Col. 0416D]

Let no other bishop be set over or superordained while a bishop lives, except perhaps in the place of one whom a capital offence has cast down.

### CHAPTER 303.—That a bishop may not choose his successor.

From the Council of Spalato, chapter 9 (First Spalato, in the fragments, chapter 8).

A bishop may not appoint another as successor in his place before the end of his life. But if anyone attempts to usurp this power, that appointment shall be void. Therefore this must not be done otherwise than with the counsel and judgment of bishops, who, after the departure of the predecessor, have authority to choose a worthy person.

### CHAPTER 304.—That no one should succeed a bishop because of his illness.

From the Register of Pope Gregory to Anatolius, deacon of Constantinople (Book IX of the *Register*, letter 41).

[Col. 0417A]

(7, q. 1, ch. *Scripsit mihi*.) Your Belovedness wrote to me that our most reverend [“our most pious lord, the most reverend,” etc.] brother John, bishop of Prima Justiniana, should be ordered to have a bishop succeed him because of the illness of the head which he suffers, lest perhaps, while that city does not have the same episcopal rights, it perish from the enemy—far be it! The canons nowhere command that a bishop should succeed because of a bishop’s illness; indeed, it is wholly unjust that a sick man should be deprived of his honor if bodily affliction comes upon him.

Rather, it should be proposed that, if anyone [“the one who”] is ill while holding office, a steward should be sought for him who can administer all his care and preserve his place in the governance [Col. 0417B] of the Church, while he himself is not removed, so that neither almighty God may be offended nor the city be found neglected.

### CHAPTER 305.—That, when a bishop suffers from a persistent illness of the head and has long been burdened by it, another may be substituted.

From the Register of Gregory, chapter 239 (Book VII, indiction 2, chapter 50).

(7, q. 1, ch. *Qualiter ordinati*.) Your fraternity has long known how the Church of Rimini, because of the bodily affliction which, as is known, prevents its bishop whom we ordained, has until now been deprived of pastoral and sacerdotal governance. Moved by the bereavement of that place’s long-absent inhabitant, we repeatedly urged him that, if he felt himself improved from the ailment of the head by which he was afflicted, he should return, with God’s help, to his Church. He was granted a reprieve and awaited during these four years.

When you clerics and citizens came from there, and likewise pressed us with petitions [“reproaching us”], and we more urgently exhorted him to return to them with the Lord’s help if he was able, he requested us in writing by petition that, because of the ailment by which he was held, he was wholly unable to undertake the governance or discharge the office of that Church, and that we should ordain a bishop for that Church. Therefore, because the care of concern for all the Churches entrusted to us constrains us not to allow the flock of the faithful to lack pastoral protection any longer, compelled by their prayers and by his renunciation based on his own incapacity, we ordered that a bishop be ordained for the Church of Rimini. Having issued the customary commands, we did not cease to urge the clergy [Col. 0417D] and people of that Church to come together in harmonious deliberation to elect a bishop for themselves.

We therefore exhort your fraternity to summon to itself the man whom all have elected with one consent, as they too are known to have asked us. Examine him with careful scrutiny in every respect; and if, with the Lord’s aid, those things which are punished by death in the text of the Heptateuch are not found in him [“which are contained in the Heptateuch, are not found,” etc.], and if his life also pleases you on the testimony of faithful persons, send him to us with the written decree of yours [“with the document of your decree”], adding also a letter of attestation, so that, by the Lord’s ordering, he may be consecrated by us as bishop of that Church.

### CHAPTER 306.—Concerning a bishop who, through illness, has fallen into mental dullness.

From the Council of Orange, chapter 2.

[Col. 0418A]

If any bishop falls into illness or some dullness of understanding, or loses the use of speech, he is not to permit a presbyter to perform those things which it is fitting for bishops to perform; rather, he is to summon a neighboring bishop, upon whom he shall lay the duties that must be performed in the Church.

### CHAPTER 307.—Likewise concerning a bishop who, because of pain in the head, frequently falls into insanity: that another is to be substituted for him, and that he himself is to be maintained from the Church’s goods.

From the Register of Gregory to Bishop Eleutherius [Etherius] (Book II of the *Register*, letter 7).

(7, q. 1, ch. *Quamvis triste*.) Although what we say is very sad to us, and brotherly compassion rather rebukes [“weighs upon”] us [Col. 0418B] than permits us to determine anything on the basis of what we have heard, nevertheless concern for the government we have undertaken strikes our heart with an urgent goad, compelling us to take great care for the Churches and, with God as author, to determine what must be done so that none of their welfare may perish.

Certain persons have reported to us that a certain bishop has incurred such an affliction of the head that, as he is wont to act with his mind alienated, groans and weeping are heard. Therefore, lest, while the shepherd is sick, the flock—God forbid!—be exposed to be torn by the teeth of the enemy, or the interests of that Church perish, we must make provision with careful foresight. And therefore, because the necessity of illness, not crime, removes a living bishop from his office, no reason permits another to be ordained in his place unless he himself refuses [the original lacks “unless”].

But if he is accustomed to have intervals of illness, he himself, by submitting a petition, should confess that he no longer has the understanding needed for this ministry and cannot undertake the other duties because illness overwhelms him, and should request that another be ordained in his place. When this is done, another who proves worthy shall be ordained bishop by the solemn election of all, provided that, for as long as life keeps that same bishop in this world, the expenses due to him are supplied from the same Church.

But if he never returns to the function of a sound mind, a faithful person of approved life is to be chosen, one who may prove fit for the governance of the Church, consider the welfare of souls, restrain the disorderly under the bond of discipline, administer ecclesiastical property, and show himself mature and [Col. 0418D] effective in all things; and that person, surviving the bishop now ill, is to be consecrated in his place.

### CHAPTER 308.—That priests of the Lord should neither presume, as the common people are accustomed to do, to swear, nor be compelled to do so.

From the decrees of Pope Cornelius (letter 2).

(2, q. 4, ch. *Sacramentum*.) We have not known that an oath has hitherto been required from bishops and the other orders except concerning the right faith, nor have we found that they have sworn voluntarily. Therefore the holy Apostle James, most emphatically forbidding oaths, says: “Before all things, my brethren, do not swear, neither by heaven, nor by earth, nor by any other oath. But let your speech be: Yes, yes; No, no; lest you fall under judgment” (James 5).

### CHAPTER 309.—Concerning a bishop tainted by an adverse report, cleansed and absolved by an oath.

From the Register of Pope Gregory to Emperor Justin [in Gratian it is addressed to a praetor; Gregory has “presbyter”] (Book II, indiction X, letter 23, §2).

[Col. 0419A]

(Q. 5, ch. *Habet hoc*.)
