This is peculiar to the envy of the ancient enemy: those whom he is unable to deceive into committing wicked deeds because they resist him [“because God resists him”], he tears apart by fabricating falsehoods for the present against their reputation. Therefore, since an adverse report had cast certain aspersions against the priestly character of our brother and fellow bishop Leo, we caused a strict and prolonged inquiry to be made whether they were true; and we found no fault in him concerning the matters alleged.

But lest anything seem to have been omitted which could leave doubt in our heart [“which might have remained doubtful to our heart”], [Col. 0419B] we made him offer strict oaths, beyond what was required, at the most sacred body of blessed Peter. We rejoiced with great exultation at the oaths which he offered, because his innocence shone forth clearly by such proof [“by a proof of this kind, his innocence,” etc.]. For this reason let Your Glory receive the aforesaid man with all charity and show him the reverence fitting for a priest, so that no doubt may remain [“lest any doubt remain in your hearts”] about matters now cleansed. Rather, you ought to adhere most devotedly in all things to the above-named bishop, so that you may seem fittingly and worthily to honor God in his person, whose minister he is.

### CHAPTER 310.—Correction of a bishop who has kept a concubine.

From the Register of Gregory to Andrew, bishop of Tarentum (Book II of the *Register*, indiction II, letter 44).

[Col. 0419C]

Whoever, conscious of his guilt, strives to appease the tribunal of the eternal Judge by fitting repentance will behold it without fear. (Distinction 33, ch. *Habuisse*.) Indeed, we have learned by manifest truth that you kept a concubine, concerning whom a contrary suspicion has also arisen that she bore children. But because judgment ought not to be definitive in ambiguous matters, we choose to commit this to your conscience.

Therefore, if, while established in sacred orders, you remember that you have been defiled by intercourse with her, having laid aside the honor of the priesthood, you must by no means presume to approach the exercise of ministry. Know that you minister at peril to your soul and will without doubt render an account to our God if, conscious of such a crime, you wish to remain in the order in which you are while concealing the truth. [Col. 0419D] Therefore we again exhort you: if you recognize that you have been deceived by the cunning of the ancient enemy, hasten, while you may, to overcome him through fitting repentance, lest—what we do not wish—you be assigned as his companion on the Day of Judgment. But if you are not conscious of this offence, you must remain in the order in which you are.

Furthermore, because you ordered a woman from the registers to be cruelly beaten with rods contrary to the order of the priesthood—although we do not judge that she died from this even after eight months—yet because you were unwilling to show regard for your order, we decree that you abstain from the administration of Masses for two months. During these months it is fitting that, suspended from office, you mourn what you have done. For it is altogether fitting that, since the examples of praiseworthy priests do not move you toward the tranquil uprightness of this life, at least the medicine of correction should compel you.

### CHAPTER 311.—Concerning a bishop cleansed and absolved by oaths.

From the Register of Gregory to Brunhild, queen of the Franks (Book II of the *Register*, letter 8).

(2, q. 5, ch. *Mennam*.) After investigating the allegations made against Menna, our most reverend brother and fellow bishop, we found him guilty in no respect. Moreover, satisfying the charge under oath at the most sacred body of blessed Peter the Apostle, he showed himself free from the matters alleged against his reputation. We therefore allowed him to return cleansed and absolved. For just as it would have been fitting, had he been guilty in any respect, to punish his fault canonically, so it was not fitting, when innocence aided him, to detain or afflict him any longer in any way.

### CHAPTER 312.—How an elderly bishop is to be corrected, and his evil advisers excommunicated.

From the same Register to Januarius, bishop of Caralis (Book VII of the *Register*, indiction II, letter 1).

The preacher of almighty God, the Apostle Paul, says: “Do not rebuke an elder” (1 Timothy 5). But this rule of his must be observed in the case of an elder only when the elder’s fault does not by his example draw the hearts of younger people to destruction. But where an elder offers younger persons an example leading to destruction, there he must be struck by strict rebuke. For it is written: “A snare of youths, all of you” (Isaiah 42). And again the prophet says: “The sinner who is a hundred years old is accursed” (Isaiah 65).

Yet such wickedness concerning your old age has reached my ears that, unless we still considered it with human forbearance, we would already have struck it with a fixed curse. For I have been told that, on the Lord’s Day, before celebrating the solemnities of Mass, you went to plough the field of the bearer of these presents; after ploughing it, you celebrated the solemnities of Mass; and after the Mass solemnities you did not fear even to tear up the boundaries of his property. What penalty this deed ought to incur, all who hear of it know.

We had, however, been uncertain about so great a perversity; but when our son Cyriacus, abbot, was questioned by us, while he was *choralis*, that is, a regional official, he declared that he knew it to be so. And because we still spare your grey hairs, we exhort you at last: come to your senses, old man—**ἀπὸ τῆς Χωρᾶς**, “from the district/countryside”—and restrain yourself from such frivolity of character and perversity of conduct. [Col. 0420D] For the nearer you become to death, the more anxious and fearful you ought to become.

Indeed, a sentence of punishment ought to have been launched against you; but because we know your simplicity together with your old age, we are silent for the present. But we decree that those by whose counsel you did these things are excommunicated for two months, provided that, if anything human should happen to them within the space of those two months, they are not deprived of the blessing of viaticum. Hereafter, however, be wary of their counsel. Guard yourself also carefully, lest, if you have been their disciple in evil when you ought to have been their teacher in good, we spare neither your simplicity nor your old age any further.

### CHAPTER 313.—Concerning the self-cleansing of Pope Leo III.

[Col. 0421A]

(2, q. 4, ch. *Auditum est*.) It has been heard, dearest brethren, and spread abroad in many places, how evil men rose up against me, sought to weaken me, and laid grave accusations upon me. For this reason this most merciful and most serene lord King Charles came to the city with his priests and nobles. Therefore I, [Leo,] pontiff of the holy Roman Church—judged by no one and compelled by no one, but of my own free will—cleanse myself in your presence before God and his angels, who know my conscience, and before blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in whose presence we stand: namely, that I neither committed nor ordered to be committed the criminal and wicked deeds which they charge against me. God is my witness, before whose judgment we shall come and in whose presence we stand.

And I do this of my own free will in order to remove evil suspicions, not as though it were found in the canons, or as though I imposed this custom or decree in the holy Church upon my successors or likewise upon our brethren and fellow bishops, but so that you may more effectively cut off rebellious thoughts.

### CHAPTER 314.—That anyone excommunicated from ecclesiastical order condemns himself if he presumes to communicate.

From the African Council, chapter 29.

(11, q. 3, ch. *Placuit universo*.) Likewise, it pleased the whole council that anyone—whether bishop or cleric—who has been excommunicated for his own neglect and presumes to communicate before his hearing during the time of his excommunication is to be judged to have pronounced a sentence of condemnation upon himself.

### CHAPTER 315.—Concerning ordained persons, if any one of them has been a striker.

From the Council of Toledo, chapter 6.

(23, q. 8, ch. *His a quibus*.) Those by whom the sacraments of the Lord are administered may not undertake judgment involving blood. Therefore such an offence must be most strictly forbidden, lest they be driven by impulses of undiscerning presumption, presume either to judge by their own sentence what ought to be punished with death, or inflict mutilations upon any persons themselves or command that they be inflicted. If anyone, forgetful of these precepts, commits anything of this kind either against the household of his Church or against any persons, let him be deprived both of the honor and place of the order granted to him, and bound under the prison-house of perpetual condemnation. Communion, however, is not to be denied him when he departs this life, because of the Lord’s mercy.

### CHAPTER 316.—That a bishop should not strike anyone with his own hand.

From the decrees of Pope Boniface (this is read after the Council of Agde, from Gratian).

(Distinction 86, ch. *Non liceat*.) A bishop may not strike anyone with his own hands; for this ought to be foreign to a priest.

### CHAPTER 317.—Concerning a bishop who neglects to correct himself and those entrusted to him.

Gregory [Augustine].

(2, q. 7, ch. *Qui nec*.) He who has neither exercised the responsibility of governance in himself, nor wiped away his own offences, nor corrected the crime of his children, ought rather to be called an impudent dog than a bishop.

### CHAPTER 318.—That a good shepherd washes his subjects from sin.

Jerome.

As lye flowing through moist ashes washes and is not itself washed, so good teaching through an evil teacher washes the souls of believers from the filth of sins.

### CHAPTER 319.—That sheep flee an evil shepherd.

From the sayings of Augustine.

As sheep flee the voice of a shepherd whom they do not know and seek deserted places, so sheepfolds flee evil shepherds.

### CHAPTER 320.—Concerning one who casts God’s nobility away from himself.

Gregory (*Homily* 9 on Ezekiel, Book I).

(Distinction 40, ch. *Adam*.) Adam, the first man, was cast out of Paradise because of sin; that is, whoever cast away from himself the nobility of God is deprived of the nobility of place.

### CHAPTER 321.—That not all who hold the places of saints are sons of saints.

From the sayings of Jerome (letter to Heliodorus).

(Distinction 40, ch. *Non est facile*.) It is not easy to stand in the place of Peter and Paul and to hold the chair of those who reign with Christ; for hence it is said: not those are sons of saints who hold the places of saints, but those who perform their works.

### CHAPTER 322.—That no one ought to glory in lineage or place.

Gregory.

(Distinction 40, ch. *Nos qui*.) We who preside ought to be known not by the dignity of places or of lineage, but by nobility of character; not by the splendor of cities, but by purity of faith.

### CHAPTER 323.—Concerning priests who offer evil examples to their sheep.

Augustine.

[Col. 0422C]

(Distinction 83, ch. *Nemo quippe*.) Certainly no one harms the Church more than one who, acting perversely, possesses the name or rank of holiness and priesthood. For no one presumes to rebuke such an offender, and the fault spreads powerfully as an example when the sinner is honored out of reverence for his order.

### CHAPTER 324.—That bishops alone should have the care of ecclesiastical affairs.

From the Apostolic Canons, chapter 39.

The bishop shall administer the care of all ecclesiastical affairs and dispose of them as under God’s observation. He may not appropriate anything whatever from them, [Col. 0422D] nor give to his own relatives what belongs to God. If they are poor, however, let him provide for them as for poor persons, but let not the Church’s affairs be plundered on their account.

### CHAPTER 325.—That a metropolitan should not presumptuously use the pallium.

From the decrees of Pope Honorius, chapter 3.

Whoever among metropolitans presumes to use the pallium in the streets or in litanies, and does not restrict that honor solely to the solemnities of Mass on the principal feasts and at the times appointed by the Apostolic See—as blessed Pope Gregory says to John, bishop of Panormus, because he maintains this grave yoke and bond upon the neck not for ecclesiastical but for a certain secular dignity—let him be deprived of the dignity which he abuses; for he justly deserves to lose a privilege who boldly usurps what is unlawful.

### CHAPTER 326.—That a bishop cannot make a testament from the goods of his Church unless he first makes restitution.

From the Council of Agde, chapter 6 (chapter 51).

(12, q. 5, ch. *Si episcopus condito*.) If any bishop, having made a testament, bequeaths anything from property belonging by ecclesiastical right, it shall not be valid unless he has made good an equal amount from the resources of his own property.

### CHAPTER 327.—That a bishop should not indiscriminately give Church property to his relatives.

From the Council of Spalato, chapter 10.

Let bishops take care, in matters concerning Church property, to avoid conduct giving rise to reproach in relation to their kinsmen, and let them maintain a measure of discretion.

### CHAPTER 328.—On the same matter.

From the same council, [Col. 0423B] chapter 5.

Since many bishops, through love for their relatives, purchase estates and slaves from property entrusted to them, in their own name or in the name of any friends, and decree that these pass into the legal ownership of their relatives; and because for this reason ecclesiastical rights are undermined and the priestly ministry is darkened—indeed, is disparaged and despised by subjects—it pleased all that this kind of avarice be avoided henceforth. We decree that the following shall be fixed and remain in force henceforth and perpetually: whatever a bishop wishes may be done with, and bestowed upon whomever he wishes, from property of his own right that he acquired before becoming bishop, or certainly that he acquired by hereditary succession during his episcopate, in accordance with canonical authority. But after he has become bishop, whatever property he may acquire from [Col. 0423C] the Church’s resources, in his own name or another’s, under any condition whatsoever, we decree shall pass not into the rights of his relatives but into the rights of the Church over which he presides.

### CHAPTER 329.—That a bishop should not presume to alienate anything from the goods of a widowed Church.

From the decrees of Pope Martin, chapter 20.

(10, q. 3, ch. *Si quis episcop.*) If any bishop, compelled by no necessity of ecclesiastical administration, presumes to sell anything from ecclesiastical property within his own clergy, or where there happens to be no presbyter, he shall be compelled to restore the property to the Church, deposed by the judgment of bishops, and deprived of his honor as one guilty of theft and robbery.

### CHAPTER 330.—Concerning priests who disdain to come to a bishop’s funeral.

From the Eighth Council of Toledo, chapter 2 (Seventh Toledo, chapter 3).

Those things that concern decency often happen not to be fulfilled through certain persons’ negligence. Therefore, since it is known what dignity the canons preserve at the funeral of a deceased bishop, we add only this, by the tradition of ancient custom: if any priest, having been summoned in accordance with the provisions of the Council of Valence (chapter 4) to come for the burial of a deceased bishop’s body, delays through sluggish will, then, upon the appeal of the clergy of the deceased bishop before the synod or metropolitan bishop, he shall have no permission whatever for one year either to celebrate Mass or to communicate.

But presbyters and other clerics who hold a higher place of honor in the same [Col. 0424A] Church whose priest has died, if they are found slow in using every diligence concerning the funeral of one already dead, or concerning the impending death of a bishop, to move a neighboring bishop, or if they appear [are proved] to neglect this through any disturbance of mind, shall be assigned to monasteries for penance for the space of a whole year.

### CHAPTER 331.—That what is given to a bishop for the redemption of souls should be left to the Church.

From the Council of Agde, chapter 6.

(12, q. 3, ch. *Pontifices*.) Whatever is given to bishops established in the high priesthood by outsiders only, whether it is left or donated to the Church [“something by outsiders, or with the Church,” etc.] or separately, is shown to be offered by the donor for the redemption of his soul, not for the priest’s personal advantage. Therefore it should be reckoned not as the bishop’s own property, but as property left to the Church’s resources; for it is just that, as the priest possesses what has been left to the Church, so also the Church should possess what is left by the priest.

### CHAPTER 332.—That no bishop should go on campaign without the council of other bishops and of the prince.

Chapter of Emperor Charles.

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and devout defender and helper in all things of the holy Apostolic See: at the exhortation of all our faithful, and especially upon the counsel of bishops and other priests, we utterly forbid all servants of God to bear arms in any matter, to fight, to go into an army, or to a campaign against the enemy, except only those who are chosen for divine ministry—that is, to perform the solemnities of Mass and carry the relics of saints. Thus one or two bishops with priest-chaplains may go, and each prince may have one priest with him who can impose penance upon those confessing sins.

### CHAPTER 333.—On the same matter.

Likewise by the same.

For the second time, instructed for more complete observance by apostolic authority and the admonition of many bishops, and taught also by the rules of the holy canons, correcting ourselves by the counsel of all of us and giving an example to our descendants, we will that no priest go on campaign except two or three bishops only, chosen by all for blessing, preaching, and reconciliation of the people; and with them, chosen priests who know how properly to impose penance upon the people, celebrate Masses, care for the sick, and administer the anointing of sacred oil with holy prayers. Above all, they are to provide that no one depart this world without viaticum.

### CHAPTER 334.—Likewise on the same matter.

Nicholas to Emperor Charles.

(23, q. 8, ch. *Reprehensibile*.) What you have added is plainly very reprehensible: namely, that the greater part of all bishops keep watch day and night with your other faithful against sea-pirates, and that bishops are thereby hindered from coming. For soldiers [“of soldiers”] of Christ ought to serve Christ, whereas soldiers of the world ought to serve the world [“but let soldiers of the world serve the world”], as it is written: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Timothy 2). But if soldiers of the world devote themselves to warfare, what is the concern of bishops, the soldiers of Christ, except that they should be free for prayers?

### CHAPTER 335.—Concerning accused bishops: how they should be summoned to a council.

From the decrees of Pope Felix, chapter 3.

(5, q. 2, ch. *Si primates*.) If primates cannot peacefully reconcile the accusers of bishops with them in a private manner, then at the lawful time they shall canonically summon them to a canonically convened synod, not within narrow time limits. First, by written notices, they shall inform them of the accusations brought against them, so that they may come prepared to answer. For if they have been driven out by force or fear, or stripped of their goods, they can neither be summoned canonically to a synod nor ought to answer their enemies before they have been canonically restored and all their possessions legally returned to them.

### CHAPTER 336.—That while a pope lives, no one may elect another without consulting him.

From the decrees of Pope Symmachus, chapter 3 (from the synod of Pope Symmachus).

If any presbyter, deacon, or cleric, while the pope is alive and without consulting him, attempts to solicit subscriptions for the Roman pontificate, promise written pledges, offer an oath, promise any support, or deliberate and decide about this matter in private gatherings, let him be deprived of the dignity of his office and of communion.

### CHAPTER 337.—Concerning the bishop’s seat.

From the Council of Carthage (Fourth Carthage, chapter 35).

[Col. 0425C]

(Distinction 59, ch. *Episcopus in ecclesia*.) In church, amid the assembly of presbyters, the bishop shall sit on a higher seat.

### CHAPTER 338.—Concerning the ordination of a bishop.

From the sayings of Theodotus, archbishop.

At the ordination of a bishop, the one who ordains must celebrate Mass, and likewise the one who is ordained.

### CHAPTER 339.—What priests of the Lord should avoid.

From the Council of Tours, chapter 7.

All things pertaining to the enticements of ears and eyes, by which the vigor of the mind may be thought capable of being softened—such as certain kinds of musicians and some other things—ought to be avoided by all priests of the Lord. For through the enticements of ears and eyes a host of vices is accustomed to enter the mind. They should also flee in their own minds the impertinent jokes of vile and obscene actors, and preach to other priests that these must be avoided.

### CHAPTER 340.—That bishops should not remain long absent from their cities for the sake of their own ease.

From the Council held at Saint-Médard in the presence of Emperor Charles, chapter 5.

Provision must be made that bishops do not withdraw to more remote places for their own ease, neglecting their ministry and abandoning their proper cities. Rather, they should either travel through their parishes with the effective discharge of their office, or reside canonically and devoutly in their cities with their spiritual children. They should also compel the presbyters entrusted to them to be ordered according to their ministry in doctrine, chastity, sobriety, and hospitality.

### CHAPTER 341.—Concerning bishops who demand payment in lieu of service without visiting their parishes.

From the Council held at Tribur in the presence of King Arnulf, chapter 26.

(10, q. 1, c. *Relata est*.) A complaint of the people was brought before the holy synod: certain bishops, unwilling to travel through their dioceses during the year either to preach or to administer confirmation, nevertheless require those who ought to provide the lodging they should have used on their journeys to redeem it by another payment. This double disgrace—negligence and avarice—was a great horror to the holy synod; and they decreed that no one should henceforth practise this device of greed, and that bishops should be more diligent in visiting their flocks. [Col. 0426B]

### CAP. 342.—On the vindication of bishops. From the council held at Altheim, in the presence of King Conrad, ch. 16.

For the love of God and neighbour, for the honour of the Catholic faithful, and especially in order to remove and utterly eradicate scandals among the multitude and the disturbances which have newly arisen and continue to arise, and also that all may know that we bishops have not, by God’s mercy, been such as we are said to be: we resolve to follow and imitate the example of St Leo the Pope, who cleared himself before the people by swearing upon the four Gospels—while preserving, nevertheless, canonical authority.

### CAP. 343.—On one who has become a bishop from being a monk. From the same council, ch. 36.

[Col. 0426C] (18, q. 1, c. *Statutum est*.) It has been decreed and reasonably confirmed by the synod in accordance with the holy Fathers that a monk whom canonical election releases from the yoke of the monastic profession and rule, and whom sacred ordination makes bishop from monk, shall, like a lawful heir, have the right thereafter to claim his paternal inheritance. But whatever he had acquired, or had been ordered to possess, he shall leave to the monastery and to the discretion of the abbot whose monk he was, according to the Rule of St Benedict. For after he is ordained bishop, whatever he is able to acquire, he shall restore to the altar at which he is consecrated and assigned, according to the holy canons.

### CAP. 344.—On one accused of some heresy: that he must recite the formula of this document in the sacred assembly. From the letter of Cyril to John of Antioch.

[Col. 0426D] I, N., by this writing which I have copied out in my own hand, profess, following the holy judgment of the Fathers of the Synod of Nicaea, three hundred and eighteen in number, and the universal council of the Synod of Chalcedon, whose definition the Apostolic See confirmed, and which the letter of the most blessed Pope Leo, addressed to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople of holy memory, expounded by a most lucid proclamation of truth: I confess one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God the Father, perfect—the same in divinity and the same in humanity—true God and true man; one and the same, from a rational soul and flesh; consubstantial with the Father according to divinity, and consubstantial with us according to human nature; like us in all things except sin; begotten of the Father before the ages according to divinity, but in these last days, for us and for our salvation, born of the Virgin Mary—who gave birth according to the humanity to the same God—one and the same Christ, Son of God, Lord, only-begotten, acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, and without separation. The difference of the natures was by no means removed because of the union; rather, the property of each nature remained intact, converging into one person, not two, but one and the same only-begotten Son, true God, Lord Jesus Christ, as the prophets of old spoke concerning him, and as Christ the Lord himself instructed us in his own person. But those who do not think thus I declare worthy of eternal anathema together with Nestorius and Eutyches, or their followers. [Col. 0427A–B]

### CAP. 345.—What sort of men ought to enter upon the priestly office. From the decrees of Pope Damasus, ch. 8.

We have also learned that men of unexamined life, even men who have had numerous marriages, freely and without restraint aspire to the aforesaid dignities according to each man’s pleasure. We lay this blame not so much upon those who attain these offices through immoderate ambition, as especially upon metropolitan bishops, who, because they do not oppose forbidden attempts, despise, so far as lies in them, the commands of our God. And, to pass over what we suspect more deeply, where is that which our God established in the Law given through Moses, saying: “My priests shall marry once” (Lev. 21)? And elsewhere: “A priest shall take a virgin as his wife, not a widow, nor a divorced woman, nor a prostitute” (1 Tim. 3). Following this, the Apostle, a preacher once a persecutor, commanded that both priest and deacon should be the husband of one wife. [Col. 0427C]

### CAP. 346.—That metropolitans should preserve their rights. Leo to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, ch. 2 (Epistle 84).

(25, q. 2, c. *Igitur secundum*.) Therefore, in accordance with the canons of the holy Fathers, framed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, we decree that the metropolitan bishops of the individual provinces, concerning whom the care of your brotherhood is exercised by our delegation, shall retain unimpaired the right of the dignity entrusted to them from ancient times; so that they may depart from the established rules neither through negligence nor presumption. [Col. 0427D]

### CAP. 347.—That no one be ordained bishop against his will. Ibid., ch. 5.

(Dist. 63, c. *Si forte*.) Therefore, when the election of the high priest is under consideration, he should in every respect be set over the rest whom the united agreement of clergy and people has requested. Thus, if votes perhaps divide among several persons, the judgment of the metropolitan shall prefer one to another who is supported by greater zeal and merits; provided only that no one is ordained against his will or without seeking the office, lest an unwilling people despise or hate an unwanted bishop, and become less devout than is fitting, because it was not permitted to have the person it wished. [Col. 0428A]

### CAP. 348.—That the primate too should confirm by his authority the person of the bishop to be consecrated. Ibid., ch. 6.

(Dist. 65, c. *De persona*.) Therefore, regarding the person to be consecrated bishop and the consent of clergy and people, the metropolitan bishop shall report to your brotherhood and make known to you what has pleased the province, so that your authority also may confirm the ordination to be duly celebrated. That authority ought to introduce no delay or difficulty into proper arrangements, lest the Lord’s flocks long lack the care of pastors.

But when a metropolitan has died and another is to be appointed in his place, the provincial bishops must assemble in the metropolitan city, so that, after the wish of all the clergy and all the citizens has been examined, the best person may be chosen from the priests or deacons of that church. The bishops of the province shall report his name to your notice, fulfilling the wishes of those requesting him when they learn that what pleased them has also pleased you. For just as we do not wish lawful elections to be burdened by any delays, so we allow nothing to be presumed without your knowledge. [Col. 0428A–B]

### CAP. 349.—That primates and metropolitans are called by the Roman Church to share in its solicitude, not in the fullness of its power. Gregory.

To the most beloved brethren, all bishops established throughout Gaul, Europe, Germany, and all the provinces: Gregory, servant of the servants of God.

[Col. 0428C] (2, q. 6, c. *Decreto*.) By our decree we command that, if any of his rivals—something we do not wish—should wickedly attempt to accuse Aedric, bishop of the Church of Le Mans, he may, after the hearing before the primate of the diocese, appeal to us if necessary; and, by our authority, may pursue and conclude his actions, either before us or before our legates sent from our side, according to the decrees of the Fathers. Let no one judge him or presume to condemn him before this. (*Above*, ch. 11.) But if—God forbid—anything grave and intolerable should be alleged against him, our judgment must be awaited, so that nothing be decided beforehand concerning one who has fled to the bosom of the holy Roman Church and implores its aid, until this has been commanded by the authority of that Church, which has so imparted its offices to other Churches that they are called to share in its solicitude, not in the fullness of its power.

Accordingly, may your affection, in whose devotion we rejoice, join its care to our dispositions, and take pains that, through no one’s presumption, concerning the aforesaid our brother, anything be done otherwise than as is set down here, whether by your provision or, should he survive, by that of your successors. For no one may lawfully either wish or be able to transgress the commands of the Apostolic See, nor the ministry of our disposition, which your charity ought to follow. Therefore, whoever wishes to oppose apostolic commands [or: decrees] shall lie prostrate in grief at his own ruin; nor shall he thereafter have a place among the priests, but shall be excluded from the holy ministry. Let no one thereafter concern himself with his judgment, since he is not doubted to stand already condemned by the holy and apostolic Church and by its authority on account of his disobedience and presumption. For he must be subjected to the penalty of a greater excommunication, to whom the discipline of the holy Church has been entrusted, and who ought not merely to obey the commands of the holy Church set over him but also to warn others not to disregard them. Let him be excluded from divine and pontifical offices who refused to obey apostolic commands. [Col. 0428C–0429A]

### CAP. 350.—That one should not flee a position of governance for the repose of contemplation. The same, to Syriacus, bishop of Constantinople (Register VI, ch. 169, ep. 5).

(8, q. 1, c. *In scriptis*.) In your writings you relate that you have earnestly sought rest. Yet by this you fittingly show that you have come to pastoral responsibility, because, just as a position of governance must be denied to those who desire it, so it must be offered to those who flee from it. And as it is written: “No one takes this honour upon himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was” (Heb. 5). And again the same outstanding preacher says: “If one died for all, then all died; and Christ died for all, so that those who live should no longer live for themselves but for him [variant: God] who died and rose for them” (2 Cor. 5). And to the shepherd of the holy Church it is said: “Simon, son of John, do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John 21).

From these words it is gathered that, if one who is capable refuses to feed the sheep of almighty God, he shows that he does not love the supreme Shepherd. For if the Father’s Only-Begotten went out from the Father’s hidden place into our public world, in order to accomplish what benefited all, what shall we say if we prefer retirement to the benefit of our neighbours? Rest, therefore, is to be sought by us from the heart; yet it must sometimes be postponed for the advantage of many. For just as we ought to flee occupation with our whole desire, so, if there is no one to preach, it is necessary willingly to undertake the burden of occupation. [Col. 0429B–C]

### CAP. 351.—That a bishop should not excommunicate for a personal injury. Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari (Register II, ch. 34).

(23, q. 4, *Inter querelas*.) Isidore complained that your brotherhood had excommunicated and anathematized him without cause. When we wished to learn from your cleric who was present why this had been done, we learned that it was for no other reason than that he had injured you. This matter deeply distressed us. For if it is so, you show that you think nothing of heavenly things, but demonstrate that you have an earthly mind [variant: earthly manner of life], in imposing the curse of anathema in revenge for a personal injury—something prohibited by the sacred rules. Henceforth, then, be watchful and diligent, and do not presume again to inflict such things upon anyone in defence of your own injury. [Col. 0429C–D]

### CAP. 352.—When a bishop is ill, another shall not be substituted unless he has departed this life, lest the beauty of the talent entrusted be destroyed. Nicholas to Albinus, bishop of Juvanum [variant: Genoa].

(7, q. 1, c. *Pontifices qui*.) Bishops afflicted by some infirmity or illness are not to be removed, nor ought others to be consecrated in their place, unless they have been taken from this life. But if they complain concerning the ministry entrusted to them, let priests perform what is lawful. In matters which they are not permitted to undertake, let the assistance of neighbouring bishops be supplied until health is restored. This must be done with careful caution, lest through the occasion of necessity ambition for usurpation spring up.

Bishops who have undertaken the care and responsibility of the Lord’s flock ought not to withdraw from its administration, lest the beauty of the talent they received be destroyed; rather, through their striving it should be salutarily increased and tripled. [Col. 0429D–0430A]

### CAP. 353.—That neither bishop nor cleric should in any way engage in hunting. The same, to the same.

[Col. 0430B] (Dist. 34, c. *Quorumdam relatione*.) Reports of certain faithful persons have informed us that Bishop Lanfredus, who is also said to be young, is devoted to hunting. This vice entangles many from the clerical roll, especially Germans and Gauls by birth, irreverent [variant: reverent]. But if this man is as we have heard, he is rightly called young: occupied with youthful desires, he is restrained by none of the gravity of old age.

Likewise: O miserable life of men, and especially of priests! When they ought to labour to win the faithful, they devote themselves to hunting wild beasts; and when they ought to catch human beings, they catch birds and animals. While they devote themselves to the deaths of living creatures, they lose the life of their own souls. O life more unhappy than every life! For in what does anyone appear more carnal than in such a life? The life of hunters gains nothing but flesh; and no one who remained in it was ever approved. For, as blessed Jerome said, “We never read that a hunter was holy.”

Woe to such bishops! Though they ought to choose Peter, Andrew, James, and John—of whom the Lord said, “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matt. 4; Mark 1)—for imitation, as men whose disciples they are, they imitate instead the rejected Nimrod, Ishmael, and Esau, who are reported to have devoted themselves to inventions of this sort (Gen. 10, 21, 25).

Nevertheless, it has also been reported to our apostolic office concerning this bishop that he maintains an immoderate familiarity with a certain daughter of his, and that an evil report has consequently arisen about him. On this account he has been admonished and rebuked by your holiness and by his fellow bishops, but has not been corrected at all. This matter is especially displeasing, and makes opinion of him worse and worse. In this he does not obey the counsels of your beatitude and his fellow bishops, and through disobedience he falls back into the fault of the first-created man.

Your brotherhood ought therefore to convene a synodal council with your bishops and suffragans, to address this bishop with words of salvation, and by pastoral authority command him wholly to abstain from the hunting of every kind of animal and bird, and entirely to restrain himself from immoderate familiarity with his daughter. If he scorns to obey, and, despite your warnings, delays to obey both by abandoning hunting and by avoiding immoderate association with his daughter, let him withdraw from your fellowship as excommunicated. But if he should still prove obstinate in this, he must cease from ministry. [Col. 0430B–0431A]

### CAP. 354.—That every metropolitan must, within three months of his consecration, send to Rome or go there for the pallium. John VIII, from the Third Council at Ravenna.

Whoever, having become metropolitan, does not within three months of his consecration—unless an unavoidable necessity intervenes—send to the Apostolic See, in order to set forth his faith and receive the pallium, shall lose the dignity entrusted to him. He shall yield the episcopal see and lack all power to consecrate for as long as he disregards the ancient custom of declaring his faith and seeking the pallium. [Col. 0431A–B]

### CAP. 355.—How true priests should be honoured, since the Lord honoured false ones. Cyprian to Rogatianus (Book III, ch. 9).

(Dist. 93, c. *Dominus noster*.) Our Lord Jesus Christ, king, judge, and priest, preserved honour for evil priests until his Passion. In that Passion he called priest the man whom he knew to be sacrilegious; and when he received a blow and was told, “Do you answer the high priest in this way?” (John 18), he said nothing insulting against the person of the high priest, but instead defended his own innocence, saying: “If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness to the wrong” (ibid.). Thus we might have an example of his humility. And he taught that true priests should be fully and lawfully honoured, since he himself acted thus toward false priests. [Col. 0431B–C]

### CAP. 356.—That the individual churches should have individual prelates. Jerome to the monk Rusticus.

(7, q. 1, c. *In apibus*.) Among bees there is one leader; cranes follow one leader in a lettered formation. There is one emperor and one judge of a province. Rome, at its founding, could not have two brothers as kings at once, and was dedicated by fratricide. In Rebecca’s womb Esau and Jacob waged war (Gen. 25). Each church has its bishop, each its archbishop, each its archdeacon; and every ecclesiastical order depends upon its own governors. [Col. 0431C]

### CAP. 357.—That at Trier and Cologne no one be elected without consulting the Roman pontiff. Nicholas to King Lothair.

[Col. 0431D]

Moreover, because it has been reported to us that whoever is to be promoted to a bishopric in your kingdom is permitted to be elected only if he enjoys your favour, we enjoin you by apostolic authority, under solemn appeal to divine judgment, not to allow anyone to be elected in the city of Trier or in Agrippine Cologne before a report on the matter has been made to our apostolic office.

### CAP. 358.—On the profession of faith. Pelagius to King Childebert.

(25, q. 1, c. *Satagendum*.) We must take pains, in order to remove the scandal of suspicion, to render the service of our confession to kings, to whom Holy Scripture commands that we also be subject. When Ruffinus, a man of distinction and envoy of your excellency, came, he confidently requested of us—as was fitting—that we should signify to you either that the *Tome* of Pope Leo of blessed memory was preserved by us in all respects, or that we should send a confession of our faith in our own words.

Since the first part of his request was easier, we fulfilled it immediately when he spoke: by a profession signed with our hand, we declared to you that, by God’s favour, we preserve in every respect the *Tome* of that bishop, written in defence of the Catholic faith. But lest thereafter—God forbid—there remain any occasion for suspicion, I also hastened to do [variant: I did] the other thing which the aforesaid illustrious man Ruffinus urged: namely, to set forth [variant: I set forth] in my own words the confession of faith which we hold. [Col. 0432A–B]

### CAP. 359.—That after a bishop has first been consecrated by election, there cannot be a second. Cyprian, in his letter to the Romans (Book IV, ep. 2, to Antonianus).

(7, q. 1, c. *Factus est*.) Cornelius was made bishop by the judgment of God and of his Christ, by the testimony of all the clergy, by the vote of the people, and by the agreement of the former priests and good men, when no bishop had been made there and the rank of the chair was vacant. Once that see was occupied and the agreement of you all confirmed, whoever thereafter wishes to become bishop must necessarily lack ecclesiastical ordination, because he does not maintain, through agreement, the unity of the Church. After the first, there cannot be a second. For whoever wishes to exist after the one consecrated by election is not merely not second, but is no bishop at all. [Col. 0432B–C]

### CAP. 360.—That one contradicts the Church who contradicts the bishop. Cyprian to Papianus (Book IV, ep. 9, to Florentius Papianus).

(7, q. 1, c. *Scire debes*.) You should know that the bishop is in the Church and the Church in the bishop; and that anyone who is not with the bishop is not in the Church. Those deceive themselves in vain who, having no peace with the priests of God, creep in and suppose that they secretly communicate with certain persons, when the Church, which is one and Catholic, has not been torn apart or divided. [Col. 0432C]

### CAP. 361.—On the unity of the Church. Cyprian.

[Col. 0432D]

Does he who does not maintain Peter’s unity believe that he holds the faith? Does he who deserts Peter’s chair, upon which the Church is founded, trust that he is in the Church?

### CAP. 362.—What is to be done with a bishop, or cleric of any rank, who has presumed to communicate after deposition. From the Council of Antioch, ch. 4.

(11, q. 4, c. *Si quis episcopus*.) If any bishop has been deposed by a synod, or a presbyter or deacon condemned by his own bishop, and presumes to undertake anything belonging to the priesthood or sacred ministry, he shall no longer be allowed either to entertain hope of restoration in another synod or to have any opportunity for defence.

[Col. 0433A]

> **Note: [Col. 0433D].** This note appears at the foot of columns 433 and 434, but the callout number (73) has not been printed in the text. Most of these matters are read in Epistle 81 of Pope Leo I, to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, ch. 1.

Moreover, all who communicate with him shall be expelled from the Church, especially if, after learning that sentence had been pronounced against him, they stubbornly communicate with him.

### CAP. 363.—That a bishop should not allege against anyone, even one who has confessed to him, what he cannot prove. From the Sixth Council of Carthage, ch. 5.

It was likewise resolved that, if a bishop should at some time say that someone had confessed a crime to him alone and that person deny it, the bishop should not consider it an injury to himself that he alone is not believed. And if, from scruple of his own conscience, he says that he does not wish to communicate with the denying person, then, as long as his own bishop does not communicate with the excommunicated person, other bishops shall not communicate with that bishop either, so that the bishop may take greater care not to allege against anyone what he cannot establish by other evidence. [Col. 0433A–B]

### CAP. 364.—On the same matter. From the First Council of Vaison, ch. 8.

(6, q. 2, c. *Si tantum episcopus*.) If only the bishop knows himself to be privy to another’s crime, he shall allege nothing so long as he cannot prove it, but shall work with the person himself toward his repentance through private rebukes. If, when rebuked, he becomes more stubborn and enters into public communion, even though the bishop lacks proof in reproving the one whom he judges guilty, the bishop shall be ordered—without condemnation, though by persons who know nothing of the matter—to withdraw for a time, for the sake of the person holding greater authority; while that other person remains in the common communion of all, so long as nothing can be proved except to the one who judges him guilty. [Col. 0433B–C]

### CAP. 365.—At what age deacons are to be consecrated. From the same council, ch. 16 (Council of Agde).

(C. 16, Dist. 77, c. *Episcopus*.) A bishop shall by no means confer the blessing of the diaconate upon persons younger than twenty-five years. Certainly, if married young men consent to be ordained, the consent of their wives is also to be sought, so that, after the marital bed has been set apart and religious observance promised, they may be ordained after both have made this conversion. [Col. 0433C]

### CAP. 366.—That bishops, presbyters, and Levites are not to have hunting dogs or hawks. From the Council of Agde, ch. 55.

(Dist. 34, c. *Episcopum*.) Bishops, presbyters, and deacons shall not be permitted to keep hunting dogs or hawks. If any person of these ranks is found [variants: detected; caught] indulging in this desire [variant: pleasure], then, if he is a bishop, he shall suspend himself from communion for three months; a presbyter shall abstain for two months; but a deacon shall cease from every office and from communion. [Col. 0433C–D]

### CAP. 367.—What is to be done with a bishop or cleric of any order unjustly deposed from his rank. From the Fourth Council of Toledo, ch. 28 (25).

(11, q. 3, c. *Episcopus, presbyter*.) If a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, unjustly deposed from his rank, is found innocent in the holy [variant: second] synod, he cannot be restored to what he was unless, before the altar, he receives from the hands of bishops the ranks he lost: if a bishop, the stole, ring, and staff; if a presbyter, the stole and chasuble [variant: paten]; if a deacon, the stole and alb; if a subdeacon, the paten and chalice. Thus also the remaining ranks shall receive the restoration of their office which they received when ordained. [Col. 0434A]

### CAP. 368.—That governors of churches should be awaited and corrected rather than immediately judged. Gregory to all bishops established throughout Gaul, Europe, and Germany (1).

(Dist. 45, c. *Licet plerumque*.) Although things deserving rebuke often happen to priests, benevolence should accomplish more in correcting them than severity, exhortation more than agitation, charity more than power, since none of us lives without reproach or sin. For if the Lord had immediately judged our teacher, the blessed Apostle Peter, after his threefold denial (Matt. 26), he would not have received from him so great a harvest as he did.

Therefore the governors of the Church ought rather to be awaited and corrected than immediately judged without consulting us, since the canons of the holy Fathers—framed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world—command that weightier affairs and more difficult outcomes of cases be suspended until our judgment is awaited and concluded under our direction. Hence it is necessary, after experience in many cases, to examine more carefully and guard against more diligently these and all other ecclesiastical matters, so that by the spirit of charity and peace every source of scandal, the presumption of the envious, and oppression of simple brethren may be removed from the Churches of the Lord. And just as none of the brethren wishes to be burdened by the judgment of others, so he should not dare inflict upon another what he does not wish done to himself. [Col. 0434A–C]

### CAP. 369.—That no bishop be compelled to appear before a secular court; and on the penalty of one who compels a bishop to come to a secular court. From the Book of Constitutions, ch. 6.

No bishop shall be compelled to appear in court to plead a case; rather, the judge shall send his officers to the bishop, so that, with the holy Gospels set before him, the bishop may say what he knows, in the manner honourable for priests.

From the same source, ch. 7. (11, q. 1, c. *Nullus episcopus*, but under the title of Pope Marcellus.) No bishop shall be brought or produced before any judge, civil or military, whether for a civil or criminal case, unless an imperial command has been issued. Any magistrate who dares to order this shall be punished by loss of his belt of office and a fine of twenty pounds of gold; those twenty pounds shall be assigned to the church whose bishop he ordered to be brought or produced. But the executor of the suit, after the loss of his belt, shall be subjected to tortures and placed on the rack. [Col. 0434C–D]

### CAP. 370.—That no bishop or cleric be a gambler or a spectator of games. Ibid., ch. 9.

Neither bishop, presbyter, deacon, subdeacon, reader, nor any other person belonging to a religious fellowship or habit shall dare to gamble, become a companion of gamblers, be a spectator, or attend any spectacle for the purpose of watching. If anyone acts against these provisions, he shall be forbidden the sacred ministry for three years. [Col. 0435A]

### CAP. 371.—That no one be excommunicated before the cause of excommunication is proved. Ibid., ch. 11.

(2, q. 1, c. *Nemo episcopus*.) No bishop and no presbyter shall excommunicate anyone before the cause has been proved for which the ecclesiastical canons command this to be done. But if anyone excommunicates another contrary to this, the person excommunicated shall, by authority of the higher priest, be restored to the grace of holy communion; while the person who unlawfully excommunicated him shall abstain for as long as seems good to the higher priest, so that he may justly suffer what he unjustly did. [Col. 0435A–B]

### CAP. 372.—That a bishop should be instructed in every knowledge of divine law. Seventh Synod, ch. 2.

Since in singing we promise God: “I will meditate on thy ordinances; I will not forget thy words” (Ps. 118), it is most salutary indeed for all Christians to observe this, but especially for those who have attained ecclesiastical dignity. Therefore we determine that every person to be promoted to the rank of bishop shall in every respect know the Psalter, so that all the clergy under him may be similarly guided and instructed by it.

The metropolitan shall inquire diligently whether he is ready to read the law attentively and not superficially: both the sacred canons and the holy Gospel, the book of the divine Apostle, and all divine Scripture; and whether he will live according to the commandments and teach the people entrusted to him. For the substance of our high priesthood consists in divinely transmitted utterances—that is, the true teaching of the divine Scriptures—as the great Dionysius testifies. But if he disputes this and does not promise willingly to act and teach in this way, he shall by no means be consecrated. For God says through the prophet: “You have rejected knowledge, and I will reject you, so that you may not serve me as priest” (Hos. 4). [Col. 0435B–C]

### CAP. 373.—That councils of bishops should be held once, not twice, each year. Ibid., ch. 6.

[Col. 0435D] (Dist. 18, c. *Quoniam quidem*.) Since there is a rule saying that regular inquiries ought to be made twice each year through an assembly of bishops in every province, the holy Fathers of the Sixth Synod determined, because of fatigue and so that those who are to assemble might have a suitable opportunity for travelling, that, every excuse removed, this should in every way take place once each year and that abuses should be corrected. We also renew this canon. If any ruler is found to hinder this, he shall be deprived of communion. But if any metropolitan neglects to do this without necessity, force, or some reasonable cause, he shall be subject to canonical penalties.

While the synod deliberates upon canonical and evangelical matters, the assembled bishops must devote themselves to meditation and diligent concern for keeping the divine and life-giving commands of the Lord. For in keeping them there is great reward (Ps. 18); because “the commandment is a lamp, the law a light, and reproof and discipline are the way of life” (Prov. 6); and: “The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. 18). Moreover, the metropolitan shall not be permitted to demand from what a bishop brings with him either an animal of burden or any other article. If he is found to have done this, he shall pay fourfold. [Col. 0435D–0436A]

### CAP. 374.—On the appointment of stewards in individual churches. Ibid., ch. 11.

(9, q. 5, c. *Cum simus*.) Since we are bound to observe all sacred rules, we must in every way preserve inviolate the rule which declares that there should be a steward (*oeconomus*) in every church. If each metropolitan appoints a steward in his own church, this is certainly good. Otherwise, by her own authority, the bishop of Constantinople has leave to appoint stewards in his church; likewise metropolitans may do so if the bishops subject to them have not taken care to establish stewards in their own churches. The same is to be observed also in monasteries. [Col. 0436A–B]

### CAP. 375.—That neither bishop nor abbot should grant church land to rulers or to his relatives. Ibid., ch. 12.

If any bishop or abbot is found transferring anything from episcopal revenues or monasteries into the hands of rulers, or conferring anything upon any person, what is established to have been given shall be void, according to the canon of the holy Apostles which says: “Let the bishop have care of all ecclesiastical property, so that he may administer it as under God’s observation.” He is not permitted to defraud them of anything, or to give to his own relatives things belonging to God. If the relatives are poor, he may give to them as poor persons, but under that pretext church property must not be defrauded.

If they put forward the excuse that a field is causing loss and yields no profit, even then that field or place shall not be granted to the rulers in those regions, but to clerics or cultivators. If he employs trickery and a ruler buys the field from a tenant or cleric, even then the sale shall be void and it shall be restored to the bishopric or monastery. The bishop or abbot doing this shall be removed: the bishop from his bishopric and the abbot from his monastery, as one who wickedly scatters what he did not gather [variant: does not gather]. [Col. 0436B–D]

### CAP. 376.—What an abbot may do concerning a reader only in his own monastery. Ibid., ch. 14.

(Dist. 69, cap. *Quoniam videmus*.) Since it is plainly necessary that order be observed in consecration, and that the promotions of priests [priesthood] be diligently maintained is altogether pleasing to God: and since we see that certain persons, having received the clerical tonsure from an early age without yet receiving the imposition of hands from the bishop, irregularly read from the ambo in the assembly, we decree that this shall henceforth by no means be done. The same also [Col. 0437A] [Note: [Col. 0437D] [ [Col. 0437] This note appears at the foot of columns 437 and 438, but the callout number (74) has not been printed in the text.] This letter of Gelasius to the Emperor Anastasius is found in volume II of the Councils.] must be observed among monks. But permission to make a reader by the imposition of hands belongs to every abbot solely in his own monastery, provided that it is known that the same abbot has received imposition of hands from a bishop, according to the custom for appointing abbots, and provided that he is a presbyter. Likewise, according to ancient custom, a chorepiscopus ought, by the bishop’s command, to promote readers.

CAP. 377.—That bishops or clerics are not to adorn themselves in glittering and splendid garments. *Ibid.*, cap. 16.

(21, q. 4, c. *Omnis jactantia*.) All ostentation and bodily adornment are foreign to the sacred order. Therefore bishops or clerics who adorn themselves in glittering and splendid garments ought to be corrected. If they persist in this, [Col. 0437B] they are to be subjected to penance; likewise also those who anoint themselves with perfumes. But since, when a root of bitterness sprang up, there arose in the Catholic Church the heresy of those who accuse Christians, *Kristianōn katēgorōn hairesis* [“the heresy of the accusers of Christians”]: and those who accepted it have not only abominated figurative paintings, *tas eikonikas zōgraphēseis* [“iconic images”], but have also rejected every reverence, offending those who live piously and religiously; and thereby there is fulfilled in them what is written: “The worship of God is an abomination to the sinner” (Prov. 15). Therefore, if any are found mocking those who are clothed in humble and religious garments, let them be corrected by penance, *di’ epitimion* [“by means of penance”]. For in former times every consecrated man lived in modest and humble clothing. Indeed, everything received not for necessity but for beauty bears the accusation of pride, as the great Basil says. Nor did anyone wear a garment variegated with silken fabrics, nor did they add ornaments of various colors to the upper parts of their garments; for they had heard in the divine language: “Those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses” (Matt. 11).

CAP. 378.—That no secular dignity, not even imperial dignity, can be equated with episcopal honor or dignity. From Gregory’s letter to Herman, bishop of Metz.

(Dist. 96, c. *Quis dubitet*.) Who can doubt that the priests of Christ are regarded as fathers and teachers of kings, princes, and all the faithful? Is it not recognized as a pitiful madness if a son should attempt to subjugate his father, or a disciple his [Col. 0437D] teacher, and to subject him by unjust bonds to his own power—him by whom he believes himself able to be bound and loosed not only on earth but also in heaven? As blessed Gregory recounts in a letter addressed to the Emperor Maurice, the Emperor Constantine the Great, lord of almost all the kings and princes of the whole world, clearly understanding this, sat last of all the bishops at the holy Synod of Nicaea and presumed to pronounce no judicial sentence over them. Rather, calling them even “lords,” he judged that they ought not to be subject to his judgment, but that he himself depended upon their decision.

Likewise, the aforesaid Pope Gelasius, seeking to persuade Anastasius not to regard the truth made known to him as an injury, added, saying (Dist. 96, *Duo sunt*): “There are indeed two powers, most august Emperor, by which this world is principally governed: namely, the sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power. Of these the burden of the priests is so much the weightier inasmuch as they will render account, in the divine judgment, even for kings themselves.” And after a few intervening words he says: “You know, therefore, that in these matters you depend upon their judgment, not that they are to be reduced to your will.”

Supported by such ordinances and authorities, many pontiffs have excommunicated some kings and others emperors. For, if a particular example concerning rulers’ persons is sought: blessed Pope Innocent excommunicated the Emperor Arcadius because he consented to the expulsion of Saint John Chrysostom from his see. Likewise another Roman pontiff deposed the king of the Franks from his kingdom—not so much on account of his own wrongdoings as because he was unfit for so great a power—and put Pippin, father of the Emperor Charles, in his place; and he absolved all the Franks from their oath of fidelity. The holy Church also acts by frequent authority in this fashion when it releases soldiers from the bond of an oath—as happens in the case of bishops who are deposed from the pontifical rank by apostolic authority.

And blessed Ambrose, though holy, was nevertheless not bishop of the universal Church; for an offense that did not seem so grave to other priests, he excommunicated the Emperor Theodosius the Great and excluded him from the Church. He also shows in his writings that gold is not more precious than lead to the degree that priestly authority is higher than royal power. Thus, near the beginning of his *Pastoral*, he writes (*On Priestly Dignity*, cap. 2): “Brethren, episcopal honor and sublimity can be equated with no comparisons. If you compare it with the splendor of kings and the diadem of princes, the comparison will fall far shorter than if you compared lead with the brilliance of gold. For when you see the necks of kings and princes bowed to the knees of priests, and, having kissed their right hands, believing themselves fortified thereby.” And shortly afterward (*ibid.*, cap. 3): “You ought to know, brethren, that we have set forth all these things beforehand in order to show [Col. 0438D] that nothing in this age is more excellent than priests, nothing higher than bishops can be found.”

Did not Pope Vigilius, of memorable memory, as blessed Gregory says, issue [promulgate] a sentence of condemnation against Theodora, then empress? Likewise Childebert, king of the Parisians, after abandoning his lawful wife Gotberga [otherwise Ingoberga] and taking as wives two sisters, Merofled and Marcovefa, was excommunicated by blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris. And because he would not repent, not long afterward he himself died by divine judgment.

## SIXTH PART OF THE DECRETUM

On the manner of life, ordination, correction, and cases of clerics.

[Col. 0439]

CAP. 1.—Whence a cleric is so called. From Jerome’s letter to Nepotian.

[Col. 0439A]

(12, q. 1, c. *Clericus*; Isidore, *Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, cap. 1.) Let the cleric who serves Christ’s Church first interpret his own designation, and, having set forth the definition of the name, strive to be what he is called. For if the Greek *klēros* is called *sors* in Latin, “lot,” clerics are so called because they belong to the Lord’s lot, or because the Lord himself is the lot—that is, the portion—of clerics. And because [otherwise: “but he who”] he is either himself the Lord’s portion or has the Lord as his portion, he ought to present himself in such a way that he may possess the Lord and himself be possessed by the Lord. He who possesses the Lord and says with the Prophet, “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. 15, 72), can possess nothing outside the Lord. But if he possesses anything else [Col. 0439B] besides the Lord, the Lord will not be his portion. For example, if he has gold, silver, estates, or assorted household goods, the Lord does not deign to become his portion along with those portions.

But if I am the Lord’s portion and the cord of his inheritance (Ps. 104), I receive no share among the other tribes; rather, like a Levite and priest, I live from tithes, and, serving at the altar, I am sustained by the altar’s offerings. Having food and clothing, I shall be content with these and, naked, follow the naked cross. Therefore I beseech you—and I shall repeat the warning again and again—not to regard the clerical office as a kind of the old military service: that is, do not seek worldly gain in Christ’s military service; do not possess more than you possessed when you began to be a cleric, lest it be said of you: “Their clerical status shall not profit them.”

CAP. 2.—That there are two kinds of clerics. From the statements of blessed Isidore concerning the kinds of clerics.

[Col. 0439C]

(*Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, cap. 3.) There are two kinds of clerics: one, ecclesiastics living under episcopal rule; the other, *acephali*, that is, persons without a head whom they know to follow. Neither the pursuits of secular occupations among laypersons nor divine religious observance among clerics restrains these men; but a shameful and wandering life alone embraces them as unbound and roving persons. They indeed fear no one [variant: “and, since they fear no one, etc.”], and pursue license to satisfy their own pleasure, borne along like brute animals by their liberty and desire. They possess the badge of religion, but not the office of religion; they resemble hippocentaurs—neither horses nor human beings—and are a mixed race and two-formed offspring, as the poet says (Virgil, *Aeneid* VI). By their foul and infamous multitude, our western region is polluted abundantly [variant: “is powerful”].

CAP. 3.—That it especially befits clerics to love God and their neighbor; and concerning their manner of life and office. A brief collected epilogue and rule for clerics.

[Col. 0440A]

By legal ordinances and the most health-giving evangelical commandments we are admonished to love the Lord our God with all our heart and our neighbors as ourselves (Deut. 6; Lev. 19; Matt. 22; Mark 12), and so forth. Therefore, if all the faithful must strive with all their strength to observe these saving commandments, how much more must those who are devoted to divine worship and ought to be the seasoning of an example of virtues to others! Accordingly, they must first of all love the Lord God with all their heart, all their soul, and all their strength, and their neighbors as themselves; and they must know that the whole Law and the Prophets hang upon these two commandments.

They must not kill or hate a brother, because, as the Apostle says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3). They must not commit adultery, theft, covet another’s property, bear false witness, or do to another what they do not wish done to themselves. They must be neither proud nor puffed up, accustomed to detraction, enslaved to drunkenness, enervated by lust, disturbed by anger, subject to any other vices, idle talkers, envious, sleepy, lazy, grumblers, whisperers, wine-bibbers, or excessive eaters. Let them avoid frauds and deceits; let them by no means practice usury; let them not swear, lest perhaps they swear falsely [commit perjury]; let them not return evil for evil. When they see any good in themselves, let them attribute it to God; when they see evil, let them attribute it to themselves.

Let them flee discord and call back those whom they know to be discordant [variant: “whom they find to be in discord”] to the concord of charity; and, in the Psalmist’s words, let them turn away from evil and do good (Ps. 36). Let them also heed the Apostle’s prohibition: “Not in revelry and drunkenness, not in beds and indecencies, not in strife and rivalry; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 13). Let them observe also that from the vices forbidden by the Apostle there springs a harvest of every vice, and that pride is the mother of these diseases.

They must also keep their souls and bodies from every defilement of flesh and spirit, so that, in the Apostle’s words, their whole spirit, soul, and body may be preserved blameless at the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ (1 Thess. 5). Let them live soberly, justly, and piously. Let them utterly reject secular business, [Col. 0440D] because, according to that same Apostle: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please him to whom he has proved himself” (2 Tim. 2). Let them love fasting, receive guests, refresh the poor, clothe the naked, visit the sick, bury the dead, bring help to those in tribulation, console the sorrowful, prefer nothing to Christ’s love, not abandon charity, and, if possible, keep peace with all people. Let them fear the day of judgment and spiritually desire eternal life. Let them commit their hope to God. In all things, according to canonical institution, let them obey their own bishop; let them not rashly criticize their teachers.

Finally, let them devote themselves to spiritual instruction—to readings, psalms, hymns, spiritual songs, and the continual practice of other good works. Let all sleep in the dormitory, except anyone prevented by illness. Let them take their meals together in the refectory and come daily to the conference. As soon as the signal is given, let all hasten to church, and let them celebrate the canonical hours together, not negligently but with every reverence. Let them enter the church not pompously but reverently. Let them not stand in choir with staffs. Let them by no means engage in idle talk, but with every devotion and reverence perform the work of divine service, knowing that the presence of angels is always there.

Let them leave the cloister only by permission. When outside, let them live irreproachably, so that they may have a good testimony from those outside and may by no unlawful acts stain their religious profession and purpose. Rather, let them season all those with whom they associate by the salt of wisdom and examples of good works. Let them by no means seek women’s company; let them not walk with wandering eyes, or with wanton, haughty bearing and loosened loins. Let them not attend shows or secular pageants, nor devote themselves to gambling [Col. 0441C] or any hunting.

For, instructed by the Apostle’s saying, “Not in costly clothing” (1 Tim. 2), let them by no means delight in costly garments. Let them take the greatest care not to linger outside the cloister except as the prior has appointed and the opportunity of the time requires. While within the cloister, let them not be idle, but devote themselves either to divine offices, their own useful tasks, or obedience to their teachers’ commands, lest, sluggish in idleness, they hear from the Apostle: “If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat” (2 Thess. 3).

Let seniors love juniors spiritually; let juniors show due obedience to seniors. Let the more learned by no means prefer themselves to the less learned, but rather build them up in charity. Nor should those distinguished by noble birth or gifts of virtue proudly exalt themselves above others. Let all in the community serve one another in turn by the office of charity. As they eat in the refectory and maintain silence with the utmost religious observance, let a reading be continuously read. Let them jointly rebuke and chastise offenders with zeal for righteousness. Let them correct negligent boys and youths with verbal discipline. Let each be instructed, according to his capacity, in the disciplines of various arts, so that no one may appear useless in the canonical community or idly consume the offerings of the faithful.

For such, indeed—or rather, in such a manner of life—ought all to be who have devoted themselves to divine offices. Therefore let them strive to read attentively, commit to memory, and, with God’s grace assisting, fulfill according to their strength these matters briefly collected here, so that they may more easily and freely carry out the greater things set forth by the holy Fathers. Let them therefore walk in the calling to which they have been called, turning neither to the right nor to the left, so that, obeying the divine commands, they may deserve, with his help, to attain Christ, in whose lot they are known to be: he who is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14).

CAP. 4.—On the tonsure of clerics. Isidore, in the book *Ecclesiastical Offices* (book II, cap. 4).

The use of ecclesiastical tonsure arose, I think, from the Nazirite practice. They first allowed their hair to grow; then, after completing the vow of their great continence [variant: “after the observance of continence had completed the vow, etc.”], they shaved their heads and were commanded to place their hair in the fire of sacrifice (Num. 6), namely, so that they might consecrate to the Lord the perfection of their devotion. The use of this example was therefore introduced by the Apostles, so that those devoted to divine worship and consecrated to the Lord might, like Nazirites—that is, holy persons of God—be renewed by cutting their hair.

For this also is commanded to the prophet Ezekiel, when the Lord says: “You, son of man, take for yourself a sharp sword, and draw it over your head and beard” (Ezek. 5). This was because he too, being of priestly descent, served God in the ministry of sanctification. We read that those Nazirites Priscilla and Aquila first did this in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 18); likewise the Apostle Paul and certain disciples of Christ who proved to be imitators in such observance (Acts 21).

Now tonsure among clerics is a certain sign represented on the body but enacted in the mind: namely, that through this sign vices may be removed in religion, and that we may strip ourselves of the crimes of our flesh as though of hair; and then, with our minds renewed, shine forth with fresh locks, stripping off, in the Apostle’s words, the old man with his deeds and putting on the new man, who is renewed in the knowledge of God (Col. 3). This renewal ought to take place in the mind, but be displayed on the head, where the mind itself is known to dwell.

But in that a circular crown is left above and below the shaven part of the head, I think the priesthood and kingship of the Church are figured in them. For among the ancients a tiara was placed upon priests’ heads. Made of fine linen, it was round, like a half-sphere; and this is signified by the shaven portion of the head. A crown, moreover, is the breadth of a golden [variant: “of gold”] circle that encircles the heads of kings. Thus both signs are expressed on the heads of clerics, so that what the Apostle Peter teaches may also be fulfilled in a bodily likeness: “You are an elect race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2).

But it is asked why, as among the ancient Nazirites, the hair is not first grown and then cut. Those who raise this question should observe the difference between that prophetic veil and this revelation of the Gospel, of which the Apostle says: “When you turn to Christ, the veil will be removed” (2 Cor. 3). For what the veil interposed between Moses’ face and the sight of the people of Israel signified, the hair of the saints signified in those times as well. The Apostle too says that hair serves as a covering. Therefore the heads of those consecrated to the Lord ought no longer to be covered by their hair (1 Cor. 11), but only uncovered, because what was hidden in the sacrament of prophecy has now been revealed in the Gospel.

CAP. 5.—I. On doorkeepers. The same author (book II, cap. 14).

Doorkeepers are those who in the Old Testament were called temple gatekeepers. They were in charge of the gates of the temple at Jerusalem and, being appointed in their turns, guarded all the inner and outer parts of the temple (1 Chron. 9, 23, 35). Thus, distinguishing between the holy and the wicked, they admit into the church only those who are faithful. For no one can enter the temple except through them. They have power both to receive the good and to reject the unworthy.

CAP. 6.—II. On readers. The same author (book II, cap. 11).

[Col. 0443B]

The order of readers received its form and beginning from the prophets. Readers, then, are those who proclaim the word of God, to whom it is said: “Cry aloud; do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58). When they are ordained, the bishop first addresses the people concerning their manner of life; then, before the people, he gives them the book of the sacred writings for proclaiming God’s word.

A person promoted to this rank must be learned in doctrine and books, adorned with knowledge of meanings and words, so that by the distinctions of clauses he may understand where a construction ends, where the sentence still hangs in suspense, and where the final sentence is closed. Thus, being practiced, he will possess the force [variant: “use”] of delivery, so as to lead the minds and understanding of all toward comprehension—distinguishing kinds of delivery and expressing the proper emotions of statements: now with the voice of one declaring, now of one grieving [variant: “commanding”], now rebuking, now exhorting, or the like, according to the kind of appropriate delivery. In this, above all [variant: “especially”], knowledge must be applied to ambiguous statements.

For many things in Scripture, unless pronounced in their proper manner, fall into the opposite sense. For example: “Who shall bring an accusation against God’s elect? God who justifies?” (Rom. 8). If this is pronounced as an affirmation, without preserving its proper mode of delivery, a great distortion arises. It should therefore be delivered as if it said: “Is it God who justifies?” The answer “No” is understood [variant: “so that ‘No’ may be understood”]. In such important matters, then, an aptitude for learning is necessary, so that each point may be pronounced properly and suitably.

For this reason the reader ought also to know the force of accents, so that he may know on which syllable the voice of the speaker is to be prolonged. For unskilled readers often err in the accents of words, and those who seem to possess learning are accustomed to mock us for our ignorance, disparaging us and swearing that we do not at all know what we are saying.

The reader’s voice, moreover, should be simple, clear, suited to every kind of delivery, full of manly vigor, avoiding a rustic and somewhat boorish sound; neither low nor excessively high, neither broken nor delicate, and conveying nothing feminine [Col. 0444A] in sound; not accompanied by bodily movement, but only by an appearance of gravity.
