For the reader must serve ears and heart, not eyes, lest he make them spectators of himself rather than hearers. An old opinion holds that readers took the greatest care of their voice for the sake of delivery, so that they might be heard amid a tumult. Hence readers were formerly called heralds or proclaimers.

CAP. 7.—III. On exorcists. The same author (book II, cap. 13).

We find that exorcists were in the first order and ministry of the Church, in accordance with the offices arranged in Solomon’s temple and later distributed by Ezra (1 Esdr. 2, 3); and those whom Ezra calls the temple’s *actores* [officials or administrators] are now exorcists in the Church of God. For under Ezra there were temple officials, sons of Solomon’s servants, who had under their care the operation of the whole temple or served the sacred offerings [variant: “services”]. Although they belonged to the order and ministry of the temple, they were far removed from the ministry of God’s altar, because neither psalmists nor doorkeepers nor sacred servants were permitted to handle the altar’s gifts—only Levites.

What, then, was their task? The temple officials had no other charge than repairing roofs and structures, so that whatever in the temple’s construction had been damaged or fallen into ruin might be repaired and restored by those same officials from the Lord’s treasuries. Therefore the temple officials are exorcists in the temple [variant: “people”] of God. For just as a prudent and good administrator knows what his lord’s estate is and the measure of all his property, and keeps with himself the original documents of the entire possession, so the exorcist gathers into his careful custody the secrets of the entire kingdom of the Lord, so that he may commit to memory, from the mysteries of Scripture, that by which he may exercise the gift granted him by the Holy Spirit, according to the Apostle’s proclamation.

For the Apostle mentions exorcists when he says: “Do all have gifts of healings?” (1 Cor. 12). When they are ordained, as the canon says (Fourth Council of Carthage), they are to receive from the bishop’s hand a booklet in which the exorcisms are written, receiving authority to lay hands upon the possessed, whether baptized or catechumens.

CAP. 8.—IV. On acolytes. [Note: [Col. 0443] This chapter is not found in printed copies of Isidore; rather, it is from the *Etymologies*.] The same author.

[Col. 0444D] (Book VII, cap. 12; and in the Council of Aachen.) *Acolythi* is Greek; in Latin they are called *ceroferarii*, “candle-bearers,” from carrying candles when the Gospel is to be read or the sacrifice offered. For then lights are kindled and carried by them, not to drive away darkness when the sun is shining at that time, but to show a sign of joy: so that under the figure of bodily light that light may be displayed of which the Gospel says: “There was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1).

CAP. 9.—V. On subdeacons. The same author (book II, cap. 10).

Subdeacons, who among the Greeks are called *hypodiaconi*, are found in Ezra, where they are called *Nathinaei* (1 Esdr. 2, 7, 8), that is, those serving the Lord in humility. From their order came that Nathanael [variant: “Nathanei”] who, instructed by divine revelation in the Gospel of John (John 1), deserved to confess the Savior, and who also shone forth faithful at the first evidence of his divinity, when the Lord declared and said: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no guile” (*ibid.*).

These receive from the people the offerings in the Lord’s temple. These obey the duties of the Levites; these also offer to the deacons at the altars of the Lord the vessels of Christ’s body and blood. Concerning them the Fathers decreed that those who handle the sacred mysteries should be chaste, abstinent from their wives, and free from every carnal impurity, according to the prophetic command: “Be cleansed, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52). Therefore, when ordained, they do not receive imposition of hands as priests and Levites do; rather, they receive only an empty paten and an empty chalice from the bishop’s hand, and from the archdeacon a pitcher of water with water, a hand-basin [variant: “ewer”], and a towel.

CAP. 10.—VI. On deacons. *Ibid.* (book II, cap. 8).

The order of deacons took its beginning from the tribe of Levi. For the Lord commanded Moses that, after the ordination of Aaron the priest and his sons, the tribe of Levi [variant: “again, the tribe of Levi, etc.”] should be appointed in the ministry of divine worship and consecrated to the Lord in place of all firstborn, and should serve Israel before Aaron and his sons in the tabernacle of God, keeping watch in God’s temple day and night. They were to carry the ark, the tabernacle, and all its vessels; they were to set their camp around the tabernacle; and when the tabernacle was moved, they were to take it down and then set it up again. From the age of twenty-five and above, they were commanded to serve in the tabernacle (Num. 1 and 3).

The holy Fathers established this rule also in the New Testament. But the beginnings of their office in the Gospel are read thus in the Acts of the Apostles: “The twelve apostles summoned the multitude of disciples and said: ‘It is not fitting that we should leave the word of God and serve tables. Therefore, brothers, choose from among yourselves seven men of good testimony, full of the Spirit [variant: ‘the Holy Spirit and wisdom’], whom we may appoint over this matter; but we shall devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.’ This saying pleased the multitude; and they immediately chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas, a convert from Antioch. They set these before the apostles, and, when they had prayed, they laid hands upon them. And the word of God increased and the number of believers multiplied” (Acts 6).

From that time the Apostles, or the successors of the Apostles, decreed that in all churches there should be seven deacons, who, being of a rank higher than the rest, should stand near Christ’s altar like pillars of the altar—and not without some mystery in the number seven. For these are the seven angels whom we read in the Apocalypse as sounding trumpets. These are the seven golden lampstands; these are the voices of thunder (Rev. 8). For they, with a clear voice like heralds, admonish all, whether to pray, bend the knee, chant psalms, or listen to readings. They cry out that we may have ears for the Lord; they also proclaim the Gospel.

Without them a priest has the name but not the office. For as consecration belongs to the priest, so the dispensation of the sacrament belongs to the minister. The former commands prayer; the latter commands chanting. The former consecrates the offerings; the latter distributes what has been consecrated. Even priests themselves are not permitted, on account of presumption, to take the chalice from the Lord’s table unless it has been handed to them by the deacons. Levites bring the offerings to the altars; Levites arrange the Lord’s table; Levites cover the ark of the covenant. For not all see the lofty mysteries covered by the Levites, lest those who ought not see should see, and those who cannot preserve them should receive them.

For this reason they stand at the altar clothed in white, that they may have a heavenly life and approach the offerings white and unstained—pure in body and incorrupt in chastity. For it is fitting that the Lord should have such ministers, who are corrupted by no contagion of the flesh but rather shine in the eminence of chastity. The Apostle Paul writes most fully to Timothy concerning the kind of deacons who should be ordained (1 Tim. 3). For, after he had spoken beforehand of the election of priests, he immediately added: “Deacons likewise irreproachable”—that is, without stain, like bishops; “chaste,” namely continent from lust; “not double-tongued,” so as not to disturb those who have peace; “not given to much wine,” because where drunkenness is, there lust and rage rule; “not pursuing shameful gain,” lest they seek earthly profit from a heavenly mystery. There is also a desire for shameful gain in thinking more about present things than future ones. After this he added: “But let these first be tested, and then let them minister, having no accusation.” These too, like bishops, ought to be tested before ordination to determine whether they are worthy, and afterward to minister.

CAP. 11.—VII. On presbyters. *Ibid.* (book II, cap. 7).

The order of presbyters took its beginning, as has been said, from Aaron’s sons. Those called priests in the Old Testament are those now called presbyters; and those called chief priests are now named bishops. *Presbyteri* means “elders,” because the Greeks call those advanced in age *presbyteroi*. To these, as to bishops, has been entrusted the dispensation of God’s mysteries. For they preside over Christ’s Church and share with bishops in the consecration of the divine body and blood; likewise in teaching the people and in the office of preaching.

The ordination and consecration of clerics are reserved to the authority of the high priest alone, lest ecclesiastical discipline, claimed by many, dissolve concord and produce scandals. For the Apostle Paul, speaking to Titus, plainly affirms that the same presbyters are truly priests under the name of bishops: “For this reason,” he says, “I left you in Crete, that you might correct what is lacking and appoint presbyters in every city as I instructed you: if anyone is without accusation, the husband of one wife, having faithful children not accused of debauchery or unsubmissive. For a bishop must be without accusation” (Titus 1). By this statement he shows that presbyters too are designated under the name of bishops.

Hence, writing to Timothy concerning the ordination of bishop and deacon (1 Tim. 3), he is entirely silent concerning presbyters, because he comprehends them under the name of bishops. For theirs is a rank joined to the first [variant: “and almost joined to the first”], just as he writes to the Philippians, “to bishops and deacons” (Phil. 1), although one city cannot have several bishops. And in the Acts of the Apostles, when he was going to Jerusalem, he summoned the presbyters of the Church, to whom, among other things, he said: “Watch over the flock in which the Holy Spirit appointed you bishops” (Acts 20).

Therefore presbyters ought to be appointed in the Church as bishops, as both the Apostle speaks to Titus (Titus 1) and the canons themselves testify. Presbyters, however, are so called from merit and wisdom, not from age (Anacletus, Epistle 2, cap. 2). Moses too is commanded to choose presbyters (Num. 11). Hence Proverbs says: “Gray hair is the glory of elders” (Prov. 20). What is this gray hair? Without doubt, wisdom, of which it is written: “The gray hair of human beings is prudence” (Wisdom 4). Although we read that human beings lived nine hundred and more years from Adam to Abraham (Gen. 5), no one before Abraham was first called a presbyter—that is, an elder (Gen. 43)—though he is shown to have lived far fewer years. Therefore presbyters are named not because of decrepit old age but because of wisdom. If this is so, it is remarkable [variant: “I wonder”] why unwise persons are appointed.

CAP. 12.—How presbyters ought to be ordained. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, cap. 3, at which Augustine was present.

(Dist. 23, cap. *Presbyter*.) When a presbyter is ordained, the bishop blessing him and holding his hand upon his head, all the presbyters present shall likewise hold their hands upon his head beside the bishop’s hand.

CAP. 13.—How deacons ought to be ordained. *Ibid.*, cap. 4.

(Dist. 23, cap. *Diaconus*.) When a deacon is ordained, the bishop who blesses him alone shall lay his hand upon his head, because he is consecrated not to the priesthood but to ministry.

CAP. 14.—On the ordination of subdeacons. *Ibid.*, cap. 5.

(Dist. 25, cap. *Subdiaconus*.) When a subdeacon is ordained, because he does not receive the imposition of hands, let him receive from the bishop’s hand an empty paten and an empty chalice; but from the archdeacon’s hand, a pitcher with water, a hand-basin, and a towel.

CAP. 15.—On the ordination of acolytes, cap. 6.

(Dist. 23, c. *Acolythus*.) When an acolyte is ordained, he is to be instructed by the bishop how he ought to perform his office; but from the archdeacon he is to receive a candlestick with a taper, so that he may know that he is assigned to light the lamps of the church [Col. 0448A]. He is also to receive an empty cruet for presenting wine for the Eucharist of Christ’s blood.

CAP. 16.—On the ordination of exorcists, chapter 7.

(Dist. 23, c. *Exorcista*.) When an exorcist is ordained, let him receive from the bishop’s hand a booklet in which the exorcisms are written, the bishop saying to him: “Receive this, commit it to memory, and have authority to lay hands upon one possessed, whether baptized or a catechumen.”

CAP. 17.—On the ordination of readers, chapter 8.

(Dist. 23, c. *Lector*.) When a reader is ordained, the bishop shall address the people concerning him, declaring his faith, manner of life, and ability. After this, in the sight of the people, he shall hand him the book from which he is to read, [Col. 0448B] saying: “Receive it, and be a herald of the word of God. If you fulfil the office faithfully and profitably, you shall have a share with those who have ministered the word of God.”

CAP. 18.—On the ordination of doorkeepers, chapter 9.

(Dist. 23, c. *Ostiarius*.) When a doorkeeper is ordained, after he has been instructed by the archdeacon concerning how he ought to conduct himself in the house of God, at the archdeacon’s prompting the bishop hands him the keys of the church from the altar, saying to him: “Act in such a way as one who must render an account to God for those things which are unlocked by these keys.”

CAP. 19.—How a psalmist is to be ordained, chapter 10.

(Dist. 23, c. *Psalmista*.) A psalmist—that is, a singer—may undertake the office of singing without the bishop’s knowledge, by the priest’s command alone, the priest saying to him [Col. 0448C]: “See that what you sing with your mouth you believe with your heart; and what you believe with your heart you prove by your works.”

CAP. 20.—How ecclesiastical offices are to be ordered, and what belongs to each person in every rank. A letter of Isidore, bishop of Seville, addressed to Ludefred, bishop of Córdoba.

(Dist. 25, c. *Perlectis*.) Having read Your Holiness’s letter, I rejoiced to learn from its report that you enjoy the health I desired for you. As for those matters which the following discourse of your eloquence has sought to set forth, I thank God that you devote care to the duty of a pastor and inquire how ecclesiastical offices should be ordered. Although all these things are known to your prudence, nevertheless, because you consult me in brotherly affection, I shall explain them insofar as I can, and shall speak of what belongs to each of the orders of the Church [Col. 0448D].

The keys of the church belong to the doorkeeper, so that he may close and open God’s temple, guard everything within and without, admit the faithful, and exclude the excommunicated and unbelievers. It belongs to the exorcist to retain the exorcisms by heart and, while performing exorcism, to lay hands upon those possessed and catechumens. It belongs to the acolyte to prepare the lights in the sacristy. He carries the candle; he prepares the vessels [variant: “the vessels presented”] for the Eucharist, and prepares the chalice [variant: “the chalices for the subdeacons”].

It belongs to the psalmist to perform the office of singing: to say blessings, praises, the sacrifice [variant: “the sacrifice of praise”], responsories, and whatever belongs to skill in singing. It belongs to the reader to pronounce the readings and to preach to the people those things which the prophets foretold [Col. 0449A]. It belongs to the subdeacon to bring the chalice and paten to Christ’s altar, hand them to the Levites, and minister to them; likewise, to hold the cruet of water, the hand-cloth, and the towel, and to provide water to bishop, priest, and Levites for washing their hands before the altar.

It belongs to the deacon to stand by the priests and minister in all that is done in Christ’s sacraments: namely, in baptism, in chrism, with paten and chalice; likewise to bring and arrange the offerings upon the altar, prepare and clothe the Lord’s table, carry the cross, preach the Gospel, and the Apostle [perhaps: “the Epistle”]. For just as readers are commanded to proclaim the Old Testament, so deacons are commanded to proclaim the New. The office of prayers and the recitation of names also belong to him [Col. 0449B]. He bids the people give ear to the Lord; he exhorts them to pray; he gives the cry; and he announces peace.

It belongs to the priest to consecrate the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood upon God’s altar, say prayers, and bless God’s gifts. It belongs to the bishop to consecrate basilicas, anoint the altar, and make chrism. He distributes the aforesaid offices and ecclesiastical orders, and he blesses consecrated virgins. Although each person has precedence in his own particular sphere, the bishop is nevertheless the chief organizer of all.

These are the orders and ministries of clerics; yet by episcopal authority they are apportioned to the care of the archdeacon and the diligence of the primicerius and treasurer. For the archdeacon commands the subdeacons and Levites. To him belong these ministries: the arrangement by the Levites of the clothing of the altar [Col. 0449C], the care of incense, and the necessary oversight of the sacrifice; determining which Levite is to read the Apostle [Gratian: “the Epistle”] and Gospel, who is to say the prayers or responsory on Sundays, or sing the solemn office. The supervision, ordering, and disputes of parishes also belong to his care; for repairs to diocesan basilicas, he makes representations to the priest. By the bishop’s command he inspects parishes and the ornaments or property of basilicas and parishes; he reports to the bishop the records of ecclesiastical manumissions. He receives the money collected from the communion, brings it to the bishop, and himself distributes to the clerics their proper shares. The misconduct of deacons is reported to the bishop by the archdeacon. He announces to the priest in the sacristy the days of fasts and solemnities, and these are publicly proclaimed in church by him [variant: “are proclaimed”].

When the archdeacon is absent, the next deacon performs his duties. The archpriest must know that he is under the archdeacon and must obey his commands as those of his bishop; and, in what belongs especially to his ministry, he must exercise oversight over all priests in the order, remain constantly in the Church, and, when his bishop is absent, celebrate the solemnities of the Mass in his place and say the collects, or appoint whomever he himself charges to do so [Col. 0449D].

To the primicerius belong the acolytes, exorcists, psalmists, and readers; the giving of the signal for the clerics’ office; oversight of honorable conduct; the office of singing [variant: “the practice of the office”]; and the careful performance of readings, blessings, psalm, praises, offertory, and responsories—determining which cleric is to say each. The ordering and manner of chanting in choir according to solemnity and season, and the arrangements for carrying lights, also belong to him. If anything necessary for repairing the basilicas in the city arises, he is to report it to the priest. He is to send the bishop’s letters concerning fast-days to parish clergy through the doorkeepers. He is to discipline clerics whom he knows to be delinquent; but the transgressions of those whom he cannot reform he is to bring to the bishop’s notice. He is to appoint the custodians of basilicas and arrange the registers of the poor. When the primicerius is absent, the person who is nearest to him either by law or by recognized competence for these duties is to carry out the matters mentioned above.

To the treasurer belong [Col. 0450B] the appointment of the doorkeepers of basilicas, preparation of incense, care of preparing chrism, care of arranging the baptistery, and preparation of lights for the sacrifice and the sacrifice [variant: “in the sacristy and for the sacrifices”].

CAP. 21.—How those to be ordained are to be examined by the bishop. From the Council of Nantes, chapter 3 [chapter 6].

(Dist. 24, c. *Quando episcopus*.) When a bishop intends to perform ordinations, all who wish to enter the sacred ministry are to be summoned on the Wednesday before the ordination itself, to the city together with the priests [variant: “archpriests”] who are to present them. The bishop must then choose from his side priests and other prudent men knowledgeable in divine law and experienced in ecclesiastical ordinances, who shall diligently investigate the life, lineage, native country, [Col. 0450C] age, education, place in which they were brought up, whether they are well educated, and whether they are instructed in the law of the Lord.

Above all, they must investigate whether they firmly hold the Catholic faith and can affirm it in simple words. Those to whom this duty is entrusted must beware lest, induced either by favour or by desire for any gift, they depart from truth, so that the bishop lays hands for reception into sacred ranks upon one unworthy and insufficiently fit. If they do so, both the man who approached unworthily shall be removed from the altar, and those who attempted to sell the gift of the Holy Spirit, already condemned before God, shall be deprived of ecclesiastical dignity. Therefore let them be examined for three consecutive days; and thus on Saturday those found approved are to be presented to the bishop.

CAP. 22.—What priests must necessarily learn and know. From the sayings of Augustine.

[Col. 0450D]

The things which priests themselves need to learn are: the book of sacraments, the lectionary, the baptismal rite, computus, the penitential canon, the Psalter, and homilies suitable for Sundays throughout the annual cycle and for every feast. If even one of all these is lacking, the title of priest can scarcely stand in him, because the Gospel’s threats are exceedingly grave, where it says: “If the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit” (Matt. XV).

CAP. 23.—On the ordinations of priests and deacons. From Letter 2 of Pope Zephyrinus, sent to the brethren throughout Egypt, chapter 10 [23].

(Dist. 75, c. *Ordinationes*.) Perform the ordinations of priests, deacons [and Levites] at a fitting time and solemnly in the presence of many persons [standing by]; appoint worthy and learned men to this task [promote them to this work], so that you may greatly rejoice in their fellowship and assistance [Col. 0451A].

CAP. 24.—That ordinations should not be performed except in a fixed and religious place. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 6 [52].

If any seek ordination, they are not to be ordained at all unless they have resided for at least one year in a fixed and religious place, or indeed in a city, so that reliable knowledge of their life, conduct, and teaching may be obtained.

CAP. 25.—That Abraham was first called a presbyter, and why a presbyter is so called. From Letter 2, chapter 22, chapter 2, of Pope Anacletus, addressed to all bishops established in Italy.

[Col. 0451B]

(Dist. 84, c. *Porro et Moysi*.) Moses too is commanded to choose presbyters, that is, elders (Num. XII). Hence Proverbs says: “Grey hair is the glory of old men” (Prov. XX). This greyness, however, signifies wisdom, concerning which it is written: “The grey hair of human beings is prudence” (Wis. IV). And although we read that from Adam to Abraham men lived nine hundred years and more (Gen. V), no one before Abraham was called presbyter—that is, elder (Gen. XLIII)—though Abraham is shown to have lived far fewer years. Presbyters, therefore, are named not on account of decrepit old age but on account of wisdom.

Aaron was the beginning of the priesthood (Exod. XXIX), although Melchizedek first offered sacrifice to God (Gen. XIV), [Col. 0451C] and after him Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. But these performed such acts by spontaneous will, not by priestly authority.

CAP. 26.—That no one is to be ordained unless he is assigned to some particular place. From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 6 (session XV).

(Dist. 70, c. *Neminem*.) No priest or deacon, nor anyone whatsoever in an ecclesiastical rank, is to be ordained absolutely, unless he is specifically designated for the church, city, estate, martyr-shrine, or monastery for which he is to be ordained. But the synod decreed that the laying on of hands of those ordained absolutely is to be held invalid and that they can minister nowhere, to the dishonour of the one who ordained them.

CAP. 27.—That ordinations ought not to be celebrated in the presence of hearers. From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 4.

[Col. 0451D]

That ordinations ought not to be celebrated in the sight of the hearers.

[Note: [Col. 0451D] This refers to catechumens, whom it calls “hearers.”]

CAP. 28.—That a priest is not to be promoted by election of the crowds. From the same council, chapter 13.

(Dist. 63, c. *Non est permittendum*.) The crowds are not to be permitted to make the elections of those who are to be promoted to the priesthood.

CAP. 29.—That it is not permitted to ordain a bishop or priest before the age of thirty, or deacons before twenty-five. From the same council, chapter 14 (Council of Agde, chapter 17).

(Dist. 77, c. *Episcopus*.) No metropolitan may presume to ordain a bishop or priest before thirty years of age—that is, before he reaches the perfection [variant: “mature age”] of manhood—or deacons before twenty-five, lest, because of their age, as sometimes happens, they be entangled in [variant: “be blamed for”] some error [Col. 0452A].

CAP. 30.—On the same matter. From the decrees of Pope Fabian sent to the Easterners.

(Dist. 78, c. *Si quis*.) If anyone has not completed thirty years of age, he is in no way to be ordained priest, even if he is exceedingly worthy; for the Lord himself was baptized at thirty years of age and then began to teach (Luke III). Therefore one who is to be ordained should not be consecrated until he reaches this lawful age.

CAP. 31.—That deacons are not to be ordained before twenty-five years of age. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 20 (Carthage III, chapter 4).

[Col. 0452B]

(Dist. 77, c. *Placuit*.) It has been decided that neither deacons are to be ordained nor virgins consecrated before twenty-five years of age, and that a reader is not to greet the people.

CAP. 32.—On the same matter. From the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 20.

(Dist. 77, c. *In veteri lege*, no. 8.) In the old law Levites are commanded to serve in the tabernacle from the age of twenty-five; the holy Fathers followed this authority in the canons. Forgetful both of divine law and of the conciliar command, we make infants and boys Levites before the lawful age and before experience of life. Therefore, lest this happen any further through us, we are admonished by the judgments both of divine law and of the canons: deacons are to be ordained at twenty-five years of age, so that, in accordance with the apostolic precept, [Col. 0452C] “they may first be proved and then minister, having no crime” (1 Tim. III).

CAP. 33.—On priests advanced without examination. From the Council of Nicaea, chapter 9.

(Dist. 81, c. *Si qui sine*.) If any priests have been advanced without examination—that is, when their sins were being investigated, they confessed them, and men, stirred contrary to the canons, attempted to lay hands upon those who confessed—the rule does not admit such persons, because the Catholic Church upholds what is beyond reproach.

CAP. 34.—On clerics made lame by a surgeon’s incision. From the Council of Lleida, chapter 20 (contained in the fragments of this council).

(Dist. 55, c. *Si quis*.) If a cleric, while ill, is made lame by a surgeon’s incision, we do not refuse his promotion to sacred orders [Col. 0452D].

CAP. 35.—On those who envy the advancement of brethren. From the African Council, chapter 54 (Council of Carthage IV, chapter 54).

(Dist. 46, c. *Clericus invidens*.) A cleric who envies the advancement of his brethren is not to be promoted while the vice remains.

CAP. 36.—That seditious persons are not to be ordained. From the same council, chapter 67.

(Dist. 46, c. *Seditionarios*.) We decree that seditious clerics are never to be ordained, just as neither usurers nor those who avenge their own injuries.

CAP. 37.—That an unlettered person, or one deficient in some bodily member, should not be promoted. From Letter 9, chapter 18 [chapter 16], of Pope Gelasius, to all bishops throughout Lucania.

[Col. 0453A]

No one may presume to promote to the clergy persons who are unlettered or deficient in any part of the body; for one lacking letters cannot be fit for sacred offices, and legal precepts have decreed that nothing defective at all is to be offered to God (Lev. XXI). Likewise, those who mutilate themselves.

CAP. 38.—On the goods of those who are granted freedom by their own masters. From the Council of Toledo, chapter 2.

Concerning the possessions or peculium of those who are granted freedom by their own masters in order that they may be promoted to ecclesiastical ranks, it has been decreed that whatever they possessed before freedom is to remain in the masters’ power, whether the masters wish to grant it to them or retain it for themselves [Col. 0453B].

CAP. 39.—On the sons of concubines. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 10 (Orléans III, chapter 9).

Concerning those who have sons by concubines, then afterwards have lawful wives, and, after their wives’ death, publicly take concubines to themselves: we have judged that this is to be observed, that just as we do not remove those who have already, through ignorance, been ordained clerics, so we now decree that no such persons are to be ordained in future.

CAP. 40.—That those entangled by demons and like afflictions are not to handle sacred things. From Letter 21 of Pope Gelasius, to all bishops throughout Lucania, chapter 21.

(Dist. 33, c. *Usque adeo*.) We have certainly learned [Col. 0453C] that unlawful practices have broken out to such an extent that the handling of most holy mysteries is entrusted to persons entangled by demons [variant: “demonic” afflictions] and similar sufferings. And shortly afterward: If divine law did not permit one wounded or infirm in body to touch holy things (Lev. XXI), how much less is it fitting that those struck in mind—which is worse—should be dispensers of the heavenly gift.

CAP. 41.—That no one of servile condition is to be ordained unless first made free. From the Council of Tribur, chapter 5.

(Chapter 29, Dist. 54, c. *Nulli*.) No one of servile condition is to be promoted to sacred orders unless he has first received lawful freedom from his own master. The charter of this freedom is to be read publicly from the ambo before ordination; and if no one objects, they shall be duly consecrated [Col. 0453D]. Moreover, when a slave not canonically consecrated has fallen from his rank, he shall be of the same condition as he was before the rank.

CAP. 42.—That those who disdain promotion by their bishops are not to remain where they please. From the Council of Carthage.

(Chapter 31, Dist. 74, c. *Si qui*.) If any clerics disdain to be promoted by their bishops, they are not to remain in the place from which they refused to depart. From the same council, chapter 31. (Dist. 74, c. *Placuit*.) It has been decided that any clerics or deacons who, for necessities concerning ecclesiastical property, do not obey their bishops when the latter wish to promote them to a higher honour in their own church, are not to minister there in the rank from which they refused to depart.

CAP. 43.—On the same matter. From the register of Pope Gelasius.

[Col. 0454A]

Those who refused to advance are to be restored as subordinates to their former inferiors; and they are to obtain the emoluments of a priest more readily than those of a deacon, so that, constrained at least by this consideration, they may endeavour to seek both the honour and gain which they flee.

CAP. 44.—That priests bear the type of the seventy disciples. Pope Anacletus, in his second decretal (Letter 2, chapter 2).

The seventy-two disciples chosen by the apostles (Luke X) are the type borne by priests; they are established in the Church in their place. It is enough that we have spoken above concerning their ordination and that of the remaining ministers.

CAP. 45.—That the worthier priests are, the more readily they are heard. Alexander, in his second decretal.

[Col. 0454B]

(1, q. 1, c. *Ipsi sacerdotes*.) Priests themselves intercede for the people and eat the people’s sins, because by their prayers they blot them out and consume them. The worthier they are, the more readily they are heard in the necessities for which they cry out.

CAP. 46.—That a cleric is not to grow his hair. Pope Anicius [Anicetus, to the bishops of Gaul].

(Dist. 23, c. *Prohibete*.) Forbid, brethren, throughout all the churches of your regions, that clerics, in accordance with the Apostle (1 Cor. XI), should grow their hair; rather, let them shave the crown of the head from above in the form of a sphere.

CAP. 47.—What sort of priests, and how, are to be ordained. Pope Zephyrinus, in his first decretal (see above, chapter 23).

[Col. 0454C]

Perform the ordinations of priests and Levites at a fitting time and solemnly in the presence of many standing by; promote worthy and learned men to this work, so that you may greatly rejoice in their fellowship and assistance. Set your hearts unceasingly upon the power of God, and recount these things and the other divine words to later generations; for “this is God, our God for ever, and he himself will guide us through the ages” (Ps. XLVII).

CAP. 48.—On the fallen and their restoration. Pope Calixtus to Bishop Benedict (Letter 2 to all the bishops of Gaul, chapter 5).

If anyone has fallen in any manner whatever, let us bear him and correct him with brotherly affection, as the blessed [Col. 0454D] Apostle says: “If a person is overtaken in some transgression, you who are spiritual instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself lest you too be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal. VI).

Moreover, holy David did penance for deadly crimes and nevertheless remained in honour. Blessed Peter likewise shed most bitter tears when he repented of having denied the Lord, yet he remained an apostle. And the Lord promises sinners through the prophet, saying: “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, I will not remember any of his iniquities” (Ezek. XVIII). Those therefore err who think that priests, after a fall, cannot minister to the Lord and enjoy their honours if they have performed fitting penance and thereafter live a good life and worthily preserve their priesthood [Col. 0455A].

Those who hold this view not only err but also appear to despise the keys entrusted to the Church, concerning which it was said: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. XVIII). Otherwise, this pronouncement either is not the Lord’s or is true. But we unhesitatingly believe that both the Lord’s priests and the remaining faithful may return to honours after worthy satisfaction, as the Lord testifies through the prophet: “Will one who falls not rise again? And will one who has turned away not return?” (Jer. VIII). And elsewhere: “I do not will,” says the Lord, “the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live” (Ezek. XXXIII).

The prophet David, doing penance, says: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a sovereign spirit” (Ps. L) [Col. 0455B]. After his repentance he both taught others and offered sacrifice to God, giving an example to teachers of the holy Church that, if they have fallen and have performed fitting penance to God, they can do both. For he taught when he said: “I shall teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly shall turn to you” (ibid.). And he offered sacrifice to God for himself when he said: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (ibid.).

CAP. 49.—That mercy is not to be forbidden. The same author (near the end of the same letter).

Flee, brethren, not only from maintaining but even from hearing a judgment that forbids mercy; for mercy is greater than all burnt offerings and sacrifices (Hos. VI).

CAP. 50.—On incontinent clerics. Pope Siricius to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona (Letter 1, chapter 7).

[Col. 0455C]

(Dist. 82, c. *Plurimos sacerdotes*.) We have learned that very many priests of Christ and Levites, after long periods of their consecration, have fathered offspring both by their own wives and through shameful intercourse; and they defend their crime by this claim [variant: “prescription”], that in the old law priests and ministers are read to have been granted permission to beget children (Lev. XXI).

Let whoever he may be—the follower of lusts and teacher of vices—tell me now: if he thinks that in the law of Moses the reins of lust were everywhere loosened by our God for sacred orders, why does God warn those to whom the Holy of Holies was entrusted, saying: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy” [Col. 0455D] (Lev. XX)? Why too were priests commanded to live apart from their homes in the temple during the year of their allotted service? (1 Chr. XXIV; Luke I.) This was plainly so that they might not be able to have carnal intercourse even with their wives, and so that, shining in integrity of conscience, they might offer an acceptable gift to God. Once the period of their service was completed, the use of a wife was relaxed solely for the sake of succession, because no one except from the tribe of Levi was commanded to be admitted to God’s ministry.

Likewise. A little later: Because some of those concerning whom we speak, as Your Holiness reported, lament that through ignorance they have fallen, we say that mercy is not to be denied them on this condition: without any increase of honour, they are to remain throughout life in the office in which they were discovered [variant: “cast down”], [Col. 0456A] provided that thereafter they endeavour to show themselves continent. But those who rely on the excuse of an unlawful privilege and assert that this was granted them by the old law should know that, by authority of the Apostolic See, they have been cast down from every ecclesiastical honour which they used unworthily; nor can they ever touch the venerable mysteries, of which they deprived themselves while craving shameful desires. Since present examples warn us to guard against the future, if any bishop, priest, or deacon should hereafter be found to be such a person—which we do not desire—let him understand now that every avenue of indulgence from us is barred to him; for wounds which have not experienced the remedy of fomentations must necessarily be cut away by iron.

CAP. 51.—That a cleric who has taken a second wife is to be deposed, chapter 11.

[Col. 0456B]

(Dist. 84, c. *Quisquis clericus*.) Any cleric who takes either a widow or indeed a second wife is immediately to be stripped of every privilege of ecclesiastical dignity, with lay communion alone granted to him. He may possess even this only if he thereafter commits nothing through which he would lose it.

CAP. 52.—What women may live with clerics, chapter 12.

(Dist. 81, c. *Feminas*.) We do not permit other women to be in clerics’ houses, except only those whom the Synod of Nicaea permitted to live with them for reasons solely of kinship.

CAP. 53.—On the promotion of monks, chapter 13.

[Col. 0456C] (16, q. 1, c. *Monachos quoque*.) We both desire and will that monks, provided that they are commended by gravity of character and by a holy rule of life and faith, should be enrolled in clerical offices.

CAP. 54.—That a penitent is not to become a cleric, chapter 14.

(Dist. 50, c. *Illud quoque*.) We also considered it necessary to provide that, just as no cleric is permitted to perform penance, so no layperson may ever, after penance and reconciliation, attain the honour of the clerical state.

CAP. 55.—That if a layman has taken a widow, he is not to become a cleric. Pope Innocent I to Bishop Victorinus [Victricius] (Letter 2, chapter 5).

(Dist. 34, c. *Si viduam licet*.) A man who, though a layman, has taken a widow as his wife, whether before baptism [Col. 0456D] or after baptism, is not to be admitted to the clergy, because he appears to be excluded by the same defect. For in baptism sins are forgiven, but the bond of a wife already taken is not dissolved.

CAP. 56.—On the same matter, chapter 6.

Nor may one who has taken a second wife become a cleric, for it is written: “the husband of one wife” (1 Tim. III); and again: “Let my priests marry once.”

CAP. 57.—On the incontinence of priests or Levites. From a letter of the same pope to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse (Letter 3, chapter 1).

(Dist. 82, c. *Proposuisti*.) You have proposed what should be observed concerning those who, placed in the ministry of the diaconate or office of the priesthood, have been shown by sons born to them to be or to have been incontinent [Col. 0457A]. Regarding these, both the discipline of divine laws and the clear admonitions of Siricius, a man of blessed memory, bishop, have decreed that those placed in such offices who are incontinent are to be deprived of every ecclesiastical honour and are not to be admitted to a ministry that ought to be fulfilled by continence alone.

CAP. 58.—That a cleric who deliberately cuts off a part of his body cannot be one, but one who does so involuntarily can. From a letter of the same pope to Felix, bishop of Nocera (Letter 4, chapter 1).

Innocent, greeting Felix, bishop of Nocera. (Dist. 55, c. *Qui partem*.) Therefore, one who deliberately cuts off from himself part of any finger is not admitted to the clergy by the canons. But those to whom this happens by some accident, while either attending to agricultural work or doing something in which they strike themselves unintentionally, the canons command both to be made clerics and, if they are found in the clergy, not to be cast out [Col. 0457B]. In the former, the will is judged: it dared to apply iron to itself, and there can be no doubt that another might do the same. But in the latter, accident has deserved pardon.

CAP. 59.—That persons ordained by heretics are not to be admitted to the clergy. Again, by the author mentioned above (Letter 22, chapter 3).

Innocent to Rufus, Eusebius, and the other Macedonian bishops. (1, q. 1, c. *Ventum est*.) We have come to the third question, which by reason of its difficulty demands a more extended discussion. We say that those ordained by heretics have their head wounded by that laying on of hands. Where a wound has been inflicted, a remedy must be applied by which health may be restored. But health restored after a wound cannot be without a scar; and where the remedy of penance is necessary, we determine that the honour of ordination can have no place [Col. 0457C].

For if, as is read, “whatever the unclean person touches shall be unclean” (Lev. XV), how can that be conferred on him which purity and cleanness are accustomed to receive? But conversely it is argued that one who has lost honour cannot confer honour, and that the other received nothing because there was nothing in the giver which he could receive. We agree, and this is certainly true: what he did not possess he could not give. He gave, indeed, the condemnation which he possessed through a perverse laying on of hands. And how one who has become a participant with the condemned ought to receive honour, I cannot discover. Yet it is said that the true and just blessing of a lawful priest removes every defect inflicted by one who is defective (Lev. IV) [Col. 0457D].

CAP. 60.—That crimes are not removed in ordinations, chapter 4.

Immediately after, in the same place. If this is so, then let sacrilegious persons, adulterers, and those guilty of every crime be admitted to ordination, since crimes and defects are thought to be removed by the blessing of ordination. Let there be no place for penance, because ordination can grant what lengthy satisfaction is accustomed to grant. But the rule of our Church is to grant only lay communion, by laying on of hands, to those coming from heretics who were nevertheless baptized there; nor do we permit any of these persons to be appointed even to the lowest honour of clerical status [Col. 0458A].

CAP. 61.—That in the Church a sin of the people is customarily passed over without punishment, chapter 6.

Therefore let Your Belovedness see that such things have hitherto been passed over, and observe that necessity, as you say, indeed required that they could not venture anything in churches now established in peace. (1, q. 7, c. *Quoties a populis*.) But, as often happens, whenever sin is committed by a people or crowd, because punishment cannot be inflicted upon everyone owing to their multitude, it is customarily allowed to pass unpunished. Therefore I say that earlier matters are to be left to God’s judgment, and that in future they must be guarded against with the greatest care.

CAP. 62.—That whoever is ordained contrary to canonical forms is to be deposed with his ordainers, chapter 3 (Letter 23, chapter 3).

[Col. 0458B]

Innocent to all bishops assembled in the synod of Toulouse. If anyone attempts to enter an ecclesiastical order, or even the priesthood itself, contrary to the forms of the canons, he and his ordainers are to be deprived of the rank and honour in which they are found. And although, dearest brethren, the Nicene rules according to which we decree that orders are to be conferred are known to Your Belovedness, I thought that some portion of what has been provided concerning ordinations should be inserted, so that we may know that future ordinations are to be celebrated according to it and that no one may be left free to interpret otherwise. First, let those things which are forbidden be set out.

CAP. 63.—On the Nicene Council, in which the aforesaid things are forbidden. The same author (ibid., chapter 4).

[Col. 0458C]

It must be forbidden that anyone from the *curiales* may enter an ecclesiastical order, if after baptism they have either been crowned or borne what is called a priesthood, or have held public shows. This too must be guarded against in regard to *curiales*: that those who have been *curiales* should not at some time be reclaimed by their own municipal councils, as we frequently see occurring. All these things, reasonably forbidden, must be observed by every means.

CAP. 64.—That no bishop may presume to promote another’s slave to clerical office. Pope Leo to all bishops throughout Campania and Picenum (Leo I, Letter 1, chapter 1).

[Col. 0458D] (Dist. 54, c. *Admittuntur passim*.) Persons are everywhere admitted to sacred order who are supported by no dignity either of birth or of character; and persons unable to obtain freedom from their masters are promoted to the height of priesthood, as if servile lowliness could lawfully attain that honour, and one is believed capable of being approved by God who has not yet been able to prove himself to his own master. There is therefore a twofold offence in this matter: the sacred ministry is polluted by the lowliness of such company, and the rights of masters are infringed insofar as unlawful usurpation is rashly committed.

Therefore, dearest brethren, let all priests of your provinces abstain from such persons; and we wish them to refrain not only from these but also from others bound either by origin [variant: “to origin”] or by some condition, unless [Col. 0459A] the request or consent of those who claim some authority over them is added. For one who is to be enrolled in the divine soldiery ought to be free from others, so that he may not be drawn away by any bonds of obligation from the Lord’s camp in which his name is enrolled.

CAP. 65.—That not only clerics, but laypeople also, ought not to exact usury, chapter 2 [3].

(14, q. 4, c. *Nec hoc*.) Nor have we thought it should be passed over that certain persons, seized by the desire for shameful gain, lend money at usury and wish to grow rich by interest. We grieve that this offense should fall not merely upon those appointed to clerical office, but also upon laypersons who wish to be called Christians; and we decree that those convicted of it be punished more severely, [Col. 0459B] so that every opportunity for sinning may be removed.

### CHAPTER 66.—That no cleric may practice usury either in his own name or in another’s, chapter 3 [4].

(Dist. 46, c. *Sicut non suo*.) We have also judged it necessary to warn that, just as no cleric should attempt to practice usury in his own name, so neither should he do so in another’s name. For it is unbecoming to employ another’s advantages in the service of one’s own crime. We ought to look to and practice only that kind of “interest” by which what we mercifully give here may be received from the Lord—who repays manifoldly and with a reward that endures forever.

### CHAPTER 67.—How presbyters or deacons who have fallen into sin ought to be reconciled. Leo to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, chapter 2 (Letter 92).

(Dist. 50, c. *Alienum est*.) It is foreign to ecclesiastical custom [Col. 0459C] that persons consecrated in the honor of the presbyterate or in the rank of the diaconate should, on account of some crime of their own, receive through the laying on of hands the remedy of penitence. This undoubtedly derives from apostolic tradition, according to what is written: “If a priest sins, who shall pray for him?” (Lev. IV). Therefore those who have thus fallen must seek private withdrawal [variant: succession or concession] in order to win God’s mercy; and, if their satisfaction is worthy, it may also be fruitful for them.

### CHAPTER 68.—That deacons are subject to the same law of continence as bishops and presbyters, chapter 3.

(Dist. 31, c. *Lex continentiae*.) The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and [Col. 0459D] presbyters. While they were laymen or readers, they could lawfully take wives and beget children. But when they attained the aforesaid ranks, what had been lawful for them ceased to be lawful. Therefore, in order that a carnal marriage may become spiritual, they must neither dismiss their wives nor possess them otherwise than as though they did not possess them (1 Cor. VII), so that the charity of marriage may remain intact while marital acts cease.

### CHAPTER 69.—That no one may solicit another’s cleric against his bishop’s will, chapter 9 (Letter 84).

(19, q. 2, c. *Alienum clericum*.) Let no one receive or solicit another’s cleric against the will of that cleric’s bishop, unless perhaps, by an agreement of charity, this is settled between the one giving and the one receiving. For he is guilty of grave injury who dares either to entice away or retain from a brother’s church that which is more useful or [Col. 0460A] more precious. Accordingly, if the matter occurs within the province, the metropolitan shall compel the fugitive cleric to return to his own church. But if he has gone farther away, he shall be recalled by the authority of the metropolitan’s command, so that no occasion may be left for either greed or ambition.

### CHAPTER 70.—That ordination may take place on Sunday morning after the continuous fast of Saturday. Letter of Leo to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria (Letter 81, chapter 1).

Leo, bishop, to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria. (Dist. 75, c. *Quod presbyteris*.) What we know was observed by our fathers with especial care, we wish also to be kept by you: namely, that priestly or Levitical ordination should not be celebrated indiscriminately on every day, but that the beginning of consecration should be chosen after Saturday and the night that dawns into the first day of the week, so that the sacred blessing may be conferred upon those who are to be consecrated while they are fasting, by persons who are themselves fasting. The same observance will be maintained if it is celebrated on Sunday morning itself, with Saturday’s fast continued; for the beginning of the preceding night does not depart from that time. That this belongs to the day of Resurrection—as is also shown in the Lord’s Passover—cannot be doubted.

### CHAPTER 71.—That priestly and Levitical ordination is to be performed on the day of Resurrection. To the same recipient (ibid.).

(Dist. 75, c. *Quod die*.) We know that ordinations of priests are celebrated on Sunday not only by custom but also through apostolic teaching, Scripture showing that, when the apostles sent Paul and Barnabas, by command of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0460C] to preach the Gospel to the Gentiles, they fasted, prayed, and laid hands upon them (Acts XIII). Thus we understand with how great a devotion both those giving and those receiving must take care that the sacrament of so great a blessing may not appear to have been carried out negligently. You will therefore act piously and laudably in conformity with apostolic institutions if you yourself preserve, throughout the churches over which the Lord has willed you to preside, this form for ordaining priests: that blessing is never bestowed upon those to be consecrated except on the Sunday of the Resurrection. Its beginning is known to be assigned from Saturday evening, and it is consecrated by such great mysteries of the divine dispensations that whatever the Lord has established more eminently has been accomplished in the dignity of this day. On this day the world received its beginning. On this day, [Col. 0460D] through Christ’s resurrection, death received its destruction and life its beginning.

### CHAPTER 72.—What bishops possess beyond chorepiscopi or presbyters. Likewise by the same author (Letter 88).

Leo, bishop of the Roman Church and Apostolic See, to all bishops of the regions of Germany and Gaul. Although chorepiscopi share with bishops the administration of many ministries, nevertheless they should know that certain things are forbidden to them by the authority of the old law, and certain others by later ecclesiastical regulations, just as they are forbidden to presbyters and deacons: namely, the consecration of virgins, the establishment of an altar, blessing, and anointing. For we do not permit them to erect altars or consecrate churches or altars; nor, by laying on hands, to confer upon believers being baptized or converts from heresy the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete; nor to prepare chrism; nor to sign the foreheads of the baptized with chrism; nor publicly to reconcile any penitent at Mass; nor to send letters of communion to anyone. These things are all unlawful for chorepiscopi, who are known to be after the example and pattern of the seventy disciples, and for presbyters, who bear the same figure; for although they possess consecration, they do not possess the summit of the episcopate. By authority of the canons all these things are prescribed as due to the supreme pontiffs alone, so that both the distinction of ranks and the lofty dignity of the chief pontiff may thereby be displayed. Nor is it permitted for presbyters, in the bishop’s presence, to enter the baptistery; or, with the bishop present, to baptize or sign an infant; or to reconcile a penitent without their own bishop’s command; or, in his presence, unless he commands it, to consecrate the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood; or, with him present, to teach, bless, greet, or indeed exhort the people.

### CHAPTER 73.—That one loses a prior dignity who usurps what he has not received. From the decrees of Pope Silverius (Letter 1, to Verg., bishop).

(25, q. 2, c. *Sic decet*.) Thus it is fitting that the faith of the holy Fathers be preserved in the Catholic Church: whoever with blameworthy rashness has usurped [variant: assumed] what he did not receive must lose what he possessed.

### CHAPTER 74.—That ordinations are not to be performed except in the fast of the Four Seasons. From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, chapter 13 (Letter 9 to the bishops throughout Lucania, chapter 13).

(Dist. 75, c. *Ordinationes*.) Ordinations also [Col. 0461C] of presbyters and deacons ought not to be performed except at fixed seasons and days: namely, in the fast of the fourth, seventh, and tenth months, and also at the beginning of Lent and on the Saturday of mid-Lent. They should know that the fasts are to be celebrated toward evening [variant: “in the fast of the week and Saturday toward evening, they should know that the ordinations themselves are to be celebrated”], and that no presbyter or deacon, for the sake of any advantage whatever, is to be preferred to those ordained before him.

### CHAPTER 75.—That an unlettered person or one deficient in a bodily member is not to be promoted to the clergy. From the same source, chapter 18.

We have learned that unlettered persons and those deficient in some part of the body are admitted to ecclesiastical service without any consideration; yet both ancient tradition and the ancient practice of the Apostolic See have not accepted this. For one lacking sacred learning cannot be fit for sacred offices, and legal precepts have decreed that nothing defective whatever is to be offered to God (Lev. XXI). Therefore, henceforth these things must by every means be avoided, and no such person is to be received into the clergy.

### CHAPTER 76.—Concerning incontinent ministers. Gregory to the citizens of Rome.

(Dist. 81, c. *Oportet*.) Priests, to whose care God’s people have been entrusted, must watch over the Lord’s sheep with great firmness of mind, lest they be torn by wolfish bites—that is, by the incitements of the devil. Nor ought I to keep silent about this—which I say with great grief of heart—that I see priests living with women; it is wicked even to say or hear this, [Col. 0462A] and it is contrary to the enactments of the holy canons. Where such cohabitation of persons dwelling together exists, the incitements of the ancient enemy are not absent. They must therefore be admonished not to be deceived by the fraud of the ancient enemy, so that, in accordance with the Apostle’s words, “Our ministry may not be blamed” (2 Cor. VI). For we must beware, brothers, of unlawful things, so that we may be able to lift pure hands to the Lord (1 Tim. II). For it is written: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. XX). But if anyone presumes to act otherwise, let him be deprived of the honor of his priesthood. Therefore, brothers, we must entirely take care not to deceive the people, lest the prophet’s saying be fulfilled in us: “My priests defile holy things and reject the law” (Zeph. III). Another prophet also rebukes them, saying: “You, O priests, who deceive [Col. 0462B] my name, and have said: ‘In what way do we deceive your name?’” (Mal. I). They were answered: “By offering polluted bread upon my altar. ‘I have no pleasure in you,’ says the Lord, ‘and I will not accept sacrifice from your hands, because you are polluted’” (ibid.).

### CHAPTER 77.—Concerning the avoidance of familiarity with women. The same author in the Register (Book VII, indiction 2, Letter 39).

(Dist. 81, c. *Legitur*. Possidius, *Life of St Augustine*.) It is read that blessed Augustine did not consent even to live with his sister, saying: “Those who are with my sister are not my sisters.” The caution of a learned man, therefore, ought to be great instruction for us.

### CHAPTER 78.—Concerning those who have fallen: that they are not to be restored. The same author to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari (Book III, Letter 26).

(Dist. 50, c. *Pervenit*.) It has also come to us that certain persons who have fallen from sacred orders are recalled to the duties of their ministry either after penance or before penance. We absolutely forbid this, and the most sacred canons also oppose it in this matter. Therefore, whoever after receiving sacred order has fallen into the sin of the flesh is to be deprived of sacred order, so that he may no longer approach the ministry of the altar.

### CHAPTER 79.—On the same subject. The same author to Constantine, bishop of Milan (Book IV, Letter 17).

We have decreed that Jobinus [variant: Jovinus], a certain deacon and abbot from Portus Veneris, be deprived of his office, and we have written that another should be ordained in his place. Likewise, we decree that the three subdeacons whom your brotherhood has reported to have fallen are always to remain removed from their office and deprived of it; nothing other than communion among the laity is to be granted them.

### CHAPTER 80.—The same, on the same subject. To the same recipient (ibid.; this is the beginning of the letter).

(Dist. 50, c. *Si lapsis*.) If permission is granted to those who have fallen to return to their order, the rigor of canonical discipline is beyond doubt broken, since, in hope of restoration, each person need not fear to conceive desires for wrongful conduct. And shortly afterward: Therefore take care above all that no entreaty persuades you in any way to recall into sacred order those who have fallen, lest punishment of this kind be thought not to be established, but merely deferred for a time.

### CHAPTER 81.—With which women priests may live. The same author to Symmachus, defender of the Church (Book I, Letter 50).

[Col. 0463A]

(Dist. 81, c. *Volumus*.) We decree that priests must be forbidden to associate with women, except only with a mother, sister, or wife who is to be governed chastely.

### CHAPTER 82.—That reordinations ought not to be performed. The same author to John, bishop of Ravenna (Book II, indiction 10, Letter 32).

What you say—that one who has been ordained should be ordained again—is utterly ridiculous. (Dist. 68, c. *Sicut semel*.) For just as a person baptized once ought not to be baptized again, so one consecrated once ought not to be consecrated again in the same order. But if anyone perhaps comes to the priesthood with a minor fault, penance ought to be imposed for the fault, while the order is nevertheless preserved.

### CHAPTER 83.—Concerning a presbyter who presumed to offer sacrifice after deposition. The same author to Venantius, bishop of Luni (Book IV, Letter 5).

(Dist. 50, c. *Accedens*.) Let your brotherhood, on proceeding to the island of Gorgona, investigate what has been reported to us concerning Saturninus, formerly a presbyter. For it has reached us that, after he had been deposed from the priestly order because of the crime of his fall, he presumed to undertake the performance of the presbyteral ministry and to offer sacrifices to almighty God. If your brotherhood finds that this has occurred, reduce him to penance, deprived of participation in the sacred body and blood of the Lord, so that he remains in that excommunication until the day [Col. 0463C] of his death and receives only viaticum at the time of his departure. But if your brotherhood finds that he is doing such penance that it is just to show him mercy by restoring him to communion among the laity even before his death, we place this in the power of your brotherhood.

### CHAPTER 84.—That the former lawful wife of a deacon may not marry another. The same author to John, bishop of Palermo (Book II, Letter 62).

Accordingly, it has reached us that Fantinus [variant: Fotinus], a defender of the Church, wished to exact punishment upon Peter, the bearer of this letter, because—so it is said—while he was a tenant, he gave in marriage the abandoned wife of a certain deacon to a husband. But this man asserts that she was not the deacon’s wife, saying that she had not come to him a virgin and that, indeed, she had not changed her religious clothing after he was promoted to sacred order; he also adds that she had lived under an evil reputation both before he came to the diaconate and afterwards. We therefore exhort your brotherhood in these words: investigate this case with the fear of God, as is fitting, by a wholly careful inquiry. If it is established that the woman in question was the deacon’s wife, then the aforesaid bearer is by every means to be delivered to the said defender and rector of the patrimony [variant: *patrimonasterium*] for punishment, and those who have been improperly joined are to be separated with suitable redress. But if she was not his wife, we wish you, by our command, to warn the said Fantinus that he must presume to do nothing against him and that a false accusation must not prejudice him before Fantinus in any respect.

### CHAPTER 85.—How those who have fallen may be restored. The same author to Secundinus, an enclosed servant of God (Book VII, indiction 2, Letter 54).

(Dist. 50, c. *Quia sanctitas tua*.) Your Holiness has asked us to write back to you concerning restoration to priestly office after a fall, saying that you have read differing canons and differing judgments on this matter—some allowing restoration, others not at all. For our part, beginning generally with the Synod of Nicaea, we venerate it together with the remaining four [ecumenical councils], which, following it, agree unanimously in all their judgments. We therefore follow the Fathers who preceded us and, with God as author, do not dissent from their sacred teaching. Beginning from the head and continuing down to the fourth minister of the altar, we recognize that this rule must be observed: the greater precedes the lesser; as one is greater in honor, so is he in culpability; and the greater the fault that follows someone, the greater must be the penalty imposed upon him. Only thus is penance afterward believed to be fruitful.

For what good is it to sow wheat and not gather its fruit? Or to build a house and not live in it? After worthy satisfaction, we believe that one who has fallen can return to honor, as the Prophet says: “Will one who falls not rise again? And will one who has turned away not return?” (Ps. XL; Jer. VIII). The same prophet says to the sinner: “On whatever day you turn and groan, then you shall be saved” (Ezek. XVIII). Hence the Psalmist says: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Do not cast me away from your presence” (Ps. L), etc. For the king and prophet trembled in terror because he had taken another man’s wife. When the prophet disclosed his crime and he did penance, he added: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation” (ibid.), etc. For had he not performed penance worthy before God, would he ever have preached to others? For he says: “I will teach the wicked your ways” (ibid.). Seeing that his sins had been cleansed by penance, he did not hesitate, by preaching, to correct [variant: heal] the sins of others. Thus he strove to offer sacrifice to God from himself when he said: “A sacrifice to God” (ibid.), etc.

These points would suffice; but every judgment is more readily believed the more it is confirmed by testimonies of sacred Scripture. For concerning this matter the prophet says: “I do not will the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live” (Ezek. XVIII). Concerning this it is said to sinners: “Sinner, on whatever day he turns and groans, all his iniquities shall be consigned to oblivion.” For if our Redeemer, who came not to destroy sinners but to justify them (Luke IX), leaves the offenses of sinners in oblivion, what human being would reserve them for condemnation, when the Apostle says: “If God justifies, who is there to condemn?” (Rom. VIII).

Let us run to the fountain of mercy and bring forward the Gospel’s judgment: “I rejoice,” he says, “over one sinner doing penance more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of penance” (Luke XV); and, leaving the ninety-nine that had not strayed, he carried the lost sheep upon his shoulder [Col. 0465A] back to the fold (ibid.). If the wandering sheep, once found, is carried on his shoulder back to the fold, why should one who has fallen not be recalled to ministry after penance? Which, then, is graver: to commit a carnal offense—without which few persons are found—or to deny the Son of God by an oath? In this sin [variant: word] we know that blessed Peter himself, prince of the apostles—at whose body we now sit unworthily—fell. Yet after denial penance followed, and after penance mercy was given, because Christ did not depose from the apostolate the one whom he had foretold would deny him. Let these words, dearest son, suffice for you: do not doubt that the one whom you see washing away sins with tears will obtain mercy in the sight of the Godhead, because he who came to redeem sinners by his blood despises no sinner who returns.

### CHAPTER 86.—What ought to be done concerning incontinent clerics. The same author to Augustine, bishop (in the response to Augustine’s second question).

(Dist. 32, c. *Si qui sunt clerici*.) If there are clerics not constituted in sacred orders who cannot remain continent, they ought to take wives and receive their stipends outside [clerical support]. For concerning the same Fathers of whom we have spoken, we know it is written that distribution was made to each according to anyone’s need (Acts IV). Provision and care must also be made for their stipend; and they must be kept under ecclesiastical rule, so that they may live with good morals, be diligent in singing psalms, and, with God’s help, keep heart, tongue, and body from all unlawful things for God.

### CHAPTER 87.—That an incontinent presbyter must not minister. Clement, in the second letter.

[Col. 0465C]

For the Lord’s ministries, however, let such men be chosen as knew their wives before ordination. But if, after ordination, it should happen that a minister enter the marital bed of his own wife, let him not cross the thresholds of the sanctuary, nor become a bearer of the sacrifice, nor touch the altar, nor receive from those offering the oblation of the holocaust, nor approach the carrying of the Lord’s body. Rather, let him only hand water to the priests for washing their hands; let him shut the doors outside [variant: “nor hand water to the priests for their hands; let him shut the doors outside”]; let him perform lesser duties; and indeed let him present a ewer at the altar [variant: “or let him not bring a chalice to the altar”].

### CHAPTER 88.—That church ornaments must not be alienated by a presbyter. Likewise by the same author.

[Col. 0465D]

(17, q. 4, c. *Si forte*.) If any presbyter or deacon steals and sells the linen cloth or veil of the sanctuary, he shall be considered like Judas Iscariot. Let the one who has done this deed out of greed know that he will receive the punishment of the aforesaid Judas.

### CHAPTER 89.—Concerning avoidance of familiarity with women. The same author, from the same source.

(Dist. 81, c. *Clericus solus*.) A cleric must not go alone to a woman’s dwelling, nor hasten there without the command of an elder. Nor may a presbyter be alone with a woman alone; rather, having brought two witnesses, he may visit a sick woman. Nor may he alone converse with a woman alone. Neither an archdeacon nor a deacon, under the pretext of humility or duty, may frequently visit the houses of matrons, [Col. 0466A] or perhaps secretly communicate something to such a matron through her clerics or household servants. If this becomes known, both he is to be deposed and she excluded from the thresholds of the church. But if there is perhaps some need of intercession, it is to be reported to the bishop; and, if she is such a person that he ought to go on her behalf for intercession, he himself shall go. Otherwise, he shall send from his side two or three persons who ought to remedy the matter.

### CHAPTER 90.—That clerics are to do nothing without their bishop’s permission. Likewise by the same author (Letter 3).

(16, q. 1, c. *Cunctis fidelibus*.) All the faithful—and especially all presbyters, deacons, and other clerics—must take heed that they do nothing without the permission of their own bishop. No presbyter is to celebrate Mass in his parish without the bishop’s command, baptize, or do anything whatever without his permission. Likewise, all the rest of the people, both greater and lesser, must do whatever is to be done by his permission; nor may they leave their own parish without his permission, or presume to remain there when arriving from elsewhere. For their souls have been entrusted to him; therefore they must do everything by his counsel and nothing without consulting him.

### CHAPTER 91.—How one ought to ascend to sacred orders. Pope Siricius to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona (Letter 1, chapter 9).

(Dist. 77, c. *Quicunque itaque*.) Whoever from childhood devotes himself to the services of the Church ought to be baptized before the years of puberty and joined to the ministry of readers. From the onset of adolescence until his thirtieth [variant: twentieth] year, if he has lived blamelessly, he must be content with one wife only, namely one received as a virgin through the common blessing of a priest; he should serve as acolyte and subdeacon. Thereafter, if he has first proved himself worthy through continence, he may advance to the rank of deacon. If he has ministered there commendably for more than five years, he may suitably receive the presbyterate. Then, after ten years, he may attain the episcopal chair, provided that throughout these periods the integrity of his life and faith has been approved.

### CHAPTER 92.—How a layman is to be promoted. The same author (ibid., chapter 10).

But one already advanced in years, prompted by a manner of life of better purpose and hastening to come from the laity into sacred service, will obtain the fruit of his desire only if, at the time when he is baptized, he is immediately joined to the number of readers or exorcists—provided it is established that he has had, or has, one wife only and that he received her as a virgin. When he has been initiated, after completing two years, he shall become an acolyte and subdeacon for another five years; and thus, if he is judged worthy during these periods, he shall be promoted to the diaconate. Thereafter, as time advances, he may not undeservedly be joined to the presbyterate or episcopate, if the election of people and clergy calls him.

### CHAPTER 93.—That one must not sit when the Gospel is read. Pope Anastasius to all the Germans (Anastasius I, Letter 1, chapter 1).

For you have reported that certain priests, in church, [Col. 0467A] sit when the Gospel is read and hear the words of the Lord and Savior sitting rather than standing; and they say that they received this from the tradition of their elders. (On Consecration, Dist. 1, c. *Apostolica*.) By apostolic authority we command that you by no means permit this henceforth. Rather, when the holy Gospels are recited in church, priests and the other [variant: all present] faithful must not sit, but stand reverently bowed in the presence of the Gospel, listen attentively to the Lord’s words, and worship faithfully.

### CHAPTER 94.—Concerning the chastity of priests and Levites. Innocent to Victricius, bishop of Rouen (Letter 2, chapter 9).

(Dist. 31, c. *Tenere debet*.) Moreover, the Church ought wholly to preserve what is worthy, modest, and honorable: priests and Levites must not have intercourse with their wives, because they are occupied by the daily necessities of ministry. For it is written: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Lev. XX–XXI). In ancient times, priests did not leave God’s temple during the year of their turn, as we read concerning Zechariah; nor did they at all touch their homes. For them the use of a wife had indeed been allowed for the succession of offspring (Luke I), since no one from another tribe, or other than from the seed of Aaron, had been commanded to approach the priesthood (Num. XVIII). How much more must these priests or Levites preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, since for them priesthood or ministry is without succession, and no day passes on which they are free either from divine sacrifices or from the office of baptism?

### CHAPTER 95.—That not all laypersons are to be excluded from becoming clerics. The same author to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse (Letter 4, chapter 3; to Felix, bishop of Nocera).

Your religiousness has consulted us concerning laypersons whom the canons forbid to be ordained. Certainly this is contained in ecclesiastical rules, but it is not laid down in such a way as to apply to all laypersons. For clerics cannot be born; they must be made. (Dist. 51, c. *Designata sunt*.) But categories have been designated from which persons cannot come to the clerical state: that is, a faithful person who has served as a soldier, a faithful person who has pleaded cases—that is, acted as an advocate—or a faithful person who has administered public office. [Col. 0467D] The reason concerning municipal councillors is clear: even if men of such a kind are found who ought to become clerics, because they are often recalled to the curia, they must be avoided on account of the trouble that frequently comes to the Church from them. But laypersons who were baptized while having wives and have subsequently ordered their lives so that their reputation is unshaken—whether they have been attached to clerics or adhered to monasteries from the time of baptism—if they have known neither concubine nor mistress, but have been watchful in every good work, are not forbidden to be admitted to the clerical portion [variant: rank]. Yet the periods established by the elders must be observed in their case, so that no one may quickly become reader, quickly acolyte, quickly deacon, and quickly priest.

### CHAPTER 96.—Concerning presbyters who beget children. The same author to Bishops Maximus and Severus (Letter 5).

[Col. 0468A]

(Dist. 81, c. *Maximilianus*.) Order those presbyters who have begotten children while in the presbyterate to be placed in the midst. Once the accusations brought against these presbyters have been examined, if they are convicted, let them be removed from priestly office; for those who are not holy cannot handle holy things, and they must be made strangers to the ministry which they have polluted by unlawful living. We are astonished, however, that their bishops should overlook these things, so that they may be judged either to restrain [variant: live with] them, or not to know that such things are unlawful.

### CHAPTER 97.—Concerning those returning from heresy. The same author to Januarius [variant: Julianus], bishop of Aquileia [Leo I, Letter 1].

[Col. 0468B] (1, q. 7, c. *Saluberrimum*.) It is most salutary, and wholly full of the benefit of spiritual medicine, that presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, or clerics of any order who wish to appear corrected and seek to return again to the Catholic faith which they formerly lost should first confess unequivocally that they have condemned both their errors and the very authors of the error.
