Their perverse opinions having also been destroyed, no opportunity for hope should remain, nor should any member of such persons be able to be corrupted by association, once their own profession has begun in every respect to oppose them. Concerning such persons, moreover, we command that the canonical provision be observed: let them count it a great benefit, if all hope of promotion has been removed from them, to remain with perpetual stability in the rank in which they are found, provided that they have not been defiled by repeated baptism.

### CHAPTER 98.—Concerning the chastity of ministers. Likewise to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica (Letter 84, chapters 3 and 4).

(Dist. 32, c. *Omnium sacerdotium*.) For the election of priests is so excellent that things which are not reckoned a fault in other members of the Church are nevertheless considered unlawful in them. For although persons outside the clerical order are free to pursue married life and the begetting of children, even subdeacons are not allowed carnal marriage, in order to display the purity of perfect continence; so that those who have wives may be as though they did not have them, and those who do not have them may remain unmarried. If this is fittingly observed in this order, which is fourth from the head, how much more must it be preserved in the first, second, and third, lest anyone be judged suitable for Levitical or presbyteral honor or episcopal eminence who is found not yet to have restrained himself from the pleasure of lust [variant: marital pleasure]?

### CHAPTER 99.—That deacons may not baptize without a bishop or presbyter. Gelasius to all bishops throughout Lucania (Letter 9, chapter 9).

We also establish a proper measure for deacons and do not permit them to attempt anything beyond the limit assigned by the paternal canons, or to appropriate in any way to their own ministry what antiquity has decreed as proper to higher orders. They must not presume to baptize without a bishop or presbyter, unless perhaps extreme necessity compels it while those aforesaid ministers are at a distance—something often permitted even to lay Christians. [Col. 0469A] They have no right, when divine services or any ecclesiastical discourse is being celebrated, to sit in the presbyterium or to exercise the distribution [variant: prerogative] of the sacred body in the sight of a bishop or presbyter, unless those persons are absent.

### CHAPTER 100.—Concerning slaves not to be received into the clergy. Gelasius likewise (ibid., chapter 16).

(Dist. 54, c. *Generalis*.) The presumption that gives rise to a general complaint must also be avoided: almost everyone complains everywhere that slaves and serfs, fleeing the legal rights and possession of their masters, under the pretext of religious life either betake themselves to monasteries or, with bishops conniving, are indiscriminately admitted to ecclesiastical service. This destructive practice must be removed by every means, lest through the institution of the Christian name either another’s property seem to be invaded or public discipline seem to be subverted—especially since it is not fitting that the dignity of clerical ministry itself should be stained by this obligation and forced, on account of the status and condition of those serving it, to litigate or, heaven forbid, appear liable to legal claims.

After such persons have been properly prohibited by a diligent injunction, any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or person known to preside over monasteries who retains such persons and judges that they need not be restored to their masters, or that they should henceforth be attached either to ecclesiastical service or to religious communities—unless they have first been freed by their masters’ will, attested by a written subscription, [Col. 0469C] or have been granted freedom by a lawful settlement—must not doubt that he will incur danger to his own rank and communion, should a truthful complaint on this matter be brought to us by anyone. For, according to the blessed Apostle, the greatest care must be taken lest the faith and discipline of the Lord be blasphemed (Rom. II; 2 Pet. II).

### CHAPTER 101.—Concerning those baptized during illness. From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 12.

(Dist. 57, c. *Si quis in aegritudine*.) If anyone has been baptized while ill, he ought not to be ordained a presbyter. For his faith is not voluntary but arises from necessity—unless perhaps his zeal and faith later prove commendable, or a scarcity of persons compels it.

### CHAPTER 102.—That a presbyter may not ordain a deacon or presbyter. From the Second Council of Seville, chapter 5.

[Col. 0469D]

(Dist. 23, c. *Quorumdam*.) In the fifth judgment, a report by the deacon of Gabrensis was brought before our examination [variant: “before our Anianus”] concerning certain clerics of that church. When one of them was being consecrated to the presbyterate and two to the ministry of Levites, their bishop, prevented by an affliction of the eyes, is said only to have laid his hand upon them, while a certain presbyter, contrary to ecclesiastical order, gave them the blessing. Although he could have been condemned by the present judgment on account of the great audacity of his presumption, had he still been alive, he had already been overtaken by the summons of death. But because he has now been left to divine judgment and cannot be accused by a human tribunal, we decree that those who survive—who received from him not the title of consecration [Col. 0470A] but rather a mark of disgrace—be deposed and justly cast out from the rank of priesthood or Levitical order which they perversely obtained, lest such an usurpation again grant itself license. For such persons are deservedly judged to be removed, because they were found to have been improperly appointed.

### CHAPTER 103.—That presbyters ought not to consecrate churches or erect altars. From the same council, chapter 7.

In the seventh inquiry it was reported to us that the most venerable late Agapius, bishop of the city of Corduba, had frequently sent presbyters or chorepiscopi (who, however, are one and the same according to the canons) to erect altars and consecrate basilicas during the bishop’s absence. [Col. 0470B] It is indeed unsurprising that a man ignorant of ecclesiastical discipline, and transferred directly from secular military service to priestly ministry, should have prescribed this. Therefore, lest such a license be further usurped among us, it was necessary to decree by common decision—for we know that, just as the consecration of an altar is unlawful for a presbyter or chorepiscopus, so too is its establishment. For in the divine Scriptures, by the Lord’s command, Moses [Aaron] alone erected the altar in God’s tabernacle; he alone also anointed it (Exod. 40), because he was God’s high priest, as it is written of him: “Moses and Aaron among his priests” (Ps. 98).

### CHAPTER 104.—Concerning slaves ordained despite their masters’ prohibition. Gelasius to the bishops Rufinus and Aprilis.

(Dist. 54, c. *Quis aut*.) For who would say that the laws of princes, the rules of the Fathers, or recent admonitions ought to be disregarded, except one who supposes that his offense may pass unpunished? [Col. 0470C] The agents of our daughter, the illustrious and magnificent woman Maxima, complained to us in a petition that her native slaves Sylvester and Candidus, contrary to the aforementioned enactments and even after objection had been made, had been ordained deacons by Bishop Lucerinus. Therefore, dearest brothers, you should investigate more carefully this violation of so great a kind. And if the complaint is found to be supported by the truth, let those who were unlawfully made clerics after objection had been raised immediately be excluded from sacred offices.

### CHAPTER 105.—Concerning the oath of the possessor. Gelasius to Bishop Justus.

Your Belovedness, having faithfully sought the truth of all the facts, [Col. 0470D] should preserve inviolate any definite settlement previously reached concerning the tracts of land over which contention is said to have arisen. Otherwise, if nothing was ever established as settled, let the party who relies upon prescription by lapse of time now offer an oath—provided, however, that the party proved to have possessed the property up to this point is allowed to take the oath.

### CHAPTER 106.—That no one should be ordained unwillingly. Gelasius to Bishop Victor.

(Dist. 74, c. *Consuluit*.) Your Belovedness has consulted us concerning the advancement of your clerics, reporting that the deacons refuse to attain the rank of presbyter, which, as you state, your church needs. Therefore, since ecclesiastical moderation and gravity do not permit unwilling persons to be made willing from unwilling persons [variant: “to become willing”], ordination can proceed thus: if you have any among the acolytes or subdeacons who are of mature age and whose life is commendable, endeavor to promote them to the presbyterate. [Col. 0471A]

### CHAPTER 107.—That one wounded and disabled does not lose his rank in the priesthood. Gelasius to Bishop Palladius.

(Dist. 55, c. *Praecepta canonica*.) The precepts of the canons by which ecclesiastical discipline is governed, just as they do not permit those physically disabled to enter the priesthood, so too, if anyone has been established in that office and is wounded, he cannot lose what he received while physically sound. For the presbyter Stephen lamented to us in a petition presented that he had [variant: “it is held that he had”], [uncertain: “in subditis”], received the dignity of the presbyterate many years ago, which he had indeed received when judged to possess an unblemished body. [Col. 0471B] But recently, because of the devastation of the province—which the savage violence of barbarians of diverse sects, and the uncertainty of their minds, brought upon Tuscia beyond all provinces [variant: “the devastation of Tuscia, which … beyond all provinces”]—while he sought to escape those threatening him with the sword by the protection of flight, he leapt over barriers set before him with sharpened stakes and, he reports, pierced [perhaps: “cut”] the lower [variant: “interior”] parts of his body. These could scarcely be cleansed even by treatment over two years. Therefore, dearest brother, restore to the aforesaid man his place and dignity, so that he may perform the most holy mysteries as he has been accustomed to do. For it is not fitting that a rank received beforehand be taken away on account of bodily infirmity which, as is shown, later befell him by accident. [Col. 0471C]

### CHAPTER 108.—That those manumitted by their masters are not to be reclaimed by the heirs after ordination. Gelasius to the bishops Crispinus and Sabinus.

(11, q. 1, c. *Sylvester*.) Sylvester and Faustinianus, clerics of the church of Grumentium, complained to us in a tearful petition that the freedom granted them through the kindness of their master was being assailed by the oppression of his heirs. Although they had served in the clerical office almost from infancy, and, while their manumitter was still alive, had nevertheless remained in that office, they were not permitted to render service in the divine ministries. Yet, if the truth follows the petition, those acting contrary to the deed of their father and author ought, as unworthy persons, to be deprived of their inheritance by law; nor should heirs be permitted to spring up against the judgment of their author. [Col. 0471D]

Therefore, dearest brothers, since they also complain that they are oppressed by the archdeacon of the said church—who promised that, in their absence, they would follow the judgment of their superior—let that person, whoever he may be, who harasses a cleric appear before your tribunal. Disregarding every [reason], and despite their being harassed contrary to divine and public laws, he thought that their proper forum could be taken away. Thus let not the rights of the Church, which ancient princes established by continual enactment, be denied to clerics who are attacked.

### CHAPTER 109.—Concerning one who undertook the guardianship of his nephew and deprived him of paternal goods. Gelasius to Bishop Fortunatus.

(Dist. 87, c. *Irreligiosum*.) We judge it altogether irreligious and detestable if anyone does not rear, with every faithfulness and with the whole sanctity of his heart, even strangers received into his guardianship. [Col. 0472A] Since the deacon Olympius of your Belovedness is said to be the maternal uncle of Felix and Olympius, and undertook to rear them as little children in the capacity of guardian, we judge it to be no less than robbery that, as they assert, he left them bereft of their parents’ small possessions, retaining some things and selling others contrary to laws and rights.

### CHAPTER 110.—That the Holy Spirit does not come at the invocation of a criminal priest. The same to Bishop Helpidius.

(1, q. 1, c. *Sacrosancta*.) The most holy religion containing Catholic discipline claims such reverence for itself that no one ought to approach it except with a pure conscience. [Col. 0472B] For how shall the heavenly Spirit, invoked for the consecration of the divine mystery, come, if the priest—and he who entreats that the Spirit be present—is rejected as full of criminal deeds?

### CHAPTER 111.—That one lacking an eye cannot obtain priestly office. Pelagius to Bishop Rufinus.

(Dist. 55, c. *Si evangelica*.) To one whose eye has been torn out, the rights of the priesthood cannot be granted according to the canons. Nor does it avail him that he lost the eye unwillingly, since no one is to be believed to have lost an eye willingly. Nor do we find that the most sacred canons made, in their rules, any exception for a circumstance of loss of an eye that would not impede [*ei*: this word is absent from the original and Gratian] a person seeking to obtain the priesthood. [Col. 0472C] Rather, we see that the Fathers established this sole prohibition: one who lacks an eye cannot obtain the priestly office.

Nor can sacred rank in any way be granted, as compensation for an injury, to the person who could provoke a priest to such anger against him that the former lost the office he held and the latter lost the possibility of his advancement.

### CHAPTER 112.—That those who need a bishop should elect him unanimously. Pelagius to Bishop Tulianus of Grumentium.

(Dist. 63, c. *Litteras charitatis*.) We received the letters of your Charity, in which you state that your deacon Latinus is being requested for the episcopate of the church of Marcellianum by the clergy and by all who assemble there. [Col. 0472D] We recall that, even before this time, the visitor and certain inhabitants of the place had reported this matter to us. But, believing that they had already received his letter of dismissal from your Charity, we wrote that he should come.

Yet since you now ask whether his person is acceptable to us and whether he ought to be released by you, nothing concerns us except that those who require a priest should unanimously choose a person against whom the canons cannot object. But we say this also: if all elect him and you are willing to release him, know that it is agreeable to us; and, if possible, let him hasten to arrive before the holy day, so that, by God’s grace, he may be ordained on that very Saturday of the great night, after baptism. Otherwise, they must wait until the fasts of the fourth month.

### CHAPTER 113.—Concerning one who married a woman previously veiled to another. Pelagius to Bishop Marcellus of Atonium.

[Col. 0473A]

(Dist. 34, c. *Valentino*.) In the case of the cleric Valentinus, whose wife had previously been veiled to another man, yet had not married him but remained a virgin, and after the death of the man to whom she had been veiled while betrothed [variant: “bridegroom”] was joined to Valentinus in marital union: because she had meanwhile received the veil, no obstacle is created to his advancement, since, so far as this particular issue is concerned, there is nothing contrary to the canonical enactments.

### CHAPTER 114.—That a priest who is a murderer cannot remain in the priesthood. John VIII to Bishop Cennemocus of Venice [in the fragments: “to the Cenomannian bishop of Utica”].

(Dist. 50, c. *Miror minus*.) I am astonished that your insufficiently instructed learning thinks that a priest can minister in the priesthood after committing homicide—or rather, what is worse, wishes to persuade us to give our assent to such presumption. [Col. 0473B] For who could be so mad and of such perverse judgment as to think that such a thing ought to be allowed, even after however great a penance, when it is wholly [variant: “entirely”] contrary to canonical discipline? Therefore, deprived of the priesthood, he ought to wash away so monstrous a crime with a fountain of tears, so that, healed at least by such remedies, he may find the aid of salvation.

### CHAPTER 115.—The same, to Emperor Louis: that one must not consent to evils.

(Dist. 10, c. *Vides*.) You see, dearest son, that what is acquired against the laws deserves to be dissolved by the laws. [Col. 0473C]

Likewise. (Dist. 86, c. *Facientis*.) Undoubtedly, one who neglects to correct what he is able to correct shares the guilt of the doer. For it is written: “Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are judged participants” (Rom. 1). And he offers acceptable sacrifice to the Lord who drives adversities away from the afflicted. To neglect, when you can overthrow the wicked, is nothing other than to foster them; nor is one free from the scruple of hidden consent who ceases to oppose manifest wrongdoing. He proves that he hates vices who condemns those in error; and he leaves himself no room for deviation who does not spare the transgressor. The first degree of innocence is to hate wicked deeds. He opens a broad entrance to offenders who joins consent with depravity; and it benefits no one not to be punished for his own sin if he must be punished for another’s.

### CHAPTER 116.—That no one may oppose the pope’s envoy. Gregory II to all bishops (Epistle 4).

[Col. 0473D]

If anyone, however—which we do not desire—should attempt, by opposing our envoy Boniface, to impede his work, or should prove hostile to the ministry entrusted to him and to his successors undertaking the same work, let him be struck by the bond of anathema under the divine sentence and be subject to everlasting condemnation.

### CHAPTER 117.—Concerning the reordination of presbyters ordained by unknown bishops. Gregory III to the presbyter Boniface (Epistle 5).

(Dist. 68, c. *Presbyteri*.) If the men by whom the presbyters whom you found there were ordained are unknown, and it is doubtful whether those who ordained them were bishops or not, then, if those presbyters themselves are men of good conduct and Catholic, instructed in ministry to Christ and in every holy law, let them receive from the Father or their bishop [variant: “suitable, from the bishop of origin”] the blessing of the presbyterate and be consecrated; and thus let them exercise the sacred ministry. [Col. 0474A]

### CHAPTER 118.—Concerning the lawful advancement of one whose finger was cut off by enemies. Stephen to Bishop Robert of Metz.

(Dist. 55, c. *Lator praesentium*.) The bearer of this letter, namely the cleric Flavinus, came to the holy Apostolic See and delivered to us the letter sent by you. In it you sought to ascertain whether, since he had recently been captured by the Northmen and had had a finger of his left hand cut off, he could or could not be promoted to ecclesiastical rank. [Col. 0474B]

Since we find that your diligence, being particularly concerned about this, seeks instruction from the Apostolic See, always desiring to follow the norm of justice, we rightly commend the zeal of your Holiness. We wish Your Reverence to know that, if it is so that he had that finger cut off by the Northmen, this will not prevent his promotion, if he is otherwise worthy. For we do not believe that your Belovedness is unaware what the sacred canons decree concerning those who suffer such a thing unwillingly at the hands of masters, physicians, or pagans. We find that the canons do not oppose such persons, if this is so. [Col. 0474C] We therefore exhort your Religiousness to act toward him in such a way that you may gain a great reward on his account and, with God’s help, fulfill this man’s desire, since no other canonical authority stands in the way.

### CHAPTER 119.—Concerning a subdeacon who took a wife after ordination. Stephen to Ado, archbishop of Vienne (among the fragments of letters of Nicholas I).

(Dist. 32, c. *De illo clerico*.) We are surprised why, by your authority, that cleric named Alvicus, whom you say had lived through the ecclesiastical orders as far as the subdiaconate, took a wife; for we have never granted anyone permission to take a wife, except those whom ecclesiastical rule permits to have wives.

### CHAPTER 120.—That a cleric who kills a pagan cannot be promoted. Nicholas to Wilfred, bishop of the Church of Morins (among rescripts of Nicholas I collected from Gratian, title 12).

(Dist. 50, c. *Clericum*.) A cleric who has killed a pagan ought not to be promoted to a higher rank [variant: “honor”]; indeed, he ought even to be deprived of what he has acquired, for he is a murderer. [Col. 0474D] Since soldiers of the world are distinct from soldiers of the Church, it is not fitting for a soldier of the Church to serve in worldly warfare, through which he must come to the shedding of blood. Finally, just as it is shameful and harmful for a layman to celebrate Masses and consecrate the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood, so it is ridiculous and unfitting for a cleric to take up arms and proceed to war, when the Apostle Paul says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2). It is as though he plainly stated the converse: “No one serving as a soldier for the world entangles himself in spiritual affairs.”

### CHAPTER 121.—That the hands of presbyters and deacons are not to be anointed with chrism when they are ordained. The same Nicholas to Radulf, archbishop of Bourges (Nicholas I, Epistle 19, chapter 3).

[Col. 0475A]

(Dist. 23, c. *Praeterea*.) You ask whether the hands of presbyters alone, or of deacons also, ought to be anointed with the liquid of chrism when they are ordained. In this holy Roman Church, in which, by God’s authorship, we serve, this is done for neither. Nor do we read anywhere—unless memory deceives us—that it was practiced by ministers of the New Law. Therefore, we send Your Holiness the canonical decrees of blessed Pope Innocent; and the opening pages of the letter sent to Decentius, bishop of Eugubium, will fully instruct you concerning the observances required in consecrations and ordinations.

### CHAPTER 122.—That no one is to be condemned except upon voluntary confession or canonical conviction. The same to Solomon, bishop of Constance.

[Col. 0475B]

(15, q. 5, c. *Presbyter, vel diaconus*.) A presbyter or deacon who, as you assert, refuses publicly to confess crimes but wishes to defend himself by oath, although the bishop knows that the crime was committed by him, cannot retain priestly or diaconal office by any penance. Yet it is astonishing how the crime could be known to have been committed by him if he has not confessed, unless perhaps a qualified accuser proves it through qualified witnesses.

Therefore, if, when the bishop investigates the case of a presbyter or deacon, that presbyter or deacon has not perhaps been convicted by the confirmation of witnesses, the crime has not been lawfully made known to the bishop unless the presbyter or deacon voluntarily confesses the crime itself. [Col. 0475C] Unless he does so, we do not at present see that the presbyter or deacon ought to be deprived of his office. Thus voluntary confession alone, or the canonical number or quality of witnesses, when bishops render judgment and the accuser proves what he alleged, deprives a cleric of his own rank.

### CHAPTER 123.—That a deacon may not sit before a presbyter. Chapter 7 of the canons of the Sixth Synod.

(Dist. 93, c. *Praecipimus*.) We command that a deacon, even if he holds some ecclesiastical dignity—that is, office—shall not sit before a presbyter, unless he represents his own patriarch or metropolitan in some matter. [Col. 0475D] For then he shall be honored as holding that person’s place. But if anyone presumptuously does this in a tyrannical manner, let him be removed from his own rank and become last of all in his order.

### CHAPTER 124.—Concerning those irrecoverably deposed, chapter 10 [variant: chapter 21].

Those who have been irrecoverably deposed for their offenses and reduced to the place of laypersons, if they turn voluntarily to God, renouncing the sin for which they were deposed and wholly separating themselves from it, should not lose clerical tonsure. But if they cling to their sin, let them let their hair grow like laymen, because they have preferred worldly life to heavenly life.

### CHAPTER 125.—That a slave may not be ordained without his master’s knowledge. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 5 (Second Council of Orléans, chapter 10).

(Dist. 54, c. *Si servus*.) If a slave is ordained deacon or presbyter while his master is absent or unaware, but the bishop knows that he is a slave, then, while the slave remains in clerical office, the bishop shall compensate the master by double satisfaction. [Col. 0476A] But if the bishop did not know him to be a slave, those who give testimony or petitioned for his ordination shall be liable to a like repayment.

### CHAPTER 126.—Concerning those who obtain freedom in such a way that their masters retain no service from them. From the Council of Toledo, chapter 74 (Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 73).

(Dist. 54, c. *Quicunque*.) Whoever receives freedom from his masters in such a way that the patron retains no service from him may freely be admitted to clerical rank, provided he is free from a capital crime, because he is known to have been released by direct manumission. [Col. 0476B] But those who have been manumitted with service retained are still bound by an obligation of service to their patrons and must by no means be promoted to ecclesiastical rank, lest, whenever their masters wish, they become slaves from being clerics.

### CHAPTER 127.—How slaves to be ordained should be made freeborn. From the Council of Reims, chapter 1.

Ecclesiastical authority openly directs, and moreover royal majesty gives its assent to canonical religion, that whenever any church determines to promote someone from its own household to sacred orders, he shall be solemnly confirmed under a charter of freedom, by the subscription or manumission of the person to whom he is subject, in the presence of canonical priests and noble laymen alike.

### CHAPTER 128.—On the same subject. From the Council of Toledo (among the fragments of the First Council of Toledo).

[Col. 0476C]

The aforementioned charters of free status should contain not only the name of the person who requests their execution, but also the names, arranged in order, of the priests and noble laymen who were present, together with marks made by their own hands. For without their attestation, a document stripped of the authority of witnesses is regarded as worthless. The place, day, year, ruler, and indiction must also be entered at the end or in the margin in this manner. [Col. 0476D]

> Done in such-and-such city, in the house of Saint Peter, on such-and-such Kalends, in such-and-such year of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the reign of such-and-such king, and with such-and-such bishop presiding in the see of the aforesaid city, or in such-and-such monastery [these four words are not in the original], in such-and-such indiction, happily, in God’s name. Amen.

For Roman authority says: “Whatever laws are promulgated without a date and consul shall not be valid.”

### CHAPTER 129.—Likewise on the same subject. From the same council (ibid.).

Laypersons must further be instructed to know that they cannot in any other place manumit their own slaves whom they have determined to enroll in the Lord’s service, except in the most holy Church and according to the manner stated above. [Col. 0477A] For how can clerics obtain freedom outside the holy Church, when they are strangers to worldly law? And how can those forbidden to proceed to a secular court be released from the yoke of slavery by a secular judgment?

But perhaps someone says: “A man is not permitted to become a cleric unless, before undertaking clerical office, he obtains free status.” He speaks the truth indeed; and therefore what can be weakened or criticized must be guarded against beforehand.

### CHAPTER 130.—Likewise on the same subject. From the same council (ibid.).

Not only those who are to be promoted to clerical rank must be manumitted in the Church, but also those whom anyone wishes to emancipate for the remedy of his soul, because this is written in the pact of the Franks.

### CHAPTER 131.—A model charter of freedom for one’s own slave. From the same council (ibid.).

Let one who releases the bond of obligation and the service due to him not doubt that a reward will come to him from the Lord in the future. Therefore I, in God’s name, for the remedy of my soul and for eternal recompense, in the church of Saint Peter, or of such-and-such saint, in the presence of the bishop or priests standing there and noble laymen, before the horn of the altar of this church, release my slave, such-and-such a person, through this charter of release and free status, from every bond of slavery. [Col. 0477B] From this day forward he shall be freeborn and remain freeborn, as though he had been born or begotten of freeborn parents.

Let him go wherever he prefers, or wherever canonical authority permits him, and let him live a free life like other freeborn persons. He shall owe none of my heirs or co-heirs, nor any other person, any service of slavery or of freed status, save God alone, to whom all things are subject and for whose love I have devoutly offered him to God’s service.

Let him possess forever as granted to him his peculium—that is, his personal property—which the Lord has given him or which he may hereafter, with God’s help, acquire [variant: “earn by labor”], so that he may do with it whatever he pleases according to the ecclesiastical enactments. [Col. 0477C]

But if anyone—which I do not believe will occur—whether I myself, or any of my heirs, or any opposing person, should attempt to act against this charter of free status or seek in any way to violate it, let that person first incur the wrath of God and be made an outsider from the thresholds of the holy Church. Moreover, let the person who brings the suit pay forty [variant: sixty] solidi and have no power to vindicate what he claims. [Col. 0477D] Rather, may this present grant of free status, confirmed by my hand or by the hands of other good men, or supported by their attestation [variant: “joined to it”], remain unshaken for all time.

### CHAPTER 132.—Concerning the ordination of slaves. From the same council, chapter 32.

(Dist. 54, c. *De servorum*.) Concerning the ordination of slaves who are indiscriminately promoted to ecclesiastical ranks, it pleased all that agreement should be maintained with the sacred canons. It was decreed that no bishop should henceforth presume to promote them to sacred orders unless they have first obtained freedom from their own masters.

If any slave, fleeing or hiding from his master, reaches ecclesiastical ranks by producing hired or corrupted witnesses, or by any trickery or fraud, it is decreed that he shall be deposed and his master shall receive him back. [Col. 0478A] But if a grandfather or father, migrating from one country to another, begets a son in that province, and the son, reared there, is promoted to ecclesiastical ranks, while it is unknown whether he is a slave, and afterwards his master arrives and legally claims him, it is ordained that, if the master wishes to grant him freedom, he shall remain in his rank. But if the master wishes to withdraw him by the chain of slavery from the Lord’s camp, he shall lose his rank, because, according to the sacred canons, a person remaining of servile condition cannot exercise the dignity of the priesthood.

### CHAPTER 133.—Concerning slaves of churches. From the same council, chapter 33 (ibid.).

[Col. 0478B]

Concerning slaves of churches, it has been decreed by common decision that archbishops established throughout the several provinces shall follow our authorization. Their suffragans, however, shall keep a copy of it with themselves; and whenever some useful person from the household of a church is found who is to be ordained, this authorization shall be read aloud from the ambo before the people. Then, in the presence of priests and all the clergy, before the horn of the altar, as our authorization provides, he shall obtain freedom with every deception removed, and only then shall he be promoted to ecclesiastical ranks.

### CHAPTER 134.—That penitents or twice-married men are not to be promoted. From the Third Council of Arles, chapter 3.

(Dist. 55, c. *Nullus poenitentem*.) Let twice-married men, penitents, and husbands of repudiated women not be promoted to the priesthood. [Col. 0478C]

### CHAPTER 135.—Concerning the possessed. From the Council of Orange, chapter 6 (First Council of Orange).

Those possessed by demons are not only not to be admitted to any clerical order; those who have been ordained are also to be removed from the office imposed upon them.

### CHAPTER 136.—Likewise, that penitents are not to be ordained. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 77 (Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 68).

(Dist. 50, c. *Ex poenitentibus*.) A cleric is not to be ordained from among penitents, even if he is good. If this happens through the bishop’s ignorance, let him be deposed from the clergy, because at the time of ordination he did not disclose that he was undergoing penance. [Col. 0478D] But if the bishop knowingly ordains such a person, let the bishop also be deprived of his episcopal power to ordain, and of that only.

### CHAPTER 137.—Whether agents and procurators ought to be ordained. From the same council, chapter 9.

Magnus, bishop of Astuaga, said: “What seems good to Your Belovedness concerning procurators and agents, including executors for minors: ought they to be ordained?”

Bishop Gratus said: “If, after all matters have been arranged and accounts rendered, their conduct of life is found approved in every respect, they should, if requested, be granted clerical honor with commendation. For if, before they are released from their business affairs or offices, they are ordained by anyone without due consideration, the Church is disgraced.”

All said: “Your Holiness has rightly determined everything; therefore this is our judgment as well.”

### CHAPTER 138.—Likewise concerning penitents. From the First Council of Toledo, chapter 2.

(Dist. 50, c. *Placuit*.) It likewise pleased us that penitents should not be admitted to the clergy, except only that, if necessity or utility requires, they may be assigned among the doorkeepers [variant: “and then be assigned”], or among the readers, provided they do not read the Gospels or the Apostle. But those already ordained shall be ranked among the subdeacons, so that they do not lay on hands or touch sacred things.

We call a person a penitent who, after baptism, has undertaken public penance for homicide or for diverse crimes and very grave sins, and has been reconciled to the divine altar under sackcloth.

### CHAPTER 139.—A layman who takes a second wife is not to become a cleric. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 8 (Third Council of Orléans, chapter 9).

[Col. 0479B]

If any layman, after a wife, has known another woman of whatever condition, he is by no means to be admitted to the clergy.

### CHAPTER 140.—That no one may presume to retain another’s parishioner. From the decrees of Pope Adrian, chapter 15 (among the eighty canons against false accusers of bishops).

No bishop may presume, without the consent of the other bishop, to retain, ordain, or judge another’s parishioner. For just as his ordination will be invalid, so also will his judgment, since we judge that no one is bound by the sentence of another judge rather than his own. For one who could not ordain him cannot in any way judge him.

### CHAPTER 141.—That one ordained by another bishop may not remain in the clergy. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 4.

[Col. 0479C]

A cleric ordained by another bishop, without the request or consent of his own bishop, shall not remain in the clergy.

### CHAPTER 142.—Concerning a bishop who ordained another bishop’s cleric against his will. From the African Council, chapter 42 (Third Council of Carthage, chapter 44).

Bishop Epigonius said: “This has been decreed in many councils, and must now be confirmed by your wisdom, dearest [variant: ‘most blessed’] brothers: no bishop may take for himself another’s cleric contrary to the judgment of the bishop whose cleric he is.

“I refer to Julian, who is ungrateful for the favors of God bestowed upon him through my insignificance. He proved himself so rash and bold that he seized a man baptized by me, who, when a most needy boy, had been entrusted to me by that same person. [Col. 0479D] He was nourished by me and grew up under my care for many years. As I said, it is established that he was baptized in my church by the hand of my insignificance. He began to be a reader in the diocese of Mapale—or rather, had read there for nearly two years. Yet for some utterly monstrous contempt [variant: ‘of my humility’] Julian seized him and, without consulting me, claimed him as though he were a citizen belonging to his own town of Vazarita. He also ordained him deacon. If this is permitted, most blessed brothers, let this permission be openly granted by you. But if not, let one so shameless be restrained, lest he involve himself in anyone’s communion.”

Bishop Numidius said: “If Julian appears to have done this without requesting or consulting Your Dignity, we all judge it to have been done unjustly and unworthily. Therefore, if Julian does not correct his error [Col. 0480A] and, with satisfaction, restore to your people the cleric whom he dared to ordain, he shall receive the judgment that, acting contrary to the decrees of the council, he has separated himself from us by his contumacy.”

Bishop Epigonius said: “Our praiseworthy brother and colleague Victor, a father in age and himself a man of most ancient standing in rank, wishes this petition to be made general for all.”

### CHAPTER 143.—That no one may retain another’s cleric. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 20 (Third Council of Carthage, chapter 2).

(Dist. 72, c. *Clericum alienum*.) Without the consent of his own bishop, let no one dare either to retain or promote another’s cleric in the church entrusted to him. The designation “clerics” also includes readers, psalmists, and doorkeepers.

### CHAPTER 144.—That no bishop may receive another’s cleric without letters from his bishop. From the same council, chapter 6 (First Council of Carthage, chapter 5).

[Col. 0480B]

The primate bishop of Vegesela said: “I submit to Your Holiness that you should decree that no one may receive a cleric belonging to another without letters from his own bishop, or retain him with himself; nor may anyone take for himself a layman from another’s people in order to ordain him without the knowledge of the bishop to whose flock he belongs.”

Bishop Gratus said: “This observance preserves peace. I remember that it was also decreed in the most holy Council of Sardica (chapters 16, 18, 19) that no one may take for himself a member of another’s people. But if he should perhaps be needed, let him ask his colleague and receive him by consent.”

### CHAPTER 145.—Concerning presbyters and deacons who travel without letters from their bishop. From the Council of Agde, chapter 5 (chapter 52).

[Col. 0480C]

Let no one extend communion to a presbyter, deacon, or cleric who travels without letters from his bishop.

### CHAPTER 146.—On the same matter. From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 41.

(De cons., dist. 5, c. *Non oportet*.) A priest or cleric ought not to travel without canonical letters.

### CHAPTER 147.—That every presbyter, when ordained, should receive letters from his ordainer. From the Council of Milevis, chapter 14.

It was further decreed that all who are henceforth ordained by bishops shall receive letters from their ordainers, subscribed by their hands, containing the year of the Lord and the day [variant: “the consul and the day”], so that no dispute may arise concerning later or earlier ordinations. [Col. 0480D]

### CHAPTER 148.—That one ordained should remain in the place for which he was ordained. From the Council of Agde, chapter 2.

Let ministers who have been ordained in particular places remain in those same places.

### CHAPTER 149.—Concerning a presbyter who confesses that he sinned before ordination. From the Council of Chalon, chapter 25 (chapter 25 of the Greek synod collected by Martin, bishop of Braga).

(25, q. 8, c. *Si quis presbyter*.) If a presbyter sinned before ordination and, after ordination, confesses that he erred beforehand, let him not offer the Eucharist; nevertheless, solely out of respect for religion, let him retain the title of presbyter. [Col. 0481A] But if he does not confess himself and is publicly convicted by another, let him not even retain the title of presbyter. The same is to be observed concerning deacons: if he confesses himself, let him retain the rank of subdeacon.

### CHAPTER 150.—Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 13 [variant: chapter 9].

(15, q. 8, c. *Qui admisit*.) If a presbyter is promoted while burdened by a carnal sin, and confesses concerning himself that he sinned before ordination, let him not consecrate the offerings, though he remains in his other duties on account of his good zeal. But if he has not confessed concerning himself and cannot be manifestly accused, let the matter be left to the judgment of his authority.

### CHAPTER 151.—Concerning the ministries of presbyters and what has been entrusted to them. From the sayings of Augustine.

[Col. 0481B]

You priests ought to know and always remember that we, to whom the care of governing souls has been entrusted, shall render an account for those who perish through our negligence; but for those whom we have won by words and examples, we shall receive the reward of eternal life. For to us the Lord said: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matt. V). If the faithful people are God’s food, we are the seasoning of that food. Know that your rank is second to, and almost joined with, our rank. For as bishops hold the place of the apostles in the Church, so indeed priests hold the place of the Lord’s other disciples. The former hold the rank of Aaron the high priest; the latter, that of his sons. Therefore you must always be mindful [Col. 0481C] of so great a dignity, mindful of your consecration, mindful of the sacred anointing which you received upon your hands, so that you neither fall away from that dignity, nor render your consecration void, nor defile by sin hands anointed with holy oil. Rather, preserving purity of heart and body, and offering the peoples an example of good living, you should provide those over whom you preside with guidance toward the heavenly kingdoms.

## CHAPTER 152.—That Each Priest Should Have One Cleric. From the Council of Nantes, chapter 8.

Let every priest who governs a people have a cleric who sings with him, reads the Epistle and the lesson, and is able to keep a school; and let him admonish his parishioners to send their sons [Col. 0481D] to church to learn the faith, so that he himself may instruct them in all chastity.

## CHAPTER 153.—On Examining the Faith of Priests. From the Council of Mâcon, chapter 3.

Before all else, the faith of priests must be examined: how they themselves believe and teach others to believe. There examples must be set forth, so that the creature may understand the Creator as far as it is at all able.

## CHAPTER 154.—How, and What, Priests Ought to Teach Those Entrusted to Them. From the Sayings of Augustine.

We exhort you to be ready to teach your peoples. Let him who knows the Scriptures preach the Scriptures; but he who does not know them should at least say to the people what he knows best: that they should turn away from evil and do good, seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord [Col. 0482A] are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers (Ps. XXXVI). But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth (Ps. XXXIII). Therefore no one will be able to excuse himself by saying that he has no tongue with which he can edify anyone. As soon as he sees any person going astray, according to his strength and ability he should draw that person back from error—by rebuking, entreating, or reproving—and exhort him to perform a good work.

## CHAPTER 155.—On the Same Matter. From the Council of Rouen, chapter 6.

First of all, it must be preached generally to everyone that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one almighty God, who made all things; and that there is one Godhead, substance, and majesty [Col. 0482B] in the three persons of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER 156.—Likewise on the Same Matter. From the Same Council, chapter 2.

Likewise it must be preached how the Son of God was incarnate by the Holy Spirit from Mary the Virgin; how, for the salvation of the human race, he suffered, was buried, rose again on the third day, and ascended into heaven; and how at the end of the world he will come to judge all people according to their own deeds; how the wicked will be sent with the devil into eternal fire, while the righteous will be with Christ in eternal life.

## CHAPTER 157.—Likewise, from the Same Source, chapter 3.

Likewise it must be preached that all people will rise again in their own flesh.

## CHAPTER 158.—That Every Priest Shall Teach His Parishioners the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer. From the Council of Reims, chapter 8.

[Col. 0482C]

Let every priest either personally teach all his parishioners the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, or direct others to teach them, so that, when they come for confession in Lent, he may have each one recite these from memory to him; and let him admit no one to holy communion before that person knows how to pronounce them from the heart. For without knowledge of these, no one can be saved. In the one are contained Christian faith and belief; in the other is expressed what we ought to pray for and ask from God. The Lord shows that no one can be saved without faith when he says: “He who believes and is baptized [Col. 0482D] shall be saved” (Matt. XVI). Yet no one can believe what he does not know and has not heard. For Paul says: “How shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard?” (Rom. X). Nor does faith in the heart alone suffice unless it is also declared in words, as the same Apostle testifies: “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (ibid.). Let no one plead dullness of mind or weakness of intellect; for these things are so small that no one is so dull or barbarous as to be unable to learn them and pronounce them in ordinary words, yet so great that anyone who can fully grasp knowledge of them may be judged to possess what is sufficient for everlasting salvation. This too must be observed: no one is to receive an infant from the sacred font in baptism until he has recited the same Creed and Lord’s Prayer before the [Col. 0483A] people [the priest]. Then the priest shall announce to all godparents that they are obliged, when their godchildren reach the age of understanding, to teach them these same things.

## CHAPTER 159.—On the Same Matter. From the Council of Chalon, chapter 3.

It must be commanded that the Lord’s Prayer, in which are contained all things necessary for human life, and the Apostles’ Creed, in which the Catholic faith is contained in its entirety, be learned by all, both in Latin and in the vernacular, so that what they confess with the mouth they may believe with the heart.

## CHAPTER 160.—On Preaching Love of God and Neighbour. From the Same Source, chapter 5.

Likewise there must be preaching on love of God and neighbour; on faith and hope in God; on humility, patience, [Col. 0483B] chastity, kindness, mercy, almsgiving, and confession, that one may forgive one’s brothers from the heart. For those who practise these and similar things shall attain the kingdom of God.

## CHAPTER 161.—On Mortal Sins. From the Same Source, chapter 3.

Likewise it must be preached for which crimes people are assigned to the devil. The Apostle enumerates them thus: fornication, impurity, licentiousness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousies, anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. Those who do such things shall not attain the kingdom of God (Gal. V). Therefore all these things must be prohibited with every effort.

## CHAPTER 162.—That No One Shall Leave the Congregation While the Priest Is Speaking. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 24.

[Col. 0483C]

(*On Consecration*, distinction 1, chapter “While the Priest Is Speaking.”) If anyone leaves the congregation while the priest is speaking in church, without grave necessity [these three words are absent in the original], let him be excommunicated.

## CHAPTER 163.—On the Same Matter. From the Canons of the Apostles, chapter 10.

(*On Consecration*, distinction 1, chapter “All the Faithful.”) All the faithful who gather in church for sacred solemnities and hear the Scriptures of the apostles and the Gospel, but do not remain in prayer until the dismissal has been completed, nor receive holy communion, ought, as persons disturbing the peace of the Church, [Col. 0483D] to be deprived of communion.

## CHAPTER 164.—Likewise on the Same Matter. From an Apostolic Canon.

All Christians who enter the church of God and hear the sacred Scriptures, but do not join the people in prayer and instead, through a certain lack of self-control, withdraw themselves from receiving holy communion, are to be removed from the church until they show the fruits of repentance through confession.

## CHAPTER 165.—On Prayers after the Address. From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 19.

It is fitting that, separately, after the address of bishops or priests, prayers first be offered over the catechumens; and, after the catechumens [Col. 0484A] have departed, prayers be made over those who are doing penance. When these too have come forward to the priest’s hand and departed, three prayers of the faithful are to be completed: the first indeed in silence, but the second and third with the customary acclamations. Then at last they shall give one another the peace. After the bishop has given the priests the kiss of peace, the laity shall then give it among themselves; and thus the holy offering shall be celebrated.

## CHAPTER 166.—What Priests Ought to Admonish. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 4.

Let priests admonish the people to give alms and to offer prayers on account of the various scourges which we continually suffer because of our sins.

## CHAPTER 167.—How Each Person Ought to Pray. From the Same Source, chapter 6.

[Col. 0484B] Likewise the people must be instructed that every day, whoever cannot do more should pray at least twice, namely morning and evening, reciting the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, or: “You who formed me, have mercy on me”; or also: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke XVIII). Let each give thanks to God for the provisions of daily life, because he has deigned to create him in his own image and distinguish him from the beasts. When these things have been done and he has worshipped God alone, his Creator, let him invoke the saints, that they may deign to intercede for him before the divine majesty. Those for whom a church building is nearby should do these things in the church; but those who are travelling, or for any reason are in woods or fields, should do so wherever the morning or evening hour [Col. 0484C] finds them, knowing that God is present everywhere, as the Psalmist says: “His dominions are in every place” (Ps. CII).

## CHAPTER 168.—How Children Ought to Obey Their Parents. From the Council at Auvergne, chapter 6 [3].

The faithful of God’s holy Church are to be admonished that sons and daughters should show obedience to their parents, the Lord saying: “Son, honour your father.” Parents themselves, moreover, must be admonished to behave with moderation toward their sons and daughters, the Apostle saying: “And you, parents, do not provoke your children to anger” (Col. 3). They must also be told that, if parents wish through natural affection to spare offences committed by their children, the Lord does not permit those children to go unpunished, unless perhaps they are subjected to penance. Yet it is lighter for children [Col. 0484D] to receive whatever punishments their parents impose than to incur God’s wrath.

## CHAPTER 169.—That All Shall Answer the Priest’s Greetings at Mass. From the Council of Orléans.

Likewise it must be made known that fitting responses to priestly greetings should be learned: not only clerics and persons consecrated to God should make the responses to the priest, but the whole people ought devoutly to answer in one voice.

## CHAPTER 170.—That a Priest Shall Not Leave His Own Church and Roam among Holy Places. From the Sayings of Augustine.

It must be forbidden that any ordained person migrate from his own parish to another, whether to the thresholds of the apostles for prayer, abandoning the care of his own church, or to the palace in order to make a petition. If he does so, such ordination or transfer is of no [Col. 0485A] validity. This must be announced to everyone: those who desire to go to the thresholds of the blessed apostles for prayer should confess their sins at home and then set out, since they must be bound or loosed by their own bishop or priest, not by a stranger.

## CHAPTER 171.—Nothing Is to Be Done without the Bishop’s Permission. From the Letter of Clement (Letter 1, near the end).

He taught that no priest ought to do anything in the parish of any bishop without that bishop’s permission. He taught that all priests ought, without delay, to obey their own bishops in all things, as the Lord ordained. He taught that no one should covet what belongs to another or presume upon what was theirs, but that each should be content with what is his own and entrusted to him. [Col. 0485B] He also instructed that no one should do to another anything which he would not wish done to himself.

## CHAPTER 172.—That Priests Shall Not Leave Places Entrusted to Them for Others. From the First Council of Arles, chapter 2.

Concerning priests or deacons who are accustomed to leave the places in which they were ordained and transfer themselves to other places, it has been decided that they shall minister in the same places to which they were assigned. If, having abandoned their own places, they wish to transfer themselves elsewhere, let them be deposed.

## CHAPTER 173.—That It Is Not Permitted for a Cleric to Be Enrolled Simultaneously in the Churches of Two Cities. From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 10, session 15.

(21, question 1, chapter “A Cleric of Two [Cities].”) A cleric may not be enrolled simultaneously in the churches of two cities, [Col. 0485C] but must minister in that city in which he was ordained from the beginning. Nor may he flee to another, as though it were superior, out of desire for empty glory. Those who do this must be recalled to their own church, in which they were first ordained, and minister there alone.

## CHAPTER 174.—That No Ordained Person Shall Be Transferred from City to City. From the Council of Nicaea, chapter 15 (and Aachen, chapter 43).

(7, question 1, chapter “It Is Not Fitting.”) Because of the great disturbance and seditions which arise, it has been decided that the custom, seemingly admitted in certain regions contrary to the rule, be entirely abolished: no bishop, priest, or deacon shall be transferred from city to city. If, after the decree of the holy and great council, anyone attempts to do such a thing [Col. 0485D] and commits himself to such an undertaking, the act shall be considered wholly void, and he shall be restored to the Church in which he was ordained bishop, priest, or deacon.

## CHAPTER 175.—On the Same Matter. From the Same Council, chapter 17.

Any priests or deacons who recklessly or dangerously depart from the church entrusted to them, having neither the fear of the Lord before their eyes nor knowledge of the ecclesiastical rule—and likewise anyone who is entirely subject to a rule—must by no means be received into another church. Rather, every compulsion must be brought to bear upon them to return to their own parishes. If they do not do so, they must be deprived of communion.

## CHAPTER 176.—That Priests Shall Not Be Sent as Envoys to Various Places, Leaving the Care of Souls Behind. From the Council of Arles, chapter 3.

[Col. 0486A]

It has been decreed that priests, as has hitherto been done, shall not indiscriminately be sent to various places by bishops, other prelates, or even laymen, lest through their absence danger to souls arise and they neglect the duties of the churches in which they are established.

## CHAPTER 177.—That Priests Ought Continually to Read and Pray. From the Sayings of Augustine.

Priests, you must be constant in reading and earnest in prayer, because the life of a righteous man is instructed by reading, adorned by prayer, and guarded from sin by assiduous reading, according to him who said: “I have hidden your words in my heart, that I may not sin against you” [Col. 0486B] (Ps. CXVIII). For these are weapons—reading and prayer—by which the devil is overcome. These are the instruments by which eternal blessedness is obtained; by these weapons vices are restrained; by these nourishments virtues are fed. But if reading is ever set aside, work of the hands must follow, because idleness is the enemy of the soul. The ancient enemy easily drags into vices anyone whom he finds free from reading or prayer. By the practice of reading you will learn both how to live yourselves and how to teach others. By the practice of prayer you will be able to benefit both yourselves and those united to you in charity. By manual labour and bodily discipline, you will both deny nourishment to vices and supply your own needs, and you will have something to give to those suffering need (Eph. IV).

## CHAPTER 178.—That Priests Shall Not Go without Their *Oraria*. From the Council of Mainz (under Leo III, chapter 28).

[Col. 0486C]

Priests shall wear their *oraria* without interruption, as a distinction of priestly dignity.

## CHAPTER 179.—That a Cleric Shall Earn His Livelihood by an Honourable Trade. From the African Council (Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 51).

(Distinction 91, chapter “A Cleric.”) Any cleric [however greatly] instructed in the word of God shall seek his livelihood through an honourable trade.

## CHAPTER 180.—On the Same Matter. From the Same Source, chapter 52.

(Distinction 91, chapter “A Cleric’s Livelihood.”) Any cleric instructed in the word of God shall provide for his food and clothing by a trade or by agriculture, provided only that this does not impair his office.

## CHAPTER 181.—What Priests Ought to Do after Completing the Morning Office. From the Council of Nantes, chapter 60.

[Col. 0486D]

In the morning, after completing the morning office, the priest shall discharge the allotted service of his duty by chanting Prime, Terce, Sext, and None. Yet afterward, at the appropriate hours and when the signals are given, they shall, insofar as possible, be completed publicly either by him or by the pupils. Then, after the hours have been performed and the sick visited, if he wishes he may go out fasting to rural work, so that he may again be able, until the appointed hour according to the season and opportunity, to assist the needs of pilgrims and guests, of various travellers, and also of the sick and dead.

## CHAPTER 182.—On the Same Matter. From the Sayings of Saint Benedict (chapter 16 of His Rule).

[Col. 0487A]

The Prophet says: “Seven times a day I have given praise to you” (Ps. CXVIII). This sacred number of seven will thus be fulfilled by us if we perform the offices of our service at the times of Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline; for concerning these the Prophet said: “Seven times a day I have given praise to you.” But concerning the night vigils the same Prophet says: “At midnight I arose to give thanks to you” (ibid.). Therefore at these times let us render praise to our Creator for the judgments of his righteousness.

## CHAPTER 183.—That Priests Shall Be Concerned for Those from Whose Goods They Share. From the Sayings of Augustine.

Priests must be admonished to consider that whatever [Col. 0487B] is given by the faithful is the redemption of sinners. Therefore they should not glory in using such resources, but rather fear what was said concerning priests in the Old Testament: that they must bear the iniquity of the people (Lev. X; Num. XVIII). Accordingly, with great fear they must be concerned for those in whose goods [gifts] they share, because it is a great danger to become the judge of another’s life when one does not know how to keep the reins of one’s own life.

## CHAPTER 184.—That Priests Shall Lodge beside the Church. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 5 (chapter 36).

Let priests by no means be allowed, or presume in any way, to lodge wherever they please; rather, they should all make it their concern to remain continually at their own churches, for the sake of the sacred mysteries or ministries to be provided to the faithful, [Col. 0487C] and they should not be permitted to reside elsewhere. Nor shall women have any lodging [variant: intercourse/association] in places to which priests have any resort. If they think little of observing this, they shall be judged as transgressors and as persons acting contrary to prohibitions.

## CHAPTER 185.—That a Priest Who Takes a Wife Shall Be Deposed. From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 1.

(Distinction 28, chapter “If a Priest [Takes a Wife],” chapter 10.) If a priest takes a wife, let him be deposed from his order. But if he has committed fornication or adultery, he must be expelled still further and reduced to penance. Likewise, if a deacon falls into the same sin, he shall be removed from the order of ministry.

## CHAPTER 186.—On the Same Matter. From the Council of Nicaea, chapter 3.

[Col. 0487D]

(Distinction 32, chapter “It Forbade in Every Respect.”) The great synod has entirely forbidden a bishop, priest, deacon, or indeed anyone whatsoever in the clergy to keep a woman introduced into his household, except perhaps a mother, sister, aunt, or only those persons who escape suspicion.

## CHAPTER 187.—On the Same Matter. From the Decrees of Pope Siricius, chapter 12 (Letter 1).

(Distinction 18, chapter “Women.”) We do not allow any women to be in clerics’ houses except those alone whom the Synod of Nicaea permitted to live with them solely because of kinship.

## CHAPTER 188.—Likewise on the Same Matter. From the Decrees of Pope Siricius, chapter 2 [chapter 3].

The bishops decreed concerning priests who indiscriminately permit women [Col. 0488A] to live with them and are, on that account, marked by suspicion of a bad reputation: if, after being admonished, they do not correct themselves henceforth, they shall, as contemners of the holy canons, be struck with canonical punishment.

## CHAPTER 189.—With What Women a Priest May Live. From the Council of Agde, chapter 4 [chapter 10].

For the safeguarding of our life and reputation, we also specially command that no cleric be joined to any unrelated woman by any kind of companionship [variant: conversation] or familiarity. Not only may an unrelated woman not come into his house, but he himself may not have licence to visit an unrelated woman. Yet he may freely live with his mother, sister, and niece, if he has or wishes to have them; for concerning these relationships it is wicked to suspect anything other than what nature has ordained. [Col. 0488B]

## CHAPTER 190.—That Female Slaves Be Removed from the Brothers’ Storeroom. From the Council of Reims, chapter 4 (Agde I).

It has been decided that female slaves or freedwomen be removed from the brothers’ storeroom, from private service, and from the same dwelling in which a cleric lives.

## CHAPTER 191.—That No Cleric Shall Have Familiarity with Unrelated Women. From the Council of Tours, chapter 6 (First Council of Tours, chapter 3).

And because no opportunity ought to be given to the devil (Eph. IV), we decree that this above all be observed: no clerics shall have familiarity with unrelated women, nor give people any occasion for evil speech or thought. For it often happens, through this unseemly occasion, that the devil—who lies in wait like a lion in his den—exults over the ruin of God’s servants. But if any cleric, after his bishop’s prohibition, presumes to persist in these attachments [illicit familiarities with unrelated women], let him be excluded from communion. [Col. 0488C]

## CHAPTER 192.—On the Same Matter. From the Council of Nantes, chapter 10 [chapter 3].

It must be forbidden and prohibited by every means that no priest keep in his house women of those classes concerning whom suspicion may arise, as is also contained in the inserted canon; nor even those whom the canons allow—mother, aunt, sister—because, at the devil’s instigation, a crime is frequently found to have been committed even with them, or with their maidservants [Col. 0488D]. But if any priest has among these a person suffering such need that the priest’s support is necessary for her, let her have a house in a hamlet or village far from the priest’s household, and let him provide there what is necessary for them. But, according to the authority of the canons, it must by every means be prohibited that any woman presume to approach the altar, minister to a priest, or stand or sit within the chancel rails.

## CHAPTER 193.—On Incontinent Clerics. From the Canons of the Apostles, chapter 22.

The discipline of the divine laws concerning priests and deacons is that incontinent persons holding such offices be deprived of every ecclesiastical honour and not admitted to a ministry [Col. 0489A] which ought to be performed only with continence.

## CHAPTER 194.—On the Same Matter. From the Same Source.

Furthermore, the Church must in every way require them to maintain what is worthy, modest, and honourable: namely, that priests and Levites do not cohabit with women, because they are occupied with the necessities of their daily ministry. It is written: “Be holy, for I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Lev. XI, XIX, XX).

## CHAPTER 195.—On Clerics Demanding Interest. From the Council of Nantes (chapter 195).

(Apostolic Canon 43; distinction 47, chapter “A Bishop.”) A bishop, priest, or deacon who demands interest from debtors must either cease or certainly be condemned.

## CHAPTER 196.—On the Same Matter. From the Council of Nicaea (chapter 17).

[Col. 0489B]

[Col. 0489B] (Distinction 47, chapter “Since Many.”) Since many who are subject to the rule pursue avarice and shameful gain, forgetting the divine Scripture which says: “He has not given his money at interest” (Ps. XIV), they lend money and demand *centesimae* [one-hundredth interest]. Therefore the holy and great synod has justly decreed that, if anyone is found after this decree to be taking interest, or conducting business by some device or in any manner, or demanding *hemiolia*, that is, one-and-a-half-fold interest, or devising anything else whatsoever for the sake of shameful gain (I Cor. V), he shall be expelled from the clergy and excluded from the rule.

## CHAPTER 197.—Likewise on the Same Matter. From the Council of Tarragona, chapter 2 (under Hormisdas).

[Col. 0489C] (14, question 4, chapter “Of the Canons.”) Whoever wishes to be in the clergy shall not engage in buying cheaply and selling dearly. If he wishes to practise this, he shall be restrained from the clergy.

## CHAPTER 198.—Likewise on the Same Matter. From the Council of Agde, chapter 1 (canon 3, chapter 16).

(14, question 4, chapter “No One.”) Likewise it has been decided that if a cleric lends money, he shall receive money; if a commodity, he shall receive the same commodity, in the amount he gave.

## CHAPTER 199.—That Priests Shall Teach the Peoples Entrusted to Them to Abstain from Interest. From the Council of Orléans [Arles], chapter 36.

Priests shall not only themselves abstain from shameful gains and interest, but shall also teach the peoples subject to them to abstain.

## CHAPTER 200.—What Interest Is. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 13 (Council of Agde, chapter 16).

[Col. 0489D]

(14, question 3, chapter “Interest Is.”) Interest is where more is demanded than was given. For example: if you have given ten solidi and demand more, or if you have given one measure of grain and exact something additional.

## CHAPTER 201.—On the Same Matter. From the Decrees of Pope Julius Sent to Usurers, chapter 131.

(14, question 4, chapter “Whoever.”) Whoever at harvest-time or vintage, not from necessity but from greed, buys grain or wine—for example, buys one measure for two denarii and keeps it until it can be sold for four or six denarii, or more—this we call shameful gain.

## CHAPTER 202.—That the Nature of Profit Either Excuses or Condemns the Trader. From the Decrees of Pope Leo (Leo I, Letter 90, to Bishop Rusticus).

[Col. 0490A]

(*On Consecration*, distinction 45, chapter “The Nature.”) The nature of profit either excuses or condemns the trader, because there is honourable gain and shameful gain. Yet it is more beneficial for a penitent to suffer losses than to be bound by the dangers of trading, because it is difficult for sin not to intervene in commerce between buyer and seller.

## CHAPTER 203.—That No One of Ecclesiastical Order Shall Enter Taverns. From the Sayings of Augustine.

The statutes of the canons forbid anyone of ecclesiastical order to enter taverns for the sake of taking food or drink, unless compelled by the necessity of travel [variant: “have permission to enter”]. But if anyone violates these prohibitions, let him, as a contemner of the holy canons, be sternly [Col. 0490B] corrected by discipline.

## CHAPTER 204.—On the Same Matter. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 25 (Third Council of Carthage, chapter 27).

(Distinction 44, chapter “Clerics Eating.”) Clerics shall not enter taverns for eating or drinking, unless compelled by the necessity of travel.

## CHAPTER 205.—Likewise on the Same Matter. From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 24.

(Distinction 44, chapter “It Is Not Fitting.”) Those devoted to sacred ministry—from priests down to deacons and the remaining ecclesiastical order, that is, subdeacons, readers, singers, exorcists, doorkeepers, and those among the continent and monks—must not enter taverns.

## CHAPTER 206.—That Those without Permission to Marry Shall Avoid Wedding Feasts. From a Letter of Pope Leo.

[Col. 0490C] Those who have no permission to take wives should avoid the feasts of other people’s weddings.

## CHAPTER 207.—That a Priest Shall Not Attend the Marriage of a Bigamist. From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 7.

(13, question [unspecified], chapter “Concerning Those Who.”) It is not fitting for a priest to dine at the wedding of a bigamist; for, since a bigamist requires penance, what priest could, for the sake of a banquet, give assent to such a marriage?

## CHAPTER 208.—That Priests, Deacons, and Other Clerics Shall Avoid Wedding Feasts. From the Sayings of Augustine (First Council of Vannes, chapter 11, and Agde, chapter 39).

(Distinction 34, chapter “Priests.”) Priests, deacons, or [subdeacons, in the original] those thereafter for whom taking wives is not lawful, should avoid even the feasts of other people’s weddings. Nor should they mingle with gatherings [Col. 0490D] where love songs, shameful verses, or obscene bodily movements are displayed in choruses [variant: dances] and dancing, lest ears and eyes devoted to sacred mysteries [variant: ministries] be polluted by the contagion of shameful spectacles and words.

## CHAPTER 209.—On the Same Matter. From the Decrees of Pope Martin, chapter 1 (Braga, chapter 60).

Priests or clerics may not watch any spectacles at weddings or banquets; rather, before entering those spectacles, they must rise and depart [variant: withdraw] from there.

## CHAPTER 210.—That No Cleric Shall Be Received in Another City without Letters of Recommendation. From the Canons of the Apostles, chapter 13.

If any cleric or layperson hastens to another city and is received without letters of recommendation, both the receiver and the person received shall be deprived of communion. [Col. 0491A]

## CHAPTER 211.—On the Same Matter. From the Council of Antioch, chapter 7 (Antioch I, under Julius).

(Distinction 71, chapter “No One without.”) No traveller shall be received without letters of peace, that is, letters of recommendation.

## CHAPTER 212.—Likewise on the Same Matter. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 8.

The Council of Antioch, and likewise that of Chalcedon, commands that fugitive and travelling clerics be neither received nor ordained except with letters of recommendation and the permission of their own bishop or abbot.

## CHAPTER 213.—That Clerics Shall Not Remain in Another City unless Their Cases Have Been Examined by the Bishop. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 35 (Third Council of Carthage, chapter 37).

[Col. 0491B]

Clerics shall not stay in another city unless the bishop of the place, or the local priests, have examined the justice of their cases.

## CHAPTER 214.—That Clerics or Monks Shall Not Wander without Letters of Recommendation. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 36 (First Council of Vannes, chapter 5).

Clerics or monks shall not be permitted to wander without letters of recommendation.

## CHAPTER 215.—On the Same Matter. From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 7 (Council of Agde, chapter 38).

Clerics shall not be permitted to wander without letters of recommendation from their own bishop. The same form of decree shall also be observed with regard to monks.

## CHAPTER 216.—That Exiled Poor Persons Shall Be Assisted Only with Letters of Peace. From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 11 (session 15).

[Col. 0491C]

We have decreed that all poor persons and persons in need of assistance, when they travel, shall be commended only by attesting letters or ecclesiastical letters of peace, and not by letters of recommendation, since letters of recommendation ought to be granted only to persons of higher rank.

## CHAPTER 217.—When Clerics Ought to Use Formal Letters. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 2 (under Sergius II, chapter 51).

Whoever comes with his superiors from other provinces into another province [“into our parishes,” in the original] shall not be permitted to minister without a formal letter. If he brings one and is found fit to minister, he shall be instructed how religiously and diligently [Col. 0491D] to perform the sacred ministry, and in what places he ought [ought not, in the original] to perform it.

## CHAPTER 218.—That Clerics or Monks Shall Not Lease Estates or Involve Themselves in Secular Affairs. From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 3 (session 15).

(Distinction 86, chapter “It Has Come [to Our Notice].”) It has come to the holy synod that certain persons who appear to have been chosen for the clergy become lessees of others’ estates for the sake of shameful gain and undertake secular business under their own management, showing contempt for God’s ministry, running about the houses of secular persons, and, through avarice, assuming care for property. Therefore it has been decreed that neither cleric nor monk may lease estates or involve himself in secular affairs, [Col. 0492A] except in the administration of ecclesiastical property.

## CHAPTER 219.—That No Layman Shall Presume to Entangle a Priest in Estate Management. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 6 (chapter 50).

Likewise it must be commanded that no layperson presume to involve the priests of his churches in shameful estate management and, according to the Apostle, secular and dishonourable trade (II Tim. II), nor presume, contrary to authority, to take them elsewhere with him, so that they are forced to neglect the ministry entrusted to them. If anyone presumes to act contrary to these prohibitions, let him be excommunicated.

## CHAPTER 220.—On Priests Who, Contrary to the Statutes of the Canons, Become Estate Managers. From the Same Council, chapter 15 (Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 173).

Likewise, concerning those priests who, contrary to the statutes [Col. 0492B] of the canons, become estate managers, enter taverns, pursue shameful gain, and practise usury in many different ways; who improperly and shamelessly frequent other people’s houses, are not ashamed to devote themselves to feasting and drunkenness, and roam indiscriminately through different markets: we have judged that henceforth they should be strictly and severely restrained, lest through their unlawful and indecent conduct both the priestly ministry be reviled and those who ought to have been examples become a scandal [reproach, in the original].

## CHAPTER 221.—That Carnal Marriage Shall Not Be Permitted Even to Subdeacons. From a Letter of Pope Leo, chapter 34 (Leo I, Letter 84, chapter 4).

With respect to those who are established outside the clerical order, it is left to free choice to pursue the married state and the begetting of children [“free choice” is absent from the original]. Yet, for the display of the purity of perfect continence, even subdeacons are not permitted carnal marriage, so that those who have wives may be as though they had none, and those who have none may remain unmarried (1 Cor. 7). If this ought to be observed in this order, which is the fourth from the head, how much more must it be maintained in the first, second, and third, lest anyone be judged fit either for Levitical ministry [“Levitical ministry” in the original], for presbyteral honour, or for episcopal preeminence, who is found not yet to have restrained himself from marital pleasure.

### CHAPTER 222.—Concerning rulers who are accustomed to make priests their officials. From the Fifth Council of Toledo, chapter 30 (Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 30).

[Col. 0492D]

(23, q. 8, c. *Saepe principes*.) Rulers often entrust their affairs, against persons liable to a charge of lèse-majesté, to priests. Since priests have been chosen by Christ for the ministry of salvation, let them consent to act as judges for kings only where remission of punishment is promised under oath, not where a sentence involving peril is being prepared.
