Therefore, if any priest, contrary to this common decision, acts as an examiner in dangers affecting others, let him be guilty before Christ of blood shed, and let him lose his own rank before the Church.

### CHAPTER 223.—Concerning one who brings a petition to the ears of the ruler without the bishop’s consent. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 7.

Nicasius, bishop of Evarista, said: I believe [Col. 0493A] that an informer ought to be cast out, not only from communion but also from the rank in which he appears to share, if he has attempted to bring trouble to the ears of the venerable ruler contrary to the laws of the Church. Therefore, if a necessary case requires recourse against the ruler, let this be done with the deliberation and counsel of the metropolitan and of the other bishops residing in the same province; they are also to accompany the departing person with their letters.

(This chapter is found altogether differently in the original of the First Council of Carthage, chapter 6; in the Victorine manuscript and in Gratian, 21, question 3, chapter *Credo*, it reads as follows:)

Nicasius, bishop of Culusium, said: I believe that my proposal pleases Your Holiness, and that you disapprove of those who serve God and are attached to the clergy approaching the business, administration, or management [Col. 0493B] of households. Bishop Gratus said: There are also the ordinances of the apostles, who say: “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles [the original: “involves”] himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2). Therefore, let clerics be without household business, or household agents entirely without clerical office. All said: We observe this.

### CHAPTER 224.—Concerning a deposed presbyter, should he presume to perform ministry. From the Council of Toledo, chapter 6.

[Note: [Col. 0493D] In the Royal manuscript the order varies, but we have not departed from the Cologne manuscript. Jean Molin also varies in the Victorine manuscript.]

If any presbyter has been degraded by his bishop, or suspended from office for specified crimes, and through contempt and pride presumes to perform some act of the ministry forbidden him, and afterward, having been corrected by his bishop, persists in the presumption he began, he is in every respect to be excommunicated and expelled from the Church. And whoever communicates with him [Col. 0493C] is likewise to know that he is excommunicated. The same is to be observed concerning excommunicated clerics, laypersons, and women. But if anyone despises all these measures and the bishop cannot correct him, let him be condemned to exile by the judgment of the king.

### CHAPTER 225.—Concerning a condemned presbyter who has troubled the emperor’s ears. From the Council of Antioch, chapter 12 (Antioch I, under Julius I).

(21, q. 5, c. *Si quis a proprio*.) If a presbyter or deacon has been condemned by his own bishop, or perhaps a bishop by a synod, and has troubled the imperial ears, he ought to have recourse to a larger council of bishops. Let him lay before the greater number of bishops whatever he believes to be just, and await their investigations and judgments. But if, slighting these provisions, they trouble the emperor, we judge them worthy of no pardon, having no opportunity for satisfaction, and with no hope whatsoever of future restoration opened to them.

### CHAPTER 226.—Concerning a presbyter who by bad examples permits evil to be suspected of him. From the Council of Agde, chapter 4 (in the fragments, chapter 3).

If any presbyter, negligent in his life, permits evil to be suspected of him by bad examples, and the people, bound by the bishop under oath or by the ban of Christianity, disclose his ill repute, yet certain accusers of his crime are lacking, he is first to be admonished privately by the bishop, then before two or [Col. 0494A] three witnesses. If he does not amend, the bishop shall admonish him in an assembly of presbyters, with public rebuke. But if he does not correct himself even thus, let him be suspended from office until worthy satisfaction has been made, lest the body of the faithful suffer scandal because of him.

(2, q. 4, c. *Si legitimi*.) But if there are no lawful accusers who undertake to prove his crimes by manifest indications, and he denies them, then, if able, he is to clear himself of the charge with seven companions of the same order. If a deacon is accused of the same crime, he is to clear himself with three.

### CHAPTER 227.—How a dispute arising between a cleric and a layperson is to be concluded. From the Council of Tribur, chapter 21.

[Col. 0494B]

(2, q. 5, c. *Si quis presbyter*.) If a presbyter has a dispute of complaint against a layperson, or a layperson against a presbyter, it is to be settled at the bishop’s command without respect of persons. The layperson, if necessary, shall clear himself by oath. The presbyter, however, in place of an oath, is to be questioned by virtue of his holy consecration; for priests ought not to swear on a slight cause. For shall the hand through which the Body and Blood of Christ are consecrated be defiled by an oath? Far be it. Since the Lord says in the Gospel to his disciples—whose office we unworthy persons hold in the holy Church—“Do not swear at all. Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes’; ‘No, no’; but what is beyond these is from evil” (Matt. 5).

### CHAPTER 228.—That a cleric having a case against a cleric must not resort to secular courts. From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 9 (session 15).

[Col. 0494C]

(1, q. 1, c. *Si clericus*.) If any cleric has a case against a cleric, he must not abandon his bishop and run to secular courts. Rather, the case shall first be heard before his own bishop; or at least, by the counsel of that bishop, the parties may obtain judgment before whomever both parties choose. But anyone who acts contrary to these provisions shall be subject to canonical corrections.

### CHAPTER 229.—Concerning presbyters who are reported ill of by their congregations, and how they ought to clear themselves. From the Council of Lleida, chapter 10 (among the fragments).

(2, q. 4, c. *Presbyter si a plebe*.) If any presbyter has been charged with an evil reputation by the people entrusted to him [Col. 0494D] and the bishop cannot establish the matter by lawful witnesses, the presbyter shall be suspended [“from office” in the council] until worthy satisfaction has been made, lest the body of the faithful suffer scandal because of him. For worthy satisfaction consists in this: that, after security has been given concerning the charge brought against him, he is shown to be innocent to those by whom he is believed guilty. This is taught to have been established by us and by our predecessors.

But whether according to the canons or at the bishop’s discretion, let him join seven colleagues to himself and swear before the sacred Gospel placed before him that the holy Trinity, and Christ the Son of God who made him and taught him what the Gospel contains, and the holy four evangelists [Col. 0495A] who wrote it, may so help him as he did not commit the aforesaid act in the manner alleged against him. Having been cleared by this satisfaction, let him thereafter exercise his ministry without fear. Some of the preceding Fathers relate that holy Pope Leo made this very satisfaction in the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle, before the most reverend Emperor Charles and the clergy and people; and that immediately thereafter the venerable ruler exercised the vengeance of fitting punishment upon the adversaries of that holy pope.

### CHAPTER 230.—That no ordained person condemned by his bishop ought to be defended by anyone. From the African Council, chapter 29 (under Boniface and Celestine).

(21, q. 5, c. *Si quis cujuslibet*.) And this too is to be requested: that they may deem fit to decree that, if a cleric of any rank has been condemned by the judgment of a bishop for any crime whatsoever, it is not lawful for him to be defended either by the churches over which he presided or by any person whatever, with a penalty of loss of property and rank imposed; and they are to decree that neither age nor sex excuses anyone.

### CHAPTER 231.—Concerning a presbyter accused by the people. From an epistle of Pope Gregory (Gregory II, epistle 13, chapter 3).

(2, q. 4, c. *Presbyter*.) Concerning a presbyter or any [priest] among the clergy accused by the people: if there are no certain witnesses to state the truth of the charge brought, an oath shall be taken, and he shall produce as witness to the purity of his innocence Him to whom all things are naked and open; and thus let him remain in his own [Col. 0495C] rank.

### CHAPTER 232.—Concerning convicted and confessing clerics, if they disdain to conclude their case within a year. From the African Council, chapter 46 (and the Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter 12).

(11, q. 3, c. *Rursus*.) It has again been decreed that, whenever clerics convicted of and confessing to some crime, either out of regard for the modesty of those who are spared, or because of reproach to the Church, or the insolent exultation of heretics and pagans, should perhaps wish to appear for their own case and assert their innocence, they must do so within one year of excommunication. But if they disdain to clear their case within a year, no voice of theirs shall thereafter be heard at all.

### CHAPTER 233.—That no ordained person presume to swear to a layperson. From the Council of Reims, chapter 5.

(22, q. 5, c. *Nullus*.) Let no one of the ecclesiastical order swear anything to any layperson upon the most holy Gospels. Rather, simply, in truth and purity, let him say: “Yes, yes; no, no.” But if anything is alleged against them by laypersons, let it be referred to the bishop in whose territory it is; and according to what those of the same order decide, let the cleric either be corrected or cleared.

### CHAPTER 234.—Concerning a presbyter discovered in some criminal sin. From the Apostolic Canons, chapter 25.

(Distinction 81, c. *Presbyter*.) A presbyter [“A bishop or presbyter” in the original] or deacon caught in fornication, perjury, theft, or homicide is to be deposed, but not deprived of communion. For Scripture says: “The Lord does not judge [this word is absent in the original; Greek: *οὐκ ἐκδικήσει*, ‘will not take vengeance’], twice for the same thing” (Nahum 1, according to another wording among the Septuagint interpreters).

### CHAPTER 235.—Concerning ordained persons, if any of them should become assailants. From the Council of Agde, chapter 3.

If anyone consecrated in some ecclesiastical rank becomes an assailant, let him be rebuked most sharply. If he does not amend, let him be deposed.

### CHAPTER 236.—Concerning presbyters degraded through their own fault. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 60.

(Distinction 81, c. *Dictum est*.) It has been reported to us that presbyters, canonically degraded because of their own negligence, live in the secular state after loss of rank and neglect the good work of doing penance. Therefore we decree that, having lost their rank, they be sent for the purpose of performing penance to a monastery, whether canonical or regular. But if any cause prevents this from being done, wherever they are, let them not cease to do penance. If, however, having lost their rank, they wish to live secularly and neglect to do penance, let them be separated from communion with the Church.

### CHAPTER 237.—How those unjustly degraded are to be restored. From the same council, chapter 28 (Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 27).

(11, q. 3, c. *Episcopus presbyter*.) A bishop, presbyter, or deacon, if unjustly cast down from his rank and found innocent at a second synod, cannot become what he was unless he receives the lost insignia of rank before the altar from the hand of bishops. If he is a bishop: the stole, ring, and staff; if a presbyter: the stole and chasuble; if a deacon: the stole and alb; if a subdeacon: the paten and chalice. So too the remaining ranks, in their restoration, are to receive the things which they had received when they were ordained.

### CHAPTER 238.—Concerning clerics who despise their own bishop. From the Council of Antioch, chapter 5 (under Julius I).

If any presbyter or deacon, despising his own bishop, separates himself from the Church, gathers separately, sets up an altar, and does not submit to the bishop’s warning, nor consent or wish to obey when summoned once and again, he is to be condemned altogether and receive no further remedy, because he cannot recover his rank. But if [Col. 0496D] he persists in disturbing and agitating the Church, let him be suppressed [“punished”] as a seditious person by external authorities.

### CHAPTER 239.—Concerning a presbyter who has made a schism against his bishop. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 11 (another version: Second Council of Carthage, chapter 8).

(11, q. 3, c. *Si quis presbyter*.) It was said by all the bishops: If any presbyter has been excommunicated or corrected by his bishop, he certainly ought to complain before neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard by them and through them he may be reconciled to his bishop. But if he does not do this, and, puffed up with pride—God forbid!—has determined to separate himself from communion with his bishop; and, making a schism separately with some persons, has offered sacrifice to God: let him be held anathematized [Col. 0497A] and lose his position. If he has no just complaint against his bishop, this is to be investigated.

### CHAPTER 240.—Concerning those who bring a false criminal charge against one of the ordained. From the same council, chapter 5 (attached to the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 3).

(2, q. 3, c. *Si quis episcopum*.) If anyone brings false charges against a bishop, presbyter, or deacon and cannot prove them, communion is to be given him only at the end [of life].

### CHAPTER 241.—That no cleric accuse another except in writing. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 10.

Moreover, this is to be observed by every ecclesiastical order without exception: no one may presume in a council or synodal assembly to assail any brother with an accusation unless he has first set down in writing, in due order and in his own hand [variant: “subscribed”], the crime charged and the grounds of litigation, and has presented it to the bishop or holy synod, so that the controversies of litigants may be concluded justly and canonically. For, as Roman authority testifies, no one may be made an accused person or brought to judgment except after a formal written accusation; since, just as punishment binds a person convicted of crime, so it binds the accuser if he does not prove what he alleged.

### CHAPTER 242.—That no member of the clergy become a hired manager for private persons. From the same council, chapter 14 (Third Council of Carthage, chapter 15).

(2, q. 3, c. *Placuit ut*.) Likewise it has been decreed that bishops, presbyters, deacons, and clerics are not to be hired agents [Col. 0497C] or managers for private persons, nor seek their living by any base or dishonourable business, because they ought to keep in view what is written: “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2).

### CHAPTER 243.—That one is not to be regarded as a cleric if, while living in a city, he does not come to the daily sacrifice. From the First Council of Toledo, chapter 5.

A presbyter, deacon, subdeacon, or any cleric assigned to the Church, if he is within a city, a place where there is a church, a fortified town, village, or estate, and does not come to the church for the daily sacrifice, is not to be regarded as a cleric if, after correction, he does not amend.

### CHAPTER 244.—On the same matter. From the Council of Vannes, chapter 5 (First Council of Vannes, chapter 14).

A cleric who dwells within the city walls and, on a day [“and on that day”], is absent from the morning hymns without illness shall be excluded from communion for seven days; for at a time when no necessity of honourable business can occupy a minister of sacred things away from his office, it is not lawful for him to refrain from what brings salvation.

### CHAPTER 245.—That all priests must be instructed, so that they may instruct others and advance themselves. From an epistle of Pope Anacletus sent to all the faithful, chapter 10 (epistle 2, chapter 1).

Therefore all who exercise the Lord’s priesthood ought to be taught, both that they may instruct others and that they may advance themselves. For it is written: “Those who are learned shall shine like the brightness of the firmament; and those who instruct many unto righteousness, like stars for everlasting eternities” (Dan. 12). And elsewhere: “The people who know their Lord shall prevail and act, and the learned among the people shall teach many” (Dan. 11). Truth itself indeed declares this and says: “Blessed is he who is not scandalized in me” (Matt. 11; Luke 7). Without doubt, he is scandalized in God who does not teach what is right [variant: “rightly”], and who scandalizes his bishop or priest.

### CHAPTER 246.—That presbyters render an annual account to the bishop of their ministry. From the Council of Mainz held by Richeulf [Riculf], archbishop of that see, chapter 10.

Every presbyter shall each year render an account of his ministry to his bishop, both concerning the Catholic faith and concerning baptism and every order of his ministry.

### CHAPTER 247.—That every presbyter oblige those subject to him to learn the faith. From the Council of Gangra, chapter 5 (First Council of Mainz, chapter 45).

[Col. 0498B]

Let priests always exhort the Christian people to learn the Creed, which is the seal of faith, and the Lord’s Prayer. We further wish those who neglect to learn these to undergo fitting discipline, whether by fasting or another correction. Therefore it is fitting that they take their children to school, monastery, or outside to the presbyters, so that they may properly learn the Catholic faith and the Lord’s Prayer and be able to teach others at home. But those unable to do otherwise should learn these in their own language.

### CHAPTER 248.—What profession presbyters or deacons ought to make to their bishop. From the Council of Toledo, chapter 27 (Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 6).

[Col. 0498C]

(Distinction 28, c. *Quando presbyt.*) When presbyters or deacons are appointed to parishes, they ought to make a profession to their bishop that they will live chastely and piously, in the fear of God, so that, bound by such a profession, they may maintain the discipline of a holy life.

### CHAPTER 249.—That monks or laypersons, however learned, must not dare to preach. From an epistle of Pope Leo (epistle 63 to Theodoret).

Concerning those unlawful measures which, in the oft-mentioned council, were presumptuously attempted against the venerable Nicene canons, we have written to our brother and fellow bishop, the bishop of the see of Antioch, adding also this point (6, q. 1, c. *Adjicimus*), which you communicated to us orally through our representatives because of the misconduct of certain monks of your region [variant: “religious order”]; and we decree this in particular: apart from the Lord’s priests, no one may dare to preach, whether monk or layperson, even if he boasts in the name of learning of whatever kind.

### CHAPTER 250.—That clerics learn the canons from their bishops. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 6 (Fourth Council of Orléans, chapter 6).

Let parish clerics receive from their bishops the necessary canonical enactments to be read, lest either they themselves [variant: “lest the matter itself, etc.”] or the people afterward excuse themselves by claiming ignorance of the measures decreed for their salvation.

### CHAPTER 251.—That no priest may be permitted to be ignorant of the canons. From an epistle of Pope Celestine, chapter 20 (Celestine I, epistle 3, section 1).

(Distinction 38, c. *Nulli sacerdotum*.) Celestine to all bishops established throughout Apulia and Calabria. No priest may be permitted to be ignorant of his canons, or to do anything that may conflict with the rules of the Fathers. For what matter will be duly observed by us if the standard of decrees and enactments is broken at the whim of certain persons by liberty allowed to the people?

### CHAPTER 252.—That presbyters, when they come to an assembly, must by no means presume to become drunk. From the Council of Nantes, chapter 10.

(Distinction 44, c. *Nullus presbyterorum*.) Let none of the presbyters, when they have gathered at the thirtieth, seventh, or third anniversary day of any deceased person, or at any summons to an assembly of presbyters, presume in any way to become drunk; nor, when asked in the name of the saints or of the person’s own soul, drink or compel others to drink, or gorge himself at another’s request [Col. 0499B]; nor presume there to recite or sing unrestrained applause, laughter, or empty tales, or to allow shameful jokes, a bear, or female performers to be made [variant: “to take place”] before him. Nor may he consent for demonic masks to be carried before him, because this is diabolical and forbidden by the sacred canons.

### CHAPTER 253.—How religiously presbyters ought to conduct themselves at a banquet. From the same council, chapter 11.

(Distinction 44, c. *Quando veniunt*.) When presbyters gather at some banquet, the first among them shall begin a verse before the table and bless the food; then they shall sit according to rank, showing honour one to another. In turn they shall bless food and drink, and one of their clerics shall read something from Holy Scripture. After the meal they shall likewise sing a holy hymn, following the Lord’s example, as he is read to have done at supper (Matt. 26; Mark 14). Thus may all presbyters restrain themselves, especially in such places, so that their ministry may not be reproached.

### CHAPTER 254.—On the same matter. From the same council, chapter 12.

Let every presbyter be especially careful, if he wishes to rejoice in his standing, not on any occasion to provoke or incite his father or any other person by any word to anger and strife, much less to fighting or slaughter; nor, if provoked, let anyone rush into these things, because in such feasts and drinking-bouts the devil always mingles himself.

### CHAPTER 255.—Likewise on the same matter. From the same council, chapter 15.

[Col. 0499D]

(Distinction 44, c. *Quando presbyteri*.) When presbyters meet together on the Kalends, after the divine ministry [variant: “mystery”] has been performed, for the necessary conference, let them not sit down at tables there as though for a full meal, almost as for lunch, lest by such dishonourable banquets they burden one another; for this is unseemly and burdensome. Often, moreover, returning late to church, they incur greater loss through reproach—because they contract mutual heaviness [variant: “truth”]—than profit there. For Paul reproved the Corinthians for gathering to eat the Lord’s Supper in an improper manner (1 Cor. 2). Likewise, those who gather for the Lord’s Supper, that is, for a conference on the word, under a pretext and join together because of the belly’s gluttony [variant: “truth”], are held blameworthy before God and human beings. Therefore, when all has been concluded, those who wish may break bread in charity in their brother’s house together with their brethren, and let each make the others drink, especially so that they do not take the cup more than a third time; and thus let them return to their churches.

### CHAPTER 256.—That neither clerics nor religious laypersons enter banquets before the third hour. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 12.

Clerics or religious laypersons ought not to enter banquets before the sacred third hour of the day; nor should clerics ever take bread except after a hymn has been said in church, and after food they should give thanks to God their creator.

### CHAPTER 257.—That presbyters be hospitable. From the Council of Nantes, chapter 3.

[Col. 0500B]

Let a presbyter care for guests, especially the poor and infirm, as well as orphans and pilgrims; according to his means, let him invite them daily to his meal and provide them lodging.

### CHAPTER 258.—On the same matter. From the same council, chapter 5.

But, to remove every occasion for extortion, we wish presbyters, who ought to show everyone a good example of charity, to be hospitable in accordance with the Lord’s and apostolic command, extending kindness to travellers, because some have pleased God through hospitality, having received angels as guests [Col. 0500C] (Heb. 13). And on the day of judgment the Lord will say to the elect: “I was a stranger and you received me” (Matt. 25). And Job says: “My door was always open to the traveller” (Job 31).

### CHAPTER 259.—On the same matter. From the council at Clermont (attached to this council).

It has been decreed that presbyters admonish their congregations to be hospitable and deny lodging to no traveller. And, in order that every occasion of extortion be removed, let them sell nothing to travellers at a higher price than [variant: “at whatever price”] they could sell it in the market. But if they wish to sell at a higher price, travellers shall report this to the presbyter, and by his order goods shall be sold to them humanely.

### CHAPTER 260.—That divine reading always be joined to priests’ meals. From the African Council, chapter 7 (Third Council of Toledo, chapter 7).

[Col. 0500D]

(Distinction 44, c. *Pro reverentia*.) Out of reverence for God and priests, the whole holy synod decrees this: because idle tales are often introduced at table, reading from the divine Scriptures shall be joined to every priestly banquet. For by this means souls are built up toward the good, and the recounting of tales [“unnecessary” in the original] is prohibited.

### CHAPTER 261.—Concerning clerics singing among feasts. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 62.

(22, q. 1, c. *Clericum*.) Clerics who sing during feasts are to be removed from office.

### CHAPTER 262.—Concerning buffoonish clerics. From the same council, chapter 80 (placed after the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 4).

(Distinction 46, c. *Clericum*.) If any cleric or monk speaks buffoonish, jocular, or laughter-provoking words, let him be rebuked most sharply.

### CHAPTER 263.—On the same matter. From Carthage, chapter 60.

Buffoonish clerics and those who make sport with obscene words are to be removed from office.

### CHAPTER 264.—That a cleric not be a surety. From the same council, chapter 70.

(From the Apostolic Canons, chapter 20.) A cleric serving as a surety is to be cast out.

### CHAPTER 265.—That a cleric not grow his hair or beard. From the same council, chapter 44.

A cleric is to grow neither hair nor beard.

### CHAPTER 266.—That a cleric not swear by a creature. From the same council, chapter 71.

(22, q. 1, c. *Clericum*.) A cleric swearing by a creature is to be rebuked most sharply; if he persists in [Col. 0501B] the fault, he is to be excommunicated.

### CHAPTER 267.—Concerning flattering clerics. From the same council, chapter 56.

(Distinction 46, c. *Clericus qui adulationibus*.) A cleric found occupied with flatteries and betrayals is to be degraded from office.

### CHAPTER 268.—That no member of the clergy bring a complaint to the emperor without the bishop’s consent. From the Council of Antioch, chapter 11.

(23, q. 8, c. *Si quis episcopus*.) If any bishop, presbyter, or person subject to the Church’s rule goes to the emperor without the counsel and letters of the bishops of the province, and especially of the metropolitan, he must be disapproved and cast out not only from communion but also from the rank in which he appears to share, because he has attempted to bring trouble to the ears of the venerable ruler contrary to the laws of the Church. Therefore, if a necessary case requires approaching the ruler, let this be done with the deliberation and counsel of the metropolitan and of the other bishops residing in the same province, who are also to accompany the departing person with their letters.

### CHAPTER 269.—That no member of the clergy make a complaint in synod except in writing. From the council held at Saint-Médard, chapter 8 (Soissons under Leo IV, beginning, chapter 269).

Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, said to his accusers: “What is your petition, brothers?”

They replied: “We ask that mercy be extended to us by your fatherhood concerning the administration of ecclesiastical orders, to which we were formerly promoted by Lord Ebbo and from which we have been suspended by your authority.”

Archbishop Hincmar said: “Do you have a written bill of complaint or petition, as ecclesiastical tradition requires?”

They answered that they had no written bill in hand.

Archbishop Hincmar said: “The custom and authority of ecclesiastical laws require writing in cases involving official acts, to such an extent that one who approaches the sacred font is commanded to give his name, and one promoted to the highest priesthood is elected by a decree confirmed by the hands of all. An ordained person is commanded to receive letters from his ordainers. Likewise, one who is separated from ecclesiastical fellowship for any offence is received or cast out by a written declaration. But [Col. 0502A] one who is accused, or one who has been excommunicated and is received or reconciled, is commanded to be accused or reconciled in writing. Thus, in other such matters, writing is required to such a degree that, as blessed Gregory writes in the memorandum to John the defender, drawing from Roman laws (*Register*, book 2, epistle 54, at the end; *Code*, book 7, title 44): ‘A judgment pronounced without a written document [variant: “in writing”] does not deserve even to bear the name of judgment.’ Therefore, brothers and sons, you must, in accordance with ecclesiastical authority, set forth your complaint in the sequence of a written petition, confirm it with your hands, and present it to the holy synod, so that an appropriate and canonical answer may be given you.”

Then the brethren wrote a petition, subscribed their names to it, and presented it [Col. 0502B] to Archbishop Hincmar, who was then presiding over the synod in the presence of the glorious King Charles together with Wenilo, archbishop of Sens [variant: “Muclo of Sens”], and Amalric, likewise archbishop of Tours [variant: “Almaric”].

### CHAPTER 270.—That presbyters not leave their parishes and migrate to others except for definite reasons. From the Council of Chalon, chapter 41.

A presbyter who leaves his own place and migrates to another is by no means to be received unless he states the reason for his migration and proves under witnesses that he has lived innocently in the parish where he was ordained. He shall also have letters in which the names of the bishop and city are impressed in lead. Once these have been examined and found to be such that trust may be placed in them, he shall be received.

### CHAPTER 271.—That accusers of clerics, if unable to prove one of the charges, are not to be admitted on the rest. From the African Council, chapter 7 (African Council 97, and Carthage 7, chapter 3).

(3, q. 10, c. *Placuit*.) Likewise it has been decreed that whenever accusers bring many charges against clerics, and cannot prove one of those first pursued, they shall not be admitted on the others.

### CHAPTER 272.—How bishops or presbyters ought to clear themselves of an imputed crime. From the Council of Worms, chapter 8 (under Adrian II, chapter 10).

(2, q. 4, c. *Si episcopo*.) If a criminal charge—that is, homicide, adultery, theft, or sorcery—has been imputed to a bishop or presbyter, for each charge he must celebrate Mass [variant: “perform the Mass”], say the secret prayer publicly, communicate, and show himself innocent of each imputation [Col. 0502D] made against him. If he does not do so, let him be excluded from the thresholds of the church for five years.

### CHAPTER 273.—That clerics not be bound by judgments of other judges. From the decrees of Pope Adrian, chapter 38 (among the eighty canons of Adrian I to Ingelram).

In a cleric’s case this rule shall be observed: he is not to be bound by a judgment not rendered by his own judge.

### CHAPTER 274.—That one publicly punished by beatings be assigned to exile if he unjustly charges another with a crime which he cannot prove. From Gregory’s Register to Anthimus, subdeacon of Campania, chapter 201 (book 9, epistle 66).

Since crimes inflicted upon innocent members of sacred orders especially deserve to be punished more severely, consider, all of you who sat in the case of John the deacon, how no punishment arising from your decision chastised Hilary [variant: “Hilarus”], his accuser. Nor should you think it a sufficient excuse that, although you wished to judge, our brother and fellow bishop Paschasius alone is said to have delayed you. For if zeal for justice had flourished in you, it could more easily and reasonably have been urged upon one person by many than many could have been delayed without cause by one. Therefore, because so great an evil of wickedness ought not to pass without fitting punishment, we wish our aforesaid brother Paschasius to be admonished first to deprive that Hilary of the office of subdeacon, which he unworthily exercises, and then, having had him publicly punished with beatings, to have him deported into exile, so that the punishment of one may be the correction of many.

### CHAPTER 275.—That ecclesiastics should not desire to hold secular powers. From an epistle of Gregory addressed to Secundinus the recluse.

For it is certain that you do not appoint anyone as leader over an army unless his labour and loyalty please you, and unless the virtue and diligence of his previous life show him fit for the post. But if command of an army is entrusted only to men of this sort, from comparison with this good matter one may infer what kind of leader of souls he ought to be. Yet it is shameful for us to say, and embarrassing, that priests seize military command who have not seen the beginning of religious warfare.

### CHAPTER 276.—That one who cannot prove his charge receive the penalty of the accused. From the Council of Braga, chapter 8 (Second Council of Braga, chapter 8).

[Col. 0503C]

(2, q. 5, c. *Placuit*.) It has been decreed that if anyone accuses a cleric of fornication, two or three witnesses are required from him according to the command of the Apostle Paul (1 Tim. 5). But if he cannot establish by the witnesses produced what he has alleged, let the accuser receive the accusation [variant, original: “excommunication”] of the accused.

### CHAPTER 277.—That, just as laypersons do not admit clerics in their own secular accusations, so neither are they to be admitted in accusations against clerics. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 5.

All the bishops in the third session acclaimed: “Indeed, it is fitting that, just as laymen do not admit priests or clerics in their accusations or in secular courts [Col. 0503D], so they likewise should not be admitted in accusations against priests or clerics, or in ecclesiastical affairs, unless this is voluntarily approved. For it is unfitting that those who reject these should be admitted by them.”

### CHAP. 278.—That no one is to admit the testimony of a layman against clerics. From the Council of Tribur, chap. 4.

(11, q. 1, c. *Testimonium*.) Let no one accept the testimony of a layman against a cleric.

### CHAP. 279.—On the preaching of presbyters. From the same council, at which King Arnulf was present.

We command you that each one of you, every two or three weeks, on Sundays or saints’ feast days, should endeavor to instruct in the church entrusted to him the people committed to him, after the Gospel has been read, with saving teachings drawn from sacred Scripture; and that he should order them not to leave the church before the final praise has been pronounced by the presbyter or deacon—that is, “Let us bless the Lord” (*Benedicamus Domino*) or “Go, the dismissal is made” (*Ite missa est*).

### CHAP. 280.—By how many witnesses ordained persons ought to be examined if they have been accused. From the Council of Carthage, chap. 20 (Council of Carthage III, chap. 2).

(15, q. 7, c. *Si autem presbyteri*.) If any presbyters or deacons have been accused, their own bishop, with the lawful number of fellow bishops from neighboring places whom the accused have requested—namely, six together with him in the case of a presbyter, three in that of a deacon—shall examine their cases, observing between the accusers and those accused the same procedure concerning days, adjournments, exclusions from communion, and examination of persons [Col. 0504B]. But the bishop of the place, even alone, shall hear and conclude the cases of the remaining clerics.

### CHAP. 281.—To whom the property of a deceased priest belongs. From the Council of Tribur, chap. 23, at which King Arnulf was present.

It has been brought before the holy council that certain laymen behave improperly toward their presbyters, so as to claim shares for themselves from the property of dying presbyters, as though from their own slaves. Therefore, by canonical authority, we forbid this to be done further; rather, just as they were made free in order to receive rank and perform the divine office, so nothing is to be exacted from them except the divine office. But let them claim nothing for themselves from the priests’ personal property; rather, let the whole be divided [Col. 0504C] into four parts: one for the bishop, another for the altar, a third for the poor, and a fourth for relatives. If the relatives are not suitable, let the bishop receive that share and distribute it carefully for the use of the Church. And if anyone presumes to act against this, let him be anathematized.

### CHAP. 282.—On clerics who died without a will. From the same council, chap. 14.

If anyone of ecclesiastical rank dies without a will and without making his wishes known, his inheritance shall pass to the Church in which he served. The same applies to religious women.

### CHAP. 283.—On clerics who wear lay clothing. From the same council, chap. 27.

Clerics are not to use lay clothing, that is, a mantle or tunic, or a cape; nor costly and unsuitable footwear [Col. 0504D], nor other vanities of novelty. Rather, clothed in a religious and becoming habit, let them go about.

### CHAP. 284.—On the same matter. From the Council of Carthage, chap. 44 (Council of Carthage IV, chap. 45).

(Dist. 42, c. *Clericus*.) A cleric should demonstrate his profession even by his dress and bearing; therefore he is to seek elegance neither in garments nor in footwear.

### CHAP. 285.—On clerics who stroll idly through markets. From the same council, chap. 48 (ibid.).

A cleric who strolls through a market [“who does not go there to buy something,” in the original] or forum for some gain is to be deposed from his office.

### CHAP. 286.—That no one of the clergy is to bear military weapons. From the Council of Meaux, chap. 18 (under Sergius II, chap. 37).

[Col. 0505A] (23, q. 8, c. *Quicunque*.) Whoever are counted among the clergy are not to take up military weapons or go about armed; rather, let them display the title of their profession through religious morals and religious dress. If they disregard this, as contemners of the sacred canons and profaners of ecclesiastical holiness, let them be punished by loss of their own rank, because they cannot serve both God and the world at once.

### CHAP. 287.—On the same matter. From the Council of Orléans, chap. 9.

Presbyters and deacons must by all means be told not to carry weapons, but rather to trust in God’s protection than in weapons.

### CHAP. 288.—That ecclesiastical persons are not to have dogs or hawks. From the Council of Meaux, chap. 8.

(Dist. 34, c. *Episcopum, presbyterum*.) It is not permitted for a bishop [Col. 0505B], presbyter, or deacon to have hunting dogs, hawks, or things of that sort. If anyone of such persons is repeatedly found indulging this desire, then, if he is a bishop, let him be suspended from communion for three months; a presbyter, for two months; but a deacon, from every office and from communion.

### CHAP. 289.—On the same matter. From the Council of Orléans, chap. 3.

(Dist. 34, c. *Omnibus servis*.) We forbid all servants of God hunting, wandering in the woods with dogs, and keeping hawks or falcons.

### CHAP. 290.—That a bishop should reconcile discordant clerics by his authority. From the African Council, chap. 59 (Council of Carthage IV, chap. 59).

[Col. 0505C] (Dist. 90, c. *Discordantes*.) A bishop shall draw discordant clerics to concord either by reason or by authority; the synod shall condemn the disobedient after a hearing.

### CHAP. 291.—On clerics who break out into mutual violence. From the Council of Lleida, chap. 6 (Council of Lleida, chap. 11).

If any clerics break out into mutual violence, let the bishop punish them more strictly in proportion as the dignity of their offices has suffered disgrace in such an offense.

### CHAP. 292.—On the same matter. From the same source, chap. 7 (among the fragments).

If a brother dares to lay a hand upon a brother, let him receive lawful discipline.

### CHAP. 293.—That seven deacons are sufficient in each Church. From the letter of Pope Fabian, chap. 2 (Letter 1, at the beginning).

[Col. 0505D]

Accordingly, there are seven deacons in the city of Rome, corresponding to the seven regions of the city, as we have received from the Fathers. Each week, on Sundays and on the solemnities of feasts, together with subdeacons, acolytes, and ministers of the succeeding orders, they are to observe the ministries entrusted to them; they are to be ready at every hour for the divine office and to carry out whatever is laid upon them. Likewise, according to what is expedient, this is to be done by you in every city, so that the divine office may be performed diligently and solemnly without any delay or negligence.

### CHAP. 294.—On the same matter. From the Council of Neocaesarea, chap. 14.

(Dist. 93, c. *Diaconi septem*.) There ought to be seven deacons [Col. 0506A], according to the rule, even if the city is very large. The book of the Acts of the Apostles likewise indicates this (Acts 6).

### CHAP. 295.—Again, on the same matter. From the Council of Bishops assembled at Ancyra and Caesarea, chap. 9.

There ought to be seven deacons according to the rule, however large the city may be; the Book of the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 6) is the authority for this rule.

### CHAP. 296.—That deacons are not to sit in the presence of presbyters. From the Council of Laodicea, chap. 20 (and the Council of Agde, chap. 65).

(Dist. 93, c. *Non oportet*.) A deacon ought not to sit in the presence of a presbyter, but is to sit by the presbyter’s command. Likewise, honor is to be shown to deacons by those subject to them—that is, subdeacons [Col. 0506B] and all clerics.

### CHAP. 297.—That deacons are not to place themselves before presbyters. From the Council of Toledo, chap. 30 (Council of Toledo IV, chap. 38).

(Dist. 93, c. *Nonnulli diaconi*.) Some deacons break out into such pride that they set themselves before presbyters and presume to stand first in the first choir, while presbyters are placed in the second choir. Therefore, so that they may acknowledge presbyters as superior to themselves, both the former and the latter are to stand in both choirs.

### CHAP. 298.—That exorcists are to lay hands upon the possessed. From the Council of Carthage, chap. 20 (Council of Carthage IV, chap. 90).

(*De consecratione*, dist. 5, c. *Omni die*.) Every day exorcists are to lay hands upon the possessed.

### CHAP. 299.—On the honor due to all orders. From the decrees of St. Pope Sylvester, chap. 4.

[Col. 0506C]

Thus, brothers, divine authority commands and affirms that from the subdeacon down to the reader all are subject to the deacon, representing only the honor due to the cardinal of the city of Rome in the Church. But presbyter, deacon, subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, reader, abbot, and monk are to render obedience to the pontiff in every place, whether in public or within the bosom of the Church.

### CHAP. 300.—On priests who do not know how to fulfill their ministry and do not wish to learn. From the Council of Orléans, chap. 6.

Priests who do not rightly understand how to fulfill their ministry, who do not strive according to their ability to learn in accordance with their bishops’ commands, and who prove contemners of the canons, are to be removed from their own office [Col. 0506D] until they have fully corrected these matters.

### CHAP. 301.—That persons found under the discipline of no bishop are not to be reckoned clerics. From the Council of Paris, chap. 10.

(Dist. 93, c. *Nulla ratione*.) Clerics or priests who are governed under the discipline and supervision of no bishop are in no respect to be regarded as such. The ancient custom of the Church has called such persons *acephali*, that is, “headless.”

### CHAP. 302.—That clerics made free by their masters should honor and serve them canonically. From the Council held at Altheim [Alteum], chap. 38.

No cleric is to be promoted to the rank of presbyter except as is written in the canons: if, for the love of God, anyone chooses one from among his slaves [Col. 0507A], teaches him letters, grants him freedom, and through intercession with the bishop makes him a presbyter; and if that man thereafter, puffed up with pride, refuses to celebrate Mass for his masters, to observe and chant the canonical hours, and to obey them justly, saying that he is free and unwilling to be subject, but acting as though he were a free man able to become the man of whomever he wishes—this holy synod anathematizes him and judges that he is to be barred from holy communion until he comes to his senses and obeys his master in accordance with the canonical precepts. But if with an obstinate mind he also despises these provisions, let him be accused before the bishop who ordained him, deposed, and made the slave of that person—namely, his master—as he had been by birth. And whoever keeps such a man with himself after learning of the aforesaid matter concerning him, and neither returns him to his master nor casts him out from himself [Col. 0507B]—whether bishop, count, cleric, or layman—being bound in fellowship with his anathema, shall suffer the penalty of excommunication.

### CHAP. 303.—On those who conceal a brother’s flight. From the sayings of Basil.

If anyone learns that a person who cannot bear ecclesiastical discipline is planning flight, and does not immediately report him, let him have no doubt that he shares in that betrayal; and he is to be separated from the assembly of the brethren until that person can be brought back.

### CHAP. 304.—On those who mistreat their presbyters. From the Council at Clermont, chap. 7.

If anyone dishonors his own presbyter, or inflicts an insult by word or deed, let him be kept from the thresholds of the church until, by worthy penitence [Col. 0507C], he makes satisfaction. For the Apostle says: “Let the presbyters who rule well be considered worthy of double honor” (1 Tim. 5). Likewise elsewhere he says: “Obey your leaders and be subject to them” (Heb. 13). And so forth.

### CHAP. 305.—That the name of the pope is to be recited in holy churches. From the Second Council of Vaison, chap. 4 (First Council of Vaison, chap. 2).

And this seemed right to us: that in your churches the name of the lord pope, whoever presides over the Apostolic See, should be recited [“our churches” in the original].

### CHAP. 306.—That presbyters and deacons living in rural districts should celebrate the chief feasts in cities. From the Council of Clermont, chap. 14.

If any presbyter or deacon who is known not to be a canon in a city, but who lives in rural districts and serves in sacred office in oratories, celebrates [Col. 0507D] the divine mysteries, we admonish him henceforth not to celebrate the principal feasts—the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, Pentecost, and any other chief feasts—anywhere except with his bishop in the city. Likewise, all lay citizens of mature age are to come to their bishops in the cities on the said feasts and there solemnly hear the divine mysteries. If any, in wicked rashness, despise these provisions, let them be excluded from communion.

### CHAP. 307.—That presbyters should be granted authority to preach among their own congregations. From the Second Council of Vaison, chap. 2 (more correctly, Council III, chap. 2).

This also seemed good to us, for the edification of all the Churches and for the benefit of the whole people: that we should grant presbyters the authority to preach not [Col. 0508A] only in cities but also in all parishes, so that, if a presbyter is prevented by some infirmity from preaching himself, the homilies of the holy Fathers may be recited by approved deacons [*probatis*, “approved,” absent from the original].

### CHAP. 308.—On clerics killed in a brawl. From the Council of Tribur, chap. 50, at which King Arnulf was present.

(23, q. 8, c. *Quicunque clericus*.) Any cleric who dies in war, in a brawl, or in the games of the pagans is not to have an offering requested for him, but is to fall into the hands of the judge. He is not, however, to be deprived of burial.

### CHAP. 309.—On presbyters accused of a capital crime who cannot clear themselves. From the same council, chap. 6 (appended to the Council of Clermont).

[Col. 0508B]

Concerning presbyters accused of the crime of fornication or some capital offense, who do not have colleagues with whom they can clear themselves [or, “purge themselves”], or, if they have perhaps fallen, how they may make satisfaction: in their judgment one must turn neither to the right nor to the left, but walk in the straight path. For in chapter one of the Council of Neocaesarea it is written: “If a presbyter takes a wife, let him be deposed from his order; but if he has committed fornication or adultery, he must be expelled further and reduced to penitence.”

### CHAP. 310.—That truthful and God-fearing men should be appointed in cities and villages. From the Council of Rouen, chap. 9.

[Col. 0508C] Let the people be admonished that on Sundays and feast days all are without exception to attend Vespers, the night vigils, and Mass; and that truthful and God-fearing men be appointed as deans in cities and public villages, to admonish the idle and negligent to hasten without excuse to God’s service. These deans themselves are to be bound by oath not, through any motive of affection, fear, kinship, or gift, to conceal negligent persons and transgressors, but to reveal their particular faults to the priests. It will be the duty of the priests, with divine zeal and love and with due discipline, to correct their vices, just as they themselves do not wish to receive the sentence of just condemnation for the errors of others. And feast days are to be celebrated from evening until evening, without servile work [Col. 0508D], with due honor.

### CHAP. 311.—That no cleric should readily be enrolled in two churches. Seventh Synod, chap. 15.

From this time onward, a cleric is not to be enrolled in two churches. For this is characteristic of commerce and shameful profit, and wholly foreign to ecclesiastical custom. For we have heard from the Lord’s own voice that “no one can serve two masters: for he will either hate one and love the other, or hold to one and despise the other” (Luke 16). For each person, according to the apostolic word, ought to remain in the condition in which he was called (1 Cor. 7), and be assigned to one Church. Things done in ecclesiastical affairs for shameful gain are alien from God; but occupations for the necessities of this life are different. From these, therefore, let anyone who wishes obtain what his body needs [Col. 0509A]. For the Apostle says: “These hands have supplied what was necessary for me and for those who were with me” (Acts 20). These provisions, indeed, are to be observed in this city; but in outlying villages an indulgence is allowed because of the scarcity of people.

### CHAP. 312.—That accusers are not to be admitted before examination. Anacletus, in his third decretal (Evaristus, Letter 2, before the middle).

(2, q. 7, c. *Si qui sunt vituperatores*.) If there are detractors or accusers of bishops or of other priests, they ought not to be heard by the judges of the Church before the suspicion or repute of their standing has been examined: with what intention, faith, rashness, manner of life, conscience [Col. 0509B], and merit they have made these accusations; whether for God, or vain glory, enmity, hatred, or greed—or not.

### CHAP. 313.—That clerics are not to be accused by laymen. Pope Telesphorus, in his first decretal to all bishops (chap. 1).

Just as secular laymen do not wish to admit clerics in their accusations and denunciations, so clerics ought not to admit them in their own complaints, because the life and manner of living of clerics and secular laymen must always be distinct and separate in all things.

### CHAP. 314.—That the common people are not to be admitted in accusations against priests. A little later in the same decretal (chap. 2).

(6, q. 1, c. *Sacerdotes*.) Priests who by their own mouth consecrate [Col. 0509C] the body of the Lord are to be obeyed [perhaps *obaudiendi*, “heeded”] and feared by all, not torn to pieces or disparaged. For the Lord’s people, who desire to be blessed, saved, and instructed by them, ought in no way to accuse them, nor should the common people be admitted to accuse them. For the people are to be taught and corrected by them, not they by the people, because “a disciple is not above his master” (Matt. 20). (A little later.) Therefore he accuses God’s ordinance who accuses or wishes to condemn the priests whom God appoints.

### CHAP. 315.—That an accuser who accuses one absent is not to be believed. In the same place, a little later (chap. 4).

We also exclude accusers and accusations which the laws of the world do not admit, and we decree that an accuser is never to be believed when he brings a charge against an absent adversary before the just examination of both parties [Col. 0509D]. Nor are those who are unfit to be admitted to an accusation to be received; and we judge all who take up arms against the Fathers—that is, priests [“that is, priests” absent from the original]—to be infamous. For all Fathers, that is, priests, are to be revered, not rejected, accused, or plotted against.

### CHAP. 316.—Only final judgments concerning clerics are to be referred to the Apostolic See. Pope Eleutherus, twelfth successor after Peter, in his first decretal to the Churches of Gaul (chap. 2 of his letter).

Therefore, concerning the accusations of clerics about which we have been consulted: because it is difficult for all their accusations to be referred to the Apostolic See, only final judgments concerning bishops are to be referred here, so that they may be concluded by the authority of this holy See [Col. 0510A], as has already been determined with the agreement of many bishops by the apostles and their successors. Nor are others to be placed over or ordained in their churches until their affairs have been justly concluded here. (3, q. 6, c. *Quamvis*.) For although it is permissible to investigate their accusations or charges before provincial bishops, metropolitans, and primates, it is not permissible to decide them otherwise than as has been stated. But the cases of the remaining clerics may be investigated and justly concluded before provincial bishops, metropolitans, and primates. The judge, however, ought to investigate everything and examine the sequence of events through full inquiry, allowing patience for questioning, presentation, and addition, so that there the action of both parties may be fully delimited.

### CHAP. 317.—That judgment is not to be given until both sides have spoken fully. In the same place (following).

[Col. 0510B]

Nor should a judge wish to forestall the disputants by his own sentence before, all matters having been completed, they have nothing further to advance in the case; and the action is to be examined until the truth of the matter is reached. He ought to question frequently, lest something that should be added perhaps remain omitted. (3, q. 3, *Induciae non modicae*.) For no small adjournments must be granted for inquiry, lest anything appear to have been done too hastily by either side, because many things occur through surprise or fraud. (2, q. 1, c. *Nihil contra*.) Nevertheless, nothing is to be done without a lawful and suitable accuser. For our Lord Jesus Christ knew Judas to be a thief; but because he was not accused [Col. 0510C], he was not expelled; and whatever he did among the apostles remained valid because of the dignity of his ministry. For if secular laws require accusers, how much more do ecclesiastical rules? For earthly and human matters teach what ecclesiastical and heavenly matters are.

### CHAP. 318.—Actions against defendants are to be pursued within the province. In the same place (chap. 3, and in Letter 1 of Felix I).

(3, q. 6, c. *Si quis clericus*.) Concerning accusers from the same province, it is thus decreed: if anyone believes that a cleric should be charged with any crimes whatever, let him pursue his action in the province in which the defendant resides, and not suppose that he may be drawn elsewhere or farther away before judges. But if the person charged considers the judge suspect, he may appeal.

### CHAP. 319.—That no judgment is to be given concerning one absent. Likewise (from Council of Carthage IV, chap. 30).

[Col. 0510D]

(3, q. 9, c. *Caveant judices*.) Let the judges of the Church also beware of pronouncing sentence while the person whose case is being examined is absent; for it will be void, indeed they themselves will have to answer before the synod for what they have done. But neither the calumny nor the voice of a betrayer is to be heard. For no one can know a debtor more fully than the person who has suffered his injury and wickedness.

### CHAP. 320.—That laymen ought not to accuse clerics. Fabian, in his second decretal to the eastern bishops (chap. 2).

(2, q. 7, c. *Sicut sacerdotes*.) Just as priests and the other clerics are excluded from accusations by secular persons, so those persons are to be excluded and kept apart from charges brought by the former [Col. 0511A]. And just as these are not admitted by them, so they are not to be admitted by these; for, as the manner of life of the Lord’s priests ought to be separate from their manner of life, so also ought their litigation to be separate, because a servant of God ought not to quarrel (2 Tim. 2). A little later. We have set this forth so that those to whom it is unknown may recognize that priests, whom the Lord chose for himself from among all people and wished to be his own, are not to be lightly treated, torn to pieces, rashly accused, or reproved, except by their masters; for the Lord wished to reserve their cases to himself and to have them judged [variant: “vindicated”] by his own judgment.

### CHAP. 321.—On the order of a case and the number of persons. Likewise (ibid., not far from the end).

(4, q. 4, c. *Nullus unquam*.) No accuser should ever presume to be at once accuser, judge, and witness, since four persons must always be present in every judgment: appointed judges, accusers, defenders, and witnesses. Likewise, establishing this by apostolic authority, we command that the sheep committed to their pastor should not dare rebuke him unless he has erred in faith; because the deeds of superiors are not to be struck with the sword of the mouth, and a disciple cannot be above his master (Matt. 10).

### CHAP. 322.—Likewise, that authority is not to be opposed. In the same place.

(11, q. 3, c. *Qui omnip.*) Whoever fears almighty God does not in any way consent to act contrary to the Gospel, the apostles, the prophets, or the institutions of the holy Fathers.

### CHAP. 323.—Where defendants ought to answer, and where they need not. The same, in his third decretal to Bishop Hilary, chap. 3.

[Col. 0511C]

(q. 6, c. *Pulsatus*.) Let the defendant state his case before his own judge; before a judge who is not his own, the defendant may remain silent if he wishes. And whenever defendants appeal, adjournments are to be granted them.

### CHAP. 324.—That insults are not to be treated as accusations. The same (ibid., a little later).

(2, q. 3, c. *De poeniten.*, dist. 1, c. *Si quis iratus*.) If anyone in anger rashly imputes any crime to another, the insult is not to be treated as an accusation. Rather, after time has been allowed for consideration, he must declare in writing that he will prove what he said in anger; so that if, having perhaps come to his senses, he is unwilling to repeat or put in writing what he said through anger, he is not to be held guilty of the crime [Col. 0511D]. (3, q. 6, c. *Qui crimen*.) Therefore, everyone who imputes a crime must put in writing that he will prove it. The case must in truth always be heard where the crime was committed. And whoever fails to prove what he alleged must suffer in himself the penalty which he sought to inflict.

### CHAP. 325.—On a foreign jurisdiction. Pope Cornelius, in his second decretal to Bishop Rufus (chap. 2).

No priest is to commit his case to a foreign jurisdiction unless an appeal has been made to the Apostolic See; rather, each is to have provincial judges known to him, unless there has arisen there some violence of a reckless multitude, or he has there hostile or suspect judges. For these reasons it is permitted to appeal and go to judges of greater authority and to other provinces [Col. 0512A]. (3, q. 9, c. *Omnia quae*.) Therefore, everything done or judged against absent persons, in any affair or place whatsoever, is utterly void; for no one condemns an absent person, and no law pronounces sentence upon one.

### CHAP. 326.—That those who allege crimes ought to accuse in person. Pope Lucius, twenty-first after Peter, in his first decretal to all bishops of Gaul and Spain (chap. 2).

(2, q. 7, c. *Criminationes*.) It has been decreed that accusations against those of greater rank are not to be brought through others, but only by those who allege the crimes, provided that they themselves appear worthy and blameless and demonstrate by public records that they are free from every suspicion and enmity, and lead a blameless life and manner of conduct [Col. 0512B]. (2, q. 6, c. *Placuit ut*.) Therefore it has been decreed that, if an appeal is made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges of greater authority, a hearing is not to be denied.

### CHAP. 327.—What accusations ought not to be received. Pope Stephen I, in his second decretal (chap. 3).

(3, q. 5, c. *Accusatores*.) We exclude accusers and accusations whom the laws of the world do not admit and whom our predecessors also forbade. For no foreigner is to be either their accuser or judge. Likewise. (The same above, chap. 315.) Let those dwelling with enemies be rejected, and all laymen, because a disposition toward enmity is wont to provoke the assault of slander. Nor are those to be admitted in your accusation who do not wish to admit you in their own denunciation. (3, q. 4, c. *Nullus anathem.*) No one is to admit or believe persons who have been anathematized, whether in what they say or write [Col. 0512C]. By “anathematized” I mean those whom bishops have anathematized in writing, or whom their decrees anathematize.

### CHAP. 328.—That no one is to be accused in writing. The same (chap. 4).

(2, q. 8, c. *Per scripta*.) No accusation against anyone is to be received in writing, but by the accuser’s own voice, if the person of the accuser is lawful and worthy, and with the person whom he wishes to accuse present; for no one who is absent can either be accused or accuse.

### CHAP. 329.—On uncertain judgments. Pope Felix I, fifteenth after Peter, in his first decretal to his fellow bishop Paternus.

(The same is given above, chap. 318.) In a doubtful matter, no certain sentence is to be judged; nor is any judgment to be held valid unless it has been conducted in due order [Col. 0512D]. If anyone believes that a cleric should be charged with any crimes whatever, let him pursue [variant: “exercise”] his action in the province in which the defendant resides, and let the accuser not suppose that he may be drawn elsewhere or farther away for judgment.

### CHAP. 330.—On the appeal of one who considers the judges suspect. The same (immediately following).

But if the person charged considers the judges suspect, he may appeal to the primates.

### CHAP. 331.—Again on the same matter, and on what accusations are not to be received. The same, in his second decretal to the bishops of Gaul.

(3, q. 7, c. *Infamis*.) A person of bad repute can be neither advocate nor representative. (3, q. 9, [Col. 0513A] c. *Absente*.) When the adversary is absent, the accuser is not to be heard, nor will a sentence pronounced by a judge when the other party is absent possess any force. Nor may an absent person accuse or be accused through another, and no relative is to be admitted as a witness. Therefore no one ought to be summoned from province to province, or to a comital court, except upon referral by the judge to whom an appeal has been made; that is, the plaintiff must always follow the defendant’s forum. But if anyone perceives a judge to be hostile to him, let him make an appeal, which must be denied to no one. (3, q. 6, c. *Peregrina*.) We forbid foreign jurisdictions by general enactment, because it is unworthy that one who ought to have fellow provincials and judges chosen by himself should be judged by outsiders.

### CHAP. 332.—On the procedure of accusation and the bond of formal registration. Pope Eutychianus to the bishops throughout Sicily (Letter 2, chap. 2).

[Col. 0513B]

We have learned, and command to be observed, the following procedure of accusation: if any cleric is charged with a crime, he is not at once to be considered guilty merely because he could be accused, lest we make innocence suspect. (2, q. 8, c. *Quisquis*.) Rather, whoever he may be who alleges a crime must come before the court, identify the defendant by name, undertake the bond of formal registration, preserve equality [of liability], yet obtain due regard for rank. Let him know that he has no license to lie, since equality of punishment calls for vengeance upon false accusers. [The printed reading *nec fore* is uncertain; the original has *patiatur, ne forte*.]

### CHAP. 333.—Who are not to be admitted to make an accusation. The same (following).

[Col. 0513C] All heretics, suspects, and excommunicated persons, as well as murderers and evildoers, thieves, sacrilegious persons, robbers, poisoners, adulterers, those who have committed abduction, borne false witness, or consulted diviners and magicians [the original reads *concurrerint*, “have resorted”], are in no way to be admitted to accusation. No infamous or sacrilegious person may ever, in any matter, give testimony against a religious Christian, even if that Christian is a humble person or slave, nor bring a Christian to charge on any ground or by any formal accusation.

### CHAP. 334.—Under how many witnesses an accusation against each rank ought to be made. From the synodal acts of Pope Sylvester.

[Col. 0513D] A cardinal presbyter is not to be condemned except on the testimony of forty-four witnesses. A cardinal deacon appointed in the city of Rome is not to be condemned except on that of thirty-six. A subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, reader, or doorkeeper is not to be condemned except, as written, on that of seven witnesses. Witnesses and accusers must be free from every infamy, have wives and children, and wholly fear [variant: “preach”] Christ. Let no one receive the testimony of a cleric against a layman. No one may presume publicly to examine any cleric except in church. No cleric, deacon, or presbyter may enter a court for any cause or presume to state a case before a girded judge, because every court is so called from bloodshed and the sacrifice of images. [Col. 0514A] And if any cleric accusing a cleric enters a court, let him incur anathema.

### CHAP. 335.—On requesting adjournments. Pope Felix, in his first decretal to Anastasius and the Egyptians, chap. 14 (Felix II, Letter 1, chap. 8).

When anyone comes to trial, if he wishes and if it is necessary, the adjournments established by the Fathers are to be granted without impediment when he requests them; and judges chosen by himself are to be allowed, so that, in the place from which the accused person comes—or, if there he fears some violence from a reckless multitude, in a suitable place chosen by him—he may, if necessity requires, have his witnesses without fear and may conclude his canonical case without impediment, since many things are wont to occur through surprise or fraud.

### CHAP. 336.—On the difference between an ecclesiastical and a secular case. The same, chap. 17 (Pope Eutychianus, Letter 2, to the bishops throughout Sicily).

[Col. 0514B]

(2, q. 6, c. *Non ita*.) Ecclesiastical affairs are not to be conducted as secular affairs are. For in secular affairs, after someone summoned by law has appeared and has begun to litigate in court, he may not withdraw before the case is concluded. But in ecclesiastical affairs, after the case has been stated, he may withdraw if necessary or if he sees that he is being overburdened.

### CHAP. 337.—On not confusing the persons in a case. From the decretal letter of Pope Damasus to Stephen, Archbishop of Mauretania (Letter 4, chap. 7).

(4, q. 4, c. *Nullus introducatur*.) No one is to be introduced personally [into the case]; rather, accusers and accused are to be heard on equal terms, as the order of the proceedings requires [Col. 0514C]. Accusers and judges are not to be the same persons, but accusers by themselves, judges by themselves, witnesses by themselves, and accused persons by themselves, each in his own proper order. For formal registration must always be made first, so that the false accuser may receive retaliation, because before formal registration no one ought to be judged or condemned, since even secular laws preserve these same rules.

### CHAP. 338.—On Bishop Maximus. From the letter of Pope Boniface to the bishops of Gaul, chap. 15 (Boniface I, Letter 2).

(3, q. 9, c. *Decernimus*.) Boniface to the bishops of Gaul. We have decreed that the judgment must take place within your province, and that a synod be assembled before the Kalends of November, so that Maximus, if he wishes to appear and is confident, may answer the accusations in person. But if he neglects to appear, let him not gain a postponement of judgment by his absence. For it is evident that one accused of a crime confesses it when, though judgment has been granted and assigned to him so many times, he does not avail himself of the opportunity to clear himself.

CAP. 339.—On rejecting intimate enemies. Pope Leo to Bishop Anatolius (Letter 76).

(24, q. 3, c. *Illud sane*.) I declare that this especially displeases me: that among the clerics under your authority [the clerics of your jurisdiction] there are said to be some who associate with [wink at] the perversity of adversaries, and that vessels of mercy are mixed with vessels of madness [wrath]. Your diligence must watchfully devote itself to investigating and restraining these persons with appropriate severity, so that excision does not spare those whom correction has been unable to benefit. For we must remember the evangelical command by which Truth itself orders that, if an eye, a foot, or a right hand causes us to stumble, it be removed from the body’s frame, because it is better to lack these members in the Church [world] than to go with them into eternal punishments (Matt. XVIII). For we resist those placed outside the Church to no purpose if we are wounded, through those who are within, in the persons whom they deceive. This pestilential forbearance, which by sparing the sins of others does not spare itself, must altogether be cast away from priestly firmness.

CAP. 340.—A bishop who has been accused is not to be abandoned by his own people before the end of the case. In the fifth synod of Pope Symmachus (from the book of Ennodius, in the Fourth Synod).

(8, q. 4, c. *Nonne directa*.) Are not the words of the canons explicit: whoever among the clergy departs from his bishop before the time of sentence on account of doubtful suspicion remains subject to manifest censure?

CAP. 341.—On the same matter, in the same source (immediately following).

Ecclesiastical law requires that a pontiff accused by others not be abandoned before the charges brought against him have been established in the light.

CAP. 342.—On the deposition of one who had usurped another’s archdeaconry. Gregory to Natalis, bishop of Salona (Book II, indiction 10, Letters 14 and 16).

(7, q. 1, c. *Eum qui contra*.) We depose from the honor of that archdeaconry the man who consented to be promoted, contrary to the rule of justice, to another man’s archdeaconry. If thereafter he presumes to minister in the same place, let him know that he is deprived of participation in sacred communion.

CAP. 343.—That unjust judgments have no force. Gregory to John, defender, c. 40 (Book XI, c. 50, or Letter 52).

[Col. 0515C]

(2, q. 1, c. *In primis*.) The assertion of a certain brother—that he was accused on false counts, that nothing was done in due order, and that he was unjustly condemned—must be carefully investigated. First, whether the judgment was held in due order; whether the accusers and witnesses were different persons; then, the character of the charges: whether it was worthy of exile or deposition; whether testimony against him was given under oath in his presence; whether the proceedings were put in writing; and whether he himself had leave to answer and defend himself. The persons of the accusers and witnesses must also be carefully investigated: what their status and reputation are; whether they are indigent; whether perhaps they bore any enmities against the aforesaid pastor; whether they gave testimony from hearsay or testified that they knew the matter personally; whether judgment was rendered in writing; and whether the sentence was read out in the presence of the parties. If these matters were not solemnly performed, and if no charge was proved that deserved exile or deposition, he is to be restored to his Church by every means.

CAP. 344.—That the individual offices of the Church are to be assigned to individual persons. Gregory to all bishops (in John the Deacon, *Life of Blessed Gregory*, no. 54).

(Dist. 89, c. *Singula ecclesiastici*.) We order that each office of ecclesiastical law be entrusted separately to each individual person. For we judge that the offices of two functions are not to be entrusted at one time to one person, however experienced. For if the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? (I Cor. XII). For just as the diversity of members, through their different functions, preserves the body’s strength and displays its beauty, so likewise the diversity of persons, through offices distributed among them, manifests both the strength and the beauty of God’s holy Church. And just as it is unbecoming for one member of the human body to perform another member’s office, so it is plainly harmful and at the same time most disgraceful if the individual ministries of affairs are not distributed among an equal number of persons.

CAP. 345.—Where ecclesiastical matters ought to be conducted. From the First Epistle of Clement (after the beginning).

(11, q. 1, c. *Si qui ex fratribus*.) If any of the brethren have disputes among themselves, they are not to be judged before secular adjudicators; rather, whatever the matter may be, it is to be settled before the priests of the Church, and they are to obey their determinations in every respect.

CAP. 346.—On the abominable crime of conspiracy. Calixtus in the second letter (chapter 1).

(11, q. 1, c. *Conspirationum*.) We have heard that the crimes of conspiracies flourish in your regions, and we have been informed that peoples are conspiring against their bishops. The cunning of this crime is abominable not only among Christians but even among pagans, and is prohibited by foreign laws. Therefore those guilty of this crime are condemned not only by ecclesiastical laws but also by secular laws—and not only those who conspire, but also those who consent to them. Our predecessors, with a very large assembly of bishops, decreed that all such persons who hold priestly rank or are clerics should lose the rank which they enjoy; they ordered the rest to be deprived of communion and made outcasts from the Church; and they judged all men of both orders alike to be infamous—not only those who commit these acts, but also those who consent to them.

(23, q. 3, c. *Justum est*.) For it is just that those who despise the divine commands and are disobedient to the injunctions of the Fathers should be corrected by sterner punishments, so that others may fear to commit such acts, God may rejoice in fraternity and concord, and all may receive an example of severity and goodness. For if—God forbid—we neglect ecclesiastical care and firmness, negligence destroys discipline and the souls of the faithful will surely be harmed.

(3, q. 4, c. *Conspiratores*.) Such persons are not to be admitted as accusers of anyone; nor can the voice either of them or of those under anathema harm or accuse anyone.

CAP. 347.—On the manner of accusing. Damasus in the second letter (Letter 4, chapter 8).

(3, q. 9, c. *Habetur*.) It is also contained in the decrees of the Fathers that it has been established that it is not canonical for any priest to be judged or condemned before he has present accusers canonically examined and receives an opportunity for defence—that is, ecclesiastical delays for clearing away the charges and other matters. Nor is the first accusation in an inquiry to be made outside his own province without apostolic authorization, to which reverence must be maintained in all cases; for the ancient rule of the Fathers also teaches this, and imperial enactments agree with it.

CAP. 348.—On the same matter. The same, in the last letter (Letter 7, to the bishops of Italy).

(3, q. 9, c. *Qui accusare*.) Whoever chooses to accuse another must make the accusation in person and not through another, after first filing the formal written accusation. Nor is anyone ever to be judged before he has legitimate accusers present and receives an opportunity to defend himself for the clearing away of the charges.

CAP. 349.—That municipal councillors are not to be promoted to the clergy. Innocent to Victricius, archbishop of Rouen (Letter 2, chapter 11).

(Dist. 51, c. *Praeterea frequenter*.) Moreover, certain of your brethren often endeavor to make clerics of municipal councillors, or of persons occupied in any public functions. Afterwards, when the emperor orders something concerning their recall, greater distress arises than the favor arising from their admission.
