For it is established that in those duties [“mimes,” *mimis*] they provide entertainments which there is no doubt were invented by the devil, and either preside over, or perhaps take part in, the apparatus of games or the troupe [“of mimes,” *mimorum*]. Indeed, as an example, consider the concern and distress of the brethren which we have often borne, in the emperor’s presence, when we repeatedly petitioned on behalf of such persons—as you yourself learned while he was with us—against whom great pressure was being applied for their return: not only lower clerics drawn from the municipal councillors, but even persons already established in the priesthood.

CAP. 350.—That what necessity has devised as a remedy must certainly cease when the necessity ceases. The same to Rufus and Eusebius, bishops of Macedonia (Letter 22, chapter 5).

[Col. 0547C]

(1, q. 7, c. *Quod pro remedio*.) The highest deliberation of the bishops was that those ordained by Bonosus should be received, lest they remain with him and lest no small scandal arise. We have overcome the ambiguities, I think.

(1, q. 1, c. *Quod pro necessitate*.) Therefore, what was established as a remedy and because of the necessity of the time clearly did not exist at first; and the old rules, handed down by the apostles or by apostolic men, which the Roman Church keeps and commands to be kept by those accustomed to heed her, did exist. But the necessity of the time urgently demanded that this be done. Therefore, what necessity has devised as a remedy must certainly cease together with the pressure that required it when the necessity ceases; for one thing is the lawful order, another an expedient usurpation to which the present time impels us. Yet the canons established at Nicaea permitted this to be done in the case of the Novatians. First, the canon instituted by the Fathers must be set forth, so that we may observe what, or in what manner, was intended or commanded by them.

(Canon 8, Synod of Nicaea.) “Concerning those who call themselves Cathari, that is, ‘the Pure,’ and who at some time come to the catholic Church, the holy and great synod has determined that, after receiving the laying on of hands, they are to remain in the clergy.” We may, however, say that this was commanded concerning the Novatians alone and does not extend to clerics of other heresies. For if they had so determined concerning all, they would have added that those returning from the Novatians and other heretics ought to be received in their own rank. That this is not so may be especially confirmed by what was said concerning the Paulianists, from whom those who come are commanded also to be baptized. When they give this order concerning the Paulianists, are all who return from heretics to be baptized by that precedent? Since no one would dare do this, reason itself shows that the command applies only to them.

CAP. 351.—On those who render void a vow of virginity. The same (Council of Ancyra under Sylvester, chapter 18).

(27, q. 1, c. *Quotquot*.) All who promise virginity and render their promise void are to be reckoned among the twice-married.

CAP. 352.—On those baptized abroad. From the Council of Elvira, chapter 24.

[Col. 0518B]

(Dist. 98, c. *Omnes qui*.) All who have been baptized abroad, because their manner of life is entirely unknown, are not to be promoted to the clergy in foreign provinces.

CAP. 353.—On slaves ordained without their masters’ consent. Gelasius to Martyrius and Justus, bishops.

The agents of the illustrious man, our son Amandianus, complain grievously that persons subject to his legal right have been ordained—some still as clerics, others already as deacons—although it is established, not only under the present enactment, which the collected authority of so many pontiffs, with the agreement of all, has perfected as a most salutary provision, that persons of this kind ought not to be admitted, but also that, if any were perhaps previously admitted through ignorance into the service of the divine warfare, they ought altogether to be removed and, stripped of the religious privilege, compelled by just admonition to return to their masters’ possessions.

Therefore, dearest brethren, investigate the persons whom the agents of the aforesaid man show to be held in clerical office; and, once their liability has been examined and proved, restore them without delay, observing the course of the laws. If anyone is already found to be a presbyter, let him remain in that rank, suffering only the loss of his peculium. But a deacon is either to provide a substitute or, if he has none, to be returned. Let the holders of the remaining offices know that no one who is proved liable can be vindicated from his condition of dependence, so that, with proper order preserved, neither the rights of masters nor ecclesiastical privileges may be disturbed on any pretext.

CAP. 354.—On the same matter. Gelasius to Herculentus, Stephen, and Justus, bishops.

For recently the agents of the illustrious woman Placidia, by a formal petition, complained that Sabinus, bishop of the city of Marcelliana or Cusilina, had taken advantage of the absence of their mistress, his patroness, and advanced Antiochus, a slave belonging by right to that patroness, as far as the honor of the priesthood; and had adorned Antiochus’ brother Leontius with the privilege of clerical office. Therefore, dearest brethren, by our authority we entrust to you the examination of the allegation between the aforesaid agents and those claimed as persons of servile condition. After the full truth has been investigated, if Leontius cannot genuinely remove the stain of injustice alleged against him by a reasoned defence, restore by every means the cleric Leontius—whom the rank already assigned does not protect under the laws—to the obligation of his condition. But Antiochus, since he can no longer be reduced from the priesthood, if he wishes to retain him in his Church in the honor which he now holds, is not to regard him as restored to himself, but is to have him as one admitted for the celebration of the ministries.

CAP. 355.—On the reverence to be shown to those ordained earlier. Pope Nicholas to Emperor Michael (Letter 8, before the middle).

(Dist. 21, c. *Denique*.) Finally, if it is read in the Epistle to the Hebrews that the lesser is blessed by the greater (Heb. VII), it follows surely that, when reason requires it, he is also cursed by the greater. Indeed, foreknowing dangerous times, those who came before us handed down a provident custom in the Churches, one which is still observed without omission in the Roman Church, which is the teacher of all Churches: no priest is to attempt to bless anything whatever while his superior fellow-priest is present. Likewise, one who stands first to pronounce a reading asks for a blessing, but no inferior dares to bless him. Why is this? Is blessing a sin? Far from it! For the Apostle speaks of those who curse, not those who bless, when he says: “They shall not possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI). But by this it is indicated by what a curb of discipline all inferiors must be restrained from judging their superiors, if they do not possess even the right of blessing them.

CAP. 356.—On a boy clothed in the monastic cowl without his own consent. Pope Nicholas I to all bishops in the kingdom of Louis (in the rescripts of Nicholas I, title 13, chapter 2).

(20, q. 3, c. *Praesens clericus*.) A cleric named Lambert, together with his father Atho—formerly a count, but now a cleric—came hastening to the thresholds of the Apostles and appeared before us. He asserted that his father, while still in lay dress [“order,” *ordine*, in the original], had built monasteries on his own estates with the intention that, after his death, this son Lambert should succeed him in his place. While Lambert was still of tender age, between eight and eleven years old, the aforesaid father, by his own decision and without regular institution, clothed him in the cowl entirely against Lambert’s will.

Then, after a certain period of time, as he says, Bishop Salomon, together with some others, made the same Lambert put on that monastic habit, without an offering by his father or a blessing received from an abbot, as is reported, against his will. Under this pretext he was deprived by his brothers of his paternal and maternal inheritance, and, contrary to all his will, as has been said, his father wished him to remain as if he were a regular monk. We investigated this affair with diligent care and, under adjuration, asked his father whether he spoke the truth. But the cleric Atho replied that he had had, and still had, the desire that his son should be a true monk and should succeed him in his place. Yet he affirmed under sworn testimony that, when he first put the cowl on him, Lambert always resisted and never consented to become a monk; but that he was eventually clothed by those pursuing him in the monastic habit by force. Atho asserted that Lambert had never at any time promised the Rule, nor had he, Lambert’s father, offered him wrapped in the altar-cloth [alternatively, “clothed in the altar-cloth”], nor had Lambert ever, after receiving the blessing from any priest or abbot as custom requires, been made subject to the Rule as a monk [alternatively, “promised to become a monk subject to the Rule”].

The aforesaid cleric Atho also declared concerning all these matters that, if at that time he had understood the monastic Rule to be one of such severe observance, he would never have compelled his son Lambert to wear the cowl. Therefore, recalling the apt words of the Psalmist, by which he declares that he will sacrifice willingly to God (Ps. LIII), and prays that the free offerings of his mouth may be pleasing in God’s sight (Ps. CXVIII), we have judged that the present cleric Lambert, as stated, ought by no means to be made a monk under such coercion. For what a person has not chosen and does not desire, he certainly does not love; and what he does not love, he easily despises. For no good exists unless it is voluntary. Thus the Lord also commanded that no staff be carried on the journey (Matt. X), a staff by which violence might be inflicted upon someone. It is therefore wiser to kindle people toward that heavenly love by preaching, with devout persuasion, contempt of the world and love of God, rather than by inflicting violence.

Accordingly, we have decreed to send this letter of our apostolate to the charity of all of you, warning and commanding that, if what these men say is true, no bishop, abbot, or assembly of the remaining monks is to compel Lambert, against his will, to be subject to monastic rules. Nor are his brothers, on this pretext, to have any permission—God forbid—to deprive him of his paternal or maternal inheritance. Rather, until, touched by divine inspiration, he submits himself to the rules of his own will, he may, removed from worldly and lay wanderings or business, be permitted to live the canonical life among religious and ecclesiastical men. For we do not think—God forbid—that religious canons are separated from the life and fellowship of holy monks, since each person, according to the Apostle, will receive his own reward according to his labor (I Cor. VIII).

CAP. 357.—That a cleric excommunicated by his own bishop is not to be received by another bishop. From the Council of Sardica, chapter 16.

Bishop Hosius said: If this also pleases everyone, namely, that if a deacon, presbyter, or any cleric is deprived of communion by his own bishop and goes to another bishop, and the bishop to whom he has fled knows that he was rejected by his own bishop, that bishop ought not grant him communion. If he does so, let him know that, when the bishops have been assembled, he will have to state his case. All said: This decree will preserve peace and safeguard concord.

CAP. 358.—That clerics should be subject to their bishops. From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 8 (session 15).

(18, q. 2, c. *Quidam monach.*) Clerics appointed in parishes [“poorhouses,” *ptochiis*, in the original], monasteries, or shrines of martyrs are to be subject to the authority of the bishop in whose city they are, according to the tradition of the holy Fathers; nor are they presumptuously to withdraw from their bishop. Those, however, who dare in any manner to abolish such an institution, or refuse to be subject to their own bishop, if they are clerics by reason of their ordination, are to be subject to the condemnations of the canons.

CAP. 359.—On the same matter. From the same source (in the same place, but from another translation).

Clerics who preside over the administration of the poor, monasteries, or shrines of martyrs are to remain under the authority of the bishops of their respective cities, according to the tradition of the holy canons; nor are they through their own rashness to decline their bishop’s governance. But those who dare in any manner to subvert such administration and do not obey their own bishop, if they are clerics, are to be subject to canonical condemnation; but if they are monks or laypersons, they are to be suspended from communion.

CAP. 360.—That clerics ought not, bypassing their bishop, resort to secular courts. From the same council, chapter 9.

(11, q. 1, c. *Si clericus*.) If a cleric has a dispute against another cleric, he is not to forsake his own bishop and resort to secular courts. Rather, the case is first to be heard before his own bishop; or indeed, if the case concerns the judgment of that bishop himself, it is to be heard before arbitrators chosen by each side. But if anyone acts contrary to this, he will be subject to canonical corrections. If a cleric has a case against his own bishop or another bishop, he is to lodge his complaint before the hearing of the provincial synod. But if a bishop or cleric has a dispute against the metropolitan bishop of that province, he is to go to the primate of that diocese, or else to the see of the imperial city of Constantinople, so that his own case may there be investigated.

CAP. 361.—That clerics are by no means permitted to move to another city, except because of persecution. From the same council, chapter 20.

It is not lawful for clerics appointed in individual Churches, as we have already decreed, to be ordained in the Churches of another city; rather, they are to remain content in the Church in which they were first found worthy to minister—except those who have lost their own cities and have migrated by necessity to other Churches. But if any bishop, after this definition, receives a cleric belonging to another bishop, the holy synod has decreed that both the bishop who receives him and the cleric who is received are to remain excommunicated until that cleric returns to his own Church.

CAP. 362.—That clerics are not to appeal to public courts. From the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 9.

(11, q. 1, c. *Placuit*.) Concerning those who serve in the various orders of the Church: if anyone incurs a criminal charge and refuses ecclesiastical judgment, he must suffer the consequences; likewise, the sons of priests are not to attend secular spectacles. It has also been decreed that any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or cleric against whom a criminal charge is brought in the Church, or against whom a civil case is initiated, if he abandons ecclesiastical judgment and wishes to clear himself in public courts, is to lose his office even if a sentence is rendered in his favor. This applies in a criminal action [“judgment,” *judicio*, in the original]; in a civil case, however, he is to lose what he won if he preferred [“wished,” *voluerit*, in the original] to retain his office.

CAP. 363.—What is to be done if an appeal is made from ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges. From the same source, chapter 10.

(2, q. 6, c. *Placuit*.) It has likewise been decreed that when an appeal is made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges, where there is greater authority, this should not prejudice those whose sentence has been annulled, if they cannot be convicted of judging with hostile intent or of being corrupted by some greed or favor.

(2, q. 6, c. *Sane*.) But if judges have been chosen by agreement of the parties, no appeal is permitted, even though their number is smaller than that prescribed.

CAP. 364.—Who are not to be admitted to give testimony. From the Seventh Council of Carthage, chapter 4.

(2, q. 2, c. *Testes autem*.) Witnesses who are ordered not to be admitted even to make an accusation are not to be admitted to give testimony; nor are persons whom the accuser has produced from his own household. Nor are persons under fourteen years of age to be admitted to give testimony.

CAP. 365.—That the sentence of judges chosen by the parties ought not to be disregarded. From the Second Council of Milevis, chapter 24.

(2, q. 6, c. *A judicibus*.) No appeal is permitted from judges whom common consent has chosen. And anyone proved, through contumacy [“inquiry,” *percont.*, in the original], unwilling to obey the judges, when this has been proved to the bishop of the first see, shall be given letters ordering that no bishop communicate with him until he obeys.

CAP. 366.—On contumacious clerics and those tardy in performing their office. From the Council of Agde, chapter 2.

(Dist. 50, c. *Contumaces*.) Contumacious clerics are to be corrected by bishops in accordance with the rank of their dignity. If any persons of a higher rank, lifted up by pride, perhaps despise communion, neglect attendance at church, or fail to perform their office, they are to be given communion as strangers; so that, when repentance has corrected them, they may be restored to the register and recover their rank and dignity.

CAP. 367.—That a cleric should not go to a secular judge without consulting his bishop. From the same council, chapter 32.

[Col. 0522D]

(11, q. 1 and 2, c. *Clericum*.) No cleric may presume, without the bishop’s permission, to prosecute anyone before a secular judge. But one against whom an action has been brought is not to answer, submit a plea, or enter into a criminal case in a secular court. If any layperson attempts through calumny to harass a Church or cleric and is defeated, he is to be barred from the thresholds of the Church and from communion with Catholics unless he makes worthy repentance.

CAP. 368.—That a presbyter or deacon suspended from communion may baptize if necessity requires. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 8 (First Council of Orléans, chapter 14).

(Dist. 81, c. *Si diaconus*.) If a deacon or presbyter has, because of his offence, withdrawn himself from communion at the altar in penitential confession, then nevertheless, if no others are available and a situation of certain necessity arises, he may baptize a person requesting baptism.

CAP. 369.—That clerics who make loans may receive repayment without usury. From the Council of Tarragona, chapter 3 (under Hormisdas).

(14, q. 4, c. *Si quis clericus*.) If a cleric lends a solidus in a time of necessity, he may receive in wine or grain that amount which at the appointed time has been decreed for sale in ordinary trade. But if he does not possess the commodity needed, he is to receive back precisely what he gave, without any increase.

CAP. 370.—That no cleric may dare remove his slave or pupil from a church. From the Council of Lleida, chapter 8.

[Col. 0523B]

(17, q. 4, c. *Nullus cler.*) No cleric may dare remove from a church, or presume to flog, his slave or pupil who has fled there for refuge. If he does so, he is to be excluded [“segregated,” *segregetur*, in the original] from the place to which he gave no honor until he has made worthy repentance.

CAP. 371.—On clerics who seek the monastic vocation. From the Council of Toledo, chapter 54 (Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 49).

(19, q. 1, c. *Clerici qui*.) Clerics who seek the vocation of monks, because they desire to pursue a better life, ought to be granted free admission by their bishop into monasteries; nor should the purpose of those who strive to pass over to the desire for contemplation be forbidden.

CAP. 372.—That clerics’ stipends are not to be alienated from the legal right of Churches. From the Seventh Council of Toledo, chapter 5.

[Col. 0523C]

(12, q. 2, c. *Saepe fit*.) It often happens that length of time obstructs the rightful claim of original ownership. Therefore, making provision, we decree that if any cleric receives a stipend from the property of any bishop’s Church by grant, he must make a written declaration under the name of a precarious grant; he must not, by prolonged retention, prejudice the Church; and he must work profitably whatever he has received for use. Thus property under divine law will not appear to be neglected on any pretext, and the clerics may receive support from the Church which they serve. If any of them refuses to do this, he will be deemed to deprive himself of his stipend.

CAP. 373.—That bishops ought to grant freedom to slaves of Churches who are made clerics. Likewise from the Ninth Council of Toledo, chapter 9.

[Col. 0523D]

(Dist. 54, c. *Qui ex familiis*.) Those who are called from the households of the Church into clerical service must receive from their bishops the gift of freedom; and, if they have distinguished themselves by merits of honorable life, only then may they perform greater offices. But those whom an incorrigible fault has marked with disgrace, perpetual servitude of condition is to bind in chains.

CAP. 374.—On eunuchs made by others and those who cut off their own sexual organs. From the decrees of Pope Martin, chapter 215 (from the decrees of Martin of Braga).

(Dist. 55, c. *Si quis per aegritudinem*.) If anyone has had his sexual organs cut by physicians because of illness, and likewise those castrated by barbarians or foolish masters, and they are judged worthy in conduct, the canon permits them to be promoted to clerical office. But if anyone in sound health, not for the discipline of religion and abstinence, but by mutilating the body fashioned by God—thinking that he can cut away from himself fleshly desires—castrates himself, we decree that he is not to be admitted to any clerical office. If he has already been promoted to the clergy, he is to be removed from his ministry and deposed.

CAP. 375.—That a deacon may not sit before a presbyter, chapter 40.

A deacon may not sit before a presbyter except by the presbyter’s command.

CAP. 376.—That one to be ordained deacon must renounce marriage, chapter 41 [chapter 39].

[Col. 0521B]

(Dist. 27, c. *Diaconus qui*.) If a man chosen as deacon declares that he is ready to enter into marriage and says that he cannot remain continent, he is not to be ordained. But if he is silent at his ordination, is ordained, and afterwards desires marriage, he is to be excluded from the ministry and removed from the clergy.

CAP. 377.—That not everyone may touch the Lord’s vessels. From the same council, chapter 42 (ibid., chapter 41).

(Dist. 23, c. *Non liceat*.) No one may touch the sacred vessels except a subdeacon or acolyte in the sacristy.

CAP. 378.—On the cutting of clerics’ hair and dignified dress. From the same council, chapter 66.

(Dist. 13, c. *Non oportet*.) Clerics ought not grow their hair long and minister in that manner. Rather, with their heads closely shorn and ears uncovered, and wearing the ankle-length tunic [“garment,” *vestem*, in the original] according to Aaron, they are to be suitably dressed.

CAP. 379.—On not ordaining unwilling persons or removing the undeserving. Pope Gregory to Natalis, bishop, in the first book of the register (Letter 19).

(Dist. 74, c. *Gesta quae*.) We have learned that the proceedings which you sent us, drawn up in the secretariat of your council, in which the honored archdeacon is adjudged, are full of the seed of disputes: since at one and the same time one person is unwillingly promoted to the order of priesthood and is removed from the office of deacon as though unworthy. And just as it is right that no one be compelled to advance unwillingly, so likewise, I think, it must be judged that no innocent person should be unjustly removed from the ministry of his rank.

CAP. 380.—What is to be done with the property of fallen clerics. Gregory to Peter, subdeacon (Book I, chapter 42).

[Col. 0524D]

(16, q. *De lapsis*.) With regard to fallen priests, levites, or anyone from the clergy, we wish you to observe this: do not involve yourself in their property through any contamination; rather, seek out very poor regular monasteries known to live according to God, and commit the fallen persons to penance in those monasteries, so that the property of the fallen may benefit the same place in which they are committed to perform penance. Thus those who are charged with concern for their correction may have support from their property. But if they have relatives, their property is to be given to their lawful relatives, provided nevertheless that sufficient provision is made for the maintenance of those committed to penance. If priests or levites, monks, clerics, or any other persons from the household of the Church have fallen, we wish them to be committed to penance, but their property is not to be withdrawn from ecclesiastical right. Yet they are to receive for their own use what will sustain them in penance, lest, if they are stripped bare, they become burdensome to the places in which they have been committed [“condemned,” *damnati*, in the text].

CAP. 381.—What penalty follows one who secretly defames another. Gregory to the clergy and people of Ravenna in the sixth book of the register (Book V, Letter 30).

Because [original adds *quidam*, “someone”], filled with the counsel of an evil spirit, someone, in the silence of night, posted in a place in the city an accusation against Castorius, our notary and representative, speaking to his discredit and also craftily opposing me concerning the making of peace; and [Col. 0525B] because whoever speaks truthfully ought not to fear making himself known, he must come forward publicly and prove whatever he presumed to say in his accusation. But if he does not come forward and make public confession, whoever he may be who presumed to do this, or who gave his consent to counsel of so great an iniquity, we decree, by the judgment of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ [original: *spiritu*, “by the Spirit”], that he be deprived of participation in His holy body and blood. And if, because he is concealed and unknown, he cannot be apprehended by discipline, yet, conscious of so great an evil and under this prohibition, he presumes to receive the body and blood of the Lord, let him, struck by the vengeance of anathema as a deceiver and pestilent man, be separated from the body of the holy Church. If, moreover, there should perhaps be such a person whom, not knowing him to be the [Col. 0525C] author and accomplice of this deed, we send letters of goodwill, let that very prayer on his behalf before almighty God be ineffectual. But if, having appeared publicly in the same city, he can prove what he said, or if, knowing that he cannot establish the charge he wrote, he openly confesses his error, let him not be deprived of participation in the Lord’s body and blood, nor be held alien from the body of the holy Church; for we acknowledge before almighty God our daily faults, so that, while preserving the moderation of discipline, we may nevertheless spare the errors of others.

### CHAPTER 382.—On bigamists and men attached to concubines. Jerome, in the letter to Oceanus (vol. II; beginning, “Sophronius Eusebius”).

[Col. 0525D]

Under no circumstances is it fitting that bigamists, or men bound by the chains of concubines, should enter upon the ministry. In Leviticus it is written and prescribed what sort of priests ought to be chosen. You have this: “And the Lord said to Moses: A priest shall take a wife who is a virgin from the stock of his fathers; but he shall not take a widow, one put away, or one abandoned by a living husband” (Leviticus 21). I have rightly understood the Lord commanding Moses that not even a bigamous wife should be suitable for a priest, lest she defile the honour of the priesthood. As He commands a husband of one wife, so He commands a wife of one husband. Therefore, if a cleric is monogamous but his wife is bigamous, do not admit him to the ministry; for he has taken a bigamous wife. The Apostle gave Titus these instructions concerning the ordination of clerics (Titus 1).

And because the book awaits its conclusion, let us return to the matter [Col. 0526A] from which we digressed. Nor, if two or three handmaids of God live together, is it fitting for a priest to enter to visit them alone. Whoever does not observe these commands is an enemy of his own soul. If, after our warnings, any cleric seeks to love *agapetae*—beloved women or spiritual companions—more than Christ, let him be summoned according to the synodal rule, and let the ordinances of the Fathers established at Nicaea be read to him. But if, converted, he abandons the aforesaid women, we have gained the greatest profit. Otherwise such a man must be anathematized by the Church. For women living with men sprout thorns, and pierce the secrets of minds with a sharp blade. Alas for the crime! It is painful to say, but it ought not to be passed over: these women vowed to marry Christ, not clerics.

### CHAPTER 383.—That Christian scholars should tolerate the solecisms of certain priests. Augustine, from *On Instructing Beginners in the Faith*, ch. 9.

[Col. 0526B]

(Distinction 38, ch. *Sedulo mon.*) Scholars must be earnestly warned that, clothed with humility, Christians should learn not to despise those whom they know avoid moral faults more than faults of speech; and that they should not dare compare, much less prefer, a practised tongue to a pure heart.

(A little later.) For it is especially useful for such persons to know that meanings are to be preferred to words as the mind is preferred to the body. From this it follows that they ought to prefer hearing truer speeches to more eloquent ones, just as they ought to prefer having wiser friends to more handsome ones. Let them also know that no voice reaches the ears of God unless it bears the affection of a friend. Thus they will not mock if they happen to observe some bishops and ministers of the Church [Col. 0526C] calling upon God with barbarisms and solecisms, or not understanding the very words which they pronounce, or punctuating them confusedly. This is not to say that such things ought not to be corrected, so that the people may say “Amen” to what they plainly understand; nevertheless, they are to be borne piously by those who have learned that, as one is blessed by sound in the forum, so one is blessed by desire in the church. Thus that kind of forensic diction may perhaps sometimes be good diction, but it can never be called a blessing.

### CHAPTER 384.—That pardon need not be sought from subjects for excess in correction. Augustine, *On the Life of Clerics* (Letter 109, to the nuns).

(Distinction 86, ch. *Quando nec.*) When the necessity of discipline compels you to speak harsh words in restraining conduct, even if you perceive that you have exceeded moderation [Col. 0526D] in those very words [original: *minoribus*, “lesser”], you are not required to ask pardon from those subject to you; lest, among those who ought to be subject, authority for governing be broken while humility is observed too much. Yet pardon must be sought from the Lord of all, who knows with what goodwill you love those whom perhaps you rebuke more than justly.

### CHAPTER 385.—Why those returning from heresy are permitted to exercise their offices. The same author, in the letter to Boniface (Letter 50, not far from the end).

(23, question 4, ch. *Ipsa pietas.*) “If,” they say, “we must repent in order to be saved because we were outside the Church and against the Church, how can we remain among you as clerics or even bishops after this repentance?” This would not happen—[Col. 0527A] indeed, as must be admitted, it ought not to happen—unless it were healed by the compensation afforded by peace itself. But let those who lie in so great a death of severance say this to themselves and grieve most humbly, so that by this certain wound of their Catholic mother they may come back to life. For when a severed branch is grafted in, another wound is made in the tree so that the branch may be received and live, though without the life of the root it was perishing. But when the received branch has grown together with the receiving tree, strength and fruit follow; if it does not grow together, that branch indeed withers, but the life of the tree remains.

There is also such a manner of grafting that, without cutting off any branch within, the branch outside is inserted—yet not without, but with at least the slightest wound to the tree. Thus also when these persons come to the Catholic root, the honour of clerical [Col. 0527B] or episcopal office is not taken from them, even after repentance for their error. Something is indeed done, as it were, in the bark of the mother-tree, contrary to the strictness of integrity; nevertheless, because “neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters” (1 Corinthians 3), when peace causes the grafted branches to grow together through prayers poured out to God’s mercy, “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4).

### CHAPTER 386.—Why public penitents are not to remain in the clergy. The same work, immediately following.

(Distinction 50, ch. *Ut constitueretur.*) The establishment in the Church that no one, after penance for any crime, should receive clerical office, return to clerical office, or remain in clerical office, was made not through despair of pardon but through the rigor of discipline. Otherwise men will dispute against the keys given to the Church, [Col. 0527C] concerning which it was said: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matthew 19). But lest, perhaps, in the case of other crimes also, a mind puffed up by the hope of ecclesiastical honour should do penance proudly, it was judged most strictly that after penance has been performed for a condemnable crime no one should be a cleric, so that the loss of temporal eminence might provide a greater and truer medicine of humility.

For holy David did penance for deadly crimes and nevertheless remained in his honour. Blessed Peter too, when he shed most bitter tears, certainly repented of having denied the Lord, and yet remained an apostle. But the later diligence of those who, where nothing would be taken away from salvation, added something to humility so that salvation might be guarded more safely, must not therefore be thought superfluous. I believe that they had experienced the feigned penitence of some [Col. 0527D], revealed by their ambitious pursuit of powerful offices. For the experience of many diseases compels the discovery of many remedies. Yet in cases of this sort, where, through grave fissures of dissension, the danger is not that of this or that individual but the ruin of whole peoples lies at hand, something must be remitted from severity, so that charity may sincerely come to the aid of healing greater evils.

### CHAPTER 387.—Why corrected Donatists were permitted to minister. In the same place, a little later.

From the beginning, the African Catholic Church observed this practice toward such persons on the judgment of the bishops who gave judgment at the Church of Rome between Caecilian and the party of Donatus. After one Donatus, who was shown to have been the author [Col. 0528A] of the schism, had been condemned, they judged that the others, once corrected, should be received in their offices even if they had been ordained outside the Church. This was not because they could possess the Holy Spirit even outside the unity of Christ’s body, but chiefly because, while outside, they might deceive those whom they could hinder from receiving that gift; and then so that their own weakness too, having been received more gently within, might become capable of healing, when no obstinacy any longer shut the eyes of the heart against the evidence of truth.

### CHAPTER 388.—On avoiding prejudgment. Augustine, in a letter to the clergy and the whole people of the Church at Hippo (Letter 137).

(2, question 1, ch. *Nomen presbyteri.*) I did not venture either to suppress or erase the title “presbyter” from the number of his colleagues, lest I seem to wrong the divine authority under [Col. 0528B] whose examination the case still remains pending, if I wished to anticipate its judgment with my own. Nor do judges do this even in secular affairs when uncertainty in a case is referred to a higher authority, so that they dare to change anything while the referral is pending. It has also been established in a council of bishops that no cleric not yet convicted ought to be suspended from communion, unless he fails to present himself for examination of his case.

### CHAPTER 389.—On the burden of the presbyterate. Augustine, in a letter to Bishop Valerius (Letter 148).

(Distinction 40, ch. *Ante omnia.*) Augustine, presbyter, greets in the Lord [Col. 0528C] his most blessed and venerable lord and father Valerius, sincerely most dear in the sight of the Lord.

Before all else, I ask that your religious prudence consider that nothing in this life—and especially at this time—is easier, lighter, or more acceptable to human beings than the office of bishop, presbyter, or deacon, if the matter is conducted superficially and flatteringly; but before God nothing is more wretched, sorrowful, or condemnable. Likewise, nothing in this life—and especially at this time—is more difficult, laborious, or dangerous than the office of bishop, presbyter, or deacon; but before God nothing is more blessed, if one serves in that office in the manner commanded by our Emperor. What this manner is, however, I learned neither in childhood nor in youth. And at the very time when I had begun to learn it, violence was done me, deservedly because of my sins. For I do not know what else to think of the fact that the second place at the helm was entrusted to me when [Col. 0528D] I did not know how to hold an oar.

### CHAPTER 390.—On the disorderly access of consecrated women. Augustine, in a letter to Eusebius (Letter 69).

[Col. 0528D]

(24, question 1, ch. *Subdiaconus.*) A subdeacon of the Spanish Church, named Primus, was removed from the clergy because, when forbidden disorderly access to consecrated women, he despised proper and sound commands.

### CHAPTER 391.—That one coming over from heretics should be received in the humility of penance. The same author, in the same letter.

(Immediately following.) If it pleases the Lord, I follow this practice: whoever, having been degraded among them for disciplinary reasons, wishes to pass over to the Catholic Church, is received in the humiliation of penance—[Col. 0529A] precisely what they themselves perhaps would compel him to undergo if he wished to remain among them.

### CHAPTER 392.—That each person should accept another’s judgment, which he himself wishes to pronounce upon another. Augustine, in a letter to Pascentius, count of Africa (Letter 174).

(32, question 6, ch. *Iniquum est.*) It is unjust for anyone to wish to judge another and not to wish to be judged himself.

### CHAPTER 393.—That clerics should not conduct secular business. Letter of Cyprian to the presbyters, deacons, and people of Furni (Letter 9, book I; otherwise Letter 66).

(21, question 3, ch. *Cyprianus.*) Cyprian greets the presbyters, deacons, and people dwelling at Furni. Long ago a council of bishops decreed that no one should name in his will any cleric or minister of God as guardian or curator [original: *constituat*, “appoint”], because each person honoured with the divine priesthood [Col. 0529B] and appointed to the clerical ministry ought to serve only the altar and sacrifices and to be free for prayers and supplications. For it is written: “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular troubles, so that he may please him to whom he has proved himself” (2 Timothy 2).

A few verses later. Our predecessor bishops, religiously considering and beneficially providing for this, decreed that no person at death should name a cleric as guardian or curator; and that if anyone did so, no offering should be made for him and no sacrifice should be celebrated for his repose. For those who wished [original: *volunt*, “wish”] to call priests and ministers away from the altar do not deserve [variant: *merentur*, “deserve”] to be named at God’s altar in the prayer of priests.

### CHAPTER 394.—On the same matter. From the same letter, somewhat earlier.

[Col. 0529C]

(21, question 3, ch. *Mollitiis.*) Those occupied with divine and spiritual matters ought not to be bound by worldly comforts, affairs, and snares, nor be free for earthly and secular occupations.

### CHAPTER 395.—Again on the same matter, in the same place, a little lower down.

(21, question 3, ch. *Hi qui in ecclesia.*) Those promoted in the Church of the Lord to clerical orders should not in any respect be called away from divine service, lest [variant: *nec*, “and not”] they be bound by troubles and secular business [original: *molestiis et laqueis saecularibus*, “by troubles and secular snares”]; nor should they withdraw from altars and sacrifices, but should serve heavenly and spiritual things day and night.

### CHAPTER 396.—On the same matter. The same author, in the same place, at the end of the letter.

Let the decree of the priests, made religiously and necessarily [Col. 0529D], be observed by us. At the same time, let an example be given to the other brethren, lest anyone call priests and ministers of God, who are devoted to His altar and Church, away to secular troubles. For it will henceforth be possible to ensure that no one further does this to clerics, if what has now been done is punished.

### CHAPTER 397.—Which clerics are to be received after a lapse and which are not. Isidore, to Bishop Massio (among the works of St Isidore, *On the Fall of a Priest and Restoration*).

What your venerable brotherhood made known in its letter: no diversity in the decrees is to be understood in judgments of this sort, since in one place it is read that after bodily lapse a rank of honour is to be restored after penance, while elsewhere, after such a fault, the privilege of the former rank [original and Victorius: *ordinis*, “of order”] is by no means [Col. 0530A] to be restored. This diversity is distinguished in the following way. The canon commands those to return to their former grades of office whose penance was preceded by satisfaction and worthy confession of sins. On the other hand, those who are not corrected from the vice of corruption [original: *correpti*, “seized/afflicted”], and who strive with a kind of superstitious rashness to vindicate the very carnal offence which they commit, receive neither the rank of honour nor the grace of communion. Thus both judgments must be decided in this way: those who have deserved reconciliation through the penance of divine mercy must necessarily be restored to a place of honour. Nor without reason do those attain the state of dignity acquired [variant: *ademptae*, “removed”] by them who are known to have received, through penance, the remedy of life.

[Col. 0530B]

### CHAPTER 398.—Why penitents are enjoined seven years of abstinence. In the same place.

Nor did the holy Fathers establish by the choice of their own will that canonical censure should command a penitent, after seven years, to return to his former status; rather, they established it according to the judgment of God. For it is read that Miriam, the prophetess and sister of Aaron, when she incurred the offence of speaking against Moses, was immediately struck with [original and Victorius: *perfusa*, “drenched with”] the mark of leprosy (Numbers 12). When Moses asked that she be healed, the Lord commanded her to go outside the camp for seven days and, after cleansing, to be admitted again within the camp.

Miriam, Aaron’s sister, therefore signifies the flesh of the priest. When it is stained, being given over to pride, by the foulest allurements [original: *contagiis*, “contagions”] of thoughts, it is cast out from the camp for seven days—that is, from the fellowship of the holy Church for seven years—where, after correction of its vices, it receives again the privilege of its former place or dignity.

And after a few words. At the end of the letter I thought this should be added: whenever a conflicting judgment is found in the acts of councils, the judgment whose authority is older and weightier should be retained.

### CHAPTER 399.—On the careful investigation of judgment. Fructuosus, bishop (in his Rule, ch. 4).

[Col. 0530C]

Every case is to be debated in the assembly of all the brethren and investigated justly and carefully, lest perhaps an innocent junior be oppressed by the deceit and malice of a senior. A superior—whether abbot or provost [Col. 0530D], as added from the original—must not be permitted to judge according to respect of persons, nor fraudulently or unjustly condemn anyone. Rather, as stated, another judgment is to be entrusted to and maintained by spiritual or truthful brethren in matters of this kind; setting God’s judgment before their eyes, they must not permit an innocent soul to be most wickedly oppressed.

### CHAPTER 400.—On those who have committed public crimes after or before ordination. From a letter of Archbishop Rabanus to Heribald, from the Council of Lleida, ch. 10 (Rabanus, ch. 1, *Book of Penitents*).

(Distinction 50, ch. *De his.*) It seemed good to us to write concerning those who hold sacred orders and confess themselves to have been defiled by capital crimes before or after ordination. In their case, it seems to me [Col. 0531A] that the following distinction must be made. Those who have been publicly detected or apprehended in perjury, theft, fornication, and other crimes of this kind are to be deposed from their proper rank according to the ordinances of the sacred canons, because it is a scandal to the people of God to have set over them persons known to be excessively vicious. For men are thereby led to speak disparagingly of God’s sacrifice, as the sons of Eli are recorded to have done when they sinned (1 Samuel 2); and rebels and opponents, through their evil examples, daily become worse.

But those who confess, by secret confession before the eyes of God and also in the presence of the priest who is to impose their penance, that they have secretly committed the aforesaid sins, and grievously lament that they have sinned—[Col. 0531B] if they strive to cleanse themselves through fasting, almsgiving, vigils, and holy prayers with tears—are to be promised hope of pardon from God’s mercy, even while retaining their rank.

### CHAPTER 401.—On injuries done to clerics and their compensation. From the *Book of Capitularies* (book V, ch. 184).

If anyone insults, strikes, or abducts a minister of the Church—a subdeacon, reader, exorcist, or acolyte [the original reads: porter]—let him make compensation threefold, as he is accustomed to compensate their relatives. But an injury to a deacon, presbyter, or bishop is to be compensated fourfold. An injury to other clerics is to be compensated as to their relatives. Likewise, an injury to monks living in a monastery according to the Rule is to be compensated twofold [Col. 0531C] according to their lineage [original: *ut*, “so that”], so that reverence may be shown to God and the Church, and peace to those who serve it.

### CHAPTER 402.—How canons ought to live in the cloister. From book V of the *Capitularies*, ch. 185 (ch. 115).

(On Constitutions, distinction 5, ch. *In omnibus.*) Therefore, in all things, insofar as human frailty permits, we decree that canonical clerics shall live canonically, observing the teaching of Holy Scripture and the instructions of the holy Fathers, and shall not presume to do anything disorderly without the permission of their bishop or master. In each bishopric they are to eat and sleep together where they have the means to do so; or those who receive stipends from ecclesiastical [Col. 0531D] property shall remain in their cloister and come every day at first morning to the reading and hear what is commanded them. Likewise, at table they shall hear a reading and render obedience to their masters according to the canons.

### CHAPTER 403.—That those who inflict injuries upon clerics are to be anathematized. In the same work, ch. 191.

Whoever, whether judge or layman, presumes to inflict an injury upon a presbyter, deacon, any cleric, or one of the younger clergy, without a hearing before the bishop, archdeacon, or archpriest, is to be held under anathema, excluded from the fellowship of all Christians.

### CHAPTER 404.—What ought to be done concerning those who secretly defame others. The same.

[Col. 0532]

Whoever secretly writes a defamatory document to injure and stain anyone, and posts it publicly or throws it down for someone to find, does not harm the person against whom the little document was posted, nor does he detract anything from that person’s reputation. But if the maker of such a document can be found, he shall be compelled to prove what he wrote. If he cannot prove what he wrote, he shall be flogged, since he preferred to defame rather than accuse.

### CHAPTER 405.—On a presbyter suffering from epilepsy. Alexander II to Genobard, Archbishop of Juvanese [alternatively: Viviers; Gratian has “Vienna”].

(7, question 2, ch. *In litteris.*) Your letter contained the following. “This cleric holds the order of the presbyterate; but because he suffers from epilepsy, and we have ourselves recognized this at present, we did not dare permit him to make the offering or celebrate Mass. Since illness is not a fault, we have resolved to seek the counsel of the decree of your authority on this matter.”

We advise, therefore, that if he is frequently afflicted by this disease, he should in every way be prohibited from making the offering and celebrating Masses. For it is improper and most dangerous that this should happen to him, so that, overcome by epileptic illness, he might fall during the consecration of the Eucharist. But if by God’s mercy he recovers, since illness and not fault is in question, we no longer forbid him to offer sacrifice.

### CHAPTER 406.—On those ordained by excommunicated persons. Urban II to Gebhard [Gebeard], Bishop of Constance.

[Col. 0532C]

(9, question 1, ch. *Ab excommunicatis.*) Permit those ordained by excommunicated bishops—provided that these bishops were formerly Catholic—if they did not receive their orders simoniacally and if the bishops themselves are found not to have been simoniacs, to remain in the orders which they received, after imposing such penance as you judge appropriate, if their more religious life and distinction in learning appear to have deserved this. But we do not permit them to ascend to higher orders unless the greatest necessity and usefulness demand it, their holy conduct has deserved it, and even then this is to be granted more rarely and with especial caution.

### CHAPTER 407.—On the manner of reconciliation. The same, to Anselm, Archbishop of Milan (Letter 4).

It seems to our judgment that, according to the tenor of our command, whenever according to the custom of your Church you begin, in giving sacred orders to others, to pronounce the blessing, you should have those whom your prudence judges must be reconciled present during the blessing and the laying on of hands. For them you shall perform all the other rites of consecration except anointing, and thus reconcile them to the sacred ministries.

### CHAPTER 408.—That no layman may exercise authority over clerics. Urban II to Count Ralph (Letter 14).

We wish you to know that no secular lord is permitted to have authority over clerics; rather, all clerics must be subject to the bishop alone. Whoever [Col. 0533A] presumes otherwise will undoubtedly be subject to canonical sentence.

### CHAPTER 409.—On one made a deacon without first being a subdeacon. Alexander II to Rumald Grimald, Bishop of Constance.

(Distinction 52, ch. *Sollicitudo.*) The concern of your charity has sought advice whether the bearer of this letter is fit or unfit to perform the office of deacon and presbyter, since he is known to have ascended to it too hastily—without the order of subdeacon—not through pride but rather through negligence. Therefore, in answer to your charity, we command that you prohibit him from priestly office until, at the next fast of the Four Seasons, you duly confer upon him the ministry of the subdiaconate; and thereafter permit him to return to the higher offices.

### CHAPTER 410.—On the sons of priests. Decree of Gregory VII and Urban II (Council of Melfi, ch. 14).

[Col. 0533B]

(Distinction 56, ch. *Presbyterorum.*) We decree that the sons of presbyters are to be excluded from the ministries of the sacred altar unless they have been found to live religiously either in monasteries or among regular canons [“regular” is absent from the original].

### CHAPTER 411.—On the stability of regular canons. Urban II to the Abbot of Saint-Ruf.

We decree that no one professing the canonical life, after he has placed a man over his own head in God’s stead, may dare, prompted by frivolity or under the pretext of a stricter religion, to leave that cloister without the permission of the abbot and the whole community. No abbot, bishop [Col. 0533C], or monk shall receive one who leaves without a joint letter of authorization.

### CHAPTER 412.—On those ordained by bishops other than their own. Urban to Hugh, Bishop of Lyons.

(9, question 2, ch. *Lugdunensi.*) The clerics of the Church [Gratian and Victorius: “diocese”] of Lyons, whom the indication in your letters shows to have been ordained by bishops of another diocese contrary to the statutes of the canons, may be received by the prudence of your religious office with the honour of their ranks, if they are otherwise found to have been canonically ordained and free of any irregularity—provided that you see that their approved life has merited this indulgence. (See Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chs. 12 and 13.) For we read that Saint Epiphanius, bishop, ordained certain clerics from the diocese of Saint John Chrysostom [Col. 0533D]. The holy man would certainly not have done this had he judged that it would harm them. Therefore, whomsoever your moderation judges should be received, you shall receive each in his own rank, after imposing a suitable penance by way of satisfaction for the Church which they offended, in view of mercy, while preserving in all things the discipline of the holy canons.

### CHAPTER 413.—That the dishonour of parents does not harm children who live honourably. Jerome, in the letter against Rufinus (book II, letter to Pammachius against the threats of John of Jerusalem).

(Distinction 56, ch. *Nasci de adulterio*; here the order of chapters varies in Victorius.) To be born from adultery is not the fault of the one who is born, but of the one who begets. Just as [Col. 0534A], among seeds, the earth which warms them does not sin, nor the seed cast into furrows, nor the moisture and warmth by which well-tempered grain springs up into a shoot; but, for example, the thief and robber who by fraud and force steals the seeds does sin. Thus the earth—that is, the womb—receives what belongs to it in the human race; it warms what it has received, gives bodily form to what it has warmed, and distinguishes the formed body into limbs. Amid those narrow confines of the sacred womb, the hand of God is always at work; and He is the same Creator of body and soul.

Do not despise the goodness of the potter who formed you and made you as He willed. He is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1), who built Himself a house in the womb of the Virgin. Jephthah, numbered among holy men by the Apostle’s voice (Hebrews 11), was the son of a prostitute (Judges 11). Esau, born of Rebecca and Isaac, was hairy in mind as well as [Col. 0534B] body (Genesis 25); just as good wheat degenerates into darnel and wild oats, because the cause of vices and virtues lies not in the seeds but in the will of the one who generates.

### CHAPTER 414.—On the same subject. Chrysostom, *Homilies on Matthew*, Homily 3 (on Matthew 1: “But Judah begot Perez”).

(Distinction 56, ch. *Nunquam.*) Let us never be ashamed of the vices of our parents, but always seek and embrace virtue alone. For such a person, even if he has a foreign mother, even if she has been defiled by fornication or stained by any such disgrace, is nevertheless neither darkened by her lowliness nor defiled by her crime. If even a fornicator himself, converted to better things, is in no way stained by his former life, much more is one born of a prostitute or adulteress not disfigured by the reproaches of his parents, if he is adorned by his own virtue.

Likewise. No one at all—no one—is to be praised or blamed for either the virtue or vice of parents; no one is truly obscure or illustrious on that account. Indeed, to speak more thoughtfully and precisely, I do not know how, but that person shines more brightly who, though born of parents altogether alien from virtue, is himself remarkable for virtue.

### CHAPTER 415.—On the same subject. Statement of Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, ch. 16.

(Distinction 56, ch. *Undecunque.*) Wherever people are born from, if they do not follow their parents’ vices and rightly worship God, they will be honourable and saved. For human seed from any sort of human being is God’s creature; it will go badly for those who use it badly, but it will never itself be evil. As good children of adulterers [original and Victorius: *adulteriorum*, “of adulteries”] are no defence of adultery, so bad children of married persons are no accusation against marriage.

### CHAPTER 416.—Again on the same matter. The same author, in a letter to the presbyter Jerome on the origin of the soul (Letter 28, in the middle).

What you wrote in your book against Rufinus—that some people malign this view because they think it unworthy that God should give souls to adulterous conceptions, and therefore seek to maintain that souls may justly be led as if to the prisons of this world on account of the merits of a life lived before the flesh—does not disturb me, as I consider many ways by which this calumny may be refuted. Your own answer, too, that the fault in wheat does not lie in the seed said to have been stolen, but in the one who stole the grain; and that the earth therefore ought not to have refused to warm the seeds in its bosom because an unclean sower cast them down by his hand—this is a most elegant comparison.

Even before I had read it, this objection concerning adulterous offspring [original: *nullas*, “no”] caused me some difficulty in this question, when I considered in general that God makes many good things even out of our evils and our sins. The creation of any animal, if it has an intelligent and devout observer, calls forth inexpressible praise for the Creator; how much more the creation not of just any animal, but of a human being?

### CHAPTER 417.—On baptism and the sacrilege of parents in their children. Augustine to Boniface, on baptism (Letter 23).

[Col. 0535B]

(1, question 4, ch. *Jam itaque.*) Once a human being exists in himself, distinct from the one who begot him, he is not held liable for another’s sin without his own consent. He nevertheless contracted guilt because he was one with, and in, the person from whom he derived it when that deed, from which he derives it, was committed. But one person does not derive it from another when each is living his own proper life and there is now ground to say: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18). But in order that he may be regenerated through the agency of another’s will when he is offered for consecration, the one Spirit through whom the person offered is regenerated accomplishes this.

### CHAPTER 418.—That an infamous person may conduct his own case. Pope Felix III, in his second decretal to the bishops of Gaul.

[Col. 0535C]

(4, question 6, and 3, question 10, ch. *Si accusatorum.*) If the persons of accusers are found culpable in the judgment of bishops, they are not to be admitted to make accusations, unless they wish to assert their own cases—and even then, not criminal or ecclesiastical cases.

### CHAPTER 419.—How accused priests ought to clear themselves. Decree and response of Pope Leo to Emperor Charles (Capitularies XLV, ch. 34, and XLVII, ch. 285).

(2, q. 5, c. *Omnibus vobis*.) We do not doubt that it is known to all of you by sight [*visu*, original and Victorius] or by hearsay that, very frequently, at the prompting of the ancient enemy, various crimes are alleged against priests. But although the manner in which a reasonable examination and satisfaction should be made concerning them by those parties was very often debated in the time of the lord Pippin, your [our] father of blessed memory, as well as in earlier times by the holy Fathers and by other men of good devotion, we have nevertheless been unable to find it fully and clearly determined.

In our own times the same matter has very often been debated by holy bishops and the other priests, and by the remaining ministers of ecclesiastical rank, yours [ours], in the kingdoms and among other peoples of God, with us acting together with them, because of the many and excessive complaints concerning this matter which have reached us from various quarters. Yet we wish all you ministers of both orders to know how the matter has been determined, by the counsel of our lord and father Leo, the Apostolic One, [Col. 0536A] and of the other bishops of the Roman Church and remaining priests; also by the authority and consent of the eastern and Greek patriarchs and of many holy bishops and priests, and likewise of all our bishops and other priests and levites, and by the counsel of all our other faithful people and counsellors.

For it has been established, by the aforesaid reason, necessity, and authority, with the counsel of all, that whenever a crime is charged against any priest, if the accuser is such a person as ought to be admitted—for the canons fully state what sort of persons ought to be admitted to accuse priests—and if, as has been said, that accuser who is canonically admissible can establish the charge before the bishops with the lawful number of men and worthy witnesses, then the case shall be judged canonically; and, if the priest is found guilty, he shall be condemned canonically.

But if the accuser cannot establish the charge by the procedure described above, this too shall be judged canonically. Therefore, if the priest is under suspicion or is not credible to his bishop, to his fellow priests, or to good and just persons from his own people or congregation, then, lest he remain under accusation or the aforesaid suspicion, he shall restore himself to the Church as cleared by an oath, sworn publicly upon the four Gospels, together with three, five, or seven good neighbouring priests—following the example of Pope Leo, who had twelve bishops in his own purgation—or with more, if this appears fitting to his bishop or is seen to be necessary because of popular disturbance [Col. 0536C]. Whoever wishes to know what kind of witnesses should be admitted for accusing priests, and what [“whatever,” original and Gratian] is to be done concerning an accuser, may find it fully in the canons.

### CHAPTER 420.—On the same matter. Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, to the beloved brother and venerable fellow-bishop John, and servant of the people of God: greetings (Letter 53).

(2, q. 4, c. *Si mala fama*.) If an evil report about a presbyter has arisen throughout a parish by resemblance or rumour, and lawful accusers and witnesses are lacking, then, lest—contrary to the Apostle—the hearts of the weak be wounded by the evil report concerning the presbyter [Col. 0536D], and lest our ministry be reviled, and lest presbyters, growing over-confident, fall more freely into sin, he shall, in accordance with the decrees of the elders, clear his reputation by an oath together with named neighbouring presbyters, whom we know to be unwilling to commit perjury.

### CHAPTER 421.—On apostate clerics. Sixth constitution from the Book of Constitutions, chapter 7.

(Justinian, imperial Novel, Constitution 6.) Whoever, whether reader, subdeacon, deacon, or presbyter, despises the honour of the clerical office and passes into another manner of life, shall be subjected, with his property, to one of two conditions: either to the municipal curial condition; or, if the city has many curials, or if he himself is of lower standing, [Col. 0537A] he shall be handed over to the *taxeotic* condition of service.

[Note: At [Col. 0537D] the Greek reads: ἢ ἐν ἀπορίᾳ πρὸς ταξεωτικὴν κατενεχθήσεται τύχην, “or, if destitute, he shall be reduced to the condition of apparitors.” Agyleus translates these words thus: “Or, being indigent, let him be degraded to the condition of court officers.”]

### CHAPTER 422.—On the chastity of clerics. Thirty-seventh constitution, chapter 28.

A cleric who is set over readers and singers, such as a subdeacon or deacon, shall not dare to contract any marriage; otherwise he shall fall from the priesthood. A reader likewise, if he contracts a second marriage, is forbidden to advance to a higher rank of ecclesiastical order. A layman too, if he is found to be joined to a wife who has had another husband, or if he is not lawfully joined, or if he himself has had another wife, can become neither subdeacon, deacon, nor presbyter. And if by clandestine arts he has slipped into consecration, he shall lose that rank.

### CHAPTER 423.—That a layman may not, without the bishop’s permission, appoint clerics in a church which he builds from his own alms. Forty-ninth constitution, chapter 2.

[Col. 0537B]

If anyone builds a church, or gives an allowance to clerics from his own resources, he may not appoint in that church whatever clerics he wishes. But if he wishes certain persons to be consecrated for himself, he shall present them to the most blessed patriarch; and, if the patriarch judges them worthy, he shall consecrate them, while if he does not approve them, he shall reject them at his discretion.

### CHAPTER 424.—On the same matter. Fiftieth constitution, chapter 1.

If anyone has an oratory in his house, he shall not dare to celebrate sacred masses in it unless he has clerics of the catholic faith assigned to him by command of the religious bishop of the city or of the most blessed patriarch. If anyone acts contrary to these provisions, his house shall be assigned to the rights of the treasury [*ficei*, probably an OCR corruption].

If clerics withdraw from churches, other clerics must be ordained in their place, so that they may receive the stipends and ecclesiastical gifts which had been supplied to those readers; and, if the former clerics later return, nothing shall be supplied to them, because their stipends have been supplied to other clerics substituted in their stead [Col. 0537C].

### CHAPTER 425.—On the condemnation of the children of priests. From the Ninth Council of Toledo, chapter 10.

(15, q. 8, c. *Cum multae*.) Since many decisions of the Fathers concerning the incontinence of the clerical order have hitherto been issued, yet the correction of their morals has in no way been able to be established, the offences committed have carried the sentence of judges so far that vengeance struck not only the perpetrators of crimes but also the offspring of those condemned. Therefore, if any person from bishop down to subdeacon, once established in office, should thereafter beget children in a detestable union [“marriage,” *conjugio*] with either a female slave or a free woman, those by whom such children are proved to have been begotten shall be condemned by canonical censure. The offspring born from this pollution shall not only receive no inheritance from their parents anywhere, but shall remain in perpetual legal servitude to the church from the disgrace of whose priest or minister they were born [Col. 0537D].

### CHAPTER 426.—That one who commits himself to a monastery cannot afterwards dispose of his possessions. Sixty-seventh constitution, chapter 1.

Whoever enters a monastery must see that his possessions [Col. 0538A] are consecrated to the monastery. Before entry, indeed, they have free power to distribute their goods as they wish. But after entering they do not have such permission, even if they have children.

### CHAPTER 427.—Before which judges the cases of clerics are to be decided. Eighty-third constitution, chapter 1.

(11, q. 1, c. *Si quis cum clerico*.) If anyone has litigation with a cleric, then, if it concerns money, he shall first approach the bishop to whose judgment the cleric is subject. The bishop shall impose a proper end upon the dispute without loss or delay. But if the bishop is unwilling to settle the suit, then the hearing of the case shall proceed to civil judges.

Where the bishop wishes to decide the case, all proceedings shall be without written pleadings, and a final judgment shall be entered by him without writings. But if litigation arises over a criminal charge, the competent officials, having been approached, shall impose upon the case a conclusion consonant with the laws; provided, however, that the hearing of the suit does not exceed two months, reckoned from the joining of issue. A cleric shall not otherwise be punished unless, having been found liable, he has first been deprived by his bishop of priesthood [“stripped,” *nudatus*, Victorius] or of clerical rank.

But if the offence is ecclesiastical, then examination and punishment of the case shall proceed according to the canons before the bishop alone; other judges shall have no participation in such cases [Col. 0538B].

### CHAPTER 428.—On one who, overwhelmed by illness, promised to become a monk. Alexander II to Udo [Hugh], bishop of Évreux, and Theodoric, bishop of Verdun.

[Col. 0538C]

(17, q. 2, c. *Cosaldus*.) Cosaldus, a presbyter and bearer of this letter, coming to the thresholds of the Apostles, laid before the Apostolic See the complaint that a certain deacon named Richerius had taken from him the benefice and altars which he had customarily held by canon in the Church of Verdun.

For he said that formerly, while ill and oppressed by the fervour of suffering, he had promised to make himself a monk; yet not in such a way as to commit himself to a monastery or abbot, nor did he put his promise in writing. He does confess, however, that he renounced the aforesaid benefice into the hand of the church’s advocate. But after recovering his health he immediately refused to become a monk. He also said that, while he lay sick, the aforesaid Richerius had been able to acquire his benefice from the bishop of Verdun because he said that Cosaldus had already become a monk.

The case was deferred to the synod of Trier, in which the aforesaid deacon Richerius was convicted of having acquired the benefice in bad faith and entered into it improperly. Therefore, since the constitution of blessed Benedict, of the canons, and especially of our father and predecessor, Pope Saint Gregory, forbids anyone to become a monk before a year’s probation, if the facts are as he has stated, we judge and command by Apostolic authority that, through your diligence and clemency, Cosaldus the presbyter, bearer of this letter [“the presbyter’s,” *presbyteri*], shall receive, possess, and retain in peace his benefices and altars [Col. 0538D].

### CHAPTER 429.—On a presbyter who had lost his church without fault. Nicholas to Airard, archbishop of Tours (in the rescripts of Nicholas I, title 1, chapter 4).

[Col. 0539A]

(2, q. 1, c. *Notum sit*.) Let it be known to your brotherly charity that this poor presbyter, named Christopher, has tearfully complained to our clemency concerning his distress. He says that he was accused of false crimes and was unreasonably expelled from his church, although neither convicted nor confessing.

For, as he reports, although your diligence conducted an inquiry three times, no fault could be found in him either concerning a charge of fornication or concerning complicity [“confession,” *confessione*, original] in homicide, of which he was accused; except that, owing to his poverty, he either was unwilling to consent to what was demanded or was unable to fulfil it. Yet his rival acted voluntarily and seized that church unjustly.

Accordingly, we strongly urge your reverence that matters which appear to have been done through the greed of Giezica, perhaps without your knowledge, be corrected by the prompt correction of your brotherly censure: namely, by restoring the said priest to his own church and by mercifully restoring to him the former dignity which he lost. Do not allow canonical ordinances to be disregarded through anyone’s rashness, since equal punishment binds the doer and the one who consents [Col. 0539B].

### CHAPTER 430.—On a deacon unjustly defamed with a crime. Pope Stephen V to Leo, bishop of Teano.

(15, q. 5, c. *De crimine*.) Your deacon most truthfully declared himself innocent of the crime charged against him. Nevertheless, if there is suspicion, and suitable accusers are found, together with witnesses of the kind prescribed by the sacred canons, let the accusers come with you and a fixed number of bishops; let the deacon Alderic himself also be summoned. If he denies the charge, let the case be examined canonically; and if he either confesses voluntarily or is proved guilty by lawful witnesses, let him be struck by canonical sentence.

But if he neither confesses voluntarily nor can lawful accusers and witnesses be found, and the bad report grows widespread, let him clear himself by a secret oath, not in a public hearing but before you and several most reverend presbyters and deacons of your church. Thereafter announce him to be of good repute, and restrain and warn the children of the Church not to presume further to defame God’s priest, fearing the curse of Ham, who mocked his father’s private parts [Col. 0539D] (Gen. VII).

### CHAPTER 431.—A manifest case does not require witnesses. The same.

(2, q. 2, c. *De manifesta*.) Witnesses are not to be sought in a case that is manifest and known to many, as blessed Ambrose writes, in expounding the Apostle’s judgment concerning the fornicator, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 5, immediately after the beginning:

> “It is not the judge’s place,” he says, “to condemn without an accuser; for the Lord, although Judas was a thief, did not cast him out because he had not been accused.”

And immediately afterwards:

> “But when the deed became known, he judged that the man ought to be expelled from the fellowship of the brethren. For all knew his crime and did not rebuke him. Publicly, indeed, he kept his stepmother in the place of a wife. In this matter there was no need for witnesses, nor could the crime be concealed by any evasion” [Col. 0540A].

And a little later:

> “Absent in body but present in the authority of the Spirit, who is absent nowhere, I have already judged, as though present, that the one who committed this deed be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh.”

### CHAPTER 432.—That property in litigation may not be given or sold. From the Book of Capitularies, chapter 357.

Property under litigation may not be given or sold.

### CHAPTER 433.—On the manner of preparing *formatae* letters, which the Synod of Nicaea ordained should be observed among bishops in drafting letters.

(Dist. 73, c. *Qualiter*.) No one with even a slight knowledge of Greek is unaware that Greek letters also express numbers. Therefore, lest any fraud of falsification should rashly be attempted in making canonical letters—which Latin custom calls *formatae*—the 318 Fathers assembled at Nicaea devised and most beneficially established the following: that such letters should employ this method of calculation or reckoning.

That is, in the calculation there are to be taken the first Greek letters of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: π, υ, α. These letters together retain the numbers 481. The first letter of the Apostle Peter, namely π, which signifies the number eighty, is also included. There shall further be taken the first letter of the writer of the letter, the second letter of the person to whom it is written, the third letter of the recipient, the fourth letter of the city from which it is written, and the number of the indiction of that time. Thus, all these Greek letters, which, as we have said, express numbers, being brought together, the letter shall contain one total sum, whatever it may be [Col. 0540C].

Moreover, the letter shall separately add the number ninety-nine, which in Greek letters signifies ἀμήν, “amen.” Thus the three aforesaid Greek letters, π, υ, α, together with the first letter of Peter’s name, π, make 501. For the first π, which is first in the name of the supreme Father, counts sixty; υ, which is first in the name of the Son, counts eighty; and α, which is first in the name of the Spirit, denotes one. If you add π, first in the name of Peter, that is, forty, you will find eighty. But ἀμήν, written at the end of the aforesaid letter, signifies 561: α counts one, μ ninety-nine, η forty-eight, and ν ninety, making ninety-nine numbers [reading and arithmetic corrupt or uncertain in the printed text; Col. 0540D]. If, however, you combine the entire total, the letter contains 660 numbers. But for those less knowledgeable, the Greek letters themselves, with their proper numerical values, seem to need to be set down.

I. α. II. β. III. γ. IV. δ. V. ε. VI. ϛ. VII. ζ. VIII. η. IX. θ. X. ι. XX. κ. XXX. λ. XL. μ. L. ν. LX. ξ. LXX. ο. LXXX. π. XC. ς. C. ρ. CC. σ. CCC. τ. CCCC. υ. D. φ. DC. χ. DCC. ψ. DCCC. ω. DCCCC. πτ. M. α.

They are counted thus: ἕν, “one”; δύο, “two”; τρία, “three”; τέσσαρα, “four”; πέντε, “five”; ἕξ, “six”; ἑπτά, “seven”; ὀκτώ, “eight”; ἐννέα, “nine”; δέκα, “ten”; εἴκοσι, “twenty”; τριάκοντα, “thirty”; τεσσαράκοντα, “forty”; πεντήκοντα, “fifty”; ἐξήκοντα, “sixty”; ἑβδομήκοντα, “seventy”; ὀγδοήκοντα, “eighty”; ἐνενήκοντα, “ninety”; ἑκατόν, “one hundred”; διακόσια, “two hundred”; τριακόσια, “three hundred”; τετρακόσια, “four hundred”; πεντακόσια, “five hundred”; ἑξακόσια, “six hundred”; ἑπτακόσια, “seven hundred”; ὀκτακόσια, “eight hundred”; ἐννεακόσια, “nine hundred”; χίλιοι, “one thousand” [Col. 0541A].

### CHAPTER 434.—Example of a *formata* letter.

(A nearly similar text is found in Dist. 73, c. *In nomine*.) In the name of π the Father, υ the Son, and α the Holy Spirit: Rathbod, humble servant of the holy Church and people of Trier, to Rotbert, bishop of the venerable holy Church of Metz, in Christ the prince of shepherds—enduring glory, with the joy of prosperity and eternity.

Observing the most salutary decrees of the 318 holy Fathers established at Nicaea, we canonically address your God-worthy and devout brotherhood, and reverently approach your holiness under the designation of a *formata* letter.
