We inform you that we have given these letters dimissory to our present presbyter, named Gislemar, who was ecclesiastically educated in our diocese and whom we advanced from the order of clerics to the grade of presbyter. Thus fortified by these canonical credentials, he may, with our permission, reside in your parish under the protection and governance of your dear charity. We entrust him to you to be cherished and governed canonically in the bosom of the holy mother Church.

We have therefore determined to authenticate this letter on both sides with Greek letters and have decided to seal it with the ring of our church. May Christ, prince of shepherds, through the intercession of blessed Peter, to whom the Lord’s flock was especially entrusted, preserve your brotherhood sound among us for a long time in guarding his flock. ἀμήν, “amen.” Total of these: 1,539. π. υ. α. ω. ρ. ο. σ. υ. θ. ἀμήν.

Given at Trier, on the Ides of October, in the year 406 of the Lord’s Incarnation, indiction IX. π. υ. α. π. δ. α. ρ. δ. θ.

### CHAPTER 435.—Likewise, another example of a *formata*.

To the most reverend and most holy Rathbod, archbishop of the holy Church of Trier: Dado of the Church of Verdun, devoted servant of Christ’s flock, wishes in the Lord, the true King, the blessedness of the highest felicity.

Although the holy catholic Church is ready to follow evangelical precepts, which say, “He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; and he who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man” (Matt. X), and so forth; and although the Apostle commands us to pursue hospitality (Rom. XII) and to share in the necessities of holy persons—nevertheless, because of those who have their conscience seared (1 Tim. IV), who call themselves simple although they are filled with diabolical cunning, who say that they travel from place to place for a work of piety although their own wickedness has made them fugitives, and who say that they are admitted to sacred ministry although they are not—[Col. 0542B] the holy Fathers have decreed that no bishop may receive an unfamiliar and unknown foreign cleric, or install him in his church, unless he has a letter from his own bishop, called in the canons a *formata*.

We therefore make known to your fatherhood that our present brother, bearer of this letter, named Adruin, was not expelled by us for his wickedness. Rather, at the request of our brothers, because he belonged to our household, we gave him freedom, canonically received from the horn of the altar, and ordained him to the rank of presbyter. We have also made for him these dimissory or commendatory letters and send him to your beloved brotherhood, that he may be able to remain in your parish under your sacred rule and protection.

I, Dado, humble bishop, in the name of π the Father, υ the Son, and α the Holy Spirit, and in the unity [Col. 0542C] of the holy Church, in which Peter was given the right of binding and loosing, absolve the presbyter Adruin of the city of Verdun, indiction IX. And I give you, venerable Archbishop Rathbod, permission to install him in whatever church of your parish you wish. May almighty God deign to preserve your beloved fatherhood, adorned with the flowers of virtues. ἀμήν, “amen.” 278: π. υ. α. π. δ. α. λ. θ. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of May, in the year 406 of the Lord’s Incarnation, indiction IX.

## SEVENTH PART OF THE DECRETUM

Concerning the separateness and tranquillity of monks and nuns; and concerning the recall and penance of those who transgress their profession of continence.

### CHAPTER 1.—That monks in each city are subject to bishops and, devoting themselves to tranquillity, should attend to fasts and prayers. From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 4 (session 15).

[Col. 0541D]

(16, q. 1, c. *Qui vere*.) Those who truly and sincerely choose the solitary life are worthy of fitting honour. But since certain monks live indiscriminately [Col. 0542D] throughout cities and likewise commend themselves to monasteries on their own presumption, it has seemed good that no one shall build or establish a monastery or a house of prayer without the knowledge of the bishop of that city.

Those who live in monasteries in each city or estate ought to be subject to the bishop, devote themselves to tranquillity, observe [Col. 0543A] fasts and prayers, and remain in the places in which they have once dedicated themselves to God. They shall neither involve themselves in ecclesiastical business nor undertake any secular activity, leaving their own monasteries only if the bishop of that city commands it because of urgent necessity. No slave shall be received into a monastery to be a monk with them without the knowledge of his own master. We decree that whoever transgresses these provisions shall be outside communion, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed. The bishop of the city, moreover, ought to provide monasteries with necessary care and solicitude.

### CHAPTER 2.—On the separateness of monks. Jerome, in his letter to the presbyter Paulinus on the instruction of clerics (Book II, Letter 14).

(16, q. 1, c. *Si cupis*.) If you wish to be what you are called, a monk—that is, one who is alone—what are you doing in cities, which are surely dwellings not of solitary persons but of many? Every vocation has its leaders. To come to your [our, original] own case: let bishops and presbyters have the Apostles and apostolic men as their examples, and, possessing their honour, strive to possess also their merit. But let us have as leaders of our vocation the Pauls, Antonies, Julians, Hilarions, and Macarii.

Have the simplicity of the dove: plot deceit against no one; and have the wisdom of the serpent, lest you be overthrown by the snares of others. There is little difference in fault between being able to deceive a Christian and being deceived. If you perceive someone always or frequently speaking to you about money—apart from almsgiving, which lies equally open to all [Col. 0543C]—regard him as a trader rather than a monk. Beyond food, clothing, and evident necessities, give nothing to anyone, nor let dogs eat the children’s bread.

### CHAPTER 3.—On the same matter. The same, in his letter to the presbyters Riparius and Desiderius (Book III, final letter, near the end).

(16, q. 1, c. *Monachus*.) A monk does not perform the office of a teacher, but of one who mourns: one who laments either himself or the world and awaits in fear the coming of the Lord. Knowing his own weakness and the fragile vessel that he carries, he fears to offend, lest he strike against something, fall, and be broken. Therefore he avoids the sight of women, especially young women; and he is so stern a disciplinarian of himself that he fears even things that are safe.

“Why,” you ask, “do you go into the desert?” Surely, that I may not hear or see you; that I may not be moved by your frenzy; that I may not endure your wars; lest the eye of a harlot capture me; lest surpassing beauty lead me to unlawful embraces.

You reply: “This is not fighting, but fleeing. Stand in the battle-line; armed, resist your adversaries, so that, after you have conquered, you may be crowned.”

I confess my weakness: I do not wish to fight on the hope of victory, lest I lose victory at some time [Col. 0543D].

### CHAPTER 4.—Likewise on the same matter. The same, in his letter to Rusticus the monk, on the labour of monks (Book II, Letter 13).

A town is a prison to me, and solitude paradise. Why should we desire the crowds of cities, who are distinguished by separateness? Moses, so that he might rule the people of the Jews, was trained forty years in the desert; a shepherd of sheep, he became a shepherd of human beings [Col. 0544A] (Exod. III). The Apostles passed from fishing in the lake of Gennesaret to fishing for human beings (Luke V). At that time they had father, net, and boat; upon following the Lord, they immediately left everything, carrying their cross daily and not even having a staff in their hand.

(16, q. 1, c. *Si clericatus*.) I say this so that, if the desire for clerical office tempts you, you may learn what you can teach and offer God a rational sacrifice (Rom. XII), lest you be a soldier before a recruit, or a teacher before a disciple. It is neither my humility nor my measure to judge others or to say anything unfavourable concerning the ministers of churches. Let them retain their own order and rank. If you hold that rank, the book addressed to Nepotian may teach you how you ought to live in it.

Now we are examining the rudiments and morals of monks—specifically of that monk who, trained in liberal studies during youth, placed Christ’s yoke upon his neck. First, it must be considered whether you ought to live alone or with others in a monastery. I prefer that you have the fellowship of holy people, that you not teach yourself, and that you not enter without a teacher upon a road you have never travelled.

### CHAPTER 5.—That a monk should always work. The same, in the same letter (after some passages).

(On Consecration, Dist. 5, c. *Nunquam de manu*.) Let the book of psalms never leave [“withdraw from,” original] your hand or your eyes; learn it word for word. Pray without ceasing. Let your mind be watchful; let body and soul alike be directed toward God, not lying open to wandering thoughts [Col. 0544C]. Conquer anger through patience. Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh. Let your mind not be idle amid various disturbances: if they take their seat in your breast, they will rule you and lead you into the greatest sin.

Do some work, so that the devil may always find you occupied. If the Apostles, though possessing authority to live from the Gospel (1 Cor. IX), worked with their hands in order not to burden anyone (1 Thess. II), and provided refreshment for others, from whom they ought to reap material things in return for spiritual things (1 Cor. IX), why do you not prepare what will serve your own needs?

Either weave a little basket of rushes, or plait a basket from pliant twigs; hoe the soil; divide garden-beds in an even line, and, after vegetable seeds have been sown or plants set out in order, channel water for irrigation. Then stand as observer of these most beautiful verses:

> See how he draws water from the brow of the sloping path;  
> It falls, raising a hoarse murmur over the smooth stones,  
> And with its streams tempers the parched fields.  
> —Virgil, *Georgics* I.103

Graft fruit-bearing trees, either by buds or shoots, so that after a short time you may pluck the sweet fruit of your labour. Make beehives, to which Solomon’s Proverbs send you (Prov. VI). Learn in these small creatures the order and royal discipline of monasteries. Let flax nets for catching fish be woven. Let books also be copied, so that the hand may work for food and the soul be satisfied by reading. “Every idler is in desires” (Prov. XIII, according to the Septuagint).

The monasteries of Egypt maintain this practice: they receive no one without work and labour, not so much for the necessities of food as for the salvation of the soul, lest people wander in destructive thoughts and, like Jerusalem in her fornication, spread their feet for every passer-by [Col. 0545A] (Ezek. XVI).

### CHAPTER 6.—That not all who live in cities will perish. And in what follows.

“What then? Will all who live in cities perish? Look: they enjoy their possessions, minister to churches, go to the baths, do not reject ointments, and yet are constantly on everyone’s lips.” To this I have already replied, and now reply briefly: in the present little work I am not discussing clerics, but instructing a monk.

### CHAPTER 7.—That fugitive monks are not to be promoted to the clergy. Augustine, in his letter to Aurelius (Letter 76).

[Col. 0545B]

(16, q. 1, c. *Legi epistolam*.) I read your kindly letter concerning Donatus and his brother, and for a long time wavered over what I ought to answer. Yet, after thinking again and again about what is useful to the salvation of those whose nourishment in Christ we serve, nothing else could occur to me except that this must not be made a route open to servants of God by which they may more easily suppose themselves chosen for something better if they have become worse.

For their own fall is thereby made easy, and an utterly unworthy injury is done to the clerical order, if deserters from monasteries are chosen for the service of the clergy, while from those who remain in the monastery we are accustomed to admit only the more tested and better men to the clergy. Unless perhaps, as ordinary people say [Col. 0545C], “A bad flute-player is a good lyre-player”; so those same ordinary people will mock us, saying, “A bad monk is a good cleric.”

It is grievous beyond measure if we raise monks to such ruinous pride [“raise,” *surrigamus*, original and Gratian] and consider clerics worthy of so serious an insult. We belong to that number, since sometimes even a good monk scarcely makes a good cleric: he may have sufficient continence yet lack necessary instruction or the integrity of a regular character.

But I believe your Blessedness decided concerning these men, according to our wish, that they had departed from the monastery in order to be useful to their fellow countrymen. Yet that is false. They went away willingly; they deserted willingly, despite our resistance, as far as we could, for their salvation.

### CHAPTER 8.—On the tranquillity of monks. The same, in his letter to Eudoxius (Letter 81).

[Col. 0545D]

To Eudoxius, beloved and most desired brother and fellow-presbyter, and to the brethren who are with you: Augustine, and the brethren who are with me in the Lord, greetings.

Whenever we think of the tranquillity which you have in Christ, we also, though occupied with various and harsh labours, find rest in your charity. For we are one body under one head, so that you may be active in us and we at leisure in you. “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; and if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it” (1 Cor. XII).

We therefore admonish, request, and beseech you through Christ’s most lofty [Col. 0546A] humility and most merciful exaltation: remember us in your holy prayers, which we believe you offer with greater vigilance and sobriety. For the darkness and tumult of secular business often wound and weaken ours. Though we do not count such business as evil, yet so many matters are imposed upon us by those who compel us to go one thousand paces and command us to go another two with them (Matt. V) that we can scarcely breathe.

Nevertheless, we trust that he “before whom the groaning of prisoners comes” (Ps. LXXVIII) will, through your assisting prayers, deliver us from every distress while we persevere in the ministry in which he has deigned to place us, together with the promised reward.

(16, q. 1, c. *Vos autem*.) But we exhort you, brothers, in the Lord to preserve your purpose and persevere to the end. If, however, mother Church requires any service [“by which service,” *qua opera*, original, Victorius, and Pannartius] from you, neither accept it in eager pride nor reject it through enticing indolence. Rather, obey God with a gentle heart, meekly bearing the one who governs you—him who guides the meek in judgment and teaches the meek his ways (Ps. XXIV). Do not prefer your own leisure to the needs of the Church; for if none of the good were willing to minister to her when she labours in childbirth, you would not have found a way to be born.

### Chapter 9.—On the vow of Count Boniface. Augustine, in his letter to Count Boniface (Letter 70).

(17, q. 2, ch. *Nos novimus*.) We know; we are witnesses that at Tubunae we spoke with you concerning your intention and will. You were alone with us—[Col. 0546C] myself and brother Alypius. For I do not suppose that the earthly cares with which you are filled have had such force that they could wholly erase this from your memory. Certainly you wished to abandon all the public affairs in which you were occupied, withdraw into holy leisure, and live the life lived by God’s servants, the monks. (After several verses, near the end.) Therefore, while we rejoiced that you held this purpose, you sailed away and took a wife. For if you did not have a wife, I would say to you what we said at Tubunae: that you should live in the chastity of continence. I would add what we then forbade from being done: that you should now withdraw yourself, so far as you could do so without disturbing the peace of human affairs, from these military matters; that you should devote yourself to this life and to the fellowship of the saints, to which you then wished to devote yourself—where the soldiers [Col. 0546D] of Christ fight in silence, not in order to kill human beings, but to overthrow “principalities and powers and spiritual forces of wickedness” (Eph. 6), that is, the devil and his angels. (After a few words.) But your wife is an obstacle to my exhorting you toward this life, since without her consent you may not live continently.

### Chapter 10.—A marriage is not dissolved if the woman married him unaware of her husband’s vow. The same author, in the same letter.

Although you ought not to have taken her after those words of yours at Tubunae, she nevertheless married you innocently and simply, knowing none of these things. And would that you could persuade her to continence, so that without hindrance you might render to God what you recognize that you owe. But if you cannot prevail with her, at least preserve [Col. 0547A] marital chastity, and pray to God, who delivers you from necessities, that what you cannot do now you may someday be able to do. Yet, to love God, not to love the world, to keep faith and seek peace even amid warfare, if you still need to be involved in it, to make good works from worldly goods and not do evil works for the sake of worldly goods—none of this is hindered by a wife, nor ought she to hinder it.

Love has commanded me to write these things to you, dearest son: the love by which I love you according to God, not according to this age; for, reflecting also on what is written, “Rebuke a wise person, and he will love you; rebuke a fool, and he will add hatred of you” (Prov. 9), I ought certainly to think of you not as foolish but as wise.

### Chapter 11.—On the peace of monks. Decree of Pope Saint Gregory (Book VII, indiction 1, Letter 18, to Bishop Marinianus).

[Col. 0547B]

(18, q. 2, ch. *Quam sit necessarium*.) How necessary it is to provide for the peace of monasteries and to make provision for their enduring security is shown by the office formerly exercised by us in the governance of a cenobium [by you, in the original]. Since we know that in very many monasteries monks have endured many injuries and burdens from prelates, the care of our brotherhood ought by wholesome regulation to arrange for their future peace, so that those living in them in God’s service may, with his grace assisting, persevere with free minds.

But lest anyone, because of a custom that especially requires correction, presume to inflict any trouble upon [Col. 0547C] monks, it is necessary that what we have taken care to enumerate below be observed by the zealous care of the brotherhood of bishops in such a way that from these matters no further occasion for disturbance can be found. Therefore, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—whose office we hold in presiding over this Roman Church—we forbid any bishop or layperson henceforth to presume, by any means or on any pretext, to diminish the revenues, possessions, charters, cells, or estates belonging to monasteries, or to employ any frauds or intrusions against them.

But if any dispute should arise between land coming to the share of their churches [Col. 0547D] and monasteries, and cannot be peacefully settled, it shall be concluded without wilful delay before chosen abbots and other God-fearing Fathers, with the holy Gospels placed in their midst. When the abbot of any community dies, no outsider shall be ordained, but one from that same community, chosen by the unanimous fellowship of the brethren according to their own will; and the person chosen shall be ordained without fraud or any venality. If they cannot find among themselves a suitable person, they shall diligently choose someone from other monasteries to be ordained in the same manner.

Once an abbot has been appointed, no person is to be set over him on any pretext, unless there are manifest crimes—may this not occur!—which the sacred canons show ought to be punished. Likewise, it must be observed that monks may not be taken away against the abbot’s will for ordination in other monasteries, [Col. 0548A] for sacred orders, or for the office of cleric.

### Chapter 12.—On the same matter. Gregory, chapter 87, to Castorius, Bishop of Rimini (Book IV, Letter 43).

(18, q. 2, ch. *Luminoso*.) On the report of Abbot Luminosus, we have learned that monks in very many monasteries have endured many injuries and burdens from prelates. Therefore the care of your brotherhood ought by wholesome regulation to arrange for their future peace, so that those living in them in God’s service may, with his grace assisting, persevere with free minds.

### Chapter 13.—That public masses are not to be celebrated in cenobia. Gregory.

We altogether [Col. 0548B] forbid public masses to be celebrated in a cenobium, lest any opportunity be afforded to the people to gather in the retreats and dwellings of God’s servants, because this is not beneficial for their souls. Nor may a bishop dare to set up a chair there, exercise any power of command, or perform any ordination whatsoever, however slight, unless requested by the abbot. Thus monks shall always remain under the authority of their abbots and, once vexations and every burden have been removed, shall forever accomplish the divine work with the utmost devotion of mind. Farewell, excellent Father; remember us.

### Chapter 14.—That a bishop should not burden a monastery. The same Gregory (indiction 1, Book VII, Letter 18, at the end).

(18, q. 2, ch. *Visitandi*.) For the purpose of visitation and exhortation, the bishop of the city may come to the monastery whenever he wishes. But the bishop shall fulfil there the office of charity in such a way that the monastery incurs no burden.

### Chapter 15.—On children offered by their parents. Letter of Gregory III to Augustine, bishop of the English (Letter 4, vol. 13, ch. 7 to Boniface).

(20, q. 1, ch. *Addidisti*.) You further asked whether, if a father or mother has entrusted a son or daughter within the enclosure of a monastery to regular discipline during the years of childhood, they may, after reaching the years of puberty, leave and be joined in marriage. We entirely prohibit this; for it is wicked that children offered to God by their parents should be given free rein to pleasures.

### Chapter 16.—On monks and virgins who do not keep their profession. Letter of Siricius, chapter 6 (Letter 1).

[Col. 0548D]

Furthermore, you report that certain monks and nuns, having cast aside their profession of holiness, have plunged into such wantonness that they first secretly mingled in illicit and sacrilegious defilement, as though under the pretext of monasteries. Then, driven into open sin by the despair of their consciences, they freely begot children from unlawful embraces—an act condemned both by public laws and ecclesiastical ordinances. We therefore command that these shameless and detestable persons be expelled from the company of monasteries and the assemblies of churches, so that, confined in their own places of detention, they may lament so great a crime with continual mourning and be refined by the purifying fire of repentance; thus, even if only at death and in view of mercy alone, [Col. 0549A] pardon may come to their aid through the grace of communion.

### Chapter 17.—On consecrated virgins, if they have fallen. From the decree of Pope Innocent I, chapter 12 (Letter 2 to Bishop Victricius).

(27, q. 1, ch. *Quae Christo*.) Likewise, women who are spiritually married to Christ and veiled by a priest, if afterward they either marry publicly or are secretly defiled, are not to be admitted to perform penance unless the man to whom they have joined themselves has departed this life. For if this rule is observed among human beings—so that any woman who marries another while her husband is alive is regarded as an adulteress and is not permitted to undertake penance unless one of them has died—how much more must it be maintained in the case of her who had first joined herself to an immortal Bridegroom and afterward chose to pass over to human marriage?

### Chapter 18.—On un-veiled virgins, if they go astray. In the same place, chapter 13.

(27, q. 1, ch. *Hae vero quae*.) But those who, though not yet covered by the sacred veil, have nevertheless always professed that they were continuing in a virginal purpose—if they should marry, although they have not been veiled—must undergo penance for some time, because they were bound to their Bridegroom by the Lord. For if among human beings a contract made in good faith is customarily not dissolved for any reason, how much more can this promise, which they have covenanted with God, not be dissolved without punishment?

### Chapter 19.—By what penance one who abandons the purpose of a monk should be cleansed. Leo, to Rusticus, Bishop of Narbonne (Letter 92, chapter 12, or Inquiry 14).

[Col. 0549C] (20, q. 3, ch. *Propositum*.) The purpose of a monk, undertaken by his own judgment or will, cannot be abandoned without sin. For what anyone vows to God, that person must also pay (Deut. 23; Ps. 49). Therefore one who, abandoning the profession of a solitary life, has fallen away to military service or marriage must be cleansed through the satisfaction of public penance. For although military service can be innocent and marriage honourable, it is nevertheless a transgression to have abandoned the choice of better things.

### Chapter 20.—That girls who abandon a voluntary purpose of virginity sin. In the same place, chapter 13.

(20, q. 1, ch. *Puellae*.) Girls who have undertaken the purpose and habit of virginity not under compulsion from parental authority but by their own voluntary judgment, if they later choose marriage, violate their undertaking, even if [Col. 0549D] the grace of consecration has not yet come to them [“even if consecration has not occurred,” original and Gratian]. They would certainly not have been deprived of that gift if they had remained in their purpose.

### Chapter 21.—On consecrated women, if they marry. In the same place, chapter 14.

There can be no doubt that a great crime is committed where both the purpose is abandoned and consecration violated. For if human agreements cannot be trampled upon with impunity, what awaits those [“them,” variant] who have corrupted the covenants of the divine sacrament?

### Chapter 22.—That monks may everywhere minister in a priestly office. From the council of Pope Boniface, the fourth after Saint Gregory.

(16, q. 1, ch. *Sunt nonnuli*.) Supported by no doctrine, certain persons, with the greatest rashness and inflamed more by zeal of bitterness than [Col. 0550A] by love, assert that monks, because they are dead to the world and live to God, are unworthy of priestly office and cannot grant penance or Christianity, nor absolve through the grace conferred in priestly office. But they are utterly mistaken. For if the ancient adversaries were proclaiming truth on this point, blessed Gregory, equal to the Apostolic See and eminent in monastic life, could never have ascended to the supreme dignity, to whom indeed the highest authority was granted for exercising the office of opening, binding, and loosing.

Likewise Augustine, disciple of that most holy Gregory and eminent preacher to the English, and blessed Martin of Pannonia, and very many other most holy men resplendent in the precious habit of monks, would never have been pledged with the episcopal ring. Yet, because [Col. 0550B] they were monks, they are reported to have exercised the aforementioned offices. Nor did Benedict, teacher of monks, in any way forbid such a thing; rather, he decreed only that they should be free from secular affairs—a requirement emphatically imposed, by apostolic teaching and the ordinances of all the holy Fathers, not only upon monks but also upon canons. Indeed, by the clear examples of the aforesaid Fathers, both are everywhere commanded, on the most evident grounds, to be dead to the world.

It is therefore dangerous to oppose the institutions and examples of so many Fathers. We believe that the authority and office of binding and loosing are by God’s work not unworthily exercised by monk-priests, if they are worthily raised to this ministry. Whoever carefully considers the status, habit, and authority of monks affirms this without hesitation and [Col. 0550C] plainly. For example, *angelus* in Greek means in Latin *nuntius*, “messenger.” Therefore monk-priests and canons, who daily proclaim God’s holy commandments, are not inappropriately called angels. But every angelic order is said to be the more exalted in dignity the more closely it beholds the brightness of God.

For, like the cherubim, monks are clothed with six wings. Two, indeed, are shown by plausible arguments in the cowl by which the head is covered. We say that the part of the tunic extending to the arms constitutes two wings; and finally, that part by which the body is covered is most certainly said to complete the number of six wings. Therefore we command that those who contend that priests of the monastic profession [Col. 0550D] must wholly be excluded from the office of priestly authority be restrained from such wicked attempts in the future, because the higher anyone is, the more powerful that person is.

### Chapter 23.—That a monk should not become a defender. Pelagius to Antonina, Patrician, and Decia (in the fragments of Pelagius II).

(16, q. 1, ch. *De praesentium*.) Let there be no distress of mind concerning the present office-holder’s not having been made a defender; for I truly find it exceedingly bitter that persons should be led from this profession into that office, in which they can by no means fulfil what monks have promised to God. For the habit of the one and the office of the other are wholly different. There are rest, prayer, and manual labour; here are the handling of cases, meetings, [Col. 0551A] proceedings, public lawsuits, and whatever the institutions of the Church or the needs of petitioners demand.

May God, however, grant that those whom you nurture in this habit or who grow up in monasteries may be such that, when they have reached mature age and proved life, they can be promoted not to the offices of litigation but to the priesthood.

### Chapter 24.—What sort of person should be chosen abbot, and by whom. Pelagius to the subdeacon Melleus [Mellitus].

(18, q. 2, ch. *Abbatem*.) We wish that the person ordained abbot in that same monastery [place] should be the one whom the choice of his community and monks, the lord of the property, and—what is more important—the order of life and merit require to be ordained.

### Chapter 25.—That a double monastery is not to be established. From the Seventh Synod, chapter 11 (seventh synodal gathering, chapter 20).

[Col. 0551B] (18, q. 2, ch. *Diffinimus*.) We decree henceforth that a double monastery is by no means to be established, because it becomes a scandal, that is, a stumbling block, to many. But if any persons wish to renounce the world together with their relatives and pursue monastic life, men should enter a cenobium of men and women a monastery of women; for in this God is pleased. Those double monasteries which have existed until now shall be organized in accordance with the rule and command of Saint Father Basil.

Monks and nuns shall not dwell in one monastery. For cohabitation leads to adultery if a monk has access to a nun, or a nun to a monk, for private conversation. A monk shall not sleep in a women’s monastery, nor shall he dine alone with a nun. When necessities of life are brought from the men’s side to the nuns living under the rule, the abbess of the women’s monastery shall receive them outside the gate, accompanied by an elderly nun. Further, if a monk should wish to see one of his female relatives, he shall speak with her in the abbess’s presence, using few and brief words, and shall quickly leave her.

### Chapter 26.—On those who were tonsured and veiled before the lawful age. From the Council of Mainz, attended by Emperor Charles and Archbishop Richulf, in the cloister of Saint Alban, chapter 20.

(*De regularibus*, title 31, ch. *Si quis*.) If anyone has been tonsured before the lawful age without the consent of his parents, and those parents do not lodge a complaint within a year with the ruler, their own bishop, or the lord’s envoy, he shall remain in that clerical state. But if, after the lawful age, someone has been made a cleric by force and has not lodged a complaint within a year with the aforesaid persons, he shall remain in the clerical state, as was said above of those persons. But if the aforesaid persons lodge a complaint within a year, those who made them clerics without their parents shall legally compensate them for whatever they inflicted against them.

Whether the person tonsured before the lawful age should remain in that tonsure or not shall lie within the parents’ authority. But if the tonsured person was another’s slave, the lord shall be legally compensated for whatever was done against him concerning his slave. Whether the tonsured person should remain [Col. 0552A] in that tonsure shall lie within his owner’s authority. But if free persons have been tonsured before or after the lawful age in the manner specified above, and have attained ecclesiastical ranks, they shall be compelled to remain in those ranks. But if a slave tonsured in the manner specified above attains ecclesiastical ranks, his owner shall be legally compensated, and, once restored to him, the slave shall remain in his rank. The same is to be observed concerning girls who are to be veiled.

### Chapter 27.—On those whom one or both parents have entrusted to holy religion. From the Council of Toledo, chapter 6 (Toledo X).

Since the outcome of lax conduct has hitherto sometimes caused an honourable decree of constitution to waver, we set forth an edict so that what is held by the authority of an indissoluble sanction may not be thought dissoluble. Therefore, whatever uncertainty may arise from ambiguity must clearly be rejected, so that henceforth nothing may remain that wavers in doubt.

(20, q. 2, *Si in qualibet*.) Therefore, if at any younger age one or both parents have given their children of either sex tonsure of religion or the clothing due to religion—certainly even where the children received it unwillingly or unknowingly—and have not at once repudiated it when it appeared upon their children, but have allowed those same children to retain such things in their presence, before the Church, and openly in the assembly, those children shall never afterward be permitted to return to secular dress. Rather, once they are shown to have had tonsure or religious clothing at any time, they shall immediately be recalled to the observance and habit of religion and compelled to serve under the strict discipline of this observance.

Parents, however, shall have permission to entrust their children to religion only until the children’s twelfth year of age. Afterward, whether the decision is by parental will or by their own devotion, the children may adopt the observance of religion through their own solitary vow. Whoever is discovered to have committed transgression by removing the tonsure or taking up secular clothing shall receive the censure of excommunication and shall always adhere to religion.

### Chapter 28.—On those who have once been assigned to the clergy or sought the monastic life. From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 7 (session 15).

(20, q. 3, ch. *Eos qui semel*.) We decree that those who have once been assigned to the clergy or sought the life of monks are to enter neither military service nor any worldly rank. Those who attempt this and do not perform penance so as to return to what they first chose for God’s sake are to be anathematized.

### Chapter 29.—That canons living among monks must either become monks or be compelled to live canonically. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 17 (Mainz I under Leo III, chapter 21).

We command that every bishop know, in each monastery, how many canons each abbot has in his monastery. Both shall jointly make full provision that, if they wish to become monks, they live according to the rule; otherwise, they are to live wholly according to the canonical rule.

### Chapter 30.—That paternal devotion or one’s own profession makes a monk. From the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 48.

[Col. 0553A]

(20, q. 1, ch. *Monachum*.) Either paternal devotion or one’s own profession makes a monk. Whichever of these has bound him [variant: “has been alleged”] shall hold him bound. Accordingly, we bar such persons from returning to the world and prohibit every return to secular life.

### Chapter 31.—On clerics who falsely claim to be monks. From the same council (*Capitularies*, Book I, chapter 77).

(*De regularibus*, title 31, ch. *Ut clerici*.) Clerics who falsely claim, in habit and name, to be monks when they are not are by every means to be corrected and reformed, so that they may be either genuine monks or genuine canons.

### Chapter 32.—That a monk may not make a vow without his abbot’s consent. From the sayings of Basil.

[Col. 0553B] (20, q. 4, ch. *Monacho*.) A monk may not make a vow without the consent of his abbot. But if he does make one, it must be broken.

### Chapter 33.—On virgins who, before age twelve and without the knowledge of their *mundiburni* [guardians; “patrons,” original], have placed the veil upon themselves. From the Council of Tribur, chapter 24.

Virgins who, before twelve years of age and without the knowledge of their *mundiburni* [guardians; *patroni*, “patrons,” original], have placed the sacred veil upon their heads, and whose *mundiburni* have consented by silence for a year and a day, shall remain in their holy purpose. If those *mundiburni* make a claim on their behalf within the aforesaid year and day, their petition shall be granted, unless perhaps, touched by the fear of God [masculine *tacti* in the text], the virgins remain in religious habit with their permission.

### Chapter 34.—That a cleric, once he has read in a church, shall thereafter remain there. From the African Council, chapter 57.

[Col. 0553C]

Likewise, it was decided that whoever has read even once in a church may not be claimed for the clergy by another church.

### Chapter 35.—On men and women transgressing a sacred profession. From the Sixth Council of Toledo, chapter 7.

(20, q. 3, ch. *Proclivis*.) The course toward pleasure is downward-sloping, and nature imitates vices. Therefore, whoever among men or women has once voluntarily put on religious dress, or if a man has been assigned to the choir of the church, or a woman has been or is assigned to a monastery of girls, shall in either sex, if a transgressor, be compelled unwillingly to return to the profession: the man shall be tonsured, and the girl shall enter the monastery [“return to the monastery,” original].

But if deserters wish to remain so under any protection, they shall by priestly sentence be regarded as excluded from the body of Christians, so that they have no place in common [“of communion,” original]. The universal synod has likewise long ago decreed that widows who abandon their profession or habit are to be condemned by the foregoing sentence.

### Chapter 36.—At what time the sacred veil should be imposed upon consecrated virgins. From the decree of Pope Gelasius, chapter 12 (chapter 14, Letter 9 to the bishops through Lucania).

(20, q. 1, ch. *Devotis Deo virginibus*.) The sacred veil shall by no means be imposed upon virgins devoted to God except at Epiphany, during the Easter Octave (*in Albis paschalibus*), or on the feasts of the apostles; nor before twenty-five years of age—unless, as has been said concerning baptism, they are seized by grave illness, lest they leave this world without this gift. If they ask for it, they are not to be refused.

### Chapter 37.—That it does not harm a bishop if, from necessity, he veils a virgin before her twenty-fifth year. From the Council of Milevis, chapter 26 (Carthage III, chapter 4; African Council, chapter 93).

[Col. 0554A]

Likewise, it was decided that if any bishop has veiled, or veils, a virgin under twenty-five years of age because the chastity of her virginity is in danger—whether from fear of a powerful suitor or a ravisher, or because she has been afflicted by some pressing apprehension of death, lest she die un-veiled—or because her parents or those responsible for her care request it, the council’s decree concerning this number of years shall not prejudice him.

### Chapter 38.—On nuns who presume to veil others. From the decrees of Pope Eutychian, chapter 13 (in the fragments, chapter 2).

[Col. 0554B] Moreover, in certain places we have found an established practice full of folly and contrary to ecclesiastical authority: namely, that certain abbesses and some nuns presume, against what is lawful, to impose the veil upon widows and virgin girls. Consequently, some women who have been unjustly veiled think that they may more freely serve their carnal desires and fulfil their own wills.

(20, q. 2, ch. *Statuimus*.) Therefore we decree that if, after this definition, any abbess or nun should break out into such audacity as to presume to veil either a widow or a virgin girl, she shall be subjected to canonical judgment until satisfaction has been made.

### Chapter 39.—At what age virgins should be veiled. From the decrees of Pope Pius.

[Col. 0554C] (20, q. 1, ch. *Virgines*.) Virgins are not to be veiled before twenty-five years of age, unless the necessity of endangered virginal chastity requires it. Nor are they to be consecrated at any time except at Epiphany, during the Easter Octave, and on the feasts of the apostles, unless death is imminent.

### Chapter 40.—That a betrothed girl may not be given to another man; but may, if she wishes, enter a monastery. From the decrees of Pope Eusebius (in the fragments, chapter 1).

(27, q. 2, ch. *Desponsatam*.) Parents may not give a betrothed girl to another man; nevertheless, she may choose a monastery if she wishes.

### Chapter 41.—That no unknown person be quickly received into a monastery of monks. From the Council of Toledo, chapter 5 (*Capitularies*, Book V, chapter 227).

[Col. 0554D] (17, q. 2, ch. *Si quis incognitus*.) If an unknown person wishes to enter a monastery, the monastic habit shall not be granted to him before three years. If, within three years, he is claimed by his master as a slave, freedman, or colonus, he shall be restored to that master with all that he brought, provided that assurance of impunity is given. But if he has not been claimed within three years, he may not afterward be claimed unless he is so far away that he cannot be found; yet the slave’s master may receive only those things which he brought into the monastery.

### Chapter 42.—On consecrated virgins who have decided to move to another monastery for a stricter life. From the Council of Tribur, chapter 26.

(12, q. 4, ch. *Virgines*.) If consecrated virgins decide, for the benefit of their souls and for a stricter life, to go to another monastery [Col. 0555A] and determine to remain there, the synod permits it. But if they seek another place in flight from discipline, they shall be compelled to return.

### Chapter 43.—In what clothing virgins should come for consecration. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 11.

(Distinction 23, ch. *Sanctimonialis*.) When a virgin dedicated to holy life is presented to her bishop for consecration, she shall be dressed in garments suited to the profession and holy life which she will always wear.

### Chapter 44.—That a slave may not become a monk without his master’s knowledge. From the Council of Arles, chapter 3.

It was decided that no slave may be received into a monastery to become a monk without the consent of his own master. We decree that anyone who violates this ordinance shall be suspended from communion, [Col. 0555B] lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed.

### Chapter 45.—That no one may, on grounds of religion, teach a slave to despise his master. From the Second Council of Braga, chapter 47 (Martin of Braga, chapter 47).

(17, q. 4, ch. *Si quis ser[vum]*.) If anyone, under the pretext of religion, teaches another person’s slave to despise his master and to withdraw from his service, that person shall be rebuked with the utmost severity and compelled to do penance.

### Chapter 46.—On fugitive clerics or monks. From the decrees of Pope Leo.

It was decided that a fugitive cleric or monk who abandons discipline should be brought back as a contemner.

### Chapter 47.—On those who, after once being tonsured, become laypeople. From the Fifth Council of Toledo, chapter 45 (Toledo IV, chapter 54).

[Col. 0555C]

All laypeople who, on receiving penance, have tonsured themselves and then, transgressing again, have become laypeople, shall, when apprehended by their bishop, be recalled to the penance which they abandoned. If any are irrevocable through penance and do not return when admonished, they shall truly be condemned before the Church as apostates by a sentence of anathema.

Likewise, those who were tonsured with their parents’ approval, or who, after losing their parents, devoted themselves to religion of their own accord and afterward adopted secular dress, shall be apprehended by the priest, perform penance first, and be recalled to the observance of religion. If they refuse to return, they shall truly be subjected to a sentence of anathema as apostates. The same rule shall be observed also [Col. 0555D] for widows, consecrated virgins, and penitent women who put on the habit of holy women and afterward either changed their clothing or entered marriage.

### Chapter 48.—That a slave may not be received into a monastery without his master’s knowledge. From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 4 (session 15).

(16, q. 1, ch. *Qui vere*.) No one may receive a slave into monasteries under the pretext of making him a monk without the knowledge of his master.

### Chapter 49.—That those consecrated to God may not contract marital unions. From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 16.

(27, q. 1, ch. *Si qua virgo*.) A virgin who has consecrated herself to God, and likewise a monk, may not contract marital unions. If they are found to have done this, they shall be excommunicated. But concerning those who confess, we decree that the bishop of the place shall have authority to grant mercy and humane consideration.

### Chapter 50.—That those who marry women dedicated to holy life shall remain without hope of marriage. From the letter of Pope Paschal, chapter 11.

(27, q. 1, ch. *Hi ergo*.) Those who knowingly join themselves in marriage to women dedicated to holy life, to the injury of Christ, shall be separated according to the censure of Christian zeal. They shall never be permitted to be bound in a marital union, but while they live they shall grievously afflict themselves in the laments of penance.

### Chapter 51.—On consecrated virgins who have violated their commitment. From the decree of Pope Gelasius, chapter 20 (Letter 9 to the bishops of Lucania, chapter 22).

[Col. 0556B]

(27, q. 1, ch. *Virginibus*.) We have learned that certain men rashly associate themselves with consecrated virgins and, after a purpose has been dedicated to God, enter into incestuous compacts and sacrilegious unions. It is right that they be immediately excluded from holy communion and not received at all except through public and approved penance. Nevertheless, if they have repented worthily, viaticum is not to be denied to them as they depart from this world [the original reads *tamen*, “nevertheless”].

### Chapter 52.—That widows may not impose the veil upon themselves without consulting their bishop, and that priests may not presume to impose it upon them, since not even bishops may do so. From the Council of Rouen, chapter 119.

It was decreed that widows ought not to be veiled. It was likewise decreed that if any priest henceforth proves a contumacious transgressor of this rule—that is, if he presumes to veil any widows, though this is not permitted even to bishops—he shall incur the peril of losing his rank. Likewise, concerning virgin girls not to be veiled by priests, it was decreed that anyone attempting this shall be condemned as a transgressor of the canons.

### Chapter 53.—That widows are under no blessing to be veiled. From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, chapter 21 (chapter 23, Letter 9 to the bishops through Lucania).

For above we judged it necessary to discuss more fully that widows are not to be veiled under any blessing. If, by their own will and changeable mind, they trample upon the chastity of their former marriage which they have professed, it concerns their own peril by what satisfaction they ought to appease God, [Col. 0556D] because, according to the Apostle, they have made void their first faith (1 Tim. 5). For just as, according to the Apostle, they were by no means forbidden to marry if they perhaps could not remain continent (1 Cor. 7), so, having deliberated with themselves, they ought to have kept the pledge of chastity promised to God.

But we ought not to lay any snare upon such persons; we should only set before them exhortations concerning eternal reward and the punishments of divine judgment, so that our conscience may be clear and their intention may render account to God for itself. We must indeed beware of what the blessed Apostle Paul testifies concerning their morals and actions (1 Tim. 5), which we refrain from explaining more fully lest the unstable sex seem less deterred than merely admonished.

### Chapter 54.—On widows who have once received the veil of consecrated life. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 3.

[Col. 0557A]

(27, q. 1, *Viduas quae*.) The holy synod decrees that widows who of their own free will receive from the altar the veil of consecrated life shall remain in that purpose. For we decree that it is not lawful, after they have once consecrated themselves to the Lord under the veil [this is absent in Gratian], and made offerings among the veiled women, for them to be permitted again to lie to the Holy Spirit.

### Chapter 55.—That no one may attempt to veil widows. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 6 (Council of Tribur, chapter 25).

(27, q. 1, ch. *Viduas*. Gelasius, chapter 13, Letter 9.) Let no bishop attempt to veil widows (1 Cor. 7), as is laid down in chapter 13 of the decrees of Pope Gelasius, [Col. 0557B] since neither divine authority nor the form of the canons has granted this. If she has professed continence by her own will, as is read in chapter 21 of the same Gelasius, her intention shall render account to God for itself; because, just as she was not at all forbidden to marry, according to the Apostle, if she could not remain continent, so, having deliberated with herself, she ought to keep the pledge of chastity promised to God.

But we, supported by the authority of the Fathers, enact and freely judge in this sacred assembly that if she has voluntarily placed upon herself a veil, even though it has not been consecrated, and has offered an oblation to God in the Church among the veiled women, whether she wishes it or not she must thereafter retain the habit of holy life, even if she wishes to affirm by oath that she put the veil upon herself with such an understanding and intention that she could remove it again.

### CHAP. 56.—On noblewomen who, after veiling themselves, later take pleasure in remaining at home amid luxuries. From the council held at Aachen in the presence of Louis the Pious, ch. 6 (in the appended capitularies, addition 2, ch. 15).

Concerning noblewomen who, after losing their husbands, suddenly take the veil and take pleasure in remaining in their own homes, alleging various necessities—concerning whom the matter has long since been discussed and decided in other assemblies before Your Serenity—we decree that they are to be admonished and instructed by the bishops with greater and diligent care, so that they may provide for their own salvation and may not, by living so indiscreetly, by exercising their own harmful liberty, and by wandering about in various places, incur danger to their souls. They should always keep before their eyes that apostolic saying: “The widow who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives” [Col. 0557D] (1 Tim. 5).

### CHAP. 57.—On those who take veiled women consecrated to God in marriage. From the Council of Orléans, ch. 23 (ch. 23, Council of Tribur).

(27, q. 1, *Si quis sacro*.) If anyone takes in marriage a woman consecrated by the sacred veil, and, after a purpose dedicated to God, mingles incestuous and sacrilegious unions, as is read in ch. 20 of the constitutions of Pope Gelasius, it is immediately right that he be cast out from holy communion and not at all received back except through public and proven penitence. Nevertheless, if they repent, the viaticum is not to be denied them when they are passing from this world. In ch. 16 of the Council of Chalcedon, those who commit this act are excommunicated; but mercy is to be bestowed, by the bishop’s authority, upon those who confess.

In ch. 6 of the letter of Pope Siricius, [Col. 0558A] it is ruled that veiled women and women consecrated to God who, casting aside their purpose of holiness, secretly join themselves in sacrilegious defilement and publicly and freely beget children through unlawful embraces, are to be expelled from the community of monasteries and the assemblies of churches—“shameless and detestable persons,” in the original and in Gratian—in order that, shut up in prisons, they may lament so great a crime with unceasing mourning. Therefore, by the word of the Lord and canonical authority, we command in this holy synod that they be separated in every way and bound by oath thereafter not to live together under one roof, nor enjoy familiar conversation except in church or in public, nor have any matter in common from which suspicion of seductive desire or scandal from a lustful act might justly arise. If there are things [Col. 0558B] that must be divided between them, let them divide them; let each provide for his or her own affairs; and let the incestuous man remain without hope of marriage.

### CHAP. 58.—On widows who have violated their professed continence. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, ch. 4.

(27, q. 1, ch. *Sicut*.) Just as the reward of chastity is good, so it must be guarded with greater observance and command: thus, if any widows, even though still in their younger years, yet left by their husband at a mature age, have devoted themselves to God and, putting aside secular clothing, have appeared in a religious habit under the witness of the bishop and the Church, but later have entered secular marriages, they shall, according to the Apostle (1 Tim. 5), incur condemnation [“shall have condemnation”], because they have appeared to have made void [“have ventured to make void,” alternatively; *nisae*, in the original] the pledge of chastity which they vowed to God [Col. 0558C].

Such persons are therefore to be separated from the communion of Christians and are not even to share a meal with Christians. For if married women are guilty of adultery when they are liable to their husbands [“are subject to guilt toward their husbands,” in the original], how much more shall widows who have altered God’s religious service be marked with the crime of adultery if they corrupt, by lustful will [“pleasure,” in the original], the devotion which they offered freely and not under compulsion to God, and pass into second marriages? Even if they have been overpowered by someone through an assault of violence, yet afterward consent to remain in marriage with the ravisher or violent man through delight in lust, they are to remain liable to the condemnation stated above. Of such women the Apostle says: “For when they have become wanton against Christ, [Col. 0558D] they wish to marry, having condemnation because they have made void their first pledge” (1 Tim. 5).

### CHAP. 59.—On the same matter. From the decrees of Pope Zephyrinus, ch. 4 (Council of Aachen, ch. 35).

Let widows not live in pleasures, but live under the authority of the bishop according to the Apostle. “Command,” he says, “that widows be irreproachable. Let a widow be enrolled who is not less than sixty years old, having testimony in good works: if she has brought up children” (1 Tim. 5), and the rest. “Avoid younger widows. For when they have become wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, having condemnation because they have made void their first pledge; at the same time they are idle, speaking what they ought not. Therefore I desire younger women to marry, bear children, [Col. 0559A] be mistresses of households, and give the adversary no occasion for reproach. For already some have turned back after Satan” (ibid.).

### CHAP. 60.—That women whose husbands have died should not veil themselves quickly. From the Council of Orléans, ch. 5 (Capitularies, book I, ch. 102).

Concerning women who lose their husbands, it is resolved that they should not, as hitherto, veil themselves indiscriminately, but should wait thirty days after their husband’s death; and, after the thirtieth day, they should choose what they ought to choose by the counsel of their bishop, or, if the bishop is absent, by the counsel of other religious priests and their friends. And the prince is to be petitioned by the sacred assembly that those who have performed public penance, and women who lose their husbands, may be granted leave by his authority to deliberate what they are to do; and we decree that they be protected and that chapters be made especially [Col. 0559B] concerning them and inserted among the chapters of secular law.

### CHAP. 61.—That the profession of widowhood be made before the bishop. From the Council of Orange, ch. 6 (First Council of Orange, ch. 27).

(27, q. 1, ch. *Viduitatis*.) We decree that a profession of preserving widowhood, made before the bishop in the secretarium, with the widow’s garment put on before the bishop, is not to be violated; and that a woman who deserts such a profession is deservedly to be condemned.

### CHAP. 62.—That no one should forbid widows to marry if they wish. From the Third Council of Toledo, ch. 10.

(32, q. 2, ch. *Hoc sanctum*.) For the benefit of chastity, which ought especially to advance through the exhortation of the council, with the assent of our glorious lord King Reccared, [Col. 0559C] this holy council confirms [“affirms,” in the original and in Gratian] that widows who choose to preserve chastity are not to be compelled by any force to enter repeated marriages. But if, before professing continence, they choose to marry, let them marry those whom they themselves freely wish to have as husbands. The same condition is to apply to virgins: they are not to be compelled to take husbands against the will either of their parents or of themselves. But if anyone hinders the purpose of chastity of a widow or virgin, he shall be excluded from holy communion and from the thresholds of the church.

### CHAP. 63.—That widows departing from their purpose of widowhood are to be excommunicated. From a letter of St Gregory the Pope sent to Boniface (Capitularies, addition 4, ch. 65, more fully).

[Col. 0559D] (27, q. 1, ch. *Viduas*.) Concerning widows departing from the purpose of widowhood, about whom, dearest brother, your charity wished to consult us: I believe that you know from Saint Paul and many holy Fathers that, unless they are converted, they have long ago been condemned. We also judge by apostolic authority that they are to be condemned and excluded from the communion of the faithful and from the thresholds of the church, until they obey their bishops and return, willingly or unwillingly, to the good which they began.

But concerning un-veiled virgins if they go astray, we have a decree of our predecessor Pope Innocent of holy memory as follows: “Those women who, though not yet covered by the sacred veil, nevertheless have always professed that they would remain in a virginal purpose—although they have not been veiled—if they marry, must perform penance for some time, [Col. 0560A] because their promise was held by the Lord. For if among human beings a contract made in good faith is customarily dissolved for no reason, how much more can this promise, which she has covenanted with God, not be dissolved without punishment,” etc.

For if virgins not yet veiled are thus punished by public penance and excluded from the assembly of the faithful until satisfaction has been made, how much more must widows—who are of more perfect age and more mature wisdom and judgment, have very often experienced the society of husbands, have assumed the religious habit, and at last have apostatized and returned to their former vomit (2 Pet. 2)—be expelled by us and by all the faithful from the thresholds of the church and from the assembly of the faithful until satisfaction, and handed over to prisons, [Col. 0560B] so that, according to the blessed Apostle Paul, “delivering such a person to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord” (1 Cor. 5). For concerning such people the Lord also speaks through Moses (Deut. 13), saying: “Remove evil from your midst.” And concerning them He says through the Prophet: “The righteous man shall rejoice when he sees vengeance; he shall wash his hands in the blood of the sinner” (Ps. 57). For of such persons and their like, and of those consenting with them, it is said: “Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are liable to judgment” (Rom. 1).

### CHAP. 64.—That veiled widows are not to enter marriages. From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, to the bishops of Sicily, ch. 9.

(27, q. 1, ch. *Neque viduas*.) Nor do we permit widows to enter marriages [Col. 0560C] who have remained in a religious purpose through long observance. Likewise, we forbid virgins to marry who have happened to spend many years of their life in a monastery.

### CHAP. 65.—On a widow who, under the pretext of religion, put on a veil for a time. From a letter of Pope Nicholas, ch. 5 (among the rescripts of Nicholas I, title 13, ch. 1).

(Dist. 27, ch. *Quod interrogasti*.) Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy fellow brother Adalwin, archbishop of the holy Church of Vienne [Vinanensis].

What you asked concerning a woman who, after the death of her husband, put the sacred veil upon her head and pretended under that veil to be a religious woman, but afterward [Col. 0560D] returned to marriage: it seems good to me, since by hypocrisy she wished to disturb the ecclesiastical rule and did not lawfully remain in her vow, that she should do penance for that wicked deception, return to what she promised, and resume the sacred service which she began. For if we consent that everyone may feign all ecclesiastical sacraments according to his own wish rather than perform them truly, the whole ecclesiastical order will be disturbed; the rights of the Catholic faith will not stand; and the sacred canons will not be duly observed.

What benefit was it to Simon Magus falsely to receive sacred baptism and pretend that he would remain in Christianity, when, after his deception had been exposed by the Apostle, what would happen to him was foretold? For he says: “May your money perish with you, for your heart is not right before [Col. 0561A] God. Therefore repent of this wickedness of yours, and pray to God, if perhaps this thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity” (Acts 8). Therefore, unless such persons come to their senses, we judge that they are to be struck with the spiritual sword. For it is not lawful to lie to the Holy Spirit, as Ananias and Sapphira lied and immediately perished (Acts 5).

### CHAP. 66.—On widows and girls who assumed the religious habit in their own homes. From the Fourth Council of Toledo, ch. 57 (Fifth Council of Paris, ch. 13; Capitularies, book VII, ch. 257).

(27, q. 1, ch. *De viduis et*.) Concerning widows and girls who changed to the religious habit in their own homes, whether through their parents or by themselves: if afterward, contrary to the ordinances of the Fathers or the precepts of the canons, they believe marriages are to be contracted, [Col. 0561B] both parties [“both women,” in Gratian] are to be suspended from communion until they correct what they have unlawfully committed. But if they neglect to make correction, they are to be separated forever from communion and from the shared meals of all Christians.

### CHAP. 67.—That Saint Gregory ordered a veiled woman who had transgressed her sacred purpose to be apprehended. From Gregory’s register, to Vitalian, bishop of Siponto (book VII of the register, ch. 9).

(27, q. 1, ch. *Si custos*.) If you had been, or had known yourself to be, a guardian of the religious habit and a bishop, the daughter of Tullianus, of glorious memory, master of the soldiers, could not, while you were stationed there, either return to secular dress after throwing aside her religious garments or send us a perverse letter. But because you are weighed down by excessive negligence and torpor, an unlawful deed has at present been committed with impunity to your disgrace. For, as we have said, if you had been vigilant, punishment of that most wicked woman ought to have reached us before her offence [Col. 0561C].

Therefore, because you are so dull and negligent that, unless you experience canonical correction in your own case, you do not know how to maintain stricter discipline in others, we shall suitably show you, if it please the Lord, in due time how vigilant you ought to be. Receiving this letter, therefore, awaken; and, at least now aroused, carry out what, until now oppressed by sloth, you have delayed.

Accordingly, with all urgency apprehend the aforesaid woman together with Sergius our defender [“defender,” in the original], immediately restore her without any excuse not only to the habit which she wickedly despised, [Col. 0561D] but also shut her up in a monastery where she can be kept under wholly strict guard. Show such care in her case that she may learn from your severity how wicked was that which she committed. If in this matter any layperson—which we do not believe—attempts by any contrivance to oppose you, suspend him from participation in the most holy communion; and hasten to report it to us, so that, after he has failed to recognize through his own reflection how execrable is what he presumes to do, he may learn it through the character of the correction. In all these matters, take care to show yourself cautious and vigilant, so that negligence may not double your fault but that diligence may in some measure lessen it.

### CHAP. 68.—On veiled widows accused of serving the pleasures of the flesh. From the Council of Meaux, ch. 2 (under Sergius II, ch. 70).

[Col. 0562A]

Those women who appear to live as religious women under the veil of religion, but who, living rather in pleasures, are reckoned dead in the eyes of God, wandering through the provinces, inquisitive [“idle”] and talkative—if they are accused of serving lusts and other pleasures of the flesh, and can be openly detected—are to be compelled by episcopal authority and royal power to remain, under religious supervision, in places where, if they perform penance, they may attain one that is both worthy and fruitful. But if they cannot be openly detected, they are to be compelled canonically to clear their bad reputation before their church; and, so that they may henceforth [Col. 0562B] live more religiously and be kept in monasteries, they are to be restrained by episcopal decree and royal authority. For of these the Apostle says: “When they have committed fornication against Christ, they wish to marry” (1 Tim. 5).

### CHAP. 69.—That those who join themselves to sacred women are to be judged sacrilegious. From the Council of Arles, ch. 7 (in the fragments).

(27, q. 1, ch. *Sciendum*.) All should know that the bodies of women consecrated to God, by the vow of their own promise and the words of the priest, are temples consecrated to God, as is proved by the testimonies of Scripture; and therefore their violators are known to be sacrilegious and, according to the Apostle, children of perdition (1 Cor. 3).

### CHAP. 70.—On those who abduct holy virgins or widows. From the Council of Meaux, ch. 6 (ch. 67).

[Col. 0562C]

Those who abduct holy virgins or widows and, advancing further in their crime, take them in marriage, are to be subjected to public penance [“according to the measure which the bishop shall judge appropriate,” in the original]. The women themselves are to be shut up in suitable places of penance and compelled to return to the religious habit. But the incestuous man [“both parties,” in the original] is to remain permanently without hope of a marital union, unless he can clear himself by showing that he did not know she was veiled [these words are absent from the original]. But if—may it not happen!—they presume to contract marriages again, they are to be subjected to a harsher punishment and driven out further. And if [“those who,” in the original] they perhaps refuse to obey salutary admonitions, let them be anathematized.

### CHAP. 71.—That clerics and laypeople should speak with sacred maidens in the presence of reputable witnesses. From the Council of Split, [Col. 0562D] ch. 10.

Let this precaution be observed with respect to all: laypeople, kept away from the private quarters of virgins, are not even to have familiar permission to approach as far as the vestibule. Nor should the superior himself converse with a woman alone, but in the presence of two or three sisters, so that access is rare and conversation brief.

### CHAP. 72.—That veiled women should observe their habit either in monasteries or in their own homes. From the decrees of Pope Eugenius, ch. 26.

(27, q. 1, ch. *Mulieres*.) Women veiled under the pretext of religion are either to live regularly in a monastery or chastely observe in their own homes the habit they have assumed.

### CHAP. 73.—That younger widows or religious women are not to be neglected by the bishop. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, ch. 102.

[Col. 0563A]

(Dist. 81, ch. *Ad reatum*.) It pertains to the guilt of a bishop or of the presbyter who presides over a parish if younger widows or religious women are subjected, for the sake of support in their present life from the Church, to the familiar associations of those men [“clerics,” in the original].

### CHAP. 74.—That every bishop should cause wandering clerics in his bishopric to return to their own bishop. From the Council of Mainz, ch. 19.

Let every bishop diligently inquire in his own parish from where the presbyters or clerics are; and if he finds any fugitive, let him cause him to return to his own bishop.

### CHAP. 75.—Likewise, on wandering clerics. From the same council, ch. 18 (ch. 22).

[Col. 0563B]

Concerning wandering or headless clerics—that is, those who are without a head, neither in the service of our Lord nor under a bishop nor under an abbot, but living without canonical or regular life—thus it is said of them in book II, ch. 3, of Isidore’s *Offices*: “Neither among laypeople, occupied with secular duties, nor among clerics does divine religion retain these men; but a base and wandering life alone embraces them as unbound and straying. Since they fear no one, they pursue the licence of satisfying their own pleasure and, like brute animals, are carried along by liberty and desire. They bear the sign of religion but not the office of religion, resembling hippocentaurs, neither horses nor men.”

We therefore wholly command that, wherever such persons are found, bishops shall without any delay bind them under canonical custody and by no means allow them any longer to live as errant wanderers according to the desires of their pleasures. But if they refuse canonically to obey their bishops, let them be excommunicated until the judgment of the bishop [“archbishop,” in the original] of that region. If those bishops too cannot correct them, let them be bound in chains until the synod, so that it may there be judged whether they are to be brought under public custody before the judgment of the prince [“our lord,” in the original] or before a universal synod [Col. 0563C].

### CHAP. 76.—That nuns should live monastically and canonically, according to the canonical life. From the same council, ch. 13, attended by Emperor Charles and Archbishop Richolf in the cloister of Saint Alban.

[Col. 0563D] We judge that abbesses together with religious women ought by all means to live rightly and justly. Those who have made profession according to the Rule of Saint Benedict are to live according to the Rule. But if they live canonically, they are to do so fully, be kept under diligent care, remain in their cloisters, and have no exit outside. The abbesses themselves likewise are to remain in the monasteries and not go out without the permission and counsel of their bishop.

### CHAP. 77.—That religious women should not leave without the abbess’s permission. From the same council, ch. 14 (Second Council of Chalon, under Charlemagne, ch. 62).

Religious women are in no way to leave the monastery unless their abbess sends them because some need requires it. Those, however, who have no male or female servants [Col. 0564A] to conduct their business are to come to the middle gate of the monastery and there conduct their business before witnesses.

### CHAP. 78.—On women who assume male clothing for the sake of continence. From the Council of Gangra, ch. 13.

(Dist. 30, ch. *Si qua mulier*.) If any woman, for the sake of a supposed continence, changes her clothing and, instead of the customary female dress, puts on male attire, let her be anathema.

### CHAP. 79.—On one who, while preserving virginity, execrates marriage. From the same council, ch. 9.

(Dist. 30, ch. *Si quis vel*.) Whoever preserves virginity or pursues continence, yet wickedly disparages marriage as though recoiling from it, and does not assume the name of virginity on account of what is good and holy, let him be anathema.

### CHAP. 80.—On women who cut their hair for the sake of religion. From the same council, ch. 17.

[Col. 0564B]

(Dist. 30, ch. *Quaecunque mulieres*.) If any woman, for divine worship as she supposes, cuts off the hair which God gave her as a reminder of subjection, thereby as though setting aside the command of obedience, let her be anathema.

### CHAP. 81.—On those who wear cloaks for the sake of continence. From the same source, ch. 12.

(Dist. 30, ch. *Si quis virorum*.) If any man, for the sake of a supposed continence, uses the dress of a cloak, as though he believed that through this he possessed righteousness, and despises those who dress reverently in *birri* [common cloaks] and other ordinary customary garments, let him be anathema.

### CHAP. 82.—That a continent person should not exalt himself against married persons. From the same council, ch. 10.

[Col. 0564C]

If any of those who preserve virginity for God exalts himself against married persons, let him be anathema.

### CHAP. 83.—That monks and nuns are not to be permitted to live together in the same monastery. From the register of Saint Gregory.

We permit monks and nuns in no place to have one monastery; nor do we permit what they call double monasteries. If anything of this sort exists, the religious bishop should ensure that the women remain in their own place and compel the monks to build another monastery. If there are many such monasteries, let the nuns be separated into some monasteries and the monks into others [Col. 0564D]. The possessions which they hold in common are to be distributed according to the rights belonging to them.

### CHAP. 84.—Bishops should frequently visit monasteries of monks and nuns. From the Council of Rouen, ch. 3.

Let the bishop frequently enter monasteries of monks and religious women; and, sitting in their assembly with serious and religious persons, diligently examine their life and conduct, and strive to correct anything found blameworthy. He should also investigate closely the chastity of religious women; and if any woman is found who, abandoning her purpose of chastity, shamelessly joins herself to a cleric or layman, she is to be restrained sharply by beatings and shut up under private custody, where she may worthily repent of the evil which she has committed [Col. 0565A].

By the authority of the holy canons he should also forbid any layperson or cleric to have access to their cloisters and secluded dwellings, and priests as well, except only for Mass. Once Mass is completed, they are to return to their own churches. Moreover, he should announce publicly and privately to all how great a crime it is for anyone to presume to violate the bride of Christ. For if a man is held guilty who violates the bride of a human being, how much more does he become guilty of treason against majesty who corrupts the bride of almighty God?

### CHAP. 85.—That abbots are subject to the authority of bishops. From the Council of Orléans, ch. 3 (First Council of Orléans, ch. 21).

(18, q. 2, ch. *Abbates*.) Abbots, in accordance with the humility of religion, are to remain under the authority of bishops, and if [Col. 0565B] they do anything outside the Rule, they are to be corrected by bishops. (And ch. *Non semel*.) Not once but several times a year bishops are to visit monasteries of monks; and, if anything needs correction, it is to be corrected. Monks, however, are to be subject to their abbots in all obedience and devotion. If anyone proves disobedient through contumacy and presumes to wander about in various places or to possess anything privately, all that he has acquired is to be taken from him by the abbots, in accordance with the Rule of Saint Benedict, for the benefit of the monastery. Those who have wandered about are, wherever found, to be brought back and confined under custody as fugitives with the assistance of the bishop.

### CHAP. 86.—On monks who beget children. From the sayings of Isidore.

[Col. 0565C] Monks who beget children are to be shut up in prison, mourning so great a crime with unceasing lamentation, so that mercy alone may be granted them, even at death, in the grace of communion.

### CHAP. 87.—On religious women who have suffered barbarian violence. From the decrees of Pope Leo (letter 87, to the African bishops, ch. 2).
