Concerning those established in the sacred purpose of virginity who have suffered barbarian violence and have lost the integrity of modesty not in mind but in body, the moderation which seems to us to be observed is that they are neither to be reduced to the rank of widows nor numbered among sacred virgins who have persevered. Yet if they persevere in all virginal observances and preserve in mind the firmness of chastity, [Col. 0565D] communion in the sacraments is not to be denied them, because it is unjust for them to be accused or marked in a matter which not their will permitted but hostile force took away.

### CHAP. 88.—On a certain abbess who lodged a complaint about soldiers quartered in her cloister. From Gregory’s register, to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples (book VII, indiction 2, ch. 107; otherwise letter 108).

Agnella, an abbess and bearer of this letter, has informed us that soldiers are quartered inside her monastery. We have been greatly surprised at the concern of your Fraternity, why you endured this patiently and did not have it corrected with all speed. Therefore we exhort you that, even now, you make it your concern urgently to press those responsible, so that they may be removed [Col. 0566A] without any excuse whatsoever, and that no one may thereafter receive access there, lest the crafty enemy, finding an opportunity, be able—God forbid—to exult in the deception of the religious habit.

### CHAP. 89.—That ecclesiastical property is not to be administered by laypeople. From the council held at Compiègne, ch. 10.

By synodal decree it has been established that lay or secular persons are not to suppose or presume that anything belonging to men dedicated to God or to the resources of the Church pertains to them except reverence; for it is taught that the care of administering such things has without question been entrusted by God to their priests. If anyone presumes to act contrary to this, let him be struck with anathema.

### CHAP. 90.—On the same matter. From the same council, ch. 3.

[Col. 0566B] No authority whatever is found ever to have been granted to laypeople, however religious, for administering anything belonging to men dedicated to God or to ecclesiastical resources.

### CHAP. 91.—That abbots are not to be compelled to attend a synod except for reasonable cause. From the Council of Tours, ch. 11.

(Dist. 18, ch. *Episcopus*, ch. 10.) A bishop ought not to compel an abbot to go to a synod unless some reasonable cause exists.

### CHAP. 92.—That communities of monks are not to be established without the bishop’s consent. From the Council of Epaone, ch. 11 (and Agde, ch. 58).

(18, q. 2, ch. *Cellulas*.) We forbid the establishment of new cells or small communities of monks without the bishop’s knowledge.

### CHAP. 93.—On sacred virgins deprived of parents. From the African Council, ch. 11 (and Third Council of Carthage, ch. 33).

[Col. 0566C]

Let sacred virgins, if deprived of the parents by whom they were guarded, be guarded by the bishop. But where the bishop is absent, let them be entrusted to the care of more serious women, so that, living together, they may guard one another and not, by wandering about indiscriminately, injure the Church’s reputation [“estimation,” in the original].

### CHAP. 94.—Who is to be placed over religious women. From the Council of Carthage, ch. 27 (Fourth Council of Carthage, ch. 97).

(18, q. 2, ch. *Qui religiosis*.) The person to be placed over religious women is to be approved by the bishop.

### CHAP. 95.—What religious women should do in the cloister. From the Council of Mainz (Second Council of Chalon, under Charlemagne, ch. 59).

[Col. 0566D]

Religious women established in a monastery are to devote themselves to reading and singing, solemnly celebrate the canonical hours together, sleep in the dormitory—all except those prevented by illness—attend chapter and the conference every day, and diligently observe the Rule established for them by the holy Fathers.

### CHAP. 96.—That no one may enter the cloisters of religious women except to perform work. From the same council, ch. 16 (Second Council of Chalon).

No vassal of the abbess, nor any servant, cleric, or layperson, may enter the cloisters of the handmaids of God, unless perhaps a necessity of work requires it.

### CHAP. 97.—That a portress is not to be chosen unless she has a good reputation. From the codex, ch. 11 (Second Council of Chalon, ch. 64).

[Col. 0567A]

A portress is not to be chosen unless she is of mature age, has a good reputation, and is of proven life.

### CHAP. 98.—That an abbess is not to leave the monastery except with her bishop’s permission. From the Council of Gangra, ch. 8 (Second Council of Chalon, ch. 57).

An abbess who has a monastery in a city is not to leave the monastery in any way except with the permission of her bishop. Whenever she goes outside, she must take the greatest care of the religious women whom she brings with her, so that they are given no occasion for sin.

### CHAP. 99.—That no abbot may preside over two monasteries. From the Council of Orange, ch. 54 (Council of Agde, ch. 57).

[Col. 0567B]

(21, q. 1, ch. *Unum*.) We forbid one abbot to preside over two monasteries.

### CHAP. 100.—That monks and nuns are not to have godparents. From the Council of Autun, ch. 5.

Let monks and nuns not presume to have spiritual co-parents (*compatres*, that is, baptismal or sponsorship kin).

### CHAP. 101.—That women may not teach in an assembly. From the Council of Carthage, ch. 1 (Fourth Council of Carthage, ch. 99).

(Dist. 22, ch. *Mulier*.) Even if learned, a woman must not dare to teach in an assembly.

### CHAP. 102.—That women may not impose penance or sit among priests at a meal. From the Council of Reims, ch. 5, in the presence of Emperor Louis.

[Col. 0567C] A woman is not to impose penance, nor place the corporal with the offering, nor set the chalice upon the altar, nor stand among the ordained in church, nor sit among priests at a meal.

### CHAP. 103.—On women adjudicating men’s cases. From the Council of Nantes, ch. 8 (under Formosus, ch. 19).

Since the Apostle says, “Let women keep silence in church, for they are not permitted to speak; for it is shameful for a woman to speak in church” (1 Cor. 14), it is astonishing that certain little women, acting shamelessly with brazen face against divine and human laws, continually attend general assemblies and public meetings and disturb the affairs of the kingdom and the interests of the commonwealth more than they arrange them. For it is unbecoming, and blameworthy even among barbarian peoples, for women to adjudicate men’s cases; and women who ought to be discussing their wool-working, textile work, and women’s concerns while sitting among their spinners, arrogate to themselves senatorial authority in a public assembly as though sitting in a court [Col. 0567D].

This disgraceful presumption seems more imputable to their supporters than to the women. Therefore, because divine laws, as has been shown above, oppose this, and human laws likewise prohibit it, so that women may pursue nothing else in public except their own cause—for the Theodosian law says: “Women are in no circumstance to have authority to conduct any cases beyond their own, nor are they to know that they may pursue another person’s case”—we therefore forbid by canonical authority that any holy virgin or widow attend general assemblies unless summoned by the prince or by her bishop, except perhaps where the consideration of her own necessity compels her; and even then only with the permission and notification [“and notification” absent from the original] of her bishop [Col. 0568A].

### CHAP. 104.—That an abbot may leave his place out of humility. From the Council of Mainz, ch. 18.

(18, q. 2, ch. *Abbas potest*.) An abbot may abandon [“leave”] his place out of humility and with the permission of the bishop. Nevertheless, the brothers are to choose an abbot for themselves from among their own number, or otherwise from outsiders. Nor should the bishop forcibly retain the abbot in his place. The community ought to choose an abbot for itself after the death of its abbot, or during his life if he departs or sins. For he himself may not appoint [Col. 0568B] anyone from among his relatives or friends without the will of the brothers.

### CHAP. 105.—That a layperson may not recite a reading in church. From the same council, ch. 9 (among the capitula of Herard, archbishop of Tours, ch. 136).

A layperson ought not to recite a reading in church or say Alleluia, but only psalms and responsories, without Alleluia.

### CHAP. 106.—That a bishop may not take away property of a monastery. From the same council, ch. 20.

(16, q. 6, ch. *Episcopo*.) A bishop may not take away a monastery’s possession, even if the abbot has sinned; rather, he should send him to another monastery under the authority of another abbot.

### CHAP. 107.—That monks are not to attend secular assemblies. From the same council, ch. 21 (First Council of Mainz, ch. 12; ch. 65 of the Rule of Saint Benedict).

[Col. 0568C]

And thereafter we decreed, as the holy Rule says, that a monastery should, where possible, be organized through deans, because those superiors often fall into pride and into the snare of the devil (1 Tim. 3). Yet we absolutely will that monks should by no means attend secular courts, nor should the abbot himself do so without his bishop’s permission; and when necessity demands, he is to go there at his bishop’s command and on his counsel. Yet he must by no means presume to stir up disputes or lawsuits there; whatever must be sought or answered, he is to do through his advocates. Abbots and monks are to keep silence until they are questioned, and when questioned they are to answer with humility and reverence; otherwise they are to avoid complaints altogether. They are to remain within their cloister, and none of them is to go outside unless, because of necessity, he is sent by the abbot on an errand of obedience; nor is he to eat or drink outside without the abbot’s permission, nor attend secular banquets.

### CHAPTER 108.—What secular business is. From the same source, chapter 22 (ibid., ch. 14).

It has seemed good to us that ministers of the Lord’s altar and monks should abstain entirely from secular business. Now there are many kinds of secular business; nevertheless, let us briefly touch on a few of them, to which belongs every form of desire—not only the impurity of the flesh, but every carnal craving. Whatever a person desires beyond what is right is shameful gain. To accept or even give unjust gifts [Col. 0569A] for some secular claim; to hire someone for payment; to love disputes, lawsuits, and quarrels; to argue in secular courts, except in defence of orphans or widows; to act as agents or administrators of secular affairs; to delight in one who hurls shameful words or deeds [perhaps “a jester,” *jocularem*]; to love gambling; to seek adornment unsuitable to one’s profession; to wish to live in luxury; to pursue gluttony and drunkenness; to possess unjust weights or measures; to carry on dishonest trade. Yet lawful business is not to be prohibited, on account of diverse necessities, since we read that the holy Apostles engaged in trade, and the Rule of Saint Benedict (ch. 57) commands provision to be made concerning through whose hands the business of the monastery is to pass. To pursue dogs and birds in hunting, and to be superfluous in all [Col. 0569B] kinds of affairs. Behold: such things, and things like them, we wholly prohibit to ministers of the Lord’s altar and likewise to monks, concerning whom the Apostle says: “No one who serves God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2).

### CHAPTER 109.—Concerning clerics or monks unjustly tonsured. From the same council, chapter 23.

Concerning clerics, we decree this: those who have hitherto been found tonsured, whether into canonical or monastic order, without their own consent, if they are free persons, are to remain as they are; and henceforth care must be taken that no one be tonsured except at the lawful age and by his voluntary will, or with his lord’s permission, or with the consent of his parents.

### CHAPTER 110.—That bishops or abbots must not permit obscene jokes in their presence. From the same source, chapter 24 (Council of Rheims I, ch. 17).

[Col. 0569C]

Bishops and abbots must not permit obscene jokes to be made in their presence, but are to have the poor at table with them, and divine reading is to resound there; they are to take food with blessing and praise of the Lord, according to the Apostle: “Whether you eat or drink, do all things to the praise of God” (1 Cor. 10).

### CHAPTER 111.—Concerning those who, deceived by bishops or others, had themselves tonsured. From the same source, chapter 23 (Council of Chalon II, ch. 17).

(16, question 7, chapter *Constituit sane*.) This holy assembly has indeed decreed that bishops or abbots who, seeking not the fruit of souls but avarice and shameful gain, have tonsured any persons whom they enticed, by deceiving them [Col. 0569D], and have not merely received but rather stolen their property by such persuasion, are to be subjected to canonical or regular penance, as pursuers of shameful gain. But those who, enticed by empty promises or persuaded by any schemes, having become bereft of judgment and unaware that they remained masters of their own possessions, laid aside their hair, are to be compelled to persevere in what they have begun. The property which is known to have been given by persons enticed and inexperienced, and to have been not merely received but seized by greedy and negligent persons, is to be returned to the heirs who are known to have been disinherited through their parents’ folly and the avarice of those who enticed them. But if, without the bishops’ or abbots’ knowledge, any of their ministers—namely, persons in the clergy—are convicted of having done this, the bishops and abbots are to be judged for negligence, [Col. 0570A] while those men are to be judged for rapacity and avarice. But what anyone justly and reasonably offers to God from his own property, the Church ought firmly to retain.

### CHAPTER 112.—That an abbess must take great care of her community. From the same source, chapter 26 (ibid., ch. 54).

An abbess is to exercise diligent care for the community entrusted to her, and provide that the nuns themselves be zealous in reading, office, and the chanting of psalms. In all good works she is to give them leadership, since she must render an account for their souls (Heb. 13) before the Lord; and she is to provide the nuns with necessities, lest perhaps need of food or drink compel them to sin.

### CHAPTER 113.—That nuns must not presume to eat or drink with men in their own houses. From the same source, chapter 27 (ibid., ch. 61).

[Col. 0570B]

Nuns ought not, in their own dwellings, to drink or eat with any male clerics or laymen, whether relatives or strangers; but if this must ever be done, it is to be done in the audience chamber. Nor may they converse with any man except in the audience chamber, and there in the presence of suitable witnesses.

### CHAPTER 114.—How an unworthy abbot is to be deposed. From the Council of Tribur, at which King Arnulf was present, chapter 15.

(31, question 1, chapter *Si quis abbas*.) If any abbot is not prudent in government, humble, chaste and sober, merciful, discerning, and does not set forth the divine commandments in word and example, he is to be removed [variant: “excluded,” *arceatur*] from his office by the bishop in whose territory he is established, by the neighbouring abbots, and by the other God-fearing persons, even if the entire community, agreeing with his vices, should wish to retain him as their abbot.

### CHAPTER 115.—What is to be done with clerics who have abandoned their tonsure and taken wives. From the same council, chapter 16.

If a cleric who has abandoned his tonsure takes a wife, provided he has no rank and was not entrusted to a monastery by his parents, then, if he is permitted to have a wife, he is to be compelled to be tonsured again and must not dare to neglect the tonsure throughout his life. But one whom his parents entrusted to a monastery, and who has begun to chant and read in church, may neither take a wife nor leave the monastery; if he leaves, [Col. 0570D] he is to be brought back; if he abandons his tonsure, he is to be tonsured again. If he has taken a wife, he is to be compelled to dismiss her.

### CHAPTER 116.—Concerning girls who of their own accord dedicated themselves to sacred religion before the lawful years. From the same council, chapter 24.

(20, question 2, chapter *Puella*.) If a girl, before her twelfth year of age, voluntarily assumes the sacred veil for herself, her parents or guardians may immediately annul the act if they wish. But if, by overlooking it, they have consented for a year and a day, they can no longer alter it. Moreover, if a young woman or young man of more mature age chooses to serve God, the parents have no authority to forbid it.

### CHAPTER 117.—That anyone who wishes may offer his daughter, granddaughter, or female relative to God. From the same council, chapter 6.

[Col. 0571A]

Whoever wishes to offer his daughter, granddaughter, or female relative to almighty God is to have permission. But if she takes a husband, she is to rear her children at home and must not presume to send any others into the monastery for upbringing, except one whom she firmly wishes to persevere in that place in God’s service, according to the enactments of the holy Fathers and canonical authority.

### CHAPTER 118.—That no one is to place his son or relative in a convent of girls to be raised. From the same council, chapter 7.

We absolutely prohibit anyone from presuming to entrust his son, grandson, or relative to a convent of girls to be raised there; nor may anyone presume to receive anyone there.

### CHAPTER 119.—That an abbot must not permit women to enter a monastery or watch celebrations there. From the Council of Urbicum.

If an abbot permits a woman to enter his monastery, or permits her to watch celebrations there, he is to be confined for three months in another monastery, content with bread and water only.

### CHAPTER 120.—That virginity is voluntary, not imposed by law or command. Ambrose, in the book *Exhortation to Virgins* (after the beginning).

(23, question 2, chapter *Integritas*.) Bodily integrity is to be sought by us; I recommend it as counsel, not prescribe it as a command. For virginity alone can be commended; it cannot be commanded: it is a matter of vow rather than precept.

### CHAPTER 121.—On the same matter. Bede, *On the Tabernacle* (book III, ch. 9).

Aaron was clothed in eight garments: linen breeches, a linen tunic, a hyacinth-blue robe, an ephod, a breastpiece, a belt, a tiara, and a golden plate. But his sons used only four of these: namely, breeches, a close-fitting linen garment, a girdle, and a tiara. Since the other garments have been discussed above, these breeches, given to Aaron’s sons to cover the shamefulness of the flesh [the original reads: “the shamefulness of the flesh is commanded to be made, that, etc.”], signify that portion of chastity which properly restrains the desire [original: “from the desire”] of marital intercourse; without it no one may either undertake the priesthood or be consecrated to the ministry of the altar—that is, unless he remains a virgin, or has dissolved the bonds of union with a wife. This kind of virtue is not necessarily imposed on anyone by God’s law, but is to be offered to the Lord by voluntary devotion; for he himself says concerning it: “Not all receive this saying” (Matt. 19). Yet he immediately invites those who are able by a gracious exhortation, saying: “Let him who is able to receive it receive it” (ibid.). And shortly afterward he promises those same persons who have left wife, other relatives, and the entanglements of this world for his sake a hundredfold reward in this life and eternal life in the age to come (ibid.).

For this reason, undoubtedly, in order to mark the distinction, Moses is not commanded to clothe his brother Aaron and his sons with him in this garment, as is said concerning the preceding garments: “You shall clothe with all these your brother Aaron and his sons with him.” Rather: “You shall make linen breeches to cover the flesh” (Exod. 28). “They,” he says, “shall cover the flesh of their shamefulness.” You shall make breeches for the high priest and his sons; you shall teach the rule of chastity; you shall declare to those who are to exercise the priesthood that they must abstain from a wife’s embrace. Yet you shall impose on no one the violent yoke of such continence. Rather, those who wish to become priests and serve the ministry of the altar must of their own accord cease to be slaves of their wives. When they have done this, and, having once undertaken the purpose of continence, agree that they will be ministers of the sanctuary and altar, divine law will be at hand. As though imposing the remaining attire suited to priests [variant: “as though imposing an attire suitable to priests”], it will abundantly instruct them how they ought to live and teach; and, rejoicing in their voluntary devotion, it will add to them the honour appropriate to the priesthood—wisdom, patience, gentleness, spiritual zeal, humility, mercy, fear of the Lord, and the other ornaments of this kind. Otherwise, as guilty of wickedness, they die; for a person certainly incurs death of the soul if, while living luxuriously, he presumes to usurp priestly rank.

### CHAPTER 122.—What is to be done with monks who take wives. Gregory to Antony, subdeacon (Register, book I, ch. 40).

(27, question 1, chapter *Et quia aliquos*.) Since we have learned that some monks have gone so far into such wickedness as publicly to acquire wives, seek them out with every vigilance, and, once found, send them back under due coercion to the monasteries of which they were monks. Nor fail to proceed likewise concerning clerics coming to monastic life, as we said above.

### CHAPTER 123.—How nuns who have fallen into adultery ought to do penance. Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari (Register, book III, chs. 6, 9).

(27, question 1, chapter *Si qua monacharum*.) If any nun, whether through earlier permission or through the evil habit of impunity, has been led into a fall of adultery or plunged into the abyss of sexual sin, we decree that, after the suitably severe punishment, she be transferred for penance to another, stricter monastery of virgins, that she may there devote herself to prayers and fasts, advance in repentance, and furnish others with a fearsome example of stricter discipline. But anyone found with women of this kind in any wrongdoing is to be deprived of communion [original Paris edition: “of all communion”], if he is a layman; if a cleric, he is also to be removed from his office and shut up in a monastery, continually to mourn his transgressions.

### CHAPTER 124.—That the defilement of a veiled virgin is reckoned as incest. Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, book I.

“If a virgin marries, she has not sinned” (1 Cor. 7)—not that virgin who has once dedicated herself to the worship of God. For if any one of these marries, she “will incur condemnation, because she has made void her first faith” (1 Tim. 5). But if someone objects that this was said of widows, how much more will it prevail concerning virgins, when even those are forbidden to whom it had once been permitted? For virgins who marry after consecration are not so much adulteresses as incestuous women.

### CHAPTER 125.—What is to be done if monks or nuns have fallen. Pelagius to Secundinus, defender.

Whoever among those who seem to serve the Church, or who are found in the habit, as stated, of monks or nuns, is discovered to be so attached to such companionships that some shameful suspicion may arise from it—which God forbid—let them be brought, through your execution of this order, Secundinus, before the bishop, so that canonical punishment may proceed against them.

### CHAPTER 126.—On the same matter. The same to Severinus.

You swore to us—which you cannot deny—that you yourself would immediately bring Juliana to us if you learned that she truly wished to leave you—Juliana whose habit and consecration you did not fear, and by corrupting whom you inflict injury upon God.

### CHAPTER 127.—Concerning virgins found in the same bed with men who do not confess defilement. Cyprian to Pomponius, *On Virgins* (book I, epistle 11 [otherwise epistle 62]).

I have read [original: “we have read”] your letter, dearest brother, which you sent through our brother Paconius, asking and desiring that we write to you what appears to us concerning those virgins who, although they once resolved to preserve their state continently and firmly, were later discovered to have remained together in the same bed with men, one of whom, you say, was a deacon. Certainly those same women who confess that they slept with men ought not to assert that they are unviolated. Since you sought our counsel concerning this matter, [Col. 0573C] etc.

(In the same place, shortly afterward.) First, therefore, dearest brother, both the superiors and the people must strive for nothing else than to fear God, not permitting our brothers to go astray, nor virgins to live with men. I do not say merely sleep together, but not even live together.

(After several lines.) Since the weaker sex and still unstable age ought in every way still to be restrained and governed by us, lest an opportunity be given to the devil who lies in wait to do harm; for we see many grave falls occur from this, and we behold very many virgins corrupted through such unlawful and destructive unions. But if they have dedicated themselves to Christ in faith, let them persevere modestly and chastely, without any occasion for scandal; thus, strong and steadfast, let them await the reward of virginity. But if they are unwilling or unable to persevere for the reward of virginity, it is better for them to marry than to fall into the fire of their sin [original: “into the fire in their sins”], and certainly not cause scandal to brothers or sisters.

(After a few lines.) Nor should anyone think herself defended by the excuse that it can be inspected and proved whether she is a virgin. For both the hands and the eye of midwives are often deceived; and even if a virgin be found uncorrupted in that part by which a woman may be so examined, she may nevertheless have sinned through another part of the body, which can be defiled but cannot be examined. Certainly the intercourse itself, the embrace itself, this intimate conversation, this shameful and foul sleeping together of two persons—how much dishonour and guilt do these confess?

### CHAPTER 128.—Likewise, concerning the examination of virgins who lay in one bed with men. The same author (ibid.).

[Col. 0574A]

You acted wisely, dearest brother, in suspending the deacon who remained with a virgin, and also the others accustomed to sleep with virgins. But if they have done penance for their unlawful intercourse and separated from one another, meanwhile let the virgins be carefully examined by midwives; and if they are found virgins, let them be admitted to received communion [original: “to received communion in the church”]. Yet this warning is to be imposed: if they afterward return to the same men, or live together with them in one house and under one roof, they are to be expelled under a graver censure and not easily received again into the church thereafter. But if any one of them has been defiled and discovered to be so, let her perform full penance, because she who committed this crime is an adulteress not of a husband but of Christ. Therefore, after a justly determined period, once confession has been made, let her return to the church. But if they persevere obstinately and refuse to separate from one another, let them know that, in such shameless obstinacy, they can never be admitted by us into the church.

### CHAPTER 129.—To the king of the English concerning the prohibition of marriage with nuns and relatives. Boniface the martyr to Hileribald [Hiltribald, Victorius edition], king of the English.

If—as God forbid—what many report is true, you have neither taken a lawful wife nor maintained abstinence for God’s sake, but, lust ruling, have disgraced the renown of your glory before God and men by the crime of fornication [Col. 0574C] and adultery, we are deeply grieved at this. For it is recognized as an outrage in God’s sight and a disgrace to one’s reputation before men. And, worse still, those who report this to us add that this shameful crime has been committed especially with nuns and virgins consecrated to God in monasteries. For this sin is undoubtedly a twofold sin. To give an example: consider how guilty before his lord is a servant who violates his lord’s wife by adultery; how much more guilty is he who has defiled, with the filth of his own lust, the bride of Christ, Creator of heaven and earth?

Likewise: among Greeks and Romans, one who was guilty of this was regarded as though he had committed blasphemy against God. If, when questioned specifically concerning this sin before ordination, he were found true [probably “found guilty”], namely that he had lain with a veiled and consecrated nun, he would be barred from every rank of God’s priests. Therefore, dearest son, you must carefully consider how grave this sin is judged in the eyes of the eternal Judge: it places its perpetrator among the servants of idolatry and excludes him from the divine ministry of the altar, even if, after completing penance, he has been reconciled to God.

### CHAPTER 130.—That incest involving nuns is worse than adultery. John IV [VIII], to Bulcred, king of the Saxons.

Since, as we have heard, the sin of fornication reigns especially among you, because men of your kingdom presume, contrary to Saint Gregory’s decree necessarily given at that time to a newly converted people, to take as wives nuns and women already dedicated to God, as well as women of their own kinship [Col. 0575A], we admonish, exhort, and command by these letters of our apostolic office that all who are subject to your jurisdiction, both laymen and clerics, henceforth and hereafter avoid this grievous crime and serious offence, perform fitting penance for what they have done, and never again commit such acts. If perhaps it seems hard to you to remedy this impiety, for which you endure such adversities, make it known to our fatherhood by your letters, so that we may rebuke, and by every means burden with decrees [variant: “reprove,” *arguamus*], those who weakly submit to such abominable conduct.

### CHAPTER 131.—Concerning the excommunication of one who had taken a veiled woman. Stephen to all the bishops throughout Italy.

[Col. 0575B]

Your fraternity perhaps does not remain ignorant how Giseltruda, the widow of Peter, despising God and casting aside the sacred veil, committed fornication with her kinsman Winnigild—something we say with great sorrow. Therefore, when we learned this, because we wished more and more to eradicate such a most abominable crime, and so establish matters that no example might be given to others, we summoned both of them to make satisfaction and repeatedly ordered them to come to us, warning them to repent of such an impious crime. Since they were unwilling to come, however, but persevered in the same disobedience and treated our warnings as nothing, we held a canonical assembly and excommunicated them; unless they hasten to make true satisfaction, we have consigned them to perpetual anathema.

### CHAPTER 132.—On the same matter. Pope Honorius to John, bishop, and Gaudius, notary of Campania.

The bearer of this letter began his petition to us with a choked voice, sighs and groans, and unceasing tears, because a certain fosterling there had, by persistent attention, deceived the petitioner’s daughter, who had entered sacred dress, until she fell into bodily fornication by committing adultery. Thus, after the crime became known, that utterly depraved man continues to live there amid the reproach of all the people dwelling in that place; and, legal pursuit having been abandoned up to this point, he is perhaps being kept unpunished through certain persons’ patronage. Therefore let your love, inflamed with divine zeal, not cease [perhaps “let it not cease”] to press the competent jurisdiction until the perpetrator of the crime is brought before the public inquiry and the most severe examination, and receives the penalty of final punishment, lest, if punishment of him is delayed, the sentence of divine judgment spread to many.

### CHAPTER 133.—Concerning the penance of a consecrated virgin if she has fallen. Pope Nicholas to Archbishop Charles and his suffragans.

Women consecrated by the sacred veil, if they have committed fornication—which we do not wish—must not presume to lay aside the veil. Rather, having submitted to the yoke of penance, they must hasten with all earnestness to strive until they may attain the grace of pardon and forgiveness.

### CHAPTER 134.—That the defilement of a consecrated virgin is sacrilege. Ambrose to a fallen virgin.

[Col. 0576A]

(Chapter 9, “Concerning the seducer of a virgin.”) O son of the serpent, minister of the devil, violator of a virgin—that is, of God’s temple—you who have perpetrated two crimes in one act: adultery, certainly, and sacrilege. Surely it is sacrilege when, with mad recklessness, you have defiled a vessel offered to Christ and dedicated to God.

### CHAPTER 135.—The lament of a violated virgin doing penance. The same author.

(In the same place, ch. 10.) Receive this lament. First, let the fiftieth Psalm never be omitted on any day, because it has been chanted in such a situation; and, going through it with tears and groaning as far as the verse, “God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart,” then also pour out before God the Judge this lamentation, not without compunction of heart:

> “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes” (Jer. 9), that I may weep for the wounds of my soul? My feast days have been turned into mourning, and my songs into lamentation. The sound of hymns and the joy of psalms have departed; grinding of teeth and weeping of eyes have succeeded. I became mute and was humbled, and I kept silence from good things, and my sorrow was renewed. My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation fire will burn (Ps. 38). Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me (Ps. 54). The deep surrounded me; at last it submerged my head into the clefts of the mountains. Alas for me, because I have become like Sodom and have been burned like Gomorrah [Col. 0576C] (Gen. 19). Who will pity my ashes? I have offended more grievously than Sodom, because it sinned without knowing the law, while I sinned against the Lord after receiving grace. If a man sins against a man, there will be one to intercede for him (1 Sam. 2). But I, who sinned against the Lord—whom shall I find to propitiate him? I conceived sorrow and gave birth to iniquity; I opened a pit and dug it, and fell into the ditch that I made. Therefore my sorrow has returned upon my head, and my iniquity has descended upon my crown (Ps. 7). My uncleanness is before my feet; I did not remember my latter end, and I fell amazingly, and there is none to comfort me. O how bitter is the fruit of lust: more bitter than gall, more cruel than a sword! How have I become a desolation? (Ps. [Col. 0576D] 72). Suddenly I failed; I perished because of my iniquity, like one rising from sleep; therefore in the city of the Lord my image has been brought to nothing. My name has been erased from the book; I have become like an owl in its dwelling, like a solitary sparrow on a building (Ps. 101): there is none to comfort me. I look to the right and see, and there is no one who recognizes me. Escape has perished from me, and there is no one who seeks my soul (Ps. 141). I have become like a ruined vessel; I heard the reproach of all who dwell around me (Ps. 30). Woe to that day on which my unhappy father begot me, and this cruel light received me! It would have been better for me not to have been born than thus to become a byword among the nations. Because of me shame has come upon all the servants of the Lord and those who worthily worship him. Mourn for me, mountains and hills; mourn, springs [Col. 0577A] and rivers, for I am a daughter of weeping. Mourn for me, beasts of the forest, creeping things of the earth, birds of heaven, and every living creature that enjoys life. For you, blessed beasts and birds of heaven, have no fear from the underworld [variant: “of the underworld”], nor must you render an account after death. But for us remains the cruel punishment of Tartarus, who, possessing understanding, sinned; therefore there is no peace for sinners (Isa. 57).

> **Note:** [Col. 0577D] Ambrose now reads thus: “My sin, my iniquity. Human offences are not comparable: [Col. 0578D] for this impiety is horrible—to promise that one will preserve the flesh as a virgin, and publicly profess chastity,” etc.

> My sin, my iniquity, are not comparable to human offences, because it is impiety: I promised to preserve my flesh as a virgin, and, though publicly professing chastity, I lied to the Lord. Therefore I have no confidence to call upon the Most High Lord, because the mouth of sinners is stopped (Ps. 62). For the Prophet sang of my evil: those who remove themselves from the Lord shall perish; he destroys everyone who prostitutes herself away from him [Col. 0577B] (Ps. 72). And again: “My tongue has cleaved to my jaws, and you have brought me down into the dust of death” (Ps. 21). Yet I shall cry to the Lord God while there is still time, while room is given, because in death there is no remembrance and in hell there is no confession (Ps. 6). Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger. For your arrows have been fastened in me, and there is no health in my flesh. Because of the face of your wrath there is no peace in my bones, because of the face of my sins. For my iniquities have passed over my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed me down. My scars have festered and worsened because of my foolishness. I have been afflicted with miseries and bowed down to the end; I roar from the groaning of my heart. My heart is troubled [Col. 0577C] within me; my strength has abandoned me, and even the light of my eyes is not with me (Ps. 37). God, you have rejected me and destroyed me; you showed me hardships and gave me the wine of compunction to drink (Ps. 59). I have been cast out from your sight; I shall no longer be added so as to rise again to your holy temple, and I have become an extermination (Isa. 24; Ps. 40). What profit is there in my blood when I go down into corruption? (Ps. 29). Will you perform wonders for the dead, or will physicians raise them up? (Ps. 87). Your word, your promise, is: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live” (Ezek. 33). To you, O God, is my conversion, you who alone can renew all things and call souls back from hell. You loose the bound and raise up the crushed; you enlighten the blind and raise the dead (Ps. 145). I have strayed [Col. 0577D] like a lost sheep; seek your handmaid (Ps. 118), lest the cruel wolf swallow me. Many say to my soul, “There is no salvation for her in her God” (Ps. 3). But your counsel is with you. How many are the days of your handmaid? When will you execute judgment for me? My soul has failed for your salvation; my eyes have failed in tears (Ps. 118); my glory has been poured out upon the earth. When will you look upon me and restore my soul? (Ps. 34). Because of iniquity you rebuked me and made my soul waste away like a spider (Ps. 38). Remember, Lord, that I am dust (Ps. [Col. 0578A] 102). See my humiliation and my labour, and forgive all my sins (Ps. 24). Forgive me, that I may be refreshed before I depart and am no more (Ps. 38). Nor shall there be redemption in hell (Job 9). You are mighty, Lord, to tear open my sackcloth and gird me with joy (Ps. 29). You are mighty, Lord, to break my bonds (Ps. 115), by which I am bound and constrained. Remove your anger from me, Lord (Ps. 84), because I have sinned cruelly against you, until you justify my cause and bring me forth into the light, O God of hosts. Grant the effect of repentance, perseverance in repentance, lest the deceiver of souls harden me. Grant this to me; deign to bestow this grace from your fountain—you who live and reign in the Trinity for ages of ages.

### CHAPTER 136.—Concerning the accusation of a virgin. Letter of Ambrose to Syagrius, bishop of Verona (*Letters*, book VIII, epistle 64, or book VI, epistle 46).

[Col. 0578B]

Had he possessed proofs, your judgment would never have demanded an inspection of your virgin’s genitals. I cannot understand, therefore, what you meant or what you aimed at in thinking that a midwife should be employed. Will it then be free to everyone to accuse; and, once proofs fail, will there be an opening for them to demand inspection of the secrets of the genitals? Shall sacred virgins always be consigned to such outrages, which are an object of horror and shame not only to sight but even to hearing?

Likewise, in the same place. A virgin of the Lord is bound by her own supports for her own proof; she needs no external dowries to prove herself a virgin. The integrity of her virginity is supported not by inspection of hidden and secret parts, but by modesty evident to all.

Likewise, in the same place. I do not think just what you included in your letter: that unless she has been inspected, virginity [original: “integrity”] is endangered and wavers uncertainly [the original reads *incerto*] concerning itself. Thus, all women who have not been inspected have been exposed to danger of shame. Thus, those who are to marry must first be inspected in order to marry. Then must those to be veiled, as more worthy of proof, first be subjected to this handling? Etc.

### CHAPTER 137.—That the body cannot be defiled unless the mind has first been defiled. Ambrose, *On Virgins*, book II.

(32, question 5, chapter *Tolerabilius*.) It is more tolerable to have a virginal mind than virginal flesh.

(After a few lines.) Both are good, if possible; if not possible, let us at least be chaste not for a human being but for God. A virgin can be prostituted; she cannot be made an adulteress. Wherever God’s virgin is, there is God’s temple; brothels do not dishonour chastity—rather, chastity even abolishes the disgrace of the place.

### CHAPTER 138.—On the same matter. Ambrose, *On the Fall of a Consecrated Virgin* (ch. 4, to a fallen virgin).

(32, question 5, chapter *Revera*.) Indeed, the flesh cannot be defiled before the mind has first been defiled.

### CHAPTER 139.—That the body is not defiled where the mind is intact. Augustine, *The City of God*, book I, chapter 18.

(32, question 5, canon *Ita ne aliquem*.) Is it feared that another person’s lust may defile someone? It will not defile her if it is another’s; but if it does defile her, it will not be another’s. [Col. 0579A] But since chastity is a virtue of the mind, and has courage as its companion—a courage by which it resolves to endure any evils rather than consent to evil—no high-minded and chaste person has it in his or her power what is done to the body, but only what the mind assents to or rejects. Who, then, being of sound mind, would suppose that a person loses chastity if, perhaps, another’s lust is exercised and satisfied upon that person’s seized or overpowered body?

Likewise, in the same place, shortly afterward. While the purpose of the mind remains—which was also the means by which the body deserved to be sanctified—violence arising from another’s lust does not take holiness away from the body itself, a holiness preserved by perseverance in one’s own continence. But if some woman, corrupt in mind and having violated the purpose she had vowed to God, proceeds to be violated by her [Col. 0579B] seducer, do we still call her holy even as she proceeds—holy in body—when that holiness of mind by which the body was sanctified has been lost and destroyed? Far be this error from us; rather, let us be warned by this that bodily holiness is thus lost even when the body remains untouched.

Likewise, in the same place (chapter 19). They extol Lucretia, that noble matron of ancient Rome, with great praises for chastity. When the son of King Tarquin had violently [“having violently overpowered [her],” original] possessed her body in lust, she disclosed the crime of that utterly wicked young man to her husband Collatinus and to Brutus, her kinsman—men most illustrious and brave—and bound them to vengeance. Then, distressed and impatient at the foul deed committed against her, she killed herself. What shall we say? Is she to be called an adulteress, or chaste? Who would struggle over this controversy? [Col. 0579C] Someone eloquently and truthfully declaiming on this subject said: “Wonderful to relate! There were two, and one committed adultery.” Splendidly and most truly said. For, observing in the union [“mingling,” original] of two bodies the utterly defiled desire of one and the most chaste will of the other, and attending not to what was done by the conjunction of bodies but to what was done by the difference of minds, he said: “There were two, and one committed adultery.”

### CHAPTER 140.—On the same subject. Augustine, *On Free Choice of the Will* (book I, chapter 5).

(32, question 5, canon *De pudicitia*.) Who could doubt that chastity is situated within the person himself or herself, since it is a virtue? Therefore not even a violent ravisher can take it away.

### CHAPTER 141.—Likewise on the same subject. Jerome on the Epistle to the Romans.

[Col. 0579D]

It cannot happen that anyone can commit adultery in body unless he has first committed adultery in heart.

### CHAPTER 142.—Likewise on the same subject. Isidore, *Synonyms*.

The body cannot be corrupted unless the mind has first been corrupted. Likewise: Flesh clean from contagion of mind does not sin.

### CHAPTER 143.—That one who abducts a consecrated virgin incurs a capital sentence. Constitution XI of the Novels.

(27, question 1, canon *Si quis rapuerit*.) If anyone abducts, solicits, or corrupts a matriculary woman (*matricularia*), deaconess, nun, or even a woman wearing religious dress or leading a religious [Col. 0580A] life, that person’s goods, and the goods of those polluted by participation in such a crime, shall be claimed for the religious house in which that woman lived, through religious bishops, stewards, provincial governors, and their officials; and the offenders themselves shall be subject to capital punishment. The woman, moreover, shall be sought everywhere and, together with her belongings, placed in the safeguarding of the monastery.

### CHAPTER 144.—On prohibiting marriage to widows and virgins long resident in a monastery. Pope Gelasius to Caesarius, chapter 4 (Symmachus, epistle 5).

(27, question 1, canon *Neque viduas*.) We do not allow widows to proceed to marriage who have remained for a long observance in a religious profession. Likewise, we prohibit virgins from marrying if they have spent many years of their lives in monasteries.

### CHAPTER 145.—On the same subject. Nicholas to Archbishop Charles and his suffragans (*Rescripts*, title 13, chapter 3).

[Col. 0580B]

(27, question 1, canon *Vidua quidem*.) A widow who has placed the sacred veil upon her head, prayed in church among the other veiled women, and offered the oblation with them—if she has professed that she will remain in this habit, pledging never to lay aside the veil of religion—must not presume to depart from religious observance.

### CHAPTER 146.—Likewise on the same subject. Augustine, *On the Good of Widowhood* (chapter 8).

(27, question 1, canon *Viduae*.) Widows who do not remain continent should marry before they profess continence and vow it to God; if they fail to fulfill it, they are justly condemned.

### CHAPTER 147.—Likewise on the same matter. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 4.

[Col. 0580C]

(27, question 1, canon *Sicut bonum*.) If any widows, even though still in their younger years and left by their husbands at an immature age, have vowed themselves to God and, having put aside lay dress, have appeared in religious habit under the witness of the bishop and the Church, but afterward have proceeded to secular marriages, they shall incur condemnation according to the Apostle (1 Tim. 5), because they have dared to make void the pledge of chastity which they vowed to God. Such persons shall remain excluded from communion with Christians and shall not even share a meal with Christians.

### CHAPTER 148.—On the same matter. To Catellinus [Catellus], priest of Rieti, and Marcellus, bishop of Amiternum [Amiternum].

Tuizia, appearing before our son, the most distinguished man Count George [Col. 0580D], acting in the place of the illustrious and most distinguished man Marcellinus, vicar, is reported to have complained that Maximus, whom she called her husband, was abandoning her without any lawful necessity or reason. Therefore, she maintained that he ought to bear the loss of as much as could be recovered from the promised betrothal gifts, as well as the other penalties which the laws impose upon those who repudiate unjustly. When this complaint had been lodged, the aforesaid Maximus was detained by public authority at the command of our aforementioned son Count George. When detained, he asserted that the case had been heard or decided by the judgment of your charity; that this woman, because she had spent no few years in the service of religious life and had been stirred by the stealthy prompting of a diabolical spirit, had laid aside the habit of a handmaid of God [Col. 0581A] and returned to secular wantonness; that she had been confined in a monastery; and that she had now secretly departed from that monastery.

Having learned of her transgression, moved by considerations of equity and in order more fully to investigate the truth of what occurred, we have found it necessary to send the said Maximus, released from the jurisdiction of the aforementioned most distinguished Count George, together with the aforesaid Tuizia, into the presence of your charity, who are said to have been the judges. We decree, that, with the person to whom our said Count George has referred this case sitting with you, you shall investigate it without any obstacle of delay. And if, because of her previous offences, you retain the often-mentioned woman by the provident care of your charity in the monastery, continuing in the measures which [Col. 0581B] you have beneficially ordained out of fear of God, place and keep her with diligence and stricter restraint in the very monastery from which she departed, granting her no permission at any time to leave.

### CHAPTER 149.—That a bishop who has become a monk cannot return to the episcopate. From the fifth session of the Synod of Constantinople of 383 Fathers, under Pope John VIII, over which Cardinal-Priest Peter, Paul bishop of Ancona, and Eugenius bishop of Ostia presided.

(7, question 1, canon *Hoc nequaquam*.) The papal envoys said: “This is by no means observed among us: whoever descends from the episcopal order to the life of monks—that is, penitents—cannot afterward return to the episcopate.” Likewise: The holy synod decreed that whoever descends from episcopal dignity to monastic life and to the place of penitence shall by no means return to the episcopate. For the monastic life is characterized by subjection and discipleship, not by teaching, presiding, or shepherding others.

### CHAPTER 150.—On the rapacity of monks. Decree of Pope Leo.

It has been reported to us that certain persons act perversely and attempt to overthrow and divide the unity of the Church: namely, abbots and monks who devote themselves, not to zeal for charity, but to zeal for plunder. They do not cease to instruct and deceive laypersons whom they can ensnare, so that they may hand over their property and possessions, in life or at death, to their monasteries [Col. 0581D], while leaving nothing of their goods to the churches to which they are known to be subject and from which they have received or receive baptism, penance, the Eucharist, and the food of life together with the milk of the flesh.

Observing, therefore, this report of discord, we wish to prevent it by every means and utterly forbid its recurrence, considering that it is not good that those who formerly were, according to the Apostle, companions in sufferings (2 Cor. 1), should be exempt from fellowship in consolations; and because “the laborer is worthy of his wages” (Matt. 10; Luke 10). Therefore we command and order that whoever henceforth wishes to enter conversion in a monastery, whether in life or at death, shall leave to the church to which he is recognized as belonging one half of all his goods and possessions [Col. 0582A] which he has determined to dispose of for the salvation of his soul. Only then may he have freedom to go and enter religious conversion in a monastery as he pleases. Whoever shall oppose, subvert, or rashly violate this our decree shall lie under the sword of anathema.

### CHAPTER 151.—On forbidding monks to wander. Alexander II to the clergy and people of Florence.

(16, question 1, canon *Juxta Chalcedonensis*.) In accordance with the tenor of the excellent Council of Chalcedon, the text of which is appended below, we command monks, however religious, to remain within their enclosure according to the rule of Saint Benedict. We forbid them to range through villages, castles, and cities; we have decreed that they must wholly abstain from preaching [Col. 0582B] to the people—unless perhaps someone, concerned for the salvation of his own soul and wishing to assume their habit, should seek their counsel within the enclosure.

### CHAPTER 152.—On a woman who put on the veil and afterward returned to marriage. Nicholas to Aluminus, bishop of Isernia [Junaria] (given above, chapter 65).

Concerning the woman about whom you asked, who, after her husband’s death, placed the sacred veil upon her head and pretended under that veil to be a nun, but afterward returned to marriage: it seems good to me that, because through hypocrisy she wished to disturb the ecclesiastical rule and did not lawfully remain in her vow, she should do penance for her shameful deception, return to what she promised, and resume the sacred ministry which she began. For if we allow [Col. 0582C] everyone to feign all ecclesiastical sacraments as he wishes, rather than to perform them truly, the whole ecclesiastical order is thrown into confusion; the rights of the Catholic faith do not stand; and the sacred canons are not properly observed.

For what good did it do Simon Magus falsely to receive sacred baptism and pretend that he would remain in Christianity, when the Apostle exposed his fraud and foretold what would befall him? For he says: “May your money perish with you, because your heart is not right before the Lord. Therefore repent of this your wickedness, and pray to God that perhaps this thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity” (Acts 8). Therefore we judge that such persons, unless they come to their senses, should be struck with the spiritual sword. For it is not [Col. 0582D] lawful to lie to the Holy Spirit, as Ananias and Sapphira lied and immediately perished (Acts 5).

### CHAPTER 153.—That one wishing to become a monk should not immediately assume the habit. From the Book of Constitutions, Constitution V, chapter 1 (title V, chapter 2).

Anyone wishing to become a monk, whether free or enslaved, shall not immediately become a monk. Rather, for three years he shall wear tonsure and the clothing of laypeople, learn the divine Scriptures, confess his condition—that is, whether he is freeborn or enslaved, or of any other condition or status—and state the reasons why he desires to migrate to the solitary life, lest they perhaps be evil and displeasing to God. The monks must also bring him words that will correct his [Col. 0583A] character and life. If, during the three years, he appears such that he seems worthy of tonsure and religious clothing, then he shall be tonsured and put on the monastic robe, whether free or enslaved; and no harassment shall be inflicted upon him either on account of servile or free condition.

But if, during the three years, anyone wishes to reclaim him as his slave and says that he fled to the monastery after stealing his property, he shall not immediately take him away. He must first prove both that the man is his slave and that he feared and fled on account of theft, an evil life, and grievous sins. If these things are true, the slave shall be returned to his master with the stolen goods, if he too is in the monastery. The master, on receiving him, shall pledge that he will inflict no evil upon him on account of what he has already done. [Col. 0583B]

But if the master proves that the alleged slave is guilty of no offence, and the slave himself has good testimony because of his chaste conduct, then, even if three years have not yet elapsed, he shall nevertheless remain in that monastery. Once the three years have elapsed and he has been numbered among the monks as a servant of God, no one thereafter shall have permission to inflict any kind of harassment upon him, whether he is truly a servant or freeborn; rather, he shall in every respect remain in the solitary life, even if he committed sin in his former life. Things stolen by theft, however, if they are found, must without doubt be returned to their owner.

### CHAPTER 154.—On a slave who, fleeing service, became a monk, chapter 2 (ibid.).

But if anyone fleeing slavery comes to a monastery and afterward leaves the venerable [Col. 0583C] place and adopts another manner of life, the master may reclaim him; and, upon proving that he is a slave, may hold him as a slave.

### CHAPTER 155.—What is to be done with the goods of one who, having become a monk, apostatizes, chapter 3 (chapter 4).

If anyone consecrates himself in a monastery and, after being clothed in religious habit, withdraws from the monastery, all his goods which he brought into the monastery shall belong to that monastery. The same is provided by another constitution: even if he brought in nothing, all his possessions shall be the property of the monastery.

### CHAPTER 156.—On the same matter, chapter 4 (chapter 7).

If anyone enters a monastery and, after religious clothing, departs and becomes a soldier, or simply becomes a layman, he shall be stripped of the military belt and shall not enjoy free status; rather, he shall be compelled to serve in the office of the provincial governor, while his property remains in the monastery.

### CHAPTER 157.—Likewise, on the same subject, chapter 6 (and *Capitularies*, book V, chapter 226).

[Col. 0584B]

If anyone has been consecrated in a monastery and afterward prefers to transfer to another monastery, his property shall be claimed by the former monastery. The heads of other monasteries shall forbid him to transfer, and he shall not be received in another monastery. This must be enforced not only by the most religious bishops, but also by the most reverend archimandrites.

### CHAPTER 158.—That one wishing to become a monk should dispose of his property before entry, since afterward it is not permitted. Constitution LXVI, chapter 1.

All who enter a monastery shall see to it that their property is consecrated in the monastery. For before entry they have free power to distribute their goods as they wish. [Col. 0584C] But after they have entered, they do not have such freedom, even though they have children.

## EIGHTH PART OF THE DECREE

On lawful marriages. On un-veiled virgins and widows. On their abductors and their separation. On concubines and the violation of marriage, and on the penance of each person.

[Col. 0583]

### CHAPTER 1.—What marriage is. From Book I, title IX, of the *Constitutions* [*Institutes*].

[Col. 0583D]

(29, question 1, *At the beginning*.) Nuptials, or marriage, are the union of a man and a woman, containing an indivisible partnership of life.

### CHAPTER 2.—When marriage comes into being. Ambrose, *Exhortation to Virginity*, book II (chapters 5 and 6 of *On the Institution of a Virgin*).

(17, question 2, canon *Cum initiatur*.) Once betrothed to a man, she receives the name of wife. For when marriage is initiated, then the name of marriage is assumed. The deflowering of virginity does not make a marriage; the marital agreement does. In short, when a girl is joined in marriage, there is marriage—not when she is known by intercourse with a man.

### CHAPTER 3.—On the same subject. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book IX, chapter 7 (chapter 8).

(27, question 2, canon *Conjuges*.) Spouses are more truly called such from the first pledge of betrothal, even though marital [Col. 0584D] intercourse is not yet known between them.

### CHAPTER 4.—Description of lawful marriage. Evaristus to the bishops of Africa, chapter 2 (epistle 1, chapter 2).

(30, question 5, canon *Aliter*.) A lawful marriage is not otherwise contracted unless the woman is sought as a wife from those who appear to have authority over her and by whom she is guarded; she is betrothed by her nearest relatives, endowed according to law, and at the proper time blessed by a priest, according to custom, with prayers and offerings. Guarded and accompanied by the paranymphs, as custom teaches, and sought from her relatives at the fitting time, she is given according to law and solemnly received. For two or three days they shall devote themselves to prayer and preserve chastity.

### CHAPTER 5.—Likewise, on the same subject.

[Col. 0585A]

When these things have been done, know that the marriages are lawful. But do not doubt that unions otherwise presumed are not marriages, but rather adulteries, concubinages, debaucheries, or fornications than lawful marriages—unless personal consent supports them and lawful vows are supplied.

### CHAPTER 6.—On the blessing of bridegroom and bride. Nicholas’s replies to the inquiries of the Bulgarians, book I (chapter 3).

(30, question 5, canon *Nostrates*.) Our people, both men and women, do not wear on their heads a band of gold or silver, or one made of any metal, when they contract nuptial bonds. Rather, after betrothals—which are promised covenants of future marriage, celebrated by the consent of those who contract them and of those under whose authority they are—[Col. 0585B] and after the bridegroom has betrothed the bride to himself by earnest-money, marking her finger of faith with a ring from himself, and has given her the dowry agreed upon by both in a written instrument containing this agreement before persons invited from both sides, then either immediately or at a suitable time, lest [Col. 0585C] anyone presume to do such a thing before the time defined by law, both are led to the nuptial covenant. First, indeed, they are placed in the Church of the Lord with the offerings which they must offer to God through the hand of the priest; and then at last they receive the blessing and the heavenly veil.

Likewise: These are, besides other matters which do not occur to memory, the solemn agreements of marriages. We do not say, however, that it is a sin if all these things do not occur in the nuptial covenant.

Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 13. (30, question 5, canon *Sponsus*.) When bridegroom and bride are to be blessed by the priest, they shall be presented by their parents or paranymphs. Having received the blessing, they shall remain virgins that night out of reverence for the blessing.

### CHAPTER 7.—Why brides are veiled. Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 19.

The veiling of women at marriage signifies that they should know themselves always to be subject and humble toward their husbands.

### CHAPTER 8.—What the emblems of brides signify. In the same place.

[Col. 0585D]

That, after the blessing, those marrying are joined to one another by the ribbons with a single bond signifies, plainly, that they should not break the structure of marital unity. Moreover, the fact that this same ribbon is intermingled with white and purple colors: white indeed signifies purity of life; purple is applied to the offspring of blood. By this sign they are reminded both that the rule of continence is to be maintained by each for a time and that, afterward, the debt due should not be refused.

Likewise: That a ring is first given by the bridegroom to the bride is done, certainly, either as a sign of mutual love or, more especially, so that their hearts may be joined by that pledge. Hence the ring is placed upon the fourth finger, because, as is reported, a certain vein in it reaches as far as the heart.

### CHAPTER 9.—That the sacrament of marriage is inviolable. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 7.

[Col. 0586A]

(32, question 7, canon *Interveniente*.) The marital covenant is not abolished by divorce, so that spouses remain spouses even when separated; and they commit adultery with those to whom they are joined even after their repudiation. Yet such is the case with a wife only in the City of our God, on His holy mountain. Who does not know that the laws of the Gentiles are otherwise? There, after a repudiation has intervened, both she marries whomever she wishes and he takes whichever woman he wishes.

### CHAPTER 10.—That concubines can become wives. In the same work (chapter 14).

(32, question 2, canon *Concubinae*.) Even concubines taken for a time, if they lie together for the sake of children, do not thereby make [Col. 0586B] their concubinage just. Yet it is plain that a marriage can be made from persons badly joined, when an honorable resolution afterward follows.

### CHAPTER 11.—That no one is chaste in body unless chaste in spirit. The same author, *On Holy Virginity* (chapter 8).

Just as no one uses the body unchastely unless wickedness has first been conceived in the spirit, so no one preserves chastity in the body unless chastity has first been implanted in the spirit.

### CHAPTER 12.—That the sacrament of marriage is inviolable. The same author, *On Marriage and Concupiscence* (book I, chapter 10).

(32, question 7, canon *Usque adeo*.) So firmly do the rights of marriage, once entered into, remain among the living that spouses remain spouses to one another even when separated, rather than becoming spouses with those to whom they have [Col. 0586C] attached themselves elsewhere.

### CHAPTER 13.—Likewise, in the same work, on the same subject.

And shortly afterward: Among the living there remains a certain marital reality which neither separation nor union with an adulterer can take away; just as the apostate soul, as though departing from its marriage to Christ, does not lose the sacrament of faith received in the laver of regeneration even when faith itself is lost. For without doubt it would be restored to one returning, if one had lost it by departing. But the person who has departed possesses it for an increase of punishment, not for the merit of reward.

### CHAPTER 14.—Likewise, in the same work, on the same subject (chapter 18).

But for those who have agreed by mutual consent to abstain forever from the use of carnal desire, far be it [Col. 0586D] that the marital bond between them should be broken. Rather, it will be firmer, in proportion as they have entered into agreements with one another which must be observed more dearly and harmoniously—not by the pleasure-seeking bonds of bodies, but by the voluntary affections of minds. For the angel did not falsely say to Joseph: “Do not fear to take Mary your wife” (Matt. 1). She is called a wife from the first pledge of betrothal, though he had neither known her through intercourse nor would know her. The designation “wife” had neither disappeared nor remained false where there had been and would be no union of flesh. Accordingly, both deserved to be called parents of Christ by reason of their faithful marriage: not only she His mother, but he also His father, as the husband of His mother—both in mind, not in flesh.

### CHAPTER 15.—On the threefold good of marriage. In the same work, near the end.

[Col. 0587A]

(27, question 2, canon *Omne*.) Therefore every good of marriage was fulfilled in those parents of Christ: offspring, fidelity, and sacrament. We recognize the offspring as the Lord Himself; the fidelity, because there was no adultery; the sacrament, because there was no divorce. (Chapter 12.) Only marital intercourse was absent there, because it could not occur in the flesh of sin without the shameful concupiscence of the flesh that arose from sin. He who was to be without sin chose to be conceived without it.

### CHAPTER 16.—That a husband may not live continently without his wife’s consent. Augustine, in his letter to Count Boniface (epistle 70).

[Col. 0587B]

We know, we are witnesses, that at Tubunae we spoke with you about your intention and will. We were alone with you, Brother Alypius and I. For I do not think that the worldly cares with which you are filled could have prevailed so greatly as utterly to erase this from your memory: namely, that you wished to abandon all the public affairs with which you were occupied, withdraw into holy leisure, and live the life lived by monks, the servants of God. When, therefore, we rejoiced that you held this purpose, you sailed away and took a wife. For if you did not have a wife, I would tell you what we told you at Tubunae: to live in the chastity of continence.

Toward the end. I would add what we then forbade: that you should now withdraw yourself, as far as you could without disturbing human peace, from these military affairs [Col. 0587C] and devote yourself to this life and fellowship of saints, to which you then wished to devote yourself, where the soldiers of Christ fight in silence—not to kill people, but to overthrow “principalities and powers and spiritual forces of wickedness” (Eph. 6), that is, the devil and his angels. But your wife is an impediment to my exhorting you to this life, since you may not live continently without her consent. For although after those words of yours at Tubunae you ought not to have taken her as wife, she nevertheless, knowing none of those things, married you innocently and simply. Would that you could persuade her to continence, so that you might render to God without impediment what you know you owe Him!

But if you cannot prevail with her, preserve at least marital chastity, and pray to God, “who delivers from necessities” (Ps. 24), [Col. 0587D] that what you cannot do now you may someday be able to do. Yet, in order that you may love God, do not love the world. Thus, even in warfare, if it is still necessary for you to be engaged in it, keep faith and seek peace; use the goods of the world to do good works, and do not do evil works for the sake of worldly goods. Your wife does not prevent this, nor ought she to prevent it. Love commanded me to write this to you, dearest son—the love by which I love you according to God, not according to this age—because, reflecting upon what is written, “Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you; rebuke a fool, and he will add hatred of you” (Prov. 19), I ought surely to think of you not as foolish but as wise.

### CHAPTER 17.—That consent makes marriage. Nicholas to Bishop Hincmar (in the replies to the Bulgarians, chapter 3).

[Col. 0588A]

(27, question 2, canon *Sufficiat*.) According to the laws, the consent alone of those whose union is at issue is sufficient. If that consent alone should happen to be lacking in marriage, all other things, even if celebrated together with intercourse itself, are vain. This is confirmed by John Chrysostom, the great teacher, who says (*Incomplete Work on Matthew*, homily 33): “Marriage is made not by intercourse, but by will.”

### CHAPTER 18.—That a widow, before professing continence, may marry whom she wishes. From the Third Council of Toledo, chapter 18.

(27, question 1, canon *Viduae*.) If widows choose to marry before they profess continence, they may marry those whom they wish by their own will to have as husbands.

### CHAPTER 19.—That a virgin or widow must not be compelled to marry one whom she does not wish. From the same source.

[Col. 0588B]

The same rule shall be observed concerning virgins: they shall not be compelled to take husbands against the will either of their parents or of themselves.

On the same subject. Ambrose on the Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 39, on chapter 7: “Let the widow marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord,” that is, let her marry the man whom she judges suitable for herself; for unwilling marriages usually have bad outcomes. “Only in the Lord” means that she should marry without any suspicion of shameful conduct, and should marry a man of her own religion.

### CHAPTER 20.—That consent is required in betrothals as in marriages. *Digest*, book XXIII, title 1.

[Col. 0588C]

In betrothals, the consent of those whose consent is required in marriages must be obtained. Yet a daughter is always understood to consent to her father [“the daughter’s father,” original], unless she clearly dissents.

### CHAPTER 21.—That a woman may lawfully marry another man if her father has handed her over to one against her will and resistance. Likewise.

Betrothals, like marriages, are contracted by the consent of the contracting parties; therefore, as in marriage, a daughter under paternal authority must consent to betrothal. She who does not oppose her father’s will is understood to consent. But permission to dissent from her father is granted when her father chooses for her a suitor unworthy in character or disgraceful. If a son under paternal authority dissents, betrothal cannot be made in [Col. 0588D] his name.

### CHAPTER 22.—Likewise, on the same subject.

In contracting betrothals, the age of the contracting parties is not fixed as it is in marriages. Therefore betrothal can take place from the beginning of age, provided it is understood that this can be done by both persons; that is, provided they are not younger than seven years.

### CHAPTER 23.—That no one may presume to abduct a woman against her parents’ will. Judgment of Pope Urban concerning the daughter of Prince Jordan.

(31, question 2, canon *Si verum esse*.) If it is established as true what the envoys of Prince Jordan reported to us—namely, that he himself, constrained and distressed, betrothed his little daughter to the son of Raynald Ridell, against her will, while she wept and resisted to the best of her strength, and without the assent of her mother and kin, who were greatly distressed—[Col. 0589A] then, since the authority of canons and laws does not approve such betrothals, as is shown below, we temper our judgment so that what we say may not seem too harsh to those ignorant of laws and canons: if the princes wish, with the consent of the daughter, mother, and kin, to complete what has been begun, we permit it. But if not, let our legate hear both parties; and, if there is no further impediment on the part of the aforesaid Raynald, let him receive from Jordan himself an oath that these things are so as stated. Then, following the determinations of canons and laws, we no longer forbid the said daughter, if she wishes, to marry another man, only in the Lord.

### CHAPTER 24.—That abduction is reckoned as fornication. Urban to King Satino [“Gratian reads Sacratio”] of Aragon.

[Col. 0589B]

(31, question 2, canon *De neptis*.) Concerning the marriage of your niece, whom, when necessity was urgent, you confirmed by a promise given in good faith that you would give to a certain knight, we decree, equity dictating, as follows: if she wholly refuses the man, as is said, and persists in the authority of that will, so that she absolutely denies that she will marry him, you shall by no means compel her, unwilling and resisting, to be joined in marriage with that man. For those whose body is one must also have one mind, lest perhaps, when a virgin is joined unwillingly to someone, she incur, contrary to the command of the Lord and the Apostle, either the guilt of discord or the crime of fornication. It is clear that the evil of this sin falls back upon the person who [Col. 0589C] joined her unwillingly. The same judgment must likewise be made concerning a man.

### CHAPTER 25.—On punishment for abduction. First Council of Paris, chapter 6.

(36, question 2, canon *Nullus*.) No one shall presume either to abduct the widow or daughter of another against the will of her parents or to suppose that she may be sought by favor of the king. Whoever does so, removed from the communion of the Church, shall be struck by the sword of anathema.

### CHAPTER 26.—How an abducted woman is to be restored. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book V, chapter 24 (chapter 26).

(27, question 2, canon *Raptus*.) Abduction, properly speaking, is illicit intercourse, so called from corruption; hence one who possesses a woman by abduction enjoys violation.

Likewise. *Capitularies*, book I, chapter 99 (chapter 105). (27, question 2, canon *Raptor*.) An abductor shall be punished by public penance. If the abducted woman’s bridegroom does not wish to receive her, and she herself did not consent to the same crime, she shall not be denied permission to marry another. But if she consented, she shall be subject to the same sentence. If, after this, the two presume to join themselves together, both shall be anathematized.

Book IV of the *Capitularies* (chapter XXII). If anyone abducts another man’s betrothed, he shall [Col. 0589D] restore her, with her legal entitlement, either to her father or to the person who ought by law to be her protector; and he shall restore, according to law, every item that he took with her.

### CHAPTER 27.—That, if a girl’s father is a slave but her grandfather freeborn, she should marry according to the choice of her grandfather rather than that of her father. Pelagius to Potentius, defender.

The girl’s father is known to be a servant of our Church, while her grandfather is of free [Col. 0590A] birth. Therefore we decree that, concerning the union of the granddaughter, greater regard shall be given to the choice of the grandfather than to that of the father, whose judgment can in no way be free.

### CHAPTER 28.—That an abducted woman is ordered to become a wife. Gregory to Pantaleon, notary (*Register*, book II, chapter 79).

Evangelus, deacon of the Church of Siponto, has complained to us that his daughter was violated by Felix—an abomination even to say. Therefore, supported by the authority of this command, you must go to the city of Siponto. With wise men there assisting you, you shall make every careful effort to discover the truth. If you find that it is so, he shall either take as wife, with nuptial instruments executed, the woman whom he [Col. 0590B] violated; or else, after corporal punishment, you shall promptly send him, deprived of communion, to a monastery where he may perform penance.

### CHAPTER 29.—On the same matter. The same author to Felix, bishop of Siponto (*Register*, book II, chapter 81).
