It has come to us that Felix, your nephew, violated the daughter of your deacon Evangelus by sexual assault. If this is true—although by law he would deserve to be punished with a severe penalty—we nevertheless soften the harshness of the law to some extent and decree this disposition: either he shall have as wife the woman whom he violated, or, if he judges that she must be refused, he shall be strictly and corporally punished, excommunicated, and confined in a monastery where he may perform penance.

### CHAPTER 30.—On prohibiting concubines. A sermon of Ambrose on Saint John, beginning, “We said on the previous Sunday” (sermon 65).

[Col. 0590C]

Someone may say: “I have no wife; therefore I have taken a maidservant as my companion.” Hear what Scripture says to Abraham: “Cast out the maidservant and her son; for the son of the maidservant shall not be heir with the son of the free woman” (Gen. 21; Gal. 4). If, therefore, the son of the maidservant is not an heir, then neither is he a son. Why, then, is such a union sought, from which a son born cannot be heir either to succession or to blood? For one who does not possess the privilege of origin cannot share in an inheritance. Why, I say, is such cohabitation sought, of which the children born are witnesses not of marriage but of adultery? Why are such adulterous offspring received, who bring shame rather than honour to their father? Scripture says: “The children of adulterers shall come to their end” (Wis. 3), [Col. 0590D] etc. Therefore, if your woman is endowed with such character as to deserve companionship, let her also deserve the name of wife. Grant your concubine freedom and the name of wife, lest you be an adulterer rather than a husband.

### CHAPTER 31.—If a concubine remains with a nobleman until his death, she is to be freed with her children by his heirs. Book Seven of the Code, chapter 15, title 3.

If anyone, being without a wife, keeps his maidservant under the designation of concubine, and continues in that relationship with her until death, and perhaps has children by her, we decree absolutely that the heirs of the deceased shall not be permitted to reduce that woman or her children—if she has borne children—into slavery; rather, after [Col. 0591A] her master’s death, she shall be released into freedom together with her offspring.

### CHAPTER 32.—That children born of a concubine who is afterwards taken as wife are legitimate children, both those born earlier and those born later. Book Three of the Sacred Institutions, title 1.

If anyone joins a woman to himself in cohabitation, not at first with marital intention, but one whom he is able lawfully to marry, and has children by her, and later, as affection develops, executes nuptial instruments with her and has sons or daughters, not only the children born after the dowry are legitimate and under the authority of their father, but the earlier children also; because they [the original reads: “and they”] have afforded to those subsequently born the occasion for the name of legitimacy. We have decided that this shall prevail even if [Col. 0591B] no children are born after the dowry instrument has been drawn up, or even if children born thereafter have been removed from this life.

### CHAPTER 33.—That betrothed women, once promised, are not to be given over immediately. Augustine, *Confessions*, Book VIII.

(27, question 2, canon *Institutum*.) It has been established that a bride already promised shall not immediately be handed over, lest a husband hold cheaply what, when delayed, he had longed for as a bridegroom.

### CHAPTER 34.—Concerning one who has had relations with a woman whom he could lawfully marry. Constitution 32 of the Novels, chapter 3.

If anyone has had relations with a woman whose marriage is not prohibited, and she has borne children by him, and he subsequently draws up dowry instruments [Col. 0591C] for her, not only shall the children already born be legitimate and under his authority, but also those begotten afterwards.

### CHAPTER 35.—That a lawful wife is not to be repudiated. Constitution 37, chapter 7.

If anyone has taken a wife with marital intention but without dowry instruments, he shall not dare to send her a repudiation without a cause recognized by the laws.

### CHAPTER 36.—That a concubine may become a lawful wife. Constitution 64, chapter 14.

If anyone has relations with a free woman without marital intention, and begets children by her, and wishes them to be legitimate children under his authority, he may draw up dowry instruments with their mother. For children who were previously natural children become legitimate and [Col. 0591D] subject to their father’s authority after the execution of dowry instruments, whether children born afterwards live or have died, or whether no other child at all is born.

### CHAPTER 37.—That prostitutes may choose an honourable life. Constitution 46 of the Novels, chapter 1.

The emperor decreed that prostitutes may choose a more honourable life without any fear, even if they have given a sworn security. Those, however, who have exacted such an oath and have lent their services against chastity shall pay, as a penalty, ten pounds of gold to those prostitutes who gave the pledges; and the penalty of ten pounds shall be demanded through the office of the governor. If the governor neglects this, he shall be compelled to pay the penalty from his own property, shall forfeit the office entrusted to him, and shall pay the penalty not only to the women but also to their heirs and other successors. This applies if it is proved that he exacted an oath from the prostitute. But if he did not exact an oath from her, he shall not be liable to that penalty.

### CHAPTER 38.—Concerning the prophet Hosea, who married a prostitute. Jerome on Hosea, Book I, on chapter 1.

(32, question 1, canon *Non est culpandus*.) The prophet Hosea is not to be blamed if he converted the prostitute whom he married to chastity; rather, he is to be praised because he made a bad woman good. For one who remains good is not himself defiled if joined to an evil person; rather, the evil person is turned toward good if she follows the example of the good. From this we understand that the prophet did not lose chastity by being joined to a prostitute; rather, the prostitute took up [Col. 0592B] the chastity which she had not previously possessed.

### CHAPTER 39.—Why marriage between relatives is forbidden. Augustine, *City of God*, Book XV, chapter 16.

Since, after the first union of the man made from dust and his spouse made from the man’s side, the human race needed the union of males and females in order to multiply through procreation, and since there were no human beings except those born from those two, men took their sisters as wives. The more ancient this was, compelled by necessity, the more blameworthy it afterwards became when forbidden by religious principle. For the most reasonable account was taken of charity: human beings, for whom harmonious relations were useful and honourable, were to be bound together by the ties of different relationships. No one person was to have many relationships concentrated in one other person; rather, individual relationships were to be distributed among individuals, so that, as it were, many persons might secure many others more diligently for social life.

“Father” and “father-in-law” are names of two relationships. Therefore, in order that each person might have one man as father and another as father-in-law, charity might extend itself more widely. Yet Adam alone was necessarily both father and father-in-law to his sons and daughters when brothers and sisters were joined in marriage. Likewise Eve, his wife, was both mother-in-law and mother to children of either sex. If there had been two women, one a mother and the other a mother-in-law, social affection would have bound itself together more abundantly. But there was then no means by which this could happen, since no human beings existed except brothers and sisters descended from those first two. It therefore had to occur when it could: once there was an abundance of people, wives were to be taken from those who were no longer sisters, so that what had formerly been a necessity would not merely cease to be necessary, but, if done, would be wicked. As the human race increased, we see this observed even among the impious worshippers of many false gods: even if marriages between siblings are permitted by their perverse laws, better custom nevertheless prefers to recoil from the licence and abhors it as though it could never have been lawful. Thus the union of male and female, so far as the human race is concerned, is a kind of nursery of the city. But the heavenly city must escape the fault of generation.

### CHAPTER 40.—Concerning three lawful marriages. Jerome.

(36, question 2, canon *Tria*.) Three lawful marriages are read of in the Scriptures. The first lawful marriage is that in which a chaste virgin, remaining a virgin, is lawfully given to a man; and the other cases follow as stated above. The second is where a virgin is found in a city by a man and forcibly joined to him: if her father wishes, that man shall endow her in whatever amount her father decides and shall pay the price for her chastity. Third, if the aforesaid daughter has been found in this manner and it is not her father’s will, he shall take her from the aforesaid man, give her to another, and endow her, and she shall be lawful to him. But the first is preferred to these two.

### CHAPTER 41.—Concerning a fourth lawful marriage. Jerome.

(27, question 2, canon *Additur*.) A fourth lawful marriage is also added: when a man’s wife has died, he may take another, but not one repudiated or betrothed to a man, but a virgin. The same applies to a woman. Hence Paul says: “The woman who is under a husband is bound by the law of her husband as long as her husband lives. Therefore, while her husband lives, she shall be called an adulteress if she is joined to another man. But if her husband has died, she is freed from the law of her husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man” (Rom. 7).

### CHAPTER 42.—That in marriage sensual and excessive intercourse is, as it were, adultery. Jerome.

In lawful marriage, adultery must be avoided: intercourse is to occur not in the measure demanded by pleasure, but in the measure required by the order of nature and the purpose of offspring. A man is not permitted to have another woman besides his wife. For if he has one, she who was lawful will not remain lawful. The Apostle Paul likewise says: “Every sin whatsoever a man commits is outside the body; but he who fornicates sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6). That is: a person living in marriage, whatever sins he commits, does not stain his own wife. But if he fornicates with others, he defiles her so that she is not lawful but, as it were, adulterous.

### CHAPTER 43.—That because of fornication one may dismiss a wife, but may not take another. Jerome, *On Matthew*, Book III, on chapter 19.

The Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, and takes another, commits adultery; and he who takes the dismissed woman commits adultery” (Matt. 19). Fornication alone overcomes affection for one’s wife; indeed, once she has divided the one flesh into another through that act and has separated herself from her husband by fornication, she ought not to be retained, lest she also bring her husband under a curse, as Scripture says: “He who keeps an adulteress is foolish and impious” (Prov. 18). Therefore, wherever there is fornication, or suspicion of fornication, the wife may freely be dismissed.

And because it could happen that someone might falsely accuse an innocent woman and, for the sake of a second marriage, lay a charge against the former wife, he is commanded to dismiss his first wife in such a way that he may not have a second while the first lives. What this means is: if you dismiss your wife not on account of lust but on account of injury, why, after experiencing the unhappy outcome of your former marriage, do you expose yourself to the danger of a new one? Furthermore, because it could happen that under the same law a wife might also repudiate her husband, the same precaution is commanded: she is not to take a second [Col. 0594A] husband. And because a prostitute, and a woman who had once been adulterous, did not fear disgrace, the husband is commanded not to marry a second time [the corrected Jerome text reads: “it is commanded to the husband a second time,” etc.], so that if he takes such a woman, he is guilty of adultery.

### CHAPTER 44.—That she is lawful who has been taken by an intervening oath. Constitution 65 of the Novels, chapter 1.

(30, question 5, canon *Si quis*.) If anyone swears upon the divine Scriptures that he will have a woman as his lawful wife, or gives such an oath in an oratory, she shall be his lawful wife, even if no dowry and no other written instrument intervenes.

### CHAPTER 45.—That a husband should be to his wife such as he wishes his wife to be to him. Augustine, *Sermons on the Words of the Lord*, tractate 47.

[Col. 0594B] If you are going to take wives, preserve yourselves for your wives. As you wish them to come to you, so they too ought to find you. What young man does not wish to marry a chaste wife? If he is to receive a virgin, who does not desire her untouched? Do you seek one untouched? Be untouched yourself. Do you seek one pure? Do not be impure. For she cannot do what you cannot do.

### CHAPTER 46.—That parents must not break the pledge of betrothal. From the Council of Elvira, chapter 54.

If any parents break the pledge of betrothal, they shall abstain from communion for three years. Nevertheless, if the same [original: “these same”] bridegroom or bride is discovered guilty of a grave crime, the parents shall be excused.

### CHAPTER 47.—That a wife is not to be taken during Lent. Nicholas’s replies to the inquiries of the Bulgarians, chapter 48.

[Col. 0594C]

(33, question 4, canon *Nec uxorem*.) We judge that neither taking a wife nor holding banquets can in any way be fitting during the Lenten season.

### CHAPTER 48.—That a priest should not dine at the wedding of a bigamist. From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 6.

(31, question 1, canon *De his*.) It is not fitting for a priest to dine at the wedding of a bigamist. For since a bigamist requires penance, what priest could, for the sake of a banquet, lend approval to such a marriage?

### CHAPTER 49.—That marriages are not to take place during Lent. Council of Laodicea, chapter 52.

(33, question 4, canon *Non oportet*.) It is not fitting to celebrate either marriages or birthdays during Lent.

### CHAPTER 50.—That a preacher of continence should not arrange marriages. Jerome to Nepotian.

[Col. 0594D]

A preacher of continence should not arrange marriages. He who reads the Apostle, “It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none” (1 Cor. 7), why does he compel a virgin to marry? He who is a priest of monogamy, why does he urge a widow to become a bigamist?

### CHAPTER 51.—Concerning those who take fiscal wives. *Capitularies*, Book III, chapter 16.

Concerning free men who take royal fiscal women as wives, and free women who take royal fiscal men: they are not to be excluded either from their parents’ inheritance, from pursuing their own legal claims, or from giving testimony on this account.

### CHAPTER 52.—That a freeborn woman who takes a slave becomes a slavewoman. Book V, chapter 20.

[Col. 0595A]

(29, question 2, canon *Si femina*.) If a freeborn woman takes a slave, knowing him to be a slave, she shall keep him; but the same law shall apply to man and woman alike.

### CHAPTER 53.—That a free person who takes a slavewoman may not dismiss her. Book VI, chapter 95 (canon 94).

(29, question 2, canon *Si quis*.) If any free person takes a slavewoman in marriage, he has no licence to dismiss her, if they were first joined by the consent of both.

### CHAPTER 54.—That a marriage between a male slave and a female slave is not dissolved even if they have different masters. Supplemental Capitularies, chapter 55.

The marriages of slaves shall not be dissolved even if they have different masters, but, remaining in one marriage, they shall serve their masters. This is to be observed in cases where there was a lawful union and it occurred by the will of the masters.

### CHAPTER 55.—Concerning a servant of the Church who wished to leave a slavewoman of the same Church. Pelagius to the subdeacon Melleus.

Dulcitia, a servant of our Church, living on the Tarpeian estate, brought the following complaint to our attention. She said that, after she had been widowed by the death of her husband, a certain Clerentius by name—said to have been born of a slavewoman of the Church—had, by various flatteries and persuasions, induced the mind of the aforesaid woman and arranged to join her to himself in union; he had also begotten a son by her. But now, after no short time of their union, when the son had already been born and brought up, and when, as is reported, no reasonable grounds existed, he had abandoned that same woman. He has proceeded to such insolence that, in order to evade the servitude due from him, he dares to assume the designation of a curial. He is also said to have had as his first wife a woman born on Church property from the Church’s tenants. From her *peculium* he is said still to possess a small field; and he is reported to have held other not inconsiderable property in his own *peculium*.

Accordingly, when you have received the force of this present order, detain the same Clarentius, investigate diligently the entire truth of the matter, and carry out whatever the Church’s interest requires concerning the aforesaid man or the Church’s property. If you find that he was born of a slavewoman of the Church, or is otherwise subject by lawful right to the Church, hasten to restore him, with all his property, to the Church estate. You shall also unite to him the aforesaid woman, whom he himself took into partnership, and he shall in no way have licence henceforth to leave her.

### CHAPTER 56.—If anyone mistakenly marries a slavewoman as a wife, thinking her free, or if a woman marries a slave as husband, such marriages do not stand. Constitution 37 of the Novels.

If anyone mistakenly takes a slavewoman as wife, thinking her to be free, or conversely if a free woman is mistakenly joined to a slave, and the truth is afterwards discovered, it must altogether be said that the marriage did not come into existence. For marriage cannot be contracted between a free person and a slavewoman, or between a slave and a free woman.

But if, through the cunning and connivance of the master, a slave or slavewoman contracts marriage with a free person—for perhaps the master joined his slavewoman, as though free, to a freeborn man and provided a dowry for her so that he might obtain, wholly or in part, the gift made on account of the marriage—then, if anything of this kind occurs, that very dowry gift shall make both the slavewoman free and the marriage valid; no law, so far as servitude is concerned, shall disturb such a marriage.

But if the master did not specifically consent to the marriage of his slavewoman or slave, yet knowingly failed to prevent it—for perhaps he does so in order later to bring an action against the free man because he took his slavewoman as wife, or against the freeborn woman because she married his slave—then, if anything of this kind occurs, although the master did not specifically consent, nevertheless, knowingly failing to prohibit it, the marriage shall stand in full legal force and the person of servile condition shall be released into free status. It is beyond doubt that children born from such marriages are both freeborn and legitimate.

### CHAPTER 57.—That a freedwoman who married her patron cannot be joined to another against his will. Chapter 25.

If a freedwoman joined to her patron in marriage renounces his marriage but wishes to enter a second marriage, she cannot do so against her patron’s will. Otherwise, if she marries against his will, there is no marriage; rather, she is regarded as joined as a prostitute.

Constitution 69, chapter 3. If anyone wishes to take his freedwoman as wife, he shall draw up dowry instruments with her, and he shall have a lawful wife, even though he himself shines with the highest rank. If children are born of such a marriage, they shall be legitimate successors and succeed their father.

### CHAPTER 58.—Concerning one who joined his slavewoman to his young son and afterwards took her away. Gregory to Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse (Register, Book III, chapter 12).

The bearer of this letter has complained tearfully that many years ago he was received [the reference to “Fontes” is uncertain] by a certain man, whom he does not know, from the Fontes on the estate of the Massanensian Church, and was forcibly joined to a girl through various persuasions. He states that he now has sons already grown young men by her; yet she is now said to have been forcibly separated from him, taken away, and sold to another person. [Col. 0596D] If this is true, your Belovedness sees how unheard-of and cruel an evil it is. We therefore urge you to investigate and examine this great wickedness with that vigour which we know you certainly possess in pious causes. If you discover that the matter is as the aforesaid bearer has represented it, you shall take care not only to restore what was wrongly done to its former condition, but also hasten by every means to impose such punishment as may appease God.

### CHAPTER 59.—That no one may have two lawful wives. Stephen V to Theodosius, bishop.

Do you instruct a barbarian people to marry two brides at the same time? Have you not read the Apostle, expounding the sacrament of the Church: “The two shall be one flesh” (1 Cor. 6; Gen. 2)? Or do your books perhaps falsely assert that three are one flesh? Cease now to waste away in such sloth, and learn to obey paternal rules, lest you be found to transgress the boundaries established by the fathers (Prov. 22), or to pass through ambition from a greater to a still greater church—an attempt for which the sacred canons deprive even laypersons of communion.

### CHAPTER 60.—That one accustomed to sleep with many women is not to be considered as having a concubine. Constitution 79 of the Novels.

No one who customarily sleeps with many women is to be understood as having a concubine. For just as one who has a lawful wife cannot have another woman while that marriage endures, so one who has one concubine cannot have others during that time.

### CHAPTER 61.—That Ishmael was not cast out because his mother was a slavewoman, but because of fraternal discord. Augustine, *On the One Baptism*, Book I (*On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 13).

(Distinction 56, canon *Ismael*.) Ishmael was not separated from the people of God because his mother was a slavewoman; rather, he was separated because of fraternal discord (Gen. 21). Nor did the status of the wife, whose son he was more truly, benefit him, since through her marital rights he was both sown in the slavewoman and received from the slavewoman.

### CHAPTER 62.—That in a relationship with a free woman, marriage rather than concubinage is to be understood. *Pandects*, Book XXIII, title 2.

In relations with a free woman, marriage rather than concubinage is to be understood, provided she has not made gain from her body.

### CHAPTER 63.—Concerning the penance of one who attempts to have two wives. Nicholas’s replies to the inquiries of the Bulgarians, chapter 51.

Whoever is found to have two wives at one time shall be compelled, while retaining the first, to relinquish the latter; moreover, he shall be compelled to undergo such penance as the priest of the place considers appropriate.

### CHAPTER 64.—That one who has a concubine is not excluded from communion if he has no other woman. From the First Council of Toledo, canon 17.

(Distinction 34, canon *Is qui non*.) If anyone who has a faithful wife keeps a concubine, he shall not receive communion. But one who has no wife and has a concubine in place of a wife shall not be excluded from communion, provided that he is content with union to one woman only, whether wife or concubine [Col. 0597D] as he chooses. Otherwise, he shall be excluded until he ceases and returns to penance.

### CHAPTER 65.—That it is, as it were, a marriage if a man uses a concubine so that he has no other and does not desire another. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 5.

(32, question 2, canon *Solet*.) It is often asked whether, when a man and a woman—neither being another’s husband or wife—are joined to one another not for the procreation of children but solely for intercourse because of incontinence, under a pledge that he will not do this with another woman, this should be called marriage. Perhaps it may not unreasonably be called a marriage if they agree to this arrangement until the death of one of them, and if they have not avoided the begetting of offspring—even though this was not their reason for joining—so as either to refuse children born to them or to perform some evil act to prevent their birth.

But if either or both of these conditions is lacking, I do not see how we can call such a relationship marriage. For if a man has taken a woman for a time, until he finds one worthy of his rank or resources, whom he may take as an equal, he is an adulterer in intention: not with the woman whom he hopes to find, but with this woman with whom he lies in such a way that he has no marital fellowship with her.

### CHAPTER 66.—That a Christian may have only one woman. Isidore, *On the Harmony of the New and Old Testaments*, chapter 3.

(Distinction 34, canon *Christiano*.) For a Christian it is lawful, I do not say to have many women, but not even two at once: only one woman, either a wife or, if a wife is lacking, a concubine in the place of a wife.

### CHAPTER 67.—That one born of a nobleman and a slavewoman is not legitimate. Pelagius to Sindula, master of soldiers.

We urge that Montanianus—who, contrary to every truth and contrary to the laws, since he was born of a slavewoman, attempts to establish himself as a legitimate son—be allowed to obtain nothing further from you by any possible deception. For it is established that the Montanianus whose estate is at issue died without children of his own and left surviving the sons of his full brother, who succeed to him by lawful right. Therefore this Montanianus, whose claim is at issue, has no standing in the succession of that deceased man. For even if he obtained imperial rescripts, these can in no way prejudice those lawful successors, because the most clement emperor himself issued general laws commanding that no rescripts obtained by one discovered to have lied in his petitions shall benefit him. Though he was a natural son, he states contrary to truth that he is legitimate—something which can by no legal reasoning be shown.

### CHAPTER 68.—That children born of lawful marriage follow their father, while those conceived in common follow their mother. *Pandects*, Book I, title 5.

When a lawful marriage has been contracted, children follow their father; those of uncertain paternity (*vulgo quaesiti*) follow their mother.

### CHAPTER 69.—Who is conceived in common. The same source.

Those are called conceived in common (*vulgo concepti*) who cannot identify their father; and also those who can identify him, but have one whom they may not lawfully have.

### CHAPTER 70.—That those born outside lawful marriage follow their mother rather than their father. The same source.

[Col. 0598D]

This is the law of nature: one born without lawful marriage follows the mother. Those who are in the womb are, in almost all civil law, understood to exist in the world of things. Thus lawful inheritances are restored to them; so that, if a pregnant woman is captured by enemies, what is subsequently born—even if she gives birth while in the possession of a purchaser in good faith—is not acquired by prescription, being treated as stolen property.

### CHAPTER 71.—That the status of children depends on the condition of the mother, not of the father. Book I, Constitution, title 4.

A person is freeborn who, immediately upon birth, is free, whether born in marriage from two freeborn parents, from freed parents, or from one freed parent and one freeborn parent. Likewise, one born of a free mother and a slave father is nevertheless born free, just as one born of a free mother and an uncertain father is free, because he was conceived in common. It is sufficient that the mother was free at the time of birth, even if she conceived while a slave; and conversely, if she conceived while free but, after becoming a slave, gives birth. For it has been decided that the child is born free, because the misfortune of the mother ought not harm one who is in the womb.

From these principles this question has also arisen: if a pregnant slavewoman is manumitted and later becomes a slave again before giving birth, does she bear a free child or a slave? Marcellus [Martianus] holds that the child is born free. For it is sufficient for one in the womb to have had a free mother even for an intermediate time; and this is true.

Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book IX, chapter 5. (32, question 4, canon *Liberi dicti*.) “Free” (*liberi*) are so called because they are born from free marriage. For children of a free man and a slavewoman are of servile status. Whoever is born always takes the inferior status of the parent.

The same, Book IX, chapter 5. Natural children are called the children of freeborn concubines, whom nature alone, not the honourability of marriage, has produced.

The same. Those who are not from lawful marriage follow their mother rather than their father.

### CHAPTER 72.—That marriage is permitted to some and not to others. Augustine, *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, chapter 22 [chapter 24].

(27, question 1, canon *Nubendi*.) Permission to marry is granted to some—namely, those who have not professed virginity or widowly chastity—but it is not granted to others, namely those who have resolved to remain virgins or continent. Fornication, however, is permitted to no one with impunity.

### CHAPTER 73.—That many things are permissible before a vow which are not permissible after a vow. Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, Book I [chapter 24].

(32, question 8, canon *Non solum*.) Not only must adultery not be committed, as some do [the original reads: “does not some”], but everyone who dismisses his wife and takes another commits adultery, even if he takes her in order to make her a Christian. Likewise, anyone not bound to a wife who has vowed continence to God must in no way sin under this pretext: he must not think that he ought to take as wife a woman who promises, because she desires his marriage, that she will become a Christian.

For what was lawful to a person before he made a vow will not be lawful after he has vowed never to do it, provided he has vowed what ought to be vowed—such as perpetual virginity, or widowly continence after marriages have been experienced and the marital bond dissolved; or, in the case of faithful and chaste spouses who vow by mutual consent and release one another from their carnal obligations. It is not lawful for one spouse to make such a vow without the other. Therefore, these vows, and whatever others are most rightly made, must under no condition be broken once persons have made them without condition.

### CHAPTER 74.—That marriage contains within itself the sacrament of Christ and the Church. Leo to Rusticus of Narbonne (Epistle 92, chapter 4).

(27, question 2, canon *Cum societas*.) Since the fellowship of marriage was established from the beginning in such a way that, beyond the union of the sexes, it also contained within itself the sacrament of Christ and the Church, there is no doubt that a woman does not belong to marriage where the nuptial mystery is shown not to have been present.

### CHAPTER 75.—That it is shameful for women not to receive the rewards of marriage. Ambrose on Luke, Book I. [Note: [Col. 0599D] Near the end, on Luke chapter 1, Ambrose discusses Elizabeth.]

(32, question 2, canon *Pudor*.) Sarah was ashamed of the age at which she gave birth, and yet rejoiced that she lacked the reproach of barrenness. For it is shameful for women not to receive the rewards of marriage, since this is their sole reason for marrying.

### CHAPTER 76.—That childbirth is the reward of marriage for women. Book II, immediately after the beginning.

(32, question 2, canon *Pudor*.) Since childbirth is the reward of marriage and the grace of wedlock for women, it was no small reason why Mary’s virginity should deceive the prince of this world.

### CHAPTER 77.—That the procreation of children alone is the bond of marriage. Augustine, *Against Julian*, Book II.

(32, question 1, canon *Non enim*.) The reality of marriage does not consist solely—as you rave—in the sexual union of male and female, although without that union marriage cannot propagate children. But other matters properly belong to marriage, by which marriages are distinguished from adulteries: namely, the fidelity of the marital bed, the ordered concern to procreate children, and—what is the greatest difference—the good use of an evil, that is, the good use of carnal concupiscence, an evil which adulterers use badly.

### CHAPTER 78.—What a husband should do if his wife can in no way render him the marital due. Gregory the Younger to Bishop Boniface (Gregory II, Epistle 13, chapter 2).

[Col. 0600C]

(32, question 7, canon *Quod proposuisti*.) You have asked what a husband should do if his wife, afflicted by illness, is never able to render him the marital due. It would be good if he remained as he is and devoted himself to abstinence; but, since this belongs to the strong, one unable to contain himself should marry instead. Yet he should not withdraw support from her whom illness prevents [the text has *quod* for *quam*] from rendering it, since no detestable fault excludes her.

### CHAPTER 79.—Concerning repudiation of a husband who cannot render the marital due to his wife. Code, Book V, chapter 19, title 10.

If a husband, from the beginning of marriage until two continuous years have elapsed, is wholly unable through natural infirmity to have intercourse with his wife, the woman or her parents may repudiate the husband without danger of losing the dowry.

### CHAPTER 80.—Concerning the same matter. Book VI of the Capitularies, chapter 91 [canon 55].

If a man and a woman have joined themselves in marriage, and afterwards the woman says that her husband is unable to have intercourse with her, then, if she can prove that this is true, she may take another husband, because, according to the Apostle, her husband was unable to render her the marital due (1 Cor. 7).

### CHAPTER 81.—Concerning the same matter. Constitution 37 of the Novels.

If anyone cannot have sexual relations with his wife, the marriage shall be dissolved even without repudiation.

### CHAPTER 82.—That marriages should be contracted for the hope of offspring. Augustine, *Against Faustus*, Book I.

[Col. 0601A]

The Manichaeans unite with women in an unchaste union merely to satisfy lust, but they receive children unwillingly, although it is for that purpose alone that marriages should be contracted. How, then, do you not forbid marriage when you try to remove from marriage that from which marriage exists? Once this is removed, husbands will disgracefully be lovers, wives prostitutes, marriage-beds brothels, and fathers-in-law procurers.

### CHAPTER 83.—That one must abstain from one’s wife on the Lord’s Day. Nicholas’s replies to the inquiries of the Bulgarians, chapter 63.

Moreover, you ask whether it is lawful for a husband to have intercourse or sleep with his wife during the night or day of the Lord’s Day. We answer: since, as we have taught above, worldly work must cease on the Lord’s Day, how much more must one guard against carnal pleasure and every pollution of the body.

### CHAPTER 84.—Concerning the same matter. Ambrose on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, on chapter 7, beginning.

(33, question 4, canon *Si causa*.) If a wife is taken for the purpose of producing children, not much time seems to be allowed for sexual use itself, since feast days and days of processions, and the very order of conception and childbirth according to the law, show that abstinence ought to be observed at those times.

### CHAPTER 85.—That a woman is subject to the authority of her husband. Ambrose [Augustine], *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, chapter 45.

(33, question 5, canon *Mulierem*.) A woman is plainly subject to her husband’s authority and possesses no authority of her own: for she can neither teach, nor testify, nor give surety, nor judge; much less can she rule.

### CHAPTER 86.—That a husband ought not to withhold the marital due from his wife. Jerome on Ezekiel, Book VII.

Let the wife beware lest, perhaps overcome by desire for intercourse, she conceal this from her husband; and let the husband beware lest he force his wife, thinking that her will in marriage must be subject to him at every time.

### CHAPTER 87.—That those intending to receive communion should abstain from their wives at that time. Jerome’s sermon for the vigil of Easter, beginning: “Today, dearest brothers, the people of Israel …” (Volume IX, sermon 33, *On Eating the Lamb*, though among the spurious works).

(33, q. 4, c. *Sciatis*.) Know, dearest brethren, that whoever renders the marital due to his wife cannot devote himself to prayer [Col. 0601D], nor eat of the flesh of the Lamb. Again, one verse later: If the loaves of the presentation could not be eaten by those who had touched their wives (1 Kings 21), how much more can that bread which came down from heaven not be profaned and touched by those who shortly before were joined in marital embraces! This is not because we condemn marriage, but because, at the time when we are about to eat the flesh of the Lamb, we ought to abstain from works of the flesh.

CAP. 88.—That husbands should not have intercourse with their wives after childbirth before the time of purification. Bede, *History of the English*, book I, chapter 27. Gregory answers Augustine (Gregory, to Augustine’s tenth question).

(Dist. 5, c. *Ad ejus vero*.) A husband ought not approach his wife after she has given birth [Col. 0602A] until the child she has borne has been weaned. But an evil custom has crept into the habits of married people: women disdain to nurse the children whom they bear and hand them over to other women to be nursed. This practice plainly seems to have been devised solely for the sake of incontinence. For, unwilling to restrain themselves, they despise nursing those whom they bear. Therefore, women who from this evil custom hand their children over to others for nursing ought not have intercourse with their husbands until the period of purification has passed. Indeed, even apart from childbirth, while they are subject to their customary menstruation, they are forbidden intercourse with their husbands; so much so that the sacred law strikes with death any man who approaches a menstruating woman (Lev. 20). Nevertheless, while a woman undergoes her customary menstruation, she ought not be forbidden to enter the church [Col. 0602B], because this superfluity of nature cannot be imputed to her as guilt; and, since she suffers it unwillingly, it is not just that she be deprived of entry into the Church.

Again (in the same place, somewhat later; 33, q. 4, c. *Vir cum*). A man who has slept with his own wife ought not enter the church unless he has washed with water; nor ought he enter immediately even after washing.

Again (a few verses later). It has always been the custom of the Romans from ancient times, after intercourse with one’s own wife, both to seek purification by washing and reverently to abstain for a little while from entering the church. In saying this, we do not reckon marriage to be a fault; but because even lawful intercourse between spouses cannot occur without pleasure of the flesh, one must abstain from entering the sacred place, since that pleasure itself can by no means exist without fault.

Again (a little later). Lawful union of the flesh ought to be for the sake of offspring, not pleasure; and bodily intercourse ought to be for the purpose of begetting children, not satisfying vices. But if anyone makes use of his wife not carried away by the desire for pleasure, but solely for the sake of begetting children, he is certainly to be left to his own judgment both concerning entry into the Church and concerning reception of the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood. For he who, placed in the fire, does not know how to burn ought not be forbidden by us to receive it. But when not love for procreating offspring but pleasure is condemned in the act of intercourse, married persons too have something to lament concerning their intercourse.

Again (at the end). Then a man who, after intercourse with his wife, has washed with water may also receive the mystery of sacred communion, when, in accordance with the previously prescribed ruling, he has also been permitted to enter the church [Col. 0602D].

CAP. 89.—That it is sometimes lawful and sometimes unlawful for a Christian to have intercourse with his wife. Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, chapter 128.

(Dist. 88, c. *Fornicari*.) It is never lawful for anyone to commit fornication; but it is sometimes lawful, and sometimes unlawful, to engage in trade. Before someone becomes an ecclesiastic, trading is lawful; once he has become one, it is not lawful. Likewise, it is sometimes lawful, and sometimes unlawful, for a Christian to have intercourse with his wife. For on account of days of procession it is sometimes not lawful to have intercourse, because one ought also to abstain from lawful things, so that what is requested may more easily be obtained. Hence the Apostle says: “By mutual consent, you ought to abstain for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Cor. 7). For under the law likewise, during a fast it is not lawful to strike or quarrel; afterwards it is lawful [Col. 0603A].

CAP. 90.—That a husband, if there is a quarrel between them, should subdue his wife. Sermon 65 of Ambrose, *On the Words of the Lord*.

If husband and wife have a dispute with one another in one house, the husband ought to labor to subdue his wife; once subdued, the wife should be subjected to her husband. Once the wife is subject to her husband, let there be peace in the house.

CAP. 91.—That a woman should be subject to her husband. Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, in the treatment of the fourth day (book V, chapter 7).

(33, q. 5, *Adam*.) Adam was deceived through Eve (Gen. 3), not Eve through Adam; the woman summoned him to guilt. It is just that he should take her under his governance [“that he should take him as governor,” original reading], lest he again fall through feminine pliancy.

CAP. 92.—Why a woman ought to veil her head. Ambrose on the First Epistle to the Corinthians (on 1 Cor. 11).

[Col. 0603B]

(33, q. 5, c. *Mulier*.) A woman ought to veil her head, because she is not the image of God, but so that she may be shown to be subject. And because transgression began through her, she ought to have this sign in church: out of reverence for the bishop she ought not have her head uncovered, but covered with a veil; nor ought she have authority to speak, because the bishop bears the person of Christ. Thus, as before a judge, so before the bishop—because he is the Lord’s vicar—she ought to appear subject on account of the origin of guilt.

CAP. 93.—That the husband ought to rule and the wife to obey. Augustine on John, first part, tractate II.

[Col. 0603C] In Scripture, “flesh” is used for a wife, just as “spirit” is sometimes used for a husband. And why? Because he governs and she is governed; he ought to rule and she to serve. For where the flesh rules and the spirit serves, the household is disordered. What household is worse than one in which a woman holds authority over a man? But that household is rightly ordered in which the husband rules and the woman obeys.

CAP. 94.—That the natural order is for a woman to serve her husband. Augustine, book of *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 153.

(33, q. 5, c. *Est ordo*.) There is a natural order among human beings: women serve men, and children serve parents; for this too is justice for them, that the lesser serve the greater.

CAP. 95.—On the same subject. Augustine, book of *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, chapter 106.

[Col. 0603D] (33, q. 5, c. *Imago*.) This is the image of God in man: that one man was made, from whom the rest arise, possessing God’s authority as, so to speak, his vicar; for every king bears the image of God. Therefore woman was not made in the image of God. For Scripture says: “And God made man; in the image of God he made him” (Gen. 1; Wis. 2). Hence the Apostle says: “A man indeed ought not to veil his head, because he is the image and glory of God; but a woman” (1 Cor. 11) therefore veils herself because she is not the glory or image of God.

CAP. 96.—Again, on the same subject. Augustine.

(33, q. 5, c. *Satis*.) From this it appears sufficiently how the law intended women to be subject to men, and wives almost servants. For when a husband gives testimony against his wife whereby she might be stoned, if this were proved true, he himself is nevertheless not in turn stoned if it is established to be false; rather, he is merely punished, fined, and commanded to remain permanently attached to her whom he had wished to be without [Col. 0604A]. But in other cases, the law commands that one who by false testimony has harmed another should suffer the same penalty which he himself would have suffered had the allegation been proved true.

CAP. 97.—That, as a man ought to be subject to Christ, so a woman ought to be subject to her husband. Jerome on the Epistle to Titus (chapter 2).

(33, q. 5, c. *Cum caput*.) Since the husband is the head of the wife, and Christ is the head of the husband, every wife who does not submit to her husband—that is, to her head—is guilty of the same offense as a husband who does not submit to his head, Christ. Moreover, the word of the Lord is blasphemed either when God’s first sentence is despised and treated as nothing (Gen. 3), or when Christ’s Gospel is dishonored because a Christian woman, subject to her husband by God’s law, desires to rule her husband contrary to law and to the order of nature—when even Gentile women serve their husbands by the common law of nature [Col. 0604B].

CAP. 98.—That a woman cannot fulfill a vow of abstinence unless her husband permits it. Augustine, book of *Questions on Numbers*, chapter 53 (book IV, *Questions on Numbers*, question 59).

(33, q. 5, c. *Noluit*.) The law did not wish a woman to vow something to God against her own person in such a way that, even in abstaining from lawful and permitted things [Col. 0604C], authority in these vows should belong to the woman rather than to the man. Thus, if while still unmarried her father had allowed her to fulfill her vows, but before she fulfills them she marries and this does not please her husband once he learns of it, she is not to fulfill them; and this entirely without sin, because God has cleansed her, as the law says—that is, judged her clean. Nor should this be considered to be done against God, since God himself commanded and willed it.

Again, in the same place, somewhat later. (33, q. 5, c. *Manifestum*.) It is clear that the law intended woman to be under her husband, so that none of her vows made for the sake of abstinence are fulfilled by her unless the husband authorizes them by permitting them. For although the law intended it to count as the husband’s sin if he first permits and afterward forbids, it still [Col. 0604D] did not say that the woman should do what she had vowed because it had first been permitted by her husband. It said that the sin was the husband’s, because he refused what he had first granted; yet it did not thereby give the woman permission that, although her husband first granted it, he should afterward be disregarded if he forbids it [“be condemned,” original reading; materially uncertain].

CAP. 99.—That adultery holds second place among punishments. From the first epistle of Clement to James.

(32, q. 7, c. *Quid in omnibus*.) What sin is graver than adultery among all sins? For it holds second place in punishments, since first place belongs to those who stray from God, even if they have lived soberly.

CAP. 100.—On adultery. Gregory, *Morals*, book XXI (chapter 9, beginning).

[Col. 0605A]

When even an unmarried woman is shamefully desired, adultery is committed.

CAP. 101.—What adultery is. Ambrose to Paternus (letter 66, beginning).

(27, q. 2, c. *Si quis*.) If someone has intercourse with a woman betrothed and delivered to him, he calls it marriage. Whoever assaults another’s chastity commits adultery; often the very name of it restrains the audacity to make an attempt.

CAP. 102.—On the same subject. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage* (chapter 4).

(32, q. 5, c. *Illae autem*.) It is called adultery when, either at the prompting of one’s own lust or with another’s consent, one has intercourse with another man or woman contrary to the marriage covenant; and thus the fidelity is broken which, even in bodily and lowly matters, is a great good of the soul [Col. 0605B]. Therefore it is certainly to be preferred even to bodily well-being, upon which this present life itself depends.

CAP. 103.—That one who commits adultery violates the temple of God. The same author, *On the Words of the Lord*, chapter 17 (sermon 16, chapter 10).

Your very body is the temple of God’s Spirit (1 Cor. 3). Now consider what you do with God’s temple. If you chose to commit adultery in a church, within its very walls, what could be more wicked than you? But now you yourself are God’s temple.

CAP. 104.—One who desires another’s wife so that, if opportunity were given, he would use her sexually is already guilty of the deed. Augustine, *On Free Will*, book I (chapter 3).

[Col. 0605C] (On Penance, dist. 1, c. *Si cui*.) Even if someone does not have the opportunity to have intercourse with another man’s wife, yet if it is somehow clear that he desires it and would do it if the power were given him, he is no less guilty than if he had been caught in the very act.

CAP. 105.—That adultery must not be committed even in the hope of begetting those to be regenerated. Augustine to Claudius, against Julian, book V (chapter 8, beginning).

(32, q. 4, c. *Sic non facienda*.) Adulteries must not be committed even with the intention of begetting persons to be regenerated, just as thefts must not be committed even with the intention of feeding holy poor persons. That, however, ought to be done not by perpetrating thefts but by making good use of the mammon of iniquity.

CAP. 106.—What adultery is. Isidore, *Book of Sentences*, chapter 39 (book II).

[Col. 0605D]

Fornication of the flesh is adultery; fornication of the soul is slavery to idols.

CAP. 107.—That one who goes from his own wife to another commits adultery. Isidore, on Exodus, chapter 29.

(32, q. 5, c. *Non moechaberis*.) “You shall not commit adultery”: that is, no one should have intercourse with women other than within the bonds of marriage in order to satisfy lust. For, specifically, one commits adultery who approaches another woman besides his own wife.

CAP. 108.—That one who has committed adultery once is guilty of it even if he will never do so again. Augustine to Valerius, *On Marriage and Concupiscence* (book I, chapter 26).

If someone commits adultery, even if afterward he never commits it again, he is guilty of adultery until the guilt itself is remitted by pardon. Therefore the sin remains, although the act which he committed is no longer present, because what was done perished with the time in which it was done [Col. 0606A].

CAP. 109.—How an adulteress ought to be repudiated. *Novels*, constitution 5, chapter 7.

If a husband believes that his wife has been convicted of adultery, he must first lodge written accusations either against the woman or against the adulterer; and, if such an accusation is proved true, then he may send a repudiation.

CAP. 110.—If the husband fails in the accusation, the same penalties are to be imposed as upon a convicted wife, chapter 8.

If a husband has in any way plotted against his wife’s life, or if, knowing that others are doing this, he has not disclosed it to the woman and has not proceeded against them according to the laws; if he has plotted against his wife’s chastity or attempted to hand her over to others for adultery; likewise, if the husband has lodged written accusations of adultery against her and cannot prove the adultery, the woman may repudiate her husband.

Again. If the husband cannot prove the accusation of adultery, he shall be subject to those penalties which the woman would have suffered if she had been convicted.

Again. If, in the same house in which the woman lives with him, he is convicted of frequently staying with another woman in contempt of her, and, having been accused once and twice—whether by his own relatives, by the woman’s relatives, or by other suitable persons—does not abstain from such disgraceful conduct, the woman may dissolve the marriage [Col. 0606B].

CAP. 111.—That a husband may kill a man whom, after forbidding him three times, he finds with his wife in one house. Chapter 14.

[Col. 0606C]

If anyone suspects that another intends to violate his wife’s chastity, the husband may send to the suspected man written attestations, and three times warn him through those attestations, containing suitable witnesses, not to be found with his wife. If, after three written attestations containing suitable persons, he finds the man whom he has warned with his wife—whether in his own house, the woman’s house, the house of that adulterer, a tavern [*propinquo*, printed reading], or a bakery—then the husband may kill him with his own hands without any penalty. But if he finds him elsewhere conversing with his wife, he should summon three suitable witnesses through whom he can prove before the judge that he found him conversing with his wife; he should hand him over to the judge, and, if the judge finds that the suspected man conversed with the woman after the three attestations, he shall punish him as an adulterer without requiring any further inquiry [Col. 0606D].

CAP. 112.—That if, after three attestations, a husband finds his wife conversing with a suspected man in a sacred place, he should seek their punishment from the bishop, chapter 15.

If, after three attestations [*testificationes*, variant], the husband finds his wife conversing with a suspected man in a sacred place, he shall hand them over to the defender of the Church [Col. 0607A] or to other clerics, so that they may be kept separately in the custody and at the risk of the defender or clerics, and so that, after hearing them, the judge may send them to the city’s religious bishop. By his authority he shall take them and inflict upon both the penalties prescribed against adulterers, without requiring anything further, if the man was found speaking with the woman after the three attestations. It is most just that neither adulterers nor abductors of women should claim the protection of sacred precincts—especially if someone has spoken within sacred precincts to another man’s wife concerning the adultery itself.

And we lay down generally that, if anyone finds his wife, daughter, granddaughter, or daughter-in-law conversing with someone and suspects that they met for an indecent purpose, he may hand both over to the defender of the Church or other clerics, to be kept separately at their risk until he makes the matter known to the judge and the judge takes the persons in accordance with the laws and investigates the case [Col. 0607B].

CAP. 113.—That after five years from its commission no one can be accused of adultery. *Code*, book XI, tractate V.

An adulterer cannot be accused after five years from the time the adultery is said to have been committed; the period is counted continuously.

CAP. 114.—That a husband cannot bring an accusation of adultery against a wife retained in marriage. Tractate XI.

No one doubts that a husband cannot bring an accusation of adultery while retaining his wife in marriage.

CAP. 115.—That only close relatives may accuse someone of adultery. Tractate XXIX.

[Col. 0607C] Lest persons acting rashly be allowed to dishonor marriages, it is decreed that the right to bring an accusation of adultery belongs only to close and necessary persons: namely, a brother, father, paternal uncle, or maternal uncle, whom genuine grief impels to accuse. Yet we impose the law upon these persons too, that they may, if they wish, suppress the accusation by abolition. Above all, the husband ought to be judge of the marital bed, and he may proceed against his wife as accused on suspicion. We decree that outsiders are to be kept far from this accusation.

CAP. 116.—Concerning King Lothair and his wife: that she is not to be convicted by trial through single combat. Pope Nicholas to King Charles (letter 49).

As we have learned from the reports of many, King Lothair intends to hold an assembly and plans to subject Queen Theutberga to his own examination and judgment. If he can produce her by the deceits of his falsehood as though she had not been his lawful wife, he wishes to separate her wholly from himself. But if he wishes to dismiss her as his own wife and afterwards accuse her as though she had committed adultery, he intends, on this account, to compel his own man and Theutberga’s man to single combat; and, if the queen’s man falls, he plans to kill her without delay.

Again. Further, whether judgment is to be made concerning the marriage bond or the charge of adultery, no reason permits Theutberga to enter into conflict with Lothair or to undertake the lawful contest of the controversy unless she is first, for a time, restored to her own control [Col. 0608A] [“restored,” original reading], joined to her own relatives, and placed where there is no fear of violence from a crowd and where it is not difficult to produce witnesses or the other persons required in such controversies by both the holy canons and venerable Roman laws. We say this in order to show what legal conflict Lothair thinks he can undertake with a woman whom he daily harasses and wears down in his inner chambers. When he wishes, he brings her to judgment; when he wishes, he returns her to confinement; and, when she has been brought out, unless she professes what he has ordered, he punishes her. Therefore she must be entrusted to her own liberty and freed from every oppression and power of the person with whom the contest is undertaken; she must be allowed freely to make use of her own resources, and she ought to avoid suspect persons while she seeks to show herself innocent of the accusations [Col. 0608B].

CAP. 117.—A confession, although extorted, is by no means to be regarded as a confession. Nicholas to Queen Theutberga (letter 48).

We do not receive as a confession this confession of yours, which not will but force extorted. Nor do we permit such an evil to spread its roots; unless it is uprooted from within, it can grow to the ruin of many. For if this is allowed, all husbands may wear down with various afflictions women whom they have lawfully received, if they hate them, and immediately compel them to say that they were not lawfully married; indeed, by inflicting intolerable punishments, they may compel them to declare a capital crime against themselves [Col. 0608C].

CAP. 118.—That the wife unjustly taken from the nobleman Radulf should be restored. John VIII to Theutberga and her son Alderic [Alberic].

Again and again we admonish you and exhort you by these present letters of our apostolic office to restore his wife without delay to the nobleman Radulf, as we have already said, and to cause her to cleave to her husband, acting according to the law of the Lord. For no law permits otherwise unless she either confesses the charge brought against her or is released from it after a lawful purgation has first been made. But if she chooses to do neither, and instead, using mere obstinacy, takes care to make no satisfaction to anyone, it is plainly clear that she undoubtedly confesses the charge which she does not clear away. For, as Pope Hormisdas writes, only those persons evade the examination of conscience who do not adhere to what is right.

Therefore, if he, or she, or you, Theutberga and Alderic, postponing obedience to the decrees of our apostolic office, should further attempt without any reasonable cause to withdraw the often-mentioned woman either from her husband’s authority or from examination under the law, then she and you, Theutberga and Alderic, until you obey our decree, are excommunicated by the judgment of almighty God and by the sentence of the princes of the apostles, blessed Peter and Paul, and are cut off from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, together with your supporters, accomplices, followers, and confederates, as violators of divine and human laws, despisers of the decrees of the Apostolic See, and persons who have broken them so often and in so many ways [Col. 0609A].

CAP. 119.—On the same matter and her purgation. John VIII to Ausbert, Archbishop of Milan.

A man of high rank named Radulf, of imperial renown, recently approached us, complaining and asserting that, inflamed by zeal for chastity, he had marked his wife, named Bava, with the stain of an indecent suspicion and had charged her, as evil report increased, with the carnal crime of adultery. After he had handed her over to her parents and relatives to purge herself according to the tenor of his own law, she was kept for more than a year under the liability of criminal accusations. Therefore, stirred by love of justice, we commanded her parents by apostolic authority that [Col. 0609B], during the month of August of the past seventh indiction, they should restore the woman to her husband, whether purged or otherwise—there being no doubt that she would undergo, if not the remedy of secular law, at least that of ecclesiastical mercy. Otherwise, they should know that they would be deprived with her of communion in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Yet they took care to do none of these things—so the aforementioned man reported when he came to us again, and so the outcome itself showed—although they respected neither the judgment of secular or divine laws nor the decree of the Apostolic See. Accordingly, we should rightly have deprived them of participation in the sacred communion, as we had threatened them; but we judged that the other party should be heard. Therefore, since we ought to be just mediators, and a mediator is not mediator of one party only, and since we do not wish to burden them by travelling farther, we exhort your holiness, acting as our delegate in the circumstances of this controversy, to summon at a fixed and announced time the venerable bishops Luitfrid of Pavia and Paul of Piacenza to a specified place. Having summoned by your messengers and letters the wife of the aforementioned Radulf, you shall without delay exercise, concerning both spouses, those measures which belong to secular and divine law, within the limits of the priestly office entrusted to you [Col. 0609C].

If, after your summons—which is plainly the third following our second—she chooses not to return to her husband after being granted the lawful and unquestionable freedom to purge herself, and evades and declines the examination of your holiness, then, acting in one accord with our spirit, exclude from communion in the sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ both her and the relatives who wickedly protect and defend her, indeed her supporters and all who communicate with them, until they obey [Col. 0609D].

CAP. 120.—Sermon of Ambrose on chastity [Note: [Col. 0609D] Sermon 49, which is by Bishop Maximus, falsely ascribed to Ambrose] concerning the Lord accused, beginning: “Perhaps it is surprising.”

No one but a chaste husband ought to hear a case concerning chastity. For chastity deserves such an arbiter, before whom modesty is not endangered.

CAP. 121.—That one should condemn sin only if one is not guilty of the same sin. Ambrose to Irenaeus (book IX, letter 76, to Studius).

[Col. 0610A]

The Lord said: “Let the one who is without sin be the first to stone the adulteress” (John 8). What is so divine, what is so just, as that the one who is free from sin should judge sins? For how can you endure one who avenges another’s sin and defends his own crime?

Again, a little later. When the woman is accused, Christ bows his head. But he raises it when the accuser has departed. Thus he wishes no one to be condemned, all to be acquitted.

CAP. 122.—On the same subject. Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*, tractate XLVIII (sermon 47, *On the Words of the Lord*, or tractate 33 on John).

The Lord says what both the gentle and the just ought to say: “Let the one who is without sin cast the first stone at the adulteress.” This is the voice of justice. Let the sinful woman be punished, but not by sinners. Let the law be fulfilled, but not by violators of the law. This is altogether the voice of justice [Col. 0610B].

CAP. 123.—How a slave accused of adultery with his mistress should be charged. *Digest*, book I, title XII.

If anyone says that his slave has committed adultery with his wife, the case shall be heard before the prefect of the city.

CAP. 124.—That a wife should not be killed for adultery according to divine laws. Nicholas to Archbishop Charles (to Archbishop Albinus of Genoa among the rescripts, title XVIII, chapter 8) and his suffragans.

(33, q. 2, *Inter haec*.) Among other things, your holiness has sought to add this question: if someone’s wife has committed adultery, may the husband kill her according to secular law? But the holy Church of God is never bound by secular laws. It has no sword except a spiritual one; it does not kill, but gives life [Col. 0610C].

CAP. 125.—On the same subject. Nicholas to Radulf, Archbishop of Bourges (title XVII, chapter 3).

(33, q. 2, c. *Interfectores*.) Those who kill their wives without judgment—since you do not add “adulterous wives,” or anything of that kind—what else are they to be regarded as but murderers? Accordingly, they are to be reduced to penance and marriage is entirely denied them, except in the case of young persons, for whom the twenty-fifth decretal rule—or rather indulgence—of blessed Pope Leo is to be observed [Col. 0610D].

CAP. 126.—On the penance of one who murdered his own wife; and that neither divine nor human law condemns anyone on the testimony of one witness, even a wholly trustworthy one. Stephen V to Hastulf.

(33, q. 2, c. *Admonere*.) We take care to admonish you with tears and much groaning of heart, son Hastulf—though you ought not to be called a son—because you have so cruelly perpetrated a wretched murder. For you killed your wife, a part of your body joined to you in lawful marriage, without cause of death: she did not resist you and did not in any way plot against your life. You did not find her doing an abominable deed with another man [Col. 0611A]; rather, stirred up by the devil and inflamed by impious fury, more cruel than every beast, you murdered her with your sword, with the brutality of robbers. And now after her death you add iniquity upon iniquity. You wish, wicked plunderer who did not spare the mother and made your own children orphans, to charge her with a cause of death after her death, through one murderous and reprobate witness.

For neither the Gospel nor any divine or human law condemns or justifies anyone on the testimony of one witness, even a suitable one. How much less, therefore, ought she to have been condemned while alive—or you excused after her death—by this most shameful and criminal man. First, the cause of the charge ought to have been investigated carefully; and then, if it had been found to be so, she ought to have undergone the punishment of vengeance according to the course of the law. For if what the adulterer falsely alleged had been true—which God forbid—you might perhaps, after eight years of penance had been completed, have dismissed her for a lawful cause, if you wished; but you ought never to have killed her [Col. 0611B]. For God does not will the death of the sinner, but that he turn to penance and live (Ezek. 33).

Therefore let our counsel please you, and do what may seem better and lighter to you. Have mercy on your soul, lest you become your own murderer. We therefore ask you to abandon this evil by which you were drawn into so monstrous a crime of sin. Enter a monastery; humble yourself under the hand of an abbot; assisted by the prayers of many brethren, observe with a suppliant spirit [Col. 0611C] all that is commanded you, if perhaps the infinite goodness of God may forgive your sins and refresh your soul before you are tormented in everlasting flames. Know most certainly that this is better and lighter.

But if you wish to perform public penance while remaining in your house or in the world—which you should not doubt would be worse, harder, and more burdensome—then we exhort you to perform it as follows. On every day on which you must do penance, drink neither wine nor any intoxicating liquor. Never at any time eat meat except at Easter and on the day of the Lord’s Nativity. You must do penance on bread, water, and salt. Persevere always in vigils, fasts, prayers, and almsgiving. Never gird yourself with weapons, nor presume to quarrel anywhere. Never take a wife, have no concubine, and commit no adultery [Col. 0611D]. Never bathe in a bathhouse, nor join yourself to festive banquets. In church, humbly place yourself apart from other Christians behind the door and doorposts, commending yourself humbly to the prayers of those entering and leaving. Consider yourself unworthy of communion in the body and blood of the Lord throughout all the days of your life. Yet, on the final day of your life, if you deserve it and if there is someone to administer it, we permit you to receive it only as viaticum, by way of pardon.

There are many other things which, in proportion to the great weight of the sin, ought to be added to you, unhappy man, more harshly and severely. But if, with the Lord’s help, you do and keep with a perfect heart all the things mercifully set forth above, we trust in God’s boundless clemency that you will receive forgiveness of your sins [Col. 0612A]. According to the gift [“word,” Victorius and Gratian] of the just and good Shepherd, holy Church will loose you from this bond of sin on earth, so that through the grace of him who acquired her by his blood you may be loosed in heaven. But if you do otherwise and despise so salutary an admonition of holy mother Church, be your own judge: you shall remain in the snare of the devil in which you are held entangled. Your blood be upon your own head. For the salvation of God’s other children, with his help we labor with all solicitude apart from communion with you and daily implore the Lord’s mercy more earnestly. He who with the Father, etc.

CAP. 127.—That a husband should not leave his wife even for religious life unless she consents. Synod of Pope Eugenius in the time of the Emperors Louis and Lothair, chapter 36.

(27, q. 1, c. *Si vir et uxor*.) If husband and wife agree together to separate solely for religious life, this must by no means be done without the bishop’s knowledge, so that each may be assigned a place separately under his provision. For if the wife is unwilling, or either one of them is unwilling, the marriage is not dissolved even for such a reason [Col. 0612B].

CAP. 128.—On the same subject. Pope Nicholas to King Charles (in the rescripts, title XVIII, chapter 2).

(27, q. 2, c. *Scripsit nobis*.) Queen Theutberga wrote to us that she wished to be stripped of rank or marital union and desired to be content with a private life alone. We wrote to her that this could not be done otherwise unless her husband Lothair chose the same life.

CAP. 129.—Marriages are not to be dissolved for the sake of religion. Gregory to the patrician Theoctista (book IX, letter 39, chapter 2).

(27, q. 2, c. *Sunt qui*.) If some say that marriages ought to be dissolved for the sake of religion, they should know that, even if human law has granted this, divine law has nevertheless forbidden it. For Truth himself said: “What God has joined, let no one separate” (Matt. 19; Gen. 2). He also said: “It is not lawful to dismiss a wife except on account of fornication” (ibid.).

Again. If husband and wife are one flesh, and the husband for the sake of religion dismisses his wife, or the woman dismisses her husband who remains in this world or perhaps falls into unlawful conduct, what sort of conversion is this, in which the same flesh partly passes into continence and partly remains in defilement? But if both agree to lead a continent life, who would dare condemn this?

Again. When good spouses desire either to increase merit or to wipe away the faults of their former life, it is permitted for them to bind themselves to continence and seek a better life. But if the wife does not follow the continence which the husband seeks, or if the husband rejects that which the wife seeks, the marriage may not be divided [Col. 0612D].

CAP. 130.—That an abstinent husband should not give his wife an occasion for fornication. Sermon of Chrysostom, on the title of Psalm 50 (near the end of the first homily on Psalm 50).

(27, q. 2, *Si tu abstines*.) If you abstain without your wife’s consent, you give her permission to commit fornication, and her sin will be imputed to your abstinence.

CAP. 131.—That the bond of marriage remains between those who have separated. Nicholas to the bishops of Brittany.

Scripture says: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19). Yet marriages, as most eminent and devout men have ordained, must be performed in their proper order. [Col. 0613A] For the rule of the Fathers concerning abducted women and persons thus joined is to be followed. Again, if a man should wish, for the sake of exaltation [or for the sake of prayer], to separate from his wife in order to be free for God, this can scarcely take place unless by the consent of both parties, so that neither of them may in any way proceed to another marriage.

### CHAPTER 132.—On the Same Matter. Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence* (book I, ch. 11).

Where husband and wife have agreed, by mutual consent, permanently to abstain from the exercise of carnal desire, far be it that the marital bond between them should be broken. Rather, it will be stronger in proportion as they have entered into agreements with one another which ought to be kept more dearly and harmoniously—not by pleasurable bonds of bodies, but by voluntary affections of souls.

### CHAPTER 133.—That Spouses Must Not Defraud One Another of the Marital Debt Even for Prayer, Except by Consent. Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages* (book I, ch. 2).

[Col. 0613B]

(33, q. 4, c. *Apostolus*.) The Apostle did not wish spouses to defraud one another of the marital debt even temporarily, so as to devote themselves to prayer (1 Cor. 7), except by consent.

Again (ch. 3): If a husband says, “I certainly dismiss my wife without any cause of fornication, but I shall remain continent,” shall we therefore say that he has done with impunity what he has done? Who would dare say this, if he understands the will of the Lord who says these things—that He did not permit a spouse to be dismissed even for the sake of continence, He who excepted only the cause of fornication?

Again (ch. 4): Behold, continence has pleased the woman, but it has not pleased the husband. [Col. 0613C] The woman has left her husband and begun to live continently; she herself, of course, will remain chaste, but she will cause the husband to become an adulterer—something the Lord does not will—for, since he has not remained continent, he will seek another woman. What shall we say to the woman? Surely what the sound doctrine of the Church says: “Render the debt to your husband” (1 Cor. 7), lest, while you seek a means of receiving greater honour, he find a means of being condemned.

### CHAPTER 134.—That Married Persons Must Vow Nothing Except by Consent. The Same, to Armentarius, Riparius, and Paulina (Letter 45).

(33, q. 5, c. *Una*.) There could be only one reason why we should not merely fail to urge you to fulfil what you have vowed, but should even forbid you to fulfil it: namely, if perhaps your wife, through weakness of mind or body, refused to undertake this with you. [Col. 0613D] For married persons ought not to make vows of this kind except by mutual consent and a common will. And if it has been done precipitately, the rashness ought rather to be corrected than the promise discharged. For God does not require a person to vow something taken from another; rather, He forbids one to appropriate what belongs to another.

### CHAPTER 135.—That, While a Wife Whom He Has Dismissed for Whatever Cause Is Alive, Another Cannot Be Taken. Bede on Mark, ch. 31.

There is one bodily fornication and one spiritual fornication. Fear of God causes a wife to be dismissed, as many are recorded to have done for the sake of religion. But no cause is prescribed by God’s law for taking another wife while the one who has been left is alive.

### CHAPTER 136.—That a Vow Made by Spouses by Mutual Consent Must Be Kept, but Not Otherwise. Augustine to Ecdicia (Letter 199).

[Col. 0614A]

(33, q. 5, c. *Quod Deo*.) What both of you had vowed to God with equal consent, you ought to have fulfilled steadfastly to the end. If he has fallen away from that purpose, at least you should persevere most firmly; I would not exhort you to do so unless he himself had consented to it. For if you had never obtained his consent, no number of years would have defended you.

Again, shortly afterwards: Your husband did not cease to be your husband because you were mutually abstaining from carnal intercourse. Indeed, you remained all the more sacredly spouses to one another, in proportion as you harmoniously observed the holier resolutions you had adopted. Therefore you ought not to do anything concerning your clothing, gold, silver, any money, or those earthly possessions of yours without [Col. 0614B] his judgment.

Again: There is a certain mode of matronly dress, distinct from a widow’s garment, which may suit faithful married women while preserving the cause or observance of religion. If your husband did not wish you to lay this aside, lest you boast as though a widow while he was alive, I think that in this matter he ought not to have been opposed to the point of the scandal of disagreement, through the evil of disobedience rather than any good of abstinence.
