For what is more absurd than for a woman to pride herself against her husband over a humble garment, when it would be more fitting for you to obey him through pure manners than to resist him through dark garments? Even if the garment of a nun pleased you, it could be assumed more acceptably with your husband respected and entreated than presumptuously by disregarding and despising him. But if he would not permit it at all, what would be lost from [Col. 0614C] your purpose? Far be it that you should displease God because, while your husband had not yet died, you did not dress like Anna but like Susanna.

### CHAPTER 137.—That After a Vow What Was Previously Voluntary Becomes Necessary. Augustine, in the Letter to Armentarius, Riparius, and Paulina (Letter 45).

I could, according to my ability, distinguish in their ranks and merits those who belong to the right hand and to the kingdom of heaven, and show how the married life of fathers and mothers of families who beget children—yet are religious and devout—differs from that life which you have vowed to God, if you now needed exhortation to make that vow. But since you have already vowed, you have already bound yourself: it is not lawful for you to do otherwise. Before [Col. 0614D] you were liable for the vow, you were free to remain inferior, although that freedom is not to be congratulated by which one is not obliged to render what is rendered with profit.

But now, because your promise is held by the Lord, I do not invite you to great righteousness, but deter you from great wickedness. For if you do not do what you vowed, you will not be such as you would have remained had you vowed nothing of the kind. You would then have been lesser, not worse. But now, God forbid, you will be as much more miserable if you break faith with God as you will be happier if you fulfil it. Nor should you repent that you made the vow; rather, rejoice that it is now lawful for you to do what had been lawful at your own loss. Therefore undertake it fearlessly and fulfil words by deeds. He who requires your vows will help you. Happy is the necessity which compels one toward better things.

There could be only one reason why [Col. 0615A] we should not merely fail to urge you to fulfil what you have vowed, but should even forbid you to fulfil it: namely, if perhaps your wife, through weakness of mind or body, refused to undertake this with you. For married persons ought not to make vows of this kind except by mutual consent and common will. And if it has been done precipitately, the rashness ought rather to be corrected than the promise discharged. For God does not require someone to vow something out of another’s property; rather, He forbids one to appropriate what belongs to another. For the divine judgment on this matter has been pronounced through the Apostle: “The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise also the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife” (1 Cor. 7).

### CHAPTER 138.—On the Virgin Demetrias. Augustine, in the Letter to Julian (Letter 143).

[Col. 0615B]

By the grace of our ministry and the mercy of the Saviour aiding us, so great a fruit has sprung up in your house that, though a human marriage had already been arranged, holy Demetrias preferred the embrace of that spiritual Bridegroom, who is fairer than the children of men. Virgins marry Him in order to possess the more abundant fruitfulness of the Spirit, not to lose bodily integrity.

We would not have known how our exhortation at that time had been received by that faithful and noble virgin, unless, after we had departed and she had shortly afterwards professed virginal holiness, we had learned, through the most joyful report and truthful testimony of your letters, that this great gift of God—which He plants and waters indeed through His servants, but Himself gives the increase (1 Cor. 3)—had come to us as labourers. [Col. 0615C]

### CHAPTER 139.—That One Does Not Err Who Gives His Daughter to a Man Who Has a Concubine. From the Decrees of Pope Leo I (Letter 91, to Bishop Rusticus, ch. 4).

(32, q. 2, c. *Non omnis*.) Not every woman joined to a man is his wife, just as not every son is heir to his father. The covenants of marriage are lawful among freeborn persons and among equals, and this was established by the Lord Himself long before Roman law began. Therefore a wife is one thing, a concubine another, just as a female slave is one thing and a free woman another (Gal. 4).

For this reason the Apostle, to make clear the distinction between these persons, adduces testimony from Genesis, where Abraham is told: “Cast out the slave woman and [Col. 0615D] her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Gen. 22). Since, therefore, the society of marriage was so constituted from the beginning that, besides the union of the sexes, it contained within itself the sacrament of Christ and the Church (Eph. 5), there is no doubt that a woman in whom no nuptial mystery is shown to have existed does not belong to matrimony.

Accordingly, if a layman of any rank [the original reads “cleric”] gives his daughter in marriage to a man who has a concubine, this is not to be understood as though he had given her to a married man—unless perhaps that woman appears to have been made free, lawfully endowed, and honoured with a public marriage. For women joined to men at their fathers’ discretion are free from blame if the women whom those men had kept were not wives; for a married woman is one thing, a concubine another.

### CHAPTER 140.—What a Lawful Wife Ought to Be. From a Letter of Pope Leo.

[Col. 0616A]

(30, q. 5, c. *Qualis*.) What sort of wife ought she to be who is to be taken according to the law? A chaste virgin, betrothed while a virgin, lawfully endowed, handed over by her parents, received by the bridegroom and by the attendants, and then, according to law and Gospel, openly and honourably taken in marriage through public nuptials. She is never to be separated on account of a human being throughout all the days of life—except by consent and for the purpose of being free for God—and, if she has committed fornication, is to be dismissed. But while she lives another is not to be taken, because adulterers shall not possess the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 6); and her penitence is to be received according to the Scriptures.

### CHAPTER 141.—That No One Is to Celebrate Marriage Secretly. From the Decree of Pope Hormisdas, ch. 6 (in the fragments).

[Col. 0616B]

(30, q. 5, c. *Nullus*.) No believer, of whatever condition, is to enter into marriage secretly; but, having received a blessing from a priest, he is to marry publicly in the Lord.

### CHAPTER 142.—At What Times Marriages Are to Be Celebrated. From the First Council of Lleida, ch. 3.

(33, q. 4, c. *Non oportet*.) Marriages ought not to be celebrated from Septuagesima until the octave of Easter; during the three weeks before the feast of Saint John the Baptist; or from the Advent of the Lord until after Epiphany. If this is done, the couple are to be separated.

### CHAPTER 143.—How Those Marrying Are to Be Blessed by a Priest. From the Council at Valence, ch. 101 (under John I, in the fragments; and Carthage IV, ch. 13).

[Col. 0616C]

(Dist. 23, c. *Sponsus*.) When bridegroom and bride are to be blessed by a priest, they are to be presented in church to the priest by their parents or attendants; and, after receiving the blessing, they are to remain virgins that night out of reverence for the blessing itself.

### CHAPTER 144.—That No Marriage Is to Take Place without a Dowry. From the Third Council of Arles, ch. 7 (in the fragments).

(30, q. 5, c. *Nullum*.) No marriage is to take place without a dowry. The dowry is to be given according to ability, and no one is to presume to marry or take a wife without public nuptials.

### CHAPTER 145.—That Bridegroom and Bride Are to Be Blessed by a Priest before Marriage. From the Decrees of Pope Soter, ch. 5.

[Col. 0616D]

Let bridegroom and bride be blessed by a priest with prayers and offerings; let them be betrothed and endowed according to the laws; let them be guarded by attendants; and let them be received publicly and solemnly. Let them also abstain for two or three days, and be instructed to preserve chastity with one another and to marry at prescribed times, so that they may beget for God and the ages children who are not illegitimate but heirs.

### CHAPTER 146.—On the Blessing of a First Marriage. From the Council of Milan, ch. 2.

At a first marriage the priest ought to celebrate Mass and bless both parties, and afterwards they are to refrain from church for thirty days.

### CHAPTER 147.—That a Faithful Husband Must Not Separate from an Unbelieving Wife.

[Col. 0617A]

The Apostle says: “If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her. And if any woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, let her not dismiss her husband. For the unbelieving husband shall be sanctified in the faithful wife, and the unbelieving wife shall be sanctified through the faithful husband” (1 Cor. 6).

### CHAPTER 148.—That There Is to Be No Dancing at Christian Weddings. From the Council of Laodicea, ch. 53.

Christians going to weddings ought not to clap or dance [βαλλίζειν, “to dance”], but to dine or take a meal reverently, as befits Christians.

### CHAPTER 149.—That No One Is to Abduct a Widow as a Wife. Gregory says (First Roman Council, under Gregory II, ch. 10).

[Col. 0617B]

(36, q. 2, c. *Si quis*.) If anyone abducts a widow to be his wife, or consents to this, let him be anathema. And all answered three times: “Let him be anathema!”

### CHAPTER 150.—That No One Is to Abduct a Virgin as a Wife. The Same.

If anyone abducts a virgin to be his wife without having betrothed her, or consents to this, let him be anathema. And all answered three times: “Let him be anathema!”

### CHAPTER 151.—On a Virgin or Widow Who Has Been Abducted. From the Decrees of Pope Eusebius, ch. 10 (ibid., ch. 11).

If anyone abducts a virgin or widow to be his wife, unless she has been betrothed to him, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER 152.—On Virgins Who Have Not Preserved Virginity before Marriage. From the Council of Elvira, ch. 5 (ch. 14).

[Col. 0617C]

Virgins who have not preserved their virginity, if they take as husbands the very men who violated them, are to be reconciled after one year of penance, because they have violated marriage alone. If they have known other men, because they have committed adultery, they are to do penance for five years and then be admitted to communion.

### CHAPTER 153.—That No One Is Permitted to Have a Concubine. From the Sayings of Augustine (book L, homily 49).

(Dist. 34, c. *Audite*.) Hear, beloved, members of Christ and children of the mother Catholic Church. What I say to the candidates, let the faithful hear. What I say to the faithful, let the candidates hear. What I say to the faithful, the candidates, and the penitents, let the catechumens also hear; let all hear, let them fear, and let no one despise it. Let your hearing be [Col. 0617D] a consolation to me, lest my grief be a testimony against you.

I say to the candidates: You are not permitted to commit fornication; let wives suffice for you. You are not permitted to have concubines. Let God hear, if you are deaf; let His angels hear, if you despise this: you are not permitted to have concubines. Even if you do not have wives, you are nevertheless not permitted to have concubines whom you later dismiss and take wives. Your condemnation will be all the greater if you wish to have both concubines and wives. You are not permitted to have wives whose former husbands are alive. Nor are you women permitted to have husbands whose former wives are alive. Those marriages are adulteries; they are not according to the law of heaven, but according to the law of the age. Nor are you permitted to have the woman who has departed from her husband through repudiation. Only for the cause [Col. 0618A] of fornication may one dismiss an adulterous wife; but while she lives, one may not take another.

### CHAPTER 154.—On Those Who Had Concubines before Marriage. Augustine Again (Sermon on Time 242).

What is this, that many men are not ashamed before marriage to keep concubines attached to themselves, whom after some years they dismiss and then take lawful wives? A little later: Therefore, before God and before His angels, I testify and declare that God has always forbidden these things and has never been pleased with them; for especially in Christian times, it has never been lawful, and never will be lawful, to have concubines.

### CHAPTER 155.—Again, on Concubines. From the Council of Arles, ch. 15.

No one is permitted at any time to have two wives, nor ever a concubine.

### CHAPTER 156.—On a Female Slave: Whether She May Become the Lawful Wife of Her Own Master. From the Decrees of Pope Julius, ch. 4 (in the fragments).

[Col. 0618B]

(29, q. 2, *Si quis ancillam*.) If anyone grants freedom to his female slave and joins her to himself in marriage, some had doubted whether such a marriage should be regarded as lawful or not. We, therefore, resolving the ancient uncertainty, have judged such unions lawful. For if all marriages are made from affection, and nothing impious or contrary to the laws can occur in such a union, why should we think that the aforesaid marriages ought to be prohibited? You all have one Father in heaven (Matt. 6), and every rich person and poor person, free person and slave, will equally [Col. 0618C] give account for themselves and their souls. Therefore we do not doubt that all persons, of whatever condition, have one law in relation to God.

### CHAPTER 157.—On One Who Has Joined His Male and Female Slaves in Marriage. From the Council of Mâcon, ch. 10.

If the master of both joins a male slave and a female slave in marriage, and afterwards, when the male slave or female slave has been freed, the one who remains in slavery cannot be redeemed, their marriages are not for that reason dissolved.

### CHAPTER 158.—On Those Married Many Times. From the Council of Braga, ch. 81. (Martin of Braga, in the chapters of the Greek synods, ch. 80, Letter 9.)

If anyone has been joined in many marriages, let him do penance. But the conduct and faith of the penitent shorten the time.

### CHAPTER 159.—That Second Marriages Are Not Denied to Laypersons, Though Those Who Contract Them Are by No Means Permitted to Enter the Clergy. From the Decrees of Pope Gelasius, ch. 24.

Just as laypersons are permitted to contract second marriages, so after them no one is permitted to enter the clerical body. For one licence is generally granted to human frailty; another manner of life ought to belong to those dedicated to the service of divine things.

### CHAPTER 160.—On Those Who Have Entered into Several Marriages. From the Council of Neocaesarea, ch. 3.

(31, q. 1, c. *De his qui*.) With regard to those who have entered into several marriages, a fixed period is indeed clearly prescribed, but their conduct and faith abbreviate the time.

### CHAPTER 161.—On Those Who Have Celebrated Marriage a Third Time. From the Decrees of Pope Hormisdas, ch. 2.

[Col. 0619A]

Let no one take more than two wives, because a third is already superfluous.

### CHAPTER 162.—On the Twice-Married. From the Council of Laodicea, ch. 1.

Those who, according to the ecclesiastical rule, have freely and lawfully entered into a second marriage and have not secretly made a marriage union [μὴ λαθρογαμίαν ποιήσαντας, “not having contracted a clandestine marriage”], ought, after a short period has elapsed, to devote themselves to prayers and fasts. We have also decreed that communion be restored to them by way of indulgence.

### CHAPTER 163.—On the Number of Husbands. From the Sayings of Jerome (vol. III, *Against Jovinian*, book I).

Where there has been a number of husbands, there ceases to be one’s own single husband.

### CHAPTER 164.—On a Freeborn Man Who Takes Another’s Female Slave as Freeborn and Afterwards Learns That She Is a Slave. From the Council at Vermeria, attended by King Pepin, ch. 7.

[Col. 0619B]

(29, q. 2, c. *Si quis ingenuus*.) If a freeborn man takes another person’s female slave, believing her to be freeborn, and that woman is afterwards discovered to be in servitude, let him redeem her from slavery if he can. If he cannot, he may take another wife if he wishes. But if he knew that she was a slave and approved this, he is afterwards to have her as his lawful wife. A freeborn woman is to act similarly concerning another person’s male slave.

### CHAPTER 165.—On a Freeborn Woman Who Takes a Male Slave as Husband. From the Same Council, ch. 8.

(29, q. 2, c. *Si femina*.) If a freeborn woman takes [Col. 0619C] a slave, knowing that he is a slave, let her keep him, because we all have one Father in heaven (Matt. 6). There shall be one law for man and woman.

### CHAPTER 166.—On Persons Lawfully Joined in Marriage, If One of Them Falls into Madness. From a Letter of Nicholas Sent to Charles, Archbishop of Mainz (in the rescript, title XVIII, ch. 7).

(32, q. 7, c. *Si qui matrimonium*.) If persons sound of mind contract marriage and madness, insanity, or some illness subsequently comes upon one of the two, the marriages of such persons cannot be dissolved on account of this illness. The same judgment is to be made concerning those whom enemies blind or mutilate.

### CHAPTER 167.—On the Lawful Marriages of Slaves. From the Second Council of Chalon, ch. 30.

(29, q. 7, c. *Dictum est*.) We have been told that certain persons, with a kind of arbitrary presumption, dissolve the lawful marriages of slaves, giving no heed to the Gospel saying: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19). Therefore it has seemed good to us that the marriages of slaves are not to be dissolved, even if they have different masters; but, remaining in one marriage, they are to serve their masters. This is to be observed where there has been a lawful union and the consent of the masters.

### CHAPTER 168.—On the Marriages of the Insane. From the Decrees of Pope Fabian, ch. 5 (at the end of the Decrees).

(32, q. 7, c. *Neque furiosus*.) Neither a madman nor a madwoman can contract marriage; but if it has been contracted, they are not to be separated.

### CHAPTER 169.—On a Betrothed Girl: Whether Another May Take Her in Marriage. From the First Letter of Pope Siricius, ch. 4.

[Col. 0620A]

(27, q. 2, c. *De conjugali*.) You have asked concerning violation of marriage whether one man may take in marriage a girl betrothed to another. We forbid this in every way, because the blessing which a priest lays upon a woman about to marry is, among the faithful, something like sacrilege if violated by any transfer.

### CHAPTER 170.—On Those Who Abduct Another’s Betrothed Women. From the Council of Meaux, ch. 5 (under Sergius II, ch. 68).

The ancient synodal judgment is to be observed concerning those who abduct another’s betrothed women. But if perhaps such a case is found to arise in the Church that bishops ought, for the requirements of salvation and religion, to deal with something more humanely—as canonical authority teaches, using its own words: “the earlier determination dealt more harshly, but the later dealt with something more humanely”—then, even if we descend to the greatest indulgence, a man who takes another’s betrothed woman is in no way to escape public penance. If he refuses to obey this, let him be anathematized without any opposition. His supporters are to do penance, by decree of the bishop, in proportion to the fault. But if, which we do not wish, someone of ecclesiastical rank has plainly shown himself a consenting party or an intermediary in such marriages, he is to be removed from his rank; and, if he has been accused on credible suspicions arising from this, he is to clear himself canonically. [Col. 0620B]

### CHAPTER 171.—On the Same Matter. From the Council at Aachen, ch. 3.

It has pleased us that those who abduct, steal, or seduce women under no circumstances are to have them as wives, even though the women afterwards agree to it, or though they have endowed them, or have received them in marriage with the consent of their parents. But if anyone wishes to have a wife, let him take her canonically and lawfully, and not abduct her. Whoever abducts, steals, or seduces her is never to have her as his wife.

### CHAPTER 172.—Again, on the Same Matter. From the Council of Meaux, ch. 10 (under Sergius II, ch. 66; Roman Council, under Gregory II, ch. 10).

Those who henceforth presume to abduct virgins or widows are, according to the synodal determination of blessed Gregory, together with their accomplices, to be anathematized; and the abductors are permanently to remain without hope of marriage.

### CHAPTER 173.—On Those Who Abduct Girls under the Pretext of Cohabitation. From the Council of Chalcedon, ch. 27 [Col. 0620D] (session 15).

(36, q. 2, c. *Eos qui rapiunt*.) The holy synod decreed that those who abduct women under the pretext of cohabitation, together with those assisting and conniving with the abductors, are, if clerics, to be deposed from their rank; if laypersons, to be anathematized.

### CHAPTER 174.—On Abducted Girls Not Yet Betrothed. From the Council of Chalon, ch. 27.

(36, q. 2, c. *De puellis*.) It is written in the Council of Chalcedon concerning girls abducted but not yet betrothed: “The holy synod decreed that those who abduct girls under the pretext of cohabitation, and those assisting and conniving with the abductors, are, if clerics, to be deposed from their rank; if laypersons, to be anathematized.” These words make clear how the authors of this [Col. 0621A] evil ought to be condemned, when participants in the plot and those who connive are struck by so great an anathema that, according to canonical authority, they cannot in any way lawfully claim as their own in lawful marriage women whom they have abducted.

### CHAPTER 175.—On the Same Matter. From the Council of Toledo.

Accordingly, it has pleased and been decreed by the sacred assembly that, if anyone abducts another man’s betrothed woman, he is to be punished with public penance and remain without hope of marriage. If she herself did not consent to the same crime, she is not to be denied permission to marry another. But if they afterwards presume to join themselves to one another, both are to be anathematized until satisfaction has been made.

### CHAPTER 176.—On the Same Matter. From the Council of Ancyra, ch. 11 (ch. 10).

(27, q. 2, c. *Desponsatas*.) It has pleased us that girls who have been betrothed and afterwards abducted by others are to be rescued and returned to those to whom they had previously been betrothed, even if it is established that force was used upon them by the abductors.

### CHAPTER 177.—On the Same Matter. From the Council of Meaux, ch. 65.

If, however, those who abducted them have not yet taken the women they abducted into marriage with the consent of their parents under the aforesaid designation of betrothal or dowry, then, once this enactment has been proclaimed for all to hear, they are to be separated from their union and subjected to public penance. The abducted women are to be lawfully restored to their parents. But after public penance has been performed, if age and incontinence require it, they may be joined in lawful marriage with the consent of both sides. For in these cases we do not establish a rule, but, to use the words of the great Leo, judge what is more tolerable. [Col. 0621C] But if one of the spouses dies, the person who has performed public penance and survives is not to presume to contract another marriage, unless perhaps the bishop foresees that some indulgence should be granted in order to avert a graver offence.

### CHAPTER 178.—On Those Who Are Joined in Marriage but Cannot Have Intercourse. From a Letter of Gregory to John, Bishop of Ravenna.

As to what you asked concerning persons joined in marriage who cannot consummate it, whether he may take another woman or she another man: it is written concerning them, “If a man and woman unite themselves, and afterwards the woman says of the man that he cannot have intercourse with her, then, if she can prove through a just judgment that this is true, she may take another; but if he has taken another woman, they are to be separated.”

### CHAPTER 179.—On the Same Matter. From the Council at Vermeria, in the Time of King Pepin, ch. 17.

If a woman declares that her husband has never had intercourse with her, let them go from there to the cross; and, if this is found true, let them be separated, and let her do what she wishes.

### CHAPTER 180.—On the Same Matter. From the Council at Compiègne, ch. 20.

(33, q. 1, c. *Si quis*.) If anyone takes a wife and has had her for some time, and the woman says that he has not had intercourse with her, while the man says that he has, the man’s assertion is to stand as true, because the husband is the head of the wife (1 Cor. 11).

### CHAPTER 181.—On the Same Matter. From the Council of Tribur, ch. 3 (Council of Tribur, ch. 41).

(27, q. 2, c. *Quidam despondit*.) If a man takes a wife but is unable to have intercourse with her, and his brother secretly violates her and makes her pregnant, they are to be separated. Yet, in consideration of their weakness, mercy is to be granted them for marriage, provided only that it is in the Lord.

### CHAPTER 182.—Again, on the Same Matter. From a Letter of Gregory.

(33, q. 50, c. *Requisisti*.) You asked concerning persons who say that, because of a cold nature, they cannot have intercourse with each other by rendering carnal service. If the man cannot use her as a wife, let him have her as a sister. But if they wish to break the bond of marriage, let both remain unmarried. For if he could not naturally be compatible with her, how will he suit another? Therefore, if the husband wishes to take another wife, the reason is clear: the devil has kindled the fuel of hatred, he has come to hate her, and thus seeks, through the falsehood of a lie, to dismiss her.

But if the woman pleads and says, “I wish to be a mother and bear children,” each of them, with the hands of seven relatives touching the most holy relics, is to state under oath that they have never been joined through carnal intercourse and made one flesh. Then it appears that the woman may contract a second marriage. I say this humanly, because of the weakness of their flesh [Col. 0622C] (Rom. 6). But the man who is of a cold nature is to remain without a wife. If he too takes another union, then those who have sworn are to be held guilty of perjury, and, after penance has been performed, are to be compelled to resume their former marriages.

### CHAPTER 183.—On Married Persons Who Desire to Leave Secular Life. From the Sayings of Bishop Basil.

[Note: [Col. 0621D] From the Eighth Synod celebrated at Constantinople under Photius, the penultimate canon, at which several bishops named Basil were present.]

If a married person wishes to enter a monastery, he is not to be received unless he has first been released by his wife, who professes chastity. For if she, while he is alive, marries another because of incontinence, she will undoubtedly be an adulteress; nor is such a man’s conversion accepted by God when the prostitution of the marital covenant follows. Therefore such persons follow Christ without fault, leaving the world, if they possess a mutual consent to chastity through an equal will. [Col. 0622D]

### CHAPTER 184.—On a Husband Who Has Allowed His Wife to Take the Veil. From the Council of Reims, ch. 4.

(33, q. 5, c. *Qui uxorem*.) A man who has allowed his wife to take the veil is not to take another wife, but is likewise to enter religious life.

### CHAPTER 185.—On a Woman Who Has Put on the Veil without Her Husband’s Permission. From the Council at Compiègne, ch. 6.

(33, q. 5, c. *Mulier si sine*.) If a woman has put a veil upon her head without her husband’s permission, and it pleases her husband, he shall receive her again into marriage.

### CHAPTER 186.—On the Same Matter. From Gregory’s Register, to Adrian, notary, book IX, ch. 46.

[Col. 0623A]

(27, q. 2, c. *Agathosa*.) Agathosa, the bearer of the present letter, complained that her husband had entered the monastery of Abbot Urbicus against her will. Since this undoubtedly concerns the fault and reproach of that same abbot, we direct your experience to investigate diligently whether perhaps he converted with her consent, or whether she promised to change her own manner of life. If you find this, ensure that he remains in the monastery, and compel her to change as she promised. But if neither is the case, and you learn that the aforesaid woman has committed no crime of fornication for which it is lawful for a husband to leave his wife, then, lest his conversion become an occasion of destruction to the wife left in the world, [Col. 0623B] we wish you to restore her husband to her, even if he has already been tonsured, all excuse being set aside. For, except for the cause of fornication, no reason permits a husband to leave his wife; because, after husband and wife are made one body by the union of marriage, one part cannot convert while the other remains in the world.

### CHAPTER 187.—On the Single Combat Which Lothair Contrived against His Wife Theutberga. Pope Nicholas (in the rescript, title XX, ch. 1).

(2, q. 4, c. *Monomachiam*.) We do not admit trial by single combat into law, for we do not find that it was commanded. Although we read that some persons undertook it, as sacred history records of holy David and Goliath (1 Sam. 17), nevertheless divine authority has nowhere ordained that it be held as law; since those who follow this and similar practices seem only to put God to the test.

### CHAPTER 188.—On the Same Matter: The Same Nicholas to Lothair (Letter 51).

(27, q. 2, c. *Scripsit*.) Therefore make every effort zealously to cherish and love your wife Theutberga as your own flesh, and be watchful not to consent under any circumstances to her leaving you. Thus, if she wishes to leave you, rebuke—indeed, correct—her, and strive in every way to recall her from such an intention. But if she seeks separation out of love for chastity and demands dissolution of the marriage bond, it is certain, as the Apostle says, that “the woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband” (1 Cor. 7).

Yet if you too, in pursuit of chastity under the pretext of religion, wish to dissolve the union—provided this is not done deceptively—we permit it. For though it is written, “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19; Gen. 2), nevertheless God, not a human being, separates when marriages are dissolved by the consent of both spouses for the sake of divine love. If, therefore, you wish this in that manner, we freely permit it and give ready consent; otherwise, we forbid your mutual separation.

### CHAPTER 189.—On Those Who Flee to Other Provinces or Follow Their Lords, Leaving Their Wives at Home. From the Council at Vermeria, ch. 6.

(34, q. 2, c. *Si quis necessitate*.) If anyone, compelled by unavoidable necessity, flees into another duchy or province, and his wife, though able and capable, refuses to follow him out of love for her parents or possessions, she is to remain unmarried at all times, as long as the husband whom she did not follow lives. [Col. 0624A]

### CHAPTER 190.—On Women Who, When Their Husbands Were Captured or Carried into Captivity, Married Other Men. From a Letter of Pope Leo, ch. 42 (Letter to Nicetas of Aquileia).

(79, c. 1, though not in precisely the same words.) Women whose husbands were captured and carried into captivity, and who married other men believing their husbands dead, ought, when their former husbands return from captivity, to be reunited with them: so that each person may be restored to what he lawfully possessed, each may receive what is his own, and the covenants of marriage may be renewed.

### Chapter 191.—That a man who appears to have taken in marriage the wife of a captive is not to be judged guilty. From a letter of the same [Pope Leo], chapter 43 (ibid., ch. 2).

[Col. 0624B] Yet he is not to be judged guilty, nor regarded as an invader of another’s right, who took the place of a husband believed no longer to exist. For in this way many things belonging to those who had been led into captivity could pass into another’s ownership; yet it is wholly just that, upon their return, their own property be restored to them. If this is rightly observed in the case of slaves, fields, houses, and possessions, how much more ought it to be done in restoring marriages, so that what has been disturbed by the necessity of war may be restored by the remedy of peace?

### Chapter 192.—That, if women refuse to return to their former husbands, they are to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion as impious persons. Of the same Leo, chapter 45 (ibid., ch. 4).

[Col. 0624C] (34, question 2, canon *Si autem*.) But if certain women are so captivated by love for their later husbands that they prefer to cling to them rather than return to a lawful union, they rightly deserve censure and are to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion. From a matter that admits excuse, they have chosen the defilement of a crime [“because they have inexcusably chosen defilement,” original text], showing that, through their own lack of self-restraint, they have approved what just remission could have expiated.

Therefore marriages should return to their former state by voluntary restoration; nor should that which necessity compelled be in any way turned into a reproach for evil intention. For just as those women who refuse to return to their husbands are to be considered impious, so those who return to the union established by God are deservedly to be praised.

### Chapter 193.—That, if husbands returning from captivity are not offended by their wives’ lack of restraint and wish to receive them again in marriage, they are to have free permission. Likewise, of Pope Leo, chapter 44 (ibid., ch. 3).

[Col. 0624D] Therefore, if husbands return after a long captivity and persist in affection for their wives so that they desire them to return to their union, what necessity brought about is to be passed over and judged blameless, and what fidelity requires is to be restored.

### Chapter 194.—What is to be done if intercourse has been impeded through diviners or sorceresses. Hincmar, bishop of Rheims.

(33, question 1, canon *Si quis per sortiarias*.) If, through diviners and sorceresses—God secretly permitting it by a judgment that is never unjust, and the devil arranging it—sexual intercourse does not take place, those to whom this happens should be urged, with contrite heart and humbled spirit, to make a pure confession to God and to the priest of all their sins. With abundant tears, more generous almsgiving, prayers, and fasts, they should make satisfaction to the Lord; and through exorcisms and the other offices of ecclesiastical remedy, the ministers of the Church should endeavor, insofar as the Lord grants it, to heal such persons. For He healed Abimelech and his household through Abraham’s prayers (Gen. 20).

[Col. 0625A] If perhaps they cannot be healed, they may separate. But after seeking other marriages, while those former spouses to whom they had been joined and whom they left remain alive in the flesh, they cannot be reconciled to them—even if the capacity for intercourse is restored to them.

### Chapter 195.—Concerning one who dismissed his wife while in paganism. From the decrees of Pope Eutychianus (fragment, decree 5).

[Col. 0625B] (28, question 1, canon *Si quis gentilis*.) If a pagan dismisses his pagan wife before baptism, after baptism it remains in his power to keep her or not to keep her.

### Chapter 196.—Concerning a baptized person whose unbelieving wife refuses conversion. From the decree of the same, chapter 6.

(28, question 1, canon *Simili modo*.) Likewise, if one of a married pair is baptized and the other is a pagan and refuses to follow, then, as the Apostle says: “If the unbeliever departs, let the unbeliever depart” (1 Cor. 7).

### Chapter 197.—Concerning one who had taken a virgin woman as wife before baptism. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 2.

[Col. 0625C] (28, question 2, canon *Si quis uxorem*.) If anyone had a virgin wife before baptism, he cannot take another after baptism while she lives. Crimes are remitted in baptism, not marriages.

### Chapter 198.—Concerning those women who, with no cause intervening, left their husbands. From the Council of Elvira, chapter 8.

Likewise, women who, with no preceding cause, leave their husbands and join themselves to another, and wish to remain in this state, are not to receive communion even at the end of life.

### Chapter 199.—Concerning a woman who has left an adulterer and taken an adulterer. Ibid., chapter 9.

(32, question 7, canon *Fidelis*.) Likewise, a believing woman who leaves her believing adulterous husband and takes another adulterer [“another,” original text] is to be forbidden to take him. But if she has taken him, she is not to receive communion until the man whom she left has departed this life—unless perhaps necessity arising from illness compels that it be given.

### Chapter 200.—That neither a person dismissed by a wife nor one dismissed by a husband may be joined to another. From the African Council, chapter 69 (and the Council of Milevis, ch. 17).

(32, question 7, canon *Placuit*.) It has been decreed that, according to evangelical and apostolic discipline, neither one dismissed by a wife nor one dismissed by a husband is to be joined to another; rather, they are to remain as they are or be reconciled to one another. If they disregard this, they are to be subjected to penance.

### Chapter 201.—Concerning one accused of committing adultery with another man’s wife while her husband lives, and known to have taken her after his death. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 69 (and the Council of Tribur, ch. 51).

[Col. 0626A] A man accused of committing adultery with another man’s wife while that husband lived, and known to have taken the same woman when he died soon afterward, is in every way to be subjected to public penance. Even after the said penance, the following rule shall be observed, if appropriate: unless perhaps that man or the woman is charged with having killed the deceased husband, or unless kinship or some other criminal act prevents it. If this is proved, they are to remain in perpetual penance, without any hope of marriage.

But if he denies having committed adultery with the same woman while her husband lived, and neither of them can be convicted of the aforesaid homicide, they shall lawfully clear their reputation from the accusation; and, if no other obstacle of the sort mentioned intervenes, they may enter into and enjoy marriage.

[Col. 0626B]

### Chapter 202.—Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Tribur, chapter 40.

(31, question 1, canon *Relatum*.) It was reported to the ears of the holy priests that a certain man had violated another man’s wife by illicit intercourse and, further, had sworn to the adulteress while her husband still lived that, if he survived the lawful husband’s death, he would take her as wife. And this was done. We therefore forbid and anathematize such a marriage.

### Chapter 203.—Concerning one who has a wife and has repeatedly committed adultery. From the Council of Elvira, chapter 7.

If a believer who has a wife has committed adultery not once but repeatedly, he is to be approached at the point of death. If he promises to cease, communion is to be given him.

[Col. 0626C]

### Chapter 204.—That Christians ought not to contract matrimonial unions with heretics. From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 31 (and the Council of Agde, ch. 67).

(28, question 1, canon *Non oportet*.) No marriage covenant ought to be made with any heretics, nor should sons or daughters be given to them; rather, their sons or daughters may be taken in marriage, provided that they promise to become Christians.

### Chapter 205.—If an unmarried layman sins with an unmarried laywoman. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 7.

If a layman has intercourse with a laywoman—that is, if both are free from the bond of marriage—he shall do penance for three years. The more often and more heedlessly he commits these sins, the more the duration and severity of the penance shall be increased.

### Chapter 206.—Concerning a wife who has committed adultery with her husband’s knowledge. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 9.

[Col. 0626D] If a wife commits adultery with the knowledge and consent of her husband, it has been decreed that communion is not to be given them even at the end of life. But if he leaves her and they are separated, and they perform worthy penance, they are to receive communion after ten years.

### Chapter 207.—Concerning an unmarried man who commits adultery with another man’s wife. From the Council of Nantes, chapter 6 (under Formosus, ch. 14).

But if a man without a wife commits adultery with another man’s wife, or if a woman without a husband does so with another man’s husband, the person who violated the marriage covenant shall do penance for seven years, as stated above. The person not bound by the law of marriage shall do penance for five years.

[Col. 0627A] For equal penance ought not to be assigned to those for whom the embrace of their own spouses could have sufficed to satisfy their desire, and to those who, lacking a spouse, fell into fornication under the compulsion of lustful passion.

### Chapter 208.—Concerning married persons who separate for some definite reason, so as to remain unmarried. From the writings of Augustine (*On the Sermon on the Mount*, book I, ch. 28).

(32, question 7, canon *Apostolus*.) The Apostle Paul says: “To those who are married I give this command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not separate from her husband; but if she separates, she should remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband” (1 Cor. 7). For she may separate for the cause which the Lord permitted.

Or, if a woman is permitted to dismiss her husband even on the ground of fornication, what shall we say concerning what follows: “And let not the husband dismiss his wife” (ibid.)? Why did he not add, “except for the cause of fornication,” which the Lord permits, unless he intended the same rule to be understood: that, if he dismisses her—which is permitted on account of fornication—he should remain without a wife or be reconciled to his wife?

And shortly afterward: The Lord permitted a wife to be dismissed for the cause of fornication; but because He permitted it, He did not command it.

[Col. 0627B]

### Chapter 209.—Concerning those who, after a repudiation, have joined themselves in marriage to others. From the decrees of Pope Innocent, chapter 26 (letter 3, ch. 6).

Your Belovedness also inquired concerning those who, after a repudiation, have joined themselves in marriage to others. It is evident that they are adulterers on both sides. Those who hasten to another union while their wives are alive—even though the marriage seems dissolved—cannot fail to appear adulterers. So much so that even the persons to whom such people are joined appear themselves to have committed adultery, according to what we read in the Gospel: “Whoever dismisses his wife and takes another commits adultery” (Matt. 5; 19).

[Col. 0627C] Therefore we have decreed that all are to be excluded from the communion of the faithful. But as for their parents or relatives, nothing of this sort can be decreed unless they are found [“are revealed,” original text] to have been instigators of the unlawful union.

### Chapter 210.—If a man’s wife has been violated and for that reason her husband plots to destroy her. From the Council of Tribur, attended by King Arnulf, chapter 46.

[Col. 0627D] If the wife of anyone has been sexually violated, and for that reason her husband plots to put her to death by capital sentence, but she, pressed by danger of death, flees to a bishop and seeks help: the bishop should exert himself with the utmost labor, if possible, to prevent her being killed. But if he cannot, he must in no way return her to the man seeking her, to be killed, since she has presented herself to him for protection. Rather, with diligent care he should send her to a place she herself chooses, so that she may live securely.

But if at some time her husband finds and claims her, he shall have power according to secular law to do what he wishes with her. Yet let him hear Saint Augustine, who says (*Sermon on the Seasons*, 243): “Since a man takes his name from strength, and a woman from softness—that is, frailty—why does every man wish his wife to be victorious against the most cruel beast of lust, when he himself falls defeated at lust’s first blow?”

A little later: “For whatever is not permitted to women against the Catholic faith is not permitted to men either.” Thus far Augustine.

[Col. 0628A] If, however, the same woman, terrified by fear, flees from the place to which the bishop sent her, and her husband asks the bishop for her once, twice, or more often, the bishop should seek her out and return her if he can secure her life. But if not, he must by no means return her. So long as she lives, the husband must in no way take another wife.

### Chapter 211.—Concerning a man who has fornicated with another’s wife while her husband lives. From a council held at Altheim, in the presence of King Conrad, chapter 5.

(31, question 2, canon *Illud vero*.) We establish and prejudge by a common decree, according to the institutions of the canons, that if anyone has fornicated with another man’s wife while her husband lived, then, when that husband dies, access to an unlawful marriage with her shall be barred to him by synodal judgment, so that he may not thereafter be joined in marriage to her whom he previously defiled by adultery. For we do not wish, nor is it consistent with Christian religion, that anyone should take in marriage one whom he previously defiled through adultery.

[Col. 0628B]

### Chapter 212.—Concerning a freeborn man who takes a freeborn woman as wife and afterward declares himself a slave. From the Council of Tribur, chapter 8.

(29, question 2, canon *Perlatum est*.) It was reported to the holy synod that a certain freeborn man had taken a freeborn woman as wife and, after begetting children, had made himself a slave on the pretext of some divorce. The question was whether he must necessarily retain the woman, and, if he retained her, whether she too ought to be subjected to slavery under secular law.

It was decided that the wife must by no means be dismissed; yet, for Christ’s law does not permit the woman to be reduced to slavery, since he made himself a slave without his wife’s consent, though she had taken him as a free man for her husband.

[Col. 0628C]

### Chapter 213.—Concerning married persons whose laws differ. From the same council, chapter 39.

A certain nobleman from Francia took as wife a noblewoman from Saxony under the law of the Saxons. He kept her for many years and begot children by her. But because Saxons and Franks do not use the same laws, he alleged that he had not betrothed, received, or endowed her under his own—that is, Frankish—law; and, having dismissed her, he took another wife.

The holy synod determined concerning this matter that he, as a transgressor of evangelical law, must be subjected to penance, separated from his second wife, and compelled to take back the first.

[Col. 0628D]

### Chapter 214.—Why adulterous husbands receive communion when adulterous wives do not. From the decrees of Pope Innocent, chapter 24 (letter 3, ch. 4).

(32, question 5, canon *Christiana*.) It was also desired to know why men who receive communion do not cohabit with adulterous wives, whereas wives, on the contrary, appear to remain in the company of adulterous husbands, although Christian religion condemns adultery in both sexes on the same grounds.

But women do not readily accuse their husbands of adultery, and hidden sins do not have punishment. Men, however, have customarily reported adulterous wives more freely to priests; and therefore, once their crime has been disclosed, communion is denied to women. Yet because men’s offence remains hidden, no one is readily excluded merely upon suspicions; indeed, he will be excluded if his disgrace is revealed. Since the ground is equal, then, when proof is sometimes lacking, the rationale for punishment remains inactive.

[Col. 0629A]

### Chapter 215.—Examination for judgment.

Concerning the charge made against me in this synod, that I committed adultery or fornication with this woman: I did not do so, nor do I acknowledge myself guilty of it. So may God help me, and this judgment.

### Chapter 216.—Separation from an incestuous union.

(35, question 6, canon *Ab isto die*.) From this day forward, you shall no longer commit adultery or fornication with this woman with whom you committed adultery or fornication, and on whose account you undertook discipline or penance; nor shall you take another wife, unless permission has been granted you by the bishop or his representative after your penance has been completed. So may God help you.

[Col. 0629B]

### Chapter 217.—Reconciliation of married persons.

(35, question 6, canon *Ab isto*.) From this day forward, you shall keep this your wife, named N., whom you unjustly dismissed, as a husband ought rightly to have his wife: in love and with due discipline. You shall not separate her from yourself by any evil contrivance, nor, while she lives, take another wife. So may God help you.

### Chapter 218.—Concerning the same matter.

From this time forward, you shall keep and embrace this your husband, whom you unjustly dismissed. You shall be subject and obedient to him in service, love, and fear, as a wife ought rightly to be subject to her husband. You shall never separate yourself from him; while he lives, you shall not join yourself to another man, either in marriage or adultery. So may God help you.

[Col. 0629C]

### Chapter 219.—Concerning a certain man’s wife who, because of suspicion of fornication, left him and afterward returned. Gregory to Secundinus, bishop of Tauromenium (*Register*, book VIII, letter 32).

Leo the *chartularius*, the bearer of this letter, came to us and stated that his wife, having left him on a charge of fornication—which, he said, had grievously agitated her—had put on religious dress; but that she had in no way been guilty, nor after entering marriage had fallen into the fault of fornication. He added that he had given his wife the most solemn oaths that he himself had remained innocent in the matter concerning which suspicion had tormented her, and that she had therefore returned of her own accord.

But because he asserts that your Fraternity deprived her and her household of communion solely because she secretly returned to him without first consulting you, we wish her household indeed to receive holy communion, and that the lady’s fault should not keep her household long under the punishment of this affliction [the original has *familiam*, “household”].

[Col. 0629D] With respect to the wife of the aforesaid bearer, you must observe this: if it is plainly established that she could prove nothing against her husband, but rather that his suspicion was removed by the oath he took, as we have learned, and that after this she returned to him of her own accord, then judicial censure toward her must also be moderated such that she is not deprived of communion for a long time.

[Col. 0630A]

### Chapter 220.—That a wife is not to separate from her husband without his consent. Pope Alexander II to Landulf in Corsica (letter 11).

(33, question 5, canon *Notificasti*.) You reported that, sick unto death and greatly terrified by the recollection and dread of your sins, you anxiously sought to become a monk. By threats and terrors of killing your wife, you extorted from her permission for this; and thus, without an abbot, you took monastic dress and sought a monastery.

Afterward, when you had recovered, overcome in penitence by your wife’s protests, wailing, and tears, and by the dispersal of your household, you returned home. After many days, at the counsel of certain wise persons, you returned to the bed of the woman just mentioned. Now you ask our counsel whether you may have relations with your wife.

[Col. 0630B] If the matter is indeed as your messenger reports, it does not seem to us that this was done reasonably or with sound judgment. For although every person seeking monastic life must act lawfully, holily, and justly, you, contrary to the laws, subjected in part to fear of death and in part to the pains of your illness, followed a wrongful path. Without receiving any permission, as is said, you left your wife and sought a monastery.

For this must be done not by coercion but by equal will and consent, as the holy Fathers say. Nor may a husband be received into a monastery unless his wife chooses a women’s monastery or, having professed continence, promptly changes her dress. For Saint Basil says as follows concerning this matter (27, question 2, canon *Si quis conjugatus*):

“If a married man wishes to enter a monastery, he is not to be received unless he has first been released by his wife after she has professed chastity. For if, while he lives, she marries another through lack of self-restraint, she will undoubtedly be an adulteress; and such a man’s conversion is not accepted by God when it results in the prostitution of the marriage covenant. Therefore such persons follow Christ without fault after leaving the world only if they have an equal, mutual consent to chastity.”

[Col. 0630C] Therefore, dearest son, consider and see whether you were thus canonically released by your wife, and whether your wife made such a promise, so that she too may fulfill the good undertaking and your shared vow. Otherwise, we ought not impose upon you the necessity of separation.

[Col. 0630D]

### Chapter 221.—Concerning those who, after dismissing their wives, entered other marriages. Nicholas to the archbishop of Ravenna.

Concerning the senator’s wife, whom you say was an adulteress, judged to have been separated from her husband because of the charge of adultery, and clothed and veiled in monastic dress: we do not know whether this judgment was decided justly or otherwise. If she appeared to be an adulteress, this matter should all the more have been investigated by her husband; and, if it was investigated by him, it ought to have been examined and determined in the presence of investigators or judges. Then, after the determination, verification, and public establishment of the matter, judgment should have been rendered upon the case, either by legal decision or canonical judgment.

[Col. 0631A] But if neither has been done, who dared to clothe her in religious dress and cover her with the sacred veil? Nevertheless, keeping the fear of God more carefully before your eyes, we command that, in the presence of your envoy or vicar, an inquiry be held through a genuine examination, with her husband present. If their case appears just and reasonable, let it stand. If it appears otherwise, as we have stated above, let their case be determined according to the will and fear of almighty God.

### Chapter 222.—Concerning the same matter. John VIII to Count Totzilo.

Moreover, those who have dismissed their wives or, while those wives live, have gone on to other marriages, we excommunicate, together with their accomplices, until they put away the later women and receive back the former wives in penitence. For, as Saint Augustine testifies, marriage was established by God, but divorce was invented by the devil. “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19), especially since this most evil custom has remained from pagan practice, among whom no one but the devil himself was teacher and author in such matters.

[Col. 0631B]

### Chapter 223.—Concerning the same matter. The same to the same.

Most prudent man, take care and make provision that those two men who have cast away the wives whom God prepared and joined to them may not be permitted to reject them; for it is impious that those joined by God’s agency in a lawful covenant should be separated at human whim—indeed, by the devil’s fraud.

The same. Memorandum to Paul, bishop.

[Col. 0631C] Take care that you give the greatest attention to the separation of married persons, so that those who have been separated since the receipt of the Apostolic See’s letters may without fault take back their former wives, after suitable penance has been imposed and those whom they subsequently took have been dismissed. If they refuse, put them outside the Church together with those who receive them into communion, until they amend what they have done.

### Chapter 224.—Concerning the English people’s practice of a second fornication. The martyr Boniface to Hiltribald, king of the English. [Alternatively: the same, likewise.]

(Distinction 56, canon *Si gens Anglorum*.) If the English people, as has been reported throughout these regions—to our reproach in Francia and Italy, and as a reproach even from pagans—should, despising lawful marriages, live a foul life of adultery and debauchery after the manner of the people of Sodom, then from such intercourse with prostitutes one must expect degenerate, ignoble peoples to be begotten, raging with lust. In the end the whole people will decline toward what is worse and more ignoble, and will finally be neither strong in secular war, nor steadfast in faith, nor honorable before human beings, nor beloved by God.

[Col. 0631D] This befell other peoples in Spain, Provence, and Burgundy, who, turning away from God, committed fornication in this way, until the Almighty Judge [alternatively, “Avenger,” original text] permitted punishments avenging such crimes to come and rage through ignorance of God’s law and through the Saracens [alternative reading: “to serve”].

### Chapter 225.—Concerning King Lothair, who had left his lawful wife and taken another. Nicholas to all archbishops established throughout Gaul and Germany. [Alternatively: the same, likewise.]

[Col. 0632A] In accordance with our decree, when we dispatched two bishops to those regions, it came to our knowledge that Lothair, having repudiated his first and lawful wife, had taken a second wife, neither awaiting a request to nor permission from our see, nor submitting anywhere to canonical judgment. What else can be understood from this except that, where he forestalled the judgment of peoples, he pronounced himself by his own judgment a transgressor?

### Chapter 226.—Concerning the deposition of two archbishops who supported Lothair in his error. Nicholas to bishops and archbishops established throughout Gaul, Italy, Germany, and all provinces (Third Roman Council under Nicholas I, ch. 1).

[Col. 0632B] (2, question 1, canon *Scelus*.) The crime committed by King Lothair—if indeed he can truly be called king, since he restrains the appetites of the body by no wholesome governance but rather yields, through slippery enervation, to their unlawful impulses—in the case of two women, namely Theutberga and Waldrada, is known to all.

Moreover, nearly the whole world, flocking from every side to the thresholds or see of the Apostles, had long reported to us that Bishops Theutgaud and Gunthar were his defenders and supporters in such conduct.

And shortly afterward: Therefore, with the holy synod decreeing together with us, they are certainly held to have been deposed in its presence, excommunicated from priestly office, and removed from the governance of the episcopate.

[Col. 0632C] Below, likewise (ch. 2). (11, question 3, canon *Teugaldum*.) The archbishops Theutgaud of Trier, primate of the province of Belgica, and Gunthar of Cologne Agrippina, now before us and the holy synod, produced an instrument strengthened by their own signatures, setting forth how they had reconsidered and judged the case of King Lothair and his two women, Theutberga and Waldrada. Before many persons present, they affirmed in their own words that they had done nothing more, less, or otherwise than this; and they publicly confessed with one voice that they had violated the sentence which our most holy brother Thado, archbishop of Milan, and our other fellow bishops had asked the Apostolic See to issue in the case of Geltrude, wife of Boso, and which we, inflamed by divine zeal, had canonically pronounced under the solemn charge of anathema.

In all these matters we found that they had in many respects transgressed apostolic and canonical ordinances and wickedly violated the norm of equity. We judge them wholly deprived of every priestly office, stripped of episcopal governance by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by the authority of Blessed Peter exercised through us, and decree that they shall remain so.

[Col. 0632D]

### Chapter 227.—Concerning Lothair’s correction. The same to King Lothair (in the reply, title VII, ch. 5).

(11, question 3, canon *Ita corporis*.) You consented so to yield to the impulses of your body, and, loosening the reins of pleasures, cast yourself at will into the pit of misery and the mire [Ps. 39], that you, who had been placed to govern peoples, have become the ruin of many.

The lawful downfall some time ago of Bishops Theutgaud and Gunthar proves this. Because they did not correct you as they should have done, but instead sought to conceal your transgression with their arguments under a certain darkened appearance of justice, and by certain elaborate inventions to bury equity, they were deposed by our authority and regularly removed from all episcopal governance.

[Col. 0633A] Below, likewise (ch. 7). (24, question 5, canon *An non districta*.) Are you not deserving to be struck with severe punishment, since you are known to imitate Lamech’s adultery and shameful conduct in having two wives? (Gen. 4.) The Lord erased this only by His saving advent after seventy-seven generations, whereas Cain’s fratricide was wiped away by the waters of the flood in the seventh generation.

### Chapter 228.—That a wife may be dismissed only for the cause of fornication. Nicholas’s replies to the questions of the Bulgarians, chapter 96.

[Col. 0633B] (32, question 5, canon *Quidquid mulier*.) Whatever your wife has plotted or done against you, or even if she has accused you, she is not to be rejected or utterly hated except for the cause of fornication; for, as the Apostle commands, she is to be loved by you as the Church is loved by God [Eph. 5].

### Chapter 229.—That a woman is not to leave her husband. Council of Gangra, chapter 14.

(Distinction 30, canon *Si qua mulier*.) If any woman, abandoning her own husband, wishes to depart because she detests marriage, let her be anathema.

### Chapter 230.—That one dismissed by a wife and one dismissed by a husband are not to marry others. Council of Milevis, chapter 17.

Neither one dismissed by a wife nor one dismissed by a husband is to be joined to another; rather, they are to remain as they are or be reconciled to one another.

[Col. 0633C]

### Chapter 231.—Concerning those who abandon the marital union without serious fault. From the Council of Agde, chapter 25.

(33, question 2, canon *Saeculares*.) Laypersons who abandon, or have abandoned, the marital union without any more serious fault, and who offer no probable grounds for separation, but dismiss their marriages so that they may presume upon unlawful or another’s unions, are, if they cast aside their wives before stating the causes of separation before the bishops of their province and before the wives have been condemned by judgment, to be excluded from communion of the Church and from the assembly of its holy people [the original has “their holy people”], because they defile the faith of marriage.

### Chapter 232.—That an uncultivated and rough husband is not to be dismissed by his wife. Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, under the heading for the fourth day (book V, ch. 7).

[Col. 0633D] “But the husband is rough [variant: *horridus*, ‘frightful’] and uncultivated.” He pleased you once. Must another husband be chosen? Even a horse loves its mate; if another is substituted, it does not know how to draw the yoke with another’s companion and thinks itself incomplete. Yet you repudiate your yokefellow, think him often to be changed, bring in a rival if he fails for a single day, and immediately, as though the cause were known when it is unknown, prosecute an injury to modesty.

### Chapter 233.—That, just as one who dismisses a chaste wife is cruel and unjust, so one who keeps a prostitute is foolish and unjust. Chrysostom on Matthew, chapter 109 (Homily 32 on Matthew, in the unfinished work).

[Col. 0634A] “Whoever dismisses his wife, except for the cause of fornication, commits adultery” (Matt. 19). Every thing is dissolved by the same causes by which it comes into being. Marriage is not made by sexual intercourse but by will; therefore it is dissolved not by bodily separation but by will. Thus one who dismisses his wife and does not take another is still a husband; for although he is now separated in body, he is still joined in will. When, therefore, he takes another, then he dismisses fully. Consequently, it is not the one who dismisses who commits adultery, but the one who takes another woman.

But just as one who dismisses a chaste wife is cruel and unjust, so one who keeps a prostitute is foolish and unjust; for the person who conceals his wife’s crime is the protector of her shamefulness.

[Col. 0634B]

### Chapter 234.—That whatever immodest or sordid acts married people perform with one another are a human vice, not the fault of marriage, but are forgiven on account of marriage. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage* (ch. 6).

(32, question 2, canon *Quidquid inter*.) Whatever immodest, shameless, or sordid acts married people perform with one another are a human vice, not the fault of marriage. Even in their excessive claiming of the marital debt, which the Apostle grants them not as a command but as a concession (1 Cor. 7), so that they may have intercourse even apart from the purpose of procreation, although depraved habits impel them to such intercourse, marriage nevertheless protects them from adultery or fornication. For this is not permitted because of marriage; it is forgiven because of marriage.

[Col. 0634C] Married people therefore owe one another not only the fidelity involved in sexual union for the purpose of begetting children—which is the primary fellowship of the human race in this mortal condition—but also a sort of mutual servitude of receiving one another’s weakness, so as to avoid unlawful intercourse. Thus, even if perpetual continence pleases one of them, it cannot be practiced without the other’s consent.

### Chapter 235.—That a spouse may lawfully be dismissed for fornication, yet the prior bond remains. Likewise [Augustine, ibid.].

To render the marital debt is no crime; to demand it beyond the necessity of procreation is a venial fault; but to commit fornication or adultery is a punishable crime.

(Ibid., ch. 7.) Marital charity must take care not to give its spouse a ground for condemnation while seeking for itself a source of greater honor. For “whoever dismisses his wife, except for the cause of fornication, makes her commit adultery” (Matt. 5). So truly is the covenant of marriage entered into a kind of sacramental reality that not even separation itself renders it void. For, while the husband from whom she was separated lives, she commits adultery if she marries another; and the man who left her is the cause of this evil.

Likewise, Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage* (ibid., same chapter). (32, question 7, canon *Interveniente*.) When divorce intervenes, the marital covenant is not abolished, so that spouses remain spouses even when separated; but they commit adultery with those to whom they are joined even after their repudiation, whether she to a man or he to a woman.

[Col. 0635A] Likewise (ibid., ch. 18). It was not lawful then, is not lawful now, and never will be lawful to pass from a living husband into another marriage. For to apostatize from the one God and go to the adulterous superstition of another has always been evil.

Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book II (ch. 4). (32, question 7, canon *Licite*.) A spouse is lawfully dismissed because of fornication, but the prior bond remains.

(Ibid., ch. 5.) For this reason, one who takes a dismissed woman is guilty of adultery, even when she was dismissed for the cause of fornication. Just as a person guilty of a crime is excommunicated while the sacrament of regeneration remains in that person, and does not lack that sacrament even if never reconciled to God, so the sacrament of marriage is not lacking while the bond remains, even if the person is never reconciled to the spouse. But she will lack it if her husband dies.

[Col. 0635B] A guilty excommunicated person, however, will never lack the sacrament of regeneration, even unreconciled, because that person never dies.

### Chapter 236.—That a wife dismissed for fornication is not to be married by another. Likewise, Book I (chap. 9).

No one is so absurd as to deny that the man is an adulterer who marries her whom her husband has cast off on account of fornication, since the Lord calls him an adulterer who marries her who has been cast off for a reason other than fornication (Matt. 19).

### Chapter 237.—That a wife is not to be dismissed lightly. Augustine, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount* (Book I, chap. 20).

(32, question 7, canon *Dominus ad illud*.) In order to establish that a wife is not to be dismissed lightly, the Lord made an exception only for the cause of fornication; but he commands that every other affliction that may arise be borne courageously for the sake of marital fidelity and chastity. He also calls an adulterer even the man who marries her who has been separated from her husband. Likewise, in the same work, a little later. (32, question 5, canon *Fieri potest*.) A husband may dismiss his wife for the cause of fornication, which the Lord wished to be excepted. But if she is not permitted to marry while the husband from whom she has departed is alive, nor he to take another wife while the wife whom he dismissed is alive, then much less is it lawful for him to commit illicit fornications with anyone whatever.

### Chapter 238.—Likewise, that a wife is not to be cast off for any bodily infirmity (ibid., chap. 27).

(32, question 5, canon *Si uxorem*.) If a man has a wife who is sterile, physically unattractive, weak in her limbs, blind, deaf, lame, or otherwise afflicted, or worn out by illnesses, pains, and labours—whatever, except fornication, can be imagined as extremely dreadful—he should bear it for the sake of fellowship and fidelity.

### Chapter 239.—That, while her husband lives, a dismissed woman cannot marry another for any reason. Jerome to the priest Amandus (vol. III, letter beginning, “A brief letter [concerning] long matters”).

(32, question 7, canon *Omnes causationes*.) The Apostle, cutting off all excuses, has most plainly determined that, while her husband lives, a woman is an adulteress if she marries another. Do not bring forward to me the violence of an abductor, a mother’s entreaty [“persuasion,” in the original], a father’s authority, a crowd of relatives, the schemes of servants, and the parents’ [“and contempt,” in the original] hostility, or losses to the household property. So long as her husband lives—even if he is an adulterer, even if a sodomite, even if covered with every disgrace, and abandoned by his wife because of those crimes—he is accounted her husband, and she is not permitted to take another man.

### Chapter 240.—That what is not permitted to women is equally not permitted to husbands. The same, to Oceanus, on the death of Fabiola (vol. I, in the epitaph of Fabiola, beginning: “Many years have passed”).

(32, question 5, canon *Praecepit*.) The Lord commanded that a wife ought not to be dismissed, except for the cause of fornication; and that, if she is dismissed, she should remain unmarried (Matt. 5). Whatever is commanded to men consequently extends also to women. For an adulterous wife is not to be dismissed while an adulterous husband is retained. Likewise, in the same place, a little later. (32, question [uncertain], canon *Apud nos*.) Among us, what is not permitted to women is equally not permitted to men, and the same servitude is assessed under equal conditions.

### Chapter 241.—On the penalty of one who marries a woman abandoned by her husband. *Capitulary*, Book V, chap. 300 (149).

(33, question 2, canon *Quicunque*.) Whoever, having abandoned his own wife—or having killed her though she was without fault—marries another, shall lay aside his arms and perform public penance. If he is contumacious, he shall be apprehended by the count, bound in irons, and put into custody.

### Chapter 242.—That reconciliation with a wife after adultery is not harsh. Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, Book II (chap. 6).

(32, question 1, canon *Quod autem tibi durum*.) What seems hard to you—that, after adultery, one spouse should be reconciled to the other—will not be hard if faith is present. Why do we still reckon as adulterers those whom we believe to have been cleansed either by baptism or healed by penance? In the old law of God these crimes were cleansed by no sacrifices; without doubt they are cleansed by the blood of the New Testament. Therefore it was then wholly forbidden to receive back a wife defiled by another husband, although David, prefiguring the New Testament, received back without defilement Saul’s daughter, whom the father of that woman had separated from him and given to another (1 Kings 18). But now, after Christ said to the adulteress, “Neither do I condemn you; go, and sin no more” (John 8), who does not understand that a husband ought to forgive, since he sees that the Lord of them both has forgiven? Nor ought he any longer to call her an adulteress whose crime, upon her repentance, he believes has been removed by divine mercy.

Likewise (ibid., chap. 8). (32, question 6, canon *Indignantur*.) Husbands are indignant if they hear that other men suffer penalties similar to adulterous women, although men ought to be punished so much more severely as it belongs to them more especially both to conquer by virtue and to govern women by example.

Likewise (ibid., chap. 9). (3, question 1, canon *Non erit turpis*.) The reconciliation of spouses, even after adulteries have been committed and purged, will not be shameful or difficult where, through the keys of the kingdom of heaven, remission of sins is not doubted to take place—not so that an adulteress may be recalled after divorce from her husband, but so that, after union with Christ, she may not be called an adulteress.

Likewise (ibid., chap. 13). (32, question 5, canon *Puto Christianum*.) I think that no Christian would deny that a man is an adulterer who has joined himself to another woman while his own wife is long ill, long absent, or desires to live continently.

Likewise (ibid., chap. 15). (33, question 2, canon *Si quod verius*.) If, as is more truly said, it is not lawful for a Christian man to kill an adulterous wife, but only to dismiss her, who is so mad as to say to him: “Do what is unlawful, so that you may be allowed to do what is unlawful”? For since both are unlawful according to Christ’s law—both to kill an adulteress and, while she lives, to take another wife—he must abstain from both; one unlawful act is not to be done for the sake of another. For if he is going to do what is unlawful, let him commit adultery rather than homicide: let him take another while his wife is alive, rather than shed human blood.

### Chapter 243.—On the same matter. Hermas, in the book *The Shepherd*, Mandate 4.

(34, question 2, canon *Ego dixi*.) I said to the shepherd: “Lord, if someone has a wife faithful in the Lord and finds her in adultery, does the husband sin if he lives with her?” And he said to me: “So long as he does not know her sin, he lives with her without fault. But if the husband learns that his wife has sinned, and the woman does not repent but remains in her fornication, and the husband lives with her, he will be guilty of her sin and a participant in her adultery.”

And I said to him: “What then, if the woman remains in her vice?” And he said: “Let the husband dismiss her, and let the husband remain by himself.”

“If the dismissed woman repents and wishes to return to her husband, will she not be received by him?” He said: “On the contrary, if her husband does not receive her, he sins and incurs a great sin upon himself. But he ought to receive the sinner who repents—yet not repeatedly. For the servants of God have one repentance. Therefore, on account of repentance, a man ought not, after dismissing his wife, to take another. The case is the same for woman and man. Nor is adultery committed only by one who defiles his flesh; he also who makes an idol commits adultery. But if she persists in these acts and does not repent, withdraw from her and do not live with her. Otherwise you too will be a participant in her sin. For this reason it has been commanded to you that each remain by himself, whether man or woman; for in such a case there can be repentance.”

### Chapter 244.—That women whose husbands have been captured and long detained, and who have married others, are to be restored to their first husbands if they return. Leo to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, chap. 1 (Letter 79).

(34, question 2, canon *Cum per bellicam*.) Since, through the calamity of war and the gravest hostile incursions, you report that certain marriages have been so divided that, when the husbands were carried away into captivity, their wives remained destitute, believing their own husbands either to have been killed or never to be freed from bondage, and, compelled by anxiety, passed into marriage with other men; and since, through the Lord’s help, circumstances have changed for the better and some of those thought to have perished have returned: your charity rightly seems uncertain what we ought to ordain concerning women joined to other husbands.

But because we know that it is written that a woman is joined to a husband by the Lord (Prov. 9), and again recognize the command that what the Lord has joined, man should not separate (Matt. 19), we must believe that the bonds of lawful marriages are to be restored. Those circumstances brought about by war having been removed, what each person lawfully possessed must be restored to him; and every effort must be made that each receive what is his own.

(Chap. 2.) Yet they are not to be judged blameworthy if they were able to pass into another’s legal right; nevertheless, it is fully consonant with justice that, when the former husbands return, what is their own should be restored to them. For if this is rightly [“duly,” in the original] observed in slaves, fields, houses, and possessions, how much more must it be done in the restoration of spouses, so that what was disturbed by the disaster of war may be restored by the remedy of peace?
