(Chap. 3.) Therefore, if husbands return after long captivity and persist in love for their wives, wishing them to return to union with them, what necessity brought about must be passed over and judged blameless, and what fidelity requires must be restored.

(Chap. 4.) But if certain women are so captivated by love for their later husbands that they prefer to cling to them rather than return to lawful union, they are rightly to be censured, so that they are deprived of communion with the Church.

### Chapter 245.—That, if a husband takes another wife while his own is captive, he is to be restored to the first. Innocent to Probus (Innocent I, Letter 9).

(34, question 2, canon *Cum in captivitate*.) While the woman Ursa was held captive, we learn that Restitutus Fontanus entered into another marriage. But, by the Lord’s favour, Ursa returned and came to us; and, with no one disputing it, she demonstrated that she was the wife of the aforesaid man. Therefore, most illustrious lord son, we have decreed, with the Catholic faith supporting us, that the marriage which had first been founded by divine grace is the true marriage, and that the union with the second woman, while the first was alive and had not been put away by divorce, can by no means be lawful.

### Chapter 246.—Therefore, so long as it is certain that the husband is alive in captivity, the wife must never marry another. *Pandects*, Book XXIV, title II.

It must be established as a general rule that, so long as it is certain that the husband remains alive in captivity, their wives have no permission to enter another marriage.

### Chapter 247.—That unbelief is fornication. Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, Book I (chap. 17).

If a man may be separated from his spouse because of bodily fornication, how much more detestable in a spouse is fornication of the mind, that is, unbelief.

Likewise (ibid., chap. 18). The fornication of an unbelieving person is greater in the heart; nor can that person’s chastity with a spouse be called true, because “whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14).

### Chapter 248.—That a wife is to be dismissed if she compels her husband to commit fornication against God. Augustine, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, Book I (chap. 22).

(28, question 1, canon *Idololatria*.) Idolatry, which unbelievers follow, and every harmful superstition, is fornication. The Lord, however, permitted a wife to be dismissed for the cause of fornication (Deut. 24; Matt. 5). But because he permitted it and did not command it, he gave the Apostle occasion to advise that one who wishes should not dismiss an unbelieving wife, so that she might perhaps thus become faithful (1 Cor. 7).

### Chapter 249.—Likewise, on the same matter (ibid., chap. 23).

If unbelief is fornication, and idolatry is unbelief, and avarice is idolatry, then it must not be doubted that avarice too is fornication. If avarice is fornication, who can now rightly separate any illicit desire whatever from the class of fornication?

### Chapter 250.—That a wife is to be dismissed where either Christ or the wife must be dismissed. Likewise.

(Immediately following.) From this it is understood that, on account of illicit desires—not only those committed in sexual immorality with other men or women, but absolutely any that cause a soul, through wrongful use of the body, to stray from God’s law and be corruptly and shamefully ruined—a husband may without sin dismiss his wife, and a wife her husband (Matt. 19). For the Lord makes an exception for the cause of fornication; and, as considered above, we are compelled to understand this fornication as general and universal.

(*Retractions*, Book I, chap. 19.) But when he says, “except for the cause of fornication,” he does not say whose fornication, whether the husband’s or the wife’s. For permission is given not merely to dismiss a fornicating wife, but also to anyone who dismisses the wife by whom he himself is compelled to commit fornication: he plainly dismisses her for the cause of fornication. For example, if a wife compels someone to sacrifice to idols, he who dismisses such a wife dismisses her for fornication—not only hers, but his own: hers, because she commits fornication; his, lest he commit fornication. Nothing, however, is more unjust than to dismiss one’s wife for the cause of fornication when one is oneself convicted of fornication. For this saying applies: “In passing judgment on another, you condemn yourself; for you do the very same things that you judge” (Rom. 2). Therefore, whoever wishes to cast off his wife for the cause of fornication must first be cleansed from fornication himself. The same, I say, applies likewise to a woman.

### Chapter 251.—On the same matter. Augustine, *On Faith and Works* (chap. 16).

(28, question 1, canon *Uxor legitima*.) A wife joined in lawful fellowship is abandoned without any fault if she refuses to remain with a Christian husband. It is not considered how most rightly she may be dismissed if she says to her husband: “I will not be your wife unless you accumulate riches for me through robbery, or unless, though now a Christian, you continue to practise the usual procuring by which you used to support our household”; or if she knows of any other criminal or shameful conduct in her husband, by which she was delighted, either satisfying her lust, obtaining an easy livelihood, or even appearing more richly dressed.

Then the husband to whom his wife says this—if, when he came to baptism, he truly repented of dead works and has, as his foundation, the faith that works through love—will beyond doubt be bound more strongly by love of divine grace than by the lust of the flesh, and will resolutely cut off the member that causes him to stumble.

### Chapter 252.—Likewise, on the same matter. Rabanus on Matthew, Book II (Augustine, Book I, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, chap. 21).

A question arises: since the Lord permits a wife to be dismissed for the cause of fornication, in what sense is fornication to be understood here? Is it to be understood as people understand it—that is, as the fornication committed in sexual immorality—or as Scripture customarily calls every unlawful corruption fornication, as stated above: such as idolatry or avarice, and thence every transgression of the law arising from illicit desire? If avarice is fornication, who can now rightly separate any illicit desire whatever from the class of fornication?

### Chapter 253.—Likewise, on the same matter. Ambrose [Augustine] to Hilary (Letter 89).

(28, question 1, canon *Si infidelis*.) “If the unbeliever departs,” says the Apostle, “let him depart; a brother or sister is not subject to bondage in such cases” (1 Cor. 7). That is, if an unbeliever does not wish to remain with a believing spouse, the believer should recognize his or her freedom, lest the believer reckon himself or herself so subject to bondage as to abandon the faith rather than lose the unbelieving spouse.

This is to be understood also concerning children and parents, brothers and sisters: all are to be left for Christ’s sake when this condition is imposed, that one must leave Christ if one wishes to keep him [“them,” in the original] with oneself. The same applies to house and fields, and [“also,” in the original] to those things possessed by proprietary right.

### Chapter 254.—That a wife is not to be dismissed because of sterility and another, fertile wife taken. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, chap. 7.

(32, question 7, canon *Tantum valet*.) The bond of companionship is so powerful that, although it was entered into for the purpose of procreation, not even the purpose of procreation dissolves it. A man might dismiss a sterile wife and marry one by whom he could have children, yet it is not lawful.

Likewise (ibid., chap. 15). The bond of marriage remains even if offspring, for whose sake it was entered into, does not follow because of manifest sterility. Thus, even if the spouses know that they will have no children, they are nevertheless not permitted to separate on account of the children themselves and join themselves to others. If they do so, they commit adultery with those to whom they join themselves. But while the marriage itself remains—[Note: Col. 0639D reads: “But while the marriage itself remains, plainly, etc.” The original reads: “But the spouses themselves plainly remain, etc.”]—with the wife’s consent, it was lawful among the ancient Fathers to take another woman, so that children might be born as common children: by the union and seed of one, but by the legal right and authority of the other. Whether this is lawful now, I would not rashly say.

### Chapter 255.—Even one who, having dismissed his wife for fornication, joins himself to another while she lives is an adulterer. Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, Book I (chap. 9).

(32, question 7, canon *Quemadmodum*.) Just as it cannot rightly be said, “If a man does not know, he does not sin”—for there are sins of the ignorant as well, though less serious than those of persons who know—so neither can it rightly be said: “If a husband has dismissed his wife for the cause of fornication and married another, he does not commit adultery.” For there is adultery also in those who marry other women after dismissing their former wives for fornication; but it is certainly less serious than that of those who dismiss their wives not for fornication and marry others.

### Chapter 256.—On one who committed adultery with his brother’s wife. *Capitulary*, Book V, chap. 21.

If any man has a lawful wife and his brother commits adultery with her, that brother and that woman who committed the adultery shall never have a marriage for as long as they live.

### Chapter 257.—That a woman who leaves her husband because of fornication should remain unmarried or be reconciled to him. Ambrose, on the First Epistle to the Corinthians (on chap. 7, before the middle).

He addresses those joined in marriage with the Lord’s pronouncement: “A wife is not to depart from her husband; but if she does depart, let her remain unmarried.” This is the Apostle’s counsel: if she departs because of her husband’s evil manner of life, she should thereafter remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband. “But if she cannot remain continent,” he says, “because she is unwilling to struggle against the flesh, let her be reconciled to her husband.”

For a woman is not permitted to marry if she has dismissed her husband for the cause of fornication, or if he has apostatized, or if, prompted by the lust of apostasy [“apostasy,” in the original], he seeks to reverse the use of a wife; because the inferior party does not at all use the same law as the superior. Yet if he has apostatized or seeks to reverse the use of a wife, the woman can neither marry another nor return to him. And the husband is not to dismiss his wife—except, understood implicitly, for the cause of fornication.

### Chapter 258.—That, however young they may be, men must not take other wives while their own wives live. First Council of Arles, chap. 10.

Concerning those who discover their wives in adultery and are themselves young believers and are forbidden to marry, it has been resolved that, so far as possible, they should be counselled not to take other wives while their own wives live, even though adulteresses.

### Chapter 259.—That God’s law does not compel a person to do evil, although evil may sometimes result from it. Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, Book II (chap. 16).

You do not doubt that it is adultery if anyone marries the wife of a living man, dismissed by her husband through a bill of divorce without any fornication on the woman’s part. What then if he sees that he will neither be admitted to baptism, if he is a catechumen, nor be able profitably to perform penance, if, being baptized, he has done this and does not correct himself and abandon what he has done; and if he wishes and is able to kill the man whose wife he married, so that this crime may be washed away by baptism or dissolved through penance, and so that even that adultery may no longer continue, the woman having been released from the law of her husband after her husband’s death—while satisfaction is made by penance for the deed already done, or it is erased by regeneration? Is Christ’s law therefore to be accused, as though it compelled homicide, because it says that marrying a woman dismissed without the crime of fornication is adultery?

### Chapter 260.—On the case of King Lothair and his wife. Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, chap. 13 (*On the Divorce of Lothair and Theutberga*, Question 13).

If perhaps, as is reported, the king in question, after contracting a marriage lawfully, engaged in sexual intercourse with some other woman, it cannot be denied that he committed adultery, even if the woman whom he married as wife may perhaps have been found guilty of the matters of which she is accused; for after entering into a lawful marriage, and before a lawful determination, he presumed to do what was unlawful.

### Chapter 261.—That no one may marry the woman with whom he committed adultery unless penance has been completed, chap. 20 (Question 21, about the middle).

It is clear from the testimonies of Scripture and the sayings of the saints that the king may, if he wishes, be able to join in marriage the concubine with whom he is said to have committed adultery: namely, if his lawfully married wife, found innocent with respect to him, has died bodily; or if she is found to be so dead in soul that his union with her is legally proved to be incest and not to be regarded under any name as marriage.

Likewise. Another point must be observed: that, before legitimate penance has been undertaken and completed according to the laws of the Church, and reconciliation obtained [“marriage,” in the original], he must much less join himself to the concubine in question. For David did not have Bathsheba, with whom he had committed adultery, as wife without penance (2 Kings 12).

### Chapter 262.—That the standard of chastity should be equal for husband and wife. Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, Book II (chap. 8).

Those who dislike preserving an equal standard of chastity between husband and wife, and who choose—especially in this matter—to be subject to the laws of the world rather than to Christ, because secular laws seem not to bind men with the same bonds of chastity as women: let them read what the emperor Antoninus, certainly not a Christian, decreed on this matter. Where a husband is not permitted to accuse his wife of the crime of adultery because he has not provided her by his own conduct with an example of chastity, so that both are condemned if the charge itself proves both equally unchaste.

For these are the words of the aforesaid emperor, found in the Gregorian Code: “Certainly,” he says, “my letter shall in no respect prejudge the case. For even if the fault lay with you that the marriage was dissolved and your wife Eupasia married according to the Julian law, she will not be condemned for adultery on account of my rescript unless it is established that adultery was committed. They will, moreover, have before their eyes the question whether, while you lived chastely, you were also an adviser to her in cultivating good morals. For it seems to me utterly unjust that a husband should demand chastity from his wife which he does not himself display.”

### Chapter 263.—That a husband ought to be an example of chastity to his wife. Augustine, book *On the Ten Strings* (chap. 3).

(32, question 6, canon *Non moechaberis*.) “You shall not commit adultery”: that is, you shall not go to any woman other than your wife. But do you demand this from your wife and refuse to render it to her? Though you ought to precede your wife in virtue, since chastity is a virtue, you fall under a single assault of lust, yet wish your wife to be victorious while you lie defeated? And although you are the head of your wife, she whose head you are goes before you to God (Exod. 20; Deut. 5). Do you wish your household to hang upside down? For the husband is the head of the woman (Eph. 5). But where the woman lives better than the man, the household hangs upside down. If the husband is the head, the husband ought to live better and to lead his wife in every good work.

### Chapter 264.—On the penance of a husband by whose connivance his wife commits adultery. Council of Elvira, chap. 70.

If, with her husband’s knowledge, a wife has committed adultery, it has been resolved that communion is not to be given to him even at the end of life. But if he leaves her, after ten years he may receive communion, if, after learning that she was an adulteress, he retained her in his house for any period.

### Chapter 265.—That a fertile wife is not to be handed over to another because of desire for children. Augustine against Julian, to Claudius, Book V, chap. 9 (also reported in *On the Good of Marriage*, chap. 18; again in *On Faith and Works*, chap. 7).

As Cato is said to have done, a fertile [*fetanda*, perhaps an erroneous reading] wife is not to be handed over by a husband who does not wish to have more children to another man.

### Chapter 266.—On dismissing an adulteress. *Code*, Book IX, title II, chap. 9 (title IX, “On the Julian Law concerning Adultery and Sexual Immorality,” Book II).

Those who retain in marriage a wife caught in adultery incur the crime of procuring; not those who have a wife merely suspected of adultery.

### Chapter 267.—On Sarah’s excuse. Haimo, on Genesis.

(32, question 1, canon *Apud misericordem*.) Sarah may be excused for having been taken into Pharaoh’s house unwillingly or under compulsion (Gen. 20), not only because the body is not defiled except through consent of the mind, but also because this was done with the husband’s agreement and permission.

### Chapter 268.—That neither several marriages are to be commended nor however many condemned. Augustine, *On the Good of Widowhood* (chap. 12).

(31, question 1, canon *Quod si dormierit*.) People are accustomed to raise a question concerning third, fourth, and still more numerous marriages. To answer briefly: I dare neither condemn any marriages nor remove from them the shame associated with their number.

Likewise, in the same work, near the end of the chapter. Nor do I dare, contrary to the sense of human modesty, to say that, whenever husbands have died, a woman may marry as often as she wishes; nor do I dare, on my own authority and apart from the authority of Holy Scripture, to condemn however many [“as many as desired,” in the original] marriages.

### Chapter 269.—That second marriages are lawful. Augustine, *Against the Opponent of the Law and the Prophets*, Book II (chap. 9).

(32, question 4, canon *Iste Abrahae*.) This man even charges Abraham with the crime of fornication in his decrepit old age, plainly because, after Sarah’s death, he married another woman (Gen. 25). Even if no sacramental meaning of a hidden matter were understood here, Abraham ought to have done this for this reason alone: lest heretics opposed to the Apostle—among whom Tertullian also stands as a supporting ally (*On Monogamy*)—should think that after a wife’s death it is a crime to marry a wife (1 Cor. 7).

Likewise (ibid., chap. 11). God, who joined male and female in marital chastity for the propagation of the human race, showed that second marriages—also permitted in the New [“in each,” in the original] Testament—are lawful.

### Chapter 270.—That, as second marriages are not condemned, neither are more numerous marriages. Jerome to Pammachius (vol. III, letter beginning: “As to what [you wrote]”).

(21, question 1, canon *Aperiant*.) Let my detractors, I beg, open their ears and see that I have approved second and third marriages in the Lord. If I have not condemned second and third marriages, could I condemn the first marriage?

Likewise, in the same work, some time later. I have not condemned those twice married; indeed, not even those married three times, or, if the term can be used, eight times married.

Likewise, not far from the end. I now proclaim freely that in the Church neither a second marriage nor even a third marriage is condemned, and that it is as lawful to marry a fifth, sixth, or further husband as it is to marry a second.

### Chapter 271.—That mothers who wish to undertake guardianship of their children should not enter another marriage, Book V, chap. 33.

Mothers who, after the loss of their husbands, seek guardianship for administering their children’s affairs must, before such confirmation of office can lawfully take effect for them, declare in the official acts, having taken an oath, that they will not enter another marriage. No woman is to be compelled into such an option; rather, she is freely to submit by her own will to the conditions we have prescribed. For if they prefer to choose other marriages, they ought not to administer the guardianships of their children.

### Chapter 272.—On the penalty of a widow who marries within the year of mourning. Thirty-seventh constitution of the *Novels*, chap. 11.

Likewise, if a woman, after her husband’s death and before the yearly period has been completed, hastens to a second marriage, she will in every respect be among the legally infamous. Yet, if she has no children from the former marriage, she may remove the infamy by presenting petitions to the emperor and being restored to her former standing by the divine decision of the prince. But she will by no means acquire property left to her by her former husband.

### Chapter 273.—That a woman who enters a second marriage is not to use the privilege of her first husband, chap. 23.

A woman who enters a second marriage does not enjoy the privileges or dignities of her former husband. But if, subject to this restriction, she contracts a second marriage, not only her own property—that is, the mother’s property—shall be subjected to her children by right of hypothec, but also the property of the stepfather, by authority of the present constitution.

### Chapter 274.—On the same matter. Eighty-fourth constitution, chap. 1.

If, after her husband’s death, a mother prefers to administer the guardianship of her children, she shall renounce second marriages before a court or by oath; she shall pledge her own property to her underage child; and then guardianship shall be entrusted to her.

### Chapter 275.—What fornication is. Augustine on the Epistle to the Galatians (on chap. 5, at the passage “Now the works of the flesh are manifest,” near the end).

Fornication is a wandering love released from lawful marriage, pursuing license for the gratification of lust.

### Chapter 276.—How great a sin are sexual beds and indecencies. Augustine to Bishop Aurelius (Letter 64).

The Vessel of Election says: “Not in revelry and drunkenness, not in beds and indecencies, not in strife and deceit” (Rom. 13). Of these three, “beds and indecencies” are judged so grave an offense that no one who has stained himself with this sin appears worthy not only of ecclesiastical ministry, but even of communion in the sacraments—and rightly so in every respect.

### Chapter 277.—That not every marriage is a true conjugal union. Jerome, Book III on the Epistle to the Ephesians (on chap. 5, about the middle).

(32, question 2, canon *Sicut non omnis*.) Just as not every assembly of heretics can be called Christ’s Church, nor is Christ their head, so not every marriage in which a wife is not joined to her husband according to Christ’s commands can rightly be called a conjugal union; rather, it is adultery.

### Chapter 278.—That every unclean defilement is called fornication. Isidore, *Sentences*, Book II, chap. 39.

Every unclean defilement is called fornication, although persons prostitute themselves to different pleasures of shamefulness. For various disgraceful acts arise from the pleasure of fornication; by these the kingdom of God is closed and a human being is separated from him [“from God,” in the original].

### Chapter 279.—That in the law every illicit sexual union is understood under the name adultery. Augustine, Book *Questions on Exodus* (in the book of seven questions, Exod. chap. 20, question 71).

Every adultery is also called fornication in Scripture; but whether every fornication can also be called adultery, I do not presently find an example of this mode of expression in the same Scriptures. But if every fornication cannot also be called adultery, I do not know whether it can be discovered where in the Decalogue that fornication is forbidden which is committed by men who do not have wives with women who do not have husbands [“husbands,” in the original].

But if every unlawful appropriation of another’s property is rightly understood under the name theft—for he who forbade theft did not permit robbery, but certainly intended the whole to be understood from the part, whatever is unlawfully taken from a neighbour’s goods—then surely, under the name adultery, every illicit sexual union and every unlawful use of those bodily members must be understood as forbidden.

### Chapter 280.—That penance is not to be imposed on married persons except by mutual consent. Second Council of Arles, chap. 22.

Penance is not to be imposed on married persons except by mutual consent.

### Chapter 281.—On the penance of married persons if they have fallen once. Council of Elvira, chap. 69.

(33, question 4, canon *Poenitentiam*.) If a man who has a wife falls once, it has been resolved that he must perform penance for five years.

Likewise, in the same place. The same is to be observed concerning women.

### Chapter 282.—On the penance of one who, having a wife, has sinned with a Jewish woman or a gentile woman, chap. 78.

If any believer who has a wife commits adultery with a Jewish woman or a gentile woman, he shall be excluded from communion. But if another exposes him, after five years of lawful penance he may be admitted to the Lord’s communion.

### Chapter 283.—What should be done concerning clergy’s wives if they sin. From the First Council of Toledo, chap. 7.

(33, question 2, canon *Placuit ut si quor.*) It has been resolved that if any wives of clerics sin—lest perhaps they have greater license for sin—their husbands shall have this authority, short of killing them: to keep and bind them in their own houses, compelling them to salutary, not deadly, fasts. Thus poor clerics are to assist one another if they lack servants. Clerics who sin with those wives themselves are not even to take food with them, unless perhaps, after penance has been performed, they return through fear of God.

### Chapter 284.—On the penance of laypersons if they commit adultery. Canons of Martin for laypersons, chap. 8 (from the Greek synods, Martin of Braga, canon 76 in general; canon 8 among those for laypersons).

If anyone’s wife commits adultery, or if a man assaults another man’s wife, he shall perform penance for seven years. And the Council of Ancyra, chap. 19: If anyone’s wife has committed adultery, or if he himself has committed adultery, he must attain completion through seven years of penance, according to the former stages.

### Chapter 285.—On the penance of clerics if they have defiled themselves by adultery. Third Synod of Orléans, in the time of King Childebert, chap. 7.

(Dist. 81, c. *Si quis clericus*.) If any cleric has committed adultery, whether he has confessed it or been convicted, he shall be deposed from his office; communion having been granted to him, he shall be confined in a monastery for the whole period of his life. [Col. 0646C]

### CHAPTER 286.—If clerics marry without consulting their bishop. Fourth Council of Toledo, ch. 43.

Clerics who, without consulting their bishop, have taken wives, or have taken in marriage a widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute, must be separated by their own bishop.

### CHAPTER 287.—That a bigamist may not enter holy orders. Apostolic Canons, ch. 22.

(Dist. 33, c. *Si quis post*.) If anyone, after baptism, has been joined in a second marriage or has kept a concubine, he cannot be a bishop, presbyter, or deacon—indeed, cannot belong at all to the number of those who serve in the sacred ministry.

### CHAPTER 288.—On the same matter: Gregory to John, bishop of Squillace (*Register*, book II, ch. 25).

[Col. 0646D]

(Dist. 34, c. *Praecipimus*.) We command that you never perform unlawful ordinations: do not allow a bigamist, or one who has not obtained a virgin as wife, or one ignorant of letters, or one defective in any part of his body, a penitent, or a person subject to any condition, to enter holy orders. If you find persons of this kind, do not dare to promote them.

### CHAPTER 289.—Likewise on the same matter. Gregory to Etherius, bishop (book II, epistle 8, to Brunhild).

You asked concerning a certain bigamist whether he could enter a sacred order; and in accordance with the canonical rule we forbade it.

### CHAPTER 290.—On the same matter. Ambrose, in the Letter to the Church of Vercelli (book X, epistle 82, after the middle).

[Col. 0647A]

(Dist. 36, c. *Qui sine crimine*.) He who is without reproach, the husband of one wife, is bound by the law governing the reception of the priesthood. But one who has repeated marriage has indeed incurred no fault of defilement, yet is stripped of the priestly prerogative. Likewise, after the verse: Let us recognize that the Apostle laid this down not only concerning a bishop and presbyter, but that the Fathers also added in the deliberation of the Council of Nicaea that no one ought to be a cleric who has entered into second marriages.

### CHAPTER 291.—That a bigamist before baptism may not enter holy orders. Ambrose, *On Duties*, book I (final chapter).

(Dist. 16, c. *Una tantum*.) Only one union, and not a repeated one, is permitted to us. Even in marriage itself there is a law: not to repeat marriage, nor to enter into the union of a second spouse. To many it seems strange why marriages repeated even before baptism create impediments to election to office and to the prerogative of ordination, when even offences are not ordinarily an obstacle if they have been remitted by the sacrament of the washing. But we must understand that, although guilt can be forgiven in baptism, the law cannot be abolished. In marriage there is not guilt but law. What belongs to guilt, therefore, is relaxed in baptism; what belongs to law is not dissolved in marriage. For how can one be an exhorter to widowhood who has himself repeatedly contracted marriages? [Col. 0647B]

### CHAPTER 292.—A literal and mystical exposition of the meaning of “the husband of one wife.” Ambrose’s *Pastoral Work* (*On Priestly Dignity*, ch. 4, beginning).

[Col. 0647C]

“The husband of one wife” (1 Tim. 3). If we look only at the surface of the letter, it forbids the ordination of a bigamist as bishop. But if we ascend to the higher sense, it forbids a bishop to appropriate two Churches. And if you search still further inward, into deeper matters, it warns that no bishop be found, under the meaning of Catholic doctrine, to have heretical belief; rather, he should associate with himself only Christian, Catholic, and orthodox faith, and [“so that” (*ut*) in the original] be called the husband of one wife only—namely, of the one Catholic Church.

### CHAPTER 293.—That bigamists or husbands of widows may not remain in the priesthood. Leo to all bishops throughout Africa, ch. 1 (epistle 87, to the African bishops, ch. 1).

[Col. 0647D] We do not permit those who have either entered into second marriages or joined themselves in marriage to widows to remain in the priesthood. And still more do we decree that the man, if he has been convicted in your judgment, who—as has been reported to us—is simultaneously the husband of two wives, or the man said to have taken another wife after dismissing his first, must be deprived of his honour.

### CHAPTER 294.—That a bishop must be the husband of one wife, not because of the sanctity of the sacrament. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage* (ch. 18).

The sacrament of marriage in our time has been reduced to one husband and one wife, so that it is not lawful to ordain as a steward of the Church anyone except the husband of one wife (1 Tim. 3). (Dist. 26, c. *Acutius*.) This was understood more keenly by those who judged that even a man who, while a catechumen or pagan, had had another wife should not be ordained. For the issue is the sacrament, not sin: for all sins are forgiven in baptism. But he who said, “If you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she does not sin” (1 Cor. 7), and, “Let her do what she wishes; she does not sin if she marries” (ibid.), sufficiently declared that marriage is no sin. Yet because of the sanctity of the sacrament, just as a woman—even if she was violated while a catechumen—cannot after baptism be consecrated among God’s virgins, so it did not seem unreasonable that a man who exceeded the singular number of wives had not committed some sin, but had lost a certain pattern of the sacrament, necessary not for the merit of a good life but for the seal of ecclesiastical ordination. [Col. 0648A]

### CHAPTER 295.—What prevents a person from being promoted to the clergy. Augustine, *On Ecclesiastical Rules*, ch. 72.

[Col. 0648B]

(Dist. 33, c. *Maritum*.) The husband, after baptism, of two married women is not to be ordained a cleric; nor one who had one woman indeed, but a concubine rather than a lawful wife; nor one who took a divorced woman, a prostitute, or a widow; nor one who, overcome by some passion or by just or unjust fear, mutilated himself in any member of his body. Nor is one to be ordained who is convicted of ever having received usury, or proved to have performed on the stage; nor one who laments mortal crimes in public penance; nor one who at any time, turned to frenzy, became insane, or was assailed by an affliction of the devil; nor one who, through ambition, offers money in imitation of Simon Magus in seeking honour (Acts 8). [Col. 0648C]

### CHAPTER 296.—On the same matter. Jerome to Oceanus (volume II, letter beginning: *Sophronius, Eusebius*).

If a cleric is monogamous but his wife is digamous, do not appoint him to office: for he has taken a digamous wife.

### CHAPTER 297.—What a widow, a repudiated woman, and a prostitute are. Jerome to Fabiola, *On the Priestly Garment* (vol. IV, letter beginning: *Usque hodie*, before the middle).

(Dist. 34, c. *Vidua est*.) A widow is one whose husband has died. A repudiated woman is one cast out while her husband lives. A prostitute is one open to the lust of many.

### CHAPTER 298.—That a digamist is not chosen for the clergy. Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, book I (vol. II, long before the middle).

[Col. 0648D]

How holy digamy is may be shown from this: a digamist cannot be chosen for the clergy.

### CHAPTER 299.—On the same matter. Jerome to Geruntia, *On Monogamy* (vol. I, letter beginning: *In veteri via*, before the middle).

We think this to be a privilege of priests alone: that no one is admitted to the altar except one who has had only one wife. For a digamist is excluded not only from the office of priesthood, but also from the alms of the Church, since she who has gone on to a second marriage is unworthy of the Church’s contribution. Yet even a layman is bound by the priestly law, since he must present himself such that he can be chosen for the priesthood; for he is not chosen if he is a digamist. Moreover, priests are chosen from the laity. [Col. 0649A]

### CHAPTER 300.—That a priest is to be chosen either monogamous or virgin. Isidore, book II, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, ch. 5.

The Church seeks a priest either ordained from monogamy or holy from virginity.

### CHAPTER 301.—The penalty for a bishop who promotes a bigamist to holy orders. Third Council of Orléans, in the time of King Childebert, ch. 10.

If any bishop knowingly presumes to promote either a bigamist or the husband of a woman previously married to the office of Levitical dignity or the presbyterate, contrary to canonical law, let him know that he is suspended from every dignity of priesthood for one year. If he should perhaps refuse to submit to the sentence, let the whole brotherhood suspend itself from communion with him until another synod. But those who were unlawfully promoted shall be reduced from their rank. [Col. 0649B]

### CHAPTER 302.—That one who has married a widow cannot be promoted. Innocent to Felix, bishop of Nuceria (epistle 4, ch. 2).

Concerning digamists, consultation ought not even to have been necessary, since the Apostle’s reading is manifest: “the husband of one wife” (1 Tim. 3) ought to be admitted to the priesthood or clergy, and that wife herself must have been taken as a virgin. For a woman who had a husband before, even though he is dead, if she has been joined to a cleric, then the cleric who took her cannot thereafter be a cleric. For the law provides that a priest cannot have a repudiated woman as wife (Lev. 21).

### CHAPTER 303.—That one who had one wife before baptism and afterwards took another may not be promoted. Innocent to Rufus, Eusebius, and the other Macedonian bishops (epistle 22, ch. 1).

[Col. 0649C]

I have learned that those said to have taken widows have not only become clerics, but have even attained to the mitres of the highest priesthood—something which no one is ignorant is contrary to the commandments of the law. For when Moses the lawgiver cries aloud, “Let the priest take a virgin as wife” (Lev. 21), and lest anything in this command should be thought ambiguous, he added, “not a widow, nor a repudiated woman.” Against this command, supported by divine authority, no defence based upon another rule can be set aside [“opposed” in the original]—except your custom, which, as you yourselves confess, has arisen from ignorance, not, to speak more modestly, from apostolic tradition and reason.

But let your charity know that we, and all the Churches throughout East and West, admit no such persons whatever, do not accept them even into the lowest place of ecclesiastical order, and remove them if they are found. (Ibid., ch. 2; Dist. 26, c. *Deinde*.) It is then asserted that a person should not be called a digamist if, while a catechumen, he had and lost a wife, and after baptism obtained another; and that she should be considered the first wife who was joined to the new man, because the former marriage was washed away with the other sins by the sacrament of baptism.

But when this is said concerning one wife, then certainly, if while still the old man he had had three wives, the woman who is fourth after baptism will be his wife, and, under this interpretation, she who is taken in the fourth place will receive the title of first—and likewise the designation of a virgin [*virginis aeque nomen*, original reading]. [Col. 0649D–0650A] Who, I ask, does not see that this is contrary to the Apostle’s command, who says that a priest must be the husband of one wife? (1 Tim. 3.)

But it is objected that in baptism whatever has occurred in a person is wholly washed away. Tell me, I speak with your forbearance: are only sins forgiven in baptism, or are things also forgiven which are fulfilled according to God’s commands and institutions? Is taking a wife a sin, or is it not a sin? If it is a sin, then—may I say it with the aforesaid indulgence—the Author himself is at fault, who, when he joined them in Paradise, blessed them so that sins might be committed (Gen. 2). But if it is not a sin, because it would be wicked to call sinful what God instituted—and Solomon added, “For a wife is prepared for a man by God” (Prov. 19)—how can what is read to have been completed by God as its author be believed to have been forgiven among sins? [Col. 0650B]

What is to be decided concerning the children of such persons? (28, q. 1, c. *Nunquid*.) Shall they not be admitted to share in the inheritance because they were begotten from a woman who was a wife before baptism? Shall they be called natural children because, in your opinion, no marriage is lawful except that contracted after baptism? When the Lord himself was asked by the Jews whether it was lawful to put away a wife, and explained that it ought not to be done, he added, “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19). And lest he be thought to have spoken of those who obtain wives after baptism, let them remember that he was questioned by Jews and answered Jews.

I ask, and ask earnestly: if one and the same woman is the wife of a man who was first a catechumen and later a believer, and he had children by her while a catechumen and other children afterwards when a believer, are they to be called brothers, or are they to have no share in the inheritance after their father’s death, since spiritual rebirth is said to have taken from them the name of sons? Since it is absurd to judge and think thus, what reason is there for defending this evil and vaunting a baseless opinion rather than strengthening it by any authority, when that which the law commanded, God joined, and the law joins could not be counted among sins? [Col. 0650C]

Likewise (ibid., shortly afterwards): Because the union of marriage is brought about by God’s command, it cannot be called sin; and what is not sin, and ought not at all to be counted among sins, remains whole. One must judge that the designation of a former wife cannot be abolished, since it was not remitted as sin, because it was completed by God’s will. [Col. 0650D]

### CHAPTER 304.—That one commits procuring who keeps slaves employed for gain. Fourth book of the *Digest*, title 2.

One commits procuring who keeps slaves employed for gain. But one who carries on this trade with free persons is in the same position, whether he conducts this business principally or uses it as an adjunct to another occupation. Thus, for example, if he is an innkeeper or stable-keeper and has such slaves serving there, who make gain through the opportunity of their service; or if he is a bathhouse keeper, or—as occurs in certain provinces—keeps hired slaves in the baths to watch clothing.

### CHAPTER 305.—That procurers may not exist in cities. Constitution 31 of the *Novels*, ch. 1.

[Col. 0651A]

This constitution commands that no one be a procurer, either in the imperial city or in the provinces; and praetors and provincial governors must enforce this prohibition. Those who have dared to be procurers contrary to the rule of the constitution are nevertheless subjected to the ultimate penalty. The constitution further commands that all instruments and surety agreements made with procurers, or made by procurers, contrary to good morals, are void and invalid.

### CHAPTER 306.—That a woman who has sold her own body or another’s may not receive communion even at the end. Council of Elvira, ch. 12.

A mother, parent, or any believing woman, if she has practised procuring—because she has sold another’s body, or [“rather” (*potius*) in the original] her own—has been judged not to receive communion even at the end. [Col. 0651B]

### CHAPTER 307.—That, in a payment made to a prostitute, the shamefulness belongs to the giver, not the receiver. *Digest*, book XII, title 4.

What is given to a prostitute cannot be recovered, as Labeo and Marcellus write, but for a novel reason: namely, not because the shamefulness belongs to both parties, but to the giver alone. For it is shameful for her to act as a prostitute, but not shameful for her, being a prostitute, to receive payment.

### CHAPTER 308.—That one joined to a prostitute becomes one body. Ambrose on the First Epistle to the Corinthians (on ch. 6; after the middle).

He who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body. He says this because one who joins himself to defilement becomes one with that to which he joins himself. For fornication makes both one, so that, as they are one in nature, so too they are one in stain. [Col. 0651C]

### CHAPTER 309.—On the correction of a certain bishop who sided with prostitutes. Honorius to Peter, bishop of Syracuse.

We have learned from the report of certain persons that your brotherhood involves itself in criminal cases, and that it is undoubtedly compelled to know, not merely from reading but also from daily practice itself, what is forbidden by the sacred canons. For we have likewise heard that it acted with equal imprudence in this matter: when more than three hundred prostitutes, at an hour when the time for the midday meal had nearly passed, proceeded with it to our most eminent son, the prefect, in the newly established bathhouse; and it stood in a crowd, pressing him with the pestilential cries of the aforesaid women of evil life, that the man who had previously been appointed their curator should be removed from them by every means, and another substituted in his place.

If this is so, it seemed preferable to weep rather than to correct these things. Yet lest so grave and enormous an outrage should seem to remain unpunished for long—since what was done was contrary both to the priestly office and to the manner of life—we have charged our son Cyriacus, the deacon, once the truth has been made known, to ensure that acts committed unlawfully and against the reverence due to modesty are cut off at the root by the canonical sword, according to ecclesiastical discipline. [Col. 0651D]

### CHAPTER 310.—That fornication after the Gospel is greater than under the Law. Jerome on Joshua, homily 5 (Origen, on Joshua, book V, homily 5, translated by Jerome, or rather by Rufinus).

[Col. 0652A]

He who fornicates after the Gospel is guilty of far greater disgrace than he who does so under the Law, because the former takes away the members of Christ and makes them members of a prostitute. Thus no one now accuses you merely as guilty of sexual violation, but condemns you for the crime of sacrilege.

### CHAPTER 311.—On the prohibition of prostitutes. Augustine, book of *Questions on Deuteronomy*, ch. 37 (ch. 23, book VII of the *Questions*).

(32, q. 4, c. *Meretrices*.) The Lord forbids both the existence of prostitutes and resort to prostitutes, whose shamefulness is publicly for sale. Yet in the Decalogue he does not seem to have expressly forbidden this under the name of adultery, since *moechia* is ordinarily understood to mean adultery alone. [Col. 0652B]

### CHAPTER 312.—On the penalty for a woman who secretly conceives after her husband’s death. Constitution 38 of the *Novels*, ch. 2.

If, after her husband’s death and before the lawful year has elapsed, a woman does not enter a second marriage, but, in the manner of prostitutes, is violated by someone, conceives, and gives birth—so that it is clear that what has been born is not the child of the deceased husband—she shall suffer the same penalties which, under the preceding constitution, are suffered by the woman who contracts a second marriage before the lawful time.

### CHAPTER 313.—That one joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her. Augustine, Sermon on the Three Charities, beginning, *De charitate nobis* (Sermon 52 *On Time*).

[Col. 0652C] “Do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute is one body?” (1 Cor. 6). And he gave testimony from Scripture, where it is written: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2). This was spoken by God, but concerning husband and wife—where it is permitted, allowed, and honourable—not where it is shameful, unlawful, and condemnable in every respect. But as one flesh is made in the lawful union of husband and wife, so one flesh is made in the unlawful union of a prostitute and her lover.

Likewise, somewhat later: Those who have no wives are, as it were, more unrestricted lovers of prostitutes. I said “as it were,” because they too are condemned if they are now believers.

### CHAPTER 314.—On women who, having committed fornication, kill their offspring. Ch. 21.

Concerning women who commit fornication and kill their offspring, and also those who take measures to expel from the womb what has been conceived: the ancient determination excludes them from the Church until the end of life. But we now determine more mercifully that they be assigned a period of ten years of penance. [Col. 0652D]

### CHAPTER 315.—That a presbyter may not attend a second marriage. From the Council of Neocaesarea, which was earlier than Nicaea, ch. 7.

(31, q. 1, c. *De his qui frequenter*.) A presbyter ought not to attend the marriage of persons entering a second marriage, especially since he is required to impose penance for second marriages. What presbyter, then, would approve those marriages for the sake of a banquet?

### CHAPTER 316.—On those who are proud of virginity. From the Council of Gangra, ch. 10.

(Dist. 30, c. *Si quis propter Deum*.) If anyone, because he has professed virginity for God’s sake, arrogantly disparages persons living in marriage, let him be anathema. [Col. 0653A]

### CHAPTER 317.—That a woman may not leave her husband while rejecting marriage. There, ch. 14.

(Dist. 30, c. *Si qua mulier*.) If any woman wishes to leave her husband, dissolving the bond of marriage by despising marriage, let her be anathema.

### CHAPTER 318.—On the same matter, ch. 15.

(Dist. 30, c. *Si quis dereliquerit*.) If anyone abandons his own children, does not feed them, and does not provide what is necessary—as piety requires—but, under the pretext of continence, thinks they ought to be neglected, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER 319.—That children may not despise their parents under the pretext of religion. There, ch. 16.

[Col. 0653B] (Dist. 30, c. *Si qui filii*.) If any children abandon their parents, especially believing parents, under the pretext of worshipping God, judging this to be right, and do not instead render due honour to their parents, so as to reverence in them their being believers, let them be anathema.

### CHAPTER 320.—That a woman’s head ought not to be shorn. Ch. 17.

(Dist. 30, c. *Quaecunque mulier*.) If any woman, judging it appropriate to religion, cuts off her hair (1 Cor. 11), which God gave her as a covering and as a reminder of subjection, as though dissolving the law of subjection, let her be anathema. [Col. 0653C]

### CHAPTER 321.—That no one may be proud because of religious dress or introduce new commandments into the Church. From the same council.

We have written these things (this is the subscription of the bishops in the Council of Gangra, ch. 21), not in order to cut off those who in the Church of God choose, according to the Scriptures, the holy purpose of continence; but to condemn those who assume its dress and are exalted in pride against persons who live more simply. We also condemn those who exalt themselves against the Scriptures and ecclesiastical canons and introduce new commandments.

But we admire virginity with humility; we declare continence with chastity and devotion to be most pleasing to God; we commend the renunciation of worldly business and occupations when joined with humility; we honour the bond of marriage which endures in chastity. We do not reject the rich who have justice and good works; nor do we reject frugality joined with humble clothing, just as we praise adornment that is unpainted and not beyond proper care of the body.

But we do not receive persons lax in dress and affected in their walk. We honour the houses of God and receive the assemblies held in them as holy and useful, without confining piety to private houses. We honour every place built in God’s name and receive a congregation assembled in church for the common benefit. We bless good works performed beyond one’s means among poor brothers in accordance with ecclesiastical traditions; and we desire that all things consistent with apostolic traditions and the commands of the sacred Scriptures be done in the Church. [Col. 0653D–0654A]

### CHAPTER 322.—On those who abduct wives for themselves. From the Council of Chalcedon, ch. 17 (Session 15, ch. 27).

(36, q. 2, c. *Eos qui*.) The holy synod decrees that those who abduct wives for themselves, or those who give them aid, if they are clerics, shall fall from their own rank; but if they are laypersons, they shall be anathema.

### CHAPTER 323.—That a layperson may not teach in the presence of clerics. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, at which Augustine was present, ch. 98.

A layperson may not dare to teach in the presence of clerics unless they themselves request it [“command it” in the original reading]. 

### CHAPTER 324.—That a woman may not teach. There, ch. 99.

(Dist. 23, c. *Mulier*.) A woman, however learned and holy, may not dare to teach men in an assembly.

### CHAPTER 325.—That a woman may not baptize. Ch. 100.

[Col. 0654B]

A woman may not presume to baptize.

### CHAPTER 326.—On young and infirm widows. Ch. 101.

Young widows who are physically weak are to be supported at the expense of the Church of which they are widows.

### CHAPTER 327.—On widows supported by the Church’s stipends. Ch. 103.

(Dist. 81, c. *Viduae*.) Widows supported by the Church’s stipend ought to be so diligent in God’s work that they assist the Church both by their merits and by their prayers.

### CHAPTER 328.—On those who leave their wives without cause. Ch. 25 (Council of Agde, ch. 25).

(33, q. 2, c. *Saeculares*.) Those laypersons who leave or have left the companionship of marriage without any graver fault, and who, proposing no plausible causes of disagreement, abandon their marriages so that they may presume to undertake either unlawful or another’s unions—unless they have first stated the grounds of dispute before the bishops of their province and have dismissed their wives only after judgment, they shall be excluded from the communion of the Church and from the holy assembly of the people, because they defile faith and marriages. [Col. 0654C]

### CHAPTER 329.—On those who leave their wives when divorce occurs. From the Twelfth Council of Toledo, ch. 8.

(32, q. 5, c. *Praeceptum Domini*.) The Lord’s command is that, except for the cause of fornication, a wife ought not to be dismissed by her husband (Matt. 5; 19). Therefore, whoever leaves his wife on any pretext apart from guilt of the aforesaid crime—because he has resolved to separate what God joined—shall remain deprived of ecclesiastical communion and excluded from the assembly of Christian people until he sincerely embraces and cherishes fellowship with his abandoned wife.

Yet those who, having been admonished by the priest once, twice, and three times to amend themselves, refuse to return to fellowship in the marriage-bed of their wives shall, by their own deserts, be separated from the office of palatine dignity; and furthermore, so long as they remain in fault, they shall lose the marks of noble rank, because they have delivered their own flesh to the yoke of discord. [Col. 0654D]

### CHAPTER 330.—That Christian women may not observe anything superstitious in wool-working. From the Council of Pope Martin, ch. 76 (ch. 75 of the Greek synods, Martin, bishop of Braga).

[Col. 0655A]

(26, q. 5, c. *Non liceat Christianis*.) Christian women may not observe any superstition in their wool-working; rather, let them call upon the Lord as helper, who gave them the wisdom of weaving.

### CHAPTER 331.—On women who commit fornication and procure abortion. From the same council, ch. 78 (77).

If any woman commits fornication and then kills the child who has been born, or takes measures to procure abortion and kill what has been conceived, or indeed strives to avoid conceiving, whether through adultery or lawful marriage, earlier canons decreed that such women should not receive communion at death [“not even in death,” another version]. Yet for mercy’s sake we judge that both such women and those who are privy to their crimes should perform penance for ten years. [Col. 0655B]

### CHAPTER 332.—On those married many times. There, ch. 81 (ch. 80).

If anyone has entered into many marriages, let him perform penance; but the manner of his life and the faithfulness of his penitence shorten the period.

### CHAPTER 333.—That the Church has no sword except a spiritual one. Nicholas to Albinus, archbishop (the same passage occurs above, ch. 124).

Among these matters your holiness has sought to add: “If a man’s wife has committed adultery, is it lawful for her husband to kill her according to secular law?” But the holy Church of God is never bound by secular law: it has no sword except a spiritual one; it does not kill, but gives life.

### CHAPTER 334.—On King Lothair and the examination of his case. The same to Radoald, bishop of Porto, and John, bishop of Ficulensis (Appendix, epistle 2).

[Col. 0655C]

(31, q. 2, c. *Lotharius*.) King Lothair declares in his memorandum that he received Waldrada from her father and later took the sister of Hubert. First investigate this with careful inquiry. If you find that the same glorious king received the aforesaid Waldrada, after dower had been given, before witnesses, in accordance with the law and rite by which marriages are customarily celebrated in every respect, and that the same Waldrada was received into his marriage by public declaration, it remains for you to investigate why she was repudiated or the daughter of Boso received.

But because the same glorious king says that he received Theutberga out of fear, recall that evangelical saying in which the Lord declares: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. 10). And again he says: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers loss of his soul?” (Matt. 16.) In these sayings of the Lord it must be considered that, if those who kill the body are not to be feared when they drive a person against justice, and if the gain of the whole world profits nothing when the soul is lost, how much less ought so great a king, through fear of one person, to have plunged into a monstrous precipice contrary to the divine command? In this, certainly, he shows himself the more blameworthy: he set love of the world before love of God.

In this matter we command you nothing else, once the king has been convicted by his own declaration, except that, relying upon our authority, you decide his case according to canonical authority. But if it is not proved that Waldrada was his lawful wife, or that, with the marriage solemnized according to custom, namely by a priest’s blessing, she was joined to our son Lothair, advise him not to take it ill that his lawful wife should be reconciled to him, if she appears innocent. Nor should he obey in this matter the voice of the flesh; rather, obeying the divine commands, he should be ashamed—indeed, fear—to rot in the filth of lust and, by following his own will, to render a strict account before Christ’s tribunal. [Col. 0656A–B]

Furthermore, I want you to know that the aforesaid Theutberga appealed to the Apostolic See twice and three times, and complained that she had been unjustly cast off by the aforesaid glorious king and forced by violence to fabricate a false crime against herself. For at that time she sent to the Apostolic See a written appeal, in which she made known that she had not yet confessed, but was being compelled to utter a false accusation against herself, adding: “If I am compelled further, know that I shall say what they wish—not from truth, but from fear of death and from the desire to escape, because I cannot do otherwise. Yet remember me as I make these things known to you.”

We therefore command you, when the same Theutberga comes to the appointed synod, as we have determined, to investigate her case by careful examination. If it is alleged against her that she confessed herself to have committed some crime, and she in reply proclaims that she suffered violence, or if she testifies that the judges were her enemies, then renew that judgment according to the standard of equity, so that she may not be crushed by the weight of injustice. [Col. 0656C]

## NINTH PART OF THE DECREE. On incestuous unions and fornication of different kinds; on the degree of kinship in which believers ought to be joined or separated; and on the correction and penance of individuals.

[Col. 0655]

### CHAPTER 1.—Between which persons incestuous union, and between which lawful marriages, may take place. First book of the *Institutes*, title ten.

[Col. 0655D]

Marriage cannot be contracted between persons who stand to one another in the place of parent and child: for example, between father and daughter, grandfather and granddaughter, mother and son, grandmother and grandson, and so on without limit. If such persons have intercourse with one another, they are said to have contracted impious and incestuous marriages. This is so true that, although they began to stand to one another in the place of parent and child through adoption, they cannot be joined to one another in marriage; indeed, the same legal position remains even when the adoption has been dissolved.

Therefore, you cannot marry a woman who has become your daughter or granddaughter by adoption, even if you have emancipated her. There is also a similar, though less extensive, restriction between persons joined by collateral kinship. Marriage between brother and sister is certainly forbidden, whether they are born of the same father and mother, or of either one of them. If any woman has become your sister by adoption, then, so long as the adoption remains in force, marriage between you and her certainly cannot stand.

(After a few words.) It is not lawful to marry one’s daughter; nor may anyone marry the granddaughter of a brother or sister, although she is in the fourth degree. For one may not marry the daughter of a person whose granddaughter one is likewise not permitted to marry. But you are not considered barred from marrying the daughter of a woman whom your father adopted, because she is joined to you neither by natural nor civil law. The children of two brothers, of two sisters, or of a brother and sister cannot be joined in marriage.  

> **Note:** [Col. 0657D] From this passage it is possible to restore the section, “But the children of two brothers,” in the *Institutes*, *On Marriage*, a passage which is commonly transmitted in a corrupt form.

Likewise: It is not lawful to marry an aunt by the father’s side, even an adoptive aunt. Likewise, nor may one marry an aunt by the mother’s side, because they stand in the place of parents; for the same reason it is true that one is also forbidden to marry a great-aunt on the father’s side or a great-aunt on the mother’s side.

Out of reverence for affinity, it is also necessary to abstain from marriage with certain persons; for instance, one may not marry a stepdaughter or daughter-in-law, because both stand in the place of daughters. Likewise: the son of a husband by another wife and the daughter of a wife by another husband—or conversely—may rightly contract marriage, even though they have a brother or sister born from a marriage subsequently contracted. If your wife, after divorce, bears a daughter by another man, that daughter is not your stepdaughter.

Likewise, if anyone has intercourse contrary to what we have said, neither husband nor wife nor marriage nor dowry is legally recognized. Accordingly, those born from that intercourse are not under the father’s power, but, so far as paternal power is concerned, are like those whom a mother has conceived promiscuously. For neither are they understood to have a father. Their intercourse is also uncertain; hence they are customarily called *spurii*, or, from the Greek expression **πωραδὴν**, “conceived promiscuously,” as though children without a father (*apatōres*) [**παρὰ τὴν απορὰν**, “from sowing,” and **ἀπατόρες**, “as it were fatherless,” etc., in the original; the Greek is materially corrupt]. It follows, therefore, that when such an union has been dissolved, there is room for recovery of the dowry. [Col. 0656D–0657C]

### CHAPTER 2.—That one who contracts marriage with persons whom one cannot or may not marry is marked with infamy. *Digest*, book III, title II.

[Col. 0657D]

If anyone has contracted marriage or betrothal with a woman whom he either cannot take as wife or is not permitted to take, he shall be marked with infamy.

### CHAPTER 3.—On the penalty for one who contracts an incestuous marriage. Constitution 32 of the *Novels*, ch. 1.

If anyone has contracted a wicked, incestuous, and damnable marriage, but has had no children from a prior lawful marriage, he shall immediately forfeit his property; the dowry given to him shall be claimed for the rights of the treasury. After public proclamation he shall also suffer the loss of his belt [a mark of status], [Col. 0658A] and be punished with exile. If he is of lower rank, he shall undergo bodily interrogation [torture], and his wife, married contrary to the same laws, shall suffer the penalties of the secular law, unless some just ignorance excuses her.

CAP. 4.—That children born from another wife are to receive the property of an incestuous father, ch. 2.

But if he has children, and has contracted incestuous marriages, while those children are legitimate children (because perhaps they were begotten from another marriage), they shall, as a punishment to their father, become legally independent and receive their father’s property; provided, however, that they furnish their father with maintenance and administer what is necessary.

CAP. 5.—That marriage cannot be contracted in the fourth degree. Ambrose, *Paterno*.

You are preparing to unite your son with his niece through your daughter, [Col. 0658B] that is, to have him take his sister’s daughter. Consider the religious significance of the names: surely he is called her maternal uncle (*avunculus*), and she his niece (*neptis*). Likewise (in the same place, a little later): What can possibly be doubted, when divine law even prohibits first cousins from entering into marital union, though they are joined [original: “associated”] to one another in the fourth degree? But this degree is the third, and it too seems excluded from the fellowship of marriage by civil law.

CAP. 6.—How degrees of consanguinity are to be reckoned. Alexander II to the clergy of Naples, ch. 55.

We have learned that even among you there has lately arisen a scruple concerning this much-discussed question of degrees of kinship. We grieve that certain destructive [Col. 0658C] interpreters and disputants have been propounding doctrines contrary to the rule of truth and sound teaching. For, sitting in the seat of pestilence (Psalm 1), they dictate laws which they do not know and teach things which they have never learned.

For, as is reported, they count the generations descending respectively from two brothers in such a way that they declare the sons of the brothers to be the fourth generation in relation to one another, their grandsons the sixth, and their great-grandsons the eighth. Thus they divide each degree of generation—which without doubt ought to be called one degree—and ignorantly attempt to split the line of descent that ought to be counted as a whole. They certainly would not break forth pestilently into the belching of this stench, if they chewed over the nourishment of Holy Scripture with the mouths of a lively intellect.

For the book of Genesis testifies that the generations of two brothers, or of grandsons, or of those thereafter descending on both sides, are not to be called different but are to be designated uniformly by the same single name, when it says: “Joseph lived one hundred and ten years, and saw Ephraim’s children to the third generation. The children also of Machir, son of Manasseh, were born upon Joseph’s knees” (Genesis 50). [Col. 0658D] If kinships were to be counted as your disputants maintain, then, since Joseph had grandsons through both Ephraim and Manasseh, Scripture would not say that he saw Ephraim’s children to the third generation, but to the sixth.

Likewise. (*Response to Augustine’s Sixth Question*.) [Col. 0659A] Blessed Gregory too, writing concerning marriages among the Angles, expressed roughly these words: “A certain law in the Roman commonwealth prescribed [Gregory: ‘permits’] that the son or daughter of two brothers or sisters might be joined in marriage; but it is altogether recognized that offspring cannot increase from this marriage. Therefore it is necessary that four or five generations should now be joined to one another.” In these words it is clearer than light that, although the distinguished teacher forbids the offspring of two brothers to be joined in marriage and permits newly converted Christians to marry in the fourth generation, the fourth generation cannot in any way, as the adherents of the perverse doctrine maintain, be found in the children of two brothers.

CAP. 7.—That consanguinity ends with six branches. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book IX, ch. 6.

[Col. 0659B]

When consanguinity, gradually separating itself through the successive orders of descendants, has withdrawn as far as the final degree and has ceased to be kinship, the law then recalls it again into the bond of marriage, as it were calling back one who has fled. Consanguinity has therefore been fixed as far as the sixth degree of descent, so that, just as the generation and condition of humankind end with the six ages of the world, so kinship of lineage may end with the same number of degrees.

CAP. 8.—Concerning the separation of Robert, king of the Franks, and his wife Bertha. Leo IX to Henry, king of the Franks.

Your father Robert, with the praise and counsel of the bishops of your kingdom, took Bertha, mother of Count Odo, as his wife. Because she was joined to him by kinship of the flesh, he and the bishops who had attended the assembly were [Col. 0659D; perhaps read: “excommunicated”; otherwise the sense is complete] by our predecessor; afterwards, coming to the Apostolic See, they underwent penance and, having made satisfaction, returned to their own places. [Col. 0659C]

CAP. 9.—That no one can purchase exemption by alms so as not to separate kindred persons. Alexander II to Mangiso, bishop of Venice.

Reconsidering the case of this man, concerning which you consulted the Apostolic See—whether he might in some merciful way retain a kinswoman unlawfully joined to him, and redeem himself by prayers, fasts, and lavish gifts of inheritance and alms—we have found no authority by which we could grant him this.

CAP. 10.—Concerning the penance of one who violated his paternal uncle’s daughter. Likewise, Alexander II to Berengar, bishop of Basel, ch. 103.

[Col. 0659D]

This penitent came to us and confessed that he had violated his paternal uncle’s daughter. We imposed on him fourteen years of penance: he is to fast in three forty-day seasons. In the Lent after Pentecost, two days each week on bread and water; in Advent, three days; and in the greater Lent, three days. He is also to abstain from entering church and from communion for two years.

CAP. 11.—That no one may unite himself in marriage with a woman of his own kin. Leo IV to the bishops of Britain.

As the Fathers have decreed, no one may dare to unite himself in marriage with a woman of his own kin; otherwise let him be anathema. Therefore the excellent decrees of blessed Gregory the Younger are to be observed.

> Note [Col. 0660D]: Gregory, Pope II, whose decrees on this matter follow shortly below, chs. 39, 59, 60, 61.

CAP. 12.—How wicked it is for blood relatives to be joined. Nicholas to Bishop Jeremiah.

Those who desire unions of blood relatives ought above all to beware lest they fall into the snare of the devil (1 Timothy 3). How wicked it is to take as wives consecrated women—who, despising marriage in the world, have devoted themselves to Christ—or a female cousin, or a woman from one’s own kinship, is plain to all who remain in the right faith of Christ.

CAP. 13.—On the observance of consanguinity. Likewise, to Archbishop Charles and his suffragans.

You asked in what generation the faithful may unite with one another; but in this matter we do not define [variant: “have not defined”] the number of generations. Rather, as we have stated above, we admonish that it be observed without hesitation. [Col. 0660B]

CAP. 14.—That the measure of guilt is to be treated according to degrees of kinship. Nicholas to Tando, archbishop of Milan.

We decree that those who have perhaps sinned—alas!—with the daughter of their paternal aunt, paternal uncle, or maternal uncle are to have the measure of their guilt treated according to the degrees of kinship, just as we previously informed you in an apostolic letter concerning those who committed this outrage with their spiritual mother.

CAP. 15.—That no one may take a wife from his own kindred. From the synod of Leo IV.

No one shall take as wife a woman of his own kindred, a veiled deaconess, or an abducted woman.

CAP. 16.—How the words “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father and mother” are to be understood. From Book III of Augustine’s *Lectures*, ch. 8 (Augustine, *Questions on Leviticus*, book III, question 58, on ch. 18).

[Col. 0660C]

“You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father and your mother” (Leviticus 18). By this expression Scripture forbade sexual intercourse with these persons, for there lies the nakedness of father and mother.

CAP. 17.—That whoever sees his sister’s nakedness shall be cut off from among his people. Augustine, *Questions on Leviticus*, ch. 75 (ibid., question 75, on Leviticus 19).

Whoever takes his sister by his father or by his mother, and sees her nakedness, it is disgrace—or reproach—and they shall be cut off in the sight of their people. He has uncovered his sister’s nakedness; they shall bear their sin. What does “has seen” mean in this passage, except that he has known her by lying with her, as the Law says: “He knew his wife,” meaning that he had intercourse with her? [Col. 0660D]

CAP. 18.—What is meant by “Children born of kindred persons shall die,” ch. 76 (ibid., following question).

(35, question 7, canon *Quid est*.) What does this mean: “Whoever lies with his kinswoman shall die childless,” when children have been born from such unions in the past and are still born today? Should this be understood as a provision of God’s law that whoever is born from them is not reckoned a child—that is, has no legal right of succession from the parents?

CAP. 19.—That whoever takes his brother’s wife, or a woman whom his kinsman has had, shall be anathema. Decree of Gregory the Younger (First Roman Council under Gregory II, chs. 5, 7, 8, 9).

[Col. 0661A]

If anyone takes his brother’s wife in marriage, let him be anathema. If anyone takes his stepmother or daughter-in-law, let him be anathema. If anyone takes his female cousin, let him be anathema. If anyone takes in marriage a woman of his own kinship, or one whom a kinsman has had, let him be anathema.

CAP. 20.—That Christians are not to unite with one another until they know themselves [to be unrelated]. Pope Zacharias, ch. 1 (Gregory I, *Response to Augustine’s Sixth Question*).

I have learned from persons coming from the regions of Germany, who assert that Pope Gregory of blessed memory, while the grace of God was enlightening them in the religion of Christianity, had given them permission to unite in the fourth generation. This is not lawful for Christians, so long as they know themselves [to be related]. Yet while they were still untrained and were being drawn to the faith, although we find nothing written on this point, we do not doubt it. [Col. 0661B]

CAP. 21.—Which persons may not be taken in marriage on account of agnation, ch. 5.

No one shall dare to unite to himself in marriage a female cousin, niece, stepmother, brother’s wife, a woman of his own kinship, or a woman whom his kinsman has had. If anyone enters such a wicked marriage and remains in it, let him know that, by apostolic authority, he is bound with the bonds of anathema, and no priest shall give him communion. But if he has repented and separated himself from such a union, let him submit to suitable penance, as the priest of the place shall judge. [Col. 0661C]

CAP. 22.—That those who take blood relatives as wives are called accursed and infamous. Pope Callixtus to the bishops of Gaul, ch. 4 (*Letter 2 to the Bishops of Gaul*).

Unions of blood relatives are forbidden, because both divine and secular laws prohibit them. In acting thus, the divine laws not only cast out those who arise from such unions, but also call them accursed. Secular laws call such people infamous and exclude them from inheritance. We, following our Fathers, mark them with infamy and judge them infamous, because they are stained with the blotches of disgrace. Nor ought we to admit as witnesses men whom secular laws reject, or their accusations.

A little later: We call those persons blood relatives whom divine, imperial, Roman, and Greek laws call blood relatives, and whom they admit to inheritance and cannot exclude. The unions of such persons are neither lawful nor able to endure, but must be rejected. [Col. 0661D]

CAP. 23.—That the infamy of incestuous persons cannot be erased, though their sins can be. Likewise, ch. 5.

Whoever is not lawfully joined, or is known to be coupled without a dowry instrument and the blessing of a priest, cannot accuse priests or persons lawfully joined, or bear testimony against them. For everyone defiled by the stain of incest is infamous and is not permitted to accuse the persons mentioned above. Therefore not only such persons are to be rejected and declared infamous, but also all who consent to them.

We judge similarly concerning abductors and those who attack their superiors. Secular laws put these persons to death; but we, with mercy leading the way, receive them to penance under the mark of infamy. We cannot erase the infamy with which they are stained, but we desire to heal their souls through public penance and satisfaction to the Church, because manifest sins are not to be cleansed by a hidden correction. [Col. 0662A]

CAP. 24.—On the ten-year penance of those who consent to incestuous persons. Council of Ancyra, ch. 24.

A certain man who had a fiancée violated her sister and made her pregnant; afterward he took the fiancée as his wife. But the woman who had been violated killed herself with a noose. Those who had known of this were ordered to be received after ten years’ satisfaction, according to the established stages of penance. [Col. 0662B]

CAP. 25.—Who are incestuous persons. From the Council of Agde, ch. 6 (Council of Epaone, ch. 30, and Third Council of Arles, ch. 2).

(35, questions 2 and 3, canon *De incestis conjunctionibus*.) We judge that the following are incestuous persons [variant: “incestuous”], not to be regarded under any name of marriage—persons whom it is ominous even to specify: anyone who defiles his deceased brother’s wife by carnal union; anyone who takes his own sister as wife; anyone who takes his stepmother; anyone who joins himself to his female cousin; anyone who has intercourse with the widow or daughter of his maternal uncle, or with the daughter of his paternal uncle, or with his own stepdaughter; or anyone who defiles by intercourse or takes as wife any woman from his own consanguinity, or one whom his blood relative has had.

Likewise, in the same chapter: Those to whom an unlawful union is forbidden shall have freedom to enter into a better marriage. [Col. 0662C]

CAP. 26.—That the faithful ought not to be joined until the seventh generation. Gregory to Bishop Felix (book XII, letter 31 or 32).

(35, questions 2 and 3, canon *Progeniem*.)
