We decree that every person among those faithfully instructed and now standing firm, planted with a secure root, shall observe his line of descent to the seventh generation; and, so long as they recognize themselves as near by affinity, they must not presume to enter into partnership in this union. Nor is it or shall it ever be lawful for any Christian to take in marriage a woman whom someone from his own consanguinity has had as wife or defiled by any unlawful intercourse, because such intercourse is incestuous and abominable to God and to all good people. [Col. 0662D] We read that the holy Fathers long ago decreed that incestuous persons are not to be regarded under any name of marriage.

CAP. 27.—That two brothers may lawfully take two sisters as wives. Bede, *History of the English*, ch. 34; and Augustine’s fifth question (Bede, book I, ch. 27).

Whether two full brothers ought to take as wives two sisters who are descended from them by a remote line. Gregory’s answer: This is lawful in every respect. For nothing is found in the sacred writings that appears to contradict this provision.

CAP. 28.—That intercourse with a stepmother is a great crime, ch. 37. Gregory answers Augustine (Gregory, same place, ch. 6).

Intercourse with a stepmother is a grave crime, because it is written in the Law: “You shall not uncover your father’s nakedness” (Leviticus 18). A son cannot indeed uncover his father’s nakedness; but because it is written, “The two shall become one flesh” (Genesis 2), he who presumes to uncover the nakedness of his stepmother—who was one flesh with his father—certainly uncovers his father’s nakedness. Intercourse with a female kinswoman is also forbidden, because through the prior union [variant: “wife”] she has become the flesh of one’s brother. For this cause John the Baptist was also beheaded (Matthew 14) and completed [original: “was crowned by”] holy martyrdom. [Col. 0663A]

CAP. 29.—That no Christian may even eat with those who defile themselves by incestuous intercourse. Council of Lleida, ch. 4.

It has been decided that those who defile themselves by incestuous intercourse, so long as they persist in that detestable and unlawful carnal cohabitation, are to be admitted to church only as far as the Mass of the Catechumens. No Christian ought to take any food with them, as the Apostle commanded (1 Corinthians 5). [Col. 0663B]

CAP. 30.—That the same judgment concerning consanguinity in the maternal line is to be held as in the paternal. Nicholas to Charles, archbishop of Mainz.

Concerning the nearness and union of consanguinity, which you say occurs among you and which we judge unlawful: we hold concerning the maternal line what we hold concerning the paternal, and in every way forbid such a union to both.

CAP. 31.—That, after worthy penance, incestuous persons may marry, lest they be overwhelmed. Nicholas to Archbishop Charles and his suffragans (in the rescript, title XVII, ch. 5; Council of Worms, ch. 33).

[Col. 0663C] (33, question 2, canon *Si quis cum*.) If anyone has committed fornication with two sisters, or with those persons concerning whom Holy Scripture issues a prohibition, and has performed worthy penance but has not been able to sustain continence in chastity, he may take a lawful wife in marriage. Likewise, a woman who has fallen into such a crime may do so, lest she be led into the abyss of fornication. But we decree this only concerning laymen and laywomen.

CAP. 32.—That a marriage is not to be dissolved on the pretext of consanguinity. Alexander II to William of Monasteriolo [Gratian reads *Monstrolico*].

(35, question 6, canon *Multorum*.) We have learned from the report of many that you wish to cast off your lawful wife and attach yourself [Col. 0663D] to another, alleging consanguinity as a pretext. Therefore, by apostolic authority we command and forbid you in any way to presume to dismiss the wife whom you now have or to take another, until a council of devout bishops has examined this case.

CAP. 33.—That a marriage is not to be dissolved for consanguinity unless proved by oath. Urban II to Cyriacus, bishop of Genoa [Gratian has: Richard, bishop of Genoa].

(35, question 6, canon *Notificamus*.) We notify you that, if three or two of the nearer relatives of the deceased or living wife of the man accused affirm this relationship by oath, or if three or two of the older men of Genoa to whom this relationship is known—men of good reputation and truthful testimony—confirm the consanguinity in the manner stated above, free from affection, fear, payment, and every evil motive, the marriage shall be dissolved without any delay. [Col. 0664A] But if relatives or outsiders merely attest the relationship in words and either refuse or are unable to prove it by oath, the marriage shall in no way be dissolved; rather, appropriate penance shall be imposed because of the disgrace or stain of sin, if perhaps they contracted some such guilt in this matter.

CAP. 34.—That there is spiritual kinship between a godfather and godchild. Nicholas’s answer to the inquiries of the Bulgarians, ch. 3.

(30, question, canon *Ita*.) A person ought to love one who receives him from the sacred font as a father. For between spiritual fathers and sons there is a gratuitous and holy [variant: “grace”; thus the text reads: “Likewise there is between spiritual brothers and sons a gratuitous and holy …”] communion, which must not be called consanguinity but rather regarded as spiritual proximity. Therefore we judge that no marital union whatsoever can exist between them, since the venerable Roman laws permit no marriage between those who are children by nature and those who are children by adoption.

Likewise: If marriage is not contracted between persons joined by adoption, how much more ought those whom regeneration through the heavenly sacrament of the Holy Spirit binds together to refrain from carnal cohabitation with one another? Thus the one whom divine grace chose to be my father’s son or my brother is called my father’s son or my brother with far greater propriety than one whom human will chose to be his son or my brother; [Col. 0664C] and we are more wisely kept apart from mutual sexual intercourse.

CAP. 35.—That, when his wife has died, no one may take her godmother as wife. The same, to Solomon, bishop of Constance (in the rescript, title XIX, ch. 4).

(30, question 4, canon *Sciscitatur*.) Your Holiness asks us whether any man may have two spiritual co-godmothers, one after the other. In this matter your brotherhood ought to remember what is written: “The two shall become one flesh” (Genesis 2). Since it is established that husband and wife become one flesh through marriage, it follows that a man becomes godfather to the woman whose godmother his wife, taken in marriage, was held to be. It is therefore clear that a man cannot be joined in union with the woman who was godmother to the woman with whom he himself became one flesh. [Col. 0664D]

CAP. 36.—That no one may take his goddaughter or co-godmother as wife. The same, to Archbishop Charles and his suffragans (ibid., ch. 5; Council of Worms, ch. 34).

(33, question 2, canon *Si quis*.) If anyone has committed fornication with a spiritual mother [variant: “co-godmother”], he is struck with the blows of anathema, as you know. Likewise we decree that he too shall be struck who commits the crime of fornication with the woman whom he received from the sacred font of baptism, or with her whom he held before the bishop when she was anointed with holy chrism; nevertheless, if he has a lawful wife, he shall not be compelled to dismiss her.

CAP. 37.—Concerning a man who took as wife a kinswoman of his concubine, betrothed to another. Alexander II to Constantine, bishop of Arezzo.

[Col. 0665A]

You wrote that a son of your Church had taken as his wife a kinswoman in the fourth degree of his concubine, namely a woman betrothed to another. For her fiancé had sworn, as you assert, to take her in marriage; and the incestuous man had also sworn to keep her in fornication. Likewise, below: Supported by apostolic authority, we have advised you in judgment that the betrothed woman be granted to her own fiancé, namely, the man joined to her by no bond of consanguinity. For it is more merciful to pardon the penalty of perjury which one incurs in order to avoid sins than the penalty of perjury together with persistence in crime or wrongdoing.

Finally, this sinner is marked by three crimes: perjury, adultery, and incest. By perjury, because he rashly presumed to swear, without the judgment of parents or judges, to observe what he could not lawfully observe. By adultery, because, while the bridegroom was alive, he coveted and seduced another man’s betrothed. By incest, because, contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, he does not fear to mingle blood with blood more closely than is permitted. [Col. 0665B] Likewise, below: You know what the sacred canons have decreed concerning such a man: if he is a layman, he is not to be promoted to the clergy; if a cleric, he is not to advance further.

CAP. 38.—That a woman contracts affinity with all the relatives of her husband. From a letter of Gregory.

(35, question 10, canon *Fraternitatis*.) Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to Venerius of Cagliari. Beloved brother, I offer due thanks to the diligent discernment of your brotherhood, because you asked what you ought to have asked and thereby gave me pleasure. I therefore answer your inquiries calmly.

You resolved to consult the Apostolic See whether a woman joined by the marital bond to a man unrelated to her belongs to his kindred; whether, if he dies, the kinship remains the same; whether the terms of kinship are dissolved under another husband; and whether offspring received [born] may lawfully enter into union with the kindred of the former husband.

For the word of the Lord is mighty and strong; it is enduring, permanent, and unchangeable—not momentary or passing. Truth itself, who is God and the Word of God, says: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matthew 24). Before God appeared among human beings in the flesh, Adam, inspired by him, said: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother, shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh” (Genesis 2). The Lord did not contradict him.

Then, when truth sprang from the earth into the earth (Psalm 84), and the visible [variant: “invisible”] appeared in humanity, he was asked whether it was lawful for a man to dismiss his wife (Matthew 19). Forbidding this, he prohibited it except where fornication alone had excluded the marital bond. He therefore immediately brought forward that same statement which, as the Word abiding with the Father before the ages, he had inspired in Adam; and he himself confirmed what man had at once uttered: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh” (Genesis 2). [Col. 0666A]

If they become one flesh, how can a relative of either belong to one without belonging to the other? This must be believed impossible. For when one dies, affinity is not erased in the survivor; nor can another marital union dissolve the affinity of the former union. Nor does it seem right that offspring of the second union should pass into participation in that former affinity, because the word of the Lord is mighty and strong. As the Prophet says: “The word of the Lord remains for ever” (Isaiah 40). And another prophet: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. He established them for age and for age of ages; he gave a command, and it shall not pass away” (Psalm 148). [Col. 0666B]

For by his word and command he can make two—male and female—into one flesh; and he has not ceased to make with himself one an innumerable multitude of both sexes, as Truth himself said: “I pray not for these alone, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they too may be one in us” (John 17).

Therefore, whoever with rash and sacrilegious boldness seeks kinship in one who has died, or seeks under another husband to dissolve the terms of affinity, or believes that offspring received from another union may lawfully be joined to the former affinity, denies that God’s word is mighty and strong. And whoever seeks to dissolve it so easily or so quickly does not believe that the word of the Lord remains for ever.

“Take earth from four places separated by a great distance, and imagine it made and glued together into a body of whatever shape or vastness you wish,” etc.

> Note [Col. 0665D]: What follows may be found in Gratian.

CAP. 39.—That no one may take a wife from his own kindred. From the Council of Worms, ch. 11 (ch. 32).

(35, question 3, canon *In copulatione*.) In unions of the faithful we do not define the number of generations; but we decree that no Christian may take a wife from his own consanguinity or kinship, for as long as the generation is remembered, known, or retained in memory. [Col. 0666C]

CAP. 40.—Concerning incestuous persons. From the Council of Agde, ch. 61 (from the Council of Epaone, ch. 30).

(35, question 2, canon *De incestis*.) We reserve absolutely no pardon for incestuous unions unless they cure the adultery by separation. If they refuse to cure it, let them be anathematized.

CAP. 41.—Likewise, on the same matter.

> Note [Col. 0666D]: Gratian attributes this to the Council of Orléans.

(35, question 8, canon *Incestuosi*.) So long as incestuous persons remain in that detestable and unspeakable crime, they are not to be counted among faithful Christians but among pagans or catechumens. That is, Christians are not to eat or drink with them; they are to do this alone, and Christians are neither to kiss nor greet them. But if they prove disobedient to their priests and refuse to separate themselves from so unspeakable a crime and return to public penance, they are to be counted among those endangered by an unclean spirit, or even among those of whom Truth himself said: “If he does not listen to you, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector” (Matthew 18). [Col. 0667A] If one of them is taken first [by death], the other, for as long as he or she lives, shall do severe penance and remain without hope of marriage.

CAP. 42.—That none of the faithful may approach a near blood relative. From the Eleventh Council of Toledo, ch. 5 (Second Council of Toledo, ch. 5).

For we also decree this salutary precaution: that no believer, so long as he recognizes through succession of descent the outlines of affinity, should desire to unite in marriage with a near relative by blood. For it is written: “No person shall approach a near relative by blood, to uncover her nakedness” (Leviticus 18). And again: “The person who does any of these things shall perish from the midst of his people” (ibid.). Those to whom an unlawful union is forbidden shall, however, have freedom to enter into a better marriage. [Col. 0667B]

CAP. 43.—That a man is equally not to be joined in marriage to his own blood relatives and to those of his wife. From the decrees of Pope Julius.

(35, question 2, canon *Aequaliter*.) A man is equally not to be joined in marriage to his own blood relatives and to the blood relatives of his wife.

CAP. 44.—That the kinship of husband and wife must be considered in the same way in respect of marriage. From the Council of Mâcon, ch. 3 (Second Council of Chalon, ch. 29).

The consanguinity to be observed in respect of a man himself must likewise be preserved under the law of marriage in his wife’s kinship; and, because it is established that the two were one flesh, each kinship must be regarded as common to both, as it is written: “The two shall become one flesh” (Genesis 2). [Col. 0667C]

CAP. 45.—At what degree abstinence is required. From the writings of Isidore (*Etymologies*, book IX, ch. 6).

Isidore in his *Etymologies* maintained that one must abstain because of consanguinity as far as the seventh generation, and thereafter enter into lawful marriage. I believe he did this because, tracing the series of genealogy, he judged that blood kinship was to be observed as far as the order of counting could be carried; and thus, for the restoration of lineage and the confirmation of the law of friendship, he decreed a return to marriage when the order of kinship ceases to be countable. [Col. 0667D]

CAP. 46.—On what branch of consanguinity lawful marriages may be contracted. From the writings of the same author (ibid., ch. 5).

(35, questions 4 and 5, canons *Series* and *Consanguinitas*.) Blessed Isidore speaks thus concerning consanguinity, whose series is divided into seven degrees:

Let son and daughter—that is, brother and sister—be the trunk itself. Once they are separately divided, these little branches emerge from the root of that trunk: grandson and granddaughter, the first; great-grandson and great-granddaughter, the second; great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter, the third; great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-granddaughter, the fourth; great-great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-great-granddaughter, the fifth; the grandson of a great-great-great-great-grandson, and the granddaughter of a great-great-great-great-granddaughter, the sixth.

[Col. 0668A] (Same place, ch. 6.) When this consanguinity, gradually separating itself in the orders of descendants, has withdrawn as far as the final degree and has ceased to be kinship, only then is it received by the law into the bond of marriage and, as it were, recalled after fleeing. Consanguinity was therefore fixed as far as the sixth degree of descent, so that, just as the generation and condition of humankind end in the six ages of the world, so kinship of lineage may end with the same number of degrees.

CAP. 47.—That consanguinity must be observed to the seventh degree. Council held at the estate of Theodonis, ch. 8.

No believer shall take his blood relative as wife up to the line of affinity—that is, up to the seventh generation—or in any manner defile her with the stain of incest. If anyone rashly presumes to do this, let him expiate the incest and do public penance according to the canonical stages. [Col. 0668B]

CAP. 48.—Likewise, on the same matter. From the Council of Lyons, ch. 10.

(55, questions 2 and 3, canon *Nulli*.) Let no one take wives from the kinship of his own blood as far as the seventh degree, nor without a priest’s blessing. Those who were previously unmarried, once blessed by a priest, may dare to marry.

> Variant in Gratian: “But those who are going to marry are [to be blessed] by a priest,” etc.

CAP. 49.—Likewise, on the same matter. From the Council of Orléans, ch. 10.

> Note [Col. 0667D]: Gratian attributes this to Pope Julius.

(35, question 3, canon *Nullum*.) We permit no person of either sex to take as wife, or to defile with the stain of incest, anyone related by blood or through a wife as far as the seventh degree of descent. [Col. 0668C]

CAP. 50.—On the same matter. From the Council of Cologne, ch. 6.

All names of kinship are contained within seven degrees, beyond which neither affinity is found nor succession can be extended further.

CAP. 51.—Likewise, on the same matter. From the Council of Meaux, ch. 7.

(35, question 2, canon *De affinitate*.) Concerning affinity of blood through degrees of kinship, it was decided that it should be observed to the seventh generation. For the inheritance of property also, by legal definitions, establishes the succession of heirs as extending to the seventh degree. They would not succeed unless this were owed to them from the stock of kinship.

CAP. 52.—That kindred persons are to be separated when two or three witnesses give testimony. From the Council of Lleida, ch. 20.

[Col. 0668D]

(35, question 6, canon *Ab isto*.) Let every dispute concerning ecclesiastical matters be settled according to the divine law by two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 17; 19). The Lord is witness when he says: “One person shall not stand against another, but every matter shall stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Matthew 18; 2 Corinthians 13).

CAP. 53.—What must be done if no one is willing to confirm consanguinity by oath. From the register of Pope Urban II.

(35, question 6, canon *Si duo*.) At Troia in Apulia a council of nearly seventy-five bishops and twelve abbots assembled [Col. 0669A]. It dealt with the line of consanguinity in married persons, although no one was willing to establish the matter asserted by an oath. It was ordered that the bishops whose diocesan subjects they were should summon them three times, at suitable intervals. Then, if two or three men establish the consanguinity by oath, or if the parties themselves perhaps confess it, the marriages are to be dissolved. But if neither occurs, the bishops are to adjure them by baptism, by faith, and by the judgment of Christ, in true obedience, to declare openly whether they acknowledge themselves to be related by blood, as rumour has it. If they deny it, they are to be left to themselves; yet they must know that, if they hold otherwise in their conscience, they are separated from the thresholds of the church, from the body and blood of the Lord, and from the communion of the faithful [Col. 0669B], and are rendered infamous, until they desist from the crime of incest. If they separate themselves at the bishops’ judgment, and are young, they are not to be forbidden to contract other marriages.

### CAP. 54.—Within what degree consanguinity ought to be separated. From the Council of Chalon, ch. 5 (Council of Mainz under Charlemagne, ch. 54).

(35, question 2, canon *Contradicimus*.) We further forbid anyone henceforth to be joined in marriage in the fourth, fifth, or sixth generation. Where such a union has been made after this prohibition and is discovered, it is to be dissolved.

### CAP. 55.—Within what degree St Gregory permitted marriages to the English nation. From the letter of John of Constantinople to Felix, bishop of Sicily.

(35, question 2, canon *Quaedam lex Romana*.) Pope Gregory [Col. 0669C], when Augustine, bishop of the English nation, asked him within what degree the faithful ought to marry, replied dispensationally as follows to the sixth question:

“A certain law in the Roman commonwealth permits either brother and sister, or the son and daughter of two full brothers, or of two sisters, to have intercourse; yet we have learned by experience that offspring cannot increase from such a marriage. Therefore it is necessary that, from the fourth or fifth generation onward, the faithful may lawfully be joined to one another.”

### CAP. 56.—That St Gregory granted this specifically to the English nation, not generally. In the same place.

But much later, when Felix, bishop of Messana in Sicily, asked whether Gregory had written to Augustine that marriages contracted in the fourth generation among the English should not be dissolved, the most humble Father Gregory [Col. 0669D] gave, among other things, the following explanation (*Epistle* 31, book XII):

“You are certainly to understand that what I wrote to Augustine, bishop of the English nation and your fosterling, as you recall, concerning unions of consanguinity, I wrote specifically, not generally, for him and for the English nation, which had recently come to the faith: lest, fearing stricter requirements, it should fall away from the good which it had begun. The whole Roman city is witness for me in this matter. Nor did I write them these instructions with the intention that, once they had been firmly established by a strong root in the faith, they should not be separated if found within their own consanguinity, or should be joined within the line of affinity—that is, as far as the seventh generation. Rather, while they were still neophytes, it was necessary first to consent to things unlawful there, instruct them by words and examples [Col. 0670A], and subsequently exclude reasonably and faithfully whatever they might do in such matters. For, according to the Apostle, who says, ‘I gave you milk to drink, not solid food’ [1 Cor. 3], we permitted these things for them at that time, not for their descendants, as has been stated, lest the good planted with a weak root should be scorched, but should gain some strength and be preserved unto perfection.”

For this reason I, John, have taken care to set this down briefly: so that those who, on the occasion of this new dispensation, cite unlawful marriages against this most learned man may understand that he did not prescribe unions in the fourth generation generally, but permitted them pardonably and at the same time temporarily.

### CAP. 57.—That outsiders ought not, except from necessity, to create discord among blood relatives. From the decrees of Pope Fabian, ch. 8 (in a fragment).

[Col. 0670B]

(35, question 6, canon *Consanguineos*.) Let no outsider accuse blood relatives or calculate consanguinity in a synod; rather, their near relatives, to whose knowledge the matter belongs—namely father, mother, sister, brother, paternal uncle, maternal uncle, paternal aunt, maternal aunt, and their descendants—should do so. But if the entire progeny has died out, the bishop shall canonically inquire of older and more truthful persons to whom the same relationship is known; and, if the relationship is found, they are to be separated.

### CAP. 58.—That no one should marry his niece. From the Roman Council. Gregory (from the decrees of Gregory II, called the Younger, ch. 6).

Whoever marries his niece is to be anathema.

### CAP. 59.—On the same matter, of the same Gregory (ch. 8).

[Col. 0670C] Whoever marries his first cousin is to be anathema.

### CAP. 60.—On the same matter (ch. 9).

Whoever marries a woman from his own kindred, or a woman whom his kinsman has had in marriage, is to be anathema.

### CAP. 61.—The oath by which kinship is to be investigated.

(35, question 6, canon *De parentela*.) Concerning that kinship which they say exists between N. and this wife, N., whatever you know or have heard from your neighbours or your older relatives, you will conceal from neither your bishop nor his envoy, by no contrivance, neither for love nor fear, nor because of reward or consanguinity, whenever he questions you concerning this matter, he having ordered it investigated. So may God help you, and these relics of the saints.

### CAP. 62.—Oath of witnesses.

(35, question 6, canon *Illud juramentum*.) Will you uphold the oath which this man has sworn concerning that kinship calculated between the son and his wife N., insofar as you know or have heard? So may God help you.

### CAP. 63.—Oath concerning an incestuous marriage.

(35, question 6, canon *Ab isto*.) From this day onward, you will not by any contrivance associate yourself with this your kinswoman N., with whom, contrary to law and right Christian conduct, you have committed adultery and incest. You will not join her to yourself either in marriage or in adultery; nor will you eat and drink with her at one table, or remain under one roof, except perhaps in church or in some public place where no evil suspicion can arise [Col. 0671A], and there, before suitable witnesses, you may speak together on account of a definite necessity. Nor will you take another wife, unless perhaps, after completing penance, permission has been granted you by your bishop or his envoy. So may God help you, and these relics of the saints.

### CAP. 64.—These chapters on the seven degrees of consanguinity St Isidore set down after careful investigation, and arranged more clearly in a diagram. Chapter 1 on the seven degrees of consanguinity. (Isidore, *Etymologies*, IX, ch. 5.)

In the first ascending degree are father and mother; in the descending degree, son and daughter. No other persons are attached to them.

In the second degree, in the ascending line, are grandfather and grandmother; in the descending line, grandson and granddaughter. In the collateral line are brother and sister; these persons are doubled. For grandfather and grandmother are reckoned both on the father’s and on the mother’s side. These persons are likewise doubled in the following degrees, in the same order, according to the substance of the persons existing in each degree [Gratian reads: “of those who stand in that degree”]. These persons are called double in the second degree because there are two grandfathers, paternal and maternal. Likewise, there are two kinds of grandchildren: those begotten by a son and those begotten by a daughter. Brother and sister come through the collateral line—that is, the brother of one’s father or the brother of one’s mother, who is called either paternal uncle (*patruus*) or maternal uncle (*avunculus*). These too are doubled in the same order.

In the third degree, above are great-grandfather and great-grandmother; below, great-grandson and great-granddaughter. Collaterally are the son or daughter of a brother or sister; paternal uncle and paternal aunt (*amita*), that is, the brother and sister of one’s father; maternal uncle and maternal aunt (*matertera*), that is, the brother and sister of one’s mother.

In the fourth degree, above are great-great-grandfather and great-great-grandmother; below, great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter. Collaterally are the grandson and granddaughter of a brother or sister; the brother and sister of a paternal cousin (*patruelis*); the paternal cousin (*patruelis*), that is, the son or daughter of a paternal uncle; the cousin (*consobrinus*, *consobrina*), that is, the son or daughter of a maternal uncle or maternal aunt; the child of a paternal aunt (*amitinus*, *amitina*); and likewise cousins born of two sisters. Added to these are the great paternal uncle and great paternal aunt—that is, the brother and sister of one’s paternal grandfather—and the great maternal uncle and great maternal aunt, that is, the brother and sister of one’s paternal or maternal grandmother.

[Col. 0672A] In the fifth degree, above are the great-great-great-grandfather and great-great-great-grandmother; below, the great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-granddaughter. Collaterally are the great-grandson and great-granddaughter of a brother or sister; the son or daughter of a paternal cousin, of a female paternal cousin, of a child of a paternal aunt, or of a cousin; and the nearer cousin (*propior consobrinus*, *propior consobrina*), that is, the son or daughter of a great paternal uncle, great paternal aunt, great maternal uncle, or great maternal aunt. There are also the great-great paternal uncle and great-great paternal aunt: these are the brother and sister of one’s maternal great-grandfather; the great-great maternal uncle and great-great maternal aunt: these are the brother and sister of one’s paternal or maternal great-grandmother, and of one’s maternal great-great-grandfather. This category cannot be explained in degrees other than those written, nor by other terms.

[Col. 0672B] In the sixth degree, above are the great-great-great-great-grandfather and great-great-great-great-grandmother; below, the corresponding great-great-great-great-grandson and -granddaughter. Collaterally are the great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter of a brother or sister; the son or daughter of a paternal cousin, a maternal cousin, a child of a paternal aunt, or a cousin; the grandson or granddaughter of a great paternal uncle, great paternal aunt, great maternal uncle, or great maternal aunt; and the son or daughter of a nearer cousin—who are called cousins. Added laterally are the son or daughter of great-great paternal uncles and aunts, or of great-great maternal uncles and aunts; the great-great-great paternal uncle and aunt. These are the brother and sister of one’s paternal great-great-grandfather; the great-great-great maternal uncle and aunt: these are the brother and sister of one’s paternal and maternal great-great-grandmother, and of one’s maternal great-great-grandfather. These too cannot be explained further than the author himself has set them out.

In the seventh degree, persons related to one another are not called by their own names in the ascending or descending direct line, but the collateral line includes the great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-granddaughter of a brother or sister, and the successive sons and daughters of cousins. The seven degrees were therefore established because, beyond them, by the nature of things, neither can names be found nor life extended through succeeding descendants. For in these seven degrees are contained all names of relationships; beyond them affinity cannot be found, nor can succession be extended further.

### ON FATHERS

The author of my line is my father; I am his son or daughter.  
My father’s father is my grandfather; I am his grandson or granddaughter.  
My father’s grandfather is my great-grandfather; I am his great-grandson or great-granddaughter.  
My father’s great-grandfather is my great-great-grandfather; I am his great-great-grandson or great-great-granddaughter.  
My father’s great-great-grandfather is my great-great-great-grandfather; I am his great-great-great-grandson or great-great-great-granddaughter.  
My father’s great-great-great-grandfather is my great-great-great-great-grandfather; I am his corresponding descendant.

### ON PATERNAL UNCLES

My father’s brother is my paternal uncle; I am his brother’s son or daughter.  
My father’s father is my great father (*pater magnus*); I am his brother’s son’s son or daughter.  
My paternal uncle’s grandfather is my great-great paternal uncle; I am his son’s or daughter’s grandson or granddaughter.  
My paternal uncle’s great-grandfather is my great-great-great paternal uncle; I am his granddaughter’s son or daughter.

### ON PATERNAL AUNTS

My father’s sister is my paternal aunt; I am her brother’s son or daughter.  
My paternal aunt’s mother is my great paternal aunt; I am her daughter’s brother’s son or daughter.  
My paternal aunt’s grandmother is my great-great paternal aunt; I am her granddaughter’s son or daughter.  
My paternal aunt’s great-grandmother is my great-great-great paternal aunt; I am her granddaughter’s grandson or granddaughter.

### ON MATERNAL UNCLES

My mother’s brother is my maternal uncle; I am his sister’s son or daughter.  
My maternal uncle’s father is my great maternal uncle; I am his sister’s son’s son or daughter.  
My maternal uncle’s grandfather is my great-great maternal uncle; I am his son’s grandson or granddaughter.  
My maternal uncle’s great-grandfather is my great-great-great maternal uncle; I am his granddaughter’s son or daughter.

### ON MATERNAL AUNTS

My mother’s sister is my maternal aunt; I am her sister’s son or daughter.  
My maternal aunt’s sister is my great maternal aunt; I am her sister’s grandson or granddaughter.  
My grandmother’s sister is my great-great maternal aunt; I am her sister’s great-granddaughter or great-grandson.  
My great-grandmother’s sister is my great maternal aunt (*promatertera*); I am her granddaughter’s son or daughter.

[Col. 0673] The little branches which advocates make in a genealogy when they divide the degrees of kinship are called diagrams (*schemata*): for example, “this one is the son, this one the father, this one the grandfather, this one the agnate,” and the rest; these are their figures.

When this consanguinity, gradually separating itself through the ranks of descendants, has withdrawn to the final degree and ceased to be kinship, the law recalls it again by the bond of marriage and in some sense calls back the fugitive. Consanguinity was therefore established as far as the sixth degree of descent, so that, just as the generation and state of humankind are completed in the six ages of the world, so the kinship of a lineage might be bounded by the same number of degrees. [Col. 0674–0675]

### CAP. 65.—On incestuous persons who despise priests’ admonitions. From the Fourth Council of Tours, ch. 4.

[Col. 0677A]

(23, question 5, canon *Incestuosi*.) Many incestuous persons, parricides, and murderers are found among us—alas! Yet some of them refuse to heed the admonitions of priests, wishing to persist in their former crimes. Such persons ought to be restrained from so depraved a custom by the discipline of secular authority, since they refused to be recalled by the saving counsels of priests.

### CAP. 66.—That marriages are not to be contracted within the seventh generation. From the Council at Koblenz, ch. 1, attended by Kings Charles and Henry.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 912, at Koblenz, by command of the venerable princes Charles and Henry, most reverend kings, eight bishops are said to have assembled: Herimann, archbishop of Cologne; Thiedo, bishop of Witeburg; Luitharius, bishop of Mundan; Doto, bishop of Osnabrück; Rihgovunno, bishop of Worms; Rithwius, bishop of Strasbourg; and Unwanus, bishop of Paderborn, together with abbots and very many men of sacred order. With Christ the Lord cooperating and confirming their decisions, seated in synodal assembly, they considered by most wholesome counsel many matters useful and beneficial to the holy Church of God. Among the things they decreed, they confirmed as especially necessary that the incest of kinship—most frequent in the pressing time through abuse, alas!—must be avoided with the utmost care [Col. 0677C]: namely, that no Christian should presume to unite in marriage within the seventh generation.

### CAP. 67.—On a woman who has committed fornication with two brothers. From the Council of Neocaesarea, ch. 2.

If a woman has married two brothers, she is to be excluded until death. Nevertheless, at the end of life, out of mercy, if she promises that, should she recover, she will dissolve the bonds of this union, she may receive the fruit of penance and be granted communion. But if the man or woman dies while persisting in such marriages, penance will be difficult for one remaining alive.

### CAP. 68.—On the same matter. From Martin’s decrees, ch. 80 (Martin of Braga, ch. 79).

[Col. 0677D] If any woman marries two brothers, or any man marries two sisters, they are to be separated from communion until death. At death, out of mercy, let them receive viaticum.

### CAP. 69.—On one who has committed fornication with two sisters, one of whom had been his wife. From the Council of Orléans, ch. 6 (Vermeria, ch. 12).

(32, question 7, canon *Qui dormierit*.) Whoever has slept with two sisters, one of whom was previously his wife, shall have neither of them; nor shall those adulterers ever be joined in marriage.

### CAP. 70.—On one who has committed fornication with two sisters; with his stepmother, his own sister, paternal aunt, maternal aunt, the daughter of his paternal or maternal uncle, the daughter of his paternal or maternal aunt, his niece, his comother, the little girl whom he received from the font, or whom he held before the bishop. From the same council.

[Col. 0678A]

If anyone has committed fornication with two sisters, or with his stepmother, his sister, his paternal aunt, his maternal aunt, the daughter of his paternal uncle or maternal uncle, the daughter of his paternal aunt or maternal aunt, his niece, his comother, his goddaughter or one whom he received from the font, or whom he held before the bishop; and if any woman has committed fornication in like manner: let such a person refrain from entering the house of God for one year, and during that year use only bread, water, and salt, except on Sundays and feast days. Let the person bear no arms, give a kiss to no one, and receive the sacrament only as viaticum. Then for six years let the person indeed enter the house of God, but use neither meat, wine, nor *sicera* [intoxicating drink], except on feast days. Concerning arms, kisses, and the sacrament, let the rule be as stated above. Thereafter, for two years, whenever the person eats meat, let the person abstain from every drink by which drunkenness may be caused; and if the person drinks, let the person not eat meat, except on principal feast days. Concerning arms, kissing, and the sacrament, let the person keep the rule already stated. From then until death, except on the feast days mentioned, let the person abstain from meat and lawfully keep three regular fast-days in every week and three Lents in the year. Let the rule concerning arms be as above, and let the person never at any time be joined in marriage.

The same penance is to be imposed upon parricides, fratricides, and blood relatives, as well as upon those who willingly, through deceit and avarice, kill an innocent person—what they call *morchidum* [variant: *morth*].

### CAP. 71.—On one who has taken his mother as wife or committed fornication with his stepdaughter. Likewise from the Council of Mainz (under Charlemagne, ch. 56).

(32, question 7, canon *Si quis*.) If anyone marries a widow and afterwards commits fornication with his stepdaughter, or cohabits with two sisters; or if any woman marries two brothers or commits fornication with father and son: we order such unions to be anathematized and dissolved, and that the parties never again be joined in marriage, but be subjected to severe discipline [perhaps “struck,” *feriri*].

### CAP. 72.—On one who unknowingly committed fornication with a stepdaughter. From the Council at Vermeria, ch. 4.

[Col. 0678D] (35, questions 2 and 3, canon *Si quis cum matre*.) If anyone has committed fornication with mother and daughter, the mother being ignorant of the daughter and the daughter of the mother, he shall never take a wife; but the women, if they wish, may take husbands. If, however, the women themselves knew of this, they shall remain unmarried forever.

### CAP. 73.—On one who had seduced a woman whom his brother afterwards unknowingly took as wife. From the same council, ch. 5 (Council of Tribur, ch. 44).

(35, questions 2 and 3, canon *Si homo*.) If a man has committed fornication with a woman and his brother, unaware of it, has taken the same woman as wife, the brother who concealed the crime from his brother is to do penance and, after penance, may marry. But the woman is to do penance until death and remain without hope of marriage.

### CAP. 74.—On the same matter. From the same council, ch. 6.

[Col. 0679A]

If one brother has committed fornication with a woman and another brother, unaware of it, has cohabited with the same woman, the woman shall do penance for the days of her life; but after penance the brother ignorant of the crime may marry if he wishes.

### CAP. 75.—On the same matter. From the Council of Mâcon, ch. 5.

It was likewise decided concerning a man who had seduced a woman whom his brother afterwards took as wife. They decreed that he who seduced her and concealed from his brother the woman whom he had seduced, because he doubled his sin, should be punished by stricter penance; that such a marriage ought to be dissolved; that the woman should never be given permission to marry; but that, out of mercy, marriage should be permitted to the others [Col. 0679B], though with penance.

### CAP. 76.—On a woman with whom both father and son committed fornication. From the Council of Tribur (ch. 43).

(34, questions 1 and 2, canon *Quidam*.) A certain man committed fornication with a woman; afterwards his son, unaware of his father’s act, violated the same woman. When the father learned this, he confessed concerning himself and his son. They decreed that it was better for those who had thus fallen to be allowed lawful marriages with fitting penance than perhaps to commit still worse offences. But the fornicatress is to remain without hope of marriage.

### CAP. 77.—On one who has committed fornication with his wife, mother, and stepdaughter. From the Council of Mainz (under Leo IV, ch. 29).

(32, question 7, canon *Si quis*.) If anyone marries a widow and afterwards commits fornication with his stepdaughter, or with two sisters; if any woman with two brothers, or with father and son; if anyone defiles his brother’s widow, his niece, stepmother, daughter-in-law, first cousin, the daughter of a maternal uncle, his widow, or his stepdaughter: we order them to be separated and never again joined in marriage [Col. 0679C].

### CAP. 78.—On a married man who has committed fornication with the daughter of his maternal aunt, maternal uncle, paternal aunt, or paternal uncle. From the Council of Tribur (*Roman Penitential*, title III, ch. 13).

It was asked whether, if anyone has cohabited with the daughter of his maternal aunt, paternal aunt, maternal uncle, or paternal uncle, he may thereafter use marriage if married, or take a wife if unmarried. It would be just, as some earlier enactments provide, that such persons should abstain from marriage forever. Yet, in view of human frailty, it has seemed right that after penance they should not be wholly deprived of marriage, though so monstrous a fornication must be punished very severely [Col. 0679D], as St Pope Nicholas and other Roman pontiffs decreed, lest in despair they sin still more.

### CAP. 79.—On father and son, maternal uncle and nephew, if they have committed fornication with one woman. From the Council of Mainz, ch. 5.

It was asked what should be done if father and son, two brothers, or maternal uncle and nephew have committed fornication with one woman. It is clear that what is found to be a grave crime must be punished by grave retribution. For every adultery is forbidden, where it is written: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20); how much more adultery with a female relative or with the wife or concubine of a relative? Hence it is written in Leviticus: “If anyone commits adultery with another’s wife, both adulterer and adulteress shall die. He who lies with his stepmother or daughter-in-law, and he who marries daughter and mother, and he who takes his sister, shall die” (Lev. 20). For if the Law ordered the shamefulness of incest to be punished by a sentence of death, how shall an incestuous person escape penance for sin in the Gospel, where perfect justice is found? Hence the Apostle: “He who has set aside the law of Moses dies without any mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses; how much worse punishments, do you think, will he deserve who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, regarded as defiled the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?” (Heb. 10) [Col. 0680B].

Accordingly Theodore judged that one who committed incest ought to do penance for twelve years; others, ten; others, seven. But, following the footsteps of the ancient Fathers, let us moderate the period of penance only for those who perform it devoutly and with tears; let the rest observe the appointed term.

### CAP. 80.—On the same matter. From the Council at Vermeria, ch. 4 (Mainz under Charlemagne, ch. 55).

(30, question 1, canon *Si quis filiastrum*.) If anyone has held his stepson or stepdaughter before the bishop for confirmation, he is to be separated from his wife and never take another; and likewise the woman.

### CAP. 81.—On those who receive their own children at baptism in order to separate from their spouses. From the Council of Chalon, ch. 45 (Second Council of Chalon under Charlemagne, ch. 31).

[Col. 0680C]

(30, question 1, canon *Dictum est*.) It has also been reported to us that certain women, some carelessly and others fraudulently, have held their own children before bishops for confirmation, in order to separate from their husbands. We therefore have judged it fitting that, if any woman has held her son before a bishop for confirmation through carelessness or any fraud, she shall do penance as long as she lives because of her deception or fraud, but she shall not be separated from her husband.

### CAP. 82.—On the same matter. Likewise from the Council of Mainz, ch. 20, held in the cloister of St Alban in the presence of Emperor Louis.

[Col. 0680D] Concerning what you asked: whether one who married his own goddaughter, one who cohabited with his spiritual comother, one who baptized his own child, and one whose wife received that child from the font, may remain afterwards in such a union when this was done in order to cause a rupture of the marriage—the answer in such cases is as follows. If anyone has married his goddaughter or spiritual comother, we judge that they must be separated and punished by severe penance. But if lawful spouses, one or both, have deliberately arranged to receive their own child from the font in order to bring about a separation, we give this counsel: if they wish to remain unmarried, that is good; but if not, severe penance is to be imposed on the deceiver [Col. 0681A], and they are to remain together. If the violator of the marriage survives, let him be punished with most stringent penance and remain without hope of marriage.

### CAP. 83.—On the same matter. From the Council of Tribur, ch. 8 (Mainz under Charlemagne, ch. 55).

No one shall receive his own son or daughter from the font of baptism, nor marry his goddaughter or comother, nor the woman whose son [or daughter, original text] he has held before the bishop for confirmation. Where this has been done, they are to be separated.

### CAP. 84.—On the same matter. From the Council of Mainz, ch. 5.

How detestable and execrable a crime it is for any Christian to violate his own goddaughter is attested by St Pope Gregory in his *Dialogues* (book IV, ch. 32), where he relates that a certain man defiled his goddaughter [Col. 0681B]. Because he neglected to do penance, he was suddenly seized by a miserable illness and expired; after burial, not only his body but even his entire tomb was consumed by invisible fire.

### CAP. 85.—On women who commit fornication with one another by some device. From Theodore’s *Penitential* (*Roman Penitential*, title III, ch. 15).

A woman committing fornication by any device, either alone or with another woman, shall do penance for two years.

### CAP. 86.—On nuns, if they commit fornication with one another. From the same source.

If a nun and another nun have committed fornication by some contrivance, they shall do penance for seven years.

### CAP. 87.—On a woman who has committed fornication with another woman. From the Council of Ancyra, ch. 8.

[Col. 0681C]

If a woman has committed fornication with a woman, she shall do penance for two years. Likewise, a woman who mixes her husband’s semen with food so as thereby to receive more of his love shall do penance.

### CAP. 88.—On those who engage in irrational conduct. From the Council of Ancyra, ch. 15.

Concerning those who have engaged, or are engaging, in irrational conduct—that is, those who have defiled themselves with animals and males—all who committed such a crime before their twentieth year shall, after completing fifteen years in penance, be deemed worthy of the communion of prayers. Then, after remaining in this communion for five years, they may at last partake of the sacraments of the offering. Their life during the period of penance [Col. 0681D] is also to be examined, and according to its character they shall receive mercy. But if they have clung insatiably to these crimes, let them spend a longer time in penance. All who, after twenty years of age and while having wives, have fallen into this sin shall, after doing penance for twenty-five years, be received to the communion of prayer. After remaining therein for five years, they may then receive the sacraments of the offering. But if any, while having wives and having passed their fiftieth year, have sinned thus, let them receive the grace of communion only at the end of life.

### CAP. 89.—On the same matter. From the same council, ch. 16.

The holy synod ordered that those who have lived irrationally and defiled others with the leprosy of an unjust crime [Col. 0682A] should pray among those endangered by an unclean spirit.

### CAP. 90.—On those who commit fornication with animals. From Theodore’s *Penitential* (ch. 17).

Concerning one who sins with an animal, some judge that the person should do penance for ten years, some for seven, some for two [or three], and some for one hundred days, according to the quality of the person.

### CAP. 91.—Likewise on those who commit fornication with quadrupeds. From the Roman Penitential.

If persons are found who sin against nature with quadrupeds or males, they are to be restrained by harsh and severe penance. Therefore bishops or priests who impose the judgment of penance should strive in every way to eradicate this evil at its root.

### CAP. 92.—On those who commit fornication like Sodomites. From Theodore’s *Penitential* (ch. 18).

[Col. 0682B] Whoever has committed fornication like the Sodomites, if a slave, shall be punished with whips and do penance for two years; if free and married, for ten years; if a private person (*privatus*), for seven years. A boy shall do penance for one hundred days if it is habitual. A married layman, if he has the practice habitually, shall do penance for fifteen years. If he belongs to the clerical orders and has the practice habitually, once deposed he shall do penance as a layman. But whoever has committed fornication with his natural brother, through so foul a mingling, shall abstain from all flesh and do penance for fifteen years; if a cleric, he ought further to be expelled.

### CAP. 93.—On clerics or monks who pursue males. From the sayings of Basil.

A cleric or monk who is a pursuer of little children, or who is caught in a shameful act through a kiss or another occasion [Col. 0682C], shall be publicly flogged and have his hair cut off; bald and shamefully smeared on the face with spittle, he shall be bound tightly with iron chains and worn down by six months’ confinement in prison. On three days each week he shall eat barley bread in the evening. After this, for another six months he shall live separately in a small cell under the supervision of a spiritual elder, applying himself to manual work and prayer, subject to vigils and tears. He shall always go about under the custody of two spiritual brothers and shall thereafter not associate with young men in any private conversation or counsel.

### CAP. 94.—On the same matter. From the sayings of Isidore.

If any youth, or any suspicious person, has played with little children [Col. 0682D], he shall be worn down by prolonged penance.

### CAP. 95.—On the same matter. From the sayings of the same.

If a brother is caught playing with boys and cultivating friendships with those of tender age, he shall be admonished a third time to remember decency and the fear of God; if he does not desist, he shall be corrected most severely.

### CAP. 96.—On one who has a spiritual compater, whose wife is not his comother, and whether, after the man’s death, he may marry his widow. From the Council of Tribur, ch. 47, attended by King Arnulf.

(30, question 4, canon *Qui spiritualem*.) One who has a spiritual compater, whose son he received from the laver of the sacred font, and whose wife is not his comother, may, after his compater’s death, take that man’s widow as wife, if they have no relationship of consanguinity [Col. 0683A]. For why should they not be joined whom neither carnal proximity nor spiritual generation separates?

### CAP. 97.—Whether anyone may take the daughter of his spiritual comother as wife. From the same council, ch. 48.

We neither define this by canonical ordinance nor reject it by any prohibition; but because some think differently about it, we mention something here. If anyone, by chance and through the occurrence of circumstances, has married the daughter of his spiritual comother, let him, after taking more mature counsel, retain her and honourably fulfil the duties of lawful marriage.

### CAP. 98.—On a certain man who violated his own spiritual goddaughter. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (book IV, ch. 32).

[Col. 0683B]

The venerable Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse, who for a long time presided over my monastery in this city, used to relate, saying that a terrible event had occurred in the province of Valeria:

“On the most holy Paschal Saturday, a certain municipal official there received in baptism the young daughter of a certain man. After the fast, he returned home, greatly intoxicated with wine, and asked that this his goddaughter remain with him. That night—an abomination even to tell—he ruined her. When he rose in the morning, guilty as he was, he began to think of going to the baths, as though bath-water could wash away the stain of sin [Col. 0683C]. He therefore went, bathed, and began to hesitate to enter the church. If he did not go to church on so great a day, he was ashamed before people; but if he went, he feared God’s judgment. Human shame therefore prevailed: he went to church, but stood trembling and afraid, every moment apprehensive of the hour when he would be handed over to an unclean spirit and tormented before all the people.

“Though he feared intensely, nothing apparently adverse happened to him in that celebration of the Mass. He went out rejoicing and entered church the next day already secure. For six successive days he went about joyful and secure, thinking that the Lord had either not seen his crime, or, having seen it, had mercifully forgiven it. But on the seventh day he died suddenly. When he had been committed to burial, for a long time a flame came forth from his tomb in the sight of all. It burned his bones until it consumed the entire tomb, and the earth gathered in the grave appeared excavated [Col. 0683D]. By doing this, almighty God showed what his soul suffered in secret, when even his body was consumed by flame before human eyes. In this matter He also deigned to give us who hear it an example of fear, so that from this consideration we may gather what the living, sentient soul suffers for its guilt, if even insensible bones are consumed by so great a punishment of fire.”

### CAP. 99.—On a certain brother who was assailed by the spirit of fornication. From the sayings of Paphnutius the hermit (*Lives of the Fathers*).

[Col. 0684A]

A certain brother was troubled by the spirit of fornication. He went to a most approved elder and begged him, saying: “Take concern for me, most blessed Father, and pray for me, for the passion of fornication grievously attacks me.” When the elder heard this, he prayed earnestly for him day and night, beseeching the Lord’s mercy. Yet the same brother came again and asked the elder to pray still more earnestly for him. Likewise, with every care, the blessed elder prayed more intently for him. But when the elder saw the monk frequently coming to him and entreating him to pray, he was deeply saddened and wondered why the Lord did not hear his prayers. That same night the Lord revealed to him the monk’s condition: his yielding through negligence and sloth, and perhaps the carnal delights of his heart. Thus it was shown to the holy elder: he saw that monk sitting down, while the spirit of fornication, in various female forms, played before him, and he himself took delight with it. He also saw an angel of the Lord standing by and gravely angered against that brother, because he did not rise or prostrate himself in prayers to the Lord, but rather delighted in his own thoughts. These things, therefore, were shown to the holy elder by revelation. He recognized that the fault and negligence of that monk were the reason his prayers were not heard. Then the elder said to him: “Because it is your own fault, brother, that you delight in evil thoughts, it is impossible for the unclean spirit of fornication to depart from you merely because others pray and entreat God for you—unless you yourself also undertake labour through fasts, prayers, and many vigils, beseeching with groaning that he may give you his mercy and the help of his grace, and that the Lord Christ may enable you to resist evil thoughts. For physicians too, who prepare and administer remedies for human bodies, may do everything with the greatest diligence; yet if the sick person does not refrain from harmful foods or from other things that usually aggravate illnesses, the care, diligence, and concern of the physicians profit him nothing. Likewise [Col. 0684D], in the ailments of the soul: although the holy Fathers, who are spiritual physicians, may with every earnestness and from their whole heart implore the mercy of Christ our Saviour for those who ask to be helped by their prayers, their prayers will not profit them unless they themselves also, with complete application of mind, both in prayer and in every spiritual work, do what is pleasing to God.”

## CHAPTER 100.—Concerning a brother’s betrothed woman, if the brother violates her. From the Council of Tribur, chapter 10, attended by King Arnulf (c. 41).

(32, q. 2, c. *Quidam*.) A certain man betrothed and endowed a wife, but could not have intercourse with her. His brother secretly violated her and made her pregnant. It was decreed that, although she could not be married to her lawful husband, nevertheless the brother may not have his brother’s betrothed woman; but the adulterer and adulteress are to undergo the penalty for fornication, while lawful marriages are not to be denied them.

## CHAPTER 101.—If anyone moves from one bishopric to another and violates a female relative, or commits any capital crime. From the same council, chapter 42.

If anyone wholly transfers from one bishopric to another, and if—it is to be hoped not!—he happens to violate the daughter of his sister, paternal aunt, maternal aunt, maternal uncle, or paternal uncle, or to commit any capital crime, the bishop in whose diocese he then resides, and under whom he is accused of such a crime, has the right and authority, according to canonical authority and our synodal ordinance, to restrain the criminal [Col. 0685B] and bring him to penitence. For through whom can the truth of the matter be investigated better than through the man under whom he lives and wishes to continue living?

## CHAPTER 102.—Concerning women who conceive while their husbands are absent. From the Council of Elvira, chapter 3 (chapter 63).

If any woman conceives by adultery while her husband is absent, and after the deed kills the child, it was decided that communion should scarcely be given her even at the end of life, because she has doubled her crime.

(From the Council of Lleida, chapter 2.) As for those women who have sought to kill fetuses wrongly conceived through adultery, whether unborn or already delivered, or who have destroyed them in their mothers’ wombs with certain potions: adulterers of either sex are to be granted communion after the completion of seven years, provided that throughout their lives they persist in tears and humility.

## CHAPTER 103.—Concerning women who secretly kill their offspring. From the Council of Arles, chapter 6.

[Col. 0685C]

Certain women, as we have heard, after conceiving through fornication and fearing that the crime they secretly committed might become known, killed the children they bore and covered them with a heap of earth, in order to cast them into water [or: and cast them into water]. How great a crime this is, the canons of the Councils of Ancyra (c. 20), Elvira (c. 63), and Lleida (c. 2) attest. These therefore decree that communion is scarcely to be given them even at the end of life; but, treating them more humanely, it was decided that such women should be received to communion after ten years’ penance.

## CHAPTER 104.—On the same matter. From the same council, chapter 10.

If any persons have smothered an infant, let them do penance for three years [Col. 0685D], one of these on bread and water. If the offender is a cleric, let him do so for four years, one of them on bread and water.

## CHAPTER 105.—Concerning those who sin against nature. Augustine, *Confessions*, book III, chapter 8.

(32, q. 7, c. *Flagitia*.) Crimes against nature, such as those of the Sodomites, are everywhere and always to be rejected and punished. If all nations committed them, they would be held guilty of the same crime under the divine law, which did not make human beings so that they should use one another in that manner. For the very fellowship which ought to exist between us and God is violated when that same nature, of which he is the author, is defiled by the perversity of lust.

## CHAPTER 106.—That it is graver to sin against nature than to commit adultery. Augustine, *Against Julian*, book V.

(32, q. 7, c. *Usus naturalis*.) Natural and lawful use is in marriage, just as unlawful use is in adultery. But use against nature is always unlawful and undoubtedly more shameful and disgraceful; the holy Apostle reproved it among both women and men (Rom. 1), intending it to be understood as more condemnable than sins committed through adultery or fornication in natural use.

## CHAPTER 107.—Concerning the penance of those who have sinned by intercourse with an animal. Canons of Martin for laypeople (from the book of synodal capitularies of the Greeks; Martin, bishop of Braga, c. 81).

If anyone before the age of twenty has sinned by intercourse with an animal of any kind, let him remain subject in humiliation at the door of the church for fifteen years; then, received for another five years into communion of prayer, let him do penance and so receive the grace of the sacrament. Others should be questioned concerning what sort of life he has lived during his penance, and thus he may obtain the mercy of communion. But if anyone after the age of twenty, while having a wife, falls into this sin, let him remain subject to humiliation for twenty-five years; and after sharing only in prayer for five years, let him thereafter receive the sacrament. If anyone has exceeded even this measure, let him receive the sacrament at his departure.

## CHAPTER 108.—Why an animal defiled by human intercourse was commanded to be killed. Augustine’s *Questions on Leviticus*, chapter 74 (q. 74, on Leviticus chapter 20).

“A woman who approaches any animal so as to be mounted by it: you shall kill the woman, and the animal shall surely die; for they are guilty.” It is asked how the animal can be guilty, when it is irrational and in no way capable of law.

Again, in the same place, a few verses later: Animals, it must be believed, were commanded to be killed because, defiled by such a crime, they revive an unworthy memory of the deed.

## CHAPTER 109.—Concerning violators of boys. Council of Elvira, chapter 71.

We have decreed that those who violate boys are not to be given communion even at the end of life.

## CHAPTER 110.—That natural use with one’s own wife is venial, whereas use with another woman or a prostitute is damnable. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage* (chapter 8).

It is worse to violate another man’s marriage than to attach oneself to a prostitute.

Again, in the same place: It is worse to lie with one’s mother than with another man’s wife.

Again, in the same place, chapter 8: Some things are necessary for wisdom, such as teaching; some for health, such as food, drink, and sleep; some for friendship, such as marriage and intercourse. For by this the propagation of the human race is sustained, and friendly fellowship within it is a great good. Therefore, whoever uses these goods, which are necessary for another purpose, otherwise than for the purpose for which they were established, sins—sometimes venially, sometimes damnably. But whoever uses them for the purpose for which they were given acts rightly.

Again, in the same place, chapter 11: When natural use exceeds the terms of marriage—that is, the need of procreation—it is venial with a wife, but damnable with a prostitute. That use, indeed, which is against nature is committed abominably with a prostitute; but it is committed more abominably when, even in things permitted for use, the proper measure is exceeded [“which is against, etc.” in the original]. Yet even a single or rare excess in what is permitted is far more tolerable than an excess in things not permitted. Therefore immoderation with one’s wife is to be tolerated, lest lust burst forth into what is not permitted. Thus even a man who approaches his wife however frequently sins far less than one who resorts even very rarely to fornication. But if a husband wishes to use a woman’s bodily member for a purpose for which it was not granted, the wife is more shameful if she permits this to be done to herself than if she permits it to be done with another woman.

## CHAPTER 111.—Concerning emissions occurring from various causes. Bede, *History of the English*, book I (Bede, chapter 27, book I of the *Ecclesiastical History*). Gregory’s reply to Augustine (at the end of the Register, chapter 11).

(Dist. 6, c. *Testamentum*, part I.) Emission sometimes occurs from surfeit, sometimes from natural excess or infirmity, and sometimes from thought. When it results from natural excess or infirmity, the illusion need not be feared at all, since the mind must grieve more that it has undergone it unknowingly than that it has done it. But when the appetite of gluttony is carried beyond measure in taking food, and the receptacles of the humours are thereby burdened, the mind incurs some guilt; yet not to the extent of being forbidden to receive the sacred mystery or to celebrate the solemnities of Mass, if perhaps a feast day requires it or necessity itself compels the performance of the ministry because no other priest is present. But if others are available who can perform the ministry, an emission caused by surfeit ought not prevent receipt of the sacred mystery; rather, in my judgment, one ought humbly refrain from offering the sacred mystery [Col. 0687C].

Again, in the same place, shortly afterward: If an emission in the mind of one asleep arises from a shameful thought entertained while awake, the soul’s guilt is evident. For it sees from what root that defilement proceeded: what it knowingly thought, it unknowingly underwent.

## CHAPTER 112.—On the same matter. Isidore, *Sentences*, book I (Isidore, chapter 6, book III, *On the Supreme Good*).

(Dist. 6, c. *Non est peccatum*, part I.) It is not sin when, unwillingly, we are deceived by nocturnal images; but it is sin if, before we are deceived, we are anticipated by the affections of thought. For images of lust that we have enacted in reality often appear in the mind during sleep, but they are harmless if they are not met with desire. One who is defiled by nocturnal illusion, though he feels himself polluted apart from any remembered shameful thoughts, should nevertheless attribute it to his own fault that he was tempted, and immediately wipe away his uncleanness with tears.

## CHAPTER 113.—Likewise on the same matter. From the *Life of Saint Dioscorus*. Saint Dioscorus said:

If an emission comes without fantasies of women, it is not sin. For an innate bodily fluid, once it has filled its proper receptacles, must necessarily be discharged through its own channels, and therefore is not imputed as sin.

## CHAPTER 114.—Whether a lesser sin should be permitted in order to avoid a graver one. Haimo, on Genesis.

It is commonly asked whether this balancing should be made: namely, whether we should permit a lesser sin in order to avoid a graver offense. For Lot wished to give his daughters over to incest, lest a greater sin against nature be committed against the men (Gen. 19). But we must attribute this to a disturbed mind. For, not knowing what he was doing or how he could rescue the guests whom he thought were men, he must be understood to have acted thus.

## CHAPTER 115.—That intercourse according to nature is a lesser evil than transgression against nature. Ambrose, book I of *On Abraham*, chapter 6.

(32, q. 7, c. *Offerebat*.) Holy Lot offered the chastity of his daughters; for although that impurity too was disgraceful, nevertheless intercourse according to nature was a lesser evil than sinning against nature.

## CHAPTER 116.—That Lot should be blamed for drunkenness rather than incest. Augustine, *Against Faustus* (book XXII, chapter 44).

[Col. 0688B]

Lot’s daughters made him drunk and had intercourse with him without his knowledge (Gen. 19). Accordingly, he is indeed to be blamed, though not for the incest itself, but to the degree deserved by that drunkenness.

## CHAPTER 117.—That Lot wished to prostitute his daughters from disturbance rather than from deliberate policy. Augustine, *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 42.

When Lot said to the Sodomites, “I have two daughters who have not yet known men; I shall bring them out to you. Use them as seems good to you, only do not commit wrongdoing against these men” (Gen. 19): since he wished to prostitute his daughters as a compensation, so that his male guests might suffer nothing of the kind from the Sodomites, it is rightly asked whether compensation among shameful acts, or among any sins whatsoever, should be accepted—so that we do something evil lest another person do a graver evil—or whether this should rather be attributed to Lot’s disturbance than to his judgment. And undoubtedly this compensation is admitted most dangerously. But if it is attributed to human disturbance and to a mind agitated by so great an evil, it is in no way to be imitated.

## CHAPTER 118.—On the same matter. In the same work, chapter 44.

Let us understand that what Lot said concerning the dishonour of his daughters is not to be taken as authoritative.

## CHAPTER 119.—That no one should have intercourse with a menstruating woman. Clement to Julius and Julian.

Let everyone take care not to have intercourse with a menstruating woman; for the law of God calls this abominable (Lev. 18).

## CHAPTER 120.—That conception during menstruation is corrupted in many ways. Augustine, *On Genesis According to the Letter*, book X, chapter 7 (chapter 17).

[Col. 0688D]

What is written, “I was a child of good natural ability, and I received a good soul” (Wis. 8), refers plainly to paternal ability or bodily temperament; then, “being better, I came into a defiled body” (ibid.): defiled, that is, either by menstrual blood—for dispositions are said to be burdened by this—or by adulterous contamination.

## CHAPTER 121.—On the same matter. Jerome on Ezekiel, book VI, on chapter 18 (middle).

Every month women’s heavy and sluggish bodies are relieved by the discharge of impure blood. If a man has intercourse with a woman at that time, the fetuses conceived are said to carry with them a defect of the seed, so that lepers and persons suffering from elephantiasis are born from such conception, and health, corrupted through smallness or deformity of the limbs, degenerates into foul bodies in either sex [the original has *sanies*, “putrid discharge,” apparently corrupt]. Men are therefore commanded to know fixed times for intercourse not only with other men’s women but also with their own wives, whom they seem to be joined to by law: when they should have intercourse and when they should refrain from their wives.

Again: Let a wife beware lest, overcome by desire for intercourse, she conceal this from her husband; and let a husband not force his wife, imagining that the will of marriage ought to be subject to him at every time.

## CHAPTER 122.—That excessively harsh penance should not be imposed on anyone. Gregory to Domitian, metropolitan (Register, book II, chapter 101, epistle 62).

[Col. 0689B]

Those who lament the sin of lust and turn fleshly pleasure into sorrow should not experience the harshness of discipline from their teachers, lest the Redeemer of the human race himself be loved less if a soul is afflicted more than it ought to be for his sake.

## CHAPTER 123.—That the disorderly movement of the members without consent is not guilt. Augustine, *City of God*, book I, chapter 23.

If the disobedience of concupiscence, which still dwells in our mortal members, moves contrary to the law of our will, as though by its own law, without guilt in the body of one asleep, how much more is it without guilt in the body of one who does not consent?

## CHAPTER 124.—That a woman should not take the veil without her husband’s consent. *Capitulary*, book V, chapter 18 (chapter 16).

If a woman puts a veil upon her head without the leave [*comiato* in the original] of her husband [Col. 0689C], then, if it pleases her husband, he may receive her again into marriage.

## CHAPTER 125.—That incestuous persons must be separated from the Church. Gregory to Felix, bishop of Sicily (Register, book XII, epistle 31).

All incestuous persons are to be separated from the thresholds of God’s holy Church until, through satisfaction and the prayers of priests, they are canonically reconciled to that holy Church. For the wicked must be separated from the good and the unjust from the righteous, so that at least through their shame they may recognize their consciences and turn from their perversities. But if they prove incorrigible, let them be separated from the faithful until satisfaction is made.

## CHAPTER 126.—That the truth of an accusation must be carefully investigated before punishment. Gregory to John, bishop of Palermo (Register, book XI, epistle 62).

[Col. 0690A]

Because there are offenses in which it is itself an offense to remit punishment, the truth must always be sought, so that it may be investigated whether guilt condemns the accused or innocence, once revealed, removes him from punishment.

(Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*, title XI, on the Gospel of Matthew, sermon 16.) There are men who commit adultery in their homes and sin in secret. Sometimes they are reported to us by their wives, often from jealousy, sometimes because the wives seek their husbands’ salvation. We do not expose them publicly, but rebuke them in private. Where the evil occurred, there let the evil die; yet we do not neglect that wound.

## CHAPTER 127.—That a husband should not practise continence against his wife’s will. Augustine on Psalm 149 [Note: [Col. 0689] Near the end, on the verse: “To bind their kings in fetters.”].

[Col. 0690B] (33, q. 5, c. *Si dicat*.) If a husband says, “I now wish to practise continence; I no longer want a wife,” he cannot do so. What if you wish it and she does not? Must she become a fornicator because of your continence? If she marries another while you live, she will be an adulteress. God does not wish to compensate such loss with such gain. Render the marital debt; and if she does not demand it, render it nevertheless. God will reckon it to you as perfect sanctification if you do not demand what is owed to you, but render what is owed to your wife.

## CHAPTER 128.—What it means to misuse one’s wife. Augustine to Valerius, *On Marriage and Concupiscence* (book II, chapter 20).

If anyone uses even his wife in that part of the body which was not established for generation, it is against nature and shameful.

## CHAPTER 129.—That by the name “body” a part of the body is understood. Augustine to Claudius against Julian, book V, chapter 4.

[Col. 0690C]

If a part of the body could not be called by the name of “body,” the Apostle would not say: “The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does” (1 Cor. 7). He plainly calls by the name “body” those very members by which sex is distinguished and intercourse is performed.
