For who would say that a man does not have authority over his own body if, in these words of the Apostle, you understand the whole body, which consists of all its members? Accordingly, according to the Apostle, even the genital member alone is called by the name “body.”

# TENTH PART OF THE DECREE. Concerning voluntary and involuntary homicides; parricides and fratricides; the killing of lawful wives, lords, and clerics; and that not everyone who kills a person is a murderer; and concerning their penance.

[Col. 0689]

## CHAPTER 1.—That all laws, both ecclesiastical and secular, forbid the shedding of human blood. Augustine, in the letter to Publicola (epistle 154).

[Col. 0689D]

(23, q. 5, c. *De occidendis hominibus*.) As to killing human beings, so that one may not be killed by them, I do not approve the course of action unless perhaps one is a soldier or is bound by public duty, so that one acts not for oneself but for others or for the state in which one also lives, having received lawful authority if it suits one’s position. Those who are restrained by some fear from doing evil may perhaps thereby themselves receive a benefit. This is why it was said, “Do not resist evil” (Matt. 5): not so that we may delight in vengeance, which feeds the mind on another’s evil, but so that we may not neglect people’s correction. Hence neither is one guilty of another’s death if, after he has built walls around his own property, someone dies by being struck through their use. Nor is a Christian guilty if his ox kills someone by goring, or his horse by kicking. Must Christians therefore not have horned oxen, hoofed horses, or dogs with teeth? Or again: because the Apostle Paul took sufficient care to make known to the tribune that certain wicked persons were preparing an ambush against him, and for that reason received an armed escort, if criminal persons had fallen upon those weapons (Acts 21), would Paul acknowledge himself guilty of their bloodshed? Far be it that things which we do or possess for a good and lawful purpose should be imputed to us if, through them and against our will, some harm comes to anyone. Otherwise household and agricultural tools ought not to be possessed either, lest anyone kill himself or another with them.

## CHAPTER 2.—Concerning the authority of a judge. Augustine, in letter 158 to Marcellinus.

I am accustomed to hear that it is within a judge’s power to mitigate a sentence and exact punishment more mildly than the laws prescribe.

## CHAPTER 3.—Likewise on the same matter, in the same letter.

Shortly afterward: I know that, in the case of the clerics of Anaunia, who were killed by pagans and are now honoured as martyrs, when the emperor was asked, he readily granted that those who had killed them and were already in custody should not suffer an equivalent punishment.

## CHAPTER 4.—That one who kills himself is a murderer. Augustine, *City of God*, book I, chapter 17.

(23, q. 5, c. *Si non licet*.) If it is not lawful for anyone acting by private authority to kill even a guilty person whom no law authorizes to be killed, then surely the person who kills himself is also a murderer. And he is made so much more guilty when he kills himself as he was more innocent in the cause for which he judged himself deserving of death. For if we rightly detest Judas’s deed, and Truth judges him in that, when he hanged himself with a noose, he increased rather than expiated the crime of that wicked betrayal, because by despairing of God’s mercy and repenting in a destructive manner he left himself no place for saving repentance, how much more ought one who has nothing in himself to punish by such a penalty refrain from killing himself? For Judas, when he killed himself, killed a wicked man; yet he ended this life guilty not only of Christ’s death but also of his own, because, although on account of his first crime, he was killed by another crime of his own.

(In the same work, chapter 18.) Why should a person who has done no evil do evil to himself and, by killing himself, kill an innocent person, lest he suffer another who is guilty, and commit his own sin against himself lest another’s sin be committed against him?

Again (chapter 20). Nowhere in the holy canonical books can we find that we have been divinely commanded or permitted to inflict death upon ourselves, whether to attain immortality itself or to avoid and escape evil itself. We must understand ourselves to be forbidden where the law says, “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20), especially because it did not add “your neighbour,” as it did when forbidding false witness: “You shall not bear,” it says, “false witness against your neighbour” (Matt. 19). Yet no one who bears false witness against himself should think himself exempt from that crime, because he derives the rule for loving his neighbour from himself, since it is written, “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. 22). But if one who testifies falsely concerning himself is no less guilty of false witness than if he did so against his neighbour, although the precept forbidding false witness forbids it against one’s neighbour—and although it can seem to the undiscerning not to forbid anyone from standing as a false witness against himself—how much more must it be understood that a person may not kill himself when, in what is written, “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20), nothing further is added, and thus surely no one to whom the command is addressed is excepted?

Again: It is written, “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20): neither another person nor, therefore, yourself. For one who kills himself kills nothing other than a human being.

(In the same work, at the end, chapter 21.) Divine authority itself has made certain exceptions—those whom God commands to be killed, either by a law given generally or by an explicit command addressed to a person for a particular time. The person who owes service to the one commanding does not himself kill, just as a sword is an instrument in the hand of one who uses it. Therefore those who waged wars under God’s authority, or who, exercising public authority according to his laws—that is, according to the command of most just reason—punished criminals with death, in no way acted against the command, “You shall not kill.” And Abraham was not merely not charged with cruel wrongdoing; he was even praised for devotion because he wished to kill his son not wickedly but obediently (Gen. 22). It is rightly asked whether Jephthah’s killing of the daughter who met her father should be understood as done at God’s command, since he had vowed to sacrifice to God whatever first met him as he returned victorious from battle (Judg. 11). Nor is Samson otherwise excused for bringing down a house’s ruin upon himself together with his enemies (Judg. 16), except because the Spirit who worked miracles through him had secretly commanded it (chapter 22). Excepting, therefore, those whom either a just law commands generally, or God himself, the source of justice, commands to be killed, whoever kills a human being—whether himself or any other—is bound by the crime of homicide.

Again (chapter 26). This we say, this we affirm, this we establish in every way: no one ought to inflict voluntary death upon himself, as though fleeing temporal troubles lest he fall into eternal ones; no one on account of another’s sins, lest by that very act he begin to have the gravest sin of his own; no one on account of his past sins, for which he has greater need of this life so that they may be healed through repentance; and no one as though from desire for the better life hoped for after death, because a better life after death does not receive those guilty of their own death.

## CHAPTER 5.—That one who kills himself should be deprived of Mass and offerings. *Capitulary*, book VII, chapter 70.

[Col. 0693A]

Concerning one who kills himself or hangs himself with a noose: it has been decided that, if anyone compassionately wishes to give alms, let him give them, and let prayers be made in psalmody; nevertheless, let him be deprived of offerings and Masses.

## CHAPTER 6.—On the same matter. Council of Auxerre, chapter 17.

Whoever of his own will throws himself into water, ties his neck, casts himself from a tree, strikes himself in frenzy, or voluntarily gives himself up to death by any means, the offerings of such persons are not to be received.

## CHAPTER 7.—That the Church kills no one. From Augustine’s *Dialogues against Petilian* (book against Petilian’s letters, chapter 49).

[Col. 0693B]

You said: “The traitor perished by a noose; he left nooses for such people.” This has no bearing at all upon us, for we do not honour as martyrs those who have tied a noose around their own necks.

## CHAPTER 8.—That compensation for a slain priest must be paid to his bishop. *Capitulary*, book V, chapter 90 (book IV, chapter 15).

Compensation for a slain priest shall be paid to the bishop to whose parish he belongs.

## CHAPTER 9.—Concerning compensation for a subdeacon, deacon, priest, bishop, or monk. Likewise, chapter 26 (book III, chapter 25).

(17, q. 4, c. *Subdiaconum*.) Whoever kills a subdeacon shall pay three hundred solidi; whoever kills a deacon, four hundred; a priest, six hundred; a bishop, [Col. 0693C] nine hundred; a monk, four hundred.

## CHAPTER 10.—Concerning the penance of one who kills a cleric or monk. Book VI, chapter 90.

(17, q. 4, c. *Qui occiderit*.) Whoever kills a monk or cleric shall lay aside his weapons and serve God in a monastery for all the days of his life, never to return to secular life; and he shall perform public penance for seven years.

## CHAPTER 11.—That a judge bears the sword for condemning criminals. Haimo, on the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 13.

(23, q. 5, c. *Sunt quaedam*.) There are certain monstrous crimes which are judged rather by the judges of the world than by bishops and governors of churches—for example, when someone kills the apostolic pontiff, a bishop, priest, or deacon. Kings and secular princes condemn persons guilty of such offenses. Therefore the judge does not bear the sword without cause (Rom. 13), when he adjudicates such crimes [the original reads *judicat*, “judges”]. They are established especially for murderers and robbers: to condemn them and to restrain others by fear of them.

## CHAPTER 12.—Concerning a man convicted of having been an accomplice in the murder of his bishop. Gelasius to Philip and Cassiodorus.

The case of Celestinus is such as I do not think you yourselves are unaware of. For this man, convicted as an accomplice in the murder of his spiritual father and bishop, as the record of the proceedings shows, was judged by everyone to be entirely unworthy of the office of the altar. For so detestable a deed, communion was forbidden him for one year, so that through suitable repentance he might remedy the breach caused by so great a crime. Even if we had by no means ordered this, he himself, reflecting all the more upon the sacrament of Christ’s body, ought to have returned to it with a more purified mind. Yet we consider that this period has either been completed or is nearly elapsed; after it, there can be no doubt that he may have access to communion, so that the synodal sentence may be lifted and he may be cleansed, to his greater benefit, through fuller satisfaction.

## CHAPTER 13.—Concerning a similar case. Gelasius to John, bishop.

We are moved by the impious presumption of Asellus, who held the office of archdeacon. For when the bishop had been mortally wounded in so grievous an occurrence, Asellus above all others ought to have guarded the church and prevented anything from being removed from the bishop’s household; yet he allowed the bishop himself to be killed amid the disturbance. He ought also to have been kept for confession, to determine whether he performed these acts of his own will or when driven by another’s instigation; and ecclesiastical property ought first to have been demanded from him, because he is said to have been the creditor of the murdered bishop. Who indeed cannot plainly understand that this was especially why it was said that the bishop had been removed so swiftly: so that he might not reveal his accomplices and so that the unknown resources of the church might more easily lie open to plundering? For the bishop’s written schedule of properties is reported to have been found, and the worthy Asellus, a good man and fitting for his rank, compelled a decree concerning himself to be pronounced first—having coerced the Church’s ministers—before a report of the death had been sent, according to ancient procedure, to the notice of the Apostolic See. What Christian can doubt how intolerable an evil this is? Although, when a bishop dies even by the common lot of humanity, his passing should first of all be announced, an appropriate visitation appointed, and only then discussion held about appointing a successor, this man alone appeared to have thought immediately of his own advancement after the murder of the bishop, rather than to have taken care to report what had happened. Although what was being done may outwardly remain concealed, the abrupt attempt to seize authority does not free from suspicion the conscience of one who thus seeks the dead man’s place. Meanwhile, lest anyone should ever dare to usurp what no one before this man had dared, by our authority let him be removed from the office he held, until we have considered more fully what ought permanently to be decided concerning such a person. If he is convicted of having taken any property belonging to ecclesiastical right, he must in every way be compelled to restore it.

## CHAPTER 14.—Concerning the penance of a priest who kills a priest. Alexander II to Amalgerius, bishop of Civita.

[Col. 0694D]

Know that, in consideration of mercy, we have imposed the following penance upon this brother, whom you sent to the Apostolic See to undergo the judgment of canonical penance for the guilt of homicide he committed. Since a priest killed a priest, he ought to do penance fourfold—that is, for twenty-eight years. We have mercifully imposed fourteen years upon him, irrevocably deposing him from the priesthood and from every ministry of the altar. He shall observe these fourteen years in the following manner: for the first three years he is to remain outside the church, except at the point of death, without communion, participation in the table, or the peace. But he shall be reconciled solely to the Lord’s Supper until the octave of Pentecost. During this present Lent he shall fast daily on bread and water for three days of each week, until Easter. From the octave of Pentecost until the feast of Saint Michael, for two days; thereafter, for three. After three years, when communion of the Church and table has been restored to him, he shall remain among the laypeople until seven full years have been completed, observing the whole period of penance in the same manner. And because it is fitting that he be under the rule of an abbot, we command you to send him to some monastery, so that there he may be saved through worthy penitence; and if it seems fit to you or to the abbot to grant him remission, if you see that he has worthily observed the penance, it may be permitted after three years.

## CHAPTER 15.—Concerning the purgation of a priest who had been accused, without accusers, of the death of his bishop. Alexander II to Rainald, bishop of Comminges.

[Col. 0695B]

With respect to the case of your priest Guilland, who has been accused of the death of his bishop, your predecessor, we have taken counsel in common. Therefore, with the unanimous assent of all the brethren present, we write to your belovedness that the aforesaid priest Guilland is to be brought before you. If reliable accusers are lacking there, then justice requiring it, without any dispute, let the priest recover both the priesthood and whatever benefices he has unjustly lost on that account. Nevertheless, we leave to your judgment the requirement that, before this, where the accuser fails, he himself furnish his purgation, with two priests joined to him. Finally, we do not wish either that he undergo, or that you in any way demand of him, the popular ordeal—unsupported by any canonical sanction—of boiling or cold [Col. 0695C] water, contact with red-hot iron, or any other popular device; for such things are altogether fabricated by envious contrivance. Indeed, by apostolic authority we most firmly forbid them.

## CHAPTER 16.—On the penance of one who killed a priest attacking him with weapons. Alexander II to the clergy of Vulturnum.

The bearer of this letter, coming to us as a penitent, reported that, at the instigation of the devil, he killed a certain armed priest who rushed upon him and struck at him. Since the canons provide that a simple penance is to be imposed for the killing of an armed priest, we have imposed a penance of ten years: from now until Easter he is to fast three days each week on bread and water, and is not to use [Col. 0695D] shoes or linen. From the octave of Pentecost until the feast of St Martin, he is to fast two days each week; and from the feast of St Martin until the Nativity of the Lord, either he is to undergo confinement, fasting daily on bread and water, or go into exile and fast three days on bread and water. From the octave of Epiphany until Lent, he is to fast two days. From Lent until Easter, he is to fast three days on bread and water; and he is to do this for five years. Moreover, he is to abstain from entering the church and from communion for seven years.

## CHAPTER 17.—Excommunication by John VIII of those suspected of the death of a Roman cleric.

Those suspected of the homicide of Roman, a religious cleric, who, having been summoned by us under the threat of canonical excommunication in June of the present eighth indiction, contemptuously failed to appear, and who for this reason were summoned a second and third time by our letters, and finally deprived of all communion through John and Leo, bishops—because they are proved hitherto to have evaded the judgment of the apostolic see, neither appearing nor sending representatives—we decree, by the authority of the Holy Spirit, that they are anathematized until the coming Kalends of October of the coming ninth indiction, when they may deserve to clear themselves canonically. If, however, they do not then show us the fullest satisfaction, let them remain bound by perpetual anathema, so that whoever henceforth communicates with them in food, drink, or prayer shall be bound together with them by an equal sentence of anathema.

## CHAPTER 18.—On those who killed two of their bishops: that they should henceforth remain without a bishop. Gelasius to the bishops Majoricus and John.

[Col. 0696B]

The double slaughter of Latin bishops has indeed confounded us by the atrocious horror of its dreadful crime, so that the resolution of our deliberation long hesitated, since we doubted whether to impose any bishop upon people whose examples were parricidal. Therefore, now avoiding, as it were, a sacrilegious usage and custom, we have judged it necessary to provide for religion to the extent that the functions of the diocese are administered by priests stationed outside it; for those dwelling there have learned to kill their shepherds with the sword. By an unheard-of crime—one which has never anywhere at all happened even in provinces afflicted by continual and varied incursions of war—[Col. 0696C] this city has been found which, without a persecutor, strikes down the bishops who minister to it the Christian faith. Care must therefore be taken that the deadly destruction there may be healed by the absence of its own bishops, and that thus at least the material of such great madness may be removed; in this way, either, having none upon whom to rage, it may desist from such recklessness, or it may not offer a dreadful contagion for others to imitate. Let the city, then, lack episcopal assistance, supplied to it from elsewhere, since it cruelly stained with shed blood the sacred dignity established in its own bosom. (The text reads *quia*, “because”; Victorius has *qui*, “those who.”) For in either case it is to be punished by this retribution: whether it commits this wickedness through domestic prompting or driven by frenzied passions from without.

## CHAPTER 19.—If a bishop has been killed, another is not to be substituted until the culprits have been discovered and punished. Nicholas to John, Archbishop of Ravenna.

[Col. 0696D]

Our apostolic office has grieved deeply over the most cruel murder of Oleobert, bishop of Gravellum, and has been afflicted with great sorrow. Yet we are no less astonished at your prudence, if it is true that your people have sent a bishop there without our permission, although, as you say, it was not lawful for one to be sent. Certainly, even if nothing else prevented it, that crime alone ought for a little while to have restrained you from quickly appointing a bishop among and for such a people, where sick sheep, imitating the crime of the Jews against the Lord and Savior, dared to cut down their own shepherd. Wait therefore a little, and investigate with utmost diligence the cause which you do not know, according to blessed Job (Job 29), lest perhaps—unless a worthy inquiry [Col. 0697A] comes first—you be found to have laid hands, God forbid, upon a head full of blood. But when the guilty have been discovered and punished, and one worthy of the office has appeared, and agreement has been reached among clergy, people, and our duke, who possesses our authority and is himself known to be one of that same people, let the election be held. Then, as was deliberated and established in synod, make this known to us; and when the elected person has been reported to our apostolic see, with the Lord’s help and after the prescribed authorization, let him be consecrated bishop by your blessedness.

## CHAPTER 20.—On those who scourge and kill bishops. Nicholas to Tado, Archbishop of Milan.

Concerning the scourgers and killers of priests—that is, robbers—who are not restrained by the secular arm, [Col. 0697B] it is fitting, according to the Lord’s command (Matt. 18), that they be approached in brotherly love a second and third time. If they do not listen to you, then, with the Church assembled, we grant authority to deprive them of the Eucharist; and if, despising priestly admonitions, they perhaps persist in their obstinacy, we grant authority to cut them off from the body of the Church under the ban of anathema. Yet you should know that, when they come to their senses and have first made worthy satisfaction, they may finally be restored to the bosom of holy mother Church.

## CHAPTER 21.—On an abbot who struck a servant once with a stick, and who died six months later. Alexander II to Aumold, Bishop of Constance.

We have learned from your letters that their bearer, namely a priest and abbot, violently provoked by anger, struck his servant once on the back with a stick, and that the man so [Col. 0697C] struck died—according to a conjecture admitted as possible—only after six months had elapsed. Consequently, he has been marked as if by the guilt of homicide; he has incurred danger to his rank and, we judge, suffered shipwreck of his dignity. In this matter—without prejudice to the privilege of your order—somewhat hasty severity seems both to have established a precedent and especially to have exceeded the measure of discernment. It seems to us that this should be moderated by a more merciful restraint. If your brotherhood hesitates concerning the discernment to be exercised here, let it read the testimony of Gregorian authority.

Likewise: We command your fraternity to restore this brother to his abbacy; and, if a year of penance has already elapsed, to restore him to priestly office and permit him to minister at the holy altars.

## CHAPTER 22.—On the penance of a woman who killed a maidservant by whipping her. From the First Council of Elvira, chapter 5.

[Col. 0697D]

(Distinction 50, chapter *Si qua femina*.) If any mistress, inflamed by jealous rage, beats her maidservant with lashes so that she expires in torment within the third day, because it is uncertain whether she killed her intentionally or by accident: if intentionally, she is to be admitted to communion after seven years; if accidentally, after five years’ periods of lawful penance. But if the maidservant becomes ill after the third day, let her receive communion.

## CHAPTER 23.—On one who ordered a woman to be beaten with sticks. Gregory to Andrew, Bishop of Taranto (*Book II*, indiction 11, letter 44).

Because you assigned a woman from the register of dependents to be cruelly beaten with sticks, contrary to the order of the priesthood, [Col. 0698A] although we do not think that she died as a result after eight months, nevertheless, because you were unwilling to have regard for your rank, we decree that you abstain from the administration of Masses for two months.

Likewise (the same pope to John, Bishop of Callipoli, letter 45): Although we do not believe that the woman from the register whom he had punished with sticks died as a result after eight months, nevertheless, because he caused her to suffer in this way contrary to the rule of his profession, suspend him from the solemn celebration of Masses for two months.

## CHAPTER 24.—On the punishment of a priest who struck a deacon. Nicholas to Hosbald, Bishop of Quadrantum.

Let your holiness endeavor to persuade your bishop to associate with himself the canonical number of fellow bishops—that is, brethren and your fellow bishops from neighboring provinces. [Col. 0698B] With them joined to you and rendering judgment, investigate diligently and make every effort to examine whether the said deacon died, as is reported, from the blow of the above-named priest or from a broken neck. If he was not struck to death by the frequently mentioned priest, but fell from a horse and died with a broken neck, then, at your discretion, impose a fitting penance upon the priest who acted imprudently in striking him, and suspend him for some time from the solemnities of Mass; afterward he may return to priestly office. But if the deacon truly died from any blow inflicted by that priest, we decree that he is in no circumstance to minister in the manner of a priest. For even if he did not intend to kill, nevertheless rage [Col. 0698C] and indignation, from which that deadly impulse proceeded, are forbidden in every person in many ways, and condemned everywhere—especially in ministers of God. But if, through your investigation, the priest is perhaps found so culpable, we command that such a benefice from his church be granted him as will provide sufficient support for both himself and his household.

## CHAPTER 25.—On the seven- or five-year penance of killers. From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 22, and the Council of Tribur, chapter 52.

For homicides committed unintentionally, the earlier ruling prescribed the completion of penance after seven years, while the later one prescribed completion of a five-year term.

## CHAPTER 26.—On examining the case of a certain priest. John VIII to Sigigod, Bishop of Narbonne.

[Col. 0698D]

The bearer of this letter, having appeared before the apostolic see, declared in a plaintive and lamenting voice that he was a priest, and that he had been suspended from the office of priesthood by bishops of the diocese subject to your holiness and subjected to certain other penances pending our special judgment. The reason, he says, is that during a disturbance a certain man seized him, lifted him from the ground by the arms, and hurled him violently against his own brother, so that this brother, driven to the ground by the weight of such an impact, fell and, thrown down and crushed, violently lost the breath of life. Finally, since those reverend bishops, as he reported, were in doubt whether he ought wholly to be deprived of the office previously entrusted to him, they decided that this should be determined and decided not by themselves but by our judgment.

But they ought to have acted in this solemn manner only if they had first themselves fully heard and carefully examined the priest’s case according to the canons, with four persons appointed for delegated judgment and persons from the venerable decrees and laws present; [Col. 0699A] then, after a written report had been made, if anything appeared doubtful or difficult to them, they should have sought our decision on the matter according to ancient custom. But since both the identity of the informant is unknown to us and no recommendation in writing from the bishops has been verified, and since moreover there is no accusation by an accuser, no confession of guilt by the accused, and no confirmation by trustworthy witnesses, we can neither credit his account alone nor pronounce against him a definitive sentence of condemnation. [Col. 0699B] Therefore, at least now, let your fraternity, vested with metropolitan authority, associate with itself six bishops subject to you or from neighboring sees, together with the bishop of the diocese to which this man belongs; let it sift so great a matter through the sieve of careful investigation; and, having found what is just, let it decide canonically and determine it by the common judgment of the brethren.

## CHAPTER 27.—Those who crush their sleeping children are to be considered killers. Stephen to Ludbert, Bishop of Mainz.

(2, question 5, *Consuluisti*.) You also asked concerning infants found dead while sleeping in one bed with their parents, whether the parents ought to clear themselves by red-hot iron, boiling water, or any other ordeal, that they did not crush them. Parents should be warned [Col. 0699C] and solemnly admonished not to place such tender children with themselves in one bed, lest through any negligence the children be suffocated or crushed, and the parents thereby be found guilty of homicide. For the sacred canons do not judge that a confession is to be extracted from anyone through the ordeal of red-hot iron or boiling water; and what has not been sanctioned by the teaching of the holy Fathers must not be presumed by superstitious invention. Public offenses, disclosed by voluntary confession or the corroboration of witnesses, are to be judged by those in authority with the fear of God before their eyes; hidden and unknown matters are to be left to the judgment of Him who alone knows the hearts of the children of men. But those proved or confessing themselves guilty of such an offense are to be punished by your moderation. For if one who destroys by [Col. 0699D] abortion a child conceived in the womb is a killer, how much more can one who kills even an infant one day old not excuse himself from being a killer?

## CHAPTER 28.—On the penance of those who have committed homicide unintentionally. Nicholas to Bishop Charles and his suffragans.

Concerning those who have committed homicide unintentionally, you have in chapter 22 of the Council of Ancyra a ruling concerning how they ought to perform penance.

Likewise: After the space of one year, killers may be permitted to enter the church.

## CHAPTER 29.—A priest who is a killer is to be deprived of priestly office. Nicholas to Tado, Archbishop of Milan.

Therefore, concerning priests who have committed homicide unintentionally and yet incur the guilt of homicide, by which [Col. 0700A] they are truly killers, we decree that, removed from priestly ministry, they are to be chastened by penance according to the sacred ordinances. After the prescribed periods of penance have passed and they have offered worthy satisfaction, let them obtain the grace of communion. The most holy canons in all respects, and the decrees of the pontiffs of the apostolic see, remain unimpaired; by these we do not deny mercy and the entrance of the Church to converts and penitents, but rather salutarily exhort and command that they be granted.

## CHAPTER 30.—On mercy to be extended to those who came upon a homicide but committed it neither by intention nor deed. Alexander II to Wilfred, Bishop of Constance.

The bearers of this letter stated that they had not at all been present at the homicide for which penance had been imposed upon them, but had merely come upon persons fighting by chance. If this is so, since they were neither involved in the homicide nor guilty of it, moved by mercy toward them, we have remitted their exile by apostolic authority.

## CHAPTER 31.—On the penance of those who commit homicide during the Truce of God. Alexander II to Adelard, Bishop of Soissons.

We do not grant authority to your decision extending to thirty years the penance for homicide committed during the Truce of God, because we do not find this in the sacred canons. Nevertheless, since the Truce of God was established by prudent and religious men to preserve peace among the people, we do not reject it in any way.

## CHAPTER 32.—A mule-driver is culpable if mules which, through inexperience or weakness, he could not restrain trample a person. *Digest*, Book IX, title II, on the Lex Aquilia, law 8.

[Col. 0700C]

If through lack of skill a mule-driver cannot restrain the rush of his mules and they trample another person, he is commonly said to be liable on the ground of fault. The same is said if, because of weakness, he could not restrain the rush of the mules. Nor does it seem unjust that weakness should be counted as fault, since no one ought to undertake a weakness that will be dangerous to others. The same rule applies to one who, because of his inexperience or weakness, cannot restrain the rush of the horse he was riding.

Likewise (Book X): Harmful play, too, constitutes fault.

## CHAPTER 33.—On the penance of one who killed three children. Pope Nicholas to Rivoladrus, bishop (letter 17).

[Col. 0700D]

Know that this Wimar hastened to the thresholds of the apostles and made known the manner of penance imposed upon him for the homicide of his three children. We moderated certain parts of it, because he hastened devoutly to seek the intercession of the prince of the apostles, our patron. For the urgency of the time called him back when he wished to go to the shrine of the blessed Archangel; and apostolic concern sent to your holiness a letter containing the terms of the rule imposed upon him.

Accordingly, it was established therein that for three years he should stand before the doors of the church, praying for his sins. Then he should remain among the hearers for four years, so that he should pass seven years [Col. 0701A] without communion in the body and blood of the Lord. During all the days of his life he is not to eat meat; during these seven years he is not to drink wine, except on Sundays and feast days. Thereafter, for five years, he is to abstain from wine three days each week, so that the term of penance extends to twelve years. It is therefore permitted to him not to abandon his own wife, lest he fall into adultery and, through the occasion of one offense, be cast by the frailty of the flesh into something worse. We have allowed him to come to you wearing shoes, and thereafter he must go barefoot for three years; he may wear garments according to the condition [“quality,” original edition] of the season and temperature of the air, and may use milk. But, discerning his conduct in this way, weigh and arrange everything carefully, so that both evangelical mercy may be recognized in him and canonical authority preserved. [Col. 0701B] Nevertheless, we permit him to eat cheese, to retain his possessions, and, after the seventh year, to persevere in the above-mentioned penance until the day of his death; nor may he bear arms except against pagans.

## CHAPTER 34.—It is not lawful for priests to fight. Letter of Pope Zachary at the head of the *Capitularies*, to all bishops established in the kingdom of the Franks (Book V, chapter 1; and Zachary, letter 3).

Even now, because of sins, you have false and erring priests. Hence all pagan nations prevailed over you while you were fighting, because there was no distinction between laypeople and priests, for whom [Col. 0701C] it is not lawful to fight. What kind of victory is given where priests celebrate the mysteries of the Lord and offer Christians the Lord’s body for the redemption of their souls, and afterward kill with their own sacrilegious hands Christians to whom they ought to minister this sacrament and pagans to whom they ought to preach Christ?

## CHAPTER 35.—A priest who is a killer is not to minister. Zachary to Boniface.

We wrote to you that no killer, adulterer, or fornicator—and no penitent—is to touch the sacred ministry, but that a priest should be such as the sacred canons declare him to be. Your fraternity asks concerning persons baptized by him and churches consecrated by him: if, while exercising the priesthood, he consecrated churches in the name of the Trinity [Col. 0701D] or likewise baptized infants, then the consecration of the churches and baptism of the infants are to be confirmed.

## CHAPTER 36.—A killer or adulterer is not to accuse a bishop. From the First Epistle of Clement to James.

(6, question 1, chapter *B. Petrus*.) The Lord taught that murderers, adulterers, all persons bound by criminal offenses, and those not equal in rank to bishops were to be forbidden from harassing or accusing bishops. He taught that no charge should be brought against them except by their equals, because it is in no way fitting that a disciple should be above his master (Matt. 10), or inflict any injury upon him.

## CHAPTER 37.—Killers, poisoners, and persons notorious for other crimes are not to be admitted to accusation. From the letter issued by Pope Adrian to Ingelrann, Bishop of the city of Metz, chapter 67 (63).

[Col. 0702A]

Murderers, evildoers, thieves, sacrilegious persons, robbers, poisoners, adulterers, those who have committed abduction, borne false witness, or resorted to diviners and magicians, are never to be admitted either to accusation or to testimony.

## CHAPTER 38.—Killers and false witnesses are to be excluded from communion. From the Council of Agde, chapter 37.

(24, question 3, chapter *Itaque*.) We have decreed that killers and false witnesses are to be excluded from ecclesiastical communion unless they wash away their committed offenses by the satisfaction of penance.

## CHAPTER 39.—On the penance of one who commits voluntary homicide. From the Council of Bishop Martin, chapter 10 (Martin of Braga, chapter 78).

[Col. 0702B]

(Distinction 50, chapter *Si quis*.) If anyone commits voluntary homicide, let him always remain prostrate at the door of the catholic church and receive communion only at the end of his life. But if he commits homicide not intentionally but by some accident, the earlier canon directed him to perform penance for seven years; the later one ordered five.

## CHAPTER 40.—What is to be done with a bull if it kills a person. Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 81, on chapter 21.

If a bull strikes a man or woman with its horn and the person dies, the bull shall be stoned and its flesh shall not be eaten; but the owner of the bull [“of the bull” is absent in the original edition] shall be innocent. Justice requires that an animal harmful to human [Col. 0702C] beings be killed. What is stated of a bull is to be understood as a part standing for the whole: it applies to any animal subject to human use that is dangerous to people.

## CHAPTER 41.—A person is not to be killed except at the command of law. *Capitulary*, Book I, chapter 64 (67).

No person shall be killed except at the command of law.

## CHAPTER 42.—On the punishment of one who kills another after making peace. Capitularies, Book III, chapter 4.

If anyone kills another after a reconciliation, he shall make compensation for him, lose the hand by which he swore falsely, and in addition pay the lord’s *ban*.

## CHAPTER 43.—No one is to punish a person except for justice. *Capitulary*, Book V, chapter 197.

Whoever, through hatred or malicious design, and not for the sake of [Col. 0702D] doing justice, punishes a person shall lose his honor and make amends, according to the laws, to the person against whom he acted unjustly, in proportion to the punishment he inflicted.

## CHAPTER 44.—On the punishment of one who kills a penitent. Capitularies, Book IV, chapter 18.

Whoever kills a person performing public penance shall pay our *ban* threefold and pay that person’s *wergild* [variant: *uverghildum*] to the deceased’s relatives.

## CHAPTER 45.—A priest is to shed neither Christian nor pagan blood. *Capitulary*, Book VII, chapter 124 (92).

Priests shall shed neither Christian nor pagan blood.

## CHAPTER 46.—The intention to kill is reckoned as homicide. Chapter 212 (151).

[Col. 0703A]

Whoever voluntarily wishes to kill a person but cannot carry it out shall be punished as a murderer.

## CHAPTER 47.—On the delay judges should grant a person before he is killed. Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, Book IX, chapter 30.

(Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chapter 17, but somewhat differently.) When Ambrose heard of a massacre full of great lamentation, and when the emperor Theodosius came to Milan and wished solemnly to enter the sacred church, Ambrose met him outside at the doors and barred his entrance over the threshold with these words:

> “Emperor, you do not know how great is the enormity of the slaughter [“killing,” original edition] you have committed; nor, after the pause following such rage, does your mind recognize the weight of its presumption. But perhaps imperial power prevents acknowledgment of sin; yet reason ought to prevail over power [variant: “lead power”].”

Likewise. In the same place, after much intervening matter, Ambrose said to the emperor:

> “Because, he says, you have entrusted your judgment to rage, and reason did not pronounce the sentence but anger rather, write a law that will annul the decrees of rage: for thirty days [the *Tripartite History* is now read: ‘so that for thirty days,’ etc.] let a sentence of death or proscription remain only in writing, and await the judgment of reason. When those days have passed and anger has ceased, let reason judge the case and determine truthfully for itself what it has learned. During these days it will be recognized whether the sentence you issued is just or unjust. If reason proves that what was issued is unjust, it shall cancel it; if just, it shall confirm it. The number of days will suffice for this examination.”

The emperor gladly accepted this warning, believed it excellent, immediately ordered the law to be written, and confirmed it by the writing of his own hand. When this had been done, Ambrose released his bond. This law is observed to this day. It reads as follows:

> “The Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius Augustus, to Flavian, Praetorian Prefect of Illyricum. If, contrary to our custom and in view of the circumstances of a case, we order more severe punishment against any persons, we do not wish them immediately either to undergo the penalty or receive sentence; rather, for thirty days their lot and fortune concerning their status shall remain in suspense.”

## CHAPTER 48.—Blessed Ambrose barred Emperor Theodosius from entering the church because of indiscriminate killing. From the *Life of St Ambrose* (by Paulinus).

[Col. 0703D]

Ambrose separated the greatest emperor from participation in communion, admonishing him to perform penance for the shedding of his own lord’s blood—and, what was more serious, of an innocent person’s blood—if he wished to provide for his standing before the Lord. The affair of the city of Thessalonica brought Ambrose no small distress when he learned that the city had almost been destroyed. For the emperor had promised him that he would grant pardon to the citizens of the aforesaid city; but while the counts dealt secretly with the emperor, without the priest’s knowledge, the city was given over to the sword until the third hour, and many innocent persons [Col. 0704A] were killed. When the priest learned what had happened, he denied the emperor permission to enter the church, judging him unworthy of the congregation of the Church or communion in the sacraments until he performed public penance.

## CHAPTER 49.—On various forms of homicide and their punishment. *Institutes*, Book IV, title III, on the Lex Aquilia.

If anyone wrongfully kills another’s slave or another’s four-footed animal belonging to the class of livestock, he shall be condemned to pay the owner the highest value that thing had in that year. The provision is not made concerning every four-footed animal without distinction, but only one belonging to the class of livestock. Accordingly, we understand that it does not cover wild beasts or dogs, [Col. 0704B] but only animals properly said to be pastured in herds, such as horses, mules, asses, oxen, sheep, and goats. The same has been held concerning swine, for swine too are included under the term “livestock,” because they too are pastured in herds.

Likewise, a little later: One is understood to kill wrongfully when one kills without any legal right. Thus, one who kills an ambushing robber is not liable, provided that he cannot otherwise escape the danger. Nor is a person liable under this law who kills by accident, provided that no fault of his is found; otherwise, indeed, a person is liable under this law no less for fault than for wrongful intent. Thus, if anyone, while playing or practicing with javelins, pierces your passing slave, a distinction is made. If this occurred through a soldier on a field where it is customary to train, no fault is attributed to him. [Col. 0704C] If another person did such a thing, he is liable for fault. The same rule applies to a soldier if he did it in a place other than that designated for the training of soldiers.

Likewise, if a pruner, by a branch thrown down from a tree, kills your passing slave: if this happens near a public or neighborhood road and he did not call out so that the accident might be avoided, he is liable for fault. But if he called out and the other person took no care to avoid danger, the pruner is without fault. He is likewise understood to be without fault if, perhaps, he was cutting away from a road or in the middle of an estate, even if he did not call out, because no outsider had any right to be in that place. Moreover, if a physician who has operated on your slave abandons treatment and the slave consequently dies, he is liable for fault. Lack of skill too is counted as fault—for example, if a physician kills your slave because he performed the operation badly [Col. 0704D] or administered medicine improperly. Likewise, if your slave is crushed by the rush of mules which a mule-driver could not restrain through lack of skill, the mule-driver is liable for fault. But even if, through weakness, he could not restrain them when another stronger person could have done so, he is equally liable for fault. The same has been held concerning one riding a horse who, through weakness or lack of skill, could not restrain its rush.

By the words of the law, “the highest value it had in that year,” this rule is expressed: if anyone kills your slave, who today is lame, maimed, or one-eyed, but who at some point in that year was sound or of high value, he is liable not for the value the slave has today but for the highest value he had [Col. 0705A] in that year. For this reason, the action under this law has been considered penal.

Likewise, in the same place somewhat later: If anyone kills one mule from a team of mules, one horse from a four-horse team, or one slave from a company of comic actors [*comoedi*, “colleagues”], the valuation is made not only of the one killed, but in addition account is taken of the amount by which those remaining have been diminished in value.

Likewise, near the end: If anyone confines (Victorius: *induxerit*, “leads into”) another’s slave or animal in such a way that it dies of hunger; drives a beast of burden so violently that it bursts; harasses livestock so greatly that it falls over a precipice; or persuades another’s slave to climb a tree or descend a well, and the slave dies while climbing or descending, [Col. 0705B] or is injured in some part of the body, an action in factum is granted against him. But if anyone throws another’s slave from a bridge or bank into a river and the slave is drowned, it may readily be understood that he caused damage by throwing him with his own body; therefore he is liable under the Lex Aquilia.

## CHAPTER 50.—On the condemnation of one who kills a lame or one-eyed person. *Institutes*, Book IV, title VI.

If anyone kills a lame or one-eyed person who was sound and of great value during that year, he is condemned to pay the highest value that person had during that year. [“That person” is inserted in the original edition.]

## CHAPTER 51.—A priest who is a killer is to be deprived of the priesthood. John VIII to Cennomoc, Bishop of Venice (the same above, Part VI, chapter 114).

[Col. 0705C]

I am astonished at your ill-informed opinion that a priest can minister in the priesthood after committing homicide—or rather, what is more absurd, that you wish to persuade us to give assent to such presumption. For who would be so mad and of such perverse judgment as to think that such a thing should be permitted even after any length of penance, when it is contrary to all canonical discipline? Therefore, deprived of the priesthood, he must wash away so enormous an offense with a fountain of tears, so that, cured at least by such remedies, he may find aid toward salvation.

## CHAPTER 52.—On the excommunication and irrevocable deposition of a bishop who committed homicide. John VIII to Emperor Louis.

The manner in which Rainald, bishop of Castrum Felicitatis, was publicly denounced concerning homicide before both the apostolic and imperial sees; how, after our beloved son Gregory the nomenclator had been sent, and the apocrisiary of our holy see was present with George, the illustrious master of soldiers, and the *venestarius* of our sacred patriarch, before our most beloved daughter, the Empress Augusta; how he was accused by the mother of the slain young man and other relatives; and how, compelled by frequent letters of excommunication from us to clear himself, he came to Rome—all this, we believe, is known to your serenity. But because, having come to Rome, he forestalled the time set for his purgation and, when a synod had been appointed for his case, fraudulently abandoned the place assigned to him by us, cast himself down like a thief over the city walls [Col. 0706A], and by evading judgment demonstrated that the accusations brought against him were true, we utterly exclude him, by the authority of almighty God, of the chief apostles, and of our own humble office, from every ecclesiastical and Christian communion.

## CHAPTER 53.—It is not homicide if a burglar breaking into a house at night is killed. Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 84.

If a thief is found breaking in and is struck dead, there is no charge of homicide against the one who struck him (Exod. 22). But if the sun has risen over him, he is guilty, and shall die the death. It is therefore understood that the killing of a thief is not homicide when the thief is killed at night, but that it is homicide if he is killed by day. This is what the text means when it says: “If the sun has risen over him” [Col. 0706B]; for it could be discerned that he had come to steal, not to kill, and therefore ought not to be killed (Digest, On the Lex Aquilia, book IV). This is also found in the ancient secular laws—though this law is older than they are—that a nocturnal thief may be killed with impunity; likewise a daytime thief, if he defends himself with a weapon [Augustine now reads: “in any manner whatever”; but, “a daytime thief, however, if with him,” etc.; and so does the ancient manuscript of St. Germain], for he is now more than a thief.

### CHAPTER 54.—That those who, out of zeal for the Church, kill excommunicated persons are not to be considered murderers. Urban II, to Godfrey, bishop of Lucca.

According to the custom of the Roman Church, which you know, impose upon those who kill excommunicated persons an appropriate measure of satisfaction according to their intention. For we do not judge them murderers because, burning with zeal for their Catholic mother, they may have happened to slaughter any of those who were excommunicated [Col. 0706C]. Yet, lest the discipline of the same mother Church become excessively harsh, prescribe for them the suitable penance of which we have spoken, by which they may be able to propitiate against themselves the eyes of divine simplicity, if perhaps, through human frailty, they have contracted any duplicity in this offense.

### CHAPTER 55.—Concerning those who kill fetuses in the womb. Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book I, chapter 15.

(32, question 2, chapter “Sometimes.”) Sometimes this lustful cruelty—or cruel lust—goes so far as to procure drugs producing sterility; and, if these accomplish nothing, it somehow extinguishes and casts out the conceived fetuses within the womb, wishing its own offspring to perish before it lives, or, if it was living in the womb, to be killed before it is born [Col. 0706D]. Indeed, if both are such persons [“such to one another,” original], they are not spouses; and if they were such from the beginning, they came together not by marriage but rather by fornication. But if both are not such, I dare say: either she is in some sense her husband’s prostitute, or he is his wife’s adulterer.

### CHAPTER 56.—Why the law did not treat an unformed embryo as homicide. Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 80, on chapter 21.

(32, question 2, chapter “But as for the unformed.”) In not wishing the killing of an unformed embryo to count as homicide, the law certainly did not reckon that which is carried in the womb in such a condition as a human being. Here the question of the soul is usually discussed: whether what is not yet formed can also be understood as not yet ensouled [Col. 0707A], and therefore whether it is not homicide because it cannot be called a being deprived of life if it did not yet possess a soul. Again, in the same place shortly afterward: If that unformed embryo already existed [“will have existed,” original], but was still in some way ensouled in an unformed manner, then, because a great question concerning the soul must not be precipitately decided by the rashness of an unexamined judgment, the law did not wish it to count as homicide, because a living soul cannot yet be said to be in that body which lacks sensation.

### CHAPTER 57.—That the soul is infused into a formed body. Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, chapter 23.

(32, question 2, chapter “Moses.”) Moses handed down: “If anyone strikes a pregnant woman and she miscarries: if it is formed, he shall give life for life; but if it is unformed, he shall be fined money” [Col. 0707B] (Exod. 21), in order to prove that there is no soul before formation. Therefore, if it is given to an already formed body, it is not born along with the seed at the conception of the body, derived from soul. For if soul exists from soul together with the seed, many souls perish daily when seed, by some discharge, does not advance to birth. But if we look more closely [“more nearly,” original], we shall see what conclusion we ought to follow.

Let us contemplate the making of Adam: for in Adam an example was given, so that it may be understood from him that the body, once formed, received a soul. For God could have mixed the soul with the clay of the earth and thus formed the body; but the reason for the arrangement was that the house first had to be constructed and then its inhabitant introduced. Certainly, because the soul is spirit, it cannot dwell in what is dry; therefore it is borne in the blood. When, then, the outlines [of the body, original] have not been joined together [Col. 0707C], where will the soul be?

### CHAPTER 58.—Concerning the unformed body. Jerome to Algasia, question 4 (vol. IV, epistle beginning: “My son Apodemius”).

(32, question 2, chapter “Just as seeds.”) Just as seeds are gradually formed in the womb, and the matter is not reckoned homicide [“a human being,” original and Gratian] until the elements are completed and assume their proper shapes and members, so a conception of the mind, unless it has burst forth into action, is still retained within the womb and quickly perishes in miscarriage [“by an enemy,” Gratian] (Exod. 21).

### CHAPTER 59.—That the good justly and piously persecute the wicked, whereas the wicked unjustly persecute the good. Augustine to Count Boniface, epistle 50.

[Col. 0707D] (23, question 4, chapter “If the Church.”) Let the schismatics ask the Apostle what Church Sarah signified when she persecuted the slave woman. For he says that our free mother, the heavenly Jerusalem—that is, the true Church of God—was prefigured in that woman who afflicted the slave woman (Gal. 4). Yet, if we examine the matter more carefully, Hagar persecuted Sarah more by her pride than Sarah persecuted Hagar by restraining her. The former wronged her mistress; the latter imposed discipline upon pride.

Then I ask: if good and holy people persecute no one but merely suffer persecution, whose voice do they suppose it is in the psalm where one reads: “I shall pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I shall not turn back until they fail” (Ps. 14)? Therefore, if we wish to speak or acknowledge the truth [Col. 0708A], there is an unjust persecution which the impious carry out against Christ’s Church, and there is a just persecution which Christ’s Church carries out against the impious. Thus the former is blessed because it suffers persecution for righteousness’ sake (Matt. 5); the latter are miserable because they suffer persecution for unrighteousness’ sake. Accordingly, the Church persecutes in love, they in rage; the Church in order to correct, they in order to overthrow; the Church in order to call back from error, they in order to hurl into error. Finally, the Church pursues its enemies and overtakes them until they fail in vanity; they pursue in order that they may advance in vanity.

Again, in the same place, after much intervening matter. (22, question 6, chapter “Schismatics.”) The schismatics say: “Upon whom did Christ inflict force? Whom did he compel?” Behold, they have the apostle Paul: let them recognize in him Christ first compelling and afterwards teaching, first striking and afterwards consoling (Acts 9). It is remarkable [Col. 0708B] how he who entered the Gospel compelled by bodily punishment labored in the Gospel more than all those who were called by word alone (1 Cor. 15); and how the greater fear that compelled him to charity was cast out by his perfect charity (1 John 4). Why, then, should the Church not compel its lost children to return, if lost children have compelled others to perish?

Moreover, even those whom they did not compel but merely seduced, if they are recalled to her bosom by frightening but salutary laws, the kindly devout mother embraces more tenderly; and she rejoices over them far more than over those whom she had never lost (Luke 15). Does it not belong to pastoral care to bring back to the Lord’s sheepfold, by the terror—or even the pain—of scourges, should they resist, those sheep which were not violently snatched away but have strayed from the flock through gentle and mild seduction [Col. 0708C], and have begun to be possessed by strangers?

Again, a little later. We have shown that Paul was compelled by Christ. Therefore the Church, in compelling these persons, imitates her Lord. She first waited, so as to compel no one, until the prophetic preaching concerning the faith of kings and nations should be fulfilled. In this connection one may also reasonably understand that apostolic saying in which blessed Paul declared: “Ready to punish every disobedience, when your prior obedience has been fulfilled” (2 Cor. 10). Hence the Lord himself, at his great supper, first commands guests to be brought in, and afterward to be compelled. For when his servants answered him: “Lord, what you commanded has been done, and there is still room,” he said: “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel whomever you find to enter” [Col. 0708D] (Luke 14). Therefore, in those who were first gently brought in, the prior obedience has been fulfilled; but in those who are compelled, disobedience is restrained.

Again, a little later. If, by the authority which the Church received through the religion and faith of kings at the time when it ought to have received it by divine gift, those who are found in the roads and hedges—that is, in heresies and schisms—are compelled to enter, they should not criticize the fact that they are compelled, but consider the end for which they are compelled.

Again, after much intervening matter. (23, question 3, chapter “Maximianus.”) Bishop Maximianus of Vaga sought assistance from the Christian emperor against the enemies of the Church, not so much for the sake of avenging himself as of protecting the Church entrusted to him. Had he neglected this, it would not have been patience worthy of praise [Col. 0709A], but negligence rightly deserving blame. For the apostle Paul likewise took thought not for his own transitory life but for the Church of God, when, against those who had conspired to kill him, he arranged for their plan to be reported to the tribune (Acts 21). As a result, an armed soldier escorted him to the place to which he was to be taken, lest he suffer their ambushes.

Again, in the same place, some time later. (23, question 5, chapter “For who?”) For who among us would wish not only any enemy to perish, but even anything belonging to him to be lost? Yet if the house of David could have peace in no other way than by the destruction of Absalom, his son, in the war which he was waging against his father—although David had earnestly commanded his men to preserve him alive and safe if they could, so that paternal affection might have someone to forgive if he repented—what remained for David except to weep for the lost man and, once peace had been obtained for his kingdom, to console his own grief? [Col. 0709B] (2 Kings 18).

### CHAPTER 60.—That no one is fit to exercise punishment unless he has overcome hatred by gentleness of love. Augustine, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, book I, chapter 37.

(23, question 4, chapter “That punishment.”) The punishment which serves correction is not forbidden; indeed, it itself belongs to mercy. Nor does it hinder that disposition by which someone is prepared to endure still more from the person whom he wishes to be corrected. But no one is fit to inflict such punishment unless he has overcome, by the gentleness of love, the hatred with which those who desire revenge ordinarily burn. For it need not be feared that parents appear to hate their little child when he is beaten by them for sinning, lest he sin further. And surely the perfection of love is set before us in imitation of God the Father himself, when it is said in what follows: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute you” (Matt. 5).

Yet it is said of God himself through the Prophet: “Whom the Lord loves he corrects; moreover, he scourges every son whom he receives” (Prov. 3; Heb. 12). And the Lord says: “The servant who does not know his master’s will and does things worthy of stripes shall be beaten with few stripes; but the servant who knows his master’s will and does things worthy of stripes shall be beaten with many” (Luke 12). Therefore, only this is required: that the one who has been given authority by the order of things should himself punish [Col. 0709D], and should punish with the intention with which a father punishes his little child, who by reason of his age cannot yet hate him.

For here a most evident example is given, by which it sufficiently appears that sin can be punished in love rather than left unpunished: so that the one whom he punishes may wish not to be made miserable by punishment but blessed by correction, while nevertheless being prepared, if need be, calmly to endure further unlawful injuries [“inflicted,” original] from the person whom he wishes to be corrected—whether he has power to restrain him or not.

(*Ibid.*, chapter 38.) Great and holy men, however, who already knew very well that this death which separates soul from body is not to be feared, nevertheless punished some sins by death, having regard to the minds of those who feared it, so that useful fear might be instilled into the living, and that death itself might not harm those punished by it [Col. 0710A], but rather the sin that might increase if they lived. Such men did not judge rashly, since God had bestowed such judgment upon them. Thus Elijah put many to death, both with his own hand and with fire obtained by divine petition (3 Kings 18; 4 Kings 1). Many other great and divinely inspired men, acting in the same spirit and taking thought for human affairs, did this without rashness.

When the disciples cited the example of Elijah to the Lord, recalling what he had done and asking that they too be given power to request fire from heaven to consume those who would not offer them hospitality, the Lord rebuked them (Luke 9). He did not rebuke the example of the holy prophet, but their ignorance of punishment (Matt. 22), observing that they did not love correction [“love,” original, manuscripts of St. Germain] [Col. 0710B], but desired vengeance from hatred. Therefore, after he taught them what it was to love one’s neighbor as oneself, and after the Holy Spirit had also been poured out—the Spirit whom, when ten days had been completed after his ascension, he sent from above as he had promised (Acts 2)—such acts of punishment were not lacking, although they were much rarer than in the Old Testament. For there, servants were for the most part held down by fear; here, free persons were chiefly nurtured by love. Thus Ananias and his wife fell dead at the words of the apostle Peter, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 5), and were not restored to life but buried.

### CHAPTER 61.—That one who unjustly persecutes a Christian is an enemy of Christ. Augustine, *Against Cresconius the Grammarian*, book III, chapter 51.

[Col. 0710C] “Whoever wickedly persecutes a Christian,” you say—Augustine has “you say,” so that these are Cresconius’s words—“is an enemy of Christ.” You speak truly, provided he does not persecute in that Christian what is hostile to Christ [“but not,” manuscripts of St. Germain]. For must not a master in his servant, a father in his son, and a husband in his wife, though both parties are Christians, persecute vices contrary to Christian truth? Or, if they do not persecute them, will they not deservedly be held guilty of negligence?

### CHAPTER 62.—That restraining one’s neighbor is loving him. Augustine to Macedonia, epistle 52.

(25, question 4, chapter “He ought.”) A person ought to love his neighbor as himself, so that, by the consolation of beneficence, the instruction of teaching, or the restraint of discipline, he may bring to the worship of God any person whom he can [Col. 0710D].

### CHAPTER 63.—That an evil will must not be left to its own freedom. Augustine to Donatus the presbyter, epistle 204.

Those who are loved must not be cruelly and with impunity left to their own evil will; but, where authority is given, they must both be prohibited from evil and compelled toward good. For if an evil will must always be left to its own freedom, why were the Israelites, when they refused and murmured, restrained from evil by such severe scourges and compelled toward the land of promise? If an evil will must be left to its own freedom, why was Paul not permitted to employ the worst will by which he persecuted the Church, but was struck down so that he might be blinded (Acts 9), blinded so that he might be changed, changed so that he might be sent, and sent so that [Col. 0711A] he might suffer for the truth the same things that he had done in error? If an evil will must always be left to its own freedom, why is a father admonished in the Holy Scriptures not only to rebuke a stubborn son with words but also to beat his sides (Sirach 7; 30), so that he may be compelled to good discipline and may love the Lord [“compelled and subdued, he may be directed”]?

### CHAPTER 64.—That people must be corrected. Augustine to the Donatists, epistle 166.

“The one that had strayed,” says the Lord, “you did not bring back; and the one that had perished you did not seek” (Ezek. 34). This the Lord himself does to you through us: whether by entreating, threatening, correcting, losses, hardships, his hidden admonitions or visitations, or the laws of temporal authorities [Col. 0711B].

### CHAPTER 65.—That not everyone who kills a person is a murderer. Chrysostom on Matthew, homily on chapter 18, in the *Unfinished Work* on Matthew chapter 5.

(23, question 8, chapter “Phinehas killed.”) Phinehas killed a man (Num. 25), and it was reckoned to him for righteousness. Abraham, however, became not merely a murderer but even a parricide—which is certainly more serious (Gen. 22)—and yet pleased the Lord all the more. Peter too committed a double homicide (Acts 5), yet what was done was a spiritual act. Therefore let us not consider deeds alone, but let us examine most diligently the time, cause, intention, difference of persons, and whatever other circumstances attend the deeds themselves. For we cannot otherwise arrive at truth [Col. 0711C].

### CHAPTER 66.—On the same matter. From the replies of Pope Adrian to certain objections, to Charles, chapter 16.

Saint Gregory recalls in his *Dialogues* how blessed Boniface, with a sorrowful utterance, struck to death that wretched man who came with a monkey and beat cymbals.

### CHAPTER 67.—Likewise on the same matter. Gregory, *Dialogues*, book I, chapter 9.

When blessed Boniface came to Fortunatus’s table, before he had sung a hymn to God, a man suddenly stood before the door with a monkey and struck a cymbal, as certain people accustomed to seeking their livelihood by the art of singing do. Hearing the sound, the holy man said indignantly: “Alas! Alas! That wretched man is dead; that wretched man is dead! I have come to the table for refreshment; I have not yet opened my mouth in praise of God, and he has come with a monkey and struck a cymbal.” Yet he added: “Go, and for the love of God [“of God,” omitted in the base text] give him food and drink; but know that he is dead.”

When the unhappy man had received bread and wine from the same house and wished to go out through the door, a huge stone suddenly fell from the roof and struck him on the crown of the head. From that blow he fell prostrate and was lifted up in their hands, already half alive. Then, on the following day, in accordance with the pronouncement of the man [“man of God,” Victorius], he entirely ended his life. From this, Peter, one must consider how great a fear ought to be shown toward holy men. For they are temples of God; and when a holy man is provoked to anger [Col. 0712A], who else is stirred to anger but the indweller of that same temple? Therefore the anger of the righteous is to be feared all the more because it is certain that he who is present in their hearts is not powerless to inflict whatever punishment he wills.

Likewise, *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 30. (23, question 8, chapter “Peter.”) Peter raised Tabitha from death by prayer (Acts 9); by rebuking Ananias and Sapphira for lying, he consigned them to death (Acts 5). It is not recorded that he prayed for their destruction, but only that he rebuked the fault they had committed. It is clear, therefore, that such things are sometimes performed by authority and sometimes granted in response to petition: by rebuke he took life from the latter two, but by prayer restored it to the former.

### CHAPTER 68.—Concerning the punishment which Pope John ordered to be inflicted upon certain persons. John VIII to Marinus and Pulcarius.

[Col. 0712B] We also enjoin upon you the charge [“the first fruits,” Victorius] of your loyalty: immediately dispatch with some ships your strongest soldiers, so that, together with our infantry, they may seize the forty Saracens who recently fled to sea in ships belonging to our Greeks and who afterward, though stripped of all their arms by our land soldiers, escaped by their strength into hiding places on Mount Circeius. For we do not wish to weary our dromons over so few Saracens, since we are urged to place every confidence in you—as, indeed, you too are said to desire.

For if from now on we perceive in your dealings with the holy Roman Church the steadfastness of your obedience and the purity of your faith joined with effective courage [Col. 0712C], then not only shall we relieve you, insofar as reason requires, of those three burdens by which you say that you are oppressed beyond custom, but, with the Lord’s strengthening, we shall also endeavor to protect you by land and sea as the proper household of Saint Peter.

### CHAPTER 69.—Concerning the defense which he made against enemies. John VIII to Empress Engelberga.

Indeed, by the power of God we shall defend what is ours better than Gaeta, and we have absolutely no need of theirs: we are building dromons along with other ships, and other engines and equipment of war; indeed, we are preparing the very spirits of men and arming them without ceasing against hostile attacks.

### CHAPTER 70.—That one who does not correct crimes when able to do so commits them. John VIII to the glorious Duke Domagoj.

[Col. 0712D]

(23, question 8, chapter “Moreover.”) Moreover, we exhort the zeal of your devotion to be stirred up all the more vigorously against the sea-robbers who, under the pretext of your name, rage against Christians, inasmuch as you know that the reputation of your name has been darkened by their wickedness. For although it may be believed that they waylay sailors against your will, nevertheless, because they are said to be capable of being restrained by you, if you do not restrain them, you will not be held innocent. For it is written: “He who does not correct crimes when he has the power to amend them, commits them himself.”

### CHAPTER 71.—How Pope John resisted the Saracens. John VIII to the emperor and empress.

[Col. 0713A]

When we had returned, we found all our coasts plundered, and many Saracens remaining even on our estates and at Terracina as though in their own house. Therefore, after remaining in the city no more than five days, although we were held by no small bodily infirmity, we went out with our faithful men. With the Lord’s help, we captured eighteen ships from them. Many Saracens were killed, and we freed nearly six hundred captives. It is therefore most necessary, when you come, that such a force of men remain on the seacoasts, by whose courage all that is ours may remain safe and places not yet plundered may not be plundered.

### CHAPTER 72.—That to punish evildoers for God is not cruelty but piety. Jerome to Riparius (vol. III, epistle beginning: “Having first received the letters”).

[Col. 0713B]

I read of the spearing of Phinehas (Num. 25), the severity [“authority,” Victorius] of Elijah (3 Kings 18; 4 Kings 1), the zeal of Simon the Canaanite (1 Macc. 13 and following), the sternness of Peter in killing Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5), and the constancy of Paul, who condemned Elymas the magician, resisting the ways of the Lord, to perpetual blindness [“severity,” Victorius] (Acts 13). It is not cruelty to punish crimes for God [Gratian: “to punish crimes for God”], but piety. Hence it is also said in the law: “If your brother, friend, or wife who is in your bosom should wish to lead you astray from the truth, let your hand be upon them and pour out their blood” (Deut. 13).

### CHAPTER 73.—That, for the suppression of evildoers, arms are to be borne in the company of bishops. Leo IV to King Louis [Lothair].

[Col. 0713C]

We shall never receive Peter and Adrian to live with us. And if—as we scarcely believe—you have regarded as nothing either our entreaties, which we sent you for their detention, or the honors of the Roman pontiff, and have loved us less than Adrian and Peter, we declare to your greatness what we have now determined for the future.

Certainly, the bishops of the Roman See, when they traveled through the various churches with their clergy for the service of Mass or, according to custom, to arrange other ecclesiastical business, carried nothing except priestly vestments, as did their clergy [Col. 0713D]; and following this practice, we too have done so until now. But it is no longer right to act thus if you determine to send men whom we neither seek nor ever wish to send. And we make this final declaration for certain: whenever we travel to any church or other place rightly subject to us, lest they exult over the danger of our death, although for divine worship or prayer we ought to carry only a stole and a chasuble, we shall order a lance, shield, and sword to be carried.

### CHAPTER 74.—That priests may pronounce death against the impious. From the history of Anastasius, librarian of the Roman Church.

Moved by great divine zeal, the most pious Emperor Michael, acting upon the exhortations of the most holy Patriarch Racephorus and of other Fathers, decreed capital punishment against the Manichaeans called Paulicians [Col. 0714A]. But he was turned away from this by other wicked counselors, under the pretext of repentance, although it was impossible for those captured by error to repent. They ignorantly maintained that priests ought not to pronounce death against the impious, opposing in every respect the divine Scriptures on this point. For if the chief of the apostles put Ananias and Sapphira to death merely for lies (Acts 5), and the great Paul cries: “Those who do such things are worthy of death” (Rom. 1)—and he says this concerning mortal sin alone—how will they not be opponents of these authorities, if they rescue from the sword persons full of every spiritual and bodily impurity and serving demons?

### CHAPTER 75.—That judges who persecute heretics and schismatics and seize their property are not to be blamed, but praised. From Augustine’s *Dialogues against Petilian*, book II, chapter 10.

[Col. 0714B]

Petilianus said: “Did the apostles persecute anyone, or did Christ hand anyone over?” Augustine replied: “I could indeed say that Satan himself is worse than all evil men, and yet the Apostle handed a man over to him for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus (1 Cor. 5). Likewise, others of whom he says: ‘Whom I have handed over to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme’ (1 Tim. 1). And the Lord drove the wicked merchants out of the temple with a whip (John 2), where the testimony of Scripture is also joined, saying: ‘Zeal for your house has consumed me’ [Col. 0714C] (Ps. 68).

“Behold, we find the Apostle one who hands over, and Christ a persecutor. Why, then, through most violent mobs, are you yourselves even unprovoked hostile to the Catholic churches wherever you can manage it, as the matter itself shows by countless examples?
