But you say that you defend your own places, and resist with sticks and blows in whatever way you can. Why have you not there heard the voice of the Lord saying: ‘But I say to you, do not resist evil’ (Matt. 5)? Or if it can happen that one sometimes rightly resists violent persons by physical force, and does not thereby violate the command which we hear from the Lord, ‘But I say to you, do not resist evil,’ why can it not likewise happen that, through duly constituted and lawful authorities, the godly man expels the ungodly, and the just man the unjust, from seats which are unlawfully usurped [Col. 0714D] or retained to the injury of God?

“For the false prophets did not suffer persecution from Elijah in the manner in which Elijah himself suffered it from a most wicked king; nor, because the Lord was scourged by persecutors, are those whom he himself drove from the temple with a whip to be compared with his sufferings. It remains, therefore, that you must admit that nothing else is to be investigated except whether you separated yourselves justly or wickedly from the communion of the whole world. For if it is found that you did so wickedly, do not be surprised if ministers of God are not lacking through whom you are scourged; because you suffer persecution, not from us, but, as it is written, from your own deeds (Wis. 2).”

Likewise (in the same book, ch. 43; 23, q. 7, c. *Si de rebus*):

“If you complain concerning ecclesiastical property or places [Col. 0715A] which you once held and do not hold, the Jews too may call themselves just and charge us with injustice, because Christians now possess the place in which the ungodly formerly ruled. What, then, is improper if Catholics possess, according to the equal will of the Lord, what heretics possessed? For that saying of the Lord applies to all such persons—that is, to all ungodly and unjust persons: ‘The kingdom of God shall be taken away from you and given to a nation producing righteousness’ (Matt. 21). Was it written in vain: ‘The righteous shall eat the labours of the ungodly’ (Ps. 104)? Therefore you ought rather to wonder that you still retain anything than that you have lost something.”

Likewise (ch. 59):

“If you have begun to possess certain things already cut off, because the Lord gave us what was taken from you, we do not therefore covet another’s goods; for by the command of him to whom all things belong, [Col. 0715B] they have become ours, and are justly ours. For you used them for separation; we, for unity. Otherwise they might charge the first people of God with coveting another’s property—those who were driven out from before them by divine power because they made evil use of that land. And the Jews themselves, from whom the kingdom was taken, according to the Lord’s words, and given to a nation producing righteousness (Matt. 21), can charge the Church of Christ with coveting another’s goods, because it possesses the places where Christ’s persecutors ruled.”

Likewise (ch. 79; 25, q. 4, c. *Qui peccat*):

“He who sins does not sin by the authority of the law, but against the authority of the law. Since you ask what is the ground for persecution, I in turn ask you whose voice it is in the Psalm that says: ‘Him who secretly slandered his neighbour, I persecuted’ [Col. 0715C] (Ps. 100). Therefore inquire into either the cause or the manner of persecution, and do not, through such ignorance, condemn persecutions of evildoers indiscriminately.”

Likewise (at the end, ch. 80):

“That Christ also persecuted bodily those whom he drove from the temple by scourging (John 2), we have already said above.”

Likewise (ch. 82):

“Nor do we persecute you except as truth persecutes falsehood.”

Likewise (ch. 83; 23, q. 5, c. *Ad fidem*):

“No one is to be compelled to the faith; but through the severity—indeed, also through the mercy—of God, faithlessness is customarily chastised by the scourges of tribulations. Because excellent conduct is chosen by freedom of will, does it follow that the worst conduct is not punished by the integrity of the law? Yet the punitive discipline of evil living is misplaced unless the preceding teaching of good living has been despised. [Col. 0715D] Therefore, if any laws have been enacted against you, you are not compelled by them to do good, but prohibited from doing evil. For no one can do good unless he chooses and loves it; and this belongs to free will.”

(Ch. 84.)

“When kings enact measures against you, believe that you are being admonished to consider why you suffer these things. If it is for righteousness’ sake, then they truly are your persecutors, while you are blessed because, having suffered persecution for righteousness, you shall possess the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 5). But if it is because of the wickedness of your schism, they are indeed your correctors, while you, like the guilty of other various crimes who pay penalties under the laws, are certainly unhappy both in this world and in the world to come.”

Likewise (ch. 88; [Col. 0716A] 23, q. 3, c. *Pro membris*):

“On behalf of Christ’s members, all those among the Catholics rage against you and resist you who are so disposed [Augustine adds: ‘still of little faith’] as Peter then was when he drew the sword in Christ’s name (Matt. 26). But there is a great difference between your persecution and theirs. You are like the servant of the priest, because, serving your leaders, you arm yourselves against the Catholic Church—that is, against Christ’s body. But these persons are such as Peter then was, who fight even bodily for Christ’s body, that is, for the Church.”

Likewise (there, ch. 92, near the end):

“If Nebuchadnezzar was not a persecutor because he most justly avenged the crime committed against holy Daniel (Dan. 6), how ought kings to avenge it when Christ’s sacraments are scornfully rejected, if the members of a prophet deserved to be so avenged because they had been exposed to danger?” [Col. 0716B]

Likewise (there, ch. 104):

“Let no one flee from God’s sacraments in a good man, nor in a bad man.”

Likewise (*Against the Letters of Petilian*, book 3, ch. 10):

“If a friend who praises is not to be believed, neither is an enemy who disparages.”

Likewise (ibid., ch. 36):

“Among us, all who are wicked either are wholly concealed, or, though known to some, are tolerated for the sake of the good to whom they are unknown and before whom they cannot be convicted, because of the bond of unity and peace (Eph. 4), lest the wheat be uprooted together with the tares (Matt. 3). Thus they bear the burden of their own wickedness (Gal. 6).”

(Augustine, ch. 8, book *On the One Baptism against Petilian*.)

“I think that no one can rightly be judged innocent who has believed a person guilty although that person has not been convicted.” [Col. 0716C]

Likewise (ch. 59):

“Who could endure his assertion that Christ’s sacraments are sacrilegious, even if, as he falsely alleges, those rites celebrated in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit according to the Gospel rite were administered by traitors? Perhaps he will now say that what is given by sacrilegious persons is no longer Christ’s sacrament. Why, then, does he not also say that the name of Christ, pronounced by sacrilegious persons, is no longer Christ’s name?”

Likewise (there, ch. 13):

“O how detestable [Augustine adds: ‘is the error of human beings’] is the error of those who think themselves laudably to imitate certain acts of distinguished men which were not rightly done, although they are strangers to those men’s virtues. Thus some may also compare themselves to the Apostle Peter if they deny Christ (Matt. 26).”

Likewise (there, [Col. 0716D] ch. 16):

“If there is such humanity in human affairs, I think we could more justly be reproached if we believed guilty rather than innocent persons unknown to us whom our enemies accuse, when they offer no proof of their charge by any testimony. For if perhaps the truth is otherwise, humanity itself is at least given its due when one man rashly suspects nothing evil of another, nor readily believes any accuser, when one who alleges a crime without witness and without any evidence has proved to be rather a slanderer hurling abuse than a truthful accuser.”

Likewise (*On the Unity of the Church against the Letter of Petilian*, ch. 2):

“If what they accuse has occurred, what sin did the ecclesiastical judges commit, since they could by no means condemn charges, even if true and brought before them, which nevertheless had not been proved to them?”

Likewise (there, ch. 17):

“But if holy and canonical Scripture proves that you have set up altars against the Church of Christ, separated yourselves by sacrilegious schism from Christian unity—which is spread throughout the whole world—and oppose Christ’s body—which is the Church spread throughout the whole world—by rebaptizing, blaspheming, and attacking it as far as you can, then you are ungodly and sacrilegious. But those who decree that you are to be deterred and restrained from so great a crime by the comparatively mild warnings of losses of property, places, honours, or money, so that, reflecting on why you suffer these things, you may recognize and flee your sacrilege and be freed from eternal condemnation, [Col. 0717A] are regarded as most diligent rulers and most godly counsellors.”

Likewise (somewhat earlier):

“Your complaint concerning persecution will be quieted if you first consider [Col. 0717B] and understand that not every persecution is blameworthy. Otherwise it would not be said commendably: ‘Him who secretly slandered his neighbour, I persecuted’ (Ps. 100). For every day we see a son complain of his father as though of his persecutor; a wife of her husband; a servant of his master; a tenant farmer of his landholder; an accused person of the judge; and a soldier or provincial of a commander or king. Yet these persons often, through a most orderly authority, restrain and check those subject to them by the fear of light punishments from graver evils; but they also often deter them from good life and good deeds through threats and violence. When, however, they prohibit evil and unlawful conduct, they are correctors and counsellors; but when they prohibit good and lawful conduct, they are persecutors [Col. 0717C] and oppressors. Even those who prohibit evil are blamed if the measure of correction exceeds the measure of the fault.”

### Chapter 76.—That it is charity to correct one’s neighbour. Augustine, vol. IX, *On the First Epistle of John*, tractate 7.

(23, q. 5, c. *Non putes*.)

“Do not think that you love your servant when you do not beat him; or that you love your son when you do not give him discipline; or that you love your neighbour when you do not correct him. This is not charity but weakness. Let charity burn with zeal to amend and correct: let good conduct delight us, but let bad conduct be corrected.”

### Chapter 77.—On the same subject. Augustine, *City of God*, book XIX, ch. 16.

[Col. 0717D]

“It is not innocence, by sparing someone, to allow him to fall into a graver evil. Therefore it belongs to the office of an innocent person not only to inflict evil on no one, but also to restrain from sin or punish sin, so that either the person previously hated may be corrected by experience, or others may be frightened by the example.”

### Chapter 78.—That no one may lawfully kill with the sword except a judge. Augustine, *Questions on the New and Old Testaments*, ch. 104.

When the Apostle Peter saw hostile persons rising up, he drew his sword and cut off the ear of the priest’s servant. Then Jesus told Peter to put his sword back into its sheath: “For everyone,” he said, “who takes the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. 16). Why did he order swords to be prepared, when he forbade striking, even marking as liable to death [Col. 0718A] [“marking him also as liable to death”] the person who had struck with the sword, although the Apostle does not seem to have struck unjustly? For, as far as the matter [Peter] was concerned, he struck someone whom he saw armed against him. He ought indeed to have resisted ungrateful servants armed to kill the Lord.

Likewise (somewhat later):

“Why, considering the action of the Apostle Peter, did the Lord say that he who uses the sword shall perish by the sword, though he does not seem to have struck unjustly? For, as Luke indicates, he struck with the Lord himself permitting it (Luke 22), and was then forbidden and heard these words. It was permitted so that he might appear able to avenge himself, but unwilling; so that the power might be shown to remain in him in which it had been before; and so that in both respects it might not be doubted that he could avenge himself. But the enemies were to know with certainty [Col. 0718B] that they had been given authority by him to do these things: he did not appear conquered, but to be handing himself over to their will. Why then was the sentence pronounced, that whoever takes the sword shall perish by the sword (Matt. 25), unless because no one, except a judge, may kill anyone with the sword? To the Apostle Peter it was permitted only to inflict pain, not to kill. Hearing this, he learned not to strike again. Furthermore [the commonly printed Augustine now reads: ‘For this reason he heard it, lest he strike again. He learned, furthermore, etc.’], because those who have become Christians are not permitted to kill: for those placed under mercy are not permitted to use harshly the law of right entrusted to the world.”

### Chapter 79.—That one who spares and fosters vices is not merciful. Augustine, to Laetarius [Lectarius; Gratian reads Lotharius].

[Col. 0718C]

(23, q. 5, c. *Qui vitiis*.)

“One who spares and indulges vices so as not to distress the will of sinners is no more merciful than one who does not wish to take a knife from a child, lest he hear the child crying, and does not fear that the child may suffer wounded or die.”

### Chapter 80.—That a Christian may not defend himself. Augustine, to the Donatist Emeritus (Letter 164).

“Our people seek protection from duly constituted authorities against the unlawful and private violence of your people—violence which even you who do not commit such acts there grieve over and lament—not in order to persecute them, but in order to defend themselves.”

### Chapter 81.—How blessed Ambrose defended a certain person, lest he be dragged from the church. From the *Life of Blessed Ambrose* (by Paulinus).

[Col. 0718D]

During his consulship, when the emperor Honorius was presenting spectacles of Libyan wild beasts in the city of Milan, and the people were flocking there, an opportunity was given to soldiers sent by Count Stilicho at the urging of Eusebius the prefect to drag a certain Cresconius from the church. When he fled to the altar of the Lord, the holy bishop surrounded him for protection with the clergy who were then present. But the multitude of soldiers, whose leaders belonged to the treachery of the Arians, prevailed against the few; and, having carried Cresconius away, they returned rejoicing to the amphitheatre, leaving the Church in no small mourning.

### Chapter 82.—How Pope Adrian fortified himself to resist King Desiderius. From the deeds of Pope Adrian.

[Col. 0719A]

When Adrian learned that the arrival of King Desiderius was near, he gathered the entire people of Tuscany, Campania, and the duchy of Perugia, together with some persons from the cities of the Pentapolis, and fortified this city of Rome. All were armed and ready, so that if the king himself should come, they might firmly resist him with God’s help and supported by the prayers of the aforesaid most holy pontiff. For His Holiness caused the churches of blessed Peter and Paul to be adorned, and brought all their *thymilia* [probably *cymbala*, “liturgical vessels/ornaments”] and decorations into this city of Rome. He caused all the doors of the church of blessed Peter to be shut, ordered bolts to be placed on the inside and the doors secured, so that if that insolent king should come without the pontiff’s safe-conduct [Col. 0719B] and permission, he would have no entrance into that church unless he broke down the doors by force, to the destruction of his own soul.

### Chapter 83.—On Pope Leo’s defence against the Saracens. From the register of Leo IV, to Louis [Lothair] Augustus.

Accordingly, since adverse reports often arrived from the Saracens’ quarter, saying that certain persons would come secretly and stealthily into the Roman harbour, we ordered our people to assemble and resolved to go down to the seashore; and we went out from Rome.

### Chapter 84.—On the same matter. Leo IV to Emperor Louis.

[Col. 0719C]

“You ought to know that we never allow our people to be oppressed by anyone; but if necessity befalls them, we immediately take vengeance for them, because in all things we must be avengers and foremost helpers of our flock.”

### Chapter 85.—Likewise on the same matter. The same, to Archbishop John.

“Know for certain that we never permit our people and subjects to be torn apart or oppressed by you. But if—which we do not expect—you disregard the words of this our warning and henceforth inflict any oppression upon the aforesaid or other persons belonging to us, we shall immediately avenge them and shall take care to seize all that is yours, with raging and cruel boldness.”

### Chapter 86.—How he sought assistance from the judge of Sardinia. The same, to the judge of Sardinia.

[Col. 0719D]

“We have thought it right to beseech Your Highness to deign to send us as many armed men—whether boys, adults, or youths—with their weapons as your magnificence shall deem fit, who may be able to carry out our daily commands.”

### Chapter 87.—That those killed in defence of Christians attain the kingdom of heaven. The same, to the army of the Franks.

“Putting aside all fear and terror, strive to act manfully against the enemies of the holy faith and the adversaries of all lands.”

Likewise:

“Wherever your ancestors have hitherto set public forces in motion, they have always proved victorious, and no multitude of people [Col. 0720A] has been able to overcome them. For we have not heard that they ever returned without the renown of victory.”

Likewise:

“We desire all your charity to know that whoever—though we say it not wishing it—shall faithfully die in this conflict of war, shall by no means be denied the heavenly kingdoms. For the Almighty knows, if any one of you dies, that he dies for the truth of the faith, the safety of his country, and the defence of Christians; therefore he shall receive from God the reward appointed beforehand.”

### Chapter 88.—On the condemnation of certain men, George, Adrian, and Peter. The same, to Lothair Augustus.

Concerning those three men, George, Adrian, and Peter, now publicly condemned and rejected: Your Sublimity directed us that they ought still to confess before another tribunal. We were wholly astonished, since, with your envoys present, a sentence had already been fixed and pronounced against them according to Roman law. And unless the feast of Easter had then been at hand, during which it is not lawful to pronounce sentence because the law forbids executions, their wickedness and unjust presumption would not have allowed them to live. For this reason, therefore, the sentence against both parties was suspended only for a time. [Col. 0720B]

### Chapter 89.—On the excommunication of Thasmo, duke of the Bavarians. The same, from the Chronicle of the Franks.

Pope Adrian, on the holy day of Easter, in the presence of Emperor Charles, anathematized Thasmo, duke of the Bavarians, unless he obeyed that emperor, his sons, and the Frankish people in all things, as he had sworn to the emperor’s father Pippin and to Charles himself. If he refused, and bloodshed or any other evil should result, responsibility would lie upon that duke and his adherents, while the aforesaid king and his followers would be free from that guilt. [Col. 0720C]

### Chapter 90.—Pope Gregory’s exhortation to defend the Roman pontiff. Gregory to Velox, master of the soldiers (Register, book XII, letter/chapter 21).

“It seemed useful that a number of soldiers be sent there, whom Your Glory should endeavour to admonish and exhort to be ready for toil.”

Likewise:

“If you learn that the unspeakable Arnulf is making incursions here or into the Ravenna region, work upon his rear in such a way—as becomes brave men—that your reputation may, with the Lord’s help, increase still further among the Roman people [the original: ‘the Republic’] through the zeal [variant: ‘quality’] of your exertion.” [Col. 0720D]

### Chapter 91.—That King Charles, at Pope Adrian’s request, undertook war against the Lombards. From the deeds of Charlemagne, according to Alcuin.

(23, q. 8, c. *Hortatu*.)

At the request and prayers of Adrian, bishop of the city of Rome, King Charles, having been persuaded, undertook war against the Lombards; this war had previously been undertaken with great difficulty when Pope Stephen was pleading with Charles’s father [Gratian: “when the pope pleaded with his father Pippin,” etc.].

### Chapter 92.—Retraction of Augustine’s statement that he did not approve compelling schismatics into communion. Augustine, *Retractions*, book II, ch. 5.

I said that it did not please me for schismatics to be violently forced into communion by the onslaught of any secular power [Col. 0721A]; and it truly did not please me then, because I had not yet experienced either how much evil their impunity dared to commit or how much the diligence of discipline could contribute to changing them for the better.

### Chapter 93.—That one must abstain from battles in Lent and at every time, unless necessity compels. Pope Nicholas, *Responses to the Bulgarians* (ch. 46).

If no necessity presses, one must abstain from battles not only during Lent but at every time. But if an unavoidable exigency presses, then even in Lent one must without doubt not refrain from preparing for war in defence of oneself, one’s country, or the laws of one’s fathers, lest a person appear to tempt God: if one has the means to act and does not take care for one’s own safety and that of others, nor guard against injuries to holy religion. [Col. 0721B]

### Chapter 94.—That officers of judges are not condemned on account of their administration. Pope Innocent, to Bishop Eusebius, ch. 3.

A question was also asked concerning those who acted in office after baptism and either employed torture alone or even pronounced a capital sentence. The elders defined nothing about these persons in the laws; for they remembered that these powers had been granted by the Lord, that the sword had been permitted for the punishment of wrongdoers, and that God’s minister had been given as an avenger in such matters. How, then, could they condemn an action which they saw had been permitted by the Lord as its author? Therefore, concerning these persons, let us maintain what has hitherto been observed, lest we appear either to overthrow discipline or to oppose the Lord’s authority. Yet all their actions shall be preserved for them when they render their account.

Likewise:

“While the authority of the laws is exercised against the wicked, the person who pronounces the sentence will be immune.” [Col. 0721C]

### Chapter 95.—That one who punishes evil does not persecute, but loves. Pelagius to the patrician Valerian.

No one persecutes except one who compels another toward evil. But one who either punishes an evil already committed or prevents it from being committed does not persecute, but loves. For if, as some think, no one is to be restrained from evil or drawn back toward good, human and divine laws must necessarily be abolished; for justice has established punishments for the wicked and rewards for the good. But evil schism must also be repressed through external authorities. [Col. 0721D]

### Chapter 96.—That a king ought to punish evils. Cyprian, *On the Ninth Kind of Abuse*.  
(This book is now extant under Augustine’s name, vol. IX.)

(23, q. 5, c. *Rex*.)

“A king ought to restrain thefts, punish adulteries, remove the ungodly from the land, not allow parricides and perjurers to live, and not allow his own sons to act wickedly.”

### Chapter 97.—That war which protects one’s country is full of justice. Ambrose, *On Duties*, book I, ch. 27.

(23, q. 3, c. *Fortitudo*.)

“Courage which in war protects one’s country from barbarians, or at home defends the weak, or protects companions from robbers, is full of justice.”

### Chapter 98.—That a soldier who kills a person in obedience to authority is not guilty of homicide. Augustine, *City of God*, book I, ch. 26.

[Col. 0722A]

(23, q. 5, c. *Miles*.)

When a soldier, obeying the authority under which he has been lawfully appointed, kills a person, he is guilty of homicide under no law of his state. Indeed, if he does not do so, he is guilty of deserting and despising authority. But if he had acted on his own initiative and authority, he would have incurred the crime of shedding human blood. Thus, for the very reason for which he is punished if he acts without orders, he will be punished if he does not act when ordered.

### Chapter 99.—That Christian kings ought to defend mother Church. Augustine, *On John*, part I, ch. 2 (Tractate 2 on John 3).

(23, q. 4, c. *Quando*.)

“When God wishes to stir up authorities against heretics, against schismatics, against destroyers of the Church, against those who reject Christ with contempt, against blasphemers of baptism, let them not be surprised that God stirs them up so that Hagar may be beaten by Sarah (Gen. 16). Let Hagar recognize herself and submit her neck; for when, humbled, she had departed from her mistress, an angel met her and said: ‘What is the matter, Hagar, Sarah’s maidservant?’ When she complained of her mistress, what did she hear from the angel? ‘Return to your mistress’ (ibid.).

“Yet they are astonished that the shepherds of the Christian faith [the original: ‘Christian authorities’] are stirred against the detestable destroyers of the Church. If they were not stirred, how would they render an account to God for their rule? Let your charity attend to what I say: it belongs to Christian kings, rulers of the age, to desire that in their times their mother the Church be at peace.” [Col. 0722B–C]

### Chapter 100.—That one sins more grievously who hands an innocent person over to authority to be killed out of envy than the one who kills him through fear of another authority. Augustine, *On John*, part II, ch. 42 (Tractate 116 on John 19).

The one who hands an innocent person over to authority to be killed out of envy sins more grievously than the authority itself if it kills him through fear of another, greater authority. For God had given Pilate such authority that he was also under Caesar’s authority. Therefore: “You would have no authority over me,” he says, “that is, whatever little authority you have, unless this itself had been given you from above. But because I know how great it is—for it is not so great that you are wholly free to act as you will—therefore he who handed me over to you has the greater sin” (John [Col. 0722D] 19).

For he handed me over to authority not through fear but through envy; you, however, are about to exercise that same authority against me through fear. A human being ought not to kill another human being even through fear, especially an innocent person; yet to do it from zeal is far worse than to do it from fear. Therefore the truthful Teacher did not say, “He who handed me over to you alone has sin,” as though Pilate had none; rather, he said, “has the greater sin,” so that Pilate too might be understood to have sin. For one sin is not nonexistent because the other is greater.

### Chapter 101.—That a person may sometimes be killed without sin. Augustine, *On Free Will*, book I, ch. 4.

(23, q. 5, c. *Si homicidium*.)

“If homicide is the killing of a person, a person may sometimes be killed without [Col. 0723A] sin. For neither the soldier who kills an enemy, nor a judge or his officer who kills a guilty person, nor someone whose weapon, perhaps against his will and unknowingly, strikes from his hand, seems to me to sin when he kills a person.”

Evodius replies: “I agree; but such persons are not usually called murderers.”

Likewise, there, ch. 5:

“The law commands a soldier to kill an enemy; if he abstains from the killing, he suffers penalties from the emperor. Shall we dare call these laws unjust, or rather no laws at all? For no law seems to me to be law unless it is just.”

Augustine, a little later:

“I see well enough that the law is fortified against charges of this kind. In the people whom it governs, it permits lesser evils lest greater ones be committed [variant: ‘lest they be committed’]. For it is much less severe that one who lies in wait for another’s life [Col. 0723B] should be killed than that one who defends his own life should be killed; and it is a much more monstrous vice for a person to submit to rape than for the person from whom that violence comes to be killed by the person upon whom he tries to inflict it. Further, a soldier killing an enemy is a minister of the law; therefore he easily fulfils his duty with no passion. The law itself, enacted for the protection of the people, cannot be accused of any passion. For the one who enacted it, if he enacted it at God’s command—that is, at the command of eternal justice—could have acted wholly free from passion. But if he established it with some passion, it does not follow that one must obey that law with passion, since a good law may be enacted [variant: ‘made’] even by a bad person.

“For instance, if someone who has acquired tyrannical power accepts a price from a person to whom it is advantageous, and decrees that no one may carry off a woman by force for marriage [Col. 0723C], the law will not thereby be bad because the one who enacted it was unjust and corrupt. Therefore that law which commands hostile violence to be repelled by the same force for the protection of citizens may be obeyed without passion. The same may be said of all officers who are subject by law and order to whatever authorities.

“But I do not see how those persons can be blameless who, although the law is blameless, kill. They are free, therefore, to kill no one for things which they can lose against their will and which for that reason they ought not to love. For perhaps someone may doubt whether, when this body is killed, the soul is taken away in any manner. But if it can be taken away, it is to be despised; if it cannot, there is nothing to fear. Who, moreover, could doubt that chastity is established in the soul itself, since it is a virtue? Therefore it cannot be taken away by a violent rapist. Whatever, then, the person who is killed was about to take away is not wholly in our power; consequently, I do not understand how it can be called ours. [Col. 0723D] Therefore I do not condemn the law that permits such persons to be killed, but I do not find how to defend those who kill them.”

Evodius replies: “Still less can I find why you seek a defence for persons whom no law holds guilty.”

### Chapter 102.—That, when a judge punishes, he does not return evil for evil. Augustine, *On Psalm 108* (on the verse “because they set themselves against me”).

The desire for vengeance is vicious, and it belongs more to a judge to distinguish this among others than for a good person to seek it for himself. Few can discern how the punishment of enemies pleases an accuser wishing to satisfy himself with enmity, and how differently it pleases a judge [the original: “it pleases”] who punishes sins with a right will. The former returns evil for evil; the latter, even when he exacts punishment, does not return evil for evil, because he returns what is just for what is unjust. But what is just is certainly good. Therefore he punishes not from delight in another’s misery—which would be evil for evil—but from love of justice, which is good for evil. [Col. 0724A]

### Chapter 103.—That an officer killing one whom a judge has ordered killed must not do it voluntarily. Augustine, *Questions on Exodus* (Question 39 on Exodus 11).

(23, q. 5, c. *Cum minister*.)

When an officer of a judge kills someone whom the judge has ordered to be killed, he is certainly a murderer if he does it voluntarily, even though he kills one whom he knows ought to have been killed by the judge. [Col. 0724B]

### Chapter 104.—That the law, not the officer, kills a person. Augustine, *Questions on Leviticus* (Question 68 on Leviticus 19).

When a person is justly killed, the law kills him, not you.

### Chapter 105.—That even wars undertaken for peace among true worshippers of God are peaceable. Augustine, *On Various Ecclesiastical Observances*, ch. 15.

(32, q. 1, c. *Apud veros Dei*.)

“Among true worshippers of God, even wars themselves are peaceable when they are waged not from greed or cruelty but from the pursuit of peace, so that the wicked may be restrained and the good supported.”

### Chapter 106.—On acts of punishment. Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels* (book I, Question 10).

[Col. 0724C]

(23, q. 5, c. *Officia*.)

“Good persons may fulfil the offices of punishment with a good intention, as may the law and the judge.”

### Chapter 107.—That Christian discipline does not condemn all wars. Augustine, to Marcellinus (Letter 5).

“If this earthly commonwealth kept Christian precepts, even wars themselves would not be waged without goodwill, so that provision might more easily be made for the conquered toward a peaceable society of piety and justice. For one whose license for wrongdoing is taken away is usefully conquered, since nothing is more unhappy than the happiness of sinners, by which punitive impunity is nourished and an evil will, like an inner enemy, is strengthened.”

Likewise, there, a little later:

“For, if possible, even wars would be waged mercifully by good people, so that, after lawless desires were subdued, these vices might be destroyed which ought to be either rooted out or repressed [the original: ‘brought down’] under a just rule. For if Christian discipline condemned all wars, the Gospel would instead have told soldiers seeking counsel for salvation to cast away their arms and withdraw entirely from military service. But it said to them: ‘Extort from no one; make false accusations against no one; be content with your wages’ (Luke 3). Since it commanded those persons to be content with their proper pay, it certainly did not forbid them military service.”

Augustine, to Macedonius (Letter 54; 23, q. 5, c. *Non est iniquitatis*):

“One who is conquered by the fellowship not of injustice but rather of humanity is a persecutor of crime precisely in order to be a liberator of the person.”

### Chapter 108.—That royal power has not been instituted in vain. Likewise (about the middle).

[Col. 0725A]

(23, q. 5, c. *Non frustra*.) Royal power, the jurisdiction of the judge (*the sword is inserted in the original*), the torturer’s claw, the soldier’s weapons, the discipline of a ruler, and even the severity of a good father, have not been established without purpose. All these have their proper limits, causes, rationales, and benefits; when they are feared, the wicked are restrained, and the peaceable live among the wicked (*quietius*, “more peacefully,” in the original). Likewise, a little later:

When one human being is killed by another, there is a great difference whether this is done from a desire to injure or to seize something unjustly, as by an enemy or a robber; or according to an order of vengeance or obedience, as by a judge or executioner; or from the necessity of escape or rescue, as when a robber is killed by a traveler, or an enemy by a soldier. And sometimes the person who caused a death is more to blame than the one who killed; for example, if someone deceives his surety, and the latter suffers the legal penalty in his place. Yet not everyone who causes another’s death is guilty: for instance, if someone seeks illicit sex and kills himself because he does not obtain it. What if a son, fearing his father’s loving blows, perishes by falling from a height? What if someone, because another has been set free—or lest another be set free—brings death upon himself? Because of such causes arising from others’ impulses (*“other deaths” in the original*), must we either consent to crime, abolish even a father’s punishment of sin—which is carried out from zeal to correct, not to injure—or restrain works of mercy? When these things happen, we ought to feel human sorrow for them; but we ought not, lest they happen, to suppress (*reprimere*, “to suppress,” in the variant) the will to do what is right.

## CHAPTER 109.—That God must be prayed to in battle. Augustine to Boniface (*Epistle* 194).

You complain bitterly of battle, so that you are in doubt; I wish to give you useful counsel for yourself and yours. Take up weapons in your hands; let prayer strike the ears of the Creator, because when battle is fought, God looks on with the heavens open (*“with open eyes” in the original*), and grants the palm of victory to the side which he sees to be just.

## CHAPTER 110.—That wars are rightly undertaken when God or some lawful authority commands. Augustine likewise (*Augustine, Book XXII, Against Faustus*, ch. 70).

(23, q. 4, c. *Ille gladium*.) “Whoever uses the sword shall fall by the sword.” But the person uses the sword who, without a higher and lawful authority either commanding or permitting it, arms himself to shed another person’s blood. Likewise, ibid., ch. 74:

Whether God or some lawful authority commands, wars are undertaken and carried on by good persons when, in the order of human affairs, they are situated where that order itself justly obliges them either to command such things or to obey in such matters. Otherwise, when soldiers came to John for baptism and said, “And what shall we do?” [Luke 3], he would have answered: “Throw away your weapons; abandon this military service; strike no one; cast no one down.” But because he knew that, when acting thus in military service, they were not murderers but ministers of the law—not avengers of their own wrongs but defenders of the public welfare—he answered them: “Extort no one, accuse no one falsely, and be content with your wages” [Luke 3].

Likewise, a little later in the same place:

Let the Manichees hear the Lord Jesus Christ commanding that payment be rendered to Caesar which John says ought to suffice for the soldier: “Render,” he says, “to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” [Matt. 22]. For taxes are paid for this purpose: that the wages necessary for soldiers may be provided for wars.

Likewise, ibid., ch. 75. (23, q. 1, c. *Qui culpatur*.) It matters for what causes and under what authorities people undertake wars that must be waged. Yet the natural order of mortals, suited to peace, requires that the authority and decision to undertake war belong to the ruler, while soldiers owe the service of carrying out military commands to the common peace and safety. But it is not permissible to doubt that a war undertaken on God’s authority ought rightly to be undertaken. Likewise, a little later in the same place:

If a just man, perhaps serving under a king who is himself sacrilegious, can rightly wage war at that king’s command—preserving the order of civic peace—because it is certain either that what he is commanded is not contrary to God’s command, or that it is uncertain whether it is so, in such a way that perhaps the injustice of command makes the king guilty while the order of service shows the soldier innocent, how much more blamelessly does one conduct himself in the administration of wars when he makes war at God’s command—God, whom no one who serves him fails to know cannot command anything evil.

## CHAPTER 111.—On the ministers of God. Jerome on Joel (on ch. 2).

(23, q. 5, c. *Non solum*.) Not only human beings are ministers and avengers of God’s wrath against those who do evil, and do not bear the sword without cause; but so also are the opposing powers called the fury and wrath of God.

## CHAPTER 112.—That one who slays cruel persons is not cruel. Jerome on Isaiah, Book V (on ch. 13, shortly after the beginning).

(23, q. 5, c. *Non est crudelis*.) One who slays cruel persons is not cruel, although he may appear cruel to those who suffer. For a robber hanging from the gallows regards the judge as cruel.

## CHAPTER 113.—That one does well who weakens the strength of a robber or pirate. The same, on Zephaniah (on ch. 1).

(23, q. 3, c. *Si quis*.) If someone strips away the strength of a robber or pirate and renders them weak, their weakness benefits them. For weakened limbs, which they previously misused, will cease from evil work.

## CHAPTER 114.—That he is God’s minister who punishes the wicked insofar as they are wicked. The same, on Ezekiel, Book III.

(On ch. 9, at the beginning.) He who strikes the wicked insofar as they are wicked, and has instruments of killing in order to slay the worst persons, is a minister of the Lord.

## CHAPTER 115.—That a judge who punishes is not a shedder of blood, but a minister of the law (23, q. 5, c. *Qui malos*). The same, on the Epistle to the Galatians, Book II, on Galatians 3, near the end.

(23, q. 5, c. *Judex*.) A judge is not the author of crime when he overcomes wicked people.

The same, on Jeremiah (on ch. 22, at the beginning). (23, q. 5, c. *Homicidas*.) To punish murderers, sacrilegious persons, and poisoners is not the shedding of blood but the administration of laws.

## CHAPTER 116.—Why a judge is so called. Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XVIII, ch. 1.

A just war is one waged by edict for the recovery of things claimed back (*“reclaimed” in the original*), or for repelling enemies. (Ch. 15.) A judge is so called because he declares law to the people, or because he decides according to law. To decide according to law is to judge justly; for one is not a judge unless justice is in him.

## CHAPTER 117.—That the king does not bear the sword without cause. Stephen to Bishop Luitward.

The king does not bear the sword without cause, for he is an avenger against all wrongdoers [Rom. 13], so that he may restrain by terror those whom he cannot correct by wholesome admonitions. Let him therefore confidently undertake what is pleasing to God. Blessed Peter will not fail him in anything with his two-edged sword, provided that he consults for his country’s safety.

## CHAPTER 118.—That everyone may lawfully defend his own body. *Pandects*, Book I, title III.

Let us repel force and injury; for it is established by law that whatever anyone does for the defense of his own body is deemed to have been done lawfully.

## CHAPTER 119.—On the just war of the Israelites against the Amorites. Augustine, *Questions on Numbers*, ch. 44.

(*Questions on Numbers*, on ch. 21.) It should indeed be noted how just wars were waged by the children of Israel against the Amorites: an innocent passage was denied them, though it ought most equitably to have been granted by the law of human fellowship.

## CHAPTER 120.—On repelling injury. Ambrose, *On Duties*, Book I, ch. 36.

Not in inflicting injury, but in repelling it, lies the law of virtue. For one who does not ward off injury from a companion when able to do so is as much at fault as one who inflicts it.

## CHAPTER 121.—That a king serves God in one way as a man, in another as king. Augustine to Count Boniface (*Epistle* 50).

(23, q. 4, c. *Si Ecclesia in fine*.) How do kings serve the Lord in fear except by religious severity in prohibiting and punishing things done contrary to the Lord’s commands? For a king serves in one way because he is a man, and in another because he is also a king. As a man, he serves by living faithfully; but because he is also a king, he serves by establishing with suitable vigor laws that command what is just and forbid what is contrary.

## CHAPTER 122.—On the penance of those who throw down their arms in battle. First Council of Arles, ch. 3.

It has been decreed that those who throw down their arms in battle are to be excluded from communion.

## CHAPTER 123.—That soldiers ought to serve God and the churches. Gregory to Theodore the physician (*Register*, Book II, Epistle 65, or ch. 103).

It seems very harsh to me that the emperor should forbid his soldiers to serve him who has bestowed all things upon him and granted him authority not only over soldiers but also over priests. If the intention is to preserve property, could not those very monasteries which received soldiers restore others’ property and retain only persons who seek conversion?

## CHAPTER 124.—That soldiers are to be tested for three years before being received into a monastery. Gregory, *Register*, Book VIII, to all bishops concerning the law of the Emperor Maurice (Gregory, Epistle 9, Book VII, to the bishops of Sicily).

(Dist. 53, c. *Legem*.) I have taken care to send to your brotherhood the law issued by the most pious emperor: perhaps those bound by military service or public responsibilities, fleeing danger in their affairs, might enter clerical dress or be converted in monasteries. It particularly urges (*exhortans*, “exhorting,” in the original) that those entangled in secular business are not to be received too hastily into the clergy of the Church, because, while living in ecclesiastical dress no differently from the way they lived before, they make no effort to flee the world but rather to change it. If such persons seek a monastery, they are by no means to be received unless first released from public obligations. But if any from the military ranks (*“men” in the original*) hasten to be converted in monasteries, they are not rashly to be received unless their life has been carefully examined. According to the monastic rule, they must be tested for three years in their own dress and then, with God as author, receive the monastic habit.

## CHAPTER 125.—That military service is not sinful unless it is for plunder and the like. Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*, Tract 19 (*Sermon on Matthew* 19).

(23, q. 1, c. *Militare*.) Military service is not sinful; but serving as a soldier for plunder is sinful. Nor is administering the commonwealth criminal; but administering it in order rather to increase one’s private estate appears blameworthy. Therefore provision has been made for wages for soldiers, lest, while expenses are being sought, plundering (*praedo*, “robber,” in the text) should rage unchecked.

Likewise, a little later in the same place: The Lord himself said, “Render to God the things that are God’s, and to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s” [Matt. 22]. Therefore what Caesar commands must be borne; what the emperor enjoins must be endured. But it becomes intolerable when he adds to it the exaction of plunder. Likewise, somewhat later in the same place:

The soldiers questioned John, saying: “What shall we also do?” He said to them: “Do not extort from anyone, nor make false accusation; but be content with your wages” [Luke 3]. Every person who serves ought to understand himself in this way. For Scripture speaks not only of those soldiers engaged in armed military service, but each person who wears the belt of his office is enrolled as a soldier of his rank. Thus this saying may be addressed, for example, to soldiers, protectors, and all governors: whoever receives publicly assigned wages and seeks more is condemned by John’s sentence as an extortioner and false accuser.

Augustine to Count Boniface (*Epistle*, among those recently discovered and appended at the end of the letters): John did not forbid soldiers to serve under arms; he commanded them to be content with their wages [Luke 3].

## CHAPTER 126.—That soldiers are not to be thought displeasing to God. The same (ibid., a little earlier).

Do not suppose that no one serving in arms of war can please God. Among them was holy David [1 Sam. 16; Ps. 88], to whom the Lord bore such great testimony; among them also were very many righteous persons of that time. Among them was also the centurion who said to the Lord: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” [Matt. 8].

## CHAPTER 127.—That soldiers should not be received into the clergy, but into the monastic habit. From the *Life of Blessed Gregory*, Book II, ch. 16 (by John, deacon of the Roman Church).

While an almost countless multitude from both ecclesiastical and secular military service was daily converging, for various reasons, upon the clerical profession, the pastor, provident in all things, judged that they should be received not into the office of ecclesiastical dignity but only to undertake the monastic vocation.

## CHAPTER 128.—That the emperor should forbid no soldier who wishes to convert. Ibid., Book III, ch. 50.

Moreover, when Maurice—then a most avaricious and rapacious ruler—at the instigation of his enemies enacted the most ruinous law, that no soldier who had been marked on the hand might be permitted to convert, he replied among other things:

“Power over all human beings has been bestowed from heaven upon the piety of my lords for this purpose: that those who seek good may be assisted; that the way to heaven may lie more widely open; and that the earthly kingdom may serve the heavenly kingdom. And behold, it is said in an open voice that one who has once been marked in earthly military service may not serve Christ unless either his service has been completed or he has been dismissed because of bodily infirmity.”

To this also (*ecce*, “behold,” in the alternative original reading) Christ responds through me, his least servant and yours, saying: “I made you from a notary into commander of the watch, from commander of the watch into Caesar, and from Caesar into emperor; and not only this, but also father of emperors. I entrusted priests to your hand, and do you withdraw your soldiers from my service?” Answer, I ask (*“therefore” in the original*), most pious lord: what answer will you give at the judgment to your Lord who speaks these vehement words? And a little later: “May therefore the merciful Lord inquire” (*alternative reading: “me”*) which of the emperors first issued such a law, and judge more carefully whether it ought to have been issued.

## CHAPTER 129.—That an emperor who forbids soldiers to convert is opposed to God. The same, to Theodore the physician (Gregory, *Register*, Book II, Epistle 64).

“Through my sins,” he says, “by whose prompting or counsel I do not know, the emperor has promulgated such a law in his commonwealth: that no one who has conducted public business, no one who has been marked by office or on the hand, or has been counted among soldiers, may be converted in a monastery unless his military service has perhaps been completed. This law was first promulgated, as those who know the ancient laws say, by Julian, whom we all know was greatly opposed to God.”

## CHAPTER 130.—On voluntary homicides and the manner of their penance. From the Council of Tribur, ch. 4 (ch. 55, though in most respects the clauses are transposed).

If anyone has committed homicide by deliberate will, he must undertake the following penance according to the decrees of Pope Melchiades and the statutes of the Council of Tribur. First, for the next forty days he is not to be permitted to enter a church; he is to walk barefoot and use no vehicle. He is to wear woolen garments without breeches, bear no arms, and during those forty days consume nothing except bread and salt, drinking pure water; nor is he to have communion in food or drink with other Christians or with another penitent before the forty days are completed, and no one else is to eat from the food he consumes. Having regard, however, to the person’s condition or infirmity, some fruit, vegetables, or legumes may be allowed as an act of mercy, according to what seems appropriate—especially if someone committed homicide under compulsion and not voluntarily. By canonical authority he is in every way forbidden during these days to have intercourse with any woman, to approach even his own wife, or to sleep with any man. He is to remain beside the church and weep for his sins before its doors. By day and night he is not to go from place to place but is to remain in one place during those forty days. If he happens to have enemies seeking his life, his penance is to be postponed until the bishop grants him peace from his enemies. If he is afflicted by illness so that he cannot perform penance worthily, the penance is to be deferred until he is restored to health. But if he is held by a prolonged illness, it belongs to the bishop’s judgment to determine how he should arrange to heal one who is guilty and ill. When the forty days have been completed, he is to wash with water, receive clothing and footwear, and cut his hair.

## CHAPTER 131.—What he must observe in the first year. From the same council, ch. 5 (ch. 56).

> Note: [Col. 0729D] The passage is obscure.

In the first year after the forty days, throughout that whole year, he is to abstain from wine, mead, honeyed beer, meat, cheese, and fatty fish, except on feast days celebrated by all the people in that bishopric. Unless he is on a long journey, in the army, staying a long time at the lord’s court (*curtim*), or detained by illness, he may then redeem Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday; *curtem* is given as *curtim* in the variant, with one denarius, or its price, or by feeding three poor persons; but only in such a way that he uses one thing out of the three—either meat, wine, or mead—and does not consume all of them. When he has returned home or recovered his health, he is to have no permission to redeem the fast. When the year’s cycle is completed, he is to be introduced into the church and granted the kiss of peace.

## CHAPTER 132.—What he must observe in the second and third years. From the same, ch. 6 (thus the codex of councils; ch. 57).

> Note: [Col. 0731D] [[Col. 0731] This note appears at the foot of columns 731 and 732, but the callout number (2) has not been printed in the text.] The codex of councils attributes this material to the preceding Council of Theodonisvilla.

In the second and third years he is likewise to fast and do penance (*jejunet poeniteat*), except that he has the authority, wherever he is, to redeem Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday at the price specified above. He is to observe all the other requirements carefully, as in the first year.

## CHAPTER 133.—What he must observe in the remaining four years. The same, on the same subject, ch. 6 (ch. 58).

Four years then remain, during each of which he is to fast three Lents. One is before Easter, together with the other Christians, abstaining from wine, mead, honeyed beer, meat and animal fat, eggs, and fatty fish. A second is before the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; if anything remains of the forty days, he is to complete it after the Mass of Saint John. A third is to be fasted before the Nativity of the Lord, as stated above. In those four years, on Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday he may eat whatever he wishes. He may redeem Monday and Wednesday at the price already mentioned; but Friday he must observe entirely on bread and water and may in no way redeem it. When these requirements have been completed, he is to receive holy communion.

## CHAPTER 134.—On the homicide and legal complaint involving bishops and the remaining orders. From the Council at Theodonisvilla, ch. 1 (under Paschal I).

At the council at Theodonisvilla, where thirty-two bishops were present—Aistulf, Archbishop of Mainz, with his suffragans; Hadabald, Archbishop of Cologne (*“Coloniensis” in the original*), with his suffragans; Ebbo, Archbishop of Reims, with his suffragans; and envoys of the remaining bishops of Gaul and Germany—because of the excessive presumption of certain tyrants raging against the Lord’s priests, and because of the recent occurrence in Gascony concerning Bishop John, who was disgracefully and unheard-of fashion murdered, it was decreed that they should, with common consent and humble devotion, petition the prince’s ears: if it pleased his piety, the accusation committed against Christ’s priests should be fully determined according to synodal statutes.

The bishops also thought it desirable, if it could wholly be settled according to their power, that those who, setting aside the fear of the Lord, presumed to rage against his ministers should be struck with a canonical sentence. But if it pleased his piety, according to the capitularies of preceding kings—where their provision mercifully imposed monetary amounts for offenses—for the consolation (*“the mitigation of penance was approved”*) of holy Church, that the aforesaid matters should be resolved by money granted by emperors to priests (*and by their successors*) for protection, and by penance according to the judgment of bishops, if his piety should approve, they would be pleased that it be determined thus.

(17, q. 4, c. *Si qui subdiaconum*.) If anyone brings a legal complaint against, wounds, or disables a subdeacon, and he recovers, let him do penance for five Lents without the attached years, and pay the bishop 300 solidi together with his composition and episcopal bans. But if he dies, let him perform each of the aforesaid Lents with the following years, and pay the bishop 400 solidi with his threefold composition and threefold episcopal bans [the original repeats: “with his composition and episcopal bans he shall compensate the bishop”].

If he brings a complaint against a deacon and the deacon recovers, let him do penance for six Lents without the attached years and pay 400 solidi with his composition and episcopal bans. But if he dies, let him perform each of the aforesaid six Lents with the following years and pay the bishop 600 solidi with his threefold composition and threefold episcopal bans.

If anyone brings a complaint against, wounds, or disables a priest, and he recovers, let him do penance for seven Lents [an alternative reading: twelve; 600 in the original] without the attached years, and pay the bishop 900 solidi with his threefold composition and threefold episcopal bans. But if he dies, a penance of twelve years is to be imposed upon him according to the canons, and he is to pay the bishop 900 solidi with his threefold composition and threefold episcopal bans.

If anyone lays an ambush for a bishop, seizes him, or dishonors him in any way, let him do penance for ten Lents with the attached years and pay the threefold composition due for a priest not killed. But if the bishop is killed by accident and not deliberately, the killer is to do penance in consultation with the bishops of the province. But if anyone deliberately kills him, he is never to eat meat or drink wine for all the days of his life; he is to lay aside the military belt and remain forever without hope of marriage.

Aistulf, bishop of Mainz, said: “If it pleases the rulers and their other faithful men, let us ask that this be approved and subscribed.” And it was approved and subscribed both by the ruler and by all the others.

## CHAPTER 135.—On the same matter. From the Council of Tribur, ch. 1.

An ecclesiastical capitulary at Tribur, approved and subscribed by Charlemagne and the leading men of Gaul and Germany.

(90.) It has pleased us and our faithful men that, just as we were admonished and asked in the preceding year at Theodonisvilla by bishops and other priests and servants of God, we should establish that bishops and their ministers—whom God has reserved by his judgment, not a human one—together with God’s priests and their fellow workers, through whose intercessions and prayers the holy Church of God seems to stand, are to remain untouched, according to the statutes of the holy canons, holy Fathers, and capitularies of preceding kings set before us.

(Ch. 1.) If anyone brings a complaint against a subdeacon and he recovers, let him perform canonical penance and pay the bishop 300 solidi. If he dies, let him do penance as the canons command and pay the bishop 400 solidi.

(Ch. 2.) If anyone brings a complaint against a deacon and he recovers, let him do penance according to the canons and pay the bishop 400 solidi. If he does not recover, let him do penance according to synodal commands and pay the bishop 600 solidi.

(Ch. 3.) If anyone mistreats and mutilates a priest, let him do penance according to the judgment of that priest’s bishop and pay the bishop 900 solidi. But if he dies, let him do penance as the synod adjudges and pay the bishop 120 [the codex of councils has 900] solidi.

(Ch. 4.) If anyone lays an ambush for a bishop, seizes him, or dishonors him in any way, let him do penance according to the statutes of the canons and pay the threefold composition due for a priest not killed, together with the penalties that appear to have been written and confirmed in the preceding chapter.

(Ch. 5.) If anyone deliberately kills a bishop, let him do penance in accordance with what was decreed at Theodonisvilla by thirty-two bishops [the codex of councils reads: “at Tribur, twenty-two bishops”], and what was there benignly approved and subscribed by us and by the leading men of all Germany and Gaul; and let him pay to the bereaved Church the money granted by us.

We have added this from our own authority: if anyone proves disobedient and contumacious toward bishops in these aforesaid sanctions of the holy canons and of our decree, let him first be struck by canonical sentence; then let him hold no benefice in our kingdom, and let his allod (*allodium*) be placed under ban. If he remains for a year and a day under our ban, let it be reduced to our fisc; let him be captured and relegated to exile, and there guarded and confined until, under compulsion, he makes satisfaction to God and holy Church for what he was unwilling to do voluntarily before.

And if these things please all of you, say so. And for a third time all cried out: “It pleases us.” The emperors and nearly all the princes of Gaul and Germany subscribed, each making his own cross. The ecclesiastical order, giving praise to God and the rulers, sang the hymn, “We praise you, O God,” and thus the synod was dissolved.

## CHAPTER 136.—On the same matter. From the Council of Mainz, ch. 19.

(17, q. 4, c. *Qui presbyterum*.) Upon one who kills a priest let a penance of twelve years be imposed according to the canons; or, if he denies it, if he is free, let him swear with seventy-two [compurgators]. But if he is a slave, let him purge himself by ordeal over twelve glowing plowshares. If convicted of the offense, let him lack the military belt until the end of his life and remain without hope of marriage.

## CHAPTER 137.—On killers of priests. From the Council of Worms, ch. 13 (Council of Mainz under Emperor Arnulf, ch. 16; and Tribur, ch. 5).

Whoever deliberately kills a priest is never to eat meat or drink wine throughout all the days of his life. He is to fast until evening, except on feast days and Sundays. He is not to take up arms, mount a horse, or enter a church for five years, but is to stand before the church doors. After five years he is to enter the church, but not yet communicate; rather, he is to stand among the hearers. When the course of twelve years has been completed, permission to communicate is to be granted him and dispensation to ride a horse allowed. In the other observances, however, he is to continue for three days each week, that he may deserve to be purified more perfectly.

## CHAPTER 138.—On priests who have been deposed and then killed. From the Council of Tours, ch. 3.

It has been reported to us that some persons who once said that they were priests, and afterward, having been degraded for their sins and performing penance, traveled through various places seeking the intercessions of the saints, have been murdered. To killers of persons of this kind we deny every ecclesiastical dignity until they have performed worthy penance for their offense according to the judgment of bishops, because they ought to do penance more severely than other murderers.

## CHAPTER 139.—On priests killed without a stole. From the Council of Tribur, ch. 26, attended by King Arnulf.

(14, q. 4, c. *Ut presbyteri*.) Priests are not to travel except clothed in a stole or *orarium*. If on a journey they are robbed, wounded, or killed while not wearing the stole, compensation is to be paid at the ordinary rate; but if they are wearing the stole, at triple rate.

## CHAPTER 140.—To whom compensation for a murdered priest belongs. From the same council, ch. 5 (*Capitularies*, Book IV, ch. 15).

(17, q. 4, c. *Omnes presbyteri*.) The compensation for a murdered priest is to be paid to the bishop to whose diocese he belonged. The bishop is to devote half of his *wergeld* (*wirigeld*) to the benefit of the church over which the priest presided, and fairly distribute the other half as alms for him, because no one seems to us to be a nearer heir of the priest than the one who joined him to the Lord.

## CHAPTER 141.—On those who commit homicide by ambush. From the Council of Nantes, ch. 2 (ch. 17).

If anyone voluntarily and by ambush kills a person, let him submit himself to continual penance. If it is established that this was done publicly, and he is a layman, let him be excluded from communion in prayers for five years. After five years, let him be received only into communion in prayers; he is not to make an offering or touch the body of the Lord. After remaining in this condition for fourteen years, he is then to be received into full communion, with offerings.

## CHAPTER 142.—Likewise, on voluntarily committed homicide. From the Council of Ancyra, ch. 21 (and Council of Tribur, ch. 54).

Those who have committed voluntary homicide are indeed to submit themselves continually to penance, but are to attain completion only near the end of life.

## CHAPTER 145.—Likewise, on the same matter. From the Council of Paris, ch. 6.

If anyone commits homicide voluntarily—not resisting violence, but using violence—and kills an innocent person simply going along his way, let him perform severe penance until the end of his life. Nevertheless, if he has performed his penance well, the viaticum of communion is not to be denied him at his departure.

## CHAPTER 144.—On homicide not voluntarily committed. From the Council of Ancyra, ch. 22 (and Council of Tribur, ch. 52).

Regarding involuntary homicides, the earlier ruling commands that completion be attained through a seven-year penance; the later ruling completes a period of five years.

## CHAPTER 145.—On the same matter. From the Council of Nantes, ch. 2 (ch. 18).

If anyone commits homicide accidentally and unwillingly, let him do penance for forty days on bread and water. When these have been completed, let him be excluded from the prayers of the faithful for two years; let him neither communicate nor make an offering. After two years, let him be admitted to communion in prayers and make an offering, but not communicate. After five years, let him be received into full communion. Abstinence from foods is to remain at the priest’s discretion.

## CHAPTER 146.—On one who commits homicide at his lord’s command. From the same council, ch. 25.

If a free person kills his lord’s slave at the lord’s command, let him do penance as for voluntary homicide.

## CHAPTER 147.—On one who kills his own slave. From the Council of Agde, ch. 62.

> Note: [Col. 0735D] And Council of Worms, ch. 38, where the wording is: “He shall cleanse the guilt of blood by excommunication or by a two-year penance.”

If anyone kills his own slave without the knowledge of a judge, let him mourn as for voluntary homicide.

## CHAPTER 148.—On a woman who, in her rage, beats her maidservant and she consequently dies. From the Council of Elvira (and Worms, ch. 39).

If a mistress, inflamed with jealous rage, beats her maidservant with scourges so that within the third day she gives up her life in suffering—because it is uncertain whether she killed voluntarily or by accident—if voluntarily, after seven years; if accidentally, after five years: having performed lawful penance, she is to be admitted to communion. If she is taken ill within the prescribed periods [“burdened by illness”], let her receive communion.

## CHAPTER 149.—On one who kills a person doing public penance. From the decrees of Pope Sylvester.

If anyone kills a person doing public penance, let him do double penance as for voluntary homicide, and let him not communicate except at the end.

## CHAPTER 150.—On those who accidentally commit homicide while doing necessary work. From the Council of Worms, ch. 5 (ch. 29).

(Dist. 50, c. *Saepe contingit*.) It often happens that, while someone engaged in necessary work is cutting down a tree, another person comes beneath it and is crushed. Therefore, if this results from the will or negligence of the person cutting the tree, he must submit himself entirely to penance as a homicide offender. But if it occurs neither by his intention nor carelessness, nor indeed knowingly, but while he may perhaps have been attending to necessary work and the other unexpectedly comes beneath the tree and is crushed by it, the woodcutter is not held guilty as a homicide offender.

## CHAPTER 151.—On the same matter. From the Council of Tribur, ch. 17 (ch. 16).

(Dist. 50, c. *Si duo*.) If two brothers are felling trees in a forest, and, as one tree is about to fall, one brother says to the other, “Take care,” and the other, while fleeing, runs into the path of the tree and dies, the surviving brother is to be judged innocent of his brother’s blood.

## CHAPTER 152.—On those who commit homicide in public war. From the Council of Mainz, ch. 2.

It is necessary, however, to admonish more carefully those who make light of killings committed in war, excusing themselves on the ground that they need not do penance for each individual act, since it was done by command of princes and so determined by God’s judgment. For we know that God’s judgment is always just and worthy of no reproach. Yet those who desire this impious killing ought to consider whether they can excuse themselves as innocent before the eyes of God—those who, because of avarice, [Col. 0736B] which is the root of all evils (1 Tim. VI) and is compared to the service of idols (Eph. V), and because of devotion to their temporal lords, have despised the eternal Lord; and, scorning His commandments, have committed homicide not by accident but deliberately.

For concerning those who killed persons unwillingly, we read that the Lord, through the lawgiver, appointed cities of refuge, to which they might flee and be saved from the avenger of their kinsman’s blood, and not die. Hence it is written in Deuteronomy: “This shall be the law for a homicide whose life is to be preserved” (Deut. XIX): “Whoever strikes his neighbor unknowingly, and is proved to have had no hatred against him yesterday or the day before, but has simply gone with him into [Col. 0736C] the forest to cut wood, and while cutting timber the axe slips from his hand, or the iron falls from its handle and strikes and kills his companion, let him flee to one of the aforesaid cities and live, lest the kinsman whose blood was shed strike down his life under the spur of grief.”

But concerning one who kills another deliberately, it is written in Exodus: “If anyone deliberately and by ambush kills his neighbor, you shall tear him even from my altar, that he may die” (Exod. XXI). And in Deuteronomy: “If anyone, hating his neighbor, lies in wait for his life, and rises up and strikes him, and he dies, and he flees to one of the aforesaid cities, the elders of that city shall send and take him from the place of refuge and deliver him into the hands of the kinsman whose blood was shed, [Col. 0736D] and he shall die; nor shall you pity him” (Deut. XIX).

If, therefore, anyone says that the man whom the Lord judged worthy of death is not guilty, how is he not opposed to God’s law, when he maintains that what the Lord commands is an accident? Yet among these matters it must be understood that there is a great difference between a lawful prince and a seditious tyrant; between one who strives to overthrow the tranquility of Christian peace and one who fights with arms against injustice in order to defend equity.

### CHAPTER 153.—Concerning those accused of homicide, if they deny it. From the Council of Tours, chapter 2.

Where it can be established that any person has committed [Col. 0737A] homicide, a judgment of penance proportionate to the offense shall be imposed upon him according to canonical authority. But if clear evidence cannot prove him to be a murderer, and he himself is unwilling to confess, let him be reserved for the judgment of almighty God, to whom all hidden things are manifest. Nevertheless, the priest shall publicly declare to him that he is unworthy of ecclesiastical communion and ought to be deprived of it until he confesses the crime he has committed and strives, through confession and fitting penance, to obtain absolution from this crime.

### CHAPTER 154.—Concerning an insane person if he commits homicide. From the same source, chapter 7 (Council of Worms, chapter 28).

If anyone, while insane, kills another, then, if he returns to a sound mind, a lighter penance is to be imposed upon him than upon one who committed such a deed while of sound mind. [Col. 0737B] Although penance must be imposed upon him, since the infirmity itself is believed to have been the cause of the sin, it is nevertheless to be lighter than for one who killed another while sane, by as much as the difference between a sane and an insane person, and between an irrational and a rational being, is evident.

### CHAPTER 155.—Concerning those who commit homicides by poison or sorcery. From the Council of Elvira, chapter 7.

If anyone has killed another by poison or sorcery, since he could not accomplish the crime without idolatry, communion is not to be granted to him except at the end.

### CHAPTER 156.—Concerning one through whose denunciation someone has been killed. From the same council, chapter 73.

(5, question 6, chapter *Delator*.) If any believer has been an informer, and through his denunciation one of the faithful has been proscribed or killed, it has been decided that he receive communion only at the end [Col. 0737C] of life. If the cause was less grave, he may receive communion within five years. If he is a catechumen, he shall be admitted to baptism after the period of five years.

### CHAPTER 157.—That there are three kinds of murderers. From the letter of Pope Clement, chapter 16 (Letter 4 to the Church of Jerusalem).

He said that there are three kinds of murderers and that their punishment would be alike. For just as he showed that the slayers of brethren are murderers, so also he declared their slanderers and those who hate them to be murderers. For he who kills, he who hates his brother (1 John III), and he who slanders him are alike shown to be murderers. He urged all to abstain from fleshly desires which wage war against the soul, and to show all persons [Col. 0737D] their good and innocent manner of life (1 Pet. II).

After much else, he urged that all love one another more earnestly from the heart; honor elders and love younger persons; instruct and love bishops, their priests, all the remaining ministers of the Church, and the whole people entrusted to them, by divine words and commandments; and that all these love their bishops with the whole strength of their souls—“direct” in the original [*dirigere orig.*]—so as to obey in all things the commands of their own eyes, which are the eyes of those [bishops] (the wording is textually awkward), even if the bishops themselves (which may it be far from them) act otherwise than is fitting (1 Pet. V), mindful, that is, [Col. 0738A] of that command of the Lord: “Do what they say; but do not do what they do” (Matt. XXIII).

### CHAPTER 158.—That murderers are to be excluded from ecclesiastical communion. From the Council of Agde, chapter 37.

(24, question 3, chapter *Itaque*.) Therefore we have decreed that murderers be removed from ecclesiastical communion unless, by satisfying penance, they have washed away the crimes they committed.

### CHAPTER 159.—Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Tours, chapter 7 (Tours I).

There is to be absolutely no communion with murderers until their crimes are washed away through the confession of their penance.

### CHAPTER 160.—Concerning those by whose counsel homicides are committed. From the sayings of Saint Augustine.

[Note: [Col. 0737D] These excerpts appear to have been taken from the exposition of Psalm LVI, at the verse “I slept, disturbed,” and the following verses.]

[Col. 0738B] They dangerously deceive themselves who suppose that only those are murderers who kill a person with their hands, and not rather those through whose counsel, deceit, and exhortation people are destroyed. For the Jews did not kill the Lord with their own hands, as it is written: “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone” (John XVIII); nevertheless, the Lord’s death is imputed to them because they crucified Him with their tongues, saying, “Crucify him” (Luke XXIII).

Accordingly, one Evangelist says that the Lord was crucified at the third hour (Mark XV), another at the sixth (John XIX): because the Jews crucified Him with their tongues at the third hour, and the soldiers with their hands at the sixth. Therefore, the one who hands over a person kills him—the Lord saying, “He who handed me over to you has the greater sin” (John XIX). Hence the Psalmist says: [Col. 0738C] “The teeth of the sons of men are weapons and arrows; their tongues are a sharp sword” (Ps. LVI). Therefore, let those by whose counsel blood is shed submit themselves to penance if they wish to deserve pardon.

### CHAPTER 161.—Concerning those who commit homicides in revenge for relatives. From the Penitential of Theodore.

Whoever kills a person in revenge for a brother or other relatives shall do penance as for voluntarily committed homicide, since Truth Himself says: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deut. XXXII; Rom. XII; Heb. X).

### CHAPTER 162.—Concerning one who kills a Jew through greed. From the Council of Mainz, chapter VI.

[Note: [Col. 0738D] Chapter 27 of the Council of Worms is read in nearly these words.]

(Distinction 50, chapter *Qui vero*.) Whoever, with premeditated hatred or through greed, kills a Jew or a pagan, because he has destroyed the image of God and the hope of future conversion, [Col. 0738D] shall do penance for forty days on bread and water.

### CHAPTER 163.—Concerning parricides and fratricides. From the Council of Tribur, chapter V.

[Note: [Col. 0738D] This is found in the Council of Worms, chapter 30.]

We decree that parricides and fratricides shall persevere for the course of one year before the doors of the church, praying for the Lord’s mercy. When the year has been completed, they shall be brought into the church, but shall remain among the hearers until another year’s period has ended. When these requirements have been fulfilled, if the fruits of penance are seen in them, let them become partakers of the body and blood of the Lord, lest [Col. 0739A] they become hardened through despair.
