They shall eat no meat on any day of their lives; they shall fast daily until the ninth hour, except on feast days and Sundays; and they shall abstain from wine, mead, and sweetened beer three days each week. They shall not dare carry arms except against pagans. Wherever they may prefer to go, they shall not be conveyed by any vehicle, but shall travel on their own feet. They shall not separate from their wives, if they have them. We place the duration of this penance in the discretion of the bishops, so that according to their conduct they may be able to extend or shorten it.

### CHAPTER 164.—Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Mainz, chapter XI (under Leo IV, chapter 20).

How detestable a crime parricide is [Col. 0739B] the Lord Himself showed in the judgment rendered between Cain and his brother Abel, when He said to Cain the parricide: “You shall be cursed upon the earth, which opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand. When you cultivate the earth, it shall not yield its fruits to you; and you shall be a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth” (Gen. IV). In this also He set a mark upon him, so that he might always live trembling, groaning, and in flight, and might not dare anywhere to have a settled place of rest.

But because in modern times fugitive parricides range through various places and give themselves over to diverse vices and the enticements of gluttony, it seems better to us that, remaining in one place, they discipline themselves with strict penance, if perhaps they may deserve to receive from the Lord’s mercy forgiveness for their crime. For it shall no longer be lawful for them to take up the military belt, nor [Col. 0739C] to make use of marriage and the bond of matrimony [“to be joined in marriage,” original], because the sacred canons do not permit this to them.

### CHAPTER 165.—Concerning those who kill their children unintentionally. From the Council of Tribur (chapter 53).

If anyone kills his son unintentionally, he shall do penance according to the rule for unintentional homicides.

### CHAPTER 166.—Concerning one who kills his lawful wife without judgment. From the decrees of Pope Pius, chapter 26.

(33, question 2, chapter *Quicunque*.) Whoever kills his own wife outside the law, or without cause and certain proof, and takes another wife, shall lay aside his arms and perform public penance. If he is contumacious and disobedient to his bishop, he shall be anathematized until he submits. The same law shall apply to one who has killed his lord.

### CHAPTER 167.—Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 1.

[Col. 0739D]

If a husband kills his wife, or a wife her husband, equal judgment shall be imposed upon them, the Lord saying: “You shall not regard the person of the poor, nor honor the countenance of the powerful” (Lev. XIX). And shortly afterward He says: “You shall hear the small as the great, nor shall you accept anyone’s person, because the judgment is God’s” (Deut. I). Therefore, if either of them denies such a charge, he or she shall be tried by the same judgment.

If the accused denies it and cannot be overcome by clear evidence: if free, he or she shall swear with twelve; if a slave, he or she shall purge himself or herself by hot iron. But if, while dying, the deceased accuses the husband before one or two hearers concerning her death, he shall not thereby be convicted; rather, if free, he shall swear with seventy-two [Col. 0740A] persons; if a slave, he shall purge himself over twelve red-hot ploughshares. The same law shall apply to a husband accusing his wife.

### CHAPTER 168.—Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Elvira, chapter LXXXV (among the fragments).

If a woman, on account of fornication, kills her husband [“by poison,” original], or causes him to be killed by any art, because she has killed her master and lord, she shall leave the world and do penance in a monastery.

### CHAPTER 169.—Concerning a wife consenting to her husband’s death. From the Council at Vermeria, chapter 3 (read at the end of the Council of Elvira).

(13, question 1, chapter *Si qua mulier*.) If a woman has plotted the death of her husband with others, and the husband himself, defending himself, has killed one of them, then, if the husband can prove that she is guilty of the plot, he may [Col. 0740B] (as it seems to us) dismiss his wife. The plotting woman, however, being subjected to penance, shall remain without hope of marriage.

### CHAPTER 170.—Concerning this matter, if several attack one person. From the same council, chapter 98.

(23, question 8, chapter *Si quatuor*.) If four or five persons, or even more, quarrel against one person, and he is wounded by them and dies, whichever of them inflicted the blow upon him shall be judged as a murderer according to the statutes of the canons. The others, however, who attacked him intending to kill him shall likewise do penance. But those who neither attacked nor wounded him, nor cooperated in counsel or assistance, but were merely present, shall be free from guilt.

### CHAPTER 171.—Concerning vengeance not to be forbidden. From the sayings of the Apostle, Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory.

[Col. 0740C]

Concerning vengeance not to be forbidden in the New Testament, Jerome says, concerning persons fit to execute vengeance (*On Ezekiel*, book III, on chapter IX): “He who strikes evil persons insofar as they are evil, and has cause to kill the utterly wicked, is a minister of God.” Likewise: “Let the law and its ministers restrain and bind enemies.” The Apostle says: “To the king as supreme, and to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good” (1 Pet. II).

Likewise Jerome (*Jerome on Jeremiah*, chapter XXII, immediately after the beginning): “To punish murderers, sacrilegious persons, and poisoners is not the shedding of blood, but the ministry of laws.” [Col. 0740D] Augustine says: “What foolishness is this—to spare one person and expose all to danger? For all are polluted when one sins; whence it is commanded in the law: ‘You shall not suffer sorcerers to live’ (Exod. XXII). Hence the prophet says: ‘They were putting to death souls that should not die.’”

Hence Gregory says: “For he kills one who is not dying, who condemns the righteous; and he endeavors to make one live who will not live, who seeks to release the guilty from punishment.” For Elijah afflicted many with death, by slaughter with his own hand and by fire divinely inspired (3 Kings XVIII; 4 Kings I). In the New Testament also Peter terribly punished Ananias and Sapphira (Acts V).

### CHAPTER 172.—Concerning those killed while breaking idols. From the Council of Elvira, chapter LX.

If anyone breaks idols and is killed there—[Col. 0741A] because this is not written in the Gospels, nor is it found ever to have been done under the apostles—it has been decided that he is not to be received into the number of martyrs.

### CHAPTER 173.—Concerning one who kills his mother, and how he ought to do penance. From the letter of Pope Nicholas to Radulf, bishop of the Holy Church of Argentia of Rhaetia.

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy Radulf, bishop of the Holy Church of Argentia of Rhaetia.

While throngs of believers from all parts of the world hasten to the thresholds of the Prince of the Apostles, a certain man named Thiothart came, bearing a letter from your blessedness, which he delivered to our pontificate. Reading its contents, we learned that he was a matricide. We grieved deeply at this deed, pouring forth many tears and lamentations. [Col. 0741B] Therefore we command, and establish by the judgments of the other Fathers, that he remain under the yoke of penance: for one year he shall not enter the church, but shall persevere before the doors of the basilica, praying and beseeching the Lord that he may be delivered from so great a crime.

When the year has been completed, he shall have permission to enter the church, but he shall stand among the hearers and shall not yet communicate. When three full years have been completed, the grace of holy communion shall be granted to him; but he shall not offer oblations until the periods of another seven years have been fulfilled. During all these years and periods he shall eat no meat and presume not to drink wine, except on feast days and Sundays, and from Easter until Pentecost. Wherever he wishes to go, [Col. 0741C] he shall not be carried by any vehicle but shall travel on foot. He shall not take up arms except against pagans. He shall fast three days each week until evening. He shall not separate from his own lawful wife, lest he fall into the abyss of fornication—a thing which we desire may not happen.

But if the end of his life approaches before the course of three years, let him become a partaker of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. Otherwise let what we have established above be carried out. Yet if in all his flourishing actions and best works you see his conduct and fountain of tears springing forth, let your watchful care show itself more merciful toward him and prove gentle to all. We pray that you may be well [Col. 0741D] in Christ.

### CHAPTER 174.—That a cleric who commits homicide must be compelled to cease from his order. From the Council of Tribur, attended by King Arnulf, chapter 11.

If any cleric, even under extreme compulsion, commits homicide, whether he is a priest or a deacon, he shall be deposed. We read in the canons of the apostles that a bishop, priest, or deacon caught in fornication, perjury, or theft shall be deposed; how much more ought one who has committed this monstrous crime to cease from his order? For whoever desires to follow Christ ought also to walk as He walked (1 John II:6). When He was cursed, He did not curse; when struck, He did not strike back; when suffering for us, He did not threaten [Col. 0742A] (1 Pet. II:23). He Himself also commanded in His Gospel: “If anyone strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also” (Luke VI:29).

For we ought not to kill, since the Lord says: “You have heard what was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not kill; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment.’ But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. V:21–22). Nor ought we to return evil for evil; rather, as the Apostle says in writing to the Romans: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Rom. XII:21). If any cleric is present where homicide has been committed and is shown to have been defiled neither by consent, counsel, nor any guilt in the homicide, nothing shall prevent him from remaining in his consecrated rank; if not consecrated, he may advance to ordination if otherwise worthy.

### CHAPTER 175.—Concerning one who, fighting against pagans in an army, kills Christian captives. From the same council attended by King Arnulf, chapter 34.

[Col. 0742B]

A victory of Christians often occurs, and the pagan side is defeated. Therefore, if Christian captives held by barbarians are killed together with the slain pagans, because in the violence of battle they cannot be distinguished, we decree that the killers should be treated more mercifully: after forty days of penance have been completed with indulgence, authority and power shall rest with the bishop to weigh the guilt and grant pardon.

### CHAPTER 176.—Concerning one who deceives a Christian slave and thus sells him. From the Council at Koblenz, attended by Kings Henry and Charles, chapter 7.

[Col. 0742C] It was likewise asked what should be done with one who has deceived a Christian person and thus sold him. All replied that such a person incurs the guilt of homicide.

### CHAPTER 177.—Concerning the penance of one who has committed fratricide. Alexander II to William of Périgueux, Durand bishop of Toledo (Toulouse), and Abbot Hugh.

The bearer of this letter, coming to us, tearfully confessed that he had incurred the crime of fratricide. Although he was the effective cause of so great a crime, he stated that it was by no means carried out by his own will. For when he had seized his brother, who was hostile to him and had laid ambushes against him, and had compelled him by a blow [Col. 0742D] with the pommel of a sword to go with him, a certain cousin who had come with him killed the brother, as he asserts, without consultation, premeditation, or even the will of the man himself.

Although your religious authority has imposed upon him a fitting and commendable penance, nevertheless, showing him the bowels of mercy, we command that, when he has returned home, he give half of all his patrimony to the poor for the remedy of his brother’s soul and his own. Likewise distributing a portion of his other inheritance for the same cause, he shall retain its use and fruits for his own necessity. When he has arranged all these things, he shall freely enter a monastery and there mortify himself by such penance for one year: namely, from Pentecost until the feast of Saint Michael, twice in each [Col. 0743A] week on bread and water; then until Lent, three days likewise on bread and water. He shall abstain from the body and blood of the Lord until three years have been completed, unless danger of death is imminent.

He shall fast throughout the entire Lent, except Sundays; he shall never bear arms in his life; and he shall not use marriage until the penance of seven years has been completed. He shall fast on Friday for as long as he lives. We have imposed all these things upon him in such a way that, if your prudence foresees that he is wholly unable to endure the severity, it may have permission to show mercy as it sees fit.

### CHAPTER 178.—Likewise concerning parricides and fratricides. Alexander to the clergy of the Church of Wilten.

Let your diligence know that we have imposed upon this Theoderic, for parricide—namely, the unintentional killing of his son—by the authority of the most blessed apostles and canons, a penance of seven years, counting within it the time already spent in penance. Thus, from now until the feast of Saint Martin, [Col. 0743B] he shall fast two days in the week, namely Wednesday and Friday, on bread and water. From Saint Martin’s feast until the Nativity of the Lord, he shall keep a continuous fast on bread and water, except Sundays and Thursday, on which he may eat Lenten food. From the octave of Epiphany until Lent, he shall fast two days each week, Wednesday and Friday, on bread and water, except principal feasts, on which he shall redeem himself by almsgiving.

In Lent, however, he shall keep a continuous [Col. 0743C] fast on bread and water, except Sundays. On Thursday alone we allow him to drink wine and eat Lenten food. After the first year has been completed, throughout every year he shall fast on bread and water two days in each week. In Lent, however, he shall keep a continuous fast on bread and water. Such fasting shall be observed in every year until the term of penance is completed. He shall abstain from meat. For one year he is denied entry to the Church; after entering the Church, he is separated from communion for three years, unless he is overtaken by fear of death. If any bishop or devout priest should wish, for the sake of mercy, to relax some remedy for him, we grant this by apostolic authority.

### CHAPTER 179.—Concerning the same matter. Gregory III to Boniface.

[Col. 0743D]

Concerning those who have killed father, mother, brother, or sister, we say that throughout their entire lifetime they shall not receive the body of the Lord, except at the end of their lives as viaticum. Let them abstain from eating meat and drinking wine as long as they live. Let them fast on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, that thus they may be able by weeping to wash away the crime they have committed.

### CHAPTER 180.—Likewise concerning the same matter and those who kill their own relatives. Nicholas to Bishop Charles and his suffragans.

We command concerning parricides and fratricides that for the course of one year they persevere before the doors of the basilica, praying for the Lord’s [Col. 0744A] mercy. When the year is completed, they shall be brought into the church, but shall stand among the hearers until a period of one year has ended, when they come to hear the solemnities of Mass or other sacred offices. When these requirements have been fulfilled, if you see the fruits of penance in them, let them become partakers of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, lest they be hardened by the darkness of despair.

They shall not eat meat on any day of their lives. They shall fast daily until the ninth hour, except feast days and Sundays. They shall not presume to take wine or cooked food except three days each week. They shall not dare carry or take up arms except against pagans; and wherever they wish to go, they shall not be conveyed by any vehicle, but should strive to travel on foot. [Col. 0744B] We place the duration of this penance in the discretion of your blessedness, so that according to their conduct you may extend or reduce it. They shall not separate from their wives, if they have them. But if they have none and cannot remain continent, let them take lawful women in marriage, lest they seem to fall into the abyss of fornication. If, however, the end of their lives arrives before the periods of the two aforesaid years are completed, viaticum shall not be denied them.

Pope Nicholas, in answer to the Bulgarians’ inquiries, chapter 24: “What a parricide—that is, one who has killed father or mother, or also one who kills brother or sister—ought to suffer is shown by the laws. But if they flee to the Church, we decree that what the bishop of the place, or the priest appointed by him, foresees shall be done.” Likewise (chapter 26): “Concerning one who kills his neighbor—that is, his blood-relative, such as a brother, cousin, or nephew—let the venerable laws retain their proper force. But if they flee to the Church, let them indeed be delivered from the penalties of death by the laws, but without doubt be subjected to such penance as the local bishop or priest sees fit.”

### CHAPTER 181.—Concerning women who kill their offspring. From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 30.

Concerning women who fornicate and kill their offspring, or who act so as to cast out those conceived in the womb: the ancient determination excludes them from the Church until the end of life; but now we decree more mercifully [Col. 0744D] that we grant them a period of ten years according to the prescribed stages of penance.

### CHAPTER 182.—Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Lleida, chapter 2.

Those who have sought to kill fetuses wrongly conceived in adultery, whether after they have been born or by administering some potions in their mothers’ wombs, shall receive communion after seven full years, in the case of adulterers of either sex; yet throughout their lives they shall persist in humility and tears. If they are clerics, they shall not be permitted to recover the office of ministry.

### CHAPTER 183.—Likewise concerning the same matter. Canons of Bishop Martin for laypeople, chapter 9 (from the Greek synodal book; Martin, bishop of Braga, chapter 77, *In universum*).

[Col. 0745A]

If any woman has fornicated and has had a child and killed it; or if she has sought to procure an abortion and kill what has been conceived; or indeed has labored not to conceive, whether from adultery or lawful marriage: the earlier canons decreed that such women be admitted to communion at death. But we, out of mercy, judge that both such women and those privy to their crimes shall do penance for ten years.

### CHAPTER 184.—Concerning a certain man who had killed his brother. Nicholas to Bishop Donno and King Charles.

A certain man of your diocese, named Hugh, came and tearfully told our pontificate [Col. 0745B] how, compelled by the ancient enemy, he had committed fratricide, and how your blessedness had placed him under the yoke of penance for so great a crime. Hearing of the wickedness of so great a calamity and the shedding of a brother’s blood, we grieved and shed no few tears.

Nevertheless, because, as he said, he prefers, at the brotherly urging of grace, to wash away the guilt of so great a stain with a fountain of tears, we decree that he promptly recover the possessions that have been taken from him for this act, lest, constrained by want through poverty, he be led to worse things. Let your holiness likewise take care that his own lawful wife, from whom he has been separated, be restored to him at once, lest he seem to fall into the abyss of fornication—which we do not wish. In all other respects, however, let him remain [Col. 0745C] subject to the measure of penance which you instructed him to perform.

### CHAPTER 185.—Concerning the penance of parricides and incestuous persons. Nicholas to Solomon, bishop of Constance.

It is clear that parricides, fratricides, and incestuous persons—concerning whom you ask whether they may be joined in marriage—are doing penance and therefore cannot be joined in a carnal union. They ought to remain chaste in mind and body throughout all the days of their lives, provided that, out of mercy even toward these persons, the twenty-fourth rule of the decretals of blessed Pope Leo is observed.

### CHAPTER 186.—Concerning a woman who had killed her children. Stephen III to Lambert, bishop of Le Mans.

Having read the letter sent to us by your holiness, which stated that this woman, named Hildegard, had killed her children [Col. 0746A] and had completed a seven-year penance, we were deeply grieved. Therefore, because you have directed us to extend to her the bowels of compassion, we desire and mercifully command that on the sacred feasts—namely, the venerable Nativity, holy Easter, Pentecost, and the feast of the Nativity of the Apostles—she shall receive the sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; and that for the days of her life she shall live enclosed in a monastery, regularly observing the monastic life.

### CHAPTER 187.—That a judge who can punish sins and does not do so is guilty of sin. Honorius to Anatolius, master of the soldiers.

The bearer of this letter tearfully petitioned us, asserting that his brother had been killed by a certain soldier of the fortress of Salerno, and that after his death he had also been despoiled of his own possessions. [Col. 0746B] By the very evidence of the facts, all plainly know and have established how impious and how injurious it is, contrary to the ordinances of the laws, that blood innocently shed should in no way be avenged upon its perpetrator.

Those who can avenge these things and, through connivance, neglect to do so should assuredly know that, if they neglect to defend innocent blood, at the future and terrible judgment this crime that has been committed will be exacted from them as participants in the deed. Therefore let your glory hasten, prompted by justice, to separate from the military body the man ensnared by the deadly crime of homicide, and hand him over to the provincial judge for punishment. Let it also without doubt restore to the aforesaid petitioner the goods violently seized by robber force, if he is the dead man’s brother, [Col. 0746C] so that, under the discipline impending from us, the man who committed the crime may always await and promptly undergo it, and the integrity of the military body may not, because of one man’s offense, be subjected to the contagion of homicide.

### CHAPTER 188.—Concerning those who inflict death upon themselves. From the First Council of Braga, chapter 34.

(23, question 5, chapter *Placuit ut si qui*.) For those who inflict death upon themselves by the sword, poison, a precipice, hanging, or any manner of violence, no commemoration shall be made in the offering, nor shall their bodies be carried to burial with psalms. For many arrogate this to themselves through ignorance. It has likewise been decided that the same be done for those who are punished for their crimes.

## ELEVENTH PART OF THE DECREE. Concerning enchanters, augurs, diviners, sorcerers, lot-casters, and the various delusions of the devil, and concerning the penance of each.

[Col. 0745]

### CHAPTER 1.—That no one should observe diviners, soothsayers, or enchanters. Decree of Gregory the Younger (Gregory II, chapter 12 of his decrees, in the First Roman Council).

[Col. 0745D]

(26, question 5, chapter *Si quis hariolos*.) If anyone observes diviners, [Col. 0746D] haruspices, or enchanters, or uses amulets, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER 2.—Concerning the same matter. From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 23.

(26, question 5, chapter *Qui divinationes*.) Those who seek divinations and follow the customs of the Gentiles, or bring such persons into their houses in order to inquire into something by magical art or for the sake of expiation, shall lie under the rule of five years, according to the appointed stages of penance.

### CHAPTER 3.—That clerics should not be enchanters. From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 36 (and the Council of Agde, chapter 68).

(26, question 5, chapter *Non oportet*.) Those devoted to sacred offices, or clerics, ought not to be magicians or enchanters, nor to make amulets, which are shown to be bonds upon their souls.

### CHAPTER 4.—What is to be done concerning lot-casters. From the Council of Agde, chapter 39 (chapter 42, and the Council of Vannes, chapter 16).

(26, question 5, chapter *Aliquanti*.) Some clerics and laypersons devote themselves to auguries and, under the name of a feigned religion, profess knowledge of divination through those lots which they call “the lots of the saints,” or promise future things by the inspection of whatever writings. Any cleric or layperson found either to consult or to teach this shall be held outside the Church.

### CHAPTER 5.—Concerning the penance of clerics who consult augurs. From the Council of Toledo, chapter 30 (Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 28).

(26, question 5, chapter *Si quis episcopus*.) If any bishop, priest, deacon, or any person of the clerical order is found to have consulted haruspices, diviners, augurs, lot-casters, those who profess magical art, or any who practice similar arts [“sublime arts,” the council manuscript reads], he shall be deposed from the honor of his dignity, undertake the care of a monastery, and there, devoted to perpetual penance, expiate the crime of sacrilege he has committed [Col. 0747C].

### CHAPTER 6.—Concerning the Pythian spirit. Ambrose on the First Epistle to the Corinthians (on chapter II).

The spirit of this world is the one by whom godless fanatics are seized [or: “carried away”]. For among worldly spirits he is the more powerful; hence he is accustomed to divine by conjectures concerning worldly things, and is called Python. This is he who is deceived through what is plausible and deceives others; he is the one who spoke through the Sibyl, following our perceptions, wishing to have a place among the heavenly beings.

### CHAPTER 7.—That the Kalends and auguries are not to be observed. Zacharias to Bishop Boniface (final letter).

Concerning the Kalends of January, other auguries, amulets, incantations, and the various other observances which, as you said, are kept in pagan fashion at [Col. 0747D] Saint Peter the Apostle’s [church] or in the city of Rome: we judge these things detestable and harmful both to us and to all Christians.

### CHAPTER 8.—That sorcerers are to be condemned. Leo IV to the bishops of Britain.

We decree that the lots by which you distinguish all matters in your provinces are nothing other than the divinations and sorcery condemned by the other Fathers. For this reason we wish them to be utterly condemned; we do not wish them henceforth even to be named among Christians, and, under the ban of anathema, we forbid these practices, so that they may be cut off.

### CHAPTER 9.—Concerning those who observe the courses of the stars and the flights of birds. Jerome on Joshua, Homily 7.

[Note: [Col. 0747] This is found in Origen, translated by Jerome, about the middle.]

[Col. 0748A]

Those who, though Christians, celebrate pagan festivals bring an anathema into the Church. And those who investigate human lives and actions from the courses of the stars; who inquire into the flight of birds and other such things formerly observed in the world: they bring the anathema of Jericho into the Church, defile the Lord’s camp, and cause God’s people to be defeated.

### CHAPTER 10.—Those who divine otherwise than according to the Lord are not to be believed. Augustine, *Questions on Deuteronomy*, book 19 (on Deuteronomy 13).

The Lord intended that even those things which are said by diviners not according to God, if what they say comes to pass, are not thereby to be accepted, so that what they command should be done [Col. 0748B] or what they worship should be worshipped.

### CHAPTER 11.—On the deposition of a cursing cleric. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 57.

(*Distinction* 46, c. *Clericus maledicus*.) A cleric who curses, especially if he is among the priests, must be compelled to seek pardon. If unwilling, he shall be degraded and shall never be restored to office without making satisfaction.

### CHAPTER 12.—On the condemnation of one who kills someone by sorcery. From the Council of Elvira, chapter 6.

If anyone kills another by sorcery—since he could not accomplish the crime without idolatry—he is not to be granted communion even at the end [of life].

### CHAPTER 13.—That human institutions are partly superstitious and partly not. Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book II (chapters 19, 20).

[Col. 0748C]

That which rests upon human institutions is partly superstitious and partly not superstitious. Superstitious is everything instituted by human beings for making and worshipping idols, whether it concerns worshipping as God a creature or any part of a creature; or consultations and certain agreed and covenanted compacts of signs with demons, such as are the contrivances of the grander arts—arts which poets usually mention rather than teach. Of this kind, though with a more permissible frivolity, are the books of soothsayers and augurs.

To this kind also belong all bindings and remedies condemned even by the medical profession: whether in charms, in certain marks called *characters*, in things hung up or bound on, or even in things in some manner danced—not for the bodily regulation, but for certain hidden or manifest significations. These they call “physical” by a more imposing [the original reads: “milder”] name, so that they may seem not to entangle people superstitiously but to benefit them by nature. Such are earrings worn at the top of each ear, rings made of ostrich bones on the fingers, or being told, when hiccuping, to hold your thumb with the right hand [the original reads: “the left thumb”].

[Col. 0749A]

To these are added thousands of utterly empty observances: if some limb twitches; if, while friends are walking together, a stone, dog, or boy passes between them. A little later: such things also include stepping on the threshold when passing before one’s own house; returning to bed if one sneezes while putting on one’s shoes; returning home if one stumbles when setting out; and, when a garment is gnawed by mice, fearing a presage of future evil more than grieving over the present loss.

Likewise, in the same work, chapter 21: Nor are those to be separated from this class of harmful superstition who, because of consideration of birthdays [variant: “natural days”], are called genethliacs, but now commonly “mathematicians” [astrologers]. For even if they trace, and sometimes accurately discover, the true position of the stars when a person is born, nevertheless they grievously err in attempting from this to foretell either our actions or their outcomes.

Likewise, on the same subject, chapter 23: Divine authority has not passed over this kind of fornication of the soul in silence; nor has it deterred the soul from it merely by saying that such practices should not be pursued because their practitioners speak falsely. Rather, it says: even if they tell you something and it comes to pass, do not believe them (Deuteronomy 13). For it does not follow that, because the image of the dead Samuel foretold the truth to Saul (1 Samuel 28), those sacrileges by which that image was presented are any less to be detested. Nor does it follow that, because the ventriloquist woman in the Acts of the Apostles bore true witness to the Apostles of the Lord, the Apostle Paul spared that spirit; instead, by rebuking and expelling that demon, he cleansed the woman [Col. 0749C] (Acts 16). Therefore all arts of this sort—whether of frivolous or harmful superstition, constituted from a pestilential association of human beings and demons, like the compacts of a faithless and deceitful friendship—must be utterly rejected and avoided by the Christian.

Likewise, in the same work, chapter 40: All the teachings of the Gentiles contain not only feigned and superstitious inventions and heavy burdens of needless labor, which each of us, when leaving Gentile society under Christ’s guidance, ought to abhor and avoid; they also contain disciplines of liberal learning more suited to the use of truth, certain highly useful precepts concerning morals, and some truths about the worship of the one God. These latter things are theirs as gold and silver—not things they themselves created, but things they extracted, as though from certain mines, from the divine providence poured out everywhere—and which they perversely and wrongfully misuse in the service of demons. When the Christian separates inwardly from their miserable fellowship, he ought to take these things from them for the proper use of preaching the Gospel. Their clothing too—that is, institutions devised indeed by human beings but nevertheless suited to human society, without which we cannot live in this life—may lawfully be taken and held for conversion to Christian use.

### CHAPTER 14.—That there is no partnership in dishonorable things. Pandects, book XVII, title II (law 57).

[Col. 0750A]

If a partnership has been formed for sorcery, it is clear that no partnership exists. For it is generally held that there can be no partnership in dishonorable matters.

### CHAPTER 15.—On not observing Egyptian days. Augustine on the Epistle to the Galatians (on chapter 4).

Let the reader understand that superstitious observances of times involve such danger to the soul that the Apostle says: “I fear for you, lest perhaps I have labored among you in vain” (Galatians 4). Although this is read in churches throughout the world with such solemnity and authority, our gatherings are full of people who obtain from astrologers the times for undertaking their affairs. Indeed, they often do not hesitate to warn us not to begin anything—whether building works [Col. 0750B] or any other undertaking whatever—on days which they call Egyptian.

### CHAPTER 16.—On not observing the Kalends of January. From a sermon of Augustine on the Kalends of January, beginning: *Dies Kalendarum*.

[Note: [Col. 0749D] Certain other fragments of this sermon are found in Augustine’s *Milleloquium*, under the heading “Kalends.”]

There are people who observe auguries on the Kalends of January so strictly that they give neither a coal from their own hearth nor any other benefit to anyone who asks; they receive diabolical New-Year gifts from others and themselves pass them on to others.

### CHAPTER 17.—That men and women ought to instruct the sons or daughters whom they have received at baptism. From Augustine’s sermon for the Sunday after Easter, beginning: *Hodiernus dies*.

[Note: [Col. 0749D] This sermon too is listed at the end of the *Milleloquium* [Col. 0750D], among the Easter sermons, no. 34. Moreover, the same material is also found in sermons *De tempore* 163, 215, and 241.]

Before all else I admonish both men and women who have received children at baptism: recognize that you have become sureties before God for those whom you appeared to receive from the sacred font. Therefore always admonish them to love chastity, preserve justice, maintain charity, and do to all what they wish done to themselves. Let them not observe auguries; let them not pay vows at trees and springs; let them flee charmers and *caragios* [term uncertain], and sacrilegious amulets, as the poisons of the devil; let them neither steal nor bear false witness. Above all, you yourselves should know the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, and teach them to those whom you have received.

### CHAPTER 18.—What is meant by “You observe days and months” (Galatians 4), etc. Augustine to Januarius (Letter 119, chapter 7).

The Apostle blames those who say: “I shall not set out today, because tomorrow is an ill-omened day [variant: ‘because it is an ill-omened tomorrow’],” or “because the moon is in such a position”; or: “I shall set out so that events may turn out favorably, because the disposition of the stars is such”; “I shall not conduct this business in this month, because that star governs my month”; or: “I shall conduct it, because it has taken charge of the month”; “I shall not plant a vineyard this year, because it is a leap year.”

No wise person, however, thinks that observers of times should be censured when they say: “I shall not set out today, because a storm has arisen”; or “I shall not sail, because winter remnants remain”; or “It is time to sow, because autumn rains have [Col. 0751A] saturated the earth”; or when they have observed perhaps certain other natural effects, concerning the movement of air and moisture and the changing qualities of seasons, in the most orderly revolutions of the stars.

### CHAPTER 19.—On the same matter: that it is a sin to observe days, months, and so forth. Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 79.

Who would think how great a sin it is to observe days, months, years, and seasons, as do those who on certain days, months, or years are willing or unwilling to begin something because, according to the empty teachings of human beings, they consider the times fortunate or unfortunate—unless we weighed its seriousness from the Apostle’s fear, when he says to such persons: “I fear for you, lest perhaps I have labored among you in vain” (Galatians 4)?

### CHAPTER 20.—On the condemnation of astrologers. Augustine, *Confessions*, book IV (chapter 3).

[Col. 0751B]

(26, question 2, c. *Illos planetarios*.) I certainly did not cease to consult those star-diviners whom they call mathematicians [astrologers], because they seemed to offer no sacrifice and to direct no prayers to any spirit for the sake of divination—although Christian and true piety consistently drives out [the original reads: “rejects”] and condemns even this practice.

### CHAPTER 21.—That lots are not to be believed. Jerome on Jonah (on chapter 1).

(26, question 2, c. *Non statim*.) We should not immediately believe in lots on the precedent of Jonah, nor join to this testimony the passage from the Acts of the Apostles in which Matthias is chosen to the apostleship by lot, since the privileges of individuals cannot establish a universal law.

### CHAPTER 22.—Who lot-diviners are. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VIII, chapter 9.

Lot-diviners are those who, under the name of a counterfeit religion, profess knowledge of divination through certain lots which they call those of the saints, or promise future knowledge by inspecting writings of any kind.

### CHAPTER 23.—On a cleric caught in sorcery. Gregory to Januarius, bishop [the original: “Bishop of Cagliari”] of Sardinia (Register, book III, letter 24).

As for the cleric Paul, who, it is often said, was caught in acts of sorcery and, despising his clerical habit, had returned to lay life and fled to Africa: if this is so, we have decided that, after corporal punishment has first been inflicted, he should be assigned [Col. 0751D] to penance.

### CHAPTER 24.—On fortune-tellers. *Capitularies*, book 7, chapter 222.

Fortune-tellers who declare that they know the future shall be beaten and expelled from the city.

### CHAPTER 25.—On correcting one who has accused a woman of practicing magic. Gelasius to Secundinus of Visinum.

We deem it altogether unseemly that grave injuries should be inflicted by the words of ministers of the Church, when laypeople for the most part avoid such conduct. For an honorable woman had learned at an opportune time from the teacher, Deacon Paul, [Col. 0752A] that she had not only been attacked by accusations, but had also implicated herself in the consciousness of the condemned art of magical abomination.

[Note: [Col. 0751D] The passage is corrupt.]

And therefore, brother, we have appointed you investigator in this matter concerning those aforementioned, so that, if this insolence proves the said deacon guilty, after it has been established that he improperly assailed the woman in an uncivil manner, you may either compel him to substantiate what he alleged or restrain him by suitable correction.

### CHAPTER 26.—That poisoners are to be condemned capitally. Pandects, book IV, title XIX.

Poisoners are to be punished capitally if, by hateful arts, poisons, or magical whispers, they have killed people or publicly sold harmful drugs.

### CHAPTER 27.—How a cleric is to be accused of sorcery. Likewise.

[Col. 0752B]

We are not a little surprised that you wish to prosecute your deacon under secular laws for the crime of sorcery. Therefore, by apostolic authority we command that, setting aside equal laws which are suited rather to slaves than to ecclesiastical orders, you receive canonical purification from him.

### CHAPTER 28.—On the condemnation of Archdeacon Paschal for his incantations. From the *Book of the Popes*.

Not long afterward Paschal was deprived of the office of archdeacon through the intervening judgment of God and of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, on account of certain incantations, little groves which he worshipped, and lots [perhaps “filth”; the printed text has *sordes*, possibly *sortes*] which he handled with other observers; [Col. 0752C] and Sergius confined him in a monastery. Five years later he died unrepentant because of hardness of heart.

### CHAPTER 29.—On lot-diviners and those who consult demons. Augustine in response to Januarius’s inquiries (Letter 119, chapter 20).

(26, question 2, c. *Hi qui*.) Those who draw lots from the pages of the Gospels: although it is preferable that they do this rather than run to consult demons, still I dislike the practice of wishing to turn divine oracles toward secular business and the vanity of this life.

[Note: [Col. 0752D] The same practice is prohibited below, chapter 52.]

### CHAPTER 30.—That bishops are to expel lot-diviners and sorcerers from their parishes; and on the empty delusion of demons. From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 1 (in a fragment).

(26, question 5, c. *Episcopi*.) Bishops and their ministers should labor with all their strength to root utterly out from their parishes the harmful art of lot-divination and sorcery, invented by the devil. If they find any man or woman devoted to such a crime, they shall disgracefully dishonor and expel them from their parishes. For the Apostle says: “After a first and second admonition, avoid a heretic, knowing that such a person is perverted” (Titus 3). Those who, abandoning their Creator, seek aid from the devil are perverted and held captive by him; therefore the holy Church must be cleansed from such a plague.

Nor should this be omitted: certain wicked women, turning backward after Satan (1 Timothy 5), deceived by demonic delusions and phantasms, believe and profess that in the nighttime they ride upon certain beasts with Diana, the goddess of the pagans, or with Herodias and an innumerable multitude of women; that they traverse great expanses of land in the stillness of the dead of night; that they obey her commands as their mistress; and that on appointed nights they are summoned to her service.

[Note: [Col. 0753] Augustine reports the same in *On Spirit and Soul*, chapter 18.]

[Col. 0753A]

But would that these women alone had perished in their perfidy and had not drawn many with them into the destruction of unbelief. For an innumerable multitude, deceived by this false opinion, believes these things to be true; and by believing, departs from the right faith and relapses into pagan error whenever it supposes that any divinity or divine power exists apart from the one God. Therefore priests must preach with every urgency to all the people in the churches entrusted to them, so that they may know these things to be entirely false, and that such phantasms are inflicted upon the minds of believers [variant: “unbelievers”] not by a divine but by a malicious spirit.

For Satan himself, who transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11), when he has captured the mind of any little woman and subjugated her to himself through unbelief and incredulity, immediately transforms himself into the appearances and likenesses of diverse persons. Deceiving in dreams the mind which he holds captive, sometimes he shows joyful things, sometimes sad; sometimes persons known, sometimes unknown; and leads it through every kind of byway. And although the spirit alone undergoes this, the unbelieving mind thinks that these things happen not in the mind but in the body.

For who is not carried outside himself in dreams and nocturnal visions, and while sleeping sees many things that he never saw while awake? But who could be so foolish and dull as to suppose that all things which occur in the spirit alone also happen in the body? Ezekiel the prophet saw the visions of the Lord in the spirit, not in the body (Ezekiel 3); and John the Apostle saw and heard the mysteries of the Apocalypse in the spirit, not in the body, as he himself immediately says: “I was in the Spirit” [the original: “as he himself says: ‘Immediately,’ he says, ‘I was in the Spirit’”]. And does Paul not hesitate to say that he was caught up in the body? (1 Corinthians 12).

[Col. 0753C]

It must therefore be publicly announced to all that whoever believes such things and things like them loses the faith. Whoever does not have right faith in God belongs not to God but to the one in whom he believes—that is, the devil. For it is written concerning our Lord: “All things were made through him” (John 1). Whoever therefore believes that anything can be done, or that any creature can be changed for better or worse, or transformed into another form or likeness, by anyone other than the Creator himself, who made all things and through whom all things were made, is without doubt an unbeliever and worse than a pagan.

### CHAPTER 31.—On worshippers of trees. From Gregory’s Register (book VII, indiction 1, letter 20, to Agnellus, bishop of Terracina).

Word has reached us that certain persons—an abomination even to mention—worship trees and commit many other illicit acts contrary to the Christian faith [Col. 0754A]. We are astonished that your brotherhood has delayed to correct this severely by punishment. Therefore, by this letter we urge that they be sought out through diligent inquiry and that, once the truth is known, you exact such punishment from them that God may be appeased and their punishment may be an example of correction to others.

### CHAPTER 32.—On worshippers of idols and their punishment. From the same source (same book, letter 66, to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari).

(26, question 5, c. *Contra idolorum*.) We strongly urge your brotherhood, in pastoral vigilance, to keep watch against worshippers of idols and against soothsayers and lot-diviners; to address the people publicly against persons of this kind; and by persuasive exhortation to call them back from the stain [Col. 0754B] of so great a sacrilege, from the prospect of divine judgment, and from the danger [variant: “food”] of the present life.

If, however, you find that they are unwilling to amend and correct themselves, we wish you to seize them with fervent zeal. If they are slaves, punish them with beatings and tortures by which they may be brought to amendment. But if they are free, they must be restrained by appropriate confinement and severe penance [the original: “directed into penance”], so that those who disdain to hear words beneficial and recalling them from danger of death may at least be restored by bodily suffering to the desired health of mind.

### CHAPTER 33.—On the same matter. From the same author to Hadrian, notary (Register, book IX, letter 47).

[Col. 0754C] (26, question 5, c. *Pervenit ad nos*.) It has come to our attention that you have prosecuted certain enchanters and lot-diviners. You should know that we found this care and zeal of yours wholly pleasing. But we took it ill that we learned you had feared that they might clandestinely prejudice us against you, contrary to the evidence of your conduct, when you ought to have been certain and known that this would advance rather to your commendation before us, not be counted against you as fault. Therefore let it be your concern diligently to seek out and correct by such strict punishment whatever enemies of Christ of this kind you find, so that we may form a better judgment of your experience and that you may commend yourself to our God—which is what must be sought above all.

### CHAPTER 34.—On those who observe pagan rites. From the Council of Braga, chapter 6 (chapter 71 of the Greek synod of Martin of Braga).

[Col. 0754D]

(26, question 5, c. *Non liceat*.) If anyone, following pagan custom, brings diviners and lot-diviners into his house as though to drive evil out or discover sorceries, let him do penance for five years.

### CHAPTER 35.—On those who give themselves to auguries and enchanters. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 89.

(26, question 5, c. *Auguriis*.) We decree that one who gives himself to auguries or incantations is to be separated from the communion of the Church [Col. 0755A]; likewise one who adheres to Jewish superstitions or festivals.

### CHAPTER 36.—On the same matter. From the Roman Penitential.

Anyone who devotes himself to auguries or divinations, or believes that certain people send storms, or any woman who performs diabolical divinations or incantations, shall do penance for seven years.

### CHAPTER 37.—On those who observe lots.

All who observe auguries or lots falsely called those of the saints, or divinations of any kind, or who make or pay a vow at a tree, stone, or any other object except at a church, shall be excommunicated [Col. 0755B]. If they come to penance, clerics shall do penance for three years and laypeople for one and a half years.

### CHAPTER 38.—On cutting down trees which the common people worship. From the Council of Nantes, chapter 8 (under Formosus, chapter 20).

Bishops and their ministers must strive with utmost zeal that trees consecrated to demons, which the common people worship and hold in such veneration that they do not dare cut off even a branch or shoot, be cut down at the roots and burned. Stones also which, deceived by demonic illusions, they venerate in ruined and wooded places, where they make and bring vows, must be dug up completely and thrown into a place where they can never be venerated by their worshippers.

Let everyone be told how great a crime idolatry is: whoever venerates and worships these things thereby denies God, renounces Christianity, and must undertake such penance as though he had worshipped idols. Everyone must be forbidden to make a vow or bring a candle or any gift elsewhere in seeking health, except to the church of the Lord his God. For it is written: “Make vows and pay them to the Lord your God” (Psalm 75). We know what great threats the Lord uttered through his prophets against the ancient people who sacrificed in groves and offered sacrifice on high places. If anyone transgresses these commands, he has lost the faith and is worse than an unbeliever (1 Timothy 5). Therefore he must by all means be cut off from communion with the holy Church and, unless he has worthily repented, not be received back.

### CHAPTER 39.—On those who sacrifice to demons. From the Penitential of Theodore.

[Col. 0755D]

For concerning those who sacrifice to demons, we have the ordinances of Bishop Theodore, in which it is written: Those who sacrifice to demons in small matters shall do penance for one year; those who do so in grave matters shall do penance for ten years.

### CHAPTER 40.—On those who observe the traditions of the pagans. From the Council of Braga, chapter 20 (chapter 72 of the Greek synod of Martin, bishop of Braga).

(26, question 5, c. *Non liceat Christianis*.) Christians may not maintain and observe the traditions of the pagans, worship the elements, the moon, or the course of the stars, or consider the empty deceit of signs [Col. 0756A] in building a house or arranging marriages. For it is written: “Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God” (Colossians 3). Whoever does this shall be most severely corrected and perform canonical penance.

### CHAPTER 41.—On women who put their children in an oven or upon a roof for health. From the Penitential of the priest Bede.

Any woman who places her son upon a roof or in an oven for relief from fevers shall do penance for one year.

### CHAPTER 42.—That it is unlawful to perform wicked observances of the Kalends. From the decrees of Bishop Martin (chapter 73 of the Greek synod).

(26, question 7, c. *Non licet iniquas*.) It is unlawful to perform the wicked observances of the Kalends, to devote oneself to idleness, or to deck houses with laurel or the greenery of trees. All this is a pagan observance.

### CHAPTER 43.—On those who presume to observe the Kalends of January according to pagan rite. From the decrees of Pope Zacharias, chapter 11.

(26, question 7, c. *Si quis Kalendas*.) If anyone presumes to observe the Kalends of January according to pagan rite; to make some additional novelty because of the new year; to prepare “months” [variant: “tables”] in his house with lamps or banquets; or to lead singers and choruses through lanes and streets: let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER 44.—On the same matter. From the Council of Rouen, chapter 3.

[Col. 0756C] If anyone on the Kalends of January does anything invented by pagans, observes days, months, and the moon, and hopes that something may turn for better or worse through their effective power, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER 45.—On swineherds, oxherds, or hunters who perform their incantations. From the same source, chapter 4.

Inquiry must be made whether any swineherd, oxherd, hunter, or others of this sort recite diabolical charms over bread, herbs, or certain wicked bindings, and hide them in a tree or cast them at a crossroads or three-way intersection in order to free their own animals from plague and disaster and destroy those of another. That all these things are idolatry no believer can doubt [Col. 0756D]; and they must therefore be eradicated most thoroughly.

### CHAPTER 46.—That Christian women may not observe superstitious practices in spinning and weaving. From the Council of Braga, chapter 11 (chapter 75 of the Greek synod of Martin of Braga).

(26, question 5, c. *Non liceat Christianis*.) Christian women may not observe vain practices in their spinning and weaving; instead, let them invoke God as their helper, who gave them the skill of weaving.

### CHAPTER 47.—That incantations may not be used in gathering herbs. From the same source, chapter 21 (ibid., chapter 74).

(26, question 5, c. *Non liceat Christianis*.) In collecting medicinal herbs it is unlawful to employ any observances or incantations [variant: “observe”], except only the divine Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, so that God and our Lord may be honored.

### CHAPTER 48.—On those who light little torches at springs or trees. From the same source, chapter 22 (Second Council of Arles, chapter 23).

If, in a priest’s parish, unbelievers light little torches or venerate trees, springs, or stones, and he neglects to uproot this practice, let the instigator or encourager of the act recognize that he has committed sacrilege. If, after warning, he neglects to correct it, he shall be deprived of communion.

[Variant/original: “let him recognize himself guilty of sacrilege; but if the lord or organizer of the act, after warning, refuses to amend, etc.”]

### CHAPTER 49.—That fortune-tellers are to be beaten and expelled. From the Council of Arles, chapter 11.

Fortune-tellers who say that they know the future shall be beaten and expelled from [Col. 0757B] the city.

### CHAPTER 50.—Likewise, on women enchanters. From the Roman Penitential.

If a woman performs diabolical divinations or incantations, she shall do penance for one year, or three Lents, or forty days, according to the gravity of the offense.

### CHAPTER 51.—On those who eat, drink, or carry something upon themselves in order to overthrow God’s judgment. From the Council of Tribur, chapter 4.

If anyone eats, drinks, or carries something on his person by which he thinks he can overturn God’s judgment, and is convicted of it, he shall receive the same sentence as magicians, soothsayers, and enchanters.

### CHAPTER 52.—On those who seek the future in tablets or books. From the Penitential of Theodore.

[Col. 0757C]

The future is not to be sought by lot from tablets or books; no one may presume to cast lots in the Psalter, the Gospel, or other things, or observe any divinations in any objects. If anyone does so, he shall do penance for forty days.

### CHAPTER 53.—On those sorcerers who hope that they can alter people’s minds. From the Roman Penitential.

Sorcerers, enchanters, storm-senders, and those who disturb people’s minds by the invocation of demons shall be anathematized and cast out. If they are willing to amend, clerics shall do penance for three years and laypeople for one year.

### CHAPTER 54.—On the same matter. From the Council of Agde, chapter 4.

[Note: [Col. 0757D] Appended at the end.]

It must be investigated whether there is any woman who claims that by certain sorceries and incantations she can [Col. 0757D] alter people’s minds—that is, turn them from hatred to love, or from love to hatred; condemn or steal away people’s goods. And if there is any woman who says that on certain nights [variant: “during the nighttime hours”] she has been transformed, with a troop of demons, into the likeness of women, rides upon certain beasts, and is numbered in their company, such a woman shall in every case be corrected with whips and expelled from the parish.

### CHAPTER 55.—On those who invoke demons to accomplish their vain practices. From the Penitential of the priest Bede.

Whoever, out of curiosity about the future, consults an invoker [Col. 0758A] of demons [variant: “is an invoker of demons”], diviners called soothsayers, or augurs who collect omens: clerics shall be removed from every office and do penance for three years; laypeople shall do penance for two years.

### CHAPTER 56.—On those who celebrate nocturnal sacrifices to demons. From the Roman Penitential.

Whoever celebrates nocturnal sacrifices to demons, or by incantations invites demons through any art to fulfill his wishes, shall do penance for three years.

### CHAPTER 57.—On those who make vows at trees or springs. From the Council of Agde, chapter 5.

Inquiry must be made whether anyone makes vows at trees, springs, or certain stones as though they were altars, or brings there a candle or any gift, as though some divine power were present there that could bring [Col. 0758B] good or evil.

### CHAPTER 58.—On those who, when the moon is eclipsed, raise their cries and practice sorcery. From the Council of Arles, chapter 5.

Whoever performs these acts when the moon is eclipsed, believing that by their cries, sorceries [variant: “their sorceries”], and sacrilegious practice they can defend themselves; and whoever attempts to hang upon their own people or themselves diviners, charmers, even diabolical amulets, diabolical characters, herbs, or amber; or presumes to honor Thursday in honor of Jupiter or the Kalends of January according to pagan custom: a monk shall do penance for five years, a cleric for four, and a layperson for two.

### CHAPTER 59.—On those who practice their vanities at funeral wakes. From the same council, chapter 3.

[Note: [Col. 0758D] Appended to the Third Council of Arles.]

[Col. 0758C]

Laypeople who keep vigil at a funeral must do so with fear, trembling, and reverence. No one there may presume to sing diabolical songs, or to engage in jokes and dancing, which pagans, under the devil’s instruction, invented. For who does not know that it is diabolical, alien not only to Christian religion but also contrary to human nature, to rejoice, become drunk, sing, and dissolve one’s mouth in laughter there—to set aside every devotion and affection of charity and seem to exult over a brother’s death—where mourning and lamentation ought to resound in tearful [variant: “faithful”] voices over the loss of a dear brother?

Indeed, in many places we read that the Fathers of the Old and New Testaments bewailed the deaths of holy men with weeping; but nowhere that they rejoiced over those who had departed this world. Thus all Egypt wept for the patriarch Jacob for seventy days. When Joseph and his brothers carried their father into the land of Canaan for burial, they held funeral rites at the threshing floor of Athael [variant: Atad], located beyond the Jordan, and filled seven days with great and vehement lamentation. The mourning was so great that the place received its name from it (Genesis 50). We also read concerning blessed Stephen that devout men buried him, or took care of him, and made great mourning over him (Acts 8).

[Col. 0758D]

Therefore such foolish joy and pestilential songs must be forbidden by God’s authority. If anyone wishes to sing, let him sing *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy”; otherwise [variant: “but otherwise”], let him be altogether silent. But if he is unwilling to be silent, on the following day let him be restrained by the priest in such a way that the rest may be afraid.

### CHAPTER 60.—On the same matter. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 10 (and the Council of Elvira, chapter 35).

It has been decided that women are to be forbidden from keeping vigil in a cemetery, since under the pretext of prayer and religion they often secretly commit crimes.

### CHAPTER 61.—On banquets held according to pagan rite. From the African Council, chapter 27 (under Celestine I).

It should also be requested that, since banquets contrary to the divine commandments are held in many places, having been drawn from pagan error (so that Christians are now compelled by pagans to celebrate them, and thus, in the times of Christian emperors, a second persecution seems secretly to be taking place [Col. 0759B]), they be ordered forbidden, and be suppressed under penalty both in cities and on estates—especially since, even on the birthdays of the most blessed martyrs, they do not fear to commit such acts in certain cities and even in the sacred places themselves. On those days, moreover—to speak of which is shameful—they practice most wicked dances through lanes and streets, so that the honor of matrons and the chastity of innumerable women who devoutly come to the most sacred day are assailed by the insults of the wanton, with the result that access even to holy religion is almost shunned.

### CHAPTER 62.—On the same matter. From the decrees of Pope Leo (Epistle 92 of Pope Leo I, to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, ch. 17).

[Col. 0759C] Those who have merely taken part in a banquet of the gentiles and eaten food sacrificed to idols may be cleansed by fasts and the laying on of hands, so that thereafter, abstaining from things offered to idols, they may be participants in Christ’s sacraments. But if they have either worshipped idols or been defiled by murders or fornications, they ought not to be admitted to communion except through public penance.

### CHAPTER 63.—That believers should not presume to eat in cemeteries. From the Second Council of Braga, ch. 70 (ch. 69 of the Greek Synod of Martin of Braga).

(*De consecratione*, distinction, ch. *Non oportet*.) Christians must not be permitted to bring meals to the graves of the dead and offer sacrifice to the dead.

### CHAPTER 64.—On those who have performed dances and transformed themselves into other forms. From the same council, ch. 80.

[Col. 0759D]

If anyone has performed dances before the churches of the saints, or has changed (transformed) his appearance by adopting female dress, or if a woman has adopted male dress, after promising amendment let him or her do penance for three years.

### CHAPTER 65.—That incantations and magical arts are snares of the devil. From the sayings of Augustine.

(26, question 7, ch. *Admoneant*.) Let priests admonish the faithful people to know that magical arts and incantations can provide no remedy for any human ailments: they can heal neither sick, lame, nor even dying living beings [Col. 0760A]. Rather, these are snares and ambushes of the ancient enemy, by which that treacherous being endeavors to deceive the human race. And if anyone practices these things, if he is a cleric, let him be deposed; if a layperson, let him be anathematized.

### CHAPTER 66.—On those who seek health not from the Savior but from his creation. Augustine, in the book *The City of God*.

All wisdom is from the Lord God, and has always been with him, and is before the age. Who has numbered the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the days of the age? Who has measured the height of heaven, the breadth of the earth, and the depth of the abyss? Who has investigated the wisdom of God, which precedes all things? Wisdom was created before all things, and the understanding of prudence from eternity. The fountain of wisdom is the word of God in the highest, and its ways are eternal commandments (Ecclus. 1). (26, question 2, ch. *Qui sine Salvatore*.) [Col. 0760B] For whoever wishes to have salvation without the Savior, and thinks that he can become wise without true wisdom, will labor in continual sickness—not sound, but sick; not wise, but foolish—and in harmful blindness will remain foolish and mad.

Accordingly, every inquiry and every cure sought from divine beings—or rather from demons themselves—in the worship of idols should be called death rather than life; and those who pursue such things, unless they correct themselves, tend toward eternal destruction. As the Psalmist says: “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Ps. 95), who daily desire, through deceived human beings, to deceive others, so as to make them sharers in their own destruction. Thus this vanity of magical arts prevailed throughout the whole world for many centuries through the tradition of evil angels [Col. 0760C]; through a certain knowledge of future things and of the underworld, divination by entrails, auguries, the things called oracles, and necromancy were devised through their inventions.

### CHAPTER 67.—On the inventors of magical art and necromancy. From the sayings of Augustine (Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VIII, ch. 9).

(26, question, ch. *Nec mirum*.)  
[Note: [Col. 0759] This passage is taken from Augustine, *The City of God*, book XVIII, chs. 17 and 18.]

Nor is it surprising concerning the tricks of magicians, whose arts of wrongdoing advanced so far that they even resisted Moses in those signs, turning staffs into serpents and water into blood (Exod. 7). It is also reported in books of the gentiles that a certain sorceress, the very famous Circe, changed Ulysses’ companions into beasts. We also read concerning the sacrifice that the Arcadians offered to their god Dycaeus, that whoever partook of it was changed into the form of beasts. But all these things were feigned by magical deceptions rather than accomplished in reality.

Therefore, in order that these errors themselves may become manifest to the ignorant, we judge it fitting first to speak, according to the tradition of the elders, about their character and inventors. Magi are those whom the common people call *malefici* (“evil-doers”) because of the greatness of their crimes. By God’s permission they disturb the elements; they trouble the minds of persons less trusting in God; and, without any draught of poison, they sometimes kill merely by the force of an incantation. Hence Lucan says:

> No mind, polluted by the corruption of swallowed poison,  
> Perishes when bewitched.

LUCAN, *Pharsalia*, book VI, line 457.

[Col. 0761A] For, having summoned demons, they dare to employ magical arts so that each person may destroy his enemies. They also use blood and often touch dead bodies with victims. Necromancers are those by whose incantations dead persons seem to be raised up, to prophesy and answer questions. For *νεκρός* (*nekros*) means “dead” in Greek, and *μαντεία* (*manteia*) means “divination.” Blood is added to the corpse in order to raise it; for demons are said to love blood. Therefore, whenever necromancy is practiced, blood is mixed with water, so that they may more easily be summoned by the color of blood.

Hydromancers are named from water. For hydromancy consists in calling up in the inspection of water [Col. 0761B] the shadows of demons, seeing their deceptive images—or images and illusions—and hearing something from them there. By the use of blood they are also said to raise up the dead below.

### CHAPTER 68.—On the various kinds of divination. From the sayings of the same author (ibid., immediately following).

(26, question 4, ch. *Igitur genus*.) Thus, the kind of divination is said to have been brought from Persia. Varro, however, says that there are four kinds of divination: earth, water, air, and fire. From these they suppose geomancy, hydromancy, aeromancy, and pyromancy to be named.

Those called *divini* are so called as though “filled with a god”; for they pretend to be full of divinity and, by a certain fraudulent cunning, conjecture future events for the deception of human beings. There are two kinds of divination: art and frenzy. Incantators are those who perform their art by words. *Arioli* are so called because near the altars of idols they utter impious prayers and offer deadly sacrifices; by these rites they receive answers from demons.

Haruspices are named as though “inspectors of the hours.” For they observe days and hours in conducting business and works, and attend to what a person ought to observe at each time. They also inspect the entrails of cattle and predict future events from them. Augurs are those who attend to the flights and cries of birds, and report other signs of things or unforeseen observations encountered by people. These are also *auspices*. For auspices are the signs observed by those traveling; and *auspicia* are so called as though “bird-observations,” and *auguria* as though “bird-chatter”—that is, the voices and language of birds. Again, *augurium* is as though *avigerium*, “what birds carry.” There are two kinds of auspices: one pertains to the eyes, the other to the ears. Flight pertains to the eyes; birds’ cries, to the ears.

[Col. 0761D] Pythonesses are named from Pythian Apollo, because he was the author of divination. Astrologers are so called because they augur from the stars. Those called genethliacs are so named from consideration of days of birth; for they set down human nativities through the twelve signs of heaven and endeavor to predict, from the courses of the stars, the dispositions, actions, and outcomes of those born. That is, they interpret under what sign a person was born and what result in life belongs to one who is born [Col. 0762A].

These are those commonly called mathematicians. The Latins call this kind of superstition “constellations,” that is, markings of the stars, according to their disposition when each person is born. But the first kind—that is, interpreters of the stars—are called magi, as is read of those who announced the birth of Christ in the Gospel (Matt. 2). Later only mathematicians were called by this name. Knowledge of this art was permitted until the Gospel, so that, once Christ had been brought forth, no one thereafter should interpret anyone’s birth from heaven.

Horoscopists are so called because they observe the hours of human births and their unlike and differing fate. Sortilegists are those who, under the name of a fictitious religion, profess knowledge of divination through certain lots which they call “lots of the saints,” or who promise future things by inspection of the learning contained in any writings whatsoever [Col. 0762B]. *Salisatores* are so called because, when any parts of their bodies have twitched, they proclaim that something prosperous or sad is thereby signified.

### CHAPTER 69.—On execrable remedies which physicians employ in their incantations. From the sayings of the same author (ibid., immediately appended).

(26, question 5, ch. *Nec mirum*.)  
[Note: [Col. 0761D] The beginning is excerpted from Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book II, chs. 20 and 23.]

To all the aforesaid things belong also the bindings of execrable remedies, which the art of physicians commends [“condemns” in Augustine and Isidore], whether in incantations, in written characters, or in any things whatsoever hung up or tied. In all these things there is an art of demons, arising from a destructive fellowship of human beings and evil angels. Therefore all must be avoided [Col. 0762C] by a Christian, and wholly rejected and condemned with every execration.

Auguries, moreover, concern birds. The Phrygians were the first to invent them. Mercury is said first to have invented conjuring trickery (*praestigium*). It is called *praestigium* because it blinds the sight of the eyes. A certain Tages [“Strages” in the original and in Victorius] is said first to have transmitted the art of haruspicy to the Etruscans. He dictated haruspicy from the hours and afterward appeared no more. For, according to a fabulous story, while a certain rustic was ploughing, he suddenly sprang forth from the clods of earth and dictated haruspicy, and died on that same day. The Romans translated those books from the Etruscan language into their own. Thus far Isidore.

Human curiosity, then, is mocked by these portents through the deception of demons, when people shamelessly desire to know what they have no rightful basis for investigating. [Col. 0762D] Therefore power is given to unclean spirits, so that through vessels suited to them—that is, depraved people—they may seduce those who despise truth and believe a lie and, in accordance with Paul’s statement, “will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears; and indeed will turn their hearing away from the truth, but will be turned to fables” (2 Tim. 4). “Burdened with sins, they are led away by various desires, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth” (2 Tim. 3).

(26, question 4, ch. *Sciendum*.) “Just as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses” (Exod. 7), so these also resist the truth: persons corrupt in mind, reprobate concerning the faith [Col. 0763A]. “But they shall advance no further; for their folly shall be manifest to all, as theirs also was.”

Nor should anyone therefore believe that anyone can accomplish anything by magical arts without God’s permission—for God either does, by just judgment, all things that occur, or permits them to occur in this way—because those magicians are read to have done things similar to Moses. Moses threw down his staff and it was changed into a serpent; and they each threw down their staffs, which were changed into serpents; but Aaron’s staff devoured their staffs (Exod. 7).

[Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 21.] Neither the magicians nor the evil angels, whose ministrations they employed, were creators of serpents. For throughout all the elements there are in bodily things certain hidden seminal principles which, when temporal and causal opportunity has been given, break forth into their proper forms according to their own modes and limits. Thus the angels who do these things are not said to be creators of animals, just as farmers are not to be called creators of crops, trees, or anything whatever growing in the earth, although they know how to provide certain visible opportunities and causes for their growth. What these persons do visibly, those beings do invisibly; but God alone is the one Creator, who implanted the causes themselves and the seminal principles in things.

(Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, ch. 27.) Furthermore, some think that it must be asked how Scripture relates that the Pythoness raised up the prophet Samuel to speak with Saul, that most impious king (1 Sam. 28), if Pythian divination is to be reckoned an error of magical art [Col. 0763C]. To them this answer may be given: it is an altogether unworthy [“malign”] deed if assent is granted according to the words of the narrative. For how could it happen that a man holy from birth [“by birth”] and righteous in the works of his life should be drawn by magical art? Or, if he was not drawn, did he consent? To believe either of these things of a righteous man is absurd [“contrary”].

For if he was brought unwillingly, righteousness has no support; but if voluntarily, he lost the spiritual merit which he had sought while placed in the flesh. This is wholly absurd, because one who departs hence righteous remains righteous. Rather, this is Satan’s trickery, by which, in order to deceive as many as possible, he pretends that even good persons are in his power. The Apostle shows this among other things when he says: “Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11).

Thus, in order to produce an error in which he himself might also glory, he presented himself under the appearance and name of a righteous man, so that he might falsely claim that the hope preached by God’s worshippers availed nothing, when he feigned that righteous persons departing hence were in his power. But some are deceived by the fact that he did not lie about the death of Saul and his sons, as though it were a great thing for the devil to foresee bodily death before its occurrence. For certain signs are accustomed to appear in those about to die, especially those from whom God’s protection seems removed; much more, then, could the devil do so, whom prophetic oracles attest to have been exalted in angelic majesty. Of his greatness the Apostle says: “Do you not know the depths of Satan?” (2 Cor. 11.) [Col. 0764A] What wonder, then, if he could foresee imminent death at hand, since this is how he deceives and wishes to be worshipped as though in God’s place? (Rev. 2.)

For Saul became so mad through his dullness that he fled to the Pythoness. Corrupted because of sin, he turned to those things which he had condemned. But if anyone, because of the historical narrative and the matters expressly stated, thinks that these things should not be passed over lest the account of the history be empty, he will indeed do rightly—provided he does not carry this over in the least to the reality of the matter, but to Saul’s perception and understanding. For having become reprobate, he could not have sound understanding.
