The historian described Saul’s mind and Samuel’s appearance, expressing what was said and seen, while leaving aside whether those things were true or false. For what does he say? “On hearing in what appearance he had been raised, he understood,” he says, “that this was Samuel” (1 Sam. 18). He reported what Saul understood; and because Saul did not understand rightly, contrary to Scripture he worshipped another than the Lord. Thinking him to be Samuel, he worshipped the devil, so that Satan might obtain the fruit of his deception. For this is what Satan strives for: to be worshipped as God.

For if Samuel had truly appeared to Saul, certainly the righteous man would not have allowed himself to be worshipped, since he had preached that God alone must be worshipped. And how could the man of God, who was in refreshment with Abraham, say to a man of pestilence, deserving the fire of Gehenna: “Tomorrow you shall be with me”? By these two points the unwise Satan disclosed the subtlety of his deception: both because, under Samuel’s appearance and name, he allowed himself to be worshipped contrary to the law, and because he falsely said that a man weighed down by sins—when there is a great distance between sinners and righteous persons—would be with Samuel [Col. 0764C], a most righteous man.

Yet, if Samuel’s name is omitted, it may seem true that Saul would be with the devil; for he passed over to the one whom he worshipped. For the devil, always hiding under a covering, gives himself away when he invents things repugnant to the persons through whom he seeks to deceive.

But if anyone objects and says, “How do those things which the diviners foretell as future come to pass? Or how can they furnish healing to the sick or inflict sickness upon the healthy, if they have no power or capacity of their own?” let him receive this answer from us: no one ought to believe them because the things they predict sometimes come to pass, or because they seem to heal the sick or harm the healthy. For this happens by God’s permission [Col. 0764D], in order that those who hear or see these things may be tested and it may appear what faith or devotion toward God they possess.

As is read in Deuteronomy, Moses by the Lord’s word commanded God’s people, saying: “If a prophet should arise in your midst, or one who says that he has seen a dream, and should foretell a sign or wonder, and what he said should occur, and he should say, ‘Let us go and follow strange gods whom you do not know, and let us serve them,’ you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer, because the Lord your God is testing you, that it may be made manifest whether you love him or not with your whole heart and your whole soul. Follow the Lord your God, fear him, keep his commandments, and obey his voice. You shall serve him, and cling to him” (Deut. 13), etc.

[Augustine, *Questions on Deuteronomy*, question 19.] Here he plainly intended it to be understood [Col. 0765A] that even those things said by diviners not according to God, if what they say should happen, are not to be accepted in such a way that the things commanded by them are done [“or even if they are done,” Victorius], or that the things worshipped by them are worshipped. Nor does God show that what happens is beyond his power; rather, as though one were asking why he permits these things, he gave the reason of testing: namely, for making known their love, whether they have it toward their God. But it is to be made known to themselves rather than to him, who knows all things before they occur.

### CHAPTER 70.—On the nature of demons. From the sayings of the same author (Augustine, *On the Divination of Demons*, book [I], ch. 3).

It should indeed be known that the nature of demons is such that, by the perception of an aerial body, they easily surpass the perception of earthly bodies [Col. 0765B]. Also, by speed—because of the greater mobility of an aerial body—they incomparably outstrip not only the running of any human beings or beasts, but even the flight of birds. Endowed with these two capacities insofar as the aerial body is concerned, namely sharpness of perception and speed of movement, they predict or report things known far beforehand which people, because of the slowness of earthly perception, marvel at.

Moreover, through the very long duration over which their life is extended, demons have acquired far greater experience of events than can come to human beings because of the brevity of life. Through these abilities bestowed by the nature of an aerial body, demons not only predict many future things, but also do many marvelous things. Since human beings cannot say or do such things, some judge demons worthy to be served and to receive divine honors—chiefly under the prompting of the vice of curiosity, through love for false and earthly happiness and temporal eminence.

But those who cleanse themselves from these desires and do not allow themselves to be struck down and carried away [“deceived and captured”] by demons, but seek and love something which remains always in the same manner, by participation in which they may be blessed, first consider that demons are not to be preferred to themselves because demons prevail through the sharper bodily perception of air [“aerial”], that is, of a subtler element. For they do not think even beasts are to be preferred to themselves because those beasts perceive many things more sharply: for example, a keen-scented dog, because by its very sharp sense of smell it finds a hidden wild beast and leads a person, as it were, to its capture [Col. 0765D]—not by a wiser intellectual understanding, of course, but by a sharper bodily sense; or a vulture, because from an unexpected distance it is summoned by a discarded corpse; or an eagle, because, flying high, it is said to see from such a distance a fish swimming under the waves and, striking down heavily with feet and talons extended, to seize it; or many other kinds of animals which wander while feeding among plants harmful to their health, yet touch none of the things by which they are harmed, whereas a human being has scarcely learned to recognize such things by experience and, because he has not tested many harmless things, fears them.

From this it is easy to infer how much sharper perception may be in aerial bodies; yet no prudent person will therefore judge demons, who possess it [Col. 0766A], to be preferable to good human beings. We say the same about swiftness of bodies: by that advantage human beings are surpassed not only by birds but also by many quadrupeds, so greatly that in comparison with them they must be reckoned leaden. Yet people do not therefore think these kinds of animals are to be preferred to themselves, though they rule them—not by bodily force but by the command of reason—by catching, taming, and bringing them under the service and benefit of their own will.

(Ibid., ch. 4.) As for that third power of demons, namely that through long experience of events they have learned how to foreknow and foretell many things, those who carefully endeavor to distinguish these matters from the truth of the truest light likewise despise it. They do not think that wicked old men, being more experienced and therefore seemingly more learned, should take precedence over upright youths; nor do they think that physicians, sailors, or farmers whose will they see to be depraved and whose habits unjust should be preferred to themselves because the former can foretell many things concerning illnesses, storms, or kinds of trees in such a way that they seem to divine them to someone inexperienced in these matters [Col. 0766B].

And because demons not only foretell certain future things but also perform certain marvelous things by the excellence of their own bodies, why should prudent people not despise this, when very many wicked and ruined persons train their bodies in such ways and can accomplish so much by various arts that those who do not know or have never seen such things can scarcely believe even reports of them? How many marvelous things have tightrope walkers and other theatrical performers done; how many have artisans, and especially mechanicians, done? Are they therefore better than good people endowed with holy piety?

We have recalled these matters so that whoever considers them without stubbornness and without a vain inclination to resist may at the same time reflect: if human beings can do so much with the underlying and grosser material of their own bodies, or of earth and water, stones and wood and various metals, that those who cannot do such things often, in astonishment at comparison with themselves, call them divine—although some of the former are more powerful in arts and some of the latter better in morals—how much better and greater things demons may accomplish through the capacity and facility of an exceedingly subtle body, that is, an aerial one, although they are most depraved in will, especially in the arrogance of pride and the evident malice of an unclean and perverse spirit [Col. 0766D].

How much the element of air, by which their bodies have power, can accomplish invisibly in producing, moving, changing, and altering many visible things, would take too long to demonstrate now; and we think that it readily occurs to anyone who considers even moderately.

### CHAPTER 71.—On the divination of demons. From the sayings of the same author (the same book, ch. 5).

First, then, since the question concerns the divination of demons, it must be known that they most often foretell things which they themselves are going to do. For they often receive power to inflict diseases, to make the very air unhealthy by corrupting it, and to suggest evil deeds to perverse people who love earthly advantages [Col. 0767A], since they are certain from those persons’ habits that they will consent to such suggestions. They suggest them in marvelous and invisible ways, penetrating by the subtlety of their bodies the bodies of unsuspecting people and mingling themselves with their thoughts through certain imaginary visions, whether people are awake or asleep.

Sometimes, however, they foretell not the things they do themselves, but things which they know by natural signs will happen—signs which cannot come within human perception. For a physician is not to be considered a diviner merely because he foresees something which one ignorant of his art does not know how to foresee. What wonder, then, if, just as the physician foresees future health, good or bad, from the disturbed or modified condition of a human body, so a demon foresees future storms from a condition and arrangement of the air known to it but unknown to us? (See *Retractations*, book II, ch. 30.)

Sometimes demons also learn with complete ease the dispositions of people, not only uttered aloud but conceived in thought, when certain signs are expressed from the mind in the body; and from this they foretell many things to persons who marvel at them because they do not know those dispositions. For just as a more excited movement of the mind appears in the face, so that something happening inwardly may be recognized outwardly even by people, so it ought not to be incredible that even gentler thoughts give certain signs through the body which cannot be known by the dull perception of human beings but can be known by the sharp perception of demons.

(From the same book, *On Divination*, ch. 6.) By this and similar capacity demons foretell many future things [Col. 0767C], although the height of that prophecy which God works through his holy angels and prophets is far removed from them. For if they foretell anything of God’s ordering, they hear it in order to foretell it; and when they proclaim what they hear from there, they do not deceive, for angelic and prophetic oracles are utterly true.

But if anyone is offended [in Augustine the reading now is “is not offended”] that demons too hear and proclaim certain such things, as though it were unworthy that what is said in order to become known to human beings should not be kept silent by evil as well as good persons: in human beings themselves we see even precepts of good life sung alike by righteous and perverse people. Nor does it do any harm; indeed, it also helps the fuller knowledge and renown of truth when even those who contradict it by perverse conduct say whatever they know of it.

In their other predictions, however, demons commonly both deceive and are deceived. They are deceived when, after they have foretold [“announced”] their own plans, something is unexpectedly commanded from above which disturbs all their counsels: just as if persons subject to certain authorities should plan something which they suppose their superiors will not prohibit, and promise that they will do it, but those in whose hands greater power lies should suddenly forbid the entire arrangement and preparation by a decision from another, higher council.

They are also deceived when they foresee certain things by natural causes, like physicians, sailors, and farmers [Col. 0768A], but far more sharply and excellently because the perception of an aerial body is more keen and alert; for these things too are unexpectedly and suddenly changed by angels who devoutly serve God Most High, through another arrangement unknown to demons. This is as if something external happened to a sick person causing death, although a physician, upon preceding signs of genuine recovery, had promised that he would live. Or as if, having observed the condition of the air, some sailors had predicted that a wind would blow for a long time, yet the Lord Christ, sailing with his disciples, commanded it to be still, “and there was a great calm” (Matt. 8). Or as if a farmer promised that a certain vine would bear fruit that year, knowing the nature of the soil and the number of the seeds, yet that year an unexpected unseasonableness of the sky dried it up, or the command of someone more powerful uprooted it.

Thus many things also belonging to the foreknowledge and prediction of demons, which are foreseen as future through lesser and more usual causes, are hindered and changed by greater and more hidden causes. But demons also deceive through the desire to deceive and through the envious will by which they rejoice in human error. Yet, lest they lose the weight of authority among their worshippers, they contrive that blame be attributed to their interpreters and conjecturers of signs whenever they have either been deceived or lied.

Sometimes, too, those malignant spirits, deceivers of human beings and enemies of their salvation, are accustomed to predict the decline of their worship and the ruin of idols, so that they may appear foreknowing what will happen in individual kingdoms or places and what adverse event may befall their own faction [Col. 0768C]. Those who read gentile histories are not ignorant of this either.

What wonder, then, if, when the destruction of times and images was already imminent—long before foretold by the prophets of the Most High God—the demon Serapis disclosed this shortly beforehand to one of his worshippers, so that in departing or fleeing he might commend his supposed divination? (Ibid., ch. 7.) For these beings are driven away, or even bound and dragged off by higher commands; and they are removed from their places, so that God’s will may be done concerning the things in which they were worshipped. He foretold long before that this would happen among all nations, and commanded that it be done through his faithful people.

Why, moreover, should a demon not have been allowed to predict this, when he already knew it was impending for himself, since this prediction also bore witness to the prophets by whom these things were written, so that prudent persons might understand how watchfully the deception of demons must be guarded against and their worship fled? Although for so long a time they had kept silent in their temples about these things to come—which they could not have been ignorant had been foretold through the prophets—when they began to draw near, demons wished to predict them, as it were, lest they seem ignorant and defeated.

### CHAPTER 72.—On the same matter. From the sayings of the same author (ibid., immediately following).

When this, then, had been foretold and written down so long beforehand—to pass over other matters in the meantime—let us cite what the prophet Zephaniah says: “The Lord will prevail against them and will destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth; and each one shall worship him from his own place, all the islands of the nations” (Zeph. 2).

A little later: Either those worshipped in the temples of the nations did not believe that these things would happen to them, and for this reason did not wish to spread them abroad through their seers and fanatics; or, although they knew with complete certainty that they would happen, they kept silence through their temples, lest even then they should begin to be abandoned and despised by discerning people, since the prophets who forbade their worship bore witness concerning the future overthrow of their temples and images. But now, after the time has come in which the prophecies of the prophets of the one God are to be fulfilled—of the God who calls these false gods and most emphatically commands that they not be worshipped—why should they not themselves have been allowed to proclaim this fact which they had discovered? Thus it might appear more clearly that previously they had either not believed these things at all [Col. 0769B], or had feared to announce them to their worshippers; but at the end, as though they had nothing further to do, they wished even there to display their own divinity, where they are now exposed as having long feigned divination. (Ibid., a little later, ch. 8.)

Yet even these things which they bring forward scarcely, rarely, and secretly ought not to move us, if some demon was compelled to disclose to its worshippers what it had learned from the sayings of the prophets or from angelic oracles; for why should this not occur, when it is not an assault upon, but a testimony to, the truth? For the one thing that ought to be demanded of those fanatics is this—and they have never produced it before, nor will they ever produce it afterward, unless perhaps they attempt to offer an invention—that their gods, through their seers, ever dared to proclaim [variant: disclose] anything against the God of Israel. Concerning this God, their most learned authors, who could read and know all those writings, sought rather to discover who he was than were able to deny that he was God. Moreover, this God, whom none of them dared to deny was the true God—for even if one denied him, he would not merely incur deserved punishments, but would also be convicted by certain effects—this God, whom, as we have said, none of them dared to deny was the true God, foretold through his seers, that is, prophets, by an open declaration, commanded by open power, and fulfilled by open truth, that those were false gods and must altogether be abandoned, and that their temples, images, and sacred rites were to be overthrown. Therefore who is so utterly foolish as not to choose rather to worship him [Col. 0769D] whose worship is not forbidden by those whom he formerly worshipped? And once he begins to worship him, he certainly will not worship those whose worship is forbidden by the one whom he worships. (Ibid., ch. 9.)

We have shortly before recalled that it was foretold by his prophets that the nations themselves would worship God after the false gods whom they formerly worshipped had been destroyed; and let us repeat it now. “The Lord,” he says, “will prevail against them and will destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth; and each one shall worship him from his own place, all the islands of the nations” (Zeph. 2). Here the islands alone are not to be understood, but rather all the nations situated in them will worship God. Nor is this surprising, since elsewhere he does not name islands, but the whole world, saying: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his presence, because the kingdom belongs to the Lord, and he himself shall rule the nations” (Ps. 21 [22]). That these things were to be fulfilled through Christ is sufficiently clear from many other testimonies, and from the very psalm from which we have cited this passage. For a little earlier he himself, speaking through the Prophet, spoke of his future passion, saying: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones; but they looked upon and gazed at me; they divided my garments among themselves, and cast lots for my clothing” (ibid.). A little later he adds the passage which we have quoted: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord,” etc.

Moreover, the testimony first cited, where it is said, “The Lord will prevail against them [Col. 0770B] and will destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth,” sufficiently shows, in the words “will prevail,” that this too was foretold: the pagans would first attack the Church and persecute the Christian name with all their power, so that, if possible, it might be wholly blotted out from the earth; and because he was to overcome them by the patience of the martyrs, the greatness of miracles, and the consequent faith of the peoples [variant: *superatura*, “was to overcome,” referring to “the patience”], it was therefore said: “The Lord will prevail against them.” For it would not be said, “he will prevail against them,” unless they resisted by attacking him. Thus it was also prophesied in the psalm: “Why have the nations raged, and the peoples devised vain things? The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. 2). And a little later it says: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession” (ibid.).

By these and similar prophetic testimonies it is shown to have been foretold that what we see fulfilled through Christ would come to pass: that the God of Israel, whom we understand to be the one true God, would be worshipped not in the one nation called Israel alone but among all nations, and would remove all the false gods of the nations both from their temples and from the hearts of their worshippers. (Ibid., ch. 10.) Let these people now go and still dare to defend their former vanities against the Christian religion, against the true worship of God, so that they may perish with a crash. For this too was foretold concerning them in the Psalms, as the Prophet says: “You have sat upon the throne, judging righteousness; you rebuked the nations and the wicked perished; you blotted out their name for ever and ever. The swords of the enemy have failed utterly, and you have destroyed their cities; their memory has perished with a crash, but the Lord remains for ever” (Ps. 9 [10]).

It is therefore necessary that all these things be fulfilled. Nor should the fact that the few who remain still dare to display their empty-talking doctrines and mock Christians as utterly ignorant move us, while we see in them the fulfilment of what was foretold. (A little below.) For since the nations raged and the peoples devised vain things against the Lord and against his Christ (Ps. 2)—when the blood of the saints was being shed and the Church was being laid waste [Col. 0771A]—they have continually diminished even to this time and thereafter daily. But against their reproaches and proud mockeries, the oracles of our God make us most steadfast; for we see, and rejoice to see, that what they say even on this matter is fulfilled. Thus he addresses us through the Prophet: “Hear me, you who know judgment, my people, in whose heart is my law: do not fear the reproaches of men, and do not be overcome by their slanders, nor regard greatly their contempt for you. For as a garment they shall be consumed in time, and as wool they shall be eaten by moths; but my righteousness remains for ever” (Isa. 51).

Thus far Augustine in that passage. It must therefore be carefully noted, and guarded against with every effort, lest in our own times—in which we see the Christian religion spread throughout the whole world—through the idleness of pastors [teachers] and the inertia of instructors, those few who still remain confuse the rite of worship due to the true God and, corrupted by demonic deceptions, practise false divinations among the people of God, deceiving the unlearned and ignorant. Thus they may abandon the truth itself, which is the light of the world and enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1), seek in these darknesses knowledge of future events, and seek from deceivers of men the salvation of their souls or bodies. God is especially angered and provoked to vengeance by such transgressions.

Therefore through Ezekiel he threatens, saying: “Woe to the foolish prophets who follow their own spirit and see nothing. Your prophets, Israel, were like foxes in deserts. Have you not seen a vain vision and uttered a lying divination? And you say, ‘The Lord says,’ when I have not spoken. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have spoken vanity and seen a lie, behold, I am against you, says the Lord God; and my hand shall be against the prophets who see vanities and divine lies. They shall not be in the council of my people, nor shall they be written in the register of the house of Israel, nor shall they enter the land of Israel” (Ezek. 13). Rebuking the laziness of teachers through the same prophet, he says: “You have not gone up to face the enemy, nor set up a wall for the house of Israel, that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (ibid.). And again: “Woe,” he says, “to the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves. Do not shepherds feed the flocks? You ate the milk [Col. 0771D] and clothed yourselves with the wool, and slew what was fat, but you did not feed my flock. What was weak you did not strengthen, what was sick you did not heal, what was broken you did not bind up, what was driven away you did not bring back, and what was lost you did not seek; but you ruled them with harshness and power. And my sheep were scattered because there was no shepherd, and they became food for all the beasts of the field, and were scattered” (Ezek. 34).

Hence it is also said through Jeremiah: “From the least even to the greatest, all pursue avarice; from prophet even to priest, all practise falsehood. And they healed the brokenness of the daughter of my people to her disgrace, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there was no peace. They were put to shame because they committed abomination” (Jer. 8). Therefore thus says the Lord God of hosts, the God of Israel: “Behold, I shall feed this people with wormwood, and give them gall-water to drink; and I shall scatter them among nations which neither they nor their fathers have known, and I shall send the sword after them until they are consumed” (Jer. 9).

How greatly the negligence of shepherds and the error of those subject to them displease almighty God is shown not only by prophetic testimonies but also by the deeds of the ancients. For in the Book of Kings one reads how an evil spirit deceived Ahab king of Israel through false prophets, so that, believing them, he perished; and how his son Ahaziah, when sick, sent messengers to consult Beelzebub, god of Ekron, whether he could live and recover from his illness (3 Kings [1 Kings] 22). On this account the prophet Elijah, sent by the Lord [Col. 0772B], rebukes him, saying: “Because you sent messengers to consult Baalzebub, the god of Ekron, as though there were no God in Israel from whom you could inquire for a word, therefore you shall not come down from the bed on which you have climbed, but you shall surely die” (4 Kings [2 Kings] 1). And he died according to the word of the Lord spoken by Elijah, and did not find the health he sought.

Therefore every care must be taken, by all means, by prelates and subjects, great and small, priests and people alike, lest anyone be deceived by the fraud, guile, and wickedness of the ancient enemy through deceptions of this kind, so that we wish to learn truth from liars and seek a remedy for our weakness from the authors of deadly diseases and death. Rather, fleeing to the living God, who gives life to all, let us hasten with devout heart through holy prayers, fasts, and almsgiving, beseeching him, in his goodness, to care for his servants, deliver us from all our enemies, and teach us to do his will, because he is the Lord our God; and to grant us his good Spirit, who may lead us in the right way and give us life in his righteousness, so that, under his instruction, offering him acceptable service throughout the whole time of our life, after this life we may through his grace merit to possess everlasting [variant: heavenly] blessedness.

### CHAPTER 73.—Concerning priests and the other ecclesiastical orders who consult magicians, soothsayers, or diviners. From the Council of Toledo, ch. 39 (Fourth Council of Toledo, ch. 28).

[Col. 0772D]

If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or any member of the clerical order is discovered to have consulted magicians, haruspices, soothsayers, augurs, lot-casters, or those who profess the magical art, or any persons practising similar arts, he is to be deposed from the honour of his rank, undergo monastic discipline, and there, given over to perpetual penance, expiate the crime of the sacrilege he has committed [variant: undergo punishment].

### CHAPTER 74.—Concerning those who utter incantations against bewitchment. From the Council of Chalon, ch. 5.

If anyone recites an incantation against a spell, or any kind of incantation whatsoever, except the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, both the person chanting and the person for whom it is chanted shall do penance for three Lents on bread and water.

### CHAPTER 75.—That one possessed by a demon may lawfully carry stones or herbs without an incantation. From the sayings of Jerome.

A person suffering from a demon may have stones or herbs without an incantation.

### CHAPTER 76.—That a priest should not delight in frivolous entertainments. From a synod in the time of Pope Eugenius and the Emperors Louis and Lothair, ch. 11.

A priest must not take pleasure in having any games performed before him. Anyone found to have transgressed must, after episcopal admonition, cease from doing so; otherwise he is to be judged according to the canons.

### CHAPTER 77.—That women should not engage in vain games on feast days, ch. 35.

There are some persons, especially women, who on feast days, holy days, and saints’ birthdays—days on which they ought to be free for God—do not take pleasure in coming to church, but arrange to come while dancing, singing shameful words, and joining in dances, thus performing an imitation of pagans. If such persons come to church with lesser sins, they return with greater sins. In such a matter every priest ought most diligently to admonish the people that on these days they should resort to church for prayer alone, because those who do such things not only destroy themselves but also aim at the destruction of others.

### CHAPTER 78.—That presbyters should not attend spectacles. From the Council of Laodicea, ch. 54.

(De consecratione, distinction 5, ch. *Non oportet ministros*.) Ministers of the altar, or any clerics whatsoever, ought not to attend spectacles presented at weddings or banquets; rather, before the theatrical performers enter, they must rise from the feast and depart.

### CHAPTER 79.—Concerning buffoonish clerics. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, ch. 59.

(Distinction 46, ch. *Clericum*.) A cleric who is buffoonish and playful in obscene words is to be removed from office.

### CHAPTER 80.—Concerning jokes to be avoided. Ambrose, *On Duties*, book 1 (ch. 23).

Although jokes are sometimes honourable and pleasant, they are nevertheless alien to the ecclesiastical rule; for how can we employ things which we do not find in the Scriptures? One must also take care in storytelling lest it bend the gravity of a more serious purpose. “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall weep” (Luke 6), says the Lord; and do we seek material for laughter, so that by laughing here we may weep there? I think that not merely unrestrained jokes but all jokes should be avoided. Yet speech full of pleasantness and grace is not unbecoming.

### CHAPTER 81.—On the same subject. From Augustine’s sermon *On Tithes*, beginning: “Christ being propitious.”

[Note: [Col. 0773] Sermon 219, *On Time*; but this passage is not taken from there.]

Admonish this, brethren: let your households not utter from their mouths songs that are shameful and sensual, enemies of chastity and decency. For it is not right that from the mouth into which Christ’s Eucharist enters there should proceed a sensual and amorous song.

### CHAPTER 82.—That in every social condition there are souls pleasing to God. From the Life of St Paphnutius.

[Col. 0774A]

Even if someone is a thief or an actor on the stage, even if he cultivates the land and appears bound in marriage, even if he is called a merchant and serves commerce, nevertheless in every condition of human life there are souls pleasing to God, possessing certain hidden [variant: cultivated] acts in which God delights. Hence it is clear that God is pleased not so much by a profession of life or an outward appearance of dress as by sincerity and disposition of mind and uprightness of deeds.

### CHAPTER 83.—Concerning an actor. Cyprian to Eucratius (book 1, letter 10, beginning: “Out of affection”).

You thought it proper to consult me, dearest brother, concerning a certain actor residing among you, who persists in the disgrace of that same profession and, as a master and teacher not of children to be educated but of children to be ruined, imparts to others what he learned wickedly: whether such a person ought to communicate with us. I think this accords neither with the divine majesty nor with Gospel discipline, that the modesty and honour of the Church should be defiled by so shameful and infamous a contagion.

For when men are forbidden in the Law (Deut. 22) to put on women’s clothing and people of this kind are judged accursed, how much greater is the crime not only of assuming women’s garments but also of representing, by the teaching of an indecent art, shameful, effeminate, and feminine gestures? Nor should anyone excuse himself on the ground that he himself has left the theatre, while still teaching these things to others. For the person who appoints substitutes and supplies many replacements for himself cannot be considered to have ceased. He instructs and teaches, against God’s ordinance, how a male may be transformed into a woman, how sex may be altered by art, and how the devil may be pleased through the sins of a corrupted and enervated body, by which he defiles God’s created form.

If he pleads need and the necessity of poverty, his need too may be assisted among the others maintained by the Church’s provisions, provided that he is content with more frugal and innocent food. Nor should he suppose that he is being paid to cease from sins, when in fact he does this not for us but for himself.

### CHAPTER 84.—That it is a vice to give one’s possessions to actors. Augustine on John, part 2 (tractate 100 on John 16).

To give one’s possessions to actors is an enormous vice, not a virtue. And you know how frequently such persons are praised with acclaim, because, as it is written: “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the doer of iniquity is blessed” (Ps. 9 [10]).

### CHAPTER 85.—That idolaters are to be converted not by force but by reason. Pope Nicholas, in response to the questions of the Bulgarians, ch. 41.

Concerning those who refuse to accept the good of Christianity and sacrifice to idols or bend the knee to them, we can write nothing else to you except that you should, by admonitions, exhortations, and reason rather than by force, convict them of the vanity of their beliefs.

### CHAPTER 86.—On the same subject. The same, ibid.

There is to be no fellowship with those who do not believe and worship idols. Yet no force whatsoever is to be applied to make them believe, for nothing that is not voluntary can be good.

### CHAPTER 87.—That an animal killed or pursued by a pagan is not to be eaten, ch. 91.

An animal which a Christian pursues but a pagan strikes and kills is not to be eaten; nor is an animal which a pagan pursues but a Christian kills.

### CHAPTER 88.—That the sun should not receive veneration as though holy. From a sermon of Pope Leo on the Nativity of the Lord, beginning: “Of today’s feast,” etc. (Sermon 7, ch. 4).

Some Christians even think they are acting very religiously when, before reaching the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter—which is dedicated to the one living and true God—they have climbed the steps leading up to the raised platform of the upper altar, turn their bodies toward the rising sun [variant in the original: turn back], bow their necks, and incline themselves in honour of the shining orb. We are greatly distressed and grieved that this happens, partly through the fault of ignorance and partly through a pagan spirit.

### CHAPTER 89.—That works are of no avail without faith. Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book 12, ch. 7.

Works of mercy avail nothing for pagans or Jews who do not believe in Christ, nor for any heretics and schismatics, where faith, love, and sober sanctification are not found.

### CHAPTER 90.—Concerning enemies of Christ to be avoided. John IX [variant: VII], to the Neapolitans, Salernitans [variant: Falerians], and Amalfitans.

[Col. 0775C]

May the conscience of your love in Christ rightly judge how far from Christ are those who, with his unbelievers, in violation of the prohibition of so great an apostle as Paul (2 Cor. 6), enter into a polluted unity of alliance. For when people are joined in any participation with the rebellions against a king, they are judged alike liable to charges of treason and condemned [variant: punished] by the same sentence. How completely alien from Christ’s body must those be judged who, allied with his enemies, tear apart his members all the more ruinously because they press closer to the Church of God?

Likewise: How detestable to God it is to make alliances with the wicked is clearly perceived from this: Jehoshaphat king of Judah, though extolled by so many praises for his previous life, is rebuked for his friendship with Ahab when the prophet Jehu says to him: “You give help to the wicked, and join in friendship with those who hate the Lord” (2 Chron. 19). “And therefore you deserved the Lord’s anger; but good works were found in you, because you removed the sacred groves from the land of Judah.” Furthermore, how pleasing it is to God to refrain from peace with the enemies of God is shown by our Psalmist, who says: “Did I not hate those who hated you, O Lord, and waste away because of your enemies? With perfect hatred I hated them; they became enemies to me” (Ps. 138 [139]).

From this, most beloved sons, it is plainly shown how great a crime it is to maintain peace with the most wicked, if so great a Prophet offered this to God as a sacrifice: that he stirred up enmities against the perverse for God’s sake [Col. 0776A]. Hence the tribe of Levi, taking up swords and passing through the midst of the camp, because it refused to spare sinners who were to be struck down, was said to have consecrated its hands to God (Exod. 32). Hence Phinehas, despising favour with his sinning fellow-citizens, struck down those coupling with Midianite women, and in his anger appeased God’s anger (Num. 25).

### CHAPTER 91.—That one baptized by pagans should be rebaptized. Gregory II to Bishop Boniface.

Concerning those whom, you asserted, had been baptized by pagans: if this is so, we command that you baptize them again in the name of the Holy Trinity. Likewise (letter 14): You asked concerning foods sacrificed to idols whether it was lawful to eat them if the life-giving sign of the cross had been made over them by the faithful. It is sufficient to answer with what the blessed apostle Paul says (1 Cor. 10): “If anyone says that this has been sacrificed to idols, do not eat it, on account of the one who informed you and on account of conscience.”

### CHAPTER 92.—That only orthodox Christians should serve in the army. From the history of Anastasius, librarian of the Holy Roman Church.

In the third year of his reign, the Emperor Justinian promulgated a law that pagans and heretics should not serve in the army, but only orthodox Christians.

### CHAPTER 93.—That Christ’s service is voluntary, not compelled. Bede, *History of the English*, book 1, ch. 26.

The king is said to have rejoiced so greatly at the faith and conversion of believers, being converted himself, that he nevertheless compelled no one to Christianity; rather, he embraced believers with a more ardent love, as fellow citizens with himself of the heavenly kingdom. For he had learned from the teachers and authors of his salvation that Christ’s service ought to be voluntary, not compelled.

### CHAPTER 94.—Concerning an exaction to be imposed upon a pagan peasant. Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari (book 3, letter 26).

“If I can discover any pagan peasant belonging to any bishop, I shall take strong action against that bishop” (23, question 6, ch. *Jam vero*). But if a peasant is found to be of such great unbelief and obstinacy that he utterly refuses to come to God, he must be burdened with so heavy a tax that the very punishment of the exaction compels him to hasten toward rectitude.

### CHAPTER 95 (see above, ch. 32).—Concerning the zeal to be exercised against worshippers of idols or soothsayers. Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Sardinia (book 7, letter 66).

[Col. 0776D]

We strongly exhort your brotherhood, by pastoral guardianship, to keep watch against worshippers of idols, haruspices, and lot-casters; to address the people publicly against persons of this sort; and, by persuasive exhortation, to recall them from the stain of so great a sacrilege, the threat of divine judgment, and the peril of this present life. If, however, you find that they refuse to amend and correct themselves of such practices, we wish you to seize them with fervent zeal. If they are slaves, punish them with beatings and tortures by which they may be brought to amendment; but if they are free, they are to be confined and bound under fitting and strict penance.

### CHAPTER 96.—Concerning food offered to idols. Ambrose on the First Epistle to the Corinthians (ch. 10).

[Col. 0777A]

Although something has become polluted incidentally—that is, through an offering to an idol—nevertheless, when the buyer does not know it, he suffers no scruple and is guiltless before God.

### CHAPTER 97.—What this means: “You observe days and months,” etc. From Ambrose’s sermon on Lent, beginning: “You have understood.”

[Note: [Col. 0777D] This is now read as Sermon 7 on the Kalends of January, beginning: “I have against …”.]

A person observes a day and a month if, on the Kalends of January, he either does not fast or does not go to church, but goes out into the field. Therefore, brethren, let us avoid with every care the festivals and holidays of the pagans, so that when they feast and are merry, we may then be sober and fasting, in order that they may understand that their merriment is condemned by our abstinence. We must avoid not only association with pagans but also association with Jews, whose very conversation is a great defilement.

### CHAPTER 98.—That Christians should not permit anything from their threshing floor or winepress to be taken for sacrifice to idols. Augustine to Publicola (letter 154).

If something is taken from a threshing floor or winepress for sacrifices to demons with a Christian’s knowledge, he therefore sins [variant: “sins before God”] if he permits it where he has the power to prevent it. But if he did not discover that it was done, or did not have the power to prevent it, he makes use of the clean remaining produce from which those things were taken.

Likewise, a little later in the same place: If someone doubts whether some meat has been sacrificed to idols, and it has not been so sacrificed, but he changes his judgment and concludes that it has not been sacrificed to idols, and eats it [Col. 0777C], he certainly does not sin; for it is not, nor is it now thought to be, meat sacrificed to idols, even if it was thought so before. For one may correct one’s judgment from falsehood to truth. But if anyone thinks good to be what is evil and acts in that belief, he certainly sins. Such are all sins of ignorance: whenever someone thinks that what is done wrongly is done rightly.

### CHAPTER 99.—That those who bind baptized persons to the sacrileges of demons are spiritual murderers. Augustine to Bishop Boniface (letter 23).

Parents, or any elders whatsoever, who attempt to bind their baptized children or any baptized little ones to the sacrileges of demons are rightly called spiritual murderers. They do not indeed cause their death in actuality, but, as far as lies in them, they become killers.

### CHAPTER 100.—That only those who leave the Church through crimes are to be mourned. Jerome to Rusticus.

[Note: [Col. 0778D] Volume 1, beginning: “That one unknown to another unknown …”.]

A pagan or a Jew, who were not in the Church and have died once, are not to be mourned; concerning them the Saviour says: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. 8). Rather, those are to be mourned who through crimes and sins depart from the Church and refuse ever to return to it because of the condemnation [variant: domination] of vices [alternate corrupt reading: “they approach condemnation”].

### CHAPTER 101.—Who may be called a devil. Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Testament* (question 90).

The devil is not a special name but a common one: for wherever the works of the devil are found, without doubt that person is to be called a devil. It is the name of an activity, not of a nature.

### CHAPTER 102.—How persons possessed by demons may be healed. Bede on Luke, book 3, ch. 5 (book 3, ch. 31, on Luke 8).

Priests of our own time who know how to cast out demons by the grace of exorcism are accustomed to say that sufferers cannot otherwise be healed unless, so far as they are able to understand, they openly disclose in confession everything that unclean spirits have produced through them while awake or asleep by sight, hearing, taste, touch, or any other sense of body or mind. This applies especially when incorporeal spirits, appearing to men in female form or to women in male dress—the demons which the Gauls call *dusii*—pretend, by an unspeakable marvel, to seek and accomplish sexual intercourse with the human body.

They also prescribe that the name by which the demon claimed to be called, and the forms of swearing by which the two parties entered a covenant of its love, must be disclosed. The matter seems very like a lie, but is so true and so well known by the testimony of many that a priest living near me related that he had begun to cure a certain nun possessed by a demon, but so long as the matter remained concealed he could make no progress with her. Once she confessed the phantom by which she was troubled, he immediately drove it away by prayers and the other necessary forms of purification; and, by adding medical care, healed with blessed salt that woman’s body from the ulcers she had contracted from the demon’s touch.

But since he was utterly unable to close one of the ulcers, which he found lodged deep in her side, so that it did not continually open, he received from the very woman whom he wished to heal the advice by which she could be healed. “If,” she said, “you sprinkle the medicine with oil consecrated for the sick and thus anoint me, I shall immediately be restored to health. For once in the spirit I saw, in a city far away which I have never seen with bodily eyes, a certain girl suffering the same affliction healed in this manner by a priest.” He did as she suggested, and immediately the ulcer consented to receive the remedy which it had previously rejected.

### CHAPTER 103.—Concerning giving communion to the possessed. From the *Collations* of Syricius, ch. 13.

We do not remember that the most holy communion was ever forbidden to the possessed by the elders; indeed, they held that, if possible, it ought even to be given them daily.

### CHAPTER 104.—That possessed clerics should not rise to higher ranks. Nicholas to Alwin, archbishop of Juvavum.

Clerics known to have been possessed by demons in youth cannot advance to a higher rank of sacred government.

### CHAPTER 105.—Concerning sexual intercourse of demons with women. Augustine, *Questions on Genesis*, question 3 (on Gen. 8).

It is more credible that righteous human beings, called either angels or sons of God, sinned with women through falling into lust than that angels, who have no flesh, could have descended to that sin—although so many things are said by many people about certain demons that are wanton toward women that it is not easy to determine a judgment on this matter.

### CHAPTER 106.—Concerning the multiplicity of demons assailing the faithful. Jerome on Joshua, homily 15. (Origen in Jerome’s translation.)

It seems to me that there is, in a sense, an infinite number of opposing powers, because in almost every individual person there are certain spirits contriving different kinds of sins within them. For example, there is one spirit of fornication, another spirit of anger, another of avarice, and yet another of pride; and if it happens that some person [Col. 0779B] is driven by all these evils, or even by more of them, he must be thought to have all these, or even more, hostile spirits within himself. Hence they must be believed to be several for each person, since individual persons do not possess only single vices or commit only single sins, but many seem to be committed by each one.

Again, it must not be supposed that one spirit of fornication seduces the man who, for example, commits fornication in Britain and the one who does so in India and elsewhere. Nor do I think there is one spirit of anger that inflames different people in different places. Rather, I think there is one prince of the spirit of fornication, but innumerable spirits obedient to him in this office; and that different spirits, serving under that prince [variant: “different spirits who serve under that prince,” etc.], [Col. 0779C] incite individual persons to sins of this sort. Likewise, I think that there is one princely spirit of anger [Col. 0780A] and innumerable agents beneath him, who kindle in each individual person sins of this kind of vice. The same is true of avarice, pride, and the remaining evils. Therefore the Apostle does not speak of one principality among the opposing powers, but of many, against whom, he writes, he and all of us wage battle (Eph. 6).

Yet I think that over all these there is, as it were, one who is more eminent in wickedness and loftier in crime, who alone, as prince and leader of them all, master of the whole abominable host [variant: “leader of the princes, and master of the whole …”], assails the entire world, while they individually incite it piecemeal to sins according to the various kinds of sins. I certainly think that all the saints who resist these spirits, the instigators of sins, conquer them, and overcome [Col. 0780B] each one of them, diminish the army of demons and, as it were, kill very many of them. For example: when one who lives chastely and modestly has overcome the spirit of fornication, that spirit which has been defeated by that saint is no longer permitted to attack another person. Rather, just as those spirits begged Jesus not to send them into the abyss—which the Lord then granted for the present dispensation (Luke 8)—so it seems consequent that each evil spirit, when conquered by the saints, is placed by Christ the just Judge either in the abyss, or in the outer darkness, or in whatever place each one deserves. This is why, with a very great number of demons already defeated, the nations are allowed to come to faith; they certainly would by no means be allowed to do so [Col. 0780C] if their legions remained whole as they had been before.

## Twelfth Part of the Decree

Concerning lying and perjury; accusers, defenders, and false witnesses; and the penance of each.

[Col. 0779]

### Chapter 1.—On the eight kinds of lies. Augustine, *On Lying*, book 1, ch. 14.

[Col. 0779C]

(22, question 2, chapter “The First Is.”) The first kind is a capital [i.e. gravely sinful] lie, [Col. 0779D] to be avoided at all costs: a lie uttered in religious teaching. No one ought under any condition to be induced to tell this lie. The second is told in order unjustly to harm someone; it is of such a kind as benefits no one and harms someone. The third benefits one person while harming another, although it does not harm through bodily uncleanness. The fourth arises solely from delight in lying and deceiving: this is pure lying. The fifth is told from a desire to please, through agreeable speech.

When all these have been wholly avoided and rejected, there follows the sixth kind, which harms no one and benefits someone: for example, if a person who knows that another’s money is to be unjustly taken lies that he does not know where it is. The seventh harms no one and benefits someone: for example, if someone lies because he is unwilling to betray a person sought for death. [Col. 0780C] The eighth kind of lie harms no one and is useful in protecting someone from bodily uncleanness.

(*Ibid.*, ch. 21.) Therefore one must not lie [Col. 0780D] in the teaching of piety, because it is a great crime and the first kind of detestable lie. One must not lie in the second kind, because no injustice must be done to anyone. One must not lie in the third kind, because no one is to be helped at another’s injury. One must not lie in the fourth kind, because of the desire for lying, which is vicious in itself. One must not lie in the fifth kind, because even truth itself is not to be proclaimed for the purpose of pleasing human beings—much less a lie, which is certainly shameful in itself because it is a lie. One must not lie in the sixth kind, for even the truth of testimony is not rightly corrupted for anyone’s temporal advantage or safety; and no one is to be led to eternal salvation by the aid of a lie. Nor is one to lie in the seventh kind, [Col. 0781A] for no person’s temporal advantage or safety is to be preferred to the fulfilment of faithfulness; nor, if anyone is so perversely affected by our rightly performed actions that he becomes worse in mind and more remote from piety, are rightly performed actions therefore to be abandoned. Nor is one to lie in the eighth kind, because among good things there are chastity of mind and bodily modesty; and among evils, what we ourselves do is worse than what we permit to be done. Among these eight kinds, a person sins less in lying insofar as he rises toward the eighth, and sins more insofar as he descends [variant: “sinks,” Vict.] toward the first. But whoever supposes that there is some kind of lie which is not sin deceives himself shamefully, when he considers himself an honourable deceiver of others.

### Chapter 2.—On the binding force of an oath. From the Eighth Council of Toledo, ch. 2.

[Col. 0781B]

Everything that enters into covenants of peace stands more firmly when the interposition of an oath confirms it. Likewise, everything that reconciles the minds of friends endures more faithfully when the bonds of a sworn pledge bind them. For everything affirmed by a witness is established more truly when the addition of an oath confirms it. Even if a witness is lacking, the assessment of swearing alone makes the innocence of the accused manifest.

### Chapter 3.—An oath is not contrary to the Lord’s command. Augustine, *On the Epistle to the Galatians* (on ch. 1, near the end; and *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, book 1, ch. 30).

(22, question 1, chapter “It Is Not Contrary.”) Swearing is not contrary to [Col. 0781C] God’s command; it arises from the evil not of the person swearing but from the unbelief of the person who compels him to swear. For this is how the Lord is understood to have forbidden swearing (Matt. 5): each person, so far as lies within him, should not swear. Yet many make a habit of having oaths in their mouths as though they were something great and pleasant. Certainly the Apostle knew the Lord’s command and nevertheless swore. Those who deny that these utterances are oaths are not to be heard. For what will they make of this: “I die daily by your glorying, brethren, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord” (1 Cor. 12)? The Greek manuscripts prove most clearly that this is an oath.

Thus, so far as lies within him, the Apostle does not swear: he does not seek an oath from a desire [Col. 0781D] or pleasure in swearing. For what is “more than” “yes, yes; no, no” (Matt. 5) comes from evil—not from the evil of the swearer, but from the weakness or unbelief of those who are otherwise moved to belief.

### Chapter 4.—One must not swear, so that we may be as far as possible from perjury. Augustine, *To Publicola* (Epistle 154).

(22, question 1, chapter “In the New Testament.”) In the New Testament it is said that we should not swear at all (Matt. 5). This seems to me to have been said not because swearing is a sin, but because perjury is a monstrous sin. He who warned us not to swear at all wished us to be far from it. Again, *ibid.*, after a few verses: Although it has been said, “Do not swear,” I do not remember having read anywhere in the holy Scriptures that we are not to receive an oath from another person.

### Chapter 5.—That it is permissible to employ an oath for the benefit of others. Augustine, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, book 1, ch. 30.

[Col. 0782A]

(22, question 1, chapter “You Do Not Do Evil.”) You do not do evil when you use an oath rightly. Although it is not good, it is nevertheless necessary in order to persuade another of what you usefully advise. But it arises from the evil of the one whose weakness compels you to swear.

### Chapter 6.—That one should swear by God, not by created things. Jerome, on Matthew, book 1.

Consider that the Saviour did not prohibit swearing by God, but by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, and one’s own head (Matt. 5). This had been granted by the Law, as it were, to little children: just as they sacrificed victims to God so that they would not sacrifice them to idols, so they were permitted to swear by God—not because [Col. 0782B] they did this rightly, but because it was better to offer this to God than to demons.

### Chapter 7.—That oaths are not to be frequent. Isidore, *Sentences*, book 2, ch. 31.

(22, question 1, chapter “It Is Not Contrary.”) It is not contrary to God’s command to swear; but when we make a practice of swearing, we incur the crime of perjury.

### Chapter 8.—That one should swear only in great necessity. From Augustine’s twenty-eighth sermon on the words of the Apostle, beginning: “The first reading which has come to us.”

(22, question 1, chapter “If Swearing Were a Sin.”) If swearing were a sin, the old Law would not say: “You shall not commit perjury, but shall render to the Lord your oath” (Lev. 19); for sin would not be commanded to us. Again, *ibid.*, after much intervening material: We do not tell you that we [Col. 0782C] do not swear; if we said that, we would lie. As far as I am concerned, I swear, but, it seems to me, compelled by great necessity. When I see that, unless I do so, I will not be believed, and that it is not advantageous for the one who does not believe me not to believe, after weighing this reason and balancing this consideration, I say with great fear: “Before God,” or “God is witness,” or “Christ knows that this is so in my mind.” And I see that this is “more,” that is, more than “yes, yes; no, no”; but this “more” comes from evil (Matt. 5), and, if not from the evil of the swearer, it comes from the evil of the unbeliever.

### Chapter 9.—Oaths contrary to nature are not to be kept. From the Eighth Council of Toledo, ch. 2.

(22, question 4, chapter “If by Public Instruments.”) If, in public records of sworn pledges [Col. 0782D] (God forbid!), some unlawful or evil condition had been attached by anyone, compelling a person either to murder his father or to commit rape upon a most sacred [variant: consecrated] virgin, would it not be more tolerable to reject the vows of a foolish promise than, by keeping useless promises, to fill up the horrible measure of crimes?

### Chapter 10.—On the same matter. Ambrose, *On Duties*, book 1, ch. 30.

(22, question 4, chapter “It Is Also Contrary.”) It is sometimes also contrary to duty to fulfil a sworn promise. Thus Herod, who swore that he would give the daughter of Herodias whatever she asked (Matt. 14), brought about John’s death lest he refuse what he had promised.

### Chapter 11.—Likewise on the same matter. From Augustine’s sermon on the beheading [Col. 0783A] of St John, beginning: “When the holy Gospel was being read.”

[Note: [Col. 0783D] Sermon 11, *On the Saints*, whose opening is: “On account of this.” At the end of volume 10.]

(22, question 4, chapter “What David Did.”) I see that David, a pious and holy man, fell into a rash oath and preferred not to do what he had sworn rather than fulfil his oath by shedding a man’s blood (1 Sam. 25). Again, *ibid.*, shortly afterward: David swore rashly, but with greater piety he did not fulfil his oath. Behold, holy David did not indeed shed a man’s blood in anger; but who can deny that he swore falsely? Of two sins he chose the lesser; but it was lesser in comparison with the greater [variant: worse]. For considered in itself, false swearing is a great evil.

### Chapter 12.—Likewise on the same matter. Isidore, *Synonyms*, book 2.

[Col. 0783B]

Break faith in evil promises; change your resolve in a shameful vow. Do not do what you vowed without due caution. A promise fulfilled by wickedness is impious.

### Chapter 13.—Likewise on the same matter. Bede, *Book of Homilies*, Homily 43 (on the beheading of St John the Baptist).

(22, question 4, chapter “If We Have Perhaps.”) If we happen to have sworn something too incautiously, the observance of which would lead to a worse outcome, we should know that it must freely be changed for a wiser course; and that, under urgent necessity, we must rather commit perjury than, in avoiding perjury, turn aside into another and graver crime. Thus David swore by the Lord to kill the foolish and impious man Nabal and to destroy everything belonging to him; but at the first intercession of the prudent woman Abigail, [Col. 0783C] he immediately withdrew his threats, recalled his sword to its sheath, and did not grieve that he had incurred any guilt by such perjury (1 Sam. 25). Again, after a verse: Not only in swearing, but in everything we do, this moderation must be more carefully observed: if we happen to fall through the snares of a crafty enemy into such a predicament that we cannot escape without some contamination of sin, we should seek the avenue of escape through which we see that we will suffer less danger.

### Chapter 14.—Whether that should be called faithfulness which is employed in committing sins. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, ch. 4.

(22, question 4, chapter “If It Is Applied to Sin.”) If faithfulness is applied to the commission of sin, it is strange that it should be called faithfulness. [Col. 0783D] Nevertheless, whatever its character, if it is violated, the act is worse—unless it is abandoned precisely so that one may return to true and lawful faithfulness; that is, so that sin may be corrected by setting right the perversity of the will. For example, if someone who cannot rob a person alone finds a companion in wrongdoing and makes an agreement with him that they will do it together and divide the spoil, but, after the crime has been committed, takes everything away alone: the other indeed grieves and complains that faith has not been kept with him. Yet in making this complaint, he ought to reflect that faith should rather have been kept with human society itself in good living, so that unjust spoil might not be made from a human being—if he recognizes how unjustly faith has not been kept with him in a partnership in sin. For the person who is faithless in both respects must certainly be judged the more criminal.

Again, *ibid.*, in the same chapter: If, after violating marital fidelity, a woman keeps faith with her adulterer, she is certainly evil; but if she does not keep faith even with her adulterer, she is worse. But if she repents of her disgrace and, returning to marital chastity, breaks the adulterous agreements and arrangements, I wonder whether even the adulterer himself would regard her as a violator of faith.

### Chapter 15.—On not keeping an unjust oath. From the fourth session of the Seventh Synod.

[Note: [Col. 0784D] Far after the beginning, it differs greatly in the Greek.]

(22, question 4, chapter “At the Fourth Session.”) John, *apocrisiarius* (envoy) of the Eastern sees, said: “The discourse of our Father Sophronius declares that it is better for one who has sworn to commit perjury than to preserve a sworn pledge in the breaking [Col. 0784B] of holy images. We say this because certain persons excuse themselves by an oath.” Patriarch Tarasius said: “Because Father Sophronius knew the goodness of God, he therefore wished to transgress an impious oath.” Again Patriarch Tarasius said: “Herod kept his oath and perished; Peter, however, denied with an oath, then turned, wept, and was saved (Matt. 26). For God forgives every sin if a person repents from the whole heart.” The holy synod said: “Thus holy Scripture teaches us.” Again Leontius, bishop of Phocaea, said: “It is written: ‘Do not love a false oath’ (Zech. 8). For this reason let our false oath be dissolved, as having no force.”

### Chapter 16.—That, of two evils, the lesser evil must be chosen. From the Eighth Council of Toledo, ch. 2.

[Col. 0784C]

(Distinction 13, chapter “Two Evils.”) Although two evils must altogether be most carefully avoided, nevertheless, if necessity arising from danger compels us to undertake [variants: “attempt”; elsewhere “rashly undertake”] one of them, we ought to dissolve that which is known to bind us with the lesser bond. Let us investigate with the sharpness of sound reason which of these is lighter and which is graver. For when we are compelled to commit perjury, we indeed offend the Creator, but we defile only ourselves. But when we fulfil harmful promises, we both proudly despise God’s commands, harm our neighbours by impious cruelty, and slaughter ourselves with the more cruel sword of death. In the former case we are struck by a double weapon of sins; in the latter, our throats are cut threefold.

### Chapter 17.—That all promises are not always to be fulfilled. Ambrose, *On Duties* (book 3, ch. 12).

[Col. 0784D]

(22, question 4, chapter “Let Each Person.”) Let everyone speak simply, possess his own vessel in holiness, and not entrap a brother by the circumlocution of words. Let him promise nothing dishonourable; or, if he has promised it, it is more tolerable not to do what was promised than to do what is shameful. Often many bind themselves by the sacrament of an oath; and although they themselves recognize that the promise should not have been made, they nevertheless do what they pledged out of regard for the oath. Such was Herod, as we wrote above: he shamefully promised a reward to the dancer and cruelly paid it (Matt. 14). [Col. 0785A] It was shameful that a kingdom should be promised for dancing; it was cruel that a prophet’s death should be granted out of reverence for an oath. How much more tolerable would perjury of this sort have been than homicide—if indeed it can be called perjury when he swore drunkenly among wine-cups and promised emasculated amid the choruses of dancers.

(*Ibid.*, shortly afterward.) The prophet’s head is brought in on a dish, and what was a matter of friendship was considered a matter of fidelity. Again: (22, question 4, chapter “Not Always.”) Not all promises are always to be fulfilled. Indeed, the Lord himself frequently changes his decision, as Scripture indicates (Num. 14).

### Chapter 18.—On penance for perjury. Third Synod of Orléans, in the time of King Childebert, ch. 8.

Concerning perjury, we have decreed that [Col. 0785B] if any cleric, in cases to be concluded under oath, gives an oath and is afterward shown by evident facts to have committed perjury, he is to be excluded from communion for two years.

### Chapter 19.—That everyone opposed to the Word of God is Antichrist. Augustine, on the First Epistle of John, Tractate 3.

However many perjurers, deceivers, evildoers, poisoners, seekers of trifles, adulterers, drunkards, usurers, slave-dealers, and all other things which we cannot enumerate the Church has—if they are opposed to Christ’s teaching, they are opposed to God’s Word. But God’s Word is Christ. Whoever, therefore, is opposed to God’s Word is Antichrist.

### Chapter 20.—That one who never swears is safe from perjury. From Augustine’s sermon on the beheading of St John the Baptist, beginning: “When the holy Gospel was being read” (at the end of volume 10).

[Col. 0785C]

To swear falsely is such a great sin that, on account of the guilt of false swearing, the Lord prohibited every oath (Matt. 5). Again, *ibid.*, somewhat later: To swear truthfully is not sin; but because to swear falsely is a great sin, one who does not swear at all is far from the sin of false swearing, whereas one who swears even truthfully approaches false swearing. Again (*ibid.*, a little farther below): Sometimes a person swears unwillingly when he thinks that what he swears is true. Indeed, his sin is not as great as that of one who knows it to be false and nevertheless swears.

### Chapter 21.—That perjury is compared with adultery. Jerome, on Malachi.

[Col. 0785D]

Let us by no means suppose that perjury, failure to pay a labourer’s wage, slandering a widow and an orphan, and oppressing a foreigner and stranger are slight sins; they are compared with evil-doing, poisonings, and adultery.

### Chapter 22.—What perjury is. Jerome, on Jeremiah, book 1 (at the beginning of ch. 4).

(22, question 2, chapter “It Must Be Noted.”) It must be noted that an oath has these companions: truth, judgment, and justice. If these are lacking, it will not be an oath at all, but perjury.

### Chapter 23.—That one convicted of perjury cannot be a witness. *Capitulary*, book 1, ch. 9 (ch. 63).

[Col. 0786A]

(22, question 5, chapter “Children.”) Children who have not reached the age of reason are not to be compelled to swear. And one who has once committed perjury is thereafter neither to be a witness nor approach the sacrament, nor serve as an oath-taker in his own case or another’s.

### Chapter 24.—Perjurers are not to be treated with such indulgence that an occasion for perjury is given. Alexander II, to the clerics Landulf and Ariald.

We may extend the hand of mercy to persons who have fallen into the crime of perjury, but we must not grant licence as an example of future destruction [variant: “prohibition”].

### Chapter 25.—On the punishment of perjury. Pope Honorius, to Hysatius, patrician and exarch of Italy.

[Col. 0786B]

We have learned from certain writings that some bishops in the regions beyond the Po declared certain things hostile to the episcopal office to Peter, son of Paul, and, by the counsel of impious persuasion, urged him to do so: asserting that he should take upon himself the guilt of perjury, so that he might consent not to King Adulubald but rather to the tyrant Ariopalt. Since the aforesaid glorious Peter refused to be swayed by the wicked persuasions of those priests—if it is lawful to call them so—but chose rather firmly to keep the sworn pledges he had given to King Cono [variant: Acono, Vict.], father of the aforesaid Adulubald; and because such a deed is hateful to God and to pious minds, so that those who ought to have prevented it from being committed instead urged its commission: when, through the nod of heavenly power and your labours, the aforesaid Adulubald has been restored to his kingdom, [Col. 0786C] be pleased, with God’s help, to send the aforesaid bishops to these Roman parts. For we shall permit such a crime to go unpunished on no account.

### Chapter 26.—On excommunication of those who draw others into perjury, and on the infamy of those who consent. From the Council of Mâcon in the time of King Guntram, ch. 21 (Council of Mâcon, ch. 1).

(22, question 5, chapter “If Anyone Is Convicted.”) If anyone is convicted of having drawn others into false testimony or perjury, or of having solicited them by any corruption, he himself shall receive no communion until death. Those, however, who are proved to have consented with him in perjury are thereafter to be excluded from all testimony and marked with infamy according to the law.

### Chapter 27.—On punishment for one who unjustly charges another with perjury. Gelasius, to the bishops Rufinus and Justus.

[Col. 0786D]

The honourable leading men of the city of Varula have petitioned us with earnest prayers, as appears in the following material. They have also affixed their own signatures, declaring that they have been harassed by the deacon Agnellus with grievous insults, so as even to assert that they were induced, as they say, into the charge of perjury. Therefore, dearest brothers, in accordance with the petitioners’ statement [variant: “petitioner”], once the aforesaid deacon has immediately been brought before your tribunal, with Laurentius, defender of the Roman Church, in attendance, and the assertion of truth has been examined: if the integrity of the petitioners is established, let the deacon either prove the accusation he has brought or know that his insolence must be punished, so that [Col. 0787A] fitting punishment may attend his exclusion for such serious excesses of infamous rashness; and let the man who has entangled himself in vulgar insults be barred from access to holy communion.

### Chapter 28.—That one who demands an oath from someone he knows will commit perjury is worse than a murderer. From Augustine’s sermon on the beheading of John the Baptist.

[Note: [Col. 0787] Sermon 11, *On the Saints*, beginning: “On account of this passage”; at the end of volume 10.]

If someone provokes you to swear, because he perhaps thinks that he can thus be satisfied—if you swear concerning the matter which he thinks you have committed and done, though perhaps you did not do it, so that evil suspicion may not remain in him—then, if you swear, you do not sin as he does who provoked you. Again, *ibid.*: If you have been provoked by another [variant: “that man”], what you swear will arise from his evil, not yours. Again, *ibid.*: The person who provokes another to swear, knowing that he will swear falsely, surpasses [Col. 0787B] a murderer. A murderer is about to kill a body; that person kills a soul—indeed, two souls: that of the person he provoked to swear and his own. You know that what you say is true and that what the other says is false, yet you compel him to swear. Behold, he swears; behold, he commits perjury; behold, he perishes. What have you gained? Indeed, you too have perished, because you wished to satisfy yourself with his death.

### Chapter 29.—To whom one should report a person known to have committed perjury. Augustine, *Questions on Leviticus* (question 1 on Leviticus 5).

(22, question 5, chapter “This Seems.”) This seems to say that a person sins when someone swears falsely in his hearing, he knows that the oath is false, and remains silent. He knows this when he was a witness to the matter sworn about, either by seeing it or by being privy to it—that is, when he learned of it in some way, either saw it with [Col. 0787C] his own eyes, or the person who swears himself informed him; for in that way he could be privy to it. But between fear of this sin and fear of betraying people there is often no small temptation. For we may call back a person prepared for perjury from so grave a sin by warning or prohibiting him. But if he will not listen, and before us swears falsely concerning a matter that we know, whether he should be denounced if, when denounced, he will incur even danger of death, is an extremely difficult question. But because the text does not specify to whom this is to be disclosed—whether to the person to whom the oath is made, to a priest, or to someone who not only cannot persecute him by inflicting punishment but can also pray for him—it seems to me that a person frees himself from the bond of this sin if he reports it to persons who can do more good than harm [Col. 0787D] to the perjurer, either in correcting him or in appeasing God for him, provided that he too employs the remedy of confession.

### Chapter 30.—That one who knowingly compels another to swear falsely is a murderer. Augustine’s sermon *On Not Swearing*, beginning: “The First Reading” (Sermon 30, *On the Words of the Apostle*).

(22, question 5, chapter “He Who Demands.”) There is a great difference, when someone demands an oath, between not knowing that the other will swear falsely and knowing it. If he does not know, and says for that reason, “Swear to me, so that I may trust you,” I do not dare say that it is not sin, though it is a human temptation. But if he knows that the other did it, knows he did it, saw him do it, and compels him to swear, he is a murderer. [Col. 0788A] For the other kills himself by his own perjury; but this man has both placed and pressed the hand of the killer [variant: “forced”].

### Chapter 31.—On the matters concerning which an oath may be made. First session of the synod of Pope Stephen III.

Christopher, *primicerius* of the notaries, said: “The most holy four Gospels, the venerable chrism, and the other mysteries of God having been brought forward, we gave one another a sworn pledge that no one else outside a Roman election should exercise the pontificate; but that, by common counsel and according to divine providence, we should choose as bishop the one given from the body of our holy Church—namely, from among the priests, cardinal deacons, in accordance with the tradition of this apostolic see.”

### Chapter 32.—On the punishment of one who swears by God’s hair or beard. Constitution 68 of the *Novellae*, ch. 1.

[Col. 0788B]

(21, question 1, “If Anyone Swears by Hair.”) If anyone swears by God’s hair or beard, or in any other way employs blasphemy against God, he shall be subjected to the ultimate punishment by the office of the urban prefect. But if anyone does not report such a person, there is no doubt that he too will likewise be restrained by divine condemnation.

### Chapter 33.—That each person should swear fasting. *Capitulary*, book 1, ch. 60 (ch. 63).

(22, question 5, chapter “Honourable.”) Whoever must swear upon holy things shall do so fasting, with every propriety and fear of God.
