### Chapter 34.—That one who swears falsely by a stone is a perjurer. From Augustine’s sermon *On Not Swearing*, beginning: “The First Reading,” etc. (Sermon 30, *On the Words of the Apostle*).

[Col. 0788C]

Is it really the case, whoever you are of wicked and perverse heart, that if you say “By God,” you swear, but if you say “God is witness,” you do not swear? For what does “By God” mean except “God is witness”? Or what does “God is witness” mean except “By God”? What is swearing except rendering what is due to God when you swear by God; rendering what is due to your salvation when you swear by your salvation; rendering what is due to your children when you swear by your children? And what do we owe to our salvation, our children, and our God, except charity, truth, and not falsehood? But especially when it is done by God, it is a true oath. For when someone says, “By my salvation,” he binds his salvation to God; when he says, “By my children,” he pledges his children to God, [Col. 0788D] so that what comes from his mouth may come upon their heads: if it is true, truth; if false, falsehood. Therefore, when a person, in an oath, names his children, his head, or his salvation, he binds to God whatever he names; how much more when he swears [some manuscripts read “commits perjury”; *ibid.*, near the end] by God himself?

Again (22, question 5, chapter “Behold, I Say”): Behold, I say to your charity: even one who swears falsely by a stone is a perjurer. Why do I say this? Because many are deceived even in this matter and think that, because what they swear by is nothing, they are not held guilty of perjury. You are certainly a perjurer, because you swear falsely by what you do not think holy. “But I do not think it holy.” You consider holy that by which [Col. 0789A] you swear. For when you swear, you do not swear to yourself or to the stone; you swear to your neighbour. You swear to a person before a stone—but are you not also before God? The stone does not hear you speaking, but God punishes you for deceiving. Again (*ibid.*, not far from the beginning): Nothing makes the tongue guilty except a guilty mind.

### Chapter 35.—That it is a lesser evil to swear truthfully by false gods than to swear deceitfully by the true God. From Augustine’s letter to Publicola (Epistle 154).

(22, question 1, chapter “It Moves You.”) You ask whether one may make use of the faithfulness of a person who has sworn by demons in order to keep it. Here I want you first to consider whether, if someone swore by false gods that he would keep faith and did not keep it, he would not seem to you to have sinned twice. [Col. 0789B] For if he kept the faith promised by such an oath, he would be judged to have sinned only because he swore by such gods. But no one would blame him for having kept faith. Now, however, because he both swore by beings by whom he ought not to have sworn and acted contrary to the faith he had pledged—which he ought not to have done—he certainly sinned twice. Accordingly, one who makes use of the faithfulness of a person known to have sworn by false gods, and uses it not for evil but for what is lawful and good, does not join himself to that person’s sin of swearing by demons, but to the good agreement by which he kept faith.

Nor do I mean here the faith by which those baptized into Christ are called believers. That faith is far different and distinct from the faithfulness of human agreements and compacts. Nevertheless, without any doubt, it is a lesser evil to swear truthfully by false gods [Col. 0789C] than deceitfully by the true God. For the holier that by which one swears, the more punishable is perjury. There is, therefore, another question: whether one who has an oath sworn to him by false gods does not sin, since the one who swears to him worships false gods. The passages you yourself recalled concerning Laban and Abimelech may support this question, if Abimelech swore by his own gods, as Laban did by the God of Nahor (Gen. 26, 31).

### Chapter 36.—That God receives an oath according to the understanding of the person to whom it is sworn. Isidore, *Sentences*, book 2, ch. 31.

(22, question 1, chapter “He Who Swears.”) By whatever verbal artifice a person swears, God, who is the witness of conscience, nevertheless takes it as the person to whom the oath is sworn understands it. [Col. 0789D] He becomes guilty in two ways: because he both takes God’s name in vain and ensnares his neighbour by deceit. An oath by which evil is unwittingly promised is not to be observed—for example, if someone pledges perpetual fidelity to an adulteress in remaining with her. It is more tolerable not to fulfil the sworn pledge than to remain in the shameful act of fornication.

### Chapter 37.—That it pleases God more not to keep a harmful oath than to keep it. Augustine, *Questions on Joshua* (question 13, on Joshua 9).

It may be asked how the Hebrews believed that an oath ought to be kept with the Gibeonites, to whom they had sworn as though they came from a distant land—as they themselves had lied. For they knew that they would be defeated if the Hebrews learned that they dwelt in that land [Col. 0790A] which they had been promised they would possess. Thus, when the Gibeonites lied that they had come to them from a far country, the Israelites swore to them. But afterwards, when they discovered that they lived there, where they were obliged by God’s command to defeat all whom they found, they nevertheless refused to break their oath. Although they had learned that the Gibeonites had lied, they preferred to spare them on account of the oath, though they could certainly have said that they had sworn as if to those whom they believed them to be, that is, persons coming from afar. Once they learned otherwise, the Lord’s command concerning them ought to have been carried out, so that they should be conquered like the rest.

But God approved this and did not grow angry [or: object] with those who spared them, although they had not asked Him who these people were, and had therefore been susceptible to their deception. Hence they should certainly be understood, although they wished to deceive men for their own safety, nevertheless not to have feared God deceitfully among His people. For this reason the Lord was not angry with those who swore or [and] spared them; so that afterwards He avenged the Gibeonites themselves, as members of His people, against the house of Saul, as the history of the kingdoms shows (2 Kings 21). And since the oath was thus kept, although it concerned persons who had lied, God was not displeased that the judgment was bent toward mercy.

For if, conversely, they had sworn that they would kill certain persons whom they believed to be Gibeonites in the land of promise, and afterwards learned that they were strangers to that land and had come to them from afar, it must by no means be thought that they would have defeated them in order to fulfill [Col. 0790C] the oath. For holy David himself, out of the mercy of sparing, even after the words by which he had sworn that he would kill Nabal (1 Kings 25)—while certainly knowing whom he was going to kill—preferred to spare him; nor did he fulfill the oath in the more severe matter, judging that it pleased God more if he did not do what, in his disturbance, he had sworn to do harmfully, than if he had carried it out.

### CHAPTER 38.—On the oath of a certain Christophorus, *primicerius*.

Third Session of the First Synod of Pope Stephen III.

Christophorus, *primicerius*, said: “When Constantine released us, I gave him this oath before everyone, saying: ‘By Almighty God, I am faithful and shall always be faithful to the holy Church of God, to blessed Peter, and to the Roman pontiff; and neither I nor my son Sergius shall ever in any way devise or undertake hostile action against the holy Roman Church and the Roman people; and I shall in no way whatsoever mention the name of Constantine himself.’ But nevertheless [only] I am certain that that oath has force, and therefore I confess to you that I have sinned on account of [or: through] the oath.”

### CHAPTER 39.—What difference there is between one who thinks a thing true and swears falsely, and one who knows or thinks it false and swears to it as true.

Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*, Sermon 28.

(22, question 2, canon *Homines*.) Men swear falsely either when they deceive or when they are deceived. For a person either thinks true what is false and swears rashly; [Col. 0791A] or knows or thinks it false and nevertheless swears to it as true, and thereby swears criminally. Yet the two perjuries which I have mentioned differ.

Suppose a man swears to something which he thinks true; he thinks it true, and yet it is false. This man does not commit perjury in his heart: he is deceived; he takes as true what is false; he does not knowingly introduce an oath concerning a false matter. Take another: he knows it to be false, says that it is true, and swears as though what he knows to be false were true. You see what a detestable beast this is, one that ought to be driven out of human affairs. For who would wish this to be done [to himself]? All people detest such things.

Take another: he thinks something false and swears as though it were true, and perhaps it actually is true. For example, so that you may understand: it rains in that place; you question a man, and [Col. 0791B] it suits his business to say, “It rained,” but he thinks it did not rain. He is asked, “Did it really rain?” “Really,” he says, and swears; and yet it did rain there. But he does not know this and thinks that it did not rain: he is perjured. What matters is how the word proceeds from the heart. It is not the tongue that makes one guilty, unless the mind is guilty.

### CHAPTER 40.—How priests ought to clear themselves by oath.

Smaragdus, *On Ecclesiastical Oppressions*, Part I.

Now—what we cannot say without injury to the holy Church of God—alas! this has been so abolished that, even in the case of an irregular accusation, scarcely any place remains for lawful defense. They do not judge that the charges unjustly brought forward should be proved, but seek only to avenge whatever has been inflicted [Col. 0791C] upon them. If a defense is sought among them, setting aside every synodal rule, they determine by their own inventions that it should take such a form as the accused cannot possibly fulfill, or one that wholly prevents them by right of office, so that they may rage more freely against God’s priests. For, according to the Apostle Paul, they are a law unto themselves (Rom. 2): they themselves are at once accusers, judges, and witnesses—not by reason, but by force.

They therefore say that the sworn defense of an accused priest has no validity unless he compels several other priests to swear with him. They cite in testimony for this what they boast that they have read was done in the acts of the Roman pontiffs. For it is found concerning the venerable pontiffs Damasus, Sixtus, and Symmachus that, when they were accused of crimes by certain perverse persons [Col. 0791D], synods of bishops having been assembled, they were cleared synodically. They confess that they understand this entirely in the sense that all the aforesaid bishops swore with the pontiffs concerning the charges brought against them, as though the pontiffs’ own defense alone did not absolve them unless the oath of their aforementioned fellow-brethren also confirmed it.

Yet it is not in fact clear to us that this should be understood in that way. Certainly, we have received that the aforesaid pontiffs were cleared by the aforementioned bishops; but upon their own petition, by their own defense alone, with the bishops also supporting them, it was established that they were free from the accusations. But if anyone has thought fit, for the innocence of some righteous person, to give an oath out of charity, in order thereby to free him from his persecutors, this is altogether approved. Nevertheless [Col. 0792A], even if under persecution by perverse persons this could have occurred, as it were, in the primitive Church, no example of it ought to have been left for the future. For by what holy council, or by what decree of a Catholic and apostolic man, it has been ordained that priests of God cannot be absolved from accusations except by the defense of fellow-brethren, we are entirely ignorant.

Since oaths are forbidden to all Christians, it is exceedingly pernicious for priests to compel others also to do what they ought both to avoid themselves and to rebuke in others.

### CHAPTER 41.—Every lie must be avoided.

Gregory, Book XVIII of the *Morals*, chapter 2.

Every lie must be avoided with the utmost care, although sometimes there is a kind of lie [Col. 0792B] of lighter fault, if someone lies in order to preserve a life. But since it is written, “A lying mouth kills the soul” (Wisdom 1), and, “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Psalm 5), even this kind of lying perfect men flee with the utmost care, lest anyone’s life be protected by their deception and they harm their own souls while striving to preserve another’s body. Yet we believe that this kind of sin is most easily forgiven. For if every fault is commonly cleansed by a subsequent work of piety, how much more easily is this wiped away when piety itself, the mother of good work, accompanies it?

### CHAPTER 42.—That no one ought to lie on the pretext of humility.

Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*, Sermon 29.

(22, question 2, canon *Cum humilitatis*.) Therefore, when you lie [Col. 0792C] for the sake of humility, if you were not a sinner before you lied, by lying you become what you had avoided. Truth is not in you unless you call yourself a sinner in such a way that you know yourself also to be one. For truth itself consists in saying what you are; how can there be humility where falsehood reigns?

### CHAPTER 43.—That lies spoken in jest are not lies.

Augustine, *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 145.

(22, question 2, canon *Quod ait*.) What Joseph said to his brothers (Gen. 44), “Did you not know that there is no man so skilled in divination as I?”—and concerning this divination he also commanded that they be told through his servant—its meaning is commonly asked. Since it was said not seriously but in jest, as the outcome showed, it should not be regarded [Col. 0792D] as a lie. For lies are performed seriously by liars, not in jest. But when things that are not so are said as a joke, they are not counted as lies.

### CHAPTER 44.—That no one should deceive another by a contrived or crafty lie.

Augustine, *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, chapter 19.

(22, question 2, canon *Nec artificioso*.) No one ought to deceive anyone either by a contrived lie or by a simple statement; for in whatever way anyone lies, “a lying mouth kills the soul” (Wisdom 1), and “the portion of all liars shall be in the lake of burning fire and sulphur” (Rev. 21).

### CHAPTER 45.—That it is not sinful to be mistaken in certain matters.

Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 21.

(22, question 2, canon *In quibus*.) In matters in which it makes no difference [Col. 0793A] for attaining the kingdom of God whether they are believed or not, and whether they are true—or thought to be true—or false: in such matters, to err, that is, to take one thing for another, is not to be judged a sin; or, if it is a sin, it is a very slight and trivial one.

### CHAPTER 46.—The difference between lying and concealing the truth.

Augustine on Psalm 5, on verse 7.

(22, question 2, canon *Ne quis*.) Let no one suppose that a perfect and spiritual man ought to lie for the sake of this temporal life, in whose death neither his own soul nor another’s is killed. But since it is one thing to lie and another to conceal the truth—one thing to say what is false and another to keep silent about what is true—if someone perhaps does not wish to betray a man even to this visible death, he ought to be prepared to conceal the truth, not [Col. 0793B] to say what is false: so that he neither betrays nor lies, and does not kill his own soul for another’s body.

In the same place, a little below. Likewise. There are two kinds of lies in which the fault is not great, though they are not without fault: when we joke, or when we lie for our neighbor. The first, in joking, is not harmful because it does not deceive; for the person to whom it is said knows that it was said in jest. The second is milder [variant: *mitius*, Vict.] because it retains some benevolence.

But that which does not have a double heart ought not even to be called a lie. For example, if a sword is entrusted to someone, and he promises to return it whenever the person who entrusted it asks for it: if that person later demands back his sword while mad, it is plainly not to be returned, lest [Col. 0793C] he kill either himself or others, until his sanity is restored. This does not have a double heart because the one to whom the sword was entrusted, when promising to return it on request, did not think that the owner might demand it while mad. It is evident that sometimes keeping silent about the truth is not blameworthy; but saying what is false is nowhere found to be permitted to the saints.

### CHAPTER 47.—That figurative speech is not a lie.

Augustine, to Oceanus.

It seems to me that figurative speech can in no way rightly be called a lie. It is not a lie when we call a day “cheerful” because it makes us cheerful, or lupin “sad” because it saddens the taster by its bitter flavor. These are not lies at all.

### CHAPTER 48.—Definition of a lie.

Augustine, *Against Lying*, chapter 12.

[Col. 0793D]

(Same work, chapter 17.) A lie is a false signification with the will to deceive. Likewise. Let a person do what he can, even for the temporal safety of human beings. But when matters have reached the point that he cannot provide for such safety without sinning, he should consider that there is nothing left for him to do when he sees that what remains is something which he cannot rightly do.

### CHAPTER 49.—That every kind of lie must be avoided.

Isidore, *Synonyms*, Book I (Book II, chapter 10).

(22, question 2, canon *Omne genus*.) Flee every kind of lie with the utmost care. Speak no falsehood either by chance or deliberately [Col. 0794A]; do not strive to lie in order to render assistance [original: *per testes*, “through witnesses”]; and do not defend anyone’s life by any deception. Beware of lying in all things. Likewise. No lie is just: every lie is sin.

### CHAPTER 50.—On the same subject.

John, in the *Lives of the Fathers*.

A lie must be avoided in every way, whether it seems to be uttered for evil or even for good; for no lie is from God, but, as the Savior says, it is from evil (Matt. 5).

### CHAPTER 51.—On the distinction between being deceived and lying, and between the will to deceive and the will to be deceived.

Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 18.

Some go so far as to maintain that even to commit perjury, and to say something false concerning matters pertaining to the worship of God and concerning God’s own [Col. 0794B] nature, is sometimes a good and pious work. To me, however, it seems that every lie is indeed a sin; but it makes a great difference with what intention, and about what matters, someone lies. For the one who lies with the intention of helping does not sin in the same way as one who lies with the intention of harming; nor does the one who sends a traveler by a lie onto a wrong road do as much harm as one who corrupts the way of life by deceptive falsehood.

Certainly, no one who says something false which he thinks true is to be judged a liar, because, so far as lies within him, he does not himself deceive but is deceived. He is therefore to be reproved not for lying but for some degree of rashness, because he too carelessly believes false things and takes them as true. Conversely, so far as lies within him, the person lies who says as true [Col. 0794C] what he thinks false. For, as regards his intention, since he does not say what he thinks, he does not speak truth, even though what he says turns out to be true. Nor is a man in any way free from lying who unknowingly speaks truth with his mouth but knowingly lies in his will.

Likewise, in the same place a little later. In considering the things that are said, it makes so great a difference in what matter someone is deceived or lies that, although, as regards a person’s will, being deceived is less evil than lying, nevertheless it is far more tolerable to lie in matters separated from religion than to be deceived in those without whose faith or knowledge God cannot be worshipped.

Likewise, same work, chapter 22. A person ought to say not only what he himself knows to be true, but also, when as a human being he errs and is deceived, what he holds in his mind, whether it is true or merely thought to be true and is not so. But everyone who lies speaks contrary to what he feels in his mind, with the will to deceive.

### CHAPTER 52.—That it is not enough to speak truth unless one also thinks so in one’s heart.

Augustine, on Psalm 14, on verse 3.

Some have truth on their lips but do not have it in their heart. For instance, if someone deceitfully points out a road, knowing that robbers are on it, and says, “If you go this way, you will be safe from robbers,” and it happens that there are indeed no robbers there: he has spoken truth, but not in his heart. For he thought otherwise and unknowingly spoke truth. Therefore it is too little merely to speak truth, unless it is also so in the heart.

### CHAPTER 53.—On the usefulness of a certain lie.

Jerome, on Psalm 8.

[Col. 0795A]

We promised brevity and have been compelled by necessity to argue at greater length: we lied, but it is a most useful lie. Would that Herod had lied and broken his oath (Matt. 14)! And so we too have now promised less and, at your request, have provided more.

### CHAPTER 54.—That it is sometimes beneficial to conceal truths.

Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, Book III, Admonition 12.

The simple are to be praised because they strive never to say false things; but they must be admonished to know that sometimes truths should be kept silent. For just as falsehood harms one who always speaks it, so truths heard have sometimes harmed certain people. Hence the Lord, tempering His speech with silence before the disciples, said: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16).

### CHAPTER 55.—On the same subject.

Augustine, *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, chapter 20 (chapter 22).

A measure must be maintained in speaking, and even useful words must sometimes be spared, as the Psalmist says: “I was humbled, and I kept silent even from good things” (Psalm 38).

### CHAPTER 56.—That error is sometimes necessary in this life.

Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 17.

When truth is considered more carefully, since error is nothing other than to think true what is false, false what is true; or to hold as certain what is uncertain, and as uncertain what is certain, whether it be false [Col. 0795C] or true; and since this is as ugly and unbecoming in the mind as it is beautiful and fitting, both in speaking and in assenting, to say “yes, yes,” “no, no”: surely this life that we live is miserable precisely because error is sometimes necessary in order that it not be lost.

### CHAPTER 57.—That keeping truth silent is sometimes useful.

Augustine on the Epistle to the Galatians, on chapter 2.

It is never permitted to say what is false, but it is sometimes useful to keep some truth silent.

### CHAPTER 58.—That perjurers are often seized by a demon at the shrines of martyrs.

From the Council of Meaux, chapter 10.

So that the manifold confusion arising from oaths and perjuries—through which the souls of many faithful persons throughout this entire [Col. 0795D] kingdom are known to have been lost—may be more attentively proclaimed to all as detestable and hateful to God. For this evil is so great that at the shrines of martyrs, where various illnesses are healed, perjurers, though they sometimes do not appear visibly to be afflicted, are nevertheless seized by demons through God’s just judgment. And, as Saint Gregory says, the sick come to these bodies and are healed; perjurers come and are tormented by a demon.

### CHAPTER 59.—On those who take God’s name in vain.

From the sayings of Jerome.

(22, question 1, canon *Habemus*.) We have it written in the law of the Lord: “You shall not commit perjury in my name, nor profane the name of the Lord your God” (Lev. 19); and, “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” (Exod. 20). Therefore all must be admonished [Col. 0796A] carefully to avoid perjury, not only at the altar or upon the relics of saints, but also in ordinary speech. Likewise. One must beware lest anyone honor gold more than the altar, when [variant: “lest he,” Vict.] the Lord says: “Fool, which is greater, the gold or the altar that sanctifies the gold?” (Matt. 23).

### CHAPTER 60.—On those who commit perjury out of greed.

From the Roman Penitential.

If anyone commits perjury out of greed, let him sell all his possessions and distribute them to the poor; and, entering a monastery, let him submit himself to continual penance.

### CHAPTER 61.—On those who commit perjury at their lords’ command.

From the Decree of Pope Pius, chapter 2 (in fragment).

(22, question 5, canon *Qui compulsus*.) Whoever, compelled by his lord, knowingly commits perjury: both are perjurers, lord and soldier. The lord, because he commanded it; the soldier, because he loved his lord more than his soul. If he is free, let him do penance for forty days on bread and water, and for the following seven years. If he is a slave, let him do penance for three forty-day periods and the prescribed fast-days.

### CHAPTER 62.—On those who commit perjury upon the hand of a bishop, or upon a consecrated or unconsecrated cross.

From Theodore’s Penitential.

(22, question 5, canon *Qui perjurat*.) Whoever commits perjury upon the hand of a bishop, or upon a consecrated cross, shall do penance for three years. But if upon an unconsecrated cross, he shall do penance for one year. Whoever has been deceived and has unknowingly committed perjury, and afterwards learns of it, shall do penance for three forty-day periods.

### CHAPTER 63.—On those who commit perjury to save their lives.

From the Roman Penitential.

[Col. 0796C]

(22, question 5, canon *Si quis coactus*.) If anyone, compelled to save his life, or for any cause or necessity, commits perjury, because he loved the body more than the soul, he shall do penance for three forty-day periods. Others judge that he should do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water.

### CHAPTER 64.—On those who have confirmed unjust vows by an oath.

From the Council of Toledo, VIII, chapter 2.

(21, question 5, canon *Necesse*.) It is necessary for one who swears wickedly to perform worthy penance, because he has taken the name of the Lord in vain against His command. For it is written in Exodus: “The Lord will not hold guiltless him who has taken the name of the Lord his God in vain” (Exod. 20). And in Leviticus: “You shall not commit perjury in my name, nor profane the name of your God; I am the Lord” (Lev. 19). Yet he must by no means do the evil which he had vowed by oath to do, because foolish vows must be broken.

### CHAPTER 65.—On not admitting a perjurer as a witness.

From the Decrees of Pope Fabian, chapter 11 (in fragment).

Whoever knowingly commits perjury shall do penance for forty days on bread and water and for the following seven years; he shall never be without penance and shall never be admitted as a witness; after this, he may receive communion.

### CHAPTER 66.—On the penance of one who has drawn others with him into perjury.

From the Decree of Pope Pelagius, chapter 11.

(22, question 5, *Si quis*.) If anyone commits perjury and knowingly leads others into perjury, he shall do penance for forty days [Col. 0797A] on bread and water and for the following seven years, and shall never be without penance. The others also, if they knew of it, shall do penance likewise; but if not, each shall do penance as for perjury not voluntarily committed.

### CHAPTER 67.—How grievously those sin who compel persons speaking to them to swear, and what it is for God to swear.

Isidore, Book II, *On the Supreme Good*, chapter 31.

Just as one who does not speak cannot lie, so one who does not desire to swear cannot commit perjury. An oath must therefore be avoided and used only in necessity. It is not contrary to God’s command to swear; but when we make a practice of swearing, we incur the crime of perjury. Therefore let one who fears committing perjury never swear.

Many, while speaking, always delight in swearing, though there ought to be only this in their mouths: “Yes, yes; no, no” [Col. 0797B]; for whatever exceeds yes and no is from evil (Matt. 5). Many commit perjury in order to deceive, so that by the credibility of an oath they may establish the credibility of their words; and thus, while deceiving, they commit perjury and lie, and deceive the unwary person. Sometimes we are also deceived by false tears, and people are believed while weeping who ought not to be believed.

Often we intend to speak without an oath, but, because those who do not believe what we say are unbelieving, we are compelled to swear; and by such necessity we develop the habit of swearing. There are many slow to believe, who are not moved to trust by a person’s word. But those who compel persons speaking to them to swear sin grievously.

Whatever artifice of words a person uses in swearing, God, who is the witness of conscience [Col. 0797C], nevertheless receives it as the one to whom the oath is sworn understands it. He will be guilty in two ways, because [who, original and Vict.] he both takes God’s name in vain and ensnares his neighbor by deceit. An oath by which evil is rashly promised must not be kept—for example, if someone pledges fidelity to an adulteress, promising to remain with her perpetually. It is more tolerable not to fulfill an oath than to remain in the shameful sin of fornication.

For God to swear is that providence by which He determines not to overturn what He has established. God’s repentance is a change of things. Not to repent is not to revoke what has been established; as in the saying, “The Lord has sworn and will not repent” (Psalm 109), that is, He will not change what He has sworn.

### CHAPTER 68.—On those who knowingly commit perjury.

From Theodore’s Penitential.

[Col. 0797D]

If anyone suspects that he is being led into perjury and nevertheless swears with consent, he shall do penance for forty days and for the following seven years, and shall never be without grave penance.

### CHAPTER 69.—That everyone ought to swear fasting.

From the Decree of Pope Cornelius, chapter 5.

(22, question 5, canon *Honestum*.) It seems honorable and just to us also that anyone who ventures to swear by holy things should do so fasting, with all propriety and fear of God; and that boys under fourteen years of age should not be compelled to swear.

### CHAPTER 70.—On the same matter.

From the Council of Orléans, chapter 10.

And this holy synod decreed that, except for the making of peace [Col. 0798A], all the faithful should approach oaths fasting.

### CHAPTER 71.—What penance perjurers ought to receive.

From the Decrees of Pope Eutychian, chapter 26.

(22, question 1, canon *Praedicandum*.) It must also be preached that the faithful should avoid perjury and abstain from it with the utmost care, knowing it to be a great crime, forbidden in the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel. Yet we have heard that some treat this crime lightly and impose upon perjurers a penance that is, as it were, slight. They ought also to know that they must impose for perjury the same penance as for adultery, fornication, voluntary homicide, and the other criminal vices.

But if anyone, after committing perjury or any criminal [Col. 0798B] sin, fears a long penance and refuses to come to confession, he must be expelled from the Church and from the communion and society of the faithful, so that no one may eat, drink, or pray with him, or receive him into his house.

### CHAPTER 72.—On those who swear by God’s hair or head, or otherwise employ blasphemy against the immortal God.

From the Decree of Pope Pius, chapter 5 (in fragment).

(22, question 1, canon *Si quis per capillum*.) If anyone swears by God’s hair or by His head, or otherwise employs blasphemy against God: if he belongs to ecclesiastical order, let him be deposed; if a layman, let him be anathematized. And if anyone swears by created things, let him be punished very severely and do penance according to the judgment of the synod [Col. 0798C]. If anyone does not report such a person, there is no doubt that he too will likewise be restrained by divine condemnation. And if a bishop neglects to correct these things, let him be rebuked by the synod [variant: very severely].

### CHAPTER 73.—On Herod’s oath.

From the sayings of Jerome, on Matthew 14.

Herod promised with an oath to give the dancing girl whatever she asked from him. If he says that he acted because of the oath, would he have done it if she had demanded the death of his father and mother—or would he not? Therefore, what he would have rejected in his own case, he ought also to have disregarded in the case of the prophet.

### CHAPTER 74.—On those who have confirmed perpetual hatred between themselves by oath.

From the Council of Lleida, chapter 7.

[Col. 0798D] (22, question 4, canon *Qui sacram*.) Whoever binds himself by oath to litigate against anyone and in no way return to peace shall, for one act of perjury, be separated from the body and blood of the Lord for one year, and shall discharge his guilt by fasts and almsgiving. But let him quickly return to charity, which covers a multitude of sins (1 Peter 6 [as printed]).

### CHAPTER 75.—On those who have sworn rashly.

From the Decrees of Pope Soter, chapter 3.

(22, question 4, canon *Si aliquid*.) If we happen rashly to have sworn something whose observance would turn to a worse outcome, we should know that it must be altered by a more salutary counsel; and that, when necessity presses, we ought rather to commit perjury than, in avoiding perjury [“for a completed [Col. 0799A] or performed oath,” original], to turn aside into another and greater crime.

### CHAPTER 76.—On those who swear fidelity to their lords.

From the letter of Bishop Fulbert to William, Duke of Aquitaine.

(22, question 5, canon *De forma fidelitatis*.) Being asked to write something on the form of fidelity, I have briefly noted for you, on the authority of books, the following. Whoever swears fidelity to his lord must always keep these six things in mind: safety, security, honor, advantage, ease, possibility.

“Safety,” namely, that he not harm his lord in his person; “security,” that he not harm him in his secrets or in the fortifications through which he can be secure; “honor,” that he not harm him in his justice or in other matters which appear to belong to his honor; “advantage,” that he not harm him in his possessions; “ease” or “possibility,” that he not make difficult for his lord a good thing which the lord could easily do, nor make impossible for him what was possible.

It is right that a faithful man avoid these injuries, but he does not thereby merit an excuse [variant: *causamentum*, “a legal excuse”]. For it is not enough to abstain from evil unless one does what is good (Psalms 33 and 36). It remains, therefore, that in these same six matters mentioned above he faithfully provide counsel and aid to his lord, if he wishes to be thought worthy of a benefice and to remain secure in the fidelity which he has sworn.

The lord likewise ought to render the same in all these matters to his faithful man. If he does not, he will deservedly be judged faithless; just as the latter, if he is found guilty of violating these matters either by doing so or consenting to it [Col. 0799C], is perjured and treacherous.

### CHAPTER 77.—How priests ought to swear.

Letter of Pope Cornelius, chapter 3 (Letter 2).

Cornelius, bishop, to Rufus, fellow-bishop: greeting in the Lord.

“Your affection, dearest brother, requires that we should respond to your inquiries on the authority of the Apostolic See. Although, because of certain troubles which have come upon us through our sins and hinder us, we hasten to do so not at length but briefly, we nevertheless entrust to your zeal the more extensive examination and investigation of the remaining ordinances of the holy Fathers. For a mind worn down and burdened by cares and troubles cannot accomplish as much good as one that is delighted and freed from oppression [Col. 0799D].

“We have not put these things forward because we wish to deny to your holiness these or other matters which we have recognized as necessary, but so that what is found here less fully may be sought more extensively. We have not known that an oath should hitherto be demanded of high priests or other ministers of God except concerning the right faith, nor have we learned that they have sworn voluntarily [original: *spontaneos*].

“Most earnestly, therefore, the holy Apostle James, forbidding oaths, says: ‘Before all things, my brethren, do not swear, neither by heaven nor by earth nor by any other oath. But let your speech be Yes, yes; No, no, lest you fall under judgment’ (James 5). And the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘You have heard that it was said to those of old: You shall not commit perjury, but you shall render your oaths to the Lord. But I say to you [Col. 0800A], Do not swear at all: neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God; nor by earth, for it is His footstool; nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King; nor by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black. But let your speech be Yes, yes; No, no. Whatever is beyond these is from evil’ (Matt. 5), that is, from the one demanding and from the one swearing.

“These things, dearest brother, the Lord Himself forbids [variant: *perhibet*, Vict.], that is, He declares that one ought not to swear. These things all the Apostles especially, these things the holy men our predecessors who presided over this holy universal apostolic Church, these things the prophets and the other holy teachers scattered throughout the world forbid oaths to be made in their preaching. If we began to enumerate their examples [Col. 0800B] or insert them in this little writing, the daylight hour would fail before we had set forth their examples on this subject.

“Following these examples, we uphold the laws of the holy Apostles and their successors, and forbid rash oaths to be made. Hence the Lord Himself, on the tablets of stone which He gave to Moses, wrote with His own hand, saying: ‘See that you do not take the name of your God in vain’ (Exod. 20), and the rest. For each person ought to keep his own conscience clean before God and retain in memory: ‘A lying mouth kills the soul’ (Wisdom 1). And the Apostle says: ‘Speak truth, each one with his neighbor, because we are members one of another’ (Eph. 4); and elsewhere: ‘Do not lie to one another’ (Col. 3).

“These are the commands of the Savior, these of the prophets, these the institutions of the holy Fathers [Col. 0800C]. Whoever treats them as vain is an enemy of his own soul, because no one does anything against the prophets, against the Apostle, or against the Gospel without danger.”

### CHAPTER 78.—On those who violate the king’s oath.

From the sayings of blessed Augustine.

(22, question 5, canon *Si quis laicus*.) If a layman, by violating the oath which he swears to his king and lord, profanes it, and afterwards wickedly and deceitfully plots against his kingdom and by some scheme lies in wait for his death, because he commits sacrilege by laying his hand upon the Lord’s anointed, let him be anathema unless he corrects himself by worthy penitential satisfaction, as has been established by the holy synod: that is, let him leave the world, lay down arms, enter a monastery [Col. 0800D], and do penance all the days of his life. Nevertheless, at the end of his life let him receive communion with the Eucharist. But if a bishop, presbyter, or deacon commits this crime, let him be deposed.

### CHAPTER 79.—On one who hears the voice of a perjurer and gives assent.

Leviticus, chapter 5.

A soul that sins and hears the voice of one swearing falsely, and is a witness of what he himself has seen or knows, if he does not report it, shall bear his iniquity.

### CHAPTER 80.—That a rash determination should be undone, but rashness corrected.

From the Council of Elvira, chapter 1 (in fragment).

(22, question 4, chapter *Definitio*.) A rash determination is laudably undone [variant: “is dissolved”], and this is not breach of faith but the correction of rashness.

### CHAPTER 81.—On the same matter.

From the same council, chapter 3 (in the same place).

[Col. 0801A]

If a girl, placed in childhood in her father’s house, binds herself by an oath without his knowledge, and if her father objects immediately upon hearing of it, her vows and oaths shall be void and may be more easily corrected.

### CHAPTER 82.—On the same matter.

From the Council of Orléans, chapter 2.

The oath of a son or daughter made without the father’s knowledge, the vows of a monk made without the abbot’s knowledge, and the oaths of a boy are void.

### CHAPTER 83.—That lying must be avoided in every way.

Gregory says.

“Do not, my son, deny the grace of God, lest you fall from good into evil, from humility into falsehood. For falsehood must be avoided in every way, whether it seems to be uttered for evil or even for good, because no falsehood is from God, but, as the Saviour says, it is from evil” (John 8).

CAP. 84.—Likewise, concerning an oath which ought, or ought not, to be kept. From the Eighth Council of Toledo, chapter 2.

For when we are compelled to commit perjury, we indeed offend the Creator, but defile only ourselves. But when we fulfil harmful promises, we both proudly despise God's commands, injure our neighbours by impious cruelty, and slaughter ourselves with a still more cruel sword of death. In the one case we are struck by a twofold weapon of sins; in the other, we are cut down threefold. It remains, therefore, that our judgment should proceed in that direction in which the way of mercy lies open. This mercy is so approved and accepted by the Lord that he desires it more than venerable sacrifices, saying himself: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6; Matthew 9).

By this granted permission of indulgence, we place the work of mercy itself within the power of the glorious prince, so that, since God has opened to him an entrance for showing mercy, he likewise may not withhold the remedies of compassion. Let these measures, moderated by princely discretion, remain so ordered that mercy is granted to those persons, yet that neither nation nor country suffers through them any danger or loss whatsoever. Let it suffice to have tempered matters under this plea of mercy.

But we decree that oaths hitherto exacted, or hereafter to be exacted, for the safety of royal authority or for the established order of nation and country, are to be observed indissolubly with every safeguard and vigilance, the religious penalty of mutilation of limbs and sentence of death being altogether removed. But lest the crafty malice of depraved minds ever provoke us ourselves into the guilt of perjury, or assert that this judgment comes from the rule of holy faith, we have taken care to append to this account both utterances of divine authority and those of the preceding Fathers.

*In the same place, a little later.* For through Jeremiah he says: “Suddenly I shall speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to uproot and destroy it. If that nation repents of its evil concerning which I spoke against it, I also shall repent of the evil which I had intended to do to it” (Jeremiah 18). And through Ezekiel: “If I say to the righteous man,” he says, “‘You shall surely live,’ and, trusting [having turned away from righteousness] in his righteousness, he commits iniquity, all his righteous deeds shall be consigned to oblivion, and he shall die in the iniquity which he has committed. But if I say to the wicked man, ‘You shall die,’ and he repents, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezekiel 33). Therefore, if our conversion so changes the divine judgment, why should the abundant tears and affliction of the miserable not temper, through compassion, so cruel a punishment?

CAP. 85.—Concerning those who conspire against their bishops. From the letter of Pope Callixtus to all the bishops of Gaul.

[Col. 0802B]

We have heard that the crimes of conspiracies flourish in your regions, and it has been reported to us that peoples are conspiring against their bishops. The craftiness of this crime is abominable not only among Christians, but is also forbidden among pagans and foreigners by law. Therefore those guilty of this crime are condemned not only by ecclesiastical laws but also by secular laws—and not only those who conspire, but those who consent to them.

Moreover, our predecessors, together with a great multitude of bishops, decreed that whoever among them is established in priestly rank or is a cleric should lose the office which he holds; but they ordered all others to be deprived of communion and made exiles from the Church—not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to them.

CAP. 86.—On the same matter. From the Council of Tongeren [otherwise, Gangra], chapter 5.

Whoever deceitfully lays his hand upon the Lord’s anointed—that is, upon his bishop, father, and shepherd—because he commits grave sacrilege, and whoever devastates and burns the Church of God, since this too is sacrilege, it has pleased the holy synod that he do penance in one place, that is, in a monastery, for all the days of his life.

CAP. 87.—Concerning clerics or monks who bind themselves by oath or conspire against their bishop. From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 18.

If any clerics or monks are found entering into a conspiracy, plotting together, or laying snares against bishops or clerics, let them be utterly expelled from their proper rank.

CAP. 88.—On the same matter. From the Council of Toledo, chapter 8 (Tenth Council of Toledo, chapter 2).

Therefore, if clerics or monks are found to have entered into a conspiracy, or through conspiracy to be devising an accusation [conspiring] against bishops or clerics, let them lose their proper rank.

## THIRTEENTH PART OF THE DECREE

Concerning robbers, thieves, usurers, and lenders at interest; hunters; cursers and quarrelsome persons; revelries and drunkenness; mad persons; Jews; and their correction.

[Col. 0803]

CAP. 1.—Concerning those who seize other persons’ property and their punishment. Pope John to Archbishop Zacharias.

[Col. 0803A]

It is decreed in the ancient statutes of the Church that one who invades another’s property shall not go unpunished, but shall restore everything with an additional amount. Thus it is written in the Gospel: “If I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19); and provision is made in secular laws: “Whoever steals another’s property shall restore to the person whose property was plundered elevenfold what was taken away.” And in the divine law we read: “Cursed is everyone who moves his neighbour’s boundary-mark,” and all the people shall say, “Amen” (Deuteronomy 27). Therefore such acts must not be presumed without punishment, nor practised without condemnation.

CAP. 2.—That the children of Israel did not commit theft in despoiling the Egyptians. Augustine, *Book of Questions* (question 39 on Exodus 11).

[Col. 0803B]

The Lord said to Moses: “Let each man ask from his neighbour, and each woman from her neighbour, vessels of gold and silver, and clothing” (Exodus 11). No one should suppose that an example is to be taken from this for despoiling one’s neighbour in this way. For God commanded this, knowing what each person ought to suffer; and the Israelites did not commit theft, but rendered service at God’s command. It is as when an officer of a judge kills the person whom the judge has ordered put to death: if he does it of his own accord, he is certainly a murderer, even if he kills someone whom he knows ought to have been killed by the judge.

CAP. 3.—What difference there is between theft and robbery. In the same place (Augustine, question 71, book 20 of *Questions*, on Exodus 11).

Secretly taking away is punishable; visibly snatching away is punishable much more severely. Therefore the commandment concerning taking from an unwilling person, whether secretly or openly, has its force. For every unlawful appropriation of another’s property is rightly understood under the name of theft. He who forbade theft did not permit robbery; rather, under the name of theft in the law of the Old Testament he intended robbery also to be understood. By a part he signified the whole: whatever of a neighbour’s goods is unlawfully taken away.

CAP. 4.—That sin is not forgiven unless what was taken is restored. Augustine, in the letter to Armentarius and Paulina (Letter 54 to Macedonius).

If another’s property, on account of which the sin was committed, is not returned when it can be returned, repentance is not performed but feigned. But if repentance is sincerely performed, the sin will not be forgiven unless what was taken away is restored—provided, as I have said, that it can be restored. For often a person who takes something loses it, whether by suffering harm from other wicked people or by living wickedly himself, and has nothing else from which to make restitution. Certainly we cannot say to such a person, “Return what you took,” unless we believe that he possesses it and denies having it.

Indeed, if he suddenly suffers some punishments because he is thought to possess what he ought to return, there is no injustice in this. For even if he has no means of repaying [returning, according to Gratian] the money taken, nevertheless, while he is compelled to repay it through bodily sufferings, he pays the penalty for the sin by which it was wickedly taken. Yet it is not inhumane to intercede even for such persons—not so that another’s property may not be restored, but so that one human being may not rage pointlessly against another.

CAP. 5.—That thefts are not to be accepted by the Church with any increment. From sayings of Gregory (chapter 4, in reply to Augustine’s questions).

There are some who commit theft while possessing resources, and there are others who offend in this matter through poverty. Therefore some must necessarily be corrected by financial penalties, some by beatings, some more strictly, and some more gently. But far be it from the Church to receive, by way of profit, what she seems to lose in temporal goods, and to seek gain from vain things.

CAP. 6.—That thieves may be convicted by seven trustworthy persons. From the book of Capitularies.

Concerning thieves and wrongdoers we have decreed that the following be observed: if five or seven persons of good faith, without prior enmity, declare under oath that the accused person is guilty, then, as he has acted contrary to law, so let him be judged according to law.

CAP. 7.—That a priest should not practise usury or rural work. From the synod of Pope Eugenius, chapter 3 (Roman synod under Eugenius II, chapter 11).

Let a priest not engage in any usurious business or rural occupations, since it is not fitting that he should appear outside his house without priestly dress.

CAP. 8.—That a cleric who lends at interest is to be deposed. From the First Council of Nicaea, chapter 17.

[Col. 0804C]

If anyone is found taking interest, or pursuing business through some device or by any means whatever, or demanding “hemiolia” and “sescupla” [increases of one-half and one-third], or devising anything else at all for the sake of shameful gain, let him be deposed from the clergy and be excluded from the rule.

CAP. 9.—That a cleric should receive no more than he lent. From the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 16.

No cleric shall receive more than he has lent: if money, money; if goods in kind, the same goods in the same quantity as he gave.

CAP. 10.—That ministers who lend at interest should abstain from communion. From the First Council of Arles, chapter 12.

[Col. 0804D]

Concerning ministers who lend at interest, it has pleased us that, according to the divinely given rule, they should abstain from communion.

CAP. 11.—That a cleric who lends at interest or trades is to be suspended from communion. From the Second Council of Arles.

If any cleric lends money at interest, wishes to become the lessee of another’s property, or carries on any form of trade for shameful gain, let him be deposed from the clergy and excluded from communion.

CAP. 12.—On the same matter. From the Council of Elvira, chapter 20.

If any cleric is discovered to be taking interest, it has pleased us that he be degraded and abstain.

CAP. 13.—Likewise on the same matter. From the Council of Tarragona, chapter 2.

Whoever wishes to be in the clergy shall not pursue the practice of buying cheaply or selling dearly. Certainly, if he wishes to carry on these practices, let him be restrained from the clergy.

CAP. 14.—On the same matter. In the same place, chapter 3.

If a cleric in need lends a solidus, let him receive from wine or grain what, for purposes of trade, has been decreed to be sold at the fixed time. But if he does not possess goods in kind, let him receive the very necessity that he gave, without any increase whatever.

CAP. 15.—On the same matter. From the Council of the Apostles, chapter 44.

A bishop, priest, or deacon who exacts interest from debtors must either desist or certainly be condemned and deprived of communion.

CAP. 16.—That one who has something from evil should make good from it. Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*, tract 35 (Sermon 35).

[Col. 0805C]

Do not wish to give alms from lending at interest and usuries.

Likewise, in the same place, somewhat later: You who possess something acquired from evil, make good from it; you who possess nothing acquired from evil, do not acquire it from evil. Let yourself be good, you who make good from evil; and when you begin to do some good from evil, do not remain evil yourself. Are your coins changed into good while you remain evil?

CAP. 17.—That everyone who receives more than he gave is a usurer. Augustine on Psalm 36 (on verse 26).

If you lend to a person—that is, if you lend your money—and expect from him more than you gave, not merely money but something more than you gave, whether it be wheat, oil, wine, or anything else whatever: if you expect to receive more than you gave, you are a usurer, and for this reason are to be condemned, not praised.

CAP. 18.—On the same matter. Jerome on Ezekiel, book 6 (on chapter 18).

They suppose indeed that usury exists only in money; foreseeing this, divine Scripture removes excess in every thing, so that you may not receive more than you gave.

Likewise, somewhat later: Others are accustomed to receive little gifts of various kinds in return for money lent at interest, and do not understand that whatever it may be is called usury and excess, if they receive back from the person to whom they gave more than they gave.

CAP. 19.—Concerning those who demand interest upon interest. Book 2 of the Codes, chapter 23.

Upon those who practise disgraceful lending at interest and unlawfully demand interest upon interest, the stigma of infamy is to be imposed.

CAP. 20.—On the same matter. Likewise, *Capitularies*, book, chapter 25.

In no way are interest payments upon interest to be demanded from debtors.

Likewise: We decree that it is in no way lawful for anyone to convert interest for past or future time into principal and again stipulate interest upon it.

CAP. 21.—Concerning the difference between shameful gain and trade. In the same place (book 1, chapter 131).

Whoever, at the time of the vintage or harvest, buys grain or wine not from necessity but from greed—for example, buys one modius for two denarii and keeps it until he can sell it for four or six denarii, or more—this we call shameful gain. If he buys it from necessity, in order to have it for himself and distribute it to others, we call it trade.

CAP. 22.—What lending at interest is. Augustine, *Book of Expressions*, chapter 34 (on Deuteronomy, book 5, expression 39).

Scripture calls money given on loan “lending at interest,” even if interest is not received.

CAP. 23.—On the same matter. In the same place, chapter 42.

“You shall lend at interest [Note: For this we now read: ‘You shall lend.’] to your brother whatever he asks and whatever he needs” (Deuteronomy 15). Here, certainly, since a work of mercy is commanded, the cruelty of usury is plainly not to be admitted.

CAP. 24.—What shameful gain is. Ambrose on the Epistle to Timothy (on chapter 3 of the First Epistle).

The Apostle calls gains shameful when, under the appearance of a pious profession, one pursues profits. For a person is found shameful when he displays himself as pure.

CAP. 25.—That it is difficult for there not to be sin between seller and buyer. Leo, to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne (Letter 92, chapter 9, *On Penance*).

The character of profit either excuses [makes honourable] or accuses a trader, for gain may be honourable or shameful. Nevertheless, it is more beneficial for one doing penance to suffer losses than to be bound by the dangers of trade, because it is difficult for sin not to intervene in commercial dealings between seller and buyer.

CAP. 26.—Concerning those who reserve, for times of high prices, crops grown for themselves by their own labour. Ambrose, *On Duties*, book 3, chapter 6.

Holy David denies that he entered into trade, because seeking increases in prices belongs not to simplicity but to cunning. And another says: “One who seeks high prices for grain is cursed among the people” (Proverbs 11). The judgment is settled, leaving nothing for dispute. Yet this kind of controversy is accustomed to be stated as follows, when one person alleges that agriculture is held praiseworthy by all; that the simple produce of the earth is tripled; that the more someone has sown, the more worthy of approval he will be; that the fuller returns of industry should not be defrauded; and that it is rather negligence and disregard of uncultivated land which are commonly reproved.

“I ploughed,” he says, “more industriously; I sowed more abundantly; I cultivated more diligently; I gathered a good yield [I gathered good yields]; I stored it carefully [being careful]; I kept it faithfully; I guarded it prudently. Now, in a time of famine, I sell; I help the hungry; I sell grain—not another’s, but my own; not at a higher price than others, indeed even at a lower price. What fraud is there here, when many might even be endangered if they had nothing to buy? Is industry charged as a crime? Is diligence condemned? Is foresight censured? Perhaps he will say: Joseph too gathered grain during abundance and sold it in dearth [the printed text: “in high price”]” (Genesis 41). “Is anyone compelled to buy at a higher price? Is force used against the buyer? The opportunity to buy is offered to all; injury is imposed on none.”

After these arguments, according to the ability of each person’s mind, another rises and says: “Agriculture is indeed good, because it supplies produce to all, because by straightforward labour it increases the fertility of lands, introducing no deceit and no fraud. If someone has sown well, he shall harvest better. The earth is fruitful: it returns multiplied what it receives. The field is faithful: it is accustomed to restore productive returns. Therefore, from the revenue of a fertile clod you should expect the recompense of your labour; from the fertility of rich soil you should hope for just profit.

“Why do you turn nature’s industry toward fraud? Why do you begrudge humankind the common fruits? Why do you diminish the abundance of the people? Why do you pursue scarcity? Why do you cause the poor to wish for barrenness? For when they do not feel the benefits of fertility—while you auction the price, while you hold back [the printed reading: *continente*; variant *condente*, ‘storing’] grain—they would rather wish that nothing were born than that you should trade upon public famine. You seek a shortage of grain, a scarcity of food; you groan over the produce of fertile ground; you weep for public fertility; you lament granaries full of crops; you investigate when the yield may be more barren, when the produce more scant. You rejoice that the curse seems to have smiled on your wishes, so that nothing might grow for anyone. Then you rejoice that your harvest has arrived; then you heap up wealth for yourself from everyone’s misery. And do you call this industry? Do you name this diligence? It is the cunning of craftiness and the cleverness of fraud. And do you call this a remedy, when it is an invention of wickedness [malice]? Shall I call it robbery, or lending at interest?

“Times are sought as though for robbery, in which you, a hard plotter, may creep into the vitals of all. The price is increased as though interest had been added to the principal. For you the interest on stored grain is multiplied; you conceal grain as a usurer, and auction it as though a seller.”

The same author, *On Naboth*: “Usurers, you receive gold and silver as a pledge, and still call debtor the person who has lent you more than he received from you? You claim that you are creditors, though you owe more.”

Likewise, chapter 14 of the book *On Tobit*: “Many, evading the commandments of the law, when they have given money to traders, demand no interest in money, but receive profits from their merchandise as though they were interest [interest payments]. Therefore let them hear what the law says: ‘You shall receive neither interest on food nor on any things whatever’” (Deuteronomy 25).

Likewise, somewhat further below: “Food is interest; clothing is interest; and whatever is added to principal is interest—whatever name you wish to give it, it is interest.”

Likewise, several verses later: “If someone thinks a banquet should be furnished, he sends to a merchant, that he may bring him a little goat flavoured with wormwood free of charge; he sends to an innkeeper, that he may procure Picene or Tyrian wine; to a butcher, that he may provide him a womb [the current text of Ambrose and Gratian reads *hilam*, ‘a trifle’]; to another, that he may supply him fruit.”

CAP. 27.—That one who demands interest from another cuts his throat without iron. The same author (the same book, chapter 15).

“Demand interest from the person whom you rightly desire to harm, against whom arms may lawfully be brought. Interest may lawfully be brought against the person whom you cannot readily defeat in war; demand interest from the person whom it is no crime to kill. He fights without iron who demands interest; he avenges himself on an enemy without a sword who has been an usurious exactor against his foe. Therefore, where there is a right of war, there is a right of usury.”

CAP. 28.—Concerning usurious clerics. Pope Gelasius to the bishops throughout Lucania, Bruttium, and Sicily (Letter 9, chapter 17).

Clerics must know that they ought to abstain from unworthy gains and desist from every contrivance or desire for any form of trade; otherwise, whatever their rank, they must at once be compelled to abstain from clerical offices.

CAP. 29.—Concerning servants of God who practise hunting and similar pursuits. Boniface to Bishop Guibert.

We forbid servants of God to engage in hunting or wild wandering with dogs, and to possess goshawks or falcons.

CAP. 30.—On the same matter, and their punishment. From the Council of Agde, chapter 55.

Bishops, priests, and deacons may not possess hunting dogs or hawks. If any such person is discovered in this inclination [pleasure], then, if he is a bishop, let him abstain [the original: “be suspended”] from communion for three months; if a priest, let him abstain for two months; if a deacon, let him cease for one month from every office or communion.

CAP. 31.—That nothing is to be given to hunters and actors. Augustine on Psalm 102, chapter 2 (on verse 6).

Why do those who give to hunters give? Let them tell me: why do they give to a hunter? They love in him that by which he is most wicked; they nourish in him that; they clothe in him that very public wickedness [Gratian reads: “make public”] through the spectacles of all. Why does one who gives to actors, one who gives to prostitutes, give? Do they not also give to human beings? Yet they do not consider there the nature, God’s work, but the wickedness of human work.

Likewise, somewhat later, on the same Psalm: One who gives to a hunter does not give to a human being, but to a most wicked craft. For if he were merely human and not a hunter, you would not give to him. You honour in him vice, not nature.

CAP. 32.—That those who see a hunter should not take pleasure in him. Augustine on Psalm 47.

People see a hunter and take pleasure in him: woe to the miserable if they do not correct themselves! For those who see a hunter and take pleasure in him will see the Saviour and mourn.

CAP. 33.—That holy persons are found to be fishers, but none to be hunters. Jerome on Psalm 90 (on verse 2).

Esau was a hunter (Genesis 29), because he was a sinner. And in the Holy Scriptures we do not find at all any holy hunter; we find holy fishers.

CAP. 34.—That it profits nothing to fast in the belly and indulge in hunting. Ambrose, homily beginning, “We said on the previous Sunday” (Sermon 33).

What does it profit to fast in one’s belly and indulge in hunting? To abstain from food and wander into sins?

Likewise, somewhat later: Do you think, brethren, that the person fasts who, at the first dawn, does not keep watch for church, does not seek out the holy places of the blessed martyrs, but rises, gathers his servants, arranges nets, leads out dogs, and searches through glades and woods? He drags servants with him, I say—perhaps servants more eager to hasten to church—and adds others’ sins to his own pleasures, not knowing that he will be guilty both of his own offence and of the destruction of his servants.

CAP. 35.—Which beasts or birds are wild, and which are not. *Institutes*, book 2, title 1.

Wild beasts, birds, and fish—that is, all animals born on land, sea, and in the sky—begin at once, when captured by anyone, to belong to that person by the law of nations. For what previously belongs to no one is granted by natural reason to the person who takes possession of it. It makes no difference whether one captures wild beasts or birds on one’s own land or another’s. Certainly, a person entering another’s land for hunting or fowling may, if the owner foresees him, be prohibited by that owner from entering.

Whatever you have captured is understood to be yours only so long as it is confined by your custody. But when it escapes your custody and returns to natural liberty, it ceases to be yours and becomes the property of the next taker. It is understood to return to natural liberty when it either escapes your sight or, though remaining in your sight, is so difficult to pursue.

The question has been raised whether a wild animal wounded in such a manner that it can be captured is immediately understood to be yours. Some have held that it is yours, and is regarded as yours so long as you pursue it; but, if you cease pursuit, it ceases to be yours and again becomes the property of the taker. Others have thought that it is yours only if you have captured it. But we confirm the latter opinion, because many things may happen that prevent you from capturing it.

The nature of bees also is wild. Thus bees that settle in your tree are not understood to be yours before you enclose them in a hive, any more than birds that have made a nest in your tree; consequently, if another encloses them, that person becomes their owner. Anyone may also take honeycombs which they have made. Certainly, while matters remain whole, if you foresee someone entering your land, you may lawfully forbid him to enter.

Likewise, if a swarm flies out from your hive, it is understood to be yours so long as it remains in your sight and its pursuit is not difficult; otherwise it becomes the property of the taker. Peacocks and doves have a wild nature; nor does it matter that by habit they fly away and return, for bees do the same, although their nature is admittedly wild. Some people also have deer so tame that they are accustomed to go into woods and return; yet no one denies that even these have a wild nature.

In animals accustomed to depart and return, this rule has been approved: they are understood to be yours so long as they retain an intention of returning. When they cease to retain an intention of returning, they cease to be yours and become the property of takers. They appear to cease having an intention of returning when they abandon the habit of returning.

Hens and geese do not have a wild nature. We may understand this from the fact that there are other hens which we call wild, and likewise other geese which we call wild. Therefore, if your geese or hens, disturbed by some chance, fly away, even if they escape your sight, wherever they are they are understood to remain yours; and anyone who retains those animals for the sake of gain is understood to commit theft.

CAP. 36.—That burnings and plunderings of ecclesiastical property are to be compensated by the payment of *emunitas*. From the letter of Pope Gregory to Queen Constantia of Gaul (book 4 of the Register, Letter 33, or chapter 77).

Since I know that Your Ladyship diligently considers the heavenly life and the remedy of her soul, I judge that I should commit a serious fault if I kept silent about matters which ought to be suggested out of fear of almighty God, and if I did not diligently admonish you, most holy lady, concerning ecclesiastical peace. The complaint of our brother and fellow bishop Julian has recently grieved me deeply, especially because the estates of his church have been plundered by most wicked raiders and burned at night, in the manner of thieves.

And since those same evil persons refused, in accordance with the decrees of our predecessor Boniface, to make compensation by *emunitas*, although secular laws also have provided similarly, as is attested by the popular law, in which it is written thus: “If anyone comes armed, with as many as four men, into another’s village to commit wrongdoing, the leader shall pay 900 solidi for his unlawful presumption, and each of his followers 80 solidi. But if they set a fire there, let them pay nine times as much, and restore the plunder fourfold.”

If secular laws have wished justice of this kind to prevail, why should divine law be inferior, when Zacchaeus was praised in the presence of Truth himself for restoring fourfold if he had defrauded anyone? (Luke 19.) Since the highest good in rulers is to cultivate justice, preserve each person’s rights, and not permit that to be done to subjects which power can do, but to maintain what is equitable—things which we trust that you love and earnestly pursue—we shall therefore send to Your Excellency’s court, in November of this present year, in the second indiction, our brother and fellow bishop Peter from the bosom of the holy Roman Church. Thus, when the brothers of that province have assembled together, let the *emunitas*, the presumption, and the sacrilege receive such an end through canonical authority and your royal dignity that henceforth the members of the devil, the sons of wickedness, may not presume such acts in the holy Church while you reign there also.

CAP. 37.—Concerning ecclesiastical property and how it ought to be restored. From the decree of Pope Eusebius, chapter 8 (Letter 2 to the Egyptians).

And secular laws also provide: “Whoever steals another’s property shall restore elevenfold to the person whose property was plundered what was taken away.” And in the divine law we read: “Cursed is everyone who moves his neighbour’s boundary-mark,” and all the people shall say, “Amen” (Deuteronomy 2). Therefore such acts must not be presumed without punishment, nor should they be practised without condemnation. Seek peace, not loss or another person’s injustice, among one another and with all persons. Therefore, if anyone has seized ecclesiastical offerings or anything consecrated to God, or has consented to those doing so, let him be judged sacrilegious, restore the loss fourfold, and do canonical penance.

CAP. 38.—That plunderers of churches are sacrilegious persons. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 3.

[Col. 0811C]

Plunderers of churches are sacrilegious persons. Hence the following decree is found in chapter 4 of the Council of Agde: “To seize something from a friend is theft; but for a church to be defrauded, deprived, or robbed is sacrilege.” For all those who act contrary to law, plunder the property of a church, or molest churches and priests against the divine enactments, are called sacrilegious; and they must without doubt be considered infamous sacrilegious persons.

CAP. 39.—On the same matter. From the second letter of Pope Pius, sent to the Italian brethren.

It has been brought to the Apostolic See that there are among you contentions and jealousies, and that some apply estates given to divine uses to human uses, withdraw them from the Lord God to whom they were given, and make them serve their own purposes. Therefore that insult of usurpation must be driven away by all, lest estates protected under heavenly sacred ordinances [the original: “dedicated to the uses of heavenly mysteries”] be harassed by certain assailants. If anyone should presume to do this, let him be regarded and judged as sacrilegious.

We have also heard that the persons who do this persecute and defame clerics and priests of the Lord, adding evil to evil and becoming worse, without understanding that the Church of God consists in priests and grows into God’s temple (Ephesians 2). Just as one who devastates the Church of God and strips, seizes, or invades its estates and gifts becomes sacrilegious, so also one who persecutes its priests is guilty of sacrilege and is judged as a sacrilegious person.

CAP. 40.—Concerning those who have mutilated limbs or burned houses. From the decrees of Pope Eutychianus (fragment).

If anyone has mutilated limbs or burned houses, ordered this to be done, or consented to the person doing it, let him know that he is excluded from the Church until he has legally and amicably made satisfaction before the bishop of the city and the other citizens to every person concerned. But if, after a second and third summons, he has not made satisfaction for all matters of which he is accused, let him be separated from the whole fellowship of Christians as a heathen and a tax collector.

CAP. 41.—That theft is the same in a small thing as in a great one. Jerome (on chapter 2 of the Epistle to Titus).

A thief is judged a thief not only in greater but also in lesser things. For attention is given not to what has been taken by theft but to the mind of the thief. Thus in fornication, fornication is not different because the woman is beautiful or ugly, a slave or free-born, poor or wealthy; whatever she may be, it is one fornication. So too in theft: however much one has taken, one incurs the crime of theft.

CAP. 42.—Concerning penance for theft. From the Penitential of Theodore.

If anyone has stolen food, clothing, or livestock out of necessity, through hunger or nakedness, let him do penance for three weeks. If he restores it, he is not to be compelled to fast.

CAP. 43.—On the same matter. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 8.

For if anyone has committed public robbery or theft, let him perform public penance for it according to the ordinances of the sacred canons. But if it was done secretly, let him do penance by the counsel of priests, because robbers, as the Apostle says, unless they perform true penance for it, shall not possess the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6). But one who has taken anything from the property of the Church is to be judged more severely. For although punishment of thieves and robbers pertains to counts, penance pertains to bishops.

CAP. 44.—On the same matter. From the Penitential of Theodore.

If anyone has committed a capital theft—that is, has taken four-footed animals or broken into houses—let him do penance for seven years and restore what was stolen. But if anyone has committed theft of lesser things once or twice, let him restore what he took and do penance for one year. If anyone has violated a tomb, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water.

Source canon references omitted from the draft: CAP. 85, I, question 1, chapter *Conspirationum* (“Conspiracies”); CAP. 86, 24, question 3, chapter *Quisquis* (“Whoever”); CAP. 87, 11, question 1, chapter *Si qui clerici* (“If any clerics”); CAP. 88, 11, question 1, chapter *Si clerici* (“If clerics”); CAP. 2, 14, question 5, chapter *Dixit Dominus* (“The Lord said”); CAP. 3, 14, question 5, chapter *Poenale* (“Punishable”); CAP. 4, 14, question 6, chapter *Si res* (“If the property”); CAP. 8, Distinction 47 and 14, question 4, chapter *Quoniam multi* (“Since many”); CAP. 9, 14, question 4, chapter *Nullus clericorum* (“No cleric”); CAP. 10, 14, question 4, chapter *Ministri* (“Ministers”); CAP. 11, chapter 14, from chapter 18 of the Nicene Synod; CAP. 12, Distinction 47, chapter *Si quis clericorum* (“If any cleric”); CAP. 13, 14, question 4, chapter *Canonum statutis* (“By the statutes of the canons”); CAP. 14, 14, question 4, chapter *Si quis clericus* (“If any cleric”); CAP. 15, Distinction 47, chapter *Episcopus* (“A bishop”); CAP. 16, 14, question 5, chapters *Nolite* (“Do not”) and *Qui habetis* (“You who have”); CAP. 17, 14, question 3, chapter *Si foeneraveris* (“If you lend at interest”); CAP. 18, 14, question 3, chapter *Putant* (“They suppose”); CAP. 21, 14, question 4, chapter *Quicunque* (“Whoever”); CAP. 25, Distinction 1, chapter *Qualitas lucri* (“The character of profit”); CAP. 26, 14, question 3, chapter *Plerique* (“Many”); CAP. 27, 14, question 4, chapter *Clerici* (“Clerics”); CAP. 30, Distinction 34, chapter *Episcopum, presbyterum* (“A bishop, a priest”); CAP. 31, Distinction 86, chapter *Qui venatoribus* (“Those who [give] to hunters”); CAP. 32, Distinction 86, chapter *Vident homines* (“People see”); CAP. 33, Distinction 86, chapter *Esau*; CAP. 34, Distinction 86, chapter *Quid prodest* (“What does it profit?”); CAP. 36, 12, question 2, chapter *Cum devotissimam* (“Since [I know] Your Devoutness”); CAP. 37, 12, question 2, chapter *In legibus* (“In the laws”); CAP. 39, 12, question 2, chapter *Praedia* (“Estates”); CAP. 40, 23, question 8, chapter *Si quis* (“If anyone”); CAP. 41, 14, question 6, chapter *Fur autem* (“But a thief”); CAP. 44, 27, question 4, chapter *Si quis furtum* (“If anyone [commits] theft”).

### Chapter 45.—That prayer is not to be made for thieves and robbers killed while stealing or plundering. From the Council of Tribur, chapter 5 (c. 31, although not in the same words).
