(13, q. 2, c. *Fures et latrones*.) If thieves and robbers are killed while stealing and plundering, it has seemed fitting that prayer should not be made for them. If, having been apprehended or wounded, they confess to a presbyter or deacon, we do not deny them communion.

### Chapter 46.—Whether those who afterwards kill a thief or robber caught in the act of plunder ought to do penance. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 1.

(13, q. 2, c. *Si fur et latro*.) If a thief or robber caught in the act of plunder can be apprehended without danger, yet is killed, then, because they were created in the image of God and baptized in his name, their killers shall not enter the church for forty days. Wearing woolen garments, they shall abstain from forbidden foods and drinks, from the marriage-bed, from the sword, and from riding. On Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday they shall use, alternately and moderately, some kind of legumes or vegetables, fruit, and small fish, with moderate beer. But if truthful witnesses establish that, without premeditation of hatred, they killed the limbs of the devil while freeing themselves and their own possessions, and that the offenders could not have been captured, we do not impose upon them penance for homicide, unless they themselves wish to do something as an act of humanity.

### Chapter 47.—On the same matter. Exodus 22.

If a thief is found breaking into or digging through a house, and, having received a wound, dies, the striker shall not be guilty of bloodshed. But if he does this after sunrise, he has committed homicide, and he himself shall die. If he does not have wherewithal to make restitution for the theft, he shall be sold. If what he stole is found alive in his possession, whether ox, ass, or sheep, he shall restore double.

### Chapter 48.—On a slave who has fled his master. From Jerome’s letter to Paschasius of Alexandria.

You asked concerning a slave who fled his master: if he should die during that flight, whether it is lawful to pray for him or not. We do not find this prohibited in the divine books; nevertheless, we know that the apostles firmly commanded that slaves should be subject to their masters in all fear, not only to the good and gentle but also to the harsh (1 Peter 2; Ephesians 6; Colossians 3; Titus 2). And in the Council of Gangra, chapter 3, it is written thus:

> “If anyone, under the pretext of divine worship, teaches a slave to despise his own master, so that he departs from his service, let him be anathema.”

Hence it may be understood that, if the person who teaches a slave to despise his own master and withdraw from his service deserved anathema, how much more the slave who spurns his master and refuses to submit to his service. Yet there is a difference between one who has done this through pride and one compelled by necessity through the cruelty of his master.

### Chapter 49.—On clerics apprehended in demolishing tombs. From the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 45.

If any cleric is caught demolishing tombs, since this crime is punished by public laws as sacrilege with blood, a man detected in such wickedness must be removed from the clerical order and assigned to three years of penance.

### Chapter 50.—On clerics or monks if they commit theft. From the Council of Agde, chapter 2.

[Note: [Col. 0813] (From the Rule of the Fathers.) Something similar is found in chapters 4 and 5 of this council.]

If any cleric or monk commits theft—which may more properly be called sacrilege—we have decreed that, if he is a younger man, he shall be beaten with rods, and, being guilty of so great a crime, shall never receive ecclesiastical office [clerical status]. But if one already ordained [cleric, original reading] is caught in this crime, he shall be deprived of the dignity of his name; after completing the satisfaction of penance, communion alone may suffice him, in view of the slightness of his deed.

### Chapter 51.—On those who steal something from the ministry of the Church. From the Roman Penitential.

If anyone has in any way stolen anything from the ministry of the Church, let him do penance for seven years.

### Chapter 52.—On cursers and their punishment. From the sayings of Jerome.

The Apostle says: “Neither cursers shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6). If anyone commits this great sin, let him do penance in proportion to the greatness of the crime he has committed, lest he be separated from the kingdom of God.

### Chapter 53.—On murmurers. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 8.

(Dist. 90, c. *Alienus sit*.) If anyone proves to be a murmurer, let him beware lest he incur the punishment of murmurers, concerning which the Apostle says: “Neither murmur, as some of them murmured and were destroyed by the destroyer” (1 Corinthians 10). In proportion to the measure and character of the sin—since the Apostle’s sentence is fully declared in this matter—let him do penance at the priest’s judgment.

### Chapter 54.—On the same matter. From the same source.

(Dist. 90, c. *Si quis monachus*.) Whoever is contentious or a murmurer shall do penance according to the prior’s discretion, in accordance with the nature of the fault [the reading is defective: *modus exstat*].

### Chapter 55.—On the same matter.

The Apostle says: “Do all things without murmurings” (Philippians 2). Let the person who murmurs be excluded from the unity of the brethren, and let his work be rejected.

### Chapter 56.—On the contentious. From the decrees of Pope Hilary I, chapter 15 (at the end).

If anyone seems to be contentious, the Apostle saying: “We have no such custom, nor has the Church of God” (1 Corinthians 11), let him be marked [*notetus*, apparently for *notetur*] until he is corrected.

### Chapter 57.—On those who are wanton in speech. From Theodore’s Penitential.

If anyone is wanton in speech [*exstiterit*], let him be purified by a three-day penance.

### Chapter 58.—On those who disagree and quarrel. From the sayings of Isidore.

If anyone is discordant, quarrelsome, and, through hatred, persists in dissension, let him remain excluded from the assembly and fellowship of the Church, as the canons command, until he returns to concord.

### Chapter 59.—On those who, through hatred, refuse to return to peace. From the same source.

If anyone hates another so that he is unwilling to return to peace, let him, as the holy Fathers established, be excommunicated and separated from the Church until he is reconciled.

### Chapter 60.—On the same matter. From the decrees of Pope Fabian, chapter 5 (in a fragment).

(Dist. 90, c. *Si quis contristatus*.) If anyone who has been offended refuses to be reconciled when the one who caused the offense makes satisfaction, let him be chastened with the severest fasts until he receives the satisfaction with a thankful mind.

### Chapter 61.—On the same matter. From the same source.

If anyone refuses to be reconciled to a brother whom he hates, let him do penance on bread and water until he is reconciled to him.

### Chapter 62.—On the same matter. From the Council of Agde, chapter 31.

(Dist. 90, c. *Placuit etiam*.) It has also pleased us that, whenever—as often happens—persons disagree through hatred or a long-standing dispute, and cannot be recalled to peace because of prolonged contention, they shall first be rebuked by the priests of the city. If, with ruinous intent, they refuse to lay aside their enmities, let them be expelled from the congregation of the Church by a most just excommunication.

### Chapter 63.—On those who love disputes and quarrels. From the same council, chapter 5 (added at the end of the Council of Agde).

[Col. 0815B]

(Dist. 90, c. *Si quis monachus*.) If anyone loves disputes and quarrels, or has inflicted open abuse upon a brother, let him be purified by prolonged penance according to the discretion of the rector and the measure of the sin.

### Chapter 64.—On those who are quick to slander. From the same source, chapter 10 (this too appended at the end of the same council).

If anyone is ready and quick to slander, saying what is untrue, let him do penance for seven days on bread and water, separated from the fellowship of the brethren.

### Chapter 65.—On the penance of one who lays hands upon a bishop. From the Council of Tongeren, chapter 5.

Whoever deceitfully lays his hand upon the Christ of the Lord—that is, upon his bishop, father, and shepherd—because he commits sacrilege; and whoever devastates and burns a church, because that too is sacrilege: the holy synod has decreed that he shall do penance in one place, that is, in a monastery, for all the days of his life.

### Chapter 66.—On cursing clerics. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 57.

(Dist. 46, c. *Clericus maledicus*.) A cursing cleric, especially among priests [or: “and especially by priests”], shall be compelled to ask forgiveness. If he refuses, let him be deposed and never restored to office without satisfaction.

### Chapter 67.—On those who slander their superiors. From the sayings of Basil (in the Shorter Rules, question 27).

[Col. 0815D] If anyone slanders the one who presides, let him do penance for seven days, separated from the assembly of the Church, as Miriam, Aaron’s sister, who had spoken against Moses (Numbers 12).

### Chapter 68.—By what means reveling and drunkenness are to be removed. Augustine, in Letter 64 to Bishop Aurelius.

(Dist. 44, c. *Comessationes*.) Reveling and drunkenness are regarded as so permissible and lawful that they are celebrated in honor even of the most blessed martyrs, not only on feast-days—which itself no one who looks upon these things with other than fleshly eyes can fail to regard as lamentable—but even daily. And shortly afterward:

Therefore, in my judgment, these practices are not to be removed harshly, not sternly, not by imperious command, but more by teaching than by ordering, more by admonishing than by threatening. For thus must one deal with the multitude; severity, however, must be exercised concerning the sins of the few. And if we threaten anything, it should be done with sorrow, threatening from the Scriptures the vengeance to come, so that it is not we ourselves who are feared through our own power, but God through our speech. Thus spiritual persons, or those near to being spiritual, will first be moved; by their authority and their very gentle yet persistent admonitions, the remaining multitude may be subdued.

### Chapter 69.—That excess in eating is greatly opposed to Christians. From the sayings of Saint Benedict.

Nothing is so contrary to a Christian as gluttony and drunkenness, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke 21).

### Chapter 70.—That the evil of drunkenness must be entirely avoided. From the decrees of Pope Eutychian, chapter 8 (at the end of Eutychian’s decrees).

[Col. 0816B]

We command Christians by every means to beware of the great evil of drunkenness, from which all vices spring. Whoever refuses to avoid it, we decree, must be excommunicated until suitable amendment.

### Chapter 71.—That bishops and their ministers must not be weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness. From the decrees of the same pope, chapter 9 (at the end of the same decrees).

Bishops and ministers of God ought not to devote themselves to reveling and excessive drinking, but should consider the judgment of the Lord saying: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke 21). They should take food and necessary sustenance moderately, so that, according to the Apostle, they may be sober and ready for God’s service (1 Thessalonians 5; 1 Timothy 3; Titus 1).

### Chapter 72.—On the same matter. From the Council of Chalon, chapter 10.

Let priests maintain sobriety and preach to the faithful that it must be maintained, because one who stuffs himself with wine to the point of mental derangement cannot freely preach sobriety. This is also to be observed regarding reveling and the other plagues pertaining to gluttony.

### Chapter 73.—On the same matter. From the Apostolic Canons, chapter 42.

(Dist. 35, c. *Episcopus*.) A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who gives himself up to gambling and drunkenness shall either cease or certainly be condemned. A subdeacon, reader, or singer who does the like shall either cease or be deprived of communion. The same applies also to a layperson.

### Chapter 74.—On the same matter. In the same place, chapter 43.

If any bishop or any ordained person is habitually drunken, let him either cease or be deposed.

### Chapter 75.—What kind of guests ought to be present at bishops’ banquets. From the decrees of Pope Eusebius, chapter 10 (appended to the end of Eusebius’s decrees).

A bishop ought to be content with moderate meals and not urge his guests to eat and drink, but rather always set an example of sobriety. From his banquet let every incentive to indecency be removed [*augmenta*, original reading, in place of *argumenta*]: no theatrical entertainments, no empty talk of performers, no foolish babbling of fools, no tricks of buffoons are to be admitted. Let travelers, the poor, and the infirm be present, so that, blessing Christ from the priestly table, they may receive a blessing. Let sacred reading be recited, followed by exhortation in a living voice, so that the diners may rejoice that they have been refreshed not only with bodily food but indeed with the nourishment of the spiritual word, and that in all things God may be honored through Jesus Christ our Lord.

### Chapter 76.—On the penance of priests and the remaining orders if they become drunk. From the Penitential of Bishop Theodore.

If any priest becomes drunk through ignorance, let him do penance for seven days on bread and water; if through negligence, for fifteen days; if through contempt, for forty days. Let a deacon or monk do penance according to his order, as has been written; likewise all other clerics and ministers shall do penance according to their rank at the priest’s judgment. Laypersons, as persons not bound by vows, if they become drunk, shall be rebuked by the priest: drunkards shall not possess the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6), drunkenness brings destruction, and he shall compel them to do penance. Whoever compels a person to become drunk under the pretext of hospitality shall be rebuked most severely and do penance for seven days; if through contempt, for thirty days. No Christian shall compel another Christian to drink more than nature requires. If he does so, let him do penance according to what is contained in the penitential.

### Chapter 77.—On the same matter. From the sayings of Bishop Fructuosus.

If anyone endowed with ecclesiastical ordination, or a monk, is found to be habitually drunken, let him do penance on bread and water for three months.

### Chapter 78.—That clerics themselves should abstain from reveling and drunkenness, and command their subjects to abstain. From the decrees of Pope Eutychian, chapter 13 (at the end of Eutychian’s decrees).

You must observe both that you yourselves abstain from drunkenness and that you preach—command—the peoples subject to you to abstain. Do not go about taverns drinking or eating; do not roam through houses or villages out of any curiosity; and do not hold banquets with women or with any impure persons, unless perhaps a head of household invites you to his home and, with his wife and children, wishes to rejoice with you in spiritual joy, receive refreshment from your words, and offer you bodily refreshment in the duty of charity. For whenever any one of the faithful refreshes you with bodily meals, it is fitting that he should be refreshed by you with spiritual fare.

### Chapter 79.—On the penance of one who has been drunk. From the Council of Agde, chapter 41.

(Dist. 35, c. *Ante omnia*.) Therefore, the person established to have been drunk shall, as the order permits, either be removed from communion for thirty days or handed over to corporal punishment.

### Chapter 80.—That wine must be avoided as poison. From the sayings of Augustine.

Avoid wine as poison, lest drunkenness overcome you and strip you of your virtues, making you naked. For wine, as Holy Scripture says, causes even the wise to apostatize (Ecclesiasticus 19). Observe how Noah, a wise and holy man, was stripped naked while sleeping through drunkenness (Genesis 9). Observe too the patriarch Lot, who through drunkenness shamefully had intercourse with his daughters (Genesis 19). Hence blessed Basil says: “Many have been seized by demons through wine; drunkenness is nothing other than a most manifest demon.”

[Note: [Col. 0817] Basil, vol. II, in the admonition to a spiritual son.]

Hence the prophet says: “Fornication and wine and drunkenness take away the heart” (Hosea 4). For drunkenness produces disturbance, begets frenzy of mind, and kindles the flame of lust, as the Apostle testifies: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is debauchery” (Ephesians 5). If anyone acts contrary to these decrees of the saints, let him perform fitting and lengthy penance, because it is one of those sins that separate a person from the kingdom of God, as the Apostle Paul says: “Neither drunkards shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6).

### Chapter 81.—On the penance of one who vomits through drunkenness. From the Roman Penitential.

A person who vomits through drunkenness, if he is a presbyter or deacon, shall do penance for forty days; if a monk, for thirty days; if a cleric, for twenty days; if a layperson, for fifteen days.

### Chapter 82.—On the same matter. From the Penitential of Bede the Presbyter.

If a layperson vomits through drunkenness, let him abstain from meat, wine, and beer for three days.

### Chapter 83.—On the penance of one who wickedly makes others drunk.

If anyone wickedly makes another drunk, let him do penance for forty days. But if he has made this a habit, let him be deprived of communion until he performs worthy penance and promises amendment.

### Chapter 84.—That drunkenness must be avoided. From the decrees of Pope Clement, chapter 35 (Letter 1 to James, the Lord’s brother).

He strongly forbade drunkenness and declared drunkards dead both in body and mind. Concerning them he said by way of example:

> “Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness and continue drinking until evening, that they may burn with wine. Lyre and harp, tambourine and flute, and wine are at your banquets; but you do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the works of his hands” (Isaiah 5).

And again:

> “Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine, men strong at mixing drunkenness, who justify the ungodly for gifts and take away from him the righteousness of the righteous. Therefore, as the tongue of fire devours stubble and the heat of flame consumes it, so their root shall be as ashes and their blossom shall rise like dust. For they have rejected the law of the Lord of hosts and blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel. Therefore the wrath of the Lord has been angered against his people; he stretched out his hand over them and struck them, and the mountains were shaken, and their corpses became like dung in the midst of the streets. In all this his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out” (ibid.).

### Chapter 85.—What evils drunkenness produces in the human body and mind. Isidore says (*On the Supreme Good*, book 2, chapter 43).

Food produces gluttony; drink produces drunkenness. Drunkenness, moreover, gives rise to disturbance of mind, frenzy of heart, and the flame of lust. Drunkenness so alienates the mind that one does not know where one is. Therefore the evil committed through drunkenness is not even felt. True is what is said according to the prophet: “Fornication and drunkenness take away the heart” (Hosea 4). For fornication, as Solomon says, makes a wise person foolish. Drunkenness, as in Lot’s case, captivates the faculty of reason (Genesis 19). Thus also in Proverbs: “The mighty,” he says, “who are wrathful, should not drink wine, lest, when they have drunk, they forget wisdom” (Proverbs 31).

For many, it is a matter of praise to drink much and not become drunk. Let such people hear the prophet speaking against them: “Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine, men strong at mixing drunkenness” (Isaiah 5). Isaiah rebukes those devoted to much wine and luxurious living, saying: “Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness and continue drinking until evening, that they may burn with wine” (ibid.). Of such people it is also said elsewhere: “Woe to you, city whose king is young, and whose princes eat in the morning” (Ecclesiastes 10). For many serve drunkenness and the pleasures of gluttony from morning until sunset, and do not understand why they were born; held fast by beastly habit, they serve only luxury and feasting the whole day.

The prophet Joel cries out to those who serve drunkenness, saying: “Awake, you drunkards, and weep; and howl, all you who drink wine in sweetness” (Joel 1). By this testimony he does not merely say, “Weep, all you who drink wine,” as though drinking were wholly unlawful, but adds “in sweetness,” which pertains to luxurious and prodigal excess. For the Apostle teaches Timothy how much is sufficient for necessity when he says: “Use a little wine” (1 Timothy 5). People become drunk not only from wine but also from other kinds of drink prepared in various ways. Hence the Nazirites, who consecrated themselves to the Lord, were commanded not to drink wine or *sicera*—intoxicating drink (Numbers 6); for both overthrow the state of the mind and make people drunk, and both equally produce the lust of the flesh. Some ascetics, just as they eat bread by weight, also drink water by measure, maintaining that abstinence even from water accords with chastity of the flesh.

### Chapter 86.—On the exemption from punishment of a madman if something has been lost through him. Book 7 of the *Institutes*, title 1.

What an infant or a madman has caused the owner to lose or has damaged is unpunished.

### Chapter 87.—Marriages are not to be contracted by mad persons; marriages already contracted are not to be dissolved. *Institutes*, book 24, title 2. (*Digest*, book 23, title 2, law 16).

Madness does not permit the contracting of marriage, because consent is necessary; but it does not invalidate a marriage rightly contracted.

### Chapter 88.—Likewise, on the same matter. Ambrose on Luke (*Digest*, book 1, title 6, law 8).

Although a madman cannot take a wife, he can nevertheless retain his marriage.

### Chapter 89.—Likewise, on mad persons (*Institutes*, book 3, title 20).

Likewise, a madman cannot conduct any legal business, because he does not understand what he does.

### Chapter 90.—That the same is to be held concerning mad children and parents. Constitutions of the Novels, chapter 4.

[Col. 0820A]

If a mad son, or any person among one’s children, is in a state of madness, the same rules are to bind them as we have stated above concerning mad parents.

### Chapter 91.—On the exemption from punishment of a madman. Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, book 1, chapter 1, in the treatise on the first day.

In judgments of this kind, guilt binds and punishment condemns persons who are voluntarily guilty, not persons compelled by necessity. For if anyone kills an innocent person in madness, he is not liable to death; indeed, by the oracle of the divine law itself, one who has inflicted death through inadvertence receives hope of impunity and an opportunity of refuge, so that he may escape. Let this then be said concerning that which appears properly to be evil. For evils are only those things that entangle the mind in guilt and bind the conscience.

### Chapter 92.—On the same matter. Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, chapter 2.

(15, q. 1, c. *Quos scimus*.) We know some people who have suddenly become mad and done much harm with sword, club, stones, and bites, and some have even killed. When apprehended by skill and brought before the courts, they were in no way found guilty, because they committed these acts not voluntarily but unknowingly, impelled by some force—I know not what. For how is one made guilty who does not know what he has done?

### Chapter 93.—That minors and mad persons cannot make a will. *Institutes*, book 2, title 12.

Minors below puberty cannot make a will, because they possess no judgment of mind; likewise mad persons, because they lack reason. Nor does it matter if a minor later becomes adult, or if a mad person later becomes sound of mind, and then dies. But if mad persons make a will during the time in which their madness has ceased, they are held to have made a valid will in law.

### Chapter 94.—Jews are not to be compelled to the Christian faith. From the Council of Toledo, chapter 58 (56).

(Dist. 45, c. *De Judaeis*.) The holy synod decreed concerning Jews that henceforth no one should have force applied to him in order to make him believe. Likewise, in the same council: Jews are to be persuaded to convert not by force but by the free choice [the capacity of free will, Gratian], rather by exhortation than compulsion.

### Chapter 95.—That no one should support Jews in their error. Likewise, chapter 57.

Whoever—bishop, cleric, or layperson—gives any Jew assistance against the Christian faith, whether by gift or favor, shall truly, as profane and sacrilegious, become anathema, excluded from the Catholic Church and the kingdom of God. For it is fitting that the person who becomes patron of Christ’s enemies should be separated from Christ’s body.

### Chapter 96.—On invalidating Jewish testimony. Likewise, chapter 63.

(2, q. 7, c. *Non potest*.) The testimony of those who are instructed falsely in the faith must be invalidated, and those who have cast away from themselves faith in the truth must not be believed.

### Chapter 97.—That public offices are not to be entrusted to Jews. Likewise (ibid., chapter 46).

(27, q. 4, c. *Constituit sanctum*.) Those who are Jews shall in no way seek public offices, because under this pretext they injure Christians. Therefore provincial judges, together with the priests, shall stop their fraudulent insinuations and shall not permit them to perform public offices. If anyone permits this, excommunication shall be pronounced against him as against a sacrilegious person; and the one who has fraudulently obtained office shall be assigned to the public registers [*caedibus*, “slaughters,” in the original reading, apparently corrupt for *codicibus*].

### Chapter 98.—That Jews must not presume to purchase Christian slaves. Likewise, chapter 65.

Jews shall not be permitted to buy Christian slaves, male or female, nor acquire any through anyone’s gift. For it is impious that the members of Christ should serve the members of Antichrist. If henceforth Jews presume to possess Christian male or female slaves, those slaves, removed from their domination, shall obtain freedom from the ruler.

### Chapter 99.—That Christians should not take part in Jewish banquets. From the Third Council of Orléans, in the time of King Childebert, chapter 13.

We forbid Christians to attend Jewish banquets. If they are proved to have attended, they shall be subject to excommunication for a year on account of such contumacy.

### Chapter 100.—That Jews should not appear in public from the Lord’s Supper until Monday. Likewise, chapter 29.

From the day of the Lord’s Supper until the second day of the Sabbath—that is, Monday—during Easter, Jews shall not presume to go about among Christians or mingle in any way with Catholic peoples, in any place [*loco*, original reading] or on any occasion, during those four days.

### Chapter 101.—That Jews are to be called to the unity of faith with all gentleness and kindness. Gregory to Peter, Bishop of Terracina (Register, book 1, letter 34).

Joseph, the bearer of this letter, a Jew, informed us that your brotherhood expelled Jews residing in the fortress of Terracina from a certain place where they customarily gathered to celebrate their festivals. They then moved to another place for the like observance of their festivals, with your knowledge and consent; and now they complain that they have once more been expelled from that same place. If this is so, we desire that your brotherhood withdraw from such a complaint, and that they be permitted, as was customary, to assemble there in the place which, as we have said, they obtained with your knowledge. For those who differ from the Christian religion must be gathered into the unity of faith through gentleness, kindness, admonition, and persuasion, lest those whom the sweetness of preaching and fear, awakened beforehand, of the Judge to come might have invited to believe should be driven away by threats and terrors.

### Chapter 102.—On Jewish slaves fleeing to a church. Gregory, Register book 3, to John, Bishop of Cagliari (letter 9).

It has reached us that male and female slaves of Jews who flee to a church on account of the faith are either restored to their unbelieving masters or money is given so that they may not be restored. We therefore exhort you by no means to permit so wicked a custom to remain. Rather, whenever any slave of the Jews flees to venerable places on account of the faith, do not allow him to suffer any prejudice; whether he was formerly a Christian or is now baptized, let him, without any loss to Christian poor persons, be defended in freedom by every means through the religious protection of ecclesiastical piety.

### Chapter 103.—On Felix, a Christian whom a Samaritan wished to subject to slavery. Likewise, to John, Bishop of Syracuse (book 7, indiction 1, letter 22).

Felix, the bearer of this letter, complained to us that, though born of Christian parents, he had been given by a certain Christian to a Samaritan—as it is a crime even to say—by way of slavery. Although neither the law’s reason nor the reverence due to religion permits persons of such superstition to possess Christian slaves in any way, he nevertheless asserts that he remained in that man’s service for nineteen years. But when your predecessor of holy memory, Maximian, learned of this, he says that Maximian, moved as was fitting by priestly zeal, freed him from the Samaritan’s wicked service.

But because the son of this Samaritan is said to have become a Christian after five years, and certain persons are endeavoring, as Felix himself says, to reduce the aforesaid Felix to his service, let your holiness investigate carefully these matters of which we have been informed. If they are found to be so, strive to protect him and permit no one to burden him under any pretext. For since the laws openly prohibit slaves belonging to a superstitious sect from being reduced to the service of masters whom they preceded in coming to the faith, how much more should this man, born of Christian parents and made a Christian from infancy, be made to endure this claim in any way?

### Chapter 104.—That Jews are to retain their old synagogues. Likewise, Gregory to Januarius, Bishop of Cagliari (book 7, indiction 2, letter 5).

Jews from your city who came here complained to us that their synagogue situated at Cagliari had been occupied, without your consent, by Peter, who, by God’s will, had been brought from their superstition to the worship of Christian faith. On the day after his baptism—that is, on Sunday during the Paschal feast—he entered it with certain undisciplined persons, causing serious scandal, and placed there an image of the Mother of God and our Lord, a venerable cross, and the white garment [*birrum album*] which he had worn when rising from the font.

Shortly afterward: By these words we exhort you that, after the image and cross have been removed from there with the reverence that is fitting, you should restore what was violently taken away. For just as the legal provision does not permit Jews to erect new synagogues, so it permits them to retain their old ones without disturbance.

### Chapter 105.—That Jews are not to be forcibly excluded from their religious observances. Likewise, to Paschasius, Bishop of Naples (book 11, letter 15).

(Dist. 45, c. *Qui sincera*.) Jews dwelling in Naples complained to us, maintaining that certain people were unreasonably endeavoring to exclude them from some solemnities of their festivals, so that they might not be permitted to observe the celebrations of their festivals, as they and their parents had been permitted to observe or celebrate them from ancient times until now. If this is indeed the truth, those persons seem to be devoting effort to an unnecessary affair.

### Chapter 106.—What is to be done if slaves of Jews wish to become Christians. Gregory to Fortunatus, Bishop of Naples (Register, book 5, chapter 131, or letter 31).

(Dist. 54, c. *Fraternitatem*.) Your brotherhood ought to be diligent if, from the service of Jews, not only a Jew but even any pagan wishes to become a Christian. Once his wish has been made known, there shall be no opportunity, through any contrivance or pretext, to sell him to any Jew; rather, the person desiring conversion to the Christian faith shall by every means be vindicated into freedom under your protection.

Concerning those who must lose slaves of this sort, lest perhaps they think their interests are unreasonably harmed, you ought carefully to observe the following. If pagans whom Jews have bought from foreign lands for trade happen, within three months—while the purchaser to whom they had been sold cannot be found—to flee to the Church, and say that they wish to become Christians, or disclose such a wish even outside the Church, let the Jews receive their price from a Christian purchaser. But if, after the three months prescribed, any slave of this sort belonging to Jews declares his wish and desires to become a Christian, and no one subsequently purchases him, then the master shall not dare to sell him under any pretext; rather, he shall without doubt be brought to the reward of freedom, because the master is said to have acquired him not to sell but to serve himself [*reservasse*, “kept,” original reading, for *comparasse*, “acquired”].

### Chapter 107.—On the zeal of Christian priests against Jews. Ambrose, in the letter to the people of Vercelli (Letter 29 to Emperor Theodosius).

It has been reported by the Count of the East, responsible for military affairs, that a synagogue was burned and that this was done at the bishop’s instigation. I do not maintain that the bishop’s assertion should have been awaited; for priests are leaders of crowds and lovers of peace, unless they themselves are stirred by an injury to God or an outrage against the Church.

Likewise: Why do you order judgment against one who is absent? You have him present; you have an accused person who confesses. I cry out that I burned the synagogue, that I gave them orders, so that there might not even be a place where Christ was denied.

Likewise: Do you not see, Emperor, that God forbids prayer to be offered for those whom you think should be defended?

Likewise: Who has the right to vindicate the synagogue? Christ, whom they killed, whom they denied? Or will God the Father vindicate those who do not receive the Father?

Likewise: If you consult your counts in monetary cases, how much more fitting is it that you consult the priests of the Lord in cases of religion?

Likewise: Everything remains intact for you. In this matter I bind myself before our God on your behalf; do not fear the oath. Can anything displease God if it is amended for the honor due to him?

Likewise: I did what could be done more honorably: I acted so that you might hear me more readily in the palace, lest, if necessary, you should hear me in the Church.

### Chapter 108.—That Jews have lost the power to wage war. Jerome on Isaiah, book 2 (on chapter 3).

[Col. 0824A]

It is no wonder that every rank of warriors has perished among the Jews, since they do not have the power to serve as soldiers under the sword or to bear arms.

### Chapter 109.—On the condemnation of Jews if they circumcise a Christian. Code, book 1.

(L. *Judaei*, C. *de Jud. et coelic.*) Jews shall be condemned both to confiscation of goods and to perpetual exile if it is established that they have circumcised a person of our faith, or ordered him to be circumcised.

### Chapter 110.—On slaves of Jews if they flee to a church. From the *Life of Blessed Gregory*, book 4, chapter 43.

As Gregory refused to have Jews forcibly baptized, so he permitted Christians in no way whatsoever to be subjected to them. Likewise, ibid., ch. 45. [Col. 0824B] He did not permit Jewish slaves who had once fled to the church ever to be returned by any persuasions whatever. Likewise, ibid., ch. 46. Gregory not only lawfully restored Christian slaves to their former freedom, but also in no way permitted pagans wishing to come to the faith to be sold.

### CHAPTER 111.—That no person of ill repute may accuse. Stephen to all bishops, ch. 1.

Let none of your accusers be a slave or freedman, nor anyone guilty of a capital offence, nor a person of ill repute. Let those also be rejected who dwell with enemies, and all laymen whom attachment of friendship is wont to incite to the harassment of calumny.

### CHAPTER 112.—That converted Jews should be honoured. Gelasius to Quinigesius, bishop.

[Col. 0824C] The most illustrious man Telesinus, although he appears to be of Jewish belief, endeavours to prove himself to us such a man that we ought deservedly to call him ours [yours], and he has made a special request concerning his parent Antonius [Antio], that we should commend him to your affection. Therefore it is fitting that you treat the aforesaid brother [brother] in accordance with our will and commands, so that he may not merely suffer oppression in any respect whatsoever, but may also rejoice that, in whatever he needs, he is aided by the support of your affection.

### CHAPTER 113.—With what care the case of Jewish slaves is to be examined. Gelasius to Syracusius, Constantius, and Laurentius, bishops.

Judas, a slave belonging to one who professes Judaism, has represented that he has now fled to the church of Venafrum, as the appended text of the petition shows. He asserts that he purchased his freedom some years ago; [Col. 0824D] and that, though a Christian from infancy, he recently had the mark of circumcision imposed upon him by the aforesaid master. Therefore let your care diligently and faithfully investigate the truth of the matter between the two parties, so that religion may not appear to have been violated rashly, nor the slave, lying by means of this allegation, seek to evade the lawful rights of his master.

### CHAPTER 114.—That Jews must be preserved, not killed. Pope Alexander II to all the bishops of Spain [Gaul].

We have been pleased by the report recently heard concerning you: how you protected the Jews dwelling among you, lest they should be killed by those who were setting out for Spain against [Col. 0825A] the Saracens. For the latter, moved by foolish ignorance, or perhaps by blind greed, wished to rage to the death of persons whom divine mercy may perhaps have predestined for salvation. Thus also blessed Gregory restrained certain people who were burning to destroy them, declaring it wicked to desire the destruction of those whom God’s mercy has preserved, so that, having lost country and freedom, condemned by the judgment passed upon their fathers for the shedding of the Saviour’s blood, they might live scattered throughout the regions of the world in prolonged penitence.

The case of Jews and Saracens is plainly different. War is justly made upon the latter, who persecute Christians and drive them from cities and their own homes; the former are everywhere ready to serve. He also restrained a certain bishop who wished to destroy their synagogue.

### CHAPTER 115.—On the same subject. To Berengar, viscount of Narbonne.

Let your prudence know that we have been pleased that you protected the Jews living under your authority, lest they be killed. For God does not delight in the shedding of blood, nor rejoice in the destruction of the wicked.

Likewise, to Wilfred [Willefred], archbishop of Narbonne. All laws, both ecclesiastical and secular, forbid the shedding of human blood.

### CHAPTER 116.—That medicine is not to be received from a Jew. From the Seventh Synod, ch. 11.

Let none of those in sacred orders, nor any layman, eat the unleavened bread of the Jews, live with them, summon them in sickness, receive medicine from them, or bathe with them in a bath. If anyone does this, if he is a cleric, let him be deposed; if a layman, let him be excommunicated.

### CHAPTER 117.—That Christians must not share banquets with Jews. From the Council of Agde, ch. 40.

(28, question 1, ch. *Omnes deinceps clerici*.) Let all clerics and laypeople avoid Jewish banquets, and let no one receive them to a banquet. For, since they do not partake of common foods among Christians, it is unworthy and sacrilegious for Christians to receive their food; since those things which we consume with the Apostle’s permission are judged unclean by them (1 Tim. IV). Thus Christians begin to be inferior to Jews if foods avoided by them are set before us and we partake of those set before us by them [“they … we partake”: thus in the original]; while they disdain what is offered by us.

### CHAPTER 118.—That Jews are not to be appointed judges or tax-collectors. From the Council of Mâcon in the time of King Guntram, ch. 16 (First Council of Mâcon, ch. 13).

Let Jews not be appointed judges over Christian peoples [“battles,” in this text; *populis*, original], nor be permitted to be tax-collectors, lest Christians appear—God forbid—to be subject to them.

### CHAPTER 119.—On the penance of those who have eaten with Jews. From the Council of Elvira, ch. 30.

If any cleric or believer has eaten with Jews, it has been decreed that he abstain from communion, so that he may be corrected.

## FOURTEENTH PART OF THE DECREE. On just or unjust excommunication: for what causes and in what order it is to be performed.

[Col. 0825]

### CHAPTER 1.—With what discernment blessed Peter taught that, in the one person of Clement, all prelates of the Church bind and loose (Letter 1 to James, brother of the Lord, immediately after the beginning).

[Col. 0825C]

“I entrust to Clement,” says blessed Peter, “the power of binding and loosing entrusted to me by the Lord, so that concerning all matters whatsoever which he decrees on earth, that decree may stand also in heaven. For he will bind what ought to be bound and loose what it is expedient to loose, as one who knows the rule of the Church thoroughly.”

### CHAPTER 2.—Likewise on the same subject (ibid., somewhat later).

O Clement, let all receive your words with such reverence that they may know you to be the envoy and herald of truth; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven (Matt. XVI), since [“since indeed,” original]—as I have said—you will bind what ought to be bound and loose what it is expedient to loose.

### CHAPTER 3.—That a prelate, following his own will, must not attempt either to loose the guilty or to bind the innocent. Gregory, Homily 26 (*Forty Homilies*).

(11, question 3, ch. *Plerumque*.) It frequently happens that a man occupies here the place of judge though his life is by no means suited to that office; and it often occurs that he either condemns the undeserving or, himself bound, looses others. Often, in loosing and binding subjects, a pastor follows the impulses of his own will rather than the merits of the cases. Thus one deprives oneself of the very power of binding and loosing when one exercises it according to one’s own desires and not according to the conduct of one’s subjects.

Often a pastor is moved toward some neighbour by hatred or favour. Those who follow either their own hatreds or their favour in the causes of their subjects cannot judge those subjects worthily. Hence the Prophet rightly says: “They put to death souls that do not die, and make alive souls that do not live” (Ezek. XIII). For the person who condemns the just puts to death one who does not die; and one who tries to acquit the guilty from punishment seeks to make alive one who will not live.

Therefore cases must be weighed, and then the power of binding and loosing exercised. One must consider what the fault is, or what repentance has followed after the fault, so that those whom almighty God visits by the grace of compunction may be absolved by the sentence of the pastor. For then is a president’s absolution true: when it follows the judgment of the inward Judge.

This is well signified by the resurrection of Lazarus after four days. It shows, namely, that the Lord first called and restored the dead man to life, saying: “Lazarus, come forth” (John II); and afterwards the man who had come out alive was loosed by the disciples, as it is written: “And when he who had been bound had come forth, he then said to the disciples, ‘Loose him, and let him go’” (ibid.). Behold: the disciples loose one already living, whom the Master had raised while dead. For if the disciples had loosed the dead man, they would have displayed a stench rather than power.

From this consideration we must understand that we ought by pastoral authority to loose those whom we recognize that our Author has made alive by reviving grace. This quickening is already known, before upright conduct, in the very confession of sin. Hence this very dead man is not told, “Come to life,” but “Come forth.” For every sinner, while hiding his fault within his conscience, lies hidden within, concealed in his inner chambers. But the dead person comes forth when the sinner voluntarily confesses his wickedness.

Thus Lazarus is told, “Come forth,” as though it were openly said to every one dead in sin: “Why do you hide your guilt within your conscience? Come forth now through confession, you who lie hidden inwardly within yourself through thought [‘denial,’ original].” Let the dead man therefore come forth—that is, let the sinner confess his fault. And let the disciples loose the one who has come forth [“come forth” inserted in the original], so that the pastors of the Church may remove the punishment deserved by one who was not ashamed to confess what he had done. I have said this briefly concerning the order of loosing, so that, with great restraint, pastors of the Church may strive either to loose or to bind.

### CHAPTER 4.—That holy persons do not sin when they strike sinners with a sentence of curse. Gregory, *Morals*, book IV, ch. 6.

(24, question 3, ch. *Cum sancti viri*.) When holy men pronounce a sentence of curse, they do not break forth into it from a desire for vengeance but from an examination of justice [“break forth,” original]. They behold inwardly God’s subtle judgment, and recognize by what curse they ought to strike the evils that arise outwardly; and they do not sin by that curse because they do not depart from the inward Judge [“judgment,” original].

### CHAPTER 5.—Likewise: that a curse is pronounced in two ways, and that unjust bonds need not be feared by the just. Gregory, *Morals*, book IV, ch. 5.

[Col. 0827D]

Holy Scripture speaks of a curse in two ways: one which it approves and another which it condemns. A curse is pronounced in one way by the judgment of justice, as it was pronounced when the first man sinned and heard: “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Gen. III); and when Abraham is told: “I will curse those who curse you” (Gen. XII). Again, because a curse is pronounced not by the judgment of justice but uttered from the rancour of vengeance, we are warned by the voice of Paul preaching, who says: “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. XII).

Augustine, *On the Word of the Lord according to Matthew*, ch. 16. (11, question 3, ch. *Coepisti*.) You have begun to regard your brother as a publican; you bind him on earth. But see that you bind justly, for justice breaks unjust bonds. When, however, [Col. 0828A] you have corrected and been reconciled with your brother, you have loosed him on earth; and when you have loosed him on earth, he shall be loosed in heaven.

### CHAPTER 6.—That the person who either binds the just or looses the unjust is abominable to God. Jerome on Paul’s Epistle to Philemon (v. 4).

(11, question 3, ch. *Si quis dixerit*.) “He who calls the just unjust and the unjust just—both are abominable before God” (Prov. XVIII). Likewise, he who says that the holy person is not holy, and again asserts that the unholy person is holy, is abominable before God.

### CHAPTER 7.—That before God it is not the sentence of priests, but each person’s life, that defends or condemns. Jerome on Matthew, book III (on ch. XVI).

“I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind [Col. 0828B] upon earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed in heaven.” Bishops and presbyters, not understanding this passage, assume something of Pharisaic arrogance for themselves, so as either to condemn the innocent or to think that they can loose the guilty, whereas before the Lord it is not the sentence of priests but the life of the accused which is examined.

We read in Leviticus concerning lepers, where they are commanded to show themselves to the priests; and, if they have leprosy, then they are made unclean by the priest (Lev. XIV). This is not because priests make men unclean, but because they have knowledge of lepers and non-lepers and can distinguish who is clean and who unclean. Therefore, just as there the priest does not make the leper clean or unclean, so here neither bishop nor presbyter binds or looses [Col. 0828C] those who are innocent or guilty; but, in accordance with his office, after hearing the varieties of sins, he knows who must be bound and who must be loosed.

### CHAPTER 8.—That a sentence unjustly pronounced is in no way to be feared. Gelasius to the Eastern bishops, on avoiding communion with Acacius.

(11, question 3, ch. *Cui est illata*.) Let the person against whom a sentence has been issued abandon his error, and the sentence is void. If it is unjust, he ought all the less to concern himself with it, because an inequitable sentence can burden no one before God and His Church. Therefore he should not seek to be absolved from a sentence by which he plainly sees that he is in no way bound.

### CHAPTER 9.—That it does not go unpunished if anyone suffers injustice. Augustine, *On the Supreme Good*.

(11, question 3, ch. *Secundum catholicam*.) According to the Catholic faith and sound doctrine, no one can harm God’s nature; nor can God’s nature unjustly harm anyone; nor does it permit anyone to suffer harm unjustly. For, says the Apostle, “He who harms shall receive what he has harmed” (Col. III).

### CHAPTER 10.—That no one is condemned except on account of an evil conscience. Augustine, *On the Sermon of the Lord on the Mount*, book II, ch. 29.

(11, question 3, ch. *Temerarium*.) A rash judgment usually does no harm to the person rashly judged. But rashness itself necessarily harms the person who judges rashly.

### CHAPTER 11.—Likewise. Augustine in a letter to the clergy of Hippo (Letter 137).

Now, if it pleases you that the name of the presbyter not be recited, [Col. 0829A] lest we give occasion to those who do not wish to come to church—as the Apostle says (2 Cor. II)—this will not be our doing. For what does it harm a man if human ignorance does not wish him to be named from that tablet, provided that an evil conscience does not erase him from the book of the living?

### CHAPTER 12.—On the same matter. Augustine to Secundinus the Manichaean (vol. VI, book *Against Secundinus the Manichaean*, ch. 1).

(11, question 3, ch. *Sent.*) Think of Augustine whatever you please; let conscience alone not accuse me in the eyes of God.

### CHAPTER 13.—That conscience alone is to be feared in judgment. Augustine on Psalm XXXVI (on v. 33).

(11, question 3, ch. *Etsi tempus*.) Even if for a time you are condemned by a human being, and if you pronounce the proconsul’s sentence [“you pronounce sentence upon Cyprian”] against Cyprian, one thing is the earthly chair, another the heavenly tribunal: from the lower he receives sentence, from the higher a crown.

### CHAPTER 14.—That the just person should hope for a reward for a curse unjustly inflicted. Augustine on Psalm XXXVII (on v. 16).

(11, question 3, ch. *Custodi*.) Keep your innocence within, where no one can oppress your cause. False testimony has prevailed against you—but among human beings. Can it prevail before God, where your case must be pleaded? When God is judge, there will be no witness other than your conscience. Between the just Judge and your conscience, fear nothing except your cause.

Likewise, Augustine on Psalm 102 (on v. 6). One who is just and is cursed unjustly shall receive a reward.

### CHAPTER 15.—That a presbyter or deacon deposed in any manner by his bishop must be examined by the bishops of the province, and before this is done may be received into communion by no one. From the Council of Sardica, ch. 117.

(11, question 3, ch. *Si episcopus forte iracundus*.) If a bishop, perhaps being irascible—which ought not to be the case—is quickly and harshly stirred against a presbyter or deacon and wishes to expel him from the Church, care must be taken lest an innocent person be condemned or lose communion. Therefore the man who has been cast out shall have the power to appeal to the neighbouring bishops, so that his case may be heard and considered more diligently; for a hearing ought not be denied to one who asks for it.

And the bishop who has cast him out, whether justly or unjustly, should patiently allow the affair to be examined, so that his sentence may either be approved by many or corrected. Nevertheless, before all matters are diligently and faithfully examined, no one ought presume to admit to communion the person separated from communion.

### CHAPTER 16.—That bishops who are violent and implacable toward their subjects should be denied communion by neighbouring bishops. From the Council of Arles, ch. 11 (Third Council of Agde).

(11, question 3, ch. *Episcopi*.) If bishops, setting aside priestly moderation, presume to excommunicate innocent persons or persons guilty of the slightest offences, or perhaps refuse to receive them back quickly to grace, they shall be admonished by letters from the neighbouring bishops of whatever province; [Col. 0830A] and if they refuse to obey, they shall be denied communion by the other bishops until the time of the synod.

### CHAPTER 17.—An example of this matter. Gregory to Magnus, bishop [Gregory has “presbyter”], of Milan (book II, indiction 11, letter 26).

(24, question 3, ch. *Comperimus*.) We have learned that Laurentius, formerly our brother and fellow-bishop, deprived you of communion although no faults of yours existed. Therefore, fortified by the authority of this our command, carry out your office without anxiety, and receive communion without any fear.

### CHAPTER 18.—That a bishop should not pronounce a hasty sentence. Gregory to Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse (book XII of the Register, ch. 26).

I recall that I have often admonished you that you ought in no way to be hasty [Col. 0830B] in pronouncing sentence; and now, behold, I have learned that your brotherhood, moved by anger, has excommunicated the most reverend man Eusebius, an abbot. This greatly astonished me.

### CHAPTER 19.—That sound reason should correct what a disturbed mind has done wrongly. Augustine to Auxilius, bishop (Letter 75).

I beg you to grant pardon to the excommunicated man who asks pardon, if he acknowledges his fault. But if you prudently see that he has committed no sin, do what it is fitting for a holy man to do: if what the man says in the psalm has happened to you—as indeed it can happen to a human being—“My eye has been troubled because of anger” (Ps. V), cry out to God: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak” [Col. 0830C] (ibid.), so that He may stretch out His right hand to you, restrain your anger, and calm your mind for seeing and doing justice. Remove the ecclesiastical records which, perhaps more disturbed than deliberate, you have made.

### CHAPTER 20.—Censure of priests who rush incautiously to prosecute faults. Rabanus, *On Ecclesiastical Afflictions*, book I.

(24, question 3, ch. *Non in perpetuum*.) We are not condemned forever when we are judged unjustly, as the Psalmist says: “Nor will He condemn him when he is judged” (Ps. XXXVI). Indeed, many priests profess that they pursue fault with zeal for God; but, while acting thus without discernment, they incur the crime of sacrilege, and while rushing headlong, as though to correct, they themselves fall much more grievously and badly.

### CHAPTER 21.—How a prelate who has unlawfully condemned a subject should be punished. From the Council of Paris in the time of Louis.

[Col. 0830D]

(24, question 3, ch. *De illicita*.) The law of the Catholic emperor Justinian concerning unlawful excommunication—Constitution 118, chapter 451—which the Catholic Church approves and observes, decreed that no bishop and no presbyter may excommunicate anyone before the cause for which ecclesiastical canons command this to be done has been proved. But if anyone excommunicates someone contrary to these provisions, the person excommunicated shall, by the authority of the higher priest, be restored to the grace of holy communion. The person who unlawfully excommunicated him, however, shall abstain from sacred communion for such time as the higher priest sees fit, so that he may justly suffer what he did unjustly.

Accordingly, Saint Gregory wrote among other things to John, bishop of Prima Justiniana, who had excommunicated unjustly (book III of the *Register*, ch. 45, letter 6):

> “After the decrees of your aforesaid sentence have first been annulled and reduced to nothing, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we decree that for a period of thirty days you are deprived of sacred communion, and that you must implore almighty God’s pardon for so great an offence with the utmost penitence and tears. But if we learn that you have carried out our sentence too negligently, know that, with the Lord’s help, not merely your injustice but also the contumacy of your brotherhood will be punished more severely. For no one is to be judged precipitately or out of due order—that is, without first being warned and summoned. Concerning the summoning of a perpetrator of manifest crimes, the law says: whoever, summoned three times by the authority of a judge, or called before a judge by three edicts, or summoned once by a peremptory citation in place of all three—that is, one which extinguishes the action—and refuses to appear before the judge by whom he was notified, may be judged as contumacious. Indeed, in all cases in which judgment has been given against a contumacious party, the proceedings cannot be reopened through appeal.”

And this rule concerning persons summoned by three authoritative citations is confirmed by Celestine, writing to Nestorius from evangelical truth; by the Synod of Ephesus, decreeing concerning the same matter (letter of the Council of Ephesus to Nestorius); and by blessed Gregory, writing to John (ch. 44) [Col. 0831C]. As for a peremptory writ, the African Council shows in the case of Cresconius that, if a summoned person refuses to amend, he is to be excluded immediately by judicial authority through his own contempt and contumacy.

Likewise, blessed Gregory, writing concerning sentence against a contumacious party to Maximus, the usurping bishop of Salona, says (Register V, letter 3, or ch. 103):

> “We exhort you to hasten to come to us, putting aside every excuse, so that, justice being preserved, Christ revealing it, we may investigate and decide according to canonical enactments these matters of which you are accused. Take care, therefore, to make no further delay in coming, lest your very absence render you more liable to the charges made, and compel us to pronounce against you a harsher judgment, as against a contumacious person, not only on account of the alleged crimes from which you evade clearing yourself, but also on account of the fault of disobedience.”

### CHAPTER 22.—What subjects ought to be like toward persons who have offended the mind of their superior. From Clement’s First Letter to James.

You yourselves ought to understand certain things, if there are matters which your bishop cannot express more openly and plainly because of the snares of evil persons. For example, if he is hostile to someone because of that person’s actions, do not wait for him to say to you, “Do not be friends with that man.” Rather, you ought prudently to observe this, comply with his will without contention, and turn away from the person toward whom you perceive him to be hostile.

Nor should you speak to those to whom he does not speak, so that anyone who is at fault, desiring to retain the friendship of all of you, may hasten more quickly to be reconciled to the one who presides over all, and thereby return to salvation when he begins to obey the admonitions of his superior. But if anyone is a friend to those to whom he is not a friend, and speaks to those to whom he does not speak, he is one of those who wish to destroy the Church of God; although he seems to be with you in body, in mind and soul he is against you, and is a far worse enemy than those who are outside and openly hostile.

### CHAPTER 23.—That one who communicates with excommunicated persons incurs a like punishment. Calixtus to the bishops of Gaul (Letter 2, ch. 2).

[Col. 0832B] (11, question 3, ch. *Excommunicatos*.) Let no one receive persons excommunicated by priests before a just examination of both parties; nor communicate with them in prayer, food, drink, or a kiss, nor say “Ave” to them. For whoever knowingly communicates with excommunicated persons in these or other prohibited ways shall himself be subject to like excommunication, according to the institution of the apostles (ch. 11, Apostolic Canons).

### CHAPTER 24.—On the same matter. Pope Fabian to the ministers of the Church (Letter 1).

(11, question 3, ch. *Sicut apostoli*.) One must not communicate with the excommunicated. If anyone knowingly so much as speaks or prays in the same house with a person to be avoided as excommunicated, he shall be deprived of communion.

### CHAPTER 25.—That no bishop may knowingly communicate with the presbyter or deacon of another bishop who has been deprived of communion. From the Council of Sardica, ch. 16.

Whether deacon, presbyter, or any cleric has been deprived of communion by his own bishop and goes to another bishop, if the bishop to whom he flees knows that he was cast out by his own bishop, he ought not grant him communion. If he does so, let him know that he will have to answer the charge when the bishops have been summoned.

### CHAPTER 26.—That ministers of every ecclesiastical rank who communicate with excommunicated persons are to be deprived of communion. From the Council of Antioch, ch. 2 (Antioch I, under Julius I).

[Col. 0832D] If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all of the clergy is found to communicate with excommunicated persons, he too shall be deprived of communion, as one who confounds the rule of the Church.

### CHAPTER 27.—That no one may receive a cleric deprived of communion unless he has either been reconciled to his bishop or cleared by synodal satisfaction. From the same council, ch. 6.

(11, question 3, ch. *Si quis a proprio*.) If anyone has been deprived of communion by his own bishop, he shall not be received by others before he has been reconciled to his bishop or has appeared before the assembled synod and made satisfaction for himself.

### CHAPTER 28.—Whoever receives into communion a cleric expelled from the Church is to be judged under the same rule. From the Second Council of Carthage, ch. 7.

[Col. 0833A]

(11, question 3, ch. *Qui merito*.) Those who have deservedly been expelled from the Church because of their crimes, if they are received into communion by any bishop, presbyter, or cleric [deacon], shall themselves be held guilty of an equal offence together with them.

On the same matter. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, ch. 73 (11, question 3, ch. *Qui communicaverit*). Whoever communicates or prays with an excommunicated person, whether cleric or layperson, shall be excommunicated.

### CHAPTER 29.—On the same matter. From the Council of Saragossa, ch. 5.

Those separated from the Church by the discipline or sentence of a bishop are not to be received by other bishops. If bishops knowingly do this, they shall not have communion.

### CHAPTER 30.—On the same matter. From the First Council of Toledo, ch. 15.

(11, question 3, ch. *Si quis laicus*.) If a layperson is suspended, no cleric or religious person shall go to him or to his house. Likewise, if a cleric is suspended, let him be avoided by clerics. If anyone is found conversing or dining with him, that person also shall be suspended. But this applies to those clerics who are under one and the same bishop [“the same,” original], and to all who have been informed about the suspended person, whether that person is any layperson or a cleric.

### CHAPTER 31.—On the same matter. From the canons of Bishop Martin addressed to laypersons (ch. 84).

It is not lawful to communicate with excommunicated persons, nor to enter their houses and pray with them. But if any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or ecclesiastic of any kind communicates with an excommunicated person, he shall be excommunicated as one who disturbs the entire discipline of the Church.

### CHAPTER 32.—Likewise on the same matter. Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Sardinia (Register, book III, letter 24).

No religious person shall associate, according to the ordinances of the canons, with those suspended from ecclesiastical communion.

### CHAPTER 33.—That no one may communicate with excommunicated persons contrary to ecclesiastical satisfaction. Gelasius to Majoricus, Seranus, and John, bishops.

Let Coelestinus, presbyter of our brother and fellow-bishop [Col. 0833D] Seranus, who, breaking forth against pontifical judgment and against the commands of the Apostolic See, presumed to administer holy communion to the aforesaid persons—although he could not be ignorant of the sentence of his own bishop—be immediately excluded from ecclesiastical office, so that none of the ministers of the Church may seek to act contrary to pontifical decrees.

### CHAPTER 34.—On the same matter. From the Rule of Saint Benedict, ch. 26.

If any brother presumes, without the abbot’s command, to associate in any way with an excommunicated brother, to speak with him, or to send him a message, he shall incur the like punishment of excommunication.

### CHAPTER 35.—That an excommunicated person may not communicate before examination; a mercifully established penance for those who have done otherwise. John VIII to the clergy and order of Salerno.

[Col. 0834A]

(11, question 3, ch. *De illis presbyteris*.) Those presbyters who, during the time of our most holy predecessor Lord Pope Nicholas, being excommunicated, presumed to handle the sacred ministry, have brought upon themselves the sentence of condemnation, as the holy canons have established. Yet, because apostolic mercy is accustomed to grant pardon to those who are corrected, we extend this indulgence to them because of the abundance of mercy: nourished by holy communion, they shall endeavour for three continuous years to fast completely from wine or vinegar every second and sixth day of each week [“at all times, on the second, fourth, and sixth days, from wine and meat completely,” thus Gratian; Col. 0834B], and not commit any further acts deserving lamentation.

### CHAPTER 36.—That no one may receive the sacraments of the Church from excommunicated persons. John VIII to Michael, king of the Bulgarians.

If you receive any sacraments from those whom we have held excommunicated, it is plain that you appear to have abandoned idolatry not in order to become Catholics, but in order to become schismatics.

### CHAPTER 37.—Likewise, that a cleric or layperson condemned by his own bishop is not to be received by others. From the Council of Nicaea, ch. 5.

With respect to persons deprived of communion, whether of the clergy or the lay order, the regular sentence pronounced by bishops throughout each province shall prevail: those cast out are not to be received by others.

### CHAPTER 38.—On the same matter. From the letter of the Council of Carthage to Pope Celestine (preserved among the decrees of the African Council, ch. 105, ch. 5).

[Col. 0834C]

We beseech you henceforth not too readily to admit to your hearing persons coming thence, and not to be willing further to receive into communion persons excommunicated by us; for your venerability readily observes that this too was determined by the Council of Nicaea. For if there provision appears to be made concerning lower clergy or laypeople, how much more did it intend this to be observed concerning bishops, lest those suspended from communion in their province appear to be restored to communion too hastily or improperly by your holiness? May your holiness also reject, as is worthy of you, the improper evasions of presbyters and subordinate clerics.

### CHAPTER 39.—Likewise on the same matter. Nicholas to Epiphanius, bishop.

[Col. 0834D]

We decree that if any presbyter is excommunicated by his own bishop for any neglect or crime, he is not to be admitted to communion by another bishop. But if he presumes to communicate before a hearing, let him know that he has brought upon himself a sentence of condemnation.

### CHAPTER 40.—On the same matter. From the Apostolic Canons, ch. 11.

(11, question 3, ch. *Sicut apostoli*.) If anyone so much as speaks or prays in a house with an excommunicated person, he shall be deprived of communion.

An example of caution: from the *Liber Pontificalis*. (Distinction 19, ch. *Anastasius*.) Anastasius II, a Roman by nationality, sat for one year, eleven months, and twenty-four days. Many presbyters and clerics withdrew themselves from communion with him because, without their counsel, [Col. 0835A] he had communicated with the deacon of Thessalonica, who was in communion with Acacius; and because he secretly wished to recall Acacius, but could not, since Acacius was struck down by divine ordinance.

### CHAPTER 41.—That no one can justly be condemned unless canonically summoned to a hearing. Alexander II to Gervasius, archbishop of Reims.

It cannot justly be done that anyone be excommunicated beforehand by any prelate before he is canonically summoned by a synodal letter to answer.

### CHAPTER 42.—That if a prelate condemns someone before the cause is proved, he himself, subject to a higher hearing, must receive what he has done. Constitution of the Novels 11, ch. 20.

(2, question 1, ch. *Nemo episcopus*.) No bishop and no presbyter may excommunicate anyone before the cause for which ecclesiastical canons command this to be done has been proved. But if anyone excommunicates someone contrary to these provisions, the excommunicated person shall, by the authority of the higher priest, return to the grace of holy communion; while the person who excommunicated unlawfully shall abstain for such time as the higher priest sees fit, so that he may justly suffer what he did unjustly.

### CHAPTER 43.—With what moderation the Apostolic See accommodates personal circumstances in pronouncing sentence. From the decrees of Gregory VII.

(11, question 3, ch. *Quoniam multos*.) Since, because our sins demand it, we see many persons perish daily on account of excommunication—some through ignorance, some through excessive simplicity, some through fear, and some [Col. 0835C] even through necessity—overcome by mercy, we temper the sentence of anathema for a time, insofar as we can. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we release from the bond of anathema wives, children, sons, male and female slaves or bondspeople, likewise peasants and servants, and all others who are not so much members of the curial class that crimes are committed by their counsel; also those who unknowingly communicate with excommunicated persons, and those who communicate with persons who communicate with excommunicated persons.

But if any ploughman, pilgrim, or traveller arrives in the land of excommunicated persons where he cannot buy, or has nothing with which to buy, we grant permission to receive from the excommunicated. And if anyone wishes to give to excommunicated persons not to sustain their pride but for humane reasons, [Col. 0835D] we do not forbid it.

### CHAPTER 44.—Whether, when any one person sins, his whole household ought to be struck with anathema. From Augustine’s letter to Bishop Auxilius (Letter 75).

(24, question 3, chapter *Si habes*.) If you have an opinion on this matter established by certain arguments or testimonies of Scripture, please teach us how a son may rightly be anathematized for his father’s sin, or a wife for her husband’s, or a slave for his master’s, or even anyone not yet born in the household, if he is born at the time when the whole household is bound under anathema and cannot be aided by the washing of regeneration in the danger of death. For this is not a bodily punishment, by which we read that certain despisers of God, together with all who shared the same impiety, were at once slain [Col. 0836A]. For then mortal bodies, themselves destined to die, were destroyed to strike terror into the living. But the spiritual punishment by which what is written is brought about—“Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven” (Matt. XVI)—binds souls, concerning which it was said: “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine; the soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. XVIII).

Perhaps you have heard that certain priests of great reputation have anathematized some sinner together with his household. But if anyone asks me whether this is rightly done, I do not know what I should answer. In cases of certain crimes committed in concert against the Church, I have never dared to do this unless I were moved most gravely.

Again, after a few intervening words: How can we render a just account either to God or to [Col. 0836B] human beings if we punish innocent souls by a spiritual penalty for another’s crime, which they do not inherit as they inherit original sin from Adam, in whom all sinned (Rom. V)? For although the son of Classicianus inherited from his father the guilt of the first man, to be cleansed in the sacred font of baptism, nevertheless who can doubt that whatever sin his father, who begot him, afterwards committed—a sin in which this son had no share—does not pertain to him? What shall I say of the wife? What shall I say of the many souls in the whole household?

### CHAPTER 45.—An example from the Apostolic See: how it publicly declares some persons excommunicated, while seeming to overlook others, whom nevertheless it warns to seek salvation through the remedy of repentance. Urban II to Gibehard, Bishop of Constance.

[Col. 0836C]

Having considered the question of excommunication, and confirming the judgment of our holy predecessor Gregory, we have, with the Lord’s inspiration, determined it as follows. In the first degree, we judge the Ravennate heresiarch, the invader of the Roman Church, to be cut off and excommunicated from all members of the Catholic Church. In the second degree are those who support their wickedness by receiving ecclesiastical orders or offices from them through arms, money, counsel, or obedience. Binding these chiefly with the bonds of anathema, we have not indeed excommunicated, in the third degree, those who communicate with them; but because they condemn themselves by communion [read: “excommunication”] with them, we by no means receive them into our fellowship without the penalty and absolution of penitence [Col. 0836D]. For it is established by the holy canons that whoever communicates with the excommunicated is excommunicated.

Yet we have prescribed the forms of repentance and absolution with such moderation that whoever has defiled himself by association, greeting, prayer, kiss, or conversation with them, whether through ignorance, fear, or the necessity of some very great and urgent business, may obtain a share in our fellowship through the remedy of a lesser penance. But those who have fallen into this either voluntarily or negligently, we wish to be received under such disciplinary restraint that fear may be instilled into others.

### CHAPTER 46.—On the same subject. Pope Nicholas to Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims.

[Col. 0837A]

(11, question 3, chapter *Excellentissim*.) The most excellent King Charles consulted our Apostolic See concerning what ought to be done with those who communicate with persons who communicate with the often-condemned woman Ingeltrude [Engiltrude], since it is clear that she, together with her communicants and supporters, is bound by an equal bond of anathema. Therefore we now charge your Beatitude, relying on our authority, to take diligent care in this matter.

And because your holiness, divinely instructed, knows very well that one thing is sinning from necessity, another from ignorance, and another deliberately; and that the latter must be punished more strictly than the first two, therefore [Col. 0837B] let it watch carefully and, with prudent discernment, judge the circumstances of each person. Thus those who sin from necessity or ignorance are to be absolved by you in our authority, provided that their ignorance or necessity is genuine and not feigned, nor arose from their own will. For, as you know well, there are many who are able but unwilling to know what is right. Hence the Psalmist says of such persons: “He would not understand, that he might act rightly” (Ps. XXXV).

But those who are bound through their own deliberate choice and, in contempt, set aside our prohibitions, we wish you by no means to absolve unless worthy satisfaction has first been made.

### CHAPTER 47.—That the Church’s judgment is ratified in heaven. Augustine on John, Part I, Tractate 44.

[Note: Milleloquium, column 0837D, attributes this to Augustine under the heading “Excommunication,” chapter 49, but it is not found there.]

When the Church excommunicates, the excommunicated person is bound in heaven; [Col. 0837C] when the Church reconciles, the reconciled person is loosed in heaven.

### CHAPTER 48.—Likewise, concerning the Church’s power. Chrysostom on the Epistle to the Hebrews, Homily 4 (on chapter II of the Epistle to the Hebrews).

(11, question 3, chapter *Nemo contemnat*.) Let no one despise ecclesiastical bonds. For it is not a human being who binds, but Christ, who gave this power and made human beings lords of so great an honor.

### CHAPTER 49.—What it means to be anathematized. From the fifth session of the Fifth Synod.

(24, question 3, chapter *Certum est*.) It is certain that whoever has been shown to be impious has in every respect been separated from God; just as one who has been anathematized has been separated as impious. For anathema signifies nothing else [Col. 0837D] than separation from God.
