In Session 8: The judgment of anathema is nothing other than separation from God. Even if an impious person had not received it verbally from anyone, by his own impiety he in fact brings anathema upon himself, separating himself from the true life.

### CHAPTER 50.—How grave is the danger of being anathematized. Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*, Sermon 68.

[Note: Milleloquium, column 0838D, attributes this to him, chapter 14, but it is not found there.]

(11, question 3, chapter *Omnis Christianus*.) Every Christian, beloved, who is excommunicated by priests is said to be delivered to Satan. How? Surely because the devil is outside the Church, just as Christ is in the Church. [Col. 0838A] Therefore one removed from ecclesiastical communion is said, as it were, to be delivered to the devil. Hence the Apostle, when he declares that certain persons had been delivered to Satan (1 Tim. I), shows that they had been excommunicated by him.

### CHAPTER 51.—The difference between excommunication and anathema. John VIII to Liutbert, Archbishop of Mainz.

You should know that Engeltrude, the wife of Boso, has repeatedly been struck not only with excommunication, which separates from fraternal fellowship, but also with anathema, which cuts off from the very body of Christ, which is the Church.

### CHAPTER 52.—How grave an anathema is. From the History of Anastasius, Librarian of the Roman Church.

When Patriarch Tarasius was elected, he said: “Anathema casts a person far from God and expels him from the kingdom of heaven, leading him into outer darkness.”

### CHAPTER 53.—That the kingdom of heaven is closed to those whom the Church shuts out. Eutychianus to the bishops throughout Sicily (Letter 2, after the opening).

[Col. 0838B]

Those to whom the kingdom of God is barred are undoubtedly also denied the Church. Concerning them the Lord, proclaiming in the Gospel the authority of the apostles and their successors, says: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you bind shall be bound” (Matt. XVIII); that is, those whom you forbid from the Church, unless they are reconciled by satisfaction, shall find the gate of the heavenly kingdom closed against them.

### CHAPTER 54.—That an ordination performed by excommunicated persons has no force. Gregory the Great to Maximus, the presumptuous claimant at Salona (Register, book III, letter 20).

There is added an unheard-of wickedness: after our prohibition, which was issued under our excommunication both against you and against those ordaining you, you are said to have been brought forth publicly by military force after priests, deacons, and the rest of the clergy had been beaten [Col. 0838C]. We can by no means call this act a consecration, because it was consecrated [variant: “celebrated”] by excommunicated persons.

### CHAPTER 55.—On the same matter. From the decrees of Pope Gregory VII.

Pope Gregory, presiding over a synod, said: “Following in the footsteps of the holy Fathers, we have judged that the ordinations of those ordained by excommunicated persons are invalid.”

### CHAPTER 56.—An example for caution. Paul, *Life of Gregory*, book IV, chapter 9.

When the people of Dalmatia unanimously chose the distinguished archdeacon, whom Gregory had transferred from the rank of presbyter to that of deacon, to be set over them, and the pontiff had approved their decree, Maximus—entangled in many crimes—invaded the episcopal see of the city of Salona by military force, through the faction of Bishop Malchus, administrator of the Apostolic patrimony. On hearing this, Gregory gravely forbade the bishops of Dalmatia and Jadera to lay hands upon him [Col. 0838D]. But Maximus, who had seized the episcopal see against the canons, did not fear also to obtain the priesthood against God through the Simoniacal heresy [Col. 0839A], from bishops only, who were excommunicated and corrupted by payment.

### CHAPTER 57.—That an excommunicated person cannot excommunicate another. Alexander II to William Marcio.

(24, question 1, chapter *Audivimus*.) We have heard that Henry, called Archbishop of Ravenna, has attempted to excommunicate you. Since, being excommunicated, he could not excommunicate you, we absolve you and yours by Apostolic authority and command you to give the matter no further concern.

### CHAPTER 58.—On the same matter. Pope Nicholas to Emperor Michael.

(24, question 1, chapter *Ait Coelestinus*.) Pope Celestine, writing to the eastern bishops, says: “If anyone was either excommunicated or deprived of the dignity of bishop or cleric by Bishop Nestorius, or by others following him, after they began to preach such things, it is manifest that he has remained and remains in our communion. Nor do we judge him removed, because the judgment of one who had already made himself liable to removal could remove no one.”

### CHAPTER 59.—On the same matter. Likewise, to the clergy of Constantinople.

(24, question 1, chapter *Aperte, inquit*.) “The authority of our See,” he says, “has expressly decreed that no bishop, cleric, or Christian of any profession who, after Nestorius or those like him began to preach such things, was deposed from his office or communion, is to be considered either expelled or excommunicated. Rather, all these have been and remain to this day in our communion, because one who wavered by preaching such things could depose or remove no one” [Col. 0839C].

Do you understand, Emperor, from the matters mentioned above that those who had formerly been removed could not remove even their own superior, not to speak of anyone at all, nor depose anyone already cast down?

### CHAPTER 60.—That we ought not communicate with the dead with whom we did not communicate in life. Leo to Rusticus, Bishop of Narbonne (Letter 92).

(24, question 2, chapter *De communione*.) In the case of those deprived of communion and so deceased, the matter must be reserved for God’s judgment, in whose hand it was to prevent their death from being delayed until the remedy of communion. But we cannot communicate with the dead with whom we did not communicate while they were alive.

### CHAPTER 61.—On the same matter. Pope Gelasius to Faustus, Master of Soldiers (Letter 4).

[Col. 0839D]

We read that Christ raised the dead; we do not read that he absolved persons dead in error. And he who alone had the assured power to do this chiefly entrusted it to the blessed apostle Peter: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. XVI). “On earth,” he says; for nowhere did he say that one dead under this bond is to be absolved.

### CHAPTER 62.—That heretics may be anathematized even after death. From Session 1 of the Fifth Synod.

[Col. 0840A]

(21, question 2, chapter *Sane profertur*.) [Note: On this subject there is much near the end of the edict sent by Emperor Justinian to Pope John II; it is printed at the end of volume I of the Councils.]

Some persons indeed maintain that heretics ought to be anathematized after death, following in this the teaching of the holy Fathers, who condemned heretics not only while living but also, since they had died in their impiety, anathematized them after death. Likewise, those who had been unjustly condemned were restored after death and inscribed in the sacred *diptychs* (διπτύχοις, “diptychs”): this was done in the case of John (Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapters 34–35) and Flavian, bishops of Constantinople of revered memory (at the Council of Chalcedon).

Likewise Augustine says (*On the Unity of the Church*): “If these books identify their betrayer as clearly as the Lord identified [Col. 0840B] Judas (John XIII), let them read in them, by name and expressly, that either Caecilianus or the ordainers of those same books were betrayers; and if I do not anathematize them, may I myself be judged to have betrayed along with them.”

Likewise: What has now been read from Gelasius of holy memory agrees with the position held from the beginning [variant in Augustine: “Augustine of holy memory consulted and decreed that it be held from the beginning,” etc.; so Gratian] in the Church: ecclesiastical tradition requires that an impious doctrine already charged and condemned, and those subject to such a doctrine, be anathematized, even though they were dead. Therefore Augustine of holy memory says: “If Caecilianus were now proved guilty of the things alleged against him, I would anathematize him even after his death.”

Likewise (Council of Africa, chapter 48): Many bishops assembled and, while disposing certain matters relating to ecclesiastical order, decreed concerning deceased bishops who leave their property to heretics that they too should be subjected to anathema after death.

Likewise (Augustine, Letter 50 to Boniface): “And if the things alleged against Caecilianus are true and could at some time be shown to us, we would anathematize him though dead.”

There are also letters of Augustine of holy memory stating that, if any persons did not hold sound views during their life, although they had not yet been condemned while living, then, once their sin has been demonstrated, they too should be subjected to anathema after death.

Likewise: “You say that I am permitted to judge even the dead, because judgment may be made not only concerning the living but also concerning the dead.”

Likewise [Note: Liberatus, chapter 10 of his *Breviary*, reports this from the letter of Ibas to Maris the Persian, a fragment of which appears in Session 10 of the Council of Chalcedon]: Rabulas, bishop of the city of Edessa, of holy memory, [Col. 0840D] who shone among the priests, anathematized Theodore of Mopsuestia in the Church even after his death.

Likewise: “Even the Church of the Romans, a few [variant: “four”] years ago, anathematized Dioscorus [Note: The passage appears corrupt or mutilated; perhaps: “who had pronounced excommunication against Leo, who was …”], who was pope of that same Church, even after his death, although he had not sinned against the faith. All Romans living here know this, especially those holding offices, who remained in communion with that same Dioscorus until his death.”

[Col. 0841A] Likewise: “If anyone looks back to the times of Theophilus of holy memory, or earlier, he will find that Origen too was anathematized after death; and your Holiness and Vigilius, the most reverent pope of elder Rome, have done this also in the present case.” [Note: Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 10 and book VII, chapter 45; Sozomen, book VIII, chapter 14; Nicephorus, book XVII, chapters 27–28; Liberatus, *Breviary*, chapter 23.]

Likewise the holy synod said: “The matters stated and presented are sufficient to demonstrate the ecclesiastical tradition that heretics ought to be anathematized even after death.”

### CHAPTER 63.—On the same matter. Session 4 of the same synod.

The holy synod said: “Various letters of Augustine of revered memory, who shone among the African bishops, have been read, signifying that heretics ought to be anathematized even after death. Such [Col. 0841B] ecclesiastical tradition was also observed by other most reverend African bishops; and the holy Roman Church likewise anathematized certain bishops even after death, although they had not been accused during life in matters of faith. The records held by us attest both facts.”

### CHAPTER 64.—That one who abducts another’s betrothed and refuses to restore her is to be excommunicated with the woman whom he abducted, if she refuses to return to her betrothed. John VIII to Rostagnus, Archbishop.

(27, question 2, chapter *Atho praesentium*.) Atho, bearer of this letter, while faithfully employed in our service, complains that a certain man has abducted a woman betrothed to him. Therefore let your fraternity, supported by our authority, convene its suffragan bishops in person, and thus by unanimous judgment, if the abductor does not restore the bride to him, let both the abductor himself and the abducted woman, if she refuses to return to her former betrothed, be deprived of all communion [Col. 0841C].

### CHAPTER 65.—That the names of excommunicated persons are to be made known. John VIII, at the Council of Ravenna, chapter 12.

(11, question 3, chapter *Curae sit omnibus*.) Let it be the concern of all bishops to make known without exception the names of excommunicated persons, both to neighboring bishops and to their own parishioners; and, placing them in a public place before the doors of the church, to impress them upon all who come. Thus, by both forms of diligence, access to the Church may everywhere be denied to excommunicated persons, and all ground of excuse removed [Col. 0841D].

### CHAPTER 66.—On the same matter. John VIII to Bishop Peter.

If Deodatus and Gregory, at the time already fixed, refuse to come to us and to make all due and canonical amendment, we shall bind them with more grievous bonds of perpetual anathema. Writing out their crimes, excommunications, and anathemas, we shall suspend them before the most holy image of the blessed apostle Peter, so that to all who come from the whole world to the Apostolic threshold their wickedness may be known and they may appear excluded from the fellowship of the holy Church.

### CHAPTER 67.—Gifts from excommunicated persons are not to be accepted. From the Council of Elvira, chapter 28.

[Col. 0842A]

It has been decreed that a bishop ought not receive gifts from one who is not in communion.

### CHAPTER 68.—That alms from one who was excommunicated are to be accepted, if he repents. Urban to Guimundus, Bishop of Aversa.

(24, question 2, chapter *Sane quod*.) We commend what your fraternity has done concerning Richard, son of Burrell, out of zeal for God and love for souls. Yet there is no need for such fear, nor for such abstention from his alms. For among the other Fathers of our faith, the blessed Leo, outstanding teacher, says (Letter 92, chapter 6): “We ought not communicate with the dead with whom we did not communicate while alive.” It follows, therefore, that with those with whom we communicated while living—if we speak by contrast [Col. 0842B]—we may communicate also when dead.

We, certainly, placed between two opposing parties, cannot communicate in any way with the impious and schismatics; but with these persons, although sinners and robbers, we communicate provisionally for the time being [Gratian reads: “therefore we bless”], because up to now they have supported the Church and promise to be more faithful in the future. Otherwise, we would have to leave the regions of this world. Under this very assurance we recently granted them absolution at the feast of the nativity of Saint Peter.

Therefore, because the aforesaid man died neither expressly excommunicated nor as one named for communicating with excommunicated persons, but in faithfulness and service to his lord, it is permissible for us, provisionally—that is, so long as we do not endure them [the reading is uncertain]—to share in his alms and to aid the soul of the deceased by the observances of Christian religion [Col. 0842C].

### CHAPTER 69.—An excommunicated person may not accuse anyone. From the Seventh Council of Carthage, chapter 1.

(4, question 1, chapter *Definimus*.) We decree that a person is not lawfully admitted to make an accusation if, after he has been excommunicated and while he still remains under that excommunication, whether cleric or layperson, he wishes to accuse someone.

### CHAPTER 70.—On the same matter. Nicholas to Emperor Michael.

(4, question 1, chapter *Quod autem hi*.) That those who had been deposed and excommunicated by our brother Ignatius could bring no judgment of condemnation [variant: “sentence of condemnation”] against him is declared by the Second Ecumenical Synod, when it says: “If an ecclesiastical charge is brought against a bishop, then the persons of the accusers must be examined, so that first heretics may not be permitted to make accusations against orthodox bishops in ecclesiastical matters.” [Note: Council of Constantinople I, chapter 6, which, as it likewise remarks somewhat above, is not found in our text.]

But lest you deny that these are heretics, hear what follows: “By heretics we mean both those who were formerly cast out of the Church and those afterward anathematized by us.” Moreover, if you still do not believe this, hear what follows: “Besides these, they say, are those who pretend to confess the sound faith, schismatics also, and those who hold separate assemblies apart from bishops in communion with us. Further, if any persons, whether clergy or laity, have been censured by the Church on certain charges and cast out or excommunicated, neither may they accuse a bishop before they have first cleared themselves of their own charge. Likewise, those who are already under a prior accusation are not admissible as accusers of a bishop or other clerics until they have shown themselves innocent of the charges brought against them” [Col. 0843A].

### CHAPTER 71.—That no one may excommunicate another unless authority has been granted him. From the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 67 [chapter 70].

We ordain and establish that no one may excommunicate or [Col. 0843B] strike any of his brothers, except one to whom authority has been granted by the abbot. Those who sin, however, are to be rebuked before all, that the rest may fear (2 Tim. V).

### CHAPTER 72.—That no one may excommunicate another’s subject, and that even a metropolitan may not presume to act in the parish of his suffragan. Calixtus, bishop of Gaul (Letter 2).

(9, question 2, chapter *Nullus alterius*.) Let no one usurp another’s boundaries, or presume to judge or excommunicate another’s parishioner. For such judgment, excommunication, or condemnation shall neither be valid nor have any force, since no one is bound or condemned by the sentence of any judge other than his own.

Likewise (9, question 3, chapter *Nullus primas*): No primate or metropolitan may presume, without counsel or judgment, to excommunicate, judge, or take any action against the church, parishioner, [Col. 0843C] or anyone from the parish of his diocesan bishop.

### CHAPTER 73.—That penance is to be imposed according to the gravity of the sin. From the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 23 [chapter 24].

The measure of excommunication or discipline must be extended according to the degree of the fault; and the degree of faults depends upon the abbot’s judgment [variant: “is to depend upon the abbot’s discretion”]. But if any brother is found guilty of lighter faults, he is to be deprived of participation at table. For one deprived of fellowship at table, the rule shall be this: he shall not lead a psalm or antiphon in the oratory, nor recite a reading, until he has made satisfaction. He shall take his meal alone after the brothers’ meal [Col. 0843D], so that, for example, if the brothers dine at the sixth hour, that brother at the ninth; if the brothers at the ninth, he in the evening—until by fitting satisfaction he obtains pardon.

In the same work, chapter 42 [chapter 44]: One excommunicated from the oratory and from the table for a grave fault, at the hour when the work of God is celebrated in the oratory, shall lie prostrate before the doors of the oratory, saying nothing; but, with his head placed on the ground, he shall lie face down and be trodden beneath the feet of all coming out of the oratory [variant: “but, with his head on the ground, let him lie face down under the feet of all coming out of the oratory; thus the printed codices read today”]. He shall do this for as long as the abbot judges satisfaction to have been made.

When ordered to come before the abbot, he shall throw himself at the abbot’s feet, then at the feet of all the brothers, that [Col. 0844A] they may pray for him. Then, if the abbot orders it, he shall be received into the choir or assigned wherever the abbot decrees; but he must by no means presume to lead a psalm, reading, or anything else in the oratory unless the abbot again orders it. At every hour when the work of God is completed, he shall cast himself to the ground where he stands and thus make satisfaction until the abbot orders him to cease this satisfaction.

But those excommunicated from the table only for lighter faults shall make satisfaction in the oratory and continue this until the abbot’s order, until he blesses them and says: “It is enough.”

### CHAPTER 74.—Why the seats of bishops ought to be set higher than those of others in church. From the letter of Pope Urban I (to all bishops, *On the Common Life of the Faithful*, chapter 4).

That the seats of bishops are found established and prepared in churches only on high, upon a throne [variant: “as a throne”], principally teaches their spiritual discernment and the power given them by the Lord to judge, loose, and bind. Hence the Savior himself says in the Gospel: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven” (Matt. XVIII), and elsewhere: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John XX).

Therefore, most beloved, we have set these things before you so that you may understand the authority of your bishops, reverence God in them, love them as your own souls, not communicate with those with whom they do not communicate, and not receive those whom they have expelled. For the judgment of a bishop is greatly to be feared, even if he binds unjustly—though he ought most earnestly to guard against doing so [Col. 0844B].

### CHAPTER 75.—How a bishop intending to excommunicate someone should address clergy and people. From the Council of Rouen, chapter 3.

[Col. 0844C]

Let your charity know, my brothers, that a certain man named N., at the devil’s persuasion [variant: “instigation”], setting aside the Christian promise [variant: “profession”] which he professed at baptism, has by apostasy turned after Satan, whom he renounced with all his works. He does not fear to lay waste and plunder Christ’s vineyard, that is, his Church, violently oppressing and killing Christ’s poor, whom Christ redeemed with his precious blood, and despoiling their goods.

Since, therefore, he ought to have been a son of this our Church over which, by God’s authorship, we preside—for in [Col. 0844D] it he was reborn through water and the Holy Spirit and numbered among God’s adopted sons, although now he is not a son of God [variant: “is a son of the devil”], in imitating the devil—we have taken care lest, through pastoral negligence, any sheep entrusted to us should perish and we should be compelled to render account for it at the fearful judgment before the Prince of Shepherds, our Lord Jesus Christ. For he threatens us terribly, saying: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I will require his blood at your hand” (Ezek. III).

We sent to him our priest and letters of admonition once, twice, and a third time, canonically inviting him to amendment, satisfaction, and penance, and reproving him with paternal affection. But he—alas! the devil hardening [Col. 0845A] his heart—has despised [variant: “despises”] salutary warnings; persisting in his begun wickedness, and puffed up by the spirit of pride, he disdains to make satisfaction to the Church of God which he has injured.

Concerning such transgressors and violators of the holy religion and peace which Christ gave and left to his disciples, we have the commands of the Lord and the Apostles, by which we are instructed what we ought to do with such offenders. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him” (Matt. XVIII; Luke XVII). A brother sins against each one of us when he sins against the holy Church. For if the holy Church is one body, whose head is Christ, while each of us is a member of another; and if, when one member suffers, [Col. 0845B] all the members suffer with it, then undoubtedly he sins against us who injures our members.

Therefore the Lord commands that a brother—that is, a Christian—sinning against us be first rebuked privately, then reproved with witnesses, and finally summoned [variant: “rebuked”] publicly in the assembly of the Church. But if he despises these three admonitions and devout corrections and refuses to make satisfaction, then, he says, “let him be to you as a heathen and a publican” (ibid.), that is, as a Gentile and pagan: he is no longer to be regarded as a Christian but as a pagan.

And elsewhere the Lord commands that a member which is detached from its proper framework, separated from the bond of charity, and scandalizes the whole body, be cut off and cast away, saying: “If your eye, hand, or foot causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it from you” (Matt. XVIII). [Col. 0845C] And the Apostle says: “Remove the evil one from among you” (1 Cor. V). And again: “If anyone is called a brother and is a fornicator, adulterer, murderer, or robber, with such a person it is not permitted even to take food” (ibid.). And John, Christ’s beloved disciple above all others, forbade even greeting such a wicked person, saying: “Do not say ‘Hail’ to him, nor receive him into your house; for whoever says ‘Hail’ to him shares in his evil works” (2 John).

Therefore, fulfilling the Lord’s and the Apostles’ commands, let us cut off from the body of the Church with the iron of excommunication the putrid and incurable member which will not receive medicine, lest the remaining members of the body be infected, as with poison, by so pestilential a disease.

### CHAPTER 76.—The first excommunication. From the same source, chapter 4.

[Col. 0845D]

Therefore, because he has despised our warnings and repeated exhortations; because, called a third time according to the Lord’s command, he has disdained to come to amendment and penance; because he has not yet acknowledged or confessed his fault, nor sought pardon by sending an embassy to us, who investigate his cause, since he is our parishioner; because he persists in his begun wickedness, the devil hardening his heart; and because, as the Apostle says, “according to his hardness and impenitent heart he stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath” (Rom. II): therefore we, by the judgment of God Almighty—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of all the saints, and also by the authority of our own humble office and the power divinely granted to us to bind and loose in heaven and on earth, separate him with all his accomplices, communicants, and supporters [Col. 0846A] from the reception of the precious body and blood and from the fellowship of all Christians. We exclude him from the thresholds of holy mother Church in heaven and on earth; we decree him excommunicated and anathematized; and we judge him condemned with the devil, his angels, and all the reprobate in eternal fire—unless perhaps he comes to his senses from the snares of the devil, returns to amendment and penance, and makes satisfaction to the Church of God which he has injured.

And let all answer three times: “Amen,” or “So be it, so be it,” or “Let him be anathema.” Twelve priests ought to stand around the bishop and hold lighted candles in their hands. At the conclusion of the anathema or excommunication they must cast these to the ground and trample them underfoot.

After this the bishop must explain this excommunication to the people in common language, so that all may understand how terribly the man has been condemned, and may know that from that hour onward he is not to be regarded as a Christian but as a pagan. Whoever communicates with him as with a Christian, eats or drinks with him, kisses him, holds familiar conversation with him—unless indeed he endeavors to call him to satisfaction and penance—receives him into his house, or prays with him, shall without doubt likewise be excommunicated [Col. 0846B].

Then letters containing the form of excommunication are to be sent to the priests throughout the parishes. They are to be commanded to announce the excommunication publicly to the people committed to them on Sundays after the reading of the Gospel, so that no one may communicate with the excommunicated person through ignorance. The excommunication must also be made known to other bishops. For the First Council of Toledo (chapter 11) commanded that written notices should promptly circulate among all bishops of the province whom they can reach, so that the excommunicated person may be publicly known. His lord, too, must be informed of the excommunication [Col. 0846C].

### CHAPTER 77.—Address for an excommunication. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 1.

You have heard, most beloved, how great and how dreadful were the works of perversity and iniquity which N., instigated by the devil, did not fear to commit; and how by apostasy he has with profane mind withdrawn from the worship of the whole Christian religion. You have heard how he was canonically summoned to make satisfaction, but delayed to come; how, though frequently admonished to come to his senses and escape the snares of the devil by which he is held fast [ensnared], he scorned to hear the most wholesome admonitions with the hardened [stopped-up] ears of his heart. The Lord says in the Gospel concerning such a contumacious brother, who refuses to accept ecclesiastical correction: “If he will not listen to the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector” (Matt. XVIII); that is, he is no longer to be reckoned among Christians but among pagans. Hence Paul, following the teaching [footsteps] of the Lord and Master, rebukes the Corinthians because they held communion with the criminal and wicked, saying: “You are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that the man might be removed from your midst” (1 Cor. V); that is, that he who committed such a crime be separated from your fellowship. And he adds: “For I indeed, absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged, as though present, him who has so acted: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are assembled together, and my spirit with the power of my Lord Jesus Christ, to hand such a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh” (ibid.). And shortly afterward: “I wrote to you not to associate with fornicators” (ibid.). And immediately he adds: “If he who is called a brother”—that is, a Christian—“is a fornicator or a robber, with such a one not even to take food” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “Put away the evil from among yourselves” [Col. 0847B] (ibid.). And: “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart” (1 Cor. VII). For one diseased sheep contaminates the whole flock, and “a little leaven corrupts the whole mass” (1 Cor. V); and very often one rotten member infects the whole body. Therefore so destructive a pest must be torn out by the roots from the body of the Church.

### CHAPTER 78.—Excommunication II. From the same council.

Therefore, instructed by the precepts of the Lord and of the apostles, by the judgment of the Father, and of his Son our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, and by the authority and power granted by God to the apostles and successors of the apostles, together with you we exclude the aforesaid most wicked man from the bounds of holy mother Church, and separate him from every Christian association and communion [Col. 0847C]; and we decree that he remain separated for ever—that is, in this present age and in the age to come. Let no Christian say “Hail” to him (2 John), or presume to kiss him. Let no priest dare celebrate Mass with him [dare celebrate while he is present], or give him the most holy body and blood of the Lord. Let no one join him in companionship or in any business. And if anyone associates with him and shares in his evil deeds, let him know that he has been struck with a like anathema; excepting those who associate with him for this purpose, that they may call him back from error and urge him to make satisfaction. Unless perhaps he comes to his senses and, inspired by God’s grace, turns to penitence and remedy, and humbly makes satisfaction by worthy amendment to the Church of God which he has injured.

### CHAPTER 79.—Excommunication III. From the Council of Tours, chapter 2.

[Col. 0847D]

Following the canonical ordinances and the examples of the holy Fathers, we separate from the bosom of holy mother Church, and condemn under the anathema of perpetual curse, violators of the churches of God—namely, plunderers, despoilers, and murderers—N., in the name of the Father and the Son, and by the power of the Holy Spirit, and likewise by the authority divinely conferred upon bishops through Peter, prince of the apostles. Let them be cursed in the city, cursed in the field; cursed be their storehouse, and cursed their remnant; cursed be the fruit of their womb and the fruit of their land. Let them be cursed when entering and cursed when going out [Col. 0848A]; let them be cursed in the house and fugitives in the field. Let all those curses come upon them which the Lord through Moses declared that he would send upon the people who transgress the divine law (Deut. XXVIII). Let them be *anathema, maranatha* (1 Cor. XVI), that is, let them perish at the second coming of the Lord. Let no Christian say “Hail” to them (2 John); let no priest presume to celebrate Mass with them or give them holy communion. Let them be buried with the burial of an ass (Jer. XXII), and let them become dung upon the face of the earth (Jer. VIII, XVI, XXV). And just as these lamps, cast from our hands, are extinguished today, so may their lamp be extinguished for ever—unless perhaps they come to their senses and make satisfaction to the Church of God, which they have injured, by amendment and worthy penitence.

### CHAPTER 80.—On the same matter. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 3 (chapter 56).

[Col. 0848B]

(11, question 3, canon *Nemo episcoporum*.) No bishop may deprive anyone of ecclesiastical communion without a certain and manifest cause of sin. Moreover, let no one impose anathema without the knowledge of the archbishop or fellow bishops, except in cases taught by canonical authority; for anathema is the condemnation of eternal death, and must be imposed only for a mortal crime, and upon one who cannot otherwise be corrected.

### CHAPTER 81.—On the same matter. From the Council of Agde, chapter 4 (chapter 3).

Bishops who, setting aside priestly moderation, presume to excommunicate innocent persons, or persons guilty only in minor matters [Col. 0848C], and perhaps, when they hasten toward restoration to favour, refuse to receive them, shall be admonished by letters from the neighbouring bishops of whatever province. If they refuse to yield [obey], they shall be suspended from the communion of their brethren until the next synod; there they shall give an account of their act, lest perhaps the excommunicated person, through the sin of the excommunicators [“through the excommunicators, sin,” thus the manuscript of the council], be overtaken by death after a long time.

### CHAPTER 82.—That no bishop should take it ill if one of his parishioners has been excommunicated by another bishop for a definite fault. From the Council at Compiègne, chapter 5.

(6, question 3, canon *Placuit*.) It has also been decided, for the common benefit and urgent necessity, that no bishop should take it ill if another bishop excommunicates one of his parishioners on account of plundering [Col. 0848D].

### CHAPTER 83.—How often persons residing in a parish who have done something against God must be summoned by the bishop to amendment. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 3.

If someone residing in a bishop’s parish has done something unjustly, the bishop shall summon him once, twice, and, if necessary, a third time, by canonical admonition through his messenger, to amendment or settlement and to penitence, so that he may make satisfaction to God and to the Church which he has injured. But if he despises and scorns the bishop’s admonition and most salutary invitation, the bishop shall strike him with the pastoral rod—that is, [Col. 0849A] with the sentence of excommunication—so that he may be separated from communion with holy Church and all Christians until suitable satisfaction and worthy amendment have been made. The same bishop must make this excommunication known to that person’s superior, to all his fellow bishops, and to all his parishioners, so that they may not receive him until satisfaction has been made.

### CHAPTER 84.—On the same matter. From the same council, chapter 6.

A bishop who, through any gift, favour, or negligence, delays [refuses] to admonish or excommunicate those who act against God and the peace of the Church—so that he may receive them when they return, or expel them from the Church when they remain contemptuous—shall himself be held excommunicated [Col. 0849B] from the college of the others, until he pronounces a sentence concerning either their amendment or their condemnation.

### CHAPTER 85.—That it is one thing to sin against God, another to sin against a human being. From the sayings of Augustine.

[Note: [Col. 0849D] Something similar occurs in Sermon 47, *On the Saints*.]

We must attend to what the Lord says: “If your brother sins against you” (Matt. XVIII). To sin against us is one thing; to sin against God is another. If someone sins against us, it is not for our own discretion. For it is written: “If a man sins against a man, God can be appeased for him; but if he sins against God, who will pray for him?” (1 Sam. II). We, by contrast, are gracious and merciful in injuries done to God, and pardon an offence against God—as though his willing and not willing were in our power—without punishment through fitting penitence; whereas [Col. 0849C] we do not allow what has been committed against us, not even an insulting word lightly uttered, to pass without revenge. Let us therefore forgive for God’s sake what has been perpetrated against us; but what has been committed against God, which we cannot forgive, let us punish according to the ordinances of the holy Fathers and canonical authority.

### CHAPTER 86.—On the same matter. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 5 (chapter 61).

Those who seize ecclesiastical property and are known not only to retain it contrary to authority, but even cruelly to despoil it—for some strip the resources of the Church through various arrangements and revenues, and mercilessly afflict, ravage, and oppress the poor, neighbours, and those dwelling nearby [Col. 0849D]—shall, as robbers excluded from the kingdom of God according to the Apostle (1 Cor. VI), be punished by public penitence for a criminal and public sin. If they refuse to do this, let the apostolic and terrible sentence be pronounced against them: “If anyone is called a brother and is a robber, let no one presume even to take food with such a person” (1 Cor. V). For it is wicked and sacrilegious, as Pope Symmachus (Third Roman Synod under Symmachus, chapter 3), and after him blessed Gregory (Register, book VIII, letter 6), writes to the subdeacon Sabinus [Gregory has “Savinus”], if anyone attempts, for the purposes of his own wicked will and gain, to retain what has been left to venerable places. According to the ordinances of the canons, he must be excluded from all ecclesiastical communion as a sacrilegious person [Col. 0850A], until he strives to correct by worthy satisfaction what he has committed.

### CHAPTER 87.—That everything offered to God is the Holy of Holies. From the decrees of Pope Boniface, chapter 5 (Addition to the calendar of Boniface’s decrees, 1).

(12, question 2, canon *Nulli liceat*.) Let no one be unaware that everything consecrated to the Lord—whether a human being, an animal, a field, or whatever has once been consecrated—shall be “the Holy of Holies to the Lord” (Lev. XXVII) and belongs by right to the priests. Therefore everyone who removes, devastates, invades, or carries off what belongs to the Lord and to the Church shall be without excuse until amendment and satisfaction to the Church; [Col. 0850B] he shall be judged a sacrilegious person, and, if he refuses to make amendment, excommunicated.

### CHAPTER 88.—On those who take away or plunder Christ’s monies. From the letter of Pope Anacletus sent to all the faithful (letter 1).

[Note: [Col. 0849] Pope Lucius says the same in his letter to the bishops of Gaul and Spain.]

“He who takes something from father or mother,” he says, “and says that this is not a sin, is a partner of a murderer” (Prov. XXVIII). Without doubt, God, who created us, is our Father. Our mother is the Church, which spiritually regenerated us in baptism. Therefore he who takes away, plunders, or defrauds Christ’s monies and those of the Church is a murderer and is accounted a murderer before God. For whoever removes the Church’s possessions commits sacrilege and must be judged as sacrilegious.

### CHAPTER 89.—On the same matter. From the decrees of Pope Lucius, chapter 10 (letter to the bishops of Gaul and Spain, chapter 6; and Anacletus, letter 1).

[Col. 0850C]

(17, question 4, canon *Omnes rapt.*) By apostolic authority we expel and condemn from the thresholds of holy mother Church those who plunder ecclesiastical property and resources, anathematizing them and judging them to be sacrilegious. And not only them, but also all who consent to them, because not only those who do such things but also those who consent are judged guilty (Rom. I). Augustine says: “He who steals or plunders anything from the Church is compared to Judas the betrayer.”

### CHAPTER 90.—On the same matter. From the Council of Gangra, chapter 8.

He who gives or receives offerings of the altar apart from the bishop or his representative—both the giver and the receiver—shall be anathema.

### CHAPTER 91.—On the same matter. From the Council at Saint-Médard, chapter 1 (from the Council of Gangra, chapter 7).

If anyone wishes to seize or distribute the offerings of the Church outside the Church, apart from the knowledge of the bishop or of the person to whom such duties have been entrusted, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER 92.—How those who commit violence against places consecrated to God are to be punished. From the decrees of Pope John, chapter 10.

Those who break into monasteries, places consecrated to God, and churches, and remove deposits or any other things from them, shall make ninefold compensation for the damage, threefold compensation for the immunity [Col. 0851A], and, as sacrilegious persons, be subjected to canonical sentence [subjected].

### CHAPTER 93.—On those who treat the house of God contemptuously. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 7.

Whoever, puffed up by the arrogance of pride, treats the house of God contemptuously, and dishonourably deals with possessions consecrated to God and placed under the protection of royal immunity for God’s honour; or presumes to violate them; or presumptuously commits arson or ravaging: as an invader and violator of the Church of God, which is the house of the living God, he shall be cut off from the communion of all the faithful.

### CHAPTER 94.—On the same matter. From the same council, chapter 6.

If anyone, by wicked cunning, takes away [Col. 0851B], defrauds, seizes, retains, or steals any gifts collected for the Church under the sacred titles of the Scriptures, and does not immediately restore to God what has been bestowed when admonished by a priest, he shall be expelled from the communion of the Catholic Church.

### CHAPTER 95.—That it is unlawful to pray with an excommunicated person. From the sayings of Isidore.

(11, question 3, canon *Cum excommunicato*.) No one may pray or speak with an excommunicated person, except concerning matters pertaining to that same excommunication; nor may anyone eat with him.

### CHAPTER 96.—On the same matter. As above (from the Rule of the Master, chapter 13).

(11, question 3, canon *Si quis frater*.) If any brother, openly or secretly, speaks with an excommunicated person, he immediately incurs with him the common punishment of excommunication [Col. 0851C].

### CHAPTER 97.—On the same matter. From the sayings of Bishop Fructuosus, chapter 14.

Let no one speak with an excommunicated person, nor support him with any compassion or pity, nor presume to strengthen him in defiance or pride.

### CHAPTER 98.—On the same matter. From the Council of Antioch, chapter 2.

It is not lawful to associate with excommunicated persons, nor with those who meet in houses while shunning the prayers of the Church, where prayer ought to be offered together. If anyone of the clergy is found to associate with excommunicated persons, he too shall be deprived of communion.

### CHAPTER 99.—On the same matter. From the Canons of the Apostles, chapter 11.

[Col. 0851D]

If anyone has prayed together with an excommunicated person, even in a house, he shall be deprived of communion.

### CHAPTER 100.—On the same matter. From the Council of Nicaea, chapter 5.

Concerning those deprived of communion, whether clergy or laypersons, the regular sentence handed down by bishops in each province shall prevail, so that those cast out are not received by others. Inquiry must be made, however, lest a person appear to have been excluded from communion through the bishop’s faintheartedness, contentiousness, or any other fault.

### CHAPTER 101.—On the same matter. From the Council of Antioch, chapter 6.

(11, question 3, canon *Si quis*.) If anyone has been deprived of communion by his own bishop, he shall not be received by other bishops before being reconciled to his own bishop [Col. 0852A].

### CHAPTER 102.—On the same matter. From the decrees of Pope Callixtus, chapter 4 (letter 2, to the bishops of Gaul).

(11, question 3, canon *Excommunicatos*.) Let no one receive persons excommunicated by priests before a just examination of both parties; nor let anyone share with them in prayer, food, drink, or a kiss, nor say “Hail” to them. For whoever knowingly associates with excommunicated persons in these or other forbidden ways shall himself be subject to like excommunication, according to the ordinance of the apostles (chapter 11, Apostolic Canon).

### CHAPTER 103.—On the same matter. From the Council of Antioch (under Julius I, chapter 2).

[Col. 0852B]

It is not lawful to associate with excommunicated persons, nor to enter houses and pray with those who do not participate in the Church’s prayer; nor may one excommunicated by one church be received into another. If any bishop, priest, deacon, or even one enrolled in the canon is found to associate with excommunicated persons, he too must be deprived of communion, as one who confounds the Church’s rules.

### CHAPTER 104.—On the same matter. From the decrees of Pope Fabian sent to the bishops of Gaul.

If anyone willingly [perhaps] associates with an excommunicated person in speech, prayer, food, or drink, he shall do penance for forty days on bread, salt, and water [“in bread and water”]. [Col. 0852C] But whoever associates with them in murders or disgraceful acts shall incur the wrath and vengeance of almighty God, whom he despises; for all these things have been forbidden him by the divine voice. According to the Apostle, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts V); and according to the offence committed, he shall do worthy penitence in accordance with the decrees of the canons. If he refuses to do penance, he shall be excommunicated.

### CHAPTER 105.—That persons excommunicated in a place shall receive communion again in that same place. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 10.

Concerning those separated from communion for their offence, it has been decided that, wherever they were excluded, they shall receive communion again in the same place.

### CHAPTER 106.—That persons excommunicated by their own bishop or priest are not to be received elsewhere into communion. From the Council of Rouen, chapter 3.

[Col. 0852D]

There are some persons who, as their offences require, are excommunicated by their own bishop, yet are presumptuously received into communion by other ecclesiastics or laypersons. This is altogether forbidden by the holy Council of Nicaea (Nicaea, chapter 5), as also by those of Chalcedon and Antioch (Antioch, chapter 2), and Sardica (Sardica, chapter 16).

### CHAPTER 107.—On the same matter. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 9 (chapter 7).

Augustine, bishop and legate of the province of Numidia, said [“Bishop Genedius said,” thus in the volume of the council] (11, question 3, canon *Qui merito*): “Deem it fitting to establish this: that if any persons perhaps have rightly been expelled from the Church because of their crimes [Col. 0853A], and are received into communion by any bishop or priest, that bishop or priest shall himself be held guilty of an equal crime with them, as they flee the regular judgment of their own bishop.” All said: “It pleases all.”

### CHAPTER 108.—On the same matter. From the same council, chapter 73.

(11, question 3, canon *Qui communicaverit*.) Whoever associates or prays with an excommunicated person, if a layperson, shall be excommunicated; if a cleric, shall be deposed (see above, chapter 28).

### CHAPTER 109.—On those who belong to another parish and commit plunderings. From the Council of Meaux, chapter 2.

Concerning those who possess a benefice or inheritance within a parish [Col. 0853B], but are parishioners of another bishop and travel from place to place, committing robberies and plunderings: it has been decided that they shall be excommunicated and shall not leave the parish before worthily making amends for what they have done. Their excommunication must be reported to their superior and their own bishop, so that they may not receive them before they return to the place where they committed the robbery and make full restitution for everything.

### CHAPTER 110.—On those who defend wrongdoers. From the sayings of Basil (from the Rule of the Easterners).

He who consents to sinners and defends another’s wrongdoing shall be accursed before God and people, and shall be corrected by a most severe rebuke. Hence a most holy Father also says: “If anyone consents to another’s error, let him know that he is to be judged guilty and excommunicated in like manner with him” [Col. 0853C].

### CHAPTER 111.—On those who neglect to prosecute their case within a year. From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, chapter 3.

(11, question 3, canon *Quicunque*.) Therefore, whoever within the space of a year has not pursued his case, civilly or publicly, before those who excommunicated him, shall be considered [shall be judged] to have closed to himself the way of a hearing. If he dies obstinately without communion, reserving their case to divine judgment according to the sentence of our predecessor blessed Leo (letter 92, chapter 6), we cannot communicate with them in death when we did not communicate with them in life.

### CHAPTER 112.—On the same matter. From the decrees of the same [pope], chapter 3.

[Col. 0853D]

Indeed, those who attempt to obtain communion before a hearing shall in no way be admitted to communion until they have bewailed their guilt by penitence, except when death is imminent. But anyone who knowingly associates with [joins himself to] an excommunicated person, and has prayed together with him even in a house, and has afforded him hiding-places of protection so that he may not be brought near [the text perhaps reads “closely”] to satisfaction, shall know himself deprived of communion in the body and blood of the Lord until he receives penitence from the excommunicator and performs penitence for his offence according to the canons.

### CHAPTER 113.—That the names of excommunicated persons should be recorded and posted on the doors of the church. From the decrees of Pope Honorius, chapter 11.

[Note: [Col. 0853] Elsewhere it is attributed to John VIII in the Council of Ravenna, chapter 12.]

[Col. 0854A]

(11, question 3, canon *Curae sit*.) Let all bishops take care to announce without exception the names of excommunicated persons both to neighbouring bishops and to their own parishioners, and, having placed those names in a conspicuous position, to impress them upon all who assemble before the doors of the church. Thus, through both forms of diligence, ecclesiastical access shall everywhere be barred to excommunicated persons, and every ground of excuse removed from all.

### CHAPTER 114.—On those who die excommunicated. From the Council of Epaone, chapter 10 (chapter 28).

(11, question 3, canon *Si episcopus*.) If a bishop is taken by death before the condemned person’s absolution, his successor may absolve the corrected [or penitent] person. And chapter 11: If an excommunicated person dies, having already confessed and having a good testimony, and he could not [will not be able to] come to the priest, but death overtook him at home or on the road, his relatives shall make an offering for him at the altar and give a redemption-payment for captives.

### CHAPTER 115.—On those who defend tenants against flogging. From the Council of Elvira, chapter 9 (in a fragment).

The holy synod decreed that bishops and ministers of bishops have the authority to flog tenants with rods for crimes, so that, through fear of the others, the guilty themselves may be corrected and may do penance even unwillingly, lest they perish eternally. But if the lords [Col. 0854C] of those tenants take this badly and wish to exact some revenge for it, or presume to defend those same tenants so that they are not punished, let them know that they are to be struck by the sentence of ecclesiastical excommunication.

### CHAPTER 116.—On bishops accused before the Roman See of associating with excommunicated persons. From the Council at Altheim [Altheum].

In the fifth year of the reign of Conrad, most pious and most Christian king, a holy general synod was assembled at Altheim, in the district of Rhaetia, in the presence, namely, of the apocrisiary of Lord Pope John, the venerable bishop Peter of the holy Church of Ostia, in order somehow [the text: “somehow, so that somehow,” etc.] to uproot the diabolical seeds that had arisen in our regions [Col. 0854D], and to suppress and remove the most wicked machinations of certain perverse people. Therefore, after a three-day fast had passed and the holy litanies had been duly celebrated, we assembled in the church of Saint John the Baptist and sat down in sorrow. Then at last the aforesaid envoy of Saint Peter and of Lord Pope John produced a document inscribed with apostolic letters, by which we were stirred, reproved, and instructed concerning all things pertaining to the true religion of the Christian faith. We humbly received all these things, as was just and fitting, carefully considered them, and embraced them in every way with devout affection. Therefore we uttered in a tearful voice the evangelical precept and most wholesome instruction by which the Pharisees and scribes were rebuked: “First cleanse what is within” (Matt. XXIII). And again: “First cast the beam out of your own eye” (Luke VI). And, reflecting upon that prophetic saying, “Evil priests are the ruin of the people,” examining and scrutinizing ourselves, and casting ourselves to the ground amid holy penitence with worthy fruit, we bewailed our innumerable negligences and most grave sins. Then, at the urging of Lord Peter, angry against ourselves and our vices, with the Holy Spirit first helping and having mercy, we gathered and established the chapters noted below for the correction both of ourselves and of the Christian people [Col. 0855A].

### CHAPTER 117.—On bishops who lead astray those subject to them by associating with excommunicated persons. From the same council, chapter 6, attended by King Conrad.

[Col. 0855B]

We know it is written by sacred authority: “Whoever associates with an excommunicated person shall be excommunicated.” In this we bishops, priests, and clerics confess that we have sinned punishably; with God’s help, we desire and command that in future we amend and avoid it.

### CHAPTER 118.—On the same matter. From the same council, chapter 7.

The holy synod resolved to remove this error from the Church as impious, because we have received from the Lord the care of souls, not of money. For this we shall render an account to the Lord, and shall receive, through his mercy, either eternal recompense or just condemnation.

### CHAPTER 119.—On bishops: that they should not be an evil example to the people. From the same council, chapter 8.

[Col. 0855C]

Bishops and priests ought to set themselves before the people as a good example, and to show it not only in words but in deeds. Therefore we have established that in no way whatsoever shall we ever again associate with excommunicated persons contrary to the sacred ordinances. We judge ourselves, so that we may not be judged by the Lord in the future (1 Cor. XI). We desire to follow the sayings and ordinances of holy Pope Gregory, and we wish to perform worthy penitence secretly in a monastery, because we could not do so publicly. In the future, by God’s favour, we desire by every means to avoid the aforesaid acts. Establishing the same rule for priests, deacons, and all the clergy, we command them, if they do not wish to be deposed from their rank, faithfully to observe it [Col. 0855D] and to preach that others observe it.

### CHAPTER 120.—On the correction of bishops who associate with an excommunicated person. From the same council, chapter 9.

By apostolic authority we confirm the sayings and commands of the holy canons, and decree that, so long as anyone is excommunicated, none of our bishops may dare to associate with him or pray with him in church. And [we address] laypeople who, as they say, followed us in error and are now following us: as we correct ourselves by chastening ourselves with penitence, and preach and open to them the way of life, let them come to their senses and escape the snares of the devil (2 Tim. II), by which they are held captive through our evil examples, and return through penitence to the true mother, the Church.

### CHAPTER 121.—On those who despise a ban imposed by bishops. From the Council of Tribur, chapter 8, attended by King Arnulf.

[Col. 0856A]

Let no one despise or transgress a ban imposed by bishops. Let him know and dread that it is written against him in the third letter of blessed Clement (*On the Offices of the Sacred and the Clergy*): “If all, of higher and lower rank alike, and the remaining peoples, tribes, and tongues, do not obey you bishops, they shall be not only infamous but also exiles from the kingdom of God, from the fellowship of the faithful, and from the thresholds of holy Church of God.” And let them hear the Lord himself saying in the Gospel: “He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects you rejects me” (Luke X). Therefore, considering evangelical and apostolic authority [Col. 0856B], seeking not monetary gain but the profit of souls, we establish and confirm that if anyone, after this decree of this holy council, is found to have violated a ban imposed by bishops, he shall be corrected by forty days’ discipline, on bread, salt, and water only.

### CHAPTER 122.—For what causes a person ought to be bound by the bond of anathema. From the same council, chapter 30.

(11, question 3, canon *Certum est*.) It was asked in the same synod for what causes anyone ought to be bound by episcopal authority with the bond of anathema. By the unanimous judgment of all, it was decreed that this should be done for these three crimes: when a person canonically ordered to come to a synod scorns to come; or, after he has come there, refuses to obey priestly [Col. 0856C] commands; or, before the examination of his case has been completed, presumptuously leaves the synod as a fugitive.

### CHAPTER 123.—On those who commit robbery and theft. From the same council, chapter 31.

Thieves and robbers testify that the tranquillity of holy Church of God is disturbed and brotherly peace attacked: they walk among us shaded by sheep’s clothing, but depart alienated in wolfish mind; driven by a savage mind, they seize the property of churches and, by plundering it, tear apart the Lord’s flock. Concerning them the Saviour says in the Gospel: “He who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold is a thief and a robber” (John X). And he adds: “The thief does not come except to steal, kill [Col. 0856D], and destroy” (ibid.). Although there he indicates heretics who steal the Church’s faith, he nevertheless shows that the peace of the churches is disturbed by the persecution of thieves and robbers. Concerning such persons the Apostle says to the Philippians: “Beware of dogs; beware of evil workers” (Phil. III). He called “dogs” those who have no shame, and “evil workers” those who do nothing suited to piety. And the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah: “I the Lord love judgment and hate robbery” (Isa. LXI). Therefore, loving what the Lord loves and hating what he hates, we establish and judge that, if anyone after these evangelical, apostolic, and prophetic words and the decree of this most peaceable synod is found to commit theft or robbery and deserves to incur death in that diabolical act, no one may presume to pray or give alms for him; nor may alms given for him be brought into the remembrance of clerics or the poor, but it shall become foul and accursed. Blessed Augustine delivers a dreadful sentence concerning such persons: “No one faithfully redeems you after your death, because you were unwilling to redeem yourself.” But if that thief or robber escapes wounded and is considered hopeless in expectation of death, and in the condition of his body and with the devout intention of his mind asks to be reconciled to the most holy mysteries, and, while life remains, confesses to God and the priest his amendment and deed, we do not deny that the grace of communion should be granted him [Col. 0857A].

### CHAPTER 124.—On those who are hanged on gibbets. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 5 (chapter 27; and the Council of Worms under Leo IV, chapter 80).

[Col. 0857B]

(13, question 2, canon *Quaesitum*.) Some brethren asked concerning those who, after confession made to God, are hanged on gibbets for their crimes: whether their bodies should be brought to churches, offerings made for them, and Masses celebrated, or not. We answer them: if communion at the end, according to canonical command, is to be given to all who make a pure confession of all their sins and do worthy penance, why do the canons forbid it to those who pay the ultimate penalty for their sins [Col. 0858A] and confess, or desire to confess? For it is written: “God does not judge twice for the same thing” (Nahum I, according to another text).

### CHAPTER 125.—On bishops who associate with excommunicated persons. From the Council at Erfurt, chapter 9, attended by King Henry.

The holy synod, with the counsel of the most serene prince, decreed that if henceforth any bishop, forgetful of his ministry, knowingly associates with an excommunicated person—whether in greeting, prayer, unjust encouragement, food, or drink—he shall be held excommunicated by the prince and by all others, until he is heard at the next synod and compelled to make satisfaction to God and his Church.

### CHAPTER 126.—On clerics who flee their churches, and servants who flee their own masters. From the Council held at Altheim, attended by King Conrad, chapter 26.

[Col. 0858B]

Saint Gregory says: “We judge that a cleric fleeing his own church, or a servant fleeing his own master and unwilling to return, is to be deprived of communion until he returns to his own church or master.” And again: “By apostolic sentence we decree that a fugitive cleric be restored to his bishop, or excommunicated, together with those who associate with him.”

## FIFTEENTH PART OF THE DECREES. On the penitence of the healthy and the sick, and by what commutation penitence may be mitigated.

[Col. 0857]

### CHAPTER 1.—What penitence is. Gregory (Homily 134 on the Gospels).

[Col. 0857C]

(On Penitence, distinction 3, canon *Poenitentia*.) Penitence is to weep for past sins and not to commit the sins for which one must weep.

### CHAPTER 2.—That a priest, when commanded by his bishop, should reconcile a penitent. From the Second Council of Carthage, chapter 4.

(26, question 6, canon *Aurelius episcopus*.) Bishop Aurelius said: “If anyone is in danger and requests reconciliation to the divine altars, then, if the bishop is absent, the priest ought certainly to consult the bishop and, by his command, reconcile the person in danger. We ought to confirm this practice by salutary counsel.” All the bishops said: “It pleases us that your holiness has deigned necessarily to instruct us [Col. 0857D].”

### CHAPTER 3.—That the measure of penitence should be assigned to penitents according to their sin. From the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 31.

(26, question 7, canon *Poenitentibus*.) Let periods of penitence be determined for penitents, at the bishop’s discretion, according to the differing kinds of sins.

### CHAPTER 4.—That a priest should not secretly reconcile a penitent without the bishop. From the same council, chapter 32.

(26, q. 6, c. *Presbyter*.) A priest is not to reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop, unless necessity compels while the bishop is absent [Col. 0858C]. In the case of any penitent whose crime is public and very widely known, and has disturbed the whole Church, hands are to be laid upon him before the apse.

### CHAPTER 5.—That a cleric ordained from among penitents is to be deposed. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 68.

(Dist. 50, c. *Ex poenitentibus*.) No cleric is to be ordained from among penitents, however good he may be. If this has occurred through the bishop’s ignorance, he is to be removed from the clergy, because at the time of ordination he did not disclose that he had been a penitent. But if the bishop knowingly ordains such a man, he too is to be deprived, at least, of the power of ordaining that belongs to his episcopal office.

### CHAPTER 6.—Concerning the rule for penitents. From the same council, chapter 74.

[Col. 0858D] (26, q. 7, c. *Sacerdos*.) A priest is to impose the rules of penance upon one who implores penance, without respect of persons.

### CHAPTER 7.—Concerning negligent penitents. From the same council, chapter 75.

More negligent penitents are to be reconciled more slowly.

### CHAPTER 8.—Concerning those who request penance and afterward become speechless. From the same council, chapter 76.

(26, q. 6, c. *Qui in infirmitate*.) If one asks for penance during illness and, by chance, when the priest who has been summoned [Col. 0859A] comes to him, is overwhelmed by illness and becomes speechless, or falls into delirium, those who heard him are to give testimony, and he is to receive penance. If he is believed to be about to die at once, he is to be reconciled by the laying on of hands, and the Eucharist is to be placed in his mouth. If he survives, he is to be reminded by the aforesaid witnesses that his request has been fulfilled, and he is to be placed under the established rules of penance for as long as the priest who gave him penance judges appropriate.

### CHAPTER 9.—That penitents may receive viaticum in death. From the same council, chapter 77.

Penitents who are ill are to receive viaticum.

### CHAPTER 10.—Concerning penitents who survive after viaticum. From the same council, chapter 78.

Penitents who, during illness, have received the viaticum of the Eucharist [Col. 0859B] are not to consider themselves absolved without the laying on of hands, should they survive.

### CHAPTER 11.—Concerning penitents who die by some accident. From the same council, chapter 79.

(26, q. 7, c. *Sacerdos poenitentiam*.) Penitents who diligently carry out the rules of penance, if they die by accident while travelling or at sea, where help cannot be given them, are to be commended to memory by prayers and offerings.

### CHAPTER 12.—That penitents may carry out and bury the dead. From the same council, chapter 81.

Penitents are to carry out and bury the Church’s dead.

### CHAPTER 13.—That penitents are always to bend the knee. From the same council, chapter 82.

[Col. 0859C] Penitents are to bend the knee even on days of remission.

### CHAPTER 14.—That penance is not to be given to married persons except by mutual consent. From the Second Council of Arles, chapter 22.

(33, q. 4, c. *Poenitentiam*.) Penance is not to be given to married persons except by mutual consent.

### CHAPTER 15.—Concerning apostates if they do not return. From the same council, chapter 25.

Those who, after the holy profession of religion, apostatize and return to the world, and afterward do not seek the remedies of penance, are absolutely not to receive communion without penance. We also order that they are not to be admitted to clerical office. Whoever he may be, after penance he is not to presume to resume secular dress [Col. 0859D]; if he does so, he is to be regarded as cut off from the Church.

### CHAPTER 16.—Concerning clerics requesting penance. From the Council of Orange, chapter 4.

Penance is not to be denied to clerics who desire it [“also,” in the original].

### CHAPTER 17.—How older persons are to receive penance, which is not readily to be entrusted to younger persons. From the Council of Agde, chapter 25.

(Dist. 50, c. *Poenitentes*.) At the time when penitents request penance, they are to receive from the priest the laying on of hands and sackcloth upon their heads, as has been established everywhere. But if they have not cut off their hair or changed their clothing, they are to be rejected; and unless they have done penance worthily, they are not to be received back. [Col. 0860A] Penance, however, is not readily to be entrusted to young people because of the frailty of their age. Yet viaticum is not to be denied to anyone at the point of death.

### CHAPTER 18.—If a priest or deacon, because of some guilt, suspends himself from the Eucharist. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 8 (First Council of Orléans, chapter 14).

(Dist. 81, c. *Si diaconus*.) If a deacon or priest, because of his guilt, withdraws himself from communion at the altar under a penitent’s confession, then, even if other ministers are lacking and a case of clear necessity arises, he may baptize one who asks for baptism.

### CHAPTER 19.—Concerning those who seek penance: if a man, he is first to be shorn; if a woman, she is first to change her dress. From the Third Council of Toledo, chapter 12.

Whoever, whether healthy or ill, asks a bishop or priest for penance: before all else, the bishop [Col. 0860B] and priest are to observe this—if the person is a man, whether healthy or ill, he is first to be shorn, or made to change his clothing into ashes and sackcloth, and then penance is to be given him. But if she is a woman, she is not to receive penance unless she has first either been veiled or changed her dress. For, when penance is carelessly bestowed upon laypeople together with women, they frequently relapse after receiving penance into deeds again deserving lamentation.

### CHAPTER 20.—How any fallen member of the clergy, thrust into a monastery to perform penance, is to be supported. Gregory to Peter the subdeacon (*Register*, book I, epistle 42).

(16, q. 6, c. *De lapsis*.) Concerning fallen priests or any member of the clergy, we wish you to observe this: do not involve yourself in their property with any taint of corruption; instead seek out very poor [Col. 0860C] regular monasteries that know how to live according to God. Entrust the fallen to those monasteries for penance, and let the property of the fallen benefit the place to which they are entrusted to perform penance, so that those who undertake concern for their correction may have support from that property. If they have relatives, their property is to be given to their lawful relatives, but in such a way that sufficient provision must be made for the maintenance of those assigned to penance. But if any priests, levites, monks, clerics, or other persons from the household of the Church have fallen, we likewise wish them to be assigned to penance; but their property is not to be withdrawn from ecclesiastical right. Yet they are to receive for their own use what will support them during penance, lest, if they are stripped bare, they become burdensome to the places [Col. 0860D] to which they have been assigned.

### CHAPTER 21.—That forgiven sins return to one who will not forgive one sinning against him. Augustine, book I, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 12.

The Lord teaches most plainly in the Gospel that sins which have been forgiven return where brotherly charity is absent. He teaches this in the case of the servant whom, when He found him owing ten thousand talents, He forgave everything as he begged; but when that servant had shown no mercy to his fellow-servant who owed him one hundred denarii, the master ordered him to repay what had been forgiven him (Matt. XVIII).

### CHAPTER 22.—Concerning those who request penance at the last moment. From the sayings of Augustine (*Fifty Homilies*, homily 41).

(De poenit., dist. 7, c. *Si quis posit*.) Certainly, whoever [Col. 0861A], placed in the final necessity of illness, receives penance and, as soon as he has been reconciled, departs from the body: I confess to you, we do not deny him what he asks, but I do not presume to say that he has departed well from here. Whether he has departed safely, I do not know. We can give penance, but we cannot give assurance. Do I say that he will be condemned? No; but neither do I say that he will be set free. Do you wish, then, to be freed from uncertainty? Do you wish to escape what is uncertain? Do penance while you are healthy. If you do so, I tell you that you are safe, because you did penance at the time when you could still sin. But if you wish to do penance when you can no longer sin, your sins have left you; you have not left your sins.

### CHAPTER 23.—That those guilty of grave crimes are to be separated from the altar by the authority of a bishop and reconciled again. Augustine likewise, in the book *On Penance*.

[Note: [Col. 0861D] From the preface of a certain penitential book, which may be found in Beatus Rhenanus’s admonition at the end of Tertullian; because it is almost wholly patched together from Augustine, it is here attributed to Augustine. Moreover, this passage is excerpted from *Enchiridion*, chapter 65, *On Penance*.]

[Col. 0861B]

(Dist. 1, c. *In actione*.) In the exercise of penance, when a deed has been committed such that its perpetrator must be separated even from Christ’s body, the measure to be considered is not so much that of time as of sorrow. For God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart (Ps. L). But because the sorrow of one heart is often hidden from another and does not come to others’ knowledge through words or any other signs, although it is before Him to whom it is said, “My groaning is not hidden from thee” (Ps. XXXVII), periods of penance are rightly established by those who preside over the Churches, so that satisfaction may also be made to the Church, in which those sins themselves are forgiven; for outside it they are not forgiven. Thus far Augustine in that passage. Therefore, when the wound of sin and the force of the disease are so great that the remedies of the Lord’s body and blood must be deferred, each person ought, by the bishop’s authority, to withdraw himself from the altar in order to perform penance, and by the same authority to be reconciled.

### CHAPTER 24.—How far one ought to accommodate penitents. Likewise from the book *On Penance* (*Fifty Homilies*, homily 50, chapter 11).

[Col. 0861D]

(Dist. 1, c. *Judicet*.) Let a person judge himself in these matters by his own will while he can, and turn his conduct toward the better, lest, when he can no longer do so, he be judged by the Lord even against his will. And when he has pronounced upon himself the sentence of the sternest remedy, let him come to the bishops, through whom the keys are administered to him in the Church; and, like a good son now beginning to be such, preserving the order of the maternal members, let him receive from the steward of the sacraments the measure of his satisfaction. In offering the sacrifice of a contrite heart, let him persist devoutly and humbly.

Yet he should do what benefits not only himself toward recovering health but also others by way of example. Thus, if his sin consists not only in a grave evil to himself but also in a great scandal to others, and if it seems expedient to the bishop for the welfare of the Church, he should not refuse to perform penance in the knowledge of many persons, or even of the whole people. He should not resist, nor add swelling through shame to a lethal and deadly wound [Col. 0862A].

(Chapter 12.) (Chapter 12.) For many are corrected like Peter, many are tolerated like Judas, and many remain unknown until the Lord comes, who will both illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the thoughts of hearts (I Cor. IV).

Likewise Augustine, in his letter to Macedonius (epistle 45, after the beginning) (Dist. 50, c. *Quamvis*):

Although it has been cautiously and beneficially provided that the place of that most humble penance be granted once in the Church, lest a remedy become cheap and consequently less useful to the sick—a remedy which is all the more salutary the less contemptible it is—who would nevertheless dare to say to God: “Why do you still spare this person who, after the first penance, again binds himself in the snares of wickedness?” [*obstringit*, perhaps *obstr.* in the original.] Who would dare to say that the saying of the Apostle is not at work in such people: “Do you not know that the patience of God [Col. 0862B] leads you to repentance?” (Rom. II). Or that, with these excepted, what is written has been limited: “Blessed are all who trust in him” (Ps. II)? Or that the saying does not apply to them: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord” (Ps. XXX)?

Since, therefore, God’s patience and mercy toward sinners are so great that one whose conduct is amended in this temporal life is not condemned eternally—He who awaits no mercy that might be shown to Him, since none is happier, none more powerful, none more just than He—what kind of people ought we to be toward people, we who do not say that this life of ours is without sin, however greatly we may extol it in praise [“commend,” variant]? And if we should say this, as it is written, we deceive ourselves [Col. 0862C] and the truth is not in us (I John I).

### CHAPTER 25.—That one cannot perfectly repent for something taken away unless it is restored, if it can be restored. Augustine, in the letter to Armentarius and Paulina (epistle 54 to Macedonius, after the middle).

(11, q. 6, c. *Si res aliena*.) If another’s property, on account of which there is sin, is not restored when it can be restored, penance is not being performed but feigned. But if it is truly performed, the sin will not be forgiven unless what was taken is restored—yet, as I said, when it can be restored.

### CHAPTER 26.—That final conversion is to be evaluated more by disposition than by time. From the decretals of Pope Celestine, chapter 20 (epistle 2 to the bishops of Gaul, chapter 27).
