Therefore true conversion to God in those at the end of life is to be assessed more by disposition than by time [Col. 0862D], as the prophet asserts thus: “If, having turned back, you groan, then you shall be saved” (Ezek. XVIII and XXXIII). Since the Lord is the examiner of the heart, penance must not be denied at any time to one who requests it, because that person binds himself to the Judge before whom he knows that all hidden things are revealed.

### CHAPTER 27.—That every believer at the end of life ought to be anointed with consecrated oil. From the decretals of Pope Callixtus.

For the blessed Apostle James wrote in his Epistle: “Is anyone among you ill? Let him summon the priests [Col. 0863A] of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person” (Jas. V). The apostles are recorded to have done this in the Gospel (Mark VI), and the practice of the Church now maintains that the sick are anointed by priests with consecrated oil and are healed when prayer accompanies it.

Not only priests may use this holy oil in their illnesses, but, as Pope Innocent I sets forth (epistle 1, chapter 8), all Christians too may use the same oil, anointing themselves or their own in time of need. Yet this oil may be made only by bishops. For the phrase, “with oil in the name of the Lord,” means oil consecrated in the name of the Lord, or certainly that, when they anoint the sick, they must also invoke the Lord’s name over them. “And if he is in sins, they are forgiven [Col. 0863B] him.”

Many are punished with bodily illness or even death because of sins committed against the soul. Hence the Apostle says to the Corinthians that, because they were accustomed to receive the body of the Lord unworthily, “therefore among you many are weak and infirm, and many sleep” (I Cor. XI). If, then, the sick are in sins and confess them to the priests of the Church, and strive with a perfect heart to abandon and amend them, they will be forgiven. For they cannot be forgiven without confession of amendment [variant: “the confession of amendment”]. Hence the following is rightly added: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (Jas. V).

### CHAPTER 28.—Concerning those who confess their sins in illness because of fear of death. From the Council of Nantes, chapter 2.

[Col. 0863C] A sick person who, under the pressure of impending death, confesses his sins is to be reconciled by the priest on this condition: if the Lord grants him life and restores health, he is to do penance according to the character of the offence, the statutes of the canons, and approved penitentials.

### CHAPTER 29.—Concerning those who, in a time of necessity, desire both penance and reconciliation. From the decretals of Pope Leo, chapter 9 (Pope Leo I, epistle 91 to Theodore).

(26, q. 6, c. *His qui in tempore*.) To those who, in time of necessity and under the urgent pressure of dangers, seek the aid of penance and then immediate reconciliation, neither satisfaction is to be forbidden nor reconciliation denied. For we can neither impose measures nor determine times upon the Lord’s mercy, before whom true conversion suffers no delay of forgiveness. The Lord says through the prophet: “When, having turned back, you groan, then you shall be saved” (Ezek. XVIII and XXXIII; Isa. XXX); and elsewhere: “Declare your iniquities first, that you may be justified.” Likewise: “With the Lord is mercy, and with him abundant redemption” (Ps. CXXIX).

[Col. 0863D] Therefore, in dispensing God’s gifts, we ought not to be hard-hearted or to disregard the groans and tears of those accusing themselves, since we believe that the affliction of repentance [variant: “the disposition to repent”] is conceived by God’s inspiration. The Apostle says: [Col. 0864A] “Perhaps God may grant them repentance, that they may recover themselves from the snare of the devil, by whom they are held captive according to his will” (II Tim. II).

### CHAPTER 30.—On the same matter. From the decretals of Pope Innocent I, chapter 22 (epistle 3 to Exuperius, chapter 2).

This too has been asked: what ought to be observed concerning those who, after baptism, [Col. 0864A] have devoted themselves all their life to the pleasures of incontinence and, at the very end of their lives, request both penance and reconciliation to communion? The earlier practice concerning them was stricter; the later, through the intervention of mercy, more lenient.

The former custom held that penance should be granted them but communion denied. For, since persecutions were frequent in those times, lest the ease with which communion was granted make people secure concerning reconciliation [Col. 0864B] and fail to recall them from falling, communion was rightly denied while penance was granted, lest everything be denied altogether; and the circumstances of the time made forgiveness harsher. But after our Lord restored peace to His Churches, once fear had been driven away, it seemed good that communion be given to those dying—through mercy, as viaticum for those departing—lest we appear to follow the harshness and severity of the Novatian heretics, who deny forgiveness. Thus final communion is granted along with penance, so that persons of this kind, even at their last moments, by the permission of our Saviour, may be rescued from everlasting destruction.

### CHAPTER 31.—Concerning those who come to their end, that they are not to be deprived of the final and necessary viaticum. From the Council of Nicaea, chapter 13.

[Col. 0864C] (26, q. 6, c. *De his vero*.) Concerning those who come to their end, even now the ancient and regular law is to be observed: if anyone is departing from the body, he is by no means to be deprived of the final and necessary viaticum. But if one who was despaired of, having received communion and become a participant in the offering, should recover again, let him be among those who receive communion in prayer only. In general, to every person at the point of departure who requests the grace of communion, the bishop ought reasonably to give it from the offering.

### CHAPTER 32.—That sins can be abolished by penance, even if someone repents in the last breath of life. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 2.

[Note: [Col. 0863] Augustine has this in *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, book [sic], chapter 80.]

[Col. 0864D] We believe without doubt that penance can abolish sins, even if, in the last breath of life, a person repents of sins committed [variant: *admissor*], and even if the sins are disclosed by public lamentation. For God’s purpose, by which He decreed to save what was lost (Luke XIX), remains immovable. Therefore, because His will is not changed, whether by amendment of life, if time is granted, or by humble confession, if life departs immediately, forgiveness of sins is faithfully to be expected from Him who does not will the death of the sinner, but that he turn back from destruction through repentance and be saved by the Lord’s mercy, and live [variant: “and, saved by the Lord’s mercy, live”] (Ezek. XI; XXXIII). Whoever thinks otherwise concerning God’s most righteous mercy [Col. 0865A] is not a Christian but a Novatian.

### CHAPTER 33.—Concerning those fallen persons at the end of life: if they ask, aid is to be given them by the gift of viaticum. From an epistle of Pope Siricius.

Whoever has fallen through carnal weakness, when he begins to depart to the Lord, is, if he asks, to be helped by the gift of viaticum through the grace of communion.

### CHAPTER 34.—Concerning sick persons who request penance but lose the use of speech before the priest arrives. From an epistle of Pope Leo (epistle 91).

Thus help must be given to persons in such need, so that neither the act of penance [Col. 0865B] nor the grace of communion is denied them, if, even after losing the use of speech [variant: “of the mouth”], they are shown by the judgment of an unimpaired mind to seek it. But if they are so burdened by illness that they cannot, in the priest’s presence, signify what they had requested a little earlier, the testimony of faithful persons standing by ought to benefit them, so that they may receive both the benefit of penance and that of reconciliation.

### CHAPTER 35.—On the same matter. From the decretals of Pope Eusebius, chapter 10.

If someone requesting penance has been deprived of the use of his tongue when the priest arrives, it is established that, if there is reliable testimony that he himself had requested penance, and if he himself can make some sign of his will by movements of some kind, the priest is to perform everything as was written above concerning the sick penitent: that is, he is to say prayers, anoint him with holy oil [Col. 0865C], give him the Eucharist, and, after he has died, provide for him as for the other faithful.

### CHAPTER 36.—Concerning the sick in danger of death. From Theodore’s Penitential (Mainz under Leo IV, chapter 26).

(26, q. 7, c. *Ab infirmis*.) From sick persons in danger of death, a pure confession of sins is to be sought by priests. Yet no fixed amount of penance is to be imposed on them; rather, it is to be made known to them, and the burden of penance is to be lightened by the prayers of friends and by works of almsgiving. And should they perhaps depart, they are not to become bound and alienated from communion or from the fellowship of forgiveness. If, rescued by God from that danger, they recover, they are carefully to observe the measure of penance imposed by their [Col. 0865D] confessor. Therefore, according to canonical authority, lest the gate of mercy seem shut to them, strengthened by ecclesiastical prayers and consolations, with the holy anointing of oil, they are to be refreshed by the communion of viaticum according to the statutes of the holy Fathers.

### CHAPTER 37.—Concerning a man who had denied Christ, and how he was released in his last moments by viaticum. Dionysius speaks in the *Ecclesiastical History* (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 34, from Rufinus’s translation).

In the *Ecclesiastical History*, Dionysius, writing in reply to Fabian, recounts a certain story. He says that a man named Serapion was in Alexandria, one of those who had lapsed, and that he had repeatedly begged to be received back but had not obtained it. [Col. 0866A] He was afterward oppressed by illness, so that for three days he lay utterly speechless. But, recovering his breath somewhat on the fourth day, he is said to have called his little daughter to him and said:

> “How long do you keep me here? I beg you, let one of the priests come quickly, so that I may be released.”

Having said this, he again remained speechless. The child ran quickly to the priest at night. The priest was ill and could not come; nevertheless, because it had been ordered that no one who had lapsed and was at the point of death was to be denied the consolation of reconciliation, especially one known to have asked for it previously, he gave the child a small portion of the Eucharist. As the child was returning, before he had yet entered the house, Serapion again said: “Have you returned, my son? Although the priest could not come, carry out what has been commanded you [Col. 0866B], so that I may depart.” When he had received the Eucharist, as though certain chains and bonds had been broken, he gave up his spirit now more joyfully. From this it is evident that no one ought to be deprived of the assistance of this good.

### CHAPTER 38.—That priests, by the bishop’s command, are to reconcile penitents for hidden sins. From the decree of Pope Evaristus, chapter 3.

(26, q. 6, c. *Presbyteri*.) Priests are, by the bishop’s command, to reconcile penitents for hidden sins and, as we stated above, to absolve and communicate the sick.

### CHAPTER 39.—Concerning a penitent who departs from the body during penance and desires reconciliation. From the First Council of Orange, chapter 3.

(26, q. 6, c. *Qui recedunt*.) It has seemed good that penitents departing from the body should receive communion without the reconciling laying on of hands; this is sufficient consolation [variant: “reconciliation”] for one dying, according to the determinations of the Fathers, who appropriately called such communion viaticum. But if they survive, they are to remain in the order of penitents, so that, after showing the necessary fruits of penance, they may receive full communion with the reconciling laying on of hands.

### CHAPTER 40.—That penitents are to be forgiven on the Thursday before Easter; but earlier, if they come to the desperate stage of illness. From an epistle of Pope Innocent I, chapter 1 (epistle 1 to Decentius, chapter 7).

(De cons., dist. 3, c. *De poenitentibus*.) Concerning penitents who are doing penance either for graver or for lighter offences, if no illness intervenes [Col. 0866D], the custom of the Roman Church shows that they are to be forgiven on the Thursday before Easter. But it belongs to the priest to judge the gravity of offences, so that he attends to the penitent’s confession and to the groans and tears of one correcting himself, and then orders forgiveness when he sees suitable satisfaction. Certainly, if anyone falls ill and reaches the point of desperation, he is to be released before Easter, lest he depart this world without communion.

### CHAPTER 41.—Concerning those who deny that sins are forgiven in the Church. From Augustine’s sayings (*Enchiridion*, chapter 83).

But whoever, not believing that sins are forgiven in the Church, despises the generosity of the divine gift and closes his final day [Col. 0867A] in this obstinacy of mind, is guilty of that unforgivable sin against the Holy Spirit, in whom Christ forgives sins.

### CHAPTER 42.—That sick persons may take food at any hour. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 23.

Sick persons may take food and drink at any hour, whenever they desire.

### CHAPTER 43.—Concerning priests who deny penance to the dying. From the decretals of Pope Julius (at the end of Julius’s decretals).

(26, q. 6, c. *Si presbyter*.) If a priest denies penance to those who are dying, he will be guilty of their souls, because the Lord says: “On whatever day the sinner turns back, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezek. XVIII). For true conversion [variant: “confession”] can occur at the final [Col. 0867B] moment, because the Lord examines not only time but also the heart (Luke XXIII), just as the thief, by the penance of a single moment, deserved to be in paradise at the hour of his final confession.

### CHAPTER 44.—That final penance is to be denied to no one. From the decretals of Pope Celestine, chapter 10 (epistle 2 to the bishops of Gaul, chapter 2).

(26, q. 6, c. *Agnovimus*.) We have learned that penance is denied to the dying and that the desires of those who, at the time of death, wish this remedy to be brought to the aid of their souls are not granted. I confess that we recoil in horror at finding anyone of such impiety as to despair of God’s mercy, as though He could not help one who runs to Him at any time and free a person endangered beneath the burden of sins by the very weight by which that person desires to be released [variant uncertain: “*se expediti*”].

What else, I ask, is this than to add death to one dying [Col. 0867C], and by one’s own cruelty to kill his soul so that it cannot be absolved? For God, most ready to help and inviting the sinner to repentance, promises: “On whatever day he turns back, his sins shall not be reckoned against him” (Ezek. XXXIII). Again: “I do not will the death of the sinner, but only that he turn back and live” (ibid.). Whoever denies penance [“hoped for” inserted in the original and in Greek] at the time of death therefore takes salvation from a person and despairs of God’s clemency, because he does not believe that God can be sufficient even for a moment to assist one who is dying.

The thief hanging on Christ’s right hand would have lost his reward on the cross [Col. 0867D] if the penance of one hour had not helped him. He repented while undergoing punishment, and through the confession of a single statement he deserved, by God’s promise, a dwelling in paradise.

### CHAPTER 45.—That at the beginning of Lent all public penitents are to come into the city and present themselves to their bishop before the church doors, barefoot and clothed in sackcloth. From the Council of Agde, chapter 9.

(Dist. 50, c. *In capite*.) At the beginning of Lent, all penitents who undertake or have undertaken public penance are to present themselves before the church doors to the bishop of the city, clothed in sackcloth, barefoot, and with faces cast down to the earth, proclaiming themselves guilty by their very dress and appearance. The deans—that is, [Col. 0868A] the archpriests of the parishes—and the penitents’ priests must be present there. They must diligently inspect the penitents’ manner of life and impose penance according to the degree of fault through the appointed stages.

After this, the bishop is to bring them into the church and, prostrate on the ground with all the clergy, chant with tears the seven penitential psalms for their absolution. Then, rising from prayer [variant: “standing up”], he is, as the canons command, to lay hands on them, sprinkle them with blessed water, first put ashes upon them, then cover their heads with sackcloth, and with groaning and repeated sighs declare to them that, as Adam was cast out of paradise, so they too are cast out of the Church because of their sins. After this he is to command the ministers to drive them out beyond the church doors. The clergy are to accompany them with the responsory: “In the sweat of thy face thou shalt eat bread” (Gen. III), etc., so that, seeing holy Church shaken and stirred by their crimes [Col. 0868B], they may not make light of penance. But at the holy supper of the Lord they are again to be presented at the thresholds of the church by their deans and priests.

### CHAPTER 46.—By what authority the measure of penance ought to be imposed on those confessing sins. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 10 (Second Council of Chalon, chapter 38).

The manner and period of penance are to be imposed by priests upon those confessing their sins, either by the ordinance of the ancient canons, the authority of the holy Scriptures, or approved ecclesiastical custom. For those who impose certain light and unusual forms of penance for grave sins “sew cushions under every elbow of the hand and make pillows under the head of every age, to catch souls,” [Col. 0868C] according to the prophetic saying (Ezek. XIII). But a distinction must be observed between those who repent publicly and secretly. Whoever sins publicly ought to be punished by public penance and, in accordance with the order of the canons, excommunicated and reconciled according to his desert.

### CHAPTER 47.—That diversity of offences produces diversity of penances. From Augustine’s sayings.

Diversity of offences produces diversity of penances. Physicians of bodies likewise prepare different medicines, so that they treat wounds in one way, disease in another, swellings in another, putrefactions in another, dimness of sight in another, fractures in another, and burns in another. Thus spiritual physicians ought to heal the wounds of souls by different kinds of treatment.

[Col. 0868D] But because it belongs to few people thoroughly to know, treat, and heal everything, so as to be able to restore an unimpaired state of health, we therefore earnestly admonish every learned priest of Christ not to arrange everything according to his own judgment, but according to the statutes of the canons and the traditions of the Fathers. He should consider the condition of each sex, age, poverty, circumstance, station, and person of everyone wishing to do penance; he should also examine the heart of the penitent; and, according to these considerations, as a wise physician, judge each individual case as seems right to him.

### CHAPTER 48.—That there are many fruits of penance. From the sayings of the same author.

There are many fruits of penance by which one attains the expiation of crimes [Col. 0869A]. Eternal salvation is not promised merely by that simple name “penance,” as in the apostolic saying: “Repent therefore,” he says, “and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts III); and in the prophetic saying: “When, having turned back, you groan, then you shall be saved” (Isa. XXX). No one will be saved because of bare groaning or the bare name of penance, but the mass of sins is overthrown through true confession, the counsel of an understanding priest, the affection of charity, and the fruit of almsgiving.

### CHAPTER 49.—Why the canons do not set out exactly, for every crime, a fixed time and measure of penance. From Jerome’s sayings.

[Note: [Col. 0869] This is found in the preface to that Penitential already mentioned above at chapter 23.]

(De poenitent., dist. 1, c. *Mensuram*.) The canons do not set out [Col. 0869B] with sufficient explicitness a measure of time for performing penance for each individual crime, so as to state separately how every offence is to be corrected; rather, they determine that this should be left to the judgment of an understanding priest. For before God, the measure of sorrow has greater force than that of time, and mortification of vices than mere abstinence from food. Therefore they command that periods of penance be shortened through the faith and conduct of penitents and consider them to be prolonged through negligence.

Nevertheless, forms of penance have been imposed [variant: “there nevertheless exist imposed forms”] for certain offences, by which other offences are to be assessed, since through those same measures it is easy to estimate the punishment and discipline of the canons.

### CHAPTER 50.—Concerning those who hasten to fulfil the penance imposed upon them. From the Roman Penitential.

[Col. 0869C]

Every person coming to penance: if you see him standing sharply and continually in penitence, deal with him more leniently at once. But do not prevent one who is able to fulfil what has been imposed upon him; rather, permit him. For those who hasten to discharge the burden owed are more deserving of praise, since fasting is a burden owed and should thus be loved by those doing penance: for if he fasts and fulfils what the priest has commanded him, he will be cleansed from his sins. But if he returns again to his former habit of sin, he is like the dog that returns to its own vomit [Col. 0869D] (Prov. 26).

Therefore every penitent ought not only to fast as much as the priest has commanded him, but also, after completing what has been enjoined upon him, ought to fast as much as seems good to him. For if he does what the priest has prescribed, only those sins which he has confessed will be forgiven. But if afterwards he fasts of his own accord, he will acquire a reward for himself and the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, one who fasts throughout the whole week for his sins should eat and drink on Saturday and Sunday whatever is set before him. Yet let him guard himself against gluttony and drunkenness, because every sensual excess arises from drunkenness. Therefore blessed Paul forbade it, saying: “Do not [Col. 0870A] become drunk with wine, in which is sensual excess” (Eph. 5)—not because sensual excess is in wine, but because it is in drunkenness.

## CHAPTER 51.—Whenever persons come to penance, priests ought to share with them in fasting and prayer. From the Penitential of Theodore.

Whenever Christians come to penance, we impose fasts upon them, and we ourselves ought to share with them in fasting for one or two weeks, or for as long as we can, lest what the Lord said to the priests skilled in the Law be said to us: “Woe to you lawyers, who burden people and lay upon their shoulders heavy and unbearable loads, while you yourselves do not touch those burdens with one of your fingers” (Luke 11).

For no one can lift up a person falling beneath a burden unless he bends down to extend [Col. 0870B] his hand to him. Nor can any physician heal the wounds of the sick unless he shares their stench. So likewise no priest or bishop can heal the wounds of sins or take sins away from souls unless he gives himself to diligent care and prayer with tears. Therefore, dearest brothers, you must be concerned for sinners, because we are members of one another.

Accordingly, if we see anyone lying in sins, let us hasten to call him back to penance by our teaching. And whenever you give counsel to a sinner, give him penance at the same time: how much he ought to fast or redeem his sins by almsgiving, lest perhaps you forget what he has already told you and must question him again; and perhaps he will be ashamed to confess his sins again, and so be found liable to yet further judgment.

## CHAPTER 52.—A person sometimes sins through an impulse of the mind and sometimes through the frailty of the flesh. From the Second Council of Chalon, chapter 32.

We have also perceived that this requires correction: certain persons, when confessing their sins to priests, do not do so fully. Since, therefore, it is established that a human being consists of two substances, namely soul and body, and sins are committed sometimes through an impulse of the mind and sometimes through the frailty of the flesh, the sins themselves must be investigated with careful inquiry, so that confession may be complete in both respects: that they confess both deeds performed through the body and those sins committed in thought alone.

[Col. 0870D] The confessor of sins should therefore be instructed to make confession concerning the eight principal vices, without which life in this world is difficult, because he has sinned at their prompting either in thought or, more grievously, in deed. Hatred, envy, pride, and the other plagues of the soul of this kind injure all the more dangerously because they creep in more subtly.

## CHAPTER 53.—Concerning incest committed secretly. From the sayings of Augustine.

If anyone has committed incest secretly and has made secret confession to a priest, let the canonical remedy be indicated to him—the remedy prescribed by the canons which he would have had to undergo [Col. 0871A] if his deed had become public. But because the offence is hidden, let the priest give him counsel so that, through secret penance, he may advance toward the salvation of his soul: that is, that he truly confess from his heart that he has sinned gravely; that by fasts and almsgiving, vigils, and sacred prayers with tears, he strive to cleanse himself; and that thus he trust, through the mercy of God, to attain hope of pardon.

## CHAPTER 54.—A distinction must be observed between those doing public penance and those doing it secretly. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 21 (Council of Reims, chapter 31, and Second Council of Chalon, chapter 38).

A distinction is to be maintained among penitents: as to which persons ought to do penance publicly and which secretly.

## CHAPTER 55.—Priests should receive with great joy one who repents from the heart. From the sayings of Bishop Basil (in the *Shorter Rules*, response to question 8).

[Col. 0871B] (26, question 7, chapter *Poenitentem*.) One who repents from the heart ought to be received as the Lord showed when he said that he summoned his friends and neighbours, saying: “Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep which I had lost” (Luke 15).

## CHAPTER 56.—Those who have already ceased to sin and have repented perfectly may be granted communion during their penance. From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 2.

(26, question 7, chapter *His qui*.) Concerning those who have sinned through various crimes and, persevering in prayer [“of confession and penance,” inserted in the original], have made their conversion from evils complete: after the appropriate period of penance has been undergone according to the nature of the offence, communion should be granted to such persons through the clemency and goodness of God.

## CHAPTER 57.—Whether those fallen in holy orders can be restored. Augustine, writing to Deacon Peter on faith, says (chapter 3):

[Col. 0871C]

Penance can be beneficial to every person in this life, whenever he performs it: however wicked, however advanced in years he may be, if he renounces his former sins with his whole heart, sheds tears for them in the sight of God—not only bodily tears but tears of the heart—and takes care to wash away the stains of evil deeds with good works, he will immediately obtain forgiveness of all sins.

For the Lord promises us this in prophetic speech, saying: “If you turn back and groan, you shall be saved” (Isa. 30). And elsewhere it is said: “My child, you have sinned; do not add sin again, [Col. 0871D] but pray also concerning your former sins, that they may be forgiven you” (Ecclus. 21). Prayer for sins would never have been enjoined upon a sinner if forgiveness were not to be granted to one who prays.

But penance benefits the sinner only if he performs it in the Catholic Church, to which God gave, in the person of blessed Peter, the power of binding and loosing, saying: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16). Therefore, at whatever age a person performs true penance for his sins and, by God’s illumination, corrects his life, he shall not be deprived of the gift of pardon. For God, as he says through the prophet, does not desire the death of the sinner so much as that he turn from his evil way and his soul live (Ezek. 33).

[Col. 0872A] Nevertheless, no one should remain longer in his sins under hope of God’s mercy, since no one, even in his body, wishes to remain ill longer under hope of future health. For those who neglect to withdraw from their iniquities while promising themselves pardon from God are sometimes so overtaken by God’s sudden wrath that they find neither time for conversion nor the benefit of forgiveness.

Therefore holy Scripture graciously forewarns each of us, saying: “Do not delay to turn to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day; for his wrath will come suddenly, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you” (Ecclus. 5). Blessed David likewise says: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden [Col. 0872B] your hearts” (Ps. 94). Blessed Paul agrees with him in these words: “Take heed, brothers, lest perhaps there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, departing from the living God; exhort one another every day, while it is called ‘today,’ lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin” (Heb. 3).

Thus he lives with a hardened heart who does not convert, whether because he despairs of forgiveness for his sins or because he hopes for God’s mercy in such a way as to remain until the end of this present life in the perversity of his crimes. Therefore, loving God’s mercy and fearing his justice, let us neither despair of forgiveness of sins nor remain in sins, knowing that the equity of the most just Judge will exact all those debts of humankind which the mercy of the most merciful [Col. 0872C] Redeemer has not forgiven. For just as mercy receives and absolves the converted, so justice will reject and punish the hardened. These are those who sin against the Holy Spirit and shall receive forgiveness of sins neither in this age nor in the age to come (Matt. 12).

Thus far Augustine. Isidore, bishop of Seville, likewise replied to an inquiry from Bishop Mason as follows, saying (Distinction 50, *Domino sancto*):

> “As to what your venerable brotherhood subsequently made known in its letter, no inconsistency is to be understood in such decretal judgments: in one place it is read that, after bodily lapse, a rank of honour is to be restored after penance; elsewhere, that after such an offence the merit of the former rank is by no means to be restored.”

This difference is to be distinguished in the following way. The canon directs those to return to their former ranks of office whose penance has been preceded by satisfaction or worthy confession of sins. On the other hand, those who are neither corrected from the vice of corruption [“of the body,” Gratian’s recension] nor cease to defend, with a kind of superstitious rashness, the very carnal offence which they commit, receive neither rank of honour nor the grace of communion.

[Col. 0872D] Therefore the two judgments must be decided thus: those who through penance have deserved reconciliation through divine mercy must be restored to a place of honour; and those who are known through the amendment of penance to have received the remedy of life rightly obtain the status of the dignity they had attained. And, lest this perhaps remain too ambiguous, let it be confirmed by the judgment of divine authority. For the prophet Ezekiel, under the figure of faithless Jerusalem, shows that former honour can be restored after the satisfaction of penance: “Be ashamed, O Judah, and bear your disgrace” (Ezek. 16). And shortly afterward: “You and your daughters shall return to your former state [‘from your iniquity’]” (ibid.).

By saying, “Be ashamed,” he shows that after the deed of shame—that is, sin—each person ought to blush, and [“after confession,” inserted in the ordinary recension] to bow down his shamefaced countenance to the ground for the crimes committed, because he perpetrated a deed deserving shame. Then he commands him to bear the disgrace of his deposition, mourning humbly for what he has sinned. [Col. 0873B] Thus, according to the prophet, he may be recalled to his former condition.

## CHAPTER 58.—The soul is nobler than many nations and more precious than many cities; therefore, if it has fallen, it should be deeply mourned. Extract from the book of St John of Constantinople to Theodore, chapter 59.

[Note: [Col. 0873D] In volume V, from the exhortation to Theodore after his fall, except that this is an old translation. Moreover, I think that this chapter-number [Col. 0874D] should be referred to the Penitential, from which these passages seem to have been drawn.]

“Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes?” (Jer. 9). Is this not said far more fittingly now by me than it was then by the prophet of God? For although not many cities nor an entire nation must be mourned, yet a soul must be wept for—a soul nobler than many nations and more precious than many cities. For if one person who does the will of God is better than a multitude of the wicked (Ecclus. 16), then you too were once better [Col. 0873C] than multitudes of Jews.

Therefore let no one wonder if I now employ more prolonged lamentations and pour forth more bitter tears than the prophet then poured forth. For I do not mourn, as I said, the ruin of a captured city or lament the captivity of a worthless populace; rather, I mourn the fall of an outstanding soul and the destruction of the temple in which Christ dwelt. This lamentation for the outstanding soul which I mourn is harsher and more bitter in proportion as it is truer.

A little later: This is surely why I weep inconsolably and grieve without ceasing whenever I remember, until I see you once more dance [or perhaps: return] to the state of your former glory. And although this seems impossible to human beings, with the Lord all things are possible (Luke 1). For he is the one “who raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dungheap, to set him with the princes of his people.” He is the one who “makes the barren woman a joyful mother of children” (Ps. 112).

[Col. 0873D] Therefore do not doubt or despair that you can be changed for the better. For if the devil had such power as to lead you from the lofty heights of virtue down into the abyss of evils, how much more will God be able to call you back to the summit of good things, and not only restore you to what you were, but make you appear far more blessed than before! Only do not lose heart or cut off hope of good things. I beg you, let what commonly happens to the ungodly not happen to you. For it is not the multitude of sins that brings a soul to despair, but ungodliness. Thus it is ungodly persons, not sinners, who despair of salvation.

These matters are drawn from elsewhere. Hence divine mercy promises, saying: “There shall be joy in heaven before the angels of God over one sinner” (Luke 15). And a little later: The Lord threatens punishment to those standing, should they fall; but to the fallen, if they desire to rise, he promises mercy. He frightens the former lest they presume in good things; he restores the latter lest they despair amid evils.

(*On Penance*, Homily 80, to the people of Antioch.) Are you righteous? Fear wrath, lest you fall. Are you a sinner? Trust in mercy, that you may rise.

(From the preceding book to Theodore.) And just as a most heavy fallen stone [the text may read *lapis*, “stone,” rather than *lapsus*, “fall”] pressing upon the neck of the soul always compels it to look downward to the earth and does not permit it to raise its eyes upward to God, so it belongs to a manly spirit to remove the burden from the neck of his soul, so that he may sing to the Lord with the prophet: “As the eyes of a maidservant are on the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are upon the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us” (Ps. 122).

[Col. 0874B] A little later: For that woman in the Gospels who found the drachma she had lost summoned her friends and neighbours to rejoice with her (Luke 15). But I shall summon your friends and mine, and our neighbours; I shall beg them to gather, not that they may rejoice but that they may mourn with me, not that they may congratulate me but that they may lament, and with voices raised to heaven make with me a mighty lament, saying to them: “Howl with me, friends; mourn and pour forth fountains of tears: not because I have lost an immense weight of gold or talents of gold, but because a friend dearer than all these things, more precious than all gold and every noble jewel, has somehow fallen and is being carried into the very depth of destruction.”

Several pages later, not far from the conclusion of the earlier exhortation: Do not despair because of your fall, lest you fall. For one who despairs of another has pardon; but one who despairs of himself has none, because he is not master of another’s mind.

A little below, with a different translation and with some changes: Thus, if a soul has once begun to despair of its salvation, it no longer knows how or into what evils it may plunge; so those seized by despair become intolerable and run through every path [Col. 0874D] of wickedness. Rise, rise, I beseech you; awaken at last, and lay aside this diabolical drunkenness. Spare all those who despair because of your despair, lest they think that they are walking the way of virtue if they do not see you return to it. Consider, I beseech you, how great is now the sorrow of the whole company of holy brethren; how great is the joy and exultation of unbelievers; and how much their influence toward the precipices of sensuality diminishes [the printed text has *decrescat*, “diminishes”; another reading is *de te crescat*, “grows because of you”]. Thereafter no one cast down by any fall will fail immediately to desire to rise and hasten at once to restore himself.

## CHAPTER 59.—No one ought to withdraw himself from consoling a wounded brother. Likewise, John of Constantinople to the same Theodore, *On the Fall*; Bacharius, chapter 60.

[Note: [Col. 0875D] Unless the heading is mistaken, the exhortation to Theodore is mutilated.]

[Col. 0875A]

Where is the mercy of the Christian religion, which our Master taught to be better than sacrifice? (Matt. 9.) Behold, a brother lies wounded by the enemy, perhaps still gasping, while you return as though unwounded and do not attempt to bring consolation to his wound. Do not be without fear, brothers: the enemy has struck one down more strongly so that his access to the rest might be easier. Why then do you despise the wounded man—or, as you suppose, the dead?

Rizpah, Saul’s concubine, was better [Note: [Col. 0875D] The passage is corrupt; perhaps it should be restored thus: “Rizpah, daughter of Aiah, Saul’s concubine, was better.”], for she guarded, clothed in sackcloth—that is, haircloth—the bodies of the dead whom David had struck down in vengeance for the Gibeonites, [Col. 0875B] until water dripped upon them from heaven (2 Sam. 21), that is, until a drop of heavenly mercy flowed down for their pardon [another reading: “until a drop flowed down”].

Judas Maccabaeus was better, for he believed that prayer ought to be offered even for his dead brothers, whom offerings to idols from the condemned city of Jamnia had brought down (2 Macc. 12). Why, I ask, has our physician placed so many kinds of ointments among the cases of his books, if there is nothing among his plasters by which the wound inflicted by the enemy can be healed?

And if it please you, let us open the school of our medicine and examine, from the beginning of the canon, the kinds of wounds and remedies. Behold, at the very entrance to the school we encounter the originators of carnal seed, who, struck by the venomous tooth of the serpent, were not immediately condemned to the penalty of death, [Col. 0875C] but were cast out from the delights of paradise—that is, from the liberty of the Church and communion in the sacred mystery [another reading: “ministry”].

## CHAPTER 60.—On the same matter. From the letter of John of Constantinople to Theodore.

Do you see from this that we are stained by the contagion of sin? Do not, I beseech you, my most blessed friend, overwhelm with the stones of despair our brother who has been plunged into the depth of a pit under the power of an unjust ruler.

Let us imitate the Ethiopian who freed the holy Jeremiah, cast into a cistern by an unjust king, by taking the assistance of thirty men and sending down to him old cloths and ropes (Jer. 38). Be readily moved by the fall and ruin of the wretched. Stretch out your hand to your brother as he lies there, confused by shame for his sin and not daring [Col. 0875D] to raise himself or lift his eyes. Fulfil the law of Moses: “Your brother’s ass has fallen beneath a burden”—that is, flesh overcome by sin; bend down, humble yourself, and lift it from its fall (Deut. 22).

Why are you ashamed to join yourself to a sinful person? Look to him who says: “Do not be excessively righteous” (Ecclus. 17). Our Master judged the man wounded by robbers not only worthy of care, but brought him to his own inn and sheepfold (Luke 10). Therefore gather up the brother whom the devil has struck cruelly. Entrust him to the innkeeper, that is, the blessed bishop, who, if he spends anything more on him, shall receive it from the Lord.

## CHAPTER 61.—On the same matter. From a letter of the same John of Constantinople to Theodore.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] This too is not found there.]

[Col. 0876A]

The Gospel saying declares: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him when you are alone with him. If he listens to you, you have gained him” (Matt. 18), together with the rest contained in the precept. Consider what it says: “Lest the sons of the uncircumcised rejoice” (2 Sam. 1). The sons of the uncircumcised are people of the world, living in the error and paganism of their foreskin. They rejoice, therefore, when they hear of the downfall of a soldier of Christ.

Let the sin, then, be concealed and correction applied. But let us offer the bandages of consolation and the ointments of heavenly hope. He himself, confessing beneath the tomb of his secrecy, should be kept confined by shame for his sin, where he is lacerated by the worm of conscience, which may smear over [the text is uncertain: *obliniat/oblingat*] all the corruptions of his sins, until he emits from himself no stench of disgraceful reputation.

## CHAPTER 62.—On the same matter. Likewise from the letter of the same John to Theodore.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] These passages too are lacking.]

How, I ask, can we despair of God’s mercy, when he even rebukes Pharaoh because he did not deign to repent, saying: “I have broken the arms of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and he has not entreated that healing might be given him and strength restored to him for grasping the sword” (Ezek. 30)?

That remarkable Solomon, who deserved to be joined to the wisdom of God [the text has *astritici Dei*, apparently corrupt] (Wis. 9), fell into the embraces of foreign women and, ensnared by the bond of lust, defiled himself even with the horror of sacrilege, because he made an image of Chemosh for the Moabite idol (3 Kgs. 11). But [Col. 0876C] because he acknowledged the fault of his error through the prophetic voice, he was never excluded from heavenly mercy. But perhaps you will say: “In neither Testament do I read either that he repented or that he obtained mercy,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER 63.—On the same matter. From the decrees of Pope Siricius, chapter 14 (Letter 1 to Himerius, chapter 14).

(Distinction 50, chapter *Illud quoque*.) We also considered it fitting to provide that, just as no cleric is permitted to perform penance [“is not permitted to perform solemn penance,” etc.], so no layperson may ever be permitted after penance and reconciliation to attain the honour of clerical office. For although they have been cleansed from the contagion of every sin, those who were formerly vessels of vices ought nevertheless not to receive the instruments for administering the sacraments.

## CHAPTER 64.—On the same matter. From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, chapter 17 (Letter 1 to the bishops throughout Lucania, chapter 20).

We have also learned that certain persons entangled in dreadful crimes, with every distinction set aside, not only do not undergo the necessary penance for atrocious deeds, but, without any correction whatever following, seek divine ministry and honour. We have learned that some persons established in orders, committing grave crimes, are not removed, although the Apostle cries aloud: “Lay hands suddenly on no one, nor share in the sins of others” [Col. 0877A] (1 Tim. 5); and the venerable ordinances of the elders declare that such persons, should they perhaps have crept in, must be expelled after deposition—both those who sinned before, and those forgetful of their sacred profession [another reading: “promise”] and violators of their holy purpose (Council of Nicaea, chapters 9 and 10).

## CHAPTER 65.—Those who imprudently travel about holy places under the pretext of religion. From the Council of Chalon, attended by King Charles, chapter 45 (Second Council of Chalon).

For many errors are committed also by some who, under the pretext of prayer, imprudently travel about Rome, Tours, and certain other places. There are priests, deacons, and others enrolled among the clergy, who live negligently and think that they are cleansed of sins and ought to perform their ministry if they reach the aforesaid places. Likewise there are laypeople who think that they may sin, or have sinned, with impunity because they frequent those places in order to pray.

There are certain powerful persons who, for the sake of acquiring wealth, obtain [another reading: “seek out”] many things under the pretext of a journey to Rome or Tours, oppress many poor people, and wish to appear to do for the sake of prayers or visits to holy places what they do solely from greed. There are poor people who do this in order to have greater occasion for begging; among these are those who wander everywhere, falsely claiming to be going there. Others are so foolish as to think that they are cleansed from sins by the mere sight of holy places, without attending to what blessed Jerome says (Letter to Paulinus, beginning “A good [Col. 0877C] man”): “It is praiseworthy not to have seen Jerusalem, but to have lived well in Jerusalem.”

With respect to all these persons, the emperor’s judgment should be awaited as to how they are to be corrected. But those who have confessed their sins to the priests in whose parishes they are, and have received from them counsel concerning the penance to be done—if they desire, by persevering in prayer, giving alms generously, ordering their conduct, and amending their lives, to visit the thresholds of the apostles or of any saints whatsoever—their devotion is to be praised in every way.

## CHAPTER 66.—Every sinner should rise as often as he falls. From the sayings of a certain hermit, Zosimus.

While a certain brother repeatedly questioned Abbot Zosimus in these words, saying, “What shall I do, Father, since I have fallen?” he replied: “Rise.” But when the man declared that he had risen and fallen again, he replied: “Rise again, still.” When the brother recounted that he had often risen and often fallen, the old man continued to use the same words, exclaiming: “Do not cease rising.”

The brother said to him: “Explain to me, Father, how long I can rise.” The old man said: “Until you die, found [another reading: ‘cast down’] either in a good work or in an evil one. For in whatever work a person is found [or ‘cast down’], in that work he will be judged.”

## CHAPTER 67.—It is just before God that a person reproach himself. From the sayings of a certain hermit, Pimen.

A certain brother questioned Abbot Pimen, saying: [Col. 0878A] “What does the Apostle mean when he says, ‘All things are pure to the pure’?” (Titus 1.) He said to him: “If anyone can attain to this saying so as to understand it, he will see himself as less than the whole creation.”

The brother said: “And how can I see myself as less than one who is a murderer?” The old man replied: “If a person can attain to this saying of the Apostle and sees someone who has perhaps killed another, he says within himself: ‘That man did only this one thing; but I commit murder every hour, killing myself.’”

When the brother asked how this could be, he replied: “This alone is a person’s righteousness: to reproach himself.” For then a person is righteous, when he condemns his own sins.

## CHAPTER 68.—No one should condemn his brother before God judges him. From the sayings of a certain hermit.

[Col. 0878B]

Abbot Isaac once came to a monastery and saw there a negligent brother; in anger he ordered him expelled from the monastery. As he was returning to his dwelling, an angel of the Lord came and stood before the door of his cell, saying: “I do not permit you to enter.”

He begged that his fault might be made known to him. The angel answered: “The Lord sent me, saying: ‘Go, say to Isaac: Where do you command us to send that brother who has sinned?’” At once he did penance, saying: “I have sinned, Lord; forgive me.”

The angel said to him: “Rise; may the Lord forgive you [the printed text has *indulget*, ‘forgives’], but do not do this again: do not condemn anyone [Col. 0878C] before the Lord judges him. Human beings have taken judgment to themselves and do not leave it to me, says the Lord.” This was said because, if it should happen that one of those who are perfect sins even in a small matter, he should not immediately be lost.

## CHAPTER 69.—Just obedience is rewarded with just rewards. From the sayings of the same author.

One of the Fathers, while in ecstasy, saw four ranks before God. The first rank consisted of sick people who gave thanks to God. The second was of those who practise hospitality and serve in this work. The third was of those who pursue solitude [“and do not see people”]. The fourth was of those who, for God’s sake, are subject in obedience to the Fathers.

This rank, which rendered obedience, was superior to those three ranks; it had a golden necklace and possessed greater glory than the rest. The old man said to the one showing him this in ecstasy: “Why does this fourth rank have greater glory than the others?” He replied: “Because all these others have some rest for fulfilling their own wills [another reading: ‘while doing, even in good works, their own wills’]. But this person who practises obedience, leaving all his own wills, depends wholly upon the will of the father who commands; therefore he has received a greater glory than the others.”

## CHAPTER 70.—Those who deliberately sin and promise themselves a kind of impunity for sin because of the distribution of alms. From the Council of Chalon, chapter 36 (Second Council of Chalon).

[Col. 0879A]

We have also thought it should not be passed over that certain persons sin deliberately, promising themselves a kind of impunity because of their distribution of alms. For almsgiving extinguishes sins, according to the saying: “Water extinguishes a blazing fire, and almsgiving extinguishes sins” (Ecclus. 3); but this applies to sins committed through necessity, chance, or any frailty whatsoever.

But sins committed deliberately in order to fulfil someone’s lust, on the calculation that they may be redeemed by alms, cannot at all be redeemed by them. Those who do this seem to hire God for a payment, so that they may be allowed to sin with impunity. Therefore no one ought to sin in order to give alms; rather, he ought to give alms because he has sinned. For the affliction and contrition of mind and body, which lust has drawn into guilt, ought to bring them back to pardon.

## CHAPTER 71.—Those who, after completing penance, return to their former wallowing places. From the decrees of Pope Siricius, chapter 10 (Letter 1 to Himerius, letter chapter 5).

(33, question 2, chapter *De his vero*.) Your charity rightly believed that the apostolic see should be consulted concerning those who, after performing penance, return like dogs and swine to their former vomit and wallowing places (Prov. 26; 2 Pet. 2), and seek again the soldier’s belt, theatrical pleasures, new marriages, and forbidden sexual unions. The children born after absolution have exposed their professed lack of continence.

Since they no longer have recourse [Col. 0879C] to doing penance, we have decided that they should be joined to the faithful only in prayer within the Church. Let them attend, though they do not deserve it, the celebration of sacred ministries; but let them be separated from the banquet of the Lord’s table, so that, corrected at least by this strictness, they may punish their own errors and offer an example to others, so that such persons may be withdrawn from obscene desires. Yet, because they fell through carnal frailty, we desire that they be helped, when they begin to depart to the Lord, through the grace of communion as viaticum. We judge that the same rule should be observed concerning women who, after penance, have bound themselves to such defilements.

## CHAPTER 72.—A penitent woman who, after her husband’s death, has presumed to marry another. From the Second Council of Arles, chapter 3 (chapter 21).

[Col. 0879D] Penitent women who, after their husbands’ deaths, have presumed to marry others, or have lived in suspect or forbidden intimacy with a stranger, are to be kept, together with that man, from the thresholds of the Church. It was also decided that this should be observed with regard to men undergoing penance.

## CHAPTER 73.—In imposing penance there must be no respect of persons. From the Second Council of Chalon, chapter 34, attended by King Charles.

Since, therefore, as the Apostle testifies, there is no respect of persons with God, and it must be avoided in all judgments (Rom. 2; Eph. 6; Col. 3; Acts 10), it must be guarded against all the more carefully in this judgment of penance, so that no priest may ever judge differently out of favour or hatred toward any person than he finds in the sacred canons, or than seems more right to him according to the authority of holy Scriptures and ecclesiastical custom.

For if physicians attempting to administer medicine to bodies do not spare those whom they wish to heal with cautery, cutting, or any other harsh treatment because of regard for a person, this must be observed still more by those who are physicians not of bodies but of souls. Penance is not to be weighed by the quantity of time, but by fervour of mind and mortification of body. For God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart (Ps. 50).

## CHAPTER 74.—Those who think that their sins can be forgiven without worthy penance. From the sayings of Augustine.

Whoever says that anyone can receive pardon from God for evil works without worthy [Col. 0880B] penance is utterly mistaken; and, being deceived, he hastens to deceive others and is bound by a double guilt: that is, his own error and another’s deception.

## CHAPTER 75.—A person ought to labour until he possesses Christ. From the sayings of Gregory.

A person ought to labour until he possesses Christ. But whoever has obtained him once need labour no longer. Yet the Lord permits his elect to labour so that they may remember the toils of tribulations and thereby guard themselves, fearing to lose such great labours. Thus God led the children of Israel through the desert for forty years so that, remembering their tribulations, they might not turn back.

## CHAPTER 76.—No bishop or priest may receive another’s penitent without letters from his own bishop. From the letter of Pope Felix, chapter 2 (third decretal letter, chapter 6).

[Col. 0880C]

Every effort must be taken, with every precaution, lest any of our brother bishops, or even priests, receive in another’s city or diocese a penitent, or one placed under a priest’s hand, or one who says that he has been reconciled, without the testimony and letters of the bishop or priest to whose parish he belongs.

### CHAPTER 77.—That penitents, according to the canons, ought not to communicate before completing penance. From the statements of Pope Pius, chapter 10.

Penitents ought not to communicate before the completion of their penance.

### CHAPTER 78.—That one unwilling to repent of a sin committed is to be regarded as a heathen and a publican. From the statements of Augustine.

[Col. 0880D]

(26, q. 7, c. *Erga eum*.) Toward one who does not repent for a sin committed, we ought to behave as the Lord commanded, saying: “Let him be to you as a heathen and a publican” (Matt. XVIII). And as the Apostle commands: “Withdraw yourselves,” he says, “from every brother who walks disorderly, and not according to the tradition which I delivered to you” (II Thess. III).

### CHAPTER 79.—That one who remembers having committed unlawful acts ought also to abstain from lawful ones. From the statements of Pope Gregory (Homily 20).

Whoever remembers that he has committed unlawful acts should make an effort to abstain even from lawful ones, so that by this means he may make satisfaction to his Creator: he who committed what was forbidden ought to cut off from himself even what was permitted.

[Col. 0881A]

### CHAPTER 80.—That after undertaking penance no one may return to secular military service. From the letter of Pope Leo, chapter 25 (Letter 92, chapter 10, *On Penance*).

(Dist. 5, c. *Contrarium vero*.) It is wholly contrary to ecclesiastical rules to return to secular military service after undertaking penance, since the Apostle says: “No one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs” (II Tim. II). Therefore, one who wishes to entangle himself in worldly military service is not free from the snares of the devil.

### CHAPTER 81.—On the same matter. From the Second Council of Arles, chapter 3 (chapter 2).

(Dist. 50, c. *Hi qui*.) Those who, after undertaking the purpose of holy religion [“If any after the purpose of holy religion,” etc.], apostatize and return to the world, and afterward do not seek the remedies of penance, are not to receive communion without penance. We also command that they not be admitted to clerical office; and whoever he may be, after penance he must not presume to adopt secular dress. If he does presume to do so, let him be regarded as outside the Church.

[Col. 0881B]

### CHAPTER 82.—That no religious or holy person is without sin. From the statements of Augustine (*On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 86).

No holy and righteous person is without sin; nevertheless, he does not on that account cease to be righteous or holy, provided that he holds fast to holiness in his disposition. For we acquire holiness not by the powers of nature, but by the assistance of resolve through God’s grace. Therefore all saints truly declare themselves sinners, because they truly have something to lament—if not the reproach of conscience, at least the changeability and instability of transgressing nature.

[Col. 0881C]

### CHAPTER 83.—That penitents ought to abstain from banquets and adornments. From the decrees of Pope Lucius, chapter 5.

That penitents ought to abstain from banquets, adornments, and white clothing; and that those at discord be driven from the church until they return to peace.

### CHAPTER 84.—That a priest must not reconcile penitents unless his bishop commands it. From the African Council, chapter 30 (chapter 10, and Carthage III, chapter 32).

(26, q. 6, c. *Presbyter*.) A priest is not to reconcile a penitent without first consulting [“without consulting,” original] the bishop, except where necessity compels because the bishop is absent.

[Col. 0881D]

### CHAPTER 85.—That ordained persons convicted of graver sins ought not, like laypeople, to receive the laying on of hands. From the Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter XXVII.

(Dist. 50, c. *Confirmatum est*.) It was likewise confirmed that, whenever priests or deacons are convicted of some graver fault for which they must be removed from ministry, hands are not to be laid upon them as upon penitents or as upon believing laypeople; nor is it ever to be permitted that those rebaptized be promoted to a clerical rank.

### CHAPTER 86.—Whether clerics who sin by a bodily offence can be restored. From Isidore’s letter to Masona.

[Col. 0882A]

[Note: [Col. 0881] This occurs above in chapter 57, and is cited in Distinction 50, *Domino sancto*.] No contradiction is to be understood in decrees of this kind: in one place it is read that a rank of honour is to be restored after penance in the case of a bodily lapse, while elsewhere, after such an offence, the standing of the former order is by no means to be restored. This difference is distinguished as follows. The canon commands those to return to their former grades of office who have first made satisfaction through penance, or made a worthy confession of their sins. On the other hand, those who neither amend the vice of the flesh nor cease striving, with a certain superstitious recklessness, to justify the very carnal offence which they commit, are to receive neither rank of honour nor the grace of communion.

### CHAPTER 87.—Concerning those who serve at God’s altar, if they suddenly fall through the lamentable frailty of the flesh. From the Council of Lleida, chapter 5.

[Col. 0882B]

(Dist. 50 and 15, c. *Hi qui altario*.) Those who serve at God’s altar, if they suddenly fall through the lamentable frailty of the flesh and, under the Lord’s regard, repent worthily—so that, having mortified the body, they offer God the sacrifice of a contrite heart—it remains within the bishop’s power either not to suspend for long those who are genuinely afflicted, or to separate the negligent from the body of the Church for a more prolonged period. Yet they are to recover the places of their offices in such a way that they cannot thereafter be promoted to higher offices. But if they return a second time, like dogs to their vomit, and, like swine, immerse themselves in wallowing mire (Prov. XXVI; II Pet. II), they are not only to be deprived of the dignity of office, but are also to receive holy communion only at the point of death.

[Col. 0882C]

### CHAPTER 88.—That married persons ought to abstain from their wives in Lent. From the Council of Elvira, chapter 5 (in fragment).

Whoever has known his wife during Lent before Easter and refuses to abstain from her is to do penance for one year, or else give the equivalent of twenty-five solidi to the Church or distribute it among the poor. If it occurred through drunkenness and not by habit, he is to do penance for forty days.

### CHAPTER 89.—Concerning those who presume to eat meat during the days of Lent. From the Eighth Council of Toledo, chapter 9.

Whoever, whether through unavoidable necessity and frailty, manifest illness, or incapacity caused by age, presumes to attempt the eating of meat during the days of Lent shall be guilty not only in respect of the Lord’s resurrection, but also excluded from holy communion on that day. This shall be added to his punishment: throughout the course of that year he is to abstain from every eating of meat, because on the sacred days he forgot the discipline of abstinence.

[Col. 0882D]

### CHAPTER 90.—Concerning a brother sinning not unto death. From the Epistle of John the Evangelist (I John V).

Whoever knows his brother to be sinning not unto death should ask for him, and God will give him life. If anyone sins unto death—because there is sin unto death—I do not say that anyone should pray for him.

[Col. 0883A]

### CHAPTER 91.—That it is difficult for one who has sinned grievously while in an ordained rank to remain in that rank. From the statements of Jerome.

Whoever does not preserve the dignity of a divine rank should be content to save his soul. For it is difficult to return to the rank in which he formerly stood.

### CHAPTER 92.—On the same matter. Again, from the same author.

Whoever sins while in an ordained rank ought to be excommunicated, because the dignity of this name is great. Yet after penance he can redeem his soul; for it is difficult to attain his former rank.

### CHAPTER 93.—On the same matter. From the statements of Augustine.

One who has fallen while in an ordained rank should, after penance, be content to baptize, give communion to the sick, and minister only at the altar.

[Col. 0883B]

### CHAPTER 94.—On the same matter. From the statements of Isidore.

In the angel set over Ephesus (Rev. II), Isidore shows the priest, in accordance with Malachi, who says: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II). For the priest’s lampstand, since the charisms of honour are understood by it, is wholly removed, according to John, when, after offences, penance having been neglected, the sins committed are not lamented. For he does not say, “Because you have fallen, I shall remove your lampstand”; but, “Unless you repent, I shall remove your lampstand.”

### CHAPTER 95.—That canonical discipline commands a penitent priest to return to his former status after seven years. Again, Isidore.

[Col. 0883C]

The discipline of the canons commands a penitent priest to return after seven years to his former status, not by the fulfilment of his own choice, but rather by the sentence of divine judgment. For it is read that Miriam, Aaron’s sister and a prophetess, when she incurred the offence of speaking against Moses, was immediately struck with the mark of leprosy. When Moses asked that she be cleansed, the Lord commanded her to go outside the camp for seven days and, after cleansing, to return again to the camp (Num. XII). Thus Miriam, Aaron’s sister, is understood as the priest’s flesh: when, devoted to pride, it is stained by the foulest errors of corruptions, it is to remain outside the camp for seven days—that is, to be cast out from the fellowship of the holy Church for seven years—and, after the correction of vices of life has been completed, to recover the standing of its place or former dignity.

[Col. 0883D]

### CHAPTER 96.—Concerning those who eat scabs or little worms, or drink urine. From Bede’s Penitential.

One who eats scabs or little worms called lice, or drinks urine or eats excrement: if they are infants or children, let them be whipped; if of adult age, let them do penance for seven days. Both are to be healed by the bishop’s laying on of hands.

### CHAPTER 97.—Concerning those who eat animals torn by beasts or strangled in snares. From Theodore’s Penitential.

Animals torn by wolves or dogs are not to be eaten; neither deer nor roe-deer, if they are found dead, unless perhaps they are first killed by a person while still alive. They are instead to be given to pigs and dogs. Birds and other animals, if strangled in nets, are likewise not to be eaten; nor those killed by a hawk and found dead in that condition, because the Acts of the Apostles commands abstinence from fornication, blood, what has been strangled, and idolatry (Acts XV).

[Col. 0884A]

### CHAPTER 98.—Concerning bees if they kill a person. Again, from the same author.

If bees kill a person, they too should quickly be killed; their honey, however, may be eaten.

### CHAPTER 99.—Concerning pigs and hens, if they eat human blood. Again, from the same author.

If pigs or hens eat human blood, they are to be killed at once; their entrails are to be thrown away, but the rest of the meat may be eaten. If their killing is delayed, however, they are not to be eaten. If they have torn the corpses of the dead, they are to be fattened and then eaten after a year’s cycle. If pigs kill a person, they are to be killed immediately and buried.

[Col. 0884B]

### CHAPTER 100.—Concerning those who eat unclean meat or carrion. Again, from the same author.

Whoever eats unclean meat, carrion, or flesh torn by beasts is to do penance for forty days. But if this occurs through the necessity of hunger, the penalty is much lighter.

### CHAPTER 101.—Concerning those who eat food touched by an unclean hand, or if a dog or another unclean animal touches food. Again, from the same author.

If someone accidentally touches food with an unclean hand, or if a dog, a *pilax* [uncertain animal], a cat, a mouse, or an unclean animal eats human blood, this does no harm. And one who, because of the necessity of hunger, eats an animal that seems unclean, whether bird or beast, is to do penance mercifully.

[Col. 0884C]

### CHAPTER 102.—Concerning those polluted by any unclean blood. Again, from the same author.

One who is polluted by blood or by anything unclean: if the person who eats does not know, the matter is slight; but if he knows, let him do penance according to the degree of pollution.

### CHAPTER 103.—Concerning those who drink blood or semen. Again, from the same author.

Whoever drinks blood or semen for any purpose is to do penance for three years.

### CHAPTER 104.—Concerning fish found dead in a river. Again, from the same author.

A fish found dead in a river is not to be eaten, because it is not a person’s catch. But if it has been caught while fishing and is found on that same day, one who has no hesitation may eat it; one who doubts, however, should not eat it.

[Col. 0884D]

### CHAPTER 105.—Concerning clerics afflicted by a demon. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 6.

If any cleric is afflicted by a demon, he is to do penance for ten years, remain among the hearers, and not be brought to sacred orders. If he lives well and is freed through God’s grace [“mercy”], he is to serve in the remaining ecclesiastical offices.

### CHAPTER 106.—Concerning those who do not preserve honour toward their parents. From the Roman Penitential.

If anyone dishonours his father or mother, he is to do penance for three years. If he raises his hand against, or strikes, either, he is to do penance for seven years.

### CHAPTER 107.—That it is unsuitable for a penitent to conduct any business. From the decrees of Pope Leo (Letter 91, chapter 9, *On Penance*).

[Col. 0885A]

(Dist. 5, c. *Qualitas*.) The character of profit either excuses or accuses a trader, for gain may be honourable or disgraceful. Nevertheless, it is more beneficial for a penitent to suffer losses than to be bound by the dangers of trade, because it is difficult for sin not to enter into the commerce between buyer and seller.

### CHAPTER 108.—That priests are to impose penance on no one from private inclination, but by authority. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 24.

After all these matters had been dealt with, the rationale of penance was examined, so that priests might understand more certainly how they ought to receive confessions and prescribe [variant: “impose”] penance upon penitents according to canonical institution.

[Col. 0885B]

### CHAPTER 109.—That every priest should know in order the eight principal vices. From the same council, chapter 5.

The doctrine of the eight principal vices was examined, so that every priest might know their differences, understand, with the Lord’s help, how to guard himself against them, and preach this to others.

### CHAPTER 110.—That priests should diligently examine the sins of those confessing. From the same council, chapter 6.

That bishops and priests should examine how they are to judge sins confessed to them and determine the time of penance.

### CHAPTER 111.—That individual priests should possess authoritative chapters for aiding penitents. From the same council, chapter 26.

[Col. 0885C]

That every priest should have chapters concerning greater and lesser vices, by which he may be able to recognize them and preach to those subject to him, so that they may beware of the devil’s snares.

### CHAPTER 112.—Concerning priests who conceal sinners’ faults or bring inadequately penitent persons to reconciliation. From the decrees of Pope Alexander I (at the end of the Decretals).

Let no priest accept a gift, or any temporal gain—indeed, spiritual loss—from anyone publicly [“publicly or,” original] sinning or incestuous, in order to conceal that person’s sin from the bishop or his ministers. Nor, through regard for any person, kinship, or friendship, sharing in another’s sins, may he refuse to make it known to the bishop. Nor may he presume to receive from any penitent grace, favour, or a gift; or bring an insufficiently worthy penitent to reconciliation and bear testimony to his reconciliation; or, through any spite, remove from reconciliation someone else more worthy in penitence. For this is simoniacal, and contrary both to God and to human beings.

[Col. 0885D]

### CHAPTER 113.—Concerning those who mutilate limbs. From the Roman Penitential.

Whoever, in a quarrel or by a blow, makes a person disabled or disfigured must pay the physician’s expenses and do penance for half a year. If he has nothing from which to make restitution, he is to do penance for one year. If a layperson maliciously sheds blood, he must repay the injured person as much as the harm done; and if he has nothing with which to repay, he must work for his neighbour while the latter is ill, and afterward do penance for forty days on bread and water.

[Col. 0886A]

### CHAPTER 114.—On the same matter. From Bede’s Penitential.

Whoever strikes his neighbour and does no harm is to do penance for three days on bread and water. If a cleric, for one year or half a year. Whoever deliberately [variant: “of his own will”] cuts off any member of another person is to do penance for three years, one of these on bread and water. Little children striking one another are to do penance for three days; but adolescents, for twenty days.

### CHAPTER 115.—Concerning those who provide guidance and lead plunderers against Christians. From the Roman Penitential.

If anyone guides raiders against Christians, so that they may plunder them, and no slaughter of Christians occurs, he is to do penance for three years. But if it does occur, having laid aside [variant: “cast aside”] arms, let him live dead to the world until death.

[Col. 0886B]

### CHAPTER 116.—Concerning those who become sorcerers through love. From Theodore’s Penitential.

If anyone becomes a sorcerer through love and destroys a person, if he is a cleric he is to do penance for one year on bread and water; if a subdeacon, for two years; if a deacon, for three years, one of these on bread and water. A layperson is to do penance for half a year. Especially if by this means anyone deceives a woman’s childbirth, each person is to add three years on bread and water, lest he be guilty of homicide.

### CHAPTER 117.—Concerning those who, unknowingly, have associated with heretics in certain matters. From the decrees of Pope Eutychian.

[Col. 0886C]

If anyone gives or receives communion from the hand of a heretic, and does not know that the Catholic Church forbids it, then, upon later learning this, he is to do penance for a full year. But if he knows and neglects this, and afterward does penance, he is to do penance for ten years; others judge seven years, and more leniently, five years. If anyone allows a heretic to celebrate Mass in a Catholic church without knowing it, he is to do penance for forty days; if he does so out of reverence for the heretic, for a full year; if for condemnation of the Catholic Church and Roman custom, let him be cast out of the Church as a heretic unless he undertakes penance. If he does, he is to do penance for ten years. If he has departed from the Catholic Church into an assembly of heretics and persuaded others to do so, then afterward does penance, he is to do penance for twelve years: four years outside the church, six among the hearers, and two more excluded from communion. Concerning such persons it is said in the canon that in the tenth year they are to receive communion without the offering. If a bishop or abbot orders his monk to chant Masses for dead heretics, it is neither permitted nor expedient to obey them. If it happens that, where a priest has chanted Mass, another recites the names of the dead and names heretics together with Catholics, if the priest realizes this after Mass, he is to do penance for a week; if he does it frequently, for a full year. But if anyone arranges a Mass for the death of a heretic and keeps that person’s relics there out of reverence for his religion, while not knowing the distinction of the Catholic faith, then, after learning it and undertaking penance, he must burn those relics there with fire and do penance for one year. But if he knows and neglects it, once moved to penance he is to do penance for ten years. If anyone departs from the Catholic faith without any necessity and afterward embraces penance wholeheartedly, according to the Nicene Council (chapter 11), he is to do penance for three years outside the church, that is, among the hearers; seven years in churches among the penitents; and two more years excluded from communion.

[Col. 0887A]

### CHAPTER 118.—Concerning those who eat or drink something touched or dipped in by unclean animals. From the Roman Penitential.

Whoever eats or drinks something dipped into by a domestic beast—that is, a dog or cat—and knows it, is to chant one hundred psalms. If he does not know it, let him fast for two days; or, if he wishes to redeem the penalty, let him chant fifty psalms. Whoever gives another a liquid in which a dead mouse or weasel has been found, if a layperson, is to do penance for seven days. If it occurs in monasteries, let three hundred psalms be chanted. Whoever later learns that he drank such a drink is to chant one hundred and fifty psalms. If anyone unknowingly eats something half-cooked, he is to do penance for three days or chant the Psalter; if knowingly, for seven days. For petty theft, one who is twenty years old is to do penance for twenty days. A child ten years old who commits some theft is to do penance for seven days.
