If anyone dips his hand into any liquid food, and does so with an unfit hand, he is to make amends by one hundred blows with the palm. If a dead mouse or weasel is found in flour, dry food, porridge, or curdled milk, everything around it is to be thrown outside, while what remains may be eaten.

[Col. 0887B]

### CHAPTER 119.—That the devil does not see the inward thoughts of the soul, but sometimes infers them from the body’s movement. From the statements of Augustine (*On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 81).

It is most certain that the devil does not see the inward thoughts of the soul. Yet experience has taught us that he gathers them from movements of the body and indications of its affections. But the secrets of the heart are known by him alone to whom it is said: “You alone know the hearts of the children of men” (II Chron. VI).

[Col. 0887C]

### CHAPTER 120.—On the same matter. Again, from the same author (ibid., chapter 82).

Not all our evil thoughts are always aroused by the devil’s prompting; sometimes they arise from the movement of our own will. Good thoughts, however, are always from God.

[Col. 0887D]

### CHAPTER 121.—Concerning those who strive to defend others in their guilt. Again, from his statements.

Let not the Church defend those guilty of blood, lest it become a participant in bloodshed.

### CHAPTER 122.—On the same matter. From the decrees of Pope Eusebius, chapter 15.

Let one who strives to defend or excuse another in that person’s guilt be excommunicated.

### CHAPTER 123.—That penance is to be given to married persons only by mutual consent. From the Second Council of Arles, chapter 6 (chapter 22).

Penance is not to be given to married persons except by mutual consent.

### CHAPTER 124.—By what means the souls of the dead ought to be released. From the statements of Gregory (Augustine, *On Care for the Dead*, book, chapter 2).

[Col. 0888A]

The souls of the dead are released in four ways: by the offerings of priests, the prayers of saints, the almsgiving of loved ones, or the fasting of relatives.

### CHAPTER 125.—Concerning the feeding of the sick. From the statements of Jerome.

There is no difference between feeding the sick and cherishing Christ. For the sick must be fed, because Christ professes himself to be sick (Matt. XXV).

### CHAPTER 126.—That past evils do no harm if present ones do not please. From the statements of Augustine.

Past evils do no harm if present ones do not please, especially if they have been expiated by many alms.

### CHAPTER 127.—Concerning those who neglect to receive guests. From the Roman Penitential.

[Col. 0888B]

Whoever does not receive guests into his house, as the Lord commanded and for which he promised the kingdom of heaven (ibid.), is to do full penance on bread and water, unless he corrects himself, for as long as he denied hospitality to guests and did not fulfil evangelical commands according to his ability—neither washing feet nor giving alms.

### CHAPTER 128.—That clerics should distribute superfluities to the poor. From the Roman Penitential.

A cleric who has superfluous goods should give them to the poor. But if he does not, thereafter, for as long as he lives, let him live withdrawn in contrition and penance.

### CHAPTER 129.—Concerning one who imputes his own sin to a brother before rebuking him privately. Again, from the same source.

[Col. 0888C]

Whoever, by imputing a sin, lays it upon a brother before rebuking him privately is to make satisfaction to him and do penance for three days.

### CHAPTER 130.—Concerning those who conceal sins for a long time. From Bede’s Penitential.

It should indeed be known that the longer anyone remains in sins, the more his penance must be increased [variant: “performed”].

### CHAPTER 131.—Concerning one who strikes another in anger. From the Council of Rouen, chapter 9.

If anyone strikes another in anger and sheds blood, if a layperson, he is to do penance for twenty days; if a cleric, for thirty. Those who hold rank, however, must be subjected to a greater penalty: a deacon, six months; a priest, one year; a bishop, two years and six months.

[Col. 0888D]

### CHAPTER 132.—Concerning those who rise to strike a person, intending to kill him, but cannot do so. From the Roman Penitential.

Whoever rises to strike a person intending to kill him is to do penance for three weeks. If he is a cleric, for six months. If he wounds him, he is to do penance for forty days. If a cleric wounds a cleric, for a full year; and he must also pay the person whom he wounded money proportionate to the wound.

### CHAPTER 133.—Concerning those who conceal a brother’s sin which is unto death. From Theodore’s Penitential.

Whoever conceals a brother’s offence which is unto death (I John V), and does not rebuke him according to the evangelical rule—first between himself and that brother alone, then before others, then by reporting the offence to the Church (Matt. XVIII), if necessary—is to do penance for as long as he concealed it.

[Col. 0889A]

### CHAPTER 134.—That it is not permitted for a deacon to give penance to anyone. From the Roman Penitential.

It is not permitted for a deacon to give penance to anyone; a bishop or priest must give it.

### CHAPTER 135.—That penance which has been delayed is not to be denied when it is sought. From the decrees of Pope Leo, chapter 21 (Letter 92, chapter 7, *On Penance*).

(Dist. 1, c. *Poenitentia quae*.) This delay may arise not from contempt for the remedy, but from fear of committing a graver sin. Therefore, when penance that has been delayed is sought more earnestly, it is not to be denied, so that in whatever way the wounded soul may attain the medicine of pardon.

### CHAPTER 136.—Concerning those who despise persons who faithfully hold agapae. From the Council of Gangra, chapter 11.

[Col. 0889B]

(Dist. 42, c. *Quis despicit*.) If anyone despises those who faithfully provide *agapae*, that is, banquets for the poor, and invite brethren for the Lord’s honour, and refuses to participate in such invitations, making light of what is done, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER 137.—Concerning those who say that they have no sins. From the African Council, chapter 70 (chapter 81, and Council of Milevis, chapter 6).

It was likewise decreed that, concerning what the holy Apostle John says, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I), whoever thinks this ought to be understood so as to say that we must say we have sin because of humility, not because this is truly so, let him be anathema. For the Apostle continues and adds: “But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity” (ibid.). Here it clearly appears that this is said not merely humbly but truthfully. For the Apostle could have said: “If we say that we have no sin, we exalt ourselves, and humility is not in us.” But when he says, “We deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us,” he sufficiently shows that one who says he has no sin speaks not truth but falsehood.

[Col. 0889C]

### CHAPTER 138.—Concerning those saints who say in the Lord’s Prayer, “Forgive us our debts.” From the same council, chapter 71 (chapter 81, and Council of Milevis, chapter 7).

[Col. 0889D]

It was likewise decreed that whoever says that saints say in the Lord’s Prayer, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. VI), not for themselves—because this petition is not necessary for them—but for others in their people who are sinners, and that therefore each saint does not say, “Forgive me my sins,” but, “Forgive us our debts,” so that the righteous person is understood to ask this for others rather than for himself, let him be anathema. For the Apostle James was holy and righteous when he said: “We all stumble in many things” (Jas. III). Why was “all” added, unless so that this statement might agree also with the psalm where it is read: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, because no living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLII)? And in the prayer of the most wise Solomon: “There is no one who does not sin” (III Kings VIII; II Chron. VI; Eccl. VII). And in the book of Saint Job: “He places a sign upon the hand of every person, so that every person may know his own weakness” (Job XXXVII). Hence even holy and righteous Daniel, when in prayer he said in the plural, “We have sinned; we have done iniquity” (Dan. IX), and the other things which he there confesses truthfully and humbly, lest he be thought—as some suppose—to have said this not of his own sins but rather of the sins of his people, later said: “While I was praying and confessing my sins and the sins of my people to the Lord my God” (ibid.). He did not wish to say “our sins,” but spoke of the sins of his people and of his own, because, as a prophet, he foresaw that there would be people who would understand so badly.

[Col. 0890A]

### CHAPTER 139.—Concerning those who afflict themselves over the death of loved ones. From the letter of Pope Anastasius I addressed to the most noble man Nerianus.

[Col. 0890B]

But we who know, believe, and teach this ought not to grieve excessively for those who die, lest what has the appearance of piety among others should be more a fault in us. For it is, in some manner, a kind of distrust to act contrary to what every preacher who loves righteousness seeks [original: “to that against which every preacher protests”], as the Apostle says: “But we would not have you ignorant, brethren, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve as the rest do, who have no hope” (I Thess. IV). Therefore, dearest brother, having considered this reasoning, we must strive, as we have said, not to afflict ourselves over the dead, but to devote our affection to the living, for whom both piety is beneficial and love fruitful. Lay aside, therefore, dearest one, sorrow, and take up the spiritual fruit of joy for the benefit of God’s holy Church and the advancement of his servants. Strive to make whatever span of this life remains illustrious through eternal and divine duties, so that he who has made you distinguished may render you more illustrious for himself through the ages.

[Col. 0890C]

### CHAPTER 140.—Concerning those who voluntarily inflict death upon themselves. From the First Council of Braga, chapter 10 (chapter 34).

(23, q. 5, c. *Placuit ut hi*.) It was decreed that for those who voluntarily bring death upon themselves by sword, poison, precipice, hanging, or any other means, no commemoration is to be made for them in the offering, nor are their bodies to be taken to burial with psalms. For many have presumed to do this through ignorance. It was likewise decreed that the same be done with those punished for their crimes.

[Col. 0890D]

### CHAPTER 141.—On the same matter. From the Council of Chalon, chapter 5 (Council of Auxerre, chapter 17).

Whoever by his own will throws [variant: “casts,” original] himself into water, hangs himself, throws himself from a tree, wounds himself with a weapon, or voluntarily consigns himself to death in any way: his offering is not to be received (the original differs slightly).

### CHAPTER 142.—Concerning those who presume to take food with unbelievers. From the Council of Elvira, chapter 50.

If a cleric or believer takes food with Jews, it was decreed that he should be excluded from communion, so that he may be corrected.

### CHAPTER 143.—Concerning those who apostatize and turn themselves to idolatry.

[Col. 0891A]

From the same council (Pope Siricius, Letter 1, chapter 3, has the same).

It was further added that certain Christians pass over to apostasy—which it is wicked even to say—and are profaned by the worship of idols and the defilement of sacrifices. We command that they be cut off from the body and blood of Christ, by which they had formerly been redeemed through rebirth; and, should they perhaps at some time come to their senses and turn to lamentation, penance is to be performed by them as long as they live, so that at their final end the grace of reconciliation may be granted them, as the Lord says: “I do not will the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XVIII).

### CHAPTER 144.—On the same matter. Again, from the same source (First Council of Arles, chapter 23).

Concerning those who apostatize, rarely present themselves at church, and do not even seek to do penance, but afterward, when seized by illness, request communion: it was decreed that communion is not to be given them unless they reveal their sound faith and produce [variant: “reveal and produce”; thus the manuscript of the council] worthy fruits of penance.

[Col. 0891B]

### CHAPTER 145.—Concerning those who take Christian slaves captive. From Theodore’s Penitential.

If anyone by any contrivance takes a person captive or sends him away, he is to do penance for three years.

### CHAPTER 146.—Concerning those who burn the house or threshing-floor of their neighbour. From the Roman Penitential.

If anyone deliberately burns by fire anyone’s house or threshing-floor, he must restore all that was taken or burned and perform penance for three years.

### CHAPTER 147.—Concerning those who indecently touch a girl or woman. From the same source.

[Col. 0891C]

If anyone touches a girl’s or woman’s breast, or their private parts, he is to do penance for five days if a cleric, three days if a layperson. A monk or priest suspended from divine ministry who commits such an act is to do penance for twenty days. For it is written: “You shall neither touch nor handle the shameful parts of women.”

### CHAPTER 148.—Concerning those who bathe with women. From Theodore’s Penitential.

If anyone presumes to bathe with women in a bath, he is to do penance for three days and must not presume to do so further.

### CHAPTER 149.—Concerning the administration of a hostel [variant: *synodochia*] and of tithes. On the same matter.

If anyone administers hostels [variant: *synodochia*] for the poor or receives the people’s tithes, and subtracts from them anything for his own profits or pursuit, as an invader of another’s property he must restore the loss and be corrected under canonical judgment, and perform penance for three years. For it is written: “The Lord seeks such a steward as appropriates nothing of his own from the goods entrusted to him.”

[Col. 0891D]

### CHAPTER 150.—That menstruating women are not to make an offering.

Women are not to make an offering during menstruation, neither consecrated women nor laywomen. If they presume to do so, they are to do penance for three weeks.

### CHAPTER 151.—Concerning women who enter a church before their blood is clean, and those who marry during those days. From Theodore’s Penitential.

A woman who enters a church before the cleansing of her blood [Col. 0892A] after childbirth, if she has borne a male child, shall do penance for 33 days; if a female, for 46. But if any woman presumptuously enters the church before the appointed time, she shall do penance on bread and water for as many days as she ought to have remained away from the church. Whoever has intercourse with her during those days shall do penance on bread and water for ten days.

### CHAPTER 152.—That monks ought not to impose penance upon laypeople. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 22.

Monks are not free to impose penance upon laypeople.

### CHAPTER 153.—That penitents are not to be reconciled before completing their penance. From the same council, chapter 23.

Penitents are not to be reconciled, unless necessity compels it, before they have performed their penance.

### CHAPTER 154.—That those who come to confession should first be questioned concerning the rancour of envy and avarice. From the Penitential of Theodore.

[Col. 0892B]

Certainly, since murders arise, as has been set forth above, from the rancour of envy, from anger, and also from avarice, we have rightly, I think, judged that we should first show how this vice itself is to be wholly corrected canonically by priestly judgment; and then, according to the order of the vices, the remedy should follow, so that, whenever a penitent wishes to be cleansed, he may without delay find in the individual chapters the means by which he may more easily be purified.

### CHAPTER 155.—Concerning those who maintain that their sins are to be confessed to God alone. From the Penitential of Theodore (and the Second Council of Chalon, chapter 33, *On Penance*).

(Distinction 1, chapter *Quidam Deo*.) Some say that sins ought to be confessed to God alone, as the Greeks do; but others judge that they should be confessed to priests, as does the whole holy Church. Both are done within the holy Church not without great profit, provided that we confess our sins both to God, who forgives sins—and this is the part of the perfected—and say with David: “I made my transgression known to you, and I did not hide my iniquity. I said: ‘I will confess my iniquities against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the ungodliness of my sin” (Psalm 31). Yet the apostolic ordinance must be followed: that we confess our sins to one another and pray for one another, that we may be saved (James 5). Thus confession made to God alone, which belongs to the righteous, cleanses sins; but confession made to a priest teaches how those sins are to be cleansed. For God, the author and giver of salvation and healing, [Col. 0892D] often bestows this through the invisible administration of his power, and often through the ministry of physicians.

### CHAPTER 156.—Concerning those who accept penance and desire more the completion of the appointed time than remission of sin. From Bede’s Penitential (Second Council of Chalon, chapter 35).

Many—though it cannot be said without sorrow—in penance await not so much the remission of sin as the completion of the appointed time. If the use of meat and wine has been forbidden them, they change not their will but their consumption of food or drink of the same kind, and indulge their pleasures so greatly that, when these things are forbidden, they are found to live more luxuriously by craving other foods or drinks. But spiritual abstinence, which ought especially to flourish in penitents, must shun the enticements [the reading is uncertain] and desire of certain foods and drinks. He, I say, is to be judged more devoted to self-denial who forbids himself not merely the consumption of certain things, but bodily pleasures altogether.

### CHAPTER 157.—That penances are to be imposed according to the ordinances of the canons and penitentials. From the Council of Mainz, chapter 20 (Second Council of Chalon, chapter 37).

Since, therefore, all councils of canons which are received ought to be read and understood by priests, and since they ought to live and preach according to them, we have judged it necessary that those things which concern the faith, and those passages which treat of rooting out vices and planting virtues, should be read by them frequently, understood well, and preached to the people.

### CHAPTER 158.—That no one may presume, for gain, to use unjust measures and unjust weights not approved by the citizens. From the same council, chapter 21.

[Col. 0893B]

That measures and weights be just, as is decreed in the divine laws (Leviticus 19; Proverbs 11 and 20), contained in the Lord’s capitulary, and established by this holy assembly, seems fitting for us all to observe. If anyone presumes, for gain, to alter just measures or just weights, he shall do penance on bread and water for twenty days.

### CHAPTER 159.—Concerning a mother who placed her infant beside the hearth, and it died through her negligence. From the Council of Tribur, chapter 14, attended by King Arnulf (chapter 37, but in other words).

If a mother places an infant beside the hearth, and another person puts water into a cauldron, and, when the water boils, [Col. 0893C] the infant is drenched and dies, the mother shall do penance for negligence, while the other person shall be free from liability.

### CHAPTER 160.—Concerning ordained men whose sins are hidden. From the Council of Toledo.

Concerning ordained men whose sins are hidden and who cannot be openly accused by anyone: if, salutarily compunct by their sins, they make secret confession to a bishop or priest, it seems good to me that, according to what has been prescribed for them, they should perform penance imposed by the bishop or priest—not lukewarmly or slowly, but fervently and diligently—and should trust that they will receive forgiveness of sins from the Lord and retain their rank.

### CHAPTER 161.—That no one may presume to impose penance or hear confession except a bishop or priest. From the Roman Penitential.

[Col. 0893D] For just as no one except bishops and priests, to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been entrusted, ought to offer sacrifice, so no others ought to usurp judgments concerning penitents.

### CHAPTER 162.—That, in the priest’s absence, a deacon may receive penitents when necessity compels. Likewise from the same source.

If necessity arises and no priest is present, a deacon may receive a penitent for holy communion.

### CHAPTER 163.—Concerning the times during which married persons ought to abstain from their wives. From the Council of Elvira.

During the three Lents of the year, on the Lord’s Day, Wednesday, and Friday, married persons [Col. 0894A] ought to abstain, and they must not have intercourse on those days while the wife is pregnant—that is, from the day on which the child first moves in the womb until childbirth; after childbirth, for 33 days if the child is a male, but if female, for 56 days.

### CHAPTER 164.—Concerning a woman who deliberately kills her child. From the same source.

If a mother deliberately kills her child, she shall do penance for fifteen years, and shall never alter her regimen except on the Lord’s Day. But a poor woman who does this because of the difficulty of supporting the child shall do penance for six years.

### CHAPTER 165.—Concerning those who marry on the Lord’s Day. From the Council of Tribur, chapter 51.

Whoever marries on the Lord’s Day shall seek forgiveness from God and do penance for four days.

### CHAPTER 166.—Concerning those who repeat sins already confessed. From the Council of Toledo.

[Col. 0894B] Those things which are repeated through frequent transgression shall be condemned by frequent sentence.

### CHAPTER 167.—Concerning the penance of the faithful: that their confession should not be public. From the letter of Pope Leo, chapter 2 (Letter 80 to the bishops of Campania, chapter 2).

I also decree that the presumption, contrary to apostolic rule, which I recently learned is being committed there by some through unlawful usurpation, be removed by every means: namely, concerning the penance requested by the faithful, that a written declaration detailing the kinds of each individual’s sins not be publicly recited, since the guilt of consciences is sufficiently disclosed to priests alone by secret confession. Although that fullness of faith may seem praiseworthy which, from fear of God, does not shrink from shame before human beings, nevertheless, because not everyone’s sins are of such a kind that those seeking penance do not fear to make them public, this objectionable custom must be removed, lest many be kept from the remedies of penance because they are either ashamed or fear that their deeds may be disclosed to enemies, by whom they could be struck under legal enactment. For that confession is sufficient which is first made to God and then also to the priest, who approaches as an intercessor for the sins of penitents. Then more persons may be moved to penance if the conscience of the confessor is not proclaimed to the ears of the people.

### CHAPTER 168.—Concerning abstinence from meat and fat during the times specified below. From the Council held at Seligenstadt, chapter 1.

All Christians shall, for fourteen days before the feast [Col. 0894D] of Saint John the Baptist, abstain from meat and blood, unless prevented by illness or by the intervening solemnity of some feast celebrated in that diocese. The same shall be observed before the Nativity of the Lord, on the vigil of Epiphany, on all vigils of the Apostles, on the vigil of the Assumption of Saint Mary, on the vigil of Saint Lawrence, and likewise on the vigil of All Saints. To the aforesaid vigils one hour for taking refreshment is added, except in illness, and except where someone wishes by a personal vow to practise a greater abstinence.

### CHAPTER 169.—At what times lawful marriages may not be contracted. From the same source, chapter 3.

Concerning lawful marriages, it has seemed good that no Christian should take a wife from Advent [Col. 0895A] of the Lord until the octave of Epiphany; from Septuagesima until the octave of Easter; during the aforementioned fourteen days before the feast of Saint John the Baptist; or on the aforesaid fast-days and on the nights preceding all solemn days.

### CHAPTER 170.—That a priest who drinks after cockcrow, unless necessity compels, must not dare to celebrate Mass on the following day. From the same council, chapter 4.

It was likewise decreed in the same council that a priest who drinks after cockcrow on summer nights shall not celebrate Mass on the following day; the same applies on winter nights, unless necessity compels.

### CHAPTER 171.—That a priest may not celebrate more than three Masses in one day. From the same council, chapter 5.

It was likewise decreed that every priest may presume to celebrate no more than three Masses in a day.

### CHAPTER 172.—That no one may throw a corporal into a fire to extinguish a blaze. From the same council, chapter 6.

[Col. 0895B]

A complaint was also made in the holy council concerning certain most foolish priests who, when they see a fire, presumptuously throw into it, in order to extinguish the blaze, a corporal consecrated by the Lord’s Body. Therefore it was decreed, under the prohibition of anathema, that this should not be done again.

### CHAPTER 173.—What is to be done if two persons are accused of adultery, one denies it, and the other confesses. From the same source, chapter 7.

[Col. 0895C] The question was asked: if two persons were accused [have been accused] of adultery, and one confessed while the other denied it, what was to be done. The holy council likewise decreed that the one who denied it should clear himself by an accepted legal proof. The one who confessed should perform fitting penance.

### CHAPTER 174.—That no one may carry a sword into church. [From the same source, chapter 8.]

It was likewise decreed in the same council that no one may carry a sword into church, except the king alone.

### CHAPTER 175.—That harmful conversations may not take place in church or in the churchyard. From the same source, chapter 9.

The holy synod also established that the evil custom, now almost universally entrenched, must be wholly prohibited: namely, that people arrange to hold their conversations in the churchyard [Col. 0895D] of a church, and then conduct them chiefly in the church itself, where it is fitting that only prayers and divine offices be performed.

### CHAPTER 176.—Concerning the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1), and special Masses: that they may be said only at their proper times. From the same source, chapter 10.

Some laypeople also, especially matrons, have the custom of hearing every day the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” and special Masses, namely those of the Holy Trinity or Saint Michael. Therefore it was decreed in the same council that this should no longer be done except at its proper time; unless some member of the faithful wishes to hear it out of reverence for the Holy Trinity, and not for some act of divination. If they wish Masses to be sung for them, they shall hear [Col. 0896A] the Masses of the day, or Masses for the welfare of the living or for the dead.

### CHAPTER 177.—Concerning the computation of consanguinity. From the same source, chapter 11.

Some wish to count degrees of consanguinity in such a way that brother and sister are first. But the holy synod established, as the ancient Fathers also decreed, that this should not be so; rather, nephew and niece—that is, the son of a brother and the daughter of a sister—are to be reckoned as first.

### CHAPTER 178.—That lay buildings may not be placed in the churchyard. From the same source, chapter 12.

It was likewise established that lay buildings adjoining churches be removed, and that none be erected in the churchyard except those of priests.

### CHAPTER 179.—That no layperson may entrust his church to a priest without the bishop’s permission. From the same council, chapter 13.

[Col. 0896B]

It was likewise decreed that no layperson may entrust his church to any priest without the bishop’s consent; rather, he shall first send the man to his bishop or the bishop’s vicar, so that it may be determined whether, in learning, age, and character, he is such a person that the people of God may be entrusted to him.

### CHAPTER 180.—What must be done if two persons are accused of adultery. From the same source, chapter 14.

The holy synod also established that, if two persons are accused of adultery, both deny it, and request permission for one of them to clear both by divine judgment, then, if one fails in this, both shall be held guilty.

### CHAPTER 181.—That the proclaimed fast is to be observed most diligently by all. From the same source, chapter 15.

[Col. 0896C]

It was likewise decreed that all must observe with the greatest diligence the proclaimed fast celebrated in whatever diocese. If anyone wishes to redeem any one of those eight prohibited things, he shall feed one poor person on that same day, according to his means.

### CHAPTER 182.—Concerning those who wish to journey to Rome. From the same source, chapter 17.

The holy synod also decreed that no one may go to Rome except with the permission of his bishop or the bishop’s vicar.

### CHAPTER 183.—That a *carina* [perhaps *carena*, a prescribed penitential term] may not be divided for a penitent. From the same source, chapter 17.

[Col. 0896D] It was also commanded under anathema that no priest may presume to divide a *carina* for any penitent unless illness intervenes.

### CHAPTER 184.—Concerning those who refuse to receive penance from priests. From the same council, chapter 18.

Because many are deceived by such folly of mind that, when accused of some capital crime, they refuse to receive penance from their priests, trusting especially that the apostolic see forgives all their sins to those who go to Rome, the holy council judged that such indulgence should not benefit them. Rather, they must first complete the penance imposed on them by their own priests according to the measure of their offence; then, if they wish to go to Rome, they shall receive permission from their own bishop and letters concerning those same matters to be carried to the apostolic see.

### CHAPTER 185.—That every penitent, while observing his *carina*, may not move from place to place. From the same source, chapter 19.

[Col. 0897A]

It was likewise decreed that every penitent, while fasting his *carina*, may not move from place to place, but shall remain where he received his penance, so that his own priest may furnish testimony concerning him. If, however, he cannot fast there because of hostile plots [“injuries,” another reading], his priest shall most carefully commend him to one of his fellow brethren, where he can fast in peace.

### CHAPTER 186.—That no priest may introduce any penitent into church. From the same source, chapter 20.

It was likewise decreed in the same council that no priest may presume, except by the bishop’s command, to introduce into [Col. 0897B] church anyone who is forbidden to enter it because of some offence.

### CHAPTER 187.—How long one ought to do penance for having done this or that. From a penitential for laypeople.

Whoever deliberately kills a person shall do penance for seven years; if he kills one undeserving of death, for ten years. If he kills a deacon, for fourteen years; if a priest, for twenty-one years. Whoever kills a person unintentionally shall do penance for three years; if in public warfare, for one year. Whoever maims a person shall do penance for three Lents. Whoever removes one of another’s principal limbs shall do penance for three and a half years. Whoever sins once sodomitically, or with an animal, shall do penance for seven [twelve] years. If he is accustomed to it, he shall do penance for fourteen years. If he fornicates once between the thighs, he shall do penance for four Lents; if accustomed to it, for three years. If [Col. 0897C] a little boy suffers this by being overpowered, he shall do penance for one Lent; if by himself, for two Lents; if he is accustomed to it, for one year.

Whoever commits adultery once shall do penance for five years; if twice, for ten years. Whoever commits abduction shall do penance for three years, one of them outside the church. Whoever violates a nun shall do penance for seven years; whoever commits incest with a blood-relative, for five years. Whoever consults diviners shall do penance for three years. Whoever is sacrilegious or perjured shall do penance for seven years. Whoever swears against peace shall do penance for one year, and redeem it with alms. Whoever persists stubbornly in hatred shall be excommunicated.

### CHAPTER 188.—The penance of women.

[Col. 0897D] If a woman marries two brothers, she shall do penance for five years. If a woman deliberately kills or aborts her child: if it is already alive, she shall do penance for twelve years; if it is not alive, for six years, and she shall always fast on Friday. If a mother, while sleeping, crushes her son or daughter, she shall do penance for three years. If an infant falls somewhere and dies, the parent shall do penance for one year. If an infant dies unbaptized through negligence, the parent shall do penance for three years, one of them outside the church, and shall always fast on Friday.

### CHAPTER 189.—The order to be observed in the penance of the year to be fasted on bread and water.

The penance of one year, to be fasted on bread and water, ought to be as follows. In every week, he shall fast three days—Monday, Wednesday, [Col. 0898A] and Friday—on bread and water. On three days—Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday—he shall abstain from wine, mead, honeyed ale, meat and fat, cheese and eggs, and every rich fish. But he may eat small fish if he can obtain them. If he cannot obtain them, he may eat only fish of one kind, legumes, vegetables, and fruit if he wishes, and drink ale. On Sundays, on the four days at the Nativity of the Lord, on one day at the Lord’s Epiphany, from Easter until the eighth day, on the Ascension of the Lord, on the four days of Pentecost, and on the Masses of Saint John the Baptist, Saint Mary, the Twelve Apostles, Saint Michael, Saint Remigius, All Saints, Saint Martin, and the feast of the saint celebrated in that diocese, he shall share fellowship with the other Christians—that is, use the same food and drink as the others. Nevertheless, he must always avoid drunkenness and distension of the belly.

### CHAPTER 190.—The manner of penance in the second year.

This is the second year after the year to be observed on bread and water, and to be fasted after it. It is to be imposed also upon those who deliberately kill churchmen; who habitually commit the Sodomitic offence; who habitually sin against nature; who deliberately commit murders in churches; who burn churches; who commit adulteries in churches; and who perpetrate other such acts. The penance of that year must be as follows: in each week he shall fast two days, namely Monday and Wednesday, [Col. 0898C] until evening; then he shall take refreshment with dry food—that is, bread and dry but cooked legumes, fruit, or raw vegetables—choosing and using one of these three; and he may drink ale, but soberly. On the third day, Friday, he shall observe bread and water. He shall also fast three Lents: one before the Nativity of the Lord, the second before Easter, and the third before the Mass of Saint John. If he cannot complete the whole Lent before the Mass of Saint John, he shall complete it afterwards. During these three Lents he shall fast two days each week until the ninth hour and eat dry food, as noted above; and on Friday he shall fast on bread and water. On Sundays, on the four days of the Nativity of the Lord, [Col. 0898D] on one day of the Lord’s Epiphany, from Easter until the eighth day, on the Ascension of the Lord, on the four days of Pentecost, and on the Masses of Saint John the Baptist, Saint Mary, the Twelve Apostles, Saint Michael, Saint Remigius, All Saints, Saint Martin, and the feast of the saint celebrated in that diocese, he shall share fellowship with the other Christians. Nevertheless, he must always avoid drunkenness and distension of the belly.

### CHAPTER 191.—Concerning those able to fast and to fulfil what is written in the Penitential.

Whoever can fast and fulfil what is written in the Penitential does well and should give thanks to God. But for one who cannot, we offer, through God’s mercy, such counsel [Col. 0899A] that neither he nor anyone else need despair or perish.

### CHAPTER 192.—Concerning the redemption of a year which one ought to fast on bread and water.

For one day which a person ought to fast on bread and water, he shall, if possible, chant fifty psalms on bended knees in church. If not, he shall do the same in a suitable place, feed one poor person, and on that day, apart from wine, meat, and fat, consume whatever he wishes.

### CHAPTER 193.—Another manner, from the same source.

But if a person is such that he cannot remain on his knees so long, he shall do this: if possible within a church, otherwise standing attentively in one place, he shall chant seventy psalms in order and feed a poor person; [Col. 0899B] and on that day, apart from wine, meat, and fat, he may consume whatever he wishes.

### CHAPTER 194.—Likewise, another manner.

Whoever bends his knees in church a hundred times—that is, asks forgiveness a hundred times—if this can be done in church, does what is most just. If it cannot be done, he shall do the same secretly in a suitable place. If he does so, on that day, apart from wine, meat, and fat, he may consume whatever he pleases.

### CHAPTER 195.—Likewise, another manner.

Whoever does not know the psalms may redeem one day for which he ought to do penance on bread and water: if rich, with three denarii; if poor, with one denarius. On that day, apart from wine, meat, and fat, he may consume whatever he wishes.

### CHAPTER 196.—Likewise, another manner.

[Col. 0899C] For one day which one ought to do penance on bread and water, he shall feed three poor persons; and on that day, apart from wine, meat, and fat, he may consume what he pleases.

### CHAPTER 197.—Likewise, another manner.

Some say that twenty *palmatae* are equivalent to one day.

### CHAPTER 198.—Concerning the redemption of one week which a person ought to fast on bread and water. From the same source.

For one week which a person ought to fast on bread and water, he shall chant three hundred psalms on bended knees in church. If he cannot do this, he shall chant three psalters attentively in church or in a suitable place. After he has chanted, apart from wine, meat, and fat, he may consume whatever he wishes.

### CHAPTER 199.—Concerning the redemption of one month which a person ought to fast on bread and water.

[Col. 0899D]

For one month which a person ought to fast on bread and water, he shall chant 1,200 psalms on bended knees. If he cannot do this with bended knee, then sitting or standing, in church if possible, otherwise in one place, he shall chant 1,680 psalms. Every day, if he wishes and does not wish to abstain, he may take refreshment at the sixth hour, except that on Wednesday and Friday he shall fast until the ninth hour. For the whole month he shall abstain from meat, fat, and wine; after chanting the aforesaid psalms, he may consume other food. The entire year is to be redeemed in this manner.

### CHAPTER 200.—Concerning those who cannot fast and do not know psalms: how they may redeem the penance of one year which they ought to fast on bread and water.

[Col. 0900A]

Whoever does not know psalms and cannot fast shall give twenty-two solidi to the poor as alms for one year which he ought to fast on bread and water. He shall fast every Friday on bread and water, and observe three Lents: forty days before Easter; forty days before the feast of Saint John the Baptist—if anything remains uncompleted before the feast, he shall complete it afterwards—and forty days before the Nativity of the Lord. During these three Lents, whatever food or drink of whatever kind is prepared for his mouth, he shall assess its price or possible value and distribute half that value as alms to the poor. He shall pray constantly and ask God that his prayer [Col. 0900B] and alms may be acceptable before the Lord.

### CHAPTER 201.—Likewise, redemption of the year which one ought to fast on bread and water. From the Penitential of Theodore.

Likewise, whoever cannot fast and observe what is written in the Penitential shall do what holy Pope Boniface established. For one day which he ought to fast on bread and water, he shall ask a priest to sing Mass for him—unless there are capital crimes, which, once confessed, must first be washed away with tears. Then he himself shall be present and hear Mass, and devoutly offer with his own hands bread and wine into the priest’s hands. He shall attentively make such responses as he knows to the priest’s salutations and exhortations, and humbly beseech God that Almighty God may mercifully deign, through his angel, to receive the offering which he and the priest [Col. 0900C] have offered to God for himself and his sins. On that day, apart from wine, meat, and fat, he may eat whatever he wishes, and thus redeem the remaining days of the year.

### CHAPTER 202.—Concerning those who cannot fast but have the means to redeem their penance.

If someone perhaps cannot fast and has the means to redeem it: if rich, for seven weeks he shall give twenty solidi; if he has not the means to give that much, he shall give ten solidi; but if very poor, he shall give three solidi. Let no one be troubled because we have ordered twenty solidi, or less, to be given: for if he is rich, it is easier for him to give [Col. 0900D] twenty solidi than for a poor person to give three. But each person should consider to whom he ought to give: whether for the redemption of captives, upon the holy altar, to the servants of God, or to the poor as alms.

### CHAPTER 203.—Concerning those who cannot fulfil what is written in the Penitential.

Whoever cannot perform penance as we have said above shall do this: if he ought to fast for three continuous years and cannot fast, he may redeem it thus. In the first year he shall distribute twenty-six solidi as alms; in the second year, twenty solidi; in the third year, eighteen solidi: these amount to sixty-four solidi. Powerful persons ought to give more, for “to whom more is entrusted, more is required” (Luke 12). Those who commit unlawful acts ought also to abstain from lawful ones, [Col. 0901A] and ought to afflict their bodies by fasts, vigils, and frequent prayers. For flesh when glad draws one toward fault, but when afflicted restores one to pardon.

### CHAPTER 204.—Concerning those who cannot fast and have nothing with which they can redeem their penance. From Bede’s Penitential.

Whoever cannot fast, has nothing with which to redeem it, and knows the psalms, shall, for one day which he ought to fast on bread and water, chant three times “Blessed are the undefiled in the way” (*Beati immaculati in via*, Psalm 118) as far as “To the Lord, when I was troubled” (*Ad Dominum cum tribularer*, Psalm 119), and six times “Have mercy on me, O God” (*Miserere mei, Deus*, Psalm 50). He shall prostrate himself on the ground seventy times and say the *Our Father* at each genuflection. But whoever does not know the psalms shall, for one day which he ought to fast on bread and water, prostrate himself on the ground a hundred times and say the *Our Father* at each genuflection.

### CHAPTER 205.—Concerning the redemption of seventy-seven years. From the Roman Penitential.

[Col. 0902A]

Likewise, in another manner: twelve individual three-day observances, each completed with three psalters and with 300 *palmatae* for each psalter, excuse one year’s penance. Two two-day observances likewise, with three psalters and 300 *palmatae* for each psalter, excuse two years. Seventy-five psalms, with an equal number of prayers for pardon during the night and with three hundred *palmatae*, excuse a two-day observance. One hundred psalms with prayers for pardon during the night and 300 *palmatae* excuse a three-day observance. One hundred and twenty special Masses, each with three psalters and three hundred *palmatae*, excuse one year. One hundred solidi given as alms excuse one year.

## SIXTEENTH PART OF THE DECREES: Concerning the duties of laypeople and their cases.

[Col. 0901]

### CHAPTER 1.—The figurative discourse of blessed Clement concerning how great and what kinds of perils the Church suffers in the world.

[Col. 0901B]

Blessed Clement, successor of the apostle Peter, says in his first letter to James, brother of the Lord, namely bishop of Jerusalem:

> “Let this world be regarded as a sea. Let the varieties of winds and whirlwinds be compared with diverse temptations. Let persecutions, tribulations, and dangers be equated with waves. Let the earthly spirits that blow either from torrents or valleys be understood as the words of false prophets, seducers, and corrupt doctrine. Let promontories and rugged places be understood as those who are judges in the powers of this world and threaten dangers and deaths. Let places between two seas, beaten by the double waves of deceptive tides, be compared with persons uncertain in mind and wavering about the truth of the promises [and, according to another reading, with those who scrutinize our faith by irrational reasoning]. Let hypocrites and deceitful persons be regarded as like pirates. And what else are the swift whirlpool, Tartarean Charybdis, shipwrecks dashed against rocks, and deadly drownings to be considered but sins? It remains, therefore, that this ship may safely enter, on a prosperous course, the harbour of the desired city, and thus pour out prayer to God, that those suffering shipwreck may deserve to be heard.”

### CHAPTER 2.—That bishops should not doubt the charge laid upon them by God to protect the people. From the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 31.

Bishops should not doubt the charge laid upon them by God to protect and defend the people. Therefore, [Col. 0901D] when they see judges and powerful persons acting as oppressors of the poor, they should first rebuke them by priestly admonition; and if they disdain to amend, [Col. 0902B] they shall be anathematized.

### CHAPTER 3.—Concerning those who commit plunder in dioceses. From the Council of Carthage, chapter 8.

If anyone despoils another person and, when admonished by the bishop, does not restore what was taken, he shall be excommunicated.

### CHAPTER 4.—That bishops should admonish authorities not to oppress the poor. From the Council of Orléans, chapter 4.

Judges or authorities [“powerful persons,” original reading] who oppress the poor, if admonished by their bishop and do not amend, shall be excommunicated.

### CHAPTER 5.—On the same matter. From the First Council of Mainz, chapter 8 (under Leo III).

That bishops may oversee, govern, administer, and dispense ecclesiastical affairs according to the authority of the canons, we will that laypeople obey bishops in their ministry: in governing the Churches of God, defending widows and orphans, and being obedient to them in preserving their Christian faith. Bishops likewise shall cooperate with counts and judges in the administration of justice, so that a just law may in no way be corrupted in any matter by anyone’s lie, false testimony, perjury, or bribe.

### CHAPTER 6.—Concerning laypeople who unjustly harass the Church or a cleric by litigation. From the Council of Agde, chapter 32.

(5, question 6, chapter *Si quis vero saecularium*.) If any layperson attempts, by a false accusation, to trouble the Church or a cleric, and is convicted, he shall be excluded from the thresholds of the church and from communion with Catholics unless he performs worthy penance.

### CHAPTER 7.—That despisers of the canons be excommunicated. From the First Council of Carthage, chapter 15 (under Julius I, chapter 14).

[Col. 0903A]

Lay despisers of the canons shall be excommunicated; clerics shall be deprived of office.

### CHAPTER 8.—Concerning transgressors of the divine laws. From the Council at Lauriacum, chapter 10 (chapter 1).

If anyone is found to be a public transgressor of the divine law, or a despiser of the holy canons because of manifest crimes, and delays to obey the episcopal constitutions of the holy Fathers, he shall be anathematized.

### CHAPTER 9.—That emperors or any powerful persons may not presume to do anything contrary to the divine command. From the Council of Pope Hadrian, chapter 16 (collected from various sources after the Second Council of Nicaea).

Therefore it is not lawful for an emperor, or for anyone maintaining piety, to presume anything contrary to the commands of the Godhead, nor to do anything opposed to evangelical, prophetic, or apostolic rules. An unjust judgment and an unjust determination, enacted by judges through royal fear or command, shall have no force. Nothing done against evangelical, prophetic, or apostolic teaching, or against their enactment or that of the holy Fathers, shall stand. Whatever has been done by unbelievers or heretics shall be wholly annulled.

### CHAPTER 10.—That no one may presume to act contrary to the canons. From the Council of Tribur, chapter 10 (from the capitula of Pope Hadrian).

(Distinction 10, chapter *Constitutiones*.) Enactments contrary to the canons, the decrees of the Roman bishops, [Col. 0903C] or good morals are of no force.

### CHAPTER 11.—Concerning imperial law. From the decrees of Pope Pius, chapter 3.

(Chapter *Lege imperatorum*.) The law of emperors is not above God’s law, but beneath it.

### CHAPTER 12.—When canonical matters are being debated, laypeople, unless religious persons, are not to be present. From the Council of Chalon, chapter 6.

When matters governed by canons are being debated, or when matters of religious rule are being examined, no laypersons ought to be present unless they are religious persons, and then only those who are summoned in their own capacity.

### CHAPTER 13.—That laypersons in a synod must not presume to teach unless the clergy command it. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, ch. 98.

[Col. 0903D] Laypersons, when clergy are present in a synod, must not presume to teach unless the clergy themselves command it.

### CHAPTER 14.—That the people are to be instructed, not followed. From the decrees of Pope Celestine, ch. 22 (Epistle III, ch. 3).

(Dist. 62, c. *Docendus*.) The people must be instructed, not followed; and, if they do not know what is permitted or not permitted, we ought to admonish them, not give our consent to them. Whoever, moreover, attempts to venture upon what has been forbidden shall find that canonical censure is by no means lacking.

### CHAPTER 15.—Concerning one who acts against a bishop’s decree. A saying of Gregory.

If anyone acts against a bishop’s decree, let him be cast out of the Church.

### CHAPTER 16.—That the emperor must be admonished to obey the ordinances of the Apostolic See. From the decrees of Pope Anastasius (Anastasius II, to Emperor Anastasius, ch. 6).

[Col. 0904A] For the love of your empire, and for the blessedness by which you may attain the kingdom [printed *quae*; read *qua*], we proclaim this more especially in fulfillment of our apostolic office: that, as is fitting and as the Holy Spirit directs, obedience be given to our admonitions, so that your commonwealth may obtain every good thing, as is promised in Exodus: “If you hear the voice of the Lord your God, and do what is pleasing before him, and obey his commandments, and keep all his righteousness, I will not bring upon you any infirmity which I brought upon the Egyptians. For I am the Lord who makes you whole” (Exod. I).

And there again the most powerful trumpet sounds:

[Col. 0904B] “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you except that you fear the Lord your God, walk in all his ways, love him, and serve the Lord your God with your whole heart and with your whole mind? Keep the commandments of the Lord your God and the righteous ordinances which I command you” (Deut. X).

Let not your piety disdain me when I offer these counsels repeatedly, keeping before its eyes the words of the Lord in the Gospel: “He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me; and he who despises me despises him who sent me” (Luke X). For the Apostle also, in harmony with our Savior, speaks thus: “Therefore he who despises these things despises not man, but God, who gave his Holy Spirit in us” (I Thess. IV).

The breast of your clemency is the sanctuary of public prosperity, so that through your earnestness—you whom he commanded to preside on earth, as it were, as his vicar—evangelical and apostolic precepts may not be resisted with harsh pride, but that those things which bring salvation may be fulfilled through obedience.

### CHAPTER 17.—A general admonition to kings. From the Register of St. Gregory, to Aldebert, king of the English, ch. 263 (Register, book IX, epistle 60).

[Col. 0904C] For this reason almighty God brings good men to the governance of peoples: that through them he may bestow the gifts of his power [*pietatis*, “mercy,” variant] upon all those set under them. We have learned that this has occurred among the English people, over whom your glory has therefore been placed, so that the good things granted to you may, by heavenly favor, also restore the people subject to you.

Therefore, glorious son, guard with a watchful mind the grace which you have received from God.

[Col. 0904D] Hasten to extend the Christian faith among the peoples subject to you. Multiply the zeal of your righteousness in their conversion; pursue the worship of idols and overthrow the buildings of their shrines. Build up the conduct of your subjects in great purity of life by exhorting, frightening, correcting, and displaying examples of good works, so that in heaven you may find as your rewarder him whose name and knowledge you have spread abroad upon earth.

He whose honor you seek and maintain among the nations will also render the name of your glory more glorious to posterity. Thus Constantine, that most pious emperor, once recalled the Roman commonwealth from perverse idol-worship, subjected it with himself to almighty God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and converted himself with the peoples subject to him to Christ with his whole mind.

[Col. 0905A] Hence it came about that this man surpassed the name of earlier rulers by his praises, and exceeded his predecessors in reputation as much as he surpassed them in good works. And now, therefore, let your glory hasten to instill knowledge of the one God—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—into the kings and peoples subject to it, so that you may surpass the former kings of your people in praises and merits; and so that, in proportion as you cleanse even the sins of others among your subjects, you may stand more secure concerning your own sins before the terrible judgment of almighty God.

A little later. Moreover, we wish your glory to know that, as we recognize from the words of almighty God in Holy Scripture, the end of the present world is now near, and the kingdom of the saints is to come—a kingdom which can never be ended by any end.

[Col. 0905B] As that end of the world approaches, many things are imminent which have not previously occurred: namely, changes in the air, terrors from heaven, storms contrary to the order [*ordinem*, “order,” variant] of the seasons, wars, famines, pestilences, and earthquakes in various places (Matt. XXIV; Luke XXI). Yet not all these things will occur in our own days; they will follow after our days. Therefore, if you learn that any of these things is happening in your land, do not let your mind be disturbed in any way. For these signs of the end of the age are sent beforehand so that we may be concerned for our souls and apprehensive concerning the hour of death, and so be found prepared in good works for the coming Judge.

### CHAPTER 18.—Another admonition of rulers. From Gregory’s Register, to Justin, praetor of Sicily, ch. 2 (Register, book I, epistle 2).

[Col. 0905C] What the tongue says, conscience bears witness to: long ago, when you were not entangled in the occupations of any office of dignity, I loved and honored you greatly. Indeed, the modesty of your very bearing compelled certain efforts, so that you ought to have been loved even by one unwilling to love you.

When I heard that you had come to administer the praetorship [*praefecturam*, “prefecture,” variant] of Sicily, I rejoiced greatly; but when I learned that a certain dissimulation had crept in between you and ecclesiastical persons, I was deeply grieved. Now, however, since both the care of administration occupies you and concern for this government occupies me,

[Col. 0905D] we can rightly love you in a special manner only insofar as we do no harm to the community at large. Therefore I beseech you by the almighty Lord, before whose dreadful judgment we must render an account of our deeds, that your glory may always keep regard for him before its eyes, and may never admit anything from which even a slight disagreement might arise between us.

Let no profits draw you into injustice. Consider how short life is; reflect upon the Judge to whom you will one day go, you who exercise judicial power. You must therefore observe carefully that we leave behind here every gain, and carry with us to judgment only the grounds arising from ruinous [*dispendiosorum*; printed *dispensativorum*] gains. We must seek, then, those advantages which death cannot take away, but which the end of the present life will show to endure forever.

### CHAPTER 19.—Likewise, an exhortation to rulers. From Gregory’s Register, to Gennadius, patrician and exarch, ch. 72 (book I, epistle 73).

[Col. 0906A] (23, q. 4, c. *Si non*.) If so great a prosperity in military undertakings had not come to Your Excellency by the merit of faith and the grace of Christian religion, it would not have been especially remarkable, since we know that such things were granted even to ancient commanders in war. But because, by God’s gift, you anticipate future victories not by carnal foresight but rather by prayers, it comes to appear wonderful that your glory proceeds not from earthly counsel but descends [*dispensat*, “is dispensed,” variant] from God above.

Where does the widespread report of your merits not travel,

[Col. 0906B] declaring that you frequently undertake wars not from a desire to shed blood, but to extend the commonwealth in which we behold God worshiped, so that the name of Christ may spread everywhere among subject peoples through the preaching of the faith? For just as the outward works of your virtues make you eminent in this life, so too the ornaments of inward character [the Register has *interna morum*, “inward things of character”], proceeding from a pure heart, glorify you in the life to come through participation in heavenly joys.

### CHAPTER 20.—How kings ought to strive to punish the sins of priests or people. From Gregory’s Register, to Brunhild, queen of the Franks, ch. 272 (book IX, epistle 64).

[Col. 0906C] Since it is written, “Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin makes peoples wretched” (Prov. XIV), a kingdom is believed to be made firm when a fault that has become known is swiftly corrected.

For reports from many persons have reached us—something which we cannot say without great affliction of heart—that certain priests in those regions conduct themselves so shamelessly and wickedly that it is disgraceful for us even to hear of it and lamentable to recount. Therefore, lest, now that report of this wickedness has extended even this far, the depravity of others strike either our soul or your kingdom with its dart of sin, we must rise eagerly to punish these matters, lest the hunger [probably *fames*, as printed; perhaps “failing” is intended] of a few be the destruction of many. For evil priests are the cause of a people’s ruin. Who, indeed, will offer himself as an intercessor for the people’s sins if the priest who ought to pray commits graver offenses?

[Col. 0906D] But since those whose duty it is to pursue these matters are stirred neither by concern to investigate nor by zeal to punish, let letters from you come to us, so that, if you command, we may send a person with the assent of your authority, who, together with other priests, ought both carefully to investigate these matters and to correct them according to God.

For the things we mention must not be ignored, because one who can correct them and neglects to do so undoubtedly makes himself a participant in the offense. Take thought, therefore, for your soul; take thought for the grandchildren whom you desire to reign happily; take thought for the provinces. Before our Creator lifts his hand to strike, consider most earnestly the correction of this crime, lest he strike more harshly afterward in proportion as he now waits longer and more mercifully.

[Col. 0907A] Know, moreover, that you will offer our God a great sacrifice of propitiation if you swiftly cut away from your territories the stain of so great a crime. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the fourth indiction.

### CHAPTER 21.—On the same subject. From the Register, to Theuderic, king of the Franks, ch. 274 (book IX, epistle 53).

The letter of Your Excellency, an index of your heart, taught in such an abundant and lucid manner how greatly prudence shines in you together with royal power that there can be no doubt about whatever praiseworthy thing report may have related concerning you.

Since you have indicated that our exhortation has so pleased your royal mind through its expressions of praise that you desire whatever you recognize to concern the worship of our God, the reverence of churches, or the honor of priests to be diligently established and preserved in every respect,

[Col. 0907B] we urge you again, for the sake of your reward [variant: “for the sake of your great reward”], by repeated exhortation, to command that a synod be assembled. As we wrote previously, cause bodily vices among priests and the depravity of the Simoniac heresy to be condemned by the judgment of all bishops and cut away from the territories of your kingdom. Do not allow them to obtain there through money more than the Lord’s commandments prescribe [variant *illis*, “them,” for *illic*, “there”].

For since all covetousness is the service of idols (Col. III), whoever does not diligently guard against it in conferring honors, especially ecclesiastical honors, subjects himself to the perdition of unbelief, even though he may appear to hold the faith which he neglects. Therefore, just as you are diligent against external enemies, be equally solicitous against the inward adversaries of souls,

[Col. 0907C] so that, by faithfully resisting the enemies of our God, you may reign happily here under his protection and afterward, led by his grace, come to eternal joys.

### CHAPTER 22.—That it is a consolation to many if prudent men attach themselves to kings. From Gregory’s Register, to Asclepiodotus, patrician of the Gauls, ch. 271 (book XII, epistle 17).

That prudent men, such as you are, attach themselves to kings is a consolation to many. For when they understand that a position has been granted them for the benefit of their souls, it is certain that they do not prefer other grounds of reward wherever they find them.

### CHAPTER 23.—That opponents of kings are to be excommunicated. From the council at Lauriacum, ch. 14 (ch. 3).

[Col. 0907D] If anyone, with a stubborn and arrogant spirit, presumes to contradict or resist royal authority—which, according to the Apostle, is only from God (Rom. XIII)—and refuses to obey its just and reasonable commands in accordance with God and ecclesiastical authority, let him be anathematized.

### CHAPTER 24.—Concerning those who do not obey a ruler. From the Council of Toledo.

In the Book of Kings it is read: “Whoever does not obey the ruler, let him surely die” (I Kings XXVI). But the Council of Agde commands that he be anathematized.

### CHAPTER 25.—Concerning those found guilty in adversity to their own people or country. From the same council (Toledo, Council VI, ch. 12, although not in the same words).

[Col. 0908A] Therefore reason has persuaded us to decree synodically that any layperson who, by going over to foreign regions, proves harmful in hostility to his own people, country, or royal power, when discovered shall thereafter be condemned to perpetual excommunication; communion shall never be granted to him except at the very end of his life.

### CHAPTER 26.—That no one may presume, while a ruler is alive, to elect another king. From the same council (ch. 17).

Although a judgment concerning such a matter was issued in an earlier council (ch. 4, Fifth Council of Toledo), which was held in the first year of our most glorious ruler, it nevertheless seems good to preserve it again, as is fitting. Therefore, while the king’s life endures, no one—whether a layperson of any rank, or one consecrated to the order of bishop, presbyter, or deacon, or devoted to the other offices of the clergy—shall by any act or deliberation provide a future king against the interest, and undoubtedly the will, of the living king. Nor shall anyone, by flattery or persuasion based upon this expectation, draw others to himself or himself consent to another.

[Col. 0908B] For Christians ought to consider it wicked and utterly detestable to make unlawful provision for a future time and, while ignorant of their own lifespan, to arrange future affairs. If anyone has already meditated upon such things in wicked deliberation with anyone whatsoever, let him know that this concession is granted him by priestly moderation: if he can do so without venial fault, he must strive without delay to disclose it to the ears of the present ruler.

[Col. 0908C] But if he remains silent and refuses to reveal the contrivances of his deliberation, let him be punished by the most severe anathema.

### CHAPTER 27.—That no one may aim at the king’s destruction. From the same Sixth Council, ch. 18 (chs. 2 and 3 of the Fifth Council of Toledo).

It is established that provision was indeed made for the safety of our rulers in the preceding general synod; but we wish to repeat what was well enacted and to strengthen by worthy authority what was beneficially ordained. Therefore, before God and the whole order of angels, before the prophets and apostles, the choir of all martyrs, the whole Catholic Church, and the assembly of Christians, we solemnly declare: let no one aim at the destruction of the king; let no one assail the ruler’s life by murder; let no one deprive him of the helm of the kingdom;

[Col. 0908D] let no one, by tyrannical presumption, usurp for himself the summit of royal power; let no one by any contrivance join the band of conspirators arrayed against him. If any one of our people, a presumptuous person of reckless daring, should be found guilty of any of these acts, let him, struck by divine anathema and without any possibility of remedy, be held condemned to eternal judgment.

### CHAPTER 28.—Concerning the faithful servants of kings. From the same Sixth Council, ch. 14.

Accordingly, as the holy council decreed in the first year of our most serene ruler (ch. 6, Fifth Council of Toledo), all who, in faithful obedience and sincere service, have obeyed the ruler’s wishes or commands and have with their whole purpose guarded and watched over the safety of the kingdom

[Col. 0909A] must not be deprived by successors, on any unjust pretext, either of their rank or of their former possessions. Rather, both now and henceforth they are to be dealt with, according to the discretion of each ruler, as their service is judged necessary to the country; and favor is to be bestowed upon them in such a way that they retain rank and authority in other matters, so that they may enjoy free discretion in all possessions justly acquired, whether to leave them to their descendants or to confer them upon those whom their will has determined.

But if anyone proves unfaithful concerning the royal person, or useless in entrusted affairs, the disposition of such a person is to rest in the ruler’s clemency, according to the judgment of posterity. For it is wicked to call into doubt the right of an authority to which, as is evident, the governance of all has been entrusted by heavenly judgment.

[Col. 0909B] If, after his death, anyone is found to have been unfaithful to his life, let him lose whatever he possessed among the goods acquired through that ruler’s generosity; those goods are to be confiscated and distributed to the faithful.

### CHAPTER 29.—Concerning the offspring of kings. From the same Sixth Council, ch. 16.

Just as the insolence of bad kings is always hateful and detestable to subjects, so the provident usefulness of good kings makes them beloved by peoples. Therefore, who could bear, or see such an erring Christian, as one who attempts to strip royal offspring or descendants of property or deprive them of dignities?

Therefore, lest this happen, let our general decree concerning the ruler’s children be promulgated; that is, let suitable ordinances be made for us concerning the descendants of the present most excellent King Chintila,

[Col. 0909C] so that the whole of his kingdom may preserve toward all his descendants what the synod held last year in this church established (ch. 4, Fifth Council of Toledo): namely, that his children be shown kindly and steadfast affection, and that, wherever the suitability of place permits, they be given protections for their rightful support, lest they be defrauded through any crafty stratagem of property lawfully expended, or procured by their parents’ rank, or owed through the generosity of rulers, the expenditures of any person, or even private ownership; and lest any grounds for injuring them be furnished to anyone by a contrivance.

For it is fitting that we should grant the peace of a conciliar decree to the descendants of him under whose rule we possess security.

### CHAPTER 30.—That whatever an agitated mind does, it considers just. From Gregory’s Register, to Emperor Maurice, ch. 23 (book II, epistle 61, or ch. 100).

[Col. 0909D] He is guilty before almighty God who is not sincere toward the most serene lord in everything he does and says. But I, the unworthy servant of your piety, speak in this petition neither as a bishop nor as a servant by right of the commonwealth, but by private right. For, most serene lord, you were my lord even at that time when you were not yet lord of all.

(St. Gregory, Register, book VIII, epistle 12, to Guidiscalcus, duke of Campania; cited also in 11, q. 3, c. *Illa praepositorum*.) The concern of superiors is useful, the caution praiseworthy, when reason does everything and

[Col. 0910A] anger claims nothing for itself. Authority must therefore be restrained by reason, and nothing must be done before an excited mind returns to tranquility. For in a time of agitation, anger considers whatever it has done to be just.

### CHAPTER 31.—That laypersons must compel presbyters who hold their churches to perform nothing but the divine office. From the sayings of Augustine.

I admonish you, most beloved, to fear God and honor priests, rendering to them the due owed to holiness, so that, with your help, they may be able, undisturbed and secure, to preach saving things and preserve ecclesiastical rule and rigor, with all clergy subject to their bishops and instructed by them.

For the Lord commanded: “Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and unto God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XXII; Mark XII; Luke XX). I give you this apostolic command: let no secular person keep a cleric in personal service; rather, let the cleric serve in mind and heart him whose seal he bears upon his head (II Tim. II), having been trained in the things commanded by his own bishop.

[Col. 0910B] For it is detestable and wicked for a cleric to be found at games, or to pass his life with hawks or in hunting, and then, wounded by such theatrical pursuits, to approach the episcopate, presbyterate, or any priestly office, filled not with good but with evil vices. For it is written: “You who love the Lord, hate evil” (Ps. XCVI).

We also exhort your Christian devotion that, according to the ordinances of the holy canons, no priest coming from elsewhere be received into churches founded by you,

[Col. 0910C] unless he has been consecrated by the bishop of your church or received from him by letters of recommendation. For many people lie to themselves; often slaves of someone, having fled from their masters, announce themselves as though they were consecrated priests, when they are not. They are ministers of the devil, not of God; and likewise are those who receive them, because it is written: “You saw a thief, and you ran with him” (Ps. XLIX), etc.

### CHAPTER 32.—That Jews must not be set over Christians. From the Council of Meaux, ch. 3.

Let Jews not dare, in the administrative capacity of stewards and tax-collectors, to govern a Christian household; nor may anyone order this to be done for them. If anyone presumes to act contrary to this: if he is a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, let him be removed from his office; if a monk, let him be deprived of communion. The same applies to a layperson. And if they persist in disobedience, let them be anathematized.

### CHAPTER 33.—That the holy Church has one Father in heaven. From the Second Council of Chalon, ch. 51.

[Col. 0910D] Since it is evident that there are persons of different conditions in the Church—nobles and persons of no rank, slaves, tenant-farmers, resident dependents, and other such classes—it is necessary that all set over them, whether clergy or laity, deal with them gently and treat them mercifully, both in demanding labor from them and in receiving taxes and certain dues. They must know that these persons are their brothers and have one Father,

[Col. 0911A] God, to whom they cry: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. VI); and one mother, the holy Church, which bears them from the undefiled womb of the sacred font. Therefore the most merciful discipline and appropriate governance must be applied to them. By living without discipline, they offend the author of discipline; systems of governance, deprived of the support of superiors in the daily provisions of life, fall apart.

### CHAPTER 34.—Concerning one who suffers tribulations for the Catholic faith. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, ch. 43.

It has been decreed that a Catholic Christian who suffers tribulations for the Catholic faith, for ecclesiastical affairs, and for the Christian religion must be honored with every honor by priests; even through a deacon, sustenance is to be supplied to him.

### CHAPTER 35.—Concerning heirs: if they do not fulfill the testator’s instructions, the bishop is to fulfill them. From the Council of Mainz, ch. 1.

[Col. 0911B] If heirs do not carry out a testator’s instructions, the bishop of that place shall canonically place under interdict the entire property left to them, together with its fruits and other revenues, so that the wishes of the deceased may be fulfilled.

### CHAPTER 36.—That laypersons, even if religious, may not administer ecclesiastical matters. From the same council, ch. 5 (Third Council of Rome under Symmachus, ch. 3).

(16, q. 7, c. *Laicis*.) Laypersons, even if religious, are never under any circumstances to be granted authority to dispose of anything belonging to ecclesiastical property.

### CHAPTER 37.—Concerning those who seek church property from kings. From the Council of Lyons, ch. 11.

[Col. 0911C] Let those who seek the property of the Church from kings and, driven by dreadful greed, seize the substance of the needy, be regarded as having obtained nothing valid; and let them be excluded from the communion of the Church whose resources they desire to take away.

### CHAPTER 38.—Concerning the case in which a bishop appoints an ecclesiastical assembly and a count a secular court for the same day. From the Council of Tribur, ch. 9, attended by King Arnulf.

When a bishop, governing the Church entrusted to him by the Lord God, proceeds on a circuit through his diocese, appoints a canonically established assembly, and summons to it the people entrusted to him; and when a count, on the same day, whether knowingly or unknowingly, appoints his own assembly with the people after the bishop has called his assembly, and commands them by ban to come there,

[Col. 0911D] everyone shall give precedence to the bishop’s assembly; and the count himself and the same people shall hasten after the bishop, knowing that they are not there to contend in seditious dispute but to keep watch for the Catholic faith—not to accumulate money, but to gather a gain of souls.

Hence, in the same epistle of blessed Clement: “It belongs to you who discharge the Lord’s embassy to teach the peoples; it belongs to them to obey you, as they obey God.” And in the epistle of Pope Alexander, successor of Evaristus: “If anyone impedes your embassy, he hinders the progress not of one person but of many. And as he harms many, so he must be rebuked by many; and because he impedes God’s cause and disturbs the state of the Church, he must be shut out from its thresholds.”

Therefore no count,

[Col. 0912A] no judge, and no person whatever, whether in clerical office or secular dress, may impede or presume to disturb the embassy of bishops.

That unanimity and concord may exist between bishops and counts, it has been decided that if a bishop residing at home wishes a gathering of the people to take place, and a count nevertheless appoints a court on precisely the same day, the decision of the one who first appointed it shall prevail, while the bishop’s dignity and authority remain intact.

### CHAPTER 39.—Concerning kings who rule well. From the sayings of Isidore (book III, *On the Supreme Good*, ch. 48).

One who rules well in temporal matters in this world reigns forever without end, and passes from the glory of this age into eternal glory. But those who exercise royal power wickedly, after glittering garments and the shining of jewels,

[Col. 0912B] descend naked and miserable to be tortured in hell.

Kings are so called from acting rightly (*recte agendo*); therefore the name of king is attained by acting rightly and lost by sinning.
