For we find that holy men also are called kings in the sacred writings because they act rightly, govern their own faculties well, and bring their opposing impulses into order by rational discernment. Therefore those are rightly called kings who know how to govern well and regulate both themselves and their subjects.

Some turn the very name of government into the savagery of cruelty; and when they have reached the height of power, they immediately fall into apostasy. They exalt themselves with such swelling pride of heart that they despise all subjects in comparison with themselves and fail to recognize those whom they happen to rule. To them Ecclesiasticus fittingly says:

[Col. 0912C] “Have they appointed you a leader? Do not exalt yourself” (Ecclus. XXXII).

When the kings of the world perceive themselves as more exalted than others, they should nevertheless know that they are mortal. They should not look to the glory of royal power by which they are raised high in this world, but direct their attention to the work which they will carry with them to hell. Therefore, if they lack glory in this age, let them do those things which they may possess without end after death.

Since the Apostle says, “There is no authority except from God” (Rom. XIII), how is it said through the prophet concerning certain rulers: “They have reigned, but not by me” (Hos. VIII)? It is as if he said: Not while I am favorable, but while I am even supremely angry [the original reads *etiam summe*]. Therefore he says further through the same prophet: “I will give you a king in my wrath” (Hos. XIII).

[Col. 0912D] From this it appears more clearly that God ordains both good and bad authority, but the good in favor and the bad in anger. When kings are good, they are a gift of God; when they are bad, they are the crime of the people. For the life of rulers is ordered according to the merit of the people, as Job testifies: “He causes a hypocrite to reign because of the sins of the people” (Job XXXIV). For when God is angry, peoples receive such a ruler as they deserve because of their sin. Sometimes kings are changed even because of the wickedness of the people, and those who formerly seemed good become wicked once they have received the kingdom.

### CHAPTER 40.—On the same matter. From the sayings of the same author (ibid., ch. 49).

One who uses royal authority rightly ought so to conduct himself toward all that, the more he shines in the height

[Col. 0913A] of honor, the more he humbles his mind within himself, setting before himself the example of David’s humility. David did not grow proud of his merits but, humbling himself, said: “I will go as one despised, and I will appear despised before the Lord who chose me” (II Kings VI).

One who uses royal authority rightly establishes a model of justice more by deeds than by words. Such a person is exalted by no prosperity and disturbed by no adversity. He does not rely on his own strength, and his heart does not depart from the Lord. He presides over the summit of royal power with a humble spirit. Wickedness does not delight him, nor does greed inflame him. Without defrauding anyone, he makes himself rich from a poor man; and what he could extort from peoples by his power, he often remits in merciful clemency.

God gave rulers preeminence for the government of peoples, and he willed them to rule those with whom they share the same condition of birth and death.

[Col. 0913B] Rule, therefore, ought to benefit peoples, not harm them; it ought not oppress them by domination, but provide for them by condescension. Thus this insignia of authority may truly be useful, and rulers may use God’s gift for the protection of Christ’s members. For faithful peoples are Christ’s members; and when rulers govern them in the best manner through the authority they receive, they assuredly render a good return to God, the giver.

A good king returns more readily from sin to justice than he passes from justice to sin, so that you may know the latter to be a lapse and the former his settled purpose. It ought to be his settled purpose never to depart from truth; but if he happens to stumble by accident, he should rise again at once.

### CHAPTER 41.—Concerning the patience of kings. From the sayings of the same author (ibid., ch. 50).

[Col. 0913C] Often a just ruler knows how to overlook even the errors of wicked people, not because he consents to their wickedness, but because he awaits a suitable time of correction, when he may be able either to amend or punish their vices.

Many are exposed as guilty of conspiracy against rulers; but God, wishing to test rulers’ clemency, permits the former to think wickedly and does not abandon the latter. From the evil of the former he does good to the latter, since the latter pardon with remarkable patience the faults which the former commit.

To return evil for evil is the reciprocity of justice. But one who adds clemency to justice does not return evil for evil to those at fault; rather, he bestows good for evil upon those who have offended.

### CHAPTER 42.—Concerning the offenses of kings. From the sayings of the same author (ibid.).

[Col. 0913D] It is difficult for a ruler to return to better things if he has become entangled in vices. Sinning peoples fear a judge; but kings, unless restrained solely by fear of God and dread of hell, freely rush headlong and, by the steep descent of license, fall into every criminal vice.

The higher anyone is placed, the greater the danger in which he stands; and the more elevated anyone is in the honor of splendor, the greater is his sin if he commits one. “The mighty will suffer mighty torments” (Wis. VI). For from one to whom more is entrusted, more is required (Luke XII), even according to the measure [*usura*, “interest/increase,” variant] of punishments.

By their examples kings easily either build up or

[Col. 0914A] overthrow the lives of their subjects. Therefore a ruler ought not to sin, lest the unpunished license of his sin make a pattern for sinning. For a king who falls into vices quickly shows the way of error. Thus it is said of Jeroboam that he “sinned and made Israel sin” (III Kings XII). Whatever his subjects commit by his example is charged to him.

Just as some follow the deeds pleasing to God of good rulers, so many readily follow their corrupt examples. Most people under wicked rulers are evil more by necessity than by choice, while obeying their commands. Yet some, just as they are ready to follow kings in evil, are slow to imitate them in good. Often the very things through which evil kings sin are the means by which good kings are justified, when they correct the greed and wickedness of their predecessors.

[Col. 0914B] For indeed they share the former rulers’ sins if they retain what those rulers plundered. Whoever follows another’s sin must necessarily follow that person’s punishment. For one whose error and vice match another’s will not be unequal in punishment.

### CHAPTER 43.—That kings are bound by laws. From the sayings of the same author (ibid., ch. 5).

(Dist. 9, c. *Justum est*.) It is just for a ruler to obey his own laws. For then he will judge his laws worthy to be observed by all when he himself shows them reverence. Rulers are bound by their own laws and cannot condemn in themselves the laws which they establish for their subjects. For the authority of their word is just if they allow that what they prohibit to peoples is not lawful for themselves.

[Col. 0914C] Secular authorities are subject to religious discipline. Although endowed with the summit of royal power, they are nevertheless bound by the bond of faith, so that they may proclaim Christ’s faith by their laws and preserve the proclamation of that faith by good conduct.

### CHAPTER 44.—Concerning the discipline of kings in the Church. From the sayings of the same author (ibid.).

(23, q. 5, c. *Principes saeculi*.) Secular rulers sometimes hold the highest offices of power within the Church, so that by that same power they may strengthen ecclesiastical discipline. Otherwise, powers within the Church would not be necessary except so that what the priest cannot accomplish by the word of teaching, authority may command [accomplish] through the terror of discipline. Often the heavenly kingdom advances through the earthly kingdom [Col. 0914D], so that those within the Church who act against the faith and discipline of the Church may be crushed [restrained] by the severity of rulers, and that princely authority may lay upon the necks of the proud that discipline which the humility of the Church is unable to exercise; and thus it deserves reverence, because it imparts the force of power [“and that it may receive reverence, force,” etc.; thus Gratian and Isidore today]. Let secular rulers know that they must render an account to God concerning the Church which they undertake to protect on Christ’s behalf. For whether the peace and discipline of the Church are increased through faithful rulers or dissolved, he who entrusted his Church to their authority will require an account from them.

### CHAPTER 45.—Why God has assigned some to freedom and others to servitude. From the sayings of the same author.

[Col. 0915A]

Because of the sin of the first man, the punishment of servitude was divinely imposed upon the human race; thus upon those whom he sees not to be suited to freedom [dignity], he more mercifully imposes servitude. And although the sin of human origin has been forgiven to all believers through the grace of baptism, nevertheless the just God has for this reason differentiated human life, making some servants and others masters: so that the license for wrongdoing among servants may be restrained by the power of masters. For if all were without fear, who would restrain anyone from evil? Hence rulers and kings were also chosen among the nations, so that through fear of them they might restrain peoples from evil and subject them to laws for right living. [Col. 0915B] As regards reason, there is no respect of persons with God (Eph. VI; Col. III), who chose the ignoble, the despised, and the things that are not, in order to destroy the things that are, so that no flesh—that is, no carnal power—may boast before him (I Cor. I). For one Lord provides equally for masters and servants. Submissive servitude is better than arrogant freedom. For many are found freely serving God while placed under wicked masters: although subject to them in body, they are nevertheless set above them in mind.

### CHAPTER 46.—That no servant may become a monk against his master’s will. From the Council of Chalcedon, canon 4 (session 15, q. 16, c. *Qui vere pureque*).

We have decreed that no servant be received into monasteries on the pretext of becoming a monk without his master’s knowledge. We decree that whoever transgresses this determination of ours shall be excommunicated.

### CHAPTER 47.—On the same matter. Gelasius to the bishops throughout Lucania, Bruttium, and Sicily (Epistle 1, c. 16).

Any bishop, priest, or deacon, or any of those known to preside over monasteries, who retains servile persons or persons bound by origin and judges that they are not to be restored to their patrons, or that henceforth they are to be assigned either to ecclesiastical service or to religious communities—unless they have first been freed, perhaps by their masters’ consent and signed instrument [“by the testimony of a written document,” original text], or by testimony, or granted through a lawful settlement—must not doubt that they will incur the loss of their office and communion.

### CHAPTER 48.—That freed slaves may not again be reduced to servitude. From the Council of Orléans in the time of King Childebert, canon 7 (Orléans V).

[Col. 0915D]

Whatever slaves are released from servitude by freeborn masters shall remain in the freedom which they then received from their masters. If such freedom is assailed by anyone, it shall be defended in justice by the Churches, except in those offenses for which the laws have ordered freedoms granted to slaves to be revoked.

### CHAPTER 49.—An example of the same matter. Gregory to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna (*Register*, book VII, epistle 21).

John, the bearer of this letter, complains that his wife, fleeing the harassment of a certain George, has remained for a long time within the venerable precincts and has thus far found no relief. Because he asserts that there is a dispute concerning her legal status [Col. 0916A], and has requested that she be commended to your brotherhood, we urge you in these words to extend protection to that woman with equity preserved, and not to allow anyone in any way to oppress her contrary to the order of justice.

### CHAPTER 50.—If a bishop has released someone belonging to the ecclesiastical household from servitude. From the Council of Agde, canon 6 (canon 7).

(12, q. 2, c. *Si quos de servis*.) If a bishop grants freedom to any servants of the Church who have deserved well, it has been resolved that his successors shall preserve the freedom conferred, together with whatever the emancipator may have bestowed upon them in freedom. Yet we order that this be kept within a limit of twenty solidi, in a small plot of land, a vineyard, or a lodging-house. If more has been given, it shall revert to the Church after the emancipator’s death.

### CHAPTER 51.—That, if necessary, the Church shall protect freed persons, canon 28 (canon 29).

[Col. 0916B]

(Dist. 87, c. *Libertos legitime*.) The Church shall protect, if necessary, freed persons lawfully made such by their masters. But if anyone, before a hearing, should wish or presume either to seize or despoil them, he shall be repelled by the Church.

### CHAPTER 52.—An example of this matter. From the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 73 (canon 71).

(Dist. 87, c. *Liberti qui a quibuscunque*.) All freed persons who have been manumitted and commended to the protection of the Church shall, as the rules of the ancient Fathers established, be protected by priestly defense from the insolence of anyone, both in their state of freedom and in the peculium which they are known to possess.

### CHAPTER 53.—On the same matter. From the *Life of Blessed Gregory*, book III, chapter 45 (by John the Deacon of the Roman Church).

[Col. 0916C]

Gregory defended the freedom of every person against the insolence of judges, nevertheless with outspoken words.

### CHAPTER 54.—On the same matter. Gregory to Leontius, former consul (*Register*, book VIII, c. 51).

I know one thing well and firmly: even if a freedman has committed some fraud in public affairs, his property ought to be confiscated, not his freedom. For in the killing of free persons—to say nothing of the offense thereby given to almighty God, to say nothing of the grave injury to your reputation—the times of our most pious emperor [Col. 0916D] are altogether darkened. For this is the difference between kings of the nations and the emperor of kings: kings of the nations are masters of slaves; the emperor, however, is lord of free Romans. Therefore, whatever you do, you must act first with justice preserved and then with freedom protected in every respect.

### CHAPTER 55.—Concerning fugitive slaves: that no one may protect them under a claim of ecclesiastical right. Likewise, to Peter the subdeacon.

We have learned that many complain concerning lost slaves, saying that if the slave of anyone, perhaps fleeing his master, declares himself to belong to ecclesiastical right, the governors of the Church immediately hold him as a slave belonging to ecclesiastical right, conducting no judicial inquiry but defending the slave’s assertion. This [Col. 0917A] displeases me as much as it departs from the judgment of truth. Therefore I wish your experience, upon learning of anything done in this way, to correct it without delay. All such slaves, if any are now held under ecclesiastical right, ought, just as they were taken without judgment, to be restored before judgment; and if Holy Church has any lawful claim upon them, then their possessors ought to be summoned through orderly legal proceedings.

### CHAPTER 56.—How one granted freedom ought to defend himself when recalled to servitude. *Capitulary*, book III, chapter 43.

If anyone has been set free by charter and is challenged as a slave by any person, he shall first produce the lawful author of his freedom and remain in his freedom. But if the lawful party is lacking [Col. 0917B], he shall be allowed to defend himself by the testimony of reputable persons who were present when he was set free. If witnesses are lacking, he shall establish that his charter, which is the third, is true and lawful by means of two other charters confirmed or written by the hand of the same chancellor. The chancellor must be one known and accepted among the people of that locality. But if the person challenged as a servant has neither the author nor testimony, and cannot find two other charters to confirm his own, then the person who challenged him shall, according to the law, prove the charter false and recover the slave.

### CHAPTER 57.—That a slave is not to be believed when accusing anyone of a crime. *Capitulary*, book VI, chapter 46.

[Col. 0917C] (2, q. 7 and 8, *On Accusations*; see the canon *Si testes*, and throughout 4, q. and 3.) A slave is absolutely not to be believed if he brings a criminal charge against anyone, even if he attacks his own master with an accusation. For even if, while under torture, he repeats what he alleged, he nevertheless ought not to be believed.

### CHAPTER 58.—Likewise, that persons of servile condition may not testify against anyone unless freeborn persons are lacking. Chapter 159.

A freedman or freedwoman shall not be admitted to give testimony against anyone in any proceedings, except in certain cases where freeborn persons are known to be unavailable, as is also permitted concerning slaves.

### CHAPTER 59.—A slave’s testimony against his master is by no means to be accepted. Book VII, chapter 208.

[Col. 0917D] If slaves have confessed the crimes of their masters, they shall in no way be heard, unless perhaps they denounce them for treason against the majesty [of the state].

### CHAPTER 60.—On the same matter. *Code*, book IV, chapter 20, title VIII (title XX, law VII).

It is beyond doubt that slaves cannot be examined either for their masters or against them, but can be examined concerning their own act.

### CHAPTER 61.—Likewise on the same matter. Book IX, chapter 1, title XX (title I, law XX).

If any member of the household, or any slave of whatever house, comes forward as informer and accuser concerning any crime, he shall, before judicial examination, at the very statement [Col. 0918A] of the crimes and beginning of the accusation, be struck down by the avenging sword, forfeiting his status, life, and property—the person to whose household or lordship he belonged.

### CHAPTER 62.—Freed persons accusing their patrons are to be punished in the same manner as slaves, title XXI (ibid., law XXI).

If freed persons presume to become accusers of those who manumitted them or of their heirs, they shall be liable to the same punishment as slaves, to suffer penalties before the commencement of the prohibited accusation.

### CHAPTER 63.—That a freed person ought to be returned to servitude for ingratitude toward a patron. Constitution 69 of the *Novellae*, chapter 2.

If a freed person is ungrateful toward his patron, his freedom must be rescinded. But it is necessary to guard against those acts of ingratitude recognized by the laws: for example, if the freed person lays hands upon his patron, or inflicts grievous insults upon him, or causes him great and intolerable harm—that is, if he pours out injuries tending to his disgrace. If the patron or his children prove any of these things, the convicted freed person shall return to his former status.

### CHAPTER 64.—Which persons are excluded from public accusation. From the Seventh Council of Carthage, canon 2.

(4, q. 1, c. *Diffinimus eum*, and 4, q. 6, c. *Omnibus quibus*.) No slaves or their own freed persons shall be admitted to make a public accusation; nor shall any marked by the stain of infamy—that is, actors or persons subject to disgraceful occupations—nor heretics, pagans, or Jews. Yet those to whom accusation is denied must not be denied the right to accuse in cases concerning themselves.

### CHAPTER 65.—That a freed person may not presume to accuse the Church of which he was formerly a slave. From the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 69 (canon 67).

[Col. 0918C]

(12, q. c. *Episcopus qui mancipium*.) A freed person shall be denied permission to accuse or testify against the Church to whose legal right he belonged. If he presumes to do so, it is resolved that he shall be returned to the servitude of the Church which he seeks to injure.

### CHAPTER 66.—On the same subject. From the Second Council of Seville, canon 9 (canon 8).

(12, q. 2, c. *Octava discussio*.) The status of freed persons who strive against their bishop or their patron Church ought rather to be abolished than preserved, so that for those whose freedom is harmful, servitude may be salutary; and those who, raised up by freedom obtained, know how to be proud, may, once it is lost, learn to obey in subjection [“restored, may learn,” original text].

### CHAPTER 67.—How freed persons and their descendants ought to deal with property entrusted to them by the Church. From the Ninth Council of Toledo, canon 16.

Freed persons of the Church and their descendants shall have no permission to transfer, by any transaction whatever, into the ownership of outsiders anything which they are known to possess by right of the Church. But if they should perhaps wish to sell anything from among these things, they shall appropriately offer it for purchase to the priest of that Church; and they may dispose of or retain the prices of those things as they please. For we by no means permit the rent or revenue of their property to pass into another’s ownership. But they shall have entirely open access to sell or give whatever they wish to their own children or relatives, who are subject to the same Church either in service or patronage [Col. 0919A].

### CHAPTER 68.—That servants fleeing to church against their masters’ will are not to be protected. Gregory to Bishop Boniface.

(17, q. 4, c. *Metuentes*.) If frightened servants flee to the precincts of the Church, they ought to seek intercession, not hiding places, lest this very presumption of delay increase their rashness in resisting. For our son, the eminent man Peter, complains that his slave has remained for some time in the church of Saint Clement; although he had arranged for assurances to be given, the slave was unwilling for any reason to leave. Therefore have the aforesaid man, in the presence of whomever he chooses to have sent with him, provide assurances [Col. 0919B] of the slave’s impunity, and make him return to his master by every means. Or if he should perhaps persist in this obstinacy, after the assurance has been given to him, let him be returned by force.

### CHAPTER 69.—On the same matter. The same author to Peter, subdeacon of Campania (*Register*, book II, epistle 1, or chapter 46).

If any slaves have fled to the monastery of Saint Severinus, or to another church of the same town, as soon as this comes to your knowledge, do not permit them to remain there in any way, but have them brought back within the city to the church. And if they have a just complaint against their masters, they must leave the churches under a suitable arrangement. But if they have committed a pardonable offense, once their masters have received an oath concerning pardon, let them be restored without delay.

### CHAPTER 70.—That no one may seize slaves of clerics as his own. From the Council of Arles, canon 6.

[Col. 0919C]

If anyone believes that slaves of clerics, fleeing to a church as their own slaves, are to be seized, he shall be struck with the most severe condemnation through all the Churches.

### CHAPTER 71.—What penalty is incurred by one who receives a fugitive slave without the master’s knowledge. *Code*, book VI, chapter 1, title IV (title I, law 4).

Whoever receives a fugitive slave in house or field without his master’s knowledge shall return him together with another slave of equal value, or twenty solidi.

### CHAPTER 72.—That one who alienates a slave from his master in any way is guilty of theft, title VI (title II, law 4).

Anyone who knowingly sells, gives, or otherwise alienates another’s slave without the master’s consent cannot thereby diminish anything of the master’s right. And if he lays hands upon or detains the slave, he commits theft.

### CHAPTER 73.—That no one may draw back into servitude a person manumitted by decree of the Apostolic See. Gregory to Anthimius, subdeacon (*Register*, book I, epistle 53).

Gaudentius [Gaudiosus in Gregory], the bearer of this letter, informed us that violence was being inflicted upon him by the agents of the holy Roman Church, over which, by God’s ordering, we preside; he asserts that they wish to claim his children as belonging by right to the aforesaid Church. For, upon documents submitted by him, we learned that Sirica, the wife of the bearer of this letter, had been granted by Aetia of blessed memory to a certain woman named Morena by deed of gift, and had been manumitted by the same Morena by letter [Col. 0920A]. We therefore consider it improper that children born of a free woman should be drawn back into servitude. Accordingly, by the present authority we command your experience to examine those documents carefully, as we too have learned from them, with an untroubled mind; so that, if the Church has no documents capable of opposing this man’s documents, it shall desist from troubling him without any further objection. For it is harsh that, if others grant freedom as a reward for their service, such freedom should be revoked by the Church, which ought to protect it.

### CHAPTER 74.—That a slave is not a fugitive if he flees to his master’s friend in order to seek intercession. *Digest*, book XXI, title I (title I, law 43).

One who flees to his master’s friend in order to entreat him is not a fugitive. Indeed, if he does not return home either with that intention or after failing to obtain help, he is not yet a fugitive.

### CHAPTER 75.—That a fleeing slave does not thereby cast off the yoke of servitude. Book XLIV, title II (book XLI, title III).

(Law XV, § *Si servus quem*.) If a slave whom I possessed flees, even if he presents himself as free, he will be regarded as possessed by his master. But this is to be understood only if, when apprehended, he is unwilling to litigate for his freedom; for if he is prepared to litigate, he will not be regarded as possessed by the master against whom he has prepared himself as an adversary.

### CHAPTER 76.—Concerning masters who become intolerable to their servants, title VIII.

[Col. 0920C] Concerning slaves who flee to a sacred temple or to statues of the emperors, the Deified Antoninus decreed that, if the cruelty of their masters appears intolerable, the masters shall be compelled to sell their slaves on favorable terms, with the price given to the masters. And rightly so: for it is in the public interest that no one use his own property badly. The words of this rescript issued to Aelius Martianus are these: “The authority of masters over their slaves ought indeed to remain unimpaired, lest anyone’s legal right be taken away. Yet it is in the masters’ interest that assistance against cruelty, hunger, or intolerable injury not be denied to those who make a just appeal. Therefore investigate the complaints of those belonging to the household of Julius Sabinus who have fled to the statue; and if you learn that they have been treated more harshly than is equitable, or subjected to disgraceful injury, order them sold, so that they may not return into their master’s power.”

### CHAPTER 77.—An example of punishment against those who falsely pretend that they have just causes. Gelasius to John, bishop of Vivanum [Vienna, according to Gratian].

(17, q. 4, c. *Uxor Felicis*.) The wife and daughter of Felix arrived at Rome, as was necessary. For we ordered this man, who had first taken refuge in the basilica of the barbarians and boasted that he had good grounds, to leave under this condition: that if he set forth his case faithfully and reasonably, we would permit nothing at all harsh or severe to be done against him. But if it were proved that he had come contrary to faith and to his master’s interest, he himself would be responsible and would be subject to appropriate discipline. When our son Orthasius, an eminent man, arrived [Col. 0921A], he was convicted on every point so completely that he could not open his mouth, and in his own voice admitted the truth of the charges made against him. He is therefore held in custody as a slave.

### CHAPTER 78.—That one is not guilty of homicide who kills another’s slave lying in ambush against him. *Digest*, book IX, title II (title II, law 4).

If I kill your slave, a robber lying in ambush against me, I shall be safe from liability. For natural reason permits a person to defend himself against danger. The Law of the Twelve Tables permits the killing of a thief caught at night, provided that this is attested by a shout. It also permits the killing of one caught by day if he defends himself with a weapon, provided likewise that this is attested by a shout.

### CHAPTER 79.—That a master is bound by equal guilt if, with his knowledge, his slave kills someone. Title IV (title IV, law II).

[Col. 0921B]

If a slave kills with his master’s knowledge, he binds the master for the whole amount; for the master himself is deemed to have killed. But if the master was unaware, the action is noxal. For he ought not to be held liable beyond surrendering the slave in compensation for the wrong.

### CHAPTER 80.—The penance of one who has killed his own slave without the judge’s knowledge. From the Council of Agde, canon 60 (canon 62).

If anyone kills his own slave without the knowledge of a judge, he shall expiate the guilt of bloodshed by excommunication or a penance of two years [“amend,” original reading].

### CHAPTER 81.—If anyone sins, punishment is to be exacted from that person, not from his property. Gregory to Peter, subdeacon of Sicily (*Register*, book I, epistle 42).

[Col. 0921C] We have learned that if anyone belonging to the household of the Church commits an offense, punishment is exacted not from the person himself but from his property. Concerning this, we command that if anyone commits an offense, punishment shall be exacted from that person, as is fitting; but his means shall be left untouched—except perhaps for some small amount that may be useful for the maintenance of the officer sent to him [Gregory has “may not be useful”].

### CHAPTER 82.—How servants ought to be admonished. Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, book II (part III, admonition 6).

Servants are to be admonished not to despise their masters, lest they offend God by proudly resisting his ordering.

### CHAPTER 83.—Likewise, an admonition to servants. Ambrose on the First Epistle to the Corinthians.

[Col. 0921D] “Let those servants who are under the yoke consider their masters worthy of all honor, lest the name of God and the teaching be blasphemed” (1 Tim. VI). The Apostle writes this concerning those who have unbelieving masters, commanding them to render every service to their masters, although the masters are estranged from piety.

### CHAPTER 84.—On the same matter. The same author, in the introduction to the Epistle to Philemon.

The Apostle commands servants to render every servile duty to their masters with all diligence, whether they have impious or pious masters.

### CHAPTER 85.—How a master ought to reconcile a slave whom he has wrongfully injured. Augustine’s sermon for Lent, *On Brotherly Concord*, beginning: “These holy days” (Homily 40, book of fifty homilies).

Sometimes a master, being human, sins against his slave. For although one is master and the other slave, both are nevertheless servants of another master, since both have been redeemed by Christ’s blood. Yet it seems harsh for me even to order or command this: that if perhaps a master sins against his slave by arguing unjustly or beating him unjustly, he should say to him, “Forgive me; pardon me.” For he ought not to do this, lest the slave begin to grow proud. What then? Let him repent before the eyes of God; before the eyes of God let him punish his own heart. And if he cannot say to his slave—for it is not appropriate—“Pardon me,” let him address him gently; for a gentle form of address is a request for pardon.

### CHAPTER 86.—Concerning a slave who retains another’s property. *Code*, book III, chapter 32, title 20 (title XXXII, law 20).

You plainly see that you must sue not the slave whom you had accustomed to retain your property, [Col. 0922B] but his master, for recovery of the property.

### CHAPTER 87.—That the master may reclaim without payment a slave secretly and wrongfully sold. Title 23 (law XXIII).

If others have disposed of your slave, taken by force or theft, without any just cause, no necessity to pay a price shall be imposed upon you when you reclaim your slave.

### CHAPTER 88.—Concerning slaves secretly cutting down trees, chapter 41, title 2 (title XLI, book 2).

If your slaves, without your knowledge or even despite your prohibition, have secretly cut down trees, you need not fear in vain that you will be liable beyond noxal surrender on their account; for masters who are ignorant or prohibiting are to be condemned for their slaves’ offenses only so that they have the power either to surrender the slave in compensation for the wrong or to bear the damages.

### CHAPTER 89.—That freed persons or slaves are innocent of offenses committed by patrons or masters, chapter 13, title V (book IV, title XIII, law 5).

Freed persons or slaves cannot be sued on account of a contract made by their patron or master.

### CHAPTER 90.—If a slave borrows money, whatever passes from it into the master’s use must be paid by the master, chapter 20, title I (title XXV, law 1).

If your slave borrows money, he binds you by the *actio institoria* only if, when you placed him in charge of some office or commercial undertaking, it can be proved that you also permitted him to do this. But if that action has no place, you will be compelled to pay, by an action on the matter itself, whatever is proved to have been applied to your benefit [Col. 0922D].

### CHAPTER 91.—On the same matter, title III (title XXV, law 3).

An *actio institoria* lies against the person whom you say placed a slave in charge of a table or bank, if it can be proved that money deposited for the business conducted through that slave was not returned.

### CHAPTER 92.—On the same matter, chapter 26, title III (title XXVI, law 3).

Even if you had lent money to Prisca without the mistress ordering, signing, or directing it, nevertheless, if that sum was applied to the mistress’s benefit in lawful expenditures, sue her before her own judge; according to the form of law, you will recover what is shown to be owed to you.

### CHAPTER 93.—That no one can bring a public accusation against his patron, book VI, chapter 6, title I (book IV, title VI, law 1).

[Col. 0923A]

You cannot institute an action affecting reputation against your patron.

### CHAPTER 94.—That no person of servile condition may, without the master’s knowledge or against his will, prejudice landholdings, book IX, chapter 16, title VIII (book VIII, title XVI, law 8).

A lien upon estates is created only by a person legally able to bind them. The law and the authorities on law declare that a slave, agent, tenant farmer, steward, or lessee cannot impose a prejudice upon possession without the master’s knowledge or against his will.

### CHAPTER 95.—Concerning the child of a female slave, if exposed without the master’s knowledge or against his will, chapter 2, title I (title LII, law I).

[Col. 0923B] If the child of your female slave has been exposed against your will or without your knowledge, you are not forbidden to reclaim him; but his restoration—if you do not reclaim him from a thief—shall take place so that whatever has justly been expended in feeding him, or perhaps in teaching him a craft, shall be reimbursed.

### CHAPTER 96.—Likewise concerning the offspring of slaves, title II (title LII, law II).

Let everyone support his own offspring; if anyone considers that it should be exposed, he shall be subject to the prescribed penalty. But we leave no right of reclamation to masters or patrons if compassionate persons have not taken up those whom the masters or patrons themselves exposed, in some manner, to death. For no one can call his own one whom he despised while perishing.

### CHAPTER 97.—That no one may claim as a slave an exposed child of any condition, title III (title LIII, law 3).

[Col. 0923C]

We decree that no one may claim for his own dominion an exposed little child—whether born of freeborn parents, descended from a freedwoman, or marked by servile condition—whether under the name of ownership, registration, or colonial status. Nor shall those who take them up to rear them be granted any permission, under any distinction [perhaps “restriction”], to take them up and provide for their upbringing so that, whether male or female, they may hold them as children, slaves, or tenant farmers. Rather, without any distinction, those reared by such persons shall be regarded as free and freeborn.

### CHAPTER 98.—Concerning condemned slaves: what of their property belongs to their masters, chapter 50, title I (book IX, title XLIX, law I).

[Col. 0923D]

It is established that the peculia of slaves condemned on capital charges are not taken from their masters; rather, the master shall recover what he proves the slave possessed.

### CHAPTER 99.—That a master may defend in court a slave charged with an offense, chapter 2, title II (book IX, title II, law 2).

If a slave is charged with any crime, the master may defend him and produce him in court to answer the accuser’s allegations.

### CHAPTER 100.—That one does not lose freedom if, through fear, one falsely claims before a judge to be a slave. *Capitulary*, book VII, chapter 342.

A person who, through fear and the pressure of some terror, has falsely declared himself to be a slave in the official records before the governor is not thereafter prejudiced in defending his status [Col. 0924A].

### CHAPTER 101.—Concerning one who bought something from another’s slave without the master’s knowledge, book V, chapter 306.

If anyone buys something from another’s slave without his master’s knowledge, and the master wishes the sale to be invalid, he shall return the price to the buyer, so that the sale has no legal force.

### CHAPTER 102.—That both the slave who proudly flees his master and the one who incites him to such flight are anathema. Jerome to Paschasius of Alexandria.

You asked concerning a slave who had fled his master whether, if he died in that flight, it was lawful to pray for him or not. We do not find this forbidden in the divine books; nevertheless, the apostles firmly commanded that slaves be subject to their masters with all fear, “not only to the good and gentle, but also to the perverse” (1 Pet. II). And in the Council of Gangra (canon 3) it is written: “If anyone, under pretext of divine worship, teaches a slave to despise his own master, so that he may leave his master’s service, let him be anathema.” It may therefore be understood that, if he deserves anathema who teaches a slave to despise his own master and depart from his service, how much more does the slave who scorns his master and refuses to submit to his service. Nevertheless, there is a difference between one who did this through pride and one compelled by necessity through his master’s cruelty.

### CHAPTER 103.—That patrons and freed persons may not be compelled to attack one another by testimony. *Digest*, book XXII (title V, law 4).

[Col. 0924C]

Neither patrons nor patronesses may be compelled to give testimony against freed persons, nor freed persons against patrons.

### CHAPTER 104.—That masters have authority over slaves to preserve or destroy them. Book XLIV, title VIII.

We may observe that among all nations alike masters have power of life and death over their slaves, and that whatever is acquired through a slave is acquired by his master.

### CHAPTER 105.—That one does not commit theft by giving away in any manner the property of one’s own female slave. *Institutes*, book II, title VI.

If the person to whom the usufruct of a female slave belongs, believing her child to be his own, sells or gives it away, he does not commit theft; for theft is not committed without an intention to steal [Col. 0924D].

### CHAPTER 106.—Concerning wrongdoing slaves. Book III, title XXX (book IV, title VIII).

From the wrongful acts of slaves—for example, if they commit theft, seize goods by violence, cause damage, or commit injury—arise noxal actions. When the master is condemned in these, he is permitted either to bear the assessed value of the action or to surrender the person in compensation for the wrong. *Noxa* means the body that caused harm—that is, the slave; *noxia*, the wrong itself, such as theft, damage, robbery, or injury. It was permitted, with the greatest reason, to discharge liability by noxal surrender; for it would have been unjust for their wickedness to injure their masters beyond their own bodies. A master sued by noxal action in the name of his slave is released by surrendering the slave to the plaintiff in compensation for the wrong, and the slave’s perpetual ownership is thereby transferred from the master. But if the slave makes good the loss of the person to whom he was surrendered, he shall, after acquiring money, be manumitted by the assistance of the praetor even against his master’s will. Likewise, somewhat later: If a master commits anything against his own slave, the slave can have no action against his master, even if he has been manumitted or alienated [Col. 0925A].

### CHAPTER 107.—Concerning what sons and slaves acquire, book III, title XXIX.

We must be reminded that property is acquired for us not only through ourselves, but also through those persons who are under our power, such as our slaves and children. Yet whatever is acquired through slaves becomes wholly ours; but whatever is acquired through children whom we have in our power through an obligation is divided according to the scheme of ownership in property—that is, according to the usufruct established by our constitution: the father has the usufruct of whatever benefit comes from an action, while ownership is reserved to the son [Col. 0925B].

### CHAPTER 108.—An example of just punishment, that no one may presume to corrupt or entice another’s slave. Book IV, title I (title II).

The following question was raised. Titius had enticed the slave of Maevius to steal certain things from his master and bring them to him; the slave reported this to Maevius. Maevius, wishing to catch Titius in the act, allowed the slave to bring certain things to him. Is Titius liable for theft, for corrupting a slave, or for neither? [Col. 0925C] When this doubt was submitted to us and we had examined the disputes of the ancient jurists on the point—some allowing neither an action for theft nor one for corrupting a slave, and others allowing only one for theft—we, opposing this kind of cunning by our decision, decreed that not only an action for theft but also an action for corrupting a slave should be granted against him. For although that slave was not made worse by the enticer, and therefore the rules establishing the action for corrupting a slave do not apply, nevertheless the corrupter’s design was introduced to destroy the slave’s integrity. Therefore a penal action is imposed upon him as though the slave had in fact been corrupted, lest, owing to such impunity, someone perpetrate the same crime against another slave who could be corrupted.

### CHAPTER 109.—Concerning a slave with whom a transaction has been conducted, tractate VI, title VII.

[Col. 0925D]

If a transaction has been conducted with a slave by his master’s command, the praetor promises an action against the master for the whole amount, since the person who contracts in this way is deemed to rely upon the master’s credit.

### CHAPTER 110.—How masters and slaves ought to comport themselves toward one another. Prosper, book II, *On the Contemplative Life*, chapter 3.

Masters, as fellow servants in Christ with their slaves, should treat them mercifully; and slaves should serve their masters from the heart, so that they fulfill the will not only of their masters but also of God, who commands this very thing.

### Chapter 111.—Concerning persons subject to ecclesiastical jurisdiction: that they may not make a testamentary document for themselves. Gelasius to Honorius, bishop.

[Col. 0926A]

(13, question 2, canon *Illud etiam*.) We also wish your sincerity not to be unaware that it has been reported to us that a certain *ampliatus conductor* [a tenant/manager named Ampliatus], who is known not only to be a servant of the Church, but also to have been so entangled in accounts for many years that, even if he were freeborn, he would in every respect be held liable until he had rendered all his accounts, has with rash audacity attempted to draw up a testamentary document, although there can be no doubt in law that his entire peculium is bound to ecclesiastical right. Therefore let your brotherhood, in our stead, oppose these presumptions, and by no contrivance whatsoever permit this to be done. And if anything human should perhaps happen to him—for he is reported to be very aged—then let your unanimity without delay deliver over his property, under a faithful inventory, only to his children, to whom the estate is shown to have been entrusted, until he is compelled to restore unimpaired the Lord’s shares for all the periods during which he is known to have administered this estate.

### Chapter 112.—That no one may judge another’s servant. Pope Telesphorus to the brother bishops.

“Who are you to judge another’s servant?” (Romans 14.) Without doubt, you are a transgressor of the law of God, of the apostles, and of the prophets, and not only of these, but also of human laws. For all laws, both divine and human, prohibit the judging of another’s servant.

### Chapter 113.—More fully on the same matter. Institutes, book IV, title IV.

[Col. 0926C]

No injury is understood to be done to slaves themselves; rather, it is considered to be done through them to their master. Yet this is not so in the same ways as through children and wives. It applies, however, where some act of robbery has been committed and where the matter plainly concerns an affront to the master—for example, if someone has beaten another’s slave; and an action is provided for this case. But if someone has insulted a slave or struck him with his fist, no action lies for the master against him.

If injury has been done to a common slave, it is fair that the assessment of the injury be made not according to the share held by each master, but according to the persons of the masters, because the injury is done to them. But if Titius has the usufruct in a slave and Maevius the ownership, the injury is understood to be done rather to Maevius.

But if injury has been done to a free person who serves you in good faith, no action will be given to you; rather, he may pursue the matter in his own name, unless he has been assaulted as an affront to you. For then an action for injury lies also to you. The same, therefore, applies to another’s slave who serves you in good faith: an action for injury is admitted as often as injury has been done to him as an affront to you.

### Chapter 114.—That subjects, being unlawfully oppressed, often seek the Church’s protection. Augustine on John, part I, tractate 44.

At times, persons subjected to an unlawful and wicked yoke flee to the Church, by which freeborn persons are kept from slavery. The bishop is appealed to; and unless he takes care to exert himself so that free status is not oppressed, he is judged merciless.

### Chapter 115.—Concerning the property of a deceased testator. Justinian’s Novels, constitution 1, chapter 1.

If anyone appoints as heir a parent, son, brother, or patron, and leaves to someone a legacy or fideicommissum recognized by the laws, then, if the written heir fulfills the will of the deceased and pays the legacy without evasion, he shall firmly possess the deceased’s inheritance and enjoy the judgment of him whose judgment he did not allow to be overturned. But if he considers that the testator’s will should be resisted and delays the legatee, so that the legatee even approaches a judge and obtains a favorable judgment, yet the heir nevertheless continues similarly to delay, and a year passes after the judicial decision, then the instituted heir shall have only the legitimate portion due to him and shall lose the remaining part.

### Chapter 116.—That the heir pay legacies within a year, chapter 4.

In every case the legacy left must be provided within a year. The beginning of the year must be the time when the defendant has been admonished by judicial judgment concerning payment of the legacy. When the year has elapsed, the heir who has not paid the legacies shall lose the testator’s inheritance.

### Chapter 117.—What a creditor ought to do when a debt is not paid on the appointed day. Constitution 4, chapter 1.

[Col. 0927C]

If anyone has lent to another and has received a surety, a mandatary, or one who has promised payment of money on the debtor’s behalf, he shall not bring his actions against such persons before proceeding against the principal debtor himself and finding him insolvent, either wholly or in part. For once the debtor is known to suffer want, whether wholly or partially, the creditor must then proceed against the sureties or mandataries.

Likewise, ibid., chapter 2: These provisions are to be understood so that a creditor has no power to claim property before he has pursued personal actions both against the principal debtor himself and against his sureties and mandataries, and it has appeared that they are unable to pay.

### Chapter 118.—What one who has borrowed money ought to do if he has no money to repay it, chapter 2 (ibid., chapter 3).

[Col. 0927D]

If anyone has borrowed money but the debtor has no money, he shall furnish the creditor with movable property, if he has any. But if he has no movable property, he must sell his immovable property, if he has any, and pay the debt from its price. If, however, he finds no buyer, then he shall furnish his creditor with the best estate he possesses and be released from the action by which he is bound. But when he has found a buyer for his estate, he shall give security to the creditor that he will pay the money owed, and after giving security he may enter into the contract of sale.

By the term “creditor” is meant not only one who has lent money to another, but also all who have any action against someone.

### Chapter 119.—What should be done with the property of one condemned capitally, chapter 10.

The property of persons condemned for a capital crime ought not to be transferred to the profit of the governor, but restored to the relatives of those punished.

### Chapter 120.—That litigants’ pleadings remain as they are until the emperor has time to administer justice. Constitution 24, chapter 2.

If a consultation is expected and the emperor, being occupied, cannot convene the senate for this purpose, the litigants’ pleadings shall remain in the same form and suffer no prejudice, even though the prescribed time has elapsed, until the emperor, having leisure, has summoned the senators.

### Chapter 121.—That pimps be permitted nowhere, and that their written instruments be void. Constitution 31, chapter 1.

[Col. 0928B]

(Constitution 14, § *Item, Si quis*.) This constitution commands that no one be a pimp, whether in the imperial city or in the provinces; and praetors and provincial governors must enforce this prohibition. For those who have dared to be pimps contrary to the rule of the constitution are subject to the ultimate penalty. The constitution also commands that all instruments and sureties entered into with pimps, or made by pimps contrary to good morals, be ineffective and invalid.

### Chapter 122.—By what punishment an incestuous marriage is punished. Constitution 32, chapter 1.

[Col. 0928C]

(Constitution 12, § 1.) If anyone contracts a wicked, incestuous, and condemned marriage, and has no children from an earlier lawful marriage, he shall immediately lose his property, and the dowry given to him shall be claimed for the rights of the fisc. After public proclamation, he shall also suffer the loss of his belt of office and be punished with exile. If he is of lower status, he shall also undergo corporal interrogation [torture]; and his wife, married contrary to the laws, shall suffer the same penalties, provided that no just ignorance excuses her.

### Chapter 123.—How grandsons and granddaughters are to divide between themselves the inheritances of grandfather or grandmother. Constitution 34, chapter 4.

(Constitution 18, § *Neque illo quidem*.) If anyone leaves grandchildren through a son and through a daughter, the grandsons and granddaughters shall alike be called to the intestate inheritance of their deceased grandfather. They shall receive not less than a third part, as before, but shall obtain a full share: grandchildren born through a daughter shall receive the same share as grandchildren begotten through a son.

Likewise (in the same section): If a grandmother dies leaving grandsons through a son and granddaughters through a daughter, all shall alike be called to their grandmother’s inheritance; and there shall be no difference whatsoever whether they are all grandsons or granddaughters, whether born through a son or through a daughter.

### Chapter 124.—What a debtor suffers who attempts, at the time of repayment, to deceive the creditor. Constitution 35, chapter 4.

(§ *Studium vero*.) If anyone, upon production of his handwriting, denies it and says that such a document is not his, the plaintiff is thereafter harassed by proof and other difficulties—

[Col. 0929A]

[Haloander: “and this one having his own handwriting, so that the plaintiff may be compelled to be involved in great business in proving it.” The Greek codex likewise has this.]

A little later: or if he acknowledges that the writing is his but says that the creditor did not count out the money to him, then, if convicted in either case, he shall pay double the amount owed. But if the judge decides contrary to the present law, he himself shall pay the plaintiff’s penalty. If anyone says that no money was counted out to him, but afterward admits it and says that he also made partial payments, then, even if he has in fact paid, he shall nevertheless pay the entire principal.

### Chapter 125.—Concerning a woman marrying within the year of mourning: that she is infamous.

[Col. 0929B]

(Constitution 22, § *Ac primae*.) If a woman, after her husband’s death and before the completion of the yearly period, hastens into a second marriage, she shall in every respect be among the infamous. But if she has no children from her prior marriage, she may indeed remove the infamy if she petitions the emperor and is restored to her former standing by the divine will of the prince; nevertheless, she shall by no means acquire the property left to her by her first husband.

### Chapter 126.—Concerning a woman who, upon marrying again, attempts to withdraw property previously given to her children, chapter 33.

(§ *Mater sane*.) If a woman has given certain property to her children and afterward enters a second marriage, and chooses, under the pretext of ingratitude, to revoke a gift once made by her, she can by no means do so unless she proves specifically either that her son plotted against her life, or laid impious hands upon her, or contrived such plots that she would be deprived of all her property.

### Chapter 127.—That a woman marrying again loses the privileges of her first husband, chapter 24.

(§ *Neque item*.) A woman who enters a second marriage does not enjoy the privileges or dignities of her first husband.

### Chapter 128.—Concerning a freedwoman who is her patron’s wife, chapter 25.

(§ *Hujusmodi eleganter autem*.) If a freedwoman joined to her patron in marriage renounces that marriage but wishes to enter a second marriage, she cannot do so against her patron’s will. Otherwise, if she marries contrary to his will, no marriage comes into being; rather, she is considered joined as a prostitute.

### Chapter 129.—Concerning a woman who, having undertaken guardianship of her children, wishes to marry again, chapter 27.

(§ *Ad haec: Si tutelam*.) If a woman administers the guardianship of her children and, after beginning the administration, wishes to enter a second marriage, she must first seek a guardian for her underage children, render to him an account of her administration, and then, after rendering the account, if she appears to be a debtor, pay her debt. Thereafter, if she wishes, she may enter a second marriage. But if, disregarding this requirement, she contracts a second marriage, not only her own property—that is, the mother’s—shall be subjected to her children under the title of hypothec,

[Col. 0930A]

but also the property of the stepfather by authority of the present constitution.

### Chapter 130.—Concerning a woman who, within the year of mourning, conceives outside marriage: that she is infamous just as if she had married. Constitution 38, chapter 2.

(Constitution 39, § end.) If, before the lawful year has passed after her husband’s death, a woman does not enter a second marriage, but, in the manner of prostitutes, is seduced by someone, conceives, and bears a child—so that it is clear that what has been born is not her deceased husband’s—she shall suffer the same penalties which, under the preceding constitution, a woman suffers who contracts a second marriage before the lawful time.

### Chapter 131.—What witnesses should be admitted when a heretic litigates against a heretic, an orthodox person against a heretic, or Catholics litigate among themselves. Constitution 42, chapter 2.

[Col. 0930B]

(Constitution 45, § end.) If a heretic litigates against a heretic, either party may bring another heretic as witness. But if an orthodox person litigates against a heretic, the testimony even of a heretic shall be valid for the orthodox person, whereas against an orthodox person only the testimony of an orthodox person shall be valid. But when orthodox persons are litigating, no heretic shall be admitted to testify.

### Chapter 132.—That one oath is enough to settle the controversy of the parties. Constitution 45, chapter 2.

(Constitution 50, § end.) After all litigants have added their oath that they demand proofs from their opponent in the whole case neither for purposes of referral nor of vexatious accusation, nor in order to harass their adversary, one oath shall suffice. For previously, in each individual heading, when a litigant demanded proofs from his adversary, he was compelled to swear repeatedly that he gave the oaths not for vexatious accusation.

### Chapter 133.—How long one summoned to court should deliberate, and that no one may spurn a judge. Constitution 48, chapter 3.

(Constitution 53, § *Sed et illud sub finem*.) If anyone has been admonished pursuant to a judge’s decision, he shall have a period of twenty-nine days after the admonition.

Likewise (§ *Ubi vero*.) A joinder of issue made within the twentieth day has no force. But if anyone rejects a judge and requests another in his place, and then wishes to reject him again in order to request some other judge, he shall not be heard.

### Chapter 134.—What one should suffer who presumes to harass his sick debtor or obstruct the funeral of one deceased. Constitution 52, chapter 1.

If anyone wishes to harass his debtor, who is sick and in danger of death, for his debt, he shall not be permitted to do so; nor may he bring any disturbance upon the debtor’s wife or children, nor place seals upon his house, unless, after the debtor’s death, a judicial decision has been established and lawful procedure has followed.

[Haloander: “not before a decree has been issued and lawful procedure, after the death of him said to owe, has been observed.”]

Nor may he obstruct the removal or funeral of the deceased debtor.

[Col. 0931A]

For if he commits anything of this kind, he loses his actions, whether his claims are just or not; he shall lose not only the amount owed to him, but shall also be compelled to pay the deceased’s heirs an equal amount for the injury done to the deceased. Nor are these penalties sufficient: a third of his property shall also be confiscated, and he himself shall be branded with infamy.

### Chapter 135.—Concerning guardians of minors. Constitution 63, chapter 1.

(Constitution 72, § end.) Before they involve themselves in the administration, a tutor or curator of any person is compelled from the outset to take an oath upon the divine Scriptures that he will do everything that he considers beneficial to the minor. We say the same concerning those who undertake curatorships.

### Chapter 136.—Concerning those who deposit their property with others. Constitution 64, chapter 1.

[Col. 0931B]

(Constitution 73, § *Si quis igitur*.) If anyone wishes to place a deposit in another’s safekeeping, three witnesses are necessary for him. For the depositary’s writing alone is insufficient for the depositor as the fullest proof that the deposit was given. The testimony must be given in such a manner that the witnesses state either that the deposit was received in their presence or that the depositary wrote that he had received it.

### Chapter 137.—With what security instruments are to be drawn up, chapter 2.

A little later: If anyone prefers to draw up an instrument without a tabellio [notary], whether concerning a loan, a deposit, or any other matter whatsoever, he shall employ three witnesses.

[Col. 0931C]

Otherwise, his writing alone is not to be believed. There is no difference whether the witnesses signed it or whether the instrument was drawn up in their presence.

### Chapter 138.—Likewise concerning the same matter, chapter 5.

(§ *Sed et si instrumenta*.) We also order that instruments drawn up before a tabellio be secured before their completion by the subscription of witnesses, as stated above, namely, inserted by the tabellio.

### Chapter 139.—How truth is to be established without a written instrument, chapter 10.

(§ end, ibid., *Nam si quis*.) If parties contract without a written instrument, they may establish the truth either by testimony or by the solemnity of an oath; namely, the plaintiff is to produce the witnesses.

### Chapter 140.—That the testament of a deceased natural father must be confirmed by the emperor for his children. Likewise.

(Constitution 74, § *Sit igitur licentia*.) Let a father be permitted in his testament to designate his natural children as his lawful successors, provided that after the parent’s death they petition the emperor, present their father’s testament, and, with the emperor’s assent, receive the paternal estate to the extent in which they are named.

### Chapter 141.—How natural children become legitimate. Likewise.

A little later: Natural children do not become legitimate, after lawful children have been born, unless their father has drawn up dowry instruments with their mother.

### Chapter 142.—Marriage is contracted by consent, even without a promise of dowry or another written instrument. Constitution 65.

[Col. 0932A]

(§ *Illud quoque ibi, quoniam autem*.) If anyone, touching the divine Scriptures, swears to a woman that he will have her as his lawful wife, or if he gives such an oath in an oratory, she shall be his lawful wife, although no dowry and no other written instrument has intervened.

### Chapter 143.—That one whose provincial governor is hostile to him may appeal to the bishop. Constitution 66, chapter 2.

If a provincial governor appears suspect to anyone and he does not wish to litigate before him alone, he may invoke the bishop, so that the bishop, sitting together with the governor, hears the case and causes the litigants to settle it either by amicable agreement

[Col. 0932B]

or by judicial hearing, provided that a judgment consistent with the laws is imposed.

### Chapter 144.—Concerning a freedman ungrateful to his patron. Constitution 69, chapter 1.

(Constitution 78, § *Statuimus*.) If a freedman is ungrateful toward his patron, his freedom must be revoked. The ingratitudes recognized by law must, however, be established—for example, if the freedman raises his hands against his patron, inflicts grievous insults upon him, or causes him serious and intolerable damage; that is, if he utters injuries tending to his dishonor. If the patron or his children prove any of these things, the convicted freedman returns to his former condition.

### Chapter 145.—If a master frees his female slave and marries her, her children also are free, even those whom she bore to him while still in slavery, chapter 3.

[Col. 0932C]

If anyone wishes to marry his freedwoman, he shall draw up dowry instruments with her, and he shall have a lawful wife, even if he himself is distinguished by the highest rank. If children are begotten from such a marriage, they shall succeed their father as lawful heirs.

(Chapter 4.) If anyone has children by his female slave and wishes to free her and, after making dowry instruments, have her as his lawful wife, his children are considered freed by the drawing up of the dowry instruments.

### Chapter 146.—Concerning one who has a case with monks and nuns. Constitution 70, chapter 1.

[Col. 0932D]

If anyone has a lawsuit with monks or nuns, he shall not dare to accuse or summon a monk or nun before a civil judge, but shall instead approach the bishop of the city. For he shall determine whether the principal person ought to appear in person [the text has *principalis persona [principali personae]*], or whether the case should be defended through stewards (*oeconomi*) or representatives (*apocrisiarii*), with all propriety; and the bishop shall pronounce a judgment consistent with laws and canons.

### Chapter 147.—How judgment is to be pronounced. Constitution 73, chapter 5.

Judges shall pronounce judgments in writing, and appeals shall not be denied to one condemned, unless perhaps someone wishes to appeal three times or was contumaciously absent. For a third appeal is barred beforehand, and those condemned in contumacy cannot appeal.

### Chapter 148.—That an arbitrator may not be chosen under the litigants’ oath, chapter 12.

In sum, we have decreed that henceforth it is not lawful for an arbitrator to be chosen under oath of the litigants. For even if he gives a judgment contrary to law, he himself will again have to render an account.

### Chapter 149.—How lawsuits should be settled, chapter 14.

All lawsuits shall be decided according to the laws and constitutions, even if our command or pragmatic sanction has established the contrary.

### Chapter 150.—What one should do who has a complaint against a cleric. Constitution 74, chapter 1.

[Col. 0933B]

If anyone has a lawsuit with a cleric concerning a monetary matter, he shall first approach the bishop to whose jurisdiction the cleric is subject. The bishop shall bring the dispute to a proper conclusion without damage or delay. But if the bishop is unwilling to settle the dispute, then the litigation of the case shall come before civil judges. Where the bishop wishes to settle the matter, all proceedings shall take place without written instruments, and he shall issue his final judgment orally, without writing.

But if litigation arises from a criminal matter, the competent authorities, once invoked, shall impose a conclusion consistent with the laws, provided that the hearing of the dispute does not exceed two months, counted from joinder of issue.

[Col. 0933C]

A cleric shall not otherwise be punished unless, having been found guilty, he has been stripped by his bishop of the priesthood or of the honor of clerical status. But if the offense is ecclesiastical, then examination and punishment of the case shall proceed solely before the bishop according to the canons, other judges having no participation in such cases.

### Chapter 151.—That no one can have several concubines at the same time. Constitution 79.

No one who customarily lies with many women is to be understood to have a concubine. For just as a man with a lawful wife cannot have another during the same marriage, so one who has one concubine cannot have others at that time.

### Chapter 152.—That a witness is not to be heard unless of reputable life, and how evasions concerning debts are to be judged. Constitution 80, chapter 1.

[Col. 0933D]

No one’s testimony shall be received unless he is of good reputation, or is commended by rank, military service, honesty of life, an honorable professional designation, or the concordant statement of other witnesses concerning his good life. But if another witness of the lowest standing is produced in court, the judge may, if he considers it appropriate, subject him to torture.

If anyone has written that he owes money to another and later says that he paid it without a written receipt, he shall not be heard, even though he produces witnesses, except according to the procedure of our constitution. The witnesses must, however, say one of two things: either that, in their presence and having been summoned for the purpose, the debtor paid the money to the creditor; or that, having been summoned for that purpose, they heard the creditor state that the money had been paid to him.

[Col. 0934A]

We do not admit the testimony of those who say that, while passing by, they heard someone state that money had been paid to him; nor is the mere presence of record-keepers sufficient unless witnesses who were also summoned have signed. Likewise, the testimony of many good persons ought to be followed. Those who have stated contrary things should be admitted if they did so through error; but if through some deceit, they should be subjected to torture.

### Chapter 153.—That the testimony of a witness thought freeborn is worthless when he is proved to be a slave, chapter 4.

If a witness produced is alleged to be a slave and he says that he is free, if indeed he claims to be freeborn, his testimony shall be written down; but afterward, if he is proved to be a slave, it shall have no force. But if he says that he is a freedman, and produces an instrument of his manumission, he shall give testimony. If, however, he says that he has documents of his status elsewhere, his testimony shall indeed be written down; but afterward, if he does not produce the documents, it shall have no force.

### Chapter 154.—That a witness known to be the enemy of the person against whom he is produced is not to be heard, chapter 5.

If anyone says that a witness produced is his enemy, then, if this is on account of a criminal case, he shall not give testimony at all. But if it is for another reason, he shall give testimony, but the objection concerning his hostility shall be raised against him.

### Chapter 155.—Concerning one who professes himself mediator between the parties.

If anyone declares himself to be a mediator between the parties and therefore says that he ought not, in doubtful testimony, to testify against either of them, but they agree that he be produced, it follows that in this case he must testify even unwillingly.

### Chapter 156.—That witnesses are not to be produced unless the opponents are present, chapter 7.

Witnesses may be produced only if the opposing party also is present, or fails to appear contumaciously, so that the party may retain the right to raise whatever objection he considers should be made.

[Col. 0934D]

But one is not considered contumaciously absent if he is absent from necessity; for perhaps he has fled into the precincts of holy places.

### Chapter 157.—Concerning a woman who, after her husband’s death, has assumed the guardianship of her children. Constitution 84, chapter 1.

If a mother, after her husband’s death, wishes to administer the guardianship of her children, she shall renounce second marriage in court without an oath, pledge her own property to her underage child, and thus guardianship shall be entrusted to her.

### Chapter 158.—That no one who does not communicate with the Church may hold public office. Constitution 99, chapter 1.

No heretic shall serve in the army or perform public duties. Likewise: we call heretics, without exception, those who do not communicate in the Church,

[Col. 0935A]

even though they appropriate the name of Christians.

### Chapter 159.—A husband intending to accuse his wife of adultery must file a formal accusation. Constitution 105, chapter 7.

If a husband considers that his wife can be convicted of adultery, he must first file formal charges against either the woman or the adulterer; and if such an accusation is proved true, he may then send repudiation.

### Chapter 160.—When a woman may send repudiation to her husband, chapter 8.

If a husband has in any way plotted against his wife’s life; or if, knowing that others were doing so, he has not disclosed it to his wife and has not vindicated her according to the laws; if he has plotted against his wife’s chastity or attempted to hand her over to others for adultery; likewise, if the husband has filed charges of adultery against her but cannot prove the adultery: the woman may send repudiation to her husband.

Likewise: if the husband does not prove his accusation of adultery, he shall be subject to the penalties that the woman would have suffered had she been convicted.

Likewise: if, in the same house in which the woman lives with him, he is found, in contempt of her, dwelling with another woman in the house; or if, while living in the same city, he is convicted of frequently dwelling in another house with another woman; and, having been accused once and twice either by his own relatives, by the woman’s relatives, or by other suitable persons, he does not abstain from such disgraceful conduct, the woman may dissolve the marriage.

### Chapter 161.—How a husband should proceed against a person whom he suspects of adultery, chapter 14.

[Col. 0935C]

If anyone suspects that another wishes to violate his wife’s honor, the husband may send to the suspected person written notices, supported by suitable witnesses, and through those notices and witnesses warn him three times not to be found with his wife. If, after three written notices supported by suitable persons, he finds the person whom he has warned with his wife—either in his own house, in the woman’s house, in the house of that adulterer, in a tavern, or in a bakery (*pistrinum*)—the husband may kill him with his own hands without any liability.

But if he catches him elsewhere conversing with his wife, he shall summon three suitable witnesses through whom he may prove before the judge that he found him conversing with his wife,

[Col. 0935D]

and hand him over to the judge. If the judge finds that the suspected man conversed with the woman after the three notices, he shall punish him as an adulterer without seeking any further proof.

### Chapter 162.—Concerning the same matter, chapter 15.

If, after three notices, the husband finds his wife conversing with the suspected man in a sacred place, he shall hand them over to the defender of the Church or to other clerics, to be guarded separately at the risk of the defender or clerics. After hearing them, the judge shall send them to the reverend bishop of the city, receive them by his authority, and inflict upon both the penalties established against adulterers, without any further inquiry, if he was found speaking with the woman after the three notices.

It is altogether just that neither adulterers nor abductors of women be protected by sacred precincts, and all the more so if someone has spoken in the sacred precincts with another man’s wife concerning the adultery itself. We further determine generally that, if anyone finds his wife, daughter, granddaughter, or daughter-in-law conversing with someone and suspects that they have met for the sake of sexual misconduct, he may hand both over to the defender of the Church or to other clerics, to be guarded separately at their risk until he informs the judge; and the judge shall receive the persons according to the laws and examine the case.

### Chapter 163.—Concerning those prevented by some necessity from appearing in court. From the Digest.

[Col. 0936B]

(Book II, title XI, § *Si quis judicio*.) If anyone has promised to appear in court and is unable to appear because of illness, a storm, or the force of a river, he is aided by an exception.

Likewise (a little later, § *Quod diximus*): What we have said, namely that relief is given also to one who did not appear because he was prevented by a storm or the force of a river, must be understood as follows. A storm may be maritime or terrestrial; and it must be such as to hinder travel or navigation. The force of a river is also to be considered even without a storm. By force of a river we mean that its size is an obstacle, whether a bridge has been swept away or a boat has not remained available.

[Col. 0936C]

Yet if someone could have avoided encountering the storm or force of the river by setting out earlier or sailing at a suitable time, but has restricted himself, should the exception not benefit him at all? This must be decided after hearing the case. For he should not be constrained so strictly that one may say to him, “Why did you not set out a very long time before the day appointed for your appearance?” But neither should he be allowed, if something is imputable to him, to allege a storm or force of a river.

For what if someone, while in Rome and at the very time appointed for his appearance, with no necessity pressing, set out for a municipality for reasons of his own choosing? Is he not unworthy of the protection of this exception? Or what if there was a storm at sea, but he could have come by land, or gone around the river?

[Col. 0936D]

It must likewise be said that the exception does not always benefit him, unless narrow circumstances did not allow travel by land or a detour; provided, however, that the river had so overflowed as to fill every place where he was required to appear, or some unforeseen disaster had destroyed that same place, or made prior knowledge dangerous to one approaching it. By what is good and equitable, the exception must also be made available to him in this case.

Likewise, an exception is given to one who wished to come to court but was detained by a magistrate, provided that he was detained without his own bad faith. For if he himself sought this or supplied the cause, the exception will not benefit him; his own bad faith will harm him. Nor will the bad faith of others who caused his detention harm him.
