But if a private person detained him, this exception will by no means benefit him.

Likewise (ibid., law IV, § *Illud*): If someone did not appear because he was hindered by a funeral in his household, an exception ought to be given to him.

### Chapter 164.—Likewise concerning judicial holidays.

(Book II, title XII, law I.) The address of the deified Marcus provides that no one shall compel his adversary to come to court during the season of harvest and vintage, because persons occupied with agricultural work ought not to be compelled into the forum. But if the praetor persists in summoning them through ignorance or negligence, then, if they come voluntarily and judgment is given while the parties are present and litigate voluntarily, the judgment shall be valid, even though the person who summoned them acted improperly.

Likewise (ibid., law III): The term “season of harvest and vintage” is also ordinarily used of matters that perish through time or death, such as theft, damage, injury, aggravated injuries alleged to have arisen from fire, collapse, shipwreck, a raft, or a ship captured by assault, and similar cases.

### Chapter 165.—Concerning agreements.

(Title XIV, law XXVII, § *Pacta quae*.) Agreements containing a disgraceful cause are not to be observed.

Likewise (ibid., law XXVIII.) Agreements made contrary to the rules of civil law are not held valid.

### Chapter 166.—Likewise, that one who contracts an unlawful marriage becomes infamous.

(Book III, title II, law XIII, § *Cum autem*.) If anyone contracts marriage or betrothal with a woman whom he either cannot or ought not lawfully marry, he shall be marked with infamy.

### Chapter 167.—Concerning payments.

[Col. 0937C]

(Title V, law XXXIX.) Anyone who makes payment on another’s behalf releases him, even against his will and without his knowledge. But what is owed to someone cannot lawfully be claimed by another without that person’s consent.

### Chapter 168.—Concerning that which is done through fear.

(Lib. IV, tit. II, l. I.) What has been done through fear I shall not hold valid. Likewise (ibid., l. III, § *Sed vim*): By force we understand grievous force, and that which is inflicted contrary to good morals, not that which a magistrate has rightly inflicted—namely, under lawful right and by virtue of the office which he holds. (Ibid., l. IX.) We must understand present fear, not a mere apprehension that it may be inflicted. (Lib. IV, tit. VI, l. III.) A person is also deemed absent through fear who is absent because he has been frightened by a justified fear of death or bodily torture. [Col. 0937D]

CAP. 169.—Who is absent on public business.

(Lib. IV, tit. VII, l. XVI.) We understand only those to be absent on public business who are absent not for their own advantage, but under compulsion.

CAP. 170.—That no one may be judge or arbitrator in his own cause.

(Lib. IV, tit. VIII, l. LVI.) Likewise. If anyone has been made arbitrator in a matter of his own, he cannot pronounce judgment.

CAP. 171.—For what sailors, innkeepers, and stable-keepers receive payment.

(Lib. IV, tit. IX, l. V.) A sailor, an innkeeper, and a stable-keeper receive payment not for safekeeping, but the sailor in order to carry passengers across, the innkeeper in order to permit travellers to remain at the inn, and the stable-keeper in order to permit beasts of burden to be stabled with him. Yet they are liable under the heading of safekeeping; for likewise the fuller and the carrier of baggage receive payment not for safekeeping but for their craft, and yet under a contract of hire they are liable for safekeeping. [Col. 0938A]

CAP. 172.—That one who kills another’s slave lying in wait for him is secure; and concerning certain other matters, book IX, title II (book IV).

Therefore, if I kill your slave when he is a robber lying in wait for me, I shall be secure. For natural reason permits a person to defend himself against danger. The Law of the Twelve Tables permits one to kill a thief caught by night, provided that he gives the alarm and calls witnesses to it. It sometimes also permits a thief thus caught to be killed if he defended himself with a weapon, provided that the act is likewise proclaimed. Likewise (ibid., l. X): He who kills another’s slave caught in adultery is not liable under this law. Likewise (ibid., § *In hac quoque*): If anyone sets fire to his stubble or thorns in order to burn them, and the fire, wandering and spreading farther, damages another’s crop or vineyard, we must inquire whether this occurred through his lack of skill or negligence; for if he did it on a windy day, he is liable in fault. For he who provides the occasion is deemed to have caused the damage. He too is guilty of the same offence who did not take care that the fire should not spread farther. But if he observed everything that he ought to have observed, or a sudden force of wind carried the fire farther, he is free from fault. Likewise (ibid., l. XXXIX): A person who finds another’s cattle in his field does not lawfully pen them up, nor drive them otherwise than—as we said above—as if they were his own; rather, he must turn them out without damage, or notify their owner to take back what is his. [Col. 0938C]

CAP. 173.—That the master also is guilty when, with his knowledge, a slave kills someone. Title IV (book II).

If a slave kills with his master’s knowledge, he binds the master for the whole amount; for the master himself is deemed to have killed. But if the master was unaware, the noxal action applies; for he ought not to be liable on account of his slave’s wrongdoing beyond surrendering him in compensation for the offence.

CAP. 174.—On the condiction where a thing has been given for a purpose and the purpose has not followed.

Likewise. Therefore, what has been given for an honourable purpose may be recovered if the purpose for which it was given has not followed. But if the recipient’s purpose was disgraceful, it may be recovered even if the purpose has followed.

CAP. 175.—That he is understood to give a mandate who permits another to be mandated to give credit to him; book XVII, title I (book XVIII).

[Col. 0938D]

He who permits another to give a mandate that credit be extended to him is understood to give the mandate.

CAP. 176.—That a partnership formed by deceit and fraud is of no effect, title II.

(Lib. III, § *Societas*.) If a partnership has been entered into through malicious deceit or for the sake of committing fraud, it is by law itself of no effect, because good faith is opposed to fraud and deceit. Likewise (ibid., l. LIII): It is manifest that what has been acquired by theft or another wrongdoing ought not to be contributed to a partnership, because fellowship in offences is disgraceful and foul. Likewise (l. LVII): If a partnership in wrongdoing has been formed, it is settled that there is no partnership. [Col. 0939A] For it is laid down generally that there is no partnership in dishonourable matters.

CAP. 177.—That one who flees to a friend in order to seek intercession is not a fugitive; book XXI, title I.

(Lib. XLIII, § *Qui ad amicum*.) He who flees to a friend in order to seek his intercession is not a fugitive; indeed, even if he goes with the intention that, unless he obtains assistance, he will not return home, he is not a fugitive.

CAP. 178.—That a thing is not alienated when it is sold for less than was directed, title II.

If anyone sells my property for less than I instructed, it is not deemed alienated.

CAP. 179.—Upon whom proof of a case rests; book XXII, title III.

The burden of proof rests upon the person who asserts, not upon the person who denies.

CAP. 180.—Which witnesses may or may not be compelled; title V, book IV.

[Col. 0939B]

No person is to be summoned against his will to give testimony in litigation against his father-in-law, son-in-law, stepfather, stepson, first cousin, female first cousin, cousin’s son, or those related in the first degree. Likewise, neither the freedman of himself, his children, parents, husband, or wife. Nor may patrons or patronesses be compelled to testify against freedpersons, nor freedpersons against their patron.

CAP. 181.—Which witnesses are not competent; book VI.

Likewise. Those persons over whom authority can be exercised so as to order them to be witnesses do not appear to be competent witnesses. Likewise (book IX): A father is not a competent witness for his son, nor a son for his father. Likewise (ibid., l. XVI): Those who have given false or inconsistent testimony, or have betrayed both parties, are punished by the judges. Likewise (ibid., l. XVII): A father and a son under his power, and likewise two brothers under the power of the same father, may both serve as witnesses in the same will or transaction, because it does no harm for several witnesses from one household to be employed in another person’s affair. Likewise (ibid., l. XVIII): From the fact that the Julian law on adultery prohibits a woman convicted of adultery from giving testimony, it follows that women also have the right to give testimony in court. [Col. 0939C]

CAP. 182.—How betrothals ought to be made. Likewise, book XXIII (title I, law II).

Betrothals, like marriages, are made by the consent of those contracting them; and therefore, as in marriage, so in betrothal a daughter under paternal power must consent. Likewise (book XII): She who does not oppose her father’s will is understood to consent. [Col. 0939D] But permission to dissent from her father is granted when a suitor unworthy in character or morally shameful is chosen for her by her father.

CAP. 183.—Likewise, concerning the differing rank and condition of those marrying; book XIII.

When a son under paternal power dissents, a betrothal cannot be made in his name. Likewise (book XIV): In contracting betrothals the age of the contracting parties is not fixed as it is in marriages. Accordingly, betrothals may be made from the beginning of childhood, provided that the act can be understood by both persons—that is, provided they are not younger than seven years. Title II (book XVI, § *Furor*): Insanity does not permit marriage to be contracted, because consent is required; but it does not dissolve a marriage rightly contracted. Likewise (book XXIV): Cohabitation with a free woman is to be understood as marriage, not concubinage, provided she has not made gain from her body. [Col. 0940A] Likewise (book XLIII, § *Quae in adulterio*): A woman caught in adultery is as though condemned by public judgment. Therefore, if she is alleged to have been condemned for adultery, she is not marked merely because she was caught, but because she was also condemned by public judgment. It must generally be determined that, so long as it is certain that a husband is alive though held captive, their wives have no permission to pass into another marriage.

CAP. 184.—That long-established customs are commonly held as law. Institutes, book I, title II.

(§ *Ex non scripto*.) What usage has approved comes into law from unwritten sources. For long-established customs, confirmed by the consent of those who use them, imitate law. Likewise. [Col. 0940B] A little later: Those things which each state has itself established are often changed, either by the tacit consent of the prince or by another law subsequently enacted.

CAP. 185.—Concerning those born of parents both freeborn, or of differing condition; title IV.

(§ *Ingenuus*.) A freeborn person—that is, one who is free immediately upon birth—is one born in wedlock either from two freeborn persons, from freedpersons, or from one freedperson and one freeborn person. But if anyone is born of a free mother and a slave father, he is nevertheless born free; just as one born of a free mother and an uncertain father, because he was conceived outside wedlock. It is sufficient that he had a free mother at the time when he is born, although she conceived while a slave. Conversely, if a woman conceives while free and then, having become a slave, gives birth, it has been decided [Col. 0940C] that the child born is free, because the mother’s misfortune ought not to harm one who is in the womb. From this another question arose: if a pregnant slavewoman is manumitted and afterwards becomes a slave again and gives birth, does she bear a free child or a slave? Marcellus holds that the child is born free; for it is sufficient for one in the womb that he had a free mother even during the intervening period, and this is correct.

CAP. 186.—That one who kills his own slave without cause should be punished equally with one who kills another’s slave, and various provisions concerning fugitive slaves. Title VIII, book I.

(§ *Nam apud omnes*.) Among all nations alike we may observe that masters possess the power of life and death over their slaves, and that whatever is acquired through a slave is acquired by the master.

[Col. 0940D] Likewise, § *Sed hoc tempore*: He who kills his own slave without cause is ordered to be punished no less than he who kills another’s slave. A little later: When Pius Antoninus was consulted by certain provincial governors concerning slaves who take refuge at a sacred shrine or at statues of the emperors, he ordered that, if their masters’ cruelty appeared intolerable, the masters should be compelled to sell the slaves on good terms, the price being given to the masters. And rightly so: for it is advantageous to the commonwealth that no one misuse his own property. The words of his rescript issued to Aelius Martianus are these: “The authority of masters over their slaves ought indeed to remain unimpaired, lest any person be deprived of his right; but it is in the masters’ interest that assistance against cruelty, hunger, or intolerable injury not be denied to those who make a just appeal. [Col. 0941A] Therefore investigate the complaints of those from the household of Julius Sabinus who have fled to the statue; and if you discover that they have either been treated more harshly than is equitable or subjected to shameful injury, order them to be sold, on condition that they do not return into their master’s power.”

CAP. 187.—That several witnesses from one household may be employed in another person’s affair; book II, title X.

§ *Pater*. Two brothers who are under the power of the same father may both serve as witnesses in one will, because it does no harm for several witnesses from one household to be employed in another person’s affair. But among witnesses there ought not to be one who is under the power of the testator.

CAP. 188.—Who may make wills; book II, title XII.

§ *Non tamen*. Not everyone is permitted to make a will; for those who are subject to another’s legal authority have no right to make a will. Likewise, § *Praeterea testamentum*: Children below puberty cannot make a will, because they possess no judgment of mind. Nor can the insane, because they lack reason. It is irrelevant if the child later reaches puberty, or the insane person later regains soundness of mind, and dies. But if insane persons make a will during a period in which their insanity has ceased, they are deemed to have made a valid will. § *Item. Surdus.* Likewise, the deaf and mute cannot always make a will. We are certainly speaking of the deaf person who hears nothing at all, not one who hears slowly or imperfectly. Likewise, a mute person is understood to be one who can utter nothing, not one who speaks slowly or imperfectly. [Col. 0941B]

CAP. 189.—Concerning the children whom a slavewoman may perhaps have borne to her master, and who, after she was subsequently manumitted and lawfully united in marriage, bore other children; book II, title II.

If anyone has joined a woman to himself in his household union, not at the outset with marital intention, though she was one with whom he could contract marriage, and has had children by her; and if afterwards, as affection developed, he has also executed nuptial instruments with her and had sons or daughters: we have decided that not only the children born after the dowry are legitimate and under their father’s power, but also the earlier children, because the later-born children have supplied them with the occasion of a lawful name; and this holds even if no children were born after the dowry instrument was executed, or even if those born [Col. 0941D] thereafter were removed from this light by death.

CAP. 190.—That what is promised for a shameful cause has no validity; title XVIII.

(Institutes, book III, title XX, § *Quod turpi*.) What is promised for a shameful cause is invalid; for example, if someone promises that he will commit homicide or sacrilege.

CAP. 191.—That force and injury must be repelled; book I, title II.

(Pandects, book I, title I, law III.) That we may repel force and injury; for this is sanctioned by law, that whatever anyone has done for the protection of his own body is judged to have been done lawfully.

CAP. 192.—That a law pardons past errors in such a way that no such thing may occur thereafter. Likewise, title II (title III, law XXII).

[Col. 0942A]

When a law grants indulgence for the past, it prohibits for the future.

CAP. 193.—Concerning those who are born in different circumstances; title V, book XII.

It is now accepted that a complete child may be born in the seventh month, on the authority of Hippocrates, a most learned man; and therefore one born in the seventh month from a lawful marriage must be believed to be a lawful son. Likewise (ibid., l. XIX): When a lawful marriage has been made, children follow the father; children conceived outside wedlock follow the mother. Likewise (ibid., l. XXIII): Those are called conceived outside wedlock who cannot identify their father, or who indeed can identify him but have a father whom it is not lawful for them to have. [Col. 0942B] Likewise (book XXIV): This is the law of nature, that one born without lawful marriage follows the mother. Likewise (book XXVI): Those in the womb are regarded in almost all civil law as already existing in the world; for lawful inheritances are restored to them. Thus, if a pregnant woman is captured by enemies, what is born, even though she gives birth while in the possession of a purchaser in good faith, is not acquired by prescription as though it were stolen property. Likewise (book I, title VI, law VIII): Although an insane person cannot take a wife, he can nevertheless retain a marriage.

CAP. 194.—Concerning an unlawful agreement. From the Theodosian law.

If persons agree concerning the commission of a crime, the infliction of violence, the doing of something prohibited by laws or by decency, or concerning someone’s property or found goods, such agreements cannot be valid. [Col. 0942C]

CAP. 195.—Concerning a thing transferred by written instrument at two different times. Likewise, book V.

If anyone gives one thing by lawful written instruments to two persons, to one earlier and to the other later, the question in such gifts is not who received earlier or later; rather, the person to whom the donor delivered the thing shall possess it. It makes no difference whether such a gift was made to relatives or to strangers.

CAP. 196.—Concerning the claim of a debt.

Although the first claimant offers an oath, nevertheless, where there is no proof of the debt, the person accused may establish his good faith by the solemnity of an oath.

CAP. 197.—Concerning the same matter.

[Col. 0942D]

If a person sued for repayment of money offers an oath, and the other party voluntarily grants him the requirement of swearing, he cannot afterwards demand the debt from him.

CAP. 198.—Who ought to swear in order to obtain a thing.

The heir of the person to whom money is said to have been lent cannot be called to an oath, because he could not know fully what his predecessor did.

CAP. 199.—Concerning expenses incurred upon things lent for use, and the obligations of a borrower for use.

Whatever has been expended upon a thing lent for use because of disease or another reason may be recovered from the owner. If a thing lent for use is lost through fire, collapse, shipwreck, or any similar accident, the person to whom it was lent is not liable on that account, unless perhaps, being able to save the borrowed thing, he preferred his own. If anyone has received from another, for use only, a slave, horse, or any other thing lent for that purpose, and has taken them to battle or where they might incur danger to life, he is rightly held by the owner liable for return of the thing lent. If anyone entrusts a thing to another to be sold at an agreed price, and while it is being offered for sale by him it perishes by any accident, the loss falls upon the person who gave it to be sold. But if the recipient loses the thing received while wishing to sell it, not at the owner’s request but with the permission of the recipient, he brings the loss of the destroyed thing upon himself. If a creditor holding a pledge deposited with him without condition has summoned his debtor three times to receive his pledges upon payment of the debt, [Col. 0943B] and the debtor, after three warnings and payment of the debt, refuses to take his pledges, the creditor shall have free power to sell the pledge.

CAP. 200.—Concerning partners.

As profit, so loss is shared among partners, unless something has been destroyed through a partner’s fault or fraud.

CAP. 201.—Concerning agreements.

Agreements made by unwilling persons contrary to laws and constitutions have, beyond doubt, no legal force. Likewise, an agreement made in bad faith ought to be void. A private agreement derogates in no respect from public law.

CAP. 202.—Which actions pass to heirs.

In criminal cases, if someone has not, before dying, been charged with and convicted of the crime of his act, then, if after his death something which he owed to another happens to be found among his successors, only that which is known to have come to the heir must be restored by the heir. Otherwise, in such a matter the heir is liable neither to punishment nor to any satisfaction. [Col. 0943C]

CAP. 203.—Who ought to swear.

The law commands that proof be required not from the possessor but from the claimant’s side, because it says that all proof ought to be sought from the person who desires to obtain the thing claimed, not from the one who maintains that he holds it lawfully—except only in the case where it is necessary to ask the possessor whether he began to possess in his own right or by succession.

CAP. 204.—Concerning the oath of witnesses, and how one who has committed such and such an offence shall be judged.

[Col. 0943D]

Before witnesses are questioned concerning the case, they must be bound by oath to swear that they will say nothing false; and greater credence is to be given to persons of higher rank than to those of lower rank. The testimony of one person, however distinguished and competent he may seem, is never to be heard.

If any freeborn person strikes a freeborn person or a slave so that blood does not flow, he shall be adjudged liable for up to three solidi for each blow. But if an ecclesiastical or royal person does this, [the penalty is] 3 solidi. Likewise, if a slave does this to an ecclesiastical, royal, or Frankish person, [he shall pay] 3 solidi, or swear with six oath-helpers. If a slave causes bloodshed to a freeborn, royal, or ecclesiastical person, [Col. 0944A] he shall be adjudged liable for three and a half solidi, or swear with six oath-helpers. Likewise, if a freeborn, royal, or ecclesiastical person breaks a slave’s bone, he shall be adjudged liable for 9 solidi, or swear with six oath-helpers. But if a slave does this to a Frankish person, [he shall pay] 36 solidi, or swear with six oath-helpers. If he does it to a royal or ecclesiastical person, [he shall pay] 9 solidi.

If a slave strikes a slave twice or three times, he shall be adjudged [to pay] 4 denarii for the sake of preserving peace. If he sheds blood, [he shall pay] three and a half solidi; if he breaks his bone, 5 solidi. If he knocks out an eye, ear, foot, or nose, [he shall pay] 18 solidi, or swear with six oath-helpers. If a freeborn man strikes a freeborn woman, he shall be adjudged liable for 18 solidi, or swear with six oath-helpers. If a freeborn man breaks a bone of a freeborn man in any limb, or pierces him through, or wounds him in the thighs, he shall be adjudged liable for 36 solidi, [Col. 0944B] or swear with six oath-helpers.

If a freeborn man knocks out a freeborn man’s thumb, [he shall pay] 50 solidi; if the thumb remains hanging there, 36 solidi. If the second finger, with which one shoots an arrow, is knocked out, 36 solidi shall be paid in compensation. If anyone cuts off another’s hand or foot, gouges out his eye, or cuts off his ear or nose, he shall be adjudged liable for 100 solidi. In every mutilation, however, if the mutilated limb remains hanging, he shall pay half of what he would have had to pay if that limb had been severed. If he knocks out the middle finger, [he shall pay] 15 solidi; likewise for the fourth or fifth finger; for a tooth, 5 solidi. If anyone wounds a person on the head so that blood falls to the ground, he shall be adjudged liable for 15 solidi. If he denies all these things, he shall swear with six oath-helpers.

If anyone kills a royal or ecclesiastical person, [Col. 0944C] he shall be adjudged liable for 100 solidi, or swear with twelve oath-helpers; if he kills a slave, [he shall pay] 36 solidi, or swear with six oath-helpers. But where a free person pays 15 solidi, a royal or ecclesiastical person shall pay half, and so proportionately as the offence increases. If a freeborn man kills a freeborn man and covers him with branches, or wishes to conceal him in a well or any place whatsoever—an offence called *mortridum*—he shall be adjudged liable for 600 solidi, or swear with seventy-two oath-helpers. Wherever the sums in solidi increase, there shall likewise be seventy-two oath-helpers.

CAP. 205.—Law concerning diverse cases. From the Theodosian law.

But whoever has thrown someone into prison in order that something might be extorted from him: whatever has been done for this reason is of no effect. Fraud exists when one thing is done and another feigned. Whoever employed fraud or fear in order that property might pass to another shall be liable under the action for force and fraud. If anyone, after attaining majority, does not choose to revoke by his silence and inaction what he did while under age, he cannot retain the remedy of restoration to his original position in that matter. [Col. 0944D]

CAP. 206.—That every layperson who injures any cleric shall be anathematized. Capitularies, book V, chapter 102.

Whoever, whether judge or layperson, presumes to inflict injury upon a priest, deacon, any cleric, or one of their juniors, without a hearing before the bishop, archdeacon, or archpriest, shall be held under anathema, excluded from the fellowship of all Christians. [Col. 0945A]

CAP. 207.—Concerning robbers, and by what graduated punishment they are to be punished. Capitularies, book VI.

We command that the following be observed concerning robbers: for a first offence he shall not die, but lose one eye; for another offence, the robber’s nose shall be cut off; for a third offence, if he has not amended, he shall die.

CAP. 208.—That infamous persons may not be witnesses, chapter 309.

It has been decided that witnesses who are accomplices in a crime, persons of ill repute, false accusers, and others prohibited by canons and law are not to be admitted.

CAP. 209.—Concerning the same matter, chapter 313.

[Col. 0945B] It has been decided that one who has confessed against himself is not to be believed against another.

CAP. 210.—The testimony of one person is not to be received, chapter 314.

The testimony of one person is not to be accepted. For if there are several witnesses on each side, the more truthful, devout, and honourable are to be selected, who shall confirm their testimony by oath that they will say nothing false.

CAP. 211.—That one who kills by night a thief carrying stolen goods is in no way guilty of homicide, chapter 343.

If a thief is caught in theft at night while carrying stolen goods with him and is killed, no complaint of homicide shall arise from this.

CAP. 212.—What must be done by one who unknowingly buys something from a thief, chapter 344.

[Col. 0945C]

If anyone unknowingly buys something from a thief, he shall seek out the seller after an interval has been granted. If he cannot find him, he shall prove himself innocent by oath and witnesses, restore what is known to be in his possession, and not cease seeking the thief. But if he wishes to conceal the thief and is afterwards discovered to have committed perjury, he shall be condemned for the crime just as that thief is.

CAP. 213.—Concerning one who kills any animal belonging to another, chapter 345.

If anyone secretly or by day kills another’s horse, ox, or any animal, denies it, and is afterwards proved to have done so, he shall make compensation as for stolen property. [Col. 0945D]

CAP. 214.—Concerning the same matter, chapter 346.

If anyone kills another’s animal where there is cause and does not deny it, he shall promptly give an equivalent animal and take the carcass of the dead one.

CAP. 215.—Concerning one who knowingly buys stolen property, chapter 347.

If anyone presumes knowingly to buy stolen property and is proved to have done so, he shall restore an equivalent to the person whose property he bought, his right of action against the other party being preserved.

CAP. 216.—Concerning one who knowingly receives stolen property of a robber for safekeeping, chapter 248.

If anyone knowingly receives stolen property from a robber to keep, he shall make compensation as a thief.

CAP. 217.—Concerning one who blocks a public road for someone, chapter 353.

[Col. 0946A]

If anyone, contrary to law, blocks for someone a public road, a paved road, or a common road, he shall make compensation according to his law and remove the obstruction which he made there. If he wishes to deny it, he shall swear with twelve such oath-helpers.

CAP. 218.—Concerning the same matter, chapter 354.

If anyone blocks a neighbourhood road or a pasture road, he shall make compensation according to his law and open that road. The same is to be done concerning a footpath.

CAP. 219.—Concerning one who maliciously pollutes a spring or well, chapter 355.

If anyone maliciously pollutes or defiles a spring in any way, he shall first restore it so that no suspicion of pollution remains in it, and shall make amends for this to the neighbours according to his law. But if it is the well of several neighbours, they shall share the compensation among themselves. [Col. 0946B]

CAP. 220.—Concerning one to whom metal or particular valuables have been lent, chapter 356.

If gold, silver, ornaments, or any valuables have been lent to someone, whether entrusted for safekeeping or for sale, and happen to be burned by fire in his house together with his own goods, he shall tender oaths together with the witnesses who received the things lent that nothing from them accrued to his own advantage, and he shall be compelled to pay nothing, except for gold and silver, which could not be burned. But if the things lent are proved to have been stolen, the person who lost the borrowed goods shall be granted time to seek out the thief by his own investigation; and, if he finds him, he shall take care to restore only his own property to the lender. The compensation for the theft, however, shall belong to the person who had received the things lent. [Col. 0946C] But if the thief is not found within the appointed time, half of the lent goods shall be returned, the owner receiving it. Both parties shall bear half the loss; and if afterwards the owner finds with the borrower anything that has been concealed, it shall be exacted from him as stolen property.

CAP. 221.—Concerning one who sells any property of another without its owner’s consent, chapter 365.

If anyone sells another’s property without its owner’s consent—whether a male slave, female slave, or any property whatever—he shall restore the very thing according to law. If he cannot find that thing, he shall restore two similar things of equal value. [Col. 0946D]

CAP. 222.—Concerning damage done, chapter 366.

If anyone knocks out one eye of another’s horse, ox, or any four-footed animal, that animal shall be valued, and he shall pay one third of its value in compensation.

CAP. 223.—Concerning one who receives a robber as a guest. Capitularies, book VI, chapter 293.

Whoever, after the Mass of Saint John in the previous year, has given lodging [the printed reading has *manumissionem*, “manumission”] to some robber: if he is a Frank, he shall swear with twelve similar Franks that he did not know him to be a robber, even if he is his father, brother, or some relative. If he cannot swear this and is convicted by another of having received the robber as a guest, [Col. 0947A] he shall be treated as a robber, because he is faithless to us and to the Franks; and he who received him is like him. But if he heard that he was a robber yet does not know it firmly, he shall swear alone that he never heard, whether truly or falsely, that he was a robber; or he shall be prepared, if that man is afterwards convicted of robbery, to be condemned likewise.

CAP. 224.—A slave is not to be heard when imputing a crime to anyone, chapter 344.

A slave is in no way to be believed if he brings an accusation against anyone or even charges his own master with a crime. For even if, placed under torture, he states what he alleges, he ought by no means to be believed.

CAP. 225.—Concerning those with whom part of plunder is found, chapter 355.

[Col. 0947B]

A person with whom a crime is established and part of the plunder is found shall immediately be compelled to name his accomplices. If he refuses to name them, he shall be subject to punishment. But if he is a person of higher rank, he shall answer for the crime and restore fourfold what had been taken or destroyed. But if part of the plunder is found with a slave, he shall receive one hundred and forty lashes, stretched out publicly, and shall not delay to name his accomplices.

CAP. 226.—That delay is to be granted in lesser offences, and that persons convicted of grave crimes who wish to appeal are not to be heard. Capitularies, book VII, chapter 181.

In civil cases and lesser crimes, delay under the laws is to be granted. Convicted murderers, adulterers, evildoers, and poisoners are not to be heard if they wish to appeal. [Col. 0947C]

CAP. 227.—If anyone entrusts his property to another for sale, chapter 298.

If anyone entrusts a thing to anyone else to be sold at an agreed price, and while it is being offered for sale by him it perishes by any accident, the loss falls upon the person who gave it to be sold. But if the recipient loses the thing received while wishing to sell it, not at the owner’s request but with the recipient’s permission, he brings the loss of the destroyed thing upon himself.

CAP. 228.—Concerning things lent, chapter 299.

If a creditor holding a pledge deposited with him without condition has summoned his debtor three times to receive his pledges upon payment of the debt, and the debtor, after three warnings and payment of the debt, refuses to receive his pledges, the creditor shall have free power to sell the pledge. [Col. 0947D]

CAP. 229.—Concerning payment of debts and set-off, chapter 303.

If anyone owes another ten solidi, and the creditor in turn owes the debtor five solidi for any reason, and the creditor comes and demands the entire ten solidi from the debtor: if that debtor proves that the other owes him five solidi, then, because the creditor sued him for the whole ten solidi, he who refused to set off the debt shall lose his case. The same rule applies to grain and other goods.

CAP. 230.—If money has been lent to a son under paternal power without his father’s knowledge, chapter 304.

[Col. 0948A]

One who has lent money to a son under paternal power, contrary to legal prohibitions and without the father’s knowledge, cannot demand it from that son either while the father lives or after his death.

CAP. 231.—Concerning sale of a pledge, chapter 313.

If a creditor, while the debtor delays payment, sells a thing pledged to him for the debt, and receives more than was owed, the excess received shall be restored to the debtor.

CAP. 232.—If anyone sells another’s property for less, chapter 308.

If anyone directs another to sell his property for ten solidi and that person sells it for eight, he shall be compelled to make up to the principal the price directed—whatever less he received from the purchaser; the sale, however, cannot be rescinded. [Col. 0948B]

CAP. 233.—That no one may act contrary to the will of the deceased, chapter 326.

All who act contrary to the will of the deceased shall be deprived of the inheritance as unworthy persons.

CAP. 234.—Concerning the same matter, chapter 327.

He who has received and claimed something left to him by will, and wishes to act contrary to the will of the deceased, shall have no permission whatsoever to do so.

CAP. 235.—Concerning one who composes a writing or insulting words to injure another’s reputation.

He who publicly composes a writing or insulting words against another’s reputation, and, when discovered, cannot prove what he has written, shall be flogged. And whoever first finds the writing shall tear it up, unless he wishes to incur the charge of being its fictitious author. [Col. 0948C]

CAP. 236.—Concerning preservation of the peace. Capitularies, book III, chapter 61.

Concerning robbers who are greatly notorious: whoever captures any one of them shall suffer no harm on that account.

CAP. 237.—Concerning preservation of peace and justice within the realm.

Concerning peace and justice within the realm: let what has often been commanded through other capitularies be fulfilled.

CAP. 238.—Concerning violation of the immunity of the Church. Capitularies, book IV, chapter 13.

If anyone, for a slight cause or without cause, kills a person in a church, he shall make composition with his life. But [Col. 0948D] if they quarrel outside, and one flees from the other into a church, and the latter kills him there while defending himself, then, if he has no witnesses to this act, he shall affirm by oath with twelve lawful oath-helpers that he killed him in self-defence. After this he shall be compelled to pay ten solidi to the share of the church which he polluted by that homicide, and in addition our ban. The person killed, however, shall lie without composition. Thereafter the killer shall receive, according to canonical judgment, a penance suitable to the crime he committed.

If his own slave commits this act, he shall be examined by the judgment of boiling water as to whether he did it willingly or in self-defence; and if his hand is burned, he shall be put to death. But if it is not burned, his master shall pay to the church according to that slave’s wergeld, [Col. 0949A] or, if he wishes, hand him over to that same church. Concerning an ecclesiastical or fiscal beneficiary slave, we decree that for the first occurrence his wergeld shall be paid on his behalf; for the second occurrence, the slave himself shall be handed over for punishment. The inheritance of a free person who is condemned to death for such a crime shall nevertheless pass to his lawful heirs. If such a homicide is committed in the churchyard of a church whose gate has been consecrated with relics of saints, it shall be amended or compensated in the same way. But if the church gate is not consecrated, compensation shall be made in the same manner as is required when an offence is committed by violating immunity.

CAP. 239.—How a free person or slave ought to clear himself of theft, chapter 27.

If a free man is accused of theft and has property of his own, he shall bind himself in the mallus before the count’s presence. [Col. 0949B] If he has no property, he shall provide sureties, who shall bind him and ensure that he is brought to the court. The first time, he may, if able, establish his innocence according to the law by oath; but if, on another occasion, two or three persons accuse him of theft, he may contend in the field against one of them with shield and staff. If a slave is accused of theft, his master shall make compensation for him or clear him by oath—unless he has committed such a theft as requires that he be handed over for punishment.

### Chapter 240.—That newly introduced unjust customs are to be abolished, ch. 45.

Concerning unjust exactions and customs newly established [Col. 0949C]—such as tributes and tolls in the middle of a road, where there is neither water, marsh, bridge, nor anything of that kind from which a payment may justly be demanded; or where ships customarily pass beneath bridges; or in the middle of a river where there is no obstruction—we decree that they be removed. Ancient customs, however, are to be reported to our attention.

### Chapter 241.—That new forests are to be relinquished, ch. 63.

Concerning our forests: wherever they may be, let inquiry be made with the greatest diligence into how they may be kept safe and protected; and let the counts be notified not to establish any forest anew. Wherever forests newly established without our command are found, they must relinquish them.

### Chapter 242.—Concerning the agreement of the laws.

[Col. 0949D] Partners may prosecute common cases on behalf of absent co-partners, provided that those present give security that whatever is adjudged will be acceptable to those absent, or provide a surety immediately, so that they do not delay in carrying out everything that has been determined.

### Chapter 243.—Concerning one who unlawfully encroaches upon boundaries.

If anyone is proved to have encroached upon boundaries, because, before anything had been settled by judgment, he invaded that which another had possessed, he shall lose not only what he wickedly encroached upon; but also, so that no one may occupy another’s property when defeated in litigation, the encroacher upon another’s right shall restore an equal extent of land to that which he presumed to invade.

### Chapter 244.—Concerning things sold.

[Col. 0950A]

When a thing has been purchased between buyer and seller for an agreed price, even though it is worth more than the amount for which it is presently sold, this alone is to be examined: whether the person proved to have purchased it employed no fraud or violence. If the seller wishes to revoke the sale, he is by no means to be permitted to do so.

### Chapter 245.—Likewise concerning the same matter.

The earlier provision of the law was that, if one of the co-partners wished to sell property for any necessity, an outsider should not have permission to purchase it. But this concession is judged preferable: that anyone may use free discretion concerning his own possessions and, passing over co-partners or relatives, have unrestricted power to sell to whomever he wishes.

### Chapter 246.—Concerning dowry property.

[Col. 0950B]

If it happens that a husband dies while his wife survives, whatever the woman had given her husband as dowry shall return to the woman’s ownership; nor shall the heirs of the deceased husband presume to claim it.

### Chapter 247.—Concerning one accused on a capital charge, Book IX.

Whoever brings against another an accusation of homicide involving danger or capital punishment shall not be heard by the judges until he has entered in writing that he will undergo the same penalty that he seeks to impose upon the accused. If he believes that another’s slaves ought to be accused, he shall bind himself by the same formal undertaking, so that he will compensate for the punishments of innocent slaves either by the penalty of his own head or by loss of his property. Before the formal accusation, no one shall be made an accused criminal. [Col. 0950C] For once the accusation has been duly entered, the accused is then to be received by the judge and placed in custody along with the accuser—yet with this proviso, that the rank of both accused and accuser be considered, and that before the investigation the judge cause each to be kept in custody in a manner appropriate to his birth or rank.

Moreover, those who have confessed their own crimes under interrogation are not to be believed by the judge if they wish to speak against others, because right and law establish that an accused person, by a voluntary confession, does not make another person accused; nor is one to be believed concerning another who has confessed himself guilty.

### Chapter 248.—Concerning defamatory libels.

Anyone who has written a defamatory document to injure and stain anyone’s reputation, and has posted it secretly or publicly [Col. 0950D] or cast it away to be found, shall not harm the person against whom the little document was posted, nor diminish anything of his reputation. But if the maker of such a document can be found, he shall be compelled to prove what he wrote. If he cannot prove even the matters he wrote, he shall be flogged, since he preferred to defame rather than accuse.

### Chapter 249.—Concerning one who has accused someone by formal indictment, Book IX.

Whoever, after first lodging a formal indictment, wishes to accuse someone of any crime shall pursue the proposed action within a year from the day on which he filed it. If he delays, he shall become infamous and be fined one fourth of his property.

### Chapter 250.—That criminal proceedings are to be concluded within a year, ch. 18.

[Col. 0951A]

Judges who have begun to hear criminal cases after a formal indictment has been filed must, from the day of indictment, grant any adjournments sought by either accuser or accused only so that the action may be concluded within the course of a year. If the accuser delays beyond a year in proving what he alleged, the accused shall be acquitted and the accuser shall undergo the penalty laid down by the earlier laws. If he is a person whose rank is such that infamy does not attach to his disgrace, he shall be assigned to exile.

Nevertheless, if, in the judge’s presence, accuser and accused so agree that complete adjournments are granted in respect of the indictment to both parties, the judge must not refuse this; but the party defeated after the adjournments shall be struck by a more severe [Col. 0951B] judgment.

### Chapter 251.—If anyone repents of having criminally accused another, ch. 20.

If anyone repents of having made a criminal accusation and of having filed an indictment concerning a matter that he could not prove, then, if he comes to an agreement with the innocent accused person, let them mutually release one another. But if the judge recognizes that the accused is guilty and that an agreement between accused and accuser has been made through corruption, he shall exact the statutory penalty for collusion.

We permit abolition of the accusation, at the accuser’s request, to be granted against the accused person’s will within thirty days after he has been committed to official custody. After that period, unless the accused consents, we decree that it is not to be granted. If the accuser in a criminal case seeks abolition within thirty days, it shall be granted by the judge even against the accused person’s will, and both accused and accuser shall depart free. But after thirty days from the accused person’s commitment to custody, unless both accused and accuser seek abolition from the judge, it is not to be granted to the accuser alone.

If witnesses have been produced at the accuser’s request and committed to custody, and abolition has been granted and the proceedings have been terminated (*penitaque*, so printed), the accuser shall pay the witnesses the expenses they incurred. For if witnesses produced by the accuser have become liable to punishment, abolition shall be denied by the judges even if the parties agree; rather, whether against the accused, if convicted, or against the accuser, if he fails to prove his case, the judge’s sentence shall impose the legally prescribed penalty: the accuser shall undergo the punishment which the accused would have suffered.

### Chapter 252.—That judges are not to rush to execute a sentence dictated by a ruler’s anger, ch. 30.

[Col. 0951D]

If a ruler, moved by any grave accusation, orders someone to be killed, the judges shall not immediately carry out what an angry ruler has commanded; rather, the person ordered to be punished shall be kept for thirty days, until the justice-loving mercy of the sovereigns intervenes.

### Chapter 253.—If another’s animal causes someone damage. From Book I of Paulus’s *Sentences*.

If another’s animal causes anyone damage or injures someone’s crops, its owner shall either pay an assessment of the damage or surrender the animal itself. The same has likewise been established concerning a dog.

### Chapter 254.—If any animal, provoked by someone, causes damage. Book IV.

[Col. 0952A]

No action is granted against either the owner or keeper to a person who by his own provocation has enraged against himself a wild beast or any other quadruped, and has thereby suffered damage.

### Chapter 255.—That sureties divide payment of a debt equally among themselves, Book V.

When several sureties are liable, even if they are proved solvent enough to pay what they promised and all may be held liable for the whole, repayment of the debt is nevertheless to be divided among them, so that each pays the amount falling to him in proportion to his share.

### Chapter 256.—Concerning those who compose writing to insult someone. From Book V.

This recklessness is punished, outside the ordinary procedure and even by relegation to an island, in the case of those authors who publish defamatory libels to insult [Col. 0952B] another person.

### Chapter 257.—That no one presume to insult a judge, ch. 11.

An appellant ought not to insult a judge; otherwise he is marked with infamy. Confessed debtors are treated as persons already judged; accordingly, the periods fixed for payment are reckoned from the day of confession.

### Chapter 258.—Concerning one lawfully summoned who refuses to come before a judge, ch. 16.

Whoever, having been summoned by three judicial summonses [*actionibus*], or called before a judge by three edicts, or summoned once by a peremptory order valid in place of all three—that is, one that extinguishes the action—refuses to appear [Col. 0952C] before the judge who notified him, may be judged as contumacious. Indeed, cases may not be reopened on appeal whenever judgment has been rendered against a contumacious party.

### Chapter 259.—Concerning one who wishes to appeal in court, ch. 19.

If, while a case is being heard by a judge, one litigant requests an oath and the other litigant, wishing to appeal from the judges, offers it, then he must appeal when the oath is offered, not after it has been sworn.

### Chapter 260.—Concerning one who, fearing prejudice, refuses to provide a surety, ch. 30.

If, in a dispute between litigants concerning the harm caused by a surety’s appearance, there is a contention about furnishing a surety, and someone fears prejudice in the wording of the security and therefore refuses to provide a surety, he may deposit a specified part of his property as a penalty. But, if judgment goes against him and he defaults, he shall lose what he deposited. [Col. 0952D]

### Chapter 261.—Concerning persons from whom property must not be accepted. Book I of the *Capitularies*, ch. 83.

It has been established that no ecclesiastic whatsoever shall henceforth presume to accept property from persons whose children or relatives may, by this unconsidered offering, be disinherited of their own property. If anyone henceforth attempts this, he shall in every way be struck by synodal or imperial sentence.

### Chapter 262.—Concerning the holdings of each church, ch. 85.

[Col. 0953A]

It has been decreed that one full *mansus* (landholding) shall be assigned to every church free from other service; and that priests established on these holdings shall render no service, other than ecclesiastical service, from tithes, offerings of the faithful, houses, courtyards, gardens situated beside the church, or the prescribed holding. If they possess anything beyond this, the service due to their lords shall be rendered from it.

### Chapter 263.—Concerning new villages and churches newly established in them, ch. 86.

It has been decreed concerning new villages and churches newly established in them that the tithes from those villages shall be assigned to those same churches.

### Chapter 264.—That no one presume to pledge sacred vessels, ch. 87.

[Col. 0953B]

Concerning sacred vessels of the Church, which we have learned are pledged in certain places by some persons: it is forbidden that this henceforth be presumed by anyone, except only when necessity compels it for ransoming captives.

### Chapter 265.—Concerning those who wish to surrender their property to the cause of God, ch. 35.

Whoever wishes to surrender his property for his soul to the cause of God shall make the transfer at home before lawful witnesses. Transfers made properly, and concerning which there is no dispute, shall remain valid.

### Chapter 266.—Concerning tolls. From Book III of the *Capitularies*, ch. 12.

[Col. 0953C] It pleases us that ancient and just tolls be exacted from merchants, whether for bridges, vessels, or markets. But no toll whatsoever shall be exacted from them in the case of new or unjust tolls—where ropes are stretched, where passage beneath bridges is made by ships, or in similar cases in which travelers receive no assistance. Likewise, no toll shall be exacted from those who, without a commercial purpose, carry their own goods from one of their houses to another, or to the palace, or to the army.

### Chapter 267.—Concerning a slave who commits any damage, ch. 44.

No one may abandon his own slave because of damage inflicted by him upon another person. Rather, according to the nature of the damage, the master shall answer for him or offer him to the claimant as compensation or punishment. But if, after committing a crime, [Col. 0953D] the slave flees so that the master cannot find him at all, the master shall endeavor to clear himself by oath that his slave’s commission of such an offence was neither by his will nor with his knowledge.

### Chapter 268.—Concerning summons according to law to the mallus, ch. 45.

If anyone is lawfully summoned to the mallus and does not come, he shall be adjudged liable for fifteen solidi if the summoner does not seize him; and likewise at the second and third summons. But if he scorns to come at the fourth summons, his property shall be placed under ban until he comes and does justice concerning the matter for which he has been summoned. If he does not come within a year, the king shall be consulted concerning the property placed under ban, so that whatever he decides concerning it may be done. The first summons shall be for seven nights, the second for fourteen nights, the third for twenty-one nights, and the fourth for forty-two nights. Likewise, a man’s benefice shall be placed under ban if he has no property of his own, until the king is consulted.

### Chapter 269.—Concerning persons condemned to death and afterwards granted life, if they seek justice, ch. 47.

Concerning persons who have been condemned to death for their offences and afterwards granted life: if they seek justice from others, or wish to seek justice against them, how judgment is to be concluded between them. First of all, concerning those cases for which they were condemned to death, they can make no claim anew, because all their property has, according to [Col. 0954B] Frankish judgment, been confiscated to the public domain. If afterwards, once life has been granted to them, they are able lawfully to acquire anything, they shall hold and defend it in their freedom according to law. They shall not, however, be received as witnesses or be numbered among the *scabini* to judge according to law. If anything has been adjudged to an oath which they must swear, and someone wishes to declare that oath false, let them contend [the printed reading is *contendant*; perhaps *concedatur*].

### Chapter 270.—That no one be compelled to go to a bridge for the sake of toll, ch. 54.

No one shall be compelled to go to a bridge or to cross a river for toll purposes when he can cross that river more conveniently [*compensius*; perhaps *competentius*] elsewhere. Likewise, in an open field, where there is neither bridge nor ferry, we command that no toll be exacted.

### Chapter 271.—Concerning exceedingly notorious robbers, ch. 61.

Concerning robbers of great notoriety: whoever apprehends one of them shall suffer no loss on that account.

### Chapter 272.—Concerning one who breaks into another person’s house, ch. 65.

If anyone breaks into another person’s house, whatever he takes by force, carries off, or steals from it, he shall make triple compensation, according to the law and pledges, to the person whose house was broken into and plundered; and in addition he shall pay the lordly ban. If a slave does this, he shall receive the higher penalty [the printed reading has *justitiam*; perhaps *sententiam*], [Col. 0954D] and, in addition, make compensation according to his law. If any person inflicts such damage upon another that he cannot make full compensation, he shall endeavor to give himself in pledge as a slave until he has completed the full compensation.

### Chapter 273.—What portion wives of the deceased ought to receive from joint labour after their husbands’ death, from Book IV, ch. 9.

We wish that the wives of deceased men, after their husbands’ deaths, receive a third part of the joint labour which they and their husbands performed together in the benefice. And concerning property which the holder of that benefice brought from elsewhere, purchased, or received as a gift from his friends, [Col. 0955A] we wish it to pass both to the deceased man’s orphans and to his wife.

### Chapter 274.—Concerning widows, wards, and the poor, ch. 15.

We command that whenever widows, wards, and poor persons come before the count in the mallus, their cases shall first be heard and decided. If they cannot themselves obtain witnesses to pursue their cases and do not know the law, the count shall assist them, giving them such a man as may maintain their plea or speak for them.

### Chapter 275.—Concerning the abduction of widows, ch. 16.

Whoever takes a widow as his wife within the first thirty days of widowhood, whether against her will or with it, shall pay our ban—that is, sixty solidi—threefold. If he takes her against her will, [Col. 0955B] he shall make the compensation required by his law, and he shall not touch her thereafter.

### Chapter 276.—Concerning one who kills a person performing public penance, ch. 17.

Whoever kills a person performing public penance shall pay our ban threefold and pay the *wergeld* to that person’s relatives.

### Chapter 277.—That a free man has authority to give his property wherever he wishes, and how he should do this, ch. 18.

If anyone wishes to surrender his property for the salvation of his soul, whether to a venerable place, to a relative, or to anyone else, then, when he is within the same county in which that property is situated, he shall endeavor to make a lawful transfer. But if, at the time he wishes to surrender it, he is outside that county—whether in the army, at the palace, or in any other place—he shall bring in suitable witnesses either from his own district or from others living under the same law as himself. If he cannot have such witnesses, then he shall use such other persons as he can find most suitable, and before them make the transfer of his property.

Once this transfer has been made, his heir shall have no power to reclaim the aforesaid property. Moreover, he himself shall provide a surety for the same investiture, so that no occasion may remain for the heir to alter this transfer, but instead an obligation may rest upon him to complete it. If he has not yet divided his property with his co-heirs, [Col. 0955D] this shall not impede him. But his co-heir, if unwilling voluntarily, shall be compelled by the count or the count’s *missus* to make the division with the person to whom the deceased wished his inheritance to pass. If he asked to transfer it to any church, his co-heir shall have with that church, concerning the aforesaid inheritance, the same legal relationship that he ought to have had with his other co-heir. This shall be observed with regard to father, son, and grandson until the lawful years; thereafter the property itself shall return to the immunity of that church.

### Chapter 278.—Concerning counterfeiters of coin, ch. 31.

Whoever is proved to have struck counterfeit coin shall have his hand cut off. Whoever consented to this: if free, shall pay sixty solidi; if a slave, shall receive sixty blows.

### Chapter 279.—Concerning tributary land, ch. 35.

[Col. 0956A]

Whoever transfers to another land liable to tribute, from which tribute used to issue to our share or to a church, the person who receives it shall in every way pay to our share the tribute formerly paid from it—unless perhaps he holds such a confirmation from the lordly authority as enables him to show that the tribute itself has been granted to him.

### Chapter 280.—Concerning censual land, ch. 37.

If anyone holds censual land which his ancestors gave either to some church or to our estate, he can by no means hold it lawfully unless the person under whose authority that church or estate belongs consents—unless he is the son or grandson of the one who transferred it and that same [Col. 0956B] land has been granted to him to hold. But in this matter consideration must be given to whether the holder is rich or poor, and whether he has another benefice or even property of his own. One who has neither should be treated mercifully, lest, stripped of everything, he fall into want; either he shall pay from it such rent as has been established for him, or he shall receive some portion of it as a benefice from which he may support himself.

### Chapter 281.—Concerning a debt pledged for the lordly work, ch. 56.

Concerning a debt pledged for our service, such consideration shall be made that a person who offended through ignorance is not compelled to pay the entire legal composition, but only such amount as seems possible. But one who offended solely through evil intent shall be compelled to pay the full composition fixed by law.

### Chapter 282.—Concerning one who, through malice or fraud, burns the house of a free person or slave. From Book V of the *Capitularies*, ch. 351.

If anyone, through any malice or fraud, by night or day sets fire to and burns the house of a free person or slave, he shall first restore all the buildings. He shall make compensation for whatever burned there; in addition, he shall be liable for forty solidi and punished by public penance according to the judgment of the priests. For however many persons escape from the fire, he shall make compensation to each according to the law and restore everything they lost there.

### Chapter 283.—That, if anyone unjustly accuses another’s slave, he shall return to the owner a slave of like kind for this deed, ch. 352.

[Col. 0956D]

If anyone unjustly accuses another’s slave, and the innocent slave suffers torture, he shall return to the owner a slave of like kind for this deed. But if the innocent slave dies under torture, he shall restore without delay two slaves of the same value to the owner.

### Chapter 284.—Concerning one who removes another person’s legal case from its place, ch. 340.

If anyone removes another’s legal case from its place, he shall return it unharmed or provide an equivalent. But if he carries it outside, conceals it, and denies it when questioned, he shall make compensation as for theft.

### Chapter 285.—Concerning sales made at a low price or with a concealed defect, ch. 352.

The following rule has been approved for sales: [Col. 0957A] whether property, slaves, or any kind of animal is sold, no one shall invalidate the sale merely because he says that he sold for a low price. Once the transaction has occurred, it shall not be altered—unless he finds a defect concealed from him by the seller. But if the seller disclosed the defect, the purchase shall stand and shall not be altered. If he did not disclose it, the buyer may rescind on that day, on the next, or on the third day. If he keeps the thing longer than three nights, he may not afterwards rescind, unless he cannot find the seller within the three days; then, when he finds him, he shall take it back, because he sold a defective thing. If the seller refuses to take it back, he shall swear with his oath-helpers that on the day when he concluded the transaction he knew of no defect in it; and the transaction shall stand.

### Chapter 286.—That one who has given earnest money for any thing is compelled to pay the price, ch. 363.

[Col. 0957B]

Whoever has given earnest money for any thing shall be compelled to complete payment of the price agreed by the buyer.

### Chapter 287.—That no one is to molest travelers passing through, ch. 364.

It has been decided that no one shall presume to molest passing travelers or dare to harm them, because some travel for the Lord’s sake and others for their own necessities. If anyone is so presumptuous as to harm, assault, despoil, injure, wound, bind, sell, or kill a traveler, he shall make compensation separately and twofold to the traveler himself, as is customary for another person; or he shall make composition, according to his own law, to the traveler’s lord or companion.

If the traveler has died and has no lord [Col. 0957C] or companion present, then the bishop or priests of that district shall, through the coercive power of the judge, receive double compensation as for a native, and assign it to their alms. In addition, the offender shall be compelled to pay sixty solidi to the fisc. If he leaves the traveler alive, he shall make double and individual compensation, as stated above, for every wrong done and everything inflicted upon him, just as compensation is ordinarily made for someone from within the province. But if he kills him, he shall make double compensation as for a free man of that province, and the money itself shall be given in alms by the aforesaid priests. For the Lord says: “You shall not afflict a stranger and sojourner” (Exod. 22).

### Chapter 288.—Concerning one who knocks out one eye of any quadruped, ch. 366.

[Col. 0957D]

If anyone knocks out one eye of another’s horse, ox, or any quadruped, the animal shall be appraised at its value, and he shall pay one third.

### Chapter 289.—Concerning one who kills someone by order of king or duke, ch. 367.

If anyone kills a person by the command of the king or of the duke who governs that province, no claim shall be made against him, nor shall he thereby become feud-liable, because the law and the lordly command killed that person and he could not refuse. The ruler and his successors shall defend him and all his descendants, so that they do not perish or suffer harm on this account. If he or his descendants suffer any harm or are killed because of it, double compensation shall be paid.

### Chapter 290.—Concerning one who produces documents in order to prove their truth by witnesses, ch. 368.

[Col. 0958A]

Whoever produces a document must prove its truth by witnesses. For it is established in all cases that the person who produces a document must affirm it.

### Chapter 291.—Concerning an ass, ox, sheep, and every beast entrusted to a friend for keeping, ch. 23.

If anyone entrusts to a friend for safekeeping an ass, ox, sheep, or any beast of burden, and it dies, is disabled, or is captured by enemies, with no one having seen this occur, an oath shall be taken between them that he did not lay his hand upon his neighbor’s property; the owner shall accept the oath, and the keeper shall not be compelled to make restitution. If it was stolen, he shall restore the loss to its owner. If it was eaten by a beast, he shall bring [Col. 0958B] to him what was killed, and shall not make restoration. Whoever borrows any of these things from his neighbor and it is disabled or dies while the owner is not present shall be compelled to make restitution. But if the owner was present, it shall not be restored, especially if it came hired for the wage of its work.

### Chapter 292.—Whoever seduces a betrothed virgin or lies with her, ch. 24.

If anyone seduces a betrothed virgin and lies with her, he shall endow her and take her as his wife.

### Chapter 293.—If the girl’s father refuses to give her, that he shall pay money according to the custom of the bride-price, ch. 25.

If the father refuses to give the virgin, he shall pay money according to the customary bride-price that virgins customarily receive.

### Chapter 294.—Concerning one who confesses theft for God’s sake, ch. 38.

[Col. 0958C]

If a person confesses, for God’s sake, the theft he has committed, he shall restore the principal and a fifth part in addition to the person against whom he sinned.

### Chapter 295.—Concerning those who take away or squander the offerings of the faithful, or who give or receive them without their own bishop’s command, ch. 84.

Those who take away from churches or from the right of priests the offerings of the faithful, or receive offerings that have been taken away, not only violate others’ vows but also commit sacrilege, and are moreover defrauders of God’s Church. For it has been recognized by the ancients that defrauding or taking anything from a church is sacrilege.

### Chapter 296.—That the life of bishops or other priests is not to be disturbed, ch. 104.

[Col. 0958D]

Let the lives of bishops be disturbed by no excesses, because it is most unworthy that those who are called the thrones of God should be agitated by any disturbance or treated unjustly. Hence it is written: “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zech. 2); and: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10); and again: “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it would be better for him to have a millstone hung about his neck and be drowned in the depth of the sea” (Matt. 18).

### Chapter 297.—That it is sacrilege to take away what rulers have granted to churches, or what individual bishops have obtained; and that clerics are not to be accused before secular judges but before their own bishops, ch. 111.

Whatever individual kings have established concerning the most holy [Col. 0959A] churches, or whatever individual bishops have obtained for ecclesiastical causes, shall be preserved in enduring perpetuity, secured under the continuing penalty of sacrilege. Clerics also shall be reserved not for secular judges but for episcopal hearing; for it is not lawful that ministers of the divine gift be subjected to temporal power.

### Chapter 298.—Concerning those who violate or disregard ecclesiastical privileges, ch. 116.

If the privileges of a venerable church are violated by anyone’s rashness or neglected through disregard, the offence shall be compensated threefold to the church against which it was committed, in accordance with the sanction of the laws; and our ban shall be paid to us threefold—that is, three times forty solidi.

### Chapter 299.—That one in whose possession a share of plunder is found shall name his associates, ch. 137.

[Col. 0959B] He in whose possession a crime is discovered and a share of plunder is found shall immediately be compelled to name his associates. If he refuses to name them, he shall be held for punishment.

### Chapter 300.—That a son or heir may not proceed against a prior determination, ch. 150.

A son or heir may not proceed against a just or lawful determination of his predecessors, because the presumption of one who attempts unjustly to overturn the acts of his elders is rightly repelled.

### Chapter 301.—Concerning those who are privy to thieves, ch. 160.

Not only the one who has committed theft, but also anyone who has been privy to it, or knowingly received property taken by theft, shall be counted among thieves and subjected to like punishment.

### Chapter 302.—Concerning one who has no children and wishes to make someone else his heir in their place, ch. 212.

[Col. 0959C]

One who has no children and wishes to make anyone else his heir shall make the transfer before the king, or before the count and *scabini*, or before the lordly envoys appointed by him in the province to administer justice.

### Chapter 303.—Concerning fugitives and travelers, that they are to be compelled, ch. 222.

Concerning fugitives and travelers: let them be constrained, so that we may know who they are and whence they have come.

### Chapter 304.—That arm-rings and coats of mail are not to be given to merchants, ch. 223.

Arm-rings and coats of mail are not to be given to merchants.

### Chapter 305.—That no one presume to summon a person to judgment without cause, ch. 228.

[Col. 0959D]

No one shall presume to summon a person to judgment without cause, unless judgment has been rendered.

### Chapter 306.—That no one presume to collect road toll or dust toll, ch. 243.

No person shall presume to collect road toll or dust toll on roads or through villages.

### Chapter 307.—Concerning one to whom judgment is not rightly given, ch. 253.

If anyone wishes to say that judgment is not rendered to him justly, he shall then come into our presence. Otherwise, he shall not presume to come into our presence in order to delay another person’s justice.

### Chapter 308.—That no one buy a horse, ox, or other animal from an unknown person, ch. 294.

No one shall buy a horse, ox, beast of burden, [Col. 0960A] or other animal unless he knows the person who sold it, whose man he is, where he resides, and who his lord is.

### Chapter 309.—Concerning a bishop against whom someone brings an action: if he himself brings any action, the case is to be concluded through episcopal judges, ch. 309.

If any bishop is sued by anyone, or brings any action himself, the case shall be concluded through bishops as judges—whether those whom the primates appoint for them, or neighboring bishops whom they themselves select by agreement.

### Chapter 310.—If a possessor is expelled by force, ch. 354.

Whoever forcibly expels a possessor before a judge’s sentence has been issued concerning the matter, even if he has the better case, shall lose the very case in dispute. The person who suffered the violence shall recover everything [Col. 0960B] in the condition in which it was, and shall hold securely what he possessed. But if someone invades that which he could have obtained by judgment, he shall both lose the case and restore to the expelled person an equal amount to that which he invaded.

### Chapter 311.—If anyone is found to have invited others to plunder, ch. 353.

If anyone invites others to plunder, so as to destroy another person’s property or seize livestock or any animals whatever, he shall restore sevenfold to the person whose property was plundered the things taken away. If those who were with him are freeborn, they shall be compelled to pay five solidi each; or, if they have nothing with which to make payment, they shall receive one hundred and fifty lashes. But if slaves commit this without their master’s will, they shall be beaten with one hundred and fifty lashes each, [Col. 0960C] and all the property shall be restored by them in full condition.

### Chapter 312.—That a person to be judged, if he prefers, is to be referred to episcopal judgment; that whatever is determined by the bishops’ sentence shall remain unalterable; and that even the testimony of one bishop is valid, ch. 366.

Whoever, whether possessor or claimant, has a lawsuit, whether at the beginning of the case, after the passage of time, while the matter is being pleaded, or when sentence has already begun to be pronounced, chooses the judgment of a bishop of the most holy law, shall immediately, without any doubt, be referred with the statements of the litigants to the bishops’ court, even if the other party objects. For the authority of most holy religion investigates and brings forth many things which, in a secular court, the snares of prescription do not permit to be produced [Col. 0960D]. Therefore, all causes handled either under praetorian or civil law, once concluded by bishops’ decisions, shall be confirmed with the perpetual force of stability. Nor may a matter decided by bishops’ judgments thereafter be reopened. Testimony given even by one bishop shall be accepted without hesitation by all judges; nor shall another be heard when a bishop’s testimony has been offered by either party. For that is established by the authority of truth, that is incorruptible, which a most holy man has declared from the conscience of an unblemished mind. We once enacted this by a salutary edict; we confirm it by a perpetual law, restraining the malicious seeds of litigation.

### CHAPTER 313.—From the third book of the Theodosian laws, chapter XII, concerning incest; chapter 410.

[Col. 0961A]

That persons born of incest are not lawful heirs, but both parties are marked by infamy.

### CHAPTER 314.—That an exchange has the same validity as a purchase; chapter 417.

An exchange, if it has not been extorted by force and fear, shall possess the same validity as a purchase.

### CHAPTER 315.—Concerning murderers, wrongdoers, poisoners, and convicted persons seeking to appeal: that they are not to be heard; from Book VII, chapter 181.

In civil causes and lighter crimes, a delay is to be granted by law. Murderers, adulterers, poisoners, if convicted and wishing to appeal, shall not be heard.

### CHAPTER 316.—Concerning the proof of causes in court; the invalidity of judgments against absentees; causes not to be reheard in court; that absentees are not to be condemned; and that absentees may neither accuse nor be accused through another; chapter 204.

[Col. 0961B]

No one can be convicted in court without witnesses or documents. A judgment rendered by a judge while the other party is absent has no validity. A cause adjudicated between parties present cannot be reopened after ten years, nor one between absentees after twenty years. In a capital case no absentee shall be condemned; nor may an absentee either accuse or be accused through another.

### CHAPTER 317.—That institutions established for perpetual benefit shall remain inviolate; chapter 227.

[Col. 0961C] What has been established for perpetual benefit shall not be altered by any change. Nor shall what has been designated for the common good be diverted to private advantage. And while the boundaries established by the fathers remain in force, no one shall condemn another; but each may exercise himself in the breadth of charity within his own proper and lawful limits, as he wishes.

### CHAPTER 318.—Concerning judges who judge contrary to law and refuse to hear the law; chapter 249.

Any judge who refuses to hear laws or statements of legal right presented to him in court, and judges contrary to them, if convicted of this, shall be committed to prison.
