### CHAPTER 319.—That it is not permitted subsequently to renew a contest concerning crimes already determined; chapter 291.

[Col. 0961D] An accusation concerning crimes of which a person has been acquitted cannot be revived by the one who brought the accusation.

### CHAPTER 320.—Concerning holding to payment those who promise a debt; chapter 297.

If anyone promises to pay money for another’s debt, he is to be held to payment of the promise he has made.

### CHAPTER 321.—Concerning those who receive another’s property in order to sell it: what is to be done; chapter 298.

If someone gives an article to anyone for sale at an agreed price, and, while it is being offered for sale by that person, it perishes through any occurrence, the loss belongs to the person who gave it to be sold. But if the recipient loses the article received, not at the owner’s request but upon his own undertaking to sell it [Col. 0962A], he bears the loss of the property lost.

### CHAPTER 322.—Concerning those who owe something to others and are themselves owed something by them: that the amounts are to be set off in payment; chapter 303.

If someone owes another ten solidi, and the debtor is, on whatever ground, owed five solidi by his creditor, and the creditor comes and demands all ten solidi from the debtor: if the debtor proves that the creditor owes him five solidi, the creditor who refused to set off the debt and sued him for the full ten solidi loses his case. The same rule applies to grain and other commodities.

### CHAPTER 323.—Concerning those who lend something to sons still under paternal authority: what is to be done; chapter 304.

A person who, contrary to the prohibitions of the laws and without the father’s knowledge, lends money to a son under paternal authority may demand it from neither the father while living nor after his death [Col. 0962B].

### CHAPTER 324.—Concerning usurpers of boundaries before a cause has been concluded by judgment; chapter 425.

If a usurper of boundaries is proved to have invaded, before anything has been determined by judgment, what another possessed, he shall not only lose what he has wickedly presumed to seize; but, lest anyone occupy another’s property, when he has been defeated in the case as a usurper of another’s right, he shall restore as much land as he presumed to invade.

### CHAPTER 325.—That not only those who commit theft, but also those who give assistance or counsel for its commission, are liable to an action for theft; chapter 340.

[Col. 0962C] Not only the person who commits a theft, but also the person through whose work or counsel the theft was committed, shall be liable to an action for theft.

### CHAPTER 326.—Who are agnates and who are cognates; chapter 341.

Agnates are those who descend through the male sex; cognates, however, through the female. Thus paternal uncles and the sons of paternal uncles are agnates and not cognates; maternal uncles and the sons of maternal uncles are cognates and not agnates.

### CHAPTER 327.—Concerning those who break into houses, plunder or storm country estates, or commit robberies: what is to be done; chapter 343.

If any persons plunder, break into, or storm houses or country estates, or commit robberies, and do this indeed as an assembled armed band [Col. 0962D], they shall be punished capitally. Under the term “weapons” are included all things by which injury may be inflicted upon a human being.

### CHAPTER 328.—Concerning those who harbor robbers or other criminals; chapter 344.

Those who shelter assailants, likewise robbers, are subject to the same penalty as the robbers themselves. For when those who receive and harbor violent offenders are removed, the desire for robbery subsides.

### CHAPTER 329.—Concerning those who commit arson; chapter 345.

If anyone maliciously sets a fire, once convicted of this crime he is ordered to be put to death by the severest penalties. But if it is proved that the fire occurred through negligence, the damage inflicted on anyone and the property destroyed by the fire [Col. 0963A] shall be made good by double compensation.

### CHAPTER 330.—That those compelled to suffer damages for an injury assessed as moderate become infamous; chapter 353.

A person compelled to suffer damages for an injury assessed as moderate, although he appears to have been civilly adjudged liable, nevertheless becomes infamous.

### CHAPTER 331.—Concerning those who violently occupy another’s property: that whatever is lost or alienated there shall be fully restored to those entitled to it; chapter 345.

If, from property which anyone has violently occupied, any items perish or are burned through any circumstance, or if slaves violently seized die, then, even though what perished does not appear to have happened through any fraud of the occupier [Col. 0963B], whatever has perished must nevertheless be restored by the person who is found to have violently occupied property belonging to another’s right.

### CHAPTER 332.—Concerning retainers or persons, free as well as enslaved, who accuse their master or reveal his secrets: what is to be done; chapter 440.

If anyone from among the household retainers or slaves of any house comes forward as informer and accuser concerning any crime, seeking the reputation, life, and property of the person to whose household or lordship he has adhered, he shall be struck by the avenging sword before witnesses are produced, before the case is examined, at the very presentation of the alleged crimes and beginning of the accusation. For such a deadly voice ought rather to be cut off than heard. We also close the mouths of such persons against accusing priests [Col. 0963C] or testifying against them—persons whom we know to be dead, not by human pronouncements but by divine utterances.

### CHAPTER 333.—Concerning causes already determined, which are by no means to be renewed; chapter 450.

Judgment must not be demanded concerning a cause that has been determined or adjudicated.

### CHAPTER 334.—Concerning one who, after truth has been discovered, investigates something further; chapter 370.

For whoever investigates anything further after truth has been discovered seeks falsehood. Therefore all must proceed cautiously.

### CHAPTER 335.—Concerning those who dissolve the marriages of slaves; chapter 472.

[Col. 0963D] It has been reported to us that certain persons, by a kind of arbitrary presumption, dissolve the lawful marriages of slaves, without attending to that Gospel saying: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19; Mark 10). Therefore it has seemed good to us that marriages of slaves shall not be dissolved, even if they have different masters, but that, remaining in one marriage, they shall serve their masters. This is to be observed where there has been a lawful union and it was contracted with the consent of their masters.

### CHAPTER 336.—Concerning those who sin deliberately; chapter 375.

Nor do we think it should be passed over that certain persons, sinning deliberately, promise themselves a kind of immunity on account of the giving of alms [Col. 0964A]. For almsgiving extinguishes sins, according to the saying: “Water extinguishes a blazing fire, and almsgiving extinguishes sins” (Sirach 3); but this applies to sins committed through necessity, chance, or some frailty. Those, however, that are deliberately committed in order to satisfy some lust, on the calculation that they may be redeemed by alms, cannot by any means be redeemed by them. For those who do this appear to hire God for a fee, that they may be permitted to sin with impunity. Therefore one must not sin in order to give alms; rather, one ought to give alms because one has sinned. The affliction and contrition of mind and body ought to bring back to pardon the mind and body that lust has drawn into guilt.

### CHAPTER 337.—That counts and judges must not admit base persons to give testimony; chapter 371.

[Col. 0964B] Counts and judges must be earnestly warned not to permit base and unworthy persons to approach before them to give testimony. Many indeed regard perjury as a trivial matter, so much so that for the satisfaction of a single day, or for any small price, they may be hired to swear an oath and do not fear at all to destroy their souls by perjury. Therefore such persons must by no means be admitted for any testimony. It should also be noted that not only those who commit perjury but also those who consent to perjurers are to be punished with a like condemnation.

### CHAPTER 338.—Concerning one who neglects to give the tithe to the church to which it is due and gives it instead to another church; chapter 377.

Whoever removes a tithe from the church to which it ought in justice to be given [Col. 0964C], and presumptuously gives it to another church because of gifts, friendship, or any other reason, shall be constrained by the count or our missus to restore the amount of that tithe with the prescribed penalty.

### CHAPTER 339.—Concerning the expulsion of bad *scabini*; chapter 378.

Let our missi, wherever they find bad *scabini*—sworn lay assessors—expel them, and with the consent of the whole people choose good ones in their place. When they have been elected, they shall make them swear that they will not knowingly judge unjustly.

### CHAPTER 340.—Concerning the selection of the best and most truthful persons; chapter 379.

In every county, those who can be found most excellent and truthful shall be chosen by our missi to make inquiries and declare the truth of a matter; and they shall assist the counts in administering justice [Col. 0964D].

### CHAPTER 341.—Concerning *scabini* who judge unjustly because of gifts, friendship, or enmity; chapter 380.

We will that any *scabinus* found to have judged unjustly because of gifts, friendship, or enmity shall be sent under sureties into our presence. Henceforth let all *scabini* be warned that none may presume even to sell a just judgment.

### CHAPTER 342.—Concerning one who transfers to his son, or to any person not yet of legal age, another’s property bought through fraudulent contrivance; chapter 381.

Whoever sells another’s property to any person, and that purchaser possesses the property through fraudulent contrivance, and transfers the purchased property to his own son or to another person not yet of legal age [Col. 0965A], in order to obstruct justice: we will and firmly command that, if the father of that minor is living, he himself shall enter the action and answer for his son. But if the father is dead, then his lawful relative, who appears rightly to be his guardian or defender, shall be compelled to answer on his behalf. The same applies to all other judicial claims pertaining to him, except his lawful inheritance, which ought lawfully to come to him by succession from his parents. If anyone despises or neglects this our command, he shall be dealt with as other contemners are. But the person who first seized the property, and likewise the purchasers—excepting only the person of the minor—shall be compelled to make amends within the realm for what they fraudulently committed [Col. 0965B], and afterwards, as contemners of our command, shall be compelled under sureties to come into our presence.

### CHAPTER 343.—Concerning one who refuses to clear himself of charges brought against him; chapter 382.

He who refuses to appear in order to refute accusations brought against him proves them true. Hence it is found written in secular laws: “A person unjustly defeated shall restore his case within three months; if he neglects to do so, the judgment pronounced against him shall remain in force.” And do not regard it as contrary, or wonder that I have spoken of secular laws in our court, since ecclesiastical and divine laws receive them.

### CHAPTER 344.—That persons received into favor by royal authority shall also be admitted by lesser authorities; chapter 383.

[Col. 0965C]

If royal authority receives any offenders either into the favor of its mercy or makes them participants at its table, assemblies of priests and peoples must also receive them into ecclesiastical communion; and what princely mercy receives must not be held alien by the priests of God.

### CHAPTER 345.—That those who disdain obedience to priests’ admonitions are to be restrained by secular power. From Book II, chapter 40; chapter 384.

Those who refuse to obey priests’ admonitions and choose to persist in their crimes ought to be restrained from so depraved a custom through the discipline of secular power.

### CHAPTER 346.—Concerning persons of unequal status joined in marriage; chapter 16.

[Col. 0965D]

Free men who marry royal fiscal women, and free women who take royal fiscal men, shall not be excluded on that account either from their parents’ inheritance, from bringing a suit, or from giving testimony.

### CHAPTER 347.—Concerning one who gives lodging to a robber; chapter 23.

Whoever gives lodging to a robber, if he is a Frank, shall swear with twelve fellow Franks that he did not know the man to be a robber. If he cannot swear, he shall be judged as a robber.

### CHAPTER 348.—Concerning men who quarrel, if one of them is struck in any manner and lies bedridden.

If men quarrel and one strikes his neighbor with a stone or fist, and the other does not die but lies in bed [Col. 0966A], then, if he rises and walks outdoors upon his staff, the striker shall be innocent; nevertheless, he shall compensate the injured man for his lost labor and medical expenses.

### CHAPTER 349.—If an animal falls into an uncovered cistern through negligence; chapter 16.

If anyone opens or digs a cistern and does not cover it, and an ox or ass falls into it, the owner of the cistern shall pay its price; but what is dead shall be his.

### CHAPTER 350.—If another’s ox wounds an ox, the owner knowing his own ox to be dangerous; chapter 17.

If one man’s ox wounds another’s ox and it dies, they shall sell the living ox and divide both the price and the carcass. But if its owner knew [Col. 0966B] that the ox was dangerous and would not keep it under guard, he shall render ox for ox and take the whole carcass.

### CHAPTER 351.—Concerning one who steals a sheep or ox; chapter 18.

Whoever steals an ox or sheep shall restore five oxen for one ox and four sheep for one sheep.

### CHAPTER 352.—Concerning a thief killed during the theft; chapter 19.

If a thief breaks into a house, or is found digging through, and dies after receiving a wound, the striker shall not be guilty of blood. But if he does this after sunrise, he has committed homicide.

### CHAPTER 353.—Concerning one who damages a field or vineyard and lets his animal graze another’s property; chapter 20.

[Col. 0966C] If anyone damages a field or vineyard and lets his animal graze another’s property, he shall make restitution, according to the assessment of the damage, from the best that he has in his field or vineyard.

### CHAPTER 354.—Concerning one who kindles a fire by which another suffers loss; chapter 21.

If a spreading fire finds sheaves and consumes heaps of grain or standing crops in the fields, the person who kindled the fire shall make good the damage.

### CHAPTER 355.—Punishment of a greedy advocate; chapter 57.

If an advocate in a case he has undertaken is found to have acted from unjust greed, he shall be separated from the assembly of honorable men and from participation in judicial proceedings; and care shall be taken that he does not assume the role of judge or legal defender.

### CHAPTER 356.—Penalty of a slave who informs against his master; chapter 177.

[Col. 0966D]

If a slave informs against his master, he shall be punished even if he proves the allegations.

### CHAPTER 357.—That all who are under anathema shall have no public voice; chapter 215.

The voice of any person under anathema shall not be received at all in accusation, testimony, or human judgment.

### CHAPTER 358.—That thieves and wrongdoers convicted by suitable witnesses shall die according to the law; chapter 257.

Concerning thieves and wrongdoers, we have decreed that this be observed: if five or seven trustworthy persons, without prior enmity, declare under oath that an accused person is guilty [Col. 0967A], then, as he acted against the law, so he shall die according to the law.

### CHAPTER 359.—That no one shall hold a debtor while disregarding the surety; chapter 334.

If anyone chooses to hold his debtor while disregarding the surety, the surety is released from the suretyship as if he were the debtor’s heir.

### CHAPTER 360.—Concerning those privy to the sins of others; chapter 336.

Those who know of others’ sins are themselves at fault unless they disclose them for the purpose of correction and salvation.

### CHAPTER 361.—That kinship or relationship shall by no means give testimony against outsiders; chapter 348.

Brothers, sisters, uterine siblings, paternal uncles, maternal uncles, maternal aunts [Col. 0968A], their children, likewise grandsons, granddaughters, cousins through paternal uncles or paternal aunts, and certain others of one’s own blood relationship, we do not permit to give testimony in court against outsiders, unless perhaps relatives of that same kinship have a lawsuit among themselves, or it is established that in the matter at issue there is otherwise a total lack of persons of free status.

### CHAPTER 362.—That what is consecrated to the Lord belongs to ecclesiastical right; chapter 394.

Things offered or consecrated to the Lord belong by right to priests. All who take them away or transfer them elsewhere are sacrilegious.

## SEVENTEENTH PART OF THE DECREE

Containing speculative statements of the holy Fathers concerning faith, hope, and charity.

[Col. 0967]

### CHAPTER 1.—How great is the dignity of the human condition, and that no one should degenerate from it into servile condition. Augustine, Treatise on the Creation of the First Human, vol. IX.

[Col. 0967B]

The dignity of the human condition is recognized as so great that the human being was created not merely by the word of one commanding, as were the other works of the six days, but by the counsel of the holy Trinity and the work of the divine majesty. Thus, from the first honor of his creation, he might understand how much he owed his Creator, since the Creator immediately granted him such a privilege of dignity in creation, that he might love the Creator more ardently in proportion as he understood himself to have been created more wonderfully by him. “Let us make,” he says, “the human being in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). This was so not only because, by the counsel of the holy Trinity, he was created from the excellence of the Creator [“was created excellently by the Creator,” Col. 0967C], but also because the Creator of all himself created him in his own image and likeness, a gift he bestowed on no other creature.

This image is to be considered more carefully in the nobility of the inner human being. First, just as God is always wholly present everywhere, giving life, moving, and governing all things—as the Apostle confirms when he says, “In him we live, move, and are” (Acts 17)—so the soul is wholly active throughout its body, giving it life, moving it, and governing it. For it is not greater in the body’s larger limbs or smaller in its lesser ones; rather, it is wholly in the smallest and wholly in the greatest. This is the image of the unity of almighty God which the soul has in itself; it also possesses a certain likeness of the holy Trinity [Col. 0967D]. First, as God is, lives, and knows, so the soul, in its own manner, is, lives, and knows.

There is also another likeness of the Trinity in the soul, which was created in the image of its Creator—the perfect and supreme Trinity, existing in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Although it is of one nature, it nevertheless possesses three capacities in itself: understanding, will, and memory [Col. 0968B]. The same thing, though in different words, is signified in the Gospel when it is said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Matt. 22), that is, with all your understanding, all your will, and all your memory. For just as the Son is generated from the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeds from Father and Son, so will is generated through understanding, and memory likewise proceeds from both of these, as any wise person can readily understand. For the soul cannot be perfect without these three, nor can any one of these three, as regards its blessedness, be complete without the other two.

And just as God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit are not three gods but one God possessing three persons, so the soul as understanding, the soul as will, and the soul as memory are not three souls in one body, but one soul possessing three capacities. In these three our inner human being wonderfully bears God’s image in his nature. From these, as from the higher capacities of the soul, we are commanded to love the Creator: that he may be loved insofar as he is understood, and that insofar as he is loved he may always be held in memory. Understanding of him alone is not sufficient unless will is made active in love; nor are these two sufficient unless memory is added, by which God always remains in the mind of one who understands and loves, so that there can be no moment in which memory does not hold him present. This is enough concerning the image.

Now understand something concerning the likeness, which must be discerned in character: just as God the Creator, who created the human being in his likeness, is charity, good, just, patient, pure, and merciful [“very merciful,” Col. 0968D], together with the other marks of virtue that are read of him, so the human being was created to possess the same virtues. The more anyone has these in himself [Col. 0969A], the nearer he is to God and the greater is the likeness of his Creator that he bears. When someone travels through the byways of vices and the divergences of crimes, he wanders away as one degenerate from this most noble likeness of his Creator. Then what is written of him comes to pass: “Though a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48).

What greater honor could there be for a human being than to be created in the likeness of his Creator and adorned with the same garments of virtues as the Creator? [“Thus there ought to be no moment in which a person, using God’s goodness and mercy, is not mindful of him.” Note: “[Col. 0969D] These words are not found in Augustine.”] Of him it is written: “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with splendor” (Ps. 92), that is, he is adorned with the splendor of every virtue and all goodness [Col. 0969B]. But what can be a greater disgrace to a human being, or a more miserable misery, than, having lost this glory of likeness to God his Creator, to fall into a shapeless and irrational likeness to brute beasts?

Therefore let each person more carefully recognize the excellence of his first creation, the venerable image of the holy Trinity in himself, and the honor of the divine likeness in which he was created. Let him strive to possess it through nobility of conduct, the exercise of virtues, and worthiness of merits, so that, when it appears what he is, he may appear like him who wonderfully created him in his likeness in the first Adam and more wonderfully restored him in the second.

### CHAPTER 2.—That, although incorporeal, the soul can nevertheless possess the likeness of a body. Augustine, *On Genesis Literally* (Book XII, chapter 33).

[Col. 0969C]

I dare profess that I do not merely suppose, but plainly know, that the soul is not corporeal. Yet whoever denies that it can possess the likeness of a body and of bodily limbs altogether may deny that the soul in dreams sees itself walking, sitting, going this way and that, or being carried and brought back in motion or even in flight—things which do not occur without some likeness of a body. Therefore, if it bears this likeness even among the dead, not corporeal but similar to a body, then it is likewise seen to be in places not corporeal but analogous to corporeal places, whether in rest or in pains. Yet I confess that I have not yet discovered that the place where the souls of the righteous rest is called “the lower regions.” And it is not without reason believed that Christ’s soul came even to those places in which sinners are tormented, in order to free from torments those whom, by his justice hidden from us, he judged ought to be freed [Col. 0969D].

### CHAPTER 3.—That Christ also, according to the flesh, was in Abraham’s loins when Levi was tithed. Augustine, *On Genesis Literally* (same work, Book X, chapter 20).

I am considerably troubled by this: although no human being’s soul is in his father’s loins, Levi was in Abraham’s loins according to the flesh and was tithed there (Heb. 7), while Christ, likewise there according to the flesh, was not tithed. Levi was there according to that seminal principle by which he was to come into his mother through sexual intercourse; according to that principle Christ’s flesh was not there, although Mary’s flesh was there according to it [Col. 0970A]. Therefore neither Levi nor Christ was in Abraham’s loins according to the soul; according to the flesh, however, both Levi and Christ were there. But Levi was there according to carnal concupiscence, whereas Christ was there according to bodily substance alone.

For in semen there are both visible corporeal substance and an invisible formative principle; both run together from Abraham—or even from Adam himself—all the way to Mary’s body, which too was conceived and arose in that manner (the variants read *cucurrit*, “ran,” and *quia*, “because,” for *quod*, “which”). Christ, however, took the visible substance of flesh from the flesh of the Virgin. The principle of his conception came not from male seed but in a far different way, from above. Therefore, according to what he received from his mother, he too was in [variant: *de*, “from”] Abraham’s loins [Col. 0970B].

Accordingly, the one who was tithed in Abraham was he who, though only according to the flesh, was nevertheless in Abraham’s loins in the same manner as Abraham himself was in his own father’s loins—that is, the one born from Father Abraham in the same manner as Abraham had been born from his own father: namely, through the law in the members resisting the law of the mind (Rom. 7) and through invisible concupiscence. Although the chaste and good laws of marriage do not allow this concupiscence to prevail except insofar as they can provide for the propagation of the human race through it, the other was not tithed there, whose flesh drew thence not the heat of the wound but the material of the remedy.

For since this tithing pertained to prefiguring the remedy, in Abraham’s flesh that which was being healed was tithed, not that from which it was healed. The same flesh, indeed—not only Abraham’s but that of the first earthly human being himself—contained both the wound of transgression and the medicine for the wound [Col. 0970C]. The wound of transgression lies in the law of the members resisting the law of the mind, which is transmitted, as it were, by a seminal principle through all flesh propagated from it. The remedy for the wound lies in what was assumed from the Virgin from that source, without concupiscent activity, in bodily material alone, through the divine principle of conception and formation: for participation in death without iniquity, and as an example of resurrection without falsehood.

### CHAPTER 4.—That all sins are removed in baptism. Augustine, *Enchiridion* (chapters 42, 43, 44).

For from a newly born infant to a decrepit old man, just as no one is to be barred from baptism, so no one fails to die to sin in baptism [Col. 0970D]. Infants die only to original sin, but adults die also to all the sins which they added by evil living to what they contracted by birth. Yet they too are often said to die “to sin,” although beyond doubt they die not to one sin but to many sins—all that they have committed as their own, whether in thought, word, or deed. For the plural number is also customarily signified by the singular, as the poet says:

> “They fill both [sides] with armed soldiery,”  
> VIRGIL, *Aeneid* II, verse 28.

Although this was done by many soldiers. And in our Scriptures one reads: “Pray, therefore, that he may take away the serpent from us” (Num. 21). It does not say “serpents,” though the people suffered from serpents; and innumerable similar examples could be cited.

Therefore, when that one original sin is also signified by another number—variant: by the plural (*plurali*)—as when infants are said to be baptized “for the remission of sins,” rather than “for remission of sin,” this is the converse form of expression, in which a singular number is signified by plural wording. So the Gospel says, when Herod had died: “For those who sought the child’s life are dead” (Matt. 2) [Col. 0971A]; it does not say, “he is dead.” And in Exodus: “They made for themselves gods of gold” (Exod. 32), although they made only one calf, of which they said: “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exod. 11). Here too the plural is used for the singular.

### CHAPTER 5.—That many sins are found in Adam’s one sin. From the same work (*Enchiridion*, chapter 45).

Although in that one sin, which entered the world through one human being and passed into all human beings (Rom. 5), and on account of which infants too are baptized, many sins can be understood if that one act is divided, as it were, into its individual members. For there is pride in it, because the human being preferred to be in his own power rather than in God’s; and sacrilege, because he did not believe God; and homicide, because he cast himself into death; and spiritual fornication, because the integrity of the human mind was corrupted by the serpent’s persuasion; and theft, because forbidden food was appropriated [Col. 0971C]; and avarice, because he desired more than ought to have sufficed him (Gen. 3); and whatever else may be discovered by careful consideration in this one act.

### CHAPTER 6.—That infants before baptism are bound by the sins of their parents. From the same work (chapter 46).

It is not implausibly said that infants are bound by the sins of their parents, not only those of the first human beings but also those of the parents from whom they themselves were born. For that divine pronouncement, “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children” (Exod. 34; Deut. 5), holds them before they begin through regeneration to belong to the New Testament. (Chapter 18.) That Testament was prophesied when Ezekiel said that children would not bear their fathers’ sins (Ezek. 18), and that in Israel the proverb would no longer be used [Col. 0971D]: “The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth are set on edge” (Jer. 31).

For each person is reborn in order that whatever sin exists in him at birth may be saved [variant: *solvatur*, “released”]. Sins later committed by evil conduct may also be healed by repentance, as we see happens even after baptism. Consequently, regeneration was instituted only because generation is defective—to such an extent that one born even from a lawful marriage says: “In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother nourished me in her womb” (Ps. 50). Here he did not say “in iniquity” or “in sin,” though this too could properly have been said, but preferred to say “iniquities” and “sins.” For even in that one sin which passed into all human beings [Col. 0972A], and which is so great that human nature was altered and turned toward the necessity of death, many sins are found, as I explained above; and there are other sins of parents which cannot alter nature in the same way, though they nonetheless bind children by guilt unless the free grace and mercy of God comes to their aid (variant: *qui etsi*, “which, although”).

### CHAPTER 7.—On the same matter. From the same work (chapter 47).

But concerning the sins of other parents, from Adam himself down to each person’s own father, through whom each succeeds to his forebears, it may not without reason be debated whether, when a person is born, he is implicated in all their evil acts and in their multiplied original offences, so that each is worse off the later he is born. Or whether God threatens the descendants with the sins of their parents unto the third and fourth generation [Col. 0972B] (Exod. XX) because, in the moderation of his mercy, he does not extend his wrath further in respect of the faults of their progenitors, lest those to whom the grace of regeneration is not granted should be crushed beneath an excessive burden in their eternal condemnation itself, if they were compelled from the beginning of the human race to contract originally the sins of all their preceding parents and pay the penalties due to them. Whether, upon a more careful and thorough investigation of the holy Scriptures, anything else on so great a matter may or may not be discovered, I do not dare rashly affirm.

### CHAPTER 8.—Original sin cannot be removed except through Christ. From the same source (ch. 48).

Yet that one sin, committed in a place and dwelling of such great happiness [“great in place and [Col. 0972C] condition of such great unhappiness,” thus in the present Augustine], was of such magnitude that in one man the whole human race was condemned originally and, so to speak, radically. It is not loosed and washed away except through the one mediator between God and men, Jesus Christ, who alone could be born in such a way that he had no need to be reborn.

### CHAPTER 9.—On the resurrection of the dead. Likewise, from the same source (ch. 84).

Now concerning the resurrection of the flesh—not as certain persons rose again and then died once more, but unto eternal life, as Christ himself rose—I do not find how I can discuss it briefly and satisfy every question customarily raised concerning this matter. Yet no Christian can in any way doubt that the flesh of all human beings who have been born and will be born, [Col. 0972D] and who have died and will die, shall rise again.

### CHAPTER 10.—On miscarried fetuses or unformed parts. From the same source (ch. 85).

Here first arises the question concerning miscarried fetuses, which have indeed already been born in their mothers’ wombs, but not yet in such a way that they can be reborn. For if we say that they shall rise again, what is said may somehow be endured with respect to those already formed. But who would not more readily suppose that unformed miscarriages perish, like seeds that have not been conceived? Yet who would dare deny—though he may not dare affirm—that the resurrection will accomplish this: that whatever was lacking in form shall be supplied? Thus there will no longer be lacking the perfection that would have come with time [Col. 0973A], just as there will not remain defects that came with time; so that nature may not be disfigured by what hostile and contrary days brought, but what was not yet whole may be made whole, just as what had been damaged shall be restored.

### CHAPTER 11.—In what condition an infant shall rise, even if, having received the vital spirit, it died before being born. From the same source (ch. 86).

Accordingly, it may indeed be investigated and debated with the greatest scrupulousness among the most learned, though I do not know whether it can be discovered by human beings, when a human being begins to live in the womb: whether there is some hidden life not yet manifested by the movements of a living being. For it seems exceedingly shameless to deny life to the offspring which are therefore cut out limb by limb and cast from the wombs of pregnant women, lest the mothers too should die if they are left dead within them [Col. 0973B]. But from the moment a human being begins to live, from that moment he can surely also die. And if dead, wherever death could have occurred to him, I cannot discover how he would not belong to the resurrection of the dead.

### CHAPTER 12.—The soul is not propagated by human seed but, once the body is formed, is created by God. Augustine says (*On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, ch. 14).

We say that human souls did not exist from the beginning among the other intellectual natures, nor were they created all at once, as Origen imagined; nor are they sown with bodies through intercourse, as the Luciferians, Cyril, and some presumptuous Latin writers affirm, as though this followed by necessity of nature. Rather, we say that the body alone is sown through the union of marriage, while by God’s judgment it is coagulated in the womb [Col. 0973C], joined together and formed; and that, once the body has been formed, the soul is created and infused, so that the human being, consisting of soul and body, may live in the womb and emerge alive from the womb, complete in human substance. But that the Creator of all things alone knows the creation of the soul.

### CHAPTER 13.—There are not two souls in one human being, but only one. Likewise Augustine (ibid., ch. 15).

We do not say that there are two souls in one human being, as a certain Jacob and other Syrian disputants write: one animal soul, by which the body is animated and which is mixed with the blood; and another spiritual soul, which supplies reason. Rather, we say that there is one and the same soul in the human being: it gives life to the body through its union with it [Col. 0973D], and orders itself by its own reason, possessing freedom of choice so that in its own substance it may choose whatever thought it wishes.

### CHAPTER 14.—Only the human being has a subsistent soul. Likewise Augustine (ibid., ch. 16).

We believe that the human being alone has a subsistent soul, by which the body lives and which retains its reason and capacities with vitality [“which, when stripped of the body, lives and retains its senses and capacities, etc.” Thus the present Augustine]. Nor does it die with the body, as the Arab [Augustine has “Aratus”] maintains; nor after a brief interval, as Zeno says, because it lives substantively.

### CHAPTER 15.—The souls of beasts end in the death of the flesh. Likewise Augustine (ibid., ch. 17).

The souls of beasts are not substances; rather, they are born with the life of the flesh itself [Col. 0974A] and end with the flesh in death. Therefore they are not governed by reason, as Plato and Alexander think, but are led toward every impulse of nature.

### CHAPTER 16.—The human soul does not die with the flesh. Likewise Augustine (ibid., ch. 10).

The human soul does not die with the flesh, because, as we said above, it is not sown with the flesh. Rather, once the body has been formed in the mother’s womb, we say that by God’s judgment it is created and infused, so that the human being may live within the womb and then come forth into the world by birth.

### CHAPTER 17.—A human being consists of two substances. Augustine (ibid., ch. 19).

A human being consists of two substances only: soul and flesh. The soul has its reason, and the flesh its senses—namely sight, hearing, taste, smell, and [Col. 0974B] touch. Yet apart from union with the soul, the flesh does not exercise these senses; while the soul, even without the flesh, retains its reason unimpaired.

### CHAPTER 18.—There is no third substance in the human being, namely spirit, as some affirm. Augustine (ibid., ch. 20).

There is no third substance in the human being, spirit, as Didymus contends; rather, spirit is the soul itself. The soul is called “spirit,” either because of its spiritual nature or because it breathes in the body. It is called “soul” because it animates the body in order to give it life. But the third thing, spirit, which the Apostle introduces together with body and soul, we should understand to be the grace of the Holy Spirit, which the Apostle prays may remain whole in us (I Thess. V), and may neither be diminished [Col. 0974C] through our fault nor driven away from us, because “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from deceit” (Wis. I).

### CHAPTER 19.—As God could make good things out of nothing, so, when he willed, through the mystery of his incarnation he also restored good things that had been lost. Gregory in his *Morals* (bk. IV, ch. 8).

Almighty God, just as he could make good things out of nothing, so, when he willed, through the mystery of his incarnation he also restored good things that had been lost.

### CHAPTER 20.—The human being was recalled to God’s grace through Christ because he sinned through weakness of the flesh; but the apostate angel cannot be restored because he fell voluntarily. From the same source (ch. 9).

He had made two creatures capable of understanding him: namely, the angelic and the human. Pride struck both, and broke them from their state of inborn uprightness [Col. 0974D]. But the one had a covering of flesh; the other bore nothing weak derived from flesh. For the angel is spirit alone, whereas the human being is both spirit and flesh. Therefore the Creator, in his mercy and in order to redeem, ought to restore to himself that creature which is known to have had some weakness in the commission of its sin; and he ought the more to reject the apostate angel, because when he fell from the strength to remain steadfast, he bore nothing weak derived from flesh. Hence the Psalmist rightly, when calling the Redeemer merciful toward human beings, also expressed the very cause of mercy, saying: “And he remembered that they are flesh” (Ps. LXXVII). As if to say: The more he saw their weakness, the less he willed strictly to punish their sins.

### CHAPTER 21.—God created three living spirits: one not covered by flesh; another covered by flesh but not dying with the flesh; a third covered by flesh and dying with the flesh. Ibid. (bk. IV, ch. 2).

[Col. 0975A]

Even unbelievers have faith—but would that it were faith in God. For if they had that faith, they would not be unbelievers. Yet for this very reason they are to be reproved in their unbelief and summoned to the grace of faith: if they believe concerning their own visible body what they have never seen, why do they not believe invisible things, which cannot be seen bodily? (Ibid., ch. 3.) For that the soul lives after the death of the flesh is evident to reason, though reason is mixed with faith. Almighty God created three living spirits: one not covered by flesh; another covered by flesh but not dying with the flesh; and a third covered by flesh [Col. 0975B] and dying with the flesh. The spirit not covered by flesh belongs to angels; the spirit covered by flesh but not dying with the flesh belongs to human beings; and the spirit covered by flesh and dying with the flesh belongs to beasts of burden and all irrational animals. Thus the human being, just as he was created in the middle, inferior to the angel and superior to the beast, has something in common with the highest and something in common with the lowest: namely, immortality of spirit in common with the angel, and mortality of flesh in common with the beast, until the glory of the resurrection swallows up even that mortality of the flesh, and the flesh, cleaving to the spirit, is preserved forever, because the spirit itself, cleaving to the flesh, is preserved in God. Yet even in the reprobate this flesh does not wholly fail amid punishments [Col. 0975C], because it subsists while always failing, so that those who sinned in spirit and flesh, while ever living in their substance, may die without end both in flesh and spirit.

### CHAPTER 22.—In his first creation the human being was endowed with free choice. Augustine (*On Spirit and Soul*, ch. 48).

The human being was entrusted with freedom of his own choice immediately in his first creation, so that, with the vigilance of mind alone exerting itself, he might, if he wished, persevere even in perfect observance in that for which he had been created. But after, through Eve, he fell from the good of nature by the serpent’s seduction (Gen. III), he lost at the same time the strength of his choice, though not his power of choosing; lest the sin which he was to amend should not be his own, and lest pardon should not justly be granted for what he had wiped away by choice. Thus freedom of choice remains for seeking salvation—that is, rational will—but only when God first admonishes and invites one to salvation, [“so that he may choose, follow, or act upon the occasion of salvation, that is, God’s inspiration. But that he attain what he chooses, follows, or acts upon as an occasion, we freely confess to be God’s work. Therefore, through God’s mercy, we have the beginning of our salvation [Note: [Col. 0975D] These words are not found in Augustine.],”] while acquiescing in the saving inspiration lies within our power. That we attain what we desire while acquiescing in the admonition [“what we desire to attain”] is a gift of God. That we do not fall, after the gift of salvation has been received, depends upon our diligence and likewise upon [Col. 0976A] heavenly assistance; but that we fall depends upon our own power and sloth.

### CHAPTER 23.—All human beings lost natural ability in Adam’s transgression. From the decrees of Pope Celestine, ch. 5 (Letter 1, to the bishops of Gaul, ch. 4).

That in Adam’s transgression all human beings lost natural ability and innocence, and that no one can rise from the depth of that fall by free choice unless the grace of God in mercy [“showing mercy”] raises him up, is declared by Pope Innocent of blessed memory, who says in his letter to the Council of Carthage (Letter 25): “For free choice, when it once suffered this and made too heedless use of its own goods, fell and was plunged into the depths of transgression; and it found no means by which it could rise from there [Col. 0976B]. Deceived forever by its own freedom, it would have lain crushed beneath this fall [“would have lain hidden beneath the ruin”], unless the coming of Christ, through his grace, had afterward raised it up—he who through the purification of new regeneration cleansed every former blemish in the washing of his baptism.”

### CHAPTER 24.—On the same matter. From the decrees of the same pope (ibid., ch. 7).

That no one makes good use of free choice except through Christ, the same teacher proclaims in his letter addressed to the Council of Milevis (Letter 26), saying: “Let the perverse doctrine of utterly depraved minds finally take heed [“O doctrine of utterly depraved minds”]: freedom itself so deceived the first human being that, while he used its reins too indulgently, he fell into the transgression [Col. 0976C] of presumption; nor could he be rescued from this unless the providence of regeneration, through the coming of Christ the Lord, restored the condition of his former freedom.”

### CHAPTER 25.—The human being was so placed in paradise that, if he remained obedient, he would at some time pass to the heavenly homeland without death of the flesh. Gregory (*Morals*, bk. IV, ch. 30).

The human being was placed in paradise for this purpose: that, if he bound himself to obedience to his Creator by the bonds of love, he might at some time pass to the heavenly homeland of angels without death of the flesh. For he was created immortal in such a way that, if he sinned, he could nevertheless die. And he was created mortal in such a way that, if he did not sin, he could also not die, and by the merit [Col. 0976D] of free choice might attain the blessedness of that region where he could neither sin nor die. Therefore, where the elect pass after the time of redemption, with death of the flesh intervening, thither without doubt our first parents too could have been transferred even without bodily death, had they remained in the state of their creation.

### CHAPTER 26.—We, born carnal in the blindness of this exile, are compared to a child born and raised in prison (bk. IV, *Dialogues*, ch. 1).

After the first parent of the human race was driven from the joys of paradise because sin demanded it, he came into the misery of this exile and blindness which we suffer [Col. 0977A], because, in sinning, he had poured himself out beyond himself and could no longer see the joys of the heavenly homeland which he had previously contemplated. For in paradise the human being had been accustomed to enjoy the words of God and, through purity of heart and loftiness of vision, to have fellowship with the spirits of blessed angels. But after he fell here, he departed from that light of mind by which he was filled. From his flesh, indeed, we are born into the blindness of this exile. We hear that there is a heavenly homeland; we hear that angels of God are its citizens; we hear that the spirits of the righteous and perfected are companions of those same angels. But all who are carnal, because they cannot know those invisible things by experience, doubt whether that exists which they do not see with bodily eyes. Such doubt certainly could not have belonged to our first parent, because, being excluded [Col. 0977B] from the joys of paradise, he recalled what he had lost since he had seen it. But these people cannot apprehend or recall what they hear, because none of them possesses, as he at least did, experience from the past.

It is as though a pregnant woman were sent to prison and there bore a child. If the child, once born, were raised and grew up in prison, and his mother, who bore him, were perhaps to name to him the sun, moon, stars, mountains, and plains, flying birds and running horses: he, born and raised in prison, knowing nothing but the darkness of the prison, would hear that these things exist; but because he did not know them by experience, he would distrust that they truly exist. So too, human beings born in the blindness of this exile, when they hear that supreme and invisible things exist, doubt whether they are true, because they know only these lowest and visible things amid which they were born [Col. 0977C]. Hence it came about that the Creator himself of invisible and visible things, the Only-Begotten of the Father, came for the redemption of the human race and sent the Holy Spirit into our hearts, so that, made alive through him, we might believe what we cannot here [“still,” or *adhuc*] know by experience. Therefore all of us who have received this Spirit as the pledge of our inheritance do not doubt the life of invisible things. But whoever is not yet firm in this faith must without doubt give credence to the words of those greater than himself and believe those who already possess, through the Holy Spirit, experience of invisible things; for a child is foolish if he thinks his mother lies about the light merely because he himself has known nothing but the darkness of prison [Col. 0977D].

### CHAPTER 27.—No one can become good through himself. From the decree of Pope Celestine (Letter 1, to the bishops of Gaul, ch. 5).

No one is good through himself unless he who alone is good grants him participation in himself. Shall we then judge rightly concerning the minds of those who think that they owe it to themselves that they are good, and do not consider him whose grace they receive daily, while trusting that without him they can attain so much?

### CHAPTER 28.—On the same matter. From the decrees of the same pope (ibid., ch. 6).

No one, even though renewed by the grace of baptism, is able to overcome the snares of the devil and conquer [Col. 0978A] the desires of the flesh unless, through God’s daily assistance, he receives perseverance in good conduct. For although he redeemed the human being from past sins, yet, knowing that he could sin again, he preserved many means for restoring him to himself, by which he might correct him even after these things, granting him daily remedies. Unless we strive relying and trusting on these, we shall by no means be able to conquer human errors. For it is necessary that, when he who assists us does not assist us again, we be conquered by him through whose assistance we conquer.

### CHAPTER 29.—On the same matter. From the decrees of the same pope (ibid., ch. 9).

That God works in human hearts and in free choice itself, so that holy thought, [Col. 0978B] pious counsel, and every movement of good will come from God, because through him we can do something good, without whom we can do nothing (John XV). The same teacher instructed us in this confession when he spoke to the bishops of the whole world concerning the help of divine grace: “What time, then,” he says, “intervenes in which we do not need his help? Therefore, in all our actions, causes, thoughts, and movements, the Helper and Protector must be invoked” (Pope Zosimus, in a letter unknown to us). For it is proud for human nature to presume anything for itself, while the Apostle cries: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers and powers of this air, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI). And again he says: “Wretched man that I am! Who will [Col. 0978C] deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VII). And again: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me was not empty; rather, I labored more than all of them. Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (I Cor. XV).

### CHAPTER 20.—Divine grace not only forgives sins, but also assists so that they are not committed. Gregory in the *Morals*.

That the grace of God not only forgives sins, but also assists so that they are not committed and the law may be fulfilled; not, as Pelagius says, merely more easily, as though it could be fulfilled with greater difficulty without the grace of God. We also embrace as properly belonging to the Apostolic See that which was established among the decrees of the Council of Carthage: namely, what was determined in the third chapter, that whoever says that the grace of God, by which we are justified through Jesus Christ our Lord, avails only for the remission of sins already committed, and not also as assistance so that they may not be committed, let him be anathema [Col. 0978D]. And again, in the fourth chapter: “Whoever says that the grace of God through Jesus Christ assists us not to sin only because through it understanding of God’s commandments is revealed and opened to us, so that we may know what we ought to seek and what to avoid, but that through it we are not also granted to love and be able to do what we have learned ought to be done, let him be anathema.”

For when the Apostle says, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (I Cor. VIII), it is altogether impious for us to believe [Col. 0979A] that we have the grace of Christ for that which puffs us up, but do not have it for that which builds up, when both are gifts of God: both knowing what we ought to do and loving in order that we may do it; so that, while love builds up, knowledge cannot puff up. For just as it is written concerning God, “He teaches the human being knowledge” (Ps. XCIII), so it is also written, “Love is from God” (I John IV). Likewise, in the fifth chapter: whoever says that the grace of justification is given to us so that we may more easily fulfill by grace what we are commanded to do through free choice, although, even if grace were not given, we could nevertheless fulfill the divine commandments without it—not easily indeed, but still could do so—let him be anathema. For the Lord was speaking even of the fruits [indeed] of the commandments, where he did not say, “Without me you can do it with greater difficulty” [Col. 0979B]; but said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV).

### CHAPTER 31.—God’s predestination is so ordered that harmful things which are predestined may be undone through the prayers of the elect (*Dialogues*, bk. I, ch. 8).

Things not predestined cannot in any way be obtained; but those things which holy men accomplish by praying are so predestined that they may be obtained by prayers. For the predestination itself of the eternal kingdom is so arranged by almighty God that the elect arrive at it through labor, in order that, by asking, they may deserve to receive what almighty God arranged before the ages to give them.

**PETER.** I should like, if possible, to have it shown more clearly to me that predestination is aided by prayers.

**GREGORY.** What I have set forth, Peter, will readily [Col. 0979C] be proved. Certainly you know that the Lord said to Abraham: “In Isaac your seed shall be called” (Gen. XXI). He had also said to him: “I have made you the father of many nations” (Gen. XXVII). And again he promised him, saying: “I will bless you, and multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore” (Gen. XXII, XXVI). From this it is plainly understood that almighty God had predestined Abraham’s seed to be multiplied through Isaac; yet it is written: “Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife because she was barren; and he heard him and gave conception to Rebekah” (Gen. XXV). If, therefore, the multiplication of Abraham’s race through Isaac was predestined, why did he take a barren wife? But it is surely evident that predestination was to be fulfilled through prayers, when he through whom the Lord had predestined to multiply Abraham’s seed obtained by prayer [Col. 0979D] that he might be able to have a son.

### CHAPTER 32.—On God’s foreknowledge and, at the same time, providence. Augustine says in the book *On Predestination*:

Every judgment embraces, according to its own nature, the things subject to it. But God’s state is always eternal and ever-present. Knowledge also, transcending every motion of time, remains in the simplicity of its presence; embracing the infinite spaces of past and future, it considers all things in its simple cognition as though they were already taking place. Therefore, if anyone wishes to weigh the presence by which God knows all things, he will more rightly judge it to be not a presence, as though of future things, but knowledge of an ever-unfailing immediacy [Col. 0980A]. Hence it is called not so much *praevidentia* (“foreseeing”) as *providentia* (“providence”), because, situated far above the lowest things, it looks out upon everything as from the lofty summit of reality.

What then are we to say? Are those things made necessary which are illuminated by the divine light, when not even human beings make necessary the things they see? Does the sight of one who sees present things add any necessity to them? Not at all. But if a worthy comparison may be made between the divine and human present, then just as human beings see certain things in this temporal present, so God sees all things in his eternal present. Therefore this divine foreknowledge does not change the nature or proper character of things; it sees them present to itself in such a way as they will at some time occur in time, and it does not confuse judgments concerning things. By the single glance of his mind he knows events that will occur necessarily and events that will occur not necessarily [Col. 0980B]. Just as someone who simultaneously sees a person walking on earth and the sun rising in heaven, though both are together, nevertheless distinguishes them in his sight and judges the one voluntary and the other necessary, so the divine gaze, looking upon all things, does not in the least disturb the quality of things—present indeed to itself, but future in relation to the condition of time.

Thus this is not opinion, but knowledge resting rather upon truth, when it knows that something will exist while not failing to know that the same thing lacks necessity of existing. If someone says here that what God sees as going to happen cannot fail to happen, and that what cannot fail to happen occurs necessarily, the answer to him would concern matters of most solid truth, but matters to which scarcely anyone may approach unless he is a contemplator of the divine [Col. 0980C]. For the same future event is established as necessary when it is referred to divine knowledge; but when weighed in its own nature, it appears altogether free and unconditioned.

For there are two necessities: one simple, as when it is necessary that all human beings are mortal; the other conditional, as when someone knows that a person is walking, it is necessary that he is walking. For what anyone knows cannot be otherwise than it is known to be. But this conditional necessity does not bring with it the simple necessity. For this necessity is produced not by the thing’s own nature, but by the addition of the condition. No necessity compels someone who walks voluntarily to walk, though, while he is walking, it is necessary that he walk. In the same way, if providence sees something as present, it must be, although it has no necessity of nature [Col. 0980D]. Yet God beholds as present those future things which arise from freedom of choice. Therefore these things, referred to the divine gaze, become necessary through the disposition of divine knowledge; but, considered in themselves, they do not cease to possess the absolute freedom of their own nature. Thus all things which God foreknows will be future will undoubtedly come to pass; but some of them arise from free choice, and although they occur by coming into existence, they do not lose their proper nature, because before they came to pass they could also have failed to come to pass.

### CHAPTER 33.—Divine eternity has neither “has been” nor “will be.” Gregory in the *Morals* (bk. IV, ch. 32).

[Col. 0981A]

But because blessed Job is filled with the holy Spirit of eternity, and eternity has neither “has been” nor “will be”: for to it, indeed, neither do past things pass away nor do future things arrive, because it sees all things in the present.

### CHAPTER 34.—Nothing that happens to human beings comes without the hidden counsel of the Almighty. Gregory says in his *Morals* (bk. XII, ch. 1):

Nothing that happens to human beings in this world comes without the hidden counsel of almighty God. For God, foreknowing all things to come, decreed before the ages how they should be ordered through the ages.

### CHAPTER 35.—On the same matter. Gregory (bk. XVI, ch. 6, though not in the same words).

[Col. 0981B]

Therefore the prophet was not false, because he made known the time of death at which that man deserved to die; nor were the Lord’s decrees overturned, because the additional years of life granted by God’s generosity were also fixed before the ages, and the span of life unexpectedly added outwardly was established inwardly without any increase in God’s foreknowledge.

### CHAPTER 36.—God fixes each person’s days beforehand, so that they can neither be diminished nor increased. Gregory in the *Morals* (bk. XII, ch. 25).

The days fixed for each person by God’s inner foreknowledge can neither be increased nor diminished, unless it happens that they are foreknown in such a way that they are longer with the best works or shorter with the worst; as Hezekiah deserved an increase of days through an outpouring of tears [Col. 0981C] (IV Kings XX; II Chronicles XXXII; Isaiah XXXVIII), and as it is written of the perverse: “Death meets the undisciplined.” But often, although long periods of life have not been predestined for an ungodly person in God’s hidden presence, he himself, desiring to live carnally, sets before his mind long days; and because he cannot attain the time he expects, he perishes as though before his days are fulfilled. Yet we may understand this differently as well. For we often see certain persons both acting perversely and reaching extreme old age. How then is it said, “He shall perish before his days are fulfilled” (Job XV), when in some persons we frequently see that their limbs already fail from advanced age, while they nevertheless do not cease to pursue the desires of their perversity [Col. 0981D]?

### CHAPTER 37.—God overlooks sins. Gregory in the *Morals* (bk. XIV, ch. 18).

Almighty God, knowing what can profit us, appears not to hear the cry of those in pain, in order that he may increase their benefit: so that life may be purified through punishment and the tranquility of rest, which cannot be found here, may be sought elsewhere.

### CHAPTER 38.—God orders all things and considers the end of all. Gregory in the *Morals* (bk. XVIII, ch. 17).

“He has set a time for darkness, and he himself considers the end of all things” (Job XXVIII). By “all things” he intended both the elect and the reprobate to be included. For God does good and orders good things; he does not do evil things, but orders those evils done by the wicked so that they do not occur without order [Col. 0982A]. He considers the end of all, patiently bears everything, and looks upon the end of the elect, by which they are changed from evil to good. He also looks upon the end of the reprobate, by which they are drawn from evil conduct to punishment deserving of them.

He saw the end of Saul the persecutor, by which, struck down, he would say: “Lord, what do you want me to do?” (Acts IX). He saw the end of the disciple who seemed obedient: that, because of the crime he had committed, he would tighten a noose about his throat (Matt. XXVII), both punish himself as a sinner and, by punishing himself more grievously, deceive himself. He saw the Ninevites sinning, but considered the end of sinners corrected by repentance (Jonah III). He also saw Sodom sinning (Gen. XVIII, XIX), but considered the end of the burning of its lust: the fire of Gehenna [Col. 0982B]. He saw the end of the Gentile world: that, possessed by the darkness of iniquities, it would one day shine with the light of faith. He also saw the end of Judea: that it would be blinded by the darkness of hardened unbelief away from that light of faith which it possessed.

### CHAPTER 39.—Likewise on predestination. From the sayings of Fulgentius (book *On Predestination*).

For God’s predestination is nothing other than the eternal preparation of his future works. Here he called preparation “predestination.” Accordingly, whether we find “preparation” or “predestination” in the sayings of the saints, we are taught that they signify one and the same thing.

### CHAPTER 40.—Likewise on predestination. From the sayings of Ambrose.

[Col. 0982C] By all these testimonies the wicked are shown to be predestined to punishment, but not predestined to sin. For God is the predestiner of those things which he will do. But those things which he has not done and will not do, he has not predestined. Since he will judge the world and condemn the ungodly to just punishment for their iniquities, he has therefore predestined them to punishment and predestined punishment for them. But he has not predestined them to sin, because God is not the author of iniquity. For just as righteousness and every good work are from God, so iniquity and every perverse work are from the devil.

### CHAPTER 41.—Likewise on predestination. From the sayings of Augustine.

[Col. 0982D] By the name “predestination” no compulsory necessity of human will is expressed; rather, the everlasting disposition of the merciful and just divine work is predetermined.

### CHAPTER 42.—Likewise on predestination. From the sayings of Isidore.

Since God is compelled by no necessity to promise anything unwillingly, no obstacle of adversity prevents him from doing what he promised either less fully than he wills or more slowly. Therefore, as he willed, he could predestine some to glory and others to punishment. But those whom he predestined to glory, he predestined to righteousness. Those whom he predestined to punishment, however, he did not predestine to guilt. Likewise, a little above: In the saints, therefore, God crowns the righteousness [Col. 0983A] which he himself freely bestowed upon them, freely preserved, and freely brought to perfection. But he condemns the wicked for impiety or injustice which he himself did not create in them. In the former he glorifies his own works; in the latter he condemns their own works.

### CHAPTER 43.—Likewise on predestination. From the sayings of Augustine.

It is fitting for believers to believe and confess that the good and just God indeed foreknew sinful human beings, because nothing future could be hidden from him. For future things would not even be future unless they were present to him. Yet he did not predestine any human being to sin; because if God predestined a person to some sin, he would not punish that person for sins. For by God’s predestination either the merciful remission of sins [Col. 0983B] has been prepared, or the just punishment of sins.

### CHAPTER 44.—Likewise on predestination. Ambrose says:

Accordingly, the wicked whom God foreknew would end this life in sin, he predestined to be punished with unending punishment. In this, just as foreknowledge of human wickedness is not blameworthy, so the predestination of most just retribution is praiseworthy, so that it may be recognized that the man whom God predestined to be punished according to the merit of sin was not predestined by him to any sin whatsoever. God therefore foreknew all human works, whether good or evil, since nothing could be hidden from him; but he predestined only the good works which he foreknew that he himself would perform in the children of grace. The future evil works of those whom he did not predestine for the kingdom but foreknew for destruction, he foreknew by his most powerful divinity and ordered by his provident goodness. [Col. 0983C]

### CHAPTER 45.—Again, on predestination. From the sayings of Augustine.

The Lord himself taught us by his own word, in that he showed that he had prepared not only the kingdom in which the good rejoice, but also the eternal fire in which the evil are tormented. For he will say to the good: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25). But to the evil he will say: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid.). Behold to what God predestined the wicked and ungodly: namely, to just punishment—not to any unjust work; to penalty, not to fault; to punishment, not to transgression; to the destruction which the wrath of the just Judge rendered to sinners, not to the destruction by which the wickedness of sinners provoked God’s wrath against itself. This the preaching of the blessed Apostle makes clear: he calls the evil persons whom God will condemn eternally “vessels of wrath,” not vessels of fault. For he says: “But if God, willing to show wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, in order to show the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory” (Rom. 9).

In this final statement it should be noted that, taking testimony from the Gospel, he says that evil persons were predestined to eternal fire, because at the judgment the Lord will say not only to the good that they are to receive the kingdom of God prepared from the foundation of the world, but also to the evil: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). From this, indeed, he proves that the Lord predestined the wicked and ungodly to punishment—from the fact that he will say to them: “Go into eternal fire.” Those, therefore, who wish to say that punishment was predestined for the unjust, but that the unjust were not predestined to punishment, should consider how they understand this author’s statements. For the person for whom punishment is prepared is surely himself prepared for punishment. [Col. 0983D–0984A]

### CHAPTER 46.—Again, on the same subject. Augustine.

God would never render destruction to vessels of wrath unless a human being were found to possess sin voluntarily; for neither would God justly inflict wrath upon a sinful human being if that person had fallen into fault by God’s predestination. [Col. 0984B]

### CHAPTER 47.—Again, on predestination. From the sayings of Fulgentius (*On Predestination*).

For just as God’s foreknowledge compels no one to sin, although he surely foreknew before the eternal ages the sins of each individual, so also his predestination compels no one to punishment, although, before anyone is born, he is predestined for punishment if he is to remain in wickedness [“is predestined, if he is to remain in wickedness,” etc.].

### CHAPTER 48.—Again, on predestination. From the sayings of Ambrose.

Just as no one can charge God with responsibility for his sin, so neither can anyone charge him with responsibility for the fact that he must be punished for sins. For a person sins by wrongdoing through his own will, but is to be punished by the just judgment of the Judge. And just as the cause of sin does not arise from God’s foreknowledge—since no one sins because God foreknew that he would sin, but because he obeyed his own desire rather than the command of God, who forbids sin—so likewise no one goes to punishment because this had previously existed in God’s predestination. Rather, because he was foreknown to remain in sins and to end this present life without the fruit of repentance, he was assigned to punishment. And just as the cause of sin is desire, by which the will of the flesh is obeyed more than the divine command, so the cause of assignment to punishment is the committing of sin, followed by no worthy satisfaction for that sin. [Col. 0984C–D]

### CHAPTER 49.—Again, on predestination. From the sayings of the same.

And Scripture says: “Consider the works of the Lord, for no one can correct the person whom he has rejected” (Eccl. 7).

### CHAPTER 50.—Again, on predestination. From the sayings of Augustine.

No one truly believes in God who doubts that heaven and earth are encompassed by his foreknowledge and that the world is governed by divine providence. And just as nothing is hidden from his wisdom, so his ordering governs and directs all things. Just as no creature is hidden in his sight.

### CHAPTER 51.—On the creation of the angels. The same Augustine (*On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, ch. 10).

[Col. 0985A]

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth, and water from nothing” (Gen. 1); and while darkness still concealed that very water and water hid the earth, the angels and all heavenly powers were made, so that God’s goodness might not be idle, but might have beings in whom to display his goodness through the many spans of time before this. Thus this visible world was made and ordered from the things that had been created [“from the matter which had been made by God.” Thus in the current text of Augustine].

### CHAPTER 52.—That nothing is incorporeal and invisible except God alone (*ibid.*, ch. 11).

Nothing in nature is to be believed incorporeal and invisible except God alone. He is believed incorporeal because he is everywhere and fills and encompasses all things. He is also invisible to all creatures because he is incorporeal. [Col. 0985B]

### CHAPTER 53.—That every creature is corporeal. Augustine (*ibid.*, ch. 12).

Every creature is corporeal. Angels and all heavenly powers are corporeal, although they do not subsist in flesh. We believe intellectual creatures to be corporeal because they are spatially circumscribed, as also is the human soul, which is enclosed by flesh, and the demons, who are of the substance [“through the substance”] of angelic nature.

### CHAPTER 54.—That all intellectual natures are immortal. Augustine (*ibid.*, ch. 13).

[Col. 0985C]

We believe intellectual natures to be immortal because they lack flesh and have nothing that can fall, so as to need resurrection after a fall.

### CHAPTER 55.—That all apostate angels possessed free choice before their fall. Gregory (*Morals*, book 5, ch. 27).

For each thing tends, as it were, toward another thing by as many steps as it is subject to motions of its mutability. But the incomprehensible nature alone does not know how to move from its own state, since it does not know how to change from him who is always the same. For if the substance of angels had been exempt from the movement of mutability, being well created by its Maker, it would never have fallen, in the case of the reprobate spirits, from the summit of its blessedness. Yet almighty God wonderfully created the nature of the highest spirits good, but mutable, so that any who would not remain might fall; while those who persevered in their created condition might remain in it with greater worth, because they stood by choice, and might possess greater merit before God because they had fixed the movement of their mutability by the steadfastness of their will. [Col. 0985C–D]

### CHAPTER 56.—Why the spirits of angels sinned without possibility of forgiveness, but sinful humanity obtained pardon. Gregory, *Morals* (book 9, ch. 36).

The spirits of angels sinned without possibility of forgiveness because they were able to stand with so much greater strength inasmuch as no admixture of flesh held them back. But humanity deserved pardon after fault because, through the fleshly body, it received something by which it was less than itself. Hence this same weakness of the flesh is, in the sight of the Judge, an argument for mercy.

### CHAPTER 57.—That guardian angels are appointed over human beings. Gregory (*Morals*, book 6, ch. 31).

[Col. 0986A]

That angels preside over human beings is attested by an angel through the prophet, who says: “The prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me” (Dan. 10). That angels are directed by the powers of higher angels is testified by the prophet Zechariah, who says: “Behold, the angel who spoke in me was going out, and another angel was going out to meet him; and he said to him: ‘Run and speak to this young man, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without walls’” (Zech. 2).

### CHAPTER 58.—That individual angels are assigned as guardians to individual human beings. From the sayings of a certain author in the *Lives of the Fathers*.

Abbot Paul the Simple possessed the grace of seeing the elders as they entered church and, from each person’s very face, perceiving whether that person’s thoughts were evil or good. When the elders came and entered the church, he saw them entering with bright faces and joyful hearts, their angels also rejoicing together with them. But he saw one man with a black and clouded body, demons dragging him from either side with a bridle placed in his nostrils, and his holy angel following sadly at a distance. Blessed Paul therefore began to weep most bitterly and to beat his breast, sitting before the church because of the man whom he had seen in this condition. All the other elders, seeing him weeping in this manner, began to entreat him, when he entered the assembly with them, to tell them if he had seen anything in them. But he refused to enter and continued weeping because of the one whom he had seen thus.

After a little while, when the dismissed assembly was leaving, he again looked around at all their faces, to see whether they departed as they had entered. He saw the man whom he had previously seen black and clouded leave the church with a bright face and a white body; the demons were following him from afar, while his holy angel was near him, cheerful and rejoicing greatly over him. [Col. 0986B–C]

### CHAPTER 59.—That God’s right hand is the elect part of the angels, and his left hand the reprobate part. Gregory (*Morals*, book 2, ch. 21).
