What, then, does it mean that the host of heaven is said to stand at his right and left? (3 Kings 22.) God, who is so within all things that he is also outside all things, is bounded by neither right nor left; rather, God’s right hand signifies the elect part of the angels, and his left hand the reprobate part. For not only the good serve God, so as to assist; the evil also serve him, so as to test [others: “so as to reject”]. Not only do those who return from fault receive help, but those who refuse to return are also weighed down. Nor does the description “host of heaven” prevent the reprobate part of the angels from being understood as included in it. For we call birds of heaven those which we know to be suspended in the air. Paul likewise says of these same spirits: “Against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6). Declaring their head, he says: “According to the prince of the power of this air” (Eph. 2).

Thus the angelic host stands at God’s right and left, because both the will of the elect spirits agrees with divine mercy and the mind of the reprobate spirits, serving its own malice, obeys the judgment of his strict justice. Hence the deceitful spirit is immediately described as having stepped forward into the midst, by whom King Ahab was deceived according to his own deserving merits. For it is not lawful to believe that a good spirit wished to serve deception when it said: “I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets” (3 Kings 22; 2 Chron. 18). But King Ahab, because of his preceding sins, deserved to be condemned by such deception, so that he who had often willingly fallen into fault might at some point be taken unwillingly for punishment. By a hidden permission of justice, malignant spirits are allowed to draw, even unwillingly, into the punishment of sin those whom, while willing, they strangle in the snare of sins.

Therefore, what is there described as the host of heaven standing at God’s right and left (3 Kings 22), is here stated as Satan’s being present among the sons of God. Behold: at God’s right stood the angels who are called sons of God; behold: at his left stand angels, because Satan also was present among them. [Col. 0986D–0987B]

### CHAPTER 60.—That unclean spirits wander in the space between heaven and earth. Gregory (*Morals*, book 2, ch. 34).

We have already said a little earlier that air is called heaven; hence we call birds “birds of heaven.” And we know that unclean spirits, who fell from the ethereal heaven, wander in this space between heaven and earth. They begrudge human hearts their ascent to heavenly things all the more because they see themselves cast down from heavenly things by the uncleanness of their pride.

### CHAPTER 61.—Whether peace is maintained in the heavenly realms. Gregory (*Morals*, book 17, ch. 7).

[Col. 0987C]

But amid these matters, it is pleasing to inquire: if the highest peace is maintained in the heavenly realms, what is meant by the angel’s saying to Daniel: “I came because of your words; but the prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me for twenty-one days; and behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me” (Dan. 10)? And shortly afterward: “Now I shall return to fight against the prince of the Persians. When I was going out, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming” (ibid.). Whom else, then, does he call princes of the nations except angels, who could resist him as he went forth? What peace can exist in the heavenly realms if a contest of battle is waged even among the angelic spirits themselves, who always stand in the presence of Truth?

Yet because definite angelic ministries have been set over the administration of each nation, when the conduct of those subject to them earns, in turn, the assistance of the presiding spirits against one another, the spirits who preside are said to come against one another. For the angel speaking to Daniel is understood to have been set over the captive people of Israel dwelling in Persia. But Michael is found to have been set over those of that same people who remained in the land of Judaea. Hence this same angel shortly afterward says to Daniel: “There is no one to help me in all these matters except Michael, your prince” (ibid.). And of him he says what we have already cited: “Behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me.” Since he is said not to be present together with him, but to come to his aid, he is plainly recognized as being set over that people which was held captive in another region. [Col. 0987C–0988A]

### CHAPTER 62.—That the devil’s will is always wicked, but his power is never unjust. Gregory (*Morals*, book 2, ch. 10).

It must be understood that Satan’s will is always wicked, but his power is never unjust, because he has his will from himself, but his power from the Lord. What he himself wickedly desires to do, God permits to be done only justly. Hence it is well said in the books of Kings: “The evil spirit of the Lord rushed upon Saul” (1 Kings 18). Behold, one and the same spirit is called both “of the Lord” and “evil”: “of the Lord,” indeed, by the permission of just power; “evil,” through the desire of an unjust will. Therefore, one who has no power except by permission need not be feared. The only force to be feared is that which, when it has permitted the enemy to rage, makes even his unjust will serve the purposes of just judgment.

But he asks that his hand be extended a little, because it is outward things that he seeks to crush. For Satan does not think he has done anything significant unless he wounds the soul, so that by striking it he may call it back from that homeland from which he himself lies cast down far away by the weapon of his pride. [Col. 0988A–B]

### CHAPTER 63.—That God speaks to the devil in four ways, and the devil to God in three ways. Gregory (*Morals*, book 2, ch. 7).

It must be understood that, as we learn in this passage, God speaks to the devil in four ways and the devil speaks to God in three ways. God rebukes the devil’s unjust ways; sets before him the righteousness of his elect; permits him, by granting leave, to test their innocence; and sometimes forbids him even to dare to test them.

He rebukes the devil’s unjust ways, as was already said: “Where do you come from?” (Job 1). He sets before him the righteousness of his elect when he says: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth?” (ibid.). He permits their innocence to be tested by granting leave, as he says: “Behold, all that he has is in your hand” (ibid.). Again, he restrains him from temptation when he says: “Only do not stretch out your hand against him” (ibid.).

But the devil speaks to God in three ways: when he either discloses his own ways, accuses the innocence of the elect with fabricated charges, or requests that the same innocence be tested. He discloses his ways when he says: “I have gone round the earth and walked through it” (ibid.). He accuses the innocence of the elect when he says: “Does Job fear God for nothing? Have you not fenced him in, and his house, and all his property round about?” (ibid.). He asks that the same innocence be tested when he says: “Stretch out your hand and touch all that he possesses, unless he bless you to your face” [that is, curse you] (ibid.). [Col. 0988C–D]

### CHAPTER 64.—That there is no palm of victory without the labor of conflict. Gregory (*Dialogues*, book 1, ch. 20).

Without the labor of conflict there is no palm of victory. How, then, are they victors except because they have fought against the snares of the ancient enemy? For the malignant spirit always attends our thought, speech, and deed, in case perhaps he may find something by which he may appear as accuser before the tribunal of the eternal Judge.

Do you wish to know how he is always present in order to deceive? Some persons now among us bear witness to the matter I relate: a man of venerable life, named Stephen, was a priest in the province of Valeria and a close relative of Boniface, our deacon and steward of the Church. One day, returning home from a journey, he spoke carelessly to his servant and commanded him, saying: “Come, devil, take off my shoes.” At these words the laces of his shoes immediately began to loosen with the greatest speed, so that it was plainly apparent that the devil himself, who had been named, had obeyed him by removing the shoes.

As soon as the priest saw this, he was greatly terrified and began to cry out in a loud voice: “Depart, wretch, depart! For I was speaking not to you but to my servant.” At his words the devil immediately departed, so that the laces were found for the most part already loosened, though in part they remained. From this it may be inferred that the ancient enemy, who is so ready for bodily acts, presses upon our thoughts with excessive snares. [Col. 0989A–B]

### CHAPTER 65.—On the creation, nature, and ministry of angels, and the fall of the apostates. Saint Isidore speaks thus in the *Book of Offices* (*On the Supreme Good*, book 1, ch. 10):

The name “angel” denotes an office, not a nature. According to their nature, they are called spirits. For when they are sent from heaven to announce matters to human beings, they are called angels from the act of announcing itself. By nature they are spirits; they are called angels when they are sent.

The nature of angels is mutable, but everlasting love makes them incorruptible. We say that angels are immutable by grace, not by nature. For if they were immutable by nature, the devil certainly would not have fallen. Thus contemplation of the Creator supports the mutability of their nature. The apostate angel was deprived of this contemplation because he wished to preserve his strength not from God but from himself.

Angels were made before every creature, when it was said: “Let there be light” (Gen. 1). For Scripture says of them: “Wisdom was created before all things” (Ecclus. 1). They are called light because they participate in eternal light; they are called wisdom because they cleave to uncreated Wisdom. Although mutable by nature, divine contemplation nevertheless does not allow them to change.

The angels were created before every creature [or, “before every creation”] of the world, and before every creation of angels the devil was created, as it is written: “He is the beginning of the ways of God” (Job 40). Hence, in comparison with the angels, he was called an archangel. For he was created first in precedence of rank, not in amount of time. It is evident that the devil held primacy among the angels through excellence of preeminence; from confidence in this he fell, so that he collapsed without restoration.

The prophet declares the excellence of this preeminence in these words: “The cedars in the paradise of God were not higher than he; the fir trees did not equal his height; no tree of paradise was comparable to him, because God made him more beautiful” (Ezek. 31). The condition of an angel differs from that of a human being. A human being was made in God’s likeness; but the archangel who fell was called the seal of God’s likeness, as the Lord testifies through Ezekiel: “You are the seal of likeness, full of wisdom, perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. 28). For the subtler his nature is, the more fully it was formed in the likeness of divine truth.

It is clear that the devil fell from heaven before the human being was created. For as soon as he was made, he burst forth into pride and was cast down from heaven. For, according to the testimony of Truth, “He was a liar from the beginning and did not stand in the truth” (John 8), because he fell as soon as he was made. He was indeed created in truth, but, by not standing, immediately fell away from truth.

By one fall of pride, while they compare themselves to God in arrogance, both the human being and the devil fell. But the human being, returning to repentance, acknowledges himself inferior to God; while the devil, not content merely with having fallen by deeming himself God’s equal, even says that he is superior to God, according to the Apostle’s statement concerning Antichrist: “He opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God or worshipped” (2 Thess. 2). The devil no longer seeks pardon because he is not moved to repentance. His members, however, often make supplication hypocritically, but because of their evil conscience they do not deserve to obtain what they seek.

Let human misery learn that God is thereby more readily moved to grant pardon, because he has compassion on frail humanity: humanity drew the weakness to sin from its lower part, that is, from the flesh in which the soul is confined. But apostate angels have no pardon because they were not burdened by any weakness of fleshly frailty that might lead them to sin. Human beings, however, return to pardon after sin because they have drawn the weight of weakness from material made of clay. Therefore, because of the frail condition of the flesh, the way back to salvation lies open to humanity, as the Psalmist says: “He knows our formation. Remember, Lord, that we are earth” (Ps. 102). And again: “Remember,” he says, “what my substance is” (Ps. 88).

After the apostate angels fell, the rest were made steadfast in the perseverance of eternal blessedness. Hence after the creation of heaven the phrase is repeated at the beginning: “Let there be a firmament.” “And the firmament was called heaven” (Gen. 1). This plainly shows that, after the angels’ fall, those who remained deserved the firmness of everlasting perseverance and blessedness, which they had previously received in a lesser degree. From this it must be recognized that the wickedness of the evil serves the benefit of the saints, because from the source of the evil’s fall the good make progress.

The number of good angels, diminished after the fall of the evil angels, will be filled up from the number of elect human beings; this number is known to God alone. Among angels there is a distinction of powers, and ministries are distributed to them according to the dignity of their ranks. Some are set above others both by eminence of authority and by knowledge of power. Thus some carry out the commands of others and obey their orders. Therefore an angel sends an angel to the prophet Zechariah and commands him what he must announce (Zech. 2).

Sacred Scripture testifies that there are nine distinctions, or orders, of angels: angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, virtues, principalities, powers, cherubim, and seraphim. The prophet Ezekiel also describes the number of these orders under an equal number of names of stones, when speaking of the primacy of the apostate angel: “Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald” (Ezek. 28). By this number of stones the orders of angels themselves are signified. Before his fall, the apostate angel had them affixed, as it were, in the garment of his adornment; seeing himself brighter than all in comparison with them, he immediately swelled with pride and raised his heart to arrogance.

Angels always rejoice in God, not in themselves. But the devil is evil because he sought not what belongs to God, but what belongs to himself. No wickedness is greater than for someone to wish to glory not in God but in himself. Angels know all things in the Word of God before they happen in actuality; and things which are still future among human beings angels already know through God’s revelation.

The transgressing angels, even after losing holiness, did not lose the lively perception of their angelic nature. For they possess sharp foreknowledge in three ways: by subtlety of nature, experience of times, and revelation from higher powers. Whenever God is angry with this world by any scourge, apostate angels are sent to perform the ministry of vengeance; nevertheless, they are restrained by divine power, lest they harm as much as they desire.

Good angels, however, are assigned to the ministry of human salvation, to administer the affairs of the world and govern all things at God’s command, as the Apostle testifies: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who will receive the inheritance of salvation?” (Heb. 1). Angels take from the upper air bodies in which they appear to human beings, and put on a solid appearance from the heavenly element, so that they may be shown more clearly to human sight.

Individual nations are believed to have angels set over them, as is shown by the testimony of the angel speaking to Daniel: “I came to announce to you, but the prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me” (Dan. 10). And later: “There is no one who helps me except Michael our prince” (ibid.). Likewise, all human beings are shown to have angels, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Truly I say to you, their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 18). Hence, when Peter in the Acts of the Apostles knocked at the door, the apostles inside said: “It is not Peter; it is his angel” (Acts 12).

If angels behold and see God—of whom the apostle Peter says: “Into whom the angels of God desire to look” (1 Pet. 1)—or, again, if they do not behold or see God, how, according to the Lord’s statement, do “their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 18)? Yet both statements are sound. For we truly believe that angels both see God and desire to see him; they both possess him and hasten to possess him; they both love him and strive to love him. For if they desire to see him in such a way that they do not enjoy the fulfillment of their desire, that desire entails necessity. Such necessity is punitive, and every punishment is far from blessed angels [variant: “but”], because punishment and blessedness never coexist. Again, if we say that they are satisfied with the vision of God, satisfaction is accustomed to produce weariness; yet we know that they cannot grow weary of the vision of God which they desire.

What, then, is the answer, except that we should believe both in a wondrous way: they both desire and are satisfied? They desire without toil, and are satisfied without weariness. So that necessity may not exist in their desire, those who desire are satisfied; and again, so that weariness may not exist in their satisfaction, those who are satisfied [variant: *satiari*, “to be satisfied”] desire. Thus angels see the Father’s face in satisfaction; but because that satisfaction knows no weariness, they always desire to look upon him.

Wherever in the holy Scriptures an angel is put in place of God, not the Father or the Holy Spirit, but the Son alone is understood, on account of the dispensation of the Incarnation. Before the coming of the Lord’s Incarnation, discord existed between human beings and angels; but Christ, when he came, made peace in himself for both angels and human beings. For at his birth the angels cried: “Peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke 1). Therefore, through Christ’s Incarnation, humanity was reconciled not only to God, but peace was also restored between angels and human beings.

That discord existed between angels and human beings before Christ’s coming is especially understood from the fact that angels greeted by human beings in the Old Testament disdain to be greeted [variant: “greeted in return”] by them. But when John did this in the New Testament, the angel not only received it reverently, but even forbade him to do it (Rev. 19, 22). For this reason the human being is disdained in the Old Testament and is not greeted in return by the angel: humanity had not yet passed over into God. But humanity is received by God and reverently greeted by the angel. For the angel Gabriel is said to have greeted Mary (Luke 1); and to John, greeting an angel, the same angel says: “See that you do not do this; for I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brethren” (Rev. 19, 22). From this it is recognized that, through the Lord’s Incarnation, peace was restored to human beings and angels. [Col. 0989C–0992D]

### CHAPTER 66.—That the number of citizens of heaven is both finite and infinite. Gregory, *Morals* (book 17, ch. 7).

The number of heavenly citizens is described as both infinite and definite, so that it may be shown to be countable to God but uncountable to us. Yet it is one thing to stand in attendance and another to minister. Those powers undoubtedly stand in attendance which do not go forth to announce particular matters to human beings. Those, however, minister who come to perform the offices of messengers; yet these too do not depart from inward contemplation. And because those who minister are more numerous than those who stand principally in attendance, the number of those in attendance is shown as though definite, while the number of those who minister is shown as infinite.

(*Ibid.*, ch. 8.) We rightly call angelic spirits God’s soldiers, because we know that they fight against the aerial powers. Yet they carry out these conflicts not by labor but by command, because whatever they seek to accomplish against unclean spirits they are able to do by the aid of him who governs all things. [Col. 0993A]

### CHAPTER 67.—That every fault is discharged before departure by the gift of an offering. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (book 4, ch. 55).

But I also think it should not be left unmentioned what I recall happened in my monastery three years ago. There was a monk named Justus, trained in the medical art [Col. 0993B], who, while I was living in that same monastery, was accustomed diligently to attend me and keep watch during my frequent illnesses. He too, overtaken by bodily sickness, was brought to the point of death. In that illness he was served by his own brother, named Copiosus, who even now in this city earns his temporal livelihood by the same medical art.

But when the said Justus knew that he had reached his end, he disclosed to his brother Copiosus that he possessed three gold coins concealed in secret. This, of course, could not remain hidden from the brothers. Searching carefully and examining all his medicines, they found the three gold coins hidden in a medicinal preparation. As soon as this was reported to me, I could not bear with equanimity so great an evil in a brother [Col. 0993C] who had lived with us in common; for the rule of my monastery had always been that all the brothers should live so communally that none of them might be permitted to possess anything of his own.

Then, struck with excessive grief, I began to consider what I should do for the dying man’s purification and what provision I should make as an example for the brothers who were living. Therefore, summoning to me Pretiosus, the steward of that monastery, I said: “See to it that none of the brothers joins himself to the dying man, nor that he receives a word of consolation from the mouth of any of them. But when, at the point of death, he asks for the brothers, let his own natural brother tell him that, because of the gold coins which he kept secretly, he is held in abhorrence by all the brothers, [Col. 0993D] so that at least in death the bitterness may pierce his mind concerning his fault and cleanse him from the sin he committed. When he has died, do not place his body with the bodies of the brothers. Instead, make a grave for him somewhere in the dung-heap, throw his body into it, and cast upon him there the three gold coins which he left, all crying together: ‘May your money be with you unto perdition’ [Acts VIII]. Then cover him with earth.”

In both these measures I intended one benefit for the dying man and the other for the living brothers: that the bitterness of death might free him from his fault, and that the severity of such a condemnation for avarice might frighten these men and prevent them from sharing in the sin [variant: “might frighten them and prevent them from the sin”]. And so it was done. When the monk came to death and anxiously sought to commend himself to the brothers, [Col. 0994A] no brother would approach him or deign to speak with him; and his natural brother told him why he was abhorred by all. At once he groaned intensely over his guilt and departed from the body in that sorrow. He was buried as I had said.

But all the brothers, disturbed by this judgment concerning him, began individually to bring out into the common store every last and worthless thing which they had always been allowed by the rule to possess, and they feared greatly lest they should have anything in their possession for which they might be reproached. When thirty days after his death had passed, my mind began to pity the deceased brother, to weigh his punishments with heavy grief, and to seek whether there might be some remedy for his deliverance. Then, calling to me Pretiosus, the steward of my monastery, I said sadly: “It has been a long time that the brother [Col. 0994B] who died has been suffering in fire. We ought to bestow some charity upon him and help him, insofar as we can, to be delivered. Go, therefore, and from this day make it your care to offer the sacrifice for him for thirty continuous days, so that no day at all is omitted on which the saving Victim is not sacrificed [variant: “offered”] for his absolution.”

He departed at once and obeyed. But while we were occupied with other concerns and did not count the days as they elapsed, the same brother who had died appeared one night in a vision to his natural brother Copiosus. When Copiosus saw him, he asked: “What is it, brother? How are you?” He replied: “Until now I have been badly off, but now I am well, because today I received communion.” Copiosus immediately went and told the brothers in the monastery [Col. 0994C] this. The brothers carefully counted the days and discovered that it was the very day on which the thirtieth offering for him had been completed. And since Copiosus did not know what the brothers had done for him, while the brothers did not know what Copiosus had seen concerning him, at one and the same time he learned what they had done and they learned what he had seen. The agreement of the vision with the sacrifice made the matter clearly evident: the deceased brother had escaped punishment through the saving Victim.

## CHAPTER 68.—That the sacred offering after death can benefit souls, if their sins are not incapable of dissolution. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (Book IV, chapter 55).

If sins are not irredeemable after death, the sacred offering of the saving Victim is accustomed to assist the souls of many even after death, so that sometimes the souls of the dead themselves seem to request it. For the aforementioned Bishop Felix asserts that he learned from a priest of venerable life, who lived until two years ago and dwelt in the diocese of the city of Centumcellae, and presided over the church of Saint John situated in the place called Tauriana, that this priest regularly bathed, whenever bodily necessity required it, in the place where hot waters give off excessive vapours.

One day, when he had entered there, he found an unknown man prepared to serve him: the man removed his shoes from his feet, took up his clothes, offered him towels upon his leaving the heat, and [Col. 0995A] performed every service with great attentiveness. As this happened frequently, the priest, going to the baths one day, said to himself: “I ought not to appear ungrateful to the man who so devoutly serves me in bathing; I must bring him something as a gift.” He therefore took with him two eucharistic loaves. As soon as he came to the place, he found the man and, as usual, availed himself of his service in everything.

Having bathed, and wishing now, once dressed, to leave, he offered to the attendant man, as a blessing, what he had brought with him, asking him kindly to receive what he offered out of charity. The man replied sadly and distressed: “Why do you give these things to me, Father? This bread is holy, and I cannot eat it. For I who you see was once the master of this place, but because of my sins I have been assigned here after death. If, however, you wish to help me, offer this bread to almighty God for me, intercede for my sins, and then know that you have been heard when you come here to bathe and do not find me.” [Col. 0995B]

At these words he disappeared, and by vanishing, he made known that he who had seemed to be a man was a spirit. The priest then afflicted himself for him in tears for a whole week, offered the saving Victim daily, and afterwards returned to the bath-house, where he did not find him. From this it is shown how greatly the sacrifice of the sacred offering benefits souls, since the spirits of the dead themselves ask the living for it and give signs by which they appear to have been absolved through it.

## CHAPTER 69.—That it is more blessed for each person to depart this life free than to seek freedom after death. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (Book IV, chapter 58).

Let all be shown that, if sins are irredeemable, even for the dead the Victim of the sacred offering can in no way be of benefit for absolution. But it must be understood that the sacred Victim benefits those dead persons who, by their manner of life here, obtained that even after death they might be aided by the good deeds performed here by others on their behalf. Meanwhile, this must be considered: the safer course is that a person should himself do while living the good which he hopes after his death will be done for him by others. For it is more blessed to depart free than to seek freedom after chains.

## CHAPTER 70.—That no one should pray for a sin which is unto death. Gregory, *Moralia* (Book XVI, chapter 31).

[Col. 0995D]

A sin is indeed carried down to hell when, before the end of this present life, it is not corrected through amendment unto repentance. Of this sin John says: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” [1 John V]. A sin unto death is a sin lasting unto death; that is, when a sin is not corrected here, forgiveness for it is sought in vain. Concerning this it is further said: “Let mercy forget him” [Job XXIV]. The mercy of almighty God is said to forget the person who has forgotten the justice of almighty God. For whoever does not now fear him as just will be unable afterwards to find him merciful. [Col. 0996A]

## CHAPTER 71.—That all souls of the elect should be believed to be in heaven, and the souls of the wicked in hell. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (Book IV, chapter 28).

“I see that my inquiry has now been answered sufficiently; but this question still presses upon my mind. Since it has been said above that the souls of the saints are already in heaven, it surely remains that the souls of the wicked also must be believed to be nowhere but in hell. Yet I do not know what truth holds on this matter. For human judgment does not admit that the souls of sinners can suffer punishment before the Judgment.”

GREGORY: “If you have believed, on the satisfying testimony of sacred Scripture, that the souls of the saints are in heaven, you must likewise in every respect believe that the souls of the wicked are in hell. For from the recompense of eternal justice, through which the just already glory, it necessarily follows in every respect that the unjust also suffer torment. For as blessedness gladdens the elect, so it must be believed that from the day of their departure fire burns the reprobate.” [Col. 0996B]

## CHAPTER 72.—That, as there is no end to the joy of the good, so there is no end to the torments of the evil. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (Book IV, chapter 44).

PETER: “May we then, I ask you, say that those who have once been plunged there will burn forever?”

GREGORY: “It is certainly and unquestionably true that, just as there is no end to the joy of the good, so there will be no end to the torments of the evil. For when Truth says, ‘These shall go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life’ [Matthew XXV], because what God promised is true, what he threatened will without doubt not be false.” [Col. 0996C]

## CHAPTER 73.—That it is not as some affirm: that God threatened sinners with eternal punishment in order to correct them from evil. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (immediately following).

PETER: “What if someone says: ‘God threatened sinners with eternal punishment precisely in order to restrain them from committing sins’?”

GREGORY: “If what he threatened is false, in order that they might be corrected from injustice, then what he promised is also false, in order that they might be induced toward justice. But who, even if mad, would dare say this? And if he threatened what he was not going to fulfill, then, while wishing to maintain that he is merciful, we are forced to proclaim him deceitful—which it is impious to say.” [Col. 0996D]

## CHAPTER 74.—Why sins committed within a finite span are punished without end. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (ibid.).

PETER: “I should like to know how it is just that a fault committed within a finite span should be punished without end.”

GREGORY: “This would be rightly said if the strict Judge weighed not human hearts but deeds. The wicked sinned within a finite span because they lived within a finite span. For, if they could, they would certainly wish to live without end, so that they might be able to sin without end. Those who never cease sinning while they live show that they wish always to live in sin. Therefore, it belongs to the great justice of the Judge that those who in this life never wished to be without sin should never be without punishment.” [Col. 0997A]

## CHAPTER 75.—That God is merciful and does not feed upon the suffering of the miserable; yet he is just and therefore is not forever satisfied by the punishment of the wicked. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (ibid.).

PETER: “But no just person feeds upon cruelty, and a sinful servant is ordered to be beaten by a just master in order that he may be corrected from wickedness. He is beaten so that he should be amended. But if the wicked, handed over to the fire of hell, do not come to correction, to what end will they burn forever?”

GREGORY: “Almighty God, because he is merciful, does not feed upon the suffering of the miserable. But because he is just, he is not forever satisfied by the punishment of the wicked. Yet all the wicked, assigned to eternal punishment, are indeed punished for their own wickedness; nevertheless, they will burn for a further purpose: namely, that all the just may both see in God the joys they receive and behold in them the punishments they escaped, so that they may know themselves eternally to be debtors to divine grace all the more, the more they see eternally punished the evils which they overcame by God’s help.” [Col. 0997B]

## CHAPTER 76.—Whether the souls of the just are received into heaven before the restoration of their bodies. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (Book IV, chapter 44).

PETER: “What you say pleases me. But I should like to know whether the souls of the saints can now, before the restoration of their bodies, be received into heaven.”

GREGORY: “We can neither affirm this of all the just nor deny it of all. For there are souls of certain just persons which are still delayed from the heavenly kingdom in certain dwelling-places [Col. 0997C]. What else is indicated by the loss entailed in this delay except that they lacked something of perfect justice? Yet it is clearer than light that the souls of the perfectly just, as soon as they leave the confines of this flesh, are received into heavenly abodes. Truth itself testifies to this, saying: ‘Wherever the body may be, there the eagles will be gathered’ [Matthew XXIV]. For where our Redeemer himself is in body, there also, without doubt, the souls of the just are gathered. Paul desires ‘to be dissolved and to be with Christ’ [Philippians I]. Therefore, whoever does not doubt that Christ is in heaven does not deny that Paul’s soul is in heaven. He also says concerning the dissolution of his body and his dwelling in the home of the heavenly country: [Col. 0997D] ‘We know that, if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands but eternal in the heavens’ [2 Corinthians V].”

## CHAPTER 77.—That on the day of judgment the just will rejoice in the glory of both soul and body. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (ibid.).

PETER: “If, therefore, the souls of the just are now in heaven, what is it that they will receive on the day of judgment as a recompense for their justice?”

GREGORY: “This is indeed increased for them at the Judgment: now they enjoy only the blessedness of souls, but afterwards also that of bodies, so that they may rejoice also in that flesh in which they endured pains and torments for the Lord. For this twofold glory of theirs it is written: ‘In their land they shall possess double’ [Isaiah LXI]. Hence also, before the day of resurrection, it is written concerning the souls of the saints: ‘White robes were given to each of them, and they were told to rest yet a little while, until the number of their fellow-servants and brothers should be completed’ [Revelation VI]. Therefore, those who have now received single robes will have double robes at the Judgment, because now they will rejoice only in the glory of their souls, but then in the glory of both souls and bodies.” [Col. 0998A]

## CHAPTER 78.—Whether the good recognize the good in the kingdom, and the evil the evil in punishment. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (Book IV, chapter 33).

PETER: “I should like to know whether the good recognize the good in the kingdom, and the evil the evil in punishments.”

GREGORY: [Col. 0998B] “The judgment on this matter is shown clearer than light in the words of the Lord [Luke XVI] which we have already cited above. There it was said: ‘There was a certain rich man, clothed in purple and fine linen, who feasted splendidly every day. And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, lying at his gate, full of sores, desiring to be filled from the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him anything; but dogs also came and licked his sores.’ It is then added that Lazarus died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom; and the rich man died and was buried in hell. Lifting up his eyes while in torment, he saw Abraham far away and Lazarus in his bosom; and he cried out: ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water [Col. 0998C] and cool my tongue.’ Abraham said to him: ‘Son, remember that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things.’

[Col. 0998D] “But the rich man, now having no hope of salvation for himself, turned to obtaining the salvation of his own people, saying: ‘I ask you, father, to send him to my father’s house; for I have five brothers, that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torment.’ These words plainly declare that both the good recognize the good and the evil the evil. For if Abraham had not recognized Lazarus, he would by no means have spoken to the rich man placed in torments about Lazarus’s past affliction, saying that Lazarus had received evil things in his life. And if the evil did not recognize the evil, the rich man in torments would by no means have remembered even his absent brothers. How could he be unable to recognize those present, when he took care to entreat even for absent persons whom he remembered?

“This also shows what you did not ask: that the good recognize the evil and the evil know the good. For the rich man is recognized by Abraham, to whom it is said, ‘Remember that you received good things in your life’; and the chosen Lazarus is recognized by the reprobate rich man, who asks that he be sent by name, saying: ‘Send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue.’ In this mutual recognition, the fullness of recompense grows for each side: the good rejoice more because they see rejoicing with them those whom they loved; while the evil, being tormented with those whom they loved in this world while despising God, are consumed not only by their own punishment but also by theirs. [Col. 0999A]

“But among the elect something more wonderful occurs. They recognize not only those whom they knew in this world, but recognize as if seen and known the good whom they have never seen. For when they see the ancient Fathers in that eternal inheritance, those whom they had always known by their deeds will not be unknown to them in sight. Since all there behold God in a common brightness, what can they fail to know there, where they know him who knows all things?

“For a certain man among us, venerable in life, very devout and praiseworthy, when he died three years ago—as other devout persons who were present testified—at the hour of his departure began to see the prophet Jonah, as well as Ezekiel and Daniel. Saying that they had come to him, and lowering his eyes, he rendered them the service of reverence; then he was taken from the flesh. From this it is plainly understood what knowledge there will be in that incorruptible life, if this man, still placed in the flesh, recognized holy prophets whom he had certainly never seen. It also often happens that a soul about to depart recognizes those with whom, according to the character of its sins or rewards, it is to be assigned to one dwelling-place; many see at that departure those whom they will have as companions either in the kingdom or in punishment.” [Col. 0999B]

## CHAPTER 79.—Whether a purgatorial fire which cleanses souls from sins after death should be believed in. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (Book IV, chapter 39).

PETER: [Col. 0999C] “I should like to learn whether a purgatorial fire ought to be believed to exist after death.”

GREGORY: “In the Gospel the Lord says: ‘Walk while you have the light’ [John XII]. Through the prophet he also says: ‘In an acceptable time I heard you, and on a day of salvation I helped you’ [Isaiah XLIX]. Explaining this, the apostle Paul said: ‘Behold, now is the acceptable time’ [2 Corinthians VI], and so forth. Solomon also says: ‘Whatever your hand is able to do, do it earnestly, for there will be neither work nor deliberation nor knowledge nor wisdom in hell, to which you are hastening’ [Ecclesiastes IX]. David likewise says: ‘For his mercy is for ever’ [Psalm CXXXVII].

“From these statements it is certainly clear that as each person departs from here, so he is presented at the Judgment. Yet it must be believed that, before the Judgment, there is a purgatorial fire for certain light sins, because Truth says: [Col. 0999D] ‘If anyone speaks blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, it shall be forgiven him neither in this age nor in the age to come’ [Matthew XII]. This saying implies that certain sins can be forgiven in this age and certain others in the age to come. For when this is denied of one kind, the consequent sense is clearly that it is granted concerning some kinds.

“Yet, as I have said, this must be believed possible only concerning small and very slight sins, such as habitual idle speech, immoderate laughter, the sin involved in managing household affairs—which can scarcely be conducted without fault even by persons who know how sins ought to be avoided—or an error of ignorance in matters not grave. All these burden a person even after death if they have not been forgiven while he is still in this life.

“For Paul says that Christ is the foundation [1 Corinthians III], and adds: ‘If anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble, the fire will test what sort each person’s work is. If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire’ [ibid.]. Although this may be understood of the fire of tribulation applied to us in this life, nevertheless, if someone takes it to refer to the fire of future purification, he must consider carefully that Paul said that one may be saved through fire—not one who builds upon this foundation iron, bronze, or lead, that is, greater sins and therefore harder sins, already then incapable of being forgiven, but wood, hay, and stubble, that is, the smallest and lightest sins, which fire easily consumes. [Col. 1000A] Yet this must be understood: there no one will obtain even purification from the smallest sins unless, while still in this life, he has deserved by good deeds to obtain it there.” [Col. 1000B]

## CHAPTER 80.—That there is one fire of hell, but it does not torment all in one manner. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (Book IV, chapter 43).

PETER: “I ask you: should it be believed that there is one fire of hell, or that, as great as the diversity of sins is, so many fires also must be thought prepared?”

GREGORY: “There is indeed one fire of hell, but it does not torment all sinners in one manner. For each person will feel there as much punishment as his fault requires. Just as in this world many stand beneath one sun, yet do not all feel the heat of that same sun equally, because one is scorched more and another less, so there in one fire there is not one degree of burning. For what diversity of bodies accomplishes here, diversity of sins accomplishes there: they have a fire not unlike one another, and yet it burns each one differently.” [Col. 1000C]

## CHAPTER 81.—How many kinds of offering ought to be made for the dead. From Augustine’s sayings (*Enchiridion*, chapter 110).

There are four kinds of offering. For the very good, they are thanksgivings—that is, people give thanks to God because they lived well. For those not very good, they are made that full remission may occur. For those not very evil, they are propitiations, that condemnation may be more tolerable. For the very evil, even though they are no help to the dead, they are whatever consolations may be available to the living.

## CHAPTER 82.—Why the souls of the saints do not pray for sinners when they see them burning in eternal fire. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (Book IV, chapter 44).

[Col. 1000D]

PETER: “And where is their holiness, if they do not pray for their enemies whom they will then see burning? For surely they were told: ‘Pray for your enemies’ [Matthew V].”

GREGORY: “They pray for their enemies at the time when they can turn their hearts to fruitful repentance and save them in that conversion. For what else ought one pray for enemies except what the Apostle says: that God may give them repentance for the acknowledgment of truth, and that they may recover themselves from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive according to his will? [1 Timothy II].”

PETER: “And how then will they pray for persons who can by no means any longer be changed from wickedness to works of righteousness?”

GREGORY: [Col. 1001A] “The reason why no prayer is then made for persons condemned to eternal fire is the same reason why even now holy people do not pray for deceased unbelieving and impious persons: they shrink from having the merit of their prayer rendered vain before the presence of the just Judge for those whom they already know to be assigned to eternal punishment. If even now just people living do not pity dead and condemned unjust persons, when they themselves still know that they are liable to suffer something subject to judgment in their flesh, how much more strictly will they then behold the torments of the wicked, when, stripped of every corruption of life, they themselves will cling more closely and more firmly to justice. For their minds are so absorbed by the force of strictness through their adherence to the most just Judge that they are entirely unable [variant: “unwilling”] to approve anything that departs from the exactness of that eternal rule.” [Col. 1001B]

## CHAPTER 83.—That life is spoken of in two ways, and death likewise understood in two ways. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (Book IV, chapter 45).

PETER: “There is now nothing to be answered against the plain argument, but this question moves my mind: how is the soul called immortal, when it is clear that it dies in perpetual fire?”

GREGORY: “Because life is spoken of in two ways, death too must be understood in two ways. It is one thing to live in the Lord, and another to live in that by which we are made or created; that is, it is one thing to live blessedly and another to live essentially. Therefore the soul is understood to be both mortal and immortal. It is mortal because it loses blessed life. It is immortal because it never ceases to live essentially and cannot lose the life of its nature, even when it has been condemned to perpetual death. Placed there, it will lose blessedness but will not lose existence. Thus it is always compelled [variant: “it always comes about”] to suffer death without death, failure without failure, and an end without end.” [Col. 1001C]

## CHAPTER 84.—That both elect and reprobate are led to common places in their torments. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (Book IV, chapter 35).

That both elect and reprobate whose cause has been shared in conduct are also led to common places would be adequately established for us by the words of Truth even if examples were lacking. For Truth itself says in the Gospel concerning the elect: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” [John XIV]. For if there were not a differing recompense in that eternal blessedness [Col. 1001D], there would be one dwelling-place rather than many. Therefore there are many dwelling-places, in which distinct ranks of the good rejoice together because of their fellowship in merits; and yet all labourers receive one denarius [Matthew XX]. They are distinguished by many dwelling-places because both the blessedness which they receive there is one and the quality of recompense which they attain through diverse works is different.

The same Truth, announcing the day of judgment, says: “Then I shall say to the reapers: Gather the tares and bind them into bundles for burning” [Matthew XIII]. The reapers, namely the angels, bind the tares into bundles for burning when they join like persons to like persons in similar torments: [Col. 1002A] so that the proud burn with the proud, the lustful with the lustful, the greedy with the greedy, the deceitful with the deceitful, the envious with the envious, and the unbelieving with the unbelieving. Therefore, when those alike in guilt are brought to like torments, because the angels assign them to places of punishment, they bind, as it were, bundles of tares for burning.

## CHAPTER 85.—That there are many dwelling-places in the house of God. Gregory, *Moralia* (Book IV, chapter 42).

Truth says in the Gospel: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” [John XIV]. Yet in these many dwelling-places the diversity of rewards will in some manner itself be harmonious, because such is the force of love joining us in that peace that whatever a person has not received in himself, he rejoices to have received in another. Hence those who do not labour equally in the vineyard nevertheless all receive the denarius equally [Matthew XX]. Thus there are many dwelling-places with the Father, yet unequal labourers receive the same denarius, because one blessed happiness of joy will belong to all, even though the loftiness of life will not be one and the same for everyone. [Col. 1002B]

## CHAPTER 86.—That mercy does not subsequently restore to pardon the person whom sin has once dragged to punishment. Gregory, *Moralia* (Book VIII, chapter 14).

“As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so he who descends to hell shall not ascend” [Job VII]. A cloud is suspended in the heights, but when thickened it is driven by the wind to move; then it is dispersed by the sun’s heat, so that it vanishes. Such, indeed, are human hearts, which rise to high things through the capacity of reason bestowed upon them; but, driven by the blast of the evil spirit, they are pulled now here, now there by the perverse motions of their desires. Yet by the strict [variant: “strictly fixed”] gaze of the heavenly Judge they melt as by the sun’s heat, and once delivered over to places of punishment they do not return further to the exercise of action.

Therefore the holy man, expressing the course of human pride and its ruin, says: “As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so he who descends to hell shall not ascend.” As though he spoke plainly, saying: “He fails in his ascent who, through pride, tends toward destruction; and if sin has once dragged him to punishment, mercy does not thereafter restore him to pardon.” [Col. 1002C]

## CHAPTER 87.—That God is called jealous, angry, repentant, merciful, and foreknowing. Gregory, *Moralia* (Book XX, chapter 24).

How, then, is God jealous, when he is touched by no anguish of mind in guarding our chastity [Col. 1002D]? How does he become angry, when he is moved by no disturbance of soul in punishing our vices? How is he repentant, when he does not grieve that he has done what he once did? How does he have mercy, when he never has a sorrowful heart? How is he foreknowing, when only things that are future are foreknown?

And we know that nothing is future to God: before whose eyes things past are not absent, things present do not pass away, and things future do not arrive. For everything which has been or will be for us lies before his sight, and everything that is present is something he can know rather than foreknow. Yet he is called jealous, angry, repentant, merciful, and foreknowing: he is called jealous in a human manner because he guards the chastity of each soul, although he is not touched by anguish of mind; because he strikes sins, he is said to be angry, although he is moved by no disturbance of soul; because he himself, immutable, changes what he wills, he is said to repent, although he changes the matter but not his counsel; and when he aids our misery, he is called merciful. [Col. 1003A]

## CHAPTER 88.—Why God permits his elect to die in such a way that he does not show during their life how holy they are. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (Book IV, chapter 24).

PETER: “What is this, I ask you: almighty God permits certain persons to die in such a way, yet after death does not allow it to remain hidden what holiness they possessed?”

GREGORY: “Since it is written, ‘Whatever death overtakes the just man, his justice shall not be taken from him,’ what harm is it to the elect, who without doubt are tending to perpetual life [Col. 1003B], if for a brief time they die harshly? Perhaps there is sometimes even a fault in them, though a very small one, which ought to be cut away by that very death. Hence the reprobate receive power against the living; but when the latter die, this is punished more severely in the reprobate: that they exercised the power of their cruelty against the good. Thus that same executioner who was permitted to strike the venerable deacon while he lived was not permitted to rejoice over him when dead.

“Sacred Scripture likewise bears witness to this. A man of God was sent against Samaria, and because he ate on the journey in disobedience, a lion killed him upon that same journey [3 Kings XIII]. But immediately it is written there: ‘The lion stood beside the donkey and did not eat the corpse’ [ibid.]. This shows that the sin of disobedience was forgiven in death itself, because the same lion which had presumed to kill the man living did not presume to touch him slain. The lion that had dared to kill did not receive permission to eat the slain man’s corpse, because the man who had been guilty in life was already just through death, his disobedience having been punished. Therefore the lion which had first killed the sinner’s life afterwards guarded the corpse of the just man.” [Col. 1003C]

## CHAPTER 89.—That death without death comes upon the wretched. Gregory, *Moralia* (Book IX, chapter 48).

Thus death without death, an end without cessation, comes upon the wretched, because death lives, the end always begins, and failure does not know how to fail. Therefore, because death kills and does not extinguish; pain tortures but in no way removes fear; flame burns but does not at all dispel darkness: so far as can be inferred from the experience of the present life, these punishments have no consistent order, since they do not in every respect retain their own character. [Col. 1003D]

## CHAPTER 90.—That in hell the fire does not give light to sinners for consolation, but rather in order to torment them more. Gregory, *Moralia* (ibid., chapter 49).

Although the fire there does not shine for consolation, it nevertheless shines in some respect in order to torment more severely. By the illumination of the flame, the reprobate will see with themselves in torment all their followers, for love of whom they sinned, so that those who loved their carnal life contrary to the Creator’s commandments may be afflicted, to the increase of their own condemnation, also by the destruction of those persons. [Col. 1004A]

## CHAPTER 91.—On the same matter. In the *Moralia* (same chapter).

[Col. 1004A]

Just as fire knows how to burn for the consolation of the elect, yet does not know how to burn for their punishment, so, conversely, the flame of Gehenna neither shines for the reprobate with the grace of consolation, yet does shine for punishment: so that the punishment may both gleam before the eyes of the damned with no clarifying brightness and, for the increase of their pain, show them how they are being tortured. What is remarkable here, if we believe that the fire of Gehenna contains at once the punishment of darkness and of light, when experience teaches us that even the flame of torches gives a dim light? Then the consuming flame burns those whom fleshly pleasure now defiles. Then the abyss of hell, opening without limit, devours those whom empty pride now exalts; and those who here fulfilled the will of the crafty persuader through whatever vice will then, as reprobates with their leader, reach torments [Col. 1004B] (ibid., ch. 50). And although the natures of angels and human beings are far different, one punishment entangles those whom one guilt binds in sin.

### CHAPTER 92.—That the human soul can be immortal in such a way as to be able to die, and mortal in such a way as to be unable to die. Gregory, *Morals* (book IV, ch. 7).

Since, therefore, the present time of our mortality perishes not in such a manner that it is ill, but in such a manner that it is not, we must ask what it is that is desired to perish not in such a manner that it is not, but in such a manner that it is ill. For the human soul, or angelic spirit, is immortal in such a way that it can die, and mortal in such a way that it cannot die. For it loses blessed life, whether through vice or through punishment; but it does not lose essential life, either through vice or through punishment [Col. 1004C]. It fails in the quality of its living, but, even in dying, it does not experience a total destruction of its subsistence. Thus, to put it briefly, it is both immortally mortal and mortally immortal.

### CHAPTER 93.—That the fire of Gehenna is corporeal and requires no material other than the torment of the reprobate. Gregory, *Morals* (book XV, ch. 14).

In a wonderfully forceful way, the fire of Gehenna is described in a few words. For corporeal fire, in order to be fire, needs corporeal fuel. When it must be preserved, it is undoubtedly nourished by piled-up wood; it cannot exist unless kindled, nor endure unless fed. But the fire of Gehenna, although corporeal and physically burns the reprobate cast into it, is neither kindled by human effort nor fed with wood [Col. 1004D]. Rather, having been created once for all, it endures unquenchably; it needs no kindling and lacks no heat. Thus it is rightly said of this wicked man: “A fire not kindled shall devour him” (Job 20). For the justice of the Almighty, foreknowing things to come, created from the very beginning of the world the fire of Gehenna, which would one day begin to exist as punishment for the reprobate, but would never end its burning even without wood. It must further be known that all the reprobate, because they sinned together in soul and body, are there tormented alike in soul and body.

### CHAPTER 94.—Why a soul remaining in the body, and departing from it, cannot be seen. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (book IV, ch. 5).

**GREGORY.**—What wonder is it, Peter, if you did not see the soul departing, when you do not see it even while it remains in the body [Col. 1005A]? When you are speaking with me now, because you cannot see my soul within me, do you therefore suppose that I am without life? The nature of the soul is invisible, and it departs invisibly from the body just as it remains invisibly within the body.

**PETER.**—But from the actual movements of the body I can judge the life of the soul remaining in it, since, if the soul were not present in the body, the limbs of that body could not move. Tell me by what movements or acts I may perceive the soul’s life after the flesh, so that from things seen I may infer the existence of what I cannot see.

### CHAPTER 95.—That no one ought to doubt the existence of invisible things which minister to the invisible God. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (ibid., ch. 6).

**GREGORY.**—As the power of the soul gives life to and moves the body, so the divine power fills all things that it has created: it gives life to some by inspiring them, grants others the capacity to live, and bestows on others only the fact that they exist. Since you do not doubt the existence of God—the Creator and Governor, filling and encompassing, transcending and subsisting, uncircumscribed and invisible—so you ought not to doubt that he has invisible servants. For those things which minister to him ought to tend toward the likeness of him to whom they minister, so that things which serve the invisible are not to be doubted to be invisible [Col. 1005B]. And what are these things whose existence we believe, if not the holy angels and the spirits of the righteous? Therefore, just as, by observing the body’s movement, you mentally discern the life of the soul which remains in the body, so you ought to discern from the Most High the life of the soul departing from the body: for it can live invisibly, since it must remain in the service of the invisible Creator.

**PETER.**—Everything is rightly said, but the mind recoils from believing what it cannot see with bodily eyes.

### CHAPTER 96.—That no visible things can be seen or known except through invisible things. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (ibid.).

**GREGORY.**—Since Paul says, “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Hebrews 11), that is properly said to be believed which cannot be seen. For what can be seen can no longer be believed. Yet, to bring you briefly back to yourself: no visible things are seen except through invisible things. Behold, the eye of your body looks upon all bodily things; yet the bodily eye itself would see nothing bodily unless an incorporeal thing sharpened it for seeing [Col. 1005D]. Take away the mind, which is not seen, and the eye that had seen lies open in vain. Remove the soul from the body: undoubtedly the eyes remain open in the body. If, then, they saw by themselves, why do they see nothing when the soul has departed? Understand from this, therefore, that even visible things themselves are seen only through invisible things.

Let us also set before the eyes of the mind a house being built: huge masses are raised; great columns hang suspended in machines. Who, I ask you, performs this work? Is it the visible body, which draws those masses with its hands, or the invisible soul which gives life to the body? Take away, indeed, that which is not seen in the body, and immediately all those things remain motionless which appeared to be visible bodies of metal moving. In this matter we must consider [Col. 1006A] that even in this visible world nothing can be ordered except through an invisible creature. For just as almighty God, by breathing upon or filling rational beings, gives life to and moves invisible things, so these invisible things themselves, by filling them, move and give sensation to the fleshly bodies which are seen [“gradually give life,” *sensim vivificant*].

**PETER.**—I confess that I am willingly overcome by these arguments; I am now almost compelled to suppose that these visible things scarcely exist at all, whereas before I took upon myself the role of those weak in faith and doubted invisible things. Everything you say, then, pleases me; but just as I recognize the life of the soul remaining in the body from the body’s movement, so I desire to recognize the soul’s life after the body through certain manifest attesting facts.

### CHAPTER 97.—That an incorporeal spirit is afflicted in hell by corporeal fire. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (book IV, ch. 29).

[Col. 1006B]

**GREGORY.**—If the incorporeal spirit of a living human being is held in a body, why should it not, after death, though it is an incorporeal spirit, also be held by corporeal fire?

**PETER.**—In every living person an incorporeal spirit is held in the body because it gives life to the body.

### CHAPTER 98.—That an incorporeal spirit can give life and be held where it is tormented by corporeal fire. From Gregory’s *Dialogues* (immediately following).

**GREGORY.**—If an incorporeal spirit, Peter, can be held in that which it gives life to, why should it not also be held, by way of punishment, where it is put to death? We say that a human spirit is held by fire in the sense that it is in the torment of fire, living and feeling [Col. 1006C]. For it suffers the fire precisely in that it sees it; and because it sees itself being burned, it burns. Thus a corporeal thing burns an incorporeal thing, while from visible fire invisible heat and pain are drawn, so that through corporeal fire the mind is tormented, though incorporeal, by an incorporeal flame.

Nevertheless, from Gospel sayings we can infer that the soul suffers the fire not only by seeing it but also by experiencing it. For by the voice of Truth the rich man is said to have been buried in hell after his death (Luke 16). That his soul is held in fire is indicated by the rich man’s voice, as he entreats Abraham: “Send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame” (ibid.). Therefore, since Truth declares the condemned sinful rich man to be in flames [Col. 1006D], who that is wise can now deny that the souls of the reprobate are held in fires?

**PETER.**—See: my mind is bent toward acceptance by reason and testimony, but, released again, returns to its resistance. For I do not understand how an incorporeal thing can be held and afflicted by a corporeal thing.

### CHAPTER 99.—On apostate spirits: that they must be believed incorporeal. In the same place.

**GREGORY.**—Tell me, I ask you: do you suppose the apostate spirits cast down from heavenly glory to be corporeal or incorporeal?

**PETER.**—What person of sound mind would say that spirits are corporeal?

### CHAPTER 100.—That the fire of Gehenna must be believed corporeal. In the same place.

**GREGORY.**—Do you acknowledge the fire of Gehenna to be corporeal [Col. 1007A], or incorporeal?

**PETER.**—I do not doubt that the fire of Gehenna is corporeal, in which bodies are certainly tormented.

### CHAPTER 101.—On the text, “No one has ever seen God,” and how it is to be understood. Gregory, *Morals* (book XVIII, ch. 5).

John says, “No one has ever seen God” (1 John 4). Yet, when I look again at the fathers of the Old Testament, I learn from the testimony of sacred history itself that many of them saw God. Jacob indeed saw the Lord and said: “I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved” (Genesis 32). Moses saw the Lord, of whom it is written: “The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak to his friend” (Exodus 33). Job saw the Lord, saying: “By the hearing of the ear I heard you, but now my eye sees you” (Job 42). Isaiah saw the Lord, saying: “In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne” (Isaiah 6). Micaiah saw the Lord, saying: “I saw the Lord sitting upon his throne, and all the host of heaven standing beside him on his right and on his left” (3 Kings 22).

What, then, does it mean that so many fathers of the Old Testament testified that they had seen God, while it is nevertheless said of this Wisdom which is God: “It is hidden from the eyes of all living beings” (Job 28), and John says: “No one has ever seen God” (1 John 4)? Is it not plainly to be understood that, so long as one lives here in mortality, God may be seen through certain images, but cannot be seen through the very form of his nature: so that the soul, inspired by the grace of the Spirit, sees God through certain figures, yet does not attain to the very power of his essence [Col. 1007C]?

Hence Jacob, who testifies that he saw God, saw him only in an angel (Genesis 32). Hence Moses, who spoke with God face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak to his friend (Exodus 33), says amid the very words of his conversation: “If I have found grace in your sight, show me yourself plainly, that I may see you” (ibid.). Certainly, if the one with whom he spoke were not God, he would have said, “Show me God,” not “Show me yourself.” But if the one with whom he spoke face to face was God, why did he ask to see the one he saw? From this request, however, it is gathered that he thirsted to behold through the uncircumscribed brightness of God’s nature the one whom he had already begun to see through certain images; so that the heavenly essence itself might be present to the eyes of his mind, and no created temporal image might stand before him for the vision of eternity [Col. 1007D].

Thus the fathers of the Old Testament saw the Lord, and yet, according to John’s declaration, “No one has ever seen God” (1 John 4); and according to blessed Job’s statement, “Wisdom, which is God, is hidden from the eyes of all living beings” (Job 28). For those who remain in this mortal flesh could both see him through certain circumscribed images and could not see him through the uncircumscribed light of eternity (Job 38). But if, for some who still remain in mortal flesh yet grow by an inestimable power, the eternal brightness of God can be seen by a certain keenness of contemplation, etc. [Col. 1008A].

### CHAPTER 102.—On the twofold punishment of the damned. From Isidore (book I, *On the Highest Good*, ch. 28).

The punishment of the damned in Gehenna is twofold: sorrow burns their mind and flame their body, in just reciprocity, so that those who devised in mind what they would accomplish in body may be punished together in soul and body. The fire of Gehenna has light in one respect and lacks it in another: it has light for damnation, so that the ungodly may see what causes them grief; and it lacks light for consolation, lest they see what would cause them joy. A fitting comparison is made from the furnace of the three youths as an example of the fire of Gehenna. For just as that fire [Col. 1008B] did not burn for the punishment of the three youths, but did burn to consume the cords of their bonds (Daniel 3), so the fire of Gehenna will shine for the wretched to increase their punishments, so that they may see what causes them grief, and will not shine for consolation, lest they see what would cause them joy. There is much difference between the misery of this life and that of the life to come. There, there is misery because of the torture of pains, and darkness because of the deprivation of light. Of these, one—that is, misery—exists in this life; the other does not. But in hell both exist.

### CHAPTER 103.—On the punishments of the ungodly. From the same author (ibid., ch. 29).

Just as bundles of wood are gathered together with like material for burning, so on the Day of Judgment those guilty of like sins will be joined to their like, so that punishment may bind together as though into a bundle those whom like conduct made alike in evil. Just as every saint will be glorified in the future judgment according to the measure of his virtues, so every ungodly person will be condemned according to the measure of his crimes. Nor will order be lacking in the future punishment of damnation; rather, there will be a distinction of punishments according to the kinds of crimes, as the prophet affirms.

Punishment is also added to the dead through the sufferings of those dear to them, as the Gospel account declares concerning the rich man in hell (Luke 16); and, for the increase of Judas’s punishment, the psalm likewise says: “Let his children be driven about in distress and beg” (Psalm 108). The ungodly are to be punished more severely in judgment by mental anguish because they will see the righteous to have attained the blessedness of glory [Col. 1008D]. The devil is to be cast down in the sight of all, when, before the gaze of all good angels and human beings, he is to be thrown with those who belong to his party into eternal fire.

When the devil is lifted up in order to be condemned, many of the elect who are to be found in the body when the Lord comes for judgment will be shaken with fear as they see the ungodly one punished by such a sentence. They are to be purified by that terror; for if any sin from the body still remains in them, they will be purified by the very fear with which they behold the devil condemned. Hence Job says: “When he is lifted up, the angels will fear, and, terrified, they will be purified” (Job 41). That many may perish on the Day of Judgment who now appear elect and holy is stated by the Prophet: “The Lord will call judgment by fire, and it will devour the great deep and consume part of the house” (Amos 7). For part of the house will be devoured, because hell will swallow up even those who now boast that they are in the heavenly commandments [Col. 1009A]. Of these the Lord also says: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons in your name, and perform many mighty works?’ Then I will confess to them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity; I do not know who you are’” (Matthew 7).

### CHAPTER 104.—On Antichrist. From the same author (ibid., ch. 25).

Everyone who either does not live according to the rule of Christian profession or teaches otherwise is an Antichrist. Yet many will not live to see the times of Antichrist, and nevertheless will be found among the members of Antichrist. Before Antichrist comes, many of his members have gone before him and, by the merit of their evil conduct, have anticipated their own head, according to the Apostle’s statement that the mystery of iniquity is already at work even before he is revealed (2 Thessalonians 2).

The greatness of the signs under Antichrist will cause even the elect, if possible, to be led into error (Matthew 24). But if they are elect, how are they to be led into error? They will therefore lapse briefly into wavering error because of the multitude of miracles; nevertheless, they are not to be cast down from their steadfastness by the impulse of terrors and signs. Thus the phrase “if possible” is added because the elect cannot perish; rather, quickly returning to their senses, they will restrain the error of their hearts by faith, knowing that the Lord foretold this so that, when adversaries do these things, the saints may not be disturbed [Col. 1009C].

When Antichrist comes, he will perform miracles and signs so astonishing that even in the elect a certain scruple of heart will arise; yet reason will quickly overcome it in them, through which they will know that the same signs are performed for the deception of the reprobate and the testing of the elect. At that time the saints will be glorious through patience, not through miracles, as the earlier holy martyrs were. For they will endure persecutors who also perform miracles. Accordingly, they will sustain a harsher war, since they must fight not only against persecutors but also against those resplendent with miracles.

In Antichrist’s time the Synagogue will rage against the Church more grievously than it persecuted Christians at the coming of the Savior himself [Col. 1009D]. Although the devil, even while bound, has already exercised great cruelty against the martyrs (Revelation 20), he will nevertheless be more cruel in Antichrist’s time, when he will also be loosed (ibid.). For if he could do such great things while bound, how great will be his deeds when released? The nearer the devil sees the end of the world, the more cruelly he carries out persecutions, so that, seeing himself about to be condemned at once, he may multiply companions with whom he will be consigned to the fires of Gehenna. The shorter the time the devil sees remaining before his condemnation (Revelation 12), the more he is stirred to the great fury of persecution, by divine justice permitting it: so that the righteous may be glorified, the wicked made more defiled, and the devil’s sentence of condemnation become harsher.

### CHAPTER 105.—That even the elect will be endangered at the coming of Antichrist before the Day of Judgment. Gregory, *Morals* (book XIV, ch. 12).

[Col. 1010A]

“In his days the last shall be astonished, and horror shall seize the first” (Job 18). For he will then be unleashed with such unrestrained wickedness against the righteous that even the hearts of the elect will be struck by no slight fear. Hence it is written: “So that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error” (Matthew 24). This is said not because the elect will fall, but because they will tremble amid great terrors.

Both the last elect and the first are said to engage in the contest of righteousness against him, because those who are found elect at the end of the world are to be struck down in bodily death; and those who came forth from the earliest ages of the world—namely Enoch and Elijah—will be called back into the midst and will endure the violence of his cruelty in their still mortal flesh [Col. 1010B] (Malachi 4; Matthew 11 and 17; Mark 9). The last are astounded and the first afraid at his powers unleashed in such might, because, though they despise all his temporal power insofar as he is lifted up by the spirit of pride, nevertheless, insofar as they themselves are still in mortal flesh, in which they can be temporally tortured, they dread the very sufferings which they courageously endure. Thus at one and the same time there is in them steadfastness from virtue and fear from the flesh: although they are elect, so that they cannot be conquered by torments, yet, because they are human, they fear the very torments which they overcome.

### CHAPTER 106.—Again, on Antichrist. Gregory, *Morals* (book XV, ch. 28).

[Col. 1010C]

For he saw that at the end of the world Satan, entering a human being whom Holy Scripture calls Antichrist, is exalted with such pride, rules with such power, and is elevated through such signs and wonders in an appearance of holiness that his deeds cannot be rebuked by a human being, because to the power of terror he also adds signs of displayed holiness. And he says: “Who will rebuke his way before him?” (Job 21). That is, who among human beings will dare to rebuke the one whose very sight he fears to endure? Yet not only Elijah and Enoch, who are brought forth to rebuke him, but all the elect also rebuke his way when they despise him and resist his malice through strength of mind.
