### CHAPTER 107.—Again, on Antichrist. Gregory, *Morals* (book XV, ch. 30).

[Col. 1010D]

In this passage “man” means human wisdom; but since all are more than innumerable, we must ask why he is said to draw innumerable persons before him and all persons after him (Job 21), unless it is because the ancient enemy, entering the reprobate man at that time, seizes under the yoke of his dominion all whom he finds carnal. Even now, before he appears, he draws innumerable, though not all, carnal persons, because every day many are recalled from fleshly conduct to life, and some return to the state of righteousness through brief repentance, others through long repentance. Now he seizes innumerable persons while he does not display to human beings the astonishing signs of his falsehood; but when he has performed for the eyes of carnal persons wonders that they find marvellous, then he draws after him not innumerable persons, but all [Col. 1011A], because those who delight in present goods submit themselves to his power without reserve.

But, as we have said, since it is greater to draw every person than innumerable persons, why is it first said that he draws every person, and then, by way of increase, innumerable persons are added? Reason requires that what is less be stated first, and what is greater afterward as an increase. Yet it must be known that in this passage it was more to say “innumerable” than “all.” For he draws every person after him because, in three and a half years, he binds beneath the yoke of his domination [variant: “damnation”] all whom he finds pursuing a fleshly way of life. But he drew innumerable persons before him because, through the course of five thousand years and more, although he could by no means draw all carnal persons, nevertheless those whom he seizes before him as innumerable are far more numerous over so long a period than all whom he will find to seize over so brief a time [Col. 1011B]. It is therefore well said: “He draws every person after him, and innumerable persons before him,” because even then he takes fewer when he has taken all, and now he plunders more when he invades the hearts of all.

### CHAPTER 108.—That in the last times all Israelites ought to be converted through Elijah’s preaching. Gregory, *Morals* (book XXXV, ch. 15).

But at the end all Israelites will flock to the faith when they have recognized Elijah’s preaching; they will return to the protection of him from whom they fled, and then that outstanding feast will be celebrated through the manifold gathering of peoples.

### CHAPTER 109.—Why it is more often ill with the good in this life. Gregory, *Morals* (book V, ch. 1).

[Col. 1011C]

Since divine judgments are very hidden, why it is sometimes ill with the good in this life and well with the wicked is more obscure still when the good fare well here and the wicked fare ill. For when the good fare ill and the wicked well, perhaps this is understood: that the good, if they have committed any sins, receive their recompense here, so that they may be more fully freed from eternal condemnation; while the wicked receive here the good things they do for this life, so that afterward they may be drawn away to torments alone. Thus the rich man burning in hell is told: “Remember, son, that you received your good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things” (Luke 16).

But when the good fare well here and the wicked fare ill, it becomes very uncertain whether the good receive good things in order that, stirred by them, they may grow toward something better, or whether, by a just and hidden judgment, they receive here the reward for their works and so are emptied of the rewards of the life to come [Col. 1011D]; and whether adversities strike the wicked in order that, through correction, they may be defended from eternal punishments, or whether their punishment begins here in order to bring them at last, when it is completed, to the final torments of Gehenna.

### CHAPTER 110.—That all the faithless also rise for torments, not for judgment. Gregory, *Morals* (book XXVI, ch. 24).

All unbelievers also rise, but for torments, not for judgment. For their case is not then examined, since they approach the presence of the strict Judge already bearing the condemnation of their unbelief. Those who retain the profession of faith but lack works corresponding to that profession are reproved in order that they may perish [Col. 1012A]. But those who did not retain even the sacraments of faith do not hear the Judge’s rebuke in the final examination, because, having already been judged by the darkness of their unbelief, they do not deserve to be reproved by the accusation of him whom they despised. The former at least hear the Judge’s words because they at least retained the words of his faith; the latter do not receive even the eternal Judge’s words in their condemnation because they were unwilling to preserve reverence for him even in words. The former perish according to the law because, being under the law, they sinned; to the latter nothing is said of the law in their perdition because they made no effort to possess any law.

### CHAPTER 111.—That all human beings ought to rise again. Augustine (*On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, ch. 7).

There will be a resurrection of all human beings. If it will be of all, then all die, so that death, given in Adam [variant: “derived from Adam”], may rule over all his children; and that privilege may remain with the Lord which is said of him alone: “You will not give your Holy One to see corruption” (Psalm 15; Acts 2). We have received this reasoning on the authority of a great multitude of the Fathers. Yet since there are other equally Catholic and learned men who believe that those found alive at the Lord’s coming will be changed to incorruption and immortality while the soul remains in the body, and that their laying aside mortality through transformation rather than death is reckoned to them as resurrection from the dead, whichever view anyone accepts, he is not a heretic unless he becomes one through contentiousness. For it is sufficient under the rule of the Church to believe that there will be a resurrection of the flesh from death.

### CHAPTER 112.—How the statement that the living and the dead are to be judged is to be understood. The same Augustine (ibid., ch. 8).

[Col. 1012C]

When we say in the Creed that, at the Lord’s coming, the living and the dead will be judged, we believe that it signifies not only the righteous and sinners, as Diodorus thinks, but also those who will be found alive in the flesh. For this reason they are held to be destined to die—or to be transformed, as others wish—so that, raised or immediately refashioned from the dead, they may be judged [variant in the modern Augustine text: “so that they may be judged before the dead”].

### CHAPTER 113.—That apostate angels and ungodly people, after torments, as though purged by punishments, are not granted fellowship with the righteous. Again, Augustine (ibid., ch. 9).

After the resurrection and judgment, let us not believe in the restoration which Origen deliriously proposes: namely, that demons or ungodly people, after torments, as though purified by punishments, may either—the former—return to the angelic dignity in which they were created, or—the latter—be granted the fellowship of the righteous, because this supposedly accords with divine mercy, lest anything among rational creatures perish, but everything be saved in whatever way. Rather, let us believe the Judge and just Rewarder of all, who said: “The ungodly will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25), so that they may receive the fruit of their deeds. And again: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid.) [Col. 1012D].

### CHAPTER 114.—That the resurrection will take place at the age of perfect youth, which needs no further development. From Isidore (book I, *On the Highest Good*, ch. 26).

The beginning of the saints’ peace is in this life, not its perfection. But then peace will be complete, when, with the infirmity of the flesh absorbed, they have become strong for the contemplation of God [Col. 1013A]. The resurrection of the dead, as the Apostle says, will be “unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4): namely, at an age of youth which needs no development and which, without declining toward defect, is from either aspect both full and strong in perfection.

Although faithful people are now called sons of God, nevertheless, because they still endure this bondage of corruption, they remain subject to the yoke of servitude. They will receive the full freedom of the children of God when “this corruptible shall put on incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15). God is now known through a mirror (1 Corinthians 11); but in the future every elect person will be presented face to face (ibid.), so as to contemplate the very form which he now strives to see through a mirror [Col. 1013B]. In this life the Church of God is said to be completed by the number of the elect who belong to the right hand and of the reprobate who will go to the left; but at the end of the age the tares will be separated from the wheat (Matthew 13).

### CHAPTER 115.—That the strict Judge, coming for judgment, sees the sinner in order to strike, not to save. Gregory, *Morals* (book VIII, ch. 13).

The strict Judge, coming for judgment, both does not see in order to save and sees in order to strike; for the one whom, in the present life, he does not regard with the mercy of his dispensation because he wishes to correct him by waiting, he afterward destroys by regarding him in justice. For now every sinner does not fear God and yet lives; he blasphemes and yet prospers, because the merciful Creator, whom he wishes to correct by waiting, does not wish to punish by looking upon him, as it is written: “Overlooking human sins for the sake of repentance” (Wisdom 11) [Col. 1013C].

But when the sinner is regarded, he cannot stand; for when the strict Judge investigates merits minutely, the guilty person cannot withstand the torments. This also accords with the language of the righteous, whose mind is always attentive in anxiety to the coming examination. For they fear all that they do, carefully considering before what great Judge they will stand. They contemplate the power of his greatness and weigh how tightly bound they are by the guilt of their own weakness. They count their evil deeds and set against them the good gifts of the Creator’s grace. They consider how strictly he judges evil deeds and how minutely he weighs good works, and they know without doubt that they would perish if judged with mercy set aside [Col. 1013D]. For even this very thing—that we seem to live rightly—is guilt, if, when he judges our life, divine mercy does not excuse it in itself.

### CHAPTER 116.—That on the Day of Judgment two orders will be divided into four. From Isidore (*On the Highest Good*, book I, ch. 27).

There are two classes or orders of human beings in judgment: the elect and the reprobate. Yet they are divided into four. There is one order of the perfect, who judge with God, and another which is judged. Yet both will reign with Christ. Likewise, the order of the reprobate is divided into two: those who are evil within the Church will be judged and condemned, while those found outside the Church will not be judged [Col. 1014A], but only condemned.

Thus the first order of those who are judged and perish is opposed to that order of the good which consists of those who are judged and reign. The second order of those who are not judged and perish is opposed to the order of the perfect, in which are those who are not judged and reign. The third order, of those who are judged and reign, is contrary to the order consisting of those who are judged and perish. The fourth order, of those who are not judged and reign, is opposed to the contrary order in which are those who are not judged and perish. The ungodly person is punished by a twofold sentence: either he is struck here with blindness because of his merits, so that he does not see the truth; or he will be condemned at the end in order to pay the punishments due.

### CHAPTER 117.—That the book of life is the very sight of the coming Judge, because, on seeing him, each person will immediately understand whatever he has done. Gregory, *Morals*, book XXIV, ch. 9 (Augustine, *City of God*, book XX, ch. 14).

[Col. 1014B]

“Books were opened, and another book was opened, which is that of life; and the dead were judged from the things written in the books” (Revelation 20). For the book of life is the very sight of the coming Judge, in which every commandment is, as it were, written; because whoever sees him immediately understands, with conscience bearing witness, whatever he has not done. The books are said to be opened because the lives of the righteous are then seen, in whom heavenly commands are discerned as impressed by deeds. “And the dead were judged from the things written in the books,” because, in the displayed life of the righteous, as though in the opening out of books, they read the good which they themselves refused to do, and are condemned by comparison with those who did it [Col. 1014C]. Therefore, lest each person then weep upon seeing in them what he did not do, let him now attend to what he should imitate in them; and the elect do not cease to do this.

### CHAPTER 118.—On the glory of the saints after death. From Isidore (book I, *On the Highest Good*, ch. 33).

In the future the hearts of the righteous will not be made sorrowful by a compassionate feeling of grief for the damned, where the saints’ joy in contemplating God will be so great that it will give no entrance to sorrow. As white appears more beautiful when compared with black, so the rest of the saints, compared with the condemnation of the wicked, will be more glorious; so too justice compared with injustice, and virtue with vice. Therefore the glory of the saints increases while the ungodly are condemned to their deserved punishment. After the resurrection, an ascent to heaven in the flesh is promised to the saints, Christ saying to the Father: “I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17) [Col. 1014D]. For if we are members of the Head, and Christ is one both in himself and in us, then certainly where he ascended, we too shall ascend.

### CHAPTER 119.—That after judgment has ended, a new heaven and a new earth will begin to exist. From the same author (Augustine, *City of God*, book XX, ch. 14).

As blessed Augustine says, once the judgment has been accomplished and completed, this heaven and this earth will then cease to exist, when a new heaven and a new earth begin to exist (Rev. 21). For this world will pass away by a transformation of things, not by utter destruction. Hence the Apostle also says: “For the form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. 7); therefore the form passes away, not the nature.

### CHAPTER 120.—Against those who say: if, after judgment has been rendered, there will be a conflagration of the world, where then can the saints be, so that they are not touched by the flame of the fire? From the sayings of the same author (Augustine, *City of God*, book XX, ch. 18).

[Col. 1015A]

Blessed Augustine resolves this question. “Perhaps someone,” he says, “may ask: if this world is to burn after the judgment has been rendered, before a new heaven and a new earth are put in its place (Rev. 21), where will the saints be during the very time of this conflagration, since, having bodies, they must necessarily be in some bodily place? We may reply that they will be in the higher regions, to which the flame of that fire will not rise, just as the flood-water did not rise there. For their bodies will be such that they will be where they wish to be; and, having become immortal and incorruptible, they will not fear the fire of that conflagration, [Col. 1015B] just as the corruptible and mortal bodies of the three men were able to remain alive and unharmed in the burning furnace” (Dan. 3).

### CHAPTER 121.—That no one should suppose that he can redeem his sins by alms unless he strives to amend his life. Augustine (*Enchiridion*, ch. 70).

Certainly one must beware lest anyone suppose that those unspeakable crimes, committed by persons who will not possess the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 6), may be perpetrated daily and redeemed daily by almsgiving. For one’s life must be changed for the better, and God must be propitiated through alms for past sins—not, as it were, bought so that one may always be permitted to commit them with impunity. For He has given no one license to sin (Ecclus. 15), although in His mercy He blots out sins already [Col. 1015C] committed, provided that fitting satisfaction is not neglected.

### CHAPTER 122.—That light sins are forgiven us by the Lord’s Prayer, provided that we forgive our debtors as we wish to be forgiven. Augustine (ibid., ch. 71).

For daily, brief, and slight sins, without which this life cannot be lived, the daily prayer of the faithful makes satisfaction. It belongs to those who say, “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. 6), who have already been reborn to such a Father by water and the Holy Spirit (John 3). This prayer wholly removes these smallest and daily sins. It also removes those from which even a life of the faithful, though wickedly lived, departs after being changed for the better through repentance—provided that, just as it is truly said, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6), since [Col. 1015D] there are not lacking debts to be forgiven, so it is truly said, “As we forgive our debtors” (ibid.); that is, what is said must be done. For forgiving a person who seeks pardon is itself an act of almsgiving.

### CHAPTER 123.—That almsgiving is given not only when some comfort is given to a needy person, but also when pardon is granted to a sinner or correction to one in error. Augustine (ibid., ch. 72).

Accordingly, for everything done through beneficial mercy, the Lord’s saying applies: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11). Not only does one give alms who gives food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, lodging to the stranger, hiding-place to the fugitive, visitation to the sick or imprisoned, redemption to the captive, support to the weak, guidance to the blind, consolation to the sorrowful, [Col. 1016A] healing to the unhealthy, a way to the wanderer, counsel to the deliberating [or: distraught; Latin reads *deliberanti [deliranti]*], and whatever is necessary to anyone in need; but one also gives alms who grants forgiveness to a sinner. And a person who corrects with a blow one over whom authority is given him, or restrains him with some discipline, yet forgives from his heart the sin by which he was injured or offended, or prays that it may be forgiven him—not only in forgiving and praying, but also in rebuking and inflicting some corrective punishment—gives alms, because he bestows mercy.

For many benefits are conferred upon unwilling persons when regard is had for their advantage rather than their wish, since they are found to be enemies to themselves, while their true friends are rather those whom they think enemies. They repay good with evil through their error, whereas a Christian ought not [Col. 1016B] to repay evil, even for evils (Rom. 12; 1 Thess. 5; 1 Pet. 3). Thus there are many kinds of almsgiving; by performing them we are helped so that our debts may be forgiven us (Matt. 6).

### CHAPTER 124.—It belongs to the perfect children of God to repay good for evil. Augustine (ibid., ch. 73).

But among these there is nothing greater than forgiving from the heart what someone has sinned against us. It is a lesser thing to be well disposed toward, or even to confer a benefit upon, one who has done you no harm. But it is far greater, and the act of most magnificent goodness, that you should also love your enemy, and always wish good—and do it when you can—to one who wishes you evil and, if able, does it; hearing Jesus say: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you; and pray for [Col. 1016C] those who persecute you” (Matt. 5). But these are gifts of the perfect children of God [the text of Augustine reads: “but since these are gifts of the perfect…”], toward which every believer ought indeed to strive, bringing the human mind to this disposition by praying to God and by striving and wrestling with himself.

### CHAPTER 125.—How the words of the Lord’s Prayer, “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive,” etc., are fulfilled by the imperfect. Augustine (immediately following).

Nevertheless, because so great a good is not possessed by so large a multitude as we believe is heard when the Lord’s Prayer says, “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6), the words of this promise are undoubtedly fulfilled if a person who has not yet advanced so far as to love his enemy nevertheless, when asked by the person who sinned against him [Col. 1016D] to forgive him, forgives him from the heart. For when he prays and says, “As we forgive our debtors” (ibid.), he surely wishes that he himself, when asking, may be forgiven; that is: forgive our debts when we ask you, as we forgive our debtors when they ask us.

### CHAPTER 126.—That almsgiving avails nothing when life is not amended. Augustine (ibid., ch. 75).

Certainly those who live most wickedly, take no care to correct such a life and conduct, and do not cease amid their very crimes and disgraceful deeds to give alms frequently, flatter themselves in vain on the ground that the Lord says: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11). They do not understand how extensive the force of this saying is; [Col. 1017A] but, in order to understand, let them attend to whom He said it. For the Gospel is written thus:

“While He was speaking, a Pharisee invited Him to dine at his house; and He entered and reclined at table. But the Pharisee began to say within himself, wondering why He had not washed before the meal. And the Lord said to him: ‘Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and dish, but what is within you is full of robbery and iniquity. Fools! Did not He who made what is outside make also what is inside? Nevertheless, give alms from what remains, and behold, all things are clean for you’” (ibid.).

Are we then to understand this as meaning that all things are clean for Pharisees who do not possess faith in Christ, even if they have not believed in Him or been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit (John 3), merely if [Col. 1017B] they have given alms—as these persons suppose alms must be given? Yet all whom the faith of Christ does not cleanse are unclean, concerning which it is written: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15). And the Apostle says: “To the unclean and unbelieving nothing is clean, but their mind and conscience are defiled” (Titus 1). How then could all things be clean for Pharisees if they gave alms but were not believers? Or how could they be believers [variant: *infideles*, “unbelievers”] if they had not wished [variant: *voluissent*, “had wished”] to believe in Christ and be reborn in His grace? And yet what they heard is true: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11).

### CHAPTER 127.—That one who intends to ask forgiveness should not be called an enemy. Augustine (ibid., ch. 74).

[Col. 1017C]

Now, a person who asks the one against whom he has sinned, if he is moved by his sin to make the request, is not yet to be reckoned an enemy, so that loving him should be difficult, as it was difficult when he was practicing hostilities.

### CHAPTER 128.—Sins are not forgiven unless one forgives from the heart a person who sins against oneself. Augustine (immediately following).

Whoever does not forgive from the heart a person asking and repenting of his sin must by no means suppose that his own sins are forgiven by the Lord, because Truth cannot lie. What hearer—or reader—of the Gospel can fail to know who said, “I am the truth” (John 14)? When He had taught the prayer, He strongly commended this statement placed within it, saying: “For if you forgive people [Col. 1017D] their sins, your heavenly Father will forgive you your offenses. But if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6). Whoever does not awaken at so great a thunderclap is not asleep, but dead. Yet He is powerful even to raise the dead.

### CHAPTER 129.—Again, how almsgiving ought to be bestowed. Augustine (ibid., ch. 76).

But the person who wishes to give alms in an orderly manner ought to begin with himself and first give them to himself. For almsgiving is a work of mercy, and it has been said most truly: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30). For this reason we are reborn: that we may please God, to whom that which we contracted by being born rightly displeases. This is the first alms which we have given ourselves, [Col. 1018A] because, miserable as we were, we sought ourselves through the mercy of the merciful God, confessing His just judgment by which we were made miserable, of which the Apostle says: “Judgment indeed came from one unto condemnation” (Rom. 5). And, giving thanks for His great love—of which the same preacher of grace says, “But God commends His love toward us, in that while we were still sinners Christ died for us” (ibid.)—we may both judge truthfully concerning our own misery and love God’s love which He Himself bestowed, and may live devoutly and rightly.

When the Pharisees passed over this judgment and love of God (Luke 11), they nevertheless tithed, in addition to [the text prints *praeter*, apparently for *propter*, “in addition to”] the alms which they gave, even the smallest produce of their fruits (Matt. 23). Therefore [Col. 1018B] they did not give alms beginning with themselves and first exercising mercy upon themselves, as these persons suppose alms must be given. Because of this order of love it was said: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22). Therefore, after He had reproved them because they washed themselves outwardly but were inwardly full of robbery and iniquity, warning them of a certain almsgiving which a person ought first to give himself, and to cleanse the inward parts, He said: “Nevertheless, give alms from what remains, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11).

Then, to show what He had urged and what they had neglected to do—lest they should think that He was ignorant of their alms—He said: “But woe to you, Pharisees”; as though saying, “I indeed admonished [Col. 1018C] you to give alms through which all things might be clean for you; but woe to you who tithe mint and rue and every herb” (ibid.). “For I know these alms of yours; do not suppose that I have now admonished you concerning them, while you have passed over judgment and the love of God.” By this almsgiving you could be cleansed of every inward defilement, so that the bodies which you wash might also be clean for you. This is what “all things” means: both inward and outward things. As elsewhere we read: “Cleanse what is within, and what is without will be clean” (Matt. 23). But lest He should seem to reject those alms which are made from the fruits of the earth, He said: “These things you ought to have done”—that is, judgment and the love of God—“and not to have passed over those things” (Luke 11), that is, alms from earthly fruits.

### CHAPTER 130.—Lest anyone suppose that, by giving alms, impunity for sin is granted him. Augustine (ibid., ch. [not specified]).

[Col. 1018D]

Therefore let not those deceive themselves who suppose that, by the most lavish alms from their produce or from money of any kind, they can buy impunity while continuing in the enormity of their crimes and the wickedness of their disgraceful deeds. For they not only do these things, but love them so that, if only they can, they desire always to remain in them with impunity. But “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10); and one who hates his soul is not merciful but cruel. For by loving it according to the world, he hates it according to God. Therefore, if he wished to give it alms, through which all things would be clean for it, he would hate it according to the world and love it according to God. But no one [Col. 1019A] gives any alms unless he receives from Him who has no need that from which to give. Therefore it is said: “His mercy will go before me” (Ps. 58).

### CHAPTER 131.—One should pray for enemies just as for the gravest sins. Augustine (ibid., ch. 78).

Which sins are light and which grave must be weighed not by human but by divine judgment. For we see that some things were conceded in forgiveness even by the Apostles themselves. Such is what the venerable Paul says to married persons: “Do not deprive one another, except by agreement for a time, that you may be free for prayer; and return again to the same, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control” (1 Cor. 7). It might be thought not to be a sin, namely, to have intercourse with one’s spouse [Col. 1019B] not for the purpose of begetting children—which is a good of marriage—but also for carnal pleasure, so that the weakness of those lacking self-control may avoid the deadly evil of fornication, adultery, or any other impurity, shameful even to mention, into which lust can draw them under Satan’s temptation. Thus, as I said, this might be thought not to be a sin, unless he had added: “But I say this by way of concession, not of command” (ibid.). But who can now deny it to be a sin, when apostolic authority acknowledges that pardon is granted to those who do it?

There is something similar where he says: “Does any one of you, having a dispute against another, dare to be judged before the unrighteous and not before the saints?” (1 Cor. 6). And a little later: “Therefore, if you have secular lawsuits,” he says, [Col. 1019C] “appoint as judges those who are held in contempt in the Church. I say this to your shame: is there really not among you one wise person who can judge between brother and brother [the text earlier reads: ‘judge his brother’]? But brother contends at law with brother, and this before unbelievers” (ibid.). For here too it might be thought not to be a sin to have a lawsuit against another, but only to wish it judged outside the Church, unless he had immediately added: “Indeed, it is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another” (ibid.). And lest someone should excuse himself in this way, saying that he has a just claim but suffers wrong, which he wishes a judge’s decision to remove from him, he immediately meets such thoughts or excuses and says: “Why do you not rather [Col. 1019D] suffer wrong? Why do you not rather allow yourselves to be defrauded?” (ibid.).

Thus we return to what the Lord says: “If anyone wishes to take your tunic and contend with you in court, let him have your cloak also” (Matt. 5). And elsewhere He says: “From him who has taken what is yours, do not demand it back” (Luke 6). He therefore forbade His own to have lawsuits with others concerning secular matters; from this teaching the Apostle says that it is a fault (1 Cor. 6). Nevertheless, when he permits such lawsuits to be settled in the Church between brothers, with brothers judging, but severely forbids them outside the Church, it is evident here too what is granted by way of pardon to the weak.

Because of these and similar sins, and others, though less serious, which arise from offenses of words and thoughts—as the Apostle James acknowledges and says, “For we all offend in many ways” [Col. 1020A] (James 3)—we must pray to God daily and frequently, saying, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6), and not lie in what follows: “As we forgive our debtors” (ibid.).

### CHAPTER 132.—That some sins are grave which people consider light. Augustine (ibid., ch. 79).

There are certain sins which would be thought very slight unless Scripture showed them to be more serious than people suppose. For who would think a person saying to his brother, “Fool,” liable to Gehenna, unless Truth said so? (Matt. 5). Yet He immediately applied a remedy to this wound, adding the command of fraternal reconciliation. For He immediately says: “Therefore, if you offer your gift at the altar, and [Col. 1020B] there remember that your brother has something against you” (ibid.), etc.

Or who would judge it so great a sin to observe days, months, years, and seasons (Gal. 4), as those do who, on particular days, years, or months, are willing or unwilling to begin something because, according to vain human teachings, they deem the times favorable or unfavorable, unless we measured the magnitude of this evil by the Apostle’s fear? To such persons he says: “I fear for you, lest perhaps I have labored among you in vain” (ibid.).

### CHAPTER 133.—What kind of sin is called an “outcry” in Holy Scripture. Augustine (ibid., ch. 50).

To this is added the fact that sins, however great and horrible, when they become customary, are believed to be either small [Col. 1020C] or no sins at all—to such an extent that they seem not only not to be concealed, but even now to be proclaimed and publicized. Thus, as it is written: “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and he who commits iniquity is blessed” (Ps. 9). Such iniquity is called an “outcry” in the divine books. Thus you have in the prophet Isaiah concerning the evil vineyard: “I expected it to produce judgment, but it produced iniquity; and not righteousness, but an outcry” (Isa. 5). Hence also that passage in Genesis: “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied” (Gen. 18). For those shameful deeds were not only no longer punished among them, but were even openly practiced as though by law.

So in our times many evils, although not such as these, have already come into open custom, so that because of them we dare not merely [Col. 1020D] excommunicate a layman, but not even depose a cleric. Therefore, when some years ago I was expounding the Epistle to the Galatians, at the very place where the Apostle says, “I fear for you, lest perhaps I have labored among you in vain” (Gal. 4), I was compelled to cry out:

> “Woe to the sins of humankind! We shudder only at those which are unusual; but sins now customary—for the cleansing of which the blood of the Son of God was shed—although they are so great as wholly to shut the kingdom of God against themselves, by living with them often we are compelled to tolerate them all, and by tolerating them often even to commit some of them. And would that, O Lord, we may not commit all that we have been unable to forbid. But see [variant: *videro*, ‘I shall see’] whether excessive grief has incautiously compelled me to say something.”

### CHAPTER 134.—That we sin for two reasons. Augustine (ibid., ch. 82).

[Col. 1021A]

I shall now say what I have indeed already often said in other places in my little works. We sin for two reasons: either because we do not yet see what we ought to do, or because we do not do what we already see ought to be done. Of these two, the former is the evil of ignorance; the latter, of weakness. We ought indeed to fight against both; but we are certainly overcome unless we are helped by God, so that we may not only see what must be done, but also, as health comes, the delight of righteousness may overcome within us the delights of those things through desiring to possess which or fearing to lose which we sin knowingly and with full sight. Then we are not only sinners—as we were even when we sinned through ignorance—[Col. 1021B] but also transgressors of the law, when we do not do what we already know ought to be done, or do what we already know ought not to be done.

Therefore we ask not only that He forgive us if we have sinned, for which we say, “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6), but also that He grant [the text has *concedat*, with variant *ut regat*, “that He govern us”] that we may not sin, for which we say, “Do not lead us into temptation” (ibid.). We must pray to Him of whom it is said in the psalm: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation” (Ps. 26): that illumination may remove ignorance, and salvation weakness.

### CHAPTER 135.—Without God’s mercy, a person performs fruitless repentance. Augustine (ibid., ch. 82).

[Col. 1021C]

For even repentance itself, when there is proper reason for it to be undertaken according to the custom of the Church, is often not undertaken because of weakness. For shame is fear of displeasing others, when human esteem gives greater pleasure than the righteousness by which a person humbles himself in repentance. Therefore God’s mercy is necessary not only when repentance is performed, but also in order that it may be performed. Otherwise the Apostle would not say concerning some: “Lest perhaps God grant them repentance” (2 Tim. 2). And that Peter might weep bitterly, the Evangelist first said: “The Lord looked upon him” (Luke 22).

### CHAPTER 136.—The sin of one who does not believe that all sins can be forgiven in the holy Church will be unforgivable. Augustine (ibid., ch. 83).

[Col. 1021D] But one who, not believing that sins are forgiven in the Church, [Col. 1022A] despises so great a liberality of the divine gift and closes his final day in this obstinacy of mind, is guilty of that unforgivable sin against the Holy Spirit, in whom Christ forgives sins. On this difficult question I have argued as fully as I could in a little book written for this purpose alone.

### CHAPTER 137.—Concerning things belonging to a venerable institution: they are not to be alienated (*Novels* of Constantine, 7, § “But if,” and following).

Let absolutely all priests refrain from alienating ecclesiastical property, fearing the penalties threatened by the Leonine constitution: namely, that one who has acquired property belonging to a venerable institution must restore it to the person to whom it previously belonged, together with its fruits and other profits [Col. 1022B] accruing in the meantime. But the steward of a church who is found to have derived any profit from such a prohibited alienation, or to have caused loss to the church, shall be removed from office, so that he may not thereafter be a steward. Not only he, but also his successors shall be bound by this law—whether the chief steward alienated the property, or whether, seeing the bishop alienate it, he did not prevent him, and much more if he consented.

The notary who drew up an instrument for such prohibited transactions must be consigned to perpetual exile. Magistrates who admitted the same instruments, and officials who assisted in them, shall be notified by public record; and donations, or at least alienations, effected through official acts shall be invalidated. Not only magistrates but other persons of rank also shall forfeit their property. The constitution, however, remits matters done in the past. It excepts certain contracts, explained in the following chapters, through which immovable property of churches may be alienated.

A *xenodochium* is a venerable institution in which strangers are received; a *ptochotrophium*, a venerable institution in which poor and infirm persons are fed; a *nosocomium*, a venerable institution in which sick persons are treated; an *orphanotrophium*, a venerable institution in which children bereft of parents are fed; a *gerontocomium*, a venerable institution in which poor persons infirm solely through old age are cared for; a *brephothrophium*, a venerable institution in which infants [Col. 1022D] are nourished.

[Col. 1021]

## NOTES ON IVO’S *DECRETUM*

### PREFACE TO THE READER

[Col. 1021]

[Col. 1021] Ivo’s *Decretum*, which had long lain hidden and, unknown to all theologians and jurists, was so greatly desired, was first arranged to be printed in the preceding century by the most distinguished man Jean Du Moulin, for the highest good of the whole Church, as he himself explained in his preface. But since he had only a single manuscript copy available to him, and not enough leisure to compare the original texts of councils and Fathers with it, he could not produce an edition that was altogether accurate or complete.

This was the desire of all learned people, who regretted that so great a work swarmed with so many errors. Yet no one thought of investigating or restoring it: some were occupied with other works; others—of whom there are the greatest number in this century—devoted themselves wholly to new authors and works, entirely neglecting the ancient ones, which is greatly to be lamented. Since we had heard that the work was about to be submitted to the press, we set our hand to the undertaking, though abruptly, lest it be printed again [Col. 1023] with its errors and so great an injury be done to our Ivo—or rather, to the Church.

Yet, having undertaken the work while the printers were hastening and the press was already running, we could not accomplish everything necessary to complete so great a task and satisfy our own wishes. But, reader, receive briefly what has been accomplished in this labor, so far as the constraints of time allowed.

First, having obtained a very ancient manuscript of Ivo’s *Decretum* from the distinguished library of Saint-Victor at Paris, we compared the printed edition with it, and from it made many annotations and corrections. Next, since modern editions of councils and Fathers differ in some matters from the ancient ones, we endeavored to compare almost every chapter of the *Decretum* with several manuscripts and printed copies, both ancient and modern. We have recorded this divergence in these notes: where slight, within brackets; where greater, more fully.

The origin of so many blemishes is easy to conjecture. Ivo was not the first compiler of canonical collections. Thus, having borrowed the greater part of his *Decretum* from earlier collectors of canons, he ought not to have altered their very words, since they were accepted by all. It is also credible that copies of that age conformed to Ivo’s *Decretum*; or, if some differed from it, this occurred through the fault of scribes, who often—as happens among most modern printers—because they had not learned letters, were unable to write correctly. Therefore Ivo used the copies that came to hand, when compelled to do so because he could not obtain better corrected ones. Yet it is also evident in many places that he used fuller manuscripts and manuscripts different from ours.

As for the diversity of citations, this too was characteristic of the copies of that age, in which even Gratian himself, later than our Ivo, was mistaken. Our later centuries have corrected this to some extent, though not without great labor. Nor should anyone be surprised that he cited many testimonies from councils and Fathers which no longer exist today, since many things have now disappeared that were available in those times, as many other things have perished through the injury of time, to the great loss of the Church. Many also still lie hidden, which, like very many already in our age, will someday be drawn out of darkness through the efforts of scholars.

Moreover, many citations which had been added only generally have been restored to their proper places. We have nevertheless put them within brackets, lest alteration be made in the printed copy, and indeed in the manuscripts. Many citations also, both from Holy Scripture and from the holy Fathers, have been added. We were greatly assisted in this work both by that remarkable manuscript of Saint-Victor at Paris and by numerous manuscript and printed volumes, of new and ancient editions, of councils and Fathers from the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés at Paris. Without them this work could scarcely have been corrected.

Furthermore, we have deliberately omitted here certain notes found in Gratian: first, because this has already been notably done by the Roman correctors and we did not wish to do what had already been done, although those notes properly belong in this place and concern Ivo before Gratian; and secondly, because time was not available, since we began the undertaking late and when the press was already hurrying. These notes, whatever their quality, will therefore suffice for the present, until fuller and more polished ones are prepared by learned persons—which we earnestly desire.

## NOTES ON THE PROLOGUE

[Col. 1023A]

**Excerptiones.** In the preceding edition and in the manuscript of Saint-Victor at Paris, as also in all manuscript and printed copies of Ivo’s *Panormia* and letters, the reading is *Exceptiones* (“Exceptions”). But because more recent writers, when citing it, such as Antonio Agustín and others, used *Excerptiones* (“Extracts”), it has here been printed on the judgment of certain persons.

Moreover, printers had appended this preface—which truly belongs here, as is clear to everyone—to the end of the earlier editions of Ivo’s letters, and not without reason, since it is also found among the manuscripts. Yet because it is not a letter, nor is it found addressed to anyone, but occurs at the beginning of Ivo’s *Decretum*, indeed also of the *Panormia*, in all manuscript and printed copies, we have removed it from the letters. Juretus also correctly observed this. Among his notes on Ivo’s letters he mentions this preface, which had been published among the letters as no. 288, and elucidates it with a note which, because it is noteworthy, [Col. 1023B] we have inserted here. Thus he says:

> **Exceptions of ecclesiastical rules.** In the preceding edition the printer appended this treatise to the end of these letters; many old manuscripts do not contain it. In certain others it is found interwoven into the middle portion of the book. In truth, it is not properly a letter, but a prologue which Ivo once prefixed to his *Decretum*; for he testifies that he collected ecclesiastical canons in Letter 262 to Pontius.
>
> There are two different volumes bearing Ivo’s name and having the same preface. One, called the *Panormia*, is an epitome, as it were, of the other, larger work, which is entitled simply the *Decretum*. Vincent of Beauvais mentions it in the *Speculum*, book XXVI, ch. 84, where he says that Hugh of Châlons composed from the same abbreviated volume of decrees a portable little book called the *Summa decretorum of Ivo*.
>
> In an old copy belonging to Servin, however, the following title is prefixed to this treatise: “Preface to the Canons of Lord Ivo, bishop of Chartres, containing a remarkable [Col. 1024A] introduction to the discerning understanding and reception of the holy judgments and dispensations of the canons. Its principal and chief purpose seems to be that any ecclesiastical teacher who interprets and moderates sacred rules in such a way as to refer everything that he teaches or expounds to the realm of charity neither sins nor errs, since, in providing for the salvation of his neighbors, he intends to reach the end due to sacred institutions.”
>
> In certain other copies the following title is attached in a more compact verbal form: “On the understanding and dispensation of ecclesiastical discipline.” Since this prologue was appended to the first edition, I willingly allow it to be added here, lest the reader lack anything; for it is indeed most worthy of reading.
>
> Incidentally, I should note that in earlier years this same preface, although greatly abridged, was attributed to Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, and appended to his letters in the appendix to the *Library of the Holy Fathers*, first published at Paris in 1579. This misled subsequent editors, as may be supposed, because they found that fragment inserted in an ancient manuscript of Hildebert.
>
> Add that Hildebert testifies in one of his letters that he had planned to collect and arrange extracts of decrees in one volume, but that the work had not yet been brought to completion. Such a work, he says, requires a mind free from cares, and the episcopate had deprived him of that freedom. He had nevertheless completed a good part of it and would lay aside his episcopal office in order to finish what remained. But this preface has more of the flavor of Ivo’s style than Hildebert’s. Moreover, no antiquarian, so far as I know, has recorded that canonical collections by Hildebert were ever published.

**“They strive to increase salvation.”** Thus from an old copy.

**“But to dispense the remedy of health to all according to its proper moderation.”** These words have been added from ancient copies.

**“Or is overcome by apparitors. Spiritual.”** Corrected [Col. 1025A] on the authority of old manuscripts. The previous printing incorrectly had: “or is overcome by parents. Spiritual.”

**“They escape unharmed.”** Thus, better, from an old copy, rather than the earlier corrupt reading, *illi eu*.

**“And become proud.”** This is more correct from the manuscript than the previous “and are proud.”

**“When there is power over wicked peoples.”** Other books, with the order of words disturbed, read: “when there is power of wicked peoples.”

**“Or hold the same opinion as Nestorius,” etc.** This entire period was expanded and restored with the aid and authority of Servin’s ancient copy; for in the others it is corrupt. It is also frequently defective in Gratian, canon 14, cause 1, question 7, owing to the fault of the ancient translator of St Cyril.

**“To depart a little from what is due.”** These words too were rendered not quite suitably through the fault of the same translator; nevertheless, the sense is easily grasped.

**“From the synod attended by King Charles.”** Other books read: “which Charles attended, king.” There are several similar passages in Ivo’s *Decretum*, from which it is clear that kings in that age attended the celebration of synods. For in Part Three, ch. 227, one reads: “From the Council of Beauvais, in the presence of Louis.” In Part Fourteen, ch. 117: “From the council at Altheim, which King Conrad attended.” And ch. 121: “From the Council of Tribur, which King Arnulf attended.” Likewise ch. 125: “From the council at Erfurt, which King Henry attended.” And in the final chapter: “From the council at Altheim, which King Conrad attended.” Evidently bishops made use of the prince’s counsel. For a canon of the said council at Erfurt says: “The holy synod decreed with the counsel of the most serene prince.” Kings and priests, moreover, ought to meet together for the sake of peace and public welfare.

**“And Pope Gelasius says.”** Thus in an old copy. The earlier reading, “and the gloss of the popes says,” was inept, evidently arising from an erroneous interpretation of abbreviated writing found in certain parchments: *Et pap. Gl. dicit.*

## TO PART I

[Col. 1025C]

CAP. 1. In the manuscript codex of Saint-Victor, the general heading of this first part appears only before the third chapter, which begins “We believe,” etc., as also in the *Panormia*, in which, however, the first part begins directly with this chapter, “We believe,” the two preceding chapters having been omitted.

CAP. 150. That passage is not by Gregory, but by Pope Zachary, Epistle 9, before the middle, where he says: “For likewise concerning that false bishop of whom you said that he was the son of an adulterous cleric and a murderer, etc., [he is not to] handle [the sacred things]; nor is a penitent, or such a person as the sacred canons forbid to be a priest.” Concerning baptism, etc.

CAP. 180. “Of souls.” In the original there is added: “which we desire to rescue.”

CAP. 246. “Is born with the flesh.” This passage seems to require restoration from Saint Gregory as follows: “If he is not born with the flesh, why is he held bound by sins in that flesh which has been derived from Adam?”

CAP. 290. “That the bishop,” etc. It seems it should be read: “That where there is a bishop and a community,” etc.

CAP. 293. “But children to whom,” etc. This reading varies in the original volumes of the councils. In the Paris and Cologne editions it stands thus: “But children, to whom the term [for] puberty belongs because they are still under age,” etc.

“That this should not be sufficient to them.” In the Paris and Cologne editions the particle “not” is lacking.

“Whoever shall violate these [ordinances] of the bishops.” In the Paris and Cologne editions: “Whoever shall violate this ordinance.”

CAP. 295. This chapter does not appear to belong to that Council of Tribur whose canons survive. For chapter 22 of the Council of Tribur concerns the careful inquiry to be made when some free faithful person is accused of an infamous crime. In chapter 16 it is forbidden that anyone sell burial for the dying. Concerning chrism, however, and the other matters contained in this chapter, there is nothing.

CAP. 297. This letter, like many other letters of the supreme pontiffs, is not divided into chapters.

“By authority.” In the original councils it reads “by veneration.”

CAP. 305. “Investigate the sayings of the earlier [fathers].” In the Cologne and Paris councils it reads: “Investigate the sayings of our earlier Fathers.”

“In the Church of Isauria.” In the royal Paris editions it reads: “In the Churches of Isauria.” In the Cologne edition: “the Churches of Isauria, Ephesus, [those] of Symeon, Jerusalem, and also of other cities; likewise the bishops of those cities.”

“That they should by no means admit themselves to marriage.” In the original it stands thus: “That women or men who, for any reason, have received their own children should by no means thereafter enter into marriage.”

“Throughout the world.” In the councils there is added: “And the error of all may increase.”

[Col. 1026B] “From the first, therefore,” etc. It reads thus: “From the first nourishment of consecrated salt, and entrance into the holy Church, up to the confirmation of the Holy Spirit through chrism. From this first gift of the Holy Spirit up to the seventh.”

AD PART II.

CAP. 25. “If nevertheless,” etc. In Augustine it reads thus: “If, nevertheless, the mind is without an inclination to sin; for one who still retains the will to sin is made more heavily burdened,” etc.

“Of the Lord’s mer…” Read thus: “Let him approach the mercy of the Lord, who is accustomed to pardon sins upon devout confession.” Moreover, Algerus and Gratian also cite this passage as Saint Augustine’s, although some doubt whether it is by Saint Augustine. But Saint Augustine has an entire chapter on this subject, namely Book I, chapter 3, of the *Questions of Januarius*.

CAP. 63. “Leaven.” After this word the Saint-Victor manuscript has the following: “Here he found Manichaeans in the city, whom he also carried away into exile.”

CAP. 67. [Col. 1026C] This is the second chapter of the first decretal epistle of Pope Anacletus, at its beginning, and it reads thus: “But when they offer sacrifice to the Lord,” etc.

“From the forehead.” In the original: “on the forehead.”

CAP. 68. “Water [and] salt,” etc. Before these words, the Saint-Victor manuscript has this heading: “On the consecration of salt and water.”

CAP. 70. This is Epistle 2 of Pope Sixtus I, chapter 1. At the end the following seem to be added from the original: “And those also who have not sinned may suffer evil things or perish, because the just man very often perishes for the impious.”

CAP. 74. “Is ministered.” The original adds: “and divine worship is celebrated with every honor and propriety by priests and the remaining ministers of the Church.”

CAP. 75. “Granted.” After that final word the Saint-Victor manuscript, as also Gratian, has: “Therefore, dearest brother, we have taken care to answer, as far as we were able, all these matters which your charity wished to have explained by us.”

CAP. 123. “Which belongs to the bishop.” These words are not found in Clement’s epistle.

“Whoever obeys him.” The original reads thus: “For whoever obeys his bishops appears indeed to confer some grace upon God; but whoever does not obey them, undoubtedly,” etc.

CAP. 131. “And likewise vom…” In the original it reads: “gives birth, which vom…,” etc., as also in Gratian.

AD PART III.

CAP. 6. In the original this chapter varies slightly at the end.

CAP. 45. “Concerning churches,” etc. What was absent from the earlier edition has been supplied from the manuscript codex of Saint-Victor.

CAP. 58. “Or by some such [sin],” etc. In the Saint-Victor manuscript it reads only: “or separated by such a sin.”

CAP. 59. “Have been burned.” This chapter, which is chapter 9 of the Council of Mainz under Stephen V and King Arnulf in the Paris councils, reads thus: “If they have been burned, it is meanwhile permissible to celebrate Masses in chapels until they themselves,” etc.

“Otherwise we strictly forbid.” These words are not found in the aforesaid chapter 9.

CAP. 60. “It is read in the Book of Kings.” We have added this from the original and Gratian, although it is not so necessary.

CAP. 61. “They were holding divine [services].” In the council: “they were consecrating [them] with divine supplications.”

“It is read thus,” etc. This passage is corrupt and should be restored as follows: “But if, as is read in the Council of Laodicea, chapter 26, that those who,” etc.

CAP. 68. In the council this chapter reads thus: “That the ordering of Masses, as it is performed in the metropolitan church, should likewise, in God’s name, be observed throughout the whole province of Tarragona, both in the order of the Mass itself and in chanting or ministering,” etc. But in the Paris edition it reads: “Concerning the ordering of Masses: that as it shall be in the metropolitan Church, so throughout all,” etc., as above.

CAP. 72. [Col. 1027B] This chapter is not found in Saint Augustine, but is taken from the Rule of Tarnat, chapter 15, §4, as the Reverend Father Hugo Maynardus of the Order of Saint Benedict, well known for his *Concordia regularum*, most learnedly observed at chapter 39. As for what that Rule of Tarnat is, one should consult Maynard himself in the preliminaries to this *Concordia*, where he treats clearly of the various rules and their authors.

CAP. 79. “Reborn.” In the original: “Arenata” [“sanded”].

CAP. 92. “Their masters.” These two words are not in the Saint-Victor manuscript.

CAP. 99. “It must be investigated.” In the Saint-Victor manuscript this is a distinct chapter bearing the heading: “Concerning priests who have acquired property for themselves from the revenues of the Church, built structures there, and placed women there,” from the Council of Reims, chapter 10.

CAP. 104. “Concerning the boundaries of cemeteries.” In all manuscripts, both of the councils and of Gratian and the *Panormia*, this chapter begins with: “As of old,” etc. In the *Panormia* it is cited from the Council of Antioch, chapter 5; in Gratian its heading is: “Let him be excommunicated who attempts to violate the boundaries of a church.”

CAP. 105. Nearly the same is found in the Council of Agde, chapter 66, but it has *diaconicon* instead of *diaconion*.

CAP. 149. The same is found in the middle of the sixth Roman synod under Pope Symmachus.

AD PART IV.

CAP. 16. This chapter occurs somewhat differently in the councils. Thus Mainz reads: “We have decreed that all Sundays be observed with every reverence, that people abstain from servile work, and that there be no market on them, nor any judicial hearing at which someone may be judged to death or punishment.” But in the Council of Frankfurt, chapter 21, it reads: “That Sunday be observed from evening until evening.”

CAP. 18. This chapter is from the second version of this council, derived from Isidore Mercator; in the earlier version it stood thus: “Since there are some who bend the knee in prayer on the Lord’s Day and on the days of Pentecost, in order that all things may be observed uniformly in every place, it has pleased the holy council that vows be rendered to the Lord standing.” In the margin beside the word “council,” with an asterisk, stands: “From Easter until the octave of Pentecost, standing,” etc. The manuscript codex of Saint-Victor followed this version; but the original reads thus:

“Since there are some who bend the knee on the Lord’s Day and on the days of Pentecost, in order that all things may be observed in every parish, the holy synod has decreed that prayers be offered to God standing.”

CAPS. 20, 21, 22. These are not found in this council, but in chapter 81 of Charlemagne’s Aachen capitulary and in Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 81, although somewhat differently.

CAP. 31. “Fasts.” In the royal Paris councils it reads: “The additions to fasts, through,” etc.

CAP. 32. This is found in Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 52, in the Life of Abbot Apollinis, not Apollonius. It reads thus: “But it is not permitted to break the catholic and general fasts without grave necessity. For on Wednesday the Savior is betrayed, and on Good Friday he is crucified. Therefore, whoever breaks them at once betrays and crucifies the Savior.”

CAP. 65. “Also acts under the name of Peter the Apostle, apocryphal.” These words are not read in the original.

“Gospel under the name of Barnabas.” Before this, the original has: “An apocryphal Gospel under the name of Matthias. An apocryphal Gospel under the name of Peter the Apostle.” And in the margin stands: “It is remarkable that no mention is made here either of the Gospel of Nicodemus.”

CAP. 84. At the end of this chapter the Saint-Victor manuscript adds, I do not know why: “Likewise: Theft is said not to be a grave fault, not by its own valuation, but in comparison with the greater sin, namely adultery.” These words neither belong to this passage nor are found in Bede.

CAP. 88. This chapter is taken from chapter 1 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, according to Maynard, whose notable annotation on that chapter may be seen at the beginning of the *Concordia regularum*, §1; we refer the reader to it, since we are not publishing commentaries here.

“Instruments of virtues.” The common reading, from Smaragdus and Saint Dunstan, is: “Examples and instruments of virtues.”

CAP. 109. “Concerning the chapters.” The original reads: “Concerning the authenticity and number of the chapters of the Council of Nicaea, which,” etc.

CAP. 152. At the end of this chapter the Saint-Victor manuscript also has: “Likewise, the celebration of a single day is rightly observed only with lamps lit inside and outside.”

CAP. 171. At the end of this chapter the Saint-Victor manuscript also adds: “Likewise: Then at Constantinople Priscian of Caesarea investigated profoundly the art of grammar.”

CAP. 225. These responses are from Adrian’s Epistle 14; see Binius’s note there. Moreover, in Saint Ambrose, *On Tobit*, Book I, chapter 20, it reads: “But concerning bodily pledges, Saint Ezra also taught us,” etc.; and in the margin stands: “Nehemiah V, that is, II Esdras V.” But in *On the Holy Spirit*, Book II, chapter 7, Saint Ambrose has: “Ezra taught us, saying in the fourth book: ‘And on the second day you again created the spirit of the firmament.’” In the margin, however, is “III Esdras VI.” In many editions it is found in the third book, as here, but this is an error, as may be seen in Ezra, I Esdras IV, chapter 6, from which this testimony was taken.

CAP. 243. This entire canon is cited according to its sense, not word for word.

AD PART V.

CAP. 3. Before this chapter another occurs in the Paris manuscript codex of Saint-Victor; but because it appears below in Part VI, chapter 316, it seemed pointless to place it here.

CAP. 5. This chapter is not found in the Saint-Victor manuscript.

CAP. 8. “They condemned.” After this word the councils read thus: “because, remaining obstinate against the privilege of the Roman primatial see, he did not wish to return from his superstitions in order that he might be saved by the first apostolic see, and, setting,” etc.

“Dioscorus [made] it itself,” etc. The original reads: “Dioscorus had dictated that excommunication, which had already been made.”

CAP. 11. “Because of the greater [excommunication],” etc. These words and what follows to the end of the chapter are not found in the Saint-Victor manuscript.

CAP. 14. On this and the other letters of Leo IV to Emperor Lothair, see Benii’s note on the Life of Leo IV.

CAP. 16. This occurs in nearly the same words at the beginning of the Life of Adrian II in the Paris councils.

CAP. 18. “You think.” In the Paris edition: “you think [plural].”

CAP. 19. In certain witnesses this chapter differs from the original.

CAP. 38. At the end of this chapter the manuscript codex of Saint-Victor also has the following:

“Benedict [writes] to all bishops throughout Gaul and Europe. Let whoever wishes to oppose the apostolic decrees lie prostrate in the sorrow of his own ruin; nor henceforth let him have a place among priests, but let him be banished from the holy mystery. Let no one take concern for his judgment, since he is already beyond doubt condemned by the holy Church and apostolic authority, and by his own disobedience and presumption; for he must be expelled by the overthrow of greater excommunication, he to whom the discipline of the holy Church has been entrusted, who ought not only to obey the commands of the holy Church set over him, but also to warn others not to transgress them. Let him be excluded from divine and pontifical offices who refused to obey apostolic commands.”

CAP. 40. This chapter is from Pope Adrian’s letter to Tarasius, Patriarch of Constantinople, in the second action of the Seventh Synod; and the whole is cited according to sense, not word for word.

CAP. 54. “Likewise.” Before this paragraph the Saint-Victor manuscript has a heading of this sort: “Disputed judgments are to be referred either to the primate or to the apostolic see.”

CAP. 75. [Col. 1029B] “Is ordained.” In the Paris councils: “Is promoted.” What follows as far as “§ And elsewhere. Grieving,” etc., is not read in the original.

CAP. 76. “To be excluded.” After this word the following must be added from the original: “Those who perpetrate such a deed not without danger.”

CAP. 120. The original has it in somewhat different words, but with the same sense.

CAP. 165. “Who afterward,” etc. These words and what follows are not in the Saint-Victor manuscript, the *Panormia*, or Gratian.

CAP. 200. This letter is found in Book III of the Council of Nicaea.

CAP. 215. It occurs after the First Council of Seville, among the fragments, chapter 1, and in Burchard, Book I, chapter 115; but where the council has *numerus* (“number”), Burchard has *numerum*.

CAP. 216. It occurs in the original somewhat differently and more briefly.

CAP. 243. “He acted unjustly.” At the end of this chapter, through the carelessness of scribes, five or six hasty lines had been added. They do not belong here, nor are they found in the Saint-Victor manuscript, but occur above, chapter 54 of this part; we have therefore deleted them.

CAP. 270. The original has it somewhat differently, but the sense is the same.

CAP. 289. “To accuse them.” The original reads: “To accuse their elders”; for “is known” it has “is not known,” as also Gratian.

“Let them not give testimony.” In the original and in Gratian it reads: “Let them offer testimony, but, being present, let them truthfully give testimony concerning what they have seen and known, and not concerning,” etc.

CAP. 292. “But if,” etc. These words to the end are not in the original.

CAP. 296. “Let no one [bring charges against] the priests of the Lord.” The original reads thus: “Let no one bring slanders against the priests of the Lord—how much more [must he not bring] accusations not produced from the root of charity!”

CAP. 308. [Col. 1029D] This passage is wholly different in Gregory, though the sense is the same.

CAP. 313. This chapter occurs somewhat differently at its beginning in Gratian. Moreover, it is not found in the Decrees of Leo, but in very ancient pontificals, and is found in Baronius, *Annals*, vol. IX, under the year 800, no. 8.

CAP. 358. “Let us serve kings.” In the latest editions of Gratian it reads “let us serve laws”; in some old printed editions, “let us serve the laws of religion”; in the Saint-Germain manuscript, “laws”; but in the volumes of councils—the Cologne edition of 1606 and the royal Paris edition of 1644—it reads “kings.” On both readings, see the Archdeacon on that passage of Gratian. Moreover, this is Epistle 16 of Pelagius I, where there is also his profession of faith that he sent to Childebert.

AD PART VI.

CAP. 7. “That he may commit [it] to memory.” In Isidore it reads: “And he commends the kingdom of God to memory through the testimonies of the Scriptures, from which he may exercise the gift.” Also in the Council of Aachen under Stephen V and Louis the Pious, chapter 4.

CAP. 11. “To the sole [authority],” etc. In Isidore it reads: “But solely on account of authority, the ordination of clerics belongs to the high priest,” etc.

CAP. 20. “The archpriest,” etc. These words down to “To the primicerius” are not in the Saint-Victor manuscript. In agreement with this is what Molinaeus placed in the margin: “These things are not found in the royal codex, and have always seemed suspicious to me, because the archpriest is made subject to the archdeacons; no one even moderately familiar with the ancient canons of councils can be ignorant that this is not ancient.” JOHN MOLINAEUS. Yet they occur in the fragments of the First Council of Toledo, fragment 8; see the margin of that fragment.

CAP. 24. It is found somewhat differently in the original: “But those who are requested from our parishes to be ordained either to a title or absolutely are by no means to be ordained, unless [they are] either in a settled and religious clergy,” etc.

CAP. 41. This canon differs greatly from the original, but the judgment is the same; indeed, it agrees most closely with chapter 88 of Book I of the *Capitularies*.

CAP. 48. “They dispute against the keys.” The original reads: “They appear to dispute and act against the keys that have been delivered.”

CAPS. 70, 71. These two chapters were reversed in Ivo, but have been restored to their proper order from the original and Gratian.

CAP. 103. “Moses alone.” In the margin, with an asterisk, stands “Aaron,” but I cannot conjecture whence Molinaeus took it, unless perhaps from some corrupt codex. For the volumes of the councils have “Moses,” and the margin cites Exodus XL, where only Moses is discussed, to whom God had commanded the erection of that altar, not Aaron, as is clearly evident from the entire chapter.

CAPS. 123, 124. These two canons do not properly belong to the Sixth Ecumenical Synod, which issued no canons at all. Rather, the one hundred and three canons circulated under the name of that Sixth Synod were issued by a certain lesser council held ten years later at Constantinople in Trullo, commonly called the Quinisext Council. It is found in the volumes of councils under the name of the Constantinopolitan lesser council, or the Quinisext Council under Sergius. Thus Binius in his notes on these councils. Moreover, in Ivo they occur somewhat differently in wording, yet with the same sense.

CAP. 134. It is cited according to sense, not word for word, as in very many others.

CAP. 165. The Greek original reads:

“All the faithful who enter and listen to the Scriptures, but do not remain for the prayer and the holy communion, are to be excluded as causing disorder in the Church.”

CAP. 223. It is not found, but occurs in an altogether different sense in the Council of Carthage and in Gratian.

CAP. 231. [Col. 1030D] It occurs among the letters of Gregory II in this form: “But concerning a priest, if any priest has been accused by the people,” etc.

CAP. 238. “But he who his own,” etc. These words were not in the old edition, but seemed necessary to add in order to complete the sense.

CAP. 242. “The same, chapter 15.” Thus it reads in some old books: “That bishops, priests, and deacons are not to be *cond.* or *pr. priu.* [materially uncertain abbreviations], nor seek their livelihood through any such business as would make it necessary for them to travel about or to be called away from ecclesiastical duties.” Thus Binius notes in the Council of Cologne.

CAP. 243. “If he is corrected.” In the original it reads: “If, having been corrected, he refuses through satisfaction to obtain pardon from the bishop.”

CAP. 244. “Because,” etc. These words have been added from the original for the sake of the sense.

CAP. 283. This is not found, but something similar occurs in the Council of Metz under Stephen V, chapter 6: “And that no cleric carry arms or put on lay clothing, that is, wear collars or mantles without a cape.”

CAP. 292. This chapter is taken from the Rule of Saint Aurelian, chapter 13, as Hugo Maynard rightly noted in the *Concordia regularum*, chapter 75, §3.

CAP. 295. This chapter is the same as, and from the same council as, the preceding one, but from the second edition, as may be seen in the councils; see also the letter of Pope Evaristus and Gratian, distinction 93, chapter “Deacons who, as it were.”

CAP. 356. On this matter see Maynard’s notable note in the *Concordia regularum*, chapter 66, p. 985.

Commentary on CAP. 358. These differ from the Greek original, which reads as follows:

“Let the clergy of poorhouses and monasteries remain under the authority of the bishops in each city, according to the tradition of the holy Fathers; and let them not grow insolent toward, or rebel against, their own bishop. But those who dare to overturn such an ordinance in any manner and do not submit to their own bishop—if they are clerics, let them be subject to the penalties of the canons; but if monks or laymen, let them be excluded from communion.”

CAP. 359. It is the same as the preceding chapter, but from the ancient translation, which does not occur in the councils, as the Roman correctors rightly note in Gratian, 18, question 2, chapter “Certain monks.”

CAP. 362. The first three lines of this chapter, down to the words “likewise it pleased,” are not found in this council.

CAP. 373. “But those whom,” etc. This passage was corrupt but has been restored from the original. It had read: “But those whom he shall have ordained amid disgraceful acts”; and in the Saint-Victor manuscript someone wishing to emend it had restored it badly as: “But those whom he shall have bound in disgraceful acts.”

CAP. 393. This and the next three chapters vary slightly in our printed editions of Saint Cyprian, but the sense is the same.

CAPS. 397 and 398. They differ slightly in the original, which reads: “But what your fraternity subsequently made known to us in the letters, namely that it is read in the canon of Ancyra, chapter 19: ‘After a bodily fall, the rank of honor is to be restored after penance.’ And elsewhere it is read: ‘After an offense of this kind,’” etc.

CAP. 399. See Maynard’s notes on the *Concordia regularum*, chapter 34, p. 542: “This chapter is taken from the Rule of Saint Fructuosus,” concerning which Maynard himself discusses extensively in the preliminaries to the *Concordia regularum*.

CAP. 400. It occurs at the end of the Council of Lleida, though not very correctly, as Antonio Agustín notes in his annotations on the penitential book of Rabanus Maurus, where this canon occurs.

“But whoever concerning the aforesaid…” Thus it varies in Rabanus and in the councils: “But whoever among the aforesaid men, through secret confession, [has] wicked acts secretly committed by himself before,” etc.

“If they themselves,” etc. In the aforesaid [sources]: “If they have truly repented and themselves,” etc.

CAP. 410. It is not found, but something similar occurs in the Council of Clermont under Urban II, chapter 25, in these words: “Let not the sons of priests, deacons, subdeacons, or canons be promoted to orders or other ecclesiastical ranks unless he is a monk or regular canon.” And among the additions to this council another canon reads: “Nor should it be permitted that the sons of priests, or children otherwise born from concubines, be promoted to the rank of priest, unless they had professed the religious life in some monastery.” So also in the Council of Poitiers, book [or section] c. 9, and it is reported in chapter 1, “On age and qualification,” etc.

CAP. 421. Compared with the Greek original, it is entirely different; thus it reads in Latin: “Once they have been made deacons or priests in accordance with this [rule], they are in no way to abandon the priesthood. We decree this not only concerning a deacon and priest, but also that, if anyone becomes a subdeacon or perhaps a reader, he is in no way to abandon his former *schema* (σχῆμα, ‘state, habit’) or pass to another manner of life, knowing that if he does any such thing, in accordance with what has already been decreed by us, he shall be assigned to the curia if he has property, or, if he lives in poverty, to official service.”

CAP. 428. “Before one year.” On the one-year probation of monks, see Maynard’s notable note on chapter 65 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, p. 938 of the *Concordia regularum*, where he also mentions this chapter.

CAP. 429. This chapter differs slightly from the original; nevertheless, it is fuller in Ivo.

AD PART VII.

CAP. 1. “And not to communicate,” etc. In the latest editions of the councils it reads: “Let them take part neither in ecclesiastical nor in secular affairs, nor be troublesome in any matter.” This differs slightly from the Greek text:

“Nor are they to trouble themselves with, or take part in, ecclesiastical or worldly affairs, after leaving their own monasteries,” etc.

CAP. 5. [Col. 1032B] “The book of Psalms,” etc. In the original and Gratian it reads: “Let the book never depart from hand and eyes; let the Psalter be learned word for word; let prayer be without ceasing; let the mind be watchful.” In the Saint-Victor manuscript, instead of “let it be watchful,” it reads “watchful, and the mind.”

CAP. 33. The sense of that chapter is found in the original, though in somewhat different words.

*Mundiburdis.* This is a German word signifying guardians and curators.

CAP. 57. “And incest,” etc. These final words, which are also in the Saint-Victor manuscript, are not in the council or Gratian.

CAP. 62. “To maintain chastity.” Another reading has: “Let them maintain chastity, and let no widow be compelled by force to enter a repeated marriage.”

CAP. 65. This chapter occurs defective and mutilated in the Councils and is divided by Gratian into two. From this one may conjecture that the person who collected these rescripts of Nicholas I from Gratian and inserted them into the Councils had not seen Ivo, from whom that passage seems capable of being restored in full.

CAP. 68. [Col. 1032C] It is given here somewhat more fully than in the original.

CAP. 85. This chapter differs slightly from the original, where it reads “according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.” In the original and the Saint-Victor manuscript, as also in Gratian, it reads only “according to the Rule.” I believe that the Rule of Saint Benedict, which was then preeminent, was called *the Rule* κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν, “preeminently.”

CAP. 93. “Under the bishop’s supervision.” In the African and Carthaginian [texts] it reads: “Under the oversight of the bishop, or of the priest when the bishop is absent, in a monastery of virgins or of more serious women,” etc.
