CAP. 101. In the original and Gratian it reads: “Although learned and holy, a woman must not presume to teach men in an assembly.”

CAP. 109. “Or with the consent of their parents.” These words are absent from the original.

CAP. 127. In some respects it differs from the original, but the principal points are noted in the margin.

CAP. 129. The letters of Saint Boniface the martyr were printed at Mainz in 1605 by Serrarius.

CAP. 139. “We therefore rather… and should thus not be lost,” etc. This passage is corrupt and should be restored as follows: “Hence we should rather admit that bodily chastity is not lost while the chastity of the mind remains, even if the body is violated; bodily chastity is lost when the chastity of the mind is violated, even if the body remains untouched.”

“For indicating,” etc. The original reads: “For indicating in the union of two bodies,” etc.

CAP. 153. This chapter differs greatly from current exemplars, though the sense is the same.

AD PART VIII.

CAP. 69. “It is not permitted.” The original adds: “Who are also called *spurii* [illegitimate children], from παρά τὴν σποράν, that is, ‘from the sowing.’” But the marginal gloss has: “or from παρὰ τὸ σπείρειν, ‘from sowing,’ or from παρὰ τὴν σποράδην [‘scattered, irregularly sown’]. Plutarch.”

CAP. 73. “Widowly.” This word is not in the printed originals of Saint Augustine, nor in the very ancient manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

CAP. 85. “How much,” etc. We have added these words from the original because they clarify the sense more fully.

CAP. 90. The heading of this chapter, I think, had through the scribes’ negligence been placed at the end of the preceding chapter, as though it belonged to that chapter; but we have restored it to its proper place.

CAP. 91. This passage was plainly corrupt, but has been restored from the original.

CAP. 98. “That a woman should be under a man.” It differs somewhat from both manuscript and printed originals. It reads thus: “The law did not wish a woman to make a vow while under her father before marriage, or while under her husband after marriage; thus in some matter, etc., [concerning] her own [vow], that is, in abstaining from some lawful things, so that in such vows feminine authority may not prevail” (Saint-Germain manuscript: “may prevail”). “So that” (Saint-Germain manuscript) “if they are still unmarried,” etc., “and it shall be altogether…” The word “law” is not in the manuscript or printed editions.

CAP. 101. [Col. 1033B] In the original the sense is more complete.

CAP. 103. “The body itself.” The original reads: “Your body itself is in you a temple of the Holy Spirit,” as is noted in the margin. The same reading occurs in the manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

CAP. 116. “With the person.” Thus it reads in the original: “When [he] wearies and daily wears away the person whom,” etc.; “when he wishes, he brings [her] to judgment; when,” etc.; “he had commanded—who can say under how great evils she is brought in and made subject?”

CAP. 152. “After penance.” In both versions of this council it reads: “After one year they ought to be reconciled without penance.”

CAP. 153. “What I say to the competent.” In the original: “What I say to the competent, let the faithful hear, [as also] penitents. What I say to the faithful, I say also to the competent and penitents.”

“Let wives suffice you.” The original continues: “or not even wives.”

CAP. 162. “According to the ecclesiastical rule.” In Greek it is κατὰ τὸν ἐκκλησιαστικὸν κανόνα, “according to the ecclesiastical canon.” That ecclesiastical canon is from the Council of Neocaesarea, mentioned above by Ivo, chapter 160; here Binius should be consulted on this canon of the Council of Laodicea.

CAP. 170. “They abduct.” The original continues: “or take [women] with the consent of their parents.”

“Penance.” The original adds: “and let him legally pay a fine to the betrothed man”; in the margin stands: “perhaps *multam*, ‘a fine.’”

“Rejected.” There is added: “and if he cannot be canonically approved according to the statutes of the holy Fathers, he must be compelled to clear himself.”

CAP. 178. In Gratian, 27, question 2 and 33, question 1, chapter “But what you asked,” it is cited from Gregory the Younger; likewise in the *Capitularies*, Book VI, chapter 55.

CAP. 181. This chapter is not found in Tribur, except that its sense is nearly the same, though not altogether alike. It also differs greatly in Gratian.

CAP. 203. At the end of this chapter the following seem to be added from the original: “If, after being restored, he has again committed adultery, it has pleased [the council] that he should no longer be admitted to the communion of peace.” In the other version: “that he should no longer be given [communion],” etc.

CAP. 213. The same words are not found in Tribur, but the sense is nearly the same.

CAP. 228. “Which is the apostolic precept.” These words have been added to clarify this passage.

CAP. 232. “A like …” In the original it reads: “a like [thing] is required both by an ox and a horse,” etc.; and above, where “another” stands, it often has “otherwise”; for “will fail” it has “will have been lacking.” Thus also in two Saint-Germain manuscripts.

CAP. 235. “Thus the bond remaining in itself.” The original adds: “A wife is dismissed on account of fornication from the bond of marriage; nor will she lack that bond, even if,” etc.

CAP. 261. This chapter was wholly corrupted. Hence Molinaeus had placed in the margin of the preceding edition “an obscure passage,” because at that time the works of Hincmar had not yet been printed. We have restored it from recently published copies.

CAP. 286. “They shall have taken wives.” These two words are not in the original.

CAP. 295. “By seeking honor.” Nor are these two words in the original.

CAP. 301. This chapter is not found in the cited place, but something similar is in the same council, chapter 7.

CAP. 303. “And it is not a sin,” etc. This passage is corrupt and should be restored from the original and Gratian as follows: “And that which is not a sin ought by no means to be believed to be absolved among sins.”

CAP. 315. “At a marriage.” The council has “at a banquet,” which seems more fitting. For the Greek exemplar has: Εἰς γάμοις διγαμοῦντων μὴ ἑστιᾶσθαι, “not to feast at the weddings of those entering a second marriage”; or, “not to feast at the marriage of one who takes two wives”; or, “not to attend the banquet of a second marriage”; or, “not to dine at the wedding of a bigamist,” as the three translations have it.

AD PART IX.

CAP. 1. “With these,” etc. In the original it reads: “With these the father is uncertain.”

CAP. 8. Baronius, *Annals*, vol. II, under the year 998, no. 1, gives this chapter differently: “Your father,” etc., “by our predecessor Gregory V, together with the bishops who attended the assembly, were rebuked, in order that afterward to the see,” etc. But in one manuscript it reads “excommunicated,” as we noted in the margin; this must be read so, otherwise the sense is incomplete.

CAP. 16. “And of the mother.” We have added these words from the original because they are necessary for the sense.

CAP. 46. Before this chapter the Paris manuscript of Saint-Victor has the following: “From the epistle of Pope Gregory sent to the bishops of Gaul. We decree that each person observe his own lineage to the seventh generation, and for as long as they recognize themselves as related by affinity, we deny them access to conjugal union.”

CAP. 69. “Nor they themselves,” etc. The original reads: “Neither that adulterous sister nor that man who committed adultery with her may ever take others.”

CAP. 113. This chapter is taken from Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 68, though somewhat more explicitly. It reads thus: “See that none who at night has had an image of a woman dare approach the holy sacraments. Let none among you, affected by visions and imaginations, have dreams; for emissions of seed occurring without imaginations happen by chance and do not arise from each person’s free choice of mind, but without the will. For they proceed from nature and are discharged from superabundant matter. Accordingly, they are not liable to sin. But visions and imaginations proceed from the free will of choice and are evidence of an evil mind.” From this it is evident that this chapter should be understood of nocturnal pollutions resulting from preceding shameful thoughts, if they occur through our fault and not from infirmity; as is clearer from the testimony of Saint Gregory in our Ivo, Part II, chapter 52, where he wonderfully elucidates this question. On this see also Cassian, *Conferences* 22, chapters 4, 5, and 6; and Saint Thomas, Part III, question 80, article 7.

CAP. 120. This chapter differs in the text of Saint Augustine.

AD PART X.

CAP. 25. “To attain the perfect [state].” In Greek it reads τοῦ τελείου μετέχειν, “to partake of the perfect [state],” a phrase which this council frequently uses for communion, to which penitents, after completing penance, were admitted, so that they might understand themselves to have been admitted with the other faithful to perfect grace and full communion. Thus Binius on this council, from Baronius. On this subject see canon 18 of the Council of Nantes under Formosus.

CAP. 31. “The Truce of God.” In the margin of this chapter, the preceding edition had: “The Truce of God seems to be the proper name of some place.” But this is incorrect, as is evident to anyone moderately familiar with the reading of the councils; we have therefore deleted it on the judgment of experts. The *treva*, *trevia*, or *treuga Dei* was a kind of truce instituted by the Church, during which it was necessary to abstain from every quarrel, hostility, and harassment of whatever kind. Much could be said concerning it, but the haste of the printers prevents us. Instead of all else, let the reader consult the notable note found in the appendix to the Council of Clermont under Urban II, at the end of volume XXVI of the latest Paris edition of the Councils, printed by the Royal Press in 1644.

AD PART XII.

CAP. 77. “For each person [is bound],” etc. In the original it reads: “For each person, just as one standing before the altar has the fear of God before his eyes and keeps his own conscience clean before God, must by no means fail to remember that [which he retains in memory], because the mouth which lies,” etc.

CAP. 85. *They ordered.* After this the original adds: “And they judged all men of both orders to be infamous, and not only,” etc.

TO PART XIII.

CAP. 10. *According to the form divinely given.* These words are not found in Ivo, but have been restored from the original and Gratian for the sake of the sense.

CAP. 50. This chapter occurs in the second rule of the Fathers in the Floracensis manuscript codex [Col. 1035B], whose beginning is: “When we had assembled in the name of the Lord with our brethren,” as Maynard rightly observes.

CAP. 62. *By priests,* etc. The words down to *they shall have been unwilling* have been added from the original to complete the sense.

CAP. 77. In the Rule of St. Fructuosus, chapter 17, at the end, speaking of monks, it reads as follows: “If any drunkard be found in the monastery, he shall be subject to the preceding sentence; likewise anyone who, without the permission of the abbot or provost, sends letters anywhere, or receives letters sent by another.” So Maynard notes on chapter 50 of the *Concordance of Rules*, §13.

TO PART XIV.

CAP. 3. *Of the judge.* The original has *of judgment*.

Before *the rectitude of the work.* In the original it reads: “before the operation of rectitude.”

CAP. 4. *Inwardly.* The original inserts parenthetically: “because they ought to be struck with a curse.”

CAP. 5. *For otherwise,* etc. The original reads thus: “For a curse is pronounced in one way by the judgment of justice, in another by the rancour of vengeance. For a curse pronounced by the judgment of justice,” etc. [Col. 1035C]

CAP. 34. *To send him a mandate.* Here *mandate* means the same as message, notification, or embassy. Thus it denotes communicating something through an intermediary. Better in French: *lui mander quelque chose* [“to send someone word of something”]. Maynard says more in his notes on this chapter.

CAP. 75. From this and the following chapter was briefly compiled the form for pronouncing an anathema—that is, solemn excommunication for more serious offences—which appears in the third part of the Roman Pontifical, chapter “On the Order of Excommunicating and Absolving.”

CAP. 88. *Marriage.* The original adds: “and says that this is not a sin.”

CAP. 95. [Col. 1036A] *Unless those,* etc. These words are not found in Isidore; but it is not clear on what basis they were added by Burchard and Ivo.

CAP. 107. This chapter differs slightly from the original.

CAP. 110. This chapter is also cited by Burchard as taken from the sayings of Basil; but it is taken from St. Isidore in Gratian, 11, question 3, chapter *Qui consentit* [“He who consents”]. Yet it occurs in neither source, but in the Rule of the Orientals and in the Rule of St. Pachomius, as Maynard, a most diligent investigator of antiquity, rightly observed in the *Concordance of Rules*, chapter 74. We have accordingly restored the citation of this chapter.

CAP. 124. *Why do the canons forbid them.* The original is shorter: “why not those who,” etc. This is also the reading in the Mainz and Worms collections.

TO PART XV.

CAP. 19. *First let him cut his hair.* The following words are absent from the original: “Or let him change his dress into ashes and haircloth, unless first either.” The following are likewise absent: “Or she shall have been veiled, or.”

[Col. 1036B] *For laymen more often.* After this, the words “with women” are absent.

CAP. 22. There is a considerable difference of wording in the original.

CAP. 29. *And in ‘per...’,* etc. These words are corrupt. The original is better: “in the pressing imminence of danger.”

CAP. 36. *Lest [obl...],* etc. In the Mainz collection it reads: “Lest, bound by excommunication, they become estranged from the fellowship of the good.”

*Anointing of oil.* In the Mainz collection it reads: “Anointing of God.” The rest is similar.

CAP. 57. At the end, *it became known.* In the original and in Gratian it reads: “It became known, namely what is read in Canon 19 of Ancyra: after a bodily fall, the rank of honour is to be restored after penance; but elsewhere it reads: ‘After such a…,’” etc. See above on chapters 397 and 398, Part VI.

CAP. 141. This chapter varies slightly in the original.

TO PART XVI.

CAP. 8. *Crimes.* The original differs somewhat [Col. 1036C], reading: “If anyone be found to be a despiser of just and reasonable ecclesiastical judgments concerning ecclesiastical matters, or be proved, puffed up and swollen, to be an opponent or mocker of ecclesiastical admonitions and the constitutions of the holy Fathers, if he obeys episcopal admonitions,” etc.

CAP. 23. *Ecclesiastical authority.* The original adds: “and civil law.”

We compared very many chapters of Part Seventeen with the originals; but owing to want of time we were unable to note the variation, which is nevertheless not very great. Thus, with the printers pressing us excessively, we have been compelled to end here.

# PANORMIA, OR DECRETUM

[Note: [Col. 1037] It does not distinguish the *Panormia* from the *Decretum*. See the Dissertation on Ivo’s *Decretum*, above, col. XLIX, EDITOR.]

OF LORD IVO, BISHOP OF CHARTRES, restored, corrected, and amended through the work and diligence of Melchior of Vosmediano, Doctor of Arts and Sacred Theology, now newly enriched with a most ample index composed with the utmost diligence by the same Lord Doctor Vosmediano.

(Louvain, from the press of Antonio Maria Bergagne, sworn bookseller, 1557, duodecimo, with the king’s favour and privilege for six years.)

[Col. 1037]

# DEDICATORY EPISTLE

To PHILIP, the most great Catholic King of the Spains, England, France, and Naples, etc., and defender of the faith, MELCHIOR OF VOSMEDIANO, Doctor of Arts and Sacred Theology, chaplain to the same royal majesty and superintendent of the royal-court hospital.

Our forefathers, most great Philip, Catholic King, strove with the utmost diligence to seek out the most approved authors from every quarter; and, sparing no expense, to have those whom they had found copied, and to preserve with immense care what had been copied. Hence it came about that among them that ardent pursuit of letters increased daily, and the minds of eminent men were stimulated to read them. We therefore owe much to those who undertook this public care, since, aided by their labours, our studies are advanced more and more each day.

This certainly befell me when, at the ecumenical Council of Trent, at which I was present for almost six complete years, I came upon the *Panormia*, or *Decretum*, of the most learned Ivo, bishop of Chartres. Yet I could not obtain the object of my desire: though I sought it with no small labour at the council, among Venetian booksellers, and elsewhere, I was unable to find it. While possessed by a great longing for the book, and residing among the English in London at the royal court of Your Majesty, I did not cease to search for it in public and private libraries. But what I could not find by searching I discovered by chance—and not one copy, but two: one printed about sixty years earlier; the other, a manuscript on parchment in very ancient characters.

These were so welcome to me that, forgetful of my English journey, I thought the book I had found far outweighed a labour otherwise not slight. And lest so great a labour should perish, and time—most precious of things—slip away through our hands, I set myself to the task: I read and reread, and examined the book—or rather, the two copies—with great care. Finding them filled with fine learning, holy laws, and the most holy institutions of the Fathers, I adorned them with a most ample index, which they lacked, compiled by myself; and I resolved to publish to the light a book most precious and most useful and necessary to the Christian commonwealth, corrected throughout, lest so great a treasure should remain hidden and a lamp, concealed beneath a bushel, lie there benefiting no one.

In this matter I spared neither labour nor sleepless nights, so that this book, purged of the almost innumerable errors with which it swarmed, might shine forth no longer in borrowed dress, as it had done, but rather in its own; and might pass through every hand. It had been written for the benefit of all with immense zeal, the greatest diligence, and remarkable genius by the most learned Ivo.

Since, therefore, it is a most ancient custom to dedicate books to a prince, to whom could or ought I dedicate this one but to you, Philip, greatest of princes and best of kings, who summoned me, though thinking of no such thing, wholly into your royal household? Or to whom should a book wholly concerned with justice and law more deservedly be dedicated than to you, mightiest of kings, who rule innumerable kingdoms and dispense law among nations so numerous and diverse?

Finally, since the office of justice is, as Aristotle says, to distribute to each according to his worth, to preserve ancestral customs and institutions, to uphold written laws, to be truthful in controversies, and to stand by agreements, to whom could this *Panormia*, concerning laws both most true and most holy, be more fittingly dedicated than to you? From it you may have readily at hand the decrees, enactments of the Fathers, and statutes of the ancients that can benefit the commonwealth; and the laws by whose rule those who live under your dominion—which, by God’s gift, is the most extensive in the whole world—ought to order their lives.

Or to whom should I dedicate this most beautiful book of most holy laws, of the Roman Church and its holy author—or rather, to whom would the author himself, were he alive, dedicate it—than to you, O king, defender of the Catholic faith? You left your most extensive dominions, including, among many other possessions, the provinces of the two Sicilies and of the Indies, which are beyond number, and came to the Britons scattered throughout the world, in order there, together with the most serene Mary, your wife, a heroine of incomparable virtue, to propagate the faith and cause it, if not dead, certainly almost extinguished, to live again—indeed, as it were, to raise it from death to life.

You performed this office of a true Christian prince with such moderation of spirit, such patience and gentleness, such skill and prudence, that within very few days the Christian faith, already an exile from the Britons, was recalled; the most extensive schism was abolished; and the name of the supreme pontiff, the vicar on earth of Christ God, best and greatest—though heretics may rage—which among them it had been unlawful even to hear, both came to be heard and was held in honour, as was fitting. The churches [Col. 1039], once full of people and then regarded as though deserted, we saw, not many days later, adorned by your care and solicitude with crowds of worshippers and innumerable sacrifices of the Mass, with much giving of thanks to God. This was not without the groaning of many wicked men, though some rejoiced.

For the Lord had left there seven thousand men who had not bent their knees before Baal. He had also heard the blood crying beneath the altar of the blessed martyr John Fisher, bishop of Rochester, a man of incomparable holiness and distinguished learning; and of Thomas More, most deserving Chancellor of England; and of the Carthusian monks and others who, for preserving the truth of the Catholic faith, most steadfastly underwent the torment of death, that they might enjoy eternal life with God.

For the Lord had raised you up, best of kings and greatest of princes, over these sheep of the British people: that you might feed them, strengthen what was weak, heal what was sick, bind up what was broken, bring back what had been cast away, and finally seek what had perished. Inflamed with zeal for the house of God and for the Christian faith, in which you burn, you have performed all these things in such a way that you seem not merely to have acted as an excellent king, but to have been a shepherd of souls and an apostle.

For you so govern the reins of the kingdom that you seem to be king alone; and you have applied yourself so fully to planting and propagating Christian faith and religion, and to uprooting that most destructive schism, that you are accounted both an apostle and a shepherd of souls. You have so assisted in performing each office that you seem deficient in neither.

I do not say these things in order to sing your praises, which even in your great modesty you do not willingly hear; but so that we may refer to the glory of God, best and greatest, the deeds which we have seen. Receive, therefore, best of kings, this work under your patronage; and regard not what sort of gift it is from its offerer, but with what mind it is offered to you. Farewell, most great Philip, defender and propagator of the Catholic faith; and may God preserve you safe for us, grant you victory and health, and cause you to reign for many years.

Brussels, 15 March 1557.

[Col. 1039]

# LORD MELCHIOR OF VOSMEDIANO TO THE CHRISTIAN READER

I am not of the opinion, Christian and candid Reader, that more is owed to those who add to discoveries than to the discoverers themselves; although I know that much is owed to both: to the latter because they discovered, and to the former because they preserved the discoveries from perishing.

In this matter I have rendered a service to our holy Ivo, bishop of Chartres, a most learned jurist. Though he flourished in the year 1090 from the birth of Christ our God, and had come forth into print about sixty years ago, he was so mutilated, torn, and defective that one would have judged it to be not Ivo’s *Panormia*, or *Decretum*, but another’s. This circumstance moved my mind so greatly that, when I found him in such a condition in London—him whom I had long before sought anxiously—I resolved, pitying the state of a man who had deserved well of both the civil and ecclesiastical commonwealth, to cleanse him thoroughly, rescue him from errors, and recall him from darkness to light.

But when I undertook the task, what had seemed easy on the title page later appeared most difficult. I found so many passages depraved, so corrupt, so badly cited—or rather, uncited—that I scarcely hoped I could overcome so great a labour. But since unremitting labour conquers all things, under God’s guidance I undertook the work; and with His assistance I removed the innumerable errors with which the copy abounded.

Moreover, many materials cited by our Ivo from general and provincial councils, many from the Fathers, and many from decrees of the supreme pontiffs, were presented without identifying the sources from which they had been drawn. You will find that I have restored them all by my own efforts. More than fifty citations from councils were missing; one hundred and thirty from sacred doctors; and almost as many from pontifical enactments. All of these, not without great vigils and labours, I restored to their sources, identifying in the margin the authors, books, and chapters.

In addition, I supplied one hundred missing summaries and inserted throughout the work divisions of chapters, besides many other things which I myself restored and corrected. In short, in place of Ivo as an old man—mute, torn, maimed, and filthy—we restore to you, Christian Reader, a young man, speaking, adorned, whole in all his limbs, and elegant: so that you may recognize him, speak with him, and enjoy his most delightful companionship with pleasure and profit.

And lest anything be lacking for sweet and easy converse with him, I compiled for every book an alphabetical index of subjects and titles, arranged in the same alphabetical order. I also added a third index, far richer, in which the principal topics and the more notable opinions scattered throughout the work are indicated with such skill and diligence that from this index alone, industrious reader, you may easily behold not Ivo’s shadow, as before, but living Ivo himself; understand the man’s profound learning; and admire, with the greatest benefit, the ornaments of that divine genius.

Finally, I added two letters by the same author, never previously published, so that Ivo might come forth complete. Though he came after Isidore, who first brought the decrees of the Fathers together into one great volume, and after Burchard, bishop of Worms, who attempted the same undertaking seventy years before our Ivo, he worked so successfully and acutely in the same field that jurists used this Decretum of Ivo before the time of Gratian, just as they now use Gratian’s. And deservedly so, since he possessed a most penetrating intellect, the weightiest and richest learning, and no ordinary eloquence.

For from him you learn how to preside over all justly, holily, uprightly, becomingly, and equitably; how to repel snares, remove discords, prevent injury, punish crimes, restrain sins with due severity, and finally impose rewards upon the good and just penalties upon the wicked according to the diversity of their merits.

You have, then, Christian Reader, our Ivo: among theologians a most learned jurist, and among jurists a theologian of the greatest weight; a man of varied reading; no longer mutilated, maimed, overflowing with errors, or corrupt as before, but perfect, whole, genuine, and corrected; no longer naked as before, but now adorned, as with garments, by many indexes and annotations. Enjoy him, therefore, most pious and Christian Reader. If you find anything that pleases you less, attribute it to me—for being human, I think nothing human alien to me. But if you find anything pleasing, give thanks to God and pray to Him for me. Farewell.

Brussels, 15 March 1557.

[Col. 1041] Christian Reader, I found in my most ancient manuscript copy this letter of Lord Ivo concerning those who, wishing to dismiss adulterous wives, desired to attach themselves to others. Since it had never been printed, I had it put into print and added to the *Panormia*, lest you be deprived of it.

Farewell, and pray to God for me.

To UMBERT [read: DAIMBERT], by the grace of God Archbishop of Sens, Ivo, humble minister of the Church of Chartres, offers service with humble devotion.

Concerning the people of Jerusalem, etc.

(This letter now appears among Ivo’s letters as number 125. See the following volume, col. 136.)

# MELCHIOR OF VOSMEDIANO TO THE PIOUS READER

Christian Reader, I had arranged to publish two letters of Lord Ivo, most learned in both branches of law, which I had found in my most ancient copy. One of them, to Umbert, I was able, though with difficulty, to read and to transcribe. But the other, addressed to Ulric, had characters not merely worn away but almost erased. In many places I was unable to read them at all—not by sunlight, not in the full sun, not by intense light, nor by subdued light—so thoroughly did I despair of ever being able to publish it.

But since affliction gives understanding, by divine assisting grace I came upon an experiment by which what could not be read at all could readily be read and transcribed. This I did, so that you may enjoy it and assist me by your prayers before God, best and greatest.

Farewell. Brussels.

Ivo, by the grace of God minister of Chartres, to his beloved brother in Christ ULRIC, greeting.

Your letter contains, etc.

(See among Ivo’s letters in the following volume, col. 160.)

[Col. 1041]

# [PANORMIA]

## HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE OF THE PANORMIA OF IVO, BISHOP OF CHARTRES, CONCERNING THE MANIFOLD DISTINCTION OF THE SCRIPTURES CONTAINED UNDER THE ONE UNITY OF CHASTE UTTERANCES

(This prologue consists of 42 chapters, of which chapters 1–34 reproduce word for word the prologue prefixed to the *Decretum*. We give the sequence of rubrics together with the beginning of each chapter. Chapters 35–42, which concern the *Panormia* alone, are presented in full. EDITORS OF THE FATHERS.)

CAP. I. [Col. 1041A] Exceptions to ecclesiastical rules, etc.

CAP. II. On the intention of the divine page. “For all ecclesiastical discipline has,” etc.

CAP. III. That charity is the teacher of every good. “Therefore whoever is an ecclesiastic,” etc.

CAP. IV. Likewise: “The attentive and diligent reader will understand this,” etc.

CAP. V. On admonition. “And the first admonition indeed,” etc.

CAP. VI. On indulgence. “Indulgence, however, so far as it appears to us,” etc.

CAP. VII. On precepts and prohibitions. “Therefore precepts and prohibitions,” etc.

CAP. VIII. A cleric after completing penance for a condemnable crime [Col. 1041B], etc.

CAP. IX. “Such is that passage in the Gospel,” etc.

CAP. X. On dispensation. “Likewise, many leaders of churches,” etc.

CAP. XI. Neophytes are forbidden the priesthood. [Col. 1042A] “Just as the holy Roman Church,” etc.

CAP. XII. Which constitutions can be moderated, and which cannot. “Likewise Pope Leo, mentioned above,” etc.

CAP. XIII. Vengeance is not always to be exercised against those who sin (Augustine, to Boniface). “If, they say, we must repent that we were outside the Church and against the Church,” etc.

CAP. XIV. Hidden offences are to be punished lightly, but manifest offences more severely by the Church (AUGUSTINE, *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, book III, chapter 2). “When anyone’s crime is known,” etc.

CAP. XV. What is sinned by a multitude, or by one who has the multitude as accomplice, is not punished by the Church but deferred (ibid.). [Col. 1042B] “For correction by many cannot be salutary,” etc.

CAP. XVI. Because of a large body of people, a crime remains unpunished (ibid.). [Col. 1043A] “Indeed, when the contagion of sin has seized a multitude,” etc.

CAP. XVII. On the same subject. “But the crowd of the wicked,” etc.

CAP. XVIII. Those who receive baptism from heretics are to be confirmed by the laying on of hands (POPE LEO I, Letter 77, to Nicetas, chapter 7). “I am accustomed to hear that it lies in the judge’s power,” etc.

CAP. XIX. What is granted because of necessity will cease when the necessity has ceased (POPE INNOCENT I, Letter 22, chapter 5). “This was the chief deliberation of the priests,” etc.

But the canons established at Nicaea allowed this to be done in the case of the Novatians. First, the canon enacted by the Fathers must be set forth, so that we may perceive what was meant or commanded by them, and in what manner.

CAP. XX. “Concerning those who call themselves Cathars, that is, ‘the pure,’ and who at some time come to the Catholic Church, it has pleased the holy and great Synod that, after receiving the laying on of hands, they should thus remain in the clergy.”

CAP. XXI. By a similar dispensation, the blessed Pope Gregory orders that those returning from the Nestorian heresy be received in their ranks, writing thus to the bishops of the Catholic Church in Ireland.

CAP. XXII. “Therefore, concerning the truth of Christ’s Nativity,” etc.

CAP. XXIII. By dispensation, some things are tolerated which the strictness of the canons condemns (CYRIL, Letter to Maximus, deacon of Antioch). [Col. 1043C] “We have something similar in the letter of Cyril,” etc.

CAP. XXIV. On the same subject (same letter). “But lest we be thought to love contention,” etc.

CAP. XXV. On the same subject (CYRIL, Letter to Januarius and Armichus, priests). “Dispensations of matters,” etc.

CAP. XXVI (ibid.). “And I write these things, knowing that your piety,” etc.

CAP. XXVII (ibid.). “Therefore, let not your piety shrink back,” etc.

CAP. XXVIII. The Roman pontiffs have employed the same moderation of discernment, etc.

CAP. XXIX. [Col. 1043D] Certain Roman pontiffs also, etc.

CAP. XXX. “But for repressing certain presbyters,” etc.

CAP. XXXI. “For since very many bishops,” etc.

CAP. XXXII. Those who fall after ordination, having performed fitting penance, are to be restored (CYRIL, Letter to John of Antioch). “Very many bishops also,” etc.

CAP. XXXIII. “Whatever the emperor,” etc.

CAP. XXXIV. “We might bring forward many reasons concerning matters of this sort,” etc.

CAP. XXXV. The first part of this book contains material concerning faith and the various heresies; the sacrament of faith and baptism; the ministry of baptizing, consecrating [Col. 1044A], and confirming; those who have been confirmed; the observance proper to each; and what baptism confers, what confirmation confers; the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood; the Mass; and the holiness of the other sacraments.

CAP. XXXVI. The second part contains material concerning the constitution of the Church and the offerings of the faithful; the dedication and consecration of churches and altars; burial and presbyters and their churches; tithes; lawful possession; those who take refuge in a church; sacrilege; the guardianship of freed persons; the alienation and sharing of church property; writings and authoritative councils; customs; fasting; and almsgiving.

CAP. XXXVII. The third part contains material concerning the election and [Col. 1044B] consecration of the pope and archbishops; orders; clergy; and laypersons who are to be or not to be ordained; the transfer of bishops; those ordained who are not to be reordained; the continence of the ordained; those ordained and those ordaining simoniacally, including those who are in every case to be deposed and those who are to be mercifully reconciled; the profession of heretics; those fallen while in holy orders, including those who ought not to minister and those who may mercifully be admitted to ministry; homicidal clerics who ought not to minister; usurers; slaves ordained in ignorance, including those who ought to remain in orders and those who ought not; drunken and buffoonish clerics; monks; the age at which parents may oppose their children’s religious life, and that at which they may not; widows; veiled virgins; and abbesses. [Col. 1044C]

CAP. XXXVIII. The fourth part contains material concerning the primacy and dignity of the Roman Church; the convocation of councils; the manner in which a province is to be constituted; the authority of primates and metropolitan bishops; where clerics’ disputes and causes ought to be heard; restoring those despoiled; accusation—its order, the persons by whom it may or may not be made, and those against whom it may or may not be made; witnesses—who they are, how many they must be, how they must testify, and in what business they ought or ought not to testify; truces, when and for how long they are to be granted; and those who evade proceedings, how long and on what grounds they should be awaited. It also concerns what sort of judges they ought to be and when they ought to pronounce [Col. 1044D] judgment; appeals, when and on what grounds they ought to be made; and the penalty for appeals made improperly.

CAP. XXXIX. The fifth part contains material concerning clerics accused of infamy alone and without witnesses, and by how many hands they ought to clear themselves; the causes and affairs of laypeople; summoning those to be excommunicated; lawful and unlawful excommunication; absolution; those bound to excommunicated persons by faithlessness or oath, and which persons may be released from that oath without perjury; heretics to be excommunicated after death; and what may be communicated to those excommunicated not by name.

CAP. XL. The sixth part contains material concerning marriages: at what time, between what persons, and for what reason they ought to be made; the three things that make a marriage complete; complete and incomplete marriage; concubines; spouses where one has vowed continence without the other or assumed the religious habit; wives who, after their husbands were taken into captivity, married others; marriage between persons of the same religion or faith—that is, among Gentiles and among Jews—whereas marriage cannot take place between persons who are not of the same religion or faith; the grounds on which marriage ought not to be dissolved; what sort of union does not make a marriage; and separation in marriage for a cause other than fornication. [Col. 1045A]

CAP. XLI. The seventh part contains material concerning separation of marriage on account of carnal fornication; the man who fornicates with another man’s wife, and why he cannot have her as his wife after her husband’s death; killers of their own spouses; spiritual fornication, on account of which a wife may lawfully be dismissed; reconciliation of spouses; the duties husbands owe to wives and wives to their husbands when they are reconciled; the subjection [Col. 1045B] wives owe to their husbands; the reason why marriage ought not to take place between relatives; the fact that one man cannot marry two co-mothers, one after the other; the case of one who has had relations with his goddaughter or her mother, or has baptized her son, or whose wife has raised her son or stepson from the sacred font, or held him for confirmation, and therefore has sought separation; in what branch of consanguinity marriages may take place; accusation of consanguinity and the persons by whom it must be made; inquiry into kinship; incestuous marriage; separation; and degrees of consanguinity, set forth in direct and collateral order. [Col. 1046A]

CAP. XLII. The eighth part contains material concerning voluntary and involuntary homicide, and what may be done without sin; what one who kills any cleric ought to make amends for; whether one who strikes a pregnant woman and causes an abortion has committed homicide or not; incantations and the various kinds of magical art; the nature of demons; lots; the observance of days and months; oaths, whether they ought to be kept or not and what obligations accompany them; and every kind of lie. [Col. 1046B]

# HERE BEGINS THE PANORMIA OF IVO, BISHOP OF CHARTRES

[Col. 1045] BOOK ONE: On faith, the various heresies, baptism, and the ministry of those to be baptized and baptized, consecrated and signed, etc.

# [PANORMIA OF IVO]

## CAP. I

[Col. 1045C]

We believe that there is one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. He is Father because He has a Son; Son because He has a Father; Holy Spirit because He is from the Father and the Son. Therefore the Father is the principle of the Godhead: just as He was never not God, so He was never not Father. From Him the Son was born; from Him the Holy Spirit is not born, because He is not the Son; nor is He unbegotten, because He is not the Father; nor was the Holy Spirit made, because He is not from nothing, but from God the Father and God the Son.

God the Father is eternal because He has an eternal Son, of whom He is the eternal Father; the Son is eternal because He is coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit; the Holy Spirit is eternal because He is coeternal with the Father and the Son. The Trinity is not confused into one person, as Sabellius says; nor is the Godhead separated or divided in nature, as Arius blasphemes. Rather, the Father is one person, the Son another person, and the Holy Spirit another person. Yet God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one in nature, in the holy Trinity.

## CAP. II. On the incarnation of Christ

It was not the Father who assumed flesh, nor the Holy Spirit, but the Son alone, so that He who was, in the Godhead, the Son of God the Father might become, in humanity, the son of man; and so that the name of Son might not pass to another who was not Son by birth. Thus He who was Son by birth from God became Son of man: born, according to the truth of His nature, Son of God from God, and, according to the truth of His nature, son of man from a human being. Thus, as the truly begotten One, He possessed the name of Son by birth in both respects—not by adoption, not merely by appellation—and was true God, true man, true Son.

## CAP. III

(23, question 3, chapter *Quidam autem* [“But certain persons”].) Therefore we do not confess two Christs or two Sons, but one Son, God and man. For this reason we call Him the Only-Begotten; and He remains in two natures, as the truth of those natures bestowed upon Him, the natures neither confused nor mingled, as the Timotheans wish, but united in fellowship. Therefore God assumed man; man passed into God—not by a change in the visible character of nature, as the third Apollinarians say, but by God’s condescension—so that God, in assuming man, was not changed into human substance, nor man, when glorified, into divine substance or God. For mutability or visibility of nature brings about both diminution and abolition of substance. [Col. 1046D]

We believe that the Trinity is joined without confusion and distinguished without separation. Thus the Son of God was born from a human being and not through a human being; that is, not from intercourse with a man, as Ebion says, but drawing flesh from the body of a virgin, and not bringing it with Him from heaven, as Marcion, Origen, and Eutyches affirm; nor existing in a phantom—that is, without flesh—as Valentinus teaches; nor *Aorchi*, that is, merely imagined or supposed. Rather, He had a true body: not flesh alone from flesh, as Marcianus says, but one Son, true God from divinity and true man from flesh; in His divinity the Father’s Word and God, and in His humanity soul and flesh. His soul was not without sense and reason, as Apollinaris taught; [Col. 1047B] nor was His flesh without a soul, as Anomoeus taught; rather, He had a soul with its reason and flesh with its senses, by which senses He endured real pains in the passion of His flesh and before the passion.

## CAP. IV. On Christ’s birth, against Artemon and the other heretics

Nor was He so born from the Virgin that, by being born as man, He received the beginning of His Godhead, as though He had not been God before being born from the Virgin, as Artemon, Beryllus, and Marcellus taught. Rather, the eternal God was born as man from the Virgin.

## CAP. V. On Christ’s birth, against heretics

Nothing created or servile is to be believed to exist in the Trinity, as Dionysius, the fountainhead of Arius, wished; nothing unequal, as Eunomius taught; nothing equal merely by grace, as Aetius wished; nothing earlier or later, or lesser, as Arius said; nothing alien or ministerial to another, as Macedonius taught; nothing inserted by persuasion or stealth, as the Manichaean taught; nothing bodily, as Melito and Tertullian taught; nothing given bodily form, as the Anthropomorphite and Vadian taught; nothing invisible to itself, as Origen taught; nothing visible to creatures, as Fortunatus taught; nothing diverse in character or will, as Marcion taught; nothing derived from the essence of the Trinity or from the nature of creatures, as Plato and Tertullian taught; nothing singular in office or communicable to another, as Origen taught; nothing confused, as Sabellius taught. Rather, all is perfect, because one is from the whole; yet not solitary, as Silvanus and Praxeas presume—that damnable Pentapolitan doctrine. [Col. 1047D]

## CAP. VI. What *homoousion* means, against the heretic Nestorius

Therefore the Son is *homoousion*—of the same substance—in the divinity of the Father; the Holy Spirit is *homoousion* with the Father and the Son. One Son is *homoousion* with God and man, remaining God in man; God in glory with the Father; desirable to be seen by angels; and, like the Father and the Holy Spirit, worshipped by angels and every creature. He is not a man on account of God, nor Christ together with God, as Nestorius blasphemes, but man in God and God in man.

## CAP. VII. On the faith of Trinity and unity, to be kept inviolate

[Col. 1048A] Saint Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book I, chapter 4.

[Note: [Col. 1047D] *De Consecratione*, distinction 3, chapter *Omnes*. It also shows what properly pertains to the Father, what to the Son, and what to the Holy Spirit.] All the Catholic interpreters of the old and new divine books whom I have been able to read, and who wrote before me on the Trinity—which is God—have aimed, according to the Scriptures, to teach that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit intimate the unity of one and the same substance in inseparable divine equality. Therefore they are not three gods, but one God. Although the Father begot the Son, and therefore the Son is not the one who is the Father; and the Son was begotten of the Father, and therefore the Father is not the one who is the Son; and the Holy Spirit is neither Father nor Son, but only the Spirit of the Father and the Son; and the Father is coeternal with the Son, himself also coequal and belonging to the unity of the Trinity [Col. 1048B]. Yet it was not this same Trinity that was born of the Virgin Mary, crucified under Pontius Pilate, buried, rose on the third day, and ascended into heaven, but the Son alone; nor was it this same Trinity that descended in the form of a dove upon Jesus when he was baptized, or on the day of Pentecost after the Lord’s ascension, when there came a sound from heaven as though a mighty rushing wind were borne along, and divided tongues like fire, but the Holy Spirit alone; nor was it this same Trinity that said from heaven, “You are my Son,” either when he was baptized by John (Matt. 3), or on the mountain when three disciples were with him (Matt. 17), or when the voice sounded, saying, “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John 12); rather, it was the voice of the Father addressed to the Son alone [Col. 1048C]. Although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, just as they are inseparable, also work inseparably. [Note: [Col. 1048D] What follows from here to the end of this chapter is not found in the chapter *Omnes quos*, *De Consecratione*, distinction 3.]

For by what understanding does a human being comprehend God, when that very understanding by which he wishes to comprehend him has not yet comprehended itself? But if one has already comprehended this, let him attend carefully and observe that in its own nature there is nothing better than it; and let him see whether he discerns there any outlines of shapes, brilliance of colors, comely magnitude, separation of parts, extension of bulk, movements through intervals of space, or anything of that sort. Surely we find none of these in that in which we find nothing better in our nature—that is, in our understanding, by which we apprehend wisdom, insofar as we are capable. Therefore, what we do not find in that which is better in us, we ought not seek in him who is far better than what is better in us [Col. 1048D], so that we may understand God, if possible, as far as we can: good without quality, great without quantity, creator without need, present without position, containing all things without outward condition, wholly everywhere without place, eternal without time, making mutable things without any change in himself, and suffering nothing. Whoever thinks of God in this way, even if he cannot yet altogether discover what he is, nevertheless piously takes care, so far as possible, not to think something of him that he is not. Yet he is without doubt substance—or, if this is better called *essence*—which the Greeks call *ousia* [οὐσία] [Col. 1049A].

## CHAPTER VIII. On the sacrament of baptism; on original sin and its remedy. St Augustine to Peter the deacon, chapter 26.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Firmissime*.) Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that every human being conceived through the sexual union of man and woman is born subject to impiety with original sin, subject to death, and for this reason born by nature a child of wrath, of which the Apostle says: “For we were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest.” From this wrath no one is freed except through faith in the Mediator between God and humankind, the man Jesus Christ, because he himself is the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world.

## CHAPTER IX. That infants who are in their mothers’ wombs are condemned, and adults unless they are baptized. [Col. 1049B] Likewise St Augustine to Peter, chapter 27.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Firmissime*.) “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3). Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt: not only persons already exercising reason, but also infants who either begin to live in their mothers’ wombs and die there, or have already been born from their mothers and depart from this world without the sacrament of holy baptism, which is given in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, are to be punished by the everlasting punishment of eternal fire. For, although they have committed no sin by their own act, they have nevertheless incurred the condemnation of original sin through carnal conception [Col. 1049C].

## CHAPTER X. Just as sins are now remitted in baptism, so formerly they were remitted in circumcision. Or: Before Christ’s coming, faith, sacrifice, and circumcision had the same efficacy as baptism now has. St Gregory, *Morals on Job*, book IV, chapter 2.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Quod autem*.) What the water of baptism accomplishes among us, faith alone accomplished among the ancients for infants; the efficacy of sacrifice for adults; and, for those sprung from Abraham’s lineage, the mystery of circumcision.

## CHAPTER XI. Original sin is now remitted in baptism, formerly in circumcision. St Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book II, [Col. 1049D] chapter 11.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Ex quo*.) From the time circumcision was instituted among the people of God, it was then the seal of the righteousness of faith in God and availed for the sanctification and cleansing of infants from original and ancient sin, just as baptism likewise began to avail, from the time it was instituted, for the renewal of the human being.

## CHAPTER XII. The faith of those presenting infants benefits them in baptism. Or: What baptism benefits infants who die immediately after baptism. St Augustine, *On Free Will*, book III, chapter 23.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Illud perscrutari*.) People are accustomed to inquire what benefit the sacrament of Christ’s baptism brings infants, since after receiving it they often die [Col. 1050A] before they are able to know anything on their own. In this matter it is sufficiently, piously, and rightly believed that the faith of those by whom the infant is presented for consecration benefits the infant. The Church’s most salutary authority commends this, so that from this each person may recognize how his own faith benefits him, when it is beneficial also on behalf of others who do not yet possess power over themselves.

## CHAPTER XIII. Resolution of the preceding canon. Infants are baptized by another’s faith and profession. St Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 24.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Parvuli*.) Infants are baptized while another makes profession for them, because they do not yet know how to speak or believe. So too with the sick, mute, and deaf: another makes profession in their place and answers for them while they are baptized.

## CHAPTER XIV. A similar rule concerning the sick, who cannot speak. Or: The sick are to be baptized on another’s testimony. [Col. 1050B] Third Council of Carthage, chapter 34.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Aegrotantes*.) If sick persons cannot answer for themselves, they are to be baptized when they have given testimony of their own will; the same procedure is to be followed for penitents.

## CHAPTER XV. An argument from the contrary sense of the preceding canon. Or: Those who can answer are not baptized unless they answer at baptism. St Augustine, *On Baptism*, book V, chapter 24.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Cum pro parvulis*, § *At si pro eo*.) If someone else answers in baptism for one who can answer for himself, it does not have the same validity. From this rule comes the saying in the Gospel which, whenever it is read, naturally instructs everyone: “He is of age; let him speak for himself” (John 9) [Col. 1050C].

## CHAPTER XVI. General baptism is to be celebrated only on the Saturday of holy Easter and at Pentecost. Or: Let no one be baptized on the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, or the festivals of apostles or saints, unless necessity requires it. Pope Leo I, letter 1 to Imerius of Tarragona.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Non ratione*.) It is not by the reason of any authority, but by rash presumption alone, that, as you assert, countless multitudes indiscriminately and freely receive the mystery of baptism on Christ’s Nativity or Manifestation, and also on festivals of apostles or martyrs. This privilege is specially reserved among us, and in all Churches, for the Lord’s Passover together with holy Pentecost [Col. 1050D].

## CHAPTER XVII. That there are two times for baptizing: namely, Easter and Pentecost. Likewise Pope Leo, letter 1 to bishops established throughout Sicily.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Duo tempora*; and chapter *Non potest*, in the same distinction.) You clearly recognize that, in the baptism of those chosen, who according to apostolic rule are to be examined by exorcisms, sanctified by fasts, and instructed by frequent preaching, only two seasons are to be observed: Easter and Pentecost.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Why Christ our Lord wished to be baptized on the feast of Epiphany, and that one grace is bestowed in the baptism of the Holy Spirit, by which we are reborn, and another in John’s baptism. Likewise Pope Leo, letter 4 to bishops established throughout Sicily.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Si quis autem*.) If anyone thinks that the feast of Epiphany—which in its proper order is to be venerated with due honor—has the privilege of baptism because they suppose that the Lord came to the baptism of Saint John on that day, let him know that that baptism had a different grace and a different rationale; nor did it belong to that same power by which those are reborn through the Holy Spirit, of whom it is said: “Who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God” (John 1). For the Lord [Col. 1051B], needing no remission of sin and seeking no remedy of rebirth, wished to be baptized just as he wished to be circumcised and to have an offering for purification offered for himself: so that he who had been made of a woman, as the Apostle says, might also be made under the law (Gal. 4), which he had not come to abolish but to fulfill, and by fulfilling to bring to an end, as the blessed Apostle proclaims, saying: “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10). But he established in himself the sacrament of his baptism, because, holding primacy in all things (Col. 1), he taught that he himself is the beginning. And he ratified the power of regeneration when from his side flowed the blood of redemption and the water of baptism.

## CHAPTER XIX. That baptism may be administered at every time when necessity is pressing. [Col. 1051C] Leo I, letter 4.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Si quis ex necessitate*.) Moreover, those who are pressed by the necessity of death, illness, siege, persecution, or shipwreck ought to be baptized at every time. Therefore we enjoin this upon your charity: do not hereafter depart in any transgression from apostolic institutions; for it cannot go unpunished after this if anyone considers apostolic rules to be neglected in any respect.

## CHAPTER XX. Catechumens are to be baptized at the Easter and Pentecost solemnities. Council of Gerona, chapter 4.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *De catechumenis*.) Concerning the baptism of catechumens, it is decreed that they are to be baptized at the solemnity of Easter or Pentecost; at other solemnities, only the sick are to be baptized [Col. 1051D].

## CHAPTER XXI. Unless necessity compels, let no one presume to baptize between Easter and Pentecost. Gelasius to the clergy and people of Taranto.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Venerabilis*.) Let no bishop presume to administer the venerable sacrament of baptism except at the Easter solemnity and Pentecost, apart from those suffering illness, whom, when the danger of death presses, must be assisted by such remedies lest they perish eternally.

## CHAPTER XXII. GREGORY TO AUGUSTINE.

There is absolutely no prohibition against baptizing either the woman herself, if she is in danger of death, even at the very hour when she gives birth, or the child that is born [Col. 1052A], at the same hour in which it has been born.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That only priests ought to baptize. Or: Let no one except a priest presume to baptize. Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 24.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Constat*.) It is established that baptism has been entrusted to priests alone; nor is it lawful even for deacons to perform its ministry without a bishop or presbyter, except in cases where, in their remote absence, the extreme necessity of illness compels it. This is also often permitted to lay faithful persons.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That laypersons ought to baptize in necessity. [Col. 1052B] Gelasius to bishops established throughout Lucania and Sicily.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *In necessitate*.) Christian laypersons are often permitted to baptize.

## CHAPTER XXV. A woman ought in no manner to baptize. Or: Let no woman presume to baptize.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Mulier*.) Let no woman presume to baptize.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Even laypersons may baptize when necessity compels. Augustine to Fortunatus.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *In necessitate*.) In an emergency, when bishops, presbyters, or any ministers cannot be found and the danger to the person requesting it is pressing, lest he end this life without this sacrament, we are accustomed to hear that even laypersons administer the sacrament which they have received [Col. 1052C].

## CHAPTER XXVII. A pagan can baptize. Or: Baptism administered by a pagan is not to be repeated. From the Decrees of Bishop Isidore.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Romanus*.) The Roman pontiff judges not the person who baptizes, but the Holy Spirit to supply the grace of baptism, even though the one who baptizes is a pagan.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. A heretic can baptize. Or: Baptism administered in the name of the Trinity is not repeated. St Augustine to Orosius, book II, question 65.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Quamvis*.) Although there is one baptism both among heretics—that is, those who baptize in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and in the Catholic Church, nevertheless, because they are baptized outside the Church, they receive baptism not unto salvation but unto destruction: they possess, indeed, the form of the sacrament, but deny its power [Col. 1052D].

## CHAPTER XXIX. A Jew can baptize. Or: Baptism is not repeated if it is administered by a Jew. Nicholas, in response to the Bulgarians’ inquiries, chapter 3.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *A quodam*.) You assert that many persons in your country have been baptized by a certain Jew, though you do not know whether he was a Christian or a pagan, and you ask what is to be done about this. Certainly, if they were baptized in the name of the holy Trinity, or even only in the name of Christ, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles [Col. 1053A], it is one and the same baptism, because it belongs not to them but to him, as Saint Ambrose explains.

## CHAPTER XXX. That baptism administered by good and evil ministers is always good. Or: Baptism is administered equally through a good and through an evil minister. St Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, book III, chapter 69.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Si inter*.) Although among good ministers one is better than another, the baptism given through the better minister is not better; likewise, one given even through an evil minister is by no means evil, when he gives the same baptism. Therefore, through unequal ministers God’s gift is equal, because it belongs not to them but to him.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Not the merits of ministers, but Christ’s power, works in baptism. [Col. 1053B] Augustine, *Tractates on John*, tractate V.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Baptismus*.) Baptism is such as he is in whose power it is given, not such as he is through whose ministry it is given. Likewise: What did the Baptist know of the Lord? He knew that the power of the Lord’s baptism would pass from the Lord to no human being, though the ministry would certainly pass on. The power passes from the Lord to no one, but the ministry passes to good and evil persons. Likewise: I say, and we all say, that those through whom baptism is administered ought to be righteous, because the ministers of so great a Judge ought to be righteous. They are righteous ministers if they wish to be. But if those sitting in Moses’ chair did not wish to be righteous [Col. 1053C], my teacher made me secure, he of whom his Spirit says: “This is he who baptizes.” Likewise: Those whom Judas baptized, Christ baptized. Therefore, if a drunkard baptized, if a murderer baptized, if an adulterer baptized—if it was Christ’s baptism—Christ baptized. I do not fear the drunkard, adulterer, or murderer, because I look to the dove through whom it is said to me: “This is he who baptizes.” Again, a murderer administered Christ’s baptism. This sacrament is so holy that it is not defiled even when a murderer ministers it.

## CHAPTER XXXII. The baptism and sacrilege of heretics are not sacraments. Or: It is found that the apostles said, “my ministry,” “my Gospel,” but never “my baptism.” [Col. 1053D] St Augustine, *On the One Baptism*, book III, chapter 11.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Nunc autem*.) Now, just as heresy belongs to heretics, just as their error belongs to them, and just as the sacrilege of their dissension belongs to them, so also the baptism—which is Christ’s—ought to be called theirs.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Of the same argument as the preceding. St Augustine, ibid., book V, chapter 13.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Cum tantum*.) Since baptism given through a contemptible person has precisely as much efficacy as baptism given through an Apostle, it is recognized to be neither his nor the other’s, but Christ’s. Likewise: We find the apostles speaking of “my glory” (Phil. 2), although it was of course imparted and bestowed by the Lord; but none of them ever at all called baptism “mine” [Col. 1054A]. For not all glory is equal; not all minister equally; not all are endowed with equal prudence; in the Gospel one works better than another; and therefore one may be called more learned than another even in the doctrine of salvation itself. But no one can be called baptized more or less than another, whether baptized by an inferior or a superior.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the same matter. St Augustine, *On Baptism*, book IV, chapter 15.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Satis*.) We have sufficiently shown that, for baptism consecrated by Gospel words, neither the error of the giver nor that of the recipient concerning the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit—that is, if either thinks otherwise than heavenly doctrine teaches—has any bearing on baptism.

## CHAPTER XXXV. That every person approaching baptism ought first to do penance, if there is opportunity. Or: One who does not repent of the old life does not pass into the new life. [Col. 1054B] St Augustine, *On the Remedy of Penance*, book II, chapter 2.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Omnis*.) Everyone who has become master of his own will, when approaching the sacrament of the faithful, cannot begin the new life unless he repents of the old life. Infants alone are exempt from this repentance when they are baptized, for they cannot yet exercise free choice.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the same. St Augustine, letter 108, to Seleucianus.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Agunt*.) Before baptism people do penance for former sins, but still are baptized, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles, when Peter spoke to the Jews and said: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 1) [Col. 1054C].

## CHAPTER XXXVII. For how many days before baptism ought a Jew to do penance? Or: A forty-day abstinence is added for Jews who are to be baptized. St Gregory, to Faustinus the defender, book VII, letter 24.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Ne, quod absit*.) Lest, God forbid, a long delay should be able to turn Jewish minds back, baptize them, with our brother the bishop of that place, after penance and abstinence have been imposed for forty days, either on Sunday or, should a particularly celebrated feast perhaps occur, under the protection of Almighty God’s mercy [Col. 1054D].

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. That, by the Lord’s authority, persons ought to be catechized before baptism. Or: The office of catechizing ought to precede baptism. Rabanus, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, book I, chapter 25.

Before baptism, the office of catechizing ought to come first in a person, or the catechumen should first receive the rudiments of faith. Likewise: Jesus himself first anointed the eyes of the man born blind with mud made from spittle, and then sent him to the waters of Siloam, because the candidate for baptism must first be admitted as a believer through faith, so that he may know in what grace he shares and to whom he thereafter becomes indebted.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. At what time catechumens are to be brought for exorcism. Or: For how many days before baptism ought a catechumen to be instructed? [Col. 1055A] Second Council of Braga, chapter 8.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Ante viginti*.) Twenty days before baptism, catechumens are to come for the cleansing of exorcism; throughout those twenty days they are to be taught spiritually in every respect the Creed, namely, “I believe in God the Father.”

## CHAPTER XL. In every church, catechumens who are to be baptized may be exorcized. Or: The priests of each church may perform catechisms. Pope Nicholas to John, Archbishop of Ravenna.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Catechismi*.) Catechisms of those to be baptized may be conducted by the priests of each Church [Col. 1055B], just as they are shown to be solemnly conducted in this holy Roman Church, in which, by God’s ordering, we perform the ministry of our service.

## CHAPTER XLI. What exsufflation signifies in baptism, and why those to be baptized are exorcized and exsufflated. Rabanus, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, book I, chapter 27.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Postquam*.) After the candidate for baptism has, by confession of the true faith, entrusted himself to another’s lordship, and by renunciation withdrawn himself from the service of his former possessor, the cruel power is breathed out from him, so that, through the devout ministry of the priest, the malignant spirit may flee and yield place to the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the same. [Col. 1055C] Augustine, *On the Creed*, book I.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Sicut nostis*.) As you know, infants too are exsufflated and exorcized, in order that the hostile power of the devil, which deceived humankind so as to possess human beings, may be driven from them. Therefore it is not God’s creature in infants that is exorcized or breathed upon, but he under whom those born subject to sin are placed.

## CHAPTER XLIII. Why the candidate for baptism is signed on heart and forehead. Rabanus, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, book I, chapter 27.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Postea*.) Afterwards the candidate for baptism is marked with the sign of the holy cross both on the forehead and on the heart, so that the apostate devil himself, recognizing in his vessel the sign of his former destruction, may know that it is henceforth alien to him [Col. 1055D].

## CHAPTER XLIV. Why prayers are said over those to be baptized, and what the salt placed in the mouth signifies. Rabanus, ibid.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Ex hinc*.) Thereafter prayers are said over him so that he may become a catechumen. Then blessed salt is given into the mouth of the candidate for baptism, so that, seasoned by the symbolic salt of wisdom, he may be free from the stench of wickedness; so that he may no longer decay through the worms of sins, but may instead be kept unharmed for receiving greater grace.

## CHAPTER XLV. Why salt is given in initiation to catechumens. Bede, on 1 Kings, book I, chapter 27.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Sal coelestis*.) We are commanded to offer, in all the sacrifices of our deeds, the salt of heavenly wisdom [Col. 1056A] by which catechumens are initiated.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Why candidates for baptism are exorcized again. Rabanus, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, book I, chapter 27.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Dehinc*.) They are then exorcized again, so that the devil, recognizing his own wickedness and fearing God’s just judgment over himself, may withdraw from the person and no longer strive by his artifice to overthrow him, lest he attain baptism; but rather, rendering honor to God his Creator, may restore God’s work to God his Creator.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On the same. Priests drive away demons by exorcizing. Gregory, homily 29 on the Gospels.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Sacerdotes*.) When priests, through the grace of exorcism, lay hands on believers and forbid malignant spirits to dwell in their minds, what else do they do but cast out demons? [Col. 1056B]

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Why the ears and nostrils are touched with spittle. Rabanus, as above.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Postea*.) Afterwards their nostrils and ears are touched with spittle, and the Gospel word is spoken to them which Jesus said when he healed the mute and deaf man: touching his tongue with spittle and putting his finger into his ear, he said, “Ephpheta,” that is, “Be opened” (Mark 7). For this sacrament is performed here so that, through the symbolic spittle and touch of the priest, divine wisdom and power may bring about the salvation [Col. 1056C] of that catechumen: that his nostrils may be opened to receive the fragrance of the knowledge of God, and his ears opened to hear God’s commands and to answer with understanding in the inward heart.

## CHAPTER XLIX. Why the bishop touches the nostrils, not the mouth, of those to be baptized. Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book I, chapter 1.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Propter gloriam*.) For the glory of the gift and work, the bishop touches not the mouth but the nostrils. Why the nostrils? So that you may receive the sweet fragrance of eternal piety.

## CHAPTER L. Why the candidate is anointed by the priest on the breast and between the shoulders. Rabanus, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, book I, chapter 27.

Then he is anointed by the priest so that the sacred baptism received with faith may be preserved [Col. 1056D]. His breast is then anointed with sanctified oil, with invocation of the holy Trinity, so that no remnants of the hidden enemy may remain in him, but his mind may be strengthened in faith in the holy Trinity. He is also anointed between the shoulders with the same oil, so that he may be protected on every side and strengthened by God’s grace to perform good works.

## CHAPTER LI. Why the baptized are anointed by the priest. Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book I, chapter 2.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Venisti*.) You came to the font and entered it. Consider what you saw, what you said, and recall it carefully. The Levite met you; the presbyter met you. You were anointed as an athlete of Christ, so that you might approach baptism as a catechumen.

## CHAPTER LII. Words of error uttered through ignorance do not prevent the sanctification of water. [Col. 1057A] Augustine, *On the One Baptism*, book VI, chapter 25.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Si non sanctificatur*.) Let the font be consecrated and the catechumen approach baptism. If water is not sanctified when a sinner, through ignorance, utters certain erroneous words, then many brothers—not only evil but also good—in the Church itself do not sanctify water.

## CHAPTER LIII. Words of error uttered through ignorance nevertheless do not prevent the sanctification of water. Or: An unlearned minister sanctifies water through the Gospel words by which baptism is consecrated, even though in that consecration he may utter many things contrary to the faith. Augustine, *On the One Baptism*, book V, chapter 25.

[Col. 1057B] (*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Si non sanctificatur*, near the beginning.) For the prayers of many are corrected daily when recited to more learned persons, and much is found in them contrary to the Catholic faith. If it is discovered that some persons were baptized while these prayers were being said over the water, are they commanded to be baptized again? Why not? Because the affection of the one praying generally overcomes a defect in the prayer; and because those, or at any rate all, Gospel words without which baptism cannot be consecrated have such power that, through them, whatever defective matter contrary to the rule of faith is said in the prayer is annulled, just as a demon is expelled in Christ’s name. Certainly, if a heretic offers a defective prayer, he does not have the good affection of charity by which such ignorance may be overcome. Thus any person in the Catholic Church who is unclean, envious, or malevolent—as Cyprian here censures such people—and offers even, as often happens, a prayer in which he speaks contrary to the rule of faith, is like him. For many people introduce into prayers compositions not only by unlearned and talkative persons but also by heretics; and, through the simplicity of ignorance, not wishing to distinguish them, they use them while believing that they are good. Yet what is perverse in them does not annul what is right there; rather, it is annulled by what is right [Col. 1057C].

## CHAPTER LIV. The malice of the one blessing does not pass into the water of baptism. Augustine, *On Baptism*, book III, chapter 10.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Non est aqua*.) Water over which God’s name is invoked is neither profane nor adulterous, even if it is invoked by profane and adulterous persons, because neither the creature itself nor the name itself is adulterous [Col. 1057D].

## CHAPTER LV. What the mysteries celebrated at the baptismal font signify. Or: How the words are to be understood: “Do you believe in God, in the holy Church, in the remission of sins, and in the resurrection of the flesh?” Augustine, homily 3 to the newly baptized.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Prima igitur*.) In the first and second instruction, therefore, we spoke only about those things which, before you came to the font, we delivered to you according to the ordinances of the Catholic rule. We interpreted, insofar as God deigned to grant it, what the anointing signified—the anointing applied to different parts of your bodies and signifying different meanings [Col. 1058A]—when we showed that by the oil of sanctification you had been prepared to hear the fullness of faith, called with your whole heart to the sweet fragrance of Christ, and fortified for renouncing the devil.

But now we shall speak about the inward mysteries celebrated in the sacred font itself. For after you had given the most certain pledge that you renounced all his pomps and works and every diabolical fornication, you descended into the sacred font: the font of redemption, the font sanctified by heavenly power. Likewise: Before immersing you bodily in this font, we asked: “Do you believe in God the Father almighty?” You answered: “I believe.” Again we asked: “Do you also believe in Jesus Christ his Son, who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary?” You answered: “I also believe.” Likewise we asked: “And [do you believe] in the Holy Spirit?” You likewise answered: “I believe.” This we did according to the command of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior, who, when ascending to the Father in heaven, commanded the disciples—that is, the apostles—saying: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

Likewise: When we asked, “Do you believe the holy Church, remission of sins, and resurrection of the flesh?” we did not ask in the manner in which one believes in God: “Do you believe *in* the holy and Catholic Church?” It is holy and Catholic because it rightly believes in God. Therefore we did not say that you should believe in the Church as in God; rather, understand us to have said, and to say, that while living in the holy Catholic Church, you should believe in God [Col. 1058C]. You should also believe in the resurrection of the flesh which is to come.

## CHAPTER LVI. What it is to believe. Or: It is not time, but faith itself—the sacrament of faith—that makes an infant faithful. Augustine, letter 23, to Boniface.
