(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Nihil est*.) To believe is nothing other than to have faith. Thus, when it is answered that an infant believes, though he does not yet possess the effect of faith, the answer is that he has faith by reason of the sacrament of faith; and that he turns to God by reason of the sacrament of conversion, because the response itself pertains to the celebration of the sacrament. Likewise, although an infant does not yet possess that faith which consists in the will of believers, nevertheless the sacrament of that very faith already makes him faithful [Col. 1058D]. For just as it is answered that they believe, so they are called faithful—not because they assent in mind to the thing itself, but because they receive the sacrament of that thing.

## CHAPTER LVII. Why a threefold immersion ought to be performed in baptism. Augustine, homily 4.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Postquam*.) After you promised to believe, we immersed your heads in the font three times. This order of baptism is celebrated with a twofold signification of mystery. You were rightly immersed three times, because you received baptism in the name of Jesus Christ, who rose from the dead on the third day. For that immersion repeated three times expresses the type of the Lord’s burial, through which you were buried with Christ in baptism and rose with Christ in faith; so that, washed from sins, you might live in Christ by imitating him in the holiness of virtues [Col. 1059A].

## CHAPTER LVIII. On the same; concerning those who are immersed once rather than three times in baptism. Apostolic Constitutions, canon 150.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Si quis*.) If any presbyter or bishop does not celebrate the threefold immersion of the one mystery, but immerses only once in the baptism which he is commanded to administer, into the Lord’s death, let him be deposed. For the Lord did not say to me, “Baptize into my death,” but: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit” (Matt. [Col. 1059B] 28).

## CHAPTER LIX. It is permissible to immerse once in baptism. Or: One immersion in the name of the holy Trinity is sufficient. Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 5.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Propter*.) To avoid the scandal of schism or the practice of heretical doctrine, let us maintain the threefold immersion of baptism.

## CHAPTER LX. That either may be done: one immersion or three. Gregory to the bishops of Spain.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *De trina*.) Nothing truer can be answered concerning the threefold immersion of baptism than what you yourselves think: within one faith, a differing custom does no harm to the holy Church. We, however [Col. 1059C], who immerse three times signify the mysteries of the three-day burial, so that, when the infant is raised from the water for the third time, the resurrection of the three-day period may be expressed. But if someone should perhaps think that this is done for reverence toward the supreme Trinity, neither does it in any way prevent the candidate for baptism from being immersed once in water. For, since one substance exists in three substances, it can in no way be blameworthy to immerse an infant in baptism either three times or once: in three immersions the Trinity of persons may be signified, and in one the unity of the Godhead.

## CHAPTER LXI. On the same. Jerome, *Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians*, chapter 4.

(*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter *Eodem modo*.) In the same manner we are baptized into the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit [Col. 1059D], and are immersed three times, so that the one sacrament of the Trinity may be manifest. Likewise: Although baptism is administered three times on account of the mystery of the Trinity, it is nevertheless reckoned one baptism.

## CHAPTER LXII. Concerning those who are immersed only once in the name of Christ. Or: That one must not baptize in the name of the Father alone, in the name of the Son alone, or in the name of the Holy Spirit alone. Pelagius
To Gaudentius.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Multi*.) Many people claim that they are baptized in the name of Christ alone, even with a single immersion. But the evangelical command, handed down by the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ himself, instructs us to confer holy baptism upon every person in the name of the Trinity, with a threefold immersion, as our Lord Jesus Christ said to his disciples: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). If those of the aforesaid heretics who are said to live near the places under your care perhaps confess that they were baptized only in the name of the Lord, then, without any uncertainty or doubt, you shall baptize them, when they come to the Catholic faith, in the name of the Holy Trinity.

### CHAPTER LXIII. At baptism we must immerse three times with invocation of the Trinity. Pope Zacharias to Bishop Boniface.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *In synodo*.) At the synod of the English it is recognized that this was most firmly decreed, commanded, and carefully demonstrated: whoever had been immersed without invocation of the Trinity did not possess the sacrament of regeneration. This is wholly true, because if anyone has been immersed in the font of baptism without invocation of the Holy Trinity, that person is not a complete Christian unless baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The priests at the aforesaid synod also wished this to be observed: anyone who failed to name even one person of the Trinity in baptism could not have performed a true baptism. This is certainly true, because one who has not confessed one name of the Holy Trinity cannot be a complete Christian. For whoever confesses the Father and the Son but has not confessed the Holy Spirit has neither the Father nor the Son; and whoever confesses the Father and the Holy Spirit but has not confessed the Son has neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit, and is empty of divine grace.

### CHAPTER LXIV. Those not baptized in the name of the Trinity must be baptized. Gregory, book IX of the *Letters*, letter 61.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Hi vero*.) Those heretics who are in no way baptized in the name of the Trinity—such as the Bonosians and Cataphrygians—must be baptized when they come to the holy Church. For the former do not believe in Christ the Lord, and the latter perversely believe that the Holy Spirit is a certain insignificant man, Montanus; and many others resemble them. What they received while established in error was not baptism, since they did not receive it in the name of the Holy Trinity.

### CHAPTER LXV. Priests baptize validly even when they make mistakes in Latin. Or: On a priest who, through ignorance of Latin, erred in the invocation of the Trinity. Pope Zacharias, in a decretal letter.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Retulerunt*.) Your messengers reported that in that province there was a priest wholly ignorant of Latin. When baptizing, unable to speak Latin and mangling the language, he would say: “I baptize you in the name of the *Patria* [fatherland/father], and the *Filia* [daughter], and the *Spiritua sancta* [holy spirit].” Your reverend brotherhood therefore considered rebaptizing. But, most holy brother, if he who baptized, introducing neither error nor heresy, but solely through ignorance of Roman speech and through mangling the language, said these words while baptizing, as we have stated above, we cannot agree that the person should be baptized anew.

### CHAPTER LXVI. Why one baptized is anointed by the priest on the head. Rabanus, book I, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, ch. 21.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Postquam*.) After the baptized person has come up from the font, he is immediately signed by the presbyter upon the head with holy chrism, together with the accompanying prayer, so that he may become a participant in Christ’s kingdom and may be called a Christian from Christ.

### CHAPTER LXVII. On the same matter: what is said over the baptized person. Ambrose, book II, *On the Sacraments*, ch. 7.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Emersisti*.) You were immersed; you came to the priest. What did he say to you? “God,” he says, “the almighty Father, who has regenerated you from water and the Holy Spirit and granted you forgiveness of your sins, may he himself anoint you unto eternal life.” See where you were anointed: “unto eternal life,” he says.

### CHAPTER LXVIII. Why ointment is placed upon the baptized person’s head. Ambrose, *On Those Initiated into the Mysteries*, ch. 6.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Accepisti*.) You receive the mystery—that is, the ointment upon the head. Why upon the head? Because “the understanding of the wise man is in his head” (Eccl. 2). There follows the spiritual seal, which you heard read today, which remains after the font, in order that perfection may be accomplished when, through the priest’s invocation, the Holy Spirit is poured out.

### CHAPTER LXIX. What the white garment placed over the baptized person’s head signifies. Or: Why a white garment is given to Christians. Rabanus, book I, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, ch. 29.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Post bapt.*.) After baptism, a white garment is given to the baptized Christian. It signifies Christian innocence and purity, which, after the old stains have been washed away, the person must preserve unstained through devotion to holy conduct, so as to appear before Christ’s tribunal. All who are reborn are clothed in white garments as a mystery of the Church’s resurrection. Likewise: baptized persons use white garments, so that the garment of the glory of their second regeneration may display outwardly what the dark covering of ancient error had marred in the appearance of their first birth. After the holy anointing, moreover, the person’s head is covered with a mystical veil, so that he may understand that he possesses the diadem of a kingdom and priestly dignity.

### CHAPTER LXX. On the same matter. Ambrose, book *On Those Initiated*.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Accepisti*.) After baptism you received white garments, as an indication that you had put off the pleasures of sins and put on the chaste coverings of innocence.

### CHAPTER LXXI. For how many months Jews are to remain among the catechumens. Council of Agde, ch. 34.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Judaei*.) If Jews, whose faithlessness frequently returns to its vomit, wish to come to the Catholic laws, they shall enter the threshold of the Church as catechumens for eight months. If they are known to come in sincere faith, only then may they receive the grace of baptism. But if during the prescribed period they should incur the danger of illness and be given up for lost, they shall be baptized.

### CHAPTER LXXII. Just as Jews are not to be compelled to the faith, so those converted are not to be allowed to depart from it. Fourth Council of Toledo, ch. 56.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *De Judaeis*.) Concerning the Jews, the holy synod decreed this: henceforth no one is to have force imposed upon him in order to believe. “For God has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills” (Rom. 9). Such persons are not to be saved unwillingly, but willingly, so that the order of justice may remain intact: just as each human being perished by obeying the serpent through his own free choice, so each is saved through faith by the conversion of his own mind when called by God’s grace. Therefore they should be summoned to conversion not by force but through free choice; they should be invited, not driven.

But those who were long ago compelled into Christianity—as happened in the time of the most religious prince Sisebut—are known already to have been joined to the divine sacraments, received baptismal grace, been anointed with chrism, and become partakers of the Lord’s body and blood. They must be compelled to retain the faith which they received either through force or necessity, lest the Lord’s name be blasphemed and the faith they received be regarded as cheap and contemptible.

### CHAPTER LXXIII. Baptized Jewish children are not to live with their parents. Or: Believers are to be separated from association with their parents, lest they be entangled in their errors. Likewise, Fourth Council of Toledo, ch. 59.

(28, question 1, ch. *Judaeorum*.) We decree that baptized Jewish sons or daughters be separated from their parents’ company, lest they be further entangled in their parents’ errors. They are to be entrusted either to monasteries or to God-fearing Christian men or women, so that under their manner of life they may learn the worship of faith and, being established in a better condition, may advance both in morals and in faith.

### CHAPTER LXXIV. Jews coming to the faith are to have no association with unbelievers. Likewise, Fourth Council of Toledo, ch. 61.

(28, question 1, ch. *Saepe mal.*.) Associations with the wicked often corrupt even the good, much more those inclined toward vices. Therefore Hebrews transferred to the Christian faith are henceforth to have no communion with those who still remain in the old rite, lest perhaps they be overthrown through sharing with them. Accordingly, any baptized persons among them who henceforth do not avoid association with unbelievers shall themselves be handed over to Christians, while the others shall be assigned to public beatings.

### CHAPTER LXXV. On the many Jews who frequently return to Judaism. Likewise, Fourth Council of Toledo, ch. 58.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Plerique*.) Many who were formerly brought over from the Jews to the Christian faith are now blaspheming Christ. Not only have they practiced Jewish rites, but they also perform abominable circumcisions. At the counsel of our most pious and religious lord, King Sisemund, this holy council decrees that such transgressors, corrected by episcopal authority, be recalled to the worship of Christian doctrine, so that priestly discipline may restrain those whom their own will does not amend. Those whom they have circumcised, if they are their children, shall be separated from their parents’ society; if slaves, they shall be granted freedom in compensation for the injury to their bodies.

### CHAPTER LXXVI. On the baptism of pagans. Before baptism we must renounce the devil and his works. Rabanus, book I, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, ch. 27.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Primum*.) First the pagan should be asked whether he renounces the devil and all his damnable works and every deceit, so that he may first reject error and then draw near to truth. Thus, in accordance with the Apostle, he may put off “the old man according to the former manner of life, which is corrupted according to the desires of error” (Eph. 4), renouncing impiety and worldly desires (Tit. 2).

### CHAPTER LXXVII. When necessity compels, the same sponsor may serve at catechizing and confirmation. From the Decrees of Pope Hyginus, ch. 10.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *In catech.*.) At catechizing, baptism, and confirmation, one and the same sponsor may be made if necessity requires it. This is not, however, Roman custom; rather, individuals are received one by one by individual sponsors.

### CHAPTER LXXVIII. Not more than one person, but one alone, is to receive a child at baptism. From the Decrees of Pope Leo at Saint-Médard.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Non plures*.) Not more than one person, whether man or woman, is to approach to receive an infant from baptism. The same is also to be done at confirmation.

### CHAPTER LXXIX. One who is neither baptized nor confirmed must not hold another at chrism or baptism. Council of Mainz, ch. 2.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *In baptismo*.) At baptism or chrism, one who has not been baptized and confirmed cannot receive another as a child.

### CHAPTER LXXX. An abbot or monk may not have godmothers. Council of Auxerre, ch. 25.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Non licet*.) It is not permitted for an abbot or monks to receive infants from baptism or to have godmothers.

### CHAPTER LXXXI. On the same matter. *Capitulary*, title VII, ch. 15.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Monachi*.) Monks are not to make for themselves godfathers or godmothers, nor are they to kiss women.

### CHAPTER LXXXII. Those who receive little children at baptism stand surety for them before God. From a sermon of Saint Augustine after Easter beginning, “This day.”

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Vos ante*.) Before all else, I admonish you, both men and women, who have received children at baptism: recognize that you have stood as sureties before God for those whom you received from the sacred font. Therefore always admonish them to preserve chastity, love justice, and maintain charity. Above all, both hold yourselves and teach to those whom you received from the sacred font the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer.

### CHAPTER LXXXIII. Neither rebaptisms nor reordinations are to be permitted. First Council of Carthage, ch. 33.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Non liceat*.) Rebaptisms, reordinations, and transfers of bishops are not to be permitted.

### CHAPTER LXXXIV. On the same matter. Augustine, letter 203, to Maximinus.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Rebaptiz.*.) To rebaptize a heretical person who has received these signs of holiness transmitted by Christian discipline is altogether sinful. But to rebaptize a Catholic is a most monstrous crime.

### CHAPTER LXXXV. One baptized by heretics is not to be rebaptized. Bede, homily 36 on John, ch. 3.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. 51, *Sive haereticus*.) Whether heretic, schismatic, or criminal, anyone baptized with confession of the Holy Trinity cannot be rebaptized by good Catholics, lest the confession or invocation of so great a name seem to be annulled.

### CHAPTER LXXXVI. Baptism administered in the name of the Trinity is not repeated. Augustine, *On Ecclesiastical Rules*, ch. 52.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Si qui*.) For this reason the Catholic Church ought not to repeat baptism because it was given among heretics: otherwise it would seem to judge that what belongs to Christ belongs to them, or that they do not possess what, once received within, they certainly could not lose by going outside.

### CHAPTER LXXXVII. One who departs from the Church loses neither baptism nor the right to administer it. Augustine, book II *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, ch. 13.

(1, question 1, ch. *Quod quidam*.) The sacrament of baptism is possessed by the one who is baptized, and the sacrament of administering baptism is possessed by the one who is ordained. Just as a baptized person does not lose the sacrament of baptism if he departs while baptized, so also an ordained person does not lose the sacrament of administering baptism if he departs from unity. No sacrament is to be treated with injury. If one departs from the wicked, both depart; if one remains among the wicked, both remain. Therefore, just as baptism is accepted which the person who departed from unity could not lose, so baptism given by one who, in departing, did not lose the sacrament of administering it must also be accepted.

### CHAPTER LXXXVIII. Those baptized by heretics must be reconciled. Or: How those baptized by heretics in the name of the Trinity are received by the Church. Gregory, book IX, letter 61, to Quirinus.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Ab antiqua*.) From the ancient institution of the Fathers we have learned that all who are baptized among heretics in the name of the Trinity, when they return to the holy Church, are to be restored to the bosom of Mother Church either by anointing with chrism, by the laying on of hands, or by profession of faith alone. Accordingly, the West restores Arians by laying on of hands, while the East restores them to entrance into Catholicism through anointing with holy chrism.

### CHAPTER LXXXIX. On the same matter. Gregory III to Boniface.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Illi*.) Those baptized amid the diversity and corruption of the languages of the nations, nevertheless having been baptized in the name of the Trinity, must be confirmed by the laying on of hands and anointing with sacred chrism.

### CHAPTER XC. Those who say that they were baptized in the name of the Trinity are not to be rebaptized, but only reconciled. Pope Pelagius to Bishop Gaudentius.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Nullus*.) But if a clear confession by those wishing to convert should establish before your charity that they were baptized in the name of the Trinity, then, when the grace of reconciliation alone has been imparted, you shall hasten to reconcile them to the Catholic faith. Thus, with such ordering or dispensation observed, nothing may appear to have been undertaken in a spirit of rashness otherwise than as evangelical authority commands.

### CHAPTER XCI. Baptism whose form is known to have been completely conferred is not repeated. Leo I, letter 90 to Rusticus, ch. 60.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Hi de quibus*.) Concerning those of whom you wrote, who know that they were baptized but profess that they do not know what faith those who baptized them held: since they received the form of baptism in whatever manner, they are not to be rebaptized. Rather, receiving through the laying on of hands the power of the Holy Spirit, which they could not receive from heretics, they are to be joined to Catholics.

### CHAPTER XCII. Those concerning whom it is unknown whether they are baptized are to be baptized. Gregory IV to Boniface.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Parvulos*.) Little children who have been taken away from their parents, and concerning whom it is unknown whether they have been baptized, you ought to baptize according to the tradition of the Fathers if no one capable of testifying is present.

### CHAPTER XCIII. On the same matter. Fifth Council of Carthage, ch. 6.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Placuit*.) It has been decreed concerning infants that whenever completely reliable witnesses cannot be found to testify without doubt that they were baptized, and the infants themselves are not old enough to answer without any uncertainty concerning the sacraments entrusted to them, they are to be baptized. Likewise concerning churches: whenever doubt exists about their consecration, the same procedure is to be followed, so that they may be consecrated without hesitation.

### CHAPTER XCIV. On the same matter. What is not proven to have been done is not understood to be repeated; therefore one whose baptism is doubtful is to be baptized anew. Leo I, letter 90 to Rusticus.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Si nulla*.) If there are no indications among relatives or household members, clergy or neighbors, by which those under inquiry may be shown to have been baptized, action must be taken so that they may be reborn, lest they plainly perish. In such cases, reason does not permit what is not shown to have been done to appear repeated. Those who can remember coming to Church with their parents may recall whether they themselves received what was given to their parents. But if even this lies outside memory, what is unknown to have been conferred seems to be conferred upon them; for rash presumption does not intervene where there is diligent piety.

### CHAPTER XCV. Baptism avails for salvation even if infants are not presented in that faith. Augustine, letter 23 to Boniface.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Non illud*.) Do not be troubled that some bring little children for receiving baptism, not in the faith that they may be regenerated by spiritual grace unto eternal life, but because they suppose that by this remedy they may retain or recover bodily health for a time. The children are not therefore deprived of regeneration because they are presented by such persons with this intention.

### CHAPTER XCVI. On those ordained through ignorance before being baptized. Council of Compiègne, ch. 5.

(1, question 1, ch. *Si presbyter*.) If an ordained presbyter discovers that he has not been baptized, he is to be baptized and ordained again, and all whom he previously baptized.

### CHAPTER XCVII. On the same matter. From the sayings of Bishop Isidore.

(1, question 1, ch. *Si presbyteri*; it is *palea* in Gratian.) If anyone is ordained through ignorance before being baptized, those baptized by him ought to be rebaptized, and he himself is not to be ordained. But the Roman pontiff judges not the person who baptizes; rather, he believes that the Spirit of God ministers baptismal grace even if the one baptizing is a pagan.

### CHAPTER XCVIII. On those who compel presbyters to give money for balsam. Nothing should be demanded either for dedicating basilicas or for conferring the Church’s sacraments. Council of Chalon, ch. 5.

(1, question 1, ch. *Statuimus*.) Certain brethren said that ancient custom in their churches was for presbyters to give two or four denarii for purchasing balsam to make chrism, or for purchasing lamps to be burned in the church. Therefore we all unanimously decree that, just as nothing is to be received for dedicating basilicas or conferring orders, so likewise presbyters are to give chrism without receiving anything for balsam or for purchasing lamps. Bishops, therefore, are to buy balsam from ecclesiastical resources and lamps for each of their churches.

### CHAPTER XCIX. It is permissible to anoint the chrism-cloth again and place it upon another baptized person. Council at Beauvais, ch. 8.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Si quis*.) If anyone wishes to anoint the chrism-cloth again and place it upon another baptized person, it is not improper.

### CHAPTER C. Baptisms may not be consecrated with old chrism. Council of Lyons, ch. 3.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Si quis de alio*.) If anyone should attempt to baptize with chrism other than the new chrism received by the gift or permission of his own bishop, unless he does so under the pressure of impending death, he is plainly shown by his rash audacity to have pronounced upon himself the sentence of his own condemnation.

### CHAPTER CI. Presbyters are to request chrism from their own bishop, personally or through another of the same order. Council at Valence, ch. 2.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Presbyteri*.) Presbyters who govern diocesan churches are to request chrism before the solemnity of Easter not from just any bishops but from their own bishop, and not through a junior cleric but personally or through one of the same order.

### CHAPTER CII. Why baptism is consecrated in water and never in wine. Haimo, on Romans I.

Perhaps someone asks why baptism is consecrated only in water and never sometimes in wine. Blessed Ambrose answers: “For this reason it is uniformly performed in water: so that it may be understood that, just as water washes away the dirt of a body or garment, so baptism cleanses and removes the stains of the soul and the defilements of vices.”

### CHAPTER CIII. Before chrism is poured in for sprinkling, water may be taken from the font. *Capitulary*, book VI, ch. 77.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *In Sabbato*.) On the holy Saturday of Easter and Pentecost, if anyone wishes to receive consecrated water for sprinkling in his house, he shall receive it before the infusion of chrism.

### CHAPTER CIV. By what reasoning we know that the Apostles were baptized. Or: Christ’s disciples are believed to have been washed by his baptism. Augustine, letter 108 to Seleucianus.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Quando ab Hierosol.*.) When the Lord Jesus left Jerusalem with his disciples for the land of Judea and remained there with them, he baptized—not personally, but through his disciples. We understand that these disciples had been baptized either with John’s baptism, as some suppose, or, more credibly, with Christ’s baptism. Likewise, the Lord answered Peter: “He who has been washed does not need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean.” Hence it is understood that Peter had already been baptized.

### CHAPTER CV. All the Apostles are believed to have been baptized with Christ’s baptism. Augustine, book III, *On the Soul and Its Origin*, ch. 9.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Si eos*.) If we maintain that those of whom it is not written whether they were baptized or not departed this life without baptism, we wrong the Apostles themselves. Apart from the Apostle Paul, we do not know when they were baptized; but that they were baptized may be made known to us by the Lord’s saying to blessed Peter: “He who has been washed does not need except to wash his feet” (John 13).

### CHAPTER CVI. All the unbaptized who die for Christ die baptized. Augustine, *City of God*, book XIII.

Whoever dies in confession of Christ without having received the washing of regeneration gains for the forgiveness of sins as much as if he had been washed in the sacred font of baptism.

### CHAPTER CVII. Although a catechumen lives rightly, without baptism he cannot be saved. Augustine, *Against the Donatists*, ch. 22.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Catechumenus*.) We do not believe that a catechumen who dies, even in good works, has life, except only when martyrdom completes the sacrament.

### CHAPTER CVIII. On the same matter. Augustine, *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, ch. 74.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Catechum.*, § *Baptizatus*, and 15, question 1, ch. *Firmissime*.) The baptized person confesses his faith before the priest and answers when questioned. The martyr does the same before the persecutor: he confesses and answers when questioned. The former, after confession, is sprinkled with water; the latter is sprinkled with blood or immersed in fire. The former receives the Holy Spirit through the bishop’s laying on of hands; the latter becomes a dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit, since it is not he who speaks, but the Holy Spirit who speaks in him. The former communicates in the Eucharist in remembrance of the Lord’s death; the latter dies together with Christ himself. The former confesses that he renounces the deeds of the world; the latter renounces both the world and life itself. To the former all sins are forgiven; in the latter they are extinguished.

### CHAPTER CIX. The shedding of blood fulfills the role of baptism. Augustine, ibid.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Baptismi*.) Blessed Cyprian derives no slight proof from the thief to whom, though unbaptized, it was said, “Today [you shall be] with me in paradise” (Luke 23), that suffering can sometimes fulfill the role of baptism. On considering this matter again and again, I find that not only suffering for Christ’s name can supply what baptism lacks, but also faith and conversion of heart, if in the constraints of time one cannot obtain baptism’s mystery. For that thief was not crucified for Christ’s name but for his own criminal deeds; nor did he suffer because he believed, but believed while suffering. Thus the Apostle’s saying, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10), is shown in that thief to have great force even without the visible sacrament of baptism.

Yet this is fulfilled invisibly only when the mystery of baptism is excluded not by contempt for religion but by necessity. Just as the Almighty’s kindness supplied in that thief what the sacrament of baptism lacked, because it was lacking through necessity rather than pride or contempt, so in baptized infants who die the same grace of the Almighty must be believed to supply what they could not do through no impious will but through the incapacity of age: they could neither believe with the heart unto righteousness nor confess with the mouth unto salvation. Baptism can indeed be present where confession of heart is lacking. Conversion of heart can indeed be present without baptism having been received; but it cannot be present where baptism is despised. In no way is conversion of heart toward God to be asserted where God’s sacrament is despised.

### CHAPTER CX. Baptism consists not so much in the washing of the body as in the faith of the heart. Prosper, in the book of *Sentences*.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Verus bapt.*.) True baptism consists not so much in washing of the body as in faith of the heart, as apostolic teaching declares: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15). And elsewhere: “Baptism saves—not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience to God” (1 Pet. 3).

### CHAPTER CXI. Whatever is within a mother’s body is not baptized with her. Augustine, *Against Julian*, book VI, ch. 5.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Si ad matris*.) If that which is conceived in a mother belonged to her body so as to be reckoned a part of her, then an infant whose mother had been baptized while carrying him in her womb, under the pressure of some danger of death, would not himself be baptized. But now, since he too is baptized, he is certainly not regarded as baptized twice. Therefore, while he was in the womb, he did not belong to the maternal body.

Likewise, if everything in a person when he is baptized and sanctified must be thought sanctified and baptized, you will say that the things in him which are discharged through the intestines and bladder by bodily evacuation are themselves baptized and sanctified. You will say that a person situated in his mother’s womb is baptized and sanctified if a pregnant woman is compelled by necessity to receive this sacrament, and therefore that one already born ought no longer to be baptized. Finally, you will say that fevers are baptized and sanctified when sick persons are baptized.

### CHAPTER CXII. Why one in a mother’s womb is not baptized with her. Isidore, book I, *On the Highest Good*, ch. 25.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Qui in maternis*.) Those in maternal wombs cannot be baptized with their mother because one who has not yet been born according to Adam cannot be reborn according to Christ. Regeneration cannot be spoken of in the case of one whom generation has not preceded. Those who live wickedly in the Church and do not cease to communicate, believing themselves cleansed by such communion, should learn that it profits them nothing for cleansing.

## ON THE SACRAMENT OF CONFIRMATION

### CHAPTER CXIII. After baptism, the sacrament of confirmation is to be conferred. Pope Urban I, letter 2.

(De Consecratione, distinction 5, ch. 1, *Omnes fideles*.) All the faithful, after baptism, must receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of bishops’ hands, so that they may be found fully Christian.

### CHAPTER CXIV. The sacrament of laying on of hands is greater than baptism. Pope Miltiades to the bishops of Spain.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *De his*.) Concerning what you asked—whether the sacrament of bishops’ laying on of hands or baptism is greater—know that both are great sacraments. And just as one of them is allotted to the greater persons, namely the supreme pontiffs, and cannot be performed by lesser persons, so it is to be revered and maintained with greater veneration. Yet these two sacraments are so joined that, unless death intervenes, they can in no way be separated from one another, and one cannot rightly be performed without the other.

### CHAPTER CXV. The sacrament of laying on of hands cannot be performed by anyone but bishops. Pope Eusebius, letter 3, to the bishops of Tuscany.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Manus*.) The sacrament of laying on of hands also must be held in great veneration. It cannot be performed by anyone except the chief priests. It is read and known that, even in the time of the Apostles, it was performed by none other than the Apostles themselves; nor can it ever be performed, or ought to be performed, by any except those who hold their place. If another arrangement is presumed, it is to be considered invalid and void, and will never be reckoned among the Church’s sacraments.

### CHAPTER CXVI. Presbyters may anoint the baptized with chrism. Innocent I, letter 1, to Bishop Decentius.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Presbyter*.) Presbyters, whether the bishop is absent or present, may anoint with chrism those whom they baptize. But, although the chrism has been consecrated by the bishop, they may not sign the forehead with that oil; this belongs to bishops alone when they impart the Paraclete.

### CHAPTER CXVII. Presbyters may not anoint baptized persons on their foreheads. Or: Only bishops may confirm. Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, book I, letter 3, epistle 5.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Presbyteri*.) Presbyters must not presume to sign baptized infants on their foreheads with sacred chrism. But presbyters anoint the baptized on the breast so that bishops may afterward confirm them on the forehead.

### CHAPTER CXVIII. Why the sacrament of confirmation is conferred upon the baptized. Rabanus, book I, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, ch. 31.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Novissime*.) Finally, the Paraclete is conferred upon the baptized by the chief priest through the laying on of hands, so that through the Holy Spirit he may be strengthened to preach to others the same gift which he himself received in baptism, being granted the grace of eternal life. The baptized person is signed with chrism by the priest upon the crown of the head; by the bishop, however, upon the forehead. The first anointing signifies the descent of the Holy Spirit upon him, to consecrate a dwelling for God; the second declares that the sevenfold grace of the same Holy Spirit, with every fullness of holiness, knowledge, and power, comes upon the person.

### CHAPTER CXIX. Only those who are fasting are to come to confirmation. Council of Orléans, ch. 3.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Et jejuni*.) Let persons of mature age come fasting to confirmation, and let them be instructed first to make confession, so that cleansed they may receive the gift of the Holy Spirit; for no one will ever be a Christian unless he has been chrismated by episcopal confirmation.

### CHAPTER CXX. Bishops likewise are to confirm the baptized only while fasting, unless necessity exists. Council of Meaux, ch. 6.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Et episcopi*.) Bishops are to confer the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands only while fasting, except in the case of sick persons and those in danger of death. Just as baptism ought to be celebrated with fasting at the two seasons, namely Easter and Pentecost, so the bestowal of the Holy Spirit should also fittingly be celebrated by bishops who are fasting.

### CHAPTER CXXI. No one is to be confirmed a second or third time. Council of Tarragona, ch. 6.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Dictum est nobis*.) We have been told that certain laypeople are confirmed twice, three times, or even more often by bishops who are unaware of it. Therefore it seems to us that confirmation, like baptism, must by no means be repeated. It has been decreed that those baptized or confirmed twice or more often are to serve most devoutly not the world but God alone, under a religious or clerical habit.

### CHAPTER CXXII. What penance is to be imposed upon those baptized twice or three times. Or: On those ignorantly baptized twice. Theodore’s *Penitential*, ch. 14.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Qui bis*.) Those baptized twice through ignorance need not do penance for this, except that according to the canons they cannot be ordained unless some grave necessity compels it. But those who knowingly are baptized again have, as it were, crucified Christ again: they shall do penance for seven years, fasting on the fourth and sixth days and observing four Lents.

> Note: Gratian reads “three Lents” at [Col. 1071D].

The same applies if it was done because of some vice; if they thought it was for purification, they shall likewise do penance for three years.

## ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST AND THE CELEBRATION OF MASSES

### CHAPTER CXXIII. Christ’s body and blood are not born for us by nature but are made for us by consecration. Ambrose, book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Panis et calix*.) Bread and the cup become mystical for us not by just any means, but by a definite consecration; they are not born so. Therefore, what is thus made for us, although it is bread and cup, is nourishment for resurrection, not a sacrament of religion: that which we bless and for which we give thanks to the Lord in every one of his gifts, not only spiritual but also bodily.

### CHAPTER CXXIV. Before the blessing there is the appearance of bread and wine; after the blessing there is the body and blood of Christ. Ambrose, *On Those Initiated into the Mysteries*, ch. 5.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Ante benedictionem*.) Before the blessing [Col. 1071D], one appearance is named; after the blessing, the body is signified. Likewise, Christ is in that sacrament. Likewise, whoever eats this body will receive forgiveness of sins.

### CHAPTER CXXV. Under the appearance of bread and wine we honour Christ’s invisible flesh and blood. Augustine in Prosper’s book of *Sentences*.

(De Consecratione, distinction 4, ch. *Nos autem*.) Under the appearance of bread and wine which we see, we honour invisible realities, that is, Christ’s flesh and blood; nor do we apprehend these two appearances [Col. 1072C] in the same manner as we apprehended them before consecration, when we faithfully confess that before consecration they are bread and wine, formed by nature. But after consecration they are Christ’s flesh and blood, consecrated by the blessing.

### CHAPTER CXXVI. Berengar’s confession concerning the body and blood of the Lord.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Ego Berengarius*.) I, Berengar, unworthy deacon of the Church of Saint Maurice of Angers, acknowledging the true Catholic and apostolic faith, anathematize every heresy, especially that concerning which I have until now been defamed: namely, the heresy which attempts to maintain that the bread and wine placed upon the altar, after consecration, are only a sacrament and not the true body and blood [Col. 1072D] of our Lord Jesus Christ, and that they cannot be physically handled or broken by the hands of priests, or crushed by the teeth of the faithful, except in the sacrament alone.

But I assent to the holy Roman and apostolic faith. With mouth and heart I profess, concerning the sacraments of the Lord’s table, that I hold the same faith which the Lord and the venerable Pope Nicholas and this holy synod, by evangelical and apostolic authority, handed down as the faith to be maintained and confirmed to me: namely, that the bread and wine placed upon the altar, after consecration, are not only a sacrament but also the true [Col. 1073A] body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and that they are physically handled, broken, and crushed by the teeth of the faithful not only in the sacrament but in truth, by the hands of priests. Swearing by the holy and *homoousian* Trinity and by these most holy Gospels of Christ, I pronounce those who have come against this faith, together with their doctrines and followers, worthy of eternal anathema. And if I myself should ever presume to entertain or preach anything contrary to these things, may I be subject to the severity of the canons. Having read and reread it, I wrote this voluntarily.

Pope Nicholas sent throughout the cities of Italy, Gaul, and Germany, and to whatever [Col. 1073B] places the report of Berengar’s perversity had earlier reached, this confession of his faith concerning the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, made by Berengar at Rome before one hundred and thirteen bishops, so that the Churches which had previously grieved over one who was hostile and perverse might afterwards rejoice over one who had returned and been converted.

### CHAPTER CXXVII. The sacrament does not change its appearance because of believers’ error. Or: Why are the appearances of the elements retained, when it is truly the body and blood of Christ? Ambrose, book VI of *On the Sacraments*, ch. 1.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Forte dicas*.) Perhaps you will say: “How is it true flesh, how true blood, when I do not see the likeness of flesh, nor see the reality of blood?” First of all, I tell you of Christ’s word, which works so as to be able to change and transform the kinds and established order of nature.

Next, when [Col. 1073C] his disciples could not bear Christ’s saying, but withdrew upon hearing that he would give his flesh to be eaten and his blood to be drunk, Peter alone said: “You have the words of eternal life; how can I withdraw from you?” (John 6). Therefore, lest more should say this, and lest there should be, as it were, a certain horror of error, while the grace of redemption remained, you receive the sacrament under a likeness. But you attain the glory and power of the true nature. “I,” he says, “am the bread that came down from heaven” (ibid.).

### CHAPTER CXXVIII. Augustine in Prosper’s book of *Sentences*.

If you ask the manner in which this can occur, I answer briefly for the present: the mystery of faith can beneficially [Col. 1073D] be believed; it cannot profitably be investigated.

### CHAPTER CXXIX. Visible creatures are invisibly transformed into Christ’s body and blood. Eusebius of Emesa.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Quia corpus*, § *Invisibilis*.) The invisible priest, by his word and secret power, transforms visible creatures into the substance of his body and blood, saying thus: “Take, this is my body” (Matt. 26). And, the sanctification having been repeated: “Take and drink; this is my blood” (ibid.). Therefore, just as at the command of God who gives orders, the heights of the heavens, the depths of the waters, and the vast expanses of the earth suddenly came into being from nothing, so in spiritual sacraments, where power has commanded, the effect obeys with equal power.

### CHAPTER CXXX. What sacrifice is, and what sacrament is. [Col. 1074A] Augustine, book X of *The City of God*, ch. 5.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Sacrificium*.) A visible sacrifice is a sacrament of an invisible sacrifice—that is, a sacred sign; elsewhere, a sacrament is the visible form of invisible grace.

### CHAPTER CXXXI. What a sign is. Augustine, book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, ch. 1.

A sign is a thing which, besides the appearance it presents to the senses, causes something else to come into knowledge through itself.

### CHAPTER CXXXII. After consecration, not the substance but the appearance remains. Gregory, in a Paschal homily.

[Col. 1074B] (De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Species*.) “Appearance” and “likeness” are names of those things which existed before, namely, bread and wine. Hence, at the end of every Mass, prayer is made and it is said: “Bring about in us, Lord, we beseech you, what your sacraments contain, so that we may receive in the reality of things what we bear under an appearance.”

For the priest asks that Christ’s body, which is now borne under the appearance of bread and wine, may someday be received in manifest vision as it truly is. Concerning this vision the Lord says in the Gospel according to John: “He who loves me is loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him” (John 14). Although some explain, not implausibly, that in this place the reality of flesh and blood means their effect itself, that is, the forgiveness of sins.

### CHAPTER CXXXIII. How the words, “Unless anyone eats the flesh of the Son of Man and drinks,” are to be understood. Or: We must receive Christ’s body and blood not carnally but spiritually. [Col. 1074C] Augustine, on Psalm 54.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Prima*.) “The first heresy,” he says, “arose among Christ’s disciples, as it were, from the hardness of his saying. For when he said, ‘Unless anyone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he shall not have eternal life’ (John 4), they did not understand and said: ‘This saying is hard; who can hear it?’ (ibid.). Saying, ‘This saying is hard,’ they separated themselves from him, and he remained with the Twelve.

“When those people departed, he instructed those who [Col. 1074D] remained: ‘It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life’ [ibid.]. Have you understood spiritually? They are spirit and life. Have you understood carnally? Even so, they are spirit and life, but they are not spirit and life for you, because you do not understand spiritually.

“To understand spiritually what I have spoken: you are not going to eat this body which you see, nor drink that blood which those who will crucify me will shed. I have commended some sacrament to you; spiritually understood, it gives you life. But ‘the flesh profits nothing’ [ibid.], in the sense in which they understood it and replied. For they understood flesh as flesh sold in a corpse or cut up in a butcher’s shop.

“But Jesus, knowing this, said: ‘Does this scandalize you, [Col. 1075A] because I said, “I give you my flesh to eat and my blood to drink”? What then if you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before?’ (John 4). What is this? By this he resolved what had disturbed them; by this he disclosed that over which they had been scandalized. They would indeed have understood, but those others thought that he would distribute his body. He said that he would ascend into heaven, surely intact. ‘When you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before,’ then certainly you will see that he does not distribute his body in the way you think; or then you will understand that his grace is not consumed by bites.

“Again: until the world ends, the Lord is above; nevertheless, the truth of the Lord is also here with us. For the body in which he rose must be in one place, but his truth is spread everywhere [Col. 1075B].”

### CHAPTER CXXXIV. How Christ’s body that hung upon the cross is received, and how it is not. Augustine, letter to Irenaeus.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Non hoc corpus*.) “You are not going to eat this body which you see, nor drink that blood which those who crucify me will shed”—the same body indeed, and not the same body: the same invisibly, not the same visibly. Hence it is added: “If it must be celebrated visibly, it must nevertheless be understood invisibly.”

### CHAPTER CXXXV. What it is to eat Christ’s body and drink his blood. Augustine, sermon on the words of the Gospel.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Quid est*.) What is [Col. 1075C] it to eat Christ? It is not merely to receive his body in the sacrament. For many receive it unworthily, of whom the Apostle says: “Whoever eats and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 2).

But how is Christ to be eaten? As he himself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 5); then he drinks and eats. But whoever does not remain in me, nor I in him, even if he receives the sacrament, acquires great torment.

### CHAPTER CXXXVI. To believe in Christ is to eat and drink Christ. Augustine, book *On the Remedy of Penance*.

Why do you prepare tooth and stomach? Believe, and you have eaten. [Col. 1075D] For to believe in him is to eat bread and wine; whoever believes in him eats him.

### CHAPTER CXXXVII. The sacrament and the reality of the sacrament constitute the sacrifice. Augustine in Prosper’s book of *Sentences*.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Hoc est*.) This is what we say and strive in every way to establish: the sacrifice of the Church is made in two ways and consists of two things—of the visible appearance of the elements and the invisible flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; of sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, that is, Christ’s body. Just as Christ’s person consists and is made up of God and man, since Christ himself is true God and true man, because every thing contains in itself the nature and reality [Col. 1076A] of those things from which it is made.

But the sacrifice of the Church is made of two things: sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, that is, Christ’s body. Therefore, Christ’s body is both sacrament and the reality of the sacrament.

Likewise: His flesh is that which we receive in the sacrament, covered by the form of bread; and his blood is that which we drink under the appearance and taste of wine—flesh indeed of flesh, and blood, the sacrament of blood [text uncertain]. By flesh and blood, both invisible, intelligible, and spiritual, is signified the visible, tangible body of our Lord Jesus Christ, full of the grace of all virtues and of divine majesty.

Likewise: Therefore, just as the heavenly bread, which is truly Christ’s flesh, is in its own manner called Christ’s body, although it is in reality the sacrament of that body of Christ which was visible, tangible, mortal, and laid upon the cross; and as the offering of the flesh itself, performed by the priest’s hands, is called Christ’s passion, death, and crucifixion—not in the truth of the thing but by signifying mystery—so the sacrament of faith, understood as baptism, is faith.

### CHAPTER CXXXVIII. In how many ways Christ’s flesh is understood. Or: Christ’s flesh and blood are understood in two ways. Jerome, on the Epistle to the Ephesians, ch. 1.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Multipliciter*.) Christ’s flesh and blood, he says, are understood in many ways: either that spiritual and divine flesh of which he himself says, “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” [Col. 1076C] (John 6), and, “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have eternal life” (ibid.); or the flesh which was crucified and the blood which the soldier’s spear shed.

### CHAPTER CXXXIX. What does the breaking of the host and the drinking of blood signify? Or: When the host is broken, Christ’s passion is recalled to memory. Augustine in Prosper’s book of *Sentences*.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Cum frangitur*.) When the host is broken, when blood from the cup is poured into the mouths of the faithful, what else is signified except the offering of the Lord’s body upon the cross and the pouring out of his blood from his side?

### CHAPTER CXL. Why three parts are made from Christ’s body. Or: What the part placed in the cup signifies, what the part eaten at the altar signifies, and what the third part reserved until the end signifies. Pope Sergius.

[Col. 1076D] (De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Triforme*.) The Lord’s body is threefold. The part placed in the cup signifies Christ’s body already risen; the part eaten, his body still walking upon the earth; the part remaining upon the altar until the end of Mass [Note: [Col. 1075D] Now no part of the host remains on the altar until the end of Mass.], the body lying in the tomb, because until the end of the age the bodies of the saints will be in the tomb.

### CHAPTER CXLI. Eating and drinking the flesh and blood is a commemoration of the Lord’s death. Ambrose, on 1 Corinthians, ch. 5.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Quia morte*.) Since we have been freed by the Lord’s death [Col. 1077A], mindful of this fact, in eating and drinking the flesh and blood which were offered for us, we signify or sanctify it.

### CHAPTER CXLII. How the statement, “Christ was offered once and is offered daily,” is to be understood. Augustine on Psalm 21.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Semel*.) Christ died once, the just for the unjust; and we know, hold as certain, and retain with unshaken hope that Christ, having risen from the dead, now dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him (Rom. 6). These are the Apostle’s words, yet they are not forgotten. What was done once occurs in our remembrance every year. Whenever Easter is celebrated, is Christ killed as often? Yet the annual commemoration represents [Col. 1077B] what was once done and thus moves us as though we saw the Lord present upon the cross.

### CHAPTER CXLIII. On the same subject. Augustine, letter 23 to Boniface.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Semel immolatus*.) Christ was offered once in himself, and yet is offered daily in the sacrament. This must be understood thus: in the manifestation of his body, distinct from all his members, true God and true man hung upon the cross only once, offering himself to the Father as a living sacrifice—passible, mortal, efficacious for the redemption of the living and the dead, namely, of those whom the height of the divine counsel judged, foreknew, predestined, and called to be redeemed, by the means and at the times at which this [Col. 1077C] was fittingly to occur.

### CHAPTER CXLIV. The victim once offered is daily offered in remembrance of its death. Ambrose, on the Epistle to the Hebrews.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *In Christo*.) In Christ there is a victim offered once, powerful for eternal salvation. What, then, of us? Do we not offer every year, but in remembrance of his death? And there is one victim, not many. How is it one and not many? Because Christ was offered once; but this sacrifice is an image of that one, and it is always the same thing.

Therefore this is the sacrifice; otherwise, since it is offered in many places, are there many Christs? By no means; rather, there is one Christ, wholly present here and wholly present there. For as that which is offered everywhere [Col. 1077D] is one body and not many bodies, so too there is one sacrifice. That high priest is he who offered the victim cleansing us. We also offer even now that same victim which was then offered and cannot be consumed. What we do is done in commemoration of what was done; for he says, “Do this in commemoration of me.”

### CHAPTER CXLV. They ought not receive Christ’s body and blood except fasting, necessity excepted. Augustine, in the book of *Responses to Januarius*.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Liquido apparet*.) It is plainly evident that when the disciples first received the Lord’s body and blood, they did not receive them fasting. Yet must the universal Church be criticized because it is received by those fasting? For the Holy Spirit [Col. 1078A] approved that, in honour of so great a sacrament, the Lord’s body should enter a Christian’s mouth before other foods. This custom is therefore observed throughout the world.

For the fact that the Lord gave it after food does not mean that brothers who have eaten breakfast or supper ought to assemble to receive that sacrament, or that they ought, as did those whom the Apostle rebukes and corrects, to mingle these things with their meals. Indeed, the Saviour wished, more emphatically, to impress the profundity of that mystery as the final thing upon the hearts and memories of the disciples from whom he was departing for his passion. Therefore, he did not prescribe the order in which it was thereafter to be received, so that he might reserve this matter for the Apostles through whom he would order the Churches.

For if he had instructed that it should always be taken or received after other foods, I believe no one would have changed that custom. But when the Apostle, [Col. 1078B] speaking of this sacrament, says, “Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you may not assemble for judgment,” he immediately adds: “The remaining matters I shall arrange when I come” (1 Cor. 11 [the citation prints “II”]). From this it is understood that, since it would have been excessive for a letter to set forth for them the whole order of practice, what the Church throughout the world observes was ordered by him and is not varied by any difference of hours.

### CHAPTER CXLVI. Concerning those who erred in various ways while offering sacrifice. From the decrees of Pope Julius to the bishops throughout Egypt—chapter 1 of the Council of Braga.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Cum omne*.) Since every crime and sin is removed by sacrifices offered to God [Col. 1078C], what afterwards will be given to the Lord for the expiation of sins when error is committed in the offering of the sacrifice itself? For we have heard that some, held by schismatic ambition, contrary to divine ordinances and apostolic institutions, consecrate milk instead of wine in the divine sacrifices; that others distribute the Eucharist dipped [in the cup] to the people as the completion of communion; that some offer squeezed wine for the sacrament of the Lord’s cup; and that others preserve throughout the year a linen cloth dipped in must, and at the time of sacrifice wash part of it in water and thus offer it.

How contrary this is to evangelical and apostolic teaching, and how hostile to ecclesiastical custom, may readily be demonstrated from the very source of truth, from which the ordered mysteries of the sacraments themselves proceeded. For when the teacher of truth commended the true sacrifice of our salvation to his disciples [Col. 1078D], we know that he gave not milk but only bread and a cup under this sacrament. For it is read in the truth of the Gospel: “Jesus took bread and a cup, and blessing them gave them to his disciples” (Matt. 26).

Therefore, let milk cease to be offered in sacrificing, because the manifest and evident example of evangelical truth has shone forth: nothing other than bread and wine may be offered. Nor have those who distribute to the people the dipped Eucharist as the completion of communion accepted testimony brought forward from the Gospel, where he commended his body and blood separately to the Apostles. For the commendation of the bread is recorded separately, and separately that of the cup [Col. 1079A].

We do not read that Christ gave dipped bread to others, except only to that disciple whom the dipped morsel of the Master identified as the betrayer—not to signify the institution of this sacrament. But the people’s communicating from pressed grapes, that is, from grapes’ berries, is altogether very confused. If necessity should arise, however, the cluster should be pressed into the cup and mixed with water, because the Lord’s cup, according to the command of the canons, must be offered mixed with wine and water.

For we see the people understood in the water, but Christ’s blood shown in the wine. Therefore, when water is mixed with wine in the cup, the people are united to Christ, and the multitude of believers is joined and bound to him in whom it believes. This union and joining of water and wine is so mixed in the [Col. 1079B] Lord’s cup that the mixture cannot be separated. For if someone offers wine alone, Christ’s blood begins to be without us; but if there is water alone, the people begin to be without Christ. Therefore, when a cluster alone is offered, in which only the efficacy of wine is displayed, the sacrament of our salvation, which is signified by water, is neglected.

For the Lord’s cup cannot be water alone or wine alone, unless both are mixed. Therefore, because from this point a very extensive and manifold judgment of the Fathers has already flowed, henceforth every such error and presumption must cease, lest the perverse and disordered offspring weaken the settled truth. Accordingly, henceforth no one shall be permitted to offer anything in the divine rites other than, according to the judgment of the ancient councils, bread only and a cup mixed with wine and water [Col. 1079C]. Whoever thereafter acts otherwise than prescribed shall abstain from offering sacrifice until, corrected through the lawful satisfaction of penance, he returns to the office of his rank which he has lost.

### CHAPTER CXLVII. A priest must always have the Eucharist prepared for the sick. Council of Worms, ch. 5.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Presbyter*.) Let the priest always have the Eucharist prepared, so that when anyone becomes ill, or a little child is ill, he may communicate him at once, lest he die without communion.

### CHAPTER CXLVIII. By whom the Lord’s sacraments are to be handled. Pope Clement, letter 2.

[Col. 1079D] (De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Tribus gradibus*, § *In tanta*.) Certainly, only so many offerings are to be made upon the altar as should suffice for the people. What remains is not to be kept until the next day, but is to be consumed with fear and trembling through the diligence of the clergy.

### CHAPTER CXLIX. One who receives Eucharistic communion daily is neither censured nor praised. Augustine, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, ch. 53.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Quotidie*.) I neither praise nor blame receiving Eucharistic communion every day. Yet I urge communion on every Lord’s day, provided that one’s mind is not inclined toward sinning. For if it still has the will to sin, I say that one is burdened rather than purified by reception of the Eucharist [Col. 1080A]. Therefore, though a sinner is pricked by remorse, if he nevertheless has no will henceforth to sin, let him who is about to communicate make satisfaction by tears and prayers and, trusting in God’s mercy, approach the Eucharist fearless and secure. But I say this of the person not burdened by mortal sins.

### CHAPTER CL. Each of the faithful should communicate three times a year. Or: All ought to communicate three times yearly—at Easter, Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord—unless they are bound by criminal sin. From Pope Fabian’s letter, ch. 3.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Et si non frequentius*.) Even if people do not communicate more frequently, they should do so three times a year—at Easter, Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord—unless perhaps someone is impeded by certain more serious crimes.

### CHAPTER CLI. Before sacramental communion, each person should abstain from his own wife. Or: For how many days one must abstain from wives before sacramental communion. [Col. 1080B] Council of Elvira, ch. 3.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Omnis homo*.) Every man ought to abstain from his own wife for three, four, or eight days before holy communion. A person who has not communicated on these three occasions—Easter, Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord—is not to be counted among Catholics.

### CHAPTER CLII. Actors and magicians who persist in their vice are not to be admitted to communion. Or: Sacred mysteries are not to be entrusted to magicians and actors. [Col. 1080C] Cyprian, letter 5 to Eucratius.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Pro dilectione*.) Because of your affection and reverence, dearest brother, you judged that I should be consulted as to what I think concerning that actor and magician who lives among you and still persists, at his present age, in the disgrace of his profession; who, a master and teacher not of boys to be educated but of boys to be ruined, imparts to others what he himself wickedly learned. Should sacred communion be given to such persons together with other Christians?

I think that communion with you is not fitting for them, nor does it accord with the divine majesty or Gospel discipline that the modesty and honour of the Church should be defiled by such foul and disgraceful contagion.

### CHAPTER CLIII. Laymen and women must not carry Christ’s body to someone to be communicated. Or: Priests must administer the divine sacraments only in person. [Col. 1080D] Council of Reims, ch. 1.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Pervenit*.) It has come to our notice that certain priests so greatly disparage the divine mysteries that they hand the sacred body of the Lord to a layman or woman to carry out to the sick, and that the holy of holies is entrusted to persons forbidden to enter the sanctuary or approach the altar. How horrible and detestable this is, the prudence of all devout persons recognizes. Therefore, the synod utterly forbids such rash presumption to occur any further; rather, the priest himself must in every case communicate the sick person. [Col. 1081A] If he acts otherwise, he shall endanger his ecclesiastical rank.

### CHAPTER CLIV. What penance is to be imposed on one who vomits the sacrament. From Bede’s penitential.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Si quis*.) If anyone, through drunkenness or gluttony, vomits the Eucharist, let him do penance for eleven days. Clerics, monks, or deacons are to do penance for forty days; priests for seventy days; bishops for ninety days. If he vomits because of illness, let him do penance for seven days.

### CHAPTER CLV. The penance of a priest through whose negligence some of Christ’s blood spills. From the Decrees of Pope Pius, ch. 3.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Si per negligentiam*.) If, through negligence, something from the Lord’s cup [Col. 1081B] drips onto the ground, it shall be licked up with the tongue and the board scraped. If there is no board, so that the place may not be trodden upon, it shall be scraped away and consumed by fire; the ashes shall be deposited at the altar, and the priest shall do penance for forty days. If [the spill reaches] as far as the third [degree; wording uncertain], he shall do penance for nine days; if as far as the fourth, for twenty days. The linen cloths touched by the drop shall be washed three times by a minister, with a cup placed below; the water of washing shall be consumed and deposited beside the altar.

### CHAPTER CLVI. The penance of one who does not guard the sacrifice properly. Council of Arles.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Qui non bene*.) Whoever does not [Col. 1081C] guard the sacrifice properly, and a mouse or another animal eats it, shall do penance for forty days. But whoever loses it in the church, or if a part of it falls and cannot be found, shall do penance for thirty days.

### CHAPTER CLVII. Which prefaces are to be sung at Mass. Pope Gelasius to all bishops of Germany and Gaul.

(De Consecratione, distinction 2, ch. *Invenimus*.) When, in God’s name, we had convened in the Roman Church a synod of bishops and the other faithful fellow-priests of God, and were considering more carefully the matters handed down by the ecclesiastical Fathers, your letter arrived; and, that it might possess greater authority, [Col. 1081D] living voices had also preceded it. You asked us to communicate to you by letter the order of prefaces which the holy Roman Church had hitherto possessed.

Then, greatly rejoicing at your good desire and zeal, and diligently rereading the sacred Roman order and the sacred enactments of our predecessors, we found that only these nine prefaces are to be received in the sacred catalogue—those which long-standing antiquity has preserved until now in the Roman Church: one for the Paschal white garments; another for the Ascension of the Lord; a third for Pentecost; a fourth for the Nativity of the Lord; a fifth for the Manifestation of the Lord; a sixth for the Apostles; a seventh for the Holy Trinity; an eighth for the Cross; and a ninth to be said only for the fast in Lent [Col. 1082A]. The holy Roman Church holds and observes these prefaces; we have commanded you to observe them.

### CHAPTER CLVIII. Unless two persons are present, a priest must not presume to celebrate Mass. Or: A priest ought not celebrate Mass unless two persons respond to him. From the Decree of Pope Soter, ch. 10.

(De Consecratione, distinction 1, ch. *Hoc quoque*.) This too has been decreed: no priest may presume to celebrate the solemnities of Mass unless two persons are present and responding to him, so that he may be counted the third. For when he says in the plural, “The Lord be with you,” and in the secret prayers, “Pray for me,” it is most plainly fitting that his greeting should be answered.

### CHAPTER CLIX. Nocturnal emissions occur in sleepers in four ways. Or: On the manifold kinds of nocturnal emissions. [Col. 1082B] Gregory to Augustine, bishop of the English, ch. 2 of Augustine’s questions.

(De Consecratione, distinction 6, ch. *Testamentum*, § *sed est in eadem*.) In a dream-induced emission, careful discernment is very necessary; one must weigh subtly from what cause it occurs to the sleeping person’s mind. For pollution sometimes occurs from overindulgence, sometimes from natural excess, illness, or thought.

Indeed, when it results from natural excess or illness, such an emission is not at all to be reckoned [culpable], because the mind, unaware, has suffered it rather than done it, and therefore should be grieved rather than blamed. But when the appetite of gluttony exceeds due measure in taking food, and consequently the receptacles of humours are burdened, [Col. 1082C] the mind bears some guilt from this—yet not so far as to be forbidden from receiving Christ’s body or celebrating the solemnities of Mass, when perhaps either a feast day requires it or necessity itself compels the ministry because no other priest is available.

But if others are present who can perform the ministry, the person affected by an emission caused by overindulgence ought, in my judgment, humbly to abstain from receiving the sacred ministry, if the sleeping mind has been disturbed by an obscene image. For some are ordinarily subject to emissions in such a way that, even while their mind is asleep in the body, it is defiled by obscene images. In this matter one thing is shown: the mind itself is altogether not guilty; nevertheless, it becomes entirely free by its own judgment [Col. 1082D] when, although it remembers having seen nothing while the body slept, it recollects in its waking state that it had succumbed to gluttony.

But if the sleeper’s emission arises from an obscene thought entertained while awake, the mind’s guilt is evident. For it sees from what root that defilement proceeded: what it knowingly thought, it unknowingly suffered. Because of such pollution, one ought to abstain from the sacred mystery that day.

### CHAPTER CLX. Of what material the cup and paten ought to be made. Council of Reims, ch. 6.

(De Consecratione, distinction 1, ch. *Ut calix*.) The Lord’s cup, together with its paten, should be made, if not wholly of gold, at least of silver. But if anyone is so poor, let him at least have a pewter cup. A cup, however, is not to be made of bronze or brass, because the force of wine [Col. 1083A] produces verdigris in it and likewise provokes vomiting. No one may presume to sing Mass using a wooden or glass cup.

### CHAPTER CLXI. The altar sacrifice is to be consecrated not on silk but on pure linen. Sylvester, in the brief epilogue of the Council of Rome.

(De Consecratione, distinction 1, ch. *Consulto*.) In addition to the matters stated above, we have established by the considered judgment of all that no one may presume to celebrate the altar sacrifice upon a silk cloth or a dyed cloth, but upon pure linen, consecrated by a bishop—linen, that is, produced and woven from earth-grown flax [Col. 1084A]. For the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was buried in a clean linen shroud (Mark 15; Luke 23).

### CHAPTER CLXII. The divine mysteries must not be supplied for wedding adornments. Council of Orléans, ch. 8.

(De Consecratione, distinction 1, ch. *Ad nuptiarum*.) Divine ministrations are not to be supplied for wedding adornment, lest, when they are polluted by the touch of wicked persons or by the display of worldly luxury, they appear unworthy for the office of sacred ministry.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1083]

## ON THE ESTABLISHMENT OF CHURCHES AND THE OFFERINGS OF THE FAITHFUL

[Col. 1083]

### CHAPTER I. On the Catholic Church. Isidore, book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, ch. 1.

“Church” is a Greek name, translated into Latin as “convocation,” because it calls all people to itself. It is called “Catholic,” that is, universal, because it is established throughout the whole world; or “Catholic” because it is universal in the same doctrine for God’s building.

### CHAPTER II. Churches have been enlarged through the benefactions of kings and rulers. From the Decrees of Pope Miltiades, ch. 12.

Finally, kings, governors, and magistrates not only granted adjoining lands, but themselves made gifts throughout all the kingdoms of the earth, from which the needy, who possessed nothing in the world, might be supported; churches might be built and restored; God and his Church might fittingly be served; and provision might be supplied without want to his servants.

### CHAPTER III. By Constantine’s authority, the Roman emperor holds the primacy of the whole world. From the Decrees of the same [pope], ch. 10.

Eminent among these, the most devout Constantine was the first openly to embrace the true faith. He granted those living throughout the world under his empire permission not only to become Christians, but also decreed that churches should be built and estates bestowed upon them. Finally, the aforesaid prince established immense gifts and the construction of the church of the first see of the blessed prince of the Apostles; indeed, he left the imperial seat over which [Col. 1083D] the Roman rulers presided, and granted it to blessed Peter and his successors for their benefit.

CAP. IV. That founders of basilicas have no authority over the property which they have bestowed upon churches. Council of Toledo, c. 32.

(10, q. 1, c. *Noverint*.) Let founders of basilicas know that they have no authority over the property which they confer upon those churches; rather, according to the ordinances of the canons, just as the church itself, so also its endowment belongs to the bishop’s administration. [Col. 1084B]

CAP. V. Whoever presumes to retain offerings made to churches, or bequests left by testament, is to be excommunicated.

(13, q. 2, c. *Clerici*.) Clerics or laypersons who presume to retain their parents’ offerings, donations, or testamentary bequests, or who believe that what they themselves have given to churches or monasteries may be taken away, are, as the holy synod has decreed, to be excluded from the churches as murderers of the poor until they return it.

CAP. VI. That no one ought to build a church without consulting the bishop. Or: Without the bishop’s designation, a new church is not to be dedicated. Council of Orléans, c. 3.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *Nemo ecclesiam*.) Let no one build a church before the bishop of the city comes, publicly sets up the cross there, and marks out the churchyard; and before this, let the person wishing to build determine what will suffice for lights, maintenance, and the wages of custodians. Having made the donation manifest, let him thus build the house; and after it has been consecrated, let him sprinkle the precincts of the same church with holy water. [Col. 1084C]

CAP. VII. Concerning the offerings of the faithful: into how many portions they are to be divided, and what is to fall to each. Gelasius II to the bishops throughout Lucania and Bruttium.

(12, q. 2, c. *Quatuor*.) It is fitting that four portions be made, both from revenues and from the offerings of the faithful, insofar as the resources of each church allow. One is for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth to be applied to the fabric of the church. [Col. 1084D]
