CAP. VIII. On the same matter. Four portions ought to be made from the church’s income. Gregory, response to Augustine’s first question.

(12, q. 2, c. *Mos est*.) GREGORY TO AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF THE PEOPLE OF CANTERBURY. It is the custom of the Apostolic See to give instructions to bishops when they are ordained. From the church’s income, or from those things which are added to the altar through the offerings of the faithful, four portions ought to be made: one, namely, for the bishop and his household, because of hospitality and the reception of pilgrims; another for the clergy; a third for the poor; and a fourth for repairing churches. [Col. 1085A]

CAP. IX. Four portions of the church’s revenues and offerings are to be entrusted to the administering priest. Decree of Nicholas, c. 9.

(12, q. 2, c. *De redditibus*.) From the revenues of first-fruits, tithes, or offerings, the bishop shall make four parts. He shall retain one for himself, distribute the second to the clergy, apply the third to the fabric or ornaments of the church, and distribute the fourth to the poor. No layperson, however, may presume to hold or possess such things without the bishops’ consent. If they do so, they are to be deprived of communion. [Col. 1086A]

## ON THE CONSECRATION OF A CHURCH

[Col. 1085]

CAP. X. Church dedications are to be celebrated for eight days. Or: Each year the solemnity of dedication is to be celebrated for eight days. [Col. 1085B] Pope Felix V to all bishops.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *Solemnitates ecclesiarum*.) The solemnities of the dedications of churches and of priests are to be celebrated solemnly every year. The Lord himself gave the example, for, in giving all a model for doing this, he came with the other people to celebrate the same festival of dedication, as it is written: “The Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem, and it was winter; and Jesus was walking in the Temple, in Solomon’s portico” (John 10). That the Dedication is to be celebrated for eight days you will find in the Book of Kings, where the temple’s dedication is completed (2 Kings 3). [Col. 1085C]

CAP. XI. The dedication of churches whose consecration is doubtful is to be repeated. Likewise Pope Felix to all the orthodox.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *Solemnitates*, § *De ecclesiarum*.) Whenever there is doubt concerning a church’s dedication, and there is neither a reliable written record nor trustworthy witnesses by whom its consecration may be known, know without any doubt that it is to be consecrated. Such hesitation does not entail a repetition, since what is not known to have been done is not shown to be repeated.

CAP. XII. Churches, together with their endowments, are subject to the bishop’s authority. Council of Toledo, c. 3.

(10, q. 1, c. *Sic quidam*.) Many, contrary to the ordinances of the canons, ask that churches which they have built be consecrated on terms that they consider the endowment they have given to the church not to belong to the bishop’s administration. This practice, having been carried out in the past, is displeasing and is forbidden for the future; rather, all things are to belong to the bishop’s administration in accordance with ancient custom. [Col. 1085D]

CAP. XIII. The consecration of churches ought not to occur without Mass. From the Decrees of Pope Evaristus, c. 4.

All basilicas must always be consecrated with Mass.

CAP. XIV. When a church once consecrated to God is to be consecrated again. From the decrees of Pope Julius, c. 4.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *De fabrica*.) If the structure of any church has been destroyed, it is to be restored. If the solemnity of consecration must be repeated in a place in which the sanctuaries have not been destroyed, we judge that no obstacle exists if exorcised water is not sprinkled over it, because we know that, at the consecration of every church in which an altar of the Holy Spirit is not set up, there is nevertheless the celebration of Masses. Therefore, if a basilica of any saint has not been renewed even from its foundations, then, without any doubt, when the solemnity of Masses has been celebrated in it, the sanctification of the whole consecration will be fulfilled. But if the sanctuaries which it possessed have been removed, it will again receive the reverence of sanctification through their restoration and the solemnity of Masses. [Col. 1086B]

CAP. XV. That places dedicated to God ought not to become secular dwellings. Or: Monasteries once dedicated remain monasteries forever. Council of Chalcedon, c. 24.

(19, q. 3, c. *Quae semel*.) Places once dedicated to God or established as monasteries are to remain such forever; they may no longer become secular dwellings. [Col. 1086C]

CAP. XVI. Dedicated church timber may not be converted to lay use. From the Decrees of Pope Eugenius, c. 3.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *Ligna*.) Timber from a dedicated church ought not to be used for another work, except for another church; it may be burned, or used for the benefit of brothers in a monastery. It must not, however, be admitted to lay use.

CAP. XVII. Without the bishop’s permission no altar is to be set up in a consecrated church. From the Decrees of Pope Hormisdas.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *Nullus presbyter*.) No priest may erect another altar in a consecrated church unless it has been sanctified by the bishop of the place or by his delegate, so that there may be a distinction between what is sacred and what is not sacred. Nor may he pretend that a dedication has occurred when it has not. If he does so, if he is a cleric, he is to be deposed; if a layperson, anathematized. [Col. 1086D]

CAP. XVIII. Churches whose consecration is uncertain are to be consecrated. Council of Meaux, c. 8.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *Ecclesiae vel altaria*.) Churches or altars whose consecration is doubtful are to be consecrated, and superfluous altars are to be destroyed.

CAP. XIX. If the bodies of the dead are buried in a church already consecrated, Masses may be celebrated there if only faithful persons have been buried. Council of Cologne.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *Ecclesiam*.) It is not permitted to sanctify the altar of a church in which the bodies of unbelieving dead persons are buried. But if it was previously consecrated, Masses may be celebrated in it. [Col. 1087A]

CAP. XX. When a church is to be consecrated again, and when it is only to be exorcised with salt. From the Decrees of Pope Eugenius, c. 4.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *Si motum*.) If the altar has been moved, the church is to be consecrated anew. If the walls are altered but not the altar, it is only to be exorcised with salt.

CAP. XXI. That, because of adultery and homicide, a whole church ought to be consecrated. From the Decrees of the same pope, c. 6.

(c. 1, *De Consecratione ecclesiae*, in VI.) If a church has been violated by homicide or adultery, it is to be purified with the greatest care and consecrated anew.

CAP. XXII. A church in which a pagan is found buried is not to be consecrated. [Col. 1087B] Council of Orléans, c. 6.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *Ecclesia*.) It is not permitted to consecrate a church in which a pagan is buried, nor to celebrate Masses there; rather, the body must be cast out and the place cleansed. [Col. 1088A]

CAP. XXIII. Concerning a church in which the bodies of believers and unbelievers are buried. Council of Cologne, c. 3.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *Ecclesiam*.) It is not permissible to sanctify a church in which the bodies of unbelieving dead persons are buried. But if it appears suitable for consecration, after the bodies have been removed and the walls or timbers of that place razed, it is to be rebuilt.

CAP. XXIV. On the same matter. Council of Cologne, c. 3.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *Ecclesiam*, § *Sed si haec*.) [Col. 1088B] If it has previously been consecrated, Masses may be celebrated there, provided that those buried in it were believers.

## ON BURIALS

[Col. 1087]

CAP. XXV. On burial in churches, and that no one may dare violate graves. [Col. 1087B] Council of Meaux, c. 10.

No one may presume to bury any dead person in a church as though by hereditary right, except one whom the bishop or priest judges worthy because of the quality of that person’s conduct and life. Nor may anyone cast the bones of any dead person out of his grave, or dare in any way, through rash presumption, to violate anyone’s burial-place. Rather, let each person await the coming of his Judge in the place prepared and granted to him by God. [Col. 1087C]

CAP. XXVI. Even under compulsion we ought not to receive payment for burial. Jerome, *Hebrew Questions*, c. 23.

(13, q. 2, c. *Postquam pretio*.) After Ephron was overcome by payment so as to sell the burial-place and receive silver—although Abraham compelled him—the letter *vau*, which among them is read as *o*, was taken away from his name, and instead of Ephron he was called Ephrau. Scripture thereby signifies that the man who could sell the memorial of the dead was not of consummate and perfect virtue. Therefore let those who voluntarily sell graves, and are not compelled to receive a price but extort something from unwilling persons, know that their name is altered and that something of their merit perishes, since even that man who accepted it unwillingly is secretly reproved. [Col. 1088B–C]

CAP. XXVII. Nothing is to be demanded for burial. Pope Gregory.

We absolutely forbid either asking or exacting anything, lest, what is exceedingly irreligious, the Church be called venal, or you appear to rejoice in human deaths if you seek in any way to gain profit from their corpses.

## ON PRIESTS AND THEIR CHURCHES

[Col. 1087]

CAP. XXVIII. That altars of alleged revelations invented through people’s dreams are rejected. Or: Altars erected without saints’ relics are to be overthrown. [Col. 1087D] Council of Africa, c. 14.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *Placuit ut*.) Likewise, it has been decreed that altars which are set up here and there in fields and villages as though memorials of martyrs, but in which no body or relics of a martyr are shown to have been deposited, are, if possible, to be overthrown by the bishops who govern those places. If this is not permitted because of popular disturbances, the people are nevertheless to be warned not to frequent them, so that those of sound judgment may not be held there captive by any superstition. No memorial of martyrs is to be accepted there as authentic unless either a body, certain relics, or the origin of some habitation, possession, or suffering is handed down by a most trustworthy tradition. For altars set up anywhere through dreams and through the empty supposed revelations of any persons are entirely rejected. [Col. 1088D]

CAP. XXIX. That every person wishing to enter religious life is to be committed to the monasteries of the church within whose parish he is subject. From the Decrees of Pope Leo IX.

It has been reported to us that there are certain persons acting perversely who try to overthrow and divide the unity of the Church—namely abbots and monks who, watching not with the zeal of charity but with the zeal of rapacity, do not cease to teach and seduce laypeople whom they can ensnare, so that in life or at death they may convey their goods and possessions to those monks’ monasteries, while leaving nothing of their property to the churches to which they are seen to belong and from which they received or receive baptism, penance, the Eucharist, and also the nourishment of life with milk. [Col. 1089A] Seeing this breeding-ground of discord, we wish to restrain it in every way and absolutely forbid its future occurrence. We consider that it is not good for those who were once companions in sufferings, according to the Apostle, to be exempt from sharing in consolations; and because the worker is worthy of his wage, we therefore command and order that whoever henceforth wishes to enter religious life in a monastery, whether in life or at death, shall leave to the church to which he is known to belong one half of all goods and possessions which he decrees are to be disposed of for the salvation of his soul. Then, and only then, may he have permission to go and enter the monastery of his choice. Whoever proves to be an opponent, violator, or rash transgressor of this our decree shall be subject to the sword of anathema. [Col. 1089B]

CAP. XXX. The solemnities of Mass are to be celebrated only in sacred places. Council of Tribur, c. 4.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *Missarum*.) We decree that the solemnities of Mass are to be celebrated not just anywhere, but in places consecrated by bishops or where the bishop himself has permitted.

CAP. XXXI. How Mass may be celebrated in a burned church. The same council, in the same place.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *Concedimus*.) We also permit that, if churches have anywhere been set on fire and burned—as has very often happened, through the demands of our sins, at the hands of Northmen, Slavs, Bulgars, evil Christians, or in any other manner—Masses may meanwhile be celebrated in chapels with a consecrated altar-board, until those churches can be restored. On a journey, if no church is available, we permit the celebration under the open sky or in tents, provided that a consecrated altar-board and the other sacred mysteries pertaining to that office are present. We wholly forbid it otherwise. [Col. 1089C]

CAP. XXXII. Altars are not to be anointed with chrism unless they are made of stone. Council of Hippo, c. 6.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *Altaria primo*.) If altars are not stone, they are not to be consecrated by anointing with chrism. For the celebration of divine offices, their fellow-provincials must observe the order maintained by the metropolitans. [Col. 1089D]

CAP. XXXIII. That we have the anointing of the altar from the old law. Or: Sacrifices are to be offered only upon an altar and in places consecrated to God. From the Decrees of Felix sent to all bishops.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *Sicut non alii*.) It is clear to all who know the precepts of the New and Old Testaments that the consecration of churches and the celebration of Masses ought not to occur anywhere except in places consecrated to the Lord, unless there is great necessity. We read that Moses, at the Lord’s command, made and consecrated the tabernacles with their table and altar and the other vessels and utensils required for the performance of divine worship; and we know that he consecrated them not only with divine prayers, but, at the Lord’s command, anointed them with holy oil. [Col. 1090A]

CAP. XXXIV. That altars ought not to be consecrated unless relics are placed in them. Council of Africa, c. 1.

Altars in which it is not shown that sacred bodies or relics of martyrs are present are to be destroyed by the bishop of the place.

CAP. XXXV. A priest may not presume to celebrate Mass at the altar at which the bishop celebrated on the same day.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *In altari*.) A priest may not presume to celebrate Mass on that day at the altar at which the bishop has sung Mass.

CAP. XXXVI. That no one may transfer the bodies of saints from place to place.

[Col. 1090B]

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *Corpora*.) Henceforth let no one presume to transfer the bodies of saints from one place to another without the counsel of the ruler, the bishops’ consent, and the permission of the holy synod.

CAP. XXXVII. Changes of episcopal sees may be made owing to the necessity of the times. Pope Gregory to John, bishop of Trani.

(7, q. 1, c. *Temporis qualitas*.) The condition of the times urges us to transfer episcopal sees, formerly established in specified cities, to other places of the same diocese which we judge safer, so that the inhabitants may live more securely and the danger from barbarians may more easily be avoided. Therefore we command you, our brother and fellow-bishop John, to move your see from the city of Bellitranum to the place called Renati, to Saint Andrew the Apostle, so that you may be freer from hostile attack and may arrange there the customary observance of the festival days. [Col. 1090C]

CAP. XXXVIII. For what reasons the places of saints are to be moved. Augustine.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *Tribus*.) The places of saints are to be transferred for three reasons: first, when the necessity of persecutors presses upon those places; second, when the sites are difficult; third, when they are burdened by association with wicked persons.

CAP. XXXIX. It is permitted to pray in private oratories, but not to celebrate Mass. [Col. 1090D] Council of Orléans, c. 3.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 1, c. *Unicuique*.) Every believer may have an oratory in his own house and pray there; it is not permitted to celebrate Masses there.

CAP. XL. At what hour Mass is to be celebrated. From the letter of Pope Telesphorus, c. 6.

Celebrations of Mass are not at all to be held before the third hour of the day, because at that same hour the Lord was crucified and the Holy Spirit is recorded as having descended upon the apostles, except on the night of the Nativity.

CAP. XLI. Until the Mass of the catechumens, no one is to be forbidden to enter the church. Council of Carthage IV, c. 14.

A bishop is not to forbid anyone—heretic or Jew—from entering the church and hearing the word of God until the Mass of the catechumens. [Col. 1091A]

CAP. XLII. Individual priests ought to have their own churches. Pope Dionysius, letter 2.

(13, q. 1, c. *Ecclesias*.) We have assigned individual churches to individual priests and have determined that each shall have his own proper right. Thus no one may invade the boundaries or rights of another parish; rather, each is to be content with his own boundaries and guard the church and people committed to him in such a way that before the tribunal of the eternal Judge he may render an account of all entrusted to him, and receive not judgment but glory for his acts.

CAP. XLIII. On the same matter. Council of Reims, c. 3.

[Col. 1091B]

Each priest is to be content with the one church to which he was ordained, and no one may presume to minister in two churches.

CAP. XLIV. One church cannot be divided between two priests. Council of Reims, c. 8.

(21, q. 2, c. *Sicut in unaquaque*.) Just as each church ought to have one priest, so the church itself, which is called his bride, cannot be divided among several priests; rather, it shall have only one priest, who governs it chastely and sincerely. Therefore we forbid anyone to presume to divide a church among two or more priests, because the Church of Christ ought to be wife and bride, not a prostitute, as Pope Calixtus testifies. [Col. 1091C]

CAP. XLV. What punishment awaits a priest who leaves his church through ambition for a better one. Or: Whoever seeks another’s church, once expelled from it, also loses his own. From the Council of Meaux.

(7, q. 1, c. *Si quis*.) If anyone of the priestly order, despising a lesser church, has ambitiously and improperly aspired to a more important one, the canonical determination is to be maintained against him: that is, he shall lose both.

CAP. XLVI. Without bishops’ consent, laypersons are not to expel priests from churches. Council of Chalon, c. 10.

(16, q. 7, c. *Inventum est*.) It has been found that many, in the rashness of their own judgment and, what is more serious, driven by greed, grant or take churches from priests without their bishops’ consent. Therefore, with the canonical rule observed, no one may give a church to any priest without his bishop’s consent. If he has justly acquired it, he may lose it only for grave fault, before the bishop and with canonical severity. [Col. 1091D]

CAP. XLVII. On the same matter. Laypersons may not expel priests from churches. Council of Mainz, c. 28.

Laypersons are not to expel priests from churches or appoint them without their bishops’ consent.

CAP. XLVIII. [Col. 1092A] From the same council.

No one at all may demand gifts from priests for the repair of a church.

CAP. XLIX. Those who attempt to acquire a church by gifts are to be expelled from the clergy. Council of Rouen, c. 5.

(7, q. 1, c. *Sancitum est*.) It has been decreed and forbidden in every way that, if any priest is found to have given or to be giving gifts or other money to a cleric or layperson, or to have bought with a price the vacant church of another priest, he is, because of this greed, robbery, or presumption for the sake of shameful gain, to be expelled from the clergy and excluded from the rule.

CAP. L. That a priest or any cleric shall leave to his own church whatever he acquires after the day of ordination, unless it comes to him by gift or hereditary right. Or: What is acquired by the rector of a church who had nothing at the time of promotion is presumed to have been acquired from the goods of the church. [Col. 1092B] Council of Reims, c. 6.

(c. 1, *extra* *De peculio*.) It must be investigated whether, when a priest who possessed no patrimony at the time he was promoted to ecclesiastical rank subsequently buys estates, they belong by right to the church to which he was promoted while possessing nothing, according to canonical authority. [Reading uncertain: *esse definitur*, “they are determined to belong.”]

CAP. LI. Concerning things purchased by priests: they are to draw up the document in the church’s name. Council of Agde, c. 54.

(12, q. 4, c. *Presbyter*.) When a priest holds a diocese, he is to draw up in the name of the church the document for things which he purchases, so that they may not be separated from the administration of the church which he governs. [Col. 1092C]

CAP. LII. Concerning those who, having initially possessed nothing, acquire something during their administration. Council of Carthage.

(12, q. 3, c. *Placuit*.) It has been decreed that bishops, priests, deacons, or any clerics who are ordained possessing nothing, but buy lands or any estates in their own names during their episcopate or clerical office, are to be liable to the charge of unlawful seizure of the Lord’s property, unless they convey those very things to the church to which they are assigned. But if something comes to them through another person’s free gift or through inheritance from relatives, they may do with it what they wish. [Col. 1092D]

CAP. LIII. Things acquired by a bishop after consecration are to be left to the holy church. Council of Carthage, c. 48.

(c. *ut unusquisque*, *extra* *De peculio*.) Each priest is to leave to his own church the property which he acquires after the day of consecration.

CAP. LIV. No disgraceful song is to be performed around churches. Council of Carthage.

We entirely forbid the performance of disgraceful or lascivious songs around churches and in church precincts; this is to be avoided everywhere.

CAP. LV. On images in churches. Council of Elvira, c. 2.

(*De Consecratione*, dist. 3, c. *Venerabiles*.) It has been decreed that paintings ought not to be made in churches, lest that which is worshipped or adored be painted upon the walls. [Col. 1093A]

CAP. LVI. Likewise on images. Gregory, letter 2, to D., the recluse.

(*Ibid.*) For it is one thing to adore an image, another to learn from the narrative of an image what ought to be adored. What Scripture is to those who can read, an image provides to the uneducated who look upon it: those who are ignorant see in it what they ought to follow; those who do not know letters read in it. Thus, especially among the nations, an image serves in place of reading. You, who dwell among the nations, ought carefully to have considered this, lest, while you were incautiously inflamed by a right zeal, you should create scandal among fierce minds. Therefore, what was placed in churches not to be adored but only to instruct the minds of the ignorant ought not to have been broken. And since antiquity has not without reason permitted the histories of saints to be painted in venerable places, if you had tempered zeal with discernment, you would without doubt have obtained beneficially what you intended and would not have scattered the flock which had been gathered; rather, you could have gathered it, so that the unblemished name of shepherd might prevail, and blame for a steward might not fall upon you. [Col. 1094A]

## ON TITHES

[Col. 1093]

CAP. LVII. That tithes which God has ordained are to be paid to God. [Col. 1093B] Council of Mainz, c. 37.

(16, q. 2, c. *Admonemus*.) We admonish and command that tithes, which God has ordained to be given, must by no means be neglected. For one must fear lest anyone who withholds from God what is due to him perhaps have his necessities taken away by God because of his sin.

CAP. LVIII. Those unwilling to give tithes to priests are to be excommunicated; and from what tithes are to be paid. Council of Rouen, c. 3.

(16, q. 7, c. *Omnes decimae*.) All tithes of the land, whether from crops or from the fruit of trees, belong to the Lord and are consecrated to him. Cattle, sheep, and goats that pass under the shepherd’s rod—whatever comes as the tenth—shall be consecrated to the Lord. Neither good nor bad shall be selected, nor shall one be exchanged for another. If anyone makes an exchange, both what is exchanged and that for which it is exchanged shall be consecrated to the Lord and shall not be redeemed. But because many are now found unwilling to give tithes, we decree that, according to the command of our Lord Jesus Christ, they are to be admonished once, a second time, and a third. If they do not amend, they are to be bound by the bond of anathema until suitable satisfaction and amendment are made. [Col. 1093C]

CAP. LIX. Abbots and bishops are not to pay tithes from their own estates. [Col. 1093D] Council of Mainz, c. 28.

(17, q. 1, c. *Questi sunt*.) Certain brothers further complained that there were some bishops and abbots who would not allow tithes to be given to the church where their tenants hear Mass. Therefore this holy assembly decreed that bishops and abbots are to have tithes brought to the churches from the fields and vineyards which they hold for their use or maintenance.

> [Note: [Col. 1093] Gratian reads: “which they hold for the support of themselves and of the brothers, they are to have [the tithes] brought to their churches.”]

But their households are to bring their tithes where their children are baptized and where, throughout the whole yearly cycle, they hear Mass.

CAP. LX. That tithe is to be given by authority of the old law. Or: Let tithes be paid after the example of the ancients. [Col. 1094B] Council of Mainz, c. 8.

(16, q. 7, c. *Decimas*.) Abraham’s acts and Jacob’s promises show that tithes are to be given to God and to God’s priests. Then the law established it, and all holy teachers recall it: the Israelites were to give to the Lord tithes of livestock, crops, and all first-fruits—he who freed them from the ten plagues with which he struck the Egyptians, and in the final plague destroyed the firstborn of all, while granting favour to his own people so that, having obtained money, they might despoil Egypt. Concerning these tithes the venerable teacher Augustine said: “Tithes are required as a debt.” [Col. 1094C]

For if God were to say: “Surely the human being is mine; the land which you cultivate is mine; the seeds which you sow are mine; the animals which you work are mine; the warmth of the sun is mine. And since all things are mine, you, who furnish the smaller part, will scarcely deserve a tenth alone; yet I reserve nine for you—give me the tenth. If you do not give me the tenth, I shall take the nine from you; but if you give me the tenth, I shall multiply the nine.” Therefore, since the Jewish people observed the commandment of tithes with such diligence that they gave a tenth even of the smallest things—namely rue, mint, and cumin, as the Lord himself testifies (Matt. 23)—why does not the evangelical people fulfil the same command with greater zeal, they whose worship of the priests is greater and whose worship through the sacraments is purer? [Col. 1094D]

They are therefore to be given so that, appeased by this devotion, God himself may grant abundantly what is necessary, as we have shown above; so that priests and teachers of the Church, relieved of concern for bodily needs, without which this life cannot be lived, may be freer for meditation upon the divine law, the administration of doctrine, and the performance of spiritual service; and so that the people’s gift may be offered to the Lord in daily oblation, and may also advance the canonical provisions for the support of the poor and the restoration of churches. For, according to the canons, four portions must be made from the offerings of the faithful: one for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth for restoration of the church. [Col. 1095A]

CAP. LXI. Three portions are to be made from tithes: two for the clergy and the third for the bishop. Or: Let founders of basilicas recognize that they have no authority over church property.

(10, q. 1, c. *De his*.) The ordinances of the ancient canons are to be observed concerning what parishioners offer to the church in lands, vineyards, slaves, and livestock: all such things are subject to the bishop’s authority. But of what is offered at the altars, one third is to be faithfully offered to the bishops and two thirds to the clergy. Tithes, however, according to some, are received by bishops one third each year, or the whole in the third year; but we, following the Romans, hold that bishops receive one fourth each year, the whole amount in the fourth year. [Col. 1095B]

CAP. LXII. Tithes are not to be redeemed by the people. Council of Mainz, c. 3.

(16, q. 7, c. *Decimas*.) Bishops must forbid the tithes which the people have customarily given from being redeemed from them by any payment. [Reading uncertain: *consuevit*.]

CAP. LXIII. By divine law all things are common; by the law of human enactment, however, this is mine and that another’s. Augustine, Tractate VI on John, chapter 1.

(Dist. 8, c. *Quo jure*.) By what law do you defend the Church’s estates: divine or human? Divine law is found in the Scriptures; human law in the laws of kings. Whence does anyone possess what he possesses? Is it not by human law? For by divine law, “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. 23). The Lord made poor and rich alike from one clay, and one earth supports poor and rich alike. Thus, by human law it is said: “This estate is mine; this house is mine; this slave is mine.” Human laws are the laws of emperors. Why? Because God has distributed those human laws to humankind through the emperors and kings of the age. Take away the laws of emperors, and who would dare say: “That estate is mine; that slave is mine; that house is mine?” But if people have received laws in order that they may hold these things, they have received the laws of kings. Do you want us to recite the laws so that you may hear them [variant: “Do you want us to be silent about the laws so that you may rejoice?”]?

[lacuna]

[Col. 1096B] Let the laws be read in which the emperors have openly commanded that those who, outside communion with the Catholic Church, usurp for themselves the Christian name and refuse to maintain peace with the author of peace, may dare to possess nothing in the name of the Church. “But what have we to do with the emperor?” Yet, as I have already said, the matter concerns human law; and nevertheless the Apostle wished kings to be served and honoured, and said: “Honour the king” (1 Pet. 2). Do not say, “What have I to do with the king?” What, then, have you to do with property? Possessions are held through the laws of kings. You said, “What have I to do with the king?” Do not call possessions yours, because you have renounced those very human laws by which possessions are held.

## ON PRESCRIPTION AND POSSESSION

[Col. 1095]

CAP. LXIV. Rural parishes are to remain undisturbed with the bishop who has possessed them for thirty years without violence. [Col. 1095C] Council of Chalcedon, c. 17.

(16, q. 3, c. *Per singulas*.) In every rural church, parish, or possession, they are to remain undisturbed with the bishops who retain them, especially those who have governed them while holding them without violence for thirty years. But if a dispute concerning them has arisen or arises within thirty years, those who claim that they have been injured may bring a case concerning them before the provincial synod.

CAP. LXV. Dioceses possessed by bishops for thirty years are to remain theirs. Pope Gelasius I, letter 3 to the Sicilians.

(16, q. 3, c. *Praesulum*, § *Permaneant*.) It was also decided to add this: if—God forbid!—the resources of churches and also dioceses are possessed by certain bishops, they shall vindicate for themselves by right what the thirty-year law establishes. For the authority of our sons the rulers has likewise been promulgated: after thirty years, no one may appeal concerning that which the passage of time fixed by kings has barred.

CAP. LXVI. Prescription of forty years is granted to religious houses. Gregory to Peter the subdeacon.

(Dist. 16, q. 5.) If the monastery of Saint Theodore is found to have possessed without disturbance for forty years the boundaries concerning which a dispute has been raised, do not permit it henceforth to suffer any claim, even if something might have belonged to the holy Roman Church; rather, secure its peace by every means. [Col. 1096C]

CAP. LXVII. Thirty-year possession must be observed within one province. Council of Toledo IV, c. 33.

(16, q. 3, c. *Quicunque*.) Any bishop who has possessed another bishop’s diocese for thirty years without any challenge, even though according to legal right it may appear not to be a diocese belonging to him, cannot be sued for its recovery. This applies only within one province, however; beyond it, in no way, lest, while a diocese is being defended, the boundaries of provinces be confused.

CAP. LXVIII. Thirty-year possession is to be secure; possession of a territory does not remove its assembly. [Col. 1096D] Fourth Council of Toledo, canons 34 and 24.

(16, q. 3, c. *Sicut dioecesim*.) Just as thirty-year possession removes another’s diocese, so it does not remove the assembly of a territory. Therefore newly established basilicas shall without doubt belong to that bishop whose assembly they are shown to be.

CAP. LXIX. Boundaries that have been defined cannot be prescribed away by time. Gelasius to Justus, bishop.

(16, q. 4, c. *Dilectio tua*.) Let your charity strive to ascertain faithfully the truth of every matter. If, concerning the boundaries over which a dispute is said to have arisen, a definite ruling was long ago issued, let it be preserved inviolate. Otherwise, if nothing was ever established as settled, then let whichever party relies upon prescription by time offer an oath; provided, however, that you permit the party proved to have possessed them hitherto to offer the oath.

CAP. LXX. Concerning those who burn churches. From the Decrees of Pope Eugenius.

(17, q. 4, c. *Si quis*.—*Palea*.) If anyone burns a church, let him do penance for fifteen years, diligently restore it, and give its value to the poor.

CAP. LXXI. Let one who dishonourably deals, through arrogant pride, with possessions consecrated to God be deprived of the communion of the faithful. [Col. 1098A] Council of Mainz, canon 7.

(Dist. 30, c. *Si quis per superbiam*, with what follows.) Whoever, puffed up by arrogant pride, treats the house of God as contemptible, and dishonourably handles or presumes to violate possessions consecrated to God and established for God’s honour under the king’s protection of immunity; or, with reckless daring, perpetrates burnings or devastations: let him, as an invader and violator of the Church, which is the house of the living God, be cut off from communion with all the faithful.

## CONCERNING THOSE WHO FLEE TO A CHURCH

[Col. 1097]

CAP. LXXII. If an abductor flees to a church with the woman abducted, what is to be done? Council of Orléans, canon 4.

(36, q. 1, c. 3, *De raptoribus*.) Concerning abductors of women, we have judged that the following is to be established: if an abductor flees to a church with the woman abducted, and it is established that the woman herself suffered violence, she is immediately to be freed from the abductor’s power and returned to her parents; and, once immunity from death or punishment has been granted to the abductor, he is to have free permission to depart.

[Note: [Col. 1097D] Gratian reads thus: “or he is to be subjected to servitude, or he is to have free permission to redeem himself.”]

But if the woman’s parents refuse to obey the churchmen, let them be excommunicated.

CAP. LXXIII. Before security has been received, a fugitive is not to be compelled to leave the church precinct. Council of Orléans, canon 3.

[Col. 1097C] (17, q. 4, c. *Id constituimus*, § *Servus etiam*.) A slave who has fled to a church on account of any offence, if he has received from his master, for the offence committed, an ecclesiastical oath, shall immediately be compelled to return to his master’s service; and after, upon the giving of the oath, he has been handed over to his master, if he who is accused is proved to have suffered anything for that same offence, he shall, for contempt of the Church and breach of faith, be regarded as excluded from the communion of Catholics, as has been set out above. But if a slave, defended by the church on account of his offence, has received from his master, at the clergy’s demand, an oath guaranteeing immunity, the master may seize him if he refuses to leave.

CAP. LXXIV. After security has been pledged, slaves are to be restored to their masters. [Col. 1097D] Gelasius to Boniface, bishop.

(Summarized from 17, q. 4, c. *Metuentes*.) A slave, after an oath has been pledged to him, is to be returned even against his will.

CAP. LXXV. No one is to attempt to drag away a person fleeing to a church. From the Book of Capitularies.

(17, q. 4, c. *Reum ad eccl.*) No one may dare drag away a slave fleeing to a church, or to the church precinct, the workshops of religious brethren, the court, or the bishop’s house, because these places are held by the ancient canons to possess immunity; nor may anyone give him up from there for punishment or death, so that the honour of God and of His saints may be preserved above all things. Rather, the rulers of churches should strive to obtain for him, upon oath, peace, life, and bodily safety. Nevertheless, he must lawfully make amends for whatever wrong he has done; and if the pursuer refuses to obey the masters of the Church, let him be constrained canonically.

CAP. LXXVI. Let a cleric who presumes to beat his slave or pupil when he has fled to the church be excluded from the church. Council of Lérida, canon 5.

(17, q. 4, c. *Nullus cleric.*) Let no cleric dare drag out or presume to flog his slave or pupil fleeing to a church. If he does so, let him be excluded, until he has made worthy penance, from the place to which he gave no honour. [Col. 1098C]

CAP. LXXVII. On what condition enemies fleeing to a church are to be returned. Council of Chalcedon, canon 5.

(17, q. 4, c. *Metuentes*.) Likewise, it was decreed in the Council of Mâcon that those who flee from their enemies to a church, a church precinct, a house, or the enclosure of religious persons are not to be dragged away from there until they have first received from their persecutor, upon sacred objects, security against death, mutilation, and every kind of punishment. If they are slaves of those from whom they flee, this is to be done on condition that satisfaction is made to the person whose property they have criminally harmed. If, however, one who first swore upon sacred objects is convicted of having violated his oath, let him, as guilty of perjury, be deprived of communion until he makes satisfaction. [Col. 1098D]

CAP. LXXVIII. From the church precinct, enclosed by thirty paces, a fugitive is not to be dragged away unless security has first been given. First Council of Toledo, canon 12.

(17, q. 4, c. *Definivit*.) Concerning those who, through any fear or terror, seek refuge in a church, this second council, with the concurrence and command of our lord King Eringius, has decreed that no one may dare drag away those taking refuge in the holy church, nor inflict upon persons remaining in a holy place any injury, damage, or spoliation. Rather, those who seek a church are in every respect to be permitted to go forth within thirty paces from the church doors; throughout the entire circuit of each church, reverence is to protect those thirty paces. Yet those who flee there must in no way enter private houses or houses far removed from the church; but, proceeding within this holy distance of thirty paces without taking shelter in private houses, they shall have access so that they may leave those places for the necessary use of nature, and may not be constrained by any unavoidable necessity, since they have committed themselves to the Lord’s enclosures for protection. [Col. 1100A]

If anyone attempts to violate this decree, let him be subject to ecclesiastical excommunication and struck by the sentence of royal severity. Yet if, in accordance with the ordinances of the ancient canons, those who demand the return of persons who have taken refuge have given oaths, and the priest of that church has not removed them from the church doors, either their flight, if it occurs, is to be sought by the priest, or a judgment of damages is to be imposed upon such priests according to the decision of the prince.

## CONCERNING SACRILEGE

[Col. 1099]

CAP. LXXIX. On the several kinds of sacrilege and their punishment. [Col. 1099B] John VIII, in the book of Gothic law.

(17, q. 4, c. *Quisquis*.) Sacrilege is committed if anyone breaks into a church, or into the thirty ecclesiastical paces surrounding a church, or into houses situated within the aforesaid thirty paces, by plundering or carrying anything away from them; likewise by anyone who inflicts injury upon, or takes property from, unarmed clerics, monks, or church persons devoted to God. Chapels situated within the circuit of the walls of fortified places are not protected or included within this observance. Likewise, sacrilege is committed by taking what is sacred from a sacred place, or what is not sacred from a sacred place; for what cannot be counted as the crime of sacrilege must be redressed under the provisions of secular laws or according to the custom of the country. [Col. 1099C]

CAP. LXXX. On the punishment of sacrilege. The same, in the same book.

(17, q. 4, c. *Quisquis*.) Having examined the Roman laws where they treat of sacrilege, we find that Emperor Justinian established the compensation for sacrilege at ten pounds of the finest gold. But we command that a lighter law, established by Charles, be observed: namely, for the prince’s settlement for sacrilege, thirty pounds of assayed silver, that is, an amount of the purest silver equal to six hundred solidi. Therefore, whoever is found guilty of sacrilege shall pay this lighter settlement to the bishops, abbots, or persons to whom the complaint of sacrilege rightly pertains. If the guilty person refuses to do so, let him remain subject to excommunication until he pays the aforesaid settlement of six hundred solidi. If he dies in this obstinacy, his body is not to be carried to burial with psalms and hymns. We command that this law be written at the end of the code of secular law. Thus far the pope’s law. [Col. 1100B]

CAP. LXXXI. Let those who attempt to violate the bounds of a church be excommunicated. [Note: [Col. 1099D] Note that several exceptions are made by the laws: *Extra*, “On the immunity of churches,” c. *Int.*] [Col. 1100C] Council of Agde, canon 28.

(17, q. 4, c. *Sicut antiquitus*.) As was established long ago by the holy Fathers, we establish that a major church shall have a circuit of sixty paces, while chapels or smaller churches shall have thirty. Whoever attempts to violate this boundary, or drags away from it a human person or his goods, unless he is a public robber, shall be excommunicated until he makes amends and restores what he has taken.

## CONCERNING THE PROTECTION OF FREE PERSONS

[Col. 1099]

CAP. LXXXII. The Church protects freed persons in their liberty. [Col. 1099D] Council of Agde, canon 29.

(Dist. 87, c. *Liberos*.) Let the Church, if necessary, protect persons lawfully made free by their masters. If anyone, before a hearing, wishes or presumes either to seize or despoil them, let them be protected by the Church.

CAP. LXXXIII. The Church must protect persons lawfully emancipated. Or thus: Let freed persons who are being reduced to slavery be defended by priests. Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 71.

(Dist. 87, c. *Liberti*.) Freed persons, whoever may have manumitted them, who have been commended to the Church’s protection, are, as the rules of the ancient Fathers have established, to be protected by priestly defence against every person’s insolence, both in their condition of liberty and in the peculium which they are known to possess. [Col. 1100D]

CAP. LXXXIV. It is unlawful to drag away those who flee to a church. First Council of Orange, canon 6.

(Dist. 87, c. *Eos*, § *In ecclesia quoque*.) If anyone attempts by force to reduce to slavery, compulsory service, or the condition of a tenant farmer persons manumitted in church or commended to the Church by testament, he shall be restrained by ecclesiastical punishment.

## CONCERNING THE ALIENATION AND EXCHANGE OF CHURCH PROPERTY

[Col. 1101]

CAP. LXXXV. A bishop ought not alienate or give away church property without the counsel of the clergy. [Col. 1101A] Council of Toledo, canon 4.

(12, q. 2, c. *Sine except.*) This holy synod grants no bishop permission to alienate church property, since this is also forbidden by the more ancient canons. But if they give from churches belonging to their own parish something that does not burden the Church, for the support of monks, let it remain valid. They are permitted, while preserving the Church’s right, to provide temporarily what they can for the need of strangers, clerics, or the poor.

CAP. LXXXVI. On the same matter. Council at Valencia. Pope Leo.

[Col. 1101B] (12, q. 2, c. *Sine except.*, § *Irrita episcopo*.) A bishop’s gift, sale, or exchange of church property shall be void without the approval and signature of the clergy.

CAP. LXXXVII. Things done without consultation are easily corrected by successors. Or thus: An exchange of church property made in an unauthorized case, or without observing the legal solemnity, must be revoked by the successor. [Col. 1102A] From the council at Beauvais.

(Extra, *De rerum permut.*, c. *Ut commutationes*.) Let exchanges of church property be very carefully guarded against and, if they ever must take place, examined with the greatest precision. Those made without due consideration—transactions which a predecessor bishop unlawfully admitted, or which others unlawfully carried out—are to be corrected by his successor, in accordance with the decrees of Pope Hilary’s canons.

CAP. LXXXVIII. On those who initially possess nothing but acquire something during their administration. Council of Braga, canon 35.

[Col. 1102B] (2, q. 3, c. *Placuit*.) Any priest who, from the right of his benefice, in any manner attempts permanently to alienate gold, silver, garments, gems, if there are any or if any are acquired, or any movable things intended for divine ornament, shall be punished, as donor, alienator, and seller, by loss of his office.

## WHICH BOOKS ARE RECEIVED BY THE CHURCH

CAP. LXXXIX.

Nothing is to be read or sung in the Church except what possesses divine authority and what the authority of the orthodox Fathers has sanctioned. Nor are false names of angels to be venerated, but only those taught by prophetic and evangelical Scripture: namely, Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael.

XC. At what times books are to be read in church. [Col. 1103A] Pope Gelasius I, with seventy bishops, decreed.

In Septuagesima they appoint the Pentateuch until the eleventh day before Easter. From the fifteenth day before Easter they appoint Jeremiah until the Lord’s Supper. At the Lord’s Supper they read three lessons from Jeremiah’s Lamentation, “How solitary she sits”; three lessons from Saint Augustine’s Treatise on Psalm VII, “Hear my prayer when I make supplication”; and three from the Apostle where he says in the Epistle to the Corinthians, “When you come together into one” (1 Cor. II). The second lesson begins thus: “Likewise after he had supped” (Luke XXII). The third: “Now concerning spiritual things, brethren, I would not have you ignorant” (1 Cor. X).

On Parasceve [Good Friday], there are three lessons from Jeremiah’s Lamentation, three from Saint Augustine’s Treatise on Psalm LX, “Hear, O Lord, my supplication,” and three from the Apostle where he says in the Epistle to the Hebrews, “Let us hasten to enter into that rest.” The second lesson begins: “For every high priest”; the third: “Of whom we have much to say.” [Col. 1103B]

On Holy Saturday, there are three lessons from Jeremiah’s Lamentation; three from Saint Augustine’s Treatise on Psalm LXIII, “Hear my prayer”; and three from the Apostle where he says in the Epistle to the Hebrews, “Christ being come, a high priest.” The second lesson begins where he says, “For the testimony”; the third, “Having a shadow.”

On the Lord’s Easter, homilies appropriate to that day are read. During the week, homilies. On the octave of Easter they appoint the Acts of the Apostles, the Catholic Epistles, and the Apocalypse until the octave of Pentecost. On the octave of Pentecost they appoint the books of Kings and Chronicles until the Kalends of August. On the first Sunday of August they appoint Solomon until the Kalends of September; then they appoint Job, Esther, Tobit, Ezra, and Judith until the Kalends of October. On the first Sunday of October, the book of Maccabees is appointed until the Kalends of November. On the first Sunday of November they appoint Ezekiel, Daniel, and the Minor Prophets until the Kalends of December. On the first Sunday of December they appoint the prophet Isaiah until the Nativity of the Lord.

At the Nativity of the Lord, they first read three lessons from Isaiah: the first, “At the first time”; the second, “Comfort ye”; the third, “Arise.” Then sermons or homilies appropriate to the day are read. [Col. 1103C]

On the feast of Saint Stephen, homilies for that day; likewise on the feast of Saint John; likewise on the feast of the Innocents; likewise on the feast of Saint Sylvester. On the octave of the Lord’s Nativity, homilies for that day. On the first Sunday after the Lord’s Nativity, they appoint the Epistles of Paul until Septuagesima. At Epiphany, three lessons from Isaiah: the first begins, “All ye that thirst”; the second, “Arise, be enlightened”; the third, “I will greatly rejoice in the Lord.” Then sermons or homilies appropriate to the day are read. [Col. 1103D]

CAP. XCI. Which books and councils are received by the Roman Church. From the Decrees of the same.

(Dist. 16, c. *Sancta*.) The holy Roman Church, after those Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments which we have received according to the rule, does not prohibit the reception also of the following writings: the holy Council of Nicaea of 318 Fathers, held under Emperor Constantine Augustus, through Maximus, at which the heretic Arius was condemned; the holy Council of Constantinople, held under Emperor Theodosius the Elder Augustus, at which the heretic Macedonius received his due condemnation; the first holy Council of Ephesus, at which Nestorius was condemned with the consent of the most blessed Pope Celestine, under Cyril, bishop of the see of Alexandria, and Arcadius, a bishop sent from Italy; the holy Council of Chalcedon, held under Emperor Marcian Augustus and Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, at which the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies, together with Dioscorus and his accomplices, were condemned. [Col. 1104A]

Moreover, whatever councils have hitherto been established by the holy Fathers, besides the authority of those four, we decree are both to be guarded and received.

Now there follows a list of the shorter works of the holy Fathers received in the Catholic Church: the works of blessed Cyprian, martyr and bishop of Carthage; likewise, the works of blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria; likewise, the works of blessed Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus; likewise, the works of blessed John, bishop of Constantinople; likewise, the works of blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria; likewise, the works of blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers; likewise, the works of blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan; likewise, the works of blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo; likewise, the works of blessed Jerome, priest; likewise, the works of blessed Gregory, bishop; likewise, the works of blessed Prosper, a most devout man; likewise, the works of blessed Pope Leo sent to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople. If anyone disputes their text even to a single point and does not receive them with reverence in all things, let him be anathema. [Col. 1104B]

Likewise, we decree that the works and treatises of all orthodox Fathers who in no respect departed from communion with the holy Roman Church nor were separated from its faithful preaching, but remained sharers, by God’s grace, in that communion until the last day of their lives, are to be read. Likewise, the decretal letters which the most blessed popes of the city of Rome issued at different times in response to consultations from different Fathers are to be received with reverence.

Likewise, the acts of the holy martyrs, resplendent in manifold tortures and in the wondrous triumphs of their confessions. Who among Catholics could doubt that they endured great things in their struggles, and bore all things not through their own powers but through God’s grace and help? Yet, in accordance with ancient authority or custom, they are not read in the holy Roman Church, with singular caution, because the names of those who wrote them are entirely unknown, and because it is thought that they were written by unbelievers with superfluities of speech, or in a fashion suited to actors, rather than according to the true order of events. Such are the passions of a certain Cyricus and his mother Julitta, of Gregory, and of others of this kind, said to have been written by heretics. Therefore, as stated above, lest even a slight occasion for mockery arise, they are not read in the holy Roman Church. [Col. 1104D]

Nevertheless, together with the aforesaid Church, we venerate with every devotion all martyrs and their glorious struggles, which are known more to God than to human beings. Likewise, we receive with all honour the *Lives of the Fathers*—of Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the hermits—which the most blessed Jerome wrote. Likewise, the acts of blessed Sylvester, bishop of the Apostolic See: although we do not know the name of their author, we know that they are read by many Catholics in the city of Rome, and many churches follow this practice because of its antiquity.

Likewise, the writing concerning the discovery of the Lord’s Cross and other writings concerning the discovery of John the Baptist are certain revelations, and some Catholics read them. But when these come into Catholic hands, the judgment of the blessed Apostle Paul must come first: “Test all things; hold fast that which is good” (1 Thess. XIX). [Col. 1105A]

Likewise, Rufinus, a devout man, published many books of ecclesiastical work and translated some writings. But because blessed Jerome criticized him in certain matters concerning freedom of the will, we hold those views which we know the aforesaid blessed Jerome held; and this applies not only to Rufinus but to all whom the frequently named man rebuked out of zeal for God and devotion to the faith.

Likewise, we receive for reading certain works of Origen which the most devout Jerome does not reject. But we declare that all the rest, together with their author, are to be rejected.

Likewise, the *Chronicles* of Eusebius of Caesarea and the books of his *Ecclesiastical History* are not to be rejected altogether, on account of their exceptional knowledge of events useful for instruction, although in the first book of his narrative he wove [material uncertain in the transmitted text] and afterwards composed one book in praise and defence of the schismatic Origen. [Col. 1105B]

Likewise, we commend Orosius, a most learned man, because he arranged matters greatly necessary for us against pagan calumnies and wove them together with remarkable brevity. Likewise, we commend with distinguished praise the Paschal work of the venerable Sedulius, which he composed in heroic verse. Likewise, we do not despise Vincentius’s laborious work, but imitate it.

But the Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church in no way receives the writings mentioned above which were composed by heretics. Of these, we believe that a few which have come to mind and which Catholics must avoid ought to be set down below. [Col. 1105D]

CAP. XCII. Ecclesiastical history is commended. Cassiodorus, in the prologue to the *Tripartite History*.

Ecclesiastical history, which is proved most necessary for all Christians, was wonderfully written by three Greek authors: namely, the venerable bishop Theodoret and the two most eloquent men Sozomen and Socrates. Trusting Epiphanius Scholasticus to render them into Latin, we judged it necessary, with the Lord’s help, to bring their selected statements together in a single treatment and make one narrative from three authors.

Likewise, whoever, with the Lord’s help, comes to these works may read without fear, gaining much usefulness and knowledge, if he carefully commits to memory what is set forth in these twelve books. [Col. 1106A]

CAP. XCIII. The Book of Wisdom is commended. Augustine to Prosper and Hilary, *On the Life of the Saints*.

The judgment of the Book of Wisdom ought not to have been rejected. It has deserved, for so many years, to be read in the Church of Christ from the rank of lectors in the Church of Christ, and to be heard with reverence as possessing divine authority by all Christians—from bishops down to the lowest faithful laity, penitents, and catechumens.

Likewise, anyone wishing to be instructed by the sayings of commentators ought to place before all commentators this Book of Wisdom, where it is read: “He was taken away lest wickedness should change his understanding” (Wis. IV). For the outstanding commentators even in times near to those of the apostles preferred it in this manner: using it as a witness, they believed that they adduced nothing except divine testimony. Likewise, the Book of Wisdom, which has deserved to be read in the Church of Christ for so great a number of years, ought to suffer no injury, because it withstands those who are deceived by human merits. [Col. 1106B]

CAP. XCIV. On Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*. Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book II.

We accept Eusebius’s treatment of the history of times and the questions of the divine books which are required for its use.

XCV. On the books of Jerome and Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book III, chapter 7.

[Col. 1106C] Jerome and Gennadius, seeking ecclesiastical writers throughout the whole world, treated them in order and gathered their studies into a catalogue of one volume.

CAP. XCVI. On Dionysius the Areopagite. Bede, *On the Acts of the Apostles*.

Dionysius the Areopagite, having been ordained bishop, gloriously governed the Church of the Corinthians and left many volumes of his own intellect which pertain to the Church’s benefit and remain to this day. He received the surname Areopagite from the place over which he presided, the Areopagus.

CAP. XCVII. On Saint Benedict.

(Gregory, *Dialogues*, book II.) Benedict wrote a Rule for monks, outstanding in discernment and eloquent in expression. [Col. 1106D]

CAP. XCVIII. On the writings of Gelasius.

Gelasius composed five books against Nestorius and Eutyches, and also treatises in Ambrose’s manner. Likewise, two books against Arius. He also composed prefaces and prayers for the sacraments in guarded language, and many letters on the faith in polished language.

CAP. XCIX. Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to Secundus, bishop.

During the sacred solemnities of the Masses, I expounded forty readings of the holy Gospel which are customarily read in this Church on appointed days. The exposition of some of them, dictated by me, was read to the assembled people by a notary; but I myself spoke before the people to explain others, and they were taken down as I spoke. Likewise, because these homilies were delivered in order, he took care to arrange them in two codices: the first twenty which were delivered, and the latter twenty likewise. [Col. 1107A]

CAP. C.

You say that you neither possess nor receive the Council of Sardica or other decrees of the holy Fathers. We are not readily given the means of believing this, especially since the whole Church receives the Council of Sardica, which was held among you in your regions. On what grounds, then, could it be fitting that this holy Church of Constantinople should object to it and, as has been said, not receive it?

CAP. CI. [Col. 1107B] Pope Agatho to all bishops.

All enactments of the Apostolic See are to be received as though confirmed by the very voice of the divine command.

CAP. CII. Acts of the Fifth Synod, day 3.

We follow in all things the holy Fathers and doctors of the Church: Athanasius, Hilary, Basil, Gregory the Theologian and Gregory of Nyssa, Ambrose, Augustine, Theophilus, John of Constantinople, Cyril, Leo, and Proclus; and we receive everything they set forth concerning the right faith and the condemnation of heretics. We also receive other holy and orthodox Fathers who preached the right faith without reproach in the holy Church of God until the end of their lives. [Col. 1107C]

CAP. CIII. By the authority of the Roman pontiff, the eight holy councils are confirmed. *Liber Diurnus*: Profession of the Roman Pontiff.

(Dist. 16, c. *Sancta*.) I confess that I shall preserve without any mutilation, down to the smallest point, the eight holy ecumenical councils—namely, the Nicene; the second Constantinopolitan; the first Ephesian; the fifth and sixth; likewise the Constantinopolitan sixth; likewise the Nicene fourth and fifth; and the eighth Constantinopolitan—and shall hold them worthy of equal honour and veneration. I confess that I shall in every way follow and proclaim what they preached and established, and condemn with mouth and heart whatever they condemned.

CAP. CIV. On the four principal councils, in the preface to the canons.

[Col. 1107D]

At what time did the canons of general councils begin? As Isidore says in the sixth book of the *Etymologies*, chapter 18: they began in the times of Emperor Constantine. Among other councils, however, four venerable synods are acknowledged to exist, which pre-eminently comprise the whole faith, like the four Gospels and the four rivers of Paradise.

The first of these was the Nicene Synod of 318 bishops, held under Emperor Constantine Augustus. In it was condemned the blasphemy of Arian perfidy, which Arius, the Alexandrian priest, asserted concerning the inequality of the Trinity. That holy synod declared the Son of God to be consubstantial with God the Father. This synod was held in the time of Sylvester, pope of Rome, Macarius, bishop of Jerusalem, and Alexander of Alexandria.

Concerning this synod Pope Leo says in his letter to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople:

> “Let no synodal councils flatter themselves on account of the multiplication of their assembly, nor let any number of priests, however much greater and more abundant, dare either compare itself with or prefer itself to the 318 bishops, since the Nicene Synod has been consecrated by so great a divine privilege that, whether ecclesiastical judgments are held by fewer or by more, whatever differs at all from their constitution is void of all authority.”

Blessed Ambrose likewise extols this Nicene Council without measure in his book *On the Trinity*, in these words:

> “Of councils, that especially is to be followed in which 318 priests, chosen as it were by Abraham’s judgment, victorious through the harmonious strength of faith, raised a trophy after the faithless had been subdued throughout the whole world. Therefore it seems to me a divine thing that in councils we possess by the same number the oracle which we possess in the history of piety as an example.” [Col. 1108B]

CAP. CV. The canons of the Apostles are to be received. Pope Zephyrinus, letter 1, to the bishops throughout Sicily.

(Dist. 16, c. *Sexaginta*.) Sixty apostles set down authoritative judgments and, together with very many other bishops, declared that they must be observed. Athanasius of Alexandria to Mark, pope and successor of Sylvester.

CAP. CVI. Letter of Athanasius requesting the chapters of the Nicene Council.

[Col. 1108C]

(Dist. 16, c. *Septuaginta*.) We desire that, through these present legates, we may deserve to receive from the authority of your Church of the Holy See the seventy chapters of the Nicene Council, which, by order of my lord Alexander, I brought as decrees of all the bishops from the aforesaid synod, and which have been burned by fire.

Likewise, eighty chapters were discussed in the aforesaid synod in our presence: namely, forty published by Greeks in the Greek language and forty likewise published by Latins in the Latin language. But it seemed good to the 318 bishops, filled with the Holy Spirit, in the aforesaid council—especially to the already mentioned Alexander and to the representatives of the Apostolic See—that ten chapters should be joined to others and inserted in suitable places, and that the chapters of so great and excellent a council should be made seventy in number, after the pattern of the seventy disciples or the seventy languages of the whole world, so that they might instruct the whole world of Christians. [Col. 1108D]

CAP. CVII. Only twenty chapters of the Nicene Council are extant. Stephen to Lullus, bishop of Mainz, chapter 20.

(Dist. 16, c. *Viginti*.) Only twenty chapters of the Nicene Council are held in the Roman Church, but through what neglect the others have disappeared is uncertain. Many think that they were inserted in the Council of Antioch.

CAP. CVIII. On the second synod. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 16.

(Dist. 15, c. *Canones*, § *Secunda*.) The second synod, of 150 Fathers, was assembled at Constantinople under Theodosius the Elder. Condemning Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit is God, it showed that the Holy Spirit is consubstantial with the Father and the Son, and gave the form of the Creed which the entire confession of Greeks and Latins proclaims in the churches. This synod was held in the time of Damasus, pope of Rome, Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, and Nestorius of Constantinople. [Col. 1109A]

CAP. CIX. On the third synod. The same, in the same place.

(Dist. 15, c. *Canones*, § *Tertia*.) The third synod, the first Ephesian, of 200 bishops, was held under Theodosius the Younger Augustus. It condemned with a just anathema Nestorius, who asserted two persons in Christ, showing that the one person of our Lord Jesus Christ remains in two natures. This synod was held in the time of Celestine, pope of Rome, Juvenal, bishop of Constantinople, and Cyril of Alexandria. [Col. 1109B]

CAP. CX. On the fourth synod. The same, in the same place.

(Dist. 15, c. *Canones*, § *Quarta*.) The Fourth Synod, that of Chalcedon, was held under the Emperor Marcian by 430 bishops. In it Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, who declared that the Word of God and the flesh were one nature, and his defender Dioscorus, formerly bishop of Alexandria, and likewise Nestorius once more, together with the remaining heretics, it condemned beforehand by the unanimous judgment of the Fathers; this synod proclaiming that Christ God was so born of the Virgin that in him we confess the natures of both the divine and the human substance. This synod was held in the time of Leo, pope of Rome; Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem; and Anastasius of Constantinople. These are the four principal synods, which most fully contain the nature of the faith; [Col. 1109C] as also are any councils which the holy Fathers, filled with the Holy Spirit, decreed. After the authority of these four, all remain established in full force.

## CHAPTER CXI. On the Fifth Synod. Bede, *On Times*, ch. 38.

The Fifth [Synod was held] at Constantinople, in the time of Pope Julius, under the Emperor Justinian, against Theodore and all heretics. [Col. 1109D]

## CHAPTER CXII. On the Synod of Aquileia.

The synod held at Aquileia, because of its ignorance of the faith, hesitated to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Council, until, instructed by the salutary admonitions of blessed Pope Sergius, it too consented to agree with the other Churches of Christ in accepting it.

## CHAPTER CXIII. On the dates of the councils. Bede, ibid.

(Dist. 16, c. *Sexta*.) The Sixth Synod was celebrated at Constantinople and recorded in the Greek language, in the time of Pope Agatho, under the execution and presidency of the most pious Emperor Constantine within his palace, while at the same time the legates of the Apostolic See and 150 bishops were sitting. [Col. 1110A]

## CHAPTER CXIV. On the same. Bede, ibid.

Leo the Younger received the holy Sixth Synod, which by God’s providence was recently celebrated in the imperial city, written in the Greek tongue, under the execution and presidency of the most pious and most merciful Emperor Constantine the Great.

## CHAPTER CXV. On the same. Anastasius the Librarian, in the prologue to the *History of the Roman Pontiffs*.

I consider it sufficient for the praise of Theophanes the chronicler that he was approved by the Apostolic See, when, that is, its vicars assembled for the second time with 350 Fathers in the city of Nicaea and celebrated an ecumenical synod. Indeed, his praise is also found in that same holy Eighth Council. [Col. 1110B]

## CHAPTER CXVI. On the same. Pope Adrian to Charles, ch. 25.

We have accepted that Seventh Synod; for if we had not received it, the Greeks would have returned to their former vomit of error, and we should have to render an account for the destruction of so many thousands of Christian souls.

## CHAPTER CXVII. Constitutions of the Sixth Synod. Sixth Synod, ch. 2.

(Dist. 16, c. *Quoniam sanctae*, § *Item confirmatus*.) We confirm the canons and synods of the holy Fathers: the First Nicene, the Antiochene, the Neocaesarean, [Col. 1110C] the Gangran, the Antiochene, the Laodicean, the Constantinopolitan, the First Ephesian, the Chalcedonian, the Sardican, and the Carthaginian; also the shorter works of Theodosius; of Alexander, bishop and martyr; of Gregory Thaumaturgus, or Trincegistus, bishop of Neocaesarea; of Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria; of Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia; of Gregory of Nyssa; Gregory the Theologian; Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium; Timothy, bishop of Alexandria; Germanus, bishop of Constantinople; Cyprian, bishop of Carthage; and his synod at Nichephotio.

“What you say” [Note: [Col. 1109D] Dist. 16, chapter *Quod dicitis*.], namely that we neither possess nor receive the Council of Sardica or the decretals of the holy Fathers, is not readily granted credence by us; especially since the Council of Sardica, which was held among you in your own regions and which the whole Church receives, how could it reasonably have happened that this holy Church of Constantinople should reject it and, as has been said, fail to retain it? That in ecclesiastical matters the authority of the canons and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs are to be preferred to the sayings of Augustine, Jerome, and others.

## CHAPTER CXVIII. The writings of others are not to be preferred to the decretals of the Roman pontiffs. Leo IV to the bishops of Britain.

(Dist. 20, c. *De libellis*.) It is not fitting for anyone to judge from the books and commentaries of others while abandoning the canons of holy councils or the rules of the decretals [Col. 1111A] which are held by us together with the canons and are used in all ecclesiastical judgments: namely, those of the Apostles, of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Sardica, and Carthage; together with these, the rules of the Roman bishops Sylvester, Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, Gelasius, Hilary, Symmachus, Simplicius, Hormisdas, and Gregory the Younger. These altogether are those by whom bishops judge, and by whom bishops and likewise clerics are judged.

For if some unusual matter should arise or occur which cannot at all be settled through these, then the sayings of those whom you mention—Jerome, Augustine, Isidore, or other similar holy doctors—if they can be found, are to be retained or promulgated with generous judgment; or such matters should be referred to the Apostolic See. For this reason I do not fear to declare more plainly and loudly that anyone—bishop, cleric, or layperson—who does not without reservation receive the ordinances of the holy Fathers mentioned above, which among us are entitled “canons,” is convicted and shown neither usefully nor effectively to preserve or believe the Apostolic faith, the Catholic faith, or the holy and true four Gospels of Christ. [Col. 1111B]

## CHAPTER CXIX. Falsehoods are not admitted in the canonical Scriptures. Augustine, Epistle 8, to Jerome.

(Dist. 9, c. *Ego solis*.) I have learned to render such fear and honor only to those books of Scripture which are now called canonical: I most firmly believe that no author of any of them erred in writing anything. If I encounter in them anything that appears contrary to truth, I shall suppose nothing else than that either the manuscript is defective, or the translator has failed to grasp what was said, or I myself have not understood it. [Col. 1111C] [Note: [Col. 1111D] Gratian reads this text differently. Nevertheless, the same sense is preserved in both places.]

But I read other authors in such a way that, however great their holiness and learning, I do not think something true merely because they thought it so, but because they have been able to persuade me, whether through canonical authorities or probable reasons, that it does not depart from the truth.

## CHAPTER CXX. The writings of commentators are subordinate to the canonical Scriptures. [Col. 1111D] Augustine, prologue to Book III of *On the Trinity*.

(Dist. 9, c. *Noli meis*.) Do not submit to my writings as though they were canonical Scriptures; but in those Scriptures, when you find something that you did not believe, believe it without hesitation. In these writings, however, do not hold firmly even what you did not previously regard as certain unless you have understood it to be certain.

## CHAPTER CXXI. On the same. Augustine to Jerome.

It seems to me most ruinous to believe that anything in the sacred books is false; that is, that the persons through whom that Scripture was administered or written down for us lied in any respect in their books. Whether a writer of the sacred Scriptures ought to have lied is another question—indeed, it is not another question but no question at all. [Col. 1112A]

## CHAPTER CXXII. On the same. Examples of pontiffs.

In the time of Pope Sergius, the Emperor Justinian ordered a council to be held in the imperial city. The legates of the Apostolic See attended it and, having been deceived, subscribed to it. He also compelled the pope himself to subscribe; but the pope by no means consented, because certain chapters contrary to ecclesiastical practice had been appended to them.

## CHAPTER CXXIII. On the teaching of apocryphal books which the holy Fathers condemned to eternal condemnation.

(Dist. 15, c. *Sancta*, § *In primis*.) We confess that the Synod of Rimini, convened by the Caesar Constantius, son of Constantine, through the agency of the prefect Taurus, has from that time and for ever been condemned. [Col. 1112B]

Likewise: the *Itinerary* under the name of the Apostle Peter, which is so called; the eight apocryphal books of Saint Clement; the apocryphal *Acts* under the name of the Apostle Andrew; the apocryphal *Acts* under the name of the Apostle Thomas; the apocryphal *Acts* under the name of the Apostle Peter; the apocryphal *Acts* under the name of the Apostle Philip; the apocryphal Gospels under the name of the Apostle Thaddaeus; the apocryphal Gospels under the name of the Apostle Barnabas; the apocryphal Gospels under the name of the Apostle Thomas, which the Manichees use; the apocryphal Gospels under the name of the Apostle Bartholomew; the apocryphal Gospels falsified by Lucian; the apocryphal Gospels falsified by Hircius; the apocryphal book *On the Infancy of the Saviour*; [Col. 1112C] the apocryphal book *On the Nativity of the Saviour and Saint Mary*, or *On the Midwife of the Saviour*; the apocryphal book called *The Shepherd*; all books composed by Lentitius, disciple of the devil, apocryphal; the apocryphal book called *The Foundation*; the apocryphal book called *The Treasure*; the apocryphal book *On the Daughters of Adam, or Genesis*; the apocryphal poem in pentameter verse concerning Christ, composed from Virgilian verses; the apocryphal book called the *Acts of Thecla and Paul*; the apocryphal book called *Nepotis*; the apocryphal book of Proverbs transcribed by heretics and marked with the name of Saint Sixtus; the apocryphal *Revelation of Paul*; the apocryphal revelation called that of the Apostle Thomas; the revelation called that of Stephen, apocryphal; [Col. 1112D] the book called the *Passing of Saint Mary*, apocryphal; the book called the *Penitence of Adam*, apocryphal; the apocryphal book under the name of the giant Diogenes, who, according to heretics, is said to have fought a dragon after the Flood; the apocryphal book called the *Testament of Job*; the apocryphal book called the *Penitence of Origen*; the apocryphal book called the *Penitence of Cyprian*; the apocryphal book called *Jamne and Mambre*; the apocryphal book called the *Lots of the Apostles*; the apocryphal Book of Susanna; the apocryphal Book of the Canons of the Apostles; the *Physiologus*, composed by heretics and attributed in advance to blessed Ambrose, [Col. 1113A] apocryphal; the *History* of Eusebius Pamphilus, apocryphal; the works of Tertullian, or Africanus, apocryphal; the works of Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla, apocryphal; the works of Jovinian and Gallus, apocryphal; all the works of Faustus the Manichee, apocryphal; the works of the other Clement of Alexandria, apocryphal; the works of Cassian, the Gallican presbyter, apocryphal; the works of Victorinus of Poitiers, apocryphal; the works of Faustus of Riez in Gaul, apocryphal; the works of Frumentius, apocryphal; the Letter of Jesus to Abgar, apocryphal; the Passion of Cyricus and Julitta, apocryphal; the Passion of George, apocryphal; the writing called *Solomon’s Contradiction*, apocryphal; all phylacteries, which, as their fabricators claim, were not written by an angel but rather by a demon, apocryphal.
