These writings and those like them, which Simon Magus, Nicolaus, [Col. 1113B] Cerinthus, Marcion, Basilides, Elion, Paul of Samosata, Photinus, and Bonosus, who fell away into similar error; also Montanus with his most obscene followers; Apollinaris, Valentinus or the Manichee, Faustus, Sabellius, Arius, Macedonius, Eunomius, Novatus, Sabatius, Callixtus, Donatus, Eustachius, Julian, Pelagius, Julian, Celestine of Latium, Maximianus, Priscillian of Spain, Lampedius, Dioscorus, Eutyches, Peter and another Peter—one of whom polluted Alexandria, the other Antioch—Acacius of Constantinople with his companions, and all heresies which they and their disciples or schismatics taught or wrote down, whose names we do not retain: these we confess to be not merely rejected, but expelled from every Catholic and Roman Church, and, together with their authors and the followers of those authors, condemned for ever under the indissoluble bond of anathema. [Col. 1113C]

## CHAPTER CXXIV. Except for fifty chapters, the Canons of the Apostles are reckoned among the apocrypha. Leo IX, letter to Nicetas, abbot of the Monastery of Studios.

(Dist. 16, c. *Clementis*.) The holy Fathers numbered the First Book of Clement, the *Itinerary* of the Apostle Peter, and the Canons of the Apostles among the apocryphal writings, except for fifty chapters, which they decreed should be joined to the rules of the Orthodox faith.

## CHAPTER CXXV. Likewise, on the Canons of the Apostles. [Col. 1113D] Sixth Synod, ch. 2.

(Dist. 16, c. *Placuit*.) It pleased this holy synod that from now on the eighty-five Canons of the Apostles should be confirmed and valid.

The letter of Isidore at the beginning of the canons: “Isidore, servant of Christ, to his fellow servant the reader: ‘On account of their authority, we have placed before the other councils the canons called Apostolic, although some call them apocryphal, because more persons receive them, and the holy Fathers strengthened their decisions by synodal authority and placed them among the canonical constitutions.’”

Likewise, the first order concerning the holding of a council, as mentioned above, is inserted; and afterwards there is a summary, arranged in its proper order and interpolated, of the Canons of the Apostles and of apostolic decrees from Saint Clement to Saint Sylvester, [Col. 1114A] together with those of various councils.

## CHAPTER CXXVI. On the *Lives of the Fathers*. Pope Adrian to Charlemagne, ch. 17.

The *Lives of the Fathers* are by no means read in the Church without reliable authors. For those entitled as works of orthodox authors are received and read. Indeed, the sacred canons judge that the passions of holy martyrs may be read in church when their anniversary days are celebrated.

## CHAPTER CXXVII. On apocryphal writings. Augustine, *Against Faustus*, Book III, ch. 2.

The Manichees read apocryphal Scriptures, composed, I do not know by what authors of fables, under the names of the Apostles—writings which might have deserved to be received into the authority of the holy Church in the age of their authors, if holy, righteous, and learned persons then living had been able to examine them and recognize that they spoke truthfully.

There, however, they read that the Apostle Thomas, while a stranger and wholly unknown at a certain wedding-feast, was struck on the palm by a servant and invoked continual and cruel vengeance upon the man. For when that servant had gone out to a spring to draw water for the guests, he was killed by a roaring lion; and a dog brought to the tables at which the Apostle himself reclined the hand with which the servant had struck the Apostle’s head with a light blow, torn from the body in accordance with the Apostle’s own wish and imprecation. [Col. 1114B]

## CHAPTER CXXVIII. On the same. Likewise, ch. 128.

That blessed Mary had as her father a certain priest named Joachim, from the tribe of Levi, is not canonical. [Col. 1114C]

## CHAPTER CXXIX. On the same. Jerome, *On the Education of a Daughter*.

Let her avoid all apocryphal writings; and if she should ever wish to read them, not for the truth of doctrines but out of reverence for the signs, let her know that they are not the works of those whose names they bear, and that much corrupt matter is mixed into them; it requires great prudence to seek gold in mud.

## CHAPTER CXXX. A bishop should not read pagan books. Fourth Council of Carthage, ch. 16.

[Col. 1114D] (Dist. 37, c. *Episcopus*.) A bishop shall not read the books of pagans or heretics, except when necessity and occasion require it.

## CHAPTER CXXXI. Priests who, neglecting the Gospels, read comedies are rebuked. Jerome to Amandus, *On the Prodigal Son*.

(Dist. 37, c. *Sacerdotes*.) We see priests of God, neglecting the Gospels and prophecies, reading comedies, singing the amorous words of bucolic verses, holding Virgil in their hands, and turning into a sin of pleasure what in boys is a matter of necessity.

## CHAPTER CXXXII. Blessed Jerome is beaten by an angel because he was reading a book of Cicero. Bede, Book II, *On the Afflictions of the Church*.

(Dist. 37, c. *Legimus*.) We read concerning blessed Jerome [Col. 1115A] that, while he was reading a book of Cicero, he was rebuked by an angel because, though a Christian man, he gave attention to pagan fictions.

## CHAPTER CXXXIII. Clerics are not to be forbidden to read secular literature. Bede, on II Kings.

(Dist. 37, c. *Turbat acumen*.) He disturbs the intellectual keenness of readers and compels it to fail who thinks that they should altogether be prohibited from reading secular literature; wherever useful discoveries are found in books, they may take them as their own. Otherwise Moses and Daniel would not have been allowed to be instructed in the wisdom or learning of the Egyptians and Chaldeans, whose superstitions and luxuries they abhorred; nor would the teacher of the Gentiles himself have inserted verses of poets either in his writings or in his utterances. [Col. 1115B]

## CHAPTER CXXXIV. Secular literature should be read so that it is not unknown. Ambrose, prologue to the *Exposition on Luke*.

(Dist. 37, c. *Legimus*.) We read certain things lest they be neglected; we read lest we be ignorant; we read not in order to retain them, but in order to reject them.

## CHAPTER CXXXV. Grammar should be studied in order that the sacred Scriptures may be understood. [Col. 1116A] Jerome, in the Letter to Titus, Book VII.

(Dist. 37, c. *Si quis artem*.) If anyone knows the art of grammar, or dialectic in order to possess the method of speaking correctly and to distinguish falsehood from truth, we do not disapprove. Geometry also, arithmetic, and music contain truth in their respective disciplines; but that learning is not the learning of piety. The learning of piety is to know the Law, understand the Prophets, believe the Gospel, and not be ignorant of the Apostles.

## CHAPTER CXXXVI. On the same. The same, ibid.

(Dist. 73, c. *In fine*.) The instruction of grammarians can contribute to life when it is employed for better purposes. [Col. 1116B]

## CHAPTER CXXXVII. Why Christians are forbidden to read poetic fictions. Isidore, Book III of *On the Highest Good*, ch. 13.

(Dist. 73, c. *Ideo prohib.*) Christians are therefore forbidden to read the fictions of poets because, through the pleasures of stories, they stir the mind toward incentives to lust. For one sacrifices to demons not only by offering incense, but also by eagerly accepting their utterances.

# ON LAWS

[Col. 1115]

## CHAPTER CXXXVIII. The law of emperors cannot dissolve ecclesiastical rights. [Col. 1115C] Pope Nicholas to bishops assembled in council at Convicinum.

(Dist. 10, c. *Lege impp.*) Imperial law is not to be used in every ecclesiastical controversy, especially since it is sometimes found to conflict with evangelical ordinance.

## CHAPTER CXXXIX. On the same. The same, ibid.

(Dist. 10, c. *Lege impp.*, § *Lex impp.*) The law of emperors is not above the law of God, but beneath it.

## CHAPTER CXL. On the same. Supplementary Capitularies, ch. 17.

(Dist. 10, c. *Lege impp.*, § *Imperiali judicio*.) [Col. 1115D] Ecclesiastical rights cannot be dissolved by imperial judgment—not that we should say that imperial laws, by which the Church often makes use of defense against heretics, against tyrants, and against the wicked, are to be wholly rejected; but rather that we maintain that they, since they must be subordinated to evangelical, apostolic, and canonical decrees, can cause no prejudice to those decrees.

## CHAPTER CXLI. The emperor may do nothing contrary to evangelical rules. Eighth Synod of Pope Symmachus.

It is not lawful for an emperor, or for anyone who safeguards piety, to presume anything contrary to the divine commandments or to do anything opposed to evangelical, prophetic, and apostolic rules.

## CHAPTER CXLII. What a law ought to be. [Col. 1116C] Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book V, ch. 10.

(Dist. 4, c. *Erit autem lex*.) A law shall be honorable, just, possible, consonant with the custom of the country, appropriate to place and time, necessary, useful, and clear; it shall contain nothing, through obscurity, hidden within its provision; and it shall be written not for any private advantage but for the common benefit of citizens.

## CHAPTER CXLIII. Laws must be judged when they are made, not when they have been made. Augustine, *On True Religion*, ch. 13.

(Dist. 10, c. *In istis*.) In these temporal laws, although people judge concerning them when they establish them, yet once they have been established and confirmed, it is not lawful for a judge to judge the laws themselves, but only according to them.

## CHAPTER CXLIV. Why they are called Theodosian Laws. [Col. 1116D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, ch. 1.

(Dist. 7, c. *Firmiter*, § *Postea*.) The younger Emperor Theodosius arranged, after the model of the Gregorian and Hermogenian Codes, a code made from the enactments of the Emperor Constantine, organized under the title of each individual emperor; and he called them Theodosian from his own name.

## CHAPTER CXLV. On the laws of Justinian.

(*Digest*, *On the Origin of Law*.) The Emperor Justinian corrected with remarkable brevity the excessive prolixity and useless inconsistency of Roman laws. For he compressed into twelve books all the constitutions of the emperors, which had certainly been contained in many volumes, [Col. 1117A] and ordered this volume to be called the Code of Justinian.

Again, he reduced the laws of the individual magistrates or judges, which had extended to nearly two thousand books, to a total of fifty books; and he called this the Code of the *Digest*, or *Pandects*, because Justinian gave different names to different volumes of law. For he newly composed four books of *Institutes*, in which the text of all laws is briefly comprised. He likewise decreed that the new laws which he himself had enacted, reduced into one collection, should be called the Code of *Novels*. Likewise: at that time, in Constantinople, Priscian of Caesarea conducted a profound investigation of the art of grammar.

## CHAPTER CXLVI. On the same. [Col. 1117B] Anastasius the Librarian, in the *History of the Roman Pontiffs*.

(§ *Quibus*, c. *De n. co. compen.*, ch. 146.) The Emperor Justinian removed conflicting rules, making a single code and calling it the *New Institutes*, in which he does not permit a ruler in the province over which he presides to hold possessions, build a house, or inherit from a person not related to him, unless that person is his kinsman.

## CHAPTER CXLVII. Enactments of emperors, made with an intention to establish law, have the force of general law unless they are made for specified persons; for then they do not extend beyond those persons. *Institutes*, Book I, ch. 2.

(Law *Quod principi*, § *Quodcunque*; *Digest*, *On the Constitutions of Princes*, § *Quodcunque*; *Institutes*, *On Natural, Gentile, and Civil Law*.) [Col. 1117C] Whatever the emperor establishes by letter, decrees upon hearing a case, or commands by edict is undoubtedly law; these are called constitutions. Certainly, some of these are personal and are not to be drawn into precedent, because that is not what the emperor intends. For what he has granted someone on account of merits, or if he has imposed a penalty on someone, or aided someone exceptionally, does not go beyond that person.

## CHAPTER CXLVIII. Preface to the Fifth Capitular.

The preceding four little books contain certain chapters of the glorious emperors Charles and Louis. Likewise, for the love of almighty God, of holy Church, of her servants, and of the whole people, we took care faithfully to investigate the matters which we learned had later been enacted by the faithful rulers of the holy Church of God—Pippin, Charles, and Louis—but had not been inserted in the aforesaid books; and we did not delay to collect and arrange them in the three following books together with their codes, and to write them down for the possession of the most noble kings Louis, Lothair, and Charles, namely the sons of the most pious Emperor Louis, [Col. 1117D] and for delivery to all the faithful of Christ.

Likewise, after these things had thus been accomplished, at the beginning of the first book was placed the letter of Zacharias, addressed, as it contains, to all bishops and to the remaining ranks of the ecclesiastical order, to all dukes and counts, and to all God-fearing persons established throughout Gaul and the provinces of the Franks. It is followed by the synodal assemblies which Boniface, legate of the holy Roman and Apostolic Church and archbishop of the Church of Mainz, canonically held in the place of the aforesaid Pope Zacharias together with Charles the Great, prince of the Franks, so that all may know that these aforesaid capitula of the rulers have been confirmed by the highest apostolic authority. [Col. 1118A]

## CHAPTER CXLIX. The laws of emperors must be observed. Leo III to Lothair Augustus.

(Dist. 10, c. *De capitulis*.) Concerning imperial capitula or commands, which must inviolably be observed and preserved by us, by our pontiffs, and by our predecessors, we profess by every means that, as far as we have been able and are able, through Christ’s favor, we shall preserve them now and for ever. And if anyone perhaps has said or shall say otherwise to you, know certainly that he is a liar. [Col. 1118B]

## CHAPTER CL. It is not lawful to despise the laws of rulers or the rules of the Fathers. Gelasius to Bishops Rufinus and Aprilius.

(Dist. 10, c. *Quis autem*.) Who would say that the laws of rulers, the rules of the Fathers, or modern admonitions should be despised, except one who considers himself free to pass over so grave an offence with impunity?

## CHAPTER CLI. The laws must be observed by all Roman rulers. The same to King Theodoric.

(Dist. 10, c. *Certum*.) It is certain that Your Magnificence wishes, for the increase of your prosperity, that the laws of Roman rulers, which you have commanded to be observed in the affairs of men, should be observed above all in relation to reverence for the blessed Apostle Peter. [Col. 1118C]

## CHAPTER CLII. Roman law must not be corrupted by anyone’s rashness. Leo IV to Lothair Augustus.

(Dist. 10, c. *Vestram*.) We entreat your clemency that, just as Roman law has hitherto flourished without all storms and is remembered to have been corrupted for the sake of no person whatsoever, so now it may retain its strength and proper vigor.

## CHAPTER CLIII. The laws of emperors may be employed in aid of the Church. Augustine, *Against Petilian*.

(Dist. 10, c. *Si in adjutorium*.) If you think that the laws of earthly empire ought to be taken up in your aid, we do not blame you: Paul did this when, against those acting unjustly, he declared that he was a Roman citizen. [Col. 1118D]

## CHAPTER CLIV. He who does not obey the just laws of emperors incurs punishment; conversely, he who refuses to obey laws issued against God’s truth gains a reward. Augustine, Epistle 50, to Boniface.

(Dist. 9, c. *Imperatores*, § *Quicunque*.) Whoever refuses to obey the laws of emperors issued for God’s truth incurs great punishment. But whoever refuses to obey the laws of emperors issued against God’s truth gains a great reward.

## CHAPTER CLV. One must not oppose a custom to which canonical authority is not contrary. [Col. 1119A] Nicholas to the Emperor Michael.

(Dist. 12, c. *Scit sancta*.) The holy Roman Church knows that differing customs according to place and time do no harm to the salvation of believers, if canonical authority does not oppose them, when one faith working through love commends all to one God.

## CHAPTER CLVI. Different customs established in different churches are to remain if they are not against the faith and agree with truth. Leo III to Lothair Augustus.

(Dist. 12, c. *Ridiculum*.) Concerning the customs which you have wished to object to us, writing that different churches have different customs: if canonical authority has not opposed them—on account of which we ought to oppose them—we make no judgment concerning them and do not resist them. Likewise, to Archbishop Hincmar: It is ridiculous and a sufficiently abominable disgrace that we should allow traditions received of old from the Fathers to be broken. [Col. 1119B]

## CHAPTER CLVII. A custom that assumes nothing contrary to the faith is praiseworthy. Pope Pius.

(Dist. 11, c. *Consuetudinem*.) We commend a custom which is known to assume nothing contrary to the Catholic faith.

## CHAPTER CLVIII. Where authority is lacking, the custom of the people and the institutions of the elders are observed as law. Augustine to the presbyter Consentius.

[Col. 1119C] (Dist. 11, c. *In his rebus*.) In matters concerning which divine Scripture establishes nothing certain, the custom of God’s people and the institutions of the elders are to be held as law; and, just as transgressors of divine laws, so also despisers of ecclesiastical customs are to be restrained.

## CHAPTER CLIX. A custom is inviolable when it is shown to conflict neither with human laws nor with sacred canons. From the sayings of Basil, ch. 28.

We have received certain institutions of the churches from Scripture, others from apostolic institution confirmed through successors in ministry, and others strengthened by custom and approved by use. Equal observance and the same disposition of piety are owed to both kinds. [Col. 1119D] Who, then, even slightly acquainted with sacred Scripture could doubt this? For if we venture to regard as nothing the customs of the Church handed down by the Fathers apart from Scripture, it will become plainly evident, through contempt for them, how great a loss religion will suffer.

For, to begin with these: what Scripture taught believers to mark themselves with the sign of the saving cross? What Scripture commended the lengthy words of prayer and consecration, divided in three parts, over the bread and cup? For we have learned in secret not only what is contained in the Gospel or set forth by the Apostle, but we add many other things which lend great force, as it were, to the mysteries. What written form granted that we should worship facing east? We bless the baptismal font with the oil of anointing. To this is added that we immerse three times, that we anoint the baptized with oil, and that we instruct them to renounce Satan and his angels. Whence come these and many other matters of this kind, unless they have been observed in the ministries, by the custom of the Fathers, with more reverent care in silent and mystical tradition than published in writing? [Col. 1120A]

## CHAPTER CLX. Book I of the *Institutes*, ch. 1.

(*Institutes on Natural, Gentile, and Civil Law*, § *Ex non scripto*.) Unwritten law arises from usage approved by practice. For customs established over a long period and approved by the consent of those who use them imitate law. Likewise, the enactments which each city establishes for itself are often changed either by the tacit consent of the ruler or by another law subsequently passed.

## CHAPTER CLXI. What is usage, and what is custom? [Col. 1120B] Isidore, *Etymologies*, V.3.

(Dist. 11, c. *Mos est*.) Usage (*mos*) is a custom approved by antiquity, or an unwritten law. Likewise, custom (*consuetudo*) is a kind of law established by manners and accepted in place of law when law is lacking. It makes no difference whether it rests on writing or reason.

## CHAPTER CLXII. Custom and usage must be observed if they are contrary neither to law nor to reason. Or thus: Whatever is done contrary to long-standing custom ought to be restored. Code, Book VIII, title 1.

(Dist. 12, c. *Consuetudo*.) The preceding custom and the reason which prompted that custom must be observed; and whatever is done contrary to long-standing custom, the governor of the province shall restore to its customary condition. [Col. 1120C]

## CHAPTER CLXIII. Usage and custom cannot prevail over law and reason. Ibid., title II, Book VIII.

Custom and usage have no slight authority, but they do not have such force as to prevail either over reason or over law.

## CHAPTER CLXIV. A harmful custom must be uprooted. Pope Nicholas to Hincmar.

(Dist. 8, c. *Mala autem*.) An evil custom is to be avoided no less than a ruinous corruption. Unless it is speedily uprooted, it is appropriated by wicked persons as a right of privilege; and transgressions and various presumptions, if not quickly checked, begin to be revered as laws and perpetually observed as a customary privilege. [Col. 1120D]

## CHAPTER CLXV. A bad usage is overcome by reason and law. The same, in the *Synonyms*.

(Dist. 11, c. *Usus auctor*.) Let usage yield to authority. Let law and reason overcome bad usage when truth is manifest; let custom yield to truth. Surely, who doubts that custom yields to manifest truth? Likewise, let no one prefer custom to reason and truth, because reason and truth always exclude custom if reason and truth prevail.

## CHAPTER CLXVI. Every custom must be subordinated to truth. [Col. 1121A] Augustine, Book IV of *On Baptism*, chs. 5–6.

(Dist. 8, c. *Si consuetudinem*.) If perhaps you set custom in opposition, the bishop should have observed what the Lord says: “I am,” he says, “the truth” (John 14); he did not say, “I am custom,” but “the truth.” And certainly, to use the judgment of blessed Cyprian: Every custom, however ancient and however widespread, must by no means be preferred to truth; and usage contrary to truth must be abolished.

## CHAPTER CLXVII. Once truth has been revealed, custom must yield to it. Augustine, in *On the Baptism of Infants*.

Once revelation has been made, then let error yield to truth, because Peter also, who circumcised, yielded to Paul as he preached the truth. [Col. 1121B]

## CHAPTER CLXVIII. Things approved neither by authorities nor by the customs of the universal Church must be cut away. Or thus: A usage which is not strengthened by authority and is observed in other places rarely or never must be wholly rejected, even though it is not contrary to the faith. [Col. 1122A] Augustine to Januarius in reply to an inquiry, Epistle 119, ch. 19.

All such things as are neither contained in the authority of the holy Scriptures, nor found established by councils of bishops, nor strengthened by the custom of the universal Church, but vary innumerably according to the differing customs of different places—so that the reasons which people followed in establishing them can scarcely or never at all be discovered—I consider, where opportunity is given, ought without any doubt to be cut away. For although it may not be possible to discover how they are contrary to the faith, nevertheless they burden religion itself, which God’s mercy willed to be free through sacraments very few and very clear, with slavish burdens, so that the condition of the Jews is more tolerable: although they do not recognize the time of freedom, they are nevertheless subject to legal sacraments, not to human presumptions. [Col. 1122B]

# ON THE OBSERVANCE OF THE SABBATH AND THE LORD’S DAY

[Col. 1121]

## CHAPTER CLXIX. The Sabbath is not to be kept as a day of rest. Gregory to the citizens of Rome, Book II, Epistle 3.

(*On Consecration*, Dist. 3, c. *Pervenit*.) It has come to my attention that certain persons of perverse spirit have sown among you certain wrong doctrines contrary to the holy faith, so that they forbade any work to be done on the Sabbath day. What else should we call them but preachers of Antichrist? For when he comes, he will wish both Sabbath and Lord’s Day to be observed free from all work, because he will pretend that he has died and risen again and will wish the Lord’s Day to be held in veneration. And because he compels the people to Judaize, in order to draw them back to the outward rite of the Law and subject them to the unbelief of the Jews, he will wish the Sabbath to be observed. [Col. 1121C]

### CHAPTER CLXX. On Sundays no buying or selling, litigation, judicial proceedings, or oaths are to take place; rather, they are to be observed from evening to evening. Council of Compiègne, ch. 2.

(*Extra*, On feast-days.) We decree that on every Sunday, from evening to evening, all unlawful work shall be abstained from with every reverence and observance; that no market [Col. 1122B] shall be held on those days; that no legal hearing shall take place in which anyone is sentenced to punishment or death; and that no oath shall be sworn on them, except for the making of peace.

### CHAPTER CLXXI. On the same matter. From the same council, ch. 8.

[Col. 1122C] (*On Consecration*, distinction 3, opening.) Let no market be held anywhere on the Lord’s Day.

### CHAPTER CLXXII. On the same matter. From the same council, ch. 6.

Three kinds of cart-service work may be performed on Sunday: namely, the killing of enemies, carts carrying provisions, or compulsory public service; and, if necessity should arise, the conveying of anyone’s body to burial.

### CHAPTER CLXXIII. On neither the Lord’s Day nor the days of Pentecost should the knees be bent in prayer. Council of Orléans, ch. 13.

(*On Consecration*, distinction 3, ch. *Quoniam*.) On Sundays and other feast-days, from evening until evening, they are not to bend the knee, but are to pray standing, bowed forward.

## ON FASTING

[Col. 1121]

### CHAPTER CLXXIV. For seven weeks before Easter, clerics are to abstain from meat and luxuries. Telesphorus, in his decretal.

[Col. 1121D] (Distinction 4, ch. *Statuimus* [Note: [Col. 1121D] This agrees with ch. *Denique*, in the same distinction; but at the end of that chapter it is said: “Although these matters have been established by laws, nevertheless, because they have not been approved by common usage, those who do not observe them are not to be charged as guilty of transgression.” Otherwise [Col. 1122D] it is the contrary—unless perhaps someone says that these were laid down not as decrees but as written exhortation. A decree creates obligation; exhortation, however, leaves the will free.].) Know that it has been established by us and by all the bishops assembled in this holy and apostolic see that, during the full seven weeks before holy Easter, all clerics called to the Lord’s [Col. 1122D] lot are to fast from meat; for, just as the life of clerics ought to be distinct from the conduct of laypeople, so too distinction ought to be made in fasting. Therefore, during these seven weeks all clerics are to fast from meat and luxuries, and are to strive to cleave to the Lord day and night through hymns, vigils, and prayers.

### CHAPTER CLXXV. At what times fasts are to be observed. [Col. 1123A] Pope Calixtus to Bishop Benedict.

(Distinction 76, ch. *Jejunium*.) The fast which you learned to observe among us three times a year, we have now decreed should more fittingly be observed in the four seasons, so that, as the year turns through four seasons, we too may hold a solemn fast four times throughout the year’s four seasons.

### CHAPTER CLXXVI. A fast is not to be observed on Sunday or Thursday. Pope Miltiades to the bishops of Spain.

(*On Consecration*, distinction 3, ch. *Jejunium*.) No one should observe a fast on the Lord’s Day or on the fifth weekday [Thursday], so that [Col. 1123B] there may be a true, not false, distinction between the fasting of Christians and that of pagans, those who do not truly believe, and heretics.

### CHAPTER CLXXVII. Out of reverence for the Lord’s burial, we ought to fast on Saturday. Innocent I to Decentius.

(*On Consecration*, distinction 3, ch. *Sabbato*.) The clearest reasoning shows that Saturday should indeed be a fast-day. For if we celebrate the Lord’s Day because of the venerable resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ not only at Easter, but also observe the image of that day in every week, then, just as we fast on Friday because of the Lord’s Passion, we ought not to pass over Saturday, [Col. 1123C] since it appears enclosed between the sorrow and joy of that time. For it is certainly established that during these two days the apostles were in grief and hid themselves through fear of the Jews; and undoubtedly they fasted during those two days mentioned, to such an extent that the Church’s tradition has it that sacraments are not celebrated at all during those two days. This pattern must likewise be kept every week, because the commemoration of that day must always be observed. But if they think that one ought to fast only once, on one Saturday, then Sunday and Friday too must surely be observed only once, at Easter.

### CHAPTER CLXXVIII. That a fast is not to be observed in July and August. From the Council of Elvira, ch. 23.

[Col. 1123D] It was decided that fasts or abstinences should be observed in each month, except during the days of the two months July and August, because of their weakness.

### CHAPTER CLXXIX. Wednesday and Friday fasts are to be observed. From the *Life of Abbot Apollonius* in Palladius.

(*On Consecration*, distinction 3, ch. *Jejunia*.) The lawful fasts—namely, Wednesday and Friday—are not to be relaxed unless some grave necessity arises; for on Wednesday Judas had conceived the betrayal of the Lord, and on Friday the Savior was crucified. Therefore anyone who relaxes the prescribed fasts on these days without some necessity will seem either to betray the Savior together with his betrayer, or to crucify him together with those who crucified him.

### CHAPTER CLXXX. In which months and in which weeks of those months the Ember fasts are to be appointed. [Col. 1124A] Council of Mainz, ch. 34.

(Distinction 76, ch. *Constituimus*.) We decree that the Four Seasons of the year [the Ember Days] be observed by everyone with fasting: in March, the first week; in June, the second; in September, the third; and in December, the fourth week, which falls before the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord. On Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday all are to come to church at the ninth hour, with litanies for the solemnities of the Mass.

### CHAPTER CLXXXI. On the same matter. Council of Salegunstadt.

(Distinction 76, ch. *De jejunio*.) Concerning the uncertain date of the [Col. 1124B] Ember fasts, we establish this certainty: if the Kalends of March fall on Wednesday or earlier, the fast is to be observed in that same week. But if the Kalends of March fall on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, the fast is to be deferred to the following week. Similarly, if the Kalends of June fall on Wednesday or earlier, the fast is to be observed in the following week; and if they fall on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, the fast is to be reserved for the third week. It must also be known that, if according to the second rule just stated the fast of June falls on the vigil of Pentecost, it is to be observed there; but during that solemn week of Pentecost itself, because it is not fitting to observe both the vigil and the fast, [Col. 1124C] then, on account of the solemnity of the Holy Spirit, dalmatics are to be worn, Alleluia is to be sung, and “Let us bend the knee” is not to be said.

In the same way it is established concerning the fast of the seventh month that, if the Kalends of September fall on Wednesday or earlier, the fasts are to be observed in the third week; but if they fall on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, fasting is to take place in the fourth week. In December, however, this is to be observed: the fast is to be celebrated on the Saturday immediately before the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, because if the vigil falls on Saturday, it is not fitting to observe the vigil and the fast together.

### CHAPTER CLXXXII. By what calculation Lent is shown to be the tenth of the year, and concerning the observance of Lent. [Col. 1124D] Gregory, Homily 16 on the Gospels.

(*On Consecration*, distinction 5, ch. *Quadragesima*.) Lent must be observed with the utmost care, so that the fast during it, apart from Sundays, which are excluded from abstinence, must under no circumstances be relaxed, unless illness prevents someone; for those days themselves are the tithe of the year. From the first Sunday of Lent until the Lord’s Easter, six weeks are counted, amounting to forty-two days. When the six Sundays are subtracted from abstinence, no more than thirty-six days remain for abstinence. For example: if the year comprises three hundred and sixty-five days and we afflict ourselves for thirty-six days, we give God, as it were, the tithe of the year. And in order that the sacred [Col. 1125A] number of forty days, consecrated by our Savior’s holy fast, may be completed, four days of the preceding week must be added to make up the forty days: namely, Wednesday, which is designated the beginning of the fast, the following Thursday, Friday, and Saturday. Unless we add these four days to the preceding thirty-six, we would not have forty days of abstinence. We are also commanded by almighty God to give tithes of all our goods. Therefore, so that the whole tithe may be duly paid by us, let us take the tenth of the year and, in it, by confessing our sins, correcting ourselves, fasting, praying, and giving alms, cleanse them away; and let us tithe our flesh, that we may be able to reach holy Easter in safety.

### CHAPTER CLXXXIII. At what times the knees are to be bent. [Col. 1125B] Council of Orléans, ch. 13.

(Distinction 30, ch. *Si quis presb.*, § *Placuit*.) Let presbyters announce to the people that during Lent and the Ember fast they ought to bend the knee only at the solemnities of the Mass, and never on Sundays or other feast-days. Nor should anyone ever presume to pray on one bent knee, as the Jews are read to have done in mockery of the Lord during his Passion; rather, let both knees be placed upon the ground. For the Apostle says: “I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Eph. III).

### CHAPTER CLXXXIV. Before the solemnities of the Mass, chanted at about the ninth hour during Lent, no one may eat. [Col. 1125C] Council of Chalon, ch. 5.

(*On Consecration*, distinction 1, ch. *Solent plures*.) Many people who think themselves to fast during Lent [Col. 1126A] eat as soon as they hear the signal for the ninth hour. Such people are by no means to be regarded as fasting if they eat before the evening office has been celebrated. Rather, they must gather for Mass, and, after hearing the solemnities of the Mass and the evening offices, and after giving alms, they are to take food. But if someone is so constrained by necessity that he cannot come to Mass, then, after the time appointed for the evening office has elapsed, having completed his prayer, let him break his fast.

### CHAPTER CLXXXV. Daily fasts are to be preferred to fasts doubled or tripled. Augustine, Letter 65 to Eustochium, on the guardianship of virginity.

(*On Consecration*, distinction 5, ch. *Sint tibi*.) Let your fasts be daily, and let your meals avoid fullness. [Col. 1126B] For it profits you nothing to carry an empty stomach for two or three days if it is then equally stuffed up, if fasting is compensated for by satiety. At once the filled mind grows sluggish, and the watered soil of this body brings forth thorns and thistles.

### CHAPTER CLXXXVI. On the same matter. Jerome to Nepotian, on the life of clerics.

Let your fasts be pure, continuous, and moderate: that is, be hungry every day and eat every day.

### CHAPTER CLXXXVII. Jerome, same work.

A sparing diet and a continually hungry stomach are preferable to three-day fasts.

### CHAPTER CLXXXVIII. Jerome, same work.

A fast is despised when it is renewed in the evening by a filling of food.

### CHAPTER CLXXXIX. Isidore.

[Col. 1126C]

A perfect fast is when our outward person fasts and the inward person prays.

## ON ALMSGIVING

[Col. 1125]

### CHAPTER CXC. Almsgiving is to be joined to fasting.

[Col. 1125C]

On days of fasting almsgiving should be performed, and whatever food or drink a person would have consumed had he not fasted, he should distribute to the poor. For to fast and save the food of one’s midday meal for supper is not an increase of reward but of food.

### CHAPTER CXCI. Almsgiving from lawful possessions or honestly acquired goods is pleasing to God. Gregory, Letter 110, book VII, to Syagrius.

[Col. 1125D] (14, question 5, ch. *Eleemosyna*.) That almsgiving is pleasing in the eyes of our Redeemer which is not amassed from unlawful and defiled sources, but is bestowed from lawful possessions and goods honestly acquired.

### CHAPTER CXCII. On the manifold kinds of almsgiving. Albinus, or Alcuin.

(Distinction 45, ch. *Tria*.) There are three kinds of almsgiving. One is bodily: to give to a needy person whatever you can. The second is spiritual: to forgive the one by whom you have been injured. The third is to correct offenders and lead one who errs into the way of truth.

### CHAPTER CXCIII. The almsgiving of the heart is preferable to almsgiving with money. Augustine, Homily 6, book I of the *Homilies*.

(Distinction 45, ch. *Duae sunt*.) There are two kinds of almsgiving: [Col. 1126C] one of the heart and another of money. The almsgiving of the heart is to forgive the injury done to oneself. For sometimes you wish to give something to a person in need and do not have it; but the power to forgive a sin is available to you as much as you wish. The almsgiving of the heart is far greater than the almsgiving of the body. The almsgiving of charity suffices without earthly substance; but that which is given bodily does not suffice at all if it is not bestowed with a kind heart.

### CHAPTER CXCIV. Almsgiving cannot be made from money acquired simoniacally. [Col. 1126D] Gregory, Letter 110, book VII.

(1, question 1, ch. *Non est*.) Nor is it to be regarded as almsgiving if what has been received from unlawful sources is distributed to the poor; for one who receives badly with the intention of distributing well, as it were, is burdened rather than helped.

### CHAPTER CXCV. Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*.

Whoever uses transient things more restrictively than the customs of those among whom he lives permit is either intemperate or superstitious. But whoever uses them so as to exceed the bounds of the good customs of those among whom he lives either signifies something or is immoral. For in all such matters [Col. 1127A] it is not the use of things but desire that is at fault. Therefore careful attention must be paid to what suits places, times, and persons, lest we rashly condemn offenses. It can happen that a wise person, without any fault of greed or gluttony, uses a most costly food, while a fool burns with the most shameful flame of appetite even for the cheapest food; and a sounder person would prefer, after the manner [Col. 1128A] of the Lord, to eat fish rather than lentils after the manner of Esau, Abraham’s grandson, or barley after the manner of beasts of burden. For the many animals that eat cheaper foods are not therefore more self-controlled than we are. In all such things, what we do must be approved or disapproved not from the nature of the things we use, but from the manner in which we use and desire them.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1127]

## ON THE ELECTION OF THE SUPREME PONTIFF

### CHAPTER I. How, and by what persons, the election of the supreme pontiff is to be made. [Col. 1127B] From the Decrees of Pope Nicholas, ch. 1.

(Distinction 23, ch. *In nomine Domini*.) In the name of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, in the year 1059 from his Incarnation, in the month of April, in the twelfth indiction: with the most holy Gospels set before us, and with the most reverend and blessed apostolic Pope Nicholas presiding in the patriarchal Lateran basilica called the Constantinian; with the most reverend bishops, abbots, and venerable presbyters and deacons also seated, the same venerable pontiff, decreeing by apostolic authority concerning the election of the supreme pontiff, said:

“Your blessedness knows, most beloved brothers and bishops—and it has not escaped even the lower [Col. 1127C] members—how many adversities this apostolic see, which I serve by God’s appointment, endured after the death of our predecessor, Lord Stephen of pious memory; and through how many repeated blows and frequent batterings it has passed at the hands of the money-changers of the simoniacal heresy, so that the pillar of the living God seemed almost to totter, and the net of the supreme Fisherman was compelled, as storms swelled, to sink into the depths of shipwreck. Therefore, if it pleases your brotherhood, we ought, with God’s help, wisely to meet future dangers and provide for the ecclesiastical order hereafter, lest recurring evils—God forbid!—prevail.

“Accordingly, instructed by the authority of our predecessors and of other holy [Col. 1127D] Fathers, we decree and establish that, upon the death of the pontiff of this universal Roman Church, the cardinal bishops shall first confer together most diligently concerning the election; they shall then summon the cardinal clerics of Christ; and thus the remaining people and clergy shall join in consenting to the new election, taking particular care lest the disease of venality creep in under any pretext. Thus the most religious men are to be leaders in the election of the pontiff to be promoted, while the others are followers. Certainly this is seen to be the right and lawful order of election if, after considering the established rules and acts of the various Fathers, that saying also of our blessed predecessor Leo is recalled: ‘No principle allows those to be reckoned among bishops who have neither been elected by the clergy, nor sought by the people, [Col. 1128B] nor consecrated by the bishops of their province with the judgment of the metropolitan.’

“Since the apostolic see is preferred to all Churches throughout the world and therefore cannot have a metropolitan over itself, the cardinal bishops undoubtedly perform the role of metropolitan; that is, they raise the bishop-elect to the summit of the apostolic office. Let him be chosen from that Church itself, if a suitable person is found; but if no one is found there, let him be taken from another, while preserving the due honor and reverence of our beloved son Henry, who at present is held to be king and, God granting, is hoped to be the future emperor—as we have already granted to him and his successors who shall personally obtain this right from this apostolic see.

[Col. 1128C] “But if the perversity of wicked and unjust persons should so prevail that a pure, sincere, and gratuitous election cannot be made in the city, the cardinal bishops, together with religious Catholic clerics and laymen, even though few, shall have the right and authority to elect the pontiff of the apostolic see wherever they judge most fitting. Clearly, after the election has been made, if a storm of war or any hostile effort of persons, out of malicious intent, prevents the elected person from being enthroned in the apostolic see according to custom, nevertheless the elect shall possess the authority of pope to govern the holy Roman Church and administer all its resources—as we know that blessed Gregory did before his consecration.

[Col. 1128D] “But if anyone, contrary to this decree of ours promulgated by synodal judgment, is elected, or even ordained or enthroned, through sedition or by any contrivance, let him, together with his authors, supporters, and followers, be separated by divine authority and by the authority of the holy apostles Peter and Paul from the thresholds of God’s holy Church under perpetual anathema, as an antichrist, an invader, and a destroyer of all Christianity. Let no hearing whatsoever ever be reserved for him on this matter; rather, from every ecclesiastical rank he previously held, let him be deposed without reconsideration. Whoever adheres to him, shows him any reverence as though he were pontiff, or presumes in any respect to defend him, shall be subjected to the same sentence. Whoever violates this decree [Col. 1129A] of ours and presumes, contrary to this statute, to throw the Roman Church into confusion and disorder by his presumption, shall be condemned under perpetual anathema and excommunication, and reckoned with the impious who do not rise in judgment. May he feel against himself the wrath of almighty God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; may he feel in this life and the life to come the fury of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, whose Church he presumes to confound. ‘Let his dwelling be desolate, and let there be none to live in his tents’ (Ps. 68). ‘Let his children be orphaned and his wife widowed’ (Ps. 108). Let him and his son be driven away in commotion; let them beg and be cast out from their dwellings. Let the moneylender search out all his substance, and strangers plunder [Col. 1129B] the fruits of his labor’ (ibid.). Let the whole world fight against him; let all the elements be hostile to him; let the merits of all who rest in the earth confound him and show open vengeance upon him in this life. But may the grace of almighty God protect those who observe this decree of ours, and may the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul loose them from the bonds of all sins.”

Nicholas, bishop of the holy catholic and Roman Church: to this decree promulgated by us, as is written above, I have subscribed. Boniface, by the grace of God bishop of Albano: I have subscribed. Humbert, of the holy Church of Silva Candida (*Silvae Condinae*, perhaps an OCR corruption of *Candidae*): I have subscribed. Peter, bishop of the Church of Ostia: I have subscribed. And [Col. 1129C] the other bishops, seventy-four in number, together with presbyters and deacons, subscribed.

Pope Stephen: because the holy Roman Church over which, by God’s appointment, we preside suffers violence from many persons upon the death of a pontiff—violence inflicted for this reason, that the pontiff’s consecration takes place without the emperor’s knowledge and without the presence of his envoys, and that envoys sent by the emperor do not attend according to canonical rite and custom to prevent scandals—we desire that, when a pontiff is to be appointed, the bishops and the whole clergy shall assemble and elect the person to be ordained in the presence of the senate and people; and that the person thus elected shall be consecrated in the presence of all the imperial envoys. No one, at peril to himself, may dare by some novel invention to extort oaths or promises [Col. 1129D] other than those required by ancient custom, lest the Church be scandalized or the honor due to the imperial office be diminished.

### CHAPTER II. If the pope cannot decide beforehand concerning the election of his successor. Or: Whose votes ought to prevail in the election of the supreme pontiff. From the Decrees of Pope Symmachus, ch. 4.

(Distinction 79, ch. *Si transitus*.) If—God forbid!—the pope’s death should occur unexpectedly, so that they cannot decide beforehand concerning the election of his successor, as was established above, then, if the election of the whole ecclesiastical order comes together in one, the bishop-elect is to be consecrated. If, however, as often happens, factions begin to differ, the judgment of the greater number shall prevail concerning those over whom contention has arisen; provided, nevertheless, that anyone who has decided concerning the election because he was won over by a promise, rather than by right judgment, shall be deprived of the priesthood.

### CHAPTER III. No bishop may do anything contrary to the decrees of the Roman pontiffs. From the *Liber Diurnus* of the Roman Pontiffs.

(25, question 1, ch. *Omnia decretalia*.) I profess that I shall more diligently and vigorously confirm all canonical decrees of our predecessor pontiffs which they established synodically and which have been approved; preserve them undiminished; and, as they were established by them, keep them in the stability of their force. Whatever persons or things they condemned or rejected, I shall condemn and reject by a like sentence.

### CHAPTER IV. The authority of the apostolic see cannot enact anything contrary to the statutes of the saints. From the same book.

(25, question 1, ch. *Contra statuta*; compare ch. *Cum isto*.) I profess that I shall neither diminish nor alter anything of the tradition which I find handed down and preserved by my most approved predecessors, nor admit any innovation; but, frequently as their disciple, I profess that with all the efforts of my mind I shall follow, observe, and venerate those things which I find canonically transmitted.

### CHAPTER V. No one is to be elected to a bishopric unless he is established in sacred orders. [Col. 1130C] Council of Benevento, ch. 1. Pope Urban.

(Distinction 70, ch. *Nullus*.) Let no one be elected to a bishopric unless he is found to be living religiously in sacred orders. By sacred orders we mean the diaconate and presbyterate; indeed, these alone are read to have existed in the primitive Church. We have the apostolic precept concerning these alone. Subdeacons, however, since they too serve at the altars, we permit where necessity requires, but very rarely, and only if they are of proven life, religious character, and learning. We firmly permit this only with the authorization of the Roman pontiff or metropolitan.

### CHAPTER VI. If several are chosen, which person should be preferred. From the Decrees of Leo, ch. 1.

[Col. 1130D] (Distinction 63, ch. *Clerici* and the following chapter.) When the election of the supreme pontiff is under consideration, he shall be preferred above all whom the agreement of clergy and people has jointly requested. Thus, if perhaps divided parties have cast their votes for another, the judgment of the metropolitan shall prefer one candidate to the other who is supported by greater favor and merit. Yet no one is to be ordained against the will of those who neither seek him nor ask for him, lest an unwilling people despise or hate a bishop whom they did not desire and become less devout than is proper, because they are not permitted to have the one whom they wished.

## ON THE ELECTION AND CONSECRATION OF BISHOPS AND PRESBYTERS

[Col. 1131]

### CHAPTER VII. The clergy are to choose their bishop not from another but from their own Church, unless no worthy person is found in their own.

[Col. 1131A]

(Distinction 61, ch. *Nullus invitis*.) Let no bishop be given to an unwilling people; rather, the consent and desire of clergy, people, and order must be sought. Only then may a person from another Church be chosen, if among the clergy of the city itself for which a bishop is to be ordained no worthy person—something we do not believe can happen—can be found. For the local clergy must first be rejected before persons from other churches are deservedly preferred. Let each person have the fruit of his own service in the Church in which he has spent his life through every office. Let no one intrude upon another’s service in another Church, nor dare to claim for himself the reward due to another. Clerics must have the freedom to resist if they see themselves oppressed, so that they need not fear to reject someone whom they know is being imposed on them from outside. For they ought to have a due reward and a free judgment concerning the person who is to rule them.

### CHAPTER VIII. A lay person is to have no voice in the election of a bishop. Eighth Synod, ch. 11, from the Apostolic Canon.

The promotions and consecrations of bishops are to be carried out, in agreement with earlier councils, by election and decree of the clergy and by the college of bishops: this holy and universal synod has defined, established, and lawfully promulgated it. No lay prince, powerful person, or other layperson of any rank may insert himself into the election or promotion of a patriarch, metropolitan, or any bishop, lest an irregular and unsuitable election, [Col. 1131C] contention, or confusion result; especially since it is fitting that none of those in authority or any other layperson should possess power in such matters, but should remain silent and attend to himself until the election of the future pontiff is canonically brought to its conclusion by the college of the Church. If, however, some layperson is invited by the Church to deliberate and cooperate, it is permissible for such a layperson, should he wish, to comply respectfully with those assembled. For in this way the clergy of the Church lawfully promote for themselves a worthy shepherd for their salvation.

On the same matter.

(Distinction 63, ch. *Nullus*, § *Quisquis*.) Whoever among secular princes, powerful persons, or laypersons of another [Col. 1131D] rank attempts to act against the common, concordant, and canonical election of the ecclesiastical order shall be anathema until he obeys and consents to what the Church has shown itself to desire concerning the election and ordination of its own bishop.

### CHAPTER IX. A person who has attained the episcopal office through royal appointment is not to be received by his fellow provincial bishops. Canons of Paris under Emperor Louis.

(Distinction 61, ch. *Si per ordinationem*.) If anyone, in excessive rashness, presumes to seize the summit of this honor through royal appointment, he deserves in no way to be received by the bishops of that locality who share his province and who know that he has been improperly ordained. [Col. 1132A] If any fellow-provincial bishop presumes to receive him contrary to this prohibition, let him be separated from his brethren and removed from the charity of them all.

### CHAPTER X. With the assent of the others, a bishop is to be ordained with three fellow-provincial bishops. From the Decrees of Anicetus, ch. 1.

(Distinction 64, ch. *Comprovinciales*.) If an archbishop dies and another archbishop is elected to be ordained, all bishops of the same province shall gather at the metropolitan see so that he may be ordained by all of them. For he who must preside over them all ought to be chosen and ordained by all of them. The remaining fellow-provincial bishops, however, if necessity requires and the others consent, may be consecrated bishops by three at the archbishop’s command; but it is better that he himself, together with all, choose the worthy person and jointly consecrate him bishop. Although this has been allowed under pressure of necessity, what has been commanded and stated concerning the consecration of an archbishop—namely, that all the suffragans must ordain him—may in no respect be changed, because the one who presides over them must be appointed by all the bishops over whom he presides. But if it has been presumptuously done otherwise, it undoubtedly lacks force, because his ordination will be invalid.

### CHAPTER XI. Archbishops, after their consecration, must receive the pallium from the apostolic see and set forth their faith. Or: Within three months every metropolitan should endeavor to set forth his faith and request the pallium from the Roman Church. From the Decrees of Pope Damasus, ch. 1.

[Col. 1132C] (Distinction 100, ch. *Quoniam quidam*.) Since certain metropolitans, refusing to set forth their faith to the holy apostolic see according to ancient custom, neither request nor receive the use of the pallium, and consequently the consecration of bishops for bereft churches is delayed not without danger, it has been decided that any metropolitan who, within three months after his consecration, does not send to the apostolic see to set forth his faith and receive the pallium shall forfeit the dignity entrusted to him. After a second and third warning, other metropolitans may, with the counsel of the Roman pontiff, assist bereft Churches by ordaining bishops. If, however, it occurs through the negligence of the bishop who is to be consecrated [Col. 1132D] that a Church remains bereft for more than three months, let him be deprived of communion until he either yields the place or no longer delays presenting himself for consecration. But if through his negligence he keeps the Church bereft for more than five months, let him receive the gift of consecration neither there nor elsewhere; indeed, let him yield by the judgment of his metropolitan.

### CHAPTER XII. At what hour episcopal ordinations ought to take place. Anacletus, Letter 2, to the bishops of Italy.

(Distinction 75, ch. *Ordinationes*.) Episcopal ordinations are to be celebrated by apostolic authority by all the bishops in the same province, [Col. 1133A] who, gathering together, are to conduct a careful inquiry; fasting is to be observed with every prayer; and on the Lord’s Day, at the third hour, while praying and laying hands upon them together with the holy Gospels which they are to preach, they are to anoint their heads with sacred unction after the manner of the prophets, following the example of kings, and after the manner of the apostles and Moses. For all sanctification consists in the Holy Spirit, whose invisible power is mingled with holy chrism; and in this rite they are to celebrate the solemn order.

### CHAPTER XIII. Why ordinations of priests are celebrated on the Lord’s Day. Leo I, Letter 79.

(Distinction 75, ch. *Quod die Dominico*.) That ordinations of priests are celebrated on the Lord’s Day derives not only from custom but, as we know, from apostolic teaching also. Scripture makes this clear: when the apostles, by the command of the Holy Spirit, sent Paul and Barnabas to preach the Gospel to the Gentiles, they fasted and prayed and laid hands on them (Acts XIII). Thus we may understand how greatly the devotion both of those giving and of those receiving must be attended to, lest the sacrament of so great a blessing seem to be performed negligently. You will act piously and reverently in accordance with apostolic institutions if you yourself preserve this form for the ordination of priests throughout the Churches over which God has willed you to preside: that blessing be granted to those to be consecrated only on the Sunday of the Resurrection. Its beginning is known to be assigned from Saturday evening, [Col. 1133C] and it has been consecrated by such great mysteries of the divine dispensations that whatever the Lord has established in a more remarkable manner has been accomplished in the dignity of this day. On this day the world received its beginning; on it, through Christ’s resurrection, death received its destruction and life its beginning.

### CHAPTER XIV. What the pontiff, deacon, and notary must do at the ordination of a bishop.

When a bishop is being ordained, the pontiff shall lay his hand upon him; the minister shall read the Gospel lesson; and the notary shall write the letter of confirmation.

### CHAPTER XV. A metropolitan is not to consecrate any bishop without at least three bishops, with the other bishops giving their assent. [Col. 1133D] From the Council of Orléans, ch. 1.

(Distinction 53, ch. *Extra*, and distinction 55, ch. *Non debet*, ch. *Nec episcopi*; *Extra*, On the times of ordination.) No bishop may presume to ordain a bishop without the metropolitan’s permission, nor may a metropolitan bishop do so without three fellow-provincial bishops; and the other fellow-provincial bishops are to be consulted, so that they may indicate by their reply that they consent. If there is any doubt between parties, the metropolitan shall follow the greater number in the election.

### CHAPTER XVI. Episcopal sees ought not to be separated from one another by a great distance. Gregory, ch. 8 of the *Responses to the Questions of Augustine of Canterbury*.

(Distinction 80, ch. *Fraternitatem*.) We desire your brotherhood [Col. 1134A] so to ordain bishops that the bishops themselves are not separated from one another by a great distance, so that there may be no necessity preventing them from being able to assemble for a bishop’s ordination. For the ordination of a bishop must by no means take place with fewer than three or four bishops assembled.

### CHAPTER XVII. On bishops not being ordained by fewer than three bishops. Anacletus, in the *Decrees*, ch. 1.

(Distinction 66, ch. *Porro*.) If all cannot assemble together, let them give their consent through prayers, so that they may not be absent in spirit from the ordination itself. Moreover, James, called the Just, the first bishop of Jerusalem and called the Lord’s brother according to the flesh, was ordained by the apostles Peter, James, and John, [Col. 1134B] thereby giving their successors the rule that no one is ever to be ordained by fewer than three bishops, with all the rest giving assent, and that the ordination be celebrated by common vote.

### CHAPTER XVIII. What bishops are to do in the ordination of another bishop, and how a bishop is to be ordained. Council of Carthage IV, ch. 2.

(Dist. 23, c. *Episcopus*.) When a bishop is ordained, two bishops shall lay their hands upon him and hold the book of the Gospels over both his head and crown; and while one pronounces the blessing over him, all the other bishops present shall touch his head with their hands.

CAP. XIX. From the sayings of Theodore, archbishop.

[Col. 1134C] At the ordination of a bishop, he who ordains must celebrate Mass, and likewise he who is ordained.

CAP. XX. From the First Council of Orange, c. 10.

(Dist. 53, c. *De abjectione*.) Concerning the degradation and ambition of one whom two bishops have presumed to ordain in your provinces: it has been decided concerning those who so presume that, wherever it happens that two bishops consecrate a third, both he and his authors shall be condemned, so that the more cautiously those things which were established in ancient times may be observed.

CAP. XXI. Those to be ordained shall assemble for examination on Wednesday. Council of Nantes, c. 3.

(Dist. 24, c. *Quando episc.*) When a bishop intends to perform ordinations, all who wish to enter the sacred ministry of the Church [Col. 1134D] must be summoned on the Wednesday before the ordination to one city, together with the presbyters who are to present them. Then the bishop must choose from his own side priests and other prudent men who are not ignorant of the divine law and are trained in ecclesiastical ordinances, to investigate carefully the life, family, country, age, education, place where they were brought up, whether they are adequately learned, and whether they are instructed in the law of the Lord, of those to be ordained; above all, whether they firmly hold the Catholic faith and can affirm it in simple words. Those to whom this care is entrusted must beware lest, enticed either by favour or by desire for any gift, they depart from the truth and place before the bishop’s hands one unworthy and insufficiently qualified to receive sacred orders. [Col. 1135A] If they do so, both he who has approached unworthily shall be removed from the altar, and those who have attempted to sell the gift of the Holy Spirit, already condemned before God, shall be deprived of ecclesiastical rank. Therefore let them be carefully examined for three consecutive days, and on Saturday those found approved shall be presented to the bishop.

CAP. XXII. Those to be ordained deacons or presbyters shall promise to live chastely. Fourth Council of Toledo, c. 26.

(Dist. 28, c. *Quando presb.*) When presbyters or deacons are appointed through the parishes, they must make a profession to their bishop that they will live chastely and purely in the fear of God; and, once he has bound them by such a profession, they shall maintain holy discipline.

CAP. XXIII. When ordained, presbyters shall receive an official written document from the bishop. [Col. 1135B] Fourth Council of Toledo, c. 26.

(Dist. 38, c. *Quando presb.*) When presbyters are ordained in parishes, let them receive an official document from their bishop, so that they may come instructed to the churches assigned to them and not offend through ignorance concerning the divine sacraments themselves; so that, when they come to litanies or to a council, they may render account to their bishop of how they celebrate the office entrusted to them and baptize.

CAP. XXIV. What priests need to know. From the sayings of Augustine.

(Dist. 38, c. *Quae ipsis*.) The things necessary for priests [Col. 1135C] themselves to learn are: the book of sacraments, the lectionary, the baptismal rite, computus, penitential canons, the Psalter, and homilies suitable throughout the course [Col. 1136A] of the year for Sundays and each feast day. If one of all these is lacking, the title of priest will scarcely stand in him, because most perilous are the evangelical threats by which it is said: “If a blind man leads a blind man, both fall into a pit” (Matt. XIII).

CAP. XXV. On the times for ordination. From the Decrees of Pope Gelasius, c. 4.

(Dist. 76, c. *Ordinat. presb.*) Ordinations of presbyters and deacons must not be performed except at fixed times and on fixed days: namely, at the fast of the fourth month, the seventh, and the tenth; also at the beginning of Lent, on the middle day of the week, and at the Saturday fast, about evening. Let them know that these ordinations are to be celebrated then, nor may they dare, for the sake of any convenience, [Col. 1136B] to confer either the presbyterate or the diaconate upon those who have been ordained before them.

CAP. XXVI. From the Council of Meaux, c. 6.

Let none who seek ordination be ordained unless they have remained for at least one year in a fixed and religious place, or in a city, so that certainty concerning their life, conduct, and teaching may be known.

CAP. XXVII. No one is to be ordained without a title. Council of Chalcedon, c. 6, session 11.

(Dist. 70, c. *Neminem*.) No presbyter or deacon, nor anyone established in an ecclesiastical rank, ought to be ordained absolutely—that is, without a particular appointment—unless he who is ordained clearly receives the public designation of ordination in a church of his city or estate, or at a martyr-shrine or monastery. But the synod decreed that such laying on of hands upon those [Col. 1136C] ordained absolutely shall be held invalid, and that they may minister nowhere, to the dishonour of the ordainer.

## ON THE AGE OF THOSE TO BE ORDAINED

[Col. 1135]

CAP. XXVIII. A bishop or presbyter is not to be ordained before his thirtieth year. [Col. 1135C] Council of Agde, c. 16.

(C. *Episcopus*, § *Presbyterum*.) No metropolitan shall presume to ordain a bishop or presbyter before thirty years of age—that is, before he has reached the age of a fully mature man—lest through age, as sometimes happens, they be blamed for some error.

CAP. XXIX. A presbyter shall not be ordained before the age of thirty. [Col. 1135D] From the decrees of Pope Fabian to the Easterners, in the Council of Neocaesarea.

(Decr. 78, c. 30, *Presbyter*, and dist. *Si quis*.) If anyone has not completed thirty years of age, he shall in no way be ordained presbyter, even if he is very worthy; for the Lord himself was baptized at thirty years of age and then began to teach (Matt. IV). Therefore the man to be ordained ought not to be consecrated before this lawful age.

CAP. XXX. When a deacon is to be ordained. Third Council of Carthage, c. 4.

(Dist. 77, c. *Placuit*.) It has been decided that neither deacons be ordained before twenty-five years of age, even if [Col. 1136C] they are very worthy, nor virgins consecrated; and that a reader shall not give the greeting to the people.

CAP. XXXI. The Levitical blessing shall not be conferred on those under twenty-five years. Fifth Council of Toledo, c. 19.

(Dist. 77, c. *In veteri*.) In the old Law Levites are commanded to serve in the tabernacle from their twenty-fifth year (Num. VIII); the holy Fathers followed its authority in the canons. We, too, not unmindful of the precept of the divine law, make infants and boys Levites before their lawful age and experience of life. Therefore, lest this continue to be done by us, we are admonished by the judgments both of the divine law and of the canons that deacons be ordained at twenty-five years of age, so that, according to the Apostle’s command, they may first be tested and then minister, having no crime against them (I Tim. III).

CAP. XXXII. From the Decrees of Nicholas, c. 6.

A grave danger threatens us concerning those ordained under twenty years, because they boast of victory before they seem, or know how, to fight: that is, before they can experience the inciting darts of nature, they grasp in their conscience, through desire, the offices of sacred chastity. Therefore the sacred canons have ordained that a subdeacon [Col. 1137A] shall not be ordained before fourteen years, nor a deacon before twenty-five, nor a presbyter before thirty. Thereafter, if he is worthy, he may be chosen for the episcopate; and we likewise command this to be observed.

CAP. XXXIII. How a presbyter is ordained. Fourth Council of Carthage, c. 3.

(Dist. 23, c. *Presbyter*.) When a presbyter is ordained, while the bishop blesses him and holds his hand over his head, all the presbyters present shall also place their hands upon his head beside the bishop’s hand.

CAP. XXXIV. How a deacon is ordained. From the same council and the same chapter.

[Col. 1137B] (Dist. 23, c. *Diaconus*.) When a deacon is ordained, the bishop alone who blesses him shall place his hand upon his head, for he is consecrated not to the priesthood but to ministry.

CAP. XXXV. How a subdeacon is ordained. From the same council, c. 5.

(Dist. 23, c. *Subdiaconus*.) When a subdeacon is ordained, because he does not receive the laying on of hands, let him receive from the bishop’s hand an empty paten and an empty chalice; but from the hand of the archdeacon let him receive a cruet with water, a water-basin, and a hand-towel.

CAP. XXXVI. How an acolyte is ordained. From the same council, c. 6.

[Col. 1137C] (Dist. 23, c. *Acolythus*.) When an acolyte is ordained, he shall indeed be taught by the bishop how he ought to perform his office. But from the archdeacon let him receive a candlestick with a candle, that he may know himself to be assigned to kindle the lights of the church. Let him also receive [Col. 1138A] an empty cruet for supplying the blood of the Lord at the Eucharist.

CAP. XXXVII. How an exorcist is ordained. From the same council, c. 7.

(Dist. 23, c. *Exorcista*.) When an exorcist is ordained, let him receive from the bishop’s hand a booklet in which the exorcisms are written, the bishop saying to him: “Receive this and commit it to memory; and have authority to lay hands upon one possessed, whether baptized or a catechumen.”

CAP. XXXVIII. How a reader is ordained. From the same council, c. 8.

(Dist. 23, c. *Lector*.) When a reader is ordained, the bishop shall address the people concerning him, declaring his faith, life, and aptitude; after this, before the people, he shall hand him the codex from which he is to read, saying: “Receive this, and be a herald of the word of God; if you faithfully and profitably fulfil your office, you shall have a share with those who have ministered the word of God.”

CAP. XXXIX. How a doorkeeper is ordained. From the same council, c. 9.

(Dist. 23, c. *Ostiarius*.) When a doorkeeper is ordained, after he has been instructed by the archdeacon concerning how he ought to conduct himself in the house of God, at the archdeacon’s prompting the bishop hands him the keys of the church from the altar, saying: “So act as one who will render account to God for the things opened by these keys.”

CAP. XL. How a psalmist is ordained. From the same council, c. 10.

[Col. 1138C] (Dist. 23, c. *Psalmista*.) A psalmist, that is, a singer, may undertake the office of singing without the bishop’s knowledge, by the command of a presbyter alone, the presbyter saying to him: “See that you sing with your mouth what you believe with your heart, and prove by works what you believe with your heart.”

## ON THE OFFICES OF THOSE WHO ARE TO BE ORDAINED

[Col. 1137]

CAP. XLI. The office of bishops and the rest in the Church. [Col. 1137C] Isidore, letter to Leofrid of Córdoba.

(Dist. 25, c. *Perlectis*.) Having read the letters of your holiness, I rejoiced to learn from their report that you enjoy the health for which I had hoped. As for the matters which the discourse of your expression has endeavoured to set forth subsequently, I give thanks to God that you devote care to the pastoral office, inquiring how and in what manner ecclesiastical offices are to be ordered. And although all things are known to your prudence, nevertheless, because you consult me in brotherly affection, I shall explain, insofar as I can, and shall speak concerning all the ranks of the Church and what belongs to each. To the doorkeeper belong the keys of the church, so that he may close and open the temple of God, guard everything within and without, receive the faithful, and exclude the excommunicated and unbelievers. To the exorcist belongs the duty of retaining the exorcisms by heart and laying hands upon the possessed and catechumens in exorcizing them. To the acolyte [Col. 1138C] belongs the preparation of lights in the sanctuary: he carries the candle, and he prepares what is to be supplied for the eucharistic chalice. To the psalmist belongs the office of singing: namely, reciting blessings, praises, the sacrifice, responsories, and whatever belongs to the skill of singing. [Col. 1138D] To the reader belongs the duty of pronouncing the readings and preaching to the peoples the things foretold by the prophets. To the subdeacon belongs the duty of carrying the chalice and paten to the altar of Christ, handing them to the Levites, and ministering to them; likewise of holding the cruet, water-basin, and hand-towel, and supplying water to bishop, presbyter, and Levites for washing their hands before the altar. To the deacon belongs the duty of assisting the priests and ministering in all that is done in the sacraments of Christ—in baptism, chrism, paten, and chalice. He is also to bring and arrange the offerings upon the altar, set in order and clothe the Lord’s table, carry the cross, and preach the Gospel and the Apostle to the peoples. For just as readers are commanded to proclaim the Old Testament, so the deacon is commanded to proclaim the New. [Col. 1139A] To him likewise belongs the office of the prayers and the recitation of names. He calls upon people to keep their ears attentive to the Lord; he exhorts them to pray; he cries aloud and announces peace. To the presbyter belongs the duty of consecrating the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood upon God’s altar, saying prayers, and blessing God’s gifts. To the bishop belongs the consecration of basilicas, anointing of the altar, and preparation of chrism. He distributes the aforesaid offices and ecclesiastical orders; he blesses consecrated virgins; and although each person has advanced through the several orders, he nevertheless is their overseer in all.

These are the orders and ministries of the clerics, which are distributed solely by pontifical authority, under the care of the archdeacon and the oversight of the primicerius and treasurer. [Col. 1139B] The archdeacon commands the subdeacons and Levites. The following ministries belong to him: arranging the vesting of the altar; through the Levites, care for incense and the necessary provision for the sacrifice; determining which Levite is to read the Apostle and Gospel, which is to say the prayers or sing the responsory on Sundays or at a solemnity. The care and ordering of parishes, and disputes, also belong to his charge; concerning the repair of diocesan basilicas he makes representations to the bishop. By the bishop’s command he visits the parishes, their ornaments and property, and the records of ecclesiastical manumissions; he also reports to the bishop the money collected, receives from the communion, and brings it to the bishop; and he distributes to the clerics their respective portions. [Col. 1140A] The misconduct of deacons is reported to the bishop by the archdeacon; and he announces to the bishop in the sanctuary the days of fasts and solemnities, which are publicly proclaimed in the church by the bishop. When the archdeacon is absent, the next deacon fulfils his office.

To the primicerius belong the acolytes, exorcists, psalmists, and readers. He gives the signal for the clerics’ office, oversees uprightness of life and the office of singing, and determines which cleric ought diligently to perform the readings, psalm, praises, offertory, and responsory; he also regulates the order and manner of chanting in choir according to solemnity and season, and arranges the carrying of lights. If anything is necessary for the repair of the basilicas in the city, he shall report it [Col. 1140B] to the bishop. He shall send the bishop’s letters concerning fast days to parishioners through the doorkeepers; he shall discipline clerics whom he knows to be delinquent; and he shall report to the bishop the offences of those whom he cannot correct. He appoints the basilica officials and arranges the rolls. When the primicerius is absent, the person who is nearest to him either by law or by learning shall carry out these matters. By these examples it is clear that to the treasurer belongs the appointment of doorkeepers for basilicas, the preparation of incense, care for making chrism, care for arranging the baptistery, and preparation of lights in the sanctuary and for the sacrifices.

## ON THE QUALIFICATIONS OF THOSE TO BE ORDAINED

[Col. 1139]

CAP. XLII. One made lame by a surgeon’s incision is not prohibited from sacred orders. [Col. 1139C] Council of Lleida, c. 20.

(Dist. 55, c. *Si quis in infirmitate*.) If a cleric, while ill, is made lame by a surgeon’s incision, we do not deny his advancement to sacred orders.

CAP. XLIII. One who deliberately cut off part of a finger is not to be ordained. Innocent to Felix, bishop of Nocera.

(Dist. 55, c. *Qui partem*.) Therefore, one who deliberately cuts off part of any finger from himself is not admitted to the clergy by the canons. But if this happens to someone by an accident while he is engaged in agricultural work or doing something else, and he wounds himself unintentionally, the canons command that such persons be made clerics; and if they are found already in the clergy, they are not to be expelled. For in the former cases the will is judged, since it was itself the cause of cutting with iron—a deed which another might not hesitate to do as well. But in the latter cases he deserves pardon.

CAP. XLIV. One who accidentally cuts off his finger is not prohibited from the clergy. Stephen to Robert, bishop of Alet.
