(Dist. 55, c. *Lator praesentium*.) The bearer of this letter, namely the cleric Flavinius, coming to the holy apostolic see, brought us the letter sent by you. In it you sought to inquire whether, since he had recently been captured by the Northmen and had a finger of his left hand cut off, he might be advanced to ecclesiastical order or not. Finding also that your zeal, anxious in this matter, seeks instruction from the apostolic see and always desires to follow the norm of justice, we rightly commend the earnestness of your holiness. We wish your reverence to know that, if it is so that his finger was cut off by the Northmen, this will not harm him in being advanced, provided that he is otherwise worthy. For we do not believe it is unknown to your affection what the sacred canons judge concerning those who willingly suffer such a thing at the hands of masters, physicians, or pagans. [Col. 1140D] We find nothing that ought to stand in his way, if this is so. We urge your religious devotion to act concerning him in such a manner that it may both gain a great reward for this and, with God’s help, accomplish his desire by the authority of this canonical institution, without opposition.

## WHICH LAYMEN OUGHT TO BE ORDAINED

[Col. 1141]

CAP. XLV. Those who had wives at the time of baptism are not prohibited from becoming clerics if they later live religiously. [Col. 1141A] Innocent I to Felix, bishop of Capua, ep. 4, c. 4.

(Dist. 33, c. *Laici*.) Laymen who were baptized while having wives, and who have thereafter so ordered themselves that their reputation is in no respect shaken; or who, from the time of baptism, have joined the clergy or adhered to monasteries—if they have known neither concubine nor mistress, and have been vigilant in all their works—are not prohibited from being admitted to the lot of clerical office. Yet the periods established by the elders must be observed in their case, so that no one becomes a reader too soon, an acolyte too soon, a deacon too soon, or a priest too soon.

CAP. XLVI. Those who receive freedom from their masters, with no service reserved, are admitted to clerical rank. [Col. 1141B] Fourth Council of Toledo, c. 72.

(Dist. 54, c. *Quicunque*.) Whoever receive freedom from their masters in such a way that their patron retains for himself no service from them, if they are free of capital crime, may freely be admitted to clerical order, since they are known to have been released by an unconditional manumission. But those who have been manumitted while service is retained must in no way be advanced to ecclesiastical order, because they are still bound under their patrons’ servitude, lest, whenever their masters wish, clerics become slaves.

CAP. XLVII. The unlettered and those bodily impaired shall not be advanced to the clergy. Pope Gelasius, c. 16.

[Col. 1141C] (Dist. 36, c. *Illitteratos*.) Let no one presume to advance to clerical order those who are unlettered, or impaired or mutilated in some part of the body; for one lacking sacred letters cannot be fit for the offices, and the precepts of the Law permit nothing defective whatsoever to be offered to God. The same has been decreed concerning those who mutilate themselves.

CAP. XLVIII. No one in a servile condition is to attain sacred orders. Council of Tibur, c. 5.

(Dist. 54, c. *Nulli*.) No one of servile condition shall be advanced to sacred orders unless he first obtains lawful personal freedom from his masters. The charter of this freedom shall be read publicly from the ambo before ordination; and, if no one objects, they shall be consecrated in due form. But a slave not canonically consecrated, after he has fallen from his rank, shall be of the condition he was in before his rank.

CAP. XLIX. Husbands of widows or men who have had multiple marriages, if advanced to the priesthood, are to be excluded from the priestly title and from all ecclesiastical offices. Leo, in the Decrees, c. 4.

(Dist. 83, c. *Quisquis*.) Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to all bishops. Whoever have been advanced to the priesthood either as husbands of widows or as men having had multiple marriages, we command, by the authority of the apostolic see, that they be excluded from all ecclesiastical offices [Col. 1142A] and from the priestly title.

CAP. L. In the Decrees of Hilary, c. 2.

Hilary, bishop of the Roman Church, presiding in synod, said: “Above all, care must be taken that no one who has not taken a virgin as wife should aspire to sacred ranks. Those also must be rejected who enter a second wife’s marriage contrary to the apostolic precepts.”

CAP. LI. Sons of presbyters are prohibited from sacred offices. From the decrees of Gregory and Urban II, concerning priests’ sons.

(Dist. 56, c. *Presbyt. filios et Osius*.) We decree that sons of presbyters are to be removed from the sacred mysteries of the altar, unless they have proved themselves to live religiously in cenobitic or regular monasteries.

CAP. LII. Those born of priests who presided over the apostolic see. [Col. 1142B] From the *Book of the Popes*.

(Dist. 56, c. *Osius*.) Felix III, a Roman by nationality, was the son of the presbyter Felix; he held office from the times of King Odoacer to the times of King Theodoric. Likewise Gelasius, an African by nationality, son of Bishop Valerius, sat for four years, eight months, and twenty-nine days. Likewise Agapitus, a Roman by nationality, son of the presbyter Gordian, sat for eleven months and twenty-three days. Likewise Silverius, a Campanian by nationality, bishop of Rome and son of Ormisda, sat for one year, five months, and nine days. Likewise Deusdedit, a Roman by nationality, son of the subdeacon Stephen, sat for three years and twenty-two days. Likewise John IV, a Dalmatian by nationality, son of [Col. 1142C] Venantio the scholar, sat for one year, nine months, and nineteen days. Likewise Theodore, a Greek by nationality, son of Theodore, bishop from the city of Jerusalem, sat for six years, five months, and eighteen days.

CAP. LIII. Sons of priests are not prohibited from the episcopate if other virtues are found in them. Urban, archbishop, to Bartholomew of Tours.

(Dist. 56, c. *Cenomanensem*.) The bishop-elect of Le Mans, because he is said to be the son of a priest, we do not reject for the present if other virtues concur in him; rather, with merits supporting him, we patiently receive him—not, however, that this be adopted as a rule in future, but that provision may be made for the Church’s present danger.

CAP. LIV. Because when many things speak for someone and only one against him, his promotion ought not to be impeded by that one thing, as Pope Urban II wishes to the bishop of León.

(Dist. 56, c. *Cenomanensem*.) Because, coming simply to the apostolic see, you have humbly confessed the sin which seemed to impede the office of your episcopate—namely, that you were born of a mother not lawfully married, whom your father is known to have known while his own wife was alive—we, through the grace of apostolic mildness, recognizing both your profession and the testimony of the brethren who are with you, and hearing of your religious life, free you from the bond of this sin and confirm you in the office of the priesthood which you have received, immune from the other crimes that impede the priesthood.

CAP. LV. A rank received in bodily soundness is not lost through a subsequent infirmity. Gelasius to Bishop Palladius.

(Dist. 55, c. *Praecepta canonica*.) The canonical precepts by which ecclesiastical discipline is governed do not permit the infirm to enter the priesthood; yet if anyone has already been established in it and is wounded, he cannot lose what he received when bodily sound. For the presbyter Stephen, in a petition to us, lamented that he had been deprived of what he possessed among those subject to him. Many years ago he had received the dignity of the presbyterate, when his body was indeed judged unblemished. But recently, because of the devastation of the province of Tuscany, which beyond all provinces the savagery of barbarians of diverse sects and their unsettled minds had brought upon it, he sought to escape the threatening swords by the protection of flight. Leaping over fences set with sharp stakes, he reported that he had impaled the lower parts of his body, which could scarcely be cleansed even with treatment for two years. Therefore, dearest brother, restore to the aforesaid man his place and dignity, so that he may exercise the most holy mysteries as he was accustomed. For it is not fitting that an order received beforehand be taken away on account of a later bodily injury, which he is shown to have suffered by accident.

CAP. LVI. Those castrated by physicians, barbarians, or their masters are not excluded from the clergy.

[Col. 1143C]

(Dist. 55, c. *Si quis per aegritudinem*.) If anyone, through illness, has had his genitals cut by physicians, likewise those castrated by barbarians or masters, if worthy in conduct, the canon admits them to advancement to clerical office. But if anyone in health, not for the discipline of religion and abstinence but through cutting off the body fashioned by God, thinking that he can cut away from himself carnal desires, has castrated himself, we decree that he is not to be admitted to any clerical office. If, however, he had already been advanced to the clergy, let him be barred from his ministry and deposed.

CAP. LVII. Although some eunuchs have intercourse and emit semen, it is nevertheless sterile for generation. [Col. 1143D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book X.

“Eunuch” is Greek, meaning *spado* (“castrated man”). Some of them have intercourse, yet there is no power in their semen. They have fluid and emit semen, but it is empty and ineffective for begetting.

CAP. LVIII. Pope Innocent I, epistle 22 to the bishops of Macedonia.

(I, q. c. *Ventum circa fin.*) It is the law of our Church that those coming from heretics, although baptized there, receive communion only as laymen through the laying on of hands; and that none from among them be appointed even to the lowest honour of the clergy.

CAP. LIX. A bigamist is not to be ordained. Third Council of Orléans, c. 8.

(Dist. 55, c. *Nullus*.) Let bigamists, penitents, and husbands of repudiated women not be advanced to the priesthood. Those possessed are not only not to be admitted to the clergy, but, if found in it, are to be removed from office.

CAP. LX. No cleric is to be ordained from among penitents. Fourth Council of Carthage, c. 68.

(Dist. 50, c. *Ex poenitentibus*.) No one from among penitents, however good he may be, is to be ordained a cleric. If it has happened through the bishop’s ignorance, he shall be deposed from the clergy, because at the time of ordination he did not disclose that he was undergoing penance.

CAP. In a case of necessity, penitents are admitted to the clergy. Second Council of Toledo, c. 2.

(Dist. 50, c. *Placuit*.) It has been decided that penitents are not to be admitted to the clergy except when necessity or utility requires it, so that they may be assigned among the doorkeepers or readers, but may not read the Apostle or the Gospels. But those who were ordained beforehand shall be counted among the subdeacons, provided that they do not lay on hands or touch sacred things. By a penitent we mean one who, after baptism, for homicide or for various crimes and very grave sins, undergoing public penance in haircloth, has been reconciled to the divine altar.

CAP. LXII. Council of Orléans, c. 8.

If anyone among the laity, after his wife, has known another woman of whatever condition, he is in no way to be admitted to the clergy.

CAP. LXIII. No one shall admit a man from overseas to the clergy unless he is identified by the letters of five bishops. [Col. 1144C] Pope Anastasius, letter to the bishops of Germany and Burgundy.

(Dist. 98, c. *Transmarinos*.) Do not admit men from overseas or unknown persons to the honour of the clergy unless they are identified by written testimonials of five or more bishops, because many things are accustomed to happen through fraud. Therefore these matters too must be guarded against with the utmost care.

CAP. LXIV. Clerics are not to be ordained by the bishop of another city. Pope Innocent I, ep. 2, to Victricius of Rouen.

(Dist. 71, c. *De aliena*.) Let no one presume to judge or ordain a cleric from another church, unless, at that bishop’s request, he is willing to grant it; this also seems to be contained in the Nicene synod. [Col. 1144D] A cleric expelled from his own church shall not be received by another church.

CAP. LXV. Without letters of recommendation, a cleric shall not minister outside his own church. Council of Chalcedon, c. 23.

(Dist. 5, c. *Hortamur*.) If any cleric or layman goes hastily to another church and is received without letters of recommendation, both the receiver and the one received shall be deprived of communion.

CAP. LXVI. Travelling clerics are not received without a *formata* [credential letter]. Council of Orléans, c. 8.

(Dist. 7, c. *Nullum*.) It is commanded in the Council of Antioch and likewise in that of Chalcedon that fugitive and travelling [Col. 1145A] clerics shall be received or ordained by no one unless they have letters of recommendation and the permission of their own bishop or abbot.

CAP. LXVII. No one shall receive a monk without the abbot’s permission. [Col. 1146A] Council of Agde, c. 27.

Clerics or monks shall not be free to wander about without letters of recommendation.

## ON THE TRANSFER OF BISHOPS OR PRIESTS

[Col. 1145]

CAP. LXVIII. From the Decrees of Pope Callistus.

[Col. 1145A]

(7, q. 1, c. *Scias frater*.) Callistus, bishop of the city of Rome, to all bishops. If a bishop is to be transferred for the sake of usefulness, he does not have authority for this by himself; rather, let it be done at the invitation of the brethren and by the authority of this holy [Col. 1145B] see, not for ambition’s sake but for utility or necessity.

CAP. LXIX. Transfers of bishops may be made for necessity or usefulness. Pope Anterus to the bishops of Baetica and Toledo.

(7, q. 1, c. *Mutationes*.) Anterus, bishop of Rome, to all bishops. Know that transfers of bishops may be made for common utility or necessity, but not at anyone’s personal will or by domination. Saint Peter, our master and prince of the apostles, was transferred from the city of Antioch to Rome for usefulness, so that he might be more effective there. Eusebius also was transferred from a certain small city to Alexandria for usefulness; [Col. 1145C] likewise Felix was transferred from the city in which he had been ordained to Ephesus, by election of the citizens on account of his teaching and good life, through the common council of bishops, the remaining priests, and the apostles. For one does not pass from city to city, nor is one transferred from a lesser to a greater city, who does this not by his own choice or ambition, but is transferred to a more important place through some necessity, or the usefulness of others, and by council. Nor is one transferred from a lesser city to a greater who does this not from ambition or personal will, but who has been transferred and enthroned humbly by others, with the authority of this holy see, whether by force, because he has been driven from his own see, through necessity, or for the usefulness of a place or people. For just as bishops have authority regularly to ordain bishops and other priests, so, whenever necessity or usefulness compels it in the aforesaid manner, they have authority to transfer and enthrone them, yet not without the authority of the most holy Roman see. [Col. 1145D] For the cause of usefulness and necessity is one thing, that of avarice, presumption, and personal will another.

CAP. LXX. A bishop shall pass from church to church not through ambition but by synodal authority. Fourth Council of Carthage, c. 27.

(7, q. 1, c. *Episcopus de loco*.) A bishop shall not pass through ambition from an undistinguished place to a distinguished one, nor any cleric of lower rank. Yet if the usefulness of the Church requires it to be done, by a decree presented to the bishops [Col. 1146A] on behalf of that person by clergy and laity, he may be transferred in the presence of a synod, provided that another bishop is appointed in his place. Priests of lower rank or other clerics may migrate to other churches with the consent of their bishops.

CAP. LXXI. From the sayings of Augustine.

It must be forbidden that any ordained person migrate from his own parish to another, or go to the thresholds of the apostles for prayer while abandoning the care of his own church, or go to the palace to pursue a petition. If he does so, such a departure is of no validity. This must be enjoined upon all: those who desire to go to the thresholds of the apostles for prayer should confess their sins at home and then depart, because they are to be bound or absolved by their own bishop or priest, not by a stranger.

CAP. LXXII. From the Council of Orléans, c. 2.

Concerning presbyters or deacons who are accustomed to leave [Col. 1146C] the places in which they were ordained and transfer themselves elsewhere: it has been decided that they shall minister in those places; but if they wish to transfer themselves from their own places to another, they shall be deposed.

CAP. LXXIII. It is not lawful for a cleric to be enrolled in two churches. Council of Chalcedon, c. 12.

(Dist. 70, c. *Sanctorum canon.*, § *Omnino autem*.) It is not lawful for a cleric to be enrolled simultaneously in the churches of two cities; rather, he shall minister in that in which he was originally ordained, and shall not flee to another as though to a more important one through desire of vain glory. Whoever does this must be recalled to his own church, in which he was first established, and minister there alone.

CAP. LXXIV. From the Council of Arles, c. 12.

[Col. 1146D]

It has been established that presbyters, as has hitherto been done, shall not indiscriminately be moved through different places, neither by bishops nor by prelates, lest, perhaps through their absence, both the danger to souls and the offices of the churches in which they are established be neglected.

CAP. LXXV. From the Second Council of Chalon.

A presbyter who has left his proper place and migrated to another is not to be received unless he has stated the reason for his migration and, under witnesses, has proved that he lived innocently in the parish in which he was ordained. He must also have letters bearing the names of the bishop and the city. Once these matters have been examined, and he is found to be such that credence may be given to him, he is to be received.

## ON THOSE ORDAINED NOT BEING REORDAINED

[Col. 1147]

### CHAPTER LXXVI. One consecrated once ought not to be consecrated again. Gregory to John, bishop of Ravenna, book VIII, letter 32.

[Col. 1147A]

(Distinction 68, canon *Sicut semel*.) What you say—that one who has been ordained should be ordained again—is altogether ridiculous. For just as one baptized once ought not to be baptized again, so one consecrated once cannot be consecrated again in the same order. But if anyone has perhaps come to the priesthood despite a minor fault, penance ought to be imposed for the fault, while the order itself is to remain intact.

### CHAPTER LXXVII. One who departs from the Church loses neither baptism nor the right to confer it. Augustine, *Against Parmenian*, book II.

(1, question [1], canon *Quod quidam*.) Both are sacraments, [Col. 1147B] and each is given to a person by a certain consecration: the former when he is baptized, the latter when he is ordained. Therefore neither may be repeated in the Catholic Church. For if, when persons come over from that party, their superiors too are received after correcting the error of the schismatics for the sake of peace, and it seems necessary that they should perform the same offices which they had performed, they are not to be ordained again. Just as baptism remained whole in them, so did ordination; for the defect lay in the separation, which has been corrected by the peace of unity, not in the sacraments, which, wherever they are, are themselves what they are.

Thus, when the Church judges it expedient that their superiors, on entering the Catholic communion, should not administer their honours there, the sacraments of ordination themselves are nevertheless not taken away from them, but remain upon them. [Col. 1147C] For this reason hands are not laid upon them among the people, lest injury be done not to a human being but to the sacrament itself. Concerning those separated from the unity of the Catholic Church, there is now no question that they possess and can confer these sacraments; but they possess them harmfully and confer them harmfully. They are outside the bond of peace. Injury must be done to neither sacrament.

Just as one who departs from unity does not possess it rightly, yet still possesses it, and therefore it is not given back to him when he returns, so one who has it from Bonosus does not confer it rightly, yet nevertheless confers it; and therefore what one receives from him is not repeated when one comes to unity.

### CHAPTER LXXVIII. Augustine, *On the One Baptism*.

(1, question [1], canon *Quod quidem*, § *Sed tamen aliud*.) It is one thing not to have something, another not to have it lawfully or to usurp it unlawfully. Therefore the sacraments of [Col. 1147D] Christ and the Church are not thereby deprived of being sacraments merely because they are used unlawfully, not only by heretics but by all the wicked and impious. Those persons, however, are to be corrected or punished; the sacraments themselves are to be acknowledged and venerated.

### CHAPTER LXXIX. Priests invoke the Lord’s name, but the Lord grants the blessing. Augustine, book of *Questions*, question 2, from the Old Testament.

(1, question [1], canon *Dictum est*.) Augustine in the book *Questions on the Old Testament*: The Lord said in Numbers to Moses and Aaron: “You shall put my name upon the children of Israel, and I, the Lord, will bless them,” so that he may transmit to people the grace bestowed through the ministry of the ordainer [the ordained]; neither the priest’s will can be absent nor can it be beneficial, but rather the merit of the one seeking blessing.

Let us observe from this how great is the dignity of priestly rank or office. It is said, among other things, concerning the most wicked Caiaphas, the murderer of the Saviour: “He did not say this of himself; but, being high priest that year, he prophesied” (John II). By this it is shown that the Holy Spirit, giver of graces, does not follow the person—whether worthy or evil—but the order of transmission. Thus, although someone may be of good merit, he nevertheless cannot bless unless he has been ordained or performs the ministry of an office; but it belongs to God to grant the effect of the blessing.

### CHAPTER LXXX. How one condemned by a synod is restored as innocent in a second synod. [Col. 1148B] Fourth Council of Mainz, canon 28, and Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 27.

(11, question [1], in canon *Episcopus*, canon 80.) If a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, unjustly deposed from his rank, is found innocent in a second synod, he cannot be restored to what he was unless he receives before the altar, from the hands of bishops, the ranks he lost: if a bishop, the *horarium*, ring, and staff; if a presbyter, the *horarium* and paten; if a deacon, the *horarium* and alb; if a subdeacon, the paten and chalice. Likewise, the remaining ranks are to receive that restoration of themselves which they received when they were ordained.

### CHAPTER LXXXI. Those returning from heretics must be reordained. Urban II to Peter, bishop of Pistoia, and to Rusticus, abbot.

[Col. 1148C] (1, question 7, canon *Daibertum*. *Concordance*, canon *Odardus*, Extra, *On Dissolution*.) We have learned from his own confession that Daibert was ordained deacon by Nezelon—though Nezelon was simoniacal, he did not ordain him simoniacally. The judgment of blessed Pope Innocent has declared that Nezelon was a heretic and, as is established, ordained by heretics. Since he had nothing, he could give nothing to the man on whom he laid hands.

Therefore, strengthened by the authority of so great a pontiff and confirmed by the testimony of Pope Damasus, who says that what has been wrongly done must be repeated, we have constituted Daibert—who has departed from heretics in body and spirit and labours, to the extent of his powers, for the benefit of the Church—a deacon anew, when the necessity of the Church required it. We judge this not to be a repetition, but solely the complete bestowal of the diaconate, [Col. 1148D] since, as we have said, one who had nothing could give nothing.

### CHAPTER LXXXII. The Roman Church received primacy from the Lord. Anacletus to the bishops of Italy, letter 2.

(Distinction 21, canon *In Novo Testamento*.) In the New Testament, after Christ the Lord, the priestly order began with Peter, because the pontificate in Christ’s Church was first given to him. The Lord said to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Mark XVI). Thus he first received from the Lord the power to bind and loose, [Col. 1149A] and he first brought the people to faith through the power of his preaching.

The other apostles received honour and authority in equal fellowship with him, and wished him to be their chief. At the Lord’s command they too were scattered throughout the whole world and preached the Gospel. When they died, bishops arose in their places. Their ordination ought to be performed in the aforesaid order and manner. Whoever receives them and their words receives the Lord. But whoever despises them also despises him by whom they were sent and whose embassy they exercise; and he himself is unquestionably despised by the Lord.

When the apostles saw that the harvest was [Col. 1150A] plentiful and the labourers few, they asked the Lord of the harvest to send labourers into his harvest. Hence the seventy disciples were chosen by them; presbyters bear their type and were established in the Church in their place.

### CHAPTER LXXXIII. From the Decrees of Pope Clement, canon 30.

The bishop, indeed, said that he represented the apostles and was to teach the law of the Lord; he indicated that presbyters ought to hold the place of the remaining disciples; and he preached that whoever caused one of these to stumble would incur a most severe punishment. He instructed all to love and assist one another, and that no one should withdraw himself from giving assistance.

## ON THE CONTINENCE OF THOSE TO BE ORDAINED

[Col. 1149]

### CHAPTER LXXXIV. Acts of the second synod of Pope Stephen, canon 4: the Western, not the Eastern, Church made a vow of chastity.

[Col. 1149B]

(Distinction 31, canon *Aliter*.) The tradition of the Eastern Churches is one thing, that of this holy Roman Church another. Their priests, presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons enter into marriage. But throughout the whole Church of the West, none of the clergy, from subdeacon to bishop, has permission to contract marriage.

### CHAPTER LXXXV. At Paphnutius’s urging, the Nicene synod did not decree that presbyters should not sleep with their wives. *Tripartite History*, book II, chapter 14.

(Distinction 31, canon *Nicaena*.) The Nicene synod, wishing to correct the life of persons dwelling in the Churches, [Col. 1149C] established laws which we call canons. In discussing these, some thought it appropriate to introduce a law that bishops, presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons should not sleep with the wives whom they had married before consecration.

But the confessor Paphnutius rose and objected. Confessing marriage to be honourable and saying that chastity consists in intercourse with one’s own wife, he urged the council not to establish such a law, asserting that the matter was burdensome and would become an occasion of fornication either to the clergy themselves or to their spouses. Although Paphnutius himself had no experience of marriage, he set this forth; the synod praised his opinion and decreed nothing on this subject, but left it to each person’s will, not as a necessity.

### CHAPTER LXXXVI. Priests are to abstain from the embrace of their wives not permanently, but at the time of the offering. [Col. 1149D] Sixth Synod, canon 23.

(Distinction 31, canon *Quoniam*.) Since we have learned that the Roman canonical order transmits that those ordained deacons or presbyters confess that they will no longer have intercourse with their wives, we, following the ancient canon of apostolic diligence and the constitution of holy men, have decreed that lawful marriages are henceforth to remain valid. In no way are we dissolving their marriages with their wives or depriving them, at a fitting time, of mutual companionship.

Therefore anyone [Col. 1150B] found worthy of subdiaconal, diaconal, or priestly ordination is in no way to be forbidden to ascend to such a rank because he lives with his wife; nor is he to be compelled at his ordination to profess that he must abstain from intercourse with his lawful wife. Likewise: those who minister at the altar must be continent in all things at the time of the offering of the holy gifts, so that they may obtain from God what they simply ask. Therefore, if anyone presumes, contrary to the apostolic canons, to deprive any presbyter or deacon of contact and communion with his lawful wife, let him be deposed. Likewise, let a presbyter or deacon who dismisses his wife on account of religion be excommunicated. If he persists in this, let him be deposed.

### CHAPTER LXXXVII. Deacons are not to be barred from ministry on account of marriage, if at ordination they state that they cannot remain continent. [Col. 1150C] Council of Ancyra, canon 10, according to the second translation.

(Distinction 28, canon *Diaconi*.) Any deacons who, at their very ordination, have declared and said that they wish to enter marriage because they cannot remain thus, are to remain in their ministry if they subsequently take a wife, because the bishop gave them permission. But any who kept silent, received the laying on of hands, and professed continence, and afterwards became bound by marriage, must indeed cease from ministry.

### CHAPTER LXXXVIII. If deacons are chaste, they are not forbidden to be appointed to ministry. [Col. 1150D] Council of Toledo, canon 2.

It was decreed that deacons, if either unmarried or chaste, may be appointed to ministry even if they have wives.

### CHAPTER LXXXIX. One who has not promised chastity is not to be compelled to separate from his wife.

(Distinction 31, canon *Ante triennium*.) Three years ago the subdeacons of all the Churches of Sicily had been forbidden to have intercourse in any way with their wives, in the manner of the Roman Church. This seems to me harsh and unsuitable: that one who has not adopted the practice of continence and has not promised chastity should be compelled to separate from his wife and thereby—God forbid!—fall into worse conduct.

It therefore seems to me that, from the present day, all bishops should be told not to presume to make anyone a subdeacon [Col. 1151A] unless he has promised to live chastely. Thus, evils previously not voluntarily sought by a settled intention are not to be forcibly exacted, and future evils may cautiously be prevented. Those who, after the prohibition issued three years ago, have lived continently with their wives are to be praised and rewarded, and exhorted to remain in goodness. But we do not wish those who, after the prohibition was made, have refused to abstain from their wives to be promoted to sacred order, because no one ought to approach the ministry of the altar unless his chastity has been proved before he undertakes the ministry.

### CHAPTER XC. No one is to be made a subdeacon unless he promises to live chastely. [Col. 1151B] Leo IX, against the vice-abbot of the monastery of Stoudios.

(Distinction 28, canon *Nullum*.) Among us, no one is to be admitted even to the rank of subdeacon unless he professes perpetual continence, even from his own wife; nor is anyone permitted to take a wife after attaining that rank.

### CHAPTER XCI. A presbyter who takes a wife is to be deposed from his order. Council of Neocaesarea, canon 1.

(Distinction 28, canon *Presbyter*.) If a presbyter takes a wife, let him be deposed from his order. But if he commits fornication or enters into a second marriage, he must be expelled from the Church and reduced to penance among the laity.

### CHAPTER XCII. Priests are commanded always to preserve chastity. [Col. 1151C] Bede, on Luke, book I, chapter 2.

(Distinction 31, canon *Sacerdotibus*.) Priests are commanded to abstain from their wives and to preserve chastity always, so that they may always be able to stand at the altar.

### CHAPTER XCIII. Those who serve the divine sacraments ought to be continent. Second Council of Carthage, canon 2.

(Distinction 31, canon *Episcopos*.) It was decreed, as is fitting, that bishops, deacons, presbyters—the most holy prelates, priests of God, and Levites—or those who serve the divine sacraments, ought to be continent in all things.

### CHAPTER XCIV. Priests and Levites must not have intercourse with their wives. Innocent I to Victor, bishop of Rouen, letter 2, chapter 9.

[Col. 1151D] (Distinction 31, canon *Tenere debet Ecclesia*.) The Church must by every means maintain that priests and Levites do not have intercourse with their wives, because ministers of God are occupied with daily duties. For it is written: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Leviticus XI). In ancient times they did not depart from the temple of God during the year of their course, as we read of Zechariah (Luke I), nor did they at all visit their homes.

To them, indeed, marital intercourse had been relaxed for the succession of offspring, and because no one was commanded to approach the priesthood from another tribe or apart from Aaron’s seed [variant: “no one was permitted to approach”]. How much more must these priests or Levites observe chastity from the day of ordination, since their priesthood or ministry [Col. 1152A] has no succession and no day passes on which they are free either from divine sacrifices or from the office of baptism.

### CHAPTER XCV. Those abstaining from their wives are admitted to sacrifices. Innocent to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse.

(Distinction 31, canon *Eos ad sacrificia*.) It is lawful for those who do not perform the carnal act, even with a wife, to be admitted to sacrifices.

### CHAPTER XCVI. A priest, who must always pray, must always abstain from marriage. Jerome, *Against Jovinian*.

(Distinction 31, canon *Si laicus*.) If a layman, and indeed any believer, cannot pray unless he abstains from marital intercourse, a priest, for whom sacrifices must always be offered, [Col. 1152B] must always pray. If he must always pray, therefore he must always abstain from marriage.

### CHAPTER XCVII. A deacon is not to be ordained unless he has professed chastity. Pope Martin in the book of Martin, bishop of Braga, from Greek synods.

(Distinction 27, canon *Diaconus*.) If a deacon chosen has made a declaration regarding contracting marriage and has said that he cannot remain in chastity, he is not to be ordained. But if he is silent at ordination, is ordained, and afterward desires marriage, let him be excluded from ministry and cease from the clergy.

### CHAPTER XCVIII. A deacon living with his wife, or an incontinent presbyter, is to be removed from office. Pope Hormisdas to bishops throughout the provinces.

[Col. 1152C] (Distinction 1, canon *Si quis diaconus*.) If any deacon or presbyter, after receiving the Levitical blessing, is found incontinent with his wife, let him be removed from office.

### CHAPTER XCIX. A subdeacon must observe continence. Gregory to Boniface, bishop of Reggio, book III, letter 5.

(Distinction 32, canon *Subdiaconis tuis*.) We have decreed that what we have established regarding each of your subdeacons is to be observed, and you are not to permit our ruling to be violated by anyone’s obstinacy or rashness.

### CHAPTER C. Carnal marriage is forbidden to subdeacons. Innocent to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica.

[Col. 1152D] To display the purity of such complete continence, not even subdeacons are permitted carnal marriage; so that those who have wives may be as though they had none, and those who do not have wives may remain unmarried.

### CHAPTER CI. Those who have marital relations after the diaconate are to lose benefice and office. Urban II, in the synod at Meaux.

(Distinction 33, canon *Eos qui*.) Those who, after the diaconate, wish to engage in marital relations are removed by us from every sacred order; and we decree that they are to be deprived of office and ecclesiastical benefice. If, when admonished by the bishop, they do not correct themselves, we grant princes permission to reduce their women to servitude. But if bishops consent to their depravity, let them be punished by exclusion from their own office.

### CHAPTER CII. Those wishing to take a wife must do so before the order of subdiaconate. [Col. 1153A] Sixth Synod, canon 7.

(Distinction 32, canon *Si quis*.) If any of those approaching the clergy wish to be joined to a woman under the law of marriage, let them do so before the order of subdiaconate.

### CHAPTER CIII. Subdeacons and those thereafter are to be excluded from the dignity of their ranks if they refuse to be continent. Patriarch Dominic of Grado.

(Distinction 32, canon *Erubescant*.) Let the ungodly be ashamed and clearly understand us: by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, those established in the three sacred ranks of presbyterate, diaconate, and subdiaconate, who have not put away women and have not lived chastely, are excluded from the dignity of those same ranks. We speak, indeed, of manifest cases. [Col. 1153B] But God is the knower and judge of secret matters.

### CHAPTER CIV. No one is to approach sacred orders unless he is a virgin or of proven chastity. Urban II, in the synod at Meaux.

(Distinction 32, canon *Nemo*.) No one is to be permitted to approach sacred order unless he is either a virgin or of proven chastity, and has had, up to the subdiaconate, one wife who was a virgin.

### CHAPTER CV. Those in the three ranks are also to abstain from their wives. Council of Carthage, canon 4.

(Distinction 32, canon *Placuit*.) It was decreed that bishops, presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons, in accordance with earlier statutes, are also to abstain from their wives. If they do not do so, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office. The other [Col. 1153C] clergy, however, are not to be compelled to this, but ought to observe the custom of each individual church.

### CHAPTER CVI. Ministers of the altar are under the same law of continence as bishops and presbyters. Leo to Rusticus of Narbonne, letter 90, chapter 3.

(Distinction 31, canon *Lex continentiae*.) The law of continence for ministers of the altar is the same as that for bishops and presbyters. While they were laymen or readers, they were lawfully able both to take wives and to beget children; but when they attained the aforesaid ranks, what had been lawful for them ceased to be lawful. Therefore, in order that a carnal marriage may become spiritual, they must leave their wives and have them as though they did not have them, so that both the chastity of their marriages may be preserved and the acts of marriage may cease.

### CHAPTER CVII. Those in minor orders may take a wife unless prevented by a vow or religious habit. [Col. 1153D] Leo XI against Nicetas, abbot of Stoudios.

(Distinction 32, canon *Seriatim*.) Let us set forth in order and plainly what the holy Roman Church says concerning the ranks of clerics:

“Clerics—namely doorkeepers, readers, exorcists, and acolytes—if they are found outside a monastic vow and habit and do not wish to profess continence, are permitted to take a virgin as wife with priestly blessing. But they may not take a widow or a divorced woman, because for that reason they cannot thereafter be promoted to the subdiaconate; nor may a layman who has not taken a virgin as wife, or a man married twice, ascend to the clergy.

“If anyone of the aforesaid orders desires to approach the subdiaconate, he cannot do so [Col. 1154A] without his wife’s consent, so that their carnal marriage may thereafter become spiritual, no one compelling them. Nor afterward may the wife be joined carnally to her husband, nor may she marry anyone during his lifetime or after his death.”

### CHAPTER CVIII. Those outside sacred orders may take wives and receive their stipends externally. Gregory to Augustine, bishop of the English.

(Distinction 32, canon *Si qui vero sunt*.) If there are clerics established outside the sacred orders who cannot remain continent, they ought to take wives and receive their stipends externally.

### CHAPTER CIX. Canons of the Apostles, canon 27.

We command that those who enter the clergy unmarried may, if they wish, take wives—but readers [Col. 1154B] and singers only.

### CHAPTER CX. Clerics may not take a wife from another sect. Council of Chalcedon, canon 14.

(Distinction 32, canon *Quoniam in quibusdam*.) Since in certain provinces readers and psalmists have been permitted to take wives, the holy synod decrees that none of these may take a wife from another sect.

### CHAPTER CXI. Readers must either take wives or profess continence. Council of Carthage, canon 3.

(Distinction 32, canon *Lectores*.) When readers reach the years of puberty, they are to be compelled either to take wives or to profess continence.

### CHAPTER CXII. Women may not live with clerics except those who by a natural bond exclude every suspicion. [Col. 1154C] Council of Nicaea, canon 3.

(Distinction 32, canon *Interdixit*.) The holy synod has wholly forbidden any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone whatsoever in the clergy to have an introduced woman living with him, except perhaps a mother, sister, aunt, or such other suitable persons as escape suspicion.

### CHAPTER CXIII. A presbyter must not reject his own wife on the pretext of religion. Canons of the Apostles, canon 6.

(Distinction 28, canon *Si quis decuerit*.) Let no bishop or presbyter reject his own wife under the pretext of religion. If he rejects her, let him be excommunicated.

### CHAPTER CXIV. A presbyter should love his wife as a sister and flee from her as an enemy. [Col. 1154D] Gregory, book IV of the *Dialogues*.

(Distinction 32, canon *Presbyter*.) A certain presbyter governed a church entrusted to him with great fear of the Lord. From the time he received his order, he loved his presbytera—that is, his wife—as a sister, but guarded against her as an enemy. He never permitted her to approach him more closely, nor did he allow her any occasion to come near him; he had wholly cut off from her any familiar intercourse with himself.

For holy men have this characteristic: in order always to remain far from unlawful things, they often cut off even lawful things from themselves. Accordingly, lest this man incur guilt through her, he even refused to let her provide him with necessities.

### CHAPTER CXV. A bishop or presbyter must not cast off his own wife from his care. [Col. 1155A] Leo IX against Nicetas, abbot, concerning the teaching of Stoudios.

(Distinction 31, canon *Omnino*.) We absolutely confess that it is not lawful for a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or subdeacon to cast off his own wife from his care on account of religion. Rather, he should supply her with food and clothing, but should not lie with her carnally in the customary way. We read that the holy apostles acted thus, blessed Paul saying: “Do we not [Col. 1156A] have authority to lead about a sister, a woman, as do the brother of the Lord and Cephas?” (I Corinthians VIII).

See, foolish man: he did not say, “Do we not have authority to embrace a sister, a woman?” but “to lead about,” namely so that she might be supported by them from the remuneration of preaching; yet thereafter there was to be no further carnal marriage between them.

Ambrose, on Second Corinthians, chapter 116.

All the apostles, except John and Paul, had wives.

## ON THOSE ORDAINED SIMONIACALLY AND THEIR ORDAINERS

[Col. 1155]

### CHAPTER CXVI. A bishop purchasing or selling a benefice is to be suspended from ecclesiastical office and benefice. [Col. 1155B] From the Apostolic Canons, canon 30, title 3.

(1, question 3, canon *Si quis*.) Any bishop, presbyter, or abbot who obtains this dignity through money is to be deposed, together with his ordainer; he is to be cut off in every way from holy communion and is to be anathema, like Simon Magus at the hands of Peter.

### CHAPTER CXVII. One who ordains or is ordained for money is excluded from the priesthood. Third Council of Braga, canon 8.

(1, question [1], canon *Qui per pecuniam*.) Whoever, for conferring upon anyone a rank of priesthood, receives either any gift or a promise of a gift before he is ordained, or, even after he has been ordained, presumes to receive any compensation for this very thing—whether the one who gave or the one who received—shall, according to the judgment of the Council of Chalcedon, incur the penalty of his rank.

### CHAPTER CXVIII. A bishop who performs an ordination for money is condemned. Council of Chalcedon, canon 2.

(1, question 1, canon *Si quis episcopus*.) If any bishop, having received money, performs an ordination and reduces to a price an ordination which cannot be priced—whether he promotes a fellow bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone else numbered among the clergy, or, having received money, ordains an *oeconomus*, that is, a defender or *paromanarius*—whoever has devised this and is convicted is himself to incur the penalty of his rank. And one ordained in this manner is to receive no benefit from such disgraceful commerce and consecration, but is to be deprived both of the dignity and of the charge which he acquired through money. Moreover, anyone who acted as an intermediary in transactions so shameful and unlawful, if he is a cleric, is to fall from his own rank; if he is a layman or monk, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER CXIX. Those who sell or buy God’s gifts are alike condemned by God. Gregory, Homily 39 on the Gospels.

Christ drives sellers and buyers from the temple (Matthew XXI), because he condemns both those who confer the laying on of hands for a reward and those who endeavour to buy God’s gift. Likewise, sellers [Col. 1156B] in the temple are those who distribute for reward what is due to certain persons by right. For to sell justice is to observe it in return for receiving a reward. Buyers in the temple, however, are those who wish to render to their neighbour what is just, but despise the matter lawfully owed and buy sin by paying a price to patrons.

### CHAPTER CXX. What it is to sell doves. Gregory, Homily 4 on the Gospels, 40.

To sell doves is to give for reward, rather than for merit of life, the laying on of hands by which the Holy Spirit is given.

### CHAPTER CXXI. On the several kinds of simoniacs. Gregory, *Gospel Treatise*.

(1, question 1, canon *Sunt nonnulli*.) There are some who receive no monetary rewards for ordination and yet bestow sacred orders for human favour, seeking from this generosity only the recompense of praise. Such persons do not give freely what they received freely, because from the bestowed office of holiness they seek the coin of favour.

Therefore, in describing the just man, the prophet rightly says: “Blessed is he who shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isaiah XXXIII). He does not say, “who shakes his hands free from a gift,” but adds, “from every gift,” because one kind of gift comes through service, another through the hand, another through the tongue. A gift through service is improperly bestowed subjection; a gift through the hand is money; a gift through the tongue is favour. Therefore, one who confers sacred orders shakes his hands free from every gift when, in divine matters, he seeks not only no money but also no human favour.

### CHAPTER CXXII. Do not permit sellers or buyers of ecclesiastical honours to exercise any power of their order. Urban to Herman, bishop of Metz.

Do not permit those who sell or buy ecclesiastical honours, or married priests, deacons, and subdeacons, to possess any power of their ordination in the Church so long as they remain in their error.

### CHAPTER CXXIII. One who buys ecclesiastical benefices is shown also to buy churches. From the Decrees of Pope Paschal, canon 18.

(1, question 3, canon *Si quis autem*.) But whoever objects [Col. 1157A] that consecrations are not bought, but only the things themselves which come from consecration, is proved entirely foolish. For since a physical church, or a bishop, abbot, or anything of that sort, in no way flourishes without physical and external possessions—just as the soul does not live bodily without the body—whoever sells one of these, without which the other cannot be possessed, cannot avoid selling both.

Yet the sacred canon completely determines this rejection, when it forbids even a church’s steward or defender, or one subject to a rule, to be ordained for money, to such an extent that it strikes even the intermediaries with the sword of anathema.

### CHAPTER CXXIV. Those who do not exercise freely the grace received from God are sellers of doves. [Col. 1157B] From Bede’s Homilies on John, chapter 2.

(1, question 3, canon *Non solum*.) Not only are those sellers of doves and makers of God’s house into a house of commerce who, in conferring sacred orders, seek payment in money, praise, or honour; but so also are those who exercise, not with a single-minded intention but for the sake of any human recompense, a spiritual rank or grace in the Church which they received by the Lord’s gift. This is contrary to the saying of the apostle Peter: “Whoever speaks, let him speak as the words of God; whoever ministers, let him minister as from the strength which God supplies, so that in all things God may be honoured through Jesus Christ” (I Peter IV).

Therefore, whoever is such a person, if he does not wish to be removed from the Church at the Lord’s command, should remove these things from his actions, lest he make God’s house a house of commerce.

### CHAPTER CXXV. No mercy is to be extended to simoniacs in preserving their dignity. [Col. 1158A] Nicholas the Younger.

(1, question 1, canon *Erga*.) We decree that no mercy is to be shown toward simoniacs in maintaining their dignity. Rather, according to the sanction of the canons and the decrees of the holy Fathers, we wholly condemn them and decree by apostolic authority that they are to be deposed.

### CHAPTER CXXVI. On one ordained by a person whom he knows to be simoniacal. From the same source.

(1, question 1, canon *De caetero*.) Henceforth we decree that if anyone in the future permits himself to be consecrated by one whom he does not doubt to be simoniacal, both consecrator and consecrated are to incur an equal sentence [Col. 1158B] of condemnation. Both are to be deposed, perform penance, and remain deprived of their own dignity.

### CHAPTER CXXVII. On the several kinds of simoniacs. Nicholas, *Decrees*, canon 11.

(1, question 2, canon *Statuimus*.) Nicholas, bishop, to all bishops. We decree concerning the threefold heresy of simoniacs: namely, simoniacs who ordain or are ordained simoniacally; simoniacs ordained simoniacally by non-simoniacs; and simoniacs ordained non-simoniacally by simoniacs.

Simoniacs ordained simoniacally, or simoniacal ordainers, are to fall from their proper rank according to ecclesiastical canons. Simoniacs ordained simoniacally by non-simoniacs are likewise to be removed from the office wrongly received. But simoniacs ordained non-simoniacally by simoniacs, we mercifully permit, by the laying on of hands and according to the necessity of the time, to remain in office.

## ON THE PROFESSION OF HERETICS

[Col. 1157]

### CHAPTER CXXVIII. No one is to receive a repentant heretic unless the bishop of that place has reconciled him. [Col. 1157C] Pope Sylvester, *Decrees*, canon 2.

Pope Sylvester, sitting in a general synod, said: “We decree that no one shall receive a repentant Arian presbyter unless the bishop of that place has reconciled him and, with the most holy chrism, confirmed him through the episcopal laying on of hands by the grace of the Holy Spirit, which cannot be given by heretics.”

### CHAPTER CXXIX. The priests of heretics are not considered worthy of episcopal honours. Innocent, in the *Decrees*, to Alexander, bishop, canon 3.

(1, question 1, canon *Arianos*.) Innocent, bishop of Rome, to Alexander, bishop of Antioch: “Since we receive Arians and other plagues of this kind—when their lay members are converted to the Lord—under the form of penance and through sanctification by the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands, it does not appear that their clergy ought to be received [Col. 1158C] with the dignity of priesthood or of any ministry.

“For we allow them only valid baptism, received in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. We judge that they do not possess the Holy Spirit through that baptism or through those ministries, because when their founders departed from the Catholic faith, they lost the fullness of the Spirit which they had received. Nor can those who, through the faithlessness of their impiety, have lost the faith of the Lord give its fullness—which [Col. 1158D] operates especially in ordinations. Therefore it cannot be that we should judge their profane priests worthy of God’s honours, when we receive their lay people as imperfect, as I have said, under the form of penance, in order to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit.

“Your gravity should make known to your fellow bishops—either through a synod, if possible, or through the public reading of our letter—what you have so necessarily inquired about and what we have answered so plainly, so that it may be observed by the common agreement and earnestness of all fellow bishops.”

### CHAPTER CXXX. Those returning from heretics are to be reordained. [Col. 1159A] Innocent I to the bishops of Macedonia, letter 22.

(1, q. 7, c. *Per illicitam*; 1, q. 1, c. *Ventum*.) INNOCENT to the bishops RUFUS and EUSEBIUS:

“Those ordained by heretics have their heads wounded by that imposition of hands. Where a wound has been inflicted, a remedy must be applied by which health may be recovered. Yet the health which follows the wound cannot exist without a scar; and where the remedy of penance is necessary, there can be no place for the honour of ordination. For if, as it is written, ‘Whoever touches an unclean thing shall be unclean’ (Lev. 22), how can that be bestowed upon him which is accustomed to receive cleanliness and purity?

“But the Church maintains that one who has lost honour cannot confer honour, nor has the recipient received anything, because there was nothing in the giver which he could receive. We agree, and this is certainly true: what a person did not possess, he could not give. He did indeed give the condemnation which he possessed through a perverse imposition of hands; and how one made a participant in condemnation ought to receive honour, I cannot discover. Yet it is truly said that the true and righteous blessing of a lawful priest can remove every defect which had been imposed by one who was defective. If this is so, let sacrilegious persons, adulterers, and persons guilty of every crime be admitted to ordination; for it is thought that crimes or defects are removed by the blessing of ordination. Let there be no place for penance, since ordination can confer what prolonged satisfaction is accustomed to confer.

“Yet the law of our Church grants only lay communion through imposition of hands to those coming from heretics who were nevertheless baptized among them; and it appoints none of these, even to the least honour of the clergy.” [Col. 1159B–C]

## CHAPTER CXXXI. From Leo’s Decrees, chapter 6

Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to JANUARIUS, bishop, and to all persons of whatever rank:

“A cleric who, abandoning Catholic communion, has joined himself to heretical perversity, if he wishes to return to the Church and Catholic communion, must first unequivocally acknowledge that he condemns his errors and their very authors; he must speak fully and openly in written declarations signed by his own hand. Then he shall be received in the rank in which he was, without any promotion. He should nevertheless regard it as a great benefit if, all hope of promotion having been taken away, he remains permanently and securely in the order in which he is found—provided only that he has not been defiled by repeated baptism.

“He incurs no slight guilt before the Lord who judges that such persons ought to be promoted to sacred orders. If promotion, even after a great and serious examination, is granted to those free from blame, it is much less lawful to grant it to those under suspicion. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we command that henceforth all carefully observe what has both been commendably proposed and beneficially ordained for the welfare of the whole Church.” [Col. 1159D–1160A]

## CHAPTER CXXXII. From Cyril’s example, addressed to John of Antioch

“I profess, under the name [given above], in the writing which I have written with my own hand, that I follow the holy judgment of the 318 Fathers of the Synod of Nicaea, and the universal council of the Synod of Chalcedon, whose definition the Apostolic See confirmed, and which the letter of the most blessed Pope Leo, sent to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople of holy memory, set forth with the clearest proclamation of truth.

“I confess one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God the Father: the same perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity; true God and true man; the same consisting of a rational soul and flesh; consubstantial with the Father according to divinity, and the same consubstantial with us according to humanity, like us in all things except sin; begotten of the Father before the ages according to divinity, but in the last days, for our salvation, born of the Virgin Mary, who gave birth to the same God according to humanity.

“I confess one and the same Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, known in two natures without confusion, without change, without division, without separation; the difference of the natures having in no way been removed because of the union, but rather the property of each nature being preserved, converging into one person, not into two; one and the same Son, the only-begotten, true God, Lord Christ, as the prophets of old spoke concerning him, and as Christ the Lord himself taught us through himself.

“But those who do not think thus, I pronounce worthy of eternal anathema together with Nestorius and Eutyches, or their followers.” [Col. 1160B–C]

## CHAPTER CXXXII bis. An act performed by excommunicated persons cannot be called a consecration. Gregory to Maximus of Salona

An unheard-of crime is reported: after our prohibition, which was issued also under our excommunication and that of those ordaining you, you are said to have been brought forward publicly by military force, priests and deacons having been beaten. We can in no way call this thing a consecration, because it was performed by excommunicated persons. [Col. 1160D]

# CONCERNING THOSE WHO FALL AFTER THEIR ORDINATION

[Col. 1159]

## CHAPTER CXXXIII. Those fallen from sacred orders cannot be restored. Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, book III, letter 26

(Dist. 50, c. *Pervenit*.) It has also come to our attention that certain persons fallen from sacred orders are recalled to the duties of their ministry, whether after penance or before penance. We entirely forbid this, and in this matter the most sacred canons oppose it. Therefore, whoever, after receiving sacred order, has fallen into a sin of the flesh, shall so lose sacred order that he may no longer approach the ministry of the altar. [Col. 1160D–1161A]

## CHAPTER CXXXIV. Priests, deacons, or subdeacons living in the crime of fornication must not enter the church. Gregory to the Italians and Teutons

(Dist. 81, c. *Si qui presbyteri sunt*.) If there are any priests, deacons, or subdeacons lying in the crime of fornication, we forbid them, on the part of Almighty God and by the authority of St Peter, to enter the church until they repent and amend their conduct. But if any prefer to persist in their sin, let none of you presume to hear their office; for their blessing is turned into a curse, and their prayer into sin, as the Lord testifies through the prophet: “I will curse your blessings” (Mal. 7 [an OCR or citation error; cf. Mal. 2:2]).

Those who refuse to obey this most salutary command incur the sin of idolatry, as Samuel testifies and blessed Gregory teaches: “Disobedience is the sin of divination, and refusal to submit is the crime of idolatry” (1 Sam. 15). Therefore, whoever professes himself a Christian yet scorns to obey the Apostolic See incurs the sin of paganism. [Col. 1161A–B]

## CHAPTER CXXXV. The Mass of a priest who has a concubine must not be heard. Nicholas [Junior] and Alexander, book III, *On Those Who Have Fallen*

(Dist. 32, c. *Nullus*, and c. *Praeter*.) Let no one hear the Mass of a priest whom he knows without doubt to have a concubine or a woman secretly introduced into his household. Hence the holy synod itself established this chapter under excommunication, saying:

“Whoever among priests, deacons, or subdeacons, after the decree concerning clerical chastity made by our predecessor of blessed memory, the most holy Pope Leo, openly takes a concubine, or does not dismiss one whom he has taken, we command and forbid, on the part of Almighty God and by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, that he shall not chant Mass, read either Gospel or Epistle at Mass, remain in the presbytery at the divine offices with those who have been disobedient to the aforesaid constitution, or receive any share from the Church, until, God granting, a sentence upon such matters proceeds from us.” [Col. 1161B–C]

## CHAPTER CXXXVI. A person whose crime has been manifest cannot be restored to the priesthood. Nicholas to Charles, archbishop, and the Council of Worms

(Dist. 50, c. *Sacerdotes*.) If priests fall into the snare of fornication and the commission of their crime has been shown to be manifest, they cannot retain the honour of priesthood, according to the authority of canonical institution. [Col. 1161D]

## CHAPTER CXXXVII. Whoever has preferred pleasure to office must be removed by every means. Innocent to Exuperius of Toulouse

(Dist. 82, c. *Proposuistis*.) You have asked what ought to be observed concerning those who, placed in the ministry of deacon or office of priest, have been shown to be incontinent or to have begotten children. The discipline of the divine laws is clear on this matter, and the manifest instructions of Siricius, bishop of blessed memory, have issued: those placed in pontifical offices who are incontinent are to be deprived of every ecclesiastical honour and must not be admitted to a ministry which ought to be discharged by continence alone. [Col. 1162A]

## CHAPTER CXXXVIII. A bishop, priest, or deacon who takes a wife or retains one already taken is to be deprived of office and benefice. Alexander II to bishops and King Da[?]mat

(Dist. 81, c. *Si quis amodo*.) If henceforth any bishop, priest, or deacon takes a woman or retains one whom he has taken, let him fall from his proper rank until he comes to satisfaction; let him not remain in the choir of those chanting, nor possess any portion of ecclesiastical property. [Col. 1162A–B]

## CHAPTER CXXXIX. On the same matter. Alexander II to the same persons

(Dist. 81, c. *Si quis sacerdotum*.) If any priest, deacon, or subdeacon stubbornly abandons his office and chooses a woman for himself, then, just as he voluntarily abandons his office on account of fornication, so he must be compelled, even unwillingly, to relinquish his benefice on account of his transgression.

## CHAPTER CXL. On the same matter. Alexander II to the people of Milan

(Dist. 81, c. *Eos etiam*.) We also judge that those who have abandoned the divine office so that they may be permitted to fornicate, and who, departing from God, serve the devil and his works, ought, just as they most justly make themselves strangers to office, to be deprived of the benefices of the churches. [Col. 1162B–C]

## CHAPTER CXLI. Whoever falls after his ordination remains deposed. Pope Martin to Amandus

(Dist. 50, c. *Qui semel*.) Whoever once falls into transgression after ordination shall thereafter be deposed and shall be able to attain no rank of priesthood.

## CHAPTER CXLII. Gregory to Venantius, bishop of Luni

We decree that the deacon-abbot whom you judge to have fallen at Portus Veneris ought not, and cannot in any way, be restored to sacred order. You ought to assign him, deprived of sacred order, to penance. If thereafter his conduct and manner of life deserve it, let him obtain a place of precedence among the monks, wherever you have decreed it. The subdeacons likewise, whom the same fault binds, having been irrevocably deposed from their office, are to receive communion among the laity. At Portus Veneris, in the place of the fallen man, you shall ordain another deacon who ought to discharge this office. [Col. 1162C–D]

## CHAPTER CXLIII. A cleric convicted or confessing that he has committed adultery is to be confined in a monastery. Synod of Orléans, chapter 7; Third Council of Orléans

(Dist. 81, c. *Si quis*.) If any cleric confesses that he has committed adultery or is convicted of it, he shall be removed from his office and, communion being granted him, shall be confined in a monastery for the whole term of his life.

## CHAPTER CXLIV. On the same matter. Pelagius to Constantine, defensor

(Dist. 81, c. *Romanus*.) Romanus, a cleric of the Church of Thiana, has, because of the crime of adultery which he is said to have committed, been deprived of clerical rank and confined in a monastery here in the city of Rome, by your order, in order to perform penance. [Col. 1163A]

## CHAPTER CXLV. Those who have fallen cannot be restored to their order. Gregory to Constantine, bishop of Milan

(Dist. 50, c. *Si lapsis*.) If permission is granted to those who have fallen to return to their order, the force of canonical discipline is undoubtedly broken, since in hope of returning a person does not fear to conceive desires for wicked conduct. And shortly afterward: Make every effort to guard against this above all things: let no entreaty whatsoever persuade you to recall persons fallen in sacred order, lest the punishment of such persons be believed not to have been established, but merely to have been deferred for a time. [Col. 1163A–B]

## CHAPTER CXLVI. After a fall, a priest cannot for any reason be restored to sacred order. Gregory in the *Decretals*, to Sabinian, book VII, letter 25

(Dist. 50, c. *Presbyterum*.) Gregory to Sabinianus, bishop:

“Know that the priest concerning whom your brotherhood consulted us through the envoy’s mission cannot, after his fall, either remain in sacred order or be recalled to it for any reason. Yet he must be dealt with more leniently because of the crime committed, since he is said to have confessed readily of his own accord.” [Col. 1163B–C]

## CHAPTER CXLVII. This determines the contrary position and holds that those who have fallen may be restored. Gregory to Secundus, book VII, letter 53

(Dist. 50, c. *Quia sanctitas*.) Your Holiness requested that we write to you concerning rising again to priestly office after a fall. You say that you have read different canons on this subject, giving different judgments: some allowing restoration after a fall, others not at all.

For we, beginning generally with the Synod of Nicaea, venerate it together with the other four [councils], which, following it, agree unanimously in all their judgments. We follow these earlier Fathers, because by God’s authority we do not depart from their sacred teaching. Beginning from the head down to the fourth ministry of the altar, we know that this rule must be observed: just as the greater precedes the lesser in honour, so it is also in crime. The greater the fault that follows a person, the greater the punishment to which he is bound; and then penance is believed to be fruitful.

For what advantage is there in sowing wheat and not gathering its fruit, or building a house and not dwelling there? After worthy satisfaction, we believe that a person who has fallen can return to honour, as the Prophet says: “Will he who falls not rise again?” (Ps. 40 [citation as printed]); and: “Will one who has turned away not return?” (Jer. 8).

What is more serious: to commit a carnal offence, without which few are found, or to deny the Son of God on oath? Yet we know that the blessed prince of the apostles himself, Peter—at whose body we unworthy persons sit—fell into this sin. But repentance followed his denial, and pardon followed repentance, because Christ did not cast him out of the apostleship, though he had foretold that Peter would deny him.

Let these statements suffice for you, my son, so that, when you see someone wiping away his sins with tears, you may not doubt that he obtains mercy in the sight of the Godhead. For he who came to redeem sinners with his own blood despises no sinner who returns.” [Col. 1163C–1164A]

## CHAPTER CXLVIII. Clerics may be restored to their orders after a fall. Pope Calixtus in the *Decretals*, to the bishops of Gaul

[Col. 1164B] (Dist. 50, c. *Ponderet*, § *Errant*.) CALIXTUS, pope of Rome, to the beloved bishops established throughout Gaul:

“Those who think that the Lord’s priests, after a fall, cannot minister to the Lord or enjoy their honours if they have performed worthy penance, thereafter led a good life, and worthily preserved their priesthood, are mistaken. Those who hold this opinion not only err, but also seem to despise the keys entrusted to the Church, concerning which it was said: ‘Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven’ (Matt. 16). Otherwise, this statement either does not belong to the Lord or is not true.

“But we believe without hesitation that both the Lord’s priests and the rest of the faithful can return to honours after worthy satisfaction, as the Lord testifies through the Prophet: ‘Will he who falls not rise again?’ (Ps. 40); and: ‘Will one who has turned away not return?’ (Jer. 8). And elsewhere the Lord says: ‘I do not will the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live’ (Ezek. 18). Through the prophet David, while he was doing penance, he says: ‘Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a ruling spirit’ (Ps. 50).

“For David himself, after his penance, both taught others and offered sacrifice to God, giving an example to the teachers of the holy Church that, if they have fallen and have performed penance worthy of God, they may do both. For he taught when he said: ‘I shall teach transgressors your ways, and the ungodly shall turn to you’ (ibid.). He offered sacrifice for himself when he said: ‘A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit’ (ibid.). Seeing that his crimes had been cleansed by repentance, the Prophet did not hesitate to heal the faults of others by preaching, the Lord delivering him.

“The pouring out of tears restrains the passion of the soul; when satisfaction has been fulfilled, the soul is turned away from wrath. Where sins abound, mercy also abounds. For with God there is mercy, and with him plentiful redemption (Ps. 129). Let a person therefore be cleansed from sin; by the grace of God he rises from his fall and remains in his former office, in accordance with the authorities cited above. Let him see that he sins no more, so that the judgment of the Gospel may remain with him which says: ‘Go, and do not sin any more’ (John 8).

“Therefore, brothers, refuse not only to maintain but even to hear a judgment that forbids mercy, because mercy is greater than all burnt offerings and sacrifices.” [Col. 1164B–D]

## CHAPTER CXLIX. Who are to be restored after a fall, and when. Isidore to Massanus, bishop, chapter 1

(Dist. 50, c. *Domino*.) ISIDORE, bishop, sends greetings to the holy lord and brother, blessed in his merits, Bishop MASSANUS:

Your venerable brotherhood made known in letters that in chapter 19 of the Council of Ancyra it is read that, after a bodily fall, a rank of honour is to be restored after penance. Elsewhere, however, it is read that after such an offence the standing of the former order is by no means to be restored. This difference is resolved in the following way.

The canon commanded those to return to their former ranks whose penance had been preceded by satisfaction, or by a worthy confession of sins. Conversely, those who are neither corrected from the defect of corruption nor cease to defend with a certain superstitious rashness the very carnal offence which they commit receive neither the rank of honour nor the grace of communion.

The judgment must therefore be determined thus: those must necessarily be restored to the place of honour who deserve, through penance, to have received reconciliation from divine mercy. Those who are known through the amendment of penance to have received the remedy of life shall deservedly attain the rank of dignity formerly acquired.

Lest this be more ambiguous, the statement is confirmed by the authority of Scripture. The prophet Ezekiel, under the figure of faithless Jerusalem, shows that former honour can be restored after satisfaction in penance: “Be ashamed, O Judah, and bear your disgrace” (Ezek. 16). And shortly afterward: “You and your daughters shall return to your former state” (ibid.).

By saying “be ashamed,” he shows that after confession—that is, after the act of sin—a person ought to blush for the work of sin; and that after confession of crimes committed, he ought with a shamefaced countenance to cast himself upon the ground because he perpetrated a deed worthy of shame. Then he commands that, after disgrace and the lowering of one’s name or dignity, he return to his former state. Therefore, when someone is ashamed after the deed which caused his shame, and, bearing his disgrace, mourns his deposition with humility, he can, according to the prophecy, be recalled to his former condition.

Likewise, John the Evangelist wrote among other similar things to the angel of the Church of Ephesus: “Remember from where you have fallen, repent, and do the first works. Otherwise I shall come and remove your lampstand from its place” (Rev. 2).

See: so far as I have been able, I have explained by sacred testimonies the ancient judgment of the Council of Ancyra, plain and full of authority, showing that he can be restored in his own order who has learned through satisfaction in penance to mourn his own offences. But you should know that he who neglects and does not mourn what he has done, and commits shameful acts without any shame of religion or fear of divine judgment, cannot in any way be restored to his former rank.

At the end of this letter I thought it should be added that whenever a conflicting judgment is found in the acts of councils, the judgment of that council is to be maintained whose authority is older or more weighty. [Col. 1165A–1166A]

## CHAPTER CL. One who confesses having sinned before ordination must not offer sacrifice; one convicted, however, is to be deposed. Martin, bishop of Braga, from a Greek synod

(15, q. 8, c. *Si quis presbyter*.) If any priest has sinned before ordination and, after ordination, confesses the sins in which he had previously erred, he shall not offer [the Eucharistic sacrifice], but for the sake of religion he shall retain the name of priest. If, however, he does not himself confess but is publicly convicted by another, he shall not even retain the name of priest. The same is to be observed concerning deacons: if he himself has confessed, he shall retain the rank of subdeacon. [Col. 1166A–B]

## CHAPTER CLI. A priest who confesses that he fell carnally before ordination must not thereafter offer sacrifice. From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 1

(15, q. 8, c. *Qui admisit*.) If a priest, having previously committed a bodily sin, is promoted and confesses of himself that he sinned before receiving order, he shall not consecrate the offerings, though he remains in his other duties because of his good zeal. But if he has not confessed of himself and cannot plainly be charged, the matter shall be left to the judgment of his authority.

## CHAPTER CLII. Who can, or cannot, be restored after a fall. Rabanus, book *On Penance*, chapter 1

(Dist. 50, c. *De his vero*.) It seemed to us necessary to write concerning those who possess sacred orders and admit that they were defiled by capital crimes before or after ordination. In their case, as it seems to me, this distinction ought to be made: those who have been discovered or apprehended publicly in perjury, theft, fornication, and other crimes of this kind are to be deposed from their proper rank according to the provisions of the sacred canons, because it is a scandal to the people of God to have such persons set over them, persons known to be excessively vicious.

For by this means people are drawn away from the sacrifice of God, just as Eli is read to have acted of old toward his sinful sons (1 Sam. 2); and those rebellious and opposed become daily worse through their wicked examples. But those who confess, by a secret confession before the eyes of God, sins of the aforesaid kind committed secretly by themselves—while the priest who is to impose penance upon them also repents—and who lament that they have sinned grievously, or strive to cleanse themselves through fasts, almsgiving, vigils, and sacred prayers with tears: to these, while their rank is retained, hope of forgiveness is to be promised from the mercy of God. [Col. 1166C–D]

# CONCERNING A HOMICIDAL CLERIC

[Col. 1167]

## CHAPTER CLIII. After committing homicide, one cannot exercise priestly office. John VIII to the bishop of Le Mans [Coenomanensis], Utic[?]

(Dist. 50, c. *Miror*.) I am astonished that your insufficiently instructed learning thinks that a priest can minister in the priesthood after committing homicide—or, more absurdly, wishes to persuade us that we should assent to such presumption. For who, however merciful and however perversely minded, would decree such a thing, or grant it even after any amount of penance, when it is contrary to all canonical discipline? Therefore, deprived of priesthood, he ought to wash away so monstrous a crime with a fountain of tears, so that, healed at least by such remedies, he may find the aid of salvation. [Col. 1167A]

## CHAPTER CLIV. One who commits homicide accidentally is, by dispensation, to remain in his order. Urban II to Gwarnerius, bishop of Narbonne

(Dist. 50, c. *Clerico*.) A boy is said to have been killed by a stone thrown by a cleric. For love of God and of you, we permit him to remain in the same order, provided that he always remains in penance and in the fear of the Lord. [Col. 1168A]

## CHAPTER CLV. Stephen V to Sigebert, bishop of Corsica
