(Dist. 30, c. *Quia*.) You do well in regarding yourself as liable because, having been captured by Saracens, you appear to have killed men. But since you are known not to have killed voluntarily, you are in no way judged subject to canonical penalty on that account.

# CONCERNING USURY

[Col. 1167]

## CHAPTER CLVI. A cleric discovered to receive usury is degraded. Council of Elvira, chapter 20

(Dist. 47, c. *Si quis*.) If any cleric is discovered to receive usury, it is decided that he be degraded and abstain.

## CHAPTER CLVII. A deacon, priest, or bishop demanding usury is to be deposed unless he ceases. Apostolic Canons

(Dist. 47, c. *Episcopus*.) A bishop, priest, or deacon who exacts usury from debtors must either be condemned or cease and be deprived of communion.

## CHAPTER CLVIII. A cleric must not receive more than he lent. Council of Agde

(Dist. 14, q. 4, c. *Nullus clericorum*.) Let no cleric receive more than he has lent: if money, money; if goods in kind, goods in kind. Let him receive the same amount that he gave, and whatever else [he receives], only as much as he gave. [Col. 1167C]

## CHAPTER CLIX. For money lent, a cleric may receive goods in kind at a just price. Pope Martin, from the Council of Tarragona, chapter 2

(14, q. 4, c. *Si quis clericus*.) If a cleric, in a time of need, has lent a solidus, let him receive in wine or grain what, for purposes of trade, is decreed to be sold at the appointed time. But if he does not have the goods in kind which are needed, let him receive exactly what he gave, without any increase. [Col. 1168B]

## CHAPTER CLX. Whatever is exacted beyond what was given is usury. Jerome, book VI on Ezekiel

(14, q. 3, c. *Putant*.) Some think that usury exists only in money. But divine Scripture, foreseeing this, removes excess in every matter, so that you receive no more than you gave. Likewise, others customarily receive various sorts of little gifts in exchange for money lent at interest, and do not understand that whatever they receive beyond what they gave is called usury and excess.

## CHAPTER CLXI. When more than is owed is exacted, usury is received. Council of Agde, chapter 1

[Col. 1168C] (14, q. 1, c. *Usura*.) Usury exists where more is demanded than is given; for example, if you give ten solidi and demand more, or give one measure of grain and exact something additional.

## CHAPTER CLXII. One who buys cheaply in order to sell dearly pursues shameful gain

(14, q. 4, c. *Quicunque*.) Whoever, at the time of harvest or vintage, buys grain or wine not from necessity but out of greed—for example, buys a measure of wine for two denarii and keeps it until it can afterward be sold for four, six, or more—this we call shameful gain.

# CONCERNING SLAVES NOT TO BE ORDAINED

[Col. 1167]

## CHAPTER CLXIII. Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 82

[Col. 1167D]

If any slave, fleeing or hiding from his master, or by employing witnesses hired or corrupted with money, or by any cunning or fraud, attains ecclesiastical ranks, it is decreed that he shall be deposed and his master shall take him back.

But if a grandfather and father, migrating from one country to another, have begotten a son in that province, and that son, brought up there and promoted to ecclesiastical ranks, has been unaware whether he is a slave, and afterward his master comes and legally establishes his claim to him: if the master wishes to grant him freedom, he shall remain in his rank. But if the master wishes to draw him away from the camp of the Lord with the chain of slavery, he shall lose his rank. [Col. 1167D–1168D]

## CHAPTER CLXIV. If a slave secretly enters the priesthood, he is to be punished by loss of his peculium. Pope Gelasius to the bishops Maranus and Justus

(Dist. 54, c. *Ex antiquis*.) The agents of our son Amandus, an illustrious man, complain grievously that persons owing service to his legal authority have been ordained, some as clerics and some as subdeacons. Not only ought such persons not to have been admitted after the recent council—which is known to have been completed by an assembly of so many bishops, with the assent of all to its most beneficial provision—but even if any had previously, through ignorance, been admitted into the service of the divine army, they should altogether be dismissed and stripped of religious privilege, and by a just admonition compelled to return to their masters’ possessions.

Therefore, dearest brothers, examine those whom the agents of the aforesaid men identify as holding clerical office; and, if they are found to be detained persons liable to service, restore them without delay, observing the course of the laws. Thus, if anyone is already found to be a priest, he shall remain in that rank, suffering only the loss of his peculium. A deacon, however, shall either provide a substitute or, if he has none, be himself surrendered. Let the holders of the remaining offices know that no one convicted may be exempted from this liability, so that, this order being maintained, neither the rights of masters nor privileges may be disturbed in any respect. [Col. 1169A–B]

## CHAPTER CLXV. A slave made a cleric remains liable to slavery. Gelasius to Ercul[?], Stephen, and Justus, bishops

(Dist. 54, c. *Frequens*.) The agents of the illustrious woman Placida have complained in a petition that Sabinus, bishop of the city of Marcelliana or Clusium, taking advantage of the absence of their mistress, advanced Antiochus, a slave belonging by law to their patroness, as far as the honour of priesthood, and adorned his brother Leontius with the privilege of clerical office.

Therefore, dearest brothers, by our authority we entrust to you the inquiry into the charge between the aforesaid agents and those claimed as persons of lowest condition. After the truth of everything has been examined, if Leontius cannot by a valid defence remove the stain alleged against him, present him by every means to undergo the consequence of his legal status; his specified rank does not protect him under the laws.

Antiochus, however, because he can no longer be recovered [for servitude] through the priesthood, if his mistress wishes to place him in his own church in the rank which he now holds, she shall regard him not as restored to herself but as accepted for the performance of ministries. [Col. 1169B–1170A]

## CHAPTER CLXVI. When a slave is to be ordained, and when not. Constitution V, Novella 23

(Dist. 54, c. *Si servus*.) If a slave has been enrolled among the clergy with his master’s knowledge and without the master’s objection, by that very fact he becomes freeborn and free. But if the consecration was performed without the master’s knowledge, the master may prove the slave’s status and recover his own slave, but only within one year.

If, however, the slave has been ordained, whether with the master’s knowledge or without it, according to the provisions which we have stated, he earns freedom through the honour of clerical status itself. If afterward he abandons ecclesiastical ministry and returns to lay life, he shall be drawn back into slavery. [Col. 1170B]

# CONCERNING THE LIFE OF CLERICS

[Col. 1169]

## CHAPTER CLXVII. A bishop may not keep dogs for hunting. Council of Orléans, chapter 8

(Dist. 34, c. *Episcopum*.) It is not lawful for a bishop, priest, or deacon to have hunting dogs, hawks, or things of this kind. If any such person is repeatedly discovered indulging in this pleasure, then, if he is a bishop, he shall be deprived of communion for three months; a priest, for two months; and a deacon shall be suspended for one month from every office and from communion. [Col. 1169C]

## CHAPTER CLXVIII. Clerics who bear military arms are to be punished by loss of their rank. From the same council, chapter 18

[Col. 1169D] (24, q. 8, c. *Quicunque ex clero*.) Whoever appears to belong to the clergy must not take up military weapons or go about armed, but must demonstrate the name of his profession by religious conduct and religious dress. If they disregard this, then, as despisers of the sacred canons and profaners of ecclesiastical holiness, let them be punished by the loss of their own rank; for they cannot serve God and the world at the same time.

## CHAPTER CLXIX. A bishop or priest who consults magicians or diviners is to be deprived of honour. Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 30

(26, q. 5, c. *Si quis episcopus*.) If any bishop, priest, deacon, or other person in clerical orders is discovered to have consulted haruspices, diviners, augurs, lot-casters, those professing the magical art, or any persons practising similar arts, let him be suspended from the honour of his rank and undertake the care of a monastery. There, devoted to perpetual penance, he shall atone for the sacrilegious crime which he has committed. [Col. 1170C]

## CHAPTER CLXX. A deacon, priest, or bishop devoted to drunkenness and gaming is, unless he stops, to be deprived of communion. Apostolic Canons, chapter 13

(Dist. 35, c. *Episcopus*.) A bishop, priest, or deacon devoted to gaming or drunkenness must either stop or be deposed. A subdeacon, reader, or singer who does the same is to be deprived of communion; likewise a layperson. [Col. 1170D]

## CHAPTER CLXXI. Board games must be avoided. Augustine, Sermon on the Litany

Flee the game of the board, a luxury opposed to the salvation of the soul and a seedbed of sins, not only on these days but at all times.

## CHAPTER CLXXII. “Let him take himself.” Council of Carthage

(Dist. 46, c. *Clericos*.) We decree that clerics who are buffoons and jokers using obscene words are to be removed from office. [Col. 1171A]

## CHAPTER CLXXIII. A cleric who is a flatterer or traitor is to be degraded from office. From the same council

(Dist. 46, c. *Clericus*.) A cleric who is discovered to engage in flattery and treachery is to be degraded from office. [Col. 1172A]

# CONCERNING RELIGIOUS

[Col. 1171]

## CHAPTER CLXXIV. Monks living in cities ought to be subject to the bishop. Council of Chalcedon, chapter 3
(16, q. 1, c. *Qui vere.*) Those who truly and sincerely choose the solitary life are worthy of fitting honour. Yet since certain monks live indiscriminately throughout cities, and likewise establish monasteries, commending themselves on their own presumption, it has pleased us that no one shall build or establish monasteries or a house of prayer without the knowledge of the bishop of that city. Those who are in monasteries throughout the several cities or estates ought to be subject to the bishop, to devote themselves to peace, and to keep fasts and prayers in the places where they once devoted themselves to God, remaining there; nor are they to take part in ecclesiastical affairs or to undertake any secular business, leaving their own monasteries, unless perhaps they are commanded to do so by the bishop of that city because of urgent necessities. Nor is anyone’s slave to be received [Col. 1171C] into a monastery in order to become a monk with them, except with the owner’s own knowledge. We have decreed that those who transgress these provisions are outside communion, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed. It is therefore proper for the bishop of the city to extend necessary care and concern to the monasteries.

### CHAPTER CLXXV. Monks ought not to be among popular crowds. Jerome, to the presbyter Paulinus.

(10, q. 1, c. *Si cupis esse.*) If you wish to be what you are called—a monk, that is, one who is alone—what are you doing in cities? Cities are surely not dwellings of solitary persons, but of many. Each calling has its own leaders; and, to come to our own case, let bishops and presbyters have as their models the apostles and apostolic men, whose honours they possess, and whose merit they should strive to possess as well. But let us have as leaders of our calling the Pauls and the Anthonys, the Julians, the Hilarys, and the Macarii. Have the simplicity of the dove, so that you contrive deceit against no one; and the cunning of the serpent, so that you are not overthrown by the snares of others. There is little difference in fault between being able to deceive and being deceived. Whenever you find someone calling himself a Christian always or frequently talking to you about money—apart from almsgiving, which lies equally open to all—regard him as a merchant rather than a monk. Beyond food, clothing, and evident necessities, give nothing to anyone, lest dogs eat the children’s bread.

### CHAPTER CLXXVI. A monk has the office not of a teacher but of a mourner. Jerome, to the presbyters Riparius and Desiderius.

(16, q. 1, c. *Monachus.*) A monk does not have the office of a teacher but of a mourner: one who mourns either himself or the world [Col. 1172B], and awaits the Lord’s coming in fear. Knowing his own weakness and the fragile vessel that he bears, he should fear offending, lest he grow fat, fall, and be broken. Therefore he should especially avoid the sight of women, and above all of young women; and he should discipline himself so strictly that he fears even things that are safe.

“Why,” you ask, “do you go into the wilderness?” Plainly, so that I may neither see nor hear you, nor be stirred by your madness, nor suffer your wars. “So that the eyes of a harlot may not capture me, nor a most beautiful appearance lead me to unlawful embraces,” you will answer. This is not fighting but fleeing. Stand armed in the battle-line and resist your adversaries, so that, after you have conquered, you may be crowned. I confess my weakness. I do not wish to fight in hope of victory, lest I lose victory at some point.

### CHAPTER CLXXVII. Jerome, to the monk Rusticus.

[Col. 1172C]

To me a town is a prison, and solitude paradise. Why do we desire the throng of cities? What judgement do we make concerning this solitude? Moses, in order to preside over the Jewish people, was trained for forty years in the wilderness. A shepherd of sheep became a shepherd of human beings. The apostles passed from fishing on the Lake of Gennesaret to fishing for human beings. Then they had father, net, and little boat; when they followed the Lord, they immediately left everything, carrying their cross daily and not even having a staff in hand.

### CHAPTER CLXXVIII. Jerome, to the same person.

Do some work, so that the devil may always find you occupied. Thus the apostles, although they had the right [Col. 1172D] to live by the Gospel, worked with their hands so as not to burden anyone; and supplied relief to others, from whose prosperity they ought to reap material things. Why do you not prepare what will be needed for your own use? Every idle person lives amid desires. The monasteries of the Egyptians have this custom: they receive no one without work and labour, not so much for the necessities of livelihood as for the salvation of the soul, lest people wander among destructive thoughts and, like adulterous Jerusalem, spread their legs to every passer-by.

### CHAPTER CLXXIX. Monks should neither assume ecclesiastical duties through greedy ambition nor reject them through enticing idleness. Augustine, to Eustochius.

(16, q. 1, c. *Vos autem.*) But we exhort you, brothers [Col. 1173A], in the Lord to preserve your purpose and persevere until the end of life. If Mother Church should desire any service from you, neither undertake it in greedy pride nor reject it through alluring idleness; rather, obey God with a gentle heart and meekness, bearing him who governs us, who directs us meekly in judgement, and teaches the meek his ways. Do not place your leisure before the needs of the Church; for if, when she is in labour, no good persons were willing to minister to her, you would not find how you yourselves could be born.

### CHAPTER CLXXX. Deserters from monasteries should not be chosen for service in the clerical ranks. Augustine, to Aurelius, Letter 76.

(16, q. 1, c. *Ex his.*) From those who remain in the monastery, we are accustomed to admit into the clergy only the more proven and better men [Col. 1173B]. Otherwise, perhaps, as ordinary people say, “A bad flute-player makes a good *symphoniacus* [musician],” so the same common people will mock us by saying, “A bad monk makes a good cleric.” It is greatly to be lamented if we raise monks to such noisy arrogance and judge clerics—among whose number we are—to deserve such grave insult, when even a good monk sometimes scarcely makes a good cleric, if he has sufficient continence but lacks the necessary instruction or the integrity proper to his character.

### CHAPTER CLXXXI. The person whom his own community and the owner of the property request to be ordained should be made abbot, not an outsider. Pope Gregory.

[Col. 1173C] (18, q. 2, c. *Abbatem et quam sit,* § *Defuncto.*) When the abbot of any community has died, no outsider is to be ordained, but someone from the same community whom the united fellowship of brothers has chosen by its own free will; and the person chosen is to be ordained without deceit or any simoniacal payment. If they cannot find among themselves a suitable person, they shall diligently choose from other monasteries someone likewise to be ordained for them. Once an abbot has been appointed, no person is to be set over him for any reason, unless crimes exist—God forbid!—which the sacred canons show are punishable. Likewise it must be observed that monks ought not to be taken from a monastery against the abbot’s will for ordination in other monasteries, for sacred orders, or for clerical office.

### CHAPTER CLXXXII. The monastic commitment voluntarily undertaken cannot be abandoned. Leo, to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne.

(20, q. 3, c. *Propositum.*) A monastic commitment voluntarily undertaken by one’s own judgement or will cannot be abandoned without sin. For what anyone vows to God, that person must also fulfil. Hence, one who has abandoned the profession of solitude and descended into military service and marriage must be purified by the satisfaction of public penance. For although military service is innocent and marriage can be honourable, nevertheless it is a transgression to have abandoned the choice of better things.

### CHAPTER CLXXXIII. No one should become a monk before a probation of one year. Calixtus III, to Hugh of Trier and Theoderic of Verdun.

[Col. 1174A] (17, q. 2, c. *Nos,* § *Benedicti.*) The canonical rule of blessed Benedict—which is also the ordinance especially of our father and predecessor, St Gregory the pope—forbids anyone to become a monk before a probation of one year.

### CHAPTER CLXXXIV. No one should be admitted into a monastery before a probation of three years. From the Decrees of Boniface.

(17, q. 2, c. *Si aliquis.*) If an unknown person wishes to enter a monastery, the monastic habit shall not be granted to him before three years have passed. If, within three years, he is claimed by his owner as a slave, tenant, or freedman, he shall be returned to that owner with everything that he brought, provided a pledge of immunity from punishment has been given. But if he has not been claimed within three years, he cannot afterwards be claimed, unless he is so far away that he cannot be found; nevertheless [Col. 1174B] the slave’s owner shall receive the goods which he brought to the monastery.

### CHAPTER CLXXXV. A minor who enters a monastery cannot be reclaimed by his parents after a year. Council of Mainz, canon 20.

(C. 2, *On religious life and transfer to religion.*) If anyone has been tonsured before lawful age without the consent of his parents, and those parents have not protested within a year to the ruler, to the person’s own bishop, or to the lord’s representative, he shall remain in that clerical state, as was said above concerning the person in question. But if private persons make a claim within a year, they themselves, or their parents, shall discharge by law whatever obligation they have incurred against them. Whether the person tonsured before lawful age ought to remain in the same tonsure or not shall rest [Col. 1174C] in the parents’ power. If the tonsured person is anyone’s slave, whatever has been contracted against the owner with respect to that slave shall be made good to the owner by law. Whether the person tonsured remains in that tonsure shall be in the power of his owner. But if free persons, whether before or after lawful age, have been tonsured in the manner treated above and have attained ecclesiastical grades, they shall be compelled to remain in those grades. If, however, a slave tonsured in the manner specified above has attained ecclesiastical grades, compensation shall be made to his owner by law, and, once returned to him, the slave shall remain in his rank. This is also to be observed concerning girls who are veiled.

### CHAPTER CLXXXVI. Tonsure or religious dress assumed in childhood may be invalidated by parents. Council of Toledo, canon 6.

(20, q. 2, c. *Si in qualibet.*) If, while children are still minors, either one or both parents have given them, of either sex, the dress owed to the religious life or tonsure; or if, although the children were unwilling or unaware when they received it, the parents have not immediately rejected it when they saw it, but have allowed those children to retain such things before themselves, or before the bishop and publicly in an assembly, then it shall never afterwards be lawful for the children to return to secular dress. Once it is established that they have at any time had tonsure or religious dress, they shall immediately be recalled to the observance and habit of religion [Col. 1175A] and compelled to serve under the strict discipline of this observance.

Parents, however, shall have permission to give their children to religion only up to the fourteenth year of age. Afterwards, whether with parental consent or by their own devotion, the children may lawfully assume the observance of religion through a solitary vow [Col. 1176A]. Whoever is discovered to have committed transgression by removing tonsure or assuming secular dress shall receive the censure of excommunication and shall always adhere to religion.

## CONCERNING VIRGINS, WIDOWS, AND ABBESSES

[Col. 1175]

### CHAPTER CLXXXVII. Until twelve years of age, a girl is subject to her father’s will. Council of Tribur, canon 24.

(20, q. 2, c. *Puella.*) Virgins who, before the age of twelve, have placed the sacred veil upon their heads without the knowledge of their guardians (*mundiburdi*), and whose guardians have consented by remaining silent for a year and a day, shall remain in their holy commitment. But if those guardians lodge a claim for them within the said year and day, their petition shall be granted, unless the girls, perhaps touched by fear of God, remain in the religious habit with their permission.

### CHAPTER CLXXXVIII. From the Council of Carthage, canon 11.

When a consecrated virgin is presented to her bishop for consecration, she shall be brought wearing such garments as she will always use—garments suited to her profession and sacred life.

### CHAPTER CLXXXIX. The veil is imposed upon virgins only on specified days. From the Decrees of Gelasius, canon 21.

(20, q. 1, c. *Devotis virginibus.*) The sacred veil shall not be imposed upon devoted virgins except on Epiphany, during the Easter octave in white garments, or on the feast-days of the apostles [Col. 1175C]; nor before the age of twenty-five, unless, as has been said concerning baptism, they are seized by a grave illness and beg that this gift not be withheld, lest they depart from the world without it.

### CHAPTER CXC. Virgins are not to be consecrated before the twenty-fifth year. From the Decrees of Pope Pius.

(20, q. 1, c. *Virgines.*) Virgins are not to be veiled before the age of twenty-five, except perhaps where virginal chastity is endangered by necessity. Nor are they to be consecrated at another time than Epiphany, the Easter octave in white garments, and the feast-days of the apostles, unless the urgency of death requires it.

### CHAPTER CXCI. From the Decrees of Pope Pius and the Council of Milevis, canon 16.

[Col. 1175D]

Likewise, it has been decided that if any bishop veils a virgin below the age of twenty-five because virginal chastity is endangered, because a powerful suitor or some abductor is feared, or because she is troubled by the anxious danger of death lest she die un-veiled—whether at the request of her parents or of those to whose care she belongs—the provision made concerning this number of years shall not count against him.

### CHAPTER CXCII. She who has vowed virginity will incur condemnation if she marries. Jerome, to Lucian.

(Dist. 22, c. *Si nupserit.*) “If a virgin marries, she has not sinned.” This does not refer to the virgin who has once dedicated herself to the service of God; for if any one of these marries, she will incur condemnation because she has made her first faith void. If they object that this is said of widows, how much more does it apply to virgins; it will apply with greater force to those to whom marriage is not allowed even though it was once allowed to the others.

### CHAPTER CXCIII. Virgins who marry after consecration commit incest.

(Dist. 27, c. *Virgines.*) Virgins who marry after consecration are not so much adulteresses as incestuous women.

### CHAPTER CXCIV. An abbess who presumes to veil a virgin or widow is to be excommunicated. From the Decrees of Pope Eutychian, canon 13.

(20, q. c. *Statuimus.*) We have nevertheless found that in certain places there has been introduced a practice full of folly and contrary to ecclesiastical authority: namely, that some abbesses and certain consecrated women presume, against what is lawful, to impose a veil upon widows and virgin girls. Consequently, some women who have been unjustly veiled believe that they may more freely serve their carnal desires and fulfil their pleasures. Therefore we decree that, if after this definition an abbess or any consecrated woman proceeds to such audacity as to presume to veil either a widow or a girl, she shall be subjected to canonical judgement until she has made satisfaction.

### CHAPTER CXCV. Boniface the martyr, to Hildrivald, king of the English.

Among Greeks and Romans, a person would be regarded as having committed almost blasphemy against God if he were guilty in this matter: if, when specifically questioned before ordination about this sin, he were found guilty of having lain with a veiled and consecrated nun, he would be barred from every grade of God’s priesthood. Therefore, my son, one must carefully consider [Col. 1176D] how weighty this sin appears in the eyes of the eternal Judge: it places its perpetrator among the servants of idolatry and casts him out from the divine ministry of the altar, even if, after performing penance, he has previously been reconciled to God.

### CHAPTER CXCVI. From the Council of Rouen, canon 9.

(27, q. 1, c. *Viduas autem.*) It has been established that widows ought not to be veiled. Likewise it has been established that, if henceforth any presbyter proves to be a contumacious transgressor of this rule—namely, if he presumes to veil any widows, though this is not lawful even for bishops—he shall incur the peril of losing his rank. The same has been established concerning virgin girls: they are not to be veiled by presbyters. If anyone attempts to do this [Col. 1177A], he shall be condemned as a transgressor of the canons.

### CHAPTER CXCVII. Widows are in no way to be veiled. Pope Martin, in a council.

(27, q. 1, c. *Viduas autem.*) Let no pontiff attempt to veil widows, as is established in chapter 13 of the Decrees of Gelasius; neither divine authority nor the rule of the canons has granted this. If a widow has of her own will professed continence, however, she shall—as the intent of Gelasius is stated for her in his chapter 21—render an account to God. For, just as, according to the apostle, if she could not contain herself, she was by no means forbidden to marry, so, after deliberating with herself, she must keep for God the pledged faith of chastity. But we, supported by the authority of the Fathers, enact and freely judge in this sacred assembly that if she has voluntarily placed upon herself a veil, even though it was not consecrated, and has offered an oblation to God in the Church among the veiled women, whether she wishes it or not, she must thereafter retain the habit of sacred life—even if she seeks to confirm by oath that she put the veil upon herself with the intention and understanding that she might put it off again.

### CHAPTER CXCVIII. It is not lawful for widows, after receiving the veil, to depart from their sacred commitment. Council of Orléans, canon 3.

(27, q. 1, c. *Viduas quae.*) The holy synod decrees that widows who have received the sacred veil from the altar by their voluntary choice of sacred conversion shall remain in the same commitment. For we determine that it is not lawful that, after they have once consecrated themselves to God under the veil [Col. 1177C] and offered an oblation among the veiled women, they should again be permitted to lie to the Holy Spirit.

### CHAPTER CXCIX. A widow is not permitted to abandon her vow after professing continence. Nicholas, to Archbishop Charles.

(27, q. 1, c. *Vidua.*) A widow who has placed the sacred veil upon her head, prayed in church among the other veiled women, and offered an oblation with them, if she has professed that she will remain in the same habit, pledging never to remove the veil of religion, must not presume to depart from religious observance.

### CHAPTER CC. Widows who wish to marry should do so before professing continence. Augustine, *On the Good of Widowhood*.

[Col. 1177D] (27, q. 1, c. *Viduae.*) Widows who wish to practise continence should marry before they vow their profession of continence to God; if they do not fulfil that vow, they are rightly condemned.

### CHAPTER CCI. No one is permitted to violate a profession of widowhood made before the bishop, after the habit has been assumed. Council of Orange, canon 6.

(27, q. 1, c. *Viduitatis.*) We declare that a profession to preserve widowhood, made before the bishop in the secretarium, after widow’s dress has been put on before the bishop, must not be violated; and we decree that a woman who abandons such a profession is deservedly to be condemned.

### CHAPTER CCII. The manner and solemnity of making the profession shall be observed in this order. Council of Toledo, canon 5.

(27, q. 1, c. *Omnes.*) All women coming to sacred religion shall cover their heads with a mantle and make a written and confirmed profession—a document—after which they shall not be permitted to relapse into the audacity of transgression. Any of them found to have given either their will or their dress over to transgression shall incur sentence of excommunication; and, after their habit has again been changed, they shall remain confined in monasteries under the hardships of severe penance until they close their final day.

### CHAPTER CCIII. Widows and virgins cannot pass into marriage after undertaking the religious commitment. Gelasius, in the Decrees, to Sicily.

(27, q. 1, c. *Neque viduas.*) We do not permit widows to enter marriage after they have persisted for a long time in the observance of a religious commitment. Likewise, we forbid virgins to marry if they have spent many years of their lives in monasteries [Col. 1178B].

### CHAPTER CCIV. Concerning widows and virgins who depart from their religious commitment. Pope Gregory, to Boniface.

(27, q. 1, c. *Viduas a proposito.*) Concerning widows departing from their commitment to widowhood, about whom, dearest brother, your affection has consulted us: I believe you know that, according to St Paul and many holy Fathers, unless they return, they have long ago been condemned. We too judge that they must be condemned by apostolic authority and excluded from the communion of the faithful and from the thresholds of the church, until they obey their bishops and return, willingly or unwillingly, to the good which they began.

Concerning un-veiled virgins, if they go astray, we have the following decree from our predecessor Pope Innocent of holy memory: “Those who are not yet covered with the sacred veil, but have nevertheless always presented themselves as remaining in the commitment of virginity, although they have not been veiled, if they marry, must at some time perform penance, because their promise was binding before the Lord. For if, among human beings, a contract made in good faith is not customarily dissolved for any reason, how much more can a pledge contracted with God not be dissolved without punishment,” etc.

For if virgins not yet veiled are thus punished by public penance and excluded from the assembly of the faithful until they come to make satisfaction, how much more should widows—who are of more mature age and wisdom [Col. 1178D] and judgement, who have often experienced the company of men, have assumed the religious habit, and finally apostatized and returned to their former vomit—be removed by us and by all the faithful from the thresholds of the church and the assembly of the faithful until satisfaction, and handed over to prisons, in accordance with the blessed apostle Paul: “Hand such a person over to Satan, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord” (1 Cor. III). For concerning such persons the Lord speaks through Moses: “Remove the evil from your midst” (Deut. XIII). And through the Prophet he says: “The righteous shall rejoice when he sees vengeance upon the wicked; he shall wash his hands in the blood of the sinner” (Ps. LI). For it is said of such persons and of those like them who consent to them that not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those doing them, are guilty [Col. 1179A] (Rom. I).

### CHAPTER CCV. A woman who has pretended to be a consecrated woman may not marry. Nicholas, to Adalwin, archbishop of Vienne.

(Dist. 27, c. *Quod interrogasti.*) NICHOLAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy fellow-brother ADALWIN, archbishop of the holy Church of Vienne.—Concerning what you asked about a woman who, after the death of her husband, placed a sacred veil upon her head and pretended, under that veil, to be a consecrated woman, but afterwards returned to marriage: it seems good to me that, because she wished through hypocrisy to disturb the ecclesiastical rule and did not lawfully remain in her vow, she should do penance [Col. 1179B] for her wicked deception, return to what she promised, and remain in the sacred service which she began.

### CHAPTER CCVI. On the same matter.

(Dist. 27, c. *Nam si consenserimus.*) For if we agree that everyone may counterfeit all ecclesiastical sacraments as he wishes, rather than perform them truly, the entire ecclesiastical order will be disturbed; the ordinances of the Catholic faith will not stand, nor will the sacred canons be rightly observed. What advantage did it bring Simon Magus falsely to receive holy baptism and to pretend that he would remain in Christianity, when, through the apostle, his deceit was exposed and what would become of him was foretold? For he says: “May your money perish with you; for your heart [Col. 1179C] is not right before God. Therefore repent of this wickedness of yours, and pray to God that perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity” (Acts VIII). Therefore, unless such persons come to their senses, we judge that they should be struck with the spiritual sword. For it is not lawful to lie to the Holy Spirit, as Ananias and Sapphira lied and immediately perished (Acts V).

### CHAPTER CCVII. Those who violate the bodies of consecrated women are children of perdition. Council of Arles, canon 4.

(27, q. 1, c. *Sciendum.*) All must know that the bodies of women consecrated to God are temples consecrated to God through the vow of their own promise and the words of the priest, as is demonstrated by the testimonies of Scripture. Therefore those who violate them are known to be sacrilegious and, according to the Apostle, children of perdition [Col. 1179D] (2 Thess. II).

### CHAPTER CCVIII. The Apostle stated what sort of widows should be chosen (1 Tim. V).

“Command,” he says, “that widows be irreproachable; let a widow be chosen who is not less than sixty years old . . . having testimony in good works, if she has brought up children,” etc. “Avoid younger widows. For when they have become wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, incurring condemnation because they have made their first faith void; and at the same time they are idle . . . speaking what they ought not. Therefore I wish younger women to marry, bear children, be heads of households, and give the adversary no opportunity for reproach. For some have already turned aside after Satan.”

### CHAPTER CCIX. Abbesses professed according to the Rule of St Benedict shall live separately and shall not go out without their bishop’s permission. Council of Mainz, canon 13.

Abbesses, together with the consecrated women, we judge ought altogether to live rightly and justly. Those, however, who have made profession according to the Rule of St Benedict shall live apart. But if they live canonically, let them live fully under diligent care and supervision, remain in their cloisters, and have no departure outside. The abbesses themselves also shall remain in their monasteries and shall not go outside without the permission and counsel of their bishop.

### CHAPTER CCX. An abbess must exercise the greatest care over the nuns whom she takes outside. Council of Mainz, canon 26.

[Col. 1180B] An abbess shall by no means leave her monastery except with her bishop’s permission; and whenever she goes outside, she shall exercise the greatest care over the consecrated women whom she takes with her, so that no occasion for sin may be given them.

### CHAPTER CCXI. What an abbess’s care for consecrated women ought to be. Council of Grat., canon 8.

An abbess shall take diligent care of the community entrusted to her and ensure that the consecrated women are zealous in reading and the office, in the chanting of psalms; and she shall lead them in good works, since she will render an account for their souls before the Lord. She shall provide the consecrated women with necessary provisions [Col. 1180C], lest perhaps they be compelled to sin through want of food or drink.

### CHAPTER CCXII. Consecrated women shall not leave the monastery unless their abbess sends them because of urgent necessity. Council of Mainz, canon 14.

Consecrated women shall by no means leave the monastery, except perhaps when their abbess sends them because of some urgent necessity.

### CHAPTER CCXIII. A woman who changes her clothing for supposed continence and takes male attire shall be anathematized. From the Council of Gangra, canon 14.

If any woman, on account of what is thought to be continence, changes her clothing and, instead of the customary female dress, takes male attire [Col. 1180D], let her be anathema.

### CHAPTER CCXIV. What penalty is owed by a woman who cuts her hair. The same council, canon 17.

If any woman, for divine worship as she supposes, cuts off the hair which the Lord gave her as a reminder of subjection, thereby dissolving the commandment of obedience, let her be anathema.

### CHAPTER CCXV. The bishop ought often to visit monasteries of consecrated women. Council of Rouen, canon 3.

(18, q. 4, c. *Non semel.*) The bishop shall frequently enter the monasteries of monks and consecrated women and, sitting in their assembly with weighty and religious persons, shall carefully examine their life and [Col. 1181A] conduct; if he finds anything blameworthy, he shall diligently correct it. He shall also investigate closely the chastity of the consecrated women; and if any woman is found who, abandoning her purpose of holiness, shamelessly has intercourse with a cleric or layman, she shall be strictly restrained by beatings and shut up under private custody, where she may worthily repent of what she has done wrongly. It shall also be forbidden by the authority of the holy canons that any layman or cleric have access to their cloisters and [Col. 1182A] private dwellings; nor shall presbyters enter except only for Mass, and, once Mass has been completed, they shall return to their own churches. Let everyone be publicly and privately informed how great is the danger incurred by one who presumes to defile the bride of Christ. For if one who violates a human being’s bride is held guilty, how much more does one who corrupts the bride of almighty God become guilty of majesty?

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1181]

Concerning the primacy of the Roman Church; the right of metropolitans and bishops; their ordination; and episcopal exaltedness.

### CHAPTER I. Concerning the privileges granted by Emperor Constantine to Pope Sylvester. From the constitution of Emperor Constantine.

From the testament of our Constantine, we grant to the holy apostles themselves, my lords, the most blessed Peter and Paul; through them, to our father Sylvester, supreme pontiff and pope of the universal city of Rome; and to all his successor pontiffs who shall sit in the see of blessed Peter until the end of the world. We presently confer the Lateran palace of our empire, which is preferred to and surpasses all palaces throughout the whole world; then the diadem, that is, the crown of our head; likewise the *phrygium*, and also the shoulder-band, that is, the *lorum* which customarily encircles the imperial neck; moreover [Col. 1181C] the purple cloak, scarlet tunic, all imperial vestments, the rank of imperial magistrates and horsemen, imperial sceptres, all standards, and the various imperial ornaments; indeed, all the distinction of imperial majesty and the glory of our power.

For the most reverend clerics serving in the various orders of that same most holy Roman Church, we decree that they shall possess that singular height of power and pre-eminence by which our most ample senate is seen to be adorned with glory: namely, that they be made patricians and consuls, decorated with the other imperial dignities, and appointed to them. And just as the imperial military service is organized, so we have decreed that the clergy and the holy Roman Church shall be ordered.

Likewise, in the same place: The most blessed pope did not permit himself to use a crown of gold upon the crown which he wears for the glory of blessed Peter. But we placed with our own hand upon his most sacred head the *phrygium*, gleaming with white brilliance and signifying the Lord’s resurrection; and, holding his bridle out of reverence for blessed Peter, we performed for him the office of groom. We decree that all his successors shall use this same *phrygium* distinctively in processions, in imitation of our empire. Therefore, lest the pontifical summit become cheapened but rather be adorned even more abundantly than the dignity and glorious power of earthly empire, behold: we assign and leave over both our palace, as stated above, and the city of Rome, and all provinces, places, and cities of Italy and the western regions to the oft-mentioned most blessed pontiff, our father Sylvester, universal pope [Col. 1182B], and to the authority and dominion of his pontifical successors, to be administered by the firm imperial sanction of this our divine, sacred, and pragmatic constitution. We grant that they shall remain by right of the holy Roman Church.

Therefore we have judged it appropriate that our empire and royal power be transferred and moved to the eastern regions, and that in the province of Byzantium a city bearing our name be built in a most suitable place, and that our empire be established there. For where the primacy of priests and the head of the Christian religion has been established by the heavenly Emperor, it is not just that an earthly emperor should hold power.

### CHAPTER II. The Roman Church received primacy not from the apostles but from the Lord himself. Anacletus, in the Decrees, Letter 3 to bishops.

(Dist. 25, c. *Sacrosancta.*) ANACLETUS, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops and the other priests of Christ, greeting.—The most holy Roman and Apostolic Church obtained primacy not from the apostles but from the Lord our Saviour himself, as he said to the blessed apostle Peter: “You are Peter,” and the rest (Matt. XVI). Therefore this Apostolic See, the hinge and head of all Churches, was established by the Lord and by no other; and just as a door is governed by its hinge, so, by the authority of this holy See, all Churches are governed as the Lord disposes [Col. 1182D]. Accordingly, if more difficult cases arise among you, refer them, as it were, to the summit of this holy See as to their head, so that they may be concluded by apostolic judgement.

### CHAPTER III. No synod but Christ established the primacy of the Roman Church. Gelasius, in the Decrees, canon 1.

(Dist. 21, c. *Quamvis.*) GELASIUS, bishop of the city of Rome, to all bishops. Although the Churches throughout the world are one bridal chamber of Christ, the holy Roman Church, Catholic and Apostolic, has been set above the other Churches by no synodical enactments, but has received primacy by the Gospel utterance of our Lord and Saviour: “You are Peter,” says the Lord, “and upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matt. XVI). It also received as its companion the most blessed apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, who, not at a different time, as heretics babble, but at one and the same time and on one and the same day, striving at Rome under Caesar Nero, was crowned with a glorious death together with Peter. Together they consecrated the aforesaid Roman Church to Christ the Lord and, by their presence and triumph, set it above all churches in all cities throughout the world. Thus the first see of the apostle Peter is the Roman Church, having neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of the sort [Col. 1183B].

### CHAPTER IV. In the Decrees of Anacletus, canon 3.

(Dist. 22, c. *Sacrosancta,* § *Prima.*) Therefore, by heavenly favour, the first see is the Roman Church, which, as has been mentioned, the most blessed Peter and Paul consecrated by martyrdom.

### CHAPTER V. The first see is subject to no one’s judgement. Innocent, in the Decrees.

(9, q. 3, c. *Nemo.*) Pope Sylvester, sitting in a general synod, said: “No one shall judge the first see when it desires to administer justice. For it shall be judged by no one: neither by the emperor, nor by all the clergy, nor by kings, nor by the people.”

### Chapter VI. Inferiors may not take cognizance of the cases of superiors. [Col. 1183C] Nicholas to the Emperor Michael, in the Decretals, ch. 1.

NICHOLAS, servant of the servants of God, to his most pious and beloved son MICHAEL, ever Augustus, beloved of God.

Now, by divine inspiration, it will neither weary us nor be impossible for us to show you—if only you are willing to hear—that no one can rightly be subjected to judicial determinations by persons of lower rank or order. For in the time of the Augusti Diocletian and Maximian, Marcellinus, bishop of the city of Rome, who afterwards became a distinguished martyr, was so compelled by pagans that, entering their temple, he placed grains of incense upon the coals. On account of this deed, after a council of numerous bishops had assembled and an inquiry had been made, that pontiff himself confessed that he had done it. Yet none of them dared to pronounce sentence upon him, while all repeatedly said to him: “Judge your own case by your own mouth, not by our judgment.” And likewise: “Do not submit yourself to be heard in our judgment, but gather your case into your own bosom.” And again: “For by yourself,” they say, “you shall be justified, or by your own mouth you shall be condemned.” And again they say: “The first see shall be judged by no one.”

Likewise, in the same source: “But when, at a certain time, some persons attempted to bring certain accusations of ill repute against Pope Sixtus, and it had been said in the council at which the Emperor Valentinian was present that it was not lawful to pronounce sentence against the pontiff, the emperor himself immediately rose and entrusted to the judgment of the aforesaid pontiff the judging of his own case. For no pontiff of the lesser or inferior cities is found subject to the judgments of his own acts.”

### Chapter VII. Superiors cannot be condemned by the judgment of inferiors. Nicholas to the same person, from the same chapter.

(Distinction 21, ch. *In tantum*.) Likewise, in the same source. The holy Fathers at Chalcedon so abhorred this presumption that they condemned Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, without any restoration, chiefly for this among other reasons: because, setting his mouth in heaven and his tongue passing over the earth, he pronounced excommunication against holy Pope Leo. Thus, in the sentence issued against him, they seem especially to mention this, saying that the second offense greatly surpassed the former iniquity: “For he presumed to pronounce excommunication against the most holy and most blessed Archbishop Leo of the great Roman Church.”

Was an inquiry made into whether Dioscorus had pronounced that excommunication justly or unjustly? Certainly not. Rather, without any controversy, he was punished for this: though inferior, he attempted to assail one superior to himself with every kind of injury. Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, bears witness to this, saying: “Dioscorus was not condemned on account of the faith, but because he excommunicated Lord Archbishop Leo.”

### Chapter VIII. The first see judges the cases of others. Pope Symmachus, in Synod V, in the book of Eunod[ius].

(9, question 3, ch. *Aliorum*.) God perhaps willed that the cases of other men should be decided by men; but He reserved the bishop of this see, without question, for His own judgment. He willed that the successors of blessed Peter should owe their innocence to heaven alone, and should preserve an unviolated conscience for the scrutiny of the most subtle controversy [variant: of the most subtle examiner].

### Chapter IX. On the same matter. Gelasius, bishop, to the Dalmatians.

(9, question 3, ch. *Cuncta per mundum*.) GELASIUS, bishop, to all. The whole Church throughout the world knows that the most holy Roman Church has the lawful right to judge concerning every Church; nor is it permitted to anyone to judge concerning its judgment. For appeals may be made to it from any part of the world, but no one is permitted to appeal from it.

### Chapter X. No one is permitted to judge what the pope has decreed or to revoke his sentence. Pope Nicholas to the Emperor Michael.

(17, question 4, ch. *Nemini*.) NICHOLAS, pope, to all bishops. No one is permitted to judge the judgments of the Apostolic See or to revoke its sentence, clearly because of the primacy of the Roman Church divinely conferred by Christ’s gift upon the blessed Apostle Peter.

### Chapter XI. The judgment of the Apostolic See is not to be revoked by anyone. [Col. 1185A] Nicholas to the Emperor Michael.

(9, question 3, ch. *Patet profecto*.) It is certainly clear that the judgment of the Apostolic See, than whose authority there is none greater, is not to be revoked by anyone, nor is anyone permitted to judge concerning its judgment. In accordance with this, Pope Boniface writes to Rufus and the other bishops established throughout Thessaly:

“No one has ever boldly raised hostile hands against the Apostolic summit, from whose judgment it is not lawful to appeal; nor does anyone become rebellious in this matter except one who has wished to be judged concerning himself.” And blessed Pope Gelasius says: “The canons have never commanded that the judgment of that same Church—that is, the Roman Church—should be judged, nor have they established that its sentences ought to be dissolved; rather, they commanded that its decrees should be followed.”

### Chapter XII. In the Decretals of Pope Julius, ch. 2.

(9, question 3, ch. *Cuncta*.) JULIUS, bishop of the Apostolic See, to all bishops. The most holy Roman Church has, by a singular privilege granted to it, the power to open and close the gates of the heavenly kingdom for whom it wills.

## On Synodal Councils

[Col. 1185]

### Chapter XIII. Two assemblies are to be held each year by the bishops. [Col. 1185B] Pope Leo to Anastasius of Thessaly, epistle 6.

(Distinction 18, ch. *De conciliis*.) Concerning episcopal councils, we decree nothing other than what the holy Fathers beneficially ordained: that two assemblies be held each year, in which judgment shall be rendered concerning all complaints that commonly arise among the various orders of the Church. But if perhaps a case concerning grave offenses should arise among those who preside themselves—may this not happen!—which cannot be determined by provincial examination, the metropolitan shall take care to inform your fraternity of the character of the entire affair, so that, if the matter has not been settled by your judgment in the presence of the Fathers, whatever it may be shall be referred to our cognizance.

### Chapter XIV. No synod may be assembled without the authority of the Roman pontiff. [Col. 1185C] Isidore, ch. 8.

(Distinction 17, ch. *Synodum episcoporum*.) The authority for convening synods has been entrusted by a special power to the Apostolic See; nor do we read that any general synod has been valid which was not convened or supported by its authority. Canonical authority bears witness to this, ecclesiastical history confirms it, and the holy Fathers affirm it.

### Chapter XV. For the correction of morals and the settlement of controversies, an episcopal council is to be held twice yearly.

(Distinction 18, ch. *Propter*, first section.) For ecclesiastical advantages, concerning matters that admit doubt and controversy, it has seemed most fitting that councils of bishops should be held twice yearly in every province. The first is to be held after the third week following the feast of Easter, so that in the following fourth week—that is, in mid-Pentecost—the synod may assemble, the metropolitan having summoned the bishops of his province.

### Chapter XVI. On the same matter. Council of Antioch, ch. 16.

(Distinction 18, ch. *Propter*, § “The second, however.”) The second synod shall be held on the Ides of October, that is, on the fifteenth day of October, which the Greeks skilled in winter weather call *hyperberetaios* [uncertain reading]. At these councils the presbyters, deacons, and all who consider themselves injured shall be present and shall undergo the examination of the synod.

### Chapter XVII. Until the next synod, a bishop summoned by the metropolitan who neglects to attend the synod without grave necessity shall abstain from communion. Council of Agde, ch. 35.

(Distinction 18, ch. *Si episcopus*.) If a metropolitan bishop sends letters to the bishops of his province inviting them either to the ordination of a brother or to a synod, they shall not delay to be present on the appointed day, setting aside all other matters except grave bodily illness or some royal command. If they are absent, then, as the ancient authority of the canons commanded, they shall be deprived of the fellowship of their brethren and of communion with the Church until the next synod.

### Chapter XVIII. A bishop summoned by the metropolitan who scorns to come to a synod shall be deprived of communion. [Col. 1186C] Council of Clermont, ch. 15.

(Distinction 18, ch. *Si quis episcoporum*.) Any bishop who, except for an unavoidable cause or necessity connected with the holding of a council, absents himself shall be deprived of communion for one year.

### Chapter XIX. A person oppressed by grave necessity shall send a representative to the synod in his place. From the Decretals of Pope Felix, epistle 2 to the bishops of Gaul.

(5, question 1, ch. *Si aegrotans*.) If a bishop is ill, or some grave necessity detains him, he shall send a representative to the synod in his place, accepting, without prejudice to the truth of the faith, whatever the synod decrees.

### Chapter XX. On the precedence of a metropolitan and a primate. Council of Chalon, ch. 6.

(Distinction 18, ch. *Placuit*.) Likewise, it was resolved that the other metropolitans, preserving the primacy of the metropolitan bishop, should yield place to one another according to the date of their ordination.

### Chapter XXI. From the Council of Auvergne.

First, it was resolved that whenever the holy synod assembles according to the statutes of the Fathers, no bishop shall dare first to bring forward any case, until matters pertaining to amendment of life, the strictness of the rule, and the remedy of souls have been concluded. [Col. 1187A]

### Chapter XXII. Examples from Pope Boniface to the bishops of Gaul.

If a dispute arises among bishops of the same council concerning ecclesiastical law or other affairs, their metropolitan, after considering the matter in council with certain others, shall first pronounce judgment. If both parties do not acquiesce in his judgment, then the primate of the region shall be heard between them; and whatever accords with the ecclesiastical canons and our laws shall be done, and neither party shall dare to oppose his decision. [Col. 1188A]

## How Provinces Are to Be Constituted

[Col. 1187]

### Chapter XXIII. What obedience is to be shown to primates and patriarchs.

[Col. 1187A]

(Distinction 19, ch. *Provinciae*.) Provinces were for the most part divided long before the coming of Christ; and afterwards that division was renewed by the apostles and by blessed Clement, our predecessor. In the chief cities of the provinces—where formerly the primates of secular law and the foremost judicial authority existed, to whom those dwelling throughout the remaining cities resorted when necessary, if they could not or were not permitted to flee to the court of emperors or kings, and to whom they appealed, whenever need required, concerning their oppressions or injustices, as was prescribed in their law—the divine and ecclesiastical laws commanded that patriarchs or primates, who have one and the same form though their names differ, should be established in those same cities or places. Bishops, if necessary, should have recourse to them and appeal to them; and those cities, and no others, should enjoy the title of primacies.

The remaining metropolitan cities, which had lesser judges, although these were greater than counts, were to have their own metropolitans, who should rightly obey the aforesaid primates, just as had been ordained in secular law. These should enjoy not the title of primates, but that either of metropolitans or archbishops. And although individual metropolitan cities have their own provinces and ought to have their own metropolitan bishops, just as they formerly had metropolitan secular judges, nevertheless, as stated above, they were commanded then and are commanded now to have primates. To them, after the Apostolic See, the most important affairs are referred; there those in need are relieved and justly restored; those who unjustly oppress are rightly reformed and supported; and the cases of bishops and the judgments of the highest affairs are most justly concluded, with the authority of the Apostolic See preserved. [Cols. 1187B–1188B]

### Chapter XXIV. How many cities each province has. Pelagius in the Decretals, ch. 1.

(6, question 3, *Scitote*.) PELAGIUS, pope of Rome, to all bishops. Know that a province properly consists of ten or eleven cities, one king, an equal number of subordinate authorities under him, one metropolitan, and ten or eleven suffragan bishops as judges. All cases are to be referred to their judgment and decided by all of them with concordant voice, unless an appeal is made by the persons to be judged to a higher authority. Therefore no province ought to be degraded or dishonored; rather, each should have within itself its priestly judges and bishops, each according to his order. Whoever has a case shall be judged by the judges of his own province and not by outsiders, unless, as has already been stated, an appeal has been made by those being judged. [Col. 1188C]

## On the Dignity and Power of Primates and Archbishops

[Col. 1187]

### Chapter XXV. None are to be called primates except those who hold the primary sees. [Col. 1187D] Pope Anicetus to the bishops of Gaul.

(Distinction 99, ch. *Nulli*.) No archbishops are to be called primates except those who hold the chief cities, whose bishops the apostles and successors of the apostles have regularly established as patriarchs and primates—unless some people should thereafter be converted to the faith, for whom it is necessary to establish a primate because of the multitude of bishops. Those, however, who have acquired other metropolitan sees are not to be called primates, but metropolitans.

### Chapter XXVI. No metropolitan may presume to conduct the cases of others without a council of the bishops of his province.

(19, question 3, ch. *Si autem aliquis*.) If any metropolitan becomes puffed up and, without the presence of all the provincial bishops or their counsel, wishes to deal with their cases or other cases—except only those pertaining to his own parish—or to burden them, he shall be sternly corrected by all, lest he dare to presume such things thereafter. But if he appears incorrigible and disobedient to them, his contumacy shall be reported to this Apostolic See, to which the determination of all bishops’ judgments has been committed, so that punishment may be exacted from him and the rest may fear.

But if, because of excessive distance, inconvenient conditions, or the hardship of the journey, it is burdensome to bring his case to this See, then the case shall be referred to his primate and judged by him under the authority of this holy See. [Col. 1188D]

### Chapter XXVII. No primate or archbishop may excommunicate anyone from another’s parish. [Col. 1189A] Pope Calixtus, epistle 2, to the bishops of Gaul.

(19, question 3, ch. *Nullus primas*.) No primate or metropolitan shall presume to excommunicate, judge, or take any action concerning the church or parish of a diocesan bishop, or anyone belonging to his parish, without that bishop’s counsel or judgment. Rather, they shall observe what has been established by the apostles, Fathers, and our predecessors, and confirmed for us: namely, if any metropolitan bishop attempts to do anything outside the affairs pertaining solely to his own parish without the counsel and consent of all the bishops of his province, he shall be subject to peril to his rank, and what he has done shall be held void and without effect. [Col. 1189B]

### Chapter XXVIII. It is not lawful to act in another’s parish unless summoned by him. Celestine to the bishops of Gaul.

(9, question 3, ch. *Nullus*.) No primate, no metropolitan bishop, and none of the other bishops may enter another’s city or approach an estate that does not belong to him, nor may anyone administer, ordain, or judge in another bishop’s parish contrary to that bishop’s direction, unless summoned by the one to whose jurisdiction it is known to belong—if he wishes to retain the honor of his rank. If he presumes otherwise, he shall be condemned, and not he alone, but also those cooperating with and consenting to him; for, just as ordination, so also his judgment and the administration of other matters are forbidden. [Cols. 1189B–1190A]

### Chapter XXIX. A metropolitan shall do nothing in a suffragan’s parish without his counsel. Nicholas to Radulf, Archbishop of Bourges.

(19, question 3, ch. *Conquestus*.) Our brother Sigedodus, Archbishop of Narbonne, has complained to our Apostolic See that you compel his clerics to come before your tribunal against his will, and that, without consulting him, you dispose of matters belonging to his Church as though by right of your patriarchate. Neither antiquity, to which the holy Fathers decreed reverence, permits this, nor does the authority of the sacred canons allow it at all—unless perhaps they have appealed to you as their patriarch concerning cases which they cannot determine among themselves, or unless, after their bishop has died, they wish you to administer the goods of their Church by your judgment.

For we determine that primates or patriarchs have no privilege beyond other bishops except insofar as the sacred canons grant it and ancient custom has conferred it upon them, so that, according to the Nicene rules, churches preserve their privileges—unless the Apostolic See has decreed to honor a church or its ruler with some episcopal privilege. [Col. 1190B]

## On the Affairs and Cases of Clerics

[Col. 1189]

### Chapter XXX. No cleric may enter a secular court on account of any case. [Col. 1189C] From the Decretals of Sylvester, ch. 10, in the Roman Synod.

(11, question 1, ch. *Nullus clericus*.) No cleric, deacon, or presbyter may enter a court on account of any case, nor presume to plead a case before a girded judge, since every court is, as it were, named from bloodshed. If any cleric accusing a cleric enters a court, let him incur anathema.

### Chapter XXXI. No cleric may be summoned before a secular judge except with the permission of his own bishop. Marcellinus, pope, in the Decretals, ch. 2.

(11, question 1, ch. *Clericum*.) MARCELLINUS, bishop of Rome, to all bishops. A cleric of any order shall not presume, without his own pontiff’s permission, to bring anyone before a secular judgment; nor is a layperson permitted to accuse any cleric. [Col. 1189D]

### Chapter XXXII. No cleric is to be brought before a secular judgment. Cornelius in the Decretals, ch. 2.

(11, question 1, ch. *Continua*.) CORNELIUS, bishop, to RUFUS, fellow bishop. No priest shall commit his case to a foreign judgment unless an appeal has been made to the Apostolic See. Rather, each shall have judges from his own province and known to him, unless he fears violence from a reckless multitude or has judges hostile or suspect to him. For these reasons it is permitted to appeal and resort to judges of higher authority and to other provinces. [Col. 1190C]

### Chapter XXXIII. A case is to be heard only within the province and by fellow-provincials. Stephen in the Decretals, ch. 2.

(3, question 6, ch. *Ultra*.) STEPHEN, bishop, to all bishops. The right of accusation shall not proceed beyond the boundaries of provinces. Every accusation shall be heard within the province and determined by provincial bishops, unless an appeal has been made solely to the Apostolic See.

### Chapter XXXIV. How one wishing to accuse a priest ought to proceed. Anacletus to the bishops of Italy, epistle 2.

[Col. 1190D] (2, question 7, ch. *Accusatio*, § “But if anyone.”) ANACLETUS, bishop of the city of Rome, to all bishops.—If anyone is stirred up against pastors or their churches, or has cases against them, let him first have recourse to them in a spirit of charity, so that, admonished in private conversation, they may heal what must be healed and amend in charity what they recognize should justly be amended. But if anyone, before doing this, presumes to attack, accuse, or harass them, let him be excommunicated and by no means absolved until, through fitting satisfaction, he has performed penance; for injury to them concerns Christ, whose embassy they exercise.

### Chapter XXXV. Whoever complains privately against a bishop before meeting him personally shall be deprived of communion. [Col. 1191A] Alexander in the Decretals, ch. 1, epistle 1.

(2, question 7, ch. *Si quis erga*.) ALEXANDER, bishop of the Apostolic Church, to all orthodox believers: If anyone believes himself to have any complaint, however just, against a bishop or the administrators of a church, he shall not first approach primates or other judges. Rather, he shall meet personally with those by whom he thinks himself injured—not once, but very often—so that he may receive from them an explanation satisfying his claim of justice. If he acts otherwise, let him be deprived of communion both by them and by others, as one who despises the apostles and the other Fathers.

### Chapter XXXVI. The people ought not rebuke or reproach a priest. [Col. 1191B] Pope Pius, epistle 1, to bishops.

(6, question 1, ch. *Oves pastorem*.) Let sheep not reproach their shepherd; let the people not accuse their bishop; let the populace not rebuke him, for “a disciple is not above his master” (Luke 6). Bishops are to be judged by God, who chose them as eyes for Himself. For they are not to be reproved, accused, or attacked by subjects or by persons of corrupt life.

### Chapter XXXVII. Laypersons are not to be admitted in accusations against bishops.

(2, question 7, ch. *Non est a plebe*.) Therefore a bishop is not to be reproved or accused by common people, even if he is disorderly; for the life of rulers is ordered in accordance with the merits of their subjects.

### Chapter XXXVIII. Examples from Pope Calixtus, ch. 1.

[Col. 1191C]

Teachers, therefore, who are also called Fathers, are to be borne with rather than reproved, unless they have erred in the true faith.

### Chapter XXXIX. Sheep ought not accuse their shepherd unless he has departed from the faith. [Col. 1192A] Pope Eusebius to the bishops of Alexandria, epistle 2.

(2, question 7, ch. *Oves suo pastori*.) The sheep entrusted to their shepherd ought not reproach him unless he has departed from the true faith, nor can they accuse him in any way; for the acts of shepherds are not to be struck with the sword of speech, even though they may appear rightly deserving of reproof.

### Chapter XL. Examples from Pope Anacletus, written to all priests of Christ, ch. 1.

(From chs. *Si haereticus* and *Quod dicitur*, 29, question 7.) A teacher departing from the faith is to be corrected by the faithful; but for blameworthy conduct he is rather to be endured than rigorously dealt with, since the rulers of the Church are to be judged by the Lord, as the Prophet says: “God stood in the assembly of gods; but in the midst he judges gods” (Psalm 81 [82]).

### Chapter XLI. Sheep ought not accuse their shepherd unless he has departed from the faith. Fabian in the Decretals, ch. 2.

(2, question 7, ch. *Oves*.) FABIAN, bishop, to all bishops. By apostolic authority we decree and command that the sheep entrusted to their shepherd shall not dare to reproach him unless he has erred in the faith. But if he has strayed from the faith, he shall first be corrected privately by his subjects. If he appears incorrigible—may this not happen!—he shall be accused before his primates or before the Apostolic See.

But in regard to his other actions, he is rather to be endured by all, even by those subject to him, than accused or publicly disparaged. For when subjects offend against such rulers, they oppose the ordinance of Him who has borne with them; as the Apostle says: “He who resists authority resists the ordinance of God” (Romans 13). [Cols. 1192B–C]

## On the Restoration of Those Despoiled

[Col. 1191]

### Chapter XLII. Bishops despoiled of their sees are forbidden to be summoned to judgment. Zephyrinus to the bishops of Egypt, in the Second Decretal.

It has been reported to the Apostolic See through your *apocrisiaries* [envoys] that certain of our brethren—namely bishops—are being driven from their churches and their own sees, their household goods are being taken from them, and they are then summoned to judgment naked and despoiled. This lacks every rational basis, since the enactments of the apostles and their successors, the commands of emperors, and the constitutions of laws forbid precisely this practice. [Col. 1191D]

### Chapter XLIII. No despoiled person may be accused until first restored. Zephyrinus to the bishops of Egypt, epistle 2.

(2, question 2, ch. *Praeceptum est*.) It has therefore been commanded in the ancient enactments that bishops expelled and despoiled of their property should recover their own churches and first have all their possessions restored to them. Only then, if anyone wishes justly to accuse them, let him do so at equal risk. The judges are to be bishops of sound judgment, meeting in the Church, where there are witnesses for each of those who appear to have been oppressed.

Likewise: they ought not answer before all their goods have been restored most fully, in accordance with the laws, to them and to their churches. [Col. 1192C]

### Chapter XLIV. Before restoration, no one ought to be summoned to a case. Felix I to the bishops of Gaul, epistle 2.

[Col. 1192D] (3, question 2, ch. *Si episcopus*.) If a bishop has been despoiled of his own goods or of the goods of the church entrusted to him, or—may this not happen, for it ought to be foreign to all believers—has been expelled from his own see, or has been confined in some detention by his fellow citizens, then he shall first be restored canonically to his former condition, with every privilege of his office. All that has been taken from him through the plots of his enemies shall be restored in full according to law. He may not be summoned or judged unless he himself freely chooses, because of his own necessity, to come—yet not to be judged.

Therefore he shall in no way be compelled by anyone before everything which he had lost through the instigations of his enemies has been restored, by lawful procedure, to his control by an honorable council.

### Chapter XLV. One who has been despoiled ought neither to be summoned to a synod nor judged in any matter. [Col. 1193A] Eusebius to the bishops of Alexandria and Egypt, epistle 2.

(2, question 2, ch. *In scripturis*.) Pope Eusebius, in his second decretal: “In your writings we find that some bishops in your regions have been accused by their own sheep, some on suspicion and others on definite grounds; that some have consequently been despoiled of their goods and others driven from their own see. You should know that they cannot be summoned either to a provincial or to a general synod, nor judged in any matter, before all that has been taken from them has been fully restored by law to their control.”

### Chapter XLVI. On the same matter. Julius I, ch. 1.

[Col. 1193B] (2, question 2, ch. *Nullus potest*.) Likewise, a person who has been despoiled or expelled cannot be summoned to a case or judged, because, once stripped, he does not possess the privilege by which he may be despoiled.

### Chapter XLVII. Before the joining of issue, everything must be restored to the possessor. Pope John.

(2, question 2, ch. *Antiquitus*.) Therefore it was decreed in ancient times that, before the joining of issue, the superior or primate should restore to the possessor all possessions, everything taken from him, and all their fruits. Likewise: it is decreed in the ancient statutes of the Church that one who seizes another’s property shall not go unpunished, but shall restore everything with multiplication.

Therefore it is written in the Gospel: “If I have defrauded anyone, I restore fourfold” (Luke 17 [the printed citation appears incorrect]). And secular laws provide: “Whoever steals another’s property shall restore elevenfold to the person whose property has been plundered all that was taken.” [Col. 1193C]

### Chapter XLVIII. Before restoration, no one ought to be summoned to a case. Pope Felix to the bishops of Gaul, epistle 2.

(3, question 2, ch. *Si episcopus*, § “The prelate, however.”) The prelate shall be restored to his former status with every honor. Then, having freely and securely arranged and ordered his own affairs, he shall come in due course, within four, five, six, or seven months according to his means—and not earlier—when summoned for the time assigned by a lawful and canonical council, to answer the case; and, if this appears just, he shall answer the allegations of the accusers. [Col. 1194A]

### Chapter XLIX. No one ought to be accused while despoiled of his goods. From the Decretals of Pope Felix.

(2, question 2, ch. *Nullus episcoporum*.) No bishop who has been despoiled of his goods or violently or fearfully driven from his own see may, before everything taken from him has been restored according to law, before he has peacefully enjoyed his offices for a year or more, and before he has been regularly restored to his own see, be accused, judged, or condemned according to the institution of the canons. [Col. 1194B]

### Chapter L. After restoration, a period of respite must be granted. Eusebius to the bishops of Alexandria and Egypt, Second Decretal.

(3, question 2, ch. *Prius*.) First, therefore, all things must be fully restored to them according to law, and the churches taken from them restored with every privilege. Afterwards, not within a narrow period, but with a period of time granted to them equal to that during which they appear to have been despoiled or expelled, they may be summoned to a synod and heard by all the bishops of their province.

### Chapter LI. In the Decretals of Felix, ch. 10.

One who has been driven from his see by force, terror, or fear, or despoiled of his goods, shall not be summoned to a synod before all things have been fully restored to him according to law. [Col. 1194C]

### Chapter LII. After restoration, a period of respite must be granted.

(3, question 2, ch. *Tandiu*.) And for as long as he appears to have been deprived of his goods while expelled or despoiled, he shall remain in his own see peacefully and with authority, administering all things.

## On Accusations

[Col. 1193]

### Chapter LIII. An accusation must not be made in writing. [Col. 1193D] Stephen in the Decretals, ch. 2.

(2, question 8, ch. *Per scripta nullus*.) STEPHEN, bishop of the holy apostolic and universal Roman Church, to all bishops. No accusation against anyone shall be accepted in writing, but only in the accuser’s own voice, provided that the accuser is a lawful and qualified person, and in the presence of the person whom he wishes to accuse; for no absent person can accuse or be accused through another.

### Chapter LIV. Persons absent can neither be accused nor judged. Felix I to the bishops of Gaul, epistle 2.

(3, question 9, ch. *Absente adversario*.) FELIX, bishop, to all bishops. When the opposing party is absent, the accuser shall not be heard; nor shall a sentence pronounced by a judge while the other party is absent possess any validity. Nor can an absent person accuse or be accused through another. [Col. 1194D]

### Chapter LV. An accusation must not be made in writing. Council of Carthage, ch. 60; Pope Calixtus, ch. 2.

(2, question 8, ch. *Per scripta*.) Therefore no teacher shall be accused in writing. We decree that no credence be given to an accuser who brings forward a case while the opposing party is absent, before both parties have been heard.

### Chapter LVI. In criminal cases, an accuser or accused person must appear personally. Pope Adrian, ch. 1.

(5, question 7, ch. *Quaerendum*; 5, ch. *Si plures*, § *De accus.*; 3, ch. *In criminalibus*.) In criminal cases, an accuser may accuse no one except in person, nor is an accused person permitted to defend himself through another person.

### Chapter LVII. Persons of greater age may not accuse unless they are of sound faith and conduct. [Col. 1195A] Felix to the bishops of Gaul, Decretal 2, epistle 2.
