(2, question 7, ch. *Quaerendum*; 50, ch. *Si plures*, § *De accus.*) If both sides have come to plead the case, since one ought not be heard without the other, inquiry must be made at judgment as to the conduct, faith, and suspected character of the accusers, and with what intention they act. For they must not be admitted unless they are men of good conduct and sound faith, entirely free from suspicion, distinguished by good life, and not infamous.

### Chapter LVIII. Priests can be accused only by suitable and proven men. Anacletus to the bishops of Gaul, epistle 2.

[Col. 1195B] (2, question 7, ch. *Accusatio quoque*.) The accusation concerning which you have wished to consult us must be made only by suitable and most thoroughly proven men, free both from suspicions and from secular crimes. For the Lord did not wish the ministers of His sacred body to be defamed or calumniated by contemptible, rejected, or unsuitable persons; rather, He Himself drove sinful priests from the temple with His own scourge.

### Chapter LIX. Unless their reputation has been examined, accusers of bishops are not to be heard. Evaristus to the bishops of Africa, epistle 2.

(2, question 7, ch. *Si qui sunt*.) If there are detractors or accusers of bishops or other priests, they ought not be heard by judges of the Church before suspicion concerning their reputation or standing has been examined: with what intention, faith, rashness, life, conscience, and merit they have presumed these things—whether for God, vain glory, enmity, hatred, or some other greed. [Col. 1195C]

### Chapter LX. A person who voluntarily transgresses his own law cannot accuse those acting rightly before his return. Anacletus in the Decretals, epistle 1, *On Oppressed Bishops*.

(3, question 4, ch. *Beatus*.) ANACLETUS, bishop of the city of Rome, to all bishops. The right to accuse or testify shall be denied to those who have neglected the dignity of the Christian religion and name, and the norm of their own law or their own profession, or matters regularly prohibited. For voluntary transgressors and violators of their own law are called apostates. Every apostate is to be rejected and may not be admitted either to accuse those acting rightly or to give testimony.

### Chapter LXI. Neither clerics in accusations against laypersons nor laypersons in accusations against clerics are to be admitted. Fabian to the bishops of the East, ch. 2, Decretal epistle 2.

(2, question 7, ch. *Sicut sacerdotes*.) FABIAN, bishop, to all bishops of the city of Rome. Just as priests and the remaining clerics are excluded from accusation by secular laypersons, so laypersons are to be excluded and kept apart from accusations by clerics; and just as clerics are not admitted by laypersons, so laypersons are not admitted by clerics. For, just as the conduct of the Lord’s priests ought to be separate from their conduct, so also should litigation be; since “the servant of the Lord ought not to quarrel, but to be gentle toward all.” [Col. 1196A]

### Chapter LXII. Enemies cannot accuse. Stephen II in the Decretals.

(3, question 5, ch. *Accusatoribus*.) Let associates of enemies and all laypersons be rejected, because the attachment of friendship is accustomed to incite slanderous harassment. Nor are those laypersons to be admitted to our accusation who wish to receive you into their own defamation.

### Chapter LXIII. Heretics, Jews, or pagans cannot accuse Christians. Pope Gaius, in the Decretals, ch. 1.

(2, question 7, ch. *Pagani*.) GAIUS, pope, to Bishop FELIX. Pagans, heretics, and Jews cannot accuse Christians or bring a charge of defamation against them.

### Chapter LXIV. A person who fails on the first count is not admitted on the others. [Col. 1196B] Seventh Council of Carthage, ch. 3.

(3, q. 10, c. *Placuit*.) It has been decided that whenever many charges are brought by accusers against clerics, and they are unwilling to prove one of those on which they first proceeded, they shall thereafter not be admitted to the others.

CAP. LXV. Recent enemies may not be accusers or witnesses. Fabian in the *Decretals*, ch. 2.

(3, q. 5, c. *Accusatores*.) POPE FABIAN, to all the faithful. We decree that those who are suspect, or who were enemies yesterday, the day before yesterday, or long ago, are not to be admitted to make an accusation, since they have become suspect; nor those whose conduct is not good, whose life is blameworthy, or who are doubtful in the right faith. Likewise, those whose faith, life, and free status are unknown, or who are stained by marks of disgrace or entangled in crimes. Nor should, or can, those accuse priests who cannot rightly become priests and are not of their order. Dearest brethren, prohibit, insofar as you can, such accusations and unjust or novel rivalries, because contention must especially be avoided.

CAP. LXVI. Which persons are to be considered infamous. Stephen in the *Decretals*, epistle 1, ch. 1.

(6, q. 1, c. *Infames*.) STEPHEN, bishop of the holy Roman Church, to his most beloved brother and familiar friend HILARY. We call infamous those persons who are marked by infamy for some fault; and all who reject the rule of Christian religion and law and despise ecclesiastical ordinances. Likewise thieves, sacrilegious persons, and all entangled in capital crimes; violators also of tombs, and those who willingly violate the ordinances of the apostles and their successors and of the other holy Fathers; and all who take arms against the Fathers, since throughout the world they are marked by infamy. Likewise, the incestuous, murderers, perjurers, kidnappers, evildoers, poisoners, adulterers, deserters from public wars, those who seek to hold positions unworthy of them, or unjustly take away the property of the Church; those who calumniate or accuse brethren and do not prove their charges; those who provoke the minds of rulers to anger against the innocent; all who have been anathematized or expelled from the Church for their crimes; and all whom ecclesiastical or holy laws pronounce infamous. All these, indeed, as well as slaves before lawful emancipation, penitents, bigamists, those who serve the civil curia, those not physically whole, those who do not possess a sound mind or understanding, those disobedient to the decrees of the holy Fathers, and those manifestly insane: none of these may anywhere be advanced to sacred orders, nor may they lawfully be admitted in any way to accusation or testimony.

CAP. LXVII. The accused, unless they have first cleared themselves, cannot accuse others. From the *Decretals* of Pope Stephen to bishops, epistle 2.

[Col. 1197B] (3, q. 11, c. *Neganda primo*.) Accused persons must be denied permission to bring criminal charges before they have freed themselves from the crime with which they are pressed. For their confession against others is not to be believed when they themselves have been charged with crimes, unless they have first proved themselves innocent. For the declaration of an accused person against anyone is dangerous and ought not to be admitted. Persons closely involved, those who confess voluntarily, and those entangled in crimes ought not to be admitted; nor those who were enemies yesterday or before.

CAP. LXVIII. From book IX of the same laws.

Certainly, those who have confessed their own crimes under examination, if they wish to speak thus concerning others, are not to be believed by the judge; for right and law establish that, by a voluntary confession, an accused person does not make another accused, nor is one who has confessed himself criminal to be believed concerning another.

CAP. LXIX. The declaration of an accused person against anyone must not be admitted. Pope Julius in the *Decretals*, epistle 18.

(15, q. 3, c. *Nemini*, and *De accusat.*) No one’s confession concerning himself can be believed regarding another’s crime, because the declaration of such a person—and of every accused person—is dangerous and ought not to be admitted.

CAP. LXX. Infamous persons cannot accuse those of good repute. Pope Eugenius, epistle 2.

(3, q. 4, c. *Alieni*.) Likewise, we cannot and ought not to receive one who is a companion in another’s error, who departs from the course of his own voluntary purpose, or who is disobedient to the sacred rules and constitutions of the Fathers.

CAP. LXXI. Those who are not to be admitted as accusers. Pope Stephen in the *Decretals* to bishops, epistle 2.

(3, q. 4, c. *Nullus*.) Let none of the anathematized be received, nor let what they say or write be believed by anyone. By “anathematized” I mean those whom their bishops have anathematized in writing, or whom their ordinances anathematize.

CAP. LXXII. One who persists in excommunication is not to be admitted to accusation. Council of Carthage VII, ch. 1.

(4, q. 1, c. *Definimus*.) We determine that one who, after having been excommunicated, remains still under that excommunication, whether cleric or layman, is not lawfully to be admitted to accuse.

CAP. LXXIII. Those who persist in schism or excommunication are held to be heretics. Nicholas to Emperor Michael.

(4, q. 1, c. *Quod autem*, § *Si vero*.) If an ecclesiastical charge has been brought against a fellow bishop, then the persons of the accusers must be examined, so that, first of all, heretics may not be permitted to bring accusations against orthodox bishops in ecclesiastical affairs. But lest you deny that these are heretics, hear what follows: “We call heretics,” they say, “both those who were formerly cast out of the Church and those subsequently anathematized by us.” Further, if you still do not believe even this, hear what is added: “Besides these, they say, are those who pretend to have sound faith or refuse to confess it; likewise schismatics, and those who separately hold assemblies apart from bishops in communion with us.” Then also, if they have been reproved and cast out or excommunicated by the Church on certain grounds, whether from the clerical or lay order, they too may not accuse a bishop before first freeing themselves from their own crime.” Likewise, those who remain under a prior accusation are not acceptable to accuse a bishop or other clerics before they have shown themselves innocent of the charges brought against them.

CAP. LXXIV. An insult is not to be treated as an accusation. Fabian, pope, to Bishop Hilary, epistle 3.

(3, q. 3, c. *Si quis iratus*.) If anyone, in anger, rashly casts or imposes some charge upon another, the insult is not to be regarded as an accusation. But after time for consideration has been allowed, if he declares in writing that he will prove what he said in anger, then, should he perhaps come to his senses and be unwilling to repeat or put in writing what he said in wrath, he is not to be regarded as guilty of a crime.

CAP. LXXV. On the penalty of one who fails in an accusation.

(2, q. 3, c. *Omnis*.) Therefore everyone who brings a charge shall state in writing that he will prove it. Indeed, a case must always be heard where the crime was committed. And whoever does not prove what he alleges shall himself suffer the penalty that he had sought to inflict.

CAP. LXXVI. One who accuses another in court shall name the accused and undertake the formal liability of the accusation. Pope Sixtus.

(2, q. 8, c. *Quisquis*.) We declare and command that this order of accusation be observed: if any cleric is charged with a crime, he is not immediately to be considered guilty merely because he could be accused, lest we make innocence subject to accusation. Rather, whoever brings the charge must come before the court, name the accused, undertake the bond of formal accusation, and accept the corresponding penalty—due regard nevertheless being had for rank. Thus he will know that he has no license to lie, since likeness of punishment demands vengeance upon calumniators.

CAP. LXXVII. Pope Damasus, epistle 1.

(4, q. 4, c. *Nullus*, § *Inscriptio*.) A formal accusation must first be made, so that the calumniator may receive retaliation; for before a formal accusation no one ought to be judged or condemned, since even secular laws maintain this.

CAP. LXXVIII. Stephen to the bishops of Gaul, in the *Decretals*.

(*L. Infamis*, and 3, q. 7, c. *Infames*, ff. *De postulat.*) For an infamous person can be neither advocate nor legal representative.

CAP. LXXIX. Stephen, in the Second Decretal, to all bishops.

No foreigner shall become either their accuser or their judge.

CAP. LXXX. No one may perform two roles in a case.

(4, q. 4, c. *Nullus in primo*.) DAMASUS, pope of Rome, to STEPHEN, archbishop. Accusers and judges must not be the same persons; rather, accusers separately, judges separately, witnesses separately, and each person accused separately in his own proper place according to due order.

CAP. LXXXI. No one can simultaneously be accuser, witness, or judge. Fabian in the *Decretals*, ch. 4.

(4, q. 4, c. *Nullus*.) Let no one ever presume to be at once accuser, judge, and witness, since in every trial four persons must always be present: chosen judges, qualified accusers, suitable defenders, and lawful witnesses. Judges ought to employ fairness; witnesses, truth; accusers, zeal to establish the case; defenders, mitigation to diminish the case.

CAP. LXXXII. No judgment is to stand unless lawfully conducted. St. Gregory to John, defender, book II, epistle 50.

(2, q. 1, c. *In primis*, § *Quia igitur*.) Since a certain brother asserts that he has been accused on false charges and that nothing was done in due order, but that he was unjustly condemned, this must be carefully investigated. First, whether the judgment was conducted in due order; whether some were accusers and others witnesses. Then the nature of the charges must be examined: whether it was worthy of exile or deposition; whether testimony against him was given under oath in the presence of the accused; whether proceedings were committed to writing; whether he had leave to answer or defend himself. The persons making accusation and testimony must also be carefully examined—what their condition and character are—lest perhaps they had enmities against the aforesaid pastor; whether they gave testimony from hearsay, or testified that they knew the matter directly; whether the judgment was written down; and whether the sentence was always read aloud in the presence of the parties. If these things were not solemnly performed, and the charge worthy of exile or deposition was not proved, he is to be restored to his church by every means.

ON WITNESSES TO BE ADMITTED IN ACCUSATIONS.

CAP. LXXXIII. Those excluded from accusation, or who have not yet reached fourteen years, cannot be witnesses. Council of Carthage VII, ch. 4; Pope Nicholas.

(4, q. 3, c. *Testes*.) We decree that those whom it has been commanded are not to be admitted to accusation, or whom the accuser himself produces from his own household, are not to be admitted to give testimony; nor are persons to be admitted as witnesses before the fourteenth year of their age.

CAP. LXXXIV. Recent enemies cannot be witnesses. Anacletus in the *Decretals*, epistle 3.

(3, q. 5, c. *Accusatores*.) Those who were enemies yesterday or the day before yesterday cannot be witnesses, lest in anger they desire to harm, or, having been injured, wish to take revenge. Therefore the disposition of the accuser and witnesses must be free of offense and not suspect.

CAP. LXXXV. Blood-relatives or household members may not give testimony against strangers. Pope Calixtus in the *Decretals*, epistle 2, to the bishops of Gaul.

(3, q. 5, c. *Consanguinei*.) Blood-relatives shall not give testimony against strangers, nor household members coming from the same house; but if they wish and mutually consent, relatives may testify only among themselves and not against others. Nor may suspect witnesses be admitted, because the affection arising from kinship, familiarity, and condemnation commonly hinders truth. Carnal love, fear, and greed often dull human judgment, so that people regard gain as piety and money as the reward of prudence.

CAP. LXXXVI. Those forbidden to be elected to the priesthood cannot accuse priests or testify against them. Damasus in the *Decretals*, epistle 3, to Stephen, archbishop.

(2, q. 7, c. *Testes*.) Witnesses must be free of every infamy, suspicion, or manifest stain, furnished with a true fullness of faith, and such as divine authority commands to be chosen for the priesthood. For, as the authority of the ancients has handed down, those who ought not, and cannot, be advanced to that honor cannot accuse priests or testify against them. Likewise, murderers, evildoers, thieves, sacrilegious persons, kidnappers, poisoners, adulterers, those who have committed abduction, borne false witness, or resorted to diviners and magicians, are in no way to be admitted either to accusation or testimony.

CAP. LXXXVII. Neither traitor nor calumniator can accuse. Pope Iguinus in the *Decretals*.

Let neither the voice of a traitor nor that of a calumniator be heard. No one’s confession concerning himself can be believed regarding another’s crime, because the declaration of such a person is dangerous and ought not to be admitted.

CAP. LXXXVIII. Companions in error and those disobedient to the sacred rules of the Fathers cannot accuse.

(3, q. 4, c. *Alieni erroris*.) Likewise, we cannot and ought not to receive companions in another’s error, one departing from the course of his voluntarily adopted purpose, or one disobedient to the sacred rules and constitutions of the Fathers.

In the decrees of Pope Sylvester, chapter 3.—Sylvester I, pope, in the brief epilogue of the Roman council.

CAP. LXXXIX. No cleric is to be examined in public. Pope Sylvester in the *Decretals* and at the Roman council.

(11, q. 1, c. *Testimonium*.) Pope Sylvester, sitting in a general synod, said: “No layman may dare bring a charge against a cleric. Nor may anyone receive the testimony of a cleric against a layman. Let no one presume to examine any cleric publicly, except in the Church.”

CAP. XC. No cleric of lower rank may presume to accuse one of higher rank, nor may a layman accuse a bishop. Pope Sylvester in the *Decretals*, ch. 3.

By the unanimous consent and subscription of all, it was established that no layman may bring any charge against a bishop or anyone constituted in orders; and that a presbyter may in no way presume to make an accusation against a bishop, a deacon against a presbyter, a subdeacon against a deacon, an acolyte against a subdeacon, an exorcist against an acolyte, a reader against an exorcist, or a doorkeeper against a reader.

CAP. XCI. By how many witnesses a bishop, presbyter, or other clerics are to be convicted.

(2, q. 5, c. *Praesul*.) A bishop shall not be condemned except on the testimony of seventy-two witnesses. A cardinal presbyter shall not be condemned except on forty witnesses; a cardinal deacon of the city of Rome, except on twenty-seven witnesses. A subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, reader, or doorkeeper shall not be condemned except on seven witnesses. The witnesses and accusers, moreover, must be without any infamy.

CAP. XCII. An infamous or sacrilegious person cannot accuse a devout Christian. Eutychian in the *Decretals*, epistle 2, to the bishops of Sicily.

(3, q. 4, c. *Nulli unquam*.) No infamous or sacrilegious person may ever, in any matter whatever, give testimony against a devout Christian—even though that Christian be of humble and servile condition—nor assail a Christian by any claim, action, or formal accusation.

CAP. XCIII. Witnesses may testify only concerning matters they know personally and truly. Pope Calixtus, epistle 2, to the bishops of Gaul.

(3, q. 9, c. *Testes*.) Witnesses shall not submit testimony by any written document; rather, being present, they shall truthfully testify concerning what they have known and seen. Nor shall they testify concerning other cases or affairs, but only concerning matters known to have occurred in their presence.

CAP. XCIV. Gregory to John the defender, ch. 40.

(*C. Licet*, *Extr. De test.* and *Barb. l. Test. c. De test.*, and 3, q. 9, c. *De his*.) It must be investigated whether they gave testimony from hearsay or testified that they knew the matter directly; whether judgment was committed to writing and the sentence read aloud in the presence of the parties. If these things were not solemnly performed, and a case worthy of exile or deposition was not proved, they are to be restored to their church by every means.

CAP. XCV. Pope Pius, eighth from Peter, to the brethren throughout Spain.

“The Apostle,” he says, “declares that a formal accusation against a presbyter is not to be received without two or three qualified witnesses” (1 Tim. V). If these precautions must be observed concerning presbyters and other faithful persons, how much more concerning bishops? “Every word stands on the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Matt. XVIII).

CAP. XCVI. Stephen V to Astulf.

(2, q. 4, c. *Veniens*; *extr. De testibus*.) Neither the Gospel nor any divine or human law condemns or acquits anyone on the testimony of a single witness, even a qualified one.

CAP. XCVII. By how many witnesses each cleric must be convicted. Second Council of Braga, ch. 9.

(2, q. 4, c. *Placuit*.) It has been decided that if anyone charges a cleric with the stain of fornication, two or three testimonies are required according to the command of the Apostle Paul. If he cannot establish by testimony what he said, the accuser shall incur excommunication.

CAP. XCVIII. A person appearing for judgment is not to be denied a postponement. Felix to Anastasius, ch. 14.

(3, q. 3, c. *Cum accusatus*.) Pope Felix, in his first Decretal. When the accused comes to judgment, if he wishes and if it is necessary, the postponement established by the Fathers shall be granted without hindrance at his request, and judges chosen by himself shall be assigned to him.

CAP. CXIX. An accused person may, if afraid, choose for himself a suitable place in which he can have witnesses without fear.

Let him choose a suitable place in the locality from which the accused person comes; or, if he fears there the violence of a reckless crowd, let him choose a place where, without fear, if necessary or if he requests it, he may have witnesses and bring his canonical case to conclusion without obstruction, since many things commonly happen through deception.

CAP. C. Before the conclusion of a case, departure by appeal is permitted. Pope Eutychian to the bishops of Sicily, epistle 2.

(2, q. 6, c. *Non ita*.) Ecclesiastical affairs are not to be conducted as secular ones are. In secular matters, after someone summoned by law has appeared and begun to contend in court, he may not withdraw before the case is completed. But in ecclesiastical matters, after stating his case he may withdraw if necessary, or if he sees that he is being unduly burdened.

ON POSTPONEMENTS.

CAP. CI. On postponements to be granted to bishops accused in criminal cases. Damasus, bishop, to Stephen, archbishop, epistle 3.

(3, q. 3, c. *Induciae*.) Postponements of six months or more are to be granted to bishops accused in criminal matters.

CAP. CII. For how many months postponements are to be granted to bishops. Felix in the *Decretals*, ch. 20.

(3, q. 3, c. *De induciis*, § *Induciae vero*.) FELIX, pope of Rome, to ANASTASIUS, bishop. Postponements must be granted not within a narrow period but over a long interval, so that the accused may prepare themselves, meet all their fellow communicants established in the provinces, prepare witnesses, and fully arm themselves against plotters. Some have directed that, to repel the machinations of impediments, prepare their answers, confirm witnesses, and seek the counsel of bishops and friends, a year and six months be granted. Others, with whom most agree, prescribe a year. But I find no period of less than six months.

CAP. CIII. On granting postponements, chapter one. Eleutherius in the *Decretals*, ch. 1.

(3, q. 3, c. *Induciae primo*.) ELEUTHERIUS, bishop of the Roman Church, to all bishops. Ample postponements for inquiry are to be given, lest anything appear to be done hastily by either party, for many things result from deception.

CAP. CIV. A definitive sentence must be given only after the case has been examined.

(30, q. 5, c. *Judicantem*, § *Nec litigantibus*.) A judge ought not to anticipate the litigants with his judgment until, after all matters have been completed, they have nothing left to propose in dispute; and the action should be examined until the truth of the matter is reached. There must be frequent questioning, lest anything perhaps remain omitted that ought to be added.

ON THOSE EVADING JUDGMENT.

CAP. CV. Judgment must not be evaded. Pope Boniface to the bishops of Gaul.

BONIFACE, bishop, to PATROCLUS, REMIGIUS, MAXIMUS, HILARY, SEVERUS, VALERIUS, JULIAN, CASTORIUS, LEONTIUS, JOHN, MONTANUS, MARINUS, and the other bishops established in Gaul and in the seven provinces of Valentia. Clerics of the city approached us, presenting a petition and charges which they assert that Maximinus committed, the entire province bearing witness. Although examination had repeatedly been assigned to him, he evaded the judgments, and, not trusting his conscience, did not hasten—if he was innocent—to clear himself after all matters had been examined. We have learned from the records of our own documents that this had repeatedly been decreed. By the contrary course he proved concerning himself the things that were said, because examination had been assigned by my provincial predecessors countless times to refute them. He is also said to have avoided the assembly and altogether refused to appear. No one doubts that the guilty person evades judgment just as the innocent person seeks it in order to be acquitted. But the crafty quibbling of those who believe that matters should be conducted through cunning schemes has never acquired the name of innocence. For whoever is thought to evade judgment by delays confesses everything.

Yet one day the man thus reported will come before judgment; and it does him no good to have evaded it so often. His acts and offenses pursue him wherever he flees, and, if true, so do the crimes alleged against him. Indeed, I ought already to have pronounced a suitable sentence in our judgment for his charged deeds, since he has thought that an investigation and decreed judgment could be mocked by evading it. But, lest perhaps some herald might judge that nothing should be reserved for one absent, though he has been sought by us, we preferred to defer speaking, granting an interval of time, since even his accusers asserted this.

A decree is made concerning his aims and behavior: Maximinus is to be regarded as committing acts all the more deserving of condemnation the more slowly he presents himself for an appointed judgment. They charge him with being wrapped in Manichaean darkness, and with having been stained long ago by a shameful sect so that he cannot wash it away from his soul. Producing synodal records of the filthy proof and acts alleged against him, they assert that he is everywhere entangled in crimes; that he had no regard for soundness of mind; that in frenzy and insane rashness he sought recourse, even to the tribunals of secular judgment, for the issue under inquiry—a course most shameful in a base person—and that he proceeded to the harms of homicide, as the records brought forth in public declare. They lament with excessive grief, to the dishonor of the city, that such a man, after such and so many offenses, still claims the title of bishop in his hiding places and, by claiming the holy name for himself, wishes to defile it.

Therefore, dearest brethren, because this man did not wish to present himself to be heard—lest perhaps, convicted by his clerical accusers, he might be unable to defend himself—we judge that he must finally be struck by a sentence of condemnation appropriate to a bishop’s judgment when he has appeared. Although, when these things become known to him, we know that this entails the loss of that title for one reported never to have possessed the shame proper to the priesthood and never to have lost his office even for a short time, we have nevertheless granted him a delay and decreed that you must hold judgment within the province and convene a synod before the Kalends of November [1 November], so that, if he wishes to appear and is confident, he may answer in person to the allegations. If he neglects to appear, he shall not profit from a delay of sentence on account of absence. For it is evident that one confesses the crime who does not use the opportunity granted and repeatedly assigned for clearing himself. It makes no difference whether all the things alleged are proved in a hearing held in his presence, since his repeatedly contrived absence is itself established by his own declaration. We shall send letters through all the provinces, lest he plead ignorance as an excuse, so that he may be compelled to come into the province and present himself there for the appointed judgment. Whatever your charity determines ought to be decreed in this matter, once it has been reported to us, must necessarily be confirmed by our authority.

CAP. CVI. One who was unable to come to a case on the appointed day is not to be suspended from communion. Third Council of Carthage, ch. 7.

(4, q. 5, c. *Quisquis episcoporum*.) Bishop Aurelius said: “Whoever brings a charge against a bishop shall bring his case to the primate of that province; nor shall the person against whom the charge is brought be deprived of communion unless, summoned by letters to state his case before the judgment of chosen judges on the appointed day, he fails to appear—namely, within one month from the day on which it is established that he received the letters. But if he proves genuine causes of necessity which manifestly made him unable to appear, he shall retain full opportunity to state his case within a second month. Yet after the second month he shall not communicate until he has cleared himself. If he refuses to appear at a general council within a year, so that the case may be concluded there, he shall be judged to have pronounced a sentence of condemnation against himself. During the time when he does not communicate, he shall not communicate in his own church or parish either.

“But if his accuser has never been absent on the days appointed for stating the case, the latter shall not be removed from communion by withdrawing himself. If, however, he is absent at any time, then, once the bishop has been restored to communion, the accuser himself shall be removed from communion. Yet the accuser is not thereby deprived of the opportunity of pursuing the case, provided that he proves not that he was unwilling to appear on the appointed day, but that he was unable to do so. It was further decided that, when he begins proceedings before the judgment of bishops, if the person bringing the case is guilty, he shall not be admitted to accuse unless he is willing to pursue his own cases, not merely ecclesiastical ones.”

CAP. CVII. A presumption lies against one who evades judgment by delays. Pope Julius in the *Decretals*, ch. 2.

(c. *Nullus*, § *De praesumptionibus*.) JULIUS, prelate of the Roman Church, to all bishops. No one doubts that the guilty evade judgment just as the innocent seek it in order to be acquitted. Nor is one free from suspicion who charges another with calumnies and is suspected of having spoken falsely when, summoned to judgment in order to prove what he alleged, he delays coming.

ON JUDGES AND THEIR SENTENCES.

CAP. CVIII. In the decrees of Felix, ch. 1.

FELIX, bishop of the nourishing Roman Church, to ANASTASIUS and the other bishops. Judges ought to be such that they are free from every suspicion and desire, from the root of charity, to pronounce their sentence.

CAP. CIX. Where each person is to be judged by those whom he has chosen as judges. Julius I, in the *Decretals*, ch. 34.

(2, q. 1, c. *Judices autem*.) JULIUS, bishop, to all bishops: There shall be no judges other than those chosen by the person charged, or those whom this holy see, or its primates by authority of this holy see and with his consent, have delegated.

CAP. CX. Judges must first examine with what intention a person makes an accusation before they receive it.

Judges must first examine the suspicion and the cause, or the intention with which the accuser acts, and then undertake the judgment. For the intention arising from kinship, enmity, fear, love, hatred, and desire commonly obstructs a profession of truth and inflicts harms upon brethren.

CAP. CXI. No one can be condemned unless convicted or confessing. Emperor Constantine.

(2, q. 1, c. *Judex*.) A judge examining a criminal person shall not pronounce a capital sentence before the accused himself confesses or is convicted through innocent witnesses.

CAP. CXII. No one is to be condemned by mere suspicion or before a true and just judgment. Melchiades in the *Decretals*.

(2, q. 1, c. *Primo semper*.) First always investigate everything carefully, so that you may decide with justice and charity, condemning no one before a true and just judgment. Judge no one by the judgment of suspicion; but first prove the matter and then pronounce a charitable sentence; and do not do to another what you do not wish done to yourselves.

CAP. CXIII. A doubtful matter is not to be determined by a certain sentence. Claims not demonstrated by certain proofs are not to be believed. Victor in the *Decretals*, ch. 1.

(11, q. 3, c. *Grave*, or *quamvis*; 30, q. 5, *Si quis*.) POPE VICTOR, to THEOPHILUS, bishop. We have heard that some among ours and yours conduct diverse judgments and judge uncertain matters. Dearest brethren, let us by no means judge uncertain matters until the Lord comes, who will bring hidden things to light, illuminate the secrets of darkness, and reveal the counsels of hearts. Hence Augustine, in the book *On Penance*: “Although things may be true, they are nevertheless not to be believed unless established by manifest proofs, unless convicted by manifest judgment, unless made public through judicial procedure.”

CAP. CXIV. On the same matter. Sixtus in the *Decretals*, ch. 1.

(11, q. 3, c. *De sent.*; 2, q. 3, c. *Quamvis*; 3, q. 5, c. *Si quis*.) SIXTUS, pope of Rome, to the bishops established throughout Spain. Let no pontiff presume to judge uncertain matters. And although things may be true, they are nevertheless not to be believed unless established by certain judgments, unless convicted by manifest judgment, unless made public through judicial procedure.

CAP. CXV. In the decrees of Eleutherius, ch. 1.

(2, q. 1, c. *Nihil* and *De Manifest.*, § *Quia Dominus*.) Our Lord Jesus Christ knew Judas to be a thief; but because he was not accused, he was not cast out. Rather, whatever he did among the apostles remained in place by virtue of the dignity of his ministry.

CAP. CXVI. A sentence must not be pronounced hastily. Eucharistius [perhaps Evaristus] in the *Decretals*, ch. 2.

(2, q. 1, c. *Deus*, l. *quia*, c. *Comminati*.) POPE EVARISTUS, to all bishops. The almighty Lord, in order to restrain us from the hasty pronouncement of sentence, although all things are naked and open to his eyes, did not wish to judge the evils of Sodom and Gomorrah merely from what he had heard, before he had openly learned whether what was said was true. Thus he himself says: “I will go down and see whether they have completed in deed the outcry that has come to me; and if not, that I may know” (Gen. XVIII). Almighty God, to whom nothing is hidden but to whom all things are manifest even before they happen, deigned to investigate these matters personally for no other reason than to give us an example: that we should not be hasty in examining and judging the affairs of brethren, and that no one should dare to believe evil concerning anyone before proving it.

By his example we are warned never to be hasty in pronouncing sentence, nor rashly and carelessly to judge matters unproved and unexamined in any fashion. The voice of Truth says: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged; for with whatever judgment you judge, you shall be judged,” and the rest (Matt. VII). Let reports of evils move no one; let no one ever believe a casual report without certain proof. Rather, let him carefully investigate what he hears beforehand and do nothing precipitately. For if the Lord, knower of all things, though knowing everything, would neither believe nor judge the evils of the Sodomites—whose outcry had reached even to heaven—until he himself had truly learned by deed those things which he had carefully investigated with trustworthy witnesses, how much more ought we, human and sinful persons, to take care, since the judgments of God are unknown to us, and neither judge nor condemn anyone before true and just proof. The Apostle bears witness when he says: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? Before his own master he stands or falls” (Rom. XIV).

CAP. CXVII. A manifest case does not require judicial procedure. Pope Stephen V to Leo, bishop of Tyana.

(11, q. 1, c. *De manifesta*.) In a case manifest and known to many, witnesses need not be sought. Thus Saint Ambrose, in his letter to the Corinthians, explains the Apostle’s pronouncement concerning fornication: “It is not the part of a judge,” I say, “to condemn without an accuser.” For although the Lord knew Judas to be a thief, because he was not accused he did not cast him out. But when that deed became known, he judged that the man should be expelled from the fellowship of the brethren. For all knew his crime and did not reprove him. He openly had his stepmother as a wife; in this matter neither witnesses were needed nor could the crime be denied by any evasion. And shortly afterward: “Absent in body, but present in authority of spirit—which is absent nowhere—I have already judged, as though present, that the man who committed this be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh” (1 Cor. V).

CAP. CXVIII. The confession of ministers must not be extorted, but voluntary.

(15, q. 6, c. *Si quandoque*.) ALEXANDER, pope, fifth from Peter, in the first book of his Decretals. If any writings have in any manner been extorted from priests or authorities of the Church through fear, fraud, or force, as though they might thereby free themselves, whatever has been written or devised by them through ingenuity, we decree that such writings have no force to their prejudice or harm. Nor, by the authority of God and the holy apostles and their successors, do we ever permit them to suffer on their account any infamy, calumny, or deprivation of their goods.

CAP. CXIX. Nothing is to be judged before it is demonstrated by certain judgments. Pope Eleutherius, in Decretal 1.

(30, q. 5, c. *Judicantem*.) A judge ought to examine everything and investigate the order of events by full inquiry, granting patience for questioning, proposing, and rejecting, so that the action of both parties may there be fully brought to light. Likewise: judgment is not to be given until both sides have completed their pleadings.

ON APPEALS.

CAP. CXX. A person may appeal before sentence has been given. From the Decretal of Pope Fabian to Bishop Hilary, ch. 27.

(2, q. 7, c. *Si quis judicem*.) But if any bishop regards the judge as suspect and sees that he is being oppressed, let him freely appeal to the Apostolic See.

### CHAPTER CXXI. No affliction should be added to one already afflicted.

(2, q. 7, c. *Appellantem*.) No affliction, whether through detention or the injurious custody of imprisonment, should be inflicted upon one who appeals; rather, the appellant must be permitted to remedy a flawed case by means of appeal.

### CHAPTER CXXII. An appeal must not be denied to one whom a sentence has consigned to punishment. [Col. 1208D] Pope Fabian to Hilary, Epistle 3.

(2, q. 7, c. *Liceat*. l. *Non tant.* § *De appel.*) It must also be permitted to appeal in criminal cases, and the right to appeal must not be denied to one whom a sentence has assigned to punishment.

### CHAPTER CXXIII. An accused person shall be heard only in his own forum. Pope Fabian to Hilary, Epistle 3.

(3, q. 6, c. *Pulsatus*.) Let the accused state his case before his own judge. Before one who is not his own judge, the accused may remain silent if he wishes; and whenever accused persons appeal, they are to be granted a postponement. Let no one be bound by a sentence pronounced outside his proper court. [Col. 1209A]

### CHAPTER CXXIV. Bishops charged in more serious cases shall appeal to the Apostolic See. From the Decree of Pope Gregory to the Eastern bishops, chapter 27.

(2, q. 6, c. *Omnes episc.*, and c. *Ad Romanam*.) Let all bishops who are attacked or accused in certain more serious causes, whenever necessary, freely appeal to the Apostolic See and flee to it as to a mother, so that they may be mercifully supported, defended, and freed by it, as has always been the case.

### CHAPTER CXXV. A bishop accused or judged by his fellow-provincial bishops shall appeal to the Apostolic See. [Col. 1209B] Pope Sixtus to Bishop Gratian, Epistle 1.

(3, q. 6, c. *Accusatus*.) Likewise, from the statements of Pope Sixtus: It was decreed that a bishop accused or judged by his fellow-provincial bishops in any cause should willingly appeal and approach the pontiff of the Apostolic See, who shall arrange for his case to be reconsidered either personally or through his vicars.

### CHAPTER CXXVI. One oppressed by his own metropolitan shall appeal to the primates or to the universal See; or: One who believes himself oppressed by his own metropolitan shall appeal to the higher See. Victor to Theophilus, Epistle 1.

(2, q. 6, c. *Si quis*.) Likewise Bishop Victor: If anyone believes himself oppressed by his own metropolitan, let his case be judged before the patriarch, or the primate of the diocese, or the See of the Apostolic Universal Church.

### CHAPTER CXXVII. Within what period each person must appeal after sentence has been pronounced. [Col. 1209C] From the laws of Theodosius, chapter 20.

(2, q. 6, c. *Propter superfluam*.) Because appellants have been granted excessive latitude, lest they seem to possess unrestricted discretion in reconsidering or revoking judgments, periods for appeal and prescribed penalties have been established. Whoever wishes to appeal before the judge who heard his case and to seek recourse to another must appeal within the days [unspecified in the supplied text], and within those same five days must reach, without any pretense, the judge to whom he has appealed. The very day on which he received the letters shall be specifically counted among those five days. But if the journey is longer, then, in addition to those five days, the number of days in which the journey can be made shall be counted.

### CHAPTER CXXVIII. Dismissory letters shall be sent from the judge appealed from to the judge to whom appeal has been made. [Col. 1209D] From the same laws, chapter 36.

(2, q. 6, c. *Ab eo*.) From the person from whom appeal has been taken, dismissory letters shall be sent to the one competent to hear the appeal; these are commonly called *apostoli*. Their request and receipt must be made ex officio within the fifth day. The foregoing has already explained the securities and penalties concerning appellants who fail, within the prescribed periods, to request, receive, or submit dismissory letters: they shall be barred from bringing an action by prescription and compelled to bear the penalty of appeal.

### CHAPTER CXXIX. Concerning those who appeal merely in order to delay the cause. From the same laws, chapter 27.

(2, q. 6, c. *Quicunque*.) Whoever appeals not in confidence of a just cause, but merely in order to postpone proceedings and prevent sentence from being pronounced against him; or whoever, having confessed his own act, wishes to appeal so as not to be removed—such appeals shall not be admitted. [Col. 1210A]

### CHAPTER CXXX. When a possessor appeals while the outcome of the cause remains uncertain, the fruits of the possession shall be sequestered. From the same laws, chapter 37.

(2, q. 9, c. *Quoties*.) Whenever, after the case has been heard, the possessor appeals from the judge, the fruits of the possession in dispute are properly sequestered while the outcome of the subsequent hearing remains uncertain. But if the claimant appeals, this cannot be demanded from him, since what he does not possess cannot be sequestered. If the appeal concerns urban estates, slaves, or beasts of burden, their possessions, rents, or transport charges are customarily deposited; this applies even where the matter concerns a ship’s sailor. [Col. 1210B]

### CHAPTER CXXXI. One who appeals unjustly must in every case be punished. From the same laws, chapter 38.

(2, q. 6, c. *Omnimodo*.) Whenever an appeal is declared unjust, the appellant must in every case be punished: he shall be compelled to repay the expenses incurred by his opponent in pursuing the matter, not singly but fourfold.

### CHAPTER CXXXII. From which judges appeal is permitted; or: Let one who refuses to obey his judges be excommunicated. Council of Spalato/Milevis, chapter 24.

[Col. 1210C] (2, q. 6, c. *A judicibus*, and c. *Quisquis*.) No one may appeal from judges chosen by common consent. Whoever is proved, through contumacy, unwilling to obey the judges, once this has been demonstrated to the bishop of the First See, shall be given letters directing that none of the bishops communicate with him until he obeys.

### CHAPTER CXXXIII. When a judgment is dissolved by appeal, it should not harm the person who did not judge with an unjust intention. Third Council of Carthage, chapter 10.

(2, q. 6, c. *Hoc etiam placuit*.) It was decreed that, whenever an appeal is made from any ecclesiastical judges to other judges of greater authority, the dissolution of their sentence shall not harm those whose judgment it was, unless they can be convicted either of having judged with hostile intent or of having been corrupted by some greed or favor. Certainly, if judges were chosen by agreement of the parties, even if their number was smaller than the prescribed number, appeal shall not be permitted. [Col. 1210D]

### CHAPTER CXXXIV. Fellow-provincial bishops and metropolitans may hear bishops’ cases, but may not decide them. Zephyrinus, in the Decree, chapter 1.

(3, q. 6, c. *Quoniam*.) Although fellow-provincial bishops may lawfully investigate the case of an accused bishop, they are nevertheless not permitted to decide it without consulting the Roman pontiff.

### CHAPTER CXXXV. An accused person cannot be condemned unless convicted or voluntarily confessing; and if the accused is a bishop, they must not pronounce a sentence of condemnation but refer the matter to the Apostolic See. [Col. 1211A] Pope Felix I [perhaps Zephyrinus], in the Decree to Paternus.

(2, q. 1, c. *Primates accus.*) ZEPHYRINUS, archbishop of the city of Rome, to all bishops. Patriarchs or primates examining an accused bishop shall not pronounce a definitive judgment until they have been supported by Apostolic authority, unless the accused confesses himself guilty or is convicted by unimpeachable witnesses who have been examined according to rule. Such witnesses must be no fewer in number than those disciples were.

### CHAPTER CXXXVI. Fellow-provincial bishops and metropolitans may hear bishops’ cases, but may not determine them. [Col. 1211B] Pope Eleutherius, in the Decree.

(2, q. 6, c. *Quamvis*.) Concerning, therefore, the accusations against clerics about which we have been consulted: because it is difficult to bring all their accusers before the Apostolic See, definitive judgments concerning bishops shall nevertheless be referred here, as has already been determined by the apostles and their successors with the assent of many bishops. Nor shall others be placed over, or ordained in, their churches before their affairs have been justly concluded here. Accusations and proceedings may indeed be discussed before fellow-provincials, metropolitans, and their primates; but they may not be definitively decided otherwise than as stated above. The cases of other clerics, however, may lawfully be both heard and justly concluded before provincial bishops, metropolitans, and primates. [Col. 1212A]

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 1211]

## CONCERNING CLERICS ACCUSED BY MERE ILL REPUTE WITHOUT WITNESSES

[Col. 1211]

### CHAPTER I. A person of ill repute who, after three warnings, does not amend himself shall be suspended from office until he has cleared himself. [Col. 1211B] Council of Agde, chapter 4.

(C. *Si quis*, extr. *De purg.*; and 2, q. 5, c. *Si legitimi*.) [Col. 1211C] If any presbyter, neglectful of his life, has by bad examples allowed evil suspicion to arise concerning himself, and the people, bound by the bishop through an oath or a ban of Christianity, have made his ill repute known, while definite accusers of his crime are lacking, he shall first be admonished privately by the bishop and then before two or three witnesses. If he does not amend himself, the bishop shall admonish him publicly in the assembly of presbyters. If he still does not correct himself, he shall be suspended from office until proper satisfaction has been made, lest the people suffer scandal on his account.

But if there are no lawful accusers seeking to prove his crimes by manifest indications, and he denies them, then, if able, he shall clear himself of the charge together with seven companions of the same order. [Col. 1211D] If a deacon is accused of the same crime, he shall clear himself together with three companions.

### CHAPTER II. On the purgation of clerics if they cannot be convicted. Council of Seville, chapter 10.

(2, q. 5, c. *Presbyter*.) If any presbyter has been defamed by unfavorable report among the people committed to him, and the bishop cannot establish the charge by lawful witnesses, the presbyter shall be suspended until proper satisfaction has been made, lest the faithful people suffer scandal on his account. Proper satisfaction consists in this: that, after proper assurance has been given, he is shown innocent of the charge laid against him before those by whom he is believed guilty. This is taught to have been established by us and by our predecessors.

[Col. 1212B] But, whether according to the canons or at the bishop’s discretion, let him associate with himself seven colleagues and swear before the holy Gospel laid before him that the Holy Trinity and Christ the Son of God, who made him and taught what the Gospel contains, and the four holy Evangelists [Col. 1212C] who wrote it, may so help him as he did not commit the aforesaid act in the manner alleged against him. Once cleared by this satisfaction, let him safely exercise his ministry. Some of the Fathers before us relate that, according to Pope Leo, this satisfaction was made in the basilica of the Apostle Saint Peter before the most reverend Emperor Charles, clergy, and people; and that the venerable prince thereafter promptly exacted fitting vengeance upon the enemies of that holy pope.

### CHAPTER III. How priests ought to clear themselves. Decretal, and Leo to Charles.

(2, q. 4, c. *Omnibus vobis*.) We do not doubt that it is known to all of you by sight or report that, at the instigation of the ancient enemy, various crimes are very often alleged against priests. Yet although the manner in which a reasonable examination and satisfaction concerning such charges should be made was frequently discussed in the time of your lord father of blessed memory, Pippin, and in earlier times by the holy Fathers and other persons of good devotion, we have not been able to find it repeatedly and clearly settled.

In our own times this same matter has often been discussed, because of the many and excessive complaints that have reached us from diverse regions, by holy bishops, other priests, and the remaining ministers of ecclesiastical rank living in your kingdoms or elsewhere under God’s rule, together with ourselves acting with them. [Col. 1213A] We wish all of you ministers of both orders to know how, by the counsel of our lord and father Pope Leo, of the other bishops and priests of the Roman Church, of the Eastern and Greek patriarchs, of many bishops, of all priests, and also by the authority and consent of our bishops, all Roman priests and levites, the other faithful, and our councils, this has been determined.

It has therefore been established, by reason, necessity, and the aforesaid counsel, that whenever a crime is alleged against a priest, if the accuser is of a kind who ought to be admitted—for the canons fully state what persons are to be admitted to accuse priests—then, if that canonically admissible accuser can prove the charge before the bishops with the lawful number of men and good witnesses, the matter shall be canonically judged, and, if the priest is found guilty, he shall be canonically condemned. But if the accuser cannot prove it under the aforesaid conditions, that too shall be canonically judged.

If, however, the priest is suspect and not credible to his bishop, to his fellow priests, or to good and just persons among his people or dependents, or remains under the charge or aforesaid suspicion, he shall clear himself with three, five, or seven good neighboring priests, following the example of Pope Leo, who had twelve bishops at his purgation—or more, if his bishop considers it advisable, or sees it necessary because of popular disturbance. [Col. 1213B–C] Together with other good and just persons, he shall restore himself cleansed to the Church by an oath taken before the people upon the four Gospels. Whoever wishes to know what witnesses ought to be received in accusations against priests, and what must be done concerning accusation, can find this fully in the canons.

### CHAPTER IV. Concerning Leo and the manner in which he cleared himself. From the Purgation of Pope Leo.

(2, q. 5, c. *Auditum*.) Beloved brothers, it has been heard and widely reported in many places how evil men rose against me, sought to weaken me, and brought grave accusations against me. For this reason this most merciful and serene lord Charles came to the city with his priests and nobles.

Therefore I, Leo, pontiff of the holy Roman Church, judged and compelled by no one, but of my own free will, clear myself before you in the presence of God and his angels, who know the conscience, and before the blessed Prince of the Apostles, in whose presence we stand: I neither committed nor ordered committed those criminal and wicked acts which they allege against me. God is my witness, before whose judgment we shall come and in whose presence we stand.

I do this of my own free will in order to remove evil suspicions, not as though I were imposing this custom or decree upon my successors, or upon our brothers and fellow bishops in the holy Church, [Col. 1213D–1214A] but so that you may more effectively cut off rebellious thoughts from yourselves.

### CHAPTER V. Concerning Bishop Leo, whom blessed Gregory caused to undergo purgation. From the Register of Pope Gregory to Emperor Justin, and Epistle 23 to the presbyter Justin.

(3, q. 5, c. *Habet*.) The envy of the ancient enemy has this characteristic: those whom, with God resisting him, he cannot deceive into committing wicked acts, he presently seeks to tear apart by falsely counterfeiting reports concerning them. Therefore, since an unfavorable rumor had spread certain allegations contrary to the priestly calling against our brother and fellow bishop Leo, we had them investigated for a long time by a strict inquiry to determine whether they were true. We found in him no fault concerning the matters alleged. [Col. 1214B]

But, lest anything seem to have been omitted that could leave doubt in our mind, we caused him, beyond what was required, to make solemn oaths at the most sacred body of the blessed Apostle Peter. When these had been made, we rejoiced greatly that such innocence had been clearly displayed. Therefore let Your Glory receive the aforesaid man with all charity and show him the reverence fitting for a priest; let no doubt remain concerning matters now cleared. You must adhere most devotedly in every respect to the aforesaid bishop, so that in his person you may fittingly and properly appear to honor God, whose minister he is.

### CHAPTER VI. How blessed Gregory the Great caused Bishop Menna to clear himself by oath. [Col. 1214C] From the Register to Queen Brunhild, chapter 332.

(2, q. 5, c. *Mennam*.) After investigating the allegations made against our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Menna, we found him guilty in no respect. Moreover, in making satisfaction under oath at the most sacred body of the blessed Apostle Peter, he showed that the charges made against his reputation did not apply to him. We therefore permitted him to return, cleared and released. For just as it would have been right, had he been guilty in any respect, to punish his fault canonically, so it was not right to keep or afflict him longer in any way when innocence came to his aid.

### CHAPTER VII. Concerning the case of the presbyter Gillandus. [Col. 1214D] Alexander II to Romuald, bishop of Como.

(2, q. 4, c. *Super causas*.) We have taken counsel concerning the case of your presbyter Gillandus, who has been defamed regarding the death of your predecessor, the bishop. Therefore, by the unanimous agreement of the brethren present, we write to your belovedness that the aforesaid presbyter Gillandus is to be brought before you. If definite accusers are lacking, then, justice so dictating and without any controversy, the presbyter shall recover both the priesthood and all benefices which he unjustly lost on that account.

### CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the same person.

(2, q. 5, c. *Mennam*, § *Purgationem*.) Nevertheless, where the accuser withdraws, we leave to your judgment whether the same man should make purgation before you together with two priests joined to him. We absolutely forbid, by Apostolic authority, that either he should perform, or you should in any manner require, the popular practice unsupported by any canonical sanction: the ordeal of boiling or cold water, contact with red-hot iron, or any other popular contrivance; for all such things are fabricated or invented entirely by envy. [Col. 1215A]

### CHAPTER IX. If a priest is accused by the people, let him affirm his innocence by oath. Gregory III to Boniface.

(2, q. 5, c. *Presbyter*.) Concerning a presbyter or any priest accused by the people: if there are no definite witnesses who can speak the truth concerning the charge brought, let him take an oath publicly and bring forward as witness to the purity of his innocence Him to whom all things are naked and open; and thus let him remain in his own rank. [Col. 1215B]

### CHAPTER X. If a presbyter has a complaint against a layperson, or a layperson against a presbyter, how proceedings should be conducted.

(2, q. 5, c. *Si quis presbyter*.) If a presbyter has a disputed complaint against a layperson, or a layperson against a presbyter, let it be settled at the bishop’s command without regard to persons. Let the layperson, if necessary, clear himself by oath. Let the presbyter, in place of an oath, be questioned upon his holy consecration, because priests ought not to swear for a trivial cause. For shall the hand through which Christ’s body is consecrated be defiled by an oath? Far be it!

For the Lord says in the Gospel to his disciples, whose office we unworthy persons hold in the holy Church: “Do not swear at all; but let your speech be ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no.’ Whatever exceeds this is from evil” (Matt. 5). [Col. 1215C]

### CHAPTER XI. No cleric shall presume to swear anything to a layperson. Council of Rheims, chapter 5.

(22, q. 5, c. *Nullus*.) No one of the ecclesiastical order shall swear anything to any layperson upon sacred things or upon the holy Gospels; rather, with simplicity, purity, and truth, let him say: “Yes, yes; no, no.” But if laypersons bring any charge against them, it shall be referred to the bishop in whose territory the matter lies; and according to what those of the same order determine, it shall either be corrected or cleared. [Col. 1215D]

### CHAPTER XII. Laypersons are not to judge concerning presbyters. Nicholas to the Bulgarians, chapter 28.

(Dist. 28, c. *Consulendum*.) You decree that consultation is necessary as to whether you ought to support and honor a presbyter who has a wife, or cast him out from among you. We reply that, although such men are indeed greatly blameworthy, you should nevertheless imitate God, who, as the Gospel testifies, makes his sun rise upon good and evil and sends rain upon just and unjust alike (Matt. 5). You ought not cast them out from among you for this reason, since the Lord did not cast Judas, though he was a lying disciple, out of the number of the apostles.

But you who are laypersons are neither to judge concerning presbyters nor to investigate anything concerning their life; whatever it may be must be reserved for the judgment of bishops. [Col. 1216A]

### CHAPTER XIII. A presbyter or deacon shall not be removed without examination by counsel. Nicholas to the same persons.

(15, q. 8, c. *Sciscitantibus*.) You ask whether you should receive Communion from a priest caught in adultery, or merely stained by public report of it. We answer: No matter how defiled a person may be, he cannot defile the divine sacraments, which cleanse every contamination. Nor can the sun’s ray, passing through sewers and latrines, acquire any contamination from them. Therefore, whatever the priest may be, holy things cannot be polluted.

Accordingly, Communion must be received from him until he is rejected by the judgment of bishops, because evil men, in administering good things, harm themselves alone. A burning wax torch harms itself, but gives light to others in darkness; from the very thing by which it confers benefit upon others, it brings loss upon itself. Receive Christ’s mysteries therefore without fear from every priest, because all things are cleansed in faith. For it is faith that conquers this world, because it is effected by the merit not of the giver but of the recipient. [Col. 1216B]

### CHAPTER XIV. Whoever wishes to accuse another of homicide must undergo the penalty of retaliation. From Book VII of the Code.

(L. *Si quis*, and c. *De accus.*) Whoever attacks another with a dangerous and capital accusation of homicide shall not be heard by the judges until he has formally undertaken in writing to undergo the same penalty that he seeks against the accused. [Col. 1216C]

### CHAPTER XV. Whoever wishes to accuse a slave shall bind himself to the penalty of retaliation.

(L. *Si quis servos*, c. *De accus.*) And if anyone believes that another person’s slaves ought to be accused, let him bind himself by the same formal undertaking, so that he shall compensate for punishments inflicted upon innocent slaves either by the penalty of his own head or by loss of his property. Whoever, after filing the required undertaking, wishes to accuse anyone charged with any crime must pursue the proposed actions within one year from the day on which he filed it. If he delays, he shall become infamous and be fined one quarter of his goods.

### CHAPTER XVI. Accusations must be proved before judicial sentence.

[Col. 1216D]

No one can be convicted in judgment without witnesses or judicial proof. A sentence given by a judge while one party is absent has no validity. A cause judged between persons present cannot be reopened after ten years, nor between absent persons after twenty years. In a capital case, no absent person shall be condemned. Nor can an absent person be accused through any accuser.

### CHAPTER XVII. Who ought to swear.

The law directs that proof be required not from the possessor but from the claimant’s side, because it says that all proof is to be sought from the person who desires to obtain the thing claimed, not from the one who intends to hold it by right. Yet, apart from that matter, it is necessary to question the possessor whether he began to possess in his own person or through a predecessor. [Col. 1217A]

### CHAPTER XVIII. He who affirms must prove: this is the affirmative rule, not he who denies: this is the negative rule.

(L. II, with the appended gloss, *Digest*, On Proofs; and the summary of Bartolus.) The burden of proof rests on the person who affirms, not on the person who denies.

### CHAPTER XIX. Witnesses shall not give testimony except concerning matters which they know personally and truthfully.

(3, q. 9, c. *Testes in principio*.) Testimony ought to be given in such a way that witnesses state what was received or deposited in their presence, or what they recorded having received as deposited.

### CHAPTER XX. Witnesses are not to be received against an absent party.

[Col. 1217B]

(In the name of the Lord, extr. *De testim.*) Witnesses shall not be produced otherwise than with the opposing party also present, or failing to appear contumaciously, [Col. 1218A] so that the customary exception which he considers appropriate may be available for him to raise. A person who is absent from necessity, however, is not deemed contumaciously absent—for instance, one who has fled for refuge among holy places.

### CHAPTER XXI. Testimony is invalid without an oath. Law of Theodosius.

(C. *Nuper*, extr. *De testim.*; 4, q. 3, c. *Jurisjurandi*, and c. *Testes*.) Before witnesses are questioned concerning a case, they must be bound by oath to swear that they will say nothing false. Greater credit shall be given to persons of higher standing than to those of lower condition. The testimony of one witness, however distinguished and qualified the person may seem, shall in no way be heard.

### CHAPTER XXII. The testimony of one person is invalid.

[Col. 1218B] (C. *Veniens*, extr. *De testim.*; 4, q. 3, c. *Si testes*, etc., *De test.*) Let the testimony of one person not be accepted. If there are several witnesses on each side, let those who are more truthful, devout, and honorable be chosen, and let them confirm their testimony by oath, swearing that they will say nothing false.

## CONCERNING THE CAUSES AND AFFAIRS OF LAYPERSONS

[Col. 1217]

### CHAPTER XXIII. To whom it is permitted to choose the judgment of a bishop of the most sacred See. [Col. 1217C] Emperor Theodosius VI.

(11, q. 1, c. *Omnes*.) Therefore all causes treated either under praetorian law or civil law shall be settled by bishops’ judgments, which shall be confirmed with the enduring force of law. No one may thereafter reopen a matter decided by bishops’ judgments. Even testimony given by one bishop shall be accepted without hesitation by all judges; nor shall any other person be heard when the testimony of a bishop has been pledged by either party.

For that testimony is confirmed by the authority of truth; that shall be regarded as uncorrupted which a most holy man has uttered in the conscience of an unstained mind. We once enacted this by a salutary edict; [Col. 1217D] we now establish it by a perpetual law, suppressing the malicious seeds of litigation.

### CHAPTER XXIV. Judges shall not readily allow persons of low condition to come forward as witnesses. Emperor Theodosius.

Counts and judges must be especially admonished not to permit low and unworthy persons to come before them as witnesses, because many regard swearing as nothing at all: they can be hired to swear for one day’s satiety or for any small price, and do not at all fear the loss of their souls. Therefore we by no means admit such persons, because not only those who commit perjury, but also those who consent to perjuries, must be condemned to the same perdition.

### CHAPTER XXV. Let no one’s testimony be received except that of a person commended by good reputation or rank. Constitution XXX, chapter 1.

(§ *Sancimus*, c. *De test.*) Let no one’s testimony be received unless he is held in good repute, or is commended by rank, military service, uprightness of life, an honorable professional title, or the concurring statement of other witnesses concerning his good life. But if a witness of the lowest condition is produced in court, the judge may, if he thinks fit, subject him to torture. [Col. 1218C]

Likewise: We do not admit the testimony of persons who claim, while passing by, to have heard someone say that money had been taken from him; nor is the mere presence of public record-keepers sufficient, unless witnesses summoned for the purpose have also signed.

### CHAPTER XXVI. What if a witness is said to be a slave?

(L. *Si testis*, c. *De test.*, § *De vero*.) If a witness produced is said to be a slave but declares himself free, his testimony shall be taken if he claims freedom by birth; afterward, if he is proved to be a slave, it shall be of no effect. But if he says that he is a freedman, then, if he produces the document of his manumission, let him give testimony. If he says that the documents proving his status are elsewhere, his testimony shall nevertheless be written down. If he subsequently fails to produce the documents, it shall be of no effect. [Col. 1218D]

### CHAPTER XXVII. Slaves shall not be received as witnesses against their masters. From the law of Theodosius.

(L. *Servos*, q., and l. *Ex quibus*.) A slave is never to be believed if he brings an accusation against anyone or attacks his own master with a criminal charge. Even if, while subjected to torture, he sets forth what he alleges, he must in no way be believed.

### CHAPTER XXVIII. A heretic may accuse a heretic and testify against him. [Col. 1219A] Constitution of the Novels, Novel 45, chapter 2.

(2, q. 7, c. *Si haereticus*.) If a heretic litigates against a heretic, either may bring a heretical witness. But if an Orthodox person litigates against a heretic, a heretic’s testimony shall be valid in favor of the Orthodox person. Against an Orthodox person, however, only an Orthodox person’s testimony shall be valid. When Orthodox persons are litigating, no heretic shall be admitted to give testimony.

Chapter 5. If anyone says that a produced witness is an enemy, then, if the hostility arises from a criminal cause, he shall not testify at all. But if it arises from another occasion, he may testify, though the objection to his testimony shall be raised. [Col. 1219B]

### CHAPTERS XXIX–XXX. Accomplices in a crime are not admitted as witnesses. Novel 308.

(C. *Veniens*, extr. *De test.*) It was decreed that witnesses shall not be admitted if they are accomplices in the crime, children, calumniators, or others prohibited by law and the canons.

### CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning an accused person who confesses: he is not to be believed against another.

It was decreed that one who has confessed concerning himself is not to be believed concerning another.

### CHAPTER XXXII. The persons who cannot be compelled to testify against relatives. Novel 313 and Council of Mâcon, chapter 6.

[Col. 1219C] (L. *Julia*, *Digest*, *De test.*; and 4, q. 8, c. *Placuit*, § *In lege Julia*.) No one shall be required against his will to give testimony in litigation against his father-in-law, son-in-law, stepfather, stepson, first cousin, female first cousin, the child of a first cousin, or those related in a closer degree. Likewise, no one shall be required to testify against his own freedman, or the freedmen of his children, parents, husband, or wife. Likewise, neither patrons nor patronesses shall be compelled to testify against freedpersons, nor freedpersons against patrons.

### CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning qualified and unqualified witnesses.

(L. *Idonei*, *Digest*, *De test.*) Likewise, those persons do not appear to be qualified witnesses whom one can compel to be witnesses.

### CHAPTER XXXIV. Concerning the same.

(L. *Testes*, *Digest*, *De test.*) A father is not a qualified witness for his son, nor a son for his father. [Col. 1219D]

### CHAPTER XXXV. Concerning the same.

(L. *Qui falso*, *Digest*, *De test.*) Likewise, those who have given false or inconsistent testimony, or testified for both parties, are punished by the judges.

### CHAPTER XXXVI. Concerning the same.

(L. *Pater*, *Digest*, *De test.*) Likewise, a father and a son subject to his authority; likewise, two brothers subject to the authority of the same father, may certainly serve as witnesses in the same will or the same transaction, because there is no objection to using several witnesses from one household in another person’s affair.

### CHAPTER XXXVII. Women have the legal right to give testimony in court.

(L. *Ex eo*, *Digest*, *De test.*) Likewise, from the fact that the Julian law on adultery prohibits a woman convicted of adultery from giving testimony, it follows that women also have the legal right to give testimony in court. [Col. 1220A]

### CHAPTER XXXVIII. Concerning free men or women who marry persons attached to the fisc.

Free men who marry royal women attached to the fisc, and free women who marry royal men attached to the fisc, shall not be excluded from inheritances from their parents, from bringing a claim, or from giving testimony in this matter.

### CHAPTER XXXIX. One under anathema cannot accuse or testify. Novel 215.

(2, q. 7, c. *In sancta*.) The voice of anyone under anathema shall in no way be heard in accusation, testimony, or a human court.

### CHAPTER XL. Concerning a slave who accuses his master. [Col. 1220B] Novels 166–167.

If a slave denounces his master, he shall be punished even if he proves the charges.

### CHAPTER XLI. Concerning postponements to be granted to an accused person or accuser.

Judges who have begun to hear criminal matters after the formal filing of an accusation must, if either accuser or accused requests a postponement, grant it from the day of the filing within one year, so that the action may be completed within the yearly term. But if the accuser delays for a year in proving what he alleged, the accused shall be acquitted and the accuser shall incur the penalty provided in the preceding laws.

### CHAPTER XLII. No postponement is to be granted to murderers, adulterers, and the like. [Col. 1220C] From Book VII, chapter 196.

In civil causes or lighter crimes, postponement must be granted according to law. Murderers, adulterers, sorcerers, and poisoners, if convicted and wishing to appeal, shall not be heard.

### CHAPTER XLIII. A sentence rendered against a genuinely or even fictitiously contumacious party is valid. From Book V.

(L. *Tres denunt.*, c. *Quocunque*, and 24, q. 4.) Whoever, having been summoned to the judge by three authoritative summonses or three edicts, or called by a single peremptory summons serving for all—which is to say, one that extinguishes the action—does not wish to make the required satisfaction before the judge by whom he has been summoned, may be judged as contumacious. Indeed, matters may not be reconsidered by appeal whenever judgment has been rendered against a contumacious party. [Col. 1220D]

### CHAPTER XLIV. A person who refuses to appear in order to refute allegations against him proves them true. Chapter 340.

He proves to be true the things alleged against him who refuses to be present to refute them. Hence it is found written in secular laws: “One unjustly defeated shall restore his cause within three months.” If he neglects to do so, the sentence rendered against him shall stand. Nor should this be objectionable to you, or cause surprise, that I have spoken of secular laws in our judgment, because ecclesiastical and divine laws receive them.

### CHAPTER XLV. Concerning slaves who accuse their masters. [Col. 1221A] The Emperors Arcadius and Honorius Augusti to Exitio, Constitution, Book VI.

(Law *If anyone from the household*, ch. *Who may not accuse*.) If anyone from among the dependants or slaves of any household emerges as an informer and accuser concerning any crime, seeking the reputation, life, and property of the person to whose household connection or lordship he has been attached, let him be struck by the avenging sword at the very presentation of the charges and beginning of the accusation, before witnesses are produced or judges examine the matter. For such a death-dealing voice ought rather to be cut off than heard; indeed, we shut the mouths of such persons against accusing priests or giving testimony against them, whom we know to be dead not by human but by divine pronouncement.

## CHAPTER XLVI. A person acquitted of a particular crime cannot be accused again of the same matter. [Col. 1221B] Council of Mainz.

(Ch. *Concerning those*, Extra, *On accusations*.) An accusation concerning crimes of which someone has been acquitted cannot be revived by the person who made the accusation. Judgment ought not to be demanded in a case that has been settled or adjudicated. But if someone rejects a judge and requests another in his place, and then prefers to reject him again, he is not to be heard in requesting a judge for himself. Judges, moreover, shall pronounce their judgments in writing, and the liberty of appeal is not to be denied to the condemned person, unless perhaps someone has preferred to appeal three times, or has been contumacious in his absence. For a third appeal is barred, and persons condemned for contumacy cannot appeal.

## CHAPTER XLVII. A slave who has fled, if he conducts himself as free and is prepared to litigate for his freedom, is not deemed to be possessed by his master.

[Col. 1221C]

If a slave whom I possessed has fled and conducts himself as free, he is deemed to be possessed by his master; but this is to be understood only if, when apprehended, he is not prepared to litigate for his freedom. For if he is prepared to litigate, he is not deemed to be possessed by his master, against whom he has made himself an adversary.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Through a slave, tenant, or agent, prejudice cannot be caused against the owner against his will. Emperors Theodosius and Honorius, Augusti, to Pope John.

(Law *Nexum*, ch. *If any property*.) No encumbrance of estates is created except by a person legally able to bind them. Moreover, both right and the authority of the laws declare that no prejudice can be imposed upon possession, without the owner’s consent or knowledge, through a slave, agent, tenant, manager, or lessee. [Col. 1221D]

## CHAPTER XLIX. One who, through fear of a governor, falsely declares himself a slave may afterwards defend his status.

A person who, through fear and the pressure of some terror, has falsely declared himself to be a slave in the governor’s official records is not thereby prejudiced from subsequently defending his status.

## CHAPTER L. If anyone buys something from a slave without the master’s knowledge, the master may return the price, and the sale is void.

If anyone buys something from another’s slave without his master’s knowledge, and the master does not wish the purchase to stand, he shall return the price to the buyer, so that the sale has no validity. [Col. 1222A]

## CHAPTER LI. A person claiming his slave from a possessor in good faith must reimburse necessary expenses. Emperor A., to Claudius.

(Law *If against your will*, ch. *On exposed infants*.)
