If, without your consent and knowledge, the offspring of your female slave has been exposed, you are not prohibited from reclaiming him; but restitution, if you reclaim him other than from a thief, shall be made in such a way that whatever has justly been expended in feeding him, or perhaps in training him in a trade, shall be reimbursed.

## CHAPTER LII. One who has exposed his own child cannot afterwards reclaim it from the person who gathered it up and reared it. Emperors Valentinian and Gratian, Augusti, to Probus.

(Law *Let each person*, ch. *On exposed infants*.) Let every person nourish his own offspring. If he considers it should be exposed, he shall be subject to the punishment established for this; nor do we leave masters or patrons any right of reclamation if a will friendly to mercy has gathered up those whom they themselves exposed, in a manner of speaking, to death. He could not call his own one whose perishing he had despised. [Col. 1222B]

## CHAPTER LIII. On the same matter.

(Ibid., 3, *We decree*, ch. *On exposed infants*.) We decree that no one may claim into his ownership a child who has been exposed—whether the little child was born of freeborn parents, of freed stock, or of servile condition—whether under the designation of slave, adscriptitius, or tenant of a holding. Nor is permission at all granted to those who took them up in order to rear them to take them up subject to a distinction and provide for their upbringing, whether male or female, in order that they may hold them in the status of freedpersons, slaves, tenants, or adscriptitii. Rather, without any distinction, those reared by such persons are to appear free and freeborn. [Col. 1222C]

## CHAPTER LIV. One who gives away or sells the offspring of his female slave, believing it to be his own, does not commit theft.

If the person to whom the usufruct of a female slave belongs sells or gives away her offspring, believing it to be his own, he does not commit theft. For theft is not committed without an intent to steal.

## CHAPTER LV. The property of persons condemned for capital crimes shall pass to their relatives. [Col. 1222D] Code, book IX.

(Law *On prescribed property*, ch. *The property of the condemned*.) The property of persons condemned for capital crime ought not to be carried off for the governor’s profit, but restored to the relatives of those punished.

## CHAPTER LVI. Praetors must prevent anyone from being a pimp.

This constitution commands that no one be a pimp, either in the imperial city or in the provinces; and praetors and governors must prohibit this. For those who have dared to be pimps contrary to the rule of the constitution are subject to the ultimate penalty. The constitution also commands that all instruments and sureties entered into with pimps, or made by pimps contrary to good morals, are ineffective and invalid. [Col. 1223A]

## CHAPTER LVII. One who contracts marriage and has no children from a prior lawful marriage shall forfeit his property, and the dowry of an incestuous marriage shall be claimed by the fisc.

(Law I, *Whoever contrary to*, ch. *On incest*.) If anyone contracts a wicked, incestuous, and condemned marriage, and has no children from a prior lawful marriage, he shall immediately forfeit his property, and the dowry given to him shall be claimed for the rights of the fisc. After public proclamation, he shall also suffer loss of his belt of office and be punished by exile. But if he is of lower status, he shall undergo corporal examination; and his wife, married contrary to the laws, shall suffer the same penalties, unless she is excused by some just ignorance.

## CHAPTER LVIII. On the same matter.

[Col. 1223B]

(Law *If the deceased*, ch. *On one’s own and legitimate children succeeding intestate*.) If anyone leaves grandchildren through a son and grandchildren, male or female, through a daughter, they shall equally be called to the intestate inheritance of their deceased grandfather. They shall receive not less than a third part, as before, but grandchildren through a daughter shall obtain a full share; those born through a daughter shall receive such a share as grandchildren born through a son receive. Likewise, if a grandmother dies leaving grandchildren through a son and grandchildren through a daughter, all shall equally be called to their grandmother’s inheritance. There shall be no difference whatever whether all are grandsons or granddaughters, or whether they were born through a son or through a daughter.

## CHAPTER LIX.

(Institutes, *On natural and civil law*, § *From unwritten law*.) Law comes from unwritten usage which custom has approved. For long-standing customs, confirmed by the consent of those who use them, imitate law. Likewise, the enactments which each city establishes for itself are often changed, either by the tacit consent of the emperor or pope, or by another law subsequently enacted. [Col. 1223C]

## CHAPTER LX. Freedpersons who are called freeborn; who may make a testament, and who may not.

(32, question 5, ch. *Freedpersons*; and Institutes, *On freeborn persons*.) A freeborn person (*ingenuus*) is one who is free from the moment of birth, whether born in marriage from two freeborn parents, from freedpersons, or from one freedperson and one freeborn parent. But if anyone is born of a free mother and a slave father, he is nevertheless born free, just as one born of a free mother and an unknown father, because he was conceived promiscuously. It is enough that he had a free mother at the time of his birth, even if she conceived while a slave. Conversely, if she conceived while free and then, having become a slave, gives birth, it has been held that the child is born free, because the misfortune of the mother ought not to harm one who is in the womb. Hence the further question has been raised whether, if a pregnant slave is manumitted and afterwards again made a slave before giving birth, she gives birth to a free child or a slave. Marcellus holds that the child is born free. For it is enough for one in the womb to have had a free mother even for an intermediate period, in order to be born free; and this is true.

Not everyone is permitted to make a testament. Those who are immediately subject to another’s legal authority have no right of making a testament. Likewise, minors below puberty cannot make a testament, because they have no judgment of mind. Likewise, persons of unsound mind cannot do so, because they lack reason; nor does it matter if a minor afterwards reaches puberty, or a person of unsound mind afterwards recovers reason, and then dies. But persons of unsound mind who make a testament during an interval in which their madness has ceased are deemed to have made it lawfully. Likewise, a mute person and a deaf person cannot always make a testament. It plainly speaks of the deaf person who hears nothing at all, not one who hears imperfectly; and “mute” means one who cannot utter anything, not one who speaks with difficulty. When the law grants something in respect of the past, it forbids it for the future. [Col. 1223D–1224A]

## CHAPTER LXI. A child born in the seventh month is called legitimate; or thus: each expert is to be believed in his own field. [Col. 1224B] Title 5.

(Law *Seventh month*, § *On status*.) It is now accepted that a fully formed child may be born in the seventh month, on the authority of Hippocrates, a most learned man. Indeed, one born in the seventh month from a lawful marriage must be believed to be a legitimate son.

## CHAPTER LXII. A legitimately born child follows the father as to status and origin; one not legitimately born follows the mother.

(Law *When legitimate*, § *On status*; and 32, question 5, ch. *Freedpersons*.) When lawful marriage has taken place, children follow their father; those conceived promiscuously follow their mother.

## CHAPTER LXIII. Who are called conceived promiscuously.

(Law *Those sought promiscuously*, § *On status*.) Likewise, those are called conceived promiscuously who cannot identify their father, or who indeed can identify him but have a father whom they are not permitted to have.

## CHAPTER LXIV. Who are said to be born according to the law of nature.

(Law *Natural law*, § *On status*.) Likewise, natural law provides that one born outside lawful marriage follows the mother.

## CHAPTER LXV. Before birth, an offspring is said to exist in the natural order because something may be left to it.

(Law *Those in the womb*, § *On status*.) Likewise, those who are in the womb are understood, throughout almost the whole civil law, to exist in the order of things. Thus even lawful inheritances are restored to them, so that if a pregnant woman has been captured by enemies, the child born—even though she gives birth while with a purchaser in good faith—is not acquired by usucaption, as being stolen property. [Col. 1224D]

## CHAPTER LXVI. Property promised in writings belongs to the person who already holds it by force of the writings, whether he is the first or last heir in order.

If someone has given one thing by lawful writings to two persons, first to one and afterwards to another, the question in these gifts is not who received first and who later, but who, upon delivery by the donor, possessed the thing: that person shall possess the thing delivered to him. It makes no difference whether such a gift was made to relatives or strangers.

Although a later claimant offers an oath, the person accused may, even when there is no proof of the debt, establish his good faith by the solemnity of an oath. If a person sued for money spontaneously offers an oath, and the other voluntarily allows him the necessity of swearing, he cannot afterwards demand the debt from him. [Col. 1225A]

The heir of one said to have lent money cannot be called upon to swear an oath, because he could not fully know what his predecessor did.

## CHAPTER LXVII. In things lent for use, accidental loss is not included unless fault intervenes.

(Law *If for a certain purpose*, § *Accordingly*.) Whatever has been expended on a thing lent for use because of illness or another reason may be claimed from the owner. If the thing lent is lost through an act of God, fire, collapse, shipwreck, or any similar event, the person to whom it was lent is not liable on that account, unless perhaps, though able to save the thing lent, he preferred his own property.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. A thing lent is lost to its lender when the loss or damage results from a use other than that for which it was lent.

(Law *If for a certain purpose*, § *But meanwhile*.) If anyone receives from another a slave, horse, or any other thing lent merely for use in service, and takes them into battle or to a place where they incur danger to life, he is rightly held liable by the owner for restoration of the thing lent.

## CHAPTER LXIX. A contract made solely for the benefit of the person delivering the thing is lost at that person’s risk.

(Law *If for a certain purpose*, no. *It must be seen*; and Law *You asked*, clause *In what manner*.) If someone entrusts an article to another for sale at a stated price, and while it is being offered for sale by that person it perishes for any reason, the loss falls upon the person who gave it to be sold. But if the recipient loses the thing received while wishing to sell it, not at the owner’s request but with his permission, he incurs the loss of the thing himself. [Col. 1225C]

If a creditor holding a pledge deposited with him without condition summons his debtor three times to redeem his pledges by paying the debt, and the debtor, after three warnings, refuses to redeem them upon payment of the debt, the creditor has free authority to sell the pledge.

If another’s animal causes damage to anyone or injures someone’s crops, its owner shall either pay the assessed damage or surrender the animal. The same rule has been established concerning a dog. But no action is granted against either the owner or keeper when someone, by his own provocation, has incited a wild beast or any other quadruped against himself and it causes damage. [Col. 1225D]

## CHAPTER LXX. All sureties, jointly and severally, are bound to pay when the principal obligor does not pay.

(Law *Among sureties*, § *If there are several*; and from Hadrian’s letter.) When there are many sureties, even though all are found able to pay what they promised and might all be bound for the whole amount, repayment of the debt must nevertheless be divided among them, so that each pays what falls to him in proportion to his share.

Whoever is proved to have struck counterfeit coin shall have his hands cut off; whoever consents to this, if free, shall pay sixty solidi, but if a slave, shall receive sixty blows. A person in whose possession the crime is discovered and a share of the plunder is found shall immediately be compelled to name his accomplices. If he refuses to name them, he shall be liable to punishment. [Col. 1226A]

A son or heir may not act against a just or lawful determination made by his predecessors, because the presumption of one who attempts unjustly to overthrow the acts of his elders is rightly repelled. Not only the person who committed theft, but also anyone who was an accomplice or knowingly received goods offered from theft, shall be counted among thieves and be subject to like punishment.

## CHAPTER LXXI. No property shall be bought unless the seller’s reliability, and other matters of this sort, have been ascertained.

(Law *Civil*, ch. *On theft*; and Law *The greater*, ch. *On forgery*.) No one shall buy a horse, ox, beast of burden, or any animal unless he knows the person who sold it, whose it is, where he lives, and who is his lord.

## CHAPTER LXXII. Damage caused by accident falls, more or less, upon the owner of the thing causing it.

[Col. 1226B]

(Ch. *If an ox*, Extra, *On injuries and damage caused*.) If one man’s ox wounds another man’s ox and it dies, he shall sell the living ox and divide both its price and the carcass. But if its owner knew that the ox was dangerous and did not keep it confined, he shall give ox for ox and receive the entire carcass (Exodus XXI).

## CHAPTER LXXIII. A thief shall restore even fivefold the price of the theft.

Whoever steals an ox shall restore five oxen for one, and four sheep for one sheep.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. A daytime thief is not killed without guilt, but a nighttime thief is.

(Ch. *Breaking through*, Extra, *On homicide*; and Law *Therefore*, § *The law under the Lex Aquilia*.) If a thief breaks into a house or is found tunnelling beneath it, and dies after receiving a wound, the person who struck him shall not be guilty of blood. But if he does this after sunrise, he has committed homicide. [Col. 1226C]

## CHAPTER LXXIV. Though a thief damages what is least valuable, he must make restitution from what is best.

If anyone damages a field or vineyard and lets his beast graze another’s property, he shall restore, as compensation for the damage, whatever best produce he has in the vineyard or field.

## CHAPTER LXXV. An arsonist is liable for damage resulting from a fire.

If fire that has escaped encounters sheaves and catches heaps of grain or standing crops in the fields, the person who kindled the fire shall pay the damage.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. Ownership of certain things is acquired by natural law, of others by civil law. [Col. 1226D] Institutes 52, title 1.

Wild beasts, birds, fish, and all animals born upon land, in the sea, and in the sky begin at once, when captured by anyone, to belong to that person by the law of nations. For what previously belongs to no one is, by natural reason, granted to the occupier. Nor does it matter whether one captures wild beasts or birds on one’s own land or on another’s. Of course, a person entering another’s land for hunting, taking possession, or another purpose may be forbidden entry by the owner if the latter foresees it.

Whatever of these animals you have captured is understood to be yours only so long as it is restrained by your custody. When it escapes your custody and returns to natural freedom, it ceases to be yours and becomes the property of the next occupier. It is understood to have returned to natural freedom when either it has escaped your sight or, though remaining in sight, its pursuit is difficult. [Col. 1227A]

The question has been asked whether a wild animal so wounded that it can be captured is immediately understood to be yours. Some have held that it is yours, and is deemed yours so long as you pursue it; but if you cease pursuit, it ceases to be yours and again becomes the property of the next occupier. Others held that it becomes yours only if you capture it. But we do not confirm the latter opinion, because many events may occur which prevent you from capturing it.

Bees also are wild by nature. Accordingly, bees which settle in your tree are no more understood to be yours before you enclose them in a hive than birds which nest in your tree. Therefore, if someone else encloses them, he becomes their owner. Anyone may also remove whatever honeycombs they have made. Yet, while the matter remains intact, if you see someone entering your land, you may lawfully forbid him entry. A swarm in your hive is likewise understood to be yours so long as it is in your sight and its pursuit is not difficult; otherwise it becomes the property of the next occupier. [Col. 1227B]

Peacocks and doves are wild by nature, and it is irrelevant that by habit they often fly away and return. For bees do the same, though they are admittedly wild by nature. Some people likewise keep deer so tame that they customarily go into the woods and return; yet no one denies that these too are wild by nature. [Col. 1228A]

For animals which habitually come and go, the approved rule is that they are deemed yours so long as they have the intention of returning. Once they cease to have the intention of returning, they also cease to be yours and belong to occupiers. They are deemed to cease having the intention of returning when they abandon their custom of returning.

Hens and geese are not wild by nature; this may be understood from the fact that there are other hens which we call wild hens, and likewise other geese which we call wild geese. Therefore, if your geese or hens, alarmed by some accident, fly away, they are nevertheless understood to be yours wherever they may be, even if they escape your sight; and one who keeps those animals for gain is understood to commit theft. [Col. 1228B]

# ON THE SENTENCE OF EXCOMMUNICATION, AND ON THE POWER OF BINDING AND LOOSING.

[Col. 1227]

## CHAPTER LXXVII. Saint Peter hands on to Clement the power of binding and loosing. [Col. 1227C] Clement to James.

“Blessed Peter said: ‘I hand over to Clement the power of binding and loosing delivered to me by the Lord, so that whatever he decrees on earth concerning all matters may be decreed also in heaven. For he will bind what ought to be bound and loose what it is expedient to loose, as one who knows precisely the rule of the Church.’

“Likewise: ‘O Clement, let all receive your words with such reverence that they may know you to be the law through the preaching of truth; and whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall also be loosed there. For, as I have said, you will bind what ought to be bound and loose what it is expedient to loose.’” [Col. 1227D]

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. One whose life does not accord with his office may loose others while himself bound. Gregory, Homily 26 on the Gospels.

(11, question 3, ch. *Often*.) It frequently happens that one occupies the place of judge whose life is least in harmony with that office; and it often occurs that he either condemns the innocent or, himself bound, looses others. In loosing and binding those subject to him, the pastor often follows the impulses of his own will, rather than the merits of the cases.

## CHAPTER LXXIX. One who exercises the power of binding and loosing unjustly deprives himself of that power. Gregory, from the same homily.

(11, question 3, ch. *He himself binds*; and ch. *Often*, § *Hence it happens*.) Hence it follows that one deprives himself of the power of binding and loosing when he exercises it according to his own wishes and not according to the conduct of those subject to him. It often happens that a pastor is moved toward some neighbour by hatred or favour. [Col. 1228C]

## CHAPTER LXXX. On the same matter. Gregory, from the same homily.

(11, question 3, ch. *To judge*; and ch. *Often*, § *To judge*.) Those who follow their own hatreds or favour in the cases of their subjects cannot judge their subjects worthily. Hence the prophet rightly says: “They put to death souls that do not die” (Ezekiel XIII). For one puts to death a person who is not dying when he condemns the just; and one attempts to give life to a person who will not live when he tries to absolve the guilty from punishment. Cases, therefore, must be weighed, and then the power of binding and loosing exercised. One must see what fault preceded and what repentance followed the fault, so that those whom almighty God visits by the grace of compunction may be absolved by pastoral judgment. [Col. 1228D]

## CHAPTER LXXXI. The absolution of one who presides is not true unless it follows the judgment of the inner Judge. Saint Gregory, Homily 56 on the Gospels.

(11, question 3, ch. *Then true*.) Then the absolution of the one who presides is true when it follows the judgment of the inner Judge. This is well signified by the raising of Lazarus, dead four days, which shows that the Lord called and gave life to the dead man, saying: “Lazarus, come forth” (John XI). Afterwards, the man who had come out alive was loosed by His disciples, as it is written: “And when he who had been bound had come forth, Jesus then said to the disciples: ‘Loose him, and let him go’” (ibid.).

Behold, the disciples loose one already alive, whom the Master had raised when dead. For if the disciples loosed the dead man, they would display a creative power rather than a ministry. From this consideration we ought to understand that we must not loose by pastoral authority those whom we know our Author has made alive through the grace that raises the dead. This enlivening is already recognized, before uprightness of conduct, in the very confession of sin. Therefore the dead man is not told, “Come back to life,” but, “Come forth.” [Col. 1229A]

For every sinner, while concealing his fault within his conscience, lies hidden inwardly in his secret chambers. But the dead man comes forth when the sinner voluntarily confesses his wickedness. Therefore Lazarus is told, “Come forth,” as though it were openly said to every dead person in sin: “Why do you conceal your guilt within your conscience? Come forth through confession, you who lie hidden inwardly within yourself through conscience.” Let the dead person therefore come forth—that is, let the sinner confess his fault—and let the disciples loose him when he comes forth, so that the pastors of the Church should remove the penalty deserved by one who is not ashamed to confess what he has done. I have said these things briefly concerning the order of loosing, so that pastors of the Church may strive to loose or bind only with great moderation. [Col. 1229B]

## CHAPTER LXXXII. Holy men pronounce certain curses not from a desire for vengeance, but from love of justice. Gregory, *Morals*, book IV, chapter 6.

(24, question, ch. *When holy men*.) When holy men pronounce a sentence of cursing, they do not burst forth into it from a desire for vengeance but from the assessment of justice. They behold the subtle judgment within and know with what curse outwardly arising evils ought to be struck; and they do not sin by that curse, because they do not dissent from the inner Judge.

Likewise, Sacred Scripture records a curse in two ways: one which it approves and another which it condemns. A curse is pronounced in one way by the judgment of justice, as was proved when the first human being sinned and heard, “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Genesis III), and when Abraham is told, “I shall curse those who curse you” (Genesis XII). Again, because a curse is pronounced otherwise—not by a judgment of justice but through the rancour of vengeance—and is punished, we are admonished by Paul’s preaching to refrain from it when he says: “Bless, and do not curse” (Romans XII). [Col. 1229C–D]

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. Justice will break unjust bonds. Augustine, Sermon 16, on Matthew.

(11, question 3, ch. *You have begun*.) You have begun to regard your brother as a publican; you bind him on earth, but see that you bind justly. For justice breaks unjust bonds. But when you have corrected and been reconciled with your brother, you have loosed him on earth; he shall be loosed also in heaven.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV. Before God, one who pronounces a sentence at variance with conduct is accursed. Jerome, on the Epistle to Philemon.

(11, question 3, ch. *If anyone says*.) Whoever calls the just unjust, and again the unjust just, is abominable before God in either case. Likewise, one who says that a holy person is not holy, and again asserts that an unholy person is holy, is abominable before God. [Col. 1230A]

## CHAPTER LXXXV. Jerome on Matthew, book III.

“I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven” (Matthew XVI). Bishops and presbyters, not understanding this passage, assume for themselves something of the arrogance of the Pharisees, so that they either condemn the innocent or imagine that they can loose the guilty. Yet before God, it is not the knowledge of priests but the life of the accused that is examined.

We read in Leviticus concerning lepers, where they are commanded to show themselves to the priests; and if they have leprosy, then they are made unclean or clean by the priest (Leviticus XIII). This is not because priests make persons unclean, but because they possess knowledge of lepers and can discern who is clean and who unclean. [Col. 1230B]

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. The judgment of a pastor does not make a person guilty or innocent. Jerome on Matthew, chapter XVI.

(11, question 3, ch. *How the priest*.) Therefore, just as the priest does not make a leper clean, so a bishop or presbyter neither binds the innocent nor looses the guilty; but, by virtue of his office, when he has heard the varieties of sins, he knows who ought to be bound and who ought to be loosed.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. Augustine on John, part I, tractate 10, book IV, chapter *When*.

[Col. 1230C]

When the Church excommunicates, the excommunicated person is bound in heaven; when the Church reconciles, the reconciled person is loosed in heaven.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. Ecclesiastical bonds are not to be despised. Chrysostom, on the Epistle to the Hebrews, tractate 4.

(From the same source, and 11, question 3, ch. *Let no one despise*.) Let no one despise ecclesiastical bonds. It is not a human being who binds, but Christ, who gave this power and made human beings worthy of such great honour.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. We separate from God those whom we declare impious. From the Fifth Synod, act 5, book IV.

[Col. 1230D] (24, question 3, ch. *It is certain*.) It is certain that one declared impious is in every way separated from God, just as one anathematized is separated as impious. For anathema signifies nothing other than separation from God.

## CHAPTER XC. What care bishops should exercise toward those who act unjustly, and how they should punish them. Council of Meaux, chapter 3.

A bishop in whose parish someone resides who has done something unjust shall summon him, once, twice, and a third time if necessary, by his messenger and through canonical admonition, to admonition or settlement and to repentance, so that he may make satisfaction to God and to the Church which he has injured. But if he despises and scorns this admonition and most salutary invitation, the bishop shall strike him with the pastoral rod—that is, with the sentence of excommunication—so that he may be separated from the communion of the holy Church and of all Christians until suitable satisfaction and worthy amendment. The bishop must make this excommunication known to that man’s superior, to all his fellow bishops, and to all his parishioners, so that they do not receive him until satisfaction has been made. [Col. 1231A]

## CHAPTER XCI. How one who acts perversely, has been admonished, and is not corrected is to be punished. Council of Rouen, chapter 3.

Let your charity know, most dear brothers, that a certain man, named N., at the devil’s persuasion, setting aside the Christian promise which he confessed in baptism, has by apostasy turned back after Satan, whom he renounced along with all his pomps. He does not fear to lay waste Christ’s vineyard—that is, His Church—violently oppressing and killing Christ’s poor, whom He redeemed with His precious blood, and plundering their goods.

We sent our priest and letters of admonition to him once, twice, and three times, canonically inviting him to amendment, satisfaction, and repentance, correcting him with fatherly affection. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him” (Matthew XVIII). Whoever sins against the holy Church sins against each one of us as a brother. For if the holy Church is one body, whose head is Christ, while we individually are members one of another, and if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it, then undoubtedly he sins against us who harms our members. [Col. 1231B–C]

The Lord therefore commands that a brother—that is, a Christian—who sins against us first be rebuked privately. But if he despises these three admonitions and godly corrections, and scorns to make satisfaction, then after these things, He says: “Let him be to you as a heathen and a publican” (ibid.); that is, as a Gentile and pagan, so that he is now regarded not as a Christian but as a pagan.

And elsewhere the Lord commands that a member which is loosened from its union, separated from the bond of charity, and causes scandal to the whole body, be cut off and cast away, saying: “If your eye, hand, or foot causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it from you” (ibid.). And the Apostle says: “Put away the evil person from among yourselves” (I Corinthians V). And again: “If anyone called a brother is a fornicator, adulterer, murderer, robber, with such a person it is not permitted even to eat” (ibid.). John, Christ’s disciple chosen above the rest, forbade greeting such a wicked person, saying: “Do not even say ‘Hail’ to him, nor receive him into your house. For whoever says ‘Hail’ to him shares in his evil works” (II John X). [Col. 1231C–D]

Therefore, fulfilling the Lord’s and the apostles’ commands, let us cut off from the body of the Church with the sword of excommunication the putrid and incurable member which will not receive medicine, lest the remaining members of the body be killed by the poison of so pestilential a member.

## CHAPTER XCII. The form of excommunication and the words by which someone is to be declared excommunicated. [Col. 1232A] Council of Orléans.

Therefore, instructed by the Lord’s and the apostles’ commands, by the judgment of God the Father, the Son our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit, and by the authority and power granted by God to the apostles and their successors, together with you we exclude the aforesaid man from the thresholds of the holy mother Church; we separate him from the fellowship of the good and from Christian communion; and we decree that he is separated for eternity, that is, in the present age and in the age to come.

Let no Christian say “Hail” to him or presume to kiss him. Let no priest dare celebrate Mass with him or administer to him the most holy body and blood of the Lord. Let no one join him in companionship or in any business. And if anyone associates with him and shares in his evil deeds, let him know that he is struck with a like anathema—except those who join him for this purpose: to recall him from error and call him to satisfaction—unless perhaps he comes to his senses and, inspired by God’s grace, turns to the remedy of repentance and humbly makes satisfaction to the Church of God which he has injured through worthy amendment. [Col. 1232B]

## CHAPTER XCIII. For what faults a person is to be deprived of communion. Council of Meaux, chapter 3.

(11, question 3, ch. *Let no bishop*.) Let no bishop deprive anyone of ecclesiastical communion without a definite and manifest cause of sin. Moreover, let no one presume to place anyone under anathema without the knowledge of the archbishop or fellow bishops, except in cases authorized by canonical authority; for anathema is a condemnation to eternal death and ought to be imposed only for a mortal crime, and upon one who cannot otherwise be corrected. [Col. 1232C]

## CHAPTER XCIV. Whoever communicates with excommunicated persons is excommunicated. Pope Calixtus to the bishops of Gaul.

(11, question 3, ch. *The excommunicated*.) Let no one receive persons excommunicated by priests before a just examination of both parties; nor communicate with them in prayer, food, drink, or a kiss, nor say “Hail” to them. For whoever knowingly communicates with excommunicated persons in these or other prohibited ways is himself subject, according to the institution of the apostles, to a like excommunication. [Col. 1232D]

## CHAPTER XCV. Excommunicated is the person who communicates with excommunicated persons. Pope Fabian, Epistle 2.

(11, question 3, ch. *As the apostles*.) One must not communicate with excommunicated persons. If anyone communicates with an excommunicated person by setting aside the rules, knowingly speaking with him even in the same house or praying with him, that person shall be deprived of communion.

## CHAPTER XCVI. On the same matter. From Martin’s Canon, addressed to the laity.

(11, q. 3, c. *Cum excom.* and *Qui commun.*) [Col. 1233A] It is not permitted to communicate with excommunicated persons, nor, upon entering their houses, to pray with them. But if any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or any ecclesiastic communicates with excommunicated persons, he too is to be excommunicated, as one disturbing all ecclesiastical discipline.

### CHAPTER XCVII. Clerics who communicate with excommunicated persons are to be deprived of communion. Council of Antioch, canon 2.

(*Extr. de Sent. excommun.*, and c. *Signif.*) If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or any member of the clergy is caught communicating with excommunicated persons, he himself also is to be deprived of communion, as one who confounds the rule of the Church.

### CHAPTER XCVIII. Whoever communicates with excommunicated persons incurs the penalty of excommunication. [Col. 1233B] Second Council of Carthage, canon 7.

(11, q. 3, c. *Qui merito*.) Those who have rightly been expelled from the Church because of their crimes, if they are received into communion by any bishop or presbyter, bind those persons themselves by the same liabilities, since they evade the regular judgment of their own bishop.

### CHAPTER XCIX. On the same matter, c. *Qui communicaverit*. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 73.

(11, q. 3, c. *Qui communicaverit*.) Whoever communicates or prays with an excommunicated person, if a layman, is to be excommunicated; if a cleric, he is to be deposed.

### CHAPTER C. A person excommunicated by one bishop ought not be received into communion by another. Council of Sanc[?], canon 15.

[Col. 1233C] Whether deacon, presbyter, or any cleric has been deprived of communion by his own bishop and goes to another bishop: if the bishop to whom he flees knows that he has been rejected by his own bishop, he ought not grant him communion. If he does so, let him know that, when the bishops are assembled, he will have to answer the charge.

### CHAPTER CI. A person excommunicated by his own bishop is not to be received by another. Council of Antioch, canon 6.

(11, q. 3, c. *Si quis a proprio episc.*) If anyone has been deprived of communion by his own bishop, he is not to be received by others before he has been reconciled to his own bishop, or at least has hastened to the assembled synod and made satisfaction on his own behalf.

### CHAPTER CII. Concerning those who presume to communicate during their excommunication. [Col. 1233D] Nicholas, to Epiphanius, bishop, at the African council.

(11, q. 3, c. *Placuit*.) We decree that, if anyone has been excommunicated by his own bishop for some neglect or crime, he is not to be communicated by another bishop. But if, before the hearing, he has presumed to communicate, let him recognize that the sentence of his condemnation has been imposed upon him.

### CHAPTER CIII. On the same matter. Apostolic Canon 11, and Isidore.

(11, q. 3, c. *Cum excommun.*) If anyone has so much as spoken or prayed in a house with an excommunicated person, he is to be deprived of communion.

### CHAPTER CIV. What penance is due from priests who, while excommunicated, presume to handle the sacred mystery. [Col. 1234A] John VIII, to the clergy and orders of Salerno.

(11, q. 3, c. *De illis presbyteris*.) Concerning those presbyters who, while excommunicated in the time of our most holy predecessor, Lord Pope Nicholas, presumed to handle the sacred mystery: they brought upon themselves the sentence of condemnation, as the sacred canons prescribe. Yet, because apostolic mercy is accustomed to grant pardon to those who are corrected, we extend to them this indulgence, on account of the abundance of mercy: strengthened by holy communion, they are to strive, for three continuous years, every week and at all times, to fast completely from either wine or meat on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, and never again to commit deeds requiring lamentation. [Col. 1234B]

### CHAPTER CV. Those who receive sacraments from excommunicated persons are schismatics.

If you receive any sacraments from persons whom we regard as excommunicated, it is plain that you seem to have abandoned idolatry not as the other Catholics have done, but in such a way that you become schismatics.

### CHAPTER CVI. Concerning those who communicate with excommunicated persons. Nicholas to Ignarus, Archbishop of Rheims.

(11, q. 3, c. *Excell. rex Car.*) The most excellent King Charles consulted our apostolic see concerning what should be done about those who communicate with persons who communicate with Engeltrude, a woman repeatedly condemned, since it is evident that she, together with her communicants and supporters, [Col. 1234C] is bound by an equal bond of anathema. Therefore we now charge your blessedness that, relying on our authority, you should take care in this matter. Since your divinely instructed holiness knows well that one thing is sinning through ignorance and another is sinning deliberately—and that the latter is to be punished more strictly than the two former cases—let it watch carefully and judge the circumstances with prudent discernment, so that those who offend from necessity or ignorance may be absolved through you by our authority.

This is so, however, only if their ignorance or necessity itself has been genuine and not feigned, and has not arisen from their own will; for, as you well know, many are able but unwilling to know what is right. Hence the Psalmist says of such persons: “He was unwilling to understand, so as to do good” [Col. 1234D] (Psalm 35). But those who bind themselves by their own deliberate choice and, in contempt of our prohibitions, set them aside, we will by no means have absolved by you unless worthy satisfaction has first been made.

### CHAPTER CVII. Those who communicate with excommunicated persons are to be punished according to the manner of their sin. Urban II, to Genebald, bishop of Constance.

(11, q. 3, c. *Sanctis quippe*.) The holy canons plainly provide that whoever communicates with an excommunicated person is to be excommunicated. Yet we determine the manner of penance and absolution with this moderation: whoever has incurred contamination through ignorance, fear, necessity arising from some very great and especially necessary business, cohabitation, greeting, prayer, or a kiss, is to receive, as a participant in our society, the remedy of a lighter penance. But those who have fallen into it willingly, spontaneously, or negligently, we will have received under such discipline and restraint that fear may be instilled into others. [Col. 1235A]

### CHAPTER CVIII. Priests are regarded as the fathers and teachers of kings and princes. Gregory to Herman, bishop of Metz.

(Dist. 96, c. *Quis dubitet*.) Who can doubt that the priests of Christ are regarded as the fathers and teachers of kings, princes, and all the faithful? Would it not be recognized as pitiable madness if a son attempted to subject his father, or a disciple his teacher, to himself, and to make him subject to his own power by unjust bonds—him by [Col. 1235B] whom he believes that he himself may be bound and loosed not only on earth but also in heaven?

Thus Blessed Gregory recalls in a letter addressed to Emperor Maurice. Constantine the Great, emperor and lord of nearly all the kings and princes of the whole world, clearly understood this. At the holy Council of Nicaea, sitting last after all the bishops, he presumed to pronounce no judgment upon them; indeed, calling them his lords, he judged that they ought not be subject to his judgment, but that he depended on their decision. The aforementioned Pope Gelasius also sought to persuade Anastasius not to regard as an injury the truth impressed upon his mind, adding:

### CHAPTER CIX. The helm of this world is governed by the sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power.

[Col. 1235C]

(Dist. 95, c. *Duo quippe*.) “There are indeed two powers, Emperor Augustus, by which this world is chiefly governed: the consecrated authority of pontiffs and royal power. The burden of priests is so much the weightier, in that they will render account, in the divine judgment, even for the kings of men themselves.” And after a few intervening words he says: “You know, therefore, that you depend upon their judgment, not that they are to be reduced to your will.”

Supported by such institutions and authorities, many pontiffs have excommunicated kings and emperors. For if an example concerning princely persons in particular is sought: Blessed Pope Innocent excommunicated Emperor Arcadius because he consented to the expulsion of Saint John Chrysostom from his see. Another Roman pontiff deposed the king of the Franks from his kingdom, not so much for his own wickedness as because he was unfit for so great a power; he set Pepin, father of Emperor Charles, in his place and absolved all the Franks from their oath of fidelity. The holy Church also acts thus on frequent authority when it absolves soldiers from the bond of the oath made to bishops who are deposed from episcopal rank by apostolic authority.

And Blessed Ambrose, though holy, was not bishop of the universal Church; nevertheless, for a fault which did not seem so grave to other priests, he excommunicated and excluded from the Church [Col. 1236A] the great Emperor Theodosius. In his writings he also shows that gold is not more precious than lead to the same degree that the priestly rank is higher than royal power. At approximately the beginning of his *Pastoral* he writes:

“Honour, brothers, and the exalted dignity of the episcopate cannot be compared with anything at all. If you compare it with the splendour of kings and the diadem of princes, it will stand far above them, as the brightness of gold surpasses the substance of lead. For you see the necks of kings and princes bowed at the knees of priests; having kissed their right hands, they believe themselves fortified by their prayers.”

And shortly afterward: “You ought to understand, brothers, that we have set forth all these things in advance in order to show that nothing in this world is more excellent than priests, nothing more exalted than bishops.” [Col. 1236B]

Did not, as Blessed Gregory says, Pope Julius of revered memory pronounce a sentence of condemnation against Theodora and against the Empress? Likewise, when Charibert, king of Paris, had abandoned his lawful wife Theoberga and taken as wives two sisters, Metroflidis and Marcovena, he was excommunicated by Blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris; and, since he refused to repent, he died not long afterward by divine judgment.

### CHAPTER CX. We are not bound by an oath of fidelity to excommunicated persons. Gregory, Roman Synod VII.

(15, q. 6, c. *Nos sanctorum*.) Following the ordinances of our predecessors, by apostolic authority we absolve from their oath those who are bound to excommunicated persons by fidelity or oath, until those persons make satisfaction; and we forbid them to observe fidelity toward them. [Col. 1236C]

### CHAPTER CXI. Before they are reconciled, no one is compelled to maintain fidelity toward excommunicated persons. Urban VII, to the bishops of Vaison and Die.

(15, q. 6, c. *Juratos*.) Forbid the soldiers who have sworn allegiance to the knight Hugh to serve him while he is excommunicated. If they invoke their oaths, they should be admonished that they must serve God rather than men; for they are bound by no authority to render the fidelity which they swore to a Christian prince who opposes God and His saints and tramples their commands underfoot. [Col. 1236D]

### CHAPTER CXII. For these three offences anyone is to be deprived of communion. Council of Tribur, canon 30.

(11, q. 3, c. *Certum*.) It was asked in the same synod for what causes any person ought to be bound by episcopal authority with the bond of anathema. By the unanimous decision of all it was decreed that this should be done for these three offences: when a person, canonically ordered to come to a synod, scorns to come; or, after coming there, refuses to obey priestly commands; or, before the examination of his case has been completed, presumes to depart as a fugitive from the synod.

### CHAPTER CXIII. Whatever is consecrated to the Lord belongs by right to the priest. [Col. 1237A] From the Decree of Pope Boniface, canon 5.

(12, q. 7, c. *Nulli liceat*.) No one may be ignorant that everything consecrated to God—whether a human being, an animal, a field, or anything whatever once consecrated—will be a most holy thing to the Lord and belongs by right to priests. Therefore everyone who takes away, devastates, invades, or seizes that which belongs to the Lord and the Church is to be judged guilty of sacrilege, without excuse, until amendment and satisfaction have been made to the Church. And if he refuses to make restitution, he is to be excommunicated.

### CHAPTER CXIV. Those who attack pilgrims or poor persons not bearing arms are to be excommunicated. [Col. 1238A] From the Decree of Nicholas, canon 16.

(22, q. 3, c. *Illi qui peregrinos*.) Nicholas, pope of Rome, to all bishops: Those who plunder pilgrims or supplicants of any saint, whether clerics, monks, women, or unarmed poor persons; who seize their goods; or who attack them with evil intent, are to be struck with the bond of anathema unless they make worthy amendment. Moreover, the peace which we formerly called the truce is to be observed as it was established by the archbishops and bishops of each province. Whoever violates it is to be subject to excommunication. Therefore the aforesaid holy synod judged that all such provisions contained authentically in the sacred canons ought to be observed.

## CONCERNING WHETHER HERETICS ARE TO BE EXCOMMUNICATED AFTER DEATH.

[Col. 1237]

### CHAPTER CXV. Heretics are to be excommunicated even after death. [Col. 1237B] Fifth Synod, session 1.

(24, q. 2, c. *Sane secundo in prim.*) Some people indeed maintain that heretics ought not to be anathematized after death and claim to follow in this the teaching of the holy Fathers, who not only condemned living heretics but also restored after death those who had been unjustly condemned, writing them in the sacred diptychs. This was done in the case of John and Flavian, devout bishops of Constantinople.

### CHAPTER CXVI. On the same matter. [Col. 1237C] The same Synod, session 5, and Augustine.

(24, q. 2, c. *Sane secundo*, § *Etsi forte*.) If these books identify their deliverer as plainly as the Lord identified Judas, let it be read in them by name and expressly that either Caecilian or the ordainers of those same books were deliverers; and unless I anathematize them, may I myself be judged to have delivered them with those persons.

What has now been recited, Augustine of holy memory established should fittingly be held as having been so from the beginning in the Church. For the impious doctrine has already been condemned and denounced, and the Church’s tradition requires that those liable to such a doctrine be anathematized, even if they were dead. Therefore Augustine of holy memory said: “If Caecilian were now convicted of the things alleged against him, I would anathematize him even after death.” [Col. 1237D]

Likewise: “Many bishops were assembled. While making certain provisions concerning various matters belonging to ecclesiastical order, they decreed concerning deceased persons who leave their property to heretics that they too should be subject to anathema after death.”

There are also letters of Saint Augustine of holy memory stating that, if persons did not hold sound views during their life, even if they had not yet been condemned while living, nevertheless, once their sin had been shown, they should be subjected to anathema even after [Col. 1238B] death. Likewise: “If the charges made against Caecilian are true and could at some time be shown to us, we would anathematize him though dead.” Likewise: “You say that I may judge even concerning the dead, because judgment may be made not only concerning the living but also concerning the dead.”

Likewise: “Rambulas, bishop of the city of Edessa, of holy memory, who shone among priests, anathematized Theodore of Mopsuestia in the Church even after his death.” Likewise: “The Church of the Romans also, a few years ago, excommunicated Dioscorus, who had been pope of that same Church, even after his death, though he had not sinned in faith. All the Romans living here know this, especially those who hold offices, who also remained communicants of that same Dioscorus until his death.” [Col. 1238C]

Likewise: “If anyone goes back to the time of Theophilus of holy memory or earlier, he will find that Origen was anathematized after death. Your Holiness has now done the same in this case, as has the most religious Pope Vigilius of elder Rome.” Likewise: “The holy synod said: What has been said and produced is sufficient to demonstrate the ecclesiastical tradition: heretics must be anathematized even after death.”

### CHAPTER CXVII. Heretics are to be excommunicated even after death. The same Synod, session 4.

(24, q. 2, c. *Sane*.) The holy synod said: “Various letters of Augustine of revered memory, who shone among the African bishops, have been read, showing that heretics too must be anathematized after death. Other most reverend African bishops likewise observed such ecclesiastical tradition; and the holy Roman Church anathematized certain bishops even after death, though they had not been accused of error in faith during their lives. The proceedings held among us attest both points.” [Col. 1238D]

### CHAPTER CXVIII. Those who refused to be absolved by the Church in this life cannot be absolved by it after death. [Col. 1239A] Leo, to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, epistle 90.

(24, q. 2, c. *De communione*.) Concerning those deprived of communion and so deceased, their case must be reserved to the judgment of Him in whose power it was that the deaths of such persons should not be delayed until the remedy of communion. But those with whom we did not communicate while they lived, we cannot communicate with when they are dead.

### CHAPTER CXIX. The Church can bind or loose the living, but not the dead. Pope Gregory to Faustus, master of the soldiers.

(24, q. 11, c. *Legatur*.) We read that Christ raised the dead; we do not read that He absolved them while in error. And He alone had the power to do so, yet He commands the blessed Apostle Peter in particular: “Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound,” etc. [Col. 1239B] (Matthew 16). “Upon earth,” He says; for in the matter of binding He never said that a dead person was to be loosed.

### CHAPTER CXX. The offering of one who hastened to repentance but could not find a priest ought not be rejected. Council of Epaone, canon 11.

(26, q. 6, c. *Ad poenitent.*) If an excommunicated person dies after having confessed, has a good testimony, and was unable to come to a priest because death overtook him at home or on the road, his relatives are to make an offering for him at the altar and give a ransom for captives.

### CHAPTER CXXI. A person remaining bound after the bishop’s death is to be loosed by his successor. [Col. 1239C] Council of Epaone.

(11, q. 3, c. *Si episcopus*.) If a bishop is taken by death before the absolution of one whom he has condemned, his successor may absolve the corrected or penitent person.

### CHAPTER CXXII. Communion is not to be denied to those hanged on gibbets. Council of Worms.

(13, q. 2, c. *Quaesitum*.) Certain brothers asked concerning those who are hanged on gibbets for their crimes, after making confession to God, [Col. 1240A] whether their bodies should be brought to churches, offerings made for them, and masses celebrated for them, or not. We answer: if, according to the commands of the canons, communion is to be given at the end to those who make a pure confession of all their sins and do worthy penance, why should the canons forbid communion or burial to those who pay the ultimate penalty for their sins, and who confess or desire to confess? For it is written: “God does not judge twice for the same thing” (Nahum 1:9, according to the Septuagint).

### CHAPTER CXXIII. We ought not abstain after death from the alms of one with whom we did not refuse communion during life. Urban to Bishop Julimundus.

[Col. 1240B] (24, q. 2, c. *Sane primo*.) Certainly, we commend your fraternity’s action concerning Richard, son of Borrell, undertaken out of zeal for God and love for souls. But you need not fear so greatly, nor need you abstain so strictly from his alms. For Blessed Leo, an outstanding teacher among the Fathers of our faith, says: “Those with whom we do not communicate while alive, we ought not communicate with when dead.” It follows, therefore, that those with whom we communicated while living—if we may speak by contrast—we may also communicate with when dead.

We are plainly placed between two opposing parties, the impious and the schismatics. With schismatics we can in no way communicate; but with the others—that is, sinners and robbers—we communicate dispensatorily, because until now they have supported the Church and promise to be more faithful in the future. Otherwise we would have to depart from the regions of this world. On this undertaking also we recently granted them absolution at the feast of Saint Peter’s Nativity. Since, therefore, the aforesaid man was neither expressly excommunicated nor known by name as a communicant with excommunicated persons, but remained in the faith and service of his lord, it is permitted for us to share, dispensively—that is, for as long as we tolerate them—the alms he gives, and to assist the soul of the deceased in every way proper to Christian religion. [Col. 1240C]

## CONCERNING LAWFUL AND UNLAWFUL EXCOMMUNICATION.

[Col. 1239]

### CHAPTER CXXIV. What penalty is imposed upon one who unlawfully excommunicates another. [Col. 1239D] Council of Paris under Louis.

(24, q. 3, c. *De illicita*.) Concerning unlawful excommunication, the law of the Catholic Emperor Justinian—which the Catholic Church approves and observes—decreed in Constitution 123, chapter 30, book I, that no bishop or presbyter may excommunicate anyone before the cause has been proved for which the ecclesiastical canons order this to be done. If anyone excommunicates another contrary to this, the excommunicated person is to be restored to the grace of holy communion by the authority of the higher priest. [Col. 1240D] But the person who has excommunicated unlawfully is to abstain from sacred communion for as much time as seems right to the higher priest, so that he may justly suffer what he has unjustly done.

On this subject Saint Gregory wrote, among other things, to Bishop John, who had excommunicated unlawfully:

“Since the decrees of your aforesaid sentence have first been attempted and reduced to nothing, by the authority of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we decree that you are deprived of sacred communion for thirty days, during which you must implore from almighty God forgiveness for so great an offence with the utmost penitence and tears. If we discover that you have carried out this sentence of ours too laxly, know that, with the Lord’s help, not merely your injustice but also the contumacy of your brotherhood must be punished more severely. For no one is to be judged hastily or in an irregular order—namely, without having been warned or convicted.” [Col. 1241A]

The law says concerning the summons preceding such proceedings against manifest crimes:

“Whoever has been summoned before a judge by three judicial citations, or called by three edicts, or by a single peremptory summons in place of all three—that is, one which extinguishes the case—and has refused to appear before the judge by whom he was notified, may be judged as contumacious. Indeed, in every case in which judgment has been given against a contumacious party, the proceedings may not be reopened by appeal.”

[Col. 1241B] Celestine, writing to Nestorius from evangelical truth, the Council of Ephesus deciding concerning the same matter, and Blessed Gregory writing to John, approve this ruling about summons by three citations. Regarding a party’s own written statement, the African council demonstrates in the case of Cresconius that, if a summoned man refused to repent, he was immediately excluded by judicial authority through his own contempt and contumacy. Likewise Blessed Gregory, writing on a judicial sentence against a contumacious person, says to Maximus, the presumptuous bishop of Salona:

“We exhort you to hasten to come to us, setting aside every excuse, so that, justice being observed, by Christ’s revelation we may investigate and decide according to canonical ordinances the matters of which you are accused. Take care, however, not to delay your coming any longer, lest your absence itself make you more liable to the allegations, and lest this matter compel us to pronounce against you, in council, a harsher judgment as against a contumacious person—not only because of the alleged crimes which you evade purging, but also because of the fault of disobedience.” [Col. 1241C]

### CHAPTER CXXV. Concerning those who communicate with excommunicated persons without fault. From the Decree of Gregory VII.

(11, q. 3, c. *Quoniam multos*.) Since, through our sins, we see many daily perish because of excommunication—some through ignorance, some through excessive simplicity, some through fear, and some even through necessity—overcome by mercy, we temper, so far as we can and for a time, the sentence of anathema. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we withdraw from the bond of anathema wives, children, sons, servants, maidservants, slaves, peasants, attendants, and all others who are not so much members of the court that crimes are committed by their counsel, as well as those who unknowingly communicate with excommunicated persons.

If any supplicant, pilgrim, or traveller comes into the land of excommunicated persons, where he cannot buy or has nothing with which to buy, we grant permission to receive from excommunicated persons. And if anyone wishes to give to excommunicated persons, not in support of their pride but from humanity, we do not forbid it. [Col. 1241D]

### CHAPTER CXXVI. A son is not to be anathematized for his father’s sin. [Col. 1242A] Augustine to Bishop Auxilius, epistle 75.

(24, q. 3, c. *Si habes*.) If you have reached a conclusion concerning this matter established by certain arguments or testimonies of Scripture, please deign to teach us how a son is rightly anathematized for his father’s sin, a wife for her husband’s sin, a slave for his master’s sin, or anyone in a household who has not yet even been born, if he is born at the time when the whole household has been bound by anathema, so that the person cannot be helped through the washing of regeneration in danger of death.

For this is a bodily punishment, by which we read that certain despisers of God, together with all who shared in the same impiety, were slain at the same time. At that time mortal bodies, which would in any case sometime die, were sometimes destroyed in order to terrify the living. But the spiritual penalty constituted by the saying, “Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound in heaven” (Matthew 16), binds souls, concerning which it has been said: “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine; the soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18). [Col. 1242B]

Perhaps you have heard that certain priests of great name have anathematized some sinners along with their household; perhaps, if they had been questioned, they would have been found able to give an adequate reason for it. But if anyone asks me whether it is rightly done, I do not find what I should answer. I have never dared to do this, except when I was most gravely moved by the crimes of certain persons committed unanimously against the Church.

Likewise, how can we give a just account either to God or to human beings if we punish innocent souls with spiritual punishment for another’s crime which they do not inherit, as they inherit original sin from Adam, in whom all sinned? For the son of Classianus, although he inherited from his father the stain of the first human being, to be cleansed in the sacred font of baptism, nevertheless no one can doubt that whatever sin his father who begot him later committed, in which this son was not a participant, does not reach him. What shall I say concerning a wife? What shall I say concerning so many souls in an entire household? [Col. 1242C]

### CHAPTER CXXVII. One who has been unjustly expelled may appeal to neighbouring bishops. [Col. 1242D] Council of Sardica, canon 17.

(11, q. 3, c. *Si episcopus forte*.) If perhaps a bishop—who ought not to be so—being quick-tempered, is swiftly and harshly moved against a presbyter or deacon and wishes to expel him from the Church, provision must be made that an innocent man is not condemned or deprived of communion. Therefore the expelled person has the power to appeal to neighbouring bishops, so that the case may be heard and more diligently examined; for he ought not to be denied a hearing.

The bishop who expelled him, whether justly or unjustly, should patiently accept that the matter be investigated, so that his sentence may be confirmed by several bishops or corrected. Yet before all matters have been carefully and satisfactorily examined, no one may presume to admit to communion, before a hearing, one who has been deprived of communion. [Col. 1243A]

### CHAPTER CXXVIII. Concerning bishops who excommunicate innocent persons or persons guilty only of very slight offences.

(11, q. 3, c. *Episcopi*.) If bishops, setting aside priestly moderation, presume to excommunicate innocent persons or persons guilty of very slight offences, or perhaps refuse to receive those hastening to the grace of baptism, they are to be admonished by letters from neighbouring bishops of any province. If they refuse to obey, communion is to be denied them by the other bishops until the time of the synod.

### CHAPTER CXXIX. If someone excommunicates unlawfully, he condemns himself, not the other person. From an epistle of Gregory the Great to the bishop of Milan, book II.

(24, q. 3, c. *Comperimus*.) We have learned that Lawrence, formerly our brother and fellow bishop, deprived you of communion although no faults existed in you. Therefore, fortified by the authority of this our command, perform your office securely and receive communion without any fear. [Col. 1243B]

### CHAPTER CXXX. Let no one excommunicate another in a fit of rage. Gregory to Maximinus, bishop of Syracuse.

I recall that I have frequently admonished you that you should by no means be hasty in pronouncing a sentence. But now, behold, I have learned that your brotherhood, stirred by rage, excommunicated the most reverend man Abbot Eusebius. This greatly astonished me.

### CHAPTER CXXXI. What one has done in a disturbed state of mind, one should correct when tranquil. [Col. 1243C] Augustine to Bishop Auxilius, epistle 75.

I ask you to pardon an excommunicated man who begs pardon, if you recognize his fault. But if you wisely perceive that he has committed no sin, do what it becomes a holy man to do. If it happens to you—as it may to a human being, who is certainly human—that you may say with the Psalmist, “My eye is troubled because of anger” (Psalm 6), cry out to God: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak” (ibid.), so that He may extend His right hand to you, restrain your anger, and calm your mind for seeing and doing justice. Remove the ecclesiastical acts which, perhaps more agitated than thoughtful, you have performed.

### CHAPTER CXXXII. A person is bound or loosed by his manner of life, not by a sentence. [Col. 1243D] Rabanus, *On the Afflictions of the Church*, book I.

(23, q. 3, c. *Non in perpetuum*.) We are not condemned forever when we are judged unjustly, as the Psalmist says: “He will not condemn him when he is judged” (Psalm 36). Many priests indeed profess that they persecute guilt out of zeal for God; but, when they act in this manner without discernment, they incur the crime of sacrilege. And while they rush headlong, as though to correct others, they themselves fall far more grievously and disastrously. [Col. 1244A]

### CHAPTER CXXXIII. An excommunicated person cannot excommunicate another. Alexander II to Valerian, bishop and martyr.

(23, q. 1, c. *Audivimus*.) We have heard that Henry, called Archbishop of Ravenna, has attempted to excommunicate you. Since an excommunicated person could not excommunicate another, by apostolic authority, absolving you and your people, we command that you never concern yourselves further about it.

### CHAPTER CXXXIV. From the time when a bishop teaches against the faith of the Church, he may excommunicate no one. Pope Nicholas to Bishop Michael.

[Col. 1244B] (24, q. 1, c. *Ait Coelestinus*.) Pope Celestine, writing to the Eastern bishops, says: “If anyone has been excommunicated or stripped of the dignity either of bishop or cleric by Bishop Nestorius or by others who follow him, from the time when they began to preach such things, it is manifest that this person has remained and remains in our communion. Nor do we judge him removed, because the sentence of one who had already made himself liable to removal could remove no one.”

### CHAPTER CXXXV. Those excommunicated by heretics are not regarded as excommunicated. Pope Nicholas to the clergy of Constantinople.

(24, q. 1, c. *Aperte, inquit*.) “The authority of our see,” he says, “has plainly decreed that no bishop, cleric, or Christian of any profession, who has been deprived of office or communion by Nestorius or his like from the time when they began to preach such things, is to be regarded as deposed or excommunicated. Rather, all these persons were and remain in our communion, because one who was wavering by preaching such things could not depose or remove anyone.” [Col. 1244C]

Do you understand, Emperor, from the matters mentioned above, that one who had formerly been removed could not remove anyone else—not, to say the least, even his own superior—and that one already cast down could not depose another?

### CHAPTER CXXXVI. A person who delays for a year to pursue the case of his excommunication denies himself a hearing. From the Decree of Pope Gelasius, canon 2.

(11, q. 3, c. *Quicunque*.) Therefore, whoever within the space of a year has not pursued his case, whether in a civil or public manner, before those who excommunicated him, is to be regarded as having closed the door of a hearing against himself. If, with an obstinate mind, he dies without communion, we reserve his case to divine judgment, in accordance with the sentence of our predecessor Blessed Leo: those with whom we did not communicate while alive, we cannot communicate with when dead. [Col. 1244D]

# BOOK SIX.

[Col. 1243]

## CONCERNING WEDDINGS AND MARRIAGES.

[Col. 1243]

### CHAPTER I. Definition of marriage. [Col. 1243D] Constitutions, book II, chapter 8.

(29, q. 1, in *inst.* *De nupt.* at the beginning, and c. *Illud*, [Col. 1244D] and *Extr.* *De praesent.*) Marriage, or matrimony, is the union of a man and a woman, entailing an indivisible partnership of life.

### CHAPTER II. Weddings may not be celebrated during the days of Lent. [Col. 1245A] Council of Lleida, canon 3.

(33, q. 4, c. *Non oportet*.) Weddings ought not be celebrated from Septuagesima until the octave of Easter, during the three weeks before the feast of Saint John, or from the Advent of the Lord until after Epiphany. If this is done, the couple are to be separated.

### CHAPTER III. On the same matter. Nicholas, *Responses to the Bulgarians*, chapter 48.

(33, q. 4, c. *Nec uxorem*.) We judge that it is in no way permissible either to take a wife, to hold banquets, or to have sexual intercourse during the Lenten season.

### CHAPTER IV. Permission to marry is not granted to those who have resolved to observe continence. [Col. 1245B] Augustine, *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, chapter 122.

(27, q. 1, c. *Nubendi*.) Permission to marry is granted to some—that is, to those who have not professed virginity or widowly chastity—but it is not granted to others, namely, those who have resolved to be virginal and continent. Fornication, however, is granted to no one with impunity.

### CHAPTER V. Secret marriages may not be celebrated. From the Decree of Pope Hormisdas, ch. 6.

(30, q. 5, ch. *Nullus*.) Let no believer, of whatever rank, contract marriage secretly; rather, having received a blessing from the priest, let him marry publicly in the Lord.

### CHAPTER VI. No one may take a wife without a public marriage. Council of Arles, ch. 6.

[Col. 1245C] (30, q. 5, ch. *Nullum*.) Let no marriage take place without a dowry; the dowry shall be provided according to means. Nor may anyone presume to marry or take a wife without public nuptials.

### CHAPTER VIII. Whoever swears to a woman upon the Scriptures that he will marry her is bound to betroth her. Novel Constitutions, ch. 1.

If anyone, having touched the divine Scriptures, swears to a woman that he will have her as his lawful wife, or if he has secretly given a sacramental pledge in an oratory, she shall be his lawful wife, even though no dowry and no other written instrument has intervened.

### CHAPTER VIII. Why women are veiled when they are married. Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, bk. II, ch. 19.

(30, q. 5, ch. *Feminae*.) Women are veiled when they are married [Col. 1245D] so that they may know that they must always be subject and humble toward their husbands. Likewise: those who marry, after the blessing, are joined together in one life as though by a mutual bond, namely, lest they break apart the structure of conjugal unity. Moreover, this veil is intermingled with white and purple colour. White indeed signifies purity of life; purple is applied to the prospect of offspring through blood, so that by this sign both parties may be reminded that continence and the law are to be observed for a time, and that afterwards the marital debt is not to be refused. Likewise: at a first marriage a ring is given by the bridegroom to the bride, doubtless either as a sign of mutual love, or, more especially, so that their hearts may be joined by their pledge. Hence the ring is placed on the fourth finger [Col. 1246A], because, as is reported, a certain vein of blood in it reaches as far as the heart.

### CHAPTER IX. Marriages ought to be celebrated publicly. Nicholas, in reply to the consultations of the Bulgarians.

(30, q. 5, ch. *Nostrates*.) Among our people neither men nor women wear upon their heads a band of gold or silver, or one made from any metal, when they contract the bonds of marriage. But after betrothals, which are a promise of the future marriage, the agreements are also concluded with the consent of those who contract them and of those under whose authority they are; and after the bridegroom has betrothed the bride to himself by giving her earnest-money and marking her with a ring upon the finger of faith, and has delivered to her, in the presence of those invited by both parties, the dowry agreed by them both, together with a written instrument containing this agreement, then either at once or at a fitting time—so that he may not presume to do such a thing before the time fixed by law—both are led to the marriage rites. First, indeed, they are placed in the church of the Lord with the offerings which they ought to offer to God through the hand of the priest; and thus at last they receive the blessing and the heavenly veil.

### CHAPTER X. Why brides are not handed over immediately. Augustine, *Confessions*, bk. IV.

(27, q. 2, ch. *Institutum*; law *Quod dicimus*, and *Fidejussor*, § *De solut.*) It has been established that brides already pledged are not handed over immediately, lest a husband hold cheap that which, when deferred, he had longed for as bridegroom.

### CHAPTER XI. Concerning those whose consent is required in betrothals. Digest, bk. XXIII, title I.

[Col. 1246C] (Law *In sponsal.*, § *De sponsal.*) In betrothals the consent of those whose consent is required in marriages must be sought. Nevertheless, a daughter is understood always to consent to her father, unless she clearly dissents.

### CHAPTER XII. Betrothals are contracted with the consent of the daughter, who ought to consent to her father, though she could object if she had a just cause for objecting. Digest, from the same book and title.

(Law *Sponsal. cum se.*, § *eod.*) Betrothals, like marriages, are made by the consent of those contracting them; therefore, as in marriages, so also in betrothals a daughter under paternal authority must consent. She who does not oppose her father’s will is understood to consent. But permission to dissent from her father is granted when a bridegroom unworthy in character or shameful in conduct [Col. 1246D] is chosen for her by her father. If a son under paternal authority dissents, a betrothal cannot be made in his name.

### CHAPTER XIII. No age is fixed for entering into betrothals. Digest, from the same book and title.

(Law *In sponsal.*, § *De sponsal.*) In contracting betrothals, the age of the contracting parties is not fixed as it is in marriages. Therefore betrothals may be effected from the beginning of age, provided that it is understood that this may be done by both persons—that is, provided they are not younger than seven years.

### CHAPTER XIV. Marriage begins at betrothal. Ambrose, *On the Institution of Virgins*, chs. 5–6.

(27, q. 3, ch. *Cum initiatur*, or *Conjug. pactio*.) [Col. 1247A] A woman betrothed to a man receives the name of wife. For when marriage is begun, the name of marriage is assumed. It is not the defloration of virginity that makes marriage, but the marital agreement. In short, marriage exists when the girl is joined in marriage, not when she is known through intercourse with a man.

### CHAPTER XV. From the first pledge of betrothal they are more truly called spouses. Isidore, *Etymologies*, bk. IX, ch. 7.

(27, q. 2, ch. *Conjuges*.) They are more truly called spouses from the first pledge of betrothal, even though conjugal intercourse is not yet known between them.

### CHAPTER XVI. Marriage exists even without carnal union and intercourse. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, bk. I, ch. 11, and *On Marriage and Concupiscence*.

(27, q. 2, ch. *Conjux*.) A spouse is so called from the first pledge of betrothal. Joseph had not known her by intercourse, was not going to know her, had not lost her, and had not remained false; yet there was the designation “spouse,” where there had been, and was not going to be, a union of flesh. For this reason both deserved to be called the faithful parents of Christ: not only she his mother, but he also his father, just as he was the spouse of his mother—both in mind, not in flesh.

### CHAPTER XVII. When a betrothed woman has been handed over and taken into use, she is properly called a wife. Ambrose to Paternus, Epistle 66.

(27, q. 2, ch. *Si quis*.) If anyone makes use of a woman betrothed and handed over to him, it is called marriage.

### CHAPTER XVIII. A girl betrothed to one man cannot be taken by another. Pope Siricius to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, Epistle 1, ch. 4.

(27, q. 2, ch. *De conjugali*.) You have asked concerning violation of the marital bond whether one man may take in marriage a girl betrothed to another. We anathematize such a marriage and forbid it by every means, lest it occur; for that blessing which the priest places upon a bride is, among unbelievers, like a kind of sacrilege if it is violated by any transgression.

### CHAPTER XIX. Betrothed girls must be restored to their former betrothed. Council of Ancyra, ch. 11.

(27, q. 2, ch. *Desponsatas*.) It has been decreed that girls who have been betrothed and afterwards abducted by others should be recovered and restored to those to whom they had previously been betrothed, even if it is established that violence [Col. 1247D] was inflicted upon them by their abductors.

### CHAPTER XX. How bridegroom and bride should approach the blessing. Fourth Council of Carthage, ch. 13.

(30, q. 5, ch. *Sponsus*.) When bridegroom and bride are to be blessed by the priest, they shall be presented in church to the priest by their parents or by the *paranymphi* (wedding attendants). Having received the blessing, they shall remain virgins that night out of reverence for the blessing.

### CHAPTER XXI. At what times spouses should abstain. Ambrose on the Epistle to the Corinthians, ch. 71.

(33, q. 4, ch. *Si causa*.) If a wife is taken for the purpose of begetting children, not much time seems to be granted for the act itself, since feast-days, [Col. 1248A] days of procession, and the very process of conception and childbirth, according to the law, show that abstinence ought to be observed at such times.

### CHAPTER XXII. Second marriages, like first marriages, are shown to be lawful. Augustine, *Against the Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets*, bk. II, ch. 21.

(31, q. 1, ch. *Deus masculum*.) God, who joined male and female in marital chastity for the propagation of the human race, has also shown that second marriages, which are permitted in each Testament, are lawful.

### CHAPTER XXIII. That woman does not belong to a marriage with whom the nuptial rite is not celebrated. From the Decree of Pope Leo II and Epistle 90 to Rusticus.

(27, q. 2, ch. *Cum societas*.)
