Since the society of marriage was established from the beginning in such a way that, besides the union of the sexes, marriage possesses within itself the sacrament of the union of Christ and the Church, there can be no doubt that a woman is not party to a marriage in whose case it is shown that the nuptial rite was absent.

### CHAPTER XXIV. The bearing of children shall be women’s sole reason for marrying. Ambrose on Luke, bk. I, ch. 1.

(32, q. 2, ch. *Pudor*.) It is a shame for women not to have the rewards of marriage, for whom this is the sole reason for marrying.

### CHAPTER XXV. On the same matter. Ambrose on Luke, bk. II.

(32, q. 2, ch. *Pudor*, § *Cum*.) Since childbirth is the reward of marriage and the grace of wedlock for women, [Col. 1248C] there was no slight reason why Mary’s virginity should deceive the prince of this world.

### CHAPTER XXVI. On the same matter. Jerome.

(32, q. 2, ch. *Sicut et venial.*) Spouses therefore owe one another not only the fidelity of joining in sexual intercourse for the begetting of children—since this is the first fellowship of the human race in this mortal condition—but also a mutual acceptance of weakness, in order to avoid illicit intercourse: a sort of mutual servitude, so that if perpetual continence pleases one of them, it cannot be undertaken without the consent of the other. Likewise: to render the conjugal debt is no sin; but to demand it beyond the necessity of procreation [Col. 1248D] is a venial fault.

### CHAPTER XXVII. Those who unite with one another solely because of incontinence are spouses. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, ch. 5.

(32, q. 2, *Solet*.) The question is commonly asked: when a man and woman, neither being the husband or wife of another, unite with each other not for the begetting of children, but solely because of the incontinence of intercourse, while maintaining the fidelity that he does not do this with another woman and she does not do this with another man—whether these should be called marriages. Perhaps this may not improperly be called a marriage, if this arrangement pleases them until the death of one of them, and if they do not avoid the generation of offspring, even though they were not joined for that purpose: that is, if they do not wish to prevent children from being born to them, or do not wickedly act in some way to prevent their birth. But if either or both of these conditions is absent, I do not see how we can call these marriages. For if a man takes a woman to himself temporarily until he finds another worthy of his rank or his means whom he may take in marriage, he is an adulterer in his very intention—not with the woman whom he hopes to find, but with the woman with whom he lies in this manner, since he does not have marital fellowship with her.

### CHAPTER XXVIII. No one may dismiss a barren wife and take another for the sake of fertility. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, ch. 7.

(32, q. 7, ch. *Tantum*.) So powerful is the social bond that, although it is contracted for the sake of procreation, it is not dissolved even for the sake of procreation itself.

### CHAPTER XXIX. The reality of marriage does not consist in the union of male and female. Augustine, *Against Julian*, bk. I.

[Col. 1249B] (32, q. 1, ch. *Non enim*.) The reality of marriage does not lie only in the union of male and female, as you foolishly maintain, although without that union marriage cannot propagate children. But there are other things properly belonging to marriage by which marriages are distinguished from adulteries: namely, fidelity to the marriage-bed, care to beget children in an orderly manner, and—what is the greatest difference—the good use of an evil, that is, the good use of the concupiscence of the flesh, which adulterers use badly.

### CHAPTER XXX. The threefold good of marriage was present in the parents of Christ. Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, bk. II, ch. 2.

(27, q. 4, ch. *Omnes*; Dist. 31, *Si sint*.) Thus every good of marriage was fulfilled in the parents of Christ: fidelity, offspring, sacrament. We recognize the offspring as the Lord himself; fidelity, because there was no adultery; sacrament, because there was no divorce. Only marital intercourse was absent there, because in flesh of sin it cannot occur without the shameful concupiscence of the flesh that arose from sin. He willed to be conceived without this, because he was to be without sin.

### CHAPTER XXXI. Clandestine marriages should not be contracted. Evaristus, bishop of Africa, Epistle 1.

A lawful marriage is not otherwise made unless the woman is sought from those who are seen to have authority over her and by whom she is guarded; unless she is betrothed by parents and nearest relatives, endowed according to law, and at the proper time blessed by a priest, as is customary, with prayers and offerings; unless, guarded by wedding attendants as custom teaches, she is sought from her relatives at a suitable time, endowed according to law, and solemnly received. Let them devote themselves to prayer for two or three days and observe chastity. But unions presumed otherwise are doubtless not marriages but adulteries, cohabitations, seductions, or fornications rather than lawful wedlocks, unless their own will supports them and lawful vows come to their aid.

### CHAPTER XXXII. Those who do not complete the solemn agreements of marriage commit an offence. Nicholas in reply to the consultations of the Bulgarians, ch. 32.

These, besides other matters which do not occur to memory, are the solemn agreements of marriage. We say that it is a sin if all these do not occur within the marriage bond.

### CHAPTER XXXIII. How many lawful marriages there are, and that by the father’s will an abductor may marry the woman he abducted. Jerome.

(36, q. 2, ch. *Tria*.) Three lawful marriages are read of in the Scriptures. The first lawful marriage is when a chaste virgin is lawfully given, while still a virgin, to a lawful man, and the remaining things mentioned above follow. The second is when a virgin is found by a man in a city and joined to him by force: if her father wishes, that man shall endow her in whatever amount the father judges, and shall give the price for her chastity. The third is when the aforesaid daughter has been found, but her father does not consent: he shall take her from the aforesaid man, give her to another, and endow her; and she shall be his lawful wife. But the first is preferred to these two.

### CHAPTER XXXIV. When a wife has died, a man may take another, but not a divorced or betrothed woman.

(27, q. 2, ch. *Additur*.) Thus a fourth lawful marriage is added. When his wife has died, he may take another, but not one divorced or betrothed to a husband: she must be free. The same applies to a woman. Hence Paul also says: “The woman who is under a husband is bound by the law of her husband as long as her husband lives. Therefore, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is joined to another man. But if her husband has died, she is released from the law of her husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man” (Rom. VII).

## BETWEEN WHICH PERSONS MARRIAGE MAY EXIST

[Col. 1249]

### CHAPTER XXXV. A woman given to a man who has a concubine is joined in lawful marriage. From the Decree of Leo, Epistle 9 to Bishop Rusticus.

[Col. 1249D] (32, q. 2, ch. *Non omnis*.) Not every woman joined to a man is his wife, just as not every son is heir to his father. But the bonds of marriage are lawful among freeborn persons and among equals; and this was established by the Lord himself long before Roman law began. Therefore a wife is one thing and a concubine another, just as a female slave is one thing and a free woman another (Gal. IV). [Col. 1250D] For this reason the Apostle, in order to make clear the distinction between these persons, adduces the testimony from Genesis, where Abraham is told: “Cast out the slave-woman and her son, for the son of the slave-woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Gen. XXI). Therefore, if a layman of whatever position gives his daughter in marriage to a man who has a concubine, this is not to be understood as though he had given her to a married man—unless, perhaps, that woman appears to have been made free, lawfully endowed, and honoured with public nuptials. For women joined to men by their fathers’ decision [Col. 1251A] are free from blame. If the women whom men had were not wives in marriage, it is because a married woman is one thing and a concubine another.

### CHAPTER XXXVI. These things must be observed when contracting a marriage. Pope Leo.

(30, q. 5, ch. *Qualis*.) What sort of wife ought she to be who is to be taken according to the law? A chaste virgin, betrothed while a virgin, lawfully endowed, handed over by her parents, received by the bridegroom and wedding attendants; and thus, according to law and Gospel, honourably and plainly taken into marriage through public nuptials. On no day of her life is she to be separated for a human reason, except by mutual consent and for the purpose of devotion to God; and, if she has committed fornication, she is to be dismissed. But while she lives another woman is not to be taken, because adulterers shall not possess the kingdom of God (I Cor. VI); and her repentance is to be received according to the Scriptures.

### CHAPTER XXXVII. A marriage between a patron and his freedwoman is acknowledged to be lawful. From the Decree of Pope Julius, ch. 4.

(29, q. 2, ch. *Si quis*.) If anyone grants freedom to his female slave and joins her to himself in marriage, some doubt whether such nuptials should be considered lawful or not. We, therefore, resolving the ancient uncertainty, have judged such marriages to be lawful. For if all marriages arise from affection, and nothing impious or contrary to the laws can occur in such a union, why should we judge the aforesaid marriages to be forbidden?

### CHAPTER XXXVIII. A slave may contract marriage.

[Col. 1251C]

(19, q. 2, ch. *Omnibus*.) We all have one Father in heaven, and rich and poor, free and slave alike will render an account for themselves and their souls. Therefore we do not doubt that all, of whatever condition they may be, have one law insofar as God is concerned. Therefore, just as a freeborn person cannot be dismissed, so neither can a slave, once joined in marriage, thereafter be dismissed.

### CHAPTER XXXIX. Marriage remains between slaves whom their master joined, when one is afterwards freed and the other remains a slave. Council of Mâcon, ch. 10.

[Col. 1252A] If the master of both has joined a male slave and a female slave in marriage, and afterwards the male or female slave is freed, the one who remains in slavery cannot be redeemed; therefore their marriage is not dissolved.

### CHAPTER XL. Masters must not dissolve lawful marriages of slaves on their own authority. Council of Chalon, ch. 30.

(29, q. 2, ch. *Dictum est*.) It has been reported to us that certain persons, by a presumptuous exercise of power, dissolve lawful marriages of slaves, without attending to the Gospel passage: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. XIX). Therefore it seemed good to us that marriages of slaves should not be dissolved, even if they have different masters, but that, remaining in one marriage, they should serve their respective masters. This is to be observed where there has been a lawful union and it was entered into with the consent of their masters.

### CHAPTER XLI. Concerning one who married as his wife a female slave whom he believed to be free. Council at Verberie, ch. 6.

(29, q. 2, ch. *Si quis ingenuus*.) If a freeborn man takes another’s female slave as his wife, believing her to be freeborn, and that woman is later discovered to be in slavery, he should ransom her from slavery if he can. If he cannot, he may take another woman if he wishes. [Col. 1252C] But if he knew that she was a slave and had approved this, he is thereafter to have her as his lawful wife. Likewise a freeborn woman must act in the same manner regarding another’s male slave.

### CHAPTER XLII. A woman may not dismiss as husband one whom she knowingly took as a slave. From the same council, ch. 8.

(29, q. 2, ch. *Si femina*.) If a freeborn woman takes a slave, knowing that he was a slave, she must keep him, because we all have one Father in heaven, and one law shall apply to man and woman.

## CONCERNING CONCUBINES

[Col. 1251]

### CHAPTER XLIII. It is not permitted to have a concubine. Augustine, Homily 49.

[Col. 1251D] (Dist. 34, ch. *Audite*.) Hear, dearest brethren, members of Christ and children of mother Church. Let the faithful hear what I say to the candidates; let the candidates hear what I say to the faithful; let both candidates and faithful, and penitents, hear what I say; let catechumens hear; let all hear and fear, and let no one despise it. May your hearing be a comfort to me, and may my grief not be testimony against you. I say to the candidates: it is not lawful for you to fornicate; let wives suffice you; it is not lawful for you to have concubines. Let God hear, if you are deaf. Let his angels hear, if you despise this. It is not lawful for you to have concubines; and even if you do not have wives, it is nevertheless not lawful for you to have concubines [Col. 1252D] whom you later dismiss and then take wives. Your condemnation will be all the greater if you wish to have both concubines and wives. Likewise Augustine: What is to be said also of the fact that many men are not ashamed, before marriage, to attach concubines to themselves, whom after some years they dismiss and then take lawful wives? Therefore, before God and his angels, I solemnly attest and proclaim that God has always forbidden these things, that they have never pleased him, and that, especially in Christian times, it has never been lawful and never will be lawful to have concubines.

### CHAPTER XLIV. On the same matter. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*.

(Ch. *Solet quaeri*; and 32, q. 2, ch. *Si aliquam*.) If a man takes a woman to himself temporarily, until he finds one worthy of his rank and resources whom he may marry as his equal, he is an adulterer in intention itself—not with the woman whom he seeks to find, but with the woman with whom he lies, since he does not have marital fellowship with her.

### CHAPTER XLV. What is called a just concubinage. Augustine, ibid.

(32, q. 2, ch. *Ut concubinae*.) Likewise, in the same place: it is clear that concubines taken temporarily, if they cohabit for the sake of children, make their concubinage just; and that marriage may indeed arise from persons badly joined, when an honourable agreement subsequently follows.

### CHAPTER XLVI. A man who is accustomed to sleep with many women is not understood to have a concubine. Novel Constitution 89.

No one is understood to have a concubine who is accustomed to sleep with [Col. 1253B] many women. For just as a man who has a lawful wife cannot have another woman while that marriage continues, so also a man who has one concubine cannot have others at the same time.

### CHAPTER XLVII. A mother’s condition does not separate anyone from the people of God, but one’s own fault does. Augustine, *On the One Baptism*.

(Dist. 56, ch. *Ismael*.) Ishmael was not separated from the people of God because his mother was a slave, but because of fraternal discord; nor did the status of the wife, whose son he was more properly, benefit him, because through her marital rights he was both begotten in a slave woman and received from a slave woman.

### CHAPTER XLVIII. Habitual union with a free woman constitutes marriage. Digest, bk. XXIII, ch. 2, and Baldus.

[Col. 1253C] (Law *In liberae*, § *De tit. nupt.*) In the habitual union with a free woman, marriage, not concubinage, is to be understood, unless she has practiced prostitution.

### CHAPTER XLIX. One who has no wife ought to have a concubine in her place. First Council of Toledo, ch. 17.

(Dist. 34, ch. *Is qui non*.) If anyone has both a faithful wife and a concubine, let him not communicate. But one who has no wife and has a concubine in place of a wife is not to be excluded from communion, provided that he is content with union to one woman only—either a wife or a concubine, as he prefers. But he must put away other women, until he ceases and returns to penitence.

### CHAPTER L. On the same matter. Isidore, *On the Differences between the Old and New Testaments*.

[Col. 1253D] (Dist. 34, ch. *Christiano*.) I say that it is not lawful for a Christian to have several women, nor even two at the same time, but only one: either a wife, or, in the fixed place of a wife, if a spouse is lacking, a concubine.

### CHAPTER LI. On the same matter. Code, bk. IV, ch. 15, title 4.

(*Authentica*, ch. *Servo*, and *De natis*.) If a man without a wife keeps his female slave as a concubine and continues in that union until his death, and perhaps has children by her, we decree in every way that the heirs of the deceased are not permitted to reduce either her or her children—if she has borne children—to slavery; rather, after the master’s death she, together with her offspring, shall be released into freedom.

### CHAPTER LII. On the same matter. Constitutions, bk. XIV, ch. 4.

(Law *Nuper*, ch. *De nat. lib.*) If anyone has a union with a free woman not in marital affection and begets children by her, and wishes to have those children as legitimate children under his authority, he may execute dowry instruments with their mother. For children who were formerly natural become legitimate and subject to their father’s authority after the execution of the dowry instruments, whether children subsequently born live or die, or whether no other child at all is begotten.

### CHAPTER LIII. What abduction is. Isidore, *Etymologies*, bk. V, ch. 26.

[Col. 1254B] (27, q. 2, ch. *Raptus*, and 28, q. 2, ch. *Raptus*.) *Raptus* (“abduction”) is illicit intercourse, so called from corruption. Hence he who obtains a woman by abduction engages in illicit intercourse.

### CHAPTER LIV. Abductors of a widow or virgin, together with those who support them, are excommunicated. Gregory Junior.

(36, q. 2, ch. *Si quis*.) If anyone abducts a widow or steals away a wife, let him be anathema. If he abducts a virgin, unless he betroths her as his wife, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER LV. What punishment there is for the abduction of girls. Council of Chalon, ch. 27.

(30, q. 2, ch. *De puellis*.) Concerning girls abducted though not yet betrothed, it is written in the Council of Chalcedon: “The holy synod decreed that those who abducted girls under the pretext of living together, together with those assisting and conniving with the abductors, are, if clerics, to be deposed from their rank; but, if laypeople, to be anathematized.” These words make clear how the perpetrators of this evil must be condemned, when the accomplices in the plan and those who connive are struck with so great an anathema that, according to canonical authority, abducted women can in no way be claimed by them as lawful wives.

### CHAPTER LVI. After the abductor’s or abducted woman’s penance, let marriage be permitted to those left unmarried. Council of Meaux, ch. 65.

[Col. 1254D] (36, 2, ch. *Si autem*.) But if they have not yet taken into marriage, with consent, the women whom they abducted under the pretext of betrothal or dowry, then, once this decree has been proclaimed in everyone’s hearing, they shall be separated from their union and subjected to public penance. The abducted women shall be lawfully restored to their parents. But after public penance has been completed, if age demands relief for incontinence, let them be joined in lawful marriage by the agreement of both parties. We do not establish a rule in these cases; rather, to use the words of the great Leo, we judge this to be the more tolerable course. But if one of the spouses dies and the person who performed public penance survives, he or she must not presume to marry again, unless perhaps the bishop foresees grounds for granting some indulgence, so that a graver offence may be removed.

### CHAPTER LVII. It is not a sin to take a prostitute as one’s wife. Jerome on Hosea, bk. I, on ch. V.

(32, q. 1, ch. *Non est culpandus*.) The prophet Hosea is not to be blamed if he converts the prostitute whom he took to modesty; rather, he is to be praised for making a good woman out of a bad one. For a person who remains good is not himself defiled if he is associated with an evil person; rather, the evil person is converted to good if she follows the examples of the good. From this we understand that the prophet did not lose his modesty when joined to the prostitute, but that the prostitute assumed the modesty which she had not previously possessed.

### CHAPTER LVIII. Prostitutes may choose a better life, even if they have sworn to remain in that occupation, because an oath made contrary to good morals is not binding. Novel Constitution; and Baldus, bk. I, Emperor Beneventanus.

[Col. 1256A] (Ch. *De nuptiis*.) The Emperor decreed that prostitutes may choose a more honourable life without any affection, even though they have furnished a sworn security. But those who exacted such an oath and lent their services against chastity shall pay, as a penalty, ten pounds of gold to those same prostitutes who made the sworn pledges. The penalty of ten pounds shall be demanded through the office of the provincial governor. If the governor neglects this, he shall be compelled to pay the penalty from his own property, be removed from the office entrusted to him, and pay the penalty not only to the women but also to their heirs and other successors—provided it is proved that he exacted an oath from the prostitute. But if he himself did exact an oath from a prostitute, he shall be liable to the penalty.

## CONCERNING SECOND MARRIAGES

[Col. 1255]

### CHAPTER LIX. Second marriages, like first marriages, are shown to be lawful. Augustine, *On the Good of Widowhood*, ch. 11.

[Col. 1255B] (31, q. 1, ch. *Quod si dormierit*.) People are accustomed to raise a question concerning third and fourth, and still more numerous, marriages. To answer briefly: I dare neither condemn any marriages nor remove from them the modest restraint arising from their number. Likewise: I do not dare, against the sense of human modesty, to say that a woman may marry whenever she wishes after her husbands have died; nor, because of the authority of Holy Scripture, do I dare from my own heart to condemn marriages however numerous.

### CHAPTER LX. How Abraham is excused from the charge of fornication. Augustine, *Against Faustus*, bk. II, ch. 5.

(32, q. 4, ch. *Iste Abrahae*.) This man even charged Abraham with fornication in his decrepit old age, no doubt because, after Sarah’s death, he took another wife. Even if no sacrament of a hidden reality were understood in this, Abraham ought to have done it for this reason alone: so that heretics hostile to the people of God—notably Tertullian, who stands with them—might not think that taking a wife after one’s wife has died is a crime.

### CHAPTER LXI. Second marriages, like first marriages, are shown to be lawful. Augustine, *Against the Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets*, bk. II, ch. 2.

[Col. 1255D] (31, q. 2, ch. *Deus masculum*.) Likewise, God, who joined male and female in marital chastity for the propagation of the human race, also showed that second marriages, which are permitted in the New Testament as well, are lawful.

### CHAPTER LXII. Neither second, nor third, nor subsequent marriages are to be condemned. Jerome to Pammachius, vol. II, in the *Apology*.

(31, q. 1, ch. *Aperiant*.) Let my detractors, I pray, open their ears and see that I have allowed second and third marriages in the Lord; I have not condemned second and third marriages, nor could I condemn a first marriage. Likewise: I do not condemn twice-married persons; indeed, if the word may be used, not even thrice-married persons, nor persons married eight times. Likewise: I now proclaim in a free voice that in the Church neither second marriage nor even third marriage is condemned, and that it is as lawful to marry a fifth, sixth, or further husband as it is a second husband.

### CHAPTER LXIII. A twice-married man does not sin, but loses the prerogative of the priesthood. Ambrose to Vercelli, 82, bk. X.

(Dist. 26, ch. *Qui sine*, and Dist. 34, ch. *Cognoscamus*.) A man without fault who is the husband of one wife is to be held fit for receiving the law of priesthood. But one who has repeated marriage has indeed committed no defiling fault, yet is deprived of the priestly prerogative. Likewise, let us recognize that the Apostle established this not only concerning bishops and presbyters, but that the Fathers also added in the deliberation of the Council of Nicaea that no cleric ought to be one who has entered into a second marriage.

### CHAPTER LXIV. A man is reckoned twice-married if he had one wife before baptism and another after baptism. Ambrose, *On Duties*, bk. I.

[Col. 1256D] (Dist. 26, ch. *Una tantum*.) Only one union, not repeated, is permitted to us; and even in marriage there is a law against repeating marriage and entering into union with a second wife. Many find it surprising that repeated marriage even before baptism creates impediments to eligibility for office and to the prerogative of ordination, when even sins do not usually hinder if they have been remitted by the sacrament of the washing. But we must understand that guilt can be forgiven in baptism, whereas a law cannot be abolished. In marriage there is not guilt but law. Therefore what belongs to guilt is remitted in baptism; what belongs to law is not dissolved in marriage. How can one who himself has frequently married be an exhorter to widowhood?

### CHAPTER LXV. One who had one wife before baptism and another after baptism may not be ordained. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, ch. 28.

[Col. 1257A] (Dist. 26, ch. *Unius*, and ch. *Acutius*.) The sacrament of marriage in our time has been reduced to one husband and one wife, so that it is not lawful to ordain as a steward of the Church anyone except a man who is the husband of one wife.

### CHAPTER LXVI. One who had one wife before baptism and another after baptism may not be ordained. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, ch. 18.

(Dist. 26, ch. *Acutius*.) Those understood this more keenly who judged that not even a man who had another wife while a catechumen or pagan ought to be ordained. For the question concerns a sacrament, not sin. All sins are indeed forgiven in baptism; but he who said, “If you take a wife, you have not sinned; if a virgin marries, she does not sin; and let her do what she wishes—she does not sin if she marries” (I Cor. VII), made sufficiently clear that marriage is not sin. But because of the holiness of the sacrament, just as a woman who has been violated, even while a catechumen, cannot be consecrated among God’s virgins after baptism, so it did not seem unreasonable that one who has exceeded the singular number of wives should be understood not to have committed any sin, but to have lost a certain norm of the sacrament necessary not for the merit of a good life but for the seal of ecclesiastical ordination.

### CHAPTER LXVII. A presbyter should not dine at the wedding of a twice-married man. Council of Neocaesarea, ch. 6.

[Col. 1257C] It is not fitting for a presbyter to dine at the wedding of a twice-married man, because, since a twice-married man requires penance, what presbyter could give consent to such a marriage?

### CHAPTER LXVIII. What a widow, a repudiated woman, and a prostitute are. Jerome to Fabulus.

(Dist. 34, ch. *Vidua*; 45, ch. *Disciplina*; 60, ch. *Latores*, *Extra De Sent. Excom.*) A widow is one whose husband has died; a repudiated woman is one cast off while her husband lives; a prostitute is one open to the lust of many men.

### CHAPTER LXIX. On the same matter. The Emperors Valens, Theodosius, and Arcadius to Pope Tatianus.

(Law *Matres*, ch. *Quando*.) Mothers who, having lost their husbands, seek the guardianship of the affairs to be administered for their children must, before legal confirmation of such an office can come to them, declare in the records, upon a sworn oath, that they will not enter another marriage. Certainly no woman shall be compelled to make such a choice; rather, she shall freely submit herself to the conditions that we prescribe. For if she prefers to choose another marriage, she ought not to administer the guardianships of her children.

### CHAPTER LXX. On the same matter. Novel Constitution 27, ch. 11.

[Col. 1258A]

(l. I, c. *De secundis*, and l. *Solet*, c. *Mulier quae ante annum*.) If a woman, before the completion of a year after her husband’s death, hastens to a second marriage, she shall in every respect be among the infamous. Yet if she has no children from the former marriage, she may remove the infamy if she presents petitions to the emperor and, by the divine nod of the prince, is restored to her former reputation; but she shall by no means acquire the property left to her by her former husband.

### CHAPTER LXXI. A woman hastening to a second marriage is not to use the privileges of her former husband.

A woman who has entered into a second marriage is not to use the privileges or dignities of her former husband.

### CHAPTER LXXII. A woman who has guardianship of her children must first render an account of the guardianship and pay what she owes before entering a second marriage.

[Col. 1258B]

If a woman has administered the guardianship of her own children and, after beginning that administration, wishes to enter a second marriage, she must first seek a guardian for her underage children and render to him an account of her administration. After rendering the account, if she is found to be a debtor, she must pay her debt. Then, if she wishes, she may enter a second marriage. But if, disregarding this requirement, she contracts a second marriage, not only the property of the woman herself—that is, the mother—shall be subject to her children by way of hypothec, but also the property of the stepfather, by the authority of the present constitution.

### CHAPTER LXXIII. On the same matter. [Col. 1258C] Constitution, book LXXXIV, chapter 1.

(l. I, c. *De secundis nuptiis*.) If, after her husband’s death, a mother prefers to manage the guardianship of her children, she shall renounce second marriages in court under oath; she shall pledge her own property to her underage child, and only then shall the guardianship be entrusted to her.

### CHAPTER LXXIV. On the same matter. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*.

(32, q. 7, c. *Usque adeo*.) The rights of a marriage once contracted remain so fully among the living that persons who have separated are still more truly spouses to one another than to those with whom they have joined themselves. And afterward:

There remains among the living a certain marital bond [Col. 1258D] which neither separation nor union with another can remove. Thus an apostate soul, as though withdrawing from the marriage of Christ, does not lose the sacrament of faith received in the washing of regeneration, even when faith itself has been lost. For it would undoubtedly be restored to one who returned, if the departing person had lost it; but the one who has departed retains it for an increase of punishment, not as a reward for merit.

## CONCERNING THE MARRIAGE OF THOSE ONE OF WHOM, WITHOUT THE OTHER, HAS VOWED CONTINENCE

[Col. 1257]

### CHAPTER LXXV. The marital bond is not dissolved on account of perpetual continence, to be observed by the consent of both spouses.

[Col. 1257D]

(32, q. 7, c. *Usque adeo*.) But where spouses have agreed by mutual consent to abstain perpetually from the carnal use of concupiscence, far be it that the marital bond between them should be broken. Rather, it shall be stronger, in proportion as the agreements they have made with one another—agreements to be kept more dearly and harmoniously—are maintained not by the pleasurable bonds of bodies but by the voluntary affections of minds.

### CHAPTER LXXVI. Husband and wife may not separate for religious reasons without the knowledge of the bishop. [Col. 1259A] Pope Eugenius, from a synod, chapter 36, under Louis and Lothair.

(27, q. 2, c. *Si vir*.) If husband and wife agree to separate from one another solely for the religious life, this must by no means occur without the bishop’s knowledge, so that they may be assigned separately to a place provided by him. For even if the wife so wishes, or either of them does, the marriage is not dissolved even for such a reason.

### CHAPTER LXXVII. A woman may not undertake vows of continence unless her husband has chosen the same life. Nicholas to King Charles.

(27, q. 2, c. *Scripsit nobis*.) Queen Theutberga wrote to us that she wished to be stripped of rank and marital union, and desired to be content with a private life alone. We wrote to her that this could not be done otherwise than if her husband Lothair chose the same life.

### CHAPTER LXXVIII. Marriages ought not to be dissolved for religious reasons. From Gregory’s letter to the patrician Theotista, book IX.

(27, q. 2, c. *Sunt qui*.) If some say that marriages ought to be dissolved for the sake of religion, it must be understood that, although human law has allowed this, divine law nevertheless forbids it. For Truth himself said: “What God has joined,” etc. (Matt. XIX). He also said: “It is not lawful to put away one’s wife except on account of fornication” (ibid.).

Likewise: If husband and wife are one flesh, and for the sake of religion the husband puts away his wife, or the woman her husband, who remains in the world—or perhaps passes into unlawful conduct—what sort of conversion is this, in which the same flesh passes in part to continence and in part remains in defilement? But if both agree to lead a continent life, who would dare to condemn this?

Likewise: When good spouses desire either to increase their merit or to erase the faults of their former life, it is permitted for them to bind themselves to continence and seek a better life. But if the wife rejects the continence desired by the husband, the marriage may not be divided, because it is written: “The woman does not have power over her own body, but the husband; likewise, the husband does not have power over his own body, but the woman” (I Cor. VII).

### CHAPTER LXXIX. A husband may not practise continence without his wife’s consent. Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*.

(27, q. 2, c. *Si tu abstines*.) If you abstain without [Col. 1259D] your wife’s consent, you grant her permission to commit fornication, and her sin will be imputed to your abstinence. The Apostle did not wish spouses to deprive one another even temporarily of the carnal obligation, for the purpose of giving themselves to prayer, except by mutual consent.

Likewise: If a husband says, “I do indeed put away my wife without any cause of fornication, but I shall remain continent,” shall we therefore say that he has done with impunity what he has done? Who would dare say this, if he understands the will of the Lord who says it? For he did not permit a spouse to be put away even for the sake of continence, he who made an exception only for the cause of fornication.

Likewise, suppose continence pleased the wife but did not please the husband. The woman leaves her husband and begins to live continently—she herself, of course, intending to remain chaste, but doing what the Lord does not wish: making her husband an adulterer [Col. 1260A], because, since he does not practise continence, he will seek another woman. What shall we say to the woman? Shall we not say what the Church’s sound doctrine says: “Render the marital due to your husband, lest, while you seek a means of being more highly honoured, he find a means of being condemned.”

### CHAPTER LXXX. A husband cannot annul vows of continence which, with his assent, his wife has promised to God. Augustine to Ecdicia, Letter 199.

(33, q. 5, c. *Quod Deo*.) What you both vowed to God by equal consent, you ought to have fulfilled steadfastly unto the end. If he has fallen away from that purpose, you at least must persevere most steadfastly. I would not exhort you to this unless he himself had consented to it. For if you had never obtained his consent, no number of years would have justified you.

Likewise: Your husband had not ceased to be your husband because you both abstained from carnal intercourse; indeed, you remained spouses to one another all the more sacredly insofar as you harmoniously kept more sacred resolutions. Therefore you ought to have done nothing concerning your clothing, gold, silver, any money, or any of your earthly goods without his judgment.

Likewise: There is a manner of dress appropriate to the condition of a married person, distinct from widow’s clothing, which can suit married believers while preserving the cause or observance of religion. If your husband wished you to lay this aside, so that you should not boast as though a widow while he was living, I think the matter ought not to have been carried to the scandal of discord, through the evil of disobedience rather than the good of that abstinence. For what is more absurd than for a woman to be proud against her husband because of humble clothing, when it would have been more advantageous for you to obey him in white morals than to resist him in black garments? Even if the garment of a nun pleased you, you could have assumed it more acceptably to your husband by consulting and persuading him than by presuming it without consulting him and in contempt of him. But if he did not permit it at all, what would your purpose have lost? Far be it that you should thereby displease God because, while your husband had not yet died, you did not dress like Anna but like Susanna.

### CHAPTER LXXXI. Married persons who vow chastity by a common vow must observe it. Augustine to Armentarius and Paulina.

I could, according to my limited ability, distinguish by their merits and grades those same persons belonging to the right hand and to the kingdom of heaven, and show how the married life of fathers and mothers of households who beget children, yet are religious and devout, differs from the life which you have vowed to God, if you were now to be exhorted to vow it. But because you have already vowed, you have already bound yourself: it is not lawful for you to do otherwise. Before you were liable for the vow, you were free to remain at a lower level, although that freedom is not to be congratulated by which a thing is not owed that would be repaid with gain.

But now, because your promise is held by God, I deter you not toward great righteousness, but from great wickedness. For if you do not do what you have vowed, you will not be such as you would have remained had you vowed nothing of the kind: then you would have been lower, not worse; but now [Col. 1261A] you will be as much lower—God forbid—if you break faith with God as you will be more blessed if you pay your vow. Nor indeed should you repent of having made the vow; rather, rejoice that what had been permitted with loss is no longer permitted to you. Therefore undertake it without fear and fulfil in deeds what you have sufficiently said; he who requires your vows will help you.

Blessed is the necessity that compels one to better things. There is only one reason why we would not merely refrain from exhorting you, but would positively forbid you, to fulfil what you have vowed: namely, if perhaps your wife refused, through weakness of mind or body, to undertake this with you. For such things ought not to be vowed by married persons except by common consent and mutual will. And if it has nearly been done, rashness must rather be corrected than the promise dissolved. God does not require that someone fulfil what he has vowed from another’s property; rather, he forbids one to usurp another’s property. For the divine judgment on this matter was pronounced through the Apostle: “The wife does not have power over her own body, but the husband; likewise, the husband does not have power over his own body, but the wife” (I Cor. VII).

### CHAPTER LXXXII. He who has allowed his wife to take the veil may not take another wife. Council of Reims, chapter 4.

(32, q. 5, c. *Qui uxorem*.) He who has allowed his wife to take the veil shall not take another wife, but shall likewise be converted.

### CHAPTER LXXXIII. A woman may not undertake vows of continence unless her husband has chosen the same life. Pope Nicholas to Lothair.

(27, q. 2, c. *Scripsit nobis*.) Therefore, take the utmost care diligently to cherish and love your wife Theutberga as your own flesh, and carefully ensure that you never consent under any arrangement for your wife, as your own flesh, to depart from you. Hence, if she wishes to depart from you, rebuke—indeed, correct—her, and strive in every way to call her back from such an intention.

But if she seeks separation through love of chastity and demands dissolution of the marital union, the Apostle plainly says that “the woman does not have power over her own body, but the husband” (I Cor. VII). Yet if you yourself also, pursuing chastity under the pretext of religion, wish to dissolve the union—provided only that this is not done deceitfully—we permit it. For although it is written, “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. XIX), God, and not man, separates when marriages are dissolved for the sake of divine love by the consent of both spouses [Col. 1261D]. Therefore we freely permit this course and readily give our assent. Otherwise, we forbid your mutual separation.

### CHAPTER LXXXIV. He who has taken religious dress without his wife’s consent must be compelled to return to her. Gregory to Adrian. Note of Panormitanus, book IX, Letter 44.

(87, q. 2, c. *Agathosa*.) Agathosa, the bearer of this letter, has complained that her husband has entered the monastery of Abbot Urbicus against her will. Since this undoubtedly pertains to the fault and reproach of that abbot, we command your experience to investigate carefully [Col. 1262A] whether he perhaps entered religious life with her consent, or whether she promised to change her own life. If you find this, provide that he remain in the monastery and compel her to change as she promised.

But if none of this is so, and you find that the aforementioned woman has committed no crime of fornication on account of which it is lawful for a husband to put away his wife, and lest his conversion become an occasion of ruin to the wife left in the world, we wish you to restore her husband to her, even if he has been tonsured, all excuse being set aside. For except on account of fornication, a husband is permitted on no ground to put away his wife. Since, after marital union, husband and wife become one body, they cannot in part be converted and in part remain in the world.

### CHAPTER LXXXV. A woman’s consent to vow continence to God must not be extorted. Alexander II to Landulf.

(33, q. 5, c. *Notificasti*.) You have informed us that you were ill to the point of death and, greatly terrified by remembrance and fear of your sins, anxiously sought to become a monk. You extorted from your wife permission for this by threats and by terror of killing her; thus you took a monk’s habit without an abbot and sought a monastery. Thereafter, when you had recovered health, utterly overcome by your wife’s objections and tears and by the dispersal of your household, you are said to have returned home and, after many days, by the counsel of certain wise persons, returned to the bed of the aforesaid woman. Now you seek our counsel as to whether you may have intercourse with your wife.

If the matter is as your messenger relates, it does not seem to us that this was done reasonably or soundly. For although every person pursuing monastic life must do so lawfully, holily, and justly, you, contrary to the laws, exhausted partly by threats and terror of death directed against your wife and partly by the sufferings of your illness, followed a wrong path: you departed and sought monasteries without having received any permission, as is said. This ought not to be done by force, but by equal will and consent, as the holy Fathers say. Nor is a husband to be received into a monastery unless his wife chooses a women’s monastery or, having professed continence, quickly changes her habit [Col. 1262D].

For holy Bishop Basil says thus on this matter: “If a married man wishes to enter a monastery, he is not to be received unless he has first been released by his wife’s profession of chastity. For if, while he lives, she marries another through incontinence, she will undoubtedly be an adulteress; nor is the conversion to God of such a husband accepted, when it entails the prostitution of the marital covenant. Such persons, therefore, follow Christ without fault after leaving the world only if they have consent by equal will. Therefore, dearest son, consider and see whether you have been released from your wife in this canonical manner and whether your wife has so promised. If so, you and she should complete the good undertaking and your vow. Otherwise we ought not to impose upon you the necessity of separation.”

## CONCERNING WOMEN WHO, WHILE THEIR HUSBANDS ARE IN CAPTIVITY, MARRY ANOTHER

[Col. 1263]

### CHAPTER LXXXVI. A woman who, after her husband has been carried into captivity, married another must be reunited to the former husband when he returns. [Col. 1263A] Pope Leo, chapter 45.

Women whose husbands were captured and carried into captivity, and who married other men because they believed their husbands had been killed, ought, when their former husbands return from captivity, to be reunited to them. Thus what each lawfully possessed may be restored and preserved; each person may receive what is his own; and the covenants of marriage may be renewed.

### CHAPTER LXXXVII. A woman who married another believing her husband dead is compelled, upon his return, to go back to the former husband. Leo to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia.

(34, q. 2, c. *Cum per bellicam*.) You say that, through the calamity of war and the most grievous assaults of hostile invasion, certain marriages have been divided in such a way that husbands were taken away into captivity, while their abandoned wives believed that their own husbands had been killed or that, owing to cruel domination, they would never be liberated. Compelled by anxiety, they passed into marriage with others. Now that the state of affairs has, by God’s help, changed for the better, and some of those believed to have perished may have returned, your Charity seems rightly to be uncertain what we should decree concerning the women joined to other husbands.

But since we know what is written, that a woman is joined to her husband by the Lord, and since we recognize the command that those whom the Lord has joined no human being may separate, we must hold that the covenants of lawful marriages are to be restored. With the effects of war removed, justice requires that what each person lawfully brought should be restored to him. Accordingly, every effort must be made that each receive what is his own. Yet the person who assumed the place of a husband who was believed no longer to exist must not be judged guilty or treated as an invader of another’s right.

For many things belonging to those carried off into captivity may have passed into another’s ownership; nevertheless, justice fully requires that their property be restored to them when they return. If this is rightly observed in slaves, fields, houses, and possessions, how much more must it be done in restoring married persons: what the disaster of war disturbed must be restored by the remedy of peace. Indeed, if husbands returning after long captivity continue to love their wives and desire them to return to their fellowship, what necessity has brought about must be forgiven and judged blameless, and what fidelity requires must be restored.

### CHAPTER LXXXVIII. On the same matter. Leo, Letter 77.

(34, q. 2, c. *Cum per*, § *Si autem*.) But if some women are so captivated by love for their later husbands that they prefer to cling to them rather than return to the lawful union [Col. 1264A], they are rightly to be censured and deprived of ecclesiastical communion. For, out of a matter that was excusable, they have chosen the contamination of crime, showing that, because of their own incontinence, they approved what a just remission could have expiated.

Marriages, therefore, should return to their original state through voluntary restoration. What the condition of necessity extorted must by no means be turned into a reproach of bad will. For just as women who refuse to return to their husbands are to be regarded as impious, so those who return to the former affection are rightly to be praised.

### CHAPTER LXXXIX. When the first husband or wife returns from captivity, the marriage is restored. Pope Innocent to Bishop Rolo, Letter 9.

(34, q. 2, c. *Cum in captivitate*.) While the woman Ursa was held captive, we learn that another marriage was contracted with Restituta at Fontanum. But when Ursa returned by the Lord’s favour, she came to us and established, with no one disputing it, that she was the wife of the man in question. Therefore, illustrious son, we decree—with Catholic faith supporting us—that the marriage is that which was first founded by divine grace; and that the union with the second woman, while the first survives and has not been put away by divorce, is in no way lawful.

### CHAPTER XC. On the same matter. *Pandects*, book XXIV, title 2.

(L. *Uxoris*, § *De divor*.) It is generally determined that, so long as it is uncertain whether husbands in captivity are alive, their wives have no permission to enter another marriage.

### CHAPTER XCI. A woman who refuses to follow a husband carried into captivity must remain unmarried as long as he lives. [Col. 1264C] Council at Vermer.

(34, q. 2, c. *Si quis necessitate*.) If anyone, compelled by unavoidable necessity, flees into another duchy or province and his wife, though able and capable, refuses to follow him out of love for her relatives or possessions, she must remain unmarried for the entire time that the husband whom she did not follow remains alive.

### CHAPTER XCII. An insane man or woman cannot contract marriage. From the Decree of Pope Fabian, chapter 5.

(32, q. 7, c. *Neque furiosus*.) Neither an insane man nor an insane woman can contract marriage; but if a marriage has been contracted, it is not to be separated.

### CHAPTER XCIII. Marriages may not be dissolved because of illness or bodily injury. Nicholas to Charles, bishop of Mainz.

(32, q. 7, c. *Hi qui*.) Those who contracted marriage while healthy, if one of the two is thereafter afflicted by mental derangement, madness, or some illness, cannot have their marriage dissolved because of that illness. The same is to be understood of those blinded by enemies or mutilated in their limbs.

### CHAPTER XCIV. The believing party must not put away an unbelieving spouse. [Col. 1265A] Paul the Apostle.

(28, q. 1, c. 1, § *Item, Apost.*) If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with [Col. 1266A] him, let him not put her away. And if any woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, let her not put him away. For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the believing woman, and the unbelieving woman is sanctified through the believing husband (I Cor. VII).

## MARRIAGE OUGHT TO BE BETWEEN PERSONS OF THE SAME RELIGION

[Col. 1265]

### CHAPTER XCV. Those who had one wife before baptism and another after baptism are regarded as bigamists. [Col. 1265A] Pope Innocent to Rufus and Eusebius, bishops of Macedonia.

(28, q. 1, c. *Nunquid*.) Are those born of the woman who was a wife before baptism not to be admitted to a share in the inheritance, and are they to be called natural children? Or is marriage not lawful, as it seems to us, except that contracted after baptism? The Lord himself, when questioned by the Jews whether it was lawful to put away a wife, explained that it ought not to be done and added: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. XIX). And, lest he be thought to have spoken of persons who receive wives after baptism, let them remember that he was questioned by Jews and answered Jews.

### CHAPTER XCVI. Those who had one wife before baptism and another after baptism are regarded as bigamists. Pope Innocent to the same persons.

(28, q. 1, c. *Nunquid*.) I anxiously ask whether the children of one and the same wife, whom he received while still a catechumen and by whom, once a believer, he later had other children [Col. 1265C], are to be called brothers; or whether, after their father’s death, they have no share in the inheritance and division of the family estate, because spiritual regeneration is said to have taken from them the name of children. Since it is absurd to judge and think thus, what reason is there for defending and asserting this evil by empty opinion rather than strengthening it by any authority, when what the law commands and God has joined cannot be counted among sins?

### CHAPTER XCVII. After baptism, it is within a believer’s power to take back the wife whom he had previously put away. From the Decree of Eutychian.

(28, q. 1, c. *Si quis*.) If a pagan puts away his pagan wife before baptism, after baptism it shall be within his power either to have her or not to have her. Similarly, if one of the spouses is baptized and the other remains pagan and does not wish to follow, as the Apostle says: “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart” (I Cor. VII).

### CHAPTER XCVIII. While the first wife lives, after baptism a man may not take another. Council of Meaux, chapter 1.

(28, q. 2, c. *Si quis*.) If anyone had a virgin wife before baptism, he cannot have another after baptism while she lives. Crimes are absolved in baptism, not marriages.

### CHAPTER XCIX. A fraudulent change of status does not separate a contracted marriage. Council of Tribur, chapter 8.

(29, q. 2, c. *Perlatum est*.) It was reported to the holy synod that a freeborn man had taken a freeborn woman as wife and, after they had produced children, had made himself a slave under the pretext of some divorce. The question was whether he must necessarily retain the woman and, if he retained her, whether she too ought to be subjected to servitude under secular law. It was decided that the wife must by no means be put away; nevertheless, the woman is not, under Christ’s law, to be reduced to slavery, since he made himself a slave without his wife’s consent, whereas she had received him as a free man for her husband.

### CHAPTER C. Even unbelievers are spouses, and a believer may lawfully put away an unbeliever. Augustine to Pollentius, *On Adulterous Marriages*, chapter 13.

(28, q. 1, c. *Jam nunc*.) Let us now consider what the Apostle says: “But to the rest I speak, not the Lord”—that is, he is about to speak concerning unequal marriages, where both parties were not Christians. It seems to me that he said this as an admonition. For because a believing spouse may lawfully leave an unbelieving spouse, it is not the Lord but the Apostle who forbids this to be done. What the Lord forbids to be done is altogether unlawful.

For the Apostle gives warning so that many may have an occasion of being gained: believing spouses, though granted permission, should not use it in leaving unbelievers. Yet you think that even unbelievers may not be put away by believers because the Lord forbids it. I do not say, however, that it is expedient; the Apostle warns against its being done, and gives the reason why it is not expedient although it is lawful. For what do you know, woman, whether you will save your husband? Or what do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife? He had also said above: “The unbelieving husband is sanctified in the believing woman,” and “the unbelieving woman is sanctified in the brother,” that is, the Christian. “Otherwise,” he says, “your children would be unclean, but now they are holy” (I Cor. VII). Thus he seems to have exhorted them to gain spouses and children for Christ, even by examples that had already occurred.

Therefore the reason has been clearly stated why it is not expedient for believing persons to put away even unbelieving spouses. It is not because the marital bond made with such persons must be maintained; rather, the Apostle forbids departure from unbelieving spouses in order that they may be sought in Christ. For many things are done not by a command of law but by free charity; and those things are more pleasing in our acts of service when, although we were allowed not to perform them, we perform them for love’s sake.

Thus the Lord himself, having shown that he was not obliged to pay the tax, nevertheless paid it, lest he give offence to those whose customs he accommodated for their eternal salvation. Further, the Apostle’s words show how he commends this: “For though I am free from all, I made myself the servant of all, that I might gain the more” (I Cor. IX). A little earlier he had said: “Do we not have the right to eat and drink? Do we not have the right to take about with us a woman who is a sister, as also the other apostles, the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas? Or do only I and Barnabas have no power to do this? Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not drink of its milk?” (ibid.). And shortly afterward: “If others share in the rights of our authority, do not we still more? But we have not used this authority; rather, we endure all things lest we give any hindrance to the Gospel of Christ” (ibid.).

### CHAPTER CI. It is lawful, but not expedient, to leave unbelieving spouses. [Col. 1267B] Augustine to the same person.

(28, q. 1, c. *Sic enim*.) Likewise: Thus believing men and women are neither forbidden by the Lord to leave unbelieving wives or husbands nor commanded to do so. For if they had been commanded to put away such wives, there would have been no room for the Apostle’s counsel warning that this should not be done. A good servant never forbids what the Lord commands.

Likewise: When, therefore, he began to preach the Gospel to the gentiles and found gentiles joined in marriage, of whom not both believed but one man or woman did, while the unbeliever consented to dwell with the believer, the believer ought neither to have been forbidden by the Lord to put away the unbeliever nor commanded to do so. They were not forbidden, because justice permits departure from one committing fornication, and the fornication of an unbelieving person is greater in the heart; nor can that person’s chastity with a spouse be called true, because “whatever is not from faith is sin.” Yet the believer possesses true chastity even with an unbelieving spouse who does not possess true chastity.

Nor, indeed, ought believers to have been commanded to separate from unbelievers, because the two gentiles were not joined contrary to the Lord’s command. Therefore, since the Lord neither forbids nor commands a believer to depart from an unbeliever, while the Apostle—not the Lord—tells the believer not to depart, the Apostle undoubtedly has the Holy Spirit, by whom he could give useful and faithful counsel concerning marriage. Hence, after he had said concerning the woman whose husband had died, “But she will be happier if she remains as she is, according to my counsel” (I Cor. VII), lest anyone suppose this counsel human and not divine, and therefore to be disregarded, he added: “I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (ibid.).

Accordingly, even those things which God does not command but which his holy servant usefully recommends are recommended through the Lord’s own inspiration. Far be it that any Catholic should say that what the Holy Spirit recommends is not recommended by the Lord, since he himself is Lord and the works of the Trinity are inseparable. For the Apostle says: “Concerning virgins, I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel” (ibid.). This is not so that we should consider this counsel alien to the Lord, since he immediately continues: “As one who has obtained mercy from God to be faithful” (I Cor. VII).

Therefore he gives faithful counsel according to God, in that Spirit of whom he says: “I think that I too have the Spirit of God.” Nevertheless, the command of the Lord who commands is one thing, and the faithful counsel of a fellow servant, inspired and granted to him by the Lord according to the mercy of charity, is another. In the former case it is not lawful to do otherwise; in the latter it is lawful, though in such a way that what is lawful is in part expedient and in part not expedient.

It is expedient when it is permitted not only by the justice which is before God, but also when no hindrance to anyone’s salvation results from it—for example, when the Apostle gives virgins counsel not to marry, concerning which he testifies that he has no command of the Lord. It is lawful to do otherwise—that is, to marry and retain the lesser good of continence in marriage—and that lawful course is also expedient, because the honourable estate of marriage receives bodily weakness that would otherwise fall into forbidden and unlawful conduct, and obstructs no one’s salvation. Yet it would be more expedient and more honourable if a virgin embraced the counsel to which no command compels her.

But what is lawful is not expedient when it is indeed permitted, yet use of that right presents others with an obstacle to salvation. Such is the matter of which we have long been speaking: the departure of a believing spouse from an unbelieving one. The Lord does not prohibit it by a command of law, because it is not unjust before him; but the Apostle forbids it by counsel of charity, because it brings an obstacle to the salvation of unbelievers. They are not only most disastrously scandalized and offended; moreover, when they enter other marriages while those who put them away are still living, they are bound in adulterous unions from which they are difficult to free.

Therefore, where what is lawful is not expedient, one cannot say, “If she puts away the unbeliever, she does well; if she does not put him away, she does better,” as it is said: “He who gives in marriage does well, and he who does not give in marriage does better” (ibid.). For in that case not merely one course, but both alike are lawful. Thus no one is compelled to either course by a command of the Lord; moreover, each is expedient, though one less and the other more. Therefore, by the Apostle’s counsel, whoever can accept it is called to that which is more expedient.

But here, when the question concerns putting away or not putting away an unbelieving spouse in a marriage with a believer, both courses are alike lawful according to the justice which is before the Lord; therefore the Lord prohibits neither. Yet both are not expedient because of human weakness; therefore the Apostle forbids what is not expedient. The Lord thereby gives him freedom to forbid it, because the Lord does not forbid what the Apostle advises, nor does the Apostle forbid what the Lord commands. If this were not so, the Apostle would neither advise anything contrary to the Lord’s prohibition nor forbid anything contrary to his command.

Accordingly, in these two cases—one concerning marrying or not marrying, the other concerning putting away or not putting away an unbelieving spouse—there is something similar and something dissimilar. The similarity is that there he says, “I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel”; and here he says, “I speak, not the Lord” (I Cor. VII). “I have no commandment of the Lord” is equivalent to “The Lord does not say”; and “I give counsel” is equivalent to “I speak.”

But the dissimilarity is this: concerning marrying and not marrying, it can be said, “This may rightly be done, but that is better,” because both are expedient, though one less and the other more. But concerning putting away or not putting away an unbelieving spouse, because one of these is not expedient and the other is expedient, it ought to be said: “He who puts away does well, and he who does not put away does better.” But it ought not to be said, “He does not put her away because it is not expedient.” Thus we can say that it is better not to put away an unbelieving spouse, although it is lawful also to put such a spouse away [Col. 1269B], just as we rightly say that what is lawful and expedient is better than what is lawful but not expedient.

For these reasons, when I was expounding the Lord’s discourse which he delivered at length on the mountain, and came to the question whether spouses should be dismissed or not dismissed, I introduced the Apostle’s counsel—not the Lord’s command—where he says: “But to the rest I speak, not the Lord” (ibid.), warning those who had unbelieving spouses not to dismiss them if they consented to live with them. This, indeed, ought to have been urged, not commanded, because people ought not to be restrained from doing what is lawful, though it be not advantageous, with as great a weight as they are restrained from what is unlawful. But if the Apostle sometimes deigns to urge even things which ought to be commanded [Col. 1269C], he does so out of indulgence toward weakness, not to prejudice the command. Thus he said: “I write these things not to shame you, but I admonish you as my dearest children” (I Cor. IV).

What difficulty is there where he says: “Behold, I Paul say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. V)? Does he also say here, “Behold, I say, not the Lord”? These things are therefore not alike, because it is neither unworthy nor contrary for the Apostle to urge those same things which the Lord commands. For we urge those whom we love to carry out the Lord’s precepts or commands. But when he says, “I say, not the Lord,” he shows that the Lord does not forbid what he himself was forbidding. The Lord would have forbidden it if it had been unlawful [Col. 1269D].

Therefore, according to what we have said and discussed at length above, it was lawful in justice, but it was not fitting to do what was lawful on account of free good will. But you, to whom it seems that what the Lord does not forbid but the Apostle does is unlawful, just as unlawful as what the Lord forbids: when you wished to explain what was meant by the saying, “I say, not the Lord,” spoken to believers whose spouses were unbelievers, you said that the Lord commanded that marriages of persons of different religions should not be joined together. You even introduced the Lord’s testimony when he says: “You shall not take a wife for your son from the daughters of foreigners, lest she lead him after foreign gods and his soul perish” [Col. 1270A] (Exod. XXXIV). You also added the Apostle’s words where he says: “A woman is bound to her husband as long as her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is free and may marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (I Cor. VII), which you explained by adding: “That is, a Christian.”

You then continued and added: “This, therefore, is the Lord’s command in both the Old and the New Testament; and this the Lord commands, this the Apostle teaches: that marriages remain joined only among those of the same religion and faith. Why, then, contrary to the Lord’s command, contrary to holy teaching, contrary to the precept of the Old and New Testament, does the Apostle command that marriages of persons of different faiths should remain joined? Because,” you say, “Paul, preacher and apostle of the Gentiles, commands—not merely advises—those already placed in marriage [Col. 1270B] that, if one of the spouses has believed and the other does not believe but nevertheless consents to live with the believer, the believer should not dismiss the other.”

By these words you show quite clearly that this case is one thing and that case another. You show quite clearly that that case is another. For that case concerns marriages not yet initially contracted: that a woman should not marry except a man of her own religion, nor a man take such a wife. This, as you say, the Lord commands, the Apostle teaches, and both Testaments prescribe. But who could deny that this case is different? For there the question is not of persons being joined, but of persons already joined. Both were of one and the same unbelief when they were joined; but when the Gospel came, either the husband believed without the wife or the wife without the husband.

If, then, this is another case—as is evident beyond any scruple of doubt [Col. 1270C]—why is it not permissible for a believing husband to remain in marriage with an unbelieving wife? Does not the Lord command this also, just as the Apostle does? Unless perhaps the Apostle’s highly faithful statement has no force here: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (II Cor. XIII). And Christ is certainly the Lord. Do you understand what we are saying? Or shall I at some point dwell more carefully on explaining this? Attend, so that we may set the matter requiring explanation, as though placed before the eyes for demonstration, in plainer speech.

Behold, two spouses were of one unbelief when they were joined. No question concerning them pertains to that command of the Lord, apostolic teaching, and precept of the Old and New Testament by which a believer is forbidden to enter marriage with an unbeliever. They are already spouses, and both are still unbelievers. They are still such as they were before they were joined and such as they were when they were joined. A preacher of the Gospel comes; either the husband or the wife believes, but the unbeliever consents to live with the believer. Does the Lord command the believer to dismiss the unbeliever, or does he not? If you say, “He commands it,” the Apostle protests: “I say, not the Lord.” If you say, “He does not command it,” I ask the reason. Nor will you give me the reason which you inserted in your writings, namely, that the Lord forbids believers to be joined with unbelievers; for that is by no means the reason here, since we are speaking of those already joined, not of persons to be joined [Col. 1271A]. Thus you have not found your reason why the Lord does not forbid what the Apostle forbids. For you now see, as I judge [Col. 1272A], that this is not the reason you thought it was.

## WHY MARRIAGE OUGHT NOT TO BE DISSOLVED, AND WHY THERE IS NO MARRIAGE WITHOUT THE CONSENT OF BOTH

[Col. 1271]

### CHAPTER CII. Marriage is contracted by consent and is not invalidated if the custom of the country is not observed. Council of Tribur, canon 15.

[Col. 1271A]

(C. I, *Extra De Sponsa*.) A certain nobleman of France took as wife a noblewoman of Saxony according to Saxon law. He kept her for many years and begot children by her. But, because Saxons and Franks do not use the same laws, he alleged that he had not betrothed, received [Col. 1271B], or endowed her according to his own—that is, Frankish—law; having dismissed her, he took another woman. Concerning this, the holy synod decreed that he, as a transgressor of evangelical law, should be subjected to penance; separated from the second wife; and compelled to take back the first.

### CHAPTER CIII. Whatever kind of man he may be, once he has been accepted, he is not to be dismissed. Ambrose, *Hexameron*, book V, chapter 7.

(32, q. 5, c. *Horrendus*.) A husband who has once been accepted is dreadful and uncouth: is another husband to be chosen? A horse loves its mate; if its mate is changed, it does not know how to draw the yoke with another. It does not regard another’s mate as its own whole companion. Do you reject your marital companion and think that he ought often to be changed? Change him; and if he departs for a single day, bring in a rival, and immediately, without knowing the cause, punish as though known the affront to your modesty.

### CHAPTER CIV. Whatever kind of woman she may be, once she has pleased her husband, she is not to be dismissed. Augustine, *On the Sermon of the Lord on the Mount*.

(32, q. 5, c. *Si uxorem*.) If anyone has a wife—whether barren, physically unattractive, weak in her limbs, blind and deaf, lame, or, indeed, exhausted by any other illnesses, pains, and labours—and however intensely dreadful anything may be imagined apart from the cause of fornication, he should endure it for the sake of fellowship and fidelity.

### CHAPTER CV. It is not lawful for anyone to dismiss a barren wife and take another for the sake of fertility. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 7.

(32, q. 7, c. *Tantum valet*.) The social bond has such force that, although it is formed for the purpose of procreation, it is not dissolved even when that very purpose of procreation fails. For a man could dismiss a barren wife and take another by whom he might have children; yet this is not lawful. Again: the bond of marriage remains even if offspring, for whose sake it was entered upon, does not follow because of manifest barrenness; so that, even when the spouses know that they will not have children, they may nevertheless neither separate from one another even for the sake of children nor join themselves to others. If they do so, they commit adultery with those to whom they join themselves.

But while the marriage itself remains, it was clearly permitted by right and authority among the ancient patriarchs, with the wife’s consent, to introduce another woman by whom common children might be born—through intercourse with one woman and the seed of the other. Whether this is also permitted now, I would not rashly say [Col. 1271D].

### CHAPTER CVI. No one may dismiss a wife unless the cause of discord is first proved before the Church. Council of Carthage IV, canon 30.

[Col. 1272A]

(33, q. 2, c. *Saeculares*.) If lay persons dismiss their marital union without any graver fault—or, having dismissed it, propose no plausible grounds of discord—and for that reason abandon their marriages in order to undertake either unlawful unions or unions belonging to another, then, if they cast away their wives before stating the causes of their discord before the bishops of their province [Col. 1272B], and before being condemned by judgment, they are to be excluded from the communion of the Church and the holy assembly of the people, because they defile faith and marriage.

### CHAPTER CVII. The consent of the contracting parties is sufficient for marriage. Nicholas to Archbishop Hincmar.

(27, q. 2, c. *Sufficiat solus*.) According to the laws, the consent alone of those whose union is at issue is sufficient. If that consent alone is lacking in marriage, perhaps all the other things, even if celebrated together with sexual intercourse itself, are void—as the great teacher John Chrysostom attests when he says: “It is not intercourse but will that makes marriage.”

### CHAPTER CVIII. A girl is not compelled to marry by her father’s oath if she has never given her consent. Pope Urban, concerning the daughter of Jordan.

[Col. 1272C]

(31, q. 2, c. *Si verum*.) If what the envoys of Prince Jordan have reported to us is found to be true—namely, that he himself, compelled and distressed, betrothed his little daughter to the son of Ramald Ridelli while she was unwilling, weeping, and resisting to the extent of her strength, and while her mother and kindred did not consent but were greatly distressed—then, since the authority of canons and laws does not approve such betrothals, as will be shown below, we moderate our judgment lest what we say appear too harsh to those ignorant of laws and canons. Thus, if the prince wishes, with the consent of his daughter, her mother, and her kindred, to complete what was begun, we permit it. But otherwise, let our legate hear both parties [Col. 1272D]; and if there is nothing on the part of the aforesaid Ramald that further hinders it, let him receive from Jordan himself an oath that these matters stand as stated. Thereafter, following the enactments of canons and laws, we do not forbid his aforesaid daughter, if she wishes, to marry another man, provided only that it be in the Lord.

### CHAPTER CIX. Those who are to become one body ought also to be of one mind; therefore no one is to be joined to another against her will. Urban, concerning the daughter of the king of Aragon.

(31, q. 2, c. *De neptis*.) Concerning the marriage of your niece, whom, under a pledge of faith, you promised to give to a certain knight when your necessity was pressing, we decree, equity so requiring, that if she wholly refuses that man, as is said, and persists in that determination of her will, so that she utterly declines to marry him, you are in no way to compel her, unwilling and resisting, to be joined in marriage to the same man. For those whose body is one ought also to have one mind [Col. 1273A; 1274A], lest, if a virgin is joined unwillingly to someone, evil should evidently recoil upon the man who joined her against her will, contrary to God and the Apostle’s command. The same is to be maintained in like manner concerning a man.

## CONCERNING THE SEPARATION OF MARRIAGE BECAUSE OF ERROR AS TO STATUS

[Col. 1273]

### CHAPTER CX. Error as to status invalidates marriage. *Novellae*, constitution 33.

[Col. 1273A]

If anyone through error marries a female slave as his wife, believing her free, or conversely if a free woman is through error joined to a slave, and the truth is afterward discovered, it must certainly be said that no marriage came into being. For marriages cannot be contracted between a free man and a slave woman, or between a slave man and a free woman. But if through the cunning and connivance of the master, a male or female slave contracts marriage with a free person—for example, the master joined his female slave as though free to a freeborn man and provided her with a dowry, in order that he might gain the whole donation made in consideration of the marriage, or a part of it—then, if anything of this kind occurs, the very giving of the dowry makes the slave woman free, and the marriage stands: no law, so far as slavery is concerned, invalidates such a marriage.

But if the master has not specifically consented to the marriage of his female or male slave, while knowing nevertheless that they have cohabited—perhaps he does this in order later [Col. 1274A] to bring an action against the free man because he has taken his slave woman as wife, or against the freeborn woman because she has married his slave—then, if such a case occurs and the master has not specifically consented, but knowingly has not forbidden the matter, the marriage stands in full legal force [Col. 1274B]; and the person of servile condition is released into freeborn status, the law being without doubt open to that effect, since children born from such marriages are both freeborn and legitimate.

### CHAPTER CXI. Concerning a man who has taken as wife a female slave whom he thinks free. Council of Verneuil, canon 6.

(29, q. 2, c. *Si quis ingenuus*.) If a freeborn man has taken another’s female slave as wife and thinks that she is freeborn, and that woman is afterward discovered to be in slavery, he should redeem her from slavery if he can.
