If he cannot, he may take another, if he wishes. But if he knew nevertheless that she was a slave and had approved the arrangement, he should keep her as his lawful wife. A freeborn woman should do likewise with respect to another’s male slave.

## CONCERNING IMPOTENCE FOR INTERCOURSE

[Col. 1273]

### CHAPTER CXII. A man whose own wife cannot render the marital due because of bodily illness may take another. Gregory the Younger to Bishop Boniface.

[Col. 1273C]

(32, q. 7, c. *Quod proposuisti*.) You have asked what is to be done concerning a wife who, stricken by illness, is unable to render the marital due to her husband. It would be good if she remained as she is, in order to devote herself to continence; but because this belongs to the great, he who cannot contain himself should rather marry. Yet he should not withdraw assistance from her whom illness hinders, though no detestable fault excludes her.

### CHAPTER CXIII. A wife may take another husband because of her husband’s impotence to render the marital due. Code, book V, title 19, chapter 10.

(L. *In causis*, c. *De repudiis*, c. *Litterae*, and *Extra* [Col. 1273D], *De frig.*) If, from the beginning of the marriage, reckoning up to two continuous years, a husband is altogether unable through natural weakness to have intercourse with his wife, the woman, or her parents, may send repudiation to the husband without danger of losing the dowry.

### CHAPTER CXIV. On the same matter. *Capitularies*, title VII, chapter 20.

(22, q. 2, c. *Non est*, and *Extra De frig.*) If a man and woman have joined themselves in marriage, and afterward the woman says that the husband cannot have intercourse with her, then, if she can prove it true, she may take another [Col. 1274C], because, according to the Apostle, that man who was her husband was unable to render the marital due.

### CHAPTER CXV. If a woman proves that she has never been known by her husband, they are to be separated. Gregory to John, bishop of Ravenna.

(27, q. 2, c. *Quod autem*; 33, q. 1, c. *Licet mul.*) As to your question concerning those who are joined in marriage but cannot have intercourse, whether he may take another woman or she another man: it is written concerning them, “If a man and woman join themselves, and afterward the woman says of the man that he cannot have intercourse with her, then, if she can prove by lawful judgment that this is true, she may take another. But if he takes another woman, they are to be separated.”

### CHAPTER CXVI. A woman whom her husband has been unable to know because of frigidity may marry another. Gregory II to John, bishop of Ravenna.

[Col. 1274D]

(34, q. 1, c. *Requisisti*.) You have inquired concerning those who say that, because of a cold nature, they cannot have sexual intercourse with one another. If this man cannot use her as a wife, let him keep her as a sister. But if they wish to break the marital bond, both are to remain unmarried. For if he could not naturally be compatible with this woman, how will he suit another? Therefore, if the man wishes to take another wife, it is plainly evident that, prompted by the devil’s tinder of hatred, he hated her; and that he therefore contrives the falsehood of a lie in order to dismiss her [Col. 1275A].

But if the woman pleads and says, “I wish to be a mother and bear children,” each of them, with seven hands of relatives touching the most holy relics, is to declare under oath that they were never joined by sexual intercourse and made one flesh. Then the woman seems able to contract a second marriage. I say this humanly, on account of the weakness of their flesh; but the man who is of a cold nature is to remain without a wife. If he too takes another union, then those who swore are to be held guilty of perjury, and, after penance has been performed, they are to be compelled to resume their former marriages.

### CHAPTER CXVII. What is to be done concerning those who, hindered by magical practices, cannot have intercourse. Hincmar, bishop of Rheims.

[Col. 1275B]

(33, q. 1, c. *Si quis per*.) If, by sorceries and magical practices—God’s hidden but never unjust judgment permitting it, and the devil preparing it—intercourse does not take place, those to whom this happens are to be urged to make a pure confession to God and the priest of all their sins, with contrite heart and humbled spirit; and, through abundant tears, more generous almsgiving, prayers, and fasts, to make satisfaction to the Lord. By exorcisms and the other ministries of the Church’s medicine, ministers of the Church should endeavour to heal such persons, insofar as the Lord grants—he who healed Abimelech and his household through Abraham’s prayers [Col. 1276A]. If perhaps they cannot be healed, they may be separated. But after they seek other marriages, while those to whom they had been joined in the flesh remain alive, they cannot be reconciled to their former spouses whom they left, even if the ability to have intercourse should be restored to them.

### CHAPTER CXVIII. The procedure for this separation. Council of Verneuil, canon 27.

(C. *Laudabilem*, *Extra De frig. et malefic.*) If any woman declares that her husband has never had intercourse with her, they are to go from there to the cross; and if this is true, they are to be separated. Then let it be done as she wishes.

### CHAPTER CXIX. The husband’s statement is to stand as true if the wife denies that she has been known by him. Council of Compiègne, canon 20.

[Col. 1276B]

(33, q. 1, c. *Si quis*.) If anyone has taken a wife and had her for some time, and the woman says that he has not had intercourse with her, while the man says that he has, the man’s statement is to stand as true, because the man is the head of the woman.

## CONCERNING SEPARATION OF MARRIAGE FOR A CAUSE OTHER THAN FORNICATION

[Col. 1275]

### CHAPTER CXX. Concerning a man who sleeps with his brother’s betrothed. Council of Tribur, canon 41.

[Col. 1275C]

(27, q. 1, c. *Quidam desponsavit*.) If a man takes a wife but is unable to have intercourse with her, and his brother secretly violates her and makes her pregnant, they are to be separated. Yet, consideration being given to his weakness, mercy is to be granted him with regard to marriage, provided only that it be in the Lord.

### CHAPTER CXXI. Those who commit any of the following offenses are to be separated and never again joined in marriage. Council of Mainz, canon 6.

(32, q. 7, c. *Si quis viduam*.) If anyone takes a widow as wife and afterward commits fornication with his stepdaughter, or with two sisters while one remains his wife [Col. 1275D]; or if any woman does so with two brothers, or with a father and son; if anyone defiles his brother’s widow, his niece, stepmother, daughter-in-law, female cousin, maternal uncle’s daughter, her widow, or his stepdaughter: we command that they be separated and never afterward joined in marriage.

### CHAPTER CXXII. Marriage cannot be contracted before the age of consent. Pope Nicholas.

(30, q. 2, c. *Ubi non est consens.*) Where the consent of both is absent, there is no marriage. Therefore, those who give a girl in the cradle to boys, or conversely, accomplish nothing unless both children consent after they have reached years of discretion. There is no marriage unless the consent of both takes place, even if father and mother have done and wished it.

### CHAPTER CXXIII. One received from the sacred font is the child of the person who receives him or her. Pope Nicholas, in response to the Bulgarians.

[Col. 1276C]

(30, q. 3, c. *Ita diligere*.) A person ought to love the one whom he receives from the sacred font as a father. Again: between spiritual brothers and children there is a gratuitous and holy communion which is not to be called consanguinity, but rather regarded as spiritual kinship. Therefore we judge that no legally valid marriage can be contracted between them, since the venerable Roman laws do not permit marriages even between those who are children by nature and those who are children by adoption. Again: marriage is not contracted between those whom adoption joins; how much more ought those whom the regeneration of the Holy Spirit binds through [Col. 1276D] the heavenly sacrament to abstain from carnal cohabitation with one another. Therefore, he says, the one whom divine grace has chosen to be my father’s son or my brother is called my father’s son or my brother far more fittingly than one whom human will has chosen to be so; and they are more wisely separated from mutual bodily intercourse.

### CHAPTER CXXIV. A woman who has lifted her stepson from the sacred font is not to be separated from her husband. Nicholas, bishop of Salonica.

(30, q. 1, c. *Nosse*.) You desire to know whether a woman who has lifted from the sacred font her husband’s son, born by another woman, may afterward be joined with the same husband. We decree that they may be joined, because, according to the sacred canons, a spouse ought not to dismiss the other spouse under any pretext of religion except by the consent of both. It pertains, moreover, to the great ruin of a wife that, hating her husband or not considering his infirmity [Col. 1277A], she commits impiety under the appearance of piety—especially since the Apostle commands: “Do not deprive one another, except by consent for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and return again to the same, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control” (I Cor. VII).

Therefore, if it is not proved that this was done by the consent of both spouses, they are not to deprive one another, but are to return to the same, especially since the Apostle says: “The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does” (I Cor. VII).

### CHAPTER CXXV. He who held his stepson before the bishop is to be separated from his wife. Council of Verneuil, canon 4.

[Col. 1277B]

(30, q. 1, c. *Si quis filiast.*) If anyone has held his stepson or stepdaughter before the bishop for confirmation, he is to be separated from his wife and is not to take another.

### CHAPTER CXXVI. Those who hold their stepchildren before the bishop are not to be separated from their wives. Pope Nicholas to Rodolph, bishop of Bourges.

(30, q. 1, c. *De his qui*.) Concerning those who have held their stepchildren at confirmation before bishops—that is, who support over themselves the children of their wives by an earlier husband while they are being anointed with chrism by bishops—if this takes place knowingly, as you assert, it is indeed a sin, but it is not to be punished as far as separation of marriage. Yet they should mourn and, cleansing this by worthy penance, say to the Lord [Col. 1277C]: “Do not remember the sins of our ignorance” (Ps. XXIV).

### CHAPTER CXXVII. Husbands are to be separated from wives who, by some accident, received their own children from the sacred washing. Pope Deusdedit to Gordian, bishop of Seville.

(30, q. 1, c. *Pervenit*, and *Imo quia*.) DEUSDEDIT, bishop of the holy Roman and apostolic Church, to GORDIAN, fellow bishop and most beloved brother of the Church of Seville.

A deacon of your holiness came to us bearing a letter stating that, on the past Sabbath of Easter, because of the great press of people, certain men and women unknowingly received their own children from the sacred washing [Col. 1277D]. You therefore wish to know whether, because of an occurrence of this sort, husbands and wives ought to return to their own marital use or not. We, saddened by the matter, investigated the statements of our predecessors.

We found in the archives of this apostolic see that such things had previously occurred in the Churches of Isauria, Ephesus, Jerusalem, and others as well; and that the bishops of those churches and cities, wishing to know from this apostolic see whether husbands and wives should return to their own bed, were instructed and confirmed in writing by holy fathers of blessed memory—Julius, Innocent, and Celestine—with the agreement of many bishops and priests, in the church of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles. They forbade such things, decreeing that women and men who had received their own children for any reason should by no means receive one another in marriage [Col. 1278A], but should be separated, lest such a vice grow throughout the world at the devil’s persuasion.

You know that, just as there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, so there are seven gifts of baptism: from the first feeding with consecrated salt and entrance into the church up to confirmation through chrism. From the first of these to the seventh, no Christian ought to receive his own comother in marriage; and whoever presumes to do so is to be bound by the bond of anathema until he has performed worthy penance.

### CHAPTER CXXVIII. A spiritual daughter can in no way marry a carnal son. Pope Zacharias to Theodore, bishop of Rheims.

[Col. 1278B]

(30, q. 3, c. *Pictatium*.) ZACHARIAS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend and holy brother THEODORE, bishop of Pavia.

We receive the *pictatium* which your venerable brotherhood presented to us, by which you wished to ask whether it is lawful for a son, whose father has received another man’s daughter from sacred baptism—that is, the spiritual daughter of that same father, a thing dreadful to say—to take her in marriage. You assert that this has occurred outrageously among you. But your brotherhood knows well that the Lord commanded Moses, saying: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father, your mother, or your sister. It is your nakedness” (Lev. XVIII).

Therefore, since we are commanded to abstain from our own blood kindred, we ought much more, setting aside every excuse or pretext, to guard ourselves with the utmost strictness from the spiritual daughter of our father [Col. 1278C], lest anyone who has entered upon such an offense and has not restrained the reins of lust incur the wrath of divine judgment. Thus everyone must altogether beware of the commission of such a crime, lest they perish eternally.

But your brotherhood should by every means endeavour to separate this man who, despising the salvation of his soul, has joined himself in an impious marriage through this pernicious rashness, and to subject him to worthy penance, so that, by the Lord’s help, you may win his soul, rescued from eternal condemnation. You also reported concerning children proved to have been born from these persons, whether they may be joined in marriage. But why should they be forbidden marriage or compelled to perform penance for such a matter [Col. 1278D], since they are not to be condemned on this account? For neither father shall bear punishments for son nor son for father, as the Lord says through the prophet: “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. XVIII). But, dearest brother, enough has been said concerning these matters. Take care, however, not to permit those subject to you to act otherwise, lest you be found to have departed from the straight path.

### CHAPTER CXXIX. No one is to marry his spiritual comother. From the Decree of Gregory the Younger.

(33, q. 2, c. *Si quis*.) If anyone takes his spiritual comother in marriage, let him be anathema.

## BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 1279]

## CONCERNING THE SEPARATION OF CARNAL MARRIAGE BECAUSE OF CARNAL FORNICATION

### CHAPTER I. He who dismisses his wife for a reason other than fornication is deprived of communion.

[Col. 1279A]

(32, q. 5, c. *Praeceptum*.) It is the Lord’s command that, except for the cause of fornication, a wife ought not to be dismissed by her husband. Therefore whoever, apart from the fault of the aforesaid crime, abandons his wife for any reason, since he has purposed to separate those whom God joined, is to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion and remain excluded from the assembly of Christian people until he sincerely embraces and cherishes fellowship with the wife he abandoned. Yet if, after being admonished once, twice, and three times by a priest to reform, they refuse to return to the partnership of their marital bed, they themselves, by their own deserts, are also to be excluded from the office of palatine dignity; moreover, they are to lose the marks of noble rank [Col. 1279B] for as long as they remain in fault, because they have handed over their own flesh to the knife of discord.

### CHAPTER II. Whether husband leaves wife or wife leaves husband because of fornication, the other is forbidden to have another spouse. Augustine, *On the Epistle to the Corinthians*.

(32, q. 7, c. *Apostolus*.) The Apostle Paul said to those who are married: “I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not leave her husband; but if she does leave, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband” (I Cor. VII). For she may leave for the cause which the Lord permitted. But if a woman may dismiss her husband even for the cause of fornication, what shall we answer concerning what he says afterward: “And let not a husband dismiss his wife”? Why did he not add, “except for the cause of fornication,” which the Lord permits, unless because he wishes the corresponding rule to be understood: that if he dismisses her, as is permitted for the cause of fornication, he should remain without a wife or be reconciled to his wife? And shortly afterward: the Lord permitted a wife to be dismissed for the cause of fornication, but because he permitted it, he did not command it [Col. 1279C].

### CHAPTER III. A husband may not dismiss his wife except for the cause of fornication. Jerome to Oceanus, in the epitaph of Fabiola.

(32, q. 5, c. *Praecipit Dominus*.) The Lord commands that a wife ought not to be dismissed except for the cause of fornication, and that, if dismissed, she should remain unmarried (Matt. V). Whatever is commanded to men applies correspondingly [Col. 1279D] to women. For an adulterous wife is not to be dismissed while an adulterous husband is retained. Again: among us, what is not permitted to women is equally not permitted to men, and the same service is assessed under equal condition.

### CHAPTER IV. He commits adultery who presumes to marry a woman dismissed by her husband. Augustine, *On the Sermon of the Lord on the Mount*.

(32, q. 2, c. *Dominus ad illud*.) In order to establish that a wife should not be dismissed lightly, the Lord excepted only the cause of fornication [Col. 1280A]. But whatever innumerable troubles may arise besides this, he commands that they be endured courageously for the fidelity of marriage and for chastity; and he calls even the man adulterous who marries a woman separated from her husband. Again: it may happen that a man dismisses his wife for the cause of fornication, which the Lord willed to be excepted. Yet if she is not permitted to marry while the husband from whom she departed is living, nor he to take another while the wife whom he dismissed is living, much less is it lawful for him to commit unlawful fornications with anyone whatsoever.

### CHAPTER V. A marriage proved once to have been contracted is dissolved for no reason. Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book II, chapter 4.

(32, q. 7, c. *Licite*.) A wife may lawfully be dismissed because of fornication, but the bond with the former wife remains. Consequently, he who marries a dismissed wife is guilty of adultery, even if she was dismissed for the cause of fornication. Just as a person guilty of crime is excommunicated while the sacrament of regeneration remains in him, and lacks no sacrament even if he is never reconciled to God, so, while the bond remains in him, he does not lack the sacrament of marriage, even if he is never reconciled to his husband. She will, however, lack it if her husband dies. But a person guilty of excommunication—indeed, even though unreconciled—will never lack the sacrament of regeneration, because God, to whom he is joined in baptism, never dies [Col. 1280B].

### CHAPTER VI. The marriage bond cannot be dissolved by fornication. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*.

[Col. 1280C]

(32, q. 7, c. *Interveniens*.) When divorce intervenes, the marriage covenant is not abolished: spouses remain spouses even when separated, and adultery is committed with those to whom either is joined even after divorce. Yet such is the rule concerning a wife only in the city of our God, on his holy mountain. Who does not know that the laws of nations are otherwise, where, after divorce has intervened, she may marry whom she wishes and he may take whom he wishes? Again: to pass from a living husband into another marriage was not lawful then, is not lawful now, and never will be lawful. For to apostatize from one God and go to another’s adulterous superstition is always evil.

### CHAPTER VII. A husband may dismiss his wife for the cause of fornication, but may not take an adulterous wife. Jerome on Matthew, chapter XIX.

[Col. 1280D]

(32, q. 1, c. *Dixit Hieron.*) Jerome: The Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever dismisses his wife, except for fornication, and takes another, commits adultery; and he who takes a dismissed woman commits adultery” (Matt. XIX). Fornication alone overcomes a husband’s affection for his wife [Col. 1281A]—that is, when she divides into another flesh the one flesh she shared with him, and by fornication separates herself from her husband. She ought not to be retained, lest she bring her husband also under a curse, Scripture saying: “He who keeps an adulteress is foolish and impious” (Prov. XVIII). Therefore, wherever there is fornication or suspicion of fornication, a wife is freely dismissed.

And because it could happen that someone might slander an innocent woman and, because of a second marital union, charge the former union with guilt, he commands that the first wife be dismissed in such a way that he does not have a second while the first lives. For what he says amounts to this: if you dismiss her not because of lust but because of injury, why, having experienced the misfortune of the first marriage, introduce yourself to the danger of a new one? Likewise, because it could happen under the same law that a wife might give repudiation to her husband, the same precaution is prescribed: she is not to take a second husband. And because a prostitute, or a woman who has once been an adulteress, did not fear for her own sake, the husband is commanded not to marry a second time [Col. 1281B]. If he takes such a woman, he is under the charge of adultery.

### CHAPTER VIII. He who refuses to dismiss his adulterous wife is a patron of shameful conduct. Chrysostom on Matthew, homily 26.

[Col. 1281C]

(32, q. 1, c. *Sicut crudelis*.) Just as he who dismisses a chaste woman is cruel and unjust, so he who keeps a prostitute is foolish and unjust. For the person who conceals his wife’s crime is the patron of her shameful conduct.

### CHAPTER IX. After the husband’s death, the adulterer may not take the adulteress in marriage. Council of Tribur, canon 40.

(31, q. 1, c. *Relatum*.) It has been reported to the ears of the holy priests that a certain man violated another’s wife by fornication and, moreover, while her husband was alive, gave an oath to the adulteress that, after the death of her lawful husband, if he himself survived, he would take her as wife. This was done. Therefore we forbid and anathematize such a union.

### CHAPTER X. No one may take in marriage a woman whom he has defiled by adultery. Council held at Alphes, ch. 6.

(31, q. 1, c. *Illud*.) By a common decree, in accordance with the institutions of the canons, we define and judge that, if anyone has committed fornication with another man’s wife while her husband is alive, then, when the husband dies, access to that unlawful union shall be barred to him by synodal judgment, lest he thereafter be joined in marriage to her whom he had first defiled by adultery. [Col. 1281D]

### CHAPTER XI. A woman defiled by adultery is not to be taken in marriage by that same man. Pope Leo.

(31, q. 1, c. *Nullus ducat*.) For we do not wish it, nor is it consistent with the Christian religion, that a man should take in marriage the woman whom he had previously defiled through adultery. [Col. 1282A]

### CHAPTER XII. After completing penance, a man may take as wife the widow whom, while her husband was alive, he defiled through adultery. Council of Tribur.

(31, q. 1, c. *Si quis vivente*.) He who is accused of having committed adultery with another man’s wife while her husband was alive, and who is known to have taken that same woman after the husband’s death shortly thereafter, must by every means be subjected to public penance. Concerning him, moreover, after the aforesaid penance, if it is fitting, this rule shall be observed: unless perhaps he or the woman is charged with having killed the husband who had died, or unless kinship or any other criminal impediment stands in the way. If this is proved, they are to remain perpetually in penance, without any hope of marriage. But if he denies having committed adultery with that woman while her husband was living, and neither of them can be convicted of the aforesaid homicide, let them lawfully clear the repute of their character, and let them enter into and enjoy the marriage, provided that no other reason, as we have said, prevents it. [Col. 1282B]

### CHAPTER XIII. If an adulteress against whom her husband plots death flees to a bishop, he is not to return her to her husband, but is to place her in a safe location where she can live securely. Council of Tribur, ch. 3.

If any man’s wife has been violated, and on that account her husband plans to destroy her by a capital sentence, but she, under imminent danger of death, has fled to a bishop and sought help, the bishop should labor most diligently, if he can, to prevent her killing. But if he cannot, he must by no means be permitted, when the husband demands her, to hand over for killing one who has offered herself to him for protection; rather, with careful solicitude, he is to send her to a place she herself chooses, where she can live safely.

But if at some time her husband finds and reclaims her, he will have, according to secular power, whatever authority he wishes to exercise against her. Yet let him hear Augustine saying:

> “Since a man takes his name from strength (*virtus*), and a woman from softness, that is, frailty, why does every man wish his wife to be victorious against the most cruel beast of lust, when he himself is overcome at the first blow of lust? For whatever is not permitted to women against the Catholic faith is not permitted to men either.”

But if that same woman, terrified by fear, flees from the place to which the bishop has sent her, and her husband demands her from the bishop once, twice, or more often, let the bishop seek to preserve her life, if he can, and return her. But if he cannot, let him not return her at all. The husband, however, so long as she lives, must by no means take another wife. [Cols. 1282C–1282D]

## CONCERNING THOSE WHO KILL THEIR WIVES

[Col. 1281]

### CHAPTER XIV. No one may kill his adulterous wife. Nicholas to Albinus, archbishop.

(33, q. 2, c. *Inter haec*.) Among these matters, your holiness has taken care to add the question whether, if any man’s wife has committed adultery, her husband may lawfully kill her according to human law. But God’s holy Church is never bound by worldly laws: she has no sword except the spiritual one, by which she does not kill but gives life. [Col. 1282D]

### CHAPTER XV. Marriage is altogether forbidden to those who kill their wives. Nicholas to Rodulf, archbishop of Bourges.

(33, q. 2, c. *Interfectores*.) Those who kill their own wives without judgment—you do not add, “adulterous wives,” or anything of that kind—what else are they to be regarded as but murderers? Accordingly, they must be reduced to penance, and marriage must altogether be denied them, excepting young men, concerning whom the twenty-fifth rule of the Decretals of blessed Pope Leo—or rather, its indulgence—is to be observed. [Col. 1283A]

### CHAPTER XVI. The penance of Astulf, who killed his own wife. Stephen V to Astulf.

[Col. 1283B] We are concerned, son Astulf, to admonish you with tears and great groaning of heart; yet you ought not to be called a son, since three times you have cruelly committed unhappy murder. For you killed your wife, a part of your own body, lawfully joined to you in marriage, without any capital cause: she did not resist you in any way, she did not plot against your life, and you did not find her committing an abominable act with another man. Rather, stirred up by the devil and inflamed with impious fury, more savage than any beast, you slew her cruelly with your sword in the manner of robbers.

And now, after her death, you add iniquity to iniquity, you wicked plunderer of your own children: you did not spare their mother and made your children orphans. [Col. 1283C] You wish, after her death, to introduce against her a cause of death; through one murderer and reprobate witness you wish to accuse the dead woman. Since neither the Gospel nor any divine or human law condemns or acquits anyone upon the testimony of one witness, even a competent one, how much less should she, through that most shameful and criminal man, have been condemned while alive or accused by you after her death.

The accusation should first have been carefully investigated; and then, if it had been established, she should have received the vengeance of punishment in accordance with the course of the law. For if it had been true—far be it!—as that adulterer lied, then perhaps, after seven years of completed penance, you could have dismissed her for an approved cause, had you wished; but you ought by no means to have killed her. For God does not will the death of a sinner, [Col. 1283D] but that he be converted to penance and live.

Therefore let our counsel please you, and do what may seem the lighter and better course. Have mercy on your soul, lest you become your own murderer. We therefore ask you to abandon this evil by which you were drawn into so monstrous a crime of sin. Enter a monastery, humble yourself under the hands of an abbot, and, aided by the prayers of many brothers, observe with a suppliant spirit all that may be commanded you. Perhaps the infinite goodness of God will forgive your sins and refresh your soul before you are tortured in everlasting flames. Know with certainty that this is the better and lighter course.

But if you wish to perform public penance while remaining in [Col. 1284A] your own house or in the world—which, do not doubt, will be worse, harsher, and more burdensome for you—we exhort you to do the following. On every day during which you must do penance, drink neither wine nor any intoxicating drink; never eat meat at any time, except at Easter and on the day of the Lord’s Nativity. Perform penance on bread, water, and salt. Persevere continually in vigils, fasts, prayers, and almsgiving. Never gird yourself with weapons, nor presume to engage in a quarrel anywhere. Never take a wife; do not keep a concubine; and do not dare to commit adultery. Never bathe in a bathhouse. Never join the banquets of the rejoicing. In church, humbly place yourself apart from the other Christians behind the door and doorposts. Simply commend yourself to the prayers of those entering and leaving. Consider yourself unworthy of communion in the body and blood of the Lord throughout all the days of your life. Yet on the final day of your life, if you are worthy, we permit you to receive it only by concession as viaticum, if there is someone to administer it to you. [Col. 1284B]

There are many other things that, in proportion to the great weight of your sin, unhappy man, ought to be added to you more harshly and severely. But if, with God’s help, you do and keep with a perfect heart all these things mercifully prescribed to you, we trust in God’s boundless mercy that you will obtain forgiveness of your sins. According to the saying of the just and good Shepherd, holy Church releases you from this bond of sin [Col. 1284C] on earth, so that, through the grace of Him who purchased her with His own blood, you may be released in heaven.

But if you do otherwise and despise this most health-giving admonition of holy mother Church, be your own judge: you will remain in the devil’s snare, in which you are held entangled. Your blood be upon your own head. We, being separate from fellowship with you, strive with every diligence for the salvation of God’s other children, with His help; we labor earnestly and implore the Lord’s mercy more attentively each day.

### CHAPTER XVII. Rather let a man take another wife while his wife lives than shed human blood. Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, ch. 2.

[Col. 1284D] (33, q. 2, c. *Si quod*.) If what is truer is said, a Christian man may not kill his adulterous wife, but only dismiss her. Who is so insane as to say to him: “Do what is unlawful, so that you may be permitted to do what is unlawful”? For since both acts are unlawful according to Christ’s law—both killing an adulteress and taking another wife while she lives—he must refrain from both, not do one unlawful thing in place of another. If he is going to do what is unlawful, let him now commit adultery rather than homicide: let him take another wife while his own lives, rather than shed human blood. But if both are impious, he ought not to commit one through the other, but avoid both.

## CONCERNING ADULTERY

[Col. 1285]

### CHAPTER XVIII. Charlemagne repudiated his first wife and took a second, by whom he had three sons and three daughters. Charlemagne, according to Alcuin.

[Col. 1285A] At his mother’s urging, Charles took as wife the daughter of Desiderius, king of the Lombards. For an uncertain reason he repudiated her after one year, and took in marriage Hildegard, a woman of the highest nobility from the people of the Suevi. By her he begot three sons—namely Charles, Pippin, and Louis—and as many daughters.

### CHAPTER XIX. A man does not sin less merely because he alone lacks the opportunity. Augustine, *On Free Choice*.

(Dist. 1, c. *Si cui*.) Even if someone does not have the opportunity [Col. 1285B] to sleep with another man’s wife, yet if it is in some way plain that he desires it and would do it if the power were given him, he is no less guilty than if he were caught in the act itself.

### CHAPTER XX. Adulteries are not to be committed even with the intention of begetting children. Augustine to Claudius against Julian.

(32, q. 4, c. *Sicut non sunt*.) Just as adulteries are not to be committed even with the intention of begetting children, so thefts are not to be committed even with the intention of feeding holy poor persons. This should indeed be done, not by perpetrating thefts but by making good use of the mammon of iniquity.

### CHAPTER XXI. Adultery occupies second place among punishments. Clement to James, Epistle 1.

(32, q. 7, c. *Quid in omnibus*.) What sin is graver than adultery? For it occupies second place among punishments; the first place is held by those who depart from God, even if they have lived soberly. [Col. 1285C]

### CHAPTER XXII. When adultery is said to be committed. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*.

(32, q. 5, c. *Illae autem*.) Adultery occurs when, either at the prompting of one’s own lust or with another’s consent, one has intercourse with a man or woman other than one’s spouse, contrary to the marriage covenant. Thus the fidelity is broken which, even in bodily and lowly matters, is a great good of the soul. Therefore it certainly ought not to be placed below even bodily health, which this present life itself contains. [Col. 1285D]

### CHAPTER XXIII. He commits adultery who has intercourse with anyone outside the marriage covenant. Isidore on Exodus, ch. 29.

(32, q. 5, c. *Non moechaberis*.) “You shall not commit adultery”; that is, no one is to have intercourse with women other than his wife in order to satisfy lust. For he commits adultery spiritually who approaches another woman besides his own.

### CHAPTER XXIV. A wife ought not to be placed under her husband’s power, but in free custody, when judgment is to be given either on the marital covenant or on a charge of adultery. Nicholas to King Charles.

[Col. 1286A] As we have learned from the report of many people, King Lothair has resolved to hold an assembly and intends to subject Queen Theutberga to examination according to his own judgment. If, by the deceptions of his falsehood, he can have her represented as not having been his lawful wife, he wishes to separate her completely from himself. But if he wishes to dismiss her as his own wife, and then accuse her as though she had committed adultery, and thereby drive his own man and Theutberga’s man to single combat, he intends, if the queen’s man falls, to kill her without delay.

Likewise, moreover, whether judgment is to be given concerning the covenant of spouses or concerning the crime of adultery, there is no basis upon which Theutberga can enter into a contest with Lothair or undertake a lawful trial of the dispute unless she is first restored to her own authority and to her own kinsfolk. A place must also be arranged among them where no force of a crowd need be feared and where it is not difficult to bring forward witnesses or the other persons whom both the holy canons and the venerable Roman laws require in controversies of this kind. [Col. 1286B]

We have not said this in order to show what legal contest Lothair imagines he can enter, when he daily harasses and crushes in his private chambers the person with whom he is in conflict; when, whenever he wishes, he brings her before judgment, whenever he wishes returns her to confinement, and, when she has been brought out, punishes her unless she professes what he has commanded. Therefore she must be committed to her own liberty and freed from every oppression and power of the person with whom the contest is undertaken; she must be allowed freely to use her own resources, and persons who are suspect must be avoided, she who desires to demonstrate that she is free from the accusations made against her. [Col. 1286C]

### CHAPTER XXV. A confession extracted by force ought not to be admitted in judgment. Nicholas to Queen Theutberga.

We by no means receive this confession of yours—which was extracted not by your will but by force—as a confession; nor do we permit the reproach to spread its roots, since, unless it is uprooted at once, it can bring ruin upon many. For if this is permitted, all husbands may torment with various afflictions the women whom they have lawfully obtained, if they hate them; immediately compel them to say that they were not lawfully taken as wives; indeed, compel them by intolerable punishments to declare some moral crime against themselves. [Col. 1286D]

### CHAPTER XXVI. A cleric may not engage in trade; and this states the times when a husband may have intercourse with his wife. Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, ch. 27.

(Dist. 38, c. *Fornicari*.) People are never permitted to commit fornication; but they are sometimes permitted to trade. Before a man becomes an ecclesiastic, he may trade; once he has become one, he may not. A Christian is sometimes permitted to have intercourse with his wife, and sometimes not permitted. For on days of processions intercourse is sometimes not permitted, since even lawful things must be abstained from, so that what is requested may be obtained more easily. Hence the Apostle says: “By mutual consent, abstain for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Cor. 7). For according to the law it is permitted to yield and quarrel during a fast—thus printed—but afterwards it is not permitted. [Cols. 1287A, 1288A]

## CONCERNING SPIRITUAL FORNICATION

[Col. 1287]

### CHAPTER XXVII. What fornication of the flesh and of the soul are. Isidore, *Sentences*, 39.

Fornication of the flesh is adultery. Fornication of the soul is slavery to idols.

### CHAPTER XXVIII. What adulterous marriage is. Augustine, Book I.

If a wife may be separated from her husband because of fornication of the flesh, how much more detestable is fornication of the mind in a spouse—that is, unbelief? The fornication of an unbelieving person is greater in the heart, and such a person’s chastity with a spouse cannot be called true, because “whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14). [Col. 1287B]

### CHAPTER XXIX. A wife who seeks to compel her husband to evil may lawfully be dismissed. Augustine, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*.

(28, q. 1, c. *Idololatria*.) Idolatry, which unbelievers follow, and every harmful superstition are fornication. The Lord permitted a wife to be dismissed on account of fornication; but because He permitted it, He did not command it. He gave the Apostle occasion to exhort that one who wishes may not dismiss an unbelieving wife, since in this way she may perhaps become a believer. [Col. 1287C]

Likewise: If unbelief is fornication, and idolatry is unbelief, and avarice is idolatry, there is no doubt that avarice too is fornication.

### CHAPTER XXX. On the same subject. Augustine, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, Book I.

(28, q. 1, c. *Idololat.*, § *Quis ergo*.) Who, then, can rightly separate any unlawful desire from the category of fornication, if avarice is fornication? From this it is understood that, on account of unlawful desires—not only those committed in sexual violations with men and women other than one’s spouse, but indeed any desires whatsoever that cause a soul to depart wickedly from God’s law and to be corrupted ruinously and shamefully—a husband may without sin dismiss his wife, and a wife her husband. For the Lord makes an exception for the cause of fornication, which, as considered above, they are compelled to understand as general and universal fornication.

But when He says, “except for the cause of fornication,” He does not say which person’s—fornication of the man or of the woman. For it is not only permitted to dismiss a wife who commits fornication; whoever dismisses the wife by whom he himself is compelled to commit fornication also dismisses her for the cause of fornication. For example, if a wife compels a man to sacrifice to idols, he who dismisses such a wife dismisses her for the cause of fornication: not only hers, but his own as well—hers, because she commits fornication; his, lest he commit fornication. [Col. 1287D]

### CHAPTER XXXI. One who commits fornication cannot dismiss his wife on account of fornication.

(20, q. 6, c. *Nihil iniquius*.) Nothing is more unjust [Col. 1288A] than to dismiss one’s wife on account of fornication when one is oneself convicted of fornication. For this saying applies: “In passing judgment on another, you condemn yourself” (Rom. 2). Therefore, whoever wishes to cast away his wife because of fornication must first be cleansed and free from fornication himself. I would say the same likewise concerning a woman.

### CHAPTER XXXII. A wife who is willing to remain with her faithful husband may be left without fault. Augustine, *On Work and Faith*, ch. 16.

(28, q. 1, c. *Uxor legitima*.) A wife joined in lawful companionship may be left without fault if she is unwilling to remain with her Christian husband. It is not considered in what way she may most rightly be dismissed, if she says to her husband: “I will not be your wife unless you provide me riches from robbery; or unless, though now a Christian, you continue the customary pimping by which you supported our household; or unless you do some other wicked or shameful thing which I knew in you, and by which I took pleasure, satisfied my lust, procured an easy living, or even went about more elegantly dressed.”

Then the man to whom his wife says these things, if he has truly repented of dead works when he came to baptism, and has as his foundation the faith which works through love, will undoubtedly be bound more strongly by love of divine grace than by the luxury of the flesh, and will resolutely cut off the member that causes him to stumble. [Cols. 1288B–1288C]

### CHAPTER XXXIII. One must not depart from the faith out of love for anyone. Ambrose to Hilary.

(28, q. 1, c. *Si infidelis*.) “If the unbeliever departs,” says the Apostle, “let him depart; a brother or sister is not subject to bondage in such cases.” That is, if the unbeliever is unwilling to remain with the believing spouse, let the believer recognize his or her freedom, and not consider himself or herself subject to bondage in such a way as to abandon the faith in order not to lose an unbelieving spouse.

This is to be understood also of believers and parents, and of brothers and sisters: all are to be left for Christ when the condition is imposed that one must abandon Christ in order to keep them. It is therefore also to be understood of a house and fields—that is, those things possessed by financial right. [Col. 1288D]

### CHAPTER XXXIV. A woman who makes an idol and does not repent is to be dismissed by her husband. Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriage*, Book II.

(28, q. 1, c. *Non solum*.) It is not only the person who defiles his or her flesh who commits adultery; the person who makes an idol also commits adultery. If she persists in these deeds and does not repent, leave [Col. 1289A] her and do not live with her. Otherwise you too will be a participant in her sin. For this reason you have been commanded to remain by yourselves, whether man or woman. For in such a case repentance is possible. [Col. 1290A]

## CONCERNING THE RECONCILIATION OF SPOUSES

[Col. 1289]

### CHAPTER XXXV. Once adultery has been purged by penance, reconciliation of the marriage may take place. Augustine to Pollentius, Book II, ch. 6.

(32, q. 1, c. *Quod autem*.) What seems harsh to you—that a spouse should be reconciled after adultery—will not be harsh if faith is present. Why do we still count as adulterers those whom we believe have been cleansed by baptism or healed by penance? Under the old law these crimes were not cleansed by any sacrifices to God; [Col. 1289B] under the law of the New Testament they are cleansed beyond doubt by blood. Therefore it was then altogether forbidden to receive back a wife defiled by another man, although David, as a prefiguration of the New Testament, received without defilement the daughter of Saul, whom the father of that same woman had separated from him and given to another.

But now, after Christ said to the adulteress, “Neither do I condemn you; go, from now on sin no more” (John 8), who does not understand that the husband ought to forgive what he sees the Lord of them both has forgiven, and that he ought no longer to call her an adulteress whose crime, upon her repentance, he believes to have been erased by divine mercy?

### CHAPTER XXXVI. Husbands ought to be punished more severely for adultery than women. Augustine to the same, Book II, ch. 6.

(32, q. 1, c. *Indignantur*.) Husbands are indignant if they hear that adulterous men suffer penalties similar to adulterous women, although men ought to be punished much more severely, inasmuch as it pertains more to them both to conquer by virtue and to govern women by example. [Col. 1289C]

### CHAPTER XXXVII. On the same subject. Augustine to the same, Book II, ch. 6.

(32, q. 1, c. *Non erit turpis*.) The reconciliation of spouses will not be shameful or difficult even after adulteries have been committed and purged, where, through the keys of the kingdom of heaven, forgiveness of sins is not doubted to occur: not so that an adulteress is recalled after divorce by her husband, but so that, after union with Christ, she is no longer called an adulteress. [Col. 1290A]

### CHAPTER XXXVIII. Whether a husband may return to an adulterous woman. Hermas, *The Shepherd*, Book I, ch. 4.

(34, q. 2, c. *Ego dixi*.) I said to the Shepherd: “Lord, if anyone has a woman faithful in the Lord and finds her in adultery, does the husband sin if he has intercourse with her?”

And he said to me: “So long as he does not know of her sin, he is without fault in being with her. But if the husband learns that his wife has sinned and the woman has not done penance, but remains in her fornication, and the husband has intercourse with her, he will be guilty of her sin and a participant in her adultery.”

And I said to him: “What, then, if the woman remains in her vice?”

And he said: “Let the husband dismiss her, and let the husband remain by himself.”

And I said: “What if the dismissed woman does penance and wishes to return to her husband? Will she not [Col. 1290C] be received by her husband?”

He said: “Indeed, if her husband does not receive her, he sins and incurs a great sin. Therefore he ought to receive the sinner who has done penance, but not repeatedly. For God’s servants have one penance. Therefore, on account of penance, he ought not, after dismissing his wife, to take another. The same rule applies to the woman and to the man.”

## CONCERNING THE SACRAMENT AND OATH OF RECONCILIATION

[Col. 1289]

### CHAPTER XXXIX. Purging of an imputed adultery.

[Cols. 1289C–1289D]

Concerning that which has been charged against me in this synod—that I had committed adultery or fornication with this woman—I have not done so, nor do I know myself to be guilty. So may God help me at that judgment.

### CHAPTER XL. Separation from an incestuous union, and oath of separation.

From this day forward, with this woman with whom you committed adultery or fornication, on account of which you underwent discipline or penance, you shall no longer commit adultery or fornication with her; nor shall you take another wife unless, after you have completed your penance, permission has been granted you by the bishop or his representative. So may God help you!

### CHAPTER XLI. Reconciliation of married persons, and oath of reconciliation.

[Cols. 1290C–1290D]

(35, q. 6, c. *Ab isto secundo*.) From this day forward, you shall keep this your wife N., whom you unjustly dismissed, as a husband ought to have his wife: with love and fitting discipline. You shall not separate her from yourself by any evil device, nor, while she lives, take another. So may God help you!

### CHAPTER XLII. Oath of reconciliation of an adulteress.

From this time forward you shall keep and embrace this your husband, whom you unjustly left; you shall be subject and obedient to him in service, love, and fear, as a wife ought rightly to be subject to her husband. You shall never separate yourself from him, nor, while he lives, join yourself to another man either in marriage or in adultery. So may God help you!

## THAT WOMEN OUGHT TO BE SUBJECT TO MEN

[Col. 1291]

### CHAPTER XLIII. Women ought to be subject to their husbands. Augustine, *Questions on Genesis*.

[Col. 1291A] There is a natural order among human beings: women should serve men, and children their parents, because there is no justice in the greater serving the lesser.

### CHAPTER XLIV. The husband is the head of the wife. Augustine, *Questions on the Old Testament*.

(33, q. 5, c. *Haec imago*.) This image is in man: that one man was made, from whom the rest arise, having God’s rule, as it were His vicar, because the man bears the image of the law of the one God [better reading: “every law bears the image of God”]. Therefore woman was not made in the image of God; for thus it says: “And God made man; in the image of God He made him” (Gen. 1). Hence also the Apostle says: “A man indeed ought not to cover [Col. 1291B] his head, because he is the image and glory of God; but a woman covers hers, because she is not the glory or image of God” (1 Cor. 11).

### CHAPTER XLV. On the same subject. Augustine, *Question 33 on Deuteronomy*, Book IV.

(33, q. 5, c. *Satis hinc apparet*.) From this it is sufficiently apparent how the law wished wives to be subject to men and almost their servants: it established that a husband might give testimony against his wife by which she would be stoned if it were proved true; yet he, in turn, is not stoned if it is proved false, but is only chastised and fined, and is ordered to remain joined to the woman whom he had wished to be without.

In other cases, however, one who harms anyone by false testimony is ordered, if that is proved, to suffer the same penalty that the other person would have suffered if the charge had been true. [Col. 1291C]

### CHAPTER XLVI. The husband is the head of the wife. Jerome, in the Epistle to Titus.

(33, q. 5, c. *Cum caput*.) Since the husband is the head of the wife, and Christ is the head of the husband, any wife who is not subject to her husband—that is, to her own head—is guilty of the same offense as a husband who is not subject to Christ, his own head. The word of the Lord is blasphemed either when God’s first judgment is despised and considered worthless, or when Christ’s Gospel is dishonored, when a woman who is Christian and by God’s law subject to her husband desires to rule contrary to the law and faith of nature, although even Gentile women serve their husbands by the common law of nature.

### CHAPTER XLVII. A woman ought in all things to follow her husband’s decision. Augustine, *Questions on Numbers*, Book IV, ch. 59.

(33, q. 5, c. *Noluit itaque*.) Therefore the law did not wish a woman to vow anything to God concerning her own person, so that in the woman’s vows no authority should prevail, even concerning abstinence from things lawful and permitted, except that of the man. Thus, if a father permitted an unmarried daughter to fulfill vows, and before she fulfilled them she married, and this became known to her husband and did not please him, she was not to fulfill them, and this entirely without sin, because, as it says, God “cleansed” her—that is, declared her clean. Nor should this be thought to be done against the Lord, since the Lord Himself commanded and willed it. [Cols. 1291D–1292A]

### CHAPTER XLVIII. Vows of abstinence which a woman has promised with her husband’s permission she is not bound to keep if he later forbids them. Augustine, *Questions on Numbers*, Book IV.

(33, q. 5, c. *Manifestum*.) It is clear that the law intended a woman to be under her husband, so that none of her vows made for the purpose of abstinence should be fulfilled by her unless her husband gave authorization by permitting them. For although the law intended that it should count as the husband’s sin if he first permitted and later forbade them, it nevertheless did not say that the woman should do what she had vowed because her husband had formerly permitted it. It called it the husband’s sin because he refused what he had previously consented to; yet it did not thereby grant permission to the woman to disregard what her husband had formerly allowed her, if he later forbade it. [Col. 1292B]

### CHAPTER XLIX. A woman has no authority, but is subject in everything to her husband’s dominion. Ambrose, in the book *Questions on the Old and New Testament*.

(33, q. 5, c. *Mulierem*.) A woman is plainly subject to her husband’s dominion and has no authority: she may neither teach nor be a witness, give assurance, or judge. [Col. 1292C]

### CHAPTER L. On the same subject. From Ambrose, *Hexameron*, Book V, ch. 7.

(33, q. 5, c. *Adam*.) Adam was deceived through Eve, not Eve through Adam. It is just that the woman who called him into fault should be taken under his governance, lest he again fall through the woman’s own pliancy.

### CHAPTER LI. On the same subject. Ambrose, on the Epistle to the Corinthians, ch. 11.

(33, q. 1, c. *Mulier debet*.) A woman ought to cover her head because she is not the image of God, but in order that she may be shown to be subject (1 Cor. 11). And because transgression began through her, she ought to bear this sign in church: out of reverence for the bishop, she should not have her head uncovered, but covered with a veil. She does not have authority to speak, because the bishop represents the person of Christ. Therefore, as before Christ the Judge, so before the bishop, who is the Lord’s vicar, she ought to appear subject on account of original guilt. [Col. 1292D]

## WHY MARRIAGE DOES NOT TAKE PLACE BETWEEN BLOOD RELATIVES

[Col. 1291]

### CHAPTER LII. Why it was established that we should not take blood relatives as wives. Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XV, ch. 15.

(35, q. 1, c. *Cum igitur*.) Since the human race [Col. 1292D], after the first union of the man made from dust and his wife made from the man’s side, required the union of males and females in order to multiply by begetting, and since there were no human beings except those born from those two [Col. 1293A], brothers took their sisters as wives. Certainly, the more ancient this was under compulsion of necessity, the more blameworthy it later became when religion forbade it.

For the most proper account was taken of charity: human beings were to be bound together in harmonious fellowship by the bonds of diverse relationships, and one person was not to have all relationships in one other person. Instead, the individual relationships were to be distributed among different persons, so that more numerous bonds might bind more persons more diligently into social life. “Father” and “father-in-law” are names of two relationships. Thus, in order that each person might have one man as father and another as father-in-law, charity might extend itself more widely. But one Adam was necessarily both to his sons and daughters when brothers and sisters were joined in marriage. Likewise Eve, his wife, was both mother-in-law and mother to children of each sex. [Col. 1293B] If there had been two women, one a mother and the other a mother-in-law, social affection would have been united more abundantly. But that was impossible when no human beings existed except the brothers and sisters from those first two people.

Therefore this had to occur when it became possible: once there was an abundance from which wives could be taken who were no longer sisters. Thus not only would necessity be absent, but, as we observe even among impious worshippers of many false gods when the human race has grown, although fraternal marriages are exchanged under perverse laws, better custom nevertheless prefers to abhor that permission and opposes it as though it could never have been allowed.

Accordingly, the union of man and woman, insofar as it concerns the human race, is a kind of seedbed of the city. But the heavenly city must escape the evil of generation. [Col. 1293C]

### CHAPTER LIII. Between which persons marriages are incestuous. *Institutes*, Book I, ch. 10.

(Institutes, *On Marriage*, § “Between Such Persons.”) For between those persons who occupy the place of parents or children, marriage cannot be contracted with one another—for example, between father and daughter, grandfather and granddaughter, mother and son, or grandmother and grandson—and so on without limit. If such persons should have intercourse with one another, they are said to have contracted wicked and incestuous marriages. And these rules are so true that, although persons may have begun to stand to one another in the place of parents or children through adoption, [Col. 1293D] they cannot be joined to one another in marriage; indeed, the same legal rule remains even after the adoption has been dissolved. Therefore, a woman who has begun to be your daughter or granddaughter by adoption you may not take as wife, even though you have emancipated her.

Among persons joined by a collateral degree of kinship there is likewise a similar observance, but not so extensive. Certainly marriages between brother and sister are forbidden, whether they were born of the same father and mother, or of one of the two only. But if a woman has begun to be your sister by adoption, then, so long as the adoption subsists, marriage between you and her certainly cannot stand. It is unlawful to take one’s daughter as wife; nor may anyone take the granddaughter of his brother or sister [Col. 1294A] as wife, although they are in the fourth degree. For one may not take the granddaughter of a person whose daughter one may not lawfully take as wife. But you do not appear to be prevented from taking as wife the daughter of a woman whom your father adopted, since she is joined to you neither by natural nor by civil law. The children of two brothers or two sisters, or of a brother and sister, however, cannot be joined in marriage. Likewise, one may not take as wife an aunt, even an adoptive aunt, nor a maternal aunt, because they are regarded as standing in the place of parents. For the same reason it is true that one is also forbidden to take as wife a great-aunt or great-maternal-aunt. Out of reverence for affinity, too, it is necessary to abstain from certain marriages: for instance, it is unlawful to take a stepdaughter or daughter-in-law as wife, because both stand in the place of daughters. Likewise, a husband’s son by [Col. 1294B] another wife and a wife’s daughter by another husband—or conversely—may properly contract marriage, although they have a brother or sister born from a marriage contracted later.

If, after divorce, your wife has borne a daughter by another man, that daughter is not your stepdaughter. Likewise, if anyone has entered into a union contrary to what we have said, neither husband nor wife, neither nuptials nor marriage, nor dowry, is recognized. Consequently, those born from such intercourse are not under their father’s power; but, as regards paternal authority, they are in the same position as those whom a mother has conceived indiscriminately. For such persons are not understood to have a father. Their intercourse is also uncertain; hence children are commonly called *spurii*, perhaps from the Greek word meaning “separated,” children conceived without a father.

## CHAPTER LIV. Your son and your daughter’s granddaughter cannot become spouses even under civil law. Ambrose to Paternus.

You would join your son with your daughter’s granddaughter—that is, have him take his sister’s daughter. Ask the whole host of relationship-names: that man is called her maternal uncle, and she his niece. Moreover, how can there be doubt, when even divine law forbids first cousins, who are joined to one another in the fourth degree, from entering into marital union? This is also the degree which appears to be excluded from the fellowship of marriage by civil law.

## CHAPTER LV. Between whom marriage is forbidden on account of consanguinity. Alexander II to the metropolitan clergy.

We have learned that, among you, a scruple concerning the degrees of kinship in this much-discussed question has recently arisen, [Col. 1294D] concerning which we grieve that certain pernicious interpreters and disputants are laying down doctrines contrary to the rule of truth and sound teaching. Sitting in the chair of pestilence, they dictate laws which they do not know and teach matters which they have by no means learned. For, as is reported, they count the lines of descent proceeding on both sides from two brothers in such a way that they forbid their children in the fourth generation, their grandchildren in the sixth, and their great-grandchildren in the ninth, to intermarry. Thus they divide each degree of generation—which without doubt ought to be called one degree—and, by unskilled reckoning, endeavor to cut up the line of descent.

Certainly they would not plunge so pestilently into the rites of this foul error if they ruminated upon the nourishment of sacred Scripture with the appetite of a living mind. For [Col. 1295A] the book of Genesis testifies that the generations descending on both sides from two brothers or grandchildren, and thenceforward, should not be called different generations but should uniformly be called one and the same generation. It says: “Joseph lived a hundred years and saw Ephraim’s children to the third generation. The children also of Machir, son of Manasseh, were born upon Joseph’s knees” (Gen. 50). But if generations had to be reckoned as your disputants assert, since Joseph had grandchildren through each of the two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, Scripture would by no means say that he saw Ephraim’s children to the third generation, but to the sixth. Likewise, blessed Gregory, writing on the marriages of the English, used nearly these words.

## CHAPTER LVI. The English are permitted to marry in the fourth or fifth generation.

[Col. 1295B]

A certain Roman law in the commonwealth permits the son or daughter of two brothers or sisters to be joined in marriage. But it is altogether known that offspring cannot flourish from this marriage. Hence it is necessary that they should be joined to one another in the fourth or fifth generation. In these words it is clearer than light that, while the eminent teacher forbids the offspring of two brothers to be joined in marriage, he permits neophytes in the fourth generation. Thus, despite what adherents of a perverse doctrine maintain, the fourth generation can be found among the children of two brothers.

## CHAPTER LVII. On the prohibited degrees among relatives. From the Decree of Gregory the Younger.

(35, question 3, chapter *De incest.* and book *Frat.*) If anyone takes his brother’s [Col. 1295C] wife in marriage, let him be anathema. If anyone takes his stepmother or his daughter-in-law, let him be anathema. If anyone takes his first cousin, let him be anathema. If anyone takes in marriage a woman of his own kin, or one whom his kinsman had, let him be anathema.

## CHAPTER LVIII. Germans may marry up to the fourth generation. Pope Zachary to bishops.

(35, question 3, chapter *Quaedam lex Roman.*) From people [Col. 1296A] from the regions of Germany I have learned the assertion that Pope Gregory of blessed memory, while divine grace was enlightening them unto the religion of Christianity, granted them permission to marry in the fourth generation. This is not lawful for Christians. Yet, while they were inexperienced persons to be invited to the faith, we do not doubt that this was done, although we find it nowhere written.

## CHAPTER LIX. The same degrees are forbidden by God.

(Law *Nemini*, chapter *De nupt.*, and 35, question 2, chapters *Progenies*, *Nulli*, and *In copul.*) Let no one dare join to himself in marriage a first cousin, a *neptis* (granddaughter or niece), a stepmother, a brother’s wife, a woman of his own kin, or one whom his kinsman had. If anyone enters into this wicked union and remains in it, let him know that he is bound by the bonds of the apostolic authority’s anathema, and let no [Col. 1296B] priest grant him communion. But if he is converted and separated from such a union, let him be subjected to such fitting penance as the local priest judges appropriate.

## CHAPTERS LX–LXI. Whether two full brothers ought each to take a sister, descended from them by a remote line.

Bede, *History* 33 and *Tractate* 8; Augustine, Gregory’s Responses.

This is lawful in every way. For nothing is found in the sacred writings that appears to contradict this chapter.

## CHAPTER LXII. On the same subject. Gregory’s response to Augustine, chapter 19.

(35, question 3, chapters *De nupt.* and *De incest.*) To have intercourse with one’s stepmother is a grave crime, because it is written: [Col. 1296C] “You shall not uncover your father’s nakedness.” A son cannot uncover his father’s nakedness. But because it is written, “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2), whoever has presumed to uncover the nakedness of a stepmother who was one with his father undoubtedly uncovers his father’s nakedness. Intercourse with a kinswoman is likewise forbidden, because through the prior union she has become the flesh of one’s brother. For this reason John the Baptist too was beheaded and completed his course in holy martyrdom.

# MARRIAGE IS NOT CONTRACTED BETWEEN SPIRITUAL CO-MOTHERS.

[Col. 1295]

## CHAPTER LXIII. It is unlawful for anyone to have two spiritual co-mothers. Nicholas to Solomon, bishop of Constantinople.

(30, question 3, chapter *Sciscitatur.*) Your Holiness asks us whether a man may have two spiritual co-mothers, one after the other. In this matter, your brotherhood ought to remember what is written: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2). Therefore, since it is established that husband and wife become one flesh through marriage, it follows that the husband is made spiritual co-father to that woman whose co-mother his wife, taken in marriage, appeared to be. Hence it is clear that a man cannot be joined in intercourse to a woman who was his co-mother, with whom he had become one flesh.

## CHAPTER LXIV. Let him who commits these crimes be punished, yet not be compelled to leave his lawful wife. Nicholas to Solomon, bishop of Constantinople.

(33, question 20, chapter *Si quis.*) If anyone has committed fornication with a spiritual mother, [Col. 1296D] let him, as you know, be struck with the blows of anathema. Likewise, we decree that he be punished who has committed the crime of fornication with a woman whom he received from the sacred font of baptism, or with her whom he held before the bishop when she was anointed with holy chrism. Nevertheless, if he has a lawful wife, he is not to be compelled to leave her. For what God has joined, man ought not to separate.

## CHAPTER LXV. A woman who fraudulently held her own son before the bishop is not to be separated from her husband, but is to do penance. Council of Chalon, chapter 4.

(30, question 1, chapter *Dictum.*) We have also been told that certain women, some negligently and others fraudulently, in order to be separated from their husbands, have held their own sons before bishops for confirmation. We therefore judged it fitting that, if any woman has held her own son before a bishop for confirmation through negligence [Col. 1297A] or any fraud, she is to do penance throughout her life for her deception or fraud; nevertheless, she is not to be separated from her husband.

## CHAPTER LXVI. Those who take their goddaughter or spiritual mother as wife are to be separated and subjected to severe penance. Council of Mainz, chapter 10.

(30, question 1, chapter *De eo quod interrogastis.*) Concerning your question whether one who has taken his goddaughter as wife, one who has had intercourse with his spiritual mother, one who has baptized his own son, or one whose wife received that son from the font, might afterward remain in such a union, so that a marriage might be broken apart: the answer concerning such persons is this. If anyone has taken his goddaughter [Col. 1297B] or spiritual co-mother as wife, we judge that they must be separated and subjected to severe penance. But if lawful spouses, one or both, have deliberately arranged to receive their own son from the font so that a separation may result, we give this counsel: if they wish to remain unmarried, it is good. But otherwise, severe penance is to be imposed on the plotter, and they are to remain together. And if the violator of marriage survives, let him be punished with the most stringent penance and remain without hope of marriage.

## CHAPTER LXVII. A man may take the wife of his spiritual co-father, if she herself was not his spiritual co-mother. Council of Tivoli, chapter 47.

(30, question 4, chapter *Qui spiritualem.*) He who has a spiritual co-father because he received that man’s son from the washing of the sacred font, while that man’s wife is not his co-mother, may, after his co-father has died, take his widow as wife, if there is no closeness of consanguinity. [Col. 1298B] For why? May not persons be joined whom no carnal proximity or spiritual generation separates?

# ON CONSANGUINITY AND AFFINITY.

[Col. 1297]

## CHAPTER LXVIII. Affinity is not extinguished in the survivor. Pope Gregory to Venerius, bishop of Cagliari.

(35, question 30, chapter *Fraternitatis.*) GREGORY, servant of the servants of God, to VENERIUS of Cagliari.

Beloved brother, I offer thanks to God for your brotherhood’s diligent discernment, because you have asked what you ought to ask and have made me glad. Therefore I answer calmly the matters inquired of. You have resolved to consult the Apostolic See [Col. 1297C] whether a woman joined in marital union to a man outside her family becomes related to his kin; whether, after his death, that kinship remains the same; whether the terms of relationship are dissolved under another husband; or whether children born to her may lawfully enter into union with the kin of her former husband.

For the word of the Lord is mighty and strong, enduring, abiding, and unchangeable—not momentary or passing. Truth itself, who is God and the Word of God, says: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. 14). Before God appeared among human beings in the flesh, Adam, inspired by him, said: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2). The Lord did not contradict this. Then, when Truth sprang from the earth onto the earth and appeared visibly in humanity, he was asked whether it was lawful for a man to put away his wife (Matt. 19). Forbidding this, he prohibited it, except perhaps where fornication alone excluded the marital union. Therefore he immediately brought forward the same pronouncement which, existing with the Father before the ages, the Word had inspired in Adam; and he himself confirmed what the first man had uttered: “Therefore a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2).

If they become one flesh, how can anyone be more closely related to one of them without being related to the other? [Col. 1298B] It must be believed that this cannot happen. For when one has died, affinity is not extinguished in the survivor, nor can another marital union dissolve the affinity of the former union. Nor does it seem right that the offspring of another union should enter into the affinity of the former husband, because the word of the Lord is mighty and strong; and, as the prophet says: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 143). “He established them for ever and ever; he gave a decree which shall not pass away.” For after his word and command, God made two into one flesh—that is, male and female—and he did not cease to make the innumerable multitude of both sexes one with himself, as Truth itself said: “I pray not for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us” (John 17).

Whoever, with rash and sacrilegious boldness, seeks to extinguish kinship after a death, to dissolve it under the designation of another affinity, or believes that the offspring of another union may lawfully be associated with it, denies that the word of God concerning the prior relationship is mighty and strong. And one who so easily and so quickly seeks to dissolve it does not believe that the word of God remains forever. Construct the earth from four places separated [Col. 1298D] from each other by a great interval, and imagine it, when made and joined together, as a body of whatever form or immensity you wish.

## CHAPTER LXIX. The same rule of consanguinity is to be observed regarding one’s own relatives and those of one’s spouse. Isidore, from the Council of Mâcon, chapter 3.

(35, question 3, chapter *Sane.*) Certainly, the consanguinity which must be observed in one’s own spouse must likewise, under the law of marriage, be observed in the spouse’s kinship, since it is established that the two were one flesh; therefore both kindreds must be regarded as common to them, as it is written: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 9).

## CHAPTER LXX. Let no one henceforth be joined in marriage in the fifth or sixth generation. Council of Chalon, chapter 5.

(35, question 3, chapter *Contradicimus.*) We also prohibit anyone henceforth from being joined in marriage in the fourth, fifth, or sixth generation. Wherever a union contracted after the prohibition is found, let it be separated.

## CHAPTER LXXI. On the same subject. Gregory to Augustine of Canterbury, chapter 6; and John of Constantinople to Felix, bishop of Sicily.

(35, question 3, chapter *Quaedam.*) When Pope Gregory was asked by Augustine, bishop of the English people, in what generation the faithful ought to marry, he gave this dispensatory reply: “A certain earthly law of the Roman commonwealth permits the son and daughter either of a brother and sister or of two full brothers or two sisters [Col. 1299B] to unite. But experience has taught us that offspring cannot increase from such a marriage. Hence it is necessary that the faithful may lawfully be joined to one another in the fourth or fifth generation.”

## CHAPTER LXXII. On the same subject. Gregory to the same person, and John.

(35, question 5, chapter *Ad sedem.*) But after a long time, when Felix and Messarius, bishops of Sicily, asked him, Gregory wrote to Augustine that marriages contracted by the English in the fourth generation were by no means to be dissolved.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. The English are permitted to marry in the fourth or fifth generation. From Gregory, Book XII, Epistle 31.

[Col. 1299C] (35, question 3, chapter *Quodam.*) The most humble father Gregory gave, among other things, this explanation: “Understand that what I wrote to Augustine, bishop of the English people and, as you remember, your fosterling, concerning unions of consanguinity, I wrote both particularly and generally for him and the English people, who had recently come to the faith, lest they should withdraw from the good which they had begun through fear of stricter measures. The city of Rome itself is my witness. Nor did I write these injunctions to them with the intention that, once they had been established with a firm root in the faith, if they were found within their own consanguinity [Col. 1300A] they should not be separated, or that they should be joined within a line of affinity—that is, as far as the seventh generation. Rather, while those persons were still neophytes, it was first necessary to tolerate what was unlawful among them and to instruct them by words and examples. For, as the Apostle says: ‘I gave you milk to drink, not solid food’ (1 Cor. 3), we allowed these matters to them at that time, not to later generations, as has been set forth, lest the good that had been planted with a still-weak root should be uprooted, but rather might be strengthened somewhat and preserved unto perfection. Nor, therefore, did I judge John to be censured on that account, so that those who, on the occasion of this new dispensation, promote unlawful marriages against this most learned man may recognize that I did not understand marriage in the fourth generation as a general rule, but permitted it pardonably and temporarily.”

## CHAPTER LXXIV. Why consanguinity is observed to the sixth degree. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book IX, chapter [uncertain].

(35, question 4, chapter *Consanguinitas.*) When consanguinity, gradually separating itself in the ranks of descendants, has withdrawn as far as the final degree and has ceased to be proximity, the law again calls it back to the bond of marriage and, in some fashion, recalls the fugitive. Consanguinity was therefore set to the sixth degree of generation, so that, just as generation and every condition are completed in the six ages of the world, so the proximity of lineage might be bounded by that number of degrees.
