## CHAPTER LXXV. How many degrees of consanguinity are to be reckoned. From the Decree of Isidore.

[Col. 1300C] (35, question 5, chapter *Ad sedem.*) Isidore, in his *Etymologies*, declares that one must abstain from consanguinity as far as the seventh generation and then enter into lawful marriage. I think he did this because, tracing the sequence of genealogy, he judged that blood-relationship should be observed as far as they could carry the order of reckoning; and so he decreed that marriage should be resumed, to preserve the claim of lineage and friendship, when the order of kinship could no longer be counted.

# IN WHICH BRANCH OF CONSANGUINITY LAWFUL MARRIAGES MAY BE CONTRACTED.

[Col. 1299]

## CHAPTER LXXVI. How the degrees of consanguinity are divided. From the Decree of Isidore.

(35, question 3, chapter *Series.*) Blessed Isidore speaks thus concerning consanguinity, whose sequence is divided into six degrees. The son and daughter—that is, brother and sister—are the trunk. Once they have been separately divided, these little branches proceed from the root of that trunk: grandson and granddaughter, the first; great-grandson and great-granddaughter, the second; great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter, the third; great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-granddaughter, the fourth; fourth-great-grandson and fourth-great-granddaughter, the fifth; the grandson of the fourth-great-grandson and the granddaughter of the fourth-great-granddaughter, the sixth. When this consanguinity, gradually separating itself in the ranks of descendants, [Col. 1300D] has withdrawn to the final degree and has ceased to be proximity, then the law first calls it back to the bond of marriage and, in some manner, recalls the fugitive. Consanguinity was therefore established to the sixth degree of generation, so that, just as generation and the human condition are completed in the six ages of the world, so the proximity of lineage might be bounded by the same number of degrees.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. Every person must observe his own descendants to the seventh generation. Gregory to the bishops of Gaul, Book XII, Epistle 31.

(35, question 3, chapter *Progeniem.*) We decree that every person must observe his own descendants to the seventh [Col. 1301A] generation; and so long as they know themselves to be close in affinity, we deny them access to marital union. If they do so, let them be separated.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. On the same subject. From the Council at Theodon, chapter 8.

Let no one of the faithful take his kinswoman as wife as far as the line of affinity—that is, to the sixth generation—or in any way defile her with the stain of incest. But if anyone rashly presumes to do this, let him pay the penalty for incest and publicly do penance according to the canonical degrees.

## CHAPTER LXXIX. Let no one take a wife from the closeness of his own blood to the seventh degree. Council of Lyons, chapter 10.

(35, question 3, chapter *Nulli ex propinq.*) Let no one take wives from the closeness [Col. 1301B] of his own blood to the seventh degree, nor without a priest’s blessing. Those who are to marry should dare to marry only after receiving the priest’s blessing, and should presume no other course.

## CHAPTER LXXX. Let no one take a wife from the closeness of his own blood or that of his wife to the seventh degree. Council of Orléans, chapter 10.

(35, question 3, chapter *Nullum in utroq.*) We permit no person of either sex to take a wife from the closeness of his own blood or that of his wife to the seventh degree of lineage, or to be defiled with the stain of incest. We add further that, just as it is unlawful for any Christian to take a spouse from his own consanguinity, so also it is unlawful to take a spouse from the consanguinity of his wife, [Col. 1301C] on account of the unity of the flesh.

## CHAPTER LXXXI. On the same subject. Council of Cologne, chapter 6.

All names of relationships are contained within seven degrees, [Col. 1302A] beyond which neither affinity is found nor succession can be extended further.

## CHAPTER LXXXII. Let no one take a wife from his own kin to the seventh generation. Council of Meaux, chapter 7.

(35, question 2, chapter *De affinitate.*) Concerning affinity through consanguinity in the degrees of kinship, it has seemed right that observance should extend to the seventh generation. For the inheritance of property, established by legal definitions, also extends the succession of heirs to the seventh degree. They would not succeed unless this were owed to them by the line of kinship.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. One may not leave one’s wife unless consanguinity has been proved before the Church. Alexander II to William of Monst[ers?].

(35, question 6, chapter *Multorum relatione.*) By the report of many we have learned that you wish to cast off your own wife and attach yourself to another, alleging an occasion of consanguinity. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we command and forbid you in any way to presume to leave the wife whom you now have or to take another, until you have examined the just cause before a council of devout bishops.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV. Every controversy must be settled by two or three witnesses. Council of Lleida, chapter 20.

(35, question 6, chapters *Ab isto* and *Cum in Hilerd.*) Let every controversy concerning ecclesiastical matters be settled, according to [Col. 1302C] divine law, by two witnesses. The Lord is witness when he says: “One witness shall not stand against another, but every word shall stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deut. 19).

# WHO MAY ACCUSE A MARRIAGE, AND ON THE OATH OF RECONCILIATION.

[Col. 1301]

## CHAPTER LXXXV. Only blood relatives—or, if the line has died out, elderly and truthful persons—may reckon kinship in a synod. From the Decree of Pope Fabian, chapter 8.

(35, question 6, chapter *Consanguineos.*) Let no outsider accuse blood relatives [Col. 1301D] or reckon consanguinity in a synod, but only relatives to whose knowledge it pertains: namely father and mother, sister, brother, paternal uncle, maternal uncle, paternal aunt, maternal aunt, and their descendants. But if the whole line has died out, the bishop shall make canonical inquiry among older and more venerable persons to whom the same relationship is known; and, if the relationship is found, they shall be separated.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. Who must establish kinship by oath. Urban to Richard, bishop of Genoa.

(35, question 6, chapter *Notificamus.*) We inform you that after three or two of the nearer relatives of the deceased wife of the accused person—or of his living wife—have established this relationship by oath, or after four or two of the older Genoese, [Col. 1302C] to whom this kinship is known and who are of good reputation and truthful testimony, have done so, setting aside affection, fear, payment, and every evil motive, marriages are to be dissolved without delay when consanguinity has been established in the manner aforesaid. But if relatives or outsiders merely assert the relationship [Col. 1302D] in words and refuse or are unable to prove it by oath, the marriage is by no means to be dissolved; rather, suitable penance is to be imposed upon them for the infamy or stain of sin, if perhaps they have incurred any in this matter.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. Oath of the accuser. Council of Rome under Gregory.

(35, question 6, chapter *De parentela.*) Concerning that relationship which they say exists between this man and this woman, his wife: whatever you know or have heard about it from your neighbors or your older relatives, you will conceal neither by any contrivance, nor for love, fear, reward, or consanguinity, from your bishop or the envoy whom he has ordered to investigate these matters, whenever he questions you concerning this [Col. 1303A]: “So may God help you, and these relics of the saints.”

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. The third oath.

(35, question 6, chapter *Illud.*) That oath which this man swore concerning the kinship reckoned between his son and that son’s wife N.: you shall observe it to the extent that you know or have heard: “So may God help you.”

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. Oath concerning separation for incest, and oath of reconciliation.

(35, question 6, chapter *Ab isto primo.*) From this day forward [Col. 1304A] you will not, by any contrivance, associate yourself with this kinswoman of yours, N., with whom, contrary to law and right Christianity, you committed adultery and incest. You will not associate her with yourself either in marriage or adultery, nor eat with her at one table, except perhaps in church or in some public place where no evil suspicion can arise, and there you may speak together before suitable witnesses for a definite necessity. Nor will you take another wife, except perhaps after completing the penance assigned to you by your bishop or his envoy: “So may God help you, and these relics of the saints.”

# ON THE DEGREES OF KINSHIP.

[Col. 1303]

## CHAPTER XC. Names of degrees above, below, and in the collateral line among living persons. Isidore, *On the Seven Degrees of Consanguinity*.

(35, question 5, chapter *Primo gradu.*) In the first degree, the upper line contains father and mother; the lower line, son and daughter. No other persons are joined with them. In the second degree, the upper line contains grandfather and grandmother; the lower, grandson and granddaughter. In the collateral line are brother and sister. These persons are doubled: grandfather and grandmother are understood both on the father’s and on the mother’s side. In succeeding degrees too, these persons are similarly doubled in accordance with the nature of those existing in each degree. The persons in the second degree are therefore called double, because there are two grandfathers, paternal and maternal. Likewise, there are two kinds of grandchildren, those begotten through a son and those through a daughter. Brother and sister come in the collateral line—that is, the father’s brother or the mother’s brother, called paternal uncle or maternal uncle. They too are doubled in this order.

In the third degree, above are great-grandfather and great-grandmother; below, great-grandson and great-granddaughter. Collaterally are the son or daughter of a brother or sister; paternal uncle and paternal aunt—that is, the father’s brother and sister; maternal uncle and maternal aunt—that is, the mother’s brother and sister. In the fourth degree, above are great-great-grandfather and great-great-grandmother; below, great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter. Collaterally are the grandson of a brother or sister; paternal-cousin niece; paternal cousin, male and female—that is, the son or daughter of a paternal uncle; first cousin, male and female—that is, the son or daughter of a maternal uncle and maternal aunt; and the son or daughter of a paternal aunt. Also first cousins [Col. 1303D] born from two sisters. Added to these are great-paternal-uncle and great-paternal-aunt—that is, the brother and sister of the paternal grandfather; and great-maternal-uncle and great-maternal-aunt—that is, the brother and sister of the paternal and maternal grandmother.

In the fifth degree, above are great-great-great-grandfather and great-great-great-grandmother; below, great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-granddaughter. Collaterally are the great-grandson and great-granddaughter of a brother or sister; male and female paternal cousins; the sons and daughters of paternal aunts; and first cousins, male and female. More closely, there are first cousins, male and female—that is, the son or daughter of a great-paternal-uncle, great-paternal-aunt, great-maternal-uncle, or great-maternal-aunt. Added are great-great-paternal-uncle and great-great-paternal-aunt: these are the brother and sister of the maternal great-grandfather; great-great-maternal-uncle and great-great-maternal-aunt: these are the brother and sister of the paternal and maternal great-grandmother, and of the great maternal grandmother. This classification cannot be explained by degrees or terms other than those written.

In the sixth degree, above are fourth-great-grandfather and fourth-great-grandmother; below, fourth-great-grandson and fourth-great-granddaughter. Collaterally are the *adnepos* and *adneptis* of a brother or sister; *fratres patrueles* and *sorores matrueles* (paternal-cousin brothers and maternal-cousin sisters); *amitini* and *amitinae* (children of a paternal aunt); and *consobrini* and *consobrinae* (cousins). Also listed are the grandson of a nearer *consobrinus*, and the son and daughter called *consobrini*. Added in the collateral line are *propatrui*, *proavunculi*, and *promaterterae* (great-paternal uncles, great-maternal uncles, and great-maternal aunts), together with a son or daughter, an *adpatruus*, and an *adamita*. The latter are the brother and sister of the paternal great-great-grandfather; an *abavunculus* and *abmatertera* are the brother and sister of the paternal and maternal great-great-grandmother and of the maternal great-great-grandfather. This too cannot be explained further than the author himself has set it out.

In the seventh degree, persons related in the direct line above and below are not called by their former proper names, but the collateral line contains the great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter of a brother or sister, and the sons and daughters of first cousins in succession. Therefore seven degrees were established because, beyond them, by the nature of things, names can no longer be found nor succession extended. All names of relationships are contained in these seven degrees, beyond which affinity cannot be found nor succession further extended.

# BOOK EIGHT.

[Col. 1303]

# ON HOMICIDE.

## CHAPTER I. It is not sinful to kill a person in the exercise of an office. Augustine to Publicola, Epistle 154.

(23, question 5, chapter *De occidendis hominibus.*) Concerning the killing [Col. 1304D] of human beings, I do not approve the counsel that no one should be killed by them, unless perhaps he is a soldier or holds a public office, so that he does not do this for himself, but for others or for the state, of which he too is a part, having received lawful authority when it suits his office. Those who are restrained by some fear from doing evil perhaps also receive a benefit thereby. Thus it was said: “Let us not resist evil,” not so that we may delight in vengeance, which feeds the mind upon another’s evil, but so that we may not neglect the correction of people.

Therefore, one who has built a circuit of walls around his property is not guilty of another’s death if someone dies after being struck by one of those walls in its use. Nor is a Christian guilty if his ox kills someone by goring, or his horse by kicking. Otherwise Christians ought not to have oxen with horns, horses with hooves, or dogs with teeth. Or again, because the Apostle Paul took sufficient care to bring to the tribunes’ attention the ambush prepared against him by certain desperate men, and consequently received armed escorts, would Paul have acknowledged his own guilt in the shedding of their blood if those wicked persons had fallen upon them? Far be it that things which we do or possess for a good or lawful purpose should be imputed to us if, through them and contrary to our will, some harm happens to another person. Otherwise no household or agricultural tools should be possessed, lest someone kill either himself or another with them. Why mention more, when I cannot finish by mentioning them? Whatever is good or lawful in human use can inflict destruction; yet even the destruction of that thing itself is not permitted without the authority of law.

## CHAPTER II. Those who waged wars by God’s authority did not in any way transgress the commandment not to kill. Augustine, *City of God*, Book I, chapter 17.

(23, q. 5, c. *Si non licet*.) If it is not lawful for anyone, by private authority, to kill a human being—even an innocent person, for whose killing no law grants permission—then certainly one who kills himself is also a murderer; and he becomes so much the more guilty when he kills himself, the more innocent was the cause for which he thought himself to be killed. Likewise: it is not lawful for a person to kill himself, since in the words written, “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20), nothing further is added; nor, indeed, is the very person to whom the command is given to be understood as excepted. Likewise: “You shall not kill”—neither yourself nor another. For one who kills himself kills nothing other than a human being. Likewise: the same divine authority has indeed made certain exceptions. [Col. 1305D] But excepting those whom God commands to be killed—whether by a law given generally, or by an express command addressed to a person [Col. 1306A] for a particular time—those who kill either as ministers owing service to the one commanding, as a sword is an instrument to its user, have in no way acted against the command, “You shall not kill”: this applies to those who have waged wars under God’s authorization, or who, bearing the office of public authority, have punished criminals with death according to His laws, that is, by the command of most just reason. Nor was Abraham merely not charged with the crime of cruelty: he was even praised by the name of piety because he was willing to kill his son, not wickedly but obediently. And it is rightly asked whether Jephthah’s killing of the daughter who came to meet her father should be regarded as done at God’s command, when he had vowed to sacrifice to God whatever first met him as he returned victorious from battle. Nor is Samson otherwise excused for crushing himself together with his enemies beneath the collapse of the house, except because the Spirit, who performed miracles through him, [Col. 1306B] secretly commanded this.

Therefore, excepting those whom either a just law generally, or God Himself, the fountain of justice, commands to be killed, whoever kills a human being—himself or anyone whatsoever—is bound by the guilt of murder. Likewise: this we say, this we affirm, this we approve in every way: no one ought voluntarily to inflict death upon himself, as though fleeing temporal troubles lest he fall into everlasting ones; no one on account of others’ sins, lest by that very act he begin to have a most grievous sin of his own; no one on account of his past sins, for which he has all the greater need of this life so that they may [Col. 1306C] be healed by repentance; no one as though from longing for the better life hoped for after death, because the better life after death does not receive those guilty of their own death.

## CHAPTER III. On the same subject. Jerome, *On Jonah*, chapter 1.

(23, q. 5, c. *Non est nostrum*.) It is not ours to accept death [of our own choosing], but willingly to receive it when inflicted by others. Hence, even in persecutions, it is not lawful to perish by one’s own hand, except where chastity is endangered; rather, one must submit one’s neck to the striker.

## CHAPTER IV. On the same subject. Augustine, to Publicola, letter 3, chapter 4.

[Col. 1306D] All laws, both ecclesiastical and secular, prohibit the shedding of human blood.

## CONCERNING ONE WHO KILLS A CLERIC.

[Col. 1305]

## CHAPTER V. Heinous crimes should be punished by secular judges.

[Col. 1305D]

(23, q. 5, c. *Sunt quaedam*.) There are certain heinous crimes which are judged more properly by the judges of the world than by bishops and rulers of churches. For example, when someone kills an apostolic pontiff, a bishop, a priest, or a deacon, the rulers of the world condemn persons guilty of such acts. Thus they do not bear [Col. 1306D] the sword without cause, since they judge crimes of this kind. For they are established especially for murderers and robbers, that they may condemn them and cause others to be restrained by fear of them.

## CHAPTER VI. What killers of priests are bound to pay. *Capitularies*, book V, chapter 20.

Priests who commit homicide shall make payment according to the assessment of the bishop to whose diocese they belong.

## CHAPTER VII. Those who kill clerics are to be fined according to the diversity of ranks. [Col. 1307A] *Capitularies*, book V, chapter 20.

(17, q. 1, c. *Qui subdiacon.*) Whoever kills a subdeacon shall pay 300 solidi; whoever kills a deacon, 400; a priest, 600; a bishop, 900; a monk, 400.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the same subject.

(17, q. 4, c. *Qui occiderit*.) Whoever kills a cleric or monk shall lay aside his weapons and serve God in a monastery all the days of his life, never to return to the secular world; and he shall perform public penance for seven years.

## CHAPTER IX. What punishment should be inflicted on one who kills a human being from hatred rather than zeal for justice. [Col. 1307B] *Capitularies*, book V, chapter 109.

Whoever, through hatred or evil intent and not for the sake of administering justice, kills a human being shall lose his [Col. 1308A] rank and make amends, under the laws, to the person against whom he acted unjustly, according to the penalty which he inflicted.

## CHAPTER X. A sentence of death is not to be carried out until after thirty days. Cassiodorus, preface to the *Tripartite History*, book IX, chapter 30.

There is a law of this kind: The Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, Augusti, to Flavianus, Praetorian Prefect of Illyricum: “If, contrary to our custom, we have ordered more severe punishment to be exacted upon any persons in view of the case, we do not wish them immediately to undergo punishment or receive their sentence; rather, for thirty days their fate and fortune are to remain in suspense over their bed.”

## CHAPTER XI. Those who, with zeal for mother Church, take up arms against excommunicated persons are not murderers. Urban II to Bishop Godfrey.

[Col. 1308B] (23, q. 5, c. *Excommunicatorum*.) For they do not consider murderers those who, burning with zeal for their Catholic mother, happen to slaughter any of those who are excommunicated.

## CONCERNING ONE WHO STRIKES A PREGNANT WOMAN.

[Col. 1307]

## CHAPTER XII. One who procures an abortion is not a murderer before a soul has been infused into the body. [Col. 1307B] Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*.

(32, q. 2, c. *Quod vero*.) If Moses or the law did not wish an unformed fetus to count as homicide, then certainly it did not regard that which is carried in the womb as a human being. Hence the question concerning the soul is commonly debated: [Col. 1307C] whether whatever has not been formed can also be understood not to be animate; and therefore homicide does not occur, because it cannot be called deprived of life if it did not yet have a soul. Likewise, if that unformed fetus already existed, but was still in some manner animated without form, then, because there is a great question concerning the soul, judgment must not be rashly pronounced without examination. Therefore the law did not wish it to count as homicide, because a living soul cannot yet be said to be in a body lacking sensation.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the same subject. Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, chapter 38.

[Col. 1307D] (32, q. 2, c. *Moyses*.) Moses handed down: “If anyone strikes a woman with child and causes an abortion: if it is formed, he shall give life for life; but if it is unformed, he shall be fined money,” in order to demonstrate that there is no soul before form. [Col. 1308B] Therefore, if it is given to an already formed body, the soul is not born in the conception of the body as something derived together with the seed. For if soul and body exist together in the seed, then many souls perish every day when seed, by some discharge, does not proceed to birth. But if we consider more closely, [Col. 1308C] we shall see what conclusion we ought to follow. Let us contemplate the making of Adam. For in Adam an example was given, so that it may be understood from him that the soul was received by an already formed body. God could indeed have mingled the soul with the clay of the earth and thus formed the body. But reason opposed this, because the dwelling first had to be put together, and then its inhabitant introduced. The soul, certainly, because it is spirit, cannot dwell in a dry place; therefore it is said to dwell in the blood. When, then, the bodily features have not been joined together, where will the soul be?

## CHAPTER XIV. On the same subject. Jerome to Algasia, question 4.

(32, q. 2, c. *Sicuti semina*.) Just as seeds are gradually [Col. 1308D] formed in the womb, and homicide is not counted until the elements have been completed and receive their forms and limbs, so a conception of the mind, unless it has burst forth into deeds, is still retained in the womb and quickly perishes through the enemy.

## WHEN HOMICIDE IS A SIN AND WHEN IT IS NOT; AND CONCERNING LAWFUL AND UNLAWFUL WAR.

[Col. 1307]

## CHAPTER XV. Christians ought to persecute what is contrary to truth. [Col. 1307D] Augustine, *Against Cresconius the Grammarian*, book I.

(23, q. 4, c. *Quisquis Christianus*.) Every Christian who does not persecute an unjust person is an enemy of Christ. You speak truly, if he does not persecute in that person what is hostile to Christ. For a master in his servant, a father in his son, and a husband in his wife—though both parties are Christians—ought to persecute only vices contrary to Christian truth. Or will they not, if they fail to persecute them, rightly be held guilty of negligence?

## CHAPTER XVI. How a person ought to love his neighbor as himself. Augustine to Macedonius, chapter 52.

(23, q. 4, c. *Debet homo*.) A person ought to love [Col. 1309A] his neighbor as himself, so that he may lead any person whom he can to worship God, whether by the comfort of beneficence, the instruction of teaching, or the restraint of discipline.

## CHAPTER XVII. Our neighbors, whom we ought to love, are to be prevented from evil and compelled to good where power is granted. Augustine to the Donatist priests.

(23, q. 4, c. *Nimirum*; c. *Haeretici*; and c. *Displicet*.) Those who are loved are not to be cruelly left with impunity to their evil will; rather, where power is granted, they are both to be restrained from evil and compelled to good. For if an evil will must always be left to its own liberty, why were the Israelites, when they refused and murmured, restrained from evil with such harsh scourges and compelled toward the land of promise? [Col. 1309B] If an evil will must always be left to its own liberty, why was Paul not permitted to employ the very evil will by which he persecuted the Church? Instead, he was struck down in order to be blinded, blinded in order to be changed, changed in order to be sent, and sent in order to suffer for the truth what he had done in error. If an evil will must always be left to its own liberty, why is a father instructed in the Holy Scriptures to rebuke his son not only with harsh words but also to strike his sides, so that he may be compelled to good discipline and be loved by the Lord? (Prov. 1.)

## CHAPTER XVIII. Certain things were permitted in the Old Testament which are forbidden in the New. Chrysostom, *On Matthew*, homily 18.

[Col. 1309C] (23, q. 8, c. *Occidit Phinees*.) Phinehas killed a man (Num. 25), and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. Yet Abraham, who became not only a murderer but even a parricide—which is certainly more grievous—was more and more pleasing to God. Peter too committed a double homicide; he performed so great a spiritual work that it was done. Therefore we should not look merely at actions, but most diligently investigate the time, the cause, the intention, the differences among persons, and whatever else attends the actions themselves. For we cannot otherwise attain the truth.

## CHAPTER XIX. Peter consigned Ananias and Sapphira to death by rebuking them. [Col. 1309D] Gregory, *Dialogues*, book VIII, chapter 30.

(23, q. 8, c. *Petrus*.) Peter, who raised dead Tabitha by prayer, consigned lying Ananias and Sapphira to death by rebuking them. For it is not recorded that he prayed for their destruction, but only that he rebuked the fault which they had committed. It is therefore clear that such acts are sometimes performed by authority and sometimes by petition: by rebuke he took life from these persons, and by prayer restored it to that woman.

## CHAPTER XX. Whoever does not correct crimes which he is able to correct commits them himself. John VIII to Hermann.

(23, q. 8, c. *Praeterea*.) Moreover, we exhort the zeal of your devotion that you may be so much the more vigorously inflamed against the sea-robbers who, under the pretext of your name, rage against [Col. 1310A] Christians, as you know that the reputation of your name has been obscured by their wickedness. For, although it may be believed that they lie in wait for voyagers without your wishing it, since they are said to be capable of being restrained by you, unless you check them, you will not be held innocent. For it is written: “Whoever is able to correct crimes and does not correct them commits them himself.”

## CHAPTER XXI. To punish crime for God is not cruelty but piety. Jerome to Riparius.

(23, q. 8, c. *Legi*.) I have read of Phinehas the Syromastes (“Syrian-slayer”), the authority of Elijah, the zeal of Simon the Canaanite, Peter’s severity in slaying Ananias and Sapphira, and Paul’s constancy in condemning with everlasting severity Elymas, the great opponent of the ways of the Lord. It is not cruelty to punish crimes for God, but piety. Thus the law also says: “If your brother, friend, or wife who sleeps in your bosom should seek to corrupt the truth, let your hand be upon them, and shed their blood.”

## CHAPTER XXII. A servant or son is not loved when he is not corrected. Augustine, *Treatises on the Epistle of John*, chapter 7.

(23, q. 5, c. *Non putes*.) Do not suppose that you love your servant when you do not beat him; or that you love your son when you do not discipline him; or that you love your neighbor when you do not correct him. This is not charity, but weakness. Let charity burn to amend and correct: if conduct is good, let it delight; if bad, let it be amended.

## CHAPTER XXIII. No one except a judge may kill anyone. Augustine, *Questions on the New and Old Testament*, chapter 103.

Why, then, was the sentence given that whoever takes the sword shall perish by the sword, unless because no one, except a judge, may kill anyone with the sword? But the Apostle Peter was permitted only so far as to cause pain, not to kill. Having heard this, he was not to strike again. Moreover, it was said that, once people have become Christians, they may not kill. For those placed under mercy may not harshly employ the law of right entrusted to the world.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Some things were commanded under the old law, others under the new.

[Col. 1310D]

Formerly the law commanded “eye for eye”; now, to one striking the cheek, we offer the other also. At that time it was commanded to warriors: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one” (Ps. 44). Now Peter heard: “Put your sword into its sheath; for whoever strikes with the sword shall die by the sword” (John 18).

## CHAPTER XXV. One who spares and indulges vices so that they may be nourished is not merciful. Augustine to Lotharius.

(23, q. 5, c. *Qui vitiis*.) Whoever spares and indulges vices so that they may be nourished, lest he grieve the will of sinners, is no more merciful than one who does not wish to take a [Col. 1311A] knife from a child lest he hear him crying, and does not fear lest he be wounded and suffer or be killed.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Catholics may seek defense against heretics from constituted authorities. Augustine to Demetrius.

(23, q. 3, c. *Nostri adversus*.) Our people seek redress from constituted authorities against your people’s unlawful and private acts of violence—acts which you yourselves there, who commit such things, grieve over and lament—not in order that they may persecute them, but in order that they may defend themselves.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On account of the Saracens, the pope orders the people to assemble and meet them at the seashore. From the Register of Leo IV to the Emperor Louis.

(23, q. 8, c. *Igitur, cum*.) Therefore, since adverse [Col. 1311B] reports often arrive from the regions of the Saracens, certain persons said that the Saracens would come secretly and stealthily into the Roman harbor. On this account we order our people to assemble, have decreed that they descend to the shore of the sea, and have departed from Rome.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The pope ought to be the avenger and chief helper of his flock. Leo IV to Emperor Louis.

(23, q. 8, c. *Scire vos*.) You ought to know that we never allow our people to be oppressed by anyone; but if any necessity arises, we immediately take vengeance, because in all things we ought to be avengers and chief helpers of our flock.

## CHAPTER XXIX. We ought not to persecute Jews, but Saracens. Alexander II to the bishops of Spain.

[Col. 1311C]

(23, q. 8, c. *Dispar*.) The case of the Jews and of the Saracens is certainly different. War is justly waged against those who persecute Christians and drive them from their cities and their own homes. The Jews, however, are prepared to serve; indeed, I restrained a certain bishop who wished to destroy their synagogue.

## CHAPTER XXX. One who dies in defense of Christians obtains the heavenly kingdom from God. Pope Nicholas to the Frankish army.

(23, q. 8, c. *Omni timore*; and q. 5, c. *Omnium*.) [Col. 1311D] Casting aside every fear and terror, strive to act courageously against the enemies of the holy faith and adversaries of all religion. Likewise: wherever your ancestors have moved the public army, they have always emerged victorious, and no multitude was able to overcome them. For we have not heard that they ever returned without the renown of victory. Likewise: we wish the charity of all of you to know that whoever among you—though we say it without wishing it—shall faithfully die in this contest of war, the kingdoms of heaven will by no means be denied to him. For the Almighty knows, if any one of you dies, that he has died for the truth of the faith, the salvation of his country, and the defense of Christians. Therefore he will receive from Him the reward for which he waits.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Pope Adrian excommunicates the duke of the Bavarians unless he keeps the oath which he gave to Pepin. From the Frankish Chronicle.

[Col. 1312A]

Pope Adrian, on the holy day of Easter, in the presence of Emperor Charles, anathematized Tarmo, duke of the Bavarians, unless in all things he obeyed that emperor, his sons, and the Frankish people, as he had sworn to his father Pepin and to himself. If he should refuse and bloodshed or any other evil should occur, it would rest upon that duke and his kinsmen; and the aforesaid king and his people would be free from that guilt.

## CHAPTER XXXII. At Pope Adrian’s entreaties, Charles undertook war against the Lombards. From the *Deeds of Charlemagne* according to Alcuin.

[Col. 1312B] (23, q. 8, c. *Hortatu*.) Urged by the exhortation and prayers of Pope Adrian, bishop of the city of Rome, King Charles undertook war against the Lombards. Earlier, his father had undertaken it, at the pope’s entreaty, only with great difficulty.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. The king must suppress thefts and crimes. Cyprian, *On the Nine Abuses*.

(23, q. 5, c. *Rex*.) A king ought to suppress thefts, punish adultery, remove the impious from the land, not permit parricides and perjurers to live, and not allow his sons to act impiously.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. One who protects his country from barbarians is full of justice. Ambrose, *On Duties*, book I.

[Col. 1312C]

(23, q. 3, c. *Fortitudo*.) Courage, which either in war protects one’s country from barbarians, or at home defends the weak, or protects companions from robbers, is full of justice.

## CHAPTER XXXV. One who kills a human being in obedience to authority is not guilty of homicide. Augustine, *City of God*, book I.

(23, q. 5, c. *Miles*.) When a soldier, obedient to the authority under which he has been lawfully appointed, kills a human being, he is guilty of homicide under no law of his state; indeed, unless he does so, he is guilty of abandoning and despising the command. But if he had acted by his own will and authority, he would have incurred the crime of shedding human blood. Thus, for that for which he is punished if he acts without orders, he would be punished if he failed to act when ordered. And if this is so at an emperor’s command, how much more so at the command of the Creator. Therefore, one who hears that it is not lawful to kill should do so if the one whose commands may not lawfully be despised has commanded it.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the same subject. Pelagius to the patrician Valerian.

No one persecutes except one who compels to evil. But one who either punishes a deed or prevents it from being done does not persecute but loves. For if, as some think, no one is to be restrained from evil or drawn back to good, human and divine laws must necessarily be annulled—laws which establish punishment for the wicked and rewards for the just. Schism, moreover, is an evil that must be suppressed even through external authorities.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. When necessity presses, it is permissible to undertake war even during the days of Lent. Pope Nicholas, in response to the Bulgarians’ inquiries.

[Col. 1313A]

(23, q. 8, c. *Si nulla*.) If no necessity presses, one must abstain from battles not only during Lent but at all times. But if unavoidable necessity presses, then even in Lenten time preparations for war must undoubtedly not be spared in defense both of oneself and one’s country, or of ancestral laws; lest a person appear to tempt God if he has something he can do and does not take care for his own safety and that of others, nor prevent harm to holy religion.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. One who kills a guilty person in the exercise of office does not sin. Augustine, *On Free Choice of the Will*, book I.

[Col. 1313B] (23, q. 5, c. *Si homicidium*.) If killing a human being is homicide, one may sometimes kill without sin. For when a soldier kills an enemy, a judge or his officer kills a guilty person, or a weapon happens to fly from someone’s hand unwillingly and without his knowing it, they do not seem to me to sin when they kill a human being. Yet I do not agree that such persons are called murderers. Likewise, a soldier is commanded by law to kill an enemy. If he excuses himself from this, he suffers punishment from the emperor. Shall we dare to call these laws unjust—or rather, no laws at all? For no law seems to me to be a law unless it is just.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. One who voluntarily kills persons whom a judge orders killed is a murderer. Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, chapter 27.

(23, q. 5, c. *Cum minister*.) When an officer of a judge [Col. 1313C] kills one whom the judge or the law has ordered to be killed, certainly, if he does it voluntarily, he is a murderer—even if he kills someone whom he knows ought to have been killed by the judge.

## CHAPTER XL. Offices of punishment can be discharged with a good intention. Augustine, *Questions on Matthew*, book III.

(23, q. 5, c. *Officia vindictae*.) Offices of punishment can be discharged with a good intention, as can the law and the judge.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the same subject. Augustine, *Questions on Leviticus*, chapter 71.

When this person is killed, the law kills him, not you.

## CHAPTER XLII. The commands of patience must be observed by strength of mind, not by an outward display of the body. Augustine to Marcellus.

[Col. 1313D] (23, q. 1, c. *Paratus*. § *Corripiendo*.) If this earthly commonwealth observed Christian precepts, its wars too would be waged not without benevolence, but so that the defeated might more readily be provided for within the peaceable fellowship of piety and justice. For one from whom the license of wrongdoing is taken is conquered more usefully, since nothing is more unhappy than the happiness of sinners, by which penal impunity is nourished and an evil will, like an inward enemy, is strengthened. Likewise: if it were possible, even wars would be waged mercifully by good people, so that, with lawless desires subdued, these vices might be destroyed which ought, under just rule, either to be eradicated or punished. For if Christian discipline condemned all wars, the Gospel would rather have said to soldiers seeking counsel for salvation that they should throw away their weapons and withdraw altogether from military service. But it said to them: “Do not extort from anyone; do not make a false accusation against anyone. Let your pay suffice you” (Luke 3). By commanding that their own pay should suffice them, it certainly did not forbid them to serve as soldiers.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the same subject. Augustine to Count Boniface.

(33, q. 5, c. *Officia, vindicta*.) I do not want you to hesitate, lamenting a grave battle; I shall give useful advice to you and yours. Take up arms in your hands; let prayer strike the ears of the Creator, because, when battle is joined, God watches from open heaven, and to the side which He sees to be just He grants both victory and the palm.

## CHAPTER XLIV. To whom it is said that he takes up the sword. Augustine, book II, chapter 2.

[Col. 1314B]

(23, q. 4, c. *Ille gladium*.) “Whoever uses the sword shall fall by the sword.” But that person uses the sword who, with no higher and lawful authority either commanding or compelling, arms himself against another’s blood.

## CHAPTER XLV. What is rightly blamed in war. Augustine, from the same work.

(23, q. 1, c. *Quod culpatur*, § *Sive Deo*.) Whether commanded by God or by some lawful authority, wars are undertaken by good persons when they find themselves in that order of human affairs in which the order of things itself justly binds them either to command such acts or to obey in such matters. Otherwise, when soldiers came to John for baptism and said, “And what shall we do?”, he would have answered, “Throw away your weapons, abandon this military service, strike no one, overthrow no one” (Luke 3). But because he knew that by serving as soldiers they were not murderers but ministers of the law, not avengers of their own injuries but defenders of public safety, he answered them: “Do not extort from anyone; make no false accusation against anyone; let your pay suffice you” (ibid.). Likewise: let the Manichees hear our Lord Jesus Christ, commanding that this tribute be rendered to Caesar which John says is sufficient for the soldier. “Render,” he says, “to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22). For tributes are paid to Caesar for this purpose: that the pay necessary for the soldier may be supplied for wars.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On the same subject. Augustine, *Against Faustus the Manichean*, book XXII, chapter 74.

[Col. 1314D] (23, q. 1, c. *Quod culpatur*.) Likewise, it matters for what causes and under what authorities people undertake wars that are to be waged. Yet the natural order adapted to the peace of mortals requires that the authority and counsel for undertaking war should reside with rulers. Soldiers, however, ought to owe the service of carrying out military commands to peace and the common safety. And it is not lawful to doubt that a war undertaken at God’s command ought rightly to be undertaken.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On the same subject. Augustine, against the same author, ibid.

(23, q. 1, c. *Quod culpatur*, § *Non enim*.) When a just man happens to serve as a soldier under even a sacrilegious human king, he may rightly wage war at that king’s command if, preserving the order of peace, it is certain that what he is commanded is not contrary to God’s command; or if it is not certain whether it is so, in such a way that perhaps the injustice of the command makes the king guilty, while the order of service shows the soldier innocent. How much more innocently does one engage in the administration of wars when he wages war at God’s command, whom no one who serves Him is unaware can command anything evil!

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Not only human beings, but also opposing powers, are avengers of God’s wrath. Jerome on Joel, chapter 2.

(23, q. 5, c. *Non solum*.) Not only human beings are ministers and avengers of God’s wrath against those who do evil—hence they do not bear the sword without cause—but also the opposing powers which are called the fury and wrath of God.

## CHAPTER XLIX. One who slays cruel persons is not such as he appears to those who suffer. Jerome on Isaiah, chapter 13.

(23, q. 5, c. *Non est crudelis*.) One who slays cruel persons is not cruel, though he appears cruel to those who suffer. For a robber hanging from the gallows considers the judge cruel.

## CHAPTER L. It benefits a robber or pirate if someone disables his limbs. Jerome on Zephaniah, chapter 1.

(23, q. 3, c. *Si quis*.) If someone removes the strength of a robber or pirate and renders him weak, his weakness benefits him. For his disabled limbs, which he formerly did not use well, will cease from evil work.

## CHAPTER LI. One who strikes evil persons insofar as they are evil is a minister of God. Jerome on Ezekiel, book IV.

(23, q. 5, c. *Qui malos*.) One who strikes evil persons insofar as they are evil, and has implements of killing in order to kill the worst persons, is a minister of the Lord.

## CHAPTER LII. A judge does not become the author of crime by overcoming people. Jerome on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 5.

(23, q. 5, c. *Judex*.) A judge is not the author of crime by overcoming people.

## CHAPTER LIII. One who punishes murderers, sacrilegious persons, and poisoners does not shed blood. Jerome on Jeremiah, chapter 22.

[Col. 1315D]

(23, q. 5, c. *Homicidas*.) To punish murderers, sacrilegious persons, and poisoners is not the shedding of blood, but the ministry of the laws.

## CHAPTER LIV. What a just war is. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XVIII, chapter 2.

(23, q. 2, c. *Justum bellum*.) A just war is one waged by edict either to recover property or to repel enemies. A judge is so called because he declares law to the people, or because he determines matters by law. To determine matters by law is to judge justly. For one is not a judge unless justice is in him.

## CHAPTER LV. A king bears the sword because he is an avenger against the wicked. Stephen to Bishop Lotharius.

[Col. 1316A]

For a king does not bear the sword without cause. He is an avenger against all wicked persons, in order to restrain by fear those whom he cannot correct by salutary admonitions. Let him therefore confidently undertake what pleases God. For Peter will in no respect be absent with his two-edged sword, provided that he consults for the safety of his country.

## CHAPTER LVI. On the same subject. *Pandects*, book I.

(Dist. 1, c. *Jus naturale*; book I, *On Sentences of Excommunication*, § *Vim*.) Let us repel force and injury. For this is established by law: whatever anyone has done for the defense of his own body is considered to have been done lawfully.

## CHAPTER LVII. Harmless passage was denied to the children of Israel, and therefore they waged just wars. Augustine on Numbers, chapter 44, question 44.

[Col. 1316B]

(23, q. 2, c. *Notandum est*.) It should certainly be noted how just wars were waged by the children of Israel against the Amorites. For harmless passage was denied them, though it ought most equitably to have been open by the law of human society.

## CHAPTER LVIII. One who does not repel an injury to an ally is like one who inflicts it. Ambrose, *On Duties*, book I, chapter 36.

(23, q. 3, c. *Non inferenda*.) The law of virtue is not to inflict injury but to repel it. For one who, if able, does not repel injury from an ally is as blameworthy as one who inflicts it.

## CHAPTER LIX. A king serves in one way because he is a human being, and in another because he is king. Augustine to Count Boniface.

[Col. 1316C]

What difference is there between Arians and Donatists? How do kings serve the Lord in fear, except by religious severity in prohibiting and punishing those things contrary to the Lord’s commands? For they serve in one way because they are human beings, and in another because they are kings. As human beings, they serve by living faithfully; as kings, they serve by establishing with fitting rigor laws that command what is just and prohibit what is contrary.

## CHAPTER LX. Military service is not a sin. Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord in Matthew*, sermon 19.

(23, q. 1, c. *Militare*.) To serve as a soldier is not an offense, but to serve as a soldier for plunder is sin. It is not criminal to administer the commonwealth; but to administer it in order rather to increase one’s private estate and wealth appears blameworthy. Hence certain provisions of pay have been established for soldiers, lest, when expenses are sought, plunder should run rampant. Likewise, the Lord himself said: “Render to God the things that are God’s, and to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s” (Matt. 22). Therefore what Caesar commands must be borne; what he orders must be endured. But it becomes intolerable when tax collectors heap up plunder. Likewise, soldiers asked John, saying: “What shall we do?” He said to them: “Do not extort from anyone, nor make false accusation, but be content with your pay” (Luke 3). Every person who serves should understand himself in this way. For Scripture speaks not only of those who serve in armed military service, [Col. 1317A] but whoever wears the belt of his office is enrolled as a soldier of his rank; and this statement can be made, for example, to soldiers, protectors, and all rulers [Col. 1318A] whatsoever who receive publicly allotted pay: if he seeks more, he is condemned by John’s sentence as an accuser and extortioner.

## CONCERNING DIVINATIONS AND INCANTATIONS.

[Col. 1317]

## CHAPTER LXI. Let one who observes diviners or enchanters be anathematized. From the Decree of Gregory III, chapter 12.

[Col. 1317A]

(26, q. 5, c. *Si quis ariolos*.) If anyone observes diviners, haruspices, or enchanters, let him be anathematized; or if anyone uses amulets (*philacteria*), let him be anathematized.

## CHAPTER LXII. One who seeks divinations must do penance for five years. Council of Ancyra, chapter 23.

(26, q. 5, c. *Qui divinationes*.) Those who seek divinations and follow pagan custom, or bring persons of this kind into their homes in order to inquire into something by magical art or for the sake of expiation, shall lie under the rule of five years, according to the established grades of penance.

## CHAPTER LXIII. Persons devoted to sacred offices must not become magicians or enchanters. Council of Laodicea.

(26, q. 5, c. *Non oportet*.) Those devoted to sacred offices, or clerics, ought not to be magicians or enchanters, nor to make amulets (*philacteria*), which are proved to be bonds upon their souls.

## CHAPTER LXIV. A bishop or priest who consults magicians or haruspices is to be deprived of office. Third Council of Toledo, chapter 28.

(26, q. 5, c. *Si quis episcopus*.) If any bishop, priest, deacon, or anyone of the clerical order is discovered to have consulted haruspices, enchanters, diviners, augurs by art, sacrilegious persons, those who profess magical art, or any persons practicing similar things, he shall be suspended from the honor of his rank, receive the discipline of a monastery, and there, devoted to perpetual penance, expiate the crime of sacrilege which he has committed.

## CHAPTER LXV. Things done by the tricks of magicians are shown to be not real but phantasmal. Augustine, *City of God*; Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VIII, chapter 9.

[Col. 1317D]

(26, q. 5, c. *Nec mirum*.) Nor is it surprising concerning the tricks of magicians, whose arts of maleficence advanced so far that they even resisted Moses in those signs, changing rods into dragons and waters into blood. It is also reported in books of the pagans that Circe, a most famous sorceress, changed Ulysses’ companions into beasts. We also read concerning the sacrifice which the Arcadians offered to their god Lycaeus, that whoever partook of it was changed into the forms of beasts. But all these things were fabricated by magical tricks rather than accomplished in the reality of things. Therefore, so that these errors may become evident to the ignorant through an account of their nature and inventors according to the tradition of the ancients, we consider it fitting first to speak of them.

Magicians are those commonly called evildoers (*malefici*) because of the magnitude of their crimes. They are persons who, by God’s permission, disturb the elements, trouble the minds of people less confident in God, and, without any draught of poison, kill merely by the force of an incantation; whence Lucan also says:

[Col. 1318B]

> A mind unpolluted by any corruption of swallowed poison  
> perishes when bewitched.

Therefore, having summoned demons, they dare to claim that they can destroy any enemies of their own by evil arts. They also use blood and often touch corpses with sacrificial victims. Necromancers are those by whose incantations dead persons seem to be revived in order to give divinations and answer questions. For *nekros* is Greek for “dead” (*mortuus* in Latin), and *manteia* means “divination”; to raise them, blood is added to the corpse. For demons are said to love blood. Therefore, whenever necromancy is practiced, gore is mixed with water, so that they may be more readily summoned by the color of blood. Hydromancers are named from water. Hydromancy consists in [Col. 1318C] summoning up the shadows of demons by inspecting water, seeing their illusory images there, and hearing something from them there; with blood added, they are even said to raise the dead from the underworld.

## CHAPTER LXVI. On the various kinds of divination. Augustine, *City of God*; Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VIII, chapter 9.

(26, q. 4, c. *Igitur.*) Thus, the kind of divination is reported to have been brought in by the Persians. Varro, however, says that there are four kinds of divination: earth, water, air, and fire. Hence he thinks the names geomancy, hydromancy, pyromancy, and aeromancy were given. Diviners (*divini*) are so called as though filled with God. For they pretend that they are full of divinity, and by a certain fraudulent craft conjecture future events to men. There are, moreover, two kinds of divination: art and frenzy. Incanters are those [Col. 1318D] who perform their art by words. They are called *arioli* because they utter wicked prayers around the altars of idols and offer deadly sacrifices; by these observances they receive responses from demons. They are called haruspices, as it were, “inspectors of the hours.” For they observe days and hours in conducting business and works, and attend to what a person ought to observe in each particular season. They also inspect the entrails of animals and foretell future events from them. Augurs are those who attend to the flight and cries of birds, and report other signs or unexpected observations that occur to people. So too are auspices. For auspices are the things which travelers observe. Auspices and auguries are so called as it were from *avium aspicia* and *garria*, that is, the sightings and cries, or tongues, of birds. Likewise, *augurium* is as though *avigerium*, what birds carry out. There are two kinds of auspices: one pertaining to the eyes, the other to the ears [Col. 1319A]—to the eyes, namely the flight of birds; to the ears, the cry of birds. Pythonesses are so called from Python Apollo, because he was the originator of divination. Astrologers are so called because they make auguries from the stars. Genethliacs are named because of their consideration of birthdays. For they describe the births of human beings through the twelve signs of heaven, inasmuch as they try, from the course of the stars, to foretell the characters, deeds, and events of those being born—that is, under what sign a person was born, or what result in life belongs to one born at such a time. These are commonly called mathematicians; the Latins call this kind of superstition “constellations,” that is, notations of the stars and of how they stand when a person is born.

But the first kind, namely interpreters of the stars, are called [Col. 1319B] magi, as is read of those in the Gospel who announced the birth of Christ; afterward only mathematicians were called by this name. Knowledge of this art was permitted until the coming forth of the Gospel, so that, once Christ had appeared, no one thereafter should interpret a birth from heaven. Horoscopists are those who observe the hours of human births according to unequal and varying fate. Sortilegists are those who, under the name of a fictitious religion, profess the knowledge of divination through certain things which they call “lots of the saints,” or foretell future events by examining the sentences of any Scriptures whatsoever. *Salitores* are so called because, when any parts of their limbs twitch, they foretell that something favorable or sad is thereby signified to them.

## CHAPTER LXVII. Things done by the tricks of magicians are shown to be not real but phantasmal. Augustine, *City of God*.

[Col. 1319C]

(26, q. 5, c. *Nec mirum*, § *Ad haec.*) To all the foregoing belong also the bindings of execrable remedies, which the art of physicians does not approve, whether in incantations, in characters, or in any things whatsoever that are hung up or tied. In all these matters there is an art of demons arising from a certain pestilential partnership of human beings and evil angels. Therefore all such things must be avoided by a Christian and wholly rejected and condemned with every execration. The Phrygians first invented auguries from birds. Mercury, however, is said to have first invented magical illusion (*praestigium*). [Col. 1319D] It is called *praestigium* because it blinds the sharpness of the eyes. A certain Tages is said to have first transmitted the art of haruspicy to the Etruscans. Though lifeless, he dictated the discipline of haruspicy and afterward did not appear. For, according to the fable, while a certain farmer was ploughing, he sprang from the clods of earth and dictated haruspicy; on that same day he also died. The Romans translated these books from the Etruscan tongue into their own.

By these portents, then, human curiosity is deceived through the fraud of demons when people imprudently seek to know what they have no right whatever to investigate. Power is therefore given to unclean spirits that they may capture the perverse—that is, seduce wicked people, those who despise the truth and believe a lie—and, in Paul’s words: “They will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their [Col. 1320A] own desires they will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears; and indeed they will turn away their hearing from the truth and be turned toward fables” (II Tim. IV). “Burdened with sins, they will be led away by various desires, always learning and never arriving at a knowledge of truth” (II Tim. III). “Now just as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth: people corrupt in mind, reprobate concerning the faith. But they will proceed no further; for their folly will be manifest to all, as theirs also was” (II Tim. III).

Nor should anyone therefore believe that any persons can accomplish anything by magical arts without God’s permission, because everything that happens happens either by His just judgment or because He permits it to happen. The aforesaid magicians are read to have done things similar to those done by Moses, who threw down [Col. 1320B] his rod and it was turned into a serpent; each of them also threw down his rods, and they were turned into serpents. But Aaron’s rod devoured their rods. Therefore neither the magicians nor the evil angels, through whose ministry they performed those things, were creators of serpents. For in bodily things throughout all the elements there are certain hidden seminal principles which, when a temporal and causal opportunity has been given, break forth into their fitting forms according to their own modes and limits. Thus the angels who do these things are not called creators of animals, just as farmers are not to be called creators of crops, trees, or anything whatever that grows from the earth, although they know how to provide certain visible opportunities and causes so that such things may grow. What these people do visibly, those beings do invisibly. But God alone is Creator, who implanted in things the causes themselves and their seminal principles.

Furthermore, some think it should be asked how Scripture relates that the pythoness raised up the prophet Samuel for a conversation with Saul, that most impious king, if Pythian divination is to be reckoned among the errors of magical art. They may be answered thus: it would be an altogether unworthy act if assent were given to this according to the words of the narrative. For how could it happen that a man holy by birth and righteous in the works of his life should be drawn by magical art? Or, if he was not drawn, did he consent? To believe either of these things about a righteous man is contrary to reason. For if [Col. 1320D] he was brought unwillingly, righteousness has no protection; but if voluntarily, his consent lost the spiritual merit which, while placed in the flesh, he had sought. This is most absurd, because one who departs hence righteous remains righteous.

Rather, this is Satan’s illusion, by which, in order to deceive the worst people, he pretends that even honor is in his power. The Apostle shows this among other things when he says: “Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (II Cor. XI). Thus, in order to produce an error in which he might be glorified, he put himself forward in the appearance and name of a righteous man, so that he might falsely represent the hope preached by the worshipers of God as accomplishing nothing, when he pretended that the righteous departing hence were in his power. But some are deceived by the fact that he did not lie concerning the death of Saul and his son—[Col. 1321A] as if it were a great thing for the devil to foresee the death of the body before its occurrence, since certain signs commonly appear in those about to die, especially those from whom God’s protection seems to have been removed. How much more could this be done by the devil, concerning whom prophetic oracles testify that he was exalted in angelic majesty. Of his greatness the Apostle says: “Do you not know the height of Satan?”

What wonder, then, if he could foresee death that was near and impending, when this is the means by which he deceives and wishes to be worshiped as though he had divine power? For Saul was made mad with such great dullness that he fled to a pythoness. Corrupted by sin, he turned to those things which he had condemned. But if anyone, because of the narrative and the matters expressed in words, thinks that they should not be passed over lest the account of the history be empty, he will indeed do rightly, provided that he does not at all force it into the meaning of truth, but refers it to Saul’s sight and understanding. For, having become reprobate, he could not possess a sound understanding. The historian describes Saul’s state of mind and Samuel’s appearance, setting forth what was said and seen, while passing over whether these things were true or false. What, he says, did Saul understand when he heard in what appearance the one summoned had arisen? “He understood,” it says, “that this was Samuel” (I Reg. XVIII). It reports what he understood; and because he did not understand rightly, contrary to Scripture he worshiped someone other than the Lord, and, thinking that he worshiped Samuel, he worshiped the devil, so that Satan might obtain the fruit of his deception. For this is what he strives for: to be worshiped as God.

For if Samuel had truly appeared to him, surely that righteous man would not have allowed himself to be worshiped—he who had preached that the Lord alone is to be worshiped. And how could a man of God, who was in refreshment with Abraham, have said to a man of pestilence worthy of the burning of Gehenna: “Tomorrow you will be with me” (ibid.)? By these two indications the heedless Satan exposed the subtlety of his own deception: because he allowed himself to be worshiped under Samuel’s appearance and name, contrary to the law and by a man burdened with sins; and because, though there is a great distance between sinners and the righteous, he lied that Saul would be with the most righteous Samuel. Yet it may appear true if Samuel’s name is omitted: for Saul was to be with the devil, since he passed over to the one whom he worshiped.

Therefore the devil, always hiding beneath a veil, reveals himself while he fabricates things that attach to the persons through whom he seeks to deceive. But if he objects to anyone and says: How do the things which those diviners foretell as future come about? Or how can they provide remedies to the sick or inflict illness on the healthy, if they possess no power or capacity of their own? Let him receive this answer from us: no one ought therefore to believe them because sometimes what they foretell comes about, [Col. 1322A] or because they seem to heal the sick or injure the healthy. This is by God’s permission, so that those who hear or see these things may be tested, and it may become apparent what faith or devotion toward God they possess. As is read in Deuteronomy, Moses, by the word of the Lord, commanded God’s people, saying:

> “If a prophet arises in your midst, or one who says that he has seen a dream, and foretells a sign and wonder, and what he has spoken comes about, and he says: ‘Let us go and follow foreign gods and serve them,’ you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer, because the Lord your God is testing you, that it may be made manifest whether you love Him or not. Follow the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul; fear Him, keep His commandments, and hear His voice. You shall serve Him and cleave to Him” (Deut. [Col. 1322B] XIII).

Here He plainly intended it to be understood that even things said by diviners not according to God, if what they say happens, are not to be received as such; nor are things to be done which they command, even if they occur, nor are those things to be worshiped which they worship. God does not show that these occurrences lie outside His power; rather, as though He were asked why He permits them, He explained the cause of the testing: namely, to discover whether they have love toward their God. This is to be discovered by themselves rather than by Him who knows all things before they happen.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. In how many ways demons foreknow future events. Augustine, *On the Divination of Demons*, chapter 3.

[Col. 1322C] (26, q. 4, c. *Sciendum est.*) It should indeed be known that the nature of demons is such that, by the perception of an aerial body, they easily surpass the perception of earthly bodies; and, because of the greater mobility of an aerial body, they incomparably exceed in speed not only the movement of any beings, such as humans or beasts, but even the flight of birds. Endowed with these two things, insofar as pertains to an aerial body—namely, keenness of perception and swiftness of motion—they foretell or report far in advance things at which human beings marvel because of the slowness of earthly perception. Demons have also acquired, through the very long time over which their life extends, a far greater experience of events than humans can attain because of the brevity of life. Through these powers bestowed by the nature [Col. 1322D] of an aerial body, demons not only predict many future things but also perform many wonders. Since human beings cannot say or do these things, some judge demons worthy of being served and of receiving divine honors—chiefly because the vice of curiosity investigates them, out of love for false and earthly happiness and temporal preeminence.

# ON SORTILEGY

[Col. 1321]

## CHAPTER LXIX. On those who devote themselves to auguries and divinations. Council of Agde, chapter 42.

[Col. 1321D]

(26, q. 5, c. *Aliquanti.*) Certain clerics and laypersons [Col. 1322D] devote themselves to auguries and, under the name of a fictitious religion, profess knowledge of divination through those things which they call the lots of the holy Fathers, or promise future events by examining any Scriptures whatsoever. Any cleric or layperson found either consulting or teaching these things shall be held excluded from the Church.

## CHAPTER LXX. A lot is nothing other than divination and is decreed to be sorcery. Leo IV, to the bishops of Britain.

(25, q. 5, c. *Sortes.*) We decree that the lots by which you make decisions throughout your provinces are nothing other than the divinations and sorcery condemned by the Fathers. Therefore we desire that they be condemned altogether; we forbid, under an anathema, that they be named any longer among Christians and command that they be cut off.

## CHAPTER LXXI. The punishment of soothsayers. *Capitulary*, book VII, chapter 27.

[Col. 1323B] Soothsayers who declare that they know future events shall be beaten and cast out of the city.

## CHAPTER LXXII. A person devoted to auguries and incantations is to be separated from the Church. Council of Carthage, chapter 79.

(26, q. 5, c. *Auguriis.*) We command that one devoted to auguries or incantations be separated from the assembly of the Church; likewise one who adheres to Jewish superstitions or festivals.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. One must not believe indiscriminately in lots on the example of Jonah and Matthias. Jerome, on the prophet Jonah, chapter 1.

(26, q. 2, c. *Non exemplo*, and c. *Non statim.*) We ought not immediately to believe in lots on the example of Jonah, nor join to this testimony that passage in the Acts of the Apostles where Matthias is chosen an apostle by lot, since the privileges of individuals cannot establish a common law.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. Divine oracles are not to be applied to secular business. Augustine, to Januarius, Letter 119.

(26, q. 2, c. *Hi qui.*) Those who read lots from the pages of the Gospels—although it is to be wished that they do this rather than run to consult demons—nevertheless I disapprove of this custom: wishing to turn divine oracles toward secular business and the vanity of this life.

## CHAPTER LXXV. Bishops should strive by every means to eliminate the arts of sortilege and magic. Council of Ancyra, chapter 4.

[Col. 1323D] (26, q. 5, c. *Episcopi.*) Bishops and their ministers should strive with all their strength completely to root out from their parishes the pernicious art of sortilege and sorcery invented by the Devil; and if they find any man or woman who practices such wickedness, they should shamefully dishonor and expel them from their parishes. For the Apostle says: “Avoid a heretical person after a first and second correction, knowing that one who is such is perverted” (Tit. VIII [sc. III]). Those who, having abandoned their Creator, seek aid from the devil are perverted and held captive by the devil. Therefore the holy Church must be cleansed of such a pestilence.

Nor should this be omitted: certain wicked women, turning back after Satan, believe and profess that during the hours of the night [Col. 1324A] they ride upon certain beasts with Diana, the goddess of the pagans, or with Herodias, and with an innumerable multitude of women; that in the silence of the dead of night they travel across great stretches of land; that they obey her commands as their mistress; and that on certain nights they are summoned to her service. But would that these women alone had perished in their faithlessness and had not dragged many others into the destruction of unbelief. For an innumerable multitude, deceived by this false opinion, believe these things to be true; by believing, they depart from the true faith and fall into pagan error, when they suppose that there is any divinity or divine power apart from the one God.

Therefore priests ought to preach with all diligence to the people in the churches entrusted to them, so that they may know that these things are altogether false, and that such phantasms are imposed upon the minds of unbelievers not by a divine spirit but by an evil one. For Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light (II Cor. XI). When he has captured the mind of any little woman and subjected her to himself through unbelief, he immediately transforms himself into the forms and likenesses of various persons; and, mocking in dreams the mind which he holds captive, now showing joyful, now sad, now familiar, now unfamiliar persons, he leads it through every byway. And although the unbelieving spirit alone undergoes this, she supposes that these things happen not only in the mind but also in the body. For who is not carried outside himself in dreams and nocturnal illusions, and while sleeping sees many things which he never saw while awake? Who, then, is so foolish and dull as to think that all these things which happen in the spirit alone [Col. 1324C] also happen in the body?

The prophet Ezekiel saw the visions of the Lord in the spirit, not in the body (Ezek. III); and John the Apostle saw and heard the mysteries of the Apocalypse in the spirit, not in the body, as he himself said: “Immediately,” he says, “I was in the spirit” (Apoc. I). And Paul does not dare to say that he was caught up in the body (II Cor. XII). Therefore it must be publicly announced to all that whoever believes such things and things like them loses the faith; and whoever does not have the right faith in God belongs not to Him but to the one in whom he believes—that is, the devil. For it is written of our Lord: “All things were made through Him” (John I). Whoever, therefore, believes that anything can be done, or that any creature can be changed or transformed for better or worse, [Col. 1324D] or into another form or likeness, by anyone other than the Creator Himself who made all things and through whom all things were made, is beyond doubt an unbeliever and worse than a pagan.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. A sorceress corrected with scourges is to be expelled from the parish. Council of Agde, chapter 3.

Inquiry must be made whether there is any woman who says that by certain sorceries and incantations she can alter people’s minds—for example, turn hatred into love or love into hatred, or destroy or steal away people’s goods. And if there is one who says that, transformed into the likeness of a woman with a troop of demons, she rides on certain beasts on specified nights and is numbered in their company, such a woman is in every way to be corrected with scourges and expelled from the parish.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. What is a lot? Augustine, on Psalm XXX.

(26, q. 2, c. *Sors non est aliquid.*) A lot is not something evil, but a matter of human uncertainty indicating the divine will. For the Apostles also cast lots when Judas, after betraying the Lord, perished and, as is written of him, “went to his own place” (Acts I); then it began to be asked who should be appointed in his place. They were chosen by human judgment, and one of the two was chosen by divine judgment. God was consulted concerning which of the two He wished to appoint, and the lot fell upon Matthias (ibid.).

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. One must not believe indiscriminately in lots on the example of Matthias. Bede, on the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 1.

[Col. 1325B]

(26, q. 2, c. *Non exemplo.*) One must not believe indiscriminately in lots on the example of Matthias [Col. 1326A] or because the prophet Jonah was reproved by lot, since, as Jerome says, the privileges of individuals cannot possibly establish a common law. Likewise: if any persons, compelled by some necessity, think that God ought to be consulted by lots on the example of the Apostles, let them observe that the Apostles themselves acted only in an assembly of the brethren, with weeping and prayers poured out to God.

## CHAPTER LXXIX. Christian and true piety rejects and condemns astrologers. Augustine, *Confessions*, IV.

(26, q. 2, c. *Illos planetarios.*) I did not cease to consult those astrologers whom they call mathematicians, because apparently no sacrifice was offered by them and no prayers were addressed to any spirit for the sake of divination; nevertheless Christian and true piety consistently rejects and condemns them.

# ON THE OBSERVANCE OF DAYS AND MONTHS

[Col. 1325]

## CHAPTER LXXX. It is a grave sin to observe days, months, and years.

[Col. 1325B]

(26, q. 7, c. *Quis existimaret.*) Who would suppose how great a sin it is to observe days, months, years, and seasons—as do those who, on particular days, months, or years, are willing or unwilling to begin something because, according to these people’s empty teachings, they consider the times favorable or unfavorable—unless we weighed the greatness of this evil from the Apostle’s fear, when he says to such persons: “I fear for you, lest perhaps I have labored among you in vain” (Gal. IV).

## CHAPTER LXXXI. On the same matter. Augustine, to Januarius, book I.

(26, q. 7, c. *Non observetis*, and *Quis existimaret.*) The Apostle rebukes this when someone says: “I shall not set out because it is an unfavorable day, or because the position of the stars is such; I shall not conduct business in this month because that star has told me the month is unfavorable; or I shall conduct it because it has made the month favorable. I shall not plant a vineyard in this year [Col. 1326B] because it is a leap year.” But no wise person considers those observers of times blameworthy who say: “I shall not set out today because winter still lingers,” or, “It is the time for sowing because the earth has been saturated by autumn rains”; nor those who note, in the most orderly revolution of the stars, the natural effects connected with the movement of the seasons and with the changing qualities of times [Col. 1326C].

## CHAPTER LXXXII. The sortilegist Paschal is deposed from the archdeaconry on account of incantations and sacred groves which he venerated. From the *Book of the Popes*.

Not long afterward Paschal was deprived of the office of archdeacon, by the intervening judgment of God and of the blessed prince of the Apostles, because of certain incantations and sacred groves which he venerated, or lots which he practiced with other observers. Shut up by Sergius in a monastery, after five years he died unrepentant because of hardness of heart.

# ON LAWFUL AND UNLAWFUL OATHS

[Col. 1325]

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. An oath is to be made for a covenant of peace. Council of Toledo VIII, chapter 2.

[Col. 1325D]

(22, q. 1, c. *Omne.*) Everything which enters into covenants of peace stands more firmly when it is strengthened by the addition of an oath. And everything which reconciles the minds of friends endures more faithfully when the bonds of a solemn oath bind them. For everything which a witness confirms is established more truly when the addition of an oath affirms it. Even if a witness is lacking, the attestation of an oath alone makes the faithfulness of the innocent person manifest.
