## CHAPTER LXXXIV. Swearing is not to be forbidden, nor sought as though it were a good. Augustine, on the Epistle to the Galatians.

(22, q. 1, c. *Non est contra.*) An oath is not contrary to the commandment of God when it arises not from the evil of the person swearing but from that of the unbeliever by whom he is compelled to swear. For the Lord is understood here to have prohibited swearing in such a way that, so far as lies in oneself, whoever one may be, one should not swear. Many do swear as a habit, considering it some great or pleasant thing. Certainly the Apostle knew the Lord’s commandment, yet he swore. Nor should those be heard who do not consider these to be oaths. For what will they make of this: “I die daily, by your glory, brethren, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord” (I Cor. XV)? The Greek copies prove most clearly that this is an oath. Therefore, so far as lies in him, the Apostle does not swear; for we are forbidden to swear from desire or love of swearing. Although an oath is more than “Yes, yes; no, no,” and therefore is from evil (Matt. [Col. 1327A] V), it is not from your evil but from the weakness and unbelief of those who are not otherwise moved to faith.

## CHAPTER LXXXV. Perjury is a sin, not swearing. Augustine, Letter 154.

(22, q. 1, c. *In Novo Testamento.*) In the New Testament it is rightly said that we should not swear at all. This seems to me to have been said not because swearing is a sin, from which He wished us to be far removed by admonishing us not to swear at all. Likewise: although it has been said that we should not swear, I do not remember ever having read in the holy Scriptures that we should not receive an oath from another person.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. Swearing is not a sin. Augustine, *On the Sermon of the Lord on the Mount*.

[Col. 1327B] (22, q. 1, c. *Tu malum.*) You do no evil when you use an oath rightly. Though it is not good, it is nevertheless necessary in order to persuade another person of what you usefully urge; but it arises from the evil of the one by whose weakness you are compelled to swear.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. Swearing is permitted to the weak. Jerome, on Matthew, chapter V, book I.

(22, q. 1, c. *Considera.*) Observe that the Savior did not forbid swearing by God, but by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, and your head. This was allowed by the law, as it were, to little children: just as they sacrificed victims to God so that they would not sacrifice them to idols, so they were permitted to swear by God—not because they did this rightly, but because it is better to render this to God than to idols or demons.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. God does not forbid swearing, but perjury. Isidore, *Sentences*, book II, chapter 31.

(22, q. 1, c. *Non est contra.*) To swear is not contrary to the Lord’s commandment; but when we make a practice of swearing, we incur the crime of perjury.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. Swearing is not a sin. Augustine, *Sermons on the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 28.

(22, q. 1, c. *Si peccatum.*) If swearing were a sin, the old law would not say: “You shall not commit perjury; you shall render to the Lord your oath” (Lev. XIX). For it would not command us to sin. Likewise: We do not say to you that we do not swear. For if we said this, we would lie. So far as concerns me, I do not swear. But, as it seems to me, when compelled by great necessity—when I see that unless I do so I will not be believed, and that it is not beneficial to the person who does not believe me that he should not believe—I shall, after weighing and considering this reason, say with great fear before God either, “God is my witness,” or, “Christ knows.” This is how it stands in my mind; and I see that the very fact that it is something more than “yes” and “no” is from evil—although it is not from evil: it is from the evil of the swearer, not of the unbeliever.

## CHAPTER XC. It is better not to fulfill vows of a foolish promise than to commit a crime. Council of Toledo VIII, chapter 2.

(22, q. 4, c. *Si publicis.*) If, God forbid, in public instruments of oath an unlawful or evil condition had been attached by anyone—one which compelled a person either to kill the soul of his father or to commit violation upon a most holy virgin—would it not be more tolerable to reject the vows of a foolish promise than, by keeping useless promises, to complete the horrible measure of crimes?

## CHAPTER XCI. At times it is not expedient to fulfill a promised oath. Ambrose, *On Duties*, book I.

(22, q. 4, c. *Est etiam.*) It is also sometimes contrary to duty to fulfill a promised oath, as in the case of Herod, who swore that he would give the daughter of Herodias whatever she asked and, lest he refuse what he had promised, granted the death of John.

## CHAPTER XCII. It was an act of piety that David did not kill Nabal as he had sworn. Augustine, on the Beheading of St. John.

[Col. 1328B]

(22, q. 4, c. *Quod David.*) When the holy Gospel is read, I see that David, a pious and holy man, fell into a rash oath and preferred not to do what he had sworn rather than fulfill his oath by the shedding of human blood.

## CHAPTER XCIII. On the same matter. Isidore, chapter *In flum.* [reading uncertain].

(22, q. 4, ibid., and c. *Juravit David.*) David swore rashly, but with greater piety he did not fulfill his oath. Behold: David, though bound by an oath, did not shed human blood; but who can deny that he swore falsely? Of two sins he chose the lesser; yet it was lesser only in comparison with the former. For considered in itself, to swear falsely is a great evil.

## CHAPTER XCIV. An oath by which evil is rashly promised must not be observed. From the Decretals of Pope Sother, chapter 3.

(22, q. 4, c. *Si aliquid.*) If perhaps we happen rashly to swear something whose observance tends toward a worse outcome, we should know that it may freely be changed by wiser counsel; and, when necessity presses, we should rather commit perjury than, in changing one perjury, turn aside into another and graver crime. Thus David swore by the Lord to kill Nabal, a foolish and impious man, and to destroy everything belonging to him. But at the first intercession of Abigail, a prudent woman, he immediately withdrew his threats, recalled his sword into its sheath, and did not regret that he had incurred any guilt by such perjury.

## CHAPTER XCV. Of two evils, the lesser should be chosen when neither can be avoided. From the same Decretals and the same chapter.

(22, q. 4, c. *Non solum.*) Not only in swearing, but in everything that we do, this restraint must be more diligently observed: if perhaps we have fallen into such a snare through the ambushes of a crafty enemy that we cannot rise without some contamination of sin, we should seek that way of escape in which we perceive that we shall suffer less danger.

## CHAPTER XCVI. A pledge admitted in order to commit sin is not to be called good faith. Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*.

[Col. 1329A]

(22, q. 4, c. *Si ad peccatum.*) If a pledge is employed in admitting sin, it is astonishing if it is called good faith. Yet whatever sort it may be, if one also acts against it, the deed is worse—unless it is abandoned precisely in order to return to true and lawful fidelity, so that the sin is corrected by amending the perversity of the will. For example, if a person cannot rob a man alone, finds a companion in wrongdoing, and makes an agreement with him that they will do it together and divide the spoils, but after committing the crime takes everything away alone, the other is indeed grieved and complains that faith has not been kept with him. But in that very complaint he ought rather to consider [Col. 1329B] that he himself should have kept faith with human society by living rightly, so that unjust spoil might not be made from a human being—if he recognizes how unjustly faith was not kept with him in the partnership of sin. The person faithless in both respects must certainly be judged the more criminal.

## CHAPTER XCVII. If faith is not kept in order that persons may return to good, it is not thereby called violated. Augustine, from the same book, chapter 4.

(22, q. 4, c. *Mulier.*) Likewise, if a woman, having violated marital fidelity, keeps faith with an adulterer, she is certainly evil; but if she does not keep faith even with the adulterer, she is worse. But if she repents of her shameful act and, returning to marital chastity, breaks off adulterous pacts and agreements, I wonder whether even the adulterer himself would regard her as a violator of faith.

## CHAPTER XCVIII. An unlawful oath is not to be kept. Seventh Synod, act 4.

[Col. 1329C]

(22, q. 4, c. *Joannes.*) John, envoy of the eastern sees, said: “The discourse of our father Sophronius signifies that it is better for one who has sworn to commit perjury than to keep an oath requiring the breaking of holy images.” We say this because some excuse themselves by an oath.

## CHAPTER XCIX. On the same matter. Tarasius, patriarch.

(22, q. 4, c. *Tharasius.*) Because Father Sophronius knew the goodness of God, he therefore chose to transgress an impious oath.

## CHAPTER C. On the same matter. From the same source.

[Col. 1329D] (22, q. 4, c. *Tharas.*, § *Secundo.*) Herod kept his oath and perished. Peter denied with an oath, was converted and wept, and was saved. For the good God forgives everything if anyone repents with the whole heart. The holy synod said: “Thus Scripture teaches us.” Likewise: Leontius, bishop of Phocaea, said: “It is written: ‘Do not love a false oath.’” For this reason our false oath is dissolved, as though possessing no force.

## CHAPTER CI. It is more tolerable not to fulfill an oath than to do what is shameful. Ambrose, *On Duties*, book III, chapter 12.

(22, q. 4, c. *Unusquisque*, § *Saepe.*) Very often people bind themselves by the sacrament of an oath and, though they themselves realize that they ought not to have promised it, nevertheless do what they promised out of regard for the oath. So, as we have written above concerning Herod, he shamefully promised a reward to the dancing girl and cruelly paid it. It was shameful that a kingdom should be promised for a dance; cruel that the death of a prophet should be given under the religious obligation of an oath. How much more tolerable would such perjury have been in regard to the oath—if it could indeed be called perjury—when he had sworn while drunk among the wine-cups and, after swearing, had promised amid the choruses of dancers. The prophet’s head is brought in upon a dish, and what belonged to friendship was considered an act of fidelity.

## CHAPTER CII. Not all promises must be fulfilled. Ambrose, *On Duties*, book III, chapter 12.

(22, q. 4, c. *Non Semper*.) Not all promises are always to be fulfilled. Indeed, the Lord himself frequently changes his decision, as Scripture indicates. [Col. 1330B]

CAP. CIII. Before the age of reason, some persons should not be compelled to swear. *Capitularies*, book I, ch. 9.

(22, q. 5, c. *Parvuli*.) Children who have not reached the age of reason are not to be compelled to swear; and whoever has once committed perjury is thereafter neither to serve as a witness nor to approach the sacrament, nor to swear in his own case or another’s.

CAP. CIV. No one is to be compelled to swear before the age of fourteen. Pope Cornelius, Council of Elvira, ch. 5.

(22, q. 5, c. *Pueri*.) Boys under fourteen years of age are not to be compelled to swear.

CAP. CV. On the same matter. Council of Elvira, ch. 3.

[Col. 1330C]

(22, q. 5, c. *Pueri*, § *Puella*; and 32, q. 2, c. *Mulier*.) If a girl, being of a childish age and living in her father’s house, has bound herself by an oath without his knowledge, and if, as soon as her father hears of it, he objects, her vows and oaths shall be void, and the matter shall be more easily set right.

CAP. CVI. On the same matter. Council of Orléans, ch. 2.

An oath of a daughter made without her father’s knowledge, the vows of a monk made without his abbot’s knowledge, and the oaths of a boy are void.

CAP. CVII. On the same matter. Augustine, sermon on the beheading of John the Baptist.

If someone provokes you to swear, perhaps because he thinks that he can thereby receive satisfaction, if you swear concerning the matter which you think you have committed and done, though perhaps you did not do it—so that no evil suspicion may remain in that place—then, if you swear, you do not sin in the same way as the person who provoked you. Likewise: if you have been provoked by another, the evil involved in your swearing comes from his wrongdoing, not your own. [Col. 1330D]

CAP. CVIII. A person who knowingly compels another to commit perjury is worse than a murderer. Augustine, *On the Saints*, sermon 2.

(22, q. 5, c. *Ille qui*.) The man who provokes another to swear, knowing that he will swear falsely, surpasses a murderer. For the murderer is about to kill a body; but this man kills a soul—indeed, two souls: that of the man whom he has provoked to swear, and his own. You know that what you say is true, that what the other says is false, and yet you compel him to swear. Behold: he swears; he commits perjury; behold, he perishes. What have you gained? Indeed, you too have perished, because you wished to satisfy yourself upon his death. [Col. 1331A]

CAP. CIX. Who must judge false that which someone swears. Augustine, *Questions on Leviticus*.

(22, q. 5, c. *Hoc videtur*.) This seems to say that a person sins if someone swears falsely in his hearing, he knows that the other swears falsely, and he remains silent. But he knows that it is being done only if he was a witness to the matter sworn about: either he saw it or was privy to it—that is, he knew it in some manner, either saw it with his own eyes or was told it by the very person who swore. For he could thus have acquired knowledge by being informed. Yet between fear of this sin and fear of the destruction of persons there is often no small temptation. For we may recall one ready to commit perjury from so grave a sin by warning or forbidding him. But if he does not listen, and in our presence swears falsely concerning a matter we know, whether he ought to be restrained by being denounced, even if in doing so he incurs danger of death, is a most difficult question. But because he has not stated here to whom this should be disclosed—whether to the person to whom the oath is sworn, or to a priest, or to someone else who cannot prosecute him—it seems to me that he frees himself from the bond of sin if he reveals it to persons more able to benefit than to harm the perjurer, either in order to correct him or to appease God on his behalf; and he himself should also apply the remedy of confession. [Col. 1331B]

CAP. CX. He does not sin who demands an oath without knowing it to be false. Augustine, *On Perjury*.

[Col. 1331C] (22, q. 5, c. *Qui exigit*.) It makes a great difference, when someone demands an oath, whether he does not know that the other will swear falsely or knows it. If he does not know, and for that reason says, “Swear to me, so that he may have confidence in it,” I do not dare to call it a sin; nevertheless, it is a human temptation. But if he knows that the other did it—if he knows he did it, saw him do it, and compels him to swear—he is a murderer. For the other kills himself by his perjury; but this man has both placed and pressed the hand of the killer.

CAP. CXI. Concerning one who swears falsely what he thinks true. Augustine, *Sermons on the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 28.

(22, q. 2, c. *Homines*.) People swear falsely either when they deceive or when they are deceived: either a person thinks true what is false and swears rashly, or he knows, or thinks, that it is false and nevertheless swears that it is true, and thus swears wickedly. But the two kinds of perjury I have mentioned differ. One swears because he thinks the matter for which he swears is true. He thinks it true, yet it is false. For the former commits perjury in intention; this one is deceived and regards as true what is false. He does not knowingly impose an oath concerning a false thing.

Take another person: he knows it is false, says it is true, and swears as though true that which he knows to be false. You see what a detestable beast this is, to be exterminated from human affairs. Who would wish it to exist? All people detest such things.

Take another case: a person thinks something false and swears that it is true; perhaps it really is true. For example, that you may understand: it is raining in that place. You ask a man, and he replies that it has rained; and it suits his purpose to say, “It is raining,” but he thinks that it has not rained. Thus it is truly said, “It is raining,” and he truly swears; indeed it is raining there. Yet he does not know this and thinks it has not rained: he is perjured. It matters how the word proceeds from the mind. The tongue is not guilty unless the mind is guilty. [Col. 1331D–1332A]

CAP. CXII. Concerning one who swears by verbal cunning. Isidore, *Sentences*, book II, ch. 26.

(22, q. 5, c. *Qui jurat*.) By whatever artifice of words anyone may swear, God, who is witness of the conscience, nevertheless takes it in the sense in which the person to whom the oath is sworn understands it. But he is guilty in two ways: he both takes the Lord’s name in vain and ensnares his neighbour by deceit.

CAP. CXIII. Not all promises are to be fulfilled. Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*, book II, ch. 31.

(22, q. 4, c. *Non est observandum*.) An oath by which evil is heedlessly promised is not to be observed—for example, if someone promises an adulteress perpetual fidelity in remaining with her. It is more tolerable not to fulfil the oath than to continue in the disgrace of fornication. [Col. 1332B]

CAP. CXIV. What God’s swearing and God’s repentance are. From the sayings of Isidore.

God’s swearing is that providence by which he determines not to uproot what has been established. God’s repentance is a change of things. Not to repent, however, is not to revoke what has been established, as in the words: “He has sworn, and he will not repent” (Psalm 109 [110]); that is, he will not change what he has sworn.

CAP. CXV. To swear by God is to render what is due to God. Augustine, sermon *On Perjury*, First Reading, etc.

Whoever is of a wicked and perverse heart—if you say, “By God,” you swear; if you say, “God is witness,” you do not swear. For what is “By God” except “God is witness”? Or what is “God is witness” except “By God”? And what is swearing except rendering what is due to God?

Since you swear by your health, render what is due to your children when you swear by your children. But what do we owe to our health, to our children, to our God, except charity, truth, and not falsehood? Above all, when it is done by God, that is a true oath. For when someone says, “By my health,” he binds his health to God. When he swears by his children, he pledges his children to God, so that what goes forth from his own mouth may come upon their heads: if it is true, what is true; if false, what is false. Therefore, in invoking his children, his head, or his health in an oath, a person binds whatever he invokes. How much more, then, when he swears by God himself! [Col. 1332C–D]

CAP. CXVI. One who swears falsely upon a stone is perjured. Augustine, *Sermons on the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 28.

(22, q. 5, c. *Ecce dico*.) Behold, I say to your charity: even he who swears falsely upon a stone is perjured. I say this because many are deceived even in this and think that, since what they swear by is nothing, they are not bound by the crime of perjury. He is altogether perjured, because he swears falsely by that which you do not think holy. Even if you do not think it holy, the person to whom you swear thinks it holy. For when you swear, you do not swear to yourself or to the stone; you swear to your neighbour, to a human being before the stone. But are you not also before God? The stone does not hear you speaking, but God punishes you for deceiving. [Col. 1333A] Likewise: the tongue is not guilty unless the mind is guilty.

CAP. CXVII. It is permissible to rely on the pledged word of one who swears by demons in order to keep it. Augustine, Letter 154 to Publicola.

(22, q. 1, c. *Movet*.) You are troubled about whether one may rely on the pledged word of someone who has sworn by demons in order to keep it. Here I first want you to consider whether, if someone swore by false gods that he would keep faith and did not keep it, he would not seem to you to have sinned twice. For if he kept the faith promised by such an oath, he would nevertheless be judged to have sinned because he swore by such gods. Yet no one would blame the fact that he kept faith.

But because he swore by beings by whom he ought not to have sworn, and then acted against his pledged word, doing what he ought not to have done, he plainly sinned twice. Accordingly, one who relies on the pledged word of a person known to have sworn by false gods—and relies on it not for evil but for a lawful and good purpose—does not associate himself with the sin of the one who swore by demons, but with the good agreement by which he kept faith.

I do not here mean the faith by which believers, baptized into Christ, are called faithful. That faith is far different and quite distinct from the fidelity of human agreements and compacts. Yet without any doubt it is a lesser evil to swear truthfully by false gods than deceitfully by the true God. The more holy that by which an oath is sworn, the more punishable is perjury.

Another question is whether a person who makes another swear to him by false gods does not sin, because the person who swears to him swears by the false gods whom he worships. The testimonies which you yourself cited concerning Laban and Abimelech may support this question—if Abimelech swore by his own gods, as Laban swore by his gods, Sukkoth or Nahor. [Col. 1333A–C]

CAP. CXVIII. An oath by which something is promised heedlessly is to be kept. From the decretal of Pope Soter, ch. 3; Bede, on the feast of the Beheading of John the Baptist.

(22, q. 1, c. *Si aliquid*.) If we happen perhaps to have sworn something too incautiously, the observance of which would lead to a worse result, we should know that it must be altered by wiser counsel; and, if necessity presses, that we must commit perjury rather than, in avoiding perjury, turn aside into another crime.

CAP. CXIX. Of two evils, the lesser is to be chosen. Council of Toledo, ch. 2.

[Col. 1333D]

(Dist. 12, c. *Duo mala*.) Although two evils must be avoided altogether with the greatest caution, yet if necessity arising from danger compels us to commit one of them, we ought to choose that by which we are known to be bound with lesser guilt. Let us investigate, with the keenness of sound reason, which of them is lighter and which more serious. For when we are compelled to commit perjury, we indeed offend the Creator, but we stain only ourselves. When, however, we fulfil harmful promises, we both despise God’s commands and injure our neighbours by impious cruelty, and we slaughter ourselves with a more cruel sword of death. Here, indeed, we are destroyed by the twofold weapon of sins. [Col. 1334A]

CAP. CXX. Oaths are to be taken by persons who are fasting. Pope Cornelius.

(22, q. 5, c. *Qui in sanctis*.) Whoever has to swear in holy matters shall do so fasting, with every propriety and fear of God.

CAP. CXXI. When one is to swear. Council held at Saint-Médard.

(22, q. 5, c. *Decrevit*.) This holy synod decreed also that, except when making peace, all the faithful are to approach oaths fasting. [Col. 1334B]

CAP. CXXII. What must be observed in fidelity. From a letter of Bishop Philibert.

(22, q. 5, c. *De forma*.) Having been admonished to write something concerning the form of fidelity, I have noted for you briefly, on the authority of books, the following matters which recur frequently. Whoever swears fidelity to his lord ought to keep six things in mind: safety, security, honour, advantage, ease, and possibility.

Safety: namely, that he cause no injury to his lord’s person. Security: that he cause him no injury regarding his secrets or the fortifications by which he may be secure. Honour: that he cause him no injury concerning his justice or other matters that appear to belong to his honour. Advantage: that he cause no injury to his possessions. Ease or possibility: that he not make difficult for his lord a good thing which the lord could readily do, nor make impossible for him something that was possible.

That a faithful man avoid these harms is just; for it is not enough to abstain from evil unless one does what is good. It remains, therefore, that in these six matters aforesaid he give his lord counsel and aid, if he wishes to appear worthy of benefice and to remain secure in the fidelity which he has sworn. The lord likewise ought to render the same in all these things to his faithful man. If he does not, he will deservedly be judged faithless; just as one caught violating these duties, whether by acting or consenting, will be faithless and perjured. [Col. 1334B–C]

CAP. CXXIII. What companions an oath ought to have. Jerome on Jeremiah, ch. IV, book II; Ambrose, *On Duties*.

[Col. 1334D]

(22, q. 2, c. *Animadvertendum*.) It must be observed that an oath has these companions: truth, judgment, and justice. If these are lacking, it is not an oath at all, but perjury.

ON LYING.

[Col. 1333]

CAP. CXXIV. How many kinds of lying there are. Augustine, *On Lying*, ch. 14.

[Col. 1333D]

(22, q. 2, c. *Primum est capitale*.) The first and most serious lie, which must be shunned from afar, is that committed in religious teaching. No one ought under any condition to be brought to this sort of lie.

The second is a lie intended unjustly to harm someone: such a lie benefits no one and harms someone.

The third benefits one person while harming another, although it does not harm bodily purity.

The fourth is lying solely out of delight in lying and deceiving: a remarkable kind of lie.

The fifth is committed from the desire to please by agreeable speech. All these are to be completely avoided and rejected.

The sixth kind follows: it harms no one and benefits someone—for example, if a person knows where another’s money is, when it is about to be taken unjustly, and falsely says that he does not know.

The seventh harms no one and benefits someone—for example, if a person lies because he is unwilling to betray someone sought for death.

The eighth kind of lie harms no one and serves to protect someone from bodily impurity.

Therefore one must not lie in the teaching of piety, because it is a great crime and is the first kind of detestable lie. One must not lie in the second kind, because injury must be done to no one. One must not lie in the third kind, because no one is to be helped at another’s injury. One must not lie in the fourth kind because of the lust for lying, which is vicious in itself. One must not lie in the fifth kind, because, if even truth itself is not to be proclaimed from the desire to please people, how much less is a lie, which is shameful in itself simply because it is a lie.

One must not lie in the sixth kind. For the truth of testimony is not rightly corrupted for anyone’s temporal advantage or safety. Nor is anyone to be led to eternal salvation by the aid of a lie. Nor must one lie in the seventh kind, because no one’s temporal benefit or safety is to be preferred to the fulfilment of faith; nor is anyone so wrongly moved by our good actions that he thereby becomes worse in mind and farther removed from piety. Nor must one lie in the eighth kind, because among goods the chastity of the mind is preferred to bodily modesty, and among evils what we ourselves do is more blameworthy than what we permit to be done to us.

But among these eight kinds, a person sins less in lying insofar as he is farther from the first. Whoever thinks that there is some kind of lie that is not a sin will shamefully deceive himself when he supposes himself to be an honourable deceiver of others. [Col. 1334D–1335C]

CAP. CXXV. What a lie is. Gelasius, from the words of Augustine.

[Col. 1335D]

(22, q. 2, c. *Beatus*, § *Est enim*.) A lie is a false signification by speech, with the intention of deceiving. Likewise: let a person do what he can for the temporal safety of people. But when he reaches the point at which he cannot provide for such safety except by sinning, he should consider that there is nothing he can do, when he sees that no righteous course remains for him.

CAP. CXXVI. We must not provide for another’s safety by our own sin. From Isidore’s synod, *On the Dialectic of Man and Reason*.

(22, q. 2, c. *Omne genus*.) Flee every kind of lie with the utmost care. Speak no falsehood either accidentally or deliberately; do not make it your purpose to lie even in order to do a service; and do not defend anyone’s life by any deception. Beware lying in everything: no lie is just; every lie is sin. [Col. 1336A]

CAP. CXXVII. On the same matter. Ambrose, 22, q. 5.

(22, q. 2, c. *Cavendum*.) Lying must be avoided in every way, whether it seems to be uttered for evil or for good; for every lie is not from God, but, as the Saviour says, “is from evil” (Matthew 5).

CAP. CXXVIII. No one may lie under the pretext of humility. Augustine, *Sermons on the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 2.

(22, q. 2, c. *Cum humilitatis*.) For when you lie for humility’s sake, if you were not a sinner before you lied, you become one by lying—what you had previously avoided. But the truth of life does not exist unless you call yourself a sinner in such a way that you know yourself to be one. Truth itself is that you say what is. For how can truth exist where falsehood reigns? [Col. 1336B]

CAP. CXXIX. Statements made in jest of things that are not so are not counted as lies. Augustine, *Questions on Genesis*, book I.

(22, q. 2, c. *Quod ait*.) As for Joseph’s statement to his brothers, “Did you not know that no man is so skilled in divination as I?” (Genesis 44), and as for his ordering that this also be said to them by his servant concerning the divination cup, it is commonly asked what he meant. Perhaps, because it was said not seriously but in jest, as the outcome showed, it is not to be regarded as a lie. For lies are seriously enacted by liars, not in jest. When things that are not so are said as a joke, they are not counted as lies. [Col. 1336B–C]

CAP. CXXX. A perfect person ought not to lie to preserve another’s temporal life. Augustine on Psalm 5, on the verse “You will destroy,” etc.

(22, q. 2, c. *Ne quis*.) Let no one suppose that a perfect and spiritual person ought to lie for this temporal life, in whose death neither his own soul nor another’s is killed. But lying is one thing and concealing truth another; saying what is false is one thing and keeping truth silent another. If someone perhaps does not wish to betray a person even to this visible death, he ought to be prepared to conceal the truth, not to state what is false, so that he neither betrays nor lies, nor kills his own soul for another’s body.

Likewise: there are two kinds of lies in which the fault is not great, yet they are not without fault: when we joke, or when we lie to our neighbour. The first, in joking, is not harmful because it does not deceive: the person to whom it is said knows that it was said in jest. The second is less serious because it retains some goodwill.

But that which does not have a double heart ought not even to be called a lie. For example, if a sword is entrusted to someone and he promises to return it when the person who entrusted it asks for it back, but the owner later demands his sword while in a rage, clearly it should not be returned to him, lest he kill himself or others, until his sanity is restored. This does not involve a double heart, because the person to whom the sword was entrusted, when he promised to return it, did not imagine that its owner might demand it back while raging. Clearly, therefore, one is not to be blamed for sometimes concealing the truth; but permission to state what is false is nowhere found among the saints. [Col. 1336C–1337A]

CAP. CXXXI. On the same matter.

No one may speak falsehood; but it is sometimes useful to keep some truth silent.

CAP. CXXXII. To be mistaken in matters not pertaining to faith is either no sin or a slight sin. Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 21.

(22, q. 2, c. *In quibus*.) In matters in which it makes no difference for attaining the kingdom of God whether they are believed or not, and whether they are thought true or false, error—that is, taking one thing for another—must not be regarded as sin; or, if it is a sin, it is the smallest and lightest. [Col. 1337A]

CAP. CXXXIII. On the same matter. Augustine, from the same work, etc.

[Col. 1337B]

(22, q. [2], c. *Homines*, and c. *De eo qui falsum*.) Certainly no one should be judged a liar who says what is false while thinking it true. For, so far as he is concerned, he does not lie and does not deceive; rather, he is deceived. Therefore he is not to be accused of the rashness of lying because he carelessly believes false things and takes them for true. Conversely, so far as he is concerned, the person lies who says what is true while thinking it false. For, as regards his mind, because he does not say what he thinks, he does not speak the truth, even though what he says proves to be true; nor is one in any way free from lying who unknowingly speaks truth with his mouth but knowingly lies in his intention.

Likewise: in considering the matters of which people speak, it makes so great a difference in what matter one is deceived or lies that, although being deceived is less evil than lying, so far as a person’s will is concerned, it is nevertheless much more tolerable to lie in matters separated from religion than to be deceived in matters without knowledge or belief of which God cannot be worshipped.

Likewise: a person ought to say what he holds in his mind, not only when he knows what he knows to be true, but even when he himself, being human, errs and is deceived, whether the thing is true or merely thought to be true and he does not know it. But everyone who lies speaks contrary to what he thinks in his mind, with the intention of deceiving. [Col. 1337B–1338B]

CAP. CXXXIV. One lies who says what is true while thinking it false.

Some have truth on their lips but not in their heart. For example, if someone deceitfully points out a road, knowing that robbers are on it, and says, “If you go this way, you will be safe from robbers,” and it happens that there really are no robbers. He has spoken truth, but not in his heart; for he thought otherwise and unknowingly spoke truth. Thus it is not enough to speak truth unless the heart is also so disposed.

ON THE ELECTION OF THE PONTIFF.

[Col. 1337]

CAP. CXXXV. The emperor has the right to elect the pontiff. From the Eighth Synod, in *Ecclesiastical History*.

[Col. 1337C]

(Dist. 63, c. *Adrianus*.) Pope Adrian of Rome requested Charlemagne to come to defend the possessions of the Church. Charles, coming to Rome, besieged Pavia; leaving his army there, he was honourably received at Rome by Pope Adrian on the holy feast of the Resurrection. After the holy feast of the Resurrection he returned, captured Pavia and King Desiderius, then returned to Rome and convened a synod there with Pope Adrian in the Lateran patriarchate, in the church of Saint Saviour.

This synod was celebrated by 153 bishops, religious persons, and abbots. Pope Adrian and the whole synod gave Charles the right and power of electing the pontiff and appointing the Apostolic See. They also granted him the dignity of the patriarchate. Moreover, it decreed that archbishops in every province should receive investiture from him; and that no bishop should be consecrated by anyone unless he were approved and invested by the king. Whoever acted contrary to this decree, it bound by the bond of anathema; and unless he repented, it ordered his goods to be confiscated. [Col. 1337C–D]

CAP. CXXXVI. The election of the Roman pontiff belongs by right to the emperor. Pope Leo.

(Dist. 63, c. *In synod*.) Pope Leo, in a synod assembled at Rome in the church of Saint Saviour, following the example of blessed Adrian, bishop of the Apostolic See, who granted to Lord Charles, most victorious king of the Franks and Lombards, the dignity of the patriciate, the ordering of the Apostolic See, and the investiture of bishops: I likewise, Leo, bishop and servant of the servants of God, together with all the Roman clergy and people, establish and confirm, and by our apostolic authority grant and bestow upon Lord Otto I, king of the Germans, and his successors in this kingdom of Italy for ever, the power of electing a successor and appointing the pontiff of the supreme Apostolic See; and, consequently, that archbishops and bishops may receive from him investiture and consecration, as they ought—excepting those whom the emperor has granted to pontiffs and archbishops.

Henceforth, no one of whatever rank or religious profession shall have power, without the consent of that emperor, to elect either the patrician or the pontiff of the supreme Apostolic See, or to appoint any bishop. This, however, shall be done without any payment, so that he himself may be both patrician and king. If any bishop is elected by the clergy and people, he shall not be consecrated unless he is approved and invested by the aforesaid king. If anyone attempts anything contrary to this apostolic authority, we decree that he shall be subject to excommunication and, unless he repents, punished by irrevocable exile or struck with the ultimate penalties. Amen. [Col. 1338C–D]

WHICH BOOKS ARE TO BE READ IN CHURCH, AND AT WHAT TIMES.

[Col. 1339]

CAP. CXXXVII.

[Col. 1339A]

During Septuagesima, *In principio* (“In the beginning”) is sung, and the Pentateuch of Moses is read until the Passion of the Lord. Septuagesima signifies the Babylonian captivity—that is, confusion—in which we are while we are held captive in the world. When we leave it, we must return to Jerusalem, that is, to the house of peace, from which the devil captured us. Although we ought always to remember our captivity, this is especially necessary on these days, when we read and sing of the expulsion of our father Adam from Paradise; of Noah’s peril in the Flood; of Abraham, who departed from his land; and of hardships of this kind. For as Adam was made at the beginning of the world, so at the beginning of the year and of the ecclesiastical office we undertake to read and sing concerning him.

From the Passion of the Lord until Easter, Jeremiah is read, because in his manifest lamentation he prefigured the Passion of our Redeemer. From the octave of Easter, the Acts of the Apostles are read for fifteen days, and the Apocalypse is sung—that is, *Dignus est, Domine* (“Worthy are you, O Lord”)—because what had been revealed to Saint John concerning the death of the Lamb, the apostles preached.

Afterward the Catholic Epistles are read until the Ascension of the Lord, and from the Psalms is sung *Si oblitus* (“If I have forgotten”), because David prophesied the Passion of the Lord which the apostles preached. From the Ascension until Pentecost, the feast is sung, but the Apocalypse is read, because he was revealed to be the Son of God when he ascended into heaven in the sight of all; and from that day many things that had previously been closed were openly revealed.

From the octave of Pentecost until the Kalends of August, the books of Kings are read, and *Deus omnium* (“God of all”) is sung. For as Saul and David and others fought for their law against the Philistines and Goliath, so we, after Pentecost—that is, after receiving in baptism the gift of the Holy Spirit—must fight against vices and demons. Hence the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6). [Col. 1339A–C]

From the Kalends of August until the Kalends of September, Solomon is read and sung—that is, Wisdom—with the responsories *In principio*. August is the sixth month, hot and the middle of the year. In the sixth age, in which the Lord came, we ought indeed to live because of his wisdom, since Wisdom itself, which came forth from the mouth of the Most High, has been heard among us; and thus the human heart should grow warm and burn in meditation upon it. For God came to cast fire upon the earth (Luke 11 [cf. Luke 12:49]). Or because, as each person is kindled by the heat of vices, he ought then to possess wisdom more fully, where one must guard oneself more wisely in proportion as the maturity of age has greater power to resist.

In September, Job, Tobit, Esther, and Judith are read and sung. These are those who endured every adversity. So also, in the seventh age, in which the world will end, we ought to bear every adversity for the Lord more patiently.

From the Kalends of October until November, the books of the Maccabees are read and *Adaperiat* (“May he open”) is sung. This eighth month signifies the joy of the resurrection, because, just as the Jews, when their battles had ended and the Temple had been restored, blessed the Lord with hymns and thanksgivings, so too in the glory of the resurrection, when the battles of the devil have been destroyed, the saints and righteous in the Lord.

Therefore, from the Kalends of November until the Advent of the Lord, Ezekiel, Daniel, and the twelve prophets are read, with the responsories *Vidi Dominum* (“I saw the Lord”). For Ezekiel saw the four living creatures, that is, the four evangelists, who taught the world the Lord’s birth, Passion, resurrection, Ascension, and so forth. Daniel likewise foretold that the Lord would come, saying: “I was looking in a vision,” etc. (Daniel 7). Likewise the other prophets foretold that the Lord would be born; and therefore they are read before his Advent, because he is the Saviour of the world whose birth they proclaimed.

From Advent until Christmas, Isaiah is read; and the more elegantly he prophesied concerning the Lord, the nearer to his Nativity he is read. From the octave of the Lord until Septuagesima, the Epistles of Paul are read with the responsory *Domine, ne in furore* (“O Lord, do not in your wrath”), because what David prophesied, the Apostle preached in agreement. [Col. 1339C–1340B]

CHAPTER I. CAP. CXXXVIII. Concerning those who obtain office through simony or otherwise improperly. Council of Chalon.

(Dist. 1, q. 1, c. *Si quis per pecuniam*.) We decree that anyone ordained simoniacally shall fall entirely from the office which he unlawfully usurped. Likewise, if anyone has acquired by money—through the accursed burning desire of avarice—a prebend, priory, diaconate, honour, or any ecclesiastical promotion, such as chrism (that is, holy oil), the consecration of altars or churches, he shall lose the honour improperly acquired. Buyer, seller, and intermediary shall be struck by the mark of infamy. Nothing shall be demanded from anyone either before or afterwards, whether for hospitality or under the pretext of any custom; nor shall anyone presume to give anything, because this is simoniacal. Rather, each person shall freely enjoy the dignity he has received, without any diminution. [Col. 1340C]

CHAPTER II. CAP. CXXXIX. One excommunicated by his own bishop is not to be received by another. From the same council.

[Col. 1340D]

(2, q. 3, c. *Si quis*.) We altogether forbid those excommunicated by their own bishops to be received by others. Anyone who presumes to communicate with an excommunicated person before that person has been absolved by the one who excommunicated him shall be held liable to the same sentence.

CHAPTER III. CAP. CXL. Priests are not to appear outside their homes without their proper dress. Pope Innocent.

(21, q. 4, c. *Praecipimus*.) We also command that bishops and clerics alike strive to please God and people in the disposition of their minds and in their bodily attire; and that they offend not the sight of onlookers—whose pattern and example they ought to be—whether by excess, slashing, or colour of garments, or by their tonsure. Rather, they should show what befits their holiness. If, after being admonished by their bishops, they refuse to amend, let them be deprived of ecclesiastical benefices. [Col. 1341A]

CHAPTER IV. CAP. CXLI. Laypeople who dare plunder the goods of dying bishops are excommunicated. Innocent II.

(12, q. 2, c. *Illud*.) We command that what was established in the holy Council of Chalcedon be observed without exception: namely, that the property of departing bishops be plundered by no person whatsoever, but remain freely under the administration of the steward or clerics for the use of the Church and of the bishop’s successor. Let that detestable and savage rapacity therefore cease. Whoever presumes to attempt this shall be subject to excommunication. [Col. 1341B]

CHAPTER V. CAP. CXLII. A subdeacon who marries is to lose office and benefice. Innocent II.

(Dist. 28, c. *Decernimus*.) We decree that those who, being in the order of the diaconate or above, take wives or keep concubines shall lose office and ecclesiastical benefice. For since they ought to be and be called the temple of God, the vessels of the Lord, and the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, it is unworthy that they should serve beds and impurities. Following the footsteps of our predecessors Gregory VII, Urban, and Paschal, Roman pontiffs, we command that no one hear the Masses of those whom the people know to have wives or concubines. [Col. 1341C]

CAP. CXLIII. Whoever takes a wife after professing continence is to be separated from her. Innocent II.

(27, q. 1, c. *Ut autem lex*.) That the law of continence and purity pleasing to God may be extended among ecclesiastical persons and sacred orders, we decree that bishops, priests, deacons, or subdeacons, regular canons and monks, as well as converts and professed religious, who dare, in violation of their holy commitment, to unite wives to themselves, shall be separated. Since such a union is known to have been contracted contrary to ecclesiastical rule, we judge that it is not a marriage. Those separated from one another shall perform fitting penance for so great transgressions. We decree the same concerning religious women if—God forbid!—they should attempt to marry. [Col. 1341D]

CHAPTER VI. CAP. CXLIV. Regular monks and canons are forbidden to devote themselves to civil law and medicine.

[Col. 1342A]

But, as we have learned, a perverse and detestable custom has taken root: monks and regular canons, after receiving the habit and making their profession, spurn the Rule of the worthy masters Augustine and Benedict and study secular law and medicine for the sake of temporal gain. For, inflamed by the fires of avarice, they make themselves advocates in lawsuits, though they ought to devote themselves to psalmody and hymns; trusting in the protection of their eloquent speech, by the variety of their pleadings they confound right and wrong, lawful and unlawful. Indeed, the imperial constitutions attest that it is absurd—nay, shameful—for clerics to wish to be experts in forensic disputes. We decree by apostolic authority that such transgressors are to be severely punished. Likewise, neglecting the care of souls and paying no attention whatever to the purpose of their order, they promise health for detestable money and make themselves physicians of human bodies. And since the shameless eye is the messenger of the shameless heart, religion ought not to discuss those matters of which decency fears to speak. Therefore, that the monastic and canonical order pleasing to God may be inviolably preserved in its holy purpose, we forbid by apostolic authority any further presumption in this matter. Bishops, abbots, and priors who consent to and do not correct so great an enormity shall be deprived of their own honors and barred from the thresholds of the Church.

## CHAPTER CXLV. Tithes are not to be possessed by laymen. Gregory VII.

[Col. 1342C]  
(16, q. 7, c. *Decimas*.) By apostolic authority we also forbid the possession by laymen of tithes of churches which canonical authority shows to have been granted for pious use. Whether they received them from bishops, kings, or any other persons, unless they restore them to the Church, let them know that they commit the crime of sacrilege and incur the danger of eternal damnation. We command also that laymen who hold churches either restore them to bishops or be subject to excommunication.

## CHAPTER VIII. CHAPTER CXLVI. No one is to be appointed provost, archbishop, archpriest, or archdeacon unless he is a priest or deacon.

[Col. 1342D]  
(Dist. 60, c. *Innovamus*.) We renew and command that no one be appointed archdeacon or dean unless he is a deacon or priest. Archdeacons, deans, or provosts who are below the aforesaid orders, if they disdain to be ordained in obedience, shall be deprived of the office they have received. We also forbid these honors to be conferred upon young men or upon those below sacred orders, but [require that they be conferred upon] those distinguished by chastity and merit of life. We command that every priest who has the means be content with one church; and we command also that every church, if its means suffice, have its own priest.

## CHAPTER VIII. CHAPTER CXLVII. It establishes the periods of truce and the penalties for violators. The persons here enumerated also enjoy full security in time of war.

[Col. 1343A]  
(Dist. 60, ibid.; *Extra*, *De treugis*, and c. *Si quis*.)

We command also that priests, clerics, monks, pilgrims, merchants, and peasants going and returning, those engaged in agriculture, the animals with which ploughing is done and which carry seed to the field, and sheep, be secure at all times. We command that the Truce be inviolably observed by all from sunset on Wednesday until sunrise on Monday; from the Advent of the Lord until the octave of Epiphany; and from Septuagesima until the octave of Pentecost. But if anyone attempts to break the Truce, let him be subject to anathema; and let no bishop presume to absolve him, except when danger of death is imminent, until he is presented before the apostolic presence and receives its command. If any such person dies, although viaticum is not to be denied him if he asks for it and repents, he shall nevertheless lack ecclesiastical burial. If anyone attempts to break the Truce, after a third warning, if he has not made satisfaction, his bishop shall pronounce upon him the sentence of excommunication and notify the neighboring bishops of it in writing. No bishop shall admit an excommunicated person to communion; rather, each shall confirm the written sentence. Whoever presumes to violate this shall be liable to the loss of his order. And because “a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Eccles. IV), we command that bishops, having regard only for God and the salvation of the people, laying aside all timidity, give one another mutual counsel and assistance in firmly maintaining peace; nor shall they neglect this through anyone’s friendship or hatred. If anyone is found timid in this work of God, let him incur loss of his own dignity.

## CHAPTER IX. CHAPTER CXLVIII. Martial tournaments, to which men come by agreement to compete in displays of strength, are condemned.

We altogether forbid those detestable fairs at which knights customarily assemble by agreement and rashly engage one another in displays of their strength and daring, [Col. 1343D] whence deaths of men and dangers to souls frequently arise. If any of them dies there, although viaticum is not to be denied him if he asks for it and repents, he shall nevertheless lack ecclesiastical burial.

## CHAPTER X. CHAPTER CXLIX. Whoever strikes a cleric is to be excommunicated and absolved only by the Roman pontiff.

(17, q. 4, c. *Si quis suadente*.) Likewise, it has pleased us that if anyone, at the devil’s prompting, incurs this guilt of sacrilege by laying violent hands upon a cleric or monk, let him be subject to anathema; and let no bishop presume to absolve him, except when danger of death is imminent, until he is presented before the apostolic presence [Col. 1344A] and receives its command.

## CHAPTER XI. CHAPTER CL. No one is to be dragged away from a church.

(17, q. 4, c. *Definivit*.) We command also that no one whatsoever dare lay hands upon those who have taken refuge in a church or cemetery. If he does so, let him be excommunicated.

## CHAPTER XII. CHAPTER CLI. The Church of God requires wise, honorable, and religious persons for its governance.

It is beyond doubt that ecclesiastical orders are matters not of blood but of merit; and the Church of God does not await as a successor by hereditary right anyone according to the flesh, but for its governance and the administration of its offices [Col. 1344B] requires honorable, wise, and religious persons.

## CHAPTER CLII. Ecclesiastical benefices must not be claimed by hereditary right. Pope Innocent II.

(8, q. 1, c. *Apostolica*.) By apostolic authority we forbid anyone to presume to claim or demand churches, prebends, provostships, chapels, or any ecclesiastical offices by hereditary right. If any wicked person, or one guilty of ambition, presumes to attempt this, he shall be punished with the due penalty and shall lose what he seeks.

## CHAPTER XIII. CHAPTER CLIII. Both canon and civil law condemn unions of blood relatives.

[Col. 1344C]

We absolutely forbid unions of blood relatives. For such incest, since through the prompting of the enemy of the human race it has now almost become customary, is abhorred by the enactments of the holy Fathers and by the most holy Church. The laws of the secular realm likewise declare those born of such cohabitation infamous and exclude them from inheritance.

## CHAPTER XIV. CHAPTER CLIV. Whoever burns houses through favor or hatred toward anyone is to be excommunicated.

(23, q. 8, c. *Pessimam*.) By the authority of God and of the blessed Peter and Paul, we utterly condemn and forbid the most wicked and horrible evil of arson. For this plague and hostile devastation surpasses all other depredations; no one is ignorant how harmful it is to the people of God, nor how much injury it brings to souls and bodies. Therefore we must rise up and labor by every means, so that so great a calamity and destruction may be rooted out and extirpated for the salvation of the people. If anyone, therefore, after the promulgation of this our constitution, from wicked intent, hatred, or vengeance, sets fires or causes them to be set, or knowingly gives counsel and aid to those setting them, let him be excommunicated. If an arsonist dies, let him lack ecclesiastical burial, nor let him be absolved unless he first restores, according to his means, the damage which he caused, and thereafter reforms himself, etc.

Volume back matter

[Col. 1345]

# UNIVERSAL INDEX OF ALL MATTERS CONTAINED IN IVO’S *DECRETUM*

The first number indicates the part; the second, the chapter.

[Note: [Col. 1345] This index refers only to the *Decretum* of Ivo of Chartres in columns 47–1022. For each entry, the first number refers to the part; the second number refers to the *caput*.]

## A

### Abbot and abbess

An abbot ought to detest avarice, part 7, chapter 150. What sales an abbot may make, 3, 163. One abbot is by no means to be placed over two monasteries, 3, 164. An abbot ought not to give away land belonging to his monastery, 5, 375. He may appoint a reader in his monastery, 5, 376. What sort of man an abbot ought to be, and by whom he ought to be elected, 7, 24, 104. An abbot ought to be subject to the bishop, 7, 85. A bishop ought not to compel an abbot to attend a synod, 7, 91. An abbot may leave his own position, 7, 104. How an unworthy abbot is to be excluded and deposed, 7, 114. An abbess ought to take great care of her convent, 7, 112. She ought not to leave the monastery without the bishop’s permission, nor nuns without the abbess’s permission, 7, 76, 77.

### Abraham and Sarah

Why a priest is so called, 6, 25. Christ according to the flesh was in Abraham’s loins when Levi was tithed, 17, 3. The entry of Sarah, Abraham’s wife, to Pharaoh is excused, 8, 267.

### Abstinence

Abstinence from meat and wine is praiseworthy, 1, 42; 1, 206; 4, 24, 25. Hunger for meat is not to be condemned, 4, 30, 48. Concerning the penance to be imposed upon those who eat scabs, little worms, unclean meat, or carrion, or drink urine, 15, 99, 100. Concerning those who eat or drink anything touched or dipped by unclean animals, 15, 101; 2, 118. At what times abstinence from meat and blood is religiously observed, 15, 168. Gluttony, or eagerness for food, is altogether to be avoided, 4, 23, 54.

### Acolyte

The office of acolytes or acolyths, 1, 69; 2, 43; 6, 8, 20. How acolytes are to be ordained, 6, 15.

### Accuser and accused; likewise accusation and condemnation

A false accuser is to be condemned, 16, 283; 6, 240. An enemy cannot be an accuser, 5, 55, 239; nor may an infamous person, 13, 111; nor an excommunicated person, 16, 357. He who accuses prelates is infamous, 5, 253. An accused person ought not to charge his accuser with a crime before he has cleared himself of the accusation made against him, 5, 274. An accusation must by no means be made by criminals, 5, 276. Who is criminal and who infamous, 5, 286, 290. Accused bishops are to be granted a delay of six months, 5, 287, 296. The common people are not to be admitted in accusations against priests, 6, 314. How the accuser of a cleric is to be rejected, 6, 271. A written accusation is not to be received when the accused is absent, 5, 293; 6, 228. No one is to be condemned unless he has confessed and been convicted, 6, 122; 38, 88. An accused person is to be punished who refuses to prove what he alleges, 6, 276. Accusers are to be examined, 6, 315. Insults are not to be regarded as accusation, 6, 324. An accuser cannot simultaneously be witness and judge, 6, 321, 337. Where accused persons ought to answer, 6, 323. An accuser must accuse in person, 6, 326. What accusations ought to be rejected, 6, 327, 331. Which accusers are to be excluded, 6, 333; 16, 64. Under how many witnesses an accusation should be made, 6, 334. The manner and order of accusation, 6, 332, 321, 347, etc. Infamous accused persons may argue their own case, 6, 419, etc. Concerning two persons accused of adultery, 15, 173, 180. What must be avoided in an accusation of a virgin, 7, 136. An accusation of adultery is permitted only to relatives and necessary persons, 8, 15. A confession extorted by force from an accused person is by no means to be regarded as a confession, 8, 117.

### Accusation and accuser

He may condemn a sin who is not guilty of the same sin, 8, 121. How a slave is to be accused of adultery, 8, 123. A murderer or adulterer cannot accuse a bishop, 10, 36. Murderers, poisoners, and the like are not to be admitted as accusers, 10, 37. What one who accuses another of homicide ought to do, 16, 247. Concerning one who repents of having criminally accused another, 16, 251. Absentees are neither to be accused nor condemned, [Col. 1346] 16, 316. No one is to be accused of a crime of which he has been absolved, 16, 319. Concerning one who refuses to clear himself of charges brought against him, 16, 343.

### Adam and Eve

Adam and Eve were created without sin, 1, 25. Adam was cast out of Paradise, 5, 320. Through Adam’s sin the penalty of servitude was inflicted upon the human race, 16, 45. In the one sin of Adam several sins are found, 17, 5. Adam sinned through the weakness of the flesh, 17, 20, 56. In Adam’s transgression all human beings lost natural capacity and innocence, 17, 24.

### Pope Adrian

He fortified himself against the designs of the king of the Lombards, 9, 82. His pious care in adorning churches, 9, 82. In the presence of Emperor Charlemagne, he excommunicated a certain Thasmo, duke of Bavaria, 9, 89.

### Adultery

Adultery must be guarded against and abhorred, 6, 42; 8, 105. What adultery is, 8, 101, etc., 106. The enormity and gravity of adultery, 8, 99, 103. Whoever desires another’s wife commits adultery, 8, 104. How adultery is committed, 8, 107, 255. Adulterous spouses are to be repudiated, 8, 109. How a husband may lawfully kill an adulterer, 8, 111. An adulterer cannot be accused after five years, 8, 113. A wife who leaves an adulterer ought not to marry an adulterer, 8, 199. Communion is to be denied adulterers unless they repent, 8, 203. Concerning a wife who, with her husband’s knowledge, commits adultery, 8, 206, 264. How a husband ought to proceed against a suspected adulterer, 16, 159, 161. Concerning a man without a wife, if he commits adultery with another man’s wife, 8, 207. A husband ought not to destroy his violated wife if she flees to a bishop, 8, 216. Adulterers are to be excommunicated, 8, 214; 9, 19. Excommunication and abjuration of adultery, 8, 214; 9, 19. Whoever has committed adultery with his brother’s wife can never enter into the bond of marriage with her, 8, 256. Men whose wives are alive, even if adulteresses, are advised not to take other wives, 8, 258. An adulterous wife is to be put away, 8, 299.

### The Churches of Alexandria and Antioch

After Rome, they hold second place among all churches, 5, 45. The foundation of the Churches of Alexandria and Antioch, 5, 45.

### Alleluia

Laypeople ought not to sing Alleluia, 7, 105.

### Altar

Relics of saints ought to be placed in the altar, 3, 270. What ought to be offered at the altar, 2, 16, etc., 34. The altar is a figure of Christ’s body, 2, 7. How the altar is to be adorned and covered with linen cloths and hangings, 2, 132. Laypeople ought not to sit beside the altar, nor women approach it, 2, 135. An altar is to be consecrated by a bishop, 3, 20. It ought to be of stone and anointed with chrism, 3, 30. To whom belong the things brought to altars, 3, 202.

### Ambrose, Saint

He forbade Emperor Theodosius to enter church because of the slaughter of the Thessalonians, 5, 48. He defended a certain man from being dragged out of the Church, 10, 81. His short works are approved by the Church, 4, 64. You will find Saint Ambrose frequently cited in this *Decretum* of Saint Ivo.

### Anathema

See Excommunication.

### Good and evil angels

The name “angel,” 3, 250. It denotes an office, not a nature, 17, 65. The apostate angel could not be restored because he fell voluntarily, 17, 20, 36. Concerning the creation of angels, 17, 51, 65. Apostate angels had free will before their fall, 17, 55. Intellectual natures, that is, angels, are immortal, 17, 54. Human beings have guardian angels, 17, 57, 58. Whether peace exists among angels, 17, 61. Concerning the fall of angels, 17, 65, 66. Apostate angels are incorporeal, [Col. 1347] 17, 99. Apostate angels and wicked human beings will never be released from punishments, 17, 113.

### English people

The English formerly practiced shameful unions, 8, 224.

### Soul

The soul is invisible, 17, 94. The soul is infused into the formed body, 10, 5; 17, 12. The nobility of the soul, 15, 58; 17, 1. The soul’s fall must be lamented, 15, 58. The soul is incorporeal, yet may have the likeness of a body, 17, 2. The soul is not formed from human seed, 17, 12. There is one soul, not two, in one person, 17, 13. Human beings alone have a substantial soul which is immortal, 17, 14, 16. How the soul is said to be mortal and immortal, 17, 83, 92.

### Antichrist

What will he do when he comes? He will command the Sabbath to be observed, 4, 6. Everyone contrary to Christ’s word is Antichrist, 12, 19. On the coming of Antichrist, 17, 104, 106, etc. Elijah with Enoch, and all the elect, will resist him, 17, 106.

### Apostate

On the conversion and perversion, or hardening, of apostates, 15, 15; 143, 144.

### Apostles

The apostles baptized, 1, 309. Why they did not build a church in Judaea, 3, 4. Apostolic life, 3, 199. The dignity of the apostolate, 5, 24. Canons of the apostles, 4, 105.

### Appeals

The apostolic see may freely be appealed to when necessity demands, 5, 3, 257, 261, 295. When an appeal ought to be made, 5, 284; 15, 259. Letters of appeal are to be accepted, 5, 282. What appeals ought to be rejected, 5, 283. Concerning the possession of appellants and unjust appellants, 5, 284, 285. Appeal to a bishop is permitted, 15, 143. For what crimes an appeal is not to be granted, 15, 226, 315.

### Holy water

Use of holy water. Holy water is to be made every Sunday, 2, 118.

### Free will

Human beings are endowed with free will, 1, 25; 17, 22. An evil will must not be left to its own freedom, 10, 63.

### Archdeacon and archpriest

The office of archdeacon, 3, 134. An archdeacon and archpriest ought to go before the bishop when he visits his diocese, 5, 196. Whether the archpriest is subject to the archdeacon, 6, 20. An usurper of an archdeaconry is to be deposed, 6, 342.

### Arius and the Arians

Arius, sacrilegious and impious, is condemned at the Council of Nicaea, 4, 113, 116. The Council of Sardica [concerning] the Arians, 4, 8.

### Arts

Masters ought to be appointed to teach the liberal arts, 6, 214.

### Authority

### Augustine, Saint

The humility of Saint Augustine, 4, 7, 73. He avoided the company of women, 6, 77. Augustine was a learned man, 6, 77. He defended Caecilianus, 14, 62. His works are Catholic and authentic, 4, 64. The Rule of Saint Augustine, 1.

### Bannition

Concerning bannition according to the law at the mallus, part 16, chapter 268.

### Baptism

A human being ought to be baptized, 1, 27. Baptism of blood, 1, 27; likewise, 1, 177, 211. Baptism outside the Church is of no benefit, 1, 36, 37. Baptism is the sacrament of faith, 1, 30; or of the faithful, 1, 76. The effect, form, and time of baptism, 1, 45, etc., 107, etc. A person to be baptized is not to be baptized at Epiphany, 1, 47, 58; nor at the Nativity of the Lord or saints’ feasts, except at Easter and Pentecost, apart from necessity, 1, 47, 58. What must be done when it is unknown whether someone has been baptized, 2, 48, 146, 169, 236, 238. Circumcision among the ancients had the same efficacy as baptism among us, 1, 49, 50. On the minister of baptism, 1, 52, 64, etc., 150, 191. Why baptism is performed in water, 1, 64. Whether it can be performed with wine, 1, 64. Heretics’ error concerning baptism, 1, 53. A baptistery or font for baptizing is consecrated, 1, 110, etc. A baptistery is not permitted in monks’ churches, 1, 55. When danger of death presses, an unbaptized woman who has expelled or is expelling a fetus may be baptized, and so may its offspring if living, 1, 62. No payment is to be demanded for baptism, 1, 71. Adults ought to be baptized after first performing penance, 1, 76. At baptism one must renounce the devil, etc., 1, 78, etc., 189. The creed of faith is to be believed, 1, [Col. 1348] 78, 81, 88. Those to be baptized are exsufflated, and why, 1, etc., 90. Likewise they are exorcized, 1, etc., 90. Those being baptized and those baptized are signed with the cross, 1, 95, 142. Blessed salt is given to them, 1, 99; and saliva is used before baptism, 1, 104, etc. They are also anointed with chrism and holy oil, 1, 108, 140, 149, 193. Whether water is sanctified by faulty words, or by words uttered by profane or evil persons, etc., 1, 115. The baptized are clothed in a white garment, 1, 143, etc. Whether persons baptized in Christ’s name are to be baptized again, 1, 148, 261. Diversity or ignorance of languages does not impede baptism, 1, 149, 237. Baptism conferred by a heretic or another unworthy minister, or received deceptively, is valid, 1, 150, 160, 162. What must be supplied after such baptism has been conferred, 1, 150, 160, 162; likewise, 1, 165. Unbelievers are not to be compelled by force to baptism, 1, 181. Infants in the womb are not to be baptized, 1, 184. The ceremonies of baptism are explained, 1, 193, 229. Through baptism all sins are wiped away, 17, 4. See the holy effect of baptism. For more on baptism, see part I of his *Decretum*.

Basilica attendants and matricularians are to be appointed in churches by the primate, 6, 20.

What wars are just, 10, 122. The Israelites’ just wars against the Amorites, 10, 119. Those who throw down arms in battle ought to abstain from communion, 10, 122. Concerning those who commit homicide in war, 10, 152.

### Benedict, Saint

He wrote an illustrious and discerning Rule for monks, 4, 91. His sister Saint Scholastica was buried in the tomb which he had prepared for himself.

### Beneficiary and benefice

The obligation of beneficiaries, 3, 35. They ought not to exchange, sell, or appropriate to themselves the property of churches entrusted to them, 3, 161, 166, 169. A priest ought not to usurp a title or benefice, 3, 269. Priests and beneficiaries ought to show concern for those in whose gifts and goods they share, 6, 183. A beneficiary who promised during illness to become a monk may be released from his promise and recover his benefices, 4, 428.

### Berengar

His heresy against the truth of Christ’s body in the Church is anathematized, 2, 10.

### Beasts, birds, fish, etc.

What beasts or birds are wild, and what are not, 13, 95. Concerning those who eat animals torn apart by wild beasts or strangled, 15, 97. If bees kill a person, they too are to be killed, 15, 98. If pigs or hens have eaten human blood, they are to be killed, 15, 99. A fish found dead in a river is not to be eaten, 15, 104. Concerning one who kills his neighbor’s animal, 16, 213; or causes him damage, 16, 222, 288. Concerning animals causing damage, 16, 253, 254. Concerning animals entrusted to a friend for safekeeping, 16, 291. The souls of cattle are not substances; they die with the flesh, 17, 15.

### Bigamist and bigamy

Who is a bigamist or digamist, 1, 292. A bigamist ought not to be promoted to sacred orders, 6, 134, 139, 382; 8, 159, 287, 298. Those who do not keep promised virginity are to be counted among bigamists, 6, 35. A priest ought not to dine at a bigamist’s wedding, 8, 48. Bigamists ought to devote themselves to prayer and fasting, 8, 162. Bigamy is not praised, 6, 268. A bigamist before baptism cannot approach sacred orders either, 8, 291. Bigamists or husbands of widows ought not to remain in the priesthood, 8, 293. A bishop who promotes a bigamist is to be punished, 8, 301. A priest ought not to attend second marriages, 8, 48, 315.

### Blasphemer and blasphemy

On the penalty and punishment of blasphemers, 12, 32, 72. Blasphemers are to be apprehended, 16, 171.

### Good and evil; good and evil persons

Good people justly persecute evil people, but evil people unjustly persecute good people, 10, 59. Punishing evil people is not cruelty, 10, 72. Whoever punishes evil does not persecute but loves, 17, 95. What ought to be done concerning good people condemned to death, 16, 119. No one can make himself good by himself, 17, 27. Whether good people recognize the good in heaven, or evil people the evil in punishments, 17, 78. Why good people are more often afflicted in this life, 17, 109. Good is to be returned for evil, 17, 124.

Catechumens are to be baptized at Easter or Pentecost unless ill, 1, 60, 63, 197. Before baptism they ought to renounce the devil, 1, 78; and they are to be catechized, 6, 82. Which Catholics will be saved, 1, 40. Catholics who suffer tribulation for the Catholic faith are especially to be honored, 16, 34.

What is permitted or forbidden to chorepiscopi, 6, 72. Their office, 6, 72.

### Christ

Christ is one God, not *Theophoros* (Θεοφόρος), that is, “God-bearer,” 1, 3. What is to be believed concerning him, 1, 3. Christ truly [is so], 1, 3. One person in Christ, 1, 17, 26. Christ, impassible, is daily sacrificed in the sacrament, and how, 2, 4. Christ sends his image to King Abgar of the city of Edessa, 4, 83. Christ’s enemies are to be avoided, 11, 90. Service to Christ ought to be voluntary, not compelled, 11, 93. Each person ought to labor until he possesses Christ, 15, 75. For more concerning Christ, see under “Word of the Incarnation.”

### Cleric, ecclesiastic, and clergy

Etymology of “cleric,” 6, 1. Different kinds of clerics, 6, 1. The obligation and office of clerics, 6, 1. They ought to wear the tonsure, 6, 4, 46, 378; 7, 115. They ought not to grow their hair long, 6, 4, 46, 378; 7, 115; likewise, 6, 265. The dress of clerics, 6, 283. What must be done concerning incontinent clerics, 6, 50, 57, 76, 86, 193. When a cleric is to be deposed, 6, 51. A penitent ought not to become a cleric, 6, 54, 134, 136; 15, 5. Those ordained by heretics ought not to be admitted into the clergy, 6, 59; nor those who have married a widow, 6, 55. Clerics ought to abhor usury, 6, 65, 195, 369. They ought to be continent and chaste, 6, 68, 76; 16, 422. They ought not to marry without consulting the bishop, 8, 286. They ought to avoid familiarity with women, 6, 191, 3. Female servants must be excluded from the dwelling in which a cleric lives, 6, 190. Clerics ought not to entangle themselves in secular affairs, 6, 3, 218, 242, 264, 275, 393; 7, 108. Clerics are not to be solicited without their bishop’s consent, 6, 69. The illiterate, eunuchs, curiales, and those baptized with excessive difficulty are not to be admitted to the clergy, 6, 75, 37, 349, 352. Not all laypeople are to be excluded from the clergy, 6, 95. Clerics ought not to go to wars or bear arms, 6, 120, 286; 7, 28. A cleric who has killed is not to be promoted to a higher rank, 6, 120, 286; 7, 28. A buffoonish cleric is to be removed from office, 12, 79. That cleric ought not to remain in the clergy who, against the will of his own bishop, has been ordained by another bishop, 6, 141. A cleric may not be enrolled simultaneously in several churches, 6, 173, 174, 311. Clerics’ disputes are to be resolved and settled before a bishop, not before secular judges, 6, 227, 345, 360, 362, 367, 427, 150; 16, 297. A cleric ought not to swear an oath to a layperson, 6, 233. Clerics cannot accuse another except in writing, 6, 241. They ought not to lodge complaints before princes, 6, 268. They ought to know the canons, 6, 250. How they are to be restrained and punished, 6, 274, 275, 301, 303, 308, 366, 421. A cleric excommunicated by his own bishop is by no means to be received by another, 6, 357. Clerics may not transfer to another city or desert their churches except in time of persecution, 6, 361; 14, 126. In cases before ecclesiastical judges, a cleric may likewise appeal to other ecclesiastics, 6, 363. Clerics receiving stipends from the church ought to spend them profitably, 6, 372. They ought not to wander about, 7, 74, 75. One who has contracted a second marriage cannot become a cleric, 8, 159. What must be done concerning clerics’ wives if they sin, 8, 283. On the penance of adulterous clerics, 8, 295. Clerics ought not to be enchanters or sorcerers, 11, 3.
