They ought to work continuously, 7, 5. Monasteries of monks are to be visited by bishops, 7, 14, 84. Monks are not permitted to return to the world, 7, 30. They ought to detest avarice and robbery, 7, 150. They ought not to impose penances upon laypeople, 15, 152. They ought not to lease possessions or involve themselves in secular business, 6, 218; 7, 23, 107. Monks and nuns ought not to have godfathers or godmothers, or receive children from baptism, 1, 132; 7, 100; nor enter into marriage, 7, 15, 49, 122. Otherwise they are to be severely punished, 7, 15, 49, 122. Monks ought not to kiss women, 1, 33, 53. A monk may become a presbyter, 7, 22; indeed, also a bishop, 5, 343. When a monk may be enrolled in clerical offices, 6, 53. Children ought not to become monks against their will, 6, 356. A bishop who has become a monk may not thereafter return to the episcopate, 7, 149.

Monastery.

Monasteries ought not to be dwellings for clerics or secular persons, 3, 17, 22. Exchange of monasteries, 3, 28; and transfer, 31. Monasteries are to be built with the bishop’s permission, 3, 157, 165; 7, 92. Nunneries ought to be far from monasteries of monks, 3, 158. Monasteries ought not to be harassed or burdened, 3, 183; 7, 14, 106. One who enters a monastery cannot thereafter dispose of his property, 6, 426; but may do so beforehand, 7, 58. One ought to take pride in the religious habit, 8, 321. The property of an apostate monk belongs to the monastery, 7, 155.

Coinage.

The hand of one who has struck counterfeit coin is to be cut off, 16, 278.

Nun or consecrated virgin. See also *Sacred Veil*.

At what time virgins are to be veiled, 7, 36. Bishops ought to keep especially vigilant watch over nuns, 7, 93. How nuns ought to live, 95. They ought not to eat with secular persons, 7, 113. One ought not approach nuns without cause, 6, 390; 6, 96. They must be spoken with very cautiously, 7, 71. They ought not handle consecrated things, 2, 72. How the incontinence of nuns is to be restrained, 7, 16, 123, 125. How a nun who has fallen ought to undergo penance, 7, 133, 135. They may not contract marriage, 7, 51, 57. What the portress of nuns ought to be, 7, 97.

Single combat.

On single combat or individual contest, 8, 187.

Death and the dead. See also *Burial* and *Cemetery*.

If the first human being had remained obedient, he would have passed to heaven without death, 17, 25. How many kinds of offerings for the dead must be performed, 17, 81. Masses are to be celebrated for the dead, 3, 66. Offerings of the dead are not to be withheld, 3, 155, 218. On the care to be given for the dead, 4, 217. What is to be done during the funeral vigil, 11, 59. The practice of burial for the dead, 3, 213, 274, 278. What benefit ecclesiastical burial provides, 3, 214. One ought not give the kiss to the dead, 3, 277. On cemeteries, and how much space they ought to have, 3, 104. In how many ways the souls of the dead ought to be released, 15, 124. Nothing is to be undertaken against the will of the deceased, 16, 233. One ought not grieve over the death of loved ones, 15, 139. Why the elect sometimes die harshly, 17, 88. For the wretched, death becomes a state without death, 17, 89.

Moses.

[Col. 1369]

The miracles of Moses, 2, 72. He appointed presbyters, 6, 25. Commended for holiness, 6, 50.

Woman. See *Female*. Murmuring. See *Defamation*. Music.

Priests ought to keep apart from certain kinds of musicians, 5, 339.

Mute person.

How one is to be baptized, 1, 230, 232. On a mute penitent, 15, 8, 34.

## N

Necessity.

Necessity has no law, 2, 76; 3, 141. When necessity ceases, that which necessity discovered as a remedy also ceases, 6, 350. In necessity it is lawful for suspended presbyters and deacons to baptize, 6, 368.

Grandson and granddaughter.

No one ought to marry his own granddaughter, 9, 58. In reckoning consanguinity, grandson and granddaughter are counted in the first degree, 15, 177. How grandsons and granddaughters are to divide inheritances among themselves, 16, 123.

Council of Nicaea.

Three hundred and eighteen Fathers attended it, 16, 433. The acts of the Nicene council were sent to St. Sylvester, pope, 4, 209. The dignity and authority of the Council of Nicaea, 4, 72; 3, 128. How many chapters or articles the Council of Nicaea contains, 4, 232, 108.

Innovations.

The Church never approves innovations, 4, 196.

Marriage.

Instituted and blessed by God, 1, 42. Continence is preferable to marriage, 1, 42. Divine mysteries ought to be absent from weddings, 2, 143. Between what persons lawful weddings may be made, 9, 1. A woman entering a second marriage cannot reclaim property that she gave to her children; moreover, she loses the privileges of her first husband, 1, 126, 127. Whatever fault married persons commit is not the fault of marriage or wedding, 8, 234. Those who ought to avoid marriage, 6, 206; 8, 50—namely, clerics, 6, 206; 8, 50. Marriage is not to be abhorred, 7, 79, 82. The threefold good of marriage: offspring, fidelity, and sacrament, 8, 15. Marriage is a sacrament of Christ and the Church, 8, 74. The reward of marriage is women’s childbearing, 8, 76. Wherein the reality of marriage consists, 77. At what time weddings are to be celebrated, 8, 142. Those marrying are to be blessed by a priest, 8, 143, 146. One who has married more than once ought to do penance, 8, 158, 339. Second marriages are permitted to laypeople, 8, 159, 269. A mother nursing her children ought not to enter another marriage, 8, 271.

## O

Obedience and disobedience.

Not to obey is a great sin, 5, 36. Just obedience is rewarded with just recompense, 15, 69.

Offering.

Offerings are to be made in the Church by Christians, 2, 34, 41. The offerings of estranged brethren, and of those who oppress the poor, are to be rejected, 2, 47, 48. What offerings benefit, 2, 113. To seize the offerings of the faithful is a great crime, 3, 140. Things offered to God are consecrated, 3, 195. Whatever is offered to God is the Holy of Holies, 14, 87, and belongs by right to priests, 16, 362. Menstruating women, whether nuns or laywomen, ought not to make offerings, 15, 150. Those who take away the offerings of the faithful are sacrilegious, 16, 295, 362.

October.

It is called Hyperberethaeus, 5, 154. A synod is to be assembled in October, 5, 154. On Sundays in October the books of Maccabees are read, 4, 63.

Divine Office. See *Prayer*. Good works.

Works are of no benefit without faith, 11, 89. God is pleased not so much by one’s profession of life or appearance of habit as by sincerity, the disposition of the mind, and uprightness of deeds, 11, 82.

Prayer.

For whom prayers are to be offered, 2, 120. How one ought to pray, 6, 167. Prayer joined with almsgiving is very beneficial, 166. The Lord’s Prayer is to be recited, 6, 158, 159. The usefulness of prayer, [Col. 1370] 6, 177. The Divine Office is to be recited by clerics and priests, 6, 181, 243. At what hour, 6, 177.

Oratories.

In private oratories neither Masses are to be celebrated nor clerics appointed, 3, 76. Nor are relics of saints to be placed there, 78. Oratories are to be built with the bishop’s permission, 3, 192. In oratories and churches nothing is to be done except prayer, 3, 275.

Sacrament of order, or sacred ordinations.

How and where ordinations ought to be celebrated, 6, 23, 24; and at what time, 6, 70, 74, 91; but not in the presence of catechumens, 6, 27. Sacred orders are to be conferred by one’s own bishops, 6, 42, 142, 412. No one is to be ordained without a title, 7, 26. Orders conferred by excommunicated persons, or by those who call themselves bishops, are invalid, 14, 54; 5, 220. Those who are not to be ordained, 6, 35, 379; 8, 302, 303. A man who has married a widow cannot be promoted to sacred orders, 6, 55. Whether managers, procurators, and even executors for wards ought to be ordained, 6, 137. It is not lawful for persons already ordained to be reordained, 1, 152; 6, 88. When it becomes lawful, 6, 117. In ordinations crimes are not removed, 6, 60. One who ordains or is ordained contrary to the canons is to be deposed, 62. A penitent ought not to be ordained, 6, 106. One whose finger has been amputated by enemies may lawfully be ordained, 6, 118. Sacred orders are neither to be sold nor bought, 2, 84; 5, 85, 91, 95, 109, 122, 208. Those who desire promotion to sacred orders are to be examined, 3, 143; 6, 21, 33. Those who ordain unworthy persons ought to lose the right of consecrating, 1, 507. The sale of orders is an inexpiable offense, 5, 132. Unlawful ordinations are not to be presumed, 5, 212. Those who have received only the laying on of hands from a bishop and the remainder of ordination from a presbyter are to be deposed, 5, 213.

Origen.

How he is to be read, 4, 142. His absurdities concerning the restoration of demons and the impious are refuted by Augustine, 17, 113. Some of his minor works are to be accepted; the rest are to be rejected together with their author, 4, 64. The book called *The Penance of Origen* is apocryphal, 4, 65. Pope Gelasius called Origen a schismatic, 4, 64.

Original sin. See *Original Sin*. Orphan and ward.

An orphanage (*orphanotrophium*), that is, a venerable place in which orphaned children, deprived of parents, are fed, 17, 137. The cases of wards are to be heard and decided first, 6, 274.

Hosea the prophet.

He is not to be blamed for having taken a prostitute as wife, 8, 38.

Doorkeeper.

His office, 6, 5. How a doorkeeper is ordained, 6, 18, 20.

Otto.

The constitution of Emperor Otto with the Roman pontiff, 5, 52.

## P

Pagans or gentiles and idolaters; also false gods.

Neither gentiles nor Jews are to be mourned, 11, 110. Pagans are to be baptized in illness if they request it, 1, 224. Yet they are not to be compelled by force to baptism, 1, 181. There is no salvation for them outside the Church, 1, 38, 39. They are to be brought back not by force but by reason, 11, 85. Idolatry is altogether to be detested, as are pagan rites, 11, 31, 45. Their vain observances and ceremonies are to be rejected, 11, 40. On things sacrificed to idols, 11, 91. One must not eat meat from an animal which a pagan has either killed or pursued, 11, 87. Exaction is to be made from a rustic pagan, 11, 94. On zeal against idolaters and diviners, 95. It is a lesser evil to swear truthfully by false gods than to swear falsely by the true God, 12, 35. One baptized by pagans is to be rebaptized, 11, 91.

Altar cloths. See *Corporals*. Blessed bread.

Blessed bread, or *eulogiae*, for the people, 2, 37. Prayer for blessing bread, 2, 37. Blessed bread is also called the “crown of the offering,” 17, 68. What kind of bread is fitting to offer at Mass, 2, 38.

Pope or supreme pontiff.

The pope is called apostolic, 15, 184. Pontiffs are called thrones of God, 16, 296. Authority of the supreme pontiff, 5, 13, 15, 44, 47, 378. His election ought to be canonical, 5, 14. In the election of a pope, the emperor’s legates need not be awaited, 5, 16. The judgment of the supreme pontiff is not to be reconsidered by anyone, 5, 19. The supreme pontiff once wished his own case to be examined in the presence of the emperor’s legates, 5, 22. The pope is not to be reproved or judged, 5, 8, 23. No one ought to separate himself from his communion, 25, 361. Judgments of bishops are to be strengthened by his authority, 5, 29. Decrees of Roman pontiffs are to be observed without omission, 5, 34, 40. Constitutions made contrary to papal decrees are invalid, 5, 37. The pope is Peter’s successor, 5, 16. A simoniacal pope is to be excommunicated, [Col. 1371] 5, 80. In pronouncing sentence, the supreme pontiff accommodates himself to the circumstances of persons, 14, 43. The bishop of the first see is to be called pope, 5, 57. On one who has extorted a false letter from him, 5, 50. How the supreme pontiff is to clear himself of concealed accusations, 5, 313, 342. While a pope lives, no one is to be elected, 5, 336. The supreme pontiff professes his faith, 5, 358. The remarkable goodwill and affection of supreme pontiffs toward the kings of France, 5, 358, 378. The pope’s name is to be recited in churches, 6, 305. Final judgments concerning clergy are to be referred to the pope, 6, 316.

Paphnutius.

St. Paphnutius prays for a certain sluggish monk tormented by an unclean spirit, 9, 99.

Parish and parish priest.

Parishes are to be governed according to the Roman Church, 3, 47. A parish is not to be divided among several presbyters or parish priests, 3, 48. On the condition of parishes, 3, 97. Parishioners ought to attend the sacred service in the parish church on Sundays, 2, 122. A bishop may convert a parish into a monastery, 3, 168, 170. A parish remains with the bishop who has governed it for thirty years, 3, 106.

Parricide.

On parricide and fratricide, 10, 163, 177, 184. Penance is to be imposed upon one who kills in avenging his parents, 10, 161; likewise upon those who kill their children or wives, 10, 165. On a wife who has killed her husband, 10, 168. On the penance of a matricide, 10, 173.

Little children. See *Infants*. Easter.

How it is to be celebrated, 2, 111; 3, 2, 114. On what day Christians are to observe Easter, 4, 3, 119. Sacred orders are to be conferred at the Easter of the Resurrection, 6, 70. On Thursday before Easter, penitents are to receive absolution, 15, 40. On the reading performed in churches on Easter Day and within its octave, 4, 63.

Baptized at Easter. See *Baptism*. Passion of the Lord.

It is commemorated in the Mass, 2, 15.

Paten. See *Sacred Vessels*. Father and mother. Godfather or sponsor.

Godfather and godmother (*matrinus*, also *matrina*) in baptism are so called because they are sponsors or bearers, 1, 118. Their faith benefits little children, 1, 118. If the person to be baptized can answer, the godfather should be absent, 1, 124. The duty and office of sponsors, 1, 134. Sponsors ought to be confirmed, believers, and so forth, 1, 220. On a father and mother who have sponsored their own children, 1, 305, 306. On those who receive their own infants from baptism, so that they are separated from their wives, 9, 80. One godfather or godmother suffices to sponsor an infant, 1, 218. An abbot or monk cannot be a sponsor, 1, 132. Spiritual kinship arises from baptism between spiritual fathers and children, 1, 135; consequently they cannot contract marriage with one another, 1, 135. On whether a wife who has lifted from the sacred font her husband’s son begotten by another woman may afterward lawfully unite with him, 1, 136. One man cannot have two spiritual co-mothers, 1, 137. Fornicators joined by spiritual affinity are anathematized, 1, 138.

The poor and poverty. See also *The Vice of Property*.

The cases of poor widows and wards are to be heard and decided first, 16, 274. Alms are distributed to the poor not only when some consolation is given to them, but also when pardon is granted to a sinner or correction given to one in error, 17, 123. Immovable property of a poorhouse (*ptochotrophium*: a place in which the poor are fed) may be alienated, 17, 137. A certain monk of St. Gregory named Justus, corrupted by the vice of private property, is not buried in a sacred place, 17, 67.

Peace.

Peace is to be maintained, 16, 235.

Mortal and venial sin.

What sins condemn a person, 6, 161. It is one thing to sin against God and another to sin against a human being, 14, 85. Light sins are forgiven by the Lord’s Prayer, 17, 122. No one should suppose that sins are redeemed by alms unless he also reforms his life, 17, 121. Sins are not forgiven unless one forgives from the heart one who sins against oneself, 17, 128. Some sins are grave that are regarded as light, 17, 132. What kind of sin is called a “cry” in Holy Scripture, 133. Sin arises from two causes, ignorance and weakness, 17, 134. A person sometimes sins through an impulse of mind and sometimes through the frailty of the flesh, 15, 52. As often as a sinner falls, so often must he rise again, 15, 66. No saint or righteous person is without sin, 15, 82, 138. The longer one remains in sins, the more one’s penance must be increased, 15, 130. One who has committed a grave sin is to be separated from Christ’s body, 15, 23. The sin of one who denies that all sins can be forgiven in the Church is unforgivable, [Col. 1372] 17, 136. Sins are not remitted without fitting penance, 15, 74. Those aware of others’ sins commit an offense if they do not disclose the sins, 16, 360. God overlooks sins, 17, 37. Why he punishes all things without end, 17, 74.

Original sin.

Every human being is born with it, 1, 25, 228, 246. The remedy for original sin, 1, 25. It cannot be remitted except through Christ, 17, 8.

Pilgrimages and pilgrims.

Those undertaking pilgrimages to holy places ought not to be harassed by anyone, 4, 60; 15, 287. On those who travel under the pretext of religion, 15, 65. On *Romipetae*, that is, those who seek Rome, 15, 182, 184. On Roman and Tours pilgrimages, 15, 65. Pilgrims and fugitives are to be constrained, 16, 303. On the administration of a *xenodochium*, a place in which pilgrims are received, 15, 149. Immovable property of a *xenodochium* may be alienated, 17, 137.

Exchange and commutation.

Grants by precarious tenure or exchanges made by a vacant church are invalid, 3, 227. Exchanges of ecclesiastical property, 3, 231. How the transfer of bishops may lawfully take place, 5, 183. On the commutation and redemption of penances, 15, 192. Exchange has the same validity as purchase, 16, 314.

Persecutions.

One who unjustly persecutes a Christian is an enemy of Christ, 10, 61.

Peter, apostle (St.).

His preeminence and prerogative, 5, 269. The *Itinerary of Peter*, and likewise his *Acts*, are apocryphal, 4, 65. On the death of blessed Peter, 4, 140.

Plague. See *Scourges of God*. Penance and penitents.

What penance is, 15, 1. There is no salvation for sinners without penance, 1, 30, 31. Penance is to be imposed according to the nature of the sin, 14, 73; 5, 3. The penance imposed on those who do not communicate fasting, 2, 25; on those who vomit the Eucharist through drunkenness, 2, 35; on those who vomit the sacrifice which is afterward consumed by dogs, or who do not guard the sacrament well, 2, 57. Prayers are to be offered for penitents, 6, 165. Public penitents are not to be admitted into the clergy, 6, 386. Why a penance of seven years is imposed, 6, 398; 8, 284; 1, 245, 293. A penance of five years is imposed on married persons who have fallen, 8, 281. A penance of fourteen years for one who has defiled his paternal uncle’s daughter, 9, 10; but ten years for one who consents to incest, 9, 24. The penance of incestuous parricides, 9, 70. Penance ought not to be imposed too harshly, 9, 122. On the absolution of penitents, 15, 2, 38. On the rule for penitents, 15, 6, 12, 19. Penitents in illness ought to receive the viaticum, 15, 9. A presbyter ought not reconcile a penitent without consulting his bishop, except in urgent necessity, 15, 4, 84, 186. On negligent penitents, 15, 7. Penance is to be given to married persons only with their consent, 15, 14. The penance of elders is not lightly to be imposed on younger persons, 17. On the penances of ecclesiastics, 15, 20. On the uncertainty of the salvation of one who has received penance in extreme necessity, 22. Penitents ought to be treated with accommodation, 24. What true conversion is, 15, 26. On those who desire penance in necessity, 29. The efficacy and effect of penance, 15, 32, 48. On a penitent who dies during the penance itself, 15, 39. Penance is not to be denied to the dying, 15, 43, 44. On Ash Wednesday public penitents must present themselves to the bishop before the doors of the church, barefoot and clothed in haircloth, 45. Penance is not to be performed negligently, 50. Fasts are to be imposed upon penitents, 51, 185, 191. A measured meal is to be allowed those doing penance publicly or secretly, 15, 54. Priests ought willingly to receive those who repent from the heart, 55.

Communion is to be given to penitents after their penance has been completed, 15, 56, 77. On those who, after completing penance, return to their former sins, 15, 71. In imposing penance, there must be no respect of persons, 15, 73. After penance no one may return to secular military service, 80. Penitents are to abstain from banquets, ornaments, and even certain lawful things, 15, 79, 83. No bishop or presbyter ought to receive another’s penitent without letters from that person’s own bishop, 15, 76. The unrepentant person is to be regarded as a gentile or a publican, 78. It is difficult for one who sins while holding an office to remain in that office, 15, 91. After seven years of penance, a priest may return to his former status, 95. It is not fitting for a penitent to conduct any business, 15, 107. Priests ought not reject the faults of penitents or bring them to reconciliation in an unworthy manner, 112. On the penance of sorcerers, 15, 116. On feigned penance, 15, 156. On penance to be imposed upon a mother who has been negligent concerning her child, 15, 159; or who has killed that child, 15, 163. The *carena* [penitential term; meaning uncertain] is not to be divided for a penitent; while fasting, the penitent is not to move his *carena* from place to place, [Col. 1373] 15, 183, 185. On the duration and varieties of penances, 187. On the condemnation of one who killed a public penitent, 16, 276. Without God’s mercy, a person will perform penance fruitlessly, 17, 135.

Pollution. See *Nocturnal Emission*. Weight and measure.

No one ought to give unjust weights or measures, 13, 158.

Possession and possessor.

Three years’ possession excludes objections. A possession of forty years is not to be reclaimed, 3, 148. How possession is valid, 3, 179. Possession of another diocese for fifty years is secure, 5, 175. The possessory oath, 6, 205. On things acquired by children and slaves, 16, 107. Whoever has possessed a thing delivered by a donor shall possess that which has been delivered to him, 16, 194. On avoiding possession and occupation of others’ property, 16, 331. On a possessor expelled by force, 16, 310. Proof is required not from the possessor but from the claimant’s party, 16, 203.

Power. See *Judge*. See also *King*. Predestination.

Predestination is the preparation of a gratuitous gift, 1, 35. How predestination is ordered, 17, 31.

Preaching. See *Word of God*. Robber. See *Thief*. Prelate. See *Bishop*. Pragmatic sanction.

By a pragmatic sanction nothing is to be taken from churches, 3, 188.

Presbyter. See *Priest*. Primate or patriarch.

Who the primates are, 5, 54, 273. The right of the primate, 5, 56. On the ordination of primates or patriarchs, 5, 53, 288. In what order they are to be approached, 5, 242. Judges of bishops, 245, 258, 267. Bishops ought not answer a primate in court unless the things taken from them are restored, 5, 246, 248, 255. Primates are to be acknowledged by bishops, 5, 269. Primates and metropolitans are called by the Roman Church to share in, not to possess the fullness of, its power, 5, 349. The authority to consecrate belongs to the primate, 348. When appeal is to be made to primates, 6, 330. Bishops’ cases are to be heard before primates, 16, 309.

Prince. See *King*. Psalmist. See *Cantor*. Battle. See *War*. Purgatory.

The souls assigned to purgatory are relieved through the sacrifice of the Mass, 17, 67, 68. A notable example on this subject in St. Gregory, concerning one of his monks, who was freed from the punishments of purgatory after a trental of Masses had been completed for him, 17, 67, 68. Whether purgatory exists, 17, 79.

## Q

Lenten season.

Whence it derives its authority, Part 4, ch. 2. How Lent is to be observed, 2, 111; 4, 1, 45, 46. Fasting is required during it, 4, 29, 34, 41. One must also abstain from meat, 15, 89. Likewise, during Lent one must fast from fleshly pleasures, 4, 47; 15, 88, 163. During Lent one must abstain from warfare, 10, 93. Wives are likewise not to be taken and marriages are not to be celebrated then, 8, 47, 49, 142. The feasts of holy martyrs are not to be celebrated throughout the whole of Lent, 4, 43. Communion is to be received on every Sunday of Lent, 2, 29.

**The fifty-day period before Easter.**

From Quinquagesima until Easter one must fast, 4, 29, 25.

## R

**Robbery.**

What distinction there is between robbery and theft, 13, 3. On compensation for robbery and theft, 16, 272. On those who commit theft and robbery, 14, 125; 16, 327. On others in whose possession a share of the plunder has been found, 15, 225, 299.

**Abductor and abducted person.**

How abductors of nuns are to be punished, 7, 70, 143. Virgins forcibly abducted and violated do not lose their virginity, 7, 87. No one ought to presume to abduct a woman against her parents’ wishes, 8, 23. Abduction is regarded as sexual violation, 8, 24, 26. What abduction is, 8, 24, 26. Abductors are to be excommunicated, 8, 25, 133, 332; 14, 64. The abducted woman must be restored, 8, 26. The abducted woman is commanded to become a wife, 8, 28. On girls abducted before betrothal, 8, 174. An abducted betrothed woman is to be excommunicated if she refuses to return to her fiancé, 14, 64. On the abduction of widows, 16, 275.

**Rebaptizing.**

One must not rebaptize, Part 1, chs. 137, 152, 160, 162, 172, 233, 234. Those who have been rebaptized are not to be ordained, 1, 245. One must by no means communicate with them, 1, 249.

**Reconciliation**

[Col. 1374]

The manner of reconciliation, 6, 407. Reconciliation of married persons, 8, 217. It is not harsh to be reconciled after adultery, 8, 242. Penitents are not to be reconciled until their penance has been completed, 15, 153.

**Kings, princes, and authorities.**

They ought to be subject to divine laws, 4, 190; 16, 11. They must not oppress the poor; otherwise they incur excommunication, 16, 4. The derivation of the name “kings,” 16, 39. On the office and virtues of a king, 40. On the sins of princes, 42. Christian kings and princes are subject to pontiffs in eternal matters, just as pontiffs are subject to princes in temporal matters, 4, 188. Kings may undertake nothing contrary to divine laws, 4, 231; 5, 235; 16, 9. They are not to be obeyed if they command anything against God, 5, 7, 16, 23, 24, 28. No secular dignity—not even royal or imperial dignity—is comparable to episcopal eminence, 5, 378. Those whom the king receives into favor must likewise be admitted to communion by others, 16, 344. The princes of the land ought not to judge bishops or ecclesiastics, 5, 378. They may contract exchanges with the Church, 3, 184. They ought not to entrust their own business affairs to priests, 6, 222. A cleric who causes trouble in the ears of a prince is to be excluded from communion and rank, 6, 225. A king must punish evils, 10, 96; and defend the Church, 10, 99. The authority of a king and judge has not been instituted in vain, 10, 108. A king serves God differently as a man and differently as king, 121. While a king is alive another is not to be elected, 16, 26. On the offspring of kings, 29. An exhortation to princes to discharge their office properly, 16, 16, 18, 20. On good royal advisers, 16, 22. No one ought to aim at the destruction of princes, 27.

**The kingdom of heaven.** See *Eternal life*.

**Holy relics.**

On their veneration, 3, 54, 57, 78. The relics of saints honor the places where they are kept, 3, 81. The bodies of saints are not to be translated, 3, 273.

**Rhaeticius, Saint, of Autun.**

Also called bishop of Edua; he wrote a commentary on the Song of Songs, greatly commended by St. Jerome, 4, 103.

**Remission of sins.**

It is supremely necessary for everyone, 1, 40. On redemption and remission of penances, 15, 192, 193.

**Repudiation.**

A lawful wife is by no means to be repudiated, 8, 35. Once repudiation has intervened, one must not enter into marriage with another, 8, 209. When a wife may send repudiation to her husband, 16, 160.

**Commonwealth.**

Who is absent on account of the commonwealth, 16, 169.

**Restitution.**

Those who seize the property of others must make restitution, 3, 149; 13, 1. Church property plundered, unlawfully bought, or retained must be restored, 3, 182, 185, 206; 13, 37. Things taken from a bishop must be returned to him, 5, 246. A sin is not erased unless what has been taken is restored, 13, 4; 15, 25. A church taken from a presbyter through no fault of his own must be restored, 6, 429.

**Resurrection.**

The good and the evil will rise again, 1, 29. The dead will rise, 17, 9. Even an infant will rise, although dead before being born, 17, 11. The resurrection will occur at the perfect age, 17, 114.

**Quarrels.** See *Dissensions*.

**Robert, king of the Franks.**

On the advice of bishops, he left his wife who was related to him by affinity, 9, 8.

**Rogation Days and Litanies.**

Rogation Days, or Litanies, are to be observed before the feast of the Lord’s Ascension, with fasting and abstention from servile labor, 4, 11, 14, 40. Institution of the Rogation Days, 4, 40. The Greater Litanies are to be celebrated according to the custom of the Holy Roman Church on the twenty-fifth of April, 4, 39. The practice of the Litanies with fasting, 14, 116.

**Roman Church.** See *Roman Church*.

## S

**Saturday.**

Work is to be done on Saturday, Part 4, ch. 6. One must also fast, 4, 28. The fast of Holy Saturday is to be continued until night, 4, 42.

**Priest.**

The office and ministry of priests, 1, 67, 353; 2, 69, 120; 3, 129; 6, 11, 45, 151, 310, 389. Priests ought to preside over judicial proceedings, 4, 245. They are to catechize, preach, and teach the people, 1, 87; 6, 154, 247, 279, 307; and baptize, 1, 90. But they may not ordain or consecrate churches, 6, 102, 103. Those who lay on hands cast out demons, 1, 103. The dignity of priests, 2, 100; 5, 5, 18, 345; 6, 45. Before God, what is sought is not priests’ judgment but their manner of life, 2, 109. They ought especially to excel in purity, chastity, and sobriety, [Col. 1375] 1, 110; 5, 48, 345; 6, 68, 94, 98, 332; and also in learning, 5, 202; 6, 22, 245. Priests and other ministers of the Church who are vicious, incontinent, criminal, possessed by demons, and so forth, handle the sacred mysteries, 1, 150; 2, 90, 125; 6, 87. The vices of priests do not remain unpunished before God, 2, 116. Priests must demand nothing for administering the sacraments, 1, 71, 92; 5, 126. A presbyter who was baptized during illness is not ordained, 1, 227; 6, 101. On an unbaptized presbyter, 1, 268. Married presbyters are not to be rejected by the people, 2, 82, 128; 3, 258. Defiled priests do not defile the divine mysteries, 2, 83, 93, 98. The Church is the heir of priests, 3, 94; 6, 281, 282. The gravity and wisdom of priests, 6, 245, 161, 25. When a priest is to be deposed, 3, 86, 103; 6, 96, 185, 193, 234. What order is to be maintained among priests, 5, 17; 6, 299; 3, 55. The order of priests is twofold, 5, 58, 44. Priests hold the place of the seventy-two disciples, 5, 58, 44. They are bound to assemble for a bishop’s funeral, 5, 330. On the ordination of priests, 6, 12, 28, 47. At what age it is to be performed, 6, 29. How deacons and presbyters who have fallen into crime are to be reconciled, 6, 67. A deposed priest must no longer offer sacrifice, 6, 83, 224. A wounded priest does not lose his rank in the priesthood, 6, 107. The Holy Spirit does not come at the invocation of a criminal priest, 110. A layman cannot be ordained a priest, 111. A priest who is a homicide cannot minister, 6, 114; 10, 29, 35, 51. Priests ought not to abandon their churches and wander about, 6, 170, 172, 176, 270. They ought to devote themselves to prayer, 6, 177. Their dress, 178, 283; 10, 139. They ought to establish their dwelling near the church, 6, 184. How a priest should be corrected and ought to clear himself, 6, 225, 229, 231, 239, 309, 419. What must be done with a priest who admits that he fathered children before or after receiving sacred orders, 6, 149, 400. It is fitting that each presbyter have one cleric, 6, 151. Each year they are bound to render their bishop an account of their ministry, 6, 246, and to make a profession when they are appointed through parish priests, 248. How priests ought to clear themselves by oath, 12, 40, 77. They may proclaim death against the impious, 10, 74. Whoever does not honor priests is to be punished, 6, 304. A priest ought not to fight, 10, 34, nor shed blood, 10, 45. To be raised to the presbyterate, a man must either be married only once or be a virgin, 8, 300.

**Sacraments.**

They are always to be venerated, even when administered by the unworthy, 2, 93. The effect of the sacraments, 2, 97. The wounded or infirm must not handle sacred things; likewise those tormented by demons, 6, 40.

**Sacrifice.**

What the Church’s sacrifice is and of what it consists, 9, 2. The power of the Church’s sacrifice, 2, 11, 97. Sacrifice should, if possible, be performed by a holy priest, 2, 107.

**Sacrilege and the sacrilegious person.**

Who are sacrilegious persons, 3, 140. A violator of a sacred place is sacrilegious and, as such, must be punished and excommunicated, 13, 38; 14, 88, 92, 89; 16, 295, 297. The same judgment is to be made concerning plunderers of churches, 13, 38; 14, 88, 92, 89; 16, 295, 297. A violator of an oath is sacrilegious, 12, 78; likewise a violator of a consecrated woman, 7, 69, 57, 134. One who demolishes tombs is also deemed sacrilegious, 13, 49. A cleric or monk who commits theft is sacrilegious, 50. Those who indiscriminately criticize the lives of priests are sacrilegious, 14, 20. On compensation and the allocation of the penalty for sacrilege, 3, 98.

**Secular persons.** See *Laypersons*.

**Eternal salvation.** See *Eternal life*.

**Saints and righteous persons.**

Those who live in holy places are not to be considered saints, but rather those who perform the works of saints, 5, 321. The souls of saints and the elect are in heaven, where they enjoy everlasting joys, just as the souls of the wicked are tortured by everlasting punishments in hell, 17, 72. Whether the souls of the righteous are received into heaven before the restoration of their bodies, 17, 76, 84. On the glory of saints after death, 17, 118. A reward is rendered to the righteous and holy for curses unjustly inflicted upon them, 14, 14. The souls of saints and righteous persons rest in heaven, whereas those of the impious are tortured in darkness, 17, 71.

**Schismatics.**

Schismatics who end their lives outside the Catholic Church will go into eternal fire, 1, 38, 39. Schismatics are to be compelled to communion, 10, 92.

**Scholars.**

They ought to show honor to ecclesiastics, 10, 283.

**Writings of the Fathers.** See *Books*.

**Holy Scripture.**

What it contains and for what purpose, 1, 1. The difference between Holy Scripture and the writings of the holy Fathers, 4, 236. What the sacred Scriptures are, 1, 1. They are to be read in church, 3, 262. Catalogue of sacred books, 4, 61, 62. When sacred books are to be read, 63. Divine oracles are by no means to be applied to secular affairs, 11, 29. What should be resorted to when Holy Scripture lacks authority, 4, 70. Contemptuous despisers of Holy Scripture are to be excommunicated, [Col. 1376] 4, 220. The authority of sacred writings, 4, 227, 233.

**Examination.**

It is to be conducted by the bishop and clergy, 1, 290.

**Burial.** See *The dead*.

**Slave.** See *Freedperson*.

**Simony.**

It is wholly prohibited, 2, 84. It is to be detested and eradicated as though it were heresy, 1, 295; 5, 92, 108. Simony is of three kinds: one by service, another by money, and another by speech, 5, 86. Simoniacal ordinations are invalid, 5, 81. The simoniacal ordainer and ordained person are to be excommunicated, 5, 78, 82. The work of a simoniac is altogether worthless; it provokes wrath rather than God’s favor, 5, 111.

**Pope Sixtus.**

The emperor Valentinian showed great deference to the supreme pontiff Sixtus and gave him jurisdiction to judge his case, 5, 8.

**Sun.**

Before entering the Church of the Apostles, certain persons venerated the sun, 11, 88.

**Diviner.** See *Soothsayer*.

**Sozomen, or Solomenus.**

His history is rejected, 4, 81.

**Spectacles.**

They are to be avoided, 4, 8, especially by priests, 11, 8.

**Holy Spirit.**

What it is to utter a word against the Holy Spirit, 2, 104. One who denies that sins are remitted in the Church of God is guilty of sin against the Holy Spirit, 15, 41.

**Bridegroom, bride, and betrothal.**

How bridegroom and bride are blessed, 8, 6. Why the bride is veiled, 8, 7. What the insignia of brides are and what they signify, 8. What consent is found in betrothal, 8, 20; not age, 8, 20. Betrothals are pledged agreements for future marriages, 8, 6. The faith pledged in betrothal must in no way be violated, 8, 46. How betrothals should be contracted and concerning the conditions of those marrying, 16, 182, 183. Brides are not to be handed over to their husbands immediately, 8, 33. On those who receive brides, 8, 170. On a woman betrothed to one brother and violated by his brother, 9, 100. A seducer of a betrothed woman must provide her with a dowry and take her as his wife, 16, 292.

**Statue.** See *Law*. Also see *Decrees*.

**Stephen.**

There was a certain presbyter whom Pope St. Gregory reports to have been torn apart by the devil, 17, 64.

**Subdeacon.**

His office, 2, 43, 79; 6, 9, 20. The rite by which he is to be ordained, 6, 4. Subdeacons must not enter the sanctuary or touch the Lord’s vessels, 3, 105. Nor may they take wives, 6, 119, 221.

**Superstition.**

Superstitions and vain observances are to be avoided, 4, 1, 24; 11, 41, 42. Superstitious observance in wool-working must be avoided, 8, 330; 11, 46. Very many human practices are superstitious, 11, 13.

For more on this matter, see under *Soothsayer*.

**Suspension.**

A suspended person may baptize, 15, 13. A presbyter who strikes a deacon is suspended, 10, 24. Ecclesiastics who strike others incur suspension, 10, 24; likewise, 10, 21, 28, 35.

**Creed.**

The creed of faith, 1, 81. It is to be recited eight days before Easter, 1, 223. A presbyter is bound to teach parishioners the Creed together with the Lord’s Prayer, 6, 158. The Ephesian Creed, 1, 3.

## T

**Tavern.**

Ecclesiastics ought not to frequent taverns, 6, 203. The sources from which innkeepers, sailors, and stable-keepers may receive payment, 17, 171.

**Bull or ox.**

On a goring bull that kills someone, 10, 40. On an ox that wounds another ox, 16, 330. Whoever has stolen an ox or a sheep is bound to restore five oxen for one ox and four sheep for one sheep, 351.

**Tolls and imposts.**

Tolls may be exacted from merchants, 16, 266. No one may be compelled to go to a particular place in order to pay a toll, 16, 270. What tolls are prohibited, 16, 306.

**Time.**

Curious observance of times is to be rejected, 4, 1. God has fixed each person’s days, so that they can neither be diminished nor increased, 17, 36.

**Land.**

On tributary land, 16, 279; and land subject to a census-tax, 280.

**Testament and testator.**

[Col. 1377]

Persons subject to ecclesiastical law may not make a testament, 16, 111. On the property of a deceased testator, 16, 115. A prince ought to confirm the testament of one who designates his natural children as his lawful successors, 16, 140. Who may make testaments, 16, 188.

**Witness and testimony.**

An evident case needs no witnesses, 6, 431. Those not to be admitted to give testimony, 6, 364; 16, 181, 337. False witnesses are to be excommunicated, 10, 38. A perjurer cannot be a witness, 12, 23; nor can an infamous person, 16, 208; nor an excommunicated person, 16, 357. Whoever solicits someone to give false testimony is to be excommunicated, 12, 26. On the differing status of witnesses according to differences of persons, 16, 131. A witness must be of respectable life, 16, 152. The testimony of a slave is invalid, 153. A hostile witness is not to be heard, 154. On a witness acting as intermediary between the parties, 16, 155. Witnesses must not be produced unless the opposing parties are present, 156. What witnesses are or are not to be compelled, 16, 80. Several witnesses from one household may be used in another person’s case, 16, 187. On the oath of witnesses, 16, 204. The testimony of one person is by no means to be accepted, 16, 210. A document must be proved by witnesses, 16, 290. Against outsiders, parents or relatives must not be witnesses, 16, 361.

**Theodore of Mopsuestia.**

Although dead, he was nevertheless anathematized by Rabbula, bishop of Edessa, 14, 62.

**Emperor Theodosius.**

Excommunicated by blessed Ambrose, 5, 378; 10, 48.

**Theophany.** See *Epiphany*.

**Treasurer and primicerius.**

Their dignity and office, 6, 20, 29.

**Fear or dread.** Also *Force*.

On what is done through force or fear, 16, 168. Whoever employs fraud or fear so that property may pass to him [read *ad eum* for the evidently corrupt printed *ad odium*], both the user of force and the user of fraud are liable to an action, 16, 205. Whoever does not now fear God as just cannot afterward find him merciful, 17, 70.

**Title.**

A presbyter must not usurp a title upon a title, 3, 269.

**Tonsure.**

No one should be tonsured except at lawful age and of free will, 7, 109, 111. On those who receive tonsure or enter religious life before lawful age, 7, 26.

**Clerical tonsure.** See *Cleric*.

**Traditions.**

Ecclesiastical traditions are to be observed, 4, 67, 195. They must by no means be altered, 4, 197. Their despisers are to be excommunicated, 198. Many things were handed down by the Apostles but not written, 4, 209.

**Trier and Cologne.**

No one there is to be elected bishop without consulting the Roman pontiff, 5, 357.

**Trinity.**

What the most holy Trinity is, 1, 2. The most holy Trinity was not incarnate; the Son alone was incarnate, 1, 2, 13. Man was created in the likeness of the supreme Trinity, 17, 1.

**Guardianship and guardian.**

A guardian ought not deprive wards of their goods, 6, 190. A woman who is guardian of her children, if she wishes to marry a second time, must provide a guardian for her children, 16, 129, 157. A guardian or curator of wards must swear that he will administer everything which he judges advantageous for the wards, 16, 135.

## U

**Usury.**

It is not lawful to practice usury, 6, 65, 195. What usury is, 200. Usurers are infamous persons, 13, 19. He who demands usury fights without iron, 13, 27.

## V

**Sacred vessels, chalices, patens.**

Sacred vessels are to be handled by sacred persons, 2, 70; 3, 264. The material of sacred vessels, 2, 131; 3, 282. Sacred vessels are not to be alienated, 3, 187. How old sacred vessels are to be handled, 3, 266. Formerly golden priests used wooden chalices; now, conversely, wooden priests use golden chalices, 3, 282. It is not lawful for just anyone to touch sacred vessels, 6, 377. They are not to be given as pledges, 16, 264.

**Sacred veil.** See *Nun*.

**Sacred veil.**

The sacred veil, also called a *syndon* (“shroud”), is not to be sold, 2, 65, nor used to cover a tomb, 2, 12; 3, 277.

**Hunting and fishing.**

Ecclesiastics ought to avoid hunting and such pursuits, 13, 29. Nothing is to be given to hunters and actors, 31. Hunters are to be avoided, 13, 32. Some holy fishermen are found, but no holy hunters, 13, 33.

**Selling.** See *Buying*.

**The divine Word.** See *Incarnation*.

**Word or discourse of God, or preaching of the word of God.**

[Col. 1378]

How the word of God is to be esteemed and heard, 2, 106. A person who negligently hears the word of God is as guilty as if, through his negligence, he allowed Christ’s body to fall to the ground, 2, 106. On every Sunday the people ought to come to the preaching of the divine word, 2, 119. Preaching is to be given during the solemn celebration of Mass, 120. Entrance into church must be forbidden to no one when God’s word is proclaimed to the people, 3, 33. When God’s word is preached, one must not leave the church, 9, 162.

**Truth and what is true.**

To speak truth is insufficient unless one so feels in one’s heart, 12, 52. Sometimes it is beneficial to do the truth, 54. Truth is established by writings or testimony, without an oath, 16, 139. Better and true things should always be chosen with care, 16, 340. Once another’s truth has been ascertained, it is not to be investigated further, 16, 334.

**Sacred vestments.**

Worn-out sacred vestments are to be burned, 2, 66; 3, 266. Ecclesiastical garments must be consecrated, 2, 74, and must not be removed outside the church, 2, 139; 6, 88.

**Widow.**

What a widow is, 8, 297. Widows are not to be veiled, 7, 52, 55. When and how they may be veiled, 60, 61. Consecrated widows must remain in their commitment, 8, 54. They are not to enter marriage, 7, 64, 144. Before professing continence, they may marry, 7, 62, 818. How an incontinent widow is to be punished, 7, 58, 63, 65, 68, 152. A widow must by no means be abducted as a wife, 8, 149. She must not enter a second marriage until a year has elapsed after her husband’s death, 8, 272. The Church ought to support young widows, 8, 326.

**Pope Vigilius.**

He bound the empress Theodora with the bond of excommunication, 5, 378. He also struck Origen with an anathema, although he was already dead, 10, 62.

**Punishment.**

It is not to be forbidden, 10, 171. Whoever is able to punish sins and neglects to do so is guilty of sin, 10, 187. One who has committed an offense must be punished in his person, not in his property, 16, 81. Punishment of a greedy advocate, 16, 355.

**Wine.** See *Drunkenness*.

**Husband and wife.**

It is fitting for a wife to be buried with her husband in the same tomb, 3, 223. A husband ought to be an example of chastity to his wife, 8, 263. When spouses may abstain from the marital obligation, 4, 47, 83, 87, 89. For the sake of prayer spouses must not defraud one another of the conjugal obligation, 8, 133, unless by mutual consent, 8, 133. A husband may receive his wife back into marriage if she has been veiled without his permission, 8, 185. On one who married a wife formerly veiled, 6, 113. A husband may not live continently without his wife’s consent, 8, 16, 127, 130, nor enter a monastery, 8, 183. A wife is not to separate without her husband’s permission, 8, 220, 229. A husband may dismiss his wife on account of fornication, 8, 43. A wife should not leave her husband without cause, 8, 198. A wife is not to be taken away from her husband, 8, 58; and if she is taken away, she must be restored, 8, 118. A wife cannot make a vow of continence if her husband refuses, 8, 98; 9, 127, nor should she be veiled without his will, 124. Married persons must make no vows except by mutual consent, 8, 134. A husband who has allowed his wife to be veiled cannot take another wife, 8, 184. How a wife becomes lawful, 8, 44. She ought not cut her hair, 7, 80. A husband should be to his wife such as he wishes his wife to be to him, 8, 45. No one is permitted to have two wives at the same time, 8, 59, 66; 5, 135. Whoever has had two is bound to dismiss the later one and do penance, 63. On men and wives at festivals, 8, 51. One spouse is to be repudiated if incapable of rendering the marital obligation, 8, 78. A husband must not have intercourse with a pregnant woman, 8, 88; 15, 263. A wife ought to be subject to her husband, and a husband ought not withhold the marital obligation from his wife, 8, 86, 85, 90, 93. An adulterous wife must not be killed according to divine law, 8, 124. A believing husband must not separate from an unbelieving wife, 8, 147.

**Virginity and virgin.**

Virginity is not a commandment, 7, 120. The body is not corrupted unless the soul is corrupted, 7, 137, 11. Marriage is not permitted to virgins, 8, 72. No one ought to abduct a virgin as a wife, 8, 150. One must not be proud of virginity, 8, 316. On the penance of virgins who have not preserved virginity, 8, 152.

**The virgin Demetrias.**

A noble virgin, at the urging of St. Augustine, consecrated the integrity of her body to Christ, 8, 138.

**Consecrated virgin.** See *Nun*.

**Force.** See *Fear*.

**Visible and invisible.**

The signs of divine things are visible, but the things themselves are invisible, [Col. 1379] 2, 8. Nothing is invisible and incorporeal except God alone, 17, 52. Invisible things cannot be seen or known except through visible things, 17, 96. There are invisible beings that minister to the invisible God, 17, 95.

**Eternal life, or the kingdom of heaven.**

Catholics who live well will have eternal life, 1, 40. How they obtained the kingdom of God, 6, 160. Those who pour out their lives in defense of Christians will attain the kingdoms of heaven, 10, 87.

**Common life.**

Praise of common life, 3, 139; 5, 229.

**Vow.**

A vow to enter religious life must be fulfilled, 7, 9, 19. A vow [Col. 1380] to preserve virginity must be kept, 29. A vow made by a religious person without the consent of his superior is invalid, 7, 32. Many things are permitted before a vow that are not permitted afterward, 8, 73, 137. Foolish vows are not to be kept, 12, 64. That vow must be kept which spouses have vowed by mutual consent, 8, 136.

## W

**Waldrada.** See *Lothair*.

## X

**Xenodochium** (*hostel for strangers*).

On the administration of a hostel for the poor, 15, 149.

See further *Pilgrim*.

[Col. 1379]

# A MOST COPIOUS INDEX TO THE *PANORMIA*, ARRANGED ACCORDING TO THE ORDER OF CHAPTERS AND BOOKS

[Note: [Col. 13479] This index refers only to the *Panormia* of Ivo of Chartres in columns 1041–1344.]

## A

The first admonition—“if you wish to be perfect”—does not threaten punishment but promises a reward, ch. 5 of the Prologue.

The admonition, “if you wish to be perfect,” places perfection in a person’s will, ibid. — The admonition, “if you wish to be perfect,” becomes necessary after a vow, though it had formerly been voluntary, ch. 5 of the Prologue.

When the Apostle said, “I became as a Jew to the Jews, that I might gain the Jews,” he said this not from the disposition of one lying, but from the disposition of one sympathizing, ch. 9 of the Prologue.

Words of error uttered through ignorance do not hinder the sanctification of water, ch. 53, book I, and ch. 53, ibid.

If anyone wishes to receive consecrated water for sprinkling a house, he must receive it on Holy Saturday or Pentecost before the infusion of chrism, ch. 103, book I.

When water is mixed with wine in the Lord’s chalice, the people are united with Christ, and the multitude of believers is joined and united to him in whom it believes, ch. 147, book I.

Superfluous altars are to be destroyed, ch. 18, book II. — Altars discovered through dreams or empty revelations are wholly rejected, ch. 28, book II.

Abbots or monks are rebuked when they teach laypersons to transfer their goods or possessions, in life or in death, to their monasteries, while passing over the churches from which they received baptism and the other sacraments, ch. 29, book II.

If altars are not of stone, they are not to be consecrated by anointing with chrism, ch. 32, book II. — Altars in which neither holy bodies nor relics of martyrs are proved to be present are to be destroyed by bishops, ch. 34, book II. A presbyter must not presume to celebrate Mass on the same day at an altar at which a bishop has sung Mass, ch. 35, book II.

False names of angels are not to be venerated, but only those taught by prophetic and evangelical Scripture: namely, Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael, ch. 89, book II.

Apocryphal writings and their authors were condemned by the holy Fathers, ch. 123, book II.

Manicheans read apocryphal writings, ch. 127, book II.

Apocrypha are not to be read for the truth of doctrine, ch. 129, book II. — Apocrypha are not by the persons whose names are placed in their titles, ibid. — Many corrupt elements are mixed into the Scriptures in apocryphal books, ibid.

To seek gold in mud is a mark of great prudence, ibid.

No written rule has prescribed worship toward the east, yet the Church observes it, ch. 159, book II.

An archbishop is to be ordained by all the bishops of his province, because one who presides over them ought to be established by all the bishops over whom he presides, ch. 10, book III.

When an acolyte is ordained, he is to be instructed by the bishop what he ought to do in his office; but he is to receive from the archdeacon [Col. 1380] a candlestick with a candle and an empty cruet for presenting wine, ch. 36, book III.

What the office of archdeacons is, ch. 41, book III.

It is one thing not to possess something; it is another not to possess it by right, or to usurp it unlawfully, ch. 78, book III.

The Apostles received honor and authority equal in partnership with Peter, and wished him to be their chief, ch. 82, book III.

Bishops arose in the place of the Apostles, ibid.

The seventy disciples were chosen by the Apostles; presbyters bear their type and were appointed in their place in the Church, ibid.

No one may approach the ministry of the altar unless his chastity has been approved before assuming the ministry, ch. 89, book III.

All the Apostles had wives, except John and Paul, ch. 116, book III.

If any bishop or cleric consults haruspices, augurs, soothsayers, diviners, or magicians, he is to be deposed from his rank and confined in a monastery, ch. 169, book III.

A bishop, presbyter, or deacon devoted to gambling or drunkenness must either cease or be deposed, ch. 170, book III.

The Apostles passed from fishing in the Lake of Gennesaret to fishing for human beings, ch. 177, book III.

That man is to be appointed abbot whom his own community has requested and elected, ch. 181, book III.

Augustine says of himself that he is among the number of clerics, ch. 180, book III.

An abbess who presumes to veil a virgin or widow is to be excommunicated, ch. 194, book III.

Abbesses who have made profession according to the Rule of Saint Benedict are to live separately, ch. 209, book III.

Abbesses are to remain in their monasteries and not go outside without the bishop’s permission, ch. 209, book III, and ch. 210.

An abbess must take the greatest care of the nuns whom she takes outside with her, ch. 210, book III.

What sort of care an abbess ought to have toward nuns, ch. 211, book III.

The holy Fathers decreed reverence for antiquity, ch. 29, book IV.

An accusation is not to be received in writing, but in the accuser’s own voice, ch. 53, book IV, and ch. 55.

An accuser is not to be heard in the absence of the opposing party. — A person absent cannot accuse through another, nor be accused through another, ch. 54, book IV.

Except in person, an accuser cannot accuse anyone in criminal cases; nor can an accused person in such cases defend himself through another, ch. 56, book IV.

In a judicial proceeding, one must inquire what manner of life, faith, and reputation accusers possess, and with what intention they accuse. — Accusers are not to be admitted unless they are men free from every suspicion and of good life, ch. 57, book IV.

Priests cannot be accused except by men of the most proven character, ch. 58, book IV.

Accusers of bishops or priests are not to be heard unless their reputations have been examined, ch. 59, book IV.

Permission to accuse or testify is to be denied to apostates, ch. 59. — Apostates are called those who voluntarily transgress their own law, ch. 59, book IV.

Enemies cannot accuse, ch. 62, book IV. — Pagans, heretics, and Jews cannot accuse, ch. 63, book IV.

Where clerics are accused on several counts, if the accuser cannot prove one of the earlier charges, he is not to be admitted on the remaining charges, ch. 64, book IV.

Recent enemies cannot be accusers, chs. 65 and 67, book IV.

Infamous persons must not be admitted to make accusations, ch. 66, book IV.

Accused persons are not to accuse others before clearing themselves, ch. 69, book IV.

Infamous persons cannot accuse those of good reputation, ch. 70, book IV.

Who may not be received in an accusation, ch. 71, book IV.

Those are called anathematized whom bishops have anathematized in their writings, or who anathematize their enactments, ch. 71, book IV.

One who persists under excommunication is not admitted to make an accusation, ch. 72, book IV.

Whoever accuses another in court must declare him guilty and submit himself to the consequences of a formal accusation, ch. 76, book IV.

No foreigner is to become an accuser or judge, ch. 79, book IV.

Accusers and judges are not the same persons, chs. 80 and 81, book IV.

Carnal love, fear, and greed often dull human understanding and pervert judgments, so that people consider profit to be piety and money to be the reward of prudence, ch. 85, book IV.

Traitors and calumniators cannot accuse. — Accomplices in another’s error and those disobedient to the holy Fathers are not to be admitted to accuse, ch. 87, book IV.

A cleric of lower rank must by no means bring an accusation against a cleric of higher rank, ch. 90, book IV. — An accusation against a presbyter is not to be received except under two or three witnesses, ch. 95, book IV. — An accuser who fails to prove an offense against a presbyter is to be excommunicated, ch. 97, book IV.

An accused person may choose for himself a suitable place where he can have witnesses without fear, ch. 99, book IV.

An action is to be examined until the truth of the matter is reached, ch. 104, book IV.

A bishop who regards a judge as suspect is to appeal to the Apostolic See, ch. 120, book IV.

No affliction or imprisonment is to be added to one making an appeal, ch. 121, book IV.

An appeal must not be denied to one whom a sentence has consigned to punishment, ch. 122, book IV.

An accused person is to be heard only in his own forum, ch. 123, book IV.

Bishops burdened by more serious cases are to appeal to the Apostolic See, chs. 124, 125, and 126, book IV.

After sentence has been pronounced, an appeal must be made within five days, ch. 127, book IV.

Letters of dismissal are to be directed from the person appealed from to the person to whom the appeal has been made. — Such letters of dismissal are commonly called “apostolic letters,” ch. 128, book IV.

Appeals that are not to be admitted, ch. 129, book IV.

What penalty follows for one who appeals unjustly, ch. 130, book IV.

It is not lawful to appeal from judges chosen by common consent, ch. 132, book IV.

When a sentence is set aside by appeal, it ought not harm one who judged without an unjust intention, ch. 133, book IV.

No one absent is to be condemned in a capital case, ch. 16, book V.

An anathematized person cannot accuse or testify, ch. 39, book V.

If adulterers, magicians, or convicted persons wish to appeal, they are not to be heard, ch. 42, book V.

A person acquitted of a particular crime cannot be accused again of the same crime, ch. 46, book V.

A person who is anathematized is, as an impious person, separated [Col. 1382] from God. — *Anathema* signifies nothing other than separation from God, ch. 89, book V. — Anathema is condemnation to eternal death and should be imposed only for a mortal crime, and upon one who cannot otherwise be corrected, ch. 93, book V.

No bishop may strike anyone with an anathema without a certain and manifest cause of sin, ch. 93, book V.

After death, those who leave their property to heretics are subject to anathema, ch. 116, book V. A son is not to be anathematized for his father’s sin, ch. 136, book V.

**People of God.** A person’s maternal condition does not separate him from the people of God, but his own fault does, ch. 47, book VI.

What the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 7, “To the rest I say, not the Lord,” seems to me to have been said by him as an admonition, ch. 100, book VI.

Roman laws, deserving of reverence, do not permit marriages to be contracted between those who are children by adoption, ch. 123, book VI.

An adulterer cannot marry the adulteress after her husband’s death, ch. 9, book VII.

No woman whom a man has defiled through adultery may be taken by him as wife, chs. 10 and 11, book VII.

A woman whom a man has defiled through adultery may afterwards, once widowed and after penance has been completed, be taken by him as wife, ch. 12, book VI.

If an adulterous woman, through fear of death threatened against her by her husband, has fled to a bishop, the bishop must by no means return her, but send her to a place she herself chooses, where she may live safely, ch. 13, book VII. — No one may lawfully kill his adulterous wife, ch. 14, book VII.

It is more permissible to commit adultery than homicide; hence Augustine says: “For if he is going to do what is unlawful, let him commit adultery rather than commit homicide,” ch. 17, book VII.

Adulteries must not be committed even with the intention of begetting children, ch. 20, book VII.

Adultery holds the second place among punishments, ch. 21, book VII.

Adultery occurs when one has intercourse, whether prompted by one’s own lust or with another’s consent, contrary to the marital covenant, ch. 22, book VII.

He commits adultery spiritually who approaches another woman besides his own, ch. 23, book VII.

Once adultery has been cleansed by penance, reconciliation of spouses may take place, chs. 37 and 38, book VII. — David received back without defilement his wife Michal, whom Saul, her father, had given to another, even under the old law, ch. 38, book VII.

Adulterous men ought to be punished more severely than women, insofar as it belongs more especially to them both to overcome by virtue and to govern women by example, ch. 36, book VII.

The reconciliation of adulterers is neither shameful nor difficult, ch. 37, book VII.

Adam was deceived through Eve, and Eve was not deceived through Adam, whom the woman summoned to sin, ch. 50, book VII.

Anathema upon anyone who takes as wife his brother’s wife, or his stepmother, daughter-in-law, first cousin, a woman of his own kin, or a blood-relative, chs. 57, 59, and 62, book VII.

Anathema if anyone has fornicated with his spiritual mother, or with a woman whom he sponsored at baptism, or with one whom he held at holy chrismation, ch. 64, book VII.

Affinity is not extinguished while the person through whom it was contracted survives, even if the other person has died, ch. 68, book VII. — Affinity is not found beyond the seventh degree, nor can succession be extended further, ch. 80, book VII.

Whoever procures an abortion before a soul has been infused into the body is not judged a homicide, chs. 12, 13, and 14, book VIII.

Abraham pleased God not merely as a homicide, but as a parricide, ch. 18, book VIII.

A servant or son who is not corrected is not loved, ch. 22, book VIII.

Pope Adrian anathematized the duke of the Bavarians on the day of holy Easter, in the presence of Emperor Charles, unless he obeyed that emperor, his sons, and the Frankish people, as he had sworn, ch. 31, book VIII.

If anyone observes diviners, haruspices, or enchanters, or uses amulets (*phylacteria*), let that person be anathema, ch. 61, book VIII. — If any bishop or cleric consults diviners or magicians, let him be deprived of his rank, ch. 64, book VIII. — They are called *arioli* (“diviners”) because they utter wicked prayers around the altars of idols, offer deadly sacrifices, and receive answers from demons through these observances, ch. 66, book VIII. — Augurs are so called because they attend to the flight and cries of birds, as well as other signs of things and unexpected omens that meet human beings. — Haruspices [Col. 1383] are called, as it were, “inspectors of hours”; for they observe days and hours in conducting affairs and works, and attend to what a person ought to observe at each particular time, ch. 68, book VIII. — Haruspices inspect the entrails of cattle and make predictions from them, ch. 66, book VIII.

Auspices are the signs which persons setting out on a journey observe; they are called *auspicia*, as though *avium spicia* (“observations of birds”), and auguries, as though *avium garria* (“bird-chatter”), that is, the cries and language of birds. — Astrologers are so called because they make auguries from the stars, ch. 66, book VIII.

Let anyone devoted to auguries or incantations be separated from the Church, ch. 72, book VIII.

No one may be ordained archdeacon or dean unless he is a deacon or priest. — Archdeaconries and deaneries must not be granted to young men or to persons below holy orders, but to those distinguished by chastity and merit of life, ch. 146, book VIII.

## B

Baptism is administered in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, ch. 9, book I.

The water of baptism has among us the force that faith had among the ancients for little children, the efficacy of sacrifice for adults, and circumcision for those descended from Abraham’s stock, ch. 10, book I.

Baptism removes original sin, ch. 11, book I. — Baptism does not benefit one able to answer for himself if another answers on his behalf, unless he himself answers for himself, ch. 15, book I.

General baptism is not to be celebrated except on the holy Saturday of Easter and Pentecost, ch. 16, book I; likewise chs. 17 and 20, book I.

The Lord wished to be baptized, not because he needed remission of sin, but in order to fulfill the law. — The baptism of John and the baptism of Christ do not have the same efficacy, ch. 18, book I.

In cases of necessity—death, illness, siege, persecution, or shipwreck—baptism may be given at any time, ch. 19, book I.

A mother may baptize her son when danger of death is urgent, ch. 22. — No one may presume to baptize except a priest, necessity being excepted, ch. 23, book I. — Laypersons are often permitted to baptize, chs. 23 and 24, book I. — A woman may not presume to baptize, ch. 25, book I. — (Understand this as excluding necessity, as ch. 22, book I, makes clear.) — Under compelling danger, baptism is permitted to laypersons in the absence of a bishop or priest, ch. 26, book I.

A pagan may administer baptism, and it is not repeated, ch. 27, book I.

A heretic may baptize, and baptism administered in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is not repeated, ch. 28, book I.

Baptism administered by a Jew in the name of the Trinity or in the name of Christ is valid and is not repeated, ch. 29, book I. — Whether administered by an evil minister or a good one, baptism is always good, chs. 30–34, book I.

An adult about to receive baptism must first repent of the old life, in order to begin a new one, chs. 35–36, book I. — Jews who are to receive baptism must first abstain for forty days, ch. 37, book I.

A person to be baptized must first be catechized and instructed in matters of faith, ch. 38, book I. — A person to be baptized must be taught twenty days before baptism, so that he knows the Creed, namely, “I believe,” ch. 39, book I. — The candidate is exsufflated, so that through the pious ministry of the priest the evil spirit may flee and yield to the Holy Spirit, chs. 41–42, book I. — The candidate is signed with the cross both on heart and forehead, so that the devil, recognizing the sign of his own destruction, may know that henceforth the person is no longer his, ch. 43, book I. — Blessed salt is placed in the candidate’s mouth, so that, seasoned with the salt of wisdom through this symbolic salt, he may be free from the stench of wickedness, ch. 44, book I. — Those to be baptized are exorcized again, so that the devil, fearing God’s just judgment, may depart from the person, ch. 46, book I. — The noses and ears of those to be baptized are touched with the priest’s symbolic saliva, so that through it and its touch their nostrils may be opened to receive the fragrance of the knowledge of God, and their ears to hear God’s commands, ch. 48, book I. — The breast and shoulders of those baptized are anointed, so that the mind may be strengthened and fortified on every side, ch. 50, book I.

The wickedness of the person blessing does not pass into the water of baptism, ch. 54, book I.

What the mysteries performed in the baptismal font signify, ch. 55, book I.

A triple immersion is made in the water of baptism: because baptism is given in the name of the Trinity; because Christ rose on the third day; and because he remained in the tomb for three days, ch. 57, book I.

Anyone who does not immerse three times in the water of baptism is to be deposed, ch. 58, book I. — It is lawful to immerse once in baptismal water; this is contrary to the preceding statement, ch. 59, book I.

[Col. 1384] Both a triple immersion may be performed in baptismal water, because the Trinity is signified in it, and a single immersion, because the unity of the Godhead is signified in it; note that this text reconciles the two preceding passages, ch. 60, book I.

It is not lawful to baptize only in the name of the Father, only in the name of the Son, or only in the name of the Holy Spirit, ch. 62, book I. — Those baptized “in the name of the Lord” must without doubt be baptized in the name of the holy Trinity, ch. 62, book I. — The Gospel command enjoins baptism in the name of the Trinity and with triple immersion, ch. 62, book I. — One baptized without invocation of the Trinity does not possess the sacrament of regeneration, ch. 63, book I. — One baptized in the name of the Father and Son, but not in the name of the Holy Spirit, has not been baptized; for if anyone confesses the Father and the Son but not the Holy Spirit, he has neither the Father nor the Son, ch. 63, book I. — Heretics baptized other than in the name of the Trinity who come to the Church are to be baptized, because those who received no baptism under an erroneous naming of the holy Trinity did not receive baptism at all, ch. 64, book I. — One baptized “in the name of the fatherland and daughter and holy spirit” is not to be rebaptized, if the baptizer did not intend to introduce error or heresy, ch. 65, book I.

A baptized person is signed by the priest on the crown of the head with holy chrism, so that he may become a participant in Christ’s kingdom, ch. 66, book I. — What the priest is to say to the baptized person after baptism, ch. 67, book I. — A white garment is put upon the baptized person, signifying Christian innocence and purity; therefore those reborn are clothed in white garments, chs. 69–70, book I.

Jews to be baptized are to enter the threshold of the Church among the catechumens for eight months, and then be baptized, and not earlier unless danger arises, ch. 71, book I. — Baptized Jews, even if baptized by force, are nevertheless to be compelled to retain the faith which they received by force or necessity, ch. 72, book I. — Force is not to be applied to make Jews come to baptism; rather, they are to be called, not driven, ch. 72, book I. — Baptized sons or daughters of Jews are to be separated from their parents, lest they be entangled in their errors, chs. 73–74, book I. — Baptized Jews who return to the vomit are to be corrected by pontifical authority and recalled to the observance of Christian doctrine; if they circumcise their sons, they are to be separated from their society; but if they circumcise slaves, the slaves are to be granted freedom because of the bodily injury, ch. 75, book I. — A pagan about to be baptized is to be asked whether he renounces the devil and all his works and deceits, ch. 75, book I.

One who leaves the Church does not lose the right to administer baptism, ch. 87, book I.

Those baptized among heretics in the name of the Trinity who return to the Church are received in the West through laying on of hands, but in the East through anointing with holy chrism, ch. 88, book I. — Those baptized in the name of the Trinity, if this is manifest from a clear confession, are not to be rebaptized, ch. 90, book I. — Those baptized by persons whose faith is unknown, if they received the form of baptism, are not to be rebaptized, but received through laying on of hands, ch. 91, book I.

Little children removed from their parents, where it is unknown whether they were baptized, are to be baptized, chs. 92–93, book I. — A person for whom there is no evidence that he was baptized is to be baptized anew, ch. 94, book I.

The baptism of a child is efficacious for the salvation of the soul, even if the intention of those presenting the child is not to offer him except for the recovery of bodily health, ch. 95, book I.

If a priest ordained has not been baptized, both he and all whom he previously baptized are to be baptized, and he is to be ordained again, chs. 96–97, book I.

Nothing may be accepted in payment for balsam to make chrism, ch. 98, book I.

Nothing may be accepted in payment for dedicating basilicas, ch. 98, book I.

In baptism it is not lawful to use old chrism, but new, ch. 100, book I.

Baptism must be performed in water and not in wine, because as bodily dirt is washed away by water, so the stains of the soul are washed away through baptism, ch. 102, book I.

It is more credible that the apostles were baptized with Christ’s baptism than that they were baptized with John’s baptism, chs. 104–105, book I.

Those not baptized who die for Christ die baptized, ch. 106, book I. — A person who ends his life in martyrdom for Christ is called baptized, ch. 108, book I. — Suffering fulfills the place of baptism, as in the case of the holy thief, ch. 109, book I. — According to Cyprian, faith and conversion of heart also supply the place of baptism when necessity prevents baptism, ch. 109, book I.

The mystery of baptism is then invisibly fulfilled when not contempt for religion but a circumstance of necessity prevents baptism. — Baptism may be present where confession of the heart is lacking. — Conversion of heart [Col. 1385] may indeed be present without baptism having been received, but it cannot be present when baptism has been despised, ch. 109, book I.

True baptism consists not so much in washing of the body as in faith of the heart, ch. 110, book I.

Whatever is in the mother’s body is not baptized with the mother, ch. 111, book I.

Children still in their mothers’ wombs cannot be baptized, because, not yet having been born, they cannot be reborn, ch. 112, book I.

Priests may anoint baptized persons with chrism, ch. 116, book I.

Baptism must be celebrated by fasting persons at the two seasons, namely Easter and Pentecost, ch. 120, book I.

Baptism must on no account be repeated, ch. 121, book I.

Persons baptized twice unknowingly need no penance, except that under the canons they cannot be ordained unless great necessity compels it, ch. 122, book I. — Persons baptized twice knowingly are to do penance for seven years, fasting on Wednesday and Friday and during three Lents; if they did this through some vice, likewise; but if they believed it was done for purification, they are to do similar penance for three years, ch. 122, book I.

Blessed Benedict wrote the Rule for monks, outstanding in discernment and lucid in style, ch. 96, book II.

Scripture has not taught us to bless the baptismal font with oil for anointing; this comes from the silent and mystical tradition of the Fathers. — Scripture has not taught us to immerse the baptized three times, anoint them with oil, or make verbal renunciation of Satan and his angels; these come from ecclesiastical custom and the tradition of the Fathers, ch. 159, book II.

Bigamists, penitents, and husbands of repudiated women are not to be promoted to the priesthood, ch. 59, book III.

To confer the effect of blessing belongs to God, ch. 79, book III.

I do not condemn bigamists; indeed, if it may be said, neither trigamists nor octogamists, ch. 62, book VI. — I now declare openly that bigamy is not condemned in the Church, nor even trigamy; and that it is as lawful to marry a fifth or sixth husband as a second, ch. 62, book VI.

A bigamist does not sin by contracting marriage, but is deprived of the prerogative of the priesthood, ch. 63, book VI. — Whoever repeats marriage does not incur the fault of defilement, but is deprived of the priestly prerogative, ibid. — The Synod of Nicaea decreed that no cleric should be one who has entered a second marriage, ch. 63, book VI.

A person who had another wife before baptism is considered a bigamist, ch. 64, book VI. — Through baptism guilt may be forgiven, but law cannot be abolished. In marriage, what is guilt is forgiven in baptism; what belongs to law in marriage is not dissolved, ch. 64, book VI. — A bigamist who had one wife before baptism and another after baptism is not to be ordained, ch. 66, book VI.

It is unfitting for a priest to dine at the wedding of a bigamist, ch. 67, book VI. — Those who had one wife before baptism and another after baptism are considered bigamists, chs. 95–96, book VI.

In baptism crimes are absolved, not marriages, ch. 98, book VI. — In baptism guilt may be forgiven, but law cannot be abolished, ch. 64, book VI. — In baptism what is guilt is remitted, but what belongs to law in marriage is not dissolved, ch. 64, book VI.

In war one must not spare for the defense both of oneself and of one’s country or ancestral laws, ch. 37, book VIII.

Wars are undertaken by good persons when, whether God or some legitimate authority commands them to order such things, the just order itself binds them either to issue such commands or to obey in such matters, ch. 45, book VIII.

The authority and decision to undertake war belong to rulers; the natural order of mortals, adapted to peace, demands this, ch. 46, book VIII.

Soldiers ought to carry out military commands in service of the common peace and safety, ch. 46, book VIII. — That a war which must be waged under God’s authority is rightly undertaken may not lawfully be doubted, ibid.

A just man may lawfully fight under a sacrilegious king, and how, ch. 47, book VIII.

A just war is one waged by proclamation to recover property or to repel enemies, ch. 54, book VIII.

The Israelites waged just wars against the Amorites because passage was denied them, though it ought most equitably to have been open to them by the right of human society, ch. 57, book VIII.

Which persons and animals are safe in time of war, ch. 147, book VIII.

## C

Charity is the teacher of every good. — Have charity, and do what you will, ch. 3, Prologue.

A cleric who has performed penance for a condemnable crime is not to remain a cleric or enter the clerical state, ch. 8, Prologue.

[Col. 1386] Whoever thinks according to the flesh fails to carry out what he intends when he defers to persons of higher rank, or is overcome by age, gain, or display, ch. 9, Prologue.

The Apostle circumcised Timothy, yielding to the need of the moment, in order to avoid scandal among the Jews dwelling there, ch. 9, Prologue.

Where grave cases involve not the danger of this or that individual but the slaughter of peoples, something must be relaxed from severity, so that charity may sincerely assist in averting greater evils, from St. Augustine, ch. 10, Prologue.

Correction cannot be salutary against many persons, or against one who has a multitude as allies, ch. 13, Prologue.

Cathar heretics, after receiving the laying on of hands, are to remain in the clergy, ch. 13, Prologue.

Personal enactments are not drawn into precedent, because the prince does not will this even in that case, ch. 30, Prologue.

Circumcision removed original sin among the ancients, chs. 10 and 11, book I.

Priests of any church may conduct the catechisms of baptismal candidates, ch. 40, book I.

To believe is nothing other than to have faith, ch. 56, book I.
