Diversity in the custom of the holy Church does no harm to unity of faith, ch. 60, book I.

To anoint the chrism cloth and place it upon another baptized person is not absurd, ch. 99, book I.

Priests governing diocesan churches must seek chrism from their own bishop, not through juniors, but in person or through others of the same rank, ch. 101, book I.

We do not believe that a deceased catechumen has life unless he ended his life in martyrdom, ch. 107, book I.

Conversion of heart to God cannot be said to exist when God’s sacrament is despised, ch. 109, book I.

All the faithful ought to receive the sacrament of confirmation after baptism, ch. 113, book I.

The sacrament of confirmation is greater than baptism, ch. 114, book I. — The sacrament of confirmation cannot be performed by priests rather than bishops, chs. 114–115, book I. — The sacrament of confirmation can be performed only by the highest priests; if anything else has been presumed, it is to be held void, ibid.

Priests must not presume to sign baptized infants on the forehead with holy chrism, but on the breast; bishops, however, on the forehead, ch. 117, book I.

The sacrament of confirmation is given to the baptized person so that he may be strengthened by the Holy Spirit to preach to others. — The baptized person is signed by a priest with chrism on the crown of the head, to signify the descent of the Holy Spirit upon him, consecrating him as God’s dwelling. — But he is signed on the forehead by a bishop, so that it may be declared that the sevenfold grace of that same Spirit, with all fullness of holiness, knowledge, and power, comes upon the person, ch. 118, book I.

Let them come fasting for confirmation. — Before confirmation, those of mature age are to be instructed to make confession. — Unless someone has been chrismated in episcopal confirmation, he will never be a Christian, ch. 119, book I. — Bishops do not administer confirmation except while fasting, necessity being excepted, ch. 120, book I.

Confirmation must not be repeated. — Persons confirmed twice or more are to live most religiously, not in the world, but only under clerical or monastic habit, ch. 121, book I.

After blessing, Christ’s body is what before blessing was bread. — Christ is in the sacrament of the Eucharist. — Christ’s body becomes remission of sins for the one who eats it, ch. 124, book I.

We honor Christ’s flesh and blood in the form of bread and wine which we see. — After consecration, Christ’s flesh and blood are what the blessing consecrated, while before consecration they were bread and wine, ch. 125, book I.

After consecration, the bread and wine placed upon the altar are the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and not merely a sacrament. — The body and blood of Christ are handled, broken, and ground by the teeth of the faithful not only sacramentally and perceptibly, but in truth by the hands of priests. — Berengar’s confession and condemnation of his heresy, ch. 126, book I.

The invisible priest, by his word and secret power, changes visible creatures into the substance of his body and blood, saying: “This is my body,” and “Drink: this is my blood,” ch. 129, book I.

The priest asks that Christ’s body, now borne under the form of bread and wine, may someday be apprehended by manifest vision as it truly is, ch. 132, book I. — How the eating of the Lord’s body and blood spiritually rather than carnally is to be understood, ch. 133, book I. — How the body of Christ which hung on the cross is received, and how it is not, ch. 134, book I.

[Col. 1387] To eat Christ is to abide in him, ch. 136, book I. — To eat Christ is to believe in him, ch. 137, book I.

Christ’s person consists of and is constituted from God and man, ch. 138, book I.

Christ’s body is both sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, ibid.

In the sacrament we receive flesh covered by the form of bread, while we drink blood under the form and taste of wine, ch. 138, book I.

Christ’s flesh may be understood in two ways: either as spiritual and divine, of which he himself says, “My flesh truly is food,” etc.; or as that flesh which was crucified, ch. 139, book I.

By eating Christ’s flesh and drinking his blood, we signify the flesh and blood offered for us, ch. 142, book I.

Christ’s death, which happened once, occurs in our memory every year whenever Easter is celebrated; the annual commemoration represents what was done long ago and thus moves us as though we saw the Lord present on the cross, ch. 143, book I. — Christ was sacrificed once in himself, and yet is sacrificed daily in the sacrament, ch. 144, book I.

If anything drips from the Lord’s chalice through a priest’s negligence, what penance is to be imposed upon him, ch. 156, book I. — The chalice with paten must be made of gold, silver, or tin, ch. 161, book I.

The body of our Lord Jesus Christ was buried in a clean linen shroud, ch. 162, book I.

Emperor Constantine left the imperial see to blessed Peter and his successors, ch. 3, book II.

Constantine decreed that churches should be built and estates granted to them, ch. 3, book II.

The performance of indecent or lascivious songs near churches or in church courtyards is forbidden, ch. 54, book II.

The Roman Church receives the Council of Nicaea, the First Council of Constantinople, the First Council of Ephesus, and Chalcedon after the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, ch. 91, book II. — The Roman Church does not read the history of Cyricus and his mother Julitta, ch. 91, book II.

The eight holy councils are confirmed by the authority of the Roman pontiff, ch. 103, book II. — The canons of general councils began from the time of Emperor Constantine, ch. 104, book II. — Among the other councils, four synods are acknowledged to be venerable, which principally encompass the entire faith, like the four Gospels. — The Council of Nicaea is of the highest authority, ch. 104, book II.

Sixty Canons of the Apostles are to be received, ch. 105, book II.

Seventy decrees of the Council of Nicaea. — Eighty chapters of the Council of Nicaea were treated: forty published in Greek and forty in Latin; but, by the Fathers’ counsel, they were reduced to seventy in the pattern of the seventy disciples, ch. 106, book II. — Only twenty chapters of the Council of Nicaea are preserved in the Roman Church; through what neglect the rest were lost is uncertain, though many think that they were inserted into the Council of Antioch, ch. 107, book II.

The Second Ecumenical Council, Constantinople I, under the senior Emperor Theodosius, ch. 108, book II.

The Council of Naples, second after the Nicene Council, gave the creed its form for the Greek and Latin Church, ch. 108, book II.

The Council of Ephesus was held under the younger Theodosius against Nestorius, ch. 109, book II. — In Christ there is one person in two natures, ch. 109, book II.

The Council of Chalcedon: under whom and when it was held, ch. 110, book II.

The Fifth Ecumenical Council, Constantinople II: when and under whom it was held, ch. 111, book II.

The Council of Aquileia, because of ignorance of the faith, hesitated to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Council, ch. 112, book II.

The Sixth Ecumenical Council, Constantinople III: under whom they were held, ch. 113, book II. — The Sixth Ecumenical Council was accepted by Leo the Younger, ch. 114, book II.

The holy Sixth Synod confirms the canons of the holy Fathers, many synods both general and provincial, and the writings of certain doctors, ch. 117, book II. — The whole Church receives the Council of Sardica, ibid. — In ecclesiastical matters, the authority of the canons and decrees of the Roman pontiffs are to be preferred to the sayings of Augustine, Jerome, and others, ibid.

The sacred canons and decrees of the Roman pontiffs are preferred to the writings of holy doctors, ch. 118, book II. — After the sacred canons and decrees of Roman pontiffs, [Col. 1388] the sayings of holy doctors are to be held in high esteem, ibid.

When in canonical Scriptures you find something you did not believe, believe it without hesitation; but in the writings of others, do not hold firmly what you did not previously know to be certain unless you have understood it to be certain, ch. 120, book II.

The book of the Canons of the Apostles is apocryphal, chs. 123–124, book II. — The holy Fathers decreed that fifty chapters of the Canons of the Apostles should be joined to the rules of orthodox faith, ch. 124, book II. — The synod regards eighty-five chapters of the Canons of the Apostles as authentic and confirmed, ch. 125, book II.

Clerics are not altogether prohibited from reading secular literature, ch. 133, book II.

Diverse customs are not to be resisted when canonical authority does not stand against them, chs. 155–156, book II. — That custom is commended which assumes nothing contrary to faith, ch. 157, book II.

Contemptuous violators of ecclesiastical customs are to be restrained like transgressors of divine laws, ch. 158, book II.

If we were to esteem customs of the Church not transmitted by the Fathers through Scriptures as nothing, religion would suffer great harm, ch. 159, book II. — No Scripture has taught that the faithful should be marked with the saving sign of the cross, just as it has not taught many other things which we preserve through hand-to-hand tradition, ibid.

Custom is a kind of law established by practice, received as law when written law is lacking; nor does it matter whether it rests on reason or on written authority, ch. 161, book II. — A prior custom and the reason which commended it are to be maintained, ch. 162, book II.

If anything is done against an established custom, the governor shall restore matters to their customary practice, ch. 162, book II.

Custom, however ancient, ought not to prevail over reason or law, ch. 164, book II. — Bad custom must be avoided no less than a pernicious corruption, ibid. — Unless bad custom is uprooted very swiftly, it is venerated as law and assumed as a privilege, ibid. — Let custom yield to truth, ch. 165, book II. — Let no one set custom before reason and truth, ibid. — Reason and truth always exclude custom, ibid. — Custom must be subordinated to truth, ch. 166, book II.

Clerics are called “the Lord’s portion.” — The life of clerics ought to be distinct from lay conduct, not only in other matters but also in fasting, ibid., ch. 174, book II.

A person made lame by a physician’s incision is not barred from promotion to holy orders, ch. 46, book III.

Those freed by their patron without any retained obligation of service may enter the clerical order, ch. 46, book III.

No one who is illiterate or impaired in any bodily part may presume to be promoted to clerical order; understand this, as they teach, of one who cut himself, not of one cut by another, chs. 43, 44, and 47, book III.

Those castrated by physicians, barbarians, or their masters are not excluded from the clergy, ch. 56, book III. — A man who castrated or mutilated himself in order to cut off carnal desires is not to be admitted to the clergy; if he was previously promoted to the clergy, he is to be deposed from his ministry, ch. 56, book III.

Persons from overseas or unknown persons are not to be admitted even to the lowest clerical dignity unless they are identified by signed certificates from five bishops, ch. 63, book III.

No one may presume to judge or ordain a cleric belonging to another church. — A cleric expelled from his own church is not to be received by another, ch. 64, book III. — A cleric may not minister in a church other than his own without letters of recommendation, ch. 65, book III. — A cleric or layperson without letters of recommendation is not to be received in another church; otherwise, both the receiver and the person received are to be deprived of communion, chs. 65–66, book III. — Fugitive and itinerant clerics are not to be received or ordained by anyone without letters of recommendation, ch. 66, book III. — Clerics and monks without letters of recommendation are not to be free to wander about, ch. 67, book III. — A cleric may not transfer from church to church unless the Church’s welfare requires it, with a decree concerning him submitted to the bishops by clerics and laity and in the presence of a synod, ch. 70, book III. — Clerics or priests of lower rank may transfer to other churches with the permission of their bishops, ch. 70, book III. — A cleric may not be enrolled simultaneously in two churches, but must minister in the one in which he was initially ordained; nor may he flee to another as though to a better one out of desire for vain glory, ch. 73, book III.

Caiaphas, the killer of our Savior, ch. 79, book III.

No cleric may keep a woman introduced into his household, except perhaps his mother, sister, aunt, or other suitable persons, ch. 112, book III.

Anyone who says that it is not consecrations that are bought, but the things themselves which arise from [Col. 1389] consecration, is shown to be utterly foolish, ch. 123, book III.

No person coming from heretics may be appointed to any clerical dignity, even the least, ch. 130, book III.

What is done by excommunicated persons can in no way be called a consecration, ch. 133, book III.

The rule concerning clerical chastity established by Saint Leo is cited, ch. 135, book III.

A cleric convicted of or confessing adultery is to be confined in a monastery for his entire lifetime, having been deposed from office, chs. 143–144, book III.

Whenever divergent rulings are found in the acts of councils, the ruling of that council whose authority is judged older or greater is to be followed, ch. 149, book III.

A cleric who commits homicide by accident may, by dispensation, remain in his order, ch. 154, book III. — A cleric receiving usury is to be degraded, ch. 156, book III. — A cleric may not receive more than he lent, ch. 158, book III. — No cleric may receive more than he lent: if money, money; if goods in kind, goods in kind, ibid.

A cleric who lent money may receive goods in kind for it, provided they are at a just price, ch. 159, book III.

Clerics are not to go armed or take up military weapons; if they do so, they are to be punished by loss of their rank, ch. 168, book III.

Clerics who are charioteers or entertainers using obscene language are to be removed from office, ch. 172, book III. — A cleric occupied with treachery and flattery is to be degraded from office, ch. 173, book III.

Regard as a merchant rather than a monk any Christian whom you perceive always or frequently speaking to you about money—apart from almsgiving, which is open equally to all—ch. 175, book III.

The grant made by Emperor Constantine to blessed Sylvester and his successors, and the privileges conferred, ch. 1, book IV.

Two episcopal councils are to be held every year, ch. 13, book IV.

The authority to convene a council has been entrusted by special power to the Apostolic See. — We read that no general council is valid unless convened or supported by its authority, ch. 14, book IV.

Councils of bishops are to be held twice each year in every province: one after the third week following the feast of Easter, the other on the Ides of October, chs. 15–16, book IV.

When a council has assembled, the primacy of the metropolitan being preserved, the other bishops are to sit according to the date of their ordination, ch. 20, book IV. — Once a council has been convened, no case is to be introduced before matters concerning amendment of life, rigor of discipline, and remedy for the soul have been completed, ch. 21, book IV.

No cleric—whether deacon or priest—may plead any case before a secular judge, ch. 30, book IV. — *Curia* (“court”) is said to derive, as it were, from *cruor* (“blood”), ibid. — A cleric accusing a cleric in a secular court incurs anathema, ibid. and ch. 31. — No cleric is to be dragged before secular judgment, ch. 32, book IV.

Every case is to be heard within the province and decided by those of the province, ch. 33, bk. IV.

Clerics are not to be admitted in accusations against laypeople, nor laypeople in accusations against clerics, ch. 61, bk. IV.

An insult uttered by someone in anger is not to be treated as an accusation, ch. 74, bk. IV.

A case must always be tried where the crime was committed, ch. 75, bk. IV.

A cleric is not to be examined publicly except in church, ch. 89, bk. IV.—No one is to admit a cleric’s testimony against a layperson, nor may a layperson dare to bring a charge against a cleric, ibid.

The cunning quibbling of those who think that affairs should be conducted by crafty counsels has never borne the name of innocence, ch. 105, bk. IV.

A person unable to appear in a case on the appointed day is not to be suspended from communion, ch. 106, bk. IV.

No one is to be condemned before a true and just judgment, ch. 112, bk. IV.

Whenever judgment has been given against a contumacious person, the proceedings cannot be reopened by appeal, ch. 43, bk. V.—A sentence duly pronounced against a contumacious person, even if only fictively, is valid, ibid.

Contumacious persons who have been condemned cannot appeal, ch. 46, bk. V.

In things lent, an accidental loss is not chargeable unless fault intervened, ch. 67, bk. V.—A borrowed thing must be restored if the person to whom it was lent took it into battle or somewhere where danger to life is incurred, ch. 68, bk. V.

[Col. 1390] A contract made solely for the benefit of the person delivering the thing perishes at that person’s risk, ch. 69, bk. V.

By confession, come out, you who inwardly lie hidden within yourself through conscience, ch. 81, bk. V.—Therefore let the dead person come forth—that is, let the sinner confess the fault; and let the disciples loose the one who comes forth in such a manner that the shepherds of the Church ought to remove from him the penalty he deserved, since he is not ashamed to confess what he has done, ibid.

Whatever has been consecrated to God belongs by right to the priest, ch. 113, bk. V.—Whatever has once been consecrated to God shall be a most holy thing to the Lord and belongs by right to the priests, ch. 113, bk. V.—Whoever devastates or takes away what has been consecrated to God is sacrilegious, ibid.

Communion is not to be denied to those hanging on gallows, ch. 122, bk. V.

How proceedings are to be conducted against a contumacious person, ch. 124, bk. V.

No marriage is to be made without a dowry, and the dowry is to be made according to means, ch. 6, bk. VI.

They are called spouses from the first pledge of betrothal, even though marital intercourse between them remains unknown, ch. 15, bk. VI.

There was a faithful marriage between the most blessed Mary, our Lady, and Saint Joseph, although there had been, and was to be, no bodily union whatever, ch. 16, bk. VI.

Marriage is said to exist if anyone has intercourse with a woman betrothed and delivered to him, ch. 17, bk. VI.

Spouses ought to abstain from sexual intercourse on feast days and days of processions, and during the time of conception and childbirth, ch. 21, bk. VI.

Married persons owe one another fidelity, and also the service of accepting one another’s weakness, in order to avoid illicit intercourse, ch. 26, bk. VI.—To render the marital debt is no crime; but to demand it beyond the need of procreation is a venial fault, ch. 26, bk. VI.

Those who unite solely on account of incontinence are spouses, ch. 27, bk. VI.

Lust of the flesh is a shameful thing that resulted from sin, ch. 30, bk. VI.

A lawful marriage is not effected except by those who appear to have authority over the woman herself, ch. 31, bk. VI.—Clandestine marriages ought not to take place, ibid.—Marriages solemnly contracted are unquestionably lawful; those otherwise presumed are not marriages, but rather adulteries, irregular unions (*contubernia*), sexual defilements, or fornications than lawful marriages, ibid.

There are three lawful marriages, ch. 33, bk. VI.—A fourth marriage is lawful in addition to those three lawful kinds when, after his wife’s death, a man takes another woman who has neither been repudiated nor betrothed to another man, ch. 34, bk. VI.

What solemnities are to be observed in contracting marriage, ch. 36, bk. VI.

It has never been lawful, and never will be lawful, to keep concubines, ch. 13, bk. VI.—Whoever keeps a concubine while intending to obtain another wife is an adulterer in intention itself, chs. 44, 45, and 46, bk. VI.—No one is understood to have a concubine who habitually sleeps with many women, ch. 46, bk. VI.—A person who keeps a concubine as a wife is not to be excluded from communion, ch. 49, bk. VI.

A concubine is called a wife not solemnly taken, as the Gloss says in the chapter *Christiano*, Distinction 34.—Whoever keeps a concubine is to put her away and not communicate until he turns to penitence, ch. 49, bk. VI.

The marital bond is not broken by perpetual continence to be observed by the agreement of both spouses, ch. 75, bk. VI.

One spouse cannot vow perpetual continence unless both have done so, ch. 77, bk. VI.

Marriages ought not to be dissolved for the sake of religion, ch. 78, bk. VI.—Marriage may not be divided if the wife rejects the continence sought by the husband, ibid., ch. 78, bk. VI.

He who made fornication alone an exception did not will that a spouse be dismissed even for the sake of continence, ch. 79, bk. VI.

The more holy was your continuance together as spouses, the more holy were the mutually agreed observances which you kept, ch. 80, bk. VI.

Once man and woman have become one body through marital union, one cannot be converted in part and remain in the world in part, ch. 84, bk. VI.

A wife’s consent to vow continence to God ought not to be extorted by force or threats.—If a married man wishes to enter religious life, he is not to be received into a monastery unless he has first been released by his wife, who professes chastity, ch. 85, bk. VI.

A deceitful condition does not separate a contracted marriage, ch. 99, bk. VI.

That faithful spouses do not make use of the permitted liberty of leaving unbelieving spouses may be an occasion for the gain of many. —It is not expedient to leave unbelieving spouses.—Even unbelievers are spouses, and it is lawful for a believer to leave an unbeliever, ch. 100, bk. VI.—It is lawful, but not expedient, to depart from unbelieving spouses, ch. 101, bk. VI.

A person who has had relations with his stepdaughter or niece, etc., is never to be joined in marriage, ch. 121, bk. VI.

There is no marriage where there is no consent of both parties, even if father and mother have arranged and wished it.—No Christian ought to take his godmother (*commater*) in marriage, ch. 127, bk. VI.

Since we are commanded to abstain from our own blood-relations, it is all the more fitting that, with every occasion or pretext set aside, we guard ourselves under the most extreme restraint from the spiritual daughter of our father, ch. 126, bk. VI.—If anyone takes a spiritual godmother (*commater spiritualis*) as wife, let him be anathema, ch. 129, bk. VI.

The Lord commands that the countless troubles of spouses, should any arise, be borne courageously for the faith of marriage and for chastity, ch. 4, bk. VII.

The bond of marriage cannot be dissolved by fornication; for, even when divorce intervenes, the matrimonial covenant is not abolished.—It is neither then lawful, nor ever will be lawful, to pass into marriage from a living husband, ch. 6, bk. VII.

Marriage is forbidden to those who kill their own wives, ch. 15, bk. VII.

Charlemagne repudiated his first wife and took a second, by whom he had three sons and three daughters, ch. 25, bk. VII.

A confession extorted by force is not to be admitted in judgment, ch. 25, bk. VII.

It has been ordained that blood-relatives are not to be taken as wives, so that charity may extend itself more widely.—The union of male and female, insofar as it concerns humankind, is the seedbed of the state, ch. 52, bk. VII.

One may not marry the granddaughter of a person whose daughter one is likewise not permitted to marry.—Between which persons marriage may not be contracted, ch. 53, bk. VII.

Your son and the daughter of your sister cannot become spouses; this is the third degree, which appears also to be excluded from matrimonial union by civil law, ch. 54, bk. VII.—In marriage, the son or daughter of two brothers or of two sisters is not to be united; indeed, it is recognized that offspring cannot arise from such a marriage.—Marriage in the fourth generation is permitted, chs. 56–71, bk. VII.

A man may not have two godmothers (*commatres*) as wives, ch. 63, bk. VII.

The degree of consanguinity observed in respect of one’s own husband is likewise to be observed among the wife’s kindred, ch. 69, bk. VII.

No one is to be joined in marriage in the fourth or fifth generation, ch. 70, bk. VII.—The faithful may lawfully be joined in marriage in the fourth or fifth generation, ch. 71, bk. VII.—Saint Gregory granted the English permission to marry in the fourth or fifth generation until they should be strengthened in the faith, but not thereafter, ch. 72, bk. VII.—Consanguinity is observed as far as the sixth degree, so that, just as the world’s generation and every state end in six ages, so kinship of blood may be limited by the same number of degrees, chs. 73 and 75, bk. VII.—Saint Isidore holds that in lawful marriage one must abstain from consanguinity as far as the seventh generation, ch. 74, bk. VII.—The seven degrees of consanguinity are to be counted from son and daughter onward, as Saint Isidore says, ch. 75, bk. VII.

No one is to enter marital union within the seventh generation; if they do so, they are to be separated, chs. 76, 77, 78, 79, and 81, bk. VII.—Just as a Christian may not take a spouse from his own blood up to the seventh generation, so neither may he take a spouse from the blood-kindred of his wife, because of the unity of flesh, ch. 79, bk. VII.

No one is to reckon relatives except relatives and blood-kindred themselves; in their absence, however, older and more truthful persons to whom the relationship is known are to be consulted, ch. 84, bk. VII.

Christians ought to oppose things contrary to truth, ch. 15, bk. VIII.

The crimes which a person can correct but does not correct, that person himself commits, ch. 20, bk. VIII.

To punish crimes for God’s sake is not cruelty but piety, ch. 21, bk. VIII.

Charity works toward amendment and correction: if conduct is good, let it delight; if it is bad, let it be corrected, ch. 22, bk. VIII.

Catholics may seek defense against heretics from the constituted authorities, ch. 26, bk. VIII.

The army of Christians and Christian soldiers should strive to act manfully against enemies and adversaries of the holy faith and of all religions, ch. 30, bk. VIII.

[Col. 1392] King Charles undertook war against the Lombards at the urging of Pope Adrian, ch. 32, bk. VIII.

A person who slays cruel persons is not cruel, but appears cruel because he is severe toward those who suffer, ch. 49, bk. VIII.

What Caesar commands must be borne; what he orders must be endured. But it becomes intolerable when tax-collectors heap up exactions, ch. 60, bk. VIII.

Clerics or persons devoted to sacred offices ought not to be magicians or enchanters, nor make amulets (*philacteria*), which are proved to be bonds upon their souls, ch. 63, bk. VIII.

Whoever believes that anything can be done, or that any creature can be changed or transformed for better or worse into another kind or likeness, except by the Creator himself who made all things and through whom all things were made, is without doubt an unbeliever and worse than a pagan, ch. 75, bk. VIII.

## D

Ecclesiastical discipline is chiefly concerned to destroy whatever raises itself against the knowledge of Christ, or to build up what pertains to the edification of faith and the uprightness of morals, or to cleanse by remedies of penitence that which defiles it, ch. 2 of the Prologue.

The doctors of the Church are spiritual physicians and do not disagree either with themselves or among one another: when they prohibit unlawful things, command necessary things, commend the highest things, and grant indulgence for venial matters, ch. 3 of the Prologue.

No dispensation is to be admitted in matters in whose observance salvation is attained, or in whose neglect certain death follows, ch. 9 of the Prologue.—A dispensation, decided upon by the authority of the presiding authorities, may take precedence over the discipline of strictness, ibid.

In doubtful or obscure matters, we ought to follow that which is found neither contrary to Gospel precepts nor opposed to the decrees of the holy Fathers, ch. 10 of the Prologue.

The severity of discipline must not sleep in the face of a known crime, ch. 12 of the Prologue.

By a certain dispensation, some things condemned by the rigor of the canons are tolerated, chs. 21 and 22 of the Prologue.—By a certain dispensation, some things are tolerated so that we may not suffer the loss of everyone, ch. 23 of the Prologue.

Let the person who has authority grant a dispensation where necessity requires it for the Church’s benefit, ch. 29 of the Prologue.

Dispensations admitted by salutary deliberation ought themselves to cease when necessity ceases, ch. 29 of the Prologue.

The Godhead is not separate or divided in nature, as Arius blasphemes, ch. 1, bk. I.

God is good without quality; great without quantity; Creator without need; present without position; containing all things without external condition; wholly everywhere without place; eternal without time; making mutable things without any change in himself; and suffering nothing.—God is undoubtedly substance—or, if it is better so called, essence, which the Greeks call *ousia* (οὐσία), ch. 7, bk. I.

The dedications of churches and priests are to be solemnly celebrated every year, ch. 10, bk. II.—The dedication of a church is to be repeated when its consecration is doubtful, ch. 11, bk. II.—Places dedicated to God are to remain so forever and are not again to become secular dwellings, ch. 15, bk. II.

In celebrating divine offices, bishops of the same province are to observe the order maintained by the metropolitans, ch. 32, bk. II.

The tithes which God has ordained to be given are to be given to God, ch. 57, bk. II.

Those unwilling to pay tithes are to be excommunicated, ch. 58, bk. II.

Bishops and abbots are not to pay tithes from their own estates, ch. 59, bk. II.

Households are to bring tithes to those churches where their children are baptized and where they hear Mass throughout the year, ch. 59, bk. II.

Tithes are to be given to God and to priests, ch. 60, bk. II.

Tithes are demanded as a debt, ibid.

“Give me a tenth; I preserve nine for you. If you do not give me a tenth, I shall take nine from you,” ibid.

“If you give me a tenth, I shall multiply nine for you,” ibid.

Tithes are therefore to be given to God so that, being appeased by this devotion, God may grant more abundantly the things that are necessary, ibid.

Tithes are to be divided into three portions: one third is to be given to bishops and two thirds to clerics, ch. 61, bk. II.

Tithes are not to be redeemed by the people, ch. 62, bk. II.

Dionysius the Areopagite left many volumes pertaining to the Church’s benefit, ch. 95, bk. II.

[Col. 1393] Daniel and Moses were educated in Egyptian and Chaldean letters, ch. 133, bk. II.

On the Lord’s Day, with every veneration and observance, one must abstain from every unlawful work, ch. 170, bk. II.—On the Lord’s Day it is lawful neither to trade, judge, litigate, nor swear, ibid. and ch. 171, bk. II.—Three works may be performed on Sunday, ch. 172, bk. II.—On Sundays or feast days, from evening to evening, knees are not to be bent; rather, we must pray standing and bowed, ch. 73, bk. II.

A bishop may do nothing contrary to the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, ch. 3, bk. III.

Whatever has been most notably established by the Lord occurred on the Lord’s Day: on it the world took its beginning, on it death its end, and life received its beginning, ch. 13, bk. III.

Deacons and presbyters are to make a profession to their bishop that they will live chastely and piously, ch. 22, bk. III.

Deacons are not to be ordained before twenty-five years of age, even if they are very worthy, ch. 30, bk. III.

Deacons are to be ordained at twenty-five years of age, after first being tested according to the apostolic precept, chs. 31 and 32, bk. III.

When a deacon is ordained, the bishop alone is to lay his hand upon his head, ch. 34, bk. III.

Deacons are commanded to preach the New Testament, just as readers are commanded to preach the Old, ch. 41, bk. III.

The canons do not admit to the clergy a person who deliberately cuts off a finger or part of a finger; if it happens by accident, however, he may be admitted, chs. 43 and 44, bk. III.

Deacons and subdeacons are not to be compelled at their ordination to profess that they must abstain from intercourse with a lawful wife, ch. 86, bk. III.

If deacons declared at their ordination that they wished to enter marriage, they are to remain in ministry if they subsequently take a wife; otherwise not, ch. 87 and ch. 97, bk. III.

Deacons who have wives are not prohibited from being appointed to ministry if they are chaste, ch. 88, bk. III.

A deacon or presbyter found incontinent with his wife is to be removed from office, ch. 98, bk. III.

Those who, after the diaconate, wish to live with their wives are to lack both office and ecclesiastical benefice, ch. 101, bk. III.

Those who buy and sell God’s gifts are condemned, ch. 119, bk. III.

When you see someone blotting out sins by weeping, do not doubt that he obtains mercy in the sight of the Godhead; for he who came to redeem sinners with his blood despises no sinner who returns, ch. 147, bk. III.

Dioscorus was not condemned on account of the faith, but because he excommunicated Lord Archbishop Leo, says Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, ch. 7, bk. IV.

When a doubt arises concerning ecclesiastical law, recourse must first be had to the metropolitan and then to the primate, ch. 22, bk. IV.

Teachers, who are also called fathers, are to be borne with rather than reproved, unless they have erred in the right faith, ch. 38, bk. IV.

A doctor or pastor of the Church who departs from the faith is to be corrected by the faithful; but for blameworthy morals he is to be tolerated rather than rigorously constrained, chs. 40 and 41, bk. IV.

A doubtful matter is not to be decided until it has been demonstrated, ch. 113, bk. IV.

The goods of persons condemned for a capital crime belong to their relatives, not to the governor, ch. 55, bk. V.

A thing given by lawful instruments, even though it has been given to two persons, belongs nevertheless to the person who has possessed it upon delivery by the donor, ch. 66, bk. V.

How much and when someone is liable for damage, ch. 72 and the following four chapters, bk. V.

Wrongdoing occurs in three ways: through necessity, ignorance, or deliberate intent; the last of these is to be punished more severely than the first two, ch. 106, bk. V.

A woman betrothed to a man has received the name of spouse.—The deflowering of virginity does not make a marriage, but a marital agreement does, ch. 14, bk. VI.

A betrothed girl who is abducted is to be restored to her first fiancé, even if the abductor has used force upon her, ch. 19, bk. VI.

God does not require fulfillment if someone vows something belonging to another, but rather forbids the usurpation of another’s property, ch. 81, bk. VI.

Although the Lord showed that he was not obliged to pay tribute, he nevertheless paid it, lest he scandalize those whose eternal salvation he was promoting by accommodating himself to custom, ch. 100, bk. VI.

Those who stray from God, even if they have lived soberly, hold the first place among punishments, ch. 21, bk. VII.

A person loves his neighbor as himself if he leads any person whom he can—whether by the solace of beneficence, the instruction of teaching, or the restraint of discipline—to worship God, ch. 16, bk. VIII.

[Col. 1394] One loves one’s neighbor by not permitting him his evil will, but rather, where authority is given, by forbidding him evil and compelling him to good, ch. 77, bk. VIII.

Whoever dies in defense of Christians attains the heavenly kingdom, ch. 30, bk. VIII.

To disable the limbs of a robber or pirate benefits them, so that, their limbs being disabled—limbs which they previously used badly—they may cease from evil work, ch. 50, bk. VIII.

Those who seek divinations, or seek anything by magical art from such persons, are to undergo five years’ penance, ch. 62, bk. VIII.—There are many kinds of divination, ch. 66, bk. VIII.—A kind of divination is said to have been brought from Persia, ibid.—They say that there are four kinds of divination: earth, water, air, and fire; hence they call them geomancy, hydromancy, pyromancy, and aeromancy.—Diviners (*divini*) are so called as though filled with God; for they pretend to be full of divinity and, by a certain craft and fraud, predict future things to people, ibid.—The kinds of divination are art and frenzy, ibid.

The Devil, always lying hidden under a covering, betrays himself when he fabricates things that adhere to the persons through whom he strives to deceive, ch. 67, bk. VIII.

Because of the superior mobility of their aerial bodies, demons incomparably surpass not only the movements of any things, such as humans or beasts, but even the flight of birds, ch. 68, bk. VIII.—In respect of their aerial bodies, demons are endowed with such acuteness of sense and swiftness of motion that they foretell or report things known much earlier, which human beings marvel at because of the slowness of earthly perception, ch. 68, bk. VIII.—Demons also gain, through the very long period to which their life extends, far greater experience of things than can come to humans because of the brevity of life, ibid.—Demons not only predict many future things, but also perform many wonders through those powers allotted to the nature of an aerial body, ibid.

Those who profess, consult, or teach the knowledge of divination, auguries, or lots are to be held outside the Church, ch. 69, bk. VIII.

Divine oracles are not to be turned to secular affairs, ch. 74, bk. VIII.

To observe days, months, or years in such a way that one refuses to begin something on certain days or in certain months is a grave sin, chs. 80 and 81, bk. VIII.

The good God forgives everything if one repents from the whole heart, ch. 100, bk. VIII.

Deacons who take wives or keep concubines are to lack ecclesiastical office and benefice, ch. 142, bk. VIII.

We forbid, by apostolic authority, tithes to be possessed by laypeople.—Laypeople who hold tithes, whether from bishops or kings, incur the crime of sacrilege and the danger of eternal damnation unless they restore them to the Church, ch. 145, bk. VIII.

## E

The translations of bishops were once strictly forbidden by apostolic sanctions; later they were permitted for the greater benefit of the Church, ch. 26 of the Prologue.—Many translations of bishops from one city to another have occurred because of necessity and the advantage of the times, as is proved by many examples, ch. 28 of the Prologue.

That many bishops were deprived of their sees and later restored is proved by many examples, ch. 29 of the Prologue.

The Church is holy and catholic because it believes rightly in God, ch. 55, bk. I.

Translations of bishops are not permitted, ch. 83, bk. I.

Churches concerning whose consecration there is uncertainty may be consecrated without hesitation, ch. 93, bk. I.

Bishops are to purchase balsam from their own resources, ch. 98, bk. I.

A presbyter must always have the sacred Eucharist ready for the sick.—Formerly the Eucharist was given to infants, ch. 148, bk. I.

What remains of the sacred Eucharist is not to be kept until the next day, ch. 149, bk. I.—Augustine neither praises nor condemns receiving the Eucharist daily, ch. 150, bk. I.—Augustine urges reception of the Eucharist on Sundays, provided that the mind is not disposed toward sinning; if anyone is so disposed, he is burdened rather than purified, ibid.—How one approaching the Eucharist may do so fearless and secure, ibid., ch. 150, bk. I.—Every believer, unless held by a crime, is to receive the Eucharist each year at Easter, Pentecost, and Christmas, chs. 151–152, bk. I.—A person about to receive the Eucharist is to abstain from his own wife for three, four, or eight days before receiving it, ch. 152, bk. I.

The Eucharist is not to be administered to actors or to magicians persisting in vice, ch. 133, bk. I.—The Eucharist [Col. 1395] is not to be entrusted to a layman or woman for carrying to the sick, ch. 154, bk. I.

A presbyter is to convey the Eucharist to the sick in person; if he does otherwise, he incurs peril to his rank, ch. 154, bk. I.—If anyone vomits the Eucharist through drunkenness or gluttony: if a layperson, cleric, monk, or deacon, let him do penance for the same number of days; if a presbyter, for seventy days; if a bishop, for ninety; but if this occurs through illness, let him do penance for seven days, ch. 155, bk. I.—If a mouse or another animal eats the Eucharist, the priest is to do penance for forty days; and for thirty days if he loses it, or if a part falls and is not found, ch. 157, bk. I.

*Ecclesia* is a Greek word which in Latin means “convocation,” and why it is called “catholic,” ch. 1, bk. II.

Kings and governors supplied the means from which churches were built and the poor maintained, ch. 2, bk. II.

Emperor Constantine bestowed immense gifts upon churches, ch. 3, bk. II.

The founders of basilicas have no authority over the property which they conferred upon churches; that authority belongs to bishops, ch. 4, bk. II.

Those who presume to retain things given or bequeathed by will to churches are to be excommunicated and regarded as killers of the poor, ch. 5, bk. II.

A new church is not to be dedicated without the bishop’s designation and without an endowment, ch. 6, bk. II.

Church offerings and revenues are to be divided into four portions: one for the bishop, another for the clerics, a third for the poor, and a fourth for the fabric or maintenance of the building, chs. 7, 8, and 9, bk. II.

A church and its endowment are under the bishop’s authority, ch. 12, bk. II.

Church consecrations ought not to take place without Mass, ch. 13, bk. II.

When a church once consecrated to God is to be consecrated again, and when it is not, ch. 14, bk. II.

Timber from dedicated churches must not pass into lay use, ch. 16, bk. II.

In a consecrated church, an altar is not to be erected without the bishop’s permission, ch. 17, bk. II.

Churches or altars whose consecration is doubtful are to be consecrated, ch. 18, bk. II.

It is not lawful to celebrate Mass in a church in which the bodies of unbelievers are buried; it is lawful, however, if an altar had previously been consecrated there, ch. 19, bk. II.

A church is to be consecrated anew if its altar has been moved; but if the walls, rather than the altar, are altered, it is only to be exorcised with salt, ch. 20, bk. II.

A church violated by homicide or adultery is to be consecrated anew and purified, ch. 21, bk. II.

A church in which a pagan has been buried may neither be consecrated nor have Mass celebrated in it, ch. 22, bk. II.

A church in which the bodies of unbelieving dead are buried may not be sanctified, ch. 23, bk. II.

If individual priests have churches, let each have one and not more: a most excellent and holy rule, but very badly observed, ch. 43, bk. II.

A priest is to be content with the one church to which he has been ordained, ch. 43, bk. II.

One church cannot be divided between two priests, ch. 44, bk. II.

Those who violate church boundaries are to be excommunicated, ch. 81, bk. II.

Ecclesiastical censure is to restrain those who attempt violently to oppress freed persons, ch. 84, bk. II.

Church property may not be alienated, ch. 85, bk. II.

A gift or sale of ecclesiastical property made by a bishop without the subscriptions of the clerics is void, ch. 86, bk. II.—An imprudently made exchange of ecclesiastical property is to be corrected by successors, ch. 87, bk. II.

If gold, silver, jewels, or movable goods accrue to churches, they may not be alienated, ch. 88, bk. II.

Nothing is to be read or sung in church unless it is of divine authority or has been approved by the authority of orthodox Fathers, ch. 89, bk. II.

One book of Ezra is numbered among the canonical books, ibid.

Augustine approves Eusebius’s book concerning times, ch. 94, bk. II.

The letter of Jesus to Abgar is apocryphal, ch. 123, bk. II.

A bishop is not to read books of the gentiles.—He may, however, read books of heretics when necessity and circumstances require it, ch. 130, bk. II.

The alms pleasing to God are those spent from permitted and honestly acquired goods, not those from unlawful goods, ch. 191, bk. II.

There are three kinds of almsgiving: one bodily, which is given to the needy; another spiritual, forgiving the person by whom one has been injured; and a third, correcting the offender and restoring the erring person to the way of truth, ch. 192, bk. II.—There are two alms: one of the heart, namely forgiving that by which you have been injured; the other of money, ch. 193, bk. II.—The alms of charity suffices without earthly substance; but an alms given bodily does not suffice at all if it is not bestowed with a kindly heart, ch. 193, bk. II.—It is not to be regarded as almsgiving if what is received from unlawful goods is distributed to the poor; for one who receives badly with the intention of distributing well is burdened rather than helped, ch. 194, bk. II.

No one is to be chosen bishop unless he is found to be living religiously in holy orders, ch. 5, bk. III.

No bishop is to be ordained over unwilling persons who do not ask for him, lest an unwilling people despise or hate an unwanted bishop, chs. 6 and 7, bk. III.

Clergy and people are not to choose a bishop from another church rather than their own unless a worthy person cannot be found there.—No layperson may dare to interfere in the election, promotion, or consecration of bishops, chs. 1 and 8, bk. III.

A person who has obtained the episcopal office by royal appointment is not to be received by the bishops of his province, ch. 9, bk. III.

A bishop is to be consecrated by three bishops of the same province, chs. 10, 12, 15, 16, and 17, bk. III.—Episcopal ordinations are to be celebrated on the Lord’s Day, at the third hour, with sacred anointing, by all bishops in the same province, ch. 12, bk. III.

What the pontiff, notary, and deacon ought to do in a bishop’s ordination, ch. 14, bk. III.

A bishop is in no way to be ordained by fewer than three bishops, with all the rest giving consent, ch. 17, bk. III.

When a bishop is ordained, two bishops are to lay hands on him and hold the book of the Gospels over his head and crown, while one pronounces the blessing over him, ch. 18, bk. III.—The bishop being ordained and the bishop ordaining are alike to celebrate Mass, ch. 19, bk. III.

Two bishops must not presume to consecrate a third, ch. 20, bk. III.

No one may presume to ordain a bishop before he is thirty years old, ch. 28, bk. III.

When an exorcist is ordained, he is to receive from the bishop’s hand a booklet in which the exorcisms are written, together with what more the bishop is to say, ch. 37, bk. III.

The office of bishops, presbyters, and others in the Church of God, ch. 41, bk. III.

Some eunuchs have intercourse, possess fluid, and emit semen, but it is empty and incapable of generation, ch. 57, bk. III.

Persons possessed by spirits (*energumenoi*) are not only not to be admitted to the clergy; if discovered, they are to be removed from office, ch. 59, bk. III.

If a bishop is to be transferred, this is to occur by apostolic authority, not from ambition, but for utility or necessity, ch. 68, bk. III.

Transfers of bishops may occur because of common necessity or utility, not by the personal wish or lordship of any individual, ch. 69, bk. III.—A bishop is not said to be transferred from city to city, nor from a lesser to a greater one, when he does this not by his own choice or ambition, but from some necessity or utility, at the urging and counsel of superior persons. Nor is one transferred from a lesser city to a greater who does this neither from ambition nor by his own will, but has been transferred and enthroned by others, with the authority of this holy see, not proudly but humbly, whether by force, having been driven from his own see, compelled by necessity, or for the benefit of the place or people, ch. 69, bk. III.

Bishops have regular authority to ordain bishops and other priests whenever utility or necessity compels, in the manner stated above; they also have authority to transfer and enthrone them, but not without the authority of the most holy Roman see, ibid.

A bishop is not to pass from an undistinguished see to a distinguished one out of ambition, ch. 70, bk. III.

How a bishop, presbyter, or deacon condemned by a synod, if found innocent at a second synod, ought to be restored, ch. 80, bk. III.

The ordination of bishops must take place in the prescribed order, ch. 82, bk. III.—Whoever receives the words of bishops receives their Lord; and whoever despises them despises him by whom they were sent and whose embassy they carry out, and is himself despised by the Lord, ibid.

Bishops hold the place of the apostles, and presbyters that of the seventy disciples, ch. 83, bk. III.

The Synod of Nicaea appeared to introduce a law requiring bishops, presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons not to sleep with the wives they had married before consecration; the venerable confessor Paphnutius opposed it and prevailed, so that they should not be continent, ch. 85, bk. III.—Bishops, deacons, and presbyters ought to be continent, ch. 93, bk. III.—Bishops, presbyters, and ministers of the altar may not take wives, ch. 106, bk. III.

[Col. 1397] A bishop or presbyter is not to put away his own wife for the sake of religion, ch. 113, bk. III.

Bishops, presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons may not cast off their own wives from their care, but should instead provide them with food and clothing; they are not, however, to lie carnally with them as a matter of habit, ch. 115, bk. III.

Any bishop, presbyter, or abbot who buys or sells a benefice is to be deposed from it and is to be anathema, ch. 116, bk. III.

Those are buyers in God’s temple who, while wishing to pay their neighbor what is just, despise a thing owed by law and, having paid a price to patrons, purchase sin, ch. 119, bk. III.

A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who takes a woman or keeps one whom he has taken is to be deprived of office and benefice, chs. 138, 139, and 140, bk. III.

A bishop captured by Saracens who kills Saracens not voluntarily is in no way canonically judged, because he did not kill voluntarily, ch. 155, bk. III.

A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who exacts interest is to be condemned or deprived of communion, ch. 157, bk. III.—A bishop, presbyter, or deacon is not to keep dogs or hawks for hunting; if he does otherwise, what penalty he is to incur, ch. 167, bk.

III.

The bishop of a city ought to show monasteries the necessary care and solicitude, ch. 167, book III.

Bishops and presbyters should take as their example the apostolic men, whose offices they possess, and should strive also to possess their merit, ch. 175, book III.

Bishops should frequently visit monasteries of monks and nuns and correct whatever needs correction, ch. 215, book III.

A bishop summoned by the metropolitan to a council, unless prevented by grave bodily illness or a royal command, is to be deprived of communion if he scorns to come, chs. 17 and 18, book IV. — A bishop whom serious necessity prevents from attending a council to which he has been summoned should send a representative in his place, ch. 19, book IV.

Anyone accusing a bishop before first meeting him privately and personally is to be deprived of communion, ch. 36, book IV. — The people must not accuse a bishop, nor must the common crowd rebuke him, because the disciple is not above the master, ch. 36, book IV. — Bishops are to be judged by God, who chose them as eyes for himself, ibid. — Bishops are not to be rebuked, accused, or assailed by their subjects, or by persons of depraved life, ibid. and ch. 37, book IV.

The rulers of the Church are to be judged by the Lord, according to the saying: “But God judges in the midst,” ch. 40, book IV.

If anyone buys something from a slave without the owner’s knowledge, the owner may repay the price, and the purchase shall not stand, ch. 50, book IV.

No one ought to buy a beast of burden or any animal unless he knows the person selling it, ch. 71, book V.

Bishops and presbyters who do not understand this passage, “I will give you the keys,” etc., assume something of the Pharisees’ arrogance, so as either to condemn the innocent or to imagine themselves able to absolve the guilty; whereas with God it is not the learning of priests but the life of the accused that is sought, ch. 85, book V.

When the Church excommunicates, the excommunicated person is bound in heaven; when the Church reconciles, the reconciled person is loosed in heaven, ch. 86, book V.

Let no one despise ecclesiastical bonds: it is not a human being who binds, but Christ, who gave this authority and made human beings worthy of so great an honor, ch. 88, book V.

What the care of bishops ought to be toward wrongdoers, and how they ought to deal with and excommunicate them, chs. 90 and 91, book V.

The form of excommunication and the words by which an excommunicated person is denounced and declared, ch. 92, book V. — Those may communicate with an excommunicated person who associate with him for this reason: to recall him from error and urge him to make satisfaction, ibid. — One must not communicate with excommunicated persons; otherwise one will oneself be excommunicated, chs. 94, 95, 103, book V. — Whoever knowingly speaks or prays together with an excommunicated person, even in a house, is to be deprived of communion, chs. 95, 96, and the following three, book V.

A person excommunicated by one bishop must not be received into communion by another bishop, chs. 100, 101, 102, book V.

Excommunicated priests who have dared to handle the sacraments are to be assigned penance: for three years they are to fast completely from either wine or meat on the second, fourth, and sixth days of every week, chs. 104 and 105, book V.

Those communicating with excommunicated persons are to be punished, some more lightly and some more severely, ch. 106, book V. — Those who communicate with excommunicated persons are to be punished according to the measure of their sin, ch. 107, book V.

Blessed Pope Innocent excommunicated the Emperor Arcadius because he consented to the removal of Saint John Chrysostom [Col. 1398] from his see, ch. 109, book V. — Blessed Ambrose, though holy, was not bishop of the universal Church; nevertheless, he excommunicated the Emperor Theodosius the Great and excluded him from the Church, ibid.

Pope Julius excommunicated Theodore and Augustus, ibid.

Charibert, king of the Parisians, was excommunicated by Blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris, because he had taken two sisters as wives, ibid.

We are not bound by an obligation of fidelity to excommunicated persons, ch. 110, book V. — No one is compelled to keep faith with excommunicated persons, ch. 111, book V.

Anyone may excommunicate for one of three crimes, ch. 112, book V.

Let those be excommunicated who do evil to pilgrims or to the envoys of any saint, ch. 114, book V. — Whoever violates a truce or peace established by the bishops of a province is to be subject to excommunication, ibid.

Many persons are excommunicated after death, and who they are, ch. 116, book V. — An excommunicated person who hastens to repentance but cannot find a priest should not have the bond of excommunication refused to him, ch. 120, book V.

At their death one should not withhold alms from persons with whom we did not cease to communicate during their life, ch. 123, book V.

One who unlawfully excommunicates another: by what penalty he is to be punished, ch. 124, book V.

Wives, children, sons, maidservants, slaves or bondsmen, as well as peasants and servants, etc., who share in intercourse with excommunicated persons are not excommunicated, ch. 125, book V.

What punishment bishops deserve who excommunicate innocent persons or persons guilty of only the smallest offenses, ch. 128, book V.

If anyone unlawfully excommunicates another, he condemns himself, not the other person, ch. 129, book V. — Let no one, moved by rage, excommunicate anyone, ch. 130, book V.

An excommunicated person cannot excommunicate another, ch. 133, book V.

Once a bishop teaches the faith of the Church, he may excommunicate another, ch. 134, book V.

Persons excommunicated by heretics are not regarded as excommunicated, ch. 135, book V.

Whoever delays for a year in pursuing the cause of his excommunication thereby renounces his hearing, ch. 136, book V.

She is an abandoned wife who is cast out while her husband is living, ch. 68, book VI.

The holy Church of God is never bound by worldly laws; it has no sword but the spiritual one, by which it does not kill but gives life, ch. 14, book VII.

The bishop as the Lord’s vicar, ch. 51, book VII.

Enormous crimes are to be punished by secular judges, ch. 5, book VIII.

Bishops and archbishops should receive investiture from the emperor, but consecration from those from whom it is due, ch. 136, book VIII.

The more elegantly Isaiah prophesied concerning the Lord, the nearer he is read to the Lord’s birth, ch. 137, book VIII.

A person excommunicated by his own bishop is not to be received by another, ch. 139, book VIII.

Whoever communicates with an excommunicated person is held liable under the same sentence, ch. 139, book VIII.

Bishops and clerics should endeavor to please God and human beings in the disposition of their minds and the bearing of their bodies, ch. 140, book VIII. — Bishops and clerics should not offend the sight of those to whom they ought to be an example and model by extravagance, cut, or color of clothing, nor by their tonsure, ibid.

No one is to plunder the goods of deceased bishops, ch. 141, book VIII. — The goods of deceased bishops are to remain freely at the disposal of the steward or clerics for the use of the Church and of the bishop’s successor, ibid.

Bishops, presbyters, deacons, or subdeacons, regular canons, monks, converts, and professed religious who have taken wives are to be separated from them, ch. 143, book VIII.

Every church, if its resources permit, should have its own priest, ch. 146, book VIII.

If anyone takes refuge in a church or cemetery, no one may drag him away, under pain of anathema, ch. 150, book VIII.

The Church of God does not await, by hereditary right according to the flesh, any successor; rather, for its governance and the administration of its offices, it requires honorable, wise, and religious persons, ch. 151, book VIII.

No one may presume to claim or demand ecclesiastical prebends, provostships, chapels, or any ecclesiastical offices by hereditary right; if anyone presumes to do so, he is to be deprived of what he has sought, ch. 152, book VIII.

## F

Profession of faith, ch. 1, book I.

The Son assumed flesh, not the Father nor the Holy Spirit, so that he who, in the divinity of God the Father, was the Son of God, might himself become [Col. 1399] in humanity the Son of Man; nor was the name “Son” to pass to another who was not a son by birth, ch. 2, book I. — The Son is true God and true man, ch. 2, book I.

The Son is one according to Godhead and humanity, not two sons nor two Christs. — The Son remains one in two natures, not confused or mixed, as the Timotheans maintain, but united in fellowship. — The Son of God was born from a human being (a woman), and not through a man; that is, not from intercourse with a man, as Ebion says, but drawing flesh from the Virgin’s body and not bringing it with him from heaven, as Marcion, Origen, and Eutyches affirm. — The Son had a rational soul of his own and flesh with its own senses, through which he endured real sensations of the pains of his flesh in his Passion and before the Passion. — The Son always existed: eternal God, man born of the Virgin, chs. 3 and 4, book I.

The faith of those by whom an infant is presented for baptism benefits infants.

The faith of one benefits another, ch. 12, book I. The same, chs. 13 and 14, book I.

The sacrament of faith makes an infant a believer, ch. 56, book I.

The mystery of faith can profitably be believed; it cannot profitably be investigated, ch. 128, book I.

No one may dare to drag away anyone fleeing to a church, to a church courtyard, or to the workshops of regular brethren. — No cleric may dare either to remove or beat a slave or pupil fleeing to a church, chs. 75, 76, and 77, book II.

A person fleeing into the church courtyard, enclosed within thirty paces, is not to be dragged away unless security has first been given, ch. 78, book II.

It can happen that, without any fault of greed or gluttony, a wise person uses the most costly food, while a foolish person burns with the foulest flame of appetite for the meanest food; and it is healthier for anyone to prefer, following the Lord’s example, to eat fish than lentils, following Esau, Abraham’s grandson, or barley, following beasts of burden, ch. 195, book II.

The sons of presbyters are to be excluded from the sacred mysteries unless they have been proved to live religiously in monastic communities, ch. 51, book III.

Profession of the true faith by Cyril against the heretics Eutyches and Nestorius, and their followers, ch. 132, book III.

Do some work, so that the devil may always find you occupied, ch. 178, book III.

Those uncertain in the right faith cannot accuse, ch. 65, book IV.

Theft is not committed without an intention to steal, ch. 53, book V. — A person does not commit theft who gives away or sells fruit which he thinks belongs to his maidservant, ibid.

A son is presumed legitimate if he is born in the seventh month from a lawful marriage, ch. 61, book V.

Each surety is to pay what falls to him in proportion, ch. 70, book V.

The hand of one who mints false coin is to be cut off, ch. 70, book V.

Anyone who is aware of theft, or receives goods offered from theft, is to be reckoned among the thieves, ibid., ch. 70, book V.

The Lord commands that a brother—that is, a Christian—who sins against us first be privately corrected; then rebuked with witnesses; and finally publicly confronted in the assembly of the Church, ch. 91, book V.

The Roman pontiff deposed the king of the Franks, not so much for his own wrongdoings as because he was unfit for so great a power; and he substituted in his place Pippin, father of Emperor Charles, ch. 109, book V.

Fornication is permitted to no one with impunity, ch. 4, book VI.

Women are veiled when they marry so that they may know that they ought always to be subject and humble toward their husbands, ch. 8, book VI.

The bearing of children by women is the sole cause of marrying, chs. 24 and 25, book VI.

Happy is the necessity that compels one toward better things, ch. 81, book VI.

A madman and a madwoman cannot contract marriage; but if marriage has been contracted, they are not to be separated, ch. 92, book VI.

Between spiritual children and brothers there is a certain holy communion, which ought rather to be regarded as spiritual kinship than called blood relationship, ch. 123, book VI.

A legal marriage cannot take place between spiritual children, ibid. — More appropriately called my father’s son or my brother is he whom divine grace, rather than human will, chose to be his son or my brother; and they are more wisely separated from another bodily union, ch. 123, book VI.

A woman who lifted a godchild from the sacred font is not to be separated from her husband, ch. 124, book VI. — A man who held a godchild before a bishop is to be separated from his wife, ch. 125, book VI. — Men who hold godchildren before a bishop are not to be separated from their wives, ch. 126, book VI.

[Col. 1400] Those who received their own children from the holy washing by some accidental occurrence are to be separated from their wives, ch. 127, book VI. — A spiritual daughter can in no way marry a natural son, ibid.

The Lord permitted a wife to be dismissed on account of fornication; but because he permitted it, he did not command it, ch. 20, book VII. — Wherever there is fornication or suspicion of fornication, a wife may freely be dismissed, ch. 7, book VII.

Thefts must not be committed with the intention of feeding holy poor persons, ch. 20, book VII.

Human beings are never permitted to commit fornication, ch. 36, book VII.

Fornication of the flesh is adultery; fornication of the soul is slavery to idols, ch. 27, book VII. — Fornication of the mind is more detestable than fornication of the flesh, ch. 28, book VII. — Fornication is idolatry and every harmful superstition, ch. 29, book VII.

It is permitted to dismiss a fornicating wife, and the wife through whom a husband is compelled to commit fornication, ch. 30, book VII. — A wife who compels her husband to sacrifice to idols is dismissed on account of fornication, ibid.

That women should serve men is the natural order among human beings.

That children should serve parents and the younger should serve the older is the natural order among human beings, ch. 43, book VII.

The law has ordained women to be subject and almost servants, ch. 45, book VII.

Two full brothers may take two sisters as wives, ch. 60, book VII.

Women who fraudulently held their children before a bishop for the reception of chrism are not to be separated from their husbands, but are to do penance as long as they live, ch. 65, book VII. — A man who took his goddaughter as wife, or married a spiritual co-mother (*commater*), and one who baptized his own son, and one whose wife he received from the font, are to be separated and punished with severe penalties, ch. 66, book VII.

Courage that either defends one’s homeland from barbarians in war, or at home defends the weak or companions from robbers, is full of justice, ch. 34, book VIII.

Faith accepted for the purpose of committing sin ought not to be called faith, ch. 98, book VIII.

If an adulteress does not keep faith with an adulterer as she should keep marital faith, faith is not violated, ch. 97, book VIII.

The form of fidelity, and the six things to be observed in it: safety, security, honorableness, usefulness, ease, and possibility, ch. 122, book VIII.

No one is permitted to speak falsely; but it is sometimes useful to keep some true thing silent, ch. 131, book VIII.

## G

Pope Gelasius wrote five books against Nestorius, two against Arius, and others, ch. 98, book II.

Pope Gregory wrote forty homilies on the Gospels, ch. 99, book II.

Knowledge of grammar and dialectic is not disapproved, ch. 135, book II. — Geometry, arithmetic, and music possess truth within their own disciplines; nevertheless, that knowledge is not the knowledge of piety, ibid. — The teaching of grammarians can benefit life when it is taken up for better uses, ch. 136, book II.

Everyone ought to bend the knee at the solemnities of Mass only in Lent and in the fast of the Four Seasons. — Let no one presume to pray with one knee bent, as the Jews are read to have done in mockery of the Lord during his Passion, ch. 183, book II.

Those who do not exercise freely the grace which they receive from God are sellers of doves, ch. 124, book III.

If a gentile dismisses his gentile wife before baptism, after baptism it is within his power to keep or not keep her, ch. 97, book VI.

Gentile women serve their husbands by the common law of nature, ch. 40, book VII.

A person uses the sword who, without any superior and lawful authority commanding or compelling him, arms himself against someone’s blood, ch. 44, book VIII.

Genethliacs are so called because they consider natal days. — Genethliacs attempt to foretell people’s character, actions, and fortunes from their nativities through the twelve signs of heaven, according to the courses of the stars; that is, under what sign a person was born, or what outcome of life belongs to one born at such a time, ch. 66, book VIII.

## H

To heretics coming to the Church only lay communion is to be granted through the laying on of hands, ch. 16, prologue. — Heretics coming to the Church should not be admitted even to the lowest clerical rank, ch. 16, prologue.

Pope Gregory orders those returning from the Nestorian heresy to be received in their ranks, ch. 19, prologue.

The heresy of Arius, ch. 1, book I. — The heresy of Sabellius, ch. 1, book I. — The heresy of the Timotheans. — The heresy of the third party, the Apollinarists. — The heresy of Marcion. — The heresy of Origen. — The heresy of Eutyches. — The heresy of Valentinus. The heresy of the Aorchori. The heresy of Marcian and Apollinaris, ch. 3, book I. — The heresy of Artemon, the heresy of Beryllus, the heresy of Marcellus, ch. 4, book I. — The heresy of Dionysius, source of Arius. — The heresy of Eunomius. — The heresy of Ethni. — The heresy of Arius. — The heresy of Macedonius. — The heresy of Mani. — The heresy of Melito. — The heresy of Tertullian. — The heresy of the Anthropomorphites. — The heresy of Vadianus. — The heresy of Origen. — The heresy of Fortunatus. — The heresy of Marcion. — The heresy of Plato. — The heresy of Tertullian. — The heresy of Origen. — The heresy of Sabellius. — The heresy of Sylvanus. — The heresy of Praxeas. — The heresy of the Pentapolitans, ch. 5, book I.

The heresy of Nestorius, ch. 6, book I and ch. 109, book II. — The first heresy arose among Christ’s disciples when he said: “Unless anyone eats my flesh,” etc., ch. 133, book I.

The heresy of Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit is God, is condemned at the second Nicene synod, the First Council of Constantinople, ch. 108, book II. — The heresy of Eutyches, who maintained that the Word of God and the flesh have one nature, is condemned, ch. 110, book II.

The Son is *homoousios* (“of the same substance”) in the divinity of the Father; the one Son is *homoousios* with God and humanity; the Holy Spirit is *homoousios* with the Father and the Son, ch. 6, book I.

Horoscopists are so called because they observe the hours of human births by varied and differing practice, ch. 66, book VIII.

When the host is broken, the sacrifice of the Lord’s body on the cross is signified; and when the blood is poured into the mouths of the faithful, the outpouring of his blood from his side is signified, ch. 140, book I.

The part of the host placed in the chalice represents the body that rose again; the part eaten, the body still walking upon earth; the part remaining on the altar until the end, the body lying in the tomb, ch. 141, book I.

As many whole offerings are to be offered at the altar as ought to suffice for the people, ch. 149, book I.

The Ecclesiastical History, written by the Greeks Theodoret, Sozomen, and Socrates, is very necessary, ch. 92, book II.

Jerome was rebuked by an angel because he read a book of Cicero, ch. 131, book II.

To heretics coming from places where they were baptized, only lay communion is to be granted through the laying on of hands; nor may anyone among them be promoted to the clergy, ch. 58, book III.

Although heretics unlawfully use the sacraments of Christ’s Church, they are nevertheless sacraments, ch. 78, book III.

No one may receive a repentant heretic unless the bishop of that place has reconciled him, ch. 128, book III.

One who has lost honor cannot confer honor, ch. 130, book III.

Those returning from heretics must be reordained, ibid.

If a heretic who has joined himself to heretical perversity wishes to return to Catholic communion, he must first renounce his errors and their authors; then he is to be received in the rank in which he was, without any promotion, ch. 131, book III.

Anyone who promotes to sacred orders persons returned from heretics incurs no light offense before the Lord, ch. 131, book III.

Heretics may not bring accusations against orthodox bishops in ecclesiastical matters, ch. 73, book III.

We call heretics both those who were formerly cast out of the Church and those whom we have afterward anathematized, ibid.

Heretics are called those who pretend the sound faith or refuse to confess it, ibid.

A heretic may accuse another heretic and bear witness against him, ch. 28, book V.

The testimony of a heretic is valid on behalf of an orthodox person, but not against an orthodox person, ibid.

A delay is to be granted to murderers in civil cases or in lesser crimes, ch. 42, book V.

Grandchildren through a son and grandchildren through a daughter succeed equally to the inheritance of a grandfather or grandmother, ch. 58, book V.

Heretics are to be excommunicated even after death, ch. 115, book V.

Church tradition wills that even dead heretics be excommunicated, chs. 116 and 117, book V.

The inheritance of property, established by legal definitions, extends the succession of heirs to the seventh degree; for they would not succeed unless it were owed them from the stock of kinship, ch. 81, book VII.

We do not regard as murderers those who, burning with zeal for the Catholic mother against excommunicated persons, have happened to kill some of them, ch. 11, book VIII.

Saint Peter committed a double homicide, ch. 18, book VIII.

[Col. 1402] A person who kills another in obedience to authority is not guilty of homicide, ch. 35, book VIII.

To kill a human being is sometimes not a sin: as when one does this by virtue of office, when a soldier kills an enemy, a judge or officer a criminal, or when a weapon happens to fly from someone’s hand unwillingly and unknowingly. Such persons do not seem to me to sin when they kill a human being, ch. 38, book VIII.

An officer of a judge is a murderer if he kills voluntarily a person whom the judge or the law ordered to be killed, ch. 39, book VIII.

When this man is killed, the law kills him, not you, ch. 41, book VIII.

To punish murderers, sacrilegious persons, and poisoners is not the shedding of blood, but the administration of the laws, ch. 53, book VIII.

Hydromancers are named from water: hydromancy consists in looking into waters to summon the shadows of demons and see images of their deceptions, and there hear something from them; by using blood, they are also said to raise the dead from the underworld, ch. 65, book VIII.

Herod shamefully promised a reward to the dancing girl, and cruelly paid it, ch. 101, book VIII.

In Herod it is shameful that a kingdom is promised for a dance, and cruel that a prophet’s death is given under the religious pretext of an oath, ibid.

## I

What is not known to have been done is not shown to have been repeated, ch. 11, book II.

Ecclesiastical rights cannot be dissolved by an imperial judgment, ch. 140, book II.

An emperor, or anyone maintaining piety, may do nothing contrary to evangelical, prophetic, and apostolic rules, ch. 141, book II.

Some ecclesiastical institutions are established by Scripture; others by apostolic institution, confirmed through successors in ministry; and others strengthened by custom, ch. 159, book II.

The incontinent are to be deprived of every ecclesiastical honor, ch. 137, book III.

They are to be called infamous persons, ch. 66, book IV. — Such are those who cast aside the rule of Christian law and despise ecclesiastical ordinances, ibid.

No one ought to be tried or condemned before the formal accusation, ch. 77, book IV.

An infamous person can be neither an advocate nor a legal representative, ch. 78, book IV.

In a trial four things must always be present: the persons involved—namely, chosen judges, qualified accusers, defenders, and lawful witnesses, ch. 81, book IV.

What is to be observed and considered in a trial, ch. 82, book IV.

No infamous or sacrilegious person, however humble or servile the Christian may be, may dare to accuse any Christian, ch. 92, book IV.

What must be sought in a trial, ch. 94, book IV.

A reprieve of six months is to be granted to bishops accused of crimes, chs. 101 and 102, book IV.

A substantial delay for investigation is to be granted, lest anything seem to be done hastily, ch. 103, book IV.

In a trial questioning should be repeated frequently, lest something that ought to be added perhaps remain omitted, ch. 104, book IV.

Unless matters are proved by manifest evidence, they are not to be believed, even if true, chs. 113 and 114, book IV.

A person of ill repute who, after a third warning, does not correct himself is to be suspended from office until he clears himself, ch. 1, book V. — A presbyter is to be suspended until worthy satisfaction has been made, ch. 2, book V.

If a presbyter has been defamed in connection with a bishop’s death and reliable accusers are lacking, his full benefices are to be restored, ch. 7, book V.

A person who has exposed his own infant cannot later reclaim it from one who has undertaken to nourish it, ch. 52, book V.

A freeborn person is one who is free immediately upon birth, ch. 60, book V.

A freeborn person is one born of a free mother and a slave father, ibid. — So also is one who had a free mother when born, even though she conceived while a slave, ibid.

One born illegitimately follows the status of the mother, ch. 64, book V.

Marriage cannot be contracted between a free person and a slavewoman, or between a slave and a free woman, ch. 10, book VI.

If unfaithfulness is fornication, idolatry unfaithfulness, and greed idolatry, then there is no doubt that greed also is fornication, ch. 29, book VII.

To repel injury and not inflict it is the law of virtue, ch. 58, book VIII. — Whoever does not repel an aggressor from his companion when able to do so is as much at fault as the person who acts, ibid.

Incantators are so called because they perform their art by words, ch. 66, book VIII.

[Col. 1403] Secular laws pronounce persons born of incest infamous and exclude them from inheritance, ch. 153, book VIII.

Arsonists are declared to be excommunicated, ch. 154, book VIII.

The plague of fire and hostile devastation surpass every other kind of plundering; no one is ignorant how destructive it is to God’s people and how much injury it inflicts upon souls and bodies, final chapter, book VIII.

Against the disaster of fire, one must altogether rise up and labor, so that so great a ruin may be rooted out and destroyed for the people’s safety, ibid.

If an arsonist dies, he is to be deprived of ecclesiastical burial and is not to be absolved unless he first restores, according to his means, the loss he inflicted, ch. 154, book VIII.

If after this promulgation anyone sets fires, or causes them to be set, from evil purpose, hatred, or vengeance, or knowingly gives counsel and aid to those setting them, he is to be excommunicated, final chapter, book VIII.

## J

To swear in human contracts out of necessity is not evil; but whoever does not swear is farther removed from perjury than one who swears on any occasion whatever, ch. 9, prologue.
