The life of our Lord Jesus upon earth is moral instruction, ch. 9, prologue.

It is in the judge’s power to soften a sentence and judge more mildly than the laws, ch. 16, prologue.

We have divine law in the Scriptures, human law in the laws of kings, ch. 63, book II.

By human law everyone possesses what he possesses, ibid.

By divine law the earth and its possession belong to the Lord, ch. 63, book IV.

By human law this estate is mine, this house is mine, this slave is mine, ibid.

God has distributed human laws to humankind through emperors and kings of the world, ibid.

Take laws away from the emperor, and who would dare say, “That estate is mine; that slave is mine”? ibid.

Possessions are held through the laws of kings. Therefore do not say, “What have I to do with the king?” What then have you to do with a possession? ibid.

The Emperor Justinian condensed two thousand Roman laws into fifty books, ch. 145, book II. — He called the new laws which he himself enacted the *Code of Novels*, ibid. — He removed contradictory rules, ch. 146, book II.

Law comes from what is unwritten and has been approved by use, ch. 160, book II.

Let clerics fast seven full weeks before holy Easter, ch. 174, book II. — During all seven weeks, clerics should abstain from meat and luxuries and endeavor day and night to cleave to the Lord by hymns, vigils, and prayers, ch. 174, book II.

No one ought to observe a fast on the Lord’s Day or Thursday, and why, ch. 176, book II. — We ought not to omit Saturday, because it seems enclosed between the sorrow and joy of that season, ch. 177, book II.

Fasts or abstinences were decreed to be observed in each month, except July and August because of their weakness, ch. 178, book II. — The fourth and sixth days are not to be relaxed without some necessity, ch. 179, book II.

When the fasts of the Four Seasons are to be observed in March and in other months if the Kalends of March fall on Wednesday or earlier, ch. 185, book II.

Let your fasts be daily, and your meal avoid satiety, ch. 185, book II.

If fasts are compensated by fullness, it does you no good to carry an empty stomach for two or three days if it is afterward stopped up, ibid.

Let fasts be pure, continuous, and moderate: that is, to be hungry every day and to eat every day, ch. 186, book II.

A hungry stomach and sparing food are preferable to three-day fasts, ch. 187, book II.

A fast is despised when it is refreshed in the evening by a filling of food, ch. 188, book II. — It is perfect when our outward person fasts and the inward person prays, ch. 189, book II.

On days of fasting, alms are to be given, and the food and drink which each person would have used had he not fasted should be distributed to the poor, ch. 190, book II.

To fast and save the food of lunch for supper is an increase not of reward but of food, ch. 190, book II.

To sell justice is to preserve it in return for receiving a reward, ch. 119, book III.

Judges ought to employ equity, witnesses truth, and accusers intent, to enlarge the case, ch. 81, book IV. — Whoever is thought to evade judgment by delays thereby confesses everything, [Col. 1404] ch. 105, book IV. — Judgment is not to be evaded, ibid.

A presumption arises against one who evades judgment by delays, ch. 107, book IV.

Judges ought to be such that they are free from every suspicion and desire to pronounce their judgment from the root of charity, ch. 108, book IV.

The judges ought to be those chosen by the person accused, or those appointed by the holy see, ch. 109, book IV.

Before accepting an accusation, judges ought first to establish with what intention each person has acted deceitfully, ch. 110, book IV.

A judge is not to pronounce a capital sentence before the accused either confesses or is convicted, ch. 111, book IV.

Matters which are uncertain are in no way to be judged, ch. 113, book IV.

Unless matters are proved by manifest evidence, they are not to be believed, however true they may be, chs. 113 and 114, book IV.

Although Judas was a thief, because he was not accused he was not expelled; rather, whatever he did among the apostles, he remained by virtue of the dignity of his ministry, ch. 115, book IV.

Matters are not to be judged, even if true, unless they are established by manifest proof and publicly set forth in judicial order, chs. 114 and 115, book IV.

It is not the judge’s role to condemn without an accuser, ch. 115, book V.

Let the judge investigate carefully before he hears, rather than doing anything precipitately, ch. 116, book IV.

We ought not to judge or condemn anyone before true and just proof, ibid.

It is not the judge’s role to condemn without an accuser, ch. 117, book IV.

A manifest case does not require judicial procedure, ibid.

Before passing sentence, the judge ought to examine, question, investigate, and set everything forth, chs. 119 and 120, book IV.

No judgment is to be made until both sides have completed their pleadings, ibid.

Let a presbyter swear by his holy consecration, ch. 10, book V. — Priests ought not to swear for a trivial cause, lest the hand by which Christ is consecrated be defiled by an oath, ibid.

No cleric may dare to swear upon the holy Gospels; rather, he should use simple speech: “yes, yes; no, no,” ch. 11, book V.

The Lord cast down Judas, although he was a lying disciple and not lord of the apostles, ch. 12, book V.

Judgment must not be demanded in a case that has been settled or judged, ch. 46, book V.

Those who follow either their own hatreds or favors in the cases of their subjects cannot judge worthily concerning those subjects, ch. 80, book V.

A case adjudicated between persons present cannot be reopened after ten years, ch. 10, book V.

A case adjudicated between absentees cannot be reopened after twenty years, ibid.

Judges should not readily permit low and unworthy persons to approach an oath, ch. 24, book V.

Within a year from the day of filing, judges ought to grant a delay if the accuser or accused asks for one, ch. 41, book V.

Law comes from what is unwritten and has been approved by use, ch. 59, book V.

Whoever calls the just unjust, and conversely the unjust just, both are abominable before God, ch. 84, book V.

What the oath of separation from a woman with whom someone has committed adultery or fornication ought to be, ch. 40, book VII. — What the oath for reconciliation with an adulterous spouse ought to be, ch. 41, book VII. — What the oath for reconciliation with an adulterous husband ought to be, ch. 42, book VII.

The form of the accuser’s oath, ch. 86, book VII.

The oath of witnesses, ch. 87, book VII.

The formula of the oath of reconciliation, ch. 88, book VII.

A judge is not the author of a crime, nor [is he such] by convicting persons, ch. 52, book VIII. — He is called a judge because he declares law to the people, or because he adjudicates according to law, ch. 54, book VIII. — He is no judge if justice is not in him, ch. 54, book VIII.

To judge justly is to adjudicate according to law, ibid.

This principle of law obtains: whatever anyone does for the defense of his body is deemed to have been done lawfully, ch. 56, book VIII.

Whoever departs this life righteous remains righteous, ch. 67, book VIII.

Whoever serves Jewish superstitions or festivals is to be separated from the Church, ch. 72, book VIII.

It is permitted to take an oath for a covenant of peace, ch. 83, book VIII.

An oath which results not from the evil of the person swearing but from that of the unbeliever by whom he is compelled to swear is not contrary to God’s commandment, chs. 84 and 88, book VIII.

[Col. 1405] That the Lord prohibited swearing is to be understood thus: so far as lies within each person, one should not swear, ch. 84, book VIII.

The Apostle swore when he said, “I die daily by your glory, brethren,” ibid.

Not to swear at all was said in the New Testament, not because swearing is a sin, but because perjury is an enormous sin, ch. 85, book VIII.

Although an oath is not good, it is nevertheless necessary in order to persuade another person of what you usefully urge upon him, ibid. and ch. 89, book VIII.

The Savior did not forbid swearing by God, but swearing by heaven, earth, and one’s head, ch. 87, book VIII.

Swearing had been permitted by the Law, not because they did this rightly, but because it is better to render this to God than to idols or demons, ibid.

Things ratified by an unlawful oath must be rescinded, not fulfilled, chs. 90, 91, book VIII.

Holy David swore, and preferred not to do what he had sworn rather than fulfill his oath by shedding a man’s blood, chs. 92, 93, book VIII.

An oath by which an evil thing is rashly promised is not to be kept; but, when necessity presses, it is preferable to commit perjury rather than, by changing one perjury into another, be diverted into a graver crime, ch. 94, book VIII.

David swore and incurred perjury, but did not grieve over it, ibid.

For one who has sworn, it is better to commit perjury than to keep an oath involving the breaking of holy images, chs. 98, 99, book VIII.

Herod kept his oath and perished; Peter denied with an oath, then turned and wept and was saved, ch. 100, book VIII.

A false oath is dissolved, as having no force at all, ch. 100, book VIII.

Children below the proper age are not to be compelled to swear, ch. 103, book VIII.

One who has committed perjury cannot be a witness, ibid.

Boys are not to be compelled to swear before their fourteenth year, ch. 104, book VIII.

The oath by which a girl in her childhood binds herself in her father’s house is of no force if, as soon as he learns of it, her father annuls it, ch. 105, book VIII.

The oaths of a son or daughter made without their father’s knowledge, and those of a monk made without his abbot’s knowledge, are void, ch. 106, book VIII.

If another person provokes you to swear, the fact that you swear will arise from his evil, not from your own, ch. 107, book VIII.

One who provokes another to swear and knows that he will swear falsely is worse than a murderer: for the murderer is going to kill a body, whereas that man kills a soul—indeed, two souls, both that of the person whom he provoked to swear and his own, chs. 108 and 110, book VIII.

If someone swears falsely, judgment must be made by persons who are more able to help than to harm through the perjury, ch. 109, book VIII.

One who demands an oath from someone whom he does not know will swear falsely does not sin, ch. 110, book VIII.

A person swears rashly if he thinks true what is false, or thinks false what is true, ch. 111, book VIII.

A false oath is a detestable beast and must be banished from human affairs, ch. 111, book VIII.

He is perjured who swears as true what he thinks false, even if what he swears is true, ibid.

Whatever verbal art a person may use in swearing, God, who is the witness of conscience, takes it in the sense in which the person to whom the oath is made understands it, ch. 112, book VIII.

One who swears falsely is guilty in two ways: because he takes the Lord’s name in vain and deceives his neighbor, ch. 112, book VIII.

An oath by which an evil thing is rashly permitted is not to be kept, chs. 113, 118, book VIII.—It is more tolerable not to fulfill it than to persist in the disgrace of fornication, ibid.

God’s swearing is that providence by which He determines not to undo what He has established, ch. 114, book VIII.

To swear is nothing other than to render what is due to God, ch. 115, book VIII.—To swear by one’s children is to pledge them to God, so that what proceeds from the swearer’s mouth may come upon their heads, ch. 115, book VIII.

One who swears falsely upon a stone is perjured, ch. 116, book VIII.—It is permissible to rely upon the pledge of one who swears by demons in order to keep it, ch. 117, book VIII.

He who swore by those by whom he ought not to have sworn—namely, by false gods—and acted contrary to his pledged faith by doing what he ought not to have done, certainly sinned twice. Accordingly, one who relies on the pledge of the person who swore by false gods, and does so not for evil but for what is lawful and good, does not share in the sin of the person who swore by demons, but in the good agreement of the person who kept faith, ch. 117, book VIII. [Col. 1406]

To swear truthfully by false gods is a lesser evil than to swear deceitfully by the true God, ibid.—Perjury is punishable in proportion as that by which one swears is more holy, ibid.

When we are compelled to swear, we offend the Creator and merely stain ourselves; but when we fulfill harmful promises, we both despise God’s commands, injure our neighbors by impious cruelty, and slaughter ourselves with the more cruel sword of death, ch. 119, book IV.

He who must swear upon holy things should swear fasting, with all honesty and fear of God, chs. 120, 121, book VIII.

An oath ought to have three companions: truth, judgment, and justice, ch. 123, book VIII.

## L

A change of law occurs from necessity, ch. 29 of the prologue.

The privileges of a few do not make a common law, ch. 29 of the prologue.—Whatever the emperor has established by letter, decreed after taking cognizance, or commanded by pronouncement, is held to be law, ch. 30 of the prologue.

Civil laws are sometimes inserted among the canons, not so that an ecclesiastical judge may condemn anyone by them, but so that he may learn what penance a crime deserves when, under those laws, it is punished by mutilation of limbs or death, ch. 31 of the prologue.

What the first book together with the other seven contains, ch. 32 and the following chapters to the end of the prologue, ch. 32 of the prologue.

Presbyters are to give chrism without receiving anything for lights, ch. 98, book I.

Let them purchase lights for each of their own churches, ch. 89, book I.

The Church is to protect persons lawfully manumitted, chs. 82, 83, book II.

The canonical books received by the Church, ch. 89, book II.

Which books are to be read in the Church and at what time, ch. 90, book II.

We read some things lest we neglect them; we read lest we be ignorant; we read not in order to retain, but in order to reject, ch. 134, book II.

Imperial law is not to be used in every ecclesiastical controversy, ch. 138, book II.

Imperial laws sometimes conflict with evangelical enactment, ibid.

The law of emperors is not above the law of God, but beneath it, ch. 130, book II.

The Church often uses the laws of emperors against heretics and tyrants, ch. 140, book II.

Imperial laws are not to be rejected altogether; only those which seem to conflict with evangelical, apostolic, and canonical decrees are to be set aside, ch. 140, book II.

What sort of thing law ought to be, and with what circumstances it should be endowed, ch. 142, book II.

Laws may be judged when they are being enacted; but after they have been enacted and confirmed, a judge may not judge the laws themselves, but must judge according to them, ch. 143, book II.

That which the emperor establishes by letter, decrees after taking cognizance, or commands by edict is held to be law, unless it was done for a specific person; for then it does not extend beyond that person, ch. 147, book II.

The laws of emperors and pontiffs must be observed, ch. 149, book II.—The rules of princes or Fathers may not be disregarded, ch. 150, book II.—The laws of Roman rulers are to be observed not only in human affairs but also in matters concerning reverence for blessed Peter, ch. 151, book II.

Roman law must not be corrupted by anyone’s rashness, ch. 152, book II.

It is permissible to employ imperial laws in aid of the Church, ch. 153, book II.

Whoever does not obey imperial laws issued for God’s truth incurs great punishment; conversely, he gains great reward if he does not obey laws issued against God’s truth, ch. 154, book II.

When a reader is ordained, the bishop shall address the people concerning him, indicating his faith, life, and character; he shall hand him the codex, and [the chapter states] what further the bishop is to say to him, ch. 38, book III.

Laymen who had wives at the time of baptism are not forbidden to be admitted to the clerical estate if, after baptism, they have lived religiously and devoutly, ch. 45, book III.

A layman who, after his wife, has known another woman is not to be admitted to the clergy, ch. 62, book III.

When readers reach the years of puberty, they are to be compelled either to take wives or to profess continence, ch. 111, book III.

Those who have fallen cannot be restored to their order, chs. 145, 146, book III.

[Col. 1407] We believe that one who has fallen can return to honor after worthy satisfaction, ch. 147, book III.

Those who have fallen may be restored after worthy satisfaction, ibid. and ch. 148, book III.

We believe that priests of the Lord who have fallen, and the rest of the faithful, can return to honors after worthy satisfaction, ibid.

The shedding of tears restrains the passion of the mind; once satisfaction has been made, the mind turns away from anger, ibid.

After a fall, who can return to their former rank and honor, and who cannot, ch. 119, book III.

We call gain shameful when someone, not from necessity but from greed, buys grain or wine at harvest-time or vintage and keeps it until it can be sold, ch. 162, book III.

The luxurious game of tables, a seedbed of sins, is to be avoided at all times, ch. 171, book III.

A layman ought not to accuse a cleric in a secular court, ch. 31, book IV.—No one may bring an accusation against either a bishop or anyone in orders, ch. 90, book IV.

Dismissory letters are commonly called apostolic letters, ch. 128, book IV.

We receive secular laws in our judgment because ecclesiastical and divine laws receive them, ch. 44, book V.

Praetors ought to prohibit everyone from acting as a procurer, ch. 56, book V.

The instruments and surety agreements of procurers, made contrary to good morals, are invalid, ch. 57, book V.

A person born legitimately follows the father; one not born legitimately follows the mother, ch. 62, book V.

He deprives himself of the power of binding and loosing who exercises it according to his own wishes and not according to the conduct of those subject to him, ch. 79, book V.

A lawful wife is she concerning whom, after touching the divine Scriptures, an oath is made that she will be held as a lawful wife, ch. 79, book VI.

Freedom is not to be congratulated when it results in there being no obligation to render what is returned with profit, ch. 81, book VI.

What is lawful is expedient when it is permitted not only on account of justice before God, but also when it causes no impediment to human salvation; but what is lawful is not expedient when it is indeed permitted, yet the exercise of that power brings an impediment to others’ salvation, ch. 101, book VI.

King Lothair sought, by deceitful artifices, to put away Queen Theutberga as though she had not been his lawful wife, ch. 24, book VII.

Every law has the image of God, ch. 44, book VII.

All laws, ecclesiastical as well as secular, forbid the shedding of human blood, ch. 24, book VIII.

In the old law the penalty of retaliation was commanded; in the new, however, that we offer the other cheek to one who strikes one cheek, ibid.

Human and divine laws must be abolished if, as some suppose, no person is either to be restrained from evil or drawn back to good, ch. 36, book VIII.

A rule which is not just does not seem to me to be a law, ch. 38, book VIII.

The art of physicians does not commend bindings as execrable remedies, whether in incantations, characters, or any things whatsoever that are hung up or bound; in all these things is the art of demons, arising from a baneful association of human beings and evil angels. Hence all such things must be avoided by a Christian and utterly rejected and condemned with every execration, ch. 67, book VIII.

The order of books that must be observed in the ecclesiastical office, which books are to be read, and at what time, ch. 137, book VIII.

Laymen who hold churches must either restore them to the bishops or be subject to excommunication, ch. 145, book VIII.

## M

The rank of marriage is voluntary, not necessary, ch. 6 of the prologue.

The rank of marriage and perfection of life must be considered before they are undertaken; after they are undertaken, one must persevere in them, ch. 6 of the prologue.

The experience of many diseases compels the discovery of many remedies, ch. 8 of the prologue.

All commands and prohibitions are to be observed in the same way as everything enacted by the eternal law, ch. 9 of the prologue.

Monks are not to kiss women, ch. 8, book I.

Mass is not to be celebrated except in places consecrated by bishops, or where they themselves permit it, ch. 30, book II.

Mass may be celebrated in a burned church or basilica with a consecrated altar-board until the church itself is restored, ch. 31, book II.

[Col. 1408] Unless an urgent necessity intervenes, Mass is not to be celebrated except in places consecrated to the Lord, ch. 33, book II.

It is not permitted to celebrate Mass in a private oratory, ch. 39, book II.

Mass is not to be celebrated before the third hour, ch. 49, book II.

Until the Mass of the catechumens, no one—whether heretic or Jew—is to be forbidden to enter the church, ch. 41, book II.

One book of Maccabees is counted among the canonical books, ch. 89, book II.

That the most blessed Mary had as her father a certain priest from the tribe of Levi, named Joachim, is not canonical, ch. 128, book II.

Moses and Daniel were educated in Egyptian and Chaldean letters, ch. 133, book II.

Where the authority of divine Scripture establishes nothing, the custom of God’s people and the institutions of the elders are to be held as law, ch. 158, book II.

Long-standing customs approved by the consent of those who use them imitate law, ch. 160, book II.

They are often changed by the tacit consent of the prince or by another law enacted by the community for itself, ibid.

Custom is a practice approved by antiquity, or unwritten law, ch. 161, book II.

A mind filled to excess becomes sluggish, and the watered soil of this body produces thorns and thistles, ch. 185, book II.

Within three months of his consecration, a metropolitan must send to the apostolic see to declare his faith and receive the pallium, ch. 11, book III.

No one is to hear the Mass of a presbyter whom he knows beyond doubt to have a concubine or an introduced woman, ch. 135, book III.

No monk may establish either monasteries or a house of prayer without the permission of the bishop of the city, ch. 174, book III.

Monks who dwell in city monasteries or upon monastic estates must be subject to the bishop of the city, ch. 174, book III.—They must not mingle in popular crowds, ch. 175, book III.—Let them have as leaders of their vocation Pauls and Anthonys, Julians, Hilarys, and Macarii; possess the simplicity of the dove, devise snares against no one, and the cunning of the serpent, lest you be overthrown by their traps, ibid.

A monk does not hold the office of a teacher, but of a mourner, one who laments either himself or the world, ch. 176, book III.—He must avoid the sight of women, especially young women, and discipline himself so greatly as to fear even things that are safe, ch. 176, book III.

Moses, in order to benefit the Jewish people, was educated for forty years in the wilderness; a shepherd of sheep, he became a shepherd of human beings, ch. 177, book III.

Egyptian monasteries have this custom: they receive no one without work and labor, not so much for the necessities of sustenance as for the salvation of the soul, lest they wander in harmful thoughts and, like Jerusalem the harlot, spread their legs to every passer-by, ch. 178, book III.

If Mother Church requests any works from monks, they are neither to undertake them greedily from pride nor reject them in indolence that flatters them, but are to obey God with a gentle heart and meekness, ch. 179, book III.

Monks are not to place their own leisure above the necessities of the Church, ibid.

A bad flute-player is a good accompanist, ch. 180, book III.

“It is commonly said: a bad monk is a good cleric,” ibid.

“It is commonly said: a good monk scarcely makes a good cleric,” ibid.

A monk’s vocation, undertaken by his own choice, cannot be abandoned without sin, ch. 182, book III.

Military service, if innocent, may be an honorable marriage; nevertheless, to abandon the better choice is a transgression, ch. 182, book III.

No one is to become a monk before a probation of one year, ch. 183, book III.—An unknown person is not to become one before being tested for three years, ch. 184, book III.—One made a monk before the lawful years is to persevere in monastic life if his parents do not object within a year, ch. 185, book III.

A woman who changes her dress for the sake of continence is to be anathematized if she takes male attire, ch. 213, book III.

What penalty is owed by a woman who cuts off her hair, ch. 214, book III.

Persons of lower rank cannot condemn their superiors, ch. 17, book IV.

A metropolitan must not presume to handle the causes of others without the counsel of his fellow-provincials, ch. 20, book IV.

[Col. 1409] A metropolitan is to do nothing in the province of a suffragan bishop without that bishop’s counsel, ch. 29, book IV.

The confession of ministers must not be extorted, but voluntary, ch. 118, book IV.

Metropolitans and fellow-provincial bishops may hear bishops’ cases, but may not decide them, chs. 134, 135, 136, book IV.

One who contracts an incestuous marriage and has no legitimate children from an earlier union is to be deprived of his goods, and the goods from the incestuous marriage are to be claimed by the treasury, ch. 57, book V.

Long-standing customs approved by the consent of those who use them imitate law, ch. 59, book V.

When holy men pronounce a sentence of curse, they utter it not from a desire for vengeance but from the judgment of justice, ch. 82, book V.

Holy Scripture mentions a curse in two ways: one which it approves and another which it condemns, ibid.

Apostolic mercy customarily grants pardon to those who have been corrected, ch. 104, book V.

It is a miserable madness if a son seeks to subject his father, or a disciple his teacher, to himself, and to make him subject to his own power by unjust bonds—the very person by whom he believes that he can be bound and loosed not only on earth but also in heaven, ch. 108, book V.

We cannot admit to communion after death those whom we did not admit while they were living, chs. 118 and 136, book V.

Marriage is the union of man and woman comprising an indivisible partnership of life, ch. 1, book VI.

That woman with whom no nuptial rite is celebrated does not belong to marriage, ch. 23, book VI.

She who is given to a man who has a concubine is joined in lawful marriage, ch. 35, book VI.

Marriage between a freedwoman and her patron is lawful, ch. 37, book VI.

A slave may lawfully contract marriage, ch. 38, book VI.—A marriage between slaves whom their master has joined remains valid if one is freed while the other remains a slave, chs. 39 and 40, book VI.

Their masters cannot dissolve marriages lawfully made by slaves, ch. 40, book VI.

There is marriage between a free man and a female slave whom he knew to be such and approved, ch. 41, book VI.—There is no marriage between a freeborn man and a female slave whom he did not know to be such, if he cannot redeem her, ibid.—There is marriage between a freeborn woman and a slave whom she knew to be such, ch. 42, book VI.—Cohabitation makes her a free woman, ch. 48, book VI.

Courtesans may choose a better life even if they have sworn to remain in that most wretched profession, ch. 58, book VI.

A courtesan is a woman open to the lust of many men, ch. 68, book VI.

Mothers wishing to have guardianship of their children must first swear not to enter another marriage, ch. 69, book VI.

Mothers who choose other marriages ought not to administer the guardianships of their children, ibid.

A woman will be infamous if, before a year has elapsed after her husband’s death, she enters into a second marriage, ch. 70, book VI.—A woman who has no children by her first husband will not be infamous even if she marries a second husband before a year has elapsed after the first husband’s death, ibid.—A woman who marries a second time is not to enjoy the privileges of her first husband, ch. 71, book VI.—A woman who has guardianship of her children and wishes to enter a second marriage must first request a guardian for her underage children, render an account of her administration, pay any debt owed to them, and then marry whom she wishes, ch. 72, book VI.

One who has permitted a woman to be veiled is not to take another woman, but is likewise to be converted, ch. 82, book VI.

A woman whose husband was led into captivity and who married another man must be reunited to the first husband when he returns, ch. 86, book VI.—A woman who marries another thinking that her husband has died in war is compelled, when he returns, to return to him, chs. 87, 88, and 89, book VI.—Nor is she to be judged blameworthy or considered, beforehand, an invader of another’s right because she assumed the role of the wife of a husband believed no longer to exist, ibid.—What necessity has brought about must be dismissed and judged blameless; what fidelity demands must be restored, ibid.

Those who contracted a marriage while sound may have their marriages dissolved on account of great sickness or mutilation of their limbs, ch. 93, book VI.

A believing woman who has an unbelieving husband, if he consents to live with her, must not put him away, ch. 94, book VI.

Many things are to be done not at the law’s command but from free charity; and those things in our duties are more pleasing which, though we were permitted not to render them, we nevertheless render for the sake of love, ch. 100, book VI.

Marriage is contracted by consent and is not rendered invalid because the custom of one’s country is not observed, ch. 102, book VI.

For marriage, the consent alone of those whose union is at issue suffices; if this alone is lacking, all else, even when celebrated with intercourse itself, is in vain, ch. 107, book VI. [Col. 1410]

Marriage is made not by intercourse but by will, as the great Chrysostom testifies, ibid.

No woman is to be joined in marriage against her will, ch. 109, book VI.

There is no marriage if someone contracts with a female slave whom he thought free, ch. 110, book VI.—Error concerning status vitiates it, ch. 110, book VI.

A woman may repudiate a husband who, because of natural incapacity, is unable to have intercourse with his wife for two continuous years, ch. 113, book VI.

A woman who, joined in marriage, proves that her husband cannot know her carnally is to take another husband, chs. 114, 115, and 118, book VI.

Persons prevented by sorcery from having intercourse are to be helped by prayers, alms, and fasts, not by magical art, ch. 117, book VI.

If a woman says that her husband has not had intercourse with her, and the husband says that he has, the husband’s statement is to prevail, because the man is the head of the woman, ch. 119, book VI.

One who keeps a courtesan is foolish and unjust, chs. 7 and 8, book VII.

“You shall not commit adultery,” that is, no one after marriage is to have intercourse with other women in order to satisfy lust, chs. 23 and 51, book VII.

Woman was not made in the image of God, but man was, ch. 44, book VII.

Woman is subject to man in all things: she can neither teach, give faith, nor judge, ch. 49, book VII.—She must veil her head because she is not the image of God, but so that she may be shown to be subject, ch. 51, book VII.

Through woman transgression began, ibid.

It is not ours to accept death, but willingly to receive it when inflicted by others, ch. 3, book VIII.

A sentence of death, once pronounced, is not to be carried into execution until after thirty days, ch. 10, book VIII.

He is not merciful who spares and indulges vices so as to sustain the will of sinners, ch. 15, book VIII.

He did not prohibit military service to those whom he commanded to be content with their own pay, chs. 42, 45, book VIII.

He who strikes evil people insofar as they are evil is a minister of the Lord, ch. 51, book VIII.

Military service is not a crime, but to serve as a soldier for plunder is sinful, ch. 60, book VIII.

Certain wages have been established for soldiers, lest, while they seek expenses, plunder should rage, ibid.

To soldiers, guards, and all rulers who receive publicly decreed pay, this saying of John can be addressed: “Extort from no one, make no false accusation, but be content with your wages,” ch. 60, book VIII.

Whether the tricks of magicians are true or imaginary, ch. 65, book VIII.

Things done through magical tricks are fabricated rather than accomplished by their reality, ibid.

Magicians are those commonly called *malefici* (“evil-doers”) because of the magnitude of their crimes, ibid.—By God’s permission, they shake the elements, disturb the minds of persons less trusting in God, and kill by the force of incantation alone, without any draught of poison, ibid.—Having summoned demons, they dare to stir them up so that they may destroy any of their enemies by evil arts, ibid.—They use blood and often touch dead bodies with sacrifices, ch. 65, book VIII.

Things done by the tricks of magicians are proved to be not real but imaginary, ch. 67, book VIII.

Human curiosity is deceived by the prodigies of magicians through the deception of demons when people imprudently seek to know what it is in no way fitting for them to investigate, ibid.—Therefore power is given to unclean spirits to capture the perverse for themselves—that is, to deceive wicked people, those who despise truth and believe falsehood, ibid.

Women who believe and profess that they ride in nocturnal illusions and traverse many stretches of land by night are condemned and execrated as *striges*, chs. 75, 76, book VIII.—An innumerable multitude, deceived by this false opinion, believe these things to be true; and by believing they depart from the right faith and fall into the error of pagans, when they suppose that there is some divinity or divine power apart from the one God, ibid.—Priests ought, throughout the churches entrusted to them, to preach with every diligence to all the people, so that they may know all these things to be false and that such phantasms are inflicted upon the minds of unbelievers not by a divine spirit but by a malignant one, ibid.

An unbelieving woman, when the spirit alone undergoes this, thinks that it occurs not in the mind but in the body, ibid.

A woman who says that she can change people’s minds, turning them either from hatred to love or from love to hatred, is to be corrected with whips and expelled from the parish, ch. 76, book VIII. [Col. 1411]

Astrologers and planet-readers are expelled and condemned by Christian and true piety, ch. 79, book VIII.

Of two evils, the lesser must be chosen, chs. 95, 119, book VIII.

The eight kinds of lying, ch. 124, book VIII.

One must not lie in the teaching of piety, because it is a great crime and the first kind of detestable lie, ibid.

A lie is shameful in itself, ibid.—It is a false signification by speech with the intention of deceiving, ch. 125, book VIII.—For the temporal safety of human beings, a person should do what he can; but when he comes to the point that he cannot provide for such safety without sinning, he should consider that there is nothing for him to do, once he perceives that there remains nothing which he can do rightly, ibid.

Avoid every kind of lie most earnestly; do not defend anyone’s life by any deception whatever, chs. 126, 127, book VIII.

When you lie from humility, if you were not a sinner before you lied, you become one by lying, ch. 128, book VIII.

Lies are seriously uttered by liars; but when things which are not are said as a joke, they are not counted as lies, ch. 129, book VIII.

There are two kinds of lies in which the fault is not great, but which nevertheless are not without fault: when we joke, or when we lie to a neighbor, ch. 130, book VIII.—If someone perhaps does not wish to betray a person to this visible death, he must be prepared to conceal the truth rather than speak falsehood, so that he neither betrays nor lies, lest he kill his own soul for another’s body, ibid.

A person who says what is false while thinking it true is not to be judged a liar, for, so far as lies in him, he neither lies nor deceives, but is deceived, ch. 133, book VIII.—Everyone who lies speaks contrary to what he thinks, with the intention of deceiving, ibid.

Monks and regular canons are forbidden to devote themselves to civil law and medicine, ch. 144, book VIII.

Military tournaments, to which men assemble by agreement in order to compete in displays of their strength and boldness, are condemned, ch. 148, book VIII.

No one is to hear the Masses of those whom he knows among the people to have wives or concubines, ch. 142, book VIII.

## N

Pope Leo the Great permitted neophytes to ascend to the highest priesthood, although St. Paul sought by public preaching to exclude them from that office, ch. 10 of the prologue.

Necessity must cease when the remedy it has found itself ceases, ch. 17 of the prologue.

Divine ministries are not to be provided for the adornment of weddings, ch. 163, book I.

Nestorius the heretic asserted two persons in Christ; his heresy is condemned in the First Council of Ephesus, ch. 109, book II.

“We venerate the Nicene Synod together with the other four,” says St. Gregory, etc., ch. 147, book III.

In ecclesiastical affairs, one may withdraw statements before the other person’s death if necessary; not so in secular affairs, ch. 100, book IV.

No one can call his own a person whom he despised while perishing, chs. 52, 53, book V.

No one is to be judged hastily or prematurely—that is, without having been warned and convicted, ch. 124, book V.

At what times weddings may be celebrated, chs. 2, 3, book VI.

Permission to marry is not granted to those who have resolved to remain continent, ch. 4, book VI.

No one is to contract a secret marriage, chs. 5, 6, book VI.

For those marrying, a ring is placed on the fourth finger because a certain vein of blood is said to run from it all the way to the heart, ch. 8, book VI.

Second marriages are shown to be lawful in both Testaments, ch. 22, book VI.

The truth of marriage does not consist in the union of male and female, ch. 29, book VI.—Every good was fulfilled in the parents of Christ our Lord: in that marriage there were fidelity, offspring, and sacrament—fidelity, because there was no adultery; offspring, because our Lord Himself; and sacrament, because there was no divorce, ch. 30, book VI.

For the person who remains good is not himself defiled if he is joined to an evil person; rather, the evil person is converted to good if he follows good examples, ch. 57, book VI.

Second marriages are proved to be lawful, chs. 59 and 60, book VI.

“I dare neither condemn any marriages nor deprive them of the honor of fruitfulness,” says St. Augustine, ibid.

The bonds of marriage between living persons, however much they may attach themselves to others, are inseparable, ch. 74, book VI.

The marriage bond remains even if the offspring for whose sake it was entered into does not follow because of manifest sterility, ch. 105, book VI.

A girl is not compelled to marry someone to whom she has never given consent, even if her father’s oath intervenes, ch. 108, book VI.

Trading is sometimes permitted and sometimes not permitted: before a person becomes ecclesiastical, trading is permitted to him; once he has become so, it is not permitted, ch. 26, book VII.—Degrees of consanguinity; names of degrees, whether ascending, descending, or collateral, ch. 89, book VII.

We must consider not only deeds, but also time, cause, intention, and the differing conditions of persons; for otherwise we cannot arrive at truth, ch. 18, book VIII.

Not to correct one’s son is not charity but weakness, ch. 22, book VIII.

Necromancers are those by whose incantations dead persons appear to be raised up, to divine and answer questions, ch. 65, book VIII.—The name is derived from Greek *nekros* (νεκρός), “dead,” and *manteia* (μαντεία), “divination,” ibid.

When necromancy is performed, blood is mixed with water so that demons, said to love blood, may be more readily summoned by the color of blood, ibid.

## O

Every human being conceived through intercourse between man and woman is born with original sin, ch. 8, book I.

No one is freed from original sin except through faith in the mediator of God and men, the man Jesus Christ, ch. 8, book I.—Those conceived in sin, whether little children living in their mothers’ wombs or outside them, or adults, are condemned if they die without baptism, ch. 9, book I.

Nothing is to be accepted for ordinations, ch. 98, book I.

It is permissible to pray in a private oratory, ch. 39, book II.

Pope Gelasius calls Origen a schismatic, ch. 91, book II.

We say that Origen’s works are to be rejected together with their author, except for certain works which Saint Jerome does not reject as fit to be read, ibid.

Examiners of candidates for ordination are to investigate their life, family, country, age, education, the place where they were brought up, whether they are well educated, instructed in the law of the Lord, firmly hold the Catholic faith, and can affirm it in simple words, ch. 21, book III.

Candidates for ordination are to be examined for three consecutive days, and on Saturday those found approved are to be presented to the bishop, ibid.

Examiners of candidates for ordination must take care not to depart from truth through favor or enticement by desire for any gift, and thereby place an unworthy and less suitable person in the bishop’s hands for reception into holy orders, ibid.

Ordinations of presbyters and deacons are not to be celebrated except at the four seasons of the year, ch. 25, book III.

No one is to be ordained except in a fixed and religious place, or unless he has at least lived for one year in the city, so that certainty regarding his life, conduct, and doctrine may be known, ch. 26, book III.

No one ought to be ordained presbyter or deacon unless he deserves the designation of public ordination among those with whom he has lived, ch. 27, book III.

When a doorkeeper is ordained, the bishop shall hand him the keys of the church from the altar, and [the chapter states] what further the bishop is to say to him, ch. 39, book III.

No one of servile condition is to be promoted to holy orders unless a charter of freedom is read from the ambo before the ordination, ch. 48, book III.

A man ordained deacon by the heretic Necebo is reordained by Pope Urban II, ch. 81, book III.

Not only those ordained for money are struck with anathema, but also those who act as intermediaries for them, ch. 123, book III.

Ordained by one whom he knows to be simoniacal, both he and the ordainer shall undergo the penance of deposition and remain deprived of their respective rank, ch. 126, book III.—No one shall transfer from his own parish to another, nor leave the care of his church in order to visit the thresholds of the Apostles for prayer, nor go to the palace in order to make an appeal, ch. 71, book III.—No one ought to be ordained a second time, ch. 76, book III.—Unless a man has been ordained, even if he is of good merit, he nevertheless cannot give a blessing, ch. 79, book III.

A person in minor orders, or even a layman, if he has not married a virgin, cannot be advanced to the subdiaconate, ibid.

One who falls after ordination shall remain deposed, chs. 141–142, book III.

Everyone who is idle lives in desires, ch. 178, book III.

[Col. 1413] Let not the sheep rebuke their shepherd, ch. 36, book IV.

Origen is excommunicated after his death, ch. 116, book V.

The prophet Hosea is not to be blamed if he converted to chastity the prostitute whom he married, ch. 57, book VI.

To kill a person in the exercise of an office is not a sin, ch. 1, book VIII.

Those who have waged wars by God’s command have not transgressed the commandment against killing, ch. 2, book VIII.

He who kills himself is a murderer; and he becomes so much the more guilty when he kills himself, the more innocent was the cause on account of which he thought himself bound to die, ibid.

When Abraham was willing to kill his son, he did not act against the commandment, because he did this obediently, not cruelly, ibid.

Whoever kills any person, or himself, is implicated in the crime of homicide, excepting those whom either a just law in general, or God himself, the fountain of justice, commands to be killed, ch. 2, book VIII.

Penalty for one who kills a cleric or monk, ch. 8, book VIII.

What penalty is to be inflicted on one who kills a person out of hatred and not through zeal for justice, ch. 9, book VIII.

Phinehas killed a man, and it was accounted to him as righteousness, ch. 18, book VIII.

No one but a judge may lawfully kill anyone, ch. 23, book VIII.

Ecclesiastical orders are determined not by blood but by merit, ch. 151, book VIII.

P

Some precepts are mutable, others immutable. Mutable precepts are those which eternal law has not enacted, but which the diligence of later persons has devised for reasons of utility, not principally for attaining salvation, but for attaining it more safely. Immutable precepts are those which eternal law has enacted: when observed, they confer salvation; when not observed, they take it away. Such are: “You shall love the Lord your God and your neighbor,” ch. 7, prologue.

Precepts which speak against vices are immutable, as: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery,” etc., ch. 7, prologue.

By prohibitions certain things are forbidden in such a way that, if they had not been forbidden, neither would death result nor salvation be endangered, ch. 7, prologue.

The feigned repentance of some, prompted by their ambitious pursuit of positions of honor, ch. 8, prologue.

The rulers of churches judge many matters more strictly according to the tenor of the canons; many they tolerate because of the necessities of the times; many they dispense with for the benefit of persons or to avoid the slaughter of peoples; and many matters altered even by holy Fathers are confirmed by testimonies of Scripture, ibid.

A multitude of sinners must be struck by a general rebuke, ch. 15, prologue.

There is sin when, because of their multitude, vengeance can be exacted from all on account of a crowd, ch. 16, prologue.

Certain Roman pontiffs decreed that sons of presbyters should not be admitted to the priesthood, ch. 27, prologue.—Sons, if proved by holy conduct and integrity of life, may be promoted not only to the priesthood but even to the high priesthood, ch. 27, prologue.—Sons were high pontiffs: namely Felix III, Agapitus, Gelasius, Silverius, Deusdedit, and Theodore, son of Theodore the bishop, ch. 29, prologue.

The Father is the principle of the Godhead, ch. 1, book I.—The Son and the Holy Spirit, through an inseparable equality of one and the same substance, signify the divine unity, ch. 7, book I.—The Son and the Holy Spirit, just as they are inseparable, so they act inseparably, ch. 7, book I.

One and the same sponsor may, where necessity compels, serve in the catechumenate, baptism, and confirmation, ch. 77, book I.—According to Roman custom, one and the same person cannot serve at both baptism and confirmation, ch. 77, book I.—One, and not several, ought to receive the infant at baptism; the same applies at confirmation, ch. 78, book I.—No one can serve either at baptism or confirmation unless he has been baptized and confirmed, ch. 79, book I.—He cannot be an abbot or monk, chs. 80–81, book I.

Sponsors are sureties before God for those whom they have received from the sacred font; and what they ought to teach their godchildren, ch. 82, book I.

Only nine prefaces are to be received in the sacred catalogue, ch. 158, book I.

A presbyter, unless two persons are present and responding to him, ch. 159, book I.

Nocturnal emission can occur in four ways, ch. 160, book I.—When a nocturnal emission prevents the celebration of the sacrifice of the Mass, and when it does not, ibid.—Laypersons must not expel anyone from churches without the consent of bishops, ch. 46, book II.

Laypersons shall neither appoint presbyters nor expel them without the consent of their bishops, ch. 47, book II.

Let him require payments from presbyters for the correction of the church, ch. 48, book II.

If a presbyter has nothing at the time of his promotion to an order, but later purchases an estate, it is presumed to belong to the church, chs. 50, 52, and 53, book II.

Images are not to be made in churches, ch. 55, book II.—They are not to be broken or removed from the church, ch. 56, book II.

An image serves the nations in place of reading, ch. 50, book II.—What writing is for readers, that is an image for the unlearned, ibid.

Four portions must be made from the offerings of the faithful: one for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth for the repair of the church, ch. 60, book II.

Parishes possessed peacefully by a bishop for thirty years shall remain unchanged, chs. 64–65, book II.

A prescription of forty years is granted to religious houses, ch. 66, book II.

Thirty-year possession must be maintained within a single province, ch. 67, book II.—Thirty-year possession extinguishes another’s diocesan claim, ch. 68, book II.

He who burns a church and does not restore it shall do penance for fifteen years, ch. 70, book II.

Whoever dishonorably handles possessions consecrated to God through the arrogance of pride shall be deprived of communion with the faithful, ch. 71, book II.

The apostle Paul incorporated verses of poets into his writings, ch. 133, book II.

Christians are forbidden to read the fictions of poets because, through the pleasures of their tales, they stir the mind toward incentives to lust, ch. 137, book II.

Priscian of Caesarea examined deeply the art of grammar, ch. 145, book II.

Peter, who practised circumcision, yielded to Paul preaching the truth, ch. 167, book II.

For the election of a pope, the cardinal bishops shall first be involved; then the cardinal clerics of Christ, and the remaining people and clergy, ch. 1, book III.

The contrary is stated in ch. 8 of book III, and in the chapter *Nullus*, and in Adrian, first distinction, 63.

If the election of a pope cannot take place in the city, the cardinal bishops, together with religious clerics and Catholic laypersons, even if few, possess the right and authority to elect a pontiff of the Apostolic See wherever they judge it more suitable, ibid.

If one elected pope cannot, through the malice of opposition, be enthroned, he nevertheless obtains, as pope, authority to govern the holy Roman Church and dispose of all its resources; this we know that blessed Gregory did before his consecration, ibid.—One elected by all shall be consecrated in the presence of imperial legates, ibid.

If factions begin to differ in the election of a pope, the decision of the greater number shall prevail, ch. 2, book III.—In an election, he shall be set over all whom the united consent of clergy and people has concordantly requested, ch. 6, book III.

Presbyters and deacons shall make a profession to their bishop that they will live purely and chastely, ch. 22, book III.

No one shall presume to ordain a presbyter before thirty years of age, that is, before the age of a mature man, chs. 28 and 32, book III.

If a presbyter has not completed his thirtieth year, he shall not be ordained, even if he is highly worthy; for Christ himself chose to be baptized and began to teach at that age, ch. 29, book III.—When he is ordained, both the bishop and all presbyters present shall place their hands beside the bishop’s hand, ch. 33, book III.

A psalmist, that is, a singer, may receive the office of singing without the bishop’s knowledge, on the command of a presbyter alone; and what further the presbyter says to him, ch. 40, book III.

What the office of the *primicerius* is, ch. 41, book III.

Even though a penitent is good, he shall not be ordained a cleric; if it has happened otherwise through a bishop’s ignorance, he shall be deposed from the clergy, ch. 60, book III.—He shall not be admitted to the clergy unless necessity or usefulness alone requires it; and then he shall be assigned among the doorkeepers or readers. If he had previously been ordained, he shall be counted among subdeacons, ch. 61, book III.—A “penitent” is said to be one who, after baptism, for homicide, various crimes, or very grave sins, while performing public penance beneath haircloth, has been reconciled to God’s altar, ch. 61, book III.

Presbyters or deacons who transfer themselves from the places where they were ordained to other places shall be deposed, ch. 72, book III.

Presbyters shall not wander through different places, but shall remain in the churches in which they were appointed, ch. 71, book III.

A presbyter migrating to another place shall not be received unless he states the reason for his migration, ch. 75, book III.

After Christ the Lord, the priestly order began with Peter, ch. 82, book III.

If a presbyter takes a wife, he shall be deposed from his order; if he commits fornication, he shall be expelled from the Church, ch. 91, book III.

Presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons shall be cast down from the dignity of their ranks if they are incontinent, ch. 103, book III.

A *presbytera* is the wife of a presbyter, ch. 114, book III.

A presbyter shall love his *presbytera*, that is, his wife, as a sister, but guard against her as an enemy; he shall never permit her to come nearer to him or to minister necessities to him through her agency, ch. 114, book III.

Where the remedy of penance is necessary, the honor of ordination can have no place, ch. 130, book III.

Whoever, while professing himself a Christian, disdains obedience to the Apostolic See incurs the sin of paganism, ch. 134, book III.

Presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons who lie in the crime of fornication shall not enter the church until they have first done penance, ibid.

Let no one hear the office of presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons who are fornicators persisting in sin, ch. 134, book III.—The blessing of a fornicator is turned into a curse, and his prayer into sin, according to Malachi 2: “I will curse,” etc., ibid.

Penance followed in Saint Peter after his denial, and after penance forgiveness was granted him, because Christ did not cast down from the apostleship the man whose denial of himself he had foretold beforehand, ch. 147, book III.

Those whose repentance has been preceded by satisfaction, or by a fitting confession of sins, the canon has commanded to return to their former ranks, ch. 149, book III.—On the other hand, those who are not corrected from the vice of corruption, and who even endeavor, with a certain superstitious rashness, to defend that very carnal offense which they commit, receive neither rank of honor nor the grace of communion, ch. 149, book III.

He who knows how to bewail his own offenses through the satisfaction of penance can be restored to his own order. But recognize that he who neglects and does not mourn what he has done, and commits shameful deeds without any modesty of religion or fear of divine judgment, cannot in any way be restored to his former rank, ch. 149, book III.

A presbyter or deacon who confesses that he sinned before ordination shall not offer sacrifice if he is a presbyter; those convicted shall be deposed, ch. 150, book III.—He who confesses that he fell bodily before ordination shall not offer sacrifice, ch. 151, book III.

Every religious undertaking has its own leaders, ch. 157, book III.

If a girl entered religious life before the age of twelve, and her parents or guardians consented by their silence, she shall remain in her holy purpose, ch. 187, book III.

How the profession of religious life ought to be made, ch. 102, book III.

Peter and Paul were crowned in the city of Rome under Nero by a glorious death, not at different times (as heretics babble), but at one time and on the same day, ch. 3, book IV.

The supreme pontiff is to be judged by no one on earth, as is proved by many examples, ch. 6, book IV.

The people of God are not separated from the people of God by their mother’s condition, but by their own fault, ch. 47, book IV.

No human being judges the causes of popes, but the pope judges the causes of other persons, ch. 8, book VI.

The judgment of the pontiff of the Apostolic See is reserved to God’s judgment alone, ch. 8, book IV.

Supreme pontiffs, Peter’s successors, owe their innocence to heaven alone, ibid.

The provinces were divided long before Christ’s advent; and for the most part their division was afterward renewed by the apostles and blessed Clement, ch. 23, book IV.

The greatest affairs belong, after the Apostolic See, to the primates, ibid.

What obedience is to be shown to primates and patriarchs, ibid.

A province is that which has ten or eleven cities, one king, an equal number of lesser powers under it, one metropolitan, and ten or eleven suffragan bishops as judges, ch. 24, book IV.—None of these ought to be degraded or dishonored, but each should have within itself priestly and episcopal judges, to whose judgment all causes may be referred, ibid.

No archbishops shall be called primates except those who hold the principal cities, ch. 25, book IV.

No primate or archbishop ought to excommunicate anyone from another’s parish, ch. 27, book IV.

No primate or metropolitan can do anything in another’s parish without the bishop’s consent, ch. 28, book IV.

Primates or patriarchs have no privilege above other bishops except what the sacred canons grant and ancient custom has long conferred upon them, ch. 29, book IV.

The sheep ought not accuse their shepherd unless he has erred from the right faith, ch. 29, book IV.

The deeds of shepherds are not to be struck with the sword, although they may rightly be reproved, ibid.

He who does not prove what he alleges shall himself suffer the penalty which he had sought to inflict, ch. 75, book IV.

How a presbyter accused of a crime is to be cleared by canonical purgation, ch. 1, book V.

In canonical purgation, adequate satisfaction is made if those by whom he is believed guilty, after proper assurance concerning the alleged crime, are shown that he is innocent, ibid.

In his purgation Pope Leo had twelve bishops, ch. 3, book V.

How a presbyter is to be cleared, ibid.

Pope Leo cleared himself of the alleged crime, and how, ch. 4, book V.

How Pope Saint Gregory caused Bishop Leo to be cleared of the alleged crime, ch. 5, book V.

How blessed Gregory caused Bishop Menna to be cleared, ch. 6, book V.

For conducting a purgation, contact with boiling water or red-hot iron is forbidden, ch. 8, book V.

Let a layperson clear himself by oath, ch. 10, book V.

Laypersons are not to judge presbyters or investigate anything concerning their lives; such matters are to be reserved for the judgment of bishops, ch. 12, book V.

Proof is to be demanded not from the possessor but from the party bringing the claim, ch. 17, book V.—It ought to be required of one who desires to obtain the thing claimed, not of one who intends to hold it by right, ch. 17, book V.—The burden lies upon the one who affirms, not upon the one who denies, ch. 18, book V.

One who is unwilling to appear in order to refute accusations against him proves them true, ch. 44, book V.

No prejudice can be created against an unwilling master through an agent, slave, or tenant, ch. 48, book V.

Saint Peter hands to Clement the power of binding and loosing, ch. 48, book V.

It frequently happens that one holds the place of a judge though his life is wholly at variance with that office; and it often occurs that he either condemns the undeserving or, though himself bound, looses others, ch. 78, book V.

A person ought to love his sponsor as a father, ch. 124, book VI.

The penance of Astulf, who killed his wife without a capital cause, ch. 16, book VII.

What penance is to be imposed upon one who unjustly killed his wife, ibid.

How the purgation of an imputed adultery ought to be conducted, ch. 39, book VII.

All names of kinship are contained within seven degrees, chs. 80 and 89, book VII.

On account of past sins, this life is especially necessary, so that people may be saved by repentance, ch. 2, book VIII.

In persecutions it is not lawful to perish by one’s own hand, except where chastity is endangered; rather, one must submit one’s neck to the striker, ch. 3, book VIII.

Various penalties for those who kill clerics, ch. 7, book VIII.

Peter raised Tabitha by praying, but delivered Ananias and Sapphira to death by rebuking them, ch. 19, book VIII.

Pope Leo entered Rome against the Saracens and ordered the people to assemble against them, ch. 27, book VIII.

The pope ought in all things to be the avenger and chief helper of his flock, ch. 29, book VIII.

Only one who compels another to evil persecutes; one who punishes a deed, or forbids it from being done, does not persecute but loves, ch. 36, book VIII.

One must abstain from battles not only during Lent, but at every time when no necessity presses, ch. 37, book VIII.

Nothing is more unhappy than the prosperity of sinners, by which penal impunity is nourished and an evil will, like an inward enemy, is strengthened, ch. 42, book VIII.

When battle is joined, God looks on from open heaven and grants both victory and the palm to the side which he sees to be just, ch. 43, book VIII.

[Col. 1417] Take up arms in your hands, and let prayer strike the ears of the Creator, ibid.

The ruler is an avenger against all wrongdoers, so that he may restrain by fear those whom he cannot correct by wholesome admonitions; therefore he does not bear the sword without cause, ch. 55, book VIII.

Female diviners are called *pythonissae* from the Pythian Apollo, because he was held to be the source of divination, ch. 66, book VIII.

Mercury is said to have first invented illusion (*praestigium*), so called because it dazzles the sight of the eyes, ch. 67, book VIII.

This is Satan’s illusion: in order to deceive the greatest number, he pretends that he holds even good people in his power, ibid.

The privileges of individuals cannot make a common law, ch. 73, book VIII.

Promises are not always to be fulfilled, ch. 102, book VIII.

God’s repentance is a change of things; for God not to repent is not to revoke what he has decreed, ch. 114, book VIII.

The emperor has the right of electing the supreme pontiff, chs. 135–136, book VIII.

Pope Adrian, together with the whole synod, granted Charles the right and power to elect the pontiff and appoint the Apostolic See, ibid.

To maintain peace firmly, bishops, casting aside all lukewarmness, shall offer one another mutual counsel and assistance, ch. 147, book VIII.

Q

Things contained neither in the authorities of holy Scriptures, nor found established by councils of bishops, nor strengthened by the custom of the Church, are to be cut away, ch. 168, book II.

The Ember Days were instituted by Pope and martyr Callistus, the twelfth from Peter, ch. 175, book II.

Let us observe the fourfold solemn fast during the four Ember seasons of the year, just as the year itself revolves through four seasons, ch. 175, book II.

During the Ember fast, all shall come to church on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday at the ninth hour, with litanies for the solemn celebration of Mass, ch. 180, book II.

Lent is to be observed with the utmost strictness; the days of fasting, apart from Sundays, are in no way to be relaxed, ch. 182, book II.

Through the thirty-six fasting days of Lent, we offer God, as it were, the tithe of the year, ibid.

So that the sacred number of forty days may be completed, which our Savior consecrated by his own fast, four days of the preceding week are added, ibid.

During Lent, believers must by no means be thought to fast if they eat before the evening office is celebrated, ibid.

In Lent one must gather for Mass; after hearing the solemnities of the Mass and the evening offices, and after alms have been given, one may approach food, ch. 184, book II.

What a person did not possess, he could not give, ch. 130, book III.

One who, through fear of a governor, falsely says that he is a slave may afterward defend himself, ch. 49, book V.

What belongs to no one beforehand is granted, by natural reason, to the person who takes possession of it, ch. 76, book V.

One unjustly expelled may appeal to neighboring bishops, ch. 127, book V.

What a person has done with a disturbed mind, he should correct when calm, ch. 131, book V.

During Lent it is not lawful to hold banquets, ch. 3, book VI.

What the Lord forbids may absolutely not be done, ch. 100, book VI.

What the Lord commands, no good servant forbids, ch. 101, book VI.

Those whose body is one ought also to have one mind, ch. 109, book VI.

If, in things which we do or possess for a good or lawful purpose, some harm happens to someone without our intention through that very thing, far be it from us that it should be imputed to us, ch. 1, book VIII.

Whoever receives publicly assigned pay, if he seeks more, is condemned by John’s judgment as a false accuser and extortioner, ch. 60, book VIII.

R

The Roman Church observes, and commands to be observed, rules handed down by the apostles or apostolic men, ch. 17, prologue.

Rebaptisms and reordinations must not be performed, ch. 83, book I.

It is altogether sinful to rebaptize a heretical person who has received the signs of holiness which Christian discipline hands down, ch. 84, book I.

[Col. 1418] One baptized by a heretic in confession of the Holy Trinity ought not to be rebaptized, ch. 85, book I.

What should be done if an abductor and the abducted woman flee to a church, ch. 72, book II.

Rufinus is censured concerning freedom of the will, ch. 91, book II.

When revelation has been made, error must yield to truth, ch. 167, book II.

God’s mercy willed the religion celebrated with the fewest and most manifest sacraments to be free, ch. 168, book II.

Whoever uses transient things more restrictively than the customs of those among whom he lives permit is either intemperate or superstitious; but whoever uses them so as to exceed the bounds of the good customs of those among whom he lives either signifies something or is depraved, ch. 195, book II.

The holy and apostolic Roman Church received primacy not from the apostles but from our Lord and Savior himself, ch. 2, book IV.—The Catholic and Apostolic Church has been set above other churches not by any synodical decrees but by the evangelical declaration of our Lord and Savior, and has received primacy: “You are Peter, and upon this …,” etc., chs. 3 and 10, book IV.

The primacy of Peter. The Church has the right to judge concerning every church, and no one may judge its judgment, ch. 9, book IV.

Appeal must be made to the Roman Church from every part of the world, but no one is permitted to appeal from it, ibid. The primacy of Peter. No one is permitted to judge the judgments of the Apostolic See or retract its sentence, chs. 10 and 11, book IV.—Primacy. By the authority of the Apostolic See, there is no higher judgment, ch. 11, book IV.—Primacy. The most holy Roman Church possesses, by a special privilege granted to it, the power to open and close the gates of the heavenly kingdom to whom it will, ch. 12, book IV.

Whoever steals another’s property is required by secular law to restore it elevenfold, ch. 47, book IV.

Let not an accused person make himself guilty by voluntary confession; nor should one who has confessed himself criminal be believed concerning another, chs. 68 and 69, book IV.—No one can be condemned unless convicted or voluntarily confessing, ch. 135, book IV.

The division of things, or ownership of things, is acquired partly by natural law and partly by civil law, ch. 76, book V.

An abducted woman may marry her abductor, ch. 33, book VI.

Rape is called unlawful intercourse, from corruption; hence one who obtains a woman by abduction enjoys debauchery, ch. 53, book VI.

Clerics who abduct girls shall fall from their rank, while laypersons shall be anathematized, ch. 53, book VI.—Abductors of girls can in no way claim the women whom they abducted for lawful marriage, ch. 55, book VI.

After penance, marriage may lawfully be granted to an abductor or an abducted woman, ch. 56, book VI.

Where repudiation has been introduced among the Gentiles, she may marry whom she wishes and he may take whom he wishes, ch. 6, book VII.

For those guilty of their own death, a better life after death is not enough, ch. 2, book VIII.

A king must restrain thefts, punish adulteries, remove the impious from the land, not permit parricides and perjurers to live, and not allow his sons to act impiously, ch. 33, book VIII.—He serves in one way because he is a man, and in another because he is a king, ch. 59, book VIII.—Because he is a man, he serves by living faithfully; because he is also a king, he serves by establishing with fitting rigor laws that command what is just and prohibit the contrary, ibid.

To administer the commonwealth is not criminal; but to administer it in order rather to increase one’s private estate and riches appears condemnable, ch. 60, book VIII.

Nothing makes a tongue guilty except a guilty mind, chs. 111 and 116, book VIII.

S

The enactments of ecclesiastical rules are derived partly from the examples of Roman pontiffs, partly from the proceedings of councils of Catholic bishops, partly from the treatises of orthodox Fathers, and partly from the institutions of Catholic kings. Ivo of Chartres, in the *Panormia*, or Book of Decrees, ch. 1, prologue.

Holy utterances have one countenance, ch. 4, prologue.

A spiritual person does not fulfill what has been prescribed when, for the salvation of those whom he wishes to benefit, he providently does something more advantageous, ch. 9, prologue.

Plans of separation are vain against a multitude that sins, ch. 14, prologue.

A synod dissolves a synod for the sake of the unity and peace of the Church, ch. 29, prologue.

The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, ch. 1, book I.

You receive the sacrament in likeness, but you attain the glory and power of the true nature, ch. 127, book I.

In spiritual sacraments, where power has commanded, the effect obeys, ch. 129, book I.

A sacrament is the visible form of invisible grace, ch. 130, book I.

The visible sacrifice is the sacrament of the invisible sacrifice, ibid.

A sign is a thing which, beyond the appearance it presents to the senses, causes something else to come into knowledge through itself, ch. 131, book I.

“Species” and “likeness” are names for the things that were previously present, namely bread and wine, ch. 132, book I.

The sacrifice of the Church consists of the visible appearance of the elements and the invisible blood and flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ, of the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament—that is, the body of Christ, ch. 138, book I.

The bodies of the saints will remain in the tomb until the end of the age, ch. 141, book I.

The sacrifice of the Mass is an example of that by which Christ died on the cross, ch. 145, book I.—And the offerings are not many, but one, because Christ was offered once, ibid.—It is one, just as that which is offered everywhere is one body and not many bodies, ibid.

Various errors occur in the sacrifice of the Mass: for some consecrated milk in place of wine, while others distributed to the people the sacred Eucharist dipped [in liquid], etc., ch. 174, book I.

By sacrifices offered to God, every crime and sin is wiped away, ibid.

In divine sacrifices, it is lawful to offer only bread and a chalice mixed with wine and water, ibid.

No one shall presume to celebrate the sacrifice of the altar except upon a clean linen cloth, ch. 162, book I.

No one shall dare to bury a dead person in a church as though by hereditary right, except one whom a bishop or priest judges worthy, ch. 25, book II.

Concerning rash violation of burial: no one shall dare rashly to violate anyone’s burial, ibid.

We ought not, even under compulsion, to receive payment for a burial, ch. 26, book II.

Saint Gregory altogether forbids asking or demanding anything for burial, ch. 27, book II.

No one shall presume to transfer the bodies of saints from place to place without the permission of the ruler, the bishops, and the holy synod, ch. 36, book II.

Changes of episcopal sees may be made through necessity of the times, ch. 37, book II.

Holy places are to be changed for three reasons, ch. 38, book II.

A priest who, in contempt of a lesser church, seeks a greater one shall be deprived of both, ch. 45, book II.

Boundaries that have been fixed cannot be acquired by prescription of time, ch. 69, book II.

A slave who has fled to a church shall be compelled to return to his master, after the master has first taken an ecclesiastical oath concerning the offense committed, chs. 73–74, book II.

Sacrilege is committed in many ways, and its penalty is manifold, ch. 79, book II.—It is committed by removing a sacred thing from a sacred place, or an unsacred thing from a sacred place, ibid.

Penalty for sacrilege, ch. 80, book II.

The Book of Wisdom is approved by Augustine, ch. 93, book II. The Council of Sardica is received by the whole Church, ch. 100, book II.

The enactments of the Apostolic See are to be received as though confirmed by the voice of the divine precept itself, ch. 101, book II.

The fifth synod follows the holy Fathers and doctors; whom it follows, we too ought to follow, ch. 102, book II.

There are four principal synods, containing most fully the nature of the faith; but whatever councils the holy Fathers, filled with the Holy Spirit, enacted after the authority of these four, let them likewise remain established in all force, ch. 110, book II.

Pope Adrian accepts the seventh holy synod, ch. 119, book II.

Falsehoods are in no way admitted in canonical Scriptures, ch. 119, book II.

It is held to be most pernicious to believe that any falsehood exists in sacred books, ch. 121, book II.

Legates of the Apostolic See signed after being deceived, ch. 122, book II.

Priests of God are forbidden to read comedies and the amatory pastoral poems, neglecting the Gospels and prophets, ch. 131, book II.

The knowledge of piety is to know the law, understand the prophets, believe the Gospel, and not be ignorant of the apostles, ch. 135, book II.

The Sabbath day is not to be kept as a festival, as certain preachers of Antichrist taught, ch. 169, book II.

The Church’s tradition requires that sacraments not be celebrated at all during the two days of Good Friday and Holy Saturday, [Col. 1420] ch. 177, book II.

The Apostolic See is set above all churches throughout the world, ch. 1, book III.

I profess that I will introduce, diminish, or alter no innovation contrary to the enactments of the Fathers, my predecessors, ch. 4, book III.

We call the diaconate and presbyterate sacred orders; for these alone the primitive Church is read to have possessed, ch. 5, book III.

We do not permit subdeacons to be elected bishops except very rarely, when necessity requires, and when their life, religious character, and learning have been proven, ch. 5, book III.

Ordinations of priests are celebrated on Sunday not only by custom but also by apostolic teaching, Acts 13, ch. 13, book III.

Things necessary for a priest to learn are: the book of sacraments, lectionary, baptismal rite, computus, penitential canons, psalter, and homilies suited to Sundays and feast days, from which he may feed his sheep; if even one is lacking, the name of priest will scarcely be sustained in him, ch. 24, book III.

The sacred canons have decreed that subdeacons shall not be ordained before fourteen years of age, ch. 32, book III.

When a subdeacon is ordained, because he does not receive the laying on of hands, let him receive from the bishop’s hand an empty paten and an empty chalice; but from the archdeacon’s hand, a pitcher with water, a water-basin, and a towel, ch. 35, book III.

If a slave not canonically consecrated falls from his rank, he shall be of the condition in which he was before that rank, ch. 48, book III.

All who have been promoted to the priesthood, whether husbands of widows or men who have had numerous marriages, shall by authority of the Apostolic See be excluded from the priestly title and from all ecclesiastical offices, ch. 49, book III.

He who has not taken a virgin wife shall not aspire to sacred ranks; and those who enter upon the marriage of a second wife contrary to apostolic precepts shall be excluded from them, ch. 50, book III.

Many born of priests have presided over the Apostolic See, ch. 52, book III.

The son of a priest is not excluded from the episcopate if the other virtues are present in him, chs. 53–54, book III.

A priesthood received in a time of health is not lost when illness supervenes, ch. 55, book III.

The sacrament of baptism and the sacrament of orders cannot be repeated, ch. 77, book III.

Wherever the sacraments are, they are themselves the same, ibid.

Of those separated from the unity of the Church there is now no question that they possess sacraments and can confer them; but they possess them perniciously and confer them perniciously, ch. 77, book III.

The Holy Spirit, giver of graces, follows not the person, whether worthy or wicked, but the order of transmission, ch. 79, book III.

The will of the priest can neither harm nor benefit; rather, it is the merit of the person requesting the blessing, ch. 79, book III.

Priests, deacons, and subdeacons of the Eastern churches enter into marriage; among Western churches no one from subdeacon through bishop has permission to enter marriage, ch. 84, book III.—Those who minister at the altar ought, during the offering of the holy gifts, to abstain from the embraces of their wives, so that they may obtain what they humbly request, ch. 86, book III.

A vow of chastity is imposed on subdeacons, ch. 89, book III.

Subdeacons who refuse to abstain from their wives shall not be promoted to sacred order, ibid.

No one shall become a subdeacon unless he professes perpetual continence, even from his own wife, ch. 90, book III.

After the subdiaconate, no one is permitted to take a wife, ch. 90, book III.

Priests are always commanded to maintain chastity, ch. 92, book III.

Priests and Levites must abstain even from their own wives, ch. 94, book III.—Under the old law, during the year of their appointed service they did not leave the Temple or touch their homes, ibid.—Levites too are bound to observe chastity from the day of their ordination, ibid.

A priest, who must always offer sacrifices, must always pray and must always abstain from marriage, ch. 96, book III.

Subdeacons must observe continence, ch. 99, book III.

Carnal intercourse is forbidden to subdeacons, ch. 100, book III.

Those entering the clergy before the order of subdiaconate may take a wife, but not afterward, ch. 102, book III.
