No one is to be allowed to approach sacred orders unless he is either a virgin or of proven chastity, ch. 104, book III.

[Col. 1421] A subdeacon must abstain from his wife, ch. 105, book III.

Holy men have this as their characteristic: they generally cut off from themselves even lawful things, so that they may always remain far from unlawful ones, ch. 114, book III.

He is excluded from the priesthood who ordains for money, or for any gift or promise of a gift; and so is he who gives or promises it, chs. 117–118, book III.

Some confer holy orders without monetary payment, out of human favor, and seek as the sole recompense for that generosity the return of praise, ch. 121, book III.

Simony can be committed in three ways: by a gift of service, namely improperly rendered subjection; by a gift from the hand, namely money; and by a gift from the tongue, namely favor, chs. 121, 124, book III.

He who confers holy orders then shakes off every gift of the hand when, in divine matters, he seeks not only no money but not even human favor, ch. 124, book III.

No mercy is to be shown toward Simoniacs in retaining them in dignity, ch. 125, book III.

Pope Nicholas calls the sin of simony a heresy, and a threefold heresy, ch. 127, book III.

The priests of heretics are not considered worthy of episcopal dignity, ch. 129, book III.

One who, after sacred ordination, has fallen into sins of the flesh is not thereafter to approach service at the altar, ch. 134, book III.

A man whose crime has been made public cannot be restored to the priesthood, ch. 136, book III.

As the greater precedes the lesser in honor, so let it be in wrongdoing: he whom the greater fault follows is to be entangled in the greater punishment; and only then is his penance to be believed fruitful, ch. 147, book III.

It is a scandal to the people of God to have set over them persons known to be excessively vicious, ch. 152, book III.

Those who hold holy orders, if they are publicly discovered in perjury, theft, fornication, or other crimes of this sort, are to be deposed from their rank; the case is otherwise with those who have sinned secretly and have confessed their crimes before a priest, ch. 152, book III.

A priest cannot minister in the priesthood after committing homicide, ch. 153, book III.

If a slave has reached ecclesiastical ranks by any fraud, he is to be deposed and his master is to take him back, ch. 164, book III.

If a slave has secretly slipped into the priesthood, he is to be punished by loss of his peculium, ch. 165, book III.—Having become a cleric, he remains liable to servitude, ch. 165, book III.—If, with his master’s knowledge and without objection, he has entered the clergy, he is to become freeborn and free; but if the master was ignorant, he may prove his status within a year and reclaim his slave, ch. 166, book III.

Solitude is paradise to me, and a town a prison, ch. 177, book III.

When a nun is presented to her bishop for consecration, she is to be presented in those garments which she will subsequently wear in religious life, ch. 188, book III.

A woman who has falsely pretended to be a nun cannot marry; if she does so and does not repent, she is to be struck with the spiritual sword, chs. 205–206, book III.

Whoever violates the body of a woman consecrated to God is sacrilegious and a son of perdition, ch. 207, book III.

Nuns must be diligent in their office, reading, and the chanting of psalms, ch. 211, book III.

A nun is in no way to leave the monastery unless the abbess sends her, and only under the greatest necessity, ch. 212, book III.—She who has intercourse shamefully with a man is to be sternly restrained by beatings and kept in private confinement, where she may make worthy penance for what she has wrongly done, ch. 215, book III.

Priests are not to enter the cloisters and private dwellings of nuns except solely for Mass, ibid.

He who violates the bride of a man, if held guilty, is guilty; how much more is he made guilty of lèse-majesté who corrupts the bride of almighty God, ibid.

The Apostolic See, the hinge and head of all churches, was established by the Lord, not by anyone else, ch. 2, book IV.

By the authority of the Apostolic See, all churches are governed, by the Lord’s ordering, ibid.

Refer more difficult cases that arise to the summit of the Apostolic See, as to the head, so that they may be decided by apostolic judgment, ibid.

The first See of the Apostle Peter is the Roman Church, having neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of the kind, chs. 3–4, book IV.—The first See shall be judged by no one: neither by the emperor, nor by all the clergy, nor by kings, nor by all the people, ch. 5, book IV.

All judgments concerning bishops are commanded to be brought to conclusion at the Apostolic See, ch. 20, book IV.

[Col. 1422] One intending to accuse priests must first admonish them charitably; but if he accuses before admonishing, he is to be excommunicated, ch. 34, book IV.

Bishops deprived of their sees are forbidden to be summoned to trial, ch. 42, book IV.

Bishops who have been despoiled must first be restored and recover their own property; afterward they may be accused, chs. 43–44, book IV.—Bishops cannot be summoned either to a provincial or to a general synod before what is theirs has first been restored to them, ch. 45, book IV.

Before the joinder of issue, all things must be restored to a despoiled person, chs. 47–49, book IV.—After restoration of his property, a not inconsiderable period of respite must be granted him before, when summoned, he comes to the synod, chs. 50–52, book IV.

A sentence rendered by a judge in the absence of a party has no force, ch. 54, book IV.

Just as priests’ manner of life ought to be distinct from that of laypersons, so too ought their litigation be distinct, ch. 61, book IV.—Schismatics are called those who hold assemblies separately from bishops in communion with us, ch. 73, book IV.

Those who neither ought nor can be advanced to the same honor cannot accuse priests or testify against them, ch. 86, book IV.

A judgment must not be rendered until, all proceedings having been completed, the parties have nothing left to submit in the case, ch. 104, book IV.—It is not to be rendered hastily, ch. 116, book IV.

By the Lord’s example we are admonished, in rendering judgment, never to be hasty, ibid.

The fruits of property are sequestered when the possessor appeals, while the outcome of the case is uncertain, ch. 130, book IV.

A priest accused by the people is to establish his innocence by oath and remain in his own rank, ch. 9, book V.

No one, however defiled, can defile the divine sacraments, ch. 13, book V.

A priest, whatever he may be like, cannot contaminate what is holy, ch. 13, book V.

The sacraments may lawfully be received from a priest caught in adultery, or even one merely tainted by report of it, ibid.—Communion too is to be received from a priest of whatever character until he is rejected by the judgment of bishops, ibid.

A sentence rendered in the absence of a party has no force, ch. 16, book V.

Anyone may choose the judgment of the bishop of the most holy See, ch. 23, book V.

Priestly ordinations are celebrated on the Lord’s Day, not only by custom but also by apostolic teaching, Acts 13, ch. 13, book III.

A slave is not to be believed if he brings an accusation against anyone, even if he attacks his own master on a criminal charge, ch. 27, book V.

If a slave informs against his master, he is to be punished even if he proves the charges, ch. 40, book V.

We know priests to be dead not by human, but by divine pronouncements, ch. 45, book V.

A slave or household dependent who is an accuser or informer against his master is to be struck with the avenging sword at the very beginning of the accusation, ibid.

Slaves cannot accuse priests or testify against them, ibid.

If a runaway slave passes himself off as free and is prepared to litigate for his freedom, he will not appear to be possessed by his master, ch. 47, book V.

One who wishes to reclaim a slave, the son of his slave woman, who was exposed without his knowledge, may do so, provided that he repays the just expenses, ch. 51, book V.

He deprives himself of the power of loosing and binding who exercises it according to his own wishes rather than according to the conduct of those subject to him, ch. 79, book V. He who endeavors to absolve a guilty person from punishment attempts to give life to one who will not live, ch. 80, book V.—One must consider what the fault was and what penance followed the fault, so that pastoral judgment may loose those whom almighty God visits through grace, ibid.—Then the absolution of the presiding authority is truly such when it follows the judgment of the inward Judge, ch. 81, book V.

By pastoral authority we ought to loose those whom we know our Creator, through life-restoring grace, has made alive, ibid.

Just as a priest does not make a leper clean, so a bishop or presbyter does not make persons innocent; nor does he loose the guilty. Rather, when in the exercise of his office he has heard the varieties of sins, he knows who is to be bound and who is to be loosed, ch. 86, book V.

Priests of Christ are regarded as the fathers and teachers of kings, princes, and all the faithful, ch. 108, book V.—Constantine the Great, calling them lords, declared that they ought not to be subject to his judgment, but that he himself depended upon their decision, ibid.

[Col. 1423] “You know,” says Saint Gregory to the Emperor Anastasius, “that you depend upon the judgment of priests, not that they should wish to be reduced to your will,” ch. 109, book V.—“Gold,” says Saint Ambrose, “is not more precious than lead to the same degree that the priestly rank is higher than royal power,” ibid.

Let the necks of kings and princes be bowed to the knees of priests; having kissed their right hands, they believe themselves fortified by their prayers, ibid.

Nothing more excellent than priests, nothing more exalted than bishops, is found in this world, ibid.

Those who refused to be absolved by the Church in this life cannot be loosed by it after death, ch. 118, book V.

The Church can loose or bind the living, but not the dead, ch. 119, book V.

One who remains bound after a bishop’s death is to be loosed by the bishop’s successor, ch. 121, book V.

Betrothal is a promise of future marriage, ch. 9, book VI.

A betrothed woman is not to be handed over immediately to her bridegroom, lest a husband regard as cheap what has been given to him, whereas the bridegroom prized it when delayed, ch. 10, book VI.

At betrothals the consent of those whose consent is required in marriage must be sought, ch. 11, book VI.

Betrothals, like marriages, are made by the consent of the contracting parties. A daughter under paternal authority must consent to betrothal just as to marriage. She who does not oppose her father’s will is understood to consent, ch. 12, book VI.—Permission to dissent from her father is granted if a bridegroom unworthy in character or disgraceful is chosen for the daughter by her father, ibid.

In betrothals, the age of the contracting parties is not defined as it is in marriages, ch. 13, book VI.

Betrothal may take place if they are not younger than seven years, ch. 13, book VI.—A girl betrothed to one man cannot be taken by another; “such a marriage,” says Pope Siricius, “we anathematize,” ch. 18, book VI.

The bridegroom and bride, when they are to receive the blessing, are to be presented to the priest by their attendants, ch. 20, book VI.

After receiving the blessing, bridegroom and bride are to remain virgins that same night out of reverence for the blessing, ibid.

He who violates his brother’s betrothed woman, even if the bridegroom could not have intercourse with her, is not to have the violated woman as his bride, ch. 120, book VI.

Those seated in the chair of pestilence pronounce laws that they do not know and teach things which they have not learned at all, ch. 54, book VII.

Samson is not otherwise excused for crushing himself with his enemies in the collapse of the house, except because the Spirit, who worked miracles through him, commanded this secretly, ch. 2, book VIII.

War is justly waged against Saracens who persecute Christians and drive them from cities and their own residences, but not against Jews who are prepared to live in subjection, ch. 29, book VIII.

Pope Alexander II prevented a certain bishop who wished to destroy a Jewish synagogue from doing so, ibid.

Interpreters of the stars are called magi, as is read of those who announced Christ’s birth in the Gospel. Later only astrologers were called by this name. Knowledge of that art was permitted until the Gospel, so that, once Christ had been born, no one thereafter might interpret a nativity from heaven, ch. 60, book VIII.

Diviners are those who, under the name of a fictitious religion, profess knowledge of divination through certain things which they call “the lots of the saints,” or who predict the future by examining the statements of any writings whatever, ibid.

Those are called “leapers” (*saltatores*) who, when any parts of their limbs leap, declare that some prosperity or misfortune is thereby signified to them, ch. 60, book VIII.

Saul, corrupted because of sin, turned to the things that he had condemned—namely, to the witch of Endor, ch. 67, book VIII.—Having become reprobate, he could not possess sound understanding, ibid.—Because he did not understand rightly, contrary to Scripture he worshipped someone other than the Lord; and, thinking it was Samuel, he worshipped the devil, so that Satan might have the fruit of his deception. For this is what he strives for: to be worshipped as God, ibid.

Lots are utterly condemned and ought not even to be named among Christians, ch. 70, book VIII.

We must not immediately put faith in lots on the example of Jonah, nor connect with this testimony that passage from the Acts of the Apostles where Matthias is chosen as an apostle by lot, ch. 73, book VIII.

Bishops and their ministers should endeavor by every means to eliminate divinatory practices and magical arts, ch. 75, book VIII.

A lot is not something evil, but a thing that indicates the divine will in a human uncertainty, ch. 77, book VIII.

Lots are not to be trusted indiscriminately on the example of Jonah or Matthias, ch. 78, book VIII.—God is not to be consulted; rather, following the apostles’ example, the brethren must confer, pouring out tears and prayers to God, ibid.

Because Paschalis handled lots, practiced incantations, and worshipped sacred groves, he is deservedly deposed from the archdiaconate, ch. 82, book VIII.

Septuagesima signifies the Babylonian captivity—that is, the confusion in which we are while we are held captive in the world. Departing from it, we must return to Jerusalem, that is, to the house of peace, ch. 137, book VIII.

One ordained simoniacally is to be removed altogether from office, ch. 138, book VIII.

If anyone, through the accursed ardor of avarice and by means of money, has acquired a prebend, priory, diaconate, ecclesiastical honor or promotion of any kind, or any ecclesiastical sacrament—for example chrism, that is, holy oil, or the consecration of altars or churches—he is to lose the office evilly acquired; and buyer, seller, and intermediary are to be struck with the mark of infamy, ibid.

In the matters just mentioned, nothing is to be demanded by anyone, whether before or afterward, either for maintenance or under pretext of some custom; nor may anyone presume to give anything, since this is simoniacal. Rather, let him freely and without diminution enjoy the dignity conferred upon him, ibid.

A priest who has the means is to be content with one church, ch. 140, book VIII.

## T

In certain traditions one must yield to the necessity of the time, ch. 6, prologue.

The Trinity is not confused into one person, as Sabellius says, ch. 1, book I.

In the Trinity there is nothing created or servile, and many other matters concerning the most holy Trinity, ch. 5, book I.

The Trinity was not born of the Virgin Mary, crucified, buried, raised on the third day, or ascended into heaven; only the Son was, ch. 7, book I.—It did not descend in the form of a dove upon our Lord Jesus Christ, nor on the day of Pentecost after the Ascension; only the Holy Spirit did, ch. 7, book I.—It did not say, “You are my Son,” when Christ was baptized by John or when he was transfigured on the mountain; rather, only the Father’s voice was addressed to the Son, ch. 7, book I.

A commendation of Theophanes the Chronographer, ch. 115, book II.

A certain apocryphal work of the Apostle Thomas, ch. 127, book II.

Theodosius named the Theodosian Code after himself, ch. 144, book II.

Let us not allow the traditions that we have received from the Fathers to be violated, ch. 156, book II.

What the office of treasurer is, ch. 41, book III.

A person tonsured, male or female, at any underage period without the parents’ knowledge, is nevertheless to remain tonsured once the parents know, provided they do not disown their children, ch. 186, book III.

A person cannot be a witness if he is also the accuser, if he is produced from the household of the accuser, or if he is under fourteen years of age, ch. 83, book IV.

The disposition of witnesses and accusers must be free from hostility and suspicion, ch. 84, book IV.

Persons who were recently enemies cannot be witnesses, ibid.—Suspected persons are not to be admitted, ch. 85, book IV.—Blood relatives and members of the same household are not to give testimony against outsiders, ibid.—They must be free from all infamy, suspicion, or manifest stain; instructed in the fullness of the true faith; and such persons as divine authority commands to be chosen for the priesthood, ch. 86, book IV.

Persons of ill repute, adulterers, those who have committed abduction, and those who have resorted to diviners and magicians can be neither witnesses nor accusers, ibid.

That a bishop, a cardinal-priest, etc., must be convicted by witnesses, ch. 91, book IV.

Witnesses are not to give testimony except concerning what they have truthfully known and seen, ch. 91, book IV, and ch. 19, book V.

Neither the Gospel, nor divine law, nor human law condemns anyone on the testimony of one witness, even a suitable one, ch. 69, book IV, and ch. 25, book V.

How many witnesses are required to condemn bishops and cardinals, ch. 91, book IV.

Seventy witnesses against a bishop, according to the number of the Lord’s seventy disciples, ch. 91, book IV.

One who accuses another’s slaves of a crime must likewise submit himself to the punishment of retaliation, ch. 15, book V.—So too must one who accuses another of homicide, ch. 14, book V.

The hearing of witnesses is not to take place against an absent party, ch. 20, book V.

Before being examined regarding the case, witnesses must be bound by oath that they will say nothing false, ch. 21, book V.

The testimony of one person is not to be received, ch. 22, [Col. 1425] book V.—Nor is testimony to be received except from a person of good repute or one commended by rank, ch. 25, book V.

What must be done if a witness produced is said to be a slave, ch. 29, book V.

A witness who is an enemy by reason of a criminal case is not to testify; rather, his disqualification is to be pleaded, ch. 29, book V.

Witnesses who are accomplices in crimes are not to be admitted, ch. 30, book V.

A witness who has confessed concerning himself is not to be believed concerning another, ch. 31, book V.

Witnesses who cannot be compelled to testify against relatives, ch. 32, book V.—Those whom it is possible to order to act as witnesses are not suitable, ch. 33, book V.

A father is not a suitable witness for his son, nor a son for his father, ch. 34, book V.

Witnesses who have given inconsistent or false testimony, or betrayed either party, are not suitable, ch. 35, book V.—Nothing prohibits several persons from one household from being called in another’s case, ch. 35, book V.

A woman condemned under the Julian law is forbidden to give testimony, ch. 37, book V.—It is inferred from the Julian law that women have the right to speak in court, ibid.

Free men who take royal fiscal women as wives, and free women who take royal fiscal men as husbands, are not excluded from giving testimony, ch. 38, book V.

Not everyone is permitted to make a will, ch. 60, book V.

Those subject to another’s legal authority do not have the right to make a will, ibid.

Who may make a will, and who may not, ibid.

Every controversy concerning ecclesiastical property is to be settled on the testimony of two witnesses, ch. 83, book VII.

At what times the truce is to be observed, ch. 147, book VIII.

If anyone attempts to break the truce, let him be subject to anathema, ibid.

## U

A practice contrary to truth must be abolished, ch. 166, book II.

Usury can consist not only in money but also in other things, ch. 160, book III.—It is every excess given above what you have given, ibid.—Divine Scripture removes every excess in any matter, so that you do not receive more than you gave, ibid.

Usury is where more is demanded than is given, ch. 161, book III.

Those who are in the womb are understood to exist in the world of things, ch. 65, book V.

It is not lawful to dismiss a barren wife and marry another for the sake of fertility, ch. 28, book VI.

From whom a wife is to be sought and how she is to be given, ch. 31, book VI.

He who has both a wife and a concubine is not to receive communion, ch. 49, book VI.

It is not lawful for a Christian to have several wives simultaneously, but only one, ch. 50, book VI.

If an unmarried man keeps his slave woman as a concubine until death and has children by her, she and her offspring are to remain free after her master’s death, ch. 51, book VI.

To take a prostitute as wife is not a sin; rather, the man who does this is to be praised if he makes a good woman out of a bad one, ch. 57, book VI.

Tertullian said that it is a crime to take a second wife after one’s wife’s death, ch. 60, book VI.

Abraham lawfully took another wife after Sarah’s death, ibid.

One who abstains without his wife’s consent grants her permission to fornicate, ch. 79, book VI.

A wife ought to do nothing concerning her clothing, gold, silver, any money, or any of her earthly possessions without her husband’s decision, ch. 80, book VI.

One who has taken the monastic habit without his wife’s consent, even if he has been tonsured, is to be compelled to return to his wife, ch. 84, book VI.

A wife who refuses to follow her husband when he has been taken captive is to remain unmarried as long as he lives, ch. 91, book VI.

Wives cannot enter another marriage until it is certain that their husband is alive in captivity, ch. 90, book VI.

If a man had a virgin wife before baptism, he cannot have another while she lives after baptism, ch. 98, book VI.

A wife, even if barren, deformed, blind, lame, or worn out by illnesses and pains, is never to be dismissed, except on grounds of fornication, ch. 104, book VI.

A man might dismiss a barren wife and marry one by whom he might have children, yet this is not lawful, ch. 105, book VI.—Nor can she dismiss her husband, even if the spouses know that they will not have children, ibid.

It is not lawful, with a wife’s consent, to bring in another woman in order to beget children by her and make them common children, ibid.

It is not lawful to dismiss a wife on account of discord until the matter has been proved before the Church, ch. 106, book VI.—If a freeborn man has taken as wife a slave woman whom he believed free, and later learns that she is a slave, he is to redeem her from slavery if he can and retain her; if he cannot and wishes to do so, he may take another, ch. 111, book VI.—A husband may take another wife if his own wife, overcome by illness, is unable to render the marital debt, ch. 112, book VI.

Let no one dare dismiss his wife for any cause other than fornication; if he does so, let him be deprived of communion, ch. 1, book VII.

If a wife leaves her husband, or a husband his wife, on grounds of fornication, either is forbidden to take another, ch. 2, book VII.

It is lawful to dismiss a wife for no cause except fornication, ch. 3, book VII.

He who conceals his wife’s offense is an advocate of shamefulness, ch. 8, book VII.

While his wife is living, let a man rather take another wife than shed human blood, ch. 17, book VII.

He who takes a wife, knowing that another man can have intercourse with her, is no less guilty than if caught in the act itself, ch. 19, book VII.

When a trial is to be held, whether concerning the marital bond or the crime of adultery, a wife is to be placed in free custody and not under her husband’s power, ch. 24, book VII.

At times intercourse with one’s wife is lawful and at times unlawful; on account of procession days, intercourse is sometimes not lawful, because one must abstain even from lawful things so that what is sought may more easily be obtained, ch. 26, book VII.

A wife may lawfully leave her husband and a husband his wife, not only because of unlawful desires committed in sexual immorality with other men and women, but wholly on account of any desires whatsoever that wrongly cause the soul, while using the body, to depart from the law of God, ch. 30, book VII.

A wife who attempts to draw her husband into heresy is lawfully dismissed, ch. 30, book VII.

A man who commits fornication cannot dismiss his wife on grounds of fornication, ch. 31, book VII.

A wife who wishes to remain with her Christian husband is left without blame, ch. 32, book VII.

One must not depart from the faith out of love for one’s wife, ch. 33, book VII.

A wife must not abandon the faith lest she lose her unbelieving husband, ibid.—A woman who worships an idol and does not repent is to be dismissed by her husband, ch. 16, book VII.—She who is not subject to her husband, that is, to her head, is guilty of the same offense as a husband if he is not subject to Christ, his head, ch. 46, book VII.

Before the time of Saint Gregory it was not lawful to take a wife within the fourth degree; and Pope Zacharias says concerning this matter that it is not lawful for Christians, ch. 58, book VII.—A man may marry a co-godmother who has not herself been his co-godmother, ch. 67, book VII.—No one is to marry without a priest’s blessing, ch. 78, book VII.—It is not lawful to separate unless consanguinity has been proved before the Church, ch. 82, book VII.

The agents of divine wrath are not only human beings and ministers, but also the hostile powers called the wrath and anger of God.

## V

The *Lives of the Fathers* are by no means read in the Church without reliable authorities, ch. 120, book II.—Those written by orthodox authors are received and read, ch. 120, book II.

Virgins are not to be consecrated before their twenty-fifth year, ch. 30, book II.

Those who sell in the temple of God are persons who grant, for payment, what belongs to certain people by right, ch. 109, book III.

To sell doves is to confer the laying on of hands, by which the Holy Spirit is given, not in accordance with merit of life but for payment, ch. 120, book III.

Do not permit those who sell or buy ecclesiastical offices to exercise any authority of their order, ch. 122, book III.

Whoever sells either of two things without which the other cannot be obtained does not cease to sell both, ch. 123, book III.

There is little difference in fault between being able to deceive and being able to be deceived, ch. 175, book III.

I do not wish to fight in hope of victory, lest I should at some time lose victory, ch. 176, book III.

The sacred veil is not to be placed upon virgins unless on Epiphany, other Paschal festivals, or feasts of the apostles, and not before their twenty-fifth year, chs. 189–191, book III.

A virgin who vows virginity and then marries will incur condemnation, ch. 192, book III.

Virgins who married after consecration are incestuous, ch. 193, book III.

Among Greeks and Romans, a man who had intercourse with a veiled and consecrated woman was excluded from every rank of the priesthood, as though he had inflicted blasphemy upon God, ch. 192, book III.

Widows are not to be veiled, chs. 195, 197, book III.

Virgins are not to be [verb missing in the source] by presbyters, etc., ch. 196, book III.

Widows who have received the sacred veil may not depart from their sacred resolve, ch. 198, book III.

A widow who has professed a vow of continence cannot abandon her vow, ch. 199, book III.—Before profession, she may marry whom she wishes, ch. 200, book III.

No one may violate a profession of widowhood made before a bishop, ch. 201, book III.

Widows and virgins cannot pass into marriage after adopting the religious resolve, ch. 203, book III.

Virgins and widows who depart from their resolve of virginity and widowhood are condemned, ch. 204, book III.

A widow of not less than sixty years is to be chosen, and what kind of women widows ought to be, ch. 208, book III.

Virgins who have spent many years in monasteries are forbidden to marry, ch. 208, book III.

Affection arising from kinship, familiarity, and domination commonly obstructs truth, ch. 85, book IV.

A party defeated unjustly is to renew the action within three months, ch. 44, book V.

Those are called conceived in the common way (*vulgo concepti*) who cannot identify their father, or who can indeed identify him but have a father whom they may not lawfully have, ch. 63, book V.

Just bonds break justice, ch. 83, book V.

A person’s life, not a sentence, binds him, ch. 132, book V.

The virginity of Mary, our most blessed Lady, deceived the prince of this world, ch. 25, book VI.

If anyone abducts a widow as a wife, let him be anathema, ch. 54, book VI.

If anyone abducts a virgin, unless he betroths her as wife, let him be anathema, ibid.

A widow is one whose husband has died, ch. 68, book VI.

A husband and wife are not to separate for the sake of religion without the bishop’s knowledge, ch. 76, book VI.

[Col. 1428] A husband cannot revoke vows of continence which his wife promised with his assent, ch. 80, book VI.

He who requires your vows will himself help you, ch. 81, book VI.

Married persons ought not to vow such things except by mutual consent and will, ibid.—Even if the promise has been made rashly, the rashness is to be corrected rather than the promise dissolved, ibid.

He who makes a vow will be so much the lower if he breaks faith with God as he will be happier if he fulfils it, ibid.

A wife cannot undertake a vow of continence unless her husband does the same, ch. 83, book VI.

A husband is not to be received into a monastery unless his wife has chosen a women’s monastery or, having professed continence, has promptly changed her dress, ch. 83, book VI.

A husband, whatever he may be like, once he has been accepted, is not to be dismissed, ch. 103, book VI.—Against whom it has been proved that he could not know his wife, if, separated from her, he has taken another, he is to be separated from the second as well, ch. 115, book V.—One who is sexually incapable is to remain without a spouse, ch. 116, book VI.

Whatever is commanded to men applies consequently also to women, ch. 3, book VII.—What is not lawful for women is equally not lawful [for men], and the same servitude is assessed under equal condition, ibid.

He who marries a woman dismissed by her husband (a) commits adultery, chs. 4, 5, 7, book VII.

The husband is the head of the wife, ch. 46, book VII.

A woman cannot make a vow unless the authority of her husband or father intervenes, ch. 47, book VII.

A woman is not compelled to keep vows of abstinence which she promised with her husband’s permission if he later forbids them, ch. 48, book VII.

Good people may carry out the offices of vengeance with good intention, ch. 48, book VIII.

Force and injury must be repelled, ch. 56, book VIII.

Soothsayers who declare that they know future events are to be beaten and cast out of the city, ch. 71, book VIII.

Truth itself consists in saying what is; for how can there be truth where falsehood reigns? ch. 128, book VIII.

At times to keep truth silent, but never to speak falsehood, is what is found permitted to the saints, ch. 130, book VIII.

Some have truth on their lips but do not have it in their hearts, ch. 134, book VIII.

It is too little to speak truth unless it is also so in the heart, ibid.

[Col. 1427]

## ORDER OF MATTERS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME

Saint Ivo, Bishop of Chartres.

Historical-literary notice. I. Dissertation on Ivo’s *Decretum* and other ancient collections of canons preceding Gratian. XLIX. Preface to the 1647 edition of Ivo’s works. 9. [Col. 1428] Saint Ivo’s *Decretum*. 47. Saint Ivo’s *Panormia*. 1037. Most ample indexes to the *Decretum* and *Panormia*. 1345.
